CONCILIO PVBLICO, SENATVI ECCLESIASTICO, & toti Ecclesiæ Dei quæ est Edinburgi, Robertus Rollocus Scotus gratiam & pacem à Domino.
units.tr: To the Public Council, the Ecclesiastical Senate, and the whole Church of God at Edinburgh: Robert Rollock, a Scot, wishes grace and peace from the Lord.

units.la: CVm quis Ecclesiæ consecrat labores suos in docendo, & viua voce Euágelium prędicádo, Edinburgenses mihi plurimum semperque diligendi & obseruandi; æquum est profecto vt is eidem illi Ecclesiæ dedicet, si nō omnes, aliquota sanè partem laborum suorum, quos collocat in scribendo. Nam cùm omnibus quibus possumus modis teneamur omnibus Christi Ecclesiis consulere, tū maximè obligamur illi Ecclesiæ, qua cum Deus nos coniunxit ac ad quam nos & secreta sua providentia destinauit, & per Ministerium suū segregauit atque vocauit: Obligamur, inquam, vsque adeo, vt omnibus modis pro mesura doni & gratiæ Christi, ei nominatim Ecclesiæ prosimus. Ego autem, vt de me dicam, annis his superioribus in Euangelio Christi ministrando, & explicandis aliquot sacræ Scripturæ libris vobis inseruiui, cum tenui quidem, fateor, dono; cum fide & sinceritate ea cuius Deus est mihi conscius, cum fructu laborum meorum quem ipse Deus nouit, qui testis est mihi, me laboribus meis ipsius benedi-ctionem & gratiam semper & serió exoptauisse: Atq; hoc in vita mea tota (ipsi sit omnis gratia & gloria) imprimis quærere, vt ipsius gloriæ & salu-ti hominum aliquo certè modo passim inseruire. Sine quo studio profectò non est mihi vsqueadeo iucúda vita ista mea, morbis & ægritudinibus de-bilitata, & prope modum cõfecta sic, vt nisi gau-diû meum (quo si in vita plane omni destituamur miseri sumus) aliunde mihi petam, quàm ex ista fragili & mortali vita, nempe ex fide Christi, Do-mini ac Seruatoris mei ex spe opum gloriæ hære-ditatis ipsius in sanctis suis, ex bona denique cõ-scientia, quæ vna mecum testatur, quòd certè ve-lim Domino meo & viuere & mori: nisi, inquam, gaudium meum aliunde mihi petam, non sit cur vita ista præsenti magnoperè delectet. Sed Deo sit gratia per Christum Iesum, qui suos nunquam omni cõsolatione plane destitutos relinquit. Post aliquot alios Scripturę sacrę libros à me in Eccle-sia vestra explicatos, nouissimè sumpsi mihi ex-plicandum Iohannis Euangelium potissimùm, vt Christum in eo tam sæpè támque suauiter loquē-tem de persona sua, de officio suo; Et ipse audire, & aliis digito quasi demonstrarem. Euangelium illud Iohannis, Deo sit gratia, iam totum explica-ui, prout tulit infirmitas mea. In progressu, cùm vętum esset ad historiâ Passionis & Resurrectio-nis Domini, visum est quæ de his ab aliis Euan-gelistis prodita sunt, coniungere, non quòd non in se putarem sufficientem esse Iohannis historiâ: Sed vt in argumento cognitu tam necessario, ha-beremus partim Euangelistarû quatuor harmo-niam niam & concentu quam suauissimum: partim verò historiâ perfectissimâ ac locupletissimam. Adieci postremò ex aliis Euágeliis simul & Actis Apostolorū historiâ gloriosæ Ascensionis Domini, eámq; paucis explicaui, vt in historia Christi Domini nostri prædicanda nihil esset quod desideraretur. Sed ad vos redeo, Edinburgenses. Cùm itaque vobis prædicem, cur non etiam vobis potissimum scriberem, & vestra causa omnia facere, & per vos ac propter vos aliis Ecclesiis scripto meo prodesserem, præsertim cùm sciâ Christum habere Edinburgi, qui ipsum sincerè, & ex animo diligât, nō paucos, quibúsq; omnia acceptissima sùt, siue dicta siue scripta, per quæ quouis modo aliquid possit accedere ad lucé Euágelij Christi amplificandâ & vindicandâ. Quanquâ quid est quod à nobis proficisci potest, quod vel vestro nomine, vel aliorum lectione dignum sit? Nam de Scripto nostro nihil est quod pollicemur, nisi hoc solùm, quòd eo certè conati sumus Dominū glorificare, & Ecclesiæ ipsius prodesse: quem quidem conatū ipsummet scriptum nostrū fortasse in summa, nō dicâ simplicitate, sed, vt ingenuè fatear, infantia ac ruditate spirabit ac præ se feret. Quæso igitur, boni consulite, nō modò conatum hunc nostrum quantulumcunque, sed & voluntatē erga vos nostram, cuius testem habemus Deum nostrum: qui faxit, precor, vt omnia vobis simul conferant ad bonum per Iesum Christũ seruatorem nostrũ, cui sit omnis gloria; & in quo vos semper gaudete & valete. Edinburgi, pridie Calend. Martij 1599.
units.tr: When someone devotes his labours to the Church by teaching and by preaching the Gospel with the living voice, it is only right that he should dedicate to that same Church, if not all, at least some part of the labours he expends in writing. For although we are bound to serve all the Churches of Christ by every means we can, we are bound most of all to that Church with which God has joined us, to which by his secret providence he has assigned us, and which through his ministry has set us apart and called us. We are bound, I say, so closely that we should benefit that particular Church by every means, according to the measure of the gift and grace of Christ. As for myself, to speak of my own case, in these past years I have served you in ministering the Gospel of Christ and in expounding several books of holy Scripture, with a gift that is indeed small, I confess, but with a faith and sincerity of which God is my witness, and with a fruit of my labours which God himself knows, who is my witness that in my labours I have always and earnestly desired his blessing and grace. And in my whole life (to him be all grace and glory) I have above all sought to serve, in some way or other, the glory of God and the salvation of men wherever I could. Without this aim, indeed, this life of mine is not very pleasant to me, weakened by diseases and sicknesses and almost worn out, so that, unless I seek my joy (for we wretched men are wholly deprived of joy if we lack it altogether in life) from elsewhere than this frail and mortal life, namely from faith in Christ my Lord and Saviour, from the hope of the riches of his glory and inheritance among his saints, and finally from a good conscience, which bears witness with me that I would indeed gladly live and die for my Lord, there is, I say, no reason why this present life should greatly delight me. But thanks be to God through Jesus Christ, who never leaves his own utterly destitute of all comfort. After several other books of holy Scripture which I have expounded to you in your Church, I last of all took upon myself to expound chiefly the Gospel of John, so that I might both hear Christ himself, speaking so often and so sweetly in it about his own person and his office, and, as it were, point him out to others with my finger. I have now expounded that whole Gospel of John, by God's grace, as far as my weakness allowed. As I proceeded, when it came to the history of the Lord's Passion and Resurrection, it seemed good to join to it what other Evangelists have related about these events, not because I thought John's history was not sufficient in itself, but so that on a subject so necessary to know we might have, partly a harmony and agreement of the four Evangelists, as sweet as possible, and partly a most complete and full history. Last of all I added from the other Gospels, and from the Acts of the Apostles, the history of the glorious Ascension of the Lord, and I explained it briefly, so that in preaching the history of Christ our Lord nothing would be left wanting. But I return to you, Edinburgh people. Since I have declared to you why I should not also write chiefly for you, and do everything for your sake, and through you and on your account serve other Churches by my writing, especially since I know that Christ has at Edinburgh not a few who love him sincerely and from the heart, and for whom whatever things, whether spoken or written, by which in any way something may be added to the amplifying and vindicating of the light of the Gospel of Christ, are most acceptable. Yet what is there that can proceed from us which is worthy either of your name or of the reading of others? For concerning our writing we promise nothing except this only, that certainly in it we have striven to glorify the Lord and to benefit his Church; and this endeavour, our writing itself, perhaps, will breathe forth and display, if I may not say in total simplicity, but, to confess frankly, in infancy and roughness. I beg you therefore to take it in good part, not only this our endeavour, however small, but also our goodwill towards you, of which we have God as witness. May he grant, I pray, that all things may combine for your good through Jesus Christ our Saviour, to whom be all glory; and in whom rejoice and farewell always. Edinburgh, the day before the Calends of March, 1599.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM EVANGELII IOHANNIS.
units.tr: THE ARGUMENT OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.

units.la: Historiæ de Christo à quatuor Sanctis Euangelistis conscriptæ, summa & præcipuæ partes.
units.tr: The summary and principal parts of the history of Christ written by the four holy Evangelists.

units.la: DE Christo historici libri quatuor sunt à quatuor Euangelistis conscripti, quorum singuli continent historiam sufficientem Iohan. 20. 31, & 21. 25. Omnes verò perfectissimam. Historiæ Euangelicæ de Christo, ut à quatuor Euangelistis conscripta est, hæc ferè capita sunt.
units.tr: There are four historical books about Christ, written by the four Evangelists. Each of them contains a sufficient history (Iohan. 20. 31, and 21. 25), and all of them together are most complete. The main headings of the Gospel history of Christ, as the four Evangelists wrote it, are for the most part these.

units.la: I. Est de deitate Christi, quæ erat in principio.
units.tr: I. It is concerning the deity of Christ, which was in the beginning.

units.la: II. Est de humanitate Christi, quæ assumpta est & nata in temporis plenitudine.
units.tr: II. It is concerning the humanity of Christ, which was assumed and born in the fullness of time.

units.la: III. Est de humiliatione Christi, quæ posita est in actionibus quas obiit ad finem usque vitæ suæ : Actiones rursus, partim sunt communes, ut opera charitatis, quæ fiunt secundum legem, partim proprie sunt, ut eæ quæ Christo ex officio Mediationis incumbebant. Atque hæ rursus actiones sunt Christi primum ut Propheta est in docendo, deinde ut Rex est in operando potenter & miraculosè, tertiò ut Sacerdos est in obeundis summa voluntate omnibus necessitatibus, periculis, molestiis, denique morte ipsa acerbissima, ut nos à peccato & miseria liberaret. Sunt (fateor) actiones Christi, ut Sacerdos est, pleraque etiam perpessiones: verùm actiones non immeritò vocantur, quia ipse se submisit, & ultrò obtulit omnib. persecutionib. & perpessionibus tolerandis.
units.tr: III. It is concerning the humiliation of Christ, which consists in the actions he performed until the end of his life. These actions are again partly common, such as works of charity done according to the law, and partly proper to him, such as those which fell to Christ by the office of Mediator. These actions of Christ are again: first, as Prophet, in teaching; second, as King, in working powerfully and miraculously; third, as Priest, in undertaking with the greatest willingness all needs, dangers and troubles, and finally death itself, most bitter, so that he might free us from sin and misery. There are (I admit) many sufferings too among the actions of Christ as Priest; but they are rightly called actions, because he submitted himself and offered himself willingly to bear all persecutions and sufferings.

units.la: IIII. Caput historiæ Euangeliæ est de Christi glorificatione, primùm resurrectione, deinde in cœlos ascensione. Duo hæc posteriora historiæ Euangelicæ capita Petrus his verbis complexus est, dum de Prophetis loquens, Scrutantes, inquit, in quem aut cuiusmodi temporis articulum prænuntius ille qui in ipsis erat Spiritus Christi declararet euenturas Christo perpessiones & gloriam illam consequuturam 1. Petr. 1. 11.
units.tr: IIII. The chief part of the Gospel history is the glorification of Christ, first in his resurrection, then in his ascension into heaven. Peter summed up these two latter parts of the Gospel history in these words, when speaking of the Prophets: "Searching," he says, "into what person, or what kind of time, the Spirit of Christ which was in them was pointing to, the sufferings destined for Christ and the glory that would follow" (1 Pet. 1. 11).

units.la: Euangelij à S. Iohanne scripti, summa & partes.
units.tr: Summary and divisions of the Gospel written by John.

units.la: Iohannis Euangelista, qui post reliquos scripsit, particulare studium fuit, vt doctrinam de Christo, ipsius natura & officio comprehensam, magna ex parte Christi sermonibus à reliquis omissis, contra omnes præcipuè sui temporis hæreses confirmaret. Miracula commemorat nonnulla, de quibus reliqui prorsus tacent. Euangelium suum orditur à magnifica quadâ Christi descriptione, quæ continetur cap.1. à versu primo vsque ad 37.verf. Hinc sequitur historia humiliationis Christi à verf. 37. cap. 1. ad cap. vsque 20. Inde sequitur historia glorificationis ipsius ad finem vsque libri.
units.tr: John the Evangelist, who wrote after the others, had a particular aim: to set out the doctrine concerning Christ, his nature and office, and to confirm it, chiefly against all the heresies of his own time. To do this he left out, for the most part, sayings of Christ that the others report. He records some miracles of which the others say nothing at all. He begins his Gospel with a magnificent description of Christ, which is contained in chapter 1 from verse 1 to verse 37. From there follows the history of Christ's humiliation from chapter 1, verse 37, to chapter 20. After that follows the history of his glorification to the end of the book.

units.la: Descriptionis Christi tria sunt argumenta. Primum, est à deitate ipsius & persona filij Dei, ab initio cap. 1. ad verf. vsque 14. Secundum, est ab incarnatione ipsius siue assumpta natura humana eiusdem cap. verf.14. Tertium vero est à multiplici Iohannis Baptistæ de ipso testimonio, inde à verf. 15. cap.1. ad versum vsque 37.
units.tr: The description of Christ has three topics. The first concerns his deity and the person of the Son of God, from the beginning of chapter 1 to verse 14. The second concerns his incarnation, or the assumption of human nature, in chapter 1, verse 14. The third concerns the many testimonies of John the Baptist about him, from chapter 1, verse 15, to verse 37.

units.la: In historia humiliationis Christi commemoratio est actionum & factorum ipsius quibus sese partim sanctissimum & iustissimum virum esse docuit: partim Prophetam illum esse quem omnes Prophetæ venturum prædixerunt, manifesto ostendit: partim regem & dominum gloriæ se arguit: partim denique sacerdotem illum summum & Pontificem magnum se probauit.
units.tr: In the history of Christ's humiliation, there is a record of his actions and deeds, by which he showed himself partly to be a most holy and righteous man, partly to be that Prophet whom all the prophets foretold would come, partly to be a king and lord of glory, and partly, finally, to be that high priest and great Pontiff.

units.la: Actiones Christi, quia narrantur continua serie, Euangelista ipse videtur distribuere ex subiectis locis ad quæ ipse venit, vel in quibus commoratus est. 1. Sunt actiones ipsius in deserto, in quo commorabatur Iohannes Baptista, postquam à Iohanne est baptizatus, cap.1.37. & sequentibus. II. In reditu é deserto inter veniendum in Galilæam, cap.1.44. & sequentibus. III. In Cana Galilææ oppido, cap.2.1. & seq. IIII. Hierosolymis in primo Paschate à Baptismate ipsius, cap. 2.13. & seq. V. In territorio Iudææ, vbi cum discipulis degebat, cap.3.22. & sequentibus. VI. Inter redeundum in Galilæam per Samariam, cap. 4.1. & seq. VII. In Galilæa & nominatim Cana Galilæae oppido, cap.4.43. & sequent. VIII. Cum reuersus esset Hierosolymam in secundo Paschate à Baptismate ipsius, cap.5.1. & sequentib. IX. Cum reuersus esset in Galilæam & transiret per mare Galilææ, cap.6.1. & seq. X. Cum reuersus esset Hierosolymam in festo Tabernaculorum, cap. 7.14. & sequentib. XI. Cum abiisset trans Iordanem. danem in deserturn in quo baptizatus fuerat a Iohanne, cap. 10. 40. & sequent. xii. Cùm è deserto venisset Bethaniam quæ propè Hierosolymam erat stadiis fere quindecim, ca. 11. 17. & sequentib. xiii. Cùm abiisset illinc in regionem quæ est prope de-sertum cap. 11. 54. & sequent. xiiii. Cùm venisset Bethaniam paulo ante Pascha quod inde ab ipsius Baptismate quartũ numeratur: Nam de tertio à Baptismate Christi Paschate nulla fit mentio, ad quod non videtur Christus Hierosolymam profectus propter metum Iudæorum, cap. 12. 1. & sequent. xv. Inter veniendum Bethania Hierosolymam & Hierosolymis, cap. 12. 12 & sequent. ad caput usque 18. Hierosolymis, dum ageret ante festum Paschæ à Baptismate ipsius quartum, sciens Iesus venisse horam ipsius, ut transiret ex hoc mundo ad Patrem, non amplius publicè cum populo egit vel docendo vel operando, sed priuatim cum discipulis suis dilectis, quos partim exemplo suo ad humilitatem formauit, partim sermone quo eos docuit & consolatus est, inde à versu primo cap. 13. ad cap. usque 17. quo cap. sermonem illum suum claudit solemnibus ad Deum conceptis precibus.
units.tr: Since Christ's actions are narrated in a continuous sequence, the Evangelist himself seems to arrange them according to the places to which he came or where he stayed. 1. His actions in the desert, where John the Baptist was staying, after he was baptized by John, chapter 1, verse 37 and following. II. On his return from the desert as he came into Galilee, chapter 1, verse 44 and following. III. In the town of Cana in Galilee chapter 2, verse 1 and following. IV. At Jerusalem at the first Passover after his baptism, chapter 2, verse 13 and following. V. In the territory of Judea, where he stayed with his disciples, chapter 3, verse 22 and following. VI. While returning to Galilee through Samaria, chapter 4, verse 1 and following. VII. In Galilee, and especially the town of Cana in Galilee, chapter 4, verse 43 and following. VIII. When he had gone back to Jerusalem at the second Passover after his baptism, chapter 5, verse 1 and following. IX. When he had returned to Galilee and crossed the Sea of Galilee, chapter 6, verse 1 and following. X. When he had returned to Jerusalem for the feast of Tabernacles, chapter 7, verse 14 and following. XI. When he had gone across the Jordan into the desert where he had been baptized by John, chapter 10, verse 40 and following. XII. When he had come from the desert to Bethany, which is about fifteen furlongs from Jerusalem, chapter 11, verse 17 and following. XIII. When he had left there for the region near the desert, chapter 11, verse 54 and following. XIV. When he had come to Bethany shortly before the Passover, which is counted as the fourth from his baptism (for no mention is made of a third Passover after Christ's baptism), and to which Christ does not seem to have gone up to Jerusalem because of the fear of the Jews, chapter 12, verse 1 and following. XV. Between Bethany and Jerusalem, and at Jerusalem, chapter 12, verse 12 and following, up to the end of chapter 18. At Jerusalem, in the days before the Passover of his fourth year after baptism, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, no longer acted publicly with the people, either by teaching or by working, but privately with his beloved disciples, whom he partly formed to humility by his example and partly taught and comforted by his words, from the first verse of chapter 13 to the end of chapter 17, where he closes that discourse of his with prayers offered solemnly to God.

units.la: Postquam Prophetę in docendo & Regis in operando potenter & miraculose partes iam egisset ut plurimum: deinde sacerdotis potissimum functus est munere, dum pro nobis seipsum obtulit morti, mortuus est, sepultus est. Historiam hanc Passionis Christi habemus inde à cap. 18. ad cap. usque 20.
units.tr: Having for the most part already played the part of Prophet in teaching and of King in acting powerfully and miraculously, he then discharged chiefly the office of priest, when he offered himself to death for us, died, and was buried. We have this history of Christ's Passion from chapter 18 to the end of chapter 20.

units.la: Absoluta iam historia humiliationis Christi, sequitur historia glorificationis, hoc est gloriosæ resurrectionis Christi. Nam Iohannes de ascensione Christi nihil scriptum reliquit. Atque hæc hactenus de argumento.
units.tr: Now that the history of Christ's humiliation is complete, there follows the history of his glorification, that is, of his glorious resurrection. For John left nothing written about Christ's ascension. So much for the subject matter up to this point.

How the manna is a corporeal and spiritual food, 372. The passage about the bread of life, 373. How Christ is the bread of life, 375. Commendation of this bread from its effects, 376.

units.la: Incredulitatis fons detectus 379. Voluntas gratiosa Dei Patris erga electos in Christo fundata 380.381.
units.tr: The source of unbelief is laid bare, 379. The gracious will of God the Father towards the elect, founded in Christ, 380, 381.

units.la: Doctrinæ reprobis propositæ effectus 382. murmur Iudæorum 383. Ingenii humani impotentia circa res spirituales 385. de libero & seruo arbitrio locus 386
units.tr: The effect of the doctrine set before the reprobate, 382. The murmuring of the Jews, 383. The impotence of the human mind in spiritual matters, 385. A passage on free and enslaved will, 386.

units.la: Promissio vitæ æternæ pertinens ad Dei electos 387. Ecclesiæ dignitas sub Euangelio 388. Quid doceat suos discipulos. Deus 389 Discipulorum officium 390. Ratio communicationis discipulorum cum Deo docete: filius quomodo à Deo: quomodo Deus videatur & filius quomodo imago Patris 391. quomodo videt Patrē: quomodo etiā cognoscimus Patrem per Filium 392
units.tr: The promise of eternal life pertaining to God's elect, 387. The dignity of the Church under the Gospel, 388. What God teaches his disciples, 389. The duty of the disciples, 390. The reason for the disciples' communion with the God who teaches: how the Son is from God; how God is seen, and how the Son is the image of the Father, 391. How he sees the Father; how we also know the Father through the Son, 392.

units.la: Modus vitam æternam adipiscēdi 393. is est in Christo pane & sote vitæ 294. hæc vita in Christi morte 395. Panis huius commendatio facta comparatione cum Manna 395. quomodo ea vita reddimur participes 396. Caro Christi cur viuifica 398. qua ratione & quotmodis hęc caro fiat nobis panis vitæ seu caro viuifica 399
units.tr: The manner of obtaining eternal life, 393. It is in Christ, the bread and sun of life, 394. This life is in the death of Christ, 395. Commendation of this bread by comparison with the manna, 395. How we are made partakers of that life, 396. Why the flesh of Christ gives life, 398. By what reason and in what manner this flesh becomes for us the bread of life, or life-giving flesh, 399.

units.la: Iudæi contradicunt veritati 400. Capernaitæ noui veteribus stupidiores 401
units.tr: The Jews contradict the truth, 400. The Capernaites, newer and more stupid than the old, 401.

units.la: Christus quatuor argumentis mäducationem carnis suæ commendat à necessario 401. à natura carnis & sanguinis ipsius: seu ab vtili 302. 303. à beata illa communione quam cum eo habemus 404. à vita, quam ex eo hauri-mus 405
units.tr: Christ commends the eating of his flesh by four arguments: from what is necessary, 401; from the nature of his flesh and blood, or from what is useful, 402, 403; from that blessed communion which we have with him, 404; from the life which we draw from him, 405.

units.la: Trium viuentium, nempe Patris, Filii Dei hominis & filiorum adoptionis gradus 406. vitæ illorum viuentium connexio 407. Conuenięta & dissimilitudo Manę & Christi panis viuifici 408
units.tr: The three living beings, namely the Father, the Son of God made man, and the degrees of the adopted sons, 406. The connection of the life of those living beings, 407. The agreement and disagreement of the manna and of Christ, the life-giving bread, 408.

units.la: Concionis à Christo habitæ conclusio 409. effectus, obduratio Iudæorum 410
units.tr: The conclusion of the sermon preached by Christ, 409. The effect: the hardening of the Jews, 410.

units.la: Apologia Christi adu. iniustā discipulorum criminationem 411. Caro eius cur & quo sensu viuifica dicitur 412. Ascensio Christi duplex 413. Distinctio demonstrans quomodo Christi caro sic viuifica 414. Spiritus & caro, quid 415
units.tr: Christ's defence against the unjust accusation of the disciples, 411. Why and in what sense his flesh is called life-giving, 412. Christ's ascension is twofold, 413. A distinction showing how Christ's flesh is thus life-giving, 414. What spirit and flesh are, 415.

units.la: Apologiæ Christi altera parș in qua de litera & Spiritu, item de ministerio Spiritus & mortis 416
units.tr: The second part of Christ's defence, concerning the letter and the Spirit, and likewise concerning the ministry of the Spirit and of death, 416.

units.la: Postrema pars Apologiæ, retorquens obiectionem in obduratos 417. Iusta obduratorum reiectio 418. mysteria ista quomodo tractāda 419. Christus cur eos inuitat quos aures non habituros ad audiendū cognoscit 420. 421. qui habituri sint aures, & quæ sit arbitrii humani libertas 422
units.tr: The last part of Christ's defence, turning the objection back upon the hardened, 417. The just rejection of the hardened, 418. How these mysteries are to be handled, 419. Why Christ invites those whom he knows will not have ears to hear, 420, 421. Who will have ears, and what is the freedom of the human will, 422.

units.la: Quorundam discipulorū Christi apostasia, & apostasiæ gradus 423. remedium aduersus Apostasiam 424
units.tr: The apostasy of some of Christ's disciples, and the degrees of apostasy, 423. The remedy against apostasy, 424.

units.la: Duodecim Apostolos suos quomodo Christus excitat ad perseuerantiam 425. Liberum obsequium
units.tr: How Christ stirs up his twelve apostles to perseverance, 425. Free obedience to be rendered to God,

units.la: quium Deo deferendum 426
units.tr: to be rendered to God, 426.

units.la: Apostoli à Christo recedere nolunt 427.quia habet vitæ æternæ verba, & est filius Dei viuentis 428. Christi ad præclaram illam professionem responsio, simul attingens Iudæ diabolicum peccatum 429. cur Diabolus vocatur 430. omnium hypocritarum princeps.
units.tr: The apostles are unwilling to withdraw from Christ, 427, because he has the words of eternal life and is the Son of the living God, 428. Christ's answer to that noble confession, at the same time touching on the devilish sin of Judas, 429. Why the Devil is called the prince of all hypocrites, 430.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Prima pars.
units.tr: The first part.

units.la: Commoratio Christi in gloria, humiliationem eius in carne pro nobis ostendens 432
units.tr: Christ's sojourn in glory, showing his humiliation in the flesh for us, 432.

units.la: Secunda pars.
units.tr: The second part.

units.la: Consilium cognatorum Christi 433. quibus argumentis nititur 434. Incredulitas consilii eorundem causa 435. peßimi æstimatores pietatis 436. Christi ad cōsilium cognatorum responsio 437
units.tr: The counsel of Christ's kinsmen, 433. On what arguments it rests, 434. The unbelief behind that counsel, 435. The worst judges of piety, 436. Christ's answer to the counsel of his kinsmen, 437.

units.la: Tertia pars.
units.tr: The third part.

units.la: Professio Christi ad festum 439. quo tempore ibid. quomodo 440.
units.tr: Christ's profession concerning the feast, 439. At what time, ibid. In what manner, 440.

units.la: Quarta pars.
units.tr: The fourth part.

units.la: De dictis & factis Iudæorum circa Christum 441. Varium de eo iudicium ibid. cōspiratio primorum 442. Ecclesiæ visibilis quaenam tunc fuerit facies 443
units.tr: What the Jews said and did concerning Christ, 441. Their divided judgment of him, ibid. The conspiracy of the leaders, 442. What the visible Church then looked like, 443.

units.la: Quinta pars.
units.tr: The fifth part.

units.la: Christi cum Iudæis in festo die colloquium 444. Occasio huius colloquii 445. Quomodo Iudæorum stuporem euellere conatus sit 446. Duplex ratio cognoscendi doctrinam cœlestem 447. prior 448. posterior in ipsa doctrina consistit 449. Veræ doctrinæ nota 450. Christi sapientia & charitas, Iudæorum hypocrisis 451. Eorundem impietas & crudelitas 452. Apologia Christi, Iudæos perspicuè conuincens 453. Variis argumentis eos refellit 454. De respectu personæ & causa 455. Malitiam Iudæorum Deus coercet 456. Eorundem ingenii 457. ignorantia, falsæ opiniones 458. quæ refelluntur 459. Via ad veram veri Dei cognitionem 460. quomodo Filius cognoscat Patrem 460. Christi erga Iudæos cæcos & præfractos charitas immensa 461. Illi verò virus suum effundunt 462. Locus de hominis non regeniti ingenio 463. hora Christi qualis, & de arcana Dei suos protegentis prouidentia 463. 464. 465.
units.tr: Christ's discourse with the Jews on the feast day, 444. The occasion of this discourse, 445. How he tried to shake off their stupor, 446. The twofold way of knowing heavenly doctrine, 447. The first, 448. The second consists in the doctrine itself, 449. The mark of true doctrine, 450. Christ's wisdom and love, the Jews' hypocrisy, 451. Their impiety and cruelty, 452. Christ's defence, which convicts the Jews plainly, 453. He refutes them by various arguments, 454. On regard for person and cause, 455. God restrains the Jews' malice, 456. Their intellect: ignorance and false opinions, 457-458, which are refuted, 459. The way to true knowledge of the true God, 460: how the Son knows the Father, 460. Christ's immense love toward the blind and stubborn Jews, 461. But they pour out their poison, 462. A passage on the nature of the unregenerate man, 463. What the hour of Christ was, and on God's hidden providence protecting his own, 463-465.

units.la: Effectus apologiæ Christi, nepe fides multorum in eum 466. Oppositus effectus Pharisæorum respectu 467. quorum ministri ad Christum malo animo accedunt 468. sed irrito conatu 469. Admonitionis & communicationis Christi effectum 470
units.tr: The effect of Christ's defence, namely the faith of many in him, 466. The opposite effect among the Pharisees, 467, whose ministers approach Christ with an evil mind, 468, but with a fruitless attempt, 469. The effect of Christ's admonition and communication, 470.

units.la: Sexta pars.
units.tr: The sixth part.

units.la: Concio Christi ad populum 472. cui gratis offert gratiam salutarem 473. Potum cælestem, cuius Christus meminit, qua ratione aßequantur & hauriant sitientes electi 474. De sensu miseriæ nostræ & misericordiæ Dei 475. Verbi Dei expositiones necessariæ in Ecclesia 476 flumina aquæ viuæ 477. à quo fonte fluunt, & quibus dentur 477. qua ratione recipiantur, & quo sensu Spiritus S. dicatur non fuisse ante Christi glorificationem 478
units.tr: Christ's sermon to the people, 472, in which he freely offers saving grace, 473. The heavenly drink that Christ mentions: by what means the elect reach it and drink, 474. On the sense of our misery and God's mercy, 475. The necessary expositions of God's Word in the Church, 476. The rivers of living water, 477: from what fountain they flow and to whom they are given, 477. In what way they are received, and in what sense the Holy Spirit is said not to have been given before Christ's glorification, 478.

units.la: Varius Concionis Christi in templo effectus 479. Discrimen inter eos qui à Christo trahuntur 480. rationes eorum qui Christum reiiciunt 481. Dissidia inter Iudæos ob Christum 482. Impiorum ingenium 483. Testimonium Christo redditum à Pontificum ministris 484. Pharisæorum rabies aduersus Christum 485. quibus argumentis perui cacian suam tuetur 486. Vulgus exosum Pharisæis 487. Nicodemi zelus prudé tia spirituali temperatus 488. huic Pharisaei contradicunt 489. Sed confunduntur
units.tr: The varied effect of Christ's sermon in the temple, 479. The difference between those who are drawn by Christ, 480. The reasons of those who reject Christ, 481. The dissensions among the Jews on account of Christ, 482. The character of the impious, 483. The testimony rendered to Christ by the ministers of the priests, 484. The rage of the Pharisees against Christ, 485. By what arguments they defend their blindness, 486. The common people hated by the Pharisees, 487. Nicodemus's zeal, tempered by spiritual prudence, 488. The Pharisees contradict him, 489, but are confounded, 490.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Prima pars.
units.tr: The first part.

units.la: Primae partis circunstantiae secessus Christi in montem olearum 491. tentatio eiusdem 492. Pharisaeorum mala mens 493. gestus Christi eorum hypocrisim perstringentis 494. Loquitur Christus non ut magistratus politicus, sed ut doctor in Ecclesia 495. repetitus gestus Christi Pharisaeos vellicantis 496. Colloquium Christi cum muliere accusata 497. eiusdem responsio & dimissio 498
units.tr: Circumstances of the first part: Christ's withdrawal to the Mount of Olives, 491. His temptation, 492. The evil mind of the Pharisees, 493. Christ's gesture rebuking their hypocrisy, 494. Christ speaks not as a civil magistrate but as a teacher in the Church, 495. Christ's repeated gesture pricking the Pharisees, 496. Christ's conversation with the accused woman, 497. His answer and her dismissal, 498.

units.la: Secunda pars.
units.tr: The second part.

units.la: Christi cum Iudaeis colloquium, in quo se lucem mundi appellat 500. Pharisaei autem caecutiunt 501. Lucem vitae extinguere conantur 502. Christus autem eos sanare studet 503. caecitatem illis benigne exprobrat 504. authoritate suam stabilit 505. tum sui ipsius, tum Patris testimonio 506. Iterum, obstrepunt Christo aduersarii 507. quos refellit, nec quisquam prehendit eum 508
units.tr: Christ's discourse with the Jews, in which he calls himself the light of the world, 500. But the Pharisees grow blind, 501. They try to extinguish the light of life, 502. Christ, however, seeks to heal them, 503. He kindly reproaches them for their blindness, 504. He confirms his authority, 505, both by his own testimony and by the Father's testimony, 506. Again his adversaries shout at Christ, 507, whom he refutes, and no one seizes him, 508.

units.la: Hora Christi praefixa, & eiusdem nova concio 509. acrius quam antea excipiuntur Pharisaei 510. spe gratia illis ablata: sed proterve Christo illudunt 511. non definit tamen eos corrigere Christus 512. 513. Illi contra pergunt in suis sarcasmis, & Christus in necessariis correctionib. 514. tandem eos ad Dei tribunal pertrahit 515. Ignorantia eorundem stupenda 516
units.tr: The appointed hour of Christ, and his new sermon, 509. The Pharisees receive it more fiercely than before, 510. Hope of grace is taken from them, but they mock Christ shamelessly, 511. Yet Christ does not cease to correct them, 512-513. They, on the contrary, persist in their sarcasm, and Christ in his necessary corrections, 514. At last he brings them before God's tribunal, 515. Their astonishing ignorance, 516.

units.la: Denuntiat Christus aduersariis fore tandem ut agnoscant inuiti se a Patre missum 517. illa agnitionem exitium illis allaturam 518. De Patris & Filii in-effabili coniunctione disserit postea 518. Effectus illius concionis, Iudaeorum quorundam respectu 420. quos Christus benigne soner & hortatur ad perseverantiam 521. assiduum in cognitione veritatis progressum pollicetur 522 & veram libertatem 524
units.tr: Christ announces to his adversaries that they will at last acknowledge, though unwillingly, that he was sent by the Father, 517. That this acknowledgement will bring ruin upon them, 518. He discusses later the ineffable union of the Father and the Son, 518. The effect of that sermon among some of the Jews, 520, whom Christ kindly encourages and exhorts to perseverance, 521. He promises a constant progress in knowledge of the truth, 522, and true liberty, 524.

units.la: Incredulí Christo responsant & obloquuntur 525. caeci mendaces, superbi apparent 526. Ideo de seruitute spirituali disserit Christus 527. & seruorum peccati stipendium declarat 528. Eosdem posse a filio in libertatem vindicari ostendit 529. & modum subiicit verae libertatis 530. Sophisma Iudaeorum de Abrahamo iniquiter gloriantium refellit 531. affirmat se loqui quod vidit apud Patrem 532
units.tr: The unbelievers answer Christ and object, 525. The blind appear as liars and the proud as arrogant, 526. Therefore Christ speaks of spiritual servitude, 527, and declares the wages of sin for slaves, 528. He shows that these same men can be set free by the Son, 529, and he gives the manner of true liberty, 530. He refutes the Jews' sophism, which wrongly boasts of Abraham, 531, and affirms that he speaks what he has seen with the Father, 532.

units.la: Instantiae Iudaeorum refutatio 537. Eorundem stupor horrendus 535. ad repetitam instantiam quod sint Dei Filii responsio 536. cur tam superbe Christo insultant 537. De ignorantia locus ibid. Iudaeos ad generis sui originem revocat Christus 538
units.tr: The refutation of the Jews' objection, 537. Their dreadful stupor, 535. The answer to their repeated objection that they are the sons of God, 536. Why they insult Christ so proudly, 537. A passage on ignorance, ibid. Christ calls the Jews back to the origin of their race, 538.

units.la: Diaboli descriptio 539. De lapsu angelorum reproborum locus 540. Apostasiae comites 541. Iudaei filii Diaboli, quod homicidae sint & infideles ibid.
units.tr: The description of the Devil, 539. A passage on the fall of the reprobate angels, 540. The companions of apostasy, 541. The Jews are sons of the Devil, because they are murderers and unbelievers, ibid.

units.la: Christi gloriatio unde 542. Quid sit ex Deo esse 543. Reprobationis signum 544. Gradus peccatorum quae ab impiis in Christum Euangelio patefactum committitur 545. &c. Honor are Deum quid 546. Christus blasphemum Iudaeorum conuitiu refellit 547. promissionem illustrem proponit 548
units.tr: Whence Christ's boasting, 542. What it is to be of God, 543. A sign of reprobation, 544. The degrees of sins which the impious commit against Christ revealed in the Gospel, 545, etc. What it is to honour God, 546. Christ refutes the blasphemous insult of the Jews, 547, and sets forth a glorious promise, 548.

units.la: Iudaei magis ac magis insultantur 549. Christo rursus insultant 550. Abrahamum & Prophetas ei opponunt 551. Efficacia Christi in electis in quo consistat 552. Vo-
units.tr: The Jews are more and more insulted. They again insult Christ, 549-550, and set Abraham and the prophets against him, 551. In what the efficacy of Christ among the elect consists, 552. Vo-

units.la: 552 Vocationem suam tuetur adversus carnale praeiudicium adversariorum 553. Deum verum hostes Christi non cognoscunt 554. Christus quomodo novit Patrem, quomodo seruat sermonem Patris, & maior Abrahamo 555
units.tr: 552 He defends his calling against the carnal prejudice of his adversaries, 553. His enemies do not know the true God, 554. How Christ knows the Father, how he keeps the Father's word, and is greater than Abraham, 555.

units.la: Desiderium piorum cum gaudio & dolore coniunctum 556. Dies Christi cur expetitus ab Abrahamo 557. Cur etiam ab aliis, & effectus istius desiderii 558 Quomodo Patriarchae Christum viderint 559
units.tr: The longing of the pious, joined with joy and sorrow, 556. Why Abraham longed to see Christ's day, 557. Why others did too, and the effect of this longing, 558. How the patriarchs saw Christ, 559.

units.la: Superstitionis & impietatis fos 560. Triplex Christi aspectus 561. quomodo Christus antequam Abraham fieret 562. Veritatis testis effectus in medacii doctoribus & discipulis 563. Infirmitatis & potentiae Christi sponsoris nostri testimonium 563
units.tr: The fountains of superstition and impiety, 560. The threefold aspect of Christ, 561. How Christ was before Abraham came to be, 562. The effect of the truth's witness on the teachers and disciples of falsehood, 563. The testimony to Christ as our surety in weakness and in power, 563.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAP. IX.

units.la: Prima pars.
units.tr: First part.

units.la: In ea occurrunt miraculum de caeco illuminato antecedentia 564. nempe tempus, discipulorum quaestio 565. huius quaestionis examen & partes, de causis efficientibus & finalibus calamitatum 566. ad quaestionem, de reatu parentum & filiorum, unde poenae oriuntur, responsio 567. finalis causa calamitatis huius caeci 569. Christi cognitio & operatio 570. Nox & dies spirituales 571. Lucis spiritualis fons Christus 572. Dies corporalis praesentiae Christi, qualis 573
units.tr: This part contains the miracle of the man born blind, and what precedes it: the time, and the disciples' question 565. The examination of this question and its parts, concerning the efficient and final causes of calamities 566. The answer to the question about the guilt of parents and children, from which punishments arise 567. The final cause of this blind man's calamity 569. Christ's knowledge and working 570. Spiritual night and day 571. Christ the fount of spiritual light 572. The bodily day of Christ's presence, and what kind it was 573.

units.la: Miraculi circumstantiae quatuor Christi respectu 573. Duę respectu caeci 574. Fidei & obedientiae fructus 575
units.tr: The circumstances of the miracle, four in number, with respect to Christ 573. Two with respect to the blind man 574. The fruit of faith and obedience 575.

units.la: Secunda pars.
units.tr: Second part.

units.la: Huius quatuor sunt membra, quae miraculi consequentia continent ibid.
units.tr: This part has four members, which contain the consequences of the miracle, ibid.

units.la: 1. Disceptatio inter vicinos mirabundos 575, responsio caeci ad dubitationem & quaestionem eorum 576. instantia vicinorum & caeci amplior declaratio 577. Christus gloriam non captauit ab hominibus 578. Suis adest, unde pax conscientiae 579. Vicini ad Pharisaeos caecum illuminatum adducunt 580
units.tr: 1. A dispute among the astonished neighbours 575; the blind man's reply to their doubt and question 576; the neighbours' insistence and the blind man's fuller explanation 577. Christ did not seek glory from men 578. He is present with his own, whence comes peace of conscience 579. The neighbours bring the man who was healed to the Pharisees 580.

units.la: 2. Pharisaei inquirut de facto: & suae inquisitionis fundamentum est cultus externi violatio 581. De modo facti deinde quaerunt 582. Inter se verbis contendunt 583. Peccatum illorum multiplex, & de Sabbatho locus 584. Quorundam fanior sententia 585. De miraculis locus ibid. dissidiorum causa 586. Caecus illuminatus veritatem facti profitetur 587. De facto an fuerit inquirunt Iudaei 588. Examen & interrogationis capita 589. Parentes caeci sapienter primo, deinde insipienter respondent 590.591. Peccati eorum fos 592. Iudei rei veritatem obscurare studeni 593. Caecus illuminatus varie respondet, & tandem eos acriter pungit 594. Ei conuitiantur, & fidem catholicam obtendunt 595. De vocatione locus 596. Illuminatus caecitatem Iudaeorum miratur 597. Eosdem docet & conuincit 598.599. De miraculis Christi locus 600. Doctrinae ab illuminato caeco propositae successus 601. Pharisaei eum Synagoga eiiciunt 602. De excommunicatione vera & falsa locus 602.603
units.tr: 2. The Pharisees inquire into the fact, and the ground of their inquiry is the violation of external worship 581. They then ask about the manner of the fact 582. They contend with one another in words 583. Their sin is manifold, and there is a place for the Sabbath 584. The more sensible opinion of some of them 585. A place for miracles, ibid. The cause of the disagreements 586. The healed blind man professes the truth of the fact 587. The Jews inquire whether the fact occurred 588. The examination and the heads of the questioning 589. The blind man's parents answer wisely at first, then foolishly 590, 591. Their sin 592. The Jews strive to obscure the truth of the matter 593. The healed blind man answers variously, and at last stings them sharply 594. They revile him and put forward the catholic faith 595. A place on calling 596. The healed man marvels at the blindness of the Jews 597. He teaches and convicts the same men 598, 599. A place on Christ's miracles 600. The success of the doctrine set forth by the healed blind man 601. The Pharisees cast him out of the synagogue 602. A place on true and false excommunication 602, 603.

units.la: 3. Christus illuminatum in re-ota fide instituit 604. quomodo ille vidit Christum 605
units.tr: 3. Christ instructs the healed man in the true faith 604; how he saw Christ 605.

units.la: 4. Disceptatio Christi impiorum iudicis aduersus Pharisaeos 606. 607. Caecorum spiritualiū peccatū in quo consistit 608. Iudicium seuerū in reprobos 609. de caecitate & illuminatione mentis 610
units.tr: 4. Christ, as judge of the impious, disputes against the Pharisees 606, 607. In what the sin of spiritual blind people consists 608. Severe judgment upon the reprobate 609. On the blindness and illumination of the mind 610.

units.la: CAP. X. Prima pars.
units.tr: CHAP. X. First part.

units.la: Parabolæ de ouili, fure, pastore, occasio & partes seu capita 611. eiusdem expositio 612
units.tr: The parable of the sheepfold, the thief and the shepherd: occasion and parts or heads, 611. Its exposition, 612.

units.la: Ouile & oues 612. Ouilis ostium Christus, & cur ita nomitur 613.614.615 fures ouile Christi ingredientes, nempe Philosophi ethnici, Pharisæi, Hæretici, Superstitiosi 616. Oues Christum audiunt 617. Introire per ostium quid 618
units.tr: The sheepfold and the sheep, 612. Christ is the door of the sheepfold, and why he is so called, 613, 614, 615. Thieves who enter the fold of Christ, namely the heathen philosophers, the Pharisees, heretics and superstitious persons, 616. The sheep hear Christ, 617. What it is to enter by the door, 618.

units.la: Pastor Ouilis, eius partes & munera 619. Boni Pastoris in Ecclesia character 620
units.tr: The shepherd of the sheepfold, his parts and offices, 619. The character of the good Shepherd in the Church, 620.

units.la: Aduentus Christi pastoris in mundum finis 621. Is proprie solus pastor, cuius charitas describitur 622. Charitas illa quomodo & in quo consideranda 623
units.tr: The coming of Christ the shepherd into the world, its purpose, 621. He alone is properly the shepherd, and his love is described, 622. How and in what respects that love is to be considered, 623.

units.la: Mercenarii characteres 624. qualis sit coniunctio eius cum ouili, peccata eiusdem grauissima, & an Pastor fugiens sit mercenarius, & quomodo 625
units.tr: The marks of the hireling, 624. What kind of connection he has with the sheepfold, his most grievous sins, and whether a shepherd who flees is a hireling, and how, 625.

units.la: Christus bonus pastor, mercenario & furi oppositus, suas nouit oues 626. Electorum Dei dignitas & gloria 627. prædictio de vocatione Gentium 628. quomodo Gentes adducantur ad Ecclesiam 629. altera prædictio Christi de morte, passione & resurrectione sua 630.631. Mortis & vitæ Christi potestas à Patre 632
units.tr: Christ, the good shepherd, set against the hireling and the thief, knows his sheep, 626. The dignity and glory of God's elect, 627. Prophecy concerning the calling of the Gentiles, 628. How the Gentiles are brought to the Church, 629. Another prophecy of Christ concerning his death, passion and resurrection, 630, 631. The power of Christ's death and life from the Father, 632.

units.la: Effectus concionis Christi 633. Discrimen credentium & non credentium vnde 634. Electi & reprobi nō consentiunt 635. Ratio certa glorificandi Deum, miracula diuina & diabolica 636
units.tr: The effect of Christ's sermon, 633. Whence comes the difference between believers and unbelievers, 634. The elect and the reprobate do not agree, 635. The sure way of glorifying God; divine and diabolical miracles, 636.

units.la: Secundæ pars.

He convicts the Jews of obstinacy by various arguments 714. &c. At last he departs and hides himself from them 717.

units.la: Quarta pars.
units.tr: Fourth part.

units.tr: Though convicted by so many arguments and miracles, the Jews do not believe in Christ. The prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled in them 719. Yet many of the leading men believe in Christ, but they make no confession, not caring for the glory of God 720.

units.la: Postrema pars.
units.tr: Final part.

units.tr: Christ's arguments for winning faith to himself 721. First, from peaceful faith and from regard to the intention of the Father and the Son 722. Second, from deliverance out of darkness 723. Third, from the threat of eternal damnation 724.

units.la: CAP. XIII. Prima pars.
units.tr: CAP. XIII. First part.

units.tr: The history of the washing of the feet. Its occasion was, first, the nearness of death, 727; second, the manifold love of Christ, 728; third, the secure mind of the same. He approaches Peter, who does not rightly grasp such great humility, 730. The true washing.

units.tr: Consolation against the scandal of the cross and against Christ's absence from the earth, 750. This rests on four arguments. The first is faith in Christ, 751. The second is the fruit of faith in Christ, namely the blessed life with him in the heavenly mansions, 752. The third is the certain promise of Christ's coming, 753. The fourth is the knowledge of the way to so great a blessedness, 754.

units.tr: The repetition of the promise concerning the Holy Spirit is necessary, 770. The disciples will see Christ, 771. The benefit of this sight and the inexcusable ingratitude of the pseudo-Christians, 772. Consideration of God's love and of ours, 773. The presence of Christ, 774.

units.tr: Admonition to produce fruits worthy of union with Christ, confirmed by reasons, 794, 795. The testimony of our love towards God, 796. The illustrious and chief example of love and obedience, and the conclusion of all Christ's exhortations, 797. The new commandment of Christ, commended to the disciples: what it is, 798. The love of Christ towards his own, 799. Comparison of this with human love, 800. Why the faithful are called not servants but friends of Christ, 801, 802. The perfection of the apostolic doctrine in writing, and the foundation and efficacy of their calling, 803. The promise of being heard, made to the disciples, 804.

units.la: Tertia pars.

units.tr: The disciples are fortified in patience by various arguments. The first is taken from Christ's example, 805. The second is from the hatred of the world, 806. units.tr: Amplification of the hatred against Christ and the members of Christ, argument. The first: the world is struck with rage at the voice of truth, 809. The second: whatever pretext the world puts forward, it hates God, 810. The third: from the works of Christ, which the world mocks; there is the source of that hatred, 811. Why the wicked are inexcusable, 812.

units.tr: The first argument of the consolation proposed by Christ to his own: that the Holy Spirit will bear witness within concerning him, 813. The second: that the disciples will be his witnesses, 814.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAP. XVI.

units.la: Prima pars.
units.tr: First part.

units.tr: The conclusion of the exhortation to patience 815. The kind of afflictions 816. The foundation of persecutions 817. Why Christ spoke about the afflictions of his people 818.

units.tr: Second part.

units.tr: Consolation against sad thoughts arising from Christ's departure 819. Why God stirs up his people with scourges, by what power the Holy Spirit is given to us, and what kind of presence of Christ is better 820. units.la: Communio Patris & Filii, magnum pietatis mysterium 828. Discipulorum Christi stupor, ante Spiritus S. receptionem 829. discessus & reditus Christi effecta 830. units.tr: The communion of the Father and the Son, a great mystery of godliness 828. The amazement of Christ's disciples before the reception of the Holy Spirit 829. The parts of future blessedness: first, eternal joy 832; second, the bright light of the knowledge of Christ 833. Ter-

units.la: Tertia pars.
units.tr: Third part.

units.tr: The obedience of faith in the disciples of Christ 838. On what foundation this faith rests 839. The weakness of the same disciples 840. The rejection of vain confidence, and the conclusion of Christ's discourse 841. The condition of the Church on earth and in heaven 842.

units.la: CAP. XVII. Precatio solennis summi Sacerdotis Christi, tribus partibus constans.
units.tr: CAP. XVII. The solemn prayer of the Chief Priest, Christ, consisting of three parts.

units.la: Prima pars, continet precationem Christi pro seipso 843. huius petitionis summa, Glorificatio filii Dei 844.845. Petitionis argumenta. 1. Mortis instantis consideratio, 2. Gloriæ compensatio 846. 3. Vitæ æternæ pro electis petitio 847. Electorum, quibus vita hæc datur, descriptio 848. De vita æterna locus 849. Cognitionis veræ natura, obiectum, fructus 850. 4. Promissionis complementum 851. Christus quomodo Patrem glorificavit 852. Petitionis conclusio glorificationis locum designans 853. qua gloria petit glorificari Christus 854
units.tr: The first part contains Christ's prayer for himself (843). The sum of this petition is the glorification of the Son of God (844, 845). The arguments of the petition: (1) consideration of his impending death; (2) the compensation of glory (846); (3) the petition for eternal life for the elect (847). Description of the elect to whom this life is given (848). The place of eternal life (849). The nature, object and fruit of true knowledge (850). (4) The fulfilment of the promise (851). How Christ glorified the Father (852). The conclusion of the petition, indicating the place of glorification (853). By what glory Christ asks to be glorified (854).

units.la: Secunda pars precationè Christi pro suis discipulis continens arg. sumptis ab efficaci vocatione, ab electione æterna, abelectio ne consequentib. à præstatia eius cui Pater dedit electos, ab efficacia fidei iustificantis 855.856. Pro discipulis orat, nō pro mundo 857. Electorum in Christo consolationes 858. argumenta reliqua petitionis Christi, petita á filii Dei glorificatione, à tuta protectione electorum ante & post Christi discessum, à mundi aduersus eos odio, ab eo quòd discipuli non sint ex mundo 859.&c. præcipuum totius petitionis argumentum, ipsius Filii charitas immensa erga Patrem & erga electos 860. conseruatio electorum Dei in quo posita fit 861. conservationis discipulorum circunstantiæ 862. conclusio petitionis pro eorum salute 863. finis huius salutis & conservationis 864. De separatione nostra à mundo locus 866. Apostolatus commendatio à mittentis persona, & à fine sanctificationis Christi 867
units.tr: The second part, containing Christ's prayer for his disciples, with arguments taken from effectual calling, from eternal election, from the consequences of election, from the care of him to whom the Father gave the elect, and from the efficacy of justifying faith (855, 856). He prays for the disciples, not for the world (857). The consolations of the elect in Christ (858). units.la: COMMENTARIORVM ROBERTI ROLLOCI IN EVANGELIVM IOHANNIS
units.tr: COMMENTARY OF ROBERT ROLLOCK ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

units.la: Pars prima. ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: Part One. ARGUMENT.

units.la: Huius capitis duæ sunt partes. Primùm est descriptio magnifica & ampla τῆς λόγυ siue filij Dei ad versum vsque 37. Deinde est historia vocationis quinque discipulorum ad finem vsque capitis.
units.tr: The first part of this chapter has two parts. First, there is the magnificent and ample description of the Word [λόγος], that is, of the Son of God, down to verse 37. Then there is the account of the calling of the five disciples, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAP. I.

units.la: 1 IN principio erat sermo ille, & sermo ille erat apud Deum, erátque ille Sermo Deus.
units.tr: 1 In the beginning was that Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

units.la: 2 Hic Sermo erat in principio apud Deum.
units.tr: 2 The same was in the beginning with God.

units.la: 3 Omnia per hunc sermonem facta sunt, & absque eo factum est nihil quod factum sit.
units.tr: 3 All things were made by him, and without him was made nothing that was made.

units.la: 4 In ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux illa hominum.
units.tr: 4 In him was life, and that life was the light of men.

units.la: 5 Et lux illa in tenebris lucet, sed tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt.
units.tr: 5 And that light shineth in darkness, but the darkness comprehended it not.

units.la: DESCRIPTIONIS λόγυ & filij Dei multæ sunt partes. Prima pars continetur prima propositione, In principio erat Sermo ille. Sermo, inquâ, ille, nam articulus habet emphasin, & distinguit hunc sermonem ab aliis. Primùm igitur huius propositionis verba singula expendenda sunt, deinde verbis iam ponderatis propositionis sensus colligendus est. Primum igitur verbum quod occurrit est λόγος. Hic non est quidem sermo pronunciatus à Deo in principio, aut verbum vocale, vt loquuntur: sed est persona illa, nempe persona filij Dei per quam Deus Pater exerit efficaciam suam & voluntatem suam patefacit. Ideoque dicta est λόγος quòd Deus per eā loquatur. Neque enim vel olim loquutus est Deus Pater, vel etiam nūc loquitur, nisi per personam hanc filij. Esaias vidit Dominum, & audiuit loquentē. Iohannes noster, cap.12.41. Iehouam siue Dominum illū, qui loquutus est exponit Iesum Christum: Hæc dixit, inquit, Esaias quando vidit gloriam eius & loquutus est de eo. Sed de λόγῳ isto paulò altius quædam nobis sunt repetenda.
units.tr: There are many parts to the description of the Word [λόγος] and of the Son of God. The first part is contained in the first proposition, In the beginning was that Word. That Word, I say, because the article gives emphasis and distinguishes this Word from others. First, then, the individual words of this proposition must be weighed; then, with the words now weighed, the sense of the proposition is to be gathered. First, then, the word that occurs first is λόγος [λόγος]. Here it is not indeed a word spoken by God in the beginning, or a vocal word, as they put it; it is that person, namely the person of the Son of God, through whom God the Father exerts his power and makes his will known. It is therefore called λόγος [λόγος] because God speaks through it. For God the Father neither spoke of old, nor speaks now, except through this person of the Son. Isaiah saw the Lord and heard him speaking. Our John, ch. 12.41, identifies Jehovah, or that Lord who spoke, as Jesus Christ: These things said Esaias, when he saw his glory and spake of him. But some things about this λόγος [λόγος] must be gone over a little more deeply.

units.la: Filij Dei propria sunt epitheta duo, alterum est, quòd sit sapientia Patris, alterum quòd sit Verbum Patris. Sapientia dicitur, quia omnia arcana & recondita in Patre perfectè novit. Verbum dicitur, quia cognita illa arcana revelat, prout comodum est & tempestiuum, Angelis & hominibus. Vel, vt paulò aliter hoc efferam, quia Pater revelat arcana illa per ipsum: Ideóque Angelus apud Danielem, agnoscens filium tanquam sapientiam & sermonem Patris, ipsum interrogauit de constituto illo tempore, de quo antea in illa prophetia: quē etiam appellauit eodem loco מללונ המדבר, quasi dicas, sapientiam & sermonem Patris. Christus etiam ipse vendicat sibi hæc epitheta & attributa, ait, Nemo nouit Patrem nisi Filius, & cuicunque voluerit filius retegere. Nemo nouit Patrem, inquit, nisi Filius: hic sapientiæ Patris attributum sibi assumit: & cuicunque, inquit, voluerit filius retegere: hic Sermonis attributum sibi ascribit. Sic apud Iohannem noßtrum, habemus quòd Deum nemo vidit vnquam: Filius verò, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse nobis enarrauit. Filius, inquit, qui est in sinu Patris, ac proinde conscius omnium consiliorum Patris, ipsiusque æterna sapientia, ipse enarrauit, tanquam Sermo Patris sui. Vrtigitur paucis hæc absoluam; audimus ex Scripturis Christum stum vocari Prophetam; en tibi eius rei causam ac fundamentum: nempe quia filius λόγος Patris est ; hoc est persona illa, per quam Pater loquitur. Hactenus de prima voce consideranda nobis in prima hac propositione Euangelistæ.
units.tr: The Son of God has two proper epithets: one, that he is the wisdom of the Father; the other, that he is the Word of the Father. He is called wisdom because he knows perfectly all the hidden and secret things in the Father. He is called Word because he reveals those known secrets, as is fitting and timely, to angels and men. Or, to put it a little differently, because the Father reveals those secrets through him. Therefore the angel in Daniel, recognising the Son as the wisdom and word of the Father, asked him about the appointed time, of which he had spoken before in that prophecy; and in the same place he called him מללונ המדבר [the speaker of the word], as if to say, the wisdom and word of the Father. Christ himself claims these epithets and attributes for himself. He says: No one knows the Father except the Son, and to whomever the Son chooses to reveal him. By saying No one knows the Father except the Son, he takes to himself the attribute of the Father's wisdom; and by saying to whomever the Son chooses to reveal him, he ascribes to himself the attribute of the Word. So in our John we have that No one has seen God at any time; but the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him. The Son, he says, who is in the bosom of the Father, and therefore privy to all the counsels of the Father, and to his eternal wisdom itself, has declared him, as the Word of his own Father. So, to finish briefly: we hear from the Scriptures that Christ is called a Prophet. Here is the cause and foundation of that: namely, that the Son is the λόγος [λόγος] of the Father, that is, that person through whom the Father speaks. So far concerning the first word to be considered in this first proposition of the Evangelist.

units.la: Altera est vox principium. In principio, inquit; Principium intelligo illud pūctum temporis, quo cœpit Deus creare cælum & terrā: Nempe illud ipsum principium, de quo Moses in Genesi, In principio creauit Deus cælum & terram. Quod si λόγος erat in principio; hoc est in ipso creationis primo puncto, profectò erat ante creationem: quod si erat ante creationem, erat ab æterno. Nam Spiritus Dei in Scriptura, hac locutione significare solet æternitatem, vt Paulus, Elegit nos Deus in Christo ante quam iacerentur mundi fundamenta, hoc est ab omni æternitate. Et Petrus dicit Christum præordinatum, antè iacta mundi fundamenta: hoc est, ab æterno. Sic Proverb.8.23. vbi descriptio quædam est æternæ Dei Sapientiæ, hoc locutionis genere significatur ipsius æternitas: nempe Christum Deum fuisse ante omnia Dei opera; Ante sæculum inuncta fui: ante principium, ante primordia terræ. Quamobrem cùm dicit in principio fuisse λόγον, cùm ex hoc sequatur eum ante creationem fuisse, & ex hoc rursus ab æterno fuisse: quid aliud quæso significat quàm λόγος æternitatem?
units.tr: The other word is beginning. In the beginning, he says. By beginning I understand that point of time at which God began to create heaven and earth: namely that very beginning of which Moses speaks in Genesis, In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. But if the λόγος [λόγος] was in the beginning, that is, at the very first point of creation, then surely he was before creation; and if he was before creation, he was from eternity. For the Spirit of God in Scripture is accustomed to signify eternity by this expression, as Paul: God chose us in Christ before the foundations of the world were laid, that is, from all eternity. And Peter says that Christ was foreordained before the foundations of the world were laid, that is, from eternity. So in Proverbs 8.23, where there is a description of the eternal wisdom of God, his eternity itself is signified by this kind of expression: namely, that Christ was God before all the works of God: I was anointed before the age, before the beginning, before the beginnings of the earth. Wherefore, since he says that the Word was in the beginning, and it follows from this that he was before creation, and from that again that he was from eternity, what else, I ask, does this signify than the eternity of the λόγος [λόγος]?

units.la: Notandum nunc postremò est tertium verbum erat. Erat, inquit, non fiebat: quo verbo significatur λόγον extitisse iam tum cùm Deus inciperet omnia ex nihilo creare. Sensus igitur huius propositionis & primæ partis descriptionis est, ὁ λόγος filius (per quē Deus loquitur,) non tum demum incepit esse cùm Deus crearet mundum, neque tum cùm manifestatus est in carne: sed erat toto illo tempore à creatione mundi vsque ad manifestationem sui in carne, imò erat ab æterno. Videte igitur quale fundamentum fidei nostræ habeamus, qui in Christum credimus, nempe τὸν λόγον qui erat iam inde ab omni æternitate.
units.tr: It remains now to note finally the third word, was. He says was, not was made; by this word it is signified that the λόγος [λόγος] already existed when God was beginning to create all things out of nothing. The sense, therefore, of this proposition and of the first part of the description is this: ὁ λόγος [ὁ λόγος], the Son (through whom God speaks), did not begin to be only when God created the world, nor only when he was manifested in the flesh; but he was throughout that whole time, from the creation of the world until his manifestation in the flesh, and indeed he was from eternity. See, then, what a foundation of our faith we have, we who believe in Christ: namely τὸν λόγον [τὸν λόγον], who was already from all eternity.

units.la: Sed pergo ad secundam partem descriptionis, quæ habetur in secunda propositione, Et sermo ille erat. Est autem secunda pars descriptionis à persona τῷ λόγῳ, quam innuit dum dicit, Et sermo ille erat apud Deum. Videamus primum verba, deinde ex verbis intellectis colligamus propositionis sensum. Deum hic intelligo, non ipsam Dei, essentiam praecipuè, sed Deum Patrem: Neque enim λόγος dici potest fuisse apud naturam sive essentiam Dei, verum personam. Quid autem illud sit λόγος apud Deum Patrem esse Johannes ipse apertius exponit postea hoc cap. Vbi dicit filium in sinu Patris esse: Item filium in Patre, & Patrem in filio esse. Significat autem his locutionibus, ut sic dicam, coexistentiam, societatem ac communionem admirabilem filij cum Patre. Fundamentum huius quam dico coexistentiae, & admirabilis societatis duarum personarum, est unitas naturae communis, & essentiae divinae. [Finge enim duas personas apud homines, exempli gratia, Ioannem & Iacobum habere unam duntaxat numero animam, unum duntaxat numero corpus: Annon tum esset mirifica coniunctio harum duarum personarum? Sed cui assimulabo Altissimum] Necesse igitur est, cum sit in Trinitate unitas ista naturae ac Deitatis, coniunctissimam & arctissimam esse societatem & coexistentiam personarum, quae tamen est sine ulla ipsarum inter se confusione. Nam ipsa illa locutio, qua dicitur λόγος fuisse apud Deum, ita coniunctos & coexistentes istos natura & communi essentia significat, ut tamen intere a distinctos personis esse importet necessario. Sed quonam tendit haec locutio? nempe eo ut significet personam esse. Nam istud esse cum Patre, vel esse apud Patrem, infert necessario personam esse: Neque enim natura Dei dici potest esse vel fuisse cum Deo Patre, verum de persona hoc & vere & proprie dicitur. Quare, ut in summa dicam, his verbis descriptio est τῆς λόγου à persona ipsius coexistente cum Deo Patre: ut hic sit sensus propositionis: λόγος qui erat in principio, & erat quoque coexistens cum Deo patre; ac proinde persona in deitate una ac distincta. Vide igitur rursus dum in Christum credimus qualenam fundamentum fidei nostrae habeamus; nempe secundam ὑπόστασιν & personam in deitate.
units.tr: But I proceed to the second part of the description, which is contained in the second proposition, And that Word was. The second part of the description concerns the person of τῷ λόγῳ [τῷ λόγῳ], which he hints at when he says, And the Word was with God. Let us look first at the words, and then from the words understood let us gather the sense of the proposition. I understand God here not chiefly as the essence of God, but as God the Father: for the λόγος [λόγος] cannot be said to be with the nature or essence of God, but with the person. What it is for the Word to be with God the Father John himself explains more clearly later in this chapter, where he says that the Son is in the bosom of the Father, and likewise that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son. By these expressions he signifies, so to speak, the coexistence, the fellowship and the wonderful communion of the Son with the Father. The foundation of this coexistence and admirable fellowship of two persons, which I speak of, is the unity of a common nature and divine essence. [Imagine two persons among men, for example John and James, having only one soul in number and one body in number: would there not then be a wonderful conjunction of these two persons? But to whom shall I liken the Most High?] It is necessary, therefore, since in the Trinity there is this unity of nature and Deity, that the fellowship and coexistence of the persons should be most closely and tightly joined, yet without any confusion among them. For that very expression by which the λόγος [λόγος] is said to have been with God signifies these as joined and coexisting in nature and common essence, and yet it necessarily implies that they are distinct in person. But to what does this expression tend? Namely, that it signify a person. For to be with the Father, or to be with God the Father, necessarily implies a person; the nature of God cannot be said to be, or to have been, with God the Father, but this is said truly and properly of a person. Wherefore, to sum up, by these words there is a description of the λόγος [λόγος] from his person, coexisting with God the Father; so that the sense of the proposition is this: the λόγος [λόγος], who was in the beginning, was also coexisting with God the Father, and therefore a person within the one and distinct deity. See, then, again, as we believe in Christ, what foundation of our faith we have: namely a second ὑπόστασις [ὑπόστασις] and person in the deity.

units.la: Sed pergo nunc ad tertiam descriptionis τῆς λόγος par-
units.tr: But I now go on to the third part of the description of the Word, which...

units.la: Deus hoc loco Patre indicat.
units.tr: God here indicates him as distinct from the Father.

units.la: Filius Patri coexistes & ὁμοούσιος.
units.tr: The Son is coexistent with the Father and consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος].

units.la: Et persona distincta à Patre, nempe secunda in divina essentia. partem, quæ sumitur ab essentia & natura ipsius: hanc Deum vocat, Deum intelligo hic, non, vt superius persona, sed ipsam essentiam & naturam τῷ λόγῳ, quæ vna eadémque est Patris, filij & Spiritus Sancti: Ideóque communiter prædicatur de singulis personis; Pater est Deus, filius est Deus, Spiritus Sanctus est Deus. Verùm cùm vna eadémque numero Dei essentia prædicetur de singulis, intelligendum tamen est paulò aliter atque aliter se habere, cùm de distinctis ipsis personis dicitur.
units.tr: And he is a person distinct from the Father, namely the second in the divine essence. part, which is taken from the essence and nature of the Word. This part God calls God. Here I understand God not, as above, as a person, but the essence and nature itself of the Word [τῷ λόγῳ], which is one and the same in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Therefore it is commonly predicated of each person: the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God. But although the one and the same numerical essence of God is predicated of each, it must be understood that it stands somewhat differently when it is said of the distinct persons themselves.

units.la: Nam cùm de Patre dicitur, tum ea natura, vt non communicata aut data Patri ab alio intelligitur. Pater enim ex eo dicitur, quia essentiam & naturam suam à se habet, non autem communicatam sibi ab alio: neque enim vel filius vel Spiritus Sanctus, eam Patri communicavit. Cùm autem de filio dicitur, ea Dei natura vna & communis tum vt communicata aut data à Patre intelligitur. Nam æterna illa filij generatio consistit in illa communicatione vnius & totius naturæ Patris. Cùm denique de Spiritu Sancto dicitur eadem illa communis, & vna numero natura, tum intelligitur vt communicata & data à Patre & filio: Nam processio illa Spiritus Sancti à Patre & filio consistit in communicatione vnius & totius naturæ Patris & Filij. Qui autem sit modus communicationis huius, eam explicare non possum, ineffabilis enim est & incomprehensibilis: nobis quidem potius adorandus, quàm curiosius indagandus.
units.tr: For when it is said of the Father, that nature is understood as not communicated or given to the Father by another. For the Father is so called because he has his essence and nature from himself, not communicated to him by another; for neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit communicated it to the Father. But when it is said of the Son, that same one common nature of God is understood as communicated or given by the Father. For that eternal generation of the Son consists in the communication of the one and whole nature of the Father. Finally, when it is said of the Holy Spirit, that same common and numerically one nature is understood as communicated and given by the Father and the Son. For that procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son consists in the communication of the one and whole nature of the Father and the Son. But what the mode of this communication is, I cannot explain; for it is ineffable and incomprehensible. It is to be adored by us rather than curiously investigated.

units.la: Quare sensus huius propositionis mihi videtur esse: λόγος cùm esset in principio, essétque apud Deum, erat quoque ipse Deus. Nam ex hoc ipso quod erat apud Deum, sequitur eum fuisse quoque vna eadémque cum Deo essentia, adeóque Deum ipsum. Vide iam tertiò fundamentum fidei quàm firmum habeamus nos qui credimus in Iesum Christum: nempe eum, qui Deus sit, & vnum cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto.
units.tr: Wherefore the sense of this proposition seems to me to be this: the Word, since it was in the beginning and was with God, was also God himself. For from the very fact that it was with God, it follows that it was also one and the same essence with God, and therefore God himself. Now see, thirdly, how firm a foundation of faith we have, we who believe in Jesus Christ: namely, that he is God and one with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Sequitur nunc quarta pars descriptionis τῷ λόγῳ ab opere creationis: Priusquàm autem eam proponit, transitum sibi facit ad eam per repetitionem duarum propositionum præcedentium, quas coniunctas fundamentum quasi substernit propositioni sequenti de opere creationis. Nam si in principio erat apud Deum, opor-
units.tr: Now follows the fourth part of the description of the Word [τῷ λόγῳ], from the work of creation. Before he sets it forth, he makes a transition to it by repeating the two preceding propositions, which, joined together, lay a foundation, as it were, for the following proposition about the work of creation. For if in the beginning he was with God, it

units.la: Quarta pars descriptionis τῷ λόγῳ, abopere creationis. tuit eum non esse otiosum, verùm per ipsum omnia fa- cta esse, per ipsum inquam, non tanquam instrumen- tum, sed per ipsum, tanquam principalem efficientem, & cooperatorem æqualem tempore, æqualem dignita-te, essentia unum: verùm persona secundum. Nam sicut λόγῳ est subsistentia sua posterior & secundus ordine, prius enim subsistit pater, deinde subsistit filius à Patre genitus ab æterno. Sic etiam ordine agendi posterior est & secundus. Præcedit enim voluntas Patris, comitatur voluntas filij in rebus omnibus agendis. Inde existit hæc loquendi forma quòd pater per ipsum omnia fecerit, nempe à patre secundum, non tempore, non dignitate, sed agendi ordine. Quare sensus huius propositionis hic est: Cùm exiterit λόγῳ in principio apud Deum Patrem, non erat tum otiosus, sed Pater per eum tanquam ordine secundum omnia creauit.
units.tr: Fourth part of the description of the Word [τῷ λόγῳ], from the work of creation. was fitting that he was not idle, but that all things were made through him; through him, I say, not as an instrument, but through him as the principal efficient cause and co-worker, equal in time, equal in dignity, one in essence, yet second in person. For just as the Word has his subsistence posterior and second in order (for the Father subsists first, then the Son, begotten of the Father from eternity), so also he is posterior and second in the order of acting. For the will of the Father goes before, and the will of the Son accompanies it in all things to be done. Hence arises this form of speaking, that the Father made all things through him: namely, the Son is second to the Father, not in time, not in dignity, but in the order of acting. Wherefore the sense of this proposition is this: when the Word existed in the beginning with God the Father, he was not then idle, but the Father created all things through him, who is second in order.

units.la: Additur asseueratio per negationem contrarij. Et absque eo factum est nihil quod factum est. Sic solet Ioannes quæ primùm affirmauit asseuerare deinde per negationem contrarij: Affirmatio enim est, omnia per ipsum facta sunt; Contrarium est, sine ipso factum est aliquid; abnegatio huius est, sine ipso factum est nihil quod factum est. Sic enim asseuerat omnia per ipsum facta esse, quò maior fides habeatur affirmationi, nempe quòd omnia per λόγον creata sunt. Vides nunc quarto loco quale fundamentum fidei nostræ habeamus dum credimus in Iesum Christum, nempe in Creatorem nostrum.
units.tr: An assertion is added by denial of the contrary. And without him was made nothing that was made. John is accustomed in this way to affirm a thing first and then to assert it by denying the contrary. The affirmation is, all things were made through him; the contrary is, without him something was made; the denial of this is, without him nothing was made that was made. For thus he asserts that all things were made through him, so that greater trust may be placed in the affirmation, namely that all things were created through the Word. You now see in the fourth place what a foundation of our faith we have when we believe in Jesus Christ, namely in our Creator.

units.la: Sequitur quinta pars descriptionis à vita illa quæ in principio fuit in λόγῳ. In ipso, inquit, vita erat. hic vitam Dei intelligo & vt crassius loquar, esse Dei. Vt enim vita creaturæ est vel esse ipsius, vel actio inde profecta: vita Dei, est esse Dei, vel certè facultas qua exercet opera suæ vitæ. In principio hæc vita erat in λόγῳ, hoc est, hanc vitam habebat in se, per se ipse viuebat, viuus erat suapte natura, imò ipsa vita erat. Vt Pater est ipsa vita, eáque re distinguitur à creaturis viuis, quarum nulla per se viuit, aut sua natura viua est, sed, vt ait Paulus, per ipsum viuimus & mouemur & sumus.
