Nam cùm participatione vitæ Dei habeamus hanc vitam quam viuimus, ipse sua manu eam sustentat: de nulla enim creacreatura dici potest id quod de filio dicitur postea, dedit filio habere vitam in semetipso. Nam quemadmodum, vt i-bidem dicitur, Pater habet vitam in seipso, ita filio dedit vitam habere in semetipso. In quibus verbis apparet etiam discrimen inter Patrem & Filium: Etsi enim vterque & Pater & filius vitam habeat in semetipso & per se viuat, quia Deus est vterque: Tamen in hoc est discrimen, quod Pater vitam illam, quemadmodum essentiam & naturam suam, non habeat communicatam sibi ab alio, sed à se habeat: Filius autem vt essentiam, sic vitam etiam habeat sibi à Patre communicatam. Ideoque Pater dicitur dedisse filio vitam habere in semetipso. Sensus igitur huius quintae partis descriptionis hic est, λόγῳ Dei filius cum esset in principio apud Deum Patrem, Cum esset ipse Deus per quem Pater creauit omnia, λόγῳ, inquam, in principio vitam in semetipso habebat, & per se viuebat vt Pater. Nâ si in principio erat Deus, oportebat profecto in principio vitam in semetipso habere, & per se viuere: Est enim hoc Dei proprium. Vide rursus quale fundamentum fidei tuae habeas, qui credis in Iesum Christum: neque enim duntaxat habes in Christo vitam hanc hominis ζωήν & naturalem etiam sanctissimam, ad quam quidem non est fidei oculo conniuendum, cum eam ipsam pro nobis posuerit: sed habes ineffabilem illam Dei vitam in Seruatore tuo, in qua fides tua vel imprimis est fundanda, & in quam fide oportet penetrare, vt hinc vitam nostram spiritualem hauriamus.
units.tr: Now follows the fifth part of the description, from that life which was in the Word in the beginning. In him, he says, was life. Here I understand the life of God, and, to speak more crudely, the being of God. For as the life of a creature is either its being or the action proceeding from it, so the life of God is the being of God, or certainly the faculty by which he exercises the works of his life. In the beginning this life was in the Word, that is, he had this life in himself; he lived through himself, he was living by his own nature, indeed he was life itself. As the Father is life itself, and is distinguished by this from living creatures, none of which lives through itself or is living by its own nature, but, as Paul says, in him we live and move and have our being. For although we have the life we live by participation in the life of God, he sustains it by his own hand; for of no creature can be said what is said afterwards of the Son: he gave to the Son to have life in himself. For just as, as is said in the same place, the Father has life in himself, so he gave to the Son to have life in himself. In these words there also appears a distinction between the Father and the Son. For although both the Father and the Son have life in themselves and live through themselves, because each is God, yet this is the difference: the Father does not have that life, just as he does not have his essence and nature, communicated to him by another, but has it from himself; the Son, however, has life, as he has essence, communicated to him by the Father. Therefore the Father is said to have given to the Son to have life in himself. The sense of this fifth part of the description, then, is this: the Word of God, the Son, when he was in the beginning with God the Father, since he was himself God, through whom the Father created all things, had life in himself in the beginning and lived through himself as the Father does. For if God was in the beginning, it was surely necessary that he have life in himself in the beginning and live through himself; for this is the property of God. See again what foundation of your faith you have, you who believe in Jesus Christ. For you have in Christ not merely that life of man, [ζωήν] natural and even most holy, toward which the eye of faith is not to be closed, since he himself has put it in our place; but you have that ineffable life of God in your Saviour, in which your faith especially must be founded, and into which we must penetrate by faith, so that from it we may draw our spiritual life.

units.la: Sequitur sexta pars descriptionis τῶν λόγων ab effecto ipsius, nempe viuificatione hominis praesertim in prima illa creatione, & tum in principio, cum vita in ipso esset, ac per se viueret. Et vita, inquit, erat lux illa hominum. vita illa τῶν λόγων, quam per se viuebat, erat lux, vitam illam Dei lucem appellat. Nam vt dicitur alibi, Deus est lux, nec in eo tenebrae sunt ullae. Deus est lux incomprehensibilis, & habitat lucem inaccessam, vt loquitur Apostolus. Verum ait vita, nempe quae erat in filio erat lux illa hominum, hoc est, erat lux illa cuius participatione illuminati sunt & viuificati homines in prima statim creatione: sensum enim & motum & cognitionem acceperunt homines in prima creatione, per participationem quandam vitæ & lucis filii Dei. Nam, vt dicam quod res est, nisi lux illa & vita illa filii, vigorem sensibus & menti nostræ inderet, in rebus etiam humanis & naturali hominum iudicio obuiis plusquam stupidi ac cæci essemus. Sicut Solomon ait, Aurem audientem & oculum videntem, Iehoua fecit æquè vtrumque. Sensus igitur huius partis est hic, Cum ⟨Greek⟩ in principio vitam haberet in semetipso: vita illa erat lux illa, quæ in principio & prima statim creatione illuminauit hominem ac viuificauit sensu, motu, cognitione, omni denique vitæ genere. Vide mihi rursus quale fundamentum fidei habeamus, eum nimirum qui cum in principio esset lux & vita, hanc lucem ac vitam ineffabilem liberaliter communicauit cum humano genere, & maiestatem quasi suam ac lucem illam inaccessam tamen applicauit ad hominem, hoc est ad creaturam suam. Hoc profecto debet animos nostros & studium omne ad ipsum mirabiliter applicare: Quod quidem faciat ipse Spiritu suo pro ea qua fuit semper, & est misericordia erga humanum genus.
units.tr: Now follows the sixth part of the description of the Word, from its effect, namely the quickening of man, especially in that first creation, and then in the beginning, when life was in him and lived through himself. And the life, he says, was that light of men. That life of the Word, which it lived through itself, was light; he calls that life of God light. For as it is said elsewhere, God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all. God is incomprehensible light, and dwells in light inaccessible, as the Apostle says. But he says life, namely that which was in the Son, was that light of men; that is, it was that light by participation in which men were enlightened and quickened in the very first creation. For men received sense, motion and knowledge in the first creation, through a certain participation in the life and light of the Son of God. For, to say what is the case, unless that light and life of the Son had infused vigour into our senses and mind, we would be more than stupid and blind even in human affairs and in matters obvious to natural human judgement. As Solomon says, the hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made both alike. The sense of this part, then, is this: since the Word had life in himself in the beginning, that life was that light which in the beginning and in the very first creation enlightened man and quickened him with sense, motion, knowledge, and finally every kind of life. See again what foundation of faith we have, namely him who, since he was light and life in the beginning, liberally communicated this ineffable light and life to the human race, and applied to man, that is, to his creature, his majesty as it were and that light inaccessible. Surely this ought to apply our minds and all our zeal wondrously to him. May he himself grant this by his Spirit, according to that mercy toward the human race which he always was and is.

units.la: Sequitur nunc septima pars descriptionis ⟨Greek⟩, ex effecto illuminationis nostri etiam post lapsum, quo tempore lux illa conuersa est in tenebras.
units.tr: Now follows the seventh part of the description ⟨Greek⟩, drawn from the effect of illumination in us even after the fall, at which time that light was turned into darkness.

units.la: Etiam nunc inquit lux ista lucet in tenebris. Mutauit tempus verbi ad designandum tempus illud insecutum hominis lapsum. Tenebras vocat hominis post lapsum non regenitos Spiritu Dei. Ait igitur lucem hanc lucere in tenebris illis. Lucet autem partim luce naturali, partim cœlesti luce Verbi sui in tenebris ipsis, hominum cordibus; Sed quo succesru? Tenebræ, inquit, non comprehenderunt eam, hoc est, homines non renati Spiritu ipsius, non assequuti sunt hanc lucem. Nam, quod ad naturalem illam lucem nihil profuit ipsis, quia eam mox malicia cordis sui verterunt in tenebras, traditique sunt in mentem omnis iudicii expertem. Quod vero ad lucem verbi attinet, sine Spiritu eam apprehendere non potuerunt. Verbum enim Dei sine Spiritu Sancto tantum abest ab eo vt intelligatur ab homine non renato, vt etiam pro stultitia ab eo habeatur. Sensus igitur huius septimæ partis descridescriptionis hic est. Post creationem humani generis & primam illam illuminationem ac viuificationem lapsis iam hominibus, lux illa tamen impertit se illuminandis hominibus lapsis & miserè obtenebratis, sed ipsi homines non regeniti ipsius spiritu, quæ est eorum pertinacia, nolunt illuminari. Nam quod ad lucem naturæ & cognitionem Dei naturalem, eam in iniustitia detinent, & Deum nolunt in notitia retinere, vt loquar cum Paulo. Ideoque procurant sibi mentem reprobam iusto Dei iudicio. Quod verò ad lucem verbi eam apprehendere non possunt. Vide rursus quàm benignè applicet ad humanum genus lucem suam, etiam postquàm sua culpa in tenebras versum est. Amor hic ineffabilis filij Dei erga humanum genus debet mirum in modum accendere animos nostros ad amplectendum fide tam benignum seruatorem. Luctatur enim perpetuò Dei Filius cum ingratitudine & malicia nostra, & si nos infidi sumus ille tamen fidus manet. Sed tu, Domine, ex tanta tua liberalitate da nobis fidem.
units.tr: Even now, he says, that light shines in the darkness. He changes the tense of the verb to indicate the time that followed the fall of man. He calls "darkness" those men, after the fall, who have not been born again by the Spirit of God. He says, then, that this light shines in that darkness. It shines partly with natural light and partly with the heavenly light of his Word, in the very darkness of human hearts. But with what success? The darkness, he says, did not comprehend it, that is, unregenerate men did not attain this light through his Spirit. As for the natural light, it did them no good, because the wickedness of their heart soon turned it into darkness, and they were given over to a mind incapable of judgement. As for the light of the Word, they could not grasp it without the Spirit. For the Word of God is so far from being understood by an unregenerate man without the Holy Spirit that he even regards it as foolishness. The sense of this seventh part of the description, then, is this: after the creation of the human race and that first illumination and quickening of men who had already fallen, that light nonetheless offers itself to fallen men who are wretchedly darkened and in need of illumination. But men who have not been born again by his Spirit, through their own obstinacy, refuse to be illumined. For as regards the light of nature and the natural knowledge of God, they hold it down in unrighteousness and are unwilling to retain God in their knowledge, to use Paul's words. So they bring upon themselves a reprobate mind, by the just judgement of God. As for the light of the Word, they cannot grasp it. See again how kindly he applies his light to the human race, even after it has turned into darkness through its own fault. This ineffable love of the Son of God towards the human race ought to kindle our minds wonderfully, so that we embrace with faith so gracious a Saviour. For the Son of God struggles constantly with our ingratitude and wickedness, and although we are faithless, he remains faithful. But you, Lord, out of your great generosity, give us faith.

units.la: 6 Exstitit homo missus à Deo, cui nomen Iohannes:
units.tr: 6 There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.

units.la: 7 Is venit ad dandum testimonium, id est, vt testaretur de illa luce, vt omnes per eum crederent.
units.tr: 7 The same came for a witness, to bear witness of that light, that all men through him might believe.

units.la: 8 Non erat ille lux illa, sed missus fuit vt testaretur de illa luce.
units.tr: 8 He was not that light, but was sent to bear witness of that light.

units.la: 9 Hic erat lux illa vera quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in mundum.
units.tr: 9 That was the true light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world.

units.la: ANtequàm persequar reliquas descriptionis partes, occurrit obiectioni occupatque sinistrum quorundam hominum iudicium de Iohanne Baptista. falsò enim putarunt cum esse Messiam, ac proinde lucem illam, de qua loquitur, id quod clarius videbimus postea. Primum igitur Ioannes contexit breuem historiam de Iohanne Baptista; cui deinde, tanquàm fundamento, superstruit responsionem suam. In Narratione describitur Iohannes. 1. à missione siue legatione sua, quòd esset homo missus à Deo, fuit quidam missus. 2. à nomine ipso Iohannis, quod significat præconem gratiæ, sumptū enim est à gratia, cui, inquit, nomen Iohannes. 3. à fine legationis suæ. Is venit, inquit, ad dandum testimonium: hoc est, vt interpretantur verba sequentia, vt testaretur de luce: Idque in hunc rursus finem, vt omnes per eum, hoc est, per eius ministerium crederent. Non erat ille. Hactenus narratio fuit, cui deinde superstruitur responsio, in qua primum negat Iohannem fuisse lucem illam: deinde λόγον esse lucem illam veram affirmat. Non erat, inquit, Iohannes lux illa. Tum propositam negationem illustrat ex diuerso Iohannis officio & ministerio, Sed missus erat vt testaretur de luce: λόγος autem erat lux illa vera: hoc est quæ natura sua lux est, non autem participatione. In quo sensu ipse etiam Iohannes lux erat, hoc est per lucis illius participationem. In hoc sensu totidem luces erant Apostoli, nimirum per participationem eius, qui natura sua ac per se lux est. Lucem hanc veram, quia ex natura sua incomprehensibili eam ostendere nō potest, ideóque ex effecto demōstrat, Quæ illuminat, inquit, omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum. Illuminat, inquam, saltē naturali luce, & non luce verbi, & Spiritu suo viuifico. De Iohanne Baptista nō est consilium hoc tempore aliquid prolixius dicere, remitto lectorē ad ea quæ de eo scripta sunt à Luca in Euangelio suo. Tantum hoc de eo in præsentia: Ministerium Iohannis fuit vt prænuncius ac præcursor esset Christi. Positum autem erat partim in doctrina, partim in Baptismo. Doctrina erat, qua quidem vt præcursor aliquis tastabatur Christum venturum, imò iam præsentem digito quasi demonstrabat. Baptisma erat, quod in Christum venturum & iam venientem administrabat. Vocatio ipsius ad hoc ministerium obeundum ita se habuit. Primùm designatus erat ad ministerium istud & prima statim conceptione, idque voce ipsius Dei per Angelum, Ne timeas, ait Angelus Zachariæ, preces tuæ exauditæ sunt, uxorque tua Elizabetha pignet tibi filium, & vocabis nomen eius Ioannem, &c. Deinde à prima statim nativitate designatus erat per Prophetam Patris sui: nam Zacharias conuertens se ad Ioannem filium recens natum ait, Tu vero puerule, inquit, Propheta altissimi vocaberis. iis, Ab ipso vtero instructus erat iis rebus quæ aptum ipsum facerent & idoneum ad illud tantum ministerium, vt Nazaræatu, iuxta prædictionem Angeli; vinum sicerámque non bibet: vt eximiis donis Spiritus Sancti ad hoc, vt tanquàm Elias alter reduceret populum ad Deum suum. Denique cùm annum ageret iam quasi tricesimum missus est à Deo ad munus suum, ad quod iam antè designatus est, & instructus obeundum. Hæc de eo hactenus.
units.tr: Before I pursue the remaining parts of the description, I must meet an objection and dispel the unfavourable judgement of certain men concerning John the Baptist. For they wrongly thought that he was the Messiah, and therefore that he was that light of which he speaks, as we shall see more clearly later. First, then, John sketches a brief history of John the Baptist, and then, as upon a foundation, he builds his response. In the narrative John is described (1) from his mission or commission, since he was a man sent from God, a certain one sent; (2) from the very name of John, which means herald of grace, for it is derived from grace: whose, he says, name was John; (3) from the purpose of his commission: The same came, he says, for a witness, that is, as the following words explain it, to bear witness of that light, and this again for the purpose that all men through him, that is, through his ministry, might believe. He was not that light. So far the narrative; upon it he then builds his response, in which he first denies that John was that light, and then affirms that the Word is that true light. He was not, he says, that light, namely John. Then he illustrates the denial he has put forward by the contrasting office and ministry of John: but was sent to bear witness of that light. But the Word was that true light, that is, one which is light by its own nature, and not by participation. In this sense John himself was also a light, that is, by participation in that light. In this sense the Apostles were as many lights, by participation in him who is light by nature and in himself. Since this is the true light, and by its nature cannot be displayed as incomprehensible, he shows it by its effect: which lighteth, he says, every man coming into this world. It lights, I say, at least with natural light, and not with the light of the Word, and by its quickening Spirit. Concerning John the Baptist it is not my purpose to say anything more lengthy at this time; I refer the reader to what Luke has written about him in his Gospel. Only this for the present: the ministry of John was to be the forerunner and herald of Christ. It consisted partly in teaching and partly in baptism. His teaching was such that, as a forerunner, he testified that Christ was coming, and even pointed to him with his finger as already present. His baptism was administered to Christ who was to come and was already coming. His calling to undertake this ministry was as follows. First, he was designated for this ministry from the very moment of his conception, by the voice of God through an angel: Fear not, said the angel to Zacharias, thy prayer is heard, and thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John, and so on. Then, from the very moment of his birth he was designated through the prophecy of his father: for Zacharias, turning to John his newborn son, said, And thou, child, he said, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest. Moreover, from the womb itself he was furnished with those things which made him fit and suitable for that ministry alone: as a Nazarite, according to the prediction of the angel, he shall drink neither wine nor strong drink; and with the outstanding gifts of the Holy Spirit, so that, like another Elijah, he might bring the people back to their God. Finally, when he was about thirty years old, he was sent by God to his task, for which he had been designated beforehand and equipped to perform it. So much for him so far.

units.la: Ex hac historia Ioannis ab Euangelista nostro recitata vnum hoc duntaxat, & illud quidem tritum ac vulgare, obseruabo; Ioannes non nisi missus prius à Deo testatus est de luce. Non nisi missos à Deo testari oportet de Christo, quod vsque adeò verum est vt Paulus pro impossibili habeat id, vt quis non missus à Deo prædicet Euangelium: Quomodo, inquit, prædicabunt nisi missi fuerint? Videant igitur ministri verbi habeant argumenta quibus ipsorum conscientiæ roborentur & confirmentur quòd missi sunt à Deo. Videant vt tolerabiliter instructi sint dono prædicationis, vt ad prædicandum veniant animo inseruiendi non ventri, sed Deo & Ecclesiæ ipsius. Videant denique ne contemnant ordinariam in Ecclesia Dei vocationem. Harum rerum sibi conscij, satis instructi sunt argumentis legationis suæ. Sed quis finis esse debet ita missorum à Deo ad testandum de Christo? nempe hic, vt omnes per eos credant. Quemadmodum igitur non effugient qui currunt non missi: ita male vertet iis, per quorum incredulitatem & contumaciam fiat vt frustra currant à Deo missi. Attendant igitur singuli quomodo audiant testimonium de Christo seruatore. Sed missi à Deo consolationem vel ex hoc capiant, quòd certò habituri sunt aliquos saltem pios auditores & fideles.
units.tr: From this history of John, recited by our Evangelist, I shall note only this one point, and that a commonplace and familiar one: John bore witness of the light only after he had first been sent by God. Those who are not sent by God ought not to bear witness of Christ at all. This is so true that Paul regards it as impossible for anyone who is not sent by God to preach the Gospel: How shall they preach, he says, unless they be sent? Let ministers of the Word therefore see that they have arguments by which their consciences may be strengthened and confirmed that they have been sent by God. Let them see that they are reasonably equipped with the gift of preaching, so that they come to preach with the intention of serving not their belly, but God and his Church. Let them see, finally, that they do not despise the ordinary calling in the Church of God. Those who are conscious of these things are sufficiently furnished with the arguments of their commission. But what end ought those sent by God to bear witness of Christ to have? Surely this: that all may believe through them. Therefore, just as those who run without being sent will not escape, so it will go ill for those through whose unbelief and obstinacy it comes about that those sent by God run in vain. Let each one therefore consider how he hears the testimony concerning Christ the Saviour. But let those sent by God take comfort even from this, that they will certainly have at least some pious and faithful hearers.

units.la: 10 In mundo erat, & mundus per eum factus est: sed mundus eum non agnouit.
units.tr: 10 He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him.

units.la: 11 Ad suos venit, & sui eum non exceperunt.
units.tr: 11 He came to his own, and his own did not receive him.

units.la: 12 Quotquot autem eum exceperunt, dedit iis hoc ius vt filij Dei sint facti, nempe iis qui credunt in nomen eius:
units.tr: 12 But as many as received him, to them he gave this right, that they should become children of God, namely to those who believe in his name.

units.la: 13 Qui non ex sanguine, neque ex libidine carnis, neque ex libidine viri, sed ex Deo geniti sunt.
units.tr: 13 who were born not of blood, nor of the lust of the flesh, nor of the lust of man, but of God.

units.la: 14 Et Sermo ille factus est caro, & commoratus est inter nos (& spectauimus gloriam eius, gloriam, inquam, ut unigeniti egressi a Patre) plenus gratia & veritatis.
units.tr: 14 And that Word was made flesh and dwelt among us (and we beheld his glory, glory, I say, as of the only-begotten who came from the Father), full of grace and truth.

units.la: HActenus fuit illa occupatio; deinde Ioannes redit ad descriptionem τῶ λόγῳ instituram. Sequitur igitur descriptionis pars octaua, à præsentia τῶ λόγῳ siue filii Dei in mundo, per ipsum creato, præsentia, inquam, quæ iam inde à principio fuit, vsque ad manifestationem ipsius in carne. In mundo inquit erat, & mundus per eum factus est. Mundum intelligo vniuersum genus hominum; opponitur quidem certo ac peculiari populo Iudaico, de quo postea. Sensus igitur est: Iam inde à principio primaque rerum omnium creatione ad aduentum vsque ipsius ad peculiarem suum populum, λόγος commorabatur toto illo spatio in mundo per ipsum facto. Hæc sententia confirmatur aliis Scripturæ locis. Prouerb. 8. 30, 31. Sapientia æterna Patris, hoc est, Dei Filius, de se ita loquitur: Cum itaque sim apud eum educàs, & sim deliciæ quotidianæ; lætificàs coràm eo omni tempore, & lætificans in orbe habitabili terra eius, atque deliciis meis filios hominum. Hæc de se loquuta est Dei Sapientia antequam esset incarnata. Sic 1. Pet. 3. 18, 19. dictum est de Christo quòd Spiritu viuificatus sit, per quem etiam spiritibus qui sunt in carcere profectus prædicauit, olim immorigeris. Ex quibus verbis colligitur Christum etiam diebus Noæ secundum deitatem suam in mundo fuisse; At quomodo tum fuit acceptus à mundo? mundus, inquit, eum non agnouit. Habuit quidem tum mundus confusam aliquam Dei notitiam, sed Deum in filio suo non agnouit, quæ tamen cognitio Dei sola salutaris est: Neque tamen excusatur mundus quòd Deum in filio suo non agnouerit, cum filius etiam tum ante manifestationem sui in carne fuerit efficax in hominibus. Vide igitur vt Christus ille in quem credimus iam inde ab initio non deseruerit homines, sed eos vt ex Prouerbiis paulò ante audiuimus pro delitiis habuerit. Quod profecto efficere debet, vt nos eum mutuo pro delitiis habeamus, ipsúmque qui sic nos perpetuò complexus est, vicissim fide amplectamur. Sed tu Domine da nobis fidem.
units.tr: Hitherto that was the subject; then John returns to describe the Word. There follows the eighth part of the description, from the presence of the Word, or Son of God, in the world, which was created through him, a presence, I say, which has existed from the beginning until his manifestation in the flesh. "He was in the world," he says, "and the world was made through him." I understand by the world the whole human race; it is indeed set against the particular and peculiar Jewish people, of whom he speaks later. The sense, then, is this: from the beginning and the first creation of all things until his coming to his own peculiar people, the Word dwelt through that whole span of time in the world made through him. This sense is confirmed by other passages of Scripture. Proverbs 8:30, 31: the eternal Wisdom of the Father, that is, the Son of God, speaks of himself thus: "Then I was beside him, as one brought up with him, and I was daily his delight, rejoicing before him at all times, rejoicing in the habitable world, and my delights were with the sons of men." The Wisdom of God spoke these things of itself before it was incarnate. So too 1 Peter 3:18, 19 says of Christ that he was quickened by the Spirit, by whom also he went and preached to the spirits who are in prison, who formerly were disobedient. From these words it is gathered that Christ, according to his deity, was in the world even in the days of Noah. But how was he then received by the world? "The world," he says, "did not know him." Indeed the world then had some confused knowledge of God, but it did not know God in his Son, and yet that knowledge of God alone is saving. Nor is the world excused for not knowing God in his Son, since the Son, even before his manifestation in the flesh, was effective among men. See, therefore, how that Christ in whom we believe has not from the beginning forsaken men, but has held them, as we heard a little before from the Proverbs, as his delights. This ought surely to bring it about that we, in turn, hold him as our delight, and embrace with faith in return him who has thus always embraced us. But you, Lord, give us faith.

units.la: Sequitur nona pars descriptionis Christi ab aduentu ipsius ad suos, hoc est Iudæos, qui peculiariter Christi esse dicuntur; quia iis nominatim est promissus. Ad suos venit. Sensus est, Non agnitus à mundo tanto temporis interuallo, in plenitudine temporis. Venit λόγος ad peculiarem suum populum, hoc est; Cùm prius etiam adesset, tamen speciali quodam modo se manifestauit suis, assumpta nimirum carne nostra ex vtero Virginis. Sed quomodo quaesso est acceptus à suis? Sui, inquit, eum non exceperunt. Maior profecto est ista ingratitudo Iudæorum, quàm quæ Mundi fuit, vel ob hanc causam, quòd se speciali modo Iudæis manifestauit. Maior etiam est futura nostra ingratitudo quàm Iudæorum, si Christum ad nos venientem non exceperimus; vel ob hanc causam, quòd spiritu suo magis efficax sit in mundo hodierno die, etiam absens quoad carnem, quàm fuit inter Iudæos præsens secundum eandem carnem.
units.tr: There follows the ninth part of the description of Christ, from his coming to his own, that is, to the Jews, who are said to be Christ's in a peculiar way, because it was promised to them by name. "He came to his own." The sense is: not recognised by the world over so great a stretch of time, he came in the fullness of time. The Word came to his peculiar people; that is, although he was already present before, he nevertheless manifested himself to his own in a special way, namely by taking on our flesh from the womb of the Virgin. But how, I ask, was he received by his own? "His own," he says, "did not receive him." Certainly this ingratitude of the Jews is greater than that of the world, if only for this reason, that he revealed himself to the Jews in a special way. Our own ingratitude will be greater still than that of the Jews, if we do not receive him coming to us; and this for the reason that he is now more effective in the world, even though absent in the flesh, than he was among the Jews, present according to the same flesh.

units.la: Sequitur nunc decima pars descriptionis ab effectu ipsius in iis Iudæorum, qui ipsum venientem exceperunt. Est autem, quòd dederit iis hanc dignitatem vt filij Dei fierent. Sed verba textus sunt: quotquot eum exceperunt, dedit iis hanc dignitatem vt filij Dei fierent. Hoc est, dignatus est eos hoc iure filiorum Dei; cùm prius filij non essent. Atque id fecit non vt Minister aut præco aliquis qui ius ab illo datum pronunciat: Sed tanquam ipse habens authoritatem & potestatem faciendi ex non filiis, Dei filios. Tum verbis sequentibus clarius exprimit quibusnam dederit hanc dignitatem: nempe iis qui credunt in nomen eius. Fide enim exceptus est Christus ad suos cùm veniret. Vbi nota oportere hominem fide prius censeri iustum in Christo quàm habeatur filius Dei per adoptionem: non enim nisi iam iustificatos & innocentes declaratos per filium censet Pater filios suos in filio.
units.tr: There follows now the tenth part of the description, from his effect on those Jews who received him when he came. It is that he gave them this dignity, that they should become sons of God. The words of the text are: "As many as received him, to them he gave this dignity, that they should become sons of God." That is, he deigned to grant them this right of sons of God, when they were not previously sons. And he did this not as a minister or herald who proclaims a right given by another, but as one who himself has the authority and power to make sons of God out of non-sons. Then the following words express more clearly to whom he gave this dignity: namely, "to those who believe in his name." For Christ was received by faith when he came to his own. Here note that a man must first be counted righteous in Christ by faith before he is held to be a son of God by adoption; for the Father does not count his sons in the Son unless they are already justified and declared innocent through the Son.

units.la: Postremò describit nobis hos filios:Filij sunt in vni- uersum qui geniti sunt ex patribus suis. Itaque Dei filios ex generatione quadam sua describit. Qui, inquit, non sunt geniti ex sanguine, neque ex libidine carnis, neque ex libidine viri. Hoc est, crasso isto & naturali modo ex massa peccatrice: cuiusmodi est prima nostrum omnium & naturalis generatio. Sed qui geniti sunt ex Deo, nempe per incorruptibile illud semen verbi sui, vt loquitur Petrus, & per Spiritum, vt Christus ipse postea disserit.
units.tr: Finally he describes these sons for us: they are, in general, those who are born of their fathers. Thus he describes the sons of God from a certain generation of their own. "Who," he says, "are not born of blood, nor of the lust of the flesh, nor of the lust of man." That is, in that crude and natural manner from a sinful mass, such as is the first and natural generation of us all. "But who are born of God," namely through that incorruptible seed of his word, as Peter says, and through the Spirit, as Christ himself discourses afterwards.

units.la: De adoptione nostri in Christo quia hic locus requirit vt dicamus nonnihil, sic paucis habeto. Adoptio nostra est qua cùm non nascamur filij Dei, sed ecòtra filij irae, censemur tamen in Christo Dei Filio naturali unico, Filij Dei, ac proinde heredes. Fundamentum huius adoptionis est charitas Dei erga humanum genus admirabilis. Videte, inquit Iohannes, qualem charitatem dedit nobis Pater, nempe vt filij Dei vocemur. Sed adhuc altius quoddam est fundamentum huius charitatis, nempe charitas illa ineffabilis, qua ab aeterno prosequutus est filium suum unigenitum. Nam in illa dilectione dilexit nos, & nos gratos effecit sibi gratos in illo dilecto.
units.tr: Since this passage requires that we say something about our adoption in Christ, take this briefly. Our adoption is that by which, though we are not born sons of God but rather sons of wrath, we are nevertheless counted in Christ, the one natural Son of God, as sons of God, and therefore heirs. The foundation of this adoption is the wonderful love of God towards the human race. "See," says John, "what manner of love the Father has given us, that we should be called sons of God." But there is a still deeper foundation of this love, namely that ineffable love with which he has loved his only-begotten Son from eternity. For in that love with which he loved him, he loved us too, and made us acceptable to himself in the Beloved.

units.la: Fundamenta igitur huius adoptionis sunt primum charitas illa Dei erga Filium suum naturalem, deinde charitas erga humanum genus, qua ipsum diligit in dilecto suo. Adoptio autem quomodo superstruatur his, quasi fundamentis nunc videamus. Vt nos filij Dei censeamur primum necesse est vt Filius Dei naturalis in quo nos dilexit, frater noster fiat, assumpta carne nostra, seque, per communicationem carnis nostrae nobiscum vniat ad hoc, vt nos deinde cum Patre ipsius vniamur: deinde necesse est vt in carne nostra moriens Filius Dei auferat omnia peccata nostra, satisfaciatque pro nobis iustitiae Patris sui, ac nos credentes in ipsum iustificet: Neque enim Pater iniustos pro filiis suis censere potest. Postquam autem iustificati sumus in eo, reliquum iam est vt filij ac heredes Dei censeamur, non secus ac si ex Deo ipso geniti essemus. Atque hac ratione dicitur Filius Dei dare nobis hanc dignitatem vt fiamus Dei filij. Sic iam adoptati in filios & pro filiis habiti in Dei Filio, accipimus sensum aliquem & quasi artha arrhabonem adoptionis nostri per Spiritum regenerantem nos, complementum autem per plenam vindicationem & liberationem in resurrectione iustorum; quo quidem tempore patefiet nos filios Dei esse: Etsi enim iam sumus filij Dei, tamen nondum patefactum est quid erimus. Ideóque ait Paulus, Suspiramus expectantes adoptionem; hoc est redemptionem corporis nostri, quæ erit in aduentu capitis nostri Christi, cui sit omnis honor & gloria. Amen.
units.tr: The foundations of this adoption, then, are first that love of God for his natural Son, and second the love for the human race, by which he loves them in his Beloved. Now let us see how adoption is built upon these, as upon foundations. For us to be counted sons of God, it is first necessary that the natural Son of God, in whom he loved us, should become our brother, by taking on our flesh, and should unite himself to us through the communication of our flesh, so that we may then be united to his Father. Next, it is necessary that the Son of God, dying in our flesh, should take away all our sins, should satisfy for us the justice of his Father, and should justify us who believe in him; for the Father cannot count the unjust as his sons. Once we have been justified in him, what remains is that we be counted sons and heirs of God, just as if we had been born of God himself. In this way it is said that the Son of God gives us this dignity, that we should become sons of God. Thus, now adopted and held as sons and as children in the Son of God, we receive some sense, as it were an earnest [ἀρραβών] of our adoption, through the Spirit who regenerates us, and its completion through full vindication and liberation at the resurrection of the just; at which time it will be made plain that we are sons of God. For although we are now sons of God, it has not yet been made manifest what we shall be. Hence Paul says, "We groan, waiting for the adoption," that is, the redemption of our body, which will come at the coming of our head Christ, to whom be all honour and glory. Amen.

units.la: Deinceps planius repetita nona parte descriptionis ab aduentu λόγῳ ad suos, transitum sibi facit ad vndecimam descriptionis partem. Sic igitur apertius repetit nonam illam descriptionis partem, expresso videlicet modo quo venerit ad suos, nempe assumpta carne & natura nostra. Verba sunt: Sermo ille caro factus est. Vi-deamus primum verba. Sermo hoc loco vt supra est illa persona per quam Deus se & voluntatem suam patefacit mundo, nempe Filius Dei æternus. Caro hoc loco est homo, κατὰ συνεκδοχὴν partis pro toto. Hominem dico non qui sit persona aut indiuidum per se subsistens. Nam humanæ in Christo naturæ nulla est subsistentia in se, verum subsistentia eius est in persona Filij Dei. Non igitur per hominem intelligenda est persona hominis, sed natura hominis, Corpus humanum, & anima humana, vna cum omnibus infirmitatibus illis quæ corpus & animam humanam comitantur excepto peccato. Cuiusmodi sunt in animo perturbationes, sed citra peccatum, metus, dolor, amor; item ignorantia illa conueniens naturæ humanæ, sed absque peccato. In corpore autem conceptio, natiuitas, augmentum staturæ, defatigatio, lachrymæ, mors denique ipsa. Tertiu hic verbum occurrit, factus est. Sermo ille factus est caro, λόγος quo-hoc est homo, non quidem vlla mutatione sui, sed assumptione duntaxat naturæ humanæ in vnitatem personæ, saluis interea & distinctis manentibus proprietatibus naturæ tam assumentis quàm assumptæ. Neque enim, exempli gratia, vel infinitas diuiuæ naturæ communicata est humanæ, vel finitas humanæ communicata est diuinæ, sic de cæteris proprietatibus vtriusque naturæ sentiendum est. Sensus igitur huius partis est. Sermo ille Dei Filius ab æterno genitus factus est homo assumpta sibi natura humana, sic vt iam euaserit nostri similis in omnibus si peccatum exceperis.
units.tr: Having repeated the ninth part of the description more fully, from the coming of the Word to his own, he now moves on to the eleventh part. He repeats that ninth part more clearly, expressing the manner in which he came to his own, namely by assuming flesh and our nature. The words are: "That Word was made flesh." Let us look at the words first. "Word" here, as above, is that person through whom God reveals himself and his will to the world, namely the eternal Son of God. "Flesh" here means man, by synecdoche of part for whole. I say man, not as a person or an individual subsisting in itself. For the human nature in Christ has no subsistence in itself; its subsistence is in the person of the Son of God. Therefore "man" is not to be understood as the person of a man, but as the nature of man: the human body and the human soul, together with all those infirmities which accompany body and soul, apart from sin. Such are disturbances of the mind, yet without sin: fear, grief, love; likewise that ignorance which belongs to human nature, but without sin. In the body, these include conception, birth, growth in stature, weariness, tears, and finally death itself. Here the third word occurs, "was made." That Word was made flesh, that is, was made man, not by any change in himself, but by the mere assumption of human nature into unity of person, while the properties of both natures, the assuming and the assumed, remain safe and distinct. For, to give an example, the infinity of the divine nature was not communicated to the human, nor was the finiteness of the human communicated to the divine; and the same must be understood of the other properties of each nature. The sense of this part, then, is this: that Word, the Son of God begotten from eternity, was made man, having taken human nature to himself, so that he has now become like us in all things, sin excepted.

units.la: In hanc sententiam multa sunt scripturæ loca, vt Heb. 2.16. Assumpsit semen Abraham, & ibidem vers. 14. particeps factus est carnis & sanguinis. Philip.2.6. sumpsit formam serui, cum prius esset in forma Dei. 2. Corinth. 8.9. Cum esset dives, propter nos factus est pauper, ut vos illius pauertate ditesceretis. 1. Timoth.3.16. Deus manifestatus est in carne. Hic videmus mirificam illam humiliationem æterni Dei. Nam propter superbiam illam hominis, vt eam nimirum expiaret, inquam hominis, qui per rapinam voluit esse Deo æqualis; Filius Dei qui non duxit rapinam parem esse cum Deo, inaniuit se, assumpta serui forma, & in ea præstita Patri obedientia visque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, Obedientia, inquam, qualis nullius vnquam creaturæ extitit, non hominis, non Angeli, cum ipsi Angeli natura serui sint: At filius non seruus ipse se inaniuit, obscurata ad tempus mirum in modum illa gloria, qua Patri ab æterno æqualis fuit, idque in massa naturæ nostræ & nostra causa. Atque in filio sic humiliato conspicitur amor Patris erga nos admirabilis, neque id modo, sed in filio, in carne nostra manifestato admirabilis ille amor, qui infinitis partibus superat omnium creaturarum amorem, propius ad nos admouetur (suavis enim huius rei consideratio est) Nam filius Dei, cum e natura patris genitus sit ab æterno, habet totam illam eandem substantiam Patris sibi communicatam, quo fit vt amor Patris resideat in natura filij. Iam vero suo tempore assumit filius naturam nostram, corpus nostrum, animam nostram, cor nostrum. Quamobrem, cum Deitas corporaliter habitet in natura nostra, profecto & amor ille Dei infinitus habitet quodammodo in corde humano Christi necesse est. Nam Christi cor non solum occupat amor hic naturalis idemque purissimus ac sanctissimus, quocum ne Angelorum quidem amor est comparandus, verum etiam infinitus ille & ineffabilis essentiæ diuinæ amor in eadem corde Christi humano habitat, & cor illud ipsum Christi humanum in illa vnione naturali hypostatica factum. factum est quodammodo Dei ipsius cor. Cum igitur tam prope nos attingat vt ad nos vsque sese ita demit- tat amor ille Dei infinitus, quippe qui in corde fratris nostri, & in natura ipsa nostra hospitetur, miseri sumus profecto, si tamen nullû prorsus eius sensum habeamus in corde nostro, & nullum sane habere possumus nisi Spiritus ipsius Dei sanctus effundat in cordibus nostris illam ipsam Dei charitatem, ad hoc vt corda nostra permoueantur ad Deum illum tam amantem nostri, redamandum, & fiduciam nostram omnem in eum collocandum. Det itaque Dominus nobis suum spiritum sanctum qui ingignat cordibus nostris hunc sensum dilectionis ipsius longè suauissimum.
units.tr: Many passages of Scripture agree with this sense: Heb. 2.16, "He took on the seed of Abraham," and in the same place verse 14, "he was made a partaker of flesh and blood." Phil. 2.6, "he took the form of a servant, though he was previously in the form of God." 2 Cor. 8.9, "Though he was rich, for our sake he became poor, that through his poverty you might become rich." 1 Tim. 3.16, "God was manifested in the flesh." Here we see the wonderful humiliation of the eternal God. For on account of man's pride, which he wished to expiate, I mean the pride of the man who by robbery wished to be equal to God, the Son of God, who did not think it robbery to be equal with God, emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, and in that form rendered obedience to the Father even unto death, and the death of the cross. Obedience such as never existed in any creature, not in man, not in an angel, since the angels themselves are by nature servants. But the Son, who is not a servant, emptied himself, the glory by which he was equal to the Father from eternity being obscured for a time in a remarkable manner, and this in the mass of our nature and for our sake. And in the Son so humbled we see the Father's admirable love toward us. And not only this: in the Son, that admirable love, manifested in our flesh, which surpasses the love of all creatures by infinite degrees, is brought nearer to us (for the consideration of this is sweet). For the Son of God, since he is begotten from the nature of the Father from eternity, has the whole of that same substance of the Father communicated to him, so that the Father's love resides in the nature of the Son. Now, in its time, the Son assumes our nature, our body, our soul, our heart. Wherefore, since "the Deity dwells bodily in our nature," it must surely be that God's infinite love dwells in some way in the human heart of Christ. For not only does that natural love, which is also most pure and holy, and with which not even the love of the angels is to be compared, occupy Christ's heart; but also that infinite and ineffable love of the divine essence dwells in the same human heart of Christ, and that human heart of Christ, made by that natural hypostatic union, has in some way become the very heart of God. Since, then, that infinite love of God touches us so closely, and so condescends to us, indeed dwelling in the heart of our brother and in our very nature, we are surely wretched if we have no sense of it at all in our hearts. And we cannot have any sense of it unless the Holy Spirit of God himself pours into our hearts that very love of God, so that our hearts may be moved to love in return that God who loves us so much, and to place all our trust in him. May the Lord therefore give us his Holy Spirit, who may engender in our hearts this sense of his most sweet love.

units.la: Sequitur duodecima pars descriptionis à cõmoratione λόγου incarnati inter Iudaeos, λόγος, inquâ, pleni gratiæ ac veritatis. commoratus est, inquit, inter nos; hoc est, Visibiliter vt homo inter homines cõuersatus est inter nos, sed ea cum plenitudine gratiæ ac veritatis, quæ in nullo vnquam homine obseruata est. Gratiæ nomine intelligo omnes proprietates, vt vocant, essentiales Dei: cuiusmodi sunt, potentia, sapientia, iustitia, bonitas &c. quæ in filio Dei fuerunt ex æterna illa sui generatione: Nam æterna illa filij generatio scaturigo quasi est & fons omnium virtutum & vt sic dicam gratiarum, quæ in natura Dei insunt. Vt enim in æterna illa generatione cõmunicata filio est essentia Dei: sic quoque omnes proprietates essentiales illius essentiæ, quæ nihil sunt aliud reipsa quàm æterna illa Dei essentia, speciatim subiungit vnam aliquam ex illis proprietatibus Dei essentialibus, veritatem nimirum: quo nomine intelligo veram illam & infinitam notitiam & cognitionem quæ erat in filio Dei, non cum tantum cum manifestatus est in carne, sed ab æterno. Nam in filio, vt ait Paulus, sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ & cognitionis abscondite: Neque id mirum videri debet, quandoquidem Filium, cum sit in sinu Patris, & æterna Patris Sapientia oportet omnia scire & peruidere, quæ Pater scit, & plane cum Patre cõscium esse omnium arcanorũ & consiliorum Patris sui. Dicit eum plenum gratiæ & veritatis, quo significat omnes istas Diuinas & essentiales proprietates in eo fuisse, non
units.tr: There follows the twelfth part of the description, from the sojourn of the incarnate Word among the Jews: "the Word, full of grace and truth." "He dwelt," it says, "among us"; that is, he lived visibly among men as a man among men, but with a fullness of grace and truth that was never observed in any man. By grace I understand all the so-called essential properties of God, such as power, wisdom, justice, goodness, and so on, which were in the Son of God from that eternal generation of his. For that eternal generation of the Son is, as it were, the spring and fountain of all virtues and, so to speak, of all the graces which are in the nature of God. Just as in that eternal generation the essence of God is communicated to the Son, so also all the essential properties of that essence, which are really nothing other than that eternal essence of God, are communicated to him. He specifically adds one of those essential properties of God, namely truth. By this name I understand that true and infinite knowledge and cognition which was in the Son of God, not only when he was manifested in the flesh, but from eternity. For "in the Son," as Paul says, "are all the treasures of wisdom and hidden knowledge." Nor should this seem strange, since the Son, being in the bosom of the Father and the eternal Wisdom of the Father, must know and see all that the Father knows, and plainly be conscious together with the Father of all the secrets and counsels of his Father. He says that he was "full of grace and truth," by which he signifies that all those divine and essential properties were in him, not

units.la: {b} ad mensuram aliquam,sed supra omnem modum, hoc est,quod Paulus ait ad Colossenses, In eo inhabitat corporaliter omnis plenitudo Deitatis. Sensus igitur huius undecimae partis hic est: λόγος iam incarnatus,communoratus est ad tempus,ac versatus est in assumpta illa carne visibiliter inter Iudaeos, sic tamen ut aperte conspiceretur eum plusquam hominem esse,utpote plenum omnium diuinarum proprietatum, praesertim autem verae sapientiae & cognitionis.
units.tr: {b} to some measure, but beyond all measure. This is what Paul says to the Colossians: "In him dwells bodily all the fullness of the Godhead." The sense of this eleventh part, then, is this: the Word, now incarnate, dwelt for a time and lived visibly among the Jews in that assumed flesh, yet in such a way that it was plainly seen that he was more than man, as one full of all divine properties, and especially of true wisdom and knowledge.

units.la: Sequitur confirmatio huius plenitudinis gratiae & excellentiae filij Dei qui commoratus est inter Iudaeos. Primum argumentum a testimonio ipsius Euangelistae & aliorum qui eum oculis spectarunt. Obiter insertum est propositioni ut nos, inquit, spectauimus gloriam eius. gloriam intelligo plenitudinem gratiae, hoc est omnium virtutum & proprietatum diuinarum thesaurum, quae quidem in effectis suis se prodiderunt, nempe miraculis, transfiguratione in monte, resurrectione gloriosa, in coelos ascensione, missione denique Spiritus sancti post ascensionem. Negari tamen non potest Christum ante mortem suam gloriam hanc non nisi obscure videdam praebuisse; neque enim Spiritus ille viuificus Christi plane se exeruit, vel erga massam illam naturae nostrae, quam ipse gestauit, sic enim impossibile fuisset naturam illam glorificatam pati: Vel erga fideles, sic enim glorificati fuissent ac sanctificati non remissis prius peccatis per mortem Filij, quod fieri non potest. Reconciliatio enim per mortem & sanguinem Christi praecedit sanctificationem & glorificationem per Spiritum ipsius.
units.tr: There follows the confirmation of this fullness of grace and excellence of the Son of God, who dwelt among the Jews. The first argument is from the testimony of the Evangelist himself and of others "who beheld him with their eyes." This is inserted in passing into the proposition, "as we, he says, beheld his glory." By glory I understand the fullness of grace, that is, the treasure of all virtues and divine properties, which indeed revealed themselves in their effects: namely in miracles, in the transfiguration on the mount, in the glorious resurrection, in the ascension into heaven, and finally in the sending of the Holy Spirit after the ascension. Yet it cannot be denied that Christ, before his death, presented this glory only to be seen obscurely. For that life-giving Spirit of Christ did not fully reveal itself, either toward that mass of our nature which he bore (for thus it would have been impossible for that glorified nature to suffer), or toward the faithful (for thus they would have been glorified and sanctified before their sins were remitted through the death of the Son, which cannot happen). For reconciliation through the death and blood of Christ precedes sanctification and glorification through his Spirit.

units.la: Quos iustificauit, hos glorificauit, teste Apostolo. Sequitur in textu, Gloriam, inquam, ut vnigeniti egressi a Patre. Definitio est quaedam eius, de qua modo loquutus est, gloriae. Est autem quae testabatur eum plusquam creaturam esse, imo filium Patris vnigenitum, ac proinde Deum cum Patre ab aeterno: Vnigenitum filium vocat, quia solus genitus est e natura Patris ab aeterno: Eodem sensu dicitur proprius Dei filius. Nos autem filij Dei sumus, sed non geniti ex substantia Patris, verum gratia adoptati per vnigenitum. Neque tamen istud est inane nomen, verum cum membra simus vnigeniti filij. lij, ipsi per fidem insiti, omnium beneficiorum ipsius participes sumus. Nam si filij, etiam hæredes sumus. Hactenus fuit primum argumentum in parenthesi, quo confirmata est illa in λόγῳ incarnato plenitudo gratiæ ac veritatis.
units.tr: "Whom he justified, them he also glorified," as the Apostle testifies. The text continues, "The glory, I say, as of the only-begotten who came forth from the Father." This is a definition of the glory he has just spoken of. It is the glory that bears witness that he is more than a creature, indeed the only-begotten Son of the Father, and therefore God with the Father from eternity. He calls him the only-begotten Son because he alone was begotten from the Father's nature from eternity. In the same sense he is called the Father's own Son. We are indeed sons of God, but not begotten of the Father's substance; we are adopted by grace through the only-begotten. Yet this is no empty name, since we are members of the only-begotten Son. Grafted into him by faith, we share in all his benefits, for "if sons, then also heirs." Thus far is the first argument, put in parentheses, by which the fullness of grace and truth in the Word made flesh is confirmed.

units.la: 15 Iohannes testatus est de eo, & clamavit dicens, Hic est de quo dicebam, Is qui post me venit, antepositus est mihi: quia prior me erat.
units.tr: John bore witness of him and cried out, saying, "This is he of whom I spoke: he who comes after me has been preferred before me, for he was before me."

units.la: 16 Et ex plenitudine ipsius omnes accepimus gratiam pro gratia.
units.tr: And from his fullness we have all received, and grace upon grace.

units.la: 17 Nam lex illa per Mosen data est: gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum præstita est.
units.tr: For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.

units.la: 18 Deum nemo vidit unquam: unigenitus ille filius qui est in sinu Patris, ille nobis expositus.
units.tr: No one has seen God at any time; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known.

units.la: SEquitur alterum Iohannis Baptistæ antegressum de Christi excellentia & gratiæ plenitudine testimonium. Testimonij propositio est, Iohannes testatus est de eo, hoc est, de excellentia eius. Iohannes, ut opinio est non inconcinna de eo, ingressus est vocationem suam anno Iubilæi, qui annus erat quinquagesimus, quo Iudæi reversi sunt ad possessiones suas, & quisque ad familiam suam. Ingressus, inquam, Iohannes functionem suam præco fuit æterni illius Iubilæi, hoc est lætitiæ, id enim nomen significat: promulgauitque æternâ redemptionem humani generis in Christo iamiam venturo. Consueuit enim annus Iubilæi per vocem præconis cum tubæ sonitu promulgari. Huc, ut probabile est, alludentes Prophetæ, quos sequuti sunt Euangelistæ, Iohannem vocem clamantis dixerunt, utpote præconem æterni Iubilæi. Sequitur declaratio propositi testimonij: hic est, inquit, de quo dicebam. Demonstrat Christum non voce solum sed digito. Quid autem dicebat de eo? Qui venit post me, prælatus est mihi. ratio autem est, Quia prior me est. Sensus horum verborum est, qui me posterior est officio, & ante quem ego missus sum, ut præparem vias eius, ante factus est, hoc est, factus est prior dignitate, prælatusque est mihi. Nam vocabulum πρῶτος priorita-temillam etiam significat quæ est ordinis ac dignitatis. Sic etiam Ioannes postea hoc cap. versu 27. vocem istam in hoc sensu accipit, & verba que eo loco sequuntur immediate sic accipiendam docent: Cuius corrigiam solearum ego non sum dignus ut soluam. Ratio autem huius praerogatiné Christi est, Quia prior me fuit, inquit, hoc est, Deus fuit ab aeterno. Testimonium igitur istud Baptistae est de dignitate personae Meffiae, quam quidem tractat comparate, dum praefert eum ipse sibi: sinistrae enim fuerunt hominum opiniones de Iohanne Baptista, ex quibus vna fuit, quod effet Meffias. Ideoque labo-
units.tr: Next follows the second testimony of John the Baptist, going before, concerning the excellence of Christ and the fullness of his grace. The proposition of the testimony is, "John bore witness of him," that is, of his excellence. John, as is not an unfitting opinion, entered upon his calling in the year of Jubilee, which was the fiftieth year, when the Jews returned to their possessions, and each to his family. John, I say, entering upon his office, was the herald of that eternal Jubilee, that is, of joy, for that is what the name means; and he proclaimed the eternal redemption of mankind in Christ, who was now about to come. For the year of Jubilee was customarily proclaimed by the voice of a herald with the sound of a trumpet. Alluding to this, as is probable, the prophets, whom the evangelists followed, called John the voice of one crying, as the herald of the eternal Jubilee. Next comes the explanation of the testimony put forward: "This is he," he says, "of whom I spoke." He shows Christ not only by voice but by finger. What, then, did he say of him? "He who comes after me has been preferred before me." The reason is, "because he was before me." The sense of these words is: he who is later than me in office, and before whom I was sent to prepare his ways, has become before me, that is, has been made first in rank, and has been preferred before me. For the word prōtos signifies that priority which belongs to order and dignity. So also John later, in this chapter at verse 27, takes the word in this sense, and the words that immediately follow in that place teach that it must be so understood: "The thong of whose sandals I am not worthy to loose." The reason for this pre-eminence of Christ is, "because he was before me," that is, God was from eternity. This testimony of the Baptist therefore concerns the dignity of the person of the Messiah, which he treats comparatively, while he sets him above himself. For the opinions of men about John the Baptist were mistaken, and one of them was that he was the Messiah. Therefore he labours

units.la: rat plurimum in eo, vt discernat fe a vero Messia. Potissimum autem in tribus discrimen facit, in persona, in officio, in Baptismo. In persona, quod Christus fit dignior ipse fit Christi duntaxat testis: in Baptismo, quod cum ipse baptizet aqua, Christus baptizet Spiritu sancto & igne. Vide igitur in hoc homine studium diuinae gloriae quantum fuerit. Modo honoraretur Messias nihili fecit contemptum sui. Imo ipse se contempsit, & cum esset homo, si quis vnquam alius, praeditus insignibus donis Spiritus sancti; tamen nihili se faciens prae Messia, ea omnia contempsit. Sic omnibus semper in quacunque vocatione ob oculos ponenda Dei gloria, praesertim testibus veritatis & ministris verbi, qui lubentissime ferre debent omnem contemptum, ad hoc vt Christi gloriam promoueant, imo seipsos oportet contemnere, & quantumuis excellentibus donis sint praediti, ea omnia prae Christo debent iis vilescere.
units.tr: greatly to distinguish himself from the true Messiah. He makes the distinction chiefly in three respects: in person, in office, in baptism. In person, in that Christ is more worthy, he himself is only a witness of Christ; in baptism, in that while he baptizes with water, Christ baptizes with the Holy Spirit and with fire. See then how great was the zeal for the divine glory in this man. So far as the Messiah was honoured, he made nothing of his own contempt. Indeed he despised himself, and although he was a man, if ever there was another, endowed with outstanding gifts of the Holy Spirit, yet making himself nothing in comparison with the Messiah, he despised all those things. So in every calling the glory of God must always be kept before the eyes of all, especially of witnesses to the truth and ministers of the Word, who ought most willingly to bear every contempt, so that they may advance the glory of Christ. Indeed they must despise themselves, and however excellent the gifts with which they are endowed, all of them ought to be counted worthless before Christ.

units.la: Hactenus fuerunt duo testimonia plenitudinis quae in Christo fuit, sequitur argumentum eiusdem tertium, ab ipsius effectu, quem experiuntur in se quotquot in eum credunt qui credunt. Et nos, inquit, omnes ex plenitudine eius accepimus. Relictis iam testimoniis, quae externa sunt & extra nos, arguit illam gratiae plenitudinem ab experientia, & sensu ipso efficacis illius gratiae, quem in nobis ipsi habemus. Et nos, inquit, omnes ex plenitudine eius accepimus; q. d. argumentum certissimum plenitudinis gratiae in Christo, est hic effectus ipsius in nobis qui credimus. Fieri enim non potest quin hoc totum, quantumcunque est quod nos sentimus in nobis ipsis, profectum {a}ctum sit à plenitudine gratiæ ipsius. Sic Paulus postquam dixit omnem plenitudinem Deitatis in ipso habitare corporaliter, subiungit, & nos in ipso sumus consummati. Sed explicationis causa addit insuper, Et gratiam pro gratia, hoc est, accepimus gratiam gratuitam remissionem peccatorum, & regenerationem, propter illam gratiæ plenitudinem quæ in ipso est. Particula enim videtur notare causam, q. d. ex eo quod ipse plenus sit gratiæ accepimus nos hanc gratiam, quam in nobis ipsi persentiscimus, vel vt ad verbum reddam: N os gratiam accepimus è regione gratiæ quæ in ipso est. Nota igitur, Volumus quidem omnes Christum videre, & introspicere in illam gloriam capitis nostri Iesu Christi qui in cœlis est: aspectus enim illius gloriæ est beatitas nostra. Etsi autem non detur nobis coràm videre eã quoad hic viuimus, tamen facilè coniicere possumus quanta sit capitis gloria ex effectis, fide, regenerationis Spiritu, quæ in nobis ipsi solemus experiri. Sic Paulus excellentiam fidei supra legis opera probat ex Spiritu; hoc est donis illis Spiritus extraordinariis quæ quidē ex fide in Christum Iesum & non ex operibus legis accepta sunt. Sic & nos ex guttulis istis, vt sic dicam, gratiæ, quæ ex capitis nostri plenitudine in nos vsque distillant, etiam in vita hac, in qua per fidem incedimus, non autem per aspectum coniecturam aliquam facere possumus de plenitudine illa gratiæ & gloriæ quæ nunc est in capite nostro Christo sedente ad dextram maiestatis illius, tantisper dum in aduentu illo ipsius glorioso, in quo plenitudine ipsius implebimur, gloriam eius & maiestatem coràm contueamur: cui cum Patre & Spiritu sancto sit omnis honor & gloria. Amen.
units.tr: Thus far there have been two testimonies to the fullness that was in Christ. There follows his third argument, drawn from its effect, which all who believe in him experience in themselves. "And we," he says, "have all received from his fullness." Now, leaving aside the testimonies that are external and outside us, he proves that fullness of grace from experience and from the very sense of that effective grace which we ourselves have within us. "And we," he says, "have all received from his fullness"; as if to say: the most certain argument of the fullness of grace in Christ is this effect of his in us who believe. For it cannot be that all this, however much we feel within ourselves, has not proceeded and been drawn from the fullness of his grace. So Paul, after saying that all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in him, adds, "and in him you are complete." But for the sake of explanation he adds further, "and grace upon grace," that is, we have received grace, the free forgiveness of sins and regeneration, on account of that fullness of grace which is in him. For the particle seems to mark a cause, as if to say: because he is full of grace, we have received this grace, which we feel within ourselves; or, to render it word for word: we have received grace over against the grace which is in him. Note, therefore: we all wish to see Christ and to gaze upon that glory of our head, Jesus Christ, who is in heaven, for the sight of that glory is our blessedness. Although it is not given us to see it face to face while we live here, yet from its effects, faith and the Spirit of regeneration, which we are accustomed to experience in ourselves, we can easily conjecture how great is the glory of the head. Thus Paul proves the excellence of faith above the works of the law from the Spirit, that is, from those extraordinary gifts of the Spirit which were indeed received by faith in Jesus Christ and not from the works of the law. So also we, from these little drops, so to speak, of grace, which distil upon us even in this life, in which we walk by faith and not by sight, can make some conjecture about that fullness of grace and glory which is now in our head Christ, seated at the right hand of his majesty, until in his glorious coming, in which we shall be filled with his fullness, we behold his glory and majesty face to face: to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be all honour and glory. Amen.

units.la: Verbis deinde sequentibus subnectit modum quo acceperimus omnes ex ipsius plenitudine. Modus est per ministerium ipsius filij Dei; qui veniens euangelizauit pacem tam iis qui procul erant, quàm iis qui prope erant. Nominatur etiam Minister circuncisionis. Minisserium hoc filij Dei, quo magis gloriosum appareat, illustratur à dissimili Mosis ministerio, Lex, inquit, per Mosen data est. Lex, hoc est, ministerium mortis & condemnationis, vt loquitur Apostolus, per Mosen, seu per ministrum literæ traditum fuit. Nam quòd ad gloriam attinet, Moses eam in lege cæremoniali vmbris & typis dū-taxat adumbrauit. Gratia autem & veritas extitit per Iesum Christum: hoc est, Iesus Christus vt author fuit, ita minister fuit gratiæ & veritatis. Gratiam intelligo gratuitam peccatorum remissionem: veritatem verò, non adumbratam illam & typis inuolutam Dei in Christo notitiam, sed sine vmbris apertam, claram & manifestam. Iohannes igitur hic inter considerandum ministerium gratiæ, vult nos reflectere oculos ad ministerium mortis. Inter considerādum liberationis illud in Christo beneficium vult nos retrospicere ad miseriam illam in qua hæsimus ante liberationem. In considerando denique lucem hāc atque beatum hunc statum, in quo Dei gratia hodierno die cōsistimus, vult nos reminisci illarum tenebrarum, in quibus versabamur aliquando in regno Antichristi. Quorsum istud? nimirūm vt istis è regione sibi positis ponderemus pro dignitate maximum illud Dei erga nos beneficium, quod alioqui facere nō possumus. Paulus dum vult pro dignitate æstimare beneficium illud maximū viuificationis nostri in Christo Iesu, ex ex diametro opponit mortem illam in qua iacuimus ante illam nostri viuificationem. Cùm essemus, inquit, mortui in offensis & peccatis, vnà nos viuificauit in Christo. Dum autem ex opposita morte magnitudinem vitæ illius ponderat, vix suppetunt ipsi verba quibus efferat Dei tantam illam misericordiam. Sed Deus, inquit, qui dives est misericordia, propter multam charitatem suam qua dilexit nos, &c. Vide mihi igitur: apprehendit misericordiam, non quantulamcunque sed diuitem: apprehendit charitatem, non quantulamcunque, sed multam eam. Disse igitur, consideratio miseriæ nostræ quid faciat. Facit autem vt pluris faciamus misericordiam: dum autem magni facimus beneficium, tum afficimur sensu ineffabilis cuiusdam amoris Dei erga nos. Sensus autem iste amoris Dei, cum ineffabili lætitia coniunctus est.
units.tr: Then, in the words that follow, he adds the manner in which we have all received from his fullness. The manner is through the ministry of the Son of God himself, who, coming, preached peace to those who were far off and to those who were near. He is also called the Minister of the circumcision. That this ministry of the Son of God may appear the more glorious, it is illustrated by the unlike ministry of Moses: "The law," he says, "was given through Moses." The law, that is, the ministry of death and condemnation, as the Apostle calls it, was delivered through Moses, or through the minister of the letter. For as far as glory is concerned, Moses only shadowed it forth in the ceremonial law by shadows and types. But grace and truth came through Jesus Christ: that is, Jesus Christ was both the author and the minister of grace and truth. By grace I understand the free forgiveness of sins; by truth, not that knowledge of God in Christ which is shadowed forth and wrapped in types, but that which is without shadows, clear and manifest. John, then, while considering the ministry of grace here, wishes us to turn our eyes back to the ministry of death. While considering that benefit of deliverance in Christ, he wishes us to look back to that misery in which we were held before deliverance. Finally, in considering this light and this blessed state in which by God's grace we stand today, he wishes us to remember the darkness in which we once dwelt in the kingdom of Antichrist. To what end? Namely, that, with those things set over against it, we may weigh according to its worth that greatest benefit of God towards us, which otherwise we cannot do. Paul, when he wishes to estimate according to its worth that greatest benefit of our quickening in Christ Jesus, sets over against it, as its direct opposite, the death in which we lay before that quickening of ours. "When we were dead," he says, "in our offences and sins, he quickened us together in Christ." When from the opposite death he weighs the greatness of that life, his words hardly suffice to express that so great mercy of God. "But God," he says, "who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, etc." See, then: he grasps mercy, not a small mercy but a rich one; he grasps love, not a small love but great love. Consider, then, what the consideration of our misery does: it makes us value mercy more. And when we value the benefit highly, we are then moved by a sense of the ineffable love of God towards us. And this sense of the love of God is joined with ineffable joy.

units.la: Ex hoc versu sic enarrato oritur quæstio: Annon dicat aliquis, fuit Christus minister etiam legis? Annon legimus ab eo explicatum esse verum & genuinum legis sensum, eámque purgatam fermento Pharisæorum? Resp. Christus vt est Dei filius & Deus ab æterno vnà cum Patre & Spiritu sancto dedit legem: Vt autem mediator est, manifestatus in carne nostra proprie minister est Euangelij & gratiæ. Dico proprie, quia etiam legis minister est quatenus inseruit vel nobis præparandis sensu aliquo miseriæ nostræ ante liberationem, vel nobis in officio continendis erga Deum tam misericordè, vt ei grati simus pro tanto liberationis nostri beneficio; hic enim duplex est legis vsus in nobis qui per Christum liberamur.Quod de Christo dixi id intelligo quoque de ministris ipsius: omnes enim sum ministri gratiæ non legis, nisi rationem habeas duplicis illius vsus legis, de quo iam diximus. Et nisi obstinatio ista & naturæ tam alta securitas quæ legis comminationibus necessario perterrefacieda est, obstaret, profecto nihil præter gratiam & misericordiam Dei in Christo Iesu remissionem peccatorum, & vitam æternam ex nobis audiretur.
units.tr: This passage, explained in this way, raises a question: might someone say that Christ was also a minister of the law? Do we not read that he explained the true and genuine sense of the law and cleansed it of the leaven of the Pharisees? I answer: Christ, as the Son of God and God from eternity, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, gave the law. But as Mediator, made manifest in our flesh, he is properly a minister of the Gospel and of grace. I say "properly," because he is also a minister of the law, insofar as the law serves either to prepare us, before our deliverance, with some sense of our misery, or to keep us in our duty toward God so that we are thankful for so great a benefit of deliverance. For there is a twofold use of the law in us who are set free through Christ. What I have said of Christ I also understand of his ministers. For all of them are ministers of grace, not of the law, unless you take account of that twofold use of the law of which we have already spoken. And unless that obstinacy and that deep security of nature, which must necessarily be terrified by the law's threats, stood in the way, nothing but the grace and mercy of God in Christ Jesus, the forgiveness of sins and eternal life, would be heard from us.

units.la: Versu deinde sequenti declarat quod dixit gratiam & veritatem per Christum extitisse: hoc est, Christum fuisse munus gratiæ & veritatis. Deum, inquit, nemo vidit vnquam: hoc est, nemo vnquam ante Christi adventum in carne habuit claram illam apertamque notitiam Dei in Christo: viderunt quidè homines Deum aliquo modo per naturæ lucem; viderunt quoque eum sui, hoc est Iudæi, per lucem verbi, legis nimirum & promissionum etiam euangelicarum quæ fuerunt de Christo venturo: viderunt Iudæi adumbratum sacrificiis & figuris aliis, sed clarè & perspicuè ante Christum manifestatum in carne nō viderunt.Ideo proximè subiectum est hoc versu, Vnigenitus ille filius, hoc est, proprius Dei filius, è natura Patris ab æterno genitus, Qui est in sinu Patris, hoc est, qui coexistit cum Patre in vna eademque natura & essentia, ac proinde conscius est omnium consiliorum Patris. Nihil enim nouit Pater quod non pariter nouit filius. Ille nobis exposuit, hoc est, manifestauit & patefecit Deum, idque non tantum qua ratione est splendor gloriæ, & character personæ ipsius, hoc est, imago Patris sui, Patrem suum ad vinum referens in natura vna eademque, item in persona: qua ratione dictum est ab eo, Qui me vidit, Patrem vidit, vtpote Patris imagi- nem. Non, inquam, hac solum ratione dicitur, manifestauit nobis Deum, sed & qua ratione, Filius assumpta carne nostra propius ad nos venit, & Patrem ipsiusque voluntatem plene patefecit. Nam Pater vltimis hisce diebus loquutus est per Filium suum. Atque in hoc sensu hoc loco magis proprie videtur accipienda haec Dei per Filium manifestatio.
units.tr: In the following verse he explains what he said, that grace and truth came through Christ: that is, that Christ was the gift of grace and truth. "No one has ever seen God," he says: that is, before the coming of Christ in the flesh, no one had that clear and open knowledge of God in Christ. Men did indeed see God in some way by the light of nature. His own people, that is the Jews, saw him too by the light of the word, namely of the law and of the gospel promises concerning the Christ who was to come. The Jews saw him foreshadowed by sacrifices and other figures, but they did not see him clearly and plainly manifested in the flesh before Christ. Therefore the next verse says: "that only-begotten Son," that is, the proper Son of God, begotten from eternity of the Father's nature, "who is in the bosom of the Father," that is, who coexists with the Father in one and the same nature and essence, and therefore knows all the counsels of the Father. For the Father knows nothing that the Son does not equally know. "He has made him known," that is, he has manifested and revealed God, and not only in the way that he is the brightness of glory and the express image of his person, that is, the image of his Father, bearing witness to his Father in one and the same nature and likewise in person, in which sense he said, "He who has seen me has seen the Father," as being the image of the Father. I say that he is said to have manifested God to us not only in this way, but also in this way: that the Son, having taken on our flesh, came nearer to us and fully revealed the Father and his will. For the Father spoke in these last days by his Son. And in this sense this manifestation of God through the Son seems to be understood more properly in this place.

units.la: Nota igitur quid sit veritas. Philosophi omni aetate valde anxie in eam inquisiuerunt in Physicis suis, in Ethicis, in Mathematicis, in aliis. Verum sola ista notitia Patris in Filio proprie meretur nomen veritatis. Quid enim attinet caelum & terram & omnia animo complecti, nisi Deum in Christo redemptore cognitum habeat peccator? hoc est, nisi Deum sibi fauentem & sui miserentem condonatis omnibus peccatis habeat, cum haec sit sola illa notitia, quae tranquillat & pacatas reddit miseras conscientias. Ideo Christus, postquam dixit neminem nosse Patrem nisi Filium, & cuicunque voluerit Filius retegere, statim addit, Venite ad me omnes qui fatigati & onerati estis, & ego faciam vt requiescatis, quibus verbis significat, Deo iam per filium reuelato, peruenire pacem conscientiae & laetitiam ineffabilem ad eos quicunque in filium exonerant peccata sua.
units.tr: Note therefore what truth is. The philosophers in every age have inquired into it very anxiously, in their natural philosophy, in their ethics, in their mathematics, and in other fields. But only that knowledge of the Father in the Son truly deserves the name of truth. For what good is it to embrace heaven and earth and all things in the mind, unless the sinner has God known to him in Christ the Redeemer? That is, unless he has God favouring him and having mercy on him, with all his sins forgiven. For this alone is that knowledge which calms and pacifies wretched consciences. Therefore Christ, after saying that no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him, immediately adds: "Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest." By these words he signifies that, now that God has been revealed through the Son, peace of conscience and ineffable joy come to those who unload their sins upon the Son.

units.la: 19 Hoc etiam est testimonium Iohannis, quando miserunt Iudaei Hierosolymis Sacerdotes & Leuitas, vt interrogarent eum quisnam ipse esset.
units.tr: 19 This also is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him who he himself was.

units.la: 20 Et professus est, neque negauit: professus est, inquam, se non esse Christum illum.
units.tr: 20 And he confessed, and did not deny it: he confessed, I say, that he was not that Christ.

units.la: 21 Tunc interrogauerunt eum, Quid ergo es? Tune es Elias? ipse vero dixit, Non sum. Et illi, es tu propheta ille? qui respondit, Non.
units.tr: 21 Then they asked him, "What then are you? Are you Elijah?" And he said, "I am not." And they said, "Are you that prophet?" And he answered, "No."

units.la: 22 Dixerunt ergo ei, Quis es? vt responsum demus iis qui miserunt nos: quid dicis de teipso?
units.tr: 22 Then they said to him, "Who are you, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?"

units.la: 23 Ait, Ego sum vox clamantis in deserto, Complanate viam Domini, prout dixit Esaias Propheta.
units.tr: 23 He said, "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of the Lord,' as the prophet Isaiah said."

units.la: Haete-
units.tr: Hitherto-
