units.la: HActenus declarata & confirmata quasi obiter plenitudo illa gratię & veritatis, quæ in Christo consپecta est quo tempore commoraretur inter Iudæos: Sequitur nunc duodecima & postrema pars descriptionis {a}λόγῳ sive filij Dei à testimoniis Iohannis Baptistæ. Testimonium autem triplex est: primum testimonium est quod perhibitum est vrgentibus Sacerdotibus & Leuitis missis Hierosolymis tentandi gratia: verba sunt, Et hoc est testimonium Iohannis. Tum tempus sive occasio testimonij perhibiti subiicitur, Quàdo miserunt Iudæi Hierosolymis Sacerdotes & Leuitas vt interrogarent eum, Tu quis es? &c. Hæc est occasio, quasi dicat quo tempore eum vrgebant missi illi à Iudæis. Sed occasionem istam sic planius expono: Iohannes Baptista ingressus ministerium suum cùm annum ageret quasi tricesimum, relictis Hierosolymis, relicto templo, & toto cultu Iudaico, non quidem clàm aufugit, sed palàm discessit, séque recepit in desertum Iudææ, in regiones prope Iardenem sitas, ibíque quanta potuit voce clamauit iam aduentante Messiam (vtinam, vt hoc dicam obiter, & nos tanta possemus voce clamare ac testari Christum secundò aduentare) clamauit, inquam, & congressus suos habuit non vno aliquo in loco, sed passim in deserto. Atque hoc suo facto reipsa abrogauit legem Mosis, finem imposuit vmbris, & veritati initium dedit in Christo iam iam affuturo. Qua re cognita Iudæi consilium conuocarunt, legatos ad Iohannem miserunt, delectos non ex infimis, sed ex Sacerdotibus & Leuitis; coacti enim sunt reuereri tantum & tam grauem virum. Miserunt itaque ad Iohannem Sacerdotes qui dignitate proximè Pontificem maximum sequebantur, qui docebant, afferebát sacrificia precabantúrque pro populo, idque per vices, vt exemplo Zachariæ discimus. Coniuncti erant cum his Leuitæ, qui inferiores diaconi & ministri erat in Ecclesia. Istos, quia ipsorum munus erat inquirere in noua dogmata, emiserunt cum his mandatis, vt iuberent Iohannem desistere ab incœpto, vel si nollet, tátùm ex eo dicerent, quis esset, quídque doceret, idque rursus ad consilium referrent. Hoc igitur sibi propositum habuerunt Iudæi & quos emiserunt legati, vt lucem illam orientem statim extinguerent, nō autem vt de Messia aliquid disceret, & si de eo per somnium quasi tum cogitaret. Nam sub aduentum Messiæ mira erat Iudæorum securitas, & eo quidem miserabilior eorum conditio, quòd etsi regnum ipsis per Cæsarem ereptum esset, & gubernatores quos ille vellet populo obtrusi, tamen sub aduentum Messiæ, in quo vno futura erat, iuxta prophetas eorum liberatio, non erant de eo soliciti, neque intempus ipsum aduentus ipsius inquirebant. Det Dominus ne nos iam sub ipsius secundum aduentum, eius simus tam securi, sed vt vigilemus & exertis capitibus eum in nubibus cito venturum expectemus: nam veniet cito & non faciet moram.
units.tr: Up to this point, the fullness of grace and truth that was seen in Christ during his sojourn among the Jews has been declared and confirmed, as it were in passing. Now follows the twelfth and final part of the description of the Word [λόγῳ], that is, of the Son of God, drawn from the testimonies of John the Baptist. There are three testimonies. The first testimony is the one given when the priests and Levites were sent from Jerusalem, urgently and to test him. The words are: "And this is the testimony of John." Then the time or occasion of the testimony is added: "When the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, 'Who are you?' etc." This is the occasion, as if he said at what time those men sent by the Jews pressed him. But I explain this occasion more plainly as follows. John the Baptist, having begun his ministry at about the age of thirty, left Jerusalem and the temple and the whole Jewish worship. He did not flee secretly but departed openly, and withdrew into the wilderness of Judea, into the regions lying near the Jordan. There he cried out with as loud a voice as he could, now that the Messiah was approaching. (Would that we too, to say this in passing, could cry out with such a voice and bear witness that Christ is coming again a second time!) He cried out, I say, and held his gatherings not in any one place but everywhere in the wilderness. By this deed he in fact abrogated the law of Moses, put an end to the shadows, and gave a beginning to the truth in Christ, who was now just about to come. When the Jews learned of this, they convened a council and sent envoys to John, chosen not from the lowest ranks but from the priests and Levites. For they were compelled to show reverence to so great and so serious a man. So they sent to John priests, who ranked next in dignity after the high priest, who taught, offered sacrifices, and prayed for the people, and did so in turn, as we learn from the example of Zechariah. Levites were joined with them, who were the lesser deacons and ministers in the Church. These they sent, because it was their office to inquire into new doctrines, with these instructions: that they should order John to desist from what he had begun, or, if he would not, that they should at least learn from him who he was and what he taught, and then report back to the council. The Jews and the envoys they sent therefore had this purpose: to extinguish at once that rising light, not to learn anything about the Messiah, even if he was perhaps occupying his thoughts somewhat in a dream. For the Jews were strangely secure about the coming of the Messiah, and their condition was all the more wretched because, although the kingdom had been snatched from them by Caesar and governors whom he wished were thrust upon the people, nevertheless, with the coming of the Messiah, in whom alone, according to their prophets, their deliverance was to lie, they were not anxious about him and did not inquire into the time of his coming. May the Lord grant that we, at his second coming, not be so secure, but that we watch and, with heads raised, await him who is coming quickly in the clouds: for he will come quickly and will not delay.

units.la: Atque sic explicata est occasio testimonij huius primi: Vbi id non obscurè videre possumus Iudæos cum iam prius cæci fuerint, tamen magis cupiuisse ad aduentum & apparitionem ipsius lucis, quā vnquam antea, adeò vt Baptistam qui tanquam Lucifer oriebatur ante Solem illius iustitiæ, Messiam ipsum, Baptistam, inquam, conati sint è medio tollere. Experientia id docet verum esse: quòd si iam oculis mentis videamus aliquid, ad lucem deinde oblatam clarius simus visuri: sin iam lippitudine aliqua laborent oculi mentis, fere ad lucem oblatam magis cæcutiant. Idque hic euenire solet, quod in oculo corporis fit, qui si bene affectus sit ad lucem solis oblatam, clarius inspiciet magisque illuminabitur: sin æger sit & male affectus, luce solis oblata cæcior euadet. Quare cauendum est, ne sinamus vnquam tenebras obrepere meribus nostris, quæ si semel eas inuaserint, tum periculum est ne perpetuò in lucem impingamus; & magis magisque quotidie excæcemur, id quòd tristi exemplo Papistarum discimus hodierno die. Illi enim quò plus lucis intuentur, eò cæciores fiunt. Vt videatur Dominus præcipere ministris verbi sui hodierno die, id quod aliquando Esaiæ imperatum legimus: Ite, dicite Papistis his, Audite continenter, at ne intelligatis: & videte continenter, neque cognoscatis: facite vt pinguescat cor istorum, & aures eorum ingrauescant, oculique conniueant: ne videant oculis suis, & auribus suis audiant & corde suo intelligant, conuertanturque sanent se.
units.tr: And so the occasion of this first testimony has been explained. Here we can plainly see that the Jews, though they had been blind before, desired the coming and appearing of that light even more than ever. So much so that they tried to remove from the midst John the Baptist, who rose like the morning star before the sun of righteousness, that is, the Messiah himself. Experience teaches that this is true. If our mind's eyes already see something, they will see it more clearly when a light is brought to them. But if the eyes of the mind are already suffering some weakness, they will almost always grow more dim when a light is set before them. This happens in the eye of the body too: if it is healthy, it will see more clearly and be better lit when the light of the sun is brought to it; but if it is sick and ill-disposed, it will become blinder when the sun's light is shown to it. We must therefore take care never to let darkness creep into our minds. Once it has entered, there is danger that we will stumble into the light forever, and be blinded more and more each day. We learn this from the sad example of the Papists today. For the more of the light they look upon, the blinder they become. It seems that the Lord commands the ministers of his Word today what he once commanded Isaiah: "Go, say to these Papists: Hear continually, but do not understand; and see continually, but do not perceive. Make the heart of these people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted and be healed."

units.la: Atque hactenus fuit occasio : sequitur ipsum testimonium, quod tractatur dialogismo, interrogantibus legatis, respondente vero Iohanne. Quaerunt autem primum de persona Iohannis, deinde de officio & Baptismo. Quaerentibus de persona, Respondet Ioannes primum negate, qui non sit ipse, deinde affirmate qui sit. Primum ergo de persona quaerunt, Tu quis es? Respondet Iohannes non tam ad externum interrogatum & vocem, quam ad internam ipsorum mentem & cogitationem. Cogitabant eum Messiam esse: Itaque Ioannes negarie Messiam esse. Et confessus, inquit, est, & non negavit. Subiecta est affirmationi negatio contrarij aequipollens: ut iudicetur plane & ingenue Baptistam confessum esse. Tertio denique idem repetitur, Et confessus est se non esse Christum illum. Idem tertio repetitum, ut appareat planissimam ac sincerissimam fuisse Baptistae confessionem. Quoties enim quaestio fit de gloria soli Deo propria, an ad nos aliqua ex parte pertineat, toties nunquam satis plane & evidenter possumus profiteri eam ad nos nulla ex parte pertinere. Plenum enim periculi est, ve quam minimum diuinae gloriae nobis vendicare. Sed hic operae pretium est descendere paulo altius in animum Baptistae, ex quo profecta est tam plana tamque sincera confessio. Illud extra quaestionem positum est, Baptistam eum fuisse homine qui ut Deum vivum glorificaret, seipsum abnegavit. Erat ergo vir plenus zeli diuinae gloriae, atque sic affectus animo plane confitetur, & eodem saepius repetito asseuerat se non esse Messiam illum, hoc est ex abundantia cordis os loquitur abunde. Nobis igitur ad hoc ut plane expressque confiteamur Dei gloriam, nihil ad nos pertinere: Vendendum est primum ut nos ipsi abnegemus, & mortificetur in nobis quoad fieri poterit haec φιλαυτία; quae si in nobis regnet, profecto non tam prompte diabolus & mundus deferent nobis gloriam Deo propriam, quam auide nos eam omnem, si fieri posset, simul ac semel nobis arripiemus. Quare studendum est in tota vita mortificationi philautiae & superbiae illius quam hausimus ex primo parente nostro qui voluit esse Deo aequalis. Hactenus prima interrogatio fuit, cui respondet Iohannes se non esse Messiam illum. Deinde quaerunt, Quid ergo es? Tune es Elias? Iohannes respondet, non sum. Cur prius quaerit, An Elias sit, quam Moses, aut alius quis ex Prophetis? Illud haud-dubie intelligebant ex Malachia propheta, Eliam venturum esse ante diem Messiae. Nam apud Malachiam sic loquitur Dominus: Ecce ego mittam vobis Eliam Prophetam, antequam veniat dies ille Iehovae maximus et reverendus. Ex hoc loco existimarunt eundem illum Eliam qui aliquando vixerat sub Achab iterum venturum sub tempus Messiae, vel certe expectarunt alium aliquem cum anima Eliae orituram, qui fuit error Pharisaeorum, qui putabant quidem animas hominum immortales esse: sed bonorum et piorum hominum animas subinde in nova corpora bonorum hominum migrare. Sed sensus verborum Dei hic fuit, quasi diceret: Agnoscite hoc signo adventare Messiam: missurus sum ante eum Iohannem Baptistam praecursorem, instructum spiritu et virtute Eliae. Sic enim interpretatur hunc locum Christus ipse, et Angelus. Respondet Iohannes, ac negat se Eliam esse eum quem illi imaginati sunt, perperam interpretati locum Malachiae. Disce igitur hic fuisse in Iudaeis ignorantiam Scripturarum sub adventum Messiae. Neque tamen minum; Nam qui Scripturas sacras, hoc est, vocem ipsius Dei detorquent pro libidine sua ad inventiones suas ac mendacia sua, ut iis inserviat ac faveat, sicut a Iudaeis procul dubio factum est; hos Deus iusto iudicio spoliat omni luce ac vera Scripturarum cognitione. Id quod tristi exemplo Papistarum experimur hodierno die, qui cum non possunt simul ac semel abolere omnes Scripturas, id quod quam maxime vellent; Ad hoc ut locus esset solis traditionibus ac inventis humanis, maliciose detorquent eas ad stabiliendum mendacia sua, quo factum est, idque iusto Dei iudicio, ut vix unam aliquam Scripturae sententiam dextre possint intelligere.
units.tr: So far the occasion; now follows the testimony itself, which is handled as a dialogue, with the envoys asking and John answering. They ask first about John's person, then about his office and baptism. To the questions about his person, John first answers by denying what he is not, and then by affirming who he is. So they first ask about his person: Who are you? John answers not so much to the outward question and voice as to their inner thought and reasoning. They were thinking that he was the Messiah, so John denied that he was the Messiah. And he confessed, he says, and did not deny. To the affirmation is added the denial of the contrary, which amounts to the same thing, so that it may be judged that the Baptist confessed plainly and frankly. Lastly, a third time the same is repeated: And he confessed that he was not that Christ. The same is repeated a third time so that it may appear that the Baptist's confession was most plain and sincere. For whenever a question arises about the glory that belongs to God alone, whether it pertains to us in any part, we can never profess plainly and clearly enough that it pertains to us in no part. For there is great danger that we claim for ourselves even the smallest part of divine glory. But here it is worth going a little deeper into the mind of the Baptist, from which so plain and sincere a confession proceeded. It is beyond question that the Baptist was a man who denied himself so that he might glorify the living God. He was therefore a man full of zeal for the divine glory, and being so disposed in his mind, he confesses plainly, and by repeating it often he asserts that he is not the Messiah; that is, out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks abundantly. Therefore, if we are to confess plainly and clearly that the glory of God has nothing to do with us, we must first deny ourselves, and this self-love [φιλαυτία] must be mortified in us as far as it can be. If this self-love reigns in us, the devil and the world will certainly not be so quick to offer us the glory that is proper to God, and we will eagerly snatch up all of it, if it were possible, as soon as it is offered. Therefore we must strive all our lives to mortify the self-love and pride which we have drawn from our first parent, who wished to be equal to God. So far was the first question, to which John answers that he is not that Messiah. Then they ask: What then are you? Are you Elijah? John answers, I am not. Why do they ask whether he is Elijah before asking whether he is Moses or some other of the prophets? They undoubtedly understood this from the prophet Malachi, who said that Elijah would come before the day of the Messiah. For in Malachi the Lord speaks thus: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet, before the coming of that great and dreadful day of the LORD." From this passage they supposed that the very Elijah who had lived in the time of Ahab would come again at the time of the Messiah, or at least they expected someone else in whom the soul of Elijah would arise. This was the error of the Pharisees, who indeed believed that human souls are immortal, but that the souls of good and pious men pass from time to time into new bodies of good men. But the sense of God's words here was, as if he said: Recognise by this sign that the Messiah is coming. I will send before him John the Baptist as his forerunner, endowed with the spirit and power of Elijah. For Christ himself and the angel interpret this passage in this way. John answers, and denies that he is the Elijah whom they had imagined, having misinterpreted the passage of Malachi. Learn then that there was ignorance of the Scriptures among the Jews at the coming of the Messiah. Nor was it a small ignorance. For those who twist the holy Scriptures, that is, the very voice of God, according to their own whim, to suit their inventions and lies, so that these may be served and favoured, as undoubtedly was done by the Jews, God in his just judgment strips them of all light and true knowledge of the Scriptures. We experience this today through the sad example of the Papists. Since they cannot abolish all the Scriptures at once, which they would most dearly wish, so that there may be room for traditions and human inventions alone, they maliciously twist them to establish their lies. The result, by the just judgment of God, is that they can scarcely understand a single sentence of Scripture rightly.

units.la: Tertio denique quaerunt: Cum neque Messias, neque Elias sit, an propheta sit? Hoc est, an sit homo extra ordinem excitatus a Deo cum donis extraordinariis, cuiusmodi fuerunt veteres illi Prophetae: Vel, ut alij volunt luut,de aliquo eximio propheta intelligat, nō de Christo. Antea enim negauit Iohānes se esse Christum. Existimārūt enim insignem aliquem Prophetam esse mittendum, similem Mosi, huc detorquentes locum illum, Prophetam suscitabit vobis Iehoua Deus vester e medio vestri, e fratribus vestris sicut me; Ipsi auscultate. Qui locus de toto prophetarum choro, maximè verò de capite Christo est accipiendus. Respondet Iohannes negans se esse prophetam illum quem illi intellexerunt.Vides hoc loco Sacerdotes istos multa ac varia diuinare de Iohanne, Ecquis sit; sed ad veritatem ipsam neutiquam accedere. Caeci, si semel à via aberrare inceperint, quantò magis procedunt, tantò magis aberrant à via. Sic ignari homines & non illuminati Dei Spiritu,quò magis inquirunt in veritatem,eò magis discedunt ab ea. Qui inter gentes maximè diuini homines ac religiosi videri voluerūt, maximi idololatrae extiterunt, & vani facti sunt in ratiocinationibus suis,obtenebratúmque est desipiens cor eorum, ait Apostolus. Papistę hodierno die postquàm semel à recta via declinarunt, quo magis laborant in Theologia, eò magis aberrant à veritate. Iohannes Baptista inter respondendum nō statim istos reducit in viam, sed primum duntaxat admonet aberrare eos à via, volens nimirum ut prius ipsi palpent crassam suam ignorantiam, sentiantque se non nisi errare posse, nisi in viam ab alio rectius sentiente reuocentur. Et quidem vtile est nobis, vt prius sentiamus quàtopere aberremus à via & veritate, quàm in viam ipsam reducamur. Ita perspecta erit nobis natura nostra quàm caeca sit & quot erroribus obnoxia, gratiámque Dei à natura internoscemus, atque ita omnem gloriam cognitæ veritatis & recti iudicij, Deo in solidum tribuemus: Cui sit omnis gloria & honor. Amen.
units.tr: Finally they ask a third time: Since he is neither the Messiah nor Elijah, is he a prophet? That is, is he a man raised up by God outside the ordinary order, with extraordinary gifts, of the kind the ancient prophets had? Or, as others would have it, does the passage refer to some outstanding prophet and not to Christ? For John had earlier denied that he was Christ. They thought that some remarkable prophet was to be sent, like Moses, and they applied to this the passage: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet from the midst of you, from your brothers, like me; listen to him." This passage must be understood of the whole choir of prophets, but most of all of Christ the head. John answers, denying that he is the prophet they had in mind. You see here that these priests guess many and various things about John, who he is, but never come near to the truth itself. Blind men, once they have begun to wander from the road, the further they go, the further they stray from the way. So ignorant men, not enlightened by the Spirit of God, the more they search for the truth, the further they depart from it. Among the nations, those who most wished to be seen as divine and religious men became the greatest idolaters, and became vain in their reasonings, and their foolish heart was darkened, as the Apostle says. The Papists today, once they have turned aside from the straight way, the more they labour in theology, the further they wander from the truth. John the Baptist, in answering, does not immediately bring these men back to the way, but first only reminds them that they have strayed from it, wishing, no doubt, that they first feel their own gross ignorance and perceive that they can do nothing but err, unless they are called back to the way by one who thinks more rightly. And indeed it is useful for us to feel first how far we have strayed from the way and the truth, before we are led back to the way itself. In this way our nature will be made clear to us, how blind it is and how liable to many errors. We shall recognise the grace of God as something beyond nature, and so we shall give all the glory of the truth we have come to know, and of right judgment, wholly to God, to whom be all glory and honour. Amen.

units.la: Hactenus quis non sit respondit, nunc verò qui sit respondet: Nimirum cum cum directè quærunt qui sit. Nam prius quærebant an is esset quem ipsi falsò opinati sunt cum esse. Nunc verò, cùm vident se falli cogitationibus suis, errorem suum aegrè ferentes, non amplius diuinant, sed ipsi permittunt vt qui sit ipse prosi-
units.tr: Hitherto he has answered who he is not; now he answers who he is, namely when they ask directly who he is. For previously they asked whether he was the one whom they had mistakenly supposed him to be. But now, seeing that they are deceived in their own thoughts and bearing their error with difficulty, they no longer guess, but let him come forward and declare himself.

units.la: det. teatur. Quærunt igitur directè qui sit; Ioannes autem rogatus directè respondet. Quis es? inquiunt, ut responsum demus iis qui miserunt nos, Quid dicis de te ipso? Respondet Iohānes, Ego sum vox clamantis in deserto, Complanate viam Domini, prout dixit Esaias Propheta. Non suis verbis respondet Iohannes, esse nimirum se præcursorem illum Domini: sed verba Prophetæ in eandem sententiam citat, sibíque applicat illud Prophetæ, Vox clamantis in deserto, Parate viam Iehoua, Adæquate in solitudine aggerem Deo nostro. Idque ideo facit ut ipsum cognitum habentes, non tam suo ipsius de se testimonio, quàm Prophetarum prædictione, maius quiddam de ipso cogitarent, & maiorem ipsius verbis fidē haberent. Vbi vides Iohānem Baptistam, qui à Deo missus est, ut dictum est, supra habuisse missionis & vocationis suæ præclarum testimonium. Spiritus enim Dei certiorem eum fecit de prophetia illa Esaiæ, quod ad ipsum nominatim pertinuerit. Nullus est Propheta aut omnino Minister Euangelij, qui à Deo mittitur, quem non faciat idem Deus eo quo ipsi visum est modo certiorem de vocatione sua: Vnde sequitur admirabilis illa lætitia, libertas & bona conscientia. Sunt quidem etiam Prophetiæ, sed generales, de ministris Euangelij mittendis in postremis his temporibus. Beatus est quisquis potest illas prophetias sibi applicare. Beati pedes euangelizantium pacem, euangelizantium bona. Sed verba paulò diligentiùs considero; Ego sum, inquit, vox clamantis in deserto. Iohannes ingressus ministerium suum, ut opinio est anno Iubilæi, qui fuit quinquagesimus quisque, quo nimirum anno Iudæorum quisque redibat ad possessiones suas, & quisque reuertebatur ad familiam suam. Ingressus igitur Baptista ministerium suum eo anno, præco fuit æterni illius Iubilæi & æternæ lætitiæ ac redemptionis in Christo iamiam affuturo. Indicebatur ille annus ex lege, præconis voce vnà cum tubæ sonitu. Huc igitur, ut mihi videtur, alludens Propheta appellauit Baptistam, vocem clamantis, quasi dicat præconem æterni illius Iubilæi. Ego sum, inquit, vox clamantis. Vbi nō Hierosolymis, non in loco Iudææ celebri aliquo, non in Templo; sed in deserto Iudææ propè Iardenem; eō enim recepit se Iohannes, eoque facto significauit finem impositum esse umbris legalibus & inchoatam veritatem in Christo, quae nulli certo loco addictus est. Quid autem clamavit? Complanate viam Domini. Iohannes venit proxime ante Messiam: ceteri quoque omnes Prophetae ante eum venerunt sed multo ante eum tempore: Iohannes vero antegressus est eum proxime, clamauitque adesse Messiam, & regem illum gloriae iam aduentare, cum regno illo suo iustitiae, pacis & laetitiae. Ideoque clamauit, Complanate viam Domini. Hoc propriis verbis effertur. Resipiscite, appropinquauit enim regnum caelorum. Via igitur hoc loco, non est illa quam ingredimur: sed viae nomine intelligo cor humanum, quod est natura quasi via aspera & inaequabilis admodum; quod nisi subigatur & complanetur resipiscentia & dolore illo qui est secundum Deum, profecto Dominus ipsum ingredi non poterit. Quamobrem si velimus Dominum vel ingredi cor nostrum, vel ingressum habitare in corde nostro, resipiscamus: Imo vero sit resipiscentia nostra perpetua, ut perpetuo habitet in corde nostro Deus. Non habito aut in caelo, aut in terra, sed in paupere & contrito spiritu, inquit Dominus.
units.tr: So they ask directly who he is; and John, being asked directly, answers directly. "Who are you?" they say, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us, "What do you say about yourself?" John answers, "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make straight the way of the Lord, as the prophet Isaiah said." John does not answer in his own words that he is that forerunner of the Lord. Rather, he quotes the words of the prophet to the same effect and applies to himself that saying of the prophet: "A voice crying in the wilderness, Prepare the way of Jehovah, make level in the desert a highway for our God." He does this so that those who had known him might think something greater of him, not so much on his own testimony about himself as on the prediction of the prophets, and might put greater faith in his words. Here you see that John the Baptist, who was sent by God, as was said above, had a clear testimony of his mission and calling. For the Spirit of God made him more certain of that prophecy of Isaiah, that it pertained to him by name. There is no prophet, or indeed no minister of the Gospel, whom God sends, whom the same God does not make certain of his calling in the way that seems good to him. Hence follows that wonderful joy, freedom and good conscience. There are indeed also prophecies, but general ones, concerning the sending of ministers of the Gospel in these last times. Blessed is whoever can apply those prophecies to himself. "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring the good news of peace, who bring good tidings." But I consider the words more carefully: "I am," he says, "the voice of one crying in the wilderness." John began his ministry, as is commonly thought, in the Jubilee year, which was every fiftieth year, in which, of course, each of the Jews returned to his possessions and each returned to his family. So John the Baptist, beginning his ministry in that year, was the herald of that eternal Jubilee and of the eternal joy and redemption in Christ, which was about to come. That year was proclaimed by the law with the voice of a herald together with the sound of the trumpet. Therefore, as it seems to me, the prophet, alluding to this, called the Baptist the voice of one crying, as if to say: the herald of that eternal Jubilee. "I am," he says, "the voice of one crying." He did not cry out in Jerusalem, nor in some famous place in Judea, nor in the Temple, but in the wilderness of Judea near the Jordan; for John withdrew there, and by doing so signified that an end had been put to the legal shadows and that the truth, which is not bound to any fixed place, had begun in Christ. What did he cry out? Make straight the way of the Lord. John came immediately before the Messiah. All the other prophets also came before him, but long before him in time; John, however, went immediately before him, and cried out that the Messiah was at hand, and that the King of glory was now coming with his kingdom of righteousness, peace and joy. Therefore he cried, Make straight the way of the Lord. This is expressed in plain words: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. So the way in this place is not the road we walk on, but by the way I understand the human heart, which by nature is like a rough and very uneven road; unless it is subdued and made level by repentance and by that sorrow which is according to God, the Lord will certainly not be able to enter it. Therefore, if we wish the Lord either to enter our heart or to dwell in our heart once he has entered, let us repent. Indeed, let our repentance be continual, so that God may dwell in our heart perpetually. "I do not dwell in heaven or on earth, but in the poor and contrite spirit," says the Lord.

units.la: 24 Qui vero missi fuerant erant ex Pharisaeis.
units.tr: 24 Now those who had been sent were of the Pharisees.

units.la: 25 Et interrogauerunt eum, ac dixerunt ei, Cur ergo baptizas, si tu non es Christus, neque Elias, neque Propheta ille?
units.tr: 25 And they asked him, and said to him, Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor that prophet?

units.la: 26 Respondit eis Iohannes, dicens, Ego baptizo aqua: sed in medio vestrum stat quem vos non nostis:
units.tr: 26 John answered them, saying, I baptize with water, but there stands among you one whom you do not know.

units.la: 27 Hic ille est qui post me venit, qui mihi antepositus est: cuius solearum ego non sum dignus qui soluam corrigiam.
units.tr: 27 This is he who comes after me, who was preferred before me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen.

units.la: 28 Haec Bethabara facta sunt secus Iordanem, ubi Iohannes baptizabat.
units.tr: 28 These things were done at Bethabara beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.

units.la: HActenus fuit prima interrogatio de persona Iohannis: Sequitur altera de Baptismo ac officio ipsius. Praefatio quedam breuis praemissa est quaestioni de officio. In qua docetur in qua secta & hæresi fuerint Sacerdotes hi,ac Leuitæ,qui missi fuerant ad Iohānem. Fuerunt enim in Iudæa plures sectæ Religiosorum, vt Pharisæorum, Sadducæorum ac Essæorum, de quibus nihil in præsentia dicimus. Fuerunt igitur isti ex Pharisæis,ac proinde doctores & legis expositores: Nam sibi hoc peculiariter vendicarunt Pharisæi, vt veram doctrinam legis aliererent,falsam autem ac noua quæque dogmata impugnarent. Idcoque sibi nomen hoc Pharisæorum sumpserunt: quasi dicas,doctores & expositores legis, cum tamen reipsa sophistæ fuerint & legis corruptores. Hinc illud quod dixit Dominus de fermento Pharisæorum. Illud igitur hominum genus decebat ea quæ sequitur argumentatio & conclusio aduersus Baptistam. Sequitur interrogatio Pharisæorum. Interrogarunt eum ac dixerunt ei, Cur ergo baptizas si tu non es, &c. Apparet hic & est verisimile istos non intellexisse Iohannem respondentem, & quinam ipse esset exponentem ex Propheta Esaia: aut certe si intellexerunt, oportuit eos esse admodum maliciosos. Neque tamen amplius postulant vt Iohannes illud apertius exponeret quod de se protulit ex Propheta: sed relicto hoc responso ad illud alterum redeunt, quo nimirum ostendit Iohannes qui non esset, ex eo que maliciosè reprehendunt Baptismum Iohannis,hoc argumento: Non es Messias, vt confessus es,non es Elias,non es Propheta aliquis,ergo malè vsurpas Baptismū. Reprehensio hæc,hoc quasi fundamento nitebatur, quòd nemini licitum erat baptizare, aut innouare aliquid in religione,præterquam vel Messiæ, vel Eliæ, vel Prophetæ. Vnde illud apparet non ignorasse Iudæos mutationem religionis aliquam futuram in aduentu Messiæ:hoc obiter. Vides in his hominibus ingenium hæreticorum & sophistarum quodnam sit: Volunt quidem videri in veritatem inquirere, sicut isti Sacerdotes veritatis scilicet gratiâ quærebant de Iohanne ecquis esset? quasi verò isti fuerint solliciti aut de Iohanne, aut de Messia cognoscendo. Sed paulo post satis ostenderunt se quærere euersionem veritatis & lucis, si qua exorta fuit per Dei misericordiam. Sicut isti hoc tempore nouæ illius lucis quæ in Baptista cœpit pit splendere extinctionem quærebant: sic etiam postea gesserunt se Pharisei erga ipsum Christum, præ se ferentes veritatis desiderium. Sic hodierno die Papistæ volunt videri veritatis indagatores ac defensores acerrimi, cum reipsa sophistæ illi quærant veritatem in tenebris sepelire, & lucem Euangelij, quæ Dei misericordia & potentia infinita nouissimis hisce diebus è tenebris illis regni Antichristi splenduit, quatum in se est extinguere. Quis enim non novit tenebricosos illos Scholasticos, lucem illam verbi Dei in tenebris sophismatum & quæstionum intricatarum pene totam demersisse? Gratiæ Deo nunquam satis agi possunt, quod eruerit veritatem suam hoc sæculo nostro ex tenebris illis densissimis.
units.tr: The first question about the person of John has now been dealt with; the second concerns his baptism and his office. A brief preface is set before the question about his office, in which it is taught in what sect and heresy these priests and Levites, who had been sent to John, were. For in Judea there were several sects of religious men, such as the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes, about which we say nothing for the present. These men, then, were of the Pharisees, and therefore teachers and expounders of the law. For the Pharisees especially claimed this for themselves: that they taught the true doctrine of the law and opposed whatever was false or new. Hence they took to themselves this name of Pharisees, as if to say: teachers and expounders of the law, although in fact they were sophists and corrupters of the law. Hence what the Lord said about the leaven of the Pharisees. Such a class of men was fitting for the argument and conclusion that follows against the Baptist. Then comes the question of the Pharisees: They asked him and said to him, Why then do you baptize, if you are not, etc. It appears here, and it is likely, that these men did not understand John when he answered and explained who he was from the prophet Isaiah; or, if they did understand, they must have been extremely malicious. Yet they no longer ask that John explain more plainly what he said about himself from the prophet; instead, leaving this answer aside, they return to the other point, namely that John showed who he was not, and from this they maliciously find fault with John's baptism, by this argument: "You are not the Messiah, as you confessed; you are not Elijah; you are not any prophet; therefore you wrongly take upon yourself the baptism." This objection rested on this foundation: that no one was permitted to baptize or to introduce any change in religion, except the Messiah, or Elijah, or a prophet. From this it is clear that the Jews did not fail to know that some change of religion would come with the coming of the Messiah; but this is by the way. You see what sort of mind these men have, those of heretics and sophists. They indeed wish to seem to be inquiring after the truth, just as those priests asked about John whether he was anyone, as if for the sake of truth. As though those men were anxious to know either about John or about the Messiah! But a little later they showed sufficiently that they were seeking the overthrow of truth and light, if any had arisen by the mercy of God. Just as in that time they sought the extinction of the new light that had begun to shine in the Baptist, so afterwards the Pharisees behaved toward Christ himself, pretending a desire for the truth. So today the Papists wish to appear as the most keen investigators and defenders of the truth, when in fact those sophists seek to bury the truth in darkness and, as far as in them lies, to extinguish the light of the Gospel, which by the mercy and infinite power of God has shone in these latest days out of the darkness of the kingdom of Antichrist. For who does not know that those shadowy Schoolmen have almost wholly plunged the light of the Word of God into the darkness of sophisms and intricate questions? Thanks can never be sufficiently given to God that in this our age he has brought forth his truth from those most dense shadows.

units.la: Sequitur responsum Iohannis. Respondit eis Iohannes, dicens. potuit quidem Iohannes negare conclusionem illam Pharisæorum captiosè illatam, hoc modo: Verum est, non sum Messias, hoc enim plane profiteor, & præme fero; non sum Elias, ut vos Eliam intelligitis; non sum etiam Propheta eo sensu, quo vos eum accipitis. Non sequitur tamen, ergo non ad me pertinet Baptismi administratio. Nam ipse Elias de quo est apud Malachiam, non est ille quem vos falso imaginamini esse. Sed is sum ego de quo prædictum est, quod venturus esset cum Spiritu & virtute Eliæ ad reducendum populum ad Deum suum. Non sic quidem respondet Iohannes: sed cum sciret eos male interpretari Baptismum ipsius, quasi vero suo nomine & authoritate baptizaret: atque ita vsurparet gloriam Deo & Messiæ propriam. Huic sinistræ de Baptismo suo sententiæ imprimis occurrit: Ac primum extenuat atque eluat quodammodo suum Baptismum: Deinde demonstrat ipsis Christum verum Messiam, auocatis oculis ipsorum à se, ad inspiciendum propius ipsum Dominum. Tertiò inita comparatione præfert Christum sibi. Dicit igitur, Ego baptizo aqua, Hoc est, ministerium meum duntaxat externum est, interiorem autem illam efficaciam Baptismi non est mene penes in quempiam erogare. Verum, inquit, in medio vestri stat, quem vos nescitis, q.d. Messias ipse stat in medio vestri, palamque offert vobis videndum & amplectendum:
units.tr: John answered them, saying: John could indeed have denied the Pharisees' conclusion, which they had drawn craftily, in this way: "It is true that I am not the Messiah; I plainly profess this and openly declare it. I am not Elijah, as you understand Elijah. Nor am I a Prophet in the sense in which you take the word. Yet it does not follow that the administration of baptism therefore does not belong to me. For the Elijah of whom Malachi speaks is not the one you wrongly imagine. I am the one of whom it was foretold that he would come with the spirit and power of Elijah to bring the people back to their God." John did not answer in exactly this way. But since he knew they misinterpreted his baptism, as if he baptized in his own name and authority, and so claimed for himself the glory belonging to God and to the Messiah, he first meets this unfavourable view of his baptism. First, he diminishes and in a sense washes away his own baptism. Second, he shows them that Christ is the true Messiah, turning their eyes away from himself to look more closely at the Lord. Third, by drawing a comparison, he places Christ above himself. He therefore says, "I baptize with water." That is, my ministry is only external; to bestow that inner efficacy of baptism is not in my power. "But," he says, "there stands in the midst of you one whom you do not know": that is, the Messiah himself stands in the midst of you, openly offering himself to be seen and embraced.

units.la: C
units.tr: C

units.la: Iohannis ad Pharisæorum quæsita responsum.
units.tr: John's answer to the Pharisees' questions.

units.la: Responsi illius summa & partes. Sed vos miseri vsque-adeo caeci estis vt tantam lucem videre non possitis. Miserrimum illud est habere Christum in medio nostri lucentem, & tamen non videre eum. Sunt tamen apud nos complures eo quem dixi modo miseri, qui Christum ante oculos ipsorum quasi crucifixum, in viua illa Euangelij praedicatione, &, vt loquar cum Apostolo demonstratione illa spirituali, non tamen vident eum: quibus Deus huius saeculi excaecauit mentes, ne irradiet eos lumen Euangelii gloriae Christi, qui est imago Dei. Postquam sic digito quasi demonstrauit ipsis Christum; deinde ipsum praefert sibi. Hic est, inquit ille, qui post me venit, nempe quoad officium & vocationem. Nam ego q.d. missus sum ante faciem Domini vt praepararem viam eius. Ante me factus est, inquit, vel praelatus est mihi, nempe quod ad dignitatis gradum, vt supra annotauimus. Tum explicans hanc praerogatiuam Christi, se longissime infra eum deiicit vt ipse longe supra omne imperium, ac potestatem, potentiam & dominium collocatus est. Cuius, inquit, solearum corrigiam non sum dignus qui soluam, Hoc est, in cuius domo non sum dignus qui fungar officio aliquo maximè seruili & abiecto, sed vt dignus sim & idoneus ipse facit.
units.tr: The sum and parts of that answer. "But you are so wretched and so blind that you cannot see so great a light. It is most miserable to have Christ shining in the midst of us and yet not to see him. Yet there are among us many who are wretched in the way I have described: though Christ is before their eyes, as if crucified, in the living preaching of the Gospel and, to speak with the Apostle, in that spiritual demonstration, they do not see him. The god of this age has blinded their minds, lest the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine upon them." Having thus, as it were, pointed out Christ with his finger, he then sets him before himself. "He it is," he says, "who comes after me," namely in respect of office and calling. For I, he means, have been sent before the face of the Lord to prepare his way. "He was made before me," he says, or "he was preferred to me," namely in respect of the rank of dignity, as we noted above. Then, explaining this prerogative of Christ, he lowers himself far beneath him, so that Christ is set far above all rule and authority, power, might and dominion. "The strap of whose sandals," he says, "I am not worthy to loose." That is, I am not worthy to perform, in his house, some office even of the most servile and abject kind; but he makes me worthy and fit.

units.la: Notandum hoc, Qui maximus est in domo, id est in Ecclesia Christi, & qui donis spiritualibus maximè excellit, in se fe alioqui non est dignus vel infimo Ecclesiae loco, sed quòd dignus sit ex mera Dei gratia est qui cum dignum duxerit. Gratiam ei habeo, inquit Paulus, qui me robustum effecit, id est, Iesu Christo Domino nostro, quod me fidelem duxerit, vt qui me in ministerio constituerit. Obseruandum hoc primum in responsione Iohannis. Duo sunt, vt videtur, quae Pharisaei obiiciunt Iohanni, alterum quidem apertè, alterum verò obscurè. Aperte obiiciunt, quòd vsurpet Baptismi ministerium absque legitima vocatione: obscurè, quòd suo nomine & authoritate baptizet non secus ac si Messias esset. Iohannes praetermisso ac dissimulato illo altero, ad secundum respondet, quia nimirum agebatur hic de gloria Dei. Purgat se igitur omni Dei ac Messiae ipsius gloriae affectatione. Quemadmodum si contingat aliquando vt Diabolus bolus aut Mundus vltrò obtrudant nobis gloriam Dei, vel gloriæ aliquam partem, prudenter tum debemus cauere ne eam in nos recipiamus, cui profecto sustinendæ nos omnino impares esse triste exemplū Herodis docuit. Ita si quando eueniat vt accusemur affectatæ eiusdem Dei gloriæ, tum relictis omnibus aliis, posthabita cura omni ac defensione nostri, aut authoritatis nostræ, quæ alioqui nobis à Deo permissa est, debemus imprimis purgare nos vel suspicione omni vsurpatę Dei gloriæ: Atque vt Deo constet sua gloria in solidum, & emineat supra nos Christus, oportet nos nostraque omnia cleuare, nósque ipsos ignominiæ exponere, vt Deo nostro sit gloria. Is qui plantat non est aliquid, neque qui rigat, sed Deus qui dat incrementum.
units.tr: It is to be noted that he who is greatest in the house, that is, in the Church of Christ, and who most excels in spiritual gifts, is in himself not worthy even of the lowest place in the Church, but he is worthy by the mere grace of God, who counts him worthy. "I thank him," says Paul, "who has strengthened me, Jesus Christ our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to the ministry." This is the first thing to observe in John's answer. There are two things, as it seems, that the Pharisees object to John: one openly, the other obscurely. Openly, they object that he usurps the ministry of baptism without lawful calling; obscurely, that he baptizes in his own name and authority, as though he were the Messiah. John, passing over and dissembling the former, answers the latter, since clearly the question concerned the glory of God. He therefore purges himself of every affectation of the glory of God and of his Messiah. Just as, if it sometimes happens that the Devil or the World thrusts upon us the glory of God, or some part of it, we ought then prudently to take care not to receive it, since the sad example of Herod has taught us that we are altogether unequal to bearing it; so, if at any time it happens that we are accused of affecting that same glory of God, then, leaving aside all other concerns and putting aside all care for our own defence or our authority, which has otherwise been granted us by God, we must first purge ourselves even of the suspicion of having usurped God's glory. And so that God's glory may remain entirely his own, and Christ may stand out above us, we must humble ourselves and all that is ours, and expose ourselves to disgrace, so that glory may belong to our God. "He who plants is nothing, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase."

units.la: Deinde hic nota, Iohannes quærentibus istis de ministerio ipsius & authoritate quam habuit ad baptizandū, nulla defensione ministerij sui vsus, verùm ipsum eleuans, statim ducit eos ad Christum. Hæretici & Sophistæ toti semper in hoc fuerunt, vt si quando Deus post tenebras illas quas ipsi in Mundum inuexerunt, Deus, inquam, misertus mundi nouam aliquam lucem præter expectationem exoriri fecit, & homines quos ipsi vitum est extra ordinem excitauit, qui vexitatem suā sic oppressam vendicarent ex tantis tenebris, fuerunt, inquā, semper toti in eo, vt neglecta illa luce quæ exorta est, cū hominibus ipsis cōflictarent, assiduè quærentes de ipsorum ministerio atque vocatione. Idē faciunt Papistæ hodierno die: sed quid nobis faciendum sit e-contra, & quid respondendum Sophistis istis ex hoc loco discimus: Non ù de ministerio nostro cū istis hominibus nobis diminandū est & garriendum, illud enim est quod vnicè cupiunt vt ad rauim vsque vociferentur de successionibus, ordinationibus, antiquitatibus & cæteris id genus. Nō tam, inquā, de ministerio garriendum est, quàm pertrahendi sunt miseri ad ipsam illam lucem quæ exorta est, eique ipsis est ante oculos ponenda: En miser eam lucem quam tu in tenebris tandiu sepeliisti, En Deus per nos infirmos homines, discussis tenebris, quas tu ei offudisti, voluit eam rursus lucere. Transfer oculos tuos, ô miser, à personis hominum & tandē intuere hunc Sole qui exortus est mūdo. Sed nescio quomodo fiat, idque iusto Dei iudicio, vt, quo magis miseri isti intuentur hunc Solem, eò magis cæcutiant. Sed istos mittamus & committamus iudici suo, qui quidem à nobis est assiduis precibus inuocandus, vt ad iudicium festinet, vel ob hanc causam, vt finem controuersiarum istarum tandem faciat; neque enim de lite hac decidetur, & aduersariis os obturabitur priusquā veniat Dominus. Etiam veni Domine Iesu.
units.tr: Next, note here that John, when these men question him about his ministry and the authority he had to baptize, uses no defence of his ministry at all, but raises himself up and at once leads them to Christ. The heretics and sophists have always been wholly intent on this: whenever God, after those darkness which they themselves have brought into the world, God, I say, in pity on the world, has caused some new light to rise beyond expectation, and has raised up men, whom they themselves have thrust out of the ordinary course, to vindicate the truth so oppressed out of such darkness, they, I say, have always been wholly bent on this: to neglect that light which has risen and to wrangle with these men, constantly asking about their ministry and calling. The Papists do the same today. But from this passage we learn what we ought to do in turn, and what to answer those sophists. We must not waste our time and breath quarrelling with these men about our ministry, for that is precisely what they most desire, that we should shout ourselves hoarse about successions, ordinations, antiquities and other things of that kind. Rather, I say, we must not quarrel about the ministry so much as draw the wretched men to that very light which has risen, and set it before their eyes: "Behold, wretch, that light which you have so long buried in darkness! Behold, God through us weak men, having dispelled the darkness which you cast over it, has willed it to shine again!" Turn your eyes, O wretch, from the persons of men, and at last gaze upon this Sun which has risen on the world. But somehow it happens, and by the just judgment of God, that the more these wretched men gaze upon this Sun, the more they grow blind. But let us send them on and commit them to their judge, who is indeed to be invoked by us with constant prayers, that he may hasten to judgment, or for this reason, that he may at last bring an end to these controversies; for this dispute will not be settled, and the mouths of our adversaries will not be stopped, before the Lord comes. "Even so, come, Lord Jesus."

units.la: Hactenus sic responsum est à Iohanne Baptista. Nunc Euangelista noster, vt maiorem fidem faciat huic narrationi, notat locum in quo ista sunt gesta. Hæc, inquit, facta sunt in Bethabara trans Iordanem, vbi Iohannes baptizabat. Baptizauit Iohannes initio in Bethabara trans Iordanem, idque vt videtur non absque mysterio. Nam Bethabara significat domum transitus, siue Traiectum: ibi enim diuisit se miraculose Iordanis fluuius, vt Iosuæ cum populo aditus pateret ad terram illam promissam. Iohannes igitur primum huc aduenientes, significare voluit aduentare veram illam Bethabaram, nempe Iesum Christum, qui solus est via ad vitam, & cœli porta, per quem habemus aditum ad Deum. Neque in hoc loco duntaxat restitit Iohannes; verùm, vt postea videbimus, venit Ænon, quæ est propè Salim; neque rursus ibi perpetuò hæsit; sed nunc huc, nunc illuc perrexit, per tractum & ripam Iordanis, ductus aquarum, quibus baptizaret, commoditate.
units.tr: Thus far John the Baptist's answer. Now our Evangelist, to lend greater credibility to this narrative, notes the place where these things were done. "These things," he says, "were done in Bethabara beyond Jordan, where John was baptizing." John first baptized in Bethabara beyond Jordan, and this, as it seems, was not without a mystery. For Bethabara means the house of crossing, or the ford; for there the river Jordan miraculously divided, so that the way lay open for Joshua and the people to the promised land. John therefore, by first coming hither, wished to signify the coming of the true Bethabara, namely Jesus Christ, who alone is the way to life and the gate of heaven, through whom we have access to God. Nor did John remain only in this place; but, as we shall see later, he came to Aenon, which is near Salim; nor again did he remain there continually, but went now here, now there, through the tract and bank of the Jordan, for the convenience of the waters with which he might baptize.

units.la: 29 Postero die videt Iohannes Iesum venientem ad se, & ait, Ecce agnus ille Dei qui tollit peccatum mundi.
units.tr: 29 The next day John sees Jesus coming to him and says, "Behold that Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world."

units.la: 30 Hic est de quo dicebam, Post me venit vir qui antepositus est mihi, quia prior me erat.
units.tr: 30 "This is he of whom I said, 'After me comes a man who has been preferred before me, because he was before me.'"

units.la: 31 At ego non noueram eum: sed vt manifestus fiat Israëli, propterea veni ego baptizans aqua.
units.tr: 31 "But I did not know him, but so that he might be made manifest to Israel, therefore I came baptizing with water."

units.la: 32 Tum, inquam, testatus est Iohannes dicens, Conspexi Spiritum descendentem quasi columbam è cœlo, qui etiam mansit super eum. 33 Et ego non noueram eum, sed qui misit me vt baptizarem aqua, ille mihi dixerat, Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem, ac manentem super eum, hic est qui baptizat Spiritu Sancto.
units.tr: 32 Then, I say, John bore witness, saying: "I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and it remained upon him." 33 And I did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water had said to me, "Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit."

units.la: 34 Ego igitur vidi, & testor hunc esse filium illum Dei.
units.tr: "I therefore saw, and I testify that this is the Son of God."

units.la: SEquitur testimonium Iohannis Baptistę secundum de Messia, primum digito quasi demonstrat Agnum illum Dei: deinde de eo concionatur. Postero die, inquit, videt Iohannes Iesum venientem ad se. Iesus, cum iam tempus propè adesset quo ingrederetur destinatum sibi officium, annum iam agens quasi tricesimum Nazaretha Galilææ venit ad desertum, vbi baptizabat Iohannes, & ab eo baptizatus est. Postea ductus est à Spiritu in desertum, vbi postquam ieiunasset 40. totos dies, tentatus est à Diabolo: hinc reuersus est ad Iohannem. Hoc igitur tempore intuitus Iohannes Iesum reuersum, & venientem ad se, demonstrat hominem discipulis suis, Ecce agnus, inquit, qui tollit peccata Mundi. Demonstrat eum tanquam victimam innocentissimam immolandam pro peccatis Mundi. Ecce agnus ille. Emphasis enim est in articulo. q.d. Agnus ille qui figuratus est, agno Paschali, & omnibus veteribus sacrificiis: & de quo Prophetę omnes prædixerunt, Agnus, inquam, ille qui tollit peccatum mundi: Qui tollit, inquit, in præsenti tempore, vt significet actum continuum: Nam perpetuus est vigor sacrificii Christi, neque arescit vnquam eius sanguis, quem Iohannes dicit sic aduocatum esse coram Patre nostra causa, vt etiam sit propitiatio pro peccatis nostris. Qui tollit, inquit, peccatum mundi. Peccatum peccans intelligit, omnis peccati radicem, & ex consequenti amaros fructus inde nascentes, quę peccata multitudinis numero dicuntur. Tollit hoc peccatum cum fructibus suis, quia reatum ipsius sanguine suo aufert, & ipsum etiam paulatim abolet Spiritu suo, dum suos regenerat in dies. Mundum dicit, non vnam aliquam gentem, non vnum Israelem, sed vniuersum mundum. Nam virtus sanguinis Christi patet ad vniuersum mundum. Sic Iohannes, Cùm dixit eum propitiationem esse pro peccatis no-stris, amplificauit sacrificium illud, nec pro nostris, inquiés, tantum, sed pro peccatis totius mundi. Sic de Christo locutus est, imitatus, vt videtur, Esaiam: Vt parua pecus ducitur ad mactationem, & velut ouis coram tonsoribus suis obmutescit, neque aperit os suum. Christum autem discipulis suis tanquam Agnum & victimam mactandam demonstrari, etiam antequam reipsa mactatus esset ac passus propter redemptionem humani generis, maximè opus fuit. Nam etsi Christum venturum expectabant Iudæi, tamè passurum eum vix intelligebant, imò verò eum fore regem cum terrestri hac pompa & gloria, qui restitueturus esset regnum Israëlis perditum, somniabant. Ipsique discipuli Christi communi illo errore abducebantur. Ideoque maximè opus fuit iam primùm Christum vt victimam demonstrari: Nam iis qui prætereunt Christi crucem, nihil prodest Christus: quandoquidè Christus non, nisi vt crucifixus, sit fundamentum fœderis statuiti, cùm non nisi ipsius sanguine pacificetur illa Dei ira aduersus peccata nostra; neque rursus conscientiæ nostræ, nisi illo sanguine tranquillentur. Quare abest à nobis gloriari nisi in cruce Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Here follows John the Baptist's second testimony about the Messiah. First he points out with his finger that Lamb of God, and then he preaches about him. "On the next day," he says, "John sees Jesus coming to him." When the time was now near at hand for Jesus to enter upon the office appointed for him, being now about thirty years old, he came from Nazareth in Galilee to the desert where John was baptizing, and he was baptized by him. Afterwards he was led by the Spirit into the desert, where, after he had fasted for forty whole days, he was tempted by the Devil. From there he returned to John. At this time, therefore, John, seeing Jesus returning and coming to him, points him out to his disciples: "Behold the Lamb," he says, "who takes away the sins of the world." He points him out as a most innocent victim to be sacrificed for the sins of the world. "Behold that lamb." For the emphasis lies on the article: that is to say, that Lamb which was prefigured by the Paschal lamb and by all the old sacrifices, and of whom all the prophets foretold. "That Lamb, I say, who takes away the sin of the world. Who takes away," he says, "in the present tense, to signify a continuing act. For the power of Christ's sacrifice is perpetual, and his blood never dries up; John says that this blood speaks on our behalf before the Father, so that it is also a propitiation for our sins. Who takes away," he says, "the sin of the world." By sin he understands sin in its root, the source of every sin, and the bitter fruits springing from it consequently, which are called sins in the plural. He takes away this sin together with its fruits: he removes its guilt by his blood, and he also gradually abolishes sin itself by his Spirit, as he daily regenerates his own. He says the world, not one particular nation, not one Israel, but the whole world. For the virtue of Christ's blood extends to the whole world. So John, when he said that he is a propitiation "for our sins," enlarged that sacrifice, saying: "not for ours only, but for the sins of the whole world." He spoke of Christ, apparently imitating Isaiah: "As a lamb is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep before its shearers is dumb, so he does not open his mouth." It was very necessary that Christ be displayed to his disciples as the Lamb and victim to be slaughtered, even before he was actually slaughtered and suffered for the redemption of the human race. For although the Jews expected the coming of Christ, they hardly understood that he would suffer; indeed they dreamed that he would be a king with earthly pomp and glory, who would restore the lost kingdom of Israel. And Christ's own disciples were led astray by that common error. Therefore it was most necessary that Christ be first shown as a victim: for Christ profits nothing to those who pass over his cross, since Christ is the foundation of the established covenant only as crucified, since that wrath of God against our sins is not appeased except by his blood, nor are our consciences calmed except by that blood. Therefore it is far from us to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Hactenus demonstrauit illum Agnum: deinceps eo sic demonstrato quæd am apud discipulos suos concionatur. 1. Prædicat eius excellentiam & præstantiam præ se. 2. Profitetur suam ipsius ignorantiam. 3. Officium tamè suum profitetur esse, vt per Baptismum suum eum manifestaret Israëli. 4. Quæ inter baptizandum Christum cœlitus facta sint, enarrat. 5. Concludit hoc suum de Christo testimonium. Vt igitur redeamus, prima concionis huius pars est de præstantia Christi & Agni illius, quam comparatè tractat. Hic est ille de quo dicebam, pone me venit vir qui prælatus est mihi, quia prior me erat. Post me venit, inquit, hoc est, posterius tempore ad officiū suum vocatus est. Nam ego missus sum ante eum, vt viam eius complanarem & præpararem. Hic factus est ante me. Ad verbum sensus est, prælatus est mihi, siue, quod dicitur alibi, Validior me est. Nam particula ἔμπροσθέν, ante, hic non tempus, sed locum siue dignitatis gradum significat, quemadmodum prius expositum. Additur ratio,
units.tr: Thus far he has shown that Lamb; from now on, having so displayed him, he preaches some things to his disciples. (1) He proclaims the excellence and pre-eminence of that one before himself. (2) He confesses his own ignorance. (3) Yet he professes that his office is to make Christ manifest to Israel through his baptism. (4) He recounts what was done from heaven while Christ was being baptized. (5) He concludes this his testimony about Christ. Returning, then, the first part of this sermon concerns the pre-eminence of Christ and of that Lamb, which he treats by way of comparison. "This is he of whom I said, after me comes a man who has been preferred before me, because he was before me." "After me comes," he says, that is, he was called to his office later in time. For I was sent before him to smooth and prepare his way. "He has become before me." The sense, word for word, is "he has been preferred to me," or, as is said elsewhere, "he is mightier than I." For the particle emprosthen, "before," here signifies not time but place, or a degree of dignity, as was explained earlier. The reason is added:

units.la: Cur ista oportuit discipuli ante Christi mactationem.
units.tr: Why it was necessary for these things to be told to the disciples before Christ's slaughter.

units.la: Partes concionis Iohannis apud discipulos suos de Christo.
units.tr: The parts of John's sermon to his disciples about Christ.

units.la: De Christi præstantia.
units.tr: On the excellence of Christ.

units.la: Matt. 3.11.
units.tr: Matt. 3.11.

units.la: Galat. 6. 14. ratio, Quia prior me erat, vtpote Deus ab æterno.
units.tr: Galat. 6.14. The reason: "because he was before me," namely, as God from eternity.

units.la: Vides igitur Iohanem aue rtere oculos discipulorum à se quem plus satis sunt admirati, ad Christum ipsum. Gloria illa & gratia quam Deus communicauit cum creaturis suis, nonnunquam impedimento est nobis ne Dei ipsius gloriâ intueamur. Ideoq; remouenda est ab oculis nostris ne eos nimium in se fe defixos detineat, & couertendi sunt oculi nostri ad Dei ipsius gloriâ inspiciendam: Quam vbi semel spectauimus, tota illa gloria & totus splendor creaturæ, etiam quàm maximè excellentis, præ ea vilescit. Id experiuntur re ipsa quotquot gloriam Dei habent ante oculos. Deinde non est prætereundum silentio quod dicit, Hic est de quo dicebam, Ex hoc loco apparet discipulos Iohannis iam ante præparatos & instructos fuisse à magistro suo de Christo, quàm Christum ipsum præsentem sunt intuiti. Nos, teste Paulo, non viuimus in hac vita per aspectum Christi seruatoris, sed tota vita nostra debet esse præparatio ad aspectum illum qui futurus est longè iucundissimus. Præparant autem nos fides in eum, quem nondum videmus & amor in eum quem nondum cernimus: sicut Petrus ait, Quem cum non videritis, diligitis, & quem cum non cernatis, et tamen creditis. Quis est fructus huius præparationis quæ est per fidē & dilectionem? Exultatis, inquit, gaudio ineffabili, & glorioso, quem quidem fructum etiam in hac præsenti vita percipimus. Quòd si fides & amor in absentem hunc, tantum gaudii fructum afferunt in hac vita, quantum gaudium efficiet præsens aspectus, cùm Dominū coràm intuebimur in altera? Sic iam antea præparati & de Christo venturo certiores facti, proculdubiò eum iam demonstratum sibi, & præsentem aduidè intuiti sunt, & ex ipsius præsentia admirabilem voluptatem animo conceperunt, cùm eum esse præsentem intelligerent, de cuius excellentia sæpiùs iam inaudient. Ita nos quoque sic præparati per fidem & amorem in hac vita cùm in altera videbimus eum præsentem, in quem credidimus, & quem tantopere dileximus, dicì non potest quanto cum gaudio fruemur illo aspectu, & Redemptorem nostrum coràm intuebimur: Sic enim argumentatur Petrus, loco à nobis iam citato: Ex fide &
units.tr: You see, then, that John turns the eyes of his disciples away from himself, whom they admired more than enough, to Christ himself. That glory and grace which God has communicated to his creatures is sometimes an impediment to us, so that we do not look upon the glory of God himself. Therefore it must be removed from before our eyes, lest it hold them too fixed upon itself, and our eyes must be turned to behold the glory of God himself. Once we have seen that, all the glory and splendour of a creature, even of the most excellent, becomes worthless in comparison. All who keep the glory of God before their eyes experience this in fact. Next, it must not be passed over in silence that he says, "This is he of whom I said," From this place it appears that John's disciples had been prepared and instructed about Christ by their master before they saw Christ himself present. We, as Paul witnesses, do not live in this life by sight of Christ the Saviour, but our whole life ought to be a preparation for that sight, which is to be by far the most delightful. Faith in him whom we do not yet see, and love for him whom we do not yet behold, prepare us, as Peter says: "Whom having not seen you love, and in whom, though now you do not see him, yet believing you rejoice." What is the fruit of this preparation, which is through faith and love? "You exult," he says, "with joy unspeakable and glorious," a fruit which we indeed receive even in this present life. But if faith and love toward this absent one bring so much fruit of joy in this life, how much joy will the present sight produce, when we shall behold the Lord face to face in the other life? Thus the disciples, already prepared beforehand and made more certain about the Christ who was to come, undoubtedly saw him already shown to them and present before their eyes, and conceived in their minds an admirable delight from his presence, when they understood that he was present, whose excellence they had heard so often before. So we too, prepared in this way through faith and love in this life, when in the other life we shall see him present whom we have believed and loved so greatly, cannot say how great the joy we shall have in that sight, and we shall behold our Redeemer face to face. For Peter argues in this way in the passage we have already cited: from faith and love toward the absent one he gathers praise, glory and honour to come, when Jesus Christ shall be revealed, to whom be all honour and glory. Amen.

units.la: 1. Petr. 1. 8. amore in absentem colligit laudem, gloriam & honorem futurum, cum patefiet Iesus Christus, cui sit omnis honos & gloria. Amen.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 1. 8. In the same way he argues from faith and love for the absent Christ that praise, glory and honour will come to us when Jesus Christ is revealed, to whom belongs all honour and glory. Amen.

units.la: Sequitur concionis altera pars, in qua ipse profitetur suam ignorantiam, Et ego, inquit, non noveram eum. Qui potuit Iohannes eum ignorare, cuius erat praecursor, & quem aduentare clamauit, & in cuius nomen baptizauit? Respondeo, nouit quidem eum iam aliqua ex parte Iohannes, sed cum venientem ad se eum baptizaret, plenius, & ut sic dicam, de facie eum coepit cognoscere. Nam tum praeterquam quod ipsum coram intuitus est, accepit caelitus oraculum, ac testimonium de eo, quod filius esset Dei, quod esset is, qui baptizat Spiritu Sancto. Priorem illam notitiam, cum hac posteriori comparans Iohannes vix putat illam mereri notitiae nomen: verum ignorantiae potius nomine appellandam censet: Ideoque ab eo dictum est quod antequam ipsum baptizaret, quo demum tempore coram eum intuitus est, accepit que testimonium Patris de eo, quod, inquam, cum non noverit Christum. Notus erat iam olim aliquo tenus modo Iesus Christus Patribus & veteri populo, verum illa notitia pene nulla erat; Et si quis eam compararet cum ea quae coepit esse in Christi ipsius aduentu & manifestatione in carne; quo nimirum tempore, ut ait Paulus, mysterium illud in lucem productum est, quod a saeculis in Deo absconditum erat. Atque hoc est illud mysterium salutis nostrae per Christum quod revelatur nobis hoc ipso die: Quod quidem mysterium si tectum est, iis qui pereunt tectum est. Miserum est mori in tanta tamque illustri vitae revelatione.
units.tr: Now follows the second part of the sermon, in which he confesses his own ignorance: And I, he says, did not know him. How could John fail to know him, when he was John's forerunner, whose coming he proclaimed and in whose name he baptized? I answer: John indeed knew him already in some respect, but when he baptized him as he came to him, he began to know him more fully and, so to speak, face to face. For then, besides seeing him in person, he received from heaven an oracle and a testimony about him, that he was the Son of God, and that he was the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. Comparing that earlier knowledge with this later one, John hardly thinks the former deserves the name of knowledge; he judges it should rather be called ignorance. Hence he says that before he baptized him, when at last he saw him in person and received the Father's testimony about him, he did not know Christ, I say, as he ought to be known. Jesus Christ was indeed known in some measure of old to the Fathers and the ancient people, but that knowledge was almost nothing; and if one compares it with the knowledge that began with Christ's own coming and manifestation in the flesh, at which time, as Paul says, that mystery was brought to light which had been hidden in God from the ages. And this is the mystery of our salvation through Christ which is revealed to us on this very day. Indeed, if this mystery is hidden, it is hidden from those who perish. It is a wretched thing to die in the midst of so great and so clear a revelation of life.

units.la: Sequitur tertia pars concionis, in qua ostendit se venisse babtizantem aquâ, ad hoc ut patefieret Israeli Agnus iste alioqui non ita bene sibi cognitus. Sed, inquit, ego veni baptizans aqua, ut manifestus fiat Israeli. Iohannes Christum manifestauit externo Baptismo: quia Baptismus symbolum est Christi, & beneficiorum ipsius, ut remissionis peccatorum, ut regenerationis, ut vitae aeternae. Dicit autem se baptizare ideo ut manifestus fiat, non quidem toti mundo, sed Israeli duntaxat. Nam etsi Agnus ille erat, ut dixit supra, qui tollit peccata totius mundi,
units.tr: Then follows the third part of the sermon, in which he shows that he came baptizing with water, so that this Lamb, who was otherwise not so well known to Israel, might be made manifest to them. But, he says, I came baptizing with water, that he might be made manifest to Israel. John manifested Christ by the outward baptism, because baptism is a sign of Christ and of his benefits, such as the forgiveness of sins, regeneration and eternal life. He says, moreover, that he baptizes so that Christ may be made manifest, not indeed to the whole world, but to Israel only. For although he was the Lamb, as he said above, who takes away the sins of the whole world,

units.la: Ephes. 3. 9.

2. Cor. 4. 3. mundi, tamen Iohannes nō erat missus ad totum mundum,sed ad perditas oues Israelis.Obtinuit autem hanc praerogatiuam Israel,quia vetus erat Dei regnum & hereditas. Fateor quidem Patrem dedisse filio omnes gentes in haereditatem,vt dicitur, Pete à me,& dabo tibi gentes possessiones tuas; verum peculiari quodam modo dedit Pater filio suo regnum Israelis. Dedit enim regnum Israelis,tanquam vetus & auitum regnum:Reliquę gentes,& alia regna terrae, tantùm erant accessoria,& vt sic dicam,nouus conquaestus.Nam filius cùm primùm veniret in mundum hunc, & manifestaret se in carne nostra, inuenit quidem in ruinis illis Ecclesiae Israeliticae aliquam Ecclesiam faciem.At verò nullam Ecclesiae faciem inuenit in reliquis gentibus, sed emissis post resurrectionem Apostolis suis,eas debellauit & compulit sub obedientiā fidei. Ob hanc igitur causam quòd Israel vetus fuerit haereditas hanc obtinuit praerogatiuam, vt Iohannes ad Israelem nominatim mitteretur:Et Christus ipse, vt Petrus docet, primùm ad eum mitteretur. Etsi hactenus praerogatiua fuerit Israelis prae caeteris gentibus ,tamen voluit Deus in hoc esse parem cum caeteris gentibus ,quòd quemadmodum caeterae gentes iustificandae erant & seruandae,per solam fidem Christi:Ita etiam oporteret Israelem sola fide in filium iustificari & seruari. In hoc enim , id est in iustificationis & salutis modo,docet Apostolus nullam fuisse distinctionem. Israel autem cùm fidei iustitiam repudiaret,& iustitiam suam, quae est ex operibus, consectaretur, effecit vt neque haec praerogatiua neque aliae queuis, quae non paucae aut paruae recensentur,ipsi prodessent : Verùm infidelitate sua Israel ferè totus excidit Dei foedere : & getes quę non sectabantur iustitiā apprehenderunt iustitiam: iustitiam autem eam quae est ex fide, & suffectae sunt ac surrogatae in locum Iudaeorum. Ex hoc loco conantur nos deiicere hodierno die , homo ille peccati,& iustiarii illi,dum docent iustitiam nostram quaerendam in operibus legis & nostris ipsorum meritis. Quod si vetusillud regnum deiectum est de loco illo , in quo nos iam stamus Dei gratia, quod per solam fidem recusauit iustificati:qui possumus nos , qui recens tantùm vocati
units.tr: 2 Cor. 4. 3. of the world; yet John was not sent to the whole world, but to the lost sheep of Israel. Israel obtained this prerogative because it was the ancient kingdom and inheritance of God. I grant indeed that the Father gave the Son all the nations for his inheritance, as it is said: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your possession; but in a peculiar way the Father gave his Son the kingdom of Israel. For he gave the kingdom of Israel as an old and ancestral kingdom. The remaining nations, and the other kingdoms of the earth, were only additions and, so to speak, new acquisitions. For when the Son first came into this world and showed himself in our flesh, he indeed found in those ruins of the Israelite Church some face of a Church. But he found no face of a Church among the other nations; and after the resurrection, when he had sent out his apostles, he subdued them and brought them under the obedience of faith. For this cause, then, because Israel was the old inheritance, it obtained this prerogative, that John should be sent to Israel by name, and that Christ himself, as Peter teaches, should be sent to them first. Although Israel's prerogative above the other nations has lasted until now, yet God willed to make Israel equal to the other nations in this respect: just as the other nations were to be justified and saved solely by faith in Christ, so Israel too was to be justified and saved by faith alone in the Son. For in this, that is, in the manner of justification and salvation, the Apostle teaches that there was no distinction. But Israel, when it rejected the righteousness of faith and pursued its own righteousness, which is from works, brought it about that neither this prerogative nor any other, of which not a few or small ones are reckoned, profited them. Rather, by their unbelief Israel almost wholly fell from the covenant of God; and the nations which did not seek righteousness laid hold of righteousness, that righteousness which is from faith, and were substituted and put in the place of the Jews. From this passage that man of sin and those justiciaries today try to drive us down, while they teach that our righteousness is to be sought in the works of the law and in their own merits. But if that ancient kingdom was cast down from that place where we now stand by the grace of God, because it refused to be justified by faith alone, how can we, who have only recently been called,

units.la: Act.3.26. Salutis aeternae omnium Dei electorum par & eadem ratio. Rom.3.22. Rom.9.3. &c. Iustitiae Christianae hostes refelluntur. sumus,consistere hoc loco & dignitatis gradu, si aliunde quæramus iustificari & seruari, quàm ex fide in Iesum Christum? Anathema esto, qui docet nos non sola fide Christi iustificari & seruari. Obserua hic deinde: Iohannes cum nondum satis Christum haberet cognitum, tamen eum Baptismi symbolo indicauit Israëli. Qui a Deo missi sunt, & si noti statim imbuantur plenior ipsius notitia, tamen vtitur Deus eorum opera in se manifestando. Verùm vt postea Iohannes ad pleniorem Christi cognitionem peruenit: Ita qui dixit vt è tenebris lux exisseret, illucet magis magisque indies eorum cordibus quos ipse misit, & Christum ipsis proponit magis magisque quasi de facie cognoscendum. Nam gloria Dei non alibi lucet quàm lucet in facie Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Acts 3. 26. the same reasoning applies to all the elect of God for eternal salvation. Rom. 3. 22. Rom. 9. 3. etc. The enemies of Christian righteousness are refuted. stand in this place and in this rank of dignity, if we seek to be justified and saved from any source other than faith in Jesus Christ? Let him be accursed who teaches that we are not justified and saved by faith in Christ alone. Observe here further: John, although he did not yet know Christ sufficiently, nevertheless pointed him out to Israel by the sign of baptism. Those whom God sends, even if they are not immediately imbued with a fuller knowledge of him, God nevertheless uses their work in manifesting himself. But just as John afterwards came to a fuller knowledge of Christ, so he who said that light should shine out of darkness shines more and more, day by day, into the hearts of those whom he himself has sent, and sets Christ before them to be known more and more, as it were face to face. For the glory of God shines nowhere else than in the face of Jesus Christ.

units.la: Quare qui velit progressum facere in Dei cognitione, perpetuo nitatur pro viribus Christum propius videre: quo fiet, vt quemadmodum loquitur Apostolus, transformemur in eandem imaginem ex gloria in gloriam.
units.tr: Therefore whoever wishes to make progress in the knowledge of God must constantly strive, as far as his strength allows, to see Christ more closely; by which it will come about, as the Apostle says, that we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory.

units.la: Hactenus tres partes concionis fuerunt: sequitur quarta. Verùm Euangelista noster præfatur ac admonet Iohannem continuasse sermonem & testimonium de Agno illo. Tum testatus est Iohannes dicens, Conspexi Spiritum descendentem super eum de cælo,&c. Hoc est primum illud quod narrat Baptista incidisse extra ordinem & miraculose in Baptismum Christi. Conspexi Spiritum descendentem, nempe quo tempore eum baptizarem. Quod quo melius intelligatur, paulò altius repetenda est historia ex aliis Euangelistis. Iesus venit Nazaretha ad Iohannem qui baptizabat in deserto, cùm iam ingrederetur annum tricesimum, simulque sibi à Patre impositum munus obiret: rogauit autem Iohannem vt ipsum baptizaret. Negauit Iohannes primùm, respondítque magis opus esse sibi vt ab eo baptizaretur: nō enim iam tum ignorabat ipsum filium Dei esse. Iesus autem iussit illum missa illa facere, oportere eum se implere omne iustitiam, hoc est legitimas omnes obseruationes. Iohannes igitur cōsilio Dei iam melius perspecto, ipsum baptizauit. Egrediente autem filio Dei ex aquis & precante, aperti sunt cœli, & Spiritus Sanctus descendit corporali specie columbæ, resedítque super ipsum. Hoc autem factum est inspiciente Iohanne. Itaque ipse ait, Conspexi Spiritum descendentem tanquam columbam super eum.
