Spiritum hic intelligo non dona Spiritus sancti, sed ipsummet Dei Spiritum eundem cum Patre & filio natura ac essentia, tertiam personam in Trinitate descendentem vidit specie columbae: Non quidem quod conversus sit in illam speciem vel in columbam, sed quod ipse Spiritus servata natura sua immutabili apparuerit sub illa specie ac imagine. Sic spiritus Dei non conversus est in linguas illas dispertitas & igneas in die Pentecostes, sed ea specie apparuit. Verum de hoc quaeri potest, An vera & materialis columba fuerit haec in qua se exhibuit conspiciendum Dei Spiritus? Respondeo ex textu, videri non fuisse eam columbam veram & materialem, sed speciem duntaxat aliquam, quae incurrit in sensus exteriores.Nam quod ad corpora illa in quibus, tum olim apparere consueuerunt spirituales illae substantiae sive Dei ipsius, sive angelorum, aliquando erat materiata, ex materia nimirum elementari, vel ex nihilo facta: quae rursus redacta sunt vel in nihilum, vel in elementa ex quibus erant conflata. Horum exempla leges in historiis Abrahami, Lothi & Moßis. Aliquando vero erant nudae duntaxat species corporum, eaeque vel sensibiles incurrentes in sensus externos, vel, ut sic dicā, intelligibiles incurrentes in sensus internos ac mentem interiorem, quiescentibus interea externis illis sensibus. Qualescunque autem erant apparitiones corporum, non erant sine aliqua revelatione. Sed ut redeamus, magis placet speciem fuisse illam columbae in qua apparuit Dei Spiritus sanctus, non materia aliqua corporea. Abutuntur hoc loco & aliis similibus Papistae, ex his speciebus & imaginibus quas Deus exhibuit, colligentes licere nobis imagines facere. Sed pessime colligunt, cum nullum extet mandatum cur imitemur exemplum Dei in imaginibus faciendis: Imo vero contra diserte prohibitum sit, ne faciamus imagines, vel hac causa, quod Idololatrae inter gentes Idola sua in imaginibus colant: Sic non facies, inquit Moses, Domino Deo tuo. Sed istos mittamus ut permittamus suae vanitati, & colamus Deum nostrum, in solius filij sui imagine, & eo solo quem ipse praescripsit modo. Addit Iohannes, Spiritum illum specie columbae apparentem mansisse super eum ; Hoc erat symbolum Spiritus sancti perpetuo requiescentis super Christum, sicut est apud Esaiam, Spiritus Iehovae requiescet super eum. Spiritus Dei requiescit super Christum duplici respectu; primum respectu humanitatis, qua cum perpetuo praesens est Dei Spiritus, efficaciter operas in ea natura omnes virtutes & proprietates divinas, ut Sapientiam, iustitiam bonitatem, lucem, gloriam denique caelestem : operatur autem & numero & gradu perfectas. Aliae creaturae singulae, cum membra tantum sint, singulas aut non multas virtutes acceperunt, & eas quidem non in summo perfectionis gradu: Christus autem cum sit caput, etiam qua homo est, dona Spiritus & universa & gradibus perfecta accepit. Unde de eo praedictum est, Vnxit te Deus, Deus tuus oleo gaudii prae consortibus tuis. Deinde respectu deitatis requiescit in eo Spiritus Dei : quia Spiritus, qui est tertia persona in una deitate, perpetuo praesens est cum filio, qui est secunda persona cum eo coniunctus in mirabili naturae unius eiusdemque unitate; atque ita coniunctus, ut a filio procedat & subsistentiam suam ab eo capiat, nonsecus atque a Patre, per ineffabilem communicationem unius eiusdemque naturae. Spiritus Dei dicitur etiam habitare & manere in renatis, & in beatis Angelis, sed pertalem coniunctionem non habitat in iis, neque ex iis est, licet in iis sit. Neque etiam creaturae per eum agunt, per eum, inquam, spiritum, qui in ipsis agit. Sed Pater & filius in renatis agunt per Spiritum a se procedentem. Atque haec est illa singularis ac excellens ratio duplex qua Spiritus Dei requiescit super Christum : qua quidem ratione dictus est supra versu 14. Plenus gratiae & veritatis, ex cuius plenitudine nos omnes accipimus gratiam pro gratia.
units.tr: Hitherto there have been three parts of the sermon; the fourth follows. Our Evangelist, however, introduces it and reminds us that John continued his discourse and testimony about that Lamb. Then John testified, saying, I saw the Spirit descending from heaven upon him, etc. This is the first thing the Baptist relates as having happened outside the ordinary course and miraculously at the baptism of Christ. I saw the Spirit descending, namely at the time when I was baptizing him. So that this may be better understood, the history must be recounted a little more fully from the other Evangelists. Jesus came from Nazareth to John, who was baptizing in the desert, when he was entering his thirtieth year and at the same time taking up the office imposed on him by the Father; and he asked John to baptize him. John at first refused, and answered that he had more need to be baptized by Jesus, for he already knew that Jesus was the Son of God. Jesus, however, told him to let that be, since it was fitting that he should fulfil all righteousness, that is, all the lawful observances. John therefore, now having a clearer view of God's counsel, baptized him. As the Son of God came up out of the water and prayed, the heavens were opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in the bodily form of a dove and settled upon him. This took place while John was looking on. So he himself says, I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven upon him. By Spirit here I understand not the gifts of the Holy Spirit but the very Spirit of God himself, the same in nature and essence as the Father and the Son, the third person in the Trinity; he saw him descend in the appearance of a dove. Not indeed that he was changed into that appearance or into a dove, but that the Spirit himself, his own unchangeable nature preserved, appeared under that form and image. So the Spirit of God was not changed into those divided fiery tongues on the day of Pentecost, but appeared in that form. But it may be asked here: was this a true and material dove in which the Spirit of God presented himself to be seen? I answer from the text that it does not seem to have been a true and material dove, but merely some appearance which fell under the outward senses. For as to those bodies in which those spiritual substances, whether of God himself or of angels, used then to appear, sometimes they were materialised, made of elemental matter or out of nothing; and these were again reduced either to nothing or to the elements out of which they had been compounded. Examples of these you will read in the histories of Abraham, Lot and Moses. At other times, however, they were mere bare appearances of bodies, and these either sensible, falling on the outward senses, or, so to speak, intelligible, falling on the inward senses and the inner mind, while the outward senses meanwhile were at rest. Whatever the kind of appearances of bodies, they were never without some revelation. But to return: I prefer to hold that the form of a dove in which the Holy Spirit of God appeared was an appearance, not some corporeal matter. The Papists abuse this passage and others like it, gathering from these forms and images which God displayed that we are permitted to make images. But they gather very badly, since there is no command that we should imitate God's example in making images; indeed, it is expressly forbidden that we make images, even for this reason, that idolaters among the nations worship their idols in images: "You shall not make for yourself," says Moses, "anything of the kind for the Lord your God." But let us leave them to their vanity, and let us worship our God in the image of his Son alone, and in the one manner that he himself has prescribed. John adds that the Spirit, appearing in the form of a dove, remained upon him. This was the sign of the Holy Spirit resting perpetually upon Christ, as in Isaiah: "The Spirit of Jehovah shall rest upon him." The Spirit of God rests upon Christ in a twofold respect. First, with respect to his humanity: in that nature the Spirit of God is always present, effectively working all the divine virtues and properties, such as wisdom, righteousness, goodness, light, and, in short, heavenly glory; and he works them perfect both in number and in degree. Other creatures, each being only a member, have received single virtues, or not many, and these not in the highest degree of perfection; but Christ, since he is the head, has received the gifts of the Spirit, all of them and perfect in degree, even as man. Whence it was foretold of him: "God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows." Secondly, with respect to his deity the Spirit of God rests in him, because the Spirit, who is the third person in the one deity, is always present with the Son, who is the second person, joined with him in the wonderful unity of one and the same nature; and so joined that he proceeds from the Son and takes his subsistence from him, no less than from the Father, through the ineffable communication of one and the same nature. The Spirit of God is also said to dwell and remain in the reborn and in the blessed angels, but he does not dwell in them with such a union, nor is he from them, although he is in them. Nor do creatures act through him—through him, I say, the Spirit who acts in them. But the Father and the Son act in the reborn through the Spirit proceeding from themselves. This is that singular and excellent twofold reason by which the Spirit of God rests upon Christ; and it was by this reason that he was spoken of above, at verse 14: "Full of grace and truth, from whose fullness we all receive grace for grace."

units.la: Hactenus de primo illo quod narrat Baptista incidisse in baptismum Christi ; sequitur alterum, cuius occasio ut videtur praemissa est, Et ego, inquit, non noveram eum. An adhuc etiam postquam conspexit Spiritum descendentem quasi columbam de caelo & manentem super eum, An adhuc, inquam, erat Christus Baptistae ignotus?
units.tr: So far concerning the first thing the Baptist relates as having happened at the baptism of Christ. The second follows, of which the occasion seems to have been set out beforehand: "And I did not know him," he says. Was Christ still unknown to the Baptist even after he saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven and remaining upon him? Was Christ, I say, still unknown to the Baptist?

units.la: Profecto non perfecte innotuit Baptistæ Christus priusquam accepit illam revelationem à Patre, quòd esset filius, & baptizaret Spiritu Sancto. De causa revelationis hactenus, Baptistæ ignorantia: sequitur ipsa revelatio, Is, inquit, qui misit me ut baptizarem aqua, hoc est, Pater à quo missus sum, ut exercerem Baptismi externum ministerium ad manifestandum eo quasi symbolo filium Israëli, Pater dixit mihi, super quem videris Spiritum descendentem & manentem super eum, Hoc quasi indicio & certo signo cognosce eum, qui baptizat Spiritu Sancto. Optimè ista inter se consentiunt: Nam super quem Spiritus requiescit, oportet eum baptizare Spiritu, hoc est, in Baptismo efficacem esse per Spiritum sanctum. Sed videamus quid sit illud Christum baptizare Spiritu Sancto. Christus dicitur Spiritu Sancto baptizare, tum propter extraordinaria illa & miraculosa dona spiritus sui quæ contulit in Pentecoste & in Baptismo illo Apostolorum ipsius, tum quia cum externo illo ministerio Baptismi intus efficax est per Spiritum suum regenerantem, per quem solus Pater & filius agunt in nobis, ut ab iis solis procedit Spiritus Sanctus, ut dictum est superius. Atque hoc modo efficax fuit in Baptismo Iohannis: hoc modo efficax fuit in Baptismo per Apostolos administrato. Nam in effectu regenerationis & remissionis peccatorum discrimen ponere inter Baptismum Iohannis & Apostolorum, summæ insciciæ est, præsertim cum diserte scriptum sit Iohanem prædicasse & administrasse Baptismum respicientia in remissionem peccatorum. Fuit tamen fateor aliquid discriminis inter Iohannis & Apostolorum Baptismum: Iohannes quidem baptizavit in nomen Christi adventientis: Apostoli baptizarunt in nomen Christi præsentis. Ideoque oportuit efficaciem esse Spiritum Christi cum baptismate Apostolorum, quàm cum baptismate Iohannis; id quod vel hinc manifestum est, quia cum extraordinaria dona Spiritus, ac planè miraculosa coniuncta fuerint cum Baptismo Apostolorum, nulla eiusmodi coniuncta legimus cum Baptismo Iohannis aut discipulorum ipsius, ut constat ex sacra historia. Ex his quæ incidisse narrat Iohannes in Baptismum Christi illud perspicimus, quanta cum gloria Christus initiatus sit officio, & vnctus sit in Mediatorem. neque enim vnquam illustrior fuit patefactio trium personarum Patris, Filij, & Spiritus Sancti, quàm fuit hoc ipso tempore: Filius in natura nostra inunctus est, Spiritus Sanctus eum inunxit, Pater voce sua e coelis audita testatus est eum esse filium suum, & eum qui baptizaret spiritu sancto. Sic voluit Pater officium unigeniti filii sui iam primùm initiù honorare: Cui sit omnis honor & gloria. Amen.
units.tr: Certainly Christ had not become fully known to the Baptist before he received that revelation from the Father, that Christ was the Son and would baptize with the Holy Spirit. Hitherto, the cause of the Baptist's ignorance; now follows the revelation itself: "He who sent me to baptize with water," that is, the Father, by whom I was sent to exercise the external ministry of baptism, in order to make Christ manifest to Israel by that sign as it were, "said to me: upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. Take this as a sign and certain token by which to know him." These statements agree perfectly with one another: for upon whom the Spirit rests, he must baptize with the Spirit, that is, be effective in baptism through the Holy Spirit. But let us see what it is for Christ to baptize with the Holy Spirit. Christ is said to baptize with the Holy Spirit partly on account of those extraordinary and miraculous gifts of his Spirit which he bestowed at Pentecost and at the baptism of his apostles, and partly because, along with that outward ministry of baptism, he is inwardly effective through his regenerating Spirit, through whom alone the Father and the Son act in us, as the Holy Spirit proceeds from them alone, as was said above. And in this way he was effective in the baptism of John; in this way he was effective in the baptism administered through the apostles. For to set a difference between the baptism of John and that of the apostles with respect to the effect of regeneration and the remission of sins is the height of ignorance, especially since it is plainly written that John preached and administered baptism looking to the remission of sins. I grant, however, that there was some difference between the baptism of John and that of the apostles: John baptized in the name of the Christ who was to come; the apostles baptized in the name of the Christ who was present. Therefore the Spirit of Christ had to be more effective with the baptism of the apostles than with the baptism of John; and this is manifest even from the fact that, since extraordinary and plainly miraculous gifts of the Spirit were joined with the baptism of the apostles, we read of no such gifts joined with the baptism of John or of his disciples, as is clear from sacred history. From what John relates as having happened at the baptism of Christ we perceive how great was the glory with which Christ was initiated into his office and anointed as Mediator. For never was there a more illustrious manifestation of the three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, than at this very time: the Son was anointed in our nature, the Holy Spirit anointed him, and the Father, by his voice heard from heaven, testified that he is his Son and that he is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. Thus the Father willed to honour the office of his only-begotten Son from its very first beginning: to whom be all honour and glory. Amen.

units.la: Reliqua nunc est conclusio huius concionis, qua Iohannes concludit se vidisse, Ego igitur vidi, & quia vidit ideo testari, Iesum esse filium Dei, Et testor hunc esse. Quo loco vides testimonium Iohannis de filio Dei fundatum esse in visibili praesentia & aspectu ipso. Confirmatus iam ipso sensu & aspectu, cum fiducia & libertate testatur de filio. Sic voluit Christus primos illos testes confirmari rerum coelestium praesenti intuitu, ut qui primi missi erant ad alios confirmandos. Nam his ipsis opus est maximè firma fide, quicunque aliis fidem facere conantur: Ideo Paulus recitat ex Psalmo centesimo decimo sexto, se credere atque ideo locutum esse. Nos qui Apostolis in Ecclesia succeßimus testamur hodierno die de Christo, non quidem vidimus, non audiuimus, non manibus nostris contrectauimus, vt illi, sed tamen revelationem habemus satis claram ex testimonio eorum, qui audiuerunt, qui viderunt, qui manibus contrectauerunt. Habemus etiam illum Spiritum, qui in Scriptura loquitur, vera omnia dicere de filio Dei, &, vt Iohannes loquitur, qui testificatur Spiritum veritatem esse. Quare Christus non deserit nos qui ipsum praedicamus hoc die, aut testimonio certissimo destituit, etsi non offerat se nunc aspectui nostro, vt olim se ad captum Apostolorum suorum demisit. Sed beati sunt, teste Christo, qui non viderunt & crediderunt: cuius beatitudinis Deus in filio suo nos omnes faciat participes. Amen.
units.tr: Now comes the conclusion of this sermon, in which John concludes that he has seen: "I have seen, and so I bear witness that Jesus is the Son of God. And I testify that this is so." Here you see that John's testimony concerning the Son of God is founded on visible presence and on the very sight. Now confirmed by sense and by sight itself, he testifies about the Son with confidence and freedom. So Christ willed that those first witnesses be confirmed by the present sight of heavenly things, so that those who were first sent to confirm others. For those who try to bring faith to others have the greatest need themselves of a firm faith. Therefore Paul quotes from Psalm 116 that he believed and therefore spoke. We who have succeeded the Apostles in the Church bear witness today about Christ. We have not seen, we have not heard, we have not handled with our hands, as they did, but nevertheless we have a revelation clear enough from the testimony of those who heard, who saw, who handled with their hands. We also have that Spirit, who speaks in Scripture, to tell all true things about the Son of God, and, as John puts it, who testifies that the Spirit is truth. Therefore Christ does not desert us who preach him on this day, nor does he deprive us of the most certain testimony, even though he does not now offer himself to our sight, as once he stooped to the grasp of his Apostles. But, as Christ testifies, they are blessed who have not seen and yet have believed: may God make us all partakers of this blessedness in his Son. Amen.

units.la: 35 Postero die stabat Iohannes, & ex discipulis eius duo:
units.tr: 35 On the next day John was standing, and two of his disciples with him:

units.la: 36 Et intuitus Iesum ambulantem, dixit, Ecce agnus ille Dei.
units.tr: 36 And looking at Jesus as he walked, he said, Behold that Lamb of God.

units.la: HActenus duo fuerunt testimonia Baptistæ, sequitur tertium quod perhibuit de Christo præsentibus duobus discipulis. Testimonium hoc perhibitum est iam cum secunda vice Christus ad Iohannem venisset, postquam nimirum iam tentatus esset in deserto. In hoc testimonio tertio, primum habemus tempus quo testatus est Iohannes, deinde occasionem, postremo testimonium ipsum. Tempus est postero die, diem hunc non intelligo immediatè sequentem eum diem quo perhibitum est secundum illud testimonium: verùm diem sub- sequentem aliquem etsi mediatè non proximè. Vbi tamen hoc videmus, Iohannem cùm iam appropinquaret ad extremitatem cursus sui subinde testatum esse de Christo. Et nos quoque quibus concreditum est hoc ministerium quos mundus vellet simul ac semel è medio sublatos, appropinquamus ad finem ministerij nostri, Et Christus cito venturus est nec moram facturus. Ideoque si vnquam ante hoc opus fuit frequenti ac crebro testimonio, profectò nunc maximè in hoc fine sæculorum simul & ministerij nostri, debemus diligenter & sæpe de Christo testari, eúmque quasi digito demonstrare è cælo aduentantem. Sequitur occasio, Stabat Iohannes, & ex discipulis eius duo: & intuitus Iesum ambulantem dixit. Iohannes occasionem hanc oblatam testandi de Christo non prætermisit. Et nos omnem occasionem testandi de Christo debemus auidè arripere, ac quoties sese offert videndum & palpandum cordibus nostris: de nobis omnibus loquor, toties oportet apud alios testari de eo, & eam gratiam cum aliis communicare, ut & alij, si possit fieri, Christum Iesum cognoscant. Imprimis hoc iis incumbit, quibus concreditum est gloriosum hoc Euangelium beati Dei, & occasionem omnem, nō modò se offerentem arripere, sed non offerentem redimere. Imò ex rebus aduersariis & impedimentis occasione captare. Paulus ait, permanebo Ephesi, vsque ad Pentecosten, nam ibi ostium magnum & efficax apertum est mihi, & aduersarii multi. Ecce Paulus captauit occasionem prædicandi Christum ex obstantibus multis aduersariis. Imò denique importunè & cùm nulla est occasio, Christum debemus prædicare; Nam cùm aliis importunum est, no-
units.tr: HHitherto there have been two testimonies of the Baptist; there follows a third, which he gave concerning Christ in the presence of two disciples. This testimony was given when Christ had come to John for the second time, after he had of course already been tempted in the desert. In this third testimony we have first the time at which John testified, then the occasion, and last the testimony itself. The time is "the next day". I do not understand this to be the day immediately following that on which the second testimony was given, but some later day, though not the nearest one. Here we see that John, now approaching the end of his course, kept testifying about Christ. We too, to whom this ministry has been entrusted, whom the world would gladly remove from the midst all at once, are approaching the end of our ministry, and Christ is coming soon and will not delay. Therefore, if ever before there was need of frequent and constant testimony, certainly now, at this end of the ages and of our ministry, we ought diligently and often to testify of Christ, and as it were point him out with the finger, as he comes from heaven. The occasion follows: "John was standing, and two of his disciples; and looking at Jesus walking, he said." John did not let slip the occasion offered him of testifying about Christ. We too ought eagerly to seize every opportunity of testifying about Christ, and as often as it presents itself to be seen and felt by our hearts, I speak of all of us: so often ought we to testify of him among others, and to share that grace with others, so that others too, if it can be done, may know Christ Jesus. This above all falls to those to whom this glorious Gospel of the blessed God has been entrusted, and not only to seize every opportunity that offers itself, but to buy back the opportunity that does not offer itself. Indeed, one should catch opportunity even from adversities and hindrances. Paul says, "I will remain at Ephesus until Pentecost, for a great and effective door has been opened to me there, and there are many adversaries." Behold, Paul seized the opportunity of preaching Christ from the many adversaries who stood in the way. Indeed, finally, we ought to preach Christ even unseasonably and when there is no opportunity. For what is unseasonable to others ought to be seasonable for us.

units.la: bis debet esse opportunū. Paulus dicit Timotheo, Praedica sermonem, insta tempestiue & intempestiue. Sequitur i-
units.tr: Paul says to Timothy, "Preach the word, be urgent in season and out of season." There follows

units.la: psum testimonium, Ecce Agnus ille Dei. Haec verba profecta sunt ex sensu conscientiae conquiescentis in illo Christi sacrificio. Nam Baptista quoque homo peccator fuit, & opus habuit illo sacrificio. Demonstrat igitur Christum non filium Dei gloriosum, non Dominum gloriae, sed victimam immolādam pro peccatis nostris. Id autem facit non citra iustissimam rationem. Nam doctrina de Messia salsissimis & crassissimis opinionibus Pharisaeorum, tanquam tenebris, sepulta erat: Et nemo fuit omnium ferè qui Christum passurū credebant, praesertim mortem tam ignominiosam, nemo ferè fuit qui putaret eum morte sua expiaturum peccata nostra. Sed omnes expectabant nescio quem Messiam, qui restituturus esset perditum regnū Israelis, ipsiúmque maiori potentia & splendore auctururus quàm vnquam antea obtinuerunt: Ideoque maximè necesse fuit admoneri istos, qui communi errore seducti erant de Christi sacrificio.
units.tr: the testimony itself: "Behold that Lamb of God." These words proceed from the feeling of a conscience resting in that sacrifice of Christ. For the Baptist too was a sinful man, and needed that sacrifice. He therefore points out Christ not as the glorious Son of God, not as the Lord of glory, but as the victim to be slain for our sins. He does this not without the most just reason. For the doctrine of the Messiah had been buried, as in darkness, under the most salted and crass opinions of the Pharisees; and almost none of all men who believed that Christ would suffer, especially so shameful a death, and almost none thought that he would make atonement for our sins by his death. But all expected I know not what Messiah, who would restore the lost kingdom of Israel, and would increase it in greater power and splendour than they had ever possessed before. Therefore it was most necessary that those who were led astray by the common error be admonished about the sacrifice of Christ.

units.la: Non minus etiam necessarium est hodierno die, vt Christi sacrificium & mors perpetuò inculcetur. Nam si illi tum ignorabant Christum immolandum, nos oblitī sumus quodammodò eum immolatum & passum esse pro peccatis nostris. Quid enim sibi volunt peccata ista quibus passim abundat haec terra nostra, quid tot adulteria, tot homicidia, tot rapinae, tot sacrilegia, tot peccata denique omnis generis? quid aliud, quaeso, quàm oblitos esse nos Christum pro nobis passum esse? Quod si enim nobis in mentem veniret nos emptos esse semel tam preciosò pretio; An, quaeso, sic venderemus nos ipsi rursus sub peccatum omnis generis? Si recordaremur nos semel ablutos tam pretiosò lauacro sanguinis Dei, An sic rursus iremus contaminatum nos foedis his muti di huius inquinamentis? Paulus dum dissuadet Corinthiis fornicationem, revocat iis in memoriam quòd pretio empti sint: qua quidem re significare voluit, eos iam oblitos esse se aliquando emptos illo pretio. Sed Petrus obliuionem istam diserte expressit. postquam enim certas aliquas virtutes commendauit, subiicit; Cui haec
units.tr: It is no less necessary on this day that the sacrifice and death of Christ be constantly impressed upon us. For if those men then did not know that Christ must be slain, we have in some measure forgotten that he was slain and suffered for our sins. For what do these sins mean, with which this land of ours everywhere abounds, what do so many adulteries, so many murders, so many robberies, so many sacrileges, in short so many sins of every kind mean? What else, I ask, than that we have forgotten that Christ suffered for us? For if it came into our minds that we were bought once at so precious a price, would we, I ask, sell ourselves again under sin of every kind? If we remembered that we had once been washed with so precious a laver of God's blood, would we again go and defile ourselves with these foul pollutions of the world? When Paul dissuades the Corinthians from fornication, he reminds them that they were bought with a price; by which indeed he meant to signify that they had now forgotten that they were once bought with that price. But Peter expressly named this forgetfulness. For after he had commended certain virtues, he adds, To whom these things

units.la: 2. Pet. 1.9. hæc non adsunt, is cæcus est, nihil procul cernens, oblitus sese à veteribus peccatis suis purgatum fuisse. Volo enim de hoc omnes certiores fieri, scortationes, homicidia, cæteraque id genus peccata eorum, qui semel abluti sunt Christi sanguine, non ideo duntaxat peccata esse quòd pugnentex diametro cum expressa Dei lege, sed vel hac re maximè quòd committa sint quasi in ludibrium sanguinis Christi, & profecta ex obliuione mortis illius, qua semel sunt redempti. Quod si ita sit, & illud rursus nobis tenendum est, non ideo tantùm dolendum nobis esse quòd violatum sit à nobis Dei mandatum aliquod, verùm ideo maximè quod obliti simus nos semel purgatos illo sanguine, & contempserimus pretium redemptionis nostræ longè gloriosissimum. Quo autem deducamur facilius ad hanc resipiscentiæ formam, atque etiam cognoscamus magnitudinem peccati nostri, in id nobis in tota vita, incumbendum est, vt intelligamus quantum sit illud pretium redemptionis nostræ, æstimemúsque pro dignitate, quantum per nos fieri potest, sanguinem illum noui testamenti.
units.tr: 2 Pet. 1.9. are not present, he is blind, seeing nothing afar off, having forgotten that he was purged from his former sins. For I want everyone to be informed of this: fornications, murders, and other sins of that kind committed by those who have once been washed in the blood of Christ are sins not only because they clash directly with the express law of God, but chiefly for this reason, that they are committed as if in mockery of the blood of Christ, and proceed from forgetting that death by which they were once redeemed. If this is so, then we must hold on to this again: we ought to grieve not merely because some command of God has been violated by us, but chiefly because we have forgotten that we were once purged by that blood, and have despised the price of our redemption, which is by far the most glorious. And so that we may be led more easily to this form of repentance, and also recognise the greatness of our sin, we ought to devote ourselves throughout our whole life to understanding how great that price of our redemption is, and to valuing, as far as we can, that blood of the new covenant according to its worth.

units.la: 37 Audierunt autem eum duo illi discipuli loquentem, & sequuti sunt Iesum.
units.tr: The two disciples heard him speaking and followed Jesus.

units.la: 38 Conuersus vero Iesus, & conspicatus eos sequentes se, dixit eis,
units.tr: Jesus turned round, saw them following him, and said to them,

units.la: 39 Quid quæritis? Illi verò dixerunt ei, Rabbi (quod dicitur, si interpreteris, præceptor) vbi maris?
units.tr: What are you looking for? They said to him, "Rabbi" (which means, when translated, teacher), "where are you staying?"

units.la: 40 Dicit eis, Venite & videte. Venerunt, viderúntque vbi moraretur: & apud eum manserunt diem illum. Hora enim erat quasi decima.
units.tr: He said to them, "Come and see." They came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day. For it was about the tenth hour.

units.la: Actenus fuerunt tria testimonia Iohannis Baptistæ de Christo, à quibus vltimo loco descriptus est Dei filius. Atque in vniuersum de descriptione ... Sequitur altera pars capitis de vocatione certorum aliquot discipulorum ad agnitionem Christi, ac primùm de vocatione duorum, qui Baptistæ prius discipuli fuerunt, nempe Andreæ & alterius cuius nomen expressum ...
units.tr: So far there have been three testimonies of John the Baptist about Christ, and the last of them describes the Son of God. In general, concerning the description... There follows the second part of the chapter, on the calling of certain disciples to the knowledge of Christ, and first of the calling of two who had earlier been disciples of the Baptist, namely Andrew and another whose name is given...

units.la: de vocatio non habetur. Qua in vocatione hæc capita distinguimus: Primùm, audito hoc Baptistæ testimonio duo illi discipuli sequuntur Christum. 2. Christus conuersus eos est conspicatus. 3. Sermones cum iis confert. 4. Inuitati à Christo eunt & vident quo loco Christus habiter: manéntque apud eum die illo. Vt redeamus igitur, narrat primùm Euangelista audisse duos illos discipulos loquentem & testantem de Christo Iohannem, & secutos esse eum. Ex hac Christi prædicatione per Spiritum Sanctum in cordibus eorum excitatum est initiū quoddam fidei quo Christum sic à Iohanne demonstratum apprehenderunt, etiamque sunt insequuti. Nam haud dubiè animus discipulorum coepit eū persequi & ad ipsum applicari mirificè. Hoc igitur exemplo discimus quàm efficax sit prædicatio Christi, imò verò vel verbum vnum aut alterum de Christo ipsiúsque cruce, quàm efficax, inquam, sit in immutandis hominum cordibus. Non est profectò alius sermo quis, ab hoc sermone crucis Christi efficax ad hoc, vt ex lapideo corde, cor carneum, ex infideli fidele fiat. Concionare, si lubet, de rebus præclarè gestis ab omnibus quotquot vnquam fuerunt regibus & imperatoribus, déque eorum virtute & gloria, ista delectatione quadā ad tempus tenebunt quidem animos hominum, sed non renouabunt. Loquere autem de homine crucifixo, re in speciem ignominiosa & stulta; Tum sermo crucis qui stultitia est iis qui pereunt, Dei sapientia & potentia futura est iis qui seruantur. Imò vt prophana ista mittamus, inculca, si lubet, Dei ipsius mandata: Legis, inquit Paulus, impotentia nihil potest in carne. Quod lex non potest, vitio carnis nostræ, sermo crucis id potest. Quæ causa est tantæ huius efficaciæ? Dominus ille, de quo sermo est, Spiritus est, qui liberat cor nostrum, adeò vt si conuertatur ad eum, tollatur necessariò hoc velamen corruptionis, quod vsque adeò cordi adhæret, vt si intueamur in illam gloriam ipsius, quæ relucet in Euangelio tanquam in speculo quodam, in eandem imaginem transformari nos oportet ex gloria in gloriam.
units.tr: ...of the calling is not recorded. In this calling we distinguish the following points. First, on hearing this testimony of the Baptist, the two disciples follow Christ. Second, Christ turns and sees them. Third, he talks with them. Fourth, invited by Christ, they go and see where Christ lives, and they remain with him that day. To return, then: the Evangelist first relates that those two disciples heard John speaking and bearing witness of Christ, and that they followed him. From this preaching of Christ, the Holy Spirit stirred in their hearts a certain beginning of faith, by which they grasped Christ as John had shown him, and so they followed him. For without doubt the disciples' minds began wonderfully to pursue him and to attach themselves to him. From this example, then, we learn how effective the preaching of Christ is, indeed how effective even one or two words about Christ and his cross are in changing people's hearts. Assuredly there is no other message that, apart from this message of the cross of Christ, can turn a stony heart into a heart of flesh, and an unbeliever into a believer. Preach, if you like, about the splendid deeds of all the kings and emperors who have ever lived, and about their valour and glory; such things will hold people's minds for a time with a certain pleasure, but they will not renew them. But speak of the crucified man, a thing in appearance shameful and foolish, and then "the word of the cross, which is foolishness to those who perish, will be the power and wisdom of God to those who are being saved." Indeed, to set aside these secular matters, press home, if you like, the commands of God himself. "What the law could not do," says Paul, "being weak through the flesh, [it could not do]." What the law cannot do, because of the weakness of our flesh, the word of the cross can do. What is the cause of such great effectiveness? That Lord of whom the message speaks is the Spirit, who frees our heart, so that when it turns to him, this veil of corruption, which so clings to the heart, must necessarily be removed; so that if we gaze upon his glory, which shines forth in the Gospel as in a mirror, we are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory.

units.la: Hactenus fuit prima pars doctrinæ vocationis huius: sequitur secunda. Conuersus Iesus ac speculatus eos sequentes se,dixit.Etsi quidem primùm visus sit Iesus se subducere ab iis, tamen post paulò conuersus est ad eos. Christus videtur se subducere à nobis dum eum insequimur,nó-que deserere, quamquàm reipsa nunquam ita se subducat quin trahat nos post se: neque enim possemus eum sequi, nisi ipse nos traheret ad se. Paulus dicit se prosequi illam metam vitæ æternæ,causam addit,inquiens, Cuius etiam rei causa apprehensus sum à Christo Iesu. Nisi e-nim ipseprior nos apprehendat,immisso in nos spiritu suo sancto tanquam manu aliqua apprehendente, pro-secto nos nunquam eum apprehenderemus.Sed redeo, Christus videtur quidem nonnunquam se subducere à nobis sequentibus ipsum,sed tandem sistit gressum, sequeque ad nos conuertit.Ex quo sequitur longè iucundissima communicatio inter peccatorem & redemptorem suum.Nihil enim suauius est peccatori,qui sentit quidè onus peccati sui, quàm sermones conferre cum eo qui potest ipsum tanto onere leuare.
units.tr: So far was the first part of the teaching on this calling; the second follows. "Jesus turned and saw them following him, and said..." Although at first Jesus seemed to withdraw from them, yet after a little he turned back to them. Christ seems to withdraw from us while we pursue him, and not to abandon us, although in fact he never so withdraws that he does not draw us after him; for we could not follow him unless he himself drew us to himself. Paul says that he presses on toward that goal of eternal life, and he adds the reason, saying, "for which also I was apprehended by Christ Jesus." For unless he first apprehended us, by sending his Holy Spirit upon us as if by some hand laying hold of us, we would never apprehend him. But to return: Christ indeed sometimes seems to withdraw from us who follow him, but at last he halts his step and turns back to us. From this follows a most delightful communication between the sinner and his Redeemer. For nothing is sweeter to a sinner, who feels the burden of his sin, than to converse with one who can relieve him of such a load.

units.la: Sed videamus dialogismum hunc & communicatio-nem inter Christum & duos illos Baptistæ discipulos. Christus non expectat dum ipsi priores loquantur,sed ipse prior ad loquendum eos invitat. Quid quæritis? inquit, Christus conuersus ad nos prior nos alloquitur ac interrogat quid quæramus,qua re nobis opus sit,ea re nimirum alliciens nos ad hoc, vt eo vtamur familiariter ipsíque exponamus omnem inopiam nostram,ac necessitatem nostram. Nam etsi Christus nunc in cœlo gloriosus sedeat ad dextram patris sui, tamen non minus familiariter nobiscum loquitur hodierno die per verbum suum scriptum,& per Spiritum suum Sanctum,qui multò efficacior nunc est quàm fuit olim ante exhibitionem & glorificationem ipsius: Non minùs,inquam, familiariter nobiscum loquitur, quàm tum olim cùm inter Iudæos commoraretur,cùm loquutus est discipulis suis. Neque enim indigemus aliis Mediatoribus vel Angelis, vel Sanctis mortuis,qui intercedant inter nos & eruatorem nostrum Iesum. Quasi verò quisquam sit ex omnibus vel beatis Angelis vel Sanctis demortuis quitam afficiatur sensu infirmitatum nostrarum,quàm ipsum caput nostrum Iesus Christus.Neque profecto fi-
units.tr: But let us look at this dialogue and communication between Christ and the two disciples of the Baptist. Christ does not wait for them to speak first, but he himself invites them to speak first. "What are you looking for?" says Christ, turning to us and first addressing us, and asking what we seek, what we need; drawing us, that is, by this very question to make use of him familiarly and to lay open all our want and our necessity. For although Christ now sits gloriously in heaven at the right hand of his Father, yet he speaks with us no less familiarly today through his written word and through his Holy Spirit, who is now far more effective than he was of old before his manifestation and glorification. He speaks with us no less familiarly, I say, than when he dwelt among the Jews and spoke to his disciples. For we have no need of other mediators, whether angels or dead saints, to intercede between us and our Saviour Jesus. As though there were any one of all the blessed angels or the dead saints who is touched by a feeling of our infirmities as our Head, Jesus Christ, is. Certainly not...

units.la: Fidei scb-des ipsa alio nos deducit, quam ad ipsum Christum Mediatorem immediate:Quod vel ex hoc exemplo discipulorum istorum patet.Accensa fide in Christum per praedicationem Iohannis, non iam Iohannem rogant discipuli, ut se manu velit ducere ad Christum hominem sibi alioqui ignotum: sed relicto Iohanne statim eum sequuntur ipsi tua sponte:Ut & mulier illa sanguinis profluuio laborans neglectis discipulis qui inter ipsam & Christum medio loco interiecti erant recta ad ipsum Christum ferebatur. Nunquam dixerim istos fide in Christum praeditos esse qui non recta Christum ipsum adeunt. Sed eos mittamus & permittamus suae caecitati, si minus velint in tam clara etiam caeli luce quidquam videre.
units.tr: Faith itself, rightly exercised, leads us to no other than to Christ himself as Mediator, immediately. This is clear even from the example of those disciples. Once their faith in Christ had been kindled through the preaching of John, the disciples no longer ask John to lead them by the hand to Christ, a man otherwise unknown to them; rather, leaving John behind, they follow Christ of their own accord at once. So too the woman suffering from a flow of blood, passing by the disciples who had been placed as intermediaries between her and Christ, went straight to Christ himself. I would never say that those who are endowed with faith in Christ are those who do not come directly to Christ himself. But let us leave them, and let us leave them to their blindness, if they are unwilling to see anything even in such clear daylight.

units.la: Quaerenti Christo respondent discipuli, Rabbi, quod dicitur (si interpreteris,) Magister, Vbi moraris? Rabbi vel Rab significat excellentem aliquem, sive is excellat generis nobilitate, sive virtute & rebus gestis, sive denique doctrina & rerum cognitione:Hoc autem loco, ut in Evangeliis passim in postremo hoc significato accipitur, & Latine redditur per nomen Magistri vel Doctoris, vox ipsa ex etymo suo sonat eum qui sit instar multorum, vel unum qui propter excellentiam aequet multos.Hoc nomen ab Esaia iam olim tributum est Christo, & quidem non immerito: Nam Christus admirabilis ille est, Consiliarius ille, Princeps pacis, Pater aeternitatis, & reliqua quae tribuuntur ipsi. Christus ipse appellationem hanc tanquam sibi propriam vendicat, reprehensa ambitione Pharisaeorum, qui volebant vocari ab hominibus Rabbi, Rabbi, & admonitis discipulis ne ambiant illud nomen, Vnus enim, inquit, Doctor vester est, nempe Christus, omnes autem vos fratres estis. Sed de nomine hactenus, Rabbi, inquiunt, vbi moraris?Hoc est, vbinam locorum est hospitium vel diuersorium tuum? Quaerunt autem de hospitio ipsius, animo eum deducendi, idque eo fine, ut itineris comites aliquid ex ipso discerret. Neque enim animus erat, ut apparet ex sequentibus, vna cum ipso pernoctare. Quasi vero Christum sequuti sint magis propter hospitium quam propter ipsum met Christum discipuli. Itaque isti duo leui aliqua cognitione Christi à Magisto suo imbuti inflammantur ad proce- dendum vlterius in cognitione Christi semel inchoata. Sic rudimenta religionis Christianæ vel leuiter degu-stata à nobis, debent nos excitare ad progressum indies maiorem faciendum, tantisper dum ad perfectionem perueniamus. Nam Author ad Hebræos illud non ob-scurè significat, quòd si non fiat progressus aliquis, oportere nos retrorsum ferri ac in deterius vergere. Peccat autem maximè horribiliter qui gustum illum primum Christi ex elementis illis primis perceptum post-eâ amittit: quod peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum vocât.
units.tr: When Christ asks, the disciples answer, "Rabbi (which, translated, means Teacher), where are you staying?" "Rabbi," or "Rab," signifies someone excellent, whether he excels in noble birth, or in virtue and deeds, or finally in learning and knowledge of things. In this place, however, as often in the Gospels, it is taken in the last of these senses, and in Latin is rendered by the name of Master or Doctor; the word itself by its etymology suggests one who is equal to many, or one who by his excellence matches many. This name was already long ago given to Christ by Isaiah, and not undeservedly: for Christ is that "Wonderful, Counsellor, Prince of Peace, Everlasting Father," and the other things that are attributed to him. Christ himself claims this title as his own, rebuking the ambition of the Pharisees, who wished to be called Rabbi, Rabbi, by men; and when he had warned his disciples not to seek that name, he said, "For one is your Teacher," namely Christ, "and you are all brothers." But enough about the name. "Rabbi," they say, "where are you staying?" That is, in what place is your lodging or inn? They ask about his lodging with the intention of accompanying him, and with the aim of learning something from him as companions on the journey. For it was not their intention, as appears from what follows, to spend the night with him. As if the disciples followed Christ more for the sake of his lodging than for Christ himself! And so these two, instructed by their Master in some slight knowledge of Christ, are kindled to proceed further in the knowledge of Christ once begun. Thus the rudiments of the Christian religion, even if we have only lightly tasted them, ought to stir us to make greater progress day by day, until we come to perfection. For the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews clearly indicates that unless some progress is made, we must be carried backwards and slide into worse things. Moreover, he sins most dreadfully who, after having received that first taste of Christ from those first elements, then loses it; this sin he calls a sin against the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Rursus hoc notandum est, non contenti sunt discipuli isti duo, euanido aliquo aspectu, quin eum ad hospitiū vsque deducūt ac comitantur, auiditate scilicet quadam fruendi magis magisque ipsius præsentia & colloquio. Ne sufficiat itaque nobis si Christum semel tantùm & quasi per transennam intueamur, sed necesse est eum propius inspiciamus, comitemur eum ad hospitium vsque. Neque enim vnquam oportet capi satietate aspe-ctus ipsius longè suauissimi, ne fide quidem ipsa, per quam incedimus in hac vita, & qua Christum quasi e-minus & e longinquo prospicimus, contenti esse debe-mus: & tamen in hac præsenti vita quid fide pretiosius habemus? Stercora sunt omnia Paulo, si comparetur cū eminentia illa cognitionis Christi, hoc est, fide in Christum: sed aspectus Christi semper nobis expetendus est. Confidimus, inquit Paulus, sed probamus potius migrare è corpore, & ad Dominum ire habitatum. Hoc eò diligentiùs obseruo, quòd videam non paucos esse qui volunt videri libenter audire Christum sibi demonstrari quasi eminus, ad hoc vt aliquo numero & loco inter Christianos videantur esse: sic tamen sunt affixi huic mundo vt nunquam velint inde migrare, & ire ad Dominum habitatum, vt ipsius præsentia & aspectu suauissimo in perpetuum fruantur, quod profectò argumento est, eos nunquam Christum inspectasse ne eminus quidem: hoc est peueram fidem. Nam vera fides habet perpetuò coniunctum desiderium aliquod migrandi ex hoc corpore & habitandi cum Domino.
units.tr: Again, it should be noted that these two disciples were not satisfied, once Christ had vanished from sight, but they followed him all the way to his lodging, out of a certain eagerness to enjoy his presence and conversation more and more. So it is not enough for us to look at Christ once, as it were in passing. We must look at him more closely and accompany him all the way to his lodging. We ought never to be satiated with the sight of him, which is by far the sweetest, and we must not be content even with faith itself, by which we walk in this life and by which we see Christ as if from afar and at a distance. And yet, in this present life, what do we have more precious than faith? All things are dung to Paul when compared with that surpassing knowledge of Christ, that is, faith in Christ. But the sight of Christ must always be what we desire. We are confident, says Paul, but we would rather depart from the body and go home to the Lord. I observe this more carefully because I see that there are not a few who gladly want to be seen hearing that Christ is shown to them as if from afar, so that they may appear to be among Christians in some number and place. Yet they are so fixed to this world that they never want to depart from it and go home to the Lord, to enjoy his presence and his most sweet sight forever. This is certainly proof that they have never looked upon Christ, not even from afar. That is a false faith. For true faith always has a longing to depart from this body and dwell with the Lord joined to it.

units.la: Hactenus quæsiuerunt discipuli isti duo, de Christi hospitio: Nunc respondet Christus, Venite & videte. Quid hac inuitatione suauius? Non sic inuitauit scribam illum, qui cum dixisset, sequar te, Magister, quocunque abieris: Respondet Dominus, Vulpes lustra habent, & volucres caeli nidos, sed filius hominis non habet vbi caput reclinet. Negauit Scribae habere se hospitium aliquod in terris in quo coquiescerent, nempe quia ille Christum voluit sequi non propter Christum, sed propter hospitium. At vero isti de hospitio Christi quaerebant, non hospitij causa, sed Christi ipsius, vt eo ipsum deducentes liberius frueren-tur in itinere suauissimis ipsius sermonibus. Qui inter-rogabunt de hospitio Christi ipsius Christi causa, Christus eos benignissimè inuitabit, venientque & videbunt multas mansiones in domo Patris ipsius: Qui vero interrogabunt de Christo, non causa ipsius Christi, sed tranquillitatis, & gloriae huius mundi causa, Christus negabit illis sibi hospitium esse in terris quo diuertat, vt absterreantur ab eo sequendo, quibus ex animo sequi Christum nunquam propositum fuit.
units.tr: Up to this point those two disciples have asked about Christ's lodging. Now Christ answers: Come and see. What could be sweeter than this invitation? He did not invite in this way the scribe who, when he had said, I will follow you, Teacher, wherever you go, was answered by the Lord: Foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head. He told the scribe that he had no lodging on earth in which to rest, namely because that man wanted to follow Christ not for Christ's sake but for the sake of lodging. But these men asked about Christ's lodging not for the sake of the lodging, but for Christ himself, so that by escorting him they might enjoy his most sweet words more freely on the way. Those who ask about Christ's lodging for Christ's own sake will be most kindly invited by Christ, and they will come and see many dwellings in the house of his Father. But those who ask about Christ, not for his own sake, but for the sake of peace and the glory of this world, Christ will deny that he has a place on earth where he may lodge, so that they may be frightened off from following him, since it was never in their heart to follow Christ.

units.la: Reliqua nunc est vltima pars doctrinae vocationis huius duorum discipulorum. Venerunt & viderunt ac permanserunt cum eo toto die illo. Ratio adiecta est, hora enim erat, quasi decima. Hoc est, instabat noctis tempus, quia duae tantum horae ad occasum vsque solis restabant. Nam Iudaei dies tam aestiuos quam hyemales distribuerunt in duodecim horas quas numerarunt inde ab ortu solis, ad occasum vsque. Sed vt ad rem reuertar, significat his verbis diem inclinasse sic, vt per breue diei quod superat spatium non licuerit eis redire domum suam ad pernoctandum. Vnde illud discere licet, non curae fuisse istis hospitium in Christo deducedo, adeo abrepti erant desiderio audiendi & discendi aliquid ex ipso, hospitium tamen nacti sunt. Qui vt Christum sequantur fugiunt mundum, & quae in mundo sunt, Christus prouidebit ne his inundanis quantum necesse est, quātunque satis est, destituantur. Quaerite primum regnum caelorum & omnia alia adijcientur vobis. Sed homines Christi sequuturi, primum omnium de eo cogitant an cum Christo diuitias, honores, & omnium rerum affluentiam habituri sunt: haec cum Christo nacti eum sequuntur. Si haec deficiunt, vel non sequun-
units.tr: Now comes the last part of the teaching on the calling of these two disciples: They came and saw, and they stayed with him that whole day. A reason is added: for it was about the tenth hour. That is, the time of night was approaching, since only two hours remained before sunset. For the Jews divided both summer and winter days into twelve hours, which they counted from sunrise to sunset. But to return to the point: by these words he signifies that the day had declined in such a way that, with the brief part of the day that remained, they were not permitted to return home for the night. From this we may learn that these men were not concerned about finding lodging when they escorted Christ, so carried away were they by the desire to hear and learn something from him; yet they did find lodging. Those who follow Christ flee the world and the things that are in the world. Christ will see to it that they are not left without these earthly things as far as is necessary and sufficient. Seek first the kingdom of heaven, and all other things will be added to you. But men who are about to follow Christ think first of all about whether they will have riches, honours and an abundance of all things along with Christ. Having found these things with Christ, they follow him. If these things fail, or they do not follow

units.la: {6} Discipuli Christi comitantur, & cum eo permanent. sequuntur, vel postquam ingressi sunt iter, ab incepto desistunt. In causa est quòd mundus nunquam huc adduci possit vt putet solum Christum lucrum esse. Christus & in vita & in morte mihi lucrum est, inquit Paulus. Beatus est, qui sic eum ante oculos habeat vt mortem, vitam, cæteraque omnia despectui habeat.
units.tr: {6} Christ's disciples accompany him and remain with him, or, once they have set out on the journey, they give up what they began. The cause is that the world can never be brought to think that Christ alone is gain. Christ is gain to me both in life and in death, says Paul. Blessed is the one who keeps him before his eyes in such a way that he holds death, life and all other things in contempt.

units.la: 41 Erat Andreas frater Simonis Petri, vnus ex duobus, qui audierant illa ex Iohanne, & sequutifuerant eum:
units.tr: 41 Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who had heard these things from John and had followed him.

units.la: 42 Invenit hic prior fratrem suum Simonem, & dixit ei, Invenimus Messiam illum, quod est, si interpreteris, Christus ille.
units.tr: 42 He first found his brother Simon and said to him, We have found the Messiah, which, if you interpret it, is Christ.

units.la: 43 Et adduxit eum ad Iesum. Intuitus autem eum Iesus dixit, Tu es Simon, filius Iona: tu vocaberis Cephas, quod est si interpreteris, Petra.
units.tr: 43 And he brought him to Jesus. And Jesus, looking at him, said, You are Simon, son of Jonah; you shall be called Cephas, which, if you interpret it, is Peter.

units.la: SEquitur vocatio siue conuersio Petri: non enim hic agitur de speciali vocatione ad Apostolatum, sed de prima conuersione istorum hominum ad fidem Iesu Christi. Quia autem Deus vtitur Andrea tanquam ministro vocationis Petri, breuis itaque est præfatio de Andrea, tum sequitur vocatio Petri, cōstans primo ministerio Andreæ, deinde verbis ipsius Christi. Præfatio de Andrea hæc est: Andreas frater Simonis Petri erat vnus ex duobus illis qui ex Iohanne audierant, nempe connonem illam de Christo, Ecce Agnus Dei supra, & qui secutus est Christum domum vsque, vbi & cum eo pernoctauit, ex eóque nonnulla prout tempus ferebat didicit: Præfatio hæc valde accommoda est ad ministerium sequens. Narratur enim de Andrea quòd ipse prius audierit ex Iohanne de Christo, quòd ipse prius secutus sit Christum, & ex ipsius ore aliquid exceperit quàm ministerium hoc in vocando fratre suo obierit Simonem Petrum vocet. Oportet enim eos qui alios vocant, ipsi priores vocati sint, & eos qui alios Christum sequi iubent, ipsi priores Christum sequuti sint. Nam qui non degustauit ipse prior quàm suauis sit Dominus, nunquā futurus est aliis aptus minister suauitatis illius. Quia, inquit Paulus, habemus eundem Spiritum fidei, secundum illud 2 Cor. 4. 13.
units.tr: Next comes the calling, or conversion, of Peter. For this is not about a special calling to the apostleship, but about the first conversion of these men to faith in Jesus Christ. Since God uses Andrew as the minister of Peter's calling, the account of Andrew is brief. Then follows Peter's calling, which consists first of Andrew's ministry and then of Christ's own words. The account of Andrew is this: Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of those two who had heard from John, namely that saying about Christ, Behold the Lamb of God above, and who followed Christ to his house, where he also spent the night with him, and learned some things from him as the time allowed. This account fits the following ministry very well. For it is told of Andrew that he himself first heard about Christ from John, that he himself first followed Christ and received something from his own mouth, before he, in carrying out this ministry, calls his brother Simon Peter. For those who call others must themselves have been called first, and those who bid others follow Christ must themselves have followed Christ first. For he who has not himself first tasted how sweet the Lord is will never be a fit minister of that sweetness for others. Because, says Paul, we have the same spirit of faith, according to what is written in 2 Cor. 4. 13.

units.la: Petri vocatio seu coniuersio ad Christum.
units.tr: The calling, or conversion, of Peter to Christ.

units.la: Andreas huius gratiæ instrumentum externum.
units.tr: Andrew, the external instrument of this grace.

units.la: Idonea gratiæ Dei instrumenta. quod scriptum est Credidi & ideo loquutus sum: Nos quoque credimus, quamobrem etiam loquimur: scientes fore, ut qui excitauit Dominum Iesum nos quoque per Iesum excitet & sistat vobiscum, Esaias agens de vocatione gentium, In postremis, inquit, diebus erit ut eant populi multi dicentes, venite ut ascendamus in montem Iehoua, in domum Dei Iahakabi, ut doceat nos de viis suis. Verba notanda sunt: Ut eant, inquit: Ergo euntes ipsi alios vocabunt. ascendamus, inquit, ergo & ipsi vnà ascensuri sunt: Ut doceat nos, inquit, Ergo & ipsi vnà docebuntur. Frustra legit, frustra scribit, frustra praedicat aliis, qui non ipse particeps fit laborum suorum. Cursorem agit, ut cum Paulo loquar, qui currit in incertum: Pugilem agit qui caedit aerem. Ideo Paulus id imprimis operam dedit, ut ipse particeps fieret Euangelij, cuius praeco aliis erat. Contundo, inquit, corpus meum, & in seruitutem redigo, ne quo modo cum aliis praedicarim, ipse reprobus fiam. Alliduus erat in mortificando vetere illo homine, ad hoc vt particeps fieret sui Euangelij. Dominus det nobis vt aedificando alios, aedificemus simul & cor nostrum ipsorum.
units.tr: Suitable instruments of God's grace. As it is written, I believed, and therefore I have spoken: we also believe, and therefore we also speak, knowing that he who raised up the Lord Jesus will raise us also through Jesus and will present us with you. Isaiah, speaking of the calling of the Gentiles, says: In the last days it will come about that many peoples will go, saying, Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob, that he may teach us his ways. The words are to be noted. Let them go, he says: therefore those who go will themselves call others. Let us go up, he says: therefore they themselves will go up together. That he may teach us, he says: therefore they themselves will be taught together. In vain does a man read, in vain write, in vain preach to others, if he himself does not share in his own labours. He is like a runner, to speak with Paul, who runs without a goal; he is like a boxer who beats the air. So Paul above all took pains that he himself might become a partaker of the gospel, of which he was a herald to others. I beat my body, says he, and bring it into subjection, lest somehow, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected. He was constant in putting to death that old man, so that he might become a partaker of his own gospel. May the Lord grant us that, in building up others, we may at the same time build up our own hearts.

units.la: Deinde est quod hic obseruemus. Andreas ipse sequutus Christum, apprehensa quasi manu fratris sui eum ad Christum adducit: Vocati debemus alios vocare ad Christum. Nam illud est ingenium eorum qui credunt, vt lucem illam in corde accensam non intra se contineant, sed huc illuc eam dispergant. Andreas scintillam tantum lucis aliquam tum primum recepit, fecit tamen vt ea, quantulacunque erat, irradiaret fratrem suum. Vae igitur socordiae nostrae, qui magis illuminati quàm tum Andreas, lucis tamen nostrae alios participes non faciimus. Duae sunt notae hominis verè Christiani: prior est desiderium proficiendi in fide: posterior desiderium ducendi alios ad fidem. Author epistola ad Hebraeos postquam hortarus est ad fidem subiungit, Obseruemus alij alios, vt nos acuamus ad charitatem & bona opera, non deferentes mutuam nostri aggregationem, sicut mos est quibusdam; sed adhortantes alij alios, idque eò magis, quòd videtis diem illum appropinquare. Subiicit deinde terribilem fore illum diem iis qui haec non fecerint. Vae iis, qui cùm ipsi cognoscant Christum, aliquo certè modo ipsum aliis non indiindicarint. Quanto magis non effugient illi, qui vocationem aliorum impediunt: Sacrilegi isti, qui bonis ecclesiæ omnibus direpris tot animas quantum in se est fame cœlestis illius cibi enecant & eunt perditum.
units.tr: Next, we should observe the following. Andrew himself, having followed Christ, takes hold of his brother as if by the hand and brings him to Christ. Those who have been called ought to call others to Christ. For it is the nature of believers not to keep the light kindled in their hearts to themselves, but to spread it abroad. Andrew had then received only a small spark of light, yet he made it shine on his brother, however small it was. Woe, then, to our sloth, since we are more enlightened than Andrew was, yet we do not make others sharers in our light. There are two marks of a man who is truly Christian: the first is the desire to make progress in faith; the second is the desire to lead others to faith. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, after exhorting to faith, adds: Let us consider one another, to stir up one another to love and good works, not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the day approaching. He then goes on to say that the day will be terrible for those who have not done this. Woe to those who, although they themselves know Christ, nonetheless in some way do not point him out to others. How much less will those escape who hinder the calling of others! Those sacrilegious men, who plunder all the goods of the Church, and, as far as they are able, starve so many souls of that heavenly food, and go to perdition.

units.la: Postremo videmus hoc loco Petrum illum qui Andrea fratre fide & zelo postea, ut ex Euangelio intelligi potest, (superior cuasit, per Andream tamen mediocriter imbutum Christi cognitione ad Christum vocatum. Deus eos qui euadunt excellentissima Ecclesiæ lumina solet vocare primum per eos qui mediocribus duntaxat donis sunt præditi, & vocatos etiam confirmat per mediocres homines. Quare istos etiam mediocres excellentissimi quique audiant de Christo loquentes. Nam illud superbiæ est non venire ad Christum vocantem nos propter ministri vilitatem. Audiamus igitur etiam in speciem viles: præsertim cum hoc sciamus, ministros Euangelij fere esse homines non potentes, non sapientes secundum carnem, non nobiles; sed pauperes, insipientes, ignobiles, ut ne glorietur vlla caro coram eo, sed qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur.
units.tr: Finally, in this place we see Peter, who afterwards (as can be understood from the Gospel) surpassed his brother Andrew in faith and zeal, being called to Christ through Andrew, who had been moderately instructed in the knowledge of Christ. God usually calls the most excellent lights of the Church first through those who are endowed only with mediocre gifts, and confirms those who have been called also through ordinary men. Therefore let the most excellent hear even these ordinary men speaking about Christ. For it is pride not to come to Christ calling us because of the lowliness of the minister. Let us then listen even to those who seem lowly, especially since we know that the ministers of the Gospel are for the most part men who are not powerful, not wise according to the flesh, not noble, but poor, foolish, and ignoble, so that no flesh may glory before him, but let him who glories glory in the Lord.

units.la: Hactenus præfatio fuit: sequitur vocatio Petri, cōstat autem primum ministerio Andreæ: deinde vocatione efficaci ipsius Christi: nam Deus is est proprie, qui vocat. Ministerium Andreæ constat his partibus. Prior inuenit fratrem suum Simonem. 1. Inuento dicit, Inueni mus Messiam. 3. deduxit eum ad Christum, Quas partes sigillatim examinemus. Prima ministerii Andreæ pars est his verbis, inuenit prior Simonem fratrem: inuenit, inquit, prior, hoc est, cum Petrus prior eum non quæsiuisset, sed contra Andreas quæsiuisset Petrū & incidisset in ipsum præter ipsius expectationem. Nota igitur vocatio Dei est inexpectata, & totum ministerium eius nobis nihil tale cogitantibus cōtigit. Inuentus sum, inquit Dominus, ab iis qui me non quærebant, conspicuus factus sum iis qui de me non interrogabant. Ita Deus solet præter & contra expectationem nostram præuenire nos gratia sua, ut in solum omnis gloria ad ipsum pertineat. Sed quæstio est, annos cum præuenimur Dei gratia, naturæ aliqua vi ac potestate respondere possumus vocanti: hoc est, assensu gratiæ præuenienti? Efficax enim vocatio habet responsionem redditam à vocato tanquam resonantem Echo, sic vt Deo dicente, Quære me, respondeat vocatus, quæro te, Domine. Tale quid legimus in Davide, Tuum illud, requirite faciem meam, cogitat animus meus: faciem tuam, Iehova, requiro. Quæstio igitur est an vocati Deo respondere quis possit per naturam? Respondent Papistæ, liberum quod vocant arbitrium esse cuiusque, quo vel assentiri, vel non assentiri possit gratiæ præuenienti, siue vocationi Dei. Nos autem negamus huiusmodi libertatem, qua homo non renatus liberè assentiatur vocanti Deo. Sed audiamus ipsum Christum, in hoc ipso Evangelio loquentem postea. Veniet, inquit, tempus, & nunc est, cum mortui audient vocem filij Dei: & qui audierint viuent. Vide, mortuos vocat nos, tum cum vocamur à Dei filio. An homo mortuus potest audire vocantem? multò minus qui mortuus est mortem spiritualem potest audire, nisi ipse Filius Dei qui vocat indat ei vim ac facultatem audiendi, hoc est, vitam Dei, à qua alienatus est, infundat. Vocatio enim hæc nostra nihil est aliud quàm nova creatio: Unde Apostolus ad Ephesios, vocatos appellauit conditos in Christo Iesu. Nam quemadmodum cùm Deus vocauit lucem, eadem opera lucem nõdum existentem creauit: sic cùm Deus nos vocat, eadem opera facit nos idipsum quod vocat, indita animis nostris noua facultate per operationem Spiritus sui sancti: Nam vocat ea quæ non sunt tanquam sint. Hoc est, vno verbo quidvis potest ex nihilo efficere. Qui dixit, inquit Apostolus, vt lux è tenebris splendesceret, is est qui splenduit in cordibus nostris. Quare Deus & vocat nos tum cùm non quærimus eum, & cùm vocat dat potestatem audiendi, vt in solidum omnis gloria vocationis nostræ efficacis ad eum pertineat. Amen.
units.tr: So far this has been the preface; now comes the calling of Peter. It happens first through the ministry of Andrew and then through the effectual calling of Christ himself, for it is God who properly calls. Andrew's ministry consists of these parts. First, he finds his brother Simon. Second, he tells him, "We have found the Messiah." Third, he brings him to Christ. Let us examine these parts one by one. The first part of Andrew's ministry is in these words: "He first found his brother Simon." He "first" found him, that is, Peter had not sought him first, but Andrew sought Peter and came upon him beyond Peter's own expectation. Note, then, that God's calling is unexpected, and his whole ministry comes to us while we are thinking of nothing of the kind. "I was found," says the Lord, "by those who did not seek me; I was made visible to those who did not ask about me." So God is accustomed to anticipate us with his grace beyond and against our expectation, so that all glory belongs to him alone. But the question is this: when we are anticipated by the grace of God, can we by some power or capacity of nature respond to the one calling us, that is, give assent to the preceding grace? For an effectual calling receives from the one called an answering reply, like a resounding echo, so that when God says, "Seek me," the one called answers, "I seek you, Lord." We read something of this sort in David: "Thy word, Seek ye my face, my heart said to me; Thy face, Jehovah, will I seek." The question, then, is whether anyone can by nature answer God when called. The Papists reply that each person has what they call free will, by which he can either assent to or refuse the preceding grace, or the calling of God. We, however, deny such a freedom, by which an unregenerate man freely assents to the calling God. But let us hear Christ himself speaking later in this very Gospel: "The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and they who hear shall live." See, he calls us dead at the time when we are called by the Son of God. Can a dead man hear one who calls him? Much less can one who is dead in spiritual death hear, unless the Son of God himself, who calls, gives him the power and ability to hear, that is, pours into him the life of God from which he is alienated. For this calling of ours is nothing other than a new creation. Hence the Apostle to the Ephesians called those who are called "created in Christ Jesus." For just as when God called light, by the same act he created light that did not yet exist, so when God calls us, by the same act he makes us what he calls, implanting in our souls a new faculty through the working of his Holy Spirit. For he calls those things that are not as though they were. That is, with one word he can bring anything out of nothing. "He who said, Let light shine out of darkness, is the one who has shone in our hearts," says the Apostle. Therefore God both calls us when we are not seeking him, and when he calls he gives the power to hear, so that the whole glory of our effectual calling belongs to him alone. Amen.

units.la: Sequitur nunc altera pars Ministerij Andreæ. Inueni-mus, inquit, Messiam, qui interpretatur Christus, subiungit Iohannes Græcam interpretationem Hebraicæ vocis, vt etiam Græcis & gentibus arcanum illud Messiæ Iudæorum nomen innotesceret. Messias, Vnctus Latinè interpretatur. Sub veteri testamento in populo Dei Reges, Prophetæ, Sacerdotes inungi consueuerunt oleo materiali, vt hoc esset iis inter alia quæ significabantur ea
units.tr: Now follows the second part of Andrew's ministry. "We have found the Messiah," he says, "which is interpreted Christ." John adds the Greek rendering of the Hebrew word, so that the hidden name of the Jews' Messiah might also become known to the Greeks and the Gentiles. "Messias" is translated in Latin as "Anointed." Under the Old Testament, kings, prophets and priests in the people of God were customarily anointed with material oil, and among other things this signified to them that

units.la: Iohan. 5. 25. Resp. Ephes. 2. 10. Cofirmatio à simili. Rom. 4. 17. Quod duplici testimonio nititur. 2. Cor. 4. 6. Messiam se inuenisse, Andreas Petro renuntiat. Iudæorum expectatio, Messias. eo symbolo, sigillum promissionis de venturo illo magno Messia, magno Rege, magno Propheta, magno Sacerdote, qui inungendus erat oleo, non materiali & typico, sed gratia Spiritus Sancti, idque supra consortes suos. Decuit enim ipsum verum Regem, Prophetam & Sacerdotem inungi oleo, non typico, sed vero illo per typicum illud oleum significato. Expectabant igitur Iudaei venturum hunc Messiam, & eum in ore habebant nam & supra hoc eodem capite, Sacerdotes illi, de quibus diximus, & Leuitae quaerebant a Iohanne an esset Christus. Et mulier Samaritana postea, Scio, inquit, Messiam venturum, qui dicitur Christus. In aduentu autem suo expectabant magnum & gloriosum futurum: Vnde illa ipsa mulier ibidem, Cum venerit, inquit, nobis annuntiabit omnia.
units.tr: John 5:25. Answer: Ephesians 2:10. Confirmation from a like case. Romans 4:17. Which rests on a twofold testimony. 2 Corinthians 4:6. Andrew reports to Peter that he has found the Messiah. The Jews' expectation: the Messiah. By that token, a seal of the promise concerning that great coming Messiah, the great King, the great Prophet, the great Priest, who was to be anointed with oil, not the material and typical oil, but with the grace of the Holy Spirit, and that above his fellows. For it was fitting that the true King, Prophet and Priest should be anointed, not with a typical oil, but with that true oil which was signified by the typical oil. The Jews therefore expected this Messiah to come, and had him constantly on their lips. For even earlier in this same chapter, those priests of whom we have spoken and the Levites asked John whether he was the Christ. And afterwards the Samaritan woman said, "I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ." They expected that at his coming he would be great and glorious. Hence the same woman says in the same place, "When he comes, he will tell us all things."

units.la: Expectabant quidem igitur venturum Messiam, sed miseri venientem non acceperunt, vt 1. capite eis exprobratum est his verbis, Ad suos venit, & sui eum non receperunt. In causa erat, quia non venit cum ea gloria externa ac mundana qua illi venturum eum imaginati sunt. Sed observandum occurrit hoc loco quod Andreas nihil de Christo concionetur, de persona eius, de naturis, de officio nihil, sed admonet tantum inuentum esse a se Messiam. Non ideo detereri oportet nos a deducendis aliis ad Christum, quia non statim possumus de eo concionari, quin potius ne nihil tenearmur dicere, admoneamus Christum venisse in mundum: hortemur vt quaerant sibi homines eos qui possunt aliquid melius & vtilius dicere. Venite, inquit mulier illa Samaritana, videte virum qui dixit mihi quaecunque feci: num iste est Christus? Potius quam nihil dicamus fungamur vice capanae, quae ipsa non concionatur, sed admonet signo dato esse qui concionetur: Sic nos eos, qui a sacris cetibus abhorrent, saltem admoneamus vt ipsi quoque iis interesse velint ac audire Dei verbum praedicatum: denique proficere in fide Iesu Christi, sine qua nulla salus.
units.tr: They indeed were waiting for the Messiah to come, but, wretched as they were, they did not receive him when he came, as was reproached to them in the first chapter in these words: "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him." The cause was that he did not come with that external and worldly glory which they had imagined the coming one would have. But it is worth noticing here that Andrew does not preach anything about Christ: nothing about his person, his natures or his office, but only urges that he himself has found the Messiah. We ought not, however, to be discouraged from leading others to Christ because we cannot at once preach about him; rather, lest we are bound to say nothing, let us remind them that Christ has come into the world, and urge them to seek out for themselves men who can say something better and more useful. "Come," said that Samaritan woman, "see a man who told me all that I have done: is not this the Christ?" Rather than say nothing, let us act as the bell-ringer does, who does not preach himself but, by giving the signal, shows that there is someone who will preach. So too let us at least urge those who shrink from the sacred assemblies to be willing to attend them themselves and to hear the Word of God preached, and finally to make progress in faith in Jesus Christ, without which there is no salvation.

units.la: Sequitur nunc tertia & postrema pars ministerij, adduxit eum ad Iesum. Andreas cum iam monuisset inuentum esse Christum, non Petrum solum ad eum amandavit, sed fratrem ipse voluit deducere: quod fecisse videtur non tantum amore & studio fratris sui, sed consilio etiam discendi vna cum fratre in schola Christi. Sic & nos facere debemus quicunque alios de Christo admonemus: debemus, inquam, in schola Christi vna cum iis proficere: Venite, inquit, ascendamus ad montem Iehouæ, vt doceat nos de viis suis. Vide rursus, testatus quidem est Andreas de Christo, sed cum nollet fratris fidem nisi testimonio suo, tanquam fundamento, eum ad Christum adduxit, vt eo audito niteretur fratris fides verbis & voce ipsius Christi. Sic nobis quoque faciendum est: & Deo sit gloria, sic facimus hodierno die, testamur de Christo, sed non eo consilio vt fides hominum nitatur testimonio nostro, verum eo ad Christum ipsum remittimus in scripturis sacris loquentem: adeoque nihil loquimur in publico nisi confirmatum Dei ipsius testimonio in Scripturis suis loquentis. Contra faciunt Papistæ, qui homines ipsorum quoque fidem abducunt ab illo vnico fundamento scripturarum ad vocem Ecclesiæ Romanæ, hoc est, impurissimæ, eique maiorem authoritatem a nobis tribui volunt, quàm ipsius Dei vocem in Scripturis loquentis: cum statuant hoc præcipuum actæ vnicum argumentum veritatis scripturarum ipsarum, nempe sic dicit Ecclesia. Hoc postquam obtinuerunt, maiorè esse authoritatem Ecclesiæ quàm Scripturæ, & Ecclesiæ vocem esse regulam primariam omnis veritatis, dici non potest quot figmenta ac somnia innecta sint in Ecclesiam Dei, & quot animæ hominum perierint. Vbi enim hoc semel insedit animis miserorum hominum vocem Ecclesiæ, Scripturæ & omnis religionis regulam esse, tunc nulla superstitio, nulla hæresis tam exitialis est, quàm si visum sit Romanæ ecclesiæ obtrudere, non statim imbibant. Remedium autem vnicum aduersus hæreses omnes & superstitionem est si teneas vnicum illud fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum.
units.tr: Now follows the third and last part of the ministry: "He brought him to Jesus." Andrew, having already told his brother that Christ had been found, did not merely send Peter to him but wished to lead his brother himself. He seems to have done this not only out of love and zeal for his brother, but also with the purpose of learning together with his brother in the school of Christ. So we too ought to do, whoever we are who admonish others about Christ: we ought, I say, to make progress together with them in the school of Christ. "Come," he says, "let us go up to the mountain of Jehovah, that he may teach us of his ways."
