See again: Andrew did indeed bear witness to Christ, but since he did not want his brother's faith to rest on his testimony alone, as on a foundation, he brought him to Christ, so that, having heard him, his brother's faith might rest on the words and voice of Christ himself. So we too must do; and God be praised, this is what we do on this very day: we bear witness to Christ, but not with the purpose that men's faith should rest on our testimony; rather we send them back to Christ himself, speaking in the holy Scriptures. Accordingly we say nothing in public unless it is confirmed by the testimony of God himself, speaking in his Scriptures. The Papists do the opposite: they draw men's faith away, even their own, from that one foundation of the Scriptures to the voice of the Roman Church, that is, the most impure church, and they want that voice to be given greater authority by us than the voice of God himself speaking in the Scriptures. They lay down that this is the chief and only argument for the truth of the Scriptures themselves, namely: "the Church says so." Once they have gained this, that the authority of the Church is greater than that of Scripture, and that the voice of the Church is the primary rule of all truth, it cannot be said how many fictions and dreams have been woven into the Church of God, and how many souls of men have perished. For once this has sunk into the minds of wretched men, that the voice of the Church is the rule of Scripture and of all religion, then no superstition and no heresy is so deadly that they will not at once swallow it, if it has seemed good to the Roman church to impose it. The only remedy, however, against all heresies and superstition is to hold fast to that one foundation of the Prophets and Apostles.

units.la: Hactenus fuit ministerium Andreæ in vocatione Petri: sequuntur partes & verba ipsius Christi. Iesus, inquit, intuitus eum, non eo duntaxat modo quo solent homines intueri, sed vt Deus oculi sui acie penetras in renes ac secreta cordis Petri, facie etiam sua illuminans cor ipsius; nam omnis cognitio est in facie Iesu Christi. Intuitus igitur eum dixit, Tu es Simon filius Iona. postea Ioanna dicitur. Non quærit Christus qui vocetur,quo Patre natus sit, sed quo Petrus subolfaciat plusquàm homine, ac proinde maiore fide habeat promissioni quæ sequitur nominat Petrum,tanquam iam ante de nomine & de facie cognitum,nominat quoque Patrem ipsius. Tu,inquit,es Simon,homo vilis,filius hominis obscuri,vtpote Ionæ:qui incola fuit Berhsaidæ, qui vicus fuit in Galilæa, pater autem fuit Andreæ & Simonis,qui exercebant artem piscatoriam in mari Galilææ. Tu,inquit, vocaberis Cephas. Iohannes vocem Chaldaicam Græcè reddit,Qui interpretatur, inquit,Petrus. Nam πέτρος vel πέτρα, id est Græcis, quod Cephas fuit illis; Latinis autem est rupes vel saxum. Tu,inquit,vocaberis Cephas.Impositio hoc nouo nomine, promisit ei stabilitatem eam fidei,quæ est saxi vel petræ, quæ loco moueri non poterit. Subest enim impositioni nominis promissio,quæ ipsa quasi obsignatur nouo cognomine Cephæ vel Petri : q.d. Christus reddam te stabilem ac firmum fide, tanquam petram; Quod quo magis credas accipito hoc signum noui cognominis, vocatorque in posterum Cephas.Papistæ ideo hoc cognomentum eum accepisse ferunt quod futurus esset petra, super quam Ecclesia Christi extruenda fuit, & illi verba illa Christi Matth. 16. 18. Tu es Petrus & super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam in eam sententiam detorquent; quasi vero Christus innuerit ædificandum esse Ecclesiam super Petrum tanquam Ecclesiæ fundamentum, quum eo loco intelligatur petræ nomine, præclara illa confessio Petri de filio Dei supra quam extruenda erat Ecclesia Dei. Nam fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere præter id quod positum est, nempe Iesum Christum. Petrus, vt & alij omnes pij in Ecclesia, nihil fuit quàm viuus lapis, vt ipse appellat, in eo ædificio extructus cuius fundamentum est Christus, immobilis tamen & nunquam diuellendus ab illo ædificio, propter constantem fidem qua inseparabiliter coniunctus est cum ipso lapide fundamentali Christo. Hic obserua: Christus priusquam promittat hanc fidei constantiam, reuocat in memoriam Petro cōditionem suam præsentem, quæ quidem, comparatacum futura il Ia, vilis abiectaque erat. At cur hoc? nempe vt posita ante oculos praesente conditione diligentius ponderet dignitatem illam ad quam vocandus erat. Sic nobis nunquam cogitandum est de beata nostra conditione quae est in Christo, quin simul recordemur miseriae illius nostriae conditionis, quae fuit extra Christum. Ita enim fiet, vt pluris faciamus gratiam Christi, & Deo magis gratias simus propter tantam ipsius gratiam. Deinde notandum non statim impertit Petro illam gratiam constantiae, sed promittit se daturum in posterum. Sic Deus solet agere nobiscum, non statim largitur nobis gloriam & complementum beneficiorum, verum multo antequam largiatur promittit nobis ea beneficia, ut nimirum fide & spe viuamus, priusquam aspectu: Tum enim maxime honoratur Deus, cum verbis ipsius & promissionibus creditur. Neque tamen carent fides & spes in vita praesenti aliqua parte illius laetitiae atque pacis, qua per aspectum semel ac simul tota fruemur in vita altera. Petrus enim, vt tum coepit per fidem pendere ex promissione futuri beneficij, ita nō caruit initio quodam illius gaudij, quod postea accepto beneficio plenius percepit. Domine, da nobis fidem propter Iesum Christum, cui sit omnis honor & gloria. Amen.
units.tr: Thus far was the ministry of Andrew in the calling of Peter; there follow the actions and words of Christ himself. Jesus, it says, "looked upon him", not merely in the way men usually look at one another, but as God, piercing with the keen gaze of his eye into the reins and secrets of Peter's heart, and enlightening his heart with his own face; for all knowledge is in the face of Jesus Christ. Having looked upon him, he said, "You are Simon the son of Jonah"; he is afterwards called John. Christ does not ask what he is called or whose son he was, but Peter perceives something more than a man, and therefore has greater faith in the promise that follows. "He names Peter" as one already known beforehand by name and by face; he names his father too. "You," he says, "are Simon," a worthless man, the son of an obscure man, "namely of Jonah," who was a resident of Bethsaida, a village in Galilee; his father was the father of Andrew and Simon, who practised the trade of fishing on the sea of Galilee. "You," he says, "shall be called Cephas." John renders the Chaldee word into Greek: "which is interpreted," he says, "Peter." For [πέτρος] or [πέτρα], that is, in Greek, is what Cephas was to them; to the Latins it is a rock or a stone. "You," he says, "shall be called Cephas." By the imposition of this new name he promised him that steadiness of faith which belongs to a stone or rock, which cannot be moved from its place. For a promise lies beneath the imposition of the name, and it is, as it were, sealed by the new surname Cephas or Peter; as if he said: "Christ will make you steady and firm in faith, like a rock; and that you may believe it the more, take this sign of the new surname, and be called Cephas from now on." The Papists say that he received this surname because he was to be the rock upon which the Church of Christ was to be built, and they twist to this sense the words of Christ in Matthew 16:18, "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church"; as if Christ had indicated that the Church was to be built upon Peter as the foundation of the Church, whereas in that place by the name of rock is understood that famous confession of Peter concerning the Son of God, upon which the Church of God was to be built. For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, namely Jesus Christ. Peter, like all the other godly in the Church, was nothing but a living stone, as he himself calls it, built into that edifice whose foundation is Christ; yet he was immovable and never to be torn from that building, on account of the steadfast faith by which he is inseparably joined to the foundation stone itself, Christ. Here observe: before Christ promises this constancy of faith, he recalls to Peter's memory his present condition, which indeed, compared with the future one, was lowly and abject. But why this? Namely, so that, with his present condition set before his eyes, he might weigh more carefully the dignity to which he was to be called. So we too must never think of our blessed condition, which is in Christ, without at the same time recalling the misery of that former condition of ours, which was outside Christ. For thus it will come about that we value the grace of Christ more, and are more thankful to God for so great a grace of his. Next, note that he does not at once bestow on Peter that grace of constancy, but promises that he will give it in time to come. So God is wont to deal with us: he does not at once grant us glory and the completion of his benefits, but long before he bestows them he promises us those benefits, so that we may live by faith and hope before we live by sight. For God is then most honoured when his words and promises are believed. Yet faith and hope in the present life are not without some part of that joy and peace which we shall enjoy fully, all at once, through sight in the life to come. For Peter, just as he then began to depend by faith on the promise of a future benefit, so at the beginning he did not lack a certain measure of that joy, which he later received more fully when the benefit was given. Lord, give us faith for the sake of Jesus Christ, to whom be all honour and glory. Amen.

units.la: 44 Postero die voluit Iesus abire in Galilaeam: invenit autem Philippum & dixit ei, Sequere me.
units.tr: 44 On the next day Jesus wished to depart into Galilee, and he found Philip and said to him, Follow me.

units.la: 45 Erat vero Philippus ex Beth-saida civitate Andreae & Petri.
units.tr: 45 Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.

units.la: Ecclesiae Christianae incunabula.
units.tr: The cradle of the Christian Church.

units.la: HActenus vocati sunt ad Christum in deserto Andreas cum altero, cuius nomen non est expressum, denique tertius Simon Petrus. In hac vocatione perpaucorum hominum, apparet incunabula regni & Ecclesiae Christi obscura fuisse & tenue initium, quae tamen postea auctiora facta sunt multis ad Ecclesiam concurrentibus. Nam qualis est Christus ipse, talis Ecclesia eius est: Christus ipse initio humilis & abiectus in speciem fuit, similis surculo, vt de eo praedicatum est ab Esaia, ex arido quodam trunco nascenti; nulla erat ei forma, nullus decor, ex obscura & contempta lesse familia oriundus, cuius nihil iā reliquum fuit nisi radix, cum trunco pene emoremortuo: Verùm postea idem euectus est in summam sublimitatem, cùm Pater exuscitaret eum ex mortuis. Talis fuit etiam Ecclesiæ Christi facies, nam prima eius initia obscura fuerant, & pauci tantùm ad eam adiunge-bantur, postea autem aucta est, & vt prædixit Christus, vis illi allata est, ac violenti rapuerunt eam, postremò denique glorificabitur. Superbi homines offenduntur hac contempta & abiecta Ecclesiæ facie: sed nos ne pu- deat humilitatis & afflictionum Ecclesiæ, quin potius participes earum fiamus. Beatus est, inquit Christus, qui non fuerit offensus in me. Hæc in genere hactenus.
units.tr: Up to this point Andrew, with another whose name is not given, and finally a third, Simon Peter, had been called to Christ in the wilderness. In this calling of so few people it appears that the beginnings of Christ's kingdom and Church were obscure and of slender origin, yet they were afterwards enlarged as many came to the Church. For such as Christ himself is, such is his Church. Christ himself was at first humble and despised in appearance, like a shoot, as Isaiah foretold of him, springing from a dry stump. He had no form or comeliness, and he came from an obscure and despised family of Jesse, of which nothing remained but the root, like a trunk almost dead. Afterwards, however, he was raised to the highest exaltation, when the Father raised him from the dead. Such also was the appearance of Christ's Church: its first beginnings were obscure, and only a few were joined to it, but afterwards it grew, and, as Christ foretold, it was taken by force, and the violent seized it, and at last it will be glorified. Proud men are offended by this despised and abject face of the Church, but let us not be ashamed of the humility and afflictions of the Church; rather let us become partakers of them. Blessed is he, says Christ, who shall not be offended in me. These things so far in general.

units.la: Habemus deinceps vocationem Philippi, quæ fuit non per hominem aliquem ministrum, vt prima illa Andreæ & altera illius discipuli, deinde secunda Simonis Petri: sed per ipsummet Christum immediatè, vt nimirum doceat nos Christus posse se sine Ministerio cuiusquam vel Angeli vel hominis, quos ipsi visum est vocare ad regnum cœlorum. In vocatione Philippi primùm occurrit occasio ipsius conueniendi & inueniendi ex profectione Christi in Galilæam, 1. Inuenit Christus Philippum. 2. inuentum vocat. 3. descriptio quædam additur ciuitatis Philippi. Primùm igitur est vocationis occasio his verbis, Postero die Iesus voluit ire in Galilæa. Hoc est paulò post vocatos primum Andream & alterum illum cuius nomen non est expressum, deinde Simonem Petrum. Iesus consultum cœpit proficiscendi in Galilæam, nempe ex deserto in quo diuersabatur vnà cum Iohanne, & in quo vocati erant illi tres discipuli Iohannis. Nam quòd ad profectionem hanc Iesu, vt eā paulò altius repetam, Primùm cùm tempus Ministerij ipsius instaret profectus est Nazaretha in desertum ad Iohannem, ibique ab eo baptizatus est. Postea ductus est à Spiritu Sancto in desertum, vbi ieiunauit quadraginta dies, & tentatus est graviter à Diabolo. Inde reuersus est ad Iohannem in desertum, vbi etiam vocati sunt illi tres discipuli, de quibus iam audiuimus. Postremò rediit in Galilæam, vbi vocauit primùm ipsemet Philippum, deinde Philippi ministerio Nathanaelem. Reditus autem ille Christi in Galilæam intelligitur hoc loco: In quo quidem reditu, ait Matthæus, impletum est ... quod dictum est per Esaiam; Terra Zabulon & terra Nephtalim ad viam maris trans Iordanem Galilæa gentium : populus positus in tenebris, vidit lucem magnam, & positis in regione ac umbra mortis lux extra est. Dicam planius: Galilæi populus qui sedit in tenebris & umbra mortis, adventu illo Christi illuminatus est. Nam lumen cognitionis gloriæ Dei in sola facie Iesu Christi apparet, absque qua nulla cuiusquam gentis gloria est, nulla lux: & propter hanc Christi præsentiam legés apud Danielem Iudæam solam ex cæteris gentibus quæ mundi gloria insignes erant præ Iudæa, Iudæam, inquam, solam, decus ipsum appellari. Utinam nos grati essemus Deo propter hanc in gente nostra qualemcunque Christi præsentiam. Hactenus fuit occasio.
units.tr: We come next to the calling of Philip, which was not through any human minister, as was the first calling of Andrew and of the other disciple, and then the second, of Simon Peter, but immediately through Christ himself. Doubtless he means to teach us that Christ can, without the ministry of any man or angel, call whom he pleases into the kingdom of heaven. In the calling of Philip, the occasion of meeting and finding him first occurs, from Christ's journey into Galilee. There are three things: (1) Christ finds Philip; (2) having found him, he calls him; (3) a certain description of Philip's city is added. The occasion of the calling is first given in these words: On the next day Jesus would go forth into Galilee. That is, shortly after he had called first Andrew and the other whose name is not given, and then Simon Peter. Jesus began to set out for Galilee, namely from the wilderness in which he was staying together with John, and where those three disciples of John had been called. For to go back a little further to this journey of Jesus: when the time of his ministry was at hand, he first went from Nazareth into the wilderness to John, and was baptised by him there. Afterwards he was led by the Holy Spirit into the wilderness, where he fasted forty days and was sorely tempted by the devil. From there he returned to John in the wilderness, where also those three disciples, of whom we have already heard, were called. Lastly he returned into Galilee, where he himself first called Philip, and then through Philip's ministry Nathanael. Now that return of Christ into Galilee is meant at this place. Matthew says: In that return, what was spoken by Isaiah was fulfilled: The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, by the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles: the people sitting in darkness saw a great light, and to those sitting in the region and shadow of death light has risen. To put it more plainly: the people of Galilee who sat in darkness and the shadow of death were enlightened by the coming of Christ. For the light of the knowledge of the glory of God appears only in the face of Jesus Christ, without which there is no glory and no light of any nation. And on account of this presence of Christ, the laws of Daniel call Judea alone, of all the nations which were conspicuous for worldly glory, the glory itself, Judea, I say, alone. Would that we were thankful to God for this presence of Christ in our nation, however slight it is. So much for the occasion.

units.la: Reuersus itaque in Galilæam Inuenit Philippum. Inuenit quidem non temere, sed certo consilio. Fieri potest ut homines quorum ministerio vtitur Dominus invocandis suis præter expectationem neque certo animi consilio, inueniant quos vocent. At Christus quem nihil latere potest omniaque certa providentia & consilio facit, neminem inuenit de quo inueniendo non prius cogitauit. Inuentum igitur Philippum vocat his paucis verbis, Sequere me. Philippus autem secutus est ipsum. Unde discimus quam efficax sit verbum Christi & quanta cum potentia Spiritus coniunctum. No minore profecto nunc in vocando & regenerando homines per verbum suum quam olim in creando primum hominem per idem verbum, cum dixit, faciamus hominem in imagine nostra, & per verbum illud factus est homo. Paulus itaque comparatis inter se creatione & vocatione ait, Qui dixit ut e tenebris lux splendesceret, is est qui splenduit in cordibus nostris. q.d Quemadmodum verbo suo Deus creauit lucem, cum diceret, Esto lux, & fuit lux: ita verbo suo splendorem excitat in animis nostris, qui natura oppleti sunt tenebris. Porphyrius hostis Christi, & Iulianus Apostata, dū inciderent in loca hæc noui testamenti de vocatione discipulorum, blasphemarunt dicentes vel mentitos esse eos, qui hæc scriptis commiserunt, vel certe nimis simplices & fatuos illos, qui vno dūtaxat verbo, & tam leuiter inuitati Christum sequusequuti sunt. Sed prophani & blasphemi homines, ignorârunt quanta sit Christi in suis efficacia cum verbo suo coniuncta. Verùm quid hic miri, si prophani homines, qui eam vim Spiritus nunquam ipsi serió senserunt, adeò ad eam obstupescant, vt dum vident tam insignem mutationē fieri in cordibus hominum paulò ante prophanorum & sui similium, peregrinari sibi videantur, vt cum Petro loquar. Hæc quidem est potentia Spiritus Christi cum verbo coniuncta, sed ea non exeritur statim in omnibus iis qui verbum Christi audiunt. Maximam enim hominū partem ipsorum culpa reddit verbum duntaxat inexcusabiles: Nobis autem solis qui seruamur est Dei potentia. Quamobrem Christus nobis assiduis precibus flagitandus est, vt velit cum verbo suo efficaciam Spiritus sui ad nos interius renouandos coiungere: Sciemus autem vocationem efficacem esse hoc modo: si vocante Deo echo sit in cordibus; hoc est, si vocem illam Dei vocantis resonêt corda nostra: vt si cùm Dominus dicit, Quærite faciem meam, tum resonet cor, Faciem tuam, Iehoua requiro. Et si cùm ille dicit, Credo, resonet cor, Credo Domine, succurre incredulitati meæ.
units.tr: Having returned, then, into Galilee, he finds Philip. He finds him, indeed, not by chance but by settled counsel. It may happen that men whose ministry the Lord uses to call his own find those they call beyond expectation, and without a settled purpose of mind. But Christ, from whom nothing can be hidden, and who acts with certain providence and counsel, finds no one whom he has not first considered finding. Having found Philip, then, he calls him in these few words: Follow me. And Philip followed him. From this we learn how effective the word of Christ is, and how great the power of the Spirit joined with it. Surely no less now in calling and regenerating men through his word than of old in creating the first man through the same word, when he said, Let us make man in our image, and by that word man was made. Paul, therefore, comparing creation and calling with each other, says: He who said that light should shine out of darkness is he who has shone in our hearts. As if to say: just as God by his word created light, when he said, Let there be light, and there was light, so by his word he kindles splendour in our souls, which are overwhelmed by darkness by nature. When Porphyry, the enemy of Christ, and Julian the Apostate came upon these passages of the New Testament concerning the calling of the disciples, they blasphemed, saying either that those who committed these things to writing were liars, or at least that those men were too simple and foolish who followed Christ when invited by a single word and so lightly. But profane and blasphemous men did not know how great is the efficacy of Christ, joined with his word, in his own people. But what is so strange here, if profane men, who never seriously felt that power of the Spirit themselves, are so astonished at it that, when they see so remarkable a change take place in the hearts of men who a little before were profane and like themselves, they seem to themselves to be strangers, to use the words of Peter? This indeed is the power of the Spirit of Christ joined with the word, but it does not break out at once in all those who hear the word of Christ. For the fault of most men, indeed, makes the word merely inexcusable; but the power of God is for us alone who are saved. Therefore Christ must be entreated by us with constant prayers, that he may be willing to join to his word the efficacy of his Spirit, to renew us inwardly. We shall know, moreover, that the calling is effective in this way: if the heart answers to God calling, that is, if our hearts resound that voice of God who calls. So, when the Lord says, Seek my face, the heart answers, Your face, Jehovah, I seek. And when he says, I believe, the heart answers, I believe, Lord, help my unbelief.

units.la: Postremò, descriptio quædam est Philippi ex ciuitate ex qua erat, nempe, Beth-saida ciuitate Andreæ & Petri. Hoc additum videtur ad commendationem bonitatis ac misericordiæ Christi, qui ex ciuitate tam ignobili támque obstinata vocauerit tres tam illustres discipulos. Erat enim Beth-saida vicus quidam in Galilæa obscurus & ignobilis, sed ad ignobilitatem accessit obstinata malitia: Ideóque postea in ipsum denuntiatum est extremum iudicium: Væ tibi Chorazim, væ tibi Bethsaida. Nam si in Tyro & Sidone editæ fuissent virtutes, quæ apud vos editæ sunt, olim cum sacco & cinere sedentes resipuissent. Quare vocari istos ex Beth-saida quid aliud fuit, quàm ex ipsis inferis excitari tam illustres Apostolos? quod quidem non parum commendat misericordiam ac bonitatem Domini. Nam quo indignior vel persona vel ciuitas est, eo copiosior est gratia. Fuì prius, ait Paulus de se, blasphemus, persecutor, iniuriosus; superabundauit autem gratia. Nunquam mirifica illa gratia Dei satis præedicari potest quam 1. Timoth. 1. 13. 14.
units.tr: Lastly, there is a description of Philip from the city from which he came, namely Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter. This seems to be added to commend the goodness and mercy of Christ, who called three such illustrious disciples from so ignoble and so stubborn a city. For Bethsaida was an obscure and ignoble village in Galilee, but to its ignobility was added stubborn wickedness. Therefore afterwards the final judgment was pronounced against it: Woe to you, Chorazin, woe to you, Bethsaida. For if the mighty works that were done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. Wherefore what else was it to call those men from Bethsaida than to raise such illustrious apostles from the very depths? This indeed greatly commends the mercy and goodness of the Lord. For the less worthy either the person or the city is, the more abundant is grace. I was before, says Paul of himself, a blasphemer, a persecutor, and injurious; but grace abounded. The wonderful grace of God can never be praised enough, which he has shown towards us wretched people in this ignoble nation. 1 Tim. 1. 13. 14.

units.la: E. exeruit Deus erga nos miseros in hac gente ignobili. Quod si erga vllam gentem vnquam patefacta est Dei in Christo misericordia, & erga hanc nostram maxime. Huic igitur sit omnis gloria in saecula saeculorum. Amen.
units.tr: God has shown his mercy toward us wretched people in this ignoble nation. And if the mercy of God in Christ has ever been revealed to any nation, it has been revealed above all to this nation of ours. To him therefore be all glory for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: 46 Inuenit Philippus Nathanaelem, & dicit ei, Inuenimus illum de quo scripsit Moses in Lege, & Prophetae: nempe Iesum filium Iosephi, illum ex vrbe Nazaretha.
units.tr: Philip found Nathanael and said to him, "We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the Law, and the Prophets: namely Jesus, the son of Joseph, from the city of Nazareth."

units.la: 47 Tum dixit ei Nathanael, Ab vrbe Nazaretha potest aliquid boni esse? dicit ei Philippus, Veni & vide.
units.tr: Then Nathanael said to him, "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" Philip said to him, "Come and see."

units.la: HACtenus fuit vocatio Philippi, Sequitur vocatio & conuersio Nathanaelis, idque per ministerium Philippi. Primum igitur habemus ministerium Philippi: Deinde habemus efficacem ipsius per Christum vocationem: Ministerium Philippi constat his quasi partibus: Primum inuenit Nathanaelem, deinde cum eo inuento sermones confert de Christo. Postremo hominem ad Christum ipsum adducit. Primum igitur inuenit Nathanaelem. Nathanael, vt videtur, familiaris fuit Philippo: de eo hoc legimus in Euangelio, primum quod ministerio Philippi vocatus fuerit: deinde quod testis fuerit resurrectionis Christi, vna cum aliis discipulis, quo tempore Christus patefecit se ipsis ad mare Tiberiadis. De Nathanaele plura in Euangelio non legimus. Hunc igitur inuenit Philippus, inuenit quidem non temere aut casu. Christus enim ait Nathanaeli postea vidisse se eum priusquam Philippus ipsum vocaret, cum esset sub ficu. Inuenit tamen eum Philippus praeter expectationem suam. Unde discimus Christum semper oculo prouidentiae suae attendere ad electos Dei, & tum videre ipsos, cum ipsi cum vicissim non videant, cumque tempus efficaci vocationi destinatum, adest, efficere vt ij quorum ministerio vtitur in aliis vocandis incidat in ipsos etiam praeter expectationem & consilium suum, Dei tamen certo consilio ac prouidentia: ac eos vocent ad hoc vt & ipsi tandem quos prius vidit.
units.tr: So far was the calling of Philip. Now follows the calling and conversion of Nathanael, and this through the ministry of Philip. First, then, we have the ministry of Philip; second, we have Christ's effective calling of him. Philip's ministry consists of three parts, as it were. First, he found Nathanael; then, having found him, he talks with him about Christ; last, he brings the man to Christ himself. First, then, he found Nathanael. Nathanael, it seems, was a friend of Philip's. We read this about him in the Gospel: first, that he was called through the ministry of Philip; second, that he was a witness of Christ's resurrection, along with the other disciples, at the time when Christ showed himself to them by the Sea of Tiberias. We do not read more about Nathanael in the Gospel. Philip found him, and he found him not by chance or accident. For Christ later tells Nathanael that he had seen him before Philip called him, when he was under the fig tree. Yet Philip found him beyond his own expectation. From this we learn that Christ always looks with the eye of his providence upon the elect of God, and sees them when they do not in turn see him; and when the time appointed for effective calling has come, he brings it about that those whose ministry he uses in calling others come upon those very people, even beyond their expectation and purpose, yet by the sure counsel and providence of God; and that they call them, so that they may at last see the one whom they had not seen before.

units.la: Huius vocationis modus & ratio. vidit Deus, vicissim videant Deum, & Filium eius Iesum Christum. Neque enim Deus, quos emittit ad vocandum electos, eos perpetuò sic alloquitur, Abi, voca mihi hunc vel illum hominē, vt factum legimus Philippo diacono, qui vocauit Eunuchum illum Æthiopem. Sed interea dum Ministri vocationis Dei nihil tale cogitant, fit sæpe vt incidant in electos, & moti Spiritu Dei incipiāt loqui iis de Deo, de Christo Redemptore, de cœlis, de inferis, &c. Sequitur nunc sermo quē habet inter se mutuo. Primùm quidem Philippus paucis Christum prædicat: Inuenimus, inquit, eum de quo scripsit Moses in lege, & Prophetæ, nempe Iesum filium Iosephi, Nazarenum. Nazarenum vocat, quia in Nazaretha fuit educatus, hinc coepit cognomentum Nazareni, vt prædictum fuit à Propheta. Quòd si patriam ex qua erat oriundus Iesus intellexerit Philippus, errauit: Christus enim natus est in Bethleem Iudææ Matth. 2.1. Filium Iosephi vocat seductus communi errore & opinione Iudæorum qui Iesum filium Iosephi ex Maria putarūt esse. Vide igitur, vix quatuor verba proferre potest Philippus de Christo, quin aberret à veritate. Hinc discimus non ex opinione vulgi loquendum de Christo, sed ex certa scientia & informatione Scripturarum: videndūmque quid & quo modo quisque superædificet super illud fundamentum, vt consulit Paulus. Nam si quis superædificet super fundamentum ligna, fœnum, stipulam, damnum faciet, quo tempore opus ipsius probabitur per ignem, & exuretur. Videmus nihilominus Philippum non sine fructu aliquo & successu hæc ipsa verba protulisse. In causa erat, quia inter loquēdum rectè & sincerè sentiebat & ex simplicitate quadam animi quærebat gloriā Christi, simul & salutem Nathanaēlis. Deus bonos conatus etiam imperitorum sic approbat, vt ex sermone suo imperito atque etiam balbo fructum aliquem reportent. Malim balbutire hominem de Christo, modò sincerè & ex animo loquatur, & Dei gloriam ac salutē hominum propositam sibi habeat; quàm eloquenter multa dicere de Christo ad ostentationem & manem gloriam captandam. Admonemur igitur ne despiciamus simplices, & minus facundos ac doctos, modò sin- E ij ceri sint. Nam sinceritas illa animi & simplicitas, Pastoris præcipuum donum. Vt autem maiore Christo quem prædicat authoritatem conciliet, commendat cum testimoniis & prædictionibus Moisis in Lege, & Prophetarum.
units.tr: The manner and reason of this calling: God sees them, so that in turn they may see God and his Son Jesus Christ. For God does not always speak to those whom he sends to call the elect in this way, "Go, call for me this man or that," as we read was done with Philip the deacon, who called that Ethiopian eunuch. Rather, while the ministers of God's calling are thinking of nothing of the kind, it often happens that they come upon the elect, and, moved by the Spirit of God, begin to speak to them about God, about Christ the Redeemer, about heaven, about hell, and so on. Now follows the conversation they have with one another. First, Philip briefly preaches Christ: "We have found," he says, "him of whom Moses wrote in the law, and the prophets, namely Jesus, the son of Joseph, the Nazarene." He calls him the Nazarene because he was brought up in Nazareth; from this he took the surname Nazarene, as was foretold by the prophet. But if Philip understood the homeland from which Jesus came, he was mistaken: for Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judea, Matt. 2:1. He calls him the son of Joseph, deceived by the common error and opinion of the Jews, who thought Jesus was the son of Joseph and Mary. See, then: Philip can scarcely utter four words about Christ without going astray from the truth. From this we learn that we must not speak of Christ according to popular opinion, but from certain knowledge and instruction in the Scriptures, and we must consider what and how each man builds upon that foundation, as Paul advises. For if anyone builds upon the foundation wood, hay, or stubble, he will suffer loss, when his work is tested by fire and burned up. Nevertheless, we see that Philip uttered these very words not without some fruit and success. The reason was that while speaking he felt rightly and sincerely, and out of a certain simplicity of mind he sought the glory of Christ and at the same time the salvation of Nathanael. God so approves the good endeavours even of the unskilled that from their unskilled, even stammering, speech they gain some fruit. I would rather a man stammer about Christ, provided he speaks sincerely and from his heart and has the glory of God and the salvation of men set before him, than speak eloquently about Christ at length for the sake of display and to win empty glory. We are therefore admonished not to despise the simple and those less eloquent and learned, provided they are sincere. For that sincerity and simplicity of mind is the chief gift of a minister. And so that he may win greater authority for the Christ whom he preaches, he commends him by the testimonies and predictions of Moses in the Law and of the Prophets.

units.la: Moses in quinque libris suis, qui nomine Legis hîc intelligutur, scribit de Messia venturo pluribus in locis, vt Genes. 49.10. Deuter. 18. 15. Prophetæ plenissunt prædictionibus de Christo venturo. Nam fundamentum Apostolorum ac Prophetarum imus angularis lapis est Iesus Christus. Et fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere, præter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus. Nec est aliud nomen sub coelo datum inter homines per quod oporteat homines seruari. Denique finis Legis est Christus ad iustitiam cuiuis credenti. Fuerunt Euangelicæ promissiones multis annis, nempe quadringentis & triginta annis ante datam Legem per Mosem: Tunc, inquit Paulus, tanto post tempore lex est addita, non quidem vt iustificaret & aboleret promissionem, si enim iustificaret, aboleret promissionem necessario, sed gratia transgressionum, inquit, addita est: vt cognosceretur peccatum, & vt augeretur peccatum. Sed vbi auctum est peccatum, ibi superabundauit gratia. Atque hic quem diximus finis fuit Legis. Etsi autem non iustificet Lex, neque eo consilio & fine à Deo data sit vt iustificaret: verumtamen quia Legis notitia & iustitia illa quæ est ex operibus Legis, naturalis est, iustitia autem illa Dei, quæ est per fidem Christi ipsiusque notitia naturalis non sit aut natura nota: hinc factum est, vt iam inde ab initio homines quæsierint perpetuò iustitiam eam quæ est ex operibus, ac etiamnum hodie Papistæ, quos ego inter ψυχικούς & animales homines numero, consectantur, iustitiam autem illam Dei, quæ est per fidem Iesu Christi, omnibus modis oppugnant.
units.tr: Moses, in his five books, which here are understood by the name of the Law, writes of the coming Messiah in many places, as in Gen. 49:10 and Deut. 18:15. The prophets are full of predictions of the coming Christ. For the foundation of the apostles and prophets is Jesus Christ, the chief corner stone. No one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Nor is there any other name under heaven given among men by which men must be saved. Finally, Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes. The promises of the gospel were made many years earlier, namely four hundred and thirty years before the Law was given through Moses. Then, says Paul, so long after, the law was added, not indeed to justify and so to annul the promise, for if it justified, it would necessarily annul the promise; but it was added because of transgressions, that sin might be known, and that sin might be increased. But where sin has increased, there grace has abounded all the more. And this, as we have said, was the purpose of the Law. Although the Law does not justify, nor was it given by God with that intention and purpose that it should justify, nevertheless, because the knowledge of the Law and the righteousness which is of the works of the Law are natural, while that righteousness of God which is through faith in Christ, and its knowledge, is neither natural nor known by nature, it has come about that from the beginning men have always sought the righteousness that is of works. And even today the Papists, whom I count among the psychic [ψυχικούς] and animal men, pursue it, while they oppose by every means that righteousness of God which is through faith in Jesus Christ.

units.la: Hactenus prædicauit Christum Philippus apud Nathanaelem. Statim excipit Nathanaël, Ἀ Nazareth potest aliquid boni esse? quippe offensus eo Nazareni titulo & cognomento, cùm sciret Nazareth abiectum & contemptum in Galilæa vicum esse. Hoc igitur præiudicio vilitatis & obscuritatis loci, unde fuit Christus, præoccupatus cupatus impingit Nathanael, ac impeditur ne statim credat ad auditam illam Philippi vocem. Natura omnes ignari sumus eorum quæ ad regnum Dei pertinent, & totius rationis qua iustificamur & seruamur, adeo vt nisi Christus ipse prior illuceat nobis, nunquam futurum sit, vt Christum videamus. Sed hæc ignorantia tolerabilis est quodammodo, si cum ea comparetur qua postquam Christus cœpit illucere ϑʏχικῶς & animali homini, cum ipse sibi eripit oculos ne possit lucem illam inspicere, ipse sibi offendicula iniicit ne possit ad Christū inoffenso cursu peruenire: offenditur cruce Christi, offenditur stultitia prædicationis Euangelij, offenditur afflictionibus Ecclesiæ: offenditur malis moribus Christianorum, denique offenditur conditione vili abiectaque ministrorum. Atque his modis fit, vt qui prius ex simplicitate quadam ignarus fuit, nunc ex malitia & obstinatione animi ac cordis obduratione, vt loquitur Apostolus, euadat ignarus, & multò maius sit peccatum & grauior sequatur damnatio. Si cæci essetis, ait Christus Pharisæis, non haberetis peccatum, Nunc vero dicitis, videmus: itaque peccatum vestrum manet. Quamobrem vt assiduè precari Deum oportet, vt velit collustrare nos gratia sua in Iesu Christo, ita debemus cauere nobis diligenter ab istiusmodi præiudiciis & offensionibus, quæ aditum omnem nobis ad Christum præcludunt. Beatus, inquit Christus, qui non fuerit offensus in me.
units.tr: Thus far Philip preached Christ to Nathanael. Nathanael immediately takes it up: "Can anything good come out of Nazareth? [Ἐκ Ναζαρέθ]" Indeed he was offended by that title and surname of Nazarene, since he knew that Nazareth was a despised and contemptible village in Galilee. So Nathanael, preoccupied by this prejudice of the lowliness and obscurity of the place from which Christ came, stumbles and is hindered from believing at once the words of Philip that he had heard. By nature we are all ignorant of the things that pertain to the kingdom of God, and of the whole reasoning by which we are justified and saved, so that unless Christ himself first shines upon us, it will never happen that we see Christ. But this ignorance is in some measure tolerable if it is compared with that ignorance which arises after Christ has begun to shine, when the psychic [ψυχικῶς] and animal man himself tears out his eyes, so that he cannot look upon that light, and himself puts stumbling blocks in his own way, so that he cannot come to Christ with a unhindered course: he is offended by the cross of Christ, he is offended by the foolishness of the preaching of the gospel, he is offended by the afflictions of the Church, he is offended by the bad morals of Christians, and finally he is offended by the low and abject condition of the ministers. And in these ways it comes about that he who before was ignorant out of a certain simplicity, now, out of malice and obstinacy of mind and hardening of heart, as the Apostle puts it, becomes ignorant, and his sin becomes much greater and a heavier condemnation follows. "If you were blind," Christ said to the Pharisees, "you would have no sin; but now you say, 'We see'; therefore your sin remains." Wherefore, just as we ought constantly to pray that God will be willing to enlighten us by his grace in Jesus Christ, so we ought carefully to guard ourselves against such prejudices and offences, which close off every access to Christ for us. "Blessed," Christ says, "is he who is not offended in me."

units.la: Est præterea quod obseruo in Nathanaële: Is fuit proculdubio qui credidit in Messiam venturum, vt apparet manifestò ex illa Christi commendatione quæ sequitur, Ecce vere Israelita, in quo dolus non est. Verè Israelita esse non potuit Nathanael absque fide aliqua, nam fides est Christi stola quæ purgat corda nostra à dolo & quacunque immunditie. Etsi igitur Nathanael iam progressum aliquem fecisset in via illa quæ ducit ad Christum, nunc offenditur humilitate Nazareth, impediturque ne statim credat in Christum præsentem. Non tantum igitur iis qui iam primum ingrediuntur viam quae ad Christum, offensionibus & præiudiciis præcluditur adytus ad Christum: verum etiam ij qui progressi
units.tr: Moreover, there is something else I observe about Nathanael. He was without doubt one who believed that the Messiah would come, as is plain from the commendation of Christ that follows: "Behold a true Israelite, in whom is no guile." Nathanael could not have been a true Israelite without some faith, for faith is the robe of Christ, which cleanses our hearts from guile and every uncleanness. Although Nathanael had already made some progress on that way which leads to Christ, he is now offended by the lowliness of Nazareth and is hindered from believing at once in Christ who is present. Therefore the approach to Christ is barred by offences and prejudices not only to those who are just entering the way that leads to him, but also to those who have advanced

units.la: Animalis hominis varia scandala. Etiam qui progressus fecerunt in stadio pietatis, nonnunquam graviter impingunt. sum etiam maiorem fortassis hoc Nathanaelis progressu fecerunt in via qua venitur ad Christum, impediuntur nonnunquam, iniectis huiusmodi offensionibus, ne inceptum iter conficiant, & ad metam pergant inoffenso cursu. Praecipuum autem illud est in quod impingunt, contempta scilicet conditio Nazareth, hoc est, humilitas crucis Christi quae imponitur Ecclesiae humeris, & comes est Euangelij. Timotheus magnum quidem progressum fecit in via Christi, Paulus tamen ad eum scripsit, Ne pudeat te testimonij Domini nostri Iesu Christi, neque te pudeat mei qui sum captivus ipsius, sed esto particeps afflictionum Euangelij ex potentia Dei. Qua Dei potentia nisi confirmatus fuisset Timotheus, bonus alioqui miles Iesu Christi, profecto cecidisset ac defecisset in incepto illo cursu, eumque puduisset vinculorum Pauli atque Euangelij. Nisi potentia Dei continuo sustentemur & promoveamur, omnes nos qui cursu eo corripimus, caro & sanguis nunquam nos docebit pati pro Christo. Quaobrem perpetuo nobis connitendum est ad hoc, ut sentiamus in nobis magis magisque potentiam illam & energiam Spiritus Christi, ut cum ventum fuerit ad certamen, decertemus secundum efficacitatem ipsius agentem in nobis poterit.
units.tr: The various stumbling-blocks of the natural man. Even those who have made progress in the course of piety sometimes fall heavily, and those who have perhaps advanced further than Nathanael did on the way that leads to Christ are sometimes hindered, when such offences are thrown in their path, so that they do not finish the journey they have begun and do not press on to the goal with an unobstructed course. The chief stumbling-block they strike against is, namely, the despised condition of Nazareth, that is, the lowliness of the cross of Christ, which is laid upon the shoulders of the Church and is the companion of the gospel. Timothy made great progress in the way of Christ, yet Paul wrote to him: "Be not ashamed therefore of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner; but be thou partaker of the afflictions of the gospel, according to the power of God." Unless Timothy had been strengthened by this power of God, he, otherwise a good soldier of Jesus Christ, would certainly have fallen and failed in that course he had begun, and would have been ashamed of Paul's chains and of the gospel. Unless we are continually sustained and advanced by the power of God, all of us who run that race will never be taught by flesh and blood to suffer for Christ. Therefore we must strive constantly towards this end, that we may feel in ourselves more and more that power and energy of the Spirit of Christ, so that when the time of the contest comes we may fight it according to the working of his effectiveness within us.

units.la: Sequitur tertia pars ministerij Philippi, qui cum non posset ipse nodum dissolvere & offensam removere, hominem ad Christum recta deducit, sperans fore ut si Christum ipsum semel videat atque audiat, scrupulus omnis ex animo ipsius eximatur. Sic & qui simpliciores sunt Ministri Christi, cum non possunt removere ea omnia quae infinita sunt, quibus offenduntur hodierno die adversarii, remittere eos debent ad Christum ipsum in Euangelio suo loquentem, ut ipsum si velint audiant: Nam si quis semel penitus videret Christum, & eius lumine irradiaretur, profecto nihil moraretur ista omnia, quibus alioqui tam facile offenditur. Vocatis, inquit Paulus, praedicatio Christi crucifixi Iudaeis quidem offendiculum est: Graecis vero stultitia est, vocatis, inquam, est Dei potentia ac Dei Sapientia. Nam humilitas crucis Christi qua tantopere homines offenduntur, haud dubie gloriosa videtur ei, qui Christi luce semel est illuminatus: & vincula ipsa Christi magis honorabilia videtur, quam omnia omnium Regum diademata: & mors ipsa videtur vita, & tenebrae lux videtur. Tantum esse experimur illud, semel videre Dominum, & illuminari splendore faciei ipsius.
units.tr: There follows the third part of Philip's ministry. He could not himself untie the knot and remove the offence, so he leads the man straight to Christ, hoping that if he once sees and hears Christ himself, every scruple will be removed from his mind. So too, those who are the simpler ministers of Christ, when they cannot remove all those countless things by which the adversaries of today are offended, ought to send them back to Christ himself speaking in his gospel, so that they may hear him if they are willing. For if anyone once truly saw Christ and were enlightened by his light, he would certainly not be held back by all those things by which otherwise he is so easily offended. "But we preach Christ crucified," says Paul, "unto the Jews a stumbling-block, and unto the Greeks foolishness; but unto them which are called, I say, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God." For the lowliness of the cross of Christ, by which men are so greatly offended, undoubtedly appears glorious to one who has once been illuminated by the light of Christ; and the very chains of Christ seem more honourable than all the diadems of all kings; and death itself seems life, and darkness seems light. We experience this so truly: to see the Lord once, and to be illumined by the splendour of his face.

units.la: 48 Vidit Iesus Nathanaelem venientem ad se, & dixit de eo, Ecce vere Israelita in quo dolus non est.
units.tr: 48 Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and said of him, Behold a true Israelite, in whom is no guile.

units.la: 49 Dixit ei Nathanael, unde me nosti? Respondit Iesus, & dixit ei, Priusquam te Philippus vocaret cum esses subter ficum videbam te.
units.tr: 49 Nathanael said to him, Whence knowest thou me? Jesus answered and said to him, Before Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee.

units.la: 50 Respondit Nathanael, & dixit ei, Rabbi, tu es ille filius Dei, Tu es ille Rex Israel.
units.tr: 50 Nathanael answered and said to him, Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel.

units.la: 51 Respondit Iesus, & dixit ei, quia dixi tibi, Vidi te sub ficu, credis, maiora istis videbis.
units.tr: 51 Jesus answered and said to him, Because I said to thee, I saw thee under the fig tree, dost thou believe? Thou shalt see greater things than these.

units.la: 52 Praeterea dixit ei, Amen, amen dico vobis, ab hoc tempore videbitis coelum apertum & Angelos Dei ascendentes ac descendentes super filium hominis.
units.tr: 52 Moreover he said to him, Verily, verily I say unto you, Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.

units.la: HActenus fuit Ministerium Philippi: Sequitur efficax vocatio ipsius Christi. Primum adducit Nathanaelem, ut credat ipsum esse filium Dei & regem Israelis: deinde promittit revelationem fuiorem ei, qui credidit, dicenti, vidi te sub ficu. Sic igitur Nathanaelis fidem conciliat: Iesus, inquit, vidit Nathanaelem venientem ad se, & dixit de eo, iis nimirum qui adstabat, ita tamen, ut audiri posset ab ipso Nathanaele appropinquante ad Dominum; Nam Nathanael statim excepit dixitque, unde me nosti? dixit igitur Iesus, Ecce vere Israelita in quo dolus non est. Filius Dei qui scit quid sit in homine, Iohan. 2. 25. scrutatus est profunditates cordis Nathanaelis, animaduersaque cordis sinceritate ac rectitudine interiori, ab ea pronunciauit hominem verè Israelitam: quasi dixisset, complures sunt qui gloriatur, hac quasi larua & inani titulo Israelita; En Israelitam qui verè & in occulto Israelita est. Primum video ex hoc loco id verum esse quod dicit Paulus, Non qui est in propatulo Iudaeus, Iudaeus est, nec ea quae carnis. est in propatulo circumcisio, id est in carne, circumcisio est, sed qui in occulto Iudaeus est, & circumcisio cordis, id est in spiritu, non litera. Quasi dicat, qui nomine tenus duntaxat & professione Christianus est, non est Christianus: sed qui corde tenus Christianus est, is demum vere Christianus est. Deinde video verum esse, quod eodem loco subiungit Paulus: Cuius Iudaei laus non est ex hominibus sed ex Deo: Deus approbat vere Christianum hominem. Filius Dei commendavit Nathanaelem. Quare imprimis studendum est sinceritati cordis, ad hoc ut & vere Christiani simus, & ut a Deo approbemur: neque contenti esse debemus quantumvis gloriosa operum specie, nisi ipsi in nobis sentiamus hanc integritatem & cordis sinceritatem. Si non reperiamus in nobis ipsis ea quam volumus sinceritatem, certe doleamus, dolor enim est initium emendationis, & aliquo etiam loco est apud Deum, si verus sit & secundum Deum: Nam vel est aliqua conscientia cum non sincere agis, vel nulla. Quod si sit aliqua conscientia accusans, ac proinde Deus qui potentior est corde & conscientia tua damnans, tu profecto necesse est ferio doleas, neque placeas tibi, etiam cum omnes mortales te collaudant. Si enim nos Deus non approbat, quis approbabit? Si Deus nos condemnat, quis absoluet? Sin nulla tibi sit facti conscientia, sed placeas tibi in hypocrisi tua, tum certe egregius es hypocrita, qui scias non tantum aliorum oculos celare, verum etiam tuos ipsius, non tantum aliis mentiri, sed etiam tibi. Detrahetur tibi aliquando haec larua, & aliquando senties conscientiae stimulum velis nolis: praestat quidem citius quam serius conscientiam afficiet, ut aliquis sit respiscentiae locus. Quare ut illud repetam, studendum est perpetuo cordis sinceritati, ut laetaris & conscientiae testimonio, & Dei ipsius approbatione. Quod si Deus nos approbat, quis condemnabit? Beati mundo corde, ait Dominus, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Quo significat in mundo puroque corde apparere & resplendere Dei aeterni faciem, ut in speculo purgato fulgens imago liquide conspicitur. Sed unde ista vel conscientiae, vel Dei approbatio, cum nulla sit vel in optimis quibusque sinceritatis perfectio? An vel conscientia nostra, vel Deus approbabit quod imperfectum est? Unde fuit quòd Filius Dei approbârit Nathanaelem, ut demus quidem aliqua ex parte tamen non perfectè sincerum? Respôdeo, fides in Iesum Christum & in ipsius iustitiam ac summam perfectionem itategere illum in nobis defectum omnem, ut in conspectu Dei & rationem non veniat. Praeterea efficere, ut illa sinceritas quantulacunque & à conscientia & à Deo ipso acceptetur. Nam Deus per fidem in Christum acceptu habet tum opera renatorum imperfecta, tum imprimis ipsas personas non plane in hac vita sanctificatas. Videamus igitur primum omnium ut simus in fide Christi, per quam primum accepimus hanc inchoatam in nobis sinceritatem, nam fide purgatur corda nostra. Deinde inchoata ista sinceritas propter eandem hanc fidem à Deo acceptatur. Dominus igitur det nobis, ut ea qua decet fide Iesum Christū apprehendamus eumque in cordibus nostris penitus viventem sentiamus: Cui sit omnis honor & gloria, Amen.
units.tr: Hitherto has been the ministry of Philip; now follows the effectual calling of Christ himself. First he brings Nathanael to believe that he is the Son of God and the King of Israel; then he promises a greater revelation to him who has believed, saying, "I saw thee under the fig tree." So he wins over Nathanael's faith. Jesus, it says, saw Nathanael coming to him and spoke of him, evidently to those who stood by, yet so that it could be heard by Nathanael himself as he drew near to the Lord; for Nathanael at once took it up and said, "Whence knowest thou me?" Then Jesus said, "Behold a true Israelite, in whom is no guile." The Son of God, who knows what is in man (John 2:25), searched the depths of Nathanael's heart, and, observing the sincerity and inward uprightness of his heart, pronounced from that the man to be a true Israelite. It is as if he had said: many glory in the title of Israelite, which is a kind of mask and empty name; behold an Israelite who is truly and inwardly an Israelite. From this passage I see first that what Paul says is true: "He is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter." As if to say: one who is a Christian only in name and profession is not a Christian; but one who is a Christian in his heart is at last truly a Christian. Next I see that what Paul adds in the same place is true: "Whose praise is not of men, but of God": God approves the man who is truly a Christian. The Son of God commended Nathanael. Therefore, above all, we must labour for sincerity of heart, so that we may truly be Christians and be approved by God; and we ought not to be content with however glorious an appearance of works, unless we ourselves feel this integrity and sincerity of heart within us. If we do not find in ourselves the sincerity that we want, let us certainly grieve, for grief is the beginning of amendment, and it has some value with God too, if it is genuine and according to God. For either there is some conscience when you do not act sincerely, or there is none. If there is some accusing conscience, and therefore God, who is mightier than your heart and conscience, condemns you, then you must surely grieve, and not be pleased with yourself, even when all mortals praise you. For if God does not approve us, who will approve us? If God condemns us, who will absolve us? But if you have no awareness of your deed, and are pleased with yourself in your hypocrisy, then you are indeed an outstanding hypocrite, who knows how to hide not only the eyes of others but also your own, and to lie not only to others but also to yourself. This mask will at some time be stripped from you, and at some time you will feel the goad of conscience whether you will or no; it is better that it should touch you sooner rather than later, so that there may be room for repentance. Therefore, to repeat what I have said: we must always strive for sincerity of heart, so that we may rejoice both in the testimony of conscience and in the approval of God himself. And if God approves us, who will condemn us? "Blessed are the pure in heart," says the Lord, "for they shall see God" (Matt. 5:8). By this he signifies that the face of the eternal God appears and shines in a pure and clean heart, as a bright image is clearly seen in a polished mirror. But whence comes this approval, either of conscience or of God, since there is no perfection of sincerity even in the best of men? Will either our conscience or God approve what is imperfect? How was it that the Son of God approved Nathanael, if we grant that he was sincere only in part and not perfectly? I answer: faith in Jesus Christ, and in his righteousness and supreme perfection, covers over every defect in us, so that it does not come into the sight of God; and moreover it brings it about that this sincerity, however small, is accepted both by conscience and by God himself. For God accepts through faith in Christ both the imperfect works of the regenerate and, above all, the persons themselves, which are not wholly sanctified in this life. Let us therefore first of all see that we are in the faith of Christ, through which we first received this sincerity begun in us, for our hearts are cleansed by faith. Then this begun sincerity is accepted by God on account of that same faith. May the Lord therefore grant us to apprehend Jesus Christ with the faith that befits us, and to feel him living deeply in our hearts: to whom be all honour and glory, Amen.

units.la: Hactenus loquutus est Christus: Nunc respondet Nathanaelē, unde me nosti? Nathanaelì ante-hac non erat Christus de facie cognitus: Miratur itaque Christum de se loqui, tanquam homine noto. Hinc illud video propositum Christo fuisse, ut manifestam faceret Nathanaēli deitatem suam ex admirabili illa, & planè divina sapientia, quam cum prodidit, cùm Nathanaelem venientem ad se verè Israëlitam pronunciavit. Hoc autem ideo Christo propositum fuit, ut Nathanaēl crederet in ipsum, confiteretúrque ipsum Filium Dei & regem Israëlis, id quod postea ab eo factum legemus. Discimus igitur, præsertim nos, quibus à Deo concreditum est gloriosum hoc ministerium, quid nobis propositū habere debeamus: Nempe ut credant homines, Credere autem non possunt, nisi substernatur ante omnia fundamentum fidei, id quod fecit Christus hoc loco. Neque enim fides potest cōsistere nisi solido nitatur fundamento: quodnam autem fundamentum subiicien-dum sit, & Christus hoc loco docuit, & Paulus, dicens, fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere præter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus. Deducenda igitur fides ad Christum vt eo nitatur, præsertim autem deducenda est ad deitatem Christi;id quod factum est à Christo hoc loco. Nam fides primum ac proprie apprehendit in Christo deitatem, apprehendit quoque humanitatem, sed ratione hypostaticæ illius vnionis duarum naturarum, cuius virtute credimus etiam in Christum hominem ac proinde creaturam: quia nunquam homo Deus est. Alias vero, si consideretur humana natura seorsim adiuina, (cum tamen nunquam ab ea separetur reipsa) tum verum est quod Christus ait, postea, Spiritus est qui vivifi-cat, caro non prodest quicquam: nempe caro separatim accepta & considerata, vt male ac crasse Capernaitæ ea consideràrunt tum, cum Christus dixit comedendam esse suam carnem ad vitam æternam. Quamobrem vt in summa dicam, cum credendum nobis sit in Patrem tanquam Deum tantum, in Spiritum Sanctum tanquam Deum tantum, credendum est in Filium tanquam Deum & hominem, vtpote Mediatorem. Neque vero patres ipsi iam olim ante manifestationem filii Dei in carne, in eum crediderunt nisi suo tempore manifestandum in carne.
units.tr: Hitherto Christ has spoken. Now he answers Nathanael: "How do you know me?" Christ had not previously been known to Nathanael by sight, so Nathanael marvels that Christ speaks of him as though he were a man known to him. Here I see that Christ's purpose was to make his divinity plain to Nathanael by that wonderful and truly divine wisdom, which he showed when he declared that Nathanael, coming to him, was a true Israelite. Christ had this purpose so that Nathanael would believe in him and confess him to be the Son of God and King of Israel, which we shall read was afterwards done by him. We learn therefore, especially we to whom this glorious ministry has been entrusted by God, what we ought to aim at: namely, that men believe. But they cannot believe unless the foundation of faith is first laid down, which Christ did in this place. For faith cannot stand unless it rests on a firm foundation. What foundation ought to be laid, Christ taught here, and Paul too, saying: No one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Faith must therefore be led to Christ so that it may rest on him, and especially must be led to the divinity of Christ, which Christ did in this place. For faith first and properly apprehends in Christ his divinity, and it also apprehends his humanity, but by reason of that hypostatic union of the two natures, by whose power we believe also in Christ as man, and therefore as creature, because the man is never God. But otherwise, if the human nature is considered apart from the divine (although it is never in fact separated from it), then what Christ says afterwards is true: It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing. That is, flesh taken and considered by itself, as the Capernaites badly and crassly considered it when Christ said that his flesh was to be eaten for eternal life. Therefore, to sum up: we must believe in the Father as God only, and in the Holy Spirit as God only, but we must believe in the Son as God and man, as Mediator. Nor indeed did the fathers of old believe in him before the manifestation of the Son of God in the flesh, except as he was to be manifested in the flesh in his own time.

units.la: Hactenus Nathanaël, deinde Christus excipit, vidi priusquam te Philippus vocaret, quum esses sub ficu videbam te, addita est circumstantia loci, quo magis sapientiam suam ipsi probaret. Videmus igitur inuestiganti Nathanaëli nouam reuelationem fieri. quanto magis quis inquiret in imperuestigabiles illas opes Christi, tanto maiorem accipit reuelationem ad hoc vt magis magisque fides ipsius confirmetur, capiatque incrementum. Nam quo quis plura videt in eo Christi mysterio, eo magis credit & diligit: Ex fide & dilectione, ait Petrus, exstitit gaudium ineffabile & gloriosum. Quare hic noster labor debet esse perpetuus, vt dies noctesque cum precibus & assidua meditatione ac lectione sacrarum scripturarum inquiramus in mysterium illud Christi, vt tandem aperiantur nobis illi thesauri omnis intelligentiæ & cognitionis qui in ipso sunt: Et omnia sunt nobis pro stercoribus ducenda vt ipsum lucrifaciamus, & reperiamur in eo nô habentes nostram iustitiam, sed eam quæ per fidem est Christi. Mirum est videre vt nunquam satisfaciat sibi Paulus aliíque Christi Apostoli in experimenda illa Dei infinita in Christo misericordia. Deus, inquit, qui dives est misericordia, propter multam charitatem suam quam dilexit nos, &c. Et in exprimenda illa plenitudine gratiæ, quæ est in Christo : In quo, inquit, sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ & cognitionis abscondituri. In exprimenda denique illa gloria & hæreditate vitæ æternæ, Ut valeatis, inquit, videre quæ sunt opes gloriæ hæreditatis ipsius in sanctis. Unde est id quod tam graviter & magnifice de his loquatur : Nempe quia plurimum vidit in illo Christi mysterio, & plurimum credidit. Hæc & similia dum inter legendum occurrunt in scriptis sanctorum hominum, accendere nos debent ad inquirendum in illud mysterium, ad hoc ut magis magisque quærentes plura in dies videamus in Christo, & augescamus in cognitione, fide & lætitia.
units.tr: So far Nathanael; then Christ takes up the word: Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you. The circumstance of place is added so that he might prove his wisdom to him more fully. We see therefore that a new revelation is made to Nathanael as he inquires. The more anyone inquires into the unsearchable riches of Christ, the greater the revelation he receives, so that his faith may be more and more confirmed and may grow. For the more a man sees in that mystery of Christ, the more he believes and loves. From faith and love, says Peter, there arises joy unspeakable and full of glory. Hence our labour ought to be constant: day and night, with prayers and constant meditation and reading of the holy Scriptures, we should search into that mystery of Christ, so that at last those treasures of all understanding and knowledge that are in him may be opened to us. All things must be counted as dung for the sake of gaining him, and that we may be found in him, not having our own righteousness but that which is through the faith of Christ. It is remarkable to see how Paul and the other apostles of Christ are never satisfied in expressing that infinite mercy of God in Christ. God, he says, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, etc. And in expressing that fullness of grace which is in Christ: In whom, he says, are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Lastly, in expressing that glory and inheritance of eternal life: That you may know, he says, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints. Hence it is that he speaks so weightily and magnificently of these things: namely, because he saw much in that mystery of Christ and believed much. When such things and similar ones occur in reading the writings of holy men, they ought to kindle us to inquire into that mystery, so that by seeking more and more we may see more in Christ each day, and grow in knowledge, faith and joy.

units.la: Non est prætereundum hoc loco quod Christus vidderit Nathanaelem quo tempore Nathanael Christum vicissim non vidit : nam ne tum quidem vidit Dominum cum vocaretur ad ipsum ministerio Philippi. Christus igitur videt nos quo tempore nos ipsum vicissim non videmus : cogitat de nobis quo tempore nos de eo vicissim non cogitamus. Ut autem sic fiat necesse est, si enim vocatio nostri tantisper differretur, dum nos ipsum priores videremus; nunquam profecto segregandi essemus ab inquinamentis huius mundi. Quoniam autem ille prior nos videt, ideo suo tempore nos vocat ad se. Quod si igitur Christus vidit nos, quo tempore nos non vidimus ipsum, quanto magis nunc videt nos, & sumus nos curæ illi, cum nos vicissim ipsum videmus? Sic enim argumentatur Paulus a minori ad maius : Si cum inimici essemus reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem filii eius, multo magis reconciliati servabimur per vitam ipsius. Mirifica est illa tura Dei & charitas erga homines, præsertim postea quam vocati sunt & iustificati per sanguinem filii sui. Quam charitatem precamur, ut velit per Spiritum suum sanctum effundere in cordibus nostris, ut attacto sensu charitatis ipsius erga nos, nos vicissim eum diligamus, adeo ut possimus cum Paulo dicere amorem Christi nos constringere & totos occupare. Hoc igitur quod in Christi conspectu sumus perpetuo, nobis debet esse consolationi; debet etiam efficere, ut accurate ambulemus in hac vita tanquam in conspectu Dei, ne quid admittamus indignum oculis tantae maiestatis. Quod ut fieri possit nobis danda est opera ut cor nostrum habeamus semper conuersum ad Dominum, ad hoc, ut auferatur hoc velamen quod impositum semel cordi, ita nos excaecat ut Dominum non videamus amplius: Quem dum non videmus, necesse est inquinamentis mundi nos implicemus.
units.tr: It is not to be passed over here that Christ saw Nathanael at the time when Nathanael did not in turn see Christ; for Nathanael did not see the Lord even when he was called to him by the ministry of Philip. Christ therefore sees us at the time when we in turn do not see him; he thinks of us at the time when we in turn do not think of him. For this to happen is necessary: if our calling were delayed until we first saw him, we would certainly never be set apart from the defilements of this world. But since he sees us first, therefore at his own time he calls us to himself. If then Christ saw us at the time when we did not see him, how much more does he now see us, and are we an object of his care, now that we in turn see him? For Paul argues in this way from the less to the greater: If when we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, shall we be saved by his life. Wonderful is that tenderness and love of God towards men, especially after they have been called and justified through the blood of his Son. We pray that he will be pleased to pour out this love in our hearts through his Holy Spirit, so that, having touched the sense of his love towards us, we may in turn love him, so that we may say with Paul that the love of Christ constrains us and wholly occupies us. Therefore the fact that we are constantly in the sight of Christ ought to be a comfort to us; it ought also to bring it about that we walk carefully in this life as in the sight of God, so that we admit nothing unworthy in the eyes of such majesty. To make this possible, we must take pains to keep our heart always turned to the Lord, so that that veil which, once placed on the heart, so blinds us that we no longer see the Lord, may be taken away. While we do not see him, we must necessarily entangle ourselves in the defilements of the world.

units.la: Sequitur confessio quaedam praeclara Nathanaelis: Rabbi, inquit, tu es ille Filius Dei, Tu es Rex ille Israel prius non est praefatus honorem, cum sic sermonem exordiretur, Unde me nosti? Nunc vero observata eius excellentia ac maiestate quocum sermone habuit, Rabbi, inquit, tu es Filius Dei, &c. Praemisso nomine illo ab excellentia personae sumpto, ut supra annotavimus. Quod si maiestas illa Dei nobis innotesceret, profecto magis reuerenter de ea & sentiremus & loqueremur quam solemus, tantum abesset ab eo ut sic vulgo erumperemus in horrendas blasphemias. Sed consideremus ipsa confessionis verba, Tu, inquit, es Filius Dei. Confessio primum est personae, nempe quod sit Dei filius, factus caro. Deinde Confessio est officij, Tu es ille Rex Israel: Hoc est populi tui peculiaris & Ecclesiae tuae. Cum enim videret eum Dei Filium esse, eumque incarnatum, statim cogitauit apud se & confessus est eum esse Messiam illum promissum, quem expectabat venturum, qui vnctus est in Regem, Prophetam & Sacerdotem: Quamquam nominatim de regno Christi loquutus est. Hac confessione officij Filium Dei propius ad se applicauit; nam nisi concipiamus animo Dei Filium affectum aliquo modo erga nos, nostrum Regem, nostrum Prophetam, nostrum Sacerdotem esse, profecto non appropinquabimus ad eum. Dum vero concipimus atque apprehendimus benè affectum erga nos miseros peccatores, & amantem nostri Dei Filium, qui est tantae potentiae ac maiestatis, tum quidem appropinquamus ad eum, & fide ad eum accedimus familiariter. Hinc est illa consolatio in Christo Iesu, de qua Apostolus scribit ad Philippenses. Unde mihi persuadere videor Papistas qui negant illam Dei iustitiam, quae est per solam fidem Christi, nunquam percipere eam consolationem quae est in Christo Iesu.
units.tr: There follows a notable confession by Nathanael: Rabbi, he says, you are that Son of God, you are that King of Israel. Before, when he began his speech with How do you know me?, he had not prefaced it with any honour. But now, having observed the excellence and majesty of the one with whom he was speaking, he says: Rabbi, you are the Son of God, etc., having prefaced it with that title taken from the excellence of the person, as we noted above. If that majesty of God were made known to us, we would certainly both feel and speak of it more reverently than we usually do, and we would be far from breaking out so commonly into dreadful blasphemies. But let us consider the very words of the confession: You, he says, are the Son of God. The confession is first of the person, namely that he is the Son of God made flesh. Then the confession is of office: You are that King of Israel, that is, of your peculiar people and of your Church. For when he saw that he was the Son of God, and that he had been made incarnate, he immediately thought to himself and confessed that he was that promised Messiah whom he was expecting to come, who was anointed as King, Prophet and Priest; although he spoke by name of the kingdom of Christ. By this confession of office he drew the Son of God nearer to himself. For unless we conceive in our minds that the Son of God is in some way disposed towards us as our King, our Prophet and our Priest, we will certainly not draw near to him. But when we conceive and apprehend that he is well disposed towards us miserable sinners, and that the Son of our God, who is of such power and majesty, loves us, then indeed we draw near to him, and by faith we come to him familiarly. Hence comes that consolation in Christ Jesus of which the Apostle writes to the Philippians. From this I seem to myself to be persuaded that the Papists, who deny that righteousness of God which is through the faith of Christ alone, never perceive that consolation which is in Christ Jesus.

units.la: Quaeri hic potest, an sola illa reuelatio & obseruatio diuinae illius sapientiae Christi adduxerit Nathanaelem ad hanc tam praeclaram confessionem? Respondeo, Christus quaerit ex discipulis suis, Quem me, inquiens, dicitis esse? Respondet Petrus, Tu es Christus ille Filius Dei viuentis. Quid hic Christus? An respondet, Petre, quia vidisti opera, quae ego feci & admirabilem meam potentiam, sapientiam, &c. ideo hanc de me confessionem edidisti? Imo non sic, Sed, beatus, inquit, es Simon Bar-Iona, quia caro & sanguis haec non retexit tibi, sed Pater meus qui in caelis est. Vidit quidem Petrus multo plura miracula & opera Christi quam Nathanael: hanc tamen confessionem Petri ascripsit Christus non miraculis, sed virtutis Spiritus Dei ac Patri, qui traxit eum ad hoc ut ad filium veniret. Quare ne illa quidem admirabilis sapientia Christi quam obseruauit Nathanael, eum adduxisset eo, ut confiteretur Dominum nisi interius doctus fuisset a Deo. Finge tibi Deum palam e coelis descendere & omnia miracula in conspectu hominum edere, non efficient profecto omnia, ut vel unus aliquis homuncio credat, nisi adsit interior illa Spiritus Sancti efficacia quae auersum a Deo & Christo cor immutatur, quod quidem maius est opus Dei & magis admirabile opus, inquam, hoc in mutandis hominum cordibus, quam sunt omnia miracula externa, quam fuit hominis ipsa prima creatio. Nam regeneratione hanc quam vocant, ego maiorem existimo, quam primam illam hominis creationem. Fieri quidem potest ut admirabilia Dei opera extorqueant nonnunquam confessionem vel ipsi diabolo: sed confessio huiusmodi iam non est voluntaria, verum inuito extorta, corde non mutato quidem, sed cōsternato & vi quasi maiori ad tempus subacto, quod statim postea redibit ad ingenium suum. Quamobrem nisi Spiritus sanctus immutet prius animum, fieri non potest ut quis confiteatur præsertim Christum: Natura enim habemus Dei aliquam notitiam, etsi obscuram illam: natura etiam confitemur Deum aliquem, vbi etiam est aliqua cordis assensio. Sed cum ventum est ad Filium Dei incarnatum, crucifixum & glorificatum, hic prorsus cæcutimus, & tantum abest, vt ei assentiamur, vt è contra eum prorsus auersemur. Nemo potest dicere Dominum Christum nisi per Spiritum sanctum. Quare beatus est qui-quis sentit in se hunc liberū cordis assensum, quo confiteatur Iesum esse Filium Dei, & dicat Iesum Dominum: nam caro & sanguis non reuelarunt ista, sed {x}Οὐ-ρανὸς est. O si Pater cœlestis det nobis liberam hanc cordis assensionem & apertam hac oris confessionem, qua credamus & confiteamur cum Nathanaële Iesum esse Filium Dei & regem Israëlis!
units.tr: Here one may ask whether the mere revelation and observation of Christ's divine wisdom led Nathanael to this so remarkable confession. I answer that Christ asks his disciples, Whom do you say that I am? Peter answers, You are that Christ, the Son of the living God. What does Christ say to this? Does he answer, "Peter, did you make this confession about me because you saw the works I have done and my wonderful power and wisdom?" No, not at all. Rather he says, Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. Peter certainly saw many more miracles and works of Christ than Nathanael did, yet Christ ascribed Peter's confession not to the miracles but to the power of the Spirit of God and of the Father, who drew him to come to the Son. Therefore even that admirable wisdom of Christ which Nathanael observed would not have brought him to confess the Lord, unless he had been taught inwardly by God. Imagine God descending openly from heaven and performing all the miracles before people's eyes: all of these would certainly not bring even one poor man to believe, unless there were that inward efficacy of the Holy Spirit by which a heart turned away from God and Christ is changed. This is indeed a greater work of God, and a more admirable work, I say, in changing human hearts, than all the external miracles, or than the very first creation of man. For I consider that regeneration, as they call it, to be greater than that first creation of man. It is true that the wonderful works of God may sometimes wring a confession even from the devil himself; but such a confession is no longer voluntary, but forced from one who is unwilling, the heart not indeed changed but dismayed and for a time subdued by a kind of greater force, which soon returns to its own disposition. Therefore unless the Holy Spirit first changes the mind, it is impossible that anyone should confess, especially Christ. For by nature we have some knowledge of God, though it is obscure; by nature too we confess that there is some God, where there is also some assent of the heart. But when we come to the Son of God incarnate, crucified and glorified, here we are utterly blind, and so far from assenting to him, we turn completely away from him. No one can say that Jesus is the Lord except by the Holy Spirit. Blessed, therefore, is whoever perceives in himself this free assent of the heart, by which he confesses that Jesus is the Son of God and says that Jesus is Lord; for flesh and blood have not revealed these things, but the Father who is in heaven. O that the heavenly Father would give us this free assent of the heart and this open confession of the mouth, by which we may believe and confess with Nathanael that Jesus is the Son of God and the King of Israel!

units.la: Hactenus adductus est Nathanael eo vt credat & confiteatur; Nunc Christus admiratus eius fidem promittit reuelationem ampliorem: Quia dixi tibi, vidi te sub ficu, credis, maiora his videbis. Quæri potest hoc loco, annon leui de causa & reuelatione inductus sit Nathanael ad credendum Christum esse Filium Dei? Potuit enim Propheta aliquis tantundem Nathanaeli reuelare. Achija vxori Ieroboami ad se ingressæ, quæ naranDo in animo habuit præoccupauit expositque ea priusquam ipsa narrare posset. Elisa expositi Regi Israelis consilia quæ Rex Syriæ in conclavi priuatim tractarat. Petrus intuitus est animum & occultam fraudem Ananiæ & Sapphiræ.
