Cum igitur potuerit Propheta aliquis tantum reuelare Nathanaeli, quantum est ipsi à Christo reuelatum, cur tam cito inductus est ad credendum in eum, non tanquam Prophetam aliquem, sed tanquam Dei ipsius Filium? Respondeo primum, latum esse discrimen inter alios homines, qui Prophetæ erant ac Christum quo ad ipsam illam notitiam rerum communem alioqui: Prophetæ nihil earum rerum sciunt nisi id reuelate eis Christi Spiritu. Christus autem primū quatenus Deus omnia nouit ab æterno quæ pater, non quidè à se, sed à Patre, per se tamē non quidem per reuelationem, sed per generationē æternam, in qua Pater cū tota sua substantia comunicauit filio suo proprieprietates, vt ita loquar, quæ ipsi essentiales sunt, ipsaque adeo Dei infinita essentia, vt Sapientiam, Potentiá, &c. Quatenus autem homo est, scit omnia quæ vult, & quo tempore vult, per reuelationem non quidem alterius çuiusquam extra se, sed suiipsius. Nam cùm sit Deus & homo in vna persona, Deus qui habitat corporaliter in homine, imprimit menti humanæ omnium rerum notitiam pro captu creaturæ. Nam ne Christus quidem, qua est homo cum mente humana, capax est infinitæ illius sapientiæ, aut potentiæ, aut aliorum quæ in Deo sunt infinita. Hæc etsi in Christo homine infinita dici possint, si comparatio fiat cum aliis creaturis quibusuis (non enim huic admetitur Deus Spiritum) tamé simpliciter & respectu Dei infinita non sunt. Neque comparanda sunt cum infinita illa potentia, Sapientia, alíisque quæ in Deo essentialia sunt. Atque hoc est discrimen inter Christum & alios Prophetas ac sanctos viros qui reuelationibus claruerunt: de Christo enim dicitur, Non enim huic admetitur Deus Spiritum, hoc est dedit ei fontem ipsum Deitatis, cum omnibus donis, qui ex eo fonte promanant. Item supra de eò dictum est, quod commoratus sit inter Iudæos, plenus gratiæ & veritatis. At de aliis Paulus ait, Vnicuique nostrum data est gratia pro mensura doni Christi: Et supra hoc capite, Ex plenitudine ipsius omnes accepimus, & gratiam pro gratia.
units.tr: So far Nathanael has been brought to believe and confess. Now Christ, marvelling at his faith, promises him a fuller revelation: Because I told you that I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? You will see greater things than these. Here one may ask whether Nathanael was moved to believe that Christ is the Son of God for a slight cause and a slight revelation. For some prophet could have revealed as much to Nathanael. When the wife of Jeroboam came in to Ahijah, he anticipated her, intending to tell the matter in disguise, and declared what she was to say before she could speak. Elisha disclosed to the king of Israel the plans which the king of Syria had discussed privately in his chamber. Peter discerned the mind and the hidden fraud of Ananias and Sapphira. Since, then, some prophet could have revealed to Nathanael as much as was revealed to him by Christ, why was he so quickly moved to believe in him, not as some prophet, but as the very Son of God? I answer first that there is a great difference between other men, who were prophets, and Christ, as regards that common knowledge of things. The prophets know nothing of those things unless it is revealed to them by the Spirit of Christ. But Christ, in so far as he is God, knows from eternity all that the Father knows, not indeed from himself, but from the Father; and he has it through himself, not indeed through revelation, but through eternal generation, in which the Father, with his whole substance, has communicated to his Son those properties, so to speak, which are essential to himself, and indeed the very infinite essence of God, such as wisdom, power, and so on. But in so far as he is man, he knows all that he wills, and at the time he wills, not through a revelation from anyone outside himself, but from himself. For since he is God and man in one person, God who dwells bodily in the man impresses on the human mind knowledge of all things according to the capacity of a creature. For even Christ, as man with a human mind, is not capable of that infinite wisdom, or power, or the other things which are infinite in God. Although these may be called infinite in Christ the man, if the comparison is made with any other creatures (for God does not give the Spirit to him by measure), yet they are not infinite absolutely and in respect of God. Nor are they to be compared with that infinite power and wisdom and the other things which are essential in God. And this is the difference between Christ and the other prophets and holy men who were distinguished by revelations. For it is said of Christ, For God does not give the Spirit to him by measure, that is, he gave him the very fountain of the Godhead, with all the gifts which flow from that fountain. Likewise above it is said of him that he dwelt among the Jews, full of grace and truth. But of others Paul says, To each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ's gift; and above in this chapter, From his fullness we have all received, and grace upon grace.

units.la: Vt ad Nathanaëlem reuertamur, De eo sic æstiman-dū est: Vidit quidé Christum omnia sapere per se, nullo alio reuelante, ac proinde in eum credidit, vt filium Dei & Deum ipsum: quamquam id quoque verum est quod supra dixit Nathanaëlem à Deo non vulgariter doctum fuisse, & illustratum Spiritu Christi, vt hoc posset videre, & confiteri filium Dei. Nam Samaritana mulier de qua postea, non minorem reuelationem externa accepit adeóque etiam maiorem quàm Nathanaël, cùm diceret ei Christus, Quinque viros habuisti & nunc quem habes, non est tuus vir. Quid illa ad hæc? Video, inquit, te Prophetam esse. Nondum eum Messiâ esse ex hac reuelatione cognouit. Quare quoties reuelatur nobis hoc Christi mysterium, orandus est Deus, vt velit Spiritu suo illuminare oculos mentis nostræ, ad hoc, vt possimus videre illud abditum mysterium filij Dei. Nathanael igitur citò credidit accepta revelatione tenui aliqua, si externa respicias. Non pauci sunt qui nunquam credituri sunt, nec si millies audierint de Christo plurima: leges postea cap. 6. Christum luctatum esse cum incredulitate multitudinis, edito vtius illo opere multo maximo in ea pascenda miraculose, nihil tamen profecit. Alij sunt qui credunt tandem, sed aegrè & non nisi post multas revelationes & crebrā prædicationem. Samaritana illa mulier ægrius & tardius credidit quàm Nathanael: sed quis discreuit inter ipsos? An discrimen hoc est à natura? minimè. Natura enim, electorum & reproborum corda ante vocationem Dei efficacem ex æquo sunt clausa: neque electorum omnium quisquam est qui possit magis suis viribus resurgere ad nouam vitam, cum sit spiritualiter mortuus, quàm potuit se ipse in principio creare, cum nondum esset omnino. Quis igitur te discernit? inquit Paulus, Quid habes quod non accepisti? q.d. & respondeat, discrimen istud non est à teipso, sed à Deo, à quo solo habes illam prærogatiuam.
units.tr: To return to Nathanael, we must judge of him thus: he saw that Christ knew all things through himself, with no one else revealing them, and therefore he believed in him as the Son of God and God himself. Yet it is also true, as said above, that Nathanael was not taught in an ordinary way, but was illuminated by the Spirit of Christ so that he could see this and confess him as the Son of God. For the Samaritan woman, of whom we speak later, received an external revelation no less, and indeed greater than Nathanael's, when Christ said to her, You have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. How did she respond? I see, she said, that you are a prophet. From this revelation she did not yet recognise him as the Messiah. Therefore whenever this mystery of Christ is revealed to us, God must be prayed to, that he would be pleased by his Spirit to illuminate the eyes of our mind, so that we may see that hidden mystery of the Son of God. Nathanael therefore believed quickly, on receiving a revelation that was slight, if you look at the external matter. There are not a few who will never believe, even if they hear a thousand times the many things about Christ; you will read later, in chapter 6, that Christ struggled with the unbelief of the crowd, and though he performed that very great work of feeding the multitude miraculously, he achieved nothing. Others do believe at last, but with difficulty, and not until after many revelations and frequent preaching. That Samaritan woman believed more slowly and with greater difficulty than Nathanael. But who distinguished between them? Is this difference from nature? By no means. For by nature the hearts of the elect and of the reprobate are equally closed before God's effectual calling; and none of the elect is able to rise again to new life by his own powers, since he is spiritually dead, any more than he could create himself at the beginning, when he did not yet exist at all. Who then makes you different? says Paul: What do you have that you did not receive? As if to say, and let him answer, that this difference is not from yourself, but from God, from whom alone you have that privilege.

units.la: At Christus tamen admiratur suam ipsius gratiam & donum in Nathanaele: nam (vt hoc dicam obiter) cum admiratione fidem hominis prædicat, neque id immerito, cum admirabile quiddam sit fides, adeo vt ipse Dei filius, qui fidei largitor est, donum suum in admiratione habeat, & nosipsi quoque si consideraremus quales natura simus, quàm simus infideles natura, fidem imprimis admiraremur ac suspiceremus. Christus igitur in Nathanaele commendat donum suum, neque hoc tantum, sed etiam compensat quasi maiorum rerum revelatione. Maiora, inquit, his videbis. Vide primum immensam Dei gratiam: ex gratia accipimus donum, donum Spiritus Christi contagione carnis vitiatum: Approbat tamen Pater propter Christum, approbatum tandem nouo dono coronat. Vide deinde quanti faciat Dominus fidem semel inchoatam, nouis promissionibus perpetuo adauget, neque vnquam finit eam extingui is qui arundinem quassatam non frangit, aut linum fumigans non extinguit. Obserua rursus: Nathanael ad mediocrem revelationem tionem credit: Christus maiorem & clariorem maiestatis suæ manifestationem pollicetur. Omnes natura expetimus rerum cognitionem; cupiunt etiam non- nulli cognoscere illud Christi mysterium, sed Nathanaëlis exemplo cognoscendi rationem disce. Si vel tantillum de Christo tibi sit reuelatum, da operā primum ut illud corde credas, atque etiam si opus sit, ore confitearis. Quod si corde credas & Christum illum aliquatenus cognitum apprehendas, habes iam promissionem parefactionis maioris atque clarioris. Quod si accepta reuelatione non labores in fide cordis, satis habens si videaris tibi aliquid de Christo mente cognoscere, non habes profectò promissionem reuelationis ulterioris. Quod si tamen sæpe audiendo vel legendo plura cognoscas, neque interea credas vnquam corde, profectò cognitio illa tua nunquam solida erit, neque vnquam cor tibi constabilietur gratia. Inde est, quod videasferè idiotam aliquem in Christum serió credentem & corde sentientem magis ad ædificationem loqui de Christo, quàm eum qui sine fide & sensu multa potest de Christo garrire potius quàm loqui.
units.tr: But Christ nonetheless marvels at his own grace and gift in Nathanael. (To make this point in passing: he proclaims a person's faith with wonder, and rightly so, since faith is a wonderful thing. So much so that the Son of God himself, who is the giver of faith, holds his own gift in admiration. If we considered what we are by nature, and how unbelieving we are by nature, we too would first marvel at faith and look up to it.) Christ therefore commends his gift in Nathanael, and not only that, but he also makes up for it, as it were, by the revelation of greater things. "You will see greater things than these," he says. First, see the immense grace of God. We receive the gift by grace, a gift of the Spirit tainted by the contagion of the flesh. Yet the Father approves it for Christ's sake, and at last crowns what he has approved with a new gift. Next, see how highly the Lord values faith once begun. He constantly increases it with new promises, and he never allows it to be extinguished, for he is the one who does not break a bruised reed or quench a smoking flax. Observe again: Nathanael believes on a small revelation, and Christ promises a greater and clearer manifestation of his majesty. By nature we all desire knowledge of things, and some want to know that mystery of Christ. But learn the way of knowing from Nathanael's example. If even a little about Christ has been revealed to you, first take care to believe it in your heart, and, if need be, to confess it with your mouth. If you believe with your heart and grasp Christ, known in some measure, you already have the promise of a greater and clearer disclosure. But if, having received the revelation, you do not labour in faith of the heart, being content if you seem to yourself to know something of Christ in your mind, then you certainly do not have the promise of a further revelation. If, however, by often hearing or reading you come to know more, and yet never believe in your heart, that knowledge of yours will certainly never be solid, and grace will never establish your heart. Hence it is that one sees, as a rule, an unlearned man who seriously believes in Christ and feels it in his heart speak of Christ more for edification than one who, without faith and feeling, can chatter about Christ at length, rather than speak of him.

units.la: Hactenus fuit propositio reuelationis & cognitionis rerum maiorum: Sequitur vltimo capitis versu decia- ratio propositionis, in qua expressa fit mentio rerum earum quas dixit maiores. Declaratio fit per apostrophen ad omnes discipulos quotquot præsentes fuerūt. Preterea dixit ei, Amen, amen, &c. deinceps videbitis, &c.
units.tr: So far has been the proposition of revelation and knowledge of greater things. There follows, in the last verse of the chapter, the explanation of the proposition, in which mention is expressly made of those things which he called greater. The explanation is made by an address to all the disciples who were present: "Moreover he said to them, Verily, verily, etc.; hereafter you shall see, etc."

units.la: Hæc est declaratio & speciali promissio: vt autem consulat discipulorum incredulitati & infirmitati, cum graui asseuratione suo more, promittit Deus iureiurando, & asseueratione ad promissionem addita, arguit primum mirificam indulgentiam erga incredulitatem nostram, quæ superat captum omnium Angelorum simul & hominum. Quis enim vnquam crederet futurum, vt Deus oppignoraret nostra causa suam ipsius gloriam (id quod facit dum iurat) & vltrò obligaret se adauctuaram faciendam gloriæ suæ nisi stet promissis? Arguit deinde, si nos interea perstemus in incredulitate, admirabilem ingratitudinem nostram & duritiem cordium nostrorum, plusquam ferream. Promissiones gra-
units.tr: This is the explanation and the special promise. But in order to meet the unbelief and weakness of the disciples, God, in his customary manner, with a solemn asseveration, promises with an oath; and by adding the asseveration to the promise, he first demonstrates a wonderful indulgence towards our unbelief, which surpasses the grasp of all angels and men together. For who would ever believe that God would pledge his own glory for our sake (which he does when he swears), and would bind himself to increase and to make his glory, unless he stood by his promises? Then he shows, if we meanwhile persist in unbelief, our admirable ingratitude and the hardness of our hearts, harder than iron. The promises of grace

units.la: F Hebr.6.17. tiæ in Christo iureiurando confirmatæ sunt omnes. Hinc fiet vt quotquot condenabuntur in illo die, de iis loquor qui de promissionibus his audiuerūt aliquid in hac vita, condemnandi sint, non tam adulteri, non tam homicidij, nō tam violatæ Legis omnino, quàm incredulitatis, & summæ ingratitudinis: Quòd si enim credidissent, omnia illa de quibus dixi remissa fuissent. Damnandi igitur sunt infidelitatis, quia non crediderunt promissionibus gratiæ in Christo: damnandi sunt mirificę& incredibilis infidelitatis, quia ne iuratis quidem promissionibus crediderunt. Oportet igitur damnationem esse grauissimam, quandoquidem tam horrendum sit & nefarium. deinceps, inquit, videbitis cælum apertum. Dixit Nathanaeli soli prius, ipsum maiora his visurum: nunc vero promissionem facit omnibus qui vna aderant: vos videbitis, inquiens. Qua re significat promissiones novi testamenti in Christo sic particulares esse, vt sint quoque vniuersales: rursus sic vniuersales esse, vt sint quoque particulares; Quod vni dicit Deus, omnibus dicit, quod omnibus dicit, vni dicit. Quare cum Nathanaelem solum compellaret semel atque iterum his verbis, maiora his videbis. Ex, praeterea dixit ei, admonuit eum vt promissionem in genere concipiendam, in specie ad se applicaret; secus enim quam consolationem potuisset ex ea capere. Nulla enim consolatio est ex generali illa Papistarum fide: verùm ex speciali fiducia, hoc est ex particulari ad vnumquemque nostrum gratię & misericordiæ applicatione.
units.tr: Heb. 6.17. are all confirmed by an oath in Christ. From this it will come about that all who will be condemned on that day, and I speak of those who have heard something of these promises in this life, will be condemned not so much for adultery, not so much for murder, nor for breaking the Law in general, as for unbelief and the greatest ingratitude. For if they had believed, all those things of which I have spoken would have been forgiven. They are to be condemned, therefore, for unfaithfulness, because they did not believe the promises of grace in Christ. They are to be condemned for a wonderful and incredible unfaithfulness, because they did not believe even promises confirmed by an oath. Therefore the damnation must be most grievous, since the sin is so dreadful and wicked. "Hereafter," he says, "you shall see heaven opened." He had said before to Nathanael alone that he would see greater things than these; now, however, he makes the promise to all who were present together: "You," he says, "shall see." By this he signifies that the promises of the New Testament in Christ are so particular that they are also universal, and again so universal that they are also particular. What God says to one, he says to all; what he says to all, he says to one. Therefore, when he addressed Nathanael alone, once and again, with these words, "You shall see greater things than these," and then added, "Verily, verily, I say to you," he admonished him to conceive the promise in general, but to apply it to himself in particular. Otherwise he could not have derived any comfort from it. For there is no comfort in that general faith of the Papists, but only in a special trust, that is, in the particular application of grace and mercy to each one of us.

units.la: Venio nunc ad promissionem ipsam, Vos videbitis, inquit, cælum apertum, &c. Promittit amplioremclarionemque revelationem maiestatis, gloriæ & deitatis suæ tum demum fore, cùm videbunt ipsos Angelos filio hominis inseruire: quasi dicat: Quamquam infirmus sum alioqui, vt pote homo & filius hominis (filium enim hominis se solet appellare, tum propter veritatem humanæ naturæ, tum propter naturæ humanæ infirmitatem) tamen, inquit, videbitis deinceps cælum apertum & Angelos inter patrem & filium quasi internuncios, sursum & deorsum itantes, idque vt filio inseruiant: Ex quo clarè conspicietis maiestatem meam ac potentiam plane diuinam. Hoc euenisse legimus, post grauissi- mam illam tentationem quam in deserto sustinuit. Vbi enim Satanas eum omisit, ecce Angeli accedebant & ministrabat ei. Vide quoque de hac re Luc.22.43.Matth. 28.2. Sed intelligendum est non solum hoc signo & angelorum ministerio conspectam esse eius maiestatem plane diuinam, verum ex multis aliis rebus eam innotuisse ex omnibus factis & dictis ipsius admirabilibus, ex transfiguratione ipsius in monte. Petrus ait se oculis adspexisse maiestatem ipsius: sed quomodo ipse narrat ibidem, Acceperat enim a Deo Patre honorem & gloriam, voce ad eum delata huiusmodi a magnifica gloria, &c. Nos quoque maiestatem eandem conspicimus hoc ipso die, non quidem in huiusmodi signis, non in miraculis, non in apertis caelis, sed eam discimus ex sensu illo maximae potentiae ipsius in nobis qui credimus. Qui sensus plane arguit Christum Deum esse illum ipsum qui creauit omnia ab initio. Potentia enim haec & ἐνέργεια quam nos in nobis sentimus, a Christo manat, & ab ipsius Spiritu est. Num, inquit Paulus, experimentum quaeritis in me loquentis Christi, qui erga vos non est infirmus, sed potens est in vobis? Quibus verbis innuit potuisse eos satis experiri qui esset Christus, quam excellens esset magnitudo potentiae ipsius vel ex sensu illo potentiae ipsius qui in ipsis fuit, cuiusque ipse fuit minister etiam hodierno die, dum Christus loquitur hominibus per ministros suos, potentia & efficacia ipsius possunt experiri in se ex mirabilibus illis effectis, quae ipsi in se sentiunt, dum mutantur corda, dum credunt, dum regenerantur. Vel etiam si nolunt credere, tamen no raro attoniti reddutur, & obstupescunt. Quaeri potest hoc loco, Annon magis ad consolationem discipulorum fuisset factum, si salute ipsis, si caelos ipsos, si ministerium angelorum ipsis promisisset. Pollicitus enim duntaxat aspectum & clariorem intuitu gloriae suae, nihil de gloria ipsorum. Respondeo, Christo in animo est confirmare ipsorum fidem, si loquaris hominibus de caelo, de vita aeterna, de omni denique benedictione spiritua-li, no credent prius, quam videat ipsum Christum per quem & propter quem sunt haec omnia. Si enim serio afficiantur sensu peccati sui, & interea agnoscant Deum summè iustum esse, non prius credent se vitam adipisci posse quàm inueniant eum qui pro ipsis satisfaciat iustitiæ diuinæ, hoc est, Mediatorem Iesum Christum, Deum & hominem in vna persona. Age videamus experientiam: Ego si quando non habeo Christum animo præsentem, eúmque fide non satis firmiter apprehendo (id quod omnes sancti in se cogūtur sentire, non sine summa animi ægritudine) si quando ego Christum in conspectu non habeo, tum quidem tantùm abest vt cœlos videam & cœlestem illam gloriam, vt nihil præter angustiam, terrores ac cruciatus sentiam. Rursus, cùm affulget mihi Christus, cùm cœli apparent, cùm gloria illa cœlestis in conspectu est, tum certa fides ac spes vitæ est. Hęc ideo loquor, vt quotquot velint certi esse vitæ illius æternæ, benedictionum omniumque spiritualium, Christum primùm quærant, & ante oculos statuant, cognoscant eum Deum & hominem passum pro se & resurrexisse pro se, ex quo deinde sequetur sua sponte fiducia illa omnium beneficiorum ipsius. Cui sit omnis honor & gloria, Amen.
units.tr: I come now to the promise itself. "You shall see," he says, "heaven opened," etc. He promises a fuller and clearer revelation of his majesty, glory and deity, which will then be given when they see the angels serving the Son of Man: as if to say, "Although I am otherwise weak, as a man and a son of man (for he is wont to call himself the Son of Man, both on account of the truth of human nature and on account of the weakness of human nature), nevertheless," he says, "you will henceforth see heaven opened, and angels going up and down between the Father and the Son, as go-betweens, and this so that they may serve the Son. From this you will clearly perceive my majesty and power, truly divine." We read that this happened after that most grievous temptation which he endured in the desert. For when Satan left him, behold, angels came and ministered to him. See also on this matter Luke 22.43; Matt. 28.2. But it must be understood that his majesty was seen truly divine not only by this sign and the ministry of angels, but also was made known from many other things, from all his wonderful deeds and words, and from his transfiguration on the mountain. Peter says that he beheld his majesty with his eyes; but as he himself relates in the same place: "For he received from God the Father honour and glory, a voice being brought to him by the magnificent glory," etc. We too behold the same majesty on this very day, not indeed in such signs, not in miracles, not in opened heavens, but we learn it from that sense of his greatest power in us who believe. That sense plainly proves that Christ is God, the very one who created all things from the beginning. For this power and energy (ἐνέργεια), which we feel in ourselves, flows from Christ and is of his Spirit. "Do you seek," says Paul, "proof of Christ speaking in me, who is not weak towards you, but is powerful in you?" By these words he implies that those who had the sense of his power in themselves, of which he himself was the minister, could sufficiently experience who Christ was, and how excellent the greatness of his power was. Even today, while Christ speaks to men through his ministers, his power and efficacy can be experienced in themselves, from those wonderful effects which they feel in themselves while their hearts are changed, while they believe, while they are regenerated. Or even if they are unwilling to believe, nevertheless they are often astonished and stunned. It may be asked here: would it not have been more for the comfort of the disciples if he had promised them salvation, heaven itself, and the ministry of angels? For he promised only the sight and a clearer vision of his glory, and nothing about their own glory. I answer: Christ intends to confirm their faith. If you speak to men about heaven, about eternal life, and finally about every spiritual blessing, they will not believe before they see Christ himself, through whom and on account of whom all these things are. For if they are seriously affected by a sense of their sin, and at the same time acknowledge that God is supremely just, they will not believe that they can obtain life until they find him who satisfies divine justice on their behalf, that is, Jesus Christ the Mediator, God and man in one person. Come, let us look at experience. If at any time I do not have Christ present in my mind, and do not grasp him firmly enough by faith (which all the saints are compelled to feel in themselves, not without great distress of mind), when I do not have Christ in view, then I am so far from seeing heaven and that heavenly glory that I feel nothing but anguish, terrors and torment. Again, when Christ shines upon me, when heaven appears, when that heavenly glory is in view, then there is certain faith and hope of life. I say these things so that all who wish to be certain of that eternal life, of all blessings and of all spiritual goods, should first seek Christ and set him before their eyes, and know that he is God and man, who suffered for them and rose again for them; from which knowledge there will follow of its own accord that trust in all his benefits. To him be all honour and glory. Amen.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Capitis secundi tres sunt omnino partes.
units.tr: The second chapter has altogether three parts.

units.la: 1. Est miraculum aquæ in vinum commutatæ editum in Cana Galilææ, ad 12. versum vsque.
units.tr: 1. There is the miracle of water changed into wine, performed at Cana of Galilee, up to verse 12.

units.la: 2. Est Christi vna cum matre, fratribus & discipulis profectio in Capernaum, simulque mora quam fecit ibi, ad alteram partem 13. vers.
units.tr: 2. There is Christ's journey to Capernaum with his mother, brothers and disciples, and the stay he made there, to the second part of verse 13.

units.la: 3. Est profectio Christi in Hierusalem simulque res illic ab eo gestæ in paschate quod primum fuit post baptismum ipsius ad finem vsque capitis. Rerum autem gestarum ab eo, prima est purgatio templi ad versum vsque 23. Secunda de miraculis ipsius summatim comprehensis, inde ad finem capitis.
units.tr: 3. There is Christ's journey to Jerusalem, and the things done by him there at the Passover that was the first after his baptism, to the end of the chapter. Of the things he did, the first is the cleansing of the temple, to verse 23. The second is a summary account of his miracles, from there to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: 1 DIE autem tertio nuptiæ factæ sunt in Cana Oppido Galilææ: erátque mater Iesu illic.
units.tr: 1 On the third day a wedding took place at Cana, a town of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.

units.la: 2 Vocatus est autem etiam Iesus ac discipuli eius ad nuptias illas.
units.tr: 2 Jesus also and his disciples were invited to that wedding.

units.la: 3 Et cum defecisset vinum, mater Iesu dixit ei, Vinum non habent.
units.tr: 3 And when the wine ran short, the mother of Jesus said to him, They have no wine.

units.la: 4 Dicit ei Iesus, Quid mihi tecum mulier? nondum venit hora mea.
units.tr: 4 Jesus said to her, Woman, what is that to me and to you? My hour has not yet come.

units.la: 5 Dicit eius mater ministris, Quodcunque dixerit vobis facite.
units.tr: 5 His mother said to the servants, Do whatever he tells you.

units.la: 6 Erant autem ibi lapideae hydriae sex positae secundum purificationem Iudaeorum, capientes singulae amphoras binas aut ternas.
units.tr: 6 Now there were six stone water jars standing there, set out for the Jewish purification, each holding two or three measures.

units.la: 7 Dicit eis Iesus, Implete has hydrias aqua. Impleverunt eas igitur usque ad summum.
units.tr: 7 Jesus said to them, Fill these jars with water. So they filled them up to the brim.

units.la: 8 Tum dicit eis, Haurite nunc & offerte architriclino: obtulerunt igitur.
units.tr: 8 Then he said to them, Draw some out now and take it to the master of the feast. So they took it.

units.la: 9 Ut autem gustavit architriclinus aquam illam quae facta fuerat vinum, (nesciebat autem unde esset, sed ministri sciebant qui hauserant aquam) vocat sponsum architriclinus,
units.tr: 9 When the master of the feast tasted the water that had been made wine (he did not know where it came from, but the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom,

units.la: 10 Et dicit ei, Omnes primo loco bonum vinum apponunt, & postquam conviviae affatim biberunt, tunc id quod minus bonum est, tu servasti bonum usque adhuc.
units.tr: 10 and said to him, Everyone serves the good wine first, and when the guests have drunk freely, the inferior; but you have kept the good wine until now.

units.la: 11 Hoc initium signorum fecit Iesus in Cana oppido Galilaeae, & manifestam fecit gloriam suam, & crediderunt in eum discipuli eius.
units.tr: 11 This was the beginning of the signs that Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and he revealed his glory, and his disciples believed in him.

units.la: PRIMA PARS CAPITIS, DE CHRISTI MIRACULO IN NUPTIIS CANAE GALILAEAE EDITO.
units.tr: FIRST PART OF THE CHAPTER, CONCERNING THE MIRACLE CHRIST PERFORMED AT THE WEDDING IN CANA OF GALILEE.

units.la: PRIMA pars capitis, proponens primum illud miraculum a Christo editum, sic se habet. Christus cum tempus iam adesset, officio Mediatoris suscipiendo a Patre destinatum, annum iam ingressus tricesimum, Nazaretha venit in desertum, ubi baptizavit Iohannes Baptista: ibique ab eo baptizatus pariterque initiatus est officio. Inde ductus per Spiritum in desertum, ibi ieiunauit quadraginta dies totos, tentatus graviter a Diabolo; postea reuersus est in desertum Iordanis, vbi baptizauit Iohannes, quo loco & tempore vocauit Andream, & alterum illum discipulum cuius nomen non habemus expressum. Vocauit etiam Simonem Petrum fratrem Andreae: hinc redit in Galilaeam, vbi vocati sunt Philippus & Nathanael. Tertio die post reditum Christi in Galilaea, contigerunt nuptiae in Cana Galilaeae oppido, non procul dissito a Nazaretha vico Galilaeae, in quo habitauit Christus vna cum parentibus. Maria mater Domini ad nuptias inuitata est: Christus etiam vna cum discipulis suis vocatus est. Cum itaque nuptiis interesset, vinumque defecisset (ea enim miraculi occasio fuit) Christus primum hoc suum miraculum mutatae aquae in vinum praestantissimum edidit. In historia miraculi quinque nobis distinguenda & consideranda veniunt. 1. Occurrunt miraculi aliquot occasiones. 2. sunt partes Mariae matris Domini. 3. sunt partes Christi & ministrorum. 4. sunt partes Architriclini. 5. est historiae conclusio.
units.tr: The first part of the chapter, setting out the first miracle performed by Christ, stands thus. When the time had now come, appointed by the Father for Christ to take up the office of Mediator, having now entered his thirtieth year, he came from Nazareth into the wilderness, where John the Baptist was baptizing; there he was baptized by him and at the same time initiated into the office. Then, led by the Spirit into the wilderness, he fasted there for forty whole days, sorely tempted by the Devil; afterwards he returned to the wilderness of the Jordan, where John was baptizing, and at that place and time he called Andrew and that other disciple whose name is not recorded. He also called Simon Peter, Andrew's brother. From there he returned to Galilee, where Philip and Nathanael were called. On the third day after Christ's return to Galilee, a wedding took place at Cana, a town of Galilee, not far distant from the village of Galilee in which Christ had lived with his parents, Nazareth. Mary the Lord's mother was invited to the wedding, and Christ was invited along with his disciples. Therefore, while he was present at the wedding, and the wine had run out (for this was the occasion of the miracle), Christ first performed this miracle of his, the changing of water into the finest wine. In the account of the miracle, five things come to be distinguished and considered by us: (1) the occasions of the miracle occur; (2) the parts of Mary the mother of the Lord; (3) the parts of Christ and the servants; (4) the parts of the master of the feast; (5) the conclusion of the account.

units.la: Vt igitur reuertamur ad occasiones: sunt tres, quae singulae suo quodam loco atque ordine antecedunt ipsum miraculum, ipsumque efficiunt. Prima est nuptiarum, secunda est inuitatae Mariae, Christi & discipulorum. Tertia & postrema est defectus vini. Quod ad primam illam, quae est nuptiarum (de singulis enim ordine dicemus) notantur in ea nuptiarum tempus simul & locus. Tempus est, cum tertius ageretur dies ex quo Christus venit in Galilaeam factae sunt nuptiae. Tempus enim hoc refero ad Christi aduentum in Galilaeam. Locus fuit Cana Galilaeae oppidum, non longe a Nazaretha situm. Cana minor vocata est, vt distingueretur a Cana maiori, inter Tyrum & Sidonem sita. Ergo vt hic aliquid obseruemus obiter: Publicus & frequens hominum coetus dedit occasionem miraculo. Non enim oportuit tam insigne miraculum priuatim fieri, sed in publico ac celebri hominum coetu, quo plus prodesse posset, & ad fidem multorum & ad Dei gloriam. Nos quidem hodierno die, fateor, neque possumus neque etiam tiam debemus in publicis hominum coetibus miracu- la edere. Sed hoc certe nobis faciendum est, quod face-re & possumus & debemus: Dei opera mirifica, quae iam olim gesta sunt in congregationibus hominum, celebranda sunt, praesertim vero admirandum illud & nun-quam satis praedicandum redemptionis humanae opus, quod nullo loco, nullo tempore debet abesse nobis ab animo & abore. Sed longe secus evenit, in huiusmodi enim hominum coetibus & conviviis de quibusvis au- dimus libentius, quam de iis quae ad Deum, ad Christi, ad vitam aeternam spectant. Tristior enim & importu-nior hic sermo reputari solet, quia excitat conscientiam aliquam peccati, quam maxime sopitam esse homi-nes vellent, imo dum intersumus conviviis nostris, (quod dolendum est) similiores sumus ethnicis illis blasphemis, de quibus Petrus loquitur, & adversus quos denuciat iudicium grauissimum in adventu Domini futurum: illis, inquam, similiores sumus, quam Christianis, quos ibidem laudat, ideo quod non concurrebant cum prophanis hominibus ad eandem luxus profusionem.
units.tr: So then, to return to the occasions: there are three, each of which comes before the miracle itself in its own place and order, and together bring it about. The first is the wedding; the second is the invitation of Mary, Christ and the disciples; the third and last is the lack of wine. As to the first, the wedding (for we shall speak of each in order), the time and the place of the wedding are noted. The time was when the third day had come since Christ came into Galilee, and the wedding took place. I refer this time to Christ's coming into Galilee. The place was the town of Cana in Galilee, situated not far from Nazareth. It was called Little Cana, to distinguish it from Great Cana, which lies between Tyre and Sidon. So let us observe in passing: a public and crowded gathering of people gave occasion for the miracle. For so notable a miracle ought not to have been done in private, but in a public and well-attended gathering of people, where it could be of greater benefit, both for the faith of many and for the glory of God. We indeed, I confess, in the present day can neither perform miracles in public gatherings of men, nor ought we to. But this at least we must do, and can and ought to do: the wonderful works of God, which were done long ago, must be celebrated in assemblies of men, and especially that admirable work of human redemption, which can never be praised enough, and which should never be absent from our mind and our lips, in any place or at any time. But things turn out far otherwise. For in gatherings and feasts of this kind we hear anything whatever more gladly than what concerns God, Christ and eternal life. For such talk is commonly thought gloomy and unwelcome, because it stirs up some sense of sin, which men would most like to be lulled to sleep. Indeed, while we are present at our banquets (which is a sorrow to say), we are more like those heathen blasphemers of whom Peter speaks, and against whom he announces the most grievous judgment to come at the Lord's coming, than like the Christians whom he praises there, because they did not run with profane men into the same riot of excess. I say we are more like those heathen than like Christians.

units.la: Sequitur altera miraculi occasio. Inuitata est Maria mater Domini, inuitatus Dominus una cum discipulis suis. Maria profecto, si quae unquam alia sobria fuit maxime ac temperans, voluit tamen interesse nuptiis cognati sui, ut verisimile est. Nihil pugnat cum Christiana temperantia & sobrietate, convivari nonnunquam & animum hilarare una cum iis qui nobis & in carne & in Domino sunt coniuncti, modo fiant omnia in Domino. Imo vero sympathia ista in Christiano homine requiritur, ut gaudeat cum gaudentibus, & fleat cum flentibus. Austeritas autem illa plusquam Stoica vel Anabaptistarum, vel Monachorum pontificiorum, non commendat Christianum hominem, sed magis arguit hypocritam. Vocatus est autem etiam Iesus. Christus non ideo in mundum venit ut aboleret hominum societates & consuetudines politicas ac civiles, ut neque rationes quibus hae coluntur: verum ideo venit, ut hypocritica ista omnia corrigeret & sanctificaret. Nam iam inde a lapsu primi hominis, in nullam omnino Dei creaturam ius habet quisquis non est in Christo Iesu, & nulla re, nullis priuilegiis gaudere debet, non nuptiis, non conuiuiis, nec buccella quidem pani. Contra vero qui in Christo Iesu est, recuperauit ius quoddam in res creatas; & id quidem plenius in Christo, quàm fuit illud quod perdidit in Adamo. Quod quidem non patefiet tantisper dum hic viuemus; tum autem apparebit cum conspiciemur cum maiestate quadam imperare creaturis omnibus in coelis, cum Christo capite nostro: Omnia vestra sunt, ait Paulus, siue Paulus, siue Apollos, siue Cephas, siue mundus, siue vita, siue mors (mors enim ipsa subiecta est Christiano homini) siue praesentia, siue futura, omnia vestra sunt, Vos autem Christi, Christus vero Dei. Quod cùm ita sit, profecto quoties vimur rebus à Deo creatis, non iis in vsum nostrum debemus esse contenti nisi vnà cum iis sententiamus praesentem ipsum Dominum: Non quod corporaliter praesentem esse oporteat, sicuti interfuit his nuptiis, sed spiritualiter & fide, qui praesentiae modus est longè praestantissimus & efficacissimus. Nā per fidem praesens Christus sanctificat vsui nostro omnia, sic, vti bona iam conscientia iis vti possumus: Ex bona rursus conscientia est laetitia quae cor nostrum adaperit & soluit in gratiarum actionem. Creauit Deus cibos ad participandum cum gratiarum actione fidelibus & iis qui cognouerunt veritatem. Quibus ergo creauit cibos? nempe fidelibus, hoc est, iis qui per fidem Christum habent praesentem, ac proinde bona conscientia creatis in vsum suum cibis vti possunt. Sed quonam modo iis participare debent? nempe cum gratiarum actione, quae quidem exsistit ex laetitia bonae conscientiae. Contra vero si non sit praesens nobis Christus per fidem, tum mala conscientia participamus creaturis Dei, aut certè non bona. Quae autem laetitia hic potest esse, quae gratiarum actio, vbi non est bona conscientia? profecto non nisi belluinam dicas, & crassam aliquam. Omnis ista voluptas quae capitur ex cibo & potu non consolaretur infideles & prophanos istos, si id scirent se mala conscientia vti creaturis illis Dei: plus enim tum valeret mala conscientia ad tristitiam quàm voluptas illa tota ad consolationem. Verùm vt redeamus; Non est hoc absque singulari Dei consilio factum, quod primo filij sui miraculo voluerit matrimonij honorabile vinculum confirmari ac cohonestari. Præsciuit enim institutionem hanc suam necessariam ac laudabilem ab Antichristo ignominia afficiendam; & suborituros & subingressuros spiritus deceptores, Papistas intelligit, tradentes doctrinas daemoniorum & prohibentes contrahere matrimonium. Diabolus impurus quidem ipse est & immundus spiritus, & in eo imprimis laborat, vt quotquot sunt homines, sint immundi omnes & contaminati omni impuritatis acfoeditatis genere tam corpore quàm animo. Non autem latet eum hoc quod dicitur ad Hebraeos, honorabile esse inter quosuis coniugium & cubile impollutum. Neque illud ignorat, quod si prohibeatur hominibus coiugium, quod vel quibusvis promiscuè vel certè alicuius conditionis, vt Ecclesiae ministris, ea ratione potissimum fieri, vt omni libidinis genere se coinquinent, idque experientia ipsa satis probauit, neque dici debet vt habeatur reuerentia castis auribus quam foedis affectibus & libidinibus contaminati sunt illi Monachi & otiosi ventres in Papistarum illis speluncis ac latebris. Quamobrem postremis his temporibus id operâ dedit praecipuè, vt prohiberetur Presbyteris matrimonium, quod tamen Deus sanctificauit cuiuscunque ordinis ac sortis hominibus, ad hoc vt ipsi sancti sint ac mundi, Dei sui vsibus atque cultui; cui sit omnis gloria. Amen.
units.tr: The second occasion of the miracle follows. Mary the Lord's mother was invited, and the Lord was invited along with his disciples. Mary indeed, if any other woman ever was, was most sober and temperate, yet she wished, as is likely, to be present at the wedding of her kinsman. There is nothing contrary to Christian temperance and sobriety in sometimes feasting and cheering the spirit together with those who are joined to us both in the flesh and in the Lord, provided all things are done in the Lord. Indeed that sympathy is required in a Christian man, that he rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep. But that austerity, more than Stoic, of the Anabaptists or of the Papist monks, does not commend a Christian man, but rather marks him out as a hypocrite. And Jesus was invited. Christ did not come into the world to abolish human society and the political and civil customs, nor the reasons by which these are maintained; rather he came to correct and sanctify all those hypocritical things. For from the fall of the first man onward, whoever is not in Christ Jesus has no right at all in any creature of God, and ought to enjoy nothing and no privilege, not weddings, not feasts, not even a morsel of bread. On the contrary, he who is in Christ Jesus has recovered a certain right over created things, and indeed more fully in Christ than that which he lost in Adam. This will not indeed be made plain so long as we live here; but then it will appear, when we shall be seen ruling over all creatures in the heavens with a certain majesty, together with Christ our head: "All things are yours," says Paul, "whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death" (for death itself is made subject to the Christian man), "whether things present or things to come, all are yours." "And you are Christ's, and Christ is God's." Since this is so, truly whenever we use the things created by God, we ought not to be content to use them for our own purposes unless at the same time we realize that the Lord himself is present: not that he must be present bodily, as he was present at this wedding, but spiritually and by faith, which mode of presence is by far the most excellent and effective. For through faith the present Christ sanctifies all things for our use, so that we may use them with a good conscience. From a good conscience in turn comes the joy which opens and loosens our heart into thanksgiving. "God created foods to be partaken of with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth." To whom, then, did he create foods? Namely to the faithful, that is, to those who through faith have Christ present; and therefore, with a good conscience, they can use the foods created for their use. But in what manner ought they to partake of them? Namely with thanksgiving, which indeed arises from the joy of a good conscience. On the contrary, if Christ is not present to us through faith, then we partake of God's creatures with an evil conscience, or at least not a good one. But what joy can there be here, what thanksgiving, where there is no good conscience? Surely you can call it nothing but bestial and gross. All that pleasure which is taken from food and drink would not console those unbelieving and profane men, if they knew that they used those creatures of God with an evil conscience: for then an evil conscience would weigh more heavily in sadness than all that pleasure would in consolation. But to return. This was not done without a singular counsel of God, that by his first miracle for his Son he should have willed the honorable bond of marriage to be confirmed and graced. For he foresaw that this institution of his, necessary and praiseworthy, would be dishonored by Antichrist, and that deceiving spirits would arise and creep in, forbidding marriage and teaching the doctrines of demons; he means the Papists. The Devil is indeed himself an impure and unclean spirit, and he labors above all to make all men, whoever they are, unclean and defiled with every kind of impurity and foulness, both in body and in mind. Nor is it hidden from him what is said to the Hebrews, that marriage is honorable among all men and the bed undefiled. Nor does he fail to know that if marriage is forbidden to men, to all men without distinction or certainly to some class of men, as to ministers of the Church, this is done chiefly so that they may defile themselves with every kind of lust; and experience itself has proved this well enough. Nor should it be said that out of reverence for chaste ears we should not speak of how defiled by foul passions and lusts those monks and idle bellies are, in those dens and hiding places of the Papists. Therefore in these latter times he has especially labored to ensure that marriage be forbidden to presbyters; yet God has sanctified marriage for men of every order and rank, so that they may themselves be holy and clean, for the uses and worship of their God; to whom be all glory. Amen.

units.la: Ac discipuli eius. Vnà cum Christo inuitati sunt discipuli ipsius, id quod argumento est, Christum cùm in terris ageret frugalem fuisse admodum ac sobrium, vt qui vnà cum discipulis vixerit, & communi cum iis mensa fuerit vsus tam domi quàm foris: nempe quia regnum ipsius non erat de hoc mundo, in quo dum commoraretur omnibus modis, Dominus gloriae sese humiliauit.
units.tr: And his disciples. Along with Christ, his disciples were also invited. This is evidence that Christ, while he lived on earth, was very frugal and sober, since he lived with the disciples and shared a common table with them both at home and abroad. The reason is that his kingdom was not of this world, and while he dwelt in it, the Lord of glory humbled himself in every way.

units.la: Sequitur tertia miraculi occasio: & quidem maximè propria ac specialis, nempe defectus vini, qui incidit in finem conuiuii, vt apparebit postea. Nihil attinet curiosius in huius defectus causam inquirere, siue ea fuerit intemperantia conuiuarum & nimia profusio, siue fuerit inopia vini quæ consueuit esse in illis partibus. His omissis contenti simus hac vna causa, quæ satis apparet ex contextu historiæ, nempe manifestatione gloriæ Dei, ad quam vt miraculum ipsum, ita miraculi occasionem refero. Ad hanc causam adduxit Christus discipulos suos, cum illi paulò curiosius interrogarent de causa cæcitatis illius hominis qui cæcus fuit ânativitate; Quis peccauit, inquiunt, hic, an parentes eius? Respondet Christus, neque iste peccauit, neque parentes eius, sed oportet opera Dei manifesta fieri in eo, edito scilicet miraculo, in aperiendis miseri oculis. Ergo quoties constiterit de gloria Dei tanquam causa cur hoc vel illud fiat, causam cur fiat ne curiosè quæramus amplius: Imo ne fiagatur de nostra ipsorum reprobatione, sicut discimus, Rom.9.20,& deinceps.
units.tr: The third occasion of the miracle follows, and it is the most particular and special one: the lack of wine, which occurred at the end of the feast, as will appear later. It is pointless to inquire too closely into the cause of this shortage, whether it was the intemperance and excessive extravagance of the guests or the scarcity of wine that is usual in those parts. Setting these aside, let us be content with this one cause, which is sufficiently clear from the context of the story, namely the manifestation of the glory of God. I refer both the miracle itself and the occasion of the miracle to this end. Christ led his disciples to this cause when they asked somewhat too curiously about the cause of the blindness of the man who was blind from birth: Who sinned, they say, this man or his parents? Christ answers: Neither this man sinned, nor his parents, but the works of God must be made manifest in him, namely by performing a miracle in opening the poor man's eyes. Therefore, whenever it is established that the glory of God is the reason why this or that happens, we should not inquire any further into why it happens. Indeed, we should take care not to end up with a reprobation of ourselves, as we learn from Rom. 9.20 and following.

units.la: Hactenus fuit triplex miraculi occasio, nunc sequuntur partes Mariæ: agit autem Maria partim cum Christo, partim cum ministris convivii. Apud Christum igitur primùm quæritur de vini defectu. Vinum non habent. Non agit quidem cum Christo animo tentandi ipsum, vt edito scilicet miraculo consuleret famæ suæ & nomini, aut nuptias cohonestaret. Verùm Mariam ad rem Christo communicandam mouit, partim sympathia quædam & commiseratio erga cognatos, partim conscientia potentiæ Christi extraordinariæ: quem etsi nondum vt Dei Filium plane cognitum habuit, vt apparet ex Lucæ narratione; vbi cùm Christus reprehenderet ignorantiam Iosephi & Mariæ his verbis, Quid me quærebatis? An nesciebatis quod in domo Patris mei oportet me esse? Post hæc, inquam, verba subiectum est: Ipsi non intellexerunt sermonem quem dixerat iis. Etsi, inquam, vt Dei Filium nondum plane cognitum habuit, tamen virum admirabilem & eum, quocum esset Deus, multis experimentis iam didicit, quorum vnumquodque in animo suo recondidit, vt constat ex eodem illo capite Lucæ, vers.51. Maria autem conseruabat omnes sermones hos in corde suo. His igitur causis adducta, vt probabile est, expositum apud ipsum Christum hunc vini defectum, vt ipse qua posset ratione succurreret. Atque hæ sunt duæ illæ causæ, quibus monemur omnes, ad Dei opem imploran-
units.tr: So far there have been three occasions for the miracle. Now follow the parts played by Mary, who deals partly with Christ and partly with the ministers of the feast. First, then, she raises the matter of the lack of wine with Christ: They have no wine. She did not, indeed, approach Christ with the intention of testing him, so that by performing a miracle he might look after his own reputation and name, or lend dignity to the wedding. Rather, Mary was moved to share the matter with Christ, partly by a certain sympathy and compassion for her relatives, and partly by her awareness of Christ's extraordinary power. Although she did not yet clearly know him as the Son of God, as appears from Luke's narrative, where Christ rebukes the ignorance of Joseph and Mary with these words: Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house? After these words, I say, it is added: They did not understand the saying which he had spoken to them. So, I say, although she did not yet have a plain knowledge of him as the Son of God, nevertheless she had already learned from many experiences that he was an admirable man, and one with whom God was. She stored up each of these experiences in her mind, as is clear from the same chapter of Luke, verse 51: But Mary kept all these sayings in her heart. Moved by these causes, as is probable, she laid this lack of wine before Christ himself, so that he might help in whatever way he could. These are the two causes by which all of us are urged to implore God's help.

units.la: Luc.2.50. plorandam : nempe cognitio Dei, naturæ ipsius, misericordiæ, potentiæ & charitatis ipsius: Neque satis virium est ad preces in hac causa; nisi enim sensu infirmitatis nostræ aliquo & miseriæ commoveamur, otiosi spectatores erimus Dei, omnipotentiæ ipsius, misericordiæ, charitatis, denique omnium quæ in ipso sunt. Itaq; Paulus suspiria illa & gemitus inenarrabiles, quos dicit esse Spiritus Dei interpellantis pro nobis, educit ex afflictionibus & sensu miseriæ, dum hoc argumento consolatur afflictos, quod Spiritus Dei interpellet pro ipsis gemitibus inenarrabilibus.
units.tr: Luc. 2.50. ... to be implored: namely, the knowledge of God, of his nature, his mercy, his power and his love. Nor is there enough strength for prayer in this matter unless we are moved by some sense of our weakness and wretchedness. Otherwise we shall be idle spectators of God, of his omnipotence, his mercy, his love, and finally of all that is in him. So Paul draws those sighs and inexpressible groanings, which he says are the Spirit of God interceding for us, out of afflictions and a sense of misery, while he uses this argument to comfort the afflicted: that the Spirit of God intercedes for them with inexpressible groanings.

units.la: Sic hactenus quæsta est Maria. Respondet Christus, Quid mihi tecum mulier ? Mulierem vocat matrem suam, & hoc loco, & alibi, ut ostendat se alium esse & maiorem aliquem quam Mariæ filium, Et ut doceat Papistas nostri temporis, qui non nisi carnaliter sentiunt de Christo, deque ipsius matre, ne attribuant maiorem gloriam Mariæ, quàm ipse eam dignetur, præsertim vero ne deferant ipsius filij Dei honorem proprium vel Mariæ, vel cuiquam alij, vel homini vel angelo. Mulier, inquit, quid mihi tecum ? forma procul dubio est reprehensionis. Quod si aliquid reprehensione dignum in Maria fuit, ut fuit quidem, ut eam Papistæ vindicent ab omni peccato, profecto non peccauit in illa quam dixi sympathia & affectu, quo deficiente vino commiserata est cognatos suos, neque in eo peccauit, quod confugerit ad Christi potentiam eam, quam aliquatenus habuit perspectam. Verum in hoc primum peccauit, quemadmodum ipsa appellatio mulieris indicat, quod de Christo nimis carnaliter senserit, & de persona, & de officio ipsius: de persona quidem, quod ignoraret adhuc Dei filium esse, putaret autem suum dumtaxat filium. De officio verò, quod ignoraret eum missum a Patre ut mundum redimeret, putaret autem astringi ad ea omnia officia & obsequia, ad quæ astringi solet filiorum vulgus. Cùm Iesus annum agens duodecimum unà cum Iosepho & Maria ascenderet Hierusalem, Maria mater eius putauit non esse quod ageret aliud, nisi ut comitaretur parentes, & ab iis ac ipsorum volunta-
units.tr: So far Mary has asked. Christ answers: Woman, what have I to do with you? He calls his mother "woman", both here and elsewhere, to show that he is another and greater being than the son of Mary. He also does this to teach the Papists of our time, who think of Christ and of his mother only in a carnal way, not to attribute greater glory to Mary than he himself deigns to give her, and especially not to transfer the proper honour of the Son of God to Mary, or to anyone else, whether man or angel. Woman, he says, what have I to do with you? This is without doubt a form of rebuke. But if there was anything in Mary deserving rebuke, as there certainly was (although the Papists wish to clear her of all sin), she certainly did not sin in the sympathy and affection I have mentioned, with which, when the wine ran out, she felt pity for her relatives. Nor did she sin in having recourse to the power of Christ, of which she had some clear knowledge. Rather, she first sinned in this, as the very address "woman" indicates: that she thought too carnally both of Christ's person and of his office. Of his person, indeed, because she did not yet know that he was the Son of God, but thought him only her son. Of his office, because she did not know that he had been sent by the Father to redeem the world, but thought he was bound to all those duties and services to which the common run of sons is usually bound. When Jesus, at the age of twelve, went up to Jerusalem with Joseph and Mary, his mother thought that he had no other business than to accompany his parents and to depend entirely upon them and their will. But he answered those who sought him and reproached him: Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in anguish. He answered, I say, somewhat angrily: Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be about my Father's business? So Mary, as if he had had no other parent, demanded of him this duty of a son to a parent. But he, when it came to the business of his heavenly Father, would acknowledge neither Mary as his mother nor any creature at all, although, in other respects, no mortal has ever shown his parents the obedience that Christ showed to his. It is said that when Christ came to Nazareth he was subject to his parents. It appears that Mary also sinned in another matter, from the words that follow: My hour, she says, has not yet come. She was pressing Christ, as if he were less concerned about this matter. Therefore Christ answered that there was no need for anyone to remind him of what belonged to his office, as if he were less mindful of it. The reason he had hitherto delayed his help was not some forgetfulness, but the timing of the opportunity, because his hour had not yet come, that is, the appropriate time for acting.

units.la: Christi ad matre responsio. Iohan. 19. 26.
units.tr: Christ's reply to his mother. John 19.26.

units.la: In quo Maria peccavit. te tantum penderet. At ipse respondit quaerentibus se & expostulantibus secum, fili cur ita fecisti nobis? Ecce pater tuus & ego cruciati quaerebamus te, Respondit inquam, subiratus: Quid est quod quaerebatis me? An nesciebatis oportere me in iis esse, quae sunt Patris mei? Ergo Maria, quasi alium parentem non habuisset, requirebat ab ipso hoc filii in parentem officium. Ipse vero vbi venturum fuit ad negotia patris sui coelestis, tum neque Mariam matrem, neque quamquam creaturarum agnoscere voluit, quamuis alioqui, nemo unquam mortalium eam obedientiam praestiterit parentibus, quam Christus suis. Dictum est, Christum cum venisset Nazareth subiectum fuisse parentibus. Apparet & in alio peccatum fuisse a Maria, ex iis verbis quae sequuntur deinceps: Nondum, inquit, venit hora mea. Vrgebat Christum, quasi minus sollicitum de hac re: ideoque Christus respondit non opus esse, ut quis ipsum commonefaciat de iis quae officij erant, quasi vero minus de iis cogitaret. Causam autem cur distulerit hactenus opem suam, non fuisse incogitantiam aliquam, verum temporis opportunitatem, quod nondum venisset hora ipsius, hoc est opportunum agendi tempus.
units.tr: In what Mary sinned. ... depended only on him. But he answered those who sought him and expostulated with him: Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in anguish. He answered, I say, somewhat angrily: Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I ought to be in the things that are my Father's? So Mary, as if she had had no other parent, required of him this filial duty to a parent. But he, when it came to the business of his heavenly Father, did not wish to acknowledge Mary his mother, nor any creature at all, although, in other respects, no mortal has ever shown his parents the obedience that Christ showed to his. It is said that when Christ came to Nazareth he was subject to his parents. It appears that Mary also sinned in another matter, from the words that follow: My hour, she says, has not yet come. She was pressing Christ, as if he were less concerned about this matter. Therefore Christ answered that there was no need for anyone to remind him of what belonged to his office, as if he were less mindful of it. The reason he had hitherto delayed his help was not some forgetfulness, but the timing of the opportunity, because his hour had not yet come, that is, the appropriate time for acting.

units.la: Obserua primum in exemplo Mariae, quod cum Christus commoraretur inter Iudaeos, fuisse quamplurimos qui de ipso, ut sic dicam, nonnisi carnaliter sentirent. Commoratus quidem est fateor, ut dixi Ioan.1.14. plenus gratiae & veritatis. Verum infirmitas & quasi velum illud carnis obscurauit illam Dei gloriam in ipso habitantis corporaliter, adeo ut nisi extra ordinem & admirabiliter illuminati in eum credere non potuerint: Quandoquidem ipsemet Christus admiratus fit fidem Nathanaelis, & praedicauit beatum Simonem qui confitereturfilium Dei, quem non reuelauit ipsi caro & sanguis, sed Pater qui est in coelis. Contra vero nostris temporibus postquam iam Christus ex potentia Dei resurrexit ac reuixit, iam non amplius est infirmus Christus, sed gloriosus. Ideoque Paulus ait, quod si Christum aliquando cognouimus secundum carnem; hoc est in infirmitate naturae humanae, nunc amplius non nouimus eum secundum carnem. Cur igitur habeamus beamus Christum non in terris infirmum, sed in cœlis glorificatum, profectò fides nostra non tam operosa est ac difficilis, quàm fuit eorum, quibuscum versatus est in carne: neque cùm iam habeamus glorificatum ante oculos nostros, crux ipsius debet esse nobis tantæ offensioni, quantæ fuit olim Iudæis; quanquam incredulos Iudæos non excusamus. Sed omnis labor est in videnda illa Christi gloria, quam si semel daretur videre ac intueri, tum profectò minori negotio confirmaretur nostra in eum fides. Equidem de hoc & mihi & aliis semper cogitandum existimaui, vt si quo modo fieri possit videamus, & nouum Christum, hoc est iam glorificatum in cœlis depositā omni infirmitate, & nouum mundum: Nam vi gloriæ & resurrectionis eius, vt ait Paulus, vetera transierunt, ecce nova facta sunt omnia. Ideóque Paulus ibidem ait, se neminem secundum carnem nouisse, hoc est, secundum ista carnalia, vt genus, patriam, formam, gloriam, opes & cætera, in quibus homines se fatigant. Non damno planè ista vetera, sed præferenda noua dico, & regeneratum hominem pluris à nobis faciendum causa regenerationis, quàm causa primæ illius generationis & propinquitatis naturæ: cuius causa etiam tenemur alij alios diligere, & de nobis inuicem solliciti esse. Optárim, inquit Paulus, anathema esse à Christo pro fratribus meis, cognatis inquam meis, secundum carnem. Verùm iis non oportet tam familiariter vti quàm renatis. Illud enim est ingenium verè renati cuiusque, vt non possit familiariter vti coniunctissimo quoque, nisi videat renatum aliquo modo, & nouum hominem factum in Christo. Quod si nullo discrimine vtaris renato & non renato, ego equidem non duxerim te renatum esse, vtcunque profitearis fidem ac regenerationem in Christo Iesu.
units.tr: First observe, in the example of Mary, that while Christ dwelt among the Jews there were very many who thought of him, so to speak, only in a carnal way. He did indeed dwell among them, as I said, as the one full of grace and truth (John 1.14). But weakness, and as it were that veil of the flesh, obscured that glory of God dwelling bodily in him, so that they could not believe in him unless they were illuminated in an extraordinary and wonderful way. Indeed, Christ himself marvelled at the faith of Nathanael, and pronounced blessed Simon, who confessed the Son of God, whom flesh and blood had not revealed to him, but the Father who is in heaven. On the other hand, in our own times, since Christ has risen and revived by the power of God, Christ is no longer weak but glorious. Therefore Paul says that if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, that is, in the weakness of human nature, now we no longer know him according to the flesh. Therefore, since we see Christ not as weak on earth but as glorified in heaven, surely our faith is not as laborious and difficult as it was for those with whom he dwelt in the flesh. And since we now have him glorified before our eyes, his cross ought not to be as great a stumbling block to us as it once was to the Jews, although we do not excuse the unbelieving Jews. But all our labour lies in seeing that glory of Christ, which, if it were once granted us to see and behold, our faith in him would certainly be strengthened with much less effort. I have certainly always thought that I and others ought to consider this, so that, if in any way it can be done, we may see the new Christ, that is, Christ already glorified in heaven and stripped of all weakness, and a new world. For by the power of his glory and resurrection, as Paul says, old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new. Therefore Paul says in the same place that he knew no one according to the flesh, that is, according to those carnal things such as lineage, country, appearance, glory, wealth and the rest, in which men wear themselves out. I do not altogether condemn those old things, but I say that the new things are to be preferred, and that a regenerated man is to be valued by us more for the sake of his regeneration than for that first natural generation and kinship, for the sake of which we are also bound to love one another and to be anxious for one another. I could wish, says Paul, to be anathema from Christ for my brothers, my kinsmen, I mean, according to the flesh. But we ought not to use those natural ties as familiarly as we use those with the regenerate. For it is the character of every truly regenerate person that he cannot be familiar even with those closest to him unless he sees that they too are in some way regenerate and have become a new man in Christ. But if you treat a regenerate and an unregenerate person without any distinction, I for my part would not judge you to be regenerate, however much you may profess faith and regeneration in Christ Jesus.

units.la: Rursus obserua, Christus omni tempore curam gerit nostri, & sollicitus est de nobis, vsque adeo vt nemine egeat, neque angelo neque homine subornatore, qui faciat vnquam vt nostri recordetur, vel de nobis incipiat cogitare. Postquàm autem tempus illud aduenit præstitutum ab æterno nobis iuuandis & liberandis, tum manum admouet & nos liberat: Antequam tempus illud aduenìat, videtur quidem nobis nonnunquam, vt su-mus morae omnis impatientes, videtur, inquam, mo-ram facere & tardare; sed non tardat Dominus qui pro-misit. Nam tardare is dicitur, qui temporis opportuni-tatem negligit, quod non cadit in Dominum, cui tum opportunum est agendi aliquid tempus, cùm aduenit tempus illud quod ab aeterno est praestitutum. Cùm au-tem tempore à se praefinito nobis iuuandis & liberan-dis manum admouet, tum quidem Dei auxilium adeo tempestiuè nobis videtur ac opportunè accidere, vt li-cet in aliquam impatientiam iam ante cruperimus; ta-men nunc si optio detur nobis non alio aliquo tem-pore velimus Deum nos respexisse nobiscum eripien-dis manum admouisse. Vide postremò, saepius ita lo-quitur Christus, nondum, inquiens, venit hora mea, vt hoc loco, vt postea cap. 7.6.&8. Id ideo facit, quo si-gnificet se non facere quicquam nisi praestituto tempo-re; neque id solum (nam & homines non possunt fa-cere aliquid nisi praefinitis à Deo temporibus) verùm etiam quo significet se cognoscere opportunitates agen-di; Neque id solum, verùm etiam quo significet se ab aeterno definiuisse omnes opportunitates suas, ac pro-inde se Deum esse ab aeterno cum Patre, & Spiritu Sancto, cui cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto sit omnis honor & gloria. Amen.
units.tr: Again, observe that Christ at all times takes care of us and is concerned for us, so much so that he needs no angel or human helper to make him remember us or begin to think of us. But when that time has come which was appointed from eternity for helping and delivering us, then he stretches out his hand and sets us free. Before that time comes, it sometimes seems to us, who are impatient of any delay, that he is putting off and delaying; but the Lord who promised is not slow. For someone is said to be slow when he neglects the opportune time, and that cannot apply to the Lord, for for him the time to act is opportune only when that time which was fixed from eternity has come. But when he stretches out his hand to help and deliver us at the time he has set for himself, the help of God then appears to us so timely and so well suited that, although we had already become impatient, if we were offered the choice we would not want God to have looked upon us or stretched out his hand to rescue us at any other time. Finally, notice that Christ often speaks in this way, saying "My hour has not yet come," as here, and later in chapters 7 and 8. He does this to signify that he does nothing except at the appointed time; and not only that (for men too can do nothing except at the times God has fixed), but also to signify that he knows the opportunities for acting. And not only that, but also to signify that he has determined all his opportunities from eternity, and therefore that he is God from eternity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be all honour and glory. Amen.

units.la: Hactenus Maria egit cum Christo filio suo secun-dum carnem; nunc conuersa ad ministros, facite, inquit, quodcunque dixerit vobis. Obseruo ex his verbis repre-hensionis Christi duo effecta in animo Mariae extitisse: alterum, humiliata est & adducta ad obedientiam: alterum, vt deiecta est vna ex parte, sic ex altera erecta est ad spem eius rei quam expetiuit à filio impetran-da. Nam quod simpliciter obedientiam praecipiat ministris, id satis ostendit ipsam iam prius ad obedien-tiam formatam & humiliatam: quod autem praecipiat iis vt faciant quodcunque dixerit, non obscurè docet Christum fecisse matri suae aliquam spem obtinendi id quod petiit. Discimus igitur hoc Mariae exemplo, quòd Dominus cùm reprehendit & castigat suos, ita humiliari quidem eos, vt interea temporis excitentur fide & spe gratiae. Nam omnes castigationes & reprehensiones
units.tr: Thus far Mary has dealt with Christ her son according to the flesh; now, turning to the ministers, she says, "Do whatever he tells you." From these words of Christ's rebuke I observe that two effects arose in Mary's mind. The first is that she was humbled and brought to obedience; the second is that, while she was cast down on one side, she was on the other side raised up to hope for the thing she desired to obtain from her son. For that she simply commands the ministers to obey shows well enough that she had already been formed and humbled to obedience; but that she tells them to do whatever he says plainly teaches that Christ had given his mother some hope of obtaining what she asked. We learn therefore from Mary's example that when the Lord rebukes and chastises his people, he humbles them indeed, but in the meantime they are stirred up in faith and in hope of grace. For all the chastisements and rebukes

units.la: {a} 1. Petr. 3.9. prehensiones Domini sunt paternæ: quòd si paternæ, elucet in iis omnibus aliqua scintilla paterni fauoris & amoris: sensu autem fauoris & amoris Dei necesse est excitemur ad credendum & sperandum. Dauid quo tempore grauissimè questus est de grauima-nu & castigatione Dei, interea temporis recreari consueuit aspectu gratiæ & misericordiæ ipsius. Et nos ipsi cùm deiicimur animo ac humiliamur, sentimus tum maximè suauitatem illam Dei nostri, animíque nostri in ipso dolore maximè lætantur Dei præsentia, qui habitat in contrito corde. Deinde videmus excellens quoddam in Maria effectum indubitatæ spei: dum enim sperat impetraturam se quod petiit, tradit se totam voluntati Christi, seque ipsi prorsus subiicit. Qui sperant in Domino, ij tradunt se prorsus Domino, & quasi clausis iam oculis, patiuntur se abduci, quocunque ipsi Domino visum fit, certò interea exspectantes fore, vt nunquam pudefiant, Spes enim non pudefacit. Paulus ait se gaudere atque etiam gaudium esse de eorum quoque prædicatione, qui tamen per invidiam & contentionem non sincerè ac pure Christum prædicarunt. Paulò post significat se nihili facere vel vitam vel mortem. Vndenam hæc tanta securitas? Nouì, inquit, fore vt hoc mihi cedat saluti: & paulò post, Secundum intentam, inquit, expectationem & spem meam quòd nulla in re pudefiam. Qui non lubens ac volens subiicit se voluntati Dei, imò Deo præscribit quod de se fieri velit, non autem relinquit hoc simpliciter Dei ipsius arbitrio, profecto is homo, quisquis est, nunquam sperauit in Dominum. Spem enim sequitur simplex obedientia, & traditio quasi nostri ipsorum in manus & voluntatem Dei nostri.
units.tr: {a} 1 Pet. 3.9. of the Lord are fatherly; and if they are fatherly, some spark of a father's favour and love shines in all of them; and by the sense of God's favour and love we must necessarily be roused to believe and to hope. David, at the time when he most bitterly complained of the heavy hand and chastisement of God, was accustomed in the meantime to be refreshed by the sight of his grace and mercy. And we ourselves, when we are cast down and humbled in spirit, feel then most of all that sweetness of our God, and our souls rejoice most in the very pain at the presence of God, who dwells in the contrite heart. Next we see in Mary an excellent effect of undoubted hope: for while she hopes that she will obtain what she asked, she gives herself wholly to the will of Christ and submits herself entirely to him. Those who hope in the Lord give themselves wholly to the Lord, and, as if their eyes were already closed, they allow themselves to be led wherever it seems good to the Lord, while meanwhile they confidently expect that they will never be put to shame, for hope does not disappoint. Paul says that he rejoices, and that there is even joy in the preaching of those who nevertheless preached Christ through envy and strife and not sincerely and purely. A little later he signifies that he counts life and death as nothing. Whence comes such great confidence? "I know," he says, "that this will turn out for my salvation"; and a little later, "according to my earnest expectation and hope, that in nothing shall I be put to shame." He who does not gladly and willingly submit himself to the will of God, but rather prescribes to God what he wants done with him, and does not simply leave this to God's own judgement, that man, whoever he is, has certainly never hoped in the Lord. For simple obedience and the surrender of ourselves, as it were, into the hands and will of our God follow upon hope.

units.la: Postremò Maria postquàm ipsa didicit obedientiā, docet deinde ministros obedientiā. Qui ipsi priores didicerunt obedientiam, ij optimi euadunt aliis obedientiæ doctores. Discitur autem obedientia Dei non suauibus dulcibus & persuasoriis docentis vocibus, sed minis etiam nonnunquam opus est & castigationibus, quæ est cordis humani durities & obstinatio. Fateor igitur non fingi animos nostros ad obedientiam sine amaritudine aliqua & principia doctrinæ istius amara esse admodum nobisque ingrata: Verum semel iam flexi ac imbuti ad obedientiam, dici non potest quantopere delectemur ea. Delector, inquit Paulus, Lege Dei, quoad interiorem hominem. Adeo tam iucunda nobis incipit esse, etiam inchoata illa obedientia, ut reliquiæ illæ rebellionis, quibus tantopere antea sumus delectati, iam incipiant esse nobis ingratissimæ; Et nos iam cum Paulo incipiamus exclamare, Miser ego homo, quis me liberabit ex isto corpore mortis? Quod autem delectat nos plurimum, id libenter cum aliis communicamus: hinc igitur est, quod nos ipsi obedientes Deo facti, serio & graviter omnibus aliis obedientiam illam Dei commendemus, ut & ipsi, si possit fieri, degustent illam Dei obedientiam & probent, quæ sit voluntas Dei bona illa accepta & perfecta. Rom. 12.2.
units.tr: Finally, Mary, having learned obedience herself, then teaches the ministers obedience. Those who have first learned obedience themselves become the best teachers of obedience to others. Now the obedience of God is learned not by gentle, sweet and persuasive voices of the teacher, but sometimes there is need of threats and chastisements, because of the hardness and obstinacy of the human heart. I admit, therefore, that our souls are not shaped to obedience without some bitterness, and the first principles of this teaching are very bitter and very unwelcome to us. But once we have been bent and trained to obedience, it cannot be said how greatly we take delight in it. "I delight," says Paul, "in the law of God according to the inner man." So pleasant does even that obedience, only begun, become to us, that those remnants of rebellion, in which we had formerly taken such great delight, now begin to be most unwelcome to us; and we ourselves, now with Paul, begin to cry out, "Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?" But what delights us most, we gladly share with others. Hence it is that we, having been made obedient to God ourselves, will earnestly and seriously commend that obedience of God to all others, so that they too, if it can be done, may taste that obedience of God and prove what is the good, acceptable and perfect will of God. Rom. 12.2.

units.la: Hactenus fuerint partes Mariæ: sequuntur nunc partes Christi præcipientes & ministrorum obedientium dicto. Narratio ita habet, Erant autem ibi lapideæ hydriæ sex positæ, positæ, inquam, & dispositæ ad usum conviuarum secundum purificationem Iudæorum, hoc est, usum purificationum & lotionum Iudaicarum: Lege quidem Dei præscriptæ fuerant Iudæis aliquot purificationes, sed illi non conterent Legis Dei simplicitate, nullum finem purificationum fecerunt: Ut eorum exemplo discamus quàm nimij semper homines fuerint in externis rebus & corporalibus exercitationibus, quæ paulum aut nihil habent utilitatis, & nullius sunt pretij.
units.tr: So far have been the parts of Mary; now follow the parts of Christ giving orders and of the obedient ministers carrying out his word.
