The narrative reads thus: "Now there were set there six water-pots of stone," set, I say, and arranged for the use of the guests "according to the purification of the Jews," that is, for the use of Jewish purifications and washings. By the law of God, indeed, some purifications had been prescribed for the Jews, but they did not keep the simplicity of God's law, and "made no end of purifications." Let us learn from their example how excessive men have always been in external and bodily exercises, which have little or no usefulness and are of no value.

units.la: Rursus collocatæ sunt hæ ipsæ hydriæ in domo nuptiali proculdubio ostentationis gratia, ut scias superstitionem semper esse ambitiosam, & inventis suis homines, ac in re religionis figmentis semper quærere sibi inanem gloriam. Testis est hodierno die Papistica illa superstitio, quæ cum tota sit consarcinata ex rebus illis externis & corporalibus, illæ ipsæ rursus externæ res & corporales sunt comparatæ ad ostentationem, & ad externam pompam & gloriæ speciem, cuius aspectu fascinent ac inescent instabiles ac fluctuantes animas. Quod si qui sint, ut sunt quidem aliqui & ii non pauci, qui in tanta luce non tamen vident has impostituras & vanitatem
units.tr: Again, these same water-pots were placed in the wedding house, no doubt for the sake of display, so that you may know that superstition is always ostentatious, and that men always seek vain glory in their own inventions and in the fictions of religion. To this day that Papist superstition bears witness, which, since it is wholly patched together from those external and bodily things, those very external and bodily things are again arranged for display, and for outward pomp and the appearance of glory, by the sight of which they bewitch and entice unstable and wavering souls. But if there are some, as indeed there are some, and not a few, who even in so great a light do not yet see these impostures and this Papist vanity,

units.la: 3. Partes Christi præcipientis & ministrorum obedientium. Hydriæ lapideæ.
units.tr: 3. The parts of Christ giving orders and of the obedient ministers. The stone water-pots.

units.la: 2. Cor. 4.3-4. tem hanc Papisticam, Quid de iis aliud possum dicere quàm quod dixit Paulus, Quòd si teclum est nostrum Euan-gelium, iis qui pereunt teclum est, quibus Deus huius seculi excæcauit mentes, &c. Pergit in descriptione vasorum, eaque à genere mensurae, quod amphoram vocarunt, & ab amphorarum numero quem capiebat vnaquæque hydria, definit. Vnaquæque, inquit, hydria capiebat binas vel ternas amphoras. Amphora alio nomine Quadrantal dicebatur, a mensurae eius figura, continetque quadrantal octauam partem cadi siue modij. Sed his omissis videamus cur circumstantiæ hæ singulæ tam accuratè ab Euangelista annotatæ sunt. Primùm vasa ipsa nominantur, deinde materia ex qua facta sunt, tertiò vasorum numerus, quartò denique mensura quam capiebant singula. Hæc annotata sunt tam minutatim ad ostendendam & magnitudinem & certitudinem miraculi. Primum enim magna aquæ copia mutata est miraculosè in magnam vini copiam: deinde hæ circumstantiæ tot & tam minutæ rem certò factam esse docent, & quasi præsentem ante oculos ponunt; vt nos qui factum hoc non vidimus oculis hís nostris, credamus & credentes habeamus vitam æternam. Beati qui cum non viderint, credunt tamen.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 4.3-4. What else can I say about them than what Paul said: "If our gospel is hid, it is hid to those who perish, whose minds the god of this world has blinded," etc. He goes on to describe the vessels, and defines them by the measure called the amphora, and by the number of amphorae that each water-pot held: "Each water-pot," he says, "held two or three amphorae." The amphora was also called the quadrantal, from the shape of that measure, and it contains the eighth part of a cadus or bushel. But leaving these aside, let us see why these individual details have been so carefully noted by the Evangelist. First the vessels themselves are named, then the material of which they were made, third the number of the vessels, and fourth the measure which each held. These things are noted so minutely to show both the greatness and the certainty of the miracle. For first a great quantity of water was miraculously changed into a great quantity of wine; then these many and such minute circumstances teach that the thing was done with certainty, and put it as it were before our eyes, so that we who did not see this with our own eyes may believe, and believing may have eternal life. Blessed are they who have not seen and yet have believed.

units.la: Sequuntur partes Christi primùm, deinde Ministrorum: Christus præcipit, illi parent. Præcipit igitur primùm omnium Christus vt impleant hydrias aquâ, Implete, inquit, has hydrias aqua. Nõ opus quidem fuit Domino istorum ministerio in edendo opere suo, quorum alioqui ministerio indiguerunt conuiue. Verum visum est Domino tum vti iplorum ministerio, vt ipsorum postea testimonio vteretur in publicando suo miraculo. Dominus potest, fine rei creatæ cuiusquam ministerio omnia quæ vult facere, placet tamen adhibere in opere suo faciendo hominum ministerium, vt homines deinde de opere Domini testentur, illud prædicent aliis, & Dominum suum in eo glorificent. Illud enim merito possum affirmare, neminem esse omnino cuius ministerio Dominus vtitur in quocunq; opere siue corporali illo siue spirituali, qui non teneatur prædicare illud opus cuius ipse testis est factus. Magnū enim est illud esse σωτῆρα Domino. Iubet igitur Dominus impleri hydrias illas aquâ, quo nimirum ex iis hydriis aquā primùm impletis haurientes deinde vinum, videant ac palpent Dei opus miraculosum, ipsumque aliis praedicet Deus quos adhibet ministros in opere suo, eos non vult otiosè speculari id quod fit aut fieri, verùm vult eos admonere manum operi, ut prorsus videat sentiantque quid rei agatur, & penitus habeant persuasum de quo aliis sunt testificaturi. Nunquam admittit Deus socium aut ministrum in opere suo, nisi quem plenè perfecte informat ad hoc, ut ipse deinde maiori cum fiducia & libertate possit quod ipse persuasum habet aliis persuadere. Is est qui splendiit in cordibus nostris ad praebendum lumen cognitionis gloriae Dei in facie Iesu Christi. Et cùm huiusmodi spem habeamus multa in loquendo euidentia vtimur.
units.tr: They follow: first the parts of Christ, then those of the ministers. Christ gives the command, and they obey. Christ first of all commands them to fill the water jars: Fill these jars, he says, with water. Indeed the Lord had no need of their ministry to carry out his work, though the guests otherwise needed the ministry of others. But the Lord was pleased to use their service, so that he might afterwards use their testimony in making his miracle known. The Lord can do whatever he wishes without the ministry of any created thing, yet he is pleased to employ human ministry in doing his work, so that men may then bear witness to the work of the Lord, proclaim it to others, and glorify their Lord for it. For I can rightly affirm that there is no one whose ministry the Lord uses in any work, whether bodily or spiritual, who is not bound to proclaim the work of which he has become the witness. For it is a great thing to be a saviour [σωτῆρα] to the Lord. The Lord therefore orders those jars to be filled with water, so that, drawing from those jars once they have been filled with water, they may then draw wine, and see and handle God's miraculous work. And God, who employs ministers in his work, wishes them not merely to look idly at what is or is to be done, but to put their hand to the work, so that they may see and feel completely what is going on, and may be fully persuaded of what they are to bear witness to to others. God never admits a companion or minister into his work unless he has fully and perfectly instructed him for this purpose, so that he may then, with greater confidence and freedom, persuade others of what he himself is persuaded. It is he who has shone in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. And since we have such a hope, we use great plainness of speech.

units.la: Tertiò iubet implere ad summum hydrias illas, non autem ad dimidium. Dominus, ut mirifico suo opere ostendit potentiam suam, ita etiam liberalitatem. Nam Christus omnibus ferè à se editis miraculis, praeterquam quod confirmauit fidem hominum, ostentata in iis mirifica sua potentia, profuit etiam aliquo modo hominibus vel corporaliter vel spiritualiter. Sanavit aegrotos, eiecit daemonia, restituit visum caecis, &c. Nam opera Domini non vno tantùm modo vtilia sunt, sed multis modis: & opus vnumquodque est quasi multiplex, dum est opus potentiae, opus misericordiae ac liberalitatis, opus sapientiae, &c. Ipsi sit omnis gloria, Amen. Quaeri potest, an hac abundantia vini suppeditata, eadem opera suppeditarit Christus conuiuis materiam intemperantiae? Respondeo, Deum liberalitate sua non prouocare homines vel ad intemperantiam, vel ad profusionem quamcunque, verum ad sobrietatem, temperantiam, omnes denique virtutes alias. Quòd si Dei liberalitate abutamur ad intemperantiam, & Dei nostri gratiam transferamus ad lasciviam, hoc nobis ipsis imputandum est. Praeterea & illud addo, Deum liberalitate sua & copia rerum omnium, quibus nos cumulat, probare nos, an velimus sobriè ac temperanter vti beneficiis ipsius. Probatio enim & experimentum perimentum temperantiæ est, non quidem penuria, sed in rerum copia, & beati sunt quotquot possunt dicere cum Paulo, Nouî autem deprimi, noui etiam abundare: vbique & in omnibus initiatus sum & ad saturitatem & ad esuritionem, id est tum ad abundantiam, tum ad inopiam. Verum pauci admodum sunt qui norunt abundare: hoc est sobrie vti illa abundantia ad Dei gloriam.
units.tr: Third, he orders those jars to be filled to the brim, and not halfway. As the Lord shows his power in his wonderful work, so also his generosity. For Christ, in almost all the miracles he performed, besides confirming the faith of men, displaying in them his wonderful power, also benefited men in some way, either bodily or spiritually. He healed the sick, cast out demons, restored sight to the blind, and so on. For the works of the Lord are useful not in one way only but in many ways, and each work is in a sense manifold: it is a work of power, a work of mercy and generosity, a work of wisdom, and so on. To him be all glory, Amen. It may be asked whether, by supplying this abundance of wine, Christ at the same time supplied the guests with the occasion for intemperance? I answer that God by his generosity does not provoke men either to intemperance or to any excess, but to sobriety, temperance, and in short to all the other virtues. And if we abuse the generosity of God for intemperance, and turn the grace of our God into wantonness, this is to be imputed to ourselves. Moreover I add this also: that God, by his generosity and the abundance of all the things with which he loads us, tests us, to see whether we are willing to use his benefits soberly and temperately. For the test and proof of temperance lies not in want but in plenty; and blessed are all who can say with Paul: I know how to be abased, and I know how to abound; everywhere and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, that is, both to abound and to suffer need. But very few indeed know how to abound, that is, to use that abundance soberly for the glory of God.

units.la: Sequitur obedientia Ministrorum: Impleuerunt hydrias vsque ad summum. Non id postulant à Christo vt alia quadam ratione, & ea quidem in speciem magnificentiori, efficiat quod instituit, vt ex nihilo potius vinum creet. Verisimile enim est eos aliquid magni ab ipso expectasse, sed audientes dicto, faciunt statim quod imperat; quod quidem in Ministris laudabile est. Deus mediis in speciem simplicibus & vilibus adhibitis proferre solet opera magnifica. Quid, quæso, mirabilius est regeneratione? illam tamen efficit in nobis leui aquæ aspersione in Baptismo. Quid remissione peccatorum? illam tamen efficit dato & accepto pane & vino in cœna Domini. Quamobrem nos intuiti perpetuo Dei potentiam illam, qua potest facere quod vult & promissiones Dei quibus ostendit se velle facere quod potest, contenti sinus mediis quamuis in speciem vilibus & simplicibus. Ea est hominum natura, fateor, qua non contenti illis mediis quæ Deo placent, vt quæ non satis magnifica & splendida ipsis videantur, velint Deo in excogitandis mediis esse sapientiores. Naaman ille Syrus, non contentus simplici illa immersione septupla in Iordanem à Prophetæ Dei præscripta ad hoc vt sanitatem recuperaret & à lepra mundaretur, somniauit sibi rationem magis, vt ipsi visum est, gloriosam & magnificam. Sic Papistæ hodierno die, non contenti simplici institutione Domini in administrando Baptismum & Cœnam Domini, sua nescio quæ inuenta, quæ incantationibus similiora sunt, quam sanctis ritibus ac cæremoniis, adiecerunt, ad reddendam vt ipsis videtur institutionem magis gloriosam ac splendidam. Sed nos existimemus stultitiam Dei sapientiorem esse quàm homines cùm vniuersa sua sapientia, & infirmitatem Dei validiorem esse quàm homines cum tota sua potentia. Huic fit omnis gloria, Amen. Christus iam ad summum impletis aqua hydriis, & aqua iam secreta quadam potentia & diuina virtute ipsius in vinum conuersa, dicit Ministris, Haurite nunc & offerte Architriclino. Iussit offerri vinum hautiu non conuiuis statim, ne nondum ab illis cognito, vt videtur, vini defectu, factum ipsum & miraculum supprimeretur, sed iussit offerri illud Architriclino, qui bene sibi conscius defectus qui fuit vini, factum in admiratione habiturus fuit ac conuiuis promulgaturus. Dominus non temere & sine delecta opera sua primum omnium offerri vult ea quibusvis, verùm iis primùm omnium offerri vult ea quos nouit de operibus ipsius non tacituros, sed coram, ad gloriam nominis sui, praecones futuros: nominatim autem vult offerri ea iis qui norunt defectum ipsorum. Nam ij sunt potissimum qui magnificant opera & misericordias Domini. Qui verò nullum defectum sentiunt, etsi cumulentur quidem subinde beneficiis & operibus Dei omnibus, tamen etiam dum his vtuntur, aut potiùs abutuntur eáque denorant, os suum non aperiunt ad commendandam illam Dei tantam liberalitatem. Quamobrem nemo dicat bene in huiusmodi hominibus collocari Dei beneficia. Hactenus fuit mandatum Christi, sequitur Ministrorum obedientia. Illi igitur obtulerunt, nempe Architriclino vini haustum; Parent Ministri in omnibus, citra responsationem, placide ac liberter, id quod argumento est in Christo dum in terris ageret etiam infirmo, dignitatem tamen & maiestatem conspectam fuisse, cui aduenæ & ignoto parent etiam serui, qui vix libenti animo parent dominis suis.
units.tr: Next comes the obedience of the ministers: They filled the jars up to the brim. They do not ask Christ to effect what he has ordered by some other means, one that might seem more magnificent, so that he might create wine out of nothing instead. For it is likely that they expected something great from him, but, obeying his word, they immediately do what he commands; and this is praiseworthy in ministers. God is accustomed to bring about magnificent works by means that seem simple and mean. What, I ask, is more wonderful than regeneration? Yet he effects it in us by the light sprinkling of water in Baptism. What is more wonderful than the forgiveness of sins? Yet he effects it by the giving and receiving of bread and wine in the Lord's Supper. Therefore, fixing our gaze continually on that power of God by which he can do what he wills, and on the promises of God by which he shows that he wills to do what he can, let us be content with means, however mean and simple they may seem. This, I admit, is human nature: not content with those means which please God, because they do not seem sufficiently magnificent and splendid, men want to be wiser than God in devising means. That Syrian Naaman, not content with the simple immersion seven times in the Jordan prescribed by the prophet of God for recovering his health and being cleansed of leprosy, imagined a method more glorious and magnificent, as it seemed to him. So the Papists today, not content with the simple institution of the Lord in administering Baptism and the Lord's Supper, have added I know not what inventions, which are more like incantations than holy rites and ceremonies, in order to make the institution, as it seems to them, more glorious and splendid. But let us reckon that the foolishness of God is wiser than men with all their wisdom, and the weakness of God stronger than men with all their power. To him be all glory, Amen. Christ, now that the jars have been filled to the brim with water, and the water has been turned into wine by a hidden power and his divine virtue, says to the ministers: Draw out now, and carry it to the chief steward. He ordered the wine to be carried not at once to the guests, lest the deed and the miracle be suppressed, since the guests, as it seems, did not yet know of the shortage of wine; but he ordered it to be carried to the chief steward, who, being well aware of the shortage of wine, would hold the deed in wonder and make it known to the guests. The Lord does not wish his works to be offered rashly and without choice to just anyone; he wishes them to be offered first to those whom he knows will not keep silent about his works, but will be heralds before others, to the glory of his name. And he especially wishes them to be offered to those who know their own lack. For these are the ones who above all magnify the works and mercies of the Lord. But those who feel no lack, although they are indeed continually loaded with the benefits and works of God, yet even while they enjoy them, or rather abuse them and devour them, do not open their mouths to commend that great generosity of God. Therefore let no one say that God's benefits are well bestowed on such men. So far was the command of Christ; now follows the obedience of the ministers. They therefore offered it, namely a draught of wine, to the chief steward. The ministers obey in all things, without answering back, calmly and willingly, which is evidence that even when Christ was on earth, in his weakness, his dignity and majesty were nevertheless seen, since strangers and unknown men were obeyed, even by servants, who scarcely obey their masters with a willing mind.

units.la: Hactenus fuerunt partes Christi, simul & Ministrorum: sequuntur partes Architriclini. Primum gustauit Architriclinus aquam illam quae facta fuerat vinum: deinde nesciens unde esset, cùm tamen scirent ministri unde esset, sponsum ad se aduocat, Aduocato sponso, admiratus ipsius in agendo consilium & prudentiam, Omnes, inquit, primo loco bonum vinum apponunt, &c. Hæc capita persequamur ordine. De vino gustato ab Architriclino nihil dici-
units.tr: So far were the parts of Christ and of the ministers together; now follow the parts of the chief steward. First, the chief steward tasted the water that had been made wine; then, not knowing where it came from, although the ministers knew where it came from, he calls the bridegroom to himself, and when the bridegroom had been summoned, marvelling at his conduct and prudence in the matter, says: Everyone, he says, sets out the good wine first, etc. Let us follow these points in order. Concerning the wine tasted by the chief steward, let nothing be said-

units.la: 2. Corinth. 3.25. dicimus: ad secundum venimus. Ignarus unde esset, quod tamen sciebant Ministri, aduocat sponsum. Nunc videor mihi videre causam, cur visus sit Christus horum ministerio in hoc opere faciundo: ea autem fuit, vt illi cognoscerent opus Domini, & eo cognito de ipso testantur: Vbi vides rursus quanta sit Dei gratia illa, quam dignatur in ministerio in opere ipsius faciudo. Nam cum alij ignari sunt operis Dei, ipse conscius est operis Dei, Deumque glorificat. Ignoratio huius vini vndenam illud esset in causa cur sponsum ad se vocet Architriclinus, eumque alloquatur. Verum & altera causa addisci potest, ex sermone illo habito cum sponso, quo factum admirans ait, Omnes primo loco bonum vinum apponunt. Nempe causa est sapor vini delicatior, quo fit vt in admirationem rapiatur & admirans ita loquatur: secus enim, etsi defectus ac inopiae vini conscius, tamen opus hoc Domini silentio praeteriisset. Hinc discimus quam simus negligentes in Dei operibus praedicandis, etiam vbi sensimus defectu. Dominus autem contra variis rationibus ac modis omnibus nos prouocat ad praedicandum opus suum. Primum omnium patitur nos sentire defectum operis & auxilij sui, ad hoc vt cum auxiliatus nobis fuerit praeter expectationem nostram, pluris faciamus Dei opus & auxilium, eoque propensiores simus ad Deum glorificandum. Cum vero ne ea quidem te mouemur, vt sumus socordes natura & ingrati, tum ne silentio sepeliatur opus suum, imprimit qualitatem & conditionem aliquam operi excellentem & admirabilem, qua inuitos alioqui prouocet ad operis admirationē & praedicationem. Omnia Dei opera sunt admirabilia, etiam ordinaria haec & naturalia, habentque impressam sibi imaginem aliquam, maiestatis, potentiae, misericordiae, iustitiae, sapientiae diuinae: Vnde Paulus, Invisibilia, inquit, vt sunt potentia & diuinitas ipsius ex rebus conditis intelliguntur. Hoc adeo verū est, vt vilissima quaeque creatura vt pilus graminis, vt culex, magis ad viuum representet nobis imaginē Dei, quam omnes imagines illae Papistarū pictae, sculptae, fusae: sed stultiores imaginibus suis, ipsorū stultitię permitto ac vanitati. Dico igitur omnia Dei opera etiam haec ordinaria plane admirabilia esse & insculptam sibi habere imaginem maiestatis ipsius. Verum extraordinaria illa & miraculosa multo maxime ostendunt nobis Dei potetiam ac omnino maiestatem, eaque Deus eo artificio fabricatur, eas notas illis imprimit, vt, si quam maxime vellent homines ea silentio sepelire, non possint tamen ita usque adeo rapiatur in admirationem ipsorum. Si Guisius ille, vel si rex ipse Gallorum e medio fuisset sublatus ab Hucnofio aliquo, vt ipsi vocant, tum quidem vel ipsa conscientia hoc iis extorsisset, iusto Dei iudicio factum fuisse in eos, qui tam barbarae crudelitatis fuerunt authores, de quia nulla vnquam aetas conticescet. Sed cum rex ipse Gallorum Guisium per fraudem oppressisset: cum rursus monachus Iacobita quidam nebulo regem Gallorum, cuius maiestatem sacrosanctam esse oportuit & inviolabilem, per maiorem fraudem occiderit, quod faci-nus equidem scio a nemine bono approbari, cogitur tamen mundus hoc opus Dei admirari ipsumque praedicare in perpetuum. Et homo ille sceleratus, filius, inquā, perditionis, qui in templo Dei tanquam Deus sedet, conscientia conuictus, necesse est illud ipsum opus tam admirabile iusto Dei iudicio ascribat ipsumque praedicet, etsi quam maxime & illud Dei opus sepultū esse velit, & conscientiam operis omnem cauterio resecta[m] esse.
units.tr: 2. Corinth. 3.25. We have spoken of the wine; now we come to the second point. Though ignorant of where it came from, the servants, who did know, summon the bridegroom. Now I seem to see why Christ chose to work this miracle through the ministers: it was so that they should know the work of the Lord and, knowing it, bear witness to it. Here you see again how great is that grace of God which he deigns to show in ministers in carrying out his work. For while others are ignorant of God's work, they are aware of it and glorify God. The Architriclinus' ignorance of where the wine came from is the reason he calls the bridegroom and speaks to him. But another reason can also be gathered from the speech he made to the bridegroom, in which, marvelling at what had been done, he says: Everyone serves the good wine first. The cause is clearly the more delicate flavour of the wine, which carries him off into admiration, so that in his amazement he speaks as he does. Otherwise, though aware of the lack and want of wine, he would have passed over this work of the Lord in silence. Here we learn how negligent we are in proclaiming the works of God, even when we have felt the want. The Lord, on the other hand, challenges us by every means and in many ways to proclaim his work. First of all, he allows us to feel the lack of his work and help, so that when he has helped us beyond our expectation, we may value God's work and help more highly and be the more inclined to glorify God. When even this does not move us, for we are naturally slothful and ungrateful, then, so that his work is not buried in silence, he stamps upon it some excellent and admirable quality by which he may otherwise provoke us, unwilling as we are, to wonder at it and to proclaim it. All the works of God are admirable, even these ordinary and natural ones, and they bear impressed upon them some image of the majesty, power, mercy, justice and divine wisdom. Hence Paul says: The invisible things of him, that is, his eternal power and Godhead, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made. This is so true that the humblest creature, a hair of grass or a gnat, represents the image of God to us more vividly than all those images of the Papists, painted, carved and cast. But they are more foolish than their images, and I leave them to their own folly and vanity. I say therefore that all the works of God, even these ordinary ones, are plainly admirable and have the image of his majesty engraved upon them. But the extraordinary and miraculous works show us God's power and majesty far more, and God so fashions them and so stamps these marks upon them that, however much men might wish to bury them in silence, they cannot, so that they are carried off into admiration. If that Guise, or the king of the French himself, had been removed from the midst by some Huguenot, as they call him, then surely their own conscience would have extorted this from them, that it was done by the just judgment of God upon those who were the authors of such barbarous cruelty, a deed no age will ever pass over in silence. But when the king of the French himself had treacherously overthrown Guise, and again a certain Jacobin monk, a scoundrel, had by a greater treachery killed the king of the French, whose sacred and inviolable majesty ought to have been, a deed which I know is approved by no good man, yet the world is compelled to admire this work of God and to proclaim it forever. And that wicked man, the son, I say, of perdition, who sits in the temple of God as God, convicted by his conscience, must needs ascribe that very admirable work to the just judgment of God and proclaim it, even though he would most of all wish that work buried and every trace of it cut away with a cautery.

units.la: Sequuntur verba quibus alloquitur Architriclinus sponsum, Omnes, inquit, primo loco bonum vinum apponunt, &c. Videtur admirari hominis prudentiam in oeconomicis ac domesticis dispensandis, & eam quidem longe abliam a consuetudine omnium aliorum qui conuiuas accipiant. Quo loco vides primum eum ascribere sponso ipsiusque prudentiae factum illud Domini. Homines ignari Dei, prouidentiae ipsius, bonitatis ipsius, potentiae ipsius, si quando vident aliquid perfici hominum ministerio, de Deo nullum verbum faciunt; hominum vero prudentiam, potentiam, fortitudinem aliasque virtutes in coelos extollunt, quasi vero ipsi sua virtute dūtaxat ista egerint. huiusmodi solent esse omnes cogratulationes hominū prophanorum. Contra vero qui nouit Deū fonte omnis bonitatis, qui nouit sententiā ipsius efficacem in omnium hominum actionibus, Dei prouidentiā suspi-
units.tr: There follow the words with which the Architriclinus addresses the bridegroom: Everyone serves the good wine first, and so on. He seems to admire the man's prudence in ordering household and domestic affairs, and a prudence quite different from the custom of all others who receive guests. Here you see that he first ascribes to the bridegroom and to his prudence what was really the Lord's doing. Men who are ignorant of God, of his providence, of his goodness and of his power, when they see something accomplished by human ministry, say nothing of God; but they extol to the heavens the prudence, power, courage and other virtues of men, as if they had done these things by their own virtue alone. Such are usually all the congratulations of profane men. But he who knows God as the fountain of all goodness, who knows that his will is effective in all human actions, looks up to God's providence.

units.la: Architriclini ad sponsum verba, Dei gloriā obscurant, vt hominī gratulentur. suspiciūt, homines dūtaxat, vt instrumēta diuinæ proui-dētię agnoscūt. Huiusmodi semper cōsueuerūt esse cō-gratulationes omniū piorū, huiusmodi sunt omnes cō-gratulationes Pauli in epistolis suis: Audiui, inquit, de fide & charitate vestra, &c. Quid tū, an ista ascribit hominibus? minimè, sed agnoscit ista omnia à Deo esse profecta, atque eorū nomine gratias agit Deo. Nō lego equidē Pauli admirari vel sapientiā, vel alias quasvis virtutes hominū: At lego eū mirari hominū stultitiā: Miror, inquit, ita deserto eo qui vocavit vos in gratiā Christi trāsferri in aliud euangelium. Nunquā gloriatur de virtutibus suis, sed gloriabor inquit, in infirmitatibus meis. Deinde his ipsis verbis adūbrauit nobis Architriclinus ingeniū hominū natura fallax ac sophisticum. Omnes cuiuscūque dignitatis vocationis & ordinis sūt, optimis ac lectissimis quibusq; rebus iuxta vocatione cuiusque primū oblatis, allicere conātur credulos ac simplices ad fidē ipsis habēdam, tū vbi alectos vident, pessimis quibusq; oblatis secūdo quasi loco miseris imponūt. Hoc mercatorum est artificiū, hæc omniū deniq; sophistica est. Vnde autem hoc ingeniū tā fallax huius sæculi? nēpe à principe huius sæculi. Ita enim ille nos ad se allicere solet primum obiecta specie quadā vana ac fallaci glorię, diuitiarum, voluptatū huius mūdi, vt deinde paulatim allectos miserē decipiat, & in perniciem trahat. At Christus contrà dum ipse nos vocat ad se nō optima quæque ac gratissima statim offert, sed ingratissima, vt afflictiones, cruces, mortes denique, cū aliquo sensu tamen gloriæ cōiunctas: Sic autē vocatos coronat tandē immortali gloria.
units.tr: Architriclinus' words to the bridegroom: they obscure God's glory in order to congratulate man. They look up, and they recognise men only as the instruments of divine providence. Such have always been the congratulations of all the godly; such are all the congratulations of Paul in his epistles: I hear, he says, of your faith and love, and so on. Does he ascribe these things to men? By no means; he acknowledges that all of them have come from God and on their account gives thanks to God. I do not read that Paul admired either the wisdom or any other virtues of men; but I do read that he wondered at men's folly: I marvel, he says, that you are so quickly removed from him who called you into the grace of Christ to another gospel. He never boasts of his own virtues, but, he says, I will glory in my infirmities. Then in these very words the Architriclinus has shadowed forth for us the deceitful and sophistical nature of human beings. Everyone, of whatever dignity, calling and rank, first offers the best and choicest things, according to his calling, and tries to attract the credulous and simple to trust him; then, when they are caught, they impose the worst things on the wretched, as though in second place. This is the art of merchants, indeed the whole sophistry of mankind. But whence comes this so deceitful disposition of this age? Surely from the prince of this age. For he is wont to attract us to himself by first presenting objects with a certain empty and deceptive show of glory, of riches, of the pleasures of this world, and then, gradually, deceiving those he has caught, he drags them to ruin. Christ, on the other hand, when he calls us to himself, does not at once offer the best and most pleasing things, but the most unwelcome, such as afflictions, crosses and finally death, yet joined with some sense of glory; and those so called he at last crowns with immortal glory.

units.la: Quare ne cōformemur sæculo huic, sed cōformes simus imaginis Christi, & vt Paulus ad Ephesios loquitur, depositō mendacio loquamur veritatē quisque proximo suo: Nam sumus alij aliorum membra. Illud in natura monstrum videretur, si caput hominis falleret ipsius pedes, si oculus imponeret manui, si os fraudem facere ventri. Non minus profectò hic deformitatis est, cum alia corporis eiusdem Christi membra aliis imponunt. Sed quid dicam? non sunt omnes statim corporis Christi membra, qui sese vendicant hoc nomine, neque etiam qui sunt, si statim omnes prorsus sanctificati sunt; quare studendum sanctificationi & renouationi cordium: Hinc Paulus postquam dixit, Ne configuremini saeculo isti, cōtinuò addidit, sed transformemini per renouationem mentis vestrae, illud innuens, renouationem ac regenerationem nos separare à praesenti hoc saeculo malo, separare à fraudibus, & fallaciis omnibus, denique corporis Christi verè membra efficere.
units.tr: Therefore let us not be conformed to this age, but be conformed to the image of Christ, and, as Paul says to the Ephesians, having put away lying, let each speak truth with his neighbour, for we are members one of another. It would seem a monstrosity in nature if the head of a man deceived his feet, if the eye imposed upon the hand, if the mouth practised fraud on the stomach. Assuredly there is no less deformity when the other members of the same body of Christ impose upon one another. But what am I saying? Not all who claim the name are at once members of the body of Christ, nor, if they are, are they all at once entirely sanctified; therefore we must strive for the sanctification and renewal of our hearts. Hence Paul, after saying, Be not conformed to this world, at once added, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, indicating that renewal and regeneration separate us from this present evil age, separate us from all frauds and deceits, and in short make us true members of the body of Christ.

units.la: Hactenus fuerunt partes Architriclini; sequitur postremo miraculi conclusio: Hoc, inquit, initium signorum fecit Iesus in Cana oppido Galilaeae. Christus initiatus primum baptismo, coepit deinde docere publicè, miraculis autem doctrinam suam confirmauit. Quamobrem cum hoc primum tempore inceperit docere publicè, conueniebat ut hoc primum tempore miraculis confirmaret doctrinam suam. Duplex visus siue effectus miraculi subiicitur: Et manifestam fecit gloriam suam, & crediderunt in eum discipuli eius. Miracula proprie sunt opera quae contra naturam & ordinem secundarum causarum fiunt, ideoque solius Dei potentia fieri ea oportet. Nam nulla est omnium creatura, quae potest naturae ordinem inuertere, non homo, non diabolus, non Angelus. Quod enim ad illa quae iactatur miracula hostium veritatis, non sunt ea quidem miracula, sed illusiones & praestigiae ac fraudes à diabolo profectae, quarum causae quia ignorantur ab hominibus, ideo pro miraculis habentur, cum tamen nomen illud non mereantur. Deus enim testimonio suo, & verè miraculosis operibus suis, nunquam consuevit confirmare diaboli & hominum mendacia cum veritate ipsius ex diametro pugnantia. Quomodo potest homo peccator talia signa edere? Scimus Deum peccatores non audire; & nisi esset hic à Deo non posset quicquam facere. Sed ut redeamus, Deus potentiam suam miraculis ostendit. Hinc duo sequuntur effecta; primum est Dei ipsius gloria quae emergit ex potentia ipsius admirabili. Alterum est, fides hominum in Deum ipsiusque verbum: Videntes enim infinitam illam in miraculis potentiam, adducuntur ac inuitantur ad fidem. Verum quidem est, Dei potentiam quae in miraculis conspicitur eam esse quae cogat vel ipsum diabolum assentiri veritati. Sed est praeterea terea quod in salutari fide requiritur, hoc nempe, vt applicet quisque particulariter ad se veritatem illam promissionum Dei, eademque opera apprehendat corde Christum Iesum gratiamque ipsius promissam: Quod quidem non fit sola inspectione potentiae, sed multo magis aspectu & sensu bonitatis Dei in Christo. Nam potentia Dei sola magis abster ret quam allicit. Si autem simul cum potentia illuceat nobis bonitas in Christo, tum quidem bonitate allicimur ad latitandum sub alis potentiae. Sensus autem bonitatis & amoris Dei obtinetur per Spiritum adoptionis: Spiritus enim adoptionis testatur vna cum spiritu nostro, nos a Deo diligi, non vulgariter aut parce, sed singulariter & abunde: Charitas enim Dei effusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritu Sanctum qui datus est nobis. Prosequitur enim nos Deus non ea tantum charitate qua creator creaturam suam, sed qua pater filium solet amplecti: Diligit enim nos in illo suo dilecto, adeoque dilecti sui amorem nobiscum communicat. Quamobrem ad hoc vt credamus imprimis opus est hoc Dei Spiritu, qui solus plus virium habet ad fidem, quam omnia illa falsa & ementita Papistarum miracula. Nos igitur contenti illis miraculis Christi & Apostolorum, quibus iam olim confirmata est doctrinae euangelicae veritas, petimus a Deo illum adoptionis Spiritum, qui sentire nos doceat illam Dei in Christo dilectionem.
units.tr: Hitherto were the parts of the chief steward. There follows finally the conclusion of the miracle: "This," he says, "the beginning of signs did Jesus in Cana, a town of Galilee." Christ, having first been initiated by baptism, then began to teach publicly, and he confirmed his teaching by miracles. Therefore, since he began to teach publicly at this first time, it was fitting that at this first time he should confirm his teaching by miracles. A twofold sight or effect of the miracle is then added: "And he manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him." Miracles, properly speaking, are works that are done against nature and the order of secondary causes, and so they must be done by the power of God alone. For there is no creature at all that can overturn the order of nature: not man, not the devil, not an angel. As for the so-called miracles of the enemies of the truth, they are not miracles at all but illusions, tricks and frauds brought about by the devil, whose causes, because men do not know them, are therefore held to be miracles, though they do not deserve that name. For God has never been accustomed to confirm by his testimony, and by his truly miraculous works, the lies of the devil and of men, which fight diametrically against his truth. How can a sinful man perform such signs? We know that God does not hear sinners, and unless this man were from God he could do nothing. But to return: God shows his power by miracles. From this two effects follow. The first is the glory of God himself, which shines forth from his wondrous power. The second is the faith of men in God and in his word: for when they see that infinite power in the miracles, they are led and invited to faith. It is indeed true that the power of God seen in miracles is that which compels even the devil himself to assent to the truth. But there is something further required in saving faith, namely that each person apply to himself, individually, that truth of God's promises, and by the same work lay hold on Christ Jesus and the grace promised in him with the heart. This is not done by the mere inspection of power, but much more by the sight and sense of the goodness of God in Christ. For the power of God alone repels more than it attracts. But if along with the power the goodness in Christ shines upon us, then indeed we are drawn by goodness to shelter under the wings of power. The sense of the goodness and love of God is obtained through the Spirit of adoption: for the Spirit of adoption bears witness together with our spirit that we are loved by God, not commonly or sparingly, but singularly and abundantly, for the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. For God embraces us not only with that love with which a creator embraces his creature, but with which a father is wont to embrace his son: for he loves us in his beloved Son, and so shares the love of his beloved with us. Therefore, in order that we may believe, above all we need this Spirit of God, who alone has more power for faith than all those false and fabricated miracles of the Papists. We, then, content with those miracles of Christ and the Apostles by which the truth of the gospel doctrine was long ago confirmed, ask God for that Spirit of adoption, who may teach us to feel that love of God in Christ.

units.la: Obserua quod dicit discipulos credidisse in eum, quasi nunc primum coeperint in Christum credere: Vnde coniectura est non leuis, ante hoc tempus imbecille dun-taxat ac pusillam fuisse discipulorum fidem, ac proinde magnam extitisse erga eos Domini indulgentiam, qui arundinem quassatam non frangit, neque linum fumigans extinguit. Quare neque nos infirmos fide aspernemur, exemplo hoc indulgentiae Christi. Paulus, Eum, inquit, qui fide est infirmus assumite; & ratio subiecta est, Deus enim eum assumpsit. Illud enim intolerabilis superbiae est, reiicere eum hominem, quem Deus sibi assumpsit, cum tu non sis ipsius dominus, neque stet vel cadat ubi, sed domino suo. Sed quid fiet de infirmo isto? pendens a Christo infirma fide tandem percipiet in eo esse & ab eo deriuari in se, quibus ipse magis magisque cōfirmetur. Vnde ibidē Apostolus subiunxit hæc verba: Stabit etur autem, poterit enim Deus eum stabilire. Et alibi, Persuasum habeo hoc ipsum, fore vt qui coepit in vobis opus bonum, perficiat usque ad diem Iesu. Verùm hic non est praetermittendum, quòd effectum istud fidei, ex inspecto miraculo, non alii quàm discipulis tribuat. Discipuli sunt Christi & qui soli proficiuntur verbo & operibus Dei. Ædificantur etiam inspectis operibus naturæ & ordinariis, in quibus quoque intuentur Dei vel potentiam, vel sapientiam vel iustitiam, ipsumque in iis glorificant. Alij otiosè speculantur Dei opera, & in mediis ipsorum positi, nihil tamen iis moventur. Abutuntur quidem opere Dei ad libidinem suam, sed Deum in opere suo non vident, neque ipsum vt par est glorificat, Cui sit omnis honor & gloria: Amen.
units.tr: Observe that he says the disciples believed in him, as if they had now for the first time begun to believe in Christ. Whence there is no slight conjecture that until this time the faith of the disciples had been only feeble and small, and therefore there was great indulgence of the Lord towards them, who does not break a bruised reed nor quench the smoking flax. Let us therefore not despise the weak in faith, following this example of Christ's indulgence. Paul says: "Receive him who is weak in faith," and the reason is added: "for God has received him." For it is intolerable pride to reject the man whom God has taken to himself, since you are not his lord, and he stands or falls not before you but before his own Lord. But what will become of this weak man? Depending on Christ with a feeble faith, he will at last perceive that he is in him, and that from him there flows into himself what may strengthen him more and more. Whence the Apostle adds in the same place these words: "He shall stand, for God is able to make him stand." And elsewhere: "I am persuaded of this very thing, that he who has begun a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Jesus." But here it must not be passed over that he attributes this effect of faith, arising from a seen miracle, to the disciples alone. The disciples are Christ's, and they alone profit by the word and works of God. They are also edified by beholding the works of nature and the ordinary works, in which they too see the power, wisdom or justice of God, and glorify him in them. Others idly contemplate the works of God, and though placed in the midst of them, are moved by nothing in them. They indeed abuse the work of God for their own lust, but do not see God in his work, nor glorify him as is fitting, to whom be all honour and glory: Amen.

units.la: 12 Postea descendit Capernaum ipse & mater, & fratres & discipuli eius, manserúntque illic non multos dies.
units.tr: 12 Afterwards he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother, and his brethren, and his disciples; and they remained there not many days.

units.la: 13 Nam prope erat Pascha Iudæorum.
units.tr: For the Passover of the Jews was near. ## Christ goes up to Jerusalem; the cleansing of the temple

units.la: HActenus de miraculo, sequitur secunda pars capitis, profectio Christi versus Capernaum. Primùm in textu habemus descensionem Christi in Capernaum. Postea, inquit, descendit in Capernaum. Hoc est, absolutis iis illis nuptiis quibus intererat in Cana Galilææ, descendit Capernaum, ciuitatem nimirum cuius postea ius obtinuit: Postquam Nazaretha, in qua enutritus fuit, coepit eo indigna esse. Secundò, habemus comitatum ipsius. Comites sunt mater & fratres, hoc est, cognati ipsius secundum carnē, ex Hebraea phrasi. Cur autem hi descenderint non habemus cōpertum, nisi dicas sequutos esse Christum Capernaum, vt postea vna cum eo ascenderet Hierosolymam ad festum Paschæ proximum. Comitati sunt eum etiam discipuli ipsius, quos ordinarios habuit comites itineris sui. Tertiò habemus cōmorationis Christi tempus, in ea ciuitate, quod breue fuit: causa additur, Nā prope erat Pascha Iudæorum, cui nimirum interfuturus erat Christus. Paulus dicit, Postquàm venit plenū tēpus, emisit Deus filium suum factum ex muliere, factū legi obnoxium.
units.tr: So far concerning the miracle. There follows the second part of the chapter, Christ's journey towards Capernaum. First, in the text we have Christ's going down to Capernaum. Then, it says, he went down to Capernaum. That is, once the wedding at Cana of Galilee, which he attended, was over, he went down to Capernaum, the city which he later made his own, since Nazareth, where he had been brought up, had become unworthy of him. Second, we have his company. His companions are his mother and brothers, that is, his kinsmen according to the flesh, in the Hebrew idiom. We do not know for certain why they went down, unless you say that they followed Christ to Capernaum so that they might afterwards go up together with him to Jerusalem for the next Passover. His disciples also accompanied him, whom he regularly had as companions on his journeys. Third, we have the length of Christ's stay in that city, which was short: a reason is added, For the Passover of the Jews was near, at which Christ was certainly to be present. Paul says, "When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law" (Gal. 4.4).

units.la: catchword: obnoxium, vt eos qui legi erant obnoxij redimeret. Vbi habes causam cur oportuerit Christum interesse festo Paschæ, nempe quia factus erat obnoxius legi, idque nostra causa: Legi, inquam, non modò morali, sed etiam caeremoniali. Ob eam causam circumcisus erat, eòque factus debitor totius Legis seruandæ. Ideo etiam vnà cum populo celebrauit Pascha, ideo omnem obedientiam præstitit Patri. Mirifica enim fuit illa filij obedientia, quæ superauit omnis creaturæ siue Angelorum, siue hominum obedientiā, qui natura omnes serui sunt, cùm filius natu-ra Dominus sit & Patri æqualis. Ideo Paulus filij Dei obedientiam illā admirabilē proponit nobis tanquam exemplar & typum omnis obedictiæ, modestiæ ac humilitatis: Sit, inquit, in affectus in vobis qui fuit & in Christo Iesu, qui cùm esset in forma Dei, non duxit rapinam partem esse cū Deo, sed ipsum se exinaniuit, &c. Quod quidē exemplum vsque adeo necessario nobis sequendum est, vt alioqui nunquam futurum sit, vt participes fiamus cū illo gloriæ illius, ad quam post tantam obedientiam & ignominiam euectus est Christus. Præter hanc causam ascensionis, illud etiam mouit Christum, quòd in tanta hominum frequentia & in tam solenni festo ad quod confluxerunt omnes ex omnibus Iudæ partibus, atque etiam ex vicinis gentibus multi; plurimum se profuturum Ecclesiæ suæ intelligebat. Adeo vt nobis exemplo sit, nobis, inquam, quibus concreditum est euangelium Christi, vt quæramus ea loca & tempora, quibus maximè prodesse possimus Ecclesiæ Dei. Neque enim contenti esse debemus, si quocunque loco aut tempore prædicemus Euangelium, verùm habentes ante oculos gloriam Dei & salutem hominum, delectum & locorum & temporum oportet facere, pro mensura gratiæ nobis concessæ.
units.tr: Obnoxium, so that he might redeem those who were under the law. Here you have the reason why it was fitting for Christ to be present at the feast of the Passover: namely, because he had been made subject to the law, and that for our sake. To the law, I say, not only the moral law but also the ceremonial law. For this reason he was circumcised, and so became bound to keep the whole Law. Therefore too he celebrated the Passover together with the people, and therefore he rendered every obedience to the Father. For that obedience of the Son was wonderful, surpassing all the obedience of creatures, whether angels or men, who are all servants by nature, whereas the Son is Lord by nature and equal to the Father. So Paul sets that admirable obedience of the Son of God before us as a pattern and type of all obedience, modesty and humility: "Let this mind be in you," he says, "which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself," etc. (Phil. 2.5–7). This example must indeed be followed by us so necessarily that otherwise we shall never be made partakers with him of that glory to which Christ was raised after so great obedience and shame. Besides this reason for the going up, something else also moved Christ: that in such a great crowd of men, and at so solemn a feast, to which all came from every part of Judea, and many also from the neighbouring nations, he understood that he would be of the greatest benefit to his Church. So let it be an example to us, I say to us to whom the gospel of Christ has been entrusted, that we should seek those places and times in which we can do the most good to the Church of God. For we ought not to be content if we preach the gospel in any place or at any time; rather, keeping before our eyes the glory of God and the salvation of men, we must make a choice both of places and of times, according to the measure of grace given to us.

units.la: Ascendit igitur Iesus Hierosolymam.
units.tr: So Jesus went up to Jerusalem.

units.la: 14 Et inuenit in templo venditores boum & ouium, & columbarum, & nummularios sedentes.
units.tr: 14 And he found in the temple those who sold oxen and sheep and doves, and the money-changers sitting.

units.la: 15 Factóque flagello è funiculis, omnes eiecit è templo, & oues & boues, & argentariorum nummulos effudit, mensasque subuertit.
units.tr: 15 And when he had made a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, both the sheep and the oxen, and poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables.

units.la: 16 Et colubarū venditoribus dixit, Tollite hinc ista: Ne facite domū Patris mei, domum mercatus.
units.tr: 16 And to those who sold doves he said, Take these things away from here; do not make my Father's house a house of trade.

units.la: HActenus fuit secunda pars capitis, sequitur tertia, in qua habemus ascensionem Christi in Hierusalem, vna cum iis quæab illo illic gesta sunt tempore Paschatis. Primum eius factum occurrit, Templi purgatio, in qua explicanda hæc capita distinguimus. Primum cum venisset Hierosolymam, inuenit Christus templum Dei prophanatum. Secundo templum Dei sic prophanatum purgat. Postremo sequitur huius facti effectum duplex, primum respectu discipulorum, secundum respectu Iudæorum. Primum igitur innenit Dominus templum Dei prophanatum. Et inuenit, inquit, in templo venditores, &c. De peruersa hac consuetudine leges in Talmud Iudæorum, lib. 1. Vbi videbis durante templo illo ex antiquissima traditione Patrum die 15. mensis duodecimi consueuisse eos inferre in templum mensas, iisque numularios præficere, in eum finem, ut qui ex lege Dei offerre deberent dimidium sicli, haberent in promptu pecunias vel commutandas vel oppignerandas, vt deinde præsentibus oblationibus singulorum possent emi bestiæ sacrificandæ Domino, vt boues, oues, columbæ. Quæ etiam vt in promptu essent & ad manum, in templo cum suis venditoribus aderant præsentes. Atque hæc fuit prophanatio templi Domini, quo tempore Messias veniret in mundum. Neque eo tempore, templi solum prophanatio fuit; verum nihil tam sanctum fuit in religione Dei, quod non fuerit miserè contaminatum & corruptum: nihil in doctrina, nihil in ceremoniis sani fuit, sed omnia adeo erant vitiata, vt vel ipsa illa misera conditio omnium rerum desiderarit aduentum Messiæ, qui corruptissimum religionis statum reformaret. Christus enim is est, qui reformat & recolligit omnia. Neque equidem expecto plenam perfectamque reformationem Ecclesiæ Christianæ post tam horredam Apostasiam sub Antichristo, donec ipse secundo aduenerit. Qui quidē secundus aduentus, profecto si nos afficeremur sensu aliquo miseriæ præsentis, longè nobis desideratissimus esset. Verùm, proh dolor,
units.tr: So far was the second part of the chapter; there follows the third, in which we have Christ's going up to Jerusalem, together with the things done there by him at the time of the Passover. His first deed presents itself: the cleansing of the temple, in explaining which we distinguish these points. First, when he had come to Jerusalem, Christ found the temple of God profaned. Second, he cleanses the temple of God so profaned. Last, there follows a twofold effect of this deed: the first with respect to the disciples, the second with respect to the Jews. First, then, the Lord found the temple of God profaned. And he found in the temple, he says, those who sold, etc. You will read of this perverse custom in the Talmud of the Jews, book 1. There you will see that while that temple stood, on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, by very ancient tradition of the Fathers, they used to bring tables into the temple and set money-changers over them, to the end that those who ought to offer half a shekel by the law of God might have money ready, either to be exchanged or pledged, so that then, with the offerings of individuals present, beasts to be sacrificed to the Lord could be bought, such as oxen, sheep, doves. And that these might be at hand and within reach, their sellers were present in the temple with them. And this was the profanation of the temple of the Lord, at the time when the Messiah was to come into the world. Nor was the profanation of the temple the only thing at that time; indeed, nothing so holy remained in the religion of God that it was not wretchedly defiled and corrupted: nothing in doctrine, nothing in ceremonies was sound, but all things were so vitiated that that very wretched condition of all things called for the coming of the Messiah, who would reform the most corrupt state of religion. For Christ is he who reforms and gathers all things together again. Indeed I do not look for a full and perfect reformation of the Christian Church after so horrible an apostasy under Antichrist, until he himself comes a second time. And that second coming, surely, if we were touched by any sense of present misery, would be by far the most longed-for thing for us. But, alas,

units.la: Ephes. 1.10. lor, pauci sunt admodum qui tanguntur aliquo sensu præsentis miseriæ.
units.tr: Eph. 1.10. Alas, very few are indeed moved by any sense of present misery.

units.la: Sequitur deinde purgatio templi quod sic profanatum inuenit, facto, inquit, flagello, &c. Quærunt hic, cum Christus natura sua mansuetissimus fuerit, & summa cum lenitate docuerit etiam quàm maximè refractarios, per clementiam & æquitatem Christi, precor vos, inquit Paulus. Non litigabit, inquit Esaias, neque clamabit neque audiet quisquam in plateis vocem eius.) Cur, cùm talis fuerit, statim adhibuerit vim ad eiiciendos istos omnes è Templo? Causa non est obscura ex effectu illo qui factum hoc Christi secutus est in discipulis ipsius. Christus vidit detestandam templi Patris sui prophanationem, hinc accensus est sanctissimus ille zelus in corde filij.
units.tr: There follows then the cleansing of the temple, which he found so profaned: a whip having been made, it says, and so forth. Here people ask, since Christ was by his nature most gentle, and taught even the most stubborn with the greatest mildness, through the clemency and equity of Christ, I beseech you, says Paul (2 Cor. 10.1). He shall not strive, says Isaiah, nor cry aloud, nor shall anyone hear his voice in the streets (Isa. 42.2). Why, since he was such, did he at once use force to drive all of those out of the temple? The cause is not obscure from that effect which followed this deed of Christ in his disciples. Christ saw the detestable profanation of the temple of his Father, and from this that most holy zeal was kindled in the heart of the Son.

units.la: Zelum autem definio, indignationem propter iniuriâ, prophanationem, contumeliam factam in Deum, vel in Ecclesiam ipsius, vel in rē denique aliquam nobis charam, ex amore ardentissimo illius rei profectam. Talis fuit zelus filij Dei erga domum Patris sui. Iam verò vbi semel accensus est hic zelus, non iam amplius locus est lenitati. Sed qui accensus est zelo, manum suam quamprimùm admovet operi & conatur vlciscì illatam iniuriam. Vnde 1. Corinth. 7. 11. zelo tanquàm effectum quoddam subiicitur vltio: Imò zelum, inquit, imò vindicationem. Ex quo factum est vt quidam etiam extra ordinem vlti sint prophanos & impios. Phineas prophanos illos scortatores spiculo transfixit: Paulus Elymam magum cæcitate. Petrus verò Ananiam & Sapphiram ipsa morte percussit. Ita Christus, vt videtur, extra ordinem zelo abreptus, præter consuetudinem suam istos vi eiecit è templo Patris sui. Hoc itaque fuit zeli sanctissimi effectum, qui accensus est ex inspecta illa prophanatione templi Dei. An cùm tot prophanationes hodierno die, cùm multis modis Sabbathum Domini sanctū violetur, cùm portio illa, quâ Deus ministris verbi sui consecrauit ac sanctificauit, tam insatiabili hominum auaritia prophanetur, cùm etiam hominum ipsa corpora, quæ debent esse templa Spiritus Sancti, tot adulteriis, impuris scortationibus, ebrietatibus, denique vitiis omnis generis contaminentur; An, inquam, cùm tot passim grassentur prophanationes, putabimus tamen omnem zelum Domini extinctum plane hodierno die esse.
units.tr: Now I define zeal as indignation on account of an injury, profanation or insult done to God, or to his Church, or finally to some thing dear to us, arising from the most ardent love of that thing. Such was the zeal of the Son of God for the house of his Father. Now indeed, once this zeal has been kindled, there is no longer room for gentleness. But whoever is kindled with zeal at once puts his hand to the work and tries to avenge the injury done. Hence in 2 Corinthians 7.11 vengeance is placed, as a certain effect, alongside zeal: "Yes, zeal," he says, "yes, vindication." From this it has come about that some have even avenged profane and impious men outside the ordinary course. Phinehas pierced those profane fornicators with a spear; Paul struck Elymas the sorcerer with blindness; Peter struck Ananias and Sapphira with death itself. So Christ, as it seems, carried away by zeal outside the ordinary course, contrary to his custom, drove those men out of the temple of his Father by force. This therefore was the effect of that most holy zeal, which was kindled by the sight of that profanation of the temple of God. Shall we then think that all zeal for the Lord is wholly extinguished today, when so many profanations occur on this day, when the holy Sabbath of the Lord is violated in many ways, when that portion which God has consecrated and sanctified for the ministers of his Word is profaned by such insatiable greed of men, when even the very bodies of men, which ought to be temples of the Holy Spirit, are defiled by so many adulteries, impure fornications, drunkenness, and finally vices of every kind? Shall we, I say, when profanations rage everywhere, think nonetheless that all zeal for the Lord is plainly extinguished today?

units.la: Coniungit Christus cum vi allata grauem reprehen-sionem, præsertim eorum, qui vendebant columbas, Ne, inquit, facite domum patris mei domum mercatus. Hoc ideo factum est, vt conuicti priusin conscientiis excæcentur e templo, atque ita os ipsis occluderetur. Dominus fere non exercet iudicium cum silentio, sed simul cum iudicio immisso loquitur aliquo modo ac conuincit peccati, vt omne os obturetur & obnoxius fiat condemnationi Dei totus mundus. An putant isti, de quibus paulo ante diximus, prophanatores Sabbathi, bonorum ecclesiasticorum, suorum etiam corporum, quæ non sui iuris, sed pretio empta, sancta sunt Domino: putantne isti, se effugituros iudicium? Non effugient quidem nisi tempestiuè resipuerint. Quid igitur? an Dominus non prius admonitos & conuictos opprimet? Non faciet, imo vero iam conuicti sunt plus millies, atque hanc quidè conuictionem quam nunc tam securè contemnunt, tandem aliquando sentient efficacem. Ne facite, inquit, domum Patris mei. His verbis non tantum admonet eos profanationis ipsorum, sed etiam auctoritatis suæ, vt prorsus os iis obthuretur. Domum patris sui appellat, Ergo ipse filius, est: quòd si filius, Ergo dominus illius domus. Moses quidem, inquit, fidelis erat in tota domo Dei, sed vt famulus, Christus verò, vt filius, præest domui suæ. Quamobrem his verbis subinnuit se filium, ac proinde dominum illius domus: ideóque iure admouisse manum ad suam ipsius domum purgandam. Quare hoc loco admonet etiam eos iuris & potestatis suæ vt prorsus obthuretur ipsis os, nihilque habeant quod contradicant. Sic etiam Rom. 9. Postquam reprobi qui eo loco introducuntur responsantes & non contenti Dei voluntate, qui alij eliguntur, alij reprobantur, Deo iniustitiam ascribere volunt, Paulus cõparatione facta potestatis & authoritatis siguli in massam suam luteam, vendicat Dei ius & potestatem in massam suam, potestatem, inquam, reiiciendi hos & eligendi illos in gloriam suam: ídque facit eò, vt cognita hac authoritate, iure & potestate Dei, obthuretur os vel ipsis improimprobis. Idem hoc loco videtur Christus facere.
units.tr: Christ couples with this forceful act a severe rebuke, especially of those who were selling doves: "Do not make my Father's house a house of merchandise." This was done so that those who were first convicted in their consciences would be driven out of the temple, and so that their mouths would be stopped. The Lord seldom exercises judgment in silence. Rather, along with the judgment he sends forth, he speaks in some manner and convicts of sin, so that every mouth is stopped and the whole world is made liable to the condemnation of God. Do those men, of whom we spoke a little earlier, the profaners of the Sabbath, of church goods, and of their own bodies, which are not their own by right but were bought at a price and are holy to the Lord, do they think they will escape judgment? They will not escape, certainly, unless they repent in time. What then? Will the Lord not crush those who were first admonished and convicted? He will not fail to do so. Indeed they have already been convicted a thousand times over, and this conviction, which they now despise so carelessly, will at last be felt as effective. "Do not make," he says, "my Father's house." By these words he not only warns them of their profanation but also of his own authority, so that their mouths are completely stopped. He calls it his Father's house. Therefore he himself is the Son, and if he is the Son, then he is the lord of that house. "Moses indeed," he says, "was faithful in all the house of God, but as a servant; Christ, however, as a son, is over his own house." Wherefore in these words he hints that he is the Son and therefore the lord of that house, and so he rightly put his hand to cleanse his own house. Hence in this place he also reminds them of his right and power, so that their mouths are stopped entirely and they have nothing to contradict. So also in Rom. 9, after the reprobate, who are introduced in that place as answering back, and not content with the will of God, who chooses some and rejects others, wish to ascribe injustice to God, Paul, by comparing the power and authority of the potter over his lump of clay, claims for God the right and power over his lump: the power, I say, of rejecting these and choosing those for his own glory. He does this so that, once this authority, right and power of God is known, the mouths even of the wicked may be stopped. Christ seems to do the same thing in this place.

units.la: In hac reprehensione etiam aliud quiddam consideran-dum venit; potuerunt quidem Iudæi multa huic facto suo & prophanationi prætexere; antiquissimam nimirum Patrum traditionem, sanctum vsum, commoditatem præsentis pecuniæ, & præsentium victimarum: hæc & similia omnia Christus præoccupat & resecat hac vna prophanationis metione; Domum Patris mei, inquit, fecistis domum mercatus. Diabolus valde ingeniosus est ad suppeditandum nobis mille excusationes & infinita effugia, posteaquam Dei voluntatem sanctam iam violauimus, aut aliquid quod ipsi sanctū est, siue Sabbathū, siue templum Domini, siue bona Ecclesiastica, siue nostra ipsorum corpora profanauimus: verum hoc vno ista omnia resecantur & facillime diluuntur; Si respondeas, profanasti quod sanctum est Domino. Prophanatio nullo modo, nullo prætextu, nulla arte, vel diaboli, vel hominis excusari potest. Quare vel omnino caueda est, vel si iam profanauimus quod sanctum est Domino, illud sola resipiscentia & conuersione ad Deū emendandum est. Non est hoc prætereundū quod Christus hanc actionem quam illi opinati sunt tam sancta esse, mercatum, hoc est, prophana duntaxat actione appellet, nihili faciés scilicet omnes eorū fictos prætextus. Cuius pro-facto exemplum nobis sequendū est, in appellando res quasqʒ, siue bonas eas, siue malas nominibus suis, quod albū est, albi nomine, quod nigrū est, nigri nomine. Imò post hoc tempus idē Christus, cum semel atque iterum inueniret templū Domini prophanatū, dixit factū esse speluncam latronū: Vbi mercatum hunc, quo locus sanctus prophanatus est, non mercatū, vt hoc loco, hoc est legitimā quidem, prophana tamen actione, sed latrocinū appellauit, & mercatores pro totidē latronibus habuit. Cùm enim vel locus vel tempus, sanctum Domino prophanatur actionibus humanis & communibus, tum actiones illę ex legitimis fiunt prorsus illegitimę ac impurę. Sic ergo hodierno die exemplo Domini mei Iesu Christi proclamo mercatº qui exercetur die Dominica merū latrociniū esse: omnes deniqʒ exercitationes, quæ prophanat illū die Dño sacrū, vt impias prorsus condeno, quicquid demum prætexant homines peccatis suis,
units.tr: In this rebuke another matter also deserves consideration. The Jews could indeed have offered many pretexts for this deed of theirs and for this profanation: namely the most ancient tradition of the Fathers, the holy use, the convenience of ready money, and of the sacrifices at hand. Christ anticipates and cuts off all these and similar things by this one word of profanation: "You have made my Father's house a house of merchandise." The devil is very ingenious at supplying us with a thousand excuses and endless escapes, once we have already violated the holy will of God, or profaned something that is holy to him, whether the Sabbath, or the temple of the Lord, or church goods, or our own bodies. But by this one word all these things are cut off and most easily refuted. If you answer, you have profaned what is holy to the Lord, there is no way, no pretext, no art, whether of the devil or of man, by which profanation can be excused. Therefore either it must be carefully avoided altogether, or, if we have already profaned what is holy to the Lord, it must be made good by repentance and conversion to God alone. It must not be passed over that Christ calls this action, which they thought so holy, a "merchandise," that is, a mere profane action, plainly disregarding all their feigned pretexts. We must follow his example in naming all things, whether good or bad, by their own names: what is white we call by the name white, what is black by the name black. Indeed, later on, when Christ found the temple of the Lord profaned on a second occasion as well as the first, he said that it had been made a den of robbers. Here he did not call that merchandise, by which the holy place was profaned, a merchandise, as in this place, that is, a lawful yet profane action, but he called it robbery, and he regarded the merchants as so many robbers. For when either a place or a time that is holy to the Lord is profaned by human and common actions, then those actions, from being lawful, become wholly unlawful and impure. So, therefore, on this day, following the example of my Lord Jesus Christ, I proclaim that the trade which is carried on on the Lord's Day is nothing but robbery. Finally, I condemn utterly all the practices which profane that day, which is sacred to the Lord, whatever pretexts men may invent for their sins.

units.la: 17 Recordati sunt autem eius discipuli, scriptum esse, Zelus domus tuæ exedit me.
units.tr: 17 His disciples remembered that it was written, "The zeal of your house has consumed me."

units.la: 18 Responderunt ergo Iudæi, & dixerunt ei, Quod signum ostendis nobis, quòd ista facis?
units.tr: 18 The Jews therefore answered and said to him, "What sign do you show us, seeing that you do these things?"

units.la: 19 Respondit Iesus, & dixit eis, Destruite templum hoc, & intra triduum excitabo illud.
units.tr: 19 Jesus answered and said to them, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up."

units.la: 20 Dixerunt ergo Iudæi, Quadraginta & sex annis ædificatum est templum istud, & tu triduo illud excitabis?
units.tr: 20 The Jews therefore said, "This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?"

units.la: 21 At ille loquebatur de templo corporis sui.
units.tr: 21 But he spoke of the temple of his body.

units.la: 22 Postquam autem suscitatus fuit ex mortuis, recordati sunt eius discipuli quòd hoc sibi dixisset, & crediderunt scripturæ, & sermoni quem Iesus dixerat.
units.tr: 22 When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this to them, and they believed the Scripture and the word which Jesus had spoken.

units.la: HActenus examinauimus repræhensionem hàc Christi, sequitur nunc postremò effectus huius facti Christi, & primùm quidem, respectu discipulorum, agente nimirum in ipsis Spiritu sancto, reuocatus eius in memoriam, ille locus Dauidis, qui ex Psal. 69.10. de zelo quodam ardentissimo; quem locum Christo proprie applicant discipuli, cuius quidem zelum ferocissimum ex hoc præsenti facto collegerunt. Dauid cùm sustineret personam Christi eo loco, postquam questus est propter Dominum hæc omnia se passum esse, subiecit eius rei rationem, à zelo illo maximo, qui ipsum quasi exedit, hoc est, consumpsit eum feruore suo: causa autem fuit cur ipse se exinaniuit & in nihilum prorsus redegit. Quod fecit quidem Christus, cùm se exinaniret, forma serui accepta, permotus scilicet ineffabili illo zelo Dei patris & Ecclesiæ suæ. Simile quid contigit etiam viris illis sanctissimis, Mosi primùm, qui zelo hoc gloriæ Dei & ecclesiæ ipsius incensus, optauit à Deo ut ipsum è libro suo deleret. Deinde Paulo, qui optauit anathema esse pro fratribus suis: nempe ex zelo Dei hoc est profectum, cuius quidem ea est natura, ut homines efficiat abiicere omnem sui curam, ut Deum suum glorificent, rificent,& Ecclesiam conseruent: Quod qui non fecerit certo quodam modo, is profecto satis prodit se longè abesse à zelo illo Moßis & Pauli. Sed hoc velim apud se cogitet is, qui nimis studet seruare animam suam, fore vt prodat eam: qui verò negligit animam suam pro studio Dei sui, fore vt lucretur eam. Abiicere enim curam nostri, propter Dei zelum, est Dei custodiae fidelissimae nos metipsos committere. Vide hic praeterea, vt factum hoc Christi reuocet discipulis in memoriam illum Scripturae locum quem Christo applicant, atque ideo magis confirmetur ipsorum fides, dum cognoscunt eum esse Messiam illum, de quo omnia illa sunt praedicta à Mose & Prophetis. Hoc igitur etiam factum Domini posterius in purgando templum, & non solu prius illud miraculosum in mutando aquam in vinum, auget fidem discipulis Christi, dum vident eum esse, de quo sit à Prophetis praedictum: Quaecunque à Domino fiunt quocunque modo, adaugent fidē eis qui Domini sunt. Sed primum omnium hic deprehenderunt discipuli in Christo zelum illum, ex quo deinde factū est, vt recordarentur illius scripturae, atque ipsam Christo applicarent, ex quo denique factum est vt augesceret ipsorū fides. Aliī fortassis tum factum hoc Christi aliūde profectum calumniati sunt. Sed pij sunt & fideles qui facta Dei & piorum hominum rectè ac dextrè interpretantur, & de causis ipsorum optimè iudicant. Deus det nobis pietatem & sapientiam. Amen.
units.tr: Hitherto we have examined this rebuke of Christ. Now follows, last of all, the effect of this deed of Christ; and first, with respect to the disciples, the Holy Spirit working in them, there was recalled to their memory that passage of David from Psalm 69:10, concerning a most ardent zeal. The disciples rightly applied this passage to Christ, and from this present deed they gathered his most fierce zeal. When David, in that place, sustained the person of Christ, after he complained that he had suffered all these things on account of the Lord, he gave the reason for it: the greatest zeal, which, as it were, consumed him, that is, wasted him with its heat. The cause why he emptied himself and reduced himself to nothing was this. Christ did this indeed when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being moved, of course, by that unspeakable zeal for the Father and for his Church. Something similar happened also to those most holy men: first to Moses, who, kindled with this zeal for the glory of God and of his Church, wished that God would blot him out of his book. Then to Paul, who wished himself to be accursed for his brethren. Surely this came from the zeal of God, whose nature is such that it makes men cast off all care for themselves, so that they may glorify their God and preserve the Church. Whoever does not do this, in some measure, plainly shows that he is far removed from that zeal of Moses and Paul. But I would have him who too eagerly seeks to save his own soul consider this: he will lose it; and he who neglects his own soul for the sake of the zeal of his God will find it. For to cast off care for ourselves for the sake of the zeal of God is to commit ourselves to the most faithful keeping of God. See here, moreover, how this deed of Christ calls to the disciples' memory that passage of Scripture which they applied to Christ, and so their faith is the more confirmed, while they recognise him to be that Messiah of whom all those things were foretold by Moses and the Prophets. Therefore this later deed of the Lord, in cleansing the temple, as well as that earlier miracle of changing water into wine, increases the faith of Christ's disciples, while they see him to be the one of whom the Prophets have spoken. Whatever the Lord does, in whatever way, increases faith in those who belong to the Lord. But first of all the disciples here perceived in Christ that zeal, from which it followed that they remembered that Scripture and applied it to Christ, and from which at last their faith grew. Others, perhaps, at that time slandered this deed of Christ as having come from some other source. But those are pious and faithful who rightly and skilfully interpret the deeds of God and of pious men, and judge their causes most well. May God grant us piety and wisdom. Amen.

units.la: Hactenus de effecto primo in discipulis, sequitur alterum in Iudaeis, hoc est in multitudine Iudaeorum, qui vnà intererant templo. Commoti rei novitate, quae religionis Iudaicę reformatione aliquam praetendere videbatur, quaerunt signum & miraculum quo confirmetur authoritas & potestas illa Christi, quam in eo facto praefe tulit. Potuerunt quidē non obscurè videre miraculum in illo ipso facto eiectionis cum Christo etiam aliqua vi eiicienti prophanatores templi, & in speciem vulgari aliquo homini, nemo tamen ex iis qui eiciebantur reiiterit, repressus, scilicet, proculdubiō diuina & miraculosa plane potentia. Sed hoc miraculum nolentes videre, requirunt nouum, quo testificetur se po-
units.tr: Thus far concerning the effect on the disciples. Next comes the effect on the Jews, that is, on the crowd of Jews who were present in the temple. Moved by the novelty of the event, which seemed to promise some reform of the Jewish religion, they seek a sign and a miracle by which that authority and power of Christ, which he displayed in this act, might be confirmed. They could indeed have seen clearly that there was a miracle in the very act of expulsion, since Christ by some power expelled the profaners of the temple, and a single man, in appearance ordinary, drove them out, yet none of those who were being cast out resisted, being restrained, of course, by a plainly divine and miraculous power. But refusing to see this miracle, they demand a new one, by which he may testify that he has the power to do such great things.

units.la: H testatem habere qua talia tantaque audeat. Quod signum, inquiunt, ostendis nobis vt ista facias? Quæri potest hoc loco, an licuerit iis petere signum à Christo hoc tempore? Cui vt respondeamus, distinctio quædam temporum est facienda, & singulis temporibus quæstio accommodanda. Primum tempus fuit sub veteri testamento: secundum sub Christo & Apostolis: tertium inde ab Apostolorum diebus ad secundum vsque Christi aduentum. Quòd ad primum tempus attinet, licuit quidem tempore veteris testamenti signa petere: tum quia eo tepore iaciebatur fundamentum illud prophetarū, de quo Ephes.2.20. Ideóque opus erat miraculis ad confirmandam doctrinā illam, tum primùm quasi fundatam: tum quia eo tempore doctrina ipsa non erat ita copiosa & manifesta, Christo nondum manifestato qui patefaceret abscónditum illud mysterium; Nondum existentibus scriptis Apostolicis, sed propheticis duntaxat, in quibus non erat plane perfectéque reuelatum illud mysterium; Exi-stentibus adhuc tantum elementis quibusdam religionis, infante adhuc populo & sub paedagogo existente. His de causis opus habebat vetus ille populus diuinis testimoniis quibus confirmaretur, exacuiis, inquâ, & responsis sacerdotum & prophetarū. Quare licuit iis qui tunc temporis vixerunt petere à Deo signa & miracula. Quòd ad secundum tempus attinet, Christi nimirum & Apostolorū, quia tum primùm fundamenta reuelati in aduentu Christi mysterij iaciebatur, & doctrina noua mundo videbatur: ideo quoque tum opus erat miraculis, permissùmque primæ illi Ecclesiæ miracula à Deo petere. Sic Ecclesia congregata in vnũ, petiit à Domino signa & miracula: Da seruis tuis vt cum omni libertate loquantur sermonem tuum, manu tua extensa ad sanandum, vtque signa & miracula edante per nomen sancti filij tui Iesu. Quòd denique ad tertium tempus attinet, cùm iam fundamentum doctrinæ sit iactum à Prophetis & Apostolis, & satis confirmatum iam editis miraculis, ipsáque adeo Ecclesia iam euasserit in perfectum virum, in mensuram staturæ adulti Christi, vt loquitur Paulus, miraculis nunc nihil est opus, & sine magno scelere, & tentatione Dei postulari à quo-
units.tr: "What sign do you show us," they say, "for doing these things?" Here it may be asked whether they were permitted to ask Christ for a sign at this time.
