To answer this, a distinction of times must be made, and the question must be adapted to each period. The first period was under the Old Testament; the second under Christ and the Apostles; the third from the days of the Apostles until the second coming of Christ. As for the first period, it was indeed permitted to ask for signs in the time of the Old Testament: partly because at that time was laid the foundation of the prophets, of which Eph. 2.20; and therefore miracles were needed to confirm that doctrine, which was then, as it were, first being founded; partly because at that time the doctrine itself was not so abundant and manifest, since Christ had not yet been revealed to disclose that hidden mystery; since the Apostolic writings did not yet exist, but only the prophetic ones, in which that mystery was not plainly and perfectly revealed; and since there were still only certain elements of religion, the people being still infant and under a schoolmaster. For these reasons that old people needed divine testimonies by which it might be confirmed, namely, oracles and answers of priests and prophets. Hence those who lived at that time were permitted to ask God for signs and miracles. As for the second period, that of Christ and the Apostles, since then the foundations of the mystery revealed at the coming of Christ were first being laid, and the doctrine seemed new to the world, therefore miracles were then also necessary, and that first Church was permitted to ask God for miracles. So the Church, gathered together as one, asked the Lord for signs and miracles: "Grant to your servants that they may speak your word with all boldness, by stretching out your hand to heal, and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy Son Jesus" (Acts 4.29, 30). As for the third period, since the foundation of doctrine has already been laid by the Prophets and Apostles, and has been sufficiently confirmed by the miracles already performed, and since the Church itself has now grown into a perfect man, into the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, as Paul says (Eph. 4.13), there is now no need of miracles, and they cannot be demanded of God without great wickedness and tempting of God.

units.la: Et nouo etiam, sub initium Euangelii patefacti. Act. 4.29. 30. Hodie cur miraculis non opus. Ephes.4.13. quam non possunt. Hactenus accomodavimus quæstionem ad tria illa tempora. Ex iis quæ diximus iam apparet nihil peccasse Iudæos hac simplici petitione signi: inciderunt enim in ea tempora, quibus licuit signum petere. At à Christo tamen ipso reprehenditur eorum petitio, ut videbimus paulò post. Ergo videndum quibus modis homines peccet in petendo signa, etiam quo tempore alioqui licet ea petere. Si petant ad hoc ut curiositatem suam expleat, peccant graviter; Quomodo Herodes signum aliquod à Christo petiit: deinde si petant figura animo prætexendi ea incredulitati suæ, quasi vero futurum sit, ut ipsi statim amplectantur propositam doctrinam, si ad eam rem adducantur prius signis quot & quibus voluerint, cum tamen non sit in animo virtute amplecti etiam mille signis confirmatam: tum quidem petere signum est Deum tentare. Sic Scribæ & Pharisæi Dominum tentarunt: Quibus respondit Dominus, Generationem malam & adulterinam signum requirere, signum autem non dandum iis nisi signum illud Ionæ Prophetæ, &c. Sic Iudæi hoc loco & tempore Dominum tetarunt, signum ab eo requirentes: ideoque signum iis nullum est datum. Quare, ut uno verbo respondeam quæstioni, Peccatum est ab iis cum petiverunt signum à Christo, non quidem simpliciter, sed quia sincerè non petiuerunt. Nunc observandum est nonnihil, ex effecto operis Christi in discipulis suis & in Iudæis longè alio atque alio. Discipuli in opere Magistri sui, dum ipsum propius intuiti sunt, viderunt zelum ineffabilem, viderunt quoque miraculum, repressa scilicet ab uno homine tanta hominum multitudine. Unde factum est procul dubio, ut fides eorum prius inchoata magis confirmata fuerit. At verò Iudæi, neque zelum Christi, neque potentiam Dei miraculosam in compescendis animis multitudinis obseruarunt: ideoque manserunt incredoli. Hæc tam diversa effecta solent apparere quoties Deus extra ordinem excitat homines, cum zelo extraordinario & cum potentia Dei ac efficacia in reformando corruptum & labefactatum religionis suæ statu. Cum enim iacente in mundo in illis tenebris regni Antichristi, Deus excitaret nobis extra ordinem viros quos ipsi visum, cum donis extraordinariis & cum potentia Dei admirabili, ad mundum ex illis tenebris vindicandum, tum quidem erant, qui cum viderent illum zelum, illam fidem, illam potentiam extraordinariam, quae in illis sic splenduerunt, ad Deum sunt conuersi. Alij vero erant qui cum nollent videre, non crediderunt, illud ipsum in ore semper habentes, quod Iudaei suo tempore: Quod signum ostenditis nobis, cur ista faciatis? sane signum satis magnum atque efficax debuit esse iis, vel hoc solum, quod inuitis & frustra renitentibus Antichristo, Episcopis ordinariis, plerisque principu huius mundi, toto denique ipso mundo, reformatio tamen incepta suum progressum habuerit continuum ad hunc usque diem: & habitura est in perpetuum (Deo sit gloria) tantisper-dum impius ille illustris aduentu Domini fuerit abolitus.
units.tr: And new also, at the beginning of the Gospel revealed. Acts 4.29, 30. Why there is no need of miracles today. Eph. 4.13. Thus far we have applied the question to those three periods. From what we have said it is now clear that the Jews did not sin by this simple request for a sign, for they fell into a time when it was permitted to ask for a sign. Yet their request is rebuked by Christ himself, as we shall see a little later. Therefore we must consider in what ways men sin in asking for signs, even at a time when it is otherwise lawful to ask them. If they ask in order to satisfy their curiosity, they sin gravely, as Herod asked some sign from Christ. Next, if they ask in order to use signs as a pretext for their unbelief, as if it were really going to happen that they would at once embrace the doctrine proposed, if they are brought to that point by whatever number and kind of signs they like, while yet they have no intention of embracing, by virtue, even a doctrine confirmed by a thousand signs, then to ask for a sign is indeed to tempt God. So the Scribes and Pharisees tempted the Lord, to whom the Lord replied, "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah," etc. So the Jews at this place and time tempted the Lord by asking him for a sign, and therefore no sign was given to them. Therefore, to answer the question in one word: it was a sin on their part when they asked a sign of Christ, not indeed simply, but because they did not ask sincerely. Now it must be noted somewhat, concerning the effect of Christ's work, which was quite different in his disciples and in the Jews. The disciples, in the work of their Master, while they gazed more closely upon him, saw his ineffable zeal, and they also saw a miracle, namely, that so great a crowd of men was restrained by one man. Undoubtedly the result was that their faith, begun earlier, was more strongly confirmed. But the Jews observed neither the zeal of Christ nor the miraculous power of God in restraining the minds of the multitude, and therefore they remained unbelieving. These so different effects usually appear whenever God raises up men beyond the ordinary course, with extraordinary zeal and with the power and efficacy of God, to reform the state of religion that has been corrupted and shaken. For when, while the world lay in those darkness of the kingdom of Antichrist, God raised up for us men beyond the ordinary course, whom he saw fit, with extraordinary gifts and with the admirable power of God, to vindicate the world from those shadows, then indeed there were some who, when they saw that zeal, that faith, that extraordinary power which shone so brightly in them, were converted to God. But there were others who, because they would not see, did not believe, always having in their mouths that very thing which the Jews said in their time: "What sign do you show us, why do you do these things?" Surely a sign great and effective enough ought to have been given to them, if only by this, that although Antichrist, the ordinary bishops, most of the princes of this world, and indeed the whole world, resisted in vain and against their will, the reformation once begun has nevertheless had continuous progress to this very day, and will have it forever (to God be the glory), until that impious one is abolished by the illustrious coming of the Lord.

units.la: Sequitur nunc Christi responsum, Destruite templum hoc, & tribus diebus erigam illud. Nondum uis signum quale petebant, quia petebant animo tentandi, non sincere, neque credendi animo, sed consilio calumniandi: Dominus exponere diuinam potentiam hominum incredulorum. Verum in eos proculdubio irascitur, sicuti colligi satis potest ex illa reprehensione Scribarum & Pharisaeorum petentium, eodem quo isti animo, signum a Domino: Natio, inquit, mala & adulterina signum petit, &c. Disce igitur exemplo Christi quid nobis faciendum sit, quoties aduersarij requiunt a nobis signa & miracula, quibus vulgo probetur nostra doctrina. Signum non est dandum iis, etsi posse dari fingas, & hanc mundi aetatem posse nunc ferre, cum ne a Christo quidem ipso, si nunc praesens esset corpore aliud audirent quam illud: Natio mala & adulterina signum petit, &c. Verum ad hoc ne sint inexcusabiles, polliceatur quidem signum Iudeis longe admirabilissimum, nempe signum resurrectionis suae, Destruite, inquit, templum hoc. Q. d. futurum est, ut destruatis hoc templum corporis mei: Sed destruite, inquit, hoc templum. Templum corporis sui intelligit, ut postea Iohannes ipse exponit, verf. 21. Templi autem nomine appellat corpus suum, per allusionem ad templum Hierosolymitanum, de quo
units.tr: Now follows Christ's answer: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." He does not yet give the kind of sign they were asking for, because they asked with the intention of tempting, not sincerely, nor with a mind to believe, but with the purpose of slandering; the Lord does not expose his divine power to men who are unbelieving. Yet he is undoubtedly angry with them, as can sufficiently be gathered from that rebuke of the Scribes and Pharisees who asked for a sign from the Lord with the same mind as these: "An evil and adulterous nation," he says, "seeks a sign," etc. Learn therefore from the example of Christ what we must do whenever adversaries demand from us signs and miracles by which our doctrine may be commonly proved. A sign is not to be given to them, even if you pretend that it could be given, and that this age of the world could now bear it, since not even Christ himself, if he were now present in body, would hear anything other than that: "An evil and adulterous nation seeks a sign," etc. Yet, so that they may not be left without excuse, he does promise the Jews a sign by far the most wonderful, namely the sign of his resurrection: "Destroy," he says, "this temple." That is to say: you are going to destroy this temple of my body; but "destroy," he says, "this temple." He understands the temple of his body, as John himself afterwards explains, v. 21. But he calls his body by the name of temple, by an allusion to the temple at Jerusalem, of which

units.la: Matth. 12. 39. de quo dictum Christi male intellexerunt Iudaei, quódque erat typus & figura quaedam corporis Christi. Permittit igitur ut destruant illud templum: promittit autem se erecturum illud tertio post die. Tribus diebus erigam illud. erigam illud ipse ego mea virtute, ut possitis facile videre, si volueritis, me Deum esse, cum non possit alius hoc praestare, nisi solus Deus, idque faciam non ad consolationem vestram, sed ad grauiorem condemnationem. Nam quo manifestius exerit Deus potentiam suam, eo grauius futurum est iudicium incredulorum. Inter opera autem potentiae diuinae alia, maxime damnabit eos opus hoc admirabile resurrectionis Christi. Idem prorsus promittitur incredulis & obstinatis Scribis ac Pharisaeis, cum dicitur, Signum non dabitur ei, nisi signum Ionae Prophetae, &c. Sensus est, Quemadmodum admirabilis illa liberatio Ionae, ex faucibus quasi mortis, signū fuit Niniuitis, quo confirmatum est iis a Deo missum esse. Ita admirabilis Christi resurrectio signum futurum est, quo confirmabitur eum Dei filium esse ac verum illum Messiam.
units.tr: Matth. 12. 39. The Jews misunderstood what Christ had said about this, and it was a type and figure of Christ's body. So he allows them to destroy that temple, but promises that he himself will raise it up on the third day. In three days I will raise it up. I will raise it by my own power, so that you may easily see, if you are willing, that I am God, since no one but God alone can accomplish this. And I will do it not for your comfort but for your heavier condemnation. For the more plainly God displays his power, the heavier the judgment of unbelievers will be. Among the works of divine power, this wonderful work of Christ's resurrection will condemn them most of all. The very same thing is promised to the unbelieving and stubborn scribes and Pharisees when it is said, No sign will be given to them except the sign of the prophet Jonah, etc. The meaning is this: just as that remarkable deliverance of Jonah, out of the jaws of what was almost death, was a sign to the Ninevites by which they were assured that he had been sent by God, so Christ's wonderful resurrection will be a sign by which it will be confirmed that he is the Son of God and the true Messiah.

units.la: Quaeri potest, cur magis hoc miraculum resurrectionis quam aliud quoduis promittat? Resp. Miraculum quoduis eo refertur, ut ostendat Dei potentiam. non potest autem aliud quodcunque miraculum magis ostendere Dei potentiam, quam illud resurrectionis Christi. Nam resurrectione declarauit se filium Dei potenter, secundum Spiritum sanctificationis per resurrectionem a mortuis. Imo magis ostenditur Dei potentia hoc miraculo resurrectionis Christi, quam alio quouis. Paulus postquam meminisset admirabilis illius potentiae diuinae, quam appellat efficacitatem fortis roboris ipsius: Quonam, quaeso, argumento arguit eam efficacitatem fortis roboris ipsius? Effectu eius statuit, fateor, verbis eo loco proxime praecedentibus, excellentem illam quam vocat, magnitudinem potentiae ipsius in nobis qui credimus, hoc est viuificatione & regeneratione nostri: sed volens deinde apertius ostendere hoc Dei robur, eiusque efficacitatem, attulit potissimum opus illud resurrectionis Christi; quam exeruit, inquit, in Christo cum excitauit eum ex mortuis, & collocauit ad dextram suam in coelis. Qua quidem re significat non aliquod esse aliud effectum potentiae diuinae, quod tam arguat ipsius efficacitatē, quàm resurrectio illa Iesu Christi ex mortuis. Neque enim in vlla vnquam creatura potentiam suam sic exeruit, vt in Christo suo, neque alias vnquā vt in Christi resurrectione: Non in creatione, nō in gubernatione: Exeruit enim potentia in euehēdo eo in summam sublimitatem, lōgē supra sortem omnis creaturæ, etiā Angelorum, eo, inquā, qui deiectus erat lōgē infra conditionē omnis creaturæ. Nulla enim omniū finit vllo tempore ita humiliata, vt Dei ipsius filius: Cui sit omnis gloria. Amen.
units.tr: It may be asked why he promises this miracle of resurrection rather than any other. Answer: every miracle is meant to show God's power, and no other miracle can show God's power more than the resurrection of Christ. For by his resurrection he was declared powerfully to be the Son of God, according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection from the dead. Indeed, God's power is shown more by this miracle of Christ's resurrection than by any other. After Paul had mentioned that wonderful divine power, which he calls the working of the strength of his might, by what argument, I ask, does he prove that working of his strength? He indicates it, I admit, by its effect in the words immediately before, namely that surpassing greatness of his power towards us who believe, that is, in our quickening and regeneration. But wishing then to show this strength of God and its working more clearly, he brought forward above all that work of Christ's resurrection, which he says God exerted in Christ when he raised him from the dead and set him at his right hand in the heavens. By this he signifies that there is no other effect of divine power that proves its working as much as that resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. For God never exerted his power in any creature as he did in his Christ, nor at any other time as in the resurrection of Christ. Not in creation, not in governing; for his power was exerted in raising him to the highest exaltation, far above the lot of every creature, even of the angels, and of him, I say, who had been cast down far below the condition of every creature. For none of all creatures was ever at any time so humbled as the Son of God himself. To him be all glory. Amen.

units.la: Hactenus fuit responsio Christi ad petitionē Iudaeorum, sequitur nunc responsionis effectus duplex: Alter in Iudaeis, alter in discipulis, quod accidit non nisi suo tempore & post resurrectionē Domini. Effectum in Iudaeis apparet, ex eo quod responderet & ludibrio habet promissum illud magnum resurrectionis miraculum. Nā cūm, vt obiter admonet Euangelista, Christus locutus sit de templo corporis sui, illi eum intellexerunt locutum de templo illo suo Hierosolymitano, & existimantes impossibilem tam breui spatio tantum templum erigi potuisse, eum ludibrio habuerūt. Sed videamus spatiū hoc temporis, quod templi sui aedificationi ascribūt: Quadraginta sex annos numerant, cùm tamen reuera praesentis templi opificium absolutū fuerit spatio sex annorū: Verū illi ad rem exaggeranda numerat annos, quàm possunt, plurimos, nō omittētes illos annos, quibus opus erat impeditum. Nā anno primo Cyri coeperunt iacì fundamenta templi. Diebus Cābysis & Darij Hystaspis opus erat impeditum: Denique Darij Logimani anno sexto absolutū erat. Vide libri Ezrae cap. 3. & deinceps, ad cap. 7. Annos autem hos numerant alij quadraginta sex: verūm si supputamus numerū annorum secundū eruditissimos, non tot videbuntur numerari posse: Nā Cyrus vnā cum Cambyse regnauit annis noue, Magianno vno, Darius Hystaspis annis viginti, Darius Longimanus annis nouēdecim. Huius autē anno sexto absolutū erat templi opificiū. Quare sic supputato tempore, numerabis annos dūtaxat triginta sex. Verū non puto equidem ante finē regni gni Darij Logimani opus prorsus consummatu fuisse & reparatum. Quamobrem nonnulli ascribunt aedificationi tepli annos totos quadraginta nouem. Sciendum autem est teplum hoc, de quo tu Iudaei loquuti sunt, non fuisse tam teplum illud quod aedificatu est post reditu populi ex captiuitate Babylonica, quam teplum ab Herode rex paratum; verum illa praeterco. Video hoc loco praxin a liquam eius quod comminatur Dominus alibi, dices, Vobis datum est nosse mysteria regni coelorum, illis autem non est datum: propterea per parabolas loquor iis, quia videntes non videant, & audientes non audiant. Hoc enim loco, cum Christus locutus esset per parabolam, non intellexerunt quod loquutus est. Sed quaeres, An ignorantiae huius causa fuerit tu in Christo, ut qui obscure loquutus sit, an vero in ipsis Iudaeis? Respon. Primum ignorantiae ipsorum causam non fuisse in loquendi forma, qua tu usus est Christus, sed in originali illa ipsorum caecitate (ut de ignoratia illa quam Paulus dicit esse ex obduratione cordis nihil dica) in originali, inquam, illa caecitate qua homo sibi iam olim voluntate sua cotraxit: Nulla enim in verbo Dei loquutio vel sententia ta obscura occurrit, quin si homo stetisset in voce illa, cum qua creatus est, ea intelligere potuerit. Quapropter ignorantia hanc omne verbi Dei sibi imputet homo, non Deo. Deinde respondeo, Christum per parabola locutu Iudaeis, ad hoc ut vlcisceretur obstinatam eorum malitiam ac infidelitatem: Nam venerunt ad eum non discendi animo, sed animo contradicendi & tentandi: ideo vltus est eos per parabola. Quae sane vltio satis grauis est, cum priuet eos intelligentia eius verbi, quo oportet nutriri animas nostras ad vita aeternam. Sed tamen ut vlciscetur Deus hominum malitiam cosueuit ipsis per parabolas loqui; quod si aperte malitiosis, & infidelibus loquatur, tum quidem solet adimere ipsis oculos: hoc est subtrahere Spiritum suum sanctu & tradere deo huius mundi excaecandos, ne irradiet eos lume gloriosi euangelij. Fateor equidem Deum no solere hodie vlcisci malitia & contemptu nostrorum hominu para-bolicis istiusmodi locutionibus: Na si tectum est Euangelium nostrum, ut cum Paulo dicam, tectum est iis qui pereunt. Verum illud extra conuersiam est, in tam clara luce quamplurimos esse qui nihil videant, Deo videlicet iusto suo iudicio subtrahente ab iis Spiritum suum sanctum. Neque enim profecto si viderent, tot adulteriis, tot homicidiis, tot sacrilegiis, tot denique peccatis omnis generis sese contaminarent, quae videtur non tantum ipsis ruina, sed toti genti extremā lucis Euangelij remotione, quo iudicio aliud gravius esse non potest in hac vita. Quandiu enim lux aliqua reliqua est, tandiu spes aliqua est emendationis, conuersionis ad Deum: sublata autem omni prorsus luce, quae spes potest esse conuersionis & resipiscentiae?
units.tr: So far is Christ's answer to the request of the Jews. Now follows the twofold effect of the answer: one in the Jews, the other in the disciples, which came about only in its proper time and after the Lord's resurrection. The effect in the Jews appears from the fact that they answered him and mocked this great promised miracle of resurrection. For when Christ, as the evangelist briefly reminds us, had spoken of the temple of his body, they understood him to have spoken of that temple of theirs at Jerusalem, and, thinking it impossible for so great a temple to be built in so short a time, they mocked him. But let us look at this span of time which they ascribe to the building of their temple. They count forty-six years, although in fact the construction of the present temple was completed within a span of six years. But they count the years as many as they could, to exaggerate the matter, not leaving out those years in which the work was hindered. For in the first year of Cyrus the foundations of the temple began to be laid. In the days of Cambyses and Darius Hystaspis the work was hindered. Finally, in the sixth year of Darius Longimanus it was completed. See the book of Ezra, chapter 3 and following, up to chapter 7. Others count these years as forty-six; but if we reckon the number of years according to the most learned authorities, it will not appear possible to count so many. For Cyrus reigned together with Cambyses nine years, the Magian one year, Darius Hystaspis twenty years, Darius Longimanus nineteen years. Yet the building of the temple was completed in his sixth year. So, reckoning the time in this way, you will count only thirty-six years. However, I do not think the work was entirely finished and restored before the end of the reign of Darius Longimanus. Therefore some ascribe to the building of the temple a full forty-nine years. But it must be noted that this temple, about which you Jews spoke, was not that temple which was built after the people returned from Babylonian captivity, but the temple prepared by King Herod; yet I pass over these matters. Here I see the practice of which the Lord elsewhere speaks, saying, To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given; therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear. For in this passage, when Christ had spoken in a parable, they did not understand what he had said. But you will ask whether the cause of their ignorance lay in Christ, as though he had spoken obscurely, or rather in the Jews themselves? I answer: first, the cause of their ignorance did not lie in the form of speech which Christ used, but in that original blindness of theirs (I say nothing here of that ignorance which Paul says arises from the hardening of the heart), in that original blindness, I say, which man long ago brought upon himself by his own will. For no utterance or saying in the word of God is so obscure that man, had he stood in that state in which he was created, could not have understood it. Therefore let man impute this ignorance of every word of God to himself, not to God. Secondly, I answer that Christ spoke to the Jews in parables in order to punish their stubborn malice and unbelief. For they came to him not with a mind to learn, but with a mind to contradict and to tempt him; therefore he punished them by parables. This punishment is indeed quite severe, since it deprives them of understanding that word by which our souls ought to be nourished to eternal life. Yet God is accustomed, in order to punish the malice of men, to speak to them by parables; but if he speaks plainly to those who are malicious and unbelieving, then he is accustomed to take away their eyes, that is, to withdraw his Holy Spirit and deliver them to the god of this world to be blinded, lest the light of the glorious gospel shine upon them. I admit indeed that God does not usually today punish the malice and contempt of our people with such parabolic forms of speech; for if our gospel is hidden, as I may say with Paul, it is hidden from those who are perishing. But this is beyond dispute: in so clear a light there are very many who see nothing, God, by his just judgment, withdrawing his Holy Spirit from them. For truly, if they saw, they would not defile themselves with so many adulteries, so many murders, so many sacrileges, and finally so many sins of every kind, which seems to be not only their own ruin but the extreme removal of the light of the gospel from the whole nation, and there can be no heavier judgment than this in this life. For as long as some light remains, so long there is some hope of amendment and conversion to God; but once all light is taken away, what hope of conversion and repentance can there be?

units.la: Video hic praeterea in Iudaeis iis non nudi tantum ignorantiam sermonis Christi, quam ipsi falso concepERUNT, verum etiam cordis duritiem. Cum Deus non illuminat oculos impiorum, ad hoc ut videant & assentiantur ipsius verbo, tum insita illa caecitas & infidelitas cordis, praeterquam quod non potest capere quae sunt Spiritus Dei, etiam iis contradicit, & sapientiam Dei stultitiam ducit. Non enim tantum a Paulo dictum est, Animalem hominem non esse capacem eorum quae sunt Spiritus Dei, sed etiam ea ipsi esse stultitiam. Atque ex hac contradictione & oppugnatione veritatis augetur continua cordis induratio. Nam quoties audit quis verbum Dei, & quoties auditu oppugnat eique contradicit, vel corde vel ore, toties attrahit sibi nouam cordis duritiem: tantisperdum tandem prorsus obduratus & desperatus euadat, tradatūrque in mentem omnis iudicij expertem, amissa omni scientia simul & conscientia. fieri quidem potest, ut non statim exerat se latens illa caecitas ac incredulitas: sed aliquandiu audiat quis verbum Dei, quasi consopitus, nullo cum sensu ac motu, neque bono neque malo, sed aliud cogitans & aliud agens. Verum non futurum est ut illa cordis malitia & infidelitas semper delitescat, sed exeret se tandem erumpetque in contradictionem ac oppugnationem veritatis. Quam-obrem perpetuo luctandum nobis est cum corde nostro a Deo auerso, ut in eo fidem quamprimum sentiamus.
units.tr: I see here, moreover, that in those Jews there was not only ignorance of Christ's words, which they had understood falsely, but also hardness of heart. When God does not enlighten the eyes of the wicked, so that they see and assent to his word, then that innate blindness and unbelief of heart, besides being unable to grasp the things of the Spirit of God, also sets itself against them and counts the wisdom of God as foolishness. For Paul said not only that the natural man cannot receive the things of the Spirit of God, but also that these things are foolishness to him. And from this contradiction and opposition to the truth, a continual hardening of the heart increases. For whenever anyone hears the word of God and, having heard it, opposes and contradicts it, either in heart or in speech, he brings a fresh hardness of heart upon himself. In this way he at last becomes utterly hardened and desperate, and is handed over to a mind without judgment, having lost all knowledge and at once all conscience. It may indeed happen that this hidden blindness and unbelief do not break out at once; but for a while a man may hear the word of God as if drowsy, with no feeling or movement, neither good nor bad, thinking one thing and doing another. Yet that wickedness and unbelief of heart will not always stay hidden; at last it will show itself and break out into contradiction and opposition to the truth. Therefore we must wrestle constantly with our heart, which is turned away from God, so that we may feel faith in it as soon as possible.

units.la: Quod postremo hic obseruo est, nimirum quod haec Iudaeorum responsio satis iam arguat quo fine perierint signum,
units.tr: What I finally observe here is this: the Jews' answer itself sufficiently shows for what purpose they sought a sign.

units.la: Caecitati Iudaeorum induratio cordis ad-iuncta.
units.tr: The hardening of the heart joined to the blindness of the Jews.

units.la: Gradus impietatis.
units.tr: Degrees of impiety.

units.la: Incredulitati sua quem praessignum, nempe ne nihil haberet quod praetexerent incredulitati suae. Haec irrisio & oppugnatio veritatis, quam videmus hodie in Papistis, satis arguit quo fine & animo petant miracula, desiderent etiam in nostris hominibus bonos mores, charitate & alia, quibus probemus mundo doctrinam nostram: Nempe ut habeant quod praetexant incredulitati & obstinationi suae: & cum ratione aliqua videantur insanire. Neque enim profecto alio quam nunc sunt in nos vel religionem nostram esse animo, si darentur iis & ante oculos ipsorum edent mille miracula, quae animum incredulum primum transformant ac renovant. Quod de incredulitate dico, in genere de omnibus vitiis, totaque naturae corruptione semel accipi volo. Mira est peccati deceptio & impostura: neque enim quisquam est omnium, qui in peccato aliquo perseverat, sive adulterio, sive homicidio, sive sacrilegio, qui non habeat impromptu aliquod praetextum, vel certe aliquid, quo se excusat cur hoc vel illud perpetret, quasi vero id sit in causa cur peccet alioqui non lubens. Verum Dominus suo tempore detrahet istis miseris larvam hanc, & toti mundo patefaciet, non aliam ob causam perseverare eos in peccando quam quod peccato summopere essent oblectati. Nam mira est impii cuiusque in peccato oblectatio, quod vel propter se expetit, propter ipsum autem alia.
units.tr: Their unbelief had a pretext ready made, namely so that they would have nothing to hide behind in their unbelief. This mockery and opposition to the truth, which we see today in the Papists, sufficiently shows for what end and with what intent they seek miracles, and also demand from our people good morals, love and other things by which we might prove our doctrine to the world. Namely, they want to have something to pretend in excuse of their unbelief and obstinacy, and so that they may seem to be sane in some reasonable way. For indeed they are not otherwise disposed towards us or our religion than they are now, even if a thousand miracles were given to them and performed before their eyes, which would first transform and renew the unbelieving mind. What I say about unbelief, I want understood in general of all vices and of the whole corruption of nature. The deception and trickery of sin is wonderful. For there is no one among all who persists in some sin, whether adultery, murder or sacrilege, who does not have some pretext ready to hand, or at least something by which he excuses himself for committing this or that, as if this were the only reason he sins, when otherwise he would not do so willingly. But the Lord in his own time will strip these wretched men of this mask and will reveal to the whole world that they persist in sinning for no other reason than that they were greatly delighted with sin. For the delight of every wicked man in sin is marvellous: he seeks it for its own sake, and other things for its sake.

units.la: Hactenus fuit primus effectus responsionis Christi, nempe in cordibus Iudaeorum, sequitur secundus, in animis discipulorum, in quibus suo tempore verba Christi fuerunt efficacia. Illi enim, postquam resurrexisset Christus ex mortuis, recordati sunt, & crediderunt Scripturae, & sermoni quem Iesus dixerat eis: Hoc est, scripturae quae praedixit resurrectionem Christi ex mortuis futuram, & sermoni ipsius Christi de resurrectione sua ex mortuis.
units.tr: So far was the first effect of Christ's answer, namely in the hearts of the Jews. There follows the second, in the minds of the disciples, in whom Christ's words were at the proper time effective. For after Christ had risen from the dead, they remembered, and believed the Scripture, and the saying which Jesus had spoken to them: that is, the Scripture which foretold that the resurrection of Christ from the dead would come, and the saying of Christ himself about his resurrection from the dead.

units.la: Apparet ex hoc loco non magis intellexisse discipulos Christi quid sibi voluerit illis verbis quam Iudaeos: sed discrimen in eo fuit, quod cum Iudaei sententiam quam sibi finxerunt verborum Christi, oppugnarint, discipuli nihil obmurmurarint. Fit saepenumero, ut etiam fideles non intelligant quae dicuntur ex verbo Dei: fit autem saepius ut non sentiant corde quae intelligunt. Attamen
units.tr: It appears from this passage that the disciples of Christ understood no better what he meant by those words than the Jews did; but the difference was this: while the Jews opposed the meaning they had invented for Christ's words, the disciples murmured no objection. It often happens that even believers do not understand what is said from the word of God; but it happens more often that they do not feel in their heart what they do understand. Yet

units.la: 2. Effectus responsionis Christi in Discipulorum animis. discrimen latum est inter fideles ac infideles. Infidelesferè oppugnant veritatem: fideles verò hanc à Deo gratiam interea impetrant, vt modestia quadam componantur, donec Deus aperiat oculos ipsorum, simulque desiderium excitet intelligendi ea quæ dicuntur & cum precibus. Cùm Christus propositisset inter alias parabolam zizaniorum, turba cùm non intellexisset, nontamen inquisiuit in sententiam parabolæ: imò verò vt colligi poterit ex contextu, eam contempsit: At verò, discipuli petiuerunt seorsim à Domino vt edisceret sibi parabolam illam zizaniorum. Sed quid subsequutum est hanc quæ in discipulis fuit modestiæ gratiam? Suo tempore, cùm iam Christus resurrexisset ex mortuis, recordati sunt quod hoc dixisset eis, & crediderunt. Modestia hæc qua continetur pij, dum non intelligunt cum desiderio intelligendi coniunctum, argumento est Deum aliquando ipsis reuelaturum quod desiderant, Idque citius vel serius. Quod si quid aliter sentitis, hoc quoque Deus vobis reteget, inquit Apostolus, & beati qui esuriunt & sitiunt iustitiam, quoniam ipsi saturabuntur. Discipuli non crediderunt nisi excitato priùs Christo ex mortuis, & re iam perfecta. At beatius est re nondum perfecta credere. Beati sunt qui non viderunt & crediderunt.
units.tr: 2. The effect of Christ's answer in the minds of the disciples. A wide difference lies between believers and unbelievers. Unbelievers generally oppose the truth; but believers, meanwhile, obtain this grace from God, that they are composed with a certain modesty, until God opens their eyes and at the same time arouses a desire to understand what is said, and they pray for it. When Christ had set forth, among other parables, the parable of the tares, the crowd did not understand it, yet did not inquire into the meaning of the parable; indeed, as can be gathered from the context, they despised it. But the disciples asked the Lord privately to explain to them that parable of the tares. But what followed this grace of modesty that was in the disciples? In due time, when Christ had already risen from the dead, they remembered that he had said this to them, and they believed. This modesty, which marks the godly while they do not understand, joined with a desire to understand, is a sign that God will at some time reveal to them what they desire, and that sooner or later. "But if you think otherwise, God will also reveal this to you," says the Apostle; and blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. The disciples did not believe until Christ had first been raised from the dead and the thing was already accomplished. But it is more blessed to believe before the thing is accomplished. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.

units.la: 23 Quum autem esset Hierosolymis in Pascha, in festo, multi crediderunt in nomen eius, conspicientes signa quæ edebat.
units.tr: 23 Now when he was at Jerusalem at the Passover, at the feast, many believed on his name, beholding the signs which he did.

units.la: 24 Ipse autem Iesus non credebat eis semetipsum, eo quòd nosset omnes:
units.tr: 24 But Jesus did not commit himself to them, because he knew all men,

units.la: 25 Nec opus esset vt quisquam ei testaretur de homine: ipse enim sciebat quid esset in homine.
units.tr: 25 And had no need that any should testify of man: for he knew what was in man.

units.la: HActenus fuit factum Christi in purgando templo, simul & ipsius effecta: sequuntur omnia eius signa & prodigia summatim comprehensa cum suo effecto. Multa, inquit, signa & prodigia fecit Hierosolymis in Pascha, die festo. Summaria miraculorum Christi comprehensio, quorum effectum est, crediderunt in nomen eius multi. Sed qualisna ista fides fuerit ex verbis sequentibus intelligi potest: verùm Iesus, inquit, nö credebat ijs semetipsum. Causa autē est, eo quòd nosset omnes. Amplificatio sequitur: Nec opus esset vt quisquam ei testaretur de homine. Q.d. Et nosset quidē per se, sine opera & testimonio cuiusquam: cuius ratio est postremis verbis; Ipse enim sciebat quid esset in homine. est autem ex eo quòd Christus conscius esset cogitationum omnium animi humani, hoc est καρδιογνώστης esset. Hic obserua, fidem quæ ex miraculis duntaxat gignitur parum fidam esse: duo enim sunt veræ fidei fundamenta præcipua; alterum est potentia Dei, quæ conspicua est in soperibus ipsius, alterum est dilectio illa Dei & misericordia in Christo; Quòd si fides tantùm gignatur ex potentia ea quæ conspicitur in miraculis, profectò cùm ea fides tàtum historica sit, vt vocant, neque sanctificet cor, purgetque ipsum à dolo, crudelitate, malitia, &c. parum tuta est ac firma, cui se credat vel Christus vel Christianus aliquis. Quòd si non tantùm existat ex potentia, sed etiam ex amore ac bonitate Dei inspecta, hoc est, si sit apprehensio dilectionis in Christo, iam purgat corda nostra, eáque sanctificat ac separat à dolo, crudelitate, omniqué malicia. Ideóque tuta fidesst cuise credat Christus. Non enim habitat Christus nisi in corde sanctificato ac purgato per fidé. Deinde vide hoc loco quomodo cõueniat inter istos & Christum: Hypocritæ erant duntaxat & in pectore absconditam habebant fraudem mox eruptura, offerente se occasione quacunque, vel ex dictis vel ex factis Christi: putabat quoque ne Christū quidem videre quid lateret in ipsorum pectore: sed ipse καρδιογνώστης statim intuitus, nō tam vultus quàm animos eorū, nō se credidit eis. Nullū est hominū genus tā effros ac impudens quàm sunt hypocritæ, dū se obtrudunt Christo, seq; ingerunt in cœtus piorū, vix ipsi videntes quid clausū habeant in pectore. Ni & suos ipsorū oculos cæcat, & putat Deū nihil videre. Sed cùm Deus perpendat corda hominū, statim oculis penetrat in secreta cordis, videtq; quid mali illic abditū lateat. Se hypocritis nō credit, fugit ab eis, nihil acceptū habet, quòd ab iis profectū est. Quis quæsiuit, inquit, hoc à manu vestra, vt cõculcetis atria mea? Quare si velimus Deū habitare nobiscū & in cordibus nostris, studeamus ante omnia cordis sinceritati, ex qua Deus æstimat omnes actiones humanas, quæque habet laudem suam non ab hominibus, sed à Deo: Cui sit omnis honor, Amen.
units.tr: Thus far has been the deed of Christ in cleansing the temple, together with its effect. Now follow all his signs and wonders, summarily comprehended with their effect. He did many signs and wonders, it says, at Jerusalem at the Passover, on the feast day. This is a summary comprehension of Christ's miracles, the effect of which was that many believed on his name. But what kind of faith this was can be understood from the words that follow: but Jesus, it says, did not trust himself to them. The cause is because he knew all men. An amplification follows: And he had no need that anyone should testify of man. That is, he knew them by himself, without the work or testimony of anyone; and the reason for this is in the last words: For he himself knew what was in man. This comes from the fact that Christ was aware of all the thoughts of the human mind, that is, he was a heart-knower [καρδιογνώστης]. Here observe that faith which arises from miracles alone is of little trust: for there are two chief foundations of true faith. One is the power of God, which is seen in his works; the other is that love and mercy of God in Christ. If faith arises only from the power that is seen in miracles, then surely, since such faith is merely historical, as they call it, and does not sanctify the heart or purge it from deceit, cruelty, malice and so on, it is too weak and unstable for either Christ or any Christian to trust it. But if it arises not only from power but also from the love and goodness of God considered, that is, if it is a grasping of the love of God in Christ, then it already purges our hearts, sanctifies them and separates them from deceit, cruelty and all malice. Therefore that faith is sure, so that Christ may trust in it. For Christ does not dwell except in a heart sanctified and purged through faith. Next, see here how these men stood with Christ: they were hypocrites only, and they had in their breast a hidden fraud which was ready to burst out on any occasion offered by something Christ said or did. They thought that not even Christ could see what lay hidden in their breast; but he, the heart-knower, at once perceived not so much their faces as their minds, and did not trust himself to them. There is no kind of men so bold and shameless as hypocrites, who thrust themselves upon Christ and force themselves into the assemblies of the godly, hardly seeing for themselves what they keep shut up in their breast. They blind their own eyes and think God sees nothing. But since God weighs the hearts of men, he at once penetrates with his eyes into the secrets of the heart and sees what evil lies hidden there. He does not trust hypocrites, he flees from them, and he counts nothing as acceptable that has come from them. Who has required this at your hand, it says, to trample my courts? Therefore, if we wish God to dwell with us and in our hearts, let us above all strive for sincerity of heart, by which God judges all human actions, and which has its praise not from men but from God, to whom be all honour, Amen.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Hoc capite primùm habemus factum Christi in instituenda & conuertendo Nicodemo ad versum vsque 22. Deinde profectionem Christi in territorium Iudæa, vnà cum iis quæ facta sunt, queque accidérunt Domino, in Iudæa territorio commorante, ad finem vsque capitis.
units.tr: In this chapter we have first the deed of Christ in instructing and converting Nicodemus, up to verse 22. Then Christ's departure into the territory of Judea, together with what was done and what happened to the Lord while he stayed in the territory of Judea, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAP. III.

units.la: 1 Erat autem quidam ex Pharisæis, cui nomen erat Nicodemo, ex primoribus Iudæorum.
units.tr: 1 There was a certain man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.

units.la: 2 Hic venit ad Iesum nocte, & dixit ei, Rabbi, scimus te à Deo venisse doctorem: nemo enim potest hæc signa edere quæ tu edis, nisi Deus sit cum eo.
units.tr: 2 This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, "Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him."

units.la: Quod ad institutionem & conuersionem Nicodemi, primùm habemus præmissam hominis descriptionem quandam, deinde institutionem ipsam. Describitur homo primùm à secta sua. Erat quidam ex Pharisæis. Ac proinde doctor populi & magister in Israël. Pharisæi enim doctores ac interpretes verbi diuini haberi voluerunt, id quod ipsum nomen præse fert. Nam Pharisæus est doctor siue interpres legis. Deinde describitur à nomine proprio: Cui nomen erat Nicodemo. Postremò describitur ab honore siue magistratu suo. Erat ex primoribus Iudæorum. Erat ex eorum numero quos Sanhedrim vocabant, vel ex principibus synagogæ. Omnes enim Pharisæi erant in summa admiratione apud popupopulum, verùm non omnes statim erant principes populi vel archisynagogi. Ideóque apud Lucà nominatur quidam ex principibus Pharisæorum. Hactenus fuit hominis descriptio. De eo legimus primùm hoc capite, quòd clam noctu venerit ad Christum. Deinde de eodem legimus Ioan. 7.50.51. quòd Christum absentem & temerè damnatum à Pontificibus & Pharisæis defenderit: Nùm lex nostra condemnat quempiam nisi prius audierit ab ipso? Postremò de eodem legimus Iohan. 19.39. Quo loco, non amplius delitescens, fidem suam in Christum palàm professus est, & Christum è cruce detractum vnà cum Iosepho Arimathæensi sepeliit. De obitu eius, nihil legimus quod fide dignum sit. Circumfertur eius nomine liber de passione Christi, de quo, quia Apocryphus est, nihil nunc dicimus.
units.tr: In regard to Nicodemus's instruction and conversion, we have first a certain description of the man, and then the instruction itself. The man is described first by his sect: "There was a certain man of the Pharisees." Accordingly he was a teacher of the people and a master in Israel, for the Pharisees wanted to be regarded as the teachers and interpreters of the divine Word, as the name itself shows. For a Pharisee is a teacher or interpreter of the law. Next he is described by his proper name: "named Nicodemus." Last, he is described by his honour or office: "he was a ruler of the Jews." He was one of those whom they called the Sanhedrin, or one of the leaders of the synagogue. For all the Pharisees were held in the highest esteem among the people, but not all of them were at once rulers of the people or chiefs of the synagogue. That is why Luke calls him simply "a certain one of the rulers of the Pharisees." So much for the description of the man. We read about him first in this chapter that he came to Christ secretly by night. Next, we read about the same man in John 7:50, 51, that he defended Christ, who was absent and was rashly condemned by the chief priests and Pharisees: "Does our law condemn anyone unless it first hears from him?" Last, we read about the same man in John 19:39, where, no longer hiding, he openly professed his faith in Christ and, together with Joseph of Arimathea, buried Christ after he had been taken down from the cross. Concerning his death we read nothing that is worthy of belief. A book on the passion of Christ circulates under his name, but since it is apocryphal, we say nothing about it now.

units.la: Hactenus de hominis descriptione. Nunc videnda eius institutio in doctrina Regenerationis, simúlque ad Christum cóuerfio. Primùm venit ad Christum noctu, deinde confert cum Christo sermonem satis prolixum. Hic, inquit, venit ad Iesum nocte. Noctu venit, non autem interdiu, cùm propter metum amittédæ dignitatis suæ, tum propter pudorem: Puduisset enim virum principem & doctorem in Vrbe palam profiteri se Christi discipulum, qui à viris principibus tam vilis est habitus. Habuit tamen proculdubiò semen aliquod pietatis, quo impulsus est ad Christum quærendum: neque enim vllo naturæ instinctu, verùm secreta quadam vi Spiritus Christi huc pertractus est. Obserua igitur in exemplo huius viri quanta sit vis in prærogatiuis huius mundi; Vt dignitatis, diuitiarum, sapientiæ, nobilitatis, &c. ad impediendam Christi professionem: vel enim efficiunt vt homines non quærant omnino Christum: paucissimi enim sunt ex hoc hominum genere, qui Christum confitentur. Videtis vocationem vestram, fratres, vos videlicet non multos sapientes secundum carnem, non multos potentes, non multos nobiles, inquit Apostolus. Vel si imbuti aliquo pietatis semine confiteantur Christum, clam hoc faciant, neque audeant profiteri, id quod Nicodemo contigisse videmus hoc loco. Rursus in eodem isto homine vide quanta sit vis, vel in scintilla pietatis aliqua, ad reluctandum omnibus his impedimentis: diuergit enim semper aliquoufque, & tandem eluctatur. Nam Nicodemus quo tempore videri potuisset maxime latendum esse ipsi & erubescendum, cum videret Christum crucifixum & morte ignominiofiffima sublatum e medio, eo tempore prodiit in lucem, ac palam professus est fidem suam in Christum, quem vna cum Iofepho sepeliit. Exhis discimus, vt principibus huius mundi maxime cauendum est, ne hæ prærogatiuæ ipsis sint impedimento, quo minus Chriftu profiteantur, & aperte ingrediatur cursum pietatis; Ita rursus cauendum nobis esse, ne fi delitescens aliquod femen pietatis, vel obscure videamus in huiusmodi hominibus, etsi non statim erumpat in lucem & professionem vel actionem externam; ne, inquam, eos temere damnemus, sed perpetuo speremus de illo quatulocunq; pietatis femine. Secure enim possunt priuati homines, qui nō implicantur his difficultatibus, quibus illi, qui in luce populi sunt, de iis loqui liberius. Sed hic fi nos effemus, aliter sentiremus. Quaobre precandū nobis est ferio, pro iis quos Deus in potestate cõftituit, ac pro iis præsertim in quibus obseruamus ꝑ pietatis scintillam, vt velit Deus efficere vt illa tandem emicet ac eluctetur, superatis omnibus impedimentis.
units.tr: So much for the description of the man. Now we must consider his instruction in the doctrine of regeneration, and at the same time his conversion to Christ. First he came to Christ by night; then he held a rather lengthy conversation with Christ. "This man," it says, "came to Jesus by night." He came by night and not by day, both from fear of losing his dignity and from shame. For a man of rank and a teacher would have been ashamed to profess openly in the city that he was a disciple of Christ, since Christ was held so cheap by men of rank. Nevertheless he certainly had some seed of piety, by which he was moved to seek Christ. For he was drawn to Christ not by any natural instinct but by the secret power of Christ's Spirit. Observe therefore from the example of this man how great is the power of the advantages of this world, such as dignity, riches, wisdom, nobility, and so on, to hinder the confession of Christ. For they either bring it about that men do not seek Christ at all, for very few of this class of men confess Christ. "You see your calling, brothers, that not many of you are wise according to the flesh, not many are powerful, not many are noble," says the Apostle. Or, if they are imbued with some seed of piety and do confess Christ, they do it in secret and do not dare to profess him openly, which we see happened to Nicodemus in this place. Again, in this same man see how great is the power, even in some spark of piety, to struggle against all these hindrances. For it always breaks out somewhere and at last fights its way through. For at the very time when Nicodemus might have seemed most bound to hide and be ashamed, namely when he saw Christ crucified and removed from the midst by a most ignominious death, at that time he came forth into the light and openly professed his faith in Christ, whom he buried together with Joseph. From these things we learn that we must be most on guard against the rulers of this world, lest these advantages be a hindrance to them in confessing Christ and in openly entering the course of piety. Likewise we must be on guard in turn, lest, if we see in such men some hidden seed of piety, or see it only dimly, even though it does not at once break out into the light in profession or outward action, we rashly condemn them, I say, but always hope for whatever small seed of piety is in them. For private men, who are not caught up in those difficulties in which those who stand in the light of the people are, can speak more freely about such things. But if we were in that position, we would think otherwise. Therefore we must earnestly pray for those whom God has placed in authority, and especially for those in whom we observe a spark of piety, that God would will that it at last shine forth and fight its way through, all hindrances overcome.

units.la: Sequitur communicatio ac dialogifmus. Primus inchoat sermonem Nicodemus: Rabbi, inquit: appellat cum reuerëter. Scimus te venisse a Deo Magistrum. Scimus, inquit, non scio: Hoc est omnes nos Pharisæi scimus, non possumus non scire, tot iam editis a te miraculis. Magi, de quibus legimus Exod. 8.19 cõspecto vno pediculorū miraculo sciuerūt Dei digitū illic esse. Qui igitur fieri potuit, vt nō sciret istud Pharisæi, tot ii editis a Christo miraculis, eū ex Deo esse? Sciuerūt quidem, sed scietes noluerūt scire, cum diceret eū per Beelzebub eicere dæmonia, & vnde esset se nescire: ideóq; imputatur eis a Christo blasphemia aduersus Spiritū Sanctū. Quare videndū nobis est, ne scientes nolimus scire, hoc est ne cordis contumacia reluctemur cognitæ veritati. Scimus, inquit, te a Deo venisse Magistru. Quod si a Deo venit Magister: Ergo lætigimus. Vide igitur fundamentū authoritatis omnium doctorum in Ecclesia, nempe hoc, si a Deo Deo venerint. Vt enim Deus solus est Dominus Ecclesiæ suæ, ita qui ab eo missi sunt necesse est cum authoritate aliqua & legitima potestate sint in Ecclesia Dei. Generale istud omnes intelligunt, vel natura ducet. Verùm cùm descenditur ad speciem, ad singulos nimirum qui missi sunt, hic tota est controversia, An à Deo missi sunt? Neque natura vnquam hoc nos docebit, An à Deo missi sint? Sed necesse est, vt hoc intelligamus, illustrem ur Dei illo Spiritu qui discretionis dicitur. Secus enim non missos à Deo, tanquam missos recipiemus, contraque missos à Deo tanquam non missos reiiciemus: Spiritualis enim diiudicat omnia, ipse verò à nemine diiudicatur, hoc est, à nullo homine ψυχικῷ & animali. Quis enim novit mentem Domini, qui instructurus sit eum? Nos autem mentem Christi habemus. quasi dicat, Quam impossibile est animali homini iudicare de Dei mente, tã impossibile est iudicare de eo qui habet Dei mente, nisi eadem Dei mente, hoc est, Dei Spiritu prius illuminatus fuerit. Sed quomodo peruenit Nicodemus ad hanc scientiam & discretionem? Nempe conspexit potentiã Dei in miraculis editis à Christo. Sic, inquies, & alij Pharisæi, & tamen non sunt professi se scire eum à Deo venisse Magistrum. Respondeo, Nicodemi mens non tantum illuminata fuit à Spiritu ad hoc, vt videret tantum potentiã Dei in miraculis, sed & cor inclinatũ fuit ad hoc, vt assentiretur illi Dei potentiæ quam vidit. Pharisæi autem viderunt quidem, sed manserunt iusto Dei iudicio immoti corde: imò restiterunt illuminationi Spiritus sancti.
units.tr: The conversation and dialogue follow. Nicodemus begins the discourse: "Rabbi," he says, addressing him reverently. "We know that you have come from God as a Teacher." We know, he says, not "I know": that is, all we Pharisees know; we cannot but know, since you have already performed so many miracles. The magicians, of whom we read in Exodus 8:19, when they saw one miracle of the gnats, knew that the finger of God was there. How, then, could the Pharisees, after so many miracles performed by Christ, fail to know that he is from God? Indeed they knew, but though knowing they were unwilling to know, when they said that he cast out demons by Beelzebub and that they did not know whence he was; and therefore Christ charges them with blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Hence we must consider that we do not, knowing, refuse to know, that is, that we do not resist by the obstinacy of the heart a truth that we have come to know. We know, he says, that you have come from God as Teacher. If the Teacher has come from God, then we must heed him. See therefore the foundation of the authority of all the teachers in the Church, namely this: that they have come from God. For just as God alone is the Lord of his Church, so those who have been sent by him must necessarily have some authority and lawful power in the Church of God. All understand this general principle, or nature will lead them to it. But when we descend to the particular, that is, to each one who has been sent, here lies the whole controversy: Were they sent by God? Nature will never teach us whether they were sent by God; but we must understand this, being illuminated by that Spirit of God which is called the Spirit of discernment. For otherwise we shall not receive as sent those who were not sent by God, and conversely we shall not reject as not sent those who were sent by God. For the spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one, that is, by no man animal [ψυχικῷ]. For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ. As if to say: just as it is impossible for an animal man to judge of the mind of God, so it is impossible to judge of one who has the mind of God, unless he has first been illuminated by the same mind of God, that is, by the Spirit of God. But how did Nicodemus arrive at this knowledge and discernment? Surely he saw the power of God in the miracles performed by Christ. "Yes," you will say, "so did the other Pharisees too, and yet they did not profess that they knew he had come from God as Teacher." I answer: Nicodemus's mind was illuminated by the Spirit not only so that he saw the power of God in the miracles, but also his heart was inclined to assent to that power of God which he saw. The Pharisees, however, indeed saw it, but by the just judgment of God remained unmoved in heart; indeed they resisted the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Sed expedamus verba quibus habetur ratio, qua motus est Nicomedus ad hoc, vt crederet Christũ à Deo venisse. Nemo, inquit, potest hæc signa edere quæ tu edis, nisi Deus sit cum eo. Dicitur Deus esse cum aliquo quando potenter & benignè agit cum eo. Sic cum Iosepho dicitur fuisse, cum eruerit eum ex omnibus oppressionibus suis, & daret ei gratiam & sapientiam coram Pharaone rege Ægypti. Verum Nicodemus, si bene novisset Christum qui esset, non dixisset Deum cum eo fuisse, sed multò magis in eo fuisse, quemadmodum dixit Paulus, Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi. In eo enim inhabitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter. Videmus igitur argumentum esse à miraculis editis à Christo, ex quo concludit eum à Deo venisse. Sed quæri potest, An non hoc videatur infirmum argumentum à miraculis desumptum, cum adventus Antichristi sit ex efficacia Satanæ, cum omni potentia & signis ac prodigiis mendacibus, & cum omni fraude iniustitiæ in iis qui pereunt, pro eo quod amorem veritatis non receperunt vt salui fierent? Sic Christus, Surgent, inquit, Pseudochristi & Pseudoprophetæ & edent signa magna & miracula, ita vt seducant (si fieri possit etiam electos). Respondeo Satanā esse simiā Dei, nihilq; esse quod à Deo vel dicitur vel geritur, quod ille nō conetur aliquo modo imitari. Verbi Dei speciē quādam abutitur, miracula & opera in illusionibus & præstigiis suis repræsentat, deniq; transformat se in Angelum lucis.
units.tr: But let us examine the words by which Nicodemus (the text misprints "Nicomedus") was moved to believe that Christ had come from God. No one, he says, can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him. God is said to be with someone when he acts toward that person with power and goodness. So God was with Joseph when he delivered him from all his oppressions and gave him grace and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. But Nicodemus, if he had known well who Christ was, would not have said that God was with him, but much more that God was in him, as Paul said: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. For in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. We see, then, that the argument is drawn from the miracles Christ performed, and from them he concludes that he had come from God. But it may be asked whether this does not seem a weak argument drawn from miracles, since the coming of Antichrist is through the working of Satan, with all power, with lying signs and wonders, and with all deceit of unrighteousness among those who perish, because they did not receive the love of the truth that they might be saved. So Christ says: There shall arise false Christs and false prophets, and they shall show great signs and wonders, so as to deceive (if it were possible, even the elect). I answer that Satan is the ape of God, and there is nothing said or done by God that he does not try in some way to imitate. He abuses some semblance of the Word of God, presents miracles and works in his illusions and tricks, and finally transforms himself into an angel of light.

units.la: An, quæso, istud debet esse præiudicio verbo & operibus Dei, ne ista scilicet effectum suum consequantur, in iis quorum mentes Deus illuminauit, vt videant potētiam ac sapientiam in operibus, & in verbo veritatem? Sed hoc non satisfacit aliis quàm iis quorum mentes Deus sic illuminauit Spiritu illo qui loquitur in verbo Dei, vt videant verbi veritatem. Papistæ enim quia non xtradiantur lumine Euangelij gloriæ Dei, idque iusto Dei iudicio, ad hoc vt videant illam lucem Euangelij, ideo non contenti sunt verbi Dei authoritate tanquam primaria, ad hoc vt credant; verum Ecclesiam suam eiusque sententiam, verbo Dei, authoritate superiorem faciunt, & ab ea quasi lucem petunt principalem, quasi inspiciant lucem verbi diuini. Idem facientes, ac si accenderent candelam, hoc est obscuram aliquam lucem, cuius beneficio deinde lucem Solis, hoc est clarissimam lucem inspiciant. Nos vero, Deo sit gratia, missis iis qui in verbum Dei blasphemi sunt suo ipsorum exitio, acquiescimus in verbi Dei scripti authoritate ac luce, affirmamusque eam maiorē esse omni authoritate Ecclesiæ, eamque esse causam cur credam Ecclesiæ hoc vel illud asserenti. Est enim veræ Ecclesiæ nota eadem que causa, veritas verbi Dei: Non autem contra Ecclesiam aut Ecclesiæ authoritas, aut vox, causa est, cur ego credā voci Dei. Cui inuitis illis veritatis hostibus sua constabit authoritas, maiestas & gloria. Fieri quidem potest, quæ
units.tr: Should this, I ask, be a reason for prejudging the Word and works of God, so that they fail to achieve their effect in those whose minds God has enlightened, so that they see the power and wisdom in the works and the truth in the Word? But this answer does not satisfy anyone except those whose minds God has so enlightened by that Spirit who speaks in the Word of God that they see the truth of the Word. For the Papists, because the light of the Gospel of God's glory does not shine upon them, and that by the just judgment of God, so that they do not see that light of the Gospel, are therefore not content with the authority of the Word of God as primary for believing. Rather, they make their Church and its judgment superior to the Word of God in authority, and seek from it, as from a principal light, as though they were looking at the light of the divine Word. They act just as if they lit a candle, that is, some dim light, by whose help they then look at the light of the sun, that is, the most brilliant light. But we, thanks be to God, having cast off those who blaspheme the Word of God to their own destruction, rest on the authority and light of the written Word of God, and we affirm that it is greater than all the authority of the Church, and that it is the reason why I believe the Church when it asserts this or that. For the mark of the true Church is the same as the cause, namely the truth of the Word of God. But neither the Church nor the authority or voice of the Church is the cause why I believe the voice of God, against the will of those enemies of the truth. Their authority, majesty and glory will stand in spite of them. Indeed it may happen, through our unbelief and weakness, that some believe the Gospel and the Word of God only when moved by the voice of the Church.

units.la: 2. Tim. 3. 9. 10. incredulitas nostra ac infirmitas vt aliqui non nisi voce Ecclesiæ adducti credant Euangelio & verbo Dei. Sed cùm vox Ecclesiæ accedit, tanquam secundarius quidã testis, authoritate inferior voce Dei in verbo scripto, adiuuat tamen infirmitatem nostram in prima præsertim nostra conuersione. Verùm postquàm iam conuersi sumus,& vidimus illam verbi Dei lucem ac authoritatem,in ea conquiescimus, & nõ iam amplius propter vocem Ecclesiæ credimus verbo Dei, sed propter vocē Dei credimus voci Ecclesiæ. Viderint hoc, qui ex tenebris illis Papisticis velint se extricare.
units.tr: 2 Tim. 3. 9. 10. But when the voice of the Church comes in, as a secondary witness, inferior in authority to the voice of God in the written Word, it nevertheless helps our weakness, especially in our first conversion. But once we have been converted and have seen that light and authority of the Word of God, we rest in it, and no longer believe the Word of God because of the voice of the Church, but we believe the voice of the Church because of the voice of God. Let those who wish to extricate themselves from those Papist shadows see to this.

units.la: Obserua ex his verbis primùm; Miracula duntaxat à Deo esse. Nemo, inquit, potest edere hæc signa, nisi cum eo Deus sit. Solius enim Dei potentia potest immutare naturæ ordinem,id quod fit in veris miraculis. Nam quòd ad miracula Papistarũ, nihil sunt nisi illusiones & præstigiæ,quorum causas quia ignorant homines,ideo putant miracula esse. Conítat enim Dei potentiam nunquam concurrere ad edendum signa mendacia quibus confirmentur mendacia. Quomodo potest homo peccator talia signa edere? hoc est,homo mendax, & qui tradit falsam doctrinam. Papistarum autem illa quæ iactant miracula eò pertinent omnia, vt confirmet ipsorum mendacia. Nam quorum oculos illuminauit Deus, illud satis videt, Papistarum hæresin potiús quàm religionem consarcinatam esse ex meris mendaciis ac vanitatibus. Secūdò obserua notam legitimæ vocationis eius,nimirum quæ à Deo fit, hanc esse: Si Deus nobiscum sit, & Dei virtus & potentia in dictis & factis nostris eluceat. Paulus probans suum Apostolatum, hoc, inter cætera, indicium profert, nempe virtutem Dei. Indicia quidem Apostalatus edita sunt apud vos per omnem tolerantiam, & signa, & prodigia, & virtutes. Idem alibi cùm promittit exploraturum pseudo-apostolos qui erant Corinthi, Cognoscam, inquit, non verba istorum qui inflati sunt, sed spiritum virtutem: Non enim in verbis situm est regnum Dei, sed in Spiritu virtute. Et illud profectò negari nõ potest, cum qui est à Deo missus, cum aliqua Dei virtute & potentia missum esse, ea nimirum, quam & ipse & alii possunt certò quodam modo persentiscere. Paulus di-
units.tr: Observe from these words, first, that miracles are from God alone. No one, he says, can do these signs unless God is with him. For only the power of God can change the order of nature, which is what happens in true miracles. As for the miracles of the Papists, they are nothing but illusions and tricks, and because men do not know their causes, they think them to be miracles. For it is certain that the power of God never concurs in performing lying signs by which lies are confirmed. How can a sinful man perform such signs? That is, a liar, who hands on false doctrine. But all those miracles of the Papists that they boast of tend to confirm their lies. For God has enlightened the eyes of those who see well enough that the Papists' heresy, rather than their religion, is patched together from pure lies and vanities. Secondly, observe that the mark of his lawful calling, that is, the calling that comes from God, is this: if God is with us, and the power and might of God shine forth in our words and deeds. Paul, proving his apostleship, brings forward this, among other evidences, namely the power of God. Indeed the signs of an apostle were wrought among you in all patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works. Elsewhere too, when he promises to test the false apostles who were at Corinth, he says: I will know not the words of those who are puffed up, but their power: for the kingdom of God is not in words, but in the power of the Spirit. And surely it cannot be denied that one who is sent from God is sent with some power and might of God, namely that which he himself and others can with certainty perceive in some way.

units.la: 1. Cor. 12. cebat, Ad quod etiam enitor, decertans secundum efficacitatem ipsius agentem in me potenter. Quod non dixisset nisi vim illam Dei agentem in se ipse sensisset. Item, Quandoquidem, inquit, experimentum quaeritis loquentis in me Christi, qui non est infirmus erga vos, sed in vobis potens. Hic dubitantes de virtute Christi quae in Paulo fuit, remittit ad effectum ipse illius virtutis, quod in se ipsi senserunt. Quod profecto si non fit ad aedificationem, necesse est fit ad destructionem & mortem. Paratum, inquit, habemus quo vindicemus omnem contumaciam, postquam impleta fuerit vestra obedientia. Non enim fieri potest, ut qui a Deo missus est, frustra sit missus & sine fructu aliquo & effectu vel vitae vel mortis. Videamus igitur, cum oporteat eum aliquo modo in nobis efficacem esse, quo modo sit efficax ad vitam ne ad mortem.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 12. Paul said: For this I also labour, striving according to his working, which works in me mightily. He would not have said this unless he had felt that power of God working in himself. Likewise: Since you seek proof of Christ speaking in me, who is not weak towards you, but mighty among you. Here, doubting the power of Christ that was in Paul, he refers them to the effect of that very power, which they had felt in themselves. Which indeed, if it is not for edification, must necessarily be for destruction and death. We have ready, he says, to avenge all disobedience, once your obedience is fulfilled. For it cannot happen that one who is sent by God is sent in vain, and without some fruit and effect, either of life or of death. Let us see, then, since he must in some way be effective in us, how he is effective unto life and not unto death.

units.la: 3 Respondit Iesus & dixit ei, Amen, Amen dico tibi, nisi quis genitus fit iterum, non potest videre regnum Dei.
units.tr: 3 Jesus answered and said to him, Verily, verily I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.

units.la: 4 Dicit ei Nicodemus, Quomodo potest homo genitus qui sit senex? num potest in uterum matris suae introire & geniti?
units.tr: 4 Nicodemus saith unto him, How can a man be born when he is old? can he enter the second time into his mother's womb, and be born?

units.la: 5 Respondit Iesus, Amen, Amen dico tibi, nisi quis fuerit genitus ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest introire in regnum Dei.
units.tr: 5 Jesus answered, Verily, verily I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.

units.la: HActenus Nicodemus professus est suam de Christo sententiam, eum nimirum doctorem esse a Deo missum, quibus verbis inuitare voluit Christum ad agendum partes doctoris in se erudiendo. Christus itaque qui ad nos, ut omnia noua faceret, teste Paulo, incipit agere doctorem, & instituturus Nicodemum, orditur statim a regeneratione, qua ex veteribus noui fimus homines. Regenerationem autem ea cum necessitate proponit, ut, nisi Nicodemus, aliisque quicunque denuo fuerint geniti, impossibile esse affirmet, ut videant regnum Dei. Quo autem maiorem propositae sententiae fidem concilier, non simpliciter, sed cum graui asseueratione & iureiurando. iurando eam affirmat. Amen, Amen, inquit veritas ipsa, dico tibi, nisi quis genitus fuerit denuo, non poterit videre regnum Dei. Regnum Dei intelligo hæreditatem regni Dei: vel hæreditatem in regno Christi & Dei. Nam quem-admodum qui naturæ lege ac ordine gignuntur, illi quidem gignuntur ac nascuntur ad participandum aliqua hæreditate vel parte bonorum paternorum ac terrestrium: ita qui spiritualiter gignuntur ac nascuntur, gignuntur illi & nascuntur ad hæreditarium regnū possidendum. Benedictus Deus & Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui ex multa sua misericordia regenuit nos ad spem viam, per resurrectionem Iesu Christi ex mortuis. Tum spem illam exponens, addit: In hæreditatem quæ nec perire potest, nec contaminari, nec marcescere, nobis in cœlis servatâ. Quem-admodum enim tum primùm creati sumus & conditi in Adamo ad hanc immortalitatem, ita regenerati & denuò conditi in Christo Iesu sumus ad eandem illam immortalitatem recuperandam in Christo quam in Adamo amisimus. Arrhabonem autem hæreditatis illius nostræ habemus in hac vita, & sentimus Spiritum illum regenerationis sanctum, ut ibidem dictum est à Paulo. Hæc est igitur illa tam præclara hæreditas, quam ita denuo adipiscemur, si in Christo fuerimus regeniti.
units.tr: Hitherto Nicodemus has declared his opinion about Christ, namely that he is a teacher sent from God, and with these words he wished to invite Christ to take up the part of a teacher in instructing him. Christ, therefore, who, as Paul bears witness, came to us to make all things new, begins to act as teacher, and, about to instruct Nicodemus, he begins at once with regeneration, by which we are made new men from the old. He sets out regeneration as so necessary that he affirms it is impossible, unless Nicodemus and whoever else is born again, for them to see the kingdom of God. And so that he might win greater belief for the proposition he put forward, he affirms it not simply but with a solemn asseveration and an oath. Verily, verily, says Truth itself, I say to you, unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. By the kingdom of God I understand the inheritance of the kingdom of God, or the inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. For just as those who are begotten by the law and order of nature are indeed begotten and born to share in some inheritance or part of their father's goods, both earthly and temporal, so those who are spiritually begotten and born are begotten and born to possess an inheritance of a kingdom. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has begotten us again unto a living hope, by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. Explaining that hope, he adds: To an inheritance that cannot perish, nor be defiled, nor fade away, reserved for us in heaven. For just as we were first created and made in Adam for that immortality, so we are regenerated and made anew in Christ Jesus for the recovery, in Christ, of that same immortality which we lost in Adam. We have the pledge of that inheritance in this life, and we feel that Spirit of regeneration, which is holy, as Paul says in the same place. This, then, is that so excellent inheritance, which we shall thus obtain anew, if we have been begotten again in Christ.

units.la: Sed quæri potest cur Nicodemus ad Christum venerit noctu, ut ex eo disceret aliquid, & ab eo consolationem aliquam perciperet, Christus tamen minister aliquì gratiæ ac veritatis, tam duriter hominem statim primâ facie exceperit, comminatus eiectionem & exterminationem è regno Dei? Respondeo: Natura hæc prima hominum admodum fallax est, & imponit multis. Existimant miseri bene secum agi, si nascantur ex honestis, ex nobilibus parentibus, idque ad hæreditatem & bona huius vitæ satis ampla, ipsi cùm sint interea satis sano, pulchro & firmo corpore. Tum usque adeo arridet ipsis præsens vitæ conditio, ut nunquam velint ipsam commutare; falluntur etiam ac decipiuntur ab effectis naturæ, hoc est, corruptionis suæ, cuiusmodi sunt, nempe scortationes, idololatria, furtum, obrietas, & alia id genus, quæ opera carnis vocat & enumerat Paulus. Persuademus enim nobis hæc non
units.tr: But it may be asked why Nicodemus came to Christ by night, to learn something from him and to receive some comfort, while Christ, a minister of grace and truth, received the man so harshly at the very first meeting, threatening him with ejection and exclusion from the kingdom of God. I answer: this first nature of men is very deceptive, and it deceives many. Wretched men think they are doing well if they are born of honest and noble parents, with an ample inheritance and the goods of this life, and if they themselves are in the meantime healthy, handsome and strong in body. Moreover, the present condition of life so pleases them that they never want to change it. They are also misled and deceived by the effects of nature, that is, of its corruption, such as fornication, idolatry, theft, drunkenness and the like, which Paul calls and lists as the works of the flesh. For we persuade ourselves that these are not evils and do not deserve death, and others persuade us of the same thing.

units.la: {y} Gal.5.19. esse mala neque mereri mortem. Et alij nobis idé persuadent.Ideo Paulus cum denunciat aduersus huiusmodi carnis opera exclusionem è regno Dei,ait ad Corinthios, Ne errate,significans nimirum errorem & deceptionem esse fallacis naturæ. Et ad Ephesios,Nemo vos seducat. Cæcitas autem ista, error naturæ,iusto Dei iudicio contingit:Nam sicut visum est hominibus,Deum non cognoscere, teste Paulo,ita Deus rursus eos tradidit in mentem omnis iudicij expertem, & excæcauit adeo, vt ne ipsi quidem possint se videre,neque suum ipsorum cor valeant penitus intueri, cor, inquam,quod est sentina omnium malorum,& oppletur omni fœditate, malitia denique, in quo est sel illud amaritudinis: Cæcutiant etiam ad mortalitatem naturæ suæ, & fragilitatem rerum huius mundi,somnient vero sibi vitam mundumque perpetuum. Cùm igitur ea fit deceptio naturæ nostræ & ea cæcitas, qua putamus ista non esse mala,quæ sunt pessima,adblandimur autem nobis in istis: ideo Christus tantum mali esse admonet in hac natura nostra tam præclara,vt nobis videtur,. vt nisi gignamur denuò, nunquam futurum sit,vt videamus regnum Dei. Verùm nō prætereundum est tempus quo sic denunciauit Christus exclusionem è regno Dei. Tépus erat, quo Nicodemus de regeneratione ista nihil dū vel sensit vel suspicatus est,sed quo placuit sibi in natura illa perdita(etsi id nō negauerim ipse hoc tépore iactum fuisse in homine regenerationis aliquod seme, quo quidé accésum est de fideriū illud veniedi ad Christū,& ex eo discendi: nā istud naturæ vi fieri nō potuit) tamē hoc,quicquid erat,cōfusum erat,& exile admodū, nō adhuc cognito Christo Dei Filio: Ideóque Christus homine statim terret cōminatione exclusionis è regno cœlorū. Nā qui nondū cōuersi sunt ad inferos,iā primū detrudēdi sunt ad hoc,vt inspecta pœna peccati, discat ab eo abhorrere,quo tépore natura sese oblectat. Cōuersi vero iam abhorret à peccato, non tā propter pœnam, quàm propter ipsum peccatū,in quo tantū mali vident, vt si fingas nullos esse inferos, nullos esse cœlos,tamen peccatū propter se detestetur.
