Auget etiā odiū illud peccati & detestationē,gustus ille inchoatæ regenerationis & suauitas obedientiæ Dei, qua adeo delectantur, vt velint quidē semel totos se, si posset fieri per reliquias peccati, Deo cōsecrare, ipsiúsq; voluntati. Nihil autē grauius ferunt, quā se impediri in impleda illa obedientia. Inde est quòd sæpe suspirēt onerati cum Paulo, & cum eodē clament nonnunquam, Miser ego homo, quis me eripiet ex-ilo corpore mortis?
units.tr: {y} Gal. 5.19. Therefore Paul, when he declares against such works of the flesh that those who do them are excluded from the kingdom of God, says to the Corinthians, "Do not be deceived," clearly signifying that error and deception belong to deceitful nature. And to the Ephesians he says, "Let no one deceive you." This blindness, however, this error of nature, comes upon men by the just judgment of God. For, as Paul testifies, since men did not think fit to acknowledge God, God in turn gave them over to a mind destitute of all judgment, and blinded them so thoroughly that they cannot even see themselves, nor can they thoroughly discern their own heart: the heart, I say, which is the sink of all evils, and is filled with every foulness and malice, in which lies that gall of bitterness. They are also blind to the mortality of their nature and the frailty of the things of this world, and they dream of a life and world that last for ever. Since, then, nature is so deceived and so blind that we think those things are not evils which are most evil, and we flatter ourselves in them, Christ therefore warns that there is so much evil in this nature of ours, which seems so fine to us, that unless we are born again it will never be possible for us to see the kingdom of God. But we must not pass over the occasion on which Christ thus declared exclusion from the kingdom of God. It was a time when Nicodemus had as yet neither perceived nor suspected anything of this regeneration, but was pleased with that lost nature. (I would not deny that at this time some seed of regeneration had been sown in the man, from which the desire came to him to come to Christ and to learn from him; for this could not happen by the power of nature.) Nevertheless, whatever it was, it was confused and very slight, since Christ, the Son of God, was not yet known. Therefore Christ at once terrifies the man with the threat of exclusion from the kingdom of heaven. For those who have not yet been turned must first be thrust down to hell, so that, having looked upon the punishment of sin, they may learn to shrink from that which delights nature at this time. But those who have now been turned shrink from sin not so much because of its punishment as because of sin itself, in which they see so much evil that, even if you were to imagine that there were no hell and no heaven, they would still detest sin for its own sake. That hatred and detestation of sin is further increased by the taste of the regeneration begun in them and the sweetness of obedience to God, in which they delight so much that they would gladly consecrate themselves wholly, if it could be done despite the remnants of sin, to God and to his will. Yet they bear nothing more heavily than being hindered from fulfilling that obedience. Hence it is that they often groan, burdened, with Paul, and sometimes cry out with him, "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?"

units.la: Hactenus proposuit Christus regenerationis necessitatem summam: Nunc videamus quid respondeat Nicodemus. Nicodemus nō habens ludibrio grauem illā denuntiatione exclusionis è regno Dei, quod fecisset alij ex Pharisæis haud dubiō, sed potius perterritus illa ipsa denuntiatione, anxiē quærit de regeneratione illa, qua fieri posset, vt tantū malum semel effugiat. Vide quid sit venire ad Christū discēdi animo, & cum desiderio cognoscendi salutis via. Qui veniūt ad audiendū verbum, cum desiderio aliquo cognoscēdi via salutis suæ, illi dū videt primū (hic etenim primus est ad salutē gradus) illa viam cōminationibus iudiciorū sibi quodammodo præcludi, tū quidē deiiciūtur animo, & mortificatur in iis vetus homo, quod quidē necesse est fieri in tota hac vita. Tū deinde dū vident qui est secūdus ad salutē gradus) via illam suauibus promissionibus sibi aperiri, rursus eriguntur ac gaudent supra modū, videntúrque sibi non parū promouisse in suscepto curriculo. Qui verò nō animo & voluntate cognoscendi salutis suæ via, veniūt ad audiendū Dei verbū, sed vel carpēdi, vel fallendi tēpus, vel ideò vt videatur in numero Sanctorū esse, cùm tamen hypocritæ sint: illi quidē vt promissionibus gratiæ nihil afficiūtur, neq; gustant illā benignitatē Domini: ita cōminationes vel secure audiūt, vel irridēt, eóq; fit vt magis magísque indurētur. Cùm igitur videamus huiusmodi effecta in plerisque nostrorū hominū, quid hinc discere possumus nisi nullū esse in iis desideriū cognoscēdi salutis suæ, nullū esse veritatis amore? quē ego tantum facio, vt vel in ignaro aliquo ac idiota, ex quo genere Nicodemus, quo primum tempore ad Christum veniret, in ignaro, inquā, eum cōmendem, audeāmque illi homini quantumvis ignaro, cupido tamē discēdi & esuriēdi ac sitiēndi, polliceri illuminatione & suo tandē
units.tr: Thus far Christ has set forth the supreme necessity of regeneration. Now let us see what Nicodemus replies. Nicodemus, not treating that grave declaration of exclusion from the kingdom of God as a joke, as doubtless others of the Pharisees would have done, but rather terrified by that very declaration, anxiously asks about that regeneration by which it might be possible to escape so great an evil. See what it is to come to Christ with a mind to learn, and with a desire to know the way of salvation. Those who come to hear the word, with some desire to know the way of their salvation, when they first see (for this is the first step to salvation) that the way is in some measure closed to them by the threats of judgment, are then cast down in spirit, and the old man is mortified in them, which indeed must happen throughout this whole life. Then, when they see (which is the second step to salvation) that the way is opened to them by sweet promises, they are raised up again and rejoice beyond measure, and they seem to themselves to have advanced not a little in the course they have undertaken. But those who come to hear the word of God without a mind and will to know the way of their salvation, either to pass the time in idle chatter or to deceive, or so that they may seem to be among the number of the saints, although they are hypocrites, these are not moved at all by the promises of grace, and they do not taste that goodness of the Lord. So they hear the threats either carelessly or with mockery, and it comes about that they are hardened more and more. Since, then, we see such effects in most of our people, what can we learn from this except that there is in them no desire to know their salvation and no love of the truth? I hold this in such esteem that I commend Nicodemus, when he first came to Christ, as an ignorant man, even if he was ignorant, and I dare to promise to such a man, however ignorant, if only he has a desire to learn and a hunger and thirst, illumination and in due time the fulness of his salvation, if only he persists in his purpose. "Blessed," says Christ, "are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled."

units.la: Electorum Dei character.
units.tr: The mark of God's elect.

units.la: Reproborum nota. tepore saturitatem futurā, si modò perstiterit in propo-sito suo. Beati, inquit Christus, qui esuriunt ac sitiunt iusti-tiam, quoniam ipsi saturabuntur. Hæc hactenus.
units.tr: The mark of the reprobate. He will have future satiety, provided he perseveres in his purpose. Blessed, says Christ, are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. So much for that.

units.la: Nunc videamus in quem modum argumetetur Nicodemus: Homo qui sit senex non potest denuò gigni: At ego senex sum (sibi enim dicto illud à Christo accipit, & rectè: nam in illa applicatione cernitur vtilitas & consolatio scripturarum) Ergo non posse gigni denuò. Probat propositum ab absurdo: Non potest homo senex in vterum matris suæ secundò introire: Ergo non potest homo senex denuò gigni. Nicodemus ignorata regenerationis voce, concludit ipsius impossibilitatē, ex qua profectò deinde oportuit eū colligere apud animū suum impossibilitatem illam ingrediendi in regnū cœlorum, ac proinde serio & ex animo dolere. Qui cogitat durū esse illud regenerari & abnegare semetipsos suaque omnia; cogitet etiam velim durum esse ac arduum imprimis ingredi in regnum cœlorum, neque vnquam ingressuros se in illud regnū, nisi prius consiliū coepe-rint abnegādi se, & captū iam strenuè persequatur. Sed non est silentio praetereunda hoc loco miseranda cæcitas, nō tantum vulgi Iudæorū, sed aduentu Christi cæcitas, nō tantum vulgi Iudæorū, etiam Pharisæorū qui professi sunt se Magistros populi: tamen illi ipsi regenerationē ignorârunt. Oportuit igitur pariter ignorare naturā hāc corruptā, imò verò putârūt inclinationes istas ad malū, & motus interiores nō esse trāsgressiones Legis diuinæ. Quod eò magis mirādū est, quòd tametsi nō diserte hanc ipsam vocē regenerationis habuerūt in Lege & Prophetis, tamen de renouatione nostri & refipiscētia, quæ re eadē est cū regeneratione, passim legerūt. Quę igitur causa fuit tā crassæ ignorātiæ? nēpe illa, non contenti solo Dei verbo finxerūt sibiipsi nouā hęresin, cęremonias & traditiones suas adinuenerunt. Quo factū est, vt iusto Dei iudicio in iis rebus, quę ad salutē necessaria sunt cognoscendis, prorsus cęcutiuerint. Nā cūm nolūt homines ex solo Dei verbo sapere, Deus iusto suo iudicio plane stupidos reddit, in necessariis capitibus ac principiis religionis. Quem stuporem cernimus hodie in hæresi Papistarum, qui iusto Dei iudicio ita excæcati sunt, vt ignorent omnia illa in vniuersum doctrinæ capita, quæ de officio Christi sunt.
units.tr: Now let us see how Nicodemus argues. A man who is old cannot be born again. But I am old. (He takes this from what Christ said to him, and rightly so, for in this application the usefulness and comfort of Scripture appear.) Therefore I cannot be born again. He proves his point from the absurd: an old man cannot enter a second time into his mother's womb; therefore an old man cannot be born again. Not understanding the word regeneration, Nicodemus concludes that it is impossible. From this he ought then to have inferred in his own mind that impossibility of entering the kingdom of heaven, and so to have grieved seriously and from the heart. Let the one who thinks it hard to be regenerated and to deny himself and all that he has also think, I would have him consider, that it is hard and difficult above all to enter the kingdom of heaven, and that men will never enter that kingdom unless they first begin to deny themselves, and then pursue this resolve vigorously. But here we must not pass over in silence the pitiable blindness, not only of the common Jews but also of the Pharisees, who professed to be the teachers of the people: yet they themselves were ignorant of regeneration. It followed that they were equally ignorant of this corrupt nature; indeed they thought that those inclinations to evil and those inward motions were not transgressions of the divine Law. This is all the more surprising because, although they did not expressly have this very word regeneration in the Law and the Prophets, they nevertheless read everywhere about the renewal of ourselves and repentance, which is the same thing as regeneration. What then was the cause of so gross an ignorance? Namely this: not content with the word of God alone, they invented for themselves a new heresy and devised their own ceremonies and traditions. The result was that, by the just judgment of God, they were utterly blinded in those matters which are necessary to be known for salvation. For when men are unwilling to be wise from the word of God alone, God, in his just judgment, makes them plainly stupid in the necessary articles and principles of religion. We see this same stupor today in the heresy of the Papists, who, by the just judgment of God, have been so blinded that they are ignorant of all those general heads of doctrine which concern the office of Christ.

units.la: Nouorum Pharisæorum cæcus stupor.
units.tr: The blind stupidity of the new Pharisees.

units.la: Regeneratio quid sit nō videt, aut certè videre nolūt. Iustificationem à Christo transferunt ad homines. Quid multis? in illa hæresi omnium hæreseon, quæ vnquā fuerunt exitiali maximè, nihil est sani, vt homines eorum tristissimo & horribilissimo exemplo admoniti, discant quid sit sapere ex solo Dei verbo.
units.tr: They either do not see what regeneration is, or certainly they are unwilling to see it. They transfer justification from Christ to men. What more need be said? In that heresy of heresies, the most deadly of all that have ever existed, there is nothing sound, so that men, warned by their most sad and horrible example, may learn what it is to be wise from God's Word alone.

units.la: Respōdit Iesus. Christus nihil moratus impossibilitatē ista à Nicodemo cōclusam, constanter asseuerat ac repetit priorem illā denūtiatione parua tantum mutatione facta, addito nimirū ad superiorē sententiā regenerationis modo, idq; in gratiā Nicodemi, quem animaduertit cupidū cognoscendę veritatis, nominatim autē capitis huius de regeneratione. Impossibilitates & impedimenta omnia quæ iniiciūt sibi homines sefèq; remorantur ne cognoscat & faciat quod Deus verbo suo præcipit, non mutabūt Dei sententiā. Dominus hoc semel pronūtiauit. Amē, Amē dico tibi, nisi quis genitus fuerit denuò nō potest videre regnū Dei. Tu iam, si lubet, qui places tibi in natura ista, hoc est, volutas te tanquā sus in volutabro cœni, obiice quæcūq; visum est impedimēta regenerationis, quibus tete detineas in illa fœditate naturæ, quominus exuas veterē illū hominē & nouū induas, hoc iterū atq; iterū audies à Domino, Amē, Amē dico tibi, &c. & nisi animū mutaueris tēpestiuē, reipsa experieris te ex cœlo exclusū & ad inferos detrusū, ex quibus nulla est redēptio.
units.tr: Jesus answered. Christ, unmoved by the impossibility that Nicodemus had raised, firmly asserts and repeats the earlier declaration, with only a slight change: he adds to his former statement the mode of regeneration. He does this for Nicodemus's sake, whom he saw to be eager to know the truth, and especially for the sake of this chapter's teaching on regeneration. All the impossibilities and obstacles that men throw in their own way, and by which they hinder themselves from knowing and doing what God commands in his Word, will not change God's decree. The Lord has pronounced this once for all: Truly, truly I say to you, unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. Now you, if you please, who take pleasure in that nature, that is, who wallow like a pig in the mire of filth, raise whatever hindrances to regeneration you like, by which you keep yourself bound to that foulness of nature, so that you do not put off the old man and put on the new. Again and again you will hear from the Lord, Truly, truly I say to you, etc. And unless you change your mind in good time, you will find in fact that you are shut out of heaven and thrust down to hell, from which there is no redemption.

units.la: Sed videamus modū hūc regenerationis quē maioris explicationis gratia adiecit Dominus. Nisi, inquit, quis genitus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu. Sēsus est, nisi quis regenitus fuerit per Spiritū sanctū, cuius sigillū est Baptismi aqua; nō potest introire in regnū Dei. Quod vt melius intelligam, sciēdū est tria esse in Baptismo, quos totidē testes Christi terrestres vocat Iohānes, Spiritus, aqua & sāguis. Spiritus est Spiritus regenerationis, qui cū alioqui idē sit testis cœlestis, tamen quia habitat perpetuò in nobis, quos semel regenerauit, in testibus quoq; terrestribus numeratur. Hic efficaci regeneratione sua testatur de Christo, cuius & Spiritus, eū nepe filiū Dei esse. Nō enim potest effici illud opus regenerationis multò maximū nisi à Spiritu Dei omnipotētis. Sanguis sequitur, q est effusus ille Christi sanguis in cruce ad remissionē peccatorū & iustificationē nostri. Sanguis quoque ipso opere iustificationis & efficacia illa sua, quam fide percipimus, testatur Christu cuius est sanguis, esse filiu Dei. Necesse enim est sit sanguis Dei ad hoc vt sit efficax ad remissionē peccatoꝝ. Vocatur Christi sanguis ipsius Dei sanguis proprius. Postremo loco sequitur Aqua, quæ, vt mihi videtur, nihil aliud est, quàm aqua illa Baptismi, quæ dum repræsentat pariter & obsignat nobis Spiritū regenerationis & sanguinem iustificantem, testatur quoque vt sigillum & instrumentum quoddam Christum esse filium Dei. Vnde Baptista ait, vt manifestus fieret Israëli Christus, venire se baptizantem aqua. Quamobrem hæc tria testantur in Sacramento Baptismi Christum filium Dei esse. Hoc loco duorum tantum ex his tribus meminit Iohannes, nēpe aquæ & Spiritus, nihil de sanguine locutus est, quia etiā aqua illa Baptismi significatur & obsignatur; nēpe quia hic de regeneratione disputatur, quæ perficitur Spiritus Sancti operatione, cuius symbolum est aqua. Atque hæc est sententia huius loci, quam eò lubentiùs sequor, quòd videam Paulum eadem ista duo coniungere in regenerationis negotio. Ex sua, inquit, misericordia seruabit nos per lauacrum regenerationis, & renouationem Spiritus Sancti, quem effudit copiosè in nos, per Iesum Christum Seruatorem nostrum.
units.tr: But let us look at this mode of regeneration, which the Lord added for the sake of greater explanation. Unless, he says, someone is born of water and the Spirit. The sense is: unless someone is regenerated through the Holy Spirit, whose seal is the water of Baptism, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. To understand this better, we must know that there are three things in Baptism, which John calls three earthly witnesses of Christ: the Spirit, the water, and the blood. The Spirit is the Spirit of regeneration, and although he is otherwise the same heavenly witness, yet because he dwells perpetually in us whom he has once regenerated, he is also counted among the earthly witnesses. Here, by his effective regeneration, he testifies of Christ, whose Spirit he is, that he is the Son of God. For that work of regeneration, by far the greatest, cannot be effected except by the Spirit of almighty God. Blood follows, that is, the blood of Christ poured out on the cross for the remission of sins and for our justification. The blood also, by the very work of justification and by that efficacy which we receive through faith, testifies that Christ, whose blood it is, is the Son of God. For it must be God's own blood if it is to be efficacious for the remission of sins. Christ's blood is called the proper blood of God himself. In the last place comes the water, which, as it seems to me, is nothing other than that water of Baptism which, while it represents and at the same time seals to us the Spirit of regeneration and the justifying blood, also testifies, as a sign and instrument of a kind, that Christ is the Son of God. Hence the Baptist says that Christ came baptizing with water so that he might be made manifest to Israel. Therefore these three testify in the Sacrament of Baptism that Christ is the Son of God. Here John mentions only two of these three, namely the water and the Spirit, and says nothing about the blood, because that water of Baptism is also signified and sealed; and especially because here the subject is regeneration, which is effected by the operation of the Holy Spirit, whose symbol is water. This is the meaning of this passage, which I follow all the more gladly because I see that Paul joins these same two in the business of regeneration. According to his mercy, he says, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out abundantly upon us through Jesus Christ our Saviour.

units.la: Nihil hic moror Papistarum sophisma, qui colligunt ex hoc loco externi Baptismi absolutam necessitatem. Necessitas enim quam innuit Christus, non est ascribenda signo, sed rei significatæ: hoc est Spiritui, etsi hic cum Spiritu coiuncta sit aqua, quæ est Spiritus signum. Nam versu sequēti cum de regeneratione loquitur, aquæ non meminit, sed Spiritui duntaxat necessitatem hanc tribuendam significat. Et Marci vltimo, postquam dictum est, Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, seruabitur, subiectum est, Qui non crediderit, non seruabitur. Non est hic prætereundum quàm patienter ferat Dominus Nicodemi tarditatem, & indulgeat etiam obiicienti regenerationis impossibilitatem ac sententiam ab ipso prolatam oppugnanti quodammodò: hac enim tarditate & contradictione moueri potuit, ne aliquid ipsi gratificaretur. Sed vidit Christus in homine alioqui hebeti & cæco, amorem
units.tr: I do not here dwell on the sophism of the Papists, who gather from this passage the absolute necessity of external Baptism. For the necessity that Christ indicates is not to be ascribed to the sign but to the thing signified, that is, to the Spirit, although here the water, which is the sign of the Spirit, is joined with the Spirit. For in the following verse, when he speaks of regeneration, he makes no mention of water, but signifies that this necessity is to be attributed to the Spirit alone. And at the end of Mark, after it is said, He who believes and is baptized will be saved, it is added, He who does not believe will not be saved. Here we must not pass over how patiently the Lord bears the slowness of Nicodemus, and how he indulges him even when he objects that regeneration is impossible and in a way opposes the teaching that Christ himself has put forward. For Christ might have been moved by this slowness and contradiction to refuse him some favour. But Christ saw in a man otherwise dull and blind a love

units.la: Ioan. 3. rem quendam veritatis atque lucis, qui profecto efficiet, idque necessario, ut quis tandem illuminetur. Fieri enim non potest, ut qui accendit in corde hanc situm & hunc amorem, frustretur nos. Contrà vero qui non recipit amore veritatis, ut loquar cum Paulo, sed amat medacia, Deus iusto suo iudicio mittit ei efficaciam deceptionis eam, qua vel futilissimo mendacio credat. Inde est quod tam cito inducatur mudus illusionibus & praestigiis illis Papistarum, quae illi miracula falso nominat, ad credendum vanitati vanissimae & hominum figmentis putidissimis, denique somniis otiosorum Monachorum.
units.tr: (John 3.) of a certain truth and light, which will surely bring it about, and necessarily so, that a man is at last enlightened. For it is impossible that he who kindles in his heart this longing and this love should be deceived by us. On the contrary, he who does not receive the love of truth, to speak with Paul, but loves lies, God in his just judgment sends him the efficacy of deception, so that he believes the most trifling falsehood. Hence it is that the world is so quickly led into those illusions and tricks of the Papists, which they falsely call miracles, to believe the most empty vanity and the most putrid inventions of men, and finally the dreams of idle Monks.

units.la: 6 Quod genitum est ex carne, caro est: Et quod genitum est ex Spiritu, spiritus est.
units.tr: 6 That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.

units.la: 7 Ne mireris me dixisse tibi, Oportet vos iterum nasci.
units.tr: 7 Do not marvel that I said to you, You must be born again.

units.la: 8 Ventus quo vult spirat, & sonum eius audis, sed nescis unde veniat, & quo vadat: ita est quisquis genitus est e Spiritu.
units.tr: 8 The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes: so is everyone who is born of the Spirit.

units.la: PERSISTIT in doctrina regenerationis: Quemadmodum enim superiori versu ea explicavit a modo suo, perfici- citur scilicet non naturali modo, sed spirituali per Spiritum sanctum cuius symbolum est aqua Baptismi: Ita nunc eam explicat ab officio suo, nempe homine spirituali. Quod genitum, est, inquit, ex Spiritu, spiritus est: hoc est, homo spiritualis, quem vocamus regenitum. Non autem simpliciter istud proponit, sed quo pulchrior & excellentior appareat Spiritus sancti iste foetus, comparat eum cum impuro illo foetu carnis. Quod genitum est ex carne, caro est. Quo autem ista cuadant apertiora, videndum nobis est quid sit caro & quae eius generatio. Item quid Spiritus & quae eius generatio. Explicaturi carne, eius initium sic altius repetimus. Peccatum duplex est, Originale, quod ex utero matris: Actuale, quod in actionibus vitae positum est & ab originali profectum. Originale rursus duplex est. Primum est apostasia illa & defectio, quae non tam solius Adami quam totius humani generis, in lumbis ipsius. Ut enim Levi decimatus est in Abrahamo, hoc est in lumbis adhuc Abrahami patris sui: ita nos omnes,inquit Apostolus,in Adamo peccauimus. Hanc defectionem sequitur reatus quo obligamur omnes ad æternã damnationem,adeò vt si fingas non extare aliud in mundo peccatum, quàm hanc primam ᾱμαϱτίαν, vel ob eam solam periremus omnes. Altera pars Originalis peccati est totius humanę naturę corruptio,& quasi ruina horribilis insecuta primam illam apostasia, iustoiudicio Dei peccatum per peccatum punientis;quæ ficinuasit &occupauit totũ hominem quantus quantus est,vt à vertice ad plantam pedis nihil vel in corpore vel in anima sani sit. Hanc corruptionē sequitur etiam suus reatus &obligatio ad mortem æternã,vt videas quàm variis modis rei simus mortis & damnationis æterně. Reatum hunc Paulus ostendit,dicens,Omnes natura erāmus filij irę.
units.tr: He persists in the doctrine of regeneration. For just as in the previous verse he explained it from its mode, namely that it is effected not in a natural way but in a spiritual way, through the Holy Spirit, whose symbol is the water of Baptism, so now he explains it from its effect, namely the spiritual man. That which is born of the Spirit, he says, is spirit: that is, the spiritual man, whom we call regenerate. He does not put this forward simply, however; in order that this offspring of the Holy Spirit may appear more beautiful and excellent, he compares it with that impure offspring of the flesh. That which is born of the flesh is flesh. But so that these matters may be clearer, we must see what the flesh is and what its generation is, and likewise what the Spirit is and what its generation is. To explain the flesh, we go back to its beginning from further up. Sin is twofold: original, which comes from the mother's womb, and actual, which lies in the actions of life and proceeds from the original. Original sin is again twofold. The first part is that apostasy and defection, which belongs not to Adam alone but to the whole human race, which was in his loins. For just as Levi was tithed in Abraham, that is, while Abraham his father was still in the loins, so we all, says the Apostle, sinned in Adam. This defection is followed by the guilt by which we are all bound to eternal damnation, so that even if you imagine there were no other sin in the world than this first ἁμαρτία, we would all perish for that alone. The other part of original sin is the corruption of the whole of human nature, and a kind of horrible ruin that followed that first apostasy, God in his just judgment punishing sin by sin; this has invaded and taken possession of the whole man, however great he is, so that from the crown of the head to the sole of the foot there is nothing sound, either in body or in soul. This corruption is also followed by its own guilt and obligation to eternal death, so that you may see in how many ways we are liable to death and eternal damnation. Paul shows this guilt, saying, We were all by nature children of wrath.

units.la: Atque hæc est illa corruptio, quam Dominus noster vocat carnis nomine hoc loco. Carne enim non intelligimus malsam hanc carneā & corporeā, quam circumferimus nobiscum omnes,neq; vim nescio quam cocupiscibilem in carne,vt loquuntur Papistæ,protsus ignari communis huius nostrę miseriæ:sed carnem intelligimus totius naturę,corporis pariter atq; animę,adeoq; omnium facultatum & virium animæ corruptione, quà ipse Creator post horribile illam defectionem nobis expressit,dicens, figmentū cordis malum esse ab adolescentia ipsius. Quibus verbis significat eum iā inde ab adolescentia nihil posse cogitare,vel cum animo suo fingere nisi quod malū est: ac proinde prorsus totum infectū & corruptū esse.Propter hanc pestem scriptum est, poenituisse Iehouā quòd fecisset hominem in terra , & dolore affectum fuisse cum animo suo. Oportuit subesse ingens malum quod Creatori hac quasi poenitentia extorsit. Sed vt magnitudo eius semel ponatur in conspectu nostro, videamus quàm latè pateat hoc malũ,& quomodo(vt de corpore nihil nunc dicamus, cuius substantia etiam totam sic inuasit, vt cùm corpus hoc oportuerit esse immortale, iam caducum & mortale factum sit) quomodo, inquam, peruaserit totam animam eiusque omnes facultates ac vires,quia ibi ea maximè sentimus omnes.Non igitur tantùm infecit appetitum inferiorem , sed ipsam arcem animæ humanæ,rationem dico ipsam, ita inuasit & oc-
units.tr: And this is that corruption which our Lord here calls "flesh"; for by flesh in this place we do not understand this frail bodily substance that we all carry about with us, nor some concupiscible power in the flesh, as the Papists put it, utterly ignorant of the common misery of our condition. Rather, we understand by flesh the corruption of the whole of nature, of body and soul alike, and of all the faculties and powers of the soul, which the Creator himself expressed to us after that dreadful defection, saying that the imagination of the heart is evil from its youth. By these words he signifies that from youth onward man can think or devise nothing except what is evil, and therefore that he is wholly infected and corrupted. Because of this plague it is written that the LORD repented that he had made man on the earth, and was grieved in his heart. There must have been a great evil which wrung this, as it were, repentance from the Creator. But so that its greatness may be set once before our eyes, let us see how widely this evil extends, and how (to say nothing for now of the body, whose very substance it has so invaded that, although this body ought to have been immortal, has now become frail and mortal) how, I say, it has penetrated the whole soul and all its faculties and powers, since there we feel them all most keenly. It has not therefore merely infected the lower appetite, but has seized the very citadel of the human soul, I mean reason itself, and has so invaded and occu-

units.la: Genes. 6.6. Peccati originalis magnitudo. & occupauit, vt cùm oportuerit mentem & rationè humanâ ex præscripto verbi diuini præesse omnibus functionibus & motibus tam animi quàm corporis, mens nostra ex diametro pugnet cum mente Dei: id quod intelligit Paulus, cùm dicit, φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς ἐστὶ ἔχθρα εἰς θεόν, hoc est, quod sapientissimum est in homine non regenito, inimicitia est aduersus Deum. Ideoque alibi requirit vt iam primùm renouentur Spiritu mentis suæ: Ergo mens ipsa est corrupta, & lux illa mentis conuersa est in tenebras pugnantes cum mente & sapientia Dei in lege expressa, sed multò magis cum sapientia Euangelij, ad quam percipiendam adeo inepta est, vt etiam ei sit mera stultitia.
units.tr: Gen. 6.6. The magnitude of original sin. pied it, that whereas the mind and human reason ought, according to the prescription of the divine Word, to govern all the functions and movements of both soul and body, our mind now fights head-on against the mind of God. This is what Paul means when he says that "the mind of the flesh is enmity against God" [φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς ἐστὶ ἔχθρα εἰς θεόν]; that is, what is wisest in an unregenerate man is enmity against God. Hence elsewhere he requires that men be renewed first of all in the spirit of their mind. Therefore the mind itself is corrupted, and that light of the mind has been turned into darkness, fighting against the mind and wisdom of God expressed in the law, but much more against the wisdom of the Gospel, which man is so unfit to perceive that to him it is sheer foolishness.

units.la: Vt veniam nunc ad cor ipsum, hoc est, voluntatem & affectiones quæ habent sedem in corde, corruptio hæc ita infecit voluntatem, vt cùm oportuerit eam eligere quod bonum est & repudiare quod malum est, idque ex arbitrio & iudicio rationis præeunte, iam nō solùm aduersetur menti & voluntati ipsius Dei sanctissimæ, verumetiam pugnet cum mente ipsa humana, & iis notitiis quæ misericordia Dei in mente post lapsum hominis reseruatæ sunt & reliquæ de Deo, de rebus iustis & honestis, de rebus etiam naturalibus; pugnet, inquam, adeò vt etiam animalis homo clamet, Video meliora probóque, deteriora sequor. Quid multis? quemadmodum voluntas diaboli aduersatur voluntati Dei: ita hominis voluntas pugnat cum voluntate Dei. Nam naturâ idem volumus quod diabolus vult, & voluntatum summa est conspiratio: Vos ex patre diabolo estis & cupiditates patris vestri vultis explere, inquit Christus. Vt præterea de affectionibus dicam, quæ, quæso, omnium libera est ab hac contagione? Nónne ira, concupiscentia, φθόνος, omnes denique aliæ aduersantur Deo; adeo ut nulla sit conformitas cum lege Dei, sed summa in omnibus deformitas & ἀσχημοσύνη? Denique vt naturales quoque facultates negligere videar, affirmo nullam esse omnium non infectam ab hac lue, appetitum omnem naturalem, vim omnem cococtricem, expultricem, assimilatricē, & cæteras quas numerant physici: affirmo, inquam, omnes etiam istas corruptas esse. Vides igitur effectus.
units.tr: Now to come to the heart itself, that is, the will and the affections which have their seat in the heart: this corruption has so infected the will that, whereas it ought to choose what is good and reject what is evil, and do so by the judgment and guidance of reason going before, it now not only opposes the mind and will of God himself, most holy as it is, but even fights against the human mind itself, and against those notions which, by the mercy of God, were preserved in the mind after the fall, concerning God, concerning just and honourable things, and even concerning natural things. It fights, I say, so that even the natural man cries out: "I see the better things and approve them, but I follow the worse." In a word, just as the will of the devil opposes the will of God, so man's will fights against the will of God. For by nature we want the same thing that the devil wants, and the sum of our wills is agreement with his: "You are of your father the devil, and you will fulfil the desires of your father," says Christ. Moreover, to speak of the affections, who, I ask, is free of this contagion? Do not anger, lust, envy, and in short all the others, oppose God, so that there is no conformity with the law of God, but the utmost deformity and indecency in all of them? Finally, lest I seem to neglect the natural faculties too, I affirm that there is none of them not infected by this plague: every natural appetite, every power of attraction, of expulsion, of assimilation, and the others which the physicians enumerate. I affirm, I say, that all of these too are corrupted. So you see the effects.

units.la: Corruptio peccati originalis. quomodo grassata sit hæc pestis totū homine, præsertim autē hominis animam, quam ita tota occupauit, vt primū nihil ab homine proficisci possit, siue cogitatio sit interna, siue motus & actio corporis externa, quod non sit peccatum: deinde nullum sit peccatum tam abominandum, quod ipse non libēter perpetret, nisi cohibeatur Dei Spiritu, vel regenerante, vel certè refrænante & terrorem iniiciente: nam radix omnium scelerum etiam maximorum, est in vnoquoque nostrum, Noui, inquit Apostolus, non habitare in me (id est in carne mea) bonum. Et Esaias, Nisi Iehoua exercituum reliquos fecisset nobis superstites vt cumque paucos, vt Sedom essemus, Gomorrhæ similes essemus. Et Ieremias, Summæ benignitatis est Iehouæ, quòd non sumus absumpti, quòd nō finiuntur miserationes nostræ. Et sanè nemo est nostrum omnium, qui sibi permittatur naturæ suæ, non dedat se præcipitem in omnem fœditatem.
units.tr: Corruption of original sin: how this plague has spread through the whole man, and especially through the soul of man, which it has so entirely occupied that, first, nothing can proceed from man that is not sin, whether it be inward thought or outward motion and action of the body; and then, there is no sin so abominable that he would not willingly commit it, unless he is restrained by the Spirit of God, either regenerating him or at least curbing him and striking terror into him. For the root of all wickedness, even the greatest, is in each of us. "I know," says the Apostle, "that in me (that is, in my flesh) dwells no good thing." And Isaiah: "Unless the LORD of hosts had left us a remnant, however small, we would have been like Sodom, and like Gomorrah." And Jeremiah: "It is of the great kindness of the LORD that we are not consumed, because his compassions do not fail." And indeed there is none of us who, if he is left to his own nature, does not hurl himself headlong into every foulness.

units.la: Atque hæc de illa pestē naturæ nostræ, quæ ideo nobis magis metuenda est, quòd mirifica sit eius deceptio, non tantùm quando non erumpit foras, verumetiam cùm erumpit. Nam antequam erūpat, facilè nobis imponit, dum putamus bene agi nobiscum, cùm non sentimus impuros & prauos istos cordis motus, & videmur nobis ipsi sani esse; iacet enim ad tempus peccatū quasi mortuum. At cùm admonetur illi lex Dei, vel alia quæuis occasio offertur, tum fremere & furere incipit, ac tum, vt loquar cum Apostolo, vigere incipiunt in membris nostris ad fructum ferendum morti. Eo tempore beatus est quisquis habet partem aliquam Spiritus Dei, quæ luctetur cum illis affectionibus. Nam in natura nihil est quod iis resistat: rerum vbi efferbuit peccatum, necesse est toti cum corrapiantur in interitum: Et hoc est regnum illud quod vocant peccati in nobis. Sed multò maiori cum periculo coniuncta est illa deceptio natiuæ pestis huius, postquam iam erupit foras. Nam etiam adulteri furentes in adulterio & libidine, homicidæ sæuientes in homicidio, furesgrassantes in furto suo & rapina, nullum tamen interea conscientiæ stimulum sentire solent, ideoque miserrime decipiuntur. Ostendam tem similitudine: Est quis
units.tr: So much for that plague of our nature, which is all the more to be feared because its deception is wonderful, not only when it does not break out, but also when it does. For before it breaks out, it easily deceives us, while we think that all is well with us, since we do not feel those impure and perverse motions of the heart, and we seem to ourselves to be sound. For sin lies for a time as if dead. But when the law of God is brought to bear on it, or any other occasion is offered, then it begins to rage and fume, and then, to speak with the Apostle, the sinful passions which are aroused by the law begin to be active in our members, bearing fruit for death. At that time he is blessed who has some part of the Spirit of God that wrestles with those affections. For in nature there is nothing that resists them; when sin has once boiled up, it must necessarily sweep the whole man away to destruction. And this is that kingdom which they call sin's reign in us. But that deception of this innate plague is attended by much greater danger once it has broken out. For adulterers raging in adultery and lust, murderers raging in murder, thieves running riot in their theft and robbery, are wont meanwhile to feel no goad of conscience, and so are most wretchedly deceived. I shall show this by a comparison. Suppose someone

units.la: Rom. 7. 18. Esai. 1. 9. Threni 3. 9.

quis qui habeat in digito suo vermem, hic ad tempus quiescit neque arrodit carnem, tum miser putat digitū satis esse sanum: ar admoto aceto vel re aliqua acri & & pungenti, si excitetur vermis,& arrodere incipiat,tū miser queritur se deceptum fuisse: ita est hic,nam conscientia est quasi vermis quidam, delitescens in animo humano, ea ad tempus non commouet se, & adeo sopita iacet vt sine dolore & stimulo aliquo perpetrent hominesetiam scelera maxime nefanda,& quod miserabilius est, etiam tum quiescit saepe sine vllo motu ac stimulo, etiam tum, inquam, dum admouetur homini lex Dei, dum iudicia ex lege denunciantur, quae cum audiant multi, apud se tamen loquuntur, nihil se illis comminationibus omnibus moueri: cum tamen hi ipsi sint vel adulteri, vel homicidae, vel raptores, vel sacrilegi, &c. Imo ludibrio habent comminationes omnes ex lege Dei. At veniet dies quo efficax futura est lex Dei in miseris illis conscientiis (Illud enim certissimum est oportere semel efficacem esse legem Dei in conscientiis hominum quorumcunque excitandis: Nemine enim excipio,idque vel citius vel serius. Quod si nō in hac vita, certe in futura, & in illo die praesertim, quo iustus iudex producta in medium eadem hac lege iudicabit mundum) veniet,inquam,dies, quo excitabuntur dolores conscientiae a lege Dei, quos tam impossibile erit vincere, quam Deum ipsum. Nam lex Dei est potentia Dei ad dolores conscientiae & damnationem, non secus atque euangelium credentibus est potentia Dei ad laetitiam conscientiae & vitam aeternam. Quare patiantur homines, si sapiant, legem Dei in conscientiis suis efficacem esse dum locus est gratiae, dumque, Euangelium in propinquo est tanquam praesens remedium, quo vulneratae per legē conscientiae rursus sanentur. Quod si semel gratiae tempus praeterierit;tum necesse est dolores illos & cruciatus conscientiae perpetuos esse & vermem eorum non intermori. Hactenus de corruptione ista naturali & carne diximus, nunc dicendum est de generatione naturali. Quid, quaeso, potest gigni a carne, nisi caro? Quis edat mundū ex mundo? Ne vnus quidem nam parentes dum comunicant cum liberis suis naturam & essentiam suam, communicant simul naturæ qualitatem, & pestem hanc exitialé penitus naturæ insitam. Gloriari solent homines de iis quæ à parentibus acceperunt, vt de nobilitate generis, honoribus, diuitiis, regnis, imperiis, & id genus aliis: Sed intelligentisti vnà cum his omnibus impertiri ipsis parentes naturam veneno quasi infectam, & pestem mortiferá, quæ profecto nisi corrigatur, necesse est cum omnibus his pereat in æternum. Quamobrē mihi videntur ij parétum optimè consulere liberis suis, qui conscientiā infectæ à se naturæ liberorum, in id incumbunt præcipuè, vt corrigatur natura illa depravata & corrupta. Quod nisi faciant, persuadeant sibi fore vt imputetur ipsis non solū vitium naturæ suæ ipsorum, sed etiam vitiū illud quod inspuerunt & transmiserunt in naturam liberorum.
units.tr: has a worm in his finger. For a time it lies quiet and does not gnaw the flesh, and the wretched man thinks his finger is sound enough. But when vinegar or some other sharp and stinging thing is applied, and the worm is stirred and begins to gnaw, then the wretch complains that he has been deceived. So it is here. For conscience is like a certain worm, lurking in the human mind; for a time it does not stir, and lies so lulled that men commit even the most abominable crimes without any pain or goad. And what is more pitiable, it often lies quiet without any movement or sting even when the law of God is brought to man, when judgments are declared from the law, and many who hear them nevertheless say among themselves that they are not moved at all by all these threats, though they themselves are adulterers, murderers, robbers or sacrilegious persons, and so on. Indeed they make a mockery of all the threats of the law of God. But the day will come when the law of God will be effective in those wretched consciences. (For this is most certain: that the law of God must at some time be effective in stirring the consciences of all men without exception, and that sooner or later. If not in this life, then certainly in the next, and especially on that day when the just Judge will bring this same law into the open and judge the world.) That day, I say, will come, when the pangs of conscience will be roused by the law of God, pangs as impossible to overcome as God himself. For the law of God is the power of God unto anguish of conscience and condemnation, just as the Gospel is the power of God unto joy of conscience and eternal life for those who believe. Therefore let men, if they are wise, suffer the law of God to be effective in their consciences while there is still room for grace, while the Gospel is near at hand as a present remedy by which consciences wounded by the law may be healed again. But if once the time of grace has passed, then those pangs and torments of conscience must necessarily be everlasting, and their worm will not die. So far we have spoken of this natural corruption and of the flesh; now we must speak of natural generation. What, I ask, can be begotten of the flesh except flesh? Who can bring forth a clean thing out of an unclean? Not even one man: for parents, in communicating their nature and essence to their children, at the same time communicate the quality of that nature, and this deadly plague, which is utterly implanted in nature. Men are wont to boast of what they have received from their parents, such as nobility of birth, honours, riches, kingdoms, empires, and other things of that kind. But understand that along with all these things parents impart to their children a nature as if infected with poison, and a deadly plague, which, unless it is corrected, must certainly perish with all these things for ever. Wherefore those parents seem to me to consult best for their children who, aware that they have passed on to them a nature infected by themselves, devote themselves above all to ensuring that this depraved and corrupt nature is corrected. But if they do not do this, let them be persuaded that it will be imputed to them not only as the fault of their own nature, but also as that fault which they breathed into and transmitted into the nature of their children.

units.la: Hactenus de carne eiúsque generatione, sequitur deinde vt dicamus de Spiritu, eiúsque generatione. Spiritum intelligo Christi Spiritū, qui idem regenerationis est Spiritus. Nam Christus nō tantū promeritus est nobis omnem gratiā, verūm etiā efficax est nobis per Spiritū suū ad regenerationem. Vt igitur de eo dicamus vniuersi hil: Christus quemadmodū frater noster primogenitus est: ita pater est: Pater æternitatis vocatur, & secūdus Adamus dicitur. Hoc posito comparatione instituamus. Naturalis noster parens reus est non tantùm primæuæ illius defectionis, sed aliarum quoque infinitarum. Spiritualis parens Christus nullus defectionis reus peragi potest: quinimò omnis obedientiæ plenus est: factus est obediens patri vsque ad mortē, mortem autem crucis. Naturalis parens natura tota corruptus est: Spiritualis vero Christus non modò perfectè sanctus est etiam qua homo est, sed est ipsa quoque sanctitas, vtpote Deus ab æterno. Naturalis parens producit vi naturæ fœtum suum: Spiritualis multò magis vi Spiritus sancti qui naturæ author est, potens est gignere. Naturalis parens, cùm sit caro, gignit carnem, hoc est corruptam quandā massam: Spiritualis parēs Spiritu suo gignit spiritū, hoc est spiritualem hominē. Quisquis natus est ex Deo, peccatum non committit, hoc est ita vt regnet in eo peccatū. Ratio additur, quoniā semen ipsius in eo manet.
units.tr: Hitherto I have spoken of the flesh and its generation. Next we must speak of the Spirit and His generation. By the Spirit I mean the Spirit of Christ, who is also the Spirit of regeneration. For Christ has not only merited all grace for us, but He is also effective for us, through His Spirit, unto regeneration. To say something general about Him: Christ is our firstborn brother, and He is also our father. He is called the Father of eternity and is called the second Adam. Given this, let us draw a comparison. Our natural parent is guilty not only of that first defection but of countless others. Christ, our spiritual parent, cannot be charged with any defection; on the contrary, He is full of all obedience. He became obedient to the Father even unto death, and the death of the cross. Our natural parent is wholly corrupted by nature; but Christ, our spiritual parent, is not only perfectly holy even as man, but He is holiness itself, being God from eternity. The natural parent brings forth his offspring by the power of nature; the spiritual parent, much more, by the power of the Holy Spirit, who is the author of nature, is able to beget. The natural parent, being flesh, begets flesh, that is, a corrupt mass; the spiritual parent begets spirit by His Spirit, that is, a spiritual man. "Whoever is born of God does not commit sin," that is, so that sin reigns in him. A reason is added: "because His seed remains in him."

units.la: Efai. 9.6. Rom. 5.14. Adami primi & secundi collatio. Philip. 2.8. 1. Ioan. 3.9. Sic vocatur Spiritus sanctus, quo tanquam viuo semine instauramur & regeneramur. Imò addit, nò potest peccare, nēpe eo modo quo non renati peccant, idq;, inquit, quia natus est ex Deo: Tātū enim est illud natū ex Deo, & habere eius semē in nobis manens. Vt enim nō tenatus, non potest nō peccare: ita renatus nō potest peccare.
units.tr: Isaiah 9:6. Romans 5:14. A comparison of the first and second Adam. Philippians 2:8. 1 John 3:9. So the Holy Spirit is called the living seed, by which we are restored and regenerated. Moreover, he adds that he cannot sin, namely in the way that the unregenerate sin; and this, he says, is because he is born of God. For to be born of God, and to have His seed remaining in us, is so great a thing. For just as the unborn cannot but sin, so the one born again cannot sin.

units.la: Atq; hæc est illa Spiritus generatio, quā regeneratione vulgò appellamus: Quā quidē sic paulò rudiùs desinio: Vt si[?]ralter ratio quędā & cōmutatio naturę totius, sacta vi Spiritus S. Nō intelligo mutationē substātię ipsius velcorporis vel animæ, quasi verò per regenerationē ex hac veteri substātia gignatur aliqua noua; verūm intelligo mutationē qualitatū, quæ insunt in substātia. Verbi gratia; In intellectu regeneratione intelligo mutationē sapiētiæ carnis, in Sapiētiā Dei. In volūtate & affectibus, mutationē peruersitatis naturæ & malæ inclinationis in rectitudinē & bonā inclinationē. Mutatio ista, quę est tā tū qualitatū non tā leuiter cōtingit, quàm fortasse suspicarentur aliqui. Verūm qui eam in se serio sentiunt, nihil tā difficile factu sentiūt. Quid enim, quæso, aliud est abnegatio sui? Abneget, inquit Christus, seipsum, & tollat crucem suam quotidie, & sequatur me. Quòd si iussisset abnegare tantùm amicos, diuitias, &c. quæ extra nos sunt, id quidē difficulter satis obtineri potuisset, vt patet exemplo adolescentis illius, in Euangelio. Sed cùm iubeat abnegare nosipsos, etiā quod in nobis sapientissimū est, rationem ipsā, & sapientiā hāc carnalem totā, quæ suppeditabit tibi mille rationes, quib. conabitur persuadere ne Christū vel profitearis vel sequaris: cùm, inquā, hoc iubeat, quid difficilius factu dici potest? Finge tibi ratio nem iam conuictā cedere: cùm ventū est ad voluntatē & affectiones, illæ pertinaciter opponūt se etiā mentis iudicio; vt videas nihil difficilius esse quā regenerari, imò verò impossibile esse nisi adsit & operetur omnipotens ille Dei Spiritus. Arma, inquit Paulus, nostra nō sunt carnalia, sed diuinitus valida, & ad subuersionē munitionū, dū rationēs ratiocinationes euertimus, &c. Ecce nō expugnatur animus noster carnalibus & mūdanis armis, sed Dei ipsius potēntia, cuius ministerū est Euāgeliū hoc quod prædicamus. Sciēdū autē est, vt hoc postremo loco dicamus, nō mometo aliquo seri hāc regeneratione, sed progressu tēporis. Non enim nisi toto vitæ spatio aboleri potest vetus homo quem necesse est per totam vitam sepeliri sub afflictionibus, sub suspiriis & doloribus, adhoc vt paulatim mortificetur & corrumpatur, donec tandem exsurgamus tanquam noui homines, depositá iam & exuta omni illa corruptione, idque virtute præsentis capitis nostri Iesu Christi. Nam Christi præsentia sola est quæ nos regenerat, imperfectè quidem & per fidem in hac vita: fides enim suo quodam modo præsente nobis exhibet Christum: perfectè vero & per aspectū in altera. Scimus fore vt cum ipse patefactus fuerit, similes ei simus, quoniam videbimus eū sicuti est. Gloriosa enim illa Christi præsentia, vsque adeo in nobis efficax futura est, vt transformatura sit corpus nostrum humile, vt conforme fiat corpori ipsius glorioso. Nā sciendum est aliam esse virtutem præsentis gloriæ Christi, aliam vero totius gloriæ terrenorum principum: Quam si millies aspexeris, nihilo ipse gloriosior fies. At vero si Christi præsentis gloriam vel semel aspexeris, in eam continuò mutaberis. Cui sit omnis gloria, Amen. Atque hæc de hisce tenus.
units.tr: And this is that generation of the Spirit which we commonly call regeneration. I define it, somewhat roughly, as follows: a certain new kind of change and renewal of the whole nature, brought about by the power of the Holy Spirit. I do not mean a change of the substance itself, whether of body or soul, as if through regeneration some new substance were born out of this old one. I mean a change of the qualities that inhere in the substance. For example, in the understanding, I understand regeneration as a change from the wisdom of the flesh to the wisdom of God. In the will and the affections, I understand a change from the perversity of nature and its evil inclination to uprightness and a good inclination. This change, which concerns qualities alone, does not come about as lightly as some might suppose. But those who seriously feel it in themselves find nothing so difficult to do. For what, I ask, is self-denial but this? "Let him deny", says Christ, "himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me" (Luke 9:23). If he had commanded us to deny only friends, riches, and other things outside us, that could have been fairly easily achieved, as the example of that young man in the Gospel shows. But since he commands us to deny ourselves, even what is wisest in us, reason itself and all this carnal wisdom, which will supply you with a thousand arguments by which it will try to persuade you not to confess or follow Christ, what can be said to be more difficult to do? Suppose that reason, now convinced, gives way; when it comes to the will and the affections, these stubbornly resist even the judgment of the mind. So you see that nothing is more difficult than to be regenerated, indeed that it is impossible unless that almighty Spirit of God is present and works. "Our weapons", says Paul, "are not carnal, but mighty through God, to the pulling down of strongholds, casting down imaginations", etc. (2 Cor. 10:4–5). Behold, our mind is not conquered by carnal and worldly weapons, but by the power of God himself, whose instrument is this Gospel which we preach. We must also note, to say this last point, that this regeneration does not take place at some moment, but over the course of time. For the old man cannot be put away except over the whole span of life, and he must be buried throughout the whole of life under afflictions, under sighs and sorrows, so that he may be gradually mortified and corrupted, until at last we rise as new men, having now laid aside and stripped off all that corruption, and this by the virtue of our present head, Jesus Christ. For the presence of Christ alone is what regenerates us, imperfectly indeed and through faith in this life. For faith, in its own way, presents Christ to us as present: but perfectly, and by sight, in the other life. We know that when he shall be revealed, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). For that glorious presence of Christ will be so effective in us that it will transform our lowly body, so that it may be made conformable to his glorious body (Phil. 3:21). For we must understand that the power of Christ's present glory is one thing, and the whole glory of earthly princes is another: though you look upon the latter a thousand times, you will not become any more glorious yourself. But if you once look upon the present glory of Christ, you will continually be changed into it. To whom be all glory. Amen. And so much on these matters.

units.la: Sequenti versu Christus per occupationem remouet impedimentum quoddam de regenerationis modo. Nicodemus modum non vidit quo fiat regeneratio, ideoque impossibilem eam esse iudicauit: Christus huic occurrit, & primum quidem proponit non esse mirandū, quòd modum illum regenerationis non statim capiat: deinde similitudine à vento sumpta id explicat. q.d. Vides, ô Nicodeme, ventum quò vult spirare, & sonum eius audis, sed nescis unde veniat, & quò vadat, hoc est, modum quo spirat vetus ignoras: ita de Spiritu regenerationis sentiendum est. Spiritus Dei spirat quò vult, & ij quorum cordibus aspirat eum penitus sentiunt, nesciunt tamen vel unde veniat, vel quò vadat, hoc est, modum quo spiret ipse non habent exploratum. Sed videamus distinctius partes huius comparationis. Ventus, inquit, quò vult spirat: Hoc est, liberum motum habet, qui à nulla creaturarum aut excitari aut cohiberi potest: Ita Spiritus Dei liberè spirat quò vult, & quemadmodum Deus inducì non potest à quoquam vt quemquam eligat: ita impediri non potest Christus quo minus Spiritus suo
units.tr: In the following verse Christ, by anticipating an objection, removes a certain hindrance concerning the manner of regeneration. Nicodemus did not see how regeneration takes place, and therefore judged it impossible. Christ meets this, and first of all points out that it is not to be wondered at that he does not immediately grasp that manner of regeneration; then he explains it by a comparison taken from the wind. As if to say: You see, O Nicodemus, the wind blowing where it wills, and you hear its sound, but you do not know whence it comes or where it goes; that is, you do not know the manner in which it blows. So it must be understood of the Spirit of regeneration. The Spirit of God blows where he wills, and those in whose hearts he breathes feel him fully, yet they do not know either whence he comes or where he goes, that is, they do not have the manner in which he himself blows explored. But let us look more distinctly at the parts of this comparison. "The wind", he says, "blows where it wills": that is, it has a free movement, which can be neither stirred up nor restrained by any creature. So the Spirit of God blows freely where he wills, and just as God cannot be induced by anyone to choose anyone, so Christ cannot be prevented from regenerating whom he wills by his Spirit,

units.la: {1} Iohan. 3.2. suo regeneret quem vult, & distribuat priuatim singulis sicut vult. Secundò sonum venti audimus: Sic, vel multò magis sentimus Dei Spiritum, & audimus quasi fragorem illum qui exiitit perrupta hac petra cordis nostri, quòd difficilius discerpitur quàm saxum quodvis durissimum. Oportet igitur maximam esse vehementiam huius Spiritus perrumpentis animum nostrum eúmque perfringentis. Tertiò nescimus quo vadat ventus & unde veniat. Ventus philosophis est exhalatio fumosa subtilis sursum elevata, & frigiditate aëris repulsa, atque descendens in terram, aëreumque medium secum trahens ac omnia verrens. Obseruamus quidem è qua cœli plaga spiret, & in quâ spiret ventus, sed è qua regione terræ prodeat ventus, & ad quam vadat, propinquamne an remotam, obseruari à nobis non potest. Ita res habet in regeneratione. Scimus quidem Spiritum Sanctum esse tertiam personam in deitate. Scimus procedere cum à Patre & filio, scimus quoque ad nos peruenire. Sed modum illum quo procedit à Patre & filio, vt & modum quo peruenit ad nos, ac nos intus regeneret nescimus. Hactenus fuit comparatio, nunc restat vt aliquid ex ea obseruemus. Res ipsæ naturales deducunt nos ad fidem in res spirituales, quarum tamen rationem & modum non tenemus: Nam ignoramus etiam modum quo fiunt res etiam naturales, cùm tamen iis oporteat nos credere. An igitur quia non possumus modulo rationis nostræ simul ac semel comprehendere incomprehensibile illum modum quo fiunt res spirituales; ideo de iis desperandum est quasi nullo modo possint fieri? Sapientes huius mundi putant hic sapientiam esse, si non statim credas nisi modum ac rationem videas qua fiant omnia; hoc enim est nimis credulì & facilis credere, sint causa priùs cognita. Sed Paulus demen- tiam vocat hanc, non credere in resurrectionem corporum, cùm tamen modum eius ignores, præsertim cùm videas ex putrefacto & mortuo grano oriri spicam, cùm tamen modum ortus huius nemo sciat. At dices, id ita euenire experimur quotidiè in rebus naturalibus: dico pios sentire similiter hæc spiritualia, cùm tamen modi quo sint ea, explicare non possint. Quo sensu fit, vt credant sæpe cum vel nullus vel exiguus admodum sensus est, pendentes nimirum aliquando ex promissionibus solis, & nudo Dei verbo. In Deo laudabo verbum eius, inquit Psaltes. Sed crede ut lubet, quod si non credideris, etiam ventus, etiam stirpes & plantæ, etiam res creatæ omnes contra te ferent sententiam in illo die. Hominesferè cum vident naturalia ista, ut ventum, plantas, aliaque id genus, non feruntur supra ea, neque admonentur ex conspectis iis, de rebus spiritualibus: sed satis habent si rebus ipsis naturalibus vtantur, fruantur. Verum longè alius & melior debet esse vsus istarum rerum, ad nos nimirum ædificandos & promouendos in cursu illo, quem corripuimus ad vitam alteram, debemus enim sic argumentari apud animos nostros: Ventum quidem audimus spirantem, sed modum ignoramus quo spirat. Ita etsi regenerationis nostræ modum nescimus, tamen non minus certò regeneramur, quàm spirat ventus. Rursus ex corrupto & putrefacto semine oritur spica, cuius ortus tamè modum ego ignoro: ut ignorem, quomodo futura sit illa resurrectio ex mortuis, tamen non minus certò Dei potentia ac virtute Christi resurgam, & corpus mihi redintegrabitur ex corrupto quàm & mortuo semine, quàm spica ex corrupto & mortuo grano.
units.tr: {1} John 3.2. and from distributing to each individually as he wills. Second, we hear the sound of the wind; so, or much more so, we perceive the Spirit of God, and we hear, as it were, that roar which breaks forth when the rock of our heart is burst open, which is harder to tear apart than any very hard stone. It must therefore be that the force of this Spirit, which breaks through and shatters our mind, is very great. Third, we do not know where the wind goes or whence it comes. To the philosophers the wind is a subtle smoky exhalation, raised upward and driven back by the coldness of the air, and descending to the earth, drawing the middle air with it and sweeping everything before it. We indeed observe from which quarter of the sky the wind blows and in which direction it blows, but from what region of the earth the wind comes forth, and whether it goes to a near or a distant place, cannot be observed by us. So it is in regeneration. We know indeed that the Holy Spirit is the third person in the Godhead. We know that he proceeds from the Father and the Son, and we know that he comes to us. But we do not know the manner in which he proceeds from the Father and the Son, nor the manner in which he comes to us and regenerates us within. So far the comparison; now it remains that we note something from it. Natural things themselves lead us to faith in spiritual things, the reason and manner of which we nevertheless do not grasp. For we do not know even the manner in which natural things themselves come about, and yet we must believe in them. Is it therefore the case that, because we cannot comprehend in the measure of our reason, all at once and in a single moment, that incomprehensible manner in which spiritual things come about, we ought to despair of them, as if they could in no way come to be? The wise men of this world think that it is wisdom here not to believe immediately unless you see the manner and reason by which all things come about; for to believe only once the cause has been known first is too credulous and easy. But Paul calls it madness not to believe in the resurrection of bodies, although you do not know its manner, especially since you see the ear of corn springing up from the rotted and dead grain, though no one knows the manner of this growth. But you will say: we experience this in natural things every day; I say that the godly feel these spiritual things in a similar way, though they cannot explain the manner in which they are. In this sense it comes about that they often believe when there is either no feeling or a very small one at all, depending, of course, at times on the promises alone and on the bare Word of God. "In God I will praise his word", says the Psalmist (Ps. 56:10). But believe as you please; if you do not believe, the wind, the stalks and plants, indeed all created things will bring sentence against you on that day. Men, when they see these natural things, such as the wind, plants, and others of that kind, are not carried above them, nor are they admonished by the sight of them about spiritual things; but they are content to use and enjoy the natural things themselves. But the use of these things ought to be far different and better: namely, for building us up and advancing us in that course which we have begun towards the life to come. For we ought to reason thus within ourselves: We indeed hear the wind blowing, but we do not know the manner in which it blows. So although we do not know the manner of our regeneration, yet we are regenerated no less surely than the wind blows. Again, from corrupt and rotted seed an ear of corn springs up, yet I do not know the manner of its growth; so although I do not know how that resurrection from the dead will be, nevertheless I shall rise no less surely by the power of God and the virtue of Christ, and my body will be restored from the corrupted seed no less than the ear of corn from the corrupted and dead grain.

units.la: 9 Respondit Nicodemus, & dixit ei, Quomodo possunt hæc fieri?
units.tr: 9 Nicodemus answered and said to him, How can these things be?

units.la: 10 Respondit Iesus, & dixit ei, Tu es doctor ille Israëlis, & hæc non nosti?
units.tr: 10 Jesus answered and said to him, Are you that teacher of Israel, and do you not know these things?

units.la: CHristus modum incomprehensibilem innuebat regenerationis nostræ, Nicodemus tamen instat, Quo modo, inquiens, possunt hæc fieri? Quod est in homine optimum, ratio est qua excellimus bruta animantia, cui philosophi nimiū semper tribuerunt. Quod tamen primum omnium impedit nos quo minus credamus spiritualibus. Ratio est cum ratiocinatione sua: nam ea est natura & superbia rationis humanæ, ut nisi incomprehensibilia illa Dei comprehendat, nunquam iis credat. Deinde etiam si demus eam aliquid etiam rerum diuinarum & cœlestium percipere, tamen si non videatur illud statim congruere & sibi consentaneum esse, nunquam ei fidem habere velit. Dicimus praeterea, quanto magis sapit quis haec terrena, tanto difficilius eum credere coelestibus: Videtis, inquit Paulus, vocationem vestram, fratres, vos non esse multos sapientes secundum carne. Dicam quod mirum alicui videri posset: Nullus unquam sapiens secundum carnem credit, tantisper dum permanet sapiens. Si quis sibi videtur esse sapiens inter vos in hoc saeculo, stultus fiat ut fiat sapiens. Oportet enim stultum fieri in hoc mundo, abnegato teipso & abnegatis omnibus rebus iis quas tanti facit mundus ut sapias coelestia. Nam quo magis quis contemnit ista quae vulgo magni fiunt, eo potentius & efficacius agit in eo Deus per Spiritum & per verbum suum: ac sermo crucis Christi fit ei potentia ac Dei Sapientia. Quare ante omnia in hac vita studendum est abnegationi nostri ipsorum, eorumque nimirum quae in nobis praestantissima sunt, ad hoc ut capaces simus coelestium ac spiritualium rerum.
units.tr: Christ was pointing to the incomprehensible manner of our regeneration, yet Nicodemus presses on: "How," he says, "can these things be?" The best thing in a man is reason, the faculty by which we surpass the brute animals, and the philosophers have always credited it with too much. Yet this is the first thing that hinders us from believing spiritual things. Reason, with its own reasoning, is the difficulty: it is the nature and pride of human reason that it never believes those incomprehensible things of God unless it first comprehends them. Further, even if we grant that reason can perceive something of divine and heavenly things, it will never be willing to trust them if they do not at once appear to fit with it and agree with its own judgement. We may add that the more a man is wise in earthly things, the harder he finds it to believe heavenly things. Paul says, "Consider your calling, brothers: not many of you are wise according to the flesh." I will say what may seem strange to someone: no one who is wise according to the flesh believes, for as long as he remains wise. If anyone among you thinks himself wise in this age, let him become foolish so that he may become wise. For one must become a fool in this world, denying oneself and denying all those things which the world values so highly, if one is to be wise in heavenly things. The more a man despises those things which the common crowd holds in high esteem, the more powerfully and effectively God works in him through his Spirit and his word, and the word of the cross becomes to him the power and wisdom of God. Therefore, above all in this life, we must labour at self-denial, and at denying those things in ourselves which are most excellent, so that we may be capable of heavenly and spiritual things.

units.la: Respondit Iesus, & dixit ei, Tu es doctor ille Israelis. Christus, superbia hominis observata, (placebat enim sibi in ratiocinationibus suis, nihilque temere & sine certa ratione volunt credere) non ultra ratiocinatur cum eo, sed demolitur illam superbiam rationis humanae, qua inflatus est obiecta ei ignorantia turpissima. Nihil enim est quod magis afficit & humiliat superbos istos, qui videntur sibi aliquid scire, cum nihil sciant ut oportet, quam conscientia ignorantiae suae. Necesse autem est isti humilientur prius quam proficiant in doctrina Christi, & comprimatur quasi eis inflatum cor, exprimaturque ille ventus sapientiae, potius quam sapientia, priusquam cor ipsis consolidetur, constabiliaturque gratia Christi. Sed qualemnam ignorantiam ei obicit? nempe turpissimam, eam nimirum quae est elementorum ipsorum in ipsa arte quam profitebatur Nicodemus. Exaggeratur enim ignorantia hominis duabus circumstantiis; prior est a vocatione ipsius, quod magister & doctor fit Israelis: posterior a rebus minimis & elementis ipsis illius vocationis, ab ipso tamen ignoratis, quarum quidem rerum ignorantia turpissima est. Christus superbissimo quique in arte sua obiecturus est rerum minimarum in arte sua ignorantiam, quoties visum erit ei descendere in disceptationem: nam superbissimus quisque in arte aliqua est ignarissimus. Nihili enim fecerim illam sapientiam quae hominem inflet & intumescere faciat. Huiusmodi profecto ignorantia turpissima cum sit debet conscientia sui hominem quam maxime humiliare. Sed adeo homines nihil pudet hodierno die ignorantiae suae, etiam in arte sua, plusquam puerilis, ut fere quisque in arte & vocatione sua libenter profitetur ignorantiam suam. Sed veniet dies cum dicet idem Iesus Christus, Tu fueras magister Israelis & haec ignorabas? Tu fueras Pastor Ecclesiae, & tamen ignorabas vel elementa ipsa vocationis tuae? Tu fuevas Christianus, & tamen nihil de Christo cognoscebas? & sic de caeteris vocationibus quibuscunque, in quibus requirit Deus sapientiam secundum vocationem quamque.
units.tr: Jesus answered and said to him, Are you that teacher of Israel? Christ, having observed the pride of the man (for he took pleasure in his own reasonings and was unwilling to believe anything rashly or without a sure reason), no longer argues with him, but tears down that pride of human reason by which he was puffed up, setting before him his most shameful ignorance. For there is nothing that more humbles and mortifies those proud men, who seem to themselves to know something when they do not know what they ought, than awareness of their own ignorance. Yet these men must be humbled before they can make progress in the teaching of Christ, and their swollen heart must be pressed down, and that wind of wisdom must be squeezed out of them, rather than wisdom itself, before their heart can be firmly established and the grace of Christ confirmed in it. But what kind of ignorance does he charge him with? Most shameful indeed: the ignorance of the very rudiments of the art which Nicodemus professed. The ignorance of a man is magnified by two circumstances. The first arises from his calling, that he is made a master and teacher of Israel. The second arises from the smallest matters and the very rudiments of that calling, which he nevertheless does not know, and ignorance of these is most shameful. Christ will charge every proud man with ignorance of the smallest matters in his own art, whenever it pleases him to descend into debate, for the proudest man in any art is the most ignorant. I would think nothing of that wisdom which puffs a man up and makes him swell. Indeed, since this kind of ignorance is most shameful, the awareness of it ought above all to humble a man. But today men are so little ashamed of their ignorance, even in their own art, which is more than childish, that almost everyone willingly confesses his ignorance in his own art and calling. But the day will come when this same Jesus Christ will say, "You were the teacher of Israel, and you did not know these things? You were a minister of the Church, and yet you did not know even the rudiments of your calling? You were a Christian, and yet you knew nothing of Christ?" And so likewise of all other callings in which God requires wisdom according to each calling.

units.la: II Amen, amen dico tibi, quod scimus loquimur, & quod vidimus testamur: sed testimonium nostrum non recipitis.
units.tr: 11 Truly, truly I say to you, we speak what we know, and we testify to what we have seen; but you do not receive our testimony.

units.la: 12 Si terrena dixi vobis & non creditis: quomodo, si dixero vobis caelestia, credetis?
units.tr: 12 If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?

units.la: CHristus reprehensa Nicodemi ignorantia, quod ad regenerationem attinet, nunc incipit graviter quaeri de incredulitate Nicodemi, simul & aliorum. Primum igitur argumentum quo exaggerat incredulitatem eorum, est a certitudine doctrinae suae. Certitudinem hanc amplificat duobus gradibus; priore, Quod scimus, inquit, loquimur. Sapientia Dei omnia sciuit. Debet quidem id nos inducere ad credendum, quoties intelligimus homines loqui de rebus quas habent perspicuas, & certe in rebus aliis, cum putamus homines, quae ipsi certo sciunt, loqui, fidem iis eo maiorem habemus. Sed natura nostra non est ita affecta ad veritatem Dei; pugnamus enim natura, etiam cum agnita veritate: Saltem nos, quotquot a Deo constituti sumus in hoc ministerio, oportet dare operam ut penitus ipsi sciamus omnia ea, quae in medium afferimus, ut homines vel ad fidem adducamus, vel relinquamus inexcusabiles. Deinde certitudinem tudinem doctrinae suae superiori quodam cognitionis gradu declarat: Quod vidimus, inquit, testamur. Quo quidem significat se non modo scire quae loquitur, sed vidisse etiam: Nam scimus etiam, quae non ipsce oculis vidimus. Deum nemo vidit vnquam, Vnigenitus filius qui est in sinu Patris ille nobis expositi. Ergo filius cum in sinu Patris sit, videt perpetuo Patrem suum, & omnia ipsius consilia quaecunque spectant ad salutem humanam. Quamobrem cum videat oculis suis Christus quaecunque proposuit de Deo & salutis via, magna profecto oportuit certitudinem esse eorum quae propo-suit. Oculatus enim testis dignus est, & ei multum credi solet in aliis quoque rebus: Vt homines incredulí inaneant, quoad res spirituales, & eas quae ad salutem ipsorum pertinent: tamen Christus voluit primos illos testes Apostolos oculatos omnes esse, quo magis crederent ipsis homines, si fieri posset. Vnde Apostolus, Quod vidimus, inquit, oculis nostris, quod spectauimus, annunciamus. Et Petrus, Oculis, inquit, nostris aspeximus illius maiestatem. Verum quidem illud est, non vidisse nos quotquot post Apostolos sumus testes Christi, non vidisse, inquam, nos oculis nostris Christum, vt Apostoli eum viderunt, tamen nihil loquimur Dei populo, nisi quod ex oculatis testibus Apostolis Christi habemus. Neque facimus vt Papistae, qui obtrudunt Ecclesiae Dei figmenta sua, plane etiam pugnantia cum scriptis Prophetarum & Apostolorum: sed monemus omnes & hortamur, vt scrutentur Scripturas, & videant ipsi num eadem loquamur nos cum oculatis illis testibus qui ante nos loquuti sunt & scripserunt: secus enim fidem non requirimus habendam iis quae nos proponimus. Notandum autem, quod non simpliciter dicat loqui se quae scit, &c. sed addito iuramento id affirmat. Amen, Amen, inquiens, Id nimirum facit quo magis Nicodemus & alii credant ipsum scire & vidisse, vel si nolint credere magis inexcusabiles reddantur, vel propter hoc ipsum, iusiurandum additum est testimonio.
units.tr: Having rebuked Nicodemus's ignorance about regeneration, Christ now begins to complain seriously of the unbelief of Nicodemus and of others with him. His first argument, by which he magnifies their unbelief, is drawn from the certainty of his teaching. He enlarges this certainty by two degrees. By the first he says, "We speak what we know." God's wisdom knows all things. Surely this ought to lead us to believe whenever we understand that men are speaking about things they plainly grasp; and certainly in other matters, when we think men are speaking of what they know for certain, we place greater trust in them. But our nature is not so disposed towards the truth of God; for we struggle against it by nature, even when the truth is known. At the very least, we who have been appointed by God to this ministry must take pains to know thoroughly everything we put forward, so that we either lead men to faith or leave them without excuse. Next he sets forth the certainty of his teaching by a higher degree of knowledge: "What we have seen," he says, "we testify." By this he means that he not only knows what he speaks, but has also seen it; for we also know things which we have not seen with our own eyes. "No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has made him known." Therefore, since the Son is in the bosom of the Father, he sees his Father continually and all his counsels which concern human salvation. Hence, since Christ sees with his own eyes whatever he sets forth about God and the way of salvation, the certainty of what he sets forth must surely be great. For an eyewitness is worthy of trust, and much credence is customarily given to him in other matters too. Although unbelieving men are empty with regard to spiritual things and those which pertain to their salvation, Christ nevertheless wished that his first witnesses, the Apostles, should all be eyewitnesses, so that men might believe them the more, if that could be. Hence the Apostle says, "What we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon, we proclaim." And Peter says, "We ourselves beheld his majesty with our eyes."
