It is true that we who come after the Apostles, as witnesses of Christ, have not seen Christ with our eyes as the Apostles saw him; yet we say nothing to the people of God except what we have from the Apostles, the eyewitnesses of Christ. Nor do we act as the Papists do, who thrust their own fictions upon the Church of God, fictions plainly contrary to the writings of the Prophets and Apostles. Rather we admonish and exhort all men to search the Scriptures and see for themselves whether we speak the same things as those eyewitnesses who spoke and wrote before us; otherwise we do not ask that what we put forward be believed. It should be noted that he does not simply say that he speaks what he knows, and so on, but adds an oath to confirm it. "Amen, amen," he says. He does this, no doubt, so that Nicodemus and the others may believe that he knows and has seen; or, if they refuse to believe, so that they may be rendered the more inexcusable. Or, for this very reason, the oath is added to the testimony.

units.la: Hactenus explicata est certitudo doctrinae Christi, Miseriarum additur, Sed testimonium nostrum non recipitis. Incertis nostrae de-scriptio: & vanis quibusque fidem habemus, natura vero nunquàm habemus fidem rebus spiritualibus,quæ omnium rerum certissimæ sunt, quia nimirum vani fumus omnes & mendaces natura. Atque hinc fit vt totus ferè mundus sequatur hæreses exitiales & mendacia;paucissimi verò,& non nisi ij quos Deus afflauit suo Spiritu & Θεοδίδακτοι sunt veritatem Dei sequantur. Non esligitur quod Papistæ glorientur de multitudine sua. Nam hoc ipsum certissimum argumentum est,doctrinam ipsorum non nisi figmentum esse & vanitatem. Quòd si veritatem Dei solam proponerent, profecto non habe-rent tot sequaces, ne si millies iactitarent fundamentum illud præclarum, scilicet fidei suæ, authoritatem nimirum Ecclesiæ. Nam authoritas ecclesiæ nisi aliud maius firmiúsque testimonium subesset, nempe ipsius Dei in scripturis suis loquentis, profecto id nunquam efficeret, vt vnus aliquis firmiter crederet veritati Dei, cùm ne ipsi quidem Deo loquenti & affirmanti credamus,nisi ipse prius immutet cor da nostra nósque couertat. Ea enim est impudentia nostra ad contra naturam ipsam, quę fuit in principio ipsius diaboli qui medacij arguit Dei verbum ac veritatem. Si terrena vobis. Alterum argumentum quo exaggerat Nicodemus aliorum infidelitatem quo-ad res spirituales. Est autem ab incredulitate,etiam quo ad res terrenas: Si cùm dixi vobis terrena,non creditis, hoc est, spiritualia terrenis & crassis figuris, cuiusmodi est ventus de quo dixi vobis,adumbraui,non tamen creditis; Quid si spiritualia suis coloribus depinxero vobis,& sublimiter tractaue-ro,non demitterem me ad captum vestrum, quomodo tum credetis? Vnde licet discere eam esse in nobis per naturam difficultatem summam concipiendi res spirituales,& eas quæ ad regnum Dei pertinent(ea enim hic spiritualia intelligo)vt etiam tum cum crasso & terreno modo tractantur,tamen non percipiantur à nobis. Quàuis autem ea sit cæcitas nostra & duritics naturalis, tamen sunt,& non pauci ij quidem,qui offenduntur humili illo dicendi tractandique genere,ac dicunt, quod si sublimiori nescio quo stylo & charactere tractarentur illa spiritualia, tum quidem libenter ea amplecterentur, sed nimia dictionis humilitate, & vili abiectóque stylo
units.tr: Thus far the certainty of Christ's teaching has been explained. A further description of our wretchedness is added: "But you do not receive our testimony." We believe the uncertain and whatever is vain, but by nature we never believe spiritual things, which are the most certain of all things, because by nature we are all vain and deceitful. And hence it comes that almost the whole world follows destructive heresies and lies, while very few, and only those whom God has breathed upon by his Spirit and who are taught of God [Θεοδίδακτοι], follow the truth of God. Therefore the Papists have no reason to boast of their multitude. For this very thing is the most certain proof that their doctrine is nothing but fiction and vanity. If they set forth the truth of God alone, they would certainly not have so many followers, even if they boasted a thousand times of that famous foundation of their faith, namely the authority of the Church. For the authority of the Church would never bring it about that a single man firmly believes the truth of God, unless there lay beneath it another, greater and firmer testimony, namely that of God himself speaking in his Scriptures; for we do not even believe God himself speaking and affirming, unless he first changes our hearts and turns us. Such is our shamelessness against nature itself, the same shamelessness that was present in the beginning in the devil, who charged the word and truth of God with lying. "If I have told you earthly things." This is the second argument by which Nicodemus magnifies the unbelief of others with respect to spiritual things. It is drawn from their unbelief even concerning earthly things: if, when I have told you earthly things, you do not believe, that is, if I have shadowed forth spiritual things by earthly and crude figures, such as the wind of which I have told you, and you still do not believe; what if I were to paint spiritual things in their own colours and treat them on a lofty level, without lowering myself to your capacity? How then would you believe? From this we may learn that by nature there is the greatest difficulty in us in conceiving spiritual things, and those which pertain to the kingdom of God (for by spiritual things here I mean these), so that even when they are handled in a crude and earthly manner, they are nevertheless not grasped by us. However great our blindness and natural hardness may be, there are nonetheless not a few who take offence at this humble manner of speaking and handling things, and who say that if those spiritual things were treated in some lofty style and character, they would gladly embrace them, but that they are frightened away from that subject by the excessive lowliness of the diction and its cheap and abject style.

units.la: Incredulitatis notatio et exaggeratio. Aduersus verbi Dei & sacri ministerii receptores dictum. stylo absterreri se queruntur ab illa materie. Nemo qui velit expendere argumetum quo vsus est hoc loco Dominus, non videt merum hunc esse prætextum infidelitatis. Si enim, inquit, cum dico vobis terrena, non creditis, Si dicerem vobis spiritualia, quomodo credetis? Si non intelligimus Deum loquentem nobis nostra quasi ipsorum lingua & nostra phrasi, quomodo intelligeremus loquetem sua lingua & sua phrasi, vtpote cœlesti, quæ exsuperat captum nostrum? Si Deum offerentem sese, manibus nostris tractandum, non tamen apprehendimus, quomodo supra nubes & cœlos ipsos offerentem se deprehenderemus? Hæc obseruo ideo, vt cum sentimus in nobis ipsis istam naturæ cæcitate, discamus ignorātiā rerū spiritualiū non cœlesti doctrinæ, sed nobisipsis imputare, & petere à Deo vt semel velit illuminare oculos mentis nostræ ad hoc, vt cœlestia ista tandem videamus; quæ si daretur semel videre & degustare, tū reipsa experiremur non esse aliam omnino doctrinam, quæ repleat inanitatem istam cordium nostrorum & deformitatem reformet. Quicquid enim tradiderunt veteres illi Philosophi, illud totum non implebit inanitatem istam, neque hominem vnquam meliorem efficiet, etenim efficacitas solì verbo Dei relinquitur.
units.tr: Notation and exaggeration of unbelief. Spoken against the receivers of the Word of God and of the sacred ministry. They complain that the style frightens them off from that subject matter. Anyone who weighs the argument the Lord uses in this place can see that this is a mere pretext for unbelief. For if, he says, when I speak to you of earthly things you do not believe, how will you believe if I speak of spiritual things? If we do not understand God speaking to us in our own tongue and our own idiom, how would we understand him speaking in his own tongue and his own idiom, which is heavenly and exceeds our grasp? If God offers himself to be handled by our hands and we still do not grasp him, how would we lay hold of him when he offers himself above the clouds and the heavens themselves? I note these things so that, when we feel within ourselves this blindness of nature, we may learn to impute our ignorance of spiritual things not to the heavenly doctrine but to ourselves, and ask God to will at last to illuminate the eyes of our mind, so that we may finally see those heavenly things. If we were once granted to see and taste them, we would truly experience that there is no other doctrine at all that fills this emptiness of our hearts and reforms their deformity. For whatever those ancient philosophers handed down will not fill this emptiness, nor will it ever make a man better, since efficacy is left to the Word of God alone.

units.la: 13 Nullus enim ascendit in cœlum nisi qui descendit è cœlo, nëpe filius hominis qui est in cœlo.
units.tr: 13 No one has ascended into heaven but he who came down from heaven, that is, the Son of Man who is in heaven.

units.la: 14 Prout autem Moses extulit serpentem in deserto, ita extolli oportet filium hominis:
units.tr: 14 And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up,

units.la: 15 Vt quisquis credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam.
units.tr: 15 That whoever believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.

units.la: 16 Ita enim Deus dilexit mundum, vt filium suum vnigenitum dederit, vt quisquis credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam.
units.tr: 16 For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whoever believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.

units.la: 17 Non enim misit Deus filium suum in mundum vt damnet mundum, sed vt sernetur mundus per eum.
units.tr: 17 For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world through him might be saved.

units.la: Hactenus Dominus regenerationis doctrinam tradidit, quanto autem cum fructu audiuimus. Post{a}quam enim & causa sua & effecto ea explicauit; modu autem eius ostendit incoprehensibilem esse, nihil profecit: verum hoc responsum accepit a Nicodemo, Quomodo possunt ista fieri? Quid ad hoc Christus respondérit vidimus. Primum exprobrauit Nicodemo crassam ignorantiam, deinde coepit grauiter queri de infidelitate tum Nicodemi, tum aliorum Iudaeorum, eamque eorum miseriam duobus argumentis exaggerare. Nunc exaggerata infidelitate eorum & miseria remedium proponit, non in alio quidem quam in Christo, hoc est, in seipso. Ergo ad finem usque huius communicationis, concionatur primum de Christo unico illo remedio, deinde de vita aeterna credentium, postremo de damnatione aeterna non credentium. De Christi autem Passione & Ascensione agit, hoc est de duabus Euangelij partibus, sed ordine inuerso primum de Ascensione, deinde de Passione. Doctrinae Ascensionis Christi in coelos arrepta esse videtur occasio ex proximo loco, in quo de rebus coelestibus dictum est. Nunc itaque subiungit solum esse Christum, qui ascendat in coelos, ac proinde penetret in illa coelestia. Ascensionem hanc Christi, quo admirabilior videatur & maior, eam solius Christi propriam facit exclusis omnibus hominibus.
units.tr: Hitherto the Lord has taught the doctrine of regeneration, but with what fruit have we heard it? For after he had explained both its cause and its effect, and shown that its manner is incomprehensible, he gained nothing, but received this answer from Nicodemus: How can these things be? We have seen what Christ replied to this. First he rebuked Nicodemus for his gross ignorance, then he began to complain sharply of the unbelief both of Nicodemus and of the other Jews, and to magnify their misery by two arguments. Now, having magnified their unbelief and misery, he sets forth a remedy, and one found in no other than Christ, that is, in himself. So, to the end of this discourse, he preaches first about Christ as the one remedy, then about the eternal life of believers, and lastly about the eternal damnation of unbelievers. He speaks of Christ's Passion and Ascension, that is, of the two parts of the Gospel, but in reverse order, first of the Ascension and then of the Passion. The occasion for teaching about Christ's ascent into heaven seems to have been taken from the preceding passage, in which heavenly things were discussed. So now he adds that Christ alone is the one who ascends into heaven, and therefore penetrates those heavenly things. To make this ascension appear more wonderful and greater, he makes it the peculiar property of Christ alone, to the exclusion of all men.

units.la: Nullus, inquit, ascendit in coelum, nisi qui descendit, nempe filius hominis: Hoc est nemo hominum sua ac propria virtute ascedit in coelos. Quod adeo verum est, vt ne Christus quidem ipse, qua homo est, sua virtute ascenderit in coelos. Nam ascendere in coelos quid aliud est, quaeso, quam postquam iam resurrexeris ex mortuis, hoc est superaueris ipsam mortem & sepulchrum, tum, inquam, posteaquam hoc peregeris, ascendere in coelos, hoc est triumphum agere, & in triumpho ducere superatos illos hostes omnes, diabolum, mundum, peccatum, mortem ipsam? Nam hanc ascensionem Christi Dauid interpretatus est de triumpho, vt & Paulus eum secutus. Ascendit in sublime, captiuam duxit captiuitatem, hoc est captiuam duxit captiuorum hostium multitudinem, deque ea triumphauit. Idem iudicandum est suo quodam modo de ascensione nostrum omnium in coelos. Vide igitur quam difficile sit in coelos ascendere, quam etiam impossibile sit homini, qua homo est. Ait igitur, Nemo ascendit in cælos, nisi qui descendit è cælo. Tum quis hic sit, verbo sequenti interpretatur, expresso ipsius nomine, Filius, inquit, hominis. Christus in Euangelio se filium hominis appellat, nomine sumpto à natura illa, in qua se humiliauit, ut vel ipso nomine testaretur de natura sua vere humana, testaretur etiam de communione infirmitatum omnium quæcunque in hominem cadere possunt, solo peccato excepto: testaretur denique de humilitate illa Christi & obedientia maxima, qua victor omnem creaturam, homines, inquam, & angelos. Nemo enim omnium sic se humiliauit, & sic obediens factus est Deo, ut filius Dei.
units.tr: No one, he says, has ascended into heaven, except he who descended, namely the Son of Man. That is, no man ascends into heaven by his own power and virtue. This is so true that not even Christ himself, as man, ascended into heaven by his own power. For what else is it, I ask, to ascend into heaven, than, after you have risen from the dead, that is, after you have overcome death itself and the grave, then, I say, after you have accomplished this, to ascend into heaven, that is, to celebrate a triumph and lead in triumph all those conquered enemies: the devil, the world, sin, and death itself? For David interpreted this ascension of Christ as a triumph, and Paul followed him: He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, that is, he led captive the multitude of his captive enemies and triumphed over them. The same must be judged, in its own way, of the ascension of all of us into heaven. See then how difficult it is to ascend into heaven, and how impossible it is for man, as man. He therefore says, No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven. Then he explains who this is in the following words, by expressly naming him: the Son, he says, of Man. In the Gospel Christ calls himself the Son of Man, taking the name from that nature in which he humbled himself, so that by the very name he might bear witness that his nature was truly human, and bear witness also to his fellowship with all the infirmities that can befall a man, sin alone excepted. Finally he bears witness to that humility of Christ and his supreme obedience, by which, as victor, he overcame every creature, men, I say, and angels. For none of all men humbled himself so, and became so obedient to God, as the Son of God did.

units.la: Hic obiici potest, Qui ascendit eum dicit esse solum filium hominis, Ergo contrà filius hominis descendit: Igitur Christus in humana natura descendit è cælo? Respondeo, Verum quidem est filium hominis descendisse: Nam illud nomen filij hominis est totius personæ nomē. Secundum autem κοινωνίαν quam vocant ἰδιώματων, proprietas ea quæ proprie est alterius tantum naturæ, toti personæ, vel quod idem est utrique naturæ communicatum propter arctissimam illam duarum naturarum unionem, tribui solet. Non tamen propterea illud sequitur, proprietatem eam tribuendam esse alteri naturæ separatim. Non igitur sequitur, Qui ascendit, hoc loco dictus est filius hominis; Ergo Christus secundum humanam naturam descendit, vel humana Christi natura descendit: Verum hoc sequitur, Ergo filius hominis (quod nomen est totius personæ) descendit.
units.tr: Here it may be objected: he who ascends is said to be only the Son of Man; therefore, conversely, the Son of Man descended. Therefore Christ descended from heaven in his human nature? I answer: it is true that the Son of Man descended, for the name Son of Man is the name of the whole person. But by the communication of properties [κοινωνία ἰδιωμάτων], as they call it, a property which belongs properly to only one nature is usually attributed to the whole person, or, what is the same, it is communicated to both natures because of the very close union of the two natures. Yet it does not follow from this that such a property is to be attributed to one nature separately. So it does not follow: he who ascends is here called the Son of Man; therefore Christ descended according to his human nature, or the human nature of Christ descended. The true inference is this: therefore the Son of Man (which is the name of the whole person) descended.

units.la: Postremò hoc versu est amplificatio quædam huius Ascensionis, Qui est in cœlo. Q. d. Imò verò filius hominis est in cœlo hoc ipso momento, quo te, Nicodeme, alloquor, nedum ascensurus est posteà in cœlum. Hoc intelligendum est de deitate secundū quam Christus ubique est. Nam deitas Christi ubique est, & ubique tota & ubique vna: Nam sic diuina illa natura Patris, Filij & Spiritus sancti est ubique, ut nulla sit extensio partium, quæ sit ut vna pars sit in uno loco, altera in alio, sed tota est in omni loco, deinde nō est ita in omni loco to ta, ut plures sint dij, quare sit tota est in omni loco, ut etiā vna sit. Quare tota deitas tum cùm alloqueretur Christus Nicodemum, erat in Christo σωμαικῶς habitans, in terris, & tota deitas erat in cælo eodem illo tempore, & tamen vna eadéque numero vtrobique & vbiq; erat deitas. Quòd si hic obiiciatur vt prius, ex phrasi hac sequi humanam Christi naturam tum in cælo fuisse; dicitur enim filius hominis qui est in cælo: Respondeo, filius hominis nomen est totius personæ: nam alterius naturæ appellatio significat συνεκδοχικῶς, & κοινωνία ἰδιωμάτων, vtramque naturam in vn am personam coalescentem. Iam verò proprietas, quæ est vnius tantū naturæ, tribuitur nomini vtramque naturā significanti, siue illud nomen vtriusque naturæ vnitæ atque ideo personæ fit synecdochicum, vt dixi, siue illud nomen proprie significet vtramque naturam, ideóq; personam ipsam ex vtraque existentē. Atque hoc propter arctissimam vnionem illam, vt dixi supra, duarum naturarum coalescentium in vnam personam. Hic exemplo summi illius Pastoris discimus ostendendam quidem & exaggerandā infidelitatem ac miseriam homini, sed non hic semper subsistendū, sed transeundū continuò à miseria ipsa ad miseriæ remedium, nō quidē ad remedium aliquod a nobis inuentū, vt sunt merita hominū, vt satisfactiones, vt indulgentiæ, aliáque hominū infinita figmenta, sed ad solū Iesum Christū. Non enim aliud nomen est sub cælo, quod datum sit inter homines, per quod oportet nos seruari, Act. 4. 12. Quod si curanda sit cæcitas ipsius naturæ, qua fit vt nō valeamus intueri cœlestia illa, tum quidē tanquā certum solumque remedium huius mali, ponendus est ante oculos Christus, in cœlum quasi ascendens, eiúsque gloria demonstranda, quæ sola eam vim habet, vt transformet nos in eandem imaginem ex gloria in gloriā 2. Cor. 3. 18. Nam præbetur lumen cognitionis gloriæ Dei in sola facie Iesu Christi 2. Cor. 4. 6.
units.tr: Last, there is a certain amplification of this ascension in the words, who is in heaven. As if to say: indeed the Son of Man is in heaven at this very moment in which I speak with you, Nicodemus, and not merely is about to ascend there afterwards. This must be understood of the deity, according to which Christ is everywhere. For the deity of Christ is everywhere, and everywhere whole and everywhere one. For the divine nature of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is everywhere in such a way that there is no extension of parts, so that one part is in one place and another in another; rather it is whole in every place. Nor is it so whole in every place that there are many gods; hence it is whole in every place, yet one. Therefore the whole deity, at the time when Christ was speaking to Nicodemus, dwelt bodily [σωματικῶς] in Christ on earth, and the whole deity was in heaven at that same time; and yet the deity was one and the same in number in both places and everywhere. But if here it is objected, as before, that from this phrase it follows that the human nature of Christ was then in heaven, since he is called the Son of Man who is in heaven, I answer: the name Son of Man is the name of the whole person. For the appellation of one nature signifies synecdochically [συνεκδοχικῶς], and by the communication of properties, both natures coalescing into one person. Now a property belonging to one nature only is attributed to a name signifying both natures, whether that name, as the name of the united natures, becomes synecdochical of the person, as I said, or whether the name properly signifies both natures, and so the person itself existing from both. And this is on account of that very close union, as I said above, of the two natures coalescing into one person. Here, by the example of that highest Shepherd, we learn that the infidelity and misery of man must indeed be shown and magnified, but we must not stop there; rather we must pass continually from the misery itself to the remedy for misery. And this remedy is not something discovered by us, such as the merits of men, satisfactions, indulgences, and the countless other inventions of men, but Jesus Christ alone. For there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved, Acts 4. 12. And if the blindness of nature itself, by which we cannot look upon those heavenly things, is to be cured, then Christ must be set before our eyes as the certain and only remedy for this evil, as though ascending into heaven, and his glory must be displayed, which alone has the power to transform us into the same image from glory to glory, 2 Cor. 3. 18. For the light of the knowledge of the glory of God is given in the face of Jesus Christ alone, 2 Cor. 4. 6.

units.la: Hactenus de Ascensione Christi incælos. Sequenti versu per correctionem quandam docet oportere filium hominis pati, & extolli in crucem, priusquam ascendat in cælos. Nam nemo coronatur, nisi qui legitimè certauerit. Crucem autem & morte Christi explicat per comparationem ac similitudinem exaltati in deserto serpentis.
units.tr: So far concerning the Ascension of Christ into heaven. In the following verse, by a kind of correction, he teaches that the Son of Man must suffer and be lifted up on the cross before he ascends into heaven, for no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully. He explains the cross and death of Christ by the comparison and likeness of the serpent lifted up in the desert.

units.la: 1. Tim. 2, 5. tis æneiqui vmbra quædã fuit Christi in crucẽ tollendi. De hoc serpente narrat Moses,cùm populus obmurmu-ratione aduersus Deum suũ effecisset, vt mitteret Deus serpentes presteres qui morderent populum; vt contabescerent ac morerétur multi:misertus Dominus populi sui edixit Mosi vt sibi serpentẽ faceret æneum,eumque perticæ imponeret,eo consilio, vt quisquis morsus effet,eo aspecto sanitatẽ recuperaret.Hic Serpens man-sit diu apud populũ vsque ad dies Ezechiæ,qui contudit serpentem æneum quem fecerat Moses, eo quòd vsque addies illos Israëlitæ adolerent ei, vbi Nehuschtan appellatur, hoc est æreus, à materia. Nunc vt ista ad institutum applicemus:ita oportuit Dominũ Iesum erigi in lignum crucis,ad hoc, vt quotquot eum intueantur fide suspensum è ligno, non pereant, sed habeant vitā æternam. Mirum est aspectum crucifixi & mortui hominis ea virtute esse & efficacia,vt vitā afferat vel intuentibus. Ita tamen res habet,nam Dominus etiam mortuus,Spiritus est viuificus, & sermo crucis iis qui vocatı sunt est potentia & sapientia Dei.
units.tr: 1. Tim. 2, 5. The bronze serpent was a kind of shadow of Christ being lifted up on the cross. Moses tells of this serpent: when the people had murmured against their God, God sent fiery serpents to bite the people, so that many wasted away and died. The Lord, having pity on his people, told Moses to make a bronze serpent for himself and to set it on a pole, with the purpose that whoever was bitten, by looking at it, would recover his health. This serpent remained among the people for a long time, until the days of Hezekiah, who broke the bronze serpent that Moses had made, because until those days the Israelites burned incense to it. It was called Nehushtan, that is, "bronze," from its material. Now to apply these things to our purpose: so it was necessary that the Lord Jesus be lifted up on the wood of the cross, so that everyone who looks upon him, hanging from the wood, in faith, should not perish but have eternal life. It is wonderful that the sight of a crucified and dead man should have such power and efficacy as to bring life even to those who look at it. Yet so it is, for the Lord, even though dead, is life-giving Spirit, and the word of the cross is to those who are called the power and wisdom of God.

units.la: Contrauertitur hoc sæculo maximè, de causa vitæ nostræ, quænam demum ea sit, quæ vitam nobis procuret ac mereatur. Papistæ eam ascribunt inhærenti nescio cui iustitiæ, & operibus nostris, quæ meritoria ipsi vocant. Nos contrà tribuimus soli Christo, ipsiúsq; merito ac cruci,per fidem apprehensæ. Dicimus autem hãc regenerationem (quam ipsi vocant inhærentem iustitiam) vnà cum operibus regenerationis, esse duntaxat initium quoddam vitæ illius æternæ; quod initium vitæ æternæ, vt totam vitam æternam,ita ipsum promeritus est nobis Iesus Christus sola morte & passione sua. Nunc, si lubet, ipsum Dominum audiamus de lite hac decidentem in hanc sententiam; Extolli oportet filium hominis, vt quisquis credat in eum nõ pereat,sed habeat vitam æternam ; ita enim Deus dilexit mundum,&c. Sententiam superiorem de filio morti tradito, & in crucem sublato repetit, & clarius explicat, hoc præterea adiecto tanquã fundamento & quasi fonte,ex quo factum hoc Dei processerit ac promanarit,nẽpe dilectionem Dei ipsius vnigenitam, ita, inquit, Deus dilexit mundum, vt vnigenitam filium suum dederit. Discimus exemplo Christi non cogitandum prius de hoc facto Dei in dando filio suo unigenito, quàm percipiendus sit animo infinitus quidem amor Dei erga nos. Est enim hoc vere indicium maximi & ineffabilis amoris. Sunt, fateor, omnia Dei beneficia, etiam temporalia ista, totidem argumenta amoris erga nos diuini. Verùm si videres peccatum quantum sit, & iram Dei aduersus peccatum quanta sit, etiamsi fingas gratificari tibi omnia regna huius mundi, tamen non propterea haberes persuasum ipsius erga te amore, nisi vnà cum iis omnibus daret tibi Christum, & in eo habitante penitus in corde tuo per fidem, sentires remissionem peccatorum, in quo solo ira illa Dei aduersus peccatum pacata est. Vnde Iohannes volens amoris Dei erga nos signum indubitatum exhibere, non profert temporarium aliquod beneficium, sed solum hoc Dei beneficium maximum in tradendo morti filio: Per hoc, inquit, cognouimus charitatem, quod ille animam suam pro nobis posuit, &c. Et Paulus, Postquam charitatis suae maximae meminit, quae effusa est in cordibus nostris, per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis, statim eius argumentum subiungit his verbis: Christus cum adhuc nullis viribus essemus, suo tempore pro impiis mortuus est. Hanc circumstantiam personae nostrae, qui impij sumus, si compares cum illa persona Christi qui filius Dei vnigenitus est, habebis amorem Dei, de quo neque homo vnquam, neque Angelus cogitare potuit. Viderunt quidem Angeli lapsum humani generis, sed de tali tantoque remedio, nec suspicati quidè sunt vnquam. Quod vbi coepit per Ecclesiam innotescere imperiis ac potestatibus, ex eo tempore desiderarunt in illud introspicere, & creaturae ipsae expectant auidè plenam ipsius reuelationem. Prosequitur quidem nos etiam nunc Deus paterno amore, sed, vt ait Iohannes, nondum patefactum est quid erimus. Scimus autem fore, vt cum ipse patefactus fuerit, similes ei simus. Praeterea circumstantia ista personae nostrae, qua dicitur nos impios esse plane, arguit immutabilitatem amoris illius Dei erga nos, vel hoc ipso quòd nulla eius in nobis causa tum reperta fuerit. Quae si in nobis fuisset aliqua, vt verbi gratia, amor erga eum nostrum, ià profecta secto sublata illa causa, tolleretur effectus, hoc est, amor Dei erga nos. Sumus enim nos mutabiles natura & inconstantes. At cum in Deo solo sit causa, manente in aeternum causa, manebit effectum, hoc est, Dei erga nos amor. Quia ego Iehoua, inquit, non mutor. Habes igitur amorem immensum, simul & immutabilem, quid amplius desideres?
units.tr: In this age the question is chiefly debated: what, finally, is the cause of our life, that is, what is it that procures and merits life for us? The Papists ascribe it to I know not what inherent righteousness and to our works, which they themselves call meritorious. We, on the contrary, attribute it to Christ alone, and to his merit and cross, apprehended through faith. We say, moreover, that this regeneration (which they call inherent righteousness), together with the works of regeneration, is only a certain beginning of that eternal life; and that this beginning of eternal life, as well as the whole of eternal life, Jesus Christ has merited for us by his death and passion alone. Now, if it pleases, let us hear the Lord himself deciding this dispute to this effect: The Son of Man must be lifted up, so that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life; for God so loved the world, etc. He repeats the earlier statement about the Son delivered to death and raised up on the cross, and explains it more clearly, adding this besides, as a foundation and as it were a source from which this act of God proceeded and flowed forth, namely God's own only-begotten love. "God so loved the world," he says, that he gave his only-begotten Son. From the example of Christ we learn that we must not think about this act of God in giving his only-begotten Son before the infinite love of God toward us is grasped in the mind. For this is truly the evidence of the greatest and ineffable love. I admit that all the benefits of God, even these temporal ones, are so many arguments of his divine love toward us. But if you were to see how great sin is, and how great the wrath of God against sin is, even if you imagined that all the kingdoms of this world were granted to you, you would not therefore be persuaded of his love toward you, unless, along with all those things, he gave you Christ, and you, feeling within your heart, through faith, that Christ dwells in you, felt the forgiveness of sins, in which alone that wrath of God against sin is appeased. Hence John, wishing to show an undoubted sign of God's love toward us, does not bring forward some temporary benefit, but only this greatest benefit of God in delivering his Son to death: By this, he says, we have known love, that he laid down his life for us, etc. And Paul, after mentioning his greatest love, which has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, immediately adds its evidence in these words: Christ, while we were yet without any strength, in due time died for the ungodly. If you compare this circumstance of our person, that we are ungodly, with that person of Christ who is the only-begotten Son of God, you will have a love of God of which neither man nor angel has ever been able to think. The angels indeed saw the fall of the human race, but they never even suspected such and so great a remedy. When this began to be made known through the Church to the principalities and powers, from that time they desired to look into it, and the creatures themselves eagerly await its full revelation. God still cares for us even now with a fatherly love, but, as John says, it has not yet been revealed what we shall be. We know, however, that when he is revealed we shall be like him. Moreover, this circumstance of our person, by which we are said to be entirely ungodly, proves the unchangeableness of God's love toward us, precisely because no cause for it was found in us at that time. For if there had been some cause in us, for example, love toward him on our part, which had arisen from us, then once that cause was removed, the effect would be removed, that is, the love of God toward us. For we are changeable by nature and inconstant. But since the cause lies in God alone, and the cause remains forever, the effect, that is, the love of God toward us, will remain. "For I, the Lord," he says, "do not change." You therefore have a love that is both immense and unchangeable: what more could you desire?

units.la: Sed vt redeamus, cum tantum tamque manifestum hoc argumentum dilectionis Dei erga nos, quod dederit nobis filium vnigenitum, profecto in hoc effecto concipienda nobis est infinita Dei dilectio, adeo vt persuasum iam habentes nos a Deo diligi, illud quoque persuasum habere possimus, omnia eius beneficia ad nos pertinere, neque enim persuadere nobis possumus beneficia Dei spiritualia ad nos pertinere, vt iustificationem, vt vitam aeternam, priusquam certi simus de amore erga nos ipsius Dei. Quid enim boni expectare possumus ab infenso & irato Deo? Vnde fidem ipsam definimus primum ex persuasione illa dilectionis Dei in Christo; deinde vero ex persuasione omnium eius beneficiorum. Hanc persuasionem deinde sequitur pax quae superat omnem intellectum, & laetitia ineffabilis & gloriosa: Iustificati per fidem pacem habemus, inquit Paulus: & Petrus, Quem cum non videritis, credentes tamen in eum exultatis gaudio ineffabili ac gloriosò. Sequitur: Vt quisquis credit in eum.
units.tr: But to return: since this so great and so manifest argument of God's love toward us, that he has given us his only-begotten Son, is set forth, we must surely conceive in this effect an infinite love of God, so that, having already been persuaded that we are loved by God, we may also be persuaded that all his benefits pertain to us. For we cannot be persuaded that God's spiritual benefits, such as justification and eternal life, pertain to us, before we are certain of God's own love toward us. For what good can we expect from a hostile and angry God? Hence we define faith first from that persuasion of God's love in Christ, and then from the persuasion of all his benefits. This persuasion is followed by the peace that surpasses all understanding, and by ineffable and glorious joy: "Being justified by faith, we have peace," says Paul; and Peter: "Whom having not seen, you love; in whom, though now you do not see him, yet believing, you rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory." It follows: that whoever believes in him.

units.la: Christus datus per se quidem efficax est, tam ad fidem ipsam quam ad iustificationem & vitam aeternam. Ea enim efficacia est in morte eius, quae liberet a morte vel infinitos mundos. Vide comparationem illam quae habetur Rom. 5.15. & deinceps. Sed tamen sine fide non est in nobis efficax Christus, non quod fides nostra vel augeat vel minuat eius efficacitatem, sed quod efficacitatem illam applicet ad nos peculiariter, & tam nostram quodammodo efficiat. Vnde dictum est Euangelium potentia Dei ad salutem, sed cui? Credenti. Et Paulus precatur vt illuminatis Ephesiorum oculis mentis, videant quae sit illa excellens magnitudo potentiae ipsius in nobis qui credimus. Quibus locis significatur potentiam illam infinitam per fidem demum nostram fieri nobisque applicari: quod quidem adeo verum est, vt qui credit, iam incipiat sentire in sese vitam illam aeternam. Et vi-tam, inquit Paulus, quam nunc viuo in carne, viuo per fidem fili Dei, qui dilexit me & semetipsum tradidit pro me. Quare precamur inter audiendum Euangelium, ne simus securi, quasi vero ille sermo crucis sit nobis potentia Dei etiam non credentibus: Sed demus operam imprimis, vt dum tanta in Christo offertur gratia, eam manu fidei continuo apprehendamus nobisque applicemus. Secus enim si neglecta & elapsa fuerit semel occasio gratiae, tantum aberit vt aliquid nobis sit profutura ista quae nunc offertur gratia, vt etiam auctura sit iusta damnationem.
units.tr: Christ given is in himself indeed efficacious, both for faith itself and for justification and eternal life. For there is in his death such efficacy that it would deliver even infinite worlds from death. Look at the comparison that is found in Rom. 5.15 and following. Yet Christ is not efficacious in us without faith, not because our faith either increases or diminishes his efficacy, but because it applies that efficacy to us in a particular way and as it were makes it ours. Hence it has been said that the gospel is the power of God unto salvation, but to whom? To the one who believes. And Paul prays that, with the eyes of the mind enlightened, the Ephesians may see what is that exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe. These passages signify that this infinite power is at last made ours through faith and applied to us; and this is indeed so true that whoever believes already begins to feel that eternal life within himself. "And the life," says Paul, "that I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." Therefore, while hearing the gospel, let us pray that we may not be careless, as if that word of the cross were the power of God even to those who do not believe. Rather let us take pains above all that, while so great grace is offered in Christ, we may immediately lay hold of it with the hand of faith and apply it to ourselves. For otherwise, if the opportunity of grace is once neglected and lost, the grace now offered will be so far from profiting us that it will even increase our just condemnation.

units.la: Non enim misit Deus. Hactenus de se concionatus est Dominus, nunc incipit concionari de vita aeterna. Hoc est, de effecto mortis suae. Eius autem certitudinem persuadet Nicodemo, a Dei propositu & consilio in mittendo filio suo, idque ex oppositis declarat. Non enim misit filium suum vt condemnet mundum, sed vt seruetur mundus per eum. Vult igitur Christus nos certos esse de salute ac vita nostra, quidem vsque adeo necessarium est, vt absque ea certitudine nulla sit futura pax conscientiae, nulla securitas, nulla laetitia. Ideoque Paulus ex hac fidei certitudine cem deriuauit: Iustificati fide, inquit, pacem habemus. Ficri quidem potest vt Papistae & dubitent ipsi, & persuadeat aliis dubitandum esse: sed ideo hoc fit quod conscientia peccati & irae Dei sopita iaceat, quae si semel expergefiert (quod quidem necessario aliquando futurum est) tum nisi simul sit sensus aliquis peccati, & apprehendatur vita illa aeterna, nihil erit in hac vita quod istos consolabitur.
units.tr: For God did not send. Hitherto the Lord has preached about himself; now he begins to preach about eternal life, that is, about the effect of his death. He persuades Nicodemus of the certainty of this from God's purpose and counsel in sending his Son, and he declares it by way of contrast: For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world might be saved through him. Christ therefore wills us to be certain of our salvation and life; indeed this certainty is so necessary that without it there will be no peace of conscience, no security, no joy. Therefore Paul also drew from this certainty of faith the words: Being justified by faith, he says, we have peace. It may indeed happen that the Papists both doubt themselves and persuade others that they should doubt; but this happens because the conscience of sin and the wrath of God lies lulled to sleep, which, if it should once awake (as it will necessarily do at some time), then, unless at the same time there is some sense of sin and that eternal life is apprehended, nothing in this life will console them.

units.la: Sed videamus nunc hoc Dei consilium in mittendo filio suo. Verum quidem est quod habetur postea, Ad iudicium exercendum ego in hunc mundum veni. Et quod Simeon apud Lucam refert de Christo: Ecce positus est iste in casum & resurrectionem multorum in Israel. Sed Christus seruat quidem per se, condemnat vero per accidens, ratione nimirum contemptus nostri: Ergo non tam Christus est qui condemnat, quam contemptus Christi. Contemptus autem Euangelij & infidelitas facit, vt {quod mirum est} doctrina quae gratiae est suapte natura & salutis, efficacior sit ad condemnationem quam vel Legis vniuersa doctrina. Verum, vt dixi, non per se id facit gratia. gratia,sed per accidens. Dicam generalius, neque Legis,neque Euangelij doctrina eo fine data est proprie à Deo vt condemnet, etsi alicubi dicatur Lex ministerium mortis,sed vt seruet.Condenatio autem propriè ex inobedientia vel Legis vel Euangelij;etsi illa ipsa inobedientia sit cum discrimine aliquo.Nam Legis inobedientia respicit nudum mandatum eique repugnat. Non enim pugnat cum aliqua potentia vel efficacia regenerationis in illo mandato oblata.Lex enim non ministrat potentiam. Euangelij autem inobedientia,quae est infidelitas,pugnat aduersus potentiam regenerationis oblatae. Nam vna cum verbo Euangelij offertur Spiritus sancti potentia ad nos regenerandos. Vnde sequitur condemnationem Euangelij infinitis partibus graviore fore quam condemnationem Legis, & tolerabiliorem fore conditionem etiam Sodomae & Gomorrhae in die iudicij quam nostram,si increduli & inobedientes fuerimus.
units.tr: But let us now look at this counsel of God in sending his Son. It is true that there is a later saying: For judgment I have come into this world. And there is what Simeon reports in Luke about Christ: Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel. But Christ saves in himself and condemns only incidentally, namely by reason of our contempt. Therefore it is not so much Christ who condemns as the contempt of Christ. Now contempt of the Gospel and unbelief bring it about that, strange as it is, the doctrine which is by its nature a doctrine of grace and salvation becomes more effective for condemnation than even the whole doctrine of the Law. But, as I said, grace does not do this of itself, but incidentally. To put it more generally: neither the doctrine of the Law nor the doctrine of the Gospel was properly given by God for this end, that it should condemn, although it is said somewhere that the Law is a ministry of death, but that it should save. Condemnation, however, properly arises from disobedience either to the Law or to the Gospel, although that disobedience itself has some difference. For disobedience to the Law regards the bare command and opposes it; it does not conflict with any power or efficacy of regeneration offered in that command, for the Law does not supply power. But disobedience to the Gospel, which is unbelief, opposes the power of regeneration that is offered. For together with the word of the Gospel is offered the power of the Holy Spirit to regenerate us. Whence it follows that the condemnation of the Gospel will be infinitely heavier than the condemnation of the Law, and that the condition of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment will be more bearable than ours, if we are unbelieving and disobedient.

units.la: 18 Qui credit in eum, non condemnatur, qui vero non credit, iam condemnatus est: quia non credidit in nomen vnigeniti filij Dei.
units.tr: 18 He who believes in him is not condemned; but he who does not believe is already condemned, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.

units.la: 19 Haec est autem condemnatio, quod lux venit in mundum, sed dilexerunt homines potius tenebras quam lucem: quia sunt eorum mala opera.
units.tr: 19 And this is the condemnation: that light has come into the world, but men loved darkness rather than light, because their works were evil.

units.la: 20 Quisquis enim quae mala sunt agit, odit lucem, nec venit ad lucem ne arguantur opera ipsius:
units.tr: 20 For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be exposed.

units.la: 21 Qui vero dat operam veritati, venit ad lucem: vt manifesta fiant facta ipsius, quod secundum Deum facta fuerint.
units.tr: 21 But he who does the truth comes to the light, so that his deeds may be made manifest, because they have been done according to God.

units.la: HActenus de doctrina vitae aeternae, nunc postremo loco concionatur de condemnatione. Est autem occupatio quaedam: Atqui multi damnantur. Respondet Christus illud non fuisse consilium Dei proprie; nequeum fuisse finem cur miserit Deus filium suum, sed hoc euenire propter infidelitatem.Qui credit in eum, inquit, non condemnatur. In praesenti loquitur,ac si dicat,non condemnatur etiam nunc:ergo ia absolutus est,etsi sint eius peccata quamplurima & quam grauissima,tamen ea vi fidei est, vt non priusattingat Christū per fidem, quàm absoluatur à peccatis suis omnibus. Vnde Paulus, Nulla nunc est condemnatio iis qui sunt in Christo Iesu, &c. Nam lex Spiritus vitæ qui est in Christo Iesu liberauit nos à lege peccati & mortis. Sed idem Paulus eodem loco dum pronun- ciat ac peruulgat præsentem hàc absolutionem, nos ita demum absolui dicit, si non secundum carnem, sed secundum Spiritum incedimus. Nam mortificatio carnis & sanctimonia vitæ, etsi causę quidem non sunt absolutionis huius, seiungi tamen ab ea non possunt. Ergo qui credit in filium Dei, iam absolutus est, qui vero non credit, iā condemnatus est, condemnatus est, inquam, etsi quàm leuissimum esse videatur peccatum aliquod, tamen in eo est condemnationis materia, non quidem tam ipsius peccati causa, quàm infidelitatis, quia qui illud committit non credit in vnigenitum Dei filium, tantam nimirum personam, cui non credere inexpiabile scelus est. Apostolus ad Hebræos, postquam primo capite dignitatem personæ Christi comparatione Angelorum exaggerasset, subiecit ac conclusit principio capitis sequentis in hæc verba: Propterea oportet nos eò magis attendere ad ea quæ audiuimus: & paulò post, Non effugiemus si tantam neglexerimus salutem. Dignitas & amplitudo tum personæ filij Dei, tum beneficij ac salutis tantæ, per tantam personam comparatæ, augebunt supramodum incredulitatem nostram, vt qui multo meliori loco fuissemus, si nihil vnquam in vita de Christo audissemus, quàm si audientes neglexissemus, tamen tantam salutem acquisitam nobis, & annunciatam à tanta persona.
units.tr: Hitherto he has preached of the doctrine of eternal life; now, last of all, he preaches about condemnation. There is an objection: many are condemned. Christ answers that this was not properly God's purpose, nor was it the end for which God sent his Son; it happens because of unbelief. He who believes in him, he says, is not condemned. He speaks in the present, as if to say, is not condemned even now. Therefore he is already absolved, although his sins are very many and very grievous; yet by the power of faith it is such that a man does not first attain Christ through faith and afterwards get absolved from all his sins. Whence Paul: There is now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, etc. For the law of the Spirit of life which is in Christ Jesus has freed us from the law of sin and death. But the same Paul, in the same place, while he pronounces and proclaims this present absolution, says that we are absolved only if we walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. For the mortification of the flesh and holiness of life, although they are not the causes of this absolution, cannot be separated from it. Therefore he who believes in the Son of God is already absolved; but he who does not believe is already condemned. He is condemned, I say, even if some sin may seem as slight as possible; yet in it there is matter for condemnation, not so much because of the sin itself as because of unbelief, since he who commits it does not believe in the only-begotten Son of God, a person of such great dignity that not to believe in him is an inexpiable crime. The Apostle to the Hebrews, after he had in the first chapter magnified the dignity of Christ's person by comparison with the angels, subjoined and concluded at the beginning of the next chapter in these words: Therefore we ought the more to attend to those things which we have heard; and shortly after, We shall not escape if we neglect so great a salvation. The dignity and greatness both of the person of the Son of God and of so great a benefit and salvation, acquired through so great a person, announced by so great a person, will increase our unbelief beyond measure. We who would have been in a far better position had we never heard anything about Christ in our lives would be worse off than if, having heard, we had neglected so great a salvation acquired for us and announced by so great a person.

units.la: Sed vt paulò altius descendamus in hanc rem: dico equidem omnem inobedienti amassere præsentem damnationem, siue Legis inobedientiā, siue Euāgelij. De condemnatione Legis dictum est: Maledictus homo qui non manserit in omnibus iis quæ scripta sunt in libro Legis, vt faciat ea. Mal̃ edictus, inquit, innuens præsentem maledictionem sequi Legis transgressionem. Id quod Paulus docet, cùm dicit palam esse & reuelari in præsenti tempore iram Dei è cœlo, aduersus omnem impietatem, & iniustitiam hominum: & postea concludit obnoxium fieri totum mundum condemnationi Dei. Id quod etiā omnes
units.tr: But to go a little more deeply into this matter: I say indeed that every disobedient person already has present condemnation, whether it be disobedience to the Law or to the Gospel. Of the condemnation of the Law it has been said: Cursed is the man who does not abide in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them. Cursed, he says, implying that present curse follows transgression of the Law. This is what Paul teaches when he says that the wrath of God is plainly revealed from heaven in the present time against all the impiety and injustice of men; and afterwards he concludes that the whole world is made liable to the condemnation of God. This also all of us

units.la: Rom. 1.18. Rom. 3.19. omnes experimur in hac vita. Neque enim quisquam omnium nostrum citius transgreditur legē Dei, quàm, si non plane stupidus sit, incipiat sentire conscientiæ stimulum. Si autem nos condemnet cor nostrum, potentior est Deus corde nostro. Quid, quæso, sunt aliud omnes hi morbi quos patiuntur increduli, omnes hæc calamitates quas experiuntur, quàm sententiæ condemnationis iam latæ executio, & initia quædam inferorum, quos paulo post totos simul ac semel patietur, nisi tempestiue resipuerint. Quòd ad inobedientiam Euangelij & fidei, locus hic præsens satis ostendit præsentem damnationem eam consequi. Sed argumentum nobis considerandum est: Iam condemnatus est, inquit, quia non credidit. Non ait, quia homicidium commisit, quia adulterium, quia furtum, & alia id genus perpetrauit, significans id quod quidam recte & pie pronunciauit, Nullam esse iustitiam nisi fidem, nullum peccatum nisi infidelitatem. Neque enim peccata in legem Dei commissa tibi imputantur si credis in Euangelium. Et incredulitas causa est cur ista omnia in rationem veniant, quæ alioqui æterna obliuione sepelirentur, per & propter Christum Iesum Dominum nostrum. Cui sit omnis honor & gloria. Amen.
units.tr: Rom. 1.18. Rom. 3.19. experience in this life. For none of us transgresses the law of God more quickly than, unless he is altogether stupid, he begins to feel the sting of conscience. If our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart. What, I ask, are all these diseases which unbelievers suffer, and all these calamities they undergo, other than the execution of a sentence of condemnation already passed, and certain beginnings of hell, which they will soon suffer wholly and at once, unless they repent in good time? As for disobedience to the Gospel and to faith, this present passage sufficiently shows that present condemnation follows it. But we must consider the argument: he is already condemned, he says, because he has not believed. He does not say, because he committed murder, or adultery, or theft, or perpetrated other things of that kind; this signifies what some have rightly and piously pronounced: that there is no righteousness except faith, and no sin except unbelief. For sins committed against the Law of God are not imputed to you if you believe in the Gospel. And unbelief is the cause why all those things come into reckoning which would otherwise be buried in eternal oblivion, through and for the sake of Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be all honour and glory. Amen.

units.la: Hæc est autem. Immoratur Christus in exaggeranda illa condemnationis causa, nimirum infidelitate, dicitque, Hæc est condemnatio. Q. d. Hæc est causa condemnationis, Lux venit in mundum, &c. Causa igitur condemnationis est, quod dilexerint homines potiùs tenebras quàm lucem. Causam hanc exaggerat in præcedenti sententia: Lux, inquiens, venit in mundum. Lux est Christus qui illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum. Magnitudinem huius beneficij, qui videre velit, consideret priùs tenebras illas & ignorantiam, in qua miserè iacuit mundus ante lucis illus aduentum. Nam vt visum est eis Deum non retinere notitia: ita tradidit eos Deus in mentem omnis iudicij expertem, vt facerent quæ minimè coueniebat. Amiserant igitur homines vel communem hunc sensum, & tanquam belluæ totidem rationis expertes, deinde sunt præcipites in omne flagitium. Lex verò tantùm abfuit ab eo vt illuminaret sic iacetes in tenebris ac c&-seruaret, vt è contrà augeret magis iustā damnationē. Itaque cùm legis impotentia nihil posset in carne, Deus suo ipsius filio misso, conformato carni peccato obnoxiæ, idque pro peccato, condemnauit peccatum in carne, vt illud in legis compleretur in nobis. Quamobrem hoc est quod exaggerat infidelitatem eorum, quòd nimirum lux venit in mundum, homines tamen dilexerunt tenebras potiùs quàm lucem. Tolerabile quidem est illud, amare tenebras, sed oblata iam luce peccare in lucem, eáque reiecta tenebras eligere, hoc nunquam satis potest exaggerari, procuratque damnationem praesentissimam.
units.tr: And this is the condemnation. Christ dwells on the cause of condemnation, namely unbelief, and says, This is the condemnation. That is: this is the cause of condemnation, that the light has come into the world, etc. So the cause of condemnation is that men have loved darkness rather than light. In the preceding sentence he magnifies this cause: The light, he says, has come into the world. The light is Christ, who enlightens every man who comes into this world. Whoever wishes to see the greatness of this benefit should first consider the darkness and ignorance in which the world lay wretchedly before that light arrived. For, as it seemed good to them not to retain the knowledge of God, God handed them over to a reprobate mind, lacking all judgement, so that they did what was not fitting. Men had therefore lost even this common sense, and like beasts devoid of reason they then plunged headlong into every shameful deed. The law, however, was so far from illuminating those who lay thus in darkness, or from preserving them, that on the contrary it increased their just condemnation. Hence since the law was powerless in the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us. Therefore this is what he magnifies in their unbelief: that the light has come into the world, and yet men have loved darkness rather than light. Loving darkness is indeed bearable, but to sin against the light when it has been offered, and to choose darkness after rejecting it, can never be sufficiently magnified, and it brings about the most present condemnation.

units.la: Sed videamus quid sibi velit tenebrarum nomen. Tenebras igitur intelligo ignorantiam Dei, voluntatis ac operum ipsius, ignorantiam filij Dei, & eorum quae ad regnum Dei pertinent. Quemadmodum enim noctis tenebrae dum occupant terrā, obscurant sic oculum corporis, vt nihil videre queant ignorantiae quasi nubes, postquam incubuit menti nostrae, sic eam obnubilat, vt Deum videre non possit. Verùm tenebrae illae corporeae & externae, impediant quidem oculum corporis, quominùs videat, non autem extinguant aciem oculi: tenebrae hae spirituales & internae sic extinguunt nobis lucem mentis, vt neque videat ipsa, neque possit videre, nisi noua acie denuo infusa per Spiritum Dei. Unde autem sunt istae tenebrae? Verba Christi quae sequuntur id ostendunt, dum ait, dilexisse homines tenebras potius quàm lucem. Exstunt igitur ex corde pessimè affecto. Verum quidem id est, nos omnes iam primùm nasci in ignorantia illa Dei ac metis caecitate ea, quam hausimus ex ipsis lumbis Adami. Verum ea est cordis nostri obstinatio ac malitia, vt nemo sit omnium qui attingat priùs eam aetatem, qua potest bonum à malo discernere, quàm incipiat pertinaciter oppugnare omnem lucem cognitionis Dei. Est quidem aliqua lucis scintilla, quae cum nascimur, & quam post lapsum hominis, Deus ex magna sua misericordia reseruauit & reliquam esse voluit: hanc non priùs scintillantem percipimus, quàm pertinacia cordis eam oppugnemus, nitamurque eam solam eiicere ex animis nostris. Qui veritatem, inquit Paulus, in iniustitia detinent: &postea: Sicut uisum est iis Deũ non retinere in notitia; & apertius alibi propter ignorantiã quæ est in ipsis, ex obduratione cordis eorum. Obstinatam istam oppugnationem lucis & cognitionis Dei naturalis, iam olim Deus vtus est in gentibus, ignorantia totius honestatis ac officiorum etiam quæ homines hominibus debent. Sicut uisum est, inquit, vt Deum in notitia non retinere: ita tradidit eos Deus in mentem reprobam, &c. Brutam hanc quasi ignorantiam insequuta est conscientiæ amissio (nam conscientia particularis scientia quam habemus nobiscum factorum nostrorum bonorum vel malorum, orta ex generali mentis notitia) Conscientia amissa, sequitur, vt sic dicam, dedolentia cordis. Amisso denique omni conscientiæ dolore ac stimulo, tum, inquit Paulus, dediderunt semetipsos proteruiæ ad certatim patrandam omnem impuritatem. Hactenus de oppugnatione naturalis lucis. Est autem lux altera verbi Dei, multò clarior ac efficacior illa naturali, quæ cum illa superior id tantum efficere possit, vt homines sint inexcusabiles: hæc etiam efficax est ad vitam æternam. Hanc quoque lucem vel multò maximè & duplicatis viribus oppugnat cor nostrum, quàm primùm ipsa sese offert oculis nostris, quod manifestum est vel ex hoc ipso loco. Lux, inquit, venit in mundum, sed dilexerunt homines potius tenebras quàm lucem, procurátque iusto Dei iudicio cordis ista contumacia extremam excæcationem & indurationem. Audite, inquit, audiendo, at ne intelligatis: videte videndo, neque cognoscatis, &c.
units.tr: But let us see what the name of darkness means. By darkness I understand ignorance of God, of his will and works, ignorance of the Son of God, and of those things which pertain to the kingdom of God. For just as the darkness of night, when it covers the earth, obscures the eye of the body so that it cannot see anything, so ignorance, once it has settled upon our mind, clouds it so that it cannot see God. But those bodily and external darknesses, while they hinder the eye of the body from seeing, do not extinguish the sight of the eye itself; those spiritual and inward darknesses so extinguish for us the light of the mind that it neither sees nor can see, unless a new sight is poured in again through the Spirit of God. Whence then come these darknesses? The words of Christ that follow show this, when he says that men have loved darkness rather than light. They therefore arise from a heart that is very badly disposed. It is true that we are all born in that ignorance of God and blindness of mind which we have drawn from the very loins of Adam. But such is the obstinacy and malice of our heart that there is no one of all men who, before he reaches that age in which he can distinguish good from evil, does not begin to attack stubbornly every light of the knowledge of God. There is indeed some spark of light which we have at birth, and which God, after the fall of man, out of his great mercy has kept and willed to remain; we do not perceive this spark as it shines before we, by the obstinacy of our heart, assail it and strive to drive it alone out of our minds. Who hold the truth, says Paul, in unrighteousness; and afterwards: As they did not see fit to retain God in knowledge; and more plainly elsewhere, on account of the ignorance that is in them, from the hardening of their heart. This obstinate assault upon the light and the natural knowledge of God God long ago punished among the nations, with ignorance of all honesty and duties, even those which men owe to men. As it seemed good, he says, not to retain God in knowledge, so God gave them over to a reprobate mind, etc. This brutish, as it were, ignorance was followed by the loss of conscience (for conscience is the particular knowledge which we have with ourselves of our good or bad deeds, arising from the general knowledge of the mind). Once conscience is lost, there follows, so to speak, a deadening of the heart. When at last all the pain and sting of conscience is lost, then, says Paul, they gave themselves over to wantonness, to work every impurity with greediness. So far concerning the assault upon natural light. There is, however, another light, that of the word of God, far clearer and more effective than the natural light; and while that light alone can make men inexcusable, this one is also effective unto eternal life. Our heart assails this light too, and far more strongly and with doubled force, as soon as it presents itself to our eyes; and this is plain from this very passage. The light, he says, has come into the world, but men have loved darkness rather than light, and by the just judgement of God this obstinacy of heart brings about extreme blindness and hardening. Hear, he says, indeed by hearing, but do not understand; see by seeing, but do not perceive, etc.

units.la: Vides igitur id quod dixi, causam potissimum ignorantiæ nostræ ac cæcitatis esse cordis insitam contumaciam. Sed quæ causa est obstinationis huius? Quia, inquit, eorum opera mala sunt, quisquis enim peruersè agit, odit lucem. Sic igitur argumentatur: Qui peruersè agit, odit lucem: At eorum opera mala sunt: Ergo dilexerunt tenebras potius quàm lucem. Nota igitur, effectum malorum operum, siue malæ conscientiæ quæ existit ex malis operibus, esse cor obstinatum & obsirmatum adversus lucem, efficereque mala opera, vt quis malè sibi conscius, fugiens lucem, auidè apprehendat tenebras.
units.tr: You see then what I have said: that the chief cause of our ignorance and blindness is the obstinacy implanted in the heart. But what is the cause of this obstinacy? Because, he says, their works are evil; for whoever acts wickedly hates the light. He argues thus: whoever acts wickedly hates the light; but their works are evil; therefore they have loved darkness rather than light. Note, then, that the effect of evil works, or of the evil conscience that arises from evil works, is a heart obstinate and hardened against the light, and that evil works bring it about that a man who is conscious of his evil, fleeing the light, eagerly seizes upon darkness.

units.la: Tenebrarum spiritualium comites.
units.tr: Companions of spiritual darkness.

units.la: Lux Spiritualis, quid. bras, mentíque suæ superinducat ignorantiam, vt mala sua opera, hoc quasi superinducto & adscito tegumento ac velamine, malè sibi conscius tegat, occultétque, non tam ab oculis aliorum quàm ab oculis suipsius, ne ipse videat ea, ad hoc, vt non videns ea, non pungatur aliqua eorum conscientia: ad hoc rursus, vt nulla conscientia compunctus peccet iam strenuè & absque doloris sensu. Id enim est quod quærunt homines, vt nimirum peccent citra dolorem omnem & cum voluptate aliqua, quod vt assequatur nihil non faciunt. Cùm itaque effectum malorum operum sit ista, quam diximus, lucis oppugnatio: Quid de istis coniectare possumus, qui lucem verbi divini fugiunt, nisi homines esse male sibi conscios, & in tenebris ea perpetrare, quæ vel dicere turpe est? Quid de Papistis sentiendum, qui tamen gloriantur de bonis operibus, nisi mala ipsorum opera esse, mendacia ac figmenta infinita, fœditatem illam inclusam Monachorum ipsorum plusquam Sodomiticam: Superbiam illius intolerabilem, quæ omnia semel affulgente luce verbi Dei statim conspiciuntur in suis coloribus? Deo autem sit gratia, qui mysterium illud iniquitatis magis magisque indies revelat. Quid dicam de nostris hominibus, præsertim viris principibus, qui lucem hanc verbi Dei simul ac semel totam extinctam esse vellent, nisi homines esse istos pessimè sibi conscios, proindeque tenebris supra modum delectari?
units.tr: Spiritual light, what... and he superinduces ignorance upon his mind, so that, with this ignorance as it were superinduced and added as a covering and veil, the man who is conscious of his evil hides and conceals his evil works, not so much from the eyes of others as from his own eyes, so that he himself may not see them, and thus, not seeing them, no part of his conscience may be pricked; and again, so that, pricked by no conscience, he may then sin vigorously and without any sense of pain. For this is what men seek, namely to sin without any pain and with some pleasure, and to attain this they leave nothing undone. Since, therefore, the effect of evil works is this assault upon the light which we have described, what can we conjecture about those who flee the light of the divine word, except that they are men badly conscious of themselves, and that they perpetrate in darkness those things which it is shameful even to speak of? What should we think of the Papists, who nevertheless glory in good works, except that their works are evil, lies and countless fabrications, that hidden filth of the monks, more than Sodomitical, and that intolerable pride of theirs, all of which, once the light of the word of God shines forth, are at once seen in their true colours? But thanks be to God, who reveals more and more, day by day, that mystery of iniquity. What shall I say of our own people, especially those men of rank who would wish this light of the word of God to be extinguished altogether at once, except that these are men most badly conscious of themselves, and therefore take excessive delight in darkness?

units.la: Videamus nunc causam propositionis illius, cur quisquis male agat aduersetur luci: Causa est ab effecto lucis: Ne arguantur, inquit, opera ipsorum. Lux enim illud est quod omnia facit manifesta. Mirificæ huius lucis verbi Dei efficaciæ habes exemplum in illo homine infideli ac idiota, quem ingredi fingit Apostolus in coetum prophetantium, & argui ab omnibus, diiudicari ab omnibus, ita ut occultis cordis ipsius, quæ ne ipse quidem vidit prius, iam manifestatis, splendore nimirum illius lucis, miser procidat in faciem, & adoret Deum, simulque renunciet Deum esse in prophetantibus. Cùm igitur ea sit lucis verbi efficacia, mirum est nostros homines adeo obfirmatos esse aduersus eam, ut absque vllo con-
units.tr: Let us now see the reason for that proposition, why whoever acts wickedly opposes the light. The reason is drawn from the effect of light: lest their works be reproved, he says. For light is that which makes all things manifest. You have an example of the marvellous efficacy of this light of the word of God in that unbelieving and untaught man whom the Apostle imagines entering an assembly of prophesying men, and being reproved by all and judged by all, so that the secrets of his heart, which he himself had not seen before, are now made manifest, and by the brightness of that light the wretched man falls on his face, worships God, and at the same time declares that God is among the prophesying. Since, then, such is the efficacy of the light of the word, it is strange that our people are so hardened against it that, without any sense of conscience, they bear its brightness.

units.la: Ephes. 5. 13. 1. Corinth. 14. 24. conscientiæ sensu ferant eius splendorem. Tam periculosum est semel obfirmare animum adversus lucem. Quod vbi factum est, tum Paganus aliquis aut Idiota, citius afficietur conscientia factorum suorum, & adducetur ad resipiscentiam, inspecta illa luce, quàm tu, qui iam plus millies audiuisti de Christo, & gloriaris etiam de Christiano nomine. Tum etiam quanto magis audies verbum Dei, tanto magis excæcaberis ac indurabéris, non quidem propter lucem ipsam, sed propter rebellionem illam cordis tui, quod reluctando magis magisque indurescit. Sed qui fit, cùm hoc sit effectum lucis, qui tamen male agunt oderint lucem? Sanè nisi ipsi male sibi conscij essent, nunquam commouerentur lucis ea præsentia qua manifestantur ipsorum opera. Ergo prima cur oderunt lucem causa est quòd male sibi conscij sint. Nota igitur malorum operum, etiam ante lucē illucentem, perpetuò esse aliquam malam conscientiā, quandiu enim manet aliqua Dei notio, aut aliqua boni & mali notitia in mente, tandiu est aliqua conscientia: Manet autem semper aliqua istorum notitia, quam tamen homines quammaximè vellent extinctam. Vnde etiam illud est quod videamus istos homines, qui tamé videntur sedoluisse, & omnem plane conscientiæ sensum amisisse, videamus, inquam, istos omnia facere, vt ipsi se excæcent, ac malæ conscientiæ dolorem non sentiant. Nisi enim subesset aliqua conscientia, quæ ipsos aliquo certè modo factorum admoneret, profectò non ita facerent. Sed ista conscientiæ scintilla, quantulacunque non habet eam vim, qua efficiat resipiscentiam ac conuersionem, sed tantùm qua reddat inexcusabiles in illo die.
units.tr: Ephes. 5. 13. 1. Corinth. 14. 24. They feel its brightness in their conscience. It is dangerous to harden the mind against the light even once. Once that has happened, a pagan or an unlearned man will be more quickly stirred in conscience by his own deeds, and brought to repentance by that light, than you are, who have already heard about Christ more than a thousand times and boast even of the Christian name. Moreover, the more you hear the Word of God, the more you will be blinded and hardened, not because of the light itself, but because of that rebellion of your heart, which grows ever harder the more it resists. But how does it happen that those who act wickedly hate the light, when this is the effect of the light? Surely, unless they were conscious of their own evil, they would never be disturbed by the presence of the light by which their works are made manifest. So the first cause of their hatred of the light is that they are conscious of their evil. Note therefore that, even before the light shines, there is always some evil conscience in those who do evil works, for as long as some notion of God, or some knowledge of good and evil, remains in the mind, so long there is some conscience. But some knowledge of these things always remains, though men would most gladly have it extinguished. Hence also we see that those men, who seem to have become insensible and to have lost every sense of conscience, do everything in order to blind themselves and not feel the pain of an evil conscience. For unless some conscience remained, which at least in some way warned them about their deeds, they would certainly not act as they do. But this spark of conscience, however small, does not have the power to bring about repentance and conversion, but only the power to make them inexcusable on that day.

units.la: Qui verò sincerè agit. Propositionem illam effecti malorum operum contrario effecto bonorum explicat, quasi dicat, hoc adeo verum est, vt contrarium ex contrario sequatur, & qui sincerè agit, hoc est animo recto, & sine dolo, non hypocriticè. Nam hypocritæ, etsi audeant, qua sunt impudentia, prodire in conspectum hominum, non audent tamen, si vel micam conscientiæ habeant, operibus suis, quantumuis in speciem gloriosis, prodiit in conspectum Dei, qui solus est cordium scrutator. Qui sincere agit, venit in lucem, &c. ut manifesta fiant facta ipsius. Ratio autem est, Quod secundum Deum facta sunt. Hoc est examinata ad voluntatis divinae regulam expressam, neque id tantum, sed ex fide professa, & ad Dei gloriam destinata sunt. Ea enim tua sunt quae requiruntur ad hoc ut possint opera nostra ferre lucem. Vide igitur vim bonae conscientiae quae existit ex bonis operibus. Audet animus bene conscius prodire in conspectum Dei & sistere se apud tribunal Christi, non quidem tam ipsorum operum causa, quam fidei, in qua Deo placent opera nostra, placent, inquam, at non merentur. Nam ista inter se differunt, placere Deo, & mereri de Deo: placent quidem & accepta sunt Deo nostra bona opera, & personae primum nostrae placent per fidem Christi, sed nihil prorsus de Deo merentur, cum solius Christi fide apprehensi sit meritum, Cui sit omnis gloria iustitiae nostrae in saeculum. Amen.
units.tr: Qui verò sincerè agit. He explains the statement about the effect of evil works by the contrary effect of good works, as if to say: this is so true that the contrary follows from the contrary, and he who acts sincerely, that is, with an upright heart and without guile, not hypocritically. For hypocrites, although they dare, in their shamelessness, to come forward into the sight of men, do not dare, if they have even a crumb of conscience, to bring their works, however glorious in appearance, into the sight of God, who alone is the searcher of hearts. Qui sincere agit, venit in lucem, &c. ut manifesta fiant facta ipsius. The reason is Quod secundum Deum facta sunt. That is, they have been examined by the expressed rule of the divine will, and not only that, but they are done from a professed faith and aimed at the glory of God. For those are the things that are required for our works to be able to bear the light. See therefore the power of a good conscience, which arises from good works. A mind that is well conscious dares to come into the sight of God and to stand before the judgment seat of Christ, not so much for the sake of the works themselves as for the sake of faith, in which our works please God. They please, I say, but they do not merit. For these things differ, to please God and to merit from God: our good works indeed please God and are accepted by him, and our persons first please him through the faith of Christ, but they merit nothing at all from God, since the merit is apprehended by the faith of Christ alone, to whom be all glory for our righteousness for ever. Amen.

units.la: 22. Postea venit Iesus & discipuli eius in Iudaeae territorium, & illic degebat cum eis, & baptizabat.
units.tr: 22. After this Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea, and there he stayed with them and baptized.

units.la: 23 Baptizabat autem etiam Iohannes in Aenon prope Salim, quoniam aquae multae erant illic, & veniebant ac baptizabantur.
units.tr: 23 John also was baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there, and people came and were baptized.

units.la: 24 Nondum enim coniectus fuerat Iohannes in carcerem.
units.tr: 24 For John had not yet been thrown into prison.

units.la: 25 Orta est igitur quaestio quibusdam ex discipulis Iohannis cum Iudaeis de purgatione.
units.tr: 25 Therefore a question arose between some of John's disciples and the Jews about purification.

units.la: IESUS, ut iam antea non semel diximus, ingressus antum tricesimum venit ad Iohannem in desertum, ut ab eo baptizaretur. Baptizatus iam, & initiatus officio Mediatoris, ductus est a Spiritu in desertum, ubi quadraginta dies & noctes totas ieiunavit. Hinc reversus est ad Iohannem in desertum, quo quidem tempore vocati sunt ad Christum discipuli quidam, nominatim Iohannes, Andreas, cuius nomen non est expressum, & Simon Petrus Andreae frater. Inde reversus in Galilaeam, in itinere vocatis Philippo & Nathanaële, vnà cum his venit Nazareth, vrbem Galilææ, in qua erat educatus. Post paucos dies inuitatus ad nuptias cum Maria matre sua & discipulis, venit Cana oppidum, vbi primum illud miraculum editum est. Absolutis nuptiis profectus est Capernaum, hinc ascendit Hierosolyma celebraturus Pascha, quod primum fuit post baptisma suum, vbi docuit, pariterque edidit miracula, vbi etiam sermones illos habuit, de quibus iam proxime contulit cum Nicodemo. Atque hucusque perduxi historiam Christi. Hinc, absoluto iam primo post baptismum Paschate, venit vnà cum discipulis suis in territorium Iudææ. Atque hæc est illa profectio, quâ habemus in hoc contextu, a qua ordimur secundam capitis partem quæ cotinet hanc profectionem, vnà cum iis quæ facta sunt & acciderunt Domino commorante in Iudææ territorio. Venit igitur Hierosolymis in territorium Iudææ, vnà cum discipulis suis, & illic degebat cum eis, neque vero in otio degebat, sed per baptismum initiauit homines regno cœlorum, docens nos exemplo suo vbicunque demum locorum simus, nunquam esse prorsus vacandum a munere, sed semper agendum alioqui bonum, imprimis vero laborandum, vt homines ad Deum adducamus. Baptizabat igitur Christus, non ipse quidem suis manibus, vt habemus Iohan. 4. 2. sed baptizabat per ministerium discipulorum: Quamquam Iesus ipse, inquit, non baptizabat, sed eius discipuli. Ipse tamen Christus solus semper fuit, est, & erit, internus ille & efficax baptizator & purgator nostri per sanguine suum, ad remissionem peccatorum, & per spiritum suum ad regenerationem. Vnde sequitur non esse tam curiose & anxiè disputandum de Ministro, qualem eum esse oportet, an fidelem, pium & bonum necessario, cum efficacia baptismi a solo Christo pendeat, non ab homine, qui legitimè vocatus seruétque integram institutionē Domini, satis est. Baptizabat autem etiam Iohannes.
units.tr: JESUS, as we have said more than once already, entering upon his thirtieth year, came to John in the desert, to be baptized by him. Having been baptized and initiated into the office of Mediator, he was led by the Spirit into the desert, where he fasted forty days and nights. From there he returned to John in the desert, at which time some disciples were called to Christ, namely John, Andrew, whose name is not expressed, and Simon Peter, Andrew's brother. Then, returning to Galilee, on the way Philip and Nathanael were called, and together with them he came to Nazareth, the city of Galilee in which he had been brought up. After a few days, invited to a wedding with Mary his mother and his disciples, he came to the town of Cana, where the first miracle was performed. When the wedding was over he set out for Capernaum, and from there went up to Jerusalem to celebrate the Passover, which was the first after his baptism, where he taught and likewise performed miracles, and where he also gave those sermons about which we have just now spoken with Nicodemus.
