And so far I have carried forward the history of Christ. Hence, now that the first Passover after the baptism is finished, he came with his disciples into the territory of Judea. And this is that departure which we have in this context, with which we begin the second part of the chapter, which contains this departure together with the things that were done and happened while the Lord was staying in the territory of Judea. He came therefore to the territory of Judea from Jerusalem, together with his disciples, and there he stayed with them. Nor did he stay in idleness, but through baptism he initiated men into the kingdom of heaven, teaching us by his example that wherever we are, we must never be wholly free from our office, but must always be doing good, and above all must labour to bring men to God. Christ therefore baptized, not indeed with his own hands, as we have in John 4. 2., but he baptized through the ministry of his disciples: "Although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples," he says. Yet Christ himself alone has always been, is, and will be the inward and effective baptizer and purifier of us, by his blood for the forgiveness of sins, and by his Spirit for regeneration. Whence it follows that we need not dispute so anxiously and minutely about the minister, what kind of man he must be, whether he must necessarily be faithful, pious and good, since the efficacy of baptism depends on Christ alone and not on the man; it is enough that he be lawfully called and keep the whole institution of the Lord. Moreover John also baptized.

units.la: Hactenus profectio Christi fuit in territorium Iudææ, & de Baptismo per ipsius discipulos ibi ministrato, nunc sequitur controuersia quædā, quæ accidit Domino commorante in Iudææ territorio. Incidit autem
units.tr: Hitherto the journey of Christ has been into the territory of Judea, and about the baptism administered there by his disciples; now follows a certain controversy, which arose while the Lord was staying in the territory of Judea. It arose

units.la: I. iiij
units.tr: I. iiij

units.la: inter quosdam ex discipulis Iohannis & Iudæos, fuit verò de purgatione. Primùm narratur de Iohanne Baptista, quid ille interea temporis agebat cùm Dominus baptizaret in Iudææ territorio: éstque hic præfatio quædam, qua transit ad sequentem historiam: secundò habemus cötrouersiam ipsam: tertiò quæsimoniam discipulorum Iohannis, habitam apud Magistrum suum: quartò responsum Iohannis. De Iohanne igitur præfationis loco dicitur, quòd baptizabat eo ipso tempore in Ænon prope Salim, quo Iesus baptizabat in territorio Iudææ. Ænon & Salim vrbes erant non longè dissitæ à Iordane. Quoniam aquæ multæ erant illic. Ratio cur eo potissimum in loco baptizaret Iohannes, ab aquarum copia quæ inseruiebant vsui baptismi. Et veniebant ac baptizabantur. Quo succeßu baptizauit Iohannes in Ænon ostenditur, Eo ibi versante & baptizante non defuerunt quos baptizaret. Nondum enim fuerat coniectus Iohannes in carcerem. Ratio est ministerij Iohannis adhuc durantis per occupationem. Nunc quod occurrit obseruandum, hoc est, Iohannes quo tempore baptizaret in Ænon, satis intellexit Christum interea temporis in territorio Iudææ baptizasse, & maiori quàm ipse fecerit cum successu baptizasse, multóque plures & frequentiores venisse ad eum quàm ad se, neque tamen propterea Iohannes destitit ab officio, verùm si vnquam antea gnauiter & sedulò officium fecit, & hoc tempore faciebat, nulla cum æmulatione & inuidia aduersus Christum, cuius se tantùm præcursorem esse probè nouerat. Quo facto & exemplo Iohannis docetur nos quotquot ministerio hoc fungimur, tum cum Deo visum est excitare homines cum maioribus donis, quàm quæ accepimus nos, plúsque eorum ministerio prodesse Ecclesiæ suæ, quàm nostro, tu, inquà, non oportere nos ideo languescere & remissiores esse in officio, quòd non simus vel superiores, vel certè pares, sed sedulò interea officiū facere, perpetuò ante oculos habentes commune illud opus ædificationis Ecclesiæ Dei, & gaudetes ex animo, cum videmus illud opus promoueri, cuiuscunque demum opera illud fiat. Quid igitur? Atqui quouis modo siue in speciē siue sincerè Christus annunciatur, de hoc quoque gaudeo atque
units.tr: between some of John's disciples and the Jews, and it was about purification. First, it is told about John the Baptist, what he was doing meanwhile while the Lord was baptizing in the territory of Judea; and this is a certain preface, by which he passes on to the following history. Secondly, we have the controversy itself; thirdly, the question of John's disciples, raised before their Master; fourthly, John's answer. So concerning John, by way of preface, it is said that he was baptizing at that same time in Aenon near Salim, while Jesus was baptizing in the territory of Judea. Aenon and Salim were towns not far distant from the Jordan. Quoniam aquae multae erant illic. The reason why John baptized especially in that place is the abundance of water, which served the use of baptism. Et veniebant ac baptizabantur. By this success John's baptizing in Aenon is shown: while he was there baptizing, there were not lacking those whom he might baptize. For John had not yet been thrown into prison. This is the reason why his ministry was still continuing without interruption. Now what should be observed here is this: while John was baptizing in Aenon, he well understood that Christ meanwhile had been baptizing in the territory of Judea, and with greater success than he himself had had, and that many more and more frequent crowds came to him than to himself; yet John did not on that account cease from his office, but if he had ever before performed his office earnestly and diligently, he did so now too, with no rivalry or envy towards Christ, whose forerunner only he knew himself to be. Quo facto & exemplo of John we are taught, all of us who discharge this ministry, that when it has pleased God to raise up men with greater gifts than we have received, and to use their ministry to benefit his Church more than ours, we ought not on that account to grow slack and more remiss in our office, because we are not superior or at least equal to them; but we should diligently perform our office meanwhile, always keeping before our eyes that common work of building up the Church of God, and rejoicing from the heart when we see that work advanced, by whomsoever it is done. What then? Yet in whatever way Christ is proclaimed, whether in appearance or in sincerity, I rejoice in this too and

units.la: Ministerij Iohannis, eiusdem-que successus.
units.tr: The ministry of John, and its outcome.

units.la: Iohannis pietas & sinceritas.
units.tr: The piety and sincerity of John.

units.la: Vsus huius exempli. atque etiam gaudebo,inquit Apostolus. Praeterea ex eo quod dicitur ideo baptizasse Iohannem, quod nondum esset coniectus in carcerem, discimus Iohannem in officio fuisse assiduum, tantisper dum Dei voluntate omnis illi libertas praerepta esset. Quo quidem exemplo admonemur perpetuo dum licet & liberum est quoquo modo aliquid in officio agendum esse, dum licet ambulare ambulandum, ut officio ne desimus. Cum vero praerepta est nobis ambulandi libertas, loquendum tamen dum licet per linguam. Cum denique praereptus est nobis linguae usus, movendam tamen manum, aut aliquo gestu corporis significandum id quod volumus hominibus amplecti, ad salutem suam aeternam. Paulus quandiu potuit, semper in itineribus fuit, coniectus in vincula & Romam deiatus, ubi in custodia detinebatur, loquutus est tamen interea, neque parum etiam in aula Caesaris lingua profecit, unde gloriatur apud Timotheum: In quo, inquit, velut facinorosus affligor usque ad vincula: sed sermo Dei non est vinctus. Id quod tam obnixe fecit, ut in vinculis cum esset Romae, hoc unum expetierit, ut cum libertate loqui posset; Unde ad Ephesios cum Roma scriberet ut & ad Colossenses, egit cum iis serio, ut id a Deo precibus contenderent, non quidem ut liberaretur vinculis, sed ut in vinculis haerens linguam haberet solutam, & daretur ipsi sermo ad apertionem oris sui cum libertate, &c. De Martyribus denique legimus quod in mediis tormentis haerentes, cum lingua nihil possent, tamen vel manus significatione, vel alio aliquo gestu corporis plurimum effecisse apud populum, & non paucos coegisse ad veritatem Christi. Quare semper, dum licet, quouis modo perstandum in officio, & quo propius abest finis, eo alacrius & intensius agendum est. Ipsum arbitror, inquit Petrus, quamdiu sum in hoc Tabernaculo excitare vos per commonefactionem, quum sciam breui futurum, ut deponam hoc tabernaculum meum, sicut Dominus noster Iesus Christus declaravit mihi. Seruus si sciret dominum suum cito superventurum, annon laboraret impensissime? Annos, cum sciamus scito venturum Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum (veniet enim cito, neque tardabit) nos, inquam, in otio securi desidebimus? Vae otianti & negligenter facienti opus Domini in ad ventum Domini. At multo magis væ verberanti conseruos: quinetiam edenti & bibenti cum ebriis, væ homicidis istis, væ adulteris, væ sacrilegis, væ blasphemis, væ persecutoribus, væ aliis omnibus quos Dominus male facientes offendet in aduentu suo. Vide Matth. 24. 45. & deinceps. Orta est igitur quæstio. Sequitur nunc controuersia ipsa & quæstio. Puto equidem extitisse hanc controuersiam inter discipulos Iohannis quosdam, & eos Iudæorum qui à Christo erant baptizati, idque de Baptismo Christi, quem hic generali nomine purgationis vocat. Nam de Baptismo Christi, controuersia videmus fuisse, non autem de legalibus lotionibus & purgationibus. Verisimile est enim discipulos Iohannis Christo inuidisse Baptismū suum & gratiam illam qua multis partibus superauit ipsorum magistrum Iohanne, idque ex præposteró quodam magistri studio. Philautia ista quæ est amor nostri & nostrorum, admodum periculosa est; Adeo enim etiam bonos saepe transuersos agit, ut, cum oporteat omnes nos habere ante oculos commune illud opus ædificationis, & ipsum ante omnia respicere, ut, inquam, faciat obliuisci ferè communis operis, nos autem ipsos nostramque gloriam nimis intendere, eoque inuidere iis, quos videmus excellere alios in illo opere communi faciendo. Corinthi in initio extitisse æmulatione & inuidia huiusmodi legimus, & colligimus ex 12.cap.1.Epist.ad Cor. Quo loco operæpretium est videre, quo pacto argumentetur Paulus aduersus eos qui quòd non essent præditi ita excellentibus donis, segregârunt se à corpore. Si dicat, inquit, pes, quia non sum manus, non sum ex corpore, nu ob id non est ex corpore? hoc est, si quod inferius membrum aliquod in corpore humano, segregaret se à reliquo corpore, ideo quòd non esset statim excellentissimum aliquod membrū in corpore, ut manus, ut oculus, an id decenter ab eo fieri videretur? Idem dici potest de corpore illo Christi: Quod si membrum aliquod, cui datum est donum non ita excellens, ideo separet se à reliquo corpore, quòd non sit illi datum à Deo præstantissimum quodque donum, an id decorum videretur? Rursus illo capite argumentatur Apostolus per concessionem quandam, vt detur, inquit, inquit, hoc, omnia membra esse vnum membrum, annon tum sequeretur necessario interitus aliorum membrorum, ac proinde totius corporis? Sí totum, inquit, corpus esset oculus, ubi auditus? si totum auditus, ubi odoratus? quasi dicat: Tum quidem necesse esset vt perirent alia membra, ac proinde collaberetur totum corpus. Hactenus Paulus: Ego autem semper fui in ea sententia, quòd si cui quàm minimum, in tam praeclaro Ministerio tis antidonum sit datum, id majus esse profecto, quàm quisque tum mereatur, cùm tantum in nobis sit mortis aeternae meritum. Dicam amplius, quòd si nullum aliud donum datum sit tibi, quàm hoc solum, vt sis homo Christianus, vt remittantur tibi peccata tua, vt sis haeres vitae aeternae, profecto datum est tibi donum, cui tu par esse non potes. Paulus agit gratias Christo quòd robustum ipsum effecerit, quòd fidelem ipsum duxerit, vt qui ipsum in ministerio constituerit: Verùm considerata conditione sua illa misera, qua prius persequutor erat, blasphemus erat, iniuriosus erat, oblitus quodammodo illius doni ministerij, incipit cogitare de dono remissionis peccatorum, & salutis in Christo Iesu, qui venit in mundum, vt peccatores seruaret, ac seipsum quidem imprimis. Ponderata denique tanta erga se Dei in Christo misericordia, erumpit in laudem & gratiarum actionem quantam potest maximam. Regi autem, inquit, aeterno, immortali, invisibili, soli sapienti Deo honor sit & gloria in saecula saeculorum, Amen. Non immunes erant etiam fortasse ab omni culpa Iudaeorum illi, qui baptizati a Christo cum Iohannis discipulis de Baptismo contenderent. Cùm enim ventum est ad huiusmodi lites & contentiones, tum difficile cuiquam non peccare. Iudaeorum igitur istos, quicunque demum illi fuerunt, verisimile est Iohannis discipulos, & a Iohanne baptizatos, praefe, qui a Christo sunt baptizati, contemnisse, neque caruisse aliquo superbiae spiritu. Qui enim excellunt donis Dei, nisi idem Deus modum ipsis imponat, fere superbiunt donis illis. Id quòd contigit Corinthiis aetate Pauli. Non igitur erit alienum ab hoc instituto, si viderimus quomodo eos in ordinem cogat Apostolus eodem illo capite supra citato. Non p-
units.tr: Use of this example. "Yes, and I will rejoice," says the Apostle. Moreover, from the fact that John is said to have baptized because he had not yet been thrown into prison, we learn that John was constant in his office for as long as God's will left him any freedom. By this example we are admonished that, as long as we may and are free, we must in some way always be active in our office: while we may walk, we must walk, so that we do not fail in our duty. When the liberty to walk is taken from us, we must still speak while we may, with the tongue. When at last the use of the tongue is taken from us, we must still move the hand, or signify by some gesture of the body what we wish men to embrace for their eternal salvation. Paul, as long as he could, was always on the road. Cast into chains and carried to Rome, where he was kept in custody, he nevertheless went on speaking, and he advanced the gospel by his tongue not a little even in Caesar's court; whence he boasts to Timothy: "In which I suffer trouble, as an evildoer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound." He did this so earnestly that, while in chains at Rome, he desired this one thing, that he might be able to speak with boldness. Hence, writing from Rome to the Ephesians and likewise to the Colossians, he earnestly urged them to ask God in prayer for this, not that he might be freed from his chains, but that, while he remained in chains, his tongue might be loosed, and utterance be given him to open his mouth with boldness, and so on. Finally, we read of the martyrs that, held fast in the midst of torments and unable to do anything with the tongue, they nevertheless accomplished much among the people by a sign of the hand or some other gesture of the body, and compelled not a few to the truth of Christ. Therefore, always while it is permitted, we must persist in our office in whatever way we can, and the nearer the end, the more eagerly and intensely we must act. "I think it right," says Peter, "as long as I am in this tabernacle, to stir you up by reminding you, since I know that I shall soon put off this my tabernacle, as our Lord Jesus Christ has shown me." "If a servant knew that his lord would soon come upon him, would he not labour most diligently? Since we know that our Lord Jesus Christ will come (for he will come quickly and will not delay), shall we, I say, sit idle and secure in leisure? Woe to the one who is idle and does the work of the Lord negligently at the coming of the Lord. But much more woe to the one who beats his fellow servants, and indeed to the one who eats and drinks with drunkards: woe to those murderers, woe to adulterers, woe to the sacrilegious, woe to blasphemers, woe to persecutors, woe to all the others whom the Lord will strike when he comes, those who do evil." See Matt. 24. 45 and following. A question therefore arises. Now follows the controversy itself and the question. I think this controversy arose between certain disciples of John and those Jews who had been baptized by Christ, and that it concerned the baptism of Christ, which he here calls by the general name of purification. For we see that the controversy was about the baptism of Christ, not about the legal washings and purifications. It is likely that the disciples of John envied Christ his baptism and the grace by which in many respects he surpassed their master John, and that they did so out of a perverse zeal for their master. That self-love, which is love of ourselves and of our own, is very dangerous; for it often leads even good men astray, so that, although we ought all to keep before our eyes that common work of building up and to regard it above all, it makes us almost forget the common work, while we fix our attention too intently on ourselves and our own glory, and so begrudge those whom we see excelling others in doing that common work. We read that at Corinth in the beginning there was rivalry and envy of this kind, and we gather it from 1 Cor. 12. Here it is worth seeing how Paul argues against those who, because they were not endowed with such excellent gifts, separated themselves from the body. "If the foot shall say, Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body?" That is: if some lower member of the human body were to separate itself from the rest of the body because it was not at once the most excellent member, such as the hand or the eye, would that seem fittingly done? The same can be said of that body of Christ: if any member to which a gift not so excellent has been given should separate itself from the rest of the body, because the most outstanding gift has not been given to it by God, would that seem seemly? Again, in that chapter the Apostle argues by a certain concession: granted, he says, that all members are one member, would it not then necessarily follow that the other members perish, and therefore the whole body? "If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the smelling be?" As if he said: then indeed the other members would have to perish, and so the whole body would collapse. So far Paul. But I have always been of this opinion: that if anyone has been given even the smallest share in so excellent a ministry, this is certainly greater than what each one deserves, since in us there is nothing but the merit of eternal death. I will say more: if no other gift has been given you than this alone, that you should be a Christian man, that your sins should be forgiven, that you should be an heir of eternal life, then certainly a gift has been given you to which you cannot be equal. Paul gives thanks to Christ that he made him strong and counted him faithful, appointing him to the ministry. But, considering his own wretched condition, in which he had formerly been a persecutor, a blasphemer and an insulter, and having in a way forgotten the gift of the ministry, he begins to think of the gift of forgiveness of sins and of salvation in Christ Jesus, who came into the world to save sinners, and of himself first of all. Finally, having weighed so great a mercy of God toward himself in Christ, he breaks out into praise and thanksgiving as great as he can. "To the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever, Amen. Perhaps those too who, baptized by Christ, contended about baptism with the disciples of John were not free from all fault of the Jews. For when things come to such quarrels and contentions, it is difficult for anyone not to sin. It is likely, therefore, that those Jews, whoever they were, despised the disciples of John, who had been baptized by John, in comparison with those baptized by Christ, and that they did not lack some spirit of pride. For those who excel in the gifts of God, unless God himself sets a measure on them, are generally puffed up with those gifts. This happened to the Corinthians in Paul's time. It will not therefore be foreign to this plan if we see how the Apostle brings them into order in the same chapter cited above.

units.la: Amari itest, inquit, oculus dicere manui, Non est mihi opus te, aut rursum caput pedibus, Non est mihi opus vobis. Imo multo potius quae videntur membra corporis infirmissima esse, necessaria sunt.
units.tr: "The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you; or again the head to the feet, I have no need of you. Nay, much rather those members of the body which seem to be the weakest are necessary." (1 Cor. 12.)

units.la: 9. d. Imo sic disposuit Deus omnia corporis membra, vt infirmissimum quodque necessarium sit firmissimo & praestantissimo. Quod si ita res habeat in corpore humano, profecto in corpore Christi, ne ab excellentissimo quidem aliquo membro dici potest, non esse sibi opus vel infimo & vilissimo quoque membro. Vt enim in corpore humano vilissimum quodque membrum habet functionem quandam suam & facultatem in corpore propriam, quae ipsa non potest exerceri ab alio vllo membro in corpore. (Neque enim oculus, quod est excellentissimum quoddam in corpore nostro membrum, aut etiam caput ipsum tam variis & excellentibus ornatum dotibus, potest tamen facere officium pedis:) Itaque habet in corpore Christi. Vnusquisque accepit donum suum ad aedificationem & bonum communis corporis, etiam membrum quod omnium infimum est, accepit donum quoddam suum. Quod si attendas, non reperies, ne in praestantissimo quidem, quod etiam suo loco inseruit communi corpori. Velim igitur corpus Christi, quod est Ecclesia, animaduertat ad illa dona etiam inferiora, quae tamen vsui sunt corpori, & sine quibus non posset bene esse Ecclesiae & communi corpori. Quod si omnes ministros Ecclesiae haberet Ecclesia, dumtaxat oculos aut manus, non esset Ecclesiae, perfectum corpus, sic enim careret pedibus, quibus ingrederetur. Vt igitur perfectum sit corpus Ecclesiae videat oculo, apprehendat aliquid manu, ingrediatur pedibus. Capiat doctrinam ab eo qui accepit doctrinae donum; Exhortatione ab eo qui accepit donum exhortationis, consolatione ab eo qui accepit donum consolationis.
units.tr: 9. d. Indeed God has so arranged all the members of the body that the weakest is necessary to the strongest and most excellent. If this is so in the human body, then surely in the body of Christ no member, however excellent, can say that it has no need even of the lowest and humblest. For just as in the human body the humblest member has a function and power of its own in the body, which no other member can exercise (the eye, though it is an excellent member of our body, and even the head itself, adorned with so many and such excellent gifts, cannot perform the office of the foot), so it is in the body of Christ. Each has received his gift for the building up and good of the common body, and even the lowest member has received a gift of its own. If you look closely, you will not find one that is not also placed in its own position for the common body, even among the most distinguished. I would therefore have the body of Christ, which is the Church, attend to those lesser gifts also, which nevertheless serve the body and without which the Church and the common body could not be well. For if the Church had only eyes or hands as ministers, that is, no others, it would not be a perfect body of the Church, since it would lack the feet by which it walks. So, that the body of the Church may be perfect, let it see with the eye, take hold of something with the hand, and walk with the feet. Let it take teaching from the one who has received the gift of teaching, exhortation from the one who has received the gift of exhortation, and comfort from the one who has received the gift of comfort.

units.la: 26 Venerunt que ad Iohannem, & dixerunt ei, Rabbi, is qui tecum erat apud transsetum Iordanis, cui tu testimonium dedisti, ecce baptizat, & omnes veniunt ad eum.
units.tr: 26 And they came to John and said to him, Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you gave testimony, behold, he baptizes, and all men come to him.

units.la: Hactenus fuit illa controuersia: Nunc veniunt discipuli Iohannis ad Magistrum suum conquerendi gratia. Rabbi, inquiunt, in qui tecum erat apud traiectum Iordanis, cui tu testimonium dedisti, ecce baptizat, & omnes venient ad eum. Designant Christum circumstantiis quibusdam. 1. Qui tecum erat trans Iordanem. 2. Cui tu dedisti testimonium. Bis venit ad Iohannem Christus, ut supra diximus. Iohannes autem testatus est cum esse agnum Dei qui tolleret peccata mundi. Sed discipuli isti hic testantem de Christo, non intellexerunt. Audiuerunt quidem testantem eum, sed non crediderunt: quod si crediderint, sequuti fuissent Christum, relicto Iohanne, id quod fecerunt alij, ut Andreas, & is cuius nomen non est expressum. Male igitur illud habere potuit Iohannem, quod ipsius discipuli non statim crediderint ipsius de Christo testimonio. Verum haec eorum confessio, quod ipse testatus sit de Christo, quod non defuerit officio suo, potuit rursus hominem consolari. Minister det operam ut saltem, officio fideliter obito, extorqueat ab incredulis hanc confessionem, quod bona fide functus sit officio suo. Quod si in illo die coram illo tribunali comparuerit non ornatus hoc testimonio conscientiarum, vae ipsi. Oportet enim, si non ora, certe conscientias hominum ita constrictas habere, ut testentur de fide vitae nostrae in officio. Quamquam in illo die verum ac solidum demum gaudium erit, cum multos sistemus Christo, quos nostro ministerio lucrifecimus in terris. Quae est spes nostra, aut gaudium, aut corona de qua glorier? Annon & vos estis in conspectu Domini nostri Iesu Christi in eius adventu? Aliquid tamen didicerunt discipuli Iohannis ex Magistro suo Iohanne, nimirum tantum quantum potuit reddere eos inexcusabiles. Potuerunt enim hoc dicere, Iohannem testatum esse de Christo. Qui audiunt Christum praedicatum, neque plus fructus ex auditu reportat, quam id quod possunt dicere Ministrum Euangelij de Christo locutum esse (ut sol respondere non pauci cum quaeritur ab iis, finita iam coniunctione, quid a concionatore dictum sit: Multa, inquit, de Deo, multa de Christo loquutus est, quae tamen nos nescimus, si tamen vel hoc solum possunt dicere) didicerunt a Ministro quantum satis sit ad ipsorum iustam damnationem. Festus apud Agrippam dixit, Paulus
units.tr: So far went that dispute. Now the disciples of John come to their Master to complain. Rabbi, they say, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you gave testimony, behold, he baptizes, and all come to him. They describe Christ by certain circumstances: (1) he who was with you beyond the Jordan; (2) to whom you gave testimony. Christ came to John twice, as we said above. John indeed testified that he was the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. But these disciples did not understand him when he bore witness of Christ. They did hear him testify, but they did not believe; for if they had believed, they would have followed Christ, leaving John, as others did, such as Andrew and the one whose name is not given. It could not therefore have grieved John that his own disciples did not at once believe his testimony about Christ. Yet their acknowledgement, that he had testified of Christ and had not failed in his office, could again console him. The minister should take pains that, having faithfully discharged his office, he at least extracts from unbelievers this confession, that he has acted in good faith in his office. But if on that day he appears before that judgment seat not adorned with this testimony of consciences, woe to him. For it is necessary, if not mouths, at least the consciences of men should be so bound that they bear witness to the faithfulness of our life in our office. Yet on that day true and solid joy will at last come, when we shall present to Christ the many whom we have won by our ministry on earth. What is our hope, or joy, or crown in which I may glory? Are not you also, in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming? Still, the disciples of John learned something from their Master John, namely just so much as could render them inexcusable. For they could say that John had testified of Christ. Those who hear Christ preached, and take from the hearing no more fruit than what they can say, that a minister of the Gospel spoke of Christ (as not a few answer when asked, once the sermon is over, what the preacher said: "He spoke much of God, much of Christ, which however we do not know," if indeed they can even say this much), have learned from the minister enough for their own just condemnation. Festus said before Agrippa, in Paul's defence, that Jesus, whom the Jews said was dead, was alive.

units.la: Ministrorum verbi cogitatio perpetua. lum in defensione sua, testatum esse Iesum, quem dixerunt Iudæi mortuum, vixisse. Reportauit quidem Festus, qui non credidit prædicationi Pauli, satis magnam materiam damnationis suæ. Queruntur Christum maiori cum successu & frequentia populi baptizare quàm Iohannem. Prius inuiderunt gratiæ, nunc inuident successui. Eò nos prouehit hæc, qua laboramus, philautia, vt non modò gratiæ & personæ inuideamus, sed etiam successui & profectui Ecclesiæ Dei, qui fit personæ ministerio. Etsi enim optemus successum suum Ecclesiæ Dei, tamen volumus eum per nos fieri, vt honoris saltem aliqua pars ad nos redundet, tam studiosi sumus interea dum Deum quærimus etiam nostri ipsorum. Beatus est qui eum fecit progressum in se abnegando, quo possit simplici oculo Dei gloriam intueri, ac quibus velit instrumentis vti in ædificanda Ecclesia sua. Paulus passus est Deum vti instrumentis iis in prædicando Christo, qui etiam per contentionem & non sincere prædicarunt, existimantes se afflictionem addere vinculis ipsius. Nihil enim sibi cura esse dixit modò Christus annunciaretur, Christi gloriam in solidum ob oculos habens, interea persuadens sibi Deum nunquam fraudaturum spem suam. Quod & nos nobis persuadere possumus, si in vnicam Dei gloriam intenti fimus in vtendo illa gratia quantulacunque est, quam ipse nobis est largitus, persuadere, inquam, possumus nobis hac conditione Deum nunquam passurum vt pudefiamus, per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum, cui sit omnis honor & gloria: Amen.
units.tr: The constant thought of the ministers of the Word. Festus, who did not believe Paul's preaching, gained indeed enough material for his own condemnation. The disciples complain that Christ baptizes with greater success and a larger crowd than John. First they envied the grace, now they envy the success. This self-love, with which we struggle, carries us so far that we envy not only the grace and the person, but also the success and progress of the Church of God, which comes through the ministry of a person. For although we wish the Church of God success, we want it to come through us, so that at least some part of the honour may flow back to us; so eager are we, even while we seek God, to seek ourselves too. Blessed is he who has made such progress in self-denial that he can look upon the glory of God with a single eye, and that he is willing to use whatever instruments he pleases in building up his Church. Paul allowed God to use those instruments in preaching Christ who preached even out of contention and not sincerely, supposing that they would add affliction to his bonds. For he said that he was not concerned, provided only that Christ was proclaimed, keeping the glory of Christ wholly before his eyes, while persuading himself that God would never disappoint his hope. We too can persuade ourselves of this, if we are intent upon the sole glory of God in using that grace, however small, which he has bestowed upon us; I say we can persuade ourselves that on these terms God will never allow us to be put to shame, through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be all honour and glory: Amen.

units.la: 27 Respondit Iohannes, & dixit, Homo non potest recipere quicquam nisi fuerit ei datum e cœlo.
units.tr: 27 John answered and said, A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.

units.la: 28 Vos ipsi mihi testes estis me dixisse, Non sum ego Christus, sed missus sum qui apparerem coram eo.
units.tr: 28 You yourselves are my witnesses that I said, I am not the Christ, but I am sent before him.

units.la: 29 Qui habet sponsam, sponsus est: amicus autem sponsi, qui stat & audit eum, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi: hoc ergo gaudium meum im-pletum est. pletum est.
units.tr: 29 He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. This my joy therefore is fulfilled.

units.la: 30 Illum oportet crescere, me vero minui.
units.tr: 30 He must increase, but I must decrease.

units.la: 31 Qui super venit, supra omnes est: qui e terra est, terrenus est, & terrena loquitur, qui e coelo venit, supra omnes est.
units.tr: 31 He who comes from above is above all: he who is of the earth is earthly, and speaks of the earth; he who comes from heaven is above all.

units.la: 32 Et quod vidit & audiuit, hoc testatur: sed testimonium eius nemo recipit.
units.tr: 32 And what he has seen and heard, that he testifies; and no one receives his testimony.

units.la: Sequitur responsum Iohannis, primum, quia oculi discipulorum ipsius erant fixi tantum in eo, & admirati sunt eum tanquam Deum aliquem, quem viderunt admirabili quadam gratia imbutum esse: ideo Iohannes eorum oculos paulisper auertit a se couertitque ad coelos, ut videant Deum authorem & fontem omnis gratiae. Homo, inquit, non potest recipere quicquam nisi fuerit ei datum e coelo. Negat in hominis potestate esse adiicere sibi vel tantillum gratiae, eam autem totam caelitus venire affirmat, ac proinde Deum eius authorem solum facit, ad hoc ut discipuli ipsius oculos suos supra ipsum erigerent, Deumque glorificarent in illa gratia quam deprehenderunt in Iohanne. Atque hoc quidem Iohannis exemplo faciendum est ab omnibus iis qui excellunt alios aliqua gratia, siue in politia, siue in Ecclesia. Vulgus hominum natura nimis propensum est ad colendos eos tanquam Deos in quibus conspicatur aliquid eximij esse, neque tantum hoc faciunt qui ignari sunt Dei & Christi authoris & datoris omnis gratiae, sicuti fecisse Lystrenses legimus, qui admirati opus illud miraculosum Pauli & Barnabae, coeperunt sacrificare. Non hi solum, inquam, hoc faciunt, sed etiam ij qui de Deo & de Christo audierunt, profitenturque se scire Deum authorem omnium rerum: Nam his quoque efficax est Satanas, facitque ut homines aequo admirentur, quod fecisse Corinthios legimus post auditum ex Paulo & aliis Euangelium. Quidam dixit se esse Pauli, alter vero se esse Apollos. Remedium quoddam aduersus hoc tantum malum praesens habemus in his verbis Iohannis: Hominum oculi continuo ab hominibus transferendi sunt ad Deum omnium
units.tr: There follows John's answer. First, because the eyes of his disciples were fixed only on him, and they admired him as some god whom they saw endowed with a certain wonderful grace, John turned their eyes a little away from himself and directed them to heaven, so that they might see God, the author and fountain of all grace. "A man," he says, "can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven." He denies that it is within a man's power to add to himself even the smallest grace, and he affirms that all grace comes from heaven; accordingly he makes God alone its author, so that his disciples might lift their eyes above him and glorify God for that grace which they had discovered in John. And this is what all who excel others in some grace ought to do after John's example, whether in civil government or in the Church. The common sort of men is by nature too inclined to worship as gods those in whom they perceive something extraordinary, and not only do those do so who are ignorant of God and of Christ, the author and giver of all grace, as we read the Lystrans did, who, amazed at the miraculous work of Paul and Barnabas, began to sacrifice to them. I say that not only these do so, but also those who have heard of God and of Christ and profess that they know God to be the author of all things. For Satan is effective even among these, and makes men admire alike, as we read the Corinthians did after hearing the Gospel from Paul and others. One said he was of Paul, another that he was of Apollos. We have a present remedy against this great evil in these words of John: the eyes of men must continually be turned away from men to God, the fountain and author of all good things. So Paul: "Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase." So we say, if a comparison is made between man and God, that neither Luther is anything, nor Melanchthon is anything...

units.la: { } Act. 14. bonorum fontem & authorem. Sic Paulus, Neque is, in-quit,qui plantat est aliquid, neque is qui rigat,sed Deus qui dat incrementum. Sic nos dicimus, si comparatio fiat hominis & Dei, neque Lutherum esse aliquid, neque Melanæthonem esse aliquid, neque Caluinum ipsum, quem nos Deum facere mentiuntur aduersarij; nō dicimus, inquam, eum esse aliquid, sed dicimus Christum, a quo solo volumus nos denominari, solum, inquam, Christum esse omnia; cui sit omnis honor & gloria, Amen. Si aduertamus diligentius ad hæc Baptistæ verba, videbimus eum innuere, contentum se esse ea gratiæ mensura, quantulamcunque accepit a Deo: dicit enim, omnem gratiam a Deo dari hominibus, & eius voluntate definiri, quo significat se conquiescere in Dei voluntate, qui distribuit cuique prout vult. Natura homines supra modum appetunt dona ista Spiritus, per quæ fit vt in admiratione sint apud homines, imo magis impense his studet, quam donis illis omni exceptione maioribus, & quæ ad alteram vitam pertinent, vt sunt remissio peccatorum, regeneratio, &c. Quam quidem naturæ propensionem, vt taceam experientiam illa, quam omnes nos in nobis ipsi sentire possumus, non obscure præ se tulerunt septuaginta illi discipuli dimissi a Christo ad prædicandum Euangelium, qui quidem reuersi & reddentes rationem Domino eorum quæ fecerunt, & miraculorum quæ ediderunt per nomen ipsius, plus quidem gaudii sunt illis miraculis, suo ministerio editis, quam vita ipsa æterna. Qua re animaduersa, Christus admonuit gaudendum esse potius, quod nomina ipsorum scripta essent in cœlis. Temperari autem potest immoderatus ille appetitus istarum rerum, vel hac ratione maxime; Si cogitemus Deum, qui admensus est nobis hanc mensuram gratiæ, ita velle. Sic enim conquiescimus in Dei voluntate, eumque glorificamus. Nam ea omnium nostrum sententia de Deo nostro esse debet: quod id demum bonum sit ac iustum, & nobis ipsis & Ecclesiæ totí utile, quodcunque ipse vult. Non hoc loquor ideo, quod nolim quemquam petere a Deo gratiæ incrementum, sed hoc permitto atque adeo moneo, vt vnusquisque petat a Deo suo acceptæ gratiæ incrementum perpetuum, verum cum hac conditione, ditione, siquidem ita velit Dominus, putetque illud magis è re fore Ecclesiæ suæ. Sunt quidam qui Deo etiam inuito volunt excellere, sefeq; venditat ac si plurimùm possent, sed ij tandem in nihilum abeunt. Atque hoc primum est quod facit Baptista, in respondendo nimirum conuertit oculos discipulorum ad Deum omnis gratiæ authorem: Vos ipsi mihi testes. Deinde purgat se omni affectatione gloriæ, quæ Christi propria est, quam discipuli ipsius ignari Christi deferre ipsi voluerunt, vocárque eos ipsos in testes, annon hoc ipsi iam antea direxit, se non esse Christum, sed missum esse qui appareret coram eo. Commendationes istæ & admirationes hominum stultorum & ignarorum Dei & Christi, periculosæ sunt admodum: ideóque qui alios antecellunt aliquo Dei dono, cauere eos diligenter oportet, ne sinant eas ad se vsque pertingere, sed eas quantis possunt viribus à se arceant. Vix enim potest fieri quin ignari peccent, cùm impensè quenquam laudant. Equidem pluris fecerim iustam commendationem vniusalicuius pij & boni viri, quàm admiratione stultam totius multitudinis. His etiam verbis Baptista discipulos suos docet quod sit officium ipsius, nempe quòd non sit Christus, sed præcursor Christi. Sed videnda est doctrinæ forma: iam antea testatus est se non esse Christum, sed Christi præcursorem, vt satis apparet ex his verbis cùm dicit, Vos mihi testes estis me dixisse. Nunc iterum idem testatur ac docet, sed simul increpat eos & excitat conscientiam superioris negligentiæ atque socordiæ, ac proinde ad resipiscentiam impellit, vt dolore affecti propter negligentiam priorem, melius in posterum proficerent. Hac docendi forma debemus vti erga eos qui negligenter verbum Dei audiuerint, nam omnis emendationis vitæ ac morum principium est resipiscentia. Nihil in posterum boni ab eo expectârim, quem non pœnituit anteactæ vitæ.
units.tr: Act. 14. the source and author of all good things. So Paul says: Neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase. So we also say, when a comparison is made between man and God, that Luther is nothing, that Melanchthon is nothing, and that Calvin himself is nothing, whom our adversaries lie in saying we make into a god. I do not say, I repeat, that he is anything; I say that Christ alone, by whose name alone we wish to be called, is all things, to whom alone be all honour and glory, Amen. If we consider more carefully these words of the Baptist, we will see that he hints at being content with that measure of grace, however small, which he received from God. For he says that all grace is given to men by God and determined by his will, by which he signifies that he rests in the will of God, who distributes to each as he wills. By nature men desire beyond measure these gifts of the Spirit, through which they come to be admired among men. Indeed they pursue these more eagerly than those gifts, far greater in every respect, which pertain to the life to come, such as the remission of sins, regeneration, and so on. To pass over the experience which we can all feel in ourselves, the seventy disciples sent out by Christ to preach the Gospel clearly showed this natural inclination. When they returned and gave an account to their Lord of what they had done and of the miracles they had performed in his name, they rejoiced more in those miracles, wrought through their ministry, than in eternal life itself. Christ, noticing this, admonished them that they ought rather to rejoice because their names were written in heaven. This immoderate appetite for such things can be tempered, most of all, by this consideration: that we think of God, who has measured out to us this measure of grace, as willing it so. For thus we rest in the will of God and glorify him. Indeed, the judgment of all of us about our God ought to be this: whatever he himself wills is finally good and just and useful both to ourselves and to the whole Church. I do not say this because I would not have anyone ask God for an increase of grace; rather I permit, and indeed advise, that each one ask his God for a continual increase of the grace he has received, but with this condition: if the Lord so wills, and judges it more to the advantage of his Church. There are some who wish to excel even against God's will, and put themselves forward as though they could do very much; but in the end they come to nothing. This is the first thing the Baptist does in his reply: he turns the eyes of the disciples to God, the author of all grace: You yourselves are my witnesses. Then he cleanses himself of every pursuit of glory, which belongs to Christ alone, a glory which his disciples, ignorant of Christ, wished to confer upon him, and he calls them themselves as witnesses: did he not already say to them that he is not the Christ, but was sent to go before him? Such commendations and admirations of foolish men who are ignorant of God and Christ are very dangerous. Therefore those who surpass others in some gift of God must carefully take care not to let such praise reach them, but must ward it off with all their strength. For it is hardly possible that the ignorant will not sin when they praise someone excessively. Indeed I would value the just commendation of some one godly and good man far more than the foolish admiration of the whole multitude. By these words also the Baptist teaches his disciples what his office is, namely that he is not the Christ but the forerunner of Christ. But the form of the teaching must be considered: he had already testified that he is not the Christ but the forerunner of Christ, as is sufficiently clear from these words, when he says, You are my witnesses that I said. Now again he testifies and teaches the same thing, but at the same time he rebukes them and stirs up their conscience over their earlier negligence and dullness, and so drives them to repentance, so that, grieved over their former negligence, they might make better progress in the future. We ought to use this manner of teaching towards those who have heard the Word of God carelessly, for the beginning of all amendment of life and conduct is repentance. I would expect nothing good in the future from one who does not repent of his past life.

units.la: Habet sponsum. Hactenus se purgauit, nunc verò comparationem inter se & Christum, respondens, videtur, potissimum ei, de quo conquesti sunt discipuli, nempe Christum baptizare & omnes ad eum venire. Ait igitur Christum esse sponsum, se autem amicum ...
units.tr: He has the bridegroom. So far he has cleared himself. Now, answering, he makes a comparison between himself and Christ, and it seems to be aimed chiefly at that matter about which the disciples complained, namely that Christ baptizes and everyone comes to him. He therefore says that Christ is the bridegroom, but he himself is the friend...

units.la: Adulatio maxima pestis in Ecclesia.
units.tr: Flattery is the greatest plague in the Church.

units.la: Sponsum vnicus Ecclesiæ Christus: reliqui omnes quales sint Iohannes ostendit. cum sponsi,qui stet & audiat voce sponsi,& gaudio gau-deat propter vocem ipsius. Hanc sententiam sic expres-sit nobis familiari quadam similitudine rerum harum terreft ium,vt sponsi, sponsæ, & amici sponsi. Difficile quidem imprimis est iis , quibus res est cum sponsa Christi,hoc est Ecclesia, sic prospicere Christo in eo ne-gotio, vt nullam etiam suiipsius rationem habeant, sed ambiant Ecclesiam Dei zelotypia,& præparent quos v-ni viro ( vt virginem puram) sistant, nempe Christo,vt loquar cum Apostolo.Qui enim honorem,diuitias,huc denique mundum quærunt in ministerio, hi necessario ambiunt,non Christo, sed sibi Christi sponsam. Reme-dium aduersus tantum malum exhibuit nobis Baptista suo exemplo, qui id semper in animo habuit, solum Christum habere sponsam, ad solum Christum ea per-tinere,se autem duntaxat esse amicum sponsi;quę etiam dignitas est satis ampla,& ob quam nunquam satis Deo gratias agere quisquam potuit. Gratiam habeo ei qui me robustum effecit,&c. Qua gratia si per summam ingrati-tudinem abusi fuerimus,& ambierimus nobis ipsi spon-sam Christi,plusquam proditores sumus. Discimus etiā hic , quod etsi amicus sponsi, id est minister Euangeli, non gaudeat gaudium sponsi, neque fructum eum percipiat ex Ecclesia,qui sponsi proprius est,non tamen ca-reat gaudio quodam suo, vel ex eo quod stet & audiat vocem illam sponsi longè suauissimam , quam rursus bona fide tanquam internuncius referat sponsæ. Nam illud extra controversiam est, sponsum Christum , cum fideli amico suo multas suauissimas promissiones communicare,renunciandas sponsæ suæ,ex quibus profecto maius existit gaudium fideli amico sponsi,quàm sit totū illud gaudium quod ex vlla re mundana & caduca percipi potest. Non est comparandum cum hoc gaudio eorum gaudium, qui à regibus terræ pro more mittuntur legati ad exteras gentes, & sponsas quas ipsi sunt in vxores ducturi:& tamen ea legatione gaudere & gloriari solent homines.
units.tr: John shows that Christ is the only bridegroom of the Church, and what all the others are like: the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears the bridegroom's voice and rejoices greatly at his voice. He has expressed this sentiment to us by a familiar comparison drawn from earthly things, namely of bridegroom, bride, and the bridegroom's friend. It is indeed especially difficult for those who have to do with the bride of Christ, that is the Church, to look so after Christ's business that they have no regard for themselves at all, but instead woo the Church of God with jealousy, and prepare those whom they present as a chaste virgin to one husband, namely Christ, to use the words of the Apostle. For those who seek honour, riches, and finally the world itself in the ministry, necessarily woo not for Christ but for themselves the bride of Christ. John the Baptist showed us a remedy against so great an evil by his example, for he always kept this in mind: that Christ alone has the bride, that the bride pertains to Christ alone, and that he himself is only the friend of the bridegroom; which dignity is also quite ample, and for which no one can ever thank God enough. I give thanks to him who has made me strong, etc. If we abuse this grace through the greatest ingratitude, and woo the bride of Christ for ourselves, we are worse than traitors. We learn here also that although the friend of the bridegroom, that is the minister of the Gospel, does not rejoice in the bridegroom's joy, nor receive from the Church the fruit that belongs to the bridegroom, yet he is not without a joy of his own, arising from the fact that he stands and hears that voice of the bridegroom, far sweeter than any other, which he in turn, faithfully, as a messenger, reports to the bride. For it is beyond dispute that the bridegroom Christ communicates to his faithful friend many most sweet promises, to be announced to his bride, and from these there truly arises in the faithful friend of the bridegroom a greater joy than the whole joy that can be derived from any worldly and transitory thing. Their joy cannot be compared with this joy, of those who are sent by the kings of the earth, as is customary, as envoys to foreign nations, to bring home the brides whom they themselves are going to take as wives; and yet men are wont to rejoice and boast in that embassy.

units.la: Hactenus fuit prima cõparatio; altera sequitur, qua gratiam suam eleuat:Illum, inquit, oportet crescere,me verò minui. In priori illa comparatione, sese aliquid fecit, nempe amicum sponsi, in hac comparatione se pro nihilo ducit, & quasi ignominiae ipse exponit in conspectu discipulorum suorum, qui tamen tanti eum fecerunt. Docet autem nos suo exemplo, oportere tantum abesse nos ab eo, ut Christi sponsi gloriae aliquam partem delatam nobis assumanus, deferentibus nimirum eam stultè nescio quibus, ut è contra nosipsi ignominiae exponamus, etiam iis inspectantibus, quibus videmur aliquid esse, ad hoc ut solus Christus glorificetur.
units.tr: So far was the first comparison; the second follows, in which he exalts his grace: He must increase, he says, but I must decrease. In the former comparison he made himself something, namely the friend of the bridegroom; in this comparison he counts himself as nothing, and as it were exposes himself to disgrace in the sight of his disciples, who nevertheless esteemed him so highly. He teaches us by his example that we must be so far from assuming for ourselves any part of the glory of the bridegroom Christ that, on the contrary, we should expose ourselves to disgrace, even in the sight of those before whom we seem to be something, so that Christ alone may be glorified.

units.la: Quaeri quisquam alius & Christi minister omnium maximè tenetur de se sobrie sentire, & se ipse negare, ut possit pati, etiam cum nominis sui ignominia, Christū glorificari. Quòd si se putet aliquid esse, cùm nihil sit, profectò non patietur totam gloriam in solidum à se in Christum transferri. Videmus praeterea in hac comparatione, Christum, ubi primum illucescere coepit, tenebras offundere cuicunque alij luci, etiam clarissimae cuique luci prophetarum tenebras offundere orientem illum solem Iustitiae, etiam luci Baptistae, qui Prophetis maior fuit. Ideoque Petrus sermonem propheticum comparat lucernae in obscuro loco lucenti, vsque dum dies ille Christi illucesceret, & lucifer Euangelij exoriretur in cordibus hominum, quo exoriente significat obscurari quodammodo vniuersam illam lucem Prophetarum, non minùs quàm oriente iam sole obfuscatur lux lucernae, quae paulò ante in obscura aliqua domo suspensa, illuminauit omnia. Hoc nostro saeculo Deo sit gloria, non tam lucerna illa prophetici sermonis, quàm lucifer Euangelij splendet: nosque, si comparemur cum veteri populo, degimus quasi in aprico, sub sole meridiano, cùm illi vixerint quasi inclusi domo obscura, non habentes nisi tenuem aliquam lucernae lucem. Vae igitur illis, qui in tanta luce positi, nihil tamen vident, cuiusmodi complures sunt hodierno die apud nos: & ô beatos illos, quorum aperti sunt oculi ad videndū tantamtam lucem.
units.tr: One should ask whether any other minister of Christ is more bound than I am to think soberly of himself, to deny himself, and to be willing to suffer, even at the cost of his own name, so that Christ may be glorified. If a man thinks he is something when he is nothing, he will certainly not allow all the glory to be transferred entirely from himself to Christ. In this comparison we also see that when Christ first begins to shine, he casts shadows over every other light, even over the brightest light of the prophets, and that rising Sun of righteousness casts shadows over the light of John the Baptist, who was greater than the prophets. So Peter likens the prophetic word to a lamp shining in a dark place, until that day of Christ dawns and the morning star of the Gospel rises in men's hearts. When it rises, the whole light of the prophets is in some measure obscured, just as, once the sun has risen, the light of a lamp that hung for a while in some dark house and lit everything is dimmed. In our age, thanks be to God, it is not so much the lamp of prophetic word that shines as the morning star of the Gospel. If we are compared with the old people, we live as if in the open, under the midday sun, while they lived as if shut up in a dark house, having only the faint light of a lamp. Woe, then, to those who, placed in so great a light, nevertheless see nothing, and there are many such among us today. Blessed are those whose eyes have been opened to see so great a light.

units.la: Quiuerne venit. Hactenus fuit comparatio, nunc Baptista, & Christus antea in illo sermone, quem cum Nicodemo contulit supra cap. 3. 11. est deinceps admiratus tantum vaporem discipulorum aliorumque Iudaeo-
units.tr: He who comes from above. So far this has been a comparison. Now, in that discourse which he held with Nicodemus, above in chapter 3, verse 11, John the Baptist and Christ are considered together. Next he marvels at the great sluggishness of the disciples and of the other Jews.

units.la: Ratio. est Ecclesiae sol. rū: ab ex-rum, delabitur in quaerimoniam, in qua conqueritur de infidelitate eorum, quā exaggerat: partim ab excellentia Christi: Qui supernè venit, inquit, supra omnes est: Hoc est, Christus Dei filius excellit omnes: partim a certitudine testimonij Christi: Quod vidit & audiuit, hoc testatur, sed tamen testimonium eius nemo recipit, hoc est, fidem ei habet. Nihil est in Christo, in quo non sit argumentum fidei firmissimum. Si respicias personam ipsius, excellit omnes; & excellentia illa personae Christi vel sola movere debet nos ad credendum. Si respicias salutem illam quam comparauit nobis, & ea quoque vim suam habet ad fidem cum tanta sit. Magnitudinem hanc expressit Apostolus ad Hebraeos, Si tantam, inquit, neglexerimus salutem. Imo si respicias quod in Christo vilissimum videtur, vt crucem ipsam, gloriosissimum est, & vim habet ad fidem efficacissimam. Cum ita sit, cumque nihil sit in Christo nisi quod ad fidem valeat & gignendam & confirmandam, si tamen nolit credere quisquam, vice versa, nihil est in eo quod non valeat ad exaggerandam infidelitate ipsius & damnationem in illa die. Sed quis est omnium qui infidelitatem hominum exaggerare potest, adductis his, quae vnus Christus suppeditat, argumentis? Sane nemo, nisi qui certo aliquo modo inspexit Christum, vidit illam excellentiam & dignitate personae ipsius, expendit pondus testimonij ipsius, magnitudine salutis complexus est animo ipsius, & alia quae in ipso sunt. Is solus admiratur posse inueniri aliquem, qui non credat tot tantisque rebus. Alij vero quibus non est datum ista videre, quae se videnda offerunt in Christo, tantum absunt ab eo vt mirentur, vt e contra stultos existiment eos, qui Christo velint credere. O beatos illos quorum oculos & corda sic adaperuit Deus, vt & Christum videant, & degustent haec quae in eo tanta tamque suauia sunt! Baptista dum praedicat Christum supra omnes esse, & certissima quaeque dicere, id facit comparatione quadam facta cum terreno homine. Qui e terra est, terrenus est: hoc est, humilis & abiectus: & terrena loquitur, hoc est vana & futilia. Ita enim Christi excellentia, qua supra omnes eminet, illustratur comparatione facta cum abiecta sorte hominis terreni. Cum datum est homini semel videre ea, quæ in Christo sunt, quæ tã excellentia & gloriosa sunt, videntur tum omnia quæ in terris sunt, quantumuis gloriosa, longè infra ipsum posita esse: ideóque dum extollit & prædicat illa cœlestia, contemptim solet loqui de terrestribus hisce, & de tota gloria huius mundi, cadémque opera exaggerat illam cœlestem gloriam, & ea quæ plané admirabilia sunt in Christo, cui sit omnis honor & gloria: Amen.
units.tr: The argument of the Church's sun. He slides into a complaint, in which he laments and magnifies their unbelief, partly from the excellence of Christ: He who comes from above, he says, is above all, that is, Christ the Son of God surpasses all. Partly from the certainty of Christ's testimony: What he has seen and heard, this he testifies, but yet no one receives his testimony, that is, no one gives him faith. Nothing is in Christ in which there is not the firmest ground for faith. If you look at his person, he surpasses all, and the very excellence of Christ's person alone ought to move us to believe. If you look at the salvation which he has procured for us, this too has its own force for faith, since it is so great. The Apostle expressed this greatness in the Letter to the Hebrews: If we neglect so great a salvation. Indeed, if you look at what seems most base in Christ, such as the cross itself, it is most glorious and has a most powerful force for faith. Since this is so, and since there is nothing in Christ except what avails both to beget and to confirm faith, yet if anyone is unwilling to believe, conversely, there is nothing in him which does not avail to magnify his unbelief and his condemnation on that day. But who among all men can magnify the unbelief of men by adducing the arguments which Christ alone supplies? Surely no one, except one who has in some certain way looked upon Christ, has seen that excellence of his person and dignity, weighed the weight of his testimony, embraced in his mind the greatness of his salvation, and the other things that are in him. He alone marvels that anyone can be found who does not believe in so many and so great things. Others, to whom it has not been given to see those things which offer themselves to be seen in Christ, are so far from marvelling at him that, on the contrary, they think foolish those who wish to believe Christ. Blessed are those whose eyes and hearts God has so opened that they both see Christ and taste those things which are in him so great and so sweet! When the Baptist preaches that Christ is above all, and says the most certain things, he does so by a comparison made with an earthly man. He who is of the earth is earthly, that is, lowly and abject; and he speaks of earthly things, that is, vain and trifling things. For thus the excellence of Christ, by which he towers above all, is illustrated by comparison with the abject lot of earthly man. When it has once been given to a man to see those things which are in Christ, and which are so excellent and glorious, then all things that are on earth, however glorious they may be, seem to be placed far below him. Therefore, while he extols and proclaims those heavenly things, he is accustomed to speak contemptuously of these earthly things and of all the glory of this world, and by the same token he magnifies that heavenly glory, and those things which are plainly admirable in Christ, to whom be all honour and glory: Amen.

units.la: 33 Qui recipit eius testimonium, is obsignauit Deum veracem esse.
units.tr: 33 He who receives his testimony has set his seal to this, that God is true.

units.la: 34 Nam is demum quem misit Deus, verba Dei loquitur, non enim huic admetitur Deus spiritum.
units.tr: 34 For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for God does not give the Spirit to him by measure.

units.la: 35 Pater diligit filium, & omnia dedit ei in manum.
units.tr: 35 The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand.

units.la: 36 Qui credit in Filium, habet vitâ æternam: qui verò non obtemperat Filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum.
units.tr: 36 He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.

units.la: HActenus questus est Baptista de infidelitate discipulorum suorum aliorúmque Iudæorum: Nunc si qua spes fidei reliqua sit, vno aut altero argumento fidē in Christi testimonium illis commendat. Primum argumentum sumptum est à gloria ipsius Dei, secundum à vita nostra: sed de hoc videbimus suo loco. Primùm igitur ait: Qui recipit eius testimonium, is obsignauit Deum veracem esse: ac proinde gloriam quantam potuit maximam ipsi detulit. Nam quemadmodum maiori ignominia Deum afficere nemo potest quàm is qui ei fidem non habet, ac proinde mendacem eum facit: (Nam qui non credit Deo, mendacem eum facit) Ita qui credit Deo loquenti ac promittenti, is illa ipsa fide sua, quàm maxi-me glorificat eum, præsertim si credat promittenti, etiã cum nulla spes videtur implendæ promissionis. Imò cùm omnia videntur esse promissioni contraria, etiam natura ipsa, & communis rerum ordo, etiam sensus ipse animi nostri; Si enim tum pendeat ex nudo quasi Dei verbo & promissione, sanè quàm potest maximè Deum honorat, id quod fecisse Abraham legimus,qui contra spem sub spe credidit,Deum quod promiserat potuisse etiam facere, ac proinde gloriam Deo tribuisse dicitur.Eam puto equidem esse causam aliquâ cur non Deus posteritatem Adami ita in integrum restituat post lapsum, vt posset perfecta bona opera producere, quibus Deus glorificetur ac colatur. Maluit Deus fidem non perfectè renati, quàm opera perfectè renati: ideóque voluit hominem ex sensu imperfectionis, infirmitatis ac miseriæ suæ, perpetuò, per fidē Christi confugere ad gratuitas illas promissiones in Christo Iesu, & ab illis prorsus pendere, ea quippe re existimauit sese quàm maximè glorificari. Potentia mea, ait Paulo, per infirmitatem perficitur. Voluit Paulus esse sine omni omnino sensu infirmitatis suæ; sed id negatum est ei, quia Deus in potentia sua glorificatur per infirmitatem humanā. Papistæ nondum hoc viderunt, qui perfectam regenerationem, &(vt vocant) iustitiam primam, perfectaque regenerationis opera hominibus in hac vita tribuunt. Quemadmodum autem summè glorificatur Deus per fidem in promissiones suas in Christo factas: ita eadem fide apprehenditur iustitia quædam, maior iustitia illa operum. Iustitia illa Christi æterna nobis imputata, maior est iustitia hominum & Angelorum omnium: & vita quæ est ex illa iustitia, maior est vita ea quæ fuisset ex iustitia operum, si fingas Adamū perstitisse in illo statu innocentiæ in quo tum primùm creatus est. Quamquam autem sensus hic infirmitatis nostræ ac peccati, quod in natura reliquum est, non est sine magno dolore; tamen confugientes ad Christum ac promissiones quæ in eo sunt per fidem, sentimus lætitiam ac pacem quæ superat omnem intellectum. Quëadmodum igitur redundat Deo summa ex fide gloria; ita homo ex fide particeps fit summæ lætitiæ ac beatitudinis.
units.tr: Thus far the Baptist has complained of the unbelief of his disciples and of the other Jews. Now, if any hope of faith remains, he commends faith to them in Christ's testimony by one or another argument. The first argument is taken from the glory of God himself, the second from our life, but we shall see about this in its place. First, then, he says: He who receives his testimony has set his seal to this, that God is true, and so he has given to God the greatest glory possible. For just as no one can dishonour God with greater disgrace than the one who does not believe him, and so makes him a liar (for he who does not believe God makes him a liar), so he who believes God speaking and promising most greatly glorifies him by that very faith of his, especially if he believes the promise even when there seems to be no hope of its fulfilment. Indeed, when all things seem to be contrary to the promise, even nature itself, the common order of things, even the very sense of our mind, if still a man relies upon the bare word and promise of God, he honours God as greatly as possible. This is what we read Abraham did, who against hope believed in hope that God could also do what he had promised, and so is said to have given glory to God. I think indeed that this is some reason why God did not, after the fall, restore the posterity of Adam to such a state of integrity that they could produce perfect good works by which God might be glorified and worshipped. God preferred the faith of the not-perfectly-regenerate to the works of the perfectly regenerate, and so willed that man, from a sense of his imperfection, weakness and misery, should perpetually flee through faith in Christ to those gratuitous promises in Christ Jesus, and depend wholly upon them, for he judged that by this means he would be most greatly glorified. My power, he said to Paul, is made perfect in weakness. Paul wished to be without any sense whatever of his weakness, but this was denied him, because God is glorified in his power through human weakness. The Papists have not yet seen this, who attribute to men in this life a perfect regeneration and (as they call it) first righteousness, and perfect works of regeneration. Moreover, just as God is most highly glorified through faith in the promises made in Christ, so by the same faith is apprehended a certain righteousness, a righteousness greater than that of works. That eternal righteousness of Christ, imputed to us, is greater than the righteousness of all men and angels, and the life which comes from that righteousness is greater than the life which would have come from the righteousness of works, even if you feign that Adam had persisted in that state of innocence in which he was first created. Although this sense of our weakness and of the sin which remains in nature is not without great pain, yet, fleeing to Christ and to the promises which are in him through faith, we feel a joy and peace which surpasses all understanding. Just as, therefore, the highest glory redounds to God from faith, so man through faith becomes a partaker of the highest joy and blessedness.

units.la: Nam is quem. Reddit rationem cur obsignauit Dei veritatem is qui recipit testimonium Christi: nam is quem misit Deus, verba Dei loquitur: Qui missus est à Deo, est filius Dei; nam ipse filius Dei non tribuit sibi hunc honorem vt Pontifex fieret, vt loqueretur Dei verba: sed is dedit qui dixerat ei, Tues Filius meus, genui te hodie, de quo & alibi dictum est, Tu es Sacerdos in æternum secundum ordinem Melchisedeci. Et tamen homunciones isti currunt & loquuntur Dei nomine, non missi à Deo. Latet hic argumentum cur loquatur verba Dei, nempe quia missus; nam qui missus est, loquitur verba Dei: Et qui nō missus est, non loquitur verba Dei. Nam vt loquatur verba Dei aliquis, non satis est si eloquatur substantiam ipsam verborum Dei, nisi etiam à Deo ipso ad hoc vocatus sit & missus. Scripturæ patent omnibus: omnes legunt eas, non pauci etiam intelligūt; verùm qui intelligit, non statim ipsi surgendum est, ac pro concione populo Dei loquendum, quasi verò ipse à Deo missus sit, cùm non sit missus. Vt dicam nonnihil de vocatione: oportet vocentur ministri verbi non à mundo, non à diuitiis huius mundi, non à gloria mundi, non ab hominum libidine, sed primùm oportet vocentur à Deo, deinde ab hominibus. Vocatio Dei præcedit, cognoscitur autem per dona Dei; vocatio hominum sequitur. Paulus, Oportet, inquit, Episcopum irreprehensum esse &c. Q_d. Timothee, ne citò imponito manus cuiquam, sed vide prius an Deus vocauerit hominem. Vocatum autem à Deo cognosces ex dono & gratia Dei multiplici. Non autem satis est, si habeat cognitionis donum, cognitionis dico, vel doctrinæ, vel disciplinæ ecclesiasticæ, nisi etiam imbutus sit multis virtutibus, quæ copiosæ enumeratæ sunt ab Apostolo eo loco: hoc est, non satis est si mens sit illuminata, nisi etiam cor sit sanctificatum, plus profecto destruet quis impura vita (nam necesse est prophanum cor tandem aliquando erumpat in impuram vitam) quàm ædificabit cognitione, & tandem ipse prodet nunquam vocatū esse à Deo; id quod contigisse vides nonnullis nostrūm hominum, quos Deus ita revelauit, & quorum hypocrisin ita detexit, vt iam putent homines indignos eos ita vita, nedum tam sancto ministerio.
units.tr: For he whom gives the reason why the one who receives the testimony of Christ sets his seal to God's truth: for he whom God has sent speaks the words of God. He who has been sent by God is the Son of God; for the Son of God himself did not assume this honour to himself, to become a high priest and to speak the words of God, but he was appointed by the one who said to him, You are my Son, today I have begotten you, of whom it is also said elsewhere, You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek. And yet these little men run about and speak in God's name without having been sent by God. The argument is hidden here as to why someone speaks the words of God, namely because he has been sent. For whoever has been sent speaks the words of God, and whoever has not been sent does not speak the words of God. For it is not enough that someone should utter the very substance of God's words, unless he has also been called and sent to this by God himself. The Scriptures lie open to everyone: everyone reads them, and not a few also understand them. But the one who understands them must not at once rise up and speak to the people of God from the pulpit, as if he had been sent by God when he has not been sent. To say something about the calling: ministers of the Word ought to be called not by the world, not by the riches of this world, not by the glory of the world, not by men's lust, but first they ought to be called by God and then by men. God's calling comes first and is recognised through God's gifts; the calling of men follows. Paul says: The bishop must be blameless, and so on. And, Timothy, do not lay hands hastily on anyone, but first see whether God has called the man. You will know that he has been called by God from the manifold gift and grace of God. But it is not enough if he has the gift of knowledge (I mean knowledge, whether of doctrine or of church discipline), unless he is also imbued with the many virtues which the Apostle lists in full in that passage. That is, it is not enough that the mind is enlightened, unless the heart is also sanctified; an impure life will certainly destroy more than knowledge builds up (for an unholy heart must at some point break out into an impure life), and in the end he will show that he was never called by God. You see this has happened to some of our own men, whom God has so revealed and whose hypocrisy he has so exposed that people now think them unworthy of such a holy ministry, let alone of such a life.

units.la: Hactenus ostendit eum qui recipit testimoniū Christi, ⁊o ipso obsignare veritatem Dei, quia nimirum Christus loquitur verba Dei. Probat autem rursus Christum loqui verba Dei, à plenitudine illa omnis gratiæ, quam Pater largitus est Filio. Itaque quò credant Christo datum esse vt loquatur verba Dei, eos quasi manu deducit ad thesaurum illum omnium donorum, qui in Christo reconditus est: Nam Christus, quatenus Deus est Deique filius, accepit totam eandemque Patris essentiam sibi communicatam in aeterna illa ac effabili generatione. Accepit infinitam potentiam, sapientiam, iustitiam, veritatem & sanctitatem, bonitatem, &c. Quatenus autem homo est, cum plenitudo Deitatis habitet in ipso corporaliter, datae sunt ei virtutes hae omnes, quas diximus, etsi quidem non ea mensura, qua alioqui in Deo sunt; infinitis tamen partibus superatces eas quae vel in hominibus vel in angelis sunt. Itaque quo credant Christum loqui verba Dei, ponit ob oculos eorum, thesaurum illum omnis gratiae, quae est in Christo Iesu. Spiritus sanctus ad hoc vt stabiliatur fides nostra, demonstrat nobis in Christo non vna duntaxat gratiam, aut alteram, sed plenum thesaurum omnis gratiae. Cum fluctuaret fides Colossiensium, Apostolus non semel reduxit eos ad illud fundamentum plenitudinis Christi. Placuit Patri, inquit, vt in ipso inhabitaret omnis plenitudo. Rursus, In eo, inquit, sunt omnes thesauri sapientiae & cognitionis abscondit. Rursus, In eo, inquit, inhabitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter. Putas enim posse fidem hominis niti vento, aut re aliqua leuiuscula & euanida, vt philosophia humana, vt inuentionibus humanis: (fidem enim illam Papisticam, equidem fidei nomine nunquam appellarim) aut, Putasne sufficere quemcunque Mediatorem ad fidem constabiliendam? Quod si peccati conscientia te serio vrgeret ac pungeret, profecto nihil inuenires, in quo fundares fidem remissionis peccati, nec in Angelis quidem ipsis, aut in sanctis demortuis: Neque vllibi conquiescetes nisi apprehensa illa plenitudine Deitatis, quae est in solo Iesu Christo. Quare Apostolus ad Colossenses, postquam dixit in Christo habitare plenitudinem Deitatis corporaliter, statim subiecit in hac verba, Et istis in eo completi. Quo significauit sola illa Christi, eiusque plenitudinis apprehensione, cōpleri corda nostra, ideo que in illo solo requiescere.
units.tr: So far he has shown that the one who receives the testimony of Christ thereby sets his seal to the truth of God, because Christ indeed speaks the words of God. He next proves again that Christ speaks the words of God, from that fullness of all grace which the Father has bestowed on the Son. So, in order that they may believe that it has been given to Christ to speak the words of God, he leads them by the hand, as it were, to that treasure of all gifts which is laid up in Christ. For Christ, as he is God and the Son of God, received the whole and the same essence of the Father, communicated to him in that eternal and ineffable generation. He received infinite power, wisdom, justice, truth and holiness, goodness, and so on. And as he is man, since the fullness of the Godhead dwells in him bodily, all these virtues which we have mentioned were given to him, though not indeed in the measure in which they are in God; yet they surpass by infinite parts those which are in men or in angels. So, that they may believe that Christ speaks the words of God, he sets before their eyes that treasure of all grace which is in Jesus Christ. The Holy Spirit, to make our faith firm, shows us in Christ not one grace only, or another, but the full treasure of all grace. When the faith of the Colossians was wavering, the Apostle more than once led them back to that foundation of the fullness of Christ. It pleased the Father, he says, that in him all fullness should dwell. Again: in him, he says, are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden. Again: in him, he says, the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily. For do you think that a man's faith can rest on the wind, or on some light and fading thing, such as human philosophy or human inventions? (I would never call that Papistical faith by the name of faith.) Or do you think that any mediator is enough to establish faith? But if the awareness of sin pressed and stung you in earnest, you would certainly find nothing on which to found faith in the forgiveness of sins, not even in the angels themselves or in the holy dead. Nor would you ever find rest anywhere, unless you had grasped that fullness of the Godhead which is in Jesus Christ alone. Therefore the Apostle, to the Colossians, after saying that the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in Christ, immediately added, And you are complete in him. By this he signified that our hearts are filled by the grasp of Christ alone and of his fullness, and therefore rest in him alone.

units.la: Praeterea videmus hic Baptistam numerare in donis Spiri[?]
units.tr: Moreover, we see here the Baptist numbering among the gifts of the Spiri[?]

units.la: Ratio. Plenitudo Dei in eo corporaliter inhabitat.
units.tr: Reason. The fullness of God dwells bodily in him.

units.la: Confirmatio, ab Apostoli testimoniis.
units.tr: Confirmation, from the testimonies of the Apostle.

units.la: Coloss. 2.10.
units.tr: Coloss. 2.10.

units.la: Eloquutio & efficax. Spiritus sancti loquutionem & prædicationem ipsam verbi diuini. Postquàm enim dixit eū loqui verba Dei, continuò addidit Deum non admetiri ei Spiritum, quo quidem significauit, à Spiritu sancto inter cætera pro- secta esse illa verba Dei, non tantùm quoad materiam sermonis, sed etiam quoad ipsum sermonem, qui plenus fuit gratiæ & authoritatis. Non enim sufficit cŏt humanum ad enunciationem illius verbi, non lingua quantumuis eloquens, non ingenium, non memoria, non denique aliæ dotes, quæ à natura sunt duntaxat, quantumuis in speciem præclaræ (cùm enim hæc omnia adsunt, profectò sunt tantummodo persuasoria humanæ sapientiæ verba, non demonstratio illa spiritualis potentiæ, vt loquitur Apostolus) Non, inquam, sa- tis sunt ista, nisi spiritus Dei moueat ipsum illud cor quod cogitat, sanctificet memoriam, refingat quasi linguam, & labia. Non enim oportet putare sic Spiritum Dei indere sua verba hominibus, vt ipsa statim deferat ea, permittatque humanis instrumentis & facultatibus, vt cordi, linguæ & labiis istis humanis. Imò verò Spiritus sanctus est, qui loquitur per ista tanquam organa & instrumenta, quæ alioqui in homine naturalia sunt. Loquitur autem per ea dum mouet ipsa arcana quadam inspiratione, ipsaque sanctificat, vocémq; & verba quasi fingit ac informat. Qui experiuntur ista, sciunt vera esse præsente Dei Spiritu sciunt quanta cum παρρησία & libertate cordis, quanta cum fiducia (dum nimirum cum Dauide & cum Paulo credunt atque ideo loquuntur.) quanta denique lætitia emittant illam, non tam suam quàm Spiritus Dei vocem. Contrà verò subtrahente Deo ad tempus Spiritum suum, sciunt quanta cum cordis angustia, quanta cum instrumentorum fatigatione & tædio, quàm parua denique ædificatione, vel sui vel aliorum proferant eas voces. Quamlibet irridmeant homines, non est hominis vox sola illa quæ ratiocinationes euertit, omnemque sublimitatem quæ extollitur aduersus cognitionem Dei, & captiuam ducit omnem cogitationem ad obediendum Christo. Vel non flectit ad obediendum, certò ita attonitos reddit homines, vt etiam superbissimi quique & maxime reluctantes cogantur sentire hic esse plus quam hu-manam vocem.
