Neque enim vox illa humana dunta-xat erat, quae extorsit Agrippae regi superbo hanc con-sessionem : Propemodum persuades mihi vt fiam Chri-stianus.
units.tr: Eloquence and efficacy. The speech and preaching of the Holy Spirit itself, the divine word. For after saying that he speaks the words of God, he at once added that God does not give him the Spirit by measure, by which he signified that those words of God were issued by the Holy Spirit among other things, not only as to the matter of the discourse, but also as to the discourse itself, which was full of grace and authority. For human ability is not enough for the utterance of that word: not a tongue however eloquent, not talent, not memory, not finally other gifts which come from nature alone, however splendid in appearance (for even when all these are present, they are only persuasive words of human wisdom, not that demonstration of spiritual power of which the Apostle speaks). These things, I say, are not enough unless the Spirit of God moves the very heart that thinks, sanctifies the memory, and as it were reshapes the tongue and lips. For we must not suppose that the Spirit of God so implants his words in men that he simply hands them over and leaves them to human instruments and faculties, such as this human heart, tongue and lips. Rather, it is the Holy Spirit who speaks through these as organs and instruments, which in a man are otherwise natural. He speaks through them while he stirs them by a certain hidden inspiration, and sanctifies them, and as it were moulds and shapes the voice and the words. Those who experience this know the things to be true when the Spirit of God is present; they know with what boldness [παρρησία] and freedom of heart, with what confidence (since they believe with David and with Paul, and therefore speak), and finally with what joy they utter that voice, which is not so much their own as the voice of the Spirit of God. On the other hand, when God for a time withdraws his Spirit, they know with what anguish of heart, with what weariness and disgust of the faculties, and with how little edification either to themselves or to others they utter those words. However much men may mock, it is not the human voice alone that overturns arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and leads every thought captive to obey Christ. Or if it does not bend them to obedience, it certainly so astonishes men that even the proudest and most stubborn are compelled to feel that here is more than a human voice. For it was not merely a human voice that wrung from the proud king Agrippa this confession: Almost you persuade me to become a Christian.

units.la: Pater diligit Filium. Confirmat rursus plenitudinem illam donorum filio datam, ex amore illo imperuesti-gabili, quo Pater filium complectitur, & ex quo pro-cessit vniuersa illa gratiae, quae in filio est, plenitudo. Spiritus igitur sanctus, quo confirmat fidem tuam in testimonium Christi, deducit te primum ad verba Dei quae loquitur Christus ; deinde ad plenitudinem illam omnium donorum Spiritus sancti. Postremo, vt habeat fides fundamentum immobile ac immutabile, alias animum tuum subuehit ad fontem ipsum omnium eorum quae dedit Pater filio, nempe ineffabilem illum amorem Patris erga filium, qui primum mouit Patrem ad hoc vt haec omnia filio impartiretur. Nā, vt loquar aliquid de illo amore, etsi quantus sit a nulla creatura comprehendi potest, tamen hoc scimus, nullum amore Dei quo prosequitur creaturam vllam, cum eo comparabilem. Nam quem, quaeso, Angelorum ita dilexit, vt impartiretur illi naturam suam, & essentiales quae in ipso sunt omnes, vt sic dicam, proprietates, quas cum filio in aeterna illa generatione communicauit Pater? Cui, inquit Apostolus, Angelo vnquam dixit, filius meus es tu, Ego hodie genui te? Itaque Spiritus sanctus, vt firmum habeamus fidei fundamentum, deducit nos ad eum amorem Patris erga filium, quo fit vt nihil possit Pater negare filio suo, sed det omnia in manu ac potestate ipsius, eo fine nimirum, vt nos, hoc intellecto, toti pendeamus ex filio.
units.tr: The Father loves the Son. He confirms again the fullness of gifts given to the Son, from that unsearchable love by which the Father embraces the Son, and from which the whole fullness of grace that is in the Son has proceeded. The Holy Spirit, therefore, by whom he confirms your faith as a witness to Christ, first leads you to the words of God that Christ speaks, and then to that fullness of all the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Finally, so that faith may have a firm and unchangeable foundation, he lifts your mind to the very source of all that the Father has given to the Son, namely the ineffable love of the Father towards the Son, which first moved the Father to impart all these things to the Son. For, to say something about that love: although no creature can grasp how great it is, yet we know this, that no love of God by which he cherishes any creature is comparable to it. For whom, I ask, of the angels has he loved so as to impart to him his nature and all the essential properties, so to speak, which the Father shared with the Son in that eternal generation? To which angel, says the Apostle, did he ever say, "You are my Son, today I have begotten you"? Therefore the Holy Spirit, that we may have a firm foundation of faith, leads us to that love of the Father for the Son, by which it comes about that the Father can deny nothing to his Son, but places all things in his hand and power, with this end surely, that we, having understood this, may wholly depend on the Son.

units.la: Quod si fit in regno humano & in aula regis cuiusquam, quem intime diligat Rex, quo magis diligit Rex eum homine, eo plures ad eum confugiunt, eique fidunt. Nullus amor Regis cuiusquā, ne ergā filium quidem suum comparandus est cum illo Dei Patris amore erga filium suum Christum. Amor hominis erga hominem mutabilis est, amor Dei erga filium immutabilis est: quem amat hodie Rex aliquis, eundem potest cras odisse. At non est metuendum ne filius
units.tr: If this is so in a human kingdom, and in the court of any king whom the king loves intimately, then the more a king loves a man, the more people flock to him and trust in him. No love of any king, not even his love for his own son, is to be compared with that love of God the Father for his Son Christ. Human love towards a human being is changeable; the love of God towards the Son is unchangeable. The one whom a king loves today, he may hate tomorrow. But there is no need to fear that the Son...

units.la: Aduersus eorum incredulitate qui reliquo Christo mediatore ad aliouos intercessores confugiunt. filius Dei vnquam amittat gratiam Patris sui. Et tu profecto si credas in filium, non magis fieri potest, vt prius gratia semel accepta & vita illa aeterna, quam potest fieri vt immutetur amor ille Patris erga filium suum. Nam gratia illa, iustitia ac vita tua fundata est in illo immutabili ac incomprehensibili amore Patris erga dilectum suum, in quo te praedestinauit ad vitam, &c, vt verbo dicam, totum illud opus redemptionis nostri absoluit atque perfecit: Gratis effecit sibi gratos in illo dilecto, inquit Apostolus. Quamobrem cum hoc sit primum fundamentum fidei nostrae in Christum, amor nempe Patris erga filium; cumque Spiritus sanctus huc nos deducat in stabilienda fide nostra, nempe vt Patris illum amorem intueamur, profecto oculi nostri semper ad eum attollendi sunt, nobisque penitus est cognoscendus. Non dico hoc ideo, quod velim quemquam statim perrumpere in lucem illam inaccessam quam inhabitat Deus: sed tamen demonstrabo tibi via quandam, qua ad eum amorem tam reconditum in illa tam profunda abysso peruenies, aliquo certe modo. Vide primum ipse sentias charitatem Patris erga te, charitatem inquam, non eam tantum qua prosequitur Creator creaturam suam, sed qua prosequitur Pater filium suum, ac proinde paternam charitatem, quae intima & tenerrima solet esse. Quod si penitus animo senseris eam Patris erga te charitatem, persuadebis tibi profectam esse ab amore illo Patris in filium suum naturalem, in eoque totam residere. Nam profecto charitas illa ita diffusa in corde tuo per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est tibi, non potest residere in dilectione, qua prosequitur Angelorum aliquem. Est enim plane similis illi amori, quo diligit ac ab aeterno dilexit filium suum unigenitum, & quodammodo idem cum illo amor est, teste ipso Christo: vt charitas qua dilexisti me, sit in iis, & ego in iis. Quod si rursus velis cognoscere an te Pater diligat, videdum an tu diligas Patrem. In hoc enim est charitas, non quod nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quod ipse dilexerit nos. Dilectio enim Dei, qua nos ipse prosequitur, causa est cur nos vicissim eum diligamus. Non enim audemus ad eum accedere, prius quam ipse accedat ad nos. Ergo si sentis
units.tr: Against the unbelief of those who, leaving Christ the mediator, flee to other intercessors. The Son of God will never lose the grace of his Father. And you, certainly, if you believe in the Son, cannot be more sure that the grace once received and that eternal life will be lost than that the Father's love for his Son can be changed. For that grace, your righteousness and life are founded on the immutable and incomprehensible love of the Father towards his beloved, in whom he has predestined you to life, etc. In a word, he has accomplished and completed that whole work of our redemption: he has made us acceptable to himself in the Beloved, as the Apostle says. Therefore, since this is the first foundation of our faith in Christ, namely the love of the Father for the Son, and since the Holy Spirit leads us here to establish our faith, namely that we should look upon that love of the Father, surely our eyes must always be lifted to it, and we must come to know it thoroughly. I do not say this because I want anyone at once to break into that inaccessible light in which God dwells; but nevertheless I will show you a way by which, in some measure at least, you will reach that love, so hidden in that deep abyss. First, see that you yourself feel the Father's love for you: I say love, not only that with which the Creator embraces his creature, but that with which the Father embraces his Son, and therefore a fatherly love, which is wont to be intimate and most tender. If you have felt that love of the Father for you deep in your mind, you will persuade yourself that it has proceeded from that natural love of the Father for his Son, and rests wholly in it. For surely that love, poured so abundantly into your heart through the Holy Spirit who has been given to you, cannot rest in the affection by which he cherishes some angel. For it is plainly like that love by which he loves, and from eternity has loved, his only-begotten Son, and in a sense it is the same love, as Christ himself testifies: that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them. But if again you wish to know whether the Father loves you, you must see whether you love the Father. For in this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us. For the love of God by which he embraces us is the cause why we in turn love him. For we do not dare to approach him before he approaches us. Therefore, if you feel...

units.la: Ephes. 1. 6. — 1. Tim. 6. 16 — Ioh. 17. 26 — 1. Ioh. 4. 10 Deum à te diligi, eadem opera sentis te à Deo diligi. Quòd si sentis te à Deo diligi, profectò ex copiosa illa ac paterna dilectione facilè colligere potes dilectionē illam residere in infinita illa dilectione, qua Pater filium prosequitur.
units.tr: Eph. 1. 6. — 1 Tim. 6. 16 — John 17. 26 — 1 John 4. 10. ...that God loves you, you at the same time feel that you are loved by God. And if you feel that you are loved by God, surely from that abundant and fatherly love you can easily gather that this love rests on that infinite love by which the Father embraces the Son.

units.la: Qui credit in filium. Hoc est argumetum alterum cur credendum sit testimonio Christi, à bono ac felicitate notra.quòd si non moueat nos argumentum à gloria Dei, saltem nos moueat argumentum à vita nostra æterna: etsi imprimis mouere nos debeat gloria Dei, quæ praeferenda est etiam vitæ ac saluti nostræ. Ait igitur fidem in filium sequi vitam æternam. Non prius fide Christum amplectimur, quàm illa fide exsugamus quasi è Christo initium quoddā vitæ æternæ. Ideóque dictum est eum qui credit in filii iam habere vitam æternam.
units.tr: He who believes in the Son. This is the second argument why the testimony of Christ must be believed, from our good and happiness. If the argument from the glory of God does not move us, at least the argument from our eternal life should move us; though the glory of God ought chiefly to move us, since it is to be preferred even to our life and salvation. He therefore says that faith in the Son is followed by eternal life. We do not first embrace Christ by faith and then, by that faith, draw from Christ some beginning of eternal life. Therefore it is said that he who believes in the Son already has eternal life.

units.la: Paulus quo tempore in Christum credit, eodem plane tempore sentit se viuere. Vita quam nunc viuo in carne, viuo per fidem filij Dei. Quid sibi vult pax ista conscientiæ? quid lætitia hæc? quid desiderium vitæ? quid denique totum hoc opus regenerationis nostræ? Annon ista sunt initium vitæ illius æternæ? Etsi fatear quidem ista ipsa longè abesse à perfectione illa qua tandem aliquando fruemur; tamen eiusdem plane generis sunt cum perfecta illa bonitate, & arrhabo sunt illius perfectionis, qua tandem aliquando fruemur. Si enim ad ista diligentius attendas, videbis vel micam aliquam spiritualis huius lætitiæ, quæ comes est fidei in Christū Iesum, facilè vincere vniuersam lætitiam huius mundi. Qui vero non credit. Effectum istud fidei illustrat à contrario effecto incredulitatis, quasi dicat, Hoc adeo verum est, vt qui non credit, is vita non sit visurus. Sententia profectò grauis. Quòd si quis sensum aliquem semel haberet illius, de qua loquimur, vitæ; is grauissimè ferret priuari se tanta vita; etsi illud daretur, nullam post hanc vitam manere mortem æternam. Sed non sine præsentia mortis æternæ priuatio futura est vitæ æternæ. Quòd si quis semel degustaret illam morte, profectò ægerrimè ferret mori sese in æternū. Atqui sic viuunt homines, vt expertes sint sensus & vitæ æternæ & mortis æternæ: idcóq; sit vt hac vita præsente tātum curet, &
units.tr: Paul, at the very time he believes in Christ, at that same time feels that he is alive. The life I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God. What does that peace of conscience mean? What is this joy? What is this desire for life? What, finally, is this whole work of our regeneration? Are not these the beginning of that eternal life? Although I admit that these things are far from that perfection which we shall at length enjoy, yet they are of exactly the same kind as that perfect goodness, and they are the pledge of that perfection which we shall at length enjoy. For if you attend more carefully to these things, you will see that even a tiny particle of this spiritual joy, which accompanies faith in Christ Jesus, easily outweighs all the joy of this world. But he who does not believe: the Evangelist illustrates the effect of faith by the contrary effect of unbelief, as if to say, this is so true that he who does not believe shall not see life. Surely a grave sentence. And if anyone once had some sense of that life of which we speak, he would take it very hard to be deprived of so great a life, even if it were granted that no eternal death remained after this life. But the loss of eternal life will not occur without the presence of eternal death. And if anyone once tasted that death, he would most bitterly bear dying forever. Yet men live in such a way as to be without any sense either of eternal life or of eternal death; hence it is that in this present life they care only for this life and take their pleasure in it.

units.la: ip in deliciis habeant. Sed ira Dei. Q. d. Non tantum non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum. Qui enim non credit, iam condemnatus est, vt dixit supra hoc cap. verf. 18. Condemnatio enim illa iam coepit esse efficax per executionem iudicij aliquam & sententiae damnatoriae, tandem illo die complenda, cum thesauro illo irae toto simul ac semel reprobi cumulabuntur.
units.tr: But the wrath of God. That is to say: not only will he not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. For he who does not believe is already condemned, as he said above in this chapter, verse 18. For that condemnation has already begun to take effect through some execution of judgment and a sentence of damnation, to be finally completed on that day, when the treasure of that wrath will be heaped up, all at once and in a single moment, upon the reprobate.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Hoc capite primum narratur Christum relicta Iudaea rursum in Galilaeam profectum esse, ad verf. 4.
units.tr: In this chapter it is first related that Christ, having left Judea, went again into Galilee, down to verse 4.

units.la: Secundo transitus Christi per Samariam simul cum iis, quae in transitu ab eo sunt gesta, a versu 4. ad verf. vsque 43.
units.tr: Secondly, the passage of Christ through Samaria, together with the things done by him on the way, from verse 4 to verse 43.

units.la: Tertio, post transitum ipsius per Samariam narratur vt ingressus sit in Galilaeam & in Galilaeae oppida, nominatim Cana. Vbi cum ageret, verbo sanauit filium cuiusdam regij absentem & decumbentem in oppido Capernaum, a versu 43. ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Thirdly, after his passage through Samaria, it is related that he entered Galilee and the towns of Galilee, namely Cana. There, while he was doing this, he healed by a word the son of a certain royal official, who was absent and lying sick in the town of Capernaum, from verse 43 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAP. IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 4.

units.la: 1 Vt ergo cognovit Dominus Pharisaeos audisse ipsum plures discipulos facere & baptizare quam Iohannem:
units.tr: 1 When therefore the Lord knew that the Pharisees had heard that he was making and baptizing more disciples than John,

units.la: 2 (Quanquam Iesus ipse non baptizabat, sed discipuli eius)
units.tr: 2 (Although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did,)

units.la: 3 Reliquit Iudaeam, & abiit rursum in Galilaeam.
units.tr: 3 he left Judea and went again into Galilee.

units.la: PRIMA pars capitis de reditu Christi in Galilaeam, vna cum occasione eiusdem. Occasio autem habetur his verbis, Cognovit Dominus Pharisaeos. Correctio autem inserta est his verbis, Quanquam Iesus ipse non baptizabat, sed discipuli eius: Hoc est, visus est externo ministerio discipulorum suorum in baptizado, ipse interea solus baptizas interius sanguine suo ad remissionem peccatorum, Spiritu suo ad regenerationem. Est igitur ea occasio reditus. Pharisaei cum cepissent consilium aduersus Christum, in causa erat cur Christus relicta Iudaea, rursum abiit in Galilaeam. De prima post baptismum suum profectione in Galilaea, vide cap. 1. verf. 44. Haec autem est secunda profectio ipsius in Galilaeam. Quod ex his obseruo, hoc tantum est: Exemplo Christi, orta persecutione, Ministri Euangelij, tenentur non temere se coniicere in praesens discrimen, sed expensis primum diligenter causis, temporibus, locis, personis, caeterisque id genus circumstantiis, sese subducere ac reseruare in meliora tempora. Christus cum in terris versaretur, nunquam se temere coniecit in discrimen aliquod, quamuis Dei filius fuerit, & Deus ipse, atque adeo potuerit se seruare in medio discrimine & eripere e quouis periculo, tamen noluit tentare Deum suum: sic enim ipsi respondit tentatori Matth. 4.7.
units.tr: This is the first part of the chapter, on Christ's return to Galilee together with the occasion for it. The occasion is given in the words, "When the Lord knew that the Pharisees..." The qualification is inserted in the words, "Although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples": that is, he seemed to leave the outward ministry of baptizing to his disciples, while he himself alone baptized inwardly, with his blood for the forgiveness of sins and with his Spirit for regeneration. So the occasion of his return is this. When the Pharisees had taken counsel against Christ, that was the reason why Christ, leaving Judea, went again into Galilee. For his first departure into Galilee after his baptism, see chapter 1, verse 44; this is his second departure into Galilee. From this I observe only the following: following the example of Christ, when persecution arises, the ministers of the Gospel are bound not to throw themselves rashly into present danger, but, after carefully weighing the causes, times, places, persons and other such circumstances, to withdraw and keep themselves for better times. While Christ was on earth, he never rashly threw himself into any danger, although he was the Son of God and God himself, and could therefore have preserved himself in the midst of danger and rescued himself from any peril. Yet he would not tempt his God, and so he answered the tempter in Matthew 4.7.

units.la: 4 Oportebat autem eum transire per Samariam.
units.tr: 4 Now he had to pass through Samaria.

units.la: 5 Venit ergo in urbem Samariae quae dicitur Sichar, iuxta praedium quod dedit Iacobus Iosepho filio suo.
units.tr: 5 So he came to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob gave to his son Joseph.

units.la: 6 Erat autem ibi fons Iacobi. Iesus ergo fatigatus ex itinere, ita sedit ad fontem: hora enim erat quasi sexta.
units.tr: 6 Now Jacob's well was there. Jesus, therefore, wearied from the journey, sat down thus by the well; it was about the sixth hour.

units.la: Secunda pars capitis de transitu Christi qui fuit per Samariam, deque iis rebus quas ibi gessit quasi obiter, & inter eundum in Galilaeam. Estque haec digressio a proposita profectione in Galilaeam. Primum proponit oportuisse eum transire per Samariam, quia media iacebat inter Iudaeam & Galilaeam. Deinde narrat eum venisse in Samariam & urbem Samariae Sichar nomine, quae & Sichem dicta est. Quam quidem urbem a situ suo describit: Erat iuxta praedium, quod dedit Iacobus Iosepho filio suo. Vide Genes. 48.22. Dotibi, inquit, partem unam supra fratres tuos, quam cepi de manu Amorrhaei, gladio meo & arcu.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter concerns Christ's passage through Samaria, and the things he did there almost in passing, on his way into Galilee. This digression is from the stated departure into Galilee. First, it states that he had to pass through Samaria, because it lay between Judea and Galilee. Then it tells how he came into Samaria and into the city of Samaria named Sychar, which is also called Shechem. He describes the city by its location: it was near the field that Jacob gave to his son Joseph. See Genesis 48.22: "I have given to you one portion above your brothers, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow."

units.la: Ioan. 4. & arcu meo. Iacob his verbis ostendit se prædium vel portionem duplam Iosepho filio suo tribuisse. Veniens Christus in hanc vrbem, convertit Samaritanam mulierem primum, deinde cives Samaritanos: vt doceat Ministros euangelij suo exemplo, etiam tum cum con-uertuntur in fugam & exules agunt, non esse cessandum ipsis ab officio, sed prædicandum esse Euangelium vbicunque locorum sint. Deinde obserua, quòd in transitu & quasi cursim converterit Samaritanos. Beati sunt, vel per quos transit Christus & obiter quasi inuisit. Neque enim tanta lux transit per aliquam gentem, quin aspergat miseros homines aliqua scintilla sua. Neque tanta plenitudo percurrit aliquam gentem, quin aliqua eius certè guttala in miseros homines distillet. Beati igitur sunt hi quibus vel in transitu & obiter affulget Christus. Sed beatiores illi sunt, inter quos resider ille Sol Iustitiæ! O beatam Scotiam nostram hoc nomine præsertim! O beatam, inquam, vel, ô infelicem! Beatam quidem, si quadantenus illuminata sit: Miseram verò, si adhuc maneat in meris tenebris. Quò enim maior lux, nisi cum luce illuminatio sit aliqua, certè eò maior condemnatio est.
units.tr: John 4. "...and with my bow." By these words Jacob shows that he gave to Joseph a field or a double portion. When Christ came into this city, he first converted the Samaritan woman and then the Samaritan citizens, so that by his example he might teach the ministers of the Gospel that, even when they are driven into flight and live as exiles, they must not cease from their office, but must preach the Gospel wherever they are. Next, observe that he converted the Samaritans in passing and, as it were, hurriedly. Blessed are those through whom Christ passes and whom he visits in passing. For no light passes through any nation without sprinkling some spark of its own on wretched men; no fullness runs through any nation without some drop of it certainly distilling onto wretched men. Blessed, then, are those on whom Christ shines even in passing and in passing. But more blessed are those among whom that Sun of Righteousness actually dwells! O our Scotland, blessed especially by this name! O blessed, I say, or rather, O unhappy! Blessed indeed, if it has been illumined in some measure; but wretched, if it still remains in utter darkness. For the greater the light, unless there is some illumination together with the light, the greater is certainly the condemnation.

units.la: Erat autem ibi. Sequitur conuersio Samaritanæ mulieris, & reliquorum Samaritanorum. Conuersio autem mulieris fit per sermones vltrò citróque habitos, & inter Christum & ipsam. Occasio autem sermonis duplex præmittitur: prima est, cum esset in illo prædio, quod dedit Iacobus Iosepho filio suo, fons, qui dictus est fons Iacobi. Iesus fatigatus ex itinere, tum propter itineris longitudinem, tum propter æstum diei, erat enim hora quasi sexta, hoc est, instabat meridies: sedit ad fontem recreandi sui gratia. Iesus Christus obnoxius fuit omnibus illis infirmitatibus, quibus sumus nos, excepto peccato: animo passus est omnes molestias & curas quas nos perpetimur; corpore passus est famē, sitim, fatigationem, mortem denique ipsam. In hoc ipso tempore passus est fatigationem, famem, sitim, vt ex historia satis colligi potest. Nam & petiit potum, & misit discipulos in vrbem, qui emerent & exportarent cibum. Quamobrem maximè opportunus & aptus erat, hoc præ-
units.tr: Now he was there. There follows the conversion of the Samaritan woman and of the other Samaritans. The conversion of the woman takes place through the conversation held back and forth between Christ and her. The occasion of the talk is introduced in two ways. The first is that, while he was in that field which Jacob gave to his son Joseph, there was a well, called Jacob's well. Jesus, wearied from the journey, both because of the length of the road and because of the heat of the day (for it was about the sixth hour, that is, midday was approaching), sat down by the well to refresh himself. Jesus Christ was subject to all those infirmities to which we are subject, apart from sin: in spirit he suffered all the troubles and cares that we undergo; in body he suffered hunger, thirst, weariness, and finally death itself. At this very time he suffered weariness, hunger and thirst, as can sufficiently be gathered from the narrative. For he both asked for a drink and sent the disciples into the city to buy and bring back food. Therefore he was especially suitable and fitting at this time, in which this wretched woman happened to meet him.

units.la: Conuersio Samaritanæ mulieris & ciuium. Christi infirmitates. fertim tempore, in quem incideret misera ista mulier. Soli enim hi qui experti sunt miseriam naturæ nostræ, hi,inquam, soli afficiuntur sensu calamitatum misero- rum hominum. Alij vero qui nondum fracti sunt communibus his malis & miseriis, nihil afficiuntur miseria & calamitatibus aliorum, quas intuentur siccis oculis, & corde nihil commoto. Dico igitur miseram istam mulierem, hoc ipso beatam fuisse, quòd inciderit in eũ, qui etiam tum experiebatur miseriam communis naturæ, si modò ipsum cognouisset, siqué ipsa aliquo modo sensisset miseriam suam. Nam cùm quis, qui oneratus est peccato & miseria, inuenit Christum, eúmque fide apprehendit, nihil est eo sensu suauius. Verùm etiam si non affecta fuerit sensu miseriæ suæ, tamen hoc ipso beata fuit, quòd inciderit in eum, qui prior sensit miseriam ipsius, eámque non dimisit priùs quàm sensit & miseriam & gratuitam liberationem. Mirum hoc: Christus priùs atque adeo propiùs afficitur sensu miseriæ nostræ, quàm ipsi nos; tùmque deinde nos eius gratia afflati sentire incipimus & miseriam, & àmiseria liberationem. Deinde hoc occurrit obseruandum, quòd Christus non venerit huc temerè, neque restinguendæ sitis præsertim gratia, verùm consilio cõueniendi ipsam hanc mulierem, eámque conuertendi. Quare oportuit eam iam antea notam esse Christo, sicut de Nathanaële dixit, quòd viderit eum priusquam ipsum Philippus vocaret, dum esset sub ficu. Deus patitur electos suos, quorum in numero fuit hæc mulier, errare ad tempus instar ouium perditarum. Verùm dissimilitudo hic magna est: pastor enim, cùm aberrata reliquo grege ouis aliqua, non iam amplius videt eam, neque amplius eã custodit: at Christus, etiam cùm errat ex electis aliquis, tamen videt eum, ac conseruat prouidentia sua, tantisperdum efficaciter eum vocet, & in caulam suam addu- cat. Atque hoc est quod ait Apostolus, quòd dilexerit nos, ac reconciliauerit nos sibi, cùm inimici essemus & peccatores. Ex quo rursus colligit, argumento à minori ad maius, reconciliatos iam & vocatos multò magis seruandos abiia, id quod vocatos mirabiliter consolatur.
units.tr: The conversion of the Samaritan woman and the citizens. The infirmities of Christ. Only those who have experienced the misery of our nature are moved by the feeling of the calamities of wretched men. Others, who have not yet been broken by these common evils and miseries, are not moved at all by the misery and calamities of others, which they look upon with dry eyes and a heart unmoved. I say, therefore, that this wretched woman was blessed for this very reason, that she met him who even then experienced the misery of common nature, provided that she knew him, and provided she had in some way felt her own misery. For when someone burdened with sin and misery finds Christ and lays hold of him by faith, nothing is sweeter than that feeling. But even if she had not been affected by a sense of her own misery, she was still blessed in this very thing, that she met him who first felt her misery and did not let it go until she felt both the misery and the free deliverance. This is remarkable: Christ is affected by a sense of our misery before us, and indeed more closely than we are ourselves; and then, inspired by his grace, we begin to feel both the misery and the deliverance from misery. Next, this should be observed: Christ did not come here by chance, nor especially for the sake of quenching thirst, but with the purpose of meeting this very woman and converting her. Therefore she must already have been known to Christ, as he said of Nathanael, that he saw him before Philip called him, while he was under the fig tree. God allows his elect, of whom this woman was one, to wander for a time like lost sheep. But there is a great difference here: when one sheep strays from the rest of the flock, the shepherd no longer sees it or keeps watch over it. Christ, however, even when one of the elect wanders, still sees him and preserves him by his providence, until he effectively calls him and brings him into his fold. And this is what the Apostle means when he says that he loved us and reconciled us to himself when we were enemies and sinners. From this he further infers, by an argument from the lesser to the greater, that those who are already reconciled and called are much more to be kept safe, which wonderfully comforts those who are called.

units.la: Ioan. 1. 49
units.tr: John 1. 49
Romans 5. 8, etc.

units.la: 7 Venit mulier Samaritana, vt hauriret aquā: dicit ei Iesus, Da mihi potum.
units.tr: 7 A Samaritan woman came to draw water. Jesus said to her, "Give me a drink."

units.la: 8 Nam discipuli eius abierant in vrbem, vt cibos emerent.
units.tr: For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.

units.la: 9 Dicit igitur ei mulier illa Samaritana, Quomodo tu Iudæus cùm sis, potum à me poscis, quæ sum mulier Samaritana? (non enim vtuntur Iudæi Samaritanis.)
units.tr: So the Samaritan woman said to him, "How is it that you, a Jew, ask me for a drink, when I am a Samaritan woman? (For the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.)"

units.la: 10 Respondit Iesus, & dixit ei, Si nosses donum illud Dei, & quis sit ille, qui dicit tibi, Da mihi potum, tu petiisses ab eo, & dedisset tibi aquam viuam.
units.tr: Jesus answered and said to her, "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water."

units.la: 11 Dicit ei mulier, Domine, neque quo haurias habes, & puteus profundus est: unde ergo habes aquam illam viuam?
units.tr: The woman said to him, "Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. Where then do you get that living water?"

units.la: 12 Num tu maior es patre nostro Iacobo, qui dedit nobis hunc puteum, ex quo ipse bibit, & filij eius, & eius pecora?
units.tr: "Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well, from which he himself drank, and his sons, and his cattle?"

units.la: SEquitur altera occasio dialogi & communicationis sequentis. Venit mulier. Interea dum Christus sedet ad fontem, venit mulier Samaritana vt hauriret aquam, venit quidem, non vt conueniret Dominum, sed nihil de Deo, nihil de cælis, nihil de vita altera cogitans venit, eodem scilicet modo quo veniunt & abeunt ad has vel illas occupationes mundanas plerique omnes, tantùm cogitantes de hoc modo, déque rebus his terrestribus, nihil interea curantes superna ac cœlestia. Superna quærite, superna curate, non terrestria, clamat Apostolus. Non reprehendo equidem curam rerum illarum, sed non oportere hanc esse præcipuam. Qui vxores habent, sint vt non habentes, qui flent vt non flentes, qui gaudent vt non gaudentes, qui emunt vt non obtinentes, qui vtuntur hoc mundo vt non abutentes. Præterit enim species huius mundi. Speciem & figuram rei appellat, potiùs quàm rem aliquam firmam ac solidam. Admonet autem Apostolus principaliter ista nō ciuum.
units.tr: Now comes the second occasion for the dialogue that follows. The woman comes. While Christ sits by the well, the Samaritan woman comes to draw water. She came indeed, not to meet the Lord, but thinking of nothing of God, nothing of heaven, nothing of the life to come. She came in the same way that almost all people come and go to these or those worldly occupations, thinking only of this life and these earthly things, and meanwhile caring nothing for things above and heavenly. "Seek the things that are above, care for the things that are above, not the things that are on earth," cries the Apostle. I do not indeed condemn care for those things, but it ought not to be our chief concern. "Those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep as though they did not weep; those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; those who buy as though they did not possess; those who use this world as though not using it to the full. For the form of this world passes away." He calls it the form and figure of the thing, rather than some firm and solid reality. The Apostle, however, is principally admonishing these things not to citizens.

units.la: N esse agenda aut curanda in hac peregrinatione nostra, sed principaliter cogitandum dies & noctes de Domino, deque iis quae ad regnum Dei spectant, ac vitam illam æternam. Neque vero metuendum est, ne huiusmodi cogitatio impediat occupationes istas terrestres, cum potius nemo in vocatione sua, etiam mundana, fidelis sit censendus, nisi is quiante oculos habet Deum suum, ac vitam illam cœlestem: nemo sit iudicandus frui solida illa voluptate, quæ est in agendo, nisi is qui de cœlis cogitat. Dicitur Eunuchus ille Æthiops postquam conversus est & baptizatus ministerio Philippi, & postquam Philippus iam sublatus est ex oculis ipsius, dicitur, inquam, perrexisse in via sua cum gaudio. Gaudium hoc non percepit ex tota Æthiopia sua, aut ex gloria & opibus quibus domi fruiturus erat: sed gaudium hoc erat ex fide & spe gloriæ Dei, ac hereditatis illius cœlestis. Venit igitur misera, ut ad eam redeam, ad fontem Iacobi, secura Dei ac vitæ cœlestis, tantum cogitans de mundo hoc, deque rebus nescio quibus frivolis & vanis, quas oportuit suboriri in corde eo in quo Christus per fidem non habitavit. Sed vide clementiam Dei: inventus est ab ea quæ ipsum non quærebat. Mundus hic miserrimus, & vnusquisque suis ipsius viis incidit, meretur que propter defectionem suam, ut Deus sinat ipsum abire in extremam perditionem: & verum quidem est quod finit multitudinem abire in perditionem. De gentibus dictum est a Paulo, quod praeteritis ætatibus Deus fuerit omnes gentes suis ipsarum viis incedere. Sic quoque ipsos electos ad tempus errare, ac tum cum ipsi videtur, praeter expectationem praeuenit eos ac vocat. Quemadmodum enim sine nobis, etiam cum non essemus nos elegit: ita sine nobis, postquam sumus, tamen sine praeparatione aliqua nostra, sine meritis nostris, nos vocat: quo nimirum gloria vocationis in solidum ad ipsum pertineat. Tum enim maxime soluitur cor hominis ad Deum suum glorificandum, dum cogitat se praeuentum esse ex Dei sola misericordia, sine merito sui, imo contra meritum suum, tanta tamque praeclara vocatione. Paulus cum videret se vocatum, etiam cum prius blasphemus, cum persecutor, cum iniurious esset, in quantam, tam, Deus bone, glorificationem Dei erumpit: Regi, inquit, æterno, immortali, invisibili, soli sapienti Deo honor sit ac gloria in sæcula sæculorum. Amen.
units.tr: Nothing is to be done or cared for in this our pilgrimage, but we must principally think day and night about the Lord, and about those things which pertain to the kingdom of God and that eternal life. Nor indeed should we fear that such thinking will hinder those earthly occupations, since rather no one should be judged faithful in his calling, even a worldly one, unless he has God and that heavenly life before his eyes; and no one should be judged to enjoy that solid delight which lies in doing his work, unless he thinks of heaven. That Ethiopian eunuch, after he was converted and baptized by the ministry of Philip, and after Philip had already been taken from his sight, is said, I say, to have gone on his way with joy. He did not receive this joy from all his Ethiopia, nor from the glory and riches he was to enjoy at home; this joy came from faith and the hope of the glory of God and that heavenly inheritance. So the wretched woman came, that I may return to her, to Jacob's well, secure about God and heavenly life, thinking only of this world and of I know not what frivolous and vain things, which had to arise in that heart in which Christ did not dwell through faith. But see the mercy of God: he was found by her who was not seeking him. This most wretched world, and each one has fallen into his own ways, and deserves, because of its defection, that God should let it go on to utter perdition; and it is indeed true that he lets the multitude go on to perdition. Of the Gentiles Paul said that in past ages God suffered all nations to walk in their own ways. So too the elect themselves for a time wander, and then, when it seems good to him, he comes before them beyond their expectation and calls them. For just as he chose us without us, even when we did not exist, so, after we exist, he calls us without us, without any preparation of ours, without our merits; so that, of course, the glory of the calling may pertain wholly to him. For then the heart of man is most stirred to glorify its God, when it thinks it has been anticipated by God's mercy alone, without its own merit, indeed against its own merit, by so great and so splendid a calling. When Paul saw that he had been called, though before he had been a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man, how, good God, does he break out into the glorification of God: To the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: Hactenus fuit occasio duplex, sequitur dialogus: Primum orditur sermonem Christus, vt fatigatus ac sitibundus erat, ita potum petiit. Da mihi potum, inquit. Potum aquæ petiit, & potum aquæ bibit Dominus, filius Dei, nostra causa cum in terris versaretur vna nobiscum. Memor esto filium Dei bibisse aquam, vt tu vinum biberes. Nosti s beneficentiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi, eum videlicet propter vos pauperem factum esse, quum esset dives, vt vos illius paupertate ditesceretis. Nam nisi ipse notis fecisset ius vtendi fruendi his rebus, non possemus nos donos bona conscientia bibere vel poculum aquæ frigidæ. Omne enim ius vtendi creaturis Dei plane amisimus in Adamo, quod in Christo altero illo Adamo recuperavimus. Tu esto memor huius rei, quisquis inter potandum & supra modum bibendum, inter devorandum Dei beneficia, tamen blasphemis tuis & prophanis vocibus conculcas pretiosum illum sanguinem, quo tum tui ipsius, tum omnium aliarum rerum, quæ tibi sunt vsui, redemptio facta est. Profecto hac ipsa tua prophanitate satis arguis, tibi nondum redemptum esse ius illud earum rerum. Quid enim iudicare possumus aliud, quoties audimus & videmus tot blasphemias & prophanationes? Dicit ergo ei mulier. Mulier cum cognosceret eum Iudæum esse, idq; vel ex habitu, vel ex voce, vel aliis, indiciis, respondet, Quomodo tu Iudæus, &c. Ratio deinde vi-detur adiecta & obiter inserta ab ipso Evangelista, his verbis, Non enim vtuntur, &c. quibus significat Iudæos non habere commercium vel necessitudinis vsum cum Samaritanis, idque propter defectionem eorum a Deo primum, deinde a domo Dauidis. Responsione hac sua mulier, non tantum denegat Christo potum aquæ, sed cum irridet eum, ac false acerbeque excipit, q d. Alias vos Iudæi contemnitis Samaritanos: nunc cum opus est, petitis ab iis auxilium. Quod ad me, non est quod a me aliquid opus exspectes. Vides igitur mulierem satis acerbe in uehi m Christum. Quæ autem causa huius acerbitatis? nempe contemptus ille Samaritanorum. Omnes
units.tr: So far there have been two occasions; now comes the dialogue. First, Christ begins the discourse; since he was tired and thirsty, he asked for a drink. Give me to drink, he says. The Lord, the Son of God, who while dwelling on earth with us lived with us for our sake, asked for a drink of water and drank water. Remember that the Son of God drank water, so that you might drink wine. You know the kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that by his poverty you might be made rich. For unless he himself had granted us the right to use and enjoy these things, we could not with a good conscience drink even a cup of cold water. For we had entirely lost in Adam every right to use the creatures of God, which we have recovered in Christ, the second Adam. Be mindful of this, whoever you are, who while drinking and drinking beyond measure, while devouring God's benefits, nevertheless trample underfoot with your blasphemies and profane words that precious blood by which the redemption both of yourself and of all the other things that serve your use was made. Surely by this very profanity of yours you prove sufficiently that the right to those things has not yet been redeemed for you. For what else can we judge, whenever we hear and see so many blasphemies and profanations? Therefore the woman says to him. When the woman recognized that he was a Jew, and this from his dress, or his voice, or other signs, she answers, How is it that you, being a Jew, etc. Then the reason seems to be added and inserted in passing by the Evangelist himself, in these words, For the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans, by which he signifies that the Jews had no fellowship or use of dealing with the Samaritans, and this because of their defection first from God, and then from the house of David. By this answer the woman not only refuses Christ water to drink, but also mocks him and receives him falsely and bitterly, as if to say: at other times you Jews despise the Samaritans; now, when you need something, you ask help from them. As for me, there is no reason you should expect anything from me. You see, then, that the woman attacks Christ quite bitterly. What is the cause of this bitterness? Namely that contempt of the Samaritans. All ...

units.la: Colloquium Christi & Samaritanæ mulieris.
units.tr: The conversation of Christ and the Samaritan woman.

units.la: Potus aquæ a Christo petitus, quid donceat.
units.tr: The drink of water asked of Christ: what it signifies.

units.la: Mulieris procacitas.
units.tr: The woman's forwardness.

units.la: Contemptus omnes homines. mines sunt nos volumus natura magni fieri, volumus etiam laudari quae in nobis vitiosa sunt, nihilque est quod aegritius ferimus, quàm contemptum nostri. Hinc fit vt cum videmus nos contemni, prodamus tum acerbitatem animi maiorem, quàm cum vlla alia ratione laedimur, vel in bonis, vel in persona ipsa; facilius quamcunque aliam iniuriam quàm contemptum. Omnes nos etiam regeniti in Christo sentimus in nobis ipsi hanc superbiae & φιλαυτίας radicem. Sed si quis sit extra Christum, regnat in eo hoc malum, vt in miserrima & vili muliere: Nam natura vilissimus quisque, superbissimus est, & de se cogitat summa omnia. Disce exemplo huius mulieris quales nos reperiat Christus in prima nostri vocatione, plenos superbiae & invidiae, & vitiorum denique omnis generis, vt illi merito omne bonum nostrum acceptum feramus, ipsumque glorificemus.
units.tr: Contempt. All men are such that we want by nature to be great, and we want even to be praised for what in us is faulty; and nothing do we bear more painfully than contempt of ourselves. Hence it comes about that when we see ourselves despised, we show a greater bitterness of mind than when we are hurt in any other way, either in our goods or in our person itself; we bear any other injury more easily than contempt. All of us, even the regenerate in Christ, feel in ourselves this root of pride and self-love [φιλαυτίας]. But if anyone is outside Christ, this evil reigns in him as in this most wretched and base woman: for by nature every most base person is most proud and thinks all things of himself. Learn from the example of this woman what kind of people Christ finds us to be at our first calling: full of pride and envy, and in short of vices of every kind, so that we may rightly ascribe all our good to him and glorify him.

units.la: Respondit Iesus, si nosses donum illud Dei, &c. Quodnam sit hoc donum ipse exponit verbis sequentibus, Et quis sit qui dicit tibi. Donum igitur est ipse Christus filius, quem dedit nobis Pater. Ideoque donum appellatur. Omne donum ex dilectione donati proficiscitur: Sic autem Deus dilexit mundum, vt filium suum unigenitum daret. De hoc ineffabili amore nunc non dicam praeterea. Petiisses, inquit, ab eo, & dediset tibi aquam viuam. Aquam viuam intelligo omnem gratiam quae recondita est in Christo, charitatem Dei, iustitiam, sanctitatem, vitam denique aeternam. Comparatur enim gratia Christi aquae, quia gratia illa non secus atque aqua copiose effunditur ac deriuatur per Spiritum sanctum ex illo in nos, quemadmodum de charitate Dei dictum est, Charitas Dei effusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum, qui datus est nobis. Rursus, quemadmodum aqua restinguit sitim hanc corpoream: ita gratia Christi restinguit sitim spiritualem & ariditatem istam quae sit premente & adurente nos ita Dei propter peccatum. Respondit Iesus. In responso Christi vide quanta cum lenitate & animi mansuetudine doceat miseram & refractariam. Non quidem statim excepit eam his verbis: Quòd tu neges mihi potum aquae frigidae, ego vicissim negabo tibi potum aquae quæ viuæ. Sed oblitus acceptæ iniuriæ, oblitus etiam sitis suæ, conatur miseræ sitim aquæ viuæ inducere. Obserua primùm; licet quidem Ministris verbi petere terrestria ista, quæ sunt necessaria ad vitâ hanc toleran- dam. Habent ius suum quærendi ista nihilominus, adeóque magis fortasse quàm alij. Alij, inquit Apostolus, sui in vos iuris participes sunt, cur non potiùs nos?
units.tr: Jesus answered, If you knew the gift of God, etc. He explains what this gift is in the words that follow: and who it is who says to you. The gift, then, is Christ the Son himself, whom the Father gave to us, and so he is called a gift. Every gift proceeds from the love of the giver: for God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son. I will say nothing more here about this inexpressible love. You would have asked of him, he says, and he would have given you living water. I understand by living water all the grace that is laid up in Christ: the love of God, righteousness, holiness, and finally eternal life. For grace is compared to water because it is poured out and drawn from him into us through the Holy Spirit, abundantly like water, just as it is said of the love of God: The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. Again, as water quenches this bodily thirst, so the grace of Christ quenches the spiritual thirst and dryness that God's displeasure on account of sin presses and burns into us. Jesus answered. In Christ's answer, see with how much gentleness and meekness of spirit he teaches this wretched and obstinate woman. He did not at once meet her with these words: Since you refuse me a drink of cold water, I in turn will refuse you a drink of living water. Rather, forgetting the wrong done to him, and forgetting his own thirst, he tries to kindle in her a thirst for living water. Observe first that ministers of the word may indeed ask for those earthly things that are necessary to endure this life. They have a right to seek these things nonetheless, and perhaps more than others. Others, says the Apostle, share this right over you; why not rather we?

units.la: Verum cùm non datur iis quod necessarium est, admonentur hic Christi exemplo sui obliuisci, obliuisci sitis suæ, nuditatis suæ, famis suæ, & cogitatare de aqua illa viua ministranda, etiam iis ipsis qui negant sitientibus potum aquæ frigidæ. Profectò zelus gloriæ Dei & amor salutis hominum huc eos pertraheret, vt obliti sui, strenuè promouerent regnum Christi. Interea autem temporis persuadeant sibi Deum non obliturum famis, sitis ac penuriæ ipsorum, neque obliturum eorum homi- minum, qui illa ad se per fas & nefas trahunt, quibus alerentur Ministri verbi Dei, vt taceam eos etiam tum cùm famelici & egeni prædicant Christum, impleri tamen gaudio spiritus ineffabili. In docendo autem ignaros ac rudes, hoc primùm omnium faciendum, conandum vt quoquo modo fieri possit, inducere iis sitim aquæ huius viuæ; quam si semel serió sitirent isti, profectò potum eius libenter redimerent multis bonis terrestribus.
units.tr: But when those to whom they minister are not given what is necessary, they are admonished by Christ's example to forget themselves: to forget their thirst, their nakedness, their hunger, and to think about ministering that living water even to those very people who deny a drink of cold water to the thirsty. Surely the zeal for God's glory and the love of men's salvation would draw them on, so that, forgetting themselves, they might vigorously advance the kingdom of Christ. Meanwhile, let them persuade themselves that God will not forget their hunger, thirst and want, nor will he forget those men who drag these things to themselves by right and wrong, by which the ministers of God's word might be fed; not to mention that even when they are hungry and needy and preach Christ, they are filled with an inexpressible joy of spirit. In teaching the ignorant and unlearned, the first thing of all to be done, and to be attempted in whatever way is possible, is to kindle in them a thirst for this living water. If once these people were seriously to thirst for it, they would surely gladly buy its drink at the cost of many earthly goods.

units.la: Sitis autem hac ratione inducitur, si notam facias iis, aquam illam quam viuā dicimus; ignoti enim nulla cupido. Vbi autem primùm ceperint eam penitus cognoscere, necesse est expetant eam & requirant. Vt autem nota fiat iis aqua illa viua, non sunt deducendi homines ad paludes & impuros riuulos humanarum inuentionum, sed ad fontem ipsum Christū. Non ad purgatorium, non ad satisfactiones & merita nostra, non ad indulgentias Paparum, & cætera id genus stercora & crebri humani figmenta, sed ad Iesum Christum, in quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ & cognitionis absconditi.
units.tr: Thirst is kindled in this way: if you make known to them that water which we call living; for nobody desires what is unknown. But once they have begun to know it thoroughly, they must desire and seek it. So that this living water may become known to them, men are not to be led to swamps and to the foul streams of human inventions, but to the fountain itself, Christ. Not to purgatory, not to our satisfactions and merits, not to the indulgences of the Popes, and other dung of that kind and the frequent figments of men, but to Jesus Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

units.la: Quare primùm omnium demonstrandus est Christi ignaris hominibus, & quasi aperiendus, ita vt valeant aliquo modo introspicere in thesauros illos, qui in illo reconditi sunt, & abscônditum illud mysterium. Sed nescio quomodo fiat, vt, dum Christus etiam crucifigitur, vt cum Apostolo loquar, ob oculos nostris hominibus, paucissimi tamen sint, qui capiuntur siti aquæ illius viuæ, & desiderio illius gratiæ, quæ ex eo fluit tam copiosè. Necesse est profecto tandè aliquando sitis eos corripiat. Nunc si quis sitit, sunt tępora refrigerationis à cōspectu Domini, vt loquitur Apostolus: est ad manum aqua viua, postea elapsis iā tęporibus his refrigerationis, necesse est, quotquot contęmpserūt hæc tępora, ab ira Dei consumantur, & ad extremā sitim ac siccitatē redigātur.
units.tr: Therefore, first of all, Christ must be shown to ignorant men, and as it were opened up, so that they may be able in some way to look into those treasures that are laid up in him, and that hidden mystery. But I do not know how it happens that, although Christ is crucified, to use the Apostle's words, before the eyes of our people, yet very few are seized with thirst for that living water and with desire for that grace which flows so abundantly from him. Surely a time must come at last when thirst seizes them. Now, if anyone thirsts, there are "times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord," as the Apostle says: the living water is at hand. Afterwards, when these times of refreshing have passed, all who have despised these times must necessarily be consumed by the wrath of God and reduced to extreme thirst and dryness.

units.la: Dicit ei mulier.Respondit mulier, eúmque petit hoc dilemmate: Aqua illa quam promittis te daturum, vel est aqua istius fontis, vel alia quædam melior illa. Atqui aquam istius fontis dare non potes; nam neque habes quo haurias, & puteus profundus est. Sin dixeris te meliorem aliquam daturum, tum quidem te ipse maiorem & præstantiorem patre nostro Iacobo feceris, eo nimirum qui dedit nobis hunc puteum, ex quo ipse bibit & filii eius & pecora eius: ergo nulla omnino aquam potes mihi dare. Satis ingeniosa est mulier ad reuiciendam à se gratiam, ne ad ipsam vsque pertingat. Videmus autem in ea, tanquam in speculo aliquo, imaginem naturæ, quæ est omnium hominum. Primùm nemo omniũ est qui natura vel semel cogitet de gratia, vel de ea semel suspicetur, priusquā ea oblata fuerit: verùm omnes cogitationes omnium sunt de rebus his terrestribus &. mūdanis: nihilque in pretio est apud nos, præter has res.
units.tr: The woman says to him. The woman answers, and she attacks him with this dilemma: That water which you promise to give is either the water of this well, or some other better water. But you cannot give the water of this well; for you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. But if you say that you will give some better water, then indeed you make yourself greater and more excellent than our father Jacob, who certainly gave us this well, from which he himself drank, and his sons and his cattle: therefore you can by no means give me water. The woman is clever enough in rejecting grace from herself, so that it may not reach her at all. Yet we see in her, as in a kind of mirror, the image of nature, which is that of all men. First, there is no one of all men who by nature ever thinks even once about grace, or suspects it even once, before it has been offered. Rather, all men's thoughts are about these earthly and worldly things, and nothing is valued by us except these things.

units.la: Atque hæc est prima miseria nostra; miseri fumus & tamen ignari adeo fumus miseriæ nostræ, vt de gratia & remedio non possimus vnquā cogitare. Sed est hæc miseria maior & grauior in natura nostra. Mulier oblata iam gratia, tamen non videt eam, neque quid sit intelligit, putat Christum loqui de aqua ista terrena. Etiam cum offertur gratia & ob oculos nostros ponitur, tamē eam non possumus internoscere. Putamus spiritualia esse terrena & corporalia; vt, si cæcum aliquem producas ad solem meridianū, & queras ecquid videat, respondebit miseró sibi nihil præter meras tenebras esse obiectū: cæco enim sol est tenebræ. Ita aqua illa spiritualis & gratia Christi si offeratur & animali homini, est ei duntaxat terrenū aliquid & corporale. Sic cum Christus ftus locutus est Nicodemo de regeneratione, intellexit cum loquentem de crassa ista & naturali generatione. Atque haec est secunda pars miseriae nostrae. Verum adhuc deterior quidem est miseriae nostrae gradus. Mulier ista etiam contradicit ac resistit gratiae oblatae, qualitercunque eam intelligat, & offerentem Christum accusat blasphemiae, ut qui se maiorem patre Iacobo faciat.
units.tr: And this is our first misery: we are wretched, and yet we are so ignorant of our misery that we can never think of grace and remedy. But this misery is greater and heavier still in our nature. The woman, although grace has already been offered to her, does not see it, nor does she understand what it is; she thinks that Christ is speaking of ordinary water. Even when grace is offered and set before our eyes, we still cannot discern it. We think spiritual things are earthly and bodily. If you bring some blind man out into the midday sun and ask whether he sees anything, he will answer that nothing but pure darkness is set before his wretched self: for to the blind man the sun is darkness. So too, if that spiritual water and the grace of Christ are offered to the natural man, it is to him only something earthly and bodily. So when Christ spoke to Nicodemus about regeneration, he understood him to be speaking of that coarse, natural generation. And this is the second part of our misery. But there is an even worse degree of our misery. This woman also contradicts and resists the grace offered, however she understands it, and accuses Christ, who offers it, of blasphemy, as one who makes himself greater than our father Jacob.

units.la: Non modo non possumus videre gratiam cum offertur, quae est mentis nostrae caecitas, sed ea praeterea est pertinacia cordis, ut nolimus videre eam, verum quantis possumus viribus oppugnemus eam, simulque eos, qui eam nobis offerunt. Unde fit ut iusto Dei iudicio magis magisque excaecemur. Nam sicut non visum est hominibus Deum in notitia non retinere; ita tradidit eos Deus in mentem omnis iudicij expertem. Deveniimus igitur ac redigimur in extremas tenebras, Deo iusto suo iudicio eximente e natura etiam naturalis illius luminis reliquias. Vide igitur in quantas tenebras demersus sit homo, & quibus demum gradibus descendat in abyssum illam, & ad inferos ipsos. Nam quanto magis involuitur tenebris, tanto magis protruditur ad inferos. Quid enim aliud inferi quam tenebrae illae exteriores, ut vocat eas Dominus. Vide igitur quam loge sit homo a luce, ut illud miraculum sit stupendium maxime, cum vides hominem ex parte aliqua illuminatum esse illa in Christo cognitione. Mirantur homines dum vident miseros se proiicere in omne scelus, sed nihil novi est hic: nihil enim faciunt contra ingenium & naturam suam. Quin mirare potius, cum vides vel centesimum quemque inflecti ad quiduis quod bonum est Deoque acceptum perpetrandum. Nondum conuersi ex gentibus, cum viderent conuersos ad Christum non concurrere more solito ad eandem luxus profusionem, sic mirati sunt, ut viderentur sibi, teste Petro, peregrinari, & blasphemarent. Sed nihil de conuersis illic legimus quod & hi minimum vicissim licentiam illam immoderatam ac luxuriam getium. Non ita magnum illud est, Deum hominem nihilo fecisse (loquor cōparatè) sed magnū hoc est, imo maximum, Deum facere hominem ex malo bonum, seu regenerationem, Deum facere ex massa tenebrarum ta claram lucem. contrario enim, quod plane contrarium est facere, summi artificij est, maximeque arguit potentiam artificis admirabilem. Potentia ista quae est in nobis regenerandis, tota in Mediatore residet, per fidem autem in Mediatorem in nobis est efficax. Et quae sit, inquit Paulus, excellens illa magnitudo potentiae ipsius in nobis qui credimus. Quotquot credunt in Christum Iesum, nō citius credunt, eúmque fide apprehendunt, quàm sentiant se mirifica illa Dei potentia aliquatenus mutari, illuminari, inquam, mentem, & reformari affectus. Quotquot vero non credunt in Christum, nullam prorsus in se vel metis vel cordis mutationem & innovationem sentire possunt. Verum vt vt in specie bene vel loquantur vel faciant, ipsi in se sentiunt interea & sibi conscij sunt, quàm obstinatum & praefractum cor intus delitescat, pugnans cum externis & praeclaris illis scilicet siue factis siue dictis. Adeóque ipsi etiam fideles, quo tempore remissior fit illa fides in Christum, interque se & Christum separationem aliquam fieri sentiunt, eo ipso tempore etiā, fideles experiuntur cor sibi redire ad pristinam dutitiem, vt reipsa illud experiri possimus, regeneratione nostri, illuminationem, inquam, mentis, & cordis reformatione, non esse nisi à praesente facie Iesu Christi, dum eum fide apprehendimus. Vbi cor conuersum fuerit ad Dominum, ait Apost. tolletur velamen. Dominus vero spiritus ille est, vbi autem spiritus ille Domini, illic libertas. Et alibi, dicit Paulus Deum nobis illuxisse, ad praebendum lumen cognitionis gloriae Dei in facie Iesu Christi.
units.tr: We not only cannot see grace when it is offered, which is the blindness of our mind; but besides this there is the obstinacy of the heart, so that we are unwilling to see it, and rather with all our strength we attack it, and at the same time those who offer it to us. Hence it comes about that, by God's just judgment, we are more and more blinded. For just as it did not seem good to men to retain God in knowledge, so God gave them over to a mind devoid of all judgment. We therefore fall and are driven into the uttermost darkness, God by his just judgment taking away from our nature even the remnants of that natural light. See, then, into what darkness man has sunk, and by what degrees he descends into that abyss, and even to hell itself. For the more he is wrapped in darkness, the more he is thrust down to hell. For what else is hell but those outer darkness, as the Lord calls them? See, then, how far man is from the light, so that that miracle is most stupendous, when you see a man illumined in some part by that knowledge of Christ. Men marvel when they see themselves cast headlong into every crime, but there is nothing new here: for they do nothing contrary to their nature and disposition. Rather, marvel when you see even one in a hundred turned to perform whatever is good and acceptable to God. When the Gentiles had not yet been converted, and saw the converted to Christ no longer running with them to the same flood of profligacy, they were amazed, so that, as Peter testifies, they seemed to themselves to be strangers, and they blasphemed. But we read nothing there about the converted, that they in turn gave any slight licence to that immoderate and luxurious way of life of the Gentiles. It is not so great a thing that God made man out of nothing (I speak comparatively), but it is great, indeed the greatest, that God makes a man good out of evil, that is, regeneration; that God makes so clear a light out of a mass of darkness. For to do the opposite, which is plainly the contrary, is the mark of the highest craftsmanship, and most of all shows the admirable power of the craftsman. That power which is in us for regeneration resides entirely in the Mediator, and through faith in the Mediator it is effective in us. And what is, says Paul, that surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe. All who believe in Jesus Christ, and so apprehend him by faith, do not sooner believe than they feel that wonderful power of God working some change in them: I mean, their mind is enlightened and their affections reformed. But all who do not believe in Christ can feel no change or renewal at all in their mind or heart. Yet, however well they speak or act in appearance, they feel within themselves in the meantime, and are conscious, how obstinate and unyielding a heart lies hidden within, struggling against those outward and splendid deeds or words of theirs. And so even the faithful themselves, at the time when that faith in Christ grows weaker, and they feel some separation between themselves and Christ, at that very time also experience their heart returning to its former hardness. Thus we can indeed experience this: that our regeneration, the illumination, I mean, of mind and the reformation of heart, is nothing other than the presence of the face of Jesus Christ, while we apprehend him by faith. When the heart has turned to the Lord, says the Apostle, the veil will be taken away. Now the Lord is that Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. And elsewhere Paul says that God has shone into us, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

units.la: 13 Respondit Iesus & dixit ei, Quisquis bibit ex aqua ista, sitiet rursus:
units.tr: 13 Jesus answered and said to her, Whoever drinks of this water will thirst again:

units.la: 14 Quisquis autem biberit ex aqua illa quam ego ei dabo, non sitiet in aeternum: sed aqua illa, quā ego dabo ei, fiet in eo fons aquae salientis vitam aeternam.
units.tr: 14 But whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst for ever; but the water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up into eternal life.

units.la: 15 Dicit ei mulier, Domine da mihi aquam istam, vt non sitiam, neque veniam huc ad hauriendum.
units.tr: 15 The woman said to him, Lord, give me this water, that I may not thirst, nor come here to draw.

units.la: SEquitur responsum Domini, vt doceat hanc aquam, quam ipse daturus esset, meliorem aqua fontis Iacobi, vtque alliciat mulieris animum ad eam requirendam, proponit ipsi effectum dissimile vtriusque aquæ. Aquæ autem fontis Iacobi primum effectum ostendit, hoc nimirum, quòd non sic restinguat sitim hominis, quum postea esset siti corripiendus. Aquæ verò quam ipse daturus esset effectum docet, quòd quisquis biberit ex ea; in posterum non sitiet in æternum: ratio autem addita est, inquit, aqua illa, quam ego dabo ei, fiet in eo fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam, ac proinde in perpetuum irrigaturus hominem, cùm ex ipso homine fit proma-naturus: ideóque nunquam sit permissurus, vt is, in quo sit ipsa, aresçat, & ad extremam sitim perveniat. Argumentum hoc quo vtitur Dominus valdè accommodatum est ad ingenium humanum. Nemo enim est omnium, qui si non prorsus hebes sit, non sentiat in se plurimum imperfectionis, & infinitos defectus. Quo sit vt appetat quisque perfectionem & supplementum tot tantorúmque defectuum, adeo vt si quid occurrat quod putet quis hoc aliquo modo præstiturum, statim ad id confugiat ipsúmque persequatur. Sed dehinc miserè erratHominies circa eas res quas putát hoc efficere posse, ipsósque perficere. Quidà enim ad diuitias confugiunt, in iisque quærunt perfectionem & beatitatem, quidam ad gloriam, quidam ad voluptatem, nonnulli ad brachium humanum: Nonnulli etiam in negotio religionis ad idola, & inventa ac figmenta cerebri humani. Fieri quidem potest vt ista aut illorum aliquod, ad breue quoddam tempus tranquillet hominis animum. Sed vt de eo taceam, falsam esse istam pacem ac mendacem securitatem (nulla enim pax est improbis, ait Dominus) necesse est is sitiat rursus cuius sicr estinsta est sitis, & quò plus istarum rerū percipit, eò plus sitiat: sunt enim omnia ista friuola & ieiuna, quæ ieiunum & vacuum hominis animum adimplere nunquam poterunt. Dicâ igitur verbo quod sentio, nihil inuenies, neque in cœlis, neque in terris quo saturaberis & perficieris præter solum Iesum Christum, cum tota plenitudine illa deitatis, quæ in ipso inhabitat corporaliter. Nam qui semel gustauit quàm benignus & suauis sit Dominus, quàm parua, quæso, istarum rerum portione cōtentus est, quas tam auidè vniuersas absorbet ac devorat vulgus hominum? Magnus est quæstus pietas, cum animo sua sorte contento. In corde enim pij cuiusque, quod Deo plenum est, parū loci relinquitur terrenis his & caducis rebus, sed contentum est mediocribus.
units.tr: The Lord's reply follows. To teach that this water, which he himself was about to give, is better than the water of Jacob's well, and to draw the woman's mind to seek it, he sets before her the different effects of the two waters. He shows first the effect of Jacob's water: that it does not quench a man's thirst so thoroughly that he will not later be seized by thirst again. Then he teaches the effect of the water he himself will give: whoever drinks of it will never thirst again for ever. He adds the reason: the water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up into eternal life. Thus it will water the man for ever, since it will flow out from the man himself. Therefore he will never allow the one in whom it dwells to dry up and come to extreme thirst. The argument the Lord uses is very well suited to the human mind. For there is no one, unless he is utterly dull, who does not feel in himself a great deal of imperfection and countless defects. Hence each person seeks perfection and the remedy for so many and such great defects. So if anything presents itself that he thinks can supply this in some way, he immediately flees to it and pursues it. But men wretchedly err about those things which they think can accomplish this and make them perfect. Some flee to riches and seek perfection and blessedness in them, some to glory, some to pleasure, some to human strength. Some, in matters of religion, flee to idols and to the inventions and fictions of the human brain. It may indeed happen that these, or some of them, calm a man's mind for a short time. But, to say nothing of that, this peace is false and this security a lie (for "there is no peace for the wicked," says the Lord). Necessarily the one whose thirst seemed quenched thirsts again, and the more he gets of these things, the more he thirsts. For all these things are frivolous and empty, and they can never fill a man's hungry and empty soul. So I will say plainly what I think: you will find nothing, neither in heaven nor on earth, with which you will be satisfied and made complete, except Jesus Christ alone, with all the fullness of the Godhead that dwells in him bodily. For whoever has once tasted how kind and sweet the Lord is, how little, I ask, is he content with that portion of these things which the crowd of men swallows and devours so eagerly? Godliness is great gain, for one content with his lot. For in the heart of every godly person, which is full of God, little room is left for these earthly and perishing things, and he is content with modest things.

units.la: Vt ad Christum redeam, sapienter admodum accommodauit argumentum suum ad ingenium mulieris. Cuius exemplo discimus, nos in tractandis spiritualibus rebus, quarum natura ignari sunt homines, vti arguméntis etiam naturæ captui & ingenio humano accommodis, vt, si quo modo fieri possit, afficiantur desiderio rerum spiritualium. Omnes amant & expetunt æternitatem ac immortalitatem, etiam natura ipsa. Dicamus igitur spiritualia illa, ac ea quæ non cernuntur oculis hisce corporeis, æterna esse, vt dixit Paulus: Ea quæ non cernuntur æterna sunt, ea vero quæ cernuntur temporaria sunt.
units.tr: To return to Christ: he very wisely fitted his argument to the woman's mind. From her example we learn that in handling spiritual things, of whose nature men are ignorant, we should also use arguments suited to the grasp and mind of human nature, so that, if somehow it can be done, they may be moved by a desire for spiritual things. All men love and desire eternity and immortality, by nature itself. Let us therefore say that those spiritual things, and those which are not seen with these bodily eyes, are eternal, as Paul said: The things which are not seen are eternal, but the things which are seen are temporary.

units.la: Deinde oritur hic quæstio; qui fiat vt dicat, eū hominem qui biberit ex aqua illa, sitim in posterum nunquàm passurum, cùm hoc sentiamus omnes in nobis ipsi, quanto magis bibimus ex aqua ista viua & gratia spiritus Christi, tanto magis nos sitire? Responsio patet ex ipso contextu, Sed, inquit, aqua illa quam ego ei dabo. &c. Q. d. Sitiet quidem, sed non prius sitiet, quàm restinguetur illa sitis. Nam aqua quam ego dabo fiet in eo fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam: Hoc est, habebit in se & ad manum fontem illum aquæ, qui semper recentem aquam subministrabit & imperpetuum irrigabit hominem, nec patietur vnquam præsiti & siccitate perire hominem. Aqua quidem ista terrena, vt & res omnes aliæ terrenæ (nam hoc homine omnes simul ac semel intelligi possunt) a sitientibus epotę ad certum tempus restinguntur sitim, sed qui eas bibunt, rursus sitient. Postremò autem eò deveniunt quotquot confidunt his rebus, vt non inveniant quidquam quo sitim restinguant, sed necesse sit præsiti ac extrema ariditate pereant in æternum. Qui vero cæpit bibere ex aqua ista viua & cælesti, quoties sitiet, toties bibet; habebit enim in se fontem aquæ perennem, neque vnquam fiet vt exaresçat. Sitimus quidem aquam istam terrenam, & res omnes has terrenas cum dolore aliquo, quia nimirum non semper suppetit,quo restin-guamus sitim. At verò cùm sitimus res illas cœlestes, tû sentimus perpetuò aliquid gaudij & voluptatis, etiam cùm desideramus, etiam cùm suspiramus, etiam cùm gaudemus. Arguit autem gaudium istud nos quo mo-mento sitimus, eodem plane momento haurire nos i-stam aquam viuam, ex eáque bibere. Verùm, vt dicam quod res est, tum sactetas hæc, de qua loquitur Christus, contingeꝛ, cùm hauriemus postremum potum illum & plenum in Domini nostri aduentu. Hausto semel illo potu non sitiemus rursus, non suspirabimus amplius, nihil vltra desiderabimus, nō dolebimus in posterum, sed abstergentur omnes lachrymæ ab oculis nostris, & sincerum erit gaudium in æternum. Nunc enim gaudium Christiani hominis non est sincerum ac purum putum, sed dolori alicui semper admixtum, tum propter reliquias illas peccati, tum quia peregrinamur à Domino. At verò tum sine dolore, sine suspiriis gaudium erit purum putum ac sincerum in omnem æternitatem.
units.tr: Then the question arises: how can he say that the man who drinks of that water will never thirst again, when we all feel in ourselves that the more we drink of this living water and the grace of Christ's Spirit, the more we thirst? The answer is clear from the context itself: But, he says, the water that I will give him, and so on. That is to say: he will indeed thirst, but he will not thirst before that thirst is quenched. For the water that I will give will become in him a spring of water welling up into eternal life. That is, he will have within himself and at hand that spring of water, which will always supply fresh water and water him for ever, and will never allow the man to perish by thirst and dryness. Indeed, earthly water, like all other earthly things (for all of these can be understood together in this one word), when drunk by the thirsty quenches thirst for a certain time, but those who drink them will thirst again. Finally, however, all who trust in these things come to the point where they find nothing with which to quench their thirst, and they must perish in extreme dryness for ever. But whoever has begun to drink of this living and heavenly water will, as often as he thirsts, drink again; for he will have within himself a perennial spring of water, and it will never happen that it dries up. We thirst indeed for this earthly water, and for all these earthly things, with some pain, because naturally they are not always at hand to quench our thirst. But when we thirst for those heavenly things, we always feel some joy and pleasure, even when we long, even when we sigh, even when we rejoice. That joy shows that at the very moment we thirst, we draw that living water and drink from it at that same moment. But, to say what is the case, that satiety of which Christ speaks will come when we draw that last and full drink at the coming of our Lord. Once we have drunk that draught we will not thirst again, we will not sigh any more, we will desire nothing further, we will grieve no longer; but all tears will be wiped from our eyes, and our joy will be pure for ever. For now the joy of a Christian is not pure and unmixed, but always mingled with some sorrow, both because of the remnants of sin and because we are away from the Lord. But then, without sorrow and without sighs, joy will be pure and unmixed for all eternity.

units.la: Dicit ei mulier. Respösione hac sua mulier indicat quidem se suè saluterm aliqua correptam, audita iam effi-cacia istius aquæ, quam dixit Dominus se daturum.
units.tr: The woman said to him. By this reply the woman shows that she has been seized by some concern for her salvation, now that she has heard of the efficacy of the water which the Lord said he would give.

units.la: Verùm rursus verba subindicant non intellixisse eam qualisnam esset ista aqua. Nam quod dicit, vt non sitiam neque veniam huc ad hauriendum, satis arguit intellexisse eam corporalem & temporariam aquam, nō absimilem nimirum aquæ fontis Iacobi, & si fortassis ea præstantiorem, qua restinguatur corporalis ista sitis, cuiusque beneficio leuari possit mulier labore illo veniendi ad fontem Iacobi. Omnes volumus esse beati, omnes immortales, ad hoc enim ipsum condidit nos Deus, vt viueremus in æternum. Hinc est vt inde à creatione perpetuò appetant, etiam naturæ instinctu, omnes homines illam immortalitatem, ad quam sunt initio conditi. Verùm si qui non sunt illuminati Spiritu Dei sancto, quærunt duntaxat terrenam quandam felicitatem, volúntque manere semper in præsenti vita etiam cum miseria & summa penuria omnium rerum, tamen volunt in terris perpetuò superuiuere, & de migratione non nisi inuiti cogitant.
