Next, we see in these words of Christ, and in this example of Christ, that the godly, once it has been granted them to behold those heavenly things, are lifted far above all these heavens, and above those who cling forever to the mire of this world, however wise or glorious they may seem to be; and they look down on all these things as if from above, and make nothing of the wisdom of this world or the nobility and glory of the noble, fixing their eyes on that wisdom and glory which is seen only in heaven.

units.la: Piorum fe-lix condi-tio. in cœlis tantùm conspicitur: non raro etiam obiicere iis qui delectantur his rebus duntaxat, neque superna vnquam quærunt, ignorantiam ac cæcitatem: atque id quidem faciunt, non ob contemptum illum, sed propter commiserationem, vt si fieri posset, attacti sensu tandem ignorantiæ ac miseriæ suæ, incipiant desiderare ac expetere aspectum illum cælorum, vt desiderantes suo tempore eos alsequantur: Beati enim qui esuriunt & sitiunt iustitiam, quoniam ipsi saturabuntur.
units.tr: The happy condition of the godly. Often they also rebuke those who take delight only in these things and never seek the things above, pointing out their ignorance and blindness. They do this not out of contempt, but out of compassion, so that, if it could be done, those who have at last felt their ignorance and misery might begin to desire and long for the sight of those heavens, so that, desiring, they may attain it in due time: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.

units.la: Hactenus respondit Christus, nunc quid ad hæc discipuli, ignari quid sibi vellet cibus ille de quo loquetur, incipiunt alij alios interrogare de eo, dicuntque, num quis attulit ei cibum quo vescatur? Suspicati enim sunt cibum vel à muliere illa vel aliunde suppeditatum: Neque enim intellexerunt eum loquutum esse de cibo illo cœlesti. Non, si semel atque iterum sermo fiat nobis de rebus cœlestibus ac spiritualibus, non tamen statim eos percipiemus, ne tum quidem cum adumbrantur nobis crassis & corporeis figuris, vt generationis carnalis sup. cap.3.3. vt aquæ terrestris hoc cap.v.10. vt cibi corporalis hoc loco. Imo verò etsi assiduè inculcentur nobis, iterentúrque per totum vitæ spatium, tamen etiam tum non nisi satis crassa est ac rudis cognitio istarum rerum. Atque hinc est quòd tam parũ gaudij ac solatij ex istis intellectis percipiamus. Quòd si Christum ipsiúsque iustitiam ac vitam in ipso æternam purè intueri ac videre possemus sicuti sunt, ô lætitiam illam & pacem quam tum conciperemus animo! sed hoc non vsquequaque obtinuerit in hac mortali vita, tantisper dum corruptio ista non fuerit tota semel deposita, & immortalitas per vitam absorpta.
units.tr: Christ has answered thus far. Now the disciples, not knowing what that food of which he was speaking meant, begin to ask one another about it, and say, Has anyone brought him something to eat? For they suspected that food had been supplied to him either by that woman or from some other source; indeed they did not understand that he had spoken of that heavenly food. It is not the case that if spiritual and heavenly things are spoken of to us once or twice, we will immediately grasp them, not even when they are shadowed forth to us by gross and bodily figures, as of carnal generation (see above, chap. 3.3), as of earthly water (chap. 5.10 here), as of bodily food in this place. Indeed, even if they are constantly impressed upon us and repeated throughout the whole span of life, our knowledge of these things is still only fairly crude and rude. And hence it is that we receive so little joy and comfort from things once understood. But if we could look upon and see Christ, and his righteousness and eternal life in him, purely, as they are, oh, what joy and peace we would then conceive in our minds! But this cannot be fully attained in this mortal life, so long as that corruption has not been wholly laid aside and immortality swallowed up in life.

units.la: 34 Dicit ei Iesus, Esca mea est exequi voluntatem eius qui misit me, & perficere ipsius opus.
units.tr: 34 Jesus said to him, My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to finish his work.

units.la: 35 Nonne vos dicitis, Adhuc quadrimestre spatium superest, & messis erit? Ecce dico vobis, Attolite oculos vestros & spectate regiones: Nam albæ iam sunt ad messem.
units.tr: 35 Do you not say, There are yet four months, and then comes the harvest? Behold, I say to you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are already white for the harvest.

units.la: 36 Qui autem metit, mercedem accipit, & cogit fructum in vitam aeternam: vt & qui seminat, simul gaudeat, & qui metit.
units.tr: 36 And he who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit unto eternal life, so that he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together.

units.la: 37 Nam in hoc dictum illud verum est, Alius est qui seminat, & alius qui metit.
units.tr: 37 For in this the saying is true, One sows and another reaps.

units.la: 38 Ego misi vos ad id metendum, in quo vos non laborastis: alii laborauerunt, & vos in labores eorum introistis.
units.tr: 38 I sent you to reap that in which you have not laboured; others have laboured, and you have entered into their labours.

units.la: NVnc Dominus ignoratum ab iis cibum illum clare exponit, atque interpretatur de executione voluntatis Patris sui qui ipsum misit, deque perfectione operis ipsius. Noto hic, priusquam ad alia accedam, bonum esse perpetuo inquirere in illa spiritualia, etsi saepe in iis concipiendis a vero aberremus. Dominus enim diligit eos qui afficiuntur aliquo boni obtinendi desiderio, neque eos deserit, sed illuminat eos Spiritu suo sancto. Vide hoc primum in Christo, Ei qui est Dominus omnium, annon liberrimum fuit, quo tempore e-suriuit, recreare sese suo ipsius cibo? verum oblata iam occasione exequendi voluntatem Patris, oblitus est cibi, & accinxit se ad illud opus Patris sui: ita omnino omnibus libera sunt, in quacunque demum vocatione sint per Dominum Iesum Christum licet iis curare corpus suum, sese recreare, cibum capere, bibere, & alia id genus facere, quae ad corporis recreationem & curam attinent: etiam haec licent Ministris verbi, quibus tamen vel ipsam hanc vitam inuidet mundus. Verum sese offerente occasione & opportunitate exequendi quae ad functionem cuiusque pertinent, iam oportet obliuisci nostri ipsorum & occasionem illam arripere, imo cum dies mali sint, & occasio agendi secundum vocationem cuiusque saepe non concedatur, redimenda est occasio vel rebus charissimis quibusque, vel discrimine vitae ipsius: Redimetes occasionem, quoniam dies mali sunt, ait Apostolus. Deinde discimus occupatione ista Christi tam seriam, fuisse ei instar cibi, hoc est, ea eum delectatum esse magis quam cibo & potu, tantum abfuit ab eo vt oneri fuerit ei. Cum distrahimur curis & occupationibus secundum vocationem cuiusque, videndum est ne sint illæ occupationes nobis graues, sed sint nobis instar cibi: hoc est, cum voluptate quadam ac iucunditate occupemur in iis. Pascite Dei gregem, qui penes vos est, curam illius agentes non coacte sed libenter, inquit Petrus. Si quem alium oportet cum voluptate & alacritate animi quadam occupatum esse, & Ministrum verbi maxime: Et revera is quisquis est quem misit Dominus, fungitur officio suo serio, & cum gaudio expectans gaudium ineffabile & gloriosum in adventu Domini sui.
units.tr: Now the Lord clearly explains that food, which was unknown to them, and interprets it as the doing of the will of his Father who sent him, and the completing of his work. I note here, before I proceed to other matters, that it is always good to inquire into those spiritual things, although in conceiving them we often go astray from the truth. For the Lord loves those who are moved by some desire to obtain a good, and he does not forsake them, but enlightens them with his Holy Spirit. See this first in Christ. Was it not most free for him, the Lord of all, when he was hungry, to refresh himself with his own food? Yet when the opportunity of doing the Father's will was offered, he forgot food and girded himself for that work of his Father. So in the same way, all are free, in whatever calling they may be, through the Lord Jesus Christ, to look after their body, to refresh themselves, to take food, to drink, and to do other things of that kind which pertain to the refreshment and care of the body. These things are allowed even to ministers of the Word, although the world begrudges them even this life. But when opportunity and occasion of performing what pertains to each one's office is offered, we must then forget ourselves and seize that opportunity. Indeed, since the days are evil, and the opportunity for acting according to each one's calling is often not granted, the opportunity must be redeemed even at the cost of the dearest things, or at the risk of life itself: "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil," says the Apostle. Next, we learn from this that such serious occupation was to Christ in place of food, that is, that he was delighted by it more than by food and drink, so far was it from being a burden to him. When we are distracted by cares and occupations according to each one's calling, we must take care that those occupations are not grievous to us, but are to us in place of food: that is, that we are occupied in them with a certain pleasure and delight. "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight of it not under compulsion but willingly," says Peter. If anyone ought to be occupied with pleasure and a certain alacrity of mind, the minister of the Word most of all should be. And indeed, whoever it is whom the Lord has sent, he performs his office earnestly, and, awaiting with joy the inexpressible and glorious joy at the coming of his Lord.

units.la: Quę est spes mea, aut gaudium, aut corona, de qua glorier? Annon vos in conspectu Domini nostri Iesu Christi in adventu eius?
units.tr: What is my hope, or joy, or crown of which I boast? Are not you also, in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming?

units.la: Tertio obseruamus in Christo, eum exequutum esse cum voluptate & gaudio non voluntate suam, sed Patris sui voluntatem; perfecisse non opus suum, sed opus Patris sui. Ita videndum nobis est cuiusnam sit illud opus, in quo perficiendo occupamur etiam cum voluptate & gaudio, nostrumne an Dei opus? Quod si nos ipsos, & quæ nostra sunt quæramus in vocatione quacunque, tum quidem opus nostrum agimus, & reportamus in hac vita mercedem nostram. Sin Deum nobis proponamus ciusque gloriam in agendo, tum Dei opus agimus, interea dum nobis ipsi prosumus: Nam & Deum eo opere glorificamus, & recipiemus mercedem nostram in cœlis, idque per Iesum Christum, cui sit omnis honor & gloria. Amen.
units.tr: Thirdly, we observe in Christ that he carried out his work with delight and joy, not by his own will but by the will of his Father, and that he finished not his own work but the work of his Father. So we must consider whose work it is that we are engaged in, even when we take delight and joy in it: is it our work or God's? If in any calling we seek ourselves and what is ours, then indeed we are doing our own work and receive our reward in this life. But if we set God before us and his glory in our acting, then we are doing God's work, and at the same time we benefit ourselves. For we glorify God by that work, and we shall receive our reward in heaven, and this through Jesus Christ, to whom be all honour and glory. Amen.

units.la: Nonne vos dicitis. Hactenus in hoc sermone cum discipulis collato Dominus instituit discipulos in cura ea & diligentia, quam ipse obibat in officio sibi a Patre delegato. Nunc hortatur discipulos, adductis aliquot argumentis, vt ipsi similiter fideles sint in officio suo faciendo. Qui fideles vere sunt, ij optima conscientia & summa authoritate possunt alios admonere & hortari. Qui autem ipsi fideles non sunt, qua, quæso, conscientia possunt alios hortari & admonere? Annon necesse est interea temporis cor eorum ipsos condemnet? Quare cum Pastorum officium potissimum cernatur in admonitionibus & exhortationibus, ipsi primi omnium videant vt acquirant sibi ex officio fideliter præstito bonam conscientiam. Sed videamus summam exhorexhortationis huius, hortatur vt partes agant fidelium messorum in messe Domini: demetant messem Domini, & curam eius rei quàm fieri potest vigilantem suscipiant. Argumentum primum est à cura illa quam habent qui in demetenda messe hac terrestri versantur. Argumentatur autem in hanc formam. Nonne vos dicitis adhuc quadrimestre spatium superesse, & messis aderit? Hoc est, ita solliciti estis de messe hac terrestri, vt singulos menses, singulas septimanas, & dies singulos numeretis vsque dum adueniat messis, adeo auidè eam expectatis. Tum assumit: At messis Domini iam adest: Quod quò magis credant, demonstrat iis quasi digito omnes regiones, quae iam albae sunt ad messem. Ex quo vult concludi, in hac messe Domini laborandum esse. Notat proculdubiò curam rerum terrestrium vsque adeo excellere curam rerum coelestium, vt homines incipiant de iis serió cogitare, déque iis solliciti esse, multò prius quàm vsque veniant solaque spe earum rerum sese oblectent: Res autem coelestes vel ante pedes positas non intueantur: Imò etiam tu cum Dominus quasi è coelis clamat, Extollite oculos & spectate, ne tum quidem spectant nisi aegrè admodum. Quandiu enim clamauit Dominus nostris hominibus vt vellent inspicere messem Domini iam maturam? ideóque vellent emittere messores in agrum Domini. Sed ad hunc vsque diem nemo eorum audiuit, eóque factum est vt messis Domini penè iam putruerit. Quod si fuit aliquando in hominibus aliquis zelus, aliquod desiderium cognoscendi Christi: iam ista ita deferbuerunt vt lubenter per totam vitam patiantur se carere Christo. Scotia nostra perdita est non vno modo, sed multis: Imprimis verò perdita est propter paucitatem eorum qui emittendi sunt in messem Domini. Hinc enim origo tantae iniustitiae quae passim viget: Nam vnde sunt ista tot homicidia, adulteria, rapinae, incantationes, omnium denique rerum confusio? Sunt ista opera infructifera tenebrarum, & sic ea vocat Apostolus: hoc est, opera ignorantiae Christi. Quod si Christus passim per hanc gentem praedicaretur, & fideliter praedicaretur, profecto non essent tot vbique praedae diabolo. Cognitio enim & fides Christi sola est quae sanctificat cor, & purgat animum ab istiusmodi operibus.
units.tr: Do you not say. Hitherto in this discourse, spoken to the disciples, the Lord has taught them to show the same care and diligence that he himself displayed in the office entrusted to him by the Father. Now, by bringing forward several arguments, he urges the disciples to be likewise faithful in performing their own office. Those who are truly faithful can admonish and exhort others with the best conscience and the greatest authority. But those who are not faithful themselves, with what conscience, I ask, can they exhort and admonish others? Must not their own heart condemn them in the meantime? Therefore, since the office of ministers consists chiefly in admonitions and exhortations, let them first of all see to it that they gain for themselves a good conscience from faithfully discharging their office. But let us look at the sum of this exhortation: he urges them to play the part of faithful reapers in the Lord's harvest, to gather in the Lord's harvest and to undertake the care of this task as watchfully as possible. The first argument is drawn from the care that those who are engaged in gathering this earthly harvest show. He argues in this form: Do you not say that there are still four months to go, and the harvest will come? That is, you are so anxious about this earthly harvest that you count out every month, every week, and every single day until the harvest comes, so eagerly do you await it. Then he adds: But the Lord's harvest is already here. So that they may believe this all the more, he points out to them, as it were with his finger, all the regions that are already white for the harvest. From this he wishes it to be concluded that we must labour in this harvest of the Lord. He clearly notes that concern for earthly things so far surpasses concern for heavenly things that men begin to think of the former seriously and to be anxious about them long before they arrive, and delight themselves only with the hope of those things, while they do not look at heavenly things even when they lie right at their feet. Indeed, when the Lord cries out, as if from heaven, Lift up your eyes and look, they do not look even then, except with great difficulty. For how long has the Lord cried out to our people that they should wish to see the Lord's harvest already ripe, and therefore wish to send reapers into the Lord's field? But up to this day none of them has listened, and so it has come about that the Lord's harvest has nearly rotted. If at any time there was in men some zeal, some desire to know Christ, it has now cooled so far that they willingly suffer themselves to be without Christ for their whole lives. Our Scotland has been lost, not in one way but in many; yet above all it has been lost because of the scarcity of those who are to be sent into the Lord's harvest. For from this comes the origin of such great wickedness, which flourishes everywhere. For whence come so many murders, adulteries, robberies, enchantments, and, in short, the confusion of all things? These are the unfruitful works of darkness, and so the Apostle calls them: that is, the works of ignorance of Christ. But if Christ were preached throughout this nation, and preached faithfully, certainly there would not be so many prizes everywhere for the devil. For the knowledge and faith of Christ alone is what sanctifies the heart and purges the mind of works of this kind.

units.la: Hactenus fuit primum exhortationis argumentum, sequitur alterum. Porro qui metuit. Quòd si pudore nolunt moueri; pudor enim est tantopere curare ista terrena etiam antequam eueniant: cœlestia autem iam præsentia & ante oculos posita negligere: proposita iis mercede laboris sui eos mouet, mercede, inquam, tali quali nulli vnquam messores in terris consecuti sunt. Qui metuit, inquit, mercedem accipit, non quòd eam mereatur, sed quòd gratis detur. Quod enim à Luca cap.6.31. id est gratia dicitur, id à Matthæo dicitur μισθος, id est merces. Et Paulus aperte significat mercedem non tantum ex debito esse, sed etiam ex gratia. Atqui ei qui operatur merces non imputatur ex gratia, sed ex debito. Porrò quod ex gratia est, id mercedem appellat Deus, ac mercedis nomine promittit bonis operibus, ad subleuandam solatio aliquo carnis nostrae infirmitatem ac debilitatem, non autem ad inflandos inani gloria animos nostros. Tum quae sit ea merces designat verbis sequentibus, Cogit, inquit, fructum in vitam æternam. Nempe sibi colligit fructum, quo futurum est vt viuat in æternum. Diligentes sunt homines ad colligendum in horrea sua fruges, sque vtendi & fruendi iis in totum annum reliquum. Tam certò, qui demetit & colligit in horreum Domini animas hominum, fruetur iis non in annum vnum aut alterum, sed in æternum. Horrea hæc terrestria frangi possunt, fruges eripi possunt, vel incendio, vel furto, vel vi aliqua maiori. Decimæ etiam ministris Euangelij possunt eripi, & ereptæ sunt reipsa hodierno die, sed animæ hominum in horreum Domini collectæ nobis eripi nulla vi possunt vel diabolorum vel hominum: Verùm sistemus eas omnes Domino in aduentu suo, quo tempore in medio earum coronandus est gloria fidelis Minister. Quæ est spes mea, aut gaudium, aut corona Dei quam glorior, Annon & vos in conspectu Domini nostri Iesu Christi in aduentu eius? inquit Paulus. Vt autem certò expectet illam coronam & gaudium illud plenum futurum in illo die, Dominus dat ei quasi degustandum illud in præsenti hoc sæculo dum conscientia fruitur laborum suorum. Neque enim est illum gaudium dium conscientiæ in quoquam homine, in quacunque demum fit vocatione, maius eius hominis gaudio, qui operam suam in lucrando animas hominum Domino suo locat, vt vel inde diuinare possis quantum sit futurum fidelis Ministri gaudium in cœlis aliquando. Sed hoc quod dico de Ministris verbi generalius extendo ad quoscunque in quacunque functione: Victuri enim sunt omnes ex laboribus suis quotquot fideles extiterint in officio suo. Quamobrem ad hoc ipsum vt sit fidelis quisque in officio, vitam illam ac mercedem semper habeat ob oculos positam. Ita enim futurum est vt erigatur animus & dirigatur ad officium fideliter obeundum. Nam qui non est fidelis in officio suo, is nunquam, ne eminus quidem, intuitus est illam mercedem vitæ æternæ: Et licet qua est impudentia, loquatur aliis de vita, id quod requirit imprimis officium Ministri: tamen nunquam ipse conspexit eam vitam, ineptúsque omnino est ad sermones habendos de cœlis & de rebus cœlestibus. Dico igitur ita demum fore vt erigatur & formetur animus ad fidelitatem atque diligentiam, si semper ob oculos habeamus tantam mercedem. Quòd si autem eam ex oculis abiue sumus, nihil fere inueniri potest in rerum quod excitet nos ad fidelitatem, imò pleraque omnia dehortantur nos à diligentia & fidelitate in quacunque sumus vocatione; maximè autem nos qui in Ministerio Christi sumus constituti. Quare Ministro Euangelij præsertim ante oculos posita esse debet vita illa æterna, ac merces cœlestis gloriæ.
units.tr: So far was the first argument of the exhortation; the second follows. Moreover, he who fears. But if they are not moved by shame (for it is a shame to be so anxious about these earthly things even before they happen, and to neglect heavenly things which are already present and set before their eyes), he moves them by setting before them the reward of their labour, a reward, I say, such as no reapers ever obtained on earth. He who fears, he says, receives a reward, not because he deserves it, but because it is given freely. For what Luke calls grace in chapter 6, verse 31 [Luke 6.35], that same thing Matthew calls μισθός [misthos], that is, reward. And Paul plainly signifies that the reward is not only of debt but also of grace. But to him who works, the reward is not reckoned as grace, but as debt. Moreover, what is of grace, God calls a reward and promises under the name of reward to good works, so as to support with some comfort the weakness and frailty of our flesh, not to puff up our minds with empty glory. Then he indicates what that reward is in the words that follow: He gathers, he says, fruit unto eternal life. Clearly he gathers for himself fruit, by which he will live for ever. Men are diligent in gathering grain into their barns, so that they may use and enjoy it for the rest of the year. Just so surely, he who reaps and gathers the souls of men into the Lord's barn will enjoy them not for one year or another, but for eternity. These earthly barns can be broken into, the grain can be taken away by fire, or by theft, or by some greater force. Even the tithes of the ministers of the gospel can be taken away, and indeed they have been taken away on this very day; but the souls of men gathered into the Lord's barn can be taken from us by no force, whether of devils or of men. Rather, we shall present them all to the Lord at his coming, when the faithful minister is to be crowned with glory in their midst. What is my hope, or joy, or crown of which I boast? Are not you also, in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming? says Paul. And so that he may surely look for that crown and that full joy which will be his on that day, the Lord gives him, as it were to taste beforehand in this present age, the joy of a conscience that enjoys the fruit of its labours. For there is no joy of conscience in any man, in whatever calling he may be, greater than the joy of the man who devotes his effort to winning souls for his Lord; so that from this alone you may guess how great the joy of the faithful minister will one day be in heaven. But what I say of the ministers of the Word I extend more generally to all in whatever function: for all who have been faithful in their office will live from their labours. Therefore, to this very end, that each one may be faithful in his office, let him always keep that life and reward before his eyes. For thus it will come about that the mind is lifted up and directed to discharging its office faithfully. For he who is not faithful in his office has never, not even from afar, looked upon that reward of eternal life; and although, with what impudence!, he speaks to others about life, which the office of the minister chiefly requires, yet he has never himself seen that life, and is wholly unfit to speak of heaven and heavenly things. I say, therefore, that the mind will be raised up and shaped to faithfulness and diligence only if we always keep so great a reward before our eyes. But if we have removed it from our sight, scarcely anything can be found among things that might rouse us to faithfulness; indeed, almost everything dissuades us from diligence and faithfulness in whatever calling we are, and most of all us who have been placed in the ministry of Christ. Therefore, that eternal life and the heavenly reward of glory ought to be set before the minister of the gospel above all.

units.la: Vt qui seminat. In quo consistit hæc quam dixi merces, nunc planius docet; nempe in gaudio, quod simul gaudent suri sunt Apostoli Christi, cum veteribus illis Prophetis. Propheras seminatores vocat, quia illi primi omnium laborarunt in agro Domini, quasi arando, seminando, ac verbo præparando eum ad futuram messem. Nam enim doctrina prophetica, quæ in elementis quasi traditis posita fuit, plus præstare potuit, quàm homines præstare, perficere autem non potuit: Consummatio enim per Leuiticum sacerdotium non erat. Et Petrus comparat sermonem propheticum lucernæ splendenti in obscuro loco vsque dum dies illucescat. Apostoli
units.tr: "Just as the one who sows" (Joh. 4.36). He now sets out more plainly what this reward consists in: namely, in the joy that the sowers and the reapers, Christ's apostles, share together with those ancient prophets. He calls the prophets sowers because they were the first of all to labour in the Lord's field, as it were ploughing, sowing and preparing it by the Word for the harvest to come. For the prophetic teaching, which was laid down as something like the elements handed down, could achieve more than men could achieve, but could not bring things to completion, since perfection did not come through the Levitical priesthood. And Peter compares the prophetic word to a lamp shining in a dark place until the day dawns (2 Pet. 1.19).

units.la: Christi Messores dicuntur, qui post ingressi sunt in labores Prophetarum, & perfecerunt quod Prophetæ inchoarunt: hoc est, adduxerunt homines ad perfectam notitiam ac cognitionem Dei in Christo, ideoque messoribus comparantur, qui falce quasi Euangelij demessuerunt animas hominum iam maturas, & comportarunt in horreum Domini, hoc enim est perficere. Ergo mercedem eam, quam promittit, innuit consistere in communi Messorum & Apostolorum cum Prophetis ipsis & seminatoribus gaudio. Tum quia potuit obiici a discipulis; Quid igitur? introibimus in labores Prophetarum, & percipiemus fructum laboris alieni? Occurrit huic tempestiue Dominus, dicens prouerbium illud vulgo vsurpatum, in hoc negotio verum esse, nempe, alius est qui seminat, alius est qui metit. Deinde id ostendens, prouerbium particulariter applicat ad discipulos suos verf. sequenti: Ego misi vos ad metendum. Q.d. Ego misi vos in labores aliorum, vt percipiatis fructum laboris alieni. Nota primum quàm liberaliter egerit Dominus cum Apostolis & Ministris noui Testamenti. Prophetis non licuit frui præsente fructu laborum suorum, neque enim maturum laborum suorum fructum viderunt: At immisit Apostolus & Ministros noui Testamenti in labores eorum, ad percipiendos fructus laborum ipsorum etiam cum maiori fortasse voluptate & gaudio quàm quod ipsi Prophetæ gauisi sunt. Nam illi magis fructus spe, quàm aspectu gauisi sunt. Apostoli vero aspectu & rei ipsius præsentia. Neque liberalitas ista Domini tantum ad Apostolos & Ministros Euangelij Apostolorum successores pertinet; verumetiam ad omnes Christianos. Nam & ipsos immissos esse in labores Prophetarum significat Petrus. Illi scrutati sunt articulum temporis quo futurum esset vt Christus pateretur & glorificaretur. Non inciderunt passio & gloriificatio Domini in illorum ætatem. Scrutati tamen sunt ea ac prædixerunt. Inciderunt autem in hos postremos dies, in quos & nos incidimus. Unde dicit Petrus, Eos prophetiis & scrutationib. suis magis nobis administrasse quæ sibi ipsis. Quàm felix est nostra hodierno die conditio in præsentia tantæ lucis Iesu Christi. Sed eam plerique, neque
units.tr: Christ's apostles are called reapers, because they came afterwards into the labours of the prophets and finished what the prophets had begun. That is, they brought men to a full knowledge and acquaintance with God in Christ. They are therefore compared to reapers, who with the sickle of the gospel have cut down the souls of men now ripe and gathered them into the Lord's barn, for this is what it means to bring to completion. Therefore he indicates that the reward he promises consists in the shared joy of the reapers and the apostles with the prophets themselves, the sowers. And this is because it could be objected by the disciples: "What then? Shall we enter into the labours of the prophets and receive the fruit of another's labour?" The Lord meets this in good time, saying the proverb commonly used, that in this business it is true: one man sows, another reaps. Then, showing this, he applies the proverb particularly to his disciples in the following verse: I sent you to reap. That is: I sent you into the labours of others, so that you might receive the fruit of another's labour. Note first how generously the Lord has dealt with the apostles and the ministers of the New Testament. The prophets were not permitted to enjoy the present fruit of their labours, for they did not see the mature fruit of their work. But he sent the apostles and the ministers of the New Testament into their labours, to receive the fruits of those labours, perhaps with greater pleasure and joy than the prophets themselves had. For the prophets rejoiced more in hope of the fruit than in seeing it. But the apostles rejoiced in the sight and the actual presence of the thing. Nor does this generosity of the Lord pertain only to the apostles and the ministers of the gospel, the successors of the apostles, but to all Christians too. For Peter also signifies that they too have been sent into the labours of the prophets. Those prophets inquired into the time at which it would come about that Christ would suffer and be glorified. The passion and glorification of the Lord did not fall in their age. Yet they inquired into these things and foretold them. But they fell upon these last days, upon which we too have fallen. Hence Peter says that those prophets ministered to us through their prophecies and inquiries more than to themselves. How happy is our condition today, in the presence of so great a light of Jesus Christ! But most people neither see nor feel it, with the result that they are more wretched in the light than they were at times without it. For to grow blind in such great light, is that not the most wretched thing?

units.la: 1. Pet. 1. 10. 2. Pet. 1. 12. neque vident, neque sentiunt, quo fit vt miseriores sint cu luce, quàm erant aliquando sine ea. Nam in tanta luce caecutire, annon miserrimum est? Nota deinde, videmus in terris quoties vsuenit, vt alius seminet, alius metat, seminatorem prorsus priuari fructu laborum suorum, nihilque ipsi reliquum fieri, nisi gemitus & moerorem ac quaerimoniâ. At non ita fit hic: Gaudent Prophetae seminatores, simul etiâ tum cùm Apostoli percipiunt fructus laborum ipsorum. Nemo est omnium qui laborat in agro Domini, siue seminet, siue metat, siue plantet, siue irriget, siue denique quocunque modo promoueat regnum Dei, & adiuuet Ecclesiam Christi, cuiuscunque demum sortis sit, qui iure queri poterit se priuari fructu laborum suorum: Vnusquisque suam mercedem accipiet secundum laborem suum, ait Apostolus. Vnde non opus est vt qui laborat in agro Domini, aliis mercedem suam inuideat, aut aemuletur quouis modo iis, quibuscum Deus agere videtur liberalius. Nam & ipsi quoque recipient mercedem laborum suorum, qua plenè perfectéque iis satisfiet, ita vt nihil amplius desideraturi sint in aduentu illo Domini: Cui sit omnis honor & gloria in saeculum. Amen.
units.tr: (1 Pet. 1.10; 2 Pet. 1.12.) Note further: we see on earth how often it happens that one man sows and another reaps, and the sower is utterly deprived of the fruit of his labours, and nothing is left for him but groaning, grief and complaint. But it is not so here. The prophets who sowed rejoice, even at the very time when the apostles receive the fruits of their labours. There is no one among all who labours in the Lord's field, whether he sows, or reaps, or plants, or waters, or in whatever way he advances the kingdom of God and helps the Church of Christ, whatever his lot may be, who can rightly complain that he is deprived of the fruit of his labours. "Each shall receive his own reward according to his labour," says the Apostle (1 Cor. 3.8). Hence there is no need for one who labours in the Lord's field to envy others their reward, or to rival in any way those with whom God seems to deal more generously. For they too will receive the reward of their labours, with which they will be fully and perfectly satisfied, so that they will desire nothing more at the coming of that Lord, to whom be all honour and glory for ever. Amen.

units.la: 39 Ex vrbe autem illa multi Samaritanorum crediderunt in eum propter sermonem mulieris illius, testantis ac dicentis: Certè dixit mihi omnia quae feci.
units.tr: 39 And many of the Samaritans of that city believed in him because of the woman's word, which testified and said: "He told me all that I ever did."

units.la: 40 Quum ergo venissent ad eum Samaritani, rogarunt eum vt apud ipsos maneret: & mansit ibi duos dies.
units.tr: 40 So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.

units.la: 41 Ac multò plures crediderunt propter sermonem ipsius.
units.tr: 41 And many more believed because of his own word.

units.la: 42 Et illi mulieri dicebat, Non amplius propter tuos sermones credimus, ipsi enim audiuimus & scimus hunc esse verè seruatorem illum mundi, Christum.
units.tr: 42 And they said to the woman, "It is no longer because of your saying that we believe; for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Saviour of the world, the Christ."

units.la: HActenus fuit sermo inter Christum & discipulos mutuus: nunc redit ad Samaritanos, ac primum docetur qui effectus fuerit sermonis mulieris in ipsis ad fidem adducendis, priusquam exirent ex urbe, & venirent ad Christum de quo supra. Effectus autem est, Multi Samaritanorum crediderunt in eum, propter sermonem mulieris, &c. Res mira: Mulier fuit quae loquuta est, & abiecta ac fornicatrix, pauca aliquot verba loquuta est; & ea quidem hauddubie non explicate satis. Samaritani alij omnes fuerunt idololatrae, quorum corda penitus erant excaecata: attamen multi ex iis adducuntur ad fidem, sermone isto mulieris semel duntaxat habito & prolato. Quaprimum visum est Deo efficaciter operari in cordibus suorum per Spiritum suum sanctum, non instrumentum quantumuis in speciem abiectum, non sermo quantumuis breuis, neque satis explicatus, nō cor ipsum quantumuis fascinatum arte diaboli & male affectum, non, inquam, ista omnia prohibebunt quo minus quis ad fidem Christi adducatur. Quare quoties accedimus ad verbum Dei audiendum, non tam ista quaecunque externa spectanda sunt a nobis, quam oculus constanter in Dei potentia & efficacia figendus est.
units.tr: Hitherto the discourse has been between Christ and the disciples. Now it returns to the Samaritans, and first it is taught what effect the woman's word had on them in bringing them to faith, before they went out of the city and came to Christ, of whom we spoke above. The effect is: many of the Samaritans believed in him, because of the woman's word, and so on. A remarkable thing! It was a woman, and a despised fornicator, who spoke; she spoke only a few words, and certainly not very fully explained. All the other Samaritans were idolaters, whose hearts were utterly blinded; yet many of them are brought to faith by this woman's word, spoken and uttered only once. Therefore, since it has pleased God to work effectively in the hearts of his people through his Holy Spirit, no instrument, however contemptible in appearance, no word, however brief and not sufficiently explained, no heart, however bewitched by the devil's art and ill-disposed, will, I say, prevent anyone from being brought to faith in Christ. Hence whenever we come to hear the Word of God, we ought to look not so much at all these external things, but to fix our eye constantly on the power and efficacy of God.

units.la: Quod quia non faciunt non pauci, sed affixi sunt toti his externis, ut personis hominum, verbis, actionibus, & reliquis id genus; ideo sic offenduntur ut vel nihil fructus percipiant ex verbo dum ipsum audiunt: vel nolunt omnino audire verbum, nisi ab iis praedicetur in quibus vident externa ista, ut eloquentiam, eruditionem non vulgarem, & alia id genus.
units.tr: And since not a few do not do this, but are wholly fixed on these external things, such as the persons of men, their words, their actions and the like, they are so offended that either they receive no fruit from the Word while they hear it, or they are wholly unwilling to hear the Word unless it is preached by those in whom they see these external things, such as eloquence, uncommon learning and other things of that kind.

units.la: Hoc vitium Paulus notauit in Corinthiis, Quae ab oculos sunt aspicitur. Sed rursus hoc videndum est, quomodo factum sit ut rem tam difficilem tam facile crediderint. Dico igitur Samaritanos isto iam ad maturitatem illam de qua supra diximus peruenisse. Maturitatem enim non tam pono in maturitate quadam ipsorum, & in siti ac desiderio quod fuit in corde ipsorum, quo ipsi auide expectabant Messiam venturum & renouationem omnium; quam in maturitate quasi gratiae Dei ac Spiritus ipsius. Nam veniente Christo in hunc mundum, coepit Spiritus Dei efficacior esse quam vnquam antea aetate Patrum. Ideoque dictum est tempus aduentus. tus Domini tempus illud acceptum. Dico igitur Sama- ritanos iam tum ad maturitatem peruenisse, ac proinde facile eò adductos esse vt crederent. Hoc enim vulgò experimur, pomum iam maturum facile etiam à puero decerpi posse: cùm quod nondum maturum, nō nisi difficulter auellatur ab arbore. Tempus istud maturitatis nunc agitur in Scotia (ipsum enim definio ex annunciatione Euangelij Christi, & ex ipsius duratione) adeo vt facile esset quamplurimos ex nostris ad fidem adducere, etiam ex iis qui videntur nobis barbari maximè, adeò vtnò maturitas, sed auaritia nostrorum hominum incauta fit, cur complures apud nos non credant, sed pereant in incredulitate sua.
units.tr: Paul noted this fault in the Corinthians: Those things which are before the eyes are looked at (2 Cor. 10.7). But again we must consider how it came about that they believed so readily a thing so difficult. I say, then, that the Samaritans had already come to that ripeness of which we spoke above. For I do not place this ripeness so much in some maturity of their own, or in the thirst and desire that was in their hearts, by which they eagerly awaited the coming of the Messiah and the renewal of all things, as in a kind of ripeness of God's grace and of his Spirit. For when Christ came into this world, the Spirit of God began to be more effective than ever before, in the age of the Fathers. And therefore the time of the Lord's coming is called the acceptable time (2 Cor. 6.2). I say, then, that the Samaritans had already come to ripeness, and therefore were easily led to believe. For we commonly experience that a fruit already ripe can easily be plucked even by a boy, whereas a fruit not yet ripe is pulled from the tree only with difficulty. This time of ripeness is now going on in Scotland (for I define it by the proclamation of the gospel of Christ and by its duration), so that it would be easy to bring very many of our own people to faith, even those who seem to us most barbarous; so that it is not ripeness but the careless avarice of our people that causes many among us not to believe, but to perish in their unbelief.

units.la: Hactenus fuit effectum sermonis mulieris in Samaritanis ac gentilibus suis, nunc deinceps quid cum Christo egerint & quo successu: Rogarunt, inquit, eum vt apud ipsos maneret. Imbuti erant initio quodam etiam veritate ac genuinae in Christum fidei. Nam non est facile dicere, quomodo fiat vt cor pertrahatur ad Christum, eumque apprehendat etiam tum cùm cognitio valdè rudis est, confusa & inchoata, adeo vt sensum illum cordis sui ipsi credentes distinctè satis explicare non possunt. Vnde igitur Samaritanos fide Christi cupiunt, & in ea progressum facere. Qui enim semel coeperunt credere, hi nullum procedendi in fide modum faciunt, tanquam perdum hic viuunt. Vt modò nati infantes lac illud sermonis sincerum expetite, vt per illud adolescatis: Si quidem gustastis quam benignus sit Dominus. Quibus verbis significat Petrus, quòd qui gustarunt semel quàm suauis sit Dominus, perpetuò eos cupere illo cibo magis magísque alii atque enutriri ad vitam aeternam. Verùm tenentur Samaritani desiderio visendi Christum, vt scias quòd qui credunt in Christum & diligunt eum quem nondum viderunt, nunquàm iis plenè satisfieri tantisper dum Christum ipsum viderint. Fides per quam nunc incedimus egregium quiddam est ac excellens, Credentes, inquit Petrus, exultamus gaudio ineffabili & glorioso. Sed quiddam maius & excellentius fide est aspectus; Aspicientes enim Christum praesentem, gaudium gaudebimus multo maximum. Magnum quidem est illud, Christum habitare in terris quasi nobiscum per fidem, sed maius est nos habitare in coelis cum Christo per aspectum. Ideoque Paulus dum in terris crederet, & haberet Christum habitantem in corde per fidem, probauit potius migrare & ad Dominum ire habitatum. Mirum illud, mortem ipsam & migrationem ex isto corpore nos expetere, a qua natura omnes tato opere abhorremus, ad hoc vt cum Christo, in quem nunc credimus, praesentes habitemus, tantum boni est in praesentia, vt ipsa mors quae natura sua amara est, credenti tamen suauis sit & iucunda.
units.tr: So far we have seen the effect of the woman's words among the Samaritans, her own people. Now let us consider what they did with Christ and with what success. "They asked him," it says, "to stay with them." At first they had been imbued with some truth and genuine faith in Christ. It is not easy to say how the heart is drawn to Christ and grasps him even when its knowledge is very crude, confused and only beginning, so that believers themselves cannot explain clearly enough the feeling of their own hearts. Hence the Samaritans desire Christ and make progress in him. Those who have once begun to believe do not stop advancing in faith, as if they were living here for nothing. "Like newborn infants, long for the pure milk of the word, so that by it you may grow, if indeed you have tasted how kind the Lord is." By these words Peter means that those who have once tasted how sweet the Lord is always long for that food more and more, and are nourished by it to eternal life. Yet the Samaritans are held by a desire to see Christ, so that you may know that those who believe in Christ and love him, though they have not yet seen him, can never be fully satisfied until they have seen Christ himself. The faith by which we now walk is an outstanding and excellent thing. "Believing," says Peter, "we rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory." But something greater and more excellent than faith is sight. For when we see Christ present, we shall rejoice with a joy far greater. It is indeed a great thing that Christ dwells on earth with us, as it were, through faith; but it is greater that we dwell in heaven with Christ through sight. That is why Paul, while he believed on earth and had Christ dwelling in his heart through faith, preferred rather to depart and go to the Lord, where he dwells. It is a marvel that we desire death itself and departure from this body, which all of us by nature shrink from so greatly, so that we may dwell present with Christ, in whom we now believe. So great is the good in his presence that death itself, which is bitter by its nature, is nevertheless sweet and pleasant to the believer.

units.la: Hactenus egerunt cum Christo de commoratione ipsius apud se: deinceps quid apud eum profecerint ostenditur: Mansit, inquit, ibi duos dies. Ergo locum dedit eorum precibus & biduum commoratus est apud eos, idque non sine magno fructu, vt audiemus. Vide igitur quantum valeat desiderium Christi: facile enim impetrant isti quod desiderant, tantum valet desiderium, ob quod etiam beatos homines praedicat Christus: Beati qui esuriunt ac sitiunt iustitiam, quoniam ipsi saturabuntur. Ego enim illud ausim affirmare, causam esse cur Christus non veniat ad plerosque neque apud eos maneat, causam, inquam, esse quod plerique nullo eius tenentur desiderio. Concedo quidem auaritia nostrorum hominum ac potentiorum fieri, vt Christus non praedicetur in plerisque nostrae gentis partibus; sed illud tamen non minus verum est, sic Deum vlcisci socordiam hominum eorum, qui ipsi non desiderant Christum, nempe perauaritiam aliorum: Qui tamen ipsi quorum opera & auaritia insatiabili vtitur Deus in aliis puniendis, ne sperent impunitatem in illo die.
units.tr: So far they have dealt with Christ about his staying with them; now it is shown what they gained from him: "He stayed," it says, "there two days." Therefore he yielded to their prayers, and stayed with them two days, and that not without great fruit, as we shall hear. See then how great the power of Christ's desire is: those men easily obtain what they desire. So great is the power of desire that Christ pronounces men blessed on account of it: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled." For I would venture to affirm that the reason why Christ does not come to many, nor stay with them, is that many are held by no desire for him. I grant indeed that through the greed of our people and of the powerful it comes about that Christ is not preached in many parts of our nation; yet it is no less true that God thus punishes the indifference of those men who do not themselves desire Christ, namely by the greed of others. Yet those very men, whose work and insatiable greed God uses in punishing others, should not hope for impunity on that day.

units.la: Sequitur deinde fructus commorationis Christi apud Samaritanos; is autem duplex est. Primum, multo plures crediderunt propter sermonem ipsius. Nempe quaam qui crediderunt propter sermonem mulieris. Deinde, illi ipsi qui propter sermonem mulieris crediderunt, magis iam audito ipso Domino in fide confirmantur. Nota primum ex fructu isto facilitatis Christi bonum esse obtemperare iustis desideriis hominum petentium, vt Christus apud se commoretur & maneat: desiderium enim illud significat maturitatem ipsorum hominum.
units.tr: Next follows the fruit of Christ's stay among the Samaritans, and it is twofold. First, many more believed because of his word. That is, more than those who believed because of the woman's word. Second, those very people who believed because of the woman's word are now further confirmed in faith, having heard the Lord himself. Note first from this fruit that Christ's kindness shows it is good to yield to the just desires of men who ask that Christ may stay and abide with them; for that desire indicates the ripeness of the people themselves.

units.la: Mar. Maturi autem facile perducuntur ad credendum. Bonum igitur est cedere desideriis hominum obnixe flagitatium a comitiis & presbyteriis nostris vt commorentur apud se Ministri Euangelij Christi, addentium illud praeterea, se decimas quidem soluere quibus ali oportuit ministros Euangelij. Sed quid hic potest per nos fieri, cum decimae illae, ex quibus oportet viuere Ministros verbi, auaritia potentiorum fere vniuersae abreptae sint ab illo vsu ad quem sunt destinatae, & applicatae profanis vsibus eorum hominum? Vtinam isti tandem aliquando tangerentur ipsi desiderio aliquo Christi & verbi ipsius, quo possent & sui & aliorum facilius misereri, sed religio istis ludibrium est. Deinde nota hoc loco, plures esse modos, quibus Deus, rationem habens infirmitatis nostrae, adducit homines iam primum ad credendum: Iudaeos per aemulationem gentium prouocauit ad fidem.
units.tr: Mar. Ripe people are indeed easily led to believe. It is therefore good to yield to the desires of men who earnestly demand from our assemblies and presbyteries that the ministers of the gospel of Christ may stay with them, adding moreover that they do indeed pay the tithes by which the ministers of the gospel ought to be supported. But what can be done here by us, since those tithes, on which the ministers of the Word ought to live, have been almost entirely seized by the greed of the powerful and turned from the use for which they were destined to profane uses of those men? Would that these men might at last be touched by some desire for Christ and his Word, by which they could more readily show pity both to themselves and to others! But religion is a mockery to them. Next, note here that there are several ways by which God, taking account of our weakness, brings men to believe at the first: he provoked the Jews to faith through the emulation of the Gentiles.

units.la: Alios adducit ad fidem etiam absque verbo, per honestam aliorum conuersationem: Vnde Petrus hortatur vt vxores subiectae sint viris suis, vt etiam si qui non obediunt sermoni, per vxorum conuersationem absque sermone lucrifiant. Nonnullos denique adducit per testificationem Ecclesiae, & eius quidem vel totius, vel a-liculae...
units.tr: He brings others to faith even without the word, through the honourable conduct of others. Hence Peter exhorts that wives be subject to their husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives. Finally, he brings some to faith through the testimony of the Church, and indeed of either the whole Church or some member of it.

units.la: Nonnullos denique adducit per testificationem Ecclesiae, & eius quidem vel totius, vel aliculae membri ipsius, vt testimonio huius mutierculae adduxit ad fidem Samaritanos. Sed quibuscunque demum modis ac rationibus vtatur Deus in addu-cendis hominibus ad fidem, solidum perpetuo atque vnicum fidei fundamentum est ipsum Dei verbum: ita vt non prius inueniat fides quo nitatur, quam verbum illud Dei audierit. Ea enim est natura rerum credendarum, vt nisi ipsum Deum promittentem eas, atque etiam iureiurando confirmantem nobis eas, audiamus, non credamus: Postquam vero Deum loquentem audiuimus, tum quidem nihili facimus ea omnia per quae adducti sumus ad fidem, prae voce & verbo Dei ipsius, illisque iam relictis, incipimus niti verbo ipsius Dei, atque propter ipsum credere: ita Samaritani dicunt mulieri, Non iam credimus propter sermones tuos, ipsi enim audiuimus & scimus hunc esse seruatorem illum mundi, &c. Fateor, non coram alloquitur nos Deus his postremis temporibus, sicut Christus cum allocutus est mulierem & Samaritanam. nos reliquos, sed scripta haec Prophetarum & Apostolorum nobis sunt loco ipsissimę Dei vocis.Iudicate igitur vtrum maioris authoritatis sit Ecclesia ipsiusq; vox, an verbum istud Dei scriptum, quod nobis est loco vocis ipsius Dei.Si semel sciret miser quid esset vera fides in Christum, reipsa experiretur verbum hoc scriptum, hoc est ipsam Dei vocem amicum esse fidei fundamentum, & medium illud principale Spiritus Sancti quo ingignit fidem in cordibus nostris.Nam sine Spiritu sancto operante in cordibus nostris,neque verbum hoc scriptum, neque vox Ecclesiae quicquam prodesset nobis ad fidem. Spiritus enim sanctus intus agens praecipuus est testis omnis veritatis: Is est qui testatur nobis de scriptura authentica, is est interpretationis scripturae testis ac iudex: Testatur autem principaliter per ipsius scripturae vocem: secundo loco minusque principaliter per vocem verae Ecclesiae. Sed quid multis opus est? Ego fidem istam Papisticam nunquam fidei nomine dignam esse existimavi.
units.tr: Finally, he brings some to faith through the testimony of the Church, and indeed of either the whole Church or some member of it, just as through the testimony of this little woman he brought the Samaritans to faith. But whatever means and methods God uses in bringing men to faith, the solid and only foundation of faith is always the very Word of God, so that faith does not find anything to rest upon before it has heard that word of God. For such is the nature of the things to be believed that, unless we hear God himself promising them, and confirming them to us even with an oath, we do not believe. But after we have heard God speaking, we then count for nothing all those things through which we were led to faith, in comparison with the voice and word of God himself; and leaving them behind, we begin to rest on the word of God himself and to believe on account of it. So the Samaritans say to the woman, "Now we believe, not because of your words; for we have heard for ourselves, and know that this is truly the Saviour of the world, etc." I admit that God does not speak to us face to face in these last times, as Christ spoke with the woman, the Samaritan, and with us the rest. But these written writings of the Prophets and Apostles stand for us in place of the very voice of God. Judge therefore which has greater authority: the Church and its voice, or that written word of God, which for us takes the place of the very voice of God. If the wretched man once knew what true faith in Christ is, he would find by experience that this written word, that is, the very voice of God, is the friend and foundation of faith, and the principal means by which the Holy Spirit begets faith in our hearts. For without the Holy Spirit working in our hearts, neither this written word nor the voice of the Church would profit us anything for faith. For the Holy Spirit, working within, is the chief witness of all truth. He is the one who testifies to us about the authentic Scripture; he is the witness and judge of the interpretation of Scripture. He testifies, however, chiefly through the voice of Scripture itself, and in second and lesser place through the voice of the true Church. But why need there be many words? I have never thought that Papistical faith deserves to be called faith at all.

units.la: Nota postremo, Samaritani postquam de Christo audierunt, voluerunt eum praesentem intueri, & cognoscere an ita esset, vt narrauit mulier, eo animo proculdubio atq; consilio, vt si offenderet ita se rem habere, putarent se singulare aliquod beneficium consequutos esse. Sed postquam iam viderunt atque audiuerunt ipsum, inuenerunt omnia maiora quam quae audierant ex muliere, adeo vt nihil se audiuisse putarint ex muliere, prae iis quae ex ipso didicerunt. Nihil de Christo tam magnificè praedicari potest a quoquam, quo non maius & excellentius est quod in ipso Christo est, nosque quum eum coram videbimus, conspiciemus omnia infinitis partibus maiora & gloriosiora, quam fuerunt ea quae vnquam audiuimus aut cogitauimus de eo in hac vita, oculus enim non vidit, nec auris audiuit, nec in hominis mentem venerunt, quae parauit Deus iis qui ipsum diligunt. Ideo quoties audimus omnia de Christo praedicari ex verbo, ne cogitemus verba esse ea hyperbolica, vt vocant; quasi vero res ipsa non respondeat verborum magnitudini: verum cogitemus in Christo omnia maiora esse verbis, quae proferuntur vel a Ministris verbi, vel a Prophetis etiam & Apo-
units.tr: Note lastly that the Samaritans, after they heard about Christ, wished to see him present and to find out whether it was as the woman had reported. Doubtless their purpose and intention was that, if they found it so, they would think they had gained some singular benefit. But once they had seen and heard him, they found everything greater than what they had heard from the woman, so much so that they thought they had heard nothing from the woman in comparison with what they had learned from him. Nothing so magnificent can be said about Christ by anyone that what is in Christ himself is not greater and more excellent; and when we see him face to face, we shall behold everything infinitely greater and more glorious than the things we have ever heard or thought about him in this life. For "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the mind of man, what God has prepared for those who love him." Therefore, whenever we hear everything about Christ preached from the Word, let us not think those words are hyperbole, as they call them, as if the thing itself did not match the greatness of the words; rather let us think that everything in Christ is greater than the words that are uttered either by the ministers of the Word, or by the Prophets too, and the Apo-

units.la: {1} Cor. 2.9. & Apostolis ipsis. Illi enim saepe admonent, quae in Christo sunt ineffabilia esse: Nam cum eum coram videbimus, tum quidem cernemus omnia maiora, quam quae vnquam audiuimus, vel sperare vel cogitare potuimus, atque videbimus ea omnia inseruire saluti nostrae nobisque esse salutaria. Sic enim de Christo loquuntur Samaritani, Scimus hunc esse vere seruatorem illum mundi, Christum. Regina Sabae vidit in Solomone maiora omnia quam fuerunt ea quae fama excepit. Sed gloriae Solomonis nullam partem ipsa secum reportauit domum. Nos vero cum Christum eiusque gloriam coram cernemus, transformabimur in eandem imaginem gloriae, vt loquitur Paulus. Et vt loquitur Iohannes, quum ipse patefactus fuerit, similes ei erimus. Ei sit omnis gloria & honor, Amen.
units.tr: {1} 1 Cor. 2.9. and the Apostles themselves. For they often warn that the things in Christ are unspeakable. "When we see him face to face, we shall indeed perceive all things to be greater than whatever we have ever heard, or could hope or think, and we shall see that all these things serve our salvation and are good for us." So the Samaritans speak of Christ: We know that this is truly the Saviour of the world, Christ. The Queen of Sheba saw in Solomon that all things were greater than what report had brought to her. Yet she carried none of Solomon's glory back home with her. But we, when we behold Christ and his glory face to face, shall be transformed into the same image of glory, as Paul says. And as John says, when he shall be revealed, we shall be like him. To him be all glory and honour, Amen.

units.la: 43 Duobus autem post diebus exiit inde, & abiit in Galilaeam.
units.tr: 43 After two days, however, he left there and went away into Galilee.

units.la: 44 Ipse enim Iesus testatus fuerat, Prophetam in sua patria honorem non habere.
units.tr: 44 For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honour in his own country.

units.la: 45 Quum ergo venisset in Galilaeam, excepe-runt eum Galilaei, quum omnia vidissent quae fecerat Hierosolymis in festo: nam & ipsi venerant ad festum.
units.tr: 45 When therefore he came into Galilee, the Galileans received him, since they had seen all the things he had done at Jerusalem during the feast; for they too had come to the feast.

units.la: HAec est tertia pars capitis, in qua post digressionem redit ad id quod incepit sup. vers. 3. profectionem Christi in Galilaeam. Narrat itaque Christum ex Samaria venisse in Galilaeam, nominatim vero Cana Galilaeae oppidum. Narratur etiam miraculum quod in Galilaea editum est. Galilaeam intelligo oppida & vicos Galilaeae alios, excepta Nazareth, ad quam vel non accessit hoc tempore, vel si ad eam accessit, non est commoratus ibi diutius: Ideoque Euangelista proximo versu, per occupationem, reddit causam cur non venerit Nazarethan, vel certe in ea non substiterit. Respondet itaque Iesus propter contemptum quem passus est ibi, testatus esse Prophetam in patria sua non habere honorem, non modo, inquam, fruistrari honore iusto ac debito, sed etiam ignominia affici. De contemptu autem quem passus est Christus Nazarethæ legitimus Matth. 13. 54. &c. Marc.6.1. Luc. 4.16. Cùm in synagoga eorum ita concionaretur, ut ipsi percellerentur; tamen sic offensi sunt ad cognationem & genus ipsius, ut iis nihil profuerit admirabilis eius doctrina. Imò, ut narrat Lucas, è synagoga eiectum ad collem pertraxerunt, è quo volebant eum præcipitare: sed ipse effugit eorum manus. Proverbium hoc, quod vsurpatur à Christo, vulgò iactatum est, vel ex contemptu illo in genere, quem patiuntur semel omnes doctores ex gentilibus suis, & patria in qua nati & educati sunt: vel ex contemptu illo in specie, quem passi sunt Prophetæ Dei in Israële, vel viv est; hoc est quod obseruamus, Ij inter quos natus est quis, inter quos educatus est, & qui testes fuerunt infirmitatum ipsius, prout omnis caro infirmitatibus obnoxia est, præsertim in pueritia & adolescentia, ij, inquam, sunt à quibus ipse minimi fit, adeo ut etiam imbutus fuerit donis Spiritus sancti illustribus, quibus fere infirmiores imbui solent; tamen adeo offenduntur infirmitatibus illis quæ vitari non potuerunt, ut nullo tempore apud eos locum aut pretio. Vnde equidem existimo optimè cum consulere vocationi suæ, qui, quod fieri potest, paucissimis in hoc mundo atque vita familiariter vtitur, quíque subducto se paulatim ex hoc mundo & alienato à moribus huius mundi, quærit amicitiam & familiaritatem ipsius Dei. Notum enim est illud & verum, Nimia familiaritas parit contemptum. Vide rursus, Christus contemptus, deserit Nazarethum patriam suam. Patria & propinqui qui debent esse nobis chari, etsi quâ Deus est impertitus nobis gratiam, cum iis primum omnium debemus eam communicare, si occasio sese offerat; verùm si contingat, idque fere fit, nos contemni in patria nostra, deseramus patriam & charissimos quosque: Ædificatio enim Ecclesiæ Dei debet perpetuò esse ante oculos ministri Euangelij. Quòd si tenseris te ineptum esse ædificationi apud quemcunque populum, etsi id non fiat tua culpa, confer te alio. Quòd si loci commoditas te magis moueat, ut ibi maneas vbi nihil proficis, quàm ædificatio & promotio regni Christi, metuendum est ne donum quod acceperis amittas, vel degeneres in errores
units.tr: This is the third part of the chapter, in which, after the digression, he returns to what he began above at verse 3: Christ's departure into Galilee. He therefore tells that Christ came from Samaria into Galilee, and by name to Cana, a town of Galilee. He also relates a miracle performed in Galilee. By Galilee I understand the towns and villages of Galilee other than Nazareth, which he either did not visit at this time, or if he did visit it, did not stay there long. So the Evangelist, in the next verse, by way of anticipation, gives the reason why he did not go to Nazareth, or at least did not stay there. Jesus therefore replies, because of the contempt he suffered there, that a prophet has no honour in his own country: he means not merely that he is deprived of the just and due honour, but that he is even subjected to disgrace. Concerning the contempt Christ suffered at Nazareth, see Matt. 13.54, etc.; Mark 6.1; Luke 4.16. When he preached in their synagogue so that they were astonished, yet they were so offended by his kinship and family that his admirable teaching did him no good. Indeed, as Luke relates, they cast him out of the synagogue, dragged him to a hill from which they meant to throw him down, but he escaped their hands. This proverb, which Christ uses, was commonly current, either from the contempt in general which all teachers suffer from their own countrymen and the land in which they were born and brought up, or from the contempt in particular which the prophets of God suffered in Israel, or indeed still do. This is what we observe: those among whom a man is born, among whom he is brought up, and who have witnessed his weaknesses (since all flesh is subject to weakness, especially in childhood and youth), these, I say, are the ones by whom he is held cheapest; so that even if he is endowed with the illustrious gifts of the Holy Spirit, with which weaker men are usually endowed, they are nevertheless so offended by those weaknesses which could not be avoided that at no time does he have a place or esteem among them. Hence I indeed think that he consults his calling well who, as far as it can be done, has as little familiar dealing as possible with this world and life, and who, withdrawing himself gradually from this world and estranged from its ways, seeks friendship and familiarity with God himself. For that saying is known and true: too much familiarity breeds contempt. Note again: Christ, despised, leaves Nazareth, his country. Our country and our kinsfolk, who ought to be dear to us, although God has imparted grace to us, we ought above all to share it with them, if an opportunity offers itself; but if it happens, as it usually does, that we are despised in our own country, we should leave our country and all those most dear to us. For the edification of the Church of God must always be before the eyes of a minister of the Gospel. But if you judge yourself unfit to edify any people whatever, even if this is not your fault, go elsewhere. But if the convenience of the place moves you more to remain where you make no progress than the edification and advancement of Christ's kingdom, it is to be feared that you may lose the gift you have received, or degenerate into errors

units.la: tores rores & hæreses. Vel si retineas puritatem doctrinæ, cuadas tamen frigidus & aridus doctor. Quare migrandum est alió potius, vt aliis prosis, & tum quidem ita migrabis, si immerito in te offensi sint, vt post decessionem tuam relinquas ingratis certum iudicium futurum.
units.tr: and heresies. Or if you keep the purity of doctrine, you may nevertheless become a cold and dry teacher. Therefore it is better to move elsewhere, so that you may profit others; and you will indeed move in such a way, if they have been offended with you undeservedly, that after your departure you leave to the ungrateful a sure judgement to come.

units.la: Quum ergo venisset in Galilaeam. Narratur quomodo Christum venientem exceperint Galilæi. Quisquis ante oculos habet promotionem regni Dei, & quærit ædificationem populi, is ab aliis eiectus, proculdubio ab aliis recipietur etiam ignotis: idque fiet etiam in conspectu gratissimorum hominum a quibus eiecti sunt, cum ipsorum summo decore; adeo magnum est Dei quærere in sua cuiusque vocatione. Quum omnia vidissent. Subiicitur causa quæ eos movérit ad Christum excipiendum: causa est, viderunt signa quæ edidit Christus in festo Paschatis Hierosolymis, quo ex legis præscripto solemne fuit iis convenire festis diebus. Disce hic vsum miraculorum non tam fuisse in ministranda fide, quam in præparandis animis certa quadam reverentia ad fidem, quę verbo Dei proprie administratur, recipiendam. Miraculis etiam confirmabatur veritas verbi veteri illi populo iam recepta. Quare miracula tantum inseruiunt verbo Dei, quod est proprium & genuinum fidei instrumentum. Quamobrem, vt videbimus paulo post, Christus oculos eorum, qui plus æquo addicti erant miraculis, solitus erat auertere a miraculis ad verbum, tanquam efficacissimum fidei instrumentum. Sed annon & incolæ Nazareth vna cum his ascenderunt Hierosolyma, & viderunt hæc ipsa signa, quæ hi viderunt? Verum est. Cur igitur non sunt etiam illi signis illis præparati ad Christum & verbum ipsius recipiendum? Respondeo; Incolæ Nazareth videntur cum præiudicio aduersus Christum ascendisse; quo factum est vt nihil profuerint iis illa miracula ab eo edita Hierosolymis. Tantum est in eo positum, vt sine præiudicio vel Dei vel ministrorum ipsius, accedamus ad verbum Dei audiendum.
units.tr: When therefore he came into Galilee. It is related how the Galileans received Christ as he came. Whoever keeps before his eyes the advancement of God's kingdom and seeks the edification of the people, if he is cast out by others, will assuredly be received by others, even strangers; and this will happen even in the sight of those most grateful men by whom he was cast out, to their own great shame. So great a thing is it to seek God in one's own calling. Since they had seen all things. The cause that moved them to receive Christ is added: they saw the signs which Christ had performed at Jerusalem at the Passover feast, to which, by the prescription of the law, it was customary for them to gather on the solemn days. Learn here that the use of miracles was not so much in conferring faith as in preparing minds, with a certain reverence, to receive that faith which is properly administered by the Word of God. Miracles also confirmed the truth of the Word, already received by that old people. Hence miracles serve only the Word of God, which is the proper and genuine instrument of faith. Therefore, as we shall see a little later, Christ was accustomed to turn the eyes of those who were more than fittingly attached to miracles away from miracles to the Word, as the most effective instrument of faith. But did not the inhabitants of Nazareth also go up to Jerusalem with these, and see those same signs which these saw? True. Why then were they not likewise prepared by those signs to receive Christ and his Word? I answer: the inhabitants of Nazareth seem to have gone up with prejudice against Christ; the result was that those miracles which he performed at Jerusalem did them no good. Everything depends on this: that we come to hear the Word of God without prejudice, whether against God or against his ministers.

units.la: 46 Venit igitur Iesus rursum Cana oppidum Galilæ, vbi fecerat ex aqua vinum. Erat autem in vrbe Capernaumo regius quidam, cuius filius agrotabat.
units.tr: 46 Jesus therefore came again to Cana, a town of Galilee, where he had made wine from water. And there was a certain royal official in the city of Capernaum, whose son was sick.

units.la: 47 Is cùm audiffet Iesum venisse ex Iudæa in Galilæam, abijt ad eum, & eum rogauit vt descen-deret ac sanaret filium suum: erat enim morибudus.
units.tr: 47 When he heard that Jesus had come out of Judea into Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.

units.la: 48 Dixit ergo Iesus ei, Nisi signa & miracula videritis, non credetis.
units.tr: 48 Jesus therefore said to him, Unless you see signs and miracles, you will not believe.

units.la: 49 Dicit ei regius ille, Domine, descende priusquam moriatur puerulus meus.
units.tr: 49 The royal official says to him, Sir, come down before my little boy dies.

units.la: 50 Dicit ei Iesus, Vade, filius tuus viuit. Credidit homo sermoni quem dixerat ei Iesus: & profectus est.
units.tr: 50 Jesus says to him, Go, your son lives. The man believed the word that Jesus had spoken to him, and he went away.

units.la: NVnc deinceps narratur quomodo Iesus venerit Cana oppidum Galilææ: designat autem ac definit Cana ex primio Christi miraculo ibi edito, de quo vidimus supra cap. 2.1. & deinceps. Sed cur cùm in multa alia quoque oppida Galilææ venerit, cur inquam præsertim fit mentio Cana? Respondet hoc factum esse procul dubio ad indicandam curam & sollicitudinem Domini de oppido Cana confirmando in ea veritate ac fide quam semel accepit, edito nimirum ibi magno illo miraculo aquæ in vinum conuersæ. Nota igitur hoc loco de Christo, quòd Christus vbi semel iecit fundamentum fidei, ibi superædificet, & vbi plantauit, ibi irriget, neque citò aut temere deserat aliquam Ecclesiam. Qui cœpit in vobis opus bonum, perficiet vsque ad diem Iesu Christi, inquit Paulus. Nota rursus ex parte nostra; non satis esse, quòd semel sumus plantati, quæ est infirmitas naturæ nostræ, & ariditas cordis nostri, nisi perpetuò irrigemur per totum vitæ huius spatium. Quare nemini sit fastidio quòd sæpe audiat verbum Dei: Eadem scribere vobis, ne quidem haud piget, vobis autem tutum est, ait Apostolus. Erat autem in Capernaumo &c. Nunc sequitur narratio miraculi cuiusdam quod editum est à Domino in Galilæa: Miraculum fuit in filio regij cuiusdam iam moribundo. In narratione primum est præfatio de regio ipso, qui vi-detur fuisse quidam ex Herodis aulicis. Deinde narratur eum, cùm intelligeret Iesum ex Iudæa in Galilæam descendisse,
units.tr: Now the narrative goes on to tell how Jesus came to Cana, a town of Galilee. Cana is identified by the first miracle of Christ performed there, of which we have seen above, chapter 2.1 and following. But why, since he came to many other towns of Galilee, is mention made especially of Cana? The answer is, undoubtedly, that this was done to indicate the Lord's care and concern for the town of Cana, for confirming it in that truth and faith which it had once received, the great miracle of water turned into wine having been performed there. Note therefore in this place concerning Christ, that when Christ has once laid the foundation of faith, there he builds upon it, and where he has planted, there he waters, and he does not quickly or rashly abandon any Church. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion by the day of Jesus Christ, says Paul. Note again on our part: it is not enough that we have once been planted, which is the weakness of our nature and the dryness of our heart, unless we are continually watered through the whole span of this life. Therefore let no one be weary of often hearing the Word of God: To write the same things to you is not irksome to me, but it is safe for you, says the Apostle. And there was in Capernaum, etc. Now follows the narrative of a certain miracle which was performed by the Lord in Galilee: it was a miracle on the son of a certain royal official, who was already at the point of death. In the narrative, first there is an introduction about the official himself, who seems to have been one of Herod's courtiers. Then it is related that when he understood that Jesus had come down from Judea into Galilee,

units.la: cendiste, cendisse, exiuisse, ac dedisse ei obuiam. Tertio, sequitur communicatio habita inter ipsum & Christum. Quarto est obedientia auluci: iussus abire domum, & admonitus de vita filio restituta credidit, & profectus est. Tum, narratur quomodo cum adhuc in itinere esset, resciuerit quòd viueret filius. Hinc inquirit de tempore restitutionis filij ad sanitatem & vitam, ad hoc vt constaret à Christo sanatum esse. Postea est fructus ex miraculo redundans in totam familiam aulici. Postremò, & conclusionis loco, admonet Euangelista hoc fuisse secundum miraculum quod à Christo in Galilæa editum est. De præfatione non est quòd immoremur in ea. Tantum hoc, In ea æternitt sibi aditum ad sequentem narrationem. Quòd autem exiit ad Christum, & ei dedit obuiam, de eo quoque nihil dicimus. Sequimur communicatio. In communicatione habemus petitiones aulici, & responsiones Christi. Eum rogauit vt descenderet, ac sanaret ipsius filium. Ratio est, erat enim, &c. Hauddubie fide aliqua excitatus est ad quærendum Christum, & implorandum ipsius opem, sed in eo tamen peccauit, quòd modum ac rationem sanandi filij volebat Christo præscribere: Descende, inquiens, ac sana filium meum. Hæc fere imperfectio est fidei omnium hominum. Si credant homines Deum posse opitulari sibi, tamen nolunt illi rem totam credere ac committere: verum ipsi rationem agendi volunt Deo præscribere. Sic Naaman Syrus fide quadam impulsus ad quærendum remedium lepræ suæ à Deo Israëlis, tamè rationem remedij & restitutionem sui à propheta Dei iussu præscriptũ ipsi, cõtepsit, ipséque cogitauit de rationibus nescio quibus magis accuratis, laboriosis, exquisitis. Quare eò nitendũ nobis est in negotio fidei, vt & ipsam & rationes omnes rei perficiendæ Deo permittamus, & patiamur captiuam duci cogitationem omnem nostram ad obediendum Deo, hoc enim est proprie credere in Deum. Huiusmodi fuit fides Abrahæ tantopere commendata. Quòd si dum petimus aliquid à Deo, sed mediorum ordinariorum semper habeamus rationem in illque hæreamus; tum quidem fiet vt non credamus futurum, quod petimus. Si enim hæsisset Abraham in mediis ordinariis, profectò nunquam habuisset fidem promissioni Dei de hærede ex Sara sibi nascituro: deinde obleruaj Aulicus, ignorato Christo ipsiusque deitate, putabat non nisi præsentem potuisse seruare filium. Ignorant ij omnes Christum, iam supra hos cælos euectum & sedentem ad dexteram Patris, qui non credunt absente tam efficacem posse esse in nobis, quàm si præsens in terris ageret nobiscum, aut etiam in Cœna Domini sub speciebus panis & vini adesset. Papistæ enim, quantumuis curiosè inquirentes in personam ac in naturas Christi, tamen qui út Christus ignorant. Tertiò, nota, aulicus non nisi iam afflictus morbo grauissimo filij sui, quem vnicè dilexit, Christum quærit. Hæc est inter cæteras specialis quædam ratio qua Christus homines ad se adducit, dum exercet eos sub aliqua cruce.
units.tr: ...descended, went out, and went to meet him. Third, there follows the conversation between him and Christ. Fourth is the courtier's obedience: told to go home, and assured that his son's life was restored, he believed, and set out. Then it is related how, while he was still on the journey, he learned that his son was alive. Hence he inquires about the time of the boy's restoration to health and life, so that it might be established that he had been healed by Christ. Afterwards comes the fruit of the miracle, spreading through the whole household of the courtier. Lastly, by way of conclusion, the Evangelist notes that this was the second miracle that Christ performed in Galilee. We need not linger over the preface. Only this: in it the way is prepared for the following narrative. That he went out to Christ and met him, we also say nothing about. We come to the conversation. In the conversation we have the courtier's petitions and Christ's replies. He asked him to come down and heal his son. The reason is given: for he was, &c. Undoubtedly he was roused by some faith to seek Christ and implore his help, yet he erred in this, that he wanted to prescribe to Christ the manner and method of healing his son: Come down, he says, and heal my son. This is almost the common imperfection of the faith of all men. If men believe that God can help them, yet they are unwilling to entrust and commit the whole matter to him; they want to prescribe to God the manner of acting. So Naaman the Syrian, moved by some faith to seek a remedy for his leprosy from the God of Israel, nevertheless despised the remedy and his restoration as prescribed to him by the prophet of God at God's command, and himself thought of I know not what more elaborate, laborious and exquisite methods. Wherefore in the business of faith we must strive towards this: to permit to God both the thing itself and all the means of accomplishing it, and to suffer all our thought to be led captive to obey God; for this is properly to believe in God. Such was the faith of Abraham, so greatly commended. But if, while we ask something from God, we always keep an eye on the ordinary means and cling to them, then it will come about that we do not believe that what we ask will come to pass. For if Abraham had clung to ordinary means, he would surely never have had faith in God's promise of an heir to be born to him from Sarah.
