Next, observe: the courtier, not knowing Christ and his deity, thought that only one present could save his son. All those who do not believe that one absent can be as effective in us as if he were acting with us on earth present, or even present in the Lord's Supper under the forms of bread and wine, are ignorant of Christ, who has now been raised above the heavens and sits at the right hand of the Father. For the Papists, however curiously they inquire into the person and natures of Christ, nevertheless do not know Christ as he is. Thirdly, note that the courtier seeks Christ only now that he is afflicted with his son's most grievous sickness, whom he loved alone. This is, among others, a special reason by which Christ draws men to himself, when he exercises them under some cross.

units.la: Igitur afflicti afflictionibus illis quasi admonentur ad Deum propius accedere; & certè beati sunt, in quibus id assequuntur afflictiones, vt ad Deum propius accedant. Is enim est ipsissimus afflictionum visus, nisi malint homines per afflictiones temporarias inchoari pœnam illam sempiternam.
units.tr: Therefore the afflicted, by those afflictions, are as it were admonished to draw nearer to God; and surely they are blessed in whom afflictions achieve this, that they draw nearer to God. For this is the very purpose of afflictions, unless men would rather that through temporary afflictions that eternal punishment should be begun.

units.la: Nunc videamus quid respondeat Christus huic petitioni. Non statim directè respondet adid quod quæsitum est: sed cùm videret morbum animi magis periculosum esse, quàm morbum hunc temporarium & corporalem, morbum animi dico, incredulitatem aulici huius simul & aliorum Iudæorum, qui nolebant credere, nisi spectatis primùm miraculis: Ideo morbum illum suum aulico indicat ad hoc, vt eius primùm omnium remedium quæreat. Omnes natura cùm externa aliqua calamitate afficimur, statim ea commouemus, & Dei operam imploramus, sed morbum hunc incredulitatis vix possumus videre. Non autem citius petimus à Deo alia quæuis, quàm ipse penitus introspiciatin animos nostros: sæpe etiam admoneat nos duritiei cordis nostri ac incredulitatis. Sæpe enim ita sentimus in nobis ipsi interea dum alia à Deo postulamus, duritiem cordis tantam, vt cogamur relicto eo quod agimus, petere à Deo fidem & respiscentiam. Dixit ei regius ille. Perfistit regius in petitione sua, neque aduertens ad obiectam sibi incredulitatem, verùm cogitans tantùm de filij sui morbo, non etiam de morbo illo incredulitatis quo ipse laborabat, iterum petit à Domino vt descendat priusquam moriatur filius ipsius. Cùm vrgent res istæ mundanæ, & propius attingunt nos, tam altam impressionem faciunt in animis nostris, vt neque cogitare, neque audire, neque loqui de aliis rebus lubenter velimus, præsertim verò cœlestibus. Tum enim frustra quis loquatur nobis de fide, de infidelitate, de Christo, de vita æterna, atque etiam tum cùm res hæ cælestes publicè prædicantur in sacris cœtibus, intersunt non pauci, quorum animi inter audiendum ita abrepti sunt, & curis his mundanis distracti, vt nihil eorum quæ dicuntur intelligant. Alij sunt qui ita toti occupati sunt in his rebus terrestribus, vt ne horam quidem in septimana lubenter velint concedere verbo prædicato, quos si quis admonebit, vt intersint aliquando Ecclesiæ & cœtibus sanctorum, & vt audiant Dei verbum, hic profectò erit illis odiosus interpellator. Quid dicam? mentes omnium hominum natura terrenæ sunt adeo, vt in rebus huius mundi etiam vilissimis & leuissimis statim demergantur adeo, vt nulla re magis opus sit hominibus cuiuscumque ordinis & conditionis quàm prædicatoribus verbi Dei, qui extrahant eos ex hoc cæno, & ex his curis quibus sese implicant tam facile, & clamant assiduè cum Apostolo: Superna quærite, superna curate, non terrestria. Si enim tantisper dum sumus in hac vita, animi nostri non fuerint aliqua saltem ex parte liberati his curis, & elevati ad aspiciendum cœlos & vitam illam alteram, frustra expectabimus eam in posterum. Beati sunt qui vel cœperunt consilium emergēdi ex his terrenis, & supernà intueri.
units.tr: Now let us see how Christ answers this request. He does not reply directly to what was asked; but seeing that the sickness of the mind was more dangerous than this temporary and bodily sickness, I mean the sickness of the mind, the unbelief of this courtier and of the other Jews, who were unwilling to believe unless they first saw miracles, he therefore points out to the courtier that sickness of his, so that he may first of all seek a remedy for it. When we are afflicted by some external calamity, we are at once moved by it and implore God's help; but we can scarcely see this sickness of unbelief. Nor do we ask anything else from God more readily than that he should thoroughly look into our hearts; often he also admonishes us of the hardness of our hearts and of our unbelief. For often, while we ask other things from God, we feel within ourselves so great a hardness of heart that we are compelled to leave off what we are doing and ask God for faith and repentance. The courtier said to him. The courtier persists in his request, not heeding the unbelief charged against him, but thinking only of his son's sickness, not of that sickness of unbelief by which he himself was afflicted; again he asks the Lord to come down before his son dies. When these worldly things press upon us and touch us nearer, they make so deep an impression on our minds that we are not willing to think, hear, or speak gladly of other things, especially heavenly ones. For then in vain does anyone speak to us of faith, of unbelief, of Christ, of eternal life; and even when these heavenly things are publicly preached in sacred assemblies, there are not a few present whose minds, while listening, are so carried away and distracted by these worldly cares that they understand nothing of what is said. Others are so wholly occupied with these earthly things that they are not willing to give even an hour in the week gladly to the preached Word; if anyone admonishes them to be present at the Church and the assemblies of the saints at some time, and to hear the Word of God, he will surely be an odious interrupter to them. What shall I say? The minds of all men are by nature so earthly that they are at once plunged into the most vile and trivial things of this world, so that men of every rank and condition have no greater need than of preachers of the Word of God, who may drag them out of this mire and out of these cares in which they so easily entangle themselves, and who cry continually with the Apostle: Seek the things above, mind the things above, not the earthly. For if, while we are in this life, our minds are not freed at least in some part from these cares, and lifted up to behold heaven and that other life, we shall wait for it in vain in the future. Blessed are they who have at least begun to take counsel to emerge from earthly things and to look upon the things above.

units.la: Id quidem reprehendendum est in hoc aulico, quòd tam secure præterierit hanc Christi reprehensionem, sed hoc quoque laudandum est in homine, quòd reprehensus non excanduerit statim & conuitiatus fuerit Domino, vt solent hoc genus hominum aulicorum qui ferè delicati sunt ac superbi, & qui non ferant æquo animo repulsam aut reprehensionem. Sed humiliatus videtur metu propinquæ mortis filij sui. Metus mali alicuius impedientis compescit ferociam hominum, fa-
units.tr: Certainly this courtier is to be blamed in that he passed over so carelessly this rebuke of Christ; but this too is to be praised in the man, that when rebuked he did not at once flare up and revile the Lord, as men of this kind, courtiers who are for the most part pampered and proud, are wont to do, and who cannot bear rebuff or reproof with an even mind. But he seems humbled by fear of the approaching death of his son. Fear of some evil that threatens checks the ferocity of men,

units.la: Q citque vt multa ferant & concedant aulici quae alioqui recusassent: Sed ij demum vere beati sunt, qui Dei praesertim metu ac reuerentia ad omnia ferenda ac facienda permouentur. Quod autem ad humiliationem istam aulicorum attinet, vt hoc genus hominum in statu est maximè lubrico & instabili, ita etiam moribus etiam instabilissimis ac inconstantissimis, nunc intolerabilis est superbia, nunc humillima est animi deiectione. In causa est, quia vnā cum mundo hoc fugue dēque feruntur, neque ferè cum destituuntur à mundo Deum habent quo nitantur. Quàm bonum est illud habere cor constabilitum gratia: praesertim huic hominum generi qui in loco sunt maximè lubrico. Sic igitur institutit regius in petitione sua, sed quid ad haec Christus? V ade, inquit, fili tuus viuit. Vide lenitatem & clementiam Domini in concedendo eo quod petiuit. Non vno tantum modo peccatum est ab aulico. Ac primum quidem in eo peccatum est, quod modum sanandi filii sui Domino voluit praescribere: Descende, inquiens, priusquam moriatur filius meus. Deinde in eo quòd crediderit quidem filium suum etiam dum laborantem morbo per Christum restitui potuisse sanitati, sed non iam mortuum, per eum restitui posse vitae. Tertiò, quòd admonitus de incredulitate sua emendanda, tamen nihil ad hoc attenderit, quo tamen maximè offensus fuit Deus, & vita ipsius metu aulici aeterna maximè in discrimen vocata est. His & tot modis peccauit iste, sed quia petitio hominis profecta est ex aliquo certè fidei quasi femine; ideo concessit Dominus quod vrgebat: Vt videas quatoperè placeat Deo, vel pauxillum fidei, & quantoperè delectetur precibus ex quantulacunque fide profectis, etiamsi coniunctam habeant multiplicem imperfectionem: Cuiusmodi tum olim fuit petitio huius hominis aulici. Videmus vulgò parentes magis delectari balbutienti infantia infantium suorum quàm vniuersa eloquentia hominum eloquentissimorum. Nos omnes, quòd ad caelestia attinet, infantes sumus, & vt infantes sentimus, vt infantes loquimur. Pater autem noster caelestis magis oblectatur ruditate ista ac infantia nostra qui sumus eius filii, per Spiritum ipsius sanctum regeniti, quàm tota eloquentia hominis. ψυχὰς & animalis.Quare ne pigeat aut pudeat balbutire in eius aurem, quam vt retineamus semper apertam ac paratam ad nos audiendam nobis laborandum est. Nam si aulici isti (de homine Euangelico agitur) aulici, inquam, diligentes sint in retinenda sibi aure ac praesentia principum huius mundi: nos multò magis retineamus nobis aurem & praesentiam eius, qui rex est regum omnium. Deinde nota,hoc ipso quòd non descendit Christus cum eo, sicut petiuit, plus illi gratificatus est quàm expectare potuit. Testificatus enim est in praesentia vitae restitutum esse ipsius filium. Deus dum non obtemperat circumstantiis quibusdam, quibus in precibus nostris vtimur, quàsque etiam satis temerè praescribimus, concedit interea nobis plus quàm petiimus aut sperare potuimus, vt ex eo discamus sapere ac non praescribere ipsi leges, aut rationem agendi: Poterit enim ille melius nobis consulere, quàm nos ipsi capere possumus: fit etiam nonnunquam, vt cùm petimus temporalia, non concessis illis, largiatur nobis meliora & spiritualia, quae infinitis partibus superant temporalia quaeque: Vt illud rursus discamus, quod petimus à Deo illud totum relinquere ipsius arbitrio, & cùm tam liberalem habeat manum Dominus, non decere vt nos habeamus cor tam angustum. Angustum cor appello illud, quod non libenter credit Deo omnia, neque se planè dedit in eius voluntatem.
units.tr: and makes courtiers endure and concede many things which otherwise they would have refused. But those alone are truly blessed who are moved to endure and do all things especially by fear and reverence of God. As for this humbling of the courtiers, since this kind of men is in a most slippery and unstable condition, so also they are of most unstable and inconstant character: now their pride is intolerable, now they are in the lowest dejection of spirit. The cause is that they are carried along with the world in this flux and reflux, and scarcely, when they are forsaken by the world, do they have God to lean upon. How good it is to have a heart established by grace, especially for this class of men who are in the most slippery places! Thus, then, the king's officer persisted in his petition; but what does Christ say to this? Go, he says, your son lives. See the gentleness and kindness of the Lord in granting what he asked. Not in one respect only did the courtier sin. First, he sinned in this, that he wished to prescribe to the Lord the manner of healing his son: Come down, he says, before my son dies. Then in this, that he believed indeed that his son, while still suffering from the sickness, could be restored to health through Christ, but not that, once dead, he could be restored to life through him. Thirdly, that when admonished to amend his unbelief, he nevertheless paid no attention to it, by which yet God was most offended, and by the courtier's fear his eternal life itself was most endangered. In these and so many ways he sinned, but because the petition of the man proceeded from some faith, as it were a little seed, the Lord granted what he urged: so that you may see how greatly God is pleased by even a little faith, and how greatly he delights in prayers that proceed from however small a faith, even though they have many imperfections joined with them; such was then the petition of this courtier. We commonly see parents take more delight in the stammering infancy of their little children than in all the eloquence of the most eloquent men. We all, as regards heavenly things, are infants, and as infants we feel and as infants we speak. Our heavenly Father, however, is more delighted by this rudeness and infancy of ours, we who are his sons, born again through his Holy Spirit, than by the whole eloquence of men. [ψυχὰς] and the natural (animal) man. Therefore let it not grieve or shame us to stammer into his ear; but we must labour that we keep his ear always open and ready to hear us. For if those courtiers (the man of the Gospel is meant) are diligent in keeping for themselves the ear and presence of the princes of this world, how much more should we keep for ourselves the ear and presence of him who is King of all kings! Next, note that by the very fact that Christ did not go down with him as he asked, he granted him more than he could have expected. For he testified that his son was restored to life while he was in his presence. When God does not comply with certain circumstances which we use in our prayers, and which we too rashly prescribe, he meanwhile grants us more than we asked or could hope for, so that we may learn to be wise and not to prescribe laws or the manner of acting to him. For he can provide for us better than we are able to grasp. It also sometimes happens that when we ask for temporal things, and they are not granted, he bestows upon us better and spiritual things, which surpass temporal ones by infinite degrees. Thus we may learn again that what we ask from God we should leave entirely to his decision, and since the Lord has so generous a hand, it is not fitting that we should have so narrow a heart. I call a narrow heart that which is not willing to believe God in all things, nor has given itself wholly into his will.

units.la: Credidit homo. Hactenus fuit communicatio inter Christum & regium, sequitur effectum communicationis: Homo credit & obedit iubenti eum Christo discedere: Credidit, inquit, homo sermoni quem dixerat ei Iesus, & praefectus est. Mirum est tam citò credidisse hominem semiprophanum: Id factum videtur, quia persuasione quadam potentiae Christi, quòd is tanquam Propheta Dei aliquis potuerit seruare filium suum: praeparatus fuit eius animus iam tum cùm ad eum accederet. Magnum quidem est illud, dum ad Deum accedimus, si habeamus animum praeparatum reuerentia Dei, sensu misericordiae, persuasione potentiae & veritatis ipsius: Ita enim praeparato animo, fit, vt non prius loquatur & promittat quàm nos auidè arripiamus ad nos sermonem ipsius. ac promissionem. Abraham plenè persuasum habens Deum quod promiserat posse etiam facere, contra spem sub spe credidit, hoc est, credidit in promissionem Dei, contra impedimenta naturæ omnia. Contrà verò cum non præparatus est animus huiusmodi plena persuasione, cum promissiones Dei fiunt ad nos, non credimus iis : indéque est quod hic homo aulicus statim auditis semel duobus vel tribus verbis crediderit, nos verò non credamus, etiam cum plus millies inculcatæ sint nobis promissiones Dei in Christo. Tantum est in eo ut præparetur cor nostrum sensu aliquo maiestatis Dei nostri ac plena persuasione veritatis ac potentiæ ipsius.
units.tr: The man believed. So far we have had the communication between Christ and the royal official; now follows the effect of that communication: the man believes and obeys Christ's command to go away. He believed, it says, the word that Jesus had spoken to him, and he set out. It is remarkable that this man, half-heathen as he was, believed so quickly. This seems to have happened because of a certain persuasion of Christ's power, that he might be able, as a prophet of God, to save his son; his mind was prepared even before he came to him. Indeed it is a great thing, when we draw near to God, to have a mind prepared by reverence for God, a sense of his mercy, and persuasion of his power and truth. For when the mind is so prepared, it comes about that we eagerly seize his word and promise before he has finished speaking. Abraham, fully persuaded that God was able to do what he had promised, believed against hope in hope, that is, he believed in God's promise against all the obstacles of nature. On the other hand, when the mind is not prepared with such full persuasion, we do not believe when God's promises are made to us; and so it is that this courtier believed at once after hearing two or three words just once, while we do not believe, even though God's promises in Christ have been impressed on us more than a thousand times. It is only this that is needed: that our heart be prepared by some sense of the majesty of our God and by full persuasion of the truth and power of himself.

units.la: 51 Jam autem eo descendente, servi occurrerunt ei, & annuntiauerunt dicentes, Filius tuus vivit.
units.tr: 51 Now as he was going down, his servants met him and told him, saying, Your son lives.

units.la: 52 Percontatum est ergo ab ijs horam qua melius habuerat: & dixerunt ei, Heri circiter horam septimam dimisit eum febris.
units.tr: 52 So he asked them the hour when he began to get better. And they said to him, Yesterday at about the seventh hour the fever left him.

units.la: 53 Agnouit ergo pater id factum esse illa ipsa hora, qua dixerat ei Iesus, Filius tuus vivit, & credidit ipse, ac domus eius tota.
units.tr: 53 So the father knew that it was at that very hour in which Jesus had said to him, Your son lives; and he himself believed, and his whole household.

units.la: 54 Hoc rursus, id est secundum signum edidit Iesus quum venisset ex Iudæa in Galilæam.
units.tr: 54 This is again the second sign that Jesus did, when he had come out of Judea into Galilee.

units.la: HActenus fuit effectum communicationis, nunc de làxto nuntio agitur quod accepit Regius de filio suo restituto sanitati. Descendente eo, inquit, servi occurre- runt ei. Vide igitur, solo verbo Domini sanatur filius iste regij: Ex quo discè efficaciam verbi Dei, qui quicquid loquitur, illud potest totum effectum dare, qui vocat ea quæ non sunt tanquam sint, hoc est, qui vel solo verbo facit aliquid ex nihilo. Verbum in prima creatione omnium rerum efficax fuit ad earum subsistentiam, dixit enim, & factum est: verbum dixit ut è tenebris lux splenderet. In regeneratione, & nova quasi creatione nostri non minus efficax est. Nam verbum Evangelij est potentia Dei in salutem omni credenti. Hic rursus vide efficaciam fidei, ut uno verbo Domini sanatus est puer; sic etiam aliquo modo fide patris vitæ restitutus stitutus est filius. De efficacia fidei vide Heb. 11. 1. & deinceps: cuius ea vis est, vt qui credit se iustificatum esse in Christo, cùm tamen in se peccator sit, statim iustificatus sit: etsi Papistæ irrideant hanc iustitiam fidei, tanquam quiddam dūtaxat imaginarium. Quamlibet irrideant, ego magis lætor hac ipsa iustitia imputata mihi peccatori per fidem Christi, quàm illi possunt lætari tota illa iustitia sua, quam vocant, inhærente, atque etiam illa operum meritoriorum iustitia. Sumāt illi sibi suam, relinquant mihi meam. Verùm oportet fides hæc effi-carnon nitatur quacunque imaginatione & inuentione nostra: verùm oportet fundetur in verbo Dei, & in promissionibus eius solis, ad hoc vt sit efficax: Ex quo fit, vt efficacia ista, reipsa non tam sit fidei nostræ quàm verbi Dei fide apprehensi. Verùm verbum Dei ita demum in nobis est efficax, si ipsum fide apprehendatur: Vnde dictum est Euangelium potentia Dei in salutem, cui? credenti, inquit. Verùm quidem est verbum Dei semper comitem ipsius Dei potentiam illam mirificam & cum verbo potentiam simul offerri, sed potentia ea nō est in nobis efficax nisi per fidem. Per incredulitatem autem nostram stat quo minus verbum Dei sit potens atque efficax in nobis ad salutem...
units.tr: So far we have had the effect of the communication; now the joyful news is discussed, which the royal official received that his son had been restored to health. As he was going down, it says, his servants met him. See, then: this son of the royal official is healed by the Lord's word alone. Learn from this the efficacy of God's word, which, whatever it says, can bring about its whole effect, and which calls those things that are not as though they were, that is, which makes something out of nothing by a word alone. In the first creation of all things the word was effective in bringing them into being, for he spoke and it was done; the word said, let light shine out of darkness. In regeneration, and in a kind of new creation of ourselves, it is no less effective. For the word of the gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. Here again see the efficacy of faith: the boy was healed by the Lord's single word; so too, in a certain way, the son was restored to life by the father's faith. On the efficacy of faith see Heb. 11. 1 and following. Its power is such that the one who believes that he is justified in Christ, although he is in himself a sinner, is at once justified. Although the Papists mock this righteousness of faith as something merely imaginary, still, however much they mock it, I rejoice more in this very righteousness, imputed to me a sinner through the faith of Christ, than they can rejoice in all that righteousness of theirs, which they call inherent, and also in that righteousness of meritorious works. Let them take their own; let them leave me mine. Indeed this faith must not rest on any imagination or invention of ours, but must be founded on the word of God and on his promises alone, if it is to be effective. From this it follows that this efficacy belongs in fact less to our faith than to the word of God apprehended by faith. Yet the word of God is effective in us only if it is apprehended by faith. Hence the gospel is called the power of God unto salvation to him who believes, as it says. It is true that God's wonderful power always accompanies his word, and that this power is offered together with the word; but that power is effective in us only through faith. Through our unbelief, however, it stands in the way that the word of God is not powerful and effective in us unto salvation...

units.la: Quamobrem ne sinamus tantam potentiam cum verbo coniunctam srustra nobis offerri, sed quoties prædicatur nobis verbum Dei, demus operam vt manum fidei paratam habeamus ad ipsum, cum potentia sua admirabili, apprehendendum ad salutem, nobisque applicandum.
units.tr: Therefore let us not allow such great power, joined with the Word, to be offered to us in vain; but whenever the Word of God is preached to us, let us take care to have the hand of faith ready to lay hold of it, together with its wonderful power, for salvation, and to apply it to ourselves.

units.la: Percontatus est ergo. Quæsiuit de tempore, quo certius constaret de miraculo vitæ, nimirum restitutum filium suum non fortuna aut causa aliqua secundaria, verùm extraordinaria Dei potentia, ac verbo Christi. Atque nō est hoc factum absque speciali Dei prouidentia vt patet tam præcisè inquisierit in horam ipsam qua cœpit filius se melius habere. Ea enim est malitia Satanæ & instrumentorum ipsius, vt Dei opera mirifica quoties in lucem erumpunt, totis viribus conentur supprimere, ne Deus in iis inter homines glorificetur. Hoc etiam eò factū est à Regio, vt confirmaretur ipsius fides, qua credidit filium suum verbo Christi sanatum. Etsi enim iste
units.tr: He therefore inquired (about the hour). He asked about the time, so that it might be more certainly established that the life-giving miracle had been wrought not by chance or some secondary cause, but by the extraordinary power of God and the word of Christ. And this did not happen without a special providence of God, as is plain from the fact that he inquired so precisely into the very hour when his son began to get better. For such is the malice of Satan and of his instruments that whenever the wonderful works of God break out into the light, they strive with all their might to suppress them, so that God may not be glorified in them among men. This was also done by the nobleman so that his faith might be confirmed, by which he believed that his son had been healed by the word of Christ. For although this man...

units.la: Fidei efficacia.
units.tr: The efficacy of faith.

units.la: Eius fundamentum.
units.tr: Its foundation.

units.la: Incredulitatis virus.
units.tr: The poison of unbelief.

units.la: Fidei inchoatę confirmatio. iam crediderit, vt dictum est; tamen voluit confirmari illam fidem suam praecise notatis quibusdam circum-stantiis. Fides nostra in Deum non ita firma est vnquam in hac vita, quin subinde egeat noua confirmatione. Et haec quoque est natura fidei, vt semel apprehenso Christo, velit eum cum beneficiis suis magis magisque firmiter apprehendere. Nam quo magis ad nos applicamus Christum, eo magis existit consolatio in Christo: ideoque fit vt fides nostra semper scrutetur argumenta quibus magis magisque stabiliatur. verbi gratia; Credo iam me iustificatum esse sola illa Dei iustitia, gratis mihi imputata per redemptionem factam in Christo Iesu, & tamen nō desino propterea quaerere ex scripturis Dei argumenta omnia, quibus in hac fide confirmer: & quo plura video eius rei argumenta, eo magis accrescit mihi gaudium; adeoque satisfacit mihi haec iustitia Dei imputata mihi, non autem inhaerens in me, vt iam nolim eam cum iustitia illa inhaerente, quam olim in Adamo amisi, commutare. O magnum illud solatium animae ex iustitia illa Dei gratis imputata peccatori per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum!
units.tr: Confirmation of faith just begun. Confirmed in particular circumstances. Yet, as has been said, he had already believed, but wished to be confirmed in that faith. Our faith in God is never so firm in this life that it does not from time to time need new confirmation. And this too is the nature of faith: once it has apprehended Christ, it wishes to apprehend him with his benefits more and more firmly. For the more we apply Christ to ourselves, the more consolation arises in Christ; and therefore it comes about that our faith always seeks out arguments by which it may be made more and more steady. For example; I believe that I am already justified by that righteousness of God alone, freely imputed to me through the redemption made in Jesus Christ, and yet I do not cease on that account to seek from the Scriptures of God all the arguments by which I may be confirmed in this faith; and the more arguments of this matter I see, the more joy grows in me; and so this righteousness of God imputed to me satisfies me, not inherent in me, so that I would no longer wish to exchange it for that inherent righteousness which I once lost in Adam. O the great comfort of the soul from that righteousness of God freely imputed to the sinner through Jesus Christ our Lord!

units.la: Sequitur effectus miraculi huius in ipso homine, pariter & tota eius familia. Credidit ipse ac domus eius tota. Sed annon iam bis dictum est eū credidisse in Christum? Resp. Fides illa, de qua dictum est semel atque iterum proprie respexit sanitatem & vitam filij sui; sed haec, de qua nunc audimus, est illa iustificans fides ad quam adductus est per illud miraculum filij in vitam restituti.
units.tr: There follows the effect of this miracle on the man himself, and likewise on his whole household: He believed, he and his whole household. But has it not already been said twice that he believed in Christ? Answer: that faith of which mention has been made once and again looked chiefly to the health and life of his son; but this faith, of which we now hear, is that justifying faith to which he was brought by that miracle of his son's restoration to life.

units.la: Qui semel re ipsa experti sunt quanta sit in Christo efficacia, facile adducuntur vt in eum credant, seque totos ipsi tradant, confiteanturque eum filium Dei esse, & seruatorem animarum. Fateor quidem nos hodierno die experiri tatam iltam Christi potentia in extraordinarius miraculis edendis, quantam tum olim expertus est hic homo aulicus: sed ausim affirmare nos hoc ipso die experiri non minorem efficaciam Christi, imo dicā maiorem, in seruandis his animis nostris moribundis & laborantibus ad mortem aeternam; hoc est, in nobis regenerandis: Quique semel expertus est hanc Christi potentiam (nam non nisi potentia & spiritu Christi regeneratio neratio ista perficitur) qui, inquam, semel est expertus & degustauit hanc potentiam, is iam lubens se totum Christo commendat imperpetuum, in eoque solo fiduciam suam omnem collocat. Quare ad fidem augendam & confirmandam opus est magis magisque sentiamus efficaciam illam Christi in nobis quotidie regenerandis. Hoc secundum signum. Haec est conclusio miraculi, in qua admonet secundum esse hoc signum quod a Domino editum est in Galilaea. De primo enim vidimus supra cap. 2.1. & deinceps. Tantum hoc Spiritus Dei, qui author fuit scriptionis huius, in numerato habuit miracula omnia quae a Christo in terris sunt edita.
units.tr: Those who have once experienced in fact how great is the efficacy in Christ easily come to believe in him, and give themselves wholly to him, and confess that he is the Son of God and the Saviour of souls. I admit that we today experience the power of Christ in working extraordinary miracles only as much as this courtier once did; but I dare to affirm that we today experience no less efficacy of Christ, indeed I would say greater, in saving these our souls that are dying and labouring towards eternal death; that is, in regenerating us. And whoever has once experienced this power of Christ (for this regeneration is accomplished only by the power and Spirit of Christ), whoever, I say, has once experienced and tasted this power, gladly commits himself wholly to Christ for ever, and places all his confidence in him alone. Therefore, to increase and strengthen faith, we need to feel more and more that efficacy of Christ in us, as he daily regenerates us. This is the second sign. This is the conclusion of the miracle, in which it is noted that this was the second sign that the Lord did in Galilee. For of the first we have seen above in chapter 2, verse 1 and following. Only this: the Spirit of God, who was the author of this writing, had in view all the miracles that Christ performed on earth.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Hoc capite, primo narratur Christum relicta Galilaea in Iudaeam revertisse et Hierosolymam ascendisse, ubi habemus miraculum sanati a Christo hominis qui triginta octo annos decumbebat, ad versum usque 17. Secundo, habemus orationem Christi qua factum illud suum in homine sanando die Sabbathi defendit, authoritatem suam plenissime asseruit, et Iudaeis incredulitatem suam exprobravit ad finem capitis.
units.tr: In this chapter, the first thing related is that Christ, having left Galilee, returned into Judaea and went up to Jerusalem, where we have the miracle of the man who had lain for thirty-eight years, healed by Christ, to verse 17. Second, we have Christ's discourse by which he defends that act of healing the man on the Sabbath day, fully asserts his own authority, and rebukes the Jews for their unbelief, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: 1 POst haec erat festum Iudaeorum, & ascendit Iesus Hierosolymam.
units.tr: 1 After these things there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.

units.la: 2 Est autem Hierosolymis ad portam pecuariam, piscina quae nominatur Hebraice Bethesda, quinque porticus habens.
units.tr: 2 Now there is at Jerusalem, by the Sheep Gate, a pool called in Hebrew Bethesda, having five porches.

units.la: 3 In his iacebat multitudo magna aegrotorum, caecorum, claudorum, aridorum, expectantium aquae motum.
units.tr: 3 In these lay a great multitude of sick people, blind, lame, and withered, waiting for the moving of the water.

units.la: 4 Angelus enim descendebat certo momento in piscinam, & turbabat aquam: itaque qui primus ingressus erat post aquæ turbationem, sanus fiebat à quocunque detineretur morbo.
units.tr: 4 For an angel went down at a certain season into the pool and troubled the water. Whoever first stepped in after the troubling of the water was made whole of whatever disease held him.

units.la: 5 Erat autem quidam illic tricesimum octauum annum agens in morbo.
units.tr: 5 And a certain man was there who had been ill for thirty-eight years.

units.la: VOD ad miraculum, habemus primum ipsum miraculum, deinde quæ editum miraculum consequuta sunt. Sic igitur narrat, Post hæc, nempe quæ gesta sunt in Galilæa: Erat dies festus Iudæorum. Festum Paschatis intelligit: Et ascendit Iesus Hierosolymam. Hic opus est ut paulò altius repetamus ea quæ præcesserunt de peregrinatione Domini, vt eum inde à prima sua profectione deducamus Hierosolymam, cuius itineris & profectionis mentio fit hoc loco. Igitur Iesus Christus ingressus annum ætatis suæ tricesimum, profectus est Nazaretha Galilææ oppido, inquo educatus est, in deserto Iordanis, vbi baptizabat Iohannes, ibique inter alios à Iohanne est baptizatus, atque ita tum primum initiatus est Mediationis officio illo suo. Hinc Spiritu abductus est in desertum Iericho, vbi quoque ieiunauit quadraginta dies & quadraginta noctes totas, simulque tentatus est à Satana: Inde reuersus est ad Iohannem in desertum Iordanis, quo quidem tempore vocati sunt discipuli numero tres, Andreas, & alter quidam cuius nomen non est expressè positum, & tertius Simon Petrus. Hinc abiit in Galilæam; in itinere autè & quasi obiter vocati sunt duo discipuli, nominatim Philippus & Nathanael. Ingressus in Galilæam, venit Nazarethaim primum, inde abiit Cana inuitatus ad nuptias, vnà cum matre & discipulis suis: Vbi etiam edidit illud primum miraculum suum in vertenda aqua in vinum. Postea descendit Capernaum, vbi mansit nō multos dies, sed ascendit Hierosolymam, nam prope erat Pascha Iudæorum. Hierosolymam vbi venisset, purgauit templum, edidit multa signa; cum Nicodemo clam noctu sermonem habuit. Hierosolymis postea abiit in territorium Iudeæ vbi degebat cum discipulis, & baptizabat bat opera & ministerio discipulorum, vbi quoque orta est quæstio de purgatione. Postea, cum cognosceret quòd Pharisæi audissent de ipso quòd ibi moraretur ac baptizaret, reliquit Iudæam, atque iter rursum suscepit in Galilæam. Oportebat autem transfire in Galilæam per Samariam in medio sitam ac interiacentem. Venit ergo obiter in Samariam, vbi sermonem habuit cum Samaritana & Samaritanis, eósque ad fidē adduxit. Cum manssisset in Samaria & Sichar, quod ibi est oppidum, duos dies, abiit inde in Galilæam. Ingressus autem Galilæam, primùm, vt verisimile est, venit Nazarectham, vbi cùm male esset exceptus, relicto hoc post se, postquam testatus esset Prophetam in sua patria honorem non habere, venit in reliqua Galilææ oppida, nominatim verò Cana oppidum Galilææ, vbi fecerat ex aqua vinum. In Galilæa dum ageret, edidit illud secundum suum miraculum, secundum, inquam, quod in Galilæa editum est ab eo, curauitque mirabiliter Regij cuiusdam filium. Post hæc erat dies festus Iudæorum, & ascendit Iesus Hierosolymam. Atque hoc est illud iter Christi, cuius hic fit mentio. Hic dies festus Iudæorum putatur esse Pascha, eo quod in Samaria Christus dixerat quatuor mences abesse ad messem, quæ inter Pascha & Pentecosten in Iudæa fiebat. Alij Pentecosten opinantur fuisse, sed nos sententiam de Paschate sequimur. Sed ad rem veniamus. Iesus cum in terris his ageret, sedulò obseruauit dies festos, & legi fuit obnoxius, vt nos liberaret à seruitute legis. At postquam venit plenum tempus, emisit Deus filium suum factum ex muliere, factum legi obnoxium, vt eos qui legi erant obnoxij, &c.
units.tr: Concerning the miracle, we have first the miracle itself, and then what followed upon it. He therefore tells it thus: "After these things," namely, the things done in Galilee: "there was a feast of the Jews." He means the feast of the Passover. "And Jesus went up to Jerusalem." Here we must go back a little further over what came before concerning the Lord's journeys, so that we may trace him from his first departure to Jerusalem, of which journey and departure mention is made in this place. Jesus Christ, then, having entered his thirtieth year, set out from Nazareth, the town of Galilee in which he had been brought up, into the wilderness of the Jordan, where John was baptizing. There he was baptized by John, among others, and so was then first installed in that office of his Mediation. From there the Spirit led him into the wilderness of Jericho, where he also fasted forty days and forty whole nights, and was at the same time tempted by Satan. Then he returned to John in the wilderness of the Jordan, and at that time three disciples were called: Andrew, another whose name is not expressly given, and a third, Simon Peter. From there he went away into Galilee, and on the way, and as it were in passing, two disciples were called, namely Philip and Nathanael. Having entered Galilee, he came first to Nazareth; from there he went to Cana, invited to a wedding, together with his mother and his disciples, and there he performed that first miracle of his, turning water into wine. Afterwards he went down to Capernaum, where he stayed not many days, but then went up to Jerusalem, for the Passover of the Jews was near. When he had come to Jerusalem, he cleansed the temple, performed many signs, and held a discourse secretly by night with Nicodemus. Afterwards he went from Jerusalem into the country of Judea, where he lived with his disciples and baptized, by the work and ministry of the disciples; there also arose the question about purification. Afterwards, when he learned that the Pharisees had heard that he was staying there and baptizing, he left Judea and again took the road into Galilee. But it was necessary to pass into Galilee through Samaria, which lies in the middle and between. So he came in passing into Samaria, where he held a discourse with the Samaritan woman and the Samaritans, and brought them to faith. When he had stayed two days in Samaria and in Sychar, which is a town there, he went from there into Galilee. Having entered Galilee, he first came, as is likely, to Nazareth, where, being badly received, he left that place behind, after testifying that a prophet has no honour in his own country, and came to the other towns of Galilee, and especially to Cana, the town of Galilee where he had made wine from water. While he was active in Galilee he performed that second miracle of his, the second, I say, that he did in Galilee, and he wonderfully healed the son of a certain royal official. After these things there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. This is that journey of Christ of which mention is made here. This feast of the Jews is thought to be the Passover, because in Samaria Christ had said that there were four months until the harvest, which in Judea came between the Passover and Pentecost. Others think it was Pentecost, but we follow the opinion about the Passover. But let us come to the matter. Jesus, while he lived on this earth, faithfully observed the feasts and was subject to the law, so that he might free us from the bondage of the law. But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made subject to the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law, and so on.

units.la: Sequitur miraculum editum Hierosolymis; sed ante miraculum ipsum habemus narrationem quandam & quasi præfationem de loco in quo editum est miraculum. Deinde, de iis qui ægroti iacebant in eo loco. Tertiò, de homine nominatim, in quo editum est miraculum. Quòd itaque ad locum attinet, ait, Hierosolymis ad forum piscarium est piscina, ex qua potare, & in qua mersari solerent pecudes, quarum magnum numerum Hierosolymis esse oportuit. Describitur etiam ex nomine Hebraeo Beth-esda, hoc est, domo effusionis, quòd in eum locum magna aqua effunderetur. Fatigant se alij in eruenda nominis huius ratione, secundum literas quibus Graece scribitur. In Syro contextu declarat locum benignitatis, quod in eo Deus benigne potentiam suam exerceret in curandis quibusvis morbis populi. Describitur etiam ex ornamento quodam suo, porticibus nimirum quae exstructae erant, vt verba sequentia indicant, ideo vt multitudo aegrotorum in iis iaceret expectans aquae motum. De loco hoc id tantum est quod notamus. Locus erat illustris & tempus solenne, idque certa Dei prouidentia factum est, vt innotesceret omnibus miraculum, & Deus a multis glorificaretur, atque si fieri posset multi seruarentur. In his iacebat. Narratio est de aegrotis & multis modis male affectis, qui tum in illis porticibus iacebant. Laborarunt autem morbis & languoribus, qui tum in illis porticibus iacebant, arte humana incurabilibus. In morbis & aegritudinibus quibusvis confugiendum est ad Deum, maxime vero in iis malis, quae nulla arte & industria humana curari possunt. Quod si in his possimus nos Deo commendare, nosque totos in manum ipsius tradere, tum quidem & in vita & in morte magnum futurum est solatium. Sed cur iacebat in illis porticibus multitudo illa aegrotorum, &c. Expectabant nimirum aquae motum. Quid ita? Angelus enim descendebat certo momento, &c. De extraordinaria ista agendi ratione non sum magnopere sollicitus, neque in eam curiosius inquiro: Tatum hoc in praesentia; Populus hic tunc temporis valde confusus erat, & magna ex parte substracta est ab eo Dei praesentia. Prophetae, quos Deus extra-ordinem excitare solitus erat, non tum dabantur: Deus igitur, ne prorsus videretur abiicere populum suum, extra-ordinem & miraculose voluit sanare quosdam, vt testaretur mundo populum hunc nondum prorsus reiectum fuisse. Praeterea hoc signum quoddam erat antegrediens mirificam illam ac plane admirabilem mutationem & innovationem omnium rerum, quae paulo post futura erat in aduentu Messiae. Nunc veniamus ad narrationem illam quae spectalis est de homine eo in quo editura est praesens hoc miraculum. Erat autem quidam illic tricesimum octavum
units.tr: Next comes the miracle performed at Jerusalem; but before the miracle itself we have a certain narrative, as it were a preface, about the place where the miracle was done. Then, about those who lay sick in that place. Thirdly, about the man by name in whom the miracle was done. As to the place, he says, "At Jerusalem, by the Sheep Gate, there is a pool," from which herds used to drink and in which they used to be washed, and of which there must have been a great number at Jerusalem. It is also described by its Hebrew name, Beth-esda, that is, house of outpouring, because a great quantity of water was poured out into that place. Others weary themselves in seeking the reason for this name, according to the letters by which it is written in Greek. In the Syriac context it declares a place of kindness, because God there kindly exercised his power in healing whatever diseases the people had. It is also described by a certain ornament of it, namely the porches which had been built, as the following words indicate, so that the multitude of the sick might lie in them, waiting for the moving of the water. Concerning this place, this alone is what we note. The place was famous and the time was solemn, and this was done by the certain providence of God, so that the miracle might become known to all, that God might be glorified by many, and, if it could be done, that many might be saved. "In these lay." This is a narrative about the sick and those variously afflicted, who then lay in those porches. Now they were suffering from diseases and infirmities which, by human art, were incurable. In diseases and sicknesses of every kind one must flee to God, and above all in those evils which cannot be cured by any human art or industry. If we can commend ourselves to God in these, and deliver ourselves wholly into his hand, then indeed it will be a great comfort both in life and in death. But why did that multitude of sick lie in those porches, and so on? They were of course waiting for the moving of the water. Why so? "For an angel went down at a certain season," and so on. I am not greatly anxious about this extraordinary manner of acting, nor do I inquire into it too curiously; this is enough for the present. The people at that time were greatly confused, and for the most part the presence of God had been withdrawn from them. The prophets, whom God was accustomed to raise up outside the ordinary way, were not then given; God therefore, lest he should seem utterly to cast off his people, willed to heal some by an extraordinary and miraculous means, so that he might bear witness to the world that this people had not yet been wholly rejected. Moreover, this was a certain sign going before that wonderful and altogether admirable change and renewal of all things which was to come a little later at the coming of the Messiah. Now let us come to that narrative which concerns the man in whom this present miracle was to be wrought. "Now there was a certain man there

units.la: Personae ibi decumbentes. tum annum agens in morbum. Ac proinde incurabili morbo laboras: atque eo admirabilius oportuit miraculum esse. Quod autem tandiu laboraverit miser iste, factum est non citra specialem Dei prouidentiam. Constituit enim Deus glorificare se in restitutione huius hominis aegroti. Deus enim nonnunquam gloriae suae materiam quaerit miseriâ nostrâ,& morbis tum diuturnis tum gravibus. Caecum illum de quo apud Iohan.9.1. &c. inde a natiuitate percussit excitate, in eum finem ut opera Dei manifesta fierent in eo. Voluit & hunc miserum tot annos detineri in illo morbo tam graui, ut ipse, per miraculum in eo restituendo sanitati, glorificaretur. Et cur non iis quibus ipsi visum est modis gloriam suam quaerat in sua ipsius creatura? Itaque nos omnes, cum ex voluntate Dei occupamur gravibus aliquibus miseriis, debemus ita apud nos ipsi cogitare, velle Deum nostrum in miseria nostra glorificari. Quod si libenter fuerimus passi Deu pro iure suo in miseria & ignominia nostra sibi gloriâ quaerere, profecto cum Dei gloria coniuncta erit vita nostra & liberatio nostri saltem illa aeterna. Omnia enim conferunt in bonum diligentibus Deum.
units.tr: Persons lying there. who had been ill for thirty-eight years. Therefore you suffer from an incurable disease, and so the miracle had to be all the more remarkable. That this wretched man suffered for so long was not without the special providence of God. For God decided to glorify himself in the restoration of this sick man. God indeed sometimes seeks the matter of his glory in our misery and in diseases both lasting and grievous. That blind man of whom we read in John 9.1, etc., he struck with blindness from birth, to this end, that the works of God might be made manifest in him. He willed also that this wretched man should be held for so many years in that disease, so grave, so that by restoring him to health through a miracle he himself might be glorified. And why should he not seek his glory in his own creature by whatever means pleased him? Therefore we all, when by the will of God we are occupied with some grave miseries, ought to think within ourselves that our God wills to be glorified in our misery. If we have gladly allowed God, by his right, to seek his glory in our misery and disgrace, then surely our life will be joined with the glory of God, and our deliverance, at least that eternal one, will be too. For all things work together for good to those who love God.

units.la: 6 Hunc cum vidisset Iesus iacentem, & cognouisset eum iam multum temporis egisse in morbo, dicit ei, Cupis sanus fieri?
units.tr: Jesus saw him lying there, and knowing that he had already been ill for a long time, said to him, "Do you want to be made well?"

units.la: 7 Respondit ei aegrotus ille, Domine, non habeo qui, quum turbata fuerit aqua, immittat me in piscinam: sed interim dum ego venio, alius ante me descendit.
units.tr: The sick man answered him, "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred; while I am coming, another goes down before me."

units.la: 8 Dicit ei Iesus, Surge, attolle grabatum tuum, & ambula.
units.tr: Jesus said to him, "Rise, take up your bed, and walk."

units.la: 9 Iudaei ergo dicebant ei qui curatus fuerat, Sabbathum est, non licet tibi attollere grabatum.
units.tr: So the Jews said to the man who had been healed, "It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your bed."

units.la: Verbis his significat proculdubio Iesum commotum fuisse ad succurrendum misero, etiam ex ipsa circumstantia formae ac habitus decumbentis: item ex circumstantia temporis diuturni ex quo coepit laborare morbo. Christus qui tentatus est in omnibus similiter atque nos, absque peccato. Afficitur sensu infirmitatum nostrarum; videt etiam & nouit circumstantias singulas nostrae miseriae: Videt nos aegrotantes, in lecto decumbentes: Nouit quandiu detenti sumus morbo: Audit suspirantes ac lamentantes, hisque omnibus non minus adeoque magis mouetur, quam nos ipsi. Nouit quis sit sensus sui Spiritus is qui scrutatur corda: simul dolet nobiscum. Neque enim, vt solent vulgo homines, ita Christus intuetur miseriam nostram sine sensu aliquo & motu. Cum in miseria aliqua sumus ac dolore, si tum habeamus apud nos qui vna doleat & lugeat, id nos aliquo modo solatur ac leuat. Quantum oportet esse illud superpreflatium, cum scimus nos habere Christum Dominum ac Deum nostrum vna nobiscum quasi dolentem & dolentem miseriam nostram, eum nimirum qui solus potest nos consolari ac liberare ab omni miseria, quique liberaturus est nos suo tempore. Verum in hoc est omnis difficultas, vt videamus Dominum nostrum, & sentiamus penitus corde hanc eius tantam charitatem atque misericordiam: Qua semel percepta, dici non potest quantum consolationis secum afferat, nisque sustentet in mediis doloribus. Malim equidem in miseria esse & in mediis calamitatibus, cum sensu illo misericordiae Domini mei Iesu Christi longe suauissimo, quam extra miseriam & calamitates omnes positus esse, sic tamen vt nihil illius suauitatis degustem. Nullam equidem maiorem ista miseria vnquam putaui, qua quis expers est plane omnis sensus istius Domini tam suauis atque iucundi. Dicit ei, Cupis. Illud erat extra quaestionem cupiuisse ex animo miserum hunc & decumbentem restitui sanitati. Sed Dominus cum iam visitaret eum, & afferret ei secum praesentem gratiam, voluit praeparari hominem etiam, si posset fieri, maiori aliquo desiderio. Cum enim omni tempore teneantur homines desiderare gratiam ac liberationem, tum vero maxime debet accendi in iis desiderium, cum praesens est Dominus, & ad manum est ipsius gratia. Hoc adeo verum esse comperimus, vt Deus, in iis quibus vult efficax esse per gratiam suam, soleat vna cum oblata gratia excitare in animis eorum admirabile quoddam desiderium, cum ine-
units.tr: By these words he clearly signals that Jesus was moved to help the wretched man, both from the very circumstance of the man's posture and condition as he lay there, and from the circumstance of the long time during which he had been labouring under the disease. Christ, who was tempted in all things in like manner as we are, yet without sin, is touched by the feeling of our infirmities. He also sees and knows each circumstance of our misery. He sees us sick and lying in bed; he knows how long we have been held by disease; he hears us sighing and lamenting; and he is moved by all of these things no less than we ourselves are, indeed more. He knows what the feeling of that Spirit is who searches the hearts, and he grieves with us at the same time. For Christ does not look upon our misery, as men commonly do, without any feeling or emotion. When we are in some misery and pain, if we have someone with us who grieves and mourns together with us, this in some way consoles and relieves us. How surpassing that must be, when we know that we have Christ the Lord and our God with us, as it were grieving and suffering together with us in our misery: he who alone can console us and free us from every misery, and who is going to free us in his own time. But in this lies all the difficulty, that we should see our Lord and feel deep in our hearts this his so great charity and mercy. Once this has been perceived, it cannot be said how much consolation it brings with it, and how it sustains a person in the midst of sorrows. I would indeed rather be in misery and in the midst of calamities, with that feeling of the mercy of my Lord Jesus Christ, which is by far the sweetest, than be placed outside all misery and calamities yet so as not to taste any of that sweetness. Indeed, I have never thought any misery greater than that by which one is utterly devoid of all sense of this Lord, so sweet and pleasant. He says to him, Do you want? It was beyond question that this wretched, bedridden man wished from his heart to be restored to health. But the Lord, when he now visited him and brought him present grace, wished the man to be prepared with some still greater desire, if that could be done. For although men are always bound to desire grace and deliverance, yet this desire ought to be kindled in them especially when the Lord is present and his grace is at hand. We find this to be so true that God, in those whom he wills to be effective through his grace, is wont, together with the grace offered, to stir up in their minds a certain wonderful desire, joined with unspeakable sighs.

units.la: Rom. 8.27 inenarrabilibus suspiriis coniũctum,desiderium,inquâ, eorum qui tum seruabuntur. Ipsi qui primitias Spiritus habemus, nosipsi, inquam, apud nosipsos suspiramus adoptionem exspectátes, redemptione corporis nostri. Hoc ipso die qui nūc agitur, offertur nobis præsens gratia atque liberatio: Et hoc est tēpus illud acceptum, &nunc venerunt tempora refrigerationis à conspeċtu Domini. Et Dominus ipse quasi omnia loca obiēs visitat singulos laborantes, quæritq; à singulis an veliut sani fieri? In quibus excitatur de fideriū sanitatis aliquod, ij hauddubiè sanātur, in quibus veró nullū excitatur desiderių gratię & liberationis sui, ij rdinquuntur in miseria sua & periturî sunt tandē nisi tandem aliquando hoc in iis desiderių gratię excitetur. Quāto magis perituri sunt illi qui tā obstinatē persistūt in contemptu gratiæ tantę in Euangelio oblatæ? Neque enim fieri potest vt impunè contemnatur tam miseri- cors Domini visitatio. Respondet ei ægrotus. Ægrotus iste absque dubio non nunc primùm cœpit esse curæ Domino,sed semper erat ei curæ,nunc autem primùm, suo nimirum tempore eum sanat ac liberat. Qui enim sunt Domino curæ, & quos etiam constituit liberare, atque etiam liberat suo tempore Dominus, sinit eos in miseria prostratos iacere, destitutos omni auxilio atque ope humana, præcludere etiam videtur eis ad satis longum tempus aditum omnem ad sanitatem & liberationem, & sic cum iis agere ad tempus vt videantur reprobi esse & abiecti. Quid hic nobis faciendum? patienter ferenda sunt omnia,nitendūmque est semper vt sentiamus hanc Domini curam & prouidentiam specialem erga nos, etiam tum esse cùm videtur nos nihil curare, constantérque exspectemus liberationem suo tempore futuram. Præter eà peccat ægrotus esse in eo quòd non possit polliceri sibi aliunde liberatione quàm ex demissione sui in piscina. Verisimile enim est quòd expectârit fore vt Dominus demitteret eum in piscinā statim postquā ab Angelo turbata esset aqua, eáque ratione sola,nō alia, sanitati eum restitueret. Mens nostra qua intelligimus cœlestia ac spiritualia,vt & cor nostrum quo sentimus,ea angusta sunt admodum, neque nunc vel intelligimus vel tentimus millesimam partem eorum quę post hanc vitam & intelligemus & sentiemus. Eo verò miseriores sumus,
units.tr: Rom. 8.27 with unspeakable sighs: the desire, I say, of those who will then be saved. "We ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, we ourselves, I say, groan within ourselves, waiting for adoption, the redemption of our body." On this very day which is now being observed, present grace and deliverance is offered to us; and this is "the acceptable time," and "now the times of refreshing have come from the presence of the Lord." And the Lord himself, as it were passing by all places, visits each labouring one, and asks each one whether he wishes to be made whole. In those in whom some desire of health is stirred up, they are without doubt healed; but in those in whom no desire of grace and of their own deliverance is stirred up, they are left in their misery and will at length perish, unless at last this desire for grace is kindled in them at some time. How much more will those perish who persist so obstinately in contempt of such great grace offered in the Gospel? For such merciful visitation of the Lord cannot be despised with impunity. The sick man answers him. This sick man without doubt had not now for the first time begun to be an object of the Lord's care; he was always an object of his care, but now, in his own time, the Lord heals and frees him. For those whom the Lord cares for, and whom he has appointed to free, and whom he does free in his own time, he allows to lie prostrate in misery, bereft of all help and human aid; he even seems for a fairly long time to shut against them every access to health and deliverance, and so deal with them for a time that they seem reprobate and cast off. What must we do here? All things must be borne patiently, and we must always strive to feel this special care and providence of the Lord towards us, even when it seems that he cares nothing for us, and steadfastly wait for deliverance to come in his time. Besides this, the sick man is at fault in that he could not promise himself deliverance from any other source than being let down into the pool. For it is likely that he expected the Lord would let him down into the pool immediately after the water had been stirred by the angel, and that by that means alone, and no other, he would be restored to health. Our mind, by which we understand heavenly and spiritual things, and our heart, by which we feel them, are very narrow, and now we neither understand nor taste the thousandth part of those things which after this life we shall both understand and feel. The more wretched, therefore, we are.

units.la: In his instillat libe rationis desiderių.
units.tr: In these he instils a desire for deliverance.

units.la: Fidei suorum imbecillitatem clementer tolerat & emendat. quòd fere non audeamus polliceri nobis ipsis maiora, quàm quæ in præsentia intelligimus aut sentimus, quod quidem est summæ infidelitatis. Fidei enim ea est natura, vt eius beneficio polliceamur nobis infinitis partibus maiora, quàm quæ aut cognoscimus in præsentia, aut etiam sentimus. Est enim fides demonstratio eorum quæ non videntur. Et per eam, vt loquitur Paulus, spectamus nō ea quæ cernuntur, sed ea quæ non cernuntur. Quare laborandum nobis est semper, vt exporrigamus fidem & spem nostram quàm longissimè, vltrà ea quæ in præsentia vel videntur vel sentiuntur. Neque vero metuendum est ne modum excedamus in fide & spe nostra. Profectò enim cum patefiet nos filios esse Dei, (nondum enim hoc patefactum est) tum quidè videbimus maiora omnia quàm quæ potuimus vel credere vel sperare. Dixit ei Iesus, Surge. Vide indulgentiam ac misericordiam Domini, quod miser iste sibi polliceri non est ausus, hoc ei præstat Dominus adeo clementer, largitúrque ei plus quàm vel credere vel sperare potuit. Hoc nos solari debet, cùm sentimus fidei imperfectionē istam quam laboramus omnes, quotiescunque cogitamus de gloriosa illa restitutione, déque vita illa æterna. Neque enim tantam gloriam polliceri nobis ipsi possumus quantam debemus, neque tantum capimus consolationis quantum debemus; neque denique tribuimus Deo promittenti gloriam eam quam debemus. Sed hoc nobis solatio esse debet, quòd misericordia Domini plus videbimus quàm vnquàm credere aut sperare in vita potuimus. Quare semper recubendum est nobis in illa Dei misericordia quæ vincit incredulitatem nostram. Nam si nos infidi sumus, ille tamen fidus manet, negare seipsum non potest.
units.tr: He mercifully bears with and corrects the weakness of his people's faith, in that we scarcely dare to promise ourselves greater things than those we understand or feel at present, which is truly the height of unbelief. For it is the nature of faith that, by its benefit, we promise ourselves things greater by infinite degrees than those we know at present or even feel. For faith is the proof of things not seen. And through it, as Paul says, we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. Therefore we must always labour to stretch out our faith and hope as far as possible, beyond what is either seen or felt at present. Nor indeed need we fear lest we exceed the measure in our faith and hope. For surely when it is revealed that we are the sons of God (for this has not yet been revealed), then we shall see all things greater than we could either believe or hope. Jesus said to him, Rise. See the indulgence and mercy of the Lord: the wretched man did not dare to promise himself this, yet the Lord grants it to him so graciously, and gives him more than he could either believe or hope. This ought to console us, when we feel that imperfection of faith which we all labour under, whenever we think of that glorious restoration and of that eternal life. For we cannot promise ourselves as great glory as we ought, nor do we receive as much consolation as we ought; nor finally do we ascribe to God, who promises, the glory that we ought. But this should be our consolation: that by the mercy of the Lord we shall see more than we could ever believe or hope for in this life. Therefore we must always rest upon that mercy of God which overcomes our unbelief. For if we are faithless, yet he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself.

units.la: Erat autem Sabbathum die illo. Transitio est ad ea quæ consequuta sunt miraculum iam editum: primum offenditur Iudæi in hominem qui sanatus est, deinde offenduntur in Christum. Transitio continet rationem offensionis, dies Sabbathinus enim, in quo miraculum hoc editum est, præbuit Iudæis occasionem offensæ. Sacceptum à Iudæis. Sacceptum tis sciuit Christus factum illud suum offensioni futurum Iudæis, eo præsertim die editum; sed cum haberet bonam conscientiam, primum eo quòd non transgrederetur. deretur limites officij sui, deinde quòd proponeret sibi, tanquā finē, gloriā Patris sui, quam opportunè elucere atq; apparere in hoc miraculo die hoc tā solēni edito, nihil cōmotus est eorum iniusta offensione, neque deterritus est ea re ab officio suo faciendo. Cū in agendo, bene nobis conscij sumus quòd non transgredimur limites officij nostri, quòdque gloriam Dei nostri ante omnia quærimus; tum agamus strenuè, etiamsi totus mundus offendatur in nos. Postquam vero effecimus quod debuimus & potuimus, si non tam feliciter succedat quàm volumus, tamen ne deiiciamur neque frāgamur animo, sed fruamur bona illa cōscientia. Hæc est gloriatio nostra, inquit Paulus, quum falsō accusaretur à Corinthiis inconstantiæ, testimonium videlicet conscientiæ nostræ, quòd cum simplicitate & sinceritate Dei, non cum sapientia carnali, sed cum gratia Dei, versati sumus in mundo, potissimum autem apud vos. Conscientia enim bona magnam vim habet ad gloriationem & cōsolationem in rebus aduersis: ea autem obtinetur si non transgrediamur limites vocationis nostræ, neque id solum; fieri enim potest ut secundum vocationem faciamus, neque tamen bonam facti nostri conscientiam consequamur. Quare & illud alterum requiritur ad bonam conscientiam, nimirum, ut semper in agendo Dei gloriā ante oculos positam habeamus. Ex his duobus existit bona conscientia, qua si fruamur, etiam inmediis calamitatibus atque huius vitæ miseriis lætabimur & gloriabimur.
units.tr: It was the Sabbath on that day. This is a transition to what followed the miracle just performed. First the Jews take offence at the man who was healed, and then they take offence at Christ. The transition gives the reason for the offence: the Sabbath day on which the miracle was performed gave the Jews their occasion for offence. Christ knew that this deed of his would give the Jews offence, especially because it was done on such a solemn day. Yet, since he had a good conscience, first because he did not overstep the limits of his office, and then because he set before himself, as his end, the glory of his Father, which shines forth and appears most fittingly in this miracle performed on such a solemn day, he was not moved by their unjust offence, nor was he deterred from doing his work. When we act in this way, we are well aware that we are not overstepping the limits of our calling and that we seek above all the glory of God. Then let us act vigorously, even if the whole world takes offence at us. Once we have done what we ought and were able to do, if it does not turn out as well as we wish, we should not be cast down or broken in spirit, but enjoy that good conscience. This is our boast, says Paul, when he was falsely accused by the Corinthians of inconstancy, namely the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and sincerity of God, not in carnal wisdom but in the grace of God, we have conducted ourselves in the world, and especially among you. For a good conscience has great power to give us boasting and consolation in adversity. But it is obtained only if we do not overstep the limits of our calling, and not even that alone. For it is possible to act in accordance with one's calling and yet not attain a good conscience about one's deed. Therefore a second requirement for a good conscience is also needed, namely that in acting we always keep the glory of God set before our eyes. From these two things a good conscience arises, and if we enjoy it, we shall rejoice and glory even in the midst of calamities and the miseries of this life.

units.la: 10 Iudæi ergo dicebant ei qui curatus fuerat, Sabbathum est, non licet tibi attollere grabatum.
units.tr: 10 The Jews therefore said to him who had been cured, It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your bed.

units.la: 11 Respondit eis, Qui me sanum fecit, is mihi dixit, Attolle grabatum tuum, & ambula.
units.tr: 11 He answered them, He who made me whole said to me, Take up your bed and walk.

units.la: 12 Interrogauerunt eum ergo, Quis ille qui dixit tibi, Attolle grabatum tuum, & ambula?
units.tr: 12 Then they asked him, Who is the man who said to you, Take up your bed and walk?

units.la: 13 Is autē qui sanatus fuerat nesciebat quis esset: Iesus enim euaserat è turba quæ erat in illo loco.
units.tr: 13 But he who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had slipped away from the crowd that was in that place.

units.la: 14 Hactenus occasio fuit, sequitur offensa. Primum offenduntur Iudæi aduersus hominem qui sanatus est, quòd is grabatum suum tolleret Sabbatho. Iudæi ergo dicebant ei qui sanatus fuerat. Non iniusta videri potuisset ista reprehensio, si nihil praeterea mali latuisset sub hoc praeclaro scilicet praetextu defensionis Sabbathi. Habebant enim Iudæi expressam legem de non portandis oneribus die Sabbathi: Cauete vobisipsis & ne portetis onera die Sabbathi, aut inferatis ea in portas Hierusalem. Praeterea religio dici Sabbathinę, siue, vt nos hodierno die vocamus, Dominicæ, omnibus modis asserenda est, ad hoc vt Deus noster glorificetur ex praescripto legis suæ. Verum videntur magis eo offensi quòd sanatus esset ægrotus iste à Christo, quàm quòd tolleret grabatum suum. Quâobrem cum eo candore & simplicitate animi qua debebant, non defenderent religionem Sabbatthi, quod faciebant, non fuit id gratum Domino. Videndum nobis illud est perpetuò in reprehendendo & admonendo, vt sincerè & propter Deum id faciamus, omninóque quoties loquimur aliquid in nomine Domini, siue reprehedimus siue admonemus, siue consolamur siue exhortamur, siue denique quid loquimur, videndum nobis est vt semper habeamus Dominum ante oculos nostros, & sincerè ac serio, non in speciem & perfunctorie hoc agamus. Inde est quòd homines loquor de Ministris Euangelij, sæpe non habetes Deum ante oculos suos, tam parua cum authoritate, libertate & gratia agant partes suas in reprehensionibus, admonitionibus, consolationibus &c. Non enim est ea Dei ipsius concurrentis cum verbo suo efficacia quam requiras, nisi ipsum praesentem ex animo requirat Minister, & ex simplicitate ac sinceritate studeat agere. Tempus autem illud probet nos non quæsiuisse Deum sincerè & ex animo.
units.tr: 14 So far there was an occasion; now the offence follows. First the Jews take offence at the man who was healed, because he carried his bed on the Sabbath. The Jews therefore said to him who had been healed. This rebuke could hardly seem unjust, if nothing else wrong had lain hidden beneath this specious pretext of defending the Sabbath. For the Jews had an express law about not carrying burdens on the Sabbath day: Take heed to yourselves, and do not carry burdens on the Sabbath day, or bring them in through the gates of Jerusalem. Besides, the observance of the Sabbath, or, as we call it today, the Lord's Day, must be defended in every way, so that our God may be glorified according to the prescription of his law. But they seem to have been more offended that this sick man had been healed by Christ than that he carried his bed. Therefore, since they did not defend the religion of the Sabbath with the candour and simplicity of mind they ought to have had, what they did was not pleasing to the Lord. In rebuking and admonishing we must take care always to do it sincerely and for God's sake. Whenever we speak anything in the name of the Lord, whether we rebuke or admonish, console or exhort, or indeed whatever we say, we must see to it that we always keep the Lord before our eyes, and that we do this sincerely and earnestly, not for show or perfunctorily. Hence it is that I speak of ministers of the Gospel, who often, not having God before their eyes, carry out their parts in rebukes, admonitions, consolations and so on with so little authority, freedom and grace. For the efficacy of God himself, concurring with his word, is not such as you would seek, unless the minister himself seeks God's presence from the heart and strives to act in simplicity and sincerity. That time will prove that we have not sought God sincerely and from the heart.

units.la: Respondit eis. Excusat se homo qui sanatus fuit à Christo; vbi obscurè & defendit suum ipsius factum in obediendo Christo iubenti ipsum tollere grabatum suum, ex eo nimirum quòd tantum in ipso sanando beneficium contulerit: & asserit authoritatem Christi in iubendo, ex eo nimirum quòd is tantum, tamque extraordinariu opus perficere potuerit. Non dubium enim fuit, quin is qui tantum vel solo verbo potuit, is, inquam, iustam causam habuerit & authoritatem iubendi, vt tolleret ipse grabatum suum. Unde & illud apparet, animum homi-nis. nis vna cum corpore ex parte aliqua mutatum, vt sic dicam, & restitutum sanitati. Inde enim est haec obedientia Christo statim praestita; inde est haec reuerentia ei habita, & defensio authoritatis ipsius, quae profecto non potuerunt fieri abeo, nisi aliqua saltem ex parte corporis iam coepisset inclinare se ad Christum, & idem Christus, qui sanauit corpus, fuisset quoque efficax per Spiritum suum in animo hominis mutando. Qua quidem re beatior fuit, quàm illa ipsa restitutione ac instauratione corporis. Nam vel minima pars regenerationis & mortificationis corruptae naturae praestantior est tota sanitate corporis. Interrogauerunt eum ergo, quis ille, &c. Non quaerunt, ecquis ille qui te sanauit? sed eo dissimulato, quaerunt de eo qui causa ipsi fuit violati Sabbathi, ac reprehendunt authoritatem mandatis vt tolleret ipse gratum suum: Atque ita produnt malitiam cordis sui: malitia enim ista cordis nihil est perniciosius, vbi enim semel malitia illa ac duritia cordis contracta est, tum quidem nihil lucis vident homines, nihil operum Dei vel clarissimorum intuentur, aut si vident, certe nolunt videre; vt ignorantia sit, vt loquitur Paulus, ex obdura- tione cordis eorum, quo quidem iudicio non est aliud sub coelo grauius: Videndo videte, ait Deus apud Esaiâ, neque intelligatis, nempe non assentientes corde his quae videtis, alioqui & intelligitis. Quare quoties audimus Dei vocem, quoties videmus opera Dei admirabilia, hoc in primis nobis videndum, vt sit assensio cordis, sic vt non modo intelligamus quod dicitur, aut agitur, sed ei assentiamur toto corde, & promissiones Dei nobis ipsi specialiter applicemus, nam tum denique est cognitio salutaris. Is autem qui sanatus fuerat. Ex his apparet, quod etsi fuerit in ipso homine secretus aliquis impulsus fidei, vt diximus, tamen eum Christi notitiam aliquam distincta non habuisse. Incredibile enim est quàm lenta motione Deus quasi attrahat ad se corda etiam eorum, quorum tamen mira est ignorantia, quíque vix tria verba de eo distincte & clarè proferre possunt, vel de persona, vel de officio Christi: Vnde non sunt illi temere abiiciendi & quasi explodendi in quibus videmus aliquid zeli inesse, etiam cum summa rerum ignoratione Dominus ipse arundinem quassatam non fregit, neque linum fumigans extinxit, sed illa tenuia fidei initia fovit, adiuvit atque promovit. Ita & nobis illius exemplo faciendum est, quoties videmus etiam cum satis magna ignorantia coniunctum aliquem in aliquo zelum Dei, demus operam ut augeatur in eo homine inchoata ea Dei cognitio. Quod si semel aperti fuerint oculi eius ad Christum illum, qui etiam iam ex parte aliqua efficax est in corde ipsius secreto quodam motu Spiritus sui, ad Christum, inquam, illum clarius videndum, exsistet in eo fides mirifica cum pace & gaudio ineffabili. Qui enim zelum Dei aliquē iam habent, si postea illuminatae fuerint mentes eorum, tum dici non poterit quam excellentes futuri sint in fide & religione. Quamobrem equidem consuluerim omnibus, quibus iam est aliquis zelus Dei & amor Christi, quem tamen nondum satis cognitum ac perspectum habent, quaerant eum magis magisque cognoscere, & quoad personam, & quoad officium. Vbi enim semel cognoverint & viderint illam plenitudinem omnis gratiae, quae est in eo, profecto iam mirum in modum confirmabitur illetus Dei & amor Christi, cum gaudio, pace & laetitia ea quam mundus non intelligit.
units.tr: He answered them. The man who was healed by Christ excuses himself; and in doing so, he obscurely defends his own deed in obeying Christ's command to take up his bed. He does so on the ground that Christ had conferred so great a benefit in healing him, and he asserts Christ's authority in commanding, on the ground that Christ could perform so great and extraordinary a work. For there was no doubt that he who could do such things by a word alone had a just cause and authority to command him to take up his own bed. From this it also appears that the man's mind, together with his body, had been changed in some part, so to speak, and restored to health. For this obedience, immediately rendered to Christ, and this reverence shown to him and defence of his authority, could not have come from him unless at least in some part of his body he had already begun to incline toward Christ, and unless the same Christ who healed the body had also been effective through his Spirit in changing the man's mind. Indeed, he was happier in this than in the very restoration and renewal of his body. For the smallest part of regeneration and mortification of corrupt nature is more excellent than the whole health of the body. Then they asked him, who it was, etc. They do not ask, Who was it that healed you? but, passing over that, they ask about him who was the cause of the violation of the Sabbath, and they find fault with the authority of the command to take up his own bed. And so they betray the malice of their heart. For this malice of the heart is nothing more harmful: once such malice and hardness of heart have been contracted, men see no light, behold none of the works of God, not even the most manifest; or if they see, they certainly do not want to see. Thus there is ignorance, as Paul says, because of the hardening of their hearts, and under heaven there is no heavier judgement than this. Seeing, see, says God in Isaiah, and do not understand, that is, do not assent in the heart to what you see; otherwise you would understand. Therefore whenever we hear the voice of God, whenever we see the wonderful works of God, we must first see to this: that there is assent of the heart, so that we not only understand what is said or done, but assent to it with the whole heart and apply God's promises specially to ourselves. For then at last there is saving knowledge. But he who had been healed. From this it appears that, although there was in the man himself some secret impulse of faith, as we have said, he nevertheless did not have any distinct knowledge of Christ. For it is incredible how slowly God, as it were, draws to himself the hearts even of those whose ignorance is nonetheless remarkable, and who can scarcely utter three words distinctly and clearly about the person or office of Christ. Therefore we should not rashly cast off or, as it were, explode those in whom we see some zeal, even when their knowledge of things is very slight. The Lord himself did not break the bruised reed nor quench the smoking flax, but cherished, aided and promoted those feeble beginnings of faith. So we too must follow his example: whenever we see in someone some zeal for God, even joined with considerable ignorance, let us take pains that this beginning of knowledge of God be increased in that man. And if his eyes are once opened to Christ, who is already in some measure effective in his heart by a secret motion of his Spirit, to see that Christ more clearly, there will arise in him a wonderful faith with peace and inexpressible joy. For those who already have some zeal for God, if their minds are afterwards enlightened, can then be said to become remarkably excellent in faith and religion. Therefore I would advise all those who already have some zeal for God and love for Christ, but who do not yet have sufficient knowledge and clear perception of him, to seek to know him more and more, both as to his person and as to his office.
