For once they have known and seen that fullness of all grace which is in him, the zeal of God and the love of Christ will surely be confirmed in a marvellous way, with a joy, peace and gladness which the world does not understand.

units.la: Iesus enim. Inserit Euangelista rationem, cur ignoraretur Christus ab eo qui sanatus fuerat: quia statim sanato homine Christus se subduxit, euasitque ex turba illa quae erat in eo loco. Dominus, cum sciret personam suam offensioni fuisse Iudaeis, statim sanato homine subduxit se, ne quid praesentia sua officeret operi, ut qui illi, absque praeiudicio & respectu personae, de opere iudicarent, ut certe, quemadmodum ipse loquitur, propter opera crederent: Dominus gloriae omnibus modis consuluit infirmitati nostrae, & pessimos quosque toleravit ad hoc, ut si fieri posset, crederent ac servarentur, seque inanuit ad tempus, & iusta gloria se defraudavit, ea nimirum quae debebat percipere ex operibus suis plane stupendis, ut si quomodo fieri posset, etiam infensissimi sibi hostes servarentur. Quanquam autem quibuscunque demum rationibus hominies adducantur ad fidem, & celetur iis ad tempus ignominia crucis Domini, ne si ea primum sic iis offerat, statim offendatur ac resiliant: tamen eò tandem redeundum est, credendúmque est in eam ipsam crucem, imò gloriandū in illa cruce: fides enim Christi esse non potest, nisi habeatur in crucem & mortem Christi, quæ est gloria nostra. Beati igitur quotquot qui in crucem Christo non offenduntur. Atque hactenus offensi sunt in hominem qui sanatus fuerat, sequitur offensio in Christum. Prius narratur noua quædam huius rei occasio: indicatus est enim iis Christus ab homine qui sanatus fuerat.
units.tr: For Jesus. The evangelist gives the reason why Christ was unknown to the man who had been healed: as soon as the man was healed, Christ withdrew himself and slipped away from the crowd that was in that place. The Lord, knowing that his person was an offence to the Jews, withdrew himself at once after the man was healed, so that his presence would not hinder the work, and so that they would judge the work without prejudice or regard for the person. Indeed, as he himself says, they would believe on account of the works. The Lord of glory consulted our weakness in every way and bore with the worst of men, so that, if it were possible, they might believe and be saved. For a time he hid himself and deprived himself of his rightful glory, namely the glory he ought to have received from his truly astonishing works, so that, if it were somehow possible, even his most bitter enemies might be saved. However, by whatever means people are brought to faith, and however the shame of the Lord's cross is hidden from them for a time, lest, if it were first offered to them in this way, they be offended at once and draw back, still they must in the end return to it and believe in that very cross, and glory in that cross itself. For there can be no faith in Christ unless it rests on the cross and death of Christ, which is our glory. Blessed, then, are all who are not offended at the cross of Christ. So far they were offended at the man who had been healed; offence now follows against Christ. First a certain new occasion of this matter is related: for Christ was pointed out to them by the man who had been healed.

units.la: 14 Postea inuenit eum Iesus in templo: & dixit ei, Ecce sanus factus es: ne pecca amplius, ut ne quid deterius tibi fiat.
units.tr: 14 Afterward Jesus findeth him in the temple, and said unto him, Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee.

units.la: 15 Abiit homo ille, & nunciauit Iudæis Iesum esse a quo sanatus fuerat.
units.tr: 15 The man departed, and told the Jews that it was Jesus, which had made him whole.

units.la: 16 Ac propterea persequebantur Iudæi Iesum, & studebant eum trucidare, quod ista fecisset Sabbatho.
units.tr: 16 And therefore did the Jews persecute Jesus, and sought to slay him, because he had done these things on the sabbath day.

units.la: PVtabat homo se iam consequutum esse summam felicitatem, quòd tandiu ægrotus recuperauit tandem sanitatem suam & præter expectationem, vt solet ii qui ex magnis miseriis liberati sunt, plurimùm facere liberationem eam, & ferè summam felicitatis suæ in ea collocare. Nam nos non assueti morbis aliisque miseriis, nihili facimus prosperam istam conditionem. Verùm Dominus admonet eum nullam felicitatis partem consequutum esse, nisi vnà cum sanitate corporis aliquam animi sanitatem recipiat, mutet animum suum cum mutato corpore, & resipiscat, & ita ipsa. In nullo bono temporario, siue id sit bona valetudo corporis, siue diuitiæ, siue gloria, in nullo, inquam, huiusmodi bono nobis acquiescendum est: sed longius prouehendi sumus ad reparationem corruptæ & perditæ naturæ, nunquam nobis satisfieri debet, tantisper dum sentiamus regenerationem naturæ nostræ tam perditæ ac modis omnibus vitiatæ. Vnde mihimagis operæpretium facere videtur, qui homi-nem iam restitutū & liberatum ex corporali aliqua mi-seria adducit ad resipiscentiam& mortificationem pec-cati,quam is ipse qui eū restituit ac liberauit abeo ipso malo corporali: Et Christus procul dubio plus profuit homini isti, cùm eum ad resipiscentiam perduceret, quàm cūm curaret morbum illum corporis ac sanaret. Nam omnes istæ temporariæ liberationes,nisi adsit re-sipiscētia,quid aliud sunt quàm totidem transitiones ad grauiora quæque mala, & tandem ad ipsos inferos? Un-de dixit Dominus, Ne pecca amplius, vt ne quid deterius ti-bi contingat. Neque exiftimādum est, non posse nos gra-uiori aliquo malo premi quā quo iam oppressi sumus.
units.tr: The man thought that he had now attained the highest happiness, since he had at last recovered his health after so long an illness, and beyond all expectation. As is usual with those who have been freed from great miseries, he rated that deliverance very highly and placed almost the whole of his happiness in it. For we, not being accustomed to diseases and other miseries, make little of this prosperous condition. But the Lord warns him that he has gained no part of true happiness unless, together with bodily health, he also receives some health of soul, and changes his mind along with his changed body, and repents. In no temporal good, whether it be good health of body, riches, or glory, must we, I say, rest content with any such good; rather we must be carried further, to the restoration of our corrupted and lost nature. We must never be satisfied while we feel that the regeneration of our nature, so lost and vitiated in every way, is still incomplete. Hence it seems to me that he does more good who leads a man, already restored and freed from some bodily misery, to repentance and the mortification of sin, than he who restored and freed him from that bodily evil itself. And without doubt Christ did more good to that man when he led him to repentance than when he cured and healed that bodily disease. For all these temporary deliverances, unless repentance is present, are nothing else than so many transitions to graver evils and at last to hell itself. Hence the Lord said, Sin no more, lest a worse thing happen to you. Nor should we think that we cannot be pressed by some evil graver than that by which we are already oppressed.

units.la: Ægrotabat iste miser graviter iā totos triginta annos, & tamē denuntiauit Christus in eū grauius aliquod ma-lum. Quòd si iratus Deus iniiceret in te manum suam, tum te ipsa disceres morbos istos corporis quoscunqi, cæterásque temporarias miserias omnes temperatas el-se misericordia aliqua, tūmque confiteteris Deum ha-ctenus clementem & misericordem in te afflgendo ac humiliādo. Sic enim statim omnia mala huius vitæ e-lectis præsertim temperari aliqua misericordia: inferos vero illos nullam habere temperatam cum ira miseri-cordiam, sed extremam iram duntaxat & oppressione. Quare cauendum diligenter in miseriis his tempora-riis, ne queramur de extremo aliquo rigore; fine du-bio enim huiusmodi impatientia, & pene dicam blas-phemia procurat multos horrendos cruciatus, idque iusto Dei iudicio. Agnoscenda igitur semper Dei ali-qua misericordia etiā cūm iustus & iratus videtur, dan-dāq; opera est vt eius sensu quantulocunque in mediis hisce miseriis nos ipsi consolemur.
units.tr: This wretched man had been seriously ill now for thirty whole years, and yet Christ threatened him with some graver evil. For if God, angry, should lay his hand upon you, you would then learn that all those bodily diseases and all the other temporal miseries were tempered by some mercy, and you would confess that God had hitherto been merciful and kind to you in afflicting and humbling you. For thus all the evils of this life, especially for the elect, are tempered by some mercy; but those depths of hell have no mercy tempered with wrath, but only extreme wrath and oppression. Therefore we must take care in these temporal miseries not to complain of any extreme severity; for without doubt such impatience, and I might almost say blasphemy, brings upon us many dreadful torments, and that by the just judgement of God. Therefore we must always acknowledge some mercy of God even when he seems just and angry, and we must take pains to console ourselves, however small the sense of it, in these very miseries.

units.la: Hic obseruo præterea quamcunque afflictionem ac miseriam ex peccato promanare. Ne pecca amplius, in-quit, ne quid deterius tibi contingat. Est igitur omnis cala-mitas ex peccato,etsi non eo fine vt peccatum in iis pu-niat, suos affligat Deus. Remittit enim in Christo eiúf-que plena satisfactione simul cum peccato omnem pec-cati pœnam, siue temporariam illam, siue æternam. Il-lud enim certissimum est, quòd si Deus inciperet exige-re ab re ab aliquo vel minimum pœnæ temporariæ peccati sui nomine, quo nimirum pro peccato ipsi satisfieret, profectò ira eius ad extremum visque eum hominem persequeretur, neque prius desisteret quàm in inferos miserum detruderet, quicquid garriant Papistæ de remissione peccati, sed non pœnæ. Ergo, vt redeam, verum quidem illud est, materiam omnis afflictionis in nobis esse, nullum esse ex omnibus tam graue malum quod peccatum nostrum merito suo non procuret, etsi interea illud fieri oportear, Deum non semper punire peccatum, sed alios fines quos ipse nouit sibi propositos habere, vt mortificationem peccati in nobis reliqui, bonu nostrum, nominatim verò gloriam suam. Quare nobis videndum est, quotiescunque affligi nos contingit, vt continuò cogitemus de graviori malo atque periculo, conuertamurque ad Dominum; sic enim Deus assequitur finem suum, mortificationem reliqui in nobis peccati, & nos incipimus summa cum voluptate in mediis etiam calamitatibus sentire infinitam illa Dei in Christo Iesu misericordiam, Cui cum Patre sit omnis honor & gloria. Amen.
units.tr: Here I further observe that every affliction and misery springs from sin. Sin no more, he says, lest a worse thing happen to you. Therefore every calamity comes from sin, even if God afflicts his own not for the purpose of punishing sin in them. For God remits in Christ, and by his full satisfaction, together with sin, the whole punishment of sin, whether temporal or eternal. For this is most certain: if God were to begin to exact from anyone even the smallest temporal punishment for his sin, that is, to make satisfaction to himself for sin, then his wrath would surely pursue that man to the end, and would not cease until it thrust the wretched man into hell, whatever the Papists babble about the remission of sin but not of punishment. So, to return: it is true that the matter of every affliction lies in us, and that there is no evil so grave that our sin does not deserve to bring it upon us by its merit; yet meanwhile it must be that God does not always punish sin, but has other ends which he knows he has set for himself: to leave the mortification of sin in us, our good, and above all his own glory. Therefore we must take care that, as often as we are afflicted, we continually think of a graver evil and danger, and turn ourselves to the Lord. For thus God attains his end, the mortification of the remaining sin in us, and we begin, with the greatest joy, even in the midst of calamities, to perceive that infinite mercy of God in Christ Jesus, to whom with the Father be all honour and glory. Amen.

units.la: Abiit ille. Homo qui sanus factus fuerat, cognito iam quòd Iesus is esset qui sanauerat ipsum, abiit & muntiauit Iudæis Iesum esse qui sanum eum fecerat: hinc orta persecuutio: Propterea, inquit, persequebantur, &c. Homo iste non animo quidem prodendi Christum nuntiauit Iudæis Iesum esse qui eum sanauerat, sed animo potius honorandi eum apud omnes, vt & omnes pariter secum admirarentur diuinum hominem ac in pretio haberet. Tamen res longè aliter succedit atque ipse expectabat: oritur enim ex indicio grauis persequutio Domini. Sæpe cum pro affectu quodam animi nostri multa agimus, infeliciter succedit adeo, vt demum incipiat nos facti ac instituti nostri pœnitere. Proculdubio enim cum homo iste ortam persequutionem Christi ex relatione & indicatione à se facta videret, eum facti cœpit pœnitere. Sed sustentemus nos interea testimonio bonæ conscientiæ, tùmque quòd non transgressi sumus limites officii nostri, tum quòd gloriam Dei in eo quod secunus ante oculos nostros habuerimus, certò illud scientes, finem tandem fore felicem post finitas omnes turbas & commotiones. Nota deinde, produnt iam isti malitiam suam, cognito iam eo quòd Iesus hominem sanauerat. Hypocritę tandem euomunt illud virus quod prius latebat in corde sub prætextu & fuco religionis & zeli gloriæ Dei in asserenda sanctitate Sabbathi.
units.tr: He departed. The man who had been made whole, now knowing that Jesus was the one who had healed him, went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him whole. Hence arose the persecution: Therefore, it says, they persecuted, and so on. This man announced to the Jews that Jesus was the one who had healed him, not indeed with the intention of betraying Christ, but rather with the intention of honouring him before everyone, so that all would likewise wonder at the divine man and hold him in esteem. Yet the outcome was far different from what he himself expected: a grievous persecution of the Lord arose from the information. Often, when we do many things out of some feeling of our mind, it turns out so unhappily that at length we begin to repent of what we have done and undertaken. Surely, when this man saw that the persecution of Christ had arisen from the report and information given by himself, he began to repent of what he had done. But meanwhile let us sustain ourselves with the testimony of a good conscience, both because we have not overstepped the limits of our duty and because we have kept the glory of God before our eyes in what we have done, knowing certainly that the end will at last be happy, once all the disturbances and commotions are over. Note further that these men now reveal their malice, now that it is known that Jesus had healed the man. At last the hypocrites vomit forth that poison which had lain hidden in their heart under the pretext and disguise of religion, and of zeal for the glory of God in upholding the sanctity of the Sabbath.

units.la: 17 Iesus autem respondit eis, Pater meus usque adhuc operatur, & ego operor.
units.tr: Jesus answered them, My Father worketh hitherto, and I work.

units.la: 18 Propterea ergo magis studebant eum Iudæi trucidare, quia non solum soluebat Sabbathum, sed & Deum dixisset patrem suum, æqualem se faciens Deo.
units.tr: For this cause the Jews sought the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God.

units.la: 19 Respondit ergo Iesus, & dixit eis, Amen amen dico vobis, non potest filius à semetipso operari, id est nisi viderit Patrem operantem: quæcunque enim ille facit, hæc etiam filius pariter facit.
units.tr: Then Jesus answered and said to them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, the Son can do nothing of himself, that is, unless he sees the Father working: for whatsoever he doeth, these the Son also doeth likewise.

units.la: 20 Pater enim amat filium, & omnia monstrat ei quæ ipse facit: & opera istis maiora monstrabit ei, ut vos miremini.
units.tr: For the Father loveth the Son, and sheweth him all things that himself doeth: and he will shew him greater works than these, that ye may marvel.

units.la: IEsvs defendit factum suum, ostenditque non esse eam quam ipsi arbitrantur violationem Sabbathi. Argumentum est ex eo, quòd unum idemque sit opus suum cum Patris sui opere: vel quòd pariter cum Patre suo operetur iam inde ab æterno in hodiernum usque diem. In hunc modum Dei Patris opus nunquam est violatio Sabbathi: At opus meum unum idemque est cum Patris mei opere; Ergo opus meum non est violatio Sabbathi. Examinemus rursus huius syllogismi partes. Quòd ad primam eius partem, non eget aliqua demonstratione, ut quæ suapte natura satis fit manifesta. Deus enim nunquam violat legem à se datam, quanquam lege aliqua non tenetur Deus. Sed cum lex Dei sit imago quædam iustitiæ ipsius, suam ipsius imaginem non violat. Secunda pars syllogismi & assumptio expresse ponitur in textu: Pater meus usque adhuc operatur, & ego operor. Pater meus, inquit, & non nostep, significans eum speciali modo sibi patrem esse, seque vicissim filium eius, non communi more aliorum qui filij Dei dicuntur per gratiam adoptionis, sed suo quodam ac proprio modo, vt pote per naturam. Atque hanc fuisse mentem eius non plane ignorarunt Iudaei, vt videbimus postea. Pater meus, inquit, usque adhuc operatur; Hoc est, inde a condito mundo usque in hunc diem operatur assidue sine intermissione aliqua citra delectum aliquem diebus etiam Sabbathinarum. Et ego quidem, cum sim eius filius, vna cum eo operor: Operor autem eadem quae Pater, atque eodem modo ac similiter, vt postea videbimus. Deus finito illo opere creationis spatio sex dierum, cessauit quidem ab opere creationis die septimo. Verum ab opere administrationis & gubernationis, ita inde a condito mundo nullo vnquam die cessauit, ne illo quidem Sabbathi, in quo tum primum cessauit ab opere creationis, neque etiam adhuc cessat: continuo enim ac indesinenter res a se creatas tuetur ac sustinet, vt naturas rerum, species animantium, humanum genus imprimis: inter homines autem electos ac fideles suos. Si enim fingas vel ad momentum eum subtrahere manum suam, res protinus collaberentur: huiusmodi autem opus sustinet hoc, in sanando homine isto aegroto.
units.tr: Jesus defends his deed and shows that it is not the violation of the Sabbath that they think it is. The argument rests on this: his work is one and the same with the work of his Father, or he works together with his Father from eternity until the present day. In this form: the work of God the Father is never a violation of the Sabbath; but my work is one and the same with my Father's work; therefore my work is not a violation of the Sabbath. Let us examine the parts of this syllogism again. The first part needs no demonstration, since it is plain enough by its own nature. For God never violates the law given by himself, although God is bound by no law. But since the law of God is a certain image of his justice, he does not violate his own image. The second part of the syllogism, the assumption, is expressly stated in the text: My Father worketh hitherto, and I work. He says "My Father," not "our Father," signifying that he is Father to him in a special way, and that he is in turn his Son, not in the common manner of others who are called sons of God by the grace of adoption, but in a certain peculiar way of his own, namely by nature. The Jews did not altogether fail to grasp that this was his meaning, as we shall see later. "My Father," he says, "worketh hitherto": that is, from the founding of the world until this day he works constantly and without interruption, not excepting even the days of the Sabbaths. And I, since I am his Son, work together with him. I work the same things as the Father, and in the same way and similarly, as we shall see later. When God had finished the work of creation in the space of six days, he indeed ceased from the work of creation on the seventh day. But from the work of administration and government he has not ceased on any day since the founding of the world, not even on that Sabbath on which he first ceased from the work of creation, nor does he cease even now. For he continually and without pause preserves and sustains the things he has created, the natures of things, the kinds of living creatures, and above all the human race, and among men his chosen and faithful ones. For if you imagine him withdrawing his hand even for a moment, things would at once collapse. Such is the work he sustains in healing this sick man.

units.la: Tantum enim abest ab eo vt opus istud conseruationis creaturae violet Sabbathum, vt e contra Sabbathū ordinatum sit a Deo in eū finem, vt homines abstinentes eo die a priuatis & ordinariis suis operibus, contemplentur illa Dei opera in conseruando ac gubernando res a se creatas, sensúsque suos ad ea obseruanda prorsus convertant.
units.tr: So far is that work of preserving creatures from violating the Sabbath, that on the contrary God ordained the Sabbath for this end: that men, abstaining on that day from their private and ordinary labours, should contemplate those works of God in preserving and governing the things he has made, and turn their senses wholly to observing them.

units.la: Propterea ergo magis. Crescit persecutio: cum enim semel animus praeoccupatus est malitia, quo plus audit quis, eo fere obstinatior & malitiosior fit. Quamobrem purgandus est animus perpetuo ista malitia, ne tandem perveniat ad extremam illam & desperatam obduratio-nē. Christus satis sciuit futurum, vt isti statim audita hac doctrina tumultuarentur, neque tamen abstinet, sed pergit porro. Non cessandum est a praedicanda veritate Dei, ne si insaniant quidem mundus. Debemus, fateor, eo consilio atque animo praedicare veritatē, vt quotquot au-
units.tr: Propterea ergo magis: Therefore, "the more." Persecution grows. For once the mind is preoccupied with malice, the more one hears, the more obstinate and malicious one almost becomes. Therefore the mind must be constantly purged of this malice, lest it finally come to that extreme and desperate hardening. Christ knew well that these men would riot as soon as they heard this teaching, yet he did not refrain but went on further. The preaching of God's truth must not be given up, even if the world should go mad. I admit we ought to preach the truth with this purpose and intention: that all who hear may be converted, and that those who are converted may be kept fervent.

units.la: Veritatis patrocinium propterea non desertendum. diunt conuertantur, ac conuersi feruentur. Tamen ne putemus nos nihil egisse aut profecisse, fi contrà euenire videamus, vt homines ad prædicationem nostram obdurentur: Deus enim illa ipsa induratione in iustitia sua glorificatur. Neque putemus oportere nos meliori cum successu docere ingratum hunc mundum, quàm quo docuit ipse Dominus noster Iesus Christus. Sed cõsideremus verba ipsa: Propterea, inquit, magis studebant eum trucidare, quia non solum soluisset Sabbathum, sed & Patrem suum dixisset Deum. Christus enim dixit supra, Pater meus, quo significauit Deum sibi Patrem speciali quodam modo & ineffabili. Id fatis obferuarunt Iudæi, & ex verbis Domini collegerunt; Ex quo tutus & aliud intulerunt, nempe Iesum fe facere Deo parem. Nam fi hoc verum fit, Deum Patrem ipsius esse proprium ac naturalem, sequitur & illud eum parem esse Deo. Nam & Deus est, fi Dei filius est naturalis. Quare non male hoc ex illo collegerunt. Sed quid ad hæc Christus? Respondit ergo Iesus. Non negat quidem fe parem Deo (non enim, ait Apostolus, rapinam duxit parem esse cum Deo.) Sed quo illud ipsum magis appareat se esse Deum respfa ac Deo Patri parem, incipit præclarè concionari de Dei filio. Primùm autem concionatur de ineffabili illa communicatione, qua Pater communicat cum filio potentiam illam ac virtutem operandi ea, quæ ipse operatur: Ex qua fatis conspicitur filium esse Deum ac parem Deo Patri. De communicatione autem illa primùm in genere agit, deinde in specie. Postea concionatur de præclaro illo testimonio quo Pater filium ornauit, quo primùm tempore eum in mundum misteret: Ex quo etiam fatis arguitur & illud, filium esse Deum ac Deo parem. Postremò ratione istarum rerum tantarum, propter quas merito ipsi fides habenda fuit, reprehendit incredulitatem Iudæorum.
units.tr: The defence of the truth is therefore not to be abandoned. Yet let us not think we have accomplished nothing or made no progress if we see the opposite happen, that men are hardened by our preaching: for God is glorified in that very hardening, in his justice. Nor should we think that we ought to teach this ungrateful world with better success than our Lord Jesus Christ himself had. But let us consider the words themselves: Therefore, he says, the Jews sought the more to kill him, because he not only had broken the Sabbath, but had also called God his Father. For Christ said above, "My Father," by which he signified God to be his Father in a certain special and ineffable way. The Jews noted this well enough and gathered it from the Lord's words, and from it they drew a further inference, namely that Jesus made himself equal to God. For if this is true, that God is his Father by nature and in his own right, it follows that he is equal to God. For he too is God, if he is the natural Son of God. Wherefore they did not gather this badly from that. But what does Christ say to this? Jesus therefore answered. He does not deny that he is equal to God (for, as the Apostle says, he did not count it robbery to be equal with God). But so that this very thing may more clearly appear, that he is God and equal to God the Father, he begins to preach splendidly about the Son of God. First he preaches about that ineffable communication by which the Father imparts to the Son that power and ability to work the things which the Father himself works, from which it is sufficiently seen that the Son is God and equal to God the Father. He treats of this communication first in general and then in particular. Afterwards he preaches about that illustrious testimony with which the Father adorned the Son at the time when he first sent him into the world, from which too it is sufficiently proved that the Son is God and equal to God. Lastly, on the ground of these great things, for which he was rightly to be believed, he rebukes the unbelief of the Jews.

units.la: Primùm itaque proponit illam communicationem, cum graui quadam & assueta asseueratione; Amen, Amen, inquiens, &c. Sententia propositionis hæc est: Filius non habet eam potentiam qua operatur à semetipso, sed habet eam à Patre sibi communicatam. Vt hæc intelligamus paulò altius quædam repetenda sunt de Patre,
units.tr: First, then, he sets forth that communication with a certain weighty and customary asseveration: "Verily, verily, I say unto you," and so on. The sense of the proposition is this: the Son does not have that power by which he works from himself, but has it communicated to him by the Father. To understand these matters a little more deeply, some things must be recalled concerning the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Philip. 2.6. tre, Filio & Spiritu sancto. Deus Pater est à se, est, ad hypostaticam suam subsistentiam accipit à se essentiam illam Dei, non aliunde, nonà Filio, non à Spiritu sancto. Filius non est à se, hoc est, ad subsi- stentiam suam non accipit essentiam illam Dei à semet- ipso, sed à Patre, in æterna nimirum illa sui generatione. Spiritus sanctus non elt à se, hoc est, ad subsistentiam sua non accipit essentiam illam Dei à sese, sed à Patre & Filio, in æterna nimirum processione illa à Patre & Filio. Rursus autem vt Pater est à se, ita à se operatur hæc omnia quæ creaturas respiciunt, hoc est, vt habet essen-tiam à se, ita potentiam illam & virtutem, qua operatur, habet à se, non ab alio. Hæc enim se comitatur inuicem, à se esse, & à se operari: Si enim essentia sit à se, etiam operatio est à se: Operatio enim proficiscitur ab essentia. Filius autem, vt non est à se, sed à Patre, ita non à semetipso operatur, hoc est, non habet à se potentiam illam & virtutem qua operatur, sed habet eam à Patre sibi communicatam. Operatur quidem per se, hoc est, per virtute ac potentiam sibi propriam & naturalem, sed communicatam & datam à Patre. Aliud enim est, à se operari, aliud per se: hanc autem virtutem nulli creaturæ communicauit, vt per se agat. Neque per se agit vlla creaturarum, sed per Deum. Per ipsum enim viuimus, & movemur, & sumus. Spiritus sanctus, vt non est à se, ita non à se operatur: hoc est, vt non habet à se essentiam illam deitatis, ita non habet à se potentiam illam & virtutem qua operatur, sed accipit eam à Patre & Filio sibi communicatam. Per se quidem operatur, quia per potentiam & virtutem sibi propriam, communicatam tamen operatur. Ex his non sequitur Filium non inferiorem Patre suo, vel quoad potetiam, vel quoad operationem: Nam vna eadémque est Dei essentia in omnibus, quę non po- testpati huiusmodi inæqualitatem. Sed ex his oritur in personis tantum differentia quædam ordinis, non etiam dignitatis, vt Pater sit ordine persona prima, Filius se- cunda, Spiritus sanctus tertia. Et in operationibus si- militer, vt Pater sit principium & origo actionum o- mnium: Filius secundo loco operetur & dispenset actiones Patris : Spiritus sanctus tertio loco operetur perficiatq; & consummet operationes Patris & Filij. His itaexpositis, videamus propositionem illam communicationis. Filius, inquit,non potest a semetipso operari, hoc est, non habet potentiam illam ac virtute qua operatur a semetipso. Deinde clarius hoc ipsum effert, Non potest operari, nisi viderit Patrem operantē: hoc est, nisi acceperit potentiam illam operandi sibi a Patre communicatam. Videre enim hoc loco non est otiosum spectatorē esse operationis paternę, sed est accipere potentia vnà operandi cum Patre sibi communicatam. Similiter etiam accipitur demonstrare, de quo posteà, non est duntaxat videda opera filio proponere, sed est potestatē operandi cum filio communicare. Quaecunq; enim ille facit. Dici potuit aliquo, Ergone simul cum Patre operatur filius? Nā hoc ex verbis proximis sequitur necessario; dictū est enim proximè filiū videre Patrem suum operantē, hoc est, accipere potestatem operandi vna cum Patre. Huic igitur respondet, ac profitetur, filium, quaecunq; operatur Pater, eadem operari, hoc est, eandem planè numero esse actione Patris & filij. Addit praeterea eodem modo operari filium quo Pater, hoc est, eadem voluntate, eadem planè potentia & virtute, eodem fine propósito. Vt enim eadem est actio & eadem quidem numero, ita eadem est potentia & voluntas vtriusque.
units.tr: Philip. 2.6. God the Father is from himself. For his hypostatic subsistence he receives that essence of God from himself, not from elsewhere, not from the Son, not from the Holy Spirit. The Son is not from himself: that is, for his subsistence he does not receive that essence of God from himself, but from the Father, namely in that eternal generation of his. The Holy Spirit is not from himself: that is, for his subsistence he does not receive that essence of God from himself, but from the Father and the Son, namely in that eternal procession from the Father and the Son. Again, as the Father is from himself, so he works from himself all those things which regard creatures; that is, as he has his essence from himself, so he has from himself that power and virtue by which he works, and not from another. For these two accompany each other, to be from oneself and to work from oneself: if the essence is from itself, the operation is also from itself, since operation proceeds from essence. But the Son, as he is not from himself but from the Father, so he does not work from himself. That is, he does not have from himself the power and virtue by which he works, but has it communicated to him by the Father. He does indeed work through himself, that is, through power and virtue proper to him and natural, yet communicated and given by the Father. For it is one thing to work from oneself and another to work through oneself. But he has not communicated this virtue to any creature, so that it might work through itself. Nor does any creature work through itself, but through God: for in him we live, and move, and have our being. The Holy Spirit, as he is not from himself, so he does not work from himself: that is, as he does not have from himself that essence of deity, so he does not have from himself the power and virtue by which he works, but receives it communicated to him by the Father and the Son. He indeed works through himself, because it is through power and virtue proper to himself, though communicated, that he works. From these things it does not follow that the Son is inferior to his Father, either in power or in operation. For the essence of God is one and the same in all, and cannot admit inequality of this kind. But from these things there arises in the persons only a certain difference of order, not of dignity: the Father is first in order, the Son second, the Holy Spirit third. Similarly in the operations: the Father is the principle and origin of all actions; the Son works in the second place and dispenses the actions of the Father; the Holy Spirit works in the third place and perfects and completes the operations of the Father and the Son. With these things explained, let us look at that proposition of communication. "The Son," he says, "cannot work from himself": that is, he does not have from himself the power and virtue by which he works. Then he states this more clearly: "He cannot work unless he sees the Father working": that is, unless he has received that power of working communicated to him by the Father. For to see here is not to be an idle spectator of the Father's operation, but to receive the power of working together with the Father communicated to him. Likewise, to show, of which more later, is not merely to set forth works to the Son, but to communicate to the Son the power of working. "For whatever he doeth": someone might say, does the Son therefore work together with the Father? For this follows necessarily from the preceding words, since it was said just before that the Son sees his Father working, that is, receives the power of working together with the Father. To this he replies and professes that whatever the Father works, the Son works the same, that is, that the action of Father and Son is plainly one and the same in number. He adds besides that the Son works in the same way as the Father, that is, with the same will, the same plainly power and virtue, and the same end in view. For as the action is one and the same in number, so the power and will of both are the same.

units.la: Haec nunc aliquo modo ad nos accommodanda sunt, etsi quid potest esse simile Altissimo? Nota igitur primum , vt filius dum videt Patrem suum operantem, non tu est otiosus spectator, sed accipit potentia simul operandi cu Patre: ita & nos nō debemus esse otiosi spectatores potentię Patris & filij, quam in operando demonstrant: Verum etsi non possumus neque etiā debeamus accipere eam nobis sic communicatam vt filius accipit potentiam Patris sui prorsus eadem & totam: tamen eò nitendum est, vt sentiamus in nobis potentiam certè aliquam Patris & filij. Si enim in Christi sumus, profecto aliquā ex eo potetiam in nobis ipsi sentiemus; & eam quidem nō communem illam & vulgarē, cuius participes fiunt omnes creaturæ: verum specialem quandā potentiam quæ est ad resipiscentiam, fidem, mortificationem pecpeccati, viuificationem, vitam deniq; æternam. Quòd si autem non sentiamus in nobis ipsi illam Christi potentiam quæ est ad fidê & regenerationem, profectò Christi non iam sumus. Quòd ii quis Spiritum Christi non habet, non est eius. Quare semper eò connitendū est, vt sentiamus in nobis potentiam illam Christi, quam si semel senseximus in mediis infirmitatibus iis, quibus vndiq; circumsepti sumus, profectò eas non modò æquiori animo feremus, veruetiam in iis gloriabimur. Lubentissimè igitur gloriabor potius de infirmitatibus meis, vt inhabitet in me potentia Christi, ait Apost. Videmus deinde summā illi inter Patrem & filium in agendo conspirationem. Nobis etiam ad eam innitendum est, quo ad eius potest fieri, vt pariter cum Patre & filio operemur: nō solùm quidem vt eadem sit actio Dei & nostra. Nam necessariò hoc futurum est vel nobis inuitis: Dei enim prouidentia efficax est etiam in pessimis quibusque malorum instrumentorum operationibus: verùm multò magis vt eodem modo cum Patre & filio, quantum per ipsius gratiam fieri potest, operemur: hoc est, vt licet non possit esse eadè plane voluntas & Dei & nostri, eadè plane potentia, virtus plane eadè, idem plane respectus: tamè vt voluntates nostrae, & omnes facultates animæ nostræ voluntati diuinæ subiiciantur. In hac enim conformitate cum Deo nostro posita est felicitas nostra. Neque dici potest quàm gaudeat regeniti dum sentiunt istam cōspirationem. Delectar lege Dei, quoad interiorem hominem. Dum rursus sentiunt nondum prorsus subiectam voluntatem suam voluntati Dei inter operandum ex præscripto legis ipsius, neque se prorsus eundem cum Deo suo spectare finem operationum suarum, hoc illis molestissimum est: effecit enim vt Paulus exclamaret, Miser ego homo quis me eripiet ex isto corpore mortis? Landādus tamen est hic dolor, multóque melior est ea lætitia & voluptate non regenitorum, quam tum capiunt etiā cum toto cælo aberrant à voluntate Dei. Cogit enim dolor iste peccatorem Christum quærere, in quo solo habet liberationem ab omni peccato per mortē ipsius. Gratias habeo Deo meo per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrū, inquit Apostolus. Pater enim diligit Filium. Duo fundamenta substernit coniunctæ huic parique operationi Patris & Filij. Primum est his verbis, Pater diligit Filium: Alterum his verbis, Omnia demonstrauit ei quæ ipse fecit, Communicatio nimirum illa qua Pater cum Filio suo seque quæque omnia communicat; atque ita redit ad propositam illam communicationem. Hinc sequitur communis operatio. Verum expendamus sigillatim hæc quæ iacit fundamenta communis operationis.Pater, inquit, diligit Filium. Dilectio ista & amor quo Pater Filium prosequitur, ut infinitus est, ita incomprehensibilis & ineffabilis: Verum ita demum eius sensum percipiemus aliquem commodissime, si videamus an Pater nos ipsos diligat. Resider enim hic amor totus in filio naturali, ex eoque tanquam fonte vberrimo manat quasi ad nos. Ex eo igitur, tanquam ex effecto, de causa possumus iudicare. Cum igitur, vt ait Apostolus, charitas Dei nō instillata sit guttatim, sed effusa in cordibus nostris per Spiritum S. qui datus est nobis, quanta est, quæsio, & quam copiosa illa charitas Dei quæ æterna Filium suum, & ex qua manauit hæc Dei erga nos, quanta quanta est, dilectio tota, cuius ne centesima quidem pars est ista qua nos in Filio prosequitur charitas? Ex hoc fundamento sic posito, sequitur illud alterum, nempe demonstratio & communicatio omnium cum Filio: dilectio enim nihil potest celare dilectum: &si sit apud nos pater aliquis terrenus qui filium habeat, quem unicè diliget, is libenter cum filio suo omnem suam facultatem, & operandi aliquid peritiam & artem communicaret. Deus igitur quo maiori charitate prosequitur unigenitum suum quàm possit creatura vlla prosequi creaturam alteram aliquam quantumuis charam & sibi dilectam, Deus, inquam, sedens in hac quasi mundi officina, & operans quasi artifex quidam admirabilis, eo magis cum Filio suo omnia sua totamque facultatem & potentiam suam communicabit. Sed videamus verba textus: demonstrat, inquit, et omnia quæ ipse facit. Vt suprà dictus est Filius videre Patrem operantem, non quòd otiosus spectator sit, sed quòd accipiat à Patre operandi facultatem sibi communicatam: ita nunc dicitur Pater demonstrare Filio quæ ipse facit, non quòd nudè proponat videnda ea quæ facit Filio suo, sed quòd demonstrando omnia, communicet ea cum Filio suo. Quare communicatio omnis hic intelligenda est. Atque ita redimus ad communicationem illam quam superius propositi. Accommodemus ista nunc ad nos ipsos: ut ex dilectione illa qua Pater Filium prosequitur existit communicatio, qua Pater se suâque Filio communicat, ex qua est communis actio & operatio Patris & Filij: ita suo quodam modo ex dilectione Dei est quòd fit ministerio nostro in opere suo perficiendo (non enim nos cooperamur cum Patre ut Filius, & quamquam principales agentes, sed nos ut Ministri & servi duntaxat cooperamur) Cooperatio tamen ista ex dilectione est, si modò simul reformet Deus voluntatem & affectus nostros, ut id ipsum velimus, id ipsum spectemus quod Pater & Filius volunt & spectant. Qui autem sentit se ita operari cum Deo eique ministrare in functione sua quacunque, iam certum habet argumentum dilectionis Dei. Neque enim vtitur Deus ministerio cuiusquam hoc modo, nisi quem prius charum habuit. Habens autem argumentum dilectionis Dei in Ministerio suo fungendo, mirum in modum in agendo gaudet, etsi interea multa se obiiciant ei impedimenta. Nam ex conscientia charitatis & dilectionis Dei est ista omnis lætitia & gloriatio.
units.tr: These things must now be applied to us in some way, although what can be like the Most High? Note first that, as the Son, while he sees his Father working, is not an idle spectator but receives the power to work together with the Father, so we too ought not to be idle spectators of the power of the Father and the Son, which they show in working. Yet although we cannot, and indeed ought not, to receive that power as communicated to us in the way that the Son receives the Father's power, entirely the same and entire, still we must strive to feel in ourselves some power truly of the Father and the Son. For if we are in Christ, we shall surely feel in ourselves some power from him, and not that common and general power of which all creatures partake, but a special power, which is for repentance, faith, the mortification of sin, the quickening of life, and at last eternal life. But if we do not feel in ourselves that power of Christ which is for faith and regeneration, then surely we are not yet Christ's. If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. Therefore we must always strive to feel that power of Christ in ourselves, and once we have felt it amid the weaknesses by which we are beset on every side, we shall surely bear them with a more equable mind, and indeed we shall glory in them. Most gladly, therefore, will I glory rather in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me, says the Apostle. Next we see the highest agreement between the Father and the Son in acting. To this we too must strive, as far as it can be done, so that we may work alike with the Father and the Son, not only so that the action of God and ours is one. For this will necessarily happen even against our will, since the providence of God is effective even in the worst works of the most wicked instruments of evil. Rather, we must work in the same way as the Father and the Son, as far as can be done through his grace; that is, although the will of God and ours cannot be entirely the same, nor the power entirely the same, nor the virtue entirely the same, nor the aim entirely the same, yet our wills and all the faculties of our souls must be subjected to the divine will. For our happiness lies in this conformity with our God. Nor can one say how the regenerate rejoice while they feel this agreement. I delight in the law of God, according to the inner man. When, on the other hand, they feel that their will is not yet entirely subject to the will of God in working according to the prescription of his law, and that they do not look on the same end of their works as their God does, this is most painful to them; it made Paul cry out, Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? Yet this sorrow is to be praised, and it is far better than the joy and pleasure of the unregenerate, which they take even when they wander wide of the will of God. For this sorrow compels the sinner to seek Christ, in whom alone he has deliverance from all sin through his death. I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ our Lord, says the Apostle. For the Father loves the Son. He lays down two foundations for this joint and equal working of the Father and the Son. The first is in these words, the Father loves the Son; the second in these words, he shows him all the things that he himself does: namely, that communication by which the Father shares himself and all things with his Son, and so returns to that communication proposed above. From this follows common working. But let us weigh separately these foundations which he lays for common working. The Father, he says, loves the Son. That love and affection with which the Father pursues the Son is, as it is infinite, so also incomprehensible and unspeakable. Yet we shall most conveniently perceive some sense of it if we see whether the Father loves us. For this whole love rests in the natural Son, and from him, as from a most abundant fountain, it flows out, as it were, to us. Therefore from him, as from an effect, we can judge the cause. Since, then, as the Apostle says, the love of God has not been instilled drop by drop, but has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who is given to us, how great and how abundant is that love of God which eternally begot his Son, and from which this love of God toward us flowed, however great the whole love is, of which not even the hundredth part is that love with which he pursues us in the Son? From this foundation so laid, there follows the other, namely the demonstration and communication of all things with the Son. For love can conceal nothing from the beloved; and if there is among us some earthly father who has a son whom he loves alone, he will gladly share with his son all his means and the skill and art of doing something. So God, the more greatly he pursues his only-begotten with love than any creature could pursue another creature, however dear and beloved, God, I say, sitting in this workshop of the world, and working as a certain wonderful craftsman, will the more share with his Son all his things and his whole faculty and power. But let us look at the words of the text: he shows, he says, and all the things that he himself does. As above the Son is said to see the Father working, not because he is an idle spectator, but because he receives from the Father a faculty of working communicated to him, so now the Father is said to show the Son the things that he himself does, not because he merely sets before his Son the things to be seen that he does, but because by showing all things he shares them with his Son. Therefore all communication is to be understood here. And so we return to that communication which we proposed above. Let us now apply these things to ourselves: as from that love with which the Father pursues the Son arises the communication by which the Father communicates himself and his own to the Son, from which there is common action and working of the Father and the Son; so in a certain manner, from the love of God, it comes about that, by our ministry, his work is brought to completion (for we do not cooperate with the Father as the Son does, being principal agents, but we cooperate only as ministers and servants). Yet this cooperation is from love, if only God at the same time reforms our will and affections, so that we will the same thing and look to the same thing that the Father and the Son will and look to. Moreover, whoever feels that he works thus with God and ministers to him in whatever office he has, already has a sure argument of the love of God. For God does not use anyone's ministry in this way unless he has first held him dear. And having an argument of the love of God in discharging his ministry, he rejoices wonderfully in working, although meanwhile many hindrances oppose him. For all this joy and glorying comes from the consciousness of God's charity and love.

units.la: Et opera ipsis maiora. Reuersus iam ad propositâ illam communicationem potentiæ Patris cum Filio suo, eam deinde exaggerat comparatione facta cum opere illo & miraculo paulò ante edito, in restituendo sanitati tandiu laborantem hominem ex tam graui morbo. Opus quidem illud magnum fuit, sed Pater maiora demonstrabit Filio, hoc est potentiam operandi maiora, quàm fuit illud opus paulò ante editum, cum filio suo communicabit. Adeo, inquit, ut vos miremini. Hoc est, ut si nô crederi fitis saltem cogamini, in admiratione habere potentiam illam Dei admirabilem in operibus ipsius sese ostendentem. Bonum quidem illud est, admirari potentiam Dei & ad eam stupere, quoties se ostendit in miraculis ipsius operibus; sed admiratione ista non o? portet contentos esse, nisi etiam afficiamur sensu aliquo charitatis & misericordiæ erga nos diuinæ. Sola enim potentia nunquam id efficiet vt credamus in Deum. Ea enim est conscientia peccati & iræ Dei aduersus peccatum, vt nisi allecti suaui aliquo misericordiæ Dei in Christo sensu, nunquam velimus credere in eum, aut ad eum confugere. Simul autem sentientes misericordiam, iam libenter delitescimus sub alis potentiæ, in eáque conquiescimus.
units.tr: And greater works than these. Returning now to that communication of the power of the Father with his Son which was proposed, he then magnifies it by comparison with that work and miracle performed a little before, in restoring health to a man who had long labored under so grave a disease. That work was indeed great, but the Father will show the Son greater things, that is, he will communicate to his Son a power of working greater than that work performed a little before. So that, he says, you may marvel. That is, if you do not believe, you may at least be compelled to hold in admiration that wonderful power of God which shows itself in his works. It is indeed good to marvel at the power of God and to be astonished at it whenever it shows itself in his miraculous works; yet we ought not to be content with this admiration alone, unless we are also moved by some feeling of the divine love and mercy toward us. For power alone will never bring us to believe in God. For the consciousness of sin and of the wrath of God against sin is such that, unless we are drawn by some sweet sense of the mercy of God in Christ, we will never wish to believe in him or to flee to him. But when at the same time we feel his mercy, then we gladly hide ourselves under the wings of his power, and rest in it.

units.la: 21 Sicut enim Pater suscitat mortuos & viuificat, ita & filius quos vult viuificat.
units.tr: 21 For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills.

units.la: 22 Nec enim Pater iudicat quemquam, sed omne iudicium dedit filio:
units.tr: 22 For the Father judges no one, but has committed all judgment to the Son:

units.la: 23 Vt omnes honorent filium prout honorant Patrem: qui non honorat filium, non honorat Patrem, vt qui misit eum.
units.tr: 23 That all may honour the Son just as they honour the Father. He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him.

units.la: EXemplo quodam speciali maximi cuiusdam maximeque admiràdi operis, nempe viuificationis mortuorum, ostendit qualia nam quantaque sint opera quæ Pater demonstraturus est filio. Sicut enim Pater, inquit, suscitat mortuos, &c. Scriptura dum vult proponere nobis Dei potentiam in effectis suis maximè admirabilem, solet eam in his effectis videndam proponere, nempe viuificatione mortuorum & creatione omnium ex nihilo. Ita Spiritus sanctus volens ostendere nobis illam potentiam qua nixa est ac firmata fides Abrahæ, eam nobis ex his effectis describit: Coram eo cui credidit, Deo videlicet viuificante mortuos, & vocante quæ non sunt tanquam sint, hæc adduxit, quia effecta sunt Dei maximè admirabilia. Porrò viuificationem istam intelligo non corporalem modò, verùm spiritualem illà ex morte exsuscitatione. Nam peccatum mortis quoddam genus est spirituale. Præterea viuificatione hic tam spiritualem quàm corporalem intelligo, atque eam quidem omni tempore antecedente iudicium illud extremum, cuiusmodi est quotidiana ista regeneratio, cuiusmodi est excitatio Lazari iam mortui & sepulti: item viuificationem intelligo in illo iudicio futuram. Omnis enim viuificatio in omni tempore à potétia illa & virtute Christi proficiscitur. Sed hoc non sentiunt, nisi qui in Christum credunt. Quotquot enim credunt in Christum, illi quidem sentiunt se per fidem quasi haurire è Christo, & ex illa plenitudine quæ in eo habitat, vitam istam etiam corporalem. Paulus, cùm crederet in Christum, illud satis didicit, non potuisse fieri, vt in tot miseriis & mortibus superuiueret, nisi Christus in eo fuisset efficax ad vitam etiam hanc corporalē. Vnde fuit illa vox ex intimo sensu profecta, Vita illa Iesu manifesta fit in mortali carne nostra.
units.tr: By a particular example of a very great and most admirable work, namely the giving of life to the dead, he shows what and how great are the works which the Father is going to show to the Son. For as the Father, he says, raises the dead, etc. When Scripture wishes to set before us God's power in its effects as most admirable, it is accustomed to present it in those effects, namely in the quickening of the dead and the creation of all things out of nothing. So the Holy Spirit, wishing to show us that power on which Abraham's faith rested and was founded, describes it for us from these effects: Before him whom he believed, that is, God who quickens the dead and calls those things which are not as though they were, he brought these things about, because they are the most admirable effects of God. Moreover, I understand this quickening not only as bodily but also as that spiritual rising from death. For sin is a certain spiritual death. Further, by this quickening I understand both spiritual and bodily life, and indeed the spiritual kind at every time before that final judgment, such as this daily regeneration and such as the raising of Lazarus, already dead and buried; likewise I understand a quickening that will take place at that future judgment. For every quickening at every time proceeds from that power and virtue of Christ. But only those who believe in Christ perceive this. For all who believe in Christ feel that through faith they as if draw from Christ, and from that fullness which dwells in him, this life, even the bodily life. When Paul believed in Christ, he learned well enough that it could not come about that he should survive in so many miseries and deaths, unless Christ were effective in him for this bodily life too. Hence came that utterance, proceeding from his inmost feeling: That life of Jesus is made manifest in our mortal flesh.

units.la: Alij vero qui non credunt in Christum, etsi quidem non alia quàm eius virtute viuant vitam etiam istam quam nunc viuimus in carne mortali & animalem: tamen id non magis sentiunt quàm si boues aut aqui essent. De vita illa spirituali non est quæstio, quin ea sit à Christo, id enim in nobis ipsi experimur, non citiùs nos credere, non citiùs nos Dei misericordiam in Christo apprehendere quàm resipiscamus & regeneremur: Ea enim est virtus fidei qua purgantur corda nostra. Vnde Paulus, Et vitam quam nunc viuo in carne, viuo per fidem filij Dei qui dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me. Hactenus de ineffabili illa communicatione in genere, hoc est, de communicatione administrationis mundi & Vniuersitatis huius, omniumque in ea operum.
units.tr: Others, however, who do not believe in Christ, although indeed they live this present life in mortal and animal flesh by nothing other than his power, nevertheless perceive this no more than if they were oxen or asses. There is no question that this spiritual life is from Christ; for we experience this in ourselves: we do not believe any sooner, nor do we grasp God's mercy in Christ any sooner, than we repent and are regenerated. For this is the power of faith by which our hearts are purified. Hence Paul: "And the life which I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." Thus far concerning that ineffable communication in general, that is, the communication of the administration of this world and this universe, and of all the works within it.

units.la: Sequitur nunc specialis communicatio iudicij, quod est pars operationis Dei maximè gloriosa. Neque enim. De communicatione igitur illa generali totius administrationis mundi huius hactenus, nunc occasione proximi loci in quo viuificationis mentio facta est, quæ quidem viuificatio ad iudicem & iudicium pertinet: Iudex enim est qui dat vitam & pronuntiat sententiâ vitę: occasione, inquam, huius viuificationis quod maximorum operum exemplum statuit, de speciali communicatione specialis & gloriosissimæ partis gubernationis & administrationis mundi loquitur. Primùmque proponit Patrem non iudicare quemquam. Iudicare hoc loco, vt mihi videtur, est iudicis partes agere in adiudicando hominem vel vitæ vel morti, siue vita illa sit spiritualis, siue sit corporalis. Sed hoc videtur iniquum, iudiciam omne Patri auferre, præsertim cùm administratio in genere supra verf.17. à Filio ipso attributa sit Patri, tanquam authori omnium operum: Pater, inquit, operatur usque adhuc & ego operor: Et postea, quæcunque ille facit hæc etiam filius pariter facit, verf.19. Et viuificatio in specie quæ etiam Iudicis est & Iudicij proximè præcedente versu, attributa sit Patri tanquam authori: Vt Pater excitat, inquit, mortuos & viuificat: ita & filius viuificat quos vult. Quare locus sic exponendus est, Pater non iudicat quemquam, hoc est, non solus iudicat quemquam. Hæc phrasis est familiaris huic nostro Euangelistæ. Nō quaero, inquit, voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem eius qui misit me, hoc est, non solum meam voluntatem: postea versu 30. Si ego testor de meipso, testimonium meum non est idoneum: Postea versu 31. hoc est, si ego solus testor, testimonium meum non est idoneum. Sensus itaque huius loci est, Pater non iudicat quemquam solus, sed una cum Filio, & in persona Filij. Paulus de hoc aperte loquitur, In die quo iudicabit Dominus de occultis hominum per Iesum Christum. Addit autem, Sed omne iudicium dedit Filio. Omne quidem iudicium dedit Filio, ita tamen ut omne sibi reseruarit. Hoc vniuersale est & patet ad omnia. Quicquid enim habet Pater, illud totum & idem dat Filio, & totum ac idem sibi retinet: Totam essentiam suam eandemque dat Filio, & totam sibi retinet; Totam potentiam suam dat Filio, & totam sibi retinet, & sic de cæteris, iustitia, bonitate, totaque sanctitate ac maiestate sentiendum est. Ex quo discere modum communicationis istius, qua Pater sc suaque omnia communicat Filio. Non communicat Filio partem aliquam vel essentiæ, vel potentiæ, vel iustitiæ suæ, sed hæc tota & eadem communicat. Vnde & aliud sequitur, æqualem nimirum esse filium Patri suo, adeóque vnum cum Patre, cum & omnia acceperit à Patre & eadem omnia.
units.tr: Now follows the special communication of judgment, which is the most glorious part of God's work. For, having thus far spoken of that general communication of the whole administration of this world, now, on the occasion of the passage just before, where mention was made of quickening, which indeed belongs to the Judge and to judgment (for the Judge is he who gives life and pronounces the sentence of life), I say, on the occasion of this quickening, which he has set up as an example of the greatest works, he speaks of the special communication of the special and most glorious part of the government and administration of the world. And first he sets forth the Father judges no one. To judge here, as it seems to me, is to act the part of a judge in adjudging a man either to life or to death, whether that life be spiritual or bodily. But this seems unfair, to take all judgment away from the Father, especially since in general the administration has been attributed to the Father by the Son himself, as the author of all works: My Father, he says, works until now, and I work; and afterwards, whatever he does, these things the Son also does in like manner (v. 19). And the quickening in particular, which also belongs to the Judge and to judgment, has been attributed to the Father as its author in the verse immediately preceding: As the Father raises, he says, the dead and quickens, so the Son quickens whom he wills. Therefore the passage must be explained thus: the Father judges no one, that is, he does not judge anyone alone. This phrase is familiar to our evangelist. I do not seek, he says, my own will, but the will of him who sent me, that is, not only my own will. Afterwards, in verse 30: If I bear witness of myself, my testimony is not valid; and afterwards in verse 31, that is, if I alone bear witness, my testimony is not valid. The sense of this passage, therefore, is: the Father does not judge anyone alone, but together with the Son and in the person of the Son. Paul speaks of this plainly: On the day when the Lord shall judge the secrets of men through Jesus Christ. But he adds: But all judgment he has given to the Son. He has indeed given all judgment to the Son, yet in such a way that he has reserved all of it to himself. This is universal and extends to all things. For whatever the Father has, he gives the whole and the same to the Son, and keeps the whole and the same for himself. He gives his whole essence, and the same, to the Son, and keeps the whole for himself; he gives his whole power to the Son, and keeps the whole for himself; and so it must be understood of the rest: justice, goodness, and all holiness and majesty. From this we learn the manner of that communication, by which the Father communicates himself and all that is his to the Son. He does not communicate to the Son some part of his essence, or power, or justice, but communicates these things wholly and the same. Whence also another consequence follows: namely that the Son is equal to his Father, and therefore one with the Father, since he has received all things from the Father and the very same things.

units.la: Nunc vt accommodemus ipsi ad nos iudicium istud, quod Pater communicat Filio, sic exis-timandum est ill-ud in nobis quoque efficax esse. Vnde, quæso, tanta ita iudicia Regum & Iudicum terræ omnium politica? Vnde nisi à iudicio isto, quod Pater Filio communicat? fluit enim totum ab eo. Et Reges ac Iudices terræ nihil sunt quàm iudicij diuini ministri totidem. Sed quod nesciat hoc plerique in causa est, quòd non credant Filio eúmque cognoscant. Quòd si crederent in Filium, profectò iam sentirent in se ipsi omne iudicium derivatum Filio, eiúsque efficacia ad ipsos peruenire, maiorémque percipérent voluptatem ex regnis & administrationibus suis, maiorem etiam gratiam Deo haberent, maiorem denique diligentiam adhiberent in officio administrando, quàm fit vulgò in misera ista Dei ac Christi ignoratione. Illud enim verissimum esse iudico, nihil homini iucundius esse quàm sentire in sese Christi potentiam ac efficaciam quamcunque & modo quouis. Sunt, fateor, quamplurimę infirmitates nostræ & quæ extra nos sunt, & intra nos sunt: sed hoc vnicum est solatium ac remedium aduersus omnes infirmitates nostras, si persentiscamus Christi Domini potentiam. Paulus questus est apud Dominum de infirmitatibus suis; accepit responsionē de potentia Christi. Sed vt nihil de iudicibus terræ politicis loquamur, affirmamus neminem ex sanctis omnibus esse, ne vno quidem excepto, in quo non sit efficax iudicium istud Filio à Patre datum ad iudicium huius mundi, iudiciū, inquit, maius ac gloriosius quàm sit omne iudicium terrestre. An ignoratis, inquit Paulus, sanctos mundum iudicaturos? An ignoratis fore vt Angelos iudicemus, nedum vt quæ ad huius vitæ vsum pertinent non iudicemus? Nihili facit omnia huius mundi iudicia politica, præillo iudicio quod datum est sanctis. Sed ideo miseri sumus, quòd ignoremus ista quæ habemus in Christo priuilegia quæ & quanta sint: Quòd si ea cognosceremus & sentiremus vt oportet, profectò maior esset consolatio, maior fides in Christo Iesu.
units.tr: Now, to apply that judgment which the Father communicates to the Son to ourselves, it must be reckoned that it is effective in us too. Whence, I ask, come so many political judgments of kings and judges of the earth? Whence, except from that judgment which the Father communicates to the Son? For all of it flows from him. And the kings and judges of the earth are nothing but so many ministers of divine judgment. But most people are ignorant of this, because they do not believe in the Son and do not know him. For if they believed in the Son, they would surely already feel in themselves that all judgment is derived from the Son, and that its efficacy reaches themselves; and they would perceive greater delight in their kingdoms and administrations, would also have greater thankfulness to God, and finally would apply greater diligence in administering their office than is commonly done in this wretched ignorance of God and Christ. For I hold this to be most true: nothing is more pleasant to a man than to feel in himself the power and efficacy of Christ, in whatever manner and form. There are, I admit, very many infirmities of ours, both those outside us and those within us; but this alone is the comfort and remedy against all our infirmities, if we truly perceive the power of Christ the Lord. Paul complained to the Lord about his infirmities; he received an answer concerning the power of Christ. But, to say nothing of the political judges of the earth, we affirm that there is no one among all the saints, not even one excepted, in whom that judgment given by the Father to the Son for the judgment of this world is not effective. Do you not know, says Paul, that the saints shall judge the world? Do you not know that we shall judge angels, to say nothing of judging the things that pertain to the use of this life? This judgment, greater and more glorious than any earthly judgment, is given to the saints. All the political judgments of this world are worth nothing compared with that judgment which is given to the saints. But we are wretched because we do not know what and how great are the privileges we have in Christ. If we knew them and felt them as we ought, surely there would be greater consolation and greater faith in Christ Jesus.

units.la: Vt omnes honorent. Finis iudicij Filio communicati est, vt omnes honorent filium, prout honorant Patrem: hoc est, non tantùm simili, sed æquali prosûs honore, quèmodum omne iudicium, nō aliquotam tantùm eius partem dedit Pater filio suo. Reges terræ communicât cum suis aliquam iudicij sui & regni partem, vt secundùsquidem & inferior honor ipsis deferatur. Pater autem cœlestis cum filio suo omne iudicium communicauit, ad hoc vt par & æqualis honor ei deferatur. Discite hic finem communicati filio à Patre iudicij esse.
units.tr: That all may honour. The power of judgement has been communicated to the Son, so that all may honour the Son, just as they honour the Father. That is, they are to honour him not with a merely similar honour but with an entirely equal one, since the Father has given to his Son the whole of judgement, not just some part of it. Earthly kings share with their subordinates some part of their judgement and rule, so that a lesser honour is paid to those subordinates in proportion. But the heavenly Father has shared with his Son the whole of judgement, so that an equal and identical honour may be paid to him. Learn here that the purpose of the Father's communicating judgement to the Son is this.

units.la: S hunc vt omnes honorent filium. Quod si cui datum esset videre gloriam hanc filij, is profecto honoraret filium. Nam qui semel intuitus est illam filij gloriam, huic prae ea nihil videtur esse tota gloria Iudiciorum & Tribunaliū huius mundi. Quae enim causa est, cur homines coram terrenorum Iudicum tribunalibus Christi causam non agant intrepide? causa est nimirū, quia non vident summum illius tribunal. Quae rursus causa est, cur quidam Christum constanter ac intrepide confessi sunt coram iudicibus & tribunalibus huius mundi? causa est nimirum, quia viderunt aliquam certe partem illius gratiae ac maiestatis.
units.tr: "...that all may honour the Son." If anyone were allowed to see this glory of the Son, he would certainly honour the Son. For whoever has once looked upon that glory of the Son will see the whole glory of the courts and tribunals of this world as nothing beside it. For why do men not plead Christ's cause boldly before the tribunals of earthly judges? The reason, surely, is that they do not see his supreme tribunal. And again, why have some confessed Christ steadfastly and boldly before the judges and tribunals of this world? Surely the reason is that they saw some part at least of that grace and majesty.

units.la: Sic Stephanus in iudicio ītās conspexit cœlos apertos & filium hominis adstantem ad dexteram Dei Patris: Ideoque nihil commotus est illo iudicio Pontificis maximi aliorumque Iudaeorum, qui frendebant cordibus & stridebat dentibus; denique concorditer irruebant in eum, & eiectum ex urbe lapidabant. Et si quidem non nunc videamus extra ordinē aperiri cœlos, neque habeamus visibilem illum aspectū gloriae Christi, quem tum habuit Stephanus: tamen illud certū est, quōd si quis oculis spei & fidei conetur penetrare in cœlos, & gloriam Christi videre, certū, inquā, est ipsum aspectū glorię eū habituru, qui ministraturus sit in iudiciis, in suppliciis omnibus constantiam & patientiam. Qui non honorat filium. Ratio est cur honorandus sit Filius prout Pater, quia cū aequalis sit Filius Patri & vnum cum Patre, qui non honorat Filium, is etsi putet se extra Filium honorare Patrem; tamen non honorat eum. Omni aetate putarunt quidem homines se honorare Deum nescio quem sine Filio. Sic Iudaei & Turcae hodierno die profitentur se Deum quisq; suum impensē colere, non modo sine Filio, sed etiam cum contemptu Filij Iesu Christi. Sed cultus hic totus idololatricus est, & quod colunt illi, idolum est. Nulla enim est veri Dei cognitio nisi in facie Filij.
units.tr: So Stephen, at his trial, looked up and saw the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God the Father. Therefore he was not moved at all by the judgement of the high priest and the other Jews, who gnashed their teeth in their hearts and raged; at last they rushed together upon him, threw him out of the city and stoned him. And even if we do not now see the heavens opened outside the ordinary course, and do not have that visible sight of Christ's glory which Stephen then had, yet this is certain: if anyone tries with the eyes of hope and faith to penetrate into heaven and to see the glory of Christ, then he will certainly have that very sight of glory, which will supply him with constancy and patience in all judgements and all sufferings. He who does not honour the Son. The reason why the Son is to be honoured just as the Father is, is that the Son is equal to the Father and one with the Father. Whoever does not honour the Son, even if he thinks he honours the Father apart from the Son, does not in fact honour him. In every age men have indeed thought that they honour some God or other without the Son. So today the Jews and the Turks profess that each of them zealously worships his own God, not only without the Son but even with contempt for the Son, Jesus Christ. But this whole worship is idolatrous, and what they worship is an idol. For there is no knowledge of the true God except in the face of the Son.

units.la: Quit Paulus, lumen cognitionis gloriae Dei in facie Iesu Christi. Deus enim est per se inconspicuus; Christus autem est imago in conspicui Dei. Sed quaero ex te serio an possis Deum honorare sine Filio, & appello conscientiam tuam an id dicet tibi. Verus cultus Dei non est sine fide, & illa cordis, vt sic dicam, apprehensione. Fides autē consistere nō potest sine sensu misericordiæ Dei, id quod experieris si conscientia peccati te vrgeret, quæ interdiceret te omni prorsus accessu ad Deū, nisi inueni- res qui pro te iustitiæ & iræ diuinæ satisfaceret. Sed vt reuertar, misericordiæ Dei qui potest esse sensus absque Mediatore? Sed cùm non sit hominibus sensus peccati & miseriæ, fallunt se miserē qui cultum Dei aliquem sibi fingunt extra Christum. Neque vel Iudæos istos vel Turcas sensum peccati suiac miseriæ serium aliquem habere putauerim.
units.tr: Paul says: the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. For God is in himself invisible; but Christ is the image of the invisible God. But I ask you seriously whether you can honour God without the Son, and I appeal to your conscience whether it will tell you so. True worship of God is not without faith, and that faith is, so to speak, a grasping of the heart. Faith cannot exist without a sense of God's mercy. You will experience this if the awareness of sin presses upon you, forbidding you every approach to God, unless you find someone who will satisfy divine justice and wrath on your behalf. But to return: how can there be a sense of God's mercy apart from the Mediator? And since men do not have a sense of sin and misery, those who fashion for themselves some worship of God outside Christ deceive themselves wretchedly. Nor would I suppose that those Jews or Turks have any serious sense of their own sin and misery.

units.la: 24 Amen, amē dico vobis, qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam æter- nam, & in condemnationem non veniet: sed trans- uit à morte in vitam.
units.tr: 24 Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life.

units.la: 25 Amen amen dico vobis, aduentat tempus & nunc est, quum mortui audient vocem Filij Dei: & qui audierint viuent.
units.tr: 25 Verily, verily, I say unto you, The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they that hear shall live.

units.la: 26 Sicut enim Pater habet vitam in seipso, sic dedit & Filio habere vitam in seipso.
units.tr: 26 For as the Father hath life in himself, so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself.

units.la: DIuinceps duobus argumentis conatur Iudæos ad honorandum Filium & ad colendum inducere: primum est hoc versu, nēpe certa promissio vitæ æternæ, quam ita demū obtinebunt, si velint audire Filii & credere in Patrem. Amen, amen, inquit, dico vobis. Adhibita familiari & assueta sua asseueratione, promittit vitam æternam, idque tum ad maiorem certitudinem promissionis, tum ad maiorem fidem eorum. Qui sermonem meum audit: Hoc enim primùm fieri debet à nobis, nimirum sermo Filij audiendus, & credendus. Et credit ei qui misit me: Hoc secundo loco fieri debet. Credendum est Patri audito iam sermone Filij qui est de Patre: nequeenim fides est in Patrem, nisi priùs audito Filio qui Patrem nobis patefacit. Porrò nominatim exprimit illum honorem quem requirit à nobis, nempe fidem: Nullus enim honor exhiberi potest Deo, qui ipsi gratior est quàm est fides peccatoris sibi renuntiantis, sese
units.tr: Next he tries to lead the Jews to honour and worship the Son by two arguments. The first is in this verse, namely a sure promise of eternal life, which they will obtain only if they are willing to hear the Son and believe in the Father. Verily, verily, I say unto you. With his familiar and customary asseveration he promises eternal life, both to make the promise more certain and to strengthen their faith. He who hears my word: this is what must be done first by us, namely that the word of the Son must be heard and believed. And believes him who sent me: this must be done in the second place. Once the word of the Son, who tells of the Father, has been heard, the Father must be believed. For faith in the Father is not possible unless the Son, who reveals the Father to us, has first been heard. Furthermore, he names expressly the honour he requires from us, namely faith. For no honour can be shown to God that is more pleasing to him than the faith of a sinner who renounces himself,

units.la: Inductio ad filii cultum religiosum duobus argumentis firmata.
units.tr: Inducement to the religious worship of the Son, confirmed by two arguments.

units.la: Is cultus est fides, sed latem ... quæres (marginal, right, partly illegible) abnegantis & quaerentis misericordiam Dei in Christo Iesu: Per fidem enim obsignatur Dei veritas, & per eam vel maxime glorificatur in misericordia sua. Magis enim glorificari Deum affirmo in iustitia & salute quae est per fidem, quam in iustitia & salute quae est per operra, si fingas hominem servari posse per opera sua; Quia operanti imputatur merces ex debito: Credenti vero imputatur merces ex gratia. Affirmo enim magis glorificari Deum in iustitia illa ac salute nostra, quae ex fide est, quam alioqui, si fingas Adamum in innocentia sua perstitisse, in iustitia illa operum Adami glorificatus fuisset. Sequitur promissio, Habet, inquit, vitam aeternam: praeterea, in condemnationem non veniet: postremo, transiit a morte in vitam. Duo hic faciunt ad maiorem tum certitudinem promissionis, tum fidem nostram. Primum repetitio eiusdem rei promissae. Nam haec tria idem sunt re ipsa. Deinde praesens & praeteritum tempus. Mittit enim nos Deus in praesentem vitae possessionem, vel certe iam missos esse in eam pronuntiat. Vide hic primum, Qui honorant filium & credunt in eum, ii erunt peccatores sint, rei iudicij & irae; tamen sententiam illud iudicium filij esse efficax in se ad vitam aeternam.
units.tr: This worship is faith, but ... (partly illegible in the margin) of one who denies himself and seeks the mercy of God in Christ Jesus. For through faith the truth of God is sealed, and through faith he is especially glorified in his mercy. I maintain that God is more glorified in righteousness and salvation which is by faith than in righteousness and salvation which is by works, if you imagine a man could be saved by his own works; for to one who works, reward is imputed as a debt, but to one who believes, reward is imputed as grace. I affirm that God is more glorified in that righteousness and salvation of ours, which is of faith, than he otherwise would have been, if you imagine that Adam had persisted in his innocence, glorified in that righteousness of Adam's works. The promise follows: He has, it says, eternal life; moreover, he shall not come into condemnation; lastly, he has passed from death to life. Two things here serve both to make the promise more certain and to strengthen our faith. The first is the repetition of the same promised thing, for these three are in fact the same. The second is the present and past tenses. For God sends us into the present possession of life, or at least declares that we have already been sent into it. Notice here first that those who honour the Son and believe in him, even though they are sinners, liable to judgement and wrath, nevertheless have that judgement of the Son efficacious in itself for eternal life.

units.la: Ille insanire nobis videretur & morte dignissimus ferretur qui reus mortis staret coram iudice terreno, possetque absolui a iudice ea lege, qua agnosceret misericordiam Iudicis, veniamque supplex precaretur: neque tamen confugeret ad misericordiam iudicis, sed eam contemptui haberet.
