Annon igitur ille insanit, ac suo merito perit, qui cum possit per resipiscentiam & impetrationem misericordiae summi Iudicis Christi, denuntiatam iam mortem effugere, non tamen dignatur eam implorare? Huius tamen agnitionis Dei in Christo misericordiae defectu, mundus perit. Nam promptissima ac propensissima est ad condonandum supremi illius Iudicis misericordia.
units.tr: He would seem to us to be mad, and would be judged most deserving of death, who, condemned to die, stood before an earthly judge and could be absolved by that judge on condition that he acknowledged the judge's mercy and humbly begged for pardon, yet did not flee to the judge's mercy, but held it in contempt. Is he not then mad, and perishes by his own fault, who, though he could escape the death now proclaimed against him through repentance and by obtaining the mercy of the supreme Judge, Christ, does not deign to implore it? Yet the world perishes for lack of this recognition of God's mercy in Christ. For the mercy of that supreme Judge is most ready and most inclined to forgive.

units.la: Deinde nota, in proponenda hac promissione non nude eum dicere, Qui credit in me, viuet: sed hoc pronunciat adiectis pluribus verbis, quorum tamen nullum videbitur nobis superfluum, si consideremus quam difficulter adducamur ad credendum, quamquam simus infirmi
units.tr: Next, note that in proposing this promise he does not simply say, He who believes in me will live, but states it with several added words. None of these words will seem superfluous to us if we consider how difficult it is for us to be brought to believe, even though we are weak by nature.

units.la: Johan. 3.33. Rom. 4.4.5 firmi natura. Primùm enim vt de difficultate fidei obtinendæ aliquid dicamus, scimus nihil esse magis naturæ nostræ contrarium quàm semel illud admittere, fide iustificari & seruari hominem. Natura omnes facilè admittimus operibus hominē iustificari ac seruari, si quo modo suppeterent: Et tantopere eò propendemus vt etiam imperfectis operibus, quæ vocant regenerationis, putemus hominem iustificari ac seruari posse. Quod quidem dogma est Papistarum hodierno die prorsus exitiale. Vel hac igitur de causa primùm tot verbis promissionem suam amplificauit, hanc nimirum; si quis credat, eum seruatum iri. Deinde postquam adducti sumus eò, vt iam in genere admittamus fide hominem iustificari atque seruari: hic tota iam difficultas est in excitando fidem in cordibus nostris, quæ profectò non excitabitur, quę est nostra incredulitas, nisi concipiatur nobis promissio verbis amplissimis, & eadē re pluribus modis nobis enuntiata. Vnde etiā vel hac de causa nihil in hac promissione superfluum esse putandū est. Postremò, postquam iam cœpimus credere, cum tot tentationibus externis pariter & internis agitari soleat fides nostra, cumque eo deueniamus nonnunquam, vt nullum sensum futuræ vitæ, nullam eius arrham inueniamus reliquam in cordibus nostris; hic si promissio simul nobiscum agitaretur, & cum fide nostra concuteretur; neque nos infirmi firma & immota promissione niteremur, profectò fidem statim amitteremus. Sciendum est, quòd, etsi fides nostra infirma sit & obnoxia infinitis motibus & tentationibus; tamen ipsam Dei promissionem qua nititur fides, firmior sit fundamentis ipsis cœli & terræ; neq; quauis vi loco suo moueri possit. Id quod in tentationibus suppeditat nobis magnam consolationis materiam. Dicimus præterea, quòd etsi fides sit infirma, & à multis rebus aduersariis impetita multoties; tamen fidem hanc nostram prorsus frangi non posse & aboleri. Nam stultitia Dei sapientior est quàm hominēs, & infirmitas Dei validior est quàm homines. Petrus hoc præclarè docet: Postquam enim dixit incorruptibilem illam hæreditatem nostram nobis asseruatam esse in cœlis, ac proinde firmam certamque esse: Tum, quia obiici potuit, At ipsi nos periculis omnibus expositi sumus? Respondet Petrus, nos custodiri virtute Dei per fidem ad vitam illam & hæreditatem. Tum quia excipi potuit: At fides hęc est obnoxia multis tentationibus? Respondet Petrus, Explorationem fidei nostræ vel fidem exploratam, pretiosiorem esse exploratione auri quod perit, & tamen per ignem exploratur: Additque tandem iltam fidem compertum iri nobis esse laudi, gloriæ & honori, cùm patefiet Iesus Christus, eiusque rei signum & argumentum exhiber, quòd nimirum in hac infirmitate fidei, exultemus tamen gaudio inef-fabili & glorioso. Quod quidem argumento est maximæ gloriæ & lætitiæ futuræ aliquando in ipso aspectu Christi ac Domini nostri. Habemus igitur hic duplicem consolationem, & eam quæ est ex firmitate promissionis inuiolabilis; & eam quæ est ex tenacitate huius nostræ fidei quantumuis alioqui infirmæ, si modò vera sit fides, qua fit vt à tam certa firmaque promissione nunquam diuelli se patiatur.
units.tr: First, to say something about the difficulty of obtaining faith: we know that nothing is more contrary to our nature than to admit, once and for all, that a man is justified and saved by faith. By nature we all readily admit that a man is justified and saved by works, if only works were to hand, and we lean so strongly in that direction that we think a man can be justified and saved even by imperfect works, which they call works of regeneration. This doctrine is utterly deadly for the Papists today. For this reason alone, then, he first enlarged his promise with so many words, namely this: if anyone believes, he will be saved. Next, once we have been brought to the point of admitting in general that a man is justified and saved by faith, the whole difficulty lies in arousing faith in our hearts. Certainly it will not be aroused, since our unbelief stands in the way, unless the promise is conceived in us in very ample words and is set forth to us in many ways by the same thing. For this reason too, then, nothing in this promise should be thought superfluous. Finally, once we have begun to believe, our faith is commonly assailed both by external and by internal temptations alike, and sometimes we come to the point where we find in our hearts no sense of the life to come and no pledge of it left. If the promise were then shaken together with us and struck along with our faith, and we weak people did not rest on a firm and unmoved promise, we would certainly lose our faith at once. It must be recognised that, although our faith is weak and exposed to endless shakings and temptations, the promise of God on which faith rests is firmer than the very foundations of heaven and earth, and cannot be moved from its place by any force. This gives us great material for consolation in temptations. We also say that, although faith is weak and often attacked by many adverse things, this faith of ours can never be utterly broken and destroyed. For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men. Peter teaches this admirably. After he had said that our incorruptible inheritance is reserved for us in heaven, and therefore is firm and certain, then, because it could be objected, "But are we not exposed to all dangers?", Peter answers that we are kept by the power of God, through faith, for that life and inheritance. Then, because it could be objected, "But is this faith not subject to many temptations?", Peter answers that the testing of our faith, or faith that has been tested, is more precious than the testing of gold, which perishes, and yet is tested by fire. He adds finally that this faith will be found to be for us a cause of praise, glory and honour when Jesus Christ is revealed, and he gives this as the sign and proof of it: that namely in this weakness of faith we nevertheless rejoice with ineffable and glorious joy. This is indeed a pledge of the greatest glory and joy that is to come at some time, in the very sight of Christ our Lord. We have, then, a twofold consolation here: one from the firmness of the inviolable promise, and the other from the tenacity of this our faith, however weak otherwise, provided that the faith is true, by which it comes about that it never allows itself to be torn away from so certain and firm a promise.

units.la: Amen, amen dico vobis. Argumentum alterum quo alicere statuit Iudæos ad honorandum filium, vel credendum in eum. Est autem ab exemplo & experientia, quorundam qui credituri essent, & per fidem vitam consequuturi, ad hoc, vt si fieri posset, ad æmulationé prouocentur Iudæi. Primùm igitur ad maiorem certitudinem & fidem rei quam proponit, adhibet iuramentum sibi familiare & consuetum, Amen, amen, dico vobis, veniet tempus, nempe post mortem, resurrectionem ac glorificationem meam, tum enim cœpit esse maximè efficax Christus ad spiritualem illam vitam credentium. Et nunc est. Correctio quædam, q.d. Imò etiam nunc ante mortem & glorificationem meam, virtute tamen mortis ac glorificationis, quæ suo tempore contingent; etiam nunc, inquit, est tempus illud, quo incipiunt viuere spiritualiter credentes, nisi malis eum tempus illud pro præsenti habere, quod nō lōgè abfuit. Statim enim post mortuus fuit Christus & glorificatus. Cùm mortui. Mortui dicuntur ij, qui mortui sunt spiritualiter in peccatis & offensis. Nam peccatum genus quoddam mortis est spirituale: Est enim priuatio conformitatis cum lege Dei, ac proinde inde priuatio vitæ Dei, vt ait Apostolus, Cogitationem habentes obtenebratà, abalienatam à vita Dei. Mortui, inquit, audiet. Audire hic est credere & corde assentiri. Voce filij Dei intelligo, promissiones illas iustitiæ & vitæ æternæ gratuitò factas in Christo Iesu. Vide mihi igitur efficaciam vocis filij Dei: facit illa quidè vt mortui audiant: excitat enim fidem in cordibus hominum, cùm habeat comitem sibi Spiritum Dei sanctum. Nulla est alia vox, præter solam filij Dei vocem, quæ potest efficere, vt mortui audiant: nō voces quidē omnes philosophorum, non voces omnes falsorū doctorum. Non norunt, inquit Christus, oues meæ vocē alienorum. Sola hæc Christi vox allicit ad se cor cuiusquę prius mortuum, & prorsus expers omnis sensus. Atq; hæc est interna & efficax Dei vocatio. Et qui audierint: hoc est, quotquot crediderint in promissiones, inchoaturi sunt spiritualem illam vitam.
units.tr: Amen, amen, I say to you. This is the second argument by which he resolves to attract the Jews to honour the Son, or to believe in him. It is drawn from the example and experience of certain people who were about to believe and would obtain life through faith, so that, if it could be done, the Jews might be provoked to emulation. First, then, for greater certainty and to strengthen faith in the thing he proposes, he uses an oath familiar and customary to himself: Amen, amen, I say to you, the time is coming, namely after my death, resurrection and glorification, for then Christ began to be most effective for the spiritual life of believers. And now it is. This is a kind of correction, as if he said: Indeed, even now, before my death and glorification, yet by the power of the death and glorification which will come in their time, even now, he says, is that time in which believers begin to live spiritually, unless you prefer to regard that time as present, since it is not far off. For Christ died and was glorified immediately afterwards. When the dead. Those are called dead who are spiritually dead in sins and offences. For sin is a kind of spiritual death. It is the privation of conformity with the law of God, and therefore the privation of the life of God, as the Apostle says: "having the understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God." The dead, he says, will hear. To hear here is to believe and assent with the heart. By the voice of the Son of God I understand those promises of righteousness and eternal life made freely in Christ Jesus. See, then, the efficacy of the voice of the Son of God: it does indeed make the dead hear, for it arouses faith in the hearts of men, since the Holy Spirit of God accompanies it. There is no other voice apart from the voice alone of the Son of God that can bring it about that the dead hear: not all the voices of philosophers, nor all the voices of false teachers. My sheep do not know, says Christ, the voice of strangers. This voice of Christ alone draws to itself the heart of each person, previously dead and wholly without any sense. This is the inward and effective calling of God. And those who have heard: that is, all who have believed the promises will begin that spiritual life.

units.la: Vide hic rursus efficaciam fidei per vocem Christi, iam excitatæ in cordibus nostris. Non prius enim credimus in promissiones vitæ, quàm incipiamus viuere illā vitam, quàm renouemur ad imaginem Dei, recuperemúsque amissam illam ac deperditam Dei vitam. Et vitam, inquit Paulus, quam nunc viuo in carne, viuo per fidem Filij Dei. Verum, sciendum est non esse hanc vitam spiritualem tam à fide nostra, quàm à fonte illo vitæ qui in Christo est, qui fide apprehenditur, & de qua mox dicemus. Disce igitur ex hoc quod affert argumento, Deum fidem, & ex fide vitam nobis largiri, nō nostra ipsorum sola causa, verùm etiam aliorum, vt alij nostro, qui credimus & viuimus, exemplo, ad æmulationem prouocetur. Sic vocatæ sunt à Deo gentes, eo fine vt Iudæi ad æmulationem prouocarentur. Quoties igitur videmus alios credere in Christum, & ex fide sua spiritualem illam vitam inchoare, piè honestéque viuere, toties nobis exemplo prouocatis, eòdem aspirandum est. Nam profectò quisquis semel gustauit quàm suauis sit Dominus, quàm suauis sit illius vita quam per fidem viuimus, videt se non tantum proficere in fide, & in vita spirituali, quantum alij, illud imprimis malè eum habet. Atque qui nondum degustarunt ista, & ne primoribus quidem, vt loquuntur, labris ea attigerunt, ij, in-
units.tr: Here again see the efficacy of faith, through the voice of Christ, now aroused in our hearts. For we do not believe in the promises of life before we begin to live that life, before we are renewed to the image of God and recover the life of God that was lost and destroyed. "And the life," says Paul, "which I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God." It must be understood, however, that this spiritual life is not so much from our faith as from that fountain of life which is in Christ, which is apprehended by faith, and of which we shall speak presently. Learn, then, from what he brings forward in this argument, that God bestows faith on us, and life through faith, not only for our own sake but also for the sake of others, so that others may be provoked to emulation by our example, as we believe and live. In this way the nations were called by God, to the end that the Jews might be provoked to emulation. Therefore, as often as we see others believing in Christ and beginning from their faith that spiritual life, living piously and honourably, so often, as we are provoked by their example, we must aspire to the same. For certainly whoever has once tasted how sweet the Lord is, how sweet is that life which we live by faith, sees that he is not advancing in faith and in spiritual life as much as others do, and this above all grieves him. Those who have not yet tasted these things, and have not touched them even with the lips, as they say, are so far from being moved by the example of others that they often even mock holy life and conduct, and piety itself, and hold all the godly in derision.

units.la: § iiij quam, tantum absunt ab eo, vt exemplo aliorum com-moucantur, vt sæpe etiam sanctam vitam & conuersationem, pietatem denique ipsam irrideant, & pios quosque ludibrio habeant. Sunt enim hoc nostro sæculo irrisores pietatis & honestatis, plane similes iis qui fuerunt ex gentibus ætate Petri, qui blasphemarunt primis illis temporibus sanctam Christianorum conuersationem, dum iam non concurrerent, vt soliti erant, ad eandem luxus profusionem. Sed de his tum dixit Petrus quòd reddituti essent rationem ei qui paratus est iudicare vivos & mortuos. Quòd si tot retro sæculis, temporibus nimirum Petri & Apostolorum, paratus fuit Dominus ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos: quanto magis nunc in hoc extremo mundi quasi puncto, paratus est ad iudicandum istos? Sed isti vt irrisores sunt pietatis, ita quoque irrisores sunt iudicij illius extremi. Neque prius iudicio illo grauissimo permouebuntur, quàm eo opprimantur.
units.tr: So far are they from being moved by the example of others that they often even mock holy life and conduct, and piety itself, and hold all the godly in derision. For in this our age there are mockers of piety and honesty, plainly similar to those among the Gentiles in the time of Peter, who in those first days blasphemed the holy conduct of the Christians, since they no longer ran, as they had been accustomed, to the same flood of luxury. But Peter said of these that they would give an account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. If, so many centuries ago, in the times, namely, of Peter and the Apostles, the Lord was ready to judge the living and the dead, how much more now, at this last point of the world, is he ready to judge those men? But they, as mockers of piety, are also mockers of that final judgment. Nor will they be moved by that most weighty judgment before they are overwhelmed by it.

units.la: Sicut enim Pater. Quò magis credant eos qui creditur ri sunt victuros, demonstrat quasi digito ipsum vitæ fontem qui in Dei Filio est, in quem crediturí sunt mortui, & à quo per fidei quasi canalem vita hæc spiritualis deriuanda est. Per comparationem cum Patre factam proponit videndam Filij vitam: Sicut, inquit, Pater habet vitam in seipso, ita, &c. Quod vt intelligamus, nonnulla paulo altius repetenda sunt. Primum igitur videndum nobis est, quid sit vita in genere viuentis cuiusuis, vt Dei beatam illam vitam deinde videamus. Vitam in genere cuiusuis viuentis definio per esse, vt sic dicam, rei viuentis, quo nimirum viuens quodque, est id quod est, quo mouet se ad actiones quascunque, & vitam hominis appello illud esse hominis, quo est homo, & quo talis res est: dum enim viuit homo, & est & dicitur homo. Priuatus autem vita homo, neque est amplius, neque dicitur homo, nisi improprie admodum. Vitam igitur illam Dei beatam, vt de ea quanta possim cum reuerentia nunc dicam aliquid, vitam, inquam, Dei intelligo illud esse Dei, quo est Deus id quod est, quo intelligit, quo vult, quo amat, cæteraque agit omnia. Dicitur autem Deus solus vitam in semetipso habere, hoc est, Dei vita & esse non non est sita in alio, ab alio pendens vel fluens; neque est per participationem vitæ alterius cuiusuis viuentis, vt est vita omnis creaturæ in Deo Creatore suo, nimirum pendens ac fluens à Deo, & per participationem vitæ Dei. Per ipsum, ait Apostolus, viuimus, & mouemur, & sumus. Sed Dei vita &, vt sic loquar, esse, est in ipso Deo. Deus enim per se viuit, & per propriam vitam suam, habet, vt planius dicam, fontem omnis vitæ in se. Non viuit ex riuulis illis qui à fonte manant, vt viuunt omnes creaturæ; sed viuit ex ipso quasi omnis vitæ fonte. Quinquid Dauid, est fons vitæ. Iam verò personæ deitatis omnes, cùm sint vnus idémque Deus, vitam in semetipso habent. Pater habet vitam suam in semetipso, & in se vitæ fontem. Filius habet vitam suam in semetipso, & in se vitæ fontem. Spiritus sanctus vitam in semetipso habet, ac in se vitæ fontem. Neque alia atq; alia est vita personarum trium, sed vna eadémque omnium vita, vnus idémque in omnibus fons vitæ. Sed in hoc est discrimen: Pater habet vitam hanc in semetipso & à semetipso, non ab alio. Filius habet vitā in semetipso quidem, sed non à semetipso, verùm à Patre suo in æterna illa ac ineffabili generatione. Spiritus sanctus habet vitam in semetipso quidem, sed non à semetipso, verùm à Patre & filio in æterna illa processione sui à Patre & filio. His fundamenti loco sic positis, nunc videamus præsentis loci sensum, hunc nimirum, ac si dicat: Sicut Pater habet vitam in semetipso, ita etiam vt habeat eam à seipso: ita filius habet vitam in seipso, eandem nimirum quam Pater habet; sed ita vt filio sit à Patre data & communicata. Nunc deinde videamus vim rationis, qua, vt diximus, persuadet Iudæis, quòd qui crediturí sunt, ii sint victuri; deducit eos ad fontem illum vitæ in filio perennem & indesinenter fluentem, vt conspecto iam, si fieri posset, illo fonte, quem apprehendit fides, facilius credant vitam ex fide proficisci. Nam si semel illud obiectum fidei nostræ cernerent, illud quidem non ita mirum videretur nobis, quòd ex fide sit vita. Obiectum enim fidei nostræ scilicet Christus, non est mortuum quid, sed viuum, neque viuum beneficio viuulorum vitæ, sed beneficio sontis ipsius vitæ. Nunc vero fides pro natura sua attrahit ad se, & ad nos applicat id quod apprehendit. Quid igitur hic miri est, si fides apprehendens infinitum vitæ fontem, bauriat aliquem vitæ riuulum, ex pleno illo fonte, atque eum ad nos applicet?
units.tr: Sicut enim Pater. That those who are about to believe will live is shown by pointing, as it were with a finger, to the very fountain of life, which is in the Son of God, into whom those who are to believe, though dead, are to believe, and from whom this spiritual life is to be drawn through faith as through a channel. By the comparison with the Father he sets before us the life of the Son to be seen: Sicut, he says, Pater habet vitam in seipso, ita, &c. As the Father has life in himself, so, etc. To understand this, some things must be taken up a little higher. First, then, we must consider what life is in general, of any living thing whatever, such as God, and then we shall see that blessed life. I define the life of any living thing in general as the being, so to speak, of the living thing, by which, of course, each living thing is what it is, by which it moves itself to whatever actions; and I call the life of a human being that being of a human, by which he is a human and by which such a thing is what it is: for while a human lives, he both is and is called a human. But a human deprived of life is no longer, and is not called a human, except very improperly. Therefore, that blessed life of God, so that I may say something about it with all the reverence I can, I understand to be that being of God by which God is what he is, by which he understands, by which he wills, by which he loves, and by which he does all other things. It is said that God alone has life in himself, that is, the life and being of God are not situated in another, nor depend on or flow from another; nor are they by participation in the life of any other living thing, as is the life of every creature in God its Creator, namely depending on and flowing from God, and by participation in the life of God. "In him," says the Apostle, "we live, and move, and have our being." But the life of God, and, if I may so speak, his being, is in God himself. For God lives through himself, and through his own life he has, to speak more plainly, the fountain of all life in himself. He does not live from those little streams which flow from the fountain, as all creatures live; but he lives from himself, as it were the fountain of all life. As David says, "With thee is the fountain of life." Now indeed all the persons of the Godhead, since they are one and the same God, have life in themselves. The Father has his life in himself, and in himself the fountain of life. The Son has his life in himself, and in himself the fountain of life. The Holy Spirit has life in himself, and in himself the fountain of life. Nor is the life of the three persons different one from another, but the life of all is one and the same, one and the same fountain of life in all. But herein lies the difference: The Father has this life in himself and from himself, not from another. The Son has life in himself indeed, but not from himself; rather from his Father, in that eternal and ineffable generation. The Holy Spirit has life in himself indeed, but not from himself; rather from the Father and the Son, in that eternal procession of himself from the Father and the Son. With these things laid down as a foundation, let us now consider the sense of the present passage, namely this, as if he said: As the Father has life in himself, so also he has it from himself; so the Son has life in himself, the very same life which the Father has; but in such a way that it is given and communicated to the Son by the Father. Next let us consider the force of the reasoning by which, as we have said, he persuades the Jews that those who are about to believe will live; he leads them to that fountain of life in the Son, perennial and flowing without ceasing, so that, with that fountain now in view, if that were possible, which faith lays hold of, they may more readily believe that life proceeds from faith. For if they once saw that object of our faith, it would not seem so strange to us that life comes from faith. For the object of our faith, namely Christ, is not something dead but living, and living not by the benefit of the life of others but by the benefit of the very fountain of life. But now faith by its nature draws to itself and applies to us that which it apprehends. What, then, is so strange here, if faith, laying hold of the infinite fountain of life, draws some little stream of life from that full fountain and applies it to us?

units.la: Sed vt de hac communicatione vitæ Christi, hoc est fontis vitæ, & vitæ in nos vsque deriuatione facta, aliquid dicamus: Sciendum quidem est primum non ita communicari nobis vitam Filij, vt Filio communicatur vita Patris: Nam dedit Pater Filio vitam in semetipso habere: dedit ei vnum eundemque omnis vitæ fontem, quem in sese habet Pater: At nos participatione duntaxat accipimus vitæ aliquot riuulos: hi autem riuuli defluunt in omnem citra exceptionem viuentem creaturam, omnisque vita à Filio est & ab illo fonte deriuata, siue naturalis sit ea & caduca, siue Spiritualis & æterna. De naturalis vitæ communicatione habes Iohan. 1. 4. In ipso vita erat: En fontem vitæ in ipso Filio; Et vita erat lux illa hominum. Ecce deriuationem illius vitæ in hominies præsertim, vt naturaliter viuunt. Nam illic de communicatione naturalis vitæ loquitur, siue in prima creatione, siue in perpetua & quotidiana hominum ex hominibus generatione. De vita autem spirituali quod ex Filio fit habes Ioh. 5. 11. Vitam æternam dedit nobis Deus, & hæc vita in Filio eius est, hoc est, hæc vita spiritualis & æterna quam per fidem viuimus in Christo Filio recondita, qui ipse fons est vitæ atque authoris.
units.tr: But to say something about this communication of the life of Christ, that is, of the fountain of life, and about the derivation of life down to us: it must first be understood that the life of the Son is not communicated to us in the way that the life of the Father is communicated to the Son. For the Father gave the Son to have life in himself: he gave him the one and the same fountain of all life which the Father has in himself. But we receive by participation only some streams of life, and these streams flow down into every living creature without exception, and all life is from the Son and derived from that fountain, whether it be natural and perishable, or spiritual and eternal. Concerning the communication of natural life you have John 1:4: In him was life: behold the fountain of life in the Son himself. And the life was the light of men. Behold the derivation of that life into human beings, especially as they live naturally. For there he speaks of the communication of natural life, whether in the first creation or in the perpetual and daily generation of human beings from human beings. But concerning the spiritual life that comes from the Son, you have John 5:11: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son, that is, this spiritual and eternal life, which we live through faith, is laid up in Christ the Son, who himself is the fountain and author of life.

units.la: Vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo, inquit Paulus.
units.tr: "Your life is hidden with Christ in God," says Paul.

units.la: Verum sciendum est vitam istam naturalem à Filio Dei esse vt Deus est idem cum Patre creator omnium: Spirituale vero esse à Filio Dei quidem, sed in carne nostra manifestato. Etsi enim omnis vita proprie fluat à Deo, & à Christo proprie, qua Deus est: tamen spiritualis ista non est à Filio Dei, nisi coniuncto & personaliter vnito cum humana natura. Ita enim à Deo ordinatum est ab æterno, vt non nisi virtute hypostaticæ & personalis illius vnionis naturæ diuinæ & humanæ ad nos vsque deriuetur vita ista spiritualis. Siue enim meritum huius vitæ spectes, non meritus est nobis illam Filius, nisi in natura humana, quæ passa est & mortua: siue efficaciam huius vitæ spectes, qua nobis applicatur efficaciter. Non defuit ea in nos nisi per carnem & humanam in Christo naturam prius viuificatam & sanctificatam. Sed age, periculum huius rei faciamus, videamus quonam modo, & qua demum fide in Christum experiamur hanc vitam Christi in nobis efficacem esse, fidene in Christum Deum tantum, an vero etiam in Christum hominem cum Deo vnitum? Quod autem non sentiamus in nobis ipsi vitam illam Christi efficacem, nisi per fidem in Mediatorem, adeoque totum Christum, profecto id argumentor, totum demum Christum Deum & hominem suo quocunque modo efficacem esse in nobis ad vitam hanc quam dicimus spiritualem, eamque per totum Christum nobis communicari.
units.tr: But it must be understood that this natural life is from the Son of God as he is God, the same with the Father, the creator of all things; but the spiritual life is from the Son of God indeed, yet as manifested in our flesh. For although all life properly flows from God, and from Christ properly as he is God, nevertheless this spiritual life is not from the Son of God, except as joined and personally united with human nature. For it has been ordained by God from eternity that this spiritual life should not be derived down to us except by the power of that hypostatic and personal union of the divine and human natures. For whether you look at the merit of this life, the Son did not merit it for us except in the human nature, which suffered and died; or whether you look at the efficacy of this life, by which it is effectively applied to us, it did not reach us except through the flesh and the human nature in Christ, first quickened and sanctified. But come, let us test this matter, and let us see in what manner, and by what faith in Christ, we experience this life of Christ to be efficacious in us: is it faith in Christ as God only, or rather faith in Christ man united with God? But that we do not feel that life of Christ to be efficacious in ourselves, except through faith in the Mediator, and so in the whole Christ, is what I certainly maintain: that in short the whole Christ, God and man, is efficacious in us in whatever manner to this life which we call spiritual, and that this life is communicated to us through the whole Christ.

units.la: Hactenus digressus est aliquantulum ad hoc, vt, si quo modo fieri posset, alliceret Iudaeos ad credendum in Filium, ipsumque honorandum: Nunc redit ad iudicium illud Filio datum & communicatum, de quo supra vers.22. Iudicium hoc Filio communicatum perpetuum est ac non interruptum iam inde a creatione mundi, & duraturum ad rerum vsque omnium consummationem. Toto enim hoc temporis interuallo quod medium est inter creationem & consummationem rerum, viuificat tam naturaliter quam spiritualiter omnia viuentia. Verum in extremo illo die maxime gloriosum conspicietur hoc iudicium Filio datum, cum alios vitae, alios morti aeternae cum summa maiestate adiudicaturus est. Hactenus igitur de iudicio in genere vniuerso dictum, nunc de iudicio in specie, illo nimirum quod futurum est in extremo die, vtpote gloriosissimo agitur, de quo sic loquitur,
units.tr: Thus far he has digressed a little, so that, if it could be done in any way, he might draw the Jews to believe in the Son and to honour him. Now he returns to the judgement given and communicated to the Son, which was mentioned above at verse 22. This judgement communicated to the Son is perpetual and uninterrupted from the creation of the world, and it will last until the consummation of all things. For throughout the whole span of time between the creation and the consummation of things, he quickens all living things, both naturally and spiritually. But on that final day this judgement given to the Son will be seen in its most glorious form, when with supreme majesty he will adjudge some to life and others to eternal death. So far, then, judgement has been spoken of in general. Now we come to judgement in particular, namely that which is to take place on the last day, the most glorious of all, and of this he speaks thus:

units.la: 27 Et authoritatem ei dedit etiam iudicium exercendi, quatenus filius hominis est.
units.tr: 27 And he gave him authority also to execute judgement, inasmuch as he is the Son of man.

units.la: 28 Ne hoc miramini: nam veniet hora qua omnes qui sunt in monumentis, audient vocem eius.
units.tr: 28 Do not marvel at this, for the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice,

units.la: 29 Et prodibunt, qui bona fecerint, in resurrectionem vitae: qui vero male egerint, in resurrectionem condemnationis.
units.tr: "And they shall come forth, those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of condemnation."

units.la: ET authoritatem ei dedit etiam iudicium exercendi, quate- nus filius hominis est, hoc est, illud iudicium vltimum, quod exercebit filius, non tantum quatenus est Dei fi- lius, sed etiam quatenus est filius hominis & indutus humana illa natura. Deus est, fateor, & filius Dei pro- prie, qui iudicium illud exercebit. Nam qui creauit o- mnia, is proprie est iudex omnium. Atque haec est ma- xima Dei ipsius gloria quam obtinet in creaturis suis iudicandis & adiudicandis vel vitae vel morti aeternae. Veruntamen hanc ipsam gloriam λόγῳ Dei Filius suo quodammodo communicauit cum massa illa humanae naturae sibi personaliter vnitae, non tamen in eum modum quo Pater eam gloriam filio suo communicauit.
units.tr: And he gave him authority also to execute judgment, inasmuch as he is the Son of man. That is, the final judgment, which the Son will execute not only as he is the Son of God, but also as he is the Son of man and clothed in that human nature. It is God, I acknowledge, and the Son of God properly, who will execute that judgment. For he who created all things is properly the judge of all. And this is the greatest glory of God himself, which he obtains in judging and adjudging his creatures to either eternal life or eternal death. Nevertheless, the Word of God [λόγῳ], the Son, has in some way communicated this same glory to that mass of human nature joined to himself personally, yet not in the same manner in which the Father communicated that glory to his Son.

units.la: Nam Pater vniuersum simul ac semel iudicium dedit filio, vt dictum est, & equalem plane ac eandem gloriam: filius autem Dei eius quasi partem duntaxat aliquam communicauit cum humana natura, in qua inhabitat ipsa corporaliter: tantam nimirum gloriam, quanta capax est creatura. Nam nulla creatura, ne Christus quidem ipse, qua homo est, capax est infinitae illius & essentialis Dei gloriae: verum eam accepit gloriae parte humana illa Christi natura, quae infinitis partibus superat omnem omnium aliarum creaturarum gloriam: Extulit enim Deus etiam Christum hominem in summam sublimitatem, ac donauit ei nomen quod est supra omne nomen, vt ad nomen Iesu omne genu se flectat caelestium ac terrestrium & subterraneorum. Atqui haec est summa consolatio nostra, quod ita glorificata & angelis etiam ipsis praelatam habemus naturam istam nostram in Christo seruatore nostro. Sed est praeterea hic quod nos consoletur, quod si insiti illi fuerimus per fidem in ipsum, etiam gloriae ipsius participes sicmus, cuius quidem arrhabone etiam nunc accipimus. Quid enim aliud est sanctificatio ista nostra inchoata in hac vita quam initium illius glorificationis quae futura est in aduentu illo Christi glorioso? Videant igitur omnes quantum referat, vt fidem in Christum habeamus.
units.tr: For the Father gave the whole judgment to the Son at once, as has been said, and plainly the same glory, equal to his own. But the Son of God communicated to the human nature, in which he dwells bodily, only some part of it: namely, as much glory as a creature is capable of. For no creature, not even Christ himself as he is man, is capable of that infinite and essential glory of God. Yet that human nature of Christ received glory in its human part, a glory which surpasses by infinite degrees the glory of all other creatures. For God also exalted Christ the man to the highest sublimity and gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth. This is our greatest consolation: that we have this our nature so glorified in Christ our Saviour, and set above even the angels themselves. Yet there is also this further consolation for us: if we have been grafted into him through faith, we shall also be partakers of his glory, of which we even now receive the earnest. For what else is this sanctification of ours, begun in this life, than the beginning of that glorification which is to come at Christ's glorious coming? Let all men therefore see how much it matters that we have faith in Christ.

units.la: Sic iam propositio futuro illo iudicio quod exercebit Christus, etiam quatenus filius hominis, mirari potuerunt Iudaei, vt & re vera mirati sunt, quod tam in speciem ciem vilis & abiectus homuncio exercituus esset tantum tamque gloriosum iudicium. Huic igitur stupori & admirationi eorum occurrit Christus. Ne hoc mirami, inquit. Mirati quidem sunt illi cum audirent Christum hoc de se pronunciantem hoc tempore, sed multo magis miraturi sunt tum cum videbunt eum venturum Iudicem eo die viuorum & mortuorum. Miratur mundus dum audit nunc aliquid de futura illa Ecclesiae gloria. Sed tum cum videbit mundus liberatam glorificatam Ecclesiam eam, quam nunc persequitur, quanta erit admiratio tam insignis mutationis? Beatos illos qui possunt per patientiam expectare revelationem illius futurae gloriae, & ferre temporariam hanc huius vitae ignominiam & contemptum. Occurrens itaque Christus huic admirationi & stupori eorum, rationem huius futuri Iudicij aperte & breuiter exponit. In qua etiam exponenda fusius nobis erit immorandum, sed ita, vt nihil de ea dicamus, nisi quod verba contextus huius nobis suppeditant. In quibus quidem explicandis, necesse erit in totum fere futuri iudicij formam excurrere. Nam venit hora, inquit. De die illo, ait Christus, & hora nemo scit, ne Angeli quidem caelorum, sed Pater meus solus. Quare in diem illum non erit nobis curiosius inquirendum, quem Deus voluit nos latere, in vtilitatem proculdubio suorum, & in gloria nominis sui.
units.tr: Yet we are persuaded of this: that hour will be at hand soon, and will come more quickly than the world hopes. "The hour comes," he says, "in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice." By this voice I understand not that voice of promises which we mentioned before, by which it comes about that the dead believe and live in this very life, but another and more terrible voice, which will be heard by all, the living as well as the dead, on that day. By Christ it is called the great voice of the trumpet; by the Apostle, the last trumpet [σάλπιγξ], as it were a cry of exhortation, such as is usually the voice of sailors, by which they draw their oars together in one concerted effort; the voice of the archangel; the trumpet of God. It appears, however, that this voice will not be that of Christ the judge himself, but will be administered by Christ through the angels, for he will send his angels with the voice of a great trumpet. This voice will be heard at the very moment of Christ's coming. For Christ will not rise from the throne of his majesty and descend to judgement any sooner than this voice is sounded. For the Lord himself, with a shout, with the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven, says the Apostle. Therefore, in the second place, something must now be said about that coming in which this voice will be. And first, the Lord is to come from the highest heaven, where he now sits at the right hand of the Father. The manner of his coming will be sudden and unexpected. The clouds and the air will be his chariot. All the angels, not one excepted, will be his companions, and from their multitude, power and glory Christ's coming will be with majesty and glory, though the judge himself will be more glorious than all. On this see Matthew 24:30; 1 Thessalonians 4:16; 2 Thessalonians 1:7; Revelation 1:7. Compare these passages with one another, and you will discover each of these circumstances. Concerning this voice to be heard at the coming of the judge, what should we be reminded of, except that we should imagine ourselves always hearing it, and that we are summoned by it to that great judgement, so that the very thought alone may rouse us from this lethargy and from the body, in which almost all of us, secure about God and that future judgement, have been lulled to sleep; and that by this same thought we may become accustomed to that voice, as if we had heard it before we actually hear it in its time? For it cannot be said how terrible it will be to those who have never thought of it during their lives. Now about those who are to hear that voice: "All who are in the tombs," he says, "will hear his voice." That voice must be very effective, since even dust and ashes will be compelled to hear it. But this efficacy belongs to the Son of God himself, the future judge, who by his own hidden power will quicken and raise the dead. For with the voice of God there is always joined the wonderful power of God, which is effective in those in whom it wills to be effective. Concerning that efficacy of Christ which will be present in that judgement, let us say a few things. That powerful judge will be effective not only at the time when he descends from heaven with that great voice of the trumpet, but even immediately before his coming the wonderful efficacy of the judge will show itself in all creatures. The whole machinery of the world will then for the first time tremble, the heavens will be shaken; the Sun and Lu-

units.la: Tamen hoc nos persuasum habemus, breui affuturam illam horam & citius venturam quam speret mundus. Venit hora, inquit, qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt audient vocem eius. Vocem hanc intelligo non eam, quam prius diximus vocem promissionum, qua fit vt credant & viuant mortui in hac ipsa vita; sed aliam quandam eamque magis terribilem vocem accipio hoc loco, quae audietur ab omnibus tam viuis quam mortuis in illo die. A Christo vocatur tubae vox magna. Ab Apostolo, vltimatuba: σάλπιγξ, quasi dicas hortationis clamorem, qualis solet esse vox nautarum, qua vno veluti concentu remos adducunt: vox Archangeli: Tuba Dei. Apparet autem vocem hanc non ipsius Christi iudicis fore, verum a Christo per Angelos administratam: mittet enim Angelos suos cum voce magnae tubae. Audietur autem hæc vox in ipso puncto aduentus Christi. Non enim citius surget Christus è throno maiestatis suæ, descendetque ad iudicium, quàm edatur hæc vox. Nam ipse Dominus cum celeusmate, cum voce Archangeli & tuba Dei, descendet è cœlo, inquit Apostolus. Quare secundo iam loco de aduentu illo, in quo futura est illa vox, nonnihil erit dicendum. Ac primum venturus est Dominus è cœlo supremo, vbi nunc sedet ad dexteram Patris. Modus aduentus eius futurus est subitus ac repentinus. Pro rheda futuræ sunt illi cœli nubes & aër. Comites aduectus futuri sunt omnes Angeli, ne vno quidem excepto, ex quorum multitudine, potentia & gloria, aduentus Christi futurus est cum maiestate & gloria. Quanquam ipse iudex futurus est omnibus gloriosior. De his vide Matth. 24. 30. 1. Thess. 4. 16. 2. Thess. 1. 7. Apoc. 1. 7. Confer inter se loca illa, & singulas has circumstantias deprehendes. De voce hac in aduentu iudicis futura, quid est quod admoneamus, nisi vt videamur nobis ipsi eam perpetuò audire, eáque nos ad iudicium illud magnum citari, vt vel sola cogitatio excitet nos ex hoc veterno & corpore, quo securi Dei & futuri illius iudicij fere omnes consopiti sumus, & eadem hac cogitatione assuefiamus, quasi voci illi prius quam eam reipsa suo tempore audiuerimus. Nam dici non potest quàm terribilis futura sit iis, qui de ea nunquam in vita cogitârunt. Nunc de iis qui vocem illa audituri sunt. Qui in monumentis sunt, inquit, vocem eius audient. Oportet eam vocem admodum efficacem esse, quam cogetur audire etiam pulvis & cinis, sed efficacia est ista ipsius Filij Dei iudicis futuri, qui secreta sua potentia viuificaturus est & excitaturus mortuos. Cum voce enim Dei semper est coniuncta potentia Dei admirabilis, quæ efficax est in iis, in quibus vult eam efficacem esse. De efficacitate igitur illa Christi quæ futura est in illo iudicio, pauca quædam dicamus. Non eo tantum tempore futurus est efficax iudex ille quo descendet è cœlo, cum voce illa tubæ magna; verumetiam immediatè ante aduentū suum exercet sese iudicis efficacia in omnibus creaturis admirabilis: Tota mundi tum primum machina intremiscet, cœlorū concutientur; Sol & Lu-
units.tr: Yet we are persuaded that that hour is at hand, and will come sooner than the world expects. "The hour is coming," he says, "in which all who are in the tombs shall hear his voice." I understand this voice not as the voice of promises which we mentioned before, by which it comes about that the dead believe and live in this very life; but I take it here as another and more terrible voice, which will be heard by all, both living and dead, on that day. It is called by Christ "the great voice of the trumpet"; by the Apostle, "the last trumpet" [σάλπιγξ], as if you were to say the shout of exhortation, such as the voice of sailors usually is, when they pull their oars together in one harmonious chorus; "the voice of the archangel," "the trumpet of God." It appears, however, that this voice will not be that of Christ the judge himself, but will be conveyed by the angels on Christ's behalf: for he will send his angels with the voice of a great trumpet. This voice will be heard at the very moment of Christ's coming. For Christ will not rise from the throne of his majesty and descend to judgment any sooner than this voice is sounded. For the Lord himself, with a shout of command [κέλευσμα], with the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven, says the Apostle. Wherefore, in the second place, something must now be said about that coming, in which that voice is to be heard. First, the Lord is to come from the highest heaven, where he now sits at the right hand of the Father. The manner of his coming will be sudden and unexpected. The clouds and the air of heaven will serve as his chariot. All the angels, not one excepted, will accompany his conveyance, and from their multitude, power and glory Christ's coming will be with majesty and glory. Yet the judge himself will be more glorious than all. On these matters see Matt. 24:30; 1 Thess. 4:16; 2 Thess. 1:7; Rev. 1:7. Compare those passages with one another, and you will discern each of these circumstances. What else should we be reminded of concerning this voice to be heard at the coming of the judge, than that we should imagine ourselves always hearing it, and that we are summoned by it to that great judgment, so that the very thought alone may rouse us from this drowsiness and this body, in which almost all of us lie lulled asleep, careless of God and of that future judgment; and that we should accustom ourselves by this same thought, as if to that voice, before we actually hear it in its appointed time. For it cannot be said how terrible it will be to those who never thought of it in their lifetime. Now let us speak of those who are about to hear that voice. "Those who are in the tombs," he says, "shall hear his voice." That voice must be exceedingly effective, since even dust and ashes will be compelled to hear it; but this efficacy belongs to the Son of God himself, the judge to come, who by his own power will quicken and raise the dead. For the wonderful power of God is always joined with the voice of God, and it is effective in those in whom he wills it to be effective. Let us therefore say a few things about that efficacy of Christ which will be exercised in that judgment. He will be an effective judge not only at the time when he descends from heaven with that great voice of the trumpet; but even immediately before his coming the wonderful efficacy of the judge will be exercised upon all creatures. Then for the first time the whole machinery of the world will tremble, and the heavens will be shaken; the sun and the moon...

units.la: 1. Thes. 4. 16 & Luna, maiora illa luminaria obscurabuntur, itaut lucem non sint editura; stellae inferiores & minora lumina cadent e coelo, vel ob lucis defectum cadere videbuntur. Efficax etiam erit Iudex paulo ante adventum suum in hominibus ipsis, qui tum in viuis reperientur: Nam reprobis horrores conscientiae, quae paulo ante consolpita erat, incutiet, & ira examinabit metu & expectatione illius iudicij paulo post futuri, ut discurruri sint miseri & passim latibula quaesituri, in quibus ab ira agni abscondantur. In electis vero erit efficax Iudex ad bonam conscientiam & laetitiam, vt cum summa laetitia redemptionem plenam aduentantem expectantes capita attollant & erigant. Zacharias prophetiae suae cap. 13. verf. 11. 12. 13. vt & Iohannes in Apocal. cap. 1. 7. videntur innuere Iudicem tum etiam in electis suis efficacem fore ad dolorem & resipiscentiam, qua attacti amare super mortem eius (quam peccatis suis procurarunt) tanquam planctu pro vnigenito, plangent. Haec omnia erunt certissima signa aduentantis iudicis; de quibus omnibus potes legere Matth. 24. 29. 30. Marc. 13. 4. Luc. 21. 26. 27. 28. 1. Thes. 5. 3. 4. Apocal. 6. 16. 17. 18. Quid autem de hac Christi Iudicis efficacia, quae futura est proximè ante ipsius aduentum, dicere & admonere possumus, nisi vt tepestiue incipiamus sentire conscientiae horrores, dum tempus est gratiae, qua vulnerata conscientia sanari potest suauissimis illis de quibus diximus Christi promissionibus? Nam si secundum hoc differamus in Christi aduentu, & non nisi tum incipiamus sentire illos conscientiae horrores, nulla profecto vel vocula promissionis dabitur audire, qua leniatur dolor ille conscientiae: Tu enim nullae futurae sunt omnino promissiones gratiae: verum haec erit illa prima quae tu audietur vox terroris plena; Abite a me exe- trabiles in ignem aeternum, qui paratus est diabolo & angelis eius.
units.tr: 1. Thes. 4. 16 The sun and the moon, those greater lights, will be darkened so that they will not give light; the lesser stars and lower lights will fall from heaven, or will seem to fall because their light has failed. The Judge will also be effective among men themselves, even before his coming, among those who are found alive at that time. For he will strike terror into the reprobate, troubling the conscience that had been at ease shortly before, and his wrath will test them with fear and with expectation of that judgment which is soon to come, so that the wretched will run about and seek hiding places everywhere, where they may be hidden from the wrath of the Lamb. But the Judge will be effective among the elect to produce a good conscience and joy, so that, in great gladness, they lift up and raise their heads as they wait for the full redemption that is approaching. Zechariah in his prophecy, chapter 13, verses 11, 12 and 13, and John in the Apocalypse, chapter 1, verse 7, seem to indicate that the Judge will then also be effective in his elect to produce sorrow and repentance, so that, struck by grief over his death (which they brought about by their sins), they will mourn for him as one mourns for an only son. All these things will be most certain signs of the approaching Judge, and you may read about all of them in Matt. 24. 29, 30; Mark 13. 24; Luke 21. 26, 27, 28; 1 Thess. 5. 3, 4; Apoc. 6. 16, 17, 18. But what can we say or urge concerning this efficacy of Christ the Judge, which will come just before his coming, except that we should begin to feel the terrors of conscience in good time, while there is still the time of grace, in which a wounded conscience can be healed by those most sweet promises of Christ of which we have spoken? For if we postpone this until Christ's coming, and do not begin to feel those terrors of conscience until then, surely not even a single word of promise will be heard by which that anguish of conscience may be eased. For then there will be no promises of grace at all; rather, this will be the first voice, full of terror: "Depart from me, you accursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels."

units.la: Nunc videamus quanta sit futura Iudicis & vocis ipsius in ipso aduentu suo efficacia, eaeque in omnibus creaturis, quum primum, inquam, incipiet se commouere & descendere ad iudicium. In descendendo quidem vox illa terribilis audietur a toto mundo, & maior erit tunc vinentis iudicis efficacia, quam fuit ea quae proximè antecessit ipsius aduentum, de qua modo diximus.
units.tr: Now let us consider how great the efficacy of the Judge and of his voice will be at his coming itself, and this among all creatures, when, I say, he first begins to stir himself and descend to judgment. As he descends, that terrible voice will be heard by the whole world, and the efficacy of the living Judge then will be greater than that which immediately preceded his coming, of which we have just spoken.

units.la: Tum quidem terribilis per ignem flammantem totius mundi erit dissolutio; ita vt donec renouetur non appareat, quæ signum Christi dicitur. Tum cœlorum erit dissolutio, qua conflagrantes ποιέω, id est, tanquam rotularū stridore præteribunt: Inferiorum denique erit dissolutio, qua & elementa omnia æstuantia & terra cum operibus quæ in ea sunt exusta dissoluentur. De his omnibus vide Matth.24.3.2. Thess.1.8.2. Petr.3.7.12.13. Apocal. 20.12.&21.1. Quòd vero ad homines attinet, quàm efficax futurus fit aduentus iudicis in iis, siue tum viui, siue mortui reperientur, promptum est dicere; Nemo enim omnium eam iudicis efficaciam effugiet. Nam quòd ad eos, qui tum viui deprehenduntur ἐν ἀτόμῳ, ἐν ῥίπῃ ὀφθαλμοῦ, momento & iactu oculi mutabuntur: Electi quidem exignominia in gloriam ac immortalitatem: Reprobi vero in immortalitatem quidem, sed morte ipsa peiorem, & cum antea fuerint ignominiosi, iam multò magis quàm antea ignominiosi reddentur. Quòd ad eos qui tunc temporis in monumentis inuenientur, si quidem omnes efficacia iudicis resurgent; Electi quidē ad gloriam; Reprobi vero ad ignominiam. Quòd ad ignominiam istam reproborum, in quam vel mutabuntur viui, vel resurgent mortui, de ea non legimus ita multa in Scripturis Dei; de gloria vero Electorum & corporum ipsorum futura, plura extant in scriptis, de qua sic paucis concionatur Paulus: Seminatur corpus corruptioni obnoxium, excitatur incorruptum; Seminatur ignominiosum, excitatur gloriosum: Seminatur infirmum, excitatur potens. Tum simul ac semel comprehendens illam corporum nostrorum futuram gloriam, seminatur corpus animale, hoc est, vitam; &, vt sic dicam, esse suum habens ab anima ista ipsiusque facultatibus naturalibus; excitatur corpus spirituale, hoc est, vitam & esse suum non tam habens ab anima ista, eiusque facultatibus naturalibus. (Quanquam etiam tum eadem hæc anima nostra coniungetur cum eodem ipso corpore nostro, & per eam etiam tum viuemus) tamen corpus quod excitabitur nō tam habebit vitam & esse suum ab ea, quàm à spiritu illo Christi, qui ita, vt sic loquar, animabit & animam istam & corpus istud, vt totus homo gloriosus instar ipsius Christi cõspiciendus sit: Vt enim anima ista dum exercet functiones suas in corpore, impertit ei colorem & totam hanc externam corporis gloriam: ita tum cum Deus erit omnia in omnibus, Spiritus Christi in nobis habitans, inducet corpora nostra gloriosissima, quibusque qualitatibus.
units.tr: Then indeed there will be a terrible dissolution of the whole world by a flaming fire, so that it will not appear until it is renewed; this is called the sign of Christ. Then there will be a dissolution of the heavens, by which they will pass away burning, with a rushing sound, as with the grinding of wheels [ῥοιζηδόν]. Finally, there will be a dissolution of the lower regions, by which all the seething elements and the earth, with the works that are in it, will be burned up and dissolved. See all these things in Matt. 24. 35; 2 Thess. 1. 8; 2 Pet. 3. 7, 12, 13; Apoc. 20. 12 and 21. 1. But as far as men are concerned, it is easy to say how effective the coming of the Judge will be upon them, whether they are found alive or dead at that time; for none of all men will escape that efficacy of the Judge. For those who are found alive at that time, in an atom, in the twinkling of an eye [ἐν ἀτόμῳ, ἐν ῥίπῃ ὀφθαλμοῦ], in a moment and in the blink of an eye, will be changed: the elect indeed from dishonour into glory and immortality; but the reprobate into immortality, yet an immortality worse than death itself, and, since they were dishonoured before, they will then be made far more dishonoured than before. As for those who are found in the tombs at that time, all will certainly rise by the efficacy of the Judge: the elect to glory, but the reprobate to dishonour. As for that dishonour of the reprobate, into which the living will be changed or the dead will rise, we do not read so much about it in the Scriptures of God; but there is more in writing about the future glory of the elect and of their bodies, of which Paul preaches briefly in this way: It is sown a corruptible body, it is raised an incorruptible; it is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power. Then, once he has at one point comprehended the future glory of our bodies, it is sown a natural body, that is, a body having its life and being, so to speak, from this soul and its natural faculties; it is raised a spiritual body, that is, a body having its life and being not so much from this soul and its natural faculties. (Although even then this same soul of ours will be joined with the same body of ours, and through it we shall even then live.) Nevertheless, the body that is raised will not have its life and being so much from the soul as from that Spirit of Christ, who will, so to speak, animate both this soul and this body, so that the whole man is to be seen as glorious, like Christ himself. For just as the soul, while it exercises its functions in the body, imparts to it colour and all this outward glory of the body, so then, when God will be all in all, the Spirit of Christ dwelling in us will bring forth our most glorious bodies, with whatever qualities.

units.la: Hactenus de efficacia Christi Iudicis & ea quae immediatè adventum ipsius antecedet, & ea quae cum adventu ipsius erit coniuncta. Nunc superest una quaestio dissoluenda, atque ita transimus ad alia. Quaestio est de efficacia Christi in excitandis mortuis, utrum una eademque Christi efficacia ac potentia utrique excitandi sunt & electi & reprobi? Respondeo una eademque Dei potentia utrosque excitandos: Nam hoc est effectum solius divinae potentiae viuificare mortuos, & vocare quae non sunt tanquam sint. Verum in hoc est discrimen, quod Electi praeterquam quod potentia Christi Iudicis excitandi sunt, etiam virtute resurrectionis Christi resurgent. Illa enim Dei potentia in electis excitandis exeret se per mediam Christi resurrectionem ex mortuis. Reprobi vero potentia duntaxat & efficacia Christi Iudicis resurgent, idque inviti. Nam in reprobis suscitandis efficax quidem futurus est Deus per Christum, sed non ut seruatorem, sed ut mundi iudicem. Causa autem cur electi excitandi sunt per medium quasi resurrectionis Christi, haec est, Quia Electi crediderunt in Christum eique per fidem insiti sunt: Credentibus autem iis & Christo insitis per fidem, necesse iam est iidem effectus quodammodo in iis edantur per dietatē illam in Christo inhabitante, qui in ipso Christo capite iam sunt editi. Resurrexit Christus, resurgent & illi quoque, idque necessitate, nempe propter illam insitionem in Christo factam, quo respexit Paulus, cum dixit; Quod si Christus praedicatur ex mortuis suscitatus esse, quomodo dicunt quidam inter vos, non esse resurrectionem mortuorum? De hac insitione eiusque effectu necessario, hoc est, resurrectione nostra, semel & simul legi. Thess. 4.14. Vbi habes haec verba; Nam si credimus Iesum mortuum esse & resurrexisse (haec est illa quā diximus insitio per fidem) ita etiam Deus eos qui obdormierunt mierunt in Iesu, adducet cum eo. hic est ille effectus quem diximus, resurrectio nostra quæ futura est vnà cū Christo. Atque hæc quidem resurrectio, quæ futura est cum Christo, & vi resurrectionis Christi, sola suauis & intima futura est: cùm illa altera reproborum, quæ erit per potentiam Christi Iudicis solùm absque virtute resurrectionis Christi seruatoris, inuita ac violenta admodum sit futura: cuperent enim suo quodam modo corpora reprobo rum in æternum sine sensuali quo lætitiæ pariter & doloris in illis sepulchris suis conquiescere, potiùs quàm resurgere ad tormenta & æternos cruciatus.
units.tr: So far concerning the efficacy of Christ the Judge, both that which immediately precedes his coming, and that which will be joined with his coming. Now there remains one question to be resolved, and then we shall pass on to other matters. The question is about the efficacy of Christ in raising the dead: whether one and the same efficacy and power of Christ is to raise both the elect and the reprobate? I answer that one and the same power of God raises both; for it is the work of divine power alone to quicken the dead and to call those things which are not as though they were. But there is this difference: the elect are raised not only by the power of Christ the Judge, but they will also rise by the virtue of Christ's resurrection. For that divine power in raising the elect will show itself through the mediation of Christ's resurrection from the dead. But the reprobate will rise only by the power and efficacy of Christ the Judge, and that against their will. For in raising the reprobate God will indeed be effective through Christ, but not as Saviour, rather as Judge of the world. The reason why the elect are raised through the mediation, as it were, of Christ's resurrection is this: because the elect have believed in Christ and have been engrafted into him through faith. Now, since they believe and are engrafted into Christ through faith, it is necessary that the same effects be produced in them in some way, by that power dwelling in Christ, which have already been produced in Christ himself as the Head. Christ has risen, and they too will rise, and this by necessity, namely because of that engrafting made in Christ, to which Paul looked when he said: "But if Christ is preached as raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?" Of this engrafting and its necessary effect, that is, our resurrection, we have read once and for all in 1 Thess. 4. 14. There you have these words: "For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again (this is that engrafting through faith which we have spoken of), so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus." This is that effect which we spoke of: our resurrection, which is to come together with Christ. And indeed this resurrection, which is to come with Christ and by the virtue of Christ's resurrection, will be altogether sweet and intimate; whereas that other resurrection of the reprobate, which will be by the power of Christ the Judge alone and without the virtue of the resurrection of Christ the Saviour, will be most unwilling and violent. For they would in a certain way wish their bodies to rest for ever in those tombs, without sensual feeling of either joy or sorrow, rather than rise to torments and eternal sufferings.

units.la: Et prodibunt. Hoc loco habemus opera & mercedem operum, qui locus requirit vt paucis comprehendamus totam illam futuri iudicij formam. Congregatis iam omnibus, & efficacia præsentiæ Christi in vnum coactis ex omnibus terræ plagis, Christus Iudex sedens in throno gloriæ suæ, ministerio Angelorum suorum, separationem quandam faciet, segregabitque agnos ab hoedis, bonos à malis, electos à reprobis. In eaque quam faciet separatione, Electos ad dexteram, Reprobos ad lævam statuet: hæc enim est scripturæ in hac separatione exponeda phrasis. vide Matth. 25. 33. Paulus 1. Thes. 4. 17. huc separationis illius modum videtur innuere; Coactis iam in vnum omnibus simúlque in terra consistentibus, electi omnes rapientur in nubes, in occursum Domini in aëra, adhuc vt reprobos, vt Christi Iudicis administri & assessores sententiam eius probantes & laudantes, iudicent: 1. Cor. 6. 2. 3. Reprobi verò non rapientur in occursum Domini, sed subsistent inferius in terra, in qua terribilem illam mortis æternæ sententiam latam audient ex aëre & nubibus. Sed in ista non statuimus curiosius aut subtilius inquirere. Separatione hac facta, tum aperientur libri, quos operum libros vocare possumus, quia nihil sunt quàm opera omnium: ex quibus producitis in medium, & apertis atque manifestatis, iudicii est faciendum & ius dicendum cuique. Apoc. 20. 12. Præter hos libros etiā alius liber aperietur, qui liber vitæ appellatur. Apoc. ibid. Liber vitæ nihil est aliud quàm decretū illud Dei de æterna salute. His libris iam apertis Iudex ius dicet, sententiam feret tam de electis, quàm de reprobis. Præcipuè quidem ac proprie iudicabit secundum librum vitæ, quorum nomina inueniet in libro vitæ scripta, eos omnes vitæ æternæ adiudicabit: quorum verò nomina non inuenient scripta in libro vitæ, eos morti æternæ omnes adiudicabit. Iam verò quia per opera tanquam decreti Electionis & Reprobationis effecta manifestum erit ac patebit mundo quinam sint ij, qui in libro illo vitæ scripti sunt, & quinam sint qui in eo non sunt scripti, qui electi, qui reprobi sunt inde ab æterno: ideo scriptura habet iudicium illud futurum secundum libros operum, & opera nominatim ex quibus constabit de prima illa causa vitæ & mortis, nempe decreto Dei æterno, cùm tamen proprie ac præcipuè iudicium futurum sit secundum illud ipsum Dei decretum, quod quidem sententiæ Dei præcipuum erit fundamentum. Ideóque Iohannes ait non introituros in nouam Hierusalē, nisi qui scripti inuenientur in libro vitæ Agni; cùm tamen in Apocalypsi dictum sit prius, Dominum secundum opera ipsorum iudicaturum mortuos. Iudicio in hunc modum fa-cto, sequetur sententia: Ac primùm quidè sententia pronuntiabitur de Electis, vt est Matth. 25. 34. Venite benedicti Patris mei, & possidete hereditario iure regnum paratum vobis à iactu mundi fundamentis. Merces igitur quę adiudicabitur Electis erit regnum. De mercede ista & gloria electorum futura, vt dicam ex scripturis nonnihil, primùm consistet ca in κοινωνία illa & communione cum Deo, quæ in eo erit posita quòd Deus habitabit nobiscum, & tabernaculum eius erit cum hominibus. Imò verò in eo quòd habitabit in nobis, ita vt habitans in nobis & nos intuentes eius faciem & gloriam, futurus sit nobis per Christum hominem, templum, lux, vita, omnia deni-que in omnibus. 1. Corinth. 15. 28. Apoc. 21. 22. 23. & 22. 5. Existente iam beata hac κοινωνία, cùm quidè liberabimur ab omni miseria & infirmitate: Deus, inquit, absterget omnem lachrymam ab oculis eorum, & mors amplius non extabit, neque luctus, neque clamor, neque dolor extabit amplius. Loco autem præteritæ omnis miseriæ, succedet omnis felicitas, beata constitutio animæ, beata constitutio corporis, beata constitutio rerum quarumcunque externa-
units.tr: And they shall come forth. Here we have the works and the reward of works, and this passage requires us to set out briefly the whole form of the future judgment. When all have now been gathered together, and brought into one place by the power of Christ's presence from every corner of the earth, Christ the Judge, sitting on the throne of his glory, will by the ministry of his angels make a certain separation, and will separate the sheep from the goats, the good from the evil, the elect from the reprobate. In this separation he will set the elect on the right hand and the reprobate on the left, for this is the phrase of Scripture for describing such a separation; see Matt. 25:33. Paul in 1 Thess. 4:17 seems to hint at the manner of that separation: when all are gathered into one and standing together on the earth, the elect will be caught up in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air, so that they may judge the reprobate, as the ministers and assessors of the Judge, approving and praising his sentence; see 1 Cor. 6:2-3. But the reprobate will not be caught up to meet the Lord; they will remain below on the earth, where they will hear that dreadful sentence of eternal death pronounced from the air and the clouds. We do not, however, intend to inquire into these matters too curiously or subtly. When this separation has been made, then the books will be opened, which we may call the books of works, since they are nothing but the works of all men. These being brought forth and opened and made manifest, judgment will be made and right pronounced to each one; Rev. 20:12. Besides these books, another book will also be opened, which is called the book of life; Rev. ibid. The book of life is nothing other than that decree of God concerning eternal salvation. With these books now opened, the Judge will pronounce right and give sentence concerning the elect and the reprobate alike. He will indeed judge chiefly and properly according to the book of life: those whose names he finds written in the book of life he will adjudge all to eternal life, and those whose names are not found written in the book of life he will adjudge all to eternal death. But because, through works as the effects of the decree of election and reprobation, it will be manifest and plain to the world who are those written in that book of life, and who are those not written in it, who are elect and who are reprobate from eternity, therefore Scripture speaks of that future judgment according to the books of works, and names the works from which the first cause of life and death, namely the eternal decree of God, will be made clear; whereas properly and chiefly the future judgment will be according to that very decree of God, which will indeed be the principal foundation of the sentence of God. Therefore John says that only those found written in the book of the Lamb will enter the new Jerusalem; yet in the Apocalypse it has been said earlier that the Lord will judge the dead according to their works. Once judgment has been made in this way, sentence will follow. And first of all sentence will be pronounced on the elect, as in Matt. 25:34: Come, blessed of my Father, and possess by hereditary right the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. The reward, therefore, which will be adjudged to the elect will be the kingdom. Concerning this reward and the future glory of the elect, I will say something from the Scriptures: it will consist first in that fellowship and communion with God, which is placed in this, that God will dwell with us and his tabernacle will be with men. Indeed, it lies in this, that he will dwell in us, so that dwelling in us and beholding his face and glory, he will be to us through Christ, as man, temple, light, life, and in short all in all; 1 Cor. 15:28; Rev. 21:22-23 and 22:5. This blessed fellowship being now in existence, we shall indeed be freed from all misery and infirmity: God, it says, will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death will be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain will be any more. In place of all past misery, however, will come all happiness: a blessed condition of soul, a blessed condition of body, and a blessed condition of all external things,

units.la: Cur secundum opera electi & reprobi iudicabuntur. rum, in quibus felicitatem collocare solent homines. Nam quòd ad animam & corpus & personas nostras, participes simus gloriæ ipsius Dei, qua erimus vt ipse Christus, etsi inæqualiter animo & corpore supra modum gloriosi: 1.Corinth.15.44.Philip.3.21. Quod ad externa attinet, obtinebimus hæreditatem incorruptibilem, incontaminatam, immarcescibilem; terram & cœlum per ignes, & per purgationem renovata, & omnia denique hæreditario possidebimus; terram, inquam, & cœlû, non qualia nunc ea videmus, sed glorificata. Nam res creatæ exerto quasi capite observantes expectant reuelationem filiorum Dei, & vanitati subiectæ (non sponte) &c. sub spe quòd & ipsæ vindicabuntur ex seruitute interitus in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei. Et Petrus ait nos expectare cœlos novos ac terram novam secundum promissionem.
units.tr: Why the elect and the reprobate will be judged according to their works. of which men are accustomed to place their happiness. For as to soul and body and our persons, we shall be partakers of the very glory of God, by which we shall be as Christ himself, although unequally in mind and body, beyond measure glorious; 1 Cor. 15:44; Phil. 3:21. As to external things, we shall obtain an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading; we shall possess by inheritance, in short, all things, the earth and heaven renewed through fire and purification; the earth, I say, and heaven, not as we now see them, but glorified. For created things, with head stretched out as it were, await the revelation of the sons of God, and are subjected to vanity (not willingly), etc., in hope that they too will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God. And Peter says that we look for new heavens and a new earth according to the promise.

units.la: Hæc est illa gloria quam in genere & communiter proponit Scriptura: propriam autem cuiusque gloriam futuram secundum opera cuiusque videtur innuere 1. Corinth.3.18. Vnusquisque suam mercedem accipiet secundum suum laborem. Hæ tamen gloriæ distinctæ species cum non sint nobis in Scripturis reuelatæ, eam scrutari nefas esse duco. Atque hæc de regno illo & mercede Electorum. Quòd autem dicitur in sententia illa Iudicis regnum illud paratum esse à iactis mundi fundamentis, non est id quidem prætermittendum hoc loco. Significat igitur his verbis, iam inde ab æterno præparatum nobis esse hoc regnum, ac proinde ab æterno nos ei destinatos esse.
units.tr: This is that glory which Scripture sets forth in general and in common; but the particular glory of each one, to be given according to each one's works, it seems to hint at in 1 Cor. 3:18: Each one will receive his own reward according to his own labour. Yet since these distinct kinds of glory have not been revealed to us in the Scriptures, I consider it wrong to search into them. And so much concerning that kingdom and the reward of the elect. But as to what is said in that sentence of the Judge, that the kingdom has been prepared from the foundation of the world, this is certainly not to be passed over here. These words signify, therefore, that this kingdom has been prepared for us from eternity, and that consequently we have been destined for it from eternity.

units.la: Ergo causa prima ac principalis huius regni ac mercedis est decretum & prædestinatio Dei ab æterno; hoc est, propositum Dei in se ad hoc, vt sit hoc regnum mere gratuitum. Concedo quidè inter decretum Dei hoc, & decreti executionem, oportere meritum aliquod intervenire, vt etiam merces referatur ad meritum aliquod, id quod aduersarij maximè contendunt. Sed dico meritum hoc, non iam esse operum nostrorum, verum Christi meritum nobis per fidem applicatum, vt etiam posito illo merito regnum hoc & merces hæc gratuita sint & maneant. Voluit enim Deus ita meritû intervenire, vt tamen gratuita sit merces, vt ipse in causis huius regni atq; mercedis, sive de proposito ipsius loquaris, siue de merito Christi, glorificetur in mera sua gratia. Quod autem ad opera illa attinet, nō sunt illa quidē merita & causae, sed effecta quaedam primum propositi diuini, deinde meriti Christi; ac proinde vtrumque & propositum Dei & meritum Christi arguetia & testificantia, vt signa quaedam manifestiora & nobis notiora. Quod si igitur obiiciatur ex hoc loco, Qui bene egerunt, prodibunt ad resurrectionem vitae: Ergo bona opera merentur vitam: Respondeo non sequi, quia in antecedente bona opera accipienda sunt non pro causis vitae, sed pro effectis arguentibus ipsas vitae causas, nempe decretum Dei aeternum, meritum Christi fide apprehensum; denique iustitiam Dei per fidem imputatam. Haec enim causae sunt, quae vitam aeternam antecedunt. Opera autem bona ex his profluunt & necessario vitam aeternam antegrediuntur, quia sunt necessaria effecta illarum causarum, & media sunt quae praeparauit Deus, vt in iis ambularemus, idque ab aeterno. In tempore autem conditi sumus, hoc est, facti noua creatura in Christo Iesu ad eadem illa opera, & mihi quidem nihil videtur aliud esse sanctificatio cum operibus & actionibus suis, quam initiu vitae illius aeternae, quae in glorioso illo Christi aduentu consummabitur. Initiu autem hoc vitae, quae est pars quaedam vitae, non meretur complementum, sed via est quasi & introitus quidam ad complementum. Complementum autem est ex sola Dei gratia, vt etiam ipsa vita fiat, vt in solidum Deo sit omnis gloria. Familiare autem est scripturae, signum pro re significata capere, eique aliquid attribuere, quod proprie attribuendum est rei significatae. In hoc autem negotio res significata, quae est fides Christi, significatur nomine egregium, quae sunt bona opera: quia nomen bonorum operum magis ad viuum exprimit veritatem fidei, quam etiam illud ipsum nomen fidei, de quo falso gloriantur & quo saepe abutuntur hypocritae. Quare respondeti potest praeterea ad illud enthymema, in antecedente nomen bonorum operum improprie accipi pro fide Christi ipsiusque iustitia, cuius sunt effecta ac signa quaedam, vt sit sensus antecedentis, Qui egerunt bona, prodibunt ad resurrectionem vitae, hoc est, qui vere credi-
units.tr: Therefore the first and principal cause of this kingdom and reward is the decree and predestination of God from eternity; that is, God's own purpose that this kingdom should be purely gratuitous. I grant indeed that between this decree of God and the execution of the decree some merit must intervene, so that the reward may also be referred to some merit, which our opponents above all contend. But I say that this merit is no longer the merit of our works, but the merit of Christ applied to us through faith, so that even with that merit posited, this kingdom and this reward are and remain gratuitous. For God willed that merit should intervene in such a way that the reward nevertheless remains gratuitous, so that he may be glorified in his mere grace, whether you speak of the purpose of his will as cause of this kingdom and reward, or of the merit of Christ. As for those works, they are indeed not merits or causes, but certain effects, first of the divine purpose, and then of the merit of Christ; and accordingly they are evidence of both God's purpose and Christ's merit, as certain clearer and better-known signs to us.
