But if it be objected from this passage, Those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, therefore good works merit life: I answer that it does not follow, because in the antecedent the good works are to be taken not as causes of life, but as effects indicating the causes of life itself, namely the eternal decree of God, the merit of Christ apprehended by faith, and finally the righteousness of God imputed through faith. For these are the causes which precede eternal life. But good works flow from these and necessarily go before eternal life, because they are the necessary effects of those causes, and are the means which God prepared beforehand so that we might walk in them, and that from eternity. We are, however, created in time, that is, made a new creature in Christ Jesus, for those same works; and to me indeed sanctification with its works and actions seems to be nothing other than the beginning of that eternal life, which will be consummated at that glorious coming of Christ. This beginning of life, however, which is a part of life, does not merit its completion, but is as it were the way and a certain entrance into the completion. The completion, however, comes from the sole grace of God, so that life itself may come about, and so that all glory may belong wholly to God. Now it is familiar to Scripture to take the sign for the thing signified, and to attribute to it something which is properly to be attributed to the thing signified. In this matter the thing signified, which is the faith of Christ, is signified by the outstanding name of good works, because the name of good works expresses the truth of faith more vividly than even that very name of faith, about which hypocrites boast falsely and which they often abuse. Hence it may be further answered to that enthymeme that in the antecedent the name of good works is taken improperly for the faith of Christ and his righteousness, of which good works are certain effects and signs; so that the sense of the antecedent is: Those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, that is, those who truly believe

units.la: Ephes. 2. 10. deruntin Christum, vt dictum est supra verf.23. vbi vita æterna fidei attributa est; & veram illam fidem suam ostenderunt ex operibus suis bonis inde manantibus, illi prodibunt ad resurrectionem vitæ. Ex qua expositione apparet iam opera non esse causam vitæ, sed argumentum duntaxat & indicium veræ causæ; ac proinde de operibus nostris, tanquam signis & necessariis consequentibus, positis prore significata & antecedente suo, enuntiatam esse vitam, nempe quòd sint totidem argumenta, atque ea quidem certissima veræ fidei, vel meriti fide apprehensi primùm; deinde iustitiæ Dei per fidem imputatæ.
units.tr: Ephes. 2. 10. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus, as was said above at verse 23, where eternal life is attributed to faith. Those who have shown that true faith of theirs by the good works that flow from it will come forth to the resurrection of life. From this explanation it is now clear that works are not the cause of life, but only the evidence and indication of the true cause. Accordingly, when our works are spoken of as signs and necessary consequences, life is predicated of them as of what they signify and of their antecedent cause. That is, they are so many proofs, and most certain ones, of true faith (first of the merit apprehended by faith, and then of the righteousness of God imputed through faith).

units.la: Atque hęc de sententia absolutionis hactenus, sequitur altera, quæ in reprobos pronùtiabitur. Abite à me, exectra biles, in ignem æternum, qui paratus est diabolo & Angelis eius. Hæc est igitur merces reproborum, nempe ignis æternus. Æternus erit ignis, sed hoc tolerabile, si illi semel essent igni illo consumendi: Verùm illi in æternum sufficient materiam æterno igni, & in æternum illo igne combusrentur. Atque hoc ipsum leuius esset, si mortui essent comburendi in æternum. Verùm viui in æternum comburendi sunt miseri, neque vnquam extinguendus ignis, neque vnquam extinguenda misera illa vita. Sed id quod adiunctum est huic igni, in illa Iudicis sententia, notandum est; Ait enim iam olim paratum Reprobis, hoc est, ab æterno constitutum & ordinatum. Quare & illi pariter ab æterno illi igni parati sunt & ordinati. Et hæc prima est omnium ac maximè principalis causa mortis æternæ ac interitus reproborum; verùm non quidem vt interitus est & perditio creaturæ, sed vt pœna est & supplicium iustè à iudice infligendum, in eum finem vt Deus glorificetur in iustitia sua. Nam decretum interitus, vt interitus est, proindeque malum culpæ est non pœnæ tantùm est, vt sic dicam, permissuum: hoc est decreuit Deus ipsum permittere fieri ac euenire. Verùm quidem illud est (vt dictum est supra de prædestinatione Electorum, deque vita æterna quæ ex ea sequitur) inter decretum illud reprobationis, & executionem decreti interuenit meritu aliquod, vt mors illa æterna euadat merces quasi debita. Meritum autem hoc est operum malorum, éstque hoc inter meritum vitæ & meritum mortis discrimen: Meritum vitæ non est operum nostrorum bonorum, sed solius Christi; Meritum mortis est operum malorum. In his verò operibus quæ merentur mortem,præcipuum est ipsum infidelitatis o- pus, ex quo sunt cætera omnia. Nā omnia mala opera,vt homicidium,scortatio,furtum, &c. & infidelitatis ope- ra sunt, & manent non remissa à Deo propter infidelita-tem,nempe quia non credunt homines in Christum Ie-sum. Quare sententia huius clausulę hęc est; Qui mala e-gerunt,prodibunt in resurrectionem condemnationis; cuius qui-dem condemnationis, illa ipsa mala opera futura sunt causæ meritoriæ. Hæc ipsa enim opera non tantùm e-runt signa quædam & testimonia æterni Reprobatio-nis decreti, simúlque infidelitatis, quæ principales sunt causæ, quorúmque mala hæc opera sunt effecta ne-cessaria, sed etiam causæ erunt per se meritoriæ futu- ræ illius condemnationis atque mortis. Estque hoc di-scrimen inter bona & mala opera quòd ad illud futu-rum iudicium attinet. Secundum bona opera iudica-bit Dominus vt signa & testimonia duntaxat, non etiã vt causas meritorias. Secundum verò mala opera, iudi-cabit non vt signa duntaxat & testimonia, sed etiam vt causas condemnationis meritorias. Quamobrem in his bene sequitur : Prodibunt qui male egerunt in resurre-ctionem condemnationis: ergo mala opera intelligen-da sunt vt causæ & merita condemnationis. Sed de his hactenus.
units.tr: So much for the sentence of absolution. What follows is the other sentence, which will be pronounced against the reprobate: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels." This, then, is the reward of the reprobate, namely eternal fire. The fire will be eternal, but that would be bearable if they were to be consumed by it once and for all. But they will be kept for ever as fuel for the eternal fire, and for ever burned by it. Even this would be lighter if they were to be burned for ever after death. But the wretched are to be burned for ever while still alive, and neither the fire nor that wretched life will ever be extinguished. Yet what is added to this fire in that sentence of the Judge must be noted. He says that it was prepared for the reprobate long ago, that is, decreed and ordained from eternity. Therefore they too were likewise prepared and ordained for that fire from eternity. And this is the first and chief cause of the eternal death and perdition of the reprobate. It is not, however, the cause of their perdition as the destruction of a creature, but as the punishment and penalty justly inflicted by the judge, to the end that God may be glorified in his justice. For the decree of destruction, as destruction, and therefore as an evil of guilt and not merely of punishment, is, so to speak, permissive: that is, God decided to permit it to happen and come about. But it is true (as was said above concerning the predestination of the elect and the eternal life that follows from it) that between that decree of reprobation and its execution some merit intervenes, so that eternal death is incurred as a wage, as if owed. This merit is the merit of evil works, and herein lies the difference between the merit of life and the merit of death. The merit of life belongs not to our good works but to Christ alone; the merit of death belongs to evil works. Among the works that merit death, the chief is the work of unbelief itself, from which all the rest arise. For all evil works, such as murder, fornication, theft and so on, are also works of unbelief, and they remain unforgiven by God because of unbelief, namely because men do not believe in Christ Jesus. So the sense of this clause is: "Those who have done evil will come forth to the resurrection of condemnation"; and of this condemnation those very evil works will be the meritorious causes. For these works will not only be certain signs and testimonies of the eternal decree of reprobation, and of unbelief at the same time (which are the principal causes, of which these evil works are the necessary effects); they will also be, in themselves, meritorious causes of that condemnation and death. And this is the difference between good and evil works as far as that future judgment is concerned. The Lord will judge good works only as signs and testimonies, not also as meritorious causes. But he will judge evil works not only as signs and testimonies but also as meritorious causes of condemnation. Wherefore it rightly follows in these words: "Those who have done evil will come forth to the resurrection of condemnation; therefore evil works are to be understood as the causes and merits of condemnation." But so much for these matters.

units.la: 30 Non possum ego à meipso facere quicquam: prout audio iudico: & iudicium meum iustum est: quia non quæro voluntatem meam,sed voluntatem eius qui misit me, id est Patris.
units.tr: 30 I can do nothing of myself: as I hear, I judge; and my judgment is just, because I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me, that is, of the Father.

units.la: 31 Si ego testor de meipso, testimonium meum non est idoneum.
units.tr: 31 If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true.

units.la: 31 Alius est qui testatur de me, & scio firmum esse testimonium quod testatur de me.
units.tr: 31 There is another who bears witness of me, and I know that the witness which he bears of me is true.

units.la: SEquitur conclusio totius præcedentis doctrinæ, tam de generali illa communicatione omnium operum Dei Patris & totius administrationis, quàm de speciali comunicatione iudicij, quæ pars est quædam generalis administrationis, eáque gloriosissima. Primum itaque est generalis conclusio his verbis: Non possum ego à meipso facere quicquam. Deus Pater in æterna illa generatione filij, vt communicauit cum Filio essentiam suam totam cádémque; ita potentiam suam totá candémque: quia omnia simul operatur. Filius autem à Patre suo in eadé generatione accepit sibi comunicatam essentiam omnémque potentiá & facultatem omnia operandi. Hoc posito quasi fundamento, seusus conclusionis hic erit: Potentia ea & facultas quam habeo operandi, non est à meipso; sed eam accepi mihi comunicatá in æterna illa generatione. Filius Dei iam communicata sibi à Patre essentia & potentia, per se, hoc est, per potentiam sibi naturalem & propriam (nam quid naturale & proprium magis, quàm id quod in generatione accipimus?) omnia operatur, eáque re differta creaturis omnibus, quæ nihil agunt per se; non mouentur, non viuunt, non sentiunt; quia non habent communicatum sibi fontem omnis potentiæ ac virtutis; sed quasi riuulos quosdam, & per participationem duntaxat habent potentiam, nō autem, vt sic dicā, essentialiter. Sed nos studeamus magis sentire in nobis ipsi hanc potentiam filio communicatam, quàm de ea plura loqui. Dici enim nō potest quanta sit cōsolatio in eius sensu, etiam cum sensu maximarum infirmitatum. Lubentissime igitur, inquit Apostolus, gloriabor potius de infirmitatibus meis, vt inhabitet in me potentia Christi.
units.tr: There follows the conclusion of the whole preceding teaching, both of that general communication of all the works of God the Father and of the whole administration, and of the special communication of judgment, which is a certain part of the general administration and a most glorious one. First, then, there is the general conclusion in these words: I can do nothing of myself. In that eternal generation of the Son, God the Father communicated to the Son his whole essence, and likewise his whole power, because he works all things together. The Son, however, received from his Father in that same generation the essence communicated to him, and all power and ability to work all things. Laying this down as a kind of foundation, the sense of the conclusion here will be this: the power and ability I have to work is not from myself, but I received it communicated to me in that eternal generation. The Son of God, having had essence and power communicated to him by the Father, works all things through himself, that is, through the power natural and proper to him (for what is more natural and proper than what we receive by generation?). By this he is distinguished from all creatures, which do nothing through themselves; they are not moved, do not live, do not sense, because they do not have the fountain of all power and virtue communicated to them, but have only certain streams, and possess power by participation alone, not, so to speak, essentially. But let us strive rather to feel this power communicated to the Son within ourselves than to say much about it. For it cannot be said how great is the consolation in the sense of it, even when we feel the greatest weaknesses. Therefore, says the Apostle, I will gladly glory rather in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me.

units.la: Sequitur altera conclusio eáque speciali de comunicato iudicio; prout audio, inquit, iudico. Audire hic, vt & videre supra, Nisi viderit Patrem operantem, vers. 19. non est nudè vel otiose audire vel videre Patrem iudicantem vel quid facientem, verùm est accipere à Patre omnem potentiam & authoritatem iudicandi & faciendi. Quare sensus est, prout accipio à Patre omnem authoritatem iudicandi communicatam, ita iudico. Demus operam & nos, vt in nobis ipsi sentiamus iudicium hoc filij ad nouam & spiritualem vitam, cùm ea sit ex illa authoritate iudicij filio communicata. Nam vt semel mel dicam, nunquam de filio, deque iis rebus à Patre ipsi communicatis, otiosè audiendum est, sed semper pro gratia Dei nitendum est, vt Christum eiusque potentiam in nobis ipsi sentiamus. Iudicio huic est adiecta sua quaedam commendatio ab ipsius iustitia. Iudicium meum iustum est: Q. d. In iudicando nulli iniuriam facio, ne reprobo quidem etiam tum cum adiudico eum mortis aeternae. Ratio subiecta est, quia non quaero voluntatem meam, hoc est, meam solius: sed voluntatem eius qui misit me, id est, Patris. Vt iudicium Patris & filij vnum idemque est: ita vna eadémque est voluntas vtriusq;. Verùm ita eadem, vt à Patre & Filio communicata sit. Quare sensus est acsi dicat, Non quaero voluntatem meam solam, sed quaero Patris voluntatem, cùm vna eadémque sit & mea & Patris voluntas. Argumentum itaque est à voluntate Dei, quo probat iustitiam & æquitatem, vt, quia ex voluntate sit Dei totum hoc iudicium, ideo iustum sit. Nota igitur primùm, Dei voluntas ipsa iustissima ac rectissima est: Deinde regula est ac norma omnium actionum iustarum, adeo vt si sint ex iustissima illa voluntate Dei, statim sint iustae. Cùm olim obijcerent aduersus Electionem & Reprobationem Dei, quòd iniusta viderentur, quandoquidem inaequaliter discernat Deus de aequalibus, Paulus Apostolus deducens corruptam & responsatricem rationem humanam ad voluntatem Dei, tanquam regulam omnis iustitiae, ex ea defendit iustitiam Dei in eligendo & reprobando. Cuius vult, inquit, miseretur, quem autem vult, indurat. Multa eueniunt quotidie & nobis ipsis & aliis, quorum indignitatem nos graviter ferimus, nonnunquam etiam impatienter. Hic paulisper oculi auertendi sunt ab instrumentis quibus vtitur Deus in operibus suis perficiendis, & ad Deum ipsum authorem omnium conuertendi: Considerandúmque est actiones illas omnes etiam à Dei voluntate aliquo modo proficisci, contra quā nihil potest eorum quae eueniunt, ac proinde iustas ac bonas esse quaecunque actiones respectu voluntatis ipsius, qualescunque demum sint, si instrumentorum habeatur ratio, ideóque patienter ferendas esse. Sed quae est peruersitas naturae nostrae, etiam hoc iam cognito, quòd sint ex voluntate Dei, non tamen ideo ferimus ea libenter, sed voluntati Dei statim incipimus obstrepere. Unde Apostolus ibidem postquam voluntatem diuinam tanquam causam electionis & reprobationis attulit, cùm satis perspectum haberet quàm inimica sit humana ratio diuinae huic voluntati, eam occupat aduersus eam obiicientem. Sed illud imprimis obseruatione dignum vt responsantem rationem humanam compescat ibidem uerf. 20. Primùm cum graui reprehensione admonet hominem esse creaturam Dei creatoris, & minus quiddam respectu Dei, quàm sit lutum respectu figuli, cùm Deus eum initio ex nihilo creavit, figulus autem lutum etsi formet atque fingat quo lubet modo, tamen non ex nihilo illud creet. Quis es, inquit, ô homo, tu qui respondes Deo, &c. Deinde admonet quòd cùm sit creatura Dei, Deus in ipsum habeat absolutam potestatem, maiorem ea quam habet figulus in lutum, cùm ex eadem massa figulus possit aliud vas ad decus, aliud verò ad dedecus facere. Figulus tamen, vt neque alia quauis creatura, absolutam potestatem non habet in creaturam quancunque Dei vel vilissimam. Postremò ibidem uerf. 22. 23. admonet Deum velle omnia quae vult propter suam ipsius gloriam, quae quidem suo merito praeferenda est saluti & vitae omnium quotquot sunt creaturarum. Quare, si quando incipiet corrupta haec ratio obstrepere iustissimae voluntati Dei, cogitandum nobis est de his tribus, de quibus iam diximus, & allatis his in medium compescenda est ratio ista humana & superbia hominis aduersus Deum nostrum. Unde enim est illud, quaeso, quòd non acquiescat homo voluntati Dei, nisi ex eo primum quòd in corde dicat se non esse creaturam, ac proinde Deum non habere hanc in se potestatem? Deinde quòd Dei sui gloriam postponat sibi suaeque saluti? Quare si quis de his cogitauerit serio, profecto incipiet demum agnoscere Dei voluntatem iustissimam esse, in eaque si nò perfectè, at aliquo certè modo coquiescet, qua profecto cóformitate voluntatis nostrae cum voluntate Dei, nihil esse poterit nobis iucundius & suauius. Neque etiam aliud quoduis certius argumentum electionis nostrae dari poterit. Nam illud certissimum est, reprobam mentem nunquam sponte conquiescere in Dei voluntate, neque aliquo placendi Deo studio detincri.
units.tr: Next comes the second conclusion, and it concerns judgment that has been communicated: as I hear, he says, so I judge. To hear here, as to see above in Unless he sees the Father working (v. 19), does not mean merely hearing or seeing the Father judging or doing something idly. It means receiving from the Father all power and authority to judge and to act. So the sense is: as I receive from the Father all the authority of judging that has been communicated to me, so I judge. Let us also take pains to feel in ourselves this judgment of the Son, which concerns the new and spiritual life, since it comes from that authority of judgment communicated to the Son. To say it once for all: we must never hear about the Son, or about those things communicated to him by the Father, idly. We must always strive, by the grace of God, to feel Christ and his power in ourselves. This judgment is also given its own commendation from his justice: My judgment is just. That is, in judging I do wrong to no one; I do not even reject anyone when I pronounce him condemned to eternal death. The reason follows: because I do not seek my own will, that is, my will alone, but the will of him who sent me, that is, of the Father. Just as the judgment of the Father and of the Son is one and the same, so their will is one and the same, though it is communicated from the Father and the Son alike. So the sense is as if he said: I do not seek my will alone, but I seek the will of the Father, since my will and the Father's will are one and the same. The argument, then, is drawn from the will of God, by which he proves justice and equity: because this whole judgment proceeds from the will of God, it is therefore just. Note first, then, that the will of God is itself most just and most right. Second, it is the rule and norm of all just actions, so that whatever comes from that most just will of God is at once just. When in former times people objected against the election and reprobation of God that they seemed unjust, since God discriminates unequally between equals, the Apostle Paul, leading corrupt and argumentative human reason back to the will of God as the rule of all justice, defended from this the justice of God in electing and reprobating. He has mercy on whom he wills, he says, and whom he wills, he hardens. Many things happen every day, both to ourselves and to others, whose unworthiness we bear heavily, sometimes even impatiently. Here we must turn our eyes for a little from the instruments God uses in carrying out his works, and direct them to God himself, the author of all. We must consider that all those actions also proceed in some way from the will of God, against which nothing that happens can stand. Therefore, with respect to his will, whatever actions occur, of whatever kind they may be, are just and good, if account is taken of the instruments, and so they must be borne patiently. But such is the perversity of our nature that, even when we have come to know that these things come from the will of God, we do not bear them gladly, but at once begin to clamour against the will of God. Hence the Apostle, in the same passage, after he has brought forward the divine will as the cause of election and reprobation, since he knew well enough how hostile human reason is to this divine will, takes up arms against the objector. Yet especially worth noting is how in the same passage (v. 20) he restrains the arguing human reason. First, with grave rebuke, he reminds us that man is a creature of God the Creator, and in relation to God is something less than clay is in relation to the potter, since God created him at the beginning out of nothing, whereas the potter, though he shapes and moulds the clay in whatever way he pleases, does not create it out of nothing. Who are you, O man, he says, who answer back to God, etc.? Then he reminds us that, since man is God's creature, God has absolute power over him, greater than the power the potter has over the clay, since from the same lump the potter can make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour. Yet the potter, like any other creature, does not have absolute power over any creature of God, however humble. Finally, in the same passage (vv. 22–23), he reminds us that God wills all that he wills for his own glory, which indeed rightly takes precedence over the salvation and life of all creatures. Therefore, whenever this corrupt reason begins to clamour against the most just will of God, we must think on these three points, of which we have already spoken, and, having brought them forward, restrain that human reasoning and the pride of man against our God. For where does it come from, I ask, that man does not acquiesce in the will of God, unless first because he says in his heart that he is not a creature, and so that God does not have this power over him? And then because he puts his own salvation and his own life before the glory of God? So if anyone considers these things seriously, he will at last begin to acknowledge that the will of God is most just, and in it he will at least in some measure find rest, if not perfectly. And from this conformity of our will with the will of God nothing can be more pleasant or sweeter to us. Nor can any surer proof of our election be given than this. For it is most certain that a reprobate mind never willingly rests in the will of God, nor is it held by any zeal to please God.

units.la: Atque hactenus fuit conclusio; sequuntur nunc testimonia ex quibus illud ipsum apparet conspicitur que, nempe Iesum esse Christum illum filium Dei & aequalem Deo. Si ego testor. Sequuntur hoc loco, vt dixi, testimonia quibus id-ipsum instituit ostendere, se nimirum esse Dei filium & patrem Deo ab aeterno. Locum hunc de testimoniis aggreditur per occupationem. Dici enim potuit, Haec omnia tu ipse testaris de teipso: Ergo testimonium tuum non est idoneum; id quod ei aperte & totidem verbis obiicitur, Iohan. 8. 13. Huic occurrit Christus, ac illis hoc largitur: Si ego testor de me ipso, sequitur profecto testimonium meum non esse idoneum. Cur autem de filii Dei testimonio ita censuerint Iudaei, in causa fuit quod eum a vulgo hominum non secernebant. Scimus autem neminem audiri in iudicio testificantem in propria sua causa: Etsi enim verum dicat cum res ipsius agitur, tamen non est pro legitimo aut fide digno habendum ipsius testimonium. Sed iniqui fuerunt Iudaei in filium Dei, tum quod eum aliis hominibus adnumerarunt, tum quod testimonium eius de se non differre a communi hominum testimonio de se ipsis iudicarunt. Ideo eodem capite 8. vbi hoc ipsum obiectum est, Testimonium ipsius de se non esse legitimum ac idoneum: Respondet Christus, etiam si ego testor de me-ipso, idoneum est testimonium meum; vers. 14. Hic tamen Christus cedere videtur ad tempus iuri suo, vt, si nolint moveri ipsius authoritate propter siniistrum illud suum de ipso iudicium, saltem moveantur authoritate Dei Patris de ipso testantis. Hic locus quoque potest habere hunc sensum, ac si dixisset; Si ego solus testor de meipso, &c. Sed ego malo cum quae iam audi. Is enim amor fuit salutis humanae in Christo, cum in terris commoraretur inter Iudaeos, vt sui sueque gloriae oblitus fuerit ad tempus, imo passus fuerit se inanin ad hoc, vt, si quomodo posset fieri, homine servaret. Etenim Christus non indulsit sibi ipsi, sed sicut scriptum est, Conuitia eorum qui conuitiantur tibi, inciderunt in me. Quādoquidem suo exemplo docet nos, quotquot
units.tr: So far was the conclusion; now follow the testimonies from which that very point appears and is seen, namely that Jesus is the Christ, that Son of God, and equal to God. If I bear witness. There follow here, as I said, testimonies by which he sets out to show that he is the Son of God and equal to God from eternity. He approaches this matter of testimonies by anticipation. For it could be said, You bear witness to these things about yourself: therefore your testimony is not fit; which is openly objected to him in these very words, John 8:13. Christ meets this and grants it to them: If I bear witness about myself, it certainly follows that my testimony is not fit. The reason why the Jews judged of the testimony of the Son of God in this way was that they did not separate him from the common run of men. We know, however, that no one is heard in court when he testifies in his own cause; for even if he speaks the truth when his own affair is under discussion, his testimony is not to be regarded as lawful or worthy of belief. But the Jews were unjust toward the Son of God, both in counting him among other men and in judging that his testimony about himself did not differ from the common testimony men give about themselves. Therefore in the same chapter 8, where this very objection is raised, that his testimony about himself is not lawful and fit, Christ replies: even if I bear witness about myself, my testimony is fit (v. 14). Here, however, Christ seems for the time to yield his right, so that, if they will not be moved by his own authority, because of their perverse judgment about him, at least they may be moved by the authority of God the Father, who bears witness about him. This passage may also have this sense, as if he had said: If I alone bear witness about myself, etc. But I prefer what has already been heard. For this was the love of Christ for human salvation, that while he dwelt on earth among the Jews he forgot, for a time, himself and his own glory, indeed was willing to be emptied, so that, if in any way it could be done, he might save man. For Christ did not please himself, but, as it is written, The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen upon me (Ps. 69:9). Since by his own example he teaches us, all who…

units.la: Coelusio- ni addunt-ur testimonia de Deitate & consubstantialitate filii Dei.
units.tr: Testimonies concerning the deity and consubstantiality of the Son of God are added.

units.la: Charitas Christi erga humanum genus.
units.tr: The love of Christ toward the human race.

units.la: Rom. 15. 3. illu sequimur in glorioso isto ministerio nosipsos abnegare, vt quaeramus Dominu qui se neglexit nostra causa, quaeramus salutem hominum ad gloriam ipsius, adeo vt si quo pacto posset, nostrum decus, nostra paupertas, amissio bonorum omnium, amissio etiam vitae ipsius, seruire hominum saluti & Dei gloriae, ea re simus contenti. Si, inquit Paulus, pro libamento offerar super hostia & sacrificioque fidei vestrae, gaudeo & gratulor omnibus vobis. Fidelis quisquis est in ministerio, si sit conscientia fidei & aedificationis eorum quibus praedicauit, etiam cum suo dedecore, etiam cum morte sua, gaudet tamen & gratulatur iis, quia assequitur id quod sibi in tota vita propositum fuit, nempe fidem & aedificationem Ecclesiae Dei. Mercenarius vero non gaudet nisi quando gloriam suam, diuitias huius mundi, seque ipsum aliquo modo assequitur, quia sui causa facit omnia. Alius est qui. Correctio quaedam est subiecta superiori concessioni, Q.d. Et si testimonium meum perhibitum de me ipso non sit idoneum & hoc vobis largior: tamen est alius qui testatur de me: qui autem is sit, exptesse docebit postea 37. verf. vbi habet haec verba, Qui misit me Pater, ipse testatur de me, nisi malis haec verba sequi priora illa in hunc sensum, ac si dixisset: Si ego solus testor de meipso, testimonium, &c. At alius est praeter me, &c. Sed mihi magis placet prior, quam attuli, consequutio verborum. Testimonium hoc alterius commendat deinde a fidelitate & veritate ipsius. Scio, inquit, quod testimonium eius verum est de me. Non ait simpliciter, Testimonium eius quod testatur de me, verum est: sed addit, scio verum esse; loquitur enim cum insigni fiducia & plena animi persuasione. In causa autem fuit, quod Dominus expertus in se ipse verum esse id omne quod Pater de ipso vnquam testatus est. Quandocunque loqui contingit nos de Dei testimonio (Testimonium vero Dei, appello verbum eius, praesertim vero verbum illud promissionis) non est tum de eo frigide & ieiune loquendum, verum oportet cum παρρησίᾳ & fiducia de eo loqui. Hoc aute non alia ratione obtinemus quam quia experimur in nobis veritate illarum promissionum Dei, experimur nobis iam remissa esse peccata in Christo, nobis iam imputatam esse iustitiam, nobis datam
units.tr: Paul, in Rom. 15. 3, says that we follow him in this glorious ministry by denying ourselves, so that we seek the Lord who neglected himself for our sake, and seek the salvation of men for the glory of God; so that, if it were possible, we should be content to lose our honour, our poverty, the loss of all our goods, and even the loss of our own life, in order to serve the salvation of men and the glory of God. If I am being poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice and congratulate you all, says Paul (Phil. 2. 17). Any faithful man in the ministry who has the assurance of the faith and edification of those to whom he has preached rejoices and is glad, even with his own disgrace and even with his own death, because he attains what he has aimed at throughout his whole life, namely the faith and edification of the Church of God. But the hireling does not rejoice unless he attains in some way his own glory, the riches of this world, and himself; for he does everything for his own sake. Another is the one who bears witness: this is a correction added to the preceding concession, as if to say: "Even if my testimony borne about myself is not sufficient, and I grant you this, there is nevertheless another who bears witness about me. Who he is he will make clear later, in verse 37, where he says: The Father who sent me, he himself bears witness about me; unless you prefer to link those earlier words to this sense, as if he had said: If I alone bear witness about myself, the testimony is not true, etc. But there is another besides me, etc." But I prefer the order of words I have given first. He then commends this testimony of another from its faithfulness and truth: I know, he says, that his testimony about me is true. He does not say simply, "His testimony which he bears about me is true," but adds that he knows it is true; for he speaks with remarkable confidence and full assurance of mind. The reason was that the Lord had himself experienced that everything the Father has ever testified about him is true. Whenever it happens that we speak of God's testimony (and by God's testimony I mean his Word, especially that word of promise), we must not speak of it coldly and dryly, but we ought to speak of it with boldness [παρρησίᾳ] and confidence. We obtain this in no other way than by experiencing in ourselves the truth of those promises of God: we experience that our sins are already forgiven in Christ, that righteousness has already been imputed to us, and that eternal life has already been given to us.

units.la: Quid pios ministros Ecclesiae deceat. Philip. 2,17
units.tr: What befits godly ministers of the Church. Phil. 2. 17.

units.la: Correctio superioris concessionis.
units.tr: Correction of the preceding concession.

units.la: Quomodo loquendum de Dei testimonio. datam iam esse vita illam æterna. Paulus magna cũ fiducia & asseueratione loquitur de salute illa peccatorũ, quæ est per Christi aduentum in mundum: Fidelis est hic sermo, inquit, & modis omnibus dignus quem amplectamur{a} Christum Iesum venisse in mundum vt peccatores seruaret. Quæ causæ huius tam grauis asseurationis? Vide quæ sequuntur. Quorum, inquit, primus sum ego. Assumit ex priori sententia se peccatorem esse, vt concludat se seruatum esse per Christum. Vide mihi igitur, experientia illa & sensus salutis suæ ipsius per Christum, effecit vt ea cum fiducia & asseueratione pronuntiaret hoc Apostolus de Christo ipsiusque aduentu. Quare in his Dei promissionibus efferendis, semper danda nobis opera est, vt gratiam illam & misericordiam promissam in nobis singuli sentiamus, ad hoc vt possimus dicere cum Dauide & Paulo, Credidi & ideo loquutus sum. Tum enim cum certò loquimur & cum plena animi persuasione, verbum a nobis prolatum, potens instrumentum est in aliis ad eos confirmandos & adducendos ad fidem & veritatem.
units.tr: How one ought to speak of God's testimony. Paul speaks with great confidence and assertion about that salvation of sinners which comes through the coming of Christ into the world: This is a faithful saying, he says, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners{a} (1 Tim. 1. 15). What is the cause of so grave an assertion? See what follows: Of whom, he says, I am chief. From the earlier statement he takes up that he is a sinner, so as to conclude that he has been saved through Christ. Consider then: that experience and the sense of his own salvation through Christ led the Apostle to pronounce this about Christ and his coming with such confidence and assertion. Therefore in setting forth these promises of God we must always take care that each of us feels in himself that grace and mercy which is promised, so that we may be able to say with David and Paul: I believed, and therefore I have spoken. For when we speak with certainty and with full persuasion of mind, the word spoken by us is a powerful instrument for strengthening others, and for bringing them to faith and to the truth.

units.la: 33 Vos misistis ad Iohannem, & is testimonium dedit veritati.
units.tr: You sent to John, and he gave testimony to the truth.

units.la: 34 Ego autem ab homine testimonium non capio: sed haec dico vobis vt seruemini.
units.tr: But I do not receive testimony from man; but I say these things so that you may be saved.

units.la: 35 Ille erat lucerna ardens & lucens: vos autem voluistis ad momentum exultare in luce eius.
units.tr: He was a burning and a shining lamp; but you were willing for a time to rejoice in his light.

units.la: 36 At ego testimonium habeo maius testimonio Iohannis: opera enim quae dedit mihi Pater vt ea perficerem, ipsa inquam opera quae ego facio, testantur de me, quod Pater misit me.
units.tr: But I have a greater testimony than John's; for the works which the Father has given me to accomplish, these very works which I do, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me.

units.la: Via alium dixit testari de se, neque cum interea nominauit, putari a Iudaeis fortasse potuit Iohannem ab eo intellectum fuisse. Huic igitur statim occurrit Christus, ac primum quidem per concessionis speciem laudat testimonium illud Iohannis, quod data est veritati; deinde per correctionem quandam ipsum extenuat atque eleuat comparatione facta cum
units.tr: Because he said that another bore witness about him, and did not name him at that point, the Jews might perhaps have thought that John was the one he meant. Christ therefore immediately meets this, and first, by way of a concession, praises John's testimony, which was given to the truth; then, by a kind of correction, he diminishes and raises it up by comparing it with

units.la: {a} 1. Tim. 1. 15. illo testimonio, de quo ipse proximè fit loquutus. Ait igitur, Vos misistis ad Iohannem. De hoc vide caput primum vers.19. & deinceps: Vbi leges emissos à Consilio Hierosolymitano Sacerdotes & Leuitas ad Iohannem in deserto agentem, qui ipsum interrogarent. Ecquis esset? Et is testimonium dedit veritati. De hoc Iohannis de Christo testimonio, quàm verum ac fide dignum fuerit, vide ibidem. Ego autem. Correctio est qua eleuat illud Iohannis testimonium, Ego, inquit, ab homine testimonium non capto. Q. d. Quòd ad me meámque veritatem, ego respectu mei meèque veritatis, non opus habeo testimonio cuiusquam mortalium, neque Iohannis quidem ipsius. Nam hoc sciendum est, veritatem Dei, & id quod Deus loquitur in sese consideratum, non egere vllo testimonio vllius creaturæ, vel hominis, vel etiam Angeli, vt eo quasi fulciatur & confirmetur. Sed hæc dico. Per occupationem reddit rationem cur paulò ante commendarit ipsius Iohānis testimonium, nempe vt nihil omitteret quo commoueri possent ipsi ad credendum. Hæc dico, inquit, vt vos seruemini, hoc est, hoc quod dico de Iohannis testimonio, non ideo dico quasi ego egeam eo, sed propter vos dico, & vestræ infirmitatis gratia, vt vos eo adiuti & quasi præparati ad me peruenia tis, & ad veritatem meam. Vnde rursus egreditur in commendationem Iohannis. Ille erat, inquit, lucerna ardens & lucens. Ardens quidem in sese, lucens verò aliis. Lucernam appellat, non Solem, vt Christus à Propheta vocatus est, Sol iustitiæ. Quia Iohannes, etsi lux erat, tamen respectu exoriturę post eum illius lucis, obscura aliqua dūraxat lux erat ad instar lucernę vel candelę. Scriptura enim Dei solet proponere eam lucē, quæ in mundo fuit ante aduentum & manifestationem Christi per comparationem subobscurę cuiusdam lucis, vīpote lucernæ aut candelæ. Ita Petrus Sermonem propheticū dicit lucernam fuisse in obscuro loco splēdentem, vsqʒ dum dies illucesceret & exoriretur Lucifer in hominū cordibus. Quanquā maior fuit lux Iohannis, quàm aliicuius ex Prophetis qui ante ipsum extiterunt. Eam verò lucem, quæ subsecuta est Christi aduentum ac manifestationem, & quam Sol ille iustitiæ attulit secum in
units.tr: {a} 1 Tim. 1. 15. that testimony of which he has just spoken. He says, then, You sent to John. On this see chapter 1, verse 19 and following, where you will read that the priests and Levites were sent out by the Council of Jerusalem to John, who was active in the desert, to ask him who he was. And he gave testimony to the truth. On how true and worthy of belief this testimony of John about Christ was, see the same place. But I. This is a correction by which he raises up John's testimony: I, he says, do not receive testimony from man. As if to say: "As far as I and my truth are concerned, I, with respect to myself and my truth, have no need of the testimony of any mortal, not even of John himself. For it must be understood that the truth of God, and what God speaks as considered in himself, has no need of any testimony from any creature, whether man or even angel, to be propped up and confirmed by it. But I say these things. By a figure of anticipation he gives the reason why he had just commended John's testimony, namely so that he might leave nothing out by which they could be moved to believe. I say these things, he says, so that you may be saved; that is, what I say about John's testimony I do not say as if I needed it, but I say it on account of you, and for the sake of your weakness, so that being helped by it, and as if prepared, you may come to me and to my truth." Hence he again goes out into the commendation of John. He was, he says, a burning and a shining lamp. Burning indeed in himself, but shining for others. He calls him a lamp, not the sun, as Christ was called by the prophet the Sun of righteousness (Mal. 3. 20). For John, although he was a light, was nevertheless, in comparison with the light that was to rise after him, only a somewhat dim light, like a lamp or a candle. For Scripture of God is accustomed to set forth the light that was in the world before the coming and manifestation of Christ by comparison with a somewhat dim light, such as a lamp or a candle. So Peter calls the prophetic word a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawned and the morning star rose in men's hearts (2 Pet. 1. 19). Yet John's light was greater than that of any of the prophets who came before him. But the light which followed the coming and manifestation of Christ, and which that Sun of righteousness brought with him into the world, Scripture is accustomed to express, I say, by comparing it with the light of God and of the sun. Hence, as wide as the difference is between the light of a candle and the light of the sun and of day, so wide is the difference between the clarity of that teaching which once existed before Christ was manifested in the flesh, and that which now exists after his manifestation. Therefore there ought to be an equally great difference in comfort and in our works. For the greater the light, the greater the comfort; the light of a lamp has indeed its own comfort, but the light of day and of the sun has a much greater. Again, the greater the light supplied to us for performing our actions, the more perfect those actions ought to be. But somehow it happens, I know not how, that in our own age, in such great light of Christ and of the Gospel itself, there is still less comfort, and the works are worse than they were long ago among that ancient people, who walked and lived in that dimmer light of the Prophets. Indeed, the works of almost all men in the very noonday light are works of night and of darkness: murders, adulteries, blasphemies, thefts, robberies, sacrileges, and others of that kind, which were not heard of even among the heathen. Surely this is a great proof of intolerable impudence and wickedness, if someone who is about to commit some foul crime comes out into the sight of this sun which we see; for by day one must walk decently. How much impudence and wickedness, then, shall we judge those men to have, who in this light of truth, which is greater by infinite degrees than the light of the sun, dare to commit every sort of foulness and shame? So much so that I often used to reflect in myself that this light of the Gospel has been given to many, not so that through it they might become better and be saved, but so that they might become worse, more blind, more obstinate, and finally so that their judgment may be made heavier on that day. But you were willing for a time. He commends the light of the Baptist from its effect on the Jews themselves, though otherwise obstinate. They were indeed willing to rejoice for a time in his light. They did receive his teaching with joy; but that joy was not lasting, but soon vanished. Note, then, the efficacy of the word and light of God: it penetrates to the heart, even of hypocrites and of the reprobate, and in some way illuminates them,

units.la: Malach. 3. 10.
units.tr: Malach. 3. 10.

units.la: 2. Pet. 1. 19. in mundum, eam, inquam, solet scriptura exprimere per comparationem lucis Dei & solis. Unde quàm latum est discrimen inter lucem cadelæ & lucem Solis ac diei, tam latum est discrimen inter doctrinæ illius claritate, quę olim fuit antequam Christus manifestaretur in carne, & eam quæ nunc est post ipsius manifestationem, ut aduenientibus Quare etiam in consolatione & operibus nostris tantum discrimen esse debet. Quò enim maior est lux, eò maior est consolatio; lucernæ lux habet quidem suam consolationem, sed lux diei & solis multo maiorem habet. Rursus quò maior lux subministratur actionibus nostris perficiendis, eò perfectiores eas esse oportet. Sed fit nescio quo modo, ut in plerisque hac nostra ætate etiam in tanta luce Christi & Euangelij ipsius, sit tamen minor consolatio, deterioràque sint opera, quàm fuerunt olim veteris illius populi, agentis & ambulantis in subobscura illa luce Prophetarum. Imò vero opera noctis sunt & tenebratum fere omnium hominum in ipsa luce meridiana, homicidia, adulteria, blasphemiæ, furta, rapinæ, sacrilegia, aliaque id genus, quæ ne inter gentes quidem audita sunt. Illud profectò magnum est argumentum intolerabilis impudentiæ atque malitiæ, si quis perpetraturus fœdum aliquod facinus, prodeat in aspectum solis huius quę videmus: nam interdiu composite ambulandum est. Quantam impudentiam ergo & malitiam iudicabimus istam eorum hominum, qui in hac luce veritatis, quæ infinitis partibus maior est illa solis luce, nihil non fœditatis ac flagitij audent perpetrare? Adeo ut ego sæpenumero mecum cogitare soleam, datam esse lucem istam Euangelij plerisque, nō ut per eam meliores fiant ac seruentur, sed ut deteriores, cæciores, obstinatiores, denique ut aggrauetur eorum iudicium in illo die. Vos autem voluistis ad tempus. Commendat hanc lucem Baptistæ ab effecto suo in ipsis Iudæis, quamuis alioqui obstinatis. Voluerunt illi quidem exultare ad tempus in luce eius. Exceperunt quidem cum gaudio doctrinam eius; sed non diuturnum fuit illud gaudium, verum cito euanuit. Nota igitur efficaciā illam verbi ac lucis Dei, penetrat in cor usque, etiam hypocritarum, etiam reprobōrū, eos aliquo modo illumi-
units.tr: 2. Pet. 1. 19. Scripture commonly expresses this light in the world by comparison with the light of God and of the sun. So just as great a difference lies between the light of a lamp or candle and the light of the sun and day, so great a difference lies between the clarity of that teaching which existed before Christ was revealed in the flesh and the teaching which exists now, after his manifestation. For this reason there ought to be as great a difference in our comfort and in our works. The greater the light, the greater the comfort: a lamp's light does have its own comfort, but the light of day and of the sun has a much greater one. Again, the greater the light supplied to us for performing our actions, the more perfect those actions ought to be. Yet somehow, I know not how, it happens in most people in our own age that, despite so great a light of Christ and of the Gospel itself, there is less comfort and worse works than there were in the old people of former times, who walked and lived in that dim light of the prophets. Indeed, the works of most men are the works of night and of darkness, even in the noonday light: murders, adulteries, blasphemies, thefts, robberies, sacrileges, and others of that kind, which were not heard of even among the heathen. This is surely a great proof of intolerable shamelessness and malice: if someone about to commit some foul crime comes out into the sight of this sun which we see, for one must walk decently in the daytime. What shamelessness and malice, then, shall we judge of those men who dare to commit every kind of filth and wickedness in this light of truth, which is greater than that light of the sun by infinite degrees? So much so that I often find myself thinking that this light of the Gospel has been given to many, not so that they may become better and be saved by it, but so that they may become worse, blinder, more obstinate, and finally so that their judgment may be heavier on that day. "But you were willing," he says, "to rejoice for a time." He commends this light by its effect even on the Jews themselves, although they were otherwise obstinate. They were indeed willing to exult for a time in his light. They did receive his teaching with joy; but that joy did not last long, and soon vanished away. Note therefore the efficacy of that Word and light of God: it penetrates even to the heart, even of hypocrites and of the reprobate, and in some way illumi-

units.la: Discrimen cognitionis salutaris ante & post Christi aduentum in carne. nat,excitat in iis fidem aliquam in promissiones Dei,Et ex fide amorem Dei & laetitiam,ac gustum quendā potestatum futuri saeculi.Sed ista non diu permanent.Causam huius rei pete ex Luc. 8. 13. quia cor est ipsis quasi petrosum.Habet quidem terream aliquam superficiem; sed si paulo altius in ipsum descendas, nihil inuenies in eo,nisi petra eamque durissimam. Christus eo loco, dū exponit nobis cor illud petrosum,dicit esse cor,quod nō sit bonum & honestum,vers.15.Nunc vero corde existente petroso ac duro,fides illa excitata,radices in eo altius agere non potest.Non actis autem radicibus,necesse est herbescens illa fides statim marcescat & pereat. Quare tiam tum cum sentimus in nobis apprehensionem ista aliquam promissionum Dei in Christo cum amore & cum gaudio quodam coniunctam, non hic haerendum est, verum altius descendendum est in intimas cordis partes, & superficies ista externa transfodienda, videndumque cuiusmodi materia subtus lateat, petrosane, an terrea, bonane ac honesta, an mala? Bonum autem ac honestum cor scies maxime ex interiori illa cordis integritate, sinceritate ac simplicitate: Ea enim est cordis nostri optima qualitas, & quam Deus in Scriptura maxime commendat. Ab hac cordis sinceritate & integritate commendati sunt veteres illi Patres, Noë, Iob aliique. Dauid beatum virum praedicat in cuius corde non est dolus. Christus iam antea in hoc Euangelio Nathanaelem ab hac potissimum commendauit:Ecce vere Israelita in quo non est dolus. Sinceritatem vero istam cordis non ex alia re cognosces melius,quam ex eo respectu quem habes, dum aliquid vel cogitas, vel loqueris, vel facis. Quod si ante omnia Deum respicias in omni motu & actione, profecto iam ex sinceritate cordis motus est & actio, si Deum respicias dum credis in ipsum, hoc est si credas in Deum non propter te aut vtilitatem & commodum tuum, sed propter Deum solum. Si Deum & Christum diligas propter Deum & Christum, non propter te, hoc est, si diligas Deum vt filius, non vt mercenarius. Nam mercenarius etiam diligit herum suum, sed propter mercedem. Si in Deo lxterius non propter te, sed propter Deum. Denique vt verbo dicam, siue edis, siue
units.tr: The difference between saving knowledge before and after Christ's coming in the flesh. It arouses in them some faith in God's promises, and from faith love of God and joy, and a certain taste of the powers of the age to come. But these do not last long. Seek the cause of this in Luke 8:13, because their heart is like stone. It has indeed some earthy surface, but if you go a little deeper into it, you will find nothing in it except rock, and that very hard. Christ, when he explains to us that stony heart, says it is a heart that is not good and honest (v. 15). Now, when the heart is stony and hard, the faith that has been aroused cannot strike its roots deeper into it. And when the roots have not taken hold, that faith, though it sprouts, must immediately wither and perish. So when we perceive in ourselves some apprehension of God's promises in Christ, joined with love and a certain joy, we must not stop here. We must go down into the inner parts of the heart, pierce this external surface, and see what material lies beneath: stony or earthy, good and honest, or evil? You will know the heart to be good and honest chiefly from its inner integrity, sincerity and simplicity, for this is the best quality of our heart, and the one God especially commends in Scripture. The ancient Fathers Noah, Job and others were commended for this sincerity and integrity of heart. David calls blessed the man in whose heart there is no guile. Christ earlier in this Gospel commended Nathanael especially for this: Behold a true Israelite, in whom there is no guile. You will best know this sincerity of heart from nothing else than from the regard you have while you think, speak or do something. If above all you regard God in every motion and action, then indeed the motion and action proceed from sincerity of heart: if you regard God while you believe in him, that is, if you believe in God not for your own sake or your advantage and convenience, but for God alone; if you love God and Christ for the sake of God and Christ, not for your own sake, that is, if you love God as a son, not as a hired servant. For the hired servant also loves his master, but for the wages. If you take joy in God, not for yourself but for God. In a word, whether you eat, or drink, or do anything else, do all things to the glory of God. Now from that very regard you have in acting you can judge of this inner sincerity of heart.

units.la: Probatio cordis necessaria. fiuebibis, fiue quid facis, omnia in gloriam Dei facias: Iam ex eo ipso respectu quem habes in agendo, iudicare potes de interna ista cordis sinceritate. Nā since ritas ista vel simplicitas cordis in eo cernitur, vt quod facimus faciamus ex animo, siue id fiat erga Deum, siue erga homines fiat, sed propter Deum. Ex animo autem aliquid facimus cum cum intuemur Deum eiusq; voluntatem. Vnde ait Apostolus, facientes ex animo quod vult Deus. Atque hinc fit vt ego petendam censeam differētiam fidei temporariae & perpetuae maximè ab hac animi sinceritate, vt sit fides temporaria semper cum simulatione quadam & hypocrisi sinceritati contraria: fides autem perpetua sit sine simulatione & hypocrisi & cum sinceritate. Vnde Paulus fidem veram ac perpetuā ab hac ipsa sinceritatis differentia nominat fidem ἀνυπόκριτον. Quare, vt hæc absoluam; si contigerit vnquam fidem tuam vocari in dubium, præsertim cùm in vera fide & temporaria similia sint plurima, huc erit confugiendū, vt explores an etiam credas in Christum, eúmque diligas sincerè & ex animo, hoc est, non propter te, non propter mundum hunc; sed propter ipsum Christum eiúsque gloriam. Quòd si senseris iam te credere in Christum, etiam propter Christum, aut saltem si non poteris id statim assequi (vt omnes natura nobis ipsi sumus addicti) si senseris velle te credere in Christū propter Christum, velle te omnia facere Dei gratia & ex animo, habes profectò egregium imprimis argumentum perseuerantiæ in fide, & fidei quæ perpetua sit futura.
units.tr: The testing of the heart is necessary. For this sincerity or simplicity of heart consists in this: that we do what we do from the heart, whether it is done toward God or toward men, but for God's sake. We do something from the heart when we look to God and his will. Hence the Apostle says, doing from the heart what God wills. And from this it follows that I think the difference between temporary and perpetual faith is to be sought above all in this sincerity of mind: temporary faith is always joined with a certain pretence and hypocrisy, contrary to sincerity; but perpetual faith is without pretence and hypocrisy, and with sincerity. Hence Paul names true and perpetual faith, from this very difference of sincerity, faith ἀνυπόκριτον [unfeigned]. Therefore, to finish this point: if ever your faith happens to be called into doubt, especially since in true faith and temporary faith there are very many similarities, you must take refuge here, to examine whether you also believe in Christ and love him sincerely and from the heart, that is, not for your own sake, not for this world, but for Christ himself and his glory. But if you have perceived that you already believe in Christ, even for Christ's sake, or at least if you cannot immediately attain this (as we are all by nature inclined to ourselves), yet if you have perceived that you wish to believe in Christ for Christ's sake, wish to do all things by the grace of God and from the heart, you have surely an outstanding argument, above all, for perseverance in faith, and for faith that will be perpetual.

units.la: Hactenus argumento altero commendauit testimonium Iohannis. At ego maius habeo. Rursus per correctionem extenuat hoc Iohannis testimonium comparatione maioris cuiusdam testimonij, quod ipse habet de se. Ego, inquit, maius testimonium habeo testimonio Iohannis. Q. d. Testimonium Iohannis non est illud testimonium quo ego nitor tanquam principali: sed magis est testimonio Iohannis testimonium illud quod ego habeo. Hic locus postulat vt attingamus, sed quàm fieri potest paucissimis, illam controuersiam satis celebrem & iam diu exagitatam de authoritate scriptura. Vrum & Ecclesiæ. Id fatemur omnes pariter, scripta Prophetica & Apostolica esse Dei ipsius verbu ac veritatē. Nisi enim eo loco ea habeamus quo ipsam Dei vocem haberemus, profecto nullum est in his fidei nostrae fundamentum. Sed tota quæstio est de argumento quo constat scripta hæc esse Dei verbum & veritatem. Pontificij respondent ideo constare esse ea Dei verbum, Deïque veritatem his contineri, quia Ecclesia ita dicit. Quòd si hoc Ecclesiæ testimonium tanquam minus principale afferrent, illud quidem ferendum esset: sed hoc testimonium Ecclesiæ tāquam principale ac vnicum fere afferunt, ac loco causæ habent cur habeat authoritatem Scriptura. Notæ enim sunt eorum voces, Maior est authoritas Ecclesiæ quàm Scripturæ. Præstantior est scriptura illa quæ in corde Ecclesiæ exarata est, quàm quæ in membranis vel chartis. Nos autem respondemus, Scripta hæc Prophetica & Apostolica præcipuè intelligi ex ipsis Scripturis quòd sint verbum Dei, nósque per Spiritum Sanctum intus doceri per ipsas Scripturas tanquam organum, & medium Spiritus Sancti primarium, quòd Scripturæ sint verbum Dei. Sunt enim in iis impressæ notæ, ex quibus manifestò conspicitur eas à Deo profectas esse, atque his ipsis adeo contentæ sunt Scripturæ, si per se ipsæ ostentantur, vt præterea nihil opus habeat alio testimonio siue hominū siue Angelorum. Requiri autem dicimus non raro hominum testimonium, propter infirmitatem & cæcitatem nostram, qui non statim possumus per nos ipsi illas notas deprehendere in Scripturis sic elucentes & luculentè satis testificantes Scripturas ipsas esse Dei verbum ac veritatē. Sic tamē requiri dicimus testimonium hominum, vt interea maius sit & grauius testimonium quo nitatur Scriptura, quàm sit illud hominum omnium, adeóque totius Ecclesiæ, nēpe eas ipsas notas eáque argumenta quæ Scripturæ ipsæ nobis suppeditant. Quæ qui semel viderunt ac cognouerunt, postquam iam adducti sunt hominum testimonio, & authoritate Ecclesiæ ad ea videnda & notanda, ita in iis conquieuerunt, vt non amplius iam crediderint Scripturas esse Dei verbum ac veritate propter Ecclesiæ & hominum testificationem, sed propter hæc ipsa in Scripturis elucentia argumenta & testimonia.
units.tr: Hitherto he has commended John's testimony by a second argument. But I have a greater one. Again, by way of correction, he belittles this testimony of John by comparison with a greater testimony which he himself has concerning himself. I, he says, have a greater testimony than the testimony of John. That is: the testimony of John is not that testimony on which I lean as principal; rather, the testimony I have is greater than John's. This place requires that we touch, but in as few words as possible, upon that controversy, quite famous and long debated, about the authority of Scripture, whether it rests on the Church's testimony as well. We all alike confess that the prophetic and apostolic writings are the very Word and truth of God. For unless we had them in the place where we would have God's own voice, there would be truly no foundation of our faith in them. But the whole question concerns the argument by which it is established that these writings are the Word and truth of God. The Papists answer that it is established that they are God's Word, and God's truth is contained in them, because the Church says so. If they brought forward this testimony of the Church as less than principal, that would be bearable; but they bring it forward as principal and almost the only one, and they hold it in place of the cause why Scripture has authority. Their sayings are well known: "The authority of the Church is greater than that of Scripture"; "That writing is more excellent which is inscribed in the heart of the Church than that which is on parchment or paper." We, however, answer: these prophetic and apostolic writings are recognised chiefly from the Scriptures themselves to be the Word of God, and we are taught inwardly by the Holy Spirit through the Scriptures themselves, as an instrument and the primary means of the Holy Spirit, that the Scriptures are the Word of God. For there are impressed in them marks from which it is clearly seen that they came from God, and the Scriptures are so sufficient in themselves, if they are displayed by themselves, that they need no other testimony, whether of men or of angels. We say, however, that the testimony of men is often required because of our weakness and blindness, since we cannot at once by ourselves detect in the Scriptures those marks which shine so clearly and testify plainly enough that the Scriptures are the Word and truth of God. Yet we say that the testimony of men is required in such a way that, meanwhile, the testimony on which Scripture leans is greater and weightier than that of all men, and so of the whole Church: namely, those very marks and arguments which the Scriptures themselves supply to us. Those who have once seen and recognised these, after they have been brought by the testimony of men and the authority of the Church to see and note them, have so rested in them that they no longer believe the Scriptures to be the Word and truth of God on account of the testimony of the Church and of men, but on account of these arguments and testimonies shining forth in the Scriptures.

units.la: Hæc quæ à nobis traduntur omnia habemus ex ore ipsius Christi in hoc contextu loquentis: Ita enim ille primum: Ego, inquit, ab homine testimonium non capto, ver. 34. Ecce igitur, Christus ipsiúsque veritas non egét testimonio humano, si in se ac per se spectentur: Tum ad-dit, Sed hæc dico propter vos vt seruemini. Ecce testimonium humanum requiri ait propter nos nostramque infirmitatem, vt nihil eorum omittatur quibus nos aliquo modo duci possumus eò vt credamus & seruemur. Pohemo ait, At ego maius testimonium habeo testimonio Iohannis. Quibus verbis significat, quòd etsi quidem testimonio humano opus sit propter infirmitatem nostram; tamen non esse illud præcipuum testimonium de Christo eiúsque veritate. Sed quid opus est multis? natura ipsa verę fidei hoc quod dicimus satis arguit, quæ nisi niteretur solidiore fundamento aliquo & testimonio, quâ fit vox Ecclesiæ, hoc est hominum quantumuis sanctificatorum, profectò nunquam creditura sit iis quæ in Scripturis sacris proponuntur: Et nisi Deus reliquisset nobis alias notas, aliáque testimonia & argumenta ex ipsis Scripturis, hoc est, ex ipsius verbo depromenda, ex quibus constare posset hanc esse vocem ac veritatem ipsius, profectò testimonium Ecclesiæ nunquam fecisset huic rei fidem.
units.tr: We have all these things that we deliver from the mouth of Christ himself, speaking in this context. For he says first: I, he says, do not receive testimony from man, v. 34. Behold, then, Christ and his truth do not need human testimony, if they are viewed in themselves and by themselves. Then he adds: But I say these things for your sake, that you may be saved. Behold, he says human testimony is required on account of us and our weakness, so that nothing is omitted by which we may in any way be led to believe and be saved. Then he says: But I have a greater testimony than the testimony of John. By these words he signifies that, although human testimony is indeed needed on account of our weakness, yet it is not the chief testimony concerning Christ and his truth. But why need there be many words? The very nature of true faith argues sufficiently for what we say. Unless it leaned on some firmer foundation and testimony than the voice of the Church, that is, of men however sanctified, it would certainly never believe what is set forth in the holy Scriptures. And unless God had left us other marks, other testimonies and arguments to be drawn from the Scriptures themselves, that is, from his own word, by which it could be established that this is his voice and truth, the testimony of the Church would certainly never have given credence to this matter.

units.la: Opera enim. Sequuntur maiora testimonia, quàm fuit Iohannis illud testimonium; Primum est testimonium operum diuinorum, secundum est testimonium Patris. Opera, inquit, quæ dedit mihi Pater vt ea perficerem, hoc est, quæ communicauit mihi Pater. Nam Pater, vt iam ante dixi, in æterna illa generatione communicauit Filio omnem potestatem faciendi pariter omnia, quæ ipse facit. Sed quænam sunt hæc opera? Non vulgaria quidem illa, sed prodigiosa, & eò magis admiranda, quòd vnà cum corporibus hominum fere restitutæ, sanatæ & sanctificatæ sint animæ, vt apparuit ex sequenti vita & conuersatione eorum, qui ab ipso sanati sunt ac restituti. Nam Christus in iis sanandis ac restituendis præcipuè habuit rationem animæ & vitæ spiritualis, vt iam
units.tr: For the works. There follow greater testimonies than that testimony of John. The first is the testimony of the divine works; the second is the testimony of the Father. "The works," he says, "which the Father has given me to accomplish," that is, which the Father has communicated to me. For the Father, as I said before, in that eternal generation, communicated to the Son all power of doing equally all the things which he himself does. But what are these works? Not ordinary ones, indeed, but prodigious, and all the more admirable because, along with the bodies of men, their souls were almost at the same time restored, healed and sanctified, as appeared from the subsequent life and conduct of those whom he healed and restored. For in healing and restoring them Christ paid especial regard to the soul and the spiritual life, as we have already seen

units.la: Confirmatio authoritatis veri Dei sui testimonii pro omne testimonium humanum. vidimus in sanatione ægroti illius, de quo supra hoc capite verf.5.& deinceps: Quem cùm inueniret in templo, monuit ne rursus peccaret, verf. 14. Sed redeo. Hæc inquit, opera testantur de me, quòd Pater miserit me. Poterant enim videre Iudæi hæc opera talia esse, qualia nemo alius posset edere. Et viderunt quidem haud dubiè talia esse, & viderunt aliquatenus ex operibus eum Filium Dei esse; Iste est hæres, venite, trucidemus eum, & obtineamus hæreditatem eius. Quòd si eum hæredem agnouerunt, ergo & Dei Filium. Sic cùm calumniati essent per Beelzebub principem dæmoniorum, eiicere eum dæmonia, accusat eos peccati in Spiritum Sanctum.Quo significat eos ita illuminatos esse à Spiritu sancto, vt satis viderint Iesum esse Christum & Filium Dei; lucem autem hanc malitiosè ipsos restinxisse. Credat fortasse aliquis Iudæos istos nondum illud vidisse & cognouisse Iesum esse Christum & Dei Filium. Qui enim potuerunt non statim credere in eum quem cognouerunt promissum illum Christum & Dei Filium? Sciat hic velim, quisquis est, eam esse malitiam cordis humani, illud esse odium à natura insitum, vt quanto magis quis videat & cognoscat Deum, tanto magis eum oppugnet, tanto magis eum odio prosequatur. Hodierno die Papistæ conuicti conscientiis hanc esse veritatem quam nos profitemur, quanto magis eam vident, tanto magis oppugnant eam, & indurantur aduersus eam. Quamobrem non est hoc tam admirandum, quòd homines videntes Deum, videntes lucem, Deum & lucem non statim amplectantur; quàm petendum à Deo seriis precibus vt vna cum luce oblata velit reformare corda nostra, voluntates & affectus nostros, ad hoc vt lucem oblatam possimus amplecti.
units.tr: Confirmation of the authority of the true God's testimony over every human testimony. We have seen this in the healing of that sick man, of whom above in this chapter, verse 5 and following: When he found him in the temple, he warned him not to sin again, verse 14. But I return. These works, he says, bear witness of me, that the Father has sent me. For the Jews could see that these works were such as no one else could perform. And they certainly saw that they were such, and they saw to some extent from the works that he was the Son of God. This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize his inheritance. If they recognised him as heir, then also as Son of God. So too, when they slandered him, saying that he cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of the demons, he accuses them of sin against the Holy Spirit. By this he signifies that they had been so enlightened by the Holy Spirit that they saw well enough that Jesus was the Christ and the Son of God, but that they had maliciously extinguished this light. Perhaps someone will think that those Jews had not yet seen and recognised that Jesus was the Christ and Son of God. For how could they not immediately believe in him whom they knew to be the Christ and Son of God who had been promised? Let him know, whoever he is, I would like him to know, that such is the malice of the human heart, such is the hatred implanted by nature, that the more someone sees and knows God, the more he opposes him, and the more he pursues him with hatred. Today the Papists, convicted in their consciences that this is the truth which we profess, the more they see it, the more they oppose it and harden themselves against it. Therefore it is not so remarkable that men, seeing God, seeing the light, do not at once embrace God and the light; rather we must seek from God with earnest prayers that, together with the light offered, he would be willing to reform our hearts, wills and affections, so that we may be able to embrace the light offered.

units.la: Sed quæri potest quonam modo testata sint miracula, ea quæ à Christo edita sunt, ipsum Deum esse, Deíque Filium, cùm etiam Moses & prophetæ veteres multa ante Christum miracula ediderint, eáque maxima, quæ quidem eos diuinos homines non Deos statim arguebant? Concedo equidem edita à prophetis iam olim miracula, edita etiam ab Apostolis Christi multò maiora. Sed ingens discrimen fuisse dico inter eorum & Christi
units.tr: But it may be asked in what way the miracles which were performed by Christ bore witness that he himself is God and the Son of God, since Moses and the ancient prophets also performed many miracles before Christ, and very great ones, which did not immediately prove those divine men to be gods. I indeed concede that miracles were performed by the prophets long ago, and that miracles far greater were performed by the apostles of Christ. But I say there was a vast difference between theirs and the miracles of Christ.

units.la: Hæc opera ra sunt mi racula Christi. sti miracula. Primùm prophetę ediderunt miracula in nomine Iehouę, Dei potestate, non sua: ita etiam Apostoli in nomine Christi operati sunt, qui est Deus laudandus in sæculum. Deinde dico, quòd cùm non nisi Dei potestate ac virtute ediderint illa miracula sua, non pro suo arbitrio & voluntate sua ediderunt ea, sed pro arbitrio & voluntate Dei ipsius. Christus autem & ex potestate sua ipsius, cùm Deus esset, & voluntate sua ipsius ac arbitratu suo miracula sua edidit. Cùm enim Deus in eo σωματικῶς habitaret, quocunq; voluit tempore, quocunq; voluit miracula edidit; perinde vt qui habet animam humanam habitantem in corpore suo, potest quicquid lubet quouis tempore cogitare. Ex hoc discrimine sequitur opera ac miracula à Christo edita talia fuisse qualia nemo operatus est vnquam, & minimum ab eo editum miraculum, cùm sua ipsius potestate ac arbitrio editum fuerit, maius extitisse quàm quoduis maximum editum vel à Propheta aliquo, vel ab Apostolo. Ex quo rursus sequitur, Christi miracula cùm talia fuerint, qualia nemo vnquam edere potuit, testata esse de ipsius deitate eum Deum esse, Deiquè Filium. Hæc diligenter à nobis obseruanda sunt, vt inter legendum & audiendum legimus de miraculis Prophetarum & Apostolorum. Rursus autem de miraculis ipsius Christi, quę omnia, si externum opus spectetur, vel parum, vel nihil discriminis habere videntur. Hic excitauit mortuos, illi quoque idem fecerunt &c. Discamus interea inter ea discrimen longum latúmque statuere, & soli Christo gloriam miraculorum omnium non solùm eorum quę ab ipso edita sunt; verumetiam eorum quę ab aliis quibuscunque, cùm ipsius potestate, & ex ipsius arbitrio ac voluntate edita sint, attribuere.
units.tr: First, the prophets performed miracles in the name of Jehovah, by the power of God, not their own; so also the apostles worked in the name of Christ, who is God blessed for ever. Next, I say that since they performed those miracles only by the power and virtue of God, they did not perform them at their own discretion and will, but at the discretion and will of God himself. But Christ performed his miracles both by his own power, since he was God, and by his own will and free choice. For since God dwelt in him bodily, he performed miracles whenever and however he wished, just as a person who has a human soul dwelling in his body can think whatever he pleases at any time. From this difference it follows that the works and miracles performed by Christ were such as no one ever performed, and that the least miracle performed by him, since it was done by his own power and according to his own will, was greater than any greatest miracle performed either by some prophet or by an apostle. From this again it follows that, since Christ's miracles were such as no one could ever perform, they bore witness of his deity that he is God and the Son of God. These things we must observe carefully, so that as we read and hear of the miracles of the prophets and apostles, we also read again of the miracles of Christ himself, which all, if the outward work is considered, seem to have little or no difference. "He raised the dead; they too did the same," and so on. Let us learn meanwhile to establish between them a difference wide and long, and to ascribe to Christ alone the glory of all miracles, not only of those which were performed by him, but also of those which were performed by any others whatever, since they were performed by his power and according to his discretion and will.

units.la: 37 Et qui misit me Pater, ipse testatus est de me. Neque vocem eius vnquam audistis, neque speciem eius vidistis.
units.tr: And the Father himself, who sent me, has borne witness of me. You have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape.

units.la: 38 Et sermonem eius non habetis in vobis manentem: quia quem misit ille, huic vos non creditis.
units.tr: And you do not have his word abiding in you: for him whom he sent, you do not believe.

units.la: 39 Scrutamini scripturas, quia vos videtis vobis in ipsis vitam æternam habere: & illæ sunt quæ testantur de me.
units.tr: Search the Scriptures; for you think that in them you have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.

units.la: 40 Sed non vultis venire ad me, ut vitam habeatis.
units.tr: 40 But you will not come to me, that you might have life.

units.la: {a}HOc est alterum testimonium magnum, testimonium ipsius Patris. De hoc testimonio Patris, lege primum Matth. 3. 17. quo enim tempore baptizaretur, audita est vox è cœlis, dicens, Hic est Filius ille meus dilectus, in quo acquiesco. Lege rursus Matth. 17. 5. quo enim tempore transformaretur in monte; ecce vox è nube audita est, dicens, Hic est Filius meus dilectus in quo acquiesco, ipsum audite. De hoc quoque vide 2. Pet. 1. 17. Hic locus, de testimoniis de Christo perhibitis, requirit ut de iis, eorumque usu pauca quædam altius repetamus.
units.tr: This is the second great testimony, the testimony of the Father himself. Concerning this testimony of the Father, read first Matthew 3:17, where, at the time he was baptised, a voice was heard from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Read again Matthew 17:5, where at the time he was transfigured on the mountain, behold, a voice was heard out of the cloud, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him. See also 2 Peter 1:17 concerning this. This place, concerning the testimonies borne about Christ, requires that we go back over these, and their use, a little more thoroughly.

units.la: Filij Dei Christi hoc officium est, ut sit Mediator novi fœderis, hoc est, ut sanguine suo stabiliat fœdus istud gratiæ. Hunc honorem non sibi assumpsit, ait Apostolus, sed eum tribuit ei is qui dixit, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Ergo vocatus est à Patre ad munus illud Mediatoris. Vocatio Christi in hoc consistit, quòd ut Filius quidem Dei est, sanctificatus sit ab æterno ad hoc munus Mediatoris; ut verò homo est, ab utero matris ad idem illud munus sit sanctificatus. Hanc autem vocationem Filij sui Deus multis modis testatâ fecit hominibus: Primùm voce sua è cœlis, Tu es Filius meus, genui te hodie, ut modò diximus. Neque voce nuda testatus est hoc, sed adhibuit præterea solenne iusiurandum, quo non modò vocationem Filij sui, sed etiam excellentiam eius præ cæteris omnibus commendauit: Iurauit Iehova, & non pœnitebit eum, Tu es Sacerdos in sæculum secundum ordinem Melchisedeci. Misit quoque Angelos qui de hac ipsa vocatione testarētur. Postremò familiarem testem Iohannem Baptistam misit Christi præcursorem, qui testatus est ipsum esse Agnum illum Dei qui tolleret peccata mundi. Vides igitur usum istorum omnium testimoniorum hunc fuisse, ut confirmaretur vocatio Christi, cum nimirum missum esse à Patre Mediatore novi fœderis & nos in ipsum crederemus, quæ est novi & gratuiti fœderis conditio. Deus enim ipse, qui requirit à nobis illam fidei conditionem, omnibus modis implet eam, vt foedus omnino, & ex omni parte gratuitum esset.Qui misit me Pater. Cauendum est ne quis ex hac missione Filij colligat Filium Patre inferiorem, eúmque inaequalem natura & gloria. Fieri enim potest vt aequalis aequalem mittat ad munus inferius vtroque, modò ex consensu vtriusque partis id fiat. In hanc sententiam scribit Cyrillus, Missio, inquiens, & obedientia non tollit aequalitatem potentiae. Huiusmodi autem est missio Filij Dei: ex communi enim consilio & decreto Filius ab illa aequalitate sese ipse ad tempus dimisit, ac inaniuit se, forma serui accepta.
