Quare cum audimus eum missum esse a Patre, tantum abesse debemus ab eo, vt propterea putemus eum natura & maiestate inaequalem Patri, vt è contrà miremur in eo tantam misericordiam erga nos indignissimos, vt nostra causa, ad hoc vt nos redimeret, ab aequalitate illa sese dimiserit ad tempus. Nam sciendum est non tantùm Christum hominem obedientem fuisse Patri; sed & Christum filium Dei ad tempus obediuisse Patri suo sponte ac voluntate sua. Huic igitur sit gloria in perpetuum. Amen.
units.tr: It is the office of the Son of God, Christ, to be the Mediator of the new covenant, that is, to ratify that covenant of grace with his own blood. He did not take this honour to himself, says the apostle, but it was given to him by him who said, Thou art my Son, today have I begotten thee. Therefore he was called by the Father to that office of Mediator. The calling of Christ consists in this: that as he is the Son of God he was sanctified from eternity for this office of Mediator, and as he is man he was sanctified for the same office from his mother's womb. God, however, made this calling of his Son known to men in many ways. First, by his own voice from heaven, Thou art my Son, today have I begotten thee, as we have just said. Nor did he attest this by a bare voice alone, but he added also a solemn oath, by which he commended not only the calling of his Son but also his excellence above all others: The Lord has sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. He also sent angels who should bear witness to this very calling. Lastly, he sent as a familiar witness John the Baptist, the forerunner of Christ, who testified that he was that Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. You see, then, that the use of all these testimonies was this: that the calling of Christ might be confirmed, namely that he was sent by the Father as Mediator of the new covenant, and that we might believe in him, which is the condition of the new and free covenant. For God himself, who requires from us that condition of faith, fulfils it in every way, so that the covenant might be altogether and in every respect free. Him whom the Father sent. Care must be taken lest anyone conclude from this sending of the Son that the Son is inferior to the Father, and unequal in nature and glory. For it can happen that an equal sends an equal to a task inferior to both, provided this is done by the consent of both parties. To this effect Cyril writes: "Sending, he says, and obedience do not take away equality of power." Such is the sending of the Son of God: for by common counsel and decree the Son, from that equality, dismissed himself for a time, and emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Wherefore, when we hear that he was sent by the Father, we ought to be far from thinking therefore that he is unequal to the Father in nature and majesty; rather, on the contrary, we should marvel at such great mercy in him towards us most unworthy, that for our sake, in order to redeem us, he for a time dismissed himself from that equality. For we must understand that Christ was not only obedient to the Father as man, but also that Christ, the Son of God, of his own accord and by his own will, for a time obeyed his Father. To him therefore be glory for ever. Amen.

units.la: Sequitur reprehensio Iudaeorum ad finem vsque sermonis ipsius. In reprehensione quod obiicit iis primùm est ignorantia Dei, Neque vocem eius, inquit, audistis vnquam, neque speciem eius vidistis. Phrasis est desumpta ab hominibus qui alij aliorum prorsus sunt ignari. Sic enim loquimur vulgò, quoties arguimus summam eorum ignorantiam, eos neque de voce, neque de facie alium quem cognoscere. Hi enim sunt duo modi quibus internoscimus homines, & alios ab aliis discernimus, nempe vox & vultus. Quare sensus est, Etsi iactetis notitiam Dei; tamen eius estis ignari, adeo vt neque de voce, neque de vultu eum cognitum habeatis. Sed quaeri potest, Annon saltem agnouerunt eum de voce; An ita prorsus ignari fuerunt? Respondeo, non intelligi hoc loco nudam & simplicem ignorantiam, sed infidelitatem, qua sermoni eius non crediderunt; ideo subiicitur protinus; Et sermonem eius non habetis in vobis manentem. Hoc est, non creditis sermoni eius. Nam per fidem apprehendentem ipsum manet sermo Dei in cordibus
units.tr: The rebuke of the Jews continues to the end of his speech. In the rebuke, the first charge against them is ignorance of God: You have never heard his voice, he says, nor seen his form. The phrase is taken from people who are utterly ignorant of one another. We speak this way in ordinary talk whenever we want to show how little someone knows, saying that he could not recognise another by voice or by face. These are the two ways by which we know people and tell one from another, namely voice and face. So the sense is: although you boast of knowing God, you are ignorant of him, so much so that you have never known him by his voice or his face. But someone may ask, did they not at least know him by his voice? Were they so utterly ignorant? I answer that the passage does not mean bare and simple ignorance, but unbelief, by which they did not believe his word. That is why it is added at once: And you do not have his word abiding in you. That is, you do not believe his word. For the word of God abides in hearts through faith that grasps it.

units.la: Confirmatio, à missione filii.
units.tr: Confirmation, from the sending of the Son.

units.la: Philip. 2.7.
units.tr: Phil. 2.7.

units.la: Peccatum Iudaeorum multiplex.
units.tr: The sin of the Jews is manifold.

units.la: 1. Ignorantia Dei.
units.tr: 1. Ignorance of God.

units.la: Qualis illa fuerit. nostris : Rursus per infidelitatem stat quo minus in no-bis maneat sermo Dei. Obserua igitur frustra iactare quemquam se nosse Deum, qui non credit in eum, & in sermonem eius. Is enim tandem audiet ex Domino hæc ipsa verba; Neque vocem eius audisti vnquam, neque speciem eius vidisti. Quare inter audiendum verbum Dei imprimis cura esse debet, vt in ipsum iam cognitum credamus, nobisq; ipsum applicemus. Quia quem misit ille. Ratio est cur non habeat sermonem Patris in se manentem, quia nimirum non credunt in Filium quem misit; qui autem non honorat Filium, non honorat Patrem, vt dictum est supra hoc cap. vers. 23. Quo autem appareat alterum sequi exaltero, substernit argumentationi propositionem & fundamentum suum. Sermo Dei vniuersus est de Filio. At vos non creditis Filio; Ergo vos non creditis eius sermoni. Propositio est his verbis, Scrutamini scripturas. Ablegat eos ad scripturas, quæ nihil aliud sunt quàm sermo Dei. Rationem addit ab illo bono, nepe vita æterna, quod inde se percepturos putabant. Nam vos videmini, inquit, vobis in ipsis vitam æternam habere. Scrutamini igitur & videte nunquid illæ testentur de me. Nota primùm, dum sermonem Dei de Filio innuit, ad scripturas eos amandat. Ergo si vis audire vocem Dei loquentis, require eum ex Scripturis; neque enim vnquam reuelationem aliquam à Deo impetraturus es in hac vita extra has, quas in manibus habemus Scripturas. In quas tamen aduersarij adeo iniurij sunt, vt mendacia sua & vocem Antichristianæ Ecclesiæ iis prælatam esse velint. Sed væ illis. Nota deinde, vniuersa scriptura testatur de Christo, estque ille materia ac scopus veteris totius scripturæ. Lex enim vetus tanquam Pædagogus quidam rudiorem populum ad eum manu deducebat. Prophetæ omnes eum prædixerunt futurum. Vnde Paulus de illa iustitia Dei loquens: comprobatam dicit eam testimonio legis & Prophetarum. Item, Finis legis, inquit, est Christus. Hinc duo sequuntur, primum ex Scripturis solis, cùm illæ sufficientes sint ac perfectæ, requirendum & discendum esse Christum: Scripturas dico primùm veteres, deinde nouas. Quòd si Christum extra scripturas quæsiueris in inuentionibus & traditionibus humanis,
units.tr: What sort it was. Again, through unbelief, the word of God is prevented from abiding in us. Observe, then, that anyone who does not believe in him and in his word boasts in vain that he knows God. Such a person will at last hear from the Lord these very words: You have never heard his voice, nor have you seen his form. So, when we hear the word of God, the first care must be that we believe in him whom we now know, and apply him to ourselves. Because he whom he sent. The reason why they do not have the word of the Father abiding in them is that they do not believe in the Son whom he sent. And whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father, as was said above in this chapter, verse 23. To show that the one follows from the other, he lays down the premise and foundation of his argument. The whole word of God is about the Son. But you do not believe the Son; therefore you do not believe his word. The premise is in these words, Search the Scriptures. He sends them to the Scriptures, which are nothing other than the word of God. He adds a reason drawn from that good thing, namely eternal life, which they thought they would obtain from them. For you think, he says, that in them you have eternal life. Search, therefore, and see whether they bear witness to me. Note first that, in hinting that the word of God is about the Son, he sends them to the Scriptures. So if you want to hear the voice of God speaking, seek him in the Scriptures; for you will never obtain any revelation from God in this life apart from those Scriptures which we have in our hands. Yet our adversaries are so unjust towards them that they want their own lies, and the voice of the Antichristian Church, to be placed above them. But woe to them. Note next that the whole of Scripture bears witness to Christ, and he is the subject and aim of the whole of the Old Testament. For the old law, like a kind of tutor, led the cruder people by the hand to him. All the prophets foretold that he would come. Hence Paul, speaking of that righteousness of God, says that it is attested by the testimony of the Law and the Prophets. Likewise, the end of the law, he says, is Christ. From this two things follow. First, since the Scriptures alone are sufficient and perfect, Christ must be sought and learned from the Scriptures alone: I mean first the old, then the new. But if you seek Christ outside the Scriptures, in human inventions and traditions,

units.la: Rom. 3. 21. Rom. 10. 4. Galat. 3. 24. nis, profecto pro Christo, nihil nisi umbratile quoddam spectrum deprehensurus es. Alterum quod sequitur est ut ad legendum & audiendum scripturas eo animo accedamus, ut Christum inveniamus & cognoscamus, neque cognoscamus modo, sed in eum credamus. Neque satisfiat nobis quotiescunque contingit audire scripturas has interpretatas & explicatas, nisi eum domum quasi nobiscum & in cordibus nostris deportemus. Quod si alio animo accedamus ad eas audiedas, si animo quidem consequendi vel iustitiam vel vitam aeternam sine Christo, id quod Iudaei isti fecerunt, profecto inutiliter illud fiet. Si denique Christum ipsum non reportaverimus, non est quod placeamus nobis vel in lectione, vel in auditione, vel in cognitione omnium scripturarum.
units.tr: Rom. 3.21. Rom. 10.4. Gal. 3.24. you will certainly find, instead of Christ, nothing but some shadowy phantom. The second consequence is that we should approach the reading and hearing of the Scriptures with the intention of finding and knowing Christ, and not merely knowing him, but believing in him. We should not be satisfied whenever we happen to hear these Scriptures interpreted and explained, unless we carry him home with us, as it were, and into our hearts. If we approach them to hear them with another intention, if indeed with the intention of obtaining righteousness or eternal life without Christ, which those Jews did, this will certainly be fruitless. Finally, if we have not carried Christ himself away, there is no reason for us to be pleased with ourselves, whether in reading, in hearing, or in knowing all the Scriptures.

units.la: Sed non vultis venire ad me.Hoc secundum est peccatum, quod obiicit iis, nempe malitia & obstinatio. Occasio eius arrepta esse videtur ex verbis proximis, Q.d. Quanquam scripturae testantur de me, ac propterea vos ignari non potestis esse mei; tamen non vultis venire ad me, quod profecto necesse est ex malitia esse & obstinatione animi, cum scientes, nolitis tamen venire. Hic locus requirit, ut dicamus nonnulla de obstinatione Iudaeorum, quae contigit eo tempore potissimum quo Christus in mundum hunc venit. De hac sic praedixit Esaias 6.9.10. Tum dicit, I, & dicito populo isti, Audite continenter, at ne intelligatis, & videte continenter, neque cognoscatis; fac ut pinguescat cor populi istius, & aures eius ingraviscant, oculique eius connivent, ne videat oculis suis, & auribus suis audiat, & corde suo intelligat, convertensque sanet se. Quibus quidem verbis habemus & modum, quo induratus est hic populus, & quae secuta sunt indurationem. Modus est per auditionem, imo per cognitionem aliquam verbi Dei, neque etiam quae mentis est tantum. At ne intelligatis: haec est cordis induratio, & ex ea rursus mentis excaecatio. Indurationis haec tum est cum non intelligimus corde, hoc est, affectamur veritati etiam cognitae. Tum ait, fac ut pinguescat cor populi istius; fac nempe continenter praedicando verbum. Est igitur hic repetita praedicatio & auditio verbi. Ut pinguescat; Haec est extrema induratio cu excæcatione, quæ significatur illa, vt sic dicam, insensibilitate, quæ solet esse carnis pinguioris, cui Physici negant sensum. Sed hic mireris, quomodo ex verbo audito, item intellecto, sequatur hæc induratio. Respondeo, verum quidem esse verbum Dei per se, & suapte natura illuminare mentes nostras, & emollire atque aperire cor nostrum; sed Deo non operante efficaciter cum verbo suo per Spiritum suum sanctum in corde nostro, quæ est cordis nostri malitia, quanto magis nobis illucescit verbum, tanto magis induramur & excæcamur, idque nostro ipsorum vitio, vt vitio ægri ac lippientis oculi fit, vt ad Solem ipse magis cæcutiat. Quod autem sequitur hanc indurationem, primum est cor quod resipiscere nescit, vt vocatur à Paulo. Nam vbi peruentum est ad extremam indurationem, tum cor nescit resipiscere. Deinde ex corde quod resipiscere nescit, sequitur iusta damnatio. Fateor quidem hunc Esaiæ Prophetæ locum competere in eos qui eadem cum ipso ætate vixerunt: verùm Apostoli eundem hunc locum transcribunt ad tempus Christi & ad eum populum qui fuit eo tempore quo Christus manifestaretur in carne & commoraretur inter Iudæos; Et Paulus ait ista omnia veteri populo euenisse typicè dñtaxat, scripta verò esse ad nostri admonitionem in quos fines sæculorum occurrerunt. Neque immeritò id fecerunt Apostoli, quandoquidem in aduentu Christi, & in regno Christi demum completa est ista induratio & excæcatio. Nam quò maior est lux verbi, ac apertior mysterij illius reuelatio, eò maior est impœnitentia & cordis durities: quò autem maior impœnitentia & cordis durities, eò maior damnatio sequitur. Et experientia satis docet nullam fuisse vnquam tam horribilem indurationem & excæcationem, quàm quæ hodierno die est Papistarum, in hac tam clara Euangelij luce & prædicatione palpantium.
units.tr: But you are not willing to come to me. This is the second sin with which he charges them, namely malice and obstinacy. The occasion for it seems to have been taken from the words just before, as if he said: although the Scriptures bear witness to me, and so you cannot be ignorant of me, yet you are not willing to come to me; which must surely come from malice and obstinacy of mind, since you know and yet are unwilling to come. Here it is necessary to say something about the obstinacy of the Jews, which occurred especially at the time when Christ came into this world. Of this Isaiah foretold: 6.9.10. Then he says, Go, and say to this people, Hear continually, but do not understand; and see continually, but do not know. Make the heart of this people fat, and make its ears heavy, and shut its eyes, lest it see with its eyes, and hear with its ears, and understand with its heart, and turn and be healed. In these words we have both the manner in which this people was hardened and the consequences that followed the hardening. The manner is by hearing, indeed by a certain knowledge of the word of God, and not merely by the mind. But lest you understand: this is hardening of the heart, and from it in turn blinding of the mind. This hardening occurs when we do not understand with the heart, that is, when we are not moved by the truth even when we know it. Then he says, make the heart of this people fat; that is, by preaching the word continually. Here, then, there is repeated preaching and hearing of the word. That it may grow fat: this is the extreme hardening together with blindness, signified by that insensibility, so to speak, which is wont to belong to fatter flesh, which the physicians say lacks feeling. But here one may wonder how this hardening follows from the word heard and also understood. I answer that the word of God is indeed true in itself and by its own nature illuminates our minds, and softens and opens our hearts; but when God does not work effectively with his word through his Holy Spirit in our heart, which is the malice of our heart, the more the word shines upon us, the more we are hardened and blinded, and this by our own fault, just as the eye of a sick or bleary person becomes dimmer when it looks at the sun. What follows this hardening is first a heart that does not know how to repent, as Paul calls it. For when the extreme hardening has been reached, then the heart does not know how to repent. Next, from a heart that does not know how to repent, just damnation follows. I grant that this passage of the prophet Isaiah fits those who lived in the same age as he did; but the Apostles transcribe this same passage to the time of Christ and to the people who were there when Christ was manifested in the flesh and dwelt among the Jews. And Paul says that all those things happened to the old people only as types, but were written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. The Apostles did not do this without reason, since this hardening and blinding was finally completed at the coming of Christ and in the kingdom of Christ. For the greater the light of the word and the clearer the revelation of that mystery, the greater the impenitence and hardness of heart; and the greater the impenitence and hardness of heart, the greater the damnation that follows. And experience teaches well enough that there has never been so terrible a hardening and blinding as that which today belongs to the Papists, who grope in this so clear light of the Gospel and its preaching.

units.la: Nec vultis venire ad me vt vitam habeatis. Vnica ratio est consequendi vitam, nempe Christus & fides in eum. Putarunt tamen Iudæi, vt vidimus, se cōsecuturos vitam sine Christo. Non reprehendo hoc quòd homines promittant sibi vitam, & certò quidem promittant; sed in eo errant miseri, quòd sine Christo promittant sibi vitam. Melior est ad tempus horror conscientiæ cū magnis dubitationibus coniunctus (nam is est ad Christū gradus quidam) quàm falsa illa conscientiæ pax & carnalis securitas. Pij autem in se hoc experiuntur tum demum esse non modò certam spem vitæ, cum Christum fide amplectuntur: verùm vitam etiam ipsam in se inchoari; vbi verò eum non apprehendunt vt volunt, neque eum sentiunt in corde habitantem vt expetūt, tum profecto tantumdem decedere sentiunt de spe salutis, de gaudiis ac securitate ipsorum.
units.tr: Nor are you willing to come to me that you may have life. There is only one way to obtain life, namely Christ and faith in him. Yet the Jews, as we have seen, supposed that they would obtain life without Christ. I do not object to men promising themselves life, and surely they do promise it. Their wretchedness lies in promising themselves life without Christ. A troubled conscience, joined with great doubts, is better for a time (for it is a certain step towards Christ) than that false peace of conscience and carnal security. The godly, however, experience in themselves that there is then not only a sure hope of life, when they embrace Christ by faith, but that life itself begins within them. But when they do not grasp him as they wish, and do not feel him dwelling in their hearts as they desire, then they truly feel how much hope of salvation, joy and security is lost to them.

units.la: 41 Gloriam ab hominibus non capto.
units.tr: 41 I do not seek glory from men.

units.la: 42 Sed vos noui charitatem Dei non habere in vobis.
units.tr: 42 But I know that you do not have the love of God in you.

units.la: 43 Ego veni nomine Patris mei, nec recipitis me: si venerit alius nomine suo, illum recipietis.
units.tr: 43 I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, you will receive him.

units.la: 44 Quomodo vos potestis credere, quum gloriam ab alijs captetis, & gloriam illam, quæ à solo Deo proficiscitur, non quæratis?
units.tr: 44 How can you believe, since you seek glory from one another, and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?

units.la: Equitur tertium peccatum quod iis obiicit & quod in iis reprehendit, nempe absentia charitatis Dei, sub qua simul odium in Deum intelligit. Priusquam autem ad ipsum descendat, occupat quod occasione præcedentium verborum obiici potuit. Dixit eos noluisse venire ad se; Vnde illis in mentem venire potuit Dominum capta esse suam gloriam ab eis, quā sine eis consequi non posset. Huic respondet, & gloriam, inquit, ab hominibus nō capto. q.d. Quòd quæstus sum nolle vos venire ad me, non ideo id feci quasi verò ego indigeam gloria à vobis, neque possim satis gloriosus esse sine vobis. Quod quò melius intelligatur à nobis, sciendum est Deum illum vnum & trinum in se ita perfectum esse & sufficientem, vt in eo nihil desiderari possit ad summam felicitatem & gloriam. Hinc sequitur hoc, quod de se ait Dominus hoc loco, Gloriam ab hominibus non capto; sequitur, inquam, nihil per creaturā vel ad Dei gloriā adduci posse, nel de ea detrahi, sed Deū semper æquè gloriosum in se permanere, ante conditum mundū & creaturas æquè gloriosum fuisse atque nunc est; creaturam autem esse non posse sine eo, vel vt bene habeat se, vel vt sint omnino. In ipso viuimus, mouemur ac sumus. Ex eo & per eum, & in ipsum sunt omnia; ipsi sit gloria in sæcula, Amen. Quòd si obiiciatur, Cur ergo dicitur à nobis glorificari Deus, contráque à nobis dedecorari & ignominia affici? vt ait Paulus. Per legis transgressionem Deum dedecoras. Hinc enim videtur sequi aliquid per nos accedere ad Dei gloriam, rursúsque aliquid de ea decedere? Respondeo in Scripturis, gloriæ Dei nomine aliâs significari virtutes illas quæ in Deo sunt, vel in virtutibus excellentiam, opera eius, & intuitum ac approbationem operum Dei, quæ est in ipso Deo: nam Deus intuetur opera sua eáque approbat & se glorificat. Hanc gloriam si intelligas, profectò nihil ei potest addi, nihil ab ea potest auferri, sed sui similis perpetuò manet æquè magna semper ac gloriosa. De hac gloria loquetur Dominus postea, Pater, glorifica me apud temetipsum ea gloria quam habui apud te, priusquam hic mundus existeret. De hac gloria loquitur Dominus hoc loco. Alias gloria Dei significat illam celebrationem & agnitionem excellentiæ & gloriæ Dei, quæ est in ipso Deo, ac operum eius. Ea quidem augeri ac imminui potest, ita tamen vt nihil idcirco de propria & vera Dei gloria ac felicitate decedat, nihil ad eam accedat, nihil ea vel iuuetur vel lædatur; sed ipsa creatura vel melior vel deterior reddatur, prout agnoscit vel non agnoscit illam, quæ in Deo est, gloriam. Nam ea est felicitas creaturæ summa, Deum suum glorificare: Et ea est miseria creaturæ maxima, Deum suum non glorificare. Quare, cum tam benignè invitet nos Deus ad se glorificandum; cum (vt loquar cum Apostolo) obsecret & precetur nos Deus per seruos suos, vt reconciliemur ei, vt credamus in Dominum Iesum; nemo existimet hoc ideo à Deo fieri, quasi vero requirat de manu nostra felicitate suam; verùm eo consilio fieri vt inueniamus nos tandem felicitatem & gloriam nostram, neque putemus Deum esse nobis ideo obligatum ac devinctum quòd nos illi seruiamus & in eum credamus; sed putemus potius nos obligatos esse Deo ad ei inseruiendum. Cōsideremus igitur quanta sit misericordia Dei nostri, dum invitat nos tam benignè
units.tr: Follows the third sin, which he charges against them and rebukes in them, namely the absence of the love of God, under which he understands at the same time hatred of God. Before coming to that, however, he deals with an objection that could arise from the preceding words. He had said that they were unwilling to come to him, so it could occur to them that the Lord was seeking his own glory from them, which he could not obtain without them. To this he replies: "I do not receive glory from men." That is, as if he said: "Although I complained that you were unwilling to come to me, I did not do so as though I needed glory from you, or could not be glorious enough without you." So that this may be better understood by us, it must be known that God, one and three, is in himself so perfect and sufficient that nothing can be lacking in him for supreme happiness and glory. Hence follows what the Lord says of himself here, "I do not receive glory from men." It follows, I say, that nothing can be added to God's glory through a creature, or taken from it; God remains always equally glorious in himself, and before the world was made and the creatures existed he was as glorious as he is now. A creature cannot exist without him, either to be well or to be at all. "In him we live, move and have our being." "From him, through him and to him are all things; to him be glory for ever, Amen." But if it is objected, why then do we say that God is glorified by us, and on the contrary dishonoured and disgraced by us, as Paul says: By transgressing the law you dishonour God? For from this it seems to follow that something comes to God's glory through us, and again that something decreases from it. I answer: in Scripture the name of God's glory signifies at other times those virtues which are in God, or the excellence of his works, and the regard and approval of his works, which is in God himself; for God regards his works, approves them and glorifies himself. If you understand glory in this sense, certainly nothing can be added to it or taken from it; it remains always like itself, equally great and glorious. Of this glory the Lord will speak later: "Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before this world existed." Of this glory the Lord speaks in this place. At other times the glory of God signifies that celebration and acknowledgement of the excellence and glory of God which is in God himself, and of his works. This indeed can be increased or diminished, yet in such a way that nothing is thereby taken from God's own and true glory and happiness, nothing added to it, and it is neither helped nor harmed by it; rather the creature itself is made better or worse, according as it acknowledges or does not acknowledge the glory which is in God. For this is the highest happiness of a creature, to glorify its God, and this is its greatest misery, not to glorify its God. Wherefore, since God invites us so kindly to glorify him; since (to speak with the Apostle) God begs and entreats us through his servants that we be reconciled to him and believe in the Lord Jesus; let no one think that this is done by God as though he sought his happiness from our hand. Rather it is done with this purpose, that we may at last find our own happiness and glory. Nor let us think that God is therefore bound and obliged to us because we serve him and believe in him; rather let us think that we are bound to God, to serve him. Let us consider therefore how great is the mercy of our God, while he invites us so kindly

units.la: 2.Cor.5.20. nigne ad id quod est officij nostri, imo ad felicitatem, bonum & gloriam nostram ipsorum; & ei semper gratias agamus, Cui sit omnis gloria, Amen.
units.tr: 2.Cor.5.20. kindly to that which is our duty, indeed to our own happiness, good and glory; and let us always give thanks to him, to whom be all glory, Amen.

units.la: Hactenus sic transfiuit ad tertium peccatum; nunc sequitur ipsum peccatum. Sed, inquit, noui vos charitatem Dei, &c. Q.d. Quanquam ego gloriam à vobis non capto, neque egeo vobis aut vestro cultu; tamen vos qui negatis mihi gloriam iure mihi debitam, plane id ostenditis, charitatem Dei non esse in vobis, vos prorsus destitutos esse charitate Dei & dilectione. Nota vbi semel dilectio Dei occupauit animum hominis, dici non potest quàm sedulus euadat in Deo suo seruiendo, nihil non agit vt ipsi placere possit, & quod agit si non sentiat illud quicquid tandem sit quod facit siue domi, siue foris, si non sentiat illud Dei cultum esse aliquem (Dei autem cultus est si animo glorificandi Dei fiat) nunquam profecto eo est contentus, neq; habet veram illam ωπαρκεια, ne si quidem agendo & laborando lucretur totum hunc mundum. Postquam verò laborando in gloriam Dei & agendo quod ipsi placeat sese fatigauit, ne respirare quidem se vnquam patitur, putatque se postquam omnia fecit, adhuc tamē inutilem esse seruum, & continuo quaerit à Deo, O Domine, nunquid est aliud quod per me vis fieri? Ideo q; Moses primum, deinde post eum Christus totum illud Dei obsequium, totum cultum eius reduxit ad vnum hoc caput, nempe dilectionem Dei. Dilige, inquit, Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, ex tota anima tua, ex tota cogitatione tua. Q.d. non opus est vt sollicitus sis de obsequio Dei, hoc vnum age, dilige Deum tuum ex corde tuo, tum quod reliquum est illud totum, sua sponte dilectionem sequetur. Quòd si hoc verū sit, quòd qui diligit Deū ex toto corde suo, is semper studeat ei placere & seruire: annon è contra id verum erit, quòd qui non serio studet placere Deo, is non diligit Deum suum? Quid igitur de iis dicemus, qui in tota vita id vnum agunt vt Deo displiceant, qui contemnunt verbum ipsius, qui moechantur, qui occidunt, qui diripiunt aliena, imo qui ipsum Deū sacrilegè spoliant? Quid, inquam, de his dicemus? Annon necesse est eos destitui illa Dei charitate, & quid boni habere possunt, qui non habent in corde suo Dei dilectionem ad aliquam certè mensuram? Quare de hac dilectione Dei imprimis oportet nos sollicitos esse. Scio autem non suppeditari eam nobis à natura: via & ratio vnica eius obtinendæ, est fides in Iesum Christum. Nam quid putas aliud fidem esse, quàm sensum & gustum infinitæ misericordiæ & φιλανθρωπίας Dei in Christo? Hic sensus misericordiæ & amoris Dei erga nos, is est qui laxat corda nostra, soluitque ea in dilectionem Dei mutuam. & lætitiâ ineffabilem. Quare quod ante omnia commendo omnibus, fides est in Christum: dum iubeo eos credere, iubeo vna eademque opera omnia facere, iubeo diligere Deum, iubeo illi omnibus modis obsequentes esse; Hæc enim omnia ex fide Christi promanant, Cui sit omnis gloria in sæcula, Amen.
units.tr: Thus far he has passed over to the third sin; now follows the sin itself. "But," he says, "I know you, that you have not the love of God, etc." That is: "Although I do not receive glory from you, and have no need of you or of your worship, nevertheless you, who deny me the glory rightly due to me, plainly show that the love of God is not in you, and that you are utterly destitute of the love and affection of God." Note: when the love of God has once taken possession of a man's soul, it cannot be said how diligent he becomes in serving his God; he does everything so as to be able to please him, and whatever he does, if he does not feel that it is some worship of God (and it is worship of God if it is done with the intention of glorifying God), he is never truly content with it, and he does not have that true self-sufficiency [αὐταρκεία], not even if by acting and labouring he gains the whole world. But after he has wearied himself by labouring for God's glory and doing what pleases him, he does not even allow himself to breathe; he thinks that, after doing everything, he is still an unprofitable servant, and he constantly asks God: O Lord, is there anything else you want done through me? Therefore Moses first, and after him Christ, reduced that whole obedience of God, his whole worship, to this one head, namely the love of God. Love, he says, the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, with your whole mind. That is: there is no need for you to be anxious about the obedience of God; do this one thing, love your God with your heart, and all the rest will follow of its own accord from love. But if this is true, that whoever loves God with his whole heart always strives to please and serve him, will it not conversely be true that whoever does not earnestly strive to please God does not love his God? What then shall we say of those who in their whole life do this one thing, that they displease God; who despise his word, who commit adultery, who murder, who plunder what belongs to others, indeed who sacrilegiously rob God himself? What, I say, shall we say of these? Must they not necessarily be destitute of that love of God? And what good can they have who do not have in their heart the love of God, at least to some measure? Wherefore we must above all be anxious about this love of God. I know, however, that it is not supplied to us by nature; the one way and reason of obtaining it is faith in Jesus Christ. For what do you think faith is, other than a sense and taste of the infinite mercy and philanthropy of God in Christ? This sense of God's mercy and love toward us is what loosens our hearts and turns them into a mutual love of God and an ineffable joy. Therefore what I commend above all to everyone is faith in Christ. When I bid them believe, I bid them do all things by one and the same work; I bid them love God; I bid them be obedient to him in every way. For all these things spring from faith in Christ, to whom be all glory for ever, Amen.

units.la: Ego veni nomine Patris mei. Hoc est quartum peccatum quod illis obiicitur, iniustitia siue iniuria in Dominum: queritur enim quodammodo secum iniustè agi ab eis & se, cum nomine Patris veniat ad eos, reiici tamen: alios autem falsos Prophetas & doctores, qui suo nomine veniunt, recipiendos ab iis. Queritur ergo de graui iniuria. Neque hæc iniustitia est eorum propria, sed in omnibus hominibus est natura. Omnes enim natura hac iniuriam facimus Deo & veritati ipsius, qua eû eiúsque veritatem postponimus falsis doctoribus & medaciis, & in delectu faciedo mendacium eligimus, veritatem respuimus, atque ideo iniusti sumus & iniurij in veritatem. Neque audiendi sunt qui huic iniustitiæ prætexere solet vel simplicitatem, vel ignorantiam, vel errorem, vel quid tale. Imò verò affirmo iniustam hanc cum Deo agendi rationem, non tam ex ignorantia vlla existere, quàm ex infito penitus odio veritatis & amore mendaciorum. Vnde enim, quæso, est hoc, quòd si exsurgat quis verus doctor à Deo missus, tam ægrè, tam pauci eum audiant, eúmque sequatur? Si verò emittatur ex inferis falsus aliquis doctor, tam facilè tam multi eum exosculentur? Vnde fuit illud quòd vniuersus fere mundus sequutus fit Antichristum, & cum eo miserè defecerit à Deo? Nunc verò exorta luce Euangelij Christi, tā pauci tamen ea sequantur, & tā multi eam oppugnent? Vnde est hoc, nisi ex eo quòd insitum in natura sit hoc veritatis odium & insitus amor mendaciorum? Paulus hoc egregiè obseruauit; Pro eo, inquit, quòd non receperunt amorem veritatis, vt salui fierent; propterea mittet illis Deus efficacitatem deceptionis vt credant mendacio. Ecce Paulus dum praedicit horribilem illam & vniuersalem defectionem sub Antichristo futuram, eius causam notat hanc, nimirum quòd non receperint homines amorem veritatis. Causa est igitur odium veritatis & amor mendacij. Atque ideo ait, hanc iustam esse compensationem & vindictā Dei, quòd misurus sit eis efficaciam deceptionis & puniturus sit eos mendaciis iis, quibus tantopere natura delectantur. Sed ne longius abeamus, huius rei manifestam experientiā habemus, in his, de quibus nunc sermo est, Iudaeis: Hi aliquatenus cognouerunt Iesum Dei filium esse, vt supra admonuimus & demonstrauimus; neque tamen cognitum eum recipere voluerunt, sed applicaturi se erant ad mendacia & mendaciorum doctores: vt eorum exemplo illud planè manifestum euadat, nimirum homines etiam scientes veritatem, malitiosè tamen se opponere veritati, & hoc esse nō tam ex eo quòd ignari sint, quàm ex odio quoddam veritatis & amore mendacii à natura insito. Quare de hoc sumus omnes admonendi, ne vnquam laboremus in celando & cleuando isto pessimo naturae malo, siue in nobisipsis, siue in aliis: Et cùm audimus tot superioribus seculis, sequutos esse homines passim mendacia & tenebras in regno illo Antichristi, tū ne praetexamus tā foedę apostasię & defectioni nescio quā simplicitate. Quasi verò simplicitas & ignorantia possint eos excusare, quae getes ipsas iam olim excusare non potuerunt. Erant quidē, fateor, tum alij aliis simpliciores magisque ignari, sed nemo fuit eorum omnium qui desciuerūt à Deo, qui nō ipsō te sua ac lubēs abductus sit à caecis illis ducibus. Neque rursus cùm audimus & videmus hac nostra aetate nō paucos etiā adhuc ab Antichristo fascinati, seq; adulterę illi Ecclesię aggregare; ne tū, inquā dicamus illud errore quodā, simplicitate vel ignorantia venire, pertim cū fieri nō possit quin oēs audiāt de luce ista, quā Deus ex infinita sua misericordia hac nostra aetate & his postremis diebus excitauit; tñ tñ ab eo absut vt eā sequi velint & amplecti, vt è contra non sit ferè in regno Antichristi hodierno die qui istam lucem, suo quisque modo non oppugnet. Neque denique excusemus nos ipsos, si qui sint, qui iam aliquando decepti sunt cum reliquo mundo; sed veniam à Deo petamus quòd tam foedè ab eo defecerimus, eíque indesinenter gratias agamus quòd nos è tenebris illis trastulerit in hanc lucem suam, animúmque nostrum ab amore illo mendaciorum mutauerit in amorem veritatis, sempérque ab eo petamus impostèrum, vt adhuc magis magísque abolcat illa quæ adhuc in natura corrupta reliqua sunt semina, odii, veritatis & amoris mendaciorum. Nam etiam adhuc illius mali aliquid in nobis residuum est, quod nō prorsus abolebitur tantisperdum hic viuimus, quòdque pij sentiunt cum magno animi dolore ingemiscentes sub hoc onere mortalitatis & expetentes plenam illam in aduentu Domini sui liberationem.
units.tr: I have come in my Father's name. This is the fourth sin laid against them, injustice or wrong done to the Lord: for he complains, in a way, that he is treated unjustly by them, because he comes to them in his Father's name yet is rejected, while they receive other false prophets and teachers who come in their own name. He therefore complains of a grave wrong. This injustice is not peculiar to them but is natural to all people. For by nature we all do this wrong to God and to his truth, when we put falsehood and lying teachers before him and his truth, choose lies when we make our choice, reject the truth, and so are unjust and wrongdoers against the truth. Nor should we listen to those who commonly pretend that this injustice comes from simplicity, ignorance, error, or something of the kind. Indeed I affirm that this unjust way of dealing with God arises not so much from any ignorance as from a hatred of the truth that is wholly ingrained, and a love of lies. For where, I ask, does it come from that when a true teacher sent by God arises, so few hear him with such difficulty and follow him? And if some false teacher is sent up from the dead, how readily do so many embrace him? Whence came it that almost the whole world followed Antichrist and miserably fell away from God with him? And now, with the light of Christ's gospel risen, why do so few follow it and so many attack it? Whence is this, unless from the fact that a hatred of the truth and a love of lies are implanted in nature? Paul observed this well: because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved, therefore God will send them the working of deception, that they should believe the lie. See how Paul, while foretelling that horrible and universal defection to come under Antichrist, notes its cause: namely that people did not receive the love of the truth. The cause, then, is hatred of the truth and love of lies. And so he says that this is the just recompense and vengeance of God, that he will send them the efficacy of deception and punish them with those lies in which nature so greatly delights. But not to go further afield, we have clear experience of this in the Jews of whom we now speak. These, as we have admonished and shown above, had some knowledge that Jesus is the Son of God, yet they were not willing to receive him when they knew him, but were ready to attach themselves to lies and lying teachers: so that from their example it becomes quite plain that people, even knowing the truth, nonetheless maliciously set themselves against it, and this comes not so much from ignorance as from a certain hatred of the truth and love of lies implanted by nature. Therefore we are all to be admonished on this point, never to labour at concealing or excusing this most evil malady of nature, whether in ourselves or in others. And when we hear that in so many earlier ages people everywhere followed lies and darkness in that kingdom of Antichrist, let us not excuse so foul an apostasy and defection by some sort of simplicity. As if simplicity and ignorance could excuse them, when they could not excuse the nations themselves even in former times! It is true, I grant, that some were then simpler and more ignorant than others, but there was none of all those who fell away from God who was not led away by those blind guides of his own accord and pleasure. Nor again, when we hear and see in our own age that not a few are still bewitched by Antichrist and join themselves to that adulterous Church, should we say, I say, that this comes by some error, simplicity or ignorance, especially since it cannot be that all do not hear of that light which God in his infinite mercy has raised up in our age and in these last days; yet they are so far from wishing to follow and embrace it that, on the contrary, there is scarcely anyone in the kingdom of Antichrist today who does not, in his own way, attack this light. Finally, let us not excuse ourselves, if there are any who were once deceived along with the rest of the world; rather let us ask God's pardon that we have so foully defected from him, and give him unending thanks that he has transferred us out of those shadows into this his light, and has changed our soul from that love of lies into a love of the truth. And let us always ask him in future that he will more and more wipe out those seeds of hatred of the truth and love of lies that still remain in our corrupt nature. For some remnant of that evil is still left in us, which will not be wholly abolished so long as we live here, and which the godly feel, groaning with great distress of mind under this burden of mortality and longing for that full deliverance at the coming of their Lord.

units.la: Quomodo potestis credere? Hoc quintum est & vltimum peccatum quod Dominus in Iudaeis istis, praesertim Scribis & Pharisaeis reprehendit.
units.tr: How can you believe?

units.la: Est autem periculosissimum & fidei in Christum Iesum inimicissimum, nempe ambitio. Quomodo vos potestis credere? Q.d. Impossibile est credere quum gloriam alij ab aliis captetis, & gloriam quae est à Deo solo non quaeratis. Ergo hoc pro impossibili habendum est, quòd ambitiosus quis & studiosus gloriae mundi huius, credat in Christum Iesum. Fieri quidem potest vt aliquam habeat animi assensionem, & aliquo modo in Christum propendeat, vt de primoribus aliquot Iudaeorum legimus, Quòd crediderint quidem in eum, sed non confessi sunt, metuentes ne synagoga mouerentur: causam metus deinde addit, dilexerunt enim gloriam hominum potius quàm gloriam Dei. Illud interea manet, impossibile esse quemquam vere ac sincere credere in Christum qui venatur gloriam huius mundi. Nam necessitas quædam imposita est vere pio ac credenti cuique. Quòd si quis velit pie viuere in Christo ... necesse habeat afflictiones perpeti. Necesse enim est contemptus mundi & crux omnis generis sequatur Euangelium Christi, Esto participes, inquit Paulus, afflictionum Euangelij ex potentia Dei. Fieri quidem potest vt ad tempus
units.tr: This is the fifth and last sin which the Lord rebukes in these Jews, especially the Scribes and Pharisees. It is also the most dangerous and most hostile to faith in Christ Jesus, namely ambition. How can you believe? That is: it is impossible to believe while you seek glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone. Therefore it must be counted impossible that a man who is ambitious and eager for the glory of this world should believe in Christ Jesus. It can indeed happen that such a man has some assent of mind and leans in some way toward Christ, as we read of some of the leading Jews, that "they believed in him, but did not confess him, fearing lest they be cast out of the synagogue"; the evangelist then adds the cause of their fear: "for they loved the glory of men rather than the glory of God." Meanwhile it remains that it is impossible for anyone to believe truly and sincerely in Christ who hunts after the glory of this world. For a certain necessity is laid upon every man who is truly godly and believing. If anyone wishes to live godly in Christ ... he must suffer afflictions. For contempt of the world and the cross of every kind must follow the Gospel of Christ. "Be partakers," says Paul, "of the afflictions of the Gospel according to the power of God." It can indeed happen that for a time some believer breathes freely and has the world smiling on him, and that some minister of the Gospel is held in high esteem among men, as was said of John the Baptist above in this chapter, verse 35, that for a time many Jews rejoiced "in his light." But let whoever he is take care meanwhile that he does not hunt after that commendation and glory which is from men himself, or seek it.

units.la: 5. Iudaeorum peccatum, Ambitio.
units.tr: 5. The sin of the Jews: ambition.

units.la: Iohann. 12. 42.43. Ambitionis effectus.
units.tr: John 12. 42.43. The effects of ambition.

units.la: 2. Tim. 3. 12. 2. Tim. 1. 8. pus fidelis aliquis respiret & habeat mundum sibi arridentem, & in satis magna gloria sit apud homines etiam Minister aliquis Euangelij, vt de Iohanne Baptista dictum est supra hoc cap. verf. 35. quod ad tempus multi Iudæi exultârunt in luce eius. Verum caueat sibi interea, quisquis est, ne venetur ipse, aut expetat commendationem illam & gloriam quæ est ab hominibus.
units.tr: 2. Tim. 3. 12. 2. Tim. 1. 8. Still, the faithful man may breathe for a while and have the world smiling on him, and a minister of the Gospel may be held in great glory among men. But let him take care meanwhile, whoever he is, that he does not hunt after, or seek, that commendation and glory which is from men.

units.la: Caueat ne voluptatem capiat ex ea, verum fugiat eam, & sese quasi ab hominibus subducat. Quod à Christo factum legimus qui secessit in montem solus, cum multitudo in animo haberet eum correptum regem facere.
units.tr: Let him take care not to take pleasure in it, but flee from it, and withdraw himself as it were from men. We read that Christ did this, who withdrew alone into the mountain when the crowd intended to seize him and make him king.

units.la: Iuenim optimè comparabit se ad illam vicissitudinem & contemptum hominum, quem vice versa patietur. Quòd si interea sibi placeat & acquiescat in illa hominum æstimatione & gloria, profecto periculum erit, ne orta persequutione vel fidem plane amittat, vel certè cum Iudæis non audeat eam confiteri. Et quæ, quæso, fides illa, quæ non habet oris confessionem? Addo ad hæc, quòd si ponas crucè ne vllo quidè tepore esse fidei comitem; tamen affirmo, ne in summa quidem pace & omnium rerum affluentia fidem cum ambitione & immoderata illa gloriæ cupiditate posse consistere. Nam vnde, quæso, existit cupiditas ista gloriæ quæ captatur ab hominibus? Non aliunde profecto quàm ex innata quadam superbia & quia quis nimium sibi ipse placet, & putat se aliquid esse. Hinc fit vt cogitet debere omnes mortales de eo ita sentire, vt ipse de se sentit, & plurimi facere etiam quæ in eo sunt quàm maximè vitiosa & vituperio digna, hoc est, ipsius stercora. At quid fides, quæso? nihil profecto aliud quàm humilis quædam abiectio nostri ipsorum ad pedes Dei, vt misericordiam in Christo consequamur. Sequitur enim fides perpetuò abiectum & contritum animum ex inspecto peccato & miseria nostra. Qui igitur potest conuenire inter superbiam illam animi, ex qua est ambitio, & humilitatem hanc, ex qua existit fides? Quando igitur conuenient inter fidem & ambitionem? Non est quidè ita sentiedu de affectatione illa, vt sic dicâ, gloriæ quæ est à solo Deo, quæ cum non sit ex vlla opinione meriti sui, vt sum ex sensu abiectissimæ naturæ suæ & summa animi efficiat. modestia, profecto optime illi conueniet cum fide, quae pariter ex humilitate & modestia exsurgit. Nam qui approbationem Dei quaerit, studet ei semper placere & acceptus esse, cumque fecit omnia quae potuit, cogitat de se quam fieri potest demisse & se tatum seruum inutilem iudicat. Neque enim dico superbum illum Pharisaeum, qui gloriam a Deo & commendationem quaesiuit, qui etiam apud Deum gloriatus est de operibus suis. vide Rom. 4. 2. Huc igitur quae a nobis dicta sunt redeunt omnia, vt in tota vita studeamus humilitati, & discamus modeste de nobis ipsis sentire, vt non sit locus ambitioni & affectationi gloriae quae est ab hominibus: Atque ita sit locus fidei in Christum quod est fundamentum totius felicitatis nostrae. Neque vero ibi tantum exulat fides vbi ambitio est; verum vt facile appareat, quantu mali sit in ambitione, nulla est cu ea recte agendi ratio, nihil, vbi ea regnat recte geri potest. Nam qui quaerit gloriam ab hominibus & non a Deo, studet placere non Deo, sed hominibus, a quibus gloriam & commendationem sibi quaerit. Quisquis autem studet placere hominibus, non Deo, nihil moratur interiorem cordis in agendo sinceritatem illam, quam non vident homines a quibus gloriam quaerit. Iam vero scimus nihil recte geri quod non ex interna illa cordis sinceritate proficiscitur. Illud igitur audeo affirmare, nullum opus ambitiosi hominis eius qui quaerit gloriam ab hominibus rectum esse coram Deo. Fieri quidem potest, vt aliis prosit, sed authori suo nihil proderit. Neque enim hanc gloriam quae est ab hominibus, aut quae est huius mundi, pro lucro vnquam duxi, nisi coniuncta Dei approbatione & commendatione. Neque rursus qui quaerit gloriam eam quae est a solo Deo, is solam habet fidem, verum Dei approbatione dum quaerit quicquid facit, id recte faciat necesse est. Na qui quaerit gloriam a solo Deo, is studet placere non hominibus, sed Deo: dum aute studet placere Deo non hominibus, non tam attendit ad externam operis speciem, quam ad internam cordis sinceritatem, quam solus intuetur Deus. Nunc vero scimus quicquid proficiscitur ab hac cordis sinceritate interna, illud rectum esse Deoque gratum, quantumuis in specie.
units.tr: For he will prepare himself very well for that reversal and for the contempt of men, which in turn he will suffer. But if meanwhile he takes pleasure in that esteem and glory of men and rests content with it, there will certainly be danger that, when persecution arises, he will either utterly lose his faith or at least not dare to confess it along with the Jews. And what faith, I ask, is that which has no confession of the mouth? I add to this that even if you assume that the cross is no companion of faith at any time, yet I affirm that not even in the greatest peace and abundance of all things can faith remain together with ambition and that immoderate desire for glory. For whence, I ask, does that desire for glory which is sought from men arise? Surely from nothing other than a certain innate pride, and because a man is too pleased with himself and thinks himself to be something. Hence it comes that he thinks all mortals ought to think of him as he thinks of himself, and that many people do even those things in him which are most wicked and deserving of blame, that is, his own dung. But what, I ask, is faith? Nothing else certainly than a humble casting down of ourselves at the feet of God, so that we may obtain mercy in Christ. For faith always follows a humbled and broken spirit, arising from the sight of our sin and misery. How then can that pride of mind from which ambition comes agree with this humility from which faith arises? When, then, will faith and ambition agree? Indeed, that affectation of glory which is from God alone, if I may so call it, should not be judged in the same way; since it arises from no opinion of one's own merit, but from a sense of one's most abject nature, and produces the highest modesty of mind, it will certainly agree very well with faith, which likewise rises from humility and modesty. For he who seeks the approval of God strives always to please him and be acceptable to him, and when he has done all that he could, he thinks of himself as humbly as possible and judges himself to be an unprofitable servant. I do not mean that proud Pharisee, who sought glory and commendation from God, and who even boasted before God of his works. See Rom. 4. 2. To this end, then, all that we have said returns: that throughout our whole life we should strive for humility and learn to think modestly of ourselves, so that there may be no room for ambition and the desire for glory which is from men; and thus there may be room for faith in Christ, which is the foundation of all our happiness. Nor does faith exile itself only where ambition is; but so that it may easily appear how much evil there is in ambition, there is no right way of acting along with it, and nothing can be done rightly where it reigns. For he who seeks glory from men and not from God strives to please not God but men, from whom he seeks glory and commendation for himself. Whoever strives to please men and not God pays no heed to that inner sincerity of heart in acting, which the men from whom he seeks glory do not see. Now we know that nothing is done rightly which does not proceed from that inner sincerity of heart. I therefore dare to affirm this: no work of an ambitious man, that is, of one who seeks glory from men, is right before God. It may indeed benefit others, but it will profit its author nothing. For I have never counted this glory which is from men, or which is of this world, as gain, unless joined with the approval and commendation of God. Nor again, he who seeks that glory which is from God alone does not have faith alone; rather, while he seeks God's approval, it is necessary that whatever he does be done rightly. For he who seeks glory from God alone strives to please not men but God; and while he strives to please God and not men, he attends not so much to the outward appearance of the work as to the inner sincerity of the heart, which God alone sees. Now we know that whatever proceeds from this inner sincerity of heart is right and pleasing to God, however it may appear in outward form.

units.la: Luc. 18. 10. &c. speciem vile & exile appareat. Et illud equidem ausim dicere, quicquid agit qui gloriam à Deo quærit, quantumuis in speciem paruum fit, illud tamen maius esse coram Deo quàm fit quoduis opus etiam in speciem gloriosissimum eius hominis qui ab hominibus gloriam quærit. Fateor quidem eum non posse obtinere inter agendum eam quam velit cordis sinceritate: Atque hinc sunt illi gemitus ac lachrymæ: sed confugit ad Christum, ac perfectionem illam quæ in eo est, integritque fide in Christum illam omnem imperfectionem quæ est in opere suo; fide autem tectu opus ipsius iam placet Deo, ac suam à Deo approbatione recipit. Nolim autem illud à nobis ignorari, miseram istam caecitatem & audaciam quorundam ambitiosorum hominum, qui cùm non habeant internam in agendo cordis sinceritatem, audent tamen non ab hominibus tantum, sed etiam à Deo gloriam & commendationem quærere, vt Pharisæus ille superbus, vt Papistæ nostri temporis. Audent enim isti operum suorum impurorum mercedem etiam, iustitiam, etiam vitam æternam sibi poscere, tanquam debitam à Deo. Sed miseri isti adeo excæcati sunt, vt neque seipsi, neque Deum videant, neque impuritatem cordis sui, neque naturam Dei sanctissimam, qui nihil approbare poterit, nisi quod ex sincero corde est profectum.
units.tr: Luke 18. 10. etc. appears cheap and slight in outward appearance. And indeed I would dare to say this: whatever he who seeks glory from God does, however small it may be in appearance, is nonetheless greater before God than any work, even one most glorious in appearance, of the man who seeks glory from men. I admit that he cannot, while acting, attain the sincerity of heart that he would wish; hence come those groans and tears. But he takes refuge in Christ, and by faith in Christ he covers with the perfection that is in him all the imperfection that is in his work; and so, by faith, his work already pleases God and receives God's approval. But I would not have us ignore that wretched blindness and boldness of certain ambitious men, who, since they do not have inner sincerity of heart in acting, nevertheless dare to seek glory and commendation not only from men but also from God, like that proud Pharisee, like our Papists of this time. For they dare to demand for themselves, as due from God, the reward of their impure works: even righteousness, even eternal life. But these wretched men are so blinded that they see neither themselves nor God, neither the impurity of their own heart nor the most holy nature of God, who can approve nothing except what has proceeded from a sincere heart.

units.la: 45 Ne putate me accusaturum vos apud Patrem: est qui accusat vos, Moses, in quo vos speratis.
units.tr: 45 Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father; there is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope.

units.la: 46 Si enim crederetis Mosi, crederetis mihi: nam ille de me scripsit.
units.tr: 46 For if you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote of me.

units.la: 47 Quod si scriptis illius non creditis, quomodo verbis meis credetis?
units.tr: 47 But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?

units.la: POstquam obiecit iis peccata illa superiora; nunc comminatur denunciatque grauissimam eorum accusationem fore ab ipso Mose præsertim, cui tamen tantopere confidunt. Sensus autem est; Non solum ego accusaturus sum vos apud Patrem, verum multo magis Mosem vestrum, in quo speratis, habebitis accusatorem.
units.tr: Having charged them with those earlier sins, he now threatens and declares that their accusation will be most grievous, and that it will come from Moses himself, in whom they nevertheless trust so greatly. The sense is: not only will I accuse you before the Father, but you will have as your accuser, far more than me, Moses, in whom you hope.

units.la: Non enim his verbis simpliciter negat se accusaturum ipsos; verum vsitata sibi phrasi significat se non vel solum, vel praecipuè accusaturum, vt vidimus supra hoc capite. Ratio cur Moses sit accusaturus ipsos est, quia non credunt Mosi. Hoc rursus ostendit, quia, inquit, si crederetis Mosi, crederetis & mihi: At non creditis mihi: Ergo neque Mosi. Probatur propositio, quia Moses scripsit de me; Praeterquam enim quod totius legis Moseos Christus sit finis, Moses nonnullis in locis de Christo venturo scripsit: Quaecunque enim veritas vnquam fuit ab initio, & quaecunque vnquam fuerunt veri doctores, illi omnes de Christo testati sunt, & ad Christum quasi manu nos deduxerunt, adeò vt quinò crediderint in Christum, illi quidem habituri sint eos omnes totidem testes aduersus ipsos in illo die. Neque verò futurum est vt praetextus iste vel scripturae, vel doctorum excusat incredulos homines. Multi enim semper fuerunt & sunt hoc die hypocritae qui satisfecisse sibi videntur, si externa professione vtantur, & ficta quadam reuerentia doctores veritatis prosequantur, cuiusmodi fuerunt olim Iudaei, qui Mosis titulum infidelitati suae praetexerunt: & hodierno die Pontificij doctores illos Ecclesiae veteres semper in ore habent. Sunt etiam inter nos qui eadem nobiscum veritatem se profiteri simulant, qui protendant necessitudinem & reuerentiam nescio quam Pastorum quos Deus suo tempore delecturus est. Neque enim praetextus hic excusabit hypocritas, verum nullos habituri sunt olim acriores accusatores, quàm illos ipsos quos nunc praetexunt hypocrisi suae. Neque enim per fictam istam reuerentiam Pastorum satisfiet veris Pastoribus; neque etiam si omnia bona tua in eos profundas, tamen iis erit satisfactum, si interea non credas in Christum Iesum. Non credens enim mendaces eos facis: Nulla autem maior iniuria fieri potest vero Pastori ista, qua mendacem eum facis. Hinc igitur futurum est, vt vindex tui sit acerrimus futurus. Duplex enim persona Pastoris impolita est, & vt seruet credentes, & vt vlciscatur contumaces. Paratum habemus, inquit, & vt vlciscatur contumaciam, postquam impleta-
units.tr: For in these words he does not simply deny that he will accuse them. By his customary manner of speaking, he means that he will not accuse them alone or chiefly, as we saw earlier in this chapter. The reason why Moses will accuse them is that they do not believe Moses. He shows this again when he says: "For if you believed Moses, you would believe me also." But they do not believe me; therefore neither do they believe Moses. The premise is proved: "because Moses wrote of me." For apart from the fact that Christ is the end of the whole law of Moses, Moses also wrote in several places about the Christ who was to come. Whatever truth has existed from the beginning, and whatever true teachers have ever existed, all of them have borne witness to Christ and have led us to him as if by the hand, so that those who did not believe in Christ will have all of them as so many witnesses against them on that day. Nor will this pretext, of Scripture or of teachers, excuse unbelieving men. For there have always been, and still are on this day, many hypocrites who think they have satisfied themselves if they make an outward profession and pursue the teachers of the truth with a feigned reverence. Such were once the Jews, who put forward the name of Moses as a cover for their unbelief, and today the Papists always have on their lips the ancient Fathers of the Church. There are also among us those who pretend to profess the same truth as we do, and who put forward some kind of kinship and reverence for ministers whom God will in his time overthrow. For this pretext will not excuse hypocrites; rather, they will have no fiercer accusers than those very men whom they now put forward to cover their hypocrisy. By this feigned reverence for ministers, satisfaction will not be made to true ministers; nor, even if you pour all your goods upon them, will they be satisfied if meanwhile you do not believe in Jesus Christ. For by not believing, you make them liars, and no greater injury can be done to a true minister than this, that you make him a liar. Hence it will follow that he will be your most fierce avenger. For the twofold office of the minister is set before us: to save believers and to avenge the obstinate. He says, "We have it ready both to avenge disobedience, when"

units.la: 2. Cor. 10. 6. Apostolus, quo vindicamus omnem contumaciam, postquam impletaimpleta fuerit obedientia vestra. Quare ne vnquam contenti simus eiusmodi aliquo praetextu, sed offerente se luce veritatis, offerentibus se veris pastoribus, ne satisfiat nobis priusquam Christum inveniamus. Fieri quidem potest vt ad tempus bene fiat nobis sub ista larua, & pro religiosis scilicet reputemur: fieri etiam potest vt familiaritas bonorum & sanctorum hominum, praesertim doctorum veritatis, procuret temporales benedictiones, id quod certo evenit: improbi enim gaudent societate bonorum, non aliam ob causam nisi propter temporarias istas benedictiones. Verum tandem aliquando futurum est, vt nisi ipse bonus euadas & in Christū credas, & boni viri & benedictiones illę quęcunque temporariae futurae sint tibi totidem maledictiones. Neque vero ego me satis accepisse putarim, si aliorum & bonorum virorum gratia Deus benedicat mihi, nisi ipse interea conscius mihi sim meipsum in gratia cum Deo esse, & mea etiam causa Deum mihi benedicere. Hoc autem ita demum eueniet vt in gratia cum Deo sit aliquis, & ipsius causa, nō alterius tantūm benedictio ipsi obueniat, si in Christum Iesum credat; sic acceptae sunt Deo per sonę nostrae, & hoc est omnis boni principium & fundamentum.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 10. 6. The Apostle: "we are ready to avenge all disobedience, when your obedience is complete." Therefore let us never be content with any such pretext, but, when the light of truth is offered and true ministers are offered, let us not be satisfied until we have found Christ. It may indeed happen that for a time all goes well for us under this mask, and that we are counted religious; it may also happen that the familiarity of good and holy men, especially teachers of the truth, procures temporal blessings, and this certainly happens, for the wicked rejoice in the fellowship of the good, for no other reason than these temporal blessings. But in the end it will someday come about that, unless you yourself become good and believe in Christ, those good men and those temporal blessings, whatever they may be, will be so many curses to you. Nor would I think I had received enough if God blessed me through the favour of other good men, unless I myself was meanwhile conscious that I am in grace with God, and that God blesses me also for my own sake. This will come about only in this way: that someone is in grace with God, and that a blessing comes to him for his own sake and not for another's alone, if he believes in Jesus Christ. Thus our persons are accepted by God, and this is the beginning and foundation of all good.

units.la: Quod si illius scriptis. Ex ostensa illa conclusione (quod neimpe Mosi non credant) concludit a maiori, non posse fieri vt ipsi Christo vel ipsius verbis credat. Maiora sunt haec, primum Moses maior Christo; deinde scripta Mosis maiora verbis Christi. Ex his concludit quod si scriptis Mosis non credant, quanto minus credent verbis ipsius? Quaeri potest: An Moses Christo sit maior, & an scripta ipsius sint maiora verbis Christi, id quod hic videtur Christus innuere? Respondeo, hoc dictum esse a Christo, ex illorum sententia & iudicio. Nam reuera Christus maior est Mose, cum Moses fuerit fidelis in tota domo Dei, vt famulus, Christus autem vt Filius domui suae praeest. Et dicta Christi maiora sunt & digniora scriptis Mosis, si personas ipsas respicias, cum alioqui & dicta & scripta Mosis a Christo fuerint, ipsiusque Spiritu loquuti sunt & scripserunt Prophetae omnes veteres, per Spiritum Christi qui in ipsis erat. Notandum hic eam esse caeci-
units.tr: "Or if his writings." From the conclusion shown (namely, that they do not believe Moses), he concludes from the greater that it is not possible for them to believe Christ himself or his words. These are the greater premises: first, Moses is greater than Christ; then, the writings of Moses are greater than the words of Christ. From these he concludes that if they do not believe the writings of Moses, how much less will they believe his words? Here one may ask: is Moses greater than Christ, and are his writings greater than the words of Christ, as Christ here seems to suggest? I answer that this was said by Christ according to their opinion and judgment. For in truth Christ is greater than Moses, since Moses was faithful in all the house of God as a servant, but Christ as a Son presides over his own house. And the words of Christ are greater and more worthy than the writings of Moses, if you look at the persons themselves, since otherwise both the words and the writings of Moses were from Christ, and all the ancient prophets spoke and wrote by his Spirit, the Spirit of Christ who was in them. It should be noted here that it is the blindness and weakness of our nature that we can hardly at once recognise the very voice of God speaking, nor believe it, unless we are led and prepared to recognise and believe through the testimony of men, which is more familiar to us, and through the authority which they call the Church.

units.la: Hypocritarum conditio. tatem naturæ nostræ & infirmitatem, vt fere non statim possimus agnoscere ipsam Dei loquentis vocem, neque in eam credere, nisi adducamur & præparemur ad agnoscendum & credendum testimonio hominum quod familiarius nobis est & authoritate quam vocant Ecclesiæ. Atque hinc fit vt ignari veritatis authoritatem Ecclesiæ præferant authoritati ipsius vocis Dei. Hanc infirmitatem in se fuisse agnouit Augustinus, quo tempore à Manichęorum hæresi ad Christianismum conuerteretur: Non crederem Euangelio, inquiens, nisi me authoritas Ecclesiæ commoueret. Sed hoc in principio conuersionis nostri tolerabile est: verùm postquam testimonio & authoritate Ecclesiæ iam addùcti sumus vt agnoscamus Dei ipsius vocem, vt tum olim Iudæi isti, qui, vt obseruauimus, aliquo modo nouerunt Iesum Filium Dei esse, & hodierno die Papistę qui conuicti conscientiis, agnoscunt satis Dei vocem in Scripturis suis, si etiam tum post agnitam ipsam Dei vocem, tamen præferamus vocem hominum & testimonium Ecclesiæ (de vera Ecclesia loquor, non autem antichristiana) præferamus, inquâ, voci ipsius Dei loquentis in Scripturis suis; hoc profecto nullo modo est ferendum: imò argumentum est insignis malitiæ & impudentiæ, necnon arguit istos homines, qui authoritatem Ecclesię iactitant non tanti facere vocem veræ Ecclesiæ Dei. Nam qui Deo loquenti non vult credere, neque eius vocē pluris facere, quàm vocem omnium hominum etiam sanctissimorum, postquàm cognouit iam satis eum esse, qui in Scripturis loquatur; indicat apertè se non credere piis & sanctis hominibus. Nam si Mosi crederetis, ait Christus, mihi crederetis. His verbis significat eos, etsi vendicent fidem suam in Mosis scripta, & amorem suum erga Mosem ipsum; tamen eam esse eorum infidelitatem, vt neque scriptis ipsius credant, neque ipsum sincerè ament. Hypocritæ egregiè quidem simulare norunt & fidem & amorem, sed nihil interea est in iis sincerì. Neque ego credà profecto vnquam in hypocritis nostris Papistis aliquid sincerì esse, vel fidem, vel amorem aliquem sincerum post horrendam illam stragem Parisiensem & Gallicanam, de qua nulla vnquam ætas contiçescet. Quomodo verbis meis. His verbis significat oportuisse latens illud in ipsis Dei odium ac infidelitatem illam ad tempus tectam & dissimulatam in se totam effundi, ut qui adeo ipsis vilescat. Nam odio & felle amaritudinis plenus est hypocrita; & odium illud quod dissimulat erga alios, illud totum effundit in alios, nempe eos qui non eam prope hypocritam ipsum attingunt,& a quibus nihil commodi ad se peruenturum expectat. Putásne, miser, fore ut Papistæ illi, qui odium illud suum ad tempus dissimulatum non potuerunt tamen continere,quin erumperet etiam in Gentiles & contribules suos, etiam in consanguineos suos? Putásne fore ut tibi parcant alienigenæ & extraneo, si vnquam iis hoc à Deo permissum fuerit, iusto ipsius iudicio, ut nos in extraneorum, siue Hispanorum, siue aliorum, potestatem deueniamus? Erras, miser, si hoc putas, neque verò proderit tibi communis religio Pontificia; cùm Papistæ, etiam qui Ecclesiasticos se haberi volunt, non pepercerunt regibus suis Papistis, ut documento sunt recentes illi nefarij, impij & crudeles eorum conatus in Reges Galliarum, quos oportuit sacrosanctos & inuiolabiles esse. Sed vt inimicis Ecclesiæ Dei, siue extraneis iis quidem, siue domesticis, & salus ac pax sit Israeli & Ecclesiæ Dei, per Iesum Christũ Dominum nostrum: Cui cum Patre & Spiritu sancto sit omnis honor & gloria, Amen.
units.tr: The condition of hypocrites. And hence it happens that men ignorant of the truth prefer the authority of the Church to the authority of the very voice of God. Augustine acknowledged this weakness in himself, at the time when he was converted to Christianity from the heresy of the Manichees: "I would not believe the Gospel," he says, "unless the authority of the Church moved me." But this is tolerable at the beginning of our conversion. Yet once we have been brought by the testimony and authority of the Church to acknowledge the voice of God himself, as those Jews once did, who, as we have observed, in some way knew that Jesus was the Son of God, and as the Papists do today, who, convicted in their consciences, acknowledge the voice of God sufficiently in their Scriptures, if even then, after the voice of God itself has been acknowledged, we still prefer the voice of men and the testimony of the Church (I speak of the true Church, not the antichristian one) to the voice of God speaking in his Scriptures, this is certainly in no way to be borne. Indeed it is a sign of notable malice and impudence, and it shows that those men, who boast of the authority of the Church, do not esteem the voice of the true Church of God so highly. For he who will not believe God speaking, nor value his voice above the voice of all men, even the most holy, once he has recognised that he is indeed the one speaking in the Scriptures, plainly shows that he does not believe pious and holy men. For if you believed Moses, says Christ, you would believe me. By these words he signifies that they, although they claim their faith in the writings of Moses and their love for Moses himself, nevertheless have such unbelief that they believe neither his writings nor love him sincerely. Hypocrites indeed know very well how to feign both faith and love, but there is nothing sincere in them. Nor shall I ever believe that there is anything sincere in our hypocritical Papists, whether faith or any sincere love, after that dreadful massacre at Paris and in Gaul, which no age will ever forget. "Than my words." By these words he signifies that the hidden hatred and unbelief in them, concealed and dissimulated for a time, had to be poured out entirely, so that he who is so vile to them might be rejected. For the hypocrite is full of hatred and the gall of bitterness; and the hatred which he dissimulates towards others he pours out entirely upon others, namely upon those who do not touch the hypocrite nearly and from whom he expects no advantage to himself. Do you think, wretched man, that those Papists, who could not nevertheless contain their hatred, which they had dissimulated for a time, from breaking out even upon their fellow countrymen and kinsmen, will spare you, a foreigner and stranger, if ever it shall be permitted them by God, in his just judgment, that we fall into the power of foreigners, whether Spaniards or others? You are wrong, wretched man, if you think so, and the common Papist religion will not help you, since the Papists, even those who wish to be regarded as ecclesiastics, have not spared their own Papist kings, as the recent wicked, impious and cruel attempts against the kings of France bear witness, kings who ought to have been sacrosanct and inviolable. But may salvation and peace be to Israel and to the Church of God, both to the enemies of the Church of God, whether they are foreigners or domestic, through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit be all honour and glory, Amen.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM
units.tr: ARGUMENT

units.la: Hoc capite, primò narratur Christum abiisse trans mare Galilææ. In qua profectione habemus primum miraculum illud quinque panibus & duobus piscibus in monte cibati sunt quinquies mille viri ad versf.16.
units.tr: In this chapter, first, it is related that Christ went away across the Sea of Galilee. In this journey we have first the miracle in which five thousand men were fed on five loaves and two fishes on the mountain, at verse 16.

units.la: Secundò, narratur Christum præmisis discipulis suis è deserto versus Capernaum iuisse, non sine miraculo quo ambulauit super mare, à versu 16 usque ad 22.
units.tr: Second, it is related that Christ, after sending his disciples ahead, went from the desert towards Capernaum, not without the miracle by which he walked upon the sea, from verse 16 to verse 22.

units.la: Tertiò, habemus concionem Christi ad Capernaitas de cibo
units.tr: Third, we have Christ's sermon to the Capernaites about food

units.la: coelesti seu pane vivifico, à versu 22. usque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: heavenly, or the life-giving bread, from verse 22 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: 1 Post haec abiit Iesus trans mare Galilaeae, quod est Tiberiadis.
units.tr: 1 After these things Jesus went over the sea of Galilee, which is the sea of Tiberias.

units.la: 2 Et sequebatur eum turba multa, quia videbant eius signa quae edebat in aegrotis.
units.tr: 2 And a great multitude followed him, because they saw his signs which he did on the sick.

units.la: 3 Subiit vero in montem Iesus, & ibi sedit cum discipulis suis.
units.tr: 3 But Jesus went up into a mountain, and there he sat with his disciples.

units.la: PROPOSITIO est profectionis Christi trans mare Galilaeae. Hanc ut intelligamus, altius repetenda est paucis tota Christi peregrinatio, & perducenda est ad hunc usque locum & hanc peregrinationis eius partem. Iesus cum ingrederetur annum tricesimum, exiit Nazareth in qua educatus est, abiitque in desertum Iordanis ubi baptizavit Iohannes, à quo etiam baptizatus est, atque ita initiatus in illa functione & officio mediationis ac sacerdotij longè excellentissimo. Inde per Spiritum ductus est in desertum Iericho, ubi tentatus est à Satana, & ieiunavit quadraginta dies ac noctes totas. Hinc reversus est ad Iordanis desertum ad Iohannem, ubi vocati sunt tres discipuli, Andreas & alter cuius nomen nō est expressum, tertius deniq; Simon Petrus Andreae frater, idque ministerio Andreae, quibus cum discipulis abiit in Galilaeam; atque in eo itinere vocatus est Philippus & Nathanael. Atque haec fere habemus cap. primo huius Euangelij. Profectus in Galilaeam venit primùm Nazarethan, ubi erat mater ipsius: paulò post cum matre & discipulis invitatus est Iesus ad nuptias in Cana oppido Galilaeae celebratas; ubi occasione sese offerente illud primum suum miraculum in faciendo ex aqua vino, edidit. Cùm autem appropinquaret Paschatis festum, quod primum erat Pascha post Baptisma Iesu, iter instituit Hierusalem versus, venitque primùm Capernaum cum discipulis, hinc Hierusalem est profectus. Quò cùm venit ingressus Templum ipsum purgavit, multa signa ac miracula edidit, nominatim verò sermosermonem habuit noctu cum Nicodemo viro Pharisaeo, & vno ex principibus Iudæorum. Hæc habemus partim cap.secundo, partim cap.tertio. Post hæc exiit Iesus Hierosolymis in territorium Iudææ, vbi docuit & ministerio discipulorum baptizauit. Hinc orta est illa de qua audiuimus controuersia inter discipulos ipsius & discipulos Iohannis, ex qua rursus sequuta illa quærimonia discipulorum Iohannis, & Iohannis ad eos responsio. Hæc habemus in posteriori parte capitis tertij. Cum in territorio Iudææ ageret Iesus, intellexit insidias sibi strui a Iudæis, ideoque reditum parat in Galilæam: per Samariam autem mediam ei proficiscendum fuit. Itaque venit in Samariam, venitque Sichar quod est oppidum Samariæ, vbi primum cum Samaritana muliere, deinde cum reliquis Samaritanis sermones contulit, eósque conuertit.
