Hinc profectus est in Galilæam, ac, vt verisimile est, venit primum Nazareth, vbi male est exceptus, extractúsque ad necem: aufugit autem relicto post se hoc testimonio aduersus Nazareth, quòd Propheta non sit in honoratus, nisi in patria sua. Venit igitur inde Cana, hinc transiit per multos vicos ac oppida Galilææ. Tunc ei fit obuius Regulus ille, cuius filium laborantem ad mortem vsque verbo suo restituit sanitati & vitæ. Hæc habemus cap.4. Interea appropinquat Pascha Iudæorum quod secundum erat post Baptisma Christi: Parat igitur Dominus iter Hierusalem versus, quò etiam venit, ac per occasionem sanauit hominem, qui iam longo morbo erat consumptus. Vnde exorta est persecutio Iudæorum, & apologia clarissima Christi sese defendentis sequuta est, de qua nos proximè audiuimus capite quinto.
units.tr: The proposition is the departure of Christ across the sea of Galilee. To understand it, we must briefly go back further and trace the whole of Christ's journey up to this point and this part of it. When Jesus was entering his thirtieth year, he left Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and went into the desert of the Jordan, where John was baptizing, and he himself was baptized by John. He was thus initiated into that function and office of mediation and priesthood, which far surpasses all others. From there the Spirit led him into the desert of Jericho, where Satan tempted him, and he fasted for forty days and nights. From there he returned to John in the desert of the Jordan, where three disciples were called: Andrew, another whose name is not given, and finally Simon Peter, Andrew's brother, who was brought to Christ through Andrew's ministry. With these disciples he went away into Galilee, and on that journey Philip and Nathanael were called. These are roughly the things we have in the first chapter of this Gospel. Having set out into Galilee, he first came to Nazareth, where his mother was. Shortly afterwards, he was invited with his mother and disciples to a wedding celebrated in Cana, a town of Galilee, and there, as the occasion presented itself, he performed his first miracle, turning water into wine. Then, as the feast of the Passover drew near, which was the first Passover after Jesus' baptism, he set out towards Jerusalem. He came first to Capernaum with his disciples, and from there went up to Jerusalem. When he arrived there, he cleansed the Temple itself, performed many signs and miracles, and in particular held a discourse by night with Nicodemus, a Pharisee and one of the rulers of the Jews. We have these things partly in the second chapter and partly in the third. After this, Jesus left Jerusalem for the territory of Judea, where he taught and, through the ministry of his disciples, baptized. From this arose that controversy we have heard about between his disciples and the disciples of John, and from it followed that complaint of John's disciples and John's answer to them. We have these things in the latter part of the third chapter. While Jesus was in the territory of Judea, he learned that the Jews were plotting against him, and so he prepared to return to Galilee; but he had to travel through the middle of Samaria. So he came into Samaria, and came to Sychar, which is a town of Samaria, where he first held discourse with the Samaritan woman and then with the other Samaritans, and converted them. From there he set out into Galilee, and, as is likely, first came to Nazareth, where he was badly received and dragged out to be killed. But he escaped, leaving behind this testimony against Nazareth, that a prophet is not honored except in his own country. Therefore he came from there to Cana, and from there passed through many villages and towns of Galilee. Then that royal official met him, whose son was dying, and he restored him to health and life by his word. We have these things in the fourth chapter. Meanwhile, the Passover of the Jews, which was the second after Christ's baptism, drew near. So the Lord prepared to travel towards Jerusalem, and went there, and on the way he healed a man who had already been worn down by a long illness. From this arose the persecution of the Jews, and followed that most famous apology in which Christ defended himself, which we heard about just now in the fifth chapter.

units.la: Nunc igitur vt redeamus ad institutam propositionem huius profectionis Christi, ait Euangelista, Post hæc, nempe de quibus capite proximo præcedenti. Non sunt autem hæc sequuta illa quæ narrata sunt superiori capite immediatè, verùm intercessit multum temporis interer hæc & illa; Medio enim tempore multa fecit, & in Iudæa & in Galilæa, vbi etiā multa itinera confecit: reliqui Euangelistæ notat tempus profectionis huius. Fuit autem post illud tempus quo Iohannes Baptista in carcere decol{}lat. latus est ab Herode: Nā post hoc tēpus Herodes audiens multa magnáq; miracula à Christo edi quotidie, capitur desiderio eius videdi & apprehendendi. Quo intellecto Dominus subduxit sese, atq;, vt nostep Euágelista habet, abiit trās mare Galileæ, in desertū nimirū ac monte aliquē, vt habet postea vers.3. Mare istud Galileæ fuit lacus & Genezareth. Dictū est mare Galileæ, quia alluebat Galileam ab occidente; dictum est etiam mare Tiberiadis sumpto nomine ab oppido illo Galilææ Tiberias vocato, quod situm erat in eius ripa. Dicit Dominum abiisse trans mare Galileæ, nō quidem, vt videtur, quòd traiecerit in vlteriorem ripam; sed quòd fugiens Herodem per sinus illius maris, vt compendiosius esset iter, transierit in remotiores Galileæ partes. Atque hic est sensus huius propositionis. Quòd autem observamus, hoc solum est: Herodes iam paulò ante interfecto Iohanne, voluit etiam Christum apprehendere. Tyranni vbi semel iniecerunt manus in vnum aliquem piorum ac seruorum Dei, adeo situnt aliorum piorum quorumcunque sanguinem, vt si possent simul ac semel eos omnes de medio tollere, illud iis esset gratissimum; non aliter quàm qui multum potauit, quò magis bibit, eò magis magísque acuitur eius sitis. Habent autem pij exemplum in Christo, vt vbi id vident, subducant se se paulisper ac deflectant à via Tyranorum sic grassantium, seséque referuent ad meliora tempora. Et sequebatur eum. Declaratur hæc profectio Christi à comitibus itineris, nempe turba quæ eum sequebatur. causa additur, Quia videbant eius signa quæ edebat in ægrotis. Alij Euangelistæ narrat cum ex omnibus vicis ac ciuitatibus undique confluerent ad Christum homines, Iesum miserum eorum, docuisse eos de regno Dei, & ægrotos inter eos sanauisse. Hinc fuit illud desiderium insequendi Dominum, quod profectò non mediocre videbis esse, si circumstantias particulares animaduertas. Primùm sequuti sunt eum in desertum, tum sequuti sunt eum cum fame, inedia, postremò sequuti sunt eum sine spe aliqua pernoctādi aut requiescendi alicubi iam ingruente nocte, nā iam vesperā fuit. Vbi semel cepit aliquem desiderium Christi & regni illius cœlestis, mirum est quàm cito
units.tr: Now then, to return to the proposition we set out of this departure of Christ, the Evangelist says, After these things, namely those mentioned in the preceding chapter. But these things did not follow immediately upon those related in the previous chapter; a considerable amount of time came between this and that. For in the meantime he did many things, both in Judea and in Galilee, where he also travelled many journeys. The other Evangelists mark the time of this departure. Now it was after the time when John the Baptist was beheaded in prison by Herod. For after this time Herod, hearing that many great miracles were being performed daily by Christ, was seized with a desire to see and apprehend him. When the Lord learned of this, he withdrew himself, and, as our Evangelist says, went away across the sea of Galilee, namely into a desert and some mountain, as he says afterwards in verse 3. This sea of Galilee was the lake of Gennesaret. It is called the sea of Galilee because it washed Galilee on the west; it is also called the sea of Tiberias, taking its name from that town of Galilee called Tiberias, which lay on its shore. He says that the Lord went away across the sea of Galilee, not indeed, as it seems, that he crossed to the farther shore, but that, fleeing Herod, he passed along the bays of that sea, so that the journey would be shorter, into the more remote parts of Galilee. And this is the sense of this proposition. What we should observe is only this: Herod, having shortly before killed John, now wanted to seize Christ also. When tyrants have once laid hands on some one of the pious and servants of God, they so thirst for the blood of the other pious people, whoever they may be, that if they could remove them all at once and in one stroke, that would be most welcome to them; just as one who has drunk much, the more he drinks, the more his thirst is sharpened. But the pious have an example in Christ, so that when they see this, they may withdraw themselves for a while and turn aside from the path of tyrants who rage in this way, and reserve themselves for better times. And a great crowd followed him. This departure of Christ is described through the companions of the journey, namely the crowd that followed him. A reason is added: Because they saw the signs which he did on the sick. The other Evangelists relate that when people from all the villages and cities flocked to Christ from every side, Jesus taught them about the kingdom of God, and healed the sick among them. Hence arose that desire to follow the Lord, which will surely be seen to be no small one if you consider the particular circumstances. First they followed him into the desert; then they followed him with hunger and want; lastly, they followed him with no hope of spending the night or resting anywhere, since night was already coming on, for it was already evening. When a desire for Christ and that heavenly kingdom has once taken hold of someone, it is remarkable how quickly

units.la: Mare Galileæ, & Tiberiadis, quod & lacus Genesareth.
units.tr: The Sea of Galilee, also called the Sea of Tiberias, and the Lake of Gennesaret.

units.la: Tyrannorum ingenium.
units.tr: The disposition of tyrants.

units.la: Comites itineris Christi.
units.tr: The companions of Christ's journey.

units.la: Varius eorundem affectus. cito rapiatur supra omnia ista, quae praesenti huic vitae sunt vsui, & prae illis caelestibus contemnat illa omnia. Verum istud eorum desiderium non durauit, neque satis alte radices egit in corde; ideoque, vt videbimus postea, à Christo desciuerunt. Danda nobis opera est, vt quo primum tempore sentimus in nobis, vel fidem vel desiderium Christi, descendamus ipsi penitus in cor nostrum, videamusque an radices ibi agat illa fides aut illud desiderium. Ratio huius rei cognoscendae haec est, Si prorsus perfodiamus quasi cor nostrum, videamus ||isque, an bonus ac honestus sit ager cordis, vt est in parabola, hoc est sincerum & sine dolo aut fuco. In huiusmodi demum corde penitus radices agit fides atque desiderium Christi. Vbi vero hypocrisis est, & dolus, & respectus mundi huius nimius, ibi non est solida fides, vel solidum desiderium, vel solidum denique gaudium. Verum qualecunque demum fuerit illud istorum desiderium, condemnabit profecto torporem hunc nostrum, imo fastidium, imo contemptum verbi, qui est in nostris hominibus, qui tantum absunt ab eo, vt velint sequi Christum in montem & desertum, vt etiam domi obuiam reiiciant: vt velint secuti ventris & quietis suae cum comitatu, vt ne vnam quidem coenam, nedum vniuersas decimas, quas tam auide ad se rapiunt, ne vnam quidem horam quietis cum Christo eiusque Euangelio velint commutare. Sed quid de iis rebus loquor, quae videntur esse alicuius momenti? Nihil est profecto hic tam friuolum, tam vanum quod non praeferant Euangelio & meditationi rerum caelestium; cùm tamen hoc ignorare non possint, aut certè non debeant: At, nisi certo aliquo modo maius sit desiderium regni caelestis, quàm rerum ad hanc vitam spectantium; aut saltem connitamur, vt aliquanto maius sit illud desiderium, nunquam futurum est, vt post hanc vitam in caelestem illam Hierusalem simus commigraturi.
units.tr: The varied affections of the same. they are carried away above all those things that serve this present life, and they despise all of them in comparison with those heavenly things. But that desire of theirs did not last, nor did it strike root deeply enough in the heart; therefore, as we shall see later, they fell away from Christ. We must take pains that, as soon as we perceive in ourselves either faith or a desire for Christ, we go down into our own heart in depth, and see whether that faith or that desire takes root there. The way to know this is this: if we dig up our heart thoroughly, we see whether the soil of the heart is good and honest, as in the parable, that is, sincere and without deceit or pretence. Only in such a heart does faith and desire for Christ take deep root. But where there is hypocrisy, deceit, and too great a regard for this world, there is neither solid faith, nor solid desire, nor finally solid joy. However, whatever that desire of theirs was, it will surely condemn our own sluggishness, indeed our distaste, indeed our contempt for the Word, which is found in our people, who are so far from being willing to follow Christ into the mountain and the desert, that they even turn him away at home. They are willing to follow their belly and their own ease with their retinue, so that they will not give up even one supper, let alone all the tithes which they snatch so eagerly to themselves, nor even one hour of quiet with Christ and his Gospel. But why do I speak of these things, which seem to be of some importance? Truly, there is nothing here so trifling, so vain, that they do not prefer it to the Gospel and to meditation on heavenly things, although they cannot be ignorant of this, or at least ought not to be. But unless in some definite way the desire for the heavenly kingdom is greater than the desire for things pertaining to this life, or at least we strive so that this desire becomes considerably greater, it will never happen that after this life we shall migrate into that heavenly Jerusalem.

units.la: Subiit autem. Notatur locus in quem in hac sua profectione aut peregrinatione peruenerit. Locum vocat mon-tem. Lucas loco iam citato narrat eum venisse in desertum Bethsaidae ciuitatis. Videtur igitur hic mons fuisse in deserto Bethsaidae. Marcus loco prius citato, narrat causam hanc fuisse cur subtraxerit se à turba in hunc locū, nempe, vt ipse paulisper cum discipulis suis, post tot labores requiesceret, & cibo sumpto se recrearet. Quatenus enim homo fuit, hoc consilium cepit, vt humanam suam naturam, quæ infirmitatibus nostris fuit obnoxia, reficeret. Verum interea visum est Deo, ne tantillum quidem temporis illi concedere ad requiem, insequente iam eum multitudine etiam ad hunc vsque montem. Pij etiam quique postquam seriò iam occupati sunt in rebus Dei, cupiunt nonnunquam respirare, & à rebus gerendis vacare, nonnunquam cibum, nonnunquam somnum capere. Atque Deus hoc illis permittit vt alacriores subinde redeant ad officium & labores suos. Verum non raro, fit vt cum ipsi proponunt sibi quietem & otium, Dei voluntate interturbetur illa quies, illud otium; Et vt generaliùs dicam, dum consilium capiunt faciendi aliquid pro ratione officij, vt ex voluntate Dei impediatur conatus eorum, ob causas quas ipse nouit. Paulus ait sæpe proposuisse se venire ad Romanos, sed prohibitum fuisse vsque adhuc. Quid hic facere oporteat piis videbimus postea in exemplo Christi.
units.tr: Subiit autem. The place is noted to which he came in this journey or retreat. He calls it a mountain. Luke, in the passage already cited, says that he came into the desert of the city of Bethsaida, so it seems this mountain lay in the desert of Bethsaida. Mark, in the passage cited earlier, gives the reason he withdrew from the crowd to this place: that he might rest a little with his disciples after so many labours, and refresh himself with food. For insofar as he was man, he took this plan so that he might refresh his human nature, which was subject to our infirmities. Yet God willed that he should not be granted even a little time for rest, since the crowd was already following him as far as this mountain. Godly people too, once they are seriously occupied with the affairs of God, sometimes desire to take breath and to be free from their work, and sometimes to take food or sleep. God permits them this, so that they may return the more eagerly to their duty and labours. Yet it not infrequently happens that, when they propose to themselves rest and leisure, that rest and leisure is disturbed by the will of God; and, to speak more generally, while they resolve to do something in keeping with their office, their effort is hindered by the will of God, for causes which he himself knows. Paul says that he often proposed to come to the Romans, but was prevented until then. What the godly ought to do in this case we shall see later in the example of Christ.

units.la: 4 Propè autem erat Pascha, festum Iudæorū.
units.tr: 4 Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near.

units.la: 5 Cùm ergo sustulisset oculos Iesus, & conspexisset multam turbam ad se venire, dicit Philippo, Vnde ememus panes, vt isti vescantur?
units.tr: 5 When Jesus therefore lifted up his eyes and saw a great crowd coming towards him, he said to Philip, Where shall we buy bread, that these may eat?

units.la: 6 (Hoc autem dicebat, tentans eum, ipse enim sciebat quid esset facturus.)
units.tr: 6 (But he said this to test him; for he himself knew what he was going to do.)

units.la: 7 Respondit ei Philippus, Ducentorum denariorum panes non sufficerint eis, vt singuli eorum paululum quiddam accipiant.
units.tr: 7 Philip answered him, Two hundred denarii worth of bread will not be enough for them, so that each of them may get even a little.

units.la: 8 Dicit ei vnus ex discipulis eius, nempe Andreas frater Simonis Petri,
units.tr: 8 One of his disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, says to him,

units.la: 9 Est hic puerulus quidam qui habet quinque panes hordeaceos & duos piscículos, sed hæc quid sunt inter tam multos?
units.tr: 9 There is a certain little boy here who has five barley loaves and two small fish, but what are these among so many?

units.la: Notatus
units.tr: Noted.

units.la: NOtatur tempus quo venerit in desertum & mira-culum illud quod sequitur ediderit, nempe cum prope esset Pascha quod erat tertium Paschapost baptisma Christi. De primo enim legimus Iohan.2.13. De secundo Pascha te audiuimus Iohan.5.1. Hoc autem tertium est a baptismate Christi. Non ascendit Christus Hierosolyma ad celebrandum hoc Pascha cum Iudaeis, ut appareret ex hoc loco; metuebat enim sibi ab insidiis Iudeorum. Ideo tempore huius Paschatis voluit delitescere in deserto, seseque reseruare in horam illam a Patre destinatam. Christus, ut paulo ante diximus, cum metueret tyrannidem Herodis, secessit ad tempus: nunc vero cum metueret insidias Iudaeorum, noluit interesse huic festo eorum. Et tamen illud constat, eum probe conscium fuisse illius horae quae destinata fuit ipsius mortis & passioni. Nam ipse Dei Filius vna cum Patre ab aeterno eam destinauit. Constat etiam sciuisse eum non potuisse se tolli de medio ante destinatam illam horam, vllis insidiis, vlla machinatione aduersariorum. Noluit tamen Christus tentare Deum suum, nec temere se periculis exponere, sed voluit vt ordinariis mediis quibus effugeret manus inimicorum, seseque seruaret ad horam illam a Patre destinatam. Non quidem similiter cognitam habemus nos horam illam in qua nobis ex voluntate Dei patiendum est; scimus tamen hoc, non licere aduersariis omnibus, vel vnum capillum capitis nostri attingere, sine Dei permissione; scimus etiam semel esse moriendum nobis omnibus. Non tamen exemplo Christi tentandus est Deus, neque temere debemus nos ipsi in discrimen aliquod praesens coniicere, sed vt debemus iis mediis quae Deus nobis permisit ad nos ipsos conseruandos in illud tempus quod a Deo constitutum est. Cum autem iam aduenit illud tempus, Deus nostri nescio quomodo per circunstantias quasdam externas, per internum quendam animi motum solet suis patefacere praesentem esse horam, qua velit ipse glorificari eorum morte, quo fit vt tum etiamsi possint aufugere, seseque seruare, offerente se occasione tamen noluit vti, sed parant se ad mortem proximam. Paulus in illa per seditione Iudaeorum, priusquam Romam esset perductus, omni ratione & modis omnibus studebat sese eri-pere ex aduersariorum manibus vitamq; seruare. Vide Act.à cap. 21. ad finem usque libri. Postquam vero iam Romam perductus esset, cum ibi in vinculis detineretur ac seruaretur ad mortem proximam, nullum verbum in Scriptura legimus quòd Paulus laborauerit sese eripere ex propinqua morte. Sed cum sciret sibi patiendū esse eo tempore, certiores per literas suas fecit eos ad quos tum ipsi visum est scribere, tempus iam adesse quo sibi patiedum esset ac moriendum. Ego iam liber, inquit, & tempus meae resolutionis instat.
units.tr: The time is noted at which he came into the desert and performed the miracle that follows, namely when the Passover was near, which was the third Passover after the baptism of Christ. For we read of the first in John 2:13, and we heard of the second in John 5:1. This one is the third from the baptism of Christ. Christ did not go up to Jerusalem to keep this Passover with the Jews, as appears from this passage; for he feared the plots of the Jews. Therefore at the time of this Passover he chose to lie hidden in the desert, and to keep himself for the hour appointed for him by the Father. Christ, as we said a little before, when he feared the tyranny of Herod, withdrew for a time; now, however, since he feared the plots of the Jews, he was unwilling to take part in their feast. And yet it is certain that he was fully aware of that hour which had been appointed for his own death and passion. For the Son of God himself, together with the Father, had appointed it from eternity. It is also certain that he knew he could not be removed before that appointed hour, by any plots or schemes of his enemies. Yet Christ was unwilling to tempt his God, nor to expose himself rashly to dangers, but chose to use the ordinary means by which he might escape the hands of his enemies and keep himself for the hour appointed by the Father. We indeed do not know in the same way that hour in which we are to suffer by the will of God; yet we know this, that it is not permitted to all our adversaries to touch even a hair of our head without God's permission; we know also that we must all die once. Yet God is not to be tempted by the example of Christ, nor ought we rashly to thrust ourselves into any present danger, but we ought to use those means which God has allowed us for preserving ourselves until the time that God has appointed. When that time has come, however, God usually makes known to his own, by certain external circumstances and some inward movement of the mind, that the hour is present in which he wishes to be glorified by their death; so that, although they could escape and save themselves, when the opportunity is offered they refuse to use it, and prepare themselves for imminent death. Paul, during that uproar of the Jews, before he was brought to Rome, zealously strove by every means and in every way to snatch himself from the hands of his adversaries and to preserve his life. See Acts from chapter 21 to the end of the book. But after he had been brought to Rome, when he was kept in chains there and reserved for imminent death, we read no word in Scripture that Paul laboured to rescue himself from near death. But since he knew that he must suffer at that time, he informed by his letters those to whom it then seemed fit to write that the time was now at hand when he must suffer and die. For I am already being poured out, he says, and the time of my departure is at hand.

units.la: Hactenus fuit profectio Christi, nunc offerente se occasione miraculi ex conspecta turba Christus tentat discipulos suos, atque ita praeparat eos ad futurum miraculum. Non prius autem conspicit turbam quam incipiat cogitare de eo quo vescerentur quos sciuit famelicos esse, quaeritque à Philippo, Vnde ememus panes quibus isti vescantur? Multitudo Iudaeorum ipsa securà ventris sui, sequuta est Christum. At Christus curat ventrem eorum. Nihil est quod magis impedit nos ne Christum sequamur quàm venter: putant enim homines, si nimis serio, ut ipsi loquuntur, quaerant regnum Dei, & illa quae ad alteram vitam pertinent, fore ut interea pereat. Hinc fit ut nolint quaerere regnum Dei, nisi certa quadam lege & conditione, qua nimirum ipsis bene sit in hac vita. Vide hic indulgentiam & misericordiam Domini. Ea ipse conditione inuitat eos ad quaerendum regnum caelorum. Quaerite primò regnum Dei & iustitiam eius, & ista omnia adiicientur vobis. Pietas ad omnia utilis est, atque promissionem habeat vitae praesentis ac futurae. Verum quidem illud est, in multas magnasque angustias saepe redigi solere charissimos quosque Dei seruos. Sed illud imprimis tenendum est: Quicquid fit erga eos, illud totum in eorum bonum conuerti, siue liberalius, siue parcius cum iis agat Dominus. Si autem parcius cum iis agat Dominus, illud rursus tenendum est, nunquam Deum tentare suos, supra id quod possunt, sed praestare vna cum tentatione etiam euasionē. Paulus didicit in quibus esset, iis ipsis contentus esse: ita omnia valere se per Christum, qui ipsum corroboraret. Nota rursus, Cum quies illa, quam sibi, qua homo fuit, proposuit Dominus, esset ex voluntate Dei per sequentem multitudinem interpellata, quàm lubens cesserit voluntati Patris sui. Neque enim vel vocula est in textu, ex qua suspicari possumus Christum graviter hoc tulisse, quòd multitudo ipsius quietem interturbasset. Eò igitur aspirare debemus omnes, ut subiiciamus nostram voluntatem Dei nostri voluntati, etsi id nunquam in hac vita plenè impetremus, ut videbimus postea in exemplo discipulorum.
units.tr: Thus far was the journey of Christ. Now, when the occasion of a miracle is offered by the sight of the crowd, Christ tests his disciples and so prepares them for the miracle to come. He does not notice the crowd until he begins to think about what they might eat, since he knew they were hungry; and he asks Philip, Where shall we buy bread for these to eat? The multitude of Jews, careless of their belly, followed Christ. But Christ cares for their belly. Nothing hinders us more from following Christ than the belly: for men think that if they seek the kingdom of God too earnestly, as they themselves put it, and the things that pertain to the other life, the things of this life will perish in the meantime. Hence it comes about that they are unwilling to seek the kingdom of God except under a certain law and condition, namely that it go well with them in this life. See here the indulgence and mercy of the Lord. On this very condition he invites them to seek the kingdom of heaven: Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Godliness is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. It is true indeed that the dearest servants of God are often brought into many great straits. But this above all must be held: whatever happens to them, it all turns to their good, whether the Lord deals with them more generously or more sparingly. And if the Lord deals with them more sparingly, this too must be held: God never tempts his people beyond what they can bear, but gives, together with the temptation, also the way of escape. Paul learned in whatever state he was, to be content with it; so he could do all things through Christ, who strengthened him. Note again: when that rest which the Lord had proposed to Christ as a man was, by the will of God, interrupted by the following crowd, how gladly he yielded to the will of his Father. For there is not even a little word in the text from which we may suspect that Christ took it hard that the crowd had disturbed his rest. Therefore we should all aspire to this: to subject our will to the will of our God, although we never fully attain this in this life, as we shall see later in the example of the disciples.

units.la: Nota praeterea, Christus cùm ex monte intuitus esset multitudinem ad se aduentantem, non solùm sollicitus erat de spirituali illo cibo quo vescerentur, verùm etiā decorporali, ideóque quaerit, Unde ememus panem? &c. Dominus, dum nunc intuetur nos de coelo, non solùm ei curae sunt animae nostrae & spiritualis illa vita quo modo ipsam ali oporteat, verumetiam curae sunt corpora & temporaria ista vita quomodo ipsa tolerari possit.
units.tr: Note also that when Christ looked up from the mountain and saw the crowd coming towards him, he was concerned not only for their spiritual food but also for their bodily food, and so he asks, "Where shall we buy bread?" etc. Now, as the Lord looks down on us from heaven, he is concerned not only for our souls and that spiritual life and how it ought to be sustained, but also for these bodies and this temporal life and how it can be endured.

units.la: Nam Pater dedit filio suo non tantum omnes thesauros spiritualium benedictionum, sed etiam temporalium, quae ipse etiam per manus hominis; hoc est, per humanam in ipso naturam, tanquam oeconomus beneficiorum Dei ministret nobis. Domini est terra & plenitudo eius. Et quamvis non nunc miraculose & extra-ordinem nos alat, ut tum olim multitudinem istam: tamen non minus liberaliter & efficaciter etiam nobiscum agit Dominus hodierno die. Nam Dei providentia non minus efficax est in ordinariis rationibus quàm in extraordinariis, si nobis essent oculi quibus eam intueamur.
units.tr: For the Father has given to his Son not only all the treasures of spiritual blessings but also those of temporal ones, which he ministers to us through human hands, that is, through the human nature in him, as steward of God's benefits. "The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof" (Ps. 24). And although he does not now feed us miraculously and outside the ordinary course, as he once fed that crowd, nevertheless the Lord deals with us today no less generously and effectively. For God's providence is no less effective in ordinary means than in extraordinary ones, if only we had eyes with which to see it.

units.la: Quamobrem non tum modò, cùm nos attingit fames animae, ad Dominum veniendum est; sed etiam tum cùm corpus hoc quod gestamus esurit, vel malè habet aliquo modo, ad cum nobis est confugiendum. De nulla re, ait Paulus, solliciti estote, sed in omni re cum precibus & supplicatione cum gratiarum actione petitiones vestrae innotescant apud Deum.
units.tr: Therefore we must come to the Lord not only when the hunger of the soul assails us, but also when this body we carry hungers or is in some way unwell; to him we must flee then too. Paul says, "Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God" (Phil. 4).

units.la: Quanquam qui ante omnia quaerunt regnum coelorum & coelestia, ut hanc multitudinem, de qua sermo est, aliquo certè modo fecisse videmus, de iis Dominus maximis sollicitus est, déque temporali eorum vita iuxta promissionem suam; Quaerite primùm regnum Dei & iustitiam eius & omnia adiicientur vobis,
units.tr: Yet those who seek first the kingdom of heaven and heavenly things, as we see some of that crowd in some sense did, the Lord is concerned about them, and about their temporal life, according to his promise: "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you" (Matt. 6).

units.la: Hoc autem dicebat. Hic obiter admonet Euangelista interrogationem hanc Domini quæ speciem quandam dubitationis præ se ferebat, non ex eo fuisse quòd Dominus non sciret quid esset facturus, sed ideo interrogasse Dominum vt tentaret Philippum, fidémque hominis exploraret, Num is deficiente ordinaria ratione vellet credere potuisse à Domino extra ordinem & miraculosè saturari multitudinem. Dominus nonnunquâ, vt videtur nobis, quasi hæsitabundus nos interrogat,&c, vt videtur nobis, quasi infirmus aliquis cum suis agit in hac vita; Patitur eos affligi, & ad tempus omnibus modis tentari. Imò in ecclesia suanon exerit plenam potentiam suam quantisper in terris militat; sed finit eam sub cruce & infirmitatibus agere. Quòd si enim plenam exerceret potentiam suam in Ecclesia sua militante, profectò necesse esset eam statim plenè glorificari etiam in hac vita. Hic igitur agendi eam rationem qua vtitur Dominus rectè oportet interpretari; non enim ideo sic facit Dominus quòd non posset secus facere; sed ideo sic facit vt fidem nostram tentet, an velimus etiam in mediis tétationibus & afflictionibus credere posse Dominū nos ex iis liberare.Quare dum affligeris aliquo modo, cauc hoc imputes impotentiæ Domini, sed cogita te tentari, an velis interea credere posse Dominum te liberare. Leue quidem illud est, fidem nostram sursum attolli ad cœlos ad Dominum, eiúsque infinitam potentiam apprehendendam, cùm nulla vi deiicitur, nullis infirmitatibus obruitur. Sed hic tota est difficultas, fide assurgere & elucstari ad Dominum quo tempore multis infirmitatibus circumuenta est. Eaque fides, vt quæ sit maximè pretiosa, cùm maximè sit igni quasi afflictionum explorata, vt aurum quò sæpius igne exploratur, eò pretiosius est; ea, in quam, fides comperietur nobis esse laudi & gloriæ & honori quum patefiet Iesus Christus.
units.tr: And this he said. Here the Evangelist briefly reminds us that this question of the Lord, which bore a certain appearance of doubt, was not because the Lord did not know what he was going to do, but he asked in order to test Philip and to explore the man's faith, whether Philip, lacking ordinary means, would be willing to believe that the Lord could feed the multitude beyond the ordinary course and miraculously. The Lord sometimes, as it seems to us, questions us as if he were hesitant, and in this life he deals with his people as if he were somehow weak. He allows them to be afflicted and for a time to be tried in every way. Indeed, in his Church he does not exert his full power while it is fighting on earth, but he lets it act under the cross and under infirmities. For if he were to exert his full power in his militant Church, it would surely be necessary for it to be fully glorified at once, even in this life. Therefore we must rightly interpret the manner of acting which the Lord uses. He does not act thus because he could not act otherwise, but he acts thus in order to test our faith, whether we are willing to believe, even in the midst of temptations and afflictions, that the Lord can free us from them. So when you are afflicted in any way, beware of imputing it to the Lord's impotence, but consider that you are being tested, whether you are willing meanwhile to believe that the Lord can deliver you. It is indeed an easy thing to lift our faith up to heaven, to the Lord, and to grasp his infinite power, when it is cast down by no force and overwhelmed by no infirmities. But here lies the whole difficulty: to rise by faith and struggle up to the Lord at the very time when we are beset by many infirmities. And that faith, which is most precious, is most tested as if by the fire of afflictions, just as gold is the more precious the more often it is tested by fire; that faith will be found to be for our praise and glory and honour when Jesus Christ is revealed.

units.la: Respondit Philippus. Ad interrogatum Domini respondet primùm Philippus, ducentorum denariorum panes, &c. Ducenti isti denarij efficient summam quasi viginti coronatorum, quæ ingens fuit, eo præsertim sæculo. Tu deinde; Andreas frater Simonis Petri respondit, Est hic puerulus rnius. Huc videntur respicere discipuli vt deterreant Christum ab instituto illo suo de pascenda multitudine, quo ipsis paulisper liceret quiescere, seseque cibo reficere: Nam quietem sibi propo suerunt ac recreationem sui, ideoque grauiter tulerunt quietem illam abrumpi per multitudinis importunitatem. Christus, qua homo, etiam tum quietem sibi & suis discipulis propo suit, sed ipse æquo animo tulit aduentum multitudinis, ac oblitus sui ac famis sue ipsius, coepit sollicitus esse de saturada multitudine. In discipulis igitur habemus exemplū rebellionis huius, quæ est in nostra omnium natura, qua fit sæpe, vt non libenter subiiciamus nos voluntati Dei. Verum nobis adnitendum est vt imitemur Dominum nostrum, vt perpetuò reprimamus rebellionem istam ac naturæ inobedientiam, ac, si erumpat tamen, id quod indesinenter facit, perpetuò resipiscamus. Vno verbo; vt in perpetua lucta & perpetua resipiscentia simus. Discimus præterea ex hoc eorum responso, quàm longè absint ab eo vt credant Christum posse extra ordinem multitudinem illam pascere, cum tamen ipse exploraret eos an vellent hoc credere. Quæ autem causa est? fixos habebant oculos in ordinariis hisce mediis. Quandiu quis totus intetus est in hæc ordinaria, & impedimenta ista naturæ, tandiu nunquam credet aliquid magni à Deo fieri posse. Imò in negotio ipso salutis si toti defixi hæreamus in mediis & rationibus ordinariis, fieri non poterit vnquam, vt credamus Deū nos seruaturum. Quare Abraham vt crederet promissioni Dei de semine numeroso, oculos suos subduxit ab impedimentis illis naturæ quæ occurrebant, partim in suo ipsius, partim in Saræ vxoris corpore, & contra spem sub spe credidit. Et Paulus in mediis infirmitatibus positus, spectabat (ipso teste) perpetuò non ea quæ cernuntur, sed ea quæ non cernuntur. Quare nobis quoque eluctandū est in mediis his impedimentis, quæ vndique nos circumstant, vt videamus illam in Deo infinitam potentiam, qua potest quicquid vult facere extra ordinem.
units.tr: Philip answered. To the Lord's question Philip first replies: "Two hundred pennyworth of bread, etc." These two hundred pennies make a sum of about twenty crowns, which was a great amount, especially in that age. Then Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, answers: "There is a lad here who has five barley loaves." The disciples seem here to be looking back, as if to dissuade Christ from his purpose of feeding the multitude, by which they might for a little while be allowed to rest and refresh themselves with food. For they had proposed rest and recreation for themselves, and so they took it badly that this rest was broken by the crowd's importunity. Christ, as man, also proposed rest for himself and his disciples, but he bore the coming of the crowd with an even mind, and forgetting himself and his own hunger, began to be concerned to satisfy the multitude. In the disciples, then, we have an example of that rebellion which is in the nature of us all, by which it often happens that we do not willingly submit ourselves to the will of God. But we must strive to imitate our Lord, so that we constantly restrain that rebellion and the disobedience of our nature, and if it nevertheless breaks out, as it does unceasingly, we constantly repent. In a word, we must be in constant struggle and constant repentance. We learn further from this their answer how far they were from believing that Christ could feed that multitude beyond the ordinary course, although he was testing them whether they would be willing to believe this. And what is the cause? They had their eyes fixed on these ordinary means. As long as anyone is wholly intent on these ordinary things and these hindrances of nature, he will never believe that anything great can be done by God. Indeed, in the very matter of salvation, if we cling wholly fixed on means and ordinary reasons, it will never be possible for us to believe that God will save us. So Abraham, that he might believe God's promise of a numerous seed, turned his eyes away from those hindrances of nature which met him, partly in his own body and partly in that of his wife Sarah, and against hope he believed in hope. And Paul, placed in the midst of infirmities, looked (as he himself testifies) continually not at things which are seen but at things which are not seen. Therefore we too must struggle through these hindrances which surround us on every side, so that we may see that infinite power in God by which he can do whatever he wills beyond the ordinary course.

units.la: 10 Dixit autem Iesus, Facite vt isti discumbant. Erat autem gramen multum in eo loco. Discu-
units.tr: 10 And Jesus said, "Make them sit down." Now there was much grass in that place. They sat down

units.la: Y buerūt ergo viri illi numero quasi quinquies mille.
units.tr: So the men sat down, about five thousand in number.

units.la: II Accepit autem panes illos Iesus, & aliis gratiis distrib uit discipulis: discipuli verò discumbentibus; similiter etiam ex piscciculis illis quantum volebant.
units.tr: 11 Then Jesus took those loaves, and when he had given thanks, distributed them to the disciples, and the disciples to those who were seated; likewise also of the little fishes, as much as they wanted.

units.la: I2 Vt autē expleti sūt, dixit Iesus discipulis suis, Cogite quæ superfuerunt fragmenta, ne quid pereat.
units.tr: 12 When they were filled, Jesus said to his disciples, "Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost."

units.la: I3 Coegerunt ergo & impleuerunt duodecim cophinos fragmentis ex quinque illis panibus hordeaceis, quæ superfuerant iis qui comederant.
units.tr: 13 So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves, which remained over for those who had eaten.

units.la: HActenus fuit tentatio discipulorum; sequitur narratio miraculi tum à Christo editi. Primum præcipit Christus discipulis suis vt faciāt discumbere multitudinem per gramen quod ibi erat satis copiosum; parent discipuli, paret multitudo. In genere hoc notandū est, quàm benignè agat Dominus cum ingratis. Etsi illi disputarint cum illo per infidelitatem, neque voluerint credere potuisse eum extra ordinem multitudinem pascere, cùm tamen multa magnáque ab eo iam priùs edita miracula conspexerint: Dominus tamen in eorū etiam gratiam, vt confirmaretur eorū fides, ipsis inspectantibus & administrantibus edidit miraculum. Quòd si igitur etiam credere nolentibus ediderit miraculum; quod opus editurus est nobis si credere voluerimus? Nullum profectò opus aliud maius edi poterit in nostram gratiam, quàm opus illud salutis nostræ. Quòd si illud crediderimus posse Dominum, & velle secundum promissionem suam illud perficere; profectò futurum est, vt illud perficiat suo tempore, imò si habuerimus fidem non maiorem quàm sit granum sinapis, seruabimur: tantum enim valet & tam efficax est vel tantillum veræ fidei. Quamobrem nobis in hac vita semper luctandum est cum infidelitate, & vt sentiamus in nobis magis magisque fidei istam apprehensionem. Quod autem in specie hic obseruo, id est, primum tentauit discipulos suos Dominus, illi per infidelitatem contra-luctati sunt. Secundò eos tentat, patitur eos in illa infidelitate permanere: ita agere solet Dominus cum suis, luctatur quasi cum illorum ingratitudine. Si nos infidi sumus, ille tamen fidus manet, seipsum negare non potest. dum autem rursus tentat discipulos suos, imperat iis faciendum quod nullo pacto videbatur ipsis probabile, aut rationi consentaneum, vt nimirum discumberet multitudo ad vescendum, cum, vt ipsis videbatur, non esset quo vescerentur. Dominus dum tentat nos, saepe iubet ambulare per tenebras, dum promittit vitam, iubet mori, omniaque facere contraria vitę promissae.Sed quid hic discipuli? parent sine obmurmuratione aliqua. Facienda sunt nobis quaecunque Deus praecipit, etsi non statim videamus quorsum euasura sint, clausis tamen oculis debemus eum ducem sequi. Verùm ex hoc quòd tam promptè paruerint voci Domini, apparet spem aliquam extraordinarij operis reliquam fuisse, etsi iam prius desputauerint cum eo per infidelitatem. Qui etiam ex infidelitate disceptant cum Deo, tamen illi nonnunquam retinent spem aliquam consequendi id quod promissum est, etiam tum cum praecipit Deus quod ipsis videtur valde rationi dissentaneum & improbabile: sperant tamen & expectant bonum ac optatum finem aliquem euenturum. Rursus qui habet illam spem, illi coguntur sese Deo eiúsque voluntati totos permittere, & tamen experiuntur talem euentum, qualem hic experti sunt discipuli Christi. Ergo etsi saepe sentiamus in nobis ipsi magnam infidelitatem, tamen luctandum est cum ea, & reseruanda saltem aliqua spes, vt sperantes permittamus nos Deo, in eiúsque voluntatem nos totos dedamus, atque ita denique in mediis mortibus seruemur.
units.tr: Thus far has been the temptation of the disciples; there follows the narrative of the miracle wrought by Christ. First Christ orders his disciples to make the multitude sit down on the grass, which was fairly plentiful there; the disciples obey, and the multitude obeys. In general, it is to be noted how kindly the Lord deals with the ungrateful. Although they disputed with him through unbelief, and were unwilling to believe that he could feed the multitude beyond the ordinary course, although they had already seen many great miracles wrought by him: nevertheless the Lord, even for their sake, so that their faith might be confirmed, wrought the miracle while they watched and ministered. If then he has wrought a miracle even for those unwilling to believe, what work will he do for us if we are willing to believe? Surely no other greater work can be wrought for our benefit than that work of our salvation. And if we believe that the Lord can, and is willing, to accomplish that according to his promise, then assuredly it will come to pass that he accomplishes it in his own time; indeed, if we have faith no greater than a grain of mustard seed, we shall be saved, for even a very little of true faith is so powerful and so effective. Therefore in this life we must always struggle with unbelief, and that we may feel in ourselves more and more that apprehension of faith. But what I observe here in particular is this: first the Lord tested his disciples, and they strove against him through unbelief. Secondly he tests them, and allows them to remain in that unbelief; the Lord is wont to act thus with his people, he struggles as it were with their ingratitude. If we are faithless, he nevertheless remains faithful; he cannot deny himself. Yet when he tests his disciples again, he commands them to do what by no means seemed to them probable or consistent with reason, namely that the multitude should sit down to eat, when, as it seemed to them, there was nothing for them to eat with. When the Lord tests us, he often bids us walk through darkness; while he promises life, he bids us die, and do everything contrary to the life promised. But what do the disciples do here? They obey without any murmuring. We must do whatever God commands, even if we do not at once see whither it will turn out, yet with eyes closed we ought to follow him as our guide. Moreover, from the fact that they obeyed the Lord's voice so promptly, it appears that some hope of an extraordinary work remained to them, although they had previously disputed with him through unbelief. Those who even from unbelief dispute with God nevertheless sometimes retain some hope of obtaining what has been promised, even when God commands what seems to them highly contrary to reason and improbable: they hope nonetheless and expect that some good and desired end will come about. Again, those who have that hope are compelled to yield themselves wholly to God and to his will, and yet they experience such an outcome as the disciples of Christ experienced here. Therefore, although we often feel in ourselves great unbelief, we must still struggle against it, and some hope must at least be kept in reserve, so that in hoping we may surrender ourselves to God and give ourselves wholly to his will, and thus at last be preserved in the midst of deaths.

units.la: Accepit ergo. In secunda parte narrationis miraculi, habemus factum Christi ac discipulorum ministerium in distribuendis panibus & piscibus. Christus autem prius quàm distribuit panes illos, egit gratias suo more, exemplo suo docens nos idipsum perpetuò facere: Ad quod profectò faciendum, si nihil aliud esset quod nos moveret, vel hoc sufficeret, quòd haec temporaria Dei beneficia sint argumenta totidem paterni illius erga nos amoris. Quamobrem non debemus ea citius inspicere,
units.tr: Accepit ergo. In the second part of the account of the miracle we have Christ's action and the ministry of the disciples in distributing the loaves and fishes. Before Christ distributed those loaves, he gave thanks in his customary way, teaching us by his example to do the same always. Indeed, if nothing else moved us to do this, it would be enough that these temporal gifts of God are so many tokens of that Father's love towards us. Therefore we ought not to look at them

units.la: quàm venire debet nobis in mentem paternus ille Dei erga nos amor in Christo, quo inspecto & percepto nescisse est cor nostrum resoluatur in preces & gratiarum actionem. Praeterea precibus & gratiarum actione sanctificatur in nostrum usum cibus appositus, ut eo bona conscientia uti possimus. Sanctificatur enim per verbum Dei & preces. Neque id solum, verum, ut illa Christi gratiarum actione ac benedictione aucti sunt hi pauci panes inter edendum hoc miraculum; ita sine dubio gratiarum actio fidelis cuiusque, attrahit quasi cibo secretam e coelo benedictionem, qua haec temporaria crescunt quodammodo & efficacia fiunt in usum nostrum: ut non fit mirum prophanos istos, qui vim quasi afferunt bonis Dei creaturis, & violentas in eas manus iniciunt, non prius à Deo venia petita, neque illi gratiis actis non minus fit, inquam, etiam satis magna copiam istarum rerum e manibus illorum quasi euanescere, & in nihilum abire, neque vim habere ad eos alendos, sicuti experimur in multis impuris ac prophanis hominibus hodierno die. Quare in sumendo cibo inter vendum creaturis Dei, si velimus veram ac solidam aliquam ex iis voluptatem capere ac dulcedinem quam oportet, simul atque eas intuemur, vel attingimus, intueamur Deum in Christo Iesu, & percipiamus eam voluptatem quae est ex fide in eum, ac tum quidem sentiemus suaviorem etiam panem hordeaceum cum fide in Christum & gratiarum actione, quam sentiunt prophani illi delitias suas quascunque, sine fide & gratiarum actione. Belluina enim est ista suavitas, quae percipitur sine Christo. Notandum hoc est, quonam tempore pauci illi panes excreverint in tantam magnitudinem. Oportuit sane illud fieri tum cum eos distribuerent accumbenti turbae discipuli Christi, ut inde discas tum demum augeri dona Dei cum ea accommodamus ad usum aliorum. Paulus, cum hortatur Corinthios ad beneficentiam erga pauperes sanctos, hoc vitur argumento; ut abundetis, inquit, ad omne opus bonum. Quo significat eos demum abundare & in eos redundare Dei gratiam; ita ut penes se habeant, non modo quantum ipsis sufficiat, sed etiam quod in alios redunder, eos, inquam, qui ministrant necessitati & inopiae. plæ aliorum.Quod adeo verum esse experimur,vt ij qui non ministrant ex abundantia sua egenis & pauperibus, iis fere euanescant ista,& quotidie minora fiant, vel si etiam ij cumulentur istis bonis. Fit enim non raro, vt mali ditescant supra modum, & affluant temporalibus his bonis, abundantia illa iis in maledictionem verta-tur. Nam diligentibus Deum, quemadmodum omnia alia,ita etiam pauperes & inopia cedit in bonum.
units.tr: without the paternal love of God towards us in Christ coming to mind. Once we have considered and grasped that love, our heart, which does not know how to stay still, melts into prayer and thanksgiving. Moreover, the food set before us is sanctified for our use by prayer and thanksgiving, so that we may use it with a good conscience. For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. Not only that: just as these few loaves were increased during the meal by Christ's thanksgiving and blessing, so without doubt the faithful thanksgiving of each believer draws down, as it were with the food, a hidden blessing from heaven, by which these temporal things grow in some way and become effective for our use. It is no wonder that those profane men who, as it were, do violence to God's good creatures and lay violent hands upon them, without first asking God's pardon and without giving thanks, find that a fairly large supply of these things melts away from their hands, comes to nothing, and has no power to nourish them, as we see in many impure and profane men today. Therefore, when we eat food and take the creatures of God, if we wish to draw from them the true and solid pleasure and sweetness that we ought, then as soon as we look upon them or touch them, let us look to God in Christ Jesus and perceive the joy that comes from faith in him. Then indeed we will find even barley bread sweeter, with faith in Christ and thanksgiving, than the delights that those profane men feel, whatever they are, without faith and thanksgiving. For that sweetness is bestial which is enjoyed without Christ. It must be noted at what time those few loaves grew to such a great size. It was surely fitting that this should happen when the disciples of Christ distributed them to the crowd reclining at table, so that you may learn from this that the gifts of God are increased when we put them to use for others. When Paul urges the Corinthians to kindness towards the holy poor, he uses this argument: "that you may abound to every good work." By this he means that God's grace then abounds and overflows in them, so that they have not only enough for themselves but also something to overflow to others, namely those who minister to the need and poverty of others. We find this to be so true that those who do not share their abundance with the needy and the poor find that these things almost melt away, and become smaller every day, even if such people are loaded with these goods. For it often happens that the wicked grow rich beyond measure and abound in these temporal goods, and that abundance turns to a curse for them. For to those who love God, poverty and want, like all other things, turn to good.

units.la: Vt autem expleti. Sequitur tertium caput narrationis miraculi huius, quo mandat Dominus vt saturata iam multitudine, cogant discipuli quæ superfuerunt fragmenta,ne quid pereat;obediunt autem mandato discipuli. Notandum hoc quòd in tanta redundantia noluit Dominus vel micam vnam panis perire. Qua quidem re docet eos quibus ista redundant, vt attendant tamen ne copia illa abutantur ad luxuriam vel prodigalitatē. Nam si paulò diligentius animaduertas, videbis alium vsum redundantiæ illius,ac,vt videtur,superfluitatis(nihil enim vnquam frustra dedit Dominus cuipiam)eum quidem discere potes ex 2.Corinth.8.13.& deinceps. Ita enim ista disposuit Dominus, qui solus sapiens est,vt alios voluerit abundare, alios voluerit egere. Hic igitur vsus est redundantiæ tuæ,vt per eum suppleas defectum illum qui est in bonis fratris tui, vt fiat æquabilitas;sicut scriptum est,Qui multum collegit,non habuit amplius, & qui paulum, non habuit minus. Redundantia igitur illa non tam tua est quàm fratrum egenorum,vt non sit quod obiicias iis qui merito reprehendunt abusum illum ac profusionem beneficiorum Dei,ista omnia scilicet tua esse,posse te agere cum tuis vt lubet.Sed profundius hic malum latet,quàm tu fortasse aduertis:Tu cum ista profundis ac perdis, nihili facis etiam illum Deum acceius paternum amorem, cuius ista omnia debent tibi esse signa totidem & arrhabones. Quare si amares eum, protestò pluris faceres illa amoris illius argumenta. Nequesauet mea ista oratio auaris-qui ita amant ista bona, vt pro Deo habeant, sed amor istorum esse debet & cura,propter amorem illum Dei, cuius hæc sunt totidem indicia. Coegerunt ergo. Parent discipuli dicto Domini sui. Singula quæ hic habes augent magnitudinem miraculi, primùm tam pauci sunt panes, tum tot iis saturantur, postremò tot fragmenta supersunt. Etsi quidem hodierno die non fit cibariorum miraculosum & extraordinarium incrementum, tamen proculdubiò non possent tot homines ali iis creaturis quæ suppetunt, nisi esset secreta aliqua Dei benedictio, & secretū quoddam creaturarum incrementum interea dum iis vtimur. Neque enim possent istæ fruges quas reddit terra, tot alere quotidie, nisi Deus tribueret iis incrementum aliquod, adeo vt non tantum sufficiant, sed etiam redundent. Scriptum est enim, Non e solo pane viuit homo, sed ex omni verbo prodeunte per os Dei. Et verbo Dei sanctificantur cibi, quos Deus creauit ad participandum. Causa autem cur homines non videant Dei prouidentiam in natura & mediis ordinariis, hæc est, quia toti affixi sunt his externis, adeóque intenti iis, vt Deum eiúsque prouidentiam mirificam non videant: neque tantùm non vident, sed ne volunt quidem videre. Nā eo sumus ingenio omnes, vt abscondita quæque, siue ea in cœlo, siue in terris sint, malimus curiosè indagare, quàm Deum sese manifestò & vltro offerentem intueri. Tam sumus natura à Deo alieni.
units.tr: But when they were filled. There follows the third point of this account of the miracle: the Lord commands that, now that the crowd is satisfied, the disciples gather up the fragments that remain, so that nothing is lost; and the disciples obey the command. It must be noted that, with such an abundance, the Lord would not allow even one crumb of bread to perish. By this he teaches those to whom such things overflow that they should nevertheless take care not to abuse that plenty for luxury or prodigality. For if you look a little more carefully, you will see another use of that overflow, and of what seems to be surplus (for the Lord never gave anything to anyone in vain). You may learn this from 2 Corinthians 8:13 and following. For the Lord, who alone is wise, has so arranged things that he wills some to abound and others to be in want. So the use of your overflow is this: through it you may supply the lack that is in your brother's goods, so that there may be equality; as it is written, "He who gathered much had no more, and he who gathered little had no less." That overflow, then, is not so much yours as it is that of your needy brothers. So you have no reason to object to those who rightly rebuke the abuse and waste of God's benefits, by claiming that all these things are yours and that you may do with your own as you please. But this evil lies hidden more deeply than you perhaps notice. When you squander and waste these things, you also make nothing of that God and his paternal love, of which all these things ought to be to you so many signs and pledges. Therefore, if you loved him, you would surely value those tokens of his love more highly. Nor is this my speech aimed at the greedy, who love these goods in such a way that they regard them as gods; rather, our love and care for them ought to be on account of that love of God, of which they are so many indications. They gathered them up. The disciples obey the word of their Lord. Each of the things you have here increases the greatness of the miracle: first, the loaves are so few; then, so many are satisfied with them; finally, so many fragments are left over. Although today there is no miraculous and extraordinary increase of food, nevertheless without doubt so many people could not be fed by the creatures that are available, unless there were some hidden blessing of God and some secret increase of creatures while we use them. For the fruits that the earth yields could not feed so many every day, unless God gave them some increase, so that they not only suffice but even overflow. For it is written, "Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God" (Matt. 4). And food, which God created to be shared, is sanctified by the word of God. The reason why men do not see God's providence in nature and in ordinary means is that they are wholly fixed on these outward things, and so intent upon them that they do not see God and his wonderful providence. Not only do they not see, but they do not even want to see. For we are all by nature inclined to inquire curiously into hidden things, whether they are in heaven or on earth, rather than to behold God openly offering himself to us of his own accord. So far are we by nature estranged from God.

units.la: 14 Illi ergo quum vidissent signum quod Iesus ediderat, dicebant, Hic est vere Propheta ille qui venturus erat in mundum.
units.tr: 14 When therefore the people saw the sign that Jesus had done, they said, This is truly the Prophet that should come into the world.

units.la: 15 Iesus ergo cùm nosset venturos, & se abrepturos vt se facerent Regem, secessit rursus in montem solus ipse.
units.tr: 15 When Jesus therefore perceived that they would come and take him by force to make him king, he departed again into a mountain himself alone.

units.la: 16 Vt autem serum diei factum est, descenderunt discipuli eius ad mare:
units.tr: 16 And when evening was now come, his disciples went down unto the sea,

units.la: 17 Et ingressi nauigium ibant trans mare Capernaumum versus: iam autem erant tenebrae, nec venerat ad eos Iesus.
units.tr: 17 And entered into a ship, and went over the sea toward Capernaum. And it was now dark, and Jesus was not come to them.

units.la: 18 Et mare vento magno flante insurgebat. Equitur effectum huius miraculi in turba quæ Iesum est sequuta. Quum vidissent signum hoc, dicebant. Proficiunt quidem quadantenus, & Messiam agnoscūt, sed statim euanescunt facientes & fingentes eum sibi regem terrenum, ut appareat ex versu sequenti. Nihil est tam naturale nobis quam ut, simulatque nobis sese patefacit Deus, statim veritatem illam Dei corrumpimus ac perveertimus. Nam vix unum passum confecimus in recta via, quin deflectere incipiamus continuo in diverticula quaedam & alia. Neque hoc fit tantum ob caecitatem naturae & ignorantiam; verum ignorantia ista, ut dicitur Ephes. 4. ex obduratione cordis est: Et Roman. 1. 28. Sicut visum est iis, inquit, Deum in notitia non retinere: ita tradidit eos Deus in mentem omnis iudicij expertem. Illud igitur est quod nobis probatur, optimumque factu videtur: nempe ut deflectamus a recta via & a vero in errores, & tandem evanescamus. Quare quo primum tempore incipit nobis elucescere veritas, ac nos coepimus insistere rectę veraeque vie, imprimis solliciti esse debemus, ut in ea progrediamur. Quod ut melius faciamus & in eo persistamus, relinquenda est nobis natura ac sapientia nostra; & mordicus adhaerendum nobis est Dei verbo, a quo si semel nos diuelli patiamur, necesse est toto caelo aberremus, ut constat hodierno die tristi illa experientia adversariorum, qui sibi permittunt ut euagentur extra limites Scripturae Dei; ex quo tot commenta & mendacia in mundum inuecta sunt, ut iam terra ista ingemiscat sub tanto onere tot figmentorum. Sed adhuc diligentius notandus est error istorum, & erucendus ex imo suo fundamento. Habuerunt illi quidem promissionem Dei de Messia rege futuro: super hoc fundamento male intellecto extruxerunt mendacia sua; primum conceperunt animis Messiam venturum regem fore terrenum aliquem: deinde inuentum eum ipsi voluerunt regem creare, cum id solius Dei fuerit, ut ex Psal. 2. 6. didicimus. Atqui ego inunxi regem meum, praefeceram Sioni monti sanctitatis meae. Quum offert se nobis locus aliquis in verbo Dei, de cultu ipsius, de via salutis, is prudenter nobis tractandus est, neque quod statim prima fronte occurrit, illud semper recipiendum, sed penitus inspiciendus est locus, & conferendus cum aliis Scripturae locis vel iisdem revel phrasi similibus. In primis vero precesque coniungendae sunt, ut is qui loquitur, nempe Dei Spiritus, velit aperire nobis mentem suam quaenam ea sit eo loco. Alioqui profecto praesens periculum est ne detorqueamus Scripturas Dei exitio nostro, & affingamus iis mendacia nostra, id quod non pudet facere hodierno die Pontificios. Hanc quam diximus tractandi & exponendi Scripturas rationem non sequuntur, sed subiiciunt eas hominum iudicio : Nam Ecclesiam (& qualem illam, quaeso) praeferunt Scripturis Dei, & potestatem ei faciunt de iis iudicandi ut velit. Atque hinc fit ut verbum Dei cumulent mendaciis suis, & Deo commenta sua quaecunque impudenter affingant.
units.tr: 18 And the sea arose by reason of a great wind that blew. There follows the effect of this miracle on the crowd that followed Jesus. "When they saw this sign, they said." They make some progress, and they acknowledge the Messiah, but they immediately fade away, making and fashioning him for themselves as an earthly king, as appears from the following verse. Nothing is so natural to us as that, as soon as God reveals himself to us, we at once corrupt and pervert that truth of God. For we have scarcely taken one step on the straight way before we begin at once to turn aside into certain byways and other paths. And this does not happen merely through the blindness of nature and ignorance; rather, that ignorance, as Ephesians 4 says, comes from the hardening of the heart. And Romans 1:28: "Just as they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge, so God gave them over to a mind devoid of all judgment." That, therefore, is what pleases us and seems best to do: namely, to turn aside from the straight way and from the truth into errors, and at last to vanish away. Therefore, from the first moment that truth begins to shine upon us, and we begin to tread the right and true way, we must above all be anxious to advance in it. So that we may do this better and persevere in it, we must set aside our own nature and wisdom, and cling tightly to the word of God; if we once allow ourselves to be torn from it, we must inevitably go astray by the whole sky, as is evident today from the sad experience of our adversaries, who allow themselves to wander outside the limits of the Scripture of God. From this, so many inventions and lies have been brought into the world that this earth now groans under such a burden of so many fictions. But the error of these men must be noted still more carefully, and rooted out from its very foundation. They indeed had God's promise concerning the Messiah, a future king; on this foundation, badly understood, they built their lies. First, they conceived in their minds that the Messiah would come as some earthly king; then, having found him, they wished to make him king themselves, although that belonged to God alone, as we learn from Psalm 2:6: "Yet I have set my king upon my holy hill of Zion." When some passage in the word of God presents itself to us, concerning his worship or the way of salvation, it must be handled prudently by us. We must not always accept at once whatever first meets the eye; rather, the passage must be examined thoroughly and compared with other passages of Scripture, either the same or similar in phrasing. Above all, prayers must be joined to this, so that he who speaks, namely the Spirit of God, may be willing to open to us his mind as to what he means in that place. Otherwise there is a real danger that we will twist the Scriptures of God to our own destruction, and attach our own lies to them, as the Papists today are not ashamed to do. They do not follow this method of handling and expounding Scripture that we have described; instead, they subject the Scriptures to human judgment. For they set the Church (and what kind of Church, I ask?) above the Scriptures of God, and they give it power to judge them as it wishes. And hence it comes about that they overload the word of God with their lies, and shamelessly attach to God whatever inventions of their own they like.

units.la: Notandum est verbum quo vtitur, rapiendi vel corripiendi, quo significatur eos voluisse inuito etiam Christo regnum hoc terrenum obtrudere. Idololatrae & qui gaudent inuentionibus suis, postquam semel conceperunt cerebro cultum suum commentitum, Deo etiam inuito illum volunt obtrudi. Sic Papistae hodierno die commentitum illud cultum suum obtrudunt, non modo Deo, sed & creaturis, ut Angelis & sanctis demortuis. Verbum etiam adportat secum zelum aliquem ardentem, quo ita abrepti sunt, ut honorandi, ut ipsi putabant, Christi causa sese exposuerint manifestissimo periculo, quod oportebat tum esse ab imperio Romano, si semel hoc ab iis tentatum fuisset. Sed zelus hic praeposterus qui magis rabiei est similis quam vero zelo, nihil valet, imo non minus saepe eo offenditur Deus, quam manifesta oppugnatione Christi ac veritatis : dicoque turbam illam non minus fuisse iniuriam Christo cum hoc suo commento & praepostero quodam zelo, quam fuit illa quae postea Christum ad crucem depoliebat. Si enim, ut hoc supponamus, quod fieri tamen nullo pacto modo, Christus in se recepisset hoc regnum ipsi obtrusum, profecto de regno illo caelesti quod ingressus est, & de salute humana fuisset actum. At vero passus est Christus apertam illam illius turbae vim, & crucifixus est. Mors autem illa & transitus fuit quidam ad gloriam ipsius Christi ineffabilem, & causa fuit vitae nostrae, postquam Christus praedixit oportere se multa pati; Respondit Petrus, Propitius tibi sis, Domine, nequaquam erit tibi hoc. At Dominus conversus dixit Petro, Abscede a me Satana, scandalo es mihi, &c. Proculdubio hoc consilium Petri ex zelo erga Dominum suum profectum est. At quia ex zelo quodam præposteró fuit & temeratio, gra-uissimè tulit ipsum Dominus: Neque enim legesalibi in toto fere Euangelio tam acerbè cuiquam responsum esse à Domino, non Iudæ proditori, non ipsi Petro cum ter eum negasset: vt facile videas, nullam vnquam rem grauius ferre Dominum, quàm ementitum cultum, & obseruantiam sui ex præpostero quodam zelo profectam. Sic dico hodierno die Papistas cum zelo suo, cum bonis intentionibus suis, nihilominus, adeóque magis hostes Dei esse, quàm eos qui hodierno die ex Iudæis ob finem manent, quàm Turcas ipsos: Si enim quod illi affingunt Deo & veritati ipsius, id omne locum habe-ret & ab omnibus hodierno die reciperetur, profectò non minùs eo læderetur Dei gloria, & Ecclesiæ salus impediretur, quàm fit aperta illa oppositione coniuratorum hostium. Siquè is quem deferunt angelis & sanctis demortuis cultus ab iis reciperetur, profectò non secus nunc cælo deturbarentur omnes, quàm aliquando Angeli illi, qui stationem suam deserentes, iudicio magni Dei vinculis æternis reseruantur.
units.tr: The verb he uses, rapiendi vel corripiendi (to seize or snatch away), signifies that they wished to thrust this earthly kingdom upon him even against his will. Idolaters and those who delight in their own inventions, once they have conceived their feigned worship in the brain, want it forced upon God even against his will. So the Papists today thrust their made-up worship not only on God but also on creatures, such as angels and departed saints. The word also carries with it a certain burning zeal, by which they were so carried away that, for the honour of Christ as they supposed, they exposed themselves to the most manifest danger, which would have come from the Roman empire had this once been attempted by them. But this preposterous zeal, which is more like madness than true zeal, is worth nothing. Indeed God is no less often offended by it than by an open assault on Christ and the truth. I say that that crowd did no less injury to Christ with this invention of theirs and their preposterous zeal than did the crowd that later dragged Christ to the cross. For if, supposing (though this can in no way happen) Christ had accepted this kingdom forced upon him, then truly the heavenly kingdom he entered, and human salvation, would have been undone. But in fact Christ suffered the open violence of that crowd, and was crucified. Yet that death was a passage to the ineffable glory of Christ himself, and the cause of our life. After Christ foretold that he must suffer many things, Peter answered, "Be it far from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you." But the Lord turned and said to Peter, "Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me," and so on. Undoubtedly Peter's counsel came from zeal for his Lord. But because it was a certain preposterous zeal, it was also rashness, and the Lord took it very badly. For you will hardly find anywhere in almost the whole Gospel that the Lord answered anyone so harshly: not Judas the traitor, not Peter himself when he had denied him three times. So you may easily see that the Lord bore nothing more grievously than a feigned worship and reverence for himself arising from a preposterous zeal. So I say that today the Papists, with their zeal and their good intentions, are nonetheless, and all the more, enemies of God, more than those Jews who today remain obstinate in their unbelief, or than the Turks themselves. For if what they attribute to God and to his truth were accepted and received by all today, the glory of God would certainly be harmed no less, and the salvation of the Church would be impeded, than by that open opposition of conspiring enemies. And if the worship they ascribe to angels and departed saints were received, then certainly all would now be cast down from heaven no less than those angels who, deserting their station, are kept in eternal chains by the judgment of the great God.

units.la: Postremo loco quod obseruamus, hoc est: Apparet quidem ex hoc contextu Iudæos ante Messiæ primum illum aduentum eum seriò expectasse, sed qualem cum expectârunt futurum? id ex hoc textu satis apparet: terrenum scilicet regem aliquem & terrenum liberatorem & vindicem regni Israëlitici, aliud quid boni ex eo in aduentu ipsius non expectarunt. Ex quo apparet eos in aduentu Messiæ fuisse prorsus ἀντιθέτως. Senserunt quidem, fateor, tyrannidem potiùs quàm imperium Romanorum, qua vt liberarentur expetiuerunt sibi aduentum Messiæ iam olim promissi, sed tyrannidem peccati & mortis tum non senserunt. Ex quo illud rursus apparet, quòd licet Christum expectassent; tamen veram illam in Christo venturo consolationem illos non perspiciisse. Illud enim certum est, sine sensu peccati & miseriæ primùm, deinde liberationis in Christo Iesu ab eadem illa miseria, nullam in Christo esse veram consolationem. Nos quidem hodierno die expectamus non primum illum, sed secundum Christi aduentum. Vt igitur eum cum aliqua consolatione expectemus, da- da nobis opera est in tota vita, vt magis magisque in sensu peccati & miseriae nostrae proficiamus: alioqui profecto tantum aberit ab eo vt cum consolatione & gaudio eum Christi aduentum expectemus, vt e contra cum horroribus animi & conscientiae non tam expecte- mus illum diem, quam eum auersemur.
units.tr: Lastly, what we observe at this point is this. It appears from this context that the Jews seriously expected the Messiah before his first coming. But what kind of coming they expected is sufficiently clear from this text: namely, some earthly king and earthly liberator and avenger of the kingdom of Israel. They expected no other good from his coming. From this it appears that in their expectation of the Messiah they were entirely antithetical [ἀντιθέτως]. They did indeed feel, I grant, the tyranny of the Romans rather than their rule, and it was for deliverance from this that they longed for the coming of the Messiah promised long ago. But the tyranny of sin and death they did not feel at that time. From this again it appears that, although they looked for Christ, they did not perceive the true consolation in the Christ who was to come. For this is certain: without first a sense of sin and misery, and then deliverance in Christ Jesus from that same misery, there is no true consolation in Christ. We today look not for his first coming but for his second. So that we may await him with some consolation, we must labour all our life to make ever greater progress in a sense of our sin and misery. Otherwise, truly, we will be so far from awaiting Christ's coming with consolation and joy that, on the contrary, with horror of mind and conscience, we will not so much await that day as shrink from it.

units.la: Iesus ergo. Nunc videamus quam in partem acceperit hunc turbae conatum Dominus; nam prius eorum animum subolfecit, vt Deus exat ἀφιστάμενος, quam sese subduxit in montem, neque passus est rem tentari vel inchoari, veritus scandalum & turbas extituras. Deus, cum affingunt ipsi homines cultum aliquem suum, non citius hoc in mentem illis venit, quam ipse se subdu- cat, neque patitur eorum inuentum ad se vsque pertin- gere. Putant Papistae sese habere Christum in superstitione sua praesentem, eúmque in pane illo missatico hę- rentem adorare, &, quod grauius est, vorare: sed errant. Non enim prius coeperunt de nugis illis suis cogitare quam Christus sese subduxit, adeo vt iam vistorannis illi miseri in tenebris palpitarint, quaerentes an Deum inuenire potuerint, vt de gentibus loquutus est Apostolus: sed quanto magis eum quaesiuerunt in idolis & inuentis suis, tanto longius ab iis recessit. Habemus etiam hic in exemplo Christi, quam alieni debent esse omnes pastores ab honoribus huius mundi captandis. Quod si etiam iusti sint, non tamen debent sibi de iis placere, verum perpetuo quaerere sibi eam laudem, quae est a solo Deo. Quod si iniusti illicitique sint, adeo eos debent a- uersari, vt ne tentari quidem tale aliquid ab hominibus patiantur ipsorum causa, quantum in se est, & ne nomen quidem suum, nedum seipsos iis dent mutuo. Vide igi- tur quam similis sit Christo, Christi, vt vocatur, in terris vicarius, qui vt in omnibus aliis rebus se Antichristum esse ostendit, ita in hac re etiam, cum nulla vnquam sanctitas regnorum ac dominiorum terrenorum eum capiat.
units.tr: Jesus therefore. Now let us see how in good part the Lord took this attempt of the crowd. For he sensed their mind first, and, as God does, withdrawing [ἀφιστάμενος], he drew himself away into the mountain before the matter could be carried out, and he did not allow it to be attempted or begun, fearing the scandal and the tumults that would arise. When men devise for themselves some worship of their own, no sooner does this come into their minds than he himself withdraws, and he does not allow their invention to reach him. The Papists think they have Christ present in their superstition, and that they adore him, indeed devour him, as they hold in that mass-bread. But they are wrong. For they did not begin to think of those trifles of theirs until Christ had withdrawn himself. So for many years those wretched men have groped in darkness, seeking whether they could find God, as the Apostle said of the Gentiles. But the more they sought him in idols and their own inventions, the further he withdrew from them. We have also here, in the example of Christ, how far removed from the pursuit of the honours of this world all ministers ought to be. For even if they are just, they must not take pleasure in such honours, but must always seek that praise which comes from God alone. And if they are unjust and unlawful, they must so shun them that, as far as in them lies, they do not allow any such thing to be attempted by men for their sake, nor even their name, much less give themselves to such men in return. See then how like Christ is his vicar on earth, as he is called, who shows himself Antichrist in all other matters, and in this too, since no holiness of earthly kingdoms and lordships ever takes hold of him.

units.la: Vt autem. Hoc capite, vt initio diximus, habemus profectionem Christi transmare Galilaeae, quod est Tiberiadis. Quod quidem sic accipiendum diximus, non quòd traiecerit Tiberiadis lacum; sed quòd fugiens Herodis insidias, & descendens longius in Galilæam, per sinus, in quos proiectum erat hoc mare, proficisci voluit, quò iter breuius & compendiosius haberet.
