Hactenus ergo per vnum lacus sinum deduximus eum; diximus etiam de miraculo illo in tot pascendis tam paucis illis panibus & piscibus, quod editum est cùm venisset ad ripam vlteriorem, & ad montem qui erat in deserto Bethsaidæ. Nunc verò traiecturus alterum sinum eiusdem lacus, discipulos suos praire iubet. Habemus igitur hoc loco praecipuè nauigationem discipulorum à Domino imperatam, in qua primùm narratur eos, cùm iam serum diei factum esset, descendisse ad mare &c. Tum describitur periculum in quod coniecti erant. Tertiò, habemus Christi ad eos aduentum, ipsiusque ab iis receptionem. Quartò, tranquillam nauigationem, quæ fuit vsque dum ad portum appelIerent. Primum igitur in textu dicitur; Vt autem serum diei factum est. Matth.14.verf.22. & Marc.6.verf.45. scriptum est Dominum coegisse eos inscendere in nauigium & praeire sibi in ripam vlteriorem, interea dum ipse turbam dimitteret, & solus in montem oraret. Ergo non temerè discipuli aggressi sunt hanc nauigationem, verùm iussu Domini sui inscenderunt in nauigiū, iuerunt trans mare versus Capernaum um. Matthæus cap.14.22.scribit edixisse Dominū vt traiicerent in ripam vlteriorem. Marcus verò, cap.6.45.vt praeirent Bethsaidam in ripam vlteriorem. Iohannes verò hoc loco, vt irent versus Capernaūmum. Verùm quia Bethsaida media iacebat in itinere, oportuit Bethsaidâ ire Capernaumū: quare non dissentit Iohannes à Marco. Vide hic, discipuli Christi nihil eorum faciunt, quae faciunt, nisi ex mandato Domini sui, & tamen inter exequendum mandatum Domini sui, non satis prospera nauigatione vntur, neque satis feliciter succedit eis, iactantur tempestate, & veniunt in discrimen vitae. Non est existimandum, quòd dum facimus quae praecipit Dominus, omnia statim ex animi nostri sententia euentura sint, neque ulla impedimenta futura sint: imò verò si qui sunt qui
units.tr: But when. In this chapter, as we said at the start, we have Christ's departure across the sea of Galilee, that is, of Tiberias. We said this is to be understood not as if he crossed the lake of Tiberias, but rather that, fleeing Herod's snares and going further down into Galilee through the bays into which this sea runs, he wished to set out, so that his journey would be shorter and more direct. So far, then, we have brought him through one bay of the lake. We have also spoken of that miracle, in which so many were fed with so few loaves and fishes, which was performed when he had come to the further bank and to the mountain in the desert near Bethsaida. Now, about to cross the other bay of the same lake, he bids his disciples go on ahead. Here, then, we have chiefly the voyage of the disciples commanded by the Lord. In it, first, it is told that when evening had come they went down to the sea, and so on. Then the danger into which they were thrown is described. Third, we have Christ's coming to them and their receiving him. Fourth, the calm voyage, which lasted until they reached the harbour. First, then, the text says: When it was evening. In Matth.14.verf.22. and Marc.6.verf.45. it is written that the Lord compelled them to get into the boat and go before him to the further shore, while he himself dismissed the crowd and prayed alone on the mountain. So the disciples did not undertake this voyage rashly, but at the bidding of their Lord they got into the boat and went across the sea towards Capernaum. Matthew, ch. 14.22, writes that the Lord ordered them to cross over to the further shore. Mark, ch. 6.45, says that they should go ahead to Bethsaida on the further shore. John here says that they should go towards Capernaum. But because Bethsaida lay midway along the way, they had to pass through Bethsaida on the way to Capernaum, so John does not disagree with Mark. See here: the disciples of Christ do nothing except by the command of their Lord, and yet in carrying out their Lord's command they do not have a very favourable voyage, nor does it go very happily for them. They are tossed by a tempest and come into peril of their lives. We must not think that when we do what the Lord commands, everything will at once turn out according to our own mind, and that there will be no hindrances. Indeed, if there are any who

units.la: profectione Christi versus Capernaum. exercentur, & periculis omnis generis obiiciuntur in hac vita, ij sunt maximè qui maximè student exequi voluntatem Dei sui, & illius opere diligentissimè occupantur. Alij verò qui viuunt pro arbitrio suo, neque Deum eiusque voluntatem propositā sibi habent, prosperiore successu vtuntur ferè in rebus suis administradis. Sed respice euentum: discipuli tandem salui in portum perueniunt: ita qui Deo student placere, vtcunque fluctibus in medio quasi cursu ad tempus agitentur: tamen hoc certum est, eos saluos quidem ad portum peruenturos, felicémque rerū suarum exitum habituros. Qui verò non Deo, sed effectibus suis student placere, neque quaerunt quod ipsi acceptū est, sed quod sibi gratum est, ac viis suis non ipsius incedunt, illi profecto etsi in medio intinere non raro prosperiore successu ac nauigatione vtantur, naufragiū tamen patientur priusquā ad portū sint peruenturi. Nam sine respicientia omnes malitandem pereunt. Quare faciendum est nobis perpetuò quod facimus, ex voluntate Dei nostri, & portum illum felicem semper ante oculos habere debemus, qui profecto plus virium habere debet ad nos aliciendos ad hoc vt Deum sequamur, quàm media illa tempestas ad nos deterrēdos ab eo ne perseueremus in obedientia Dei nostri, eiusque voluntatem sequamur.
units.tr: The departure of Christ toward Capernaum. They are exercised and exposed to dangers of every kind in this life. Those who most strive to carry out the will of their God, and are most diligently occupied in his work, are the ones most troubled. Others, who live at their own pleasure and do not keep God and his will before them, enjoy a more prosperous outcome in managing their affairs. But look at the outcome: the disciples at last arrive safe in harbour. So those who strive to please God, however they may be tossed by the waves for a time in the middle of their course, yet this is certain: they will arrive safe at the harbour and have a happy end to their affairs. But those who strive to please not God but their own inclinations, who seek not what is acceptable to him but what is pleasing to themselves, and who do not walk in his ways but their own, these, indeed, though in the middle of their journey they often enjoy a more prosperous course and smoother sailing, will nevertheless suffer shipwreck before they reach the harbour. For without repentance all such men perish in the end. Therefore we must always do what we do according to the will of our God, and we ought always to keep that happy harbour before our eyes. It must surely have more power to draw us to follow God than that storm in the middle has to turn us away from him, so that we do not persevere in obedience to our God and follow his will.

units.la: Iam autem tenebrae. Sequitur periculum illud in quod incidunt inter nauigandum; his autem circumstantiis exponitur.1. Tenebrae erant.2. nec venerat ad eos Iesus. 3. ventus magnus flabat. 4. mare insurgebat. Alij quoque Euangelistae periculum in quo erant ac discrimen ex his omnibus notant, vexatos eos in promouendo nauigio, & agitatos. Sed obserua; discipuli paulo ante vsi sunt ministerio leuiori & faciliori: leuius enim erat illud iuxta mandatum Domini ministrare discumbentes turbae. At nunc incumbit iis, multò grauior ac difficiliot ministerij pars. Putasne tu fore, quisquis es, qui Christo seruis, vt semper ministerio vtaris leuiori? Multi enim sunt qui si succederent iis omnia ex animi sui sententia, & cum satis magna affluentia omnium rerum, voluptatum, diuitiarū, gloriae huius mundi, Christo libenter ministrarent. At abstinerentur à Christi ministerio. ministerio his tot tempestatibus & fluctibus, quibus iacta-ri solent Christi serui. Equidem in ea sententia sum, vt putem ex pontificiis non esse paucos, qui conuicti con-scientiis hanc esse ipsam Dei veritatem, quam nos pro-fitemur hodierno die, lubentissime ad nos transirent, si fieri posset vt vnà secum asportarent mundum hunc, vniuersam illam pompam externam, omnes denique affectus suos vitiosos. Sed quia iam vident id fieri non posse, haerent in caltris suis, hoc est, in tenebris regni Antichristiani. Sed væ eis. Tempestas haec quoque & grauis labor multos ex nostris hominibus deterret, ne ministerium Euangelij suscipiant, quod ipsum vident cō-iunctum esse cum tanta pauperie, tanto hominū con-temptu, tanta etiam persecutione: Nam afflictio ne-cessario Euangelium comitatur. Esto particeps afflictio-num Euangelij ex potentia Dei. Quod si in pace daretur iis ministrare Euangelium, illud quicquid est oneris lu-benter in se reciperent. Atque hinc fit vt hodierno die tam pauci inueniantur qui obeant munus hoc ministe-rij, neque fere ipsum aggrediatur nisi inuiti quodammodo & extrusi. Sed pessime subducunt rationes suas, qui nō sciant fideles quoq; Christi seruos, post leues labo-res, post quietem ac tranquillitatem, si quae illis aliquando contingat, non manere grauiorem tempestatem, adeo vt qui nunc in pace viuunt, & ministrant Deo, non ita magna agitatione oporteat eos praeparari aduersus futuram tempestatem, idque quod fiet hac potissimum ratione, si non patiamur animos securè conquiescere in rebus quibuscunque huius mundi, diuitiis, existimatione hominum, aut aliis id genus, verum in solo Deo nostro, vt & in pace hac externa fruamur, vera quiete, & in tepestate olim exoritura habeamus in quo conquiescamus; quo tempore illi, quicunque non tem-pestate quaesiuerunt sibi veram illa quae in Deo est tran-quillitatem, contenti externa ista & carnali pace ac se-curitate; illi, inquam, exorta iam tempestate difficulter sunt habituri in quo conquiescant. Tam magni interest non acquiescere nisi in Deo solo! Vide hic rursus, disci-puli cum intuentur tenebras exortas, tum, & propter no-stem & propter tempestatem commouentur: cum rursus audiunt ventum magnum flantem, commouentur. Cum denique insurgentes maris fluctus, commouetur; verum quo maxime perturbantur, hoc est, quod interea non conspiciant Iesum, quem si praesentem habuissent, parum commoti fuissent illis rebus omnibus. Cum quis in discrimen vitae suae adducitur, commouetur quidem iis omnibus quae minitantur praesentem mortem: verum, si modo sit sensus aliquis conscientiae, id eum pessime habebit quod Christum praesentem non habeat, quo praesente, ducet omnia mala esse leniora: ille enim lucrum est in morte, ut & in vita. Et sane mors terribilis est, non tam propter hanc separationem animae & corporis, quam propter tormentum illud quod anima destituta Christi praesentia praesentit futurum. Quare semper etiam, cum extra periculum omne positi sumus, nitendum est ut habeamus Christum praesentem, & eum oculis fidei semper per medios quasi caelos iltos penetrantes intueamur, neque ab oculis nostris unquam discedere eum patiamur; nam ubi ventum est ad periculu, ea ratione maxime eum praesentem habebimus. Extraordinarium enim illud est, & non nisi raro admodum, quod quis habeat Christum praesentem in extremo discrimine & in mortis articulo, qui eum iam antea in tota vita ipsiusque praesentiam contempsit. Extraordinarium fuit quod latro ille qui una cum eo suspensus est, eum in morte & cruce tam praesentem habuit. Vanae enim ac prophanae sunt istae hominum voces, qui non dicunt se laborare benene an male vitam transigant, modo concedatur iis vel una hora ad resipiscentiam ante extremum spiritum: Quasi vero hoc fit futurum in eorum potestate tunc temporis resipiscere, & statim Christum pro arbitrio suo de caelo deducere.
units.tr: But now it was dark. There follows the danger into which they fell while sailing, and it is set out in these circumstances: (1) it was dark; (2) Jesus had not yet come to them; (3) a great wind was blowing; (4) the sea was rising. The other Evangelists also note the peril and distress they were in from all these things: they were troubled and tossed while driving the boat forward. But observe: a little before, the disciples had performed a lighter and easier ministry, for it was less burdensome to serve the crowd at table, as Christ had commanded. But now the heavier and more difficult part of the ministry falls to them. Do you suppose, whoever you are who serve Christ, that you will always have a lighter ministry? For there are many who, if everything went as they wished, and if they had a fair abundance of all things, pleasures, riches and the glory of this world, would gladly serve Christ. But they would hold back from Christ's ministry when such storms and waves as Christ's servants are usually tossed by come upon them. Indeed I am of the opinion that among the Papists there are not a few who, convinced in their consciences that this is the very truth of God which we profess today, would most gladly come over to us, if they could carry this world with them, all that outward pomp, and finally all their vicious affections. But since they see this cannot be done, they stay in their camps, that is, in the darkness of the Antichristian kingdom. But woe to them. This storm and heavy labour also deter many of our people from taking up the ministry of the Gospel, since they see it is joined with so much poverty, so much contempt of men, and so much persecution as well, for affliction necessarily accompanies the Gospel. Be a partner in the afflictions of the Gospel by the power of God. If the Gospel could be preached to them in peace, they would gladly take on whatever burden it carries. And hence it comes about that today so few are found who undertake this office of ministry, and scarcely anyone enters upon it except, as it were, unwillingly and pushed into it. But those reckon their accounts very badly who do not know that after light labours, after rest and tranquillity, if these should ever come to them, a heavier storm does not fail to remain for faithful servants of Christ too, so that those who now live in peace and minister to God ought to prepare themselves against the coming storm with no small agitation. This will be done chiefly in this way: if we do not let our minds rest securely in any things of this world, in riches, in the esteem of men, or things of that kind, but in our God alone, so that we may enjoy this outward peace, a true quiet, and have something in which to rest in the storm that will arise one day. At that time those who have not sought for themselves, in God, that true tranquillity, but have been content with that outward and carnal peace and security, will, I say, once the storm has broken, find it hard to have anything in which to rest. So great a thing it is not to rest except in God alone! See here again: the disciples, when they see the darkness come on, are disturbed both by the night and by the storm; when again they hear the great wind blowing, they are disturbed; finally, when the waves of the sea rise up, they are disturbed. But what most troubles them is that meanwhile they do not see Jesus, whom, if they had him present, they would have been little moved by all those things. When someone is brought into danger of his life, he is indeed disturbed by all the things that threaten present death; but if there is any sense of conscience left in him, he will take it very badly that he does not have Christ present, for with Christ present he would count all evils lighter, since to him death is gain, as life is. And indeed death is terrible, not so much because of this separation of soul and body as because of that torment which the soul, deprived of the presence of Christ, foresees as coming. Therefore, always, even when we are placed outside all danger, we must strive to have Christ present, and to gaze upon him with the eyes of faith, always piercing, as it were, through those heavens, and not allow him ever to depart from our eyes; for when we come to danger, we shall have him present most of all in this way. For it is extraordinary, and very rarely the case, that someone has Christ present in the utmost peril and at the point of death, if he has despised him and his presence all his life before. It was extraordinary that that robber who was hanged together with him had him so present in death and on the cross. For those human voices are vain and profane who say they do not care whether they spend their life well or badly, provided they are granted even one hour for repentance before their last breath. As if it were in their power then to repent, and immediately to bring Christ down from heaven at their own will!

units.la: 19 Provecti vero quasi stadia viginti quinque aut triginta, conspiciunt Iesum ambulantem super mare, & appropinquantem navi: & timuerunt.
units.tr: Having sailed on about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they see Jesus walking upon the sea and drawing near to the ship, and they were afraid.

units.la: 20 Ille vero dixit eis, Ego sum, ne timete.
units.tr: But he said to them, It is I; do not be afraid.

units.la: 21 Cupide ergo receperunt eum in navigium: & statim navigium pervenit ad regionem in quam ibant.
units.tr: Gladly therefore they received him into the boat, and immediately the boat came to the land toward which they were going.

units.tr: Why death is terrible, and to whom.

units.la: Voces vanae & prophanae.

units.la: HOc tertium est caput narrationis huius, in quo ad-uenit ad eos Christus: ipsi autem lubenter & cupi-dè recipiunt. Ait igitur, Cùm prouecti fuissent quasi stadia viginti quinque aut triginta. Hoc est, quatuor fere miliaria, si numeres stadia triginta; nam octo quæque stadia efficiunt miliare, pro quo Marcus habet eos iam peruenisse nauigando ad medium vsque maris. Ex hoc stadiorum 25. numero apparet satis látum fuisse hunc maris sinum, nisi dicas progressum hunc tantùm non fuisse rectum, sed obliquum, in tanta maris agitatione. Tum, inquit, conspiciunt Iesum ambulantem super mare, & appropinquantem nauì. Non sequitur ex hoc, quòd Iesus ambulauit super mare, depositisse eum corporis humani quod ipse gerebat qualitates aliquas, aut conditiones naturales & essentiales, vt grauitatè humani & terreni corporis naturalem; verùm retentis omnibus conditionibus naturalibus ferebatur moles illa corporis Christi, naturâ grauis, super aquas, vi inhabitantis in ipso Deitatis. Quòd si mutatio aliqua facta est, ea facta est in aquis super quas ambulauit, quas verisimile est ex liquidis factas esse solidas, ad instar pauimenti cuiusdam firmi ac solidi. Vt non habeant Papistæ ex hoc loco quo defendant realem illam præsentiam suam, quæ plane tollit conditiones naturalis corporis essentiales. Conspiciunt igitur eum ambulantem super mare & appropinquantem nauì, indéque subortus est maior metus, quàm qui priùs fuit. Et timuerunt, inquit. Causa adiecta est ab aliis Euangelistis, Rati enim sunt spectrum esse. Fieri non potest cùm sese obiiciunt nobis eiusmodi res nouæ ac in solitæ, quin horrescamus, quia vel Satanam imponere nobis illusionibus suis, vel Deum aliquid mali portendere continuò immentem nobis venit. Causa autem est conscientia peccati & infirmitatis nostræ, quam solus aufert sanguis Iesu Christi. Quare si quis velit non statim peni-tentiam exhorrescere ad istiusmodi visa, quærat sibi Christum eiusque sanguinem. Sed de his satis.
units.tr: This is the third part of this narrative, in which Christ comes to them, and they receive him gladly and eagerly. He says, When they had sailed on about twenty-five or thirty stadia. That is, nearly four miles, if you count thirty stadia, for eight stadia make a mile; Mark says they had by then sailed as far as the middle of the sea. From this number of twenty-five stadia it appears that this arm of the sea was fairly broad, unless you say that this advance was not straight but oblique, in such agitation of the sea. Then, he says, they see Jesus walking upon the sea and drawing near to the ship. It does not follow from this, because Jesus walked upon the sea, that he laid aside certain qualities of the human body which he bore, or natural and essential conditions, such as the heaviness of a human and earthly body; rather, while all natural conditions were retained, that mass of Christ's body, heavy by nature, was carried over the waters by the power of the Deity dwelling in him. But if any change was made, it was made in the waters over which he walked, which it is likely were made solid from liquid, like a firm and solid pavement. So the Papists cannot get from this passage any support for their real presence, which plainly removes the essential conditions of a natural body. They therefore see him walking on the sea and drawing near to the ship, and from this arose a greater fear than before. And they were afraid, he says. The cause is added by the other Evangelists: they supposed it was a ghost. When such new and unaccustomed things present themselves to us, it cannot be but that we shudder, and immediately it comes to mind that either Satan is imposing illusions upon us, or God is portending some evil. The cause, however, is the consciousness of sin and of our weakness, which the blood of Jesus Christ alone takes away. Therefore if anyone wishes not to shrink at once in repentance from such sights, let him seek for himself Christ and his blood. But enough of these matters.

units.la: Deinde in hunc modum prostratos & territos discipulos consolatur Christus: Ego sum, inquiens, ne timete. Tum illi è vestigio recreati cupidèeum receperunt in nauem. nauigium. Obseruua,aderat quidem vnà cum discipulis suis Christus iam priùs virtute suæ deitatis : at nunc, cùm satis sciret,qua essent adhuc infirmitate, eos ponere virtutem ipsius in sola præsentia corporali, hac in parte noluit deesse eorum infirmitati. Christus ita indulget nobis, vt etiam mirabiliter toleret infirmitates nostras. Verùm,Deo sit gratia,nos qui nunc in tanta luce Euangelij viuimus, didicimus non ponere virtutem eius in præsentia aliqua corporali : verùm credimus in Christum positum longè supra omnes cælos quòd ad corpus, non minùs tamen præsentem nobiscum esse in terris virtute & deitate sua, quàm si corpore præsens adesset. Verùm præsentia hæc Christi per virtutem suam non semper est eiusdem modi. Tum enim maximè virtute sua præsens est nobis cùm maximè periclitamur, maximèque sentimus infirmitatem nostram : Potentia mea, inquit, per infirmitatem perficitur. Hoc expertus est Paulus in morte. Vita, inquiens, Iesu manifesta est in mortali carne nostra. Id etiam sentiunt in se pij quique. Verùm non est putandum Christum præsentem virtute & efficacia sua semper suos liberare, vt sic dicam, corporaliter, vt discipulos suos tum olim liberauit, sed sæpius liberare eum suos spiritualiter existimandum est. Nam Christus, inquit Apostolus, etiam in morte lucrum est. Quòd si in morte lucrum sit, seruat etiâ morientes, eósque in ipsa morte liberat, quæ profectò liberatio longè præstantissima est & suauissima. Maius pondus latet in his verbis quàm prima facie apparet. Christus enim, cùm eminus incuentur eum discipuli, antequam vocem edidisset, putarunt spectrum esse, vnde tantum abfuit ab eo, vt eius præsentia eos consolata sit, vt eos etiam magis deiecerit quàm antea. Christum dum intuentur homines emi-nus, hoc est, in operibus, vident aliqua maiestatis eius signa & indicia, neque adhuc audiunt vocem eius, ipsúmque se in verbo suo patefacientem docentémque quæ sit ipsius persona, quod officium, quis omnino cultus ipsi debeatur, statim pro Christo faciunt sibi spectrum idolum. Vnde nihil in cordibus hominum nisi pauor existere potest : Nam idolum implet animos trepida superstitione. Multiplicant dolores suos qui alienum dotant. At vero discipuli ipsius, posteaquam vocem eius inaudi-uerunt, continuo ex voce eum cognouerunt: unde insecuta est illa laetitia in corde atque avida ipsius apprehensio. Postquam iam audiuimus Christi vocem in verbo suo scripto, extra quod verbum non audietur usque ad extremum illum diem, incipiunt eum cognoscere quotquot ipsius oves sunt, simulque laetitia ingenti afficiuntur, atque avide eum ad se apprehensum trahunt. Fateor quidem hoc effectum vocis Christi nō in omnibus sine discrimine inueniri, quia Christus non loquitur similiter cordibus omnium, hoc est, non vocat intus & efficaciter eos omnes quoscunque verbo suo foris vocat. Vide hic rursus vsum afflictionum; discipuli tempestate agitati incipiunt tangi absentis Christi desiderio magno, quod quidem desiderium satis apparet tum ex eo quod praecessit, Iesus non venerat: tum ex eo quod sequitur, tupidè receperunt eum. Desiderantes autem eum, cum primum inueniunt eum, gestiunt pro laetitia, avidèque Dominum suum ad se arripiunt. Sic vsu venit; afflictiones enim gignunt in nobis desiderium. Nam non satis cognoscimus quantum bonum sit in Christo priusquam sentiamus in nobis penuriam ac egestatem nostram. Atque inde fit vt afflicta ista Ecclesia militans mirabiliter desideret secundum illum Domini aduentum. Etiam veni, Domine Iesu, Apocal. 22. 20. Postquam vero conspeximus iamdiu desideratum, mirum est quanta cum auiditate eum apprehendamus, id quod etiam fiet in illustri illo aduentu Domini, quo tempore videbimus eum electos ad se arripere mira cum auiditate. Sed quod est effectum praesentis Domini? Quàm efficax sit illa praesentia Domini ad vitam ac salutem, ex postrema parte huius historiae satis elucet, sed datur tempestas, discipuli statim ad portum appellunt. Praesentia Christi semper est efficax, adeo vt qui sentit cum habitare in corde suo per fidem, etiam in summo discrimine possit sibi persuadere se ereptum iri ex omnibus malis, sed tum demum, quàm efficax sit illa Christi praesentia, sentiemus, cùm videbimus eum in illo die cum gloria in nubibus veniente ad perfectam Ecclesiae suae liberationem. Huic igitur sit omnis gloria, Amen.
units.tr: Then Christ, having thus laid the prostrate and terrified disciples low, comforts them: "I am," he says, "do not fear." At once they were restored and gladly received him into the ship. Observe that Christ had already been present with his disciples by the power of his deity. But now, since he knew how weak they still were, and that they placed his power only in his bodily presence, he was unwilling in this respect to fail their weakness. Christ thus indulges us, and even wonderfully bears with our infirmities. Yet, thanks be to God, we who now live in such clear light of the Gospel have learned not to place his power in any bodily presence. Rather, we believe that Christ, though placed far above all the heavens as to his body, is nonetheless present with us on earth by his power and deity, no less than if he were present in the body. But this presence of Christ through his power is not always of the same kind. For he is most present to us by his power when we are in the greatest danger and most feel our weakness: "My power," he says, "is made perfect in weakness." Paul experienced this in death: "The life of Jesus," he says, "is made manifest in our mortal flesh." All the godly also feel this in themselves. Yet it is not to be thought that Christ, present by his power and efficacy, always delivers his people bodily, so to speak, as he once delivered his disciples; rather, we should understand that he more often delivers them spiritually. For Christ, says the Apostle, is gain even in death. If he is gain in death, he also preserves those who are dying and delivers them in death itself; this deliverance is truly most excellent and most sweet. A greater weight lies hidden in these words than appears at first sight. For when the disciples saw Christ from afar, before he had uttered a word, they thought he was a spirit. So far was he from comforting them by his presence that he cast them down even more than before. While people look at Christ from afar, that is, in his works, they see some signs and indications of his majesty, but they do not yet hear his voice, nor do they hear him revealing himself in his word and teaching who his person is, what his office, and what worship is due to him at all; at once they make for themselves, in place of Christ, a phantom, an idol. Hence nothing but dread can arise in men's hearts, for an idol fills the minds with trembling superstition. Those who endow another multiply their sorrows. But his disciples, after they heard his voice, at once recognised him from his voice; hence came that joy in the heart and that eager grasping of him. Now that we have heard the voice of Christ in his written word, outside which word he will not be heard until that last day, all his sheep begin to know him, and are at the same time filled with great joy, and eagerly draw him to themselves as they grasp him. I admit that this effect of the voice of Christ is not found in all without exception, because Christ does not speak in the same way to the hearts of all, that is, he does not inwardly and effectually call all those whom he outwardly calls by his word. See here again the use of afflictions: the disciples, troubled by the storm, begin to be touched by a great longing for the absent Christ, which longing appears clearly both from what went before, "Jesus had not come," and from what follows, "they gladly received him." Longing for him, when they first found him, they rejoiced, and eagerly seized their Lord to themselves. So it happens; for afflictions beget longing in us. For we do not sufficiently know how great a good is in Christ until we feel our want and poverty. And hence it comes that this afflicted Church militant wonderfully longs for the second coming of the Lord: "Even so, come, Lord Jesus" (Apoc. 22. 20). But when we have seen him long desired, it is wonderful with what eagerness we lay hold of him; and this will also happen at that illustrious coming of the Lord, when we shall see the elect seize him to themselves with wonderful eagerness. But what is the effect of the present Lord? How efficacious that presence of the Lord is for life and salvation is sufficiently clear from the last part of this history: there is a storm, and at once the disciples reach the harbour. The presence of Christ is always efficacious, so much so that he who feels that Christ dwells in his heart by faith can, even in the greatest peril, persuade himself that he will be snatched from all evils. But then at last we shall feel how efficacious that presence of Christ is, when we see him in that day coming in the clouds with glory, to the perfect deliverance of his Church. To him therefore be all glory, Amen.

units.la: 22 Postero die turba quæ substiterat cis mare, quum vidisset illic non fuisse aliud navigiolum nisi unum illud in quod ingressi fuerant discipuli eius, & Iesum non introisse cum discipulis suis in navigium, sed solos eius discipulos abiisse:
units.tr: 22 On the next day the multitude which had stood on the other side of the sea, when they saw that there had been no other little boat there except that one into which his disciples had entered, and that Jesus had not entered with his disciples into the boat, but that only his disciples had gone away:

units.la: 23 (Alia verò navigiola Tiberiade venerunt prope locum illum ubi comederant panem, postea-quam gratias egisset Dominus:)
units.tr: 23 (However, other little boats had come from Tiberias near the place where they had eaten the bread, after the Lord had given thanks:)

units.la: 24 Quum igitur, inquam, vidisset turba Iesum illic non esse neque discipulos eius, ingressi sunt & ipsi in navigia, & venerunt Capernaumum, quaerentes Iesum.
units.tr: 24 When, therefore, I say, the multitude saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they also entered the boats and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.

units.la: 25 Et eo invento trans mare, dixerunt ei, Rabbi, quando huc pervenisti?
units.tr: 25 And when they had found him across the sea, they said to him, "Rabbi, when did you come here?"

units.la: NUNC redimus ad turbam. Primum observavit Christum traiecisse illum maris sinum, & traiecisse quidem miraculose admodum: deinde sequuntur ac quaerunt eum: tertio, inveniunt eum: quarto, habent sermones cum illi mutuos ad finem fere capitis. Quod ad primum eorum quae propositimus, hoc quasi dilemmate narratur eos collegisse traiectum Domini miraculosum fuisse. Si in navigio traiecit, vel in alio quodam ab illo in quo ante eum traiecerunt ipsius discipuli, vel in eodem: at non in alio, quia non erat aliud navigium in illo portu; Non in eodem, quia viderunt eum iubentem discipulos sibi praeire ad ulteriorem ripam, neque interea abeuntem cum iis: Non traiecit in navigio illo: Ergo traiectus eius plane miraculosus fuit. Tum excipi potuit: At erant ad manum alia praeterea navigia non pauca illic. Respondet alia navigiola Tiberiade venisse, non in eum portum; sed in portum qui erat prope illum locum ubi comederat panem, postquam gratias egisset Dominus. Observa primum; Non frustra factum est quod viderunt illic non esse aliud navigium: viderunt etiam edixisse discipulis ut praeirent. Hoc in eum finem factum est vt saltem ex his & similibus circumstantiis colligeret Christi traiectum miraculosum fuisse, vt rursus notitia illa Messiæ ex primo illo miraculo inchoata, per hoc miraculum confirmaretur. Eodem quoque tendit prolixus ille sermo cum illis habitus, de quo posteavidebimus. Opus bonum quod incepit Deus in nobis cupit ad finem perducere. Qui cœpit in vobis, inquit, opus bonum, perficiet vsque ad diem Iesu Christi. Et, Vocatio Dei est absque respisentia, saltem ex ipsius parte. Nam si nos infidi sumus, ille tamen fidus manet, negare seipsum non potest. Hinc fit vt non satis habeat in conspectu nostro tantum vnum aliquod opus edere, vel semel nobis alloqui in verbo suo, adhoc inchoetur in nobis notitia ipsius, verum opus perpetuo addat operi, prædicationem prædicationi continua successione, donec vel perficiamur, vel certè deficiamus ab eo. Est quidem continuatio ista verbi prædicati in hac nostra Ecclesia & gente, argumentum indubitatum quòd velit Deus nos perficere ac cognitionem istā nostram inchoatam; adeò vt si non sit futurum vt perficiamur, illud tribuendum sit non Deo, sed metæ ingratitudini nostræ & infidelitati, qua tantam illam Dei fidem, & ergà nos misericordiam compensamus. Obserua secundò, cum de navigiis iis loquitur Euangelista quæ venerunt Tiberiade propè locum vbi comederant panem, non solùm panis & piscium illorum miraculosè auctorum; sed & precum illarum quibus impetratū est à Patre illud panis & piscium admirabile augmentum, pariter meminit: ea re commendans nobis, non tam miraculum illud quàm rationem & medium impetrati à Deo miraculi, nempe preces; vt nos quoque excitemur ad preces, ad hoc vt in nostram etiam gratiam non minùs mirifica edantur opera, quàm fuit istud, de quo nunc loquimur, miraculum. Et verum est quidem fide & precibus hodierno die non minus miraculosè ali & animas & corpora piorum, quàm tum olim turba satura est. Nam vt de animis nihil loquar quorum nutrimentum superat infinitis partibus illud miraculum tum editum; quì omnes in hac vita dum spectant non ea quæ cernuntur, sed ea quæ non cernuntur, neque ita solliciti sunt de rebus huius vitæ; sed vt præcipit Apostolus, Omni ...
units.tr: Now we return to the crowd. First, he notes that Christ crossed that arm of the sea, and crossed it in a quite miraculous manner. Next, they follow and seek him; third, they find him; fourth, they hold conversations with him, nearly to the end of the chapter. As to the first of these points, the matter is related in this kind of dilemma: they concluded that the Lord's crossing was miraculous. If he crossed in a boat, it was either in another one, different from that in which his disciples had crossed before him, or in the same one. Not in another, because there was no other boat in that harbour. Not in the same, because they saw him bidding his disciples to go ahead to the farther shore, and meanwhile not leaving with them. He did not cross in that boat. Therefore his crossing was plainly miraculous. Then it might be objected: "But there were in fact many other boats there at hand." He answers that other little boats had come from Tiberias, but not to that harbour; rather to the harbour near the place where he had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks. Observe first: it was not in vain that they saw there was no other boat there; they also saw that he had ordered the disciples to go ahead. This was done with this end, that from these and similar circumstances at least they might gather that Christ's crossing was miraculous, so that the knowledge of the Messiah, begun from that first miracle, might again be confirmed through this miracle. To the same end also tends that long discourse which he held with them, of which we shall see more later. God desires to bring to completion the good work which he has begun in us. "He who has begun a good work in you," he says, "will bring it to completion until the day of Jesus Christ." And, "The calling of God is without repentance," at least on his part. For if we are faithless, he nevertheless remains faithful; he cannot deny himself. Hence it is that he does not think it enough to perform only one work in our sight, or to speak to us once in his word, so that the knowledge of him is begun in us; rather he adds work to work and preaching to preaching in continuous succession, until either we are made perfect or we certainly fall away from him. This continuation of the preached word in this our Church and nation is indeed an indubitable argument that God wishes to make us perfect and to bring our begun knowledge to completion; so that if we are not going to be made perfect, the blame is to be laid not on God but on our ingratitude and unbelief, by which we repay that great faithfulness of God and his mercy toward us. Observe, secondly, that when the Evangelist speaks of those boats which came from Tiberias near the place where they had eaten the bread, he mentions equally not only the bread and fish miraculously increased, but also those prayers by which that wonderful increase of bread and fish was obtained from the Father. He thereby commends to us not so much that miracle as the reason and means of obtaining the miracle from God, namely prayers; so that we also may be stirred to prayer, that in our own favour no less wonderful works may be done than that miracle of which we now speak. And it is true indeed that by faith and prayer on this very day the souls and bodies of the godly are fed no less miraculously than the crowd was satisfied at that time. For, to say nothing of souls, whose nourishment surpasses that miracle then wrought by infinite degrees, all those who in this life look not at things which are seen but at things which are not seen, and are not so anxious about the things of this life, but as the Apostle teaches, in every

units.la: Philip. 1,6.
units.tr: Philip. 1,6.

units.la: Altera observatio commendatio precum.
units.tr: The second observation: the commendation of prayers.

units.la: Philip. 4,6. in re precibus & supplicatione cum gratiarum actione petitiones suas faciunt innotescere apud Deum; tum haud dubie ratione plane admirabili aluntur: neque ipsi satis sciunt, neque alij etiam unde suppeditentur iis ea quibus vitam istam suam tolerant: adeo ut ego cogar preces ex fide professas pro bono aliquo temporario ad Deum conceptas, praeferre ipsi illi bono quod per preces suas a Deo impetrant. Malo enim accipere a Deo ferias preces, quam sine precibus vniuersum hunc mundum. Nam rarius est hoc donum precum, quam donum temporarium quodcunque, & paucioribus conceditur. Neque enim omnes quotquot acceperunt a Deo temporaria ista, statim acceperunt donum illud precum & actionis gratiarum.
units.tr: Philip. 4,6. In every matter they make their petitions known to God with prayer and supplication, together with thanksgiving; then undoubtedly they are fed in a wholly admirable manner. Neither they themselves nor others know fully where the things that sustain their life in this world come from. So much so that I am compelled to set the prayers that are professed in faith and offered to God for some temporal good above that very good which they obtain from God through their prayers. For I would rather receive from God the gift of prayer than this whole world without prayer. This gift of prayer is rarer than any temporal gift, and it is granted to fewer people. Indeed, not all who have received those temporal things from God have at once received the gift of prayer and thanksgiving.

units.la: Quum ergo vidisset. Nunc quaerunt lesum, eamque sequuntur Capernaum usque: quo admonemur, quod quemadmodum Dominus animos eorum ad se pertraxit operibus suis admirabilibus, ita ipsi eum sunt sequuti: sed cum non nisi hypocritae essent, ut audiemus postea vers. 66. multi enim ex iis pedem retulerunt & defecerunt, non tam adhaeserunt ipsi Domino, quam esca quasi illi, quam iniecit ori eorum, ut solent piscess qui inescantur non piscatorem sequi, sed escam. Sic multi apud nos hodierno die non Euangelium Christi; sed escam & mundum hunc, quae etiam secum nonnunquam adportat Euangelium, sequuntur: Quo ubi primum se fructratos esse viderint, tum profecto ostendent se non magis secutos esse Christum ipsum aut Euangelium ipsius, quam sequuta est eum tum olim turba ista, quae quamprimum coepit Christus abstrahere eius animum a terrenis istis ad considerationem coelestium, tum primum ab eo defeciit. De sacrilegis istis loquor potissimum, qui bona Ecclesiastica omnia diripuerunt.
units.tr: When therefore he had seen. Now they seek Jesus and follow him as far as Capernaum. We are thereby admonished that, just as the Lord drew their minds to himself by his wonderful works, so they in turn followed him. But since they were nothing but hypocrites, as we shall hear later at verse 66, many of them turned back and fell away. They clung not so much to the Lord himself as to the bait that he had thrown into their mouths, just as fish that are enticed do not follow the fisherman but the bait. So today many among us follow not the Gospel of Christ but the bait and this world, which sometimes brings the Gospel along with it. When they see that they have been cheated, they will certainly show that they followed Christ himself or his Gospel no more than that crowd did long ago, which fell away from him as soon as Christ began to draw their minds from earthly things to the contemplation of heavenly ones. I speak chiefly of those sacrilegious men who have plundered all the Church's goods.

units.la: Et eo inuento. Dum quaerunt Dominum, ipse, etsi satis sciret plerosque eorum non nisi hypocritas esse, tamen non subduxit se, sed obtulit iis suam praesentiam, simulque dignatus est eos sermone satis prolixo: suo exemplo docens nos, non statim reiiciendos esse hypocritas, sed admittendos ad audiendum Christum in verbo suo, cum ipse Christus non negauerit praesentiam suam tum olim huic hominum generi. Sed hoc praeterea considerandum est, quod cum sciret inutilem & praesentiam & sermonem suum fore iis, tamen vltro obtulerit se iis, eòsque allocutus fuerit. Hoc non tantum ideo fecit, vt reddetentur inexcusabiles, sed hoc primum respexit, vt, si fieri posset, resipiscerent ac seruarentur : Dominus enim pro infinita sua misericordia miseretur hypocritarum, miseretur etiam reproborum : tam propensa est eius misericordia in quoscunque. Ante executionem iudicij sui omnibus modis inuitat etiam ipsos reprobos ad resipiscentiam. Vide Rom. 2. 4. An coptiam benignitatis eius & tolerantiae ac lenitatis contemnis, ignorans te benignitate Dei ad resipiscentiam deduci? Et Ro. 9. 22. Pertulit multa lenitate vasa irae coagmentata ad interitum. Cum autem ventum est ad iudicium & executionem, sic exequitur iudicium ex iustitia, vt interea etiam miserea-tur ad instar iudicis alicuius, qui bonus est vir & rectus coram Deo. Is dum tradit reum & iam damnatum in manus catnificis : interea misericordia erga damnatum hominem aliqua afficitur, ita tamen vt misericordia non sit praeiudicio iustitiae, & iubeat reum & damnatum morte multari. In Deum hoc cadit vel multo magis, in quo admirabiliter consistunt, etiam in ipsa executione iudicij sui, summa misericordia erga creaturam suam, & summa iustitia erga reum & peccatorem, vt ipsi sit gloria misericordiae simul & iustitiae in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: And when they had found him. While they seek the Lord, he himself, although he knew well that most of them were nothing but hypocrites, did not withdraw himself but offered them his presence, and at the same time condescended to address them at some length. By his example he teaches us that hypocrites are not to be rejected at once, but admitted to hear Christ in his word, since Christ himself did not deny his presence to that kind of men long ago. But this must also be considered: although he knew that both his presence and his speech would be useless to them, he nevertheless offered himself to them of his own accord and spoke to them. He did this not only so that they would be made inexcusable, but first of all he looked to this, that, if it were possible, they might repent and be saved. For the Lord, in his infinite mercy, has pity on hypocrites and has pity even on the reprobate; so inclined is his mercy toward whomever it may be. Before the execution of his judgment he invites even the reprobate to repentance by every means. See Rom. 2:4: Or do you despise the riches of his goodness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? And Rom. 9:22: He endured with much patience the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction. But when the time comes for judgment and its execution, he so carries out judgment in justice that meanwhile he also shows mercy, like some judge who is a good and upright man before God. While he hands over the accused, already condemned, into the hands of the executioner, he is nevertheless moved by some mercy toward the condemned man, yet in such a way that mercy does not prejudice justice, and he orders the guilty and condemned man to be put to death. This applies to God much more, in whom, wonderfully, there coexist, even in the very execution of his judgment, the highest mercy toward his creature and the highest justice toward the guilty sinner, so that to him there may be glory for his mercy and justice together forever. Amen.

units.la: Dixerunt ei Rabbi. Sequitur nunc dialogus & sermo inter Christum & turbam mutuo habitus : illi priores Christum alloquuntur. Rabbi, inquiunt, quando huc venisti? Quaestio non tantum est temporis, sed & modi : nam volunt videri inter quaerendum in admiratione habere eius aduentum, qui mos est hypocritarum. Nemo enim est piorum omnium, qui tantus est in verbis & gestibus, quanti sunt hypocritae. Vera pietas non est in istiusmodi ostentatione & verborum iactatione; sed in interiori sinceritate & in externo bono opere. Sed videndum est quomodo eos excerpsit Dominus.
units.tr: They said to him, Rabbi. Now follows a dialogue and discourse between Christ and the crowd, carried on in turn. The first speakers address Christ: Rabbi, they say, when did you come here? The question concerns not only the time but also the manner. For while asking, they wish to appear to be amazed at his coming, which is the custom of hypocrites. For no one among all the pious is as full of words and gestures as hypocrites are. True piety does not lie in such display and boasting of words, but in inward sincerity and in good works outwardly. But we must see how the Lord sifted them out.

units.la: 26 Respondit eis Iesus, & dixit, Amen, amen dico vobis, quaeritis me, non quia vidistis signa, sed quia comedistis panes illos & saturati estis.
units.tr: Jesus answered them and said, Verily, verily I say unto you, you seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.

units.la: 27 Operimini non cibo qui perit, sed cibo illi qui permanet in vitam aeternam, quem Filius hominis dabit vobis: hunc enim Pater obsignauit, id est, Deus.
units.tr: Work not for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you; for God the Father has sealed him.

units.la: 28 Dixerunt ergo ad eum, Quid faciemus vt operemur operibus Dei?
units.tr: Then they said to him, What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?

units.la: 29 Respondit Iesus & dixit eis, Hoc illud est opus Dei, vt credatis in eum quem ille misit.
units.tr: Jesus answered and said to them, This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.

units.la: Quod dicerent, Quamuis vos prae vobis seratis admirationem quandam signorum meorum, tamen non tam iis adducimini, vt me sequamini, quam esca illa quam accepistis, & pane quo estis saturati. Addit etiam iuramenti speciem, Amen, amen, inquit, quo significat se non loqui perfunctorie & fiete, vt ipsi sunt loquuti; sed plane serio, ad hoc vt tandem agnoscant serio se hypocrisia esse. Nam hoc est hypocritarum ingenium, vt non tantum imponat aliorum oculis, verumetiam suis ipsorum. Atque ex hoc responso Domini discimus, non tam respondendum esse verbis hypocritarum, in specie magnificis ac praeclaris, quam mentibus & cogitationibus, si vlla ratione deprehendi a nobis possint, ad hoc, vt, si fieri possit, in lucem proferantur secretae cogitationes, & ab ipsis etiam miseris conspiciantur, vt tandem resipiscant & seruentur. Hoc postremo succurrit quod hic obseruamus; Quaeritis me, inquit, non quia vidistis signa, sed quia comedistis panes. Ex hoc apparet cum Christo eiusque Euangelio coniuncta esse etiam ista terrena. Christus enim efficax est, & ad vitam aeternam, & ad praesentem hanc vitam, & quaerentibus se ac vitam in ipso aeterna, promittit etiam satis magnam copiam bonorum huius vitae. Pietas ad omnia vtilis est, vt quae promissione habeat vitae praesentis ac futurae. Vide quid hic fiat ab hypocritis, hoc cum sciant sequuntur Christum, sed non tam propter ipsum, quam propter bona ista temporaria quae
units.tr: By this he means: although you display before you a certain wonder at my signs, you are not drawn to them so as to follow me, but rather by that food which you have received and by the bread with which you have been filled. He also adds the form of an oath, Verily, verily, he says, by which he signifies that he is not speaking carelessly or in pretence, as they did; but quite seriously, so that at last they may recognise seriously that they are hypocrites. For this is the nature of hypocrites: they deceive not only the eyes of others but also their own. And from this answer of the Lord we learn that we must answer not so much the words of hypocrites, especially their splendid and fine-sounding ones, as their minds and thoughts, if by any means we can detect them, so that, if possible, their hidden thoughts may be brought into the light and seen even by the wretched themselves, so that at last they may repent and be saved. Last, what we observe here comes to mind: You seek me, he says, not because you saw signs, but because you ate the loaves. From this it appears that even earthly things are joined with Christ and his Gospel. For Christ is effective both for eternal life and for the present life, and to those who seek him and in whom life is eternal, he also promises a fairly large store of the good things of this life. Piety is useful for all things, since it has the promise of the present and the future life. See what happens here among hypocrites: they know this, and so they follow Christ, but not so much for his own sake as for those temporal goods

units.la: Hypocritis quomodo respondendum. quæ illi serió apprehendunt, Christum autem ipsum, & efficaciam illam quæ est in eo ad vitam æternam, videri tantum volunt apprehendere. Atque ita spoliant Christum præcipua illa sua efficacia, quantum in ipsis est: Nã etsi re ipsa nulla ex parte imminuatur vis illa & efficacia Christi, de qua vide Rom. 5. 12. & deinceps, in illa nimirum præclara comparatione primi Adami & secundi: tamen quia illam contemnunt hypocritæ, non minus rei futuri sunt, quàm si Christum ea omnino spoliassent. Videmus igitur quantò cum periculo hæc res coniuncta sit. Demus itaque operam, ut non tantum escam hac quæ offertur à Christo vnà cum Euangelio consecte-mur, sed multò magis ipsum Christum ac Euangelium ipsius. Atque ita demum solidum gaudium, ac voluptatem percipiemus nō modò ex illo cœlesti cibo, qui nutrit nos ad vitam æternam, verùm etiã ex hoc ipso temporario: Nam illi demum soli sunt qui percipiunt veram voluptatem vel ex his terrenis, qui vnà cum his degustant illa cœlestia, sine quibus profectò belluinus tantùm est sensus omnium quæcũque in hoc mundo sunt.
units.tr: How one should answer hypocrites. which they eagerly grasp, while they wish to appear to grasp Christ himself and that efficacy which is in him for eternal life. And so, as far as they are concerned, they rob Christ of his chief efficacy. For although in fact that power and efficacy of Christ is in no way diminished, on which see Rom. 5:12 and following, in that famous comparison of the first Adam and the second, nevertheless, because the hypocrites despise it, they are no less liable to punishment than if they had altogether deprived Christ of it. We see, therefore, how great a danger is bound up with this matter. Let us then take pains to pursue not only the food that is offered by Christ together with the Gospel, but much more Christ himself and his Gospel. Thus at last we shall receive solid joy and delight, not only from that heavenly food which nourishes us to eternal life, but also from this temporal food itself. For only those receive true pleasure even from these earthly things who taste with them those heavenly things, without which the sense of all things that are in this world is surely no more than brutish.

units.la: Operemini non cibo. De Christo venturo ab Esaia prædictum est, & à Matthæo citatum, Quòd in aduentu suo primo non sit litigaturus, neque clamaturus, neque vox eius à quoquam audienda sit in plateis; neque confracturus arundinem quassatam, & linum fumigans non extinguet, &c. Quibus verbis prædicitur, Christum in aduentu suo placidum ac misericordem fore etiam erga quoscunque, etiam erga hypocritas, etiam erga reprobos ipsos. Huius rei exemplum habes tum hoc loco, tum in toto isto qui sequitur sermone mutuò cum hypocritis istis tum habito. Vemm quidem id est, Christum grauiter & cum graui asseueratione sæpe reprehendere, vt superiori versu scilicet eum vidimus: sed quod reprehendit laborat corrigere, & cum spiritu lenitatis reprehendit perpetuò, vt vidimus in hoc textu: vt nos quoque eius exemplo nihil unquam vituperemus, nisi quod studeamus in eo emendare; alioqui cũ spiritu amaritudinis videbitur à nobis dictũ esse duntaxat quod proferimus. Spiritus enim lenitatis & mansuetudinis in reprehendendo simul instaurat eum quem reprehendimus. Et qui cum spiritu mansuetudinis reprehendit, eadem opera instaurat & erigit eum qui lapsus est. Vide Galat. 6. 1. Spiritus autem mansuetudinis obtinetur dum consideramus nos ipsos, ne nos quoque tentemur; ibidem. Spiritus autem amaritudinis causa est quod non sentiant plerique communis naturæ huius miseriâ ac infirmitatem. Vide deinde, Christus dum corrigit hoc eorum vitium, abducere eos conatur à se, à cura ventris sui, ad quærendum ipsum Christum, sed tanquam panem vitæ æternæ. Christus enim nunquam proponit se nobis sequendum, quin admoneat nos boni alicuius, quod in nos ex ipso redundet. Commodum nostrum & verum bonum nostrum semper coniunctum est cum Dei gloria. Paulus primum habet hæc verba, Magnificabitur Christus in corpore meo, sive per vitam sive per mortem. En gloriam Christi; deinde habet hæc verba: Nam & in vita & in morte mihi Christus lucrum est: En bonû & lucrû nostrum cum Christi gloria inseparabiliter coniunctû, sive viuamus, sive moriamur. Expendamus nunc verba ipsa.
units.tr: Labour not for the food that perishes. Concerning the coming of Christ, it is foretold by Isaiah and quoted by Matthew that in his first coming he will not strive nor cry out, nor will his voice be heard by anyone in the streets; he will not break a bruised reed, and will not quench smoking flax, and so on. By these words it is foretold that Christ in his coming will be gentle and merciful even towards all men, even towards hypocrites, even towards the reprobate themselves. You have an example of this both in this place and in the whole discourse that follows, in which he speaks with those hypocrites. It is true that Christ often rebukes severely and with grave asseveration, as we saw in the previous verse; but what he rebukes he labours to correct, and he always rebukes in a spirit of gentleness, as we see in this text. So too, following his example, we should never find fault except in order to amend. Otherwise what we say will seem to have been said with a spirit of bitterness only. For a spirit of gentleness and meekness in rebuking at the same time restores the one we rebuke. And whoever rebukes with a spirit of meekness, by the same act restores and raises up the one who has fallen. See Galatians 6.1. The spirit of meekness is obtained while we consider ourselves, lest we too be tempted; ibid. The spirit of bitterness, on the other hand, is caused by most people not perceiving the misery and weakness of our common nature. Note further: Christ, while he corrects this fault of theirs, tries to draw them away from himself, from concern for their belly, to seek Christ himself, but as the bread of eternal life. For Christ never sets himself before us to be followed without reminding us of some good that flows back upon us from him. Our advantage and our true good is always joined with the glory of God. Paul first has these words: Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death. Here is the glory of Christ. Then he has these words: For both in life and in death Christ is my gain: Here is our good and gain, inseparably joined with the glory of Christ, whether we live or whether we die. Let us now weigh the words themselves.

units.la: Operemini, inquit. Multum quidem iam operati sunt isti & se fatigarunt in quærendo & sequendo Christum. Sequuti enim sunt eum trans mare Capernaumũ vsque. Totus hic labor erat ventris causa susceptus. Id cum vidéret Christus eos sic laborare ob rem perituram & rem nihili: Si quidem vultis, inquit, laborare & operari: operamini non cibo qui perit, sed cibo illi qui permanet in vitam æternam. Molestum enim est laborando se fatigare quemquam ob rem nihili. Licet mundus hic putet nihil serio agendum esse in vita præter ista, quæ euanida sunt & caduca, quod ad alia & cœlestia illa pertinent. Sunt mundo, si contingat eos aliquid temporis in illis collocare nonnunquam, tantundem temporis sepe didisse putant. Paulus, Contracte, inquit, tempus est in posterum, ut qui vxores habent sint vt non habentes, & qui flent vt non flentes, & qui gaudent vt non gaudentes, & qui emunt vt non obtinentes (hoc est, quod emerunt non tanti faciant, sed reputantes se quodammodo nihil obtinuisse) qui vtuntur hoc mundo, vt non abutentes (Illud enim est abuti mundo, affixum prorsus esse & addictum mūdo ac mundanis rebus. bus: sic enim vis quædam iis affertur, cùm non in eum finem à Deo sint ordinatæ. His verbis Paulus non prorsus dissuadet curam omnem rerum terrestrium, & earū quæ pertinet ad hanc vitā, sed suadet duntaxat moderatā, vt prima ac præcipua cura semper sit rerum cœlestium.
units.tr: Labour, he says. Indeed these men have already laboured much and wearied themselves in seeking and following Christ. For they followed him across the sea as far as Capernaum. All this labour was undertaken for the sake of the belly. When Christ saw them labouring so for a thing that perishes and is worth nothing, he said: If indeed you want to labour and work, work not for the food that perishes, but for that food which endures to eternal life. For it is irksome to wear oneself out with labour for something worth nothing. Though this world thinks that nothing in life should be done seriously except those things that are fleeting and frail, the things that pertain to those others, the heavenly ones, it considers time spent on them, if it happens that they occasionally spend some time on them, to be time largely wasted. Paul says: The time is short from now on, so that those who have wives should be as though they had none, and those who weep as though they did not weep, and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, and those who buy as though they did not possess (that is, they should not value what they have bought so highly, but reckon that in a sense they have obtained nothing), those who use this world as not abusing it (for to abuse the world is to be wholly fixed and devoted to the world and worldly things, for such a thing is forced upon people when they are not ordained by God for that end). By these words Paul does not altogether dissuade us from all care for earthly things and those that pertain to this life, but he only advises moderate care, so that the first and chief concern should always be for heavenly things.

units.la: Idem alibi diligentissimè commendat omnibus industriam ac laborem, seque ipsum pro exemplo hominis maximè industrij proponit, qui die & nocte cum labore & inedia operatus sit manibus suis, ad hoc vt omnes ipsius exemplo in quacunque demum vocatione laborent, & aliquid boni in vita faciant, atque ita demum comedant panè suum, nō alienum. Non enim est panis cuiusquà proprius, ne summi quidè regis, nisi serio laboret in vocatione sua. Idè tamè Paulus, Non spectamus, inquit, ea quæ cernuntur, sed ea quæ nō cernuntur, &c. Quibus quidem verbis significat etiam tum cùm maximè serio ac sedulò manibus laboraret, oculū tamè fidei & mentem occupatam fuisse in speculando æterna illa ac cœlestia, & interea temporis gessisse sese vt municipem regni cælorum. Nam hæc contemplatio cælestium, tantum abest ab eo vt impediat ista terrestria quæ cuique incumbunt iuxta vocationem cuiusque, vt tum demum veram voluptatem capiamus ex hisce laboribus nostris, & cum iucunditate quadam operemur, cùm de Deo eiúsque gloria, ad quam nimirum tanquam scopum dirigimus omnes labores nostros, & de Christo seruatore & de vita quæ in eo est æterna cogitamus.
units.tr: Elsewhere he most diligently commends industry and labour to everyone, and he sets himself forward as an example of the most industrious man, who by day and night worked with his hands in labour and want, so that all, following his example, should labour in whatever calling they have, and do something good in life, and thus eat their bread, not another's. For no one's bread is his own, not even a highest king's, unless he labours earnestly in his calling. Yet Paul also says: We do not look at the things that are seen, but at the things that are not seen, etc. By these words he signifies that even when he was labouring most earnestly and diligently with his hands, the eye of faith and his mind were nevertheless occupied in contemplating those eternal and heavenly things, and meanwhile he conducted himself as a citizen of the kingdom of heaven. For this contemplation of heavenly things is so far from hindering those earthly duties that fall to each person according to his calling, that then at last we take true pleasure from these labours of ours, and work with a certain cheerfulness, when we think of God and his glory, to which of course we direct all our labours as to a goal, and of Christ the Saviour and of the eternal life that is in him.

units.la: Videamus nūc cui demum rei oporteat eos operari. Operamini, inquit, non cibo qui perit, sed cibo illi qui permanet. Cibū in genere capio pro quauis re, siue terrestri siue cælesti, vt pro terrenis his diuitiis, gloria, voluptatibus; vt pro Christo & omnibus iis thesauris gratiæ quæ in ipso sunt. Notandum in verbis quòd non dicat statim, operamini cibo qui permanet, sed prius dicat, operamini non cibo qui perit. Prius enim vult solui ac laxari eorū animos & cogitationes à terra ista & rebus terrenis, quàm sursum euehatur versus cælos. Neq; enim est arbor quæuis quæ tam firmiter agit radices suas in terra ista, quàm firmiter in ea defixus est animo vniuscuiusq; nostrum per naturam. Frustra conetur aliquis proceram aliquam arborem, quæ penitus egit radices in terra, statim manu apprehenso summo eius cacumine, sursum versus trahere, nisi prius demittens sese ad radicem arboris eam laxet liberetque terra cui penitus est immersa: quo iam facto facile loco dimouetur arbor & sursum attrahitur: ita fit de animis nostris, quos frustra conaberis erigere ad cælos, nisi è luto isto tam tenaci prius eos solueris: Quod cum feceris iam leuior erit labor in iis ad cœlos vsque subuehendis. Quare præmittendæ sunt perpetuo dehortationes ad relinquendam hanc terram & res istas terrenas pereuntes: deinde exhortationes adhibendæ sunt ad quærendum cælestia ac superna spectantes. Sed videamus nunc rationem illam qua Dominus liberat quasi a terra hac & rebus istis terrestribus eorum animos. Cibus hic, inquit, perit. Ergo ne eū solum quærite. Ratio est a caduca natura, & conditione cibi, & rerum denique omnium terrestrium. Ratio quidem efficax est in ipsa natura (nam Christo res est nunc cum &c. & naturalibus) nihil enim est a quo natura abhorremus magis quam a morte & interitu, & a rebus iis quibuscunque quæ mortem accersunt, cuiusmodi sunt ista terrestria omnia, si iis innitamur ac confidamus. In causa autem est cur iis tam arcte adhæreamus, quia non videmus satis caducam illam & euanidam earum rerum naturam. Neque enim, quæ est obstinatio ista cordis nostri, in quotidiana experientia eam videre volumus. Hoc igitur est quod discimus ex hoc argumento; Non prius hominem diuelli a rebus his terrestribus, quam penitus videat earum naturā quæ fit, quam caduca, quam fragilis. Quare hoc semper inculcari debet hominum auribus, euanidam esse speciem huius mundi; opus est etiam ad hanc rem experientia, vt experiantur re ipsa hanc quam dicimus vanitatem gloriæ, diuitiarum, voluptatum huius mundi. Sed frustra adhibentur omnia, nisi Dominus Spiritu suo interius mutet ac flectat animum, ad hoc vt patiatur tandem hominem videre caducam istarū rerum omnium naturam. Sed cibo illi. Hactenus dedit operam Dominus vt turbæ animos auelleret a terrestribus hisce rebus; nunc, qua ratione id fieri possit, tentat eos altius subuehere ad cælos & res cælestes. Ad hanc rem hoc argumento vti- tur: Cibus, inquit, ille cælestis permanet in vitâ æternam. Q.d. ipse quidem æternus est, & permanet ad vitam æternam; hoc est, æternos facit quoscunque, qui eo vescuntur: Argumentū est ab immortali natura, & conditione cibi illius cælestis & rerum cælestium sitem ab eius efficacia in nobis, quæ est ad vitam æterna. Argumenti hoc genus quoqj est in natura ipsa efficax, vt fuit prius illud: Nā nihil est quod magis allicere potest homine natura ipsa quàm immortalitas, neque vlla re magis cõmouetur, vt qui, teste Paulo, ad immortalitatem conditus sit à Deo. Vide de hac re exemplum mulieris Samaritanæ, quæ cum iam aliquandiu ludibrio habuisset illam aquam, quam obtulit ei Dominus, vbi primum de eius perennitate cœpit audire, statim permota est ad eam quærendam; Domine, inquiens, da mihi aquam illam vt non sitiam. Amat quidem igitur & per naturam appetit homo immortalitatem; verùm cùm venturn est ad res eas, quæ ipsæ immortales sunt, & efficiunt nos immortales, dictu mirabile est quàm hic homines execuntur: neque etiam, id quod deterius est, volunt eas videre: Nam animali homini stultitia sunt ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Hoc igitur est quod ex hoc argumento discitur, non prius nimirum homine res cœlestes appetere & sequi, quàm cognoscat & earum naturam per se immortalem esse, & eas ipsas res efficaces esse nobis ad immortalitatem, adeo vt quoties cœlestes illas res commendamus hominibus, totius immortalitatem illam cõmendemus. Sed frustra omnia, nisi Dominus & aperiat oculum mentis, & flectat cor cuiusque vt ista & possit & velit intueri & amplecti. Quod protecto nõ citius faciet, quàm incipiat sentire se immortalem iam esse factū. Ea enim est natura & efficacia illarum rerum, vt non prius cognoscantur & apprehendantur à quoquam, quàm sentiat se eorum beneficio mutatum & alio quodam modo factum esse.
units.tr: Let us now see for what purpose they ought to labour. Labour, he says, not for the food that perishes, but for that food which endures. I take "food" generally for any thing, whether earthly or heavenly, such as these earthly riches, glory, pleasures; or such as Christ and all those treasures of grace which are in him. It should be noted in the words that he does not say at once, "labour for the food that endures," but first says, "labour not for the food that perishes." For he first wishes their minds and thoughts to be loosed and freed from this earth and earthly things, before they are lifted up towards heaven. For there is no tree so firmly driving its roots into this earth as the mind of each of us is by nature fixed in it. In vain would anyone try to draw upwards a tall tree whose roots have gone deep into the earth, by seizing its top, unless first he bends down to the root of the tree and loosens it and frees it from the earth in which it is deeply immersed; once that is done the tree is easily moved and drawn upwards. So it is with our souls: you will try in vain to raise them to heaven, unless first you loosen them from this so tenacious mud. When you have done that, the labour of lifting them up even to heaven will be lighter. Therefore warnings to leave this earth and these perishing earthly things must always be sent first; then exhortations must be applied to seek heavenly and higher things. But let us now see the reason by which the Lord frees their minds, as it were, from this earth and these earthly things. This food perishes, he says. Therefore do not seek that alone. The reason is taken from the frail nature and condition of food, and indeed of all earthly things. The reason is indeed effective because of nature itself (for now he is dealing with Christ's... and with natural things); for there is nothing from which nature shrinks more than from death and destruction, and from those things whatever that bring death, such as all these earthly things are, if we lean upon them and trust in them. The cause, however, why we cling to them so closely is that we do not see enough the frail and fleeting nature of those things. For, such is the obstinacy of our heart, we do not wish to see it in daily experience. Therefore this is what we learn from this argument: a man is not torn away from these earthly things until he sees thoroughly what their nature is, how frail, how fragile. Therefore this should always be drummed into people's ears, that the form of this world is fleeting; experience too is needed for this, so that they may actually experience that vanity of glory, riches and worldly pleasures which we speak of. But all these means are in vain, unless the Lord inwardly by his Spirit changes and bends the mind, so that at last he allows the man to see the frail nature of all those things. But to that food. Hitherto the Lord has laboured to draw the minds of the crowd away from these earthly things; now, by what means this can be done, he tries to lift them higher, up to heaven and heavenly things. For this purpose he uses this argument: That heavenly food, he says, endures to eternal life. That is, it itself is eternal, and endures to eternal life; that is, it makes eternal all who feed on it. The argument is from the immortal nature and condition of that heavenly food and of heavenly things, and from its efficacy in us, which is unto eternal life. This kind of argument too is effective by nature itself, just as the former was: for nothing can attract a man more by its nature than immortality, and nothing moves him more, since, as Paul testifies, he was made by God for immortality. See an example of this in the Samaritan woman, who, though for some time she had mocked that water which the Lord offered her, as soon as she began to hear of its perpetuity was at once moved to seek it: Lord, she says, give me that water, that I may not thirst. Man certainly loves immortality and by nature desires it; but when it comes to those things which are themselves immortal and make us immortal, it is wonderful to say how these men shrink back: nor, what is worse, do they wish to see them. For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him. Therefore this is what is learned from this argument: a man does not desire and follow heavenly things until he recognises that their nature is immortal in itself, and that these very things are effective for immortality for us; so that whenever we commend those heavenly things to men, we commend the whole of immortality. But all is in vain unless the Lord both opens the eye of the mind and bends the heart of each so that he can and will look upon and embrace these things. Certainly he will do this no sooner than the man begins to feel that he is already made immortal. For such is the nature and efficacy of those things that they are not known or grasped by anyone before he feels himself changed by their benefit and made in some other way.

units.la: Quemadmodum hominis. Hactenus dedit operam Dominus, vt præpararet eorum animos ad cibum illum cœlestem recipiendum. Nunc quid reliquum est nisi hoc, vt demonstret iis cibi illius quasi promptuarium, & eum hominem qui cibum ipsum impertiatur, nēpe filium hominis? hoc est, Filium Dei factum hominem, & porrigentem nobis cælestem illum cibum per manum hominis. Neque enim ad nos vsque peruenire potest nisi per mediam humanam carnem. Disce igitur hoc Christi exemplo, quòd vbi primum iam praeparatus est animus alicuius, in cóq; excitatus est appetitus aliquis cibi illius cælestis, continuò Christus (qui cibi illius solus dator est) ficiam praeparato, digito quasi demonstrandus sit. Dico demonstrandum esse Christum & non alium quem, neque aliud quid. Nemo enim est qui pluribus verbis loquatur de vanitate rerum terrestrium, de immortalitate ac gloria cælesti, hoc est de cibo illo cælesti, quàm Papistæ: Sed cùm ventum est ad pascendos hominum animos illo cibo de quo tam multa fecit verba, Christi quandam speciem eminus quasi ostentant, mox rursus ex oculis miseri hominis subducto, iam pro Christo, pro ipsius meritis ac iustitia sola, merita hominum, satisfactiones, intercessiones, purgatoria & infinita huiusmodi dicam stercora misero comedenda proponunt. Iudaei illi qui cum Christo legis caeremonias, à Deo ipso veteri populo olim traditas, coniunxerunt & hominibus ministrarunt, impotentia ac ieiuna elementa ministrasse dicuntur. Isti cùm figmenta sua, traditiones suas ministrent, quid dicemus eos ministrare populo nisi stercora, aut si quid dici possit quod vilius aut putidius sit? Tu verò caue, ne aliò deducas homines quàm ad solum Christum Iesum, ad omnes illos thesauros sapientiae & cognitionis qui in eo sunt. Ideo additum est in textu, Hunc enim Pater signauit, id est, Deus.
units.tr: As of man. Hitherto the Lord has taken pains to prepare their minds to receive that heavenly food. What remains now but that he should show them, as it were, the storehouse of that food, and the man who distributes the food itself, namely the Son of Man? That is, the Son of God made man, who offers us that heavenly food through the hand of a man. For it cannot reach us except through the middle of human flesh. Learn therefore from this example of Christ that, as soon as a person's mind is prepared and some appetite for that heavenly food has been stirred up in it, Christ, who is the sole giver of that food, must at once be pointed out to the prepared mind, as if with a finger. I say that Christ must be pointed out, and no other person or other thing. For there is no one who speaks with more words about the vanity of earthly things and the immortality and glory of heaven, that is, about that heavenly food, than the Papists. But when it comes to feeding men's minds with that food about which they have said so much, they display some image of Christ from afar, and then soon withdraw him from the wretched man's eyes, and now, in place of Christ and his merits and his righteousness alone, they set before the wretched man to eat the merits of men, satisfactions, intercessions, purgatories, and countless filthy things of this kind, I may call them. Those Jews who joined the ceremonies of the law, once handed down to the old people by God himself, to men and served them out, are said to have served up weak and beggarly elements. These men, since they serve out their own inventions and their own traditions, what shall we say they serve to the people but dung, or anything that can be called more vile or more foul? But you must take care not to lead people anywhere other than to Christ Jesus alone, to all those treasures of wisdom and knowledge that are in him. Therefore it is added in the text: For him the Father has sealed, that is, God.

units.la: Non satis habuit Christus se ipsum semel digito quasi iis demonstrasse, sed eos adducit ad se propius, vt clare videant & internoscant characterem illum quem Pater inipso quasi impressum reliquit, hoc est, mediationis suæ, vocationem quidem illam æternam, vt est Filius Dei; Ab vtero verò matris, vt est homo, neque externam quidem duntaxat vocationem videant, sed internam etiam & efficacem per Spiritum Patris sui, & infinita illa dona cælestia ac spiritualia. Dum hanc suam vocationem
units.tr: Christ was not satisfied with having pointed them to himself once, as it were with a finger, but he draws them closer to himself, so that they may clearly see and distinguish that mark which the Father has left impressed upon him, that is, his mediatorial office: the eternal calling indeed, as he is the Son of God; but from his mother's womb, as he is man, so that they may see not merely an external calling but also an internal and effective one, through the Spirit of his Father, and those countless heavenly and spiritual gifts. While he points out this his calling by his own hand,

units.la: Galat. 4.9. nemiis demonstrat, duo innuit,& authoritatem habere se à Patre vt det cibum illum, & cibum illum ipsum ac materiam omnem felicitatis nostræ se habere in seipso reconditam, adeo vt nihil in eo desiderari possit. Hoc igitur Christi exemplo discimus, non satis esse, si digito tantùm eminus demonstremus Christum, nisi propius admoueamus animos hominum ad eum, ac demonstremus etiam sigillum illud quo obsignatus est à Patre, & dicamus cum Apostolo ad Colossenses, in eo esse thesauros omnes sapientiæ & cognitionis abscondítos.Præterea in eo habitare σωματικῶς omnem deitatis plenitudinem.Neque hoc tantùm, sed in eo quoque nos compleri esse, ita vt non opus sit nobis aliunde aliquid emendicare. Et certè qui semel in eo completi sunt, ij continuò capiuntur fastidio, imò nausea quadam totius illius cibi quem proponunt mundo Pontificij hodierno die. Nam quid causæ putas esse cur homines vulgò patiantur se pasci eo commentorum humanorum cibo? In causa est, Quòd verum illum ac genuinum cibum, hoc est Christum cum thesauro illo gratiæ quæ in ipso est, nondum videantur ne primoribus quidem labiis degustasse.
units.tr: Galat. 4.9. he hints at two things: that he has authority from the Father to give that food, and that the food itself, and all the matter of our happiness, is stored up in himself, so that nothing can be lacking in him. Therefore from this example of Christ we learn that it is not enough merely to point to Christ from afar with a finger, unless we also bring people's minds nearer to him, and show them also that seal with which he has been sealed by the Father, and say with the Apostle to the Colossians that in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
