Moreover, in him dwells bodily [σωματικῶς] all the fullness of the Godhead. Nor is this all: we are also made complete in him, so that there is no need for us to beg anything from elsewhere. And certainly those who have once been made complete in him are at once seized with disgust, indeed with a kind of nausea, at all that food which the Papists today set before the world. For what do you think is the reason why people commonly allow themselves to be fed on that food of human inventions? The reason is that they seem not yet to have tasted even with the tips of their lips that true and genuine food, that is, Christ with the treasure of grace that is in him.

units.la: Dixerunt ad eum. Dominus verbo illo, quo vsus est, operandi intellexit opus illud fidei, hoc est apprehensionem illam, applicationem, studium, desiderium, & cætera, in quibus posita est fides. Turba verò trahit operationem illam ad legis Mosaicæ observationem. Quid faciemus inquiunt (hic facere & credere contraria sunt) vt operemur opera Dei? Hoc est, opera Deo grata & placentia. Fides res est quidem quam animalis homo non intelligit, & natura de gratia Dei, de fide, de iustitia per fidem, ne suspicari quidem vnquam potuit. Inde est quòd si loquaris de his quæ superant naturæ captum, nihil intelligat. Si fidem opus voces, operis verbum statim ad opera illa legis moralia trahit; si de iustitia loquaris, intelligat iustitiam operum; quia nimirum natura corrupta eò inclinat, & fœderis operum ac legis naturalis est aliqua in hominibus post lapsum religio, qua fit vt natura homines quærant sibi legis & operum iustitiam; quamuis natura inepti sint prorsus ad eam ipsam iustitiam praestandā. Israel, inquit Apostolus, qui sectabatur legem iustitiæ, ad legem iustitiæ non peruenit. Sic Papistæ hodierno die eam sectantur, sed ad eam nunquam tunt peruenturi. Imò flagitiosissimi quique, vt homicidæ, adulteri, fures, aliíque id genus peccatores, qui non conantur se iustificare per opera sua, sed confugiunt ad misericordiam illam Dei in Christo Iesu, prius quàm isti Iustitiarij cum bonis, iustis ac meritoriis scilicet operibus suis, iustitiam assequentur.
units.tr: They said to him. By that word which he used, the Lord understood that work of faith, that is, the apprehension, application, zeal, desire and the rest, in which faith consists. But the crowd draws that activity to the observance of the Mosaic law. "What shall we do," they say (here to do and to believe are opposites), "that we may work the works of God?" That is, works pleasing and acceptable to God. Faith is indeed a thing that the natural man does not understand, and nature could never even suspect anything about the grace of God, about faith, about justification through faith. Hence, if you speak of these things which surpass the capacity of nature, he understands nothing. If you call it a work, he at once drags the word "work" to those moral works of the law; if you speak of righteousness, he understands the righteousness of works; because, of course, corrupt nature inclines that way, and after the fall there remains in men some religion of the covenant of works and of natural law, by which it comes about that nature seeks for itself the righteousness of law and works, although by nature they are wholly unfit to perform that very righteousness. "Israel," says the Apostle, "which followed after the law of righteousness, has not attained to the law of righteousness." So the Papists today pursue it, but they will never attain to it. Indeed the most shameless sinners, such as murderers, adulterers, thieves, and other sinners of that kind, who do not try to justify themselves by their own works, but flee to the mercy of God in Jesus Christ, will attain righteousness before those Righteous-men, with their good, just and meritorious works, obtain it.

units.la: Gentes, inquit Apostolus, quæ non sectabantur iustitiam, apprehenderunt iustitiam; iustitiam autem eam quæ est ex fide. Amen dico vobis, ait Christus, Publicani & meretrices præeunt vobis in regnum Dei. Vox hæc autem (Quid faciemus?) non tam esse videtur ex fiducia aliqua qua putârunt se iam impleuisse legem totam, quàm ex hæsitatione & dubitatione, cuiusmodi fuit illa vox iuuenis illius ad Christum, Magister bone, quid boni faciam vt habeam vitam æternam? Qui natura duce sectantur iustitiam operum & gloriantur de operibus, næ illos oportet in perpetua dubitatione hærere. Neque aliter potest fieri, tu quia semper conscientia admonet eos de imperfectione operum suorum; tum quia eadem conscientia admonet eos de perfectissima illa iustitia Dei, quam non possunt ferre opera nostra imperfecta. Hinc existunt illæ dubitationes & dolores illi conscientiæ: hinc sunt dubitationes illæ Papistarum hodierno die; Et id, quod peius est, hinc est illa doctrina eorum de dubitatione, quam nobis commendant, tanquam rem in se bonam, laudabilem, Deoque gratam. Contra vero qui sectantur illam iustitiam fidei, oportet eos non hunc in modum dubitare, quia hi non sunt freti operibus suis, aut iustitia aliqua sibi inhærente, sed perfecta illa Christi iustitia, qua sola se iustificari coram Deo credunt; inde est illa pax, illa lætitia: Iustificati fide, inquit Paulus, pacem habemus apud Deum. Quòd si quæ dubitatio exoritur in cordibus eorum, ea iam non ipsis est grata, sed peracerba iis accidit, quam etiam totis animis damnant, vt Deo ingratam. Vide Rom. 7. 24. Quo loco rebellio ista quæ in natura reliqua est, excusst Apostolo hanc vocem miserabilem ac plane flebilem: Mi-
units.tr: "The Gentiles," says the Apostle, "who did not follow after righteousness, have attained righteousness, but the righteousness which is of faith." "Verily I say to you," says Christ, "tax-collectors and harlots go before you into the kingdom of God." But this cry, "What shall we do?", seems to arise not so much from any confidence that they had already fulfilled the whole law, as from hesitation and doubt, such as was that cry of the young man to Christ: "Good master, what good shall I do that I may have eternal life?" Those who, with nature as their guide, pursue the righteousness of works and glory in their works, must of necessity remain in perpetual doubt. Nor can it be otherwise: partly because conscience always warns them of the imperfection of their works, and partly because the same conscience warns them of that most perfect righteousness of God, which their imperfect works cannot endure. Hence arise those doubts and those pangs of conscience: hence come the doubts of the Papists today. And what is worse, hence comes their doctrine of doubt, which they commend to us as a thing good in itself, "laudable," and pleasing to God. On the other hand, those who pursue that righteousness of faith ought not to doubt in this way, because they do not rely on their works or on any righteousness inherent in them, but on the perfect righteousness of Christ, by which alone they believe themselves justified before God. Hence comes that peace, that joy: "Being justified by faith," says Paul, "we have peace with God." But if any doubt arises in their hearts, it is not pleasing to them but comes upon them as something most bitter, which they also condemn with their whole soul, as displeasing to God. See Rom. 7.24. In that passage the rebellion that remains in nature wrung from the Apostle this wretched and utterly tearful cry: "Wretch-

units.la: Hypoeritarum miseria.
units.tr: The misery of hypocrites.

units.la: Pax & lætitia cordis credentium in Christum. {ser}ego homo, quis me eripiet ex isto corpore mortis? Sed si quae dubitatio est, quam fatemur esse multiplicem, iam ea non imputanda est iustitiae Christi, qua induimur per fidem, sed imperfectioni fidei nostrae, quae iustitiam Christi non satis firmiter apprehendit. Quanquam id nos interea consolari debet, nos, si vel tantillo fidei, quae vera sit, apprehendamus iustitiam illam Christi perfectam, nos, inquam, ea etiam imperfecta, veratamen iustificari coram Deo: nam non ta fides nostra qua apprehendimus Christum cum iustitia sua, causa est iustificationis nostri, quam fidei obiectum, nempe Christum cum iustitia sua fide apprehensus. Sed illud rursus verum est, quod quo maior est fides, eo maior sit securitas ac laetitia cordis; quo rursus minor est illa apprehensio, eo minor sit ea laetitia cordis & pax conscientiae. Atque inde est, quod fideles perpetuo aspirent cum suspiriis ad maiorem & auctiorem fidem.
units.tr: The peace and joy of heart of believers in Christ. "I am a wretched man; who will deliver me from this body of death?" But if there is any doubt, which we confess is manifold, it is not to be imputed to the righteousness of Christ, with which we are clothed through faith, but to the imperfection of our faith, which does not apprehend the righteousness of Christ firmly enough. Nevertheless this ought to console us in the meantime: that we, if we apprehend that perfect righteousness of Christ with even a little true faith, are, I say, truly justified before God even though it is imperfect. For it is not our faith, by which we apprehend Christ with his righteousness, that is the cause of our justification, but the object of faith, namely Christ with his righteousness apprehended by faith. But it is again true that the greater the faith, the greater the security and joy of heart; and again, the smaller that apprehension, the smaller that joy of heart and peace of conscience. And hence it is that the faithful perpetually breathe with sighs after a greater and fuller faith.

units.la: Respondit Iesus. Dominus operationem illam, quam antea commendauit ipse, interpretatur, non quidem de legis operibus, sed de fidei operatione: nam apprehensio illa cordis interna motus quidam est, & opus suo quodam modo, non minus quam est inanis ista externa apprehensio. Hoc illud est opus Dei, inquit. Opus Dei vocat, hoc est, quod Deus flagitat, quodque Deo gratum est imprimis. Concedo quidem esse etiam alia opera praeter fide Deo grata, vt sunt opera sanctificationis omnia; sed hoc elogium tributum est fidei nominatim, tum quia fides opus est imprimis Deo acceptum, atque adeo acceptu, vt Deus iustu ex fide reputet, quod no similiter fit in aliis operib. etiam bonis & Deo acceptis: tu quia per fide & fidei illud opus, alia quaecunque bona opera Deo placet & accepta sunt: Primum enim per fide sanctificatur, & a fide habet ea quae in ipsis est sanctitate, quia fides sanctificat cor hominis: Fide, inquit, purgatis cordibus eorum. Inde per fide quasi perficiuntur: fides enim in Iesum Christum, tegit omne imperfectionem operum nostrorum, eaque quanquam perfecta ac integra Deo sistit. Tantum autem fidei tribuo, non vt est apprehensio duntaxat a nobis profecta; sed vt est iustitia Christi fide apprehensa; hoc est, non propter apprehensionem ipsam, sed pro-
units.tr: Jesus answered. The Lord explains that work which he had himself commended earlier, not as a work of the law but as the working of faith. For that inner apprehension of the heart is a kind of motion and a work in its own way, no less than that empty external apprehension. "This is the work of God," he says. He calls it the work of God, that is, what God chiefly requires and what is especially pleasing to him. I grant that there are other works besides faith that are pleasing to God, such as all the works of sanctification. But this commendation is given to faith by name, first because faith is a work especially acceptable to God, and so acceptable that God reckons it to us for righteousness (which is not similarly the case with other works, even good works acceptable to God), and second because through faith and by that work all other good works please God and are acceptable to him. For first, they are sanctified through faith, and they have from faith whatever holiness is in them, since faith sanctifies the heart of man: By faith, he says, having purified their hearts. Then through faith they are, as it were, made perfect, for faith in Jesus Christ covers every imperfection of our works, and presents them to God as perfect and whole, though they are not. I attribute so much to faith, however, not as it is merely an apprehension proceeding from us, but as it is the righteousness of Christ apprehended by faith; that is, not on account of the apprehension itself but on account of its object.

units.la: Act. 15. 9. pter obiectum ipsius, nempe Christum cum sua iustitia. Nam quòd ad apprehensionem attinet, ipsa quoque imperfecta est, vt & alia omnia quæ à nobis proficiscuntur, quantisper sumus in hac vita: quòd verò ad obiectum apprehensionis perfectum est ac infinitum, perficitque non solùm alia omnia sanctificationis opera, sed etiam ipsam illam apprehensionem sui. Hæc illa perfectio obiecti est, quæ nos consolatur in tota vita. Nota hic quòd Christus, postquam turba loquuta est de legis operibus, nō perseguatur vlterius doctrinā legis & operū, vel fœderis quod vocat operū, quæ alioqui vtilis est ac bona: sed reuocat eos ad opus illud fidei, doctrinámq; illius operis instituit, cuius erat ipsi planè ignari, cùm ex doctrina legis cognita haberent opera legis, & iustitia sibi in operibus legis quærerent: etiā ex natura cognita ea aliquo modo haberent. Nā operū naturalis est notitia, &ad opera natura propendet, adeò vt animalis homo quærat sibi iustitiam ex iis, de iis semper cogitet, de iis & loquatur ipse perpetuò, & alios lubenter audiat loquetes. Hinc sunt illa tot volumina veterum Philosophorum de moribus & de operibus naturæ conscripta. Verùm frustra loquatur aliquis de lege eiúsque operibus huic homini, qui nondum credit: lex enim impotens est in natura corrupta. Neque enim melior euadet quisquam, audita lege, vel ad centum annos, si nihil interea de Euangelio Christi audiat. Vide Rom. 8.3. vbi dicit Apostolus, Legis impotentiam nihil posse in carne. Potens est quidem, fateor, ad reddendum deteriorem hominem, idque propter carnem, quæ ex Lege iusta arripit occasionem iniustitiæ; sed ad meliorem reddendum nihil potest sine fide. Rom. 7.8. Peccatum occasione sumpta, genuit in me omnem cupiditatem per illam legem. Quòd verò Prophetæ veteres exorsi sunt doctrinam suam à lege, id non fecerunt ideo quòd expectarent meliores futuros ea re; sed vt abigerent quasi ad Christum veterem populum, demonstrato per legem peccato ipsorum & miseria. Postquam verò iam vidimus miseriam nostram, & apprehendimus Christum cum iustitia sua, tunc vsum suum assequitur legis doctrina in eo nimirum qui credit, ac proinde regeneratur, hoc est, habet legem iam pes per fidem inscriptam cordi suo. Quare doctrina fidei est quæ proprie mutat animum hominis, Lex autem non mutat, non sanctificat, sed præparat ad fidem, quæ sola proprie regenerare & mutare hominis animum dicitur. Ergo præterita legis & legalium operum doctrina, docuit eos illud opus fidei, ut ipsi renuntiantes legi & iustitiæ operum, quærerent sibi fidem & iustitiam eam quæ est per fidem Christi.
units.tr: Act. 15. 9. on account of its object, namely Christ with his righteousness. For as regards the apprehension, it too is imperfect, as are all other things that proceed from us for as long as we are in this life; but as regards the object of apprehension, it is perfect and infinite, and it perfects not only all the other works of sanctification but even that very apprehension of itself. This is the perfection of the object which comforts us through the whole of life. Note here that Christ, after the crowd had spoken of the works of the law, does not pursue the doctrine of the law and of works any further, nor the covenant which he calls the covenant of works, which is otherwise useful and good. Instead he calls them back to that work of faith, and teaches the doctrine of that work, of which they were quite ignorant. From the doctrine of the law they knew the works of the law and sought righteousness for themselves in those works; and they had some knowledge of them even from nature. For there is a natural knowledge of works, and nature inclines toward works, so that the natural man seeks righteousness for himself from them, always thinks about them, talks about them constantly himself, and gladly hears others speaking of them. Hence come those many volumes of the ancient philosophers written on morals and on the works of nature. But one speaks in vain of the law and its works to this man, who does not yet believe, for the law is powerless in corrupt nature. Nor will anyone become better by hearing the law, even for a hundred years, if meanwhile he hears nothing of the Gospel of Christ. See Rom. 8.3, where the Apostle says that what the law could not do, it could do nothing in the flesh. It is indeed powerful, I grant, in making a man worse, and that because of the flesh, which seizes on the just law as an occasion for unrighteousness; but it can do nothing to make him better without faith. Rom. 7.8: Sin, taking occasion, produced in me every desire through that law. But as for the ancient Prophets beginning their teaching from the law, they did not do so because they expected that people would become better by it, but in order to drive the old people, as it were, to Christ, by showing them their sin and misery through the law. But once we have seen our misery and apprehended Christ with his righteousness, then the doctrine of the law attains its use in the one who believes, and so is regenerated; that is, he has the law now written on his heart by faith. Therefore it is the doctrine of faith that properly changes the mind of man. The law does not change it or sanctify it, but prepares for faith, which alone is said properly to regenerate and change the mind of man. Therefore the earlier doctrine of the law and of legal works taught them that work of faith, so that, renouncing the law and the righteousness of works, they might seek for themselves faith and that righteousness which is through faith in Christ.

units.la: 30 Dixerunt ergo ei, Quod ergo tu signum edis, ut videamus & credamus tibi? Quid operaris?
units.tr: 30 They said therefore to him, "What sign, then, do you give, that we may see it and believe you? What do you work?"

units.la: 31 Patres nostri comederunt illud Manna in deserto illo: sicut scriptum est, Panem cælestem dedit eis vescendum.
units.tr: 31 "Our fathers ate that manna in the desert, as it is written: 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat.'"

units.la: 32 Dixit ergo eis Iesus, Amen, amen dico vobis, neque Moses dedit vobis panem illum cælestem: sed Pater meus dat vobis panem illum cælestem verum.
units.tr: 32 Jesus therefore said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you that bread from heaven; but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven."

units.la: 33 Panis enim ille Dei is est qui de cœlo descendit, & dat vitam mundo.
units.tr: 33 "For the bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world."

units.la: Iam intelligunt aliquo modo illud opus Fidei; non tamen statim credunt, sed signum quærunt, non quidem animo credendi; sed, ut apparet, ex Mosis hoc quod asserunt exemplo, ventris sui causa. Volebant enim miraculose & extra-ordine pasci à Christo, ut olim populus in deserto per Mosem pastus fuit. Res est quam quis miretur, iam antea Christus reprehendit eorum hypocrisin, consuluit etiam iis, ut relicto hoc pane terreno, cœlestem & æternum sibi quærerent. Instituit denique eos in opere Fidei, & tamen isti nihilo meliores evadunt, adhuc enim adhærent pani huic terrestri, & specie quam religionis huic suo instituto prætexunt. Vsque adeo difficile est sincerum reddere cor hypocritæ, & efficere ut ipse videat dolum illum qui in corde ipsius latet penitus. Conatur quidem celare oculos aliorum, sed maxime suis oculis imponit miser. Totus mundus inspiciet cor hypocritæ & dolum illic latere tam, priusquam possit ipse hypocrita se videre. Atque inde est quod non
units.tr: They now understand that work of faith in some way, yet they do not believe at once, but seek a sign, not with any mind to believe, but, as is evident, from the example of Moses which they cite, for the sake of their belly. For they wanted to be fed by Christ miraculously and beyond the ordinary course, as the people once were fed in the desert through Moses. It is a matter to wonder at: Christ had already rebuked their hypocrisy, and had advised them that, leaving this earthly bread, they should seek for themselves the heavenly and eternal. In short, he has instructed them in the work of faith, and yet these men become no better, for they still cling to this earthly bread and to the appearance of religion which they put forward as a pretext for their purpose. So difficult is it to make the heart of a hypocrite sincere, and to bring it about that he sees the deceit lying deep in his heart. He does indeed try to hide it from the eyes of others, but the wretch deceives above all his own eyes. The whole world will see the hypocrite's heart and the deceit lurking there before the hypocrite himself can see it. And hence it is that he is not

units.la: & A pudeat cum in conspectum hominum prodire cum suo fuco & suis coloribus ementitis: Nimirum quia ipse se non intuetur, putat alios similiter non videre fucum illu & latetem sub eo dolu, & ignominiosissimos quosque affectus. Nam quae in occulto fiunt ab eo turpe est vel dicere. Rursus vide: prius ignorarunt isti fidem, nunc vero in ea institutin ac adductiad aliquam certe fidei notitiam, nolunt tamen credere, sed iniiciunt sibi ipsis remoram. Natura primum homines ignorant fidem, & quid sit illud, aliquem credere in Deum; vbi vero iam instituti sunt in fide, nolunt credere, imo vero volunt incredulimanere: Incredulitas enim occupat animum cuiusque per naturam, sed ad incredulitatem accedit aliud malum, nempe hypocrisis, qua artificiose tegunt illam incredulitatem penitus in animo latitantem. Tecta autem in hunc modum & abscondita incredulitas, difficillime eruitur ex latibulo suo, tot enim praetextus sunt, tot excusationes, tot ratiocinationes, vt fere incassum quis tentet incredulitatem illam eximere ex animo hypocritae: Illud enim affirmare, aut dicere, difficilius esse adducere ad fidem infidelem hypocritam, qui etiam se Christianum simulat, aut profitetur nobiscum Euangelium Christi, quam Turcam aliquem, & eum qui aperte est infidelis: Et minori negotio lucrifieri dico quemcumque etiam aperte adversante Christiano nomini, quam obstinatum aliquem & obstinatum Papistam, qui didicit ex Iudaeis istis obiicere nobis perpetuo vocationem nostram: Vbi, inquit, vocatio vestra? Obiicere miracula, Vbi, inquit, miracula? Scilicet credam, si persuaderetur huic vocatio nostra, si miracula a nobis ederentur, cum vnquam crediturum esse. An crediturum erant Iudaei illi si Christus edidisset ea quae ipsi voluerunt signa? Quasi vero, viderunt iam antea complura signa, viderunt donalla recentia, de quibus paulo ante diximus, non tamen crediderunt. Verum non ob eum finem, vt crederent, requirebant signa, sed ventris causa duntaxat; id quod euentus tandem probavit: Neque isti profecto, si vel mille miracula & prodigia ipsis inspectantibus ederentur, crediturl esset. Quaerunt enim non animo credendi, sed integrendi infidelitatem illam suam, hostes enim sunt Christi gratiæ & Fidei.
units.tr: ashamed to come forward into the sight of men with his paint and his false colours. Namely, because he does not look at himself, he thinks others likewise do not see the paint and the deceit lying beneath it, and all the most shameful affections. For what is done in secret is shameful even to speak of. Again, see: those men previously did not know faith, but now, once instructed in it and brought to some definite knowledge of faith, they are unwilling to believe, but place an obstacle in their own way. By nature men are ignorant of faith, and of what it is to believe in God; but once they have been instructed in faith, they are unwilling to believe, indeed they want to remain unbelievers. For unbelief occupies each person's mind by nature, but another evil is added to unbelief, namely hypocrisy, by which they artfully cover that unbelief lying hidden deep in the mind. Unbelief covered and hidden in this way is drawn from its hiding place with the greatest difficulty, for there are so many pretexts, so many excuses, so many arguments, that one nearly tries in vain to remove that unbelief from the mind of the hypocrite. For I say that it is more difficult to bring to faith an unbelieving hypocrite, who even pretends to be a Christian or professes the Gospel of Christ with us, than some Turk, or one who is openly an unbeliever. And I say that with less trouble one wins over anyone even openly opposed to the Christian name than some obstinate Papist, who has learned from those Jews to object to us constantly about our calling: "Where," he says, "is your calling?" He objects about miracles: "Where," he says, "are the miracles?" Surely, he says, I would believe if our calling were persuasive to him, if we performed miracles; but when would he ever believe? Would those Jews have believed if Christ had performed the signs they wanted? As if they had not already seen many signs, had not seen the recent gifts of which we spoke a little earlier, and yet did not believe. But they did not demand signs so that they might believe, only for the sake of their belly; which the outcome at last proved. Nor would those men surely believe even if a thousand miracles and wonders were performed before their eyes. For they seek not with a mind to believe, but to strengthen that unbelief of theirs, for they are enemies of the grace of Christ and of faith.

units.la: Sed videamus nunc Mosis hoc quod allatum est exemplum: Patres nostri comederunt. De Manna vide Exod. 16.14.& deinceps, Mane erat stratus ros circa ipsa castra populi; cumque se eleuasset stratus ille ros, ecce in superficie ipsius terræ tenue quoddam & rotundum, tenue, inquam, sicut ipsa pruina super terram: Quod videntes filij Israëlis dicebant alter ad alterum, Man-Hu, non enim sciebant quid esset. Ipsum igitur generali nomine vocabant, qui eius speciem ignorabant. Generale enim vocabulum man significat cibum aptum ad comedendum sine alio hominis labore. Vide Sapientiæ librum 16.20.vbi man huius circumlocutio est, per comparatum panem sine labore. Erat autem figura quædam Christi, ideóque spiritualis cibus dicitur, propter rem significatam spiritualem. Verum isti, non significatum illud spirituale, sed externum duntaxat signum & cibum corporeum respexerunt, commendatúrque ab iis Moses, non quòd signum vel sacramentum dederit Christi; sed quòd dederit corporeum hunc cibum. Vide igitur ipsi se producunt ostendúntque se quærere signa, non eo fine quem præxerunt, nempe vt credant, sed ventris sui gratiâ duntaxat. Hypocrita sese prodit interdum, vel verbo vel facto aliquo: abundantia enim illa cordis non potest se continere quin interdum erumpat. Et hypocrita nonnũquam in suis coloribus conspicitur. Deinde nota; laudant Mosem, sed eadem opera Christum obscurè vituperant, qui tantum aberat ab eo, vt ministraret iis eo modò cibum quo olim Moses ministrauit eum veteri populo, vt etiam dehortatus sit à quærendo cibum istum terrenum & periturum. Non amo commendationem & laudem etiam boni viri profectam ex ore impij & hypocritæ, nunquam enim sincera est, sed vitiata est perpetuò corrupto aliquo animi ipsius affectu; vel enim ventris sui gratia vt quæstum sibi ipse faciat; vel laudatio in vituperium hominis fortasse melioris. Non amo laudes Papistarum, qui dum laudant veteres illos Patres, dum laudát Apostolos Christi, dum Petrum ipsum, quem supra omnes alios laudibus cuehút, id faciunt studio ventris sui, & animo stabiliendi ineptias. suas & figmenta sua, eadémque opera veritatem & veritatis assertores vituperant & damnant.
units.tr: But let us now look at the example that Moses has brought forward: "Our fathers did eat." Concerning the manna see Exod. 16.14 and following: "In the morning there lay a layer of dew round about the camp; and when the layer of dew was gone up, behold, upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, small as the hoar frost on the ground." When the children of Israel saw it, they said one to another, "Man-hu," for they did not know what it was. So they called it by a general name, since they did not know its kind. For the general word man signifies food fit for eating, obtained without any labour of man. See the Book of Wisdom 16.20, where this periphrasis for man is "bread prepared without labour." Now it was a certain figure of Christ, and therefore it is called spiritual food, on account of the spiritual thing signified. But those people looked not at that spiritual thing signified, but only at the external sign and bodily food; and Moses is commended by them, not because he gave a sign or sacrament of Christ, but because he gave this bodily food. See then, they betray themselves and show that they seek signs, not for the purpose which they ought to have had, namely that they might believe, but only for the sake of their belly. The hypocrite sometimes gives himself away, by some word or deed, for the abundance of the heart cannot always restrain itself from breaking out; and the hypocrite is at times seen in his true colours. Next, observe: they praise Moses, but at the same time they obscurely disparage Christ, who was so far from providing them with food in the way Moses once provided it for the old people, that he even warned them against seeking that earthly and perishable food. I do not like praise, even when it comes from a good man, if it proceeds from the mouth of an impious person and a hypocrite, for it is never sincere but is always tainted by some corrupt affection of the mind: either it is for the sake of his belly, to make gain for himself, or the praise is meant to disparage a man who is perhaps the better. I do not like the praises of the Papists, who, while they praise those ancient Fathers, while they praise the Apostles of Christ, while they praise Peter himself, whom they extol above all others, do so out of zeal for their own belly and with a mind to establish their follies and their fictions; and at the same time they disparage and condemn the truth and the defenders of the truth.

units.la: Dixit ergo iis Iesus. Respondet Christus, negatque quodam modo panem illum cœlestem fuisse, qui ministratus est à Mose in deserto; cum autem quem dat Pater verè cœlestem esse dicit. Contradicit itaque, ut videtur, testimonio scripturæ proximè superiori, quo dictum est, Panem cœlestem dedit eis, ut vescerentur. Respondeo negationem istam & contradictionem non esse absolutè, sed comparatè propositam. Negat igitur comparatè, facta nimirum comparatione Mannæ cum Christo. Manna enim, qui corporalis fuit cibus, si cum Christo comparetur, qui spiritualis est cibus, quodammodo non est cœlestis, imò nihil est. At dices manna appellari escam spiritualem. Respondeo, manna ibi, vt Sacramentum fuit coniunctum cum significato, hoc est Christo qui verè est spiritualis ille cibus, acceptum esse, hic verò manna seorsim accipi à Christo pro cibo duntaxat corporali, quemadmodum Iudæi isti quibuscum Christo res erat, ipsum acceperunt. Nam ex hypothesi illorum loquitur. Nota igitur: omnia dona à Deo sunt, & cœlitus ad nos veniunt: omne munus bonum & omne bonum est profectum supernè, descendens à Patre luminum. Verùm si venias ad comparationem, tum quidem temporaria ista & terrena, quæ inseruiunt vitæ duntaxat præsenti, nihil sunt ad æterna illa & spiritualia, quæ inseruiunt alteri vitæ, imò quodammodo dici possunt esse à cœlis. Unde sequitur & aliud, nempe eum qui accepit duntaxat terrestria ista & temporaria, etiam si regna, dicas nihil tamen accepisse; si nullâ partem rerum illarum spiritualium vnà cum his accepit. Eum verò qui Christum accepit, cum mediocri tantùm portione rerum istarum terrestrium, eum, inquam, satis accepisse, etsi non statim regnum aut dominium aliquod à Deo acceperit. Sit itaque contentus sorte sua: & quidem is solus est qui sorte sua contentus viuit; nemo enim est, cõtentus sorte sua, nisi qui in Christo est: Nam pietas, inquit Apostolus, magnus quæstus est, cum animo suo contento, quo significat pietatem afferre secum veram αὐτάρκειαν & sufficientiam.
units.tr: Jesus therefore said to them. Christ answers, and in a certain manner denies that the heavenly bread was that which was ministered by Moses in the wilderness; but he says that what the Father gives is truly heavenly. So he seems to contradict the testimony of Scripture cited just before, in which it is said, "He gave them bread from heaven to eat." I answer that this denial and contradiction is not absolute but comparative. He denies, therefore, comparatively, namely by making a comparison of the manna with Christ. For the manna, which was bodily food, if it is compared with Christ, who is spiritual food, is in a certain sense not heavenly, indeed is nothing. But you will say that the manna is called spiritual food. I answer that the manna there was received as a sacrament joined with the thing signified, that is, Christ, who is truly that spiritual food; but here the manna is taken apart from Christ merely as bodily food, just as those Jews with whom Christ had to do took it. For he speaks from their hypothesis. Note therefore: all gifts are from God and come to us from heaven: "every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights." But if you come to comparison, then indeed those temporary and earthly things, which serve only the present life, are nothing compared with those eternal and spiritual things, which serve the other life, and indeed may in a certain sense be said to be from heaven. Whence it follows also this other thing: that he who has received only those earthly and temporary things, even if you call them kingdoms, has nevertheless received nothing, if he has received no part of those spiritual things along with them. But he who has received Christ, even with only a moderate portion of those earthly things, has, I say, received enough, even if he has not at once received any kingdom or lordship from God. Let him therefore be content with his lot; and indeed he alone lives content with his lot, for no one is content with his lot except he who is in Christ. For "godliness," says the Apostle, "is great gain, with a contented mind," by which he signifies that godliness brings with it true self-sufficiency and sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια].

units.la: Ioan.
units.tr: John.

units.la: Panis enim ille. Ratio est cur dixerit panem illum verè cœlestem à Patre dari. Est autem à definitione & natura panis illius verè cœlestis. Panis ille Dei, hoc est, verè panis est, qui non tantum descendit de cœlo, vt Manna, sed qui dat vitam mundo. At Pater dat eum panem qui descendit è cœlo & dat vitam mundo. Ergo Pater est qui dat verè cœlestem illum panem. Vide igitur, Christus eum qui verè panis est, hoc est, quæ verè dona sunt, definiratque æstimat ex hoc effecto spiritualis vitæ. Hoc repetito altius inuestigemus, sciendum est, Christum, dum in mundo ageret, perpetuò ob oculos suos habuisse præsentem hominum miseriam & peccatum illud in quo iacebant mortui. Quare dum ponderaret Dei erga homines beneficia, ea omnia definire solitus est & æstimare ex præsenti illa quam vidit conditione misera, sic vt quæ beneficia videret ad hoc vtilia esse, vt ex tanta morte liberarentur homines, ea pro verè donis Dei habuerit; quæ vero non id efficerent, vt homines surgerent ex morte illa in vitam, ea cum aliis illis donis comparata pro nihilo ducebat. Quid enim attinet in eum, qui naturaliter mortuus est, conferre omnia? quid attinet cibum illi porrigere, quid vestem dare, quid honore afficere, quid diuitiis cumulare? Nihilo profecto magis prosunt ista omnia ei qui spiritualiter mortuus est, si sola dentur. Tantum enim absunt ab eo vt miserum vitæ restituant, vt potius mortem illam spiritualem adaugeant. Ergo Christus merito definiuit ex illa mortis & miseriæ conditione beneficia Dei, quæ verè eo nomine appellanda sunt. Vt autem ad homines veniam; Qui habet ante oculos miseram istam conditionem, is est qui solus potest beneficia Dei quæcunque rectè definire, siue temporaria ista, siue spiritualia illa. Quisquis enim serio attingitur sensu miseriæ suæ ipsius & aliorum pariter, regnū, gloriā ac diuitias rectius definiri quam politicus aliquis, qui est sine sensu omni miseriæ, qui tamē videtur sibi solus hæc sapere. In definiendis autem Dei beneficiis, ea sola quæ possunt hominem aliquo certè modo ex tanta morte, putat verè talia esse, imprimis autem Christum ipsum in pretio habet, cuius respectu omnia ista terrena bona ei Phil. 3. 8.
units.tr: "For that bread..." This is the reason why he said that the truly heavenly bread is given by the Father. Now it is from the definition and nature of that truly heavenly bread. That bread of God, that is, is truly bread which not only comes down from heaven, as the manna did, but which gives life to the world. But the Father gives that bread which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world. Therefore it is the Father who gives that truly heavenly bread. See then, Christ defines and estimates what is truly bread, that is, what gifts are truly gifts, from this effect of spiritual life. To inquire into this more deeply, it must be understood that Christ, while he was living in the world, always had before his eyes the present misery of men and that sin in which they lay dead. Therefore, when he weighed God's benefits toward men, he was accustomed to define them all and to estimate them from that miserable condition which he saw present, so that those benefits which he saw to be useful for this, that men should be rescued from so great a death, he held to be truly gifts of God; but those which did not bring it about that men should rise from that death into life, he counted as nothing when compared with those other gifts. For what good is it to bestow everything on one who is naturally dead? What good is it to offer him food, to give him clothing, to honour him, to heap him with riches? Truly all these things profit no more one who is spiritually dead, if they are given alone. For they are so far from restoring the wretched man to life that they rather increase that spiritual death. Therefore Christ rightly defined God's benefits from that condition of death and misery, benefits which are rightly to be called by that name. But to come to men: he who has before his eyes this wretched condition is the only one who can rightly define whatever benefits of God, whether those temporary or those spiritual. For whoever is seriously touched by a sense of his own misery and that of others alike, will define kingdom, glory and riches more rightly than some politician who is without any sense of misery at all, yet who seems to himself alone to be wise in these things. But in defining God's benefits, he holds that only those things which can in some way rescue a man from so great a death are truly such; and above all he holds Christ himself in highest esteem, in comparison with whom all those earthly goods are to him but loss, indeed dung. [Phil. 3.8]

units.la: Phil. 3. 8. damna sunt totidem, imò stercora.
units.tr: Phil. 3.8: They are loss, indeed dung.

units.la: 34 Dixerunt ergo ei, Domine, da nobis semper panem istum.
units.tr: "34 They said therefore to him, Lord, give us this bread always."

units.la: 35 Dixit autem eis Iesus, Ego sum panis ille vitæ: qui venit ad me nequaquam esuriet: & qui credit in me, non sitiet unquam.
units.tr: "35 And Jesus said to them, I am the bread of life: he who comes to me shall never hunger; and he who believes in me shall never thirst."

units.la: 36 Sed dixi vobis, vos etiam vidisse me, & non credere.
units.tr: 36 But I said to you, that you have also seen me, and yet do not believe.

units.la: EXcitatum iam videtur in animis turbæ aliquod pænis illius vitæ desiderium, & eleuati sunt aliquo usque oculi mortuorum illorum (verè enim mortui erant, quo tempore starent coram Domino) Verùm vita ista, quam hi respexerunt, temporaria erat duntaxat, utpote quam tum vixerunt, & panis vitæ, quem desiderarunt, erat temporarius ille duntaxat & terrenus, quo nimirum alitur præsens ista vita. Neque enim ultra præsentem hanc vitam, & ea quæ ad ipsam pertinent, potest animalis homo porrigere cogitationes suas. quoties audit de vita aliquid, quoties audit de iis quæ vitam procurant, arrigit aures suas, & ea sibi expetit: natura enim omnes vitam expetimus, & quæ eam alunt desideramus, sed de alia vita quàm ista, de alio vitæ alimento, quàm isto præsente, ne cogitare quidem potest homo per naturam. Adeò ut mihi beati videantur esse, qui dum audiunt sermonem de vita, déque iis quæ ad vitam pertinent, qualis fuit tum Christi sermo, altius aspirant ad vitam spiritualem & alimentum spirituale, & animis feruntur supra terrestria omnia. Natura enim nunquam potuisset erigere eos ad cogitandum de iis rebus. Beatus autem est qui profecit vel tantillum in cœlestibus illis, habet enim arrhabonem perfecti post hanc vitam futuri gaudij. Dixit autem ys Iesus. Dominus cùm videt animos eorum aliquo modo iam erectos esse & aliquod vitæ similúque eorum quæ ad vitam alendam pertinent desiderium excitatum, quamquam terrestria duntaxat ipsi adhuc sapiebant, adhuc tamen conatur altius eos erigere supra ista temporaria & terrena, ad inuendum, si quo modo fieri posset, illam vitam cœlecœlestem. Quoniam autem, quæ fuit eorum infirmitas & grauitas, vt sic dicam terrena & naturalis, quæ non sinebat eos altius assurgere ad apprehendendum quasi in cœlis ipsum illum cibum, ideo Dominus sese ad eos demittens, præsentem iis cibum illum sistit in terris.
units.tr: It seems that in the minds of the crowd some longing for that life of bread has been stirred up, and the eyes of those dead men were lifted up for a while (for they really were dead, at the time when they stood before the Lord). But the life that they looked to was only temporary, since it was the life they then lived, and the bread of life they desired was only that temporary and earthly bread, by which of course this present life is nourished. For natural man cannot extend his thoughts beyond this present life and the things that belong to it. Whenever he hears anything about life, whenever he hears about the things that sustain life, he pricks up his ears and craves them, for by nature we all desire life and long for what feeds it. But by nature a man cannot even think of any life other than this one, or of any food for life other than the present kind. So those seem blessed to me who, when they hear talk of life and of the things that pertain to life, such as Christ's discourse was at that time, aspire higher to spiritual life and spiritual food, and are carried in their minds above all earthly things. For nature could never have raised them up to think about such things. Blessed, however, is the one who has advanced even a little in those heavenly things, for he has the earnest of the perfect joy that is to come after this life. Then Jesus said to them. When the Lord sees that their minds are in some measure already lifted up, and that a desire has been stirred for a life like the things that sustain life, although they still relished only earthly things, he nevertheless tries to raise them higher above those temporary and earthly things, so that, if possible, they might find that heavenly life. But because of their weakness and their heaviness, which was, so to speak, earthly and natural, which did not allow them to rise high enough to grasp that food as it were in heaven itself, the Lord therefore lets himself down to them and sets that food before them here on earth.

units.la: Ego sum, inquit, panis ille vitæ. Sic Deus agere solet nobiscum; vbi videt excitatum in nobis aliquod vitæ ternæ & rerum cœlestium desiderium, etsi quidem non sit illud perfectum, imo vero admodum exile & imperfectum sit: tamen qui arundinem quassatam non frangit, neque ellychnium fumigans extinguit, non statim reicit nos, sed desiderij illam quantulamcunque scintillam incipit fouere, & nos aliquantulum erectos pergit adhuc sursum versus trahere, ad hoc vt videamus & apprehendamus magis magisque altiora & cœlestiora: quoniam autem infirmitas nostra tanta est, vt non possimus in cœlos statim euehi; ideo Dominus sese ac cœlestia illa ad nos demittit, atque licet non nunc quidem offerat nobis suum corpus præsens videdum oculis istis corporeis; tamen sese offert percipiendum efficaciter animis per Spiritum suum sanctum, qui rursus animos nostros tam stupidos & terrenos ad cœlos erigit, & coporateam terrena & gravia suo tempore eriget. Sed obseruanda sunt nobis hæc verba paulo diligentius: dum offert se iis tanquam vitæ illum panem, illud maius est profecto quàm fortasse statim alicui prima facie videatur. Vt enim Dominus sit panis ille vitæ, oportet eum præparari atque disponi ad hoc vt sit vtile & salutare nobis alimentum. Præparatur autem & disponitur dum frangitur eius corpus & effunditur eius sanguis: Christus enim, nisi mortificatus prius carne, vt loquitur Petrus, non est aptum alimentum: sed Christus crucifixus est cibus animæ. Dicam hoc paulo clarius; Edere Christum, est credere in eum atque applicare cum magis magisque ad animos nostros. Iam vero peccator, qui conscius peccati ac miseriæ suæ, non credit in Christum nisi pro mortuum pro peccatis ipsius, quærit enim eius modi mediatorem, qui satisfaciat pro peccatis ipsius; absque autem sanguinis effusione non fit remissio. Iudæi cum Messiam expectarent fore hominem nescio
units.tr: "I am," he says, "that bread of life." God is accustomed to act thus with us: when he sees in us some desire for eternal life and heavenly things, even though it is not perfect, but indeed very slight and imperfect, yet he who does not break a bruised reed nor quench a smoking wick does not reject us at once, but begins to foster that spark of desire, however small it is, and continues to draw us, now somewhat raised up, further upward, so that we may see and grasp ever more and more the higher and more heavenly things. And since our weakness is so great that we cannot be carried up to heaven at once, the Lord lets himself and those heavenly things down to us. And although he does not now offer us his body to be seen by these bodily eyes, yet he offers himself to be received effectively by our souls through his Holy Spirit, who again raises our minds, so dull and earthly, up to heaven, and in due time will raise our earthly and heavy bodies as well. But we must observe these words a little more carefully: when he offers himself to them as that bread of life, this is certainly greater than it may perhaps seem at first sight. For the Lord can be the bread of life only if he is prepared and made ready to be useful and wholesome nourishment for us. Now he is prepared and made ready when his body is broken and his blood poured out. For Christ, unless he has first been put to death in the flesh, as Peter says, is not fit food; but the crucified Christ is the food of the soul. I shall say this a little more plainly: to eat Christ is to believe in him and to apply him more and more to our souls. Now the sinner, who is aware of his sin and his misery, does not believe in Christ unless as one dead for his sins, for he seeks a mediator of this kind, who may make satisfaction for his sins; and without shedding of blood there is no remission. The Jews, while they were waiting for the Messiah to be some glorious man, I know not who, were therefore offended at his cross and shame, and did not perceive how wretched and already lost they were, nor did they see themselves bound to sin and damnation. But if they had perceived this, they would certainly have been so far from the stumbling block of Christ's cross that their whole glorying would have been in it, and they would have said with Paul: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ."

units.la: 1.Pet.3.18 quem gloriosum, ideoque offenderentur eius cruce & ignominia, non senserunt quam miseri essent ac iam perditi, neque viderunt se obnoxios peccato & damnationi. Quod si sensissent, tum profecto tatum abfuissent a scandalo crucis Christi, ut in ea sola fuisset illis tota ipsorum gloriatio, dixissentque cum Paulo: A nobis absit gloriari nisi in cruce Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Quare maius quiddam est illud, Christum offerre se nobis comedendum, quam statim prima facie apparet. Tantundem enim est ac si dixisset, Pro vobis me trado morti omnium acerbissimae, quae debita est offensis vestris: ut vos credentes in me pro vobis iam mortuum, virtute mortis meae vivatis in aeternum. Quamobrem qui velit pro dignitate sua aestimare donum hoc quod offert Christus, quantum sit, necesse est iam primum de peccatis suis & miseria cogitet: sic enim fiet ut plures faciat Christum, quam universum hunc mundum, eumque auide ad se arripiat ad iustificationem & salutem suam aeternam.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 3.18 Therefore this offer of Christ, that he presents himself to us to be eaten, is something greater than it first appears. For it amounts to this: "I give myself up to a most bitter death, which is owed to your offences, so that you, believing in me as one already dead for you, may live forever by the power of my death." Wherefore, whoever wishes to estimate, according to its worth, the gift that Christ offers, how great it is, must first of all think about his sins and his misery: for in this way he will make Christ of more account than the whole world, and will eagerly seize him for his justification and his eternal salvation.

units.la: Qui venit ad me. Commendat illis ex effectis suis longe suavissimis panem illum, ubi etiam habes, quid sit illud, Christum edere; est autem primum ad Christum venire, deinde in Christum credere, haec enim idem sunt. Effecta igitur sunt; Non esuriet unquam, non sitiet unquam. Esurienti cuique & fame laboranti nihil gratius est quam si saturetur: sitibundo nihil acceptius, quam si restinguatur sitis. Ita esurienti & sitienti spiritualiter nihil gratius accidere potest quam si satisfiat ipsi. Itaque plena satisfactio ista & satietas suavissima offertur. Sed offertur etiam praeterea; qui enim vescuntur hoc cibo terreno, saturantur quidem, sed ad tempus; offertur autem credenti aeterna saturitas: Non esuriet, non sitiet unquam. Quae quidem saturitas aeterna sic intelligenda est, non quod non esuriemus omnino aut sitiemus postquam semel datus fuerit nobis cibus ille caelestis: Nam esuriemus quidem ac sitiemus, postea desiderabimus magis magisque illa caelestia, tantisperdum hic viuemus; sed hinc est illa aeterna saturitas, quod non prius desiderabimus quam accipiemus. Beati qui esuriunt ac sitiunt iustitiam, quoniam ipsi saturabuntur. Non autem ita fit in terrestri isto cibo, quem appetunt quidem multi, non tamen continuo suppeditatur iis. Neque vero aliter fieri potest, quin credentes in Christum paulatim impleatur gratia, cum Christus ipse sit plenus gratiæ & veritatis. Apostolus post- quam dixit in eo esse omnes thesauros cognitionis & sapientiæ, & omnem plenitudinem deitatis in eo habitare corporaliter, subiecit, Et in eo estis completi. Item Iohannes postquam dixit eum plenum gratiæ & veritatis, addidit, ex plenitudine eius omnes accepimus. Nihil est vel in cælis vel in terra tam impletum omni gratia quàm est Christus. Quare qui vult quærere sibi saturitatem ex aliis rebus quæ ipsæ ieiunæ sunt omnes, non saturabi-tur in æternum. Neque vero qui non gustauit vnquam, quàm suauis sit Dominus, sensit vnquam quid esset sanctitas. Sed quòd homines vulgò non saturantur Christo, causa est, quòd non esuriunt: non autem esuriunt, quia iam impleta sunt corda hominum alio cibi quodam genere, terrestri nimirum isto vel gloriæ, vel diuitiarum, vel voluptatum. Si loquaris ei homini qui iam plus quàm satis fuit cibi huius corporalis voravit, si, inquam, loquaris huic homini iam sic satiato ad fastidiū vsque etiam de optimo quoque & lectissimo cibi genere, profecto moueris ei nauseam: ita quoque se res habet in his de quibus loquimur. Quare iam primùm illi, qui velit saturari Christo, obdormiēda est, vt sic dicam, crapula, & euomenda ambitio sua, auaro auaritia sua, libidinoso libido sua, & sic de aliis alioqui profecto nunquam futurum est, vt gustet quisquam quàm suauis sit Dominus, sine quo nulla suauitas, nulla lætitia, nulla pax, nulla vita neque in hac vita, neque post hanc vitam.
units.tr: "Who comes to me." He commends that bread to them by its most sweet effects; and here you also have what it is to eat Christ: first to come to Christ, then to believe in Christ, for these are the same thing. The effects, therefore, follow: he shall never hunger, he shall never thirst. Nothing is more welcome to a man who is hungry and starving than to be satisfied, nor to one who is thirsty than to have his thirst quenched. So nothing more welcome can happen to one who is spiritually hungry and thirsty than to be satisfied. Thus this full satisfaction and most sweet satiety is offered. But something more is offered besides: for those who feed on this earthly food are indeed satisfied, but only for a time; to the believer, however, is offered eternal satiety: he shall not hunger, he shall never thirst. This eternal satiety is to be understood not in the sense that we shall not hunger or thirst at all once that heavenly food has been given to us. For we shall indeed hunger and thirst, and afterwards we shall desire those heavenly things more and more, as long as we live here; but the eternal satiety lies in this, that we shall not desire before we have received. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. It is not so, however, with that earthly food, which many desire, yet which is not continually supplied to them. Nor indeed can it be otherwise, but that those who believe in Christ are gradually filled with grace, since Christ himself is full of grace and truth. The Apostle, after saying that in him are all the treasures of knowledge and wisdom, and that in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily, added: And in him you are made complete. Likewise John, after saying that he is full of grace and truth, added: from his fullness we have all received. There is nothing in heaven or on earth so filled with all grace as Christ is. Wherefore whoever wishes to seek satisfaction from other things, which are all empty in themselves, will never be satisfied. Nor indeed has anyone who has never tasted how sweet the Lord is ever known what holiness is. But the reason why men in general are not satisfied with Christ is that they do not hunger; and they do not hunger because their hearts are already filled with another kind of food, namely this earthly one of glory, or riches, or pleasures. If you speak to a man who has already eaten more than enough of this bodily food, and who is so satiated that he is sick of even the best and choicest kind of food, you will certainly stir up nausea in him: so it is also in the matters of which we are speaking. Wherefore, before anything else, the one who wishes to be satisfied with Christ must, so to speak, sleep off his gluttony, and vomit up his ambition, the covetous man his covetousness, the lustful man his lust, and so on with the rest; otherwise it will never happen that anyone tastes how sweet the Lord is, without whom there is no sweetness, no joy, no peace, no life, either in this life or after it.

units.la: Sed dixi vobis. Christus considerato iam illo fructu, qui est ex fide in ipsum tam abundanti & iucundo, non continet quin erumpat in reprehensionem aliquam eorum, qui tamen noluerunt credere. Qui considerant & gustant illum fructum qui est ex fide, tam vberem, cum intuentur obstinatos istos, qui nolunt ex animi malitia credere; non mirum est, quòd se non contineant quin cuehantur in eos, qui & spoliant Deum tanta gloria, & priuant se tanto gaudio. Qui sentit illam αὐτάρκεια & sufficientiam quæ est ex solo Christi merito, iustitia & obedientia eius ipsi imputata, si interea cum videt impostores istos abducere homines à Christo ad consectandum merita sua, & quærendum iustitiam suam, quæ est ex operibus legis: si, inquam, interea in eos acerbius inuehatur, excusare profecto debet eum zelus gloriæ Dei sui. Sed quos reprehendit Dominus? eos nimirum qui viderunt, neque tamen crediderunt. In quos, quæso, inuehimur nos hodierno die? In eos potissimum qui Christum viderunt, hoc est, ante quorum oculos crucifixus est, tam clara scilicet euangelij prædicatione. Non tam inuehimur vel in Turcam, vel in Iudæum, vel in eum, qui homicidium, qui adulterium, qui sacrilegium committit; denique qui Christum vita & factis negat; ac proinde infideli detestor est, quicquid tandem profiteatur; non tam, inquam, in istos inuehimur; quam in Antichristum illum qui hostis est crucis Christi, & qui plane abrogat gratiam Dei in Christo Iesu.
units.tr: But I have told you. Christ, having already considered the fruit that comes from faith, which is so abundant and delightful, cannot help breaking out into a rebuke of those who nevertheless refused to believe. Those who consider and taste that fruit of faith, so rich, when they look upon those obstinate people who from wickedness of mind refuse to believe, it is no wonder that they cannot restrain themselves from railing against those who both rob God of so great a glory and deprive themselves of so great a joy. Whoever feels that self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια] and sufficiency which comes from Christ's merit alone, his righteousness and obedience imputed to him, if meanwhile he sees these impostors drawing men away from Christ to pursue their own merits and to seek their own righteousness, which is from the works of the law: if, I say, in the meantime he rails more bitterly against them, the zeal for the glory of his God ought surely to excuse him. But whom does the Lord rebuke? Surely those who saw and yet did not believe. Whom, I ask, do we rail against today? Chiefly those who have seen Christ, that is, before whose eyes he was crucified, through the so clear preaching of the gospel. We do not so much rail against the Turk, or the Jew, or him who commits murder, adultery or sacrilege, in short, who denies Christ by his life and deeds, and therefore detests the unfaithful, whatever they profess; we do not, I say, so much rail against these as against that Antichrist who is the enemy of the cross of Christ, and who plainly abrogates the grace of God in Christ Jesus.

units.la: Tolerabilius quidem est illud Turcam vel aperte infidelem esse quemquam; sed profiteri se fidelem esse & videri, atque interea temporis ex obstinata quadam animi malitia nolle credere, nescio quomodo fit feredu: Si cæci essetis, ait Christus, non haberetis peccatum, nunc vero dicitis, videmus; itaque peccatum vestrum permanet. Non possum satis dicere, quàta sit infidelitas & obstinatio eorum qui hodierno die viuunt, ac proinde quanta futura sit eorum damnatio. Notandum autem est verbum quod habet, dixi, id est, iam antea dixi vobis, & nunc iterum dico, quandiu non piget vos infidelitatis vestræ, tandiu non pigebit me idem vobis repetere. Quandiu non pigetmundum peccatorum omnis generis, tandiu non pigere debet pastorem repetitionis earundem rerum ac reprehensionum. Neque vero oportet expectare infideles & peccatores istos, dum priores dicant scilicet, fastidio se capitam frequentis eiusdem rei repetitionis; sed præoccupare conuenit ac dicere, hoc à se ἐxpiùs iam dictum esse, & nunc rursus dici. Neque profecto caret hoc vsu suo aliquo: præterquam enim quòd purgat pastore sanguinis eorum, dum iusto Dei iudicio intereunt, exaggerat etiam iudicium & damnationem eorum qui ad tot repetitiones non resipiscunt. Neque enim inutilis aut inanis futura est, vel vna aliqua repetitio: verum addit aliquid ad iudicij grauitatem. Multæ & crebræ repetitiones, multa iudicia cumulant, & thesaurum iræ Dei complent. Rom. 2. 5.
units.tr: It is indeed more tolerable for any man to be openly unfaithful, like the Turk; but to profess oneself faithful and to seem so, and meanwhile from a certain obstinate malice of mind to be unwilling to believe, somehow is more hard to bear: If you were blind, says Christ, you would have no sin; but now you say, We see; therefore your sin remains. I cannot say enough how great is the unbelief and obstinacy of those who live today, and therefore how great their damnation will be. Note, however, the word he uses, dixi, that is, I have said to you before, and now I say again: as long as it does not grieve you of your unbelief, so long it will not grieve me to repeat the same to you. As long as it does not grieve the world of sinners of every kind, so long ought the minister not to grieve at repeating the same things and the same rebukes. Nor ought we to wait for the unbelieving and these sinners to say, forsooth, that they are wearied with the frequent repetition of the same thing; rather it is fitting to forestall this and to say that this has been said by him more than once already, and is now said again. Nor is this without some use: for besides the fact that it clears the minister of their blood, when they perish by the just judgment of God, it also heightens the judgment and damnation of those who do not repent after so many repetitions. For no single repetition will be useless or vain; rather it adds something to the weight of judgment. Many and frequent repetitions pile up judgments and fill up the treasure of the wrath of God. Rom. 2. 5.

units.la: 37 Quicquid dat mihi Pater, ad me veniet: & eum qui venit ad me, nequaquam eiecerim foras:
units.tr: 37 All that the Father gives me will come to me, and him who comes to me I will by no means cast out.

units.la: 38 Quia descendi à cœlo vt exsequar non voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem eius qui misit me.
units.tr: 38 For I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.

units.la: 39 Hæc est autem voluntas eius qui misit me, idest, Patris, vt quicquid mihi dederit, non perdam ex eo, sed suscitem illud in vltimo illo die.
units.tr: 39 And this is the will of him who sent me, that is, of the Father, that of all he has given me I should lose nothing, but raise it up at the last day.

units.la: 40 Hæc est autem voluntas eius qui misit me, vt omnis qui conspicit filium, & credit in eum, habeat vitam æternam: & suscitem ipsum ego vltimo illo die.
units.tr: 40 And this is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day.

units.la: Hic obscurè ad altius quoddam principium infidelitatis deducit eos, nempe ad terribilem illum reprobationis fontem, ac si sic argumentaretur: Quicquid dat mihi Pater, ad me veniet: Sed vos non venitis ad me: Ergo quid dici poterit, nisi vos non datos mihi à Patre? Quicquid dat mihi Pater, &c. Hoc est, quod elegit ab æterno, & dedit mihi conseruandum: nam Pater ab æterno eligit ac seperat quos dat filio custodiendos: Vocatis, inquit Iudas, à Deo Patre sanctificatis, & Iesu Christo seruatis Iud. 1. Ad me venit. Electi necesse est veniant ad Christum, vel citius vel serius, nonnunquam etiam in ipso mortis articulo ad Deum in Christo conuertuntur. Sæpe videntur perditi esse tanquam oues errantes, qui tamen necessitate quadam redeunt ad Pastorem suum suo tempore. Obserua: Qui noluntadduci vlla ratione ad credendum, quid vetat iis nunc demonstrare terribile illud & metuendum principium infidelitatis? [nam vt fidei effectum est electionis, ita infidelitas effectum est reprobationis. Crediderunt quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam æternam.] Nunc vero infidelitatis finem non minus terribilem & horrendum, nempe æternam illam damnationem.
units.tr: Here he obscurely leads them back to a higher principle of unbelief, namely that terrible fountain of reprobation, as if he argued thus: All that the Father gives me will come to me. But you do not come to me. Therefore what can be said, except that you have not been given to me by the Father? All that the Father gives me, etc. That is, what he chose from eternity and gave me to keep: for the Father from eternity chooses and separates those whom he gives to the Son to be kept. Called, says Jude, by God the Father, sanctified and preserved in Jesus Christ (Jude 1). Will come to me. The elect must come to Christ, either sooner or later, and sometimes they are converted to God in Christ even at the moment of death. Often they seem lost, like wandering sheep, yet by a certain necessity they return to their Shepherd in their own time. Observe: for those who are unwilling to be brought to believe by any means, what forbids us to set before them now that terrible and dreadful principle of unbelief? [For as faith is the effect of election, so unbelief is the effect of reprobation. As many as were ordained to eternal life believed.] But now also the end of unbelief, no less terrible and horrible, namely that eternal damnation.

units.la: Iudas Parentheses sic corrigi velim: Nam vt fidei electionis effectum est, eamque in credibus fidelium elicit, sic etiam, et à contra perpetua et constans infidelitas, cum peccatum in infidelitate, reprobationem non obtinere arguit. tionem demonstrat. Ea enim est αὐτοκρισία, &, vt sic dicā, infensibilitas infidelitatis, ita etiam placet sibi natura in ipsa, vt nisi maiori aliqua vi excitetur consopita ipsius conscientia, etiam denuntiata, si opus sit, aeterna reprobatione, nunquam futurum sit, vt quis eam in se persentiscat. Nihil autem terribilius est, aut maiori aut tristiori sensu nos afficit, quàm reprobatio. Nam cum cogitatione ipsius coniunctus est sensus quidam ipsorum inferorum Et cum qui venit. Hactenus digito quasi demonstrauit fontem infidelitatis, nempe reprobationem, nunc vicissim finem ostendit fidei, qui est vt deiecti primum terribili illa inspectione reprobationis: deinde excitentur suaui illo intuitu vitæ æternæ. Fieri quidem potest, vt per comminationes & denuntiationes efficiatur in nobis sensus aliquis infidelitatis, aliorumque peccatorum; sed nunquam per eas solas fiet, vt malis illis purgentur corda nostra (nam hic est gradus quidam ulterior) aut propter eas solas credamus & convertamur ad Deum, nisi cum iis audiamus bona, vt dicit solet, verba & suaues promissiones, quæ vbi primùm audiuimus, iam quo acerbior fuit comminatio, eo suavior euadit promissio: neque enim quæ dulcia sunt sentit is qui non prius gustauit quæ amara sunt. Quamobrem quoties comminatur & deiicit nos Dominus, toties dicendum est, Domine, da bona verba, quæso, & suauia, vt audeam ad te propius accedere, & te intueri: quod profecto non citius feriis precibus flagitabis à Deo quàm impetrabis. Neque verò expectabis è cœlo nouas aliquas reuelationes, nouas promissiones: nam, vt ait Apostolus, Prope te est verbum & in ore tuo & in corde tuo, hoc est verbum illud fidei quod prædicamus. Quod quidem verbum fidei ex omnibus quæ vel dicuntur vel scribuntur suauissimum est, & id habet singulare, quòd cùm verba hominum quæ suauia sunt & iucunda, fere assentatoria sint & fucata, nihil hic fuci est vel assentationis, sed omnia credenti suo tempore implebuntur.
units.tr: I would have this parenthesis in Jude corrected thus: For just as faith is the effect of election, and draws it out in the believing faithful, so too the continual and constant unbelief, since sin in unbelief shows that reprobation is not obtained, demonstrates it. For this is self-judgment [αὐτοκρισία], and, as I may say, the insensibility of unbelief; so too nature is so pleased with itself that, unless the stupefied conscience is roused by some greater force, even if eternal reprobation is announced, if need be, it will never come about that anyone perceives it in himself. Yet nothing is more terrible, or affects us with a greater or sadder feeling, than reprobation. For with the thought of it there is joined a certain sense of the very depths And with him who comes. Thus far he has pointed, as it were with a finger, to the fountain of unbelief, namely reprobation; now in turn he shows the end of faith, which is that men, first cast down by that terrible sight of reprobation, may then be roused by the sweet gaze of eternal life. It may indeed happen that through threats and denunciations some sense of unbelief and of other sins is produced in us; but never through these alone will our hearts be cleansed of those evils (for this is a further step), nor do we believe and turn to God on account of these alone, unless with them we hear good words, as they say, and sweet promises; which, as soon as we have heard them, the sharper the threat was, the sweeter the promise becomes: for he who has not first tasted what is bitter does not feel what is sweet. Therefore, whenever the Lord threatens and casts us down, we must always say: Lord, give good and sweet words, I pray, that I may dare to draw nearer to you and look upon you; which assuredly you will obtain from God no more slowly by urgent prayers than you will by asking. Nor should you expect from heaven any new revelations or new promises; for, as the Apostle says, The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart: that is the word of faith which we preach. This word of faith is the sweetest of all the things that are either said or written, and it has this singular quality: while the words of men, though sweet and pleasing, are mostly flattering and feigned, here there is no pretence or flattery, but all things will be fulfilled for the one who believes, in their time.

units.la: Quia descendi.
units.tr: Because I have come down.

units.la: Quo certiorem reddat iis hanc vitam, ostendit ex voluntate Patris esse, vt viuant quotquot ad ipsum veniunt, atque id quidem ad maiorem fidem & pleniorem persuasionem semel atque iterum pronuntiatur. tiatur. Addit etiam alterum fundamentum quo rursus magis persuasum hoc ipsi habeant, nempe quòd ipse descenderit de cœlo, vt faceret voluntatem non suam, hoc est suam solius, sed voluntatem eius, hoc est Patris sui.
units.tr: To make this life more certain for them, he shows that it is the will of the Father that all who come to him should live. He states this once and again, for greater faith and fuller assurance. He also adds a second ground, by which they may hold it more firmly still: namely, that he has come down from heaven to do not his own will, that is, the will that is his alone, but the will of him, that is, of his Father.

units.la: Quod admonet eos de voluntate Patris sui, innuit difficultatem credendi, & importat dubitasse istos de vita illa quam proximè promisit se daturum ei qui ad ipsum venturus esset, & in ipsum crediturus. Atque hoc rursus importat conscientiam peccati: nam conscientia peccati quo offendimus, in causa est cur dubitemus de benevolentia & promissione Dei. Ea enim est peccati conscientia in natura insita, proindeque sensus iræ Dei, vt per naturam nunquam possumus credere nos seruatum iri: imò in ipsis regenitis quoque reliqua est aliqua peccati conscientia, ac proinde iræ sensus aliquis, vt non sine graui lucta & multis dubitationibus sæpè possint credere victuros se in æternum post hanc vitam. Neque enim tam facile illud est, polliceri sibi quemquam vitam illam æternam. Nouimus enim diaboli machinationes.
units.tr: When he reminds them of the will of his Father, he hints at the difficulty of believing, and implies that these people had doubted about that life which he had just promised to give to whoever would come to him and believe in him. This again implies a consciousness of sin. For the consciousness of sin by which we offend is the cause of our doubting God's goodwill and promise. Such consciousness of sin is implanted in nature, and with it a sense of God's wrath, so that by nature we can never believe that we shall be saved. Indeed, even in the regenerate some consciousness of sin remains, and with it some sense of wrath, so that they often cannot believe, without hard struggle and many doubts, that they will live for ever after this life. For it is not so easy to promise oneself that eternal life. We know the devices of the devil.

units.la: Sed en hic remedium: admonendi sumus perpetuò de voluntate Dei erga nos, & conandum omnibus modis ut sentiamus illam charitatem effusam in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis. De voluntate ista Dei ac Domini admonuit Dominus turbam istam. Studendum est quoque vt magis magisque pu- getur per Christi sanguinem mala conscientia, hoc est, conscientia illa peccatis quod ita demum obtinebimus, si, quantum Dei gratia fieri potest, abstinebimus à peccatis præsertim grauioribus, quæ efficiunt atque augent malam conscientiam: sed imprimis hoc fiet si credamus in Iesum Christum, in quo habemus omnium peccatorum nostrorum remissionem, etiam reliquiarum istarum, quæ perpetuò dum vixerimus in natura ista corrupta aliquo numero permansuræ sunt. Deinde hoc quoque quod admonet, se descendisse de cœlo ad hoc vt impleat Patris illam voluntatem quæ fuit de iis seruandis, importat dubitationem quandam eorum, de modo ac ratione qua implenda esset ipsius voluntas. Postquam enim admoniti de voluntate Patris erga salutem nostram, id, fatebor, magnam habet vim ad nos consolandos, sed continuò suboritur aliud dubium de via ac ratione voluntatis illius perficiendæ: nam si nos ipsos intueamur, non videbimus nisi materiam iræ; si rursus Deum respiciamus, non videbimus nisi iustitiam in eo summam, cui non potest vllo modo renuntiare. Nam de Christo Mediatore non nisi admoniti prius de eo, ne ipsi quidem Angeli potuerunt vnquam suspicari. Quare (id quod video Christum facere hoc loco) de Christo ipsiusque aduentu, cuius finis erat vt impleret Dei illam erga nos voluntatem, perpetuo certiores fieri nos oportet, & nitendum est vt nos ipsum videamus, neque videamus modo, sed vt in textu additum est, in eum credamus totis animis. Quod si fiet, non modo habebimus Dei voluntatem, quæ nobis probet ac confirmet vitam illam, non modo habebimus Christum voluntatem eam Dei exequentem, sed habebimus ipsum in nobis arrhabonem vitæ illius æternæ. Neque enim citius credemus in eum, qui est omnis vitæ author, quàm incipiemus iam ipsi viuere vitâ illam æternam, quod argumento erat nos, etsi corpora nostra in pulverem redacta fuerint, tamen suo tempore resuscitandos, & cum Christo capite illo nostro glorificandos in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But here is the remedy: we must constantly be reminded of God's will towards us, and we must strive in every way to feel that love poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. The Lord reminded that crowd of this will of God and of the Lord. We must also work that, more and more, an evil conscience is cleansed by the blood of Christ, that is, that consciousness of sin which we shall obtain only in this way: if, as far as God's grace allows, we abstain from sins, especially the grave ones which make and increase an evil conscience. But this will be done above all if we believe in Jesus Christ, in whom we have the forgiveness of all our sins, including those remnants which, as long as we live, will remain in some number in this corrupt nature. Then, when he says that he has come down from heaven in order to fulfil the will of the Father, which concerned their salvation, this too implies some doubt among them about the manner and method by which his will was to be carried out. For once we have been reminded of the Father's will towards our salvation, I admit, this has great power to console us, but at once another doubt arises about the way and means of accomplishing that will. For if we look at ourselves, we see nothing but the matter of wrath; if we look again at God, we see nothing but his supreme justice, which in no way can be set aside. Indeed, about Christ the Mediator not even the angels themselves could ever have guessed, unless they had first been instructed about him. Therefore (as I see Christ doing in this place) we must be made continually more certain about Christ and his coming, whose purpose was to fulfil God's will towards us; and we must strive not only to see him, but, as is added in the text, to believe in him with all our souls. If this is done, we shall have not only God's will, which approves and confirms that life for us, and not only Christ carrying out that will of God, but we shall have him in us as a pledge of that eternal life. For we shall not believe in him, who is the author of all life, any sooner than we begin now to live that eternal life in him. This was the proof that, although our bodies have been reduced to dust, we shall nevertheless be raised up at the appointed time, and glorified for ever with Christ, our head. Amen.

units.la: 41 Murmurabant ergo Iudæi de eo, quia dixerat, Ego sum panis ille qui è cœlo descendit.
units.tr: 41 The Jews therefore murmured at him, because he said, I am the bread which came down from heaven.

units.la: 42 Et dicebant, Nonne hic est Iesus, filius ille Iosephi, cuius nos nouimus patrem & matrem? quomodo ergo dicit iste, E cœlo descendi?
units.tr: 42 And they said, Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he say, I came down from heaven?

units.la: HOc effectum est doctrinæ Christi in incredulis Histis: primùm quidem nihil ne suspicati quidem sunt de pane illo cœlesti, de eius è cœlis descensu, quàm Christus hæc eos doceret: nunc verò vbi audiunt ista, non intelligunt, hoc est, non approbant, sed obmurmurant. Ex hoc eorum exemplo discimus, quàm vera sit illa Pauli doctrina, quando ait sapientiam illam Dei in mysterio latentem, id est occultam illam, Principes huius sæculi non cognouisse: & ea quæ præparauit Deus diligentibus se oculum hominis non vidisse, neque aurem audiuisse, neque in mentem hominis venisse. Quibus significat de mysterio hoc nullum vnquam hominum natura ne suspicatum quidem esse. Tum postea dicit, animalem hominem non esse capace eorum quae sunt Spiritus Dei. Quibus verbis significat, nec tu etiā, cum de his audit, naturale hominem ea percipere: nō quōd nō plane intelligat quae dicuntur, hoc enim esset negare illi commune istud sensum: sed hoc vult Paulus, animalem hominem spiritualia etiam certo quodam modo intellecta non approbare, non iis assentiri. Unde etiam addit postea, Sunt enim ei stultitia; hoc est stulta & friuola esse iudicat. Beatus igitur est, quisquis audit ea de quibus nē suspicatus semel fuisset vnquam, sed beatior est qui audita intelligit, hoc est, non iudicat stultitiam, sed, vt Paulus loquitur, sapientiam Dei, neque id solum, sed etiam Dei potentiam. Hoc postremum tum demum obtinetur, cum per fidem applicatis ad se spiritualibus quis sentit eam in se Dei potentiam. Nam Euangelium non est potentia Dei nisi credenti, hoc est, applicanti ad se ea quae dicuntur. Et dicebant. Hactenus propositā est eorum murmuratio, nunc propositionem eam explicat. Ac primum murmurationem aduersus id quod dictum est ab eo se e caelo descendisse; duobus enim his offenduntur, & eo quod dixerit se panem vitae esse, & eo quod dixerit se e caelo descendisse. Murmuratio autem eorum aduersus descensum eius e caelis constitit in ratiocinatione quadam, & disceptatione, quae est ex infidelitate. Nonne hic est? Q.d. Hic est Iesus filius Iosephi cuius nos novimus patrem & matrem; unde concludunt contradicentes assertioni ipsius, impossibile esse quod dixit se e caelo descendisse. Vides igitur eos se sua ratiocinatione excaecare & obdurare. Praestantissimum quidem in homine est rationis illa facultas, sed tamen infidelitatis primus fons est ratio, suppeditat enim infinita argumenta partim falsa, cuiusmodi est hoc Iudaeorum; neque enim Iesus erat filius Iosephi) partim etiam vera e natura & e medio petita, quibus omnibus praeludant sibi aditum ad Christum eiusque veritate.
