Non est quidem tam pretiosum quiddam humana ratio quam putarunt olim Philosophi veteres, neque etiam quam putant hodierno die Papistae, neque denique quae putant alii, qui verbo quidem profitentur veritatem & sapientiam Dei, sed re & factis pluris faciunt sapientiam carnis, videntúrque sibi soli sapientes esse. Quod enim in homine est, quo primùm ipse sibi imponit & cæteris animæ suæ facultatibus, ratio est. Unde etiam Paulus ascribit illi principem errorum omnium in religione, & idololatriæ, causam. Quamobrem hoc primum est quod à Paulo præscribitur ei, qui velit sapere Deo, nempe ut stultus fiat, ut fiat sapiens: hoc est, in rebus spiritualibus percipiendis renuntiet rationi suæ & prudentiæ carnis, cui quidem, fateor, in aliis rebus, ut naturalibus ac civilibus locus esse potest, sed in iis quæ ad regnum Dei pertinent & spiritualibus, corruptæ rationi non est locus. Atquæ, inquies, certitudo cognitionis esse potest
units.tr: This is the effect of Christ's teaching on the unbelieving Jews. First, they had not even suspected anything about that heavenly bread, or about its descent from heaven, before Christ taught them these things. Now, when they hear them, they do not understand, that is, they do not approve, but murmur. From their example we learn how true is that doctrine of Paul, when he says that the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery, that is, that secret wisdom, was not known by the princes of this world; and that the things which God has prepared for those who love him, the eye of man has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man. By these words he means that the nature of man has never even suspected this mystery. Then afterwards he says that the natural man is not capable of the things of the Spirit of God. By these words he means that the natural man does not perceive these things even when he hears of them: not that he does not plainly understand what is said, for to say this would be to deny him that common sense; but Paul means that the natural man does not approve of spiritual things, even when they have been understood in a certain way, and does not assent to them. Hence he adds afterwards, For they are foolishness to him; that is, he judges them to be foolish and frivolous. Blessed, then, is whoever hears those things of which he had never before even suspected anything; but more blessed is he who understands what he has heard, that is, who does not judge it to be foolishness, but, as Paul puts it, the wisdom of God, and not only that, but also the power of God. This last is obtained only when, by faith, someone applies these spiritual things to himself and feels in himself that power of God. For the gospel is not the power of God except to the believer, that is, to one who applies to himself what is said. And they said. So far their murmuring has been set forth; now he explains the statement. And first, their murmuring against what was said, that he had come down from heaven. For they are offended by these two things: both by his saying that he is the bread of life, and by his saying that he came down from heaven. Their murmuring against his descent from heaven rests on a certain reasoning and dispute, which springs from unbelief. Is not this? That is: This is Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know. From this they conclude, against his assertion, that what he said, that he came down from heaven, is impossible. You see, then, that they blind and harden themselves by their own reasoning. Indeed, that faculty of reason is the most excellent thing in man; yet reason is the first source of unbelief, for it supplies endless arguments, some false, such as this of the Jews (for Jesus was not the son of Joseph), and some true, drawn from nature and from the world, by which they all pave for themselves the way to Christ and to his truth. Human reason is not so precious a thing as the ancient philosophers thought, nor as the Papists think today, nor indeed as others think, who in word profess the truth and wisdom of God, but in deed and fact value the wisdom of the flesh more, and seem to themselves alone to be wise. For what is in man by which he first imposes on himself and on the other faculties of his soul is reason. Hence Paul also ascribes to it the chief cause of all errors in religion and of idolatry. Therefore this is the first thing Paul prescribes to one who wishes to be wise towards God: namely, that he become foolish, that he may become wise; that is, in perceiving spiritual things he must renounce his reason and the prudence of the flesh. This prudence, I admit, may have a place in other matters, such as natural and civil affairs; but in those things which pertain to the kingdom of God and are spiritual, there is no place for corrupt reason. But, you will say, can there be certainty of knowledge

units.la: sine ratione? Respondeo certitudinem fidei non niti ratione, verùm cum ratione pugnare. Abraham contra spem & naturam credidit Deum potuisse quod promiserat præstare. Non caret quidem fundamentis ac principiis quibusdam suis fides, intuetur enim in Deum ipsum, eius summam potentiam, summam veracitatem (fidelis enim est qui promisit) summam misericordiam, cæteraque denique quæ in eo longè firmissima sunt & fallere nos non possunt. Ex his ratiocinatur, colligitque certitudinem promissionum ac verbi ipsius, quod profecto non facit citius quàm incipiat animo secum persentiscere promissionum præstationem & impletionem aliquam, ut iam habeat fides, præter illa principia ex quibus pendet, etiam arrhabonem & initium quoddam rerum carum quæ fide percipiuntur, quo etiam confirmatur ipsa fides in promissiones, sperátque homo earum complementum.
units.tr: without reason? I answer that the certainty of faith does not rest on reason but is opposed to reason. Against hope and nature, Abraham believed that God was able to do what he had promised. Faith does have its foundations and principles. It looks to God himself: to his supreme power, his supreme truthfulness (for he is faithful who has promised), his supreme mercy, and everything else in him that is most firm and cannot deceive us. From these it reasons and draws the certainty of the promises and of the Word itself. Faith does not do this only after it has begun to sense within the soul some foretaste and beginning of the things promised, so that it has, besides those principles on which it depends, an earnest and a first instalment of the things that are grasped by faith. By this, faith itself is confirmed in the promises, and a person hopes for their fulfilment.

units.la: Deinde observa: Intuentur isti genus Christi, quod quidem ipsis videbatur vile & contemptibile: At que genus hoc Christi in speciem vile dum intuentur, nihil in eo vident diuinū aut spirituale, vel saltem videre nolūt. Animales homines tantum quod ob oculos est aspiciunt. Hoc conabor explicare: Res in Christo spirituales offerri solent sub vili quodam habitu ac specie contemptibili, & gloria ipsa cælestis offertur in hac vita sub integumento ignominiæ, quæ tamen in altera vita conspicietur in suis coloribus. Christi vilis est aspectus: Non est forma ei neque decor. Euangelium eius vile afflictum. Filij Dei sumus, aiit Iohannes, sed nondum patefa- ctum est quod erimus. Ministri verbi fiunt purgamenta mundi, usque omnium sordes usque adhuc. Haec igitur omnia caelestia dum intuentur filij huius saeculi, tantum in externa illa & contemptibili eorum facie haerent, & ex ea metiuntur ipsa caelestia ac spiritualia. Putant quidem isti se sagacissimos & perspicacissimos esse in rebus iudicandis; at in caelestibus nihil vident, nisi superficiem: neque enim unquam is, qui tantum sapit mundum hunc, solide intelligit aliquid in rebus divinis, neque ea unquam altius penetrant in eius animum. Soli enim filij Dei sunt, qui per superficiem hanc externam & mediam penetrare possunt in profunditates Dei, hoc est in illam abditam gloriam rerum spiritualium: Spiritus enim omnia scrutatur, etiam profunditates Dei. 1.Cor.2.10. Estque hic aspectus perspicacior ac profundior quam est omnium sapientium huius mundi, dum illuminatis oculis vident, quae sit spes illa vocationis Dei, quae opes gloriae haereditatis ipsius in sanctis, quae excellens illa magnitudo potentiae ipsius in nobis qui credimus.
units.tr: Next, observe this: those men look at the lineage of Christ, which seemed to them base and contemptible. While they look at that lineage, which is humble in appearance, they see nothing divine or spiritual in it, or at least they refuse to see it. Natural men look only at what is before their eyes. I will try to explain this. Spiritual things in Christ are usually offered under a certain cheap guise and a contemptible appearance, and heavenly glory itself is offered in this life under the covering of disgrace, yet in the other life it will be seen in its own colours. The appearance of Christ is lowly: "he has no form nor comeliness" (Isa. 53). His gospel is poor and afflicted. "We are the sons of God," says John, "but it is not yet made manifest what we shall be." "The ministers of the word become the filth of the world, the offscouring of all things, even until now." While the sons of this age look at all these heavenly things, they cling only to that outward and contemptible face, and they measure the heavenly and spiritual things by it. They think themselves very shrewd and very perceptive in judging matters. But in heavenly things they see nothing but the surface. Indeed, one who savours only this world never understands anything solidly in divine matters, and such things never penetrate deeply into his mind. Only the sons of God can pass through this outward and middle surface into the depths of God, that is, into that hidden glory of spiritual things. "For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God" (1 Cor. 2:10). This sight is keener and deeper than that of all the wise of this world, since with enlightened eyes they see what is the hope of God's calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, and what is that surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe.

units.la: 43 Respondit ergo Iesus, & dixit eis, Ne murmurate inter vos.
units.tr: Jesus therefore answered and said to them, Murmur not among yourselves.

units.la: 44 Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater qui misit me, traxerit eum: & ego suscitem ipsum in novissimo die.
units.tr: No man can come to me, except the Father who sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.

units.la: 45 Scriptum est in Prophetis, Et erunt omnes docti a Deo. Quisquis ergo audiit a Patre & didicit, venit ad me.
units.tr: It is written in the prophets, And they shall all be taught of God. Every one therefore that has heard and learned of the Father comes to me.

units.la: 46 Non quod Patrem viderit quisquam, nisi is, qui est a Deo: hic vidit Patrem.
units.tr: Not that any man has seen the Father, save he who is of God: he has seen the Father.

units.la: Quasi diceret Dominus: Vos praetexitis infidelitati vestrae genus meum, parentes meos, ignobilitatem meam: sed longe alia causa subest, eaque in vobis ipsis penitus sita, nempe impotentia quaedam vestra, qua fit ut non possitis ad me venire: nulla in vobis est inclinatio qua ad me propendeatis, vel ad Deum, sed plane averfiftis a Deo, & a me alieni. Pater autem nondum traxit vos, hoc est nondum mutauit vestram illam inclinationem, indiditque facultatem. Nemo autem ad me venire potest nisi Pater eum traxerit: argumentatio enim Domini sic habet: Nemo potest ad me venire nisi Pater qui misit me eum traxerit: At Pater nondum vos traxit; Ergo non potestis ad me venire. Hypocritae habent quae praetexant infidelitati suae & cordi pessimè affecto, externa multa: & nunc culpam conferunt in doctores, nunc in doctrinam ipsam: non enim ignoramus voces istorum hominum, Quis vos vocauit? Quae sunt miracula in Ecclesia vestra? & cætera huiusmodi. Sed sunt hi tantum praetextus quos obtendunt infidelitati suae, & cordis indurationi ac impotentiae illi quae penitus latet in animis: neque enim potest Papista venire ad veritatem, ideóque hypocritis istis ita occurrendum est, Non potes, Papista, recipere amorem veritatis, animus tuus plane alienatus est à veritate: neque enim si haec, quae petis darentur tibi omnia, posses tamen ad veritatem peruenire. Ita respondendum exemplo Christi centesimo, ut descendat tandem hypocrita ad altiora illa fundamenta ac principia in corde ipsius ita recondita, ut ipsummet hypocrita lateant. Nam quādo cū hypocrisis nobis res est, quia hypocrisis profunda admodū est, & altissimas radices agit in corde, ideo cor hypocritae semper pungendum est, euellendaque est, si fieri possit, radix illa amaritudinis. Notandum autem est quòd dicit Patre trahere nos ad filium: ex hoc enim sequitur nullam esse prorsus in nobis naturae potentiam, nullam arbitrii libertatem, nec eius quidem micam aliquam. Fateor quidem postea quam iam conuersi sumus ad Deum & regeniti, tum quidem nos nostra voluntate progredi aliquo modo ad Christum, etsi semper impedimenta & remorae iniiciantur nobis a reliquiis istis peccati, quae in carne nostra habitant. Verum in ipso primo conversionis & regenerationis nostrae puncto, nulla est plane in nobis propensio ad Christum & ad gratiam Dei quae in ipso est, imò verò propensio est in contrarium. Ideoque fit vt in illo principio conuersionis & regenerationis, praeuenente nos Dei gratia, habeamus nos vere vt loquuntur pathetice, & vis quodammodo afferatur naturae. re nostræ, trahamúrque ad Christum, non sine acerrima quadam luƈta & conflictu, hinc pugnante potentia peccati, quam Paulus vocat potestatem tenebrarum, illinc vero pugnante Dei illa potentia. Ex quarum rerum tam pugnantium congressu, oportet pugnam oriri acerrimam, cùm non possunt congredi duo aliqui antagonistæ robusti, nisi conflictus sit acerrimus. In hoc cõflictu magna solet esse animi abiectio, nonnunquàm incutiuntur horrores inferorum, quos cùm excipit lætitia aliqua, iam conuersio est facta & victoria acquisita: cernitur enim victoria ista etiam in bona aliqua inclinatione post luctam reliqua, qua quidè fit vt iam deiectum sit peccatum de regno suo.
units.tr: It is as if the Lord were saying: "You put forward my lineage, my parents, and my lowly origin as a pretext for your unbelief. But a far different cause lies underneath, one hidden deep within you: namely, a certain inability in yourselves, by which you cannot come to me. There is in you no inclination by which you lean towards me or towards God, but you are plainly turned away from God and alienated from me. The Father has not yet drawn you, that is, he has not yet changed that inclination of yours and given you the ability." And no one can come to me unless the Father draws him. The argument of the Lord runs thus: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. But the Father has not yet drawn you. Therefore you cannot come to me. Hypocrites have many outward things to put forward as pretexts for their unbelief and their very evil heart. Now they lay the blame on the teachers, now on the doctrine itself. We know well the words of such men: "Who called you? What miracles are there in your Church?" and others of this kind. But these are only pretexts which they put forward for their unbelief, and for the hardening of their heart and that inability which lies hidden deep in their souls. A Papist cannot come to the truth, and therefore the hypocrites must be met in this way: "You cannot, Papist, receive the love of the truth; your soul is wholly estranged from the truth. Even if all the things you ask for were given to you, you still could not come to the truth." So we must answer in the manner of Christ's example, so that the hypocrite may at last be brought down to those deeper foundations and principles which lie hidden in his heart, so deeply that the hypocrite himself does not see them. For when we have to do with hypocrisy, since hypocrisy is very deep and strikes its roots most deeply into the heart, the heart of the hypocrite must always be pricked, and that root of bitterness must be torn out, if it can be done. It must be noted that he says we are drawn to the Son by the Father. From this it follows that there is absolutely no power of nature in us, no freedom of the will, not even the smallest crumb of it. I admit indeed that after we have been turned to God and regenerated, we then in some measure advance by our own will toward Christ, although impediments and hindrances are always thrown in our way by those remnants of sin which dwell in our flesh. But at the very first point of our conversion and regeneration, there is plainly in us no inclination toward Christ or toward the grace of God which is in him; rather the inclination is toward the opposite. Therefore it comes about that at that beginning of conversion and regeneration, with God's grace going before us, we are, as they say in the language of feeling, and violence is in some measure done to our nature, and we are drawn to Christ not without a most bitter struggle and conflict: on one side the power of sin fights back, which Paul calls the power of darkness, and on the other side that power of God fights. From the clash of such opposing forces a most fierce battle must arise, since two strong antagonists cannot meet unless the conflict is most fierce. In this conflict there is usually great dejection of spirit, and sometimes the terrors of hell are brought on; when these are followed by some joy, the conversion is then accomplished and the victory won. For that victory is seen also in some good inclination remaining after the struggle, by which sin is now cast down from its kingdom.

units.la: Ego vero suscitabo. Coniungit cum proxima seueritate mansuetudinem & promissionem vitæ æternæ pulcherrimam, quòd nimirum qui tracti à Patre ad ipsum venerint, nunquam futurum sit vt querantur se frustra iter illud suscepisse: quod enim donorum omnium maximum est, accepturi sunt vitam æternam. Et quanquam futurum est, necessitate vt dissoluatur mortale hoc corpus (huic enim scrupulo videtur occurrere) tamen excitandum esse admonet idem hoc corpus ipsorum in vltimo die. Christus cùm videret omnes mortuos esse in peccatis & offensis, quàdo beneficium, quod mortuis dari potest, maximum omnium, sit vita; ideòque ferè vitam hanc promittit nobis in Euangelio, vtpote mortuis in peccatis & offensis. Nihil tamen his promissionibus vitæ mouentur homines hodierno die, quia nimirum non est sensus mortis, non est sensus huius miseriæ, in qua omnes natura demersi sumus. Quamobrem in excitando hoc sensu miseriæ, imprimis nobis laborandum est, vt tandem dulces ac suaues videantur nobis esse promissiones illæ vitæ æternæ. Notandum præterea est, quòd Christus, postquam demonstrauit miseris iam sentinam illam & colluuiem omnium sordium, in qua iacerent ipsi, admonuitque nondum eos inde extractos esse admota manu salutari & facta promissione omnium dulcissima, conatus est eos inde extrahere. Ita nobis ad exemplum ipsius faciendum est; post demonstratam iam hominum miseriam porrigeda est iis manus. nus & promissiones faciendæ, vt, si fieri possit, miseri ex miseria illa tandem emergant extrahanturque: Deo, qui solus potest hoc, sit gloria in Christo. Amen.
units.tr: But I will raise him up. He joins to the preceding severity both gentleness and the most beautiful promise of eternal life: namely, that those who have been drawn by the Father and have come to him will never have cause to complain that they undertook that journey in vain, for they shall receive eternal life, which is the greatest of all gifts. And although it is destined that this mortal body must be dissolved by necessity (for this seems to be the scruple he is answering), yet he reminds us that this same body must be raised up on the last day. Since Christ saw that all were dead in sins and offences, and since the benefit that can be given to the dead is the greatest of all, which is life, he therefore almost always promises us this life in the gospel, as to those dead in sins and offences. Yet people today are not moved by these promises of life, because there is no sense of death, no sense of this misery in which we have all sunk by nature. So in awakening this sense of misery, we must above all labour that the promises of eternal life may at last seem sweet and pleasant to us. It must further be noted that Christ, having shown the wretched people the sink and the cesspool of all filth in which they lay, and having warned them that they were not yet drawn out of it, since the saving hand had not been put forth, and having made the most delightful of all promises, tried to draw them out of it. So we too must follow his example: after the misery of men has been shown, hands must be stretched out to them and promises made, so that, if it can be done, the wretched may at last emerge and be drawn out of their misery. To God, who alone can do this, be glory in Christ. Amen.

units.la: Est scriptum in Prophetâ. Confirmat quod dixit proximè de tractione Patris, ex testimonio Prophetarū, præsertim Esaiæ cap.54.13. Tractionis igitur illius modum statuit in docendo & mouendo interius per Spiritum sanctum. Propheta eo in loco prædicit statum Ecclesiæ qui futurus est sub Christo & Euangelio, q.d. Non Modes, non Prophetæ tum docturi sunt Ecclesiam literaliter, vt ita dicam, sed ipse Deus docturus est eam spiritualiter. Hanc oppositionem hominum docentium, & Dei docentis habes Ierem.31.24. Non autem docebunt amplius quisque amicum suum & quisque fratrem suum, dicendo, Cognoscite Iehouam. Nam quotquot erunt, cognoscent eum à minimo eorum vsque ad maximum eorum, dictum Iehoua: me condonare iniquitatem ipsorum & peccati ipsorum non recordabor amplius. Neque vero hoc ita accipiendum est, quasi Deus neque docuerit tum olim veterem Ecclesiam, neque opus sit hominibus qui doceant in nova ista quæ nunc est sub Christo: sed hoc comparatè dictum intelligi debet, q.d. Vsque adeò excellet Ecclesia Christi hanc quæ nūc est Ecclesiā, cognitione & spiritu ac donis Spiritus, vt Ecclesia Christi omnium iudicio habitura sit Deum solum doctorem, cūm hæc Ecclesia habeat non tam Deum quàm homines doctores. Quòd autem hoc intelligendum sit de copia cognitionis & Spiritus, appareţ ex Esaiæ 11.9. Plena erit terra hæc scientia Iehouæ, velut aquis alueum maris operientibus. q.d. Erit in Ecclesia immensum mare cognitionis Dei: vt etiam prophetarut Esaiæ 54.13 Paulus vidit ætate sua Prophetiæ huius & promissionis complementum, Quòd in omnibus ditati sitis in ipso, omni loquendi facultate, omnique cognitione, adeò vt nullo dono deficiamini. Item, Nobis, inquit, Deus ea reuelauit per Spiritum suum. Spiritus enim omnia scrutatur, etiam profunditates Dei. Item, Dum palam fit, inquit, vos esse epistolam Christi subministratam à nobis, inscriptam non atramento, sed spiritu Dei viui. Et Iohannes, V nctionem habetis à sancto illo, & omnia, &c. Sed an nos vidimus huius promissionis complementum, sumus eaim & nos Ecclesia Christi iā quidem audeo dicere, clariorem Euangelij Christi doctrinam nulli vnquam populo ante propositam esse, quàm sit ea quam nos quotidie audimus in Ecclesiis nostris, item nunquam ante hac maiorem copiam Spiritus oblatam esse quàm nunc offertur: ideóque Deum fecisse suas partes. Ausim quoque id affirmare,nō fuisse in veteri illo populo tantam notitiam Christi, quanta nunc est in nostris Ecclesiis, adeò vt illud Petri in nobis verum nunc esse comperiatur, Prophetas illos veteres non sibi administrasse sed nobis qui hodierno die audimus Euangelium Christi & complementum habemus eorum quæ tum olim prædicta sunt. Sed vbi zelus, vbi amor Dei & hominum, vbi fides in Christum, vbi lætitia illa quæ percipi debet ex tanta luce, vbi opera lucis in tanta præsertim luce? Quid sibi volunt opera ista tenebrarum, quid homicidia, quid adulteria, quid sacrilegia, quid rapinæ, quid infidelitas, quid tantum istud verbi Diuini fastidium? Quòd si profectò non haberemus aliquid aliud boni sub cœlo excepta hac tam clara verbi luce, ea deberet nos vel sola consolari. Quis est qui non gaudet & recreatur cùm ex tenebris educi-vt in lucem istam solarem? At nos qui aliquando submersi in tenebris longè horribilissimis, multò clariorem lucem habemus, scilicet nimirum illum iustitiæ. Hæc nimirum satis arguunt plerosque nostrum non esse doctos à Deo: doctrina enim Dei docentis est doctrina qua interius infotmatur & illuminatur animus noster per Spiritum ipsius sanctum, vt paulò post videbimus.
units.tr: It is written in the Prophet. He confirms what he said just before about the drawing of the Father, from the testimony of the prophets, especially Isaiah 54:13. He thus states the manner of that drawing: it is by teaching and moving inwardly through the Holy Spirit. In that place the prophet foretells the state of the Church that is to come under Christ and the Gospel, as if to say: the prophets will not then teach the Church outwardly, so to speak, but God himself will teach it spiritually. You have this contrast between teaching men and God teaching in Jeremiah 31:34: And they shall no more teach every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying, Know the LORD: for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them, saith the LORD: for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more. Yet this must not be taken to mean that God did not teach the old Church in former times, or that there is no need for men to teach in the new dispensation that now exists under Christ. The statement is comparative, and should be understood as saying: the Church of Christ, as it now is, will so far excel itself in knowledge, spirit and the gifts of the Spirit, that by general consent the Church of Christ will have God alone as its teacher, although this Church has not so much God as men as its teachers. That this must be understood of the abundance of knowledge and of the Spirit appears from Isaiah 11:9: The earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea. As if to say: there will be in the Church an immense sea of the knowledge of God. So also Paul saw in his own time the fulfilment of this prophecy and promise of Isaiah 54:13: That in every thing ye are enriched by him, in all utterance, and in all knowledge, so that ye come behind in no gift. Likewise: But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit: for the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God. Likewise: Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God. And John: Ye have an unction from the Holy One, and ye know all things, etc. But have we seen the fulfilment of this promise? For we too are the Church of Christ. I dare indeed to say that the clearer doctrine of the Gospel of Christ has never been set before any people before than that which we hear every day in our churches; and likewise a greater measure of the Spirit has never before been offered than is now offered; and therefore God has done his part. I would also venture to affirm that there was not in that old people so great a knowledge of Christ as there is now in our churches, so that what Peter said is found to be true of us now: those ancient prophets did not minister to themselves but to us, who today hear the Gospel of Christ and have the fulfilment of those things that were foretold in former times. But where is zeal, where is the love of God and of men, where is faith in Christ, where is that joy which ought to be received from so great a light, where are the works of light, especially in so great a light? What do those works of darkness mean: murders, adulteries, sacrileges, robberies, unbelief, and such great contempt for this word of God? If indeed we had no other good under heaven, apart from this so clear light of the word, that alone ought to console us. Who does not rejoice and take delight when he is led out of darkness into that solar light? Yet we, who were once sunk in darkness most horrible, now have a much clearer light, namely that of righteousness. These things surely show well enough that most of us are not taught by God: for the doctrine of God teaching is a doctrine by which the mind is inwardly formed and illuminated through his Holy Spirit, as we shall see a little later.

units.la: Quisquis audiuit. Videri potuit alicui doctrinam Dei positā in nuda tantum cognitione: ideo huic occurrit Christus, docetque quòd quisquis doctus sit à Deo, oportet eum venire ad Christum, hoc est, credere corde in Christum Iesum. Vide igitur quòd cùm Deus docet quemquam, non tantùm renouet vnam aliquam animi facultatem, vt mentem solam, sed simul omnes aliqua certè ex parte reformet, descendatque penitus in cor ipsum, ibíque ignat dilectionem Dei & proximi, fidem, lætitiam, aliáque huiusmodi. Paulus, Si quis, inquit, diligit Deum, hic edoctus fuit ab eo: Ecce, definit eum, qui à Deo
units.tr: Whosoever has heard. It might seem to someone that the teaching of God consists only in bare knowledge. Therefore Christ meets this objection and teaches that whoever is taught by God must come to Christ, that is, believe in Christ Jesus with the heart. See, then, that when God teaches anyone, he does not merely renew one faculty of the soul, such as the mind alone, but reforms all of them in some measure at once, and descends deep into the heart itself, and there kindles love of God and neighbour, faith, joy, and other such things. Paul: If anyone, he says, loves God, he has been taught by him. Behold, he defines the one who is truly taught by God

units.la: Seculi nostri benedictio.
units.tr: The blessing of our age.

units.la: Seculi nostri maledictio.
units.tr: The curse of our age.

units.la: Quid doceat suos discipulos Deus.
units.tr: What God teaches his disciples.

units.la: 1. Tes. 1. 12. vere edoctus est, ex dilectione quæ in corde est, non autem ex nuda mentis notitia, de qua sic locutus est proximè ibidem. Quòd si quis, inquit, sibi videtur aliquid scire, nondum quicquid nouit, sicut oportet nosse. Quòd si igitur inter prædicandum euangelium scire velis, an Deus te doceat necne: vide an sententias cordis mutationem aliquam in te fieri, fidem in Christum ingenerari, & cor tuum ad Deum sursum trahi. quòd si hoc penitus in te senseris, iam habes argumentum quòd à Deo docearis, habeásque doctorem præstantiorem quàm sunt omnes vel homines, vel Angeli.Quòd si Deus te docet ad ministerium & prædicationem istam infirmorum hominum, non tam attendendum est ad eos, quàm ad internum illum doctorem Deum. Et sic quidem se res habet. Hoc ipso tempore efficacius docet suos Dominus etiam per infirmos homines, quàm olim per ministerium ipsorum Angelorum. Secundum ex hoc sequitur, quòd si qui à Deo docti sunt, veniant ad filium, necessariò sequitur Deum Patrem nihil docere eos, quàm Filium & Euangelium de Filio. Non aliud profecto per Spiritum suum docet nos Pater, quàm hoc ipsum quod in scripto habemus de Christo Euangelium; quantumlibet gariant Papistæ de non scriptis suis traditionibus. Euangelium autem hoc quid aliud habet, quàm Christum crucifixum & glorificatum, beneficiáque ex eius cruce & gloria profluentia? Quare Deus per Spiritum Sanctum non aliud docet nos quàm Filium, qui est splendor gloriæ paternæ. Neque enim est doctrinæ aliud fundamentum quàm Christus. Fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere præter id quod positum est, Iesus Christus. Iohannes suppeditat firmum argumentum & signum quo iudicemus de Spiritu Dei, an sit in quoquam. Ex hoc, inquit, cognoscite Dei Spiritum, Quicunque Spiritus confitetur Iesum Christum in carnem venisse (hoc est, omnia confitetur quæ vel ad personam, vel officium Christi pertinet) is ex Deo est. Quòd si hæc confessio veritatis, quæ est de Christo, signum sit indubitatum Spiritus Dei, profecto sequitur Spiritum illum non docere aliud quàm Christum. Ex quo sequitur quòd cum Spiritus ille qui est in regno Papistarum non confiteatur Christum, præsertim quoad officium ipsius
units.tr: 1 Thess. 1:12. truly taught, from the love that is in the heart, and not from bare knowledge of the mind, of which he spoke just before in the same place: But if anyone thinks that he knows anything, he does not yet know as he ought to know. If therefore, while preaching the Gospel, you wish to know whether God teaches you or not, see whether some change of mind has taken place in you, whether faith in Christ has been engendered, and whether your heart is drawn upwards to God. If you have felt this deeply in yourself, you already have proof that you are taught by God, and you have a teacher more excellent than all men or angels. If God teaches you for this ministry and preaching of weak men, attention must be paid not so much to them as to that inward teacher, God. And so indeed the matter stands. At this very time the Lord teaches his people more effectively through weak men than once through the ministry of the angels themselves. Second, it follows from this that if some have been taught by God and come to the Son, it necessarily follows that God the Father teaches them nothing but the Son and the Gospel concerning the Son. Certainly the Father teaches us through his Spirit nothing other than what we have in writing, the Gospel concerning Christ, however much the Papists may boast of their unwritten traditions. But what else does this Gospel contain than Christ crucified and glorified, and the benefits flowing from his cross and glory? Therefore God, through the Holy Spirit, teaches us nothing other than the Son, who is the brightness of the Father's glory. For there is no other foundation of doctrine than Christ. No one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, Jesus Christ. John supplies a firm argument and sign by which we may judge whether the Spirit of God is in anyone. By this, he says, know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh (that is, confesses all that pertains either to the person or to the office of Christ) is of God. If this confession of the truth concerning Christ is an indubitable sign of the Spirit of God, then surely it follows that that Spirit does not teach anything other than Christ. From this it follows that, since the spirit which is in the kingdom of the Papists does not confess Christ, especially as to his office

units.la: Quid discipulos scire vel potius sentire oportet.
units.tr: What disciples ought to know, or rather to feel.

units.la: Summa doctrinæ quam Deus suis proponit.
units.tr: The sum of the doctrine which God sets before his people.

units.la: Spiritus Christi. ipsius & iustificationem quæ est per solum ipsius sanguinem, sequitur eum non esse Christi, sed Antichristi Spiritum.
units.tr: The Spirit of Christ. his own and justification, which is through his blood alone, it follows that he is not of Christ but the spirit of Antichrist.

units.la: Non quòd Patrem. Obiici potuit occasione verborum proximè præcedentium, quòd si quis audierit & didicerit ex Deo, an non propterea oportet eum vidisse Deum doctorem illum suum? Respondet, ac si dicat, Non dico hoc, quòd sentiam quemquam vidisse Patrem, eo solo Deo docente, excepto qui est à Deo, hoc est, excepto Filio. Periphrasis enim est Filij. Tum eandem sententiam rursus exprimit. Hic, inquit, vidit Patrem, hoc est, hic solus qui est à Deo vidit Patrem. Idem enim hoc est cum eo quod dixit prius. Hic primùm ut intelligatur hæc propositio, videndum est quid sit à Deo esse: à Deo vel ex Deo dicitur quis esse, primùm propter creationem. Rom. 11.33. Ex eo sunt omnia. Ex eo deinde est aliquis propter regenerationem. Iohan. 8.47. Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit, hoc est, qui regeneratur per Spiritum eius Sanctum. Tertiò dicitur Filius Dei à Deo vel ex Deo esse, quia ab eo genitus est ab æterno, quomodo hic sumitur à Deo esse. Estque hæc descriptio quædam & periphrasis Filij ex proprietate sua. Estque hic à Deo esse, idem cum eo quod dixit supra cap. 1.18. in sinu Patris esse. Nemo novit Patrem nisi unigenitus qui est in sinu eius, ille nobis exposuit. Nunc deinde veritate propositionis huius videamus; de qua quæri potest, Annon de Angelis dicitur quòd in cælis per omne tempus videant faciem Patris, qui in cælis est? De certis quibusdam hominibus scriptum legimus quòd viderint Deum, ut de Abrahamo, Mose & aliis. Respondeo, duobus modis dici potest quis Deum videre: dicitur enim quis Deum videre, vel per se, vel per aliud. Filius solus videt Deum per se; Angeli & homines per Filium. Nemo novit Patrem nisi Filius, & cuicunque voluerit filius revelare. Ideòque dictus est imago Dei inconspicui. Sed qualisnam imago? Imaginum enim plura sunt genera: imago, quæ repræsentat tantùm qualitates & externa quædam rei alicuius lineamenta, ut homo repræsentatur picta aliqua tabula. Est imago deinde, quæ repræsentat etiam substantiam, cùm sit eiusdem speciei, ut Filius repræsentat Patrem. atque hæc est imaginis species qua in terris non reperitur cum re quam repræsentat coniunctior: sed Filius Dei repræsentat substantiā Dei Patris sui vt substantia,nō eadem specie,sed eadem planè numero:nam eadem & tota Dei Patris substantia communicata est Filio: ideóque dicitur, Splendor gloriæ eius, hoc est deitatis, & omnium essentialium proprietatum, vt misericordiæ, iustitiæ,potentiæ,sapientiæ,&c.quæ nō cōspiciuntur aut videntur à quoquam extra Christum. Nam splendor licet distinctus sit aliquo modo à luce, tamen non differt ab ea substantia.Sed repræsentat præterea Filius personam Patris, quæ non est communicabilis. Repræsentatur tamē in Filio persona Patris,in quo est ipsius expressa quædam imago. Ideóque dicitur Character persona illius. Cùm igitur habeamus tam expressam Patris imaginem tanquam coniunctam cum Patre, non est quòd queramur ideo, quòd non videamus Patrem per se, sed per aliud duntaxat, nempe per Filium; cùm Filius sit imago coæqualis,coessentialis, coæterna Patri.
units.tr: Not that the Father. An objection could be raised from the words immediately preceding: if someone has heard and learned from God, must he not have seen that teacher, God? He answers as if saying: I do not mean that anyone has seen the Father, with God alone teaching, except him who is from God, that is, except the Son. For this is a periphrasis of the Son. Then he expresses the same sentiment again: He, he says, has seen the Father, that is, he alone who is from God has seen the Father. For this is the same as what he said before. First, to understand this proposition, we must consider what it is to be from God. Someone is said to be from or of God first on account of creation: Rom. 11.33, All things are of him. Then someone is of God on account of regeneration: John 8.47, He who is of God hears the words of God, that is, he who is regenerated by his Holy Spirit. Thirdly, the Son of God is said to be from or of God because he was begotten by him from eternity, in the sense in which he is here said to be from God. This is a certain description and periphrasis of the Son drawn from his own property. To be from God here is the same as what he said above, chap. 1.18, to be in the bosom of the Father: No one has known the Father except the only-begotten, who is in his bosom; he has declared him to us. Now let us consider the truth of this proposition. It may be asked: is it not said of the angels that in heaven they continually see the face of the Father who is in heaven? We read that certain men have also seen God, as Abraham, Moses and others. I answer that someone can be said to see God in two ways: for someone is said to see God either through himself or through another. The Son alone sees God through himself; angels and men see him through the Son. No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son is willing to reveal him. Therefore he is called the image of the invisible God. But what sort of image? There are many kinds of images. There is an image that represents only the qualities and certain external outlines of a thing, as a man is represented by some painted picture. Then there is an image that also represents the substance, when it is of the same kind, as the Son represents the Father. This is the kind of image that is not found on earth more closely joined to the thing it represents. The Son of God represents the substance of God his Father as substance: not of the same kind, but plainly of the same number. For the whole and same substance of God the Father has been communicated to the Son. Therefore he is called the brightness of his glory, that is, of the deity and of all essential properties, such as mercy, justice, power, wisdom, and so on, which are not seen or perceived by anyone outside Christ. For although the brightness is in some way distinct from the light, nevertheless it does not differ from that substance. Moreover, the Son also represents the person of the Father, which is not communicable. Yet the person of the Father is represented in the Son, in whom there is a certain expressed image of him. Therefore he is called the express character of his person. Since, then, we have so express an image of the Father as joined to the Father, there is no reason to complain that we do not see the Father himself, but only through another, namely through the Son, since the Son is an image co-equal, co-essential, co-eternal with the Father.

units.la: Porrò de modo quo Filius videt Patrem,non est quòd nos curiosius inquiramus in eum; singulari quodam ac suo modo eum videt, quo nimirum nulla creatura eum videre potest. Est enim λόγος Patris quasi conceptus & verbum mentis Patris. Iam verò conceptus & verbum mentis nostræ videt mentem, quomodò nihil extra metem eam videre potest aut intelligere. De eo quod videt Filius in Patre suo, hoc est,de obiecto visus ipsius vt dicamus, videt incomprehensibilem illam & totam Patris essentiam. Cùm solus Filius per se videat Patrem, necesse est differat à creaturis etiam modo videndi, & obiecto visus. Quæri potest hic quónam modo per Filium cognoscamus Patrem, cùm dictus ipse Pater docere nos per Filium suum? Respondeo,Spiritus est Patris & à Patre primùm procedens,qui gignit in nobis notitiam Filij; ideóque per Patrem dicimur cognoscere Filium. Est quoque Spiritus ille Filij & à Filio procedens, sed primùm procedit à Patre tanquam fonte deitatis: deinde Filius manifestat Patrem vt est λόγος ,& vt est vina Patris sui imago. Vt vt est, hæc mutua revelatio Patris & Filij,qua se nobis mutuò patefaciunt,arguit coniunctionem ipsorum arctissimam, adeoque essentiam unam eandemque numero. Patri igitur cum Filio & Spiritu Sancto sit omnis honor & gloria, Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, concerning the manner in which the Son sees the Father, we need not inquire too curiously into it. He sees him in a singular way that is his own, in which no creature can see him. For he is the Word [λόγος] of the Father, as it were the concept and word of the Father's mind. Now the concept and word of our mind sees the mind, just as nothing outside the mind can see or understand it. As to what the Son sees in his Father, that is, to speak of the object of his sight, he sees that incomprehensible and whole essence of the Father. Since the Son alone sees the Father through himself, he must differ from creatures both in the manner of seeing and in the object of sight. Here it may be asked how we know the Father through the Son, since the Father himself is said to teach us through his Son? I answer: the Spirit is of the Father and proceeds first from the Father, and he begets in us the knowledge of the Son; therefore we are said to know the Son through the Father. That Spirit is also the Son's and proceeds from the Son, but he proceeds first from the Father as the fountain of deity. Then the Son makes the Father known, as he is the Word, and as he is the living image of his Father. However it is, this mutual revelation of the Father and the Son, by which they mutually disclose themselves to us, shows their most close conjunction, and therefore one and the same essence in number. To the Father, therefore, together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, be all honour and glory. Amen.

units.la: 47 Amen, amen dico vobis, qui credit in me, habet vitam aeternam.
units.tr: 47 Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me hath everlasting life.

units.la: 48 Ego sum panis ille vita.
units.tr: 48 I am that bread of life.

units.la: 49 Patres vestri comederunt Manna in deserto, & mortui sunt.
units.tr: 49 Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead.

units.la: 50 Hic est panis ille, qui e caelo descendit, ut qui eo vescitur non moriatur.
units.tr: 50 This is the bread which cometh down from heaven, that a man may eat thereof, and not die.

units.la: 51 Ego sum panis ille vivificus qui e caelo descendit. Si quis ederit ex hoc pane, vivet in aeternum: panis autem quem ego dabo, caro mea est, quam ego dabo pro mundi vita.
units.tr: 51 I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.

units.la: IAm inde a versu 45. ad hunc usque locum digressus est ab instituto; nunc redit ad illam promissionem vitae aeternae & resurrectionis quae fuit versu 44. Ego suscitabo eum in ultimo die: super structuque eam super fundamenta quae in digressione fuerunt: nempe super id quod dixit, Quisquis audivit a Patre & didicit, venit ad me. Quo innuebat, ut dixi, totam Patris doctrinam esse de Filio suo. Deinde super eo quod dixit, Non quod Patrem vidit quisquam nisi is qui est a Deo. His positis, sequitur conclusio de resurrectione & vita aeterna. Cum Filius sit talis tarusque & eo loco apud Patrem, sequitur quod quicunque crediderit in eum, habiturus sit vitam aeternam. Causa cur non credamus in promissiones a Christo & in Christo factas, est quod non videamus admirabilem illam gratiam quae est in ipso, non videamus quanti faciat eum Pater, quam Patri illi gloriae coniunctus sit. Quod si id videremus, tum quidem nihil esset tam incredibile per naturam, quod tamen non crederemus, si semel esset promissum in ipso & propter ipsum. Causa diffidentiae & incredulitatis nostrae non est in Christo, in quo sunt ea fundamenta tam certa ac firma implendae promissionis, sed est in nobis qui illa ipsa fundamenta non perspicimus. Quare nobis enitendum est perpetuò vt Christum magis magisque videamus & cognoscamus, Vt cognoscamus eum, inquit Apostolus, & vim resurrectionis ipsius, & communionem perpessionum ipsius. Quo loco Paulus summè enixus est ipse ad hoc vt ipsum vi-deret & cognosceret. Alibi suum exemplum commen-dat aliis. Colossenses seducti erant à Christo ad cōtem-plandum inania nescio quæ: philosophiam, inanem de-ceptionem, traditiones hominum, elementa mundi. Quamobrem Paulus in eo laborat, vt demonstret iis o-mnem plenitudinem in eo habitare. Omnes thesauros cognitio-nis & sapientiæ in eo absconditos. Imò omnem plenitudinem Deitatis inhabitâtis in eo corporaliter. Sed verba textus sunt consideranda. Quo magis persuadeat iis veritatem pro-missionis suæ, adhibet iurisiurandi speciem sibi familiarem; Amen, Amen: præterea in promittendo vi-tam, vtitur verbo præsentis temporis, habet vitam æter-nam. q. d. Non tam habiturus est imposterum, quàm etiam nunc habet. Nam re vera non priùs credimus in Christum quàm inchoetur in nobis illa vita æterna. Quid sibi vult pax ista, quæ superat omnem intelle-ctum, quam seniuunt credentes in se quo primùm tempore credere incipiunt? Iustificati ex fide pacem habe-mus erga Deum. Quid sibi vult gaudium quod percipiunt animis dum credunt? Credentes ei, inquit Petrus, exultatisgaudio inessabili & glorioso. Quid aliud sunt ista, quàm vitailla in nobis inchoata? Nam regnum Dei, ait Paulus, cernitur in iustitia, pace & gaudio per Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: From verse 45 onward he has departed from his subject; now he returns to that promise of eternal life and resurrection which was in verse 44: I will raise him up at the last day. He builds this upon the foundations laid in the digression: namely upon what he said, Whoever has heard from the Father and learned comes to me. By this, as I have said, he indicated that the whole teaching of the Father is concerning his Son. Then upon what he said, that no one has seen the Father except him who is from God. Having laid these down, the conclusion about the resurrection and eternal life follows. Since the Son is such, and has that place with the Father, it follows that whoever believes in him shall have eternal life. The reason we do not believe the promises made by Christ and in Christ is that we do not see the admirable grace which is in him, we do not see how highly the Father esteems him, and how closely he is joined to that glory of the Father. If we saw this, then nothing would be so incredible by nature that we would not believe it, once it had been promised in him and for his sake. The cause of our distrust and unbelief is not in Christ, in whom there are such certain and firm foundations for fulfilling the promise, but in us, who do not perceive those very foundations. Therefore we must always strive to see and know Christ more and more, that we may know him, says the Apostle, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings. In this place Paul himself strove most earnestly to see and know him. Elsewhere he commends his own example to others. The Colossians had been led away from Christ to contemplate I know not what empty things: philosophy, vain deceit, the traditions of men, the elements of the world. Therefore Paul labours to show them that all fullness dwells in him: all the treasures of knowledge and wisdom are hidden in him. Indeed, the whole fullness of the Deity dwells in him bodily. But the words of the text must be considered. To persuade them the more of the truth of his promise, he uses a form of oath familiar to him: Amen, amen. Moreover, in promising life he uses the verb in the present tense: he has eternal life; as if to say, he will not merely have it hereafter, but even now has it. For in truth we do not believe in Christ before that eternal life begins in us. What is that peace which surpasses all understanding, which believers feel the moment they first begin to believe? Being justified by faith, we have peace with God. What is that joy which they perceive in their souls while they believe? Believing in him, says Peter, you rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. What else are these things than that life begun in us? For the kingdom of God, says Paul, is seen in righteousness, peace and joy through the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Substernit præter illa iam dicta etiam aliud fundamentum promissioni huic suæ de vita æterna. Est autem illud potentia, virtus & efficacia, quæ inipso est ad vitam æternā. Ego sum panis. Hanc virtutem & efficaciam adumbrat typo panis, vtpote de quo isti tantùm cogitabant (nam id iam antea petebant vt pane in deserto imperpetuum alerentur à Christo, quemadmodum populus iam olim à Mose nutritus est cœlesti illo manna) & quidelementum est aptum ad figurandum ac repræsentandum Christum. Scimus pani inditam esse à Deo vim eam & potentiam ad alendam istam vitam, quæ non est communicata aliis rebus creatis, vt lapidibus, vt lignis, &c. Ita in Christo inst virtus ac potentia ad vitam æternam.
units.tr: He adds, besides those things already said, another foundation for this promise of his concerning eternal life. This foundation is the power, virtue and efficacy that lies in him for eternal life. I am the bread. He pictures this virtue and efficacy under the type of bread, since it is of bread that they were thinking (for they were already asking that they might be nourished by Christ with bread in the desert forever, just as the people had once been fed by Moses with that heavenly manna). Bread is also an element fit for signifying and representing Christ. We know that God has put into bread a power and strength for sustaining this life, a power not given to other created things, such as stones, wood, and so on. So in Christ there is virtue and power for eternal life.

units.la: Similitudinis huius collatio. æternam non alendam modò in viuis, sed dandam iis qui planè mortui sunt, quæ quidem vis non inest in pane isto terrestri: neque enim iam mortuo vitam impertiri potest. Rursus in Christo potentia est ad alendam vitam, non ad tempus tantùm, sed in æternum; cùm panis hic terrestris tantùm alat vitam præsentem ad tempus. Sed quo demum nomine appellabis hanc virtutem & potentiam quæ in Christo est ad vitam? Supra cap.5. postquam dixit eos qui audierint filium Dei victuros verf. 25. statim subiecit huius vitæ causam quæ est in Christo. Sicut pater, inquit, habet vitam in seipso, sic dedit & filio vitam habere in semetipso, verf.26. Ergo potentia ista & virtus tam efficax ad vitam in Christo, vita est appellanda & fons vitæ omnis. Non mirum est igitur Christum, qui vitam habet in seipso, esse panem vitæ æternæ. Quòd si panis hic terrestris & corporeus qui mortuus est, neque vitam in se habet (neque enim hæc in eo vis quæ est ad alendum nos, vita est dicenda) si, inquam, hac in se vim habeat tamen, vt ad tempus sustentet istam vitam: quanto magis Christus qui est vita ipsa & omnis vitæ fons, vim habebit ad dandam & in æternum sustinendam vitam nostram spiritualem? Neque verò hoc impedit quicquam vivificationem istam nostri, quòd Christus ipse mortuus sit. Mors enim Christi, vt audiemus posteà, tantum abest ab eo vt impediat viuificationem nostri, vt è contra sit causa cur Christus sit viuificus: hoc est, cur Christus iam glorificatus post mortem suam efficax in nobis sit ad vitam æternam: nisi enim mortuus fuisset, nos mansissemus in perpetuum in peccato & morte. Non autem sublata priùs morte potest esse vitæ locus aliquis.
units.tr: Comparison of this likeness. Christ's bread feeds eternal life not only in the living but gives it to those who are altogether dead, a power that is not in this earthly bread, for it cannot restore life to one who is already dead. Again, in Christ there is power to nourish life not just for a time but forever, whereas this earthly bread sustains the present life only for a time. But by what name will you call this virtue and power that is in Christ for life? Above, in chapter 5, after saying that those who hear the Son of God shall live (v. 25), he immediately added the source of this life, which is in Christ: As the Father, he says, has life in himself, so he has given to the Son also to have life in himself (v. 26). Therefore this power and virtue, so effective for life in Christ, must be called life, and the fount of all life. It is no wonder, then, that Christ, who has life in himself, is the bread of eternal life. But if this earthly and bodily bread, which is dead, has no life in itself (for the power in it that nourishes us should not be called life), yet if, I say, it has in itself a power to sustain this life for a time, how much more will Christ, who is life itself and the fount of all life, have power to give and to keep our spiritual life forever? Nor does it hinder this quickening of ours that Christ himself died. For the death of Christ, as we shall hear afterwards, is so far from hindering our quickening that on the contrary it is the cause why Christ is life-giving, that is, why Christ, now glorified after his death, is effective in us for eternal life. For unless he had died, we would have remained forever in sin and death. Nor can there be any place for life unless death has first been taken away.

units.la: Patres vestri. Commendat eis panem hunc vitæ facta comparatione cum Manna illo quod ipsi tanti fecerunt. Maiores vestri comederunt quidem Manna, quem cibum vos tanti facitis, & tamen mortui sunt omnes, & ex iis etiam non pauci mortui sunt spiritualiter. Hic vero panem (enim digito suo videtur demonstrare) qui de cælo descendit, ea natura est, vt qui ex eo sem el ederit non moriturus sit in æternum. Qui velit videre vim illam ac virtutem quæ est in Christo Iesu, circumferat oculos,consideretque omnia quaecunque in hac vita putat esse pretiosissima: ita enim fiet ut ex eorum vanitate Christi excellentiam & potentiam addiscat. Sed ea est caecitas nostra, ut neque vanitatem & impotentiam rerum istarum terrestrium,neque potentiam illam ac stabilitatem Christi videre possimus. Sed si penitius intuitus fueris Christi verba, habebis rationem tibi suppeditatam qua cognoscas utrumque. Patres, inquit,vestri comederunt Manna in deserto, & mortui sunt. Quibus verbis amandat illos ad pristinam illam experientiam vanitatis Mannae quod comederunt maiores in deserto. Disce igitur ex ipsa experientia non praeterita modo sed praesentia, quam vanae sunt & instabiles res hae terrestres omnes. Sed caecutimus mirifice ad omnem experientiam, verum tamen haec tamen est facillima qua poteris ad eam cognitionem pervenire. Habes etiam rationem in verbis Christi, qua cognosces Christi virtutem illam & excellentiam. Si quis, inquit, ederit ex hoc pane, vivet in aeternum. hoc est, Si quis crediderit. Ratio igitur est qua cognosces potentiam & efficaciam Christi, si crederis in eum. Crede in ea vita red dimur participes. quam potens sit Dominus. Paulo, prius quam credidisset in Christum, videbantur ei praerogatiuae illae circumcisionis, Israelis, Hebraei, tribus Benjamin, Pharisaei &c. aliquid esse, imo magni illa faciebat: Ubi vero primum coepit cognoscere Christum, tum omnia illa, quae antea visa sunt lucra, putavit totidem damna, imo stercora, prae eminentia illa cognitionis Christi Iesu. Proba igitur Christum, tum ego fallor, si non videbuntur tibi omnia ea quae tati facis in hac vita, vana esse, nihil esse, & si non in eorum omnium vanitate apparebit illa Christi potentia & excellentia.
units.tr: Your fathers. He commends to them this bread of life by a comparison with that manna which they valued so highly. Your fathers indeed ate the manna, which you value so highly as food, and yet they all died, and not a few of them also died spiritually. But this bread (for he seems to point to it with his finger) which comes down from heaven is of such a nature that whoever eats of it once will not die forever. Anyone who wishes to see that power and virtue which is in Jesus Christ, let him look around and consider all those things which he thinks most precious in this life; for in that way he will learn from their vanity the excellence and power of Christ. But such is our blindness that we can see neither the vanity and powerlessness of these earthly things nor that power and steadfastness of Christ. But if you look more deeply into the words of Christ, you will have a reason supplied to you by which you may know both. Your fathers, he says, ate manna in the desert, and died. By these words he sends them back to that former experience of the vanity of the manna which their fathers ate in the desert. Learn, then, from that experience, not only past but present, how empty and unstable all these earthly things are. But we are wonderfully blind to all experience; yet this is the easiest experience by which you can come to that knowledge. You also have, in the words of Christ, a reason by which you will know that virtue and excellence of Christ. If anyone, he says, eats of this bread, he will live forever. That is, if anyone believes. So the reason by which you will know the power and efficacy of Christ is this: if you believe in him. Believe in him, and we are made partakers of that life. Consider how powerful the Lord is. Before Paul believed in Christ, those privileges of circumcision, of Israel, of the Hebrews, of the tribe of Benjamin, of the Pharisees and so on, seemed to him to be something, indeed he valued them highly. But when he first began to know Christ, then he thought all those things which before had seemed gains to be so many losses, indeed dung, in comparison with the surpassing excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus. Therefore, test Christ; then I am much mistaken if all those things which you so value in this life do not appear to you vain and nothing, and if in the vanity of all of them that power and excellence of Christ does not appear.

units.la: Ego sum panis vivificus. Repetitio est, qua iterum demonstrat panem illum vitae. Iterum dicit eum e coelo descendisse, iterum dicit eo vescendum esse ad vitam aeternam. Repetitio haec non est inanis, & ne vocula quidem hic frustra iteratur. Nam quod iterum inculcat illum panem, in causa est quod omnes quidem volunt vivere, sed ubi quaerenda sit vita, omnes fere ignorant.
units.tr: I am the living bread. This is a repetition, by which he again sets forth that bread of life. He says again that it came down from heaven, and again that it must be eaten for eternal life. This repetition is not idle, and not even the little word here is repeated in vain. For the reason he again presses home that bread is that all indeed wish to live, but where life is to be sought, almost all are ignorant.

units.la: Signu non vivificat, sed res significata, nempe Christus.
units.tr: The sign does not give life, but the thing signified, namely Christ.

units.la: Quomodo ea vita red dimur participes.
units.tr: How we are made partakers of that life.

units.la: Phil. 3. 4. etc.
units.tr: Phil. 3. 4. etc.

units.la: Repetitio gratissima, & plane necessaria. rant, Multi extra Christum eam quærunt, alij in Christo partim, partim in aliis rebus. Quare illud non satis vnquam inculcari potest, Christum esse solum illum vitæ æternæ panem. Repetitio autem illa descensus illius panis è cœlis, de duabus rebus nos admonet; primùm de Christo, quòd non sit homo tantùm, sed etiam Dei filius in cœlis genitus à Patre ab æterno. Deinde de vita nostra nos admonet quòd in cœlis sit, cùm cœlitus ad nos descendat. Fateor quidem vitam nostram in Christo de cœlis descendisse, ideo quòd nos ad eam in cœ-lum ascendere non potuerimus, verùm in terras duntaxat inchoata est vita nostra, per Christum descendentem ad nos, quo facto Christus rursus se in cœlos recepit, vt nos quæramus in cœlis vitæ nostræ complementum. Vnde Apostolus, Superna, inquit, quærite, vbi Christus est ad dextram Dei sedens. Quòd denique comestionem istam inculcet, vide quoque quàm necessarium hoc fuerit: Postquam enim iam cognouerunt homines solum Christum esse vitam nostram, qua ratione ad eum pertineant, nō statim assequuntur. Neque enim tam leue est solum credere, ideoque illud repetendum, credendum esse, credendum esse. Præterea non tantùm repetitur fides, sed etiam inculcatur qualis esse debeat illa apprehensio Christi, illa coniunctio cum Christo; non oportet quidem eam leuem aliquam esse vel apprehensionem vel coniunctionem; verùm oportet comestionem quandam esse. Scimus in comestione cibum non leuiter attingere substantiam corporis nostri, sed penitus, vt sic dicam, incorporari in nobis, vnámque fieri nobiscum substantiam. Ita quoque oportet in coniunctione cum Christo incorporationem & insitionem in Christo fieri, nósque euadere in eius substantiam, fieri os ex ossibus eius, carnem ex carne eius. Præterea non vescendum est cibo se-duntaxat in hac vita, sed iteratò certis & præstitutis temporibus, tantisperdum sumus in hac vita, alioqui vita præsens pereat necesse est. Ita ista in Christo incorporatio non simul & semel tota fit, sed continuari eā oportet tantisperdum hic viuimus, & crescere in eo perpetuò debemus, donec euadamus in virum perfectum ad mensuram staturæ adulti Christi. Pueris quidem crescendum est & adolescendum, quousque in viros tan-dem euadant. Nos omnes pueri sumus, imo infantes su-mus, quantisper hic agimus. Quum infans essem, ut infans loquebar, ut infans cogitabam, ut infans sentiebam, inquit Paulus.
units.tr: A most welcome and altogether necessary repetition. Many seek that life outside Christ; others seek it partly in Christ and partly in other things. Therefore this point can never be pressed home enough: that Christ is the only bread of eternal life. This repetition of the descent of that bread from heaven reminds us of two things. First, about Christ: that he is not merely a man, but also the Son of God, begotten of the Father from eternity and in heaven. Second, it reminds us about our life, that it is in heaven, since it comes down to us from heaven. I confess indeed that our life in Christ has come down from heaven, because we could not ascend to it into heaven; but our life has been only begun on earth, through Christ coming down to us; and when this was done, Christ withdrew again into heaven, so that we might seek the completion of our life in heaven. Hence the Apostle: Seek those things which are above, he says, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God. Finally, see also how necessary it was that he should press home this eating: for although men have now come to know that Christ alone is our life, they do not immediately grasp how they are related to him. For believing alone is not so slight a matter, and so it must be repeated: one must believe, one must believe. Moreover, not only is faith repeated, but it is also urged what kind of apprehension of Christ, what union with Christ, ought to be; it is not right that this apprehension or union should be some slight thing; rather it ought to be a kind of eating. We know that in eating, food does not lightly touch the substance of our body, but, so to speak, is thoroughly incorporated in us, and becomes one substance with us. So too in union with Christ there ought to be an incorporation and ingrafting into Christ, and we ought to pass into his substance, to become bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh. Moreover, food is not to be eaten only once in this life, but again and again at fixed and appointed times, as long as we are in this life; otherwise present life must necessarily perish. So this incorporation into Christ is not completed all at once and in one go, but it must be continued as long as we live here, and we must always grow in him, until we pass into a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. Children indeed must grow and become adults until at last they become men. We are all children, indeed we are infants, as long as we live here. When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child, I felt as a child, says Paul.

units.la: Panis quem ego dabo. Hic definit eis panem illum quē daturus est; definit autem eum per suam ipsius carnem. Christus toto hoc loco de se loquitur ut Mediatore Deo simul & homine. Id autem negari non potest, quæ hic sibi attribuit, competere ea proprie in alteram naturam, nempe deitatem; sed ea est unio naturarum Christi hypostatica, ut non immerito quæ propria sunt unius naturæ, communicentur utrique in persona una: Et de toto Christo enuntiari potest eum descendisse de cælis, eum esse panem illum vitæ, etsi haec propria sint deitatis. Scimus hoc omnes, animam nostram quæ est in corpore nostro, corpus alioqui in se mortuum vivificare: Ita deitas in humana Christi natura habitans corporaliter, ut est, quoniam anima in corpore, humanam illam naturam totam vivificat, vita illa spirituali & plane divina: Nam alioqui naturali vita animatur corpus Christi per naturalem & humanam quæ in ipso est animam. Scimus rursus animam in corpore habitantem producere animales & vitales actiones extra corpus erumpentes in res alias, & ad id ut ministerio corporis quo iam prius vivificatum & animatum est: Ita deitas in Christo producit extra corpus ipsius Christi animatum & vivificatum iam vita Dei vitales actiones, vivificatque creaturas, idque per corpus illud & naturam humanam prius vita illa Dei vivifica-tam. Est enim deitas in Christo quasi fons vitae, natura vero humana quasi canalis per quem illius vitae cælestis quasi aqua transfunditur in creaturas usque communicatur. Quod cum ita sit, non immerito panis vitae dicitur, qui alioqui ad deitatem pertinet proprie, naturae etiam humanae tribuitur, per eamque definitur, cum illa ipsa caro Christi vivifica sit propter inhabitantem deitatem. Hoc vero non praetermittendum est, carnis nomine hoc loco non intelligi alteram duntaxat partem naturae humanae in Christo, sed totam eam, corpus, inquam, cum anima; Neque rursus naturam totam humanam nam separatam à deitate, sed eam in vnione illa hypo-statica & personali. Secus enim caro nihil prodesset, vt audiemus postea hoc eodem capite versi.63. Spiritus est qui vivificat, caro non prodest quicquam. Quòd autem per carnem potius quàm per deitatem definierit nobis panem illum vitæ, in causa esse videtur, quòd illi contemptui habuerint humanam Christi naturam, obiicientes eum Filium esse Iosephi & Mariæ. Ideo nunc tantum abesse eos debere innuit ab eo, vt offendantur ipsius carne, vt inde etiam vitam sibi expectent.
units.tr: The bread which I will give. Here he declares the bread that he is about to give, and he declares it through his own flesh. Throughout this passage Christ speaks of himself as Mediator, God and man together. It cannot be denied that the things he attributes to himself belong properly to the other nature, namely the deity. But such is the hypostatic union of Christ's natures that what is proper to one nature is not wrongly communicated to the whole person, and it can be said of the whole Christ that he came down from heaven and that he is the bread of life, although these things are properly of the deity. We all know that our soul, which is in our body, makes alive a body that would otherwise be dead in itself. So the deity, dwelling bodily in the human nature of Christ, makes that whole human nature alive, as the soul does in the body, with that spiritual and altogether divine life. For otherwise the body of Christ is animated with natural life through the natural and human soul that is in him. We know again that the soul dwelling in the body produces animal and vital actions that break out beyond the body into other things, and it does so by means of the body, which has already been made alive and animated. So in Christ the deity, through that body and human nature already quickened by the life of God, produces vital actions outside the body of Christ himself, now animated and made alive by the life of God, and it gives life to creatures. For the deity in Christ is like a fountain of life, and the human nature is like a channel through which that heavenly life flows, as water, into creatures and is communicated to them. Since this is so, he is rightly called the bread of life. That title properly belongs to the deity, yet it is ascribed to the human nature and defined through it, since that very flesh of Christ is life-giving because of the indwelling deity. But this must not be passed over: by the name of flesh here is understood not merely the other part of the human nature in Christ, but the whole of it, that is, the body with the soul. Nor is it the whole human nature taken as separated from the deity, but as it is in that hypostatic and personal union. Otherwise the flesh would profit nothing, as we shall hear later in this same chapter, verse 63: The Spirit is it that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing. As for why he defined that bread of life through the flesh rather than through the deity, the cause seems to be that they despised the human nature of Christ, objecting that he is the son of Joseph and Mary. Therefore he hints that they ought now to be so far from taking offence at his flesh, that they should look for life from it.

units.la: Postremis autem verbis rationem aperit, qua caro Christi fiat panis vitæ. Quam ego, inquit, dabo pro mundi vita. Ratio est, quia tradetur ipse morti, ad hoc vt mundus viuat. Verum quidè est, carnem Christi viuam esse in se, propter inhabitantem in ipsa deitatem; sed in nobis viuifica esse non potest nisi prius moriatur & Christus in cruce prius frangatur pro nobis: nisi enim morte afficiatur Mediator noster, manet peccatum nostrum. Quare non immerito hoc ab ipso postremo loco adiectum est, ipsius nimirum carnem morti dandam & tradendam esse, ad hoc vt nobis sit viuifica. Vnde discimus duobus modis Christi carnem viuificam esse; primùm per deitatem inhabitantem, deinde per mortem eius: Per deitatem inhabitantem viuifica est in se, per morte viuifica est in nobis. Quare tantum ab eo abesse debet, vt offendamur Christi morte, aut putemus, ideo quòd mortuus sit, minus efficacem fore eum ad vitam nostram, vt è contra mortem eius causam vitæ nostræ esse putemus. Causa enim est in morte cur Christus iam viuificatus & glorificatus efficax in nobis sit ad vitam æternam. Hoc si cognouissent Iudæi, profectò Christus humiliatus & crucifixus non fuisset iis scandalo.
units.tr: In his final words, however, he sets out the reason why the flesh of Christ becomes the bread of life. "Which I, he says, will give for the life of the world." The reason is that he will be given up to death, so that the world may live. It is true that the flesh of Christ is living in itself, because of the deity dwelling in it. But it cannot give life in us unless Christ first dies and is first broken for us on the cross. For unless our Mediator is subjected to death, our sin remains. Therefore it is rightly added at this final point that his flesh must be given and delivered to death, so that it may be life-giving to us. From this we learn that the flesh of Christ is life-giving in two ways: first through the indwelling deity, and then through his death. Through the indwelling deity it is life-giving in itself; through his death it is life-giving in us. Therefore we ought to be so far from taking offence at the death of Christ, or thinking that because he is dead he will be less effective for our life, that on the contrary we should think his death is the cause of our life. For the reason why Christ, now quickened and glorified, is effective in us for eternal life lies in his death. If the Jews had known this, certainly Christ, humbled and crucified, would not have been a stumbling-block to them.

units.la: 52 Pugnabant autem Iudæi alij aduersus alios, dicentes, Quomodo potest hic nobis carnem suam dare ad vescendum?
units.tr: 52 The Jews, however, quarrelled among themselves, saying, How can this man give us his flesh to eat?

units.la: Dixit ergo eis Iesus, Amen, amen dico vobis, nisi ederitis carnem Filij hominis, & biberitis eius sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis.
units.tr: Therefore Jesus said to them, Verily, verily I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you.

units.la: 54 Qui edit carnem meam, & bibit meum sanguinem, habet vitam æternam, & ego suscitabo ipsum in vltimo illo die.
units.tr: 54 He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day.

units.la: 55 Caro enim mea verè est cibus, & sanguis meus verè est potus.
units.tr: 55 For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.

units.la: Effectus est proximæ doctrinæ. Murmurabant prius cùm dixisset se descendisse è cælis; nunc verò pugnat, hoc est, non iam obscurè murmurant vt prius, sed aperte agunt. Pugnant enim alij aduersus alios de eo quod dixit, carnem suam esse panem illum vitæ quem daturus esset comedendum. Quanto magis audit de illis cælestibus ac spiritualibus, tanto magis commouetur. Primùm quidem murmurat obscurè, sed postea pugnat & aperte contradicit, denique persequitur veritatem ad mortem vsque. Quanto autem magis reluctantur, tanto magis obduratur. Nam sicut assensione illa qua veritati assentiuntur, emollitur animus, ita contradictione indura-ratur magis magisque, donec tandem pinguescat. Iubet Dominus Prophetam concionari continenter, audiant, inquit, continenter, sed quid tum, at ne intelligant, inquit, hoc est, ne assentiantur corde, sed reluctentur audire veritati. Quid inde? pinguescat, inquit, cor populi istius, ingraue-scat auris, oculique eius connniueant, hoc est, planè stupidus reddatur populus. Quare inter audiendum verbum semper illud attendum, ut sit cordis assensio, ne audiendo indurętur cor nostrum. Deinde ex ignorantia naturæ cometionis huius damnant eam. Non quidem peccant in eo quòd condemnent oralem illam maducationem, vtpote planè monstruosam, sed in eo quòd ignorent veram eius acceptionem, præsertim cùm iam antea Christus instituerit eos in opere Fidei, & cometionem istam interpretatus sit applicationem fidei; quod enim vocaut edere, id apertè docet nihil aliud esse quàm credere, sine discrimine enim vtitur vocibus, edendi, veniendi ad se, credendi. In hoc igitur peccarunt. Sed si compares eos cum Papistis nostri temporis, videbuntur ij magis peccare. Peccant enim in funiftra acceptione cometionis huius: peccant prætereà in eo quòd defendant tam crassam & corporalem illam manducationem; his ni- mirum Capernaitis crassiores. Nam quo magis resistūt veritati, eo magis indurantur & stupidiores reddunturn. Resistunt autem magis quàm Capernaitæ isti, ideòque crassiores euadunt & stupidiores, quàm fuerunt Capernaitæ. Sed cur cùm significatio huius comestionis tam sæpe iam inculcata sit, non tamen intellexerunt eam de spirituali comestione? Dicam quod videtur: Sensus hominis natura crassus est & terrestris, quare spiritualia non possit capere.Quòd si res spirituales exprimas verbis vulgaribus & è medio petitis, accommodatis scilicet ad intelligentiam nostram, vt si pro credere dicas edere, continuò animalis homo, quæ est eius intelligentia, tam crassè concipit animo crassam & corporalem comestionem: nam Papistas istos tam obstinatos dico habere carnalem duntaxat sensum, qui tam carnaliter & tam impiè sentiunt & loquuntur de præsentia & esu corporis Dominici in cœna Domini. Dixit ergo. Christus commendat pluribus argumentis comestionem illam corporis sui: primum est per occupationem, quo redigit eos in angustias vitæ & mortis. Est autem argumentum à consequentibus comestionis vel non comestionis, vt ita dicam, corporis sui, q.d. Quamuis irridea- tis hanc quam dico comestionem carnis meæ: tamen si non comederitis carnem filii hominis & biberitis eius sanguinem, non habetis vitam in vobis. Qui autem comederit carnem meam & biberit meum sanguinem, habet vitam æternam. Quoties loquimur de fide & de Christo, cùm videatur sermo crucis stultitia mundo, toties vita & mors ponenda sunt ante oculos hominum, vita si credant, mors si non credant, ad hoc vt, si fieri possit, afficiantur sensu aliquo vitæ & mortis, & vna ex parte metu obiectæ mortis impellantur; altera ex parte sensu vitæ blandè alliciantur credendum. Nam sensus hic vitæ & mortis non promouet fidem in Christum. Quid causæ est, quæso, nisi Euangelium fabulam tantùm putent homines vulgi, mirum non est sensus iste vitæ & mortis, cœlorum & inferorum, hinc nulla fides, nullum desiderium audiendi verbum Euangelii, sed merus duntaxat contemptus & fastidium. Quòd si quæras hic, cùm erient
units.tr: This is the effect of the preceding teaching. Before, when he had said that he came down from heaven, they murmured; now they strive, that is, they no longer murmur quietly as before, but act openly. For they dispute with one another about what he said, that his flesh is the bread of life which he would give to be eaten. The more he hears of those heavenly and spiritual things, the more he is moved. At first he murmurs quietly, but afterwards he strives and openly contradicts, and at last he persecutes the truth even to death. Yet the more they resist, the more they are hardened. For as the heart is softened by that assent by which it agrees to the truth, so by contradiction it is hardened more and more, until at last it becomes fat. The Lord bids the Prophet to preach continually: let them hear, he says, continually; but what then? Lest they understand, he says, that is, lest they assent in their heart, but resist hearing the truth. What follows?
