Make the heart of this people fat, he says, make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; that is, let the people be made utterly dull. Therefore, when the word is being heard, we must always take heed that the heart assents, lest by hearing our heart be hardened. Next, out of ignorance of the nature of this eating, they condemn it. They do not indeed sin in condemning that oral eating as altogether monstrous, but in this, that they are ignorant of its true reception, especially since Christ had already instructed them in the work of faith, and had explained that eating as the application of faith. For the word he uses for eating, he clearly teaches, means nothing other than believing; for he uses the words eating, coming to him, and believing without distinction. In this, then, they sinned. But if you compare them with the Papists of our own time, these seem to sin more. For they sin in the perverse reception of this eating; they sin further in defending that gross and bodily eating, being even grosser than these Capernaites. For the more they resist the truth, the more they are hardened and made duller. And they resist more than those Capernaites, and so they become grosser and duller than the Capernaites were. But why, since the meaning of this eating has been so often impressed upon them, did they not understand it as spiritual eating? I shall say what seems to me: the human sense is by nature gross and earthly, and so cannot grasp spiritual things. If you express spiritual things in common words taken from ordinary life, adapted of course to our understanding, as when you say to eat for to believe, the animal man, whose understanding this is, immediately conceives in his mind a gross and bodily eating. For I say these Papists are so obstinate that they have only a carnal sense, and they feel and speak so carnally and so impiously about the presence and eating of the Lord's body in the Lord's Supper. Therefore he said. Christ commends this eating of his body by several arguments. The first is by a consequence, by which he brings them into the straits of life and death. It is an argument from the consequences of eating or not eating his body, so to speak, as if he said: Although you may mock this eating of my flesh which I speak of, yet if you do not eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you have no life in you. But he who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life. Whenever we speak of faith and of Christ, since the word of the cross seems foolishness to the world, life and death must always be set before men's eyes: life if they believe, death if they do not believe. This is so that, if it were possible, they may be moved by some sense of life and death, and on the one side be driven by fear of the death set before them, and on the other be gently drawn by a sense of life to believe. For this sense of life and death does not advance faith in Christ. What is the cause, I ask, except that common people think the gospel is only a fable? It is no wonder that this sense of life and death, of heaven and hell, is lacking; hence there is no faith, no desire to hear the word of the gospel, but only mere contempt and disgust. But if you ask here, since they were ignorant of the word eating...

units.la: CC ex ignorantia vocis comestionis, intelligunt enim corporalem, non spiritualem comestionem, cur non statim explicet iis vocem, doceatque se spiritualem illam comestionem intelligere? Id enim non statim facit, sed voce hac edendi non explicata, prius aliquot argumentis conatur eos adducere ad comedendum carnem suam. Respondeo, potuisse quidem eos satis intelligere vocis significationem impropriam, quod per eam fidem designaret. Iam antea enim instituit eos in opere fidei praeterea sine discrimine usus est vocibus credendi, edidi, veniendi ad se. Verum ut haec omitta, magis laborat Dominus in eo, ut sentiant corde comestione ista, quam ut mente eam intelligant. Doctrina fidei posita est, non tam in vocibus explicandis, quam in sensu gignendo in cordibus hominum. Nam sensu semel accepto, tum facilius intelligentur voces, sive credere dicas, sive edere, sive bibere. Quae causa cur Papistae hodierno die non intelligant hanc ipsam comestionis vocem, cum eius sensus iam plus millies inculcatus sit tot modis, tot disputationibus, tot scriptis voluminibus. Non dicam vinquam obstinatos istos penitus sentire in cordibus spirituali illam comestionem, quam profecto si sentirent semel, non iam amplius sic de voce garrirent, & propter eam tot tragoedias excitarent. Quare Ministris Evangelij in hoc laborandum est praecipue ut sentiant homines penitus animis totam hanc doctrinam, quae est de fide, de Christo, deque eius beneficiis. Accepto autem semel sensu aliquo istarum rerum, mirum est quam facile assequantur etiam idiotae cognitionem rerum arduarum & sublimium in illo mysterio Christi, quam quidem alij qui videntur sibi sapere plurimum, cum sine sensu sint, non obtinent Spiritum Sanctum.
units.tr: Why, given that they misunderstand the word "eating" and take it to mean bodily rather than spiritual eating, does he not at once explain the word to them and say that he means that spiritual eating? He does not do so immediately. Instead, without explaining the word eat, he first tries to draw them, by several arguments, to eat his flesh. I answer that they could indeed grasp the figurative sense of the word well enough, namely that it signified faith. For he had already taught them about the work of faith. Moreover, he uses the words believe, eat, and come to me indiscriminately. But to set these aside, the Lord labours more to make them feel this eating in their hearts than to make them understand it with their minds. The doctrine of faith is laid down not so much in explaining words as in producing a sense of it in men's hearts. For once that sense has been received, the words are understood more easily, whether you say believe, eat, or drink. This is why the Papists today do not understand this very word eating, although its meaning has already been impressed upon them more than a thousand times, by so many modes, so many disputations, and so many volumes of writings. I will not say that these obstinate men do not at all feel in their hearts that spiritual eating; for if they had once felt it, they would not now chatter so about the word, and stir up so many tragedies over it. Therefore the ministers of the Gospel must labour above all that men feel this whole doctrine deeply in their souls, the doctrine concerning faith, concerning Christ, and concerning his benefits. Once they have received some sense of these things, it is remarkable how easily even the uneducated attain knowledge of the lofty and sublime matters in that mystery of Christ, which others who seem to themselves very wise do not obtain, because they lack feeling and do not have the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Caro enim mea vere est cibus. Hoc est secundum argumentum, quo ad fidem & comestionem eos allicit, à natura carnis & sanguinis ipsius. Si sit cibus aut potus aliquis temporarius aut paulo delicatiorem (nam natura de his temporariis & carnalibus satis iudicare possumus, eaque satis sapimus omnes) statim abripimur auiditate quadam eius, omniaque facimus, nullis sumptibus parcimus, ad hoc vel cum eum consequamur. At vero nullus vnquam fuit cibus, cum isto cibo, carne nimirum Christi, comparandus; nullus vnquam potus fuit conferendus cum hoc potu, nempe Christi sanguine. Hic est verus ac proprie vnicus cibus ac potus, non est alius praeter eum, qui vere cibus ac potus dicendus sit. Ratio est, alij cibi potusque omnes pereunt, alunt quidem, fateor, & vim alendi aliquam habent ad tempus, sed perit illa vis statim, abeuntque vel in substantiam corporis aliti, opusque habent ipsi in corpus transeuntes, suo rursus alimento, vel in excrementa abeunt: unde cibus quo vescimur hodie non sufficiet nobis sustentandis cras. At vero Christi caro & sanguis nunquam pereunt, nunquam amittunt vim illam altricem, sed semel percepta alunt in perpetuum. Expe-rire, ede eius carnem hodie, bibe sanguinem eius hodie, cras invenies vim eorum non minus recentem ad alendum te ad vitam aeternam, quam hodie expertus es: neque etiam nudiustertius minus efficacia erunt, quam hodie sunt. Imo vero progressu temporis Christus fide semel apprehensus, perpetuo efficacior fit ad vitam. Quare dictum est supra vers. 27. Operemini non cibo, qui perit, sed cibo illi qui permanet in vitam aeternam. Sequitur igitur quod cum caro Christi, sanguis Christi talis sit, tamque efficax cibus ac potus, & vere sit cibus ac potus, oportere esse in animis hominum ingens ipsorum desiderium. Quod autem in multis non sit hoc desiderium, in causa est quod nondum gustarunt quam suavis sit Dominus. Ignoti autem nulla cupido est. Qui vero semel gustavit quam suavis sit Dominus, non expletur ne toto quidem cibo huius mundi, omnibus eius voluptatibus, nisi simul Christum percipiat. Petrus, postquam hortatus est dispersos advenas ut depositā omni malitia expeterent sincerum illud lac sermonis, subiecit, Si modo gustastis quod benignus sit Dominus. Quo significat eos demum qui gustarunt semel quam benignus sit Dominus, appetere ipsum & expetere sermonem illum, qui est de ipso, cuiusque beneficio adolescunt. Quare in id incumbendum nobis imprimis, ut & nos ipsi primum degustemus suavitatem Christi, & proponamus deinde aliis gustandam, et vallecti illa suavitate iam desiderēt eo vesci magis
units.tr: For my flesh is truly food. This is the second argument, by which he draws them to faith and to eating, from the very nature of his flesh and blood. If there is any food or drink for the body, or something somewhat more delicate (for we can judge well enough from nature about such temporal and carnal things, and we all know them well enough), we are at once carried away by a certain eagerness for it, and we do everything, spare no expense, in order to obtain it. But truly, no food has ever been comparable with this food, namely the flesh of Christ; no drink has ever been comparable with this drink, namely the blood of Christ. This is the true and properly unique food and drink; there is no other that can truly be called food and drink. The reason is this: all other foods and drinks perish. They do nourish, I grant, and have some power of nourishing for a time; but that power soon passes away, and they either turn into the substance of the body they feed, which in turn needs its own nourishment, or they pass into excrement. Hence the food we eat today will not be enough to sustain us tomorrow. But the flesh and blood of Christ never perish, never lose that nourishing power, but once received they nourish for ever. Try it: eat his flesh today, drink his blood today, and tomorrow you will find their power to nourish you to eternal life no less fresh than you found it today; nor will they be less effective the day after tomorrow than they are today. Indeed, as time goes on, Christ, once laid hold of by faith, becomes ever more effective unto life. Therefore it was said above, at verse 27: Work not for the food which perishes, but for the food which endures unto eternal life. It follows, then, that since the flesh of Christ and the blood of Christ are such, and so efficacious a food and drink, and are truly food and drink, there ought to be in men's souls a great desire for them. That this desire is absent in many is because they have not yet tasted how sweet the Lord is. But there is no desire for what is unknown. Yet whoever has once tasted how sweet the Lord is is not satisfied even with the whole food of this world, with all its pleasures, unless at the same time he receives Christ. Peter, after he had exhorted the scattered strangers to put away all malice and to desire the pure milk of the word, added: If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good. By this he means that those who have once tasted how good the Lord is then desire him and that word which concerns him, by whose benefit they grow. Therefore we must above all labour at this: that we ourselves first taste the sweetness of Christ, and then set it before others to be tasted, so that, once delighted by that sweetness, they may desire to feed on him more and more, for as long as they have looked upon him present.

units.la: {1} 1. Pet. 2. 1. &c. magisque, tantisperdum eum praesentem intuiti fuerint.
units.tr: {1} 1 Pet. 2.1 etc. and more and more, for as long as they have looked upon him present.

units.la: 56 Qui edit meam carnem & bibit meum sanguinem, in me manet & ego in eo.
units.tr: 56 He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.

units.la: 57 Sicut misit me vivens ille Pater, & ego vivo per Patrem: ita etiam qui ederit me, vivet ipse quoque per me.
units.tr: 57 As the living Father sent me, and I live by the Father, so also he who eats me shall himself live by me.

units.la: 58 Hic est panis ille qui de coelo descendit: non prout comederunt patres vestri Manna, & mortui sunt: qui ederit hunc panem, vivet in aeternum.
units.tr: 58 This is the bread which came down from heaven: not as your fathers ate the manna and died; he who eats this bread shall live for ever.

units.la: 59 Haec dixit in synagoga quum doceret in urbe Capernaumo.
units.tr: 59 He said these things in the synagogue, when he taught in Capernaum.

units.la: HOc est tertium argumentum quo allicit eos ad vescendum carne sua; sumptum a beata illa communione quae est cum Christo. Scimus id, communem hunc cibum postquam eum iam comedimus, paulatim incorporari, ut sic dicam, nobis, & abire eum in substantiam corporis nostri. Ex quo dici potest quodammodo & eum esse in nobis, & nos in eo esse vicissim, cum dicatur quisque esse in sua ipsius substantia. Ita hic res habet, postquam comedimus Christum, iam fit incorporatio, non quidem ipsius in nobis, nam ipse infinitis partibus melior est substantia quam sumus nos, sed nostri in eo, fitque transmutatio quasi substantiae nostrae in ipsius substantiam, & nos efficimur ossa ex ossibus eius, & caro ex carne eius. Ex quo fit, ut merito dici possimus iam in eo esse, & ille vicissim in nobis. Ut de fide dicam, ea est eius vis, ut ubi semel credidimus in Christum, qui nunc, qua homo est, supra omnes hos coelos aspectabiles positus est, ita trahat fides Christum quasi deorsum versus ad nos, ut inhabitet in nobis & in cordibus nostris, ruissusque subuchat nos ad Christum, ut nos habitemus cum eo & in eo, euadamusque etiam dum in terris agimus, municipes caelorum. De hac communione ut dicam nonnihil: Si loquamur de communione cum Christo, de beata illa societate cum eo, qui nescit dum quid sit quam solum esse, hoc est, miserum esse, destitutum esse omni
units.tr: This is the third argument by which he draws them to eat his flesh, taken from that blessed communion which is with Christ. We know that this common food, once we have eaten it, is gradually incorporated into us, so to speak, and passes into the substance of our body. From this it can be said that in some way it is in us, and we in it in turn, since each is said to be in his own substance. So it is here: after we have eaten Christ, there takes place an incorporation, not indeed of him into us (for he is in substance infinitely better than we are), but of us into him; and a kind of transformation of our substance into his substance occurs, and we become bones of his bones and flesh of his flesh. From this it follows that we may rightly be said to be now in him, and he in turn in us. To speak of faith: its power is such that, once we have believed in Christ, who now, as man, is placed above all these visible heavens, faith draws Christ down, as it were, toward us, so that he dwells in us and in our hearts; and again it lifts us up to Christ, so that we dwell with him and in him, and while we still live on earth we become citizens of heaven. To say a little more about this communion: if we speak of communion with Christ, of that blessed fellowship with him, then the man who does not know anything but being alone, that is, being wretched, being destitute of every glory and grace, gains nothing from this word, and it profits him nothing in the sight of God. But if you speak of this communion to one who feels that he is by nature alone and naked, destitute of all grace, he is greatly moved and profited by that word, and places his happiness in participation in Christ and in that fullness which is in him. But once he has believed in him and joined himself to him through faith, he is then wonderfully delighted by his ineffable sweetness, and he will not exchange that fellowship with Christ, not even for the whole world. For he finds in him the forgiveness of sins, he finds righteousness, and all will find the treasures of every grace. It is certain that a time will at some point come when each person will feel how great his solitude is by nature, how destitute he is of all grace.

units.la: Ephes.5.30. Vis fidei. Philip.3.20. De communione nostra cum Christo, loeus. omni gloria ac gratia, illud nihil est ei, nihilq; proficies eo sermone apud eum. Sin loquaris de hac communione, ei qui sentit se solum natura ac nudum, destitutum omni gratia, is quidem multum afficitur, ac proficit illo sermone, ponitque felicitatem in participatione Christi & plenitudinis illius, quæ est in ipso. Postquam vero crediderit in eum, coniunxeritque se cum eo per fidem, iam mirum in modum delectatus eius suavitate ineffabili, non commutaturus est illam societatem Christi, nec cum toto quidem mundo. Invenit enim in eo remissionem peccatorum, invenit iustitiam, invenient omnes thesauros omnis gratiæ. Certum est illud tempus aliquando affuturum, quo sentiet quisque in quanta sit solitudine per naturam, quam sit destitutus omni gratia.
units.tr: Eph. 5.30. The power of faith. Phil. 3.20. On our communion with Christ, a locus. of all glory and grace; that word is nothing to him, and you will make no progress with him by that speech. But if you speak of this communion to one who feels that he is by nature alone and naked, destitute of all grace, he is indeed greatly moved and profited by that word, and places his happiness in participation in Christ and in the fullness which is in him. But once he has believed in him and joined himself to him through faith, he is then wonderfully delighted by his ineffable sweetness, and he will not exchange that fellowship with Christ, not even for the whole world. For he finds in him the forgiveness of sins, he finds righteousness, and all will find the treasures of every grace.

units.la: Quod si tempestiue, dum vocatur hodiernus dies & dum tempus est gratiæ, id contigerit, bene est; sin serius elapso iam tempore illo accepto, id euenerit, tum quantæ erunt angustiæ, quot lachrymæ, qui eiulatus? sed frustra omnia. Prophanus Esau vnico edulio vendidit suum ius primogeniti, hoc est, Christum & cælos. Postea sensit quid esset carere illa societate Christi & iure primogeniturae, quamuis cum lachrymis benedictionem illam exquisisset, tamen non reperit pœnitentiæ locum. Contemptores gratiæ tandem certè apud inferos sentient suo magno malo felicitatem omnem in hac κυριότητα cum Christo collocatam esse, sed nihil tum proficient.
units.tr: If this happens in good time, while "today" is still called today and the time of grace lasts, it is well. But if it happens later, after that accepted time has already passed, how great will the distress be, how many tears, what wailing? Yet all will be in vain. Profane Esau sold his birthright, that is Christ and heaven, for a single meal. Afterwards he felt what it was to lack that fellowship with Christ and the right of the firstborn. Although he sought that blessing with tears, he found no place for repentance. Despisers of grace will at last certainly feel in hell, to their great harm, that all happiness is placed in this lordship [κυριότητα] with Christ, but by then they will achieve nothing.

units.la: Sicut misit me viuens. Hoc quartum est argumentum quo allicit eos ad vescendum carne sua, sumptum a vita quam viuent per ipsum. Scimus quod qui vescuntur cibo hoc temporario, viuant per eum, nam cibi quæ sumimus hic vsus est, vt per eum viuamus: Edimus enim vt viuamus, non autem viuimus vt edamus. Quod autem non esset cibus qui periret, aleret vitam imperpetuum: sed quia cibus est qui perit, ideo perit & vita.
units.tr: "As the living Father sent me." This is the fourth argument by which he draws them to eat his flesh, taken from the life they will live through him. We know that those who eat this temporal food live through it, for the use of the food we take is that we may live through it. We eat in order to live; we do not live in order to eat. Food that did not perish would nourish life forever. But because food perishes, life too perishes.

units.la: Sic et qui vescuntur carne Christi & comedunt eum, per eum viuent. Vt autem Christus cibus est qui non peritura quotquot ederint eum, nunquam peribunt. Argumentum hoc a vita sumptum, non mouet eos qui non sentiunt quantum mali sit in morte illa spirituali. Quod qui sentiunt, promissione vitæ plurimum commouen-tur, nihilque non faciunt vt vitam consequantur : quòd si iubeantur credere in Christum ad hoc vt viuant, auidè ipsum apprehendunt, vt apprehendentes eum, ipsíque innixi, sese possint erigere ex tanta morte. Vbi autem semel crediderunt in eum, comederunt eum, tum ea suavitas existit ex apprehensione illa & quasi degustatione, vt, quemadmodum priùs sensu mortis impulsi erant ad eum quærendum, ita nunc allecti suavitate eius ac dulcedine, eum ex oculis, ex animo discedere nùquam sint passuri. Scimus ipsum gustum cibi alicuius suavius efficere in nobis eius cibi desiderium. Ex nullo cibo tam suavis est sensus, quàm est ex Christo fide semel percepto. Est autem hoc discrimen inter ipsum aliósque cibos vulgares perceptos : Alij cibi, si assiduè gustentur, quantumuis delicati, pariunt tamen fastidium sui : nulla enim est voluptas quæ non assiduitate sui fastidium pariat. At Christus, etsi continuò & indesinenter perceptus ac gustatus, nunquam tamen pariet fastidium sui. Satietas enim eius, est satietas gaudiorum, vbi omnia gaudia sunt, ibi nullum est fastidium, quod necessario est cum aliquo doloris sensu. Quare si vis permouceri ad comedendum Christum à vita illa, quam ex eo hauries, primùm gusta morte, & quasi mortuus perpetuò accede ad participandum Christo, & ita demum vitam ex eo percipies. Non enim nisi mortui in se, sentiunt vitam in eo. Quo autem magis confirmetur eorum fides in hanc vitam, quæ est per fidem Christi, proponit iis simile exemplum sui suæque vitæ, quæ est ipsi à Patre. Non minus certè viuit Filius ipse per Patrem suum viuetem, quàm is qui credit in Filium, viuet per ipsum. Tres sunt hic viuentes, Pater, Filius & Fidelis, qui hic se respiciunt inuicem, vt quemadmodum secundus, hoc est Filius, viuit per primum, nempe Patrem: ita tertius hoc est fidelis, viuet per secundum, hoc est Filium. Sed vt agamus de viis istorum omnium: Pater viuit à se, quia non habet vitâ sibi comunicaram aliunde: itè per se, quia habet vitæ illum fontem in seipso. Filius viuit quidem per se, quia habet totum semel & vniuersum illum vitæ fonte in se, sed non à se viuit: quia illum vitæ fontem habet sibi.
units.tr: So also those who eat the flesh of Christ and feed on him will live through him. Christ is food that does not perish, so all who eat him will never perish. This argument drawn from life does not move those who do not perceive how great an evil there is in that spiritual death. Those who do perceive it are greatly moved by the promise of life, and they do everything to obtain it. If they are commanded to believe in Christ in order to live, they eagerly lay hold of him, so that, grasping him and leaning on him, they may raise themselves out of so great a death. Once they have believed in him, they have eaten him. Then from that apprehension, and as it were tasting, comes such sweetness that, just as the sense of death had driven them before to seek him, so now, drawn by his sweetness and delight, they will never allow him to depart from their eyes or their minds. We know that the very taste of some food makes our desire for that food sweeter. No food gives so sweet a sense as Christ does when once perceived by faith. There is this difference between him and other common foods that are tasted: other foods, however delicate, if constantly tasted, produce weariness of themselves, for there is no pleasure that does not through constancy produce weariness of itself. But Christ, although perceived and tasted continually and without ceasing, will never produce weariness of himself. For his satiety is a satiety of joys, and where all is joy there is no weariness, which necessarily carries some sense of pain. Therefore, if you wish to be drawn to eat Christ by the life you draw from him, first taste death, and approach to share in Christ as one who is continually dead, and so at last you will receive life from him. For those who are dead in themselves feel life only in him. So that their faith in this life, which is through faith in Christ, may be further confirmed, he sets before them a similar example of himself and of his life, which he has from the Father. The Son himself lives through his living Father no less surely than the one who believes in the Son will live through him. There are three living ones here, Father, Son and believer, who look to one another, so that just as the second, that is the Son, lives through the first, namely the Father, so the third, that is the believer, will live through the second, that is the Son. But to speak of the manner of each: the Father lives of himself, because he has no life communicated to him from elsewhere, and he lives through himself, because he has the fountain of that life in himself. The Son lives through himself, because he has the whole and entire fountain of life in himself, but he does not live of himself, because he has that fountain of life from the Father.

units.la: Ex notes: Chrifius quomodo degustandus; Trium viuentium gradus; Pater cœlestis; Filius, Deus homo. bi communicatum à Patre in æterna illa generatione. Vt autem homo est, viuit illam vitam Dei per vnionem illam hypostaticam hominis cum Deo. Fideles viuunt quidem, sed neque à se, quia vitam sibi habent communicatam à Patre & Filio, neque per se, quia non habent communicatum sibi ipsum vitæ fontem, sed vitam habet tantum participatione Dei. Hoc igitur occurrit observatione dignum: Quàm certò viuit Filius per viuentem Patrem; tam certò viuit fidelis per Filium, in quo quidem est materia insignis consolationis: sed ita demùm si persuasum habeat Filium viuere per Patrē, videatque Patrem in Filio viuentem, videat Filij vitam, & Patris viam in Filij vita tanquam viua sui imagine. Nam quid attinet proponere vitam Filij quæ est per Patrem, ei, qui nihil vidit aut nouit de ea vita? At verò vbi quis semel vidit Filium per Patrem viuentem, tum hoc argumentum à Filij vita ductum ad vitam nostram confirmandam, plurimum eum consolatur, incitatque ad credendum in Filium, vt & ipse sit particeps vitæ per Filium; quod non citius profectò faciet, quàm viua illa Christi in ipsum deriuabitur, & ipse eam in se sentiet. Id suo exemplo docuit Paulus: Et vitam, inquit, quam nunc viuo in carne, viuo per fidem filij Dei, qui dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me. Tum quidem igitur reipsa cognoscet se viuere per fidem, cognoscet praeterea & sentiet quodammodo ex effecto vitæ filij in se, & filium per Patrem viuere, vitam Filij & vitam Patris in Filio videbit. Nam profunditates illæ Dei omnes, ex effectis ipsarum, quæ in nobis ipsi sentimus, percipiuntur. Verbi gratia, vita quæ in Deo est cognoscitur ex effecto illius vitæ Dei, ipsiusque sensu qui in nobis est: ita infinita illa in Deo charitas ex ipsa effusa in cordibus nostris, hoc est, ex ipsius effecto in nobis cognoscitur. Potentia illa Dei ex sensu aliquo magnitudinis ipsius in nobis qui credimus percipitur, vt loquitur Apost. Ephes. 1.19. Adeo nulla est cognitio eorum quæ in Deo sunt, nisi Deus aliquo modo perceptum nobis sit efficax. Quare ante omnia nobis laborandum est in sensu rerum spiritualium ac cœlestium. Nam quisquis optimè sensit eas, is optimè eas cognoscit. Hic est panis. A natura panis illius, qui est ipsius caro, &c. persuadet illis vitam futuram ex esu ipsius. A natura carnis & sanguinis sui
units.tr: From the notes: how Christ is to be tasted; the degrees of the three living ones; the heavenly Father; the Son, God and man. [The Son has life] communicated from the Father in that eternal generation. But as man, he lives that life of God through the hypostatic union of man with God. The faithful indeed live, but neither of themselves, because they have life communicated to them by the Father and the Son, nor through themselves, because they do not have the fountain of life communicated to themselves; they have life only by participation in God. This therefore presents itself as worthy of observation: as certainly as the Son lives through the living Father, so certainly the believer lives through the Son, in which indeed there is matter of remarkable consolation, but only if he is persuaded that the Son lives through the Father, and sees the Father living in the Son, sees the life of the Son and the way of the Father in the life of the Son as a living image of himself. For what is the point of setting before someone who has seen or known nothing of that life the life of the Son, which is through the Father? But when someone has once seen the Son living through the Father, then this argument drawn from the Son's life to confirm our life consoles him greatly and urges him to believe in the Son, so that he too may share in life through the Son. He will do this no sooner than that living life of Christ flows into him and he feels it in himself. Paul taught this by his own example: "And the life which I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." Then indeed he will truly know that he lives through faith. He will also know and in some measure feel, from the effect of the Son's life in him, that the Son lives through the Father, and he will see the life of the Son and the life of the Father in the Son. For all those depths of God are perceived from their effects, which we ourselves feel in us. For example, the life that is in God is known from the effect of that life of God and from the sense of it in us; so that infinite charity in God is known from that charity poured out in our hearts, that is, from its effect in us. That power of God is perceived through some sense of its greatness in us who believe, as the Apostle speaks, Ephesians 1.19. So there is no knowledge of the things that are in God unless God has in some way become effectually perceptible to us. Therefore before all things we must labour for a sense of spiritual and heavenly things, for whoever has best sensed them best knows them. "This is the bread. From the nature of that bread, which is his flesh," etc. He persuades them that they will have future life from eating it. From the nature of his flesh and blood

units.la: [the text continues] Sabbata, lectam fuisse. Hebraei quidem doctores scribunt hunc vsum ab ipso Mose institutum primum, deinde reparatum ab Ezra post reditum populi e captiuitate, qui etiam coniunxit cum lectione Moßs, lectiones Prophetarum, respondentes singulas singulis lectionibus Moßs & numero & materia. Lectio haec incepit a festo Tabernaculorum, absoluta autem est cum anno absoluto & decursu. Legimus etiam in more positum fuisse, vt absoluta iam lectione Moßs & Prophetarum, si quis esset in quoquam sermo exhortationis ad populum, diceret, cum bona venia praefectorum synagogae.
units.tr: [the text continues] Sabbaths, to have been read. Hebrew teachers write that this custom was first instituted by Moses himself, and then restored by Ezra after the people returned from captivity. Ezra also joined to the reading of Moses readings from the Prophets, each answering to each reading of Moses in number and subject matter. This reading began at the feast of Tabernacles and was completed with the completed year and cycle. We also read that it was the custom that, when the reading of Moses and the Prophets was finished, if anyone had a word of exhortation to the people, he would speak, with the good permission of the rulers of the synagogue.

units.la: Secundum hanc consuetudinem, videtur Christus hoc tempore concionatus esse. Sed vt redeam. Sermo igitur superior totus habitus est in synagoga, idque est quod hic obseruo. Quanquam enim Christus saepenumero in deserto sermones habuit ad populum, tamen subinde docuit in ciuitatibus Iudaeae, cum Hierosolymis esset non raro in templo docuit, in aliis ciuitatibus cum esset, in synagogis earum docuit populum. Fuitque hoc argumentum tum veritatis doctrinae Christi, quae lucem populi ferre non potuit; tum innocentiae personae ipsius qui in publicum saepe prodiit: nam qui male agunt oderunt lucem. Mox quoque Iesus quo tempore captus est a Iudaeis irrumpentibus in eum cum gladiis & fustibus, hoc argumento reprehenderit eorum factum, quod egressi essent in eum tanquam latronem aliquem, cum ipse quotidie apud ipsos docuerit in templo eorum, neque tamen prehenderunt eum. Sermo igitur praecedens totus habitus est in synagoga. Quae autem sequuntur verba, ea locutus est Dominus postquam dimissus iam esset populus.
units.tr: According to this custom, Christ seems to have preached at this time in the same way. But to return to my point: the preceding discourse was delivered entirely in the synagogue, and that is what I note here. For although Christ often preached to the people in the wilderness, he also taught from time to time in the cities of Judea. When he was at Jerusalem he often taught in the temple, and when he was in other cities he taught the people in their synagogues. This served as proof both of the truth of Christ's teaching, which the people could not bear to have brought into the light, and of the innocence of his person, since he often came forward in public. For those who do evil hate the light. Later too, when Jesus was seized by the Jews who rushed at him with swords and clubs, he rebuked their action with this argument: they had come out against him as if he were some robber, although he had taught daily among them in their temple and they had not laid hands on him. So the preceding discourse was given entirely in the synagogue. The words that follow, however, the Lord spoke after the people had already been dismissed.

units.la: Ecclesiae Iudaicae consuetudo.
units.tr: The custom of the Jewish church

units.la: 60 Multi ergo ex discipulis eius his auditis dixerunt, Durus est hic sermo: quis potest eum audire?
units.tr: 60 Many therefore of his disciples, when they had heard this, said: This is a hard saying; who can hear it?

units.la: 61 Sciens autem Iesus apud se discipulos suos de hoc murmurare, dixit ijs, Hoccine vos offendit?
units.tr: 61 But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples murmured at this, said to them: Does this offend you?

units.la: 62 Quid si igitur spectaueritis Filium hominis ascendentem eo vbi erat prius?
units.tr: 62 What if, then, you should see the Son of man ascending up where he was before?

units.la: 63 Spiritus est id quod vivificat, caro non prodest quicquam: verba quae ego loquor vobis, spiritus sunt & vita.
units.tr: 63 It is the Spirit that quickens; the flesh profits nothing: the words that I speak to you are spirit and life.

units.la: Hic est effectus scilicet egregius quem reliquit totus sermo Christi superior, non in animis modo turbae & vulgi, sed etiam in animis discipulorum ipsorum, qui ipsum secuti sunt quotidie, & docentem audiverunt. Ad impatientiam audiendi ex iis aliqui iam tandem deveniunt. Operepretium est observare quae incrementa hactenus ceperit obduratio cordis illorum inter audiendum hanc unicam Christi concionem. Vix dum inchoavit Dominus sermonem cum coeperunt murmurare & obscurè reprehendere quod dixit se panem illum qui e coelo descendit: In progressu ab obscura illa obmurmuratione deveniunt ad apertam oppugnationem doctrinae ipsius. Denique ad finem vergente oratione ab oppugnatione aperta pervenient ad impatientiam eam qua recusant eum loquentem amplius audire. Periculosum si audias vel unam aliquam concionem de Christo, nedum multas, nisi interea Dominus cum praedicatione verbi sui externa coniungat internam Spiritus sui operationem aliquam. Secus quato magis audies, tanto magis obfirmabitur animus, donec ad extremam obdurationem perveniat. In causa est constitutio ista cordis nostri pessima. Scimus oculum male affectum obiectu solis peius affectum cuadere. Nam contraria lux Solis excitat malam illam quae in oculo est qualitatem. Scimus etiam gustum felle & amaritudine infectum, ut fit in febri, quo magis percipit dulcia, eo magis infici amaritudine: nam provocatur & augescit mala qualitas illa qua infectus est gustus ab obiecto contrario. Ita res se habet in corde nostro, amarulentum est natura & caecum: quo igitur magis suavia & lucida ei obiiciuntur, eo magis amarescit & exacerbatur, excitata nimirum & aucta innata ista corruptione a contrariis obiectis, eoque insaniae tandem deveniunt quo legimus persecutores Stephani devenisse, qui audita iam praedicatione ipsius apologia, frendebant cordibus & stridebant dentibus in eum. Tandem exclamantes voce magna continuerunt tinuerunt aures suas & irruerunt concorditer in eum. Quod si indurarentur corda hominum ad auditam legē tantum, id esset tolerabile, sed indurantur etiam ad suavissimam illam Euangelij vocem. Non ignoro equidem causam indurationis huius ab ipsis induratis transferri in Dei verbum, vt factum est ab hoc populo, qui quidem durus est durum esse sermonem illum Christi, qui tamen plum. omnium suavissimus fuit & mollissimus. Scimus quidem id, Solem male affecto oculo videri subobscurum, & magis obscurum quam quod obscurum est & opacum respiciat. Lux enim solaris splendore suo obtundit aciem & excaecat oculum. Rursus scimus quod qui male affecto gustu est, ei dulcedo videatur amaritudo esse, contraque amaritudo dulcedo. Ita est hic, nam cordi male affecto & amaritudine infecto videtur quod suave est, & quod melle ipso dulcius est, amarum tamen esse. Id est igitur de quo velim omnes admoneri vt sedulo attendant, dum audiunt praesertim verbum Euangelij, vt corde continuo assentiatur verbo quod auribus excipiunt & emolliri sibi animum, & quasi mitescere ipsum sentiat. Quod si id non semper obtineri possit, secundum est hoc, vt sententiam cordis sui duritiem, caveant autem ea verbo Dei suavissimo imputent, sed dicant cum Paulo, Scimus legem Spiritualem esse: At ego carnalis sum, venditus vt subiiciar peccato. Nam sensus duritiei cordis nostri ipsorum, primus est gradus ad ipsius emendationem & conversionē. Sic enim de ea cordis duritie queri apud Deum nostrum possumus, peteretque ab eo vt per Spiritum eam velit expellere. Quod si quis perpetuo sentiat verbum Dei durum esse, expers interea sensus duritiei cordis sui, is necesse est audiendo progrediatur continuo ad maiorem cordis duritiem.
units.tr: This is, of course, the remarkable effect which the whole of Christ's preceding discourse produced, not only in the minds of the crowd and the common people, but also in the minds of the disciples themselves, who followed him daily and heard him teaching. Some of them at last come to impatience with hearing. It is worth observing what increase the hardening of their hearts has made so far, during their hearing of this one sermon of Christ. Scarcely had the Lord begun his discourse when they began to murmur and to find fault obscurely with his saying that he was the bread which came down from heaven. As he went on, from that obscure muttering they proceed to open opposition to his teaching. At last, as the speech draws to its end, from open opposition they come to that impatience by which they refuse to hear him speak any further. It is dangerous to hear even one sermon about Christ, let alone many, unless in the meantime the Lord joins to the external preaching of his Word some inward working of his Spirit. Otherwise, the more you hear without it, the more the mind will be hardened, until it reaches the utmost hardness. The cause lies in the very bad disposition of our heart. We know that an eye ill disposed is made worse by exposure to the sun, for the contrary light stirs up the bad quality that is in the eye. We know too that a palate infected with gall and bitterness, as happens in fever, tastes sweet things all the more bitterly: for the bad quality with which the taste is infected is provoked and increased by the contrary object. So it is in our heart: it is bitter by nature and blind. The sweeter and brighter things are set before it, the more it grows bitter and irritated, since that innate corruption is roused and increased by contrary objects. And so it comes at last to the madness into which we read that the persecutors of Stephen came, who, when they had heard his defence, gnashed their teeth in their hearts against him. At last, crying out with a loud voice, they stopped their ears and rushed together upon him. If men's hearts were hardened only against the hearing of the Law, that would be tolerable; but they are hardened even against that most sweet voice of the Gospel. I am not unaware that the cause of this hardening, though it lies in those who are hardened, is transferred by them onto God's Word, as happened with this people, who indeed said that the words of Christ were hard, though they were the sweetest and gentlest of all. We know, of course, that to an ill-disposed eye the sun looks rather dim, and looks darker than what is dark and opaque. For the light of the sun dulls the sight by its brightness and blinds the eye. Again, we know that to one whose taste is ill disposed, sweetness seems bitter, and bitterness seems sweet. So it is here: to a heart ill disposed and infected with bitterness, what is sweet seems bitter, even though it is sweeter than honey itself. This, then, is what I would have everyone warned about, that they attend carefully, especially when they hear the word of the Gospel, so that the heart may assent at once to the word its ears receive, and feel its own mind softened and, as it were, made gentle. But if this cannot always be obtained, the second best is this: that they should not impute the hardness of their heart to God's most sweet Word, but say with Paul: We know that the law is spiritual; but I am carnal, sold under sin. For the sense of the hardness of our own heart is the first step towards its amendment and conversion. For thus we can complain to our God of that hardness of heart, and ask him to will to drive it out by his Spirit. But if anyone constantly feels that the word of God is hard, while lacking any sense of the hardness of his own heart, he must necessarily, by hearing on, advance continually to greater hardness of heart.

units.la: Sciens autem Iesus. Christus iustificat verbū illud suum, quod illi damnabant: dicitur ergo, Sciens apud se: Non auditur, intelligens ex aliis discipulos suos de hoc murmurare. Videtur enim turba murmurasse, postquam discipuloru ab eo iam aliquantulum discessisset ac dimissa esset. Nō criminatio, inquam, dicitur: sed tantum, Sciens apud se, hoc est apud animum suum. Nouit enim omnes Dominus, nec opus habebat vt quisquam ei testaretur de homine; ipse enim sciebat quid esset in homine, supra cap. 2. 24. 25. Non opus est, ut quisquam certiorem faciat Dominum de flagitiis quæ perpetrantur apud nos quotidie, ut enarret tot cædes istas, sacrilegia, rapinas, blasphemias, caeteraque tum facta tum dicta pessima. Scit ista Dominus apud se, nouit etiam motus cordis secretissimos. Homines quæ absentibus ipsis geruntur non intelligunt, nisi per alios certiores de iis fiant. At Dominus scrutatur omnia, nouitque ea per se. Quod vel hoc vno argumento verum esse constat, quòd conscientia aliqua & dolore moueamur nonnunquam malefactorum & maledictorum nostrorum, item malarum cogitationum; quod profecto non fieret, nisi sentiremus aliquo modo præsentem & conscium nobis esse Dominum, nósque animósque nostros nudos esse in conspectu eius. Non de hypocritis loquor, qui quòd putent se celare quæ in occulto perpetrant & Deum & homines, nullam habent vel factorum, vel dictorum, vel cogitationum denique suarum conscientiam. Sed loquor de ipsis regenitis, qui prorsus ab omni malo vacui non sunt, dum hic viuitur. Quare in id nobis incumbendum est ut semper appropinquemus Deo, qui conscius est nobis omnium rerum, etiam cogitationum nostrarum. Inter audiendum autem ipsius verbum, vel imprimis id faciamus, neque tum contenti simus externa aliqua reuerentia, nisi etiam interiorem illam fidei obedientiam & sinceritatem in cordibus nostris sentiamus.
units.tr: "Knowing in himself." Christ vindicates that word of his which they were condemning. It is said, therefore: "Knowing within himself," not "understanding from others that his disciples murmured at this." For it seems the crowd had murmured after some of the disciples had already withdrawn a little from him and been dismissed. I say, it is not stated as an accusation, but only "knowing within himself," that is, in his own mind. For the Lord knew all men, and he had no need for anyone to bear witness to him about a man, for he himself knew what was in man (see above, chapter 2, verses 24 and 25). There is no need for anyone to inform the Lord of the wicked deeds committed among us every day, so as to recount all those murders, sacrileges, robberies, blasphemies, and other most evil deeds and words. The Lord knows these things within himself; he also knows the most secret movements of the heart. Men do not learn what is done in their absence unless they are informed of it by others. But the Lord searches all things, and knows them by himself. That this is true is plain from this one argument alone: that we are sometimes moved by conscience and grief for our wicked deeds and words, and likewise for our evil thoughts. This would certainly not happen unless we felt in some way that the Lord is present and privy to us, and that we and our souls lie naked in his sight. I am not speaking of hypocrites, who, because they think they hide from both God and men what they commit in secret, have no conscience at all of their deeds, words, or thoughts. I am speaking of the regenerate themselves, who are not wholly free from all evil while they live here. Therefore we must strive to draw near to God constantly, who is privy to all things, even our thoughts. Above all, when we hear his Word, we should do this, and we should not be content with some outward reverence, unless we also feel that inward obedience and sincerity of faith in our hearts.

units.la: Hoc vos offendit. Dominus expositurus quo sensu dixerit carnem suam viuificam, nempe non causa carnis ipsius seorsim ac per se sumptæ, sed causa Spiritus, hoc est, deitatis habitantis in ea: primum excessu ipsius, quo Filius hominis ascensurus est in cælos, ostendit iis deitatem in carne sua corporaliter inhabitantem. Ascensio enim in cælos proprie effectum fuit. Scriptura si quando vult demonstrare Dei potentiam illam infinitam, eam maxime proponit nobis videndam & cognoscendam in Christi resurrectione & ascensione ad cælos. Sic Paulus dicit eum declaratum Dei Filium potenter secundum Spiritum sanctificationis per resurrectionem a mortuis.
units.tr: This offends you. The Lord, about to explain in what sense he called his flesh life-giving, did so not because of the flesh taken by itself and separately, but because of the Spirit, that is, the deity dwelling in it. First, by his departure, when the Son of Man was about to ascend into heaven, he showed them the deity dwelling bodily in his flesh. For the ascension into heaven was properly an effect of power. When Scripture wishes to demonstrate God's infinite power, it especially sets it before us to be seen and known in Christ's resurrection and ascension to heaven. So Paul says that he was declared the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection from the dead.

units.la: Alibi, postquam meminit efficacitatis fortis roboris Dei, admonuit continuò eam exertam esse in Christo, cùm eum ex mortuis excitaret, & collocaret ad dexteram suam. Ita hoc loco in futurae ascensionis Christi effectu, deitatem Christi proponit iis videndam. Nam Christus sua ipsius virtute resurrexit ex mortuis & ad coelos ascendit. Sed vt de verbis aliquid dicamus, ait Filium hominis ascensurum eò vbi erat prius, nempe secundum Christi deitatem suam: nam humana Christi natura nondum ascendit in coelos. His igitur verbis aperte continetur Christum Dei Filium esse, nô quidem per adoptionem in terris genitum, sed per naturam in coelis genitum ab aeterno. Sed si dicas nomen istud Filij hominis, naturae humanae esse, non diuinae proprium, quare secundum naturam humanam in coelis erat prius: Respondeo, nomen istud etsi sumptum sit ab altera tantum natura, nempe humana, tamen nomen esse hoc loco totius personae Dei & hominis. Vulgò autem notum est proprietatem alterius naturae, praedicari solere de vtraque natura hypostaticè & personaliter vnita, propter illam nimirum vnionem naturarum duarum arctissimam. Nota ad intelligenda ea quae de Christo, supra naturam, imò contra naturam dicuntur, vt eius carnem esse viuificam, qui comedent carnem eius eum vitam adepturum, &c. Nô est haerendum in natura Christi humana, sed penetrandum altius in deitatem illam in ipsa inhabitantem. Paulus ait, Si etiam nouimus Christum secundum carnem, nunc tamen non amplius nouimus. q. d. Si nondum conuersus intuitus sum in Christi humanam naturam, eamque in speciem infirmam & carnalibus istis rebus obnoxiam, nunc non amplius eum nouimus, sed inuenimur nunc humanam illam naturam supra modum gloriosam, videmus & agnoscimus deitatem in eo habitantem. At dices, quomodò cognoscis Christum Deum vel deitatem illam Christi inuisibilem? nempe in effectis his gloriosae resurrectionis & ascensionis in coelos, in quibus eius deitatem cognoscendam proponit Scriptura. Dei Filius, inquit Apostolus, declaratus est per resurrectionem ex mortuis. At quomodo eum resurrexisse & ascendisse rescies? rem scilicet totâ hinc annis confectam, quam neque nos neque Patres nostri gestam viderunt. Beati sunt, inquit
units.tr: Elsewhere, after mentioning the efficacy of the mighty strength of God, he at once added that it was exerted in Christ when he raised him from the dead and set him at his right hand. So here, in the effect of Christ's coming ascension, he sets before them Christ's deity to be seen. For Christ rose from the dead and ascended to heaven by his own power. But to say something about the words: he says the Son of Man will ascend where he was before, namely according to his own deity, for Christ's human nature has not yet ascended into heaven. By these words it is clearly contained that Christ is the Son of God, not indeed begotten on earth by adoption, but begotten in heaven by nature from eternity. But if you say that the name Son of Man belongs to the human nature, not the divine, why was he before in heaven according to his human nature? I answer: although that name is taken from one nature only, namely the human, nevertheless here it is the name of the whole person of God and man. It is commonly known that the properties of one nature are usually predicated of both natures, hypostatically and personally united, on account of that very close union of the two natures. Note this for understanding those things said of Christ that are above nature, indeed against nature, such as that his flesh is life-giving, and that those who eat his flesh will obtain life, and so on. One must not dwell on Christ's human nature, but penetrate more deeply into the deity dwelling within it. Paul says: "Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer." That is, as if he said: if I had not yet turned my gaze to Christ's human nature, and that in appearance weak and subject to those carnal things, now I no longer know him so, but find that I now see and acknowledge the deity dwelling in that human nature, which is beyond measure glorious. But you will ask: how do you know that Christ is God, or that invisible deity of Christ? Namely from the effects of his glorious resurrection and ascension into heaven, in which Scripture sets forth his deity to be known. The Son of God, says the Apostle, was declared by the resurrection from the dead. But how will you know that he rose and ascended? It was a matter done so many years ago, which neither we nor our fathers saw done. Blessed are, he says, those who have not seen and yet have believed.

units.la: Ascensio Christi deitatis. Christus, qui non viderunt & crediderunt. Credendum est tot testimoniis Spiritus, quæ in scriptura sacra de ea re inveniuntur. Sed si vis familiare & sensibile testimonium mortis, resurrectionis & ascensionis Christi, vide an in temetipso sentias mortificationem veteris hominis & resurrectionem novi hominis: hæc cum sint certissima effecta mortis & resurrectionis Christi, non minus certò de iis testantur tibi, quàm si ipse oculis ea vidisses. vide Rom.6.3.&c. Et Ephes.2.1. &c. 1.Corinth.15.12.&c.
units.tr: The ascension of Christ proves his deity. Who have not seen and yet have believed. We must believe the many testimonies of the Spirit found in holy Scripture concerning this matter. But if you want a familiar and sensible testimony of Christ's death, resurrection and ascension, see whether you feel in yourself the mortification of the old man and the resurrection of the new man. Since these are the most certain effects of Christ's death and resurrection, they bear witness to you no less surely than if you had seen them with your own eyes. See Rom. 6.3, etc., Eph. 2.1, etc., 1 Cor. 15.12, etc.

units.la: Paulus ait se omnibus multa esse, ut Christum cognosceret & vim resurrectionis ipsius, & communionem perpessionum ipsius. Quibus verbis definit cognitionem illam Christi quam tantopere expetebat positam in sensu effectus resurrectionis & passionis ipsius, hoc est, in sensu vivificationis & mortificationis. Dicam verbo quod sentio. Non est Christi cognitio vera quæ est sine sensu efficaciæ ipsius in nobis ipsis. Neque de Christo didicit quicquam, qui non depositit veterem hominem ex parte, ex parte autem induit novum. Apostolus cum de proteruia & impuritate gentium locutus esset, subiecit continuò, Vos autem non ita didicistis Christum. Si modò eum audistis & per eum edocti fuistis, sicut est veritas in Iesu. Tum addidit, nempe deponere veterem hominem & induere novum. Quibus verbis significat eos demum vere audisse Christum, & abeo doctos esse, qui vim eius in regeneratione perceperunt.
units.tr: Paul says that he has become all things to all men, in order to know Christ and the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings. By these words he defines that knowledge of Christ, which he so eagerly sought, as lying in the sense of the effect of his resurrection and passion, that is, in the sense of vivification and mortification. I will say in a word what I think. That knowledge of Christ is not true which is without a sense of his efficacy in ourselves. Nor has anyone learned anything about Christ who has not put off the old man in part, and in part put on the new. The Apostle, after speaking of the wantonness and impurity of the Gentiles, immediately added: But you have not so learned Christ; if indeed you have heard him and been taught by him, as the truth is in Jesus. Then he added: namely to put off the old man and put on the new. By these words he signifies that those truly heard Christ and were taught by him who perceived his power in regeneration.

units.la: Spiritus est. Nunc exponit eis sententiam quam dixit supra vers.55. carnem suam vere esse cibum vel vivificam esse: explicat autem ea distinctione, q.d. quod dixi carnem meam vere cibum esse vel vivificam esse, nolo ea re carnem meam per se ac seorsim sumptam à Deitate, ut vos eam intelligitis, vivificam esse. Nam ita sumpta nullam vim habet ad vitam. Sed volo per Spiritum, hoc est, per Deitatem coniunctam & inhabitantem vivificam esse. Nam Spiritus est qui vivificat, habetur enim hoc loco utriusque partis distinctionis ratio.
units.tr: It is the Spirit. Now he explains to them the statement he made above in verse 55, that his flesh is truly food or is life-giving. He explains it with a distinction, as if to say: what I said, that my flesh is truly food or life-giving, I do not want you to understand as meaning that my flesh, taken by itself and separately from the Deity, is life-giving. For so taken it has no power for life. But I mean that it is life-giving through the Spirit, that is, through the Deity joined to it and dwelling in it. For it is the Spirit who gives life; for in this place the reason of each part of the distinction is held.

units.la: Sed ut verba examinemus. Spiritus hic non est Spiritus sanctus, tertia nimirum in Deitate persona, sed est Deus, spiritualis scilicet natura, vel vis illa Deitatis in Christo: nam vis rei alicuius dicitur ipsius rei Spiritus. Renovari Spiritu mentis vestrae, hoc est, vi & efficacia. Sic accipiendum piendum esse Spiritus nomen appareat ex aliis Scripturæ locis, vt ex sequentibus: Deus est Spiritus. Declarato filio Dei potenter secundum Spiritum sanctificationis. Mortificatus quidem carne, viuificatus autem Spiritu. Ergo sensus est, Spiritus vivificat, hoc est, Deitas in Christo inhabitans, est causa propriè cur caro sit verè cibus & viuificet. Caro autem, hoc est natura humana nihil prodest, hoc est per se quid. ac sola nullam habet viuificandi efficaciam. Vnde sequitur carnem verè cibū esse & viuificam esse, nō per se & seorsim sumptā, sed per Deitatē inhabitatē. Nota igitur, caro Christi sola ac per se accepta nihil prodest, nulla efficacia habet ad vitam. Quod de natura Christi humana dico, intelligēdū simul volo de iis pariter omnibus quæ Christus fecit & passus est in natura humana, vt de sanctissimis operibus ipsius, de precibus, de passione & morte, quæ omnia nisi à deitate inhabitante in humana natura, eamque viuificante interea dum hæc omnia facta sunt, ipsa viuificata essent, profectò nihil nobis profuissent. Si sanguis, inquit, taurorum & cinis iuuencæ aspergens inquinatos sanctificat ad carnis puritatem, quanto magis sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum æternum seipsum obtulit inculpatum Deo, purgabit conscientiam vestram à mortuis operibus ad seruiendum Deo viuo. Quibus verbis significat sanguinem Christi ex eo vim purgandi habere, quòd deitatē personaliter secum vnitam habeat. Horum quę dico experientia testis est: nam si quis satis esse putet sibi, si credat in humanam Christi naturam solam, non sentiet is profectò in se vitam ex ea fide. Neque hæretici vnquam, quotquot Christum solum hominem dixerunt, vim illam Christi quæ est ad vitam perceperunt. Ex his posi- tis sequitur Christum non esse Mediatorem secundum humanitatem tantum, caro enim per se & sola nihil prodest, sed secundum vtramque naturam personaliter vnitam. Deinde sequitur nihil valere esum illum & applicationem papisticam, quæ solius est carnis: caro enim per se nihil prodest. Nam id non audent dicere, se vnà cum humana Christi natura deuorare quoque deiratem ipsam. Quare ille esus Christi solus, qui est totius Christi & vtriusque naturæ valet ad vitam. Is autem non corporalis, sed spiritualis est per fidem.
units.tr: But let us examine the words. The Spirit here is not the Holy Spirit, the third person in the Deity, but is God, that is, the spiritual nature, or that power of the Deity in Christ, for the power of a thing is called its spirit. Compare "to be renewed in the spirit of your mind" (Eph. 4.23), that is, in power and efficacy. That the name Spirit must be taken in this sense appears from other passages of Scripture, such as the following: "God is Spirit" (John 4.24). "Declared the Son of God with power according to the Spirit of sanctification" (Rom. 1.4). "Put to death indeed in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit" (1 Pet. 3.18). So the sense is: the Spirit gives life, that is, the Deity dwelling in Christ is properly the cause why the flesh is truly food and gives life. But the flesh, that is the human nature, profits nothing, that is, it is of no avail by itself, and alone has no efficacy for giving life. Hence it follows that the flesh is truly food and life-giving not when taken by itself and separately, but through the Deity dwelling in it. Note, then, that the flesh of Christ taken alone and by itself profits nothing and has no efficacy for life. What I say of Christ's human nature I wish to be understood equally of all those things which Christ did and suffered in his human nature, such as his most holy works, his prayers, his passion and death. Unless the deity dwelling in the human nature and giving it life had quickened all these things while they were being done, they would certainly have profited us nothing. "If the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on the unclean, sanctify to the purifying of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God" (Heb. 9.13–14). By these words he signifies that the blood of Christ has power to purge because it has the deity personally united with itself. Of these things I speak, experience is the witness: for if anyone thinks it enough for himself to believe in Christ's human nature alone, he will certainly not feel life in himself from that faith. Nor have heretics ever perceived that power of Christ which is for life, as many as have said that Christ is only man. From these things it follows that Christ is not Mediator according to his humanity only, for the flesh by itself and alone profits nothing, but he is Mediator according to both natures personally united. Next it follows that the eating and application of the Papists, which concerns the flesh alone, is worth nothing, for the flesh by itself profits nothing. For they do not dare to say that together with Christ's human nature they also devour the deity itself. Therefore that eating of Christ alone, which is of the whole Christ and of both natures, is of value for life. And that eating is not bodily but spiritual, through faith.

units.la: Verba quae ego loquor vobis. Nunc explicata illa sententia de carne sua vero cibo & viuifico, duritie illa obiecta, sermonem suum purgat primum; deinde eam ipsam imputat cordibus eorum. Quod ad primum, ait, Verba quae ego loquor vobis, Spiritus & vita sunt. q. d. Verba mea non sunt dura, vt vos calumniamini, sed Spiritus & vita sunt, hoc est, ministerium Spiritus sunt, vt & ministerium iustitiae, vt loquitur Apostolus. Vide huiusmodi phrasin Rom. 1. 16. vbi dicitur Euangelium potentia Dei. Vt autem videamus quomodo dicatur Euangelium ministerium Spiritus, iustitiae, vitae; opus est intelligamus quo sensu & modo dicatur lex ministerium litera & mortis. Nam ibi ministerium spiritus & literae opposita sunt. Similiter etiam ministerium iustitiae, vitae, & ministerium mortis. Lex dicitur ministerium literae, quod iubet & prohibet, non ministret interea vim vllam animo internam quae efficax sit ad interiorem obedientiam efficiendam, sed tantum externum illud mandatum proponit literis inscriptum in tabulis lapideis, vnde & literae nomen accepit. Euangelium vero dum annuntiat remissionem peccatorum & vitam aeternam per Christum, ministrat interea potentiam Spiritus, qua excitatur in nobis fides, qua Christum primum ipsum, deinde ipsius beneficia, nobis ipsi applicamus; ideoque ministerium Spiritus appellatum est. Deinde lex ministerium mortis dicitur, quia ministerium est literae, litera enim occidit; dum enim non ministrat internam vim aliquam, sed tantum externum mandatum, irritatur magis magisque caro & corrupta ista natura, fitque magis obnoxia peccato & morti quam prius, atque eo modo docet Paulus, Legem esse mortiferam, nempe quia peccatum occasione arrepta seducit me, inquit, per illud mandatum, & per illud occidit: Euangelium vero ministerium vitae est, quia cum ministrat potentiam & Spiritum, qua excitatur fides, qua fide rursus applicatur Christus, & caro Christi viuifica, hoc est, efficax ad nos viuificandos, necesse est vna eademque opera ministret vitam credenti. Hinc Paulus pronunciauit se vitam illam quam dixit in carne, viuisse per fidem Filii Dei. Hactenus purgauit sermonem suum illa quam falso obiecerunt duritie: nunc duritiem.
units.tr: The words that I speak to you. Having explained that saying about his flesh as the true food that gives life, and having cleared his word of the hardness objected to it, he first purges his word, and then he imputes that very hardness to their hearts. As to the first point, he says, The words that I speak to you are spirit and life. As if to say: my words are not hard, as you slander them, but are spirit and life, that is, they are a ministry of the Spirit, just as the Apostle speaks of the ministry of righteousness. Compare a phrase like this in Rom. 1.16, where the gospel is called the power of God. But to see how the gospel is called a ministry of the Spirit, of righteousness, of life, we must understand in what sense and manner the law is called the ministry of the letter and of death. For there the ministry of the Spirit and the ministry of the letter are set against each other, and likewise the ministry of righteousness and of life against the ministry of death. The law is called a ministry of the letter because it commands and forbids, but meanwhile supplies no inward power of the mind that is effective for producing inward obedience, but only sets forth that outward command, written in letters on tablets of stone, whence it also takes the name "letter." But the gospel, while it announces the forgiveness of sins and eternal life through Christ, meanwhile ministers the power of the Spirit, by which faith is stirred up in us, and by faith we apply to ourselves first Christ himself and then his benefits; therefore it is called a ministry of the Spirit. Next, the law is called a ministry of death, because it is a ministry of the letter, and the letter kills. For since it ministers no inward power but only an outward command, flesh and this corrupt nature are provoked more and more, and become more liable to sin and death than before. In this way Paul teaches that the law is deadly: sin, seizing the occasion, deceives me, he says, through that commandment, and through it kills me. But the gospel is a ministry of life, because it ministers the power and Spirit by which faith is excited, and by faith Christ is applied again; and the flesh of Christ is life-giving, that is, effective for quickening us, so by one and the same work it must minister life to the believer. Hence Paul declared that the life he said he lived in the flesh, he lived by faith in the Son of God. Thus far he has purged his word of the hardness falsely objected to it; now he imputes that hardness.

units.la: Gal. 2. 20. duritiem eam imputat cordibus eorum.
units.tr: Gal. 2.20. He imputes that hardness to their hearts.

units.la: 64 Sed sunt quidam ex vobis, qui non credut. Sciebat enim a principio Iesus quinam essent qui non crediderant, & quis eum proditurus esset.
units.tr: 64 But there are some among you who do not believe. For Jesus knew from the beginning who were those that did not believe, and who would betray him.

units.la: 65 Et dicebat, Propterea dixi vobis neminem posse venire ad me, nisi fuerit ei datum a Patre meo.
units.tr: 65 And he said, For this reason I have told you that no one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father.

units.la: 66 Ex eo tempore multi discipulorum eius redierunt : nec amplius cum eo versabantur.
units.tr: 66 From that time many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him.

units.la: 67 Dixit ergo Iesus duodecim illis, Num & vos vultis abire?
units.tr: 67 Jesus therefore said to the twelve, "Do you also want to go away?"

units.la: Quasi diceret; durities ea quam dicitis in sermone meo esse, re vera est in cordibus vestris, infidelitas nimirum desperata : nam pronuntiat aliquot ex iis reprobos esse, ut apparet ex sequenti quorundam apostasia. Peccatum hoc nimis vulgare est ac vitatum, cum enim non est is effectus verbi Dei in cordibus hominum, qui debet esse, statim imputat illud vel verbo praedicato, vel personis ministrorum. Sed faciant illi quod lubet, videt interea Deus in quo demum sit culpa, ipsique imputat culpam, in quo revera haeret culpa. Ingens quidem peccatum est, fateor, cum minister superaedificat super fundamentum lignum, foenum, stipulam; ita enim polluitur sacra doctrina & Ecclesiae puritas, quod facinus non est futurum inultum. Sed quaecunque demum culpa in ministro est, illud tamen verum est, quod si fundamentum quod est Christus retineatur, siquequod de eo dicitur nullo modo sit efficax in nobis, quod, inquam, incausa etiam sit duritiesi cordis nostri. Quare ego semper maxime probaui hoc genus hominum, qui quoties non sine magno cum fructu audiunt verbum praedicatum, magis imputant sibi ac duritiei cordis sui, quam vel verbo praedicato vel ministro. Paulus cum sensisset legem Dei non satis efficacem esse in corde suo, non cum accusauit legem, sed eam asseruit tanquam spiritualem, sed autem ut carnalem damnauit venditum ut sub-
units.tr: As if he said: that hardness which you say is in my word is really in your hearts, namely a hopeless unbelief. For he pronounces that some of them are reprobate, as appears from the subsequent apostasy of some. This sin is very common and well avoided: when the word of God does not have in men's hearts the effect it ought to have, people at once impute it either to the word preached or to the persons of the ministers. But let them do as they please; meanwhile God sees where the fault really lies, and imputes the fault to the one in whom it really clings. It is indeed a great sin, I admit, when a minister builds on the foundation wood, hay and stubble; for thus sacred doctrine and the purity of the Church are polluted, and such a crime will not go unpunished. But whatever fault lies in the minister, it is nevertheless true that if the foundation, which is Christ, is retained, yet what is said about him is in no way effective in us, then, I say, the cause is the hardness of our own heart. Therefore I have always greatly approved of that kind of people who, whenever they hear the word preached with no small profit, impute the hardness of their heart to themselves rather than to the word preached or to the minister. When Paul perceived that the law of God was not effective enough in his heart, he did not accuse the law, but affirmed that it is spiritual, yet condemned himself as carnal, sold under sin.

units.la: DD iiceretur peccato. Quanto igitur magis debet illud fieri à nobis cùm non sentimus Euangelium, quod suapte natura potentia Dei est ad salutem credenti, quod est Spiritus & vita, tum, inquam, non sentimus tamen illud efficax in nobis ad Spiritum & vitam ministrandam? Sentire enim cum dolore aliquo duritiem istam cordis quæ resistit verbo Dei, est ipsa via ad remedium obtinendum: nam dolor iste ac cōtritio cordis assidua, paulatim excauat quasi petram istam duritiei, quæ est in omnium nostrum cordibus. Quòd si quis non diiudicauerit se ipse & cor suum, neque castigauerit illam quæ in eo est duritiem, profectò diiudicabitur & castigabitur à Domino. Nouerat enim. Potuit videri temerarium hoc Domini iudicium de infidelitate, atque adeò de reprobatione quorundam ex iis qui aderant tam absolutè pronuntiatum, ideóque Iohannes obiter rationem eius rei reddit, à prouidentia ipsius Domini, adeóque à prædestinatione eorum ad talem damnationem, q. d. Non mirum est Dominum de iis sic pronunciasse, ab initio enim cognouit, hoc est, ab æterno non cognouit modò, sed etiam ordinauit eos infideles fore, nominatim autem præcognouit & præordinauit proditionem Iudæ, qui unus erat ex duodecim. Obserua igitur, Christus ideò pronuntiauit istos desperata esse infidelitate, quia id præcognouit ab æterno, adeóque etiam præordinauit. Nemo debet pronuntiare absolutè de reprobatione aut etiam electione cuiusquam, nisi is solus qui id præcognouit ab æterno & præordinauit, hoc est Deus, vel certè is cui Deus aliquam decreti illius æterni videndi copiam fecit. Non autem, nisi rarissimè, Deus vnquam demonstrauit cuiquam hominum decretum reprobationis cuiusquam; fecit tamen id nonnunquam extra ordinem, sed raró. Neque etiam ita ad viuum solet demonstrare decretum illud electionis aliorum hominum. Quòd ad nos ipsos attinet, etsi non immediatè demõstret nobis decretum illud electionis nostræ æternum quod in secretissimo illo Trinitatis consilio reconditum est: tamen mediatè exhibet eis illud videndum. Apostolus præclarum habet de hac re locum: Solidum, inquit, fundamentum Dei stat: fundamentum Dei est de-
units.tr: Now, if this ought to be done by us, since we do not feel the gospel, which by its very nature is the power of God for salvation to the believer, which is Spirit and life, then, I say, do we not feel that it is effective in us for ministering Spirit and life? For to feel with some pain that hardness of heart which resists the word of God is itself the way to obtain the remedy: that sorrow and the constant contrition of heart gradually hollow out as it were a rock that hardness which is in all our hearts. But if anyone has not judged himself and his own heart, nor chastised that hardness which is in him, he will surely be judged and chastised by the Lord. For he knew. This judgment of the Lord concerning unbelief, and so concerning the reprobation of some of those who were present, might have seemed rash, since it was pronounced so absolutely; therefore John briefly gives the reason for the matter, from the providence of the Lord himself, and so from their predestination to such damnation, as if to say: it is no wonder that the Lord pronounced thus about them, for from the beginning he knew them, that is, from eternity he not only knew but also ordained them to be unbelievers; and he foreknew and predestined by name the betrayal of Judas, who was one of the twelve. Observe, then: Christ pronounced those men to be in hopeless unbelief because he foreknew this from eternity, and so also predestined it. No one ought to pronounce absolutely concerning the reprobation or even the election of anyone, except he alone who foreknew and predestined it from eternity, that is God, or at least one to whom God has granted some measure of seeing that eternal decree. But only very rarely has God ever shown any man the decree of anyone's reprobation; yet he has sometimes done so beyond the ordinary course, but rarely. Nor does he usually display in this way, to the life, that decree of election of other men. As far as we ourselves are concerned, although he does not immediately show us that eternal decree of our election, which is hidden in that most secret counsel of the Trinity, yet he does mediately set it before our eyes to be seen. The Apostle has a notable passage on this matter: The firm foundation of God stands, he says; the foundation of God is the decree of election, immovably laid by God.

units.la: 2.Tim.2.19 decretum illud electionis à Deo immobiliter fundatū. Tum addit, habens sigillum hoc, quo nimirum occluditur & obsignatur, ita vt eius videndi nulla fiat copia. Tum describitur sigillum ab inscriptionibus suis vel inscriptis in ipso sententiis. Alludit enim ad vulgarem sigillorum formam; duæ autem sunt sententiæ sigillo inscriptæ: prior est, Nouit Dominus qui sunt sui, hoc est, solus Deus ipse, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus nouit immediatè, quorum nomina inscripta sunt in illo decreto suo electionis. Nulli autem creaturæ, ne angeli quidem, eius introspiciendi immediatè copia est facta. Posterior sententia est, discedat ab iniustitia omnis qui nominat nomen Christi. Hac posteriori sententia sigillo insculpta mitigatur prior illa, & quasi corrigitur. Ac si dicat, etsi immediatè nemini copia vnquam facta sit inspiciendi decretum Electionis vel suæ vel aliorum: tamen ex fide in Christum eiúsque nominis confessione & conuersatione honesta, quæ fidei & professioni respondeat, tanquam certissimis decretis illius reconditi effectis, quis certior potest fieri de sua electione. Nam vt ibidem dicit postea vers. 11. Si quis seipsum ab his expurgaverit (nempe vitiis quorum iam antea mentio est facta) erit vas ad decus sanctificatum & accommodatum vsibus Domini. Ex his sequitur primum non temere debere quamquam pronuntiare de reprobatione cuiusquam: deinde de Electione alterius non tam certò & confidenter pronunciare, quàm de ipsius electione: nam operum istorum externa facies sæpe fallit nos, & solus Deus atque homo ipse conscius est sinceritatis illius quæ in corde est. De Electione tamen alterius debemus ex charitatis regula in meliorem partem iudicare. Postremò de electione sua cuiusque oportet vnumquemque certò pronuntiare. Cuius quidem rei Paulus habet exemplum insigne. Quæritur num Deus abiecerit populum suum vniuersum? Respondet facta instantia particulari. Instantia autem particularis facta est non in persona alicuius alterius, ne Apostoli quidem alicuius, sed instantia facta in persona sua ipsius: Nam & ego Israelita sum, ex semine Abrahæ, ex tribu Beniamin, & ego habeo personam meam esse à Deo abiectum. Qua re indicauit posse
units.tr: 2 Tim. 2.19. Then he adds, having this seal, by which, of course, it is closed and sealed, so that no opportunity of seeing it is granted. Then the seal is described by its inscriptions, or by the sentences inscribed on it. For he alludes to the common form of seals; there are two sentences inscribed on the seal. The first is, The Lord knows those who are his, that is, God alone, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, immediately knows whose names are inscribed in that decree of election of his. But no creature, not even an angel, has been granted the immediate opportunity of looking into it. The second sentence is, Let everyone who names the name of Christ depart from iniquity. By this second sentence engraved on the seal the first is softened, and as it were corrected. As if to say: although no one has ever been granted the immediate opportunity of inspecting the decree of election, either his own or that of others, yet from faith in Christ, and the confession of his name, and an upright life corresponding to faith and profession, as the most certain effects of that hidden decree, one can become more certain of his own election. For as he says afterwards in the same place, verse 21, If anyone cleanses himself from these things (namely the vices mentioned before), he will be a vessel for honour, sanctified and fit for the uses of the Lord. From this it follows, first, that we ought not rashly to pronounce concerning the reprobation of anyone; second, that we should not pronounce concerning the election of another as confidently and certainly as concerning our own; for the outward appearance of such works often deceives us, and God alone, and the man himself, is conscious of the sincerity that is in the heart. Yet concerning the election of another we ought, by the rule of charity, to judge in the better part. Lastly, each one ought to pronounce with certainty concerning his own election. Paul has a notable example of this. It is asked whether God has cast off his whole people. He answers by a particular instance.
