But the particular instance was made not in the person of some other, not even of any Apostle, but in his own person: For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin; and I hold that my person has not been cast off by God. By this he indicated that it is possible

units.la: Exemplū insigne. Rom. 11.1. aliquem atque adeo debere de Electione atque salute sua certò pronuntiare. De aliorum autem Electione & salute non ita certò. Neque verò est quod obiiciant Pastæ, Paulum certum fuisse de Electione sua extraordinaria aliqua ratione. Nam Paulus non cognouit Electionis suæ decretum illud immediatè, neque eius inspiciendi immediatè copia vnquam facta erat, vel Paulo, vel cuiquam Apostolorum, sed pernecessaria decreti Electionis effecta illud vidit, nempe quòd & omnes alij Electi vident, præsertim cùm omnes renati habeant charitatem illam Dei effusam in cordibus suis, tàquam causam persuasionis suæ aduersus res aduersarias quascunque. Sed valeant isti cum doctrina illa sua desperationis plena.
units.tr: A notable example (Rom. 11.1): that a person may and indeed must pronounce with certainty about his own election and salvation, but not so certainly about the election and salvation of others. Nor is there any force in the objection of the Papists that Paul was certain of his election by some extraordinary means. For Paul did not know the decree of his election directly, nor was any opportunity of inspecting it directly granted to Paul or to any of the apostles. Rather, he saw it by the necessary effects of the decree of election, just as all the other elect do, especially since all who are born again have that love of God poured out in their hearts as the ground of their assurance against whatever adversities arise. But let those people keep their doctrine of despair, which is full of despair.

units.la: Nouerat enim à principio. Quæri hic potest, cur Dominus cùm sciuerit iam inde à principio ex his quosdam nunquam credituros, imò præordinatos esse ad infidelitatem illam & ad perditionem, cur tamen ad fidem eos adeo sollicitè inuitarit hoc tempore? Cur tandiu eos docuerit? Respondeo id non factum fuisse vel tantum, vel primum, vt eos inexcusabiles efficeret: verùm quidem est & lucem istam naturæ, quæ est ex operibus Dei eò pertinere, vt mundus inexcusabilis reddatur, Rom. 1. & lucem illam, quæ est ex Dei verbo, eò tendere vt maior pars mundi inexcusabilis fit: sed tamen eò non respexit primùm Dominus, verùm istos voluit ad resipiscentiam adducere. Paulus in eum sensum dicit, ignoras te benignitate Dei ad resipiscentiam deduci. Item, Pertulit multa lenitate vasa iræ coagmentata ad interitum. Vult Dominus omnes homines, ne vno quidem excepto, seruari: omnium hominum est conseruator, maximè verò fidelium. Et omnes homines vult seruari & ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Quare dum homines recta tendere ad perniciem videt, eorum miseretur & verbo reuocat. Sic Dominus adeo misertus est vrbis Hierosolymorum, vt desperata ipsius conditione inspectalachrymatus sit. Dices igitur, cur non seruat eos? Cur finit perire cùm possit seruare? Respondeo, vult quidem, vt sic dicam, simpliciter salutem eorum, sed finit ac permittit tamen ipsos perire, quia id postulat iustitiae ipsius gloria. Exemplo iudicis terreni id manifestum erit. Iudex dex aliquis terrenus vult simpliciter salutem hominis rei ac damnati, alioqui reus esset sanguinis ipsius, eo quòd delectaretur pernicie creaturæ Dei, quæ ad ipsius Dei imaginem est facta. Sinit tamen eum ad supplicium trahi, quia id postulat iustitia. Ita Deus summus ille iudex, & à quo iudex quisque terrenus, vt qui sit imago quædam illius iudicis, hoc habet, vt & misericors sit & iustus: vult quidem, inquam, summus ille iudex, salutem ipsorum etiam reproborum, quia non delectatur perditione creaturæ suæ vt perditio est; sed finit tamen reprobos perire, ne misericordia ipsius præiudicio fit iustitiæ.
units.tr: For he knew from the beginning. Here one may ask why the Lord, though he had known from the beginning that some of these would never believe, indeed that they had been foreordained to that unbelief and to destruction, nevertheless invited them so earnestly to faith at this time, and why he taught them for so long. I answer that this was not done solely or primarily so that he might make them inexcusable. It is true that the light of nature, which comes from the works of God, tends to make the world inexcusable (Rom. 1), and that the light which comes from the word of God tends to make the greater part of the world inexcusable. But the Lord did not look first to that end; rather, he wished to bring these men to repentance. Paul says to this effect: do you not know that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? Likewise: he endured with much patience the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction. The Lord wills that all men, without exception, be saved; he is the preserver of all men, and most of all of believers. He wills that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. Therefore, when he sees men rushing towards ruin, he pities them and calls them back by his word. So the Lord pitied the city of Jerusalem so greatly that, looking upon its hopeless condition, he wept. You will say, then, why does he not save them? Why does he let them perish when he is able to save them? I answer: he indeed wills, so to speak, their salvation simply, but nevertheless he lets them and permits them to perish, because the glory of his justice requires it. This will be clear from the example of an earthly judge. An earthly judge wills simply the salvation of a man who is accused and condemned; otherwise he would be guilty of that man's blood, since he would take pleasure in the destruction of a creature of God, made in the image of God himself. Yet he allows the man to be led to punishment, because justice requires it. So God, that supreme judge, from whom every earthly judge (being in some sense an image of him) has this quality, is both merciful and just. That supreme judge, I say, wills the salvation even of the reprobate, because he does not delight in the destruction of his creature as destruction; yet he lets the reprobate perish, lest his mercy be prejudicial to justice.

units.la: Quum primum audit creatura de gloria Dei, quòd reprobatio sit in gloriam ipsius, sileat: nam creatura est propter gloriam ipsius, siue velit eam seruari, siue velit eam perire. Quum potius miretur quòd tam misericors sit Deus etiam erga reprobos, vt eos ad resipiscentiam tanta cum lenitate inuitet. Tātæ misericordiæ Dei magnitudinem non potuit sufficientibus verbis exprimere Apostolus, dum opes benignitatis, tolerantiæ & lenitatis Dei appellaret. Mirandum vero tibi est maximè, quòd te elegerit & vocarit, cùm alios tui similes & natura pares reprobarit. Hanc misericordiam sic expressit Paulus, Deus, qui dives est misericordia, propter multam charitatem suam qua dilexit nos, etiam cùm per offensas mortui essemus, vna viuificauit per Christum, vnáque excitauit, vnaque collocauit in cælis in Christo Iesu, vt ostenderet seculis succedentibus summas opes suæ gratiæ. Nota hic, quòd si tum Christus tā diligens fuerit & sedulus in iis adducendis ad resipiscentiam, quos tamen præcognouit ab æterno nunquā creditu ros esse, annon debent nunc Pastores & doctores in Ecclesia in id serió incumbere, vt ij seruentur, de quorū salute & resipiscentia docet eos bene sperare? Quòd si iis esset misericordiæ sensus, & amor salutis humanæ in tobis qui in Christo fuit, profectò non sic parceremus laboribus nostris, vel nobis ipsis, tantisperdum aliquos seruandi homines esset reliquum. Verum quidem est, contemptus hic verbitantus & Ministrorum, quem in pleriisque cernimus hodierno die, alienat animos Pastorum ab ipsis, sed tamen luctandum nobis est cum infidelitate hominum, exemplo Christi, exemplo
units.tr: When the creature first hears of the glory of God, that reprobation is for his glory, let him keep silent. For the creature exists for his glory, whether it wishes to be saved or to perish. Rather let it marvel that God is so merciful even towards the reprobate, that he invites them to repentance with such great gentleness. The Apostle could not express the greatness of so great a mercy of God in sufficient words, when he called them the riches of God's goodness, forbearance and long-suffering. But above all you must marvel that he has chosen and called you, when he has rejected others like you and equal to you by nature. Paul expressed this mercy thus: God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our offences, made us alive together with Christ, and raised us up together, and seated us together in the heavens in Christ Jesus, so that in the ages to come he might show the surpassing riches of his grace. Note here that if Christ was so diligent and earnest in bringing to repentance those whom he had nevertheless foreknown from eternity would never believe, ought not ministers and teachers in the Church now to apply themselves seriously to this, that those should be saved concerning whose salvation and repentance he teaches us to hope well? If we had a sense of mercy and a love for human salvation like that which was in Christ, we would certainly not spare our labours, or ourselves, so long as there remained any men to be saved. It is true that the contempt for the word and for ministers, which we see in most people today, estranges the minds of pastors from them. Yet we must struggle with the unbelief of men, following the example of Christ,

units.la: Dei ipsius, de quo scriptum legimus, Si infidi sumus, ille tamen fidus manet, seipsum negare non potest.
units.tr: and the example of God himself, of whom we read in Scripture: If we are faithless, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself.

units.la: Hactenus inserta fuit ab Euangelista ratio eius quod dixit Dominus; Esse nimirum quosdam ex iis qui non crederent. Nunc redit ad sermonem Christi, in quo ipse concludit ex antecedente illa eorum infidelitate non posse eos venire ad se: addit autem exceptionem, nisi datum sit hoc ipsis a Patre. Significat autem obscure, & intelligendum iis relinquit, quod neque datum sit, neque dandum unquam in posterum; sed haec in genere dicta sunt a Domino & ex superioribus repetita. Nemo potest, inquit, venire ad me, nisi fuerit ei datum a Patre meo. Ex his quae dicit, hoc colligendum est. Primum ubi infidelitas regnat, ibi nulla est, nec potentia quidem veniendi ad Christum. Natura autem omnes infideles sumus: Quare in natura nulla est potentia veniendi ad Christum: sequitur ergo nullam esse arbitrij libertatem, hoc est bonitatem nescio quam in natura post lapsum hominis reliquam, & potentiam, ut vocant, activam etiam ad spiritualia, & ea quae ad regnum Dei pertinent. Praeterea nota, fidem esse donum Dei, non quidem quod accedit ad aliquam potentiam, quae iam in natura est, ut est illa hominum arbitrij libertas (nam dicitur, nemo potest venire ad me, hoc est, nemo potest credere, nisi datum fuerit ei a Patre) Sed fidem esse donum ipsius illius potentiae & libertatis. Hoc dictum sit contra Papistas, qui dicunt gratia & motione praeveniente erigi & corrigi liberum arbitrium, liberamque illam cordis assensionem, quae in natura est, debilitata tamen & attenuata.
units.tr: Hitherto the Evangelist has inserted the reason for what the Lord said, namely that there are some among those who do not believe. Now he returns to the words of Christ, in which he concludes from that earlier unbelief of theirs that they cannot come to him. He adds an exception: unless it has been given to them by the Father. He indicates this obscurely, and leaves it to be understood that it has neither been given nor will ever be given in the future; but these things were said by the Lord in general and repeated from what has gone before. No one can, he says, come to me unless it has been given him by my Father. From what he says, the following is to be gathered. First, where unbelief reigns, there is neither power, not even the power to come to Christ. But we are all unbelievers by nature. Therefore in nature there is no power to come to Christ. It follows, then, that there is no freedom of the will, that is, no goodness of some sort remaining in nature after the fall of man, and no power, as they call it, active even towards spiritual things and those things which pertain to the kingdom of God. Besides, note that faith is the gift of God, not indeed because it is added to some power which already exists in nature, such as that freedom of the human will (for it is said: no one can come to me, that is, no one can believe, unless it has been given him by the Father). Rather, faith is the gift of that very power and freedom itself. Let this be said against the Papists, who say that the free will is raised up and corrected by grace and by prevenient motion, and that the free assent of the heart, which is in nature though weakened and attenuated, is thus restored.

units.la: Quaeri hic potest, Annon venerunt isti ad Christum, annô eum secuti sunt, annon eo ipso momento, quo hoc dixit Dominus, cum eo una fuerunt? qui fit igitur ut dicat, non potuisse venire eos ad se? Respondeo, non venisse eos revera ad Christum, quia corde suo non appropinquarunt ad eum. Nā non tam praesentia corporis, aut locus unus idemque id praestat, ut quis dicatur vel venire ad Christum, vel cum eo versari & manere, quàm affectio cordis, adeò ut is qui loco & corpore praesens sit, si non sit animo & affectu praesens, non dicatur praesens esse cum Christo. Contrà verò is qui corpore absens est eo loco, præsens tamen erit corde & fide, dicatur præsens esse. Sic Chanoc dictus est continenter cum Deo ambulasse, ac si in cœlis vna cum Deo vixisset, cum tamen in terris egisset. Nimirum quia cor hominis ibi fuit, vbi fuit thesaurus ipsius, hoc est, in cœlis fuit. Sic Paulus dixit, se in terea dum in terris ageret, cœlorum tamen municipem esse, quia nimirum corde tenus in cœlis erat. Verum quidem est eum alibi dicere se dum in corpore esset, peregrè abesse à Domino. Sed hoc dictum videtur comparatè, verum enim est animi ipsius simul que affectus animi præsentiam plus esse, quàm solius affectus præsentiam, vt & corporis & animi simul præsentia plus est quàm animi solius & affectus ipsius pariter. Quamobrem dum abest animus ipse à Domino, etiamsi interea affectus animi sit præsens cum Domino; tamen dicimur peregrè abesse à Domino. Verum nos etiam dum non præsentes sumus cum Domino vel corpore nostro vel animi nostri essentia, si tamen interea in eum credamus & eum diligamus etiam absentes corpore, & animi nostri essentia à Domino, exultabimus gaudio inessabili & gloriosò.
units.tr: One may ask here: did they not come to Christ, did they not follow him, were they not with him at the very moment when the Lord said this? How then does he say that they could not come to him? I answer: they did not in truth come to Christ, because they did not draw near to him in their heart. For it is not so much bodily presence, or one and the same place, that makes someone be said either to come to Christ or to be with him and remain with him, as the disposition of the heart. Thus one who is present in place and body, if he is not present in mind and affection, is not said to be present with Christ. On the contrary, one who is absent from that place in body will be said to be present if he is present in heart and faith. So Enoch is said to have walked continually with God, as if he had lived together with God in heaven, although he was living on earth. Clearly, because the heart of a man is where his treasure is, that is, he was in heaven. So Paul said that while he was living on earth he was nevertheless a citizen of heaven, because clearly he was in heaven in heart. It is true that he elsewhere says that while he was in the body he was away from the Lord as a pilgrim. But this statement seems to be made comparatively: it is true that the presence of the mind together with the affection of the mind is greater than the presence of the affection alone, just as the presence of body and mind together is greater than the presence of the mind alone and of the affection alone. Therefore, while the mind itself is away from the Lord, even though in the meantime the affection of the mind is present with the Lord, we are still said to be away from the Lord as pilgrims. But when we are not present with the Lord, either in our body or in the essence of our mind, if nevertheless in the meantime we believe in him and love him, even though absent from him in body and in the essence of our mind, we shall rejoice with unspeakable and glorious joy.

units.la: Ex eo multi discipulorum. Hæc est fœda illa istorum apostasia: neque enim patiuntur tetegi à Domino hypocrisin illam suam, ac latentem illam infidelitatem suam in lucem produci. De his igitur vide. Satis iam longo tempore etiam sine offensa versati sunt cum Christo, tandem audiunt ex eo quod incredibile ipsis videbatur de carne Christi, quòd vere cibus sit quo vesci eos oporteat ad vitam æternam, quod descenderit de cœlis. Hæc dum audiunt, primùm incipiunt titubare & offendi: dum pergit porrò Dominus, offenduntur magis. Quantò magis pergit, tantò magis offenduntur. Tum vbi Christus attingit offensionis causam, infidelitatem in corde ipsorum penitus latentem, planè deficiunt ab eo. Hypocritæ satis longo tempore sine offensa viuunt in Ecclesia, tandem oblata aliqua occasione vel ex doctrina, vel ex disciplina, vel ex personis ministrorum offendi incipiunt. Vbi semel cœperint offendi ac impingere, tum nullus est modus impingendi & titubandi. Quòd si tandem paulò seuerius cum iis agatur, & tentet quis proferre in lucem latentem illam in corde infidelitatem, quae totius offensionis causa est, tum ferre illud nequaquam possunt, quin statim & manifestè à Christo & veritate ipsius descisçant. Nunquam mihi placuerunt isti, quos semper videas vel re aliqua minima offendi, aliquid reprehendere, vel in doctrina, vel in personis doctorum. Periculum est ne siquando retegatur latens illud odium & malum infidelitatis, plane deficiant à veritate. Beati sunt, inquit Christus, qui non offenduntur in me, Beati sunt, inquam, qui inoffenso cursu pergunt. Id autem ita demum obtinebitur, si cor bene excutiatur, & latens illa offensionis causa, quam infidelitatem diximus esse, tandem è corde eradicetur. Contrà verò fides in corde radices agat, ea enim est quae facit, ut quis inoffenso pede pergat, quoque maior est fides, eo minor est perpetuò offensio. Sed rursus aduertendum est ad fidem, quonam modo radices agat in corde. Fidei aliquam speciem habuerunt isti, & (ut dictum est de discipulis Iohannis supra cap. 5. 35. quòd voluerunt ad tempus exultare in luce eius) isti voluerunt ad tempus exultare in luce Christi. Sed defecerunt ab eo postea, quod non satis altas radices egerit fides in cordibus ipsorum. Quare attendendum est ut fides radices agat in corde, attendendum ut fidei sensus aliquis in imo cordis sit, non autè in eius superficie haereat. Id ita demum fiet, si ad cor tuum attendas, quomodo ipsum afficiatur: suapte natura terra est quasi petrosa; fieri quidem potest ut ad lucè & calore verbi resoluatur superficie tenus in aliquam quasi mollitiè, sic ut verbum recipiat, credat, gaudeat: sed, ut dixi, superficie tenus omnia. Nā paulò post, cùm se offerent scādala, sive in doctrina, sive in disciplina ecclesiastica, vel in personis ministrorum, sive denique afflictionibus; statim euanescet illa fides, quia radicem non habuit, & duritiei illa cordis petrosa allidetur ad scandala illa quaecunque. Quare semper in eo laborandum, ut cor hoc nostrum bonus & honestus ager reddatur ex malo & petroso, ad hoc ut fides tandem agat in eo radices; id autem non obtinetur, nisi assiduo animi cultu, assidua exercitatione in meditando, precando, docendo, discendo. Neque enim frustra monet Apostolus,
units.tr: From this many of his disciples. This is that shameful apostasy of theirs. They did not want their hypocrisy exposed by the Lord, nor their hidden unbelief brought into the light. Consider them. For a long time they lived with Christ without offence, but at last they hear from him what seemed incredible to them about his flesh: that it is truly food, which they must eat for eternal life, and that it came down from heaven. When they hear this, they first begin to stumble and take offence, and as the Lord goes on, they are offended more. The further he goes, the more they are offended. Then, when Christ touches the cause of the offence, the unbelief lying deep in their hearts, they utterly fall away from him. Hypocrites live in the Church for a long time without offence, but at last, when some occasion is offered, whether from doctrine, from discipline, or from the persons of the ministers, they begin to be offended. Once they have begun to take offence and stumble, there is no limit to their stumbling and wavering. If at last one deals with them a little more sternly, and tries to bring to light the hidden unbelief in the heart, which is the cause of all their offence, then they cannot bear it at all, but at once and openly break away from Christ and his truth. I have never liked those people whom you always see taking offence at some trifle and finding fault with something, either in doctrine or in the persons of the teachers. There is danger that, if that hidden hatred and the evil of unbelief should ever be exposed, they will utterly fall away from the truth. Blessed are they, says Christ, who are not offended in me. Blessed are they, I say, who go on with an unstumbling course. This will be attained only if the heart is thoroughly searched, and that hidden cause of offence, which we have said is unbelief, is at last rooted out of the heart. On the other hand, let faith take root in the heart, for it is faith that makes a man go on with an unstumbling foot, and the greater the faith, the less the offence at all times. But again we must attend to how faith takes root in the heart. These men had some appearance of faith, and (as was said above of the disciples of John, in chapter 5, verse 35, that they wanted to rejoice for a time in his light) these men wanted to rejoice for a time in the light of Christ. But they afterwards fell away from him, because faith had not struck deep enough roots in their hearts. Therefore we must take care that faith takes root in the heart, and that there is some sense of faith in the innermost heart, not clinging only to its surface. This will happen only if you attend to how your own heart is affected. By its nature the earth is, as it were, stony. It can indeed happen that by the light and warmth of the word it is softened on the surface, so that it receives the word, believes, and rejoices; but, as I said, only on the surface. For a little later, when offences appear, whether in doctrine, in church discipline, in the persons of the ministers, or finally in afflictions, that faith will at once vanish, because it had no root, and the stony hardness of the heart is dashed against any such offences. Therefore we must always labour to make this heart of ours, from being evil and stony, a good and honest field, so that faith may at last take root in it. This is not attained, however, except by constant cultivation of the mind, constant exercise in meditating, praying, teaching, and learning. For the Apostle does not advise in vain

units.la: 1 Thess. 5.19 ftolus, indesinenter esse orandum.
units.tr: 1 Thess. 5.19 The Apostle: that we must pray without ceasing.

units.la: Post apostasiam illam non paucorum ex discipulis suis, Iesus conuersus ad duodecim illos selectos, quos nimirum elegit primum e reliquorum discipulorum numero, postquam totam noctem precatus esset, Luc.6. misit deinde ad praedicandum primum in Iudaeam solum. Postea ipse iam discessurus e terris in omnes terrae partes. Ideoque Apostoli dicti sunt quasi legatos totidem appellés.Conuersus igitur ad hos Dominus ita eos allocutus est, Num & vos vultis abire? Quibus quidem verbis non tradit eos plane sibi, aut sibi omnino permittit, ut si velint abeant, sed excitat eos potius ad asperfiftendum in gratia, & perseuerandum, in tanta praesertim aliorum defectione. Nam, quae est nostra natura adeo prona ad defectiones, periculum est semper, ne dum videmus deficientes aliquos, siue id fiat in moribus, siue in fide & religione, ne tum una cum iis prolabamur. Natura enim dum quis videt furem, eum sequitur, dum homicidam, sequitur eum, dum adulterum, se socium illi adiungit. Haereticus quisque post se traxit semper magnam turbam. In tanta lubricitate naturae nostrae, quae conspicitur in defectionibus aliorum, semper egemus admonitionibus, exhortationibus, comminationibus, ne cum iis una deficiamus. Nunquam profecto antehac extitit maior defectio in moribus praesertim, quam quae est hodierno die nostrorum hominum. Quare nunquam satis commonefieri possint qui stant, videant ne cadant: nam etiam optimi quique difficulter retinentur ne corruant in tam horribilibus defectionibus multorum, quas tandiu impune tulerunt. Sed verba diligentius paulo excutienda sunt. Non detinet quidem inuitos, etiamsi quodammodo excitet eos ad perseuerandum: neque enim manu apprehensis iis, ait: Nolite vos quoque: sed permittit iis liberum esse vt abeant vel non abeant, interea dum inuitat eos quodammodo ad manendum. Deus enim ita inuitat nos ad credendum, ad perseuerandum, vt liberum quodammodo relinquat nobis vtrum velimus facere. Populus enim Dei maxime omnium voluntarius est. Et Petrus hortatur presbyteros vt curam agant gregis, non coacte, sed
units.tr: After that apostasy of not a few of his disciples, Jesus turned to those twelve chosen men, whom indeed he had first chosen from the number of the rest of the disciples, after he had spent the whole night in prayer, Luke 6. Then he sent them to preach, first in Judea alone, and afterwards, as he was about to leave the earth, into all parts of the earth. Therefore the apostles were called, as it were, so many envoys. Turning to these, then, the Lord addressed them thus: Do you also want to go away? By these words he does not plainly hand them over to themselves, or wholly leave it to them, so that they may go if they wish. Rather he stirs them up to hold fast to grace and to persevere, especially in such a great defection of others. For our nature is so prone to defection that there is always danger, when we see some falling away, whether in morals or in faith and religion, that we too may slip along with them. For when a man sees a thief, he follows him in nature; when a murderer, he follows him; when an adulterer, he joins himself to him as a partner. Every heretic has always drawn a great crowd after him. Given such slipperiness of our nature, which is seen in the defections of others, we always need admonitions, exhortations, and threats, lest we fall away along with them. Certainly there has never before been a greater defection in morals, especially, than that of our people today. Therefore those who stand can never be warned enough to see to it that they do not fall; for even the best are hardly kept from falling in such horrible defections of many, which they have so long endured with impunity. But the words must be examined a little more carefully. He does not indeed hold back the unwilling, even though in a way he stirs them up to persevere. For he does not take them by the hand and say: "Do not you also go." But he allows them to be free either to go or not to go, while in a way inviting them to stay. For God so invites us to believe and to persevere that he leaves us, in a sense, free to choose what we wish to do. For the people of God are above all things willing. And Peter exhorts the elders to take care of the flock, not by compulsion, but

units.la: Psal.110.3. 1.Pet.5.2. libenter. Sunt qui putant se bene de Deo meritos esse, & ipsi exhibeant externum hunc cultum, si veniant in coetus sanctorum, audiantque eius verbum certis statisque quibusdam temporibus. Sed sciant hi, velim, Deum non detenturum inuitos ipsos. Quod si forte non sentiant magis e re sua esse quam Dei, quod Deo suo inseruiant, Respondebit Deus, vt supra, cap.5.41. Ego ab hominibus gloriam non capto. Dominus igitur non opus habet eorum cultu. Quod si ipsi autem non seruierint Domino, tum vae ipsis. Vae mihi, inquit Paulus, nisi Euangelizem. Idem de quibusdam dici potest cuiuscunque demum functionis & muneris; Vae iis nisi inseruiant Deo pro ratione functionis & vocationis suae. Paulus, Si volens, inquit, hoc faciam, hoc est, Euangelium, mercedem habeo. Atque hic excellens quaedam Dei gratia cernitur. Primum enim ex Dei gratia est, quod vocet nos ad seruiendum ipsi. Quod si non esset aliquid praeterea boni ex cultu Dei expectandum, profecto gratia ad colendum eum data ipsa per se satis magna est merces. Sed cum praeterea sit merces aeternae gloriae colentibus Deum proposita, quantum est illud inservire Deo ipsumque colere volentes ac iubentes? Sciendum autem est voluntatem istam seruiendi Deo, non esse ex nobis ipsis: nam natura nostra vero Dei cultui plane contraria est (vt ne fit qui ex his quae dicimus libertatem arbitrij inferat) sed voluntas ea qua sponte & libere ipsum colimus a Deo datur: cum enim iubet vt sponte ipsi seruiamus, tum largitur ipse eam voluntatem. Si autem rationem habeas naturae huius nostrae rebellis & refractariae, non tam dicitur quis sponte seruire Deo, quam trahi ad seruiendum ipsi, vt supra versu 44. Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum. Verbo enim, trahendi, videtur Dominus subinnuere eam quae in natura est, obstinationem & rebellionem. Paulus de se ait, se persequi metam experiendo an quoque apprehendat. At vero dum interea naturam suam considerat & naturae rebellionem, addit continuo: Cuius etiam rei gratia apprehensus sum a Christo Iesu.
units.tr: Ps. 110.3; 1 Pet. 5.2: willingly. There are some who think they have deserved well of God, and who themselves offer this external worship, if they come to the assemblies of the saints and hear his word at certain fixed times. But I would like them to know that God will not hold back the unwilling. But if perhaps they do not think it more to their own advantage than to God's that they serve their God, God will answer, as above, chapter 5, verse 41: I do not seek glory from men. The Lord therefore has no need of their worship. But if they do not serve the Lord, then woe to them. Woe is me, says Paul, if I do not preach the gospel. The same can be said of certain persons of whatever office and function: woe to them unless they serve God according to the manner of their office and calling. Paul: If I do this willingly, he says, that is, the gospel, I have a reward. And here a certain excellent grace of God is seen. For first it is by God's grace that he calls us to serve him. If there were no other good to be expected from the worship of God, the grace given to worship him would in itself be a sufficiently great reward. But since besides this the reward of eternal glory is set before those who worship God, how great is it to serve God and to be willing and commanded to worship him? It must be known, however, that this will to serve God is not from ourselves; for our nature is truly contrary to the worship of God (so that no one may draw from what we say an argument for freedom of the will). But that will by which we worship him freely and willingly is given by God. For when he commands us to serve him willingly, he himself bestows that very will. If, however, you take account of this nature of ours, rebellious and stubborn, one is not so much said to serve God willingly as to be drawn to serve him, as above, verse 44: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. For by the word "draw" the Lord seems to hint at the obstinacy and rebellion that are in nature. Paul says of himself that he pursues the goal, testing whether he too may lay hold of it. But while he considers his own nature and its rebellion, he adds at once: For this very reason I was laid hold of by Christ Jesus.

units.la: {y} Qui Deo seruiunt, liberum obsequium praestare debent.
units.tr: Those who serve God ought to render free obedience.

units.la: Vnde & a quo illa libertas.
units.tr: Whence, and from whom, comes that freedom?

units.tr: Then Simon Peter answered him, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life."

units.la: 69 Et nos credidimus, & scimus te esse Christum illum Filium Dei viventis.

units.la: 70 Respondit eis Iesus, Nonne ego vos duodecim elegi? & tamen unus ex vobis est diabolus.
units.tr: Jesus answered them, "Did I not choose you twelve? And yet one of you is a devil."

units.la: 71 Loquebatur autem de Iuda Simonis filio Iscariota: futurum enim erat ut hic proderet eum, quum esset unus ex illis duodecim.
units.tr: He was speaking of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot, for he was going to betray him, being one of the twelve.

units.la: PEtrus caeterorum nomine respondet, ut erat homo prompto ingenio, ne fit quod ex hoc loco fabricent Papistae primatum Petri & Papam suum. Summa responsionis haec est; Non est praeter te ad quem abeamus. Duo sequuntur huius sententiae argumenta; primum est a verbis ipsius, secundum est a persona ipsius. Verba, inquit, habes vitae aeternae, idque solus: ergo ad alium nullum abeundum praeter te. Verba Christi sunt, quae faciunt ut nos ad eum veniamus, & cum eo permaneamus, sed non quovis modo percepta, verum animo concepta, sic ut sentiatur ex iis vita aeterna nobis inchoata: secus enim non efficient, ut ad ipsum veniamus, imo vero abstherrebunt nos potius ab eo, quae est naturae nostrae prauitas: vel si id contingat, ut ad eum veniamus, verbis eius scilicet allectis; tamen non efficiet ut cum eo perpetuo permaneamus. Id quod nos docuit exemplum defectionis discipulorum istorum de quibus paulo ante diximus. Quod si autem efficacia fuerint Christi verba in nobis ad vitam, tum quidem alliciunt re vera ad eum animos nostros, nosque cum eo coniungunt imperpetuum, nihilque tum magis expetimus, quam ut semper ipsi adstemus & audiamus eius vocem. Amicus sponsi est qui stat & audit eum & gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi. Verum videndum nobis est, undeam sit haec quam dicimus efficacia verborum Christi; non profecto ex artificiosa aliqua verborum collocatione, non ex persuasoriis humanae sapientiae verbis, sed ex demonstratione spiritualis potentiae, qua nimirum ad oculum demonstratur, & plane sentitur illa Spiritus sancti potentia. Nam, ait Paulus, fides nostra non consistit in humana sapientia, sed in potentia Dei. Quare Paulus ipse in audiendo verbo Euangelij non verba, sed spiritualem virtutem attendebat. Sic enim de Pseudo-Apostolis Corinthiorum ipse locutus est. Veniam breui ad vos, si Dominus voluerit, & cognoscam non verba istorum qui inflati sunt, sed spiritualem virtutem: non enim in verbis situm est regnum Dei, sed in Spiritus virtute. Alterum argumentum sequitur his verbis; Et nos credidimus & cognouimus. Est autem à persona ipsius Christi, q.d. Tu es Christus ille Dei viuentis Filius, atque illud nos credimus & cognoscimus. Ergo ad quem àte alium abibimus? Sequitur autem optimè ex superiori illo argumento: nam sensus vitæ qui est ex verbis Christi, deducit nos altius ad notitiam personæ illius tantæ, cuius verba ad vitam tam efficacia sunt. Oportet enim eum Deum esse cuius verba tam efficacia sunt ad vitam. Postquam autem iam ex verborum efficacia deprehendimus filium qui fons est vitæ, & inuenimus quasi ipsum vitæ fontem, tum dici non potest quantus existat in nobis vitæ sensus. Illud interea manet, verba Christi efficacia ad vitam deducere nos ad personæ ipsius notitiam. Neque enim ego vnquam crediderim istos qui efficaciam verbi Euangelij, quæ est ad renouationem cordis, nondum senserunt, cognoscere aut certò credere Christum esse Deum, etsi alioqui de eo, de eius persona, de eius officio quamplurima verba faciant. Postquam vero degustauimus illam vitam, quæ est ex verbis Christi, tum statim cognoscimus eum Deum esse ac Dei filium. Nam vita non est aliunde, nisi ex Deo & ex verbis Dei. Ac tum denique fides nostra fundamentum quo nitatur solidum accipit, conquiescitque. Est enim Dei natura fidei nostræ solum fundamentum, quæ non potest quiescere in illa creatura, quæ pure est creatura, ne in Christi quidem ipsius natura humana sola.
units.tr: Peter answers on behalf of the others, as a man of quick wit, and so the Papists cannot make from this passage a primacy for Peter and their pope. The sum of his answer is this: there is no one besides you to whom we may go. Two arguments follow from his statement: the first is drawn from Christ's words, the second from his person. You have, he says, the words of eternal life, and only you have them; therefore we must go to no one but you. Christ's words are what bring us to him and keep us with him, but not when they are received in just any way; they must be taken into the mind, so that eternal life is felt to be begun in us through them. Otherwise they will not bring us to him; rather, the wickedness of our nature will repel us from him. Or if it should happen that we come to him, drawn by his words, still they will not make us remain with him for ever. The example of the defection of those disciples, of whom we spoke a little earlier, teaches us this. But if Christ's words are effective in us unto life, then they truly draw our souls to him and join us to him for ever, and then we desire nothing more than to stand before him always and hear his voice. The friend of the bridegroom is he who stands and hears him, and rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. Yet we must see where this effectiveness of Christ's words comes from, which we are speaking of. Certainly it does not come from any artful arrangement of words, nor from the persuasive words of human wisdom, but from a demonstration of spiritual power, by which that power of the Holy Spirit is plainly shown to the eye and clearly felt. For, as Paul says, our faith does not rest in human wisdom, but in the power of God. Therefore Paul himself, in hearing the word of the Gospel, attended not to the words but to the spiritual virtue. For he spoke in this way about the false apostles of the Corinthians: I shall come to you shortly, if the Lord will, and I shall know not the words of those who are puffed up, but the spiritual virtue; for the kingdom of God lies not in words but in the virtue of the Spirit. The second argument follows from these words: And we have believed and known. It is drawn from the person of Christ himself, as if to say: You are that Christ, the Son of the living God, and this we believe and know. To whom, then, shall we go other than you? This follows very well from the earlier argument, for the sense of life which comes from Christ's words leads us more deeply to a knowledge of that great person, whose words are so effective unto life. For he must be God whose words are so effective unto life. Now when we have discovered from the effectiveness of his words the Son, who is the fountain of life, and have found, as it were, the very source of life, then it cannot be said how great the sense of life is that exists in us. Meanwhile this remains: the effective words of Christ lead us to a knowledge of his person. For I could never believe that those who have not yet felt the effectiveness of the word of the Gospel, which renews the heart, can know or firmly believe that Christ is God, even though they may otherwise say a great many things about him, his person and his office. But once we have tasted that life which comes from Christ's words, we at once recognise him to be God and the Son of God. For life is from nowhere else than from God and from the words of God. Then at last our faith receives a solid foundation on which to rest, and it comes to rest. For the nature of God is the only foundation of our faith, and our faith cannot rest in that creature which is purely a creature, nor even in the human nature of Christ alone.

units.la: Nonne ego vos duodecim, Petrus præclaram quidè confessionem edidit & suo & aliorum discipulorum nomine, neque id immerito: vidit enim eos primum electos à Domino ex aliorum discipulorum numero: deinde vidit eos hoc ipso tempore tam præclarum conscientiæ suæ specimen dedisse: decuit igitur eam de condiscipulis Iis suis ita & sentire & loqui, quasi in finem vsque essent perseveraturi. Ita decet vnumquemque nostrum in meliorem partem & iudicare & loqui de iis quotquot tepore persecutionis egregium specimen constantiae suae dederunt: quod illi ipsi in finem vsque perseveraturi sint. Sed quid respondet Christus? non reprehendit quidem illam Petri confessionem quam dedit suo & aliorum discipulorum nomine, & professionem quam fecit constantiae & perseverantiae, tam suae ipsius quam aliorum, sed admonet quod etsi ipse duodecim illos elegerit & segregarit ex toto discipulorum numero: tamen quod mirum videri poterit, vnus ex iis diabolus sit. Ex quo discimus, quod etsi semper nobis in meliorem partem iudicandum sit de iis qui vocati sunt a Deo; praesertim iis qui constantiae suae specimen aliquod dederunt: tamen iudicium suum Deo permittere debeamus, & cogitare interea, quod possit fieri vt ex iis qui aliquo tentationis tempore specimen aliquod dederunt constantiae suae, postea possint iidem illi deficere a Deo & veritate ipsius. Interea autem debet quisque sibi cavere, ne ipse sit futurus is qui postea defecturus est, laborareque debet in confirmanda magis magisque fide sua: nam per fidem stamus. Non tam sollicitus esse debet de defectione aliorum, quam de sua ipsius perseverantia: id enim est quod Paulus primis illis temporibus reprehendit in gentibus, quae magis intentae erant ad defectionem Iudaeorum, quam in ad suam ipsorum perseverantiam. Tu, inquit, per fidem stas, ne effertor animo, sed time. Hic timor est sollicitudo de perseverantia nostra deque fidei nostrae constantia. Oportet igitur quemque imprimis attentum esse ad se. Neque enim dubium est quin eo spectarint verba haec Christi: id quod vel ex ipso apparet quod Iudam hic non designarit nominatim, sed in genere dixerit, ex iis vnum aliquem diabolum esse. Quod vero ad alios attinet, de iis id discimus hoc loco; non oportet nos in eos impingere, aut offendi eorum exemplo, quando viderimus eos, etiam qui optimi putabantur, deficere, & ipsas stellas de coelo decidere. Nam proculdubio eo spectat haec praemonitio de diabolo isto, quem vocat, vt cum vituri essent diaboli istius fo-
units.tr: "Have not I chosen you twelve?" Peter indeed made a notable confession, both in his own name and in that of the other disciples, and not undeservedly. For he saw that they had first been chosen by the Lord from among the other disciples, and then he saw that at this very time they had given such a notable proof of their conscience. It was therefore fitting that he should think and speak of his fellow disciples as if they were going to persevere to the end. So ought each of us to judge and speak in the better sense of those who, in a time of persecution, have given a notable proof of their constancy, namely that they will persevere to the end. But what does Christ reply? He does not indeed rebuke Peter's confession, which he made in his own name and in that of the other disciples, nor the profession of constancy and perseverance which he made, both for himself and for the others. But he warns that although he himself chose those twelve and set them apart from the whole number of disciples, yet, as may seem strange, one of them is a devil. From this we learn that, although we must always judge in the better sense those who have been called by God, especially those who have given some proof of their constancy, nevertheless we must leave our judgment to God, and meanwhile consider that it may happen that those who have given some proof of their constancy in some time of temptation may afterwards fall away from God and from his truth. Meanwhile each one ought to take heed to himself, lest he himself be the one who is going to fall away later, and he ought to labour to confirm his faith more and more, for by faith we stand. He ought not to be so anxious about the defection of others as about his own perseverance. For this is what Paul in those early times rebuked in the Gentiles, who were more intent on the defection of the Jews than on their own perseverance. You stand by faith, he says, so do not be proud, but fear. This fear is anxiety about our perseverance and about the constancy of our faith. It is necessary, therefore, that each man above all be attentive to himself. Nor is there any doubt that Christ's words here aimed at this, as is clear from the fact that he did not name Judas here, but spoke generally, that one of them is a devil. As for the others, we learn from this passage that we must not stumble over them, nor be offended by their example when we see them, even those who were thought the best, fall away, and the very stars fall from heaven. For this warning about that devil, whom he calls so, undoubtedly looks to this: that when they were about to undergo the foul defection of that devil,

units.la: Rom.11.20 dam defectionem, ne ea re offenderentur. Oportuit enim maius scandalum oriri ex apostasia vnius Iudæ, quàm exortum est ex totius huius multitudinis, quæ nunc defecit, ipsis inspectantibus. Quare opus fuit, vt de ea re, antequam viuueniret præmonerentur, vt cum eueniret non impingerent. Verum, vt dicam quod in re est, nisi verba Christi nobis sint verba vitæ æternæ, & excitetur in nobis per ea sensus aliquis illius vitæ, profecto futurum non est vt perstemus in fide Christi ad finem vsque. Vitæ autem illius quæ in Christo est, sensus pariter & mortis illius quæ extra ipsum est sensus, coniunget nos cum eo efficacissimè & artissimè, videbimurque nobis non viuere sine eo. Imò videbimur nobis mortui esse sine eo, cum eo autem videbimur nobis viuere in ipsa morte: vt Paulus in ipsa corporis sui mortificatione sensit in se vitam Christi, Vita, inquit, Iesu manifesta sit in mortali nostra carne in nobis.
units.tr: Rom. 11.20: they should not be offended by it. For it was necessary that a greater scandal should arise from the apostasy of Judas alone than arose from the defection of this whole multitude, which has now fallen away before their eyes. Therefore it was necessary that they be forewarned of this matter before it happened, so that when it occurred they would not stumble. But, to say what is actually the case, unless Christ's words are for us the words of eternal life, and some sense of that life is stirred up in us through them, truly it will not come about that we persevere in the faith of Christ to the end. Now the sense of that life which is in Christ, and likewise the sense of that death which is outside him, will join us to him most effectively and most closely, and we shall see that we cannot live without him. Indeed we shall seem to ourselves dead without him, but with him we shall seem to live even in death itself, as Paul felt in the very mortification of his body the life of Christ in himself: The life of Jesus, he says, may be made manifest in our mortal flesh in us.

units.la: Iohannes qui vidit diabolum hunc reiectum suo tempore & manifestatum, adiecit hoc versu quasi declarationem quandam & interpretationem verborum Christi: Loquebatur, inquit, de Iuda Simonis filio Iscariota. Sic cognominatum eum referunt ab vrbe quadam Iudæ, ex qua oriundus fuit. Vbi collige causam cur Dominus eum diabolum vocaverit: nempe proditionem ipsius. Nam verisimile est etiam tum cœpisse Iudam de tradendo Domino suo cogitare. Quod pro facto crimen iure promerebatur tam exsecrabile nomen: præsertim cum esset in persona Apostoli, & amicitiam prætenderet. Nam Pharisæum aliquem qui molitus esset ipsius mortem, diabolum non dixisset Dominus, vtpote apertum hostem. Vnde illud nota: proditionem, perfidiam, neglectum officium in persona Apostoli, Prophetæ & ministri Christi, fidem violare peccatum esse multò maximum, imò maius grauius quam esse in persona ipsius, quàm in alia quavis persona. Ideoque non potest invenire nomen aliquod adeò exsecrabile quod non commereatur in tali persona crimen & peccatu. Contra vero, si fidelis fuerit verbi Ministri Christi meriris, dari solet illi nomen in Scripturis quo excellentius fere creaturæ dari non potest, Angelusque Dei vocatur. Hinc etiam, nempe ex laude hac quæ sequitur fidelitatem, & ex ignoscendo
units.tr: John, who saw this devil cast out at his time and made manifest, added this verse as a kind of declaration and interpretation of Christ's words: "He was speaking," he says, "of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot." They report that he was so surnamed from a certain city of Judah from which he came. Here gather the reason why the Lord called him a devil: namely, his betrayal. For it is likely that even then Judas had begun to think of handing over his Lord. Such an execrable name rightly belonged to him, as a crime already committed in fact, especially since he was in the person of an apostle and pretended friendship. For the Lord would not have called a Pharisee who had plotted his death a devil, since such a man was an open enemy. Hence note this: betrayal, treachery and neglect of duty in the person of an apostle, prophet and minister of Christ, the violation of faith, is by far the greatest sin, indeed greater and graver than in the person of any other. Therefore no name can be found so execrable that such a person does not deserve it for his crime and sin. On the contrary, if he is a faithful minister of Christ's Word, he is given in the Scriptures a name than which almost none more excellent can be given to a creature: he is called an angel of God. Hence also, from this praise which follows faithfulness, and from the disgrace which follows perfidy, it can easily be seen that this office of ministry is by far the most worthy.

units.la: Proditor Christi diabolus tunc vocatur.
units.tr: The betrayer of Christ is then called a devil.

units.la: Diabolus appellandus est, apostatiqui fidem violant. ignominia quæ sequitur perfidiam, facilè videri potest munus hoc ministerij longè dignissimum esse. Nam illud certum est, quo maior laus vel quo maius vituperiu sequitur munus aliquod vel fideliter, vel perfidè obitus; eo ipsum illud munus dignius excellentiúsque est suapte natura. Id, si percurras omnia munera, quotquot in aliquo pretio sunt, videbis manifestū esse. Sed hic obstantia paulisper Iudæ proditoris ingenium. Proculdubio audita vocehac Domini sensit aliquem conscientiæ stimulum; verūtamen is stupor, ea duritiesi cordis fuit, vt non potuerit flecti ad resipiscentiam. Rursúsque ea duritiesᵗ impudentia in vultu fuit, vt non puduerit eum attollere faciem in conspectu reliquorum discipulorū, imò vero coram Domino ipso, quem tamen certum est ab eo cognitum fuisse vt Dei Filium & cordium scrutatorem. In eo igitur habes exemplum insignis hypocritæ, qui malè sibi conscius dum audit designari, sed in genere, infidelitatem suam, & opera quæ in tenebris ipse perpetrat: tamē pro duritia sua & corde quod resipiscere nescit, vt loquitur de eo Apostolus Rom. 2. 5. nihil commouetur, durities autem ea cordis obsirmat vultū aduesus omnē pudorē, adeo vt impudentereum palàm attollere audeat etiam in conspectu ipsius Dei, vt nihil dicā de Ecclesia ipsius, cuius oculis putat hypocrita sese egregie imponere. Ea quidem verbi Dei efficacia est, ait Apostolus, vt si ingrediatur & audiat prophetam infidelis quispiam aut idiota, arguatur ab eo & diiudicetur, ita vt occulta cordis eius manifesta fiant, & procidens in faciem adoret Deum. Sed ea ferè est durities cordis hypocritæ, vt nihil verbi Diuini efficacia commoueatur: tum desperatus est infidelis hypocrita, hoc est infidelis, qui tamen belle nouit fidem simulare.
units.tr: He is to be called a devil, those apostates who violate faith. Now, if you run through all the offices which are held in any esteem, you will see that it is clear that a greater praise or a greater reproach follows an office, whether it is discharged faithfully or treacherously; and so much the more worthy and excellent is that office in its own nature. But let us pause here a little over the disposition of Judas the traitor. Undoubtedly, on hearing this word of the Lord, he felt some sting of conscience; yet that stupor and hardness of heart was such that he could not be bent to repentance. Again, that hardness showed itself in his face as impudence, so that he was not ashamed to lift up his face in the sight of the other disciples, indeed before the Lord himself, whom it is certain he knew to be the Son of God and searcher of hearts. In him, then, you have an example of a notable hypocrite, who, though conscious of his guilt when he hears himself designated, though only in general terms, for his unbelief and for the works he commits in darkness, yet, because of his hardness and a heart that does not know how to repent (as the Apostle says of such a one, Rom. 2.5), is moved by nothing; and that hardness of heart hardens the face against all shame, so that he dares openly to lift it even in the sight of God himself, not to mention his Church, before whose eyes the hypocrite thinks he is brilliantly deceiving. Such, indeed, is the efficacy of God's word, says the Apostle, that if an unbeliever or an ignorant person enters and hears a prophet, he is convicted and judged by him, so that the secrets of his heart are made manifest, and falling on his face he worships God (1 Cor. 14.24, 25). But the hardness of the hypocrite's heart is such that he is moved by nothing of the efficacy of God's word: then he is a desperate hypocrite, that is, an unbeliever who nevertheless knows well how to feign faith.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM
units.tr: ARGUMENT

units.la: Hoc scilicet; Primum, narratur commoratum esse in Galilæa, ubi summaria quædam comprehensio eorum omnium quæ ab eo facta sunt, ex eo tempore quo gesta sunt ea quæ commemo-
units.tr: This, namely: First, it is related that he remained in Galilee, where there is a brief summary of all the things that he did, from the time when the things recorded in the previous chapter were done

units.la: 1. Corinth. 14.24.25. rata sunt capite superiori in illud vsque tempus quo appropin-quante iam festo Tabernaculorum, cum eo egerunt cognati ipsius vt ad festum ascenderet verf. 1.
units.tr: 1 Corinthians 14.24, 25. up to that time when, the Feast of Tabernacles now drawing near, his kinsmen urged him to go up to the feast, verse 1.

units.la: Secundò, habemus sermonem cognatorum Christi cum ipso habitum ante festum à versu 2. ad versum decimum.
units.tr: Secondly, we have the speech of Christ's kinsmen with him, held before the feast, from verse 2 to verse 10.

units.la: Tertiò, narratur Christum suo tempore clam ascendisse Hierosolyma ad festum versu 10.
units.tr: Thirdly, it is related that Christ at his own time went up secretly to Jerusalem for the feast, verse 10.

units.la: Quartò, habemus sermonem populi de eo antequam se palam conspiciendum præberet à verf. 11. ad versum 14.
units.tr: Fourthly, we have the talk of the people about him before he presented himself to be seen openly, from verse 11 to verse 14.

units.la: Quintò, occurrit sermo ipsius in templo habitus cum Iudæis festo iam medio à versu 14. ad versum 37.
units.tr: Fifthly, there occurs his teaching in the temple, held with the Jews when the feast was already half over, from verse 14 to verse 37.

units.la: Sextò, Est concio Christi ad populum die festi vltimo, vnà cum eventu suo à versu 37. vsque ad finem.
units.tr: Sixthly, there is Christ's sermon to the people on the last day of the feast, together with its outcome, from verse 37 to the end.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: 1 Ersabatur autem Iesus post hæc in Galilæa: nolebat enim in Iudæa versari, quia studebant eum Iudæi trucidare.
units.tr: And after these things Jesus walked in Galilee: for he would not walk in Judaea, because the Jews sought to kill him.

units.la: TIgitur de commoratione Domini in Galilæa dicamus paucis, durante ea incidit Pascha, quod tertiu fuit à Baptismate Domini, & ad quod celebrandum vnà cum populo non ascendit Dominus. Iudæi enim in insidiis fuerunt; durante ea multa & dixit & fecit in Galilæa, quæ ab aliis Euangelistis sunt perscripta. Causa propositæ commorationis in Galilæa reddita est his verbis, Non enim volebat in Iudæa versari. Cuius rei causa rursus assignata est: quia studebant eum Iudæi trucidare. Hic si quæras cur Dominus, cum potuerit nullo negotio sese omnibus periculis liberare, vtpote Dei Filius, quæsierit tamen latebras? Respondeo, obedientiam illam ac humiliationem quam in se vltrò ipse recepit, id postulasse, vt & obnoxius periculis fieret, & metui qui est ex periculis, ideóque ex metu fugeret instar aliorum hominum, quorum infirmitatem totam in se volens recepit, si peccatum excipiatur. Hæc autem est pars quædam infirmitatis illius & humiliationis Domini. Quòd si rursus quæras cùm nondum venisset hora illa quala qua traderetur, quam ipse vt Dei Filius probè cognouit, & ante quam horam non potuit à quoquam opprimi: cur tamen metuit sibi à periculis quibuscunque? Respondeo idem quod prius; humiliationem illam Filij Dei id postulasse. Dicam verbo, Dominus humiliatus in terris, non tam rationem habuit eius quod vt potuit, vel quod cognouit vt Deus par & aequalis Patri, quam eius quod voluit eum facere & pati Pater ipsius, cuius voluntate nostra causa est humiliatus. Ita nobis quoque illius exemplo faciendum est. Non tam aducrtendum nobis quod possit quisquam nostrum facere, vel quid futurum de nobis sit, quam quid voluerit nos Deus vel facere vel pati, & clausis oculis nostris ad omnem euentum oportet dedamus nos ipsius voluntati, ipsumque perpetuo ducem vitae nostrae sequamur.
units.tr: Therefore let us say a few words about the Lord's stay in Galilee. While it lasted, the Passover fell due, the third since the baptism of the Lord, and the Lord did not go up with the people to celebrate it, because the Jews were lying in wait for him. During this stay he said and did many things in Galilee, which the other Evangelists have recorded. The reason for his staying in Galilee is given in these words: "For he would not walk in Judaea." The cause of this is then stated again: "because the Jews sought to kill him." Here, if you ask why the Lord, who as the Son of God could have freed himself from every danger without any difficulty, nevertheless sought hiding places, I answer that the obedience and humiliation which he willingly undertook required that he be exposed to dangers and feel fear, which arises from dangers, and so flee out of fear, like other men, whose whole weakness he willingly took upon himself, apart from sin. This is indeed a part of that weakness and humiliation of the Lord. But if you ask again, since the hour had not yet come in which he would be delivered up, an hour he knew well as the Son of God, and before which no one could lay hands on him, why then did he fear for himself from whatever dangers? I answer as before: the humiliation of the Son of God required it. To put it in a word: the Lord, humbled on earth, took less account of what he could do, or what he knew as God equal and co-eternal with the Father, than of what his Father, by whose will he was humbled for our sake, willed him to do and to suffer. So we too must act after his example. We should attend less to what any one of us can do, or what will become of us, than to what God has willed us to do or to suffer. With our eyes closed to every outcome, we ought to surrender ourselves to his will and always follow him as the guide of our life.

units.la: 2. Prope autem erat festum Iudaeorum, Sceno-pegia.
units.tr: 2. Now the Jews' feast of Tabernacles [σκηνοπηγία] was near.

units.la: 3. Dixerunt igitur ad eum fratres eius, Digredere hinc, & vade in Iudaeam, vt tui quoque discipuli videant opera tua quae facis.
units.tr: 3. Therefore his brothers said to him, Depart hence and go into Judaea, that your disciples also may see the works that you do.

units.la: 4. Nemo enim in occulto facit aliquid, & quaerit ipse celebris esse: si haec facis, patefacito teipsum mundo.
units.tr: 4. For no one does anything in secret while he himself seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world.

units.la: 5. Nam neque fratres quidem eius credebant in eum.
units.tr: For neither did his brothers believe in him.

units.la: SEquitur consilium fratrum, hoc est cognatorum Christi. Primum est occasio consilij, est autem sumpta ex imminenti festo tabernaculorum. Erat autem hoc festum ex maximè solennibus vnum quod celebrari consueuit in tabernaculis, vel potius tuguriis ex viridibus arborum ramis contextis, in quibus totos septem dies degebant. Vtiliter autem huius festi erat, vt cognoscerent omnes generationes Deum fecisse vt filij Israelis habitarent in Tabernaculis cum eduxit eos ex Aegypto: ac proinde celebrarent memoriam liberationis illius tantae ex Aegypto. Erat autem celebratio memoriae illius liberationis celebrationem perpetuae memoriae liberaq-
units.tr: There follows the advice of his brothers, that is, of Christ's kinsmen. The occasion for the advice was taken from the approaching Feast of Tabernacles. This was one of the most solemn feasts, celebrated in booths, or rather huts, made of green branches woven together, in which they lived for the whole seven days. The purpose of this feast was that all generations should know that God made the children of Israel dwell in booths when he led them out of Egypt, and so should celebrate the memory of that great deliverance from Egypt. That celebration of the memory of that deliverance was a celebration of the perpetual memory of our deliverance through Christ, which ought now to be made in the Church of Christ. On this feast see Leviticus 23:34.

units.la: EE tionis nostri per Christum, quæ nunc in Ecclesia Christi fieri debet. De hoc festo vide Leuitic. 23 34. Sequitur consilium: Summa suasionis hæc est, ut digrederetur Dominus è Galilæa, utpote obscuro loco, & ascenderet in Iudæam. Argumenta suasionis duo sunt: primum est ut discipuli conspiciant opera tua quæ facis. Discipulorum nomine intelliguntur hic non duodecim illi solum, sed & omnes qui concurrerant ex locis & regionibus quibuscunque ad ipsum audiendum. Non est hoc quidem dictum studio vllo vel conuersionis vel confirmationis discipulorum Christi: sed peruerso quodam studio gloriæ & existimationis mundanæ cognati sui, nempe Iesu. Alterum argumentum est ab instituto & consilio quod ipsi falso putarunt Christi cognati sui esse in edendis miraculis suis. Tu quæris, inquiunt, ipse celebris esse. Nemo autem simul in occulto facit aliquid, & quærit ipse celebris esse. Q. d. hæc dissentanea sunt adeo, ut stultum sit velle ea inter se cohærere. Quare ne amplius in occulto facito opera tua, sed patefacito te mundo & prodito in cōspectum populi. Quo loco habemus exemplar quoddam viuum moris & consuetudinis huius sæculi. Quod si forte quis sit, quem Deus imbuit speciali aliqua gratia, siue qua prosit Ecclesiæ, siue qua vtilis sit Reipublicæ, lentur quidem dono hominis omnes eius cognati, quique cum eo aliqua necessitudine coniuncti sunt. Sed quid respiciunt interea? an Deum? an Ecclesiam? an republicam? minimè vero; sed ob oculos habent nomen & existimationem hominis cognati & amici, fortasse etiam suam vel gloriam, vel commoditatem, quæ ad ipsos per talem, tantumque hominem peruenire potest; adeo autem cæcutiunt in iis quæ spectant ad Dei gloriā, vt etiam si sit is homo alioqui studiosus gloriæ Dei, tamen putant eum non aliud spectare, quam quod ipsi spectant. Sic putarunt fratres Christi ipsum captasse inanem istam mundi gloriolam. Atque hinc fit, vt si videat cognatum suum vel amicum, non satis strenuè aliquando venari vel gloriam vel opes huius mundi, familiariter eum adeant, querantur de perdita tam pulchra occasione vel gloriæ vel commoditatis suæ: interea tempori nullum verbum audituri de Deo, de commodo vel Reipu-
units.tr: There follows the advice. The sum of their urging was that the Lord should depart from Galilee, as from an obscure place, and go up into Judea. Their argument for this urging is twofold. The first is: that your disciples may see the works that you do. By "disciples" are understood here not only the twelve, but all who had gathered from whatever places and regions to hear him. This was not said from any zeal for the conversion or confirmation of Christ's disciples, but from a perverse zeal for the glory and worldly esteem of his kinsman, Jesus himself. The second argument is drawn from the aim and purpose which they wrongly supposed Christ's kinsmen had in performing his miracles: for you seek to be known openly, they say. For no one does anything in secret and at the same time seeks to be widely known. That is to say, these things are so inconsistent that it is foolish to want them to cohere. Therefore he should no longer do his works in secret, but reveal himself to the world and come forward before the people. Here we have a living example of the custom and manners of this age. If there happens to be someone whom God has endowed with some special grace, whether one that benefits the Church or one that is useful to the commonwealth, all his kinsmen and all who are joined to him by any tie of relationship rejoice in that man's gift. But what do they look to meanwhile? God? The Church? The commonwealth? By no means; they keep before their eyes the name and reputation of their kinsman or friend, and perhaps also their own glory or advantage, which can come to them through such a man. They are so blinded in matters that concern the glory of God that, even if the man is otherwise zealous for God's glory, they think he aims at nothing but what they themselves aim at. So the brothers of Christ thought that he was seeking that empty little glory of the world. And from this it happens that if they see a kinsman or friend who has not been very eager to hunt after the glory or wealth of this world, they approach him familiarly and complain about the loss of such a fine opportunity for glory or advantage, while meanwhile they will hear not a word about God, about the good of the commonwealth or the Church.

units.la: {1} Carnalis prudentiæ exemplum. Reipublicę, vel Ecclesiæ. Hęc omnia habemus in exemplo hoc fratrum Christi. Ex quo quis non videt donum aliquod speciale diuinitus homini datum, coniunctum esse cum magno periculo, & cum graui tentatione, quæ procedit non tam ab extraneis, quàm à cognatis & necessariis ipsius, qui aliquo modo cum ipso coniuncti sunt? Neque enim pij alicuius viri omnes cognati sunt pij. Neque gratia Dei hæreditaria est, ita vt qui coniunctus est sanguine & natura, cum pio aliquo viro, statim eum participem fieri illius gratiæ & doni pij viri necesse sit. Neque enim hoc contigit Christi ipsius cognatis. Iam verò plurimum valet cognatio ista vel sola cohabitatione. Natura enim omnes lubenter audimus iobis coniunctos sanguine qualescunque demum fuerint, siue boni, siue mali. Ex quo sequitur maius periculum piis esse à cognatis ipsorum, quàm ab extraneis. Neque verò hoc vnquam latuit Satanam, qui his quasi flabellis vtitur ad permouendum animum hominis fortasse nō mali, vel ad auaritiam, vel ad inanem gloriam, vel denique ad flagitiosum aliquid persequendum. Quā- obrem cum diuinitus datum est aliquid supra fratres suos, opus est imprimis ipse studeat sinceritati animi, vt Dei gloriam in actionibus suis & occupationibus quibuscunque nunquam ex oculis sinat discedere, assuefaciatque se perpetuò suauitati illi ac iucunditati, quæ existit ex animo intento diuinæ in Christo gloriæ. Sic enim fiet, vt nihil in vita suaue existimet, neque fructum laborum suorum aliquem se consecutum esse putet, nisi sentiat se Deum in tota vita sua quærere. Quòd si non sit sincero animo quis etiam cum maximo aliquo dono, necesse est is exponatur omnibus istiusmodi tentationibus, & prædæ sit diabolo. Et cum eo bene fuisset actum si nunquam ipsi huiusmodi aliquod Dei donum fuisset concessum.
units.tr: {1} An example of carnal prudence. Of the commonwealth, or of the Church. We have all these things in this example of Christ's brothers. From it, who does not see that some special gift given by God to a man is joined with great danger and severe temptation, which arises not so much from strangers as from his kinsmen and intimates, who are in some way joined to him? For not all the kinsmen of a godly man are godly. Nor is grace hereditary, so that whoever is joined to a godly man by blood and nature must necessarily become a partaker of that grace and gift of the godly man. Indeed, this did not happen to Christ's own kinsmen. Moreover, this kinship has great power even by living together alone. For by nature we all gladly hear of those joined to us by blood, whatever they may be, good or bad. From this it follows that godly people are in greater danger from their own kinsmen than from strangers. Nor has this ever been hidden from Satan, who uses these as it were fans to stir the mind of a man, perhaps not a wicked one, to avarice, to empty glory, or finally to the pursuit of something shameful. Therefore, when something has been given by God above his brothers, he himself must above all strive for sincerity of mind, so that he never allows the glory of God to slip from his eyes in his actions and in whatever occupations he has, and accustoms himself continually to that sweetness and delight which arises from a mind intent on the divine glory in Christ. For so it will come about that he counts nothing pleasant in life, and does not think he has obtained any fruit of his labours, unless he feels that he seeks God in the whole of his life. But if anyone is not of sincere mind, even with some very great gift he must necessarily be exposed to all such temptations and become the prey of the devil. And it would have been better for him if such a gift of God had never been granted to him.

units.la: Hactenus fuit consilium fratrum Christi; nunc Euangelii obiter inserit fundamentum & causam consiliorum perversi. Non, inquit, credebant in eum fratres eius. q. d. Non cognouerunt eum Messiam esse, & Dei viuentis Filium, sed hominem duntaxat sui similem putabant, qui operibus suis miraculosis quæreret sibi gloriam hu-
units.tr: Hitherto we have heard the counsel of Christ's brothers. Now the Gospel briefly sets out the foundation and cause of their perverse counsels: "For neither did his brothers believe in him." That is, as if to say, they did not recognise that he was the Messiah and the Son of the living God, but thought him merely a man like themselves, who by his miraculous works sought glory for himself in this world.

units.la: E e ij ius mundi. In hanc enim partem interpretati sunt fratres Christi omnia & facta & dicta ipsius. Neque enim altius descenderunt opera & verba Christi in animos cognatorum ipsius. Audierunt quidem & viderunt multa, sed nihil profecerunt, ex quo vides multos quidem audire Dei verbum, multos videre Dei opera: sed non nisi paucos audire & videre cum fructu aliquo. Quod non est datum ne Christi quidem ipsius cognatis: ex quo & aliud sequitur; quorum corda non permouentur verbo & operibus Dei, eos pessimos esse aestimatores Dei, voluntatis & operum ac sermonum ipsius, eaque omnia perperam interpretari. Nam certum est assentatores istos principum, qui intersunt coetibus sanctorum non discendi, sed carpendi gratia, certum est verbum Dei nunquam afficere serio animos eorum. Quod si fieret, profecto longe aliter ipsi afficerentur erga ministros Christi. Discis etiam ex hoc loco, cognationem & sanguinis coniunctionem non id statim efficere, ut quis sit vere ac proprie coniunctus cum Christo, dicit enim, Ne fratres quidem eius crederent in eum: hoc est, qui coniuncti erant sanguine, non tamen coniuncti erant cum eo per fidem. Quis igitur dicetur vere coniunctus esse cum Christo? Si quis, inquit Paulus, in Christo est, nova creatura est 2. Corinth. 5. 17. Quare quisquis velit esse propinquus Christi, &c, ut ipse loquutus est, mater Christi, frater Christi, nova creatura sit.
units.tr: For Christ's brothers interpreted all his deeds and words in this sense. Indeed, the works and words of Christ did not sink deeply into the minds of his kinsmen. They heard and saw many things, but gained nothing from them. From this you see that many hear God's Word and many see God's works, but only a few hear and see with any fruit. This was not granted even to Christ's own kinsmen. From this another point follows: where hearts are not moved by God's Word and works, those people are the worst judges of God, of his will, of his works and words, and they interpret all of them wrongly. For it is certain that those flatterers of princes, who attend the assemblies of the saints not to learn but to find fault, are never seriously moved in their minds by the Word of God. If it were otherwise, they would certainly be affected quite differently towards the ministers of Christ. You learn also from this passage that kinship and blood relationship do not at once make a man truly and properly joined to Christ. For it says: "Not even his brothers believed in him." That is, those who were joined to him by blood were not joined to him by faith. Who then will be said to be truly joined to Christ? "If anyone is in Christ," says Paul, "he is a new creature" (2 Cor. 5:17). Therefore whoever wishes to be near to Christ, to be (as he himself put it) mother or brother of Christ, must be a new creature.

units.la: 6 Dicit ergo eis Iesus, Tempus meum nondum adest, tempus autem vestrum semper est paratum.
units.tr: 6 Jesus therefore said to them, My time is not yet come, but your time is always ready.

units.la: 7 Non potest mundus vos odisse: me autem odit, quoniam ego testor de eo, opera eius mala esse.
units.tr: 7 The world cannot hate you, but it hates me, because I testify of it that its works are evil.

units.la: 8 Vos ascendite ad hos dies festos: ego nondum ascendo ad festum, quia tempus meum nondum expletum est.
units.tr: 8 You go up to this feast; I am not yet going up to the feast, because my time is not yet fulfilled.

units.la: 9 Haec autem cum eis dixisset, mansit in Galilaea.
units.tr: 9 When he had said these things to them, he remained in Galilee.

units.la: HAEC Domini responsio est, Non aperte quidem reprehendit iudicium illud fratrum de se & consilium, lium, sed negat se ascensurum ad festum ; id nimirum quod ij consulebant vt faceret, simul etiam permittet eis, vt ipsi, si ita videatur, ad festum ascendant. Vtriusque horum argumentum sequitur, ac primum cur non sit ipse ascensurus, ratio est, quia tempus, inquit, meum nondum adest. Non est hic accipiendum tempus mortis & passionis ipsius, sed tempus ascensionis ad festum proximum. Cuius rursus ratio est, Mundus me odit: cuius denique ratio est, Quia ego testor de mundo quod opera eius mala sunt. Christus inferebat se mundo tanquam lucem, in qua apparuerunt opera tenebrarum, quae prius inuoluta erant tenebris: Vnde eum ferre non potuit mundus. Sunt deinde rationes cur permittat ipsis, vt ascendant ad festum propinquum. Tempus, inquit, vestrum semper est paratum. Cuius rei ratio est, Quia mundus non potest vos odisse, cuius rursus argumentum intelligi potest ex contrario, quia moribus plane similes erant reliquo inundo, neque arguebant opera tenebrarum infrugifera, vt loquitur Apostolus. Vides igitur hic Dominum non ita quidem permittere fratres suos sibi, neque ita secuturum esse ipsorum, vt plane non corrigat eos, quin potius obscure indicat ipsis fontem iudicij sui, & consilij impurum, nempe animum carnalem & mundanum, adhoc vt inspecto fonte consilij ac iudicij sui impuri, discant, quam iniquè iudicent ac peruerse sentiant de ipso, ac mutent animum in melius, ac corrigant ac purgent ia primum ipsum fontem. Ad hanc quoque rem simul demonstrat iis animum suum, quàm sincerus sit & alienus ab omni illa re, ambitione nominatim, quam ipsi temere & falsò imputabant. Nam hoc dum facit, non tantum ipse purgat, verum etiam eos docet ac conatur efficere sibi similes atque conformes. Non enim parum valet ad resipiscentiam ac mutationem animi, si is qui admonet aut reprehendit, simul quoque pium ac sincerum animum indicet ac ponat nobis ob oculos. Ita enim fit vt pudeat nos nostri, simul & conemur similes euadere ei qui nos docet & admonet. Ex quo discimus non ita permittendo esse à nobis malos sibi, vt interea nihil laboremus de eorum conuersione & salute. Deinde putabant fratres Christi nō nisi leve aliquid fuisse Christo ascendere ad festum. Metiebantur nimirum Christum ex se suóque animo. Christus autem radicem huius attingit carnalem animum. Sunt qui leue quid putant esse habere commercium cum hominibus cuiuscunque generis, Papistis, idololatris, homicidis, scortatoribus, deni-que quouis modo prophanis. Quid arguit illud? Animum profecto carnalem & religionem atque mores plane similes religioni ac moribus eorum quibuscum tam facile congregantur. Nam cui purior est animus, cui insidet religio ac veritas altius cordi, eum profecto necesse est ex conscientia delectum facere eorum, quibuscum viuat & commercium habeat. Hac autem. Vt verbo recusauit ascendere ad festum, ita quod dixit facto confirmat: non cedit ergo peruerso cognatorum suorum consilio, neque verbo neque facto. Quare in te Christum imitari debemus, neque verbo neque facto cedendum impiis ac mundanis consiliis, etiam coniunctissimorum hominum, quod non assequemur, nisi is sit affectus in nobis, qui in Christo fuit. Neque omnino eum nisi tanquam simiae poterimus imitari, nisi animo simili modo atque ille fuerimus affecti. Quo autem modo affectus animo fuerit Christus hoc tempore satis intelligi potest ex ipsius responsione, Me odit mundus, quoniam ego testor de eo, opera eius mala esse. Ergo animum habuit Christus non mundanum, sed coelestem ac spiritualem, unde nihil mouit eum mundanum illud eorum consilium, sed eo audito stetit quasi immobilis animo & inconcussò. Sic & animos nostros spirituales ac coelestes euectos supra omnia ista saecularia oportet esse, si futurum sit vnquam vt Christum tam constanti recusatione mundani & peruersi alicuius consilij imitemur. Quòd si carnales simus, quales fuerunt Christi illi fratres ac cognati, citius dicto dabimus locum peruersissimis quibusque consiliis. Quàm enim facile est carnalem animum mouere ad carnalia amplectenda, qui suapte natura eò totus propendet. Quamobrem in id incumbendum est Christiano cuique, vt in mediis tentationibus huius mundi positus, illud imprimis semper sibi quaerat, vt animum habeat spirituale & quantum fieri potest elevatū supra ista omnia inferiora & secularia.
units.tr: This is the Lord's answer. He does not openly rebuke the brothers' judgement about him and their counsel, but he refuses to go up to the feast, which is exactly what they were urging him to do; at the same time he allows them, if they think fit, to go up to the feast themselves. The reasoning behind each of these two points follows. First, why he himself is not going up: the reason is, my time, he says, is not yet come. Here the time of his death and passion is not meant, but the time of going up to the next feast. The reason for this in turn is, the world hates me. Finally, the reason for that is, because I testify of the world that its works are evil. Christ was presenting himself to the world as a light, in which the works of darkness appeared, works which had previously been wrapped in darkness; therefore the world could not bear him. Then there are the reasons why he allows them to go up to the coming feast. Your time, he says, is always ready. The reason for this is, because the world cannot hate you.
