The argument for this in turn can be understood from the opposite: they were entirely similar in their ways to the rest of the world, and did not reprove its unfruitful works of darkness, as the Apostle puts it. You see, then, that the Lord here does not so permit his brothers to do as they please, nor so follow their lead, that he does not correct them at all. Rather, he obscurely points out to them the source of their judgement and their impure counsel, namely a carnal and worldly mind, so that, by examining the source of their impure counsel and judgement, they may learn how unjustly they judge and how perversely they think about him, and may change their minds for the better, and correct and purify that first source. At the same time, by this he also shows them how sincere his own mind is and how far removed from all that ambition in particular, which they rashly and falsely attributed to him. For in doing this he not only purges himself, but also teaches them and tries to make them like himself and conformed to him. For it is no small help towards repentance and a change of mind when the one who admonishes or rebukes also shows and sets before us a pious and sincere mind. In this way we are ashamed of ourselves, and at the same time we strive to become like the one who teaches and admonishes us. From this we learn that we must not so permit those who are evil to remain evil that meanwhile we take no trouble about their conversion and salvation. Next, the brothers of Christ thought that going up to the feast was only a slight matter for Christ. Of course they measured Christ by themselves and their own mind. But Christ touches the root of this, the carnal mind. There are those who think it a light thing to have dealings with men of any kind: Papists, idolaters, murderers, fornicators, in short, profane men of every sort. What does that show? Surely a carnal mind, and a religion and manners entirely like the religion and manners of those with whom they so easily associate. For the one whose mind is purer, in whose heart religion and truth dwell more deeply, must of necessity make a choice from his conscience of those with whom he lives and has dealings. But (he says), as he refused in word to go up to the feast, so he confirms by deed what he said. He therefore yields neither in word nor in deed to the perverse counsel of his kinsmen. Therefore we ought to imitate Christ: neither in word nor in deed should we yield to impious and worldly counsels, even those of the closest men. We shall not achieve this unless the same disposition is in us as was in Christ. Nor can we imitate him at all, except like apes, unless we have been affected in our minds in the same way as he was. How Christ was affected in mind at this time can be well understood from his answer: the world hates me, because I testify of it that its works are evil. So Christ had a mind not worldly but heavenly and spiritual, and therefore that worldly counsel of theirs did not move him at all; on hearing it he stood as if immovable and unshaken in mind. So our minds too must be heavenly and spiritual, raised above all these worldly things, if we are ever to imitate Christ in refusing with such constancy any worldly and perverse counsel. But if we are carnal, like those brothers and kinsmen of Christ, we shall quickly give way to any most perverse counsels whatever. For how easily is a carnal mind moved to embrace carnal things, since by its very nature it leans wholly that way. Therefore every Christian must strive, placed in the midst of the temptations of this world, to seek above all this for himself: that he have a spiritual mind, raised as far as possible above all these lower and worldly things.

units.la: Sed pietatis & iustitiae studiis semper adhaerendū.
units.tr: But one must always cling to the pursuits of piety and righteousness.

units.la: 10 Vt autem ascenderunt fratres eius, tunc & ipse ascendit ad festum, non manifeste, sed velut in occulto.
units.tr: 10 But when his brothers had gone up, then he too went up to the feast, not openly, but as it were in secret.

units.la: 11 Iudæi ergo quærebant eum in festo & dicebant, Vbi est ille?
units.tr: "So the Jews sought him at the feast and said, 'Where is he?'"

units.la: 12 Et murmuratio multa erat in turba de eo: alii quidem dicebant, Vir bonus est: alii vero dicebant, Non, sed seducit.
units.tr: And there was much murmuring about him among the crowd. Some said, "He is a good man"; others said, "No, but he is leading the people astray."

units.la: 13 Nullus tamen palam loquebatur de eo, propter metum Iudæorum.
units.tr: Yet no one spoke openly about him, for fear of the Jews.

units.la: HIc habemus Christum suo tempore ascendisse ad festum: perspecta habuit Dominus singula momenta & opportunitates singulas rerum, quæ agendæ erant ex voluntate Patris sui, & non nisi suo tempore omnia egit: nos non nouimus quidem tempora a Deo præstituta, & momenta quibus vult Deus hoc vel illud geri. Id autem probè nouimus, nullo non tempore bene agendum nobis esse, & nullum autem tempus nobis datum a Deo collocandum in malis actionibus. Sed hic opus est nobis prudentia, qua bonarum actionum, quæ quoque tempore faciendæ sunt delectum faciamus, vnaquæque enim actio suum quoddam tempus habet. Quare hic consulendus est Deus perpetuò & precibus flagitandus, vt nos velit regere omni tempore pro bona sua voluntate. Circumscribitur tempus quo ascendit Dominus, item modus quo ascendit notatur. Circumscriptio temporis est his verbis, Vt ascenderunt autem fratres eius. Neque enim ipsorum tempore, quod semper paratum esse dixit supra versu 6: ascendit, neque voluit secum expectare illud suum tempus, quod dixit nondum adesse, sed permisit eos abire suo ipsorum tempore: ipse autem ascendit sine eorum comitatu suo tempore. Christus non delectatur comitatu eorum quibus omne tempus ex æquo paratum est, & omne commercium æquè acceptum est, ne si fratres quidem ipsius Domini sint. Sed est hic quod miretur aliquis, ibant enim isti ad festum celebrandum, hoc est, ad Deum ex nos esse animatos.
units.tr: Here we have Christ going up to the feast at his appointed time. The Lord perfectly knew every moment and every fitting opportunity for the things that had to be done according to his Father's will, and he did all things only at their proper time. We do not know the times fixed by God, or the moments at which he wills this or that to be done. But we know well that we must always act well, and that no time given to us by God is to be spent on evil deeds. Here, however, we need prudence, by which we choose which good actions are to be done at which time, for every action has its own time. Therefore we must always consult God and beg him in prayer to govern us at every time according to his good will. The time of the Lord's going up is defined, and the manner of his going up is noted. The time is defined by these words: "But when his brothers had gone up." For he did not go up at their time, which (as he said above in verse 6) was always ready for them, nor did he wish to wait with them for his own time, which he said had not yet come. Rather, he let them go at their own time, and he went up at his own time without their company. Christ takes no pleasure in the company of those for whom every time is equally ready and every conversation equally welcome, even if they are the Lord's own brothers. But someone may wonder at this, for those men were going up to celebrate the feast, that is, to worship God in the Church.

units.la: Tertia pars capitis, de profectione Christi ad festum. ipsius præscripto colendum: verùm non erat interea iis sincerus animus. Ne tum quidem igitur Christum itineris socium habebis,cùm accingis te ad ipsum colendum in Ecclesia ipsius, vnà cum sanctis omnibus; nisi sincero sis & sancto animo. Quamobrem hæc duo in omni instituto nostro nobis videnda sunt; Primùm vt quod facis,facias ex Dei voluntate ac mandato, hoc est, facti tui rationem habeas ex verbo & voluntate eius: deinde cùm facis ex verbo & voluntate eius, vt sincerè & ex animo facias quod facis:secus profectò Christum non habebis socium &fautorem actionum tuarum.Notatur deinde modus quo ascendit. Non manifestè,sed velut in occulto,&c. Et hæc quoque pars fuit obedientiæ & humiliationis Domini.Potuit enim palam & apertè ascendere,sed voluit clam,idque in eum finem, vt tu cum siducia procedas ad tribunal Patris sui. Metuit enim sibi ab hominibus, vt tu coram Deo securus posses consistere. Quare nemo sit qui offendatur hac Christi humiliatione. Quòd si quis servõ in se senserit tum huius partis, tum aliarum partium humiliationis ipsius in se structu, profectò tantum aberit ab eo, vt humiliatione ipsius offendatur,vt è contrà de eo maximè glorietur. Absit, inquit Paulus,gloriari nisi in cruce Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: The third part of the chapter concerns Christ's journey to the feast, to be kept according to his prescription; but meanwhile these men did not have a sincere mind. Therefore you will not have Christ as your companion on the journey either, when you prepare to worship him in his Church together with all the saints, unless you have a sincere and holy mind. Hence in every undertaking of ours two things must be seen to. First, that what you do, you do according to God's will and command; that is, you must have the reason for your deed from his word and will. Second, when you do what you do according to his word and will, you must do it sincerely and from the heart. Otherwise you will certainly not have Christ as companion and supporter of your actions. Next the manner of his going up is noted: not openly, but as if in secret, etc. This too was a part of the Lord's obedience and humiliation. For he could have gone up publicly and openly, but he chose to go secretly, and to this end, that you may go forward with confidence to the judgment seat of his Father. For he feared men on your behalf, so that you could stand secure before God. Therefore let no one be offended by this humiliation of Christ. But if anyone perceives in himself the working of this part and of the other parts of Christ's humiliation, he will certainly be so far from being offended by his humiliation that, on the contrary, he will glory in it most of all. "Far be it," says Paul, "that I should glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ."

units.la: Et Christum crucifixum Iudæis quidem offendiculum; Græcis verò stultitiam, ipsis vocatis dicit esse Dei potentiam ac Dei sapientiam. Vocatos autem intelligit eos qui fructum crucis ipsius in se percipiunt, qui vitam ex morte eius hauriunt. Videas hic latum discrimen inter Christum & fratres eius: Christus timidè ascendit, illi securè. Hic est typus quidam discriminis quodam inter pios & impios in hac vita. Pij cum timore versantur in hoc mundo.Nam omnia loca sunt quasi spinis tentationum strata, vixque pedem suum desigere possunt in aliqua parte quin pungantur. Impij verò confidenter ac securè viuunt ac versantur cum quibuscunque, cum adulteris,cum homicidis, cum latronibus, cum blasphemis, quia pares cum paribus facillimè congregantur. Sed rursus latum est discrimen inter eos. Christus quo tempore ascendit ad festum, habuit fiduciam suam in Deo suo collocatam, cognati verò eius minimè. Nam hoc certum est(vtrum autem mauis elige)quod si mundo pax est,inimicitię sunt cum Deo.Quod si id non statim intelligant homines, improbis nullam esse pacem, de vera pace loquor, in causa est sopita ista conscientia, quæ tandem suo tempore expergefiet.
units.tr: And Paul says that Christ crucified is indeed a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks, but to those who are called he is the power and wisdom of God. By "those who are called" he means those who receive the fruit of his cross in themselves and draw life from his death. Here you may see a wide difference between Christ and his brothers: Christ went up timidly, they boldly. This is a certain type of the difference between the godly and the ungodly in this life. The godly live in this world with fear, for all places are, as it were, strewn with the thorns of temptation, and they can scarcely set their foot down anywhere without being pricked. The ungodly, however, live and move about confidently and securely with whoever they meet: with adulterers, murderers, robbers, blasphemers, because like gathers readily with like. Yet again there is a wide difference between them. When Christ went up to the feast, he had placed his trust in his God; his kinsmen certainly had not. For this is certain (choose whichever you prefer): if there is peace with the world, there is enmity with God. If men do not at once understand that there is no peace for the wicked, I speak of true peace; the cause is that this conscience is lulled to sleep, but at its own time it will finally wake up.

units.la: Iudæi ergo. Hic Iohannes narrat quid rerum gereret Iudæi qui festo intererant, interea dum Christus ascenderet ad festum non manifeste sed velut in occulto. quæ-rebant, inquit, tum in festo, & dicebant, Vbi est ille? Qui enim requirebant erant illi quidem qui soliti erant ab eo pe-rɛcùm versaretur in Iudæa, præsertim temporibus solennibus & festis diebus: nunc itaque eum absentem requirunt. Vox ea quam tum vsurparunt satis indicat eos non satis diligenter & ex animo eum quæsiuisse. Est enim satis frigida. Vbi, inquiunt, est ille? Quod si ferio Messiæ sensu ac desiderio fuissent tacti, profecto vox eum requirentium magis sollicita & seria fuisset. Sunt hodierno etiam die qui Christum, qui Euangelium ipsius, qui Euangelij ministros requirunt ac desiderant, sed frigidè & perfunctoriè: cùm ne vel minimam partem temporalium istorum commutarent cum spiritualibus illis. Quod si eos serio moveret Euangelium illud gloriosum beati Dei, vel vniuersum hunc mundum, ac vitam ipsam cum eo commutarent. Expetite, inquit Petrus, sincerum illud lac sermonis, ut per illud adolescatis. Tum addit continuò, Siquidem gustastis quàm benignus sit Dominus. Qua quidem conditione satis innuit, non nisi eos qui gustant suavitatem illam Domini, posse serio expetere & desiderare sermonem illum. Et mussitatio multa. Hoc alterum est quod ab iis fiebat interea dum Christus ascenderet ad festum: murmurabant inter se multum, & murmurando sententias de Christo diuersas imò contradicentes proferebant. Alij dicebant virum bonum esse, alij vero dicebant non esse virum bonum, verùm seductorem. Ex hoc conii-cere poteris, quinam fuerint affectus quaerentium eum, cùm maior pars seductorem eum dixerit non obscurè: verùm sunt ex iis aliqui, qui rectius de eo sentiunt, eúmque virum bonum esse dicunt. Ex quo discε nullum esse populum, qui aliquid de Christo semel inaudiuit, quin ex eo aliqui saltem reperiantur quorum animi a-liquo certè modo incipiant ad eum inclinari, etiam tũ cùm eum non nisi obscurè admodum cognoscunt. Est enim nescio quæ secreta Christi efficacia in cordibus etiam idiotarum. Qua fit vt ad ipsum cum confusa quadam ipsius notitia inflectantur eorum animi. Christus enim ipse fuit, qui occulta quadam vi sua hoc discrimine fecit inter eos qui cum bonum virum esse, & eos qui seductorem cum murmurabant. Nam vt dicam de motu ac sensu cordis eorum quotquot aliquid de Deo in Christo sapiunt, maior est fere motus ac sensus qui in corde est, notitia & cognitione quæ in mente est. Vnde Petrus, quem cum non videritis, diligitis, quem cum nunc non cernatis, en tamen credentes, exultatis gaudio ineffabili ac gloriosò. Quo profecto significatur gaudium illud quod nunc ex fide est maius esse aspectu & cognitione. Ideo ineffabile gaudium dicitur ac gloriosum. Suspiria subministrata nobis à Spiritu sancto inenarrabilia dicuntur, vt scias sensum cordis ineffabilem esse ac incomprehensibilem. Quod si igitur tantum sit nunc gaudium, tantus motus in corde, ex tam tenui & obscuro intellectu, quantus erit tum motus, quantum gaudium, ex tam pleno intuitu Dei nostri in Christo Iesu?
units.tr: "So the Jews." Here John tells what the Jews who were present at the feast were doing while Christ went up to the feast not openly but as if in secret. "They sought him," he says, "at the feast, and said, 'Where is he?'" For those who were seeking him were indeed those who had been used to attend him while he was active in Judea, especially at the solemn times and feast days. Now, therefore, they seek him in his absence. The phrase they then used sufficiently shows that they did not seek him very diligently or with their whole heart, for it is rather cold: "Where is he?" they say. If they had been touched by a serious longing for the Messiah, the voice of those seeking him would surely have been more anxious and earnest. Even today there are those who seek and long for Christ, his gospel, and the ministers of his gospel, but coldly and perfunctorily, since they would not exchange even the smallest part of these temporal things for those spiritual ones. If that glorious gospel of the blessed God, or indeed this whole world and life itself, seriously moved them, they would exchange them for it. "Desire," says Peter, "the pure milk of the word, that by it you may grow." Then he adds at once, "If indeed you have tasted how gracious the Lord is." By this condition he sufficiently hints that only those who taste that sweetness of the Lord can earnestly desire and long for that word. "And much murmuring." This is the second thing they did while Christ was going up to the feast: they murmured much among themselves and, by murmuring, put forward opinions about Christ that were diverse and even contradictory. Some said he was a good man, others said he was not a good man but a deceiver. From this you may guess what the feelings of those seeking him were, since most of them openly called him a deceiver; yet among them there were some who judged him more rightly and said that he was a good man. From this we learn that there is no people which has once heard anything about Christ in which there are not at least some whose minds begin, in some way, to incline toward him, even while they know him only dimly. For there is, I know not what, secret efficacy of Christ even in the hearts of the unlearned, by which their minds are turned toward him through some confused notion of him. Indeed Christ himself, by a certain hidden power, made this distinction between those who said he was a good man and those who murmured that he was a deceiver. For to speak of the motion and feeling of the heart of all who have some understanding of God in Christ, the motion and feeling which is in the heart is generally greater than the knowledge and understanding which is in the mind. Hence Peter says, "Whom not having seen you love; in whom, though now you do not see him, yet believing, you rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory." By this he surely signifies that the joy which now comes from faith is greater than sight and knowledge. Therefore it is called unspeakable and glorious joy. The groanings supplied to us by the Holy Spirit are called unutterable, so that you may know that the feeling of the heart is inexpressible and incomprehensible. If, then, there is so great a joy now, so great a motion in the heart, from so slight and obscure an understanding, how great will be the motion, how great the joy, from the full sight of our God in Jesus Christ?

units.la: Nullus tamen. Causam affert cur murmurarint, non autem aperte loquuntur. Est autem, quod interdictum fuerit iis ne vel in ore semel haberent nomen illud Iesu, qui autem interdixerunt fuerunt principes Iudæorum, quos Iudæorum generali nomine hic intelligimus. Ex quo coniicere poteris, quo fuerint isti Principes Iudæorum animo erga Christum. Oportet sane in iis ipsis primum omnium extinctus fuerit omnis sensus Christi, & sepulta omnis ipsius memoria: vel certè in id eos incubuisse vt nullus esset ipsius sensus in se, nulla memoria: Vnde perspicuum est quanta in iis malitia fuerit: qua oppresserunt non modò lucem illam Christi in se, sed in aliis quoque. Verum quidem id est, cæci sunt duces cæcorum, sed cæcitatis & malitiæ discrimen est magnum: nam maior est perpetuo malitia in iis, qui ducunt cæcos, in iis vero qui ducuntur maior est simplicitas: et si non careant illi quoque sua quadam malitia. Maior fuit simplicitas in populo Iudaeorum; maior fuit malitia in principibus qui viderunt, neque tamen voluerunt videre. Ideo enim dixit Christus peccatum eorum manere. Sic maior est malitia doctorum & ducum caecorum, qui hodierno die in Papistino sunt; vulgi vero miseri maior est simplicitas. Nam illi neque ingredi regnum caelorum ipsi voluit, neque alios ingredi patiuntur. Pro culdubio enim, si vulgus illud Papistarum permitteretur sibi, neque coerceretur illis tormentis, inquisitionibus, aliisque id genus, transiret tandem ad lucem. Vtut est, quidam ex iis murmurant, & murmurant quidem in partem meliorem, ut tum ex Iudaeis nonnulli fecerunt. Deus illos liberet illa tanta tyrannide, & nos gratos sibi faciat ob tantam nostri liberationem. Nota deinde, misera fuit ista tum Ecclesiae Iudaicae facies, quae sola tam Ecclesia visibilis in terris extitit, misera, inquit, tum fuit etiam in luce praesentis Christi, vulgus Iudaeorum tantum de eo murmurabant, & ex iis plerique in peiorem partem. Pauci autem in meliorem, dicentes quod vir bonus esset. Principes metu opprimebant vulgus, eoque arguebant infidelitatem suam & cordis sui malitiam adversus Christum. Quare tum completum est illud quod praedictum est a Propheta, Quis credidit praedicationi nostrae & brachium Iehovae in quo revelatur? Hic si fingas ex prophanis gentibus quenquam voluisse tum se adiungere Ecclesiae Dei, quamnam habuisset tum in tanta confusione Iudaicae Ecclesiae, quae tum eo solo nomine gaudebat, quamnam, inquit, habuisset veræ Ecclesiae notam externam, qua admonitus potuisset se ad Ecclesiam Dei aggregare? Papista aliquis hic responderet, multitudinem vel iudicium multitudinis ei pro certissima verae Ecclesiae nota esse potuisse. Tum profecto cum multitudine Iudaeorum oportuisset miserum negare Christum. Puteat eos tandem istiusmodi notarum, quas defendunt verae Ecclesiae, neque pendeat amplius ex multitudinis iudicio, sed ex Dei ipsius verbo; quod quidem si sincere sonuerit in Ecclesia, & sacramentis sincere administratis confirmatum fuerit, firmius est ac certius indicium verae ac visibilis Ecclesiae, quam sunt omnia illa, quae ab iis afferri solent. Tertio observua, Iudaei hoc tempote multis malis ac miseriis oppressi, auidè quidem expectabant Messiam qui futurus erat liberator: sese tamen offerentem reiiciebant. Quae autem causa? quia talem Christum non expectabant, tam humilem, & tam in speciem abiectum. Facile est & propè naturale desiderare Christum, hoc est liberatorem & vindicem, sed natura non acquiescit in illo Christo, illa iustitia, illa salute quam Deus offert. Hinc fit vt hodierno die plerique iustitiam operum suorum, non illam gratuitam ac imputatam, salutem ex operibus suis, non merito Christi solo, sibi expectant. Quam obrem nobis ad id est enitendum, non tam vt desideremus redemptionem in Christo, quàm vt coquiescamus totis animis in ea quam Deus offert redemptione. Et nos ipsos ac nostram sapientiam omnem abnegantes ad hoc vt sit locus in negotio salutis nostrae soli Dei sapientiae quae ψυχικός & animalibus hominibus videtur stultitia. Quod qui faciant, etsi nunc non clarè ac manifestè videant causas illas cur Deo sit visum sic nobiscum agere: tamen & nunc sentient effectum causarum illarum, vtpote novam illam vitam in se inchoari, & illo die complementum percipient.
units.tr: Nullus tamen. He gives the reason why they murmured but did not speak openly. It had been forbidden them to so much as have the name of Jesus on their lips, even once. Those who forbade it were the rulers of the Jews, whom we here understand under the general name of Jews. From this you may guess what the rulers' disposition towards Christ was. Surely in them every sense of Christ must first have been extinguished and every memory of him buried, or at least they had set themselves to ensure that there was in them no sense of him and no memory. Hence it is plain how great the malice in them was, which suppressed that light of Christ not only in themselves but in others too. It is true that the blind are leaders of the blind, but the difference between blindness and malice is great. Malice is always greater in those who lead the blind, while simplicity is greater in those who are led, although even they are not free from a certain malice of their own. There was greater simplicity in the people of the Jews, and greater malice in the rulers, who saw and yet would not see. For this reason Christ said that their sin remains. So the malice of the teachers and blind leaders who today are in Papistry is greater, but among the wretched common people there is greater simplicity. For those men neither wished to enter the kingdom of heaven themselves nor allow others to enter. Doubtless, if that crowd of Papists were left to itself and not restrained by those torments, inquisitions and the like, it would at last pass over to the light. However that may be, some of them murmur, and they murmur indeed in a better direction, as some of the Jews did then. May God deliver them from that great tyranny, and make us pleasing to him for so great a deliverance of ours. Note next that wretched was the face of the Jewish Church then, which alone was then the visible Church on earth. Wretched, he says, it was even in the light of Christ's presence: the common people of the Jews only murmured about him, and most of them in the worse direction, and few in the better, saying that he was a good man. The rulers oppressed the people with fear, and by this they displayed their unbelief and the malice of their heart against Christ. Therefore that was fulfilled which was foretold by the prophet: Who has believed our preaching, and to whom is the arm of Jehovah revealed? Here, if you imagine that someone from the profane nations had then wished to join himself to the Church of God, what would he have had, in the great confusion of the Jewish Church, which then rejoiced in that name alone? What, he asks, would he have had as the external mark of the true Church, by which, being admonished, he could have joined himself to the Church of God? Some Papist would here answer that the multitude, or the judgment of the multitude, could have been for him the most certain mark of the true Church. Then indeed, along with the multitude of Jews, he would have had to deny Christ to his own wretchedness. Let them be ashamed to any longer rely on marks of that kind, which they defend as marks of the true Church, and let them no longer depend on the judgment of the multitude but on God's own Word. If that Word sounds sincerely in the Church, and the sacraments are sincerely administered, it is a firmer and more certain sign of the true and visible Church than all those things which they are wont to bring forward. Thirdly, observe: the Jews at this time, oppressed by many evils and miseries, eagerly expected the Messiah who was to come as liberator, yet they rejected him when he offered himself. What was the cause? Because they did not expect such a Christ, so humble and so abject in appearance. It is easy and almost natural to desire Christ, that is, a liberator and avenger, but nature does not rest in that Christ, in that righteousness and that salvation which God offers. Hence it happens that today most men look for the righteousness of their own works, not that free and imputed righteousness, and expect salvation from their own works rather than from the merit of Christ alone. Therefore we must strive for this: not so much that we desire redemption in Christ, as that we rest with all our souls in that redemption which God offers. We must deny ourselves and all our own wisdom, so that there may be room in the business of our salvation for the wisdom of God alone, which seems foolishness to the psychic [ψυχικός] and animal men. Those who do this, even if they do not now clearly and manifestly see the causes why God has been pleased to deal with us in this way, will nonetheless feel even now the effect of those causes, namely that a new life is begun in them, and on that day they will receive its completion.

units.la: 14 Festo autem illo iam medio ascendit Iesus in templum, ac docebat.
units.tr: 14 But when the feast was now half over, Jesus went up into the temple and taught.

units.la: 15 Et mirabantur Iudaei dicētes, Quomodo iste literas nouit, quum eas non didicerit?
units.tr: 15 And the Jews marvelled, saying, How does this man know letters, when he has never been taught?

units.la: 16 Respondit eis Iesus & dixit, Mea doctrina non est mea, sed eius qui misit me.
units.tr: 16 Jesus answered them and said, My doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me.

units.la: 17 Si quis voluerit quod ille vult facere, cognoscet de doctrina, vtrum ex Deo sit, an ego à me ipso loquar.
units.tr: 17 If anyone is willing to do his will, he will know concerning the doctrine whether it is of God, or whether I speak of myself.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Hactenus inserta sunt ea quae Iudaei agebant, interea dum Christus vel in itinere esset, vel nondum in publicum prodiret: nunc verò redimus ad ascensionem Christi quae fuit cū iam medium ageretur festū, die festi circiter quarto. Tum itaq; prodiit Christus in publicū, neque diutius latere voluit, verum se contulit in locum vrbis maximè celebrem, Templum: neque eò cùm venisset silere voluit: in occulto ascendit. Ingressus autem vrbem tandem in locum maximè frequentem ac celebrem venit, ibique omnibus audientibus docuit. Christus vitæ suæ curam non agebat, cùm officium ipsum vrgebat & offerente se occasione seruandi aliquos & glorificandi Patrem suum occasioni vitam postposuit. Debent quidem pij curam agere vitæ suæ, sed ita vt curailla stet cum officio, imò verò vt inseruiat officio. Nam propter officium data est vita ista, & quæ vitæ inseruiunt omnia, vt sapientia, honores, diuitiæ, vt nimirum Deo nostro inseruiamus prout postulat officij ratio. Quòd sanè vita nonnunquam videatur impedimento esse officio, tum abiicienda est vita & Deo committenda: imò verò redimenda est occasio agendi ex officio rebus quibusque in vita charissimis. Neque enim rectè sentiunt ij qui non putant offerri occasionem officij faciendi, nisi tum cùm vita est in tuto. Paulus dixit alicubi ostium sibi magnum apertum fuisse, hoc est occasionem prædicandi Euangelium oblatam fuisse egregiam, sed inimicos fuisse permultos; qua quidem re significauit se vix potuisse redimere oblatam illam occasionem tam pulchram, nisi vitæ præsentis dispendio. Quare sic statuendum est vnicuique qui velit fideliter fungi officio, moriendum prius, quàm non faciendum officium; Maledictus enim qui facit opus Iehouæ negligenter. Et mirabantur Iudæi. Hic transit ad mutuum illum sermonem qui habitus est inter Christum & Iudæos. Occasio autem eius habetur his verbis: Mirabantur, inquit, Iudæi. Causa addita est, quia Christus qui non didicerat litteras, eas tamen nouit, mirabantur dicit, non autem dicit, credebant iis quæ dicebat Christus; aliud enim est mirari, aliud credere: mirantur quidem fideles, sed non eo incredduli, modo, cùm enim in admirationem operum verborum Dei rapiuntur, ea quoque interea impressionem aliquam faciunt in cordibus eorum, & ad credendum ac glorificandum Deum excitant. Vide Paulum, postquam admiratus est Dei sapientiam illam inscrutabilem, qua omnes in contumacia concluserit, vt omnium misereretur, & deinceps tũ ex fide & serio glo-
units.tr: Hitherto we have inserted what the Jews were doing while Christ was either on his journey or had not yet come out in public. Now, however, we return to Christ's going up to the feast, which took place when the festival was already half over, about the fourth day of the feast. So Christ came out in public, and he no longer wished to remain hidden. He made his way into the most crowded and famous place in the city, the Temple. Nor, having come there, did he wish to keep silent; he went up in secret, but once he had entered the city he came at last into the most crowded and renowned place and taught there in the hearing of all. Christ took no thought for his own life when duty pressed upon him. When the occasion offered itself of saving some and glorifying his Father, he set his life aside. The godly ought indeed to take care of their lives, but in such a way that this care agrees with their duty, indeed that it serves their duty. For this life was given for the sake of duty, and all the things that serve life, such as wisdom, honours and riches, serve so that we may serve our God as the reasoning of our duty requires. Certainly, if life sometimes seems to be an obstacle to duty, then life must be cast aside and committed to God; indeed, the opportunity of acting from duty must be bought at the cost of whatever is dearest to us in life. Those who do not think that an opportunity of doing their duty is offered unless their life is safe do not think rightly. Paul said somewhere that a great door had been opened to him, that is, an excellent opportunity of preaching the gospel was offered, but that there were very many adversaries; by which he indicated that he could hardly have bought that fine opportunity except at the cost of his present life. Therefore, anyone who wishes to discharge his duty faithfully must settle it thus: he must be ready to die rather than leave the duty undone, for "cursed is he who does the work of the LORD negligently." And the Jews were amazed. Here he passes to the mutual discourse that took place between Christ and the Jews. The occasion of it is given in these words: "The Jews were amazed," he says. The cause is added, because Christ, who had not been taught letters, nevertheless knew them. He says they were amazed; he does not say they believed the things Christ said, for to be amazed is one thing, to believe another. The faithful indeed are amazed, but not in the unbelieving way. For when they are carried away in wonder at the works and words of God, these things also make some impression on their hearts meanwhile and stir them to believe and to glorify God. See Paul: after he had marvelled at the inscrutable wisdom of God, by which he shut up all in disobedience so that he might have mercy on all, he then broke out, from faith and with earnest zeal, into the glorifying of God.

units.la: Ierem. 48. 10.
Occasio huius colloquii.
units.tr: The occasion of this conversation.

units.la: Rom. 11. riæ Dei studio erupit in ipsius glorificationem. Ipsi, inquit, sit gloria in seculum, Amen. At verò infideles dum mirantur vel inspectis Dei operibus, vel audito eius verbo non mouentur solido aliquo sensu cordis, sed & sensus quodammodo expertes redduntur; imò excutitur illis quasi mens, vt verbum Græcum ἐξίστανται sonat, quod in hunc sensum vsurpatum est, Matth. 7.28. & alibi. Causa autem admirationis est, quia vident opus extra ordinem fieri, vt hoc loco vident Christum docere, qui tamen literas non didicit, non tamen attollunt oculos altius ad Deum, agnoscuntque hoc ab eo extra ordinem factum esse: Vnde Christus ipse istos deducit postea ad causam doctrinæ tam admirabilis, nempe Deum, à quo etiam extra ordinem eam accepit. Nonnunquam etiamcum admiratione offenduntur in Christum, vt Nazarethani percelluntur quidem doctrina Christi, sed tamen ea offenduntur: Causa autem offensionis est, quia animum præiudicio aliquo habent præoccupatum. Quamobrem nos ne tantùm in admiratione operum & verborum Dei raptamur, & stupidi reddamur atque attoniti ex iis inspectis & auditis: verum sentiamus interea penitus corde ea quæ vel facit vel loquitur Deus admirada, & credamus in ipsum cum gaudio ineffabili. Id autem fiet, si animum erigamus altius ad Deum ipsum, eius sapientiam, eius potentiá, &c. Vnde hæc quæ vel facit, vel loquitur omnia sunt profecta; siqúe animum habeamus expurgatum præiudiciis istis, quæ faciunt vt homines impingant atque offendantur, Beatus, inquit Christus, qui non offensus fuerit in me.
units.tr: Rom. 11. ...to the glory of God, with earnest zeal, breaking out into his praise: "To him, he says, be glory for ever, Amen." But unbelievers, when they are amazed, either at the works of God when they look upon them or at his word when they hear it, are not moved by any solid sense of the heart. Rather, they are in some way deprived of their senses; indeed, their mind is, as it were, shaken out of them, as the Greek word ἐξίστανται [they are beside themselves] signifies, a word used in this sense at Matt. 7.28 and elsewhere. The cause of their amazement is that they see a work done beyond the ordinary course, as they see Christ teaching here although he had not learned letters. Yet they do not lift their eyes higher to God, and they do not acknowledge that this was done beyond the ordinary course by him. For this reason Christ himself afterwards leads them on to the cause of so wonderful a teaching, namely God, from whom he also received it beyond the ordinary course. Sometimes they are even offended at Christ with amazement, as the Nazarenes were struck by the teaching of Christ but were nevertheless offended by it. The cause of the offence is that they have their minds occupied beforehand by some prejudice. Wherefore let us not only be carried away in admiration at the works and words of God, and become dumbfounded and astonished at what we have seen and heard; rather, let us meanwhile feel deep in our hearts that the things God does or says are admirable, and believe in him with inexpressible joy. This will happen if we raise our minds higher to God himself, to his wisdom, his power, and so on. From him all the things he does or says have come forth. And if we keep our minds cleansed of those prejudices which make men stumble and take offence, then "Blessed, says Christ, is he who is not offended in me."

units.la: Respondit Christus.
units.tr: Christ replies.

units.la: Christus sola admiratione eorum quæ fide permixta non fuit non contentus (quod quidem exemplum ministris Euangelij sequendum est, iis præsertim qui supra alios donis Spiritus sancti eminet) ideo patefacta causa doctrinæ suæ, ostensóque vndenam ea esset, conatur eorum cordibus solidiorem fidem inigenere. Mea, inquit, doctrina non est mea: Hoc est, doctrina quam ego doceo non est mea, neque solius, neque primum: Sed eius qui misit me: Hoc est, etiam Patris est doctrina, & quidem Patris est primum. Huius sermonis & aliorum huic similium hæc causa videtur: Pater vocauit ad ad officium Mediatoris Filium suum, vt Deum quidem ab æterno, vt hominem verò ab vtero matris. Vocatio autem in eo fuit posita, quòd communicauit illi omnē gratiam supra mensuram. Hinc fit vt Filius omnia quæ in vocatione illa sua à Patre accepit, Patri accepta referret, & gloriam eorum ipsi deferre soleat, cuius rei multa exstant exempla. Interea autem persōnæ suæ authoritatem conciliat, dum se à Patre missum esse ait; neque enim satis est, si quis proferat Dei verbū & doctrinam, nisi etiam à Deo missus sit, hoc est, legitimam habeat vocationem qua id faciat: id quidem ostendi experientia auditoris: nam fides auditoris ad duo solet dirigi, primò ad Deum ipsum authorem doctrinæ, deinde ad hominem à Deo vocatum & missum, huius vocationem nisi legitimā & à Deo esse constiterit, profecto de fide illa quæ habenda est sermoni ipsius nonnihil detrahitur. Quare ei qui vult cum fructu docere, attendendum, non solùm vt nihil offerat, nisi quod habet ex verbo Dei, sed etiam vt confirmatam apud se habeat vocationem suam. Quare semper ei consulendus est Deus, videndùmque priusquam quid proferat, vt à Deo quasi proferendi illud, venia quasi impetretur, hoc est, aliquo modo constet de ipsius voluntate, nunquid velit nos Deus loqui suo nomine.
units.tr: Christ was not content with the mere admiration of those whose wonder was not mixed with faith. (This example ought to be followed by the ministers of the Gospel, especially by those who excel others in the gifts of the Holy Spirit.) So he reveals the cause of his teaching and shows where it comes from, and he tries to produce a firmer faith in their hearts. My teaching, he says, is not mine: that is, the teaching I give is not mine, nor mine alone, nor originally mine, but his who sent me: that is, the teaching is also the Father's, and indeed it is the Father's first. The reason for this saying and others like it seems to be this: the Father called his own Son to the office of Mediator, as God from eternity and as man from his mother's womb. The calling consisted in this, that the Father gave him all grace beyond measure. Hence the Son refers to the Father everything he received from the Father in that calling, and he is accustomed to ascribe their glory to the one from whom they came, as many examples show. Meanwhile he establishes the authority of his person when he says that he was sent by the Father. For it is not enough that someone proclaims the Word and teaching of God unless he has also been sent by God, that is, has a lawful calling to do so. This is shown by the experience of hearers, for the faith of a hearer is usually directed in two ways: first to God himself, the author of the teaching, and then to the man called and sent by God. If it is not established that this man's calling is lawful and from God, then surely some of the faith that ought to be given to his preaching is taken away. Therefore one who wishes to teach with profit must take care not only to offer nothing except what he has from the Word of God, but also to have his own calling assured. Hence God must always be consulted, and before he puts anything forward, he must see to it that he obtains, as it were, leave from God to proclaim it; that is, it must in some way be established what the will of God is, whether God wishes us to speak in his name.

units.la: Si quis voluerit. Non satis habet Dominus illud semel admonuisse, suam doctrinam à Deo esse, nisi rationem quoque qua id sciant, ac veritatem à falsitate internoscant, ipsis ostendat. Est enim natura nostra adeo hebes, vt nisi omnibus modis adducamur ad veritatem cognoscendam & oculis quasi obiectam habeamus, non magis valeamus de ea iudicare, quàm cæcus de coloribus. Ratio qua cognosci potest doctrina Dei, & veritas ipsa duplex est: Prior est in ipso homine, studium nempe cognoscendi voluntatem Dei, & iam cognitam faciendi. Posterior est in doctrina ipsa, si doctrina ad Deum ante omnia referatur eumque glorisicet. De priori igitur sic ait, Si quis voluerit, &c. Hoc est, voluntatem atque animi propensionem habuerit ad seruiendum & obediendum Deo: Is cognoscet de doctrina, &c. id est, internoscet inter veram doctrinam & falsam, veramque à falsa discernet. Nota igitur: via recte iudicandi de doctrina est, si praeparetur animus studio placendi Deo & faciendi ipsius voluntatem. Scimus id natura, gustum bene affectum bene iudicare de ciborum sapore: malè verò affectum ac noxio aliquo humore vitiatum malè iudicare. Sic animus bene ac pie affectus erga Deum, recte iudicat de verbo Dei, qui est cibus animi: malè verò affectus animus, vanus ac prophanus, malè iudicat de doctrina quavis, ac imbibit continuò doctrinam quamque venenolam. Quae enim causa alia esse potest cur maior pars mundi infecta sit hodierno die mendaciis ac haeresibus exitialibus, papismo autem imprimis, peste nimirum illa vniuersali & maximè contagiosa, quae, inquam, causa potest esse alia, nisi quia animi hominum non fuerunt praeparati studio illo cognoscendi voluntatem Dei, eamque iam cognitam exequendi. Pro eo, inquit Apostolus, quod non receperunt amorem veritatis ut salui fierent, propterea mittit illis Deus efficaciam deceptionis ut credant mendacio. Et illud equidem audeo certò polliceri, quòd quisquis sit, qui ex animo velit cognoscere veritatem Dei, & secundum eam viuere, is vel non imbibiturus sit omnino illas haereses, vel, si etiam contigerit eum aliquo modo iis infici & seduci à veritate, & non permansurus sit in ea caecitate ad finem vsque; sed tandem aliquando ex ea emersurus sit, & ad lucem peruenturus. Quare quàm necessarius sit ad cognitionem animus piè sanctéque affectus, vel ex his quae diximus cognosci potest. Neque verò illud praetereundum est quòd argumenti huius quod sumptum est ab interiori cordis affectione & ad Dei obedientiam propensione, primùm fecerit mentionem: eo enim argumentorum ordine & collocatione plane significat, quòd cùm plures sint rationes perueniendi ad veritatis cognitionem, hanc ex omnibus primam esse: etsi Papistae principalem ac fere vnicam cognoscendae veritatis rationem dicitent, authoritatem ac testimonium Ecclesiae suae Romanae. Verùm, vt eos sibiipsis permittamus, asserimus nos non prius posse quemquam discernere veritatem Dei quae est in verbo scripto, quàm animus sanctificatus sit aliquo modo ac praeparatus eodem illo Spiritu qui loquitur in verbo. Tantùm valet habere animum praeparatum pio studio & amore veritatis cognoscendæ! Non autem statim id obtinetur, sed ad id opus est diutina ac multa mortificatione sapientiæ carnis ac affectuum nostrorum, quæ inimicitiæ sunt adversus Deum.
units.tr: If anyone wills. The Lord does not think it enough to have once admonished that his teaching is from God, unless he also shows them the reason by which they may know this and distinguish truth from falsehood. For our nature is so dull that unless we are led to know the truth in every way and have it set before our eyes, as it were, we are no better able to judge of it than a blind man is of colours. The way by which the teaching of God, and the truth itself, can be known is twofold. The first lies in the man himself: namely, the eagerness to know the will of God and, once known, to do it. The second lies in the teaching itself, if the teaching is referred above all to God and glorifies him. So of the first he says: If anyone wills, and so on; that is, if he has the will and inclination of mind to serve and obey God. He will know concerning the teaching, and so on; that is, he will discern between true teaching and false, and separate the true from the false. Note, then, that the way to judge rightly about teaching is for the mind to be prepared by the zeal to please God and to do his will. We know by nature that a palate well disposed judges well the flavour of food, while one that is badly disposed and spoiled by some harmful humour judges badly. So a mind well and piously disposed towards God judges rightly about the Word of God, which is the food of the mind; but a mind badly disposed, empty and profane, judges badly about any teaching whatever, and soaks up continually every poisonous doctrine. For what other cause can there be why the greater part of the world today is infected with lies and deadly heresies, and above all with Popery, that universal and most contagious plague, I say, what other cause can there be, except that the minds of men have not been prepared by that zeal to know the will of God and to carry it out once known? Because, says the Apostle, they did not receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved, therefore God sends them the power of deception, so that they should believe a lie. And indeed I dare to promise with certainty that whoever he may be who sincerely wishes to know the truth of God and to live according to it, he will either not soak up those heresies at all, or, if it should happen that he is in some way infected by them and led away from the truth, he will not remain in that blindness to the end, but will at last emerge from it and come to the light. Hence how necessary a mind piously and holily disposed is for knowledge can be seen even from what we have said. Nor must it be passed over that he first made mention of this argument, which is taken from the inner affection of the heart and the inclination towards obedience to God. For by this order and arrangement of his arguments he clearly signifies that, although there are several ways of arriving at knowledge of the truth, this one is the first of them all. Although the Papists say that the principal and almost only way of knowing the truth is the authority and testimony of their Roman Church, yet, to leave them to themselves, we assert that no one can discern the truth of God, which is in the written Word, unless his mind has first been in some way sanctified and prepared by that same Spirit who speaks in the Word. So much is it worth to have a mind prepared by a pious zeal and love for knowing the truth! Yet this is not obtained at once; for this work there is need of a long and great mortification of the wisdom of the flesh and of our affections, which are enmity against God.

units.la: 18 Qui à semetipso loquitur, gloriam propriam quærit, qui autem quærit gloriam eius qui misit ipsum, hic verax est, & iniustitia in eo non est.
units.tr: 18 He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory; but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him, the same is true, and there is no unrighteousness in him.

units.la: 19 Nonne Moses dedit vobis Legem & tamen nemo ex vobis præstat Legem? Quid me studetis trucidare?
units.tr: 19 Did not Moses give you the Law, and yet none of you keeps the Law? Why do you seek to kill me?

units.la: 20 Respondit turba, & dixit, Dæmonium habes; quis te studet trucidare?
units.tr: 20 The crowd answered and said, You have a demon; who seeks to kill you?

units.la: 21 Respondit Iesus, & dixit eis, Vnum opus feci, & omnes miramini.
units.tr: 21 Jesus answered and said to them, I did one work, and you all marvel.

units.la: 22 Attamen Moses dedit vobis circumcisionem (non quod ex Mose sit, sed quia ex Patribus) & Sabbatho circumciditis hominem.
units.tr: 22 Yet Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and on the Sabbath you circumcise a man.

units.la: 23 Si circumcisionem accipit homo Sabbatho, ut non solvatur lex Moysis, mihi indignamini quod totum hominem sanum fecerim Sabbatho?
units.tr: 23 If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath, so that the law of Moses is not broken, are you angry with me because I made a whole man well on the Sabbath?

units.la: 24 Ne iudicate secundum speciem, sed iustum illud iudicium ferte.
units.tr: 24 Do not judge according to appearance, but make the righteous judgment.

units.la: HÆc est altera via quam demonstrat, cognoscendi veritatem doctrinæ: est autem à nota quadam ac proprietate veræ doctrinæ, vera enim doctrina ad Deū dirigitur, quæritque gloriam Dei. Quæ doctrina inventa est ab homine, ea quærit gloriā hominis ipsius, non Dei: Ergo quæ doctrina quærit gloriam Dei, non autem hominis, ea necesse est non sit falsa, sed vera doctrina. Nota igitur, doctrina falsa & mendax tendit ad gloriam creaturæ; doctrina autem verax perpetuò attendit ad gloriam creatoris; éstque hæc eius certa proprietas: Hinc sequitur hanc esse veræ doctrinæ no tam adeo indubitatam, vt si quis scire cupiat, an doctrina aliqua sit vera & a Deo, quærat sibi hanc in doctrina ipsa notam. Verbi gratia: de Prædestinatione est varia doctrina: vna est quòd prædestinatio sit ex prævisis operibus, eáque est Papistarum, cuius tamen nunc eos incipit pudere. Altera est, quòd Deus prædestinauit nos in sese pro benevolo affectu voluntatis suæ sine prævisis operibus nostris, quæ est Pauli Apostoli. Iam si quis scire cupiat vtra harum sit verior, examinet vtramque ad hanc normam gloriæ divinæ, videatque vtra magis ei inseruiat, cáne quæ prævisis hominum meritis imputat Prædestinationem, an ea quæ solius Dei beneplacito & gratiæ, sine respectu prævisorum operum. Quis autem non videt magis spectare Dei gloriam eam doctrinam quæ solius Dei gratiæ ac beneplacito tribuit Prædestinationem? Ideoque Paulus cum prædestinationem & electionem soli Dei beneplacito tribuisset, subiecit hæc verba, ad laudem, inquiens, gloriæ gratiæ ipsius. Deinde de Iustificatione ac salute humana varia est doctrina: vna quæ & hanc & illam tribuit etiam hominum meritis, non soli Christi satisfactioni. Altera quæ soli fidei, hoc est, Christi satisfactioni per fidem apprehensæ vtramque tribuit. Iam si quis id scire velit vtra doctrina vera sit, id resciet ex nota illa quam diximus gloriæ Dei: cum autem nemo non videat posteriorem hanc magis spectare gloriam Dei. Commendat enim gratiam eius & misericordiam in Christo, in qua maximè gloriam sibi quærit, necesse est hæc posterior sola sit vera doctrina. Idem iudicium est de aliis doctrinæ capitibus, quæ in controversia sunt hodierno die: si quis enim diligenter attendat ad illa Papistarum doctrinam, vt debit planè eam abducere hominum animos a Deo Deique gloria ad creaturam etiam peccatricem magnificiendam. Quamobrem habes hoc loco argumenta duo, rationesque præcipuas quibus cognoscitur veritas doctrinæ: Et verbum hoc scriptum a Deo sit an non. Sunt, fateor, aliæ rationes, sed minus quam hæ præcipuæ. Christus autem rationes præcipuas & quas putauit necessarias maximè, attigit.
units.tr: This is the second way which he shows of knowing the truth of teaching. It is taken from a certain mark and property of true teaching: for true teaching is directed to God and seeks the glory of God. Teaching that is invented by a man seeks the glory of the man himself, not of God. Therefore the teaching that seeks the glory of God and not of man cannot be false, but must be true. Note, then, that false and lying teaching tends to the glory of a creature, but true teaching always attends to the glory of the Creator, and this is its certain property. Hence it follows that this mark is not so unquestionable a sign of true teaching that, if anyone wishes to know whether some teaching is true and from God, he should look for this mark in the teaching itself. For example: there are various teachings about predestination. One is that predestination is according to foreseen works, and this is the view of the Papists, though they now begin to be ashamed of it. The other is that God predestined us in himself, out of the benevolent affection of his will, without any foreseen works of ours; this is the view of the Apostle Paul. Now if anyone wishes to know which of these is the more true, let him examine both by this rule of the glory of God, and see which serves it better: whether the doctrine which imputes predestination to the foreseen merits of men, or that which ascribes it to the good pleasure and grace of God alone, without regard to foreseen works. Yet who does not see that the teaching which ascribes predestination to the grace and good pleasure of God alone looks more to the glory of God? That is why Paul, when he had ascribed predestination and election to the good pleasure of God alone, added these words: to the praise, he says, of the glory of his grace. Then, concerning justification and human salvation, there are various teachings. One ascribes both this and that also to the merits of men, not to the satisfaction of Christ alone. The other, which ascribes both to faith alone, that is, to the satisfaction of Christ apprehended by faith. Now if anyone wishes to know which teaching is true, he will learn it from that mark of the glory of God which we have mentioned; and since everyone sees that the latter looks more to the glory of God, for it commends his grace and mercy in Christ, in which he most of all seeks his own glory, it must be that this latter alone is true teaching. The same judgment holds for the other heads of doctrine that are in controversy today. For if anyone carefully attends to the doctrine of the Papists, he will plainly see that it draws men's minds away from God and the glory of God, to magnify a creature, even a sinful one. Therefore you have here two arguments and the principal reasons by which the truth of doctrine is known: both whether this written Word is from God or not. There are other reasons, I admit, but they are less important than these principal ones. Christ, however, touched upon the principal reasons, and those he thought especially necessary.

units.la: Nonne Moses. Hactenus commendauit doctrinam suam
units.tr: Nonne Moses. Hitherto he has commended his doctrine

units.la: Christi sapientia & charitas. suam; sed cùm doctrina pura non posset recipi ab impuris animis, eorum autem animi laborarent malitia adversus ipsum, qui doctor eorum erat futurus, ideóque malitiam vrget nunc, & quærit, si fieri posset, eam ex animis ipsorum evellere. Quærit igitur: Quid igitur me studetis trucidare? Verùm huic interrogationi præmittit alteram, qua quasi larvam iis detrahit, & causam quā prætendebat malitiæ suæ admisit: fuit autem ea legis ab ipso violatæ, quòd nimirum sanato homine illo, de quo cap. 5. 5. & deinceps, Sabbathum prophanauerit. Nonne Moses dedit vobis Legem? q.d. Non est ea causa quam prætexitis malitiæ vestræ & studio interficiendi me, vera causa: legem enim illam à Mose vobis datam, nemo est ex vobis qui præstet. Nulli sunt qui magis ostentant legem, déque ea gloriantur magis, quàm illi ipsi qui minimam oneris ipsius partè in sese recipiunt. Nam, ut loquutus est Christus de Scribis & Pharisæis hypocritis; Ligant onera gravia difficiliáque portatu, & imponunt in humeros hominum, digito autem suo nolunt ea movere. Et hoc genus hominum minimè omnium sentit animo internam illam legis obedientiam. Neque tamen vlli sunt, qui magis confidenter loquuntur de Deo, de Christo, de religione, quàm qui minimè omnium sapiunt Deum, Christum, religionem; neque sunt denique qui seueriores sint aliorum censores, quàm illi ipsi qui legem maximè transgrediuntur, si sit interea quod prætexant factis suis deterrimis. At qui sentit legem Dei onus esse (non quidem quòd in se onus sit, sed propter corruptam hanc naturam, onus facta sit) Qui, inquam, sentit legem sibi onus esse, & nouit quanta cum difficultate obtineatur obedientia legis, sensus Dei & misericordiæ ipsius in Christo Iesu; is profectò non nisi ægrè admodum de iis loquitur, nisi interea, quemadmodum os extra loquitur, ita & cor intus loquatur; id est, nisi sentiat intus & in corde quæ ore proferuntur, omnium autem mortalium maximè misericors est erga eos, quicunque ex infirmitate naturæ communis lapsi sunt, qui ipse maximè sentit communem hanc naturæ miseriam & infirmitatem. Sed hic considera, ut Christus tractet genus hoc hominum Legem Dei falsò prætendentium: legis illum præ
units.tr: The wisdom and love of Christ. his own. But since pure teaching could not be received by impure minds, and their minds were troubled by malice against him who was to be their teacher, he now presses that malice and seeks, if it were possible, to tear it out of their minds. He therefore asks: "Why then do you seek to kill me?" But before this question he puts another, by which he strips away their mask and draws out the cause they had pretended for their malice. That cause was the violation of the law by him, namely that, having healed that man (of whom ch. 5, v. 5 and following), he had profaned the Sabbath. Did not Moses give you the Law? As if he said: "The cause you put forward for your malice and your eagerness to kill me is not the true one, for the law given you by Moses is kept by none of you." No people boast more of the law, or glory in it more, than those who take upon themselves the smallest part of its burden. For as Christ said of the hypocritical Scribes and Pharisees: They bind heavy burdens, hard to carry, and lay them on the shoulders of men, but they themselves will not move them with a finger. This kind of men feels least of all that inner obedience to the law. Yet there are none who speak more confidently of God, of Christ, and of religion than those who know least of all about God, Christ and religion; and finally there are none who are stricter censors of others than those who most of all break the law, if meanwhile there is some pretext for their most wicked deeds. But he who feels that the law of God is a burden (not indeed because it is a burden in itself, but because this corrupt nature has made it a burden), who, I say, feels the law to be a burden to him and knows how great a difficulty there is in keeping the law's obedience, and who feels God's mercy in Jesus Christ, certainly speaks of such men only very reluctantly, unless his heart speaks inwardly as his mouth speaks outwardly; that is, unless he feels inwardly and in his heart what is uttered with the lips. And he is most merciful of all mortals towards those who have fallen through the common weakness of nature, since he himself most feels this common misery and weakness of our nature. But consider here how Christ deals with this kind of men who falsely put forward the law of God: he strips away from them the cover and mask of the law.

units.la: (continued) textum & laruam ipsis detrahit. Quæ causa? Quia non est vera iustáque causa illa quam ipsi prætexunt. Quid ita? quia maximè omnium ipsi legem transgrediuntur. Nam qui ipsi legem transgrediuntur, ídque vel palam, & elata(vt dicitur) manu,vel clàm & occultè (nam quæ occultè fiunt ab istis, turpe est vel dicere )'isti, inquam, dum reprehendunt alios, dum iudicant, dum plectunt, non habent hanc legis transgressionem pro vera, cur ita faciant,causa. Possunt eam quidem prætexere,sed vera illis causa non est. Possunt Iudices qui ipsi homicidæ sunt legem prætexere quoties iudicant vel puniunt homicidá:sed ea illis nō est vera causa. Possunt Iudices qui ipsi furaces sunt, rapaces, adulteri,legem ipsiúsque transgressionem prætexere,quoties fures & adulteros iudicant & morti adiudicant,sed ea non est eis vera causa. Quid hic faciendum? exemplo Christi detrahenda est illis larua & legis prætextus,id quod Christus olim facturus est illo die in conspectu totius mundi Quamobrem quisquis velit alterum vel reprehendere vel iudicare, vel damnare,videat hac de causa id faciat sincere, quòd legem nempe Dei transgressus sit,quòd maiestatem iam violauerit. Sinceritatem autem hanc in agendo itaque demum assequetur si ipse prior ex animo legi obediens fuerit,& Deum in lege sua fuerit reueritus: ita enim fiet,vt seriò iam permotus Dei gloria, eiúsque respectu cum altero de lege Dei violata agat Detracta hic larua transgressionis legis,Christus iam vrget veram causam, cur ipsum studeant interficere; & vrget quidem acerrima interrogatione. Subest alia perpetuò causa,vel corruptus aliquis affectus , vel respectus aliquis peruersus cur transgressores isti omnia faciant,etiam in speciem bona & honesta: ideóque detracta iam illa legis larua, ea causa vrgenda est acerrimè. Quid me , inquit Christus,studetis trucidare? Quasi diceret:Dicite mihi sincerè & ex animo,quæ causa sit cur me studeatis trucidare? Sed quid ad hoc ludæorum turba? Dæmonium,inquit, habes, &c. Inuehitur iam in personam hominis,re ipsa omissa. Respondio enim est,vt loquuntur,magis ad hominem quàm ad rem: id quod familiare est hypocritis, si quando vrgeantur acriùs & pungantur:ita enim confusis fusis omnibus, & cælo quasi terræ misto, putant se optimè effugere quæstionem, quæ est de re ipsa magis vrgentem eos & in angustias redigentem. Sed notandus est loquendi modus. Daemonium habes, inquiunt. Sic quidem loqui consueverunt Iudæi, quoties viderunt mente captum aliquem, & à ratione plane alienum. Et certè verum est, dum castigationes Dei leviores sunt & paternæ, videtur tum Deus sua ipsius manu nos castigare, dum vero graviores sunt, videtur tum nos, non sua ipsius manu castigare, sed diabolo tanquam carnifici, & iræ suæ administro tradere. Deinde vbi inuenti sunt in personam, rem ipsam negant impudenter nam hi ipsi studebant Christum è medio tollere cap.5. 18. Responsio hæc tota acerba est & illita quasi felle amaritudinis. Vnde id obseruas? cum vrgetur illa, quę in hypocritis est malitia, detracta iam larua quam malitiæ suæ prætexunt, ferre id ipsi non possunt, sed continuo venenum illud latens quo toti sunt oppleti eo munt: & quòd mireris etiam tum cum continere illud intra se & simulare maximè cupiunt; tamen continere illud intra se non possunt diutius, sed necesse est prodat illud aliquo certè modo inter respondendum. Respondit Christus. A re institutta non digreditur Dominus, neque respondet ad conuitium in personam suam iactum: defendit autem factum illud suum quo hominem illum sanauit, de quo capite 5. & iustum esse conuincit. Est autem argumentum defensionis à simili ipsorum facto sumptum: factum autem ipsorum est quod ipsi circumciderent singulis Sabbathis. V num, inquit, opus edidi, nempe opus illud in sanando homine illo ægroto de quo supra cap.5. Et omnes miramur. Non quidem propter opus ipsum plane miraculosum, sed propter opus editum die Sabbathi. Hoc verbo, mirandi, includit iram eorum aduersus se, & consilium illud interimendi ipsum. At vos ex lege illa Mosis de circumcisione (quæ lex non tam a Moë est quàm ex Patribus, Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo & cæteris, hoc enim habet in parenthesi) ex lege, inquam, illa Mosis circumciditis homines singulis sabbathis. Nam oportuit diem Sabbathi vnum-
units.tr: (continued) the pretext and mask of the law. What is the reason? Because the cause they put forward is not a true and just one. Why so? Because they themselves most of all transgress the law. For those who themselves transgress the law, and that either openly, with a high hand (as they say), or secretly and covertly (for it is shameful even to name what these men do in secret), these men, I say, when they rebuke others, when they judge, when they punish, do not have this transgression of the law as the true reason for so acting. They may indeed put it forward as a pretext, but it is not their true cause. Judges who are themselves murderers may put forward the law whenever they judge or punish a murderer, but that is not their true cause. Judges who are themselves thieves, robbers and adulterers may put forward the law and its transgression whenever they judge thieves and adulterers and condemn them to death, but that is not their true cause. What is to be done here? By the example of Christ their mask and the pretext of the law must be torn away from them, which Christ is about to do on that day in the sight of the whole world. Therefore, whoever wishes to rebuke, judge or condemn another, let him see that he does so sincerely, for this reason, namely that the other has transgressed the law of God and has already violated its majesty. But he will attain this sincerity in acting only if he himself has first been obedient to the law from the heart and has reverenced God in his law; for then, being seriously moved by the glory of God and with regard to it, he will act with the other about the violated law of God. With the mask of the transgression of the law removed, Christ now presses the true cause why they seek to kill him, and presses it with the sharpest question. There is always some other cause, either a corrupt affection or some perverse regard, for which such transgressors do everything, even things that look good and honourable; so, the law's mask having been removed, that cause must be pressed most sharply. Why, says Christ, do you seek to kill me? As if he said: "Tell me sincerely and from your heart, what is the cause why you seek to kill me?" But what does the crowd of Jews answer to this? You have a demon, they say, etc. They now rail against the man's person, leaving the matter itself aside. For this is, as they say, an answer more to the man than to the thing: a habit familiar to hypocrites when they are pressed more sharply and stung. For, everything being confused and heaven mixed as it were with earth, they think they escape the question well, which is about the matter itself and presses them more and drives them into a corner. But the manner of speaking should be noted. You have a demon, they say. Thus the Jews are accustomed to speak whenever they see someone out of his mind and quite alien to reason. And certainly it is true that while God's chastisements are lighter and fatherly, then God seems to chastise us with his own hand; but when they are heavier, then he seems to chastise us not with his own hand, but to hand us over to the devil as to an executioner and minister of his wrath. Then, when they have been caught out in person, they shamelessly deny the thing itself, for these same men were seeking to remove Christ from the midst (ch. 5, v. 18). This whole answer is bitter and smeared as it were with the gall of bitterness. Whence do you observe this? When the malice that is in hypocrites is pressed, the mask of the law which they put forward having been removed, they cannot bear it, but at once they spit out that poison with which they are wholly filled; and, though they most wish to keep it within themselves and to pretend, yet they cannot keep it within for long, but it must certainly break out in some way in their reply. Christ answered. The Lord does not depart from the matter in hand, nor does he reply to the insult cast at his person; but he defends that deed of his by which he healed the man, of whom ch. 5, and proves it to be just. The argument of his defence is taken from the like deed of theirs: their deed is that they circumcise on each Sabbath. I have done, he says, one work, namely that work of healing that sick man of whom above, ch. 5. And you all marvel. Not indeed on account of the work itself, which is wholly miraculous, but on account of the work done on the Sabbath day. By this word "marvel" he includes their anger against him and their plan to kill him. But you, by that law of Moses about circumcision (which law is not so much from Moses as from the Fathers, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and the rest, for he says this in a parenthesis), by that law of Moses, I say, you circumcise men on every Sabbath. For the Sabbath day had to be one-

units.la: Loquendi modus Iudæos familiaris.
units.tr: The manner of speaking familiar to the Jews.

units.la: Hypocritarum furor.
units.tr: The fury of the hypocrites.

units.la: Apologia Christi, Iudæos perspicue conuincens. quemque diem octauum esse, quo circumcidendi erant certè aliqui apud Iudæos. Argumentatio igitur est, Vos ex præscripto legis Mosis circumciditis homines singulis etiam Sabbathis: Ergo cur miramini, quòd ego vnum hoc opus, vno tantum ex multis, Sabbatho fecerim? Nota primùm, Christus dum ait eos mirari etiamnum ob opus illud vnum, & postea dicit eos indignari ipsi, planè innuit consilium illud interficiendi se nondum depositsse eos ex animo: etsi id quidem verbo negarint se quærere ipsum ad cædem. Malitia persecutoris non facilè deponitur, sed latet perpetuò dum opportuno tempore se proferat: atque de hac re nos Dominus facit certiores hoc loco. Nõ facilè crediderim Papistam, vtcunque ad tempus adblandiatur nobis, deponere tamen ex animo malitiam & studium etiam ad vnum interimendi quotquot hodierno die profitentur Euangelij puritatem. Sed illud rursus vide, dum argumentatur à similli eorum facto, non argumentatur quidem ab illegitimo aliquo facto, neque enim damnat illud eorum factum, aut obiicit hoc facto violatum esse Sabbathum: sed argumentatur à facto licito & quod lege nitebatur. Quàm dissimilis est hic Christus nostris hominibus, qui adulteria sua, homicidia, furta, sacrilegia & alia id genus excusant, ex aliorum factis similibus; quasi verò aliorum peccata nos onere peccatorum nostrorum levatura sint. Verum quidem est illud Christi, Væ homini illi per quem offendiculum venit: non tamen carent suo væ, suaque maledictione qui offenduntur, qui pereunt propter peccatum suum: verùm sanguis ipsorum requiretur è manibus eorum, qui in causa fuerunt cur impingerent: maximè verò requiretur è manibus virorum principum, quos oportuit præire alios bono exemplo, & alios delinquentes & errantes corrigere atque in totum reducere. Si circumcisionem. Rursus ab eodem illo facto eorum argumentatur, sed paulò aliter nunc quàm priùs considerato, nempe vt exemplo minori. Argumentum à minori ad maius, Si, inquit, circumcisionem accipit homo Sabbatho, idque legitimè & iustè: quod quidem minus beneficium est, vtpote sigillum duntaxat sanationis & renouationis animi, atque illud quidem sæpenumero ... ro minus efficax, propter peruersitatem recipientis. Cur indignamini mihi quod totum hominem quantus quantus est animo & corpore sanum fecerim Sabbatho? Nam homo ille de quo controuersia fuit, sanatus est etiam animo, remissaque sunt ei peccata sua, & sanctificatus est Christi Spiritu vna eadémque opera. Huic defensioni facti sui subiicit admonitionem de fundamento iudicij eorum sinistri & peruersi: fundamentum enim iudicij eorum fuit respectus personae Christi, quae vsque adeo ipsis vilescebat; hinc fuit quod tam peruerse iudicauerint de ipsius facto. Nota igitur: respectus personae peruerit quodcunque iudicium, facitque vt quod alioqui optimum est in se Deique gloriae maximè inseruit, pro peßimo habeatur. Quare in omnibus iudiciis facie-dis auertendi sunt oculi & sensus à personis hominum; imprimis vero id fieri debet in iudiciis iis quae fiunt de rebus caelestibus ac spiritualibus: quia natura alieniores sumus ab iis rebus quàm à terrestribus hisce & corporalibus. Quo fit vt facilè iniecto impedimento vel leuissimo quoque, impingamus ita, vt de iis rebus peruerssime iudicemus. Sic impingunt hodierno die Papistae. Quae enim ob oculos sunt aspiciunt, & in personis hominum ministrorum ac professorum toti haerent, vsque adeo vt non sit iis otium cogitādi vel semel in tota vita de veritate ipsa quam profitentur.
units.tr: Christ's defence, clearly convicting the Jews, and showing that the eighth day was the day on which some among the Jews were certainly to be circumcised. The argument, then, is this: You circumcise men on the Sabbath too, as the law of Moses prescribes. Why, then, do you wonder that I have done this one work on the Sabbath, out of many? First note that Christ, in saying that they still wonder at that one work, and then that they are angry with him, clearly implies that they have not yet laid aside their plan of killing him from the heart, although in words they denied that they sought his death. The malice of a persecutor is not easily laid aside; it lies hidden always until it comes forward at a suitable time, and the Lord makes us aware of this very matter in this place. I should not easily believe that the Papists, however much they flatter us for a time, lay aside from the heart their malice and their zeal to destroy, even to the last man, all who today profess the purity of the gospel. But look again at this: in arguing from the similar act of the Jews, he does not argue from some illegitimate act, for he does not condemn their act, nor does he charge that the Sabbath was violated by it; rather he argues from a lawful act, one that rested upon the law. How unlike these men are to Christ, who excuse their adulteries, murders, thefts, sacrileges and other such things by appeal to the similar deeds of others, as if the sins of others would relieve us of the burden of our own sins! It is true, indeed, that which Christ said: Woe to that man through whom the offence comes. Yet those who are made to stumble, who perish on account of their own sin, are not free from their own woe and their own curse; but their blood will be required at the hands of those who were the cause of their stumbling; and above all it will be required at the hands of the princes, who ought to have gone before others with a good example, and to correct the others who sin and err and bring them back altogether. If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath... Again he argues from that same deed of theirs, but now in a slightly different way from before, namely as from a lesser example, an argument from the less to the greater: If, he says, a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath, and that lawfully and justly; this is indeed a lesser benefit, since it is only a seal of the healing and renewal of the mind, and that indeed often less effective on account of the perversity of the recipient. Why are you angry with me because I have made the whole man, however great he is in mind and body, whole on the Sabbath? For that man about whom the dispute arose was healed in mind as well; his sins were forgiven him, and he was sanctified by the Spirit of Christ, all in one work. To this defence of his deed he adds a warning about the foundation of their wrong and perverse judgment. For the foundation of their judgment was regard for the person of Christ, who was so cheap in their eyes; hence it is that they judged his deed so perversely. Note, therefore: regard for the person perverts any judgment whatever, and makes what is in itself best, and most serves the glory of God, to be held the worst. Wherefore in all judgments we must turn away our eyes and senses from the persons of men; this must be done above all in those judgments which concern heavenly and spiritual things, since by nature we are more alien to those things than to these earthly and bodily ones. Hence it happens that, with the least obstacle thrown in our way, we stumble, so that we judge those things most perversely. So the Papists stumble today. For they look at what is before their eyes, and cling wholly to the persons of the men who minister and profess, so much so that they have no leisure to think, even once in their whole life, about the truth itself which they profess.

units.la: 25 Dicebant quidam ex Hierosolymitanis, Nonne hic est quem student trucidare?
units.tr: 25 Some of the Jerusalemites were saying, "Is not this the man whom they are trying to kill?"

units.la: 26 At ecce palam loquitur, & nihil ei dicunt, numnam vere cognouerunt primores hunc vere esse Christum illum?
units.tr: 26 But look, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him. Can it be that the rulers have truly come to know that this is the Christ?

units.la: 27 Sed nouimus vnde hic sit: quum autem venerit ille Christus, nemo cognituru est vnde sit.
units.tr: 27 But we know where this man is from; yet when the Christ comes, no one will know where he is from.

units.la: & Clamabat ergo Iesus in templo, docens ac dicens, Et me noftis & vnde sim noftis: & à meipso non veni, sed est verax qui misit me, quem vos non noftis.
units.tr: And so Jesus cried out in the temple, teaching and saying: "You both know me and know where I am from; and I have not come of my own accord, but he who sent me is true, and you do not know him."

units.la: 29 Ego vero noui eum, quia ab eo sum, & ille me misit.
units.tr: 29 But I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me.

units.la: NVnc mirantur quidam ex turba tantam esse patiētiam virorum principum, qui paulò ante quaerebant eum interficere: nunc autem dum pulcherrima se offert occasio, nihil tamen tentant aduersus ipsum. In hunc igitur modum argumentantur: quaerebant eum paulò ante interficere, nunc autem palam loquitur in templo: ergo cur non eum interficiunt? Cur ne hiscere quidem contra eum audent? Mirabile dictu est quo pacto Deus cohibeat malitiam illam quae in cordibus impiorum est. Illi perpetuò fouent eam quam conceperunt malitiam in pectore suo, quaerentque occasionem exequendi quod impie cogitarunt. Nunc autem occasione se offerente, ne hiscere quidem audent, non modo vinctas habent manus, sed os illis plane obturatur. Ex quo apparet eam esse Dei prouidentiam in suos, qua non modo ipsos sustentet vna quasi manu, sed etiam aduersarios ipsorum deprimat altera. Quod ut patefiat mundo, solet eum hominē (vt hoc tempore Christum) quem maxime oderunt impij in medium producere, dare ei libertatem loquendi, reprehendendi aduersarios ipsos, cum interea ij nihil mutire contra audeant: non secus acsi catenis ferreis vincti detinerētur.
