Idē nimirū facit, ac si quis prēdā leonis in cōspectū ipsius proferat, interea autē leonē ipsum vinculis cōstrictū teneat, ne in prædā suā inuolet: ita mundus hic refrenatur hodierno die ne in homines pios qui numero paucissimi sunt & virib. infirmissimi, irruptionem faciat: quod nisi fieret, an credis potuisse iampridem Ecclesiæ locum esse in terris aliquem? Hoc eos consolatur quotquot concisi sunt suæ infirmitatis, dum vident non solum sese protegi Dei manu, sed etiam eadem Dei manu impios quosque re-frænari. Nota deinde, non modo mirantur isti, sed etiam irascuntur ideo quòd principes populi nō statim ipsum prehendant ac interficiant: nam ipsi vix se continent, petunt tantum ductores qui ipsis præeant in scelere perpetrando. Hi ipsi tamen prius negabant sese quaesiuisse Dominum interficere. Non est fides habenda hostibus veritatis, qui obstinatè perseuerant in ignorantia quantumuis se verbo purgent ac simulent amicitiam, imò quantumuis serius videantur loqui. Manet enim perpetuò sub obstinata ignorantia, malitia & odium in professores veritatis: & sub tenebris illis manent operatenebrarum; quæ paulatim in lucem prodeunt, seseque exerunt. Num vere cognouerunt. Occupant rationem quam pro se afferre poterant principes, cur abstinerent ab eo. Fortassè, inquiunt, cognouerunt primores hunc verè esse Christum. Tum rationem illam statim refellunt, Nemo cognitum est unde sit Christus cùm venerit: At nouimus unde hic sit: Ergo hic non est Christus. Sine dubio dū occupāt rationē principum, ipsi quoque eadem ratione conuicti aliquo modo conscientiis tenentur, insidétque animis eorum aliqua opinio Christi ex operibus ipsius mirificis, ex authoritate verbi ipsius concepta. Sed præiudiciū hoc de cognito eo, & cognita eius tota gente non finit eos animum suum ad ipsum applicari, in eóque conquiescere. Conuincuntur conscientiæ vel maximè obstinatorum quorumque, ita ut cogantur aliquo modo assentiri veritati: sed eorum animi ita præoccupati sunt præiudiciis & præceptis sinistris opinionibus, ut ad veritatem non possint propius accedere. Multis Papistarum hoc contigit hodierno die; sed vt eos omittam: ipsi pij sæpe sentiunt multa in se impedimenta, quominus id quod maximè vellent, veritatem & Christum plenè amplectantur, voluptatémque ex eo, quam vellent, percipiant. Nota; hi ipsi, vt paulò ante dictum erat, repressi metu primorum, non audebant palam de Christo loqui. Unde & illud apparet, detentos fuisse quasi vi in illis tenebris illáque ignorantia. Nunc verò cùm suspicantur minores Christum amplexos esse, quid eos remoratur, quominus in eum ipsi quoque credant? At nunc & contra Christum & contra principes ipsos argumentantur. Verum quidem id est, metum principum magno sæpe impedimento esse vulgo hominum, ne veritatem amplectantur: sed & hoc non minus verum est, remoto illo externo impedimento satis impedimenti esse in ipsis, ga quantumuis simplices videantur, ne veritatem sequantur: & maliciam esse in ipsorum cordibus eam quę reluctetur veritatis luci, cui prius quàm locum dent fabricant sibi mille impedimenta non necessaria. Est quidem, fateor, ignorantia aliqua quæ paulò simplicior est, sed nulla est omnino absque aliqua obstinatione. Paulus dum loquitur de ignorantia gentium, Propter ignorantiam, inquit, quæ est in ipsis, ex obduratione cordis eorum. Videndum erit nunc nobis quo tandem modo argumententur; Cùm Christus, inquiunt, venerit, nemo cogniturus est unde sit. At hunc novimus unde sit: Ergo hic non est Christus. Falsissima conclusio est. Oportet ergo causa falsitatis sit in antecedente: fundamentum igitur rationis eorum ut videamus: Habebat quidem illud ex Scripturis, nominatim vero ex Mica Propheta, cap. 5. 1. At tu Bethlehem Ephratha minima ut sis in ducibus Iohuda, ex te mihi prodibit futurus dominator in Israele, cuius exortus inde à principio à diebus sæculi sunt. Sed locus ille de Christi deitate accipiendus est. Nam Christus qua Deus eo modo venit, quo nemo cognouit. Isti autem trahunt locum ad Christum hominem, ignorantes eum oportuisse Christum Deum quoque esse, non hominem tantùm, omnia de homine sunt interpretati. Quod ad Christum hominem attinet, ibidem de eo dictum est à Propheta quòd ex Bethlehem sit prodituros. Rationis ergo fundamentum, ut isti intelligebant, ipsum falsum est. Rationis assumptionem refellit ipse Christus veriu sequeti: nam quanquam Christum hominem aliquo modo cognitum habebant; tamen ne hominem quidem eo quo oportuit modo eum agnoscebant, cùm à Deo missum esse non cognoscerent, ut ipse Christus ostendit postea: ergo ex falsis illis principiis necesse est lequi salsissimam conclusionem. Nulla profectò conclusio est salsior & perniciosior quàm est ea quæ ex scriptura & verbo Dei colligitur sæpenumero. Imò verò ne ethnici quidem ipsi magis perniciosas aut magis pugnantes cum Deo ac veritate conclusiones sine verbo Dei collegerunt, quàm sunt quas isti hodierno die ex verbo Dei conantur colligere. Nullum enim est mandatum aut figmentum ipsorum tam putidum, quod non statim ascribat verbo Dei, & cuius Deum authorem non faciant. Hoc quidem non fit ex eo quòd Scriptura sit nasus cereus. ecrene, hoc est quòd suapte sponte possit duci in quem velis sensum, quasi verò nihil certi habeat: sed ipsi indo-ƈti parùmque itabiles detorquent Scripturas suo ipso-rum exitio.
units.tr: Now some of the crowd marvel at such patience in the leading men, who a little before were seeking to kill him, and yet now, when the finest opportunity presents itself, they attempt nothing against him. They argue in this way: they were seeking to kill him a little while ago, but now he speaks openly in the temple: why then do they not seize him? Why do they not even dare to open their mouths against him? It is wonderful to say how God restrains that malice which is in the hearts of the wicked. They constantly nurse the malice they have conceived in their breast, and they look for an opportunity to carry out what they have impiously planned. But now, with the opportunity offered, they do not even dare to open their mouths; not only are their hands bound, but their mouths are plainly stopped. From this it appears that such is God's providence towards his own people, that he not only sustains them with one hand, as it were, but also holds down their adversaries with the other. So that this may be made plain to the world, he is accustomed (as at this time with Christ) to bring forward into the open the man whom the wicked hate most, to give him freedom to speak and to rebuke his adversaries themselves, while meanwhile they dare not utter a murmur against him, no differently than if they were held fast in iron chains. He does the same as if someone were to display a lion's prey before its eyes while keeping the lion itself bound with chains, lest it rush upon its prey: so this world is restrained today from making an assault upon godly men, who are very few in number and very weak in strength; for if it were not so, do you think there could have been any place for the Church on earth long ago? This consoles all those who are crushed by their own weakness, while they see that they are protected not only by God's hand, but that by the same hand of God all the impious are restrained. Note next that these men not only marvel but are also angry that the princes of the people do not at once seize and kill him; for they can scarcely contain themselves, and they only seek leaders to go before them in carrying out the crime. Yet these same men earlier denied that they had sought to kill the Lord. One should not trust the enemies of the truth, who obstinately persist in ignorance, however much they purge themselves by their words and feign friendship, indeed however mildly they seem to speak. For malice and hatred against the professors of the truth remain constantly under stubborn ignorance; and those who work in darkness remain under that darkness, which gradually comes out into the light and shows itself. Did they truly come to know? They seize upon the reason which the princes could have offered for holding back from him: "Perhaps," they say, "the chief men have come to know that this is truly Christ." Then they immediately refute that reason: No one will know whence Christ is when he comes; but we know whence this man is; therefore this man is not Christ. Undoubtedly, while they seize upon the reasoning of the princes, they themselves are in some way convicted by the same reasoning and held in their consciences; some opinion of Christ, formed from his wonderful works and from the authority of his own word, dwells in their minds. But this prejudice about his being known, and about the whole nation having known him, does not allow them to apply their minds to him and rest in him. The consciences even of the most obstinate are convinced, so that they are compelled in some way to assent to the truth; but their minds are so preoccupied with prejudices and sinister opinions that they cannot draw nearer to the truth. This has happened to many of the Papists in our own day; but, to pass them over, the godly themselves often feel many hindrances in themselves, so that they do not fully embrace what they most desire, namely the truth and Christ, nor receive from it the joy which they would wish. Note: these same men, as was said a little earlier, held back by fear of the leaders, did not dare to speak openly about Christ. From this it also appears that they were held, as it were by force, in those shadows and that ignorance. But now, when they suspect that the lesser people have embraced Christ, what holds them back from believing in him themselves? Yet now they argue both against Christ and against the princes themselves. It is indeed true that fear of the princes is often a great hindrance to the common people, so that they do not embrace the truth; but it is no less true that, that external hindrance removed, there is enough hindrance in themselves, so that, however simple they may appear, they do not follow the truth; and there is in their hearts a malice which resists the light of truth, and before they give it place they build for themselves a thousand unnecessary obstacles. There is indeed, I admit, some ignorance which is somewhat more simple, but none is entirely without some obstinacy. Paul, when he speaks of the ignorance of the Gentiles, says: Because of the ignorance, he says, that is in them, from the hardening of their heart. We shall now have to see how they argue: When Christ, they say, comes, no one will know whence he is. But we know whence this man is; therefore this man is not Christ. The conclusion is most false. The cause of the falsity must therefore lie in the premise; let us see, then, the foundation of their reasoning. They indeed had it from the Scriptures, namely from the prophet Micah, chapter 5, verse 1: But you, Bethlehem Ephratah, though you are small among the leaders of Judah, from you shall come forth to me the future ruler in Israel, whose goings forth are from of old, from the days of eternity. But that passage must be understood of the deity of Christ. For Christ, as God, came in a way that no one has known. But they draw the passage to Christ as man, not knowing that Christ had to be God also, not only man, and they have interpreted everything of the man. As far as Christ as man is concerned, the prophet said of him in the same place that he would come forth from Bethlehem. The foundation of the reasoning, then, as they understood it, is itself false. The assumption of the reasoning is refuted by Christ himself in what follows: for although they had Christ as man known in some way, yet they did not recognise him even as man in the way they ought, since they did not know that he had been sent by God, as Christ himself shows afterwards; therefore from those false principles a most false conclusion necessarily follows. Certainly no conclusion is more false and more pernicious than that which is often drawn from Scripture and the word of God. Indeed, even the heathen themselves did not draw from their own reasoning, without the word of God, conclusions more pernicious or more opposed to God and truth than those which these men today try to draw from the word of God. For there is no command or invention of theirs so foul that they do not at once ascribe it to the word of God and make God its author. This does not happen because Scripture is a waxen nose, that is, because it can of its own accord be drawn to whatever sense you like, as if it had nothing certain; but the ignorant and rather unstable men twist the Scriptures to their own destruction.

units.la: Sed videamus quid ad argumentum ipsorum respon- deat Christus. Commotus mendacio eorum tam splen-dido, vocem intendit, clamatque. Primùm ironicè, vt videtur, concedit eis quod volebant, eos nempe & nosse ipsum, & vnde sit nosse: deinde & hoc & illud refutat. Primùm autem demonstrat eos non nosse vnde ipse sit, hoc modo, Ego, inquit, à meipso non sum. Hoc est, veni missus à Deo Patre, qui verax est: ac proinde & ego quoque qui missus sum ab eo verax sim oportet, hoc enim consequenter intelligitur. At vos dicitis me esse à meipso, me venille mea solius authoritate; Quare vnde sim non nostis. Ex quo demum disce, ita demum cognosci verum pastorem vnde sit, non quidem cùm cognoscitur ex qua gente, ex quibus parentibus oriundus sit, sed cùm cognoscitur quòd ex Deo sit. Hæc enim sola cognitio vtilis est ad fidem, cùm scimus à Deo vocatum & missum aliquem, armatúmque esse diuina quadam authoritate. Illa autem cognitio nihil valet ad fidem, imò verò eam sæpe impedit. Deinde arguit eos non nosse qui sit ipse. Eum, inquit, qui misit me vos non nostis. Nempe Patrem: Ergo me nō nostis. Qui enim non nouit Patrem, non filium, & contrà. Iohan. 8.19. At dices, Annon nouerunt Deum? Annon nouerunt quoque eum patrem populi sui? Resp. Sit ita, sed non propterea nouerunt Patrem Christi, qui autem non cognoscunt Deum, vt Patrem Christi, existimat Christus eos nihil de Deo, vt oportet, scire, cùm nulla sit alia nisi ea quæ in Christo est cognitio Dei salutaris. Nota hic: professi sunt eā Christiam notitiam qua quidem factum est vt magis alienarentur Christo eorum mentes. Christus itaque eam ipsorum quam prætendebant notitiam irridet. Christus irridet cœlis omnem istorum notitiam quam profitentur se habere Christi, qui non interea credunt in ipsum. At quis dicat istos qui mentiuntur Christi nomen, & falsò Christiani nomine vocantur, homicidas, inquam, adulteros, blasphemos, sacrilegos, quorum animi obstumati sunt aduersus refipiscentiam; quis dicat istos credere in Christum? Quare futurum est, vt Dominus tandem externam hanc eorum professionem falsa & amarulenta irrisione excipiat cum eorum perpetua confusione nisi tempestiue resipiscant. Ego vero noui eum. Obiecta iam istis Dei & Patris ignoratione,non delectatus scilicet eorum caecitate & miseria, imo vero misertus eorum, statim incipit viam indicare qua recta ad Dei cognitionem procedant. Est autem ea, si cognoscant ipsum qui a Deo missus est, ideoque Deum perfecte cognitum habet, cum ab eo sit missus. Ego, iuquit, noui eum. Tum causam reddit, Quia ab ipso sum & ille me misit. Posterius hoc declarat illud prius. Nam utroque idem significatur. Est autem argumentum a missione & legatione sua, qua ostendit se eum cognoscere a quo sit missus. Scimus enim hoc quod qui ablegatus est & missus ab aliquo, oporteat is probe cognoscat eum hominem a quo sit missus, exploratam etiam habeat mentem eius & consilium vniuersum. Ita filius Dei a Patre suo missus in mundum, necesse est cognoscat tum Patrem ipsum, tum mentem Patris totam ac voluntatem vniuersam de salute humani generis. Sed sunt causae, hac quae allata est a Christo, altiores ac profundiores cur Filius Dei cognoscat Patrem suum. Antea dictum est, Deum nemo vidit vnquam, vnigenitus ille Filius qui est in sinu Patris, ille nobis exposuit. Vbi habes notitiam huius, quam hic profitetur Christus causam primum, aeternam nimirum illam Filij generationem. Nam necesse est is qui ab aeterno prodiit ex Patris visceribus, plane cognita habeat perspectaque illa ipsa viscera ex quibus ab aeterno prodiit: & scrutatus sit necesse est Dei Patris immensas illas profunditates. Deinde habes eiusdem huius notitiae causam ex eo quod genitus ex Patre ab aeterno Filius non recedat ab eo vllo tempore, verum nullo non tempore maneat in sinu ipsius, hoc est maneat in coniunctione illa arctissima, non solum ineffabilis amoris, sed etiam naturae vnius eiusdemque. Ex quo sequitur oportere Patrem penitus perspectum esse Filio sub. His causis tam addas legatione illam Filij, qua quum venit tempori splenitude missus est in mundum.
units.tr: How Christ answers their argument. Christ, moved by their so splendid lie, raises his voice and cries out. First, ironically, as it seems, he grants them what they wanted, namely that they know him and know whence he is; then he refutes both this and that. First he shows that they do not know whence he is, in this way: "I am not from myself," he says. That is: "I came sent by God the Father, who is true, and so I too, who have been sent by him, must be true, for this is the necessary inference." But you say that I am from myself, that I came by my own authority alone; therefore you do not know whence I am. From this, learn at last that a true minister is known by whence he is, not when it is known from what nation or from what parents he is descended, but when it is known that he is from God. For this alone is useful for faith: when we know that someone has been called and sent by God and armed with some divine authority. That other kind of knowledge is worth nothing for faith; indeed it often hinders it. Then he proves that they do not know who he himself is. "You do not know him who sent me," he says. That is, the Father; therefore you do not know me either. For whoever does not know the Father does not know the Son, and conversely. John 8.19. But you will say: Did they not know God? Did they not know him as the Father of their own people? I answer: Granted, but they did not therefore know the Father of Christ, and Christ judges that those who do not know God as the Father of Christ know nothing about God as they ought to, since there is no other knowledge of God that saves except the knowledge that is in Christ. Note here: they professed that Christian knowledge, yet it has come about that their minds were the more estranged from Christ. Christ therefore mocks the knowledge of them that they claimed. Christ scorns in heaven all the knowledge of Christ that these men profess to have, while they do not believe in him. But who would say that those who falsely take the name of Christ, and are wrongly called Christians, — murderers, I mean, adulterers, blasphemers, sacrilegious men, whose minds are hardened against repentance — who would say that these believe in Christ? Therefore it will come about that the Lord at last meets this external profession of theirs with a false and bitter mockery, to their perpetual confusion, unless they repent in time. But I know him. Having now charged them with their ignorance of God and the Father, not taking pleasure, surely, in their blindness and misery, but rather pitying them, he at once begins to point out the way by which they may proceed straight to the knowledge of God. It is this: if they know him who was sent by God, and so has God perfectly known, since he was sent by him. "I know him," he says. Then he gives the reason: "Because I am from him, and he has sent me." The latter declares the former, for both mean the same thing. It is an argument from his sending and his mission, by which he shows that he knows the one from whom he was sent. For we know that one who has been dispatched and sent by someone must thoroughly know the man from whom he was sent, and have a clear grasp of his mind and his whole plan. So the Son of God, sent by his Father into the world, must know both the Father himself and the Father's whole mind and will concerning the salvation of mankind. But there are deeper and more profound causes, besides the one Christ has given, why the Son of God knows his Father. Earlier it was said: "No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him." There you have the knowledge of this, which Christ professes here, and the first cause, namely that eternal generation of the Son. For he who came forth from eternity from the Father's inward parts must have a clear and thorough knowledge of those very inward parts from which he came forth from eternity; and he must necessarily have searched out those immense depths of God the Father. Then you have the cause of this same knowledge in that the Son, begotten of the Father from eternity, never departs from him at any time, but at all times remains in his bosom, that is, remains in that closest union, not only of ineffable love but also of one and the same nature. From this it follows that the Father must be thoroughly known to the Son. To these causes you may add his mission, by which he was sent into the world when the fullness of time came.

units.la: Vera ad veram veri Dei cognitionem
units.tr: True to the true knowledge of the true God

units.la: Quomodo Filius cognoscat Patrem. dum cum mandatis paternis existet mirabilis quædam Filij quòd ad Patrem suum attinet cognitio. Hic nota, Christus continuò, post obiectam & reprehensam istorum ignorantiam, transiit ad informationem eorum in vera cognitione, id quod argumento est reprehensione illam proximam temperatam fuisse Spiritu, quem vocat Apostolus mansuetudinis, & amore erga humanum genus, ineffabili, adeóque à sensu miseriæ eorum multo maiore eo ipso, quem ipsi miseriæ suæ habuerunt, profectam esse. Nos igitur eius exemplo discimus quòd debemusquidem admonere homines ignorātiæ suæ, eámquegrauiter reprehendere; sed ita tamen, vt cum reprehensione institutionem coniungamus: hoc enim arguit Spiritum illum lenitatis. Sunt quibus adeo nihil curæ est ignorantia omninóque miseria aliorum hominum, vt licet oculis videant perire eos propter ignorantiam; tamen miseris & pereuntibus opem ferre nolint. Cuius generis sunt nostri homines, qui non tantùm siccis oculis pereuntes quotidie innumeros sustinent intueri, sed ipsi in causa sunt cur tot pereant ( de Sacrilegis istis loquor) qui auaritia sua perdunt hanc gentem ferè totam, hoc est, eos pro quibus Christus mortuus est, & eos quos Christus redemit suo sanguine pretioso pereuntes tot numero nolunt redimere vel vna, vt vocant, buccella proventus Ecclesiastici, quem totum ad fe iniuftiffimè traxerunt. Sunt alij qui etiam delectantur miseria hominum aliorum, ac pro deliciis quasi habent eorum ignorantiam & peccata. Quibus voluptati est sæpenumerò de his loqui, ac sermones cum aliis conferre, nihil interea dolentes eorum. De quibus equidem id pronunțio, nondum eos ipsos recte illuminatos qui cæcitate aliorum delectantur, neque rectè liberatos ex sua miseria quibus miseria aliorum est voluptati. Nam fidei, cognitionis ac liberationis nostri in Christo factæ ea est natura, vt velit omnes pariter Christum cognoscere, & omnes porrecta quasi manu sua erigere ex miseria præsenti, participésque facere gaudij ac gloriæ, qua ipse fruitur quisquis verè credit, verèque per Christum liberatus ac redemptus est.
units.tr: How the Son knows the Father. While he remains with the Father's commands, there is a certain wonderful knowledge in the Son of what concerns his Father. Here note that Christ, after reproving their ignorance, at once passed on to instruct them in true knowledge. This shows that the rebuke just before was tempered by the Spirit whom the Apostle calls the Spirit of gentleness, and that it came from an ineffable love for mankind, and from a sense of their misery far greater than the sense they themselves had of their misery. So from his example we learn that we ought indeed to admonish men of their ignorance and rebuke it sharply, but in such a way that we join instruction to the rebuke; for this is what marks that spirit of gentleness. There are some to whom the ignorance and utter misery of other men are of so little concern that, although they see with their own eyes that others are perishing through ignorance, they are unwilling to bring help to the wretched and the perishing. Of this kind are our own men, who not only look on, with dry eyes, at the countless numbers perishing every day, but are themselves the cause of so many perishing (I am speaking of those sacrilegious men), who by their greed ruin almost this whole nation, that is, those for whom Christ died, and whom Christ redeemed with his precious blood. Though they are perishing in such numbers, they will not redeem them with even one morsel, as they say, of ecclesiastical revenue, which they have drawn wholly to themselves most unjustly. There are others who even take pleasure in the misery of other men, and who regard their ignorance and sins almost as delights. They delight to talk of these things often and to discuss them with others, feeling no grief over them. Concerning such people I pronounce this: those who take delight in the blindness of others are not yet rightly enlightened themselves, nor rightly freed from their own misery, if the misery of others is a pleasure to them. For faith, knowledge and our deliverance in Christ are of such a nature that they wish all men alike to know Christ, and wish to raise all, as with an outstretched hand, out of present misery, and to make them partakers of that joy and glory which he himself enjoys, whoever truly believes and is truly redeemed and delivered through Christ.

units.la: 30 Studebant ergo eum prehendere, sed nemo iniecit in eum manum, quia nondum venerat hora illa ipsius.
units.tr: 30 They therefore sought to take him, but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.

units.la: 31 Multi vero ex turba crediderunt in eum, & dicebant, Christus cum venerit num signa plura edet iis quae iste edidit?
units.tr: 31 But many of the crowd believed in him, and said, "When the Christ comes, will he do more signs than this man has done?"

units.la: Icne isti compensant Christi erga ipsos lenitatem & animum adeo propensum! Studebant nihilominus apprehendere eum, ac apprehensum trucidare, ij ipsi nimirum qui paulo ante tam strenuè negabant se quaerere eum ad necem. Nunc adeo impotentes sunt ut vix se cohibeant, quinetiam non praeuntibus & signum quasi dantibus principibus Iudaeorum manus sceleratas in Dominum iniiciant, ut clarè videas non fidendum esse iis qui obstinatè ignari sunt. Nubes enim illa ignorantiae fovet continuo & auget illam in corde maliciam semel conceptam adversus veritatem & veritatis professores, adeo ut quantisper manet ignorantia, tantisper maneat malitia, profiteantur ac prae se ferant quicquid tandem velint. Verum, quid est quod nunc usque adeo exacerbat eorum animos in Christum? antea quidem expectabant principes suos, qui priores manus in ipsum iniicerent. Nunc sine principibus & ducibus, ipsi soli volunt in eum irruere. Adeo scilicet commouentur postremis illis Christi verbis, in quibus obiecit iis ignorantiam ipsorum, simulque obtulit in sese lucem & Dei cognitionem: neque patiuntur sibi excuti ignorantiam illam suam & mentis tenebras discuti, persequuntur autem tum lucem ipsam, tum lucis Ministros. Nam ignorantiae mentis perpetuo comes est cordis obstinatio, & mens caeca coniunctum habet cor durum ac praefractum.
units.tr: How do these men repay Christ's gentleness towards them and his so generous disposition! Nevertheless they sought to seize him, and having seized him to slaughter him: they, indeed, who only a little before had so vigorously denied that they were seeking him to kill him. Now they are so unrestrained that they can hardly hold themselves back; moreover, with the chief priests of the Jews not going before them and not giving the signal, they lay sinful hands on the Lord. So you may see clearly that one should not trust those who are obstinately ignorant. For that cloud of ignorance constantly nourishes and increases the malice once conceived in the heart against the truth and against those who profess the truth, so that as long as the ignorance remains, the malice remains too, whatever they may profess or pretend. But what is it that now so exasperates their minds against Christ to such a degree? Before, they were waiting for their leaders, who would lay hands on him first. Now, without leaders and chiefs, they themselves want to rush upon him. Clearly they are moved by those last words of Christ, in which he charged them with their ignorance and at the same time offered in himself the light and the knowledge of God. They will not allow that ignorance of theirs to be shaken off, nor the darkness of their minds to be dispelled; instead they pursue both the light itself and the ministers of the light. For a hardness of heart always accompanies the ignorance of the mind, and a blind mind has a hard and stubborn heart joined to it.

units.la: Habentes, inquit Paulus, διανοίᾳ σκοτωμένοι, ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι a vita Dei propter ignorantiam, quae est in ipsis ex obduratione cordis eorum. Quibus verbis plane significat ab obdurato corde maliciose detineri mentem in ignorantia ac caecitate. Quod quo magis appareat, sic paucis habe: Cor hominis natura sua oppletum est totum seminae omnis generis mali, homicidij, adulterij, furti &c. Hoc autem egregio suo semine vnicè se oblectat,ipsum in gremio fouet, eóque fruitur. Quo autem pacatius & liberius fruatur eo,vult ipsum obtegi & occultari ab oculis Dei, ab oculis hominum, ab oculis etiam suis, ne si quando à se conspiciatur, inquietetur aliquo modo conscientia.
units.tr: Paul says that they are "having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardening of their heart" [διανοίᾳ σκοτωμένοι, ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι]. By these words he plainly signifies that the mind is held in ignorance and blindness by a heart that is hardened through malice. To make this clearer, consider the following briefly. The human heart by its nature is filled entirely with the seed of every kind of evil: murder, adultery, theft, and so on. The heart takes its chief delight in this foul seed, nurses it in its bosom, and enjoys it. But so that it may enjoy it more calmly and freely, it wants the seed covered and hidden from the eyes of God, from the eyes of men, and even from its own eyes, lest, if it ever sees it, its conscience be disturbed in some way.

units.la: Quòd autem integit ac velat cordis illud semen pessimum, est velum illud ignorantiæ Dei, voluntatis ac veritatis ipsius. Quod verò detegit illam cordis malitiam & semen illud omnis mali, est lux veritatis & verbi Dei. Itaque amat cor ignorantiam, ac pertinaciter eam retinet immente, quæ quasi in vicinia est: odit autem lucem eamque strenuè oppugnat, lucis etiam Ministros quoscunque persequitur capitali odio. Fundamentum igitur persecutionis huius, istorum est cordis obstinatio & oppugnatio internę lucis ac ipsius Spiritus S. illuminare conantis mentem eorum obtenebratam: illud enim manet necesse est, persecutionem omnem externam oriri perpetuò ex persecutione veritatis ipsius ac lucis interna. Atque hæc ipsa causa est contemptus huius quem videmus hodierno die Ministrorum verbi Dei. Profitentur homines vt velint ore Euangelium ipsiúsque puritatem: factis tamen arguunt innatum illud veritatis ac Ministrorum veritatis odium.
units.tr: The veil of ignorance of God, of his will and of the truth itself, is what covers and conceals that most wicked seed of the heart. The light of the truth and of the word of God is what uncovers that malice of the heart and that seed of all evil. Therefore the heart loves ignorance and clings stubbornly to it, keeping it close as if it were a neighbour; but it hates the light and vigorously opposes it, and it pursues with deadly hatred whoever are ministers of the light. The foundation of this persecution, therefore, is the obstinacy of their heart and their opposition to the inner light and to the Holy Spirit himself, who strives to illuminate their darkened mind. For it necessarily follows that all outward persecution always arises from persecution of the truth itself and of the inner light. And this very cause is the contempt, which we see today, for the ministers of the word of God. Men profess with their mouths that they wish for the gospel and its purity, yet by their deeds they betray that innate hatred of the truth and of the ministers of the truth.

units.la: Hæc hactenus; nunc vt redeamus ad contextum, Studebant igitur eum apprehendere, sed nemo omnium interea immisit in illum manum. Causa fuit, Quia nondum venerat hora eius. Quo significatur eos oppressos vi diuinæ prouidentiæ. Vide igitur, diuina prouidentia inhibet quidem manum, sed animam non conuertit: nam animis suis studebant eum apprehendere ac interficere. Sic solet Deus cum improbis agere. Regit eos prouidentia sua externus, sed non reformat eos interius Spiritu suo sancto, nimirum fine, vt in conseruatione suorum à manu improborum, interea sit in ipsis impiis materia iustæ damnationis ipsorum: quæ satis magna est vel in sola cordis malitia, & in studio male agendi, quod vel solum reos coram Deo peragit. Quamobrem sciat quis sibi benè consultum esse, si illa Dei efficaci prouidentia refrænetur ipsius manus à malè agendo: si cohibeatur ipsius os à malè loquendo & cætera membra corporis ne cõspirent vnà cum animo malè affecto, ad flagitium aliquod perpetrandum. Sed interea reus est coram Deo peccati & mortis, si interea resideat in animo ipsius male agendi studium, si maneat animo cupiditas vel caedis, vel adulterij, vel alicuius denique mali. Quamobrem ne vnquam contenti simus externa ista obedientia sola, nisi etiam interna sit cordis reformatio ac obedientia; ad quam nobis perpetuò connitendum est in tota vita.
units.tr: So much for this; now let us return to the context. They therefore sought to seize him, but meanwhile no one laid a hand on him. The reason was that his hour had not yet come. This signifies that they were restrained by the power of divine providence. Notice, then, that divine providence indeed restrains the hand but does not convert the soul, for in their minds they were eager to seize and kill him. So God is accustomed to deal with the wicked. He governs them outwardly by his providence, but he does not reform them inwardly by his Holy Spirit. The purpose, of course, is that while his people are preserved from the hand of the wicked, there may meanwhile remain in the ungodly themselves matter for their own just condemnation. This matter is great enough in the malice of the heart alone, and in the zeal for doing evil, which alone makes them guilty before God. Therefore let anyone know that he has been well provided for if, by the effective providence of God, his hand is restrained from doing evil, his mouth is restrained from speaking evil, and the other members of his body do not conspire with an evil mind to commit some crime. But meanwhile he is guilty before God of sin and death, if the zeal for doing evil remains in his mind, if the desire for murder, or adultery, or indeed for any evil, remains in his soul. Therefore let us never be content with that outward obedience alone, unless there is also an inward reformation and obedience of the heart; and to this we must strive continually throughout our whole life.

units.la: Rursus vides, Christi mortem ex decreto Dei dependere. Id non vno in loco Scriptura inculcat, vt Act. 2. 23. & 4. 28. Quod non fit eo fine vt excusentur executores decreti diuini in Christo interficiendo, Herodes, Pilatus, sacerdotes, milites, Iudas denique proditor. Nā postquam dixit Christum deditum & acceptum definito consilio ac prouidetia Dei, subiecit, crucifixum tamen eum & interemptum manibus executorum sceleratis. Ergo executio decreti fuit summum scelus executorum ipsorum respectu. Sed ideo decreti diuini toties meminit Scriptura, ne Mundus offendatur morte Filij Dei, quasi verò ea pependerit ex sola libidine pessimorum hominum, quo profecto animus humanus, si non succumbat alia & superior causa, nempe decretum ipsius Dei aeternum. Ergo in morte Christi, & tota illa quam ipse passus est ignominia, oculi perpetuò attollendi sunt ad Dei eiusque prouidentiam, tanquam primam ac principem efficientem causam omnium eorum, quae acciderunt.
units.tr: Again you see that the death of Christ depends on the decree of God. Scripture repeats this in more than one place, as in Acts 2:23 and 4:28. This is not done so that the executors of the divine decree in killing Christ, Herod, Pilate, the priests, the soldiers, and finally Judas the traitor, should be excused. For after saying that Christ was delivered up and received by the definite counsel and providence of God, it adds that they crucified him and killed him by the wicked hands of his executioners. Therefore the execution of the decree was the greatest crime of the executioners themselves. But Scripture mentions the divine decree so often so that the world may not be offended by the death of the Son of God, as if it had depended only on the lust of wicked men. Certainly the human mind, unless it rests on another and higher cause, namely the eternal decree of God himself, would be offended. Therefore, in the death of Christ, and in all the disgrace he suffered, our eyes must always be lifted up to God and to his providence, as the first and principal efficient cause of all the things that have happened.

units.la: Loquor de ipsis actionibus, & actionum substantia, vt sic dicam: nam si actionum malitiam respexeris, tum quidem non efficiens, sed permittens causa dicenda est decretum Dei. Decreuit enim Deus permittere, & permisit malitiam illarum actionum ad gloriam nominis sui & humani generis salutem. Postquam sublatis oculis vidimus Dei illam prouidentiam, tum quidem conquiescit animus, nō modò in hac de qua loquimur morte Christi, spectaculo nimirum omnium indignissimo. (Quid enim vel visu, vel auditu indignius quam vel videre vel audire Dominum gloriae crucifixum?) Non, inquam, tantum in morte Christi conquiescit, sed etiam in omnibus aliis factis quae alioqui coiuncta sunt cum magna indignitate ac deformitate, si spectetur externa eorum.
units.tr: I am speaking of the actions themselves and of the substance of the actions, so to speak. For if you look at the wickedness of the actions, then the decree of God must be called not an efficient but a permitting cause. For God decreed to permit, and permitted, the malice of those actions for the glory of his name and the salvation of the human race. When we have lifted up our eyes and seen this providence of God, the mind is at rest, and not only in this death of Christ, which is certainly the most unworthy of spectacles. (For what is more unworthy to see or hear than the Lord of glory crucified?) I say that the mind is at rest not only in the death of Christ, but also in all other deeds which, if you look only at their outward appearance, are otherwise joined with great indignity and deformity.

units.la: Christi mors a Dei decreto pendet. eorum facies & instrumentorum habeatur ratio. Voluntatem enim Dei ipsiusque prouidentiam oportet esse requiem animæ omnis creaturæ, ea enim reuerentia & obedientia habenda est creatori benedicto in sempiternum. Amen. Neque verò vnius tantùm Christi mors pendebat ex voluntate Patris sui ipsiusque prouidentia, sed & omnium similiter piorum, id quod tedium difficile est nobis, qui ferè oculos habemus defixos in causis secundis, & instrumentis prouidentiæ diuinæ. Ideóque Deus consueuit omnibus sæculis, ex suis aliquem producere ac constituere in medio hostium, interea autem secreta sua prouidentia ita illorum malitiam cohibere, ut ne mouere quidem manum suam potuerint, vt hic de Christo factum legimus. Siuit nonnunquam sibi charissimos proiici in aquas, ex quibus eos liberauit, miraculosè & extra ordinem. Siuit in ignes inici vt Danielis socios, interea autem ita flammas secreta vi sua coercuit, vt ne pilus quidem vestis eorum fit exustus. Siuit bestiis obiici, vt Danielem leonibus, quorum tamen insanam rabiem compescuit. Siuit denique alios in aliis periculis exponi, ex quibus ipsos seruari potuisse mirabile fuit. Hæc omnia euenerunt, ideo vt nos ex manifestis exemplis discceremus omnia, non tam ex causis secundis, quàm ex æterna Dei Prouidentia pendere, quæ solet multa facere sine causis secundis, imò contra causas secundas quaïcunque. Postquam autem hoc iam perspectum habuerunt homines, ex Dei prouidentia ipsorum vitam, morteմque pendere, secundo loco discendum iis est ex hoc etiam Christi exemplo, quid in iis efficere debeat diuinæ prouidentiæ cognitio; non quidem stultam audaciam, qua se temerè conjiciant in manifesta pericula & procurrant extra limites vocationis suæ. Quum potius sanctam fiduciam qua summam libertate, ac absque timore officium faciant, ac si officium facere non possint, nisi cum vitæ aliquo discrimine faciant officium neglecta vita. Semper enim officium faciendum est, & vel ipsa vita nostra, redimendæ sunt occasiones eius faciendi. In quo faciendo si ex voluntate Dei contingat mori, tum vel mors ipsa suavis, quia coniunctum habet bonæ conscientiæ gaudium.
units.tr: The death of Christ depends on the decree of God. Regard must be had to their outward appearance and to the instruments. For the will of God and his providence ought to be the rest of the soul of every creature, since that reverence and obedience is due to the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen. Nor did the death of Christ alone depend on the will of his Father and on his providence, but so did the death of all the godly in the same way; this is hard for us to accept, since we keep our eyes fixed mostly on secondary causes and on the instruments of divine providence. Therefore God has been accustomed in all ages to raise up some of his own people and place them in the midst of enemies, while by his secret providence he restrains the malice of those enemies so that they cannot even move their hand against them, as we read was done here with Christ. Sometimes he allows his dearest ones to be thrown into the waters, and he delivers them from them miraculously and beyond the ordinary course. He allows them to be cast into fire, as were Daniel's companions, but meanwhile he restrains the flames by his secret power so that not a hair of their clothing is burned. He allows them to be exposed to beasts, as Daniel was to the lions, yet he restrains their raging fury. Finally he allows others to be placed in various dangers, from which it would have been remarkable for them to be saved. All these things happened so that from these plain examples we might learn that all things depend not so much on secondary causes as on the eternal providence of God, which often does many things without secondary causes, and indeed against all secondary causes. Now that men have come to see clearly that their life and death depend on the providence of God, they must learn in the second place from this example of Christ what the knowledge of divine providence ought to produce in them: not a foolish boldness, by which they rashly throw themselves into obvious dangers and run beyond the limits of their calling, but rather a holy confidence, by which they perform their duty with the greatest freedom and without fear, as if they could not perform their duty except with some risk to their life, neglecting their life. For duty must always be done, and even our life must be given up to seize the opportunities of doing it. If in doing it God's will brings it about that we die, then death itself is sweet, because it is joined with the joy of a good conscience.

units.la: Piorum omnium, vt & Christi, vita & mors à Dei arbitrio pendet.
units.tr: The life and death of all the godly, Christ's included, depend on the will of God.

units.la: Exempla in eâ rem.
units.tr: Examples of this.

units.la: Quid hoc nos meditari iu-beat. Ex turba autem multi. Hic alter quidem effectus est factorum & verborum Christi superiori plane contrarius. Multi ex turba in eum crediderunt. Ex quo discimus, quod etsi alij irrideant Euangelium, fremant aduersus ipsum: tamen aliquos semper esse, qui Euangelio credant. Quare semper spargendum est illud semen Euangelij, & cum patientia expectandus est fructus futurus suo tempore. Tum quidem si vel in vno aliquo apparuerit laboris tui fructus, habes tum quod compenset omnes labores tuos praeteritos. Plus enim momenti est in vnius alicuius animi salute, quam in omnibus omnium hominum laboribus ac sudoribus, qui omnes optime collocati sunt, si vel vna anima iis fuerit conseruata: sed notanda est causa fidei huius quae multorum fuit ex turba. Dicebant, inquit, Christus cum venerit, &c. Fidei hae maxime ex visis miraculis excitit. Quare properatio ad fidem magis fuit quam ipsa fides, quae per verbum Dei praecipue ac Spiritum ipsius sanctum gignitur in corde. Verum ex hoc apparet rem gratam adeo esse Deo fidem, ut vel minimam eius scintillam ac particulam hoc nomine dignetur. Neque quantum est hoc tantum inane nomen esse, quandoquidem vel minima verae fidei scintilla efficax sit ad hominem conseruandum, cum ea vis non insit in fide proprie, sed in Christo in quo credimus, ex cuius plenitudine tantam virium ac gratiae haurimus ore fidei quantumuis exilis, verae tamen quanta ad salutem aeternam sufficiet.
units.tr: What this bids us consider. But many of the crowd. Here is a second effect of Christ's deeds and words, quite contrary to the first. Many of the crowd believed in him. From this we learn that although others mock the Gospel and rage against it, there are always some who believe it. Therefore the seed of the Gospel must always be sown, and the fruit that is to come must be awaited with patience, in its own time. Indeed, if even one fruit of your labour appears, you have something to offset all your earlier labours. For the salvation of a single soul weighs more than all the toils and sweat of all men, which are all well spent if even one soul is preserved by them. But we must note the cause of this faith, which belonged to many of the crowd. They said, he says, "When Christ comes," etc. This faith was chiefly stirred up by the miracles they had seen. So their haste towards faith was greater than faith itself, which is begotten in the heart chiefly through the Word of God and his holy Spirit. From this it is plain that faith is so pleasing to God that he deigns to honour even its smallest spark and particle with this name. Nor is it a mere empty name, since even the least spark of true faith is effective in preserving a man, for that power lies not in faith properly speaking but in Christ in whom we believe, from whose fullness we draw such strength and grace through the mouth of faith, however slight it may be, yet of true faith, that it suffices for eternal salvation.

units.la: 32 Audierunt Pharisaei turbam istam murmurantem de eo, ac miserunt Pharisaei ac primarij sacerdotes ministros ut eum prehenderent.
units.tr: 32 The Pharisees heard the crowd murmuring about him, and the Pharisees and the chief priests sent ministers to seize him.

units.la: 33 Dixit ergo ijs Iesus, Adhuc paulisper ero vobiscum, deinde abibo ad eum qui me misit.
units.tr: 33 Jesus therefore said to them, Yet a little while am I with you, and then I go to him who sent me.

units.la: 34 Quaeretis me, nec inuenietis, & vbi ego ero, eo vos non poteritis venire.
units.tr: 34 You will seek me and will not find me, and where I am, you cannot come.

units.la: 35 Dixerunt ergo Iudaei inter se, Quo iam est iste profecturus, ut nos non inueniamus eum? num ad ad eos qui dispersi sunt inter Graecos profecturus est, & Graecos docturus?
units.tr: 35 The Jews therefore said among themselves, Where is this man about to go, that we shall not find him? Is he going to those who are scattered among the Greeks, and to teach the Greeks?

units.la: 36 Quis est hic sermo quem dixit, Quaeretis me & non invenietis: Et ubi ego ero, vos non poteritis venire?
units.tr: 36 What is this saying that he said, You will seek me and not find me, and where I am, you cannot come?

units.la: HOc est effectu amplificationis regni Christi, de qua proxime praecedeti versu audiuimus. Pharisaei hoc audito conspirant aduersus Christum, una cum sacerdotum ordine a quibus alioqui dissentiebant, ac iniussis ex communi consilio ministris eum prehendi iusserunt. Antea quidem passi sunt Christum spargere semen Euangelij & lumen accendere. Quare a vulgo Iudaeorum ignauiae eorum hoc imputatum est, sed vbi iam vident fructum aliquem existere ex iacto illo semine, vbi vident lucem illam accensam diffundi in cordibus hominum, & in fidem apertam erumpere, hoc est, vbi vident incrementum regni Christi, tum quidem id ferre non possunt. Hostes veritatis aliquanto tempore in speculis sunt, e quibus vident lucem verbi Dei accendi, ac patuntur nonnunquam incendij initia: verum vbi vident lucem accensam diffundi latius, ac propagari regnum Christi, iam progressum illum doctrinae ferre amplius non possunt, quin tandem procurrant ad restinguendum quasi incendium. Neque vero ea est celeritas, aut diligentia Ministrorum lucis ac veritatis, professorumque ipsius in ea propaganda, quae est hostium in ea opprimenda: adeo vt quis iure miretur qui possit haec lux Euangelij quae, Dei admirabili gratia, hodierno die in hac Ecclesia nostra splendet, in tanta praesertim diligentia & oppugnatione hostium veritatis, tum pontificiorum, tum sacrilegorum hominum. Et caecus fit qui non videat secretam quandam Dei potentiam hic subesse, quam nisi ego aliquo modo viderem, cuique nisi considerem, desperarem profecto de lucis ac veritatis in hac nostra Ecclesia perseuerantia, vel ad breue aliquod tempus futura. Quam etiam miror non videre ipsos hostes praesertim, in tanta professorum ac ministrorum ipsorum socordia, atque ab ea sibi metuere. Futurum enim est profecto, vt ea ipsa tanta Dei potentia, quæ tam mirificè sustentat veritatem & Ecclesiam suam aduersus ipsos, tandem eos consumat, & in nihilum redigat. Dixit ergo. Christus ministros ad se apprehendendum vocientes, hoc primùm sermone excipit, nam cum ministris Pharisæorum & sacerdotum hic sermo habitus videtur, in quo non tam cauet sibi quàm ipsis. Certiores enim facit eos de eventuro ipsis propediem quodam grauissimo malo. Christus enim quo tempore in terris ageret, perpetuò ob oculos habuit miseriam hominum inter quos commorabatur, eorumque semper adeo miserius est, vt se suamque vitam neglexerit, vt eorum curam gereret. Christus enim non indulsit sibi ipsi, Rom. 15.3. id quod facilè conspicitur ex hoc loco. Pij quidem in hoc similes sunt Christi, aliquo certè modo. Nam & ij sunt qui vident miseriam tum suam tum aliorum, & ij sunt qui miserantur alios, atque dum intuentur spiritualem illam miseriam etiam summorum regum, quot hodierno die viuunt sine Christo, sine Deo in mundo, non habent in admiratione totam illam externam pompam ac gloriam eorum, imò ne suam quidem fortem, licet in speciem abiectam, cum eorum vniuersa felicitate commutarent; imò sese feliciores eis existimant.
units.tr: This is the effect of the enlargement of Christ's kingdom, of which we heard in the immediately preceding verse. When the Pharisees heard this, they conspired against Christ together with the order of priests, with whom they otherwise disagreed, and by common counsel they ordered the ministers, though not commanded, to seize him. Before this they had allowed Christ to scatter the seed of the Gospel and kindle the light. Therefore their inertia was imputed by the common people of the Jews to this, but when they now see some fruit spring up from that sown seed, when they see that light kindled and spreading in the hearts of men and breaking out into open faith, that is, when they see the increase of Christ's kingdom, then indeed they cannot bear it. For a time the enemies of truth are on watch, from which they see the light of God's Word being kindled, and they sometimes suffer the first beginnings of the fire; but when they see the light spreading more widely and the kingdom of Christ propagating, then they can bear this advance of the doctrine no longer, and at last they rush forward to quench the fire as it were. Yet the speed and diligence of the ministers of light and truth, and of its professors in spreading it, is not such as the diligence of the enemies in suppressing it, so that one may rightly wonder how this light of the Gospel can shine in our Church today by God's wonderful grace, especially amid such diligence and assault of the enemies of truth, both Papists and sacrilegious men. He is blind who does not see some hidden power of God at work here; and unless I saw it in some way, and unless I considered it, I would certainly despair of the light and truth persisting in this our Church, or even lasting for any short time. I also wonder that the enemies themselves do not see this, and fear it, especially given the great negligence of the professors and ministers themselves. For it will surely come about that that very great power of God, which so wonderfully sustains the truth and his Church against them, will at last consume them and reduce them to nothing. So Christ, when those ministers were summoned to seize him, first met this with a word; for this saying seems to have been spoken to the ministers of the Pharisees and priests, and in it he takes care not so much for himself as for them. For he informs them of a very grievous evil that is soon to befall them. For Christ, during the time he lived on earth, always kept before his eyes the misery of the men among whom he dwelt, and their misery was always so great that he neglected himself and his own life in order to care for them. For Christ did not please himself, Rom. 15.3, as is easily seen from this passage. The godly are indeed in this like Christ, in some certain way. For they too are those who see the misery both of themselves and of others, and they are those who pity others, and while they look upon that spiritual misery of even the greatest kings, of whom so many live today without Christ and without God in the world, they do not admire all that external pomp and glory of theirs, nor even their own lot, though humble in appearance; they would not exchange it for all their happiness; indeed they count themselves happier than those.

units.la: Cùm audita Pauli apologia, dixisset rex Agrippa ad Paulo, Propemodum persuades mihi vt fiam Christianus: Tum Paulus dixit, Optarim à Deo vt & propemodum, & admodum non tu modo, sed omnes etiam qui me audiunt hodie, facti effetis tales quales ego sum, exceptis istis vinculis. Imò bene cum Agrippa actum fuisset si etiam quoad vincula illa Paulo similis fuisset. Non quidem exististi comparatio istiusmodi ex superbia aliqua vel contemptu, cum sit cum summa misericordia coniuncta, qua mouentur pij erga miseros, quàque miserentur etiam persecutorum suorum, vt hoc loco Christus. Stephanus autem dum Iudæi eum lapidarent vocem edidit nouissimam, Domine ne statuas eis hoc peccatum: & cùm hoc dixisset, obdormiuit. Memor nimirum fuit sanctissimus Dei martyr, hostium suorum magis quàm sui ipsius, ac sentiens magis eorum miseriam, quàm præsentem illam mortem, qua tum ipsi eum affecerunt.
units.tr: When Paul had made his defence and King Agrippa had said to Paul, "You almost persuade me to become a Christian," then Paul said, "I would pray to God that not only you, but also all who hear me today, might become both almost and altogether such as I am, except for these chains." Indeed, it would have gone well with Agrippa if he had been like Paul even as to those chains. Yet such a comparison does not arise from any pride or contempt, since it is joined with the greatest compassion, by which the godly are moved towards the wretched, and by which they pity even their persecutors, as Christ does in this passage. Stephen too, when the Jews were stoning him, uttered his last word: "Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge"; and when he had said this, he fell asleep. The most holy martyr of God was surely mindful of his enemies rather than of himself, and felt their misery more than that present death with which they then afflicted him.

units.la: Sed hic notandum cuius demum malivistos certiores faciat Dominus, nempe quòd ipse breui tempore futurus esset vna cum iis,id nimirū, in quo ipsi felicitatem suam posuerunt. Quare nos quoque hoc ipsum Christi exemplo debemus obiicere tanquam summum aliquod malum mundo isti ingratissimo, quod ipsi tamen summum bonum existimant: praesertim autem de hoc admonendi sunt nostri homines, ingratissimi mortalium, quòd Christus propediem sit commigraturus è nobis.
units.tr: But here we must note what evil the Lord warns them of, namely that he himself would soon be gone together with those things in which they had placed their happiness. Therefore we too should set this very example of Christ before that most ungrateful world as some supreme evil, though they themselves count it their highest good; and especially our own people, the most ungrateful of mortals, must be warned about this, that Christ will shortly migrate from us.

units.la: Et ego eos de hoc admoneo Christi nomine hoc ipso die, Euangelium Christi non nisi ad breue tempus permansurum esse apud nos. Verum ne hoc istis leue videretur (vt quidem reipsa videbatur) subiungit Christus post discessum suum correptum iri eos desiderio ipsius admirabili; quod malum rursus vt augeat, admonet eos non tamen inuenturos esse ipsum. Quod ipsum denique malum vt amplificet, admonet futurum vt ipsi non possint eò loci venire, vbi sit ipse futurus. Et ego quoque moneo, istos qui bono suo futurum sperant, quòd Christus cum Euangelio suo sit commigraturus è nobis, statim insecuturum decessum ipsius desiderium ac sitim ipsius lucis ac libertatis in Christo tantum quantum ipsi tunc temporis ferre non poterunt, etsi nunc nullum in se desiderium Christi sentiant. Desiderium enim Christi, si sit tempore lucis ac gratiae oblatae, bonum quidem est ac suave, non secus atque sitis si potus sit ad manum, qua ipsa restinguatur bona est, & cum suavitate sentitur: ita est hoc desiderium gratiae, si gratiae dies sit, ac tempus illud acceptum. Tum enim illud habet locum, Beati qui esuriunt ac sitiunt iustitiam, quoniam ipsi saturabuntur. Haec beatitudo intelligenda est tum esse, cum iustitia illa, quam esuriunt ac sitiunt, praesens offertur: tum etiam eam quasi hauriunt ac comedunt praesentem cum ineffabili nescio qua suavitate. At vero desiderium gratiae, si tum sit cum tempus offerendi gratiam iam elapsum est, tum quidem graue est ac molestum admodum. Nonaliter atque sitis haec naturalis, cum non est ad manum potus, quo ipsa restinguatur, tum si vehemens sit, cum dolore quodam vehementi à nobis sentitur. Atque hoc est quasi mundi fatum, de maiori mundi huius parte loquor, vt quo tempore offertur gratiae & dum appellatur dies hodiernus, vt Apostoli verbis vtar, interea nullum in se sentiat gratiae desiderium: quin potius nauseam eius sentiat, id quod nos experimur hodierno die. At postquam iam euanuit gratia, tum quidem solet exoriri sitis gratiae intolerabilis, neque id mirum. Nam Deus postquam propter ingratitudinem nostram abstulit à nobis verbum suum, tum solet immittere iudicia, quae velint nolint homines, vi quadam sua ingignunt iis sensum miseriae praesentis, ac desiderium liberationis. Id quod nostri homines experientur tandem suo tempore, ne sit quod somnient rursus tenebras illas regni Antichristiani, illi qui volunt inuehi in nostram gentem, futuros se immunes à certa calamitate, & in pace tum fruituros bonis suis, ac foedissimis suis affectibus, cum exulabit Christus. Imò vero pronuncio tum fore vt exerceantur continuis malis ad confusionem suam aeternam, nisi tempestiue resipuerint. Ac tum quidem, vt vere dicam, rara solet esse resipiscentia eorum hominum, qui oblatam lucem contempserunt, postquam iam lux illa adempta est eis. Neque enim prophanus Esau poenitentiae locum reperit, quamuis cum lachrymis benedictionem illam exquisisset. Neque enim desiderium hoc prophanorum hominum proficisci solet ex seria resipiscentia, aut odio peccati propter ipsum peccatum, aut amore iustitiae & Christi propter ipsum Christum, sed ex sensu miseriae praesentis à qua cupiunt se liberari, vel mala aliqua conscientia, vt fuit desiderium illud Esau, qui sine dubio cum lachrymatus est mala conscientia contempti ac spreti à se iuris primogeniti est attactus. Quare tum demum existit sitis gratiae cum absumpta est gratia. Sed sitis illa nunquam restinguetur, verum poena erit superioris contemptus atque indurationis.
units.tr: And I, in Christ's name, warn them of this very day that the gospel of Christ will remain with us only for a short time. But lest this seem a small matter to them (as indeed it did seem), Christ adds that after his departure they will be seized with a wonderful longing for him. To increase this evil again, he warns that they will not find him. And to magnify it further, he warns that they will not be able to come to the place where he will be. I also warn those who hope for their own good when Christ departs from us with his gospel: the longing for him and the thirst for the light and liberty in Christ will immediately follow his departure, to a degree they will not be able to bear at that time, even though they now feel no longing for Christ within themselves. For the longing for Christ, if it comes in a time of offered light and grace, is good and sweet, just as thirst is good and is felt with pleasure when a drink is at hand to quench it. So too is this longing for grace, if it comes on a day of grace and in that acceptable time. For then that holds true: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. This blessedness is to be understood as present when that righteousness they hunger and thirst for is offered to them; then they drink it in, as it were, and eat it while it is present, with some ineffable sweetness I know not what. But longing for grace, when it comes after the time for offering grace has already passed, is then very heavy and burdensome indeed. It is not unlike natural thirst: when there is no drink at hand to quench it, and it is intense, we feel it with a certain vehement pain. And this is, as it were, the fate of the world (I speak of the greater part of the world): while grace is offered, and while the day is called "today", to use the Apostle's words, it feels no longing for grace within itself; rather it feels nausea for it, which we experience on this very day. But once grace has vanished, there usually arises an intolerable thirst for grace, and no wonder. For God, after taking his Word from us on account of our ingratitude, usually sends judgments which, whether men will or no, by their own power engender in them a sense of present misery and a desire for deliverance. Our people will experience this in its own time, so that those who wish to be carried into our nation may not go on dreaming of returning to that darkness of the Antichristian kingdom, supposing that they will be immune from certain calamity and will enjoy their goods and their most foul desires in peace, once Christ is driven out. Rather, I declare that they will then be afflicted with continual evils to their eternal confusion, unless they repent in time. And then, to speak truly, repentance is rare among those who have despised the light offered, once that light has been taken from them. For the profane Esau found no room for repentance, although he had sought that blessing with tears. This longing of profane men does not usually proceed from serious repentance, from hatred of sin for sin's own sake, or from love of righteousness and of Christ for Christ's own sake, but from a sense of present misery from which they wish to be freed, or from some evil conscience. So it was with that longing of Esau, who doubtless wept when he was struck by the evil conscience of having despised and scorned the birthright. Therefore thirst for grace arises only when grace has been taken away. But that thirst will never be quenched; it will be the punishment of the earlier contempt and of hardening.

units.la: Dixerunt ergo Iudaei inter se. Hoc effectum est praecedentis admonitionis vel etiam comminationis, effectii, inquam, in ministris illis, qui missi erant ad apprehendum Christum. Nihil illi quidem cogitant de eius decessu: non conantur eum quasi invitum apud se retinere: non sic eum animis suis ratiocinantur. Breue tem-pus pus dicit Iesus futurum esse gratiae; recte igitur vtamur breui illo tempore, & redimamus occasionem. Verum tantum absunt ab eo, vt incipiant ludibrio habere ipsius siue admonitionem, siue comminationem. Quò futurū est, inquiunt, vt iste proficiscatur, ita vt non sit inueniēdus à nobis in posterum? num ad eos qui dispersi sunt inter Graecos iturus est? Hebraeos intelligunt qui dispersi erant inter gentes. Hic est mos huius saeculi: In comminationibus iudiciorum Dei, & in hac praesertim comminatione iudicij grauissimi, quo comminatur Deus se alio transflaturum esse hanc gratiam Euangelij, ridentes ludibundi ac si ea res sit nullius momenti. Ea enim est hominum impietas, qua non modò nihil sentiunt, nihil audiunt, nihil intelligunt prae stupore & cordis duritie, sed etiam quae non intelligunt irrid- ent ac ludibrio habent, quod est summum impietatis caput. Christus nominatim locum illum in quem iturus erat designauit, nempe caelum ipsum: Abibo, inquiens, ad eum qui misit me. Hoc est Patrem, vt postea loquitur Discipulis suis cap. 14.1. & deinceps: sed hoc isti nequaquam intellexerunt. Qui terrena duntaxat sapiunt, non intelligunt de spiritualibus, de caelesti illo loco loquentem: de terrestri vero loco aliquo, etiam transmarino, & de commigratione vel in Galliam vel in Hispaniam, vel in Italiam, vel in aliquam denique huiusmodi regionem, quantumuis longe dissitum, loquentem intelligunt, de commigratione in caelos non intelligunt. Atqui sermo Domini non caruit omnino effecto suo, ea enim fuit gratia sermonis ipsius, sicut videbimus postea, hoc cap. vers. 44. vt non aliquis sint isti eum vel manu semel attingere. Irriserunt, fateor; sed tamen conscientia eorum ita attacta fuit, vt non aliquis sint manum in eum iniicere. Quid, quae prohibet manifestam & apertam vim irrisorum istorum, quibus impleta est tota haec regio nostra? Quid, aliud, praeter conscientiam gratiae illam & maiestatem illius ipsius verbi, quam tamen apud se false irridentes ex animis suis eiectum eunt?
units.tr: Therefore the Jews said among themselves. This is the effect of the preceding admonition, or even threat, the effect, I say, upon those ministers who had been sent to seize Christ. Those men do not think at all of his departure; they do not try to keep him with them as if he were unwilling to go; they do not reason about him in this way in their minds. Jesus says that the time of grace will be short; therefore let us use that short time well and redeem the opportunity. But they are so far from this that they begin to mock both his admonition and his threat. "Where is he going," they say, "that we shall not be able to find him in future? Will he go to those scattered among the Greeks?" They mean the Hebrews who were dispersed among the nations. This is the custom of this age: in the threats of God's judgments, and especially in this threat of the most grievous judgment, by which God threatens to transfer the grace of the gospel elsewhere, men laugh and mock as if the matter were of no moment. Such is the impiety of men, by which they not only feel nothing, hear nothing and understand nothing, through stupor and hardness of heart, but also they laugh at and mock what they do not understand, which is the highest head of impiety. Christ expressly named the place to which he was going: heaven itself. "I go," he says, "to him who sent me." This means the Father, as he later speaks to his disciples in chapter 14 and following; but these men did not understand this at all. Those who savour only earthly things do not grasp that he is speaking of spiritual things, of that heavenly place. They understand him speaking of some earthly place, even one across the sea, and of a migration into France or Spain or Italy, or into some region of this kind, however far away; of a migration into heaven they do not understand. Yet the Lord's word did not wholly lack its effect, for that was the grace of his word, as we shall see later in this chapter, verse 44: they were not able to lay a hand on him even once. They mocked, I grant; but nevertheless their conscience was so touched that they could not lay hands on him. What prevents the manifest and open violence of those scoffers, by which this whole region of ours has been filled? What else but that awareness of grace and that majesty of the very word, which those who falsely mock nevertheless carry away, cast out of their minds?

units.la: 37 Vltimo autem die illo magno festi stetit Iesus, & clamauit dicens, Siquis sitit, veniat ad me & bibat.
units.tr: 37 On the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, saying: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.

units.la: 38 Qui credit in me, sicut dixit Scriptura, flumina aquæ viuæ ex ventre ipsius fluent.
units.tr: 38 He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from his belly shall flow rivers of living water.

units.la: 39 Hoc autem dixit de spiritu illo quem accepturi erant credentes in eum. Nondum enim erat Spiritus sanctus, quia nondum erat glorificatus.
units.tr: 39 But he said this about the Spirit whom those believing in him were to receive. For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.

units.la: HÆc est concio Iesu habita ad populum vltimo decimum die illo magno festi tabernaculorum; notatur circumstantia temporis, sub qua intelligi etiam frequentiam populi. Notatur quoque gestus dicentis. Clamavit, inquit: ad innuendam summam libertatem Domini qua vsus est in loquendo. Illud enim erat summæ libertatis eo die, eo modo atque gestu loqui præsertim, cum eum interea continuò persequuti sint Ministri illi Pharisæorum & Sacerdotum, qui ipsum ad necem quærebant. Sic nescio quomodo fit vt etiam pij ad exemplum Domini sui in extremis quibusque periculis ferè maximè audaces ac fortes inveniantur, vt facile quis videat non vi vlla naturæ vel humana, sed plane diuina potentia eos fulciri, sicuti Paulus de se dixit, vitam Iesu manifestam fieri in corpore suo, ac si dixisset neminem esse, cui hoc non possit constare, si modò velit animum suum advertere, se non tam suæ vitæ beneficio viuere, in tanta præsertim mortificatione corporis sui, omnibus modis afflicti, quàm vitæ Iesu ac vitæ ipsius Dei.
units.tr: This is the sermon of Jesus delivered to the people on the last, the great day of the feast of tabernacles. The circumstance of time is noted, under which the crowd of people is also to be understood. The speaker's gesture is noted too: "he cried out," it says, to show the great freedom of the Lord with which he spoke. For it was a sign of the greatest freedom on that day to speak in such a manner and with such a gesture, especially since meanwhile those ministers of the Pharisees and priests who sought his death were continually pursuing him. So somehow it happens that even the godly, after the example of their Lord, are found most bold and brave in the gravest dangers, so that one can easily see they are upheld not by any natural or human power but plainly by divine power. Paul said of himself that the life of Jesus is made manifest in his body. It is as if he had said that there is no one to whom this cannot be plain, if only he is willing to attend to his own mind: that he does not live so much by the benefit of his own life, especially amid such mortification of his body, afflicted in every way, as by the life of Jesus and the life of God himself.

units.la: Sed videamus nunc summam concionis huius Domini. Si quis sitit. In eandem planè sententiam dictum est omnia ab Esaia, Heus, qui sitis, venite ad aquas, &c. Sed hoc cum olim prædictum esset à Propheta de Christo venturo. Christus itaque in adventu suo implet quod de se prædictum fuerat. In hac concione Dominus stans in medio populi, nihil quidem ab eo exposcit, ne vitam quidem ipsam, cùm tamen eam peti intelligeret à Ministris Pharisæorum & sacerdotum, qui & ipsi cum cæteris vna stabant: sed vltrò offert gratiam populo. & quâ illam? quanimirum maximè iis opus esse sciebat. qua autem gratia opus iis maximè esse sciebat? Quo, quæso, beneficio eget is potissimum, qui sitit ista corporali enecatur?
units.tr: But let us now look at the sum of this sermon of the Lord. "If anyone thirsts." Isaiah said essentially the same thing: "Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters, etc." But this was foretold by the Prophet of the Christ who was to come. Christ, then, at his coming fulfils what had been foretold of him. In this sermon the Lord, standing in the midst of the people, asks nothing from them, not even their life itself, although he knew it was sought by the ministers of the Pharisees and the priests, who stood there with the rest. Instead he freely offers grace to the people. And what grace? Surely the grace they most needed, as he knew. What grace did he know they most needed? What benefit, I ask, does a man need most when he is perishing of bodily thirst?

units.la: Summa concionis Christi. Esai. 55.1.
units.tr: The sum of Christ's sermon. Isaiah 55.1.

units.la: Qua gratia Christus Iudæis offert. catur? annon potu quo restinguatur sitis huic si dederis omnia, potum autem non obtuleris, frustra alia omnia, siti enim coficietur. Dominus itaque cum staret in medio populi illius miseri, vidit eorum miseriam eam quam ipsi non potuerunt videre. Sensit ipse eorum ariditatem fuminam, quam tamen ipsi non senserunt. Cognovit eos siti illa spirituali perituros propediem, sino tempestive esset restincta. Ideo liberaliter offert miseris & sitientibus potum: Et quem illum Non terrestrem aliquem, sed potum quem ipsi nullo pretio vnquam redimere poterant, non argento, non auro, non aliquibus huiusmodi caducis rebus. Potum nimirum & haustum sanguinis pretiosissimi, sanguinis ipsius Dei. Potum Spiritus sancti ex sanguine illo in ipsos demanaturi videbimus postea. Quem potum, nisi quis gratis acceperit, accipere eum non poterit. Unde illo quod citauimus Esaiae capite dictum est, comparate absque pecunia, absque pretio. Hunc ipsum potum tam liberaliter, tam clementer offert nobis hodierno die Dominus per Ministros Euangelij sui. Nondum enim exaruit ille sanguis Domini, aut gratia Spiritus imminuta est aliqua sui parte. Sed cui demum offert hunc potum? Si quis, inquit, sitit. Cui offert quis corporalem aliquem potum? Annon sitienti? Dominus itaque non offert potum nisi sitienti. Fateor quidem populum eum no tum sitiuisse, ut oportuit eos sitire: sed Dominus dum dicit, Siquis sitit, &c. his ipsis verbis simul offert potum & sitim excitat. Offert gratiam desideranti, & dat gratiam desiderij, ut non sit quod ex hoc aut simili aliquo loco colligant pontificij liberum arbitrium suum: quasi vero in manu eorum fuerit & in libertate arbitrij sitire. Aut quasi eo consilio animo obtulerit iis hunc potum. Sitienti igitur offert, ut intelligatis, nonnisi sitientem primum ac serio desideratem gratiam eam obtinere posse. Petite, inquit, & dabitur vobis, pulsate & aperietur vobis. Contra vero non prius quis gratiam quam eius aliquam mensuram accipit. Beati qui esuriunt ac sitiunt iustitiam, quoniam saturabuntur. Quibus verbis significat simul cum ipso desiderio dari aliquo certe modo desideratum donum. Quid enim aliud significat voluptas ista quam inter desiderandum sentimus, quàm fruitionem rei desideratæ? An voluptas aliqua est in siti ista naturali, nisi simul cum siti bibamus & potu fruamur aliquo? Verùm quomodo ingignitur nobis sitis illa spiritualis? Paulus air, Onerati suspiramus: quo significat onus illud peccati ac miseriæ grauissimum, exprimere nobis sitim illam, ac desiderium ingens cum suspiriis & gemitibus inenarrabilibus coniunctum. Fieri enim non potest vt instabiles istæ animæ quæ viuunt sine sensu omni miseriæ, istæ, inquâ, expetant vnquam gratiam ac liberationem. Quamobrè id quod primùm omnium operatur in nobis sitim hanc ac desiderium hoc gratiæ, est sensus peccati ac miseriæ nostræ. Vnde pro siti hac, quam hoc loco dicit Dominus, vsus est alibi in simili exhortatione sensu miseriæ ac oneris peccati: Venite, inquit, ad me omnes qui defatigati estis & onerati, & ego faciam vt requiescatis. Quòd si igitur non nisi iis demum qui sitiunt, offeratur iste potus cœlestis, quid dicemus de iis qui inebriati sunt ad nauseam usque, & vsque adeo oppleti sunt vanitatis huius mundi, vt sastidiant potum illum cœlestis gratiæ? Quid ad hæc benedicta virgo, Famelicos, inquit, impleuit bonis ac diuites ablegauit inanes.
units.tr: By what grace does Christ offer himself to the Jews? Is it not like giving a man everything else that might quench his thirst, but withholding the drink? All the rest is useless, for he will waste away with thirst. The Lord, then, standing in the midst of that wretched people, saw their misery, which they themselves could not see. He felt their dreadful dryness, which they themselves did not feel. He knew that they would soon perish of that spiritual thirst, unless it were quenched in time. So he freely offers drink to the wretched and thirsty. And it is not some earthly drink, but a drink which they could never buy back at any price, not with silver, not with gold, nor with any such perishable things: the drink, that is, and the draught of the most precious blood, the blood of God himself. We shall see later that the Spirit of the Holy Spirit is to flow out upon them from that blood. Unless a man receives this drink freely, he will not be able to receive it at all. So it is said in the chapter of Isaiah that I have cited, buy without money, without price. Today the Lord offers this same drink to us so freely and so graciously through the ministers of his Gospel. For that blood of the Lord has not yet dried up, nor has the grace of the Spirit been diminished in any part. But to whom does he offer this drink at last? If anyone, he says, thirsts. To whom does anyone offer bodily drink? Is it not to the thirsty? So the Lord offers the drink only to the thirsty. I admit that that people had not yet thirsted as they ought to have thirsted. But when the Lord says, If anyone thirsts, etc., by these very words he at once offers the drink and arouses the thirst. He offers grace to the one who desires it, and gives the desire for grace, so that the Papists cannot gather from this or a similar passage that their free will has any part in it, as if it were in their hands and within the freedom of their will to thirst. Or as if the Lord had offered them this drink with such an intention. He offers to the thirsty, therefore, so that you may understand that only one who thirsts, and who desires grace earnestly and in earnest, can obtain it. Ask, he says, and it will be given you; knock, and it will be opened to you. On the contrary, no one receives grace before he receives some measure of it. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. By these words he signifies that the desired gift is given, in some certain way, together with the desire itself. For what else does that pleasure which we feel while we desire signify, but the enjoyment of the thing desired? Is there any pleasure in that natural thirst, unless we drink and enjoy some drink at the same time as we thirst? But how is that spiritual thirst kindled in us?
