Paul says, Being burdened, we groan: by which he means that the heaviest burden of sin and misery presses out in us that thirst, and a great longing joined with sighs and inexpressible groanings. For it cannot happen that those unstable souls which live without any sense of misery should ever seek grace and deliverance. Therefore, what first of all works this thirst and this desire for grace in us is the sense of our sin and misery. Hence, for the thirst which the Lord speaks of here, he elsewhere uses, in a similar exhortation, the sense of misery and the burden of sin: Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. But if this heavenly drink is offered only to those who thirst, what shall we say of those who are drunk even to nausea, and so utterly weighed down by the vanities of this world that they loathe that drink of heavenly grace? What does the blessed Virgin say to this? He has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty.

units.la: Hactenus de potu illo cœlesti, de iis quibus demum offeratur, nempe sitientibus, déque modo illo præcipuo quo gignatur in nobis sitis illa gratiæ. Nunc de modo ac ratione qua iam sitiens aliquis potum illum assequatur & hauriant. Est enim certus quidem modus, quo quis etiam sitiens ac præparatus ad potum illum accipiat. Veniat, inquit, ad me & bibat. Veniendum est rectà ad fontem omnis gratiæ Iesum Christum. Christus sitientem non amandat ad ieiuna elementa, non ad umbras, sed ad sE inuitat: vt illud sciamus, sitienti non quærendas paludes aut riuulos, quibus sitim suam sarient, sed statim veniendum ad fontem ipsum longè purissimum. Papistæ hodiemo die amandant sitientem ad paludes meritorum, satisfactionum, inuocationis angelorum, & sanctorum hominum demortuorum, ad mille denique alia huiusmodi inuenta sua. Sed væ illis. Hinc internoscas inter verum & falsum doctorem. Dicit Dominus, Veniat ad me, non ad alium quem, aut aliud quid. Quid igitur ve-rus
units.tr: So far, concerning that heavenly drink, to whom it is at last offered, namely the thirsty, and concerning that principal manner in which that thirst for grace is begotten in us. Now concerning the mode and manner in which a man who is already thirsty obtains and drinks that drink. There is indeed a certain way in which even a thirsty man, prepared for that drink, receives it. Let him come, he says, to me and drink. He must come straight to Jesus Christ, the fountain of all grace. Christ does not send the thirsty man away to empty elements, nor to shadows, but invites him to himself, so that we may know that the thirsty should not seek marshes or streams with which to slake their thirst, but should come at once to the source itself, which is by far the purest. Today the Papists send the thirsty man away to the marshes of merits, of satisfactions, of the invocation of angels and of dead holy men, and finally to a thousand other such inventions of theirs. But woe to them. From this you may distinguish a true teacher from a false one. The Lord says, Let him come to me, not to any other person or to anything else. What, then, is a true teacher?

units.la: Matth. 11. 28. rus est doctor? Qui dicit sitienti: ito recta ad Christum ipsum vitæ fontem. Falsus vero doctor est, qui vel directè vel indirectè quemquam ablegat alió quàm ad Christum. Neque ipse vnquam hausit illam aquam vitæ quæ est in ipso fonte, qui ad paludes illas impurissimas miseros ac sitientes homines remittit. Habemus igitur potum oblatum: habemus cui offeratur, nempe sitienti; habemus postremò modum quo sitiens vel siti præparatus eam consequatur, nempe si ad Christum rectà veniat. Nunc quò magis excitet illam sitim ac fidem, potus illius vberem copiam ac abundantiam ineffabilem ipsis ob oculos ponit: Qui credit in me, inquit, sicut dixit Scriptura, &c. Scriptura hæc est Esaiæ 58.11. eadem quidem sententia, etsi non eadem verbis cum hoc loco: Erit tanquam hortus irriguus & veluti scatebræ aquarum cuius non fallunt aquæ. At Christus hoc loco ait, flumina aquæ viuæ, &c. q.d. Dabo ei nō riuulum aliquem, sed fontem ipsum copiosissimum aquæ viuæ, hoc est, meipsum, qui per fidem illam habitabo in ipsius corde. Designatur hic fons copiosissimus & vberrimus per flumina hæc, quæ ex ventre eius fluent, quæque ita irrigabunt ipsum, vt instar horti cuiusdam irrigui, in quo est scatebra aquarum perennium, perpetuò virescat atque fructificet, non tantum sibi, sed & aliis; non secus atque hortus irriguus fructus in vsus hominū producit. Nota hoc loco: Christus quò magis alliciat eos ad sitiendum & credendum, aperit quasi fontem illum aquæ viuæ ex quo sunt bibituri. Diximus quidem supra sensum miseriæ necessario præcedere oportere sitim hanc gratiæ. Verùm nunc dicimus, quòd si non cum sensu illo miseriæ coniunctus merit aspectus aliquis, atque adeo sensus atque perceptio quædam illius aquæ viuæ, ex qua nobis bibendum quamquam fore vt serio ac vero eius desiderio tangatur. Sensus miseriæ, fateor, primus esse debet, sed secundo loco sit necesse est sensus ac perceptio misericordiæ aliqua, secus enim non appetemus eam sicuti oportet. Vnde Petrus, Expetite, inquit, lac sermonis sincerum: si quidem gustatis quòd benignus sit Dominus. Ecce conditione hanc ponit, guslum nempe suauitatis ac benignitatis Domini: ex quo sequitur hæc quam commendat expetitio sincerī lactis sermonis. Cūm igitur adeo necessarius sit sensus gratiae aliquis ad desiderium animo ingenuendum, ideo Dominus aequas illas gratiae quasi aperit hoc loco. Et Paulus aperit & explicat Colossensibus thesauros illos omnis sapientiae & cognitionis abscondi- tos, & plenitudinem illam deitatis corporaliter habi- tantis in Christo. Et alibi precatur vt illuminatis oculis Ephesij possint videre quae sit spes illa vocationis ipsius, &c. Atque hoc fuit argumentum Christi, fuit quoque argumentum Apostolorum ipsius, & est hodierno die argumentum Ministrorum Euangelij, quo quidem excitant in hominum cordibus desiderium gratiae, neimpe ostensio ac patefactio illius tantae quae in Christo est gratiae, vt inde, si possit fieri, sensus eius aliquis oriatur, vt ex sensu deinde desiderium existat, donec tandē percipiant homines satietatem illam gaudiorum quae est in conspectu eius. Nam cùm duo sint fere quibus excitetur desiderium hoc, atque situs haec gratiae, praedicatio miseriae ac praedicatio miserecordiae, sic Christus inter se & Moisen ac Prophetas suos, qui ante ipsum fuerunt in mundo, partitus est haec duo, vt partes praedicandi miseriam hominis, idque ex lege Dei dederit Mosi & Prophetis: sibi autē, Apostolis ac Ministris suis sumpserit partes praedicandi gratiam.
units.tr: Matth. 11. 28. A true teacher is one who says to the thirsty: go straight to Christ himself, the fountain of life. A false teacher, on the other hand, is one who, either directly or indirectly, sends anyone away anywhere but to Christ. Nor has he himself ever drunk of that water of life which is in the fountain itself, who sends wretched and thirsty men back to those most foul marshes. We have, therefore, the drink offered; we have to whom it is offered, namely the thirsty; and lastly we have the manner in which the thirsty man, or one prepared by thirst, obtains it, namely if he comes straight to Christ. Now, so that he may stir up that thirst and faith more, he sets before their eyes the abundant plenty and the unspeakable fullness of that drink: He who believes in me, he says, as the Scripture has said, etc. This Scripture is Isaiah 58.11, the same sense though not the same words as in this place: It shall be like a watered garden and like a spring of waters, whose waters do not fail. But here Christ says rivers of living water, etc., as if to say: I will give him not some little stream, but the very most copious fountain of living water, that is, myself, who by that faith will dwell in his heart. This most copious and abundant fountain is here designated by these rivers, which shall flow out of his belly, and which shall so water him that, like a watered garden in which there is a spring of perennial waters, he shall be always green and fruitful, not only for himself but for others also, just as a watered garden produces fruit for the use of men. Note this here: in order to draw them more to thirst and to believe, Christ opens, as it were, that fountain of living water from which they are to drink. We said above, indeed, that the sense of misery must necessarily precede this thirst for grace. But now we say that, unless some sight, and therefore some sense and perception of that living water, from which we are to drink, is joined with that sense of misery, the soul will not be touched with a serious and true desire for it. The sense of misery, I admit, must be first; but in the second place there must necessarily be some sense and perception of mercy, otherwise we shall not seek it as we ought. Hence Peter says, Desire the sincere milk of the word, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is kind. See, he lays down this condition, namely the taste of the sweetness and kindness of the Lord, from which follows this desire for the sincere milk of the word which he commends. Since, then, some sense of grace is so necessary for kindling the desire in the mind, therefore the Lord, in this place, as it were opens up those graces. And Paul opens and explains to the Colossians those treasures of all wisdom and knowledge hidden in Christ, and that fullness of the Godhead dwelling bodily in Christ. And elsewhere he prays that the eyes of the Ephesians, being enlightened, may be able to see what is the hope of his calling, etc. This was the method of Christ; it was also the method of his Apostles; and it is today the method of the ministers of the Gospel, who indeed stir up in men's hearts the desire for grace by setting forth and laying open that great grace which is in Christ, so that from this, if it can be done, some sense of it may arise, and from the sense then the desire may come into being, until at last men perceive that satisfaction of joys which is in his presence. For since there are almost two things by which this desire and this thirst for grace are excited, the preaching of misery and the preaching of mercy, Christ divided these two between himself and Moses and his Prophets, who were in the world before him: he gave to Moses and the Prophets the part of preaching man's misery, and that from the law of God; but he took to himself, and to his Apostles and ministers, the part of preaching grace.

units.la: Lex per Mosem data est, gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum extitit. Hoc enim est proprium ac praecipuum munus quod hodierno die incumbit Ministris Euangelij, etsi quę nunc est hominum obstinatio extorqueant iis comminationes ac denuntiationes quae sunt ex lege grauissimas.
units.tr: The law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. This is the proper and chief task that falls to the ministers of the Gospel today, even though the stubbornness of men now extorts from them the most severe threats and denunciations that the law contains.

units.la: Hoc autem dixit. Iohannes inserit expositionem praesentis allegoriae de fluminibus illis, quae dixit Dominus, aquae viuae, &c. scilicet vt ex hoc loco & aliis huiusmodi discamus opus esse Ecclesiae expositione verborum Christi, Prophetarum ac Apostolorum ipsius. Nunquam enim satis potest illud mysterium aperiri: neque sufficit lectio Scripturarum ad cognitionem & consolationem eam quam ex Scripturis capere debemus. Verum quo demum tempore adiecit Iohannes interpretationem hanc verborum Christi: nimirum quando ipse re ipsa expertus est complementum eorum & in se & aliis, postquam quam iam Christus in cælos ascendisset. Ita quicunque interpretationem Scripturarum suscipiunt, oportet eos quodammodo experiri in se ea quæ sunt scripta, ac sentire Spiritum illum de quo loquuntur, gratiam illam Spiritus, Christum ipsum, cæterAQue illa cælestia. Optima enim expositio iflarum rerum ex sensu earundem tantum existit, neque aptus est ad scrutandum profunditates Dei, quisquis spiritum Dei non habet. Verum ut ad verba ipsa veniamus: flumina aquę viuę interpretatur Spiritum illum quem accepturi erant credentes: Spiritum intelligo ipsum Dei Spiritum Sanctum cum donis suis, præsertim autem illis mirificis & extraordinariis, quæ effusa sunt in primitiuam illam Ecclesiam, post gloriosam Christi ascensionem: quæ Ioel Propheta prædixit effundenda, Petrus autem apud Lucam narrauit effusa. Dixi hic intelligendum esse ipsummet Spiritum sanctum cū donis suis, quia vbi dona & efficacia Spiritus, ibi & ipse Spiritus præsens est: & cum dantur dona, datur Spiritus, cum accipiuntur dona, accipitur Spiritus: non quidem quòd mutet locum Spiritus, sed quòd cum impleat omnia, vt qui Deus sit cum Patre & Filio, vnus idemque incipiat iam in cordibus hominum speciali aliquo modo esse efficax, & sese præsentem per dona & effecta sua manifestare. Atque hac ratione dicitur dari & mitti hominibus. Quem accepturi erant credentes in eum. Quòd si credentes demum in Christum accepturi erant Spiritū Sanctum cum donis illis suis, necesse est fontem omnium donorum Spiritus in Christo esse. Quid ita? Nam omnia dona Spiritus sancti primum a Patre data sunt Filio quatenus Deus, infinita & quantitate & numero; quatenus homo, & maiora & plura infinitis partibus quam ea quæ data sunt vlli creaturæ, hominи vel Angelo; vnde proprie & peculiarius dicitur Spiritus sanctus super eū requiescere. Vt autem Christus solus in se habet fontem illum omnium donorum sibi datum a Patre, ita solus potest donare hominibus: neque enim quisquam est hominum vel Angelorum qui donum aliquod quod a Deo accepit, aliis possit communicare. Solus enim Christus est dator omnium donorum vt qui Deus sit: solus enim Deus dator est Spiritus ac donorum Spiritus. fui. Quum ascendisset in sublime, captiuam duxit captiuitatem & dedit dona hominibus. Nam fecundu mensuram donationis Christi potest quidè aliquis ministri vice fungi in donatione illa donorum Spiritus sancti, sed efficaciter operari eam in animis non potest; potest quidem irrigare & plantare, sed Deus est qui dat incrementum. Modus autem quo recipimus Spiritus dona hic est: credimus in Christum, eiúsque sanguinem primum omnium fide apprehendimus: Tum Deus non solum imputat nobis fidem illam pro iustitia, hoc est censet nos per fidem iustos in illa Christi iustitia: sed conformes nos facit imagini Filij sui in cognitione & sanctitate. Regenerat nos per Spiritum ipsius atque sanctificat: quos iustificauit eos etiam glorificauit. Nondum enim erat. Obiici poterat, quòd statim modo accepturi erât credentes Spiritum: ergo nondum erat Spiritus sanctus ... tetur Apostolus nondum fuisse Spiritum, hoc est Spiritum sanctum cum suis donis vt prius, aut Spiritus effi-cax ad dona sua operandum in hominibus, miraculosa illa praesertim intelligit. Ratio autem est, quia Iesus nondum erat glorificatus, id est Spiritus sanctus in ipso capite non se plane manifestauit in donis suis, neque dum plane glorificauit caput ipsum Christum. Nam glorificatio capitis est Spiritum eiúsque dona supra omnem mensuram accipere. Fundamentum autem ac propositio huius rationis ista potest esse: Glorificatio (quæ nempe fit per Spiritum & dona ipsius) glorificatio, inquam, membrorum pendet à glorificatione capitis: vnde sequitur, si caput nondum erat glorificatum quo tempore interris ageret, humiliaretur & seipsum inaniret: sequitur, inquam, nondum fuisse Spiritum quo glorificarentur membra ipsius. Contrà autem glorificato iam capite, Spiritum esse necesse est quo glorificentur membra. Vide igitur proportionem inter caput & membra quòd ad Spiritum & gloriam. Proportio autem hæc est virtute coniunctionis membrorum & capitis, adeo vt, quo arctior est coniunctio membrorum & capitis, eo maior fit glorificatio membrorum. Exempli gratia, fide cum Domino ac capite nostro coniungimur in hac vita, quo maior est fides cuiusque, eo maior est necessario sanctificatioficationis mensura in quoque. Cùm autem aspectu ipso fruemur Domino nostro ac capite, & plenè perfectéque cum eo coniungemur, tum quidem perficietur glorificatio nostri ac sanctificatio in altero demum sæculo.
units.tr: He said this. John inserts an explanation of the present allegory about those rivers which the Lord called living water, etc. He does so, clearly, so that from this passage and others like it we may learn that the Church needs to expound the words of Christ and of his Prophets and Apostles. That mystery can never be opened fully, and reading the Scriptures is not enough for the knowledge and comfort which we ought to draw from them. But when, in fact, did John add this interpretation of Christ's words? Clearly when he himself had experienced in fact their fulfilment, both in himself and in others, after Christ had ascended into heaven. So whoever takes up the interpretation of the Scriptures must in some measure experience in himself what is written, and perceive that Spirit of whom they speak, that grace of the Spirit, Christ himself, and the other heavenly things. For the best exposition of these things comes only from the sense of them, and whoever does not have the Spirit of God is not fit to search the depths of God. But let us come to the words themselves. He interprets the rivers of living water as that Spirit which believers were to receive. By the Spirit I understand the Holy Spirit of God himself, with his gifts, especially those wonderful and extraordinary gifts which were poured out upon the primitive Church after Christ's glorious ascension, which the Prophet Joel foretold would be poured out, and which Peter related in Luke as having been poured out. I say here that the Holy Spirit himself with his gifts is to be understood, because where the gifts and the workings of the Spirit are, there the Spirit himself is present; and when gifts are given, the Spirit is given, and when gifts are received, the Spirit is received. Not that the Spirit changes place, but because, while he fills all things, being God together with the Father and the Son, he begins now in a special way to be effective in the hearts of men, and to manifest himself present through his gifts and effects. And in this way he is said to be given and sent to men. Which believers were to receive in him. But if believers were at last to receive the Holy Spirit with those gifts of his in Christ, it is necessary that Christ be the fountain of all the Spirit's gifts. Why so? Because all the gifts of the Holy Spirit were first given by the Father to the Son, as God, infinite both in quantity and in number; and as man, greater and more numerous, by infinite parts, than those given to any creature, man or angel. Hence the Holy Spirit is said, in a proper and more peculiar sense, to rest upon him. And just as Christ alone has in himself that fountain of all gifts given to him by the Father, so he alone can bestow them on men. For no one among men or angels can communicate to others any gift which he has received from God. Christ alone is the giver of all gifts, as he is God; for God alone is the giver of the Spirit and of the gifts of the Spirit. When he had ascended on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men. For according to the measure of Christ's bestowal, a minister may indeed act in the place of the giver in that bestowal of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, but he cannot work it effectively in souls; he can water and plant, but it is God who gives the increase. The manner in which we receive the gifts of the Spirit is this: we believe in Christ, and first of all we lay hold of his blood by faith. Then God not only imputes to us that faith for righteousness, that is, he counts us righteous through faith in that righteousness of Christ; but he also makes us conformed to the image of his Son in knowledge and holiness. He regenerates us through his Spirit and sanctifies us; those whom he justified, these he also glorified. For the Spirit was not yet. It could be objected that believers were about to receive the Spirit only now: therefore the Holy Spirit was not yet ... The Apostle affirms that the Spirit had not yet been, that is, the Holy Spirit with his gifts as before, or the Spirit effective in working his gifts in men; he especially understands those miraculous ones. The reason, moreover, is that Jesus was not yet glorified, that is, the Holy Spirit had not yet plainly manifested himself in his gifts in the Head himself, nor had he yet plainly glorified the Head, Christ himself. For the glorification of the Head consists in receiving the Spirit and his gifts beyond all measure. The foundation and premise of this reasoning may be this: the glorification of the members (which indeed takes place through the Spirit and his gifts) depends upon the glorification of the Head. Whence it follows that, if the Head was not yet glorified, while he was walking on earth, he was humbled and emptied himself, it follows, I say, that the Spirit was not yet there by whom his members might be glorified. On the other hand, with the Head now glorified, the Spirit must be there by whom the members are glorified. See therefore the proportion between the Head and the members as regards the Spirit and glory. This proportion rests on the power of the union of the members and the Head, so that the closer the union of the members and the Head, the greater the glorification of the members. For example, by faith we are joined to the Lord and our Head in this life; the greater each one's faith, the necessarily greater the measure of sanctification in each one. But when we shall enjoy our Lord and Head in his very sight, and shall be joined to him fully and perfectly, then our glorification and sanctification will at last be perfected in the age to come.

units.la: 40 Multi ergo è turba quum audissent hunc sermonem dicebant, Vere hic est Propheta ille.
units.tr: 40 Many therefore of the crowd, when they heard this saying, said, Truly this is the Prophet.

units.la: 41 Alii dicebât, Hic est Christus ille. Quidam autem dicebant, Num enim è Galilæa veniet ille Christus?
units.tr: 41 Others said, This is the Christ. But some said, Surely Christ does not come out of Galilee?

units.la: 42 Nonne Scriptura dicit, Ex semine Dauidis, & ex vico Bethlehema vbi erat Dauid, venturum illum Christum?
units.tr: 42 Does not the Scripture say that Christ comes from the seed of David, and from the village of Bethlehem, where David was?

units.la: HIc post digressiunculam proximam redimus ad precationem illam Christi, eiusque effectum habemus tribus versibus sequentibus: effectus autem varius est ac diuersus ratione diuersorum. Omnino autem, vt dicam, alij sunt qui de Christo rectius sentiunt, alij qui pejus & eum reiiciunt. Hic quidem effectus tam diuersus in diuersis ex prædicatione Christi perpetuus futurus est. Exstitit autem hoc discrimen, non ex natura ista, non ex libero arbitrio: (nam natura æqualiter in omnibus inimica est gratiæ) sed existit ex Deo miserente. Non est volentis neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei. Ita tunc temporis ex gratia Christi prædicantis factum est illud inter Iudæos discrimen. Nam ipse & minister verbi fuit, & dator gratiæ: nos verò omnes Ministri quidem verbi sumus, sed efficaciam illam relinquimus Christo. Quare oculi auditorum semper ad Christum convertêsunt, vtpote datorem Spiritus & incrementi. Neque verò temerè cuiquam datur vnquam Christi gratia, nec discrimen hoc forte fortunâ obuenire solet: verùm Dominus qui sunt sui in vnoquoque hominum corde, in quo prædicatur ipsius verbum, & iis demum quos nouit ac præcognouit ab æterno, atque adeo elegit ad vitam, dat Spiritum suum, eorumque corda aperit ad prædicationem Euangelij sui. Credidérunt, (inquit Lucas) quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam æternam. Qui autem credunt aliquando plures sunt. Legimus enim ad prædicationem Petri vnicam, quasi ter mille credidisse: aliquando pauciores. Ad prædicationem vero Pauli legimus vni Lydiæ purpurariæ adapertum esse cor vt attenderet ea quæ dicebantur à Pauio. Quare qui sentit sibi penitus aperiri cor ad prædicationem Euangelij, habet ille quidem sigillum æternæ electionis suæ, ac materiam ineffabilis gaudij. Qui vero nullo vnquam tempore sentit sibi adaperiri cor ad prædicationem Euangelij, nullâ profecto habet lætitiæ materiam, etsi habeat vniuersum hunc mundum quo possit vti pro libidine sua. Deinde ex iis ipsis qui animis aliquo modo propendebant ad Christum, vides alios longius à vera ipsius notitia abesse, alios vero propius ad eum accedere. Hoc quoque discrimen perpetuum est inter eos qui Christum ac veritatem ipsius aliquo modo profitebantur, alij enim minus, alij plus de ipso cognoscent, prout Deus dimensus fuerit gratiam suam vnicuique. Sed hoc nota: inter eos qui reiiciunt Dominum, nullum vides esse discrimen, & hoc quoque perpetuum erit, maiorque futura est consensio animorum, inter eos qui pariter reiiciunt veritatem, quàm inter eos qui eam simul amplectuntur. Ratio in promptu est, quia qui reiiciunt Christum ac veritatem ipsius, ij natura id faciunt, quæ ex se in omnibus ex æquo aduersatur Christo ac veritati ipsius. Qui vero eum amplectuntur ipsiusque veritatem, ij ex gratia id faciunt, quæ nō datur omnibus eadem mensura; verùm aliis maior, aliis minor conceditur. Discrimina, inquit Apostolus, donorum varietates sunt, sed idem Spiritus. Vnde vides non ita magnam esse gloriationis materiam hodierno die Papistis in sua illa quam prædicant summa consensione, nostra vero dissensione maxima. Religio enim Papistica planè naturalis est, & ea præscribit ad quæ natura sua proclives sunt homines. At veto veritas Christi ex gratia est, & à natura hominum tota abhorret, vt non sit quod illi magnopere gloriantur vel de sua cōsensione, vel de nostra dissensione. Sed nunc ad eos veniamus qui Christum reiiciebant, ac videamus eam, quam niuntur rationem. Scriptura dicit Christum venturum ex semine Dauid & vico Bethlehem, vbi erat Dauid: at hic est à Galilæa: Ergo non est iste Christus. Ratio eorum petitur ex Scriptura: nullum est in genere in re quauis mendacium, quod sophistæ & deceptores non obtinent fuco veritatis. Neque enim homines natura mendaces tantum sunt, sed & hypocritæ, ingeniosi in colorando specie quadam veritatis, mendacium suum. Vt ad speciem descendam, nullum est mendacium tam splendidum in negotio religionis, cui non inducant sophistæ isti aliquem veritatis colorem ex verbo ipsius Dei petitum: quasi vero Deus sit mendaciorum patronus. Neque enim in Papatu vllum est somnium vel figmentum ex omnibus, quod nô stanim ascribant sophistæ voci ipsius Dei loquentis in Scripturis suis. Præterea diligentiores sunt homines natura in scrutandis Scripturis defendendi mendacij gratia quàm vel discendi, vel confirmandi veritatem causa. Quare suspecta nobis esse debet ista tam frequens in Papistino Scripturarum allegatio, videndumque num sc res habeat, id quod Beroenses fecisse legimus. Quod qui fecerit, videbit profecto monstrosam plane ac prodigiosam Scripturarum detorsionem. Sed rursus examinemus ratione ab istis adductâ: Scriptura dicit, inquiunt, Christum venturum ex semine Davidis, ex urbe Bethlehem.
units.tr: Here, after this brief digression, we return to that prayer of Christ and its effect, which we find in the three following verses. The effect is varied and different according to the different hearers. Broadly speaking, some think rightly about Christ, and others think worse and reject him. This difference in effect among different people will last for ever as Christ is preached. This division arises neither from nature nor from free will (for nature is equally hostile to grace in all people), but from God's mercy. It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. So at that time the division among the Jews arose from the grace of Christ who preached. For he himself was both minister of the Word and giver of grace. We are indeed all ministers of the Word, but we leave that efficacy to Christ. Therefore the eyes of the hearers are always turned to Christ, as the giver of the Spirit and of increase. Christ's grace is never given at random to anyone, nor does this division usually come about by chance. Rather, the Lord, who knows those who are his, gives his Spirit in the heart of each person in whom his Word is preached, and opens the hearts of those whom he has known and foreknown from eternity, and so chose to life, to attend to his Gospel. "As many as were ordained to eternal life believed," says Luke. Those who believe are sometimes many: we read that about three thousand believed at Peter's single preaching. Sometimes they are fewer. At Paul's preaching we read that the heart of Lydia, a seller of purple, alone was opened to attend to what was said by Paul. Therefore he who feels that his heart is fully opened by the preaching of the Gospel has indeed the seal of his eternal election and the matter of unspeakable joy. But he who at no time feels his heart opened by the preaching of the Gospel has truly no matter for joy, even if he has this whole world to use at his pleasure. Again, among those who in some way inclined their minds towards Christ, you see some remaining far from the true knowledge of him, and others coming nearer to him. This difference also is permanent among those who in some way profess Christ and his truth: some know him less, others more, as God has measured his grace to each. But note this: among those who reject the Lord you see no difference, and this too will be permanent. And there will be greater agreement of minds among those who alike reject the truth than among those who embrace it together. The reason is plain: those who reject Christ and his truth do so by nature, which in everyone alike is opposed to Christ and his truth. But those who embrace him and his truth do so by grace, which is not given to everyone in the same measure, but more to some and less to others. "There are differences of gifts," says the Apostle, "but the same Spirit." Hence you see that the Papists have not much ground for boasting today in their so-called great agreement, while we have great disagreement. For the Papist religion is wholly natural, and it prescribes what men are by nature inclined to. But the truth of Christ is from grace, and wholly abhors the nature of men; so they have nothing great to boast of, either in their agreement or in our disagreement. But now let us come to those who rejected Christ, and see the argument on which they rely. Scripture says that Christ will come from the seed of David and from the village of Bethlehem, where David was. But this man is from Galilee. Therefore he is not the Christ. Their argument is drawn from Scripture: there is no lie in any kind of matter which sophists and deceivers do not cover with the appearance of truth. For men are not only naturally liars, but hypocrites too, clever at colouring their lie with some semblance of truth. To come to particulars: there is no lie so specious in matters of religion for which these sophists do not bring some colour of truth taken from the very Word of God, as if God were the patron of lies. Indeed, among the Papists there is no dream or fiction at all that the sophists do not ascribe to the voice of God speaking in their Scriptures. Moreover, men by nature are more diligent in searching the Scriptures to defend a lie than to learn or to confirm the truth. Therefore this so frequent citation of Scripture among the Papists ought to be suspect to us, and we must see whether the matter really stands so, as we read the Bereans did. Whoever does this will certainly see a plainly monstrous and prodigious distortion of Scripture. But let us examine again the argument these men have brought: "Scripture says," they say, "that Christ will come from the seed of David, from the city of Bethlehem."

units.la: Prior pars propositionis plana est ex plurimis Scripturæ locis. Posteriorem habemus in Mica: At tu Bethlehem Ephrata, minima vt sis inter duces Iehudæ, ex te mihi prodibit futurus dominator in Israele. De Christo loquutum esse Prophetam certum est. Propositio itaque manifesto vera est; veniamus deinde ad assumptionem: At hic est ex Galilæa. Assumptio falsa est: nam Iesus educatus quidè fuit ac ferè commoratus est in Galilæa: de quo Propheta Esaias 9.1. quem locum citat Matthæus 4.14. & sequentibus; Zabulon & terra Nephthalim ad viam maris trans Iordanem, Galilæa gentium, Populus positus in tenebris vidit lucem magnam & positis in regione & umbra mortis lux orta est. Sed natus fuit Bethlehem Iudæ, Matth.2.1. quod etiam isti nullo negotio discere potuerunt: at dilexerunt mendacium potius quàm veritatem: Vnde satis habuerunt acquiescere in vulgari illa & falsa quæ de loco in quo natus est Christus circumferebatur opinione; quòd scilicet ex Galilæa esset. Hoc enim ingenium est.
units.tr: The first part of the premise is plain from very many places of Scripture. We have the second part in Micah: "But you, Bethlehem Ephratah, though you are least to be among the leaders of Judah, out of you shall come forth to me the one who is to be ruler in Israel." That the prophet spoke of Christ is certain. The premise is therefore manifestly true. Let us now go on to the assumption: "But this man is from Galilee." The assumption is false. For Jesus was indeed brought up and for the most part lived in Galilee; of this the prophet Isaiah speaks (9:1), and Matthew quotes this passage (4:14 and following): "The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles; the people who sat in darkness have seen a great light, and to those who sat in the region and shadow of death a light has risen." But he was born in Bethlehem of Judah (Matt. 2:1). These men could have learned this without any trouble. But they loved a lie rather than the truth. Hence they were content to rest in that common and false opinion which was circulated about the place where Christ was born, namely that he was from Galilee. For this is the nature of such men.

units.la: HH istorum hominum qui delectantur mendaciis. Si quæ significatio vel voculæ sit, quæ inclinet ad mendacium, illud quidem auidè arripiunt, neque si quis vltrò velit eos veritatem docere, eam tamen recipere volunt. Quoties inclamamus hodierno die in aurem Papistarum, non esse quidem eum sensum huius vel illius Scripturæ, quamcunque visum est iis allegare pro mendaciis suis defendendis. Illi tamen interea surdi perseverant; quia nimirum dilexerunt mendacium potius quàm veritatem. vide 2. Thess. 2. 10. 11.
units.tr: These are the men who delight in lies. If there is any meaning or little word that inclines towards a lie, they eagerly seize it, and even if someone is willing to teach them the truth freely, they still will not receive it. As often as we cry out today into the ears of the Papists that this or that passage of Scripture, whichever they choose to allege, does not have the sense they give it to defend their lies, they still persist, deaf to us, because they have loved a lie rather than the truth. See 2 Thessalonians 2:10, 11.

units.la: 43 Dissidium ergo ortum est in turba propter eum.
units.tr: 43 So there was a division among the people because of him.

units.la: 44 Quidam autem ex ipsis volebant eum prehendere, sed nemo iniecit in eum manus.
units.tr: 44 Some of them wanted to seize him, but no one laid hands on him.

units.la: HOc est effectum tam variæ ac pugnantis istorum de Christo sententiæ. Discordia ac dissidium inter ipsos oritur. Variæ de religione opiniones atque sententiæ gignuntur inter homines discordiam. Neque verò vllum vinculum tam firmum inveniri potest, non natura, non fœdera, quòd eos inter se in religione dissentes continebit: Ne existimetis, ait Dominus, me venisse mittere pacem in terram: Non veni mittere pacem, sed gladium. Nam veni facere ut dissideat filius aduersus patrem suum, et filia aduersus matrem suam, et nurus aduersus socrum suam: Et inimici hominis erunt qui sunt domestici ipsius. Omnis quidem discordiæ fundamentum est quòd non omnes idem de Christo sentiunt. Paulus hortatus pios ad pacem & concordiam mutuam; hortationis suæ fundamenta substernit vnum Deum Patrem, vnum Dominum Iesum Christum, vnum Spiritum Sanctum, vnam fidem, vnam spem vocationis, vnum baptisma: illud nimirum innuēs, veram inter homines concordiam & pacem niti vnitate religionis. Quamobrem vbi non habetur vnitas illa fidei, ac religionis, necesse est distrahantur animi hominum alioqui coniunctissimorum. Quòd si discrepantes hominum sententiæ de re aliqua etiam communi ac prophana efficiant discordias: (nam rem velle aut nolle, inquit Ethnicus, ea demum firma amicitia est:) profecto vel multò magis in re tam sancta, in religione diuersitas uersitas opinionū necesse est abrumpat amicitiā,discor-diámque gignat.Vnde damnatur impia eorum vox,qui dictitant ita demum fore vt ciues & subditi pace con- tineantur, si libertas quam vocant conscientiæ, vnicui- que permittatur, hoc est, si concedatur cuique vt viuat ac Deum colat pro figmento animi sui. Libertatémne istam quis nunc inuehat in regionem & Ecclesiam reformatam ac semel consentientem in vna fide ac veritatis professione? hoc esset profecto semen iacere omnis discordiæ ac horrendæ dissolutionis futuræ, non modò in toto reipublicæ corpore, verumetiam in singulis familiis & reipublicæ nostræ partibus. Denique hac quasi via relaberemur omnes in meras tenebras, superioribus illis, ex quibus Deus nos liberauit, multò tristiores, idque iusto Dei iudicio. Quidam autem ex iis, Hi erant mi- nistri illi ac emissarij Pharisæorum atque sacerdotum. Nam perpetuò in insidiis fuerunt quærentes occasionem prehendedi Dominū, si quando sese offerret: nunc autem oblata occasione, vt videtur, ex præsenti illo dissidio ac tumultu, voluerunt manus in eum iniicere. Sūt enim in omni republica ac societate huius farinæ homines qui perpetuò aliquid mali machinantes ac perficere conantes captant auidè occasiones, si quando se offerunt ex seditionibus ac dissidiis in Republ. exortis. Verum isti ex eorum numero proculdubiò erant, qui Christum reiecerunt supr. 41.42. Nunc igitur iidem illi vim externam Christo afferre volunt, sceleratásque manus in eum iniicere: Ex quo discimus superstitionem & veritatis odium perpetuò coniunctam cum crudelitate, quæ suo tempore sit eruptura. Sed nemo Obstupefacti enim sunt omnes sermone illo Christi, omnis gratiæ & authoritatis pleno, vt ex eo manifestum est quod sequitur postea vers.46.
units.tr: This is the effect of such varied and conflicting opinions about Christ: Discord and dissension arise among them. Differing opinions and views about religion beget discord among men. Nor can any bond be found so firm, neither nature nor covenants, that will hold together those who differ with one another in religion: Do not think, says the Lord, that I have come to send peace on earth. I have not come to send peace, but a sword. For I have come to set a son against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law: and a man's enemies will be those of his own household. The foundation of all discord is that not all think the same about Christ. Paul, exhorting the godly to peace and mutual concord, lays as the foundations of his exhortation: one God the Father, one Lord Jesus Christ, one Holy Spirit, one faith, one hope of calling, one baptism. Clearly he meant that true concord and peace among men rest upon unity of religion. Therefore, where that unity of faith and religion is not held, the minds of men, otherwise most closely joined, must necessarily be torn apart. But if differing opinions of men about some matter, even a common and profane one, produce discords (for, as the heathen says, the agreement of wills and aversions is the true firm friendship), then surely in a matter so holy as religion, diversity of opinions must much more break friendship and beget discord. Hence the impious voice of those is condemned who keep saying that citizens and subjects will be kept in peace only if what they call liberty of conscience is granted to each person, that is, if each is allowed to live and worship God as he pleases. Who would now introduce that liberty into a region and a Church that is reformed and has once for all agreed in one faith and profession of the truth? That would indeed be sowing the seed of all discord and of a dreadful dissolution to come, not only in the whole body of the commonwealth, but also in individual families and parts of our commonwealth. Finally, by such a path we would all slide back into utter darkness, far more wretched than those former darknesses from which God has freed us, and that by the just judgment of God. Some of them were the ministers and agents of the Pharisees and the priests. For they were continually in ambush, seeking an opportunity to seize the Lord whenever it presented itself; and now, the opportunity seeming to be offered by that present dissension and tumult, they wanted to lay hands on him. For in every commonwealth and society there are men of this kind, who are always plotting and trying to bring about some evil, and eagerly catch at any opportunity arising from seditions and dissensions in the state. But these men were certainly of the number of those who rejected Christ, as above in verses 41 and 42. Now, therefore, these same men want to inflict violence on Christ and lay wicked hands on him. From this we learn that superstition and hatred of the truth are always joined with cruelty, which will break out at its appointed time. But no one [laid hands on him]. For all were astonished at that sermon of Christ, full of grace and authority, as is clear from what follows afterwards in verse 46.

units.la: ¶ Venerunt ergo Ministri ad primarios Sacerdotes & Pharisæos, qui dixerunt eis, Quare non adduxistis eum?
units.tr: Therefore the ministers came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, "Why did you not bring him?"

units.la: 46 Responderunt Ministri, Nunquam ita loquutus est homo vt hic homo.
units.tr: 46 The ministers answered, "No man ever spoke like this man."

units.la: 47 Responderunt ergo eis Pharisæi, Num & vos seducti estis?
units.tr: 47 The Pharisees therefore answered them, "Have you also been deceived?"

units.la: 48 Num quis ex primoribus credidit in eum, aut ex Pharisæis?
units.tr: 48 "Has any of the rulers believed in him, or any of the Pharisees?"

units.la: 49 Sed hæc turba quæ non novit Legem, exsecrabilis est.
units.tr: 49 "But this crowd, which does not know the Law, is accursed."

units.la: RE infecta reuertuntur Ministri ad Pharisæos & Pontifices, illi autem ex ira & indignatione quærunt cur non adduxerint hominem secum, quasi vero nihil debuerit resistere eorum voluntati. Hoc est ingenium superborum, putant nihil debere resistere suæ libidini ac suæ potentiæ, quam somniant adeo absolutam esse: Quod si autem non statim succedat quod ipsi volunt, tum quidem insanire incipiunt, & insania ista comes est superbiæ, qua Deus superbos quosque qui vendicant sibi absolutam, hoc est, plane diuinam potentiam, vlcisci solet. Tandem enim adigit eos ad insaniam. Sed quid respondent ministri, Nunquā ita loquutus est homo vt homo ille. Fatentur se attonitos & conuictos conscientia verbis Christi, eorumque authoritate & maiestate, sed non crediderunt tamen. Sunt qui eminus quasi audientes ac intuentes Christum ac Euangelium ipsius, agnoscunt quidem vim esse in iis & efficaciam maximam, conuicti nimirum conscientia, sed interea non credunt. Nam vt de vi & efficacia verbi Diuini nonnihil dicam, habet quidem illud eam vim in omnibus indifferenter piis ac impiis, quia potest eos pariter prosternere, eorumque conscientias conuincere. Virga oris sui percutiet terram, inquit Propheta: hoc est, omnes homines promiscue, verum euentus varius est. Pij conuertuntur ac seruantur, impij indurantur ac pereunt tandem. Quare Esaias continuo addidit ibidem, Spiritu labiorum suorum mortem te afficiet improbum. Quare bene aduertat quisque, quomodo audito iam verbo Euangelij dicat de aliquo, nunquam ita loquutus est homo, vt ille homo. Hoc est, quomodo perceallatur authoritate Euangelij. Videat autem ex auditu sequatur in corde conuersio. Neque enim satis est si Euangelium eiusque potentiam admireris, nisi in ve efficax sit ad fidem & salutem. Hoc postremò notandū, istos ex ministris crudelitatis factos esse quodammodò ministros Euangelij & præconcs Christi. Neque enim hoc eorum præconium plane inutile fuit, nulliusque effecti. Nam etsi fingas Pharisæos & Sacerdotes illos præterea de Christo nihil vnquam audiuisse, vel hoc solum quod Ministri isti tum de eo testati sunt, satis erit ad iustissimam eorum condemnationem, vel sola vox ista de Christo, quam vulgus hominum passim habet in ore, quòd mediator sit inter Deum & homines, quòd pro peccatis nostris mortuus sit, satis virium habitura est in illo die ad condemnandos eos, quicunque nullo vnquam tempore dignantur Euangelium hoc Christi prædicatum sua præsentia, neque cœtibus sanctorum interesse volunt. Responderunt ergo eis Pharisæi. Nunc magis commouentur in Ministros istos Pharisæi quàm prius, quippe quos suspicati sunt credidisse in Christum. Non caret suo aliquo effecto verbum Christi & gratiæ ipsius, à quocunque demum proferatur. Vel enim conuertit animum, vel indurat: animum bene affectum afficit gaudio, male vero affectum tristitia, cumque magis indurat. Non tum Christus indurabat animos Pharisæorum & Pontificum sua ipsius voce, sed Ministri ipsi Pontificum & Pharisæorum obfirmabant animos dominorum suorum. Non ministri verbi è suggestu soli sunt qui indurant istos contemptores & irrisores, quibus referta est hæc nostra natio, sed quicunque demum sunt qui audita tantùm referunt, etiam ipsorum famuli qui aliquid in commendationem gratiæ Christi loquuntur ac recitant ex ministri ore exceptum, cùm ipsi Domini concionibus populi Dei non dignentur interesse: ita autem facilè cognoscent se indurari, si inserint sibi animum nō applicari ad ea, quę de Christo audiunt ex quolibet. Hi autem, quæ est eorum malitia non tantùm indurantur ipsi, sed conantur obdurare partes ministrorum suorum animos aduersus Christum, & excutere illam eius, quæ in ipsis fuit, reuerentiam qualemcunque. Qui ipsi obdurati sunt aduersus Christum & veritatem eius, volunt omnes pariter indurari. Qui nolūt ipsi ingredi in regnum cœlorum, omnes alios absterrent ab eo, quantum in fe est. Qui denique inimici sunt veritatis, inimici sunt salutis omnium hominum, Neque Deo placent, inquit Paulus, & omnibus hominibus aduersantur: prohibentes nos gentibus loqui vt feruentur. Nam non contenti obstinati illi, de quibus ibi loquitur, Iudæi sese obfirmare aduersus Christum: verum in Iudæa tota, quoscunque poterant indurabant: Neque eo etiam contenti excurrebant in gentes, & impediebant quantum poterant salutem gentium. Quemadmodum ex nostris hominibus quidam faciunt, qui ipsi in exteris ac Papifticis regionibus, primum obdurati domum deinde redeunt, & interpellant quibus possunt modis cursum Euangelij apud nos.
units.tr: The ministers return empty-handed to the Pharisees and chief priests. They, out of anger and indignation, ask why the ministers did not bring the man with them, as if he ought not to have resisted their will at all. This is the nature of the proud: they think nothing should resist their lust and their power, which they dream is so absolute. But if what they want does not happen at once, they begin to rage, and this madness is the companion of pride, by which God is wont to punish all the proud who claim for themselves an absolute, that is, plainly divine, power. For at last he drives them into madness. But what do the ministers answer? "No man ever spoke as this man did." They confess that they were astonished and convicted in conscience by the words of Christ and by his authority and majesty, yet they did not believe. There are those who, from a distance, as though listening and looking on, acknowledge that there is great force and efficacy in Christ and his Gospel, convicted indeed in conscience, yet meanwhile do not believe. To say something about the power of the divine Word: it has this power indifferently in all, pious and impious alike, because it can equally overthrow them and convict their consciences. "He shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth," says the prophet; that is, all men without distinction. But the outcome varies. The godly are converted and saved; the wicked are hardened and at last perish. Therefore Isaiah immediately added in the same place, "With the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked." Let each one therefore notice how, once the word of the Gospel has been heard, he says of someone, "Never has a man spoken as this man did"; that is, how he is struck by the authority of the Gospel. Let him see whether a conversion of the heart follows the hearing. For it is not enough that you admire the Gospel and its power, unless it is effective unto faith and salvation. Lastly, this must be noted: these men, from being ministers of cruelty, have in a way become ministers of the Gospel and heralds of Christ. For their proclamation was by no means wholly useless and without effect. Even if you pretend that those Pharisees and priests had never heard anything about Christ before, this alone, what those ministers then testified about him, will suffice for their most just condemnation. And that one word about Christ, which common people everywhere have on their lips, that he is the mediator between God and men and that he died for our sins, will have enough strength on that day to condemn all those who never deign, by their presence, to hear this Gospel of Christ preached, and who are unwilling to attend the assemblies of the saints. "The Pharisees therefore answered them." Now the Pharisees are more stirred against these ministers than before, since they suspected them of having believed in Christ. The word of Christ and of his grace never fails to have some effect, from whomever it is uttered. For it either turns the mind or hardens it: it gladdens a well-disposed mind with joy, but a badly disposed one with sorrow, and hardens it all the more. Christ did not harden the minds of the Pharisees and chief priests by his own voice; rather, the ministers themselves of the chief priests and Pharisees strengthened their masters in obstinacy. It is not only ministers of the Word from the pulpit who harden those scorners and mockers with whom our nation is filled. Whoever merely repeats what he has heard does so too, even the servants of such men, who say and recite something in commendation of Christ's grace, taken from a minister's mouth, while they themselves do not deign to attend the sermons of the Lord's people. They will easily recognise that they are hardened if they find that their mind is not applied to what they hear about Christ from anyone at all. These men, in their malice, are not only hardened themselves, but also try to harden the minds of their ministers against Christ and to shake off whatever reverence for him was in them. Those who are obstinate against Christ and his truth want everyone to be equally hardened. Those who are unwilling to enter the kingdom of heaven themselves frighten all others away from it, as far as they can. Finally, those who are enemies of the truth are enemies of the salvation of all men. "They please not God," says Paul, "and are contrary to all men, forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles that they may be saved." For those obstinate Jews, of whom he speaks there, were not content to harden themselves against Christ. Throughout all Judea they hardened whomever they could, and not content with this, they ran out to the Gentiles and hindered, as far as they could, the salvation of the Gentiles. Just as some of our own people do: having first been hardened in foreign and Papist lands, they return home and hinder, by whatever means they can, the course of the Gospel among us.

units.la: Num quis ex primoribus. Hactenus minis egerunt, nunc ratione agunt cum Ministris suis, ad hoc vt ipsi ratione conuicti alienarentur a Christo. Argumentantur autem ab exemplo primorum. Principes populi, Pontifices, Scribæ, Pharifæi non crediderunt in eum: Ergo non est vobis credendum in eum. Propositio argumenti intelligitur: Populus ac vulgus tenetur sequi exemplum ac parere mandato principum ac gubernatorum qui Ecclesiæ præfecti sunt. Quæ quidem propositio, iusta, vt videtur, ratione nititur. Nam fi permittatur sibi vulgus in negotio religionis, neque pendeat à gubernatoribus Ecclesiæ, necesse est sequatur maxima rerum confusio. Nititur etiam Scripturæ authoritate, Deuter.17.9.10. Vbi precipitur, vt in rebus religionis ac ecclesiasticis, populus adeat sacerdotes, eósque consulat, vt faciat ex præstituto illius sententiæ quam indicauerint ipsis. Sed eo loco distum est verf. 11. vt faciat populus ex præstituto legis, quam docuerint ipsum. Quare ita demum parendum est sacerdoti, & ex præstituto diuinæ legis & ex verbo Dei præscribat faciendum aliquid. At isti, vt ipsi fatentur, recierunt Christum. Ergo eorum exemplum sequendum non fuit. Ea tamen solet esse impudentia istorum hominum, vt vel nudam authoritatem suam absque mandato verbi, imo contra mandatum verbi mundo obtrudant. Ea est Papistarum hodierno die impudentia, quibus perpetuo opponenda est veritas verbi diuini, à qua illi tam longe discesserunt: neque credendum eis, etsi milmillies dicant se nobis veritatem proponere. Sed turba hæc. Occupatio; dicere enim poterant Ministri: At turba credit in Christum, ipsúmque sequitur? Respondet cum indignatione quadam, Turba hæc non novit legem. Ex legis ignorantia dicunt profectum, quòd turba credat in li, præsertim in Christum. Ergo oportuit obduratiōnem ac infidelitate istorum proficisci ex opinione quadam superba legis Dei tam perfectè à se cognitæ. Nota igitur, superba opinio cognitionis & scientiæ indurat animum adversus Christum. Non eorum modò, qui non profitētur ipsum, sed eorum etiam qui profitentur. Nam qui inflati sunt suaipsorum scientia, ij nihil sciunt de Christo ut oportet. Neque tantùm hac opinione scientiæ suæ ipsi indurantur, sed & contemnunt simplices, ignorantiámque iis obiiciunt: hoc quoque sequitur ex opinione scientiæ suæ. Et doctores illi Papistici hodierno die eos omnes qui amplectuntur veritatem Euangelij, tanquam idiotas totidem contemnunt. Neque verò tantùm contemnunt isti hos simplices, sed & execrantur malitiosè: malitia enim coniuncta est cum contemptu. Ita doctores illi Papistici & cócilium Tridentinum hodierno die ingeminant adversus nos anathemata: sed ipsi execrabiles sunt, qui execrantur eos quibus Deus benedixit, id quod tandem aliquando reipsa verum esse comperient. Observa rursus, quod ad turbam hanc, cùm esset ea citra opinionem cognitionis suæ, neque ei consideret, animo in Christum propendebat. Facilius simplex aliquis & idiota qui nihil magni de se suaque cognitione cogitat ad credendum adducetur, quàm superciliosus aliquis Pharisæus aut Papista cum tota illa sua, de qua gloriatur, cognitione.
units.tr: "Has any of the rulers?" Hitherto they have acted by threats; now they deal with their ministers by reasoning, so that, convinced by reason, they might be estranged from Christ. They argue from the example of the leaders: the princes of the people, the chief priests, the scribes and the Pharisees did not believe in him; therefore you must not believe in him either. The premise of the argument is understood: the people and the common crowd are bound to follow the example and obey the command of the princes and rulers who are set over the Church. This premise rests, as it seems, on sound reason. For if the crowd were allowed to act on its own in matters of religion, and not depend on the governors of the Church, the greatest confusion of affairs would necessarily follow. It also rests on the authority of Scripture, Deut. 17.9, 10, where it is commanded that in matters of religion and ecclesiastical things the people should go to the priests, consult them, and act according to the sentence they pronounce. But in that passage it is also said (v. 11) that the people should act according to the law which the priests teach them. Therefore the priest is to be obeyed only so far as he prescribes something in accordance with the divine law and the Word of God. But these men, as they themselves confess, rejected Christ; therefore their example was not to be followed. Yet it is the custom of such men's impudence to thrust their bare authority upon the world, even without the command of the Word, indeed against the command of the Word. This is the impudence of the Papists today, against whom the truth of the divine Word must always be set, since they have departed so far from it. Nor are they to be believed, even if they say a thousand times over that they set forth the truth to us. "But this crowd." This is an anticipated objection: the ministers could say, "But the crowd believes in Christ and follows him?" The Pharisees answer with a certain indignation: "This crowd does not know the law." They ascribe to ignorance of the law the fact that the crowd believes, especially in Christ. Therefore the obduracy and unbelief of these men must have arisen from a proud opinion of their own perfect knowledge of God's law. Note, then: the proud opinion of one's own knowledge and learning hardens the mind against Christ. This holds not only of those who do not profess him, but also of those who do. For those who are puffed up with their own learning know nothing of Christ as they ought. Nor are they merely hardened by this opinion of their learning; they also despise the simple and throw their ignorance in their faces, and this too follows from their opinion of their own learning. Those Papist teachers today despise as so many idiots all who embrace the truth of the Gospel. Nor do they merely despise these simple folk; they also curse them maliciously, for malice is joined with contempt. Thus those Papist teachers and the Council of Trent today hurl anathemas at us. But they themselves are accursed, who curse those whom God has blessed, as they will at length discover to be true in fact. Observe again that the crowd, since it had no opinion of its own knowledge and did not think much of itself, was inclined toward Christ. A simple and unlearned man, who thinks nothing great of himself or of his own knowledge, is more easily brought to believe than some haughty Pharisee or Papist with all the learning he boasts of.

units.la: 50 Dicit eis Nicodemus, is qui venerat ad eum nocte, quum unus esset ex illis,
units.tr: 50 Nicodemus, he who had come to him by night and who was one of them, said to them,

units.la: 51 Num lex nostra condemnat quempiam, nisi prius ex ipso audierit, & cognoverit quid faciat?
units.tr: 51 Does our law condemn anyone unless it first hears from him and knows what he is doing?

units.la: 52 Responderunt & dixerunt ei, Num & tu Galilaeus es? scrutare & scito ex Galilaea prophetam non fuisse suscitatum.
units.tr: 52 They answered and said to him, Are you also a Galilean? Search and see that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee.

units.la: 53 Et profectus est unusquisque domum suam.
units.tr: 53 And each went home.

units.la: Nicodemus ex hoc concilio & numero animadversa istorum in Christum absentem petulantia ac rabie, eam ratione quadam studet compescere; ubi nota Nicodemum omnia quae ab iis dicta sunt in Christum accepisse, ad ipsum absentem condemnandum dicta esse. Ita est quicquid dicitur ab istis aduersus professores Christi ac veritatis hodierno die, id dicitur animo condemnandi Christum ipsum ac veritatem ipsius. Rursus vide; Nicodemus exsurgit ex medio istorum ac Christum absentem defendit. Christus cum veritate sua semper habitura est aliquos qui ipsum defendant; si minus Nicodemum qui & ipse crediderat Christum, certe Gamalielem qui cum in Christum non crediderit, tamen patronus fuit causae Apostolorum Christi. Quod si non Gamalielem, profecto Pilatum hominem ethnicum & prophanum, qui contra Iudaeos satis longo tempore pro Christo absoluendo laborauit. Sed videamus descriptionem hanc quae hoc loco habetur Nicodemi. Dicitur is esse qui noctu venerat ad Christum, quo significatur inde ab eo tempore, quo primum noctu venit ad Christum, percepitque aliquod semen fidei, manssisse ipsum perpetuo in fide. Vide Iohan.3.1.&sequentib. Erat tamen unus ex istis, id quod arguit semen illud fidei receptum ad hoc usque tempus suffocatum fuisse & impeditum metu amittendorum honorum huius mundi, sese non exeruisse. Hoc tamen tempore Christi absentis patronus fuit; quo significatur semen illud fidei non semper suffocatum iri, sed erupturum tandem in lucem inuito hoc mundo. Verum patrocinium hoc Christi quod suscipit, ieiunum satis videtur & frigidum. nihilo enim minus dici potuit in gratiam flagitiosissimi cuiusque quam hoc ne indicta causa damnaretur. Oportuit enim plane & aperte pronuntiare Christum iustum ac innocente, eumque vindicare ab eorum calumniis: ex quo vides quanta sit vis huius mundi, diuitiarum, honorum, voluptatum eius collectantium cum fide. Adeo enim ista aduersantur fidei, ut si contingat eam aliquando erumpere ac emergere, non prodat seferè nisi timidè & frigidè. dè. At tandem quo tempore oportuit hunc hominem maximè dissimulare fidem suam, cùm nimirum ipse ignominiosè penderet è cruce, eum tum liberrimè confessus est, ac vnà cum Iosepho Arimathæensi honorificè sepeliuit, vt videbimus postea, cap. 19. 38. & deinceps. Sic igitur exemplo huius hominis primùm discimus, bonum esse semel venire ad Christum, si non interdiu, noctu saltem, vt semel recipiatur semè illud fidei, quod deinde ex corde nunquam prorsus expungendum est.
units.tr: Nicodemus, though he is one of this council and this number, notices the insolence and rage of these men against Christ, who is absent, and by some reasoning he tries to restrain them. Note here that Nicodemus took everything they said against Christ as said to condemn Christ himself, who is absent. So whatever is said today by these men against the professors of Christ and of the truth is said with the intention of condemning Christ himself and his truth. Look again: Nicodemus rises up from the midst of them and defends the absent Christ. Christ, with his truth, will always have some who defend him. If not Nicodemus, who also had believed in Christ, then surely Gamaliel, who, although he did not believe in Christ, was nevertheless a patron of the cause of Christ's Apostles. And if not Gamaliel, certainly Pilate, a heathen and profane man, who for a fairly long time labored against the Jews to have Christ acquitted. But let us look at this description of Nicodemus given in this place. He is said to be the one who had come to Christ by night. This signifies that from the time when he first came to Christ by night and received some seed of faith, he remained in the faith perpetually. See John 3:1 and following. Yet he was one of them, which shows that this seed of faith, received up to this time, had been smothered and hindered by fear of losing the goods of this world, and had not come forth. Nevertheless, at this time he was the patron of the absent Christ, which signifies that this seed of faith would not always be smothered, but would at last break out into the light, even though the world is unwilling. Yet this patronage of Christ which he undertakes seems rather feeble and cold. For it could have been said no less in favor of the most shameless wretch, merely so that a cause might not be condemned unheard. For it was necessary to declare plainly and openly that Christ is just and innocent, and to vindicate him from their calumnies. From this you see how great is the power of this world, of its riches, honors and pleasures, to hinder faith. For these things are so opposed to faith that if faith ever happens to break out and emerge, it rarely shows itself except timidly and coldly. But at last, at the time when this man most needed to hide his faith, namely when Christ hung ignominiously on the cross, he then confessed him most freely, and together with Joseph of Arimathea he honorably buried him, as we shall see later, in chapter 19:38 and following. Thus, from the example of this man we first learn that it is good to come to Christ once, if not by day then at least by night, so that the seed of faith may be received once, which afterwards must never be entirely blotted out of the heart.

units.la: Deinde fugiendum esse amorem huius sæculi, vt qui adeo aduersetur fidei & confessioni Christi ac veritatis ipsius, vt vix emergat tandem fides, ac si emergat sese- que exerat, in confessione oris, frigidè tamen & timidè id faciat. Nonne & tu Galilæus? Vide quomodo inuehantur in Nicodemum nihil nisi vulgarem apologiam afferentem pro Christo. Ea est malitia istorum hominum qui sese semel indurarunt aduersus veritatem, vt occludant sibi aures aduersus omnem veritatis defensionem. Quòd si autem quis pro veritate dicat aliquid, quod quiuis æquus rerum æstimator putet rationi esse consentaneum, tum statim inclamant hæreticum hominem, &c. Nouimus enim istorum hominum petulantiam. Quare in omni iudicio fugienda est malitia in personam, & vindictæ cupiditas: hæc enim sunt quæ peruertunt iudicium, faciunt ex iudice alioqui legitimo, homicidam. Scrutare, & vide. Nunc ne videantur carere ratione aliqua, conantur adducta in medium ratione alienare Nicomedi animum à Christo. Ex Galilæa non est propheta: Atqui hic est ex Galilæa, Ergo non est propheta: ex quo rursus inferunt, non credendum esse in eum. Sed falsa est conclusio prior ex falsa assumptione. Neque enim Christus ex Galilæa fuit, hoc est, in Galilæa natus, quod & isti facilè intelligere potuissent, si tam diligentes fuissent in hoc scrutando, quàm seduli sunt nunc in iubendo Nicodemum scrutari, An ex Galilæa surrexerit Propheta aliquis. Nota ergo, cum conuiciis ungunt rationem, sed falsam: ita pontificij hodierno die nolunt videri carere prorsus ratione, aut insanire contra rationem. Verùm non minùs falsæ, non minùs sophisticæ sunt istorum rationes quas afferunt hodierno die ad labefactadum fidē hominum ac veri-tatē, quàm tunc temporis fuerūt illorum. Et profectus est vnusquisque. Discedunt re infecta; non est consilium adversus Dominum, semperque hostes veritatis frustrantur fine consiliorum ac factorum suorum. Vel enim nō finit eos Deus in conciliis suis aliquid concludere, vel si finit concludere, non finit tamen exequi quod impiè decreuerunt: vel si etiam exequi id sinat, tamen non si-nit assequi, quod tanquam præcipuum ac vltimum fi-nem apud animum suum intenderunt, nempe pernicie Ecclesiæ ac euersionem veritatis. Quod cùm animad-uerteret Dauid, miratus est sic tumultuari, sic medita-ri, sic consultare impios aduersus Christum & Ecclesiam ipsius. Et quis non miretur hodierno die istos hæc agi-tare aduersus Ecclesiam Christi, post tot exempla, qui-bus Deus iam inde ab initio sanis docuit hostes Eccle-siæ semper tandem confusos esse? Sed & isti quoque confundentur tandem post omnes illas victorias quas se reportare ab Ecclesia Dei gloriantur, eo nimirum die quo Dominus suos perfectè vindicabit, & inimicos suos omnes planè confunder. Huic sit omnis honor & gloria in sæcula sæculorum, Amen.
units.tr: Next, we must flee the love of this world, since it so opposes faith and the confession of Christ and of his truth that faith scarcely emerges, and if it emerges and shows itself, it does so only coldly and timidly in the confession of the mouth. Are you also a Galilean? See how they rail against Nicodemus, who brings forward nothing but a common apology for Christ. Such is the malice of these men who have once hardened themselves against the truth, so that they close their ears against every defense of the truth. But if anyone says something for the truth which any fair judge of things thinks is consistent with reason, they at once shout that he is a heretic, and so on. For we know the insolence of these men. Therefore in every judgment we must flee malice against the person and the desire for revenge, for these are what pervert judgment and turn a judge who is otherwise lawful into a murderer. Search and see. Now, lest they seem to lack any reason, they try by an argument brought forward to turn Nicodemus' mind away from Christ. No prophet is out of Galilee. But this man is from Galilee; therefore he is not a prophet. From this they further infer that one must not believe in him. But the first conclusion is false, because the assumption is false. For Christ was not from Galilee, that is, born in Galilee, which they could easily have understood if they had been as diligent in searching this out as they are now eager in ordering Nicodemus to search whether any prophet has arisen out of Galilee. Note, then, that they anoint their reasoning with insults, but it is false reasoning. So the Papists today do not wish to seem to lack reason altogether, or to rage against reason. Yet the arguments they bring forward today to shake men's faith and the truth are no less false and no less sophistical than those of their predecessors were at that time. And each went home. They depart with their purpose undone. Counsel against the Lord does not stand, and the enemies of the truth always fail, and their counsels and deeds come to nothing. For either God does not allow them to conclude anything in their councils, or if he allows them to conclude, he does not allow them to carry out what they have impiously decided, or if he even allows them to carry it out, he does not allow them to attain what they had set before their minds as the chief and final end, namely the ruin of the Church and the overthrow of the truth. When David observed this, he marveled that the impious should make such a tumult, plot such things, and take counsel so against Christ and his Church. And who would not marvel that today these men devise such things against the Church of Christ, after so many examples by which God has from the beginning taught that the enemies of the Church are always at last confounded? But these also will at last be confounded after all those victories which they boast of having won from the Church of God, namely on that day when the Lord will completely vindicate his own and will utterly confound all his enemies. To him be all honor and glory for ever and ever, Amen.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Capitis huius partes præcipuæ sunt duæ. Prima est de mulie-re in adulterio deprehensa, à Pharisæis ad Christum tentandū eum animo adducta, vt is suam de ea puniendā sententiam dice-ret, vsque ad versum 12. In secunda habetur sermocinatio Do-mini cum Iudæis varia ac multiplex, ad finem vsque capitis.
units.tr: The chief parts of this chapter are two. The first is about the woman taken in adultery, brought by the Pharisees to Christ with the intention of tempting him, so that he might state his sentence about her punishment, to verse 12. In the second there is a varied and manifold discourse of the Lord with the Jews, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: ESVS autem profectus est in mon-tem olearum.
units.tr: But Jesus went unto the Mount of Olives.

units.la: Et diluculo rursus adfuit in tem-plo, plo, & totus populus venit ad eum, & sedens docebat eos.
units.tr: And early in the morning he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him, and he sat down and taught them.

units.la: 3 Adducunt autem ad eum Scribæ & Pharisæi mulierem in adulterio deprehensam, & cum statuissent eam in medio,
units.tr: 3 Then the scribes and Pharisees bring to him a woman taken in adultery, and when they had set her in the midst,

units.la: 4 Dicunt ei, Præceptor, hæc mulier deprehensa est in ipso facto quum mœcharetur:
units.tr: 4 they say to him, Teacher, this woman was caught in the very act of adultery.

units.la: 5 In lege vero Moses mandavit nobis ut tales lapidentur: tu ergo quid dicis?
units.tr: 5 Now Moses in the law commanded us that such women should be stoned. What do you say, then?

units.la: 6 Hoc autem dicebant tentantes eum, ut possent eum accusare.
units.tr: 6 They said this, testing him, so that they might have grounds to accuse him.

units.la: NTEQVAM aggrediamur textus expositionem, de hoc admonendi sunt omnes, deesse hoc loco in exemplari Syriaco historiam adulteræ, undecim versiculis comprehensam: neque tamen ideo putandum est historiam hanc apocryphan esse, cum ab Ecclesia sit iam olim recepta, & nunc pro canonica habeatur. Primum itaque hoc capite secedit in montem olearum noctu, ut videtur, quo paulisper sese recrearet, ac precaretur suo more. Occupationes istæ tam assiduæ postulant, ut aliquando recipiamus nos in secessum, & ad tempus requiescamus; ita tamen ut interea occupetur animus exemplo Christi in Domino, in precibus, in gratiis agendis, ideo quod Deus benedixerit occupationibus & laboribus nostris, in petitionibus ideo factis, ut velit nobis multiplicare deinceps gratiam suam. Hoc nobis faciendum exemplo quoque politicorum & piorum hominum, ut Danielis, qui tribus temporibus de die, procumbes in genua sua, orabat; hoc est, toties quoties ipsi praeoccupationes licuit. Ut Dauidis, qui hanc consuetudinem respiciens, ait, Vespere & mane atque meridie meditabor & perstrepam, donec audierit vocem meam. Putant homines vulgo sibi non concedi requiem, nisi conquiescat in foedissuis libidinibus, & volutentur tanquam sues in omni immunditie. Existimant magis laboriosum esse animum suum in Deo occupari, quam si exercerentur grauissimis quibusque, ad sudorem vsque, laboribus. Adeo abhorret animus non regenitus à cogitatione rerum diuinarum ac cœlestium. Sed vt permittamus eos somniare sibi quam velint ipsi requiem; sic nobis sentiendum est, non esse veram animi nostri requiem, nisi ipsa occupetur in Deo suo. Hinc enim est quòd hæc exercitatio, quæ est in verbo prædicando, audiendo, precando, vocetur Sabbathum, hoc est, requies. Item exercitatio illa, quam in cœlo eandem perpetuò habebimus, vocetur Sabbatismus & requies Domini. Et diluculo rursus. Redit Dominus ad labores suos, ac redit quidem tempestiuè, vtpote diluculo, quò nos doceat, non perpetuò delitescendum & conquiescendum esse, ne in priuatis quidem precibus & meditationibus, more Monachorum & Eremitarum, hoc est, pigrorum ventriùs sed redeundum esse ad labores nostros quotidianos, ac redeundum tempestiuè. In quibus quidem sic oportet nos occupari exterius corpore, vt interius animo perpetuò occupemur in Deo nostro: adeo vt & in otio & in negotio occupemur in Deo nostro: ià quod faciemus profecto sine vlla iactura aut impedimento negotiorum quæ nobis procuranda sunt, imò verò faciemus cum eorum promotione, ac cum vera animi iucunditate ac lætitia, quæ non nisi ex sola Dei præsentia obtinetur.
units.tr: Before we undertake the exposition of the text, everyone should be warned that in this place the Syriac copy lacks the story of the adulteress, which is contained in eleven verses. Yet we must not therefore think that this story is apocryphal, since the Church has long since received it and it is now held to be canonical. First, then, in this chapter he withdraws by night to the Mount of Olives, as it seems, so that he might refresh himself for a little and pray in his customary way. Such constant occupations require that we sometimes withdraw into seclusion and rest for a time; yet in such a way that the mind is meanwhile occupied, after the example of Christ, in the Lord, in prayers and in giving thanks, because God has blessed our occupations and labours, and so in petitions made for this purpose, that he may wish henceforth to multiply his grace to us. We should do this also after the example of civil and godly men, such as Daniel, who knelt down on his knees and prayed three times a day, that is, as often as his occupations allowed him leisure. Likewise David, looking to this custom, says: "Evening and morning and at noon will I meditate and make a noise, until he hears my voice." Men commonly think that no rest is granted them unless they rest in their most foul lusts and wallow like swine in all filthiness. They judge it more laborious to have their mind occupied in God than to be exercised in the heaviest labours, even to the point of sweating. So far does the unregenerate mind shrink from the thought of divine and heavenly things. But, let us allow them to dream of whatever rest they themselves wish for; so we must judge that there is no true rest of our mind unless it is occupied in its God. Hence it is that this exercise, which consists in preaching the word, hearing, and praying, is called the Sabbath, that is, rest. Likewise that exercise which we shall have continually in heaven will be called the Sabbath-keeping and the rest of the Lord. And early in the morning again. The Lord returns to his labours, and he returns indeed in good time, as early in the morning, to teach us that we should not hide and rest forever, not even in private prayers and meditations, after the manner of monks and hermits, that is, of lazy bellies, but that we should return to our daily labours, and return in good time. In these we ought indeed so to be occupied in body outwardly, that inwardly in mind we are continually occupied in our God: so that we are occupied in our God both in leisure and in business; which we shall certainly do without any loss or hindrance to the affairs that must be attended to; nay rather, we shall do it with their advancement, and with true cheerfulness and joy of mind, which is obtained only from the presence of God alone.

units.la: Adducunt autem. Christus occupatus in docendo populum, tentatur. Quòd si ipse Dominus tentatus est ac impeditus, inter fungendum minissterio suo tam sancto, quid miri est, si nos multas tentationes, ac multa impedimenta experiamur in occupationibus nostris, siue politicis quidem illis, siue Ecclesiasticis? Et si vsque adeo tetemur, vt necesse habeamus redimere occasione agendi bene in vita quotidiana, rebus etiam pretiosissimis, etiam vita ipsa? In quibus tamen omnibus consolationem habemus nobis ministratam, hoc Christi exemplo, qui ante nos tentatus est, in eum finem, vt iis qui tentantur possit succurrere. Sed videamus nunc tentationem. postquam statuissent mulierem adulteram in medio, primum aiunt, Magister, hæc mulier, &c. Secundò, aiunt, In lege autem Moses mandauit. Tertiò, Tu ergo quid dicis? His subiungit Iohannes noster, Hoc dixisse eos, tensententes eum. Et iá quidem non obscurè perspici potuit ex eorum verbis, quibus in medium afferebant legem Mosis satis manifestam in hanc sententiam, Quòd lapidanda esset; quà profecto re prodebant se ipsi non animo discendi aliquid ex eo, sed animo potius ipsum tentandi interrogare. Tentabant igitur eum, vt possent ex ipsius ore materiam accusationis ac condemnationis aliquam excipere. Nam studebant eum trucidare, vt postea videbimus. Si enim cum lege Mosis respondisset lapidandam esse adulteram, tum accusassent eum, quòd sententiam tulisset contrariam professioni illi gratiæ ac mansuetudinis, quam in doctrina sua alioqui præ se ferebat: Lex enim per Mosen data est, gratia verò & veritas per Iesum Christum exstitit. Sin verò contra legem sententiam tulisset, tum accusassent quòd condemnasset legem Mosis. Expectabant autem fore, vt vel cum lege, vel contra legem responderet. In isto eorum exemplo vides ingenium calumniatorum: quærunt sibi perpetuò materiam qua accusent pios. Aucupantur eam etiam ex verbo aliquo: hoc si non statim excidat eis sua sponte, tentando conantur ipsam extorquere, vt opus sit piis magna prudentia, ne vel verbum ipsius aliquod excidat, quod iure reprehendi possit. Quòd si iniuria reprehendant aduersarij vel dictum, vel factum aliquod ipsorum, tum quidem beati sunt qui patiuntur iustitiæ causa.
