units.tr: Then they bring him. Christ, while occupied in teaching the people, is tempted. If the Lord himself was tempted and hindered in the course of so holy a ministry, what wonder is it if we experience many temptations and many hindrances in our occupations, whether civil or ecclesiastical? And if we are so troubled that we must needs redeem the opportunity of doing good in our daily life at the cost of even the most precious things, even life itself? Yet in all these things we have consolation provided for us by the example of Christ, who was tempted before us, to the end that he might be able to help those who are tempted. But let us now look at the temptation. When they had set the adulterous woman in the midst, first they say, Teacher, this woman, etc. Secondly, they say, Now Moses in the law commanded. Thirdly, What do you say, then? To this our John adds: They said this, testing him. And indeed it could be clearly seen from their words, by which they brought forward the law of Moses plainly enough to this effect, that she should be stoned; by which act they revealed that they were asking not with a mind to learn anything from him, but rather with a mind to test him. They were testing him, therefore, so that they might obtain from his own mouth some material for accusation and condemnation. For they were eager to put him to death, as we shall see afterwards. For if he had answered with the law of Moses that the adulteress must be stoned, they would then have accused him of pronouncing a sentence contrary to that profession of grace and gentleness which he otherwise displayed in his teaching: For the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. But if he had pronounced a sentence against the law, they would then have accused him of condemning the law of Moses. They were expecting that he would answer either with the law or against the law. In this example of theirs you see the character of calumniators: they always seek for themselves material with which to accuse the godly. They fish for it even from some word; if it does not immediately slip from them of its own accord, they try by testing to extract it, so that the godly need great prudence lest any word of theirs should slip out which could justly be censured. And if the adversaries rightly censure any saying or deed of theirs, then indeed blessed are those who suffer for righteousness' sake.

units.la: Iesus autem incurvatus deorsum, scribebat in terra.
units.tr: But Jesus, bending down, wrote on the ground.

units.la: 7 Quum autem perseuerarent eum interrogare, erexit se, & dixit eis, Qui vestrum immunis est à peccato, primus in eam iaciat lapidem.
units.tr: 7 When they persisted in asking him, he raised himself up and said to them, He among you who is without sin, let him first cast a stone at her.

units.la: 8 Et rursum incurvatus deorsum, scribebat in terra.
units.tr: 8 And again, bending down, he wrote on the ground.

units.la: 9 Ipsi verò cùm hæc audivissent, & à conscientia sua redarguerentur, singulatim alius post alium exierant, initio facto à senioribus usque ad vltimos, & relictus est solus Iesus, & mulier in medio stans.
units.tr: 9 But they, when they had heard these things, and were convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, one after another, beginning from the elders to the last; and Jesus was left alone, and the woman standing in the midst.

units.la: Dum ipsi scisciantur, Christus interea incuruatus scribebat in terra: nō quidem puto eum, quicquam quod alicuius esset momenti tum scripsisse, sed hoc quasi indicio voluit ostendere neglectum, imò contemptum interrogationis ipsorum, vt si proferetibus iis friuolum aliquid aut captiosum, conuersus ad parietem digito vel cultello lineas in eo duceret: ea re significans se non aduertere animum ad ea quae dicerentur. Nam praestat leuiusculum aliquid agere, imò saepe nihil agere, quàm occupari serio in respondendo iis omnibus quae proferuntur à vana & captiosa ista generatione. Praestat in nullo occupari quàm in respondendo omnibus iis quae Papista aliquis obiiceret. Illud enim esset infinitum. Nullum enim illi modum in quaerendo & haesitando faciùt, seque & alios inextricabilibus labyrinthis implicant. Quum autem perseueraret, Iesus, importunitate eorum quasi coactus, respondet tandem, sed prudenter adeo vt illi confusi descesserint; Qui vestrùm immunis est à peccato, &c. Summa responsionis haec est, quasi dicat, Ne condemnate, ne lapidate istam, nisi velitis vos ipsum condemnari. Nam hoc sequitur ex hac ipsius propositione, hoc modo; Qui vestrùm immunis est à peccato, primus in eam iaciat lapidem: At nemo vestrùm immunis est à peccato: Ergo nemo vestrùm iaciat lapidē, nisi velit eadem opera seipsum condemnare. Verùm assumptionem hanc & conclusionem relinquit singulorum conscientiis, quas proculdubio pungit & excitat hac sola propositione. Solet enim Dominus generales theses & propositiones substernere, applicationem autem particularem singulorum conscientiis relinquere; vt hanc thesin, verbi gratia, in lege sua substernit: Maledictus omnis, qui non praestiterit verba legis huius, faciendo ea. Assumptionem qua quis convincatur peccati sui, ac conclusionem qua condemnetur, relinquit conscientiae cuiusque. At ego nō praestiti: Ergo maledictus sum. Quod si quis obiiciat, an recte hic sequatur; Peccator est quis: Ergo ne iudicet, condemnet & puniat maleficum alium; quem nita enim nullus repetietur in terris iudex & vltor flagitiosorum hominum. Videtur autem Dominus sic concludere: Peccatores estis, Ergo ne proiicite lapidem
units.tr: While they were questioning him, Christ meanwhile, bending down, wrote on the ground. I do not think he wrote anything of any importance at that time; but he wished to show by this sign that he neglected, nay rather despised, their questioning: as if, while they were putting forward something trivial or captious, he turned to the wall and with a finger or a knife drew lines on it, thereby signifying that he did not give his attention to what was being said. For it is better to do something rather trivial, nay often to do nothing, than to be seriously occupied in answering all those things which are put forward by this vain and captious generation. It is better to be occupied in nothing than in answering all the objections that some Papist might raise. For that would be endless. They make no limit to their questioning and hesitating, and they entangle themselves and others in inextricable labyrinths. When, however, he persisted, Jesus, as if compelled by their importunity, at last answers, but so wisely that they departed confused: He among you who is without sin, etc. The sum of his answer is this, as if he said: Do not condemn, do not stone her, unless you wish to be condemned yourselves. For this follows from his proposition in this way: He among you who is without sin, let him first cast a stone at her; but none of you is without sin; therefore none of you should cast a stone, unless he wishes at the same time to condemn himself. But he leaves this minor premise and the conclusion to the consciences of each, which he undoubtedly pricks and stirs by this proposition alone. For the Lord is accustomed to lay down general theses and propositions, and to leave the particular application to the consciences of individuals; as, for example, he lays down this thesis in his law: Cursed is everyone who does not perform the words of this law, by doing them. The minor premise by which anyone is convicted of his sin, and the conclusion by which he is condemned, he leaves to the conscience of each. But I have not performed them: therefore I am cursed. But if anyone objects whether this follows rightly: Someone is a sinner, therefore he should not judge, condemn and punish another evildoer; for in that case no judge or avenger of wicked men would be found on earth. Yet the Lord seems to conclude thus: You are sinners, therefore do not cast the stone.

units.la: Euangelii non tollit iudicia politica & Ecclesiastica: imò stabilit, & mein eam. Respondeo non colligi ex eo peccato ipsius iudicis, simpliciter non iudicandum, condemnandum & puniendum ab ipso alterum aliquem: sed colligi & ex conditione non condemnandum ab eo, aut puniedum alterum, nisi prius ipse se condemnet, tanquam peccatorem coram Domino. Propositionis enim Domini hic Iesus videtur: Nisi quis immunis a peccato, vel certè agnoscat se peccatorem ac reum, veniamque peccatui a Deo petat, ne iudicet alterum aut puniat: At vos neque immunes estis a peccato, neque agnoscitis vos ipsi peccatores; Ergo inepti estis qui peccatrice istam condemnatis aut puniatis: requirit enim Dominus ut iudex quisque sit vel immunis a peccato, quod fieri non potest: vel certè agnoscat se peccatorem ac reum eiusdem peccati, quod damnat & punit in altero, saltem quod ad semen illud mali, quod in corde penitus delitescit. Requirit ut prius odio prosequatur peccatum quod in se est, quàm quod in altero est; quod profecto nisi faciat, sed ut doctor in Ecclesia, syncophantarum malâ mentem vellicans, saris arguit se non tam odio prosequi peccatum, quàm personam ipsam hominis. Neque verò bona conscientia iudicium potest exercere. Quod si autem agnoscat saltem semen cuiusque peccati in se haerere, & constitutens quasi ipse coram tribunali summi illius iudicis, interea dum reus aliquis peragitur pro tribunali ipsius, supplex veniam flagitet peccati sui, idque per Christum Iesum, tum profecto innocens est in Christo, ac bona conscientia iudicium potest in alterum exercere. Manet igitur illud, non prius iudicem aliquem terrenum debere alterum condemnare, quàm se condemnet. Paulus, grauiter inuectus est in hypocritas illos censores sui temporis: Quapropter inexcusabilis es, ô homo, quisquis alios damnas, &c. An hic reprehendit eos quòd omnino condemnarent alios? minimè: sed reprehendit, quòd non prius, cùm pariter rei essent, se condemnarent, quò possent deinde, bona conscientia freti, aliorum esse censores & iudices. Nam hypocritarum hoc est ingenium, abundant ipsi quidem vitiis omnis generis, & quae occulte fiunt ab ipsis turpe est vel dicere, interea temporis aliorum grauissimi ac truculentissimi censores existunt, ut habeant scilicet quod praetexant suis ipsorum vitiis, quorum ipsi secum conscij sunt.
units.tr: The gospel does not abolish civil and ecclesiastical judgments; rather, it establishes and confirms them. I answer that it does not follow from the sin of the judge himself that he must not judge, condemn and punish another person at all. It follows, rather, on the condition that he must not condemn or punish another unless he first condemns himself as a sinner before the Lord. For this is the proposition that Jesus seems to state here: unless a man is free from sin, or at least acknowledges himself a sinner and guilty and asks God for pardon for his sin, he must not judge or punish another. But you are neither free from sin nor do you acknowledge yourselves to be sinners; therefore you are foolish to condemn or punish this woman. The Lord requires that every judge be either free from sin, which cannot happen, or at least acknowledge himself a sinner and guilty of the same sin that he condemns and punishes in another, at least as regards that seed of evil which lies hidden deep in the heart. He requires that a man pursue with hatred the sin that is in himself before the sin that is in another. If he does not do this, but, like a teacher in the Church who pricks the malicious minds of the sycophants, he argues that he does not so much hate sin as the person of the man himself, he is plainly a hypocrite. Nor can he exercise judgment with a good conscience. But if he acknowledges that at least the seed of every sin clings to himself, and while another is being tried before the tribunal, places himself as it were before the tribunal of that supreme Judge and, as a suppliant, asks pardon for his sin, and does so through Jesus Christ, then indeed he is innocent in Christ, and with a good conscience he can exercise judgment on another. It remains, therefore, that an earthly judge must not condemn another until he has condemned himself. Paul sharply attacked those hypocritical censors of his time: "Therefore you are inexcusable, O man, whoever you are who condemn others," etc. Did he rebuke them because they condemned others at all? By no means; he rebuked them because, though they were equally guilty, they did not first condemn themselves, so that afterwards, relying on a good conscience, they might become censors and judges of others. For this is the character of hypocrites: they themselves abound in vices of every kind, and the things they do in secret are shameful even to mention, yet meanwhile they become the most severe and savage censors of others, so that they have something to put forward as a pretext for their own vices, of which they themselves are conscious.

units.la: Et rursum incuruatus deorsum. Christus rursus aliud agedo ostendit, quàm indigna esset responsione illa eorum interrogatio, etiam postquam iam aliquid respondit.
units.tr: And again, bending down, he wrote on the ground. By doing something else, Christ again showed how unworthy of an answer that question of theirs was, even after he had already given them an answer.

units.la: Auditis autem his. Hoc effectum est superiorum Christi verborum: ad propositionem illam Domini, assumpserunt singuli conuicti conscientiis suis, se peccatores esse, quos nondum peccati sui poenituit, ac deinde conclusserunt singuli apud conscientias suas se nihilominus mortem esse commeritos quàm miseram illam adulteram. Ex quo rursus intulerunt se salua conscientia in miseram illam aduertere non potuisse. Itaque discesserunt singuli, initio facto à senioribus vsque ad vltimos. Quo loco discis, vbi semel compuncta est & excitata Dei voce conscientia hypocritæ in alios læuientis, eum pudere sui, adeo vt neque posset iam alios damnare, neque ferre conspectum iusti illius iudicis. Nam consopita ista conscientia, quæ est absque sensu scelerum suorum, in causa est, cur tam audaces feratur ad alios condemnandos, & sese etiam sistendos in conspectu Domini. Quod quidem Christi humiliati non potuerunt hypocritæ ferre aspectu, quanto magis iidem, reliquique hypocritæ omnes, non poterunt ferre aspectum Christi gloriosi, cum venturus est ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos?
units.tr: But when they heard these things. This was the effect of the words Christ had just spoken. At that statement of the Lord, each of them, convicted by his own conscience, admitted that he was a sinner, one who had not yet repented of his sin; and then each of them concluded, in his own conscience, that he deserved death no less than that wretched adulteress. From this they again inferred that they could not, with a clear conscience, turn against that wretched woman. And so they departed one by one, beginning from the elders down to the last. Here you learn that when the conscience of the hypocrite, which rages against others, has once been pierced and stirred by the voice of God, it is put to shame, so that he can no longer condemn others nor bear the sight of that just Judge. For that drowsy conscience, which has no sense of its own crimes, is the reason why hypocrites are carried so boldly to condemn others and to present themselves before the face of the Lord. If the hypocrites could not bear the sight of the humbled Christ, how much less will they, and all the other hypocrites, be able to bear the sight of the glorious Christ, when he comes to judge the living and the dead?

units.la: Vides deinde, quid tentando Dominum promouerint, & quid interea egerint. Nectebant scilicet ipsi laqueum, quo ipsi sunt implicati. Idem faciunt hodie omnes calumniatores, quibus etsi benè succedat ad tempus, & videantur aliquid efficere, tamen tandem, laqueo illo manibus suis complicato, vitam suam finient.
units.tr: Next you see what they achieved by tempting the Lord, and what they accomplished in the meantime. Of course they were weaving the snare in which they themselves were caught. All slanderers do the same today: though they may succeed for a time and seem to accomplish something, yet at last, with that snare folded by their own hands, they will end their lives.

units.la: 10 Quum autem sese Iesus erexisset, & neminem conspiceret, præter mulierem, dixit ei, Mulier, vbi sunt illi tui accusatores? nemo te condemnauit?
units.tr: 10 When Jesus had raised himself up and saw no one but the woman, he said to her, "Woman, where are those your accusers? Has no one condemned you?"

units.la: 11 Ipsa vero dixit, Nemo, Domine. Dixit autem ei Iesus, Nec ego te condemno: vade, & ne amplius pecca.
units.tr: 11 She said, "No one, Lord." And Jesus said to her, "Neither do I condemn you; go, and sin no more."

units.la: 12 Rursum ergo Iesus eis loquutus est, dicens, Ego sum lux illa mundi: qui sequitur me, non ambulabit bulabit in tenebris, sed habebit lumen vitæ.
units.tr: 12 Again therefore Jesus spoke to them, saying, "I am the light of the world; he who follows me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life."

units.la: HIc Dominus interrogat mulierem, non quòd du- bitet an ita sit, vidit enim omnes abesse, sed vt excitet mulierem ad animadversionem tanti operis, in iis ita convincendis, & sic condemnandis vno verbo, vt neque haberent linguam, qua loquerentur, neque manum, qua proicerent lapidem, neque denique faciem, qua possent ferre præsentiam Domini, sed toti conterriti confugerent ab ipsius aspectu, quo scilicet magnitudinem operis illius mulier diligentius considerans, cum cognosceret & agnosceret mundi iudicem, ac proinde in eum crederet ad salutem. Neque dubium est quin mulier tum cœperit fidem aliquam in eum habere. Hinc autem discimus nos, quàm stupida sit natura ista, in operibus Dei etiam mirificis expendendis, vsque adeo enim stuper, vt nunquam satis excitari possit. Neque enim possunt hodierno die nostri homines satis vnquam expergefieri ad considerandum Dei iudicia ista, quæ hodierno die Dominus alia post alia continuò immittit, & quibus ingratam istam gentem cumulat. Verum hoc malum ex stupiditate duntaxat naturæ existeret, aliquo modo tolerabile esset, sed cum ex obstinata quadam malitia tum aduersus Dei opera, tum aduersus Dei verbum proficiscatur, profecto indicio est, Deum multiplicaturum iudicia sua, donec tandem frangatur ista aduersus ipsum obstinatio. Quæ immittit quidem nunc, propius ac magis magisque nos attingunt, in quo genere est hoc nouissimum iudicium, in quo tum eq circumstantiæ tum personæ nobilis occisæ, tum personæ occidentis, tum etiam actionis ipsius, vt nemo animo non plane ferreo, qui eo non commoveatur. Hæc enim est tota ista vulgi commotio. Verum non omnes eo permoti sunt, & ij quidem sunt ex principibus viris, quorum est videre, vt in tam crudele facinus animaduerterent. Quid, quæso, aliud portendit hoc, quàm Deum nunquam iudiciorum suorum finem facturum, priusquàm omnes à summo ad infimum pariter se miseros sensérint, & conditionem suam defleuerint? Ipsa vero dixit ei, Nemo Domine. Respondet
units.tr: Here the Lord asks the woman, not because he doubts whether it is so, for he saw that they had all gone, but in order to rouse the woman to consider the greatness of so great a work: that these men had been convicted and condemned by a single word, so that they had neither a tongue with which to speak, nor a hand with which to throw the stone, nor finally a face with which they could bear the presence of the Lord, but in utter terror they fled from his sight. By this the woman, considering the magnitude of that work more carefully, might recognise and acknowledge the Judge of the world, and so believe in him unto salvation. Nor is there any doubt that the woman then began to have some faith in him. Here we learn how dull our nature is in weighing even the wonderful works of God; it is so stupid that it can never be sufficiently roused. Indeed, our people today can never be wakened enough to consider these judgments of God, which the Lord continually sends upon us one after another, and with which he heaps up this ungrateful nation. But if this evil arose only from the dullness of nature, it would be somewhat tolerable; but since it proceeds from a certain obstinate malice both against the works of God and against the Word of God, it is surely a sign that God will multiply his judgments until this obstinacy against himself is broken. He indeed now sends judgments that touch us ever more nearly and closely, among which is this most recent judgment, in which the circumstances, the noble person slain, the person who slew, and the deed itself are such that no one who is not utterly stony-hearted fails to be moved by it. For this is the whole commotion of the common people. Yet not all have been moved by it, and some of them are men of rank, from whom one would expect that they would take note of so cruel a crime. What, I ask, does this portend, except that God will never make an end of his judgments until all, from highest to lowest, alike feel themselves wretched and lament their condition? "She said to him, No one, Lord." The woman answers

units.la: II mulier ac excitatur quidem ex stupore illo suo: sed quotus quisque est hodierno die apud nos, qui vel respondet, vel etiam dignatur audire Deum ex Verbo suo clamantem & expergefacientem nos? Quod argumento est, verbum hoc quod audimus quotidie, breui conuertendum in iudicium grauissimum Deus enim non feret in perpetuum hūc contemptum suae vocis. Dixit autem eis Iesus. Non, ait, absoluo te ab hoc crimine; neque enim ciuilis magistratus partes in se recipit, neque si recepisset quidem contradixisset Dei mandato tam expresso de adulteris: Leuitic.20.10. Vt non sit quod quisquam ex hoc Domini responso colligat adulterum non condemnandum morte. Quod profecto non minus ineptum esset, ac si quis colligeret haereditatem non esse diuidendam inter fratres, quod Dominus Luc. 12.14. respondit cuidam e turba petenti vt fratri diceret vt partiretur secum hereditatem. Heus tu, quis me voluit iudicem aut partitorem praefecit? Non igitur mulieri respondet, Ego te absoluo, sed ait, Nec ego te condemno. Hoc enim generalius est, non condemnat enim iudex, cum absoluit. Non condemnat quoque priuatus, cum non recipit in se partes iudicis. Verum non est hic putadum Dominum nullo pacto absoluisse mulierem. Absoluit enim eam proculdubio spiritualiter a peccato & morte aeterna. In quo illud mireris: Ij qui tanquam iusti se stiterunt coram eo, & conuenerunt ad condemnandum mulierem ream, ij, inquam, discesserunt conuicti conscientiis & condemnati: mulier autem quae in medio statuebatur, & rea peragebatur absoluta est. Ex quo illud conspicitur, quod alibi dictum legimus in Euangelio, principibus Sacerdotum & senioribus: Publicani & meretrices praecunt vos in regnum caelorum. Atqui id quoque verum est hodierno die. Nam etiam ex iis qui palam peccant inuenient gratiam potius accitius, quam hypocritae isti indurati. Tam incurabile malum est hypocrisis! Et tantum bonum est in sinceritate cordis! malim enim peccatorem etiam grauissimum ingenuè confitentem peccata sua, quam hypocritam affectatem iustitiam externam, celatem autem interiorem cordis impuritatem atque infidelitatem. Vide, & ne amplius pecces. Expectauit
units.tr: 11 The woman answers and is roused from her stupor. But how few among us today answer, or even deign to hear God calling and waking us by his Word? This is a sign that the word we hear every day will soon be turned into a most severe judgment; for God will not bear this contempt of his voice forever. Then Jesus said to them. He does not say, "I absolve you of this crime," for he does not take upon himself the part of the civil magistrate; and even if he had, he would not have contradicted God's so explicit command concerning adulterers: Leviticus 20:10. So nothing should be inferred from this answer of the Lord as to whether the adulterer should not be condemned to death. That inference would be no less absurd than if someone were to conclude that an inheritance must not be divided among brothers, because the Lord, in Luke 12:14, answered a man in the crowd who asked him to tell his brother to divide the inheritance with him: "Man, who made me a judge or divider over you?" Therefore he does not answer the woman, "I absolve you," but says, "Neither do I condemn you." This is the more general statement, for a judge does not condemn when he absolves; nor does a private person condemn when he does not take upon himself the part of a judge. Yet we must not think that the Lord in no way absolved the woman. For he surely absolved her spiritually from sin and eternal death. Here one may marvel at this: those who stood before him as if righteous, and gathered to condemn the guilty woman, these, I say, departed convicted and condemned by their consciences; but the woman who was set in the midst and was being tried as guilty was absolved. From this we see what we read elsewhere in the Gospel, said to the chief priests and elders: "The tax collectors and harlots go into the kingdom of heaven before you." And this is true today as well. For among those who sin openly, even more readily than among those hardened hypocrites, one finds grace. So incurable is the evil of hypocrisy! And so great is the good of sincerity of heart! For I would rather have a most grievous sinner who frankly confesses his sins than a hypocrite who pretends to external righteousness while concealing the inner impurity and unbelief of his heart. See, and sin no more. She waited

units.la: humile excipit. uit mulier & sustinuit aspectum Domini, tantisperdum iussa est ab ipso Domino discedere. Pharisæi autem ac Scribæ iniussi & vltrò discesserunt, neque enim ferre diutius potuerunt aspectum Domini. Causa autem fuit, quia hæc misera, etsi conscientiam quidem peccati ha- buerit, tamen purgata fuit à mala conscientia. Illi vero nequaquàm fuerunt purgati à mala conscietia, & à rea- tu peccati. Qui autem non sunt purgati à mala conscie-tia, & à reatu peccati, non audent illi coram Domino consistere. Qui autem sanguine Christi ab ea sunt pur-gati, hi etiamsi in se peccatores sint, coram Deo tamen audent consistere. Vnde Apostolus, postquàm docuit purgatam esse malam conscientiam sanguine Christi, conclu sit accedendum esse ad Deum cum vero corde, & certa persuasione fidei, & cordibus puris à conscientia mala. Postremò dicit mulieri, Ne amplius pecces: q.d. Etsi impuné tuleris hoc peccatum adulterij, tamen ne ex hac impunitate arripito occasionem peccandi amplius. Homines enim vulgò impunitate & deteriores fiunt ipsi, & malo suo exemplo deteriores faciunt alios, & animant ad peccandum. Remissiones enim istæ, quas vocant, quæ impetrantur quotidie, causa sunt tot cædium apud nos. Sed monet hic Dominus, non amplius peccandum esse. Hoc enim est non tam præpostera ista magistratus lenitate abuti, quem oportuit animaduertere in flagitia ex Dei mandato & voluntate, quàm lenitatem Dei, & diuitias benignitatis, tolerantiæ ac lenitatis eius contemnere, ignorantes se benignitate Dei ad resipiscē- dam deduci. Vnde futurum est, vt thesaurizent sibi ipsi in diem iræ ac patefactionis iusti iudicij Dei. Sed inquit, pro duritia tua & corde quod resipiscere nescit, &c. Nota præterea etiam iam absolutam à peccato & morte habemus assiduis admonitionibus, ad hoc ne peccemus amplius. Nam nisi adiuti essemus continuò admonitionibus, adhortationibus, profecto futurum esset, vt relabeƦemur & Filium Dei, vt ait Apostolus Heb.6.6. rursus crucifigeremus nobismetipsis, & ad ignominiam exponeremus.
units.tr: humile excipit. uit mulier & sustinuit aspectum Domini, tantisperdum iussa est ab ipso Domino discedere. The woman received it humbly. She stood and endured the Lord's gaze, until she was bidden by the Lord himself to depart. The Pharisees and scribes, however, withdrew without being bidden and of their own accord, for they could no longer bear the Lord's gaze. The reason was that this wretched woman, although she had a sense of sin, was nonetheless cleansed from an evil conscience. Those men, however, were by no means cleansed from an evil conscience and from the guilt of sin. Those who are not cleansed from an evil conscience and from the guilt of sin do not dare to stand before the Lord. But those who have been cleansed from it by the blood of Christ dare to stand before God, even if they are sinners in themselves. Hence the Apostle, after teaching that the evil conscience is cleansed by the blood of Christ, concludes that we must draw near to God with a true heart, in the assurance of faith, and with hearts pure from an evil conscience. Lastly, he says to the woman: Sin no more. That is to say: even if you have escaped punishment for this act of adultery, do not seize on this impunity as an occasion to sin any further. For men generally become worse through impunity, and by their evil example make others worse too and urge them to sin. Those indulgences, as they call them, which are obtained every day, are the cause of so many murders among us. But here the Lord warns that we must not sin any more. For this is not so much to abuse the magistrate's absurd leniency, which ought to punish crimes by God's command and will, as to despise the leniency of God and the riches of his goodness, forbearance and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads them to repentance. Hence it will come about that they store up for themselves wrath on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God. But he says: according to your hardness and your heart that cannot repent, etc. Note further that we have been freed from sin and death, and we are given constant admonitions so that we may not sin any more. For unless we were continually aided by admonitions and exhortations, it would surely come about that we fall back and crucify again for ourselves the Son of God, as the Apostle says (Heb. 6.6), and expose him to shame.

units.la: Rursum ergo Iesus. Dominus rursus coepit docere in tem-plo, congregata in vnum rursus multitudine. Summa
units.tr: Summary: Again, then, Jesus. The Lord again began to teach in the temple, the crowd having once more gathered together.

units.la: Secunda pars capitis, varium autem sermonis ipsius haec est. Sequimini me, Ratio est, qui sequitur me non ambulabit in tenebris, sed habebit lumen vitae: ergo sequimini me. Fundamentum huius rationis est. Ego sum lux mundi, ait Dominus. Quare de hoc fundamento, ut quod primo loco substratum sit, primum agamus. Ego sum lux mundi, inquit. Primum est quod hic consido. Dicit Iohannes Deum esse lucem, nec in eo tenebras esse ullas, hoc est, ut apparet ex argumento illius loci, Deum sanctum esse. Sanctitas autem naturae Dei haec posita est primum in vita, sive in esse, ut loquuntur, Dei incomprehensibili. Deinde in reliquis omnibus eius proprietatibus essentialibus, ut potentia, iustitia, misericordia, bonitate, laetitia, reliqua denique beatitate. Alterum est, lux illa mundi in persona Patris inconspicua est, neque ulla unquam creatura, vel angelus, vel homo, videt eam lucem in patre immediate, ut ait Paulus, Deum inhabitare lucem inaccessam quem vidit nemo hominum, neque videre potest. Et Iohannes, Deum nemo vidit unquam. Capite autem sexto post, significat de Patre loqui, non quod Patrem viderit quisquam nisi is qui est a Deo, hic vidit Patrem. Ergo lux Dei in persona Patris est inconspicua: in persona vero filii conspicua. Quamobrem dicitur imago inconspicui Dei, & splendor gloriae ipsius, hoc est totius naturae gloriosae Dei. Nam tota resplendet ac elucet in Christo filio tanquam imagine, quae essentia una eademque est cum Patre. Tertium est, quo magis percipiatur, & ad sensus ipsos corporeos propius admoveatur lux illa Dei in persona Filii, & ut dicitur 1.Iohan.1.1. videatur his oculis, contrectetur his manibus, audiatur his auribus nostris, lux illa Deitatis in persona filii ipsa, induit naturam humanam & sensibilem. Unde hae loquutiones, Deus conspicuus factus est in carne: Sermo caro factus est, & commoratus est inter nos, & spectavimus gloriam eius, gloriam, inquam, ut unigeniti egressi a Patre, plenum gratiae & veritatis. Quanto igitur magis apparebit in humana carne gloria illa Dei, in glorioso illo adventu Domini nostri Iesu Christi? Quartum, teste Apostolo, Incredulis διανοία habent obtenebratam, alienatam a vita Dei propter ignorantiam. Neque enim vita ista naturalis faciet, quo minus sit mors spiritualis, ritualis. Nā multi viuentes naturaliter, spiritualiter mortui sunt, vt loquitur Apost. de vidua, quę in luxu viuit: ita etiam hæc duo cõiuncta sunt, illuminatio mentis, ac vita illa Dei. Quare rectè vocatur ab ipso lumen vitæ. Hactenus ratio fuit ex illo fundamento. Quid igitur reliquum est, nisi vt concludatur exhortatio: Ergo sequimini me. Promittit enim lucem illam cuius beneficio participes fiemus & consortes diuinæ naturæ, vt loquitur Petrus. Sed nemo est omnium fere qui commoue-bitur promissa luce ista, nisi cuius oculi cœperunt primùm ea illuminari, & qui cœpit viuere illam Dei vitā. Quare precandum assiduè, vt illuminatis oculis mentis, possint homines videre, quæ sit spes illa vocationis ipsius, & quæ opes gloriæ hæreditatis ipsius in sanctis.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter, and the variety of his speech, is this. Follow me. The reason is this: whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life; therefore follow me. The foundation of this reason is: I am the light of the world, says the Lord. Let us therefore first deal with this foundation, since it is laid first. I am the light of the world, he says. The first point is this, which I am considering here. John says that God is light, and that there is no darkness in him, that is, as appears from the argument of that passage, that God is holy. The holiness of God's nature is set first in his life, or in his being, as they say, which is incomprehensible. Then it is set in all his other essential properties, such as power, justice, mercy, goodness, joy, and finally his blessedness. The second point is that this light of the world is invisible in the person of the Father, and no creature ever, whether angel or man, sees that light in the Father immediately; as Paul says, God dwells in unapproachable light, whom no man has seen or can see. And John: No one has ever seen God. In chapter six below, however, he signifies that he is speaking of the Father, not that anyone has seen the Father except the one who is from God; this one has seen the Father. Therefore the light of God is invisible in the person of the Father, but visible in the person of the Son. For this reason he is called the image of the invisible God and the brightness of his glory, that is, of the whole glorious nature of God. For the whole of it shines and gleams forth in Christ the Son as in an image, who is one and the same essence with the Father. The third point, so that this light of God in the person of the Son may be perceived more clearly and brought nearer to the bodily senses themselves, and, as 1 John 1.1 says, may be seen with these eyes, handled with these hands, and heard with these ears of ours, is that this light of the Deity in the person of the Son has put on human and sensible nature. Hence those expressions: God was made visible in the flesh; the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, the glory, I say, of the only begotten who came forth from the Father, full of grace and truth. How much more, therefore, will that glory of God appear in human flesh at the glorious coming of our Lord Jesus Christ? The fourth point, as the Apostle witnesses, is that unbelievers have their understanding [διανοία] darkened, alienated from the life of God through ignorance. For that natural life does not prevent spiritual, indeed ritual, death. For many who live naturally are spiritually dead, as the Apostle says of the widow who lives in pleasure. So too these two things are joined together: the illumination of the mind and that life of God. Wherefore he is rightly called by him the light of life. So far the reasoning has come from that foundation. What remains, then, except that the exhortation be concluded: Therefore follow me? For he promises that light, through whose benefit we shall become partakers and sharers of the divine nature, as Peter says. But almost no one of all men will be moved by the promise of this light unless his eyes have first begun to be illuminated by it, and he has begun to live that life of God. Therefore we must pray constantly that, with the eyes of the mind enlightened, men may be able to see what is the hope of his calling and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints.

units.la: 13 Pharisæi igitur dixerunt ei, Tu de teipso testaris, testimonium tuum non est firmum.
units.tr: 13 The Pharisees therefore said to him: You bear witness about yourself; your testimony is not true.

units.la: 14 Respondit Iesus & dixit eis, Etiamsi ego testor de meipso, firmum est testimonium meum, quia scio unde venerim, & quo vadam: vos autem nescitis unde venerim, & quo vadam.
units.tr: 14 Jesus answered and said to them: Even if I bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going; but you do not know where I came from or where I am going.

units.la: 15 Vos secundum carnem iudicatis, ego non iudico quemquam.
units.tr: 15 You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one.

units.la: 16 Quod si etiam iudicarem ego, iudicium meum firmum esset, quia solus non sum, sed ego, & qui misit me Pater.
units.tr: 16 But even if I did judge, my judgment would be true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.

units.la: 17 Sed & in lege vestra scriptum est, Duorum hominum testimonium firmum est.
units.tr: 17 And it is written in your law too, that the testimony of two men is true.

units.la: 18 Ego is sum qui testor de me ipso, & testatur de me qui misit me Pater.
units.tr: 18 I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me.

units.la: HOc est effectum illud, quod exhortatio ista Domini operatur in cordibus Pharisæorum, nempe non sequuntur eum; hinc colligitur, nihil permotos fuisse eos lucę illa, à qua argumentatus est, non, inquam, motos eos aliquo eius desiderio, ac proinde non vidisse eos, aut sensisse tenebras illas quibus erat oppressi. Disce igitur illorum exemplo, quòd qui non senserunt, quantæ sint tenebræ istæ, quæ in natura sunt, nullo illi desiderio lucis moueantur. Qui autem nullo lucis desiderio mouentur, ne si Christum quidem ipsum statuas iis ante oculos, eum sequentur. Qui vero senserunt ac palpārunt crassas iltas naturæ tenebras, illi quidem desiderio lucis afficiuntur; his autem si Christum indicaueris præsentem, statim eum ac auide arripient, vtpote vnicam illam ac solam lucem, quæ dispellit naturæ tenebras. Quare in hortationibus quæ fiunt ad Christum sequendum, perpetuo sunt præparandi animi hominum, sensu miseriæ ac tenebrarum, ac proinde desiderio liberationis atque lucis. Ita enim fiet, vt locus sit hortationibus ad Christum sequendum, & non simus similes Pharisæis istis. Verum non modo non mouentur isti lucis desiderio, verumetiam strenuè eam oppugnant. In natura nostra non modò non est lucis ac vitæ desiderium, verum etiam malitia qua oppugnamus quod non desideramus. Vnde sequitur multo grauior induratio & excæcatio: denique mens reproba, inquit Apostolus, ad perpetrandam omnem iniustitiam, scortationem, improbitatem, aliáque id genus infinita, in quæ nos vide mus hodierno die nostros homines erumpere, & quibus manifestò arguitur plerosque omnes induratos & excæcatos esse, ac proinde lucē iltam oppugnare. Hinc enim fons & hinc origo omnium horum malorum, cædium horribilissimarum, rapinarum, sacrilegiorum, quæ non cessabunt, priusquam finis factus fuerit tanti huius contemptus Dei ac verbi ipsius. Verum hoc notandum est in Pharisæis istis, non directè eos oppugnare ipsam lucem, sed negare Christum esse lucem. Tu testaris de tei-psoinquiunt, quare testimonium tuum non est firmum. Ex quo illud sequi volunt eum non esse lucem eam, quam ipse prædicat. Nota igitur, fere cum maliciosa illa lucis oppugnatione coniunctam esse hypocrisin: Nemo enim reperietur tam impudens, vt velit splendide ac manifesto lucem oppugnare: verum omnes fere fatebuntur verbo, se lucem diligere, ac veritatem, tenebras autem odisse. Iudæus hodierno die negabit Christum esse lucem. Atque ita odium illud lucis penitus animo insitum occultat. Papistæ concedunt quidem Christum esse lucem, sed negant à nobis verè prædicari Christum. Estque hic eorum prætextus quem odio lucis prætendunt. Ex professoribus etiam ipsis multi concedunt quidem verè ac sincerè à nobis Christum prædicari: Sed contumeliæ istæ quibus ministros Christi afficiunt satis testantur hanc eorum professionem tantùm fucum esse. Vita autem tam impurè ac turpiter acta satis arguit eos lucem odisse, quicquid demum de eius amore iactitent. Illud enim Christi verum manet: Quisquis peruersa agit, odit lucem. supra cap. 3. 20. Nota igitur hic hypocrisin cum malitia coniunctam.
units.tr: This is the effect that this exhortation of the Lord works in the hearts of the Pharisees: namely, they do not follow him. From this it is gathered that they were moved by nothing of that light from which he argued; that is, they were not moved by any desire for it, and therefore they had not seen or felt the darkness by which they were oppressed. Learn, then, from their example that those who have not felt how great the darkness is that is in nature are moved by no desire for light. But those who are moved by no desire for light will not follow Christ, even if you set him before their eyes. Those, however, who have felt and groped about in that thick darkness of nature are indeed affected by a desire for light; and if you point out Christ to them as present, they will immediately and eagerly seize him, as the only and sole light that dispels the darkness of nature. Therefore in exhortations to follow Christ, men's minds must always be prepared by a sense of misery and of darkness, and so by a desire for deliverance and light. For in this way there will be room for exhortations to follow Christ, and we shall not be like those Pharisees. But these men are not only not moved by a desire for light, but they also fiercely attack it. In our nature there is not only no desire for light and life, but there is also a malice by which we attack what we do not desire. Hence there follows a much graver hardening and blinding: finally a reprobate mind, as the Apostle says, for committing every kind of unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, and countless other such things, which we see breaking out among our own people today, and by which it is manifestly shown that most of them are hardened and blinded, and therefore attack that light. For from this comes the source and origin of all these evils: the most horrible murders, robberies, sacrileges, which will not cease until an end is made of this so great contempt of God and of his very Word. But this must be noted in these Pharisees: they do not directly attack the light itself, but deny that Christ is the light. You bear witness about yourself, they say; therefore your testimony is not true. From which they wish it to follow that he is not that light which he proclaims. Note, therefore, that hypocrisy is almost always joined with this malicious attack on the light. For no one will be found so shameless as to wish openly and plainly to attack the light; rather, almost all will confess with their words that they love the light and the truth and hate darkness. The Jew today will deny that Christ is the light, and so he hides that hatred of the light which is deeply implanted in his mind. The Papists indeed concede that Christ is the light, but they deny that Christ is truly preached by us; and this is the pretext which they put forward for their hatred of the light. Among the professors themselves, many concede indeed that Christ is truly and sincerely preached by us; but the insults with which they assail the ministers of Christ sufficiently bear witness that this profession of theirs is only a pretence. Their life, so impurely and shamefully lived, sufficiently proves that they hate the light, whatever they may boast about loving it. For that saying of Christ remains true: Whoever does wicked things hates the light (John 3.20). Note, then, here that hypocrisy is joined with malice.

units.la: Respondit Iesus, &c. Christus negat sequi quod illi colligunt ex eo quod ipse de se testetur, neque enim ex eo sequitur testimonium Christi non esse idoneum. Argumentum est à persona testantis, quam describit ex loco unde venerit, nempe cœlo, & in quem ascensurus est, nempe cœlum. Quibus circumstantiis innuit personam eam Deum esse ac Dei filium. Nota igitur, Dei testimonium de se idoneum est, ideòque differt ad hominum testimonio. Homines non audiuntur vt testes in sua causa, quia οἰκεῖοι sunt omnes natura, ac proinde suspectum esse debet eorum de se testimonium. At Dei de se testimonium idoneum est & per se sufficiens, adeò vt nihil indigeat creaturæ vllius testimonio. Ego, inquit, testimonium ab homine non capto: sed hæc dico vt vos seruemini. Quo significat testimonio humano ornari se, non sua, sed nostræ infirmitatis ac infidelitatis causa. Cùm verò accedunt ad Dei de se testimonium, insuper hominum testimonia, iam Dei solius de se testimonium maius est omnibus iis: ideòque ait, Ego testimonium habeo maius testimonio Iohannis Baptistæ. Hoc ideo annoto, vt magni faciamus hoc Dei de se testimonium in Scripturis loquentis, cui tamen præferunt Papistæ Ecclesiæ suæ testimonium, adeo vt negent Scripturas authenticas esse & canonicas, nisi comprobatas prius & receptas ab Ecclesia. Probat autem se talem personam esse non alio argumento quàm quod ipse sciat ita esse: ex eo enim sequitur ita esse necessariò, etsi id nesciant aut nescire velint omnes creaturæ, vt discant homines acquiescere in Dei sententia, & dicere ita esse, sicut Deus scit, ac petere. id ad ipsorum salutem pertineat, vt velit Deus etiam cum ipsis quoque eam scientiam communicare. Vos autem nescitis. Nunc, postquam reddita ratione infirmauit eorum conclusionem, ipsos reprehendit: reprehensionis autem primum caput est, vos nescitis unde venerim, & quo vadam. Obiicit eis primùm ignorantiam personæ suæ gloriosæ. Id autem ex eo colligit, quòd negent ipsius de se testimonium. Qui se irreuerenter gerunt in Christum vel verbo vel facto, qui negant eius testimonium de se vel ministrorum ipsius de ipso, illi profecto satis ostendunt nunquam se cognouisse Deum, neque gustasse quàm benignus sit Dominus, neque denique sensisse vim illam vel mortis vel resurrectionis ipsius. Si enim eum cognouissent vnquà, ac sensissent in cordibus per fidem habitantem, profecto & de ipso, & de omnibus quæ ad ipsum quoquo modo pertinent, reuerenter magis & sensissent & loquuti fuissent. Quare laborandum est, vt tandem aliquando cognoscamus Dominum, ac serio sentiamus vim mortis ac resurrectionis ipsius. Secundum caput reprehensionis est, quo exprobrat iis peruersum iudicium. Vos, inquit, iudicatis secundum carnem. Significat iniquum illud eorum de ipso iudicium. Est autem hic effectus prioris; nam qui ignari sunt rei alicuius, illi, necesse est, si velint de ea iudicium facere, peruerse iudicent. Paulus ex peruerso iudicio arguit ignorantiam. Animalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, sunt enim illi stultitia: id est iudicat ea stulta esse, ac proinde ignorat plane quæ sint. Qui autem maximè ignari sunt, ferè omnium mortalium promptissimi sunt ad iudicandum & condemnandum, ac aliorum censores sunt rigidissimi. At isti, inquit Apostolus, quæ non nouerunt, ea conuitiis incessunt.
units.tr: Jesus answered, etc. Christ denies that what they infer from his testimony about himself follows. For it does not follow that the testimony of Christ is not sufficient. The argument rests on the person who testifies, whom he describes by the place he came from, namely heaven, and the place to which he is going, namely heaven. By these circumstances he indicates that this person is God and the Son of God. Note, then, that God's testimony about himself is sufficient, and therefore it differs from human testimony. Men are not admitted as witnesses in their own cause, because all are kinsmen [οἰκεῖοι] by nature, and so their testimony about themselves ought to be suspected. But God's testimony about himself is sufficient in itself and needs no support from any creature. I, he says, do not receive testimony from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved. By this he means that he does not adorn himself with human testimony for his own sake, but for the sake of our weakness and unbelief. When men add their testimonies to God's testimony about himself, the testimony of God alone is already greater than all of them. Therefore he says, I have a testimony greater than the testimony of John the Baptist. I note this so that we may hold in high esteem this testimony of God speaking in the Scriptures, which the Papists nevertheless prefer to the testimony of their Church, so much so that they deny that the Scriptures are authentic and canonical unless they have first been approved and received by the Church. He proves that he is such a person not by any other argument than that he himself knows it to be so. For from this it necessarily follows that it is so, even though all creatures do not know this or do not wish to know it, so that men may learn to acquiesce in God's judgment, to say that it is so as God knows it, and to ask that God, who wills to share that knowledge also with them, should do so for their own salvation. But you do not know. Now, having given the reason, which weakens their conclusion, he rebukes them. The first head of his rebuke is this: you do not know where I came from and where I am going. He charges them first with ignorance of his glorious person. He infers this from the fact that they deny his testimony about himself. Those who behave irreverently towards Christ, in word or deed, who deny his testimony about himself or the testimony of his ministers about him, certainly show plainly that they have never known God, have never tasted how gracious the Lord is, and have finally never felt the power of his death and resurrection. For if they had ever known him, and had felt him dwelling in their hearts through faith, they would surely have both felt and spoken more reverently both about him and about all things that pertain to him in any way. Therefore we must labour so that at last we may know the Lord and seriously feel the power of his death and resurrection. The second head of the rebuke is that in which he charges them with a perverse judgment. You, he says, judge according to the flesh. He signifies their unjust judgment about him. This, however, is the effect of the former: for those who are ignorant of something, if they wish to pass judgment on it, must necessarily judge perversely. Paul argues from a perverse judgment to ignorance: the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, that is, he judges them to be foolish and therefore plainly does not know what they are. But those who are most ignorant are almost always the readiest of all mortals to judge and condemn, and they are the most severe censors of others. But these men, says the Apostle, revile what they do not know.

units.la: Christus deinde exaggerat hoc eorum factum à suo exemplo, Ego, inquit, non iudico quemquam. Hoc vel referendum est in speciem ad præsens hoc tempus, quo nemirem iudicabat, sed in docendo omnes laborabat: vel in genere pertinet ad totum tempus, quo Christus in terris fuit. Nam finem sibi præcipuum propositum habuit, non condemnationem sed salutem omnium. vide supra cap.3.17. Non misit Deus filium suum in mundum vt condemnet.
units.tr: Christ then magnifies this their conduct by his own example: I, he says, do not judge anyone. This may be referred, in appearance, to the present time, when he did not judge anyone but laboured in teaching all; or it pertains generally to the whole time in which Christ was on earth. For he had as his chief aim not the condemnation but the salvation of all. See above, chapter 3, verse 17: God did not send his Son into the world to condemn it.

units.la: Ignorantiæ malù detegit Christus.
units.tr: Christ exposes the evil of ignorance.

units.la: Deinde, peruersum iudicii.
units.tr: Next, the perversity of judgment.

units.la: 1. Corinth. 2.14.
units.tr: 1 Corinthians 2.14.
Jude 1.10.

units.la: Christus alia reprehensione Iudæos ad bonam mentem reuocat. net mundum, sed ut seruetur mundus per eum. Hoc sine praecipuo deficiente, idque per hominum obstinationem, tum verbum eius ad condemnationem & ad iudicium exaggerandum spectabat cap. 9. 39. Ad iudicium exercendum ego in hunc mundum veni. Misericordia ista Christi & clementia tanta, condemnat hominum summam crudelitatem, ac rigorem summum in iudicando & condemnando. Iesus Christus sensit ipse miseriam nostram, ideoque aptus fuit Pontifex, qui misereretur nostri. At homines nunc sentiunt communem istam miseriam, ideoque tantum absunt ab eo, ut commoueantur aliorum miseria, ut contra eam quantum in ipsis est adaugeant. Miseri sunt, non qui sentiunt miseriam vel suam vel aliorum. Atquia obiici potuit: At iudicium rectum ac firmum non est; Respondet, quod si etiam iudicem ego, iudicium meum firmum est. Reddit rationem à legitima ipsius forma, Ego solus non sum, nempe dum iudico: Sedego, & qui misit me Pater, scilicet simul iudicamus. Unde concludit, Ergo iudicium meum rectum est ac firmum. Fundamentum huius consequentiae petit ex lege: Testimonium duorum idoneum est, ut ait Moses: In ore duorum aut trium testium stabit omne verbum. Discè igitur, in hoc apparet mansuetudo Christi summa, quod cum iudicij ipsius rectum sit, tamè à iudicio abstinet. In hoc apparet summa hominum seueritas, quod cum iudicium ipsorum corruptum sit ac iniquum, tamen in alios homines saeuiunt.
units.tr: Christ, by another rebuke, calls the Jews back to a good mind. ... not to condemn the world, but that the world might be saved through him. This, when the chief thing is lacking, and that through the obstinacy of men, his word was aimed at heightening the condemnation: chapter 9, verse 39, For judgment I have come into this world. This mercy of Christ and so great a clemency condemns the greatest cruelty of men and the utmost rigour in judging and condemning. Jesus Christ himself felt our misery, and therefore he was a fitting High Priest who could have compassion on us. But men now feel that common misery, and yet they are so far from being moved by the misery of others that they increase it as far as in them lies. They are wretched not those who feel their own misery or that of others. But it might be objected: yet judgment is not right and sure. He answers that even if he does judge, his judgment is sure. He gives the reason from its lawful form: I am not alone, namely when I judge; but I and the Father who sent me, that is, we judge together. Hence he concludes: therefore my judgment is right and sure. He seeks the ground of this inference from the law: the testimony of two is valid, as Moses says: by the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word stand. Learn, then, that in this appears the supreme gentleness of Christ, that although his judgment is right, he yet refrains from judging. In this appears the supreme severity of men, that although their judgment is corrupt and unjust, they nevertheless rage against other men.

units.la: Sed quomodo rectum est iudicium Christi? Iudicium apud homines rectum dicitur, tum ratione habita personae, quae rea peragitur, & meritorum ipsius, tum respectu legitimae iudicij ipsius formae. Christi iudicium rectum est, non modò respectu eius quod merentur homines, qui iure ac merito ab ipso damnarentur, sed etiam respectu legitimae ipsius formae, ideoque ad formam legitimam docendam affertur in medium lex de forma iudicandi quae habetur Deut. 19.15. Hoc fit non ideo, quod Deus sit obligatus legibus quemadmodum creaturae, vel huic etiam legi nominatim: cum leges omnes in genere, & haec lex in specie imago quaedam sint iustitiae illius ineffabilis, & iudicij ac formae iudicij ineffabilis quae est apud Deum. Sed Christus ita loquitur propter Pharisæos, ad eos conuincendos, qui opinati eum purè hominem non Deum esse, voluerunt legibus iis quæ hominibus tradita sunt de iudicio ipsiusque forma, obnoxium esse. Id tantum obseruamus ex hoc loco, quod, cum Christus volens probare rectitudinem iudicij sui, formam eius legitimam afferat, non satis sit terrestribus iudiciis si ratione meriti personæ ipsius eam condemnent ac iudicent, nisi etiam forma illa legitima obseruetur, quæ est ad imaginem illius iudicij quod in cælis peragitur ineffabili ac incomprehensibili quodam modo. Quantum absunt ab hoc homicidæ isti, iudicet Dominus.
units.tr: But how is the judgment of Christ right? A judgment among men is called right both with regard to the person who is on trial and his deserts, and with regard to the lawful form of the judgment. The judgment of Christ is right not only with respect to what men deserve, since they would justly and rightly be condemned by him, but also with respect to its lawful form. Therefore, in order to teach the lawful form, he brings forward the law concerning the form of judging, which is found in Deuteronomy 19.15. He does this not because God is bound by laws as creatures are, nor even by this law by name, since all laws in general, and this law in particular, are certain images of that ineffable justice and of the ineffable judgment and form of judgment which is with God. But Christ speaks thus on account of the Pharisees, to convict those who, supposing him to be a mere man and not God, wished him to be subject to those laws about judgment and its form which have been handed down to men. We observe only this from this passage: that since Christ, wishing to prove the rectitude of his judgment, brings forward its lawful form, it is not enough for earthly judgments to condemn and judge a person on account of his merits, unless that lawful form is also observed, which is according to the image of that judgment which is carried out in heaven in an ineffable and incomprehensible manner. How far those murderers are from this, let the Lord judge.

units.la: Ego is sum qui testor. Redit ad testimonium de se, ac priori illi adiungit alterum, alterius de se, nempe Pastris. In quo vide liberalitatem ac bonitatem Domini. Illi reiecto illo ipsius de se testimonio procurarunt suo merito vt vicissim ipsi reiicerentur. At adhuc luctatur Dominus cum eorum infidelitate, ac in eorum gratiam, vt ipsi, si fieri posset, crederent, adducit testimonium etiam alterius. Quia non placuit illud suum de se. Nos si Dominus ageret nobiscum pro ratione meriti nostri, certe ties quotidie nos reiiceret: sed luctatur Dominus cum infidelitate nostra. Si infidi sumus, ille tamen fidus manet, negare seipsum non potest. Quid enim aliud significat, id quod adhuc sinat verbum suum lucere ac prædicari inter nos, quàm Deum luctari cum incredulitate nostra? Notandum hoc quòd nō adducat pro teste altero vel Prophetam aliquem, vel Iohannem Baptistam, propheta aliquo maiorem, sed Patrem suum Deum, vt ea re ostendat in Deo ipso sufficientiam esse ad testandum de se, neque opus esse vt persona aliqua trinitatis quærat sibi testem alium à personis trinitatis. Verbi gratia, vt Filius alium testem quærat quàm Patrem & Spiritum sanctum. Nam Deus est in se perfectissimus. Patrem quoque adduxit testem, vt ex tanto teste ostenderet quanta esset persona illa de qua ipse testatur; necesse enim est, vt persona ea, de qua testetur tantus testis, excellens sit admodum. Quod profecto videbimus melius, si obseruemus quodnam sit testimonium quod de ipso perhibeat, nempe quale non sit perhibitum de vllo angelo: Cui enim angelo-rum
units.tr: I am he who bears witness. He returns to testimony about himself, and he adds to his former testimony another, the testimony of another about him, namely the Father. In this see the liberality and goodness of the Lord. They, having rejected his testimony about himself, had by their own merit brought it about that they in turn were rejected. But the Lord still strives with their unbelief, and for their sake, so that they might, if it were possible, believe, he brings forward also the testimony of another, since his testimony about himself did not please them. If the Lord were to deal with us according to the measure of our merit, surely he would reject us every day. But the Lord strives with our unbelief. If we are faithless, he nevertheless remains faithful; he cannot deny himself. For what else does it signify that he still allows his word to shine and be preached among us, than that God strives with our incredulity? This is to be noted: that he does not bring forward as a second witness either some prophet or John the Baptist, greater than any prophet, but his Father, God, so that by this he may show that in God himself there is sufficiency to bear witness about himself, and that there is no need for any person of the Trinity to seek for himself another witness from among the persons of the Trinity. For example, that the Son should seek another witness than the Father and the Holy Spirit. For God is in himself most perfect. He has also brought forward the Father as a witness, so that from so great a witness he might show how great is that person about whom he testifies; for it is necessary that the person about whom so great a witness testifies should be exceedingly excellent. This we shall certainly see better if we observe what testimony he bears about himself, namely, such as has not been borne about any angel. For to which of the angels did he ever say, You are my Son, today I have begotten you?

units.la: {2.Tim.2.13} rum dixit vnquam, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te? Atque ex tanto teste arguit suam excellentiam ac dignitatem, non tantùm propter gloriam suam, sed propter eum etiam finem, ob quem venit in hunc mundum: nempe vt mundus, postquàm vidit eum plusquam hominem esse Deum esse ac Dei Filium, in ipsum crederet, ac credens seruaretur.
units.tr: {2.Tim.2.13} To which of the angels did he ever say, "You are my Son; this day have I begotten you"? And from so great a witness he proves his own excellence and dignity, not only because of his glory but also because of the purpose for which he came into this world: namely, that the world, having seen that he is more than man, that he is God and the Son of God, should believe in him and, believing, be saved.

units.la: 19 Dicebant ergo ei, Vbi est tuus ille Pater? Respondit Iesus, Neque me nostis, neque Patrem meum: si me nosset is, Patrem quoque meum nosset is.
units.tr: 19 Then they said to him, Where is your Father? Jesus answered, You neither know me nor my Father: if you had known me, you would have known my Father also.

units.la: 20 Haec verba loquutus est Iesus in gazophylacio, docens in templo: & nemo prehendit eum, quia nondum venerat illa ipsius hora.
units.tr: 20 Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, teaching in the temple: and no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.

units.la: 21 Dixit ergo iterum eis Iesus, Ego vado & quaeretis me, & in hoc peccato vestro moriemini: quo ego vado vos non potestis venire.
units.tr: Jesus therefore said to them again, I go away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin: where I go, you cannot come.

units.la: REprehendunt quoque aliquo modo quod nunc affert pro se testimonium, vt facile videas non ob defectum argumentorum eos non credidisse, cum esse lucem mundi, sed ob cordis obstinatam malitiam: hypocritae enim obdurati praetendunt se destitui argumentis, dum non recipiunt oblatam lucem. Sed dum omnia argumenta etiam firmissima quaeque ex ipsis scripturis petita reiiciunt, satis produnt obstinatam malitiam suam ac propositum animi sui in permanendo in infidelitate. Testimonium autem Patris non aperte reiiciunt, verum id reprehendere videntur, quòd Deum Patrem suum dixerit, vt supra cap. 5.18. Nam cum indignatione hoc quaerunt ex ipso, Vbi est tuus ille Pater? aliquo tamen pacto reprehendunt argumentum, neque eo adducuntur ad credendum: vt videas induratos, si non vno modo, certe alio quoduis argumentum reiicere, neque esse vllum tam firmum in se atque euidens, quod non aliqua ratione eludant. Quàm ingeniosi sunt miseri ad se indurandos & excaecandos! Respondit Iesus. Dominus non directe respondet ad interrogatum, sed perspecta illa eorum obstinata caecitate, eam iis obiicit, q.d. Non nostis
units.tr: They also, in a way, find fault with his now bringing forward testimony on his own behalf. From this you can easily see that they did not believe that he was the light of the world because of any lack of arguments, but because of the obstinate malice of their hearts. For hardened hypocrites pretend that they lack arguments while they refuse the light offered to them. But when they reject every argument, even the very strongest ones drawn from the Scriptures themselves, they sufficiently betray their obstinate malice and their settled purpose of remaining in unbelief. They do not openly reject the testimony of the Father, but they seem to find fault with it because he called God his own Father, as above in chapter 5.18. For they ask him with indignation, "Where is that Father of yours?" Yet in some way they find fault with the argument, and they are not led by it to belief. So you may see that the hardened reject any argument, if not in one way then certainly in another, and that there is none so firm and evident in itself that they do not somehow evade it. How ingenious these wretched people are in hardening and blinding themselves! Jesus answered. The Lord does not answer the question directly, but, seeing their obstinate blindness, he sets it before them, as if to say: "You do not know me, nor do you wish to know me; therefore you do not know the Father either. Why then should I point out either myself or the Father to you?"

units.la: Impii hypocritae malitiae plus quam ignorantiae peccant. me, neque noscere vultis; ideoque neque patrem nostis. Cur igitur vel meipsum vel Patrem vobis indicem? Hic disce, quomodo respondendum sit obstinato hypocritae, tum praesertim cum reiectis & eiusdem omnibus argumentis, prodit ipse suam maliciam. Obiicienda est ei malitia illa & caecitas animi, obiiciendum cor quod resipiscere nescit. Tum ne forte negarent illud sequi, nempe eos non nouisse Patrem, ideo quod Iesum non nouissent, respondet, Sime nosjetis: quasi diceret, haec adeo secum invicem coniuncta sunt, ut si quis me sciat, statim cognoscat Patrem, & e contra. Fundamentum huius rei est, quod Filius sit imago Dei inconspicui, imago, inquam, & essentiae eius: ideoque dicitur splendor gloriae Patris & persona eius, ideoque dicitur character personae ipsius. Quo autem magis conspiciatur a nobis filius, & quasi palpetur, manibus tractetur, cernatur oculis, induit naturam hanc nostram. Deus, inquit, conspicuus factus est in carne. Sed quivis fidelium experientia ipsa istud facis potest deprehendere, verbi causa, dum non sentit charitatem illam Patris diffundi per Spiritum sanctum in corde suo, nisi credat prius in Filium. Fluit enim charitas illa Dei paterna ex filio proxime. Nam in eum, tanquam caput, immensa illa charitas primum omnium tota effunditur. Deinde e capite defluit in singula membra corporis, cum ipso capite per fidem unita. Sic etiam nemo prius sentit infinitam illam Dei potentiam in regenerandis nobis quam credat in Christum. Unde Apostolus, Et quae sit, inquit, excellens illa magnitudo potentiae ipsius in nobis qui credimus, nempe in Christum, quem prius potentia illa sua admirabili ex mortuis excitavit. Eos autem qui obdormierint in Iesu, adducet cum eo, ut alibi dicit.
units.tr: Wicked hypocrites sin more through malice than through ignorance. Learn here how one should answer an obstinate hypocrite, especially when, having rejected all arguments, including his own, he betrays his malice. His malice and the blindness of his mind must be set before him, and the heart that does not know how to repent must be set before him. Then, lest they should perhaps deny the consequence, namely that they did not know the Father because they had not known Jesus, he replies, "If you knew me." It is as if he said: these things are so bound together that whoever knows me at once knows the Father, and conversely. The foundation of this is that the Son is the image of the invisible God: an image, I say, and of his essence; therefore he is called the brightness of the Father's glory and his person, and therefore he is called the character of his person. But the more the Son is seen by us, and as it were touched, handled with the hands and beheld with the eyes, the more he takes on our nature. "God," it says, "was made visible in the flesh." Indeed, any of the faithful can learn this from experience itself, for example when he does not feel that the Father's love is poured into his heart through the Holy Spirit unless he first believes in the Son. For that fatherly love of God flows from the Son immediately. For that immense love is first of all poured out wholly upon him, as upon the head, and from the head it flows down into the individual members of the body, which are united with the head itself through faith. So too no one first feels that infinite power of God in regenerating us unless he believes in Christ. Hence the Apostle says: "and what is that surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe," namely in Christ, "whom he first raised from the dead by his wonderful power." And he will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus, as he says elsewhere.

units.la: Haec verba loquutus est. Hic est effectus quidam, & eventus superioris sermonis Christi, quem obiter inserit Euangelista. Est autem, quod nemo eum apprehenderit. Exaggeratur autem ex loco, in quo tum docebat Iesus, templo nimirum & gazophylacio, qui locus erat in templo augustior, conferendis oblationibus destinatus. Mirum fuit eum non prehensum, in eo praesertim loco, in quo illi plurimum poterant. Ratio subiecta est, Quia nondum venerat hora eius: Nempe praestituta ipsi divina uina prouidentia. Quo loco, nota diuinæ prouidentiæ efficaciam. Seruat suos ab inimicis tutos, etiam cum locus, tempus, cæteraque omnia pro inimicis facere videntur contra Dei seruos. Adeo vt mundus nunquam satis miretur seruari posse eos in tanto discrimine, vt dictum est supra de Hierosolymitanis, qui admirati dixerunt, An non hic est quem student trucidare? At ecce palam loquitur, & nihil ei dicunt. Admirabile est quod cum totis hostes Ecclesiæ in mundo, tot commoditates perdendi eam ipsis oblatæ, Ecclesiam tamen inuitis illisomnibus conseruat. Qua in re profecto maximè cerni potest efficax illa ac potes Dei Prouidentia, in suis conseruandis. Hac etiam experientia animari debemus ad officium faciendum, liberè ac intrepidè loquendum veritatem, etiam in conspectu omnium hostium, etiam ipsis audientibus, etiam in eorum medio nobis consistentibus. Notandum insuper quod hoc argumento, nempe quod palam docuerit in templo eorum, neque tamen tum ipsi eum prehenderint, arguat postea Dominus innocentiam suam, simulque reprehendat Iudæos quod exierint in ipsum tanquam in latronem aliquem. Ex quo illud apparet, ante illam horam postremam, diuina prouidentia eum ita conseruatum fuisse, vt eum ne capere quidem potuerint. Cum autem veniret ea hora, qua deprehendendus fuit ex Dei consilio, & interficiendus pro peccatis nostris, conuictos fuisse conscientiis inimicos quod innocentem prehenderint. Idem quoque accidit Domini seruis: reseruantur ad horam illam à Deo ordinatam, sic vt prehendi & interfici non possint. Vbi verò iam illa hora adest, & iam traduntur in manus inimicorum ex Dei voluntate & ordinatione; tum conuincuntur conscientiis, qui iniustè tractant hos, saltem conuincentur aliquando. Neque enim quisquam adhuc fuit tyrannorum omnium, qui persecuti sunt Dei Ecclesiam, qui non iniuriæ conuictus fuerit, & condemnatus à propria conscientia ante decessum suum ex hac vita.
units.tr: He spoke these words. This is a certain effect and outcome of Christ's preceding discourse, which the Evangelist inserts in passing. What follows is that no one seized him. This is heightened by the place in which Jesus was then teaching, namely the temple and the treasury, which was a more august place in the temple, set apart for the collecting of offerings. It was remarkable that he was not seized, especially in that place where they had the greatest power. The reason is added: because his hour had not yet come, namely the hour appointed for him by the divine providence of the Father. Here note the efficacy of divine providence. It keeps its own people safe from their enemies, even when place, time and all other things seem to work for the enemies against the servants of God. So much so that the world never sufficiently marvels that they can be preserved in so great a danger, as was said above of the Jerusalemites, who, amazed, said: "Is not this the one they seek to kill? And look, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him." It is remarkable that although the enemies of the Church in the world have so many opportunities offered them for destroying it, nevertheless the Church is preserved in spite of all of them. In this matter, certainly, that effective and powerful providence of God in preserving his own can best be seen. We ought also to be encouraged by this experience to do our duty and to speak the truth freely and fearlessly, even in the sight of all enemies, even while they listen, even standing in the midst of them. It should further be noted that by this argument, namely that he had taught openly in their temple and yet they had not then seized him, the Lord afterwards asserts his innocence, and at the same time reproves the Jews because they went out against him as against some robber. From this it appears that before that last hour, divine providence so preserved him that they could not even lay hands on him. But when that hour came, in which he was to be seized according to God's counsel and put to death for our sins, the enemies were convicted in their consciences because they had seized an innocent man. The same thing also happens to the servants of the Lord: they are kept until the hour appointed by God, so that they cannot be seized and killed. But when that hour is at hand, and they are delivered into the hands of their enemies by the will and ordinance of God, then those who treat them unjustly are convicted in their consciences, or at least will be convicted at some time. For there has not yet been any of all the tyrants who persecuted God's Church who was not convicted of wrong and condemned by his own conscience before his departure from this life.

units.la: Ego vado & quæritis me. Quia nihil istos monit exhortatio illa à luce sumpta, ideo nunc comminatur iis lucis remotionem. Ego, inquit, vado. Cum nihil mouet præsentia lucis, tum denuntianda est eius remotio, excontemptu ipsius necessario sequutura. Idque hodierno die nobis in tanto omnium ordinum lucis contemptu faciendum est merito. Ne autem illud videretur illis leuiusculum, addit, Et quaeretis me. Comminatur desiderium sui insequuturum eam lucis remotionem: hoc est futurum eum sensum, eam conscientiam peccati & miseriae, praesertim vero conscientiam tanti contemptus oblatae lucis, idque ex indiciis quibus exercebuntur, ut tum quidem serio cruciandi sint desiderio Christi: non quidem quod id desiderium sit futurum Christi, propter ipsum Christum, quem etiam tum totis animis auersabuntur, aut propter odium peccati, sed propter sensum miseriae quem ferre non poterunt, qui quidem tantus futurus est, ut quaesituri sint sibi liberatorem quemcunque, etiam diabolum ipsum, si fieri posset, ut ab eo liberentur. Huiusmodi enim fuit desiderium Esau qui cum lachrymis benedictionem exquisuit. Huiusmodi fuit desiderium divitis illius gulosi, qui quoque aquae ad refrigerandam linguam suam ab Abrahamo expetuit. Huiusmodi ego desiderium hodierno die possum denuntiare futurum ac superuenturum ingratae huic genti, in cuius medio viuimus, idque ex sensu iudiciorum & peccati conscientia, praesertim tanti contemptus, qui passim conspicitur Euangelij Christi. Nam remota sine luce hac, propter ingratitudinem nostram & contemptum, insequuntur sunt procul dubio iudicia grauissima: sicuti experientia omnium temporum satis docet. Ne vero hoc rursus videatur iis leue aliquod malum, minatur aliud malum ex isto sequuturum; nempe moriendum esse iis in peccato suo, praesertim contemptu isto lucis oblatae atque infidelitate. Ideoque singulariter loquitur, in peccato, inquiens. Nam hoc peccatum erit quasi consumens quidam ignis ad eos in perpetuum exurendos, ad excitandum perpetuum, sed vanum desiderium liberationis. Hoc autem malum rursum praesupponit alterum de quo supra cap. 7.34. nempe eos quaerendo non inuenturos Christum, quem tanto pere desiderabunt, quem cum non inuenient enecabuntur siti illa excitata ex sensu peccati & miseriae grauissimo. Idem ego audeo denuntiare hodierno die aduersus nostros homines, nisi resipuerint tempestiuè. Neverò ab illa morte peccati sperent aliquam futuram vnquam libe-rationem, videntur verbis sequentibus omnem spem euadendi eis praecidere: Quò ego vado non poteritis venire. Hęc ipsa verba loquutus est Dominus discipulis suis infrà 13.13. Sed quid sibi tū voluerit statim post expositūit Petro: Non potes, inquit, nunc me sequi, sequeris autè postea. Quare nunc cōminatur, nunquam fore vt veniant isti obstinati eò loci, quò ille abiturus sit. Quamobrem praecidit illis omnem spem liberationis. Atque hoc est quod aggravat cruciatum illum, qui est apud inferos, nempe desperatio; est enim quasi poenæ pars altera; Erit tū quidem cruciatus animi simul & corporis ineffabilis, qui tamen mitigaretur certo quodam modo, si reliqua esset spes aliqua liberationis, aliquo vnquam tempore futuræ. Sed cùm nulla sit reliqua spes futuræ liberationis, cruciatus inferorum tolerabiles fiunt, accedente nimirum ad cruciatum desperatione. De hoc voluit admoneri istis tum Dominus. De hoc quoque admonendi sunt obstinati isti ac contemptores nostri temporis.
units.tr: I go away, and you will seek me. Because that exhortation, drawn from the light, has not moved them, he now threatens them with the removal of the light. I go away, he says. When the presence of the light does not move them, then its removal must be announced, which will necessarily follow from their contempt for it. And in our day, in the face of so great a contempt for the light among all orders of men, this ought rightly to be done. Lest this should seem to them a trifling matter, he adds, And you will seek me. He threatens that a longing for him will follow that removal of the light: that is, there will come upon them a sense and awareness of sin and misery, and above all an awareness of their great contempt for the light offered to them, and this by the signs by which they will be exercised, so that they will indeed be seriously tormented by a longing for Christ. Not indeed that this longing will be for Christ himself, whom even then they will reject with their whole souls, nor out of hatred of sin, but because of the sense of misery which they will be unable to bear. And this will be so great that they will seek any deliverer whatever, even the devil himself, if it were possible, so that they might be freed from it.
