Such was the longing of Esau, who with tears sought the blessing. Such was the longing of that greedy rich man, who also asked Abraham for water to cool his tongue. Such a longing, I may announce today, will come upon and overtake this ungrateful people in whose midst we live, and it will come from a sense of judgments and an awareness of sin, especially of such contempt as is everywhere seen toward the Gospel of Christ. For when this light is removed, because of our ingratitude and contempt, the most grievous judgments will undoubtedly follow, as the experience of all ages sufficiently teaches. Lest this again should seem to them some slight evil, he threatens another evil that will follow from it: namely that they must die in their sin, especially in this contempt for the light offered and in unbelief. Therefore he speaks in the singular, in sin. For this sin will be like a consuming fire to burn them up forever, to stir up a perpetual but vain longing for deliverance. This evil, moreover, presupposes another, which is spoken of above in chapter 7, verse 34: namely, that in seeking they will not find Christ, whom they will so greatly desire; and since they will not find him, they will be destroyed by that thirst which is kindled by a most grievous sense of sin and misery. I dare to announce the same thing today against our own people, unless they repent in good time. And lest they hope for any future deliverance from that death of sin, the following words seem to cut off every hope of escape from them: Where I go, you cannot come. The Lord spoke these very words to his disciples below, at chapter 13, verse 33. But what he meant by them he explained immediately afterwards to Peter: You cannot follow me now, but you shall follow afterwards. Therefore he now threatens that these obstinate men will never come to the place whither he is going. Wherefore he cuts off from them every hope of deliverance. And this is what makes more severe that torment which is in hell, namely despair; for it is as it were the second part of the punishment. There will indeed be a torment of soul and body together, unspeakable, which would nevertheless be mitigated in a certain way if some hope of deliverance remained, to come at some time. But since no hope of future deliverance remains, the torments of hell become tolerable only when despair is added to the torment. The Lord wished to warn them of this at that time, and these obstinate despisers of our own age must also be warned of it.

units.la: 22 Dicebant ergo Iudæi, Num trucidabit seipsum, qui dicat, Quò ego vado, vos non potestis venire?
units.tr: 22 Then the Jews said, "Will he kill himself, since he says, 'Where I go, you cannot come'?"

units.la: 23 Tunc dixit eis, Vos ex locis infernis estis, ego sum ex supernis: Vos ex hoc mundo estis, ego non sum ex hoc mundo.
units.tr: 23 And he said to them, "You are from beneath; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world."

units.la: 24 Ideo vobis dixi, vos morituros in peccatis vestris. Nam nisi crediderit is me eum esse, moriemini in peccatis vestris.
units.tr: 24 "Therefore I told you that you will die in your sins. For unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins."

units.la: HÆc verba per sarcasmum rhetoricum sunt dicta. Acerba enim irrisio est hoc loco: q.d. dicit iste quò vadat ipse, nos nō posse eò peruenire; quid sibi vult hoc? An ipse manum iniiciet, mortémque sibi consciscet. Quod si eò vadat, profectò fatemur nos lubenter, atque vt conceditimus, non posse eò peruenire nos quò ipse abeat; neque enim placet. Magna profectò est haec proteruia, non absimilis proteruiæ nostrorum hominū hodiernæ, qui irridènt omnes comminationes iudicio-rum Dei. Quamquam risus iste nonnunquam sardonius est, & interea stimulètur ipsis conscientia: nam alioqui cur nonnunquam tantopere fremunt, atque adeo blas-phemi sunt in seruos Dei? necesse est profecto ex con-scientia mala & perturbata ista proficiscantur. Rident tamen & miseram conscientiam omnibus modis falle-re, ac consopitam reddere nituntur. Tum dixit eis. Domi-nus suo hoc responso descendit penitus in animos eo-rum, videtque corruptionem ibi insitam, ex qua promanauit vox illa eorum tam falsa atque amara. Visam au-tem à se & deprehensam, in lucem producit, exponitque eam ipsis miseris conspiciendam. Nam mire cæcutimus ipsi in natura nostra perpendenda. Facit autem hoc com-paratè, simul enim demonstrat seipsum, unde fit & qua-lis: ut per contrariam ipsius cælestem illam naturam vi-deant magis turpitudinem suam, eamque (si fieri posset) ad exemplum naturæ ipsius cælestis corrigant. Sed ver-ba textus sunt: Vos ex locis infernis estis. Tum quæ sequun-tur manifestiora reddunt præcedentia verba: Vos ex hoc mundo estis. q.d. Vos terreni toti ac mundani estis, nihil-dum mutati, sed adhuc oppleti mundanis affectibus & naturæ corruptione. Præsertim autem designat in ipsis cæcitatem ac stupiditatem in rebus cælestibus videndis ac sentiendis: qualem paulò ante ipsi prodiderunt, cùm de cælo loquens diceret Dominus, quò ego vado, vos non potestis venire, sup. vers. 21. Verùm cum hac ignorantia ac stupiditate notat coniunctam malitiam & acerbitatem animi, qualem etiam suo illo inter se sermone collato, prodiderunt supra vers. 22. Nam hoc est ingenium impiorum, malitiosè feruntur in ea quæ ignorant, quæ neque vident, neque sentiunt. Non est enim ignorantia aliqua rerum cælestium, quæ non sociam habeat malitiam aliquam: nemo est apud nos hodie, qui non ex dictis nostrorum hominum concuntuliosis in Dei seruos ac in Deum ipsum blasphemis, ex factis sacrilegis, impiis, impuris, non videat quonam sint ipsi animo, quàm malè affecti, non videat nondum exemptos eos ex illa corruptione, in qua concepti ac nati sunt: quin potius eam auctam esse supra modum. Annon igitur qui ad hoc
units.tr: These words were spoken with a rhetorical sarcasm. The mockery here is bitter. The sense is: "This man says where he is going, and that we cannot get there. What does he mean by that? Will he lay hands on himself and kill himself?" But if he means he is going there, we freely admit, and as we concede, that we cannot reach the place he goes to, and we have no wish to. This is surely great insolence, not unlike the insolence of our own people today, who laugh at all the threats of God's judgments. Yet this laughter is sometimes sardonic, and their consciences are meanwhile stung. Otherwise, why do they sometimes rage so fiercely and even blaspheme against the servants of God? Such behaviour must certainly come from a guilty and troubled conscience. Still, they laugh and strive in every way to deceive their wretched conscience and to lull it to sleep. Then he said to them. By this answer the Lord goes deep into their minds. He sees the corruption implanted there, from which their words, so false and bitter, have come forth. He brings that corruption, once seen and detected by himself, into the light, and sets it out for the wretched men themselves to behold. For we are strangely blind ourselves when it comes to weighing our own nature. He does this by comparison, for at the same time he shows himself, whence he comes and what he is like, so that by contrast with his heavenly nature they may see more clearly their own baseness, and, if it were possible, correct it by the pattern of that heavenly nature. But the words of the text are: "You are from beneath." Then what follows makes the preceding words plainer: "You are of this world." That is to say: "You are wholly earthly and worldly, not yet changed, but still overwhelmed by worldly affections and the corruption of nature." Above all, he marks in them blindness and dullness in seeing and perceiving heavenly things, such as they had just shown when the Lord, speaking of heaven, said, "Where I go, you cannot come," see above, verse 21. Yet with this ignorance and dullness he also notes the malice and bitterness of mind that goes with it, such as they showed in the discussion they had among themselves, above, verse 22. For this is the character of the wicked: they rush maliciously against the things they do not know, do not see, and do not feel. There is no ignorance of heavenly things that does not have some malice as its companion. Today there is no one among us who does not see, from the words of our own people full of slander against the servants of God and blasphemy against God himself, and from their sacrilegious, impious and impure deeds, what state of mind they are in and how ill-disposed they are. They are not yet freed from that corruption in which they were conceived and born, but rather it has grown beyond measure. Therefore, should not those who are sent for this purpose...

units.la: Nec tamen quiete agunt.
units.tr: Yet they do not act quietly.

units.la: Christicorum rectio. hoc missi sunt à Domino, vt eruant in lucem perditam istam hominum naturam, & eam vel aboleant in hominum ipsorum salutem, vel si ipsi miseri nolint eam aboleri, deteriorem eam faciant ac indurent magis, in Dei gloriam, vt ipse etiam in indurationE eorum glorificetur: (nam glorificatur Deus in iusta cofusione omnis creaturæ) an, inquam, his tacendum est, an non potius Christi exemplo tenentur corda hominum excutere, ac malitiam illam atque prauitatem deprehendere & reprehendere? Fremat licet interea mundus, nisi ipsi proditores & salutis humanæ & gloriæ diuinæ haberi velint. Ideo vobis dixi. Ex demonstrata illis cordis eorum demus Dominum nihil deterreri à comminationibus, licet comminationes suas aduersarij irrideant & contemptui habeant: verùm eo magis vnam eandémque comminationem ingeminare. Neque enim oportet Dei Ministros abstinere à denuntiationibus, ideo quod videant se nihil proficere apud stupidum hunc & obduratum mundum, quódque videant non alium earum fructum produci in hominibus impiis, quàm acerbitatem, iram, blasphemiam, irrisionem denique. In his enim omnibus materia est duplicandarum minarum, & iudiciorum grauius denuntiandorum: neque etiam hodierno die nobis abstinendum est à minis, & à denuntiando iudicia aduersus eos, qui hæc ipsa ludibrio habent, quòd homines id ægrè ferant vel irrideant, sed eò magis pergendum in denuntiationibus, tantisperdum vel resipiant homines, vel iusto Dei iudicio pereant. Nam nisi audieritis. Mitigatio quædam sententiæ superioris, per exceptionem fidei, cum qua intelligeresipiscetiam. Dominus enim non ita irascitur vt lenitatis ac misericordiæ interea obliuiscatur, neque sic constringit eos vinculis illis mortis æternæ, vt euasionem nullam demonstret iis, si modò velint effugere, vt si perire malint pereundum illis sit ob contemptum gratiæ & misericordiæ, tam clementer oblatæ. Præterea non aliam euasionem, aliud effugium eis demonstrat quàm se: Nisi crediderItis, inquit, me eum esse: se, inquam, quem tantope-
units.tr: Christian rectitude. They have been sent by the Lord for this: to bring into the light that lost nature of men, and either to abolish it for the salvation of men themselves, or, if those wretched men are unwilling for it to be abolished, to make it worse and harden it further, to the glory of God, so that God may also be glorified in their hardening (for God is glorified in the just confusion of every creature). Should such men, I say, keep silent? Or are they not rather bound, by Christ's example, to shake men's hearts and to detect and rebuke that malice and perversity? Let the world rage meanwhile, unless they wish to be regarded as betrayers both of human salvation and of the glory of God. Therefore I have said to you. From what has been shown of their hearts, let us learn that the Lord is not deterred at all by threats, even when his adversaries mock his threats and hold them in contempt. Rather, he repeats the one and same threat all the more. For the ministers of God ought not to refrain from denouncing sin because they see that they achieve nothing before this stupid and hardened world, and because they see that no other fruit from their threats is produced in impious men than bitterness, anger, blasphemy, and finally mockery. For all these things are the very matter for doubling the threats and for pronouncing heavier judgments. Nor, even in our own day, should we refrain from threats and from announcing judgments against those who make a mockery of these very things, and who either take them badly or laugh at them. Rather we must press on all the more with threats, until men either come to their senses or perish by the just judgment of God. For unless you believe. A certain softening of the previous sentence comes through the exception of faith, with which one understands repentance too. For the Lord is not so angry that he forgets gentleness and mercy in the meantime, nor does he bind them so tightly with those chains of eternal death that he shows them no way of escape, if only they are willing to flee. Otherwise, should they prefer to perish, they would perish through contempt of grace and mercy offered so graciously. Moreover, he shows them no other escape or refuge than himself: "Unless you believe," he says, "that I am he," namely himself, I say, whom they had so greatly despised.

units.la: KK re contempserunt. Conclusi homines sub peccato & damnatione vellent quidem elabi atque effugere, sed effugium illud unicum in Christo natura aduersantur atque despiciunt. Sed vt tum Christus restrinxit istos ad hoc vnicum effugium, adeo vt si nolint eo confugere, velint nolint perituri sint.
units.tr: Men shut up under sin and condemnation would indeed like to slip away and escape, but they are hostile to and despise the one refuge offered in Christ. But as Christ then confined them to this one refuge, so that if they are unwilling to flee to it, whether they like it or not, they will perish.

units.la: 25 Dixerunt ergo ei, Tu quis es? Tum dixit eis Iesus, Id quod a principio dico vobis.
units.tr: 25 Then they said to him, "Who are you?" Jesus said to them, "The very thing I have been telling you from the beginning."

units.la: 26 Multa habeo quae de vobis loquar ac iudicem: sed qui misit me verax est, & ego quae audiui ab eo, haec loquor mundo.
units.tr: 26 I have many things to say and to judge concerning you; but he who sent me is true, and what I heard from him, these things I speak to the world.

units.la: 27 Non cognouerunt eum de Patre sibi haec dicere.
units.tr: 27 They did not understand that he was speaking to them about the Father.

units.la: ETHoc quoque responsum ex fastidio quodam & contemptu simul cum irrisione profectum est. Irriserunt antea iudicium denuntiatum, nunc irridentes gratiam illam euadendi ex morte per fidem in Christum oblatam. Contemptores iudiciorum Dei pariter contemptores sunt gratiae: fieri enim non potest, quicquid demum de fide Christi & de gratia Dei garriant homines isti, qui irridٍent comminationes iudiciorum ex verbo Dei factas, pariter irrideant & contemnant Christum, & in ipso gratiam Dei. Qui enim ludibrio habet inferos, an hic, quaeso, serio cogitat coelos esse? Nequaquam. Tum dixit eis Iesus. Respondet Dominus, non quidem totidem verbis se Christum illum esse & Dei Filium: verum quod reipsa idem est. Ita enim respondet, vt obscura sit reprehensio ignorantiae eorum ac malitiae, quod cum iam inde ab initio dixisset eis quinam ipse esset, nolunt tamen eum cognoscere & agnoscere. Quotquot nunc demum quaerunt quis sit Christus, postquam iam de eo, tam saepe, tam multa dicta sint ac praedicata; profecto si iis respondendum sit de Christo, non sine reprehensione & obiurgatione respondendum est. Vides deinde in eodem isto responso, quanta extiterit Christi constantia in se confitendo. Idem de se perpetuo ab initio ipse confessus est, non aliud hodie, aliud cras de se professus est, sed vnum idémque omni loco & tempore. Vt & prædi-dicatores verbi ipsius, Domini sui exemplo discant, idem de se sentiendum & loquendum perpetuò, neque alium Christum hodie prædicandum, alium cras, aliud Euangelium hodie, aliud cras. Filius Dei Iesus Christus qui inter vos per nos prædicatus est, non fuit etiam & non, sed fuit etiam in ipso. Ex qua Christi constantia immutabili arguit Apostolus, oportere Christianorum hominum & verba & vitam totam constantem esse & invariabilem, non autem leuem ac mobilem.
units.tr: This answer also came from a kind of disdain together with mockery. They had mocked the judgment announced; now, mocking, they mock the grace of escaping death through faith in Christ that is offered. Despisers of God's judgments are equally despisers of grace. For whatever those men may chatter about the faith of Christ and the grace of God, it cannot be that those who mock the threats of judgments made from the Word of God should at the same time not mock and despise Christ and, in him, the grace of God. For he who makes a mockery of hell, does he, I ask, seriously think that heaven exists? By no means. Then Jesus said to them. The Lord answers, not indeed in so many words that he is that Christ and the Son of God, but in what amounts to the same thing. He answers in such a way that the rebuke of their ignorance and malice is veiled, because although he had already told them from the start who he was, they still refuse to know and acknowledge him. Whoever now asks who Christ is, after so much has been said and proclaimed about him so often and at such length, surely if they are to be answered about Christ, they must be answered not without rebuke and reproof. Next, see in this same answer how great Christ's steadfastness was in confessing himself. He always professed about himself from the beginning the same thing: he did not declare one thing today and another tomorrow, but one and the same thing in every place and at every time. So that the preachers of his very word may learn from the example of their Lord to think and speak about him in the same way always, and not to preach one Christ today and another tomorrow, or one gospel today and another tomorrow. The Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, was not yes and no, but in him was yes (2 Cor. 1). From this unchanging steadfastness of Christ the Apostle argues that the words and the whole life of Christians ought to be steadfast and unchanging, not light and fickle.

units.la: Multa habeo. Hactenus responsio fuit cum reprehensione. Nunc gravius insuper respondet, ac citat quasi coram Dei tribunali, ac si dicat: Multarum rerum vobis mihi reddenda est ratio. Neque quidem aliter fieri potuit, cum fidem in ipsum sint aspernati quæ vel sola delet omnia debita. Infidelium omnium peccata manent non deleta etiam maxima, etiam minima, ne vno quidem dempto, & Dei oculis perpetuò obiecta sunt. Quod profecto si miseri ipsi persentiscerent, quantis conscientiæ horroribus agitarentur. Sed ita consopitus est mundus iste, ut non sentiat Deum irato vultu intueri omnia ipsius peccata. Et sicut loquitur Apostolus, Palam esse iram Dei adversus omnem hominum impietatem & iniustitiam. Etsi interea temporis fiat nonnunquam, ut velint nolint ipsi, aliquo conscientiæ terrore cocutiantur, sed qui mox euanescit. Sed quia me misit. q. d. Sed nunc supersedeo ratione istarum rerum à vobis exigere, contentus Patris mei iudicio, qui verax est in verbo suo omni, & veritatem suam aduersus contemptores & irrisores quoscunque asseret. Tum si forte dicerent: Quid hoc te quod veritatem suam asseret? tempestiuè huic occurrit; Et ego quæ audiui ab eo hæc loquor mundo. q. d. Ego nō aliud loquar quàm veritatem eius, vel, Hæc est ipsa veritas eius quam ego loquor. Quamobrem hanc veritatem asseret. Vide igitur, cum Deus necessariò sit assertor veritatis suæ contemptæ, cuiuscunque demum ministerio utatur in ea prædicanda, debet id profecto efficere, ne nimium nos moueant isti verbi Diuini contemptores, siue Papistæ sint, qui vel detorquent suo exitio, vel eludunt aliquo modo Dei verbum; siue etiam alij, qui tam vita quàm verbo Dei illam vocem in ore ministrorum ipsius contemnunt: Hæc enim eius iudicio permittenda sunt qui suo tempore hunc contemptum graviter vleiscetur. Sed in hoc nobis laborandum, vt persuasum apud nos habeamus nos ab ipso missos esse, & non nisi veritatem ipsius nos loqui atque prædicare; quorum vtrumque Christus hic de se pronuntiat, Non cognouerunt. Hic videtur effectus esse verborum quæ proximè loquuntur est Dominus: ignorant enim de Patre loqui, cum Patrem non expresse nominarit, sed ex effecto suo tantum eum subindicarit: Qui misit me, inquiens, Ex hac eorum ignorantia discendum est, eos nihil permotos fuisse illa Christi oratione, citantis quasi eos, & sistentis coram tribunali Dei. Nihil videmus in hoc miserò populo, per totum hunc sermonem quem confert cum iis Christus, nisi nunc malitiam cordis, nunc stuporem, nunc ignorantiam: vt sit hoc exemplum eorum formidabile toti posteritati & sæculis omnibus ventu-tis, vt discant eorum exemplo metuere deserantur à Deo, etiam interea dum ipsis loquitur per servos suos. Nam nisi etiam interea cum verbo suo coniungat efficacem Spiritus sui, profecto futurum est, vt prodamus non minorem sive malitiam, sive ignorantiam, quàm illi ipsi Iudæi, quorum tam horribile exemplum ante oculos nostros positum habemus. Debemus autem magni beneficij loco ducere, si inter prædicandum Christum sentiamus aperiri nobis oculos mentis, ad hoc vt intelligamus, quæ ex verbo Dei dicuntur, & aperiri corda, vt quæ intelleximus aliquo certè modo, etiam penitus animo sentiamus.
units.tr: I have many things. So far the answer has been given with rebuke. Now he answers more severely and summons them, as if before the tribunal of God, as though to say: you must render me an account of many things. Nor could it have been otherwise, since they have spurned faith in him, which alone wipes out all debts. The sins of all unbelievers remain undeleted, the greatest and the least alike, not one of them removed, and they are constantly set before the eyes of God. Indeed, if these wretched men actually perceived this, what horrors of conscience they would be troubled by. But this world is so lulled to sleep that it does not feel God looking upon all its sins with an angry countenance. As the Apostle says, the wrath of God is revealed against all the ungodliness and unrighteousness of men. Meanwhile it sometimes happens that, whether they will or not, they are shaken by some terror of conscience, but this soon vanishes. But because he sent me. That is: now I forbear to demand from you an account of these things, content with the judgement of my Father, who is true in all his word and asserts his truth against all contemners and mockers whatsoever. Then, if perhaps they should say, "What does it matter to you that he asserts his truth?", he meets this opportunely: And the things which I heard from him, these I speak to the world. That is: I will say nothing other than his truth, or, this is his very truth which I speak. Therefore he asserts this truth. Consider, then: since God is necessarily the asserter of his own truth when it is despised, whatever ministry he uses in preaching it, he must surely bring it about that we are not too much moved by those contemners of the divine Word, whether they are Papists, who either twist the Word of God to their own destruction or in some way mock it, or others who despise that voice of God in the mouth of his ministers, both by their lives and by their words. For these matters are to be left to his judgement, who in his time will severely avenge this contempt. But our labour must be this: to be persuaded among ourselves that we have been sent by him, and that we speak and preach nothing but his truth. Christ pronounces both of these concerning himself here. They did not know. This seems to be the effect of the words the Lord spoke just before: they did not know that he was speaking of the Father, since he had not expressly named the Father but had only hinted at him through his effect, saying, "he who sent me." From this ignorance of theirs we must learn that they were not moved at all by that speech of Christ, which summoned them as it were and set them before the tribunal of God. In this wretched people, throughout the whole discourse Christ holds with them, we see nothing but malice of heart, now stupor, now ignorance. Their example is thus to be a dreadful warning to all posterity and to all the ages to come, so that they may learn from it to fear being forsaken by God even while he speaks to them through his servants. For unless he also joins the effectual power of his Spirit to his word, it will certainly come about that we show no less malice or ignorance than those very Jews, whose most horrible example we have set before our eyes. We ought, moreover, to count it a great benefit if, while Christ is being preached, we feel the eyes of our mind opened, so that we understand what is said from the Word of God, and our hearts opened, so that what we have understood in some measure we may also feel deeply in our souls.

units.la: 28 Dixit ergo eis Iesus, Quum fuerit is Filium hominis, tunc agnoscetis me eum esse, & à me ipso nihil facere, sed prout docuit me Pater hæc loqui.
units.tr: 28 Jesus therefore said to them: When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing of myself, but speak these things as the Father has taught me.

units.la: 29 Nam qui misit me, mecum est, non reliquit me solum Pater, quia ego quæ placita sunt ei facio semper.
units.tr: 29 For he who sent me is with me; the Father has not left me alone, because I always do the things that please him.

units.la: 30 Hæc illo loquente multi crediderunt in eum.
units.tr: 30 While he was saying these things, many believed in him.

units.la: Citauit eos proximè, vt sese sisterent coram tribunali Dei: Effectus autem citationis eius proximo versu fuit; Non cognouerunt eum de Patre ipsis loqui. Cum autem fuit, loquutus est quidem de eo qui ipsum misit, atque illud ipsi audiuerunt, sed interea non cognouerunt eum loqui de Patre mittente, neque etiam id vi-dere aut cognoscere voluerunt. Ideóque Christus hoc versu denuntiat fore tandem, vt cognoscant & agnoscant, velint nolint, ipsum à Patre missum: hoc enim est quod ait, Agnoscetis me eum esse: Fore etiam vt agnoscant ipsum nihil facere à seipso, hoc est, cuius non sit author Pater, qui misit ipsum, sed omnia loqui, & omnia facere Patre suo authore. Hanc sententiam de Filio habuimus semel atque iterum supra cap. 5. primum versu 19. Non potest Filius à semetipso operari: deinde versu 30. Non possum ego à meipso facere quicquam. Nam vt Pater est fons Deitatis, ita in omnibus his actionibus externis, quæ versantur circa creaturas, idem primus fons est & author in agendo, non quidem dignitate primus, sed ordine. Verum hac de re satis multa diximus eo in loco. Videmus hic primùm, neminem esse ex improbis tam induratum adversum omnem gloriæ Christi aspectum, quin aliquando tandem cogendus sit videre eum ac præsentem intueri. Neque enim is stupor tantus est nunc, quin aliquando excutiendus sit, neque ita conniuent oculis impij, quin aliquando aperiendi sint, adeo vt cogendi sint intueri eum, à quo tantopere & oculis & animis abhorrent. Nam tum quidem non minus dolebunt propter aspectum Christi, quàm qui oculos obiectos habet igni ardenti ac comburenti. Sed dices, annon ingens lætitia est ex aspectu Christi & gloriæ ipsius? Respondeo, si hoc quidem tempestiuè fiat, & dum tempus est gratiæ, verum est. At si illud tempus gratiæ iam contemptum sit simul & elapsum, tum seriùs quidem, & non nisi cum doloris sensu intolerabili Dominum intuebuntur. Sed hoc clarius erit, si viderimus tempus illud quo demum elapso, cognoscent tandem eum missum esse à Patre. Nempe, inquit, Postquam extuleritis Filium hominis. Hoc est, postquam sublatum in crucem eum interfecerutis, tum quidem agnoscetis eum missum à
units.tr: He summoned them just before, to present themselves before the tribunal of God; the effect of this summons is stated in the next verse: "They did not know that he was speaking to them of the Father." Yet although he did speak of the one who sent him, and they heard it, they did not recognise that he was speaking of the Father who sent him, nor were they willing to see or perceive it. Therefore Christ declares in this verse that at last they will come to know and acknowledge, whether they will or not, that he was sent by the Father: this is what he means by "you will know that I am he." They will also come to acknowledge that he does nothing of himself, that is, that the Father who sent him is not the author of what he does, but that he speaks and does everything with his Father as author. We had this statement about the Son once and again above, in chapter 5: first in verse 19, "the Son can do nothing of himself," and then in verse 30, "I can of myself do nothing." For just as the Father is the fount of the Godhead, so in all these external actions which concern creatures, the same first fount and author is in acting; first not in dignity but in order. But we have said enough on this matter in that place. Here we see first that there is no one among the wicked so hardened against every sight of Christ's glory that he will not at some time be compelled to see it and to look upon him as present. For that stupor is not so great now that it will never be shaken off, nor do the ungodly close their eyes so firmly that they will never be opened, so that they will be compelled to look upon him from whom they so greatly turn away both in eyes and in minds. For then they will grieve no less at the sight of Christ than one who has his eyes set upon burning and scorching fire. But you will say: is there not great joy in the sight of Christ and of his glory? I answer: if this happens in due time, while there is still the time of grace, it is true. But if that time of grace has already been despised and has passed, then they will look upon the Lord too late, and only with an intolerable sense of grief. This will be clearer if we consider that time, when at last, after it has passed, they will come to know that he was sent from the Father. Namely, he says, "after you have lifted up the Son of Man": that is, after you have raised him on the cross and put him to death, then indeed you will acknowledge that he was sent by the Father, and that he is the Messiah, in his glorious resurrection, in his ascension into heaven, and continually from that time until the day when you see him appear in glory at the last judgement. Note, then, at what time the wicked and obstinate will at last behold Christ's glory: not before they have persecuted him, and then they will be compelled to see him with the greatest admiration and amazement, and with an unspeakable anguish of conscience, when they see that he whom they treated with such unworthy indignities in this life has been appointed their judge. No one fails to bear it grievously if the one he has killed becomes his judge. What I say of Christ the Head is true also of his body, the Church. For those persecutors will not see the glory that belongs to the members of Christ and the Church before they have persecuted them. Then they will be compelled to behold it and her glory, when they see her sitting with Christ the judge on that day to judge the world, and even those very enemies and persecutors whom they most bitterly held in this life. "Do you not know," says the Apostle, "that the saints will judge the world?" Therefore blessed are those to whom it has been given to behold in due time the glory of the Church, however lowly she now appears. For even now she has a heavenly glory. Hence in Daniel the Jewish Church, grievously afflicted by Antiochus, is called "the very glory" [Dan. 8 / 11, as printed in the author's sense], and in John: "Beloved, now we are the sons of God."

units.la: Iudicii divini efficacia.
units.tr: The efficacy of divine judgment

units.la: Gloriæ Christi tempestiuus aspectus quid efficiat. Patre, & Messiam esse in gloriosa ipsius resurrectione, & in coelos ascensione, atque perpetuo ab eo tempore ad illud usque tempus, quo videritis eum apparere in ultimo illo iudicio cum gloria. Nota igitur quo demum tempore conspiciant improbi ac obstinati Christi gloriam, nempe non prius quam ipsum persequuti fuerint, ac tum quidem cogentur eum videre cum admiratione maxima ac stupore; & cum dolore conscientiae ineffabili, cum videbunt iudicem sibi constitui eum, quem tam indignis modis tractarunt in vita ista. Nemo est qui non id ferat aegre, si quem interfecit eum habeat sibi iudicem. Quod de Christo capite loquor, id de corpore ipsius Ecclesia verum est: non enim prius videbunt persequutores illi gloriam illam, quae est membrorum Christi & Ecclesiae, quam cum fuerint eam persecuti. Tum autem cogentur eam eiusque gloriam intueri, cum videbunt ipsam sedere cum Christo iudice illo die ad iudicandum mundum, adeoque eos ipsos quos infensissimos habuerunt in hac vita hostes & persequutores. An ignoratis, inquit Apostolus, sanctos mundum iudicaturos? Quare beati sunt quibus datum est tempestiue inspicere gloriam Ecclesiae, quantumuis nunc in speciem abiectae. Nam etiam nunc caelestis quaedam est ipsius gloria. Ideoque apud Danielem etiam afflicta grauissime ab Antiocho Iudaica Ecclesia appellatur Decus ipsum: & apud Iohannem, Charissimi, nunc Filij Dei sumus.
units.tr: What the timely sight of Christ's glory brings about. He was sent by the Father and is the Messiah, as shown in his glorious resurrection, his ascension into heaven, and continually from that time until that day when you will see him appear in glory at the last judgment. Note, then, at what time the wicked and obstinate will finally behold the glory of Christ: not before they have persecuted him, and then they will be compelled to see him with the greatest wonder and amazement, and with an indescribable anguish of conscience, when they see that the one whom they treated so shamefully in this life has been appointed their judge. Anyone would take it badly if the man he had killed became his judge. What I say of Christ the head is true of his body, the Church. Those persecutors will not see that glory, which belongs to the members of Christ and the Church, before they have persecuted it. But then they will be forced to look upon it and its glory, when they see it sitting with Christ the judge on that day to judge the world, and therefore those very enemies and persecutors whom they had as their most bitter foes in this life. "Do you not know," says the Apostle, "that the saints will judge the world?" (1 Cor. 6.) Therefore blessed are those to whom it has been granted to see the glory of the Church in good time, however much it now appears abject. For even now it has a certain heavenly glory. Hence in Daniel the Jewish Church, grievously afflicted by Antiochus, is even called Glory itself; and in John: Beloved, now we are the sons of God.

units.la: Aperit deinde Christus eis causam eius quod dixit proximè, nēpe se nihil ex seipso facere, sed prout ipsum Pater qui misit eum, docuit haec loqui & facere. Id autem ideo facit, ut si fieri possit, adhuc videant stupidi praesentem illam ipsius gloriam tempestiue. Causa autem ac fundamentum est ab illa vnione ac coniunctione Patris & Filij incomprehensibili, in vna eademque essentia. Pater mecum est, inquit, neque me solum reliquit. Nota igitur causam omnium operum, quae trium personarum deitatis communia sunt, in mundo hoc creando & administrando, nempe vnionem illam atque ineffabilem coniunctionem trium personarum in vna eademque deitatis essentia. Vt autem hoc certo aliquo modo ad nos ipsi accommodemus, causa cur Deus operetur nobiscum aliquid, vel nos cum Deo vnà operemur, essinque authorem habeamus omnium actionum nostrarum, causa, inquam, haec est: quòd eum habeamus nobis praesentem per Christum, & in illa cum Christo Que si non sit, profectò nos soli ac sine Deo agemus omnia, & male agemus, quantumuis in speciem pulchrae videatur esse actiones nostrae. Vt autem hoc sedulò faciedum est omnibus in omni actione, vt Deum praesentem sibi habeant, ac ducem actionum suarum: ita ei qui statuit loqui in nomine ipsius, videndum est imprimis, vt eum habeat corde suo praesentem; vt ex eius ore quasi excipiatque dicturus sit omnia, loquaturque ex sensu & fide. Secus profectò solus relinquetur ac solus loquetur.
units.tr: Christ then explains to them the reason for what he said just before, namely that he does nothing of himself, but speaks and does these things as the Father who sent him has taught him. He does this so that, if it were possible, these dull men might still in time see his present glory. The cause and foundation of this is that incomprehensible union and conjunction of the Father and the Son in one and the same essence. The Father is with me, he says, and has not left me alone. Note, then, the cause of all the works that are common to the three persons of the Godhead in creating and governing this world: namely, that ineffable union and conjunction of the three persons in the one essence of the Godhead. To apply this to ourselves in some certain way: the reason why God works something in us, or we work together with God, and why we have God as the author of all our actions, is, I say, this: that we have him present with us through Christ, and in that [fellowship] with Christ. Which, if it is not there, we shall certainly act alone and without God, and we shall act badly, however fine our actions may appear. Just as everyone must take care in every action to have God present to them and as the guide of their actions, so the one who has determined to speak in his name must above all take care to have him present in his heart, so that he is about to say everything as if he received it from his mouth, and speaks from understanding and faith. Otherwise he will certainly be left alone and will speak alone.

units.la: Atque haec quidem causa est erroris & haeresis, quoties homines contempta Dei praesentia sibi confisi ac ingenio suo, de rebus diuinis ac caelestibus audent loqui. Quia ego quae placita sunt. Haec ratio est cur Deum Patrem perpetuò praesentem habeat, ex ipsius summa erga Patrem suum obedientia, qua fit vt mirum in modum Patri placeat. Causa praesentiae Patris cum Filio suo altior quaedam est, nempe naturae vnius eiusdemque vnio. Verum accommodauit se Dominus ad captum & aedificationem eorum quos tunc alloquebatur. Hoc enim argumento praesentiae, ab obedientia sumpto, excitari potuerunt ipsi ad obediendum Deo similiter, vt & ipsi per obedientiam suam fruerentur Dei praesentia. Notandum autem hic est, obedientiam hanc Christi esse non tantum quatenus est homo, sed vt qua Filius est. Nam cùm esset in forma Dei, non duxit rapinam parem esse cum Deo: sed ipsa se exinaniuit accepta serui forma. Loquitur autem eo loco de ipso Dei Filio, vel Deo in persona Filij, cuius obedientia oritur ex voluntate quidem sua erga Patrem suum mirifica.
units.tr: This is indeed the cause of error and heresy whenever men, despising the presence of God, trust in themselves and their own wit and dare to speak of divine and heavenly things. For I always do the things that please him. This is the reason why he always has the Father present, from the Son's supreme obedience towards his Father, by which he wonderfully pleases the Father. The cause of the Father's presence with his Son is more profound, namely the union of one and the same nature. But the Lord adapted himself to the capacity and edification of those whom he was then addressing. For by this argument of presence, drawn from obedience, they could be roused likewise to obey God, so that they too, through their obedience, might enjoy the presence of God. It must be noted here that this obedience of Christ belongs not only to him as man, but as he is the Son. For though he was in the form of God, he did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. He is speaking there of the Son of God himself, or of God in the person of the Son, whose obedience arises from his own wonderful will towards his Father.

units.la: Vt autem nos hoc ad nos ipsi applicemus aliquo pacto; obedientia est, eáque ex Dei ipsius praescripta quae conseruat nobis, ac tuetur illam Dei praesentiam quae est nobiscum. Placemus enim Deo vel maximè obedientia illa qua omnia facimus ex voluntate eius, & omnia dirigimus ad gloriam eius. Sed cùm tam perfecta à nobis haberi non possit, perpetuò confugiendum est ad perfectam illam Christi obedientiam, in qua Deus perfectè conquiescit, vt nos eum in illa Christi obedientia nobis præsentem habeamus perpetuò, & in Christo placeant Deo personæ nostræ. Hæc illo loquente. Hic effectus est sermonis Christi. Iam tandem excitati sunt, postquam multum diúque cum eorum incredulitate luctatus est. Scintilla quædam est ista ac præparatio ad fidem potius quàm ipsa fides, vt apparet ex sequentibus. Christi autem exemplum hoc, facit spem pastoribus Ecclesiæ, aliquid se consequuturos etiam ex induratis tandem aliquando: vt & ipsi perseuerent ac continuò luctentur cum hominum incredulitate, successum autem Deo committant. Videtur autem hunc animorum motum excitasse maximè illis vi verborum illorum, quæ vltimò postulit, quibusque asseruit gloriam suam. Denuntiauit eam tàdem ipsos agnoscituros, præsentem etiam aliquo modo demonstrauit. hæc eò pertinent, vt videamus efficacem esse hunc sermonem qui de Christi gloria instituitur. Est enim Christi vita ac gloria res quædam maximè efficax ad vitam nostram, & ad accedendum in cordibus hominum gloriam: efficax, inquam, etiam in verbo prædicato. Ad præbendum, inquit Paulus, lumen cognitionis gloriæ Dei in facie Iesu Christi. Facie, inquam, gestata ac ostentata mundo in verbo ipsius. Nam facies illa Christi gloriosa, quouis modo repræsentetur nobis, efficax est ex sese sine verbo, sine aspectu, quanquam tamen quidem longè efficacior erit, cùm his oculis aliquando eam coram intuebimur.
units.tr: Now, to apply this to ourselves in some way: it is obedience, and that obedience which is prescribed by God himself, that preserves for us and guards that presence of God which is with us. For we please God most by that obedience in which we do all things according to his will and direct all things to his glory. But since we cannot have obedience so perfect, we must always flee to that perfect obedience of Christ, in which God rests perfectly, so that we may always have him present with us in that obedience of Christ, and so that our persons may be pleasing to God in Christ. While he was speaking these things. This is the effect of Christ's word. At last they have been stirred, after he has struggled long and hard with their unbelief. This is a spark and a preparation for faith rather than faith itself, as appears from what follows. The example of Christ also gives hope to the ministers of the Church that they will accomplish something even with those who are at last hardened: so that they too may persevere and continually struggle with men's unbelief, while committing the outcome to God. It seems that this stirring of minds was chiefly caused by the force of those words which he finally uttered, and by which he asserted his glory. He announced that they would at last recognise it, and in some way he showed it to be present. These things tend to this, that we may see that the word which is preached concerning the glory of Christ is effective. For the life and glory of Christ is a thing most effective for our life, and for bringing the glory of God into men's hearts: effective, I say, even in the preached word. To give, says Paul, the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. In the face, I say, displayed and exhibited to the world in his word. For that glorious face of Christ, however it may be represented to us, is effective of itself without the word, without sight; though it will certainly be far more effective when we shall one day behold it face to face with these eyes.

units.la: 31 Dicebat ergo Iesus iis Iudæis qui crediderant ipsi, Si vos manseritis in sermone meo, vere discipuli mei eritis:
units.tr: 31 Then Jesus said to those Jews who had believed in him: If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples.

units.la: 32 Et cognoscetis veritatem, & veritas vos in libertatem vindicabit.
units.tr: 32 And you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.

units.la: 33 Responderunt ei, Semen Abrahamisumus, neque cuiquam seruiimus vnquam: quomodo tu dicis vos in libertatem vindicabimini?
units.tr: 33 They answered him, "We are the seed of Abraham, and we have never been in bondage to anyone. How can you say that we shall be made free?"

units.la: NVnc quid vicissim facit Dominus, postquam sensit hunc in animis eorum motum fidei qualemcunque
units.tr: Now, in turn, what does the Lord do, after he has perceived that such a movement of faith, however slight, has been stirred up in their minds?

units.la: 2 Cor. 4.6. que excitari. An eos relinquit continuò? Minimè: sed inchoatam illam fidem conatur fouere: vt discant eius exemplo pastores, non satis esse si semel inchoent in hominibus fidem, nisi etiam continuò ac omnibus eam fouerint modis, ad extremum denique perduxerint. Perfectio enim fidei est opus ministerij. Quomodo autem fouet eam, quomodo promouet? num vim ei aliquam affert, num comminatur? Minimè, hoc enim fuisset frangere arundinem quassatam, & linum fumigans extinguere, id quod à Domino nunquam est factum: sicut etiam deco iam olim praedictum fuit à Propheta. Vt sciant pastores eius exemplo, non seuerius agendum cum infantibus in fide, sed mitioribus promissionibus ducendos eos esse, non vi adigēdos, ne illud fidei & zeli initium quantulumcunque destruant. Multa enim ferenda sunt in iis qui modò initiati sunt in fide. Eum qui fide est infirmus assumite, non ad certamina disputationum. Hinc sunt illae voces tam blandae Apostolorum, tanquam matrum ad modò natos quasi infantes in fide, Filioli, inquiunt, pueruli, &c. Nam, vt verè dicam, non sunt commi- nationes istae ex lege naturalis ac genuinus fidei cibus, verum genuinus fidei cibus sunt promissiones. Commi- nationum autem usus maximus est vel ante fidem, ad hoc vt sit sensus peccati ac miseriae, vel post fidem iam satis diu confirmatam. Videamus autem nunc promissionem eam, qua allicit istos Christus ad perseueran-tiam in fide illa inchoata. Si vos manseritis. Primùm pro- mittit iis fore vt sint discipuli ipsius, si modò manserint in eo sermone, quem iam coeperunt amplecti. Notan-dum: non ait, quia coepistis amplecti sermonem meum, ideo eritis mihi discipuli: Verùm ait, si vos manseritis in sermone meo, &c. Non est itaque initiatio in sermone Christi iam primùm facta, quae statim reddit verum Christi discipulum, sed est perseuerantia. Vt res habet in scholis in quibus traduntur humaniores literae: ita hic, non statim euadit discipulus, qui inchoat scientiam aliquam humaniorem, coepitque eam profiteri: sed discipulus est qui diu haesit in scholis, assiduúsque longo tempore auditor fuit. Ita se res habet in schola Christi, in qua is demum vere discipulus est, qui perseuerat ad finem vsque. Atque perseuerantia ista non ad tempus, neque ad longum tempus, sed ad finem vsque efficit discipulum Christi. Fieri enim potest, vt qui iam diu substiterit in schola Christi, tandem deficiat. Nunquâ profecto fuit is vere Christi discipulus. Vt sit vere discipulus, ad assiduitatem & diligentem attentionem in audiendo sermone ipsius, requiritur cordis sinceritas ac veritas: adeo vt non in superficie tantum cordis, vt sic dicam, sed penitus in intimo corde recipiat doctrinā illam Christi. Et vt ipse Dominus loquitur in parabola illa seminantis, requiritur vt ager cui committitur semen verbi, bonus sit. Quare inter audiendum verbum Dei, semper excutiendum est cor, videndúmque vt verum ac simplex sit, bonum ac honestum: vt verbi illud semen deferatur penitus in imum cordis, è quo rursus fides ac gaudium enascatur.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 4.6. to be aroused. Does he leave them at once? By no means. Rather, he tries to foster that faith which has been begun, so that the ministers may learn from his example that it is not enough to kindle faith in people once, unless they also continually nurture it in every way and at length bring it to completion. For the perfecting of faith is the work of the ministry. But how does he foster it, and how does he advance it? Does he apply some force to it, or does he threaten? By no means. That would have been to break a bruised reed and to put out a smoking wick, which the Lord never did; just as it was also long ago foretold by the Prophet. So that the ministers may learn from his example that children in the faith should not be dealt with more harshly, but should be led by gentler promises and not compelled by force, lest they destroy that beginning of faith and zeal, however small it is. For much must be borne with those who have only just been initiated into the faith. Receive him who is weak in faith, but not to quarrel over disputations. Hence come those very tender words of the Apostles, like those of mothers to infants newly born: little sons, they say, little children, and so on. For, to speak truly, those threats are not the natural food of faith; the genuine food of faith is the promises. The chief use of threats is either before faith, so that there may be a sense of sin and misery, or after faith has been confirmed for long enough. Let us now look at that promise by which Christ entices them to persevere in the faith that has been begun. If you continue. First he promises that they will be his disciples, provided they persevere in the word they have now begun to embrace. Note that he does not say, "Because you have begun to embrace my word, therefore you will be my disciples." He says, "If you continue in my word," and so on. So the beginning of the Christian's acquaintance with Christ's word is not what at once makes someone a true disciple of Christ; it is perseverance. It is as in schools where the humanities are taught: one who has begun to study some humane subject and has begun to profess it does not at once become a student; the student is the one who has stayed long in the schools and been a diligent hearer over a long time. So it is in the school of Christ, in which he alone is truly a disciple who perseveres to the end. And this perseverance, not for a time, nor for a long time, but to the end, makes a disciple of Christ. For it can happen that one who has long remained in the school of Christ finally falls away; he was never truly a disciple of Christ. To be a true disciple, with constant and diligent attention in hearing his word, there is required sincerity and truth of heart, so that he receives the teaching of Christ not merely on the surface of the heart, as it were, but deep within the innermost heart. And as the Lord himself speaks in the parable of the sower, the field to which the seed of the word is committed must be good. Therefore, while hearing the word of God, the heart must always be searched, and one must see that it is true and sincere, good and honourable, so that the seed of the word may be carried deep into the bottom of the heart, from which faith and joy may in turn spring up.

units.la: Et cognoscetis. Hoc alterum est quod promittitur, & qui iam vetus est discipulus: nempe assiduus progressus in cognitione veritatis. Sed cuiusnam veritatis? multiplex enim est veritas. Omnis scientia profitetur veritatem aliquam. Nulla non Philosophiae pars suam & habet & profitetur. Sed hic aliud quoddam veritatis genus intelligendum est, nimirum ea veritas, de qua coepit dicere sup. vers. 26. Quod ipse sit missus a Patre, &c. & quam ipsi iam amplecti coeperint. Quam Paulus vocat eminentiam cognitionis Iesu Christi; eamque infinitis partibus praefert toti doctrinae Pharisaicae, rebusque omnibus aliis, quae ipsi videbantur esse aliquid aliquando. Nota igitur: non quiuis statim proficit in doctrina Christi, sed qui se in discipulum dat Christo: neque id solum, sed qui perseuerat ad finem vsque. Neque enim in scholis humanis proficiunt, nisi qui serio discipuli sunt, seseque disciplinae submittunt. Fieri quidem potest, vt qui semel audiuit aliquid de verbo illo Christi, etiam quod temere in ipsum incidit & quod audiuit non animo credendi, vt contigit Iudaeis istis, qui ad sermonem Christi crediderunt: fieri, inquam, potest, vt is praeter consilium suum incipiat credere; magna enim est efficacia sermonis Christi in eo, in quo vult Dominus esse efficax. Sed progressus non est, nisi quis se in disciplinam plinam dedat. Quòd si autem quis se semel in discipli-nam dederit verè, sincerè & ex animo, profecto tum necesse est proficiat. Estque hoc discrimen inter discipulos, qui versantur in schola Christi, & eos qui in scholis aliis. Discipuli qui versantur in scholis falsorum doctorum nihil illi quidem proficiunt vnquam in veritatis cognitione: Qui enim fieri potest, vt proficiat quis in veritate, vbi non est veritas ipsa, sed veritatis quidam praetextus? Ita Apostolus de mulierculis quibusdam sedu-ctis à fallis doctoribus loquitur: Semper, inquit, discentes, sed quexnunquam ad veritatis cognitionem venire possint. Illud equidem asseuero, nunquam fore vt quis proficiat, ne si mille totos annos sederit in schola Papistica, nisi dicas in peius. Sed vt de aliis scholis loquar, in quibus etiam verae scientiae traduntur, non omnes quidem discipuli etiam seduli & attenti in iis statim proficiunt: sunt enim quidam absurdo & infelici adeo ingenio, vt nihil possint proficere: non est autem penes praeceptorem etiam diligentissimum ingenium cuiusquam mutare, & ex indocili docile efficere. Atqui discipulus Christi etsi ingenio sit, vt ita dicam, quàm abstrusissimo, hoc est corde indurato simo, quales Christus reperire solet primùm nos omnes: omnes enim ineptissimi sumus natura ad disciplinam & doctrinam Christi capessendam: ) tamen potens est Dominus ex ineptis aptos, ex indocilibus doceles efficere, vt qui internus doctor sit; ideoque de Christi discipulis praedictum est, quòd omnes futuri sint θεοδίδακτοι. Et erunt omnes docti à Deo supra cap.6.45. Verùm quidem est vt Dominum ministerio hominum Ecclesia sua, & vt scribit Apostolus, Postquam ascendit longè supra omnes coelos, alios dedit Apostolos, alios Prophetas, alios Euangelistas, alios Pastores & Doctores: Sed nunquam ita destituit scholam suam Dominus Spiritu suo, qui ei praesens sit, neque minus efficax est, in quibus vult esse efficax, quàm si ipse suo ore doceat. Quamobrè neminem omnium quantumuis indocilem, etiam quod maius est, quantumuis durum corde indocilitas illa & duritiem abstterreat à scholis Christi, sed eum audiat, quum sciat hanc necessitatem esse vt proficiat qui in Christi schola serió eum audiuerit docentem. Dico qui
units.tr: And you shall know. This is the second promise, and it belongs to the one who is already an old disciple: namely, steady progress in knowledge of the truth. But which truth? Truth is many-sided. Every science professes some truth, and every part of philosophy has and professes its own. Here, however, another kind of truth must be understood, namely the truth of which he began to speak above at verse 26: that he was sent by the Father, etc., and which they had now begun to embrace. Paul calls this the excellence of the knowledge of Jesus Christ, and he sets it infinitely above the whole Pharisaic teaching and all the other things that once seemed to them to be something. Note, then: not everyone at once makes progress in the teaching of Christ, but only one who gives himself as a disciple to Christ, and not only that, but who perseveres to the end. For in human schools too, only those make progress who are earnest disciples and submit themselves to the discipline. It is indeed possible that someone who has once heard something of the word of Christ, even one who stumbled upon it by chance and heard it without a mind to believe, as happened to those Jews who believed at the word of Christ, may, I say, come to believe beyond his own intention; for the power of the word of Christ is great in the one in whom the Lord wills it to be effective. But there is no progress unless a person gives himself to discipleship. If indeed someone has once truly, sincerely and wholeheartedly given himself to discipleship, then he must certainly make progress. And this is the difference between the disciples who are in the school of Christ and those who are in other schools. Disciples who are in the schools of false teachers never make any progress at all in the knowledge of truth. For how can anyone make progress in truth where the truth itself is not, but only a pretence of truth? So the Apostle speaks of certain silly women seduced by false teachers: always learning, yet never able to come to the knowledge of the truth. I certainly affirm that no one will ever make progress, even if he sits a thousand whole years in a Papist school, unless you mean for the worse. But to speak of other schools, in which true sciences are also taught, not all disciples, even the diligent and attentive, make progress in them at once. For there are some with so absurd and unhappy a mind that they can make no progress at all; and it is not in the power of the teacher, however diligent, to change anyone's nature and make a docile person out of an indocile one. But the disciple of Christ, even if he has a mind as obscure as one can imagine, that is, a heart as hardened as Christ usually finds all of us at first (for we are all by nature most unfit to take hold of the discipline and teaching of Christ), nevertheless the Lord is able to make the unfit fit and the indocile docile, since he is the inner teacher; and therefore it has been foretold of Christ's disciples that they will all be taught by God [θεοδίδακτοι]. And all will be taught by God, see above ch. 6.45. It is true that the Lord uses the ministry of men in his Church, and, as the Apostle writes, after he ascended far above all the heavens, he gave some apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, some pastors and teachers. But the Lord never so abandons his school as to be without his Spirit present with it, and he is no less effective in those in whom he wills to be effective than if he taught with his own mouth. Therefore let no one, however indocile, or, what is worse, however hard of heart, be frightened away from the school of Christ by that indocility and hardness; rather let him listen, since he knows that the necessity is that he who listens earnestly to Christ teaching in his school makes progress. I say, who listens earnestly to him teaching.

units.la: Ephes. 4.10-11. serio eum docentem audiuerit: Nam complures sunt qui audiunt quotidie, non proficiunt tamen. Causa autem est, quia non serio sed perfunctorie audiunt. Cui enim dedit Deus velle, hoc est serium discendi studium, iis necessario dabit perficere, vt loquar cum Apostolo.
units.tr: Eph. 4.10-11. For there are many who hear every day and yet do not make progress. The cause is that they do not listen earnestly but carelessly. For to whom God has given the will, that is, an earnest desire to learn, to them he will necessarily give also the power to accomplish it, to use the words of the Apostle.

units.la: Et veritas vos. Hoc tertium est quod promittit permanentibus in sermone ipsius. Eltque effectus cognitionis illius quam dixit veritatis: q. d. Veritas haec cognita vos in libertatem vindicabit: non enim nuda est ca duntaxat huius veritatis contemplatio, qualis est veritatum quæ locum habet in aliis scientiis, quæ contemplatrices sunt modo, & nihil in vita quotidiana efficiūt. Fieri quidem potest vt ethicæ istæ Philosophorum scientiæ, externam vitam aliquo modo informent, sed interim animum & pravos effectus (pollicentur quantum velint) informare & mutare non possunt. Non possunt ex servo peccati efficere liberum, ne Mosis quidem ipsius lex & doctrina id potuit. Nam quamuis legeretur Moses quotidie, tamen manet velamē cordibus eorum impositum. Atqui doctrina Christi audita & exceptā animo, mutat animum, ex servo peccati liberum, imo regem facit. Participem facit sortis sanctorum in luce, liberat à potestate tenebrarum ac transfert in regnum Filij Dei. In causa est, quòd, vt ait Apostolus, Dominus Spiritus ille est, Dominus nimirum, qui est subiectum veritatis illius, non est quiddam mortuum aut inefficax, sed Spiritus est ad penetrandum in intum cordis, & ad liberandum ipsum à seruitute peccati & mortis. Vbi autem Spiritus ille Domini, illic libertas. Imo historia sola mortis & ignominiae Christi, efficacior est ad mutationem animi, quàm omnes omnium regum atque imperatorum historiae, quotquot vnquam in summa gloria & mediis triumphis vixerunt. Fieri quidem potest, vt hæ euanido quodam gaudio animum ad tempus tillent, sed nihil mutant eum, neque ex malo bonum efficiunt. Sermo autem crucis est potentia ac sapientia Dei iis qui vocati sunt.
units.tr: And the truth shall make you. This is the third thing he promises to those who abide in his word. And it is the effect of that knowledge of the truth which he spoke of: as if to say, "This truth, once known, will set you free." For this is not a bare contemplation of the truth, such as belongs to the truths of other sciences, which are merely contemplative and accomplish nothing in daily life. It is indeed possible that these ethical sciences of the philosophers shape external life in some way, but meanwhile they cannot shape and change the mind and its wicked effects, however much they promise. They cannot make a free man out of a slave of sin; not even the law and teaching of Moses itself could do that. For though Moses is read every day, the veil remains laid upon their hearts. But the teaching of Christ, heard and received in the mind, changes the mind, makes a free man out of a slave of sin, and indeed makes a king. It makes us partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light, rescues us from the power of darkness and transfers us into the kingdom of the Son of God. The reason is that, as the Apostle says, the Lord is the Spirit; that is, the Lord, who is the subject of that truth, is not something dead or ineffective, but is a Spirit who penetrates into the innermost heart and frees it from the slavery of sin and death. Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. Indeed the history of the death and shame of Christ alone is more effective in changing the mind than all the histories of all the kings and emperors who ever lived in the highest glory and among triumphs. It is indeed possible that these histories lift the mind for a time with some fleeting joy, but they change it not at all, and they do not make good out of evil. But the word of the cross is the power and wisdom of God to those who are called.

units.la: Respönderunt ei. Responsum hoc tribuendum est non iis qui crediderunt, sed aliis ex eo numero qui in duritie cordis permanserunt. Hi iam prorsum punt ad impediendum diendum cursum Euangelij & salutem eorum qui coeperunt credere, vt habuit Satan omni aetate emissarios suos, qui neque ipsi ingredi in regnum caelorum volūt, neque alios ingredi patiuntur. Sic autem argumentantur: Si vindicandi sumus in libertatem, iam serui sumus: At non sumus serui: Ergo non vindicandi in libertatem. Assumptio ostenditur: Semen Abrahae sumus, hoc est, natura liberi sumus, ex libero atque ingenuo parente orti: Deinde, nemini adhuc unquam seruituimus, hoc est in libertate illa in qua sumus nati, ex Patre nimirum libero, perstitimus ad hunc vsque diem. Sed examinemus haec argumenta: primum est: semen Abrahae sumus, hoc est, liberi sumus natura ipsa. Verum quidem hoc est, si loquaris de semine carnali tantum. Nam semen Abrahae duplex est: primum carnale, quod vi carnis tantum & natura nascitur, etsi etiam vi promissionis. At non spirituale illius promissionis, quae fuit de spirituali semine, cuius typus erat promissio de semine carnali. Secundum est spirituale semen, quod secundum Spiritum sanctum vi promissionis Spiritualis nascitur. Exant quidem isti quia hoc loco respondent semen Abrahae carnale, neque hic aliud Abrahae semen isti intellexerunt: quare neque aliam libertatem quam carnalem: id quod etiam appa-ret ex hoc contextu. Ex quo demum nota quo caecitatis & ignorantiae peruenerint Iudaei, qui iam cognitionem omnem ac sensum rerum spiritualium amiserunt. Ignorarunt Abrahamum spiritualem esse Patrem, ignorarunt promissionem illam de spirituali semine, cuius typus erat semen carnale. Ignorarunt Spiritualem illam libertatem, liberationem a peccato & morte. In hanc tantam tam crassam ignorantiam paulatim peruenerunt: Prophetarum aetate non adeo erant caeci. His quidem etiam tum considebant, tanquam meritis rerum spiritualium. Vide Esai.1. At nunc demum in aduentu Christi spirituales quidem res vllas esse putant, nō peccatum, non iustitiam, non caelos, non inferos. Exemplū in ipsum Deus, quo terreri oportet omnes posteros, vt caveant sibi tempestiue, neque sinant se paulatim excaecari atque indurari, ne tandem aliquando fiat vt amittant omnem aspectum, omnem sensum rerum spiritualium. Sed nunc videamus an cum isti intellexerint non aliud semen quam carnale, ac proinde libertatem in qua nati erant, non aliam quam carnalem & corporale, an verum sit quod ostentant, scilicet liberos natos esse? verum quidem est ex maioribus eorum aliquos liberos fuisse natos, sub Iudicibus primum, deinde sub Regibus. At isti qui libertatem istam carnalem nunc iactitant, nati erant sub imperio ac seruitute Romanorum. Quapropter hic oportet mentiantur. Sed mendacium quod sequitur magis impudens est: Neque cuiquam, inquiunt, seruiuimus vnquam. Praeterquam enim quod primum in Canaan, deinde in Aegypto, tum in Babylonia, denique in terra etiam sua non semel seruierant, hoc ipso tempore Romanis seruiebant. Sed mendacij causa fuit stupiditas quaedam ac induratio cordis, qua obfirmati sunt miseri aduersus omnem sensum iudicij ac seruitutis non spiritualis modo, sed etiam corporalis ac iudiciorum Dei externorum. Sed hoc euenjebat iis typicè, inquit Apostolus. Hac nostra autem aetate sunt, qui non minus, imò magis indurati sunt aduersus omnem protsus sensum, non modò internae ac spiritualis seruitutis, quae est sub peccato & morte; verum etiam aduersus omnem sensum iudiciorum Dei externorum, quum nemo sanae mentis sit, aut qui oculos aliqua ex parte illuminatos habeat, qui non videat familias ferè omnes, quae alicuius nominis sunt apud nos, exercet iudiciis Dei assiduis, vel hoc ipso quod peccandi finem nullum eos facere videamus, occidendi nullum finem, adulterandi nullum finem, diripiendi ac opprimendi rempublicam & Ecclesiam nullum finem. Nam peccata ista perpetua, ut de aliis Dei iudiciis & poenis, quibus eos exercet, ut consumptione Patrimoniorum, & id genus aliis, ut de his nihil dicam, peccata ista & defectiones continuae peccatorum praecedentium, totidem poenae sunt grauissimae.
units.tr: They answered him. This answer is to be attributed not to those who believed, but to others from that number who remained in hardness of heart. These now rush headlong to hinder the course of the gospel and the salvation of those who have begun to believe, just as Satan has always had his emissaries in every age, who neither wish to enter the kingdom of heaven themselves nor allow others to enter. They argue thus: If we are to be set free, then we are already slaves; but we are not slaves; therefore we are not to be set free. The minor premise is shown thus: We are the seed of Abraham, that is, we are free by nature, born of a free and freeborn parent; then, we have never yet served anyone, that is, we have remained in that freedom into which we were born, namely from a free father, down to this day. But let us examine these arguments. The first is: we are the seed of Abraham, that is, we are free by nature itself. This is true only if you speak of the carnal seed alone. For the seed of Abraham is twofold: first the carnal, which is born by the power of the flesh and nature only, though also by the power of the promise; but not the spiritual of that promise, which concerned a spiritual seed, of which the promise concerning the carnal seed was a type. The second is the spiritual seed, which is born according to the Holy Spirit by the power of the spiritual promise. These men, indeed, in this place answer that the seed of Abraham is carnal, and they understood no other seed of Abraham here; hence they understood no other freedom than carnal freedom, which also appears from this context. From this we may finally note into what blindness and ignorance the Jews had fallen, who had now lost all knowledge and sense of spiritual things. They did not know that Abraham is a spiritual father; they did not know that promise concerning the spiritual seed, of which the carnal seed was a type. They did not know that spiritual freedom, the liberation from sin and death. Little by little they had come into this so great and so gross ignorance; in the time of the prophets they were not so blind. Even then they were still clinging to these things as if they were the merits of spiritual things. See Isa. 1. But now at last, at the coming of Christ, they think there are no spiritual things at all: not sin, not righteousness, not heaven, not hell. Let God's example, by which all posterity ought to be terrified, be a warning to them to take heed in good time, and not to allow themselves to be gradually blinded and hardened, lest at last it come about that they lose every view, every sense of spiritual things. But let us now see whether, when they have understood that the seed is nothing but carnal, and therefore the freedom in which they were born is nothing but carnal and bodily, what they boast is true, namely that they were born free. It is indeed true that some of their ancestors were born free, first under the judges, then under the kings. But these men, who now boast of that carnal freedom, were born under the rule and slavery of the Romans. Therefore they must lie here. But the lie that follows is more shameless: We have never served anyone, they say. For apart from the fact that they had served, first in Canaan, then in Egypt, then in Babylon, and finally in their own land, not once only, at this very time they were serving the Romans. But the cause of the lie was a certain stupidity and hardening of heart, by which those wretched men were made obstinate against every sense of judgment and of servitude, not only spiritual but also bodily, and against the external judgments of God. But this happened to them typically, says the Apostle. In our own age there are some who are no less, indeed more, hardened against every sense whatever, not only of inner and spiritual servitude, which is under sin and death, but also against every sense of the external judgments of God; since there is no one of sound mind, or who has his eyes in some measure enlightened, who does not see that almost all the families of any name among us are being constantly exercised by the judgments of God, if only from this fact, that we see them make no end of sinning, no end of killing, no end of committing adultery, no end of plundering and oppressing the commonwealth and the Church. For these perpetual sins, not to speak of the other judgments and punishments of God by which he exercises them, such as the consuming of patrimonies and others of that kind, these sins and the continual defections from earlier sins are themselves most grievous punishments.

units.la: 34 Respondit eis Iesus, Amen, amen dico vobis, Quisquis operam dat peccato, seruus est peccati.
units.tr: 34 Jesus answered them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin."

units.la: 35 Seruus autem non manet in domo perpetuo: filius manet perpetuò.
units.tr: 35 "Now the slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever."

units.la: 36 Itaque si vos filius in libertatem vindicârit, verè liberi estis.
units.tr: 36 "So if the Son sets you free, you will be truly free."

units.la: EX multitudine Iudæorum ij qui increduli manse-runt, opponebant sese promissioni à Christo factæ iis qui cœperunt credere: potissimum autem reprehen-debant illud postremum, quod à Christo dictum est, ne Christo, pe veritatem eos in libertatem vindicaturam: Hic cum intelligerent libertatem corporalem & externam, ita concludebant: Si vindicandi sumus in libertatem, sequi-turnos seruiuisse priùs. At serui non fuimus: Ergo, &c. Assumptionem probant duobus argumentis. 1. Semen Abrahæ sumus, hoc est natura & nascendi lege liberi sumus, Abraham enim liber vixit. 2. Nullo vnquâ tem-pore seruiuimus cuiquam. Christus hic respondet, non ad argumenta eorum primùm, sed ad assertionem: quia dixerunt non esse seruos sese: seruos itaque probat eos hoc argumento; Serui estis peccati: Ergo seruì. Vbi cùm illi corporaliter in seruitutem intellexerint, Dominus spi-ritualem intelligit, ad eamque considerandam eos de-duxit. Vbi obseruua discrimen inter Deum & hominem in accipiendâ veraliberatae simul & seruitute. Homo desixus est totus in consideranda externa libertate & seruitute corporis: Deus verò internam intuetur: ita vt vel regem nihili faciat, nisi liberatū eum videat à peccato & morte per Iesum Christum. Hanc Dei naturam imitantur quicunque aliquam imaginis ipsius partem acceperunt, & quorum oculi illuminati sunt aliqua ex parte ad videndum res spirituales. Sic Paulus: Post hac, inquit, neminem nouimus secundum carnem, id est carnalia sia, vt libertatem, & seruitutem carnalem, &c. Et alibi exhortationem suam ad seruos dirigens: Seruus, inquit, vocatus es? ne sit tibi curæ. Etenim qui in Domino vocatus est seruus, libertus Domini est. Quibus verbis monet non an-xie laborandum de seruitute hac carnali, posteaquam quis semel vocatus est ad spiritualia illa & æterna. Sed cernere spiritualia longè difficillimum est. Ideo cum Paulo precandum continuò, vt illuminatis oculis vi-deamus quæ sit spes vocationis ipsius, & quæ opes gloriæ hæreditatis ipsius in Sanctis. Consideremus rursus argumentationem Christi. Serui estis peccati: Ergo servi. Antecedens probatur. Qui committit peccatum, peccati servus est. At vos committitis peccatum, Ergo servi peccati. Propositio hæc nititur vniuersali thesi quam habet Apostolus. An nescitis quod cui sistitis vosipsos servos ad obediendum, eius servi estis cui obeditis? Hinc sequitur speciale, Quisquis obedit peccato, ipsum ei seruum esse addictum. Tenendum autem hoc loco, committere peccatum, non esse peccare simpliciter. Si enim dixerimus nos non habere peccatum, fallimus nosipsos, & veritas non est in nobis. Sed committere peccatum, est magnopere delectari peccato, facere malum non quidem quod nolunt, sed quod volunt. Habere peccatum in se regnans, quos dicit Iohannes eadem illa epistola filios esse diaboli: Qui committit peccatum ex diabolo est. Vide igitur, Dominus ex operibus iudicat de interna conditione, non de habitu tantum animi vitioso, id quod fecerunt etiam ipsi Philosophi, qui alioqui libertatem arbitrii pessimo cuique tribuerunt, sed de seruili plane natura. Quare ex operibus iudicandum est de conditione cuiusque, servitus sit, peccatine an iustitiæ, hoc est, ex fructibus de arbore iudicandum est. Quod si enim opera mala sint, iudicandus est peccati seruus. Sed difficillime persuadebis pessimo cuique homini, homicidæ, adultero, &c. ipsum proptera seruum esse, quod talis sit. Putat enim eam esse libertatem veram, pro arbitrio suo pessima quæque perpetrare, quoque magis impune grassatur, eo magis se liberum esse existimat, adeo cæcutimus natura in hac miseria cognoscenda, quam plerique non agnoscent, priusquam experiunt fructum peccati sui tam acerbum percipere, Nam stipendium peccati mors.
units.tr: AMONG the great crowd of Jews, those who remained unbelieving opposed the promise made by Christ to those who had begun to believe. They objected chiefly to the last part of what Christ said, that the truth would set them free. Since they understood this as bodily and outward liberty, they argued as follows: "If we are to be set free, it follows that we were slaves before. But we were never slaves. Therefore, etc." They prove the assumption by two arguments: (1) We are the seed of Abraham; that is, by nature and by the law of birth we are free, for Abraham lived as a free man. (2) We have never at any time been slaves to anyone. Christ replies here, not first to their arguments, but to their assertion, because they said they were not slaves. He therefore proves that they are slaves by this argument: "You are slaves of sin; therefore you are slaves." When they understood this in a bodily sense as servitude, the Lord understood it spiritually, and led them to consider that. Here observe the difference between God and man in understanding both true liberty and true servitude. Man is wholly fixed on considering outward liberty and bodily servitude, but God looks upon inward liberty, so that he regards a king as nothing unless he sees him freed from sin and death through Jesus Christ. Whoever has received some part of God's image, and whose eyes have been enlightened in some measure to see spiritual things, imitates this nature of God. So Paul says: "Henceforth we know no one according to the flesh," that is, according to carnal things, such as bodily liberty and servitude, etc. And again, directing his exhortation to slaves, he says: "Were you called as a slave? Let it not concern you. For he who is called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman." By these words he warns that we should not anxiously labour over this carnal servitude, once someone has been called to those spiritual and eternal things. But to perceive spiritual things is by far the most difficult. Therefore, with Paul, we must continually pray that, with our eyes enlightened, we may see what is the hope of his calling and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints. Let us consider again the argument of Christ: "You are slaves of sin; therefore you are slaves." The antecedent is proved thus: He who commits sin is a slave of sin. But you commit sin; therefore you are slaves of sin. This proposition rests on the general thesis that the Apostle holds: Do you not know that to whom you present yourselves as slaves to obey, you are the slaves of him whom you obey? From this follows the particular: whoever obeys sin is delivered over to it as its slave. But here we must hold that to commit sin is not simply to sin. For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. Rather, to commit sin is to take great delight in sin, to do evil not indeed what one is unwilling to do, but what one wills to do. Those who have sin reigning within them, John in the same epistle calls children of the devil: He who commits sin is of the devil. See, then, that the Lord judges from works the inward condition, not merely from a vicious habit of mind, which the philosophers too did, who otherwise attributed freedom of the will to every wicked man, but from a plainly servile nature. Hence from works we must judge the condition of each person, whether it is servitude to sin or to righteousness; that is, we must judge the tree by its fruits. For if the works are evil, he must be judged a slave of sin. Yet you will with the greatest difficulty persuade the most wicked man, a murderer, an adulterer, and so on, that he is a slave for that very reason, that he is such. For he thinks that true liberty is to commit every wickedness at his own will, and the more he runs riot with impunity, the more he thinks himself free. So blind is our nature in recognising this misery, which most people do not acknowledge until they experience the bitter fruit of their sin: For the wages of sin is death.

units.la: Sed considera quid Dominus proxime denuntiet in seruos istos peccatis. Serum, inquit, non manet in domo in aeternum.
