For there is no limit to sinning once someone has begun to sin maliciously against the light. So great is the evil of hardening and blinding, even when it has only just begun. But you will say that they were provoked by the Lord's very sharp words. For he had called them children of the devil and had utterly separated them from God. But I reply that they deserved it, and their obstinacy demanded it. Unless it is laid open thoroughly, down to its foundation and its innate principle in human nature, it will certainly never be cured. For this is the first step to salvation: the recognition of our misery and of this most corrupt nature. Whoever has not recognised this, at least in some part, has certainly not taken a single step on the way of salvation. But what is it that they object? Merely a common insult. For commonly, when the Jews wished to burden someone with some great disgrace, they called him a Samaritan, that is, an impure man, corrupt in the knowledge of the truth. So they have nothing with which to accuse him of some special crime. Indeed, he had already silenced them above; yet they do not altogether keep quiet. Learn from this that the obstinate will never lack material by which to harden themselves further, and which they can throw against all the godly, and especially against those who set the light before them. Even if a minister of the word today is no less innocent than an angel, our people will never lack material for accusing, reviling, or slandering him. Rather than have none, they will object that he has a demon. These voices of theirs are not unknown to us, but Christ suffered all these things before us. "Jesus answered." The Lord, answering, does not match insult with insult, but modestly denies what they threw at him as an insult. He gives the reason for his denial from the opposite of their conduct. "I," he says, "do not have a demon." He who honours the Father necessarily does not have a demon; but I honour the Father; therefore, and so on. What it is to honour the Father the Lord himself shows in that prayer to his Father, which we shall discuss later in chapter 17, verse 4: "I have glorified you on earth." Then he teaches what this is in the following words: "I have finished the work that you gave me to do." By the work he means the redemption of mankind, in carrying out which he emptied and humbled himself, and became obedient to the Father even to death, indeed to the death of the cross. For no creature has ever humbled itself under the hand of the Father as the Son did. Note therefore that whoever truly honours God is necessarily not seized by a lying spirit. For this is the mark of a true teacher: if he seeks God's glory wholly in his teaching. Conversely, this is the mark of a false teacher: if he seeks himself rather than God in his teaching, he certainly cannot be a true teacher. From this the Lord gave these marks of true and false doctrine above, in chapter 7, verse 18: "He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory; but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him, the same is true, and there is no unrighteousness in him." Then he sets against his own conduct their opposite conduct, which is most unworthy, I say, most unworthy. For it is most unworthy to heap disgrace upon those who sincerely glorify God. And yet those who are most disgraced, and treated in every unworthy way in this age, are the very ones who most strive to please God; I mean those who humble themselves and labour to deny themselves so that they may glorify their God. Hence, says Paul, "we are toiled and reproached, because we hope in the living God." And Peter says that Christians at first were blasphemed by profane men, because they did not run with them to the same excess of dissipation as they were used to. Each of the best and holiest among us is mocked and blasphemed by the children of this age.

units.la: Sed quid Dominus ad haec, hoc loco factum hoc eorum exaggerat primum a gloria qua Pater ipsum affectus erat. Amplificatur autem ea gloria ad quam erat cuiusdam heredus a Patre a diverso facto suo in gloria sua ipsius negligenda. Est quidem hoc indignum cum ignominia afficere, quem Pater quaerit glorificare. Sed quaenam haec gloria? Glorifica me, inquit Filius Patri, apud temetipsum ea gloria, quam habui apud te priusquam hic mundus existeret. Gloriam etiam Christi graphice depinxit Apostolus. Idcirco, inquit, extulit eum Deus in summam sublimitatem, & donavit ei nomen quod est supra omne nomen, &c. Quo loco notandum Apostolum glorioso exitu humiliationis Christi, tanquam argumento, quo suadet modestiam & humilitatem qualis erat in Christo. Nam etsi non possumus nos actu humiliare ac submittere sub Deo ut Christus, tamen humiliantes nos ipsi pro mensura doni Christi exaltabimur a Deo, licet non ad parem cum Christo gloriam, at immensam tamen cuius nos capaces, quaque contenti erimus. Exaggerat quoque illud eorum factum, a iudicio illo graui, quod ob conceptum ipsius reportaturi sunt: Et iudicet, inquit. Sciendum enim est gloriam eorum apparituram simul cum ignominia impiorum, id autem maxime conspicietur ac revelabitur vna cum perpetua hostium ignominia. Amen, Amen. Omissa commina-tione Dominus conuertit se ad promissionem, idque partim in eorum gratiam, qui ex hac turba iam coeperunt credere, de quibus supra vers.30. vt nimirum eos vitrius in fide deduceret ac confirmaret: partim etiam ipsorum illorum obstinatorum, vt si fieri posset ipsi quoque ad meliorem frugem conuerterentur ac resipiscerent. Neque enim satis est ad fidem & resipiscentiam demonstrasse solâ hominis miseriam, sed vltra etiam promissionem gratiæ est faciendam & ostendendam in Christo Dei misericordia. Ideoque iam demonstrata eorum miseria, nempe quòd filij diaboli sint: quòd cum Deo nihil commune habeant, secundo loco iis gratiam ac misericordiam in Mediatore proponit atque offert. Sed videamus promissionem. Primùm assueta illa asseueratione vtitur ad certitudinem & maiorem fidem rei promissæ. Deinde promittit, sed seruanti sermonem suum, seruanti, inquam, sermonem suum promittit certam liberationem à morte. Seruanti, inquam, quia non satis est semel duntaxat annuere & assentiri verbo Christi, nisi etiam verbum illud semel receptum seruaueris apud animum tuum in perpetuum: atque ita seruaueris apud animum, vt in vita tua eluceat & exprimatur: hoc enim est seruare sermonem Dei. vide 1.Iohan.2.3. vbi eodem sensu loquitur de obseruatione mandatorum ipsius. Eritaque qui in hunc modum seruauerit sermonem ipsius, promittit fore, vt nunquam conspiciat mortem: Mortem intelligit spiritualem illam corporis simul & animæ æternam. A qua liberatum iri eum promittit, qui seruaturus sit sermonem ipsius. Promittit quoque ex parte aliqua liberationem à prima morte illa ac temporaria, qua ratione nimirum qui seruaturi sunt sermonem ipsius, in hac ipsa prima morte conspecturi sunt vitam, & mors prima quæ sua natura est stipendium peccati, conuertenda sit iis in transitum atque mediam viam quæ ducat eos ad vitam æternam. Sed expendamus effectum hunc fidei quæ habetur sermoni Christi. Desinemus mirari liberationem à morte æterna insequuturam fidem in in sermonem Christi, si efficaciam seruonis Christi quæ quantaque sit consideremus. Verbum Christi dixit Petrus supra 6.68. esse verbum vitæ æternæ, Verba vitæ æternæ habes, inquit. Verbum autem vitæ est, quia spiritus est eodem cap.verf.63. Verba quæ ego loquor vobis, Spiritus sunt & vita sunt. Vita igitur sunt, quia spiritus sunt, hoc est, coniunctam habent Spiritus Dei potentiam, qui iis vtitur tanquam efficaci instrumento ad ex citandam in cordibus fidem & nouam vitam. Neque enim putandum est verba Dei nuda & ieiuna duntaxat verba esse, cuiusmodi sunt hominum etiam eloquentissimorum, quæ nihil plane possunt ad solidam cordis atque effectuum immutationem; sed verba Dei virtutis ac potentiæ plena sunt. Ideoque Apostolus ait, Regnum Dei non est situm in verbis etiam difertissimis (cuiusmodi erat verba illa Pseudo-apostolorum illorum Corinthiorum)sed in Spiritus virtute. Verum quidem id est, sermonem crucis humilem esse, atque in speciem abiectam, sed sermo crucis, inquit Paulus, iis qui seruantur potentia Dei 1.Cor 1.18. est. Et materia illius sermonis vilis admodum videtur mundo, vtpote homo crucifixus, sed Christus crucifixus, at Apostolus, vocatis est Dei potentia & sapientia. Demum hoc intelligunt qui ipsa experti sunt. Sentiunt ij dum prædicatur hoc verbum excitari in se nouam vitam, seseque ex morte ad vitam resurgere.
units.tr: But what does the Lord say to this? In this place he first magnifies their deed by the glory with which the Father had honoured him. That glory is further enlarged by the fact that he was the Father's heir, so their conduct in neglecting his own glory is all the more serious. It is indeed an unworthy thing to treat with contempt the one whom the Father seeks to glorify. But what glory is this? "Glorify me, Son says to the Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before this world existed." The Apostle also portrays the glory of Christ vividly: "Therefore God has exalted him to the highest place and has given him the name which is above every name," and so on. Here we should note that the Apostle, to persuade us of the modesty and humility that were in Christ, sets the glorious outcome of Christ's humiliation before us as an argument. For although we cannot humble and submit ourselves under God as Christ did, yet if we humble ourselves according to the measure of Christ's gift, we shall be exalted by God. This will not be the same glory as Christ's, but it will be an immense glory, one for which we are capable and with which we shall be content. The Lord also magnifies their deed by the severe judgement which they will incur because of their attitude towards him: "and he will judge," he says. For we must understand that their glory will appear together with the shame of the wicked, and this will be seen and revealed most of all along with the everlasting shame of his enemies. Amen, amen. Having left aside the threat, the Lord turns to the promise. He does this partly for the sake of those from this crowd who had already begun to believe (of whom he spoke above, at verse 30), so that he might lead them further on in faith and strengthen them. Partly he does it for the sake of those obstinate men themselves, so that, if it were possible, they too might be turned to a better course and repent. For it is not enough, in order to bring men to faith and repentance, to have shown only human wretchedness; beyond that, the mercy of God in Christ must also be set forth and displayed in the promise of grace. Therefore, having already demonstrated their wretchedness, namely that they are the children of the devil, that they have nothing in common with God, he now offers and presents to them grace and mercy in the Mediator. But let us look at the promise. First, he uses that customary asseveration, to give certainty and greater faith to what is promised. Then he promises, but to the one who keeps his word, to the one who keeps his word, I say, he promises certain deliverance from death. "To the one who keeps," I say, because it is not enough merely to assent once to the word of Christ, unless you also keep that word once received within your mind for ever; and you keep it in your mind in such a way that it shines out and is expressed in your life. For this is to keep the word of God. See 1 John 2:3, where he speaks in the same sense of keeping his commandments. And so the one who keeps his word in this way is promised that he will never see death. By death he means that spiritual death, eternal in body and soul alike, from which he promises that the one who keeps his word will be freed. He also promises, in some measure, deliverance from that first, temporal death, in the sense that those who keep his word will, in this very first death, see life, and the first death, which by its nature is the wages of sin, will be turned for them into a passage and a middle way that leads them to eternal life. But let us consider the power of this faith which is placed in the word of Christ. We shall cease to wonder at deliverance from eternal death following faith in the word of Christ, if we consider what and how great the efficacy of the word of Christ is. Peter said above, at 6:68, that the word of Christ is the word of eternal life: "You have the words of eternal life," he says. And the word is life because it is spirit, as the same chapter says at verse 63: "The words that I speak to you are spirit and life." They are life, therefore, because they are spirit; that is, they have joined to them the power of the Spirit of God, who uses them as an effective instrument to kindle faith and new life in hearts. For we must not think that the words of God are bare and empty words only, such as the words of even the most eloquent men are, which can accomplish nothing at all towards a solid change of heart and conduct. The words of God are full of virtue and power. Therefore the Apostle says, The kingdom of God does not consist in words, even the most eloquent (such as those words of those false apostles of the Corinthians were), but in the power of the Spirit. It is true that the word of the cross is humble and in appearance abject, but the word of the cross, says Paul, is the power of God to those who are being saved (1 Cor. 1:18). And the matter of that word seems very base to the world: a crucified man. But Christ crucified, says the Apostle, is the power and wisdom of God to those who are called. At last, those understand this who have experienced it themselves. While this word is preached, they feel a new life stirred up in themselves, and they rise from death to life.

units.la: 52 Dixerunt ergo ei Iudæi, Nunc agnoscimus te daemonium habere. Abrahamus mortuus est, & Prophetæ: & tu dicis, Si quis sermonem meum seruauerit, non gustabit mortem in æternum.
units.tr: 52 The Jews therefore said to him, "Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham is dead, and the prophets too; and you say, If anyone keeps my word, he shall never taste death for ever."

units.la: 53 Num tu maior es Patre illo nostro Abrahamo, qui mortuus est? etiam Prophetæ mortui sunt, quem tu teipsum facis?
units.tr: 53 "Are you greater than our father Abraham, who is dead? The prophets too are dead. Whom do you make yourself out to be?"

units.la: Vdæi indurantur etiam ad promissionem vitæ propositam, non minus quam ad exprobrationem miseriæ, vt intelligas imprimis difficile atque arduum, induratum hominis animum & cor quasi præclusum emollitatem atque aperire. Sed videamus quid sit quod colligant ex Christi hac promissione; Nunc nimirum cognoscere dæmonium ipsum habere. Consequens probant ex eo quod verbis vsus sit quæ ipsum faciant maiorem Abrahamo & Prophetis veteribus. Id quod arguit verba illa è Spiritu esse fallaci ac deceptore. Hæc autem quærunt ex eo cum indignatione, Num tu maior es Patre nostro Abrahamo? Antecedens hoc probant ex eo quod Abraham iam mortuus sit ipse, etiam prophetæ ipsi mortui sint: tantum abfuerunt ab eo vt vitam aliis æternam vnquam promiserint. Argumentatio est: Abraham mortuus est, Prophetæ mortui sunt; At tu dicis te liberaturum alios à morte: Ergo teipsum facis maiorem Abrahamo & Prophetis. Atque hæc est eorum responsio & argumenta, Eam nos & singulas eius partes examinemus. Primum itaque quod concludunt ex eius verbis cum dæmonium habere, id non sequitur: cum concludendum fuisset eum veraci imò veracissimo spiritu imbutum ista loqui: sed ad alia: Consequens confirmat, quia ex iis ipsius verbis clarè consequitur eum se maiorem facere Abrahamo & Prophetis. Respondeo, valeat illud antecedens: & quidem verum est ea Christi verba illud non obscurè significare: non tamen sequitur quod ipsi inferre conantur. Vt autem de hac re paucis dicamus: Christus quidem dum in terris ageret, humilis ac vilis mundo visus est, & re ipsa se exinaniuit: verum in illa humilitate apparuit tamen maiestas Dei, quam vidit Iohannes noster. Speculavimus, inquit, gloriam eius, gloriam, inquam, vnigeniti egressi a Patre. Verba eius & facta eius plane stupenda arguebant homine maiorem ac augustiorem. Nunquam ita loquutus est quisquam vt ille. Abraham, Moses & Prophetæ serui erant in familia & domo Dei, & loquuti sunt vt serui: at Christus vt Filius præest domui suæ, & loquutus est vt Dominus. Scimus seruos quibus in familia aliqua provincia est demandata, imperare quidem, aliisque domesticis multa præcipere, sed non suo, verum Domini sui nomine & authoritate, omnia mandare ac præscribere. Ita hi de quibus loquimur Abraham Moses & Prophetæ loquuti sunt non suo, sed Domini sui nomine. At Christus, cum sit Dominus, loquutus est suo ipsius nomine. Eius rei exemplum habemus hoc ipso in loco, in quo promittit liberationem à morte iis té iis qui seruauerint sermonem ipsius. Nemo Prophetarum ita loquutus est vnquam, cùm ij passim proponăt seruandum sermonem, non suum, sed Domini tui: dictum Iehoua, inquiunt. At sermo quem proponit Christus nō minùs est à se quàm à Patre, ideóque tà quam suum proponit: qui seruauerit sermonem meum, inquit. Quare, vt redeam, sermo Christi satis arguebat eum maiorem homine, id quod & ipsi Iudæi aduersarij viderunt supra.Iohan.7.46. Qui enim missi erant à Pharisæis & sacerdotibus vtrisum prehenderent: Nullus vnquam homo loquutus est, inquiunt, vt homo iste. Et hi ipsi de quibus hic sermo est, ex verbis & promissione ipsius viderunt eum Abrahamo & quouis Prophetarum maiorem, sed id videre noluerunt laborantque in obscuranda ipsius gloria, quæ sese in oculos ipsorum ingerebat.
units.tr: The Jews are hardened even against the promise of life set before them, no less than against the reproach of their wretchedness, so that you may understand above all how difficult and arduous it is to soften and open a man's obstinate mind and heart, which is as it were shut. But let us see what they infer from this promise of Christ: "Now," of course, "we know that you have a demon." They prove the consequence from the fact that he has used words which make him greater than Abraham and the ancient prophets. This is what shows those words to be the words of a deceiving spirit. They ask this with indignation: "Are you greater than our father Abraham?" They prove the antecedent from the fact that Abraham is now dead, and the prophets themselves are dead: so far were they from ever promising eternal life to others. The argument is: Abraham is dead, the prophets are dead; but you say that you will free others from death; therefore you make yourself greater than Abraham and the prophets. This is their answer and their arguments. Let us examine it and each of its parts. First, then, the conclusion they draw from his words, that he has a demon, does not follow; the conclusion should have been that he is speaking under the influence of a true, indeed the truest, spirit. But they pass on to other points. The consequence is confirmed, because from his words it clearly follows that he makes himself greater than Abraham and the prophets. I answer: let the antecedent stand. It is indeed true that those words of Christ signify this not obscurely; but it does not follow what they try to infer from it. To say a few words on this matter: Christ, while he was living on earth, appeared humble and base to the world, and in fact he emptied himself. Yet in that humility there nevertheless shone forth the majesty of God, which our John saw: "We have beheld his glory," he says, "the glory, I say, of the only-begotten who came forth from the Father." His words and his deeds plainly showed him to be more than a man, and more majestic. "No one has ever spoken as this man does." Abraham, Moses and the prophets were servants in the household and house of God, and they spoke as servants; but Christ, as the Son, presides over his own house, and he spoke as Lord. We know that servants to whom some province of a household has been entrusted do give orders and prescribe many things to the other members of the household; but they do not command and prescribe everything in their own name and authority, but in the name and authority of their master. So Abraham, Moses and the prophets, of whom we speak, spoke not in their own name but in the name of their Lord. But Christ, since he is Lord, spoke in his own name. We have an example of this in this very passage, where he promises deliverance from death to those who keep his word. No prophet ever spoke in this way; they constantly set forth the word to be kept not as their own but as the word of your Lord: "Thus says the LORD," they say. But the word which Christ sets forth is no less his own than the Father's, and so he puts it forth as his own: "whoever keeps my word," he says. Therefore, to return to the point, the word of Christ sufficiently showed that he was greater than a man, as even the Jewish adversaries themselves saw above. For the men who had been sent by the Pharisees and chief priests to arrest him said, "No man has ever spoken as this man does" (John 7:46). And these very men of whom this discourse speaks saw from his words and promise that he was greater than Abraham and any of the prophets; but they were unwilling to see it, and they labour to obscure his glory, which forced itself upon their eyes.

units.la: Operæprecium est autem considerare quo demũ modo id conentur facere. Opponunt ex aduersò seruos Domino suo Abrahamum & Prophetas Christo: atque gloriolâ ipsis beneficio Domini communicatâ conatur obscurare Domini ipsius gloriam. Hoc itaque vetus est artificium diaboli, qui omnibus modis studet obscurare gloriam Filii Dei, ytpote in quo tanquam imagine eluceat gloria Patris, in quo etiam posita sit gloria tota hominum. Ex iis autem qui tam multi sunt modus hic vnus est, per quem etiam hodierno die efficax est in Papistis, qui Sanctis suis & Martyribus cum ignominia Christi diuinos honores deferunt: cuius quidem fundamentum est, vt verè dicam, non honor habitus Sanctis, non ficta illa submissio ac subiectio de qua Apostolus, Coloss.2.18.& 23. sed malitia aduersus Christum Dominum. Hostes enim sunt crucis Christi ac gratiæ, ac temere turgent carnis suæ sensu, vt ibidem loquitur Apostolus. Sed pergamus ad alia: non expectant fore vt Christus tantùm sibi sumat, vt dicat se maiorem Abrahamo & Prophetis. Itaque hoc probat, Abraham mortuus, itè Prophetæ mortui sunt: Ergo &c. Et hoc quoque argumentum vitiosum est ac laborat homonymia. Nam cùm Christus loquutus sit de morte illa spirituali, hi non nisi corporalem & temporariam hanc intelligunt. Christus cùm hic ageret in terris, ante oculos habuit perpetuò spiritualia illa, vt spiritualem mortem, vitam spiritualem habebat enim sensum plane spiritualem: de his igitur rebus perpetuo sermonem habuit, de his mundo loquutus est. Et re ipsa quidem quotquot sentiunt efficaciam Christi, sentiunt eam non tam ad vitam hanc sustinendam quàm ad illam alteram inchoandam & perficiendam suo tempore. Neque enim venit Christus ideo vt efficeret corpus animale, sed vt efficeret corpus spirituale. Est enim aliud corpus animale, aliud spirituale, ait Apostolus. Adam genuit animalia corpora, vt qui ipse animal viuum erat: Christus autem secundus Adam gignit corpora spiritualia, vt qui ipse fit Spiritus viuificus, vt vocatur ibidem ab Apostolo. Experientiam huius rei praebuit Apostolus in persona sua. Externus homo noster, inquit, corrumpitur, hoc est homo praeditus vita hac naturali & animali: at, inquit, interno (hoc est, spiritualis homo) renouatur quotidie. Sed unde haec renouatio? unde sit eodem illo capite prius docuit vers. 11. vt vita, inquit, Iesu manifesta fiat in mortali carne nostra, id quod ipse expertus est dum scripsit alibi, Si Christus habitat in vobis, corpus quidem mortuum est propter peccatum (id est, oportet quidem dissolui hoc corpus, idque propter peccatum penitus insitum, cuius stipendium est mors, vt dictum est ab eo alibi) Sed spiritus vita est, id est anima superuiuit post illam separationem ac corporis dissolutionem, idque propter iustitiam, nempe Christi, quae promerita est vitam animae, prout peccati meritum est mortem corpori. Verum ne putetur Christus seruator animae tantum non etiam corporis, subiicit continuo: Sed si Spiritus eius qui excitauit Iesum a mortuis habitat in vobis, &c. quo significat, quod si Spiritus Christi semel coeperit in nobis habitare, nunquam deserturus eum nos in posterum, ne quidem in sepulchro positos, sed tandem Deum per eum nos glorificaturum. Quare, vt redeam, efficacia Christi est ad vitam spiritualem, qua qui sentiunt, ij demum sunt qui intelligunt promissiones istas de vita, de liberatione a morte, fieri de rebus spiritualibus, easque pluris faciunt, quam si fierent de liberatione a morte hac, aut de conseruatione vitae huius. Carnales vero qui no sentiunt hanc efficaciaChristi, quae est ad nouam vitam, omnia metiuntur carnis suae sensu: neneque intelligunt promissiones has spirituales de rebus spiritualibus: aut si intelligant, non tamen iis assentiuntur, aut iis delectantur. Unde fit ut Christus & spirituales in eo benedictiones insipidae videantur crasso huic & carnali mundo, qui nihili facit quid quam praeter id quod carnalibus oculis videre & manibus contrectare potest. Atque ita examinata est a nobis eorum argumentatio: nunc videamus quid respondeat ad haec Dominus.
units.tr: It is worth considering, then, how exactly they try to do this. Over against Christ they set Abraham and the Prophets, servants of their Lord, and by means of a little glory granted to them by the Lord's kindness they try to obscure the Lord's own glory. This is therefore an old trick of the devil, who by every means strives to obscure the glory of the Son of God, in whom the glory of the Father shines as in an image, and in whom the whole glory of mankind is also placed. Among the many forms this takes, this is one, and it is still effective today among the Papists, who give divine honours to their Saints and Martyrs with dishonour to Christ. Its foundation is, to speak truly, not the honour paid to the Saints, nor that feigned submission and subjection of which the Apostle speaks in Coloss. 2.18 and 23, but malice against Christ the Lord. For they are enemies of the cross of Christ and of grace, and they puff themselves up idly with the sense of their flesh, as the Apostle says in the same place. But let us go on to other points. They do not expect that Christ would claim so much for himself as to say that he is greater than Abraham and the Prophets. So they prove this: Abraham is dead, and likewise the Prophets are dead; therefore etc. And this argument is faulty too, and suffers from an equivocation. For when Christ spoke of that spiritual death, they understand only this bodily and temporary death. Christ, while he was living on earth, always had before his eyes those spiritual things, such as spiritual death, and he had spiritual life, for he had a plainly spiritual sense; it was about these things, then, that he always spoke, and it was of these he taught the world. And indeed all who perceive the efficacy of Christ perceive it not so much for sustaining this life as for beginning and completing that other life in its time. For Christ did not come in order to produce an animal body, but to produce a spiritual body. For there is an animal body, and there is a spiritual body, says the Apostle. Adam begat animal bodies, since he himself was a living animal; but Christ, the second Adam, begets spiritual bodies, since he himself is a life-giving Spirit, as the Apostle calls him in the same place. The Apostle gave an experience of this in his own person. Our outward man, he says, is decaying, that is, the man endowed with this natural and animal life; but, he says, the inward man (that is, the spiritual man) is renewed day by day. But whence this renewal? Whence it comes he taught earlier in the same chapter, verse 11: that the life of Jesus, he says, might be made manifest in our mortal flesh; which he himself experienced when he wrote elsewhere: If Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin (that is, this body must indeed be dissolved, and that because of sin inherent in it through and through, whose wages is death, as he said elsewhere), but the spirit is life, that is, the soul survives that separation and dissolution of the body, and this because of righteousness, namely Christ's, which has merited life for the soul, just as sin has merited death for the body. But lest it be thought that Christ is the saviour of the soul only and not of the body too, he adds at once: But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, etc., by which he signifies that if the Spirit of Christ has once begun to dwell in us, he will never forsake us in future, not even when we are laid in the grave, but will at last glorify us before God through him. Wherefore, to return to the point: the efficacy of Christ is toward spiritual life, and only those who perceive it understand that those promises of life and of deliverance from death are made concerning spiritual things, and they value them more highly than if they were made concerning deliverance from this death or the preservation of this life. But carnal men, who do not perceive this efficacy of Christ which is toward new life, measure everything by the sense of their flesh; and they neither understand these spiritual promises as concerning spiritual things, or if they understand them, they do not assent to them or take delight in them. Hence it comes about that Christ and the spiritual blessings in him seem insipid to this gross and carnal world, which values nothing except what it can see with carnal eyes and handle with its hands. And so their argument has been examined by us; now let us see what the Lord answers to these things.

units.la: 54 Respondit Iesus, Si ego glorifico meipsum, gloria mea nihil est: Pater ille meus is est qui glorificat me, quem vos dicitis Deum vestrum esse.
units.tr: 54 Jesus answered, If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; it is my Father who glorifies me, whom you say is your God.

units.la: 55 Sed non novistis eum, ego vero ipsum novi: & si dixero ipsum mihi non esse notum, ero similis vestri, id est mendax: sed eum novi, & sermonem eius servo.
units.tr: 55 But you have not known him, but I know him; and if I should say that I do not know him, I should be like you, that is, a liar; but I know him, and I keep his word.

units.la: 56 Abrahamus Pater ille vester gestiit ut videret diem istum meum, & vidit & gavisus est.
units.tr: 56 Abraham, that father of yours, rejoiced that he would see my day; and he saw it and was glad.

units.la: Vrgat se primum ambitione quam ipsi obiecerunt: non negat quidem se maiorem Abrahamo & Prophetis esse: sed negat se a seipso glorificari, hoc est a seipso tantum glorificari, non praeunte Patre suo. Affirmat autem Patrem ipsum glorificare, hoc est, authorem esse glorificationis ipsius. Ideoque dictum est, Christum non tribuisse sibi hunc honorem ut fieret Pontifex, sed datum ipsi ab eo qui dixerat, Filius meus es tu, &c. Quo significat Apostolus, vocationem Christi ad officium Mediatoris a Patre authore fuisse, qui vocationem hanc Filii sui deinceps ornauit testimoniis variis, partim sua ipsius voce, partim voce Angelorum, partim autem voce hominum, voce autem imprimis praecursoris illius Iohanis Baptistae. Obserua igitur hoc loco non peccare eum qui quaerit honorem simpliciter, sed eum qui per ambitionem, hoc est per malas artes, sine authore Deo, eum venatur. David non purgat se quidem de gloria quoquomodo affectata, sed purgat se de ambitione: Iehoua, inquit, non fuit altum animus meus, neque elati oculi mei, &c. Quod si quis gloriam per ambitionem affectat, is audiat istud Christi sti hoc loco pronuntiantis gloriam illam nihil esse. Item illud Pauli dicentis, non qui semetipsum commendat probatus est, sed quem Dominus commendat. Videas quantopere de re nihili contendant ambitiosi isti. Quem vos dicitis Deum. Occupatio est, dici enim posset (id quod etiam supra obiectum est Christo) Quis est Pater ille tuus? huic occurrit Christus, eum ipsum esse Patrem suum, quem ipsi dixerunt Deum suum esse. Nota, non ait, Qui est Deus vester: Sed ait, quem vos dicitis Deum esse, hoc est falsò nuncupatis. Potuerunt quidem Iudæi & verbo & facto Deum Deíque omnia beneficia sibi vendicare iure fœderis, in quo promisit Deus Abrahamo se ipsi fore in Deum & semini ipsius. Quibus verbis se primum offert ipsi participandum, deinde omnes in se benedictiones. Potuerunt igitur isti Deum sibi vendicare iure fœderis: Sed ius illud amiserunt sua culpa; Mediatorem enim in quo percussum est fœdus reiecerunt. Tunc verbis sequentibus vel prætextum hunc diuini nominis illis adimit hoc argumento: Non nostis eum, ergo falsò dicitis eum Deum vestrum esse. Argumentum est à Dei notitia quæ non obtinetur nisi in imagine ipsius, nempe filio, qui est imago inconspicui Dei, & splendor gloriæ ac character personæ illius. Hunc filium cum ignorarent, Deum Patrem ignorare eos oportuit, sicut loquitur supra hoc cap. vers. 19. Patrem quoque meum nossetis, si me nossetis. Notitiam autem hoc loco non nudam intelligit, sed eam quæ est cum sensu Dei & misericordiæ ipsius internæ, qui extra Christum non consistit. Neque enim existit illa Dei in corde apprehensio, qua dicere quis potest, ex præscripto fœderis, Deum esse suum Deum: hæc, inquam, apprehensio sine Christo nonexistit. Glorietur de Deo, ut velint, vel Iudæi hodierno die, vel etiā Turcæ, pro Deo habent inane tantum nomen. Nota igitur inanem esse illam oris professionem de Deo, quæ sit sine notitia fidei quæ in corde est, ac proinde totam hac gloriationem ac professionem hoc uno verbo refutari posse: non nostis Deum. Ego autem novi eum. Vt Deum ibi-lis ademit: ita eum sibi contra vendicat; argumento à notitia quam ipse habet Dei sui. Vnigenitus qui est in sinu Patris, hoc est, in mirabili illa coniunctione cum Patre, nouit Patrem, nouit omnia eius secreta, nouit ac videt opera eius, vnde & Patris sapientia dicitur. Declarat autem hanc notitiam suam, vel potius professionem notitiae huius confirmat ab absurdo. Si dixero me eum non nosse, ero similis vestri, id est, mendax. Hoc est illud absurdum mendacium, nempe quod in eos a se transfert. Mendaces autem vocat eos, qui contra notitiam & mentis illuminationem loquuti sunt. Nota ergo quid sit proprie medacium in negotio veritatis ac religionis. Non tam mendacium est id, quod contra veritatem dicitur, (potest enim ex ignorantia dici,) quam quod contra veritatem agnitam dicitur: adeo ut Papista induratus adversus veritatem agnitam hodierno die, mendax sit potius dicendus, quam Turca, qui eandem illam veritatem negat. Quia hic ex ignorantia magis, ille ex obstinata malitia veritatem oppugnat. Hinc concludit ac profitetur palam se nouisse Deum. Sed novi eum, inquit. Huius notitiae argumentum assignat, nempe, quod seruet sermonem eius, obedientiam illam humillimam maximeque submissam a Filio incarnato, Patri suo praestitam significat. Verbum autem Dei explorat coniunctionem illam quae cum Deo intercedit. Prout enim unusquisque erga verbum affectus est, ita erga Deum ipsum affectus dicetur, Qui audit verbum eius, ipsumque seruat ex animo, is ostendit se cum Deo coniunctum esse fide ac dilectione. Per hoc scimus (inquit Iohannes) nos in ipso esse: nempe si sermonem eius seruauerimus. Qui verbum Dei non audit ipsum neque seruat, ostendit satis nihil sibi cum Deo negotij esse.
units.tr: He first presses the charge of ambition which they brought against him. He does not indeed deny that he is greater than Abraham and the Prophets; but he denies that he is glorified by himself, that is, that he is glorified by himself alone, without his Father going before. He affirms, however, that the Father himself glorifies him, that is, is the author of his glorification. And so it has been said that Christ did not assume this honour for himself, to become High Priest, but it was given to him by him who said, You are my Son, etc. By this the Apostle signifies that Christ's calling to the office of Mediator was from the Father as author, who afterwards adorned this calling of his Son with various testimonies, partly by his own voice, partly by the voice of angels, and partly by the voice of men, and above all by the voice of that forerunner John the Baptist. Observe therefore here that he sins not who seeks honour simply, but he who pursues it through ambition, that is, by wicked arts, without God as author. David does not indeed clear himself of glory sought in any way at all, but he clears himself of ambition: Lord, he says, my heart is not haughty, nor are my eyes lofty, etc. But if anyone seeks glory through ambition, let him hear Christ here pronouncing that glory to be nothing. Likewise that saying of Paul: not he who commends himself is approved, but he whom the Lord commends. You may see how greatly those ambitious men contend about a thing of no account. Whom you say is God. It is an occupatio: for one could say (as was also objected to Christ above), Who is that Father of yours? To this Christ replies that he himself is the Father's Son, whom they said was their God. Note: he does not say, Who is your God; but he says, whom you say is God, that is, whom you falsely name. The Jews indeed could, by word and deed, claim God and all God's blessings for themselves by right of covenant, in which God promised Abraham that he would be a God to him and to his seed. By these words he offers himself first to be shared, and then all blessings in himself. These men, then, could have claimed God for themselves by right of covenant; but they lost that right through their own fault, for they rejected the Mediator in whom the covenant was struck. Then, by the following words, he takes away from them even the pretext of the divine name, by this argument: You do not know him; therefore you falsely say that he is your God. The argument is from the knowledge of God, which is not obtained except in his image, namely the Son, who is the image of the invisible God, and the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person. Since they did not know this Son, they must have been ignorant of God the Father too, as he says above in this chapter, verse 19: You would have known my Father also, if you had known me. By knowledge here he means not bare knowledge, but that which is together with a sense of God and of his inward mercy, which does not exist apart from Christ. For that apprehension of God in the heart, by which one can say, according to the terms of the covenant, that God is his God, does not exist without Christ: this apprehension, I say, does not exist without Christ. Let the Jews today glory in God as they wish, or even the Turks, they hold only an empty name for God. Note, then, that that profession of God with the lips which is without the knowledge of faith which is in the heart is empty, and that consequently all this boasting and profession can be refuted with this single word: You do not know God. But I know him. As he took away God from them there, so he claims him for himself over against them, by an argument from the knowledge which he himself has of his God. The Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, that is, in that wonderful union with the Father, knows the Father, knows all his secrets, knows and sees his works, whence he is also called the wisdom of the Father. He declares this knowledge of his, or rather confirms by a reductio ad absurdum the profession of this knowledge: If I should say that I do not know him, I should be like you, that is, a liar. This is that absurd lie, namely the one he transfers from himself to them. He calls them liars who have spoken against knowledge and illumination of mind. Note therefore what a lie properly is in the matter of truth and religion. It is not so much a lie to say what is contrary to the truth (for this may be said out of ignorance) as to say what is contrary to truth already known: so that a Papist who is hardened against the truth now known is rather to be called a liar than a Turk who denies that same truth. For the one opposes the truth more out of ignorance, the other out of obstinate malice. From this he concludes and openly professes that he knows God. But I know him, he says. He assigns the proof of this knowledge, namely that he keeps his word, which signifies the most humble and most submissive obedience rendered by the incarnate Son to his Father. Now the word of God tests the union which exists with God. For just as each man's disposition toward the word is, so is it said to be toward God himself: he who hears his word and keeps it from the heart shows that he is joined to God by faith and love. By this we know (says John) that we are in him: namely if we keep his word. He who does not hear or keep the word of God shows well enough that he has nothing to do with God.

units.la: Hactenus ita digressus est post purgationem sui, tum redit ad institutum respondetque quod isti tanquam blasphemum acceperunt, se esse nimirum Abrahamo patre ipsorum maiorem: argumento autem ab illo defensio vehementi Abrahami videndi ipsum in carne, ostendit se maiorem eo, vel certe relinquit illud intelligendum. Abraham Pater vester. Patrem eorum appellat Abrahamum, quo indicet quam dissimiles sint Patri suo, qui Christum absentem tam serio desiderarit videre, cum ipsi praesentem eum auersentur. Gestiuit. Verbum ipsum significat desiderium ardens cum gaudio vehe-menti coniunctum. Quare desiderium Christi est cum gaudio: in causa est quòd non citiùs incipiamus desiderare Christum, &cœlestia illa, quàm eorum ex parte sal-tem aliqua fiamus participes. Nam is qui dat velle, dat quoque perficere. Christus ait, Qui esuriunt & sitiunt iusti-tiam, ipsi saturabuntur. Quo significat gustum saltem rei aliquem continuò sequi sitim ac desiderium Christi & beneficiorum eius. Quo autem hoc melius intelligamus, sciendum desiderium hoc perpetuò esse cum fide coniunctum, imo ex fide esse: fides autem perpetuò habet perceptionem aliquam & apprehensionem rei fide apprehensæ. Apprehensio autè ea est cum suauitate magna & gaudio incredibili, vt res plane suauis est ea quæ apprehenditur. Quid enim Christo suauius? Quare desiderium hoc complementi eius, quod interea ex parte per fidem apprehendimus, cum suauitate & gaudio sit oportet. Verum quidem illud est, desiderium hoc esse cũ dolore. Quid enim sibi volunt quæ locum habent inter desiderandum suspiria illa, sæpe etiam λαcτυγμᾶς? Paulus ait, In hoc suspiramus expetentes domicilio nostro superindui quod è cœlis est. Vide, desiderium cœlestis illius ædificij coniungit cum suspiriis. Est igitur illud verum, desiderium hoc coniungi cum dolore & suspiriis ex sensu peccati ac miseriæ, & ex eo quod nondum sit plena liberatio nostra. Imò cum inenarrabilibus suspiriis coniungit ipsum Paulus, dicens, Ipse spiritus interpellat pro nobis suspiriis inenarrabilibus. Sed hæc ipsa suspiria comitem habent lætitiam imò inenarrabilia suspiria coniunguntur cum gaudio ineffabili. Quare Petrus suspiriis illis Pauli inenarrabilibus è regione collocat gaudium ineffabile: Credentes, inquit, exultatis gaudio ineffabili ac glorioso. In desiderio igitur illo pij animi suspiria inenarrabilia & gaudium ineffabile mirificè coadunantur, suspiria, inquam, & gaudium, quę ne ipse quidem, qui ea sentit, potest plenè enarrare. Plus enim capit animus pij cuiusque, quàm potest os eloqui. Sed quid gestiuit Abraham videre? diem, inquit, istum meum, hoc est, tempus hoc illud primi aduentus Domini quod diei nomine insignitur: quòd is sit dies omnium mnium qui vnquam luxerunt præstantissimus. Cæterū metonymia est adiunċti pro subiecto: nam diei nomine intelligendus est ipse Christus incarnatus in tempore sine die illo manifestatus. Nunc autem quo intelligatur melius quod de Abrahamo dicitur ipsiúsque desiderio, fundamentum eius rei altius inquirendum est. Vnde igitur hoc tantum Abrahami desiderium? Sane ex nihilo existere non potuit. Vnde igitur profectum est? Paulus ait, nos qui sumus in hoc tabernaculo suspirare. Necesse igitur est desiderium & suspiria existant ex oneris alicuius sensu. Onus autem est peccati miseriæ ac mortalitatis huius, cuius meminit ibidem Paulus. Non est autem satis oneratum esse peccato & miseria: (Sumus enim omnes & singuli per naturam onerati peccato & morte:) sed oportet sit oneris huius sensus aliquis, ad hoc vt suspirius sit locus, & desiderium sit liberationis. Abrahamus igitur, si quis alius vnquam, oneratus fuit & serio sensu affectus miseriæ illius suę, quę est extra Christum, & re vera tota vita ista ipsi oneri fuit. Versatus enim est in perpetuis ærumnis vt apparet ex ipsius historia. Itaque ex sensu illius tanti onerts exstitit hoc desiderium ipsius. Sed cur desiderium fuit Christi? Sine Christo nullum est ab onere illo leuamen, Venite, inquit, ad me omnes, qui fatigati estis & onerati, & ego faciam vt requiescatis. Imò nulla alia ratione vllus vnquam Patrum onere suo leuatus est, quàm per eundem illum Mediatorem Christum, qui heri & hodie idem est & in sæcula. Quare Abrahamus desiderauit videre Christum in carne manifestatu. Legimus quidem de Abrahamo eum ardenti desiderio promissi illius seminis captum fuisse. An putandum est hoc tantum desiderium fuisse vel Isaaci vel seminis alicuius carnalis & mortalis, cuiusmodi vulgo solet esse hominum desiderium? Imo vero desiderium illud fuit capitis ipsius seminis benedicti quod ex se ventururum præcipuè promissum habuit. Promissio enim seminis fuit præcipuè Christi, in quo benedicendæ erant omnes gentes, cuius tanquam typum & figuram accepit filium Isaacum. In summa desiderium Abrahami fuit rerum præcipuè spiritualium, neque enim promissæ terræ tantò desiderio corripiebatur, quanto patriæ illius cælestis, cuius ea erat typus, unde Hebr. 11.10. Exspectabat urbem habentem fundamenta, cuius artifex & conditor est Deus. Urbem hanc habentem fundamenta opponit tetoriis illis, in quibus, inter p regrinandum in terra Canaan, degebat. Eiusmodi plane fuit desiderium aliorum Patrum omnium, nimirum rerum coelestium, Christi & benedictionum in eo. Unde Christus ipse latius hoc deciderunt extendit ad multos reges: Beati, inquit, oculi qui vident quae vos videtis. Dico enim vobis multos prophetas & reges cupiuisse videre quae vos videtis, nec vidisse, & audire quae vos auditis, nec audiuisse. Reges ipsi non putarunt sibi leviamen oneris sui in regnis suis fuisse, aut in tota huius mundi gloria positum, nisi simul Christi pacificatoris & Mediatoris dato aspectu aliquo: Et Prophetae quam anxie desiderarunt videre diem illum testatur Petrus, dum dicit eos scrutatos in quem aut cuiusmodi temporis articulum, praenuntius ille, qui in ipsis erat Spiritus Christi, declararet euentuas Christo perpessiones & gloriam illas consequuturam. Vide quantum desiderium fuerit omnium piorum omnibus seculis Christi primum in carne manifestandi, hoc est inchoatae tantum felicitatis. Quantum igitur debet esse desiderium Christi secundo venturi, hoc est perfectae beatitatis nostrae?
units.tr: Having thus digressed after clearing himself, he now returns to his subject and answers what they took as blasphemy: that he is greater than their father Abraham. To support that claim, from Abraham's eager longing to see him in the flesh, he shows that he is greater than Abraham, or at least leaves that to be understood. Abraham your father. He calls Abraham their father to show how unlike their father they are, since Abraham longed so earnestly to see Christ when he was absent, while they turn away from him now that he is present. Rejoiced. The word itself signifies an ardent desire joined with intense joy. Therefore the desire for Christ comes with joy. The reason is that we do not begin to desire Christ and those heavenly things sooner than we become in some measure partakers of them. For he who gives the will also gives the power to accomplish. Christ says, Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled. By this he means that some taste of the thing itself always follows the thirst and longing for Christ and his benefits. To understand this better, we should note that this desire is always joined with faith, indeed comes from faith, and faith always has some perception and apprehension of the thing it apprehends. This apprehension is accompanied by great sweetness and incredible joy, since the thing apprehended is altogether sweet. For what is sweeter than Christ? So this desire for that fullness of him, which we in part apprehend by faith in the meantime, must be accompanied by sweetness and joy. It is true, however, that this desire is also accompanied by sorrow. For what do those sighs mean, which occur among the longings, often even tears? Paul says, In this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our habitation which is from heaven. See, Paul joins the desire for that heavenly building with sighs. It is therefore true that this desire is joined with sorrow and sighs, arising from the sense of sin and misery and from the fact that our deliverance is not yet complete. Indeed Paul joins it with inexpressible sighs when he says, The Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. But these very sighs have joy as their companion; indeed inexpressible sighs are joined with unspeakable joy. Hence Peter sets unspeakable joy over against Paul's inexpressible sighs: you believe, he says, and rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. In that desire, then, the godly soul's inexpressible sighs and unspeakable joy are wonderfully united: sighs, I say, and joy, which not even the one who feels them can fully describe. For the mind of every godly person holds more than the mouth can express. But what did Abraham long to see? My day, he says, that is, that time of the first coming of the Lord which is marked by the name of day, because that day is the most outstanding of all the days that have ever dawned. Yet this is metonymy of the adjunct for the subject, for by the name of the day we are to understand Christ himself, incarnate in time and made manifest on that day. Now, to understand better what is said of Abraham and his desire, the ground of this matter must be sought more deeply. Whence, then, came this so great desire of Abraham? Certainly it could not arise from nothing. Whence, then, did it proceed? Paul says, we who are in this tabernacle groan. It is necessary, then, that the desire and the sighs arise from a sense of some burden. The burden is the sin and misery and mortality of this life, which Paul also mentions in that place. Yet it is not enough to be burdened with sin and misery (for we are all, each one of us, burdened by nature with sin and death), but there must also be some sense of this burden, so that there is room for sighing and a desire for deliverance. Abraham, then, if anyone ever was, was burdened and seriously affected by a sense of that misery of his which is outside Christ, and in truth his whole life was a burden to him. For he lived in constant hardships, as appears from his history. Therefore the desire arose from his sense of so great a burden. But why was the desire for Christ? Without Christ there is no relief from that burden. Come to me, he says, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Indeed, no one of the Fathers was ever relieved of his burden by any other means than through that same Mediator Christ, who is the same yesterday, today and forever. Therefore Abraham desired to see Christ manifested in the flesh. We read indeed that Abraham was seized with an ardent desire for that promised seed. Must we think that this desire was only for Isaac, or for some carnal and mortal seed, of the sort that men's common desires usually are? Nay, rather that desire was for the head of the blessed seed itself, which was chiefly promised as coming from him. For the promise of the seed was chiefly of Christ, in whom all nations were to be blessed, and of whom he received his son Isaac as a type and figure. In sum, Abraham's desire was for chiefly spiritual things. For he was not seized with so great a desire for the promised land as for that heavenly homeland, of which the land was a type; whence Heb. 11:10: He looked for a city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God. He sets this city with foundations over against those tents in which he dwelt while sojourning in the land of Canaan. Plainly of this kind was the desire of all the other Fathers, namely for heavenly things, for Christ and the blessings in him. Hence Christ himself extends this more widely to many kings: Blessed are your eyes, for they see what you see. For I tell you that many prophets and kings have desired to see what you see and have not seen it, and to hear what you hear and have not heard it. The kings themselves did not think that relief for their burden lay in their kingdoms or in all the glory of this world, unless at the same time they had some sight of Christ the peacemaker and Mediator. And how earnestly the prophets desired to see that day Peter bears witness, when he says that they searched into what time or what kind of time that prophetic Spirit of Christ, who was in them, was signifying, which would bring the sufferings of Christ and the glory that would follow. See how great was the desire of all the godly in all ages to see Christ first manifested in the flesh, that is, of a happiness only begun. How great, then, ought to be our desire for the coming again of Christ, that is, for our perfect blessedness?

units.la: Hactenus de desiderio Abrahami, sequitur eius effectus, Et vidit, inquit, scilicet diem meum: vide igitur cum desiderio fruitionem rei desideratae aliquam coniunctam esse. Sed quomodo vidit Abraham diem Christi? hoc est, primum eius aduentum? vidit quidem Christum, sed venturum, non praesentem: Vidit eum in promissione: Vidit e longinquo fidei oculis: de qua visione, Heb. 11. Neque vidit tantum venturum Christum, sed simul cum intuitu illo cor ipsius dilatatum est, ut Christum illum venturum eminus apprehenderet: Estque haec apprehensio illa fidei. Ex hac autem apprehensione sequuta est Christi in eo efficacia ad gaudium & ad alia, ut mortificationem, vivificationem, &c. Sed gaudium hoc imprimis nominavit Euangelista & pacem conscientiae, quia praecipuum hoc effectum est apprehensi Christi ac iustitiae eius. Iustificati enim fide, pacem habemus erga Deum. Gaudium igitur concepit animo Abrahamus hamus ex inspecto eminus ac apprehenso Christo. Hoc gaudiū illud est, quod absorbet omnes huius vitæ molestias ac difficultates: quod quidem Abrahamum comitatum est ad sepulchrum usque. Nota igitur Christum hominem, Christi mortem, Christi resurrectionem, non modò tum demum cœpisse efficacia esse in membris ipsius, cum ipse incarnatus est, mortuus, resurrexit reipsa: Sed efficaciam hac ac virtutem Christi hominis ab initio fuisse. Est enim Agnus ille maactatus ab origine mundi. Et Iesus Christus heri & hodie idem est, ac in sæcula. Quæ verba de perpetua illa quæ iam inde ab initio fuit virtute Mediatoris & Christi etiam hominis accipienda sunt. Sed obiicies fortasse hoc loco: Qui fit ut dicat Abrahamum vidisse Christum & gauisum, cum desiderio multorum regum & prophetarum non fuisse satisfactum dicat Christus? Nec, inquit, viderunt ea, neque audierunt ea quæ videtis & auditis. Responsio est manifesta ex eo ipso loco: Non viderunt neque audiuerunt ea quæ Apostoli eodem certè modo, id est, non plenè viderunt & audiuerunt. Viderunt quidem è longinquo, non autem ex propinquo, quomodo dicitur hoc loco Abraham vidisse: ex quo sequitur, neque eos percepisse tantum fructus ac virtutis ex Christo, quantum Apostoli & ætates illæ hominum, quæ eius primum aduentum subsequuntur sunt. Unde beatos esse Apostolos præ regibus illis ac Prophetis prædicat Dominus. Et Petrus ait Prophetas prædixisse gratiam in nos venturam. Nam licet Christus efficax semper fuerit iam inde ab initio, tamen maior extitit eius efficacia posteaquam iam manifestatus, iam passus & glorificatus fuit, quàm vnquam antea. Maior igitur est beatitas nostra quàm Patrum, maiorque efficacia offertur nunc nobis, quàm tum olim patribus. Maiorem itaque oportet esse ingratitudinem non recipientium tantam gratiam.
units.tr: So far concerning Abraham's desire; there follows its effect: And he saw, it says, my day. See, then, that with desire some enjoyment of the desired thing is joined. But how did Abraham see the day of Christ? That is, his first coming? He indeed saw Christ, but as one who was to come, not as present. He saw him in the promise, he saw him from afar with the eyes of faith. Of that vision, Heb. 11 speaks. And not only did he see Christ as coming, but at the same time as he looked, his heart was enlarged so that he apprehended from afar that Christ who was to come, and this apprehension is that faith. From this apprehension there followed in him the efficacy of Christ for joy and for other things, such as mortification, vivification, and so on. But the evangelist names this joy especially, and the peace of conscience, because this is the chief effect of apprehending Christ and his righteousness. For being justified by faith, we have peace with God. Abraham therefore conceived joy in his mind from beholding Christ from afar and apprehending him. This is the joy that swallows up all the troubles and difficulties of this life, and it indeed accompanied Abraham even to the grave. Note, therefore, that Christ as man, the death of Christ, the resurrection of Christ, did not begin to be effective in his members only when he was actually incarnate, dead and risen. Rather the efficacy and power of Christ as man was there from the beginning. For he is the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world. And Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever. These words are to be understood of that perpetual power of the Mediator and of Christ as man, which has existed from the beginning. But perhaps you will object here: how is it that Christ says Abraham saw Christ and rejoiced, when he says that the desire of many kings and prophets was not satisfied? Nor, he says, did they see the things that you see and hear the things that you hear. The answer is plain from that very passage: they did not see or hear the things that the Apostles saw and heard, at least not in the same way, that is, they did not see and hear them fully. They indeed saw from afar, but not from near, as Abraham is here said to have seen. From this it follows that they did not receive as much fruit and power from Christ as the Apostles and those generations of men which followed his first coming. Hence the Lord declares the Apostles blessed above those kings and prophets. And Peter says that the prophets foretold the grace that would come to us. For although Christ was always efficacious from the beginning, yet his efficacy has been greater since he was manifested, suffered and glorified, than it ever was before. Our blessedness, therefore, is greater than that of the Fathers, and greater efficacy is now offered to us than was offered to the fathers of old. Therefore the ingratitude of those who do not receive so great a grace must be all the greater.

units.la: 57 Dixerunt igitur ei Iudæi, Quinquaginta annos nondum habes, & Abrahamum vidisti?
units.tr: 57 The Jews therefore said to him, "You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?"

units.la: 58 Dixit eis Iesus, Amen, amen dico vobis, priusquam Abrahamus existeret ego sum.
units.tr: 58 Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly I say to you, before Abraham was, I am."

units.la: {a} Apocal. 1.
units.tr: {a} Apocal. 1.

units.la: 59 Sustulerunt ergo Iudæi lapides vt iacerent in eum: Iesus autem occultauit se & exiuit e templo, quum transiuisset per medios ipsos, & ita praeterijt.
units.tr: 59 Then they took up stones to throw at him. But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple, passing through the midst of them, and so went on his way.

units.la: RESpondent Iudæi, sed nihil ad id quod ab ipso propositum fuit. Videtur illis plane impossibile & ridiculum quod dixit de Abrahamo, quòd vel is ipsum viderit, vel ipse Abrahamum. Ratio est ab aetate ipsius, Nam nondum attigit annum quinquagesimum: Verum quidem est, nondum attigisse Dominum annum tricesimum quartum (nam post annum tricesimum tertium cum dimidio Christus sublatus est è terris) Verum hoc illi largiuntur, cum iam prope attingere annum quinquagesimum; Non potuisse tamen fieri affirmant, vt viderer Abrahamum. Quo quidem responso corporalem hunc aspectum intelligunt, cum Dominus de spirituali & fidei aspectu loquutus sit. Qui nihil vident spiritualiter, illi omnia carnali & corporali suo sensu metiuntur, neque intelligunt loquentes de aspectu spirituali aut de rebus caelestibus, frustraque cum iis de rebus huiusmodi sermo confertur, nisi visum sit interea Domino aperire eorum oculos. Si eum aspectum habuissent, quem de Abrahamo praedicat Christus, longe secus ipsum fuissent interpretati. Verum quidem illud est, vidisse eos Christum corpore praesentem, eaque re superiores fuisse Abrahamo & Patribus ipsis, quibus ea gratia non fuit concessa, sed illum aspectum sibi inutilem reddiderunt (de corporali aspectu loquor) quia vnicum eo non coniunxerunt illi fidei & interioris hominis intuitum. Neque enim beatitudo illa quam praedicat Christus de videntibus se, accipienda est de aspectu duntaxat corporali & exterioris hominis: verum vel multo magis de aspectu spirituali & interioris hominis: quem quidem excitare in nobis oportet exterior ille & corporalis aspectus. Quorsum enim attinet videre Christum praesentem hisce oculis corporeis, nisi externus aspectus excitet internum, faciatque vt cor nostrum ad ipsum magis se applicet? Vt autem haec rem in summam contrahamus: triplex omnino est Christi aspectus: primum est aspectus spiritualis duntaxat, qualis fuit ille Patrum, qualis etiam est hic noster hodierno die. Quem cum non cernatis, ait Petrus, hunc aspectu sequitur sua quae dam beatitas: Vnde Christus ad Thomam: Beati qui non viderunt & crediderunt. Alter aspectus est non modo spi- ritualis sed & corporalis, qualis fuit Apostolorum & aliorum qui in primo Domini adventu vixerunt, qualis quoque futurus est noster in illo die secundi adventus eius: hic aspectus vere beatos efficit, esque ea beatitas quam praedicat Christus. Tertius denique aspectus est corporalis duntaxat, qui ex se quidem beatus est, sed quia caret aspectu illo spirituali qui est per fidem, nihilo facit beatiores homines. Quid enim ad beatitudinem profuit istis Christus aspectus, vel Christi corporalis praesentia: Et quid quaeso proderit reprobis gloriosa illa eius praesentia in illo die, a qua ipsi tantopere abhorrebunt? Quare imprimis laborandum est illuminentur mentis oculi in hac vita, quibus videmus Christum ac in eo benedictiones, hoc est credamus tantisperdum cum praesentem viderimus etiam oculis istis corporeis, & cum eo iam perfecte beati in aeternum habitaverimus: huic sit omnis gloria, Amen. Dicit eis Iesus. Videbatur iis ridiculum quod dixit se ab Abrahamo visum aut Abrahamum ab ipso conspectum vnquam, nam haec in idem recidunt. Causa fuit, quod nondum attigerat annum quinquagesimum. Ideoque his verbis Dominus ostendit iis se antiquum antiquiorem Abrahamo, & antiquum illum dierum esse: sicut vocatur Dan.7.9. Causa autem cur ei tam paucos annos conscripserint, erat quia piditi tantum oculo carnis externam illam carnem Christi a Deitate inhabitante assumptam tantum intuebantur. Ideoque Dominus introducit eos ad videndum Deitatem (fieri possit) quiddam altius & diuinius, quam quod corporali-sensu carnis percipi queat, quod solis fidei oculis con- spicitur. Demonstrat iis deitatem illam corporaliter in ipso habitantem & eam quidem aeternam. Demonstrat iis incarnationis etiam suae vim & efficaciam, quae ab initio fuit: Iesus Christus idem est heri & hodie idem ac in secula: Et agnus est immolatus inde ab origine mundi. Haec Christi verba de Deitate ipsius proprie accipiam. Sed videamus verba.
units.tr: The Jews reply, but their answer has nothing to do with what Christ had said. It seems to them quite impossible and ridiculous that he said of Abraham either that he had seen him or that Abraham had seen him. The reason is his age, for he had not yet reached fifty years. It is true that the Lord had not yet reached thirty-four years of age (for Christ was taken from the earth after he had passed thirty-three and a half years). But the Jews grant this, since he was nearly fifty, and they say only that it could not be that he had seen Abraham. In this answer they understand a bodily sight, although the Lord was speaking of a spiritual sight, that is, of sight by faith. Those who see nothing spiritually measure everything by their carnal and bodily sense. They do not understand those who speak of spiritual sight or of heavenly things, and talk about such matters with them is wasted, unless the Lord is pleased in the meantime to open their eyes. Had they possessed the sight of which Christ speaks concerning Abraham, they would have interpreted him very differently. It is true that they saw Christ present in the body, and for that reason were superior to Abraham and the Fathers, to whom that grace was not granted. But they made that sight useless to themselves (I am speaking of bodily sight), because they did not join to it the sight of faith and of the inner man. For the blessedness that Christ describes in those who see him is not to be understood of bodily sight alone and of the outward man, but much more of spiritual sight and of the inner man. That outward and bodily sight ought indeed to stir this up in us. For what use is it to see Christ present with these bodily eyes, unless the outward sight stirs up the inward, and makes our heart apply itself more closely to him? To sum up the matter: there is altogether a threefold sight of Christ. The first is spiritual sight only, such as that of the Fathers, and such as ours is today. Peter says that, although we do not see him, a certain blessedness follows this sight, whence Christ says to Thomas: Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed. The second sight is not only spiritual but also bodily, such as that of the Apostles and of others who lived at the first coming of the Lord, and such as ours will be on the day of his second coming. This sight truly makes men blessed, and this is the blessedness which Christ proclaims. Finally, the third is bodily sight only, which in itself is indeed a blessing, but because it lacks that spiritual sight which is by faith, it makes men no more blessed. For what benefit to those men was the sight of Christ, or the bodily presence of Christ? And what, I ask, will his glorious presence on that day profit the reprobate, from which they will shrink so greatly? Therefore, above all, we must labour in this life that the eyes of the mind be enlightened, by which we see Christ and the blessings in him. That is, we must believe, until we have seen him present even with those bodily eyes, and have dwelt with him in perfect blessedness for ever. To him be all glory, Amen. Jesus said to them. It seemed ridiculous to them that he said he had ever been seen by Abraham, or that Abraham had ever been seen by him, for these come to the same thing. The cause was that he had not yet reached fifty years. So by these words the Lord showed them that he was older than Abraham, and that he is the Ancient of Days, as he is called in Daniel 7:9. But the reason they counted him as having so few years was that they looked only with the eye of the flesh upon that external flesh of Christ, assumed by the indwelling Deity. Therefore the Lord leads them to see (it may be) something higher and more divine than can be perceived by the bodily sense of the flesh, something that is discerned only by the eyes of faith. He shows them that Deity dwelling bodily in him, and that it is eternal. He shows them also the power and efficacy of his own incarnation, which has been from the beginning: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and for ever, and the Lamb has been slain from the foundation of the world. I will take these words of Christ properly of his Deity. But let us look at the words themselves.

units.la: Amen, Amen, inquit. Grauis est asseueratio ad certitudinem & fidem rei quam pronuntiaturus est, Priusquam Abraham fieret. Non air esset, est enim hoc verbum pro prië essentiae eius, quae est per se, cuiusmodi est solus Dei essentia. Ideoque ei in scripturis verbum hoc quod vocant substantiuum peculiariter attribui solet: vt & Christus statim post hoc verbum de te enuntiabit. Ergo non ait priusquam esset, sed, fierem, inquit. Verbum enim in Graeco est γενέσθαι: quod significat fieri vel nasci proprie. Quo verbo significatur quidem essentia, sed ea quae quidem non est per se, verum per alium & per ipsum per quem omnia facta sunt quae facta sunt: de se autem quod ait, Ego sum verbum, Esse quod sibi attribuit, significat se essentiam habere per se, & non per alium, vt qui sit Deus. Sed notandum quod dicit in praesenti Sum, non in praeterito Fui. Verbo hoc praesentis temporis significatur temporis continuatio & aeternitas. Quanquam alibi in Apocalypsi aeternitas haec essentiae diuinae in Christo verbis trium temporum circumscribatur, Qui est, inquit, & qui erat, & qui venturus est. Ergo hoc verbo significatur duo, primum essentia quae per se est, deinde essentia quae ab aeterno est. Ideoque fit, vt idem hic Christus noster se nominauerit Mosi, Ehje, hoc est, Qui sum. Dic, inquit, filiis Israel, quod Eheje misit te. Vide igitur in hoc responso quam longo latoque interuallo sese praeferat Christus Abrahamo, contraque Abrahamu sibi postponat. Vt hinc discamus hominem cum Deo non esse parem, neque faciendam esse comparationem creaturae cum creatore benedicto in secula. Amen. Creatura habet essentiam suam aliunde, nempe a Deo, neque per se est: at Deus per se est. Creatura est in tempore: Deus est ab aeterno. Ideoque evanescat omnis creatura in conspectu eius: Pulvis fit & cinis coram eo, vt hic ipse Abraham de se ipse dixit, dum Angelum, qui fuit Christus, alloqueretur. Quo quidem significauit indignum se esse qui consisteret in conspectu eius, & qui ipsum coram alloqueretur.
units.tr: Amen, amen, he says. It is a solemn affirmation, given to make certain and to confirm the thing he is about to pronounce: Before Abraham was, I am. He does not say "was," for this word is used of the proper essence of God, which is self-existent, such as the essence of God alone is. Therefore in the Scriptures this word, which they call the substantive, is commonly attributed to him in a special way, as Christ also afterwards pronounces this word of himself after this. So he does not say "before he was," but "before I was born," he says. For the word in Greek is γενέσθαι, which properly means to become or to be born. This word signifies an essence, but one that is not self-existent. It is rather from another, and through him through whom all things that were made were made. But when he says of himself, "I am," the I am which he attributes to himself signifies that he has his essence of himself and not from another, as God does. It should be noted that he says I am in the present tense, not "I was" in the past. By this word of the present tense is signified the continuity and eternity of time. Although elsewhere in the Apocalypse this eternity of the divine essence in Christ is marked by the words of three tenses: He who is, he says, and who was, and who is to come. So two things are signified by this word: first, the essence which is of itself, and second, the essence which is from eternity. Hence it comes about that this same Christ of ours named himself to Moses as Ehyeh, that is, I am. Say, he says, to the sons of Israel, that Ehyeh has sent you. See, then, in this answer, by how long and broad an interval Christ sets himself above Abraham, and places Abraham beneath himself. Let us learn from this that man is not equal to God, and that no comparison is to be made between the creature and the Creator, blessed for ever. Amen. The creature has its essence from elsewhere, namely from God, and is not of itself; but God is of himself. The creature is in time; God is from eternity. Therefore every creature must vanish in his sight: it becomes dust and ashes before him, as Abraham himself said of himself when he addressed the Angel, who was Christ. By this he signified that he was unworthy to stand in his sight, and to speak with him face to face.

units.la: Sustulerunt ergo. Hic effectus est responsionis Christi in incredulis istis. Paulatim indurescentes toto tempore huius dialogi tandem abeunt in apertam rabiem. Is est finis indurationis aduersus Christum & lucem Euangelij. Indurati tandem insaniunt, vt de persequutoribus illis Stephani dictum est Act.7.54. Frendebant cordibus & stridebant dentibus in eum, & postea vers.57. Exclamantes autem illi voce magna, continuerunt aures suas, & irruerunt concorditer in eum. Hanc rabiem Papistae vocant zelum. Hic igitur est zelus Papistarum rabies plusquam canina, qua saeuiunt in sanctos Dei Martyres. Isti quidem quibuscum Christo res cum erat, zelum aliquem potuerunt praetexere, zelum Abrahami, zelum Dei, zelum legis. Nam ex legeblasphemus quisque lapidandus fuit. Sed quis tamen dixerit verum hunc zelum fuisse? Paulus ipse zelu illum suum quo persequutus est initio Christianos, furorem vocauit in Apologia illa sua habita coram Agrippa rege: Et supra modum, inquit, furens aduersus eos, &c. Zelus quidem iste Pauli ex ignorantia fuit, vt ipse ait de se, Nam, inquit, ignorans id faciebam, & tamen rabies fuit ipso teste. Quanto magis est zelus Papistarum qui ex corde aduersus veritatem obdurato proficiscitur, quanto, inquam, magis rabies dicenda est, & ea quidem maliciosa. Quid tum Christus? Iesus, inquit, occultauit se. Hoc infirmitati humanae tribuendum. Quid tum? Exiuit e templo, quum transiuisset. Quod sic euaserit, proculdubio potentiae Dei in ipso habitantis, tribuendum. Quare in hac liberatione ita exerit vim suam Deus in Christo, vt interea locum aliquem relinquat humanae infirmitati. Ita oportuit cum gloria illa ac potentia Christi Dei coiunctam esse infirmitatem Christi hominis, ita, inquit, oportuit fieri nostra causa. Quod si enim statim maiestas illa Dei in Christo sese manifestasset, vt in resurrectione illa & assensione gloriosa factum est, tum profecto nulla vis ei afferri potuisset, neque crucifixus vnquam fuisset. Quamobrem nostra gloria est in infirmitate eius: Idcoque quoties aliquid huiusmodi quod infirmitatem in eo aliquam significat, occurrit: nos in eo continuo gloriemur. Exiuit, inquit, e templo. Ergo reliquit Iudaeis templum suum sine Christo illo, nimirum in quo corporaliter inhabitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis: qualia nimirum in regno Antichristi sunt hodierno die templa.
units.tr: Therefore they took up. This is the effect of Christ's answer upon these unbelievers. Gradually hardening throughout this whole dialogue, they at last break out into open fury. This is the end of hardening against Christ and the light of the gospel. Being hardened, they finally rage, as was said of the persecutors of Stephen in Acts 7:54: They gnashed their teeth at him with their hearts, and afterwards in verse 57: But they, crying out with a loud voice, held their ears shut, and rushed together upon him. The Papists call this fury zeal. So this is the zeal of the Papists, a rage more than canine, with which they rage against the holy martyrs of God. Those with whom Christ had to do could at least pretend some zeal: the zeal of Abraham, the zeal of God, the zeal of the law. For by the law every blasphemer was to be stoned. But who would say that this zeal was true? Paul himself, in his defence delivered before King Agrippa, called the zeal with which he at first persecuted Christians a fury: And being exceedingly mad against them, and so on. Paul's zeal was indeed from ignorance, as he himself says of himself: For I did it, he says, in ignorance; and yet it was a rage, by his own testimony. How much more is the zeal of the Papists, which proceeds from a heart hardened against the truth, to be called rage, and indeed malicious rage! What then did Christ do? Jesus, it says, hid himself. This must be attributed to human weakness. What then? He went out of the temple, passing through. That he escaped in this way must without doubt be attributed to the power of God dwelling in him. Therefore in this deliverance God so exerts his power in Christ that he leaves some room in the meantime for human weakness. So it was necessary, he says, that the weakness of Christ the man should be joined with that glory and power of Christ God; so, he says, it was necessary to happen for our sake. For if that majesty of God had at once manifested itself in Christ, as happened in that glorious resurrection and ascension, then surely no violence could have been done to him, nor would he ever have been crucified. Wherefore our glory is in his weakness; and so whenever something of this kind occurs which signifies some weakness in him, we shall continually glory in him. He went out, he says, of the temple. So he left to the Jews their temple without that Christ, in whom, namely, dwells bodily all the fullness of the Deity. Such are the temples today in the kingdom of Antichrist.

units.la: Mendacii doctoribus & discipulis. illa Papistarũ, cum tota illa externa sua pōpa & gloria. Quare quoties de his deque eorum externa illa gloria aliquid prædicari aut ostentari audimus, dicamus toties sine Christo esse ea, & sepulchra esse potius fœtida, in quibus sepulti iacent mortui, quàm templa, in quibus viui Deum suum laudant per Iesum Christum, cui sit omnis gloria in sæcula, Amen.
units.tr: Teachers and disciples of falsehood: those of the Papists, with all their external pomp and glory. So whenever we hear anything proclaimed or displayed about these things, and about their external glory, let us say that they are without Christ every time, and that they are rather foul sepulchres, where dead men lie buried, than temples, in which the living praise their God through Jesus Christ, to whom be all glory for ever, Amen.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Hoc capite, 1. habes miraculum apertionis oculorum cuiusdam hominis qui cæcus erat à natiuitate ad 8. verf. vsque. 11. quæ miraculum subsequuta sunt ad finem capitis.
units.tr: In this chapter you have, first, the miracle of opening the eyes of a man who had been blind from birth, up to verse 8. Second, the things that followed the miracle, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Primùm, vicini quibus notus erat cæcus, quærüt de facto miraculoso, adducúntque hominem ad Pharisæos à verf. 8. vsque ad verf. 14. Secundò, Pharisæi inquirunt de rei gesta veritate, & cũ sanato altercantur de Christo vsque ad verf. 35. Tertiò, Christus se sanato plenius patefacit ad verf. 39. Quartò, Christus Pharisæis cæcitatem voluntariam exprobrat.
units.tr: First, the neighbours, who knew the blind man, ask about the miraculous deed and bring the man to the Pharisees, from verse 8 to verse 14. Second, the Pharisees inquire into the truth of the deed, and dispute with the healed man about Christ, down to verse 35. Third, Christ reveals himself more fully to the healed man, at verse 39. Fourth, Christ rebukes the Pharisees for their wilful blindness.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: 1. ET cùm transiret vidit quendam cæcum à natiuitate:
units.tr: 1. And as he passed by, he saw a man who was blind from birth.

units.la: 2. Et interrogauerunt eum discipuli eius, dicentes, Rabbi, quis peccauit, iste, an parentes eius, vt cæcus nasceretur?
