units.tr: 2. And his disciples asked him, saying, Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?

units.la: IDEAMVS igitur primum miraculum. Ante miraculum, primùm occurrit eius occasio statim primo versu: deinde est communicatio quædam Christi & discipulorum ipsius mutua, qua instruitur discipuli & præparantur ad miraculum illud tantum recipiendum. De occasione igitur vt dicam hæc est: Christus egressus iam è templo & prætereicns,
units.tr: Let us therefore consider the first miracle. Before the miracle itself, its occasion comes first, in the very first verse, and then there is a certain mutual conversation between Christ and his disciples, by which the disciples are instructed and prepared to receive that miracle. As to the occasion, then, this is what I say: Christ, having now gone out of the temple and passing by,

units.la: Prima pars: in qua occurrunt miraculum antecedētia. teriens, vidit quendam cæcum : non euenit hoc forte-fortuna, vt putari posset, sed destinato Dei consilio. Nõ præterit nos Christus, non prætereundo intuetur nos nunquam temere Dominus; vidit cæcum à natiuitate. Circumstantia hæc temporis, quo percussus fuit hic homo cæcitate, ostendit malum illud incurabile fuisse, acproinde amplificat hoc opus Christi. Nam Christus quo maiora conspicerentur opera eius, quóque magis appareret potentia Dei in ipso, ad fidem spectantium, manum admouere solitus est ad eos morbos & infirmitates, quæ nulla vel arte vel potestate creaturæ curari aut restitui potuerunt. Nam quòd ad diaboli miracula, ego in ea sententia sum, non posse eum ordinem naturæ immutare in operibus suis, ad confirmandum mendacia, comparatis. Nam ea sola est Dei potentia qua inuertit naturæ ordinem, quam diabolo (meo iudicio)nõ accommodat ad mendacia stabilienda. Quod apparet ex eo quod dicetur hoc capite postea versu 31. Scimus Deum peccatores, hoc est falsos doctores & mendaces, non audire. Et postea vers.33. Nisi esset hic à Deo, non posset quicquam facere. Et interrogarunt. Sequitur mutuo habitus sermo Christi & discipulorum, vti diximus. Primum interrogant eum discipuli de cæco illo. Postquam, vt videtur, sermonem aliquem cum ipso contulerunt de hominis cæcitate, intellexerúntque iam inde à natiuitate cæcum, Rabbi, inquiunt, quis peccauit, &c. Sensus est, quasi dicant: Scimus id quidem peccatum in causa esse cur iste cæcus iam inde à prima natiuitate sua exiterit. Sed hoc quærimus; Cuiúsnam peccatum fuit, ipsiúsne hominis peccatum, an verò peccatum parentum? De hominis autem peccato, Qui fieri potuerit vt hominis ipsius peccatum procurauerit hanc cæcitatem, non videmus : peccare enim non potuit priusquam natus esset. Percussus est autem cæcitate hac inde ab vtero matris. De peccato verò parentum eius; Non videmus qua ratione puniat Deus in vno homine quod ab altero commissum est. Quare in hac re profitemur ignorantiam nostram nescire nos, cuiúsnam peccatum procurauerit hanc huius hominis cæcitatem. Atque hactenus sententia fuit quæstionis à discipulis propositæ, meo quidem iudicio, ea quam attuli. Hanc sententiam nunc examinemus, eiusque partes singulas. Primum itaque quòd cæcitatem hominis peccato tribuant, si hic fuisset eorum sensus quòd peccatum fuerit origo & efficiens illius cæcitatis causa, non errassent. Nam peccatum origo est ac fons, ex quo quasi scaturiunt omnes calamitates, siue eæ sint pœnæ impiorum, siue cruces & afflictiones piorum. Quoties autem intuemur eas calamitates, toties venire nobis in mentem debet peccatum, & oculus ad fontem ipsum est dirigendus. Præsertim verò in calamitatibus nostris ipsorum hoc est faciendum. Nam in aliorum miseriis nimis feré acutè cernimus originem hanc & fontem peccati, eámque grauius exaggeramus. In nostris verò ipsorum calamitatibus, aut non videmus eam originem peccati, aut si viderimus, quantum possumus eam eleuamus. Quamobrem in nostris præsertim ipsorum calamitatibus oculi sunt coniiciendi ad fontem illum peccati, vt ea ratione sollicitemur ipsi ad respicientiam. Quare si hæc fuissent tum mens discipulorum, illi quidem nò abertassent à vero. Atqui ea non fuit: nam satis apparet putasse eos peccati pœnam, (finalem causam dico, non efficientem) finalem, inquam, causam ac solam finalem fuisse cur Deus hominem cæcitate percusserit: in quo profectò vehementer erràrunt. Nam etsi, vt iam diximus, peccatum in quibuscunque calamitatibus causæ locum semper habeat, nepe efficientis & originalis: tamen non semper peccati pœna finis est is, quem intuetur Deus, dum affligit peccatorem, neque vnquam hunc finem habet propositum, nempe vt pro merito puniat ipsos, dum suos, hoc est electos affligit. Verùm hunc potius, vt mortificetur in iis peccatum, tantisperdum per mortem corporalem ipsum perfectè aboleatur. Quare non fuit Deus, in hoc suo iudicio, redigendus in eos angustias finium operum suorum, quasi verò non iure potuerit affligere hominem nisi hoc solo fine propositio: sed libertas agendi quamcunque ipse vellet ob causam, ei permittenda fuit. Neque rursus, vt de causis iustis finalibus dicam nonnihil, in causas finales Deo inter agendum propositas curiosius creaturæ indagandum est: Neque Deus ad reddendum
units.tr: The first part, containing the events that precede the miracle. Passing by, he saw a certain blind man. This did not happen by chance, as one might think, but by the settled counsel of God. Christ does not pass us by, and the Lord never looks upon us rashly without purpose. He saw a man blind from birth. This circumstance of time, in which this man was struck with blindness, shows that the evil was incurable, and therefore magnifies this work of Christ. For Christ was accustomed to put his hand to those diseases and infirmities which could not be cured or restored by any art or power of a creature, so that his works might be seen the more, and so that the power of God in him might appear the more clearly to the faith of those who looked on. As for the miracles of the devil, I am of this opinion, that he cannot change the order of nature in his works, in order to confirm lies. For God's power alone is that by which he overturns the order of nature, and this the devil (in my judgement) does not lend to establish falsehoods. This appears from what is said later in this chapter, at verse 31: we know that God does not hear sinners, that is, false teachers and liars. And afterwards, at verse 33: unless this man were from God, he could do nothing. And they asked him. There follows the mutual conversation of Christ and the disciples, as we said. First the disciples ask him about that blind man. After they had, as it seems, spoken with him about the man's blindness, and had understood that he had been blind from birth, they said, Rabbi, who sinned, and so on. The sense is as if they said: We know indeed that sin is the cause why this man has been blind from his very first birth. But this is what we ask: whose sin was it, the man's own sin, or the sin of his parents? As for the man's own sin, we do not see how the sin of this very man could have brought about this blindness, for he could not have sinned before he was born; yet he was struck with this blindness from his mother's womb. As for the sin of his parents, we do not see on what ground God punishes in one man what was committed by another. Therefore in this matter we confess our ignorance, not knowing whose sin brought about the blindness of this man. And so far was the sense of the question proposed by the disciples, in my judgement, the one I have given. Let us now examine this sense and its separate parts. First, then, that they ascribe the man's blindness to sin: had they meant that sin was the origin and efficient cause of that blindness, they would not have erred. For sin is the origin and fountain from which, as it were, all calamities spring, whether they are the punishments of the wicked or the crosses and afflictions of the godly. And whenever we look upon those calamities, sin ought to come to mind, and the eye must be directed to the fountain itself. Especially ought this to be done in our own calamities. For in the miseries of others we commonly discern this origin and fountain of sin rather sharply, and we magnify it more gravely. But in our own calamities we either do not see that origin of sin, or, if we see it, we lessen it as much as we can. Therefore, especially in our own calamities, the eyes are to be turned to that fountain of sin, so that by this means we ourselves may be stirred to repentance. So if this had been the mind of the disciples, they would not have strayed from the truth. But it was not so: for it is plain enough that they thought the punishment of sin (I mean the final cause, not the efficient cause) to be the final and only cause why God struck this man with blindness; and in this they certainly erred greatly. For although, as we have said, sin always has a place as a cause in whatever calamities there are, namely the efficient and original cause, yet the punishment of sin is not always the end which God has in view when he afflicts a sinner, nor does he always have this purpose, namely to punish them according to their deserts, when he afflicts his own, that is, the elect. Rather, he has this purpose: that sin may be mortified in them, until it is wholly abolished by bodily death. Therefore God was not, in this judgement, to be confined within the narrow limits of the ends of his works, as if he could not rightly afflict a man unless he had proposed this one end alone; rather, freedom of acting for whatever reason he himself wished must be granted to him. Nor, to say something about just final causes, is the creature to inquire too curiously into the final causes which God has proposed to himself in acting. Nor is God to be

units.la: Huius quæstionis examen & partes. Causa efficiens calamitatum. Iudicii humani de causis finalibus calamitatum prauè sententis censura. Voluntas & gloria Dei. dum nobis operum ac consiliorum suorum rationem trahendus est. Sed ita oportet reuereri occulta eius iudicia, vt contenti simus iis causis, quas Paulus adducit consiliorum & iudiciorum Dei Rom. 9. nempe voluntate eius, quae est regula omnis iustitiae verf. 18. & gloria eius verf. 22. 23. Nam in his causis generalibus nunquam falli possumus. Ex voluntate enim eius fit quicquid fit in mundo, & adgloriam eius tendit recta quicquid ex voluntate ipsius geritur. In particularibus vero causis errare ac decipi facile est. Quod si his contenti simus quas mens non potest videre, sane fiet eo, vt etiam si ipsi visum sit, Deus tandem particulares aliquas factorum suorum causas aperiat, quibus tandem inspectis & consideratis futurum est vt vsque adeo probemus eius consilia & facta quaecunque, etiam afflictiones ab eo immissas, vt cogamur fateri nihil melius, nihil nobis conducibilius potuisse accidere. Bonum fuit mihi, inquit ille, quod humiliaueris me.
units.tr: The examination of this question and its parts. The efficient cause of calamities. The censure of human judgements that have wrongly judged the final causes of calamities. The will and glory of God. to be called to account for his works and counsels. But we ought so to revere his hidden judgements that we are content with those causes which Paul adduces for the counsels and judgements of God in Romans 9: namely his will, which is the rule of all righteousness, verse 18, and his glory, verses 22 and 23. For in these general causes we can never be deceived. For by his will comes whatever comes to pass in the world, and whatever is done by his will is rightly directed to his glory. But in particular causes it is easy to err and be deceived. If, however, we are content with those things which the mind cannot see, then surely it will come about that, even if it has not seemed good to him to open to us some particular causes of his deeds, yet once those have been looked at and considered, we shall approve his counsels and all his deeds, even the afflictions he has sent, to such an extent that we are compelled to confess that nothing better, nothing more profitable for us, could have happened. It was good for me, he says, that you have humbled me.

units.la: Pergamus nunc ad alias partes interrogationis discipulorum. Quod igitur illis videtur hominem propter suum ipsius peccatum plecti hac caecitate non potuisse, praesertim cum non exti terit in rerum natura ante caecitatem illam. Resp. Exitit quidem in lumbis parentum, ideoque parentum peccatum non fuit ipsorum solum, sed etiam ipsius. Quod solum procurauit non modo corporalem illam caecitatem in ortu ipsius, sed etiam caecitatem spiritualem & mortem aeternam. Quod denique putarunt eum plecti non potuisse ob peccatum parentum & alienum, de eo sic dicemus: Deus punit iniquitatem parentum in filiis, in nepotibus, in pronepotibus, in abnepotibus, hoc est in quarta generatione eorum qui ipsum oderunt: quo loco iniquitatem intelligo non promiscue quamcunque, sed eam peculiariter, quae infringit foedus Dei, quae dissoluit spirituale illud cum ipso coniugium; vtpote spiritualem illam fornicationem, nempe idololatriam. Est enim haec comminatio addita ad legem illam, qua prohibetur idololatria, vel alioqui insignem aliquam defectionem, cuiusmodi fuit Adae in initio. Hanc tam seuere punit, vt & iniquitatem plane similem parentum iniquitati, & poenam similem in posteros. tatem pa-steros, tanquam meretricios partus, transmittat. Sed aperiendum est huius rei fundamentum quoddam altius:
units.tr: Let us now turn to the other part of the disciples' question. They think that this man could not have been punished with blindness on account of his own sin, especially since he had not existed before the blindness. Answer: he did indeed exist, in the loins of his parents, so the parents' sin was not theirs alone but his as well. That sin brought about not only his bodily blindness at birth but also spiritual blindness and eternal death. As for their view that he could not have been punished for the sin of his parents, or for another's sin, we shall answer thus. God punishes the iniquity of the parents in the children, in the grandchildren, the great-grandchildren and the great-great-grandchildren, that is, in the fourth generation of those who hate him. By iniquity here I understand not any sin whatever indiscriminately, but especially that which breaks God's covenant and dissolves that spiritual marriage with him, namely spiritual fornication, that is, idolatry. For this threat is added to the law that forbids idolatry, or to some other notable defection, such as Adam's at the beginning. God punishes this so severely that he passes on to the descendants, like the offspring of harlotry, both an iniquity wholly like the parents' iniquity and a punishment like theirs. But the foundation of this matter must be laid open at a deeper level.

units.la: Qui stant in Dei foedere & in spirituali illo coniugio, non sibi solum stant, sed & semini suo: qui desciscunt ab eo foedere & spirituali coniugio, seque eo indignos reddunt, non se solum ab eo excludunt, sed etiam semen ac posteros suos. Exclusum igitur semen & destitutum atque destitutum Dei Spiritu: non enim, nisi confoederatis largitur Deus Spiritum suum Sanctum. Destitutum itaque Dei Spiritu, ac sensui suo permissum, quid poterit aliud nisi peccare & peccatum peccato cumulare? Idololatriam suam idololatriae parentum addere, defectionem defectioni? atque ita denique necesse est sibi maledictionem & vindictam Dei accersat. Iam quod adduci poterit ex Ezech. 18. 20. anima quae peccat ipsa morietur, filius non feret propter iniquitatem patris: & pater non feret propter iniquitatem filij, &c. Id ex eo quod iam diximus manifestum euadit. Nam dum punitur semen, id fit propter iniquitatem ipsius contractam tamen vitio parentum, qui semen suum a foedere exclusterint sua iniquitate atque defectione. Addo praeterea peccatum etiam illud primum parentum, non solum esse ipsorum parentum peccatum, sed & seminis in lumbis parentum peccantium existentis. In Adamo enim omnes peccavimus. Ideoque fieri dico, ut cum punitur semen ob peccatum parentum, tum ob suum illud & commune peccatum puniri.
units.tr: Those who stand in God's covenant and in that spiritual marriage do not stand for themselves alone, but for their seed as well. Those who fall away from that covenant and spiritual marriage, and make themselves unworthy of it, exclude not only themselves but also their seed and their descendants. The seed, then, is excluded and left destitute of God's Spirit, for God gives his Holy Spirit only to those who are in covenant with him. Being therefore destitute of God's Spirit and left to their own sense, what else can they do but sin, and heap sin upon sin? They add their own idolatry to the idolatry of their parents, defection to defection, and so at last they necessarily bring upon themselves the curse and vengeance of God. Now what can be brought from Ezekiel 18:20, the soul that sinneth, it shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son, and so on? From what we have already said this becomes plain. For when the seed is punished, it is punished for its own iniquity, which it has contracted, though through the fault of its parents, who by their own iniquity and defection cut off their seed from the covenant. I add besides that the first sin of the parents is not only the sin of the parents themselves but also of the seed existing in the loins of the sinning parents. For in Adam all have sinned. Hence I say that when the seed is punished for the parents' sin, it is at the same time punished for its own and common sin.

units.la: Quare, ut in summa dicam, moriuntur filij ob duplicem iniquitatem: primum ob illam quae ipsis communis est cum parentibus, quamque perpetrarunt quodammodo in lumbis parentum peccantium cum essent: deinde, ob illam priuatam & peculiarem suam, quam exclusi a foedere ac deserti a Deo ipsi perpetrarunt eorum a parentibus suis. Quamobrem censeo, ut de hoc obiter admoneam, diligenter cauendum esse parentibus ne deficiant unquam a Deo, non solum sua ipsorum causa, sed etiam posteritatis ac seminis: ne ex ipsorum iniquitate contrahant iniquitatem filij atque posteri, ne & illi similiter defectores & idololatrae euadant, id quod ordinaria ratione fieri solet, siquae secus aliquando euenirat, illud speciali & extraordinariae cuidam Dei gratiae tribuendum, qui semen vitio parentis exclusum à fœdere ad fœdus suum reducit) ne illi, inquam, defectores evadant, & ex iniquitate & defectione vindictam & iram Dei sibi vltrò accersant.
units.tr: Therefore, to sum up, the children die on account of a twofold iniquity: first, on account of that which they share with their parents, and which they committed in a certain way in the loins of the sinning parents while they were there; and then on account of their own private and peculiar iniquity, which they committed themselves after they had been cut off from the covenant and forsaken by God, having gone astray from their parents. Wherefore I judge that I should give this brief warning: parents must take great care never to fall away from God, not only for their own sake but also for the sake of their posterity and seed, so that their children and descendants do not contract iniquity from their iniquity, and so that they themselves do not likewise become defectors and idolaters. This is what usually happens in the ordinary course of things; if on some occasion it turns out otherwise, that must be ascribed to a special and extraordinary grace of God, who brings back to his covenant the seed that was cut off from the covenant through the parent's fault. Lest they, I say, become defectors, and bring upon themselves of their own accord the vengeance and wrath of God through iniquity and defection.

units.la: 3 Respondit Iesus, Neque iste peccavit, neque parentes eius, vt cæcus nasceretur: sed cæcus natus est, vt opera Dei manifesta fiant in eo.
units.tr: 3 Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.

units.la: 4 Oportet me vacare operibus eius qui misit me, donec dies est: venit nox cum nemo potest operari.
units.tr: 4 I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.

units.la: 5 Quandiu fuero in mundo, lux sum mundi.
units.tr: 5 As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.

units.la: DOminus, responsione hac sua, non negat quidem istos peccatores, neque etiam negat peccatum originem esse cæcitatis illius: sed negat peccatum causam esse eam quam respexit Deus in percutiendo homine hoc cæcitatis malo, hoc est, negat finalem causam hanc nimirum, vt hominem propter peccatum puniret Deus. Affirmat autem finalem aliam Deo propositam in perc[?]uiendo homine: hanc nimirum vt opera Dei manifestarentur in hoc quoque homine, vt in aliis. In hunc enim finem percussus fuit cæcitate, & detentus fuit in ea cæcitate, vt hoc demum tempore opus Dei ad gloriam nominis ipsius conspiceretur in eo sanando. Duo mihi videtur agere Dominus in hac sua responsione. Primùm corrigit discipulorum errorem, negans eam causam quam illi putarunt esse cæcitatis: affirmans autem verà. Dum autem corrigit errorem, proculdubio eadem opera reprehendit discipulos iniuriæ in Deum, quod in causa iudiciorum eius nimis temerè & curiosè inquisierint, reprehendit quoque iniuriæ in miserum hominem, quòd contra charitatis officium de eo seuerius iudicauerint. Simul etiam admonet satis causæ esse omnium iudiciorum Dei in vnica gloria sua. Quare oportuisse eos in ea acquieuisse. Atque hoc primùm mihi videtur facere: secundò autem dum corrigit, simul præparat eos ad futurum miraculum, facitque iis eius spem aliquam. Nam ad Dei opera mirifica præparandi sunt animi nostri, vt ea primùm fide aliqua & spe cernamus quàm his oculis: præsertim verò ad illud opus multo maximum plenæ redemptionis nostræ in hunc modum sinus præparandi. Oportet me. In operibus illis quorum proximè meminit immoratur: ac in eorum natura præterea instituit discipulos suos. Primùm itaque hoc versu ostendit quasi demonstrat discipulis eum per quem Pater operatur omnia, nempe seipsum. Necessitatem autem sibi impositam significat operandi, causam innuit in verbo mittendi. Significat enim se misssum in mundum, ad id, ut operetur ea: ergo causa est ab officio suo, vel fine missionis suæ. Conuertit igitur eorum oculos ad operatorem sive opificem, hoc est, ad se. Id enim requiritur ut in operibus Dei oculos habeamus non tam fixos in operibus, quàm in ipso Deo & Christo, per quem Deus omnia operatur in hoc mundo. Plus enim consolationis est ex inspecto opifice, ex animadversa divina illa potentia, sapientia & misericordia eius, qui operatur, quàm ex operibus ipsis: hoc enim extremæ cæcitatis est, intueri opera tantum, non etiam operantem Deum ut in eum credamus, in eo consolationem habeamus, ipsum denique glorificemus. Donec dies est Circumscripto operatio-nem suam suo tempore ac duratione: donec dies est, inquit. Alludit autem ad vulgarem hominum consuetudinem, qui cum exorto iam sole mane surgunt, perseverantque vesperam usque in opere suo faciundo. Qua de re vide Psal. 104. 23. Prodit homo nempe exorto Sole ad opus suum, & ad culturam suam usque ad vesperam. Vespera superveniente ac post lucem diurnam incumbente iam nocte, nō operatur amplius. Ita Dominus dum dies fuit, operatus est: adveniente nocte quieuit ab opere. Diem Domini voco totum illud temporis spatium a Patre ipsi definitum ac destinatum ad complendum illud opus mediationis suæ & redemptionis humanæ. Diem hunc nō intelligo nudum tempus, vel solam temporis continuationem, sed tempus plane gloriosum & plenum lucis, non quidem terrestris huius, sed cælestis ministratæ a præsentia non alterius cuiusquis, sed ipsius Domini commorantis & operantis in hoc mundo, ut postea videbimus. Ob hanc lucem illud tempus Domini diei nomine vocatum est: quod non modò tempus, sed lucem significat. gnificat. Noctis nomine intelligo tempus illud quod subsequutum est diem præsentiæ Domini, quod instar noctis incubuit in eos nominatim, qui lucem illam, quę fuit ex præsentia Domini, contempserunt. Eorum enim tantùm respectu nox subsequuta dicitur decessionem Domini, iuxta illud quod dictum est sup. cap.6.34. Quæretis me, nec invenietis, &c. Sed de hoc postea. Nunc quæ Dominus dicit de se, certo quodam modo trahi possunt ad nos, quibus dum dies est laborandum est assiduè & diligenter in ea vocatione quam quisque diuino beneficio sortitus est. Diem nostrum intelligo spatium vitæ nostræ, quod spatium excipit nox: hoc est mors hæc temporaria: qua nos opprimente non amplius permittitur nobis in opere esse: at fere fit vt de improuiso superueniente ea nocte quotquot nihil boni in vita vnquam fecerunt, tum subitò percellantur conscientia torporis sui ac desidiæ, quæ in die fuit, hoc est in tota vita anteacta fuit. Quare ad exemplum Domini nostri assiduè in vita hac laboremus iuxta vocationem cuiusque, non tam quærentes nos ipsos laboribus nostris quàm Dominum eiusque gloriam & ædificationem communis corporis: hoc enim destinata est tanquam ad præcipuum finem suum omnis occupatio & functio quæcunque terrena. Quare vt migremus ex hac vita cum bona conscientia, laborandum: idque eo magis, quo breuis est vsura huius lucis: vt in tanta breuitate & tantis angustiis temporis, aliquid tamen confecisse videamur. Vt enim cùm contractior est dies (verbi gratia, brumalis) operarij quique eò diligentius incumbunt operi suo, dum videlicet supplet illa breuis lux: ita non est nobis torpescendum, sed vel hac ipsa breuitate excitari debemus ad maiorem diligentiam. Illud autem non est nobis ignorandum: tempus hoc vitæ nostræ, quotquot sub gloriosò beati Dei Euangelio degimus, tempus, inquam, istud nostrum vniuersum, & omni sui parte diem esse nihil in se noctis habere, sed totum lucidum esse, idque ob præsentiam Christi, qui in Euangelio suo splendet mirificè. Quare id videdum nobis ante omnia, ne dum vocatur hodiernus dies, obduremus corda nostra, sed illuminemur tanta illa Euangelij luce, ne contempta luce fiat tandem vt serius eam requiramus, cùm iam propter ingratitudinē nostram, vel ipsa auferetur à nobis, vel nos auferemur ab ea, siue mortis necessitate, siue aliqua alia ratione. Alterum enim horum procurabit necessariò ingratitudo nostra.
units.tr: THE Lord, in this answer of his, does not indeed deny that these men were sinners, nor does he deny that sin is the origin of that blindness; but he denies that sin is the cause which God had in view in striking the man with this affliction of blindness, that is, he denies that this is the final cause, namely, that God should punish the man on account of sin. He affirms, however, another final cause which God had in view in striking the man: namely, that the works of God should be made manifest in this man also, as in others. For to this end he was struck with blindness, and was held in that blindness, so that at this very time the work of God might be seen in him, in healing him, to the glory of his name. The Lord seems to be doing two things in this answer. First, he corrects the disciples' error, denying the cause they thought to be the cause of the blindness, and affirming the true one. But in correcting the error he doubtless at the same time rebukes the disciples for wrong done to God, in that they had inquired too rashly and curiously into the cause of his judgements; he also rebukes them for wrong done to the wretched man, in that, contrary to the duty of charity, they had judged him more severely. At the same time he reminds them that there is reason enough for all the judgements of God in his own glory alone, and that they ought therefore to have rested in that. This seems to me to be the first thing he does. Second, while correcting them, he at the same time prepares them for the coming miracle and gives them some hope of it. For our minds must be prepared for the wonderful works of God, so that we may see them first with some faith and hope rather than with these eyes; and especially must we be prepared in this way for that far greater work of our full redemption. I must. He lingers on those works which he has just mentioned, and in addition he instructs his disciples about their nature. First, then, in this verse he shows the disciples, as it were, that he is the one through whom the Father works all things, namely himself. He indicates the necessity of working laid upon him, and hints at the cause in the word sent. For he signifies that he was sent into the world in order to do these works; the cause, then, is from his office or from the purpose of his mission. He turns, therefore, their eyes to the worker or maker, that is, to himself. For this is required, that in God's works we keep our eyes not so much fixed on the works as on God himself and on Christ, through whom God works all things in this world. For there is more comfort from looking at the maker, from observing that divine power, wisdom and mercy of his who works, than from the works themselves; for it is the mark of extreme blindness to look only at the works, and not also at God working, so that we may believe in him, have comfort in him, and finally glorify him. As long as it is day. He limits his working to its appointed time and duration: as long as it is day, he says. He alludes to the common custom of men, who rise in the morning when the sun is already up, and persevere at their work until evening. On this see Psalm 104:23. Man goes forth to his work and his tillage when the sun has risen, and continues until evening. When evening comes, and night now presses upon the daylight, he no longer works. So the Lord, while it was day, worked; when night came, he rested from work. I call the day of the Lord that whole span of time appointed and destined for him by the Father for the completion of that work of his mediation and of human redemption. I do not understand this day as bare time, or mere continuance of time, but as a time wholly glorious and full of light: not indeed the light of this earthly world, but of heaven, supplied by the presence not of any other but of the Lord himself, dwelling and working in this world, as we shall see later. Because of this light that time is called by the name of the day of the Lord, since it signifies not only time but light. By the name of night I understand that time which followed the day of the Lord's presence, which fell like night upon those in particular who had despised that light which came from the Lord's presence. For only with respect to them is the night said to have followed the Lord's departure, in accordance with what was said above in chapter 6:34, You shall seek me, and shall not find me, and so on. But more on this later. Now what the Lord says of himself can in a certain way be applied to us: while it is day for us, we must labour constantly and diligently in that calling which each has received by divine benefit. By our day I understand the span of our life, and night follows that span: that is, this temporary death, when we are overtaken by it we are no longer permitted to be at work. And it generally happens that when that night comes suddenly, all those who never did any good in their life are then struck at once by conscience of their sloth and idleness, which were in the day, that is, in the whole of their past life. Therefore, following the example of our Lord, let us labour constantly in this life according to each one's calling, not so much seeking ourselves in our labours as the Lord, his glory and the edification of the common body; for every occupation and every earthly function is destined for this as its chief end. Therefore we must labour so that we may depart from this life with a good conscience, and all the more so because the enjoyment of this light is brief, so that in such brevity and such narrowness of time we may seem to have accomplished something. For just as when the day is shorter (for instance, in winter), labourers apply themselves all the more diligently to their work, since that brief light is all they have, so we must not grow sluggish, but ought to be stirred by this very brevity to greater diligence. Yet we must not be ignorant of this: this time of our life, all of us who live under the glorious Gospel of the blessed God, this time, I say, our whole time, and every part of it, is day, has no night in it, but is wholly bright, and this because of the presence of Christ, who shines wonderfully in his Gospel. Therefore above all we must see to this, that while today is called, we do not harden our hearts, but are illumined by that great light of the Gospel; lest, the light being despised, we at last seek it too late, when now, because of our ingratitude, it will be taken from us, or we from it, either by the necessity of death or by some other means. For our ingratitude will necessarily bring about one or the other.

units.la: Quandiu fuero. Nunc diem hunc suum ab authore suo declarat, comparatenim se Soli, vt enim Sol in luce est ac die, & idem author est illius lucis in qua est: ita Christus Sol ille iustitiæ in luce est, & in die operatur: non quidē in luce aliena, sed in luce sua ipsius, quæ ex ipsius Domini gloriosa præsentia existit: in eóque differt à creatura omni, quæ in luce est. Notanda est diligenter ista Domini sententia. Primùm, sequi ex ea videtur, quòd ante præsentiam Domini in terris, eiúsque manifestationem in carne, lux hæc cœlestis in mundo non extiterit: nam ait, quandiu ego sum in mundo, lux mundi sum. Sequitur ergo, cùm non fuit in mundo, tum non fuit lux mundi. At non sequitur hoc, Neque enim ideo, quod dum Christus est in mundo corporaliter, lux sit mundi, sequitur eum non fuisse antehac mundi lucem. Nam radij quasi illius lucis atque Solis Christi aduentantis, mundum ætate Patrum collustrárunt, non secus atque radij præcedunt Solis ortum. Et quò propius aberat eius præsentia, eò maior extitit splendor eius in mundo. Verùm exoriente demum Sole illo iustitiæ, tum plena luce illuminatus est orbis. Sed videtur sequi id quod magis absurdum est ex hac eadem sententia, nempe non esse iam amplius diem in mundo, post Christi in cœlos ascensionem. Quandiu enim, inquit, sum in mundo, sum lux mundi. Sed id non sequitur: nō enim hoc excludit lucem illam quæ subsecuta est migrationem Christi corporalem ex hoc mundo. Nam reliqui fuerunt ac sunt etiamnum radij mirifici in terris post eius decessum corporalem. Vt enim sol, dum petit occasum discedítque è conspectu nostro, relinquit post se radios suos aliquos in terris: ita multo magis relinquit Christus radios suos post se, vbi iam à nobis subduxit corpus suum. Neque minor est profectò lux ea quam relinquit post se, quàm fuit illa lux olim existens ex præsentia ipsius corporali. Quod enim deficit in præsentia, id suppletur primùm per Euangelium gelium ipsiusque lucem, in quo quasi ante oculos nostros crucifigitur Christus. Deinde per Spiritus sancti efficaciam, quae etiam nunc maior est, dum procedit a Christo glorificato, quàm tum fuit cū manauit à Christo in terris humiliato. Quamobrem Paulus de suo tempore loquens, dixit lumen cognitionis gloriae Dei in facie Iesu Christi ministratum fuisse. Quare ut tedeam ad id unde sum digressus, non sequitur ex his Domini verbis, vel lucem non fuisse ante eius adventum in mundum, vel nō manere iam etiam post eius discessum corporalem è mundo. Verùm illud ex eius verbis colligi potest, diem illum praesentiæ corporalis Domini singularem quendam fuisse diem & eo nomine iustissima de causa insigniendum, cùm eius virtute extiterit, & dies quae eum praecesserit ab origine mundi, & dies qui ipsum subsequutus est ad finem usque mundi: Virtute enim manifestationis Christi in carne & passionis ipsius in terris extitit illa lux & efficacia, quæcunque fuit ætate Patrum: Virtute deinde exhibitionis Christi existit ea lux & efficacia quae iam inde ab ascensu eius in coelos duratura est, ad secundum ipsius adventum usque.
units.tr: As long as I am. Now he declares this day to be his own, by its author. He compares himself to the Sun. For as the Sun is in light and in day, and is also the author of that light in which it is, so Christ, the Sun of righteousness, is in light and works in the day. Not indeed in another's light, but in his own light, which comes from the glorious presence of the Lord himself. In this he differs from every creature, which is in light. This saying of the Lord must be carefully noted. First, it seems to follow from it that before the Lord's presence on earth and his manifestation in the flesh, this heavenly light did not exist in the world. For he says, as long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world. It follows, then, that when he was not in the world, he was not the light of the world. But this does not follow. For it does not follow, because Christ is the light of the world while he is bodily in the world, that he was not the light of the world before. For the rays of that light, as it were, and of Christ the Sun who was coming, lit up the world in the age of the Fathers, just as rays go before the rising of the sun. And the nearer his presence drew, the greater his splendour was in the world. But only when that Sun of righteousness had at last risen was the world illumined with full light. But from this same saying there seems to follow something even more absurd, namely that there is no longer day in the world after Christ's ascension into heaven. For he says, as long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world. But this does not follow. For this does not exclude that light which came after Christ's bodily departure from this world. For wonderful rays remained on earth, and still remain, after his bodily death. For as the sun, while it sinks towards the west and withdraws from our sight, leaves behind some of its rays on the earth, so much more does Christ leave his rays behind him, when he has now withdrawn his body from us. Nor is that light which he leaves behind surely any less than the light which once existed from his bodily presence. For what is lacking in presence is supplied, first, through the Gospel and its light, in which Christ is, as it were, crucified before our eyes. Then, through the efficacy of the Holy Spirit, which is now greater, since it proceeds from the glorified Christ, than it was when it flowed from Christ humbled on earth. Therefore Paul, speaking of his own time, said that the light of the knowledge of the glory of God was given in the face of Jesus Christ. So, to return to where I digressed: it does not follow from these words of the Lord either that there was no light before his coming into the world, or that the light does not remain even after his bodily departure from the world. But from his words it can be gathered that that day of the bodily presence of the Lord was a certain unique day, and for that reason is to be marked out for the most just cause, since by its power there came into being both the days which preceded it from the beginning of the world and the days which followed it to the end of the world. For by the power of Christ's manifestation in the flesh and of his passion on earth, that light and efficacy came to be, whatever it was in the age of the Fathers. Then by the power of Christ's exhibition there exists that light and efficacy which, from his ascension into heaven onward, is to endure until his second coming.

units.la: 6 Hoc cum dixisset, spuit humi & fecit lutum ex humo, & illinuit lutum oculis caeci:
units.tr: 6 When he had said this, he spat on the ground and made clay from the dust, and smeared the clay on the eyes of the blind man,

units.la: 7 Dixitque ei, Vade ablue oculos in piscina Siloam, quod est, si interpreteris, Missus. Abiit ergo & abluit oculos, reditque videns.
units.tr: 7 And said to him, Go, wash your eyes in the pool of Siloam, which, if you interpret it, is Sent. So he went and washed his eyes, and came back seeing.

units.la: Equitur miraculū, in quo primùm sunt partes Christi, deinde hominis caeci; ex quibus sequitur effectus, visum recipit homo qui caecus fuit. Partes Christi sunt hae: primùm spuit humi. 2. fecit lutum ex sputo cum terra admisto. 3. illeuit lutum oculis caeci, adhibita scilicet eadem materia in homine isto sanando, quam adhibuit initio in humano genere creando. 4. dixit ei, vade & laua oculos in piscina Siloam, quod est si interpreteris, Missus. Erat autem is fons ebulliens non continuò, sed incertis horis diebúsque ex radicibus montis Sion, unde missus dictus est, meqiudicio, nempe quòd non iuges essent in ea aquæ, sed missæ incertis temporibus. Hæ sunt itaque partes Christi in hoc miraculo edendo: vbi vides media quæ adhibentur vel leuia in speciem vel etiam contraria sanationi oculorum. Nam illinere lutum oculis cæci quid videtur aliud quàm cæcitatem duplicare? Quorsum adhibuit ista Dominus: Certum est illud, huiusmodi mediis vsum esse eum eo fine, vt fidem hominis probaret, an vellet is constanter credere. Dominus solet in magnis operibus faciendis, vti mediis in speciem leuis momenti, vel etiam pugnatibus ex hominum iudicio cum instituto effecto vel promissione sua, etsi ex Dei consilio nihil aptius sit ad effectum illud producendum. Quorsum autem hoc? nempe vt fidem nostram exploret, vt deinde explorata fide nos seruet.
units.tr: There follows the miracle, in which the parts first belong to Christ and then to the blind man; from these the effect follows, that the man who was blind receives sight. The parts of Christ are these: first, he spat on the ground; second, he made clay from the spittle mixed with earth; third, he smeared the clay on the blind man's eyes, namely using the same material in healing this man as he used at the beginning in creating the human race; fourth, he said to him, go and wash your eyes in the pool of Siloam, which, if you interpret it, is Sent. Now that spring was not flowing continually, but welled up at uncertain hours and days from the roots of Mount Zion, and it was called "Sent" from that, in my judgement, namely because its waters were not perpetual, but were sent forth at uncertain times. These, then, are the parts of Christ in performing this miracle, where you see the means employed, which are either slight in appearance or even contrary to the healing of the eyes. For what does smearing clay on the eyes of the blind man seem to be but doubling the blindness? Why did the Lord employ these things? It is certain that he used such means for this end, to test whether the man would believe steadfastly. The Lord is accustomed, in performing great works, to use means of slight importance in appearance, or even ones that seem to men's judgement to conflict with his appointed purpose or his promise, although in God's counsel nothing is more fitting for producing that effect. And why this? Namely, to test our faith, so that, once our faith has been tested, he may preserve us.

units.la: Neque enim salus est ex quacunque demum fide, ex fide quæ nihil aduersi perferre potest, sed salus est ex fide explorata tentationibus iis quibus visum est Domino eam probare. Eidem pretiosam vocat Petrus: vt enim aurum exploratum igni pretiosum euadit, sic fides tentationibus explorata reddituR pretiosa. Nam exploratio fidei vestræ, multo pretiosior exploratione auri quod perit, & tamen per ignem exploratur, comperiatur vobis esse laudi & gloriæ & honori, cùm patefiet Iesus Christus. Nunc videamus partes hominis cæci quæ sint. Ille paret mandato, abit, lauat. Exemplum est singularis obedientiæ, præsertim in eo homine. Certum tamen est ex effectis hominem interius tractum fuisse ad Dominum, & femina quædam fidei in corde eius iacta. Quare in eo homine, nos qui in fide maiore fecimus progressum, saltem fecisse debuimus, habemus exemplum rarae obedientiæ, discimusque quibuscunque demum mediis visum fuerit Domino vti, quantumuis in speciem leuibus, quantumuis contrariis, ad perficiendum opus suum in nobis. Discimus eius exemplo primùm nobis credendum esse constanter, & fide petendum à Domino eius potentia eius misericordia, eius denique verbo, si in verbo promissio nobis aliqua facta sit, cuiusmodi est promissio illa vitæ æternæ. Deinde discimus posteaquam iam credidimus, obediendum esse voluntati eius, sic vt clausis quasi oculis eum sequamur ducem, Abeamus & lauemus.
units.tr: For salvation does not come from just any faith, from a faith that can bear no adversity; but salvation comes from faith tested by those temptations by which it has pleased the Lord to prove it. Peter calls it precious: for as gold tested by fire turns out precious, so faith tested by temptations is made precious. For the proof of your faith, much more precious than gold that perishes and yet is tested by fire, is found to be for praise and glory and honour at the revealing of Jesus Christ. Now let us see what the part of the blind man is. He obeys the command, goes away, washes. It is an example of singular obedience, especially in that man. It is certain, however, from the results, that the man was inwardly drawn to the Lord, and that a certain seed of faith had been cast into his heart. Therefore, in that man we have an example of rare obedience, and we who have made progress in greater faith ought at least to have done the same. We learn from his example that, by whatever means it has pleased the Lord to use, however slight they may appear and however contrary, he works to accomplish his work in us. From his example we learn first that we must believe steadfastly, and by faith ask of the Lord his power, his mercy, and finally his word, if some promise has been made to us in the word, such as the promise of eternal life. Then we learn, once we have believed, that we must obey his will, so that, as if with eyes closed, we follow him as our leader: Let us go and wash.

units.la: 1. Pet. 1.7. lauemus in nos piscina Siloa, hoc est sequamur Domi- num per impedimenta quæcunque externa, quæ extra nos sunt, interna quæ intra nos sunt. Vide euentum obe-dientiæ in isto homine: redyt, inquit, videns. Euentus itaque obedientiæ nostræ felix erit, non tum tantum cùm habemus certam promissionem vitæ ac liberationis, sed etiam tum cùm nullam habemus promissionem certà, vt in temporariis hisce liberationibus. Nam tû si pendeamus ab eius potentia & credamus quod possit, etsi non constet an velit: fieri quidem etiam potest vt velit, si putet idnobis esse conducibile; Vt videmus in tribus illis Danielis sociis qui pendebant ex eius potentia, non habentes interea persuasum an vellet eos Deus eripere ex flammeo illo fornaci: erepti tamen sunt ac liberati potenter. Quòd si verò nolit Deus nos eripere ex temporario aliquo discrimine, neque videat id nobis expedire: tamen nunquam propterea nos fallet fides nostra & obedientia: pro hac enim vita & liberatione temporaria, æternam nobis reponet.
units.tr: 1. Pet. 1.7. Let us wash in the pool of Siloam, that is, let us follow the Lord through whatever external hindrances are outside us and internal ones within us. See the outcome of obedience in this man: he returned, it says, seeing. The outcome of our obedience, therefore, will be happy not only when we have a sure promise of life and deliverance, but also when we have no sure promise, as in these temporary deliverances. For if we depend on his power and believe that he is able, even though it is not certain whether he is willing, it may indeed also happen that he is willing, if he thinks it expedient for us. As we see in those three companions of Daniel, who depended on his power, not having been persuaded in the meantime whether God would rescue them from that fiery furnace, yet they were rescued and delivered mightily. But if God is unwilling to rescue us from some temporary peril, and does not see that it is expedient for us, still our faith and obedience will never deceive us on that account; for in exchange for this temporary life and deliverance he will restore to us eternal life.

units.la: 8 Vicini ergo & qui prius viderant eum cæcum esse, dicebant, Nonne hic est qui sedebat & mendicabat?
units.tr: So the neighbours, and those who had earlier seen him as blind, were saying, "Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?"

units.la: 9 Alij dicebant, Hic est: alij vero, Similis est ei. Ille vero dicebat, Ego issum.
units.tr: Others said, "It is he." Others said, "He is like him." But he himself said, "I am he."

units.la: Equitur miraculum iam editum, sermo quidam mutuus inter hominem illum qui cæcus erat, iam verò sanatus, & vicinos ipsius, eos nimirum quibus cæcus ille satis erat notus. Occasio fuit ex illa dubitatione & disceptatione quam illi inter se agitabant de homine. Dicebant illi inter se mutuò, Nonne hic est qui sedebat? Considerato nimirum priori statu hominis qui à natiuitate cæcus fuit, vix adduci poterant, vt crederent eum esse, quiam videret. Nota igitur, Deus est qui potest insignem adeo in homine siue externam siue internâ mutationem facere, vt etiam ij quibus notus erat prius incipiant eum ignorare. Vt de interna mutatione dicam; Paulus mutatus admirationem non mediocrem attulit omnibus, qui eum priùs cognitum habuerunt. Petrus scribit de his qui prophani inter gentes erant initios quod cùm viderent eos qui ex Gentibus Christiani facti erant non concurrere secum ad eandem luxus profusionem, peregrinari sibi sunt visi, hoc est rem eam plane nè nouam & admirandam eis visam fuisse. Quare Deus quoties eilubet, proponit hominem mundo tanquam miraculū quoddam, in eum nimirum finem, vt nos non tam creaturam quàm Deum ipsum, stupendam eius potentiam, infinitam eius misericordiam & reliquam maiestatem admiremur & glorificemus. Admirandus enim fit Deus in suis fidelibus. Sed in hac dubitatione non caret Satan arte quadam sua: nam iniecit hanc de homine isto dubitationem, vt ignorato homine ignoraretur & obscuraretur miraculosum illud in homine sanando Dei opus. Ea enim semper fuit eius malicia in obscuris Dei operibus. Sed vide mihi quid ex hac eorum haesitatione Deus eliciat, maiorem scilicet miraculi sui lucem, quàm alioqui fuisset. Nam ex dubitatione exstitit certa personae notitia. Dubitando enim & suscitando peruenimus ad indubitatam rei veritatem. Ex certitudine personae rursus elucescit miraculum. Ita nimirum Deus ex tenebris lucem existere facit, & dubitationes istas omnes quas nobis iniicit Satan de vita & salute nostra, tandem conuertit Deus ad salutem nostram & gloriam sui nominis. Ille autem. Dubitantibus iis, ac inter se mutuò quaerentibus de homine an is sit, qui caecus erat ipse homo litem dirimit, profitetúrque se eum esse. Quo loco vides, quòd etsi illi ignorauerint hominem, tamen hominem ipsum nō ignorasse se, neque oblitum esse praecedentis miseriae suae, quòd & caecus fuerit & medicus. Suo exemplo nos admonēs, vt propter praesentem aliquam conditionem prosperam, non obliuiscamur praeteritae miseriae, sed subinde oculos ad eam reflectamus, confiteamurque, eam si opus, fit coram vniuerso hoc mundo. Memento te, sit Paulus, vos quondam gentes in carne &c. Et ipse Paulus recordatus est subinde miseriae illius suae in qua vixit, antequam ad Christum fuisset conversus: quam etiam ipsum non puduit toti posteritati prodere. Qui prius, inquit, eram blasphemus & persecutor, & iniurios. Quare perpetuò oculi reflectendi sunt ad prae-
units.tr: What follows is a conversation between the man, who was blind but is now healed, and his neighbours, who knew the blind man well. It arose from the doubt and dispute they were having among themselves about the man. They said to one another, "Is this not the man who used to sit here?" Given his earlier condition from birth, they could scarcely be brought to believe that this was the man who now sees. Note, then, that God is able to work such a remarkable change in a man, whether outward or inward, that even those who knew him before begin not to recognise him. To speak of the inward change: Paul, once changed, caused no small amazement to all who had known him before. Peter writes of those who had been profane among the Gentiles, that when they saw those who had become Christians from among the Gentiles no longer running with them into the same flood of dissipation, they thought it strange, that is, that the thing seemed to them quite new and marvellous. Therefore God, whenever he pleases, sets a man before the world as a kind of miracle, to this end, that we may admire and glorify not so much the creature as God himself, his astonishing power, his infinite mercy and his other majesty. For God is made wonderful in his faithful people. But in this doubt Satan does not lack his own craft: for he cast this doubt about the man, so that, with the man unknown, the miraculous work of God in healing him would also be unknown and obscured. For it has always been his malice to obscure the works of God. But see what God draws out of their hesitation, namely a greater light of his miracle than otherwise would have been. For out of the doubt there arose a certain knowledge of the person. For by doubting and inquiring we arrive at the undoubted truth of the matter. From the certainty of the person the miracle shines forth again. Thus God indeed causes light to arise out of darkness, and all those doubts which Satan casts upon us concerning our life and salvation, God at last turns to our salvation and to the glory of his name. Ille autem. While they doubt and ask among themselves whether this is the man who was blind, the man himself settles the dispute and declares that he is that man. Here you see that although they did not know the man, the man himself did not fail to know himself, nor has he forgotten his former misery, that he was blind and a beggar. Setting an example for us, he admonishes us that, on account of some present prosperous condition, we should not forget our past misery, but from time to time turn our eyes back to it and confess it, if need be before the whole world. Remember, says Paul, that you were once Gentiles in the flesh, etc. And Paul himself often recalled that misery of his in which he had lived before he was converted to Christ; a misery he was not ashamed to make known to all posterity. He says, I who was before a blasphemer and a persecutor and injurious. Therefore our eyes must always be turned back to our earlier misery, whether bodily or spiritual.

units.la: Responsio ad dubitationem & quaestionem vicinorum. præcedentem miseriam nostram, siue corporalem, siue spiritualem illam. Ea enim re fit, vt melius sentiamus beneficij & gratiæ magnitudinem; & ex sensu illo Deū magis glorificemus in eóque gloriemur. Sitetiam vt inspecta superiori miseria in rebus prosperis nos submisse geramus, neque altum sapiamus. Vnde enim existit hæc superbia, quam videmus intolerabilem esse in istis hominibus quos Deus euexit ad aliquem dignitatis gradum? Nimirum ex eo, quòd non recordentur prioris suæ conditionis. Quare vel hac causa vt humiles simus iam in sublimi aliquo loco constituti, nunquā recedere ab oculis nostris debet pristina & misera nostra conditio.
units.tr: The answer to the neighbours' doubt and question. For this is why we better feel the greatness of the benefit and grace, and from that feeling we glorify God the more and glory in him. Also, so that, having considered our former misery, we may conduct ourselves humbly in prosperous circumstances and not think highly of ourselves. For where does this pride come from, which we see to be intolerable in those men whom God has raised to some grade of dignity? Surely from this, that they do not remember their former condition. Therefore, for this reason alone, that we may be humble even when placed in some lofty position, our former and wretched condition ought never to leave our eyes.

units.la: 10 Dixerunt ergo ei, Quomodo apertisunt oculi tui?
units.tr: 10 They said therefore to him, How were your eyes opened?

units.la: 11 Respondit ille, & dixit, Quidam qui dicitur Iesus, lutum fecit & illenit illud oculis meis, & dixit mihi, Vade ad piscinam Siloam & ablue oculos: vt autem abij & ablui oculos, vidi.
units.tr: 11 He answered and said, A man called Jesus made clay and anointed my eyes with it, and said to me, Go to the pool of Siloam and wash your eyes. So I went and washed, and I saw.

units.la: 12 Dixerunt ergo ei, Vbi est ille? Ait, Nescio.
units.tr: 12 They said therefore to him, Where is he? He said, I do not know.

units.la: Illo proferente se eum esse qui cæcus erat, exoritur inter ipsum & vicinos communicatio quædam mutua. Illi itaque quæruntmodum tantæ mutationis in ipso factæ. Ipse ab initio rem repetit, authorem exponit, modum quo sanatus sit & restitutionis, omnes facti circumstantias enarrat. Postremò ipsum effectum sanationem oculorum ostendit. Notandum hoc quod modum quo sanatus sit tam diligenter persequatur, & circumstantias quibus visus est Dominus in eo restituendo singulas recenseat: hoc enim videtur factum ab homine, vt patefaciat iis potentiam Domini tantam in mediis tam vilibus. Nam quo viliora sunt media, quibus aliquod opus absolvit Dominus, eo magis conspicitur potentia ac gloria ipsius. Contra vero media ac instrumenta in se gloriosa reddunt Dei per eam operatis gloriam obscuriorem: ideóque Dominus semper consueuit per vilia abiectaque media maxima quæque facere, vt vel in Sacramentis ipsis Baptismi & Cœnæ Domini conspicitur.
units.tr: When he declares himself to be the one who was blind, a certain mutual conversation arises between him and the neighbours. They therefore ask how such a great change was brought about in him. He recounts the matter from the beginning, sets out the author, the manner in which he was healed and restored, and describes all the circumstances of the event. Finally he shows the effect itself, the healing of his eyes. It should be noted that he pursues so carefully the manner in which he was healed, and recounts one by one the circumstances in which the Lord was pleased to restore his sight. For this seems to be done by the man so that he may reveal to them the Lord's great power in such mean means. For the meaner the means by which the Lord accomplishes some work, the more clearly his power and glory are seen. On the contrary, means and instruments that are glorious in themselves make the glory of God, which is worked through them, more obscure. Therefore the Lord has always been accustomed to do the greatest things through mean and despised means, as is seen even in the sacraments themselves, of Baptism and the Lord's Supper.

units.la: 00 Quid enim in speciem vilius est quàm aqua,quàm aqnę aspersio,&c Et tamen,per hæc, magna operatur Dominus,Remissionem peccatorum & Regenerationem.Rursus quid leuius aut magis vulgare, quàm panis ille & potus in Cœna Domini? Et tamen per hæc tam vulgaria communionem Christi & beneficiorum eius efficit & obsignat Dominus. Sed vt narrationem istam hominis paulò diligentius perpendamus:proculdubiò,quòd nihil prætermiserit eorum quæ Dominus fecerit,eo significat magnam beneficij illius impressionem factam in animo suo. Nam cùm seria est apprehensio beneficij alicuius diuini, tum illud solemus dilatare, non piget sæpius de eo sermones conferre, præsertim verò si impressio facta sit spiritualis alicuius beneficij in nos collati. Operæpretium est videre quàm nunquam sibi satisfaciant Apostoli,dum verba faciunt de illa Dei in Christo misericordia: Deus,inquit Paulus, quì diues est misericordia. Opes benignitatis eius, & tolerantiæ, ac lenitatis. Secundum multam suam misericordiam. Unde quaeso hæc voces,nisi ex profundo misericordiæ diuinæ sensu? Sed locus Pauli ad Timotheum in primis est obseruatione dignus, in quo misericordiam illam Dei, quam erga ipsum exercuit, commemorat, in eáque amplificanda diutius immoratur,tandem erumpit in Dei glorificationę magnificam. Ex eo loco disci potest quantus fuerit diuinæ misericordiæ sensus in Apostolo. Contrà verò erga se misericordiæ sensus in Apostolo. Contrà verò ex parco isto & ieiuno sermone nostro de Dei beneficiis erga nos, de eius misericordia in Christo,satis intelligi potest quàm frigidus sit sensus, præsertim spiritualium benedictionum. Nam quòd ad tëporaria ista beneficia, lubenter admodum loquuntur homines de iis,prædicat felicitatem suam: sed vix centesimus cum homine isto sic loquitur, Iesus fecit hoc vel illud: Verum se tanquam sue felicitatis authores laudant & admirantur, non Deum. Dixerunt ergo ei, Vbi? Rursus cognito iam Christo,tanquam facti huius authore, de eo quæruntt: non quidem benevolo aliquo erga ipsum animo,vt videbimus postea, sed maleuolo. Ait homo, Nescio. Ex hoc colligi potest,Iesum non hæsisse in illo loco, dum homo redire videns à Piscina Siloam,vt scilicet reportaret ab homine facti sui gloriam, vel esset in admiratione apud multitudinem concurrentem ad videndam rei novitatem: sed se subduxisse, neque ista moratum esse, ut reipsa illud verum esse comperiatur, quod de se praedicavit Iesus cap.5.41. Ab hominibus gloriam non capto. Ita nobis omnibus Christi exemplo faciendum est. Postquam Deus in vocatione nostra quacunque aliquid magni per nos fecit, non est nobis pendendum ex hominum commendatione, sed aliquo recedendum, ubi perseveremus in vocatione nostra, expectantes approbationem, non hominu, sed Dei ipsius. Nam quem Deus commendat, inquit Apostolus, is vere probatus est. Respondet homo, Iesum abiisse a se, quo autem abierit se nescire: apparet tamen ex verbis eius superioribus & sequentibus, quibus Pharisaeos excipit, hominem hunc a Christo non plane derelictum, sed ex praesentia illa Christi quae antea fuit, reliquam fuisse saetam in homine illo fidem in Christum aliquam, & gaudium ex eius in se collato beneficio. Tantum boni est ex Christi praesentia, sive se in sua persona praesentem exhibeat, sive se offerat in Evangelij sui ministerio. Eunuchus ex praesentia Philippi tatum boni percepit, ut postquam ille iam ab eo distractus fuisset & raptus a Spiritu Domini, perrexerit in via sua cum gaudio. Dominus enim a nobis discedens, pacem suam nobis post se relinquit, ut discedes dixit discipulis suis: Pacem relinquo vobis, pacem meam do vobis, non prout mundus dat ego do vobis. Quarendum nobis, ut si vnquam futurum sit ut haec Domini nostri in externo ministerio suo praesentia auferatur, id accidat propter mundi istam ingratitudinem, quae necessario videtur decessum Evangelij procuratura, si, in quam, hoc futurum sit vnquam, sentiamus tamen post decessum Evangelij gaudium hoc ex praesentia illa Christi, quae aliquando in ministerio fuit, reliquum esse.
units.tr: 00 For what is more lowly in appearance than water, than the sprinkling of water, etc.? And yet through these the Lord works great things, the remission of sins and regeneration. Again, what is lighter or more common than that bread and drink in the Lord's Supper? And yet through these so common things the Lord effects and seals the communion of Christ and of his benefits. But let us weigh this narrative of the man a little more carefully: doubtless, that he omitted nothing of what the Lord had done signifies the great impression that benefit made on his mind. For when the apprehension of some divine benefit is earnest, then we are wont to dwell upon it; we do not hesitate to confer about it often, especially when some spiritual benefit bestowed upon us has made an impression. It is worth seeing how the Apostles never satisfy themselves when they speak of that mercy of God in Christ: God, says Paul, who is rich in mercy; the riches of his kindness, and forbearance and gentleness; according to his great mercy. Whence, I ask, these words, unless from a deep sense of divine mercy? But Paul's passage to Timothy is especially worthy of observation, in which he recalls that mercy of God which he showed toward him, and lingers at length in amplifying it, and at last breaks out into a magnificent glorification of God. From that passage one can learn how great was the sense of divine mercy in the Apostle. On the contrary, from our own sparse and meagre speech about God's benefits toward us, and about his mercy in Christ, one can understand well enough how cold our sense is, especially of spiritual blessings. For as to those temporal benefits, men speak very willingly about them and proclaim their happiness; but scarcely one in a hundred speaks thus with this man: Jesus did this or that. Rather they praise and admire themselves as the authors of their own happiness, not God. They said therefore to him, Where? Again, Christ now being known as the author of this deed, they ask about him, not indeed with any kindly feeling toward him, as we shall see later, but with ill will. The man says, I do not know. From this it can be gathered that Jesus had not stayed in that place, since the man, on returning from the pool of Siloam, was about to report the glory of his deed, or to be an object of admiration to the crowd flocking to see the novelty of the thing. Rather, Jesus had withdrawn himself and did not tarry over these things, so that what Jesus had said of himself in John 5:41 is found to be true in fact: I do not receive glory from men. So we all must do after the example of Christ. When God, in our calling, has accomplished something great through us, we must not depend on the commendation of men, but withdraw somewhere where we may persevere in our calling, awaiting approval not from men but from God himself. For, says the Apostle, the one whom God commends is truly approved. The man answers that Jesus had departed from him, but he does not know where he went; yet it appears from his earlier and later words, in which he excepts the Pharisees, that this man was not wholly abandoned by Christ, but that from that presence of Christ which had been before, some remaining faith in Christ and joy at the benefit bestowed upon him was left in that man. So much good comes from the presence of Christ, whether he shows himself present in his own person or offers himself in the ministry of his Gospel. The eunuch received so much good from the presence of Philip that, after Philip had been taken away from him and caught up by the Spirit of the Lord, he went on his way rejoicing. For the Lord, departing from us, leaves his peace with us behind him, as when he said to his disciples as he was leaving: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give to you; not as the world gives do I give to you. We must take care that if ever it should happen that this presence of our Lord in his external ministry is taken away, it should come about because of the ingratitude of the world, which seems necessarily to bring about the departure of the Gospel; and that, whenever this may happen, we should nevertheless feel, after the departure of the Gospel, that this joy from that presence of Christ which once existed in the ministry still remains.

units.la: 13 Adducunt eum ad Pharisaeos, eum, inquam, qui olim caecus fuerat.
units.tr: They bring him to the Pharisees, him, I say, who had formerly been blind.

units.la: 14 Erat autem Sabbathum quum lutum faceret Iesus & aperiret oculos eius.
units.tr: John 9:14. It was the Sabbath when Jesus made the clay and opened his eyes.

units.la: 15 Rursus ergo interrogarunt eum etiam Pharisæi, quomodo videndi facultatem esset adeptus. Ille vero dixit eis, Lutum unposuit oculis meis, & ablui oculos, & video.
units.tr: Then the Pharisees again asked him how he had received his sight. He said to them, "He put clay on my eyes, and I washed, and I see."

units.la: INterrogabant primis de Christo quem imprimis voluerunt adductū ad Pharisæos: Respondet is qui cæcus fuit, se nescire vbi esset: itaque cum non possunt deprehendere ipsum Dominum, apprehensum servum adducunt ad Pharisæos. Incertum est quo consilio aut quo modo hoc fit factum ab iis, vtrū ex malitia an ex zelo quodam præposterο. Certū hoc est, istos Christo inimicos fuisse, neque caruisse sua quadam adversus eum malitia: etsi ex vulgo fuerint isti & idiotæ. Hostes enim Christi & veritatis ipsius cuiuscunque demum conditionis sint & quovis modo illi infensi, vellent quidem apprehensum ipsum Dominum, & è cœlo deturbatum, si posset illud obtineri. Verum cum non possunt Dominum ipsum apprehendere, sæviunt in servos eos apprehensos adducunt ad Pharisæos, hoc est, coiuratos Christi hostes, qui in ipsos inquirant, & ipsos omnibus mordis diuexent. Mirum hoc potuit miraculum istud in homine, isto editum iniecisse eis aliquam conscientiam qua impedirentur ne hominem pertraheret ad iniquos illos iudices. Verum miraculum editum tantum abfuit ab eo, vt contrà magis eos irritarit aduersus Christum & hominem. Tantum absunt miracula ista quæ edit Dominus quotidie in suis illuminandis & aperiendis interniis animi oculis; tantum, inquam, absunt ab eo vt reuerentiam aliquam vel Dei vel hominum ingignant in animis aduersariorum, vt contra eos provocent ad euomendum egerendumque aduersus Dei seruos totum illud venenum quod intus delitescit. Mirifica fuit illa Stephani illuminatio, cum exclamaret, persequutoribus suis præsentibus & audientibus, cœlos apertos & se videre gloriam Dei & Iesum sedentem ad dextram gloriæ Dei. Sed an hoc continuit eorum rabiem? Contra, illi elata voce exclamarunt & ne vox eius audiretur aures continuerunt, & concorditer in eum irruerunt, eiectumque
units.tr: They first questioned the man who had been brought to the Pharisees, the one who had been blind. He replied that he did not know where Jesus was. Since they could not seize the Lord himself, they took hold of the servant and led him to the Pharisees. It is uncertain what plan or what manner lay behind this, whether it was malice or some misguided zeal. What is certain is that these men were enemies of Christ and were not without a certain malice of their own against him, even though they were of the common people and uneducated. For the enemies of Christ, and of the truth itself, whatever their rank and however hostile they are to it, would gladly seize the Lord himself and cast him down from heaven if they could manage it. But since they cannot lay hands on the Lord, they vent their fury on the servants whom they can seize and drag before the Pharisees, that is, before the sworn enemies of Christ, who will investigate them and harass them with every kind of bite. It was a remarkable miracle performed on this man, and one might have expected it to stir some conscience in them, enough to keep them from dragging him before those unjust judges. But the miracle did so little to achieve that that it rather stirred them up more against Christ and the man. Just so, the miracles which the Lord performs daily, in enlightening and opening the inner eyes of the mind, do so little to instil any reverence for God or for men in the hearts of his opponents that they are provoked to vomit forth and discharge against the servants of God all the poison that lies hidden within. Wonderful was the illumination of Stephen when, with his persecutors present and listening, he cried out that he saw the heavens opened and the glory of God, and Jesus sitting at the right hand of the glory of God. But did this restrain their rage? On the contrary, they shouted with loud voices, stopped their ears so that his voice could not be heard, rushed together upon him with one accord, cast him out of the city and stoned him.

units.la: Act. 7. 56. &c. Testes, Stephani hostes. stúmque foras lapidarunt. Ex horum numero fuit Paulus, qui tamen ex zelo quodam Iudaismi & ex ignorantia, hoc & huiusmodi alia à se facta alibi scribit. Vide igitur quantū malum sit in cæcitate ista mentis, quanto magis conspiciunt illuminatos alios, tanto magis excæcantur & indurantur & in illuminatos insaniunt.
units.tr: Acts 7:56, etc. Witnesses, enemies of Stephen. Among their number was Paul, who nevertheless, from a certain zeal for Judaism and out of ignorance, writes elsewhere of these and similar deeds done by himself. See then how great an evil there is in this blindness of mind: the more they see others enlightened, the more they are blinded and hardened, and the more they rage against the enlightened.

units.la: Erat autem Sabbathum. Reliquum est vt in hominem ad se adductum inquirant Pharisæi. Verum Euangelista noster prius fundamenta futuræ inquisitionis & accusationis subiiciunt, Sabbathum nimirum in quo editum est illud miraculum. Nam, vt postea videbimus, damnant Christum ob id quod violatum sit ab eo Sabbathum. Hoc semper visitatum fuit Hypocritis vt cum staturent oppugnare veritatem quàm maximè, & crudelitatè quàm maximam in seruos Dei exercere, tanquam fundamenta accusationis & condemnationis suæ subiecerint Deum, religionem, legem Dei. Neque vlla in re alia magis cernitur ars diaboli quàm in ista, quotiescunque vult maximè crudelis esse in membra Christi. Neque enim vlla ætate extitit maior crudelitas in hominess vllos, quàm quæ fuit in seruos Dei sub hoc prætextu religionis, legis ac voluntatis diuinæ. Testantur hoc abundè libri Martyrum. Sed hic quærat aliquis cur delegerit Dominus hunc Sabbathi diem ad opus hoc faciendum; cùm sciret hoc fore scandalo Iudæis, id quod etiam sua ipsius experientia iam didicit supra cap.ç.16. & deinceps post sanatum ægrotum illum die Sabbathi. Resp. Nihil moratus est Dominus eorum iniustam offensionem, cùm ipse sibi probè conscius esset scandalum à se non datum esse. Neque nos oportet morari hominum offensiones hodierno die in prædicando Euangelio, modò nos ipsi officium faciamus: stultum est enim putare posse adduci homines ad Christum cùm offensiones hominum omnis generis, regum, nobilium, ignobilium omnium denique. Sed respondeo rursus hoc consilio editum à Domino miraculum eo die præsertim, vt nimirum miraculum innotesceret. Scit enim Dominus inquisitionem & accusationem exoriturram ex circumstantia temporis, qua rursus futurum esset vt in lucem veniret opus illud, & manifestò cognosceretur. Pluris itaq; fecit Dominus manifestationem gloriæ Patris sui quàm eorum iniustas offensiones: neque rursus persecutio illa, quam certò sciuit euenturam, deterruit eum à quærendo gloriam Patris sui.
units.tr: It was the Sabbath. It remains for the Pharisees to inquire into the man who has been brought to them. But our Evangelist first lays down the foundations of the coming inquiry and accusation, namely the Sabbath on which this miracle was performed. For, as we shall see later, they condemn Christ because the Sabbath was broken by him. It has always been the habit of hypocrites, when they have resolved to oppose the truth as fiercely as possible and to inflict the greatest cruelty on the servants of God, to set up God, religion and the law of God as the foundations of their accusation and condemnation. Nor is the art of the devil more clearly seen in anything else than in this, whenever he wishes to be most cruel towards the members of Christ. For in no age has there been greater cruelty towards any men than that which was directed against the servants of God under this pretext of religion, of the law and of the divine will. The books of the Martyrs bear abundant witness to this. But here someone may ask why the Lord chose this day of the Sabbath to do this work, since he knew it would be a stumbling block to the Jews, as he had already learned from his own experience above, in chapter 5, verse 16 and following, after healing the sick man on the Sabbath day. I answer: the Lord did not delay on account of their unjust offence, since he himself was well aware that he had given no offence. Nor ought we, in preaching the Gospel today, to delay over men's offences, provided that we ourselves do our duty; for it is foolish to think that men can be brought to Christ while the offences of men of every kind, kings, nobles, and the lowly alike, remain. But I answer again that the miracle was performed by the Lord with this purpose, and especially on that day, namely that the miracle might become known. For the Lord knew that an inquiry and accusation would arise from the circumstances of the time, and that by this means the work would again come to light and be clearly recognised. Therefore the Lord valued the manifestation of his Father's glory more highly than their unjust offences, and that persecution, which he knew for certain would come, did not deter him from seeking the glory of his Father.

units.la: Rursus ergo interrogarunt, &c. Sequitur inquisitio: Primum quærunt modum facti, fortasse eo consilio ut ex modo expiscarentur materiam accusationis violatique Sabbathi. Nam vel hoc eos offendit quòd lutum illud fecisset eo die, quòdque factum impositiset cæci hominis oculis. Sed interea puto eos in admirationem facti aliquo modo raptos fuisse: ideóque de modo eius tam diligenter quæsiuisse. Nam eiusmodi sunt opera Domini, ut obstupefaciant aliquo certè modo etiam eos qui quàm maximè aduersus ipsa sunt indurati, adeo ut subsistant aliquantisper, ac de modo eorum inquirant. Sed hoc faciunt non quidem ut operibus Domini proficiat, sed vel curiositatis causa, vel alia quauis quam ipsi norunt. Sed in homine hoc notandum quod non pigeat eum factum illud in Domini altus repetere, vniuersamque eius exequendi rationem prosequi. Notandum etiam quod hoc fecerit quærentibus ab eo Pharisæis, hostibus nimirum & persequutoribus Christi, eorumque omnium qui nomen eius profiterentur. Notandum denique quod inter confitendum nihil immutarit, sed constanter vnum idemque de facto illo Domini erga se prædicarit. Hoc nobis faciendum est istius hominis exemplo: Confessio Domini facienda & veritatis ipsius, ac ratio spiritualis illuminationis nostri reddenda, quotiescunque de ea quærunt homines, quicunque demum ij sunt, etiamsi Pharisæi sint: hoc est inquisitores isti Pharisæis ipsis truculentiores. Denique in confessione nihil mutandum, sed constanter vnum idemque asseuerandum est; nihil minuendum est, sed amplificandum est potius Dei erga te beneficium, idque ad exemplum istius hominis. Neque enim prætermittendum est quod nunc mutato tempore dicat, se videre in præsenti tempore, cùm prius interrogatus, respondérit se visum retexisse; significat enim continuationem beneficij, ac solidum, vt ita dicam, beneficium non euanidum: ita nobis quoque amplificandum est hoc Christi beneficium in nobis spiritualiter illuminandis. Neque enim hic peccare possumus, si amplificemus Dei erga nos beneficia: Maiora enim sunt quàm quæ possunt vel animo cogitari vel lingua prædicari.
units.tr: Then again they asked him, etc. The inquiry follows. First they ask about the manner of the deed, perhaps with the aim of drawing from the manner some material for accusation and for a charge of breaking the Sabbath. For they were offended by this, that he had made the clay on that day and had put it on the blind man's eyes. But meanwhile I think they were in some way carried away in astonishment at the deed, and so they asked so carefully about its manner. For the works of the Lord are such that they astonish, in some way at least, even those who are most hardened against them, so that they pause for a while and inquire about how they were done. But they do this not in order to profit by the works of the Lord, but out of mere curiosity or for some other reason which they themselves know. In this man, however, we must note that he did not shrink from recounting that deed of the Lord from the beginning and going through the whole manner of its performance. We must also note that he did this when asked by the Pharisees, that is, by the enemies and persecutors of Christ, and by all those who professed his name. Finally, we must note that in confessing he changed nothing, but constantly affirmed one and the same thing about the Lord's deed toward him. We must follow this man's example: the confession of the Lord and of his truth must be made, and an account of our spiritual enlightenment must be given, whenever men ask about it, whoever they are, even if they are Pharisees, that is, inquisitors more savage than the Pharisees themselves.
