Finally, in confession nothing is to be changed, but one and the same thing must be constantly asserted; nothing is to be diminished, but rather God's kindness toward you is to be magnified, and this after the example of that man. Nor should we pass over what he says now, when the time has changed, that he sees at the present time, whereas before, when asked, he answered that he had recovered his sight. For this signifies the continuation of the benefit, and a solid benefit, not one that has faded away, so to speak. So too this benefit of Christ in spiritually enlightening us must be magnified in us. For we cannot sin here if we magnify God's benefits toward us, since they are greater than can be thought in the mind or proclaimed by the tongue.

units.la: 16 Dicebant ergo ex Pharisæis quidam, Homo iste non est à Deo: nam Sabbathum non seruat. Alij dicebant, Quomodo potest quispiam peccator talia signa edere? Et dissidium erat inter homines.
units.tr: John 9:16. Then some of the Pharisees said, "This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath." Others said, "How can a sinner perform such signs?" And there was a division among the people.

units.la: 17 Rursus dicunt cæco, Tu quid dicis de ipso, quòd aperuit oculos tuos? Ille autem dixit, Certè Propheta est.
units.tr: John 9:17. Again they say to the blind man, "What do you say about him, since he opened your eyes?" He said, "Surely he is a prophet."

units.la: Advito iam facti modo, inter se conferunt sermones, ut mos est Hispanicis istis Pharisæis, hoc est, inquisitoribus. Collatis iam inter se sermonibus opinione varij sunt: ac primùm ij qui magis impiè de Christo sentiunt, sententiam suam de eo pronuntiant, ut solent iti qui magis peruersè de rebus controuersis sentiunt, & quorum iudicium non est ita sanum, promptiores esse perpetuò ad loquendum. Sed quænam est eorum sententia? damnant Dominum, tanquam impium: sententiam proferunt de eo non modò quòd non sit Filius Dei, sed quòd nō sit homo qui aliquid cum Deo commercij habeat. Damnat autem ex facto illo suo, quo violatum est Sabbathum, sed non prius de facto iudicant, quod oportet fieri, modo recta sint iudicia, verùm pro confesso sumpto hoc, quòd violarit Sabbathum, ex eo inferunt, non esse eum à Deo. Ex quo vides, profectam esse totam hanc agendi rationem ex malitia, non ex vlla Sabbathi cura aut reuerentia, quanuis Sabbathū prætexerint, verùm ex malitia & obstinato odio in Christum. Nā cùm animus iudicis præoccupatus est affectu isto plane sanguinolento malitiæ & odij in personam aliquam ream, nonnum quidem inquirit in factum, nisi forte perfunctorie, & pro pessimo facto habet etiam optimū quodque, in personam autem rei malitiosè inuehitur. Sed nos inquiramus paulisper in factum istud Christi, videamusque an per ipsum Sabbathum sit violatum. Ipse Dominus pro se respondit sup. cap. 5. 17. cùm persecutio esset ob Sabbathum violatum eo facto quod fuit in homine aegroto restituendo sanitati suae. Respondit tum Dominus, Pater meus operatus est usque adhuc & ego operor.
units.tr: Now that the manner of the deed has been examined, they confer their opinions with one another, as is the custom of these Spanish Pharisees, that is, of inquisitors. Once their opinions have been compared, they differ: and first those who think more impiously about Christ declare their judgment of him, as usually happens with those who think more perversely about disputed matters, and whose judgment is not so sound, and who are always more ready to speak. But what is their opinion? They condemn the Lord as impious. They pronounce judgment on him not only in that he is not the Son of God, but in that he is not a man who has any dealings with God. They condemn him for that deed of his by which the Sabbath was broken, but they do not first judge the deed, as ought to be done, if judgments are to be sound. Instead, taking it as granted that he broke the Sabbath, they infer from this that he is not from God. From this you can see that this whole way of acting proceeded from malice, not from any care or reverence for the Sabbath, although they put the Sabbath forward as a pretext, but from malice and obstinate hatred of Christ. For when the mind of a judge is preoccupied with that utterly bloody passion of malice and hatred against some accused person, he scarcely examines the deed, except perhaps perfunctorily, and he holds even the best deed to be the worst, while he rages maliciously against the person of the accused. But let us examine this deed of Christ for a little while, and see whether the Sabbath was in fact broken by it. The Lord himself answered for himself above, in chapter 5, verse 17, when he was persecuted because of the Sabbath having been broken by the deed of restoring the sick man to health. The Lord then answered: "My Father works until now, and I work."

units.la: Quo loco duo significauit. 1. opus suum non esse hominis tantum opus, sed Dei opus, opus autem Dei non violare Sabbathum. 2. scilicet cum Patre perpetuo inde à creatione mundi ad praesentem usque diem operatum sine dietum exceptione, ne Sabbathi quidem ipsius. Quod ut intelligamus, sciendum est Dominum die septimo conquieuisse ab operibus suis, sed non omnibus, verum operibus creationis. Quod enim ad opera ista administrationis attinet, perpetuo in iis versatur, iam inde à rebus conditis, alioqui non possent res creatae consistere. Quare nos tantum abesse ab eo oportet ut putemus iis operibus violari Sabbathum, ut e contra sanctificatio sabbathi sit in eo posita, sic ut requiescamus à nostris operibus & divina illa opera contemplemur. Sic igitur respondit Dominus pro setu in illa causa, id quod nunc responderi potest, cum de hoc facto quaerit. At dices, ignorarunt Pharisaei fuisse hoc Iesu opus Dei ipsius opus? Nam Iesum Deum ac Dei filium esse non nouerunt.
units.tr: In this passage he signified two things. First, that his work was not merely the work of a man but the work of God, and that the work of God does not violate the Sabbath. Second, that the Father has worked continually, from the creation of the world until the present day, without any interruption of days, not even of the Sabbath itself. To understand this, we must note that the Lord rested from his works on the seventh day, but not from all of them, only from the works of creation. As for those works of governance, he is perpetually engaged in them from the time things were made, since otherwise created things could not continue to exist. Therefore we must be far from thinking that those works violate the Sabbath. On the contrary, the sanctifying of the Sabbath consists in this: that we rest from our own works and contemplate those divine works. So the Lord answered for himself in that case, and this is what can be answered now when they ask about this deed. But you will say: did the Pharisees not know that this work of Jesus was the work of God himself? For they did not recognise that Jesus was God and the Son of God.

units.la: Resp. Non tam ignorarunt hoc quam noluerunt agnoscere, ideoque vltimo versu huius capitis dicit Dominus: Si caeci essetis non haberetis peccatum, nunc vero dicitis, Videmus; itaque peccatum vestrum manet. Verum, ut hoc largiamur, saltem negari non potest, eos potuisse videre opus illud plane diuinum ac bonum. Ideoque si non à Deo, ab homine salte bono sanctoque profectum. Id quod homo iste idiota vidit cum dicat paulo post Iesum, quemadhuc non haberet cognitum pro Dei filio, Iesum, inquit, illum Prophetam esse; vers.17. Id quod etiam viderunt ex Pharisaeis alij quorum sententia mox afferemus. Potuerunt hoc videre, vel natura ipsa duce, restitutionem non esse violationem Sabbathi: Sabbathū enim, & dies quicunque alij sunt propter hominem, non autem homo propter Sabbathum. Sed omnis lux in iis extincta fuit, & illa quae ex verbo Dei est, & illa quae ex natura est, itaque Dei iudicio coniecti sunt in sensum reprobum.
units.tr: Answer: they did not so much fail to know this as refuse to acknowledge it. That is why the Lord says in the last verse of this chapter: "If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, 'We see'; therefore your sin remains" (John 9:41). But even granting this, it cannot be denied that they could have seen that the work was plainly divine and good, and so, if not from God, at least that it came from a man who was good and holy. This the man himself saw, when a little later he says that Jesus, whom he did not yet know as the Son of God, is a prophet: "He is a prophet," he says (v. 17). Some of the Pharisees also saw this, whose opinion we shall quote shortly. They could have seen, even with nature as their guide, that restoring a man is not a violation of the Sabbath: "the Sabbath and all other days are made for man, not man for the Sabbath." But all light was extinguished in them, both that which comes from the word of God and that which comes from nature; and so, by the judgement of God, they were given over to a reprobate mind.

units.la: Alij dicebant. Haec est aliorum ex Pharisaeis sententia, sanior nimirum, quam fuit illa prior. Contra ipsi de Christo sto rectiùs sentiunt, eúmque quodam modo absoluunt ex opere illo ipsius. Vident opus esse contra naturam, id quod & alij potuerunt videre: sed noluerunt. Vident proinde in opere illo mirificam Dei potentiam: ex opere colligunt non esse peccatorem Iesum. Peccatoré vocant Hebraei eum qui insigniter peccat, delectatúrque peccato quocunque, & peccati quasi artem facitat. Hic vero peccatorem intelligit deceptorem aliquem & medacem insignem. Sed quæri potest an satis firmũ sit hoc argumentum: facit talia opera: ergo peccator vel deceptor non est. Annon potest peccator aliquis & deceptor talia opera facere? Quod si possit, profecto argumetum hoc Pharisæorum istorum satis firmum non videtur. Respondeo primùm, hanc potentiam operandi contra naturam solius esse Dei, Deúmque solum esse eum, qui vocat ea quæ non sunt, tanquam sint, hoc est, verbo creat omnia. Rursus Deum solum esse qui viuificat mortuos, hoc est, contra naturam agit: nam hoc opus fit contra naturam: ideóque commendatur fides Abrahæ vel ex eo, quòd crediderit eam potentiam in Deo esse, qua posset suscitare naturam in suo & Sarę vxoris suæ corpore. Quare res adhuc est credere eam in Deo potentiam esse: quæ est ista infirmitas nostra. Si quæras rursus annon Prophetæ illi veteres & Apostoli ipsi post Christi ascensionem, contra naturam multa operati sunt? Respondeo non fuisse ea facta vel à Prophetis vel ab hominibus, vel à creatura vlla, sed à Deo solo, vtente tamen eorum ministerio, non quidem communicante cum iis potentiam suam, sed exercente ipso potentiam suam cum eorũ ministerio. Quemadmodũ in ministerio Euangelij res sese habet: ita quoque in miraculis edendis. Credit quidem Deus homini ac Ministro suo, verbum suum ministrandum, sed non tribuit ei Spiritum Sanctum suum, quem aliis vnà cum ministrato verbo largiatur: sed ipse reseruat sibi suum Spiritum, eúmque tribuit inter prædicandum verbũ, quibus ipse vult: ita plane res se habet in miraculis edendis. Sed quæritur tertiò, annon in miraculis quæ fiunt contra naturæ ordinem vtitur ministerio Satanæ ac falsorum doctorum, quemadmodum constat eũ vti ministerio suorum? Respondeo meo iudicio nunqua id fit, & causam addo, quia miracula & prodigia deceptorum eo pertinent, vt confirmentur mendacia. Actum quidem verū est hoc quod dicūt hic Pharisæi: Non potest homo peccator, deceptor & mendax, talia opera facere. Neque tantum dicunt hoc Pharisæi, sed & homo qui cæcus fuit, idem postea verf. 31. pronuntiat atque se & Christum defendit hoc argumento; Scimus, inquit; Deum non audire peccatores, id est, deceptores. Notandum quod dicit, Scimus, ponit enim hoc tanquam omnium iudicio ac communi sensu comprobatum, neque id deinde Pharisæi aduersarij oppugnant aut inficiantur. Postremò quæri potest, Annon à Satana & impostoribus etiam miracula contra naturam multa iam edita sunt? Annon dicit Christus aduentum Antichristi fore ex efficacia Satanæ cum omnipotentia & signis ac prodigiis? Respondeo, Sed quid additum est eo loco ad illa signa & prodigia? Cum prodigys, inquit, mendacibus, hoc est, quæ non tantum valent ad mendacium aliquod stabiliendum, sed quæ ipsa mendacia sunt: hoc est, nihil veritatis & soliditatis in sese habent, sed tantum imponunt sensibus. Quamobrem vt concludam, argumentum hoc Pharisæorum istorum satis firmum mihi videtur: in hoc tamen videntur illi peccare, quòd non satis certò & confidenter hoc pronuntiant, quemadmodum illi ex Pharisæis, alij certò ac sine hæsitatione vlla asseuerarunt Dominum non esse ex Deo: Verum isti quæstione facta dubitant an ita sit, vel certè metuunt sententiam suam de Christo liberè proferre. Metus amittendi huius mundi tam inimicus est libertatis professioni.
units.tr: Others said: this is the opinion of some other Pharisees, which is certainly saner than the former. On the contrary, these men judge rightly about Christ, and in a way acquit him on account of that work of his. They see that the work was against nature, which others also could have seen, but they were unwilling to. Therefore they see in that work the wonderful power of God, and from the work they conclude that Jesus is not a sinner. The Hebrews call a sinner one who sins outrageously, takes delight in sin of any kind, and makes a kind of craft of sin. But this man understands by a sinner a notable deceiver and liar. But one may ask whether this argument is firm enough: "He does such works; therefore he is not a sinner or deceiver." Can a sinner and deceiver not do such works? If he could, then surely this argument of those Pharisees does not seem firm enough. I answer, first, that the power to work against nature belongs to God alone, and that God alone is he who calls the things that are not as though they were, that is, who creates all things by his word. Again, God alone raises the dead, which is also against nature; for this work is against nature, and therefore the faith of Abraham is commended precisely because he believed that God had the power to raise up nature in his own body and in the body of his wife Sarah. So it is still a matter of believing that God has this power, and this is our weakness. If you ask again whether the ancient prophets and the apostles themselves, after Christ's ascension, did many things against nature, I answer that those deeds were done neither by the prophets nor by men, nor by any creature, but by God alone, who nonetheless used their ministry; not indeed communicating his power to them, but himself exercising his power through their ministry. As things stand in the ministry of the gospel, so also in the performing of miracles. God indeed entrusts his word to a man and his minister to be preached, but he does not give him his Holy Spirit, whom he might bestow together with the preached word on others; rather he keeps his Spirit for himself and gives it in preaching the word to whom he wills. So matters stand exactly in the performing of miracles. But thirdly it is asked whether, in miracles that are done contrary to the order of nature, Satan and false teachers do not make use of a ministry, as it is clear that he makes use of the ministry of his own. I answer that, in my judgement, this never happens, and I add the reason: the miracles and portents of deceivers serve to confirm lies. What these Pharisees say is indeed true: a man who is a sinner, a deceiver and a liar cannot do such works. Nor do only the Pharisees say this, but also the man who had been blind, who afterwards in verse 31 declares the same thing and defends both himself and Christ by this argument: "We know," he says, "that God does not hear sinners," that is, deceivers. Note that he says "We know," for he presents this as approved by the judgement of all and common sense, and the Pharisees, his opponents, do not then attack or deny it. Lastly it may be asked: have not many miracles against nature already been performed by Satan and impostors? Does not Christ say that the coming of Antichrist will be by the working of Satan, with all power and signs and wonders? I answer: but what is added in that place to those signs and wonders? "With lying wonders," he says, that is, wonders which not only serve to establish some lie, but which are themselves lies, having in themselves nothing of truth or solidity, and merely deceive the senses. Therefore, to conclude, this argument of those Pharisees seems to me firm enough. Yet in this they seem to err: they do not state it with enough certainty and confidence, as the others among the Pharisees, who affirmed without any hesitation that the Lord is not from God. These men, after the question was raised, doubt whether it is so, or at least fear to declare their opinion about Christ freely. The fear of losing this world is as hostile to the profession of liberty as anything.

units.la: Sed quid tandem sequitur, Et dissidium, inquit, erat inter eos. Hoc est effectum quod in his fortiter miraculum illud Christi. Verba quidem Christi & opera Christi dissidium pariunt, vt ipse loquitur: Non veni mittere pacem, sed gladium. Sed videndum an sint proprie dissidij & schismatis causa. Annon verbum Euangelij bonum est? Annon bona Christi opera in sese? Iam quod bonum est, mali causa esse proprie non potest. Quærenda igitur a-libi causa mali per se: nempe in rebellione hominum, qui non admittunt & agnoscunt vel verba vel facta Domini. Atque hæc rebellio induratorum hominum in regno Antichristi causa est hodierno die tantæ dissensionis, tot bellorum, tot denique calamitatum ac commotionum. Verùm eligenda sunt ista potius omnia dissidia, bella, distractiones animorum, & cetera, quàm pax ineunda cum iis qui in tenebris agunt, quàm redeundum in gratiam cum Euangelij hostibus. Misera siquidem ea pax & communio ea quæ est luci cum tenebris. Rursus dicunt caeco. Cùm non conueniat inter Pharisæos ipsos de Christo, conuertunt se ad hominem qui cæcus fuit, quærúntque quidnam ipse de Christo sentiat. Quærunt hoc ea spe, qua homo non erat confessus, propeditus scilicet metu ex ipsorum præsentia: sed homo tamen confitetur eum prophetam esse, hoc est, quantum de eo cognouit id professus est: Non enim adhuc didicit eum esse Dei filium. Nota igitur, quàto magis conantur isti opprimere gloriam Domini, tàto magis emergit: frustra laborant homines in opprimenda veritatis luce, idem enim faciunt ac si quis ignem conetur flatu oris extinguere. Neque enim alió spectant omnia ista martyria, omnes inquisitiones, Deo sic operante & educente lucem ex tenebris, quàm vt Euangelium Christi propagetur. Rursus in homine hoc videmus insignem confessionem & illam quidem ex notitia Christi admodum tenui profectam. Qualis igitur confessio ab iis requiritur qui vident eum filium Dei esse, qui vident eum sedentem ad dextram gloriæ Patris, qui expectant eum venturum mundi iudicem? Sed nuda notitia non efficit confessionem. Homo iste amplius quiddam de Christo corde sensit quàm mente intellexit. Unde affectus est sensu isto collati in se beneficij, & plurimum dilexit. Quare ad confessionem Domini, imprimis facit sensus beneficiorum ac dilectionis eius. Vnde Paulus de gloriatione agens, quæ est confessionis quædam species, & confessio quædam intensissima ad hoc tantum fundamentum peruenit, nempe sensum dilectionis ipsius in Christo, Charitas, inquit, Dei effusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis. Et hæc quidem de prima Pharisæorum inquisitorum actione.
units.tr: But what follows at last? "And there was a division," he says, "among them." This is the effect that this miracle of Christ had upon them. Christ's words and works, as he himself says, bring division: "I came not to send peace, but a sword" (Matt. 10:34). But we must consider whether they are properly the cause of division and schism. Is not the word of the gospel good? Are not Christ's good works good in themselves? Now what is good cannot properly be the cause of evil. We must therefore seek the cause of evil elsewhere, namely in the rebellion of men who do not admit or acknowledge either the words or the deeds of the Lord. And this rebellion of hardened men, in the kingdom of Antichrist, is the cause on this present day of such great dissension, of so many wars, and finally of so many calamities and disturbances. Yet we should choose all those divisions, wars, distractions of minds and the rest, rather than to make peace with those who walk in darkness, rather than to return to favour with the enemies of the gospel. For that peace and fellowship of light with darkness is wretched. "Again they said to the blind man." Since the Pharisees themselves did not agree about Christ, they turn to the man who had been blind and ask what he himself thinks of Christ. They ask this in the hope that he would not confess, being held back, of course, by fear of their presence; but the man nonetheless confesses that he is a prophet, that is, he professed as much as he had come to know about him, for he had not yet learned that he is the Son of God. Note, then, that the more these men try to suppress the glory of the Lord, the more it emerges. Men labour in vain to smother the light of truth, for they do the same as one who tries to extinguish fire by breathing on it. Indeed, all these martyrdoms and all these inquisitions do not aim at anything other than that the gospel of Christ be spread, God thus working and bringing light out of darkness. Again, in this man we see a notable confession, and one that springs from a very slight knowledge of Christ. What sort of confession, then, is required of those who see that he is the Son of God, who see him sitting at the right hand of the glory of the Father, who "await him as the judge of the world to come"? But bare knowledge does not produce confession. This man felt something about Christ in his heart more than he understood with his mind. He was moved by the sense of the benefit conferred on him, and he loved greatly. Therefore the sense of his benefits and of his love above all contributes to the confession of the Lord. Hence Paul, speaking of glorying, which is a kind of confession, and a most intense confession, arrives at this one foundation alone, namely the sense of God's love in Christ: "The love of God," he says, "is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us" (Rom. 5:5). And so much for the first action of the Pharisees who inquired.

units.la: 18 Non crediderunt ergo Iudæi de eo quod cæcus fuisset, & videndi facultatem esset adeptus, vsquequo vocarunt eius parentes, eius inquam qui videndi facultatem fuerat adeptus:
units.tr: So the Jews did not believe concerning him that he had been blind and had received the power of sight, until they called the parents of the man who had received the power of sight.

units.la: 19 Et interrogauerunt eos, dicentes, Hiccine est filius ille vester, quem vos dicitis cæcũ natum esse? Quomodo ergo nunc videt?
units.tr: And they questioned them, saying, "Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How then does he now see?"

units.la: HAc non successit, alia aggrediuntur via. Ex iure & facto nihil consequuntur: alij ex Pharisæis non tam condemnant quàm absoluunt Dominum: ipse quoque homo qui accepit beneficium, profitetur eum Prophetam Dei esse. Ideo nunc cùm nihil pro eis facit Domini miraculum editum, imò cùm vident illud facere ad Domini gloriam contra se, de eo incipiunt dubitare, vocaréque in controuersiam miraculum illud editúmne sit an non, ob eamque rem vocant ad se parentes hominis qui cæcus fuit, abiisque scisciantur de facto. Vide quæso quæ sit ista iudicij forma. Iam ante condemnarunt Christũ quasi non iure id fecerit. Nunc factũ ipsum vocant in quæstionem, an exiterit omnino. Idem est ac si Iudex aliquis primum condemnet quemquam vel homicidij vel furti, tum vocet factum ipsius in controuersiã an id homicidiũ vel furtũ omnino comiserit. Anno primùm quærendum iis fuit de facto ipso, an exiterit, siquidem de eo dubitarunt: deinde quærendum fuit de qualitate facti, bonúmne vel malum esset. Postremò ex qualitate facti cognita vel condemnandus vel absoluendus fuit. At illi omissa quæstione an sit, nihilquoque disceptantes de qualitate facti, statim damnant innocentem, pronuntiantque hominem impostorem à Deo alienum: postea quia non assequuntur ex facto quod volūt, imò verò gloriam Domino ex facto vident emergere, de facto an omnino fuerit, dubirant: qua agendi ratione profecto produnt malitiam suam & odiũ aduersus personam, ostendúntque se nõ iam iudicare Sabbathi vindicandi gratia, sed innocentis hominis condemnandi. Nam quotiescunque videmus peruerti legitimam iudiciorum formam, tum suspicio est odij iudicis in persona ream. Sed hic quæri potest, annon reuera ignorarunt factum, an vero simularunt ignorantiam, vt quod vellent consequerentur? Resp. vt mihi quidem videtur, sciuerunt factum, quod fuerit, sed malitiose dissimularunt, & interrogarunt parentes, vt ex parentum ipsorum ore faltassis aliquid acciperent quo factum illud quod pertinebat ad Dei gloriam obscuraretur. Hic enim mos est perpetuò Sophistis, vt obscuran dæ veritatis gratia simulent se ignorare, quæ tamen satis intelligunt, ideóque interrogent alios quasi rerum omnium ignari. Sed vt demus hoc, nō certò istos cognouisse factum illud an fuerit, tamen non sic effugient; si enim satis cognitum habuerunt factum an fuerit, cur ex eo facto tanquam indubitato Dominum iam ante condemnarunt? Non igitur possunt effugere, siue dicas cognitum fuisse iis illud factum, siue dicas nō fuisse perspectum. Si enim cognitum fuit, cur tam dissimulanter quærunt de re nota? Si ignoratum fuit, cur tam malitiosè Dominum absentem propter ipsum condemnarunt? Itaque inexcusabiles omnino sunt: vt & omnes hypocritæ & sophistæ isti, qui nunc videntur habere effugia cùm reddent rationē illi qui paratus est iudicare viuos & mortuos, tunc, inquam, inexcusabiles erunt, & os iis obturabitur.
units.tr: This did not succeed, so they tried another way. They gained nothing by right or by fact. Some of the Pharisees were not so much condemning the Lord as acquitting him, and the man himself who had received the benefit declared that he was a prophet of God. So now, since the miracle that had been performed does nothing for them, and indeed they see it being done to the Lord's glory and to their own discredit, they begin to doubt it. They call that miracle into question, whether it was performed at all, and for this reason they summon the parents of the man who had been blind and question them about the fact. Consider, I beg you, what kind of judicial procedure this is. Already they had condemned Christ, as though he had acted without right. Now they call the deed itself into question, whether it happened at all. It is as if a judge should first condemn someone for murder or theft, and then bring the act itself into dispute, asking whether he committed murder or theft at all. First, they ought to have asked about the fact itself, whether it had happened, since they doubted it. Then they ought to have asked about the nature of the deed, whether it was good or bad. Finally, once the nature of the deed was known, they ought to have either condemned or acquitted him. But they passed over the question whether it had happened, and without disputing its nature at all, they immediately condemn an innocent man and pronounce him an impostor, one estranged from God. Afterwards, because they do not achieve through the deed what they want, but see glory for the Lord coming out of it, they doubt whether the deed happened at all. This manner of acting surely betrays their malice and hatred against the person, and shows that they are no longer judging for the sake of defending the Sabbath, but for the sake of condemning an innocent man. For whenever we see the lawful form of judgment perverted, there is a suspicion of the judge's hatred against the accused. But here it may be asked: did they really not know the fact, or did they feign ignorance so as to obtain what they wanted? I answer: as it seems to me, they knew what the fact was, but maliciously dissembled, and they questioned the parents so that they might at least get something from their mouths by which that deed, which pertained to God's glory, might be obscured. For this has always been the custom of the Sophists: for the sake of obscuring the truth, they pretend to be ignorant of things which they nonetheless understand well, and so they question others as if they were ignorant of everything. But grant that they did not certainly know whether that deed had happened; still they will not escape in this way. For if they had sufficient knowledge whether the deed had happened, why did they already condemn the Lord before, on the basis of that deed as if it were beyond doubt? So they cannot escape, whether you say the deed was known to them or that it was not clear to them. For if it was known, why do they inquire so dissemblingly about a known matter? If it was unknown, why did they so maliciously condemn the Lord, who was absent, on account of it? Therefore they are wholly inexcusable, and all these hypocrites and sophists, who now seem to have excuses, will be inexcusable when they render an account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead; then, I say, their mouths will be stopped.

units.la: Et interrogarunt. Examinanda est ista interrogationis formula. Interrogatio est multiplex, tria enim multiplicant, vt fallant simplices homines. Quæsierunt enim vna vice 1. An Filius sit. 2. An cæcus natus sit. 3. Quomodo vilum receperit? Ista enim omnia simul ac semel quærunt, & confusè multa interrogant, vt vel nullam vel cer-te confusam responsionem accipiant. Nō enim ad multiplicem quæstionem simpliciter potest responderi. Sed præterea notandum in hac eorum interrogatione quod dicunt, Quem vos dicitis cæcum natum: q. d. Vos dicitis hoc, quum tamen falsum sit: non enim possunt ista consistere, cæcum esse natum hominem, & eundem nunc videre. Hac interrogandi forma conantur deterrere à veritatis professione parentes hominis, cogereque ad negandum quod verum erat, nempe cæcum natum illum suum filium. Vide igitur hic attem Sophistarum quæ est in interrogando homines simplices. Multiplicat quæstiones
units.tr: "And they questioned them." This manner of questioning must be examined. The question is manifold, for they multiply three questions in order to deceive simple people. At one time they ask: (1) Is he the son? (2) Was he born blind? (3) How did he receive his sight? They ask all these things together at once, and they put many questions in a confused way, so that they will get either no answer or a thoroughly confused one. For a multiple question cannot be answered simply. Note also, in their question, what they say: "whom you say was born blind," as if to say: "You say this, though it is false; for it cannot be that a man was born blind and now sees." By this form of questioning they try to frighten the man's parents away from professing the truth, and to force them to deny what was true, namely that this was their son who had been born blind. See here, then, the trick of the Sophists in questioning simple people: they multiply the questions.

units.la: Sophistarum ideo vt in respondendo ij perturbentur. Eáque forma quærendi vtuntur, vt facilè appareat eos non veritatis cognoscendæ gratia, sed causa capiendi eius qui respondet,& veritatis obscurandæ, scisicitari. De hoc ideo admoneo, vt, si vnquam Dei voluntate contigerit vt nostrum quisquam deueniat sub eorum inquisitionem, tum diligenter animaduertat ad ipsorum interrogata. Eius enim momenti sunt eorum interrogata & fallaciæ, vt nisi aduertantur, perniciem sæpe adferant respondenti.
units.tr: The Sophists do this so that those who answer will be thrown into confusion. They use this method of questioning so that it readily appears that they ask not for the sake of knowing the truth, but to catch the one who answers and to obscure the truth. I give this warning so that, if it should ever happen by God's will that any of us falls into their examination, he will pay close attention to their questions. For their questions and their deceits are of such weight that, unless they are noticed, they often bring ruin upon the one answering.

units.la: 20 Responderunt eis parentes eius,& dixerunt, Scimus hunc esse filium illum nostrum & cæcum natum esse:
units.tr: Their parents answered them and said: We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind.

units.la: 21 Quomodo vero nunc videat nescimus: aut quis eius aperuerit oculos. Ipse ætatem habet, ipsum interrogate, ipse de se loquetur.
units.tr: But how he now sees we do not know, nor who opened his eyes. He is of age; ask him, he will speak for himself.

units.la: 22 Hæc dixerunt parentes eius, quod timerent Iudæos: iam enim constituerant Iudæi, vt si quis eum confiteretur esse Christum, synagoga moueretur.
units.tr: His parents said these things because they feared the Jews; for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone should confess him to be Christ, he would be put out of the synagogue.

units.la: 23 Propterea parentes eius dixerunt, Ætatem habet, ipsum interrogate.
units.tr: Therefore his parents said: He is of age; ask him.

units.la: RESpondent parentes prudenter in eo, quòd ad singula interrogata distinctè respondeant. Primum dicunt, filium suum esse illum qui cæcus fuit. Secundò, confitentur cæcum natum,& rectè quidem. Nam istud negari voluerunt Pharisæi. Quòd ad tertium interrogatum, respondent quidem ad id distinctè, & in eo recte faciunt. Sed cùm respônsum hoc de modo facti, de persona agente à se reiiciant in filium suum, sanè peccant & ingratitudinem suam produnt. Non enim debebant silentio suo eum lædere, qui tanto beneficio eos affecit in persona filii ipsorum. Tenentur etiam Deo gratias agere parentes pro beneficiis in liberos suos collatis; vt enim hoc est in beneficiis Dei numerandum. merandum quòd liberos accipiant: ita hoc vel multo maius beneficium est quòd bonos accipiant liberos, hoc est, quòd spiritualiter illuminatos accipiant. Quare hic nimis ingrati sunt in Dominum. At homo ipse & filius sanè gratum se ac memore beneficij ostendit, cùm non tantùm semel atque iterum factum confessus sit, & authorem facti, sed etiam authorem facti Prophetę nomine honorauerit. Quemadmodum igitur in illis habemus exemplum ingratorum parentum in Deum, ita in isto habemus exemplum grati in Deum filij: eiúsque exemplo discimus quòd quocunque demum modo parentes nostri vel etiam cognati commoueantur beneficiis Dei in nos collatis, oporteat nos ipsos in quos collata sunt ea beneficia, iis serió assici, Deóque gratias agere perpetuò, & eum eiúsque beneficia palam profiteri. Peccant igitur quòd non confiteantur, sed hoc in iis tamen aliquo modo laudatur primùm, quod velint factū Domini in lucem prodire. Deinde quod confessionem illā transferant in testem, qui melius posset de eo testari, quā possent ipsi: nempe hominem ipsum, qui per ætatem testari posset, & de modo, & de authore facti. Sed tamē hic inuritur illis ingratitudinis & mollitiei nota à Spiritu sancto. Non enim satis est, si velimus Dei gloriam illucere, si etiam confessionem Dei illis relinquamus, qui de eo melius testari possunt: sed oportet, si grati Deo velimus esse, nos ipsi pro modulo cognitionis nostræ, si vrgeamur, ipsi ore nostro Christum ac veritatem eius confiteamur. Sed videamus fundamentum denegatæ confessionis. Hæc dixerunt, inquit, parentes eius, quòd timerent Iudæos. Metu igitur excommunicationis siluerunt. Ex hoc colligo, non negatam esse confessionem hanc ex ignorantia: imò verò sciuerunt & modum facti & authorem: sed præ metu siluerunt: eóque grauius eorum factum. Nam maius peccatum est metu silere, non confiteri, aut etiam negare veritatē, id quod Petrus fecit, qui ter Dominum abnegauit, quàm ex ignorantia non cōfiteri, aut etiam negare veritatem, id quod Paulus fecit: nam, inquit, ignoras faciebam, fidei expers. Sed multò maximum peccatum est ex malitia veritatem negare, eámque oppugnare, id quod Pharisæi illi
units.tr: The parents answer prudently in that they reply distinctly to each question. First they say that the man is their son who had been blind. Second, they confess that he was born blind, and rightly so, for the Pharisees wished to deny this. As to the third question, they do indeed answer it distinctly, and in that they act rightly. But when they refer the account of the deed, the agent of it, to their son, they surely sin and betray their ingratitude. For they ought not to have wounded by their silence him who had bestowed such a benefit upon them in the person of their son. Parents are also bound to give thanks to God for the benefits bestowed upon their children. For just as receiving children is to be counted among God's benefits, so receiving good children, that is, children who have been spiritually enlightened, is an even greater benefit. Therefore these parents are far too ungrateful toward the Lord. But the man himself and the son shows himself plainly grateful and mindful of the benefit, since he has not only confessed the deed and its author once and again, but has also honoured the author of the deed with the name of Prophet. Just as in those parents we have an example of ungrateful parents toward God, so in this man we have an example of a son grateful toward God. From his example we learn that, however our parents or even our relatives are moved by the benefits of God bestowed upon us, we ourselves, upon whom those benefits were bestowed, ought to be earnestly affected by them, always give thanks to God, and openly profess him and his benefits. Therefore the parents sin in that they do not confess, yet in them this is praised to some degree, first because they wish the Lord's deed to come to light, and then because they transfer that confession to a witness who could testify about it better than they could, namely the man himself, who by his age could bear witness both to the manner and to the author of the deed. But even so, the mark of ingratitude and softness is branded upon them by the Holy Spirit. For it is not enough, if we want God's glory to shine forth, that we leave the confession of God to those who can testify about him better; rather, if we wish to be grateful to God, we ourselves, according to the measure of our knowledge, ought, if we are pressed, to confess Christ and his truth with our own mouths. But let us look at the basis of the denied confession. "These things," it says, "said his parents, because they feared the Jews." Therefore they kept silent out of fear of excommunication. From this I gather that this refusal to confess did not come from ignorance; rather they knew both the manner of the deed and its author, but out of fear they kept silent, and so their act was all the more grievous. For it is a greater sin to keep silent out of fear, to not confess or even to deny the truth, as Peter did, who denied the Lord three times, than to fail to confess or even deny the truth out of ignorance, as Paul did; for, he says, I did it in ignorance, lacking faith. But by far the greatest sin is to deny the truth and oppose it out of malice, which those Pharisees did.

units.la: Distinctio confessionis istorum consideratio. fecerunt: hoc enim malum quoddam desperatum evadit, fitque tandem peccatum in Spiritum sanctum. Ergo ex metu factum est, quod non confessi sint Dominum & factum eius parentes eius qui caecus fuit. Cuius rursus altius est fundamentum, si ipsum lubeat introspicere: nempe φιλαυτία, id est, immoderatus quidam amor nostri ipsorum, nostrae huius vitae, honoris, commodi nostri, qua quidem fit ut natura nos ipsos & nostra propria diis habeamus, & ipsi vero Deo praeferamus. Ex hoc nostri ipsorum immoderato amore, necesse est perpetuo in metu simus amittendae huius vitae & eorum quae ad eam alendam decorandamque pertinent. Quare si velimus liberè confiteri Dominum ac sine metu, laborandum est primum, ut Deum pluris faciamus quam nos ipsos, & nos ipsos nostraque omnia abnegemus, ut Christum obtineamus. Non assequimur istud momento temporis, sed perpetuo praeparandi sumus ad confessionem Christi ac veritatis, si quando eius ex Dei voluntate usus futurus sit, praeparandi, inquam, sumus per mortificationem corruptae huius naturae, dandaque opera est, ut Deum in Christo Iesu magis magisque diligamus, & tandem constringat nos, ut Apostolus de se loquitur, charitas Christi. Hoc est nos totos occupet, ac omnes sensus nostros constrictos teneat. Ita demum parati accedemus ad liberam confessionem.
units.tr: Consideration of the distinction of their confession. They did it; for by this a certain desperate evil is escaped, and it finally becomes a sin against the Holy Spirit. So what they did, in not confessing the Lord and his work, was done out of fear. Its foundation runs deeper, if we are willing to look into it: namely self-love [φιλαυτία], that is, an immoderate love of ourselves, of this life, of our honour and our advantage, which makes us hold ourselves and our own things dear to us, even above God himself. From this immoderate love of ourselves it is necessary that we are always in fear of losing this life and whatever pertains to sustaining and adorning it. Therefore, if we wish to confess the Lord freely and without fear, we must first labour to value God more than ourselves, and to deny ourselves and all our own things, so that we may gain Christ. We do not attain this in a moment of time; we must be prepared continually for the confession of Christ and of the truth, should there ever be occasion for it by God's will. We must, I say, be prepared by mortifying this corrupt nature, and care must be taken that we love God more and more in Jesus Christ, and at last the love of Christ constrains us, as the Apostle speaks of himself, the love of Christ. That is, it must occupy us wholly and hold all our senses bound. Only then shall we come to a free confession.

units.la: 24 Secundo ergo vocarunt hominem qui fuerat caecus, & dixerunt ei, Tribue gloriam Deo, nos hunc hominem scimus peccatorem esse.
units.tr: 24 Secondly, then, they called the man who had been blind, and said to him, Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinner.

units.la: 25 Respondit igitur ille, & dixit, An peccator sit, nescio: unum scio, me cum caecus fuerim, nunc video.
units.tr: 25 He answered, then, and said, Whether he is a sinner I do not know: one thing I know, that whereas I was blind, now I see.

units.la: 26 Dixerunt autem ei rursus, Quid fecit tibi? Quomodo aperuit oculos tuos?
units.tr: 26 Then they said to him again, What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?

units.la: 27 Respondit eis, Iam vobis dixi, & non audistis: cur iterum vultis audire? Num & vos fieri vultis ipsius discipuli?
units.tr: 27 He answered them, I have already told you, and you did not listen: why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?

units.la: PErgunt in obscurando miraculo, conantúrque nunc illud assequi ex confessione ipsius hominis, qui cæcus fuit. Aggrediuntur autem cum cum hac præfatione: Tribue gloriam Deo. Hæc est præfationis quædam formula præmitti solita confessionibus vrgendis. Ita Josua vrget Achanum deprehensum cum anathemate, Fili mi, tribue nunc gloriam Iehouæ Deo Israelis. Sententia autem vsitatæ huius formulæ habetur eodem loco Josuæ: Nam subiectum est statim post, Ede, inquit ei, confessionem. Quare dare gloriam Deo hoc loco est veritatis confessionem in quaque re edere. Nam vt fide, quæ cordis est, glorificatur Deus: ita cõfessione quæ oris est glorificatur Deus vel maximè. Quare quàm pretiosa est nobis gloria Dei, tam pretiosa esse debet veritas, præsertim in religione & rebus fidei: Atque vt amamus Dei gloriam, ita veritatem debemus confiteri, & mendacium odisse. Hæc enim inter sese coniuncta sunt, gloria Dei & veritas. Huius rei ignorantia facit, vt tam temerè mentiantur homines, vel certè veritatem celent. Nos hunc hominem. Ex hoc innuunt tacitam cõclusionem, nempe nõ esse à Christo visum cæco restitutum: illud enim principium vidimus prius. Quomodo potest homo peccator signa edere? Iohan.9.16. Vide ergo vt præiudicium afferant veritati, cuius alioqui confessionem vrgent. Hic est mos hypocritarum: prætexunt quidem gloriam Dei ac veritatem: sed nihil minus audire cupiunt quàm veritatem: id quod apparet etiam ex formulis interrogandi, quibus ipsi vtûtur. Obtestantur per Deum, per eius gloriam, vt veritas proferatur; tum continuò subiiciunt aliquid quod à veritate deterreat, vel aliquo modo ei præiudicio esse possit. Ita in mediis illis obtestationibus cùm volunt videri Deum reuereri, maximè prodit scorum hypocrisis & odium veritatis. Respondit ille. In hominis qui cæcus fuit responsione duo sunt, prius re-spicit personam Christi, posterius factum: Quod ad personam, An peccator sit, inquit, nescio. Nescio equidem quàm bene sit hoc dictum. Nam cùm supra vers.17. cõfessus sit eum Prophetam esse Dei, & postea vers. 33. & deinceps argumentetur eum non esse peccatorem, quia Deus non audit peccatores; videtur hic aliquid dissimu-
units.tr: They go on to obscure the miracle, and now they try to get at it from the confession of the man who had been blind. They begin with this preface: Give glory to God. This is a set formula, customarily put before the confessions that are being pressed. So Joshua presses Achan when he is caught with the accursed thing: "My son, give now glory to the LORD God of Israel." The meaning of this familiar formula is found in the same place in Joshua, for right after it follows: "Make confession to me." So to give glory to God in this place means to make a confession of the truth in any matter. For just as God is glorified by faith, which belongs to the heart, so He is glorified most of all by confession, which belongs to the mouth. Therefore, as precious to us as the glory of God is, so precious ought the truth to be, especially in religion and matters of faith. And as we love the glory of God, so we ought to confess the truth and hate lying. For the glory of God and the truth are bound together. Ignorance of this makes men lie so rashly, or at least hide the truth. "This man, we know not whence he is." From this they insinuate an unspoken conclusion: that the miracle was not wrought by Christ upon the man who was made to see, for they had already set down the principle: "We know that God spake unto Moses; as for this man, we know not from whence he is." And, "How can a man that is a sinner do such signs?" John 9.16. See, then, how they prejudge the truth whose confession they otherwise press. This is the way of hypocrites: they put forward the glory of God and the truth, but they desire to hear the truth least of all. This also appears from the forms of questioning that they use. They adjure by God and by His glory that the truth be told, and then straightaway they add something that frightens them away from the truth, or that could in some way prejudice it. So in those adjurations, while they want to seem to reverence God, the hypocrisy of these men and their hatred of the truth are most plainly revealed. He answered. The man's answer that had been blind has two parts. The first concerns the person of Christ, the second the deed. As to the person: "Whether he be a sinner, I know not." I do not know how well this is said. For although above, at verse 17, he confessed that He is a prophet of God, and later, at verse 33 and following, he argues that He is not a sinner, because God does not hear sinners, there seems to lie some pretence of

units.la: P P lationis subesse: Vt videas quàm difficile sit pede plane inoffenso in confessionibus pergere, & non prodere interea aliquid infirmitatis humanæ. De facto autem respondet bene: nam plane confitetur factum, id quod illi negari ab eo voluerunt; vt rursus videas Deum suos ita sustinere in confessionibus edendis, vt eos prorsus deficere non patiatur: verum in rebus quæ sunt maximi momenti, suffulciat. Vt igitur prodit se infirmitas humana, ita simul se prodit potentia divina. Dixerunt autem ei. Homo iste valde sibi constat, at illi valde instant, vt scias nunquam satis posse nos muniri atque confirmari aduersus obstinatam & pertinacem diligentiam aduersariorum, & opus esse nobis vniuersa illa armatura Dei, & assiduis precibus ad hoc vt in dietentationis consistamus: Ephes. 6. 13. Respondit eis. Homo iste perspecta incredulitate & duritie cordis eorum, simul etiam proposito atque fine quo interrogarunt, nempe vt veritatem miraculi supprimerent: non exponit modum facti, quem illi quidem requirebant, sed obiicit iis primum duritiem. Iam, inquit, vobis dixi, & non audiuistis: hoc est, non credidistis ob duritiem cordis vestri. Deinde sinem ipsis propositum urget interrogatione: Cur, inquit, iterum vultis audire? An vultis eius discipuli fieri? Hæc est responsio per contemptum ironicum occupata, contrarium enim significatur. Nam innuit eos non quærere eo animo vt euadant eius discipuli, sed animo supprimendi veritatem miraculi. Habemus itaque in exemplo huius hominis, quonam modo respondendum sit obduratis istis, qui quærentes subinde in nulla quiescunt responsione, & non audiunt, vt hic dicitur, nempe hypocritis istis & induratis tandem cum nihil eos proficere videmus, obiicienda est duritie cordis sui, eruenda est profunda illa hypocrisis quæ in animo penitus latet. Sic Stephanus tandem in oratione sua, duri cervice, incircumcisi corde & auribus. Et Paulus obiicit hypocritis duritiem suam & cor quod respicere nescit. Sed interea hic conficitur in homine isto libertas magna extam exigua Christi notitia. Non enim filium Dei eum cognouit: Vt discas audaciam ac libertatem in confessionibus suis sæpe esse in idiotis ipsis, vt requiras in quo-uis
units.tr: dissimulation beneath it here, so that you may see how hard it is to go on in confessions with a foot quite unstumbled, and not to betray in the meantime some weakness of human nature. As to the deed, however, he answers well, for he plainly confesses the deed, which they wanted him to deny. Again you may see that God so sustains His people in making confessions that He does not allow them to fail utterly, but supports them in matters of the greatest moment. Thus, as human weakness shows itself, divine power shows itself at the same time. Then they said to him. This man holds his ground well, but they press him hard, so that you may know that we can never be sufficiently fortified and confirmed against the stubborn and persistent diligence of our adversaries, and that we need that whole armour of God, and constant prayer, so that we may stand in the evil day. Ephesians 6.13. He answered them. The man, perceiving their unbelief and hardness of heart, and also the purpose and end for which they questioned him, namely that they might suppress the truth of the miracle, does not explain the manner of the deed, which they indeed demanded, but first confronts them with their hardness. Now, he says, I have told you already, and you did not hear: that is, you did not believe, because of the hardness of your heart. Then he presses on them the end they had proposed, with a question: Why, he says, do you want to hear it again? Do you want to become his disciples as well? This is an answer made with ironic contempt, for the opposite is meant. For he hints that they are not asking with the mind of becoming his disciples, but with the mind of suppressing the truth of the miracle. We have, then, in the example of this man, how one ought to answer those obstinate people who, though they keep asking, never rest in any answer, and do not hear. As this is said here, namely to those hypocrites and hardened men, when we see that nothing is gaining ground with them, we must confront them with the hardness of their own heart, and drag out that deep hypocrisy which lies hidden in the mind. So Stephen at last, in his speech: stiff-necked, uncircumcised in heart and ears. And Paul confronts hypocrites with their hardness and with a heart that does not know how to look back. But meanwhile in this man there is great freedom, though his knowledge of Christ is very small. For he did not know Him as the Son of God. Learn that boldness and freedom in confessions is often found in the unlearned themselves, and seek in every

units.la: Sincera in confessione de facto.
units.tr: Sincerity in confessing the deed.

units.la: Hostium veritatis pertinax diligentia, quid nos doceat.
units.tr: The stubborn diligence of the enemies of the truth: what it teaches us.

units.la: Hypocritæ tandem acriter punguntur.
units.tr: Hypocrites are at last sharply pricked.

units.la: Ita Stephanus eos excipit. Act. 7. 51. Paulus ite. Rom. 2. 5. uis non tam notitiam multiplicem quàm cordis boni-tatem & animum bene affectum erga Dominum & ve-ritatem ipsius in confessionibus edendis, & tolerandis Christi causa calamitatibus. Nam homo iste idiota plu-rimùm dilexit Dominum, & valde commotus est miracu-lo ab ipso edito.
units.tr: So Stephen answers them, Acts 7.51; Paul likewise, Romans 2.5. For this man, unlearned as he was, loved the Lord very much, and was deeply moved by the miracle wrought by him.

units.la: 28 Itaque conuitiati sunt ei, & dixerunt, Tu discipulus illius es: nos autem Mosis discipuli sumus.
units.tr: 28 And they reviled him and said, You are his disciple; but we are disciples of Moses.

units.la: 29 Nos scimus Deum esse loquutum Mosi: hic autem unde sit nescimus.
units.tr: 29 We know that God spoke to Moses; but as for this man, we do not know where he is from.

units.la: NOn patiuntur hypocritæ larvam sibi detrahi: vide enim vt insaniunt. Iudæi postquam Stephanus obiecit eis duritiem cordis, frendent cordibus, stridént dentibus, tandémque concorditer irruunt in eum. Et dixerunt, Tu Discipulus illius es. Probri loco obiiciunt ei, quòd sit discipulus Christi. Nam eo significant eum apostasiæ fecisse à lege Mosis. Christum enim & Mosem contrarios sibi inuicem somniant. Quare si sit Christi discipulus, non amplius iam Mosis est. Nota est illa vox Papistarum, qua obiiciunt nobis continuò apostasiam & defectionem ab Ecclesia catholica. Non est, vt videmus exemplo tèporis Christi, illa vox noua, neque nostro demum sæculo vsurpata est ab hypocritis, qui ipsi à Deo & veritate desciuerunt, cùm tantùm inania nomina & titulos habeant. Nos verò Mosis sumus discipuli. Constantiam suam in lege Mosis prædicant, eámque ex aduerso opponunt defectioni hominis illius qui cæcus fuit: bene sibi consultum esse putant, si larua quadam Mosis sese induant, vt solent hypocritæ & sibi & aliis imponere vanis nominibus rerum diuinarum vel hominum vel aliarum rerum. Et Papistæ hodierno die satis se habere putant, si Catholici vocentur, & aliis id genus titulis nihil solidi habentibus insigniantur. Sed quid profuit Pharisæis nomen Mosis sine Christo, quem tanquam finem respexit lex Mosaica? Illi tamen eum sibi magistrum esse noluerunt. Quid proderit, quæso, istis Ecclesiæ catholicæ nomen? Quid Patrum nomina sine Christo, cuius ipsi membra sunt. gratiam inanem reddunt. Nam etsi nomen Christi retineant, reipsa tamen Christum negant, & diuellunt Ecclesiam à Christo. Quemadmodum olim Pharisaei illi Mosem à Christo separarunt. Sed videamus rationem cur glorientur illi se Mosis discipulos, non autem Christi esse. Est autem ratio à vocatione vtriusque & Mosis & Christi, in hanc formam: Audiendi sunt illi tatum qui à Deo vocati sunt & missi; At Moses à Deo vocatus est (hoc est quod intelligunt dum dicunt Deum illu coram allocutum esse) Christus autem non est vocatus à Deo (hoc est quod intelligunt, cum aiunt, unde hic sit, nescimus: hoc enim est de vocatione eius accipiendum) Ergo Moses, non autem Christus audiendus est. Sumunt sibi argumentationis suae fundamentum laudabile admodum: neque enim temere quiuis sunt audiendi, ne circumferamur quouis vento doctrinę. Ideo Apostolus datos ait à Christo alios Apostolos, alios Prophetas, alios Euangelistas, alios Pastores & doctores in hunc finem, ne simus amplius pueri qui fluctuemus, &c. Quare fundamentu rationis satis firmum est. Recte etiam concludunt ex eo fundamento Mosen audiendum esse. Sed male inferunt Christum non audiendum. Hic enim ad reiiciendum Christum abutuntur principio in se quidé firmo atque bono: vt discas hypocritas & sophistas pervertere principia, & ex veris principiis assumere & concludere quod falsum est. Legas in doctrina Papistarum principia in sese vera ac bona, inter quae numeratur hoc ipsum de quo nunc loquimur. Sed quis non videt eos abuti iis aduersus Doctores & Professores veritatis sincerós? Quis non videt eos abuti aliis quibusuis quae in se bona sunt, aduersus veritatem Euangelij?
units.tr: The hypocrites will not suffer their mask to be torn off: see how they rage. After Stephen charged them with hardness of heart, they gnash their teeth and grind their teeth in their hearts, and at last they rush at him together. And they said, You are his disciple. They throw it at him as an insult that he is a disciple of Christ, for by this they mean that he has apostatised from the law of Moses. They imagine Christ and Moses to be opposed to each other, so that if he is Christ's disciple he is no longer Moses'. This is a familiar cry of the Papists, who constantly charge us with apostasy and defection from the Catholic Church. As we see from the example of Christ's own time, it is not a new phrase, nor was it first used in our own age by hypocrites, who have themselves fallen away from God and truth while holding only empty names and titles. But we are disciples of Moses. They boast of their constancy in the law of Moses, and they set it over against the defection of that man who had been blind. They think they have provided well for themselves if they put on a mask of Moses, as hypocrites are wont to deceive both themselves and others with empty names of divine things, or of men, or of other things. And the Papists of today think it enough if they are called Catholics and adorned with titles of that sort, which hold nothing solid. But what did the name of Moses profit the Pharisees without Christ, to whom the Mosaic law looked as its end? Yet they did not want him as their teacher. What, I ask, will the name of the Catholic Church profit these men? What do the names of the Fathers profit without Christ, whose members they themselves are? They make grace empty. For although they keep the name of Christ, in fact they deny Christ and tear the Church away from Christ, just as those Pharisees of old separated Moses from Christ. But let us see the reason why they glory in being disciples of Moses and not of Christ. The reason is drawn from the calling of each, of Moses and of Christ, and runs in this form: those alone are to be heard who have been called and sent by God. But Moses was called by God (this is what they understand when they say that God spoke with him), whereas Christ was not called by God (this is what they understand when they say, we do not know where he is from, for this is to be taken as referring to his calling). Therefore Moses, not Christ, is to be heard. They take for the foundation of their argument a principle that is quite commendable: for not just anyone is to be heard rashly, lest we be carried about by every wind of doctrine. So the Apostle says that Christ gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, some as pastors and teachers, to this end, that we should no longer be children tossed about by waves, and so on. Therefore the foundation of the reasoning is quite firm. They also conclude rightly from that foundation that Moses is to be heard. But badly they infer that Christ is not to be heard. For here they abuse, in order to reject Christ, a principle which in itself is firm and good: so that you may learn that hypocrites and sophists pervert principles, and from true principles assume and conclude what is false. You may read in the doctrine of the Papists principles that are true and good in themselves, among which is numbered this very point of which we now speak. But who does not see that they abuse these against the teachers and true professors of the truth? Who does not see that they abuse whatever other things are good in themselves, against the truth of the Gospel?

units.la: 30 Respondit eis ille, & dixit, Atenim istud mirum est, quod vos nescitis unde sit, & tamen aperuit oculos meos.
units.tr: 30 He answered them and said, Indeed this is a marvel, that you do not know where he is from, and yet he has opened my eyes.

units.la: 31 Scimus autem quod Deus peccatores non audiat: sed si quis cultor eius est & facit quod ille vult, ille hunc audit.
units.tr: 31 But we know that God does not hear sinners; but if anyone is a worshipper of him and does his will, him he hears.

units.la: 32 Ab saeculo non est auditum aliquem aperuisse vuiffe oculos eius qui cæcus natus fuerit.
units.tr: 32 It has not been heard from the beginning of the world that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind.

units.la: 33 Nisi esset hic à Deo, non posset tale quicquā facere.
units.tr: 33 If this man were not from God, he could do nothing of the kind.

units.la: 34 Responderunt & dixerunt illi, Tu in peccatis natus es totus, & tu doces nos? Et eiecerunt eum foras.
units.tr: 34 They answered and said to him, You were born wholly in sins, and do you teach us? And they cast him out.

units.la: Miratur primùm is qui cæcus fuit eorum stupore, quòd in tanta luce editi miraculi, tamen ignorarent ex quo esset ipse, quæque esset eius vocatio. Ergo miratur quòd ignari essent vocationis ipsius. Causa est, miraculum illud ab ipso editum. Miretur aliquis stuporem hunc & ignorantiam mundi in tanta luce operum & verbi Dei. Sed quis tamen est cui mirum hoc videtur? non quiuis sine discrimine, sed quibus aperti sunt oculi ad hoc vt videant lucem illam verbi & operum Dei lògè clarissimam. Miratur Paulus Galatas ita citò trāsferri in aliud Euangelium. Mirantur autem nostri hoc imprimis, Papistas, in tanta luce Euangelij, vocare in dubiū vocationem eorum præsertim, quorum ministerio primum (parta est per orbem terrarum ista tanta Euangelij lux, vt Lutheri, Melanæthonis, Zuinglij, Caluini, & aliorum, &c. Effecta enim ipsa satis testatur vocationem eorum fuisse à Deo, siue ordinariam dicas quam in Papistino acceperunt; (erant enim vel Doctores, vel Presbyteri in ipsa Ecclesia Papistica) siue extraordinariam intelligas. Proculdubio enim extra ordinem cum donis extraordinariis in Ecclesiam missi sunt à Deo illi viri Dei. Sed obdurati Papistæ plane similes sunt Pharisæis: illi quidem vt obscurarent miraculum illud editum, vocationem Iesu in quæstionem vocarunt: Papistæ vt veritatem Euangelij & lucem eius extinguant, de ministrorum Christi vocatione disputant, & ministros Dei persequuntur. Vident enim lucem iustitiæ, quæ nobis per Christum imputatur, lucem etiam vitæ æternæ quæ est per illum solum, aliaque huiusmodi, tenebris illis, quas ipsi in mundum inuexerunt, aduersaria esse. Memorabit mundus, inquit, quia testor de eo opera eius mala esse, sup. cap. 7.7.
units.tr: The man who had been blind first wonders at their stupidity, that although the miracle had been done in such a great light, they nevertheless did not know where he himself was from, or what his calling was. So he marvels that they were ignorant of his calling. The cause is that miracle which he himself had performed. Let anyone wonder at this stupor and at the ignorance of the world amid such a great light of the works and word of God. But who is it to whom this seems strange? Not just anyone without distinction, but those whose eyes have been opened to see that light of the word and works of God, which is by far the clearest. Paul wonders that the Galatians were so quickly carried over to another gospel. But our people chiefly wonder that the Papists, in so great a light of the Gospel, call into question the calling of those through whose ministry this so great light of the Gospel was first spread over the whole world, namely Luther, Melanchthon, Zwingli, Calvin and others. For the effect itself sufficiently attests that their calling was from God, whether you call it ordinary, which they received in Popery (for they were either teachers or elders in the Papal Church itself), or understand it as extraordinary. For undoubtedly those men of God were sent by God into the Church beyond the ordinary order, with extraordinary gifts. But the hardened Papists are plainly like the Pharisees. Those indeed, in order to obscure the miracle that had been done, called into question the calling of Jesus. The Papists, in order to extinguish the truth of the Gospel and its light, dispute about the calling of Christ's ministers and persecute the ministers of God. For they see that the light of righteousness, which is imputed to us through Christ, and the light of eternal life, which is through him alone, and other things of this kind, are opposed to those darknesses which they themselves have brought into the world. The world will remember, he says, that I testify its works are evil, above, chap. 7.7.

units.la: Scimus autem. Nunc doctoris partes agit is qui cæcus fuit, probatque vocationem Iesu, quòd ea ex Deo sit. Primum autem docet Christum peccatorem non esse, quod illi dixerunt: ex eóque infert ex Deo esse. Sic itaque argumentatur: Scimus Deum non audire peccatores: at hunc audiuit, ergo hic peccator non est, ergo ex Deo est. Assumptionem probat ex facto illo admirabili, quod Deus per eum edidit. Huius argumenti partes videamus. Primum ait, Scimus Deum peccatores, &c. Hoc tanquam notum & omnium iudicio & noritia communi comprobatum proponit. Peccatores intelligit eos peculiariter in quibus regnat peccatum, prophanos & proiectos ad omnem nequitiam. Nota igitur, preces ex prophano corde profectæ non penetrant cælos, neque se ingerunt in Dei aures. In causa est; quia non nisi sancti motus cordis, sanctæ voces oris movent Deum. Non sunt omnes omnium motus statim sancti, non sancta omnium suspiria, non sanctæ omnium preces: sed illi demum motus sancti sunt, qui ex Spiritu Dei sancto existunt. Precantes omni tempore per Spiritum. Spiritus interpellat pro nobis suspiriis inenarrabilibus. Suspiria illa quæ per Spiritum sanctum excitantur sancta sunt. Quare non quiuis motus cordis, non quæuis suspiria mouent Deum. Prophanus Esau etiam cum lachrymis benedictionem exquisiuit, sed an auditus? De eo scriptum est, respipiscentiæ locum non inuenit. Nempe preces eius & lachrymæ eius prophanæ erant. Voces autem à Spiritu sancto profectæ audiuntur. Christum cum in diebus carnis suæ deprecationes & supplicationes obtulisset cum clamore valido & lachrymis exauditus est ex motu. Moses cum non clamaret ad Deum, neque vocem vllam ederet, verum commoueretur corde tantum, & preces apud animum suum conciperet, tamen exauditus est, non secus acsi clamasset. Quare voces eæ tantum quæ à Spiritu sancto proficiscuntur à Deo exauduntur. Deus enim nouit quis sit sensus Spiritus sui. Hoc est motus cordis à Spiritu sancto excitatus statim mouet Deum: Quia Spiritus Dei est qui eos in corde ciet. Rursus autem facit vt nos sentiamus Dei erga nos animum, & charitatem Dei effundit in cordibus nostris, cum sensu
units.tr: But we know. Now he who had been blind takes on the role of a teacher, and proves the calling of Jesus, that it is from God. He first teaches that Christ is not a sinner, which they had said, and from this he infers that he is from God. He argues thus: We know that God does not hear sinners; but he heard this man; therefore this man is not a sinner; therefore he is from God. He proves the assumption from that wonderful deed which God performed through him. Let us look at the parts of this argument. First he says, We know that God does not hear sinners, etc. He sets this forth as something known and approved by the judgment and common knowledge of all. By sinners he means especially those in whom sin reigns, the profane and those abandoned to every wickedness. Note, therefore, that prayers that come from a profane heart do not penetrate the heavens, nor do they force their way into the ears of God. The reason is that only holy movements of the heart and holy voices of the mouth move God. Not all movements of everyone are at once holy, nor are all sighs holy, nor all prayers holy; but those movements are holy which arise from the Holy Spirit of God. Praying at all times through the Spirit. The Spirit intercedes for us with unutterable sighs. Those sighs which are stirred up by the Holy Spirit are holy. Therefore not every movement of the heart and not every sigh moves God. Esau, though profane, sought the blessing with tears, but was he heard? Of him it is written that he found no place for repentance. Clearly his prayers and his tears were profane. But voices that come from the Holy Spirit are heard. When Christ, in the days of his flesh, had offered up supplications and entreaties with strong crying and tears, he was heard because of his reverence. Moses, when he did not cry out to God nor utter any voice, but was moved only in heart and conceived prayers in his mind, was nevertheless heard, no less than if he had cried out. Therefore only those voices which proceed from the Holy Spirit are heard by God. For God knows what is the sense of his own Spirit. This means that a movement of the heart stirred up by the Holy Spirit at once moves God, because it is the Spirit of God who stirs them in the heart. Again, he causes us to feel God's disposition toward us, and pours out the love of God in our hearts, together with a sense

units.tr: Testimonies. Ephes.6.18. Rom.8.26.

units.tr: A contrary example. Heb.12.17.

units.tr: The opposite. Heb.5.7.

units.la: Rom.8.27. su quodam gaudij ineffabilis. Spiritus autem iste Spiritus est Christi, qui fluit in nos per eius passionem, & per eius resurrectionem mediam. Quare vt sit Spiritus, necessaria est cum Christo coniunctio & vnio. Hoc igitur est primum fundamentum cur audiantur preces nostrae, nempe, fides in Christum: ex qua Spiritus sanctus in corde habitans, ex quo rursus sanctae preces quae deniique audiuntur a Deo. Fundamentum itaque omnis gratiae & aditus ad Deum, est Iesus Christus fide apprehensus. De propositione igitur hactenus.
units.tr: Rom.8.27. with a certain sense of unspeakable joy. This Spirit is the Spirit of Christ, who flows into us through his passion and through his middle resurrection. Therefore, for there to be this Spirit, union and fellowship with Christ are necessary. This, then, is the first foundation of why our prayers are heard, namely faith in Christ: from which the Holy Spirit, dwelling in the heart, and from which again the holy prayers that are at last heard by God. Therefore the foundation of all grace and access to God is Jesus Christ, apprehended by faith. So much for the proposition.

units.la: Assumptionem, nempe quod Iesus Christus auditus sit, ostendit ex insigni illo miraculo, quod comparatione omnium temporum & operum inde vsque ab origine mundi editorum amplificat. Sed quaeres annon fuit tam insigne miraculum antehac editum? Respon. ita loquutum esse hominem istum de hoc miraculo, vel propter formam editi miraculi vel propter eius, vt sic dicam, singularitatem: vel denique propter magnitudinem. Propter formam, quia Iesus sua ipsius virtute, vtpote Deus, miraculum edidit. Nullus autem Prophetarum ante ipsum sua virtute, sed virtute aliena, hoc est Christi miracula sua edidit. Sed cum ignorauerit adhuc is qui caecus fuit Iesum Dei filium esse, formam istam insolitam ac nouam qui potuit videre? Ergo vt de singularitate dicam miraculi huius quod eam spectans iste sic loquutus sit: Concedo equidem id, nos non legere in veteribus scripturis quenquam qui inde a natiuitate caecus fuit oculis restitutum esse. De Tobia legimus in Apocryphis, quod post caecitatem visum recuperarit: sed non erat Tobias caecus natus. Verum meo iudicio speculatus homo operis ipsius magnitudinem, vt de ea postremo dicamus. Fateor quidem opera in veteri testamento edita esse a Mose & Prophetis quae non videntur minora isto opere: sed quia non spectauit iste potentiam tantum in hoc miraculo edito in se sanando, sed etiam sensit misericordiam erga se multo maximam, quod nimirum ipse per hoc miraculum ex potentia Dei editum sanatus esset, ex eoque sit vt pluris faciat, & maius esse ducat hoc opus, quam omnia illa ante hac patrata. Solemus enim cum serio afficimur sensu alicuius operis & misericordiæ Dei erga nos patefactę; solemus, inquit, pluris facere illud opus, quo benefit nobis, quàm alia alioqui eo fortasse in sese maiora. hoc locum habet maximè in spiritualibus benedictionibus. Paulus ait Deũ ostendisse erga se primum omnem clementiam. Atqui non minor fuit clementia ostensa erga Petrum, cuius defectio etiam grauior erat quàm fuit Pauli peccatum. Nam Paulus ex ignorantia persecutus est Christum. Petrus verò sciens ex infirmitate tamen Dominum suum negauit. Clementia itaque nihilo minor ostensa erat erga Petrum, idque priore loco, etiamsi se primum vocet erga quem ineffabilis illa clementia patefacta fuerit. Procul dubio ex sensu beneficij vehementi in se collari sic loquutus est Paulus. Nos idem faceremus omnes si serio sensu spiritualium erga nos benedictionum attingeremur. Nam ex serio sensu proficiscitur hæc verborum magnitudo: & verum quidem est, nunquam posse inueniri à quoquam verba, quæ satis exprimant magnitudinem etiam minimi erga nos beneficij spiritualis. Sed vt de miraculis à Christo editis, nonnihil addam, verum quidem est, si simul sumas ea omnia, & maiora & plura ab eo edita esse quàm à quoquam qui antè eum fuit. Si non fecissem opera inter eos, quæ nemo alius fecit, peccatum non haberent, ait Dominus postea cap.15.24. Par quidem fuit & maxima & plurima miracula prouidentia Dei reseruari in aduentum filij Dei, vt per ea nimirum demonstraretur esse filius Dei. Hic enim vsus fuit miraculorum Christi, vt discimus ex cap.10.Iohannis, versu 25. Opera quæ ego facio in nomine Patris mei, hæc testantur de me. Item Petrus dicit Christum approbatum apud homines præstantibus factis & miraculis & ignis, quæ edidit per ipsum Deus. Hæc de miraculis Christi hactenus. Nisi esset hic à Deo. Hæc est conclusio principalis, de vocatione Iesu, quòd ea à Deo sit: coniungitur autem cum proximo argumento ab opere eius sumpto. An vero necessitas est in hoc argumento: Talia quidem operatus est vel edidit miracula cōtra naturæ ordinem: Ergo à Deo est? Vidimus supra cum examineremus argumentum quorundam ex Phariseis, qui Christum ex facto suo conati sunt absoluere, vel certè eum non condemnarunt narunt. Tantùm in eo quod dicit, non posset facere quicquam, notandum est, q.d. Non posset facere quoduis miraculum, nedum hoc antea inauditum opus. Ex quo colligimus neminem posse vel quicquam facere in opere Dei, in mutàda vel natura ista communi, vel natura corrupta, nisi à Deo mittatur ad eam rem praestàdam. Nam ut de mutatione naturę corruptæ, vt mentis illuminatione & cordis conuersione, dicam nonnihil; cum opera haec ex diametro pugnent cum natura ista corrupta, & planè admirabilia sint, quis est qui possit tam insignem mutationem facere, nisi mittatur à Deo? Vnde Paulus, Rom.10.15. Quomodo, inquit, praedicabunt nisi missi fuerint? Item, nō quòd 2.Cor 3.5. idonei simus ex nobisipsis ad cogitandum quicquam, sed quòd idonei simus, id ex Deo est. De hoc rursus admonendi sumus, non requirere nos hoc loco, vt regeniti sint ipsi verèque pij omnes quotquot mutationem istam vel in natura communi vel corrupta facturi sunt: sed hoc tantùm vt mittantur à Deo. Mittit autem Deus nonnunquam etiam hypocritas, per quos tamen magna & miraculosa operatur suo Spiritu.
units.tr: The assumption, namely that Jesus Christ was heard, he shows from that remarkable miracle, which he magnifies by comparison with all the times and works performed from the beginning of the world. But you will ask: was not a miracle as remarkable as this performed before? I answer: the man speaks of this miracle in this way either because of the form of the miracle performed, or because of its, so to speak, singularity, or finally because of its greatness. As to its form: Jesus performed the miracle by his own power, as God. But none of the prophets before him performed miracles by his own power, but by another's power, that is, Christ's miracles were his own. But since the one who had been blind did not yet know that Jesus was the Son of God, who could have seen this unusual and new form? So, to speak of the singularity of this miracle, that the man spoke thus with regard to it: I grant indeed that we do not read in the old Scriptures of anyone who had been blind from birth and was restored to sight. We read in the Apocrypha that Tobit recovered his sight after blindness, but Tobit was not born blind. But in my judgement, the man, having considered the greatness of the work itself, (to speak of it last): I admit that works were performed in the Old Testament by Moses and the Prophets which do not seem less than this work; but because he did not look only at the power displayed in this miracle in healing himself, but also felt a very great mercy towards himself, namely that he himself had been healed by this miracle, performed by the power of God, and from this it comes that he esteems this work more highly, and judges it greater, than all those performed before. For we are wont, when we are seriously affected by the sense of some work and of God's mercy revealed toward us, we are wont, he says, to value more highly that work by which we benefit, than others which in themselves may perhaps be greater. This holds especially for spiritual blessings. Paul says that God showed toward him first all mercy. Yet the mercy shown to Peter was no less, although his fall was even graver than Paul's sin. For Paul persecuted Christ out of ignorance, but Peter, knowing him, nevertheless denied his Lord out of weakness. Therefore mercy no less was shown toward Peter, and that at an earlier point, even though Paul calls himself first, toward whom that unspeakable mercy was revealed. Undoubtedly Paul spoke thus out of a vehement sense of the benefit conferred on him. We would all do the same if we were seriously touched by a sense of spiritual blessings toward us. For the greatness of his words proceeds from a serious sense: and it is true that no one has ever been able to find words that adequately express the greatness of even the smallest spiritual benefit toward us. But to add a little about the miracles performed by Christ: it is true that, taking all of them together, more and greater ones were performed by him than by anyone who came before him. "If I had not done among them works which no one else has done, they would not have sin," the Lord says later, in chapter 15.24. It was fitting that the greatest and most numerous miracles should be reserved by the providence of God for the coming of the Son of God, so that by them he might be shown to be the Son of God. For this was the use of Christ's miracles, as we learn from John chapter 10, verse 25. The works that I do in my Father's name, these bear witness of me. Likewise Peter says that Christ was approved among men by excellent deeds, miracles and signs, which God performed through him. So much for the miracles of Christ. Unless God were in him. This is the main conclusion concerning the calling of Jesus, that it is from God; but it is joined with the nearby argument taken from his work. But is there any necessity in this argument: He performed or wrought such miracles against the order of nature, therefore he is from God? We saw above, when we examined the argument of certain Pharisees, who tried to acquit Christ on account of his deed, or at least did not condemn him. Only in what he says, he could do nothing, it must be noted, that is to say: he could not do any miracle, much less this work never heard of before.
