From this we gather that no one can do anything in the work of God, either in changing this common nature or in changing corrupt nature, unless he is sent by God to accomplish that thing. For, to say a little about the change of corrupt nature, such as the illumination of the mind and the conversion of the heart: since these works are in direct conflict with this corrupt nature, and are plainly wonderful, who is able to effect so remarkable a change unless he is sent by God? Hence Paul: Rom.10.15. How, he says, shall they preach unless they have been sent? Likewise: not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything, but our sufficiency is of God, 2 Cor. 3.5. On this we must be reminded again: we do not require at this point that all those who are going to make that change, either in common or in corrupt nature, should themselves be reborn and truly godly; but only that they be sent by God. God indeed sends sometimes even hypocrites, through whom he nevertheless works great and miraculous things by his Spirit.

units.la: Tu in peccatis. Hactenus Doctoris partes in docendis Pharisæis egit idiota iste: nunc habemus quo succeßu laboraverit. Reprehendunt graviter Pharisæi, quòd docent ipsos, & doctrinam eius respuunt. argumentum est, Quia, inquiunt, in peccatis natus es totus: Id est, peccator fuisti inde ab incunabilis, cuius rei argumentum est vel caecitas illa sola in qua natus es, nam cum ea, tanquam peccati inhærentis nota, prodiisti primùm ex vtero matris tuæ. Respicere enim hoc loco videntur hominis cœcitatem, eámque peccato ascribere tanquam ipsius certam quandam poenam, vt & discipuli Christi, supra vers. 1. Nota igitur: Deus nonnunquam excitat abiectissimos quosque, & idiotas, qui doceant etiam Doctores ipsos & sapientes huius mundi, eo scilicet fine vt pudefaciat eos, & deprimat eorum altitudinem. Videtis, fratres, vocationem vestram, &c. Tum vers. sequentibus finis subiicitur, vt nimirum pudefaciat sapientes secundum carnem, potentes, nobiles. Tandè vltimus finis subiicitur vers. 29. vt nè gloriatur vlla caro coram eo. Sed videamus hic an hunc finem consilij sui in excitando homine isto idio-ta ad docendos Pharisæos assequutus sit Dominus. Imò illi consilium Dei non aduertentes, vilitate hominis vsque adeo offenduntur vt eius doctrinam respuant. Vide quàm difficile sit vincere illam altitudinem superborum & captiuas ducere eorum cogitationes ad obediendum Christo. Nos itaque eorum exemplo admoniti, & Dei consilium, non conditiones hominum, aduertentes, audiamus vel abiectissimos quosque eius nomine loquentes & vera docentes: hoc est stulti fiamus, vt fiamus sapientes, sicut loquitur Apostolus. Stulti autem fimus dum demittimus nos ipsi & abiicimus omnem opinionem sapientiæ nostræ. Et eiecerunt eum. Pergunt porrò in malitia sua, & à verbis ad facta veniunt hominemque eiiciunt, quod sic accipiendum est, non quòd vi aut magnibus hominem eiecerint; sed quòd strinxerint aduersus eum sententiam & gladium vt vocant excommunicationis, & eiectionis è synagoga sua. Vnde colligimus antiquum fuisse iudicij genus Ecclesiasticum, vsitatum etiam Christi temporibus, imò ante eam tempora inde à prima mundi creatione in Ecclesia Dei receptum.
units.tr: You were born altogether in sins. Hitherto this unlearned man has played the part of a teacher in instructing the Pharisees; now we have the outcome of his labour. The Pharisees severely rebuke him, because he teaches them, and they reject his teaching. The argument is: because, they say, you were born wholly in sins: that is, you were a sinner from the cradle, the proof of which is that blindness alone in which you were born, for with it, as a mark of inherent sin, you came out first from your mother's womb. For in this place they seem to look at the man's blindness and to ascribe it to sin, as a certain punishment due to him, just as Christ's disciples did, above, at verse 1. Note therefore: God sometimes raises up the most abject and unlearned men, who teach even the teachers and the wise of this world, clearly for this end, that he may shame them and bring down their loftiness. You see your calling, brethren, etc. Then in the following verses the end is added, namely that he may shame the wise according to the flesh, the powerful, the noble. Finally the last end is added in verse 29, that no flesh may glory before him. But let us see here whether the Lord attained this purpose of his, in raising up this unlearned man to teach the Pharisees. Indeed they, not noticing God's purpose, are so offended by the lowliness of the man that they reject his teaching. See how hard it is to overcome that loftiness of the proud and to lead their thoughts captive to obey Christ. Therefore, admonished by their example, and attending to God's purpose and not to men's condition, let us hear even the most abject men speaking in his name and teaching the truth: that is, let us become foolish, that we may become wise, as the Apostle says. We become foolish when we humble ourselves and cast off all opinion of our own wisdom. And they cast him out. They continue further in their malice, and from words they proceed to deeds, and cast the man out; which is to be understood not as though they cast the man out by force or violence, but that they drew against him the sentence and sword, as they call it, of excommunication, and of expulsion from their synagogue. Hence we gather that there was an ancient kind of ecclesiastical judgement, in use even in Christ's time, and indeed before that time, received in the Church of God from the very creation of the world.

units.la: Nam Cainum fratricidam legimus hoc iudicio à Deo ipso primùm ex Ecclesia quæ tum in familia Adami patris fuit, eiectum esse Genef.4.10. &c. Quanta autem fit eius vis, & quàm graue sit hoc iudicium apparet ex eo quod in ipso agitur. Traditur homo iam eiectus ex Ecclesia Dei in manus Satanæ qui ipse est extra Ecclesiam: in hunc autem finem non ad hoc vt homo prorsus pereat, sed ad interitum carnis, hoc est hominis, qua ex parte carnalis est, vt Spiritus saluus fiat in die Domini, hoc est, vt spiritualis homo, vel homo qua ex parte spiritualis est, saluus fiat. Ne autem videretur hæc perfunctorie geri, docuit nos Deus multis exemplis, reipsa id fieri ac euenire quod verbo dicitur. Vide exemplum Caini primum, is eiectus ex præsentia Dei; & ex Ecclesia incidens in manus Satanæ conquestus est pœnam suam intolerabilem esse. Vide exemplum incestuosi illius, quem Paulus significat pene iam absorptum dolore superabundanti. Cùm enim visum est Deo per hoc iudicium dicium efficaciter agere, tum quanti existunt horrores conscientiæ Sed plerosque excommunicationem video à Deo sibi permitti, sic vt magis magisque indurentur, neque videant, neque sentiant quo loco sint. Verum quando demum est ista grauiras sententiæ excommunicationis: & quo tempore efficax est hæc traditio in manus satanæ. Vobis, inquit Paulus, & meo Spiritu in nomine Domini nostri Iesu Christi congregatis, cum potestate Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Ergo tum est grauitas & efficacia huius iudicij, cùm legitimum est iudicium, conuocatis nimirum in vnum presbyteris & ministris Ecclesiæ legitimis, neque id solùm, sed cùm sedet vna quasi cum iis in iudicio Dominus Iesus per potestatem suam. Oportet autem illud iudicium, in quo sedet vel cui præsidet Dominus, tanquam iudex ratum esse in cœlis, & efficaciam suam tandem aliquando vel citius vel serius exercere. Hinc videre licet, an hæc excommunicatio qua eiectus est homo iste è synagoga efficax fuerit. Nimirum si eo non sedit Christus neque legitimum neque efficax fuit. Verùm an sederit Christus in hoc iudicio cognoscitur satis ex eo quod sequitur. Non enim citius eiectus est ex synagoga Iudæorum quàm acceptus à Christo, & ab eo institutus est in cognitione filij Dei & Messiæ. Ex hoc effecto possumus iudicare an anathemata illa ex Concilio Tridentino fulminata legitima sint & efficacia necne. Videmus enim Christum non prius se hominibus offerre, aut ad eos propius accedere, quàm vel eiecti sunt ex illa impia societate, vel eam ipsi sua sponte deseruerunt. Lutherus aliique eius confortes initio cùm crassos tantùm Papæ errores reprehenderent, neque dum se ab eo & Papistis prorsus segregarent, non tantùm in illo Christi mysterio viderunt quantum postea cùm eiecti & excommunicati essent. Mirum est enim quantoperè tum profecerint in cognitione illius mysterij.
units.tr: For we read that Cain, the murderer of his brother, was first cast out of the Church by God himself, which then existed in the family of Adam the father (Gen. 4.10, etc.). How great its force is, and how grave this judgement is, appears from what takes place in it. The man, now cast out of the Church of God, is handed over into the hands of Satan, who himself is outside the Church. This is done not so that the man should perish utterly, but for the destruction of the flesh, that is, of the man in so far as he is carnal, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord, that is, so that the spiritual man, or the man in so far as he is spiritual, may be saved. Lest it should seem that these things are done carelessly, God has taught us by many examples that what is said in words is really done and comes to pass. Consider first the example of Cain: cast out from the presence of God and from the Church, and falling into the hands of Satan, he complained that his punishment was intolerable. Consider the example of that incestuous man, whom Paul shows to be almost swallowed up by excessive sorrow. For when it has pleased God to act effectively through this judgement, how great the horrors of conscience then arise! But I see that most people are permitted by God to be excommunicated in such a way that they are hardened more and more, and neither see nor feel where they stand. But when, finally, is the gravity of this sentence of excommunication, and at what time is this handing over into the hands of Satan effective? To you, says Paul, and to my spirit, gathered together in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore the gravity and efficacy of this judgement lie in its being lawful, that is, when the lawful elders and ministers of the Church are gathered together into one, and not only that, but when the Lord Jesus, by his power, sits in judgement with them, as it were. Moreover, that judgement in which the Lord sits, or over which he presides, must be ratified in heaven as by a judge, and must at some time, sooner or later, exercise its efficacy. Hence it can be seen whether this excommunication by which this man was cast out of the synagogue was effective. Surely, if Christ did not sit in it, it was neither lawful nor effective. But whether Christ sat in this judgement is known well enough from what follows. For the man was no sooner cast out of the synagogue of the Jews than he was received by Christ and instructed by him in the knowledge of the Son of God and the Messiah. From this result we can judge whether those anathemas hurled from the Council of Trent are lawful and effective or not. For we see that Christ does not offer himself to men, or draw nearer to them, before they have either been cast out of that impious fellowship or have themselves deserted it of their own accord. Luther and his companions, at first, when they were rebuking only the gross errors of the Pope, and had not yet wholly separated themselves from him and the Papists, did not see into that mystery of Christ as much as they did afterwards, when they were cast out and excommunicated. For it is remarkable how greatly they then advanced in the knowledge of that mystery.

units.la: 35 Audiuit Iesus eum eiectum foras: Et cum naetum, dixit ei, Tu ne credis in Filium Dei?
units.tr: 35 Jesus heard that they had cast him out; and when he had found him, he said unto him, Dost thou believe on the Son of God?

units.la: 36 Respondit ille & dixit, Quis est, Domine, vt credam in eum?
units.tr: 36 He answered and said, Who is he, Lord, that I might believe on him?

units.la: 37 Dixit autem ei Iesus, Et vidisti eum, & ipse est qui loquitur tecum.
units.tr: 37 And Jesus said unto him, Thou hast both seen him, and it is he that talketh with thee.

units.la: 38 At ille ait, Credo Domine: Et adoravit eum.
units.tr: 38 And he said, Lord, I believe. And he worshipped him.

units.la: SEd quomodo excipit Christus hominē, quibus primum verbis? Tune credis? Instituit eum in fide Filij Dei: hoc enim est principium omnis gratiæ, fidesin Christum. Per quem, inquit Apostolus, fidem habuimus hunc aditum in gratiam hanc per quam stamus. Sed notandum quod vrgeat fidem, quæratque num credat? Ita enim interrogando, eius desiderium excitat, & præparat animum hominis ad fidem recipiendam. Notandum est etiam quòd quærat num credat in filium Dei? vult enim eum scire Messiam illum, cuius nomen vulgò in ore omnium habebatur esse Filium Dei, non tantùm filium Dauidis, sicut vulgo putabatur. Neque enim fides nostra acquiescit prius in Christo quàm penetret vsque ad Deitatem illam habitantem in eo σωματικῶς. Nam ira Dei offensi propter peccata nostra, non conquiescit nisi in sanguine illo, qui certo quodam modo sit Dei ipsius sanguis, nempe propter ineffabilem illam vnionem naturæ humanæ & diuinæ in Christo. Quare cum in eodem conquiescat Dei ira simul & fides nostra, necesse est securitatem fidei nostræ & certitudinem remissionis peccatorum tum demum esse, cùm apprehensa est illa Deitas Filij. Apprehenditur quoque humanitas & sanguis Christi, sed non nisi in illa vnione quæ est cum filio Dei. Quis est, Domine? In hoc hominis qui cæcus fuit, respondo, primum laudabile est, quòd non temere credat, id est applicet cor suū, sed primum quærat notitiam: lux enim mentis necessariò præcedit apprehensionem cordis, & fides procedit ex cognitione. Qui enim apprehendam fide, vel ad me ipse applicabo, quod non prius cognitum habeo? Verum quidem id est, profundiorem esse & maiorem non nunquam cordis sensum quàm sit mentis notitia. Ineffabilia enim suspiria excitantur in corde, ineffabile gaudium existit in corde: pax quæ superat omnem intellectum est in corde. Denique in corde sen-
units.tr: BUT how does Christ receive the man, and with what words first? "Dost thou believe?" He establishes him in faith in the Son of God, for this is the beginning of all grace: faith in Christ. Through him, says the Apostle, we have had access by faith into this grace in which we stand. But note that he urges faith and asks whether he believes. For by asking in this way he stirs up his desire and prepares the man's mind to receive faith. Note also that he asks whether he believes in the Son of God. For he wants him to know that this is the Messiah, whose name was commonly on everyone's lips as the Son of God, not merely the son of David, as was commonly thought. For our faith does not rest in Christ until it penetrates to that Deity dwelling in him bodily [σωματικῶς]. For God's wrath, provoked by our sins, does not come to rest except in that blood which in a certain manner is the very blood of God, namely because of the ineffable union of the human and divine natures in Christ. Wherefore, since God's wrath and our faith rest together in the same place, it must be that the security of our faith and the certainty of the forgiveness of sins are then at last present, when that Deity of the Son has been apprehended. The humanity and blood of Christ are also apprehended, but only in that union which is with the Son of God. "Who is he, Lord?" I answer, in the case of the man who had been blind: first, it is praiseworthy that he does not believe rashly, that is, apply his heart, but first seeks knowledge. For the light of the mind necessarily goes before the apprehension of the heart, and faith proceeds from knowledge. For how could I apprehend by faith, or apply to myself, what I do not first have known? It is true that the sense of the heart is sometimes deeper and greater than the knowledge of the mind. For unspeakable sighs are stirred up in the heart, unspeakable joy exists in the heart, the peace which passes all understanding is in the heart. Finally, in the heart are felt those things which cannot be fully known by the mind nor expressed by the tongue. Yet some knowledge of the mind is always required, at least for this, namely for application. Faith establishes a solid foundation. And this way of acting which this man followed condemns that implicit faith of the Papists. Another thing is also praiseworthy in this answer of the man: namely that he desires both to know and to believe. For this is the first operation of the Holy Spirit and the first grace, as they call it, of the Spirit: it stirs up in him a desire and thirst to understand and to believe. For this desire does not arise from the freedom of our will, but is a motion of the Holy Spirit and the beginning of our regeneration. This first grace is followed by knowledge and faith itself, which necessarily follows the first. For he who gives the willing also gives the performing. And blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Wherefore we must always come to hear the Word of God with a certain hunger and thirst and desire: for from this there will necessarily follow some increase of knowledge and faith.

units.la: Fides sterinit solidū fundamentum. sentiuntur ea, quæ tota neque cognosci possunt mente, neque lingua exprimi. Attamen requiritur perpetuò aliqua saltem notitia mentis ad hoc, ut scilicet applicatio. Atque hæc quidem agendi ratio quam secutus est homo iste, condemnat fidem illam implicitam Papistarum. Alterum quoque est laudabile in hoc hominis istius responso, nempe quòd desideret & cognoscere & credere. Hæc enim est prima Spiritus Sancti operatio & prima gratia, ut vocant, Spiritus: nempe de cupit desiderium & sitis intelligendi & credendi. Neque enim exsistit hoc desiderium à libertate arbitrij nostri, sed motus est Spiritus sancti, & initium regenerationis nostri. Hanc primam gratiam sequitur altera ipsa notitia & fides quæ primam sequitur necessario. Nam qui dat velle, dat quoque perficere. Et beati sunt qui esuriunt & sitiunt iustitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum. Quare semper cum fame quadam & siti ac desiderio veniendum est ad verbum Dei audiendum: hinc enim sequetur necessario aliquod certè notitiæ & fidei incrementum.
units.tr: Faith establishes a solid foundation. Those things are felt which cannot be wholly grasped by the mind nor expressed by the tongue. Nevertheless, some knowledge of the mind is always required at least for this, namely for application. And this way of acting which this man followed condemns that implicit faith of the Papists. Another thing is also praiseworthy in this answer of the man, namely that he desires both to know and to believe. For this is the first operation of the Holy Spirit and the first grace, as they call it, of the Spirit: it stirs up in him a desire and thirst to understand and to believe. For this desire does not arise from the freedom of our will, but is a motion of the Holy Spirit and the beginning of our regeneration. This first grace is followed by knowledge and faith itself, which necessarily follows the first. For he who gives the willing also gives the performing. And blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Wherefore we must always come to hear the Word of God with a certain hunger and thirst and desire: for from this there will necessarily follow some increase of knowledge and faith.

units.la: Et vidisti eum. Non statim ostendit, ecquis sit ille Dei filius, sed prius admonet eum negligentiæ, quòd cùm vi- derit Filium, non tamen cognoscat. Quæri potest quomodo eum vidêrit, cùm oculis eum corporeis non sit antehac intuitus, discesserat enim Christus priusquam reversus est homo à piscina Siloam. Quare alius hic videtur intuitus intelligendus, nempe intuitus gloriæ, quæ effulsit in illo opere potentiæ & misericordiæ in ipso homine editæ. Sic dixit Iohannes, se vidisse gloriam Christi, tanquam gloriam unigeniti egressi à Patre. Quare admonet eum negligentiæ, quòd cùm in illo opere videre potuerit oculis animi gloriam filij Dei, non tamen satis eam animadverterit. Sic admonedi sunt à nobis, qui cùm de Christo eiusque mysterio audiuerint, non semel sed centies, accedunt tamen ad audiendum de eo adeo ignari, ac si nihil unquam de eo auditum esset abiis. Sic enim præparantur ad maiorem attentionem & accenditur in iis studium quoddam serium audiendi ea quæ dicuntur. Tum quis sit Filius ille Dei demonstratus? Non ait, Ego is sum, sed, Qui loquitur tecum ille est. Hac nimirum descriptione & periphrasi filij Dei non ingificaciter, gnens notitiam, sed fidem in corde ex sensu tanti bene-ficij, quòd scilicet tam familiari colloquio filius Dei homunculonem illum dignatus sit. Sensus enim divini beneficij est quæ facit illam in nobis cordis applicatio-nem & apprehensionem, quam fidem dicimus. Sermo Euangelij totus est de gratia & misericordia: vnde non tantùm est sermo cognitionis, ad cognitionem faciendam in mente: sed est sermo fidei ad fidem gignendam ex sensu illius misericordiæ quæ toties resonat in Euan-gelio. Atque in eo etiam offertur, adeóque per ipsum perficitur in cordibus nostris. Ait ille, Credo. Hoc lauda-bile est in homine isto, quòd non citius cognoscat filiū Dei, quàm credat in eum. Neque enim apprehensio cor-dis continuò sequitur in quibuscunque notitiam mentis: rarum enim est illud beneficium verae fidei. Quare oportuit magnam esse efficaciam ipsius Christi in hoc homine, qua cor tam citò est adductum ad credendum in filium Dei, præsertim ita humiliatum in carne. Qua-quam non dixerim nisi fidei principium istud inchoa-tum in homine isto tam citò, ex tam tenui notitia: ut e-nim sit perfectior fides in Christum, alia multa intelli-geda sunt in illo Christi mysterio. Et adorauit eum. Fides in Dei filium erumpit in adorationem, hoc enim est pri-mū fidei effectū, humiliatio simplex cordis & reverētia Dei. Hic enim aliter res se habet, quàm solet se habere inter homines, vbi nimia familiaritas parit contemptū.
units.tr: And thou hast seen him. He does not at once show who that Son of God is, but first admonishes him of his carelessness, that although he has seen the Son, yet he does not recognise him. It may be asked how he has seen him, since he had not looked upon him with bodily eyes before, for Christ had departed before the man returned from the pool of Siloam. Therefore another kind of sight seems to be meant, namely the sight of the glory which shone forth in that work of power and mercy wrought in the man himself. So John said that he had seen the glory of Christ, as the glory of the only-begotten going forth from the Father. Therefore he admonishes him of carelessness, that although in that work he could have seen with the eyes of his mind the glory of the Son of God, yet he had not sufficiently noticed it. So we also ought to be admonished, who, though we have heard about Christ and his mystery not once but a hundred times, nevertheless come to hear about him so ignorant, as if nothing had ever been heard about him before. For in this way they are prepared for greater attention, and in them is kindled a certain earnest zeal for hearing what is said. Then, who is that Son of God who is shown? He does not say, "I am he," but, It is he who talks with you. Surely by this description and periphrasis of the Son of God, he does not stir up knowledge in the mind so much as faith in the heart, from the sense of so great a benefit, namely that the Son of God has deigned to converse with that poor little man in such familiar talk. For the sense of the divine benefit is what produces in us that application and apprehension of the heart which we call faith. The word of the Gospel is wholly about grace and mercy: hence it is not only a word of knowledge, to make knowledge in the mind, but a word of faith, to beget faith from the sense of that mercy which resounds so often in the Gospel. And in that word also it is offered, and so through it is brought to completion in our hearts. He said, I believe. This is praiseworthy in this man, that he does not know the Son of God sooner than he believes in him. For the apprehension of the heart does not always follow immediately upon knowledge in the mind, for that gift of true faith is rare. Wherefore the efficacy of Christ himself in this man must have been great, by which his heart was so quickly brought to believe in the Son of God, especially one so humbled in the flesh. Although I would not say that this beginning of faith was begun in this man so quickly out of so slight a knowledge; for in order that faith in Christ may be more perfect, many other things are to be understood in that mystery of Christ. And he worshipped him. Faith in the Son of God breaks out into worship, for this is the first effect of faith: a simple humbling of the heart and reverence for God. For here the matter stands otherwise than it usually does among men, where excessive familiarity breeds contempt.

units.la: 39 Et dixit Iesus, Ad iudicium exercendum ego in hunc mundum veni: vt qui non vident, vide-ant, & qui vident cæci fiant.
units.tr: "Jesus said, For judgment I am come into this world, that they which see not might see; and that they which see might be made blind."

units.la: 40 Audiuerunt autem hæc quidam ex Phari-sæis, qui cum ipso erant, & dixerunt ei, Num & nos cæci sumus?
units.tr: "And some of the Pharisees which were with him heard these words, and said unto him, Are we blind also?"

units.la: 41 Dixit eis Iesus, Si cæci essetis non haberetis peccatum: nunc verò dicitis, Videmus: itaque pec-catum vestrum manet.
units.tr: "Jesus said unto them, If ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth."

units.la: Nunc occasione beneficij huius collati in homine isto, nempe quòd aperuerit eius oculos, oculos, inquam, animi ad videndum filium Dei, & credendum in eum, incipit concionari de certo quodam fine aduentu brum tinens sui in mundum, id autem facit, vt videtur, conuersus ad eos qui circumstabant: finis autem est cur in mundum venerit, nempe vt iudicium exerceret, hoc est, vt regis & iudicis partes ageret (nam iudicium istud pertinet ad officium Christi regale) iudicis, inquam, partes ageret in iudicando, de aequo & iniquo, de bono & malo, & adiudicando cuique mercedem suam. De hoc Christi iudicio quodnam sit, & a quo ipsum acceperit, nempe a Deo Patre, supra vidimus cap.5. Vbi dicit, Pater non iudicat quenquam, sed omne iudicium dedit Filio, vers.22. & postea vers.27. Dedit ei authoritatem iudicium etiam exercendi, quatenus Filius hominis est. Declarat autem iudicium, de quo in genere dixit, ex particulari quodam iudicio, vel potius praeiudicio, quod filius Dei exercet in mundo ante illud magnum & extremum iudicium, quodque praecurrit illam vel salutem, vel condemnationem aeternam. Nam quotquot illuminantur in hac vita, arrham habet futurae illius vitae aeternae. Et quotquot excaecatur in hac & perseuerant in ea caecitate, nihil habent quo sibi persuadeant victuros sese post hanc vitam. Quod si tectum est Euangelium nostrum, tectum est iis qui pereunt, inquit Apostolus. Neque vero tantum in sua persona exercuit Dominus hoc iudicium, tum nimirum quum interris ageret, sed per Ministros suos illud ipsum exercet continuo ad reditum suum vltimum, & magnum ac postremum illud iudicium. Per ministros enim suos soluit & ligat, per Ministros suos excaecat & illuminat. Sed videamus qui demum sint quibus oculos adiudicat: ij sunt qui caeci sunt, hoc est, qui habentur pro caecis, ab iis nimirum qui videntur sibi sapere. Sic enim nominat eos ex sententia Pharisaeorum, qui sapienter suae praesidebant, idque cum contemptu aliorum: neque vero tantum caeci sunt hoc loco qui ex sententia Pharisaeorum sunt caeci, sed qui videntur etiam sibi ipsis caeci esse, & afficiuntur serio sensu ignorantiae, peccati ac miseriae suae: nam hi sunt quos vocat Dominus pauperes Spiritu. Et quos vocat Apostolus stultos. Item Dominus alibi oneratos dicit afflictos, dicens, Venite ad me omnes qui fatigati estis, & onerati, & ego faciam vt requiescatis. His adiudicat occu-
units.tr: Now, on the occasion of this benefit conferred on this man, namely that he has opened his eyes, the eyes, I say, of his mind, to see the Son of God and believe in him, Christ begins to preach about a certain definite end of his coming into the world. He does this, it seems, turning to those who stood around. The end is why he came into the world, namely to exercise judgment, that is, to act the part of king and judge (for this judgment belongs to the kingly office of Christ). I say, he would act the part of a judge in judging between right and wrong, good and evil, and in rendering to each his due reward. We saw above, in chapter 5, what this judgment of Christ is and from whom he received it, namely from God the Father. There he says, "The Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son" (v. 22), and afterwards, in v. 27, "He hath given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man." He then explains the judgment he spoke of in general by means of a particular judgment, or rather a preliminary judgment, which the Son of God exercises in the world before that great and final judgment, and which goes before that eternal salvation or condemnation. For all who are enlightened in this life have a pledge of that future eternal life, and all who are blinded in this life and persist in that blindness have nothing by which they can assure themselves that they will live after this life. "But if our gospel be hid," says the Apostle, "it is hid to them that are lost" (2 Cor. 4). Nor did the Lord exercise this judgment only in his own person, when he was indeed on earth, but he continues to exercise it through his ministers until his final return and that great and last judgment. For through his ministers he loosens and binds, and through his ministers he blinds and enlightens. But let us see who they are to whom he adjudges sight. They are those who are blind, that is, who are regarded as blind by those who seem to themselves to be wise. For he calls them blind according to the opinion of the Pharisees, who presided over the wise, and that with contempt for others. Yet those are not the only blind in this place who are blind by the Pharisees' judgment; those are also blind who seem blind to themselves, and who are seriously affected by a sense of their own ignorance, sin and misery. For these are the ones whom the Lord calls the poor in spirit, and whom the Apostle calls fools. Likewise the Lord elsewhere calls them burdened and afflicted, saying, Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. To these he adjudges (sight-)

units.la: Quosdam illuminat. Qui sint illuminati. los. Modus autem quo illos illuminat, est idem cum eo quo illuminauit caecum illum, nempe demonstrauit caeco illi filium Dei. Aspectus Christi in Euangelio crucifixi & glorificati illuminat oculos nostros. Ad praebendum, inquit Paulus, lumen cognitionis gloriæ Dei in facie Iesu Christi. Nā simulatq; cor conuertitur ad Dominū, tollitur velamen; & simulatque auditur vox filij Dei, mortui viuunt, vt supra dixit Dominus, cap.5.25. Nunc videndum qui sunt qui excæcantur, nempe ij, qui vident, hoc est opinione sua vident, hoc enim ex sensu Pharisæorum dictum est, vt supra admonuimus. Ergo excæcantur, qui, cum reipsa cæcutiant, miseri sint, nihil sint, videntur tamen sibi esse aliquid, neque tanguntur sensu aliquo miseriæ suæ. Hi cum non sentiant morbum, quomodo possunt quærere sibi medicum ad hoc vt sanentur? Modus autem quo hos excæcat, est per idem illud verbum Euangelij: nam eadem lux illa quæ humilibus aperit oculos mentis, superbis oculos admit. In causa est non verbum Euangelij proprie, sed ipsorum malitia, quæ (id quod de lege loquitur Apostolus, Rom.7.) occasione sumpta ex verbo Euangelij, per verbum illud irritatur ac augetur, latiusque venenum suum spargit atque infi-cit animum, non secus ac luce solis obiecta oculus aliquis male affectus deterior fit. Atque ex hoc sequitur non esse proprium Domini effectū hanc partem iudicij, quæ est in excæcando & indurando, sed ex malitia hominū existere. Ideoque supra cap.3.17. dictū est, Non misit Deus Filium suum in mundum vt condemnet mundum, sed vt seruetur mundus per eum. & cap.12.47. Non veni vt condemnem mundum, sed vt seruem mundum. Quare iudicij illa prior pars quæ est in illuminādo, Domini proprium est effectum, & verbum eius per se illuminat, per accidens autem & ratione malitiæ hominum excæcat.
units.tr: He grants sight to some. Who are the enlightened? The manner in which he enlightens them is the same as that by which he enlightened that blind man, namely by showing the Son of God to the blind man. The sight of Christ crucified and glorified in the Gospel enlightens our eyes. To give, says Paul, the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. For as soon as the heart is turned to the Lord, the veil is taken away; and as soon as the voice of the Son of God is heard, the dead live, as the Lord said above, in chapter 5, verse 25. Now we must consider who they are who are blinded, namely those who see, that is, who see in their own opinion. For this is said according to the sense of the Pharisees, as we noted above. Those therefore are blinded who, although they are really blind, are wretched and nothing, yet seem to themselves to be something, and are not touched by any sense of their misery. Since they do not feel the disease, how can they seek a physician for themselves, so that they may be healed? The manner in which he blinds these is by the same word of the Gospel: for the same light which opens the eyes of the mind to the humble closes them to the proud. The cause is not the word of the Gospel properly, but their own malice, which (as the Apostle speaks of the law in Romans 7) takes occasion from the word of the Gospel, is provoked and increased by that word, and spreads its poison more widely and infects the mind, just as an eye that is ill-disposed grows worse when exposed to the light of the sun. From this it follows that this part of judgment, which consists in blinding and hardening, is not the proper work of the Lord, but arises from the malice of men. Therefore it was said above, in chapter 3, verse 17: "God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world through him might be saved," and in chapter 12, verse 47: "I came not to condemn the world, but to save the world." Therefore that former part of judgment, which consists in enlightening, is the proper effect of the Lord, and his word of itself enlightens, but by accident, and by reason of the malice of men, it blinds.

units.la: Num & nos cæci sumus? Pharisæi comminationem illam Domini ad se ipsi applicant, scilicet male sibi concscij, quod quidem non esset reprehendendum, nisi applicantes simul insanirent. Hic quidem peccant grauiter, quare malitiosè admodum & superbè respondent Domino, vt non opus sit aliunde quærere exemplum illius partis iudicij quæ cernitur in excæcādo. Dominus enim dum de hoc iudicio apud eos prædicat, simul etiam ipsum exequitur. Nam reluctando veritati exæcantur & indurantur homines. Quòd si permoti sensu aliquo miseriæ suę sic respondissent Domino, Fatemur istud quod dicis: cæci quidem sumus, tu verò aperi oculos nostros: tum profecto fuisset executio alterius partis iudicij, quæ est in illuminando. Sed cùm tam duriter & superbè obviam veniant verbis Domini, id argumento est alteram illam & deteriorem iudicij partem, quæ est in excæcando, adueršus eos exerceri. Sic hodierno die videas passim exerceri hanc diuini iudicij partem, cùm homines cuiuscunque conditionis atque ordinis tam superbè & maliciosè excipiant veritatem Dei, & ex verbo ipsius comminationes & admonitiones. Si cæci essetis, Dominus tantum abest ab eo, ut quod dixit, retractet, ut è contra obiiciat iis duplicem cæcitatem. Cæci sunt primùm, deinde non vident se cæcos esse, id quod auget eorum miseriam. Sic autem occurrit iis eo fine, ut vel illuminentur & convertrentur, vel certè magis indurentur. Idem faciendum hodierno die ministris omnibus, exemplo Domini. Sic præcepit Dominus Esaiæ, ut prædicaret continuò, & prædicaret tantisper dum Iudæi illi obstinati prorsus excæcarentur atque indurarentur. Fateor equidem hoc videndum esse ministro in primis, ut quoscunque illuminet, & ut verbum eius sit odor vitæ ad vitam. Sed si id obtineri non poterit, pergendū tamen, ut salvetur glorificetur Deus in indurationæ quorundam; & odor sit mortis ad mortem. Nā etiam tum, cùm in iis qui pereunt est odor mortis ad mortem, Christi bona fragrantia est Deo. Sed videamus verba: Sicaci essetis. Id est, si cæci essetis atque ignari, quales putatis esse alios, hoc est, si cùm cæci sitis reipsa cæcitatem illam vestram agnoscueritis, tum quidem peccatum non haberetis, hoc est minus peccaretis, & magis esset hoc malum cæcitatis curabile. Sed quia dicitis, videmus: hoc est, opinione vestra videmini nobis ipsis clarè videre & cognoscere omnia, cùm reipsa cæci sitis, ideo peccatum vestrum manet: hoc est grauius est, & longius abest à remedio. Nota igitur cæcitatem istam animi peccatum esse, & Deum eo offendi, eoque differt à corporis cæcitate, quæ miseria mum.
units.tr: Are we blind also? The Pharisees apply the Lord's threat to themselves, being evidently conscious of their own guilt, which would not be blameworthy were it not that in applying it they at the same time show their madness. Here they sin gravely, and therefore they answer the Lord very maliciously and proudly, so that there is no need to look elsewhere for an example of that part of judgment which is seen in blinding. For while the Lord preaches about this judgment among them, he also carries it out at the same time. For men are blinded and hardened by resisting the truth. But if, moved by some sense of their misery, they had answered the Lord thus: "We confess what you say: we are indeed blind, but do you open our eyes," then surely the execution of the other part of judgment, which is in enlightening, would have followed. But since they meet the words of the Lord so harshly and proudly, this is evidence that the other and worse part of judgment, which is in blinding, is being carried out against them. Thus today you may see this part of the divine judgment exercised everywhere, when men of every condition and rank receive the truth of God, and the threats and admonitions from his word, so proudly and maliciously. "If ye were blind," the Lord is so far from retracting what he said that, on the contrary, he charges them with a double blindness. They are blind first, and then they do not see that they are blind, which increases their misery. Yet he meets them thus with the aim that they may either be enlightened and converted, or at least be hardened further. The same must be done today by all ministers, following the example of the Lord. So the Lord commanded Isaiah to preach continually, and to preach until those obstinate Jews were utterly blinded and hardened. I admit indeed that this is to be looked to first by the minister, that he may enlighten whomever he can, and that his word may be a savour of life unto life. But if this cannot be obtained, he must nevertheless go on, so that God may be saved and glorified in the hardening of some, and that it may be a savour of death unto death. For even then, when among those who perish it is a savour of death unto death, the good fragrance of Christ is pleasing to God. But let us look at the words: If ye were blind. That is, if you were blind and ignorant, as you think others are, that is, if, being blind, you had recognised that blindness of yours, then indeed you would not have sin, that is, you would sin less, and this evil of blindness would be more curable. But because you say, We see, that is, in your own opinion you seem to yourselves to see and know everything clearly, when in fact you are blind, therefore your sin remains: that is, it is graver and further from the remedy. Note therefore that this blindness of the mind is a sin, and that God is offended by it, and in this it differs from bodily blindness, which is a misery only.

units.la: Iudicium seuere exercet Christus in reprobos.
units.tr: Christ exercises severe judgment against the reprobate.

units.la: Esai.6.9.
Idem faciendum debent Christi servi.
units.tr: Christ's servants ought to do the same.

units.la: Cæcitas mentis, peccatum grauius. quædam est, sed non peccatum: cæcitas verò mentis peccatum est, & reum facit hominem mortis æternæ: quia nemo sic cæcus est, qui non priùs eruerit sibi ipsi oculos, quíque non assiduò oppugnet oblatam lucem per duritiem cordis sui. Propter ignorantiam, inquit Apostolus, quæ est in ipsis ex obduratione cordis eorum. Sed remedium huius mali est, si quis agnoscat ex animo cæcitatem & miseriam suam. Nam qui semel cœpit videre cæcitatem suam & appetere lucem, is continuò certè aliquo modo liberatur ab ea cæcitate. Illuminationis enim mētis hic primus gradus est, vt videamus nos ipsos cæcos esse. Quod si verò non viderit quis primùm omnium se cæcum esse, miser est, & peccatum eius manet. At si quis nō modò non viderit cæcitatem suam, sed etiam putauerit, cùm cæcus sit, se tamen videre, iã is miserior est, & multò grauius peccat. In hoc genere fuerunt Pharisæi: & in hoc genere sunt doctores illi Papistici hodierno die. Atque hoc genus hominum difficillimè omnium ad veritatis agnitionem perducitur, vt qui obstinati sint & induxati in illa cæcitate sua.
units.tr: Blindness of mind is a greater sin. There is a blindness that is a misfortune but not a sin. But blindness of mind is a sin, and it makes a man liable to eternal death, because no one is so blind that he has not first put out his own eyes, and who does not constantly resist the light offered him through the hardness of his heart. "Because of the ignorance that is in them," says the Apostle, "which comes from the hardening of their hearts." But the remedy for this evil is if someone acknowledges from the heart his blindness and misery. For whoever has once begun to see his blindness and to desire the light is certainly at once in some way freed from that blindness. For this is the first step of the enlightenment of the mind, that we see ourselves to be blind. But if someone does not first of all see that he is blind, he is wretched, and his sin remains. But if someone not only fails to see his blindness but even thinks that, though he is blind, he sees, then he is more wretched and sins far more gravely. The Pharisees were of this kind, and those Papist teachers are of this kind today. And this sort of people is brought to the acknowledgment of truth with the greatest difficulty of all, since they are obstinate and hardened in that blindness of theirs.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT

units.la: Hoc capite primùm occurrit parabola de fure siue latrone, & vero ouium pastore, cum ipsius explicatione atque euentu, ad versum vsque 22. Secundò, altercatio Christi cum Iudæis in festo Encæniorum habita de suo officio & persona, simul cum altercationis euentu vsque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: In this chapter there first occurs the parable of the thief or robber and the true shepherd of the sheep, with its explanation and outcome, up to verse 22. Secondly, the dispute of Christ with the Jews held at the feast of Encaenia, concerning his office and person, together with the outcome of the dispute, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: 1 Amen, Amen dico vobis, qui non ingreditur per ostium in caulam ouium, sed ascendit aliunde, ille fur est & latro.
units.tr: 1 Verily, verily, I say unto you, he that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber.

units.la: 2 Qui vero ingreditur per ostium, pastor est ouium. 3 Huic aperit ianitor, & oues vocem eius audiunt: & suas oues vocat nominatim, & educit eas.
units.tr: 2 But he that entereth in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep. 3 To him the porter openeth, and the sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out.

units.la: 4 Quùmque suas oues emiserit, antecedit eas, & oues eum sequuntur, quia norunt vocem eius.
units.tr: 4 And when he hath put forth his own sheep, he goeth before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice.

units.la: 5 Alienum autem nequaquam sequentur, sed fugient ab eo, quia non norunt vocem alienorum.
units.tr: 5 And a stranger will they in no wise follow, but will flee from him: for they know not the voice of strangers.

units.la: REo vt de parabola dicamus, eius occasio sumpta est ex Pharisæis iis, de quibus in fine capitis noni. Capita parabolæ hæc ferè sunt. 1. Est ouile. 2. Est ostiū ouilis. 3. Sunt personæ ouile ingredientes. Primùm quidem ij qui non ingrediuntur per ostium in caulam ouium, sed ascendunt aliunde, & hi latrones & fures dicuntur. Deinde est persona quæ ingreditur per ostium, ea autem est verus pastor. Quarto loco est probatio qua probat primùm hunc qui ingreditur per ostium Pastorem esse ouium: deinde eum qui non ingreditur per ostium, sed aliunde ascendit, furem esse. Probat autem duobus argumentis eum qui ingreditur per ostium pastorem esse ouium. Primū est à ianitore; ianitor aperit ei, hoc dictum est ex consuetudine illorum temporum, quibus seruus quidam obseruabat ingressum & egressum præcipui pastoris ouium. Secundum argumentum est ab ipsis ouibus, oues vocem eius audiunt; hoc est, obediunt eius voci. Hoc ostenditur verbis sequentibus. Pastor ingressus ouile suas oues nominatim vocat, nam numerus earum cùm olim non adeo copiosè magnus fuit, vt non posset eas pastor etiam singulas nominare. Pastor autem diligens erat in singulis de capite notandis & cognoscēdis, quasi de nomine. Ergo ipse nominatim vocat singulas, & vocatas educit: eductis verò præit ipse, illæ sequuntur. Causa est quia noverunt vocem eius. Deinde ostendit non esse cuin qui non egreditur per ostium, pastorem ouium ex eo quòd oues eum non sequantur, quia nimirum non nouerunt vocem eius. Atque hæc est parabola, cuius hic est scopus, vt doceat Pharisæos illos non esse veros pastores, se verò & quotquot ipsius nomine docent veros esse pastores.
units.tr: To speak of the parable: its occasion was taken from those Pharisees of whom we read at the end of chapter nine. The chief points of the parable are roughly these. (1) There is a sheepfold. (2) There is a door of the fold. (3) There are the persons who enter the fold. First are those who do not enter by the door into the sheepfold but climb up another way, and these are called robbers and thieves. Then there is the person who enters by the door, and he is the true shepherd. Fourth comes the proof, by which he first shows that the one who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep, and then that the one who does not enter by the door but climbs up elsewhere is a thief. He proves by two arguments that the one who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep. The first is from the porter: the porter opens to him. This was said according to the custom of those times, when a certain servant watched the coming and going of the chief shepherd of the sheep. The second argument is from the sheep themselves: the sheep hear his voice, that is, they obey his voice. This is shown by the words that follow. The shepherd, entering the fold, calls his own sheep by name, for their number was not formerly so great that the shepherd could not name each one of them. The diligent shepherd took care to note and know each sheep by its head, as it were by name. So he himself calls each one by name, and when they are called he leads them out; and when they are led out he goes before, and they follow. The reason is that they know his voice. Then he shows that the one who does not go out through the door is not the shepherd of the sheep, because the sheep do not follow him, clearly because they do not know his voice. And this is the parable, whose aim here is to teach that those Pharisees are not true shepherds, but that he himself, and all who teach in his name, are the true shepherds.

units.la: 6 Hanc similitudinem dixit eis Iesus. Illi verò non cognouerunt quænam illa essent quæ loquebatur eis.
units.tr: 6 Jesus spoke this parable to them, but they did not understand what the things were which he was saying to them.

units.la: 7 Iesus ergo rursum dixit eis, Amen, amen dico vobis, ego sum ostium ouium.
units.tr: 7 Jesus therefore said to them again, Verily, verily I say unto you, I am the door of the sheep.

units.la: Sequitur parabolæ expositio. Primùm allata est ab Euangelista eius occasio, nempe ignorantia præsertim Pharisæorum. Hic obiter voluit invrere eis ignorantiæ notam, qui tamen considebant supra modum cognitioni suæ, nam etsi parabola obscurior quædam fit orationis species (est enim parabola non nuda comparatio & similitudo, sed allegoria, & impropriя quædam loquendi ratio) tamen non ita obscura fuit haec parabola, quin illi si habuissent vel vnciam eius scientiæ, quam immenso pondere se habere videri volebant, potuerint eam satis intelligere. Ego autem existimo adductam esse parabolam hanc in gratiam Pharisæorum, vt ij ipsi qui putabant se omnia scire, experientia comperirent se nihil scire, ne ea quidem, quæ non ita difficilia erant. Sic tentat Deus eos qui sapientiæ suæ falsam opinionem habent. Iesus ergo rursus. Sequitur nunc expositio, in qua orditur ab ostio ouilis. De ouili ipso, primùm fuit dicendum, sed quia quid sit facile cognosci potest ex sequentibus, ideo eius expositionem omisit. Illud itaque nunc nos paucis attingemus. Ouile est Ecclesia Christi, præsertim illa invisibilis, ex iis cœtibus quos nouit Dominus, vt ex sequentibus intelligitur. Cōparantur homines qui in illa Ecclesia sunt cum ouibus variis de causis, primùm oues errabundæ sunt naturaliter & homines etiā electi, etiam vocati. Vnde cōparamur ouibus errantibus ante conuersionem nostram. Nam eratis, inquit Petrus, velut oues errantes, sed conuersi nunc estis ad pastorem & curatorem animarum vestrarum. Deinde oues exrant, ita vt earum
units.tr: The exposition of the parable follows. First, the Evangelist gives its occasion, namely the ignorance of the Pharisees above all. Here he wished in passing to level at them the mark of ignorance, though they were excessively confident in their own knowledge. For although a parable is a rather obscure form of speech (a parable is not a bare comparison and likeness but an allegory, a kind of figurative way of speaking), this parable was not so obscure that they could not have understood it well enough, had they possessed even an ounce of that knowledge which they wished to appear to have in such great measure. I think, however, that this parable was introduced for the sake of the Pharisees, so that those who believed they knew everything might discover by experience that they knew nothing, not even those things which were not so difficult. In this way God tests those who hold a false opinion of their own wisdom. "Jesus therefore said again." Now follows the exposition, which begins with the door of the sheepfold. Concerning the sheepfold itself, something should have been said first, but because what it is can easily be gathered from what follows, he has omitted its exposition. Therefore we shall touch on it briefly now. The sheepfold is the Church of Christ, especially the invisible Church, made up of those companies which the Lord knows, as is understood from what follows. Men who are in that Church are compared with sheep for various reasons. First, sheep are by nature prone to wander, and men too, even the elect and the called. Hence we are compared to sheep going astray before our conversion. For, says Peter, "you were like sheep going astray, but you have now returned to the shepherd and overseer of your souls." Next, sheep go astray, so that their salvation is despaired of, and the shepherd thinks them already lost.

units.la: { } Ecclesia Dei. Ouile, Ecclesia Dei. rum salus sit desperata, & putet pastor iam perditas esse eas. Similiter omnium hominum iudicio ex hominibus, qui in Ecclesia sunt Christi, quidam sic erant vt desperati esse videantur & perditi. Vide parabolam ouis perditae Matth. 18. 12. Luc. 15. 1. & deinceps. Tertio oues audiunt & agnoscunt vocem pastoris sui, postquam iam satis manluefactae sunt, id quod hoc loco dicitur: ita homines & electi in Ecclesia, postquam iam satis mansuefacti sunt, agnoscunt vocem pastoris sui. dico posteaquam iam satis mansuefacti sunt, quia ipsi etiam electi ante regenerationem totidem quasi ferae belluae sunt. Nemo enim nascitur ouis, sed formatur per regenerationem. Postremo in mansuetudine & simplicitate maxime est similitudo. Nam oues scimus natura mansuetum esse animal, nulli iniurium, sed multis vtile, iniuriis vero aliorum obnoxium, & in ferendis iniuriis patientissimum. Sic pij in Ecclesia innoxij sunt & prosunt etiam nocentibus, obnoxij sunt iniuriis, & patienter ferunt eas: ita tamen simplices esse debent vt oues, vt columbae, vt interea prudentes sint vt serpentes in dignoscendis & cauendis Christi hostibus. Amen, amen. Orditur primum expositionem parabolae ab ostio, asseuerat autem se ostiu esse ouium, adhibita vsitata illa & familiari sibi asseverationis specie: ita tamen obsignat quod ab eo dicitur, vt mundus no possit illud couellere. Notandae sunt phrases ipsae Christo familiares: Ego sum, inquit, panis vitae, ego sum lux mundi, ego sum illud ostium, ego sum pastor ille bonus, ego sum vitis illa vera, & similia. Quae quidem voces profectae sunt, fateor, a Christo homine, etiam vt homo est: nam ita constituitur est ab aeterno, vt filius Dei neque panis nobis sit, neque lux, &c. nisi incarnatus. Verum exsurgunt hae loquutiones ex altiori quodam principio & diuiniori, nempe maiestate illa Dei quae in ipso inhabitat corporaliter. Nulla enim creatura, vt creatura est tantum, haec de se sine blasphemia audet praedicare. Quare vel ex his loquendi generibus satis conuincitur seruatorem nostrum Dei filium esse. Sed videamus nunc ipsa verba: Ego sum, inquit, ostium ouium, hoc est, ouilis. Christus quidem praecipue hic dicitur ostium, respectu
units.tr: The Church of God. The sheepfold, the Church of God: of these the salvation may be despaired of, and the shepherd may think them already lost. In the same way, by everyone's judgment, some of those who are in Christ's Church seem desperate and lost. See the parable of the lost sheep, Matth. 18.12; Luke 15.1 and following. Third, sheep hear and recognise the voice of their shepherd once they have become sufficiently tame, which is what is said in this place. So men, even the elect in the Church, recognise the voice of their shepherd once they have become sufficiently tame. I say "once they have become sufficiently tame", because even the elect, before regeneration, are as wild beasts. For no one is born a sheep; he is formed by regeneration. Lastly, the likeness lies chiefly in gentleness and simplicity. For we know that the sheep by nature is a gentle animal, harmful to no one, but useful to many, and liable to the injuries of others, and most patient in enduring them. So the godly in the Church are harmless, and they benefit even the wicked; they are liable to injuries, and they bear them patiently. Yet they ought to be simple as sheep and as doves, while at the same time being wise as serpents in discerning and guarding against Christ's enemies. Amen, amen. First he begins the exposition of the parable with the door, and he affirms that he is the door of the sheep, using that customary and familiar form of asseveration of his. Yet he so seals what is said by him that the world cannot tear it away. The phrases themselves are familiar to Christ and ought to be noted: "I am," he says, "the bread of life; I am the light of the world; I am that door; I am that good shepherd; I am that true vine," and similar things. These words, I admit, came from Christ as man, since it was appointed from eternity that the Son of God would not be bread or light to us, and so on, unless he were incarnate. But these forms of speech arise from a certain higher and more divine principle, namely that majesty of God which dwells in him bodily. For no creature, as a creature only, dares to say these things of himself without blasphemy. Wherefore, from these very modes of speaking, it is sufficiently proved that our Saviour is the Son of God. But let us now look at the words themselves: "I am," he says, "the door of the sheep," that is, the sheepfold. Christ is called the door here chiefly with respect to the shepherds who enter in to the sheep.

units.la: Quo respectu ostium dicatur. pastorum qui ingrediuntur ad oues. Verum ostium est quoque per quod ipsæ oues ingrediuntur in ouile. Unde scripturæ allusione quadam facta ad ostium istud, de Christo sic loquuntur: Per quem etiam fide habuimus hunc aditum in gratiam hanc per quam stamus. Item, in quo habemus libertatem & aditum cum fiducia per fidem ipsius. Quamobrem Christus ostium est. Præterea tantum est ostium per quod oues ingrediuntur in illam caulam earum ouium, quæ Domino suo tantum sunt notæ, hoc est, in Ecclesiam invisibilem, eam nimirum quam hic proprie intelligimus, & ad beneficia illa Christi, remissione peccatorum & vitam æternam participanda. Fieri quidem potest ut larvatæ quædam oues, hoc est hypocritæ, ingrediantur in Ecclesiam istam visibilem, suo tempore rursus ex ea eiiciendæ: sed oues veræ nullæ ingrediuntur in Ecclesiam invisibilem, nisi per ostium Christum, hoc est, per Christum vera fide apprehensum. Porro videndum hic quomodo dicatur Christus ostium: nam hæc loquutio est impropria. Christus quidem, ut filius Dei est, ostium est primum, sed non ea tantum ratione, verum etiam ut homo est, ostium vocatur. Ita enim decretum est ab æterno ut Christus Deus & homo simul sit ostium. Ergo oportet quoque homo sit, neque id tantum, sed oportet sit homo crucifixus. Ergo ostium est qua filius Dei est crucifixus in natura hominis. Id quod sic ostenditur: Ira Dei in peccatum præclusit nobis omne aditum ad cælos, nosque conclusit sub peccato & damnatione. Crux autem Christi est quæ satisfacit iræ, atque ita satisfacit iræ & iustitiæ, ut simul promereatur gratia & misericordiam, eaque excellentia est soli iuspalmonis Christi. Pœnæ reproborum satisfaciunt quidem iræ Dei, & Deus quasi pascit se eorum supplicio in æternum: sed nihil merentur pœnæ illæ quæ sufficiunt ad satisfaciendum pro peccato. At, quæ fuit dignitas personæ Christi, illius passio etiam, præterquam quod plene satisfecerit iræ Patris, promeretur præterea nobis gratiam, & quantam illam. Id apparet ex fœdere gratiæ, in quo promittitur iustitia, eaque æterna & nunquam peritura, promittitur vita eaque æterna, non quidem degenda in terrestri aliquo paradiso, qualis vita promissa est in fœdere legali in creatione, sed agenda infinito cum gaudio & pace in paradiso caelesti. Haec ideo dico, vt videas quantum sit meritum in passione Christi. Tantum hoc addo, vt passio illa sit nobis meritoria, firma fide apprehendenda est, nobisque per fidem applicandus est Christus crucifixus. Quem profecto non apprehendimus corde citius quam sentire incipiamus meritum illud passionis Christi ad iustitiae sensum & vitae aeternae. Diximus antea Christum ostium hic intelligi praecipue respectu Pastorum, id nunc videbimus. Non est alius in ovile Christi introitus quam unicum hoc ostium. Fieri quidem potest vt fures suffodiant sibi foramina, per quae subintrediatur in ovile, sed ostium aliud nullum est in ovili; neque verus vnquam pastor per aliam viam ingressus est ovile, quam per Christum solum. Vnde Paulus ait, Ego igitur cum venirem ad vos, fratres, non veni cum eminentia sermonis aut sapientiae, hoc est, non subingressus sum per rimam aliquam ad suffurandam animos vestros, & alienandum eos a sinceritate crucis Christi. Nam, inquit, non decreveram quicquam scire inter vos nisi Iesum Christum eum que crucifixum. Ingreditur ergo per ostium Pastor, cum nihil profiteatur aut praedicat nisi solum Christum, eumque crucifixum. Sed videat Pastor ne tantum aliis praedicet Christum, verum vt ipse particeps fiat Euangelii sui, & non ingrediatur ovile tantum, vt Pastor, sed vt ovis, & vt se pascat eodem cibo quem ovibus distribuit, & primus credat iis, quae aliis credenda proponit, sicuti post Dauidem Paulus de se dixit: Et quia habemus eundem Spiritum fidei, secundum illud quod scriptum est, Credidi & ideo loquutus sum, nos quoque credimus, quamobrem etiam loquimur. Secus enim, quid prodest cuiquam praedicare Euangelium, si interea ipse reprobus fiat?
units.tr: In what respect the door is so called: the shepherds who enter to the sheep. But the door is also that through which the sheep themselves enter the fold. Hence, with some allusion to this door, they speak of Christ thus: Through whom also we have obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand. Likewise: in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through his faith. Therefore Christ is the door. Moreover, he is the only door through which the sheep enter that fold of his sheep who are known only to their Lord, that is, into the invisible Church, which is certainly the one we properly mean here, to share in those benefits of Christ, the forgiveness of sins and eternal life. It can indeed happen that certain sheep in disguise, that is, hypocrites, enter this visible Church, to be cast out of it again in due time; but no true sheep enter the invisible Church except through the door, Christ, that is, through Christ laid hold of by true faith. Further, we must consider here how Christ is called the door, for this way of speaking is figurative. Christ is indeed the first door as he is the Son of God, but he is called the door not only for that reason, but also as he is man. For it has been decreed from eternity that Christ, God and man together, should be the door. Therefore he must also be man, and not only man, but a crucified man. So he is the door in that the Son of God was crucified in human nature. This is shown as follows: the wrath of God, on account of sin, has shut against us every access to heaven, and has shut us up under sin and condemnation. But the cross of Christ is what satisfies the wrath, and so satisfies both the wrath and the justice of God that it at the same time merits grace and mercy, and this excellence belongs to the sole righteousness of Christ. The punishments of the reprobate indeed satisfy the wrath of God, and God, as it were, feeds himself on their torment forever; but those punishments merit nothing, being enough only to make satisfaction for sin. But the dignity of the person of Christ, and his passion too, besides fully satisfying the wrath of the Father, further merit grace for us, and how great a grace! This appears from the covenant of grace, in which righteousness is promised, and an everlasting righteousness that will never perish; life is promised, and eternal life, not indeed to be spent in some earthly paradise, such as the life promised in the legal covenant at creation, but to be lived in infinite joy and peace in the heavenly paradise. I say these things so that you may see how great is the merit in the passion of Christ. I add only this: that the passion may be meritorious for us, it must be grasped by firm faith, and Christ crucified must be applied to us through faith. Certainly we do not lay hold of him in our hearts sooner than we begin to feel that merit of Christ's passion for the sense of righteousness and of eternal life. We said before that Christ is understood here as the door, chiefly with respect to the shepherds; now we shall see this. There is no other entrance into the fold of Christ than this single door. It may indeed happen that thieves dig holes for themselves through which they slip into the fold, but there is no other door in the fold; nor has any true shepherd ever entered the fold by any other way than through Christ alone. Hence Paul says: For I, brethren, when I came to you, did not come with excellence of speech or of wisdom, that is, I did not slip in through some crack to steal your minds and to turn them away from the sincerity of the cross of Christ. For, he says, I had determined to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. So the shepherd enters by the door when he professes and preaches nothing but Christ alone, and him crucified. But let the shepherd take care that he does not preach Christ only to others, but becomes himself a partaker of his Gospel, and does not enter the fold only as shepherd but as a sheep, and feeds on the same food he distributes to the sheep, and first believes what he proposes to others to be believed, just as after David Paul said of himself: And since we have the same spirit of faith, according to what is written, I believed and therefore I spoke, we also believe, and therefore we also speak. Otherwise, what good is it to anyone to preach the Gospel, if meanwhile he himself becomes reprobate?

units.la: 8 Quotquot ante me venerunt, fures sunt & latrones: sed oves non auscultarunt eos.
units.tr: 8 All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them.

units.la: 9 Ego sum illud ostium: per me si quis introierit, servabitur: & ingredietur & egredietur, & pascua inveniet.
units.tr: 9 I am the door: if anyone enters by me, he will be saved, and he will go in and out, and will find pasture.

units.la: 10 Fur non venit nisi vt furetur & mactet &c. perdat oues: Ego veni vt vitam habeant & abun-dent.
units.tr: 10 The thief does not come except to steal, and to kill, and to destroy the sheep. I have come that they may have life and have it abundantly.

units.la: 11 Ego sum Pastor ille bonus: bonus pastor animam suam deponit pro ouibus.
units.tr: 11 I am that good Shepherd: the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.

units.la: HActenus de ouili & de ostio: nunc de personis ingredientibus ouile illud: ac primùm de furibus est dicendum. Fures sunt, inquit, quotquot ante ipsum venerunt. Hoc non est in genere intelligendum, sed limitandum hac restrictione, nempe (& non ingressi sunt per ostiū) de ostio enim proximè loquutus est. Ergo omnes Doctores, siue illi ex Iudaeis, siue ex gentibus erant, ex Iudaeis verò praesertim, qui ante Christum venerunt, neque ingressi sunt ad populum per ipsum, tanquam per vnicum ostium, hoc est, non posuerunt hoc vnicū doctrinae suae fundamentum, totidem fures erant. Doctores & Philosophi ex gentibus doctrinam virtutum, vitiorum, felicitatis ipsius, nulla interea Christi, vel Dei in Christo mentione facta, tradiderunt, quare vanis fuit tota illa eorum doctrina. Pharisaei Legem Mosis proposuerunt populo Dei, eiusque videri voluerunt acerrimi vindices, sed de Christo, qui finis est legis, nihil. Quamobrem & illi quoque fures erant ac latrones. Quod de temporibus quae ante Christum fuerunt, loquor, id trahendum ad tempora aduentum Christi subsequuta. Quicunque post Christum Doctores non ingressi sunt ad populum Dei per illud vnicum ostium, nempe Christum, sed subingressi sunt per rimas & foramina quae ipsi sibi suffoderunt, cum meritis scilicet hominum & Angelorum, cum satisfactionibus, cum Purgatorio, cum invocatione sanctorum & reliquis id genus somniis, illi totidem fures ac latrones & erant & sunt hodierno die, praetexat quicquid lubet, etiam Christi etiam Ecclesiae nomen. Nam non ingreditur per Christum, nisi qui per eum solum ingreditur. Verùm, vt ad verba veniamus, Quotquot, inquit. Obiici ei potuit, At multi venerunt ante te? Respondeo, Quotquot venerunt ante me, & non ingressi sunt per me, totidem fures fuerunt. Deinde, ante me, dicit. Obiici enim potuit, At antiqui fuerunt illi, qui ingressi sunt? Respond. Quàm antiqui fuerint & quàm longo tempo-
units.tr: Hitherto concerning the sheepfold and the door; now concerning the persons who enter that sheepfold. And first, concerning thieves must be spoken. "They are thieves," he says, "as many as came before him." This is not to be understood in general terms but is to be limited by this restriction, namely "and did not enter by the door," for he has just spoken of the door. Therefore all teachers, whether they were from the Jews or from the Gentiles, and especially the Jews who came before Christ and did not enter to the people through him, as through the one door (that is, did not lay this one foundation for their doctrine), were just as many thieves. The teachers and philosophers among the Gentiles delivered a doctrine of virtues, vices and happiness itself, with no mention made of Christ or of God in Christ, so all that doctrine of theirs was empty. The Pharisees set forth the Law of Moses to the people of God and wished to be seen as its most zealous defenders, but said nothing of Christ, who is the end of the Law. Wherefore they too were thieves and robbers. What I say of the times before Christ must be applied also to the times that followed his coming. Whoever after Christ has been a teacher and has not entered to the people of God through that one door, namely Christ, but has crept in through the cracks and holes they have dug for themselves, with the merits of men and angels, with satisfactions, with Purgatory, with the invocation of saints and other dreams of that kind, they were and still are today just as many thieves and robbers, however much they pretend, even to the name of Christ and of the Church. For no one enters through Christ unless he enters through him alone. But to come to the words: "as many as," he says. It could be objected to him: "But many came before you?" I answer: as many as came before me and did not enter through me were just as many thieves. Next, he says "before me." For it could be objected: "But were those who entered ancient?" I answer: how ancient they were, and how long before me they came, makes no difference, provided they did not enter through me, for they were nothing but thieves and robbers. I note this on account of the Papists, who boast of the multitude and antiquity of their teachers, as if this were enough to make them true teachers, while all the time they sell nothing but their lies to the people of God. Christ would answer those who make such a display of their multitude and antiquity in this way: they are only thieves and robbers.

units.la: Aduersus inanem superstitiosorum iactantiam. re ante me venerint, nihil refert, modo non sint ingressi per me. Non enim nisi fures & latrones fuerunt. Hæc obseruo propter Papistas, qui multitudinem doctorum suorum & antiquitatem iactitant. Quasi vero hoc satis sit ad id, vt sint ipsi veri doctores, cum interea non nisi mendacia sua populo Dei venditent. Christus istius multitudinem & antiquitate suam sic ostentantibus in hunc modum occurreret, eos fures esse & latrones tantum.
units.tr: Against the empty boasting of the superstitious. Which is what it is. [Note: a running heading, rendered here as given.] Hence we are told that Christ would meet such people in this manner, namely by declaring that they are only thieves and robbers.

units.la: Tandem autem audient acerbam istam vocem tum nimirum cum os eorum obturabitur. Sed oues non auscultarunt. Hoc per occupationem dictum videtur, At multi eos sunt sequuti? Resp. At oues eos nō sunt sequutæ: nam nulla non ætate mundi habuit Christus suas oues, etiam ingentilisimo, etiam in Papismo, quæ vocem pastoris sui, non latronum, audiuerunt. Sed nouit Dominus qui sui sunt. Videndum hic quinam dicantur oues: primum electi sunt, neque id tantum: nam etiam electi ipsi priusquam efficaciter vocati sunt, instar luporum & vrsorum sunt. Quare ad electos necesse est accedat efficax vocatio, qua curantur electi & manluefiunt, atque ita efficiuntur oues. Vocati autem statim agnoscunt vocem pastoris sui. Nam vocati omnes acceperunt eundem illum Spiritum, per quem loquitur Christus. Quamobrē non citius loquitur Christus, quàm ipsi decernant eius vocem cámque internoscant. Testatur enim Spiritus ille de voce pastoris, Cum venerit ille consolator, quem ego mittam vobis à Patre, (Spiritus, inquam, ille veritatis, qui à Patre emanat) ille testabitur de me. nempe, postquam ego loquutus fuero, testabitur me esse Seruatorem mundi. Contrà vero vocem extranei & furis non audiunt vocem. Quia idem ille Spiritus testatur de contrariis. Atqs hoc obiter dicam, hæc causa est cur inter argumenta quibus constat hanc scripturam quam habemus in manibus, scripturam, inquam, Prophetarum & Apostolorum, dictatam esse à Spiritu sancto, Deìque ipsius vocem esse ipsissimam: cur, inquam, inter ea argumenta, hoc imprimis numeretur, nempe testimonium Spiritus sanctitestantis in corde cuiusque. Nam etsi testimonium quod perhibet Ecclesia procedat quoque à Spiritu sancto, qui habitat in sanctis Dei viris, tamen nisi simul testetur Spiritus Dei spiritui meo scripturam esse Dei verbum, profectò etsi commoueri me aliquo modo oporteat voce & testimonio sanctæ Ecclesiæ, tamen non habebo hoc plane persuasum, neque iustam ex scriptura consolationem hauriam priusquam Spiritus sanctus intus me docuerit Scripturam esse verbum Dei. Vnum hic quæri potest, Annon possit etiam quis, hoc est is qui iam efficaciter vocatus est, nonnunquam deficere à vero suo pastore & auscultare vocem peregrinam? Responndeo, vocationem in hac vita non esse perfectam, neque Spiritum veritatis dari cuiquâ perfectum, verum semper quoad hic viuimus admisceri carnem Spiritui, quæ ad deficiendum nos sollicitat, & cui Deus etiam suos, tentandi eos gratia nonnunquam tradit. Atque hinc fieri dico, vt nonnunquam sibi traditus homo, qui ex parte tantum regenitus est & primitias modo Spiritus habet, aberret & deficiat à veritate; verum id non est futurum neque totaliter, vt ita loquar, neque finaliter: nam tandem victor euadet Spiritus Dei Sanctus.
units.tr: At length, however, they will hear that harsh voice, namely when their mouths are stopped. But the sheep did not listen. This seems to be said by way of anticipation: "But did many follow them?" Answer: but the sheep did not follow them, for Christ has had his sheep in every age of the world, even in the most dire times, even under Papacy, who heard the voice of their shepherd and not of robbers. But the Lord knows who are his. Here we must consider who are called sheep. First, they are the elect, and not only that, for even the elect, before they are effectually called, are like wolves and bears. Therefore an effectual calling must come to the elect, by which the elect are healed and tamed, and so become sheep. Those who are called at once recognise the voice of their shepherd, for all who are called have received that same Spirit through whom Christ speaks. Therefore Christ does not speak any sooner than they themselves discern his voice and recognise it. For that Spirit bears witness of the shepherd's voice: When that Comforter comes, whom I will send to you from the Father (that Spirit, I say, of truth, who proceeds from the Father), he shall bear witness of me. That is, after I have spoken, he will bear witness that I am the Saviour of the world. On the contrary, they do not hear the voice of a stranger or a thief, because that same Spirit bears witness against such things. I will add in passing that this is the reason why, among the arguments by which it is established that the Scripture we have in our hands, I mean the Scripture of the Prophets and Apostles, was dictated by the Holy Spirit and is the very voice of God itself, this is especially counted: namely the testimony of the Holy Spirit bearing witness in the heart of each believer. For although the testimony that the Church gives also proceeds from the Holy Spirit, who dwells in the holy men of God, nevertheless unless the Spirit of God at the same time bears witness to my spirit that Scripture is the Word of God, then, although I ought in some measure to be moved by the voice and testimony of the holy Church, I shall not have this fully persuaded, nor shall I draw true consolation from Scripture, until the Holy Spirit teaches me inwardly that Scripture is the Word of God. Here one may ask: can not even one who is now effectually called sometimes fall away from his true shepherd and listen to a foreign voice? I answer: calling in this life is not perfect, nor is the Spirit of truth given to anyone perfectly, but as long as we live here, flesh is always mixed with the Spirit, which urges us to fall away, and to which God sometimes also delivers his own, to test them. And from this, I say, it happens that sometimes a man given over to this, who is only partly regenerate and has only the first-fruits of the Spirit, goes astray and falls away from the truth. Yet this will not be so either wholly, so to speak, or finally, for in the end the Holy Spirit of God will prove the victor.

units.la: Ego sum ostium. Priusquam ad alteram personam veniat, nempe verum pastorè, repetit se ostium esse: quod fit propter torporem hunc nostrum, quibus non satis est si semel tantum demonstretur Christum ostium esse; vix enim demonstratus est Christus cùm sopor nobis continuò obrepat. Ideóque sæpius demonstrandus est nobis Christus & inculcandus auribus cum repetito clamore, ne nos tandem corripiat letalis ille somnus. Quare, vt loquar cum Apostolo, nobis tutum est quòd idem sæpius repetatur, etsi nos id soleamus ægrè ferre, non secus atque ij, qui ex longo aliquo itinere fatigati, ægrè ferunt si quis eos inquietet & ex somno expergefaciat.
units.tr: I am the door. Before he comes to the other person, namely the true shepherd, he repeats that he is the door. This is done because of our dullness, for it is not enough for us if Christ is shown to be the door only once; Christ is scarcely shown before drowsiness creeps upon us continually. Therefore Christ must be shown to us again and again, and pressed upon our ears with repeated cries, lest that deadly sleep finally seize us. Therefore, to speak with the Apostle, it is safe for us that the same thing be repeated often, although we are accustomed to take this badly, just as those who are worn out by some long journey take it badly if anyone disturbs them and wakes them from sleep.

units.la: Philip. 3.1.
units.tr: Philip. 3.1.

units.la: Vide Iohan. cap. 6. quoties hoc repetat Dominus, Ego sum panis ille vitæ. Per me si quis introierit. Vt oculos ipsis ad videndum se, aperuit proximis verbis: ita nunc eorum allicit ad se amplectendum. Frustra enim videmus Christum, nisi simul corde apprehendamus. Quare addit, qui introierit per me, id est, qui crediderit in me, ser-vabitur, vitam consequetur. Ergo id quo allicit ad se amplectendum est vita, quæ in ipso est. Nam vita etiam ista præsens suauis est, præsertim si in discrimen vocetur.
units.tr: See John 6, how often the Lord repeats this: I am that bread of life. If anyone enters through me. As he opened their eyes to see him in the words just before, so now he entices them to embrace him. For we see Christ in vain unless we also grasp him with the heart. Therefore he adds: whoever enters through me, that is, whoever believes in me, will be saved, he will obtain life. Therefore what he entices us to embrace is life, which is in him. For even this present life is sweet, especially when it is put in peril.

units.la: Introire per Christum, quid. tur. Quanto magis suauis est illa altera, si ad eam perse-quendam vrgeamur sensu peccati & mortis omninó-que miseriæ huius nostræ. Tum vitam illam explicat ab ipsius conditione. Posita autem est in duobus istis, id est securitate. 1. quòd tuta sit vita, 2. vbertate & copia, quòd omnibus bonis affluens.
