Quod ad primum, Ingredietur & egredietur, inquit: id est, in tuto ac secure aget.
units.tr: To enter through Christ: what it means. How much sweeter is that other life, if we are urged to pursue it by a sense of sin and death and the complete misery of our condition. He then explains that life from its condition. It is placed in these two things, namely security: first, that the life is safe, and second, abundance and plenty, that it overflows with all good things. As to the first, he says: He will go in and go out, that is, he will live in safety and security.

units.la: Phrasis hæc est Hebraeorum scripturis familiaris, qua significatur occupatio domi forísque, personis quidem publicis laboriosa, privatis verò tuta & tranquilla, vt quæ sint sub tutela & præsidio personarum publicarum, siue in republica, siue in Ecclesia. Quare hoc loco significatur tuta, secura & tranquilla occupatio, sub ductu pastorum, præsertim magni illius pastoris ouium Iesu Christi. Quod ad alterum illud, in quo posita est vita illa quam offert, est vbertas & copia rerum satis magna: Pascua, inquit, inueniet. Alludit ad pascua ouium, quare in vita illa hæc insunt, primum vita est secura & tuta nobis in cœlis seruata. Deinde est copiosa vita & abundans, vtpote opes gloriæ & hereditatis Dei.
units.tr: This phrase is familiar in the Hebrew Scriptures, and it signifies work at home and abroad: laborious for those in public office, but safe and peaceful for private persons, who are under the protection and defence of public officers, whether in the commonwealth or in the Church. So here it signifies a safe, secure and peaceful work, under the guidance of the ministers, and above all of that great shepherd of the sheep, Jesus Christ. As to the other point, in which the life he offers consists, it is a fairly great abundance of good things: he will find pasture, he says. It alludes to the pastures of sheep. Thus this life contains these features: first, it is a life secure and safe, kept for us in heaven; then, it is a life rich and abounding, since it is the riches of the glory and inheritance of God.

units.la: Fur non venit. Nunc quæ sit illa altera persona quæ ingreditur ouile, nempe pastor, edocet: Ego, inquit, Pastor ille bonus. Dominus & ostium est & pastor est: primùm quidem est pastor, deinde ostium, per quod oportet ingredi in ouile alios omnes pastores, nihil enim oportet eos cum ouibus & Ecclesia communicare præter solum illum pastorem ouium magnum & ea quæ ad eius gloriam pertinent. Probat se pastorem esse bonum, primùm à fine cur veniat in ouile: est autem vt viuant oues, &c. ex hoc sequi se bonum pastorem esse probat, ex fine cur fur veniat superioti plane contrario, fur non venit, nisi vt furetur & mactet, quare cùm ego veniam vt vitam habeant oues, sequitur me bonum esse pastorem. Ac primùm quidem de fure loquitur. Fur non venit.
units.tr: A thief does not come. Now he teaches who the other person is who enters the sheepfold, namely the shepherd: I, he says, am the good shepherd. The Lord is both the door and the shepherd: he is first the shepherd, and then the door, through which all other ministers must enter into the sheepfold, for they ought to have no fellowship with the sheep and the Church except through that one great shepherd of the sheep and the things that pertain to his glory. He proves that he is the good shepherd, first from the purpose for which he comes into the sheepfold. That purpose is that the sheep may live, and so from this he proves that he is the good shepherd. The purpose for which the thief comes is plainly the opposite: the thief does not come except to steal and slaughter. Therefore, since I come that the sheep may have life, it follows that I am the good shepherd. And first, indeed, he speaks about the thief: A thief does not come.

units.la: Notanda phrasis, non sic loquitur, Fur venit vt furetur, sed sic; Fur non venit, nisi vt furetur: quo locutionis genere significat hunc solum esse & vnicum finem cur veniat fur, quantumuis alios soleat prætendere. Notat ergo solere furem alios fines prætendere ouibus, vt beatitatem, salutem ipsorum, vt Christi etiam gloriam. No-
units.tr: The phrase is to be noted. He does not say, "The thief comes in order to steal," but he says, "The thief does not come except in order to steal." By this manner of speaking he signifies that this is the only and single purpose for which the thief comes, however much he is accustomed to put forward other purposes. He notes, therefore, that the thief is accustomed to put forward other purposes to the sheep, such as their blessedness and salvation, and even the glory of Christ. We note

units.la: Notatio ritualium. tat praeterea nimiam credulitatem, simplicitatem ac facilitatem esse in ouibus, quòd praetendentibus alios fines, nimis cito fidem habeant. Mirum hoc si quis videat aliquem perrumpere per tectum domus, statim coniiciet furem esse, si quis viderit lupum irrumpentem in ouile, statim dicet ipsum facere vt depraedetur ouile: At verò cùm quis videt subingredi in Ecclesiam fures istos spirituales, non deprehenduut fures esse, vsque adeo cautius in spiritualibus diiudicandis. Ideo Dominus admonet hunc solum esse finem & non alium. Et Paulus saepius se Philippensis admonuisse dicit & tunc se flentem admonere de hostibus crucis Christi. Neque hodierno die de his furibus, hoc est pontificiis, facis vnquam admoneri possumus. Sed videamus fines istos qui sese ordine sequuntur. Primus est, vt furetur, hoc est clam auferat oues é caula Domini, sibique eas, non Domino, acquirat. Bonus pastor laborat in adducendo oues in ouile Domini. Paulus de se ait: Ambio vos Dei zelotypia, praeparaui enim vos quos vni viro vt virginem puram sistam, nempe Christo. At fur quoque ambit, sed sibi, non Domino. Depereunt etiam, sed non bene, inquit Paulus. Deinde alter finis est: vt mactet. Vinctam quasi iam ouem & humeris impositam non transfert in ouile aliud vt ibi etiam pascat: sed cùm fur sit & latro, abripit eam in latibulum & speluncam suam, ibique eam mactat. Nam sibi eam furatus est & ventri suo. Nam de his ait Apostolus, quòd eorum Deus sit venter. Pastor bonus introducat in ouile Domini ouem pascit quàm potest studiosissime: at fur etiam subductam ouem statim necat. Haec enim duo coniuncta sunt: qui lucratur Domino ouem, cui pascit deinde, ac fouet quàm fieri potest tenerrime: & qui diligit Dominum, diligit ouem propter Dominum. Amas me? dixit Dominus Petro tribus vicibus: & tandem subiecit triplici Petri responsioni, Pasce oues meas. Amorem erga oues proficisci ab amore erga Dominum ipsum significans. Contrà verò haec duo coniuncta sunt. Qui quaerit, non Domino, sed sibi ouem, nō pascet, sed mactabit ouem: qui non diligit Dominū, non diligit oues eius. Quare videndum nobis est diligenter, num quos audimus tàquam Pastores, verbis suis allialliciant nos ad Dominum, an vero ad se. Videndum an praeter Christum solum aliquid ingerant in animos nostros. Quod si merita alia a Christi meritis, quod si quae destruunt illam Christi gratiam nobis proponant, tanquam fures totidem reiiciendi sunt: nisi malimus audiendo & recipiendo eos ab iis tantum mactari. At perdunt oves. Hic tertius est finis, mactando quem quaerit interitum & perditionem ouis, eumque finem sibi habet propositum, nempe interitum creaturae. Non omnes qui quosuis occidunt statim quaerunt perditionem creaturae, aut eum finem sibi propositum habent. Dominus ipse occidit ut satisfaciat iustitiae suae, non quaerens interea perditionem creaturae suae: Iustus Iudex quisque occidit hominem, sed non eo fine ut eum perdat, neque enim laetatur interea eius nece: verum necat, ut satisfiat iustitiae. At vero fures isti hoc sibi proponunt, ut pereant homines, quemadmodum enim diabolus quaerit perniciem creaturae, ita & isti. Non ingrediuntur in regnum caelorum ipsi, neque alios patiuntur ingredi: ea enim est malitia eorum, quam quidem expressit Apostolus 1. Thes. 2. 15. 16.
units.tr: Notation of ritual matters. He notes besides that there is great credulity, simplicity and readiness in the sheep, in that they too quickly believe those who put forward other purposes. It is a wonder if anyone sees a man breaking through the roof of a house: at once he will conclude that he is a thief; if anyone sees a wolf breaking into the sheepfold, at once he will say that it is doing so in order to plunder the fold. But when someone sees those spiritual thieves creeping into the Church, they do not recognise them as thieves, so much more cautious are people in judging spiritual matters. Therefore the Lord warns that this is the only purpose and no other. And Paul says that he often warned the Philippians, and that he warned them even weeping, about the enemies of the cross of Christ. Nor can we ever warn enough, in these days, about these thieves, that is, the Papists. But let us look at these purposes, which follow one another in order. The first is that he may steal, that is, secretly carry off the sheep from the fold of the Lord, and acquire them for himself and not for the Lord. The good shepherd labours in bringing the sheep into the fold of the Lord. Paul says of himself: I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy; for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But the thief also courts, but for himself and not for the Lord. They also are zealous, but not well, says Paul. Then the second purpose is that he may slaughter. Having the sheep bound, as it were, and laid on his shoulders, he does not carry it into another sheepfold to feed it there; but since he is a thief and a robber, he snatches it away into his hiding-place and den, and there slaughters it. For he has stolen it for himself and for his belly. For of such men the Apostle says that their god is the belly. The good shepherd, when he brings a sheep into the fold of the Lord, feeds it as diligently as he can; but the thief, once he has carried off the sheep, straightway kills it. For these two things are joined: he who gains a sheep for the Lord then feeds it, and cherishes it as tenderly as may be; and he who loves the Lord loves the sheep for the Lord's sake. Do you love me? the Lord said to Peter three times; and at last he added to Peter's threefold answer, Feed my sheep, signifying that love for the sheep proceeds from love for the Lord himself. On the contrary, these two things are joined: he who seeks the sheep for himself and not for the Lord will not feed the sheep but will slaughter it; he who does not love the Lord does not love his sheep. Therefore we must carefully consider whether those whom we hear as shepherds, by their words, draw us to the Lord or rather to themselves. We must consider whether they put anything into our minds besides Christ alone. If they set before us merits other than the merits of Christ, or anything that destroys that grace of Christ, they must be rejected as so many thieves, unless we prefer to be slaughtered by them through hearing and receiving them. But they destroy the sheep. This is the third purpose: by slaughtering, he seeks the death and perdition of the sheep, and he holds that purpose before himself, namely the destruction of the creature. Not all who kill anyone at once seek the destruction of the creature, or have that purpose before them. The Lord himself kills in order to satisfy his justice, not seeking in the meantime the destruction of his creature. Every just judge kills a man, but not with the purpose of destroying him; for in the meantime he does not rejoice in his death, but kills him so that justice may be satisfied. But these thieves set before themselves this aim, that men may perish; for just as the devil seeks the ruin of the creature, so do they. They do not enter into the kingdom of heaven themselves, and they do not allow others to enter. For such is their malice, which indeed the Apostle expressed in 1 Thessalonians 2:15–16.

units.la: Hactenus de fine, eoque triplici cur fur veniat, nunc de fine cur Christus venerit, qui ideo affertur, ut ostendatur ipsum bonum illum Pastorem esse. Ego veni, inquit, ut vitam habeant. Non veni, inquit Christus alibi, in mundum, ut condemnem eum, sed ut seruem mundum. Non enim potest esse hic finis adductus Christi proprius: Lux enim non proprie causa esse potest tenebrarum, vita non proprie esse causa mortis. Fateor Christum pleriisque esse lapidem offensionis, sed hoc ipsis imputandum est, qui immerito offendunt in eum, & scandalum non datum vltro accipiunt. Deinde est amplificatio huius finis, a copia quasi & abundantia illius vitae, quam secum adportat. Et, inquit, abundent. Christi beneficia non parca manu conferuntur, sed plena. Iustitia per Christum iniuria aliqua aut mediocris non datur, sed copiosa & aeterna. Vita per Christum non parca datur, sed copiosa. Videquantam & qualem offerat Apostolus. Vocat eam non quiddam leuis momenti, sed pondus. Deinde pondus dicit non temporarium, sed aeternum. Tertio, pondus æternum vocat, non rei alicuius vilis aut parui pretij, sed gloriæ, rei vtpote pretiosissimæ: Plurimi enim omnes faciunt gloriam. Quarto, vocat gloriam illam, nō quidē vulgarem aliquā, sed excellētem, neque id modò, sed excellēter excellēte κ ὑπερβολῶ εἰς ὑπερβολὴν. Causa tantæ magnitudinis & copiæ beneficiorum Christi est in ipsius partim merito, partim efficacia. Meretur enim primùm omnia magna & excellentia; deinde efficax est ad illa nobis applicanda, quia in eo habitat omnis plenitudo deitatis corporaliter. Atque hactenus de fine cur venerit: ex eo colligit se Pastorem illum bonum esse: Ego, inquit, sum Pastor ille bonus. Christus est solus proprië dicendus Pastor: nam Pastor est qui pascit. Quis autem Pastor proprië dicendus in familia? Isne qui de suo pascit aliquos, vtpote Dominus familiæ, an verò dispensator qui ex voluntate Domini cibum distribuit aliis? Annon Dominus familiæ proprië dicetur pascere familiā, & Pastor esse familiæ suæ, non autem qui dispensator est? ita est hic. Christus est qui de suo pascit familiam suam: Ministri tantum dispensatores sunt mysteriorum Dei, vt vocantur ab Apostolo. Communicatur tamen cū iis ex gratia nomen istud Domini proprium, pastoresque appellantur. Bonus Pastor. Hoc alterum argumentū est, quo se docet bonum Pastorem. Bonus ille Pastor dat animam suam pro ouibus: Ergo is est bonus Pastor. Argumentum est à summa illa charitate qua oues suas prosequitur Dominus. Nā quod moriatur pro ouibus, ex immensa charitate est. Commendat autem suam charitatem erga nos Deus, quòd cùm essemus peccatores, Christus mortuus sit pro nobis. Magnitudinē huius charitatis Paulus comparatione conatur exprimere, ibidem vers.7. Vix enim quispiam pro iusto moritur: At Christus mortuus est pro peccatoribus: quo significat in hominibus non reperiri tantam charitatem. Concedo equidē hanc dilectionem esse Christi etiam hominis: nam charitas est Christi, etiam hominis: vel in corde humano Christi, maior illa quidem, quàm sit vel hominum vel Angelorum omnium, nam magis sanctificatus est Christus homo ab inhabitante in ipso deitate, quàm quiuis etiam angelorum. At non est ea charitas, qua factum est vt
units.tr: So far concerning the purpose, and the threefold purpose for which the thief comes; now concerning the purpose for which Christ came, which is brought forward so that it may be shown that he himself is that good shepherd. I have come, he says, that they may have life. I have not come into the world, Christ says elsewhere, to condemn it, but to save the world. For this cannot be the proper purpose of Christ's coming: light cannot properly be the cause of darkness, nor life properly the cause of death. I grant that Christ is to many a stone of stumbling, but this must be imputed to them, who stumble at him unjustly, and who willingly receive an offence not given. Next comes an amplification of this purpose, drawn from the abundance, as it were, and plenty of that life which he brings with him. And, he says, that they may have it abundantly. The benefits of Christ are not conferred with a sparing hand, but in full measure. Righteousness through Christ is not given in some small or moderate measure, but abundant and eternal. Life through Christ is not given sparingly, but abundantly. See how great and of what kind the thing is that the Apostle offers. He calls it not something of slight moment but a weight. Then he calls this weight not temporary but eternal. Third, he calls it an eternal weight, not of some cheap or trivial thing, but of glory, a thing most precious indeed; for all men value glory very highly. Fourth, he calls that glory not some common glory, but an excellent one, and not only that, but exceedingly excellent [καθ' ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολήν]. The cause of so great a magnitude and abundance of Christ's benefits lies partly in his merit and partly in his efficacy. For he first merits all things great and excellent; then he is effective in applying them to us, because in him dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. And so far concerning the purpose for which he came: from this he gathers that he is that good shepherd: I, he says, am that good shepherd. Christ alone is properly to be called the Shepherd, for a shepherd is one who feeds. But who in a household is properly called the shepherd? Is it he who feeds some from his own store, such as the master of the household, or rather the steward who distributes food to others according to the master's will? Will not the master of the household properly be said to feed the household, and to be the shepherd of his household, and not the steward? So it is here. Christ is the one who feeds his household from his own store; the ministers are only stewards of the mysteries of God, as the Apostle calls them. Yet by grace that name proper to the Lord is communicated to them as well, and they are called shepherds. Good Shepherd. This is the second argument by which he teaches that he is the good shepherd. That good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep; therefore he is the good shepherd. The argument is drawn from that supreme love with which the Lord pursues his sheep. For that he dies for the sheep comes from immense love. God commends his love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Paul tries to express the greatness of this love by comparison, in the same place, verse 7: For scarcely for a righteous man will one die; but Christ died for sinners, by which he signifies that so great a love is not found among men. I readily grant that this love is also the love of Christ as man; for the love of Christ is also the love of the man Christ, or in the human heart of Christ, greater indeed than that of all men or all angels; for Christ as man was more sanctified by the Godhead dwelling in him than any of the angels. But it is not that love by which it came about that...

units.la: Colos.2.9.
1. Corinth. 4.1.

Rom.5.8. vt mortuus sit pro nobis, hominis tantùm: oportuit enim eam maiorem esse charitate cuiusuis creaturæ, quæ creatura sit tantùm. Secus enim, Filius Dei in carne nostra tam execrabilem & infamem mortem nunquam obiuisset. Quare charitas Dei fuit in persona Filij & ea quidem infinita & incomprehensibilis. Nam verba illa Pauli, quæ habetur Eph.3.18. De charitate maiori, quàm quæ in creatura sit intelligenda, Vt charitate, inquit, radi- cati & fundati valeatis assequi cum omnibus sanctis, quæ sit illa latitudo & longitudo & profunditas & sublimitas, &c. quæ melius sentiuntur animo, quàm verbis exprimuntur. Paulus eam grandem quidem verbo exprimit. Effusa, inquit, est charitas Dei in cordibus nostris: sed totam illam charitatem simul ac semel non comprehendit. Quare laborandum est vt eam corde sentiamus, quam verbo exprimere nequimus, nam suavitas omnis est ex sensu cordis. Præsertim laborandum est Pastoribus Ecclesiæ vt eam sentiant, ex sensu enim charitatis Christi, in redemptione illa per ipsum facta exiit primùm amor Christi mutuus, deinde amor ouium Christi. Et siquidem sensus hic serius sit, profecto efficiet vt pro ouibus ipsi lubeant moriantur, & vt hoc de iis quoque verum sit, quod de principe Pastore dictum est hoc loco, Pastor ille bonus dat animam suam pro ouibus. Ex serio enim illo sensu amoris Christi profecta est illa vox Pauli. Quinetiam si pro libamento offerar super hostia sacrificio quæ fidei vestræ, gaudeo & gratulor omnibus vobis. Quæ voces in cordibus Pastorum omnium Ecclesiæ Christi hærere & perpetuò resonare debent.
units.tr: Rom. 5.8. that he died for us, for man only. For it was necessary that this love be greater than the love of any creature, which is only a creature. Otherwise the Son of God would never have undergone in our flesh so detestable and infamous a death. Therefore the love of God was in the person of the Son, and that love was indeed infinite and incomprehensible. For those words of Paul in Eph. 3.18 must be understood of a love greater than any that exists in a creature: "That you may be able, being rooted and grounded in love, to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and depth and height," and so on. These things are better felt in the mind than expressed in words. Paul does indeed express it in a grand way: "the love of God has been poured out in our hearts." Yet he did not comprehend all that love at once. Therefore we must labour to feel in our hearts what we cannot express in words, for all sweetness comes from the feeling of the heart. Above all, the pastors of the Church must labour to feel it, for from the feeling of Christ's love, shown in that redemption made by him, there came forth first Christ's love for us and then the love of Christ's sheep. And if this feeling is indeed earnest, it will certainly bring it about that they are willing to die for the sheep, and that what is said here of the chief Pastor is true of them too: "The good Shepherd gives his life for the sheep." It was from that earnest feeling of Christ's love that Paul's words came: "Even if I am poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrifice of your faith, I rejoice and congratulate you all." These words ought to cling in the hearts of all the pastors of Christ's Church and sound forever.

units.la: 12 Mercenarius autem & qui non est pastor, cuius non sunt oues propria, videns lupum venientem, relinquit oues & fugit: lupus autem eas rapit & dispergit ouile.
units.tr: 12 But the hired hand, who is not a shepherd and whose own the sheep are not, seeing the wolf coming, leaves the sheep and flees; and the wolf snatches them and scatters the flock.

units.la: 13 Mercenarius autem fugit, quia mercenarius est, & non est illi cura ouium.
units.tr: 13 The hired hand flees because he is a hired hand, and the sheep are not his concern.

units.la: 14 Ego sum Pastor ille bonus, & agnosco meas, & agnoscor à meis.
units.tr: 14 I am the good Shepherd, and I know my own, and my own know me.

units.la: 15 Prout novit me Pater, ita & ego novi Patrem, & animam meam depono pro ovibus.
units.tr: 15 As the Father knows me, so also I know the Father, and I lay down my life for the sheep.

units.la: PRobat sequi ex argumento isto tantæ dilectionis suæ bonum illum Pastorem esse, adducto in medium mercenarij facto. Mercenarius tantum abest ab eo ut velit mori pro ovibus, ut videns venientem lupum, relinquat oves & fugiat. At cum ego dem animam meam pro ovibus meis, non sum mercenarius, sed verus Pastor. Christus supra oppositionem se furi, hoc est, ei qui tradit falsam doctrinam. Nunc etiam oppositionem instituit inter se & mercenarium, hoc est eum qui veritatem quidem tradit, sed nullo amore vel Dei vel gregis, verum mercedis & quæstus causa. Non quod quicunque mercedem capit, is statim fit mercenarius dicendus, capiunt enim pastores boni & iam mercedem, nam dignus est operarius mercede sua, ait Apostolus. Verum mercenarius hoc loco est, qui mercedem tanquam finem unicum & præcipuum respicit ministerij sui. Tria sunt igitur genera doctorum: primum sunt fures qui falsam & perversam doctrinam tradunt. Deinde sunt mercenarij, qui tradunt quidem veram doctrinam, sed propter mercedem tanquam præcipuum finem. Tertio, sunt veri pastores qui veritatem tradunt, non propter mercedem, sed propter Dei gloriam in Christo & hominum salutem. Sed expendamus verba, Mercenarius, inquit, tum enim definit per abnegationem pastoris, Et qui non est Pastor. Nam mercenarius etsi videatur pastorem agere, tamen vere pastor non est. Postea rationem reddit cur non sit pastor: Cuius, inquit, non sunt oves propriæ. Ex hoc sequi videtur Christum solum verum Pastorem, cuius sunt oves propriæ, cum eas ipse sanguine suo redemerit.
units.tr: He proves from this argument that he is the good Shepherd, by bringing forward the case of the hired hand. The hired hand is so far from being willing to die for the sheep that, seeing the wolf coming, he leaves the sheep and flees. But I, who give my life for my sheep, am not a hired hand but the true Shepherd. Christ has already set himself against the thief, that is, against the one who teaches false doctrine. Now he sets up a contrast between himself and the hired hand, that is, the one who indeed teaches the truth, but out of no love either for God or for the flock, only for wages and gain. This does not mean that whoever takes wages at once becomes a hired hand, for good pastors also take wages; the Apostle says, "the labourer is worthy of his wages." Rather, the hired hand here is the one who looks to wages as the sole and chief end of his ministry. There are therefore three kinds of teachers: first, thieves, who teach false and perverse doctrine; second, hired hands, who indeed teach true doctrine but have wages as their chief end; third, true pastors, who teach the truth not for the sake of wages but for the glory of God in Christ and the salvation of men. But let us weigh the words. "The hired hand," he says, is defined first by a denial of the pastor: "and who is not a shepherd." For although the hired hand may seem to act as a pastor, he is not truly a pastor. Afterwards he gives the reason why he is not a pastor: "whose own the sheep are not." From this it seems to follow that Christ alone is the true Pastor, whose own the sheep are, since he redeemed them with his own blood.

units.la: Resp. verum quidem esse ad Christum solum proprie pertinere oves, & Pastorem eum esse proprie. Sed nemo est Christianorum qui non putet omnia quæ Christi sunt, ipsius esse quodammodo, quemadmodum quæ mariti sunt, uxor in suis bonis numerat. Pastor itaque & Minister omnis cum speciali modo coniunctus sit cum grege suo & grex ipsi traditus sit a Domino, profecto necesse est ad eum magis proprie quam ad aliquem ex vulgo Christianorū pertinere oues Christi ipsi cōmisse. Ex quo sequitur & eum pastorem esse dicendum, sed secundo loco, cùm solus Christus sit vere & proprie Pastor. Sed quæri potest, annon mercenarius quoque gregem habeat sibi traditum, ideoque pastor quoque dicendus sit? Respond. Præfici illum aliquo modo gregi, sed non esse efficacem coniunctionem illam, vt quæ sit sine coniugali, vt loquuntur, affectu, sine amore ouium quibus præficitur. Quare non meretur is pastoris nomen, dicendus potiùs mercenarius, etsi ita vulgo vocetur, antequam Deus eum reuelet. Videns lupum. Hactenus descriptio fuit mercenarij, sequuntur eius effecta, primum est, videt quidem lupum venientem: Recte quidem, nam vigilis partes tenetur agere, quicunque gregi Domini præficitur. Lupum intelligo eum quem dixit supra furem, nam reipsa idem est, etsi ratio in agendo alia atque alia: fur clam furatur, lupus palam rapit. Quid deinde facit mercenarius? Relinquit oues, & fugit. Hic ostendit se mercenarium esse, & sibi non esse curam ouium, vt poltea dicetur, oportuit enim non deseruisse stationem suam, sed mansisse & admonuisse de aduentu lupi. Sed hic quæri potest, An quia mercenarius fugit, ideo quicunque fugit is statim mercenarius est? Respondeo id non continuò sequi, quia fugere generalius est, & ad bonum etiam pastorem pertinere potest. Quâ do igitur liceat fugere, & quibus de causis, non nunc quæram subtilius, sed de hoc tantùm admonebo, tum quidem licere pastori fugere, cùm manere non est tutum, neque id satis est ad id vt fugiat, verùm hoc adendum, si vel mors eius vel incarceratio, vel aliquid tali gregi magis obsit quàm prosit. Qui autem id cognoscit, non est de eo certa regula. Dominus omni æta-tem monuit suos, & interius per Spiritum suum sanctum, & exterius per oblatas circumstantias varias, quâdo vilius esset gregi, vt ipsi morerentur, quàm vt fuga se reuerentur in aliud tempus. Quare de fuga pastorum non temere iudicandum, neque qui fugiunt statim damnandi sunt. Tum quid lupus? Lupus, inquit, rapit & dissipat oues. Fur furatur, sed lupus rapit, id est, apertiùs vim affert. Sed quando rapit? cùm grex destitutus est
units.tr: Answer: it is true that the sheep belong properly to Christ alone, and that he is properly the Shepherd. Yet there is no Christian who does not think that all things which are Christ's are in some sense his own, just as a wife counts among her own goods what belongs to her husband. Therefore every pastor and minister, since he is joined with his flock in a special way and the flock has been entrusted to him by the Lord, must surely belong more properly to Christ's sheep, which have been committed to him, than to any of the common Christians. From this it follows that he is to be called a pastor as well, but in a secondary sense, since Christ alone is truly and properly the Pastor. But it may be asked: does not the hireling also have a flock entrusted to him, and so is he not to be called a pastor too? Answer: he is set over the flock in some way, but that bond is not effective, since it is without, as they say, conjugal affection, that is, without love for the sheep over whom he is set. Therefore he does not deserve the name of pastor; he is rather to be called a hireling, even though he is commonly so called, until God reveals him. "Seeing the wolf coming." Thus far is the description of the hireling; there follow his effects. First, he indeed sees the wolf coming. Rightly so, for whoever is set over the Lord's flock is bound to play the part of a watchman. By the wolf I understand him whom he called a thief above, for in reality it is the same, although the manner of acting is different: the thief steals secretly, the wolf snatches openly. What then does the hireling do? "He leaves the sheep and flees." Here he shows that he is a hireling and that he has no care for the sheep, as will be said later; for he ought not to have deserted his post, but to have remained and warned of the wolf's coming. But here it may be asked: since the hireling flees, is whoever flees at once a hireling? I answer that this does not follow directly, because fleeing is a more general matter and can pertain even to the good pastor. I shall not now inquire more subtly when and for what reasons it is lawful to flee, but I will only note this: a pastor may flee when remaining is not safe; yet that alone is not enough to make him flee, but this must be added, that his death or imprisonment, or something of the kind, would do more harm than good to such a flock. But whoever recognises this, there is no fixed rule about it. The Lord has warned his people at all times, both inwardly through his Holy Spirit and outwardly through various circumstances presented, when it would be less useful to the flock for them to die than to save themselves by flight for another time. Therefore the flight of pastors is not to be judged rashly, nor are those who flee to be condemned at once. Then what of the wolf? "The wolf, he says, snatches and scatters" the sheep. The thief steals, but the wolf snatches, that is, it uses force more openly. But when does it snatch? When the flock is abandoned by its shepherd, while the pastor is present he restrains that violence; but when the pastor is absent, the wolf rages, snatches, scatters.

units.la: RR pastore suo, pastor praesens prohibet illam violentiam; sed absente pastore grassatur lupus, rapit, dissipat. Quod & experientur nostri homines, si unquam futurum sit ministerio isto, quo tantopere carere vellent, spolientur. Tum quid mercenarius? Mercenarius autem fugit, & id facit, quia mercenarius est, hoc est, mercedem, non oves respicit: Et non est illi cura ovium. Haec est causa cur fugiat mercenarius, non tangitur cura & dilectione ovium. Quod si curae essent ipsi oves, tum si fugiens forte retrospiceret cerneretque truculenter rapi eas, & a lupo discerpi, tum profecto aegre illud spectaculum intueretur, ut si parens aliquis in conspectu suo laniari infantem suum conspiceret.
units.tr: This our own people will also experience, if ever it should come to pass that they are stripped of that ministry which they would so gladly be without. Then what of the hireling? "But the hireling flees, and he does so because he is a hireling, that is, he looks to his wages, not to the sheep; and he has no care for the sheep." This is the reason why the hireling flees: he is not moved by care and love for the sheep. For if the sheep were truly his concern, then if, while fleeing, he chanced to look back and saw them savagely seized and torn apart by the wolf, he would surely be grieved to witness that sight, as a parent would be if he saw his child mangled before his eyes.

units.la: Ego sum Pastor ille. Concludit ac repetit se Pastorem illum bonum esse, addit praeterea novum argumentum a mutua notitia, qua ipse oves suas, & oves ipsum cognoscunt. Christo hoc peculiare est, ut de eius habeat, & qua oves sunt. Christus enim is est, qui cum scrutator cordium sit, discernere potest vere pios, qui in Ecclesia ista visibili sunt ab hypocritis. Alij pastores certo internoscere non possunt, bene autem iudicant de omnibus ex externis circumstantiis. Praeterea non est ista notitia generalis duntaxat, sed cum dilectione & summa benevolentia coniuncta, ut quae sit suorum.
units.tr: I am that Shepherd. He concludes and repeats that he is the good Shepherd, and he adds a further argument from the mutual knowledge by which he knows his sheep and the sheep know him. This is peculiar to Christ, that he has knowledge of those who are his and who are the sheep. For Christ is the searcher of hearts, and so he can discern the truly godly who are in this visible Church from the hypocrites. Other ministers cannot know them for certain; they judge well of all from external circumstances. Moreover, this knowledge is not merely general but joined with love and the greatest goodwill, as belongs to those who are his own.

units.la: Dominus qui sunt sui. Quibus verbis significatur notitia & cognitio, cum applicatione cordis ac voluntatis coniuncta, quo modo pater cognoscit filium suum, aut amicus amicum suum; neque nos expertes sensus huius dilectionis relinquet: verum eam spiritum suum sanctum effundit in cordibus nostris. Atque hinc est quod nos eum mutuo cognoscamus & diligamus, ut infans cognoscit parentem suum speciali quodam modo ex sensu illo dilectionis qua parens ipsum amplectitur. Cognoscit quidem alios, sed generaliter, particulariter vero & cum affectu quodam cordis cognoscit parentem suum, & novit vocem eius, eamque discernit, ad quam auditam exultat: ita etiam sceres habet in filiis Dei: Amicus enim sponsi qui stat & audit eum, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi. Prout novit me Pater. Videtur haec illuillustratio quædam esse proximi argumenti, à simili comparatione mutuæ cognitionis, quæ est inter Deum Patrem & filium. De notitia ista Patris & Filij diximus non semel antea, tantùm hoc in præsentia: Pater nouit filium suum eúmque perpetuò ob oculos habet,necnon in delicijs habet, vicissimáq; filius in sinu Patrisui cùm sit, nouit patrem, eúmque continuò intuetur & intuen-do gaudet mirabiliter. Vide Prouerb.9.30. Tantùm hic obseruamus dignitatem eam ad quam in Christo su- mus euecti, vt nimirum euadamus similes Deo & glo- riosæ trinitati Patri, Filio & Spiritui sanćto, similes, inquam, in vnione & coniunćtione, non tantùm qua coniungimur inter nos mutuò, per spiritum & vinculù charitatis,de qua Iohan.17.21. Vt omnes vnum sint,sicut tu Pater in me,& ego in te, vt & ipsi in nobis vnum sint; verùm-etiam in vnione cum ipso Filio, vt quemadmodum Pa-ter & Filius vniuntur natura,seséque amplećtuntur mu-tua & ineffabili dilećtione: ita etiam nos cum Filio v-niamur & coniungamur, quod est caput felicitatis no-stræ. Nam ex hac vnione cum Filio,est vnio cum Patre, omninóque cum Trinitate: & ex hac est vnio nostri in-ter nos. Atque in his coniunćtionibus tribus posita est felicitas nostra ,& ius perfećtum est gaudium nostrum. Iohan.1.ep.1.4. postquam horum coniunćtionum me- minit; Hæc scribimus,inquit,vobis,vt gaudiù vestrum sit plenum. Et animam meam. Hoc argumentum est se- cundum repetitum.Repetitur autem vt effećtum,ad ar- guendam notitiam illam cum dilećtione coniunćtam ea qua filius oues suas amplećitur.de hac supra audiui-mus.Tantùm hoc in præsentia admonendum exemplo Christi: Quòd si Christus ita cognouit & dilexit oues suas,vt pro iis vitam suam dederit,tanquam pretium re- demptionis,ad eas nimirum redimendas eius exemplo: tenentur omnes pastores (qui in Ecclesia sequi vo- lunt magnum illum pastorem ouium Iesum Christū) sic ligere greges sibi comminissos, vt lubenter pro iis moriantur,si ita res ferat,ad eam veritatem quam verbo tradiderunt in cordibus eorum sanguine suo obsignan-dam, debéntque perpetuò inter docendum veritatem, consilium moriendi capere, si ita Deo visum sit. Id au-
units.tr: "The Lord knows those who are his own." These words signify a knowledge joined with the application of heart and will, as a father knows his son, or a friend his friend. Nor will he leave us without a sense of this love; rather, he pours out his Holy Spirit into our hearts. And hence it is that we know and love him in return, as an infant knows its parent in a special way from that sense of love by which the parent embraces it. It knows other people, indeed, but in a general way; it knows its parent particularly and with a certain affection of heart, and it recognises his voice and distinguishes it, and at hearing it, it exults. So too there is a similar joy among the sons of God: "For the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice" (John 3:29). "As the Father knows me" (John 10:15). This seems to be a kind of illustration of the nearer argument, drawn from the likeness of the mutual knowledge that exists between God the Father and the Son. We have spoken of this knowledge of Father and Son more than once before, so for the present only this: the Father knows his Son and always keeps him before his eyes, and holds him in his delight; and in turn the Son, being in the bosom of the Father, knows the Father, always gazes upon him, and in gazing rejoices wonderfully. See Proverbs 8:30. Here we only observe the dignity to which we are raised in Christ, namely that we should become like God and the glorious Trinity, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, like them, I say, in union and communion. This is not only the union by which we are joined to one another, through the Spirit and the bond of charity, of which John 17:21: "That they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us." It is also the union with the Son himself, so that just as the Father and the Son are united in nature and embrace one another in mutual and ineffable love, so we too are united and joined with the Son, which is the head of our happiness. For from this union with the Son comes union with the Father, and altogether with the Trinity; and from this comes our union with one another. In these three communions our happiness consists, and our joy is made full. 1 John 1:4, after he has mentioned these communions: "We write these things to you," he says, "so that your joy may be full." "And my soul." This argument is repeated a second time. It is repeated, however, as an effect, to prove that knowledge joined with love by which the Son embraces his sheep. We have heard of this above. For the present only this is to be noted from the example of Christ: if Christ so knew and loved his sheep that he gave his life for them as the price of redemption, then by his example all pastors who wish in the Church to follow that great Shepherd of the sheep, Jesus Christ, are bound so to love the flocks committed to them that they gladly die for them, should the situation so require, sealing with their blood, if need be, the truth which they have delivered by word in their hearts. And they ought continually, while teaching the truth, to take up the resolve to die, if it so pleases God. Id au-

units.la: Ad autem fiet optimè si studeant πλεονεξίαν & plenam persuasionem habere apud animos suos doctrinæ illius quam tradunt, adeo vt possint dicere cū Dauide & Paulo, Credidi atque ideo loquutus sum.
units.tr: This will be done best if they strive with great eagerness [πλεονεξίαν] and have a full persuasion in their minds of the doctrine which they deliver, so that they can say with David and Paul: "I believed, and therefore I spoke."

units.la: 16 Alias oues habeo quæ non sunt ex hac caula, illas quoque oportet me adducere: nam vocem meam audient: fiětque vnus grex & vnus Pastor.
units.tr: "I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one Shepherd." (John 10:16)

units.la: 17 Propterea Pater me diligit, quia ego depono animam meam, vt eam rursus assumam.
units.tr: "For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it up again." (John 10:17)

units.la: 18 Nemo tollit eam à me, sed ego depono eam per meipsum: potestatem habeo deponendi eam, & potestatem habeo rursus eam assumendi. Hoc mandatum accepi à Patre meo.
units.tr: "No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again. This command I have received from my Father." (John 10:18)

units.la: HActenus fuit Parabola, vnà cum ipsius declaratione, sequitur ad finem vsque huius sermonis Dominidu-plex prædictio. Prior est prædictio vocationis gentium. Posterior est prædictio passionis & resurrectionis ipsius. De vocatione gentium sic loquitur: Alias oues habeo. Sensus est, Præter has oues, quæ sunt in visibili ista caula & Ecclesia ista Iudaica, habeo alias passim inter gentes dispersas. huius rei principium paulò altius repetendum est. Inde ab initio ad primum vsque aduentum suum, habuit Dominus inter homines caulam aliquam, hoc est Ecclesiam visibilem cum externo aliquo ministerio verbi, prædicatione, administratione sacramentorum & disciplinæ, quanquam interdum obscura solita est facies huius Ecclesiæ, idque vel propter persecutionem, vel denique hæreses subingredientes. Atque hæc ecclesia visibilis primum fuit in fami-liis Patrum, vt Adami, Noë, Abrahami, Isaaci, Iacobi, &c. Deinde post descensum Iacobi in Ægyptum, diffusa est in vniuersam gentem Israëliticam. Præter visibilem istam, quam dicimus Ecclesiam, habuit Dominus perpetuò oues alias extra Ecclesiæ visibilis septa, quas elegit ad vitam æternam, vocauit interius, & Christo per fidem inseruit, denique extra ordinem seruauit. Atque hinc
units.tr: Thus far there has been the parable, together with its explanation. Up to the end of this discourse there follows a twofold prediction of the Lord. The first is a prediction of the calling of the Gentiles; the second is a prediction of his own passion and resurrection. He speaks of the calling of the Gentiles thus: "I have other sheep." The meaning is: besides these sheep which are in this visible fold and this Jewish Church, I have others dispersed among the nations. The beginning of this matter must be taken up somewhat further back. From the beginning until his first coming, the Lord had among men a certain fold, that is, a visible Church with an external ministry of the Word, preaching, administration of the sacraments and discipline, although at times the face of this Church was accustomed to be obscured, either on account of persecution or because heresies crept in. And this visible Church was first in the families of the fathers, such as Adam, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and so on. Then, after Jacob's descent into Egypt, it spread out over the whole Israelite nation. Besides this visible Church, as we call it, the Lord always had other sheep outside the enclosure of the visible Church, whom he chose to eternal life, called inwardly, joined to Christ through faith, and finally preserved beyond the ordinary way.

units.la: {y} Parabolæ de pastore & ouibus additur prædictio de vocatione gentium. hinc est(vt nunc redeamus ad institutum)quòd dicat se alias oues habere extra septa Ecclesiæ Iudaicæ. Si quæras cur non Dominus itas oues alias, quæ singulis ætatibus fuerunt, in caulam collegerit & alias aggregauerit, imò verò cur exclusérit eas quasi macerie extructa? Respondeo, non inquirendum esse curiosè in consilia Domini, aut factorum ipsius rationes quærendas. Idcirco possumus dicere, ea re voluisse Dominum ostendere mundo, se non astringi ordinariis mediis, sed posse se homines extra ordinem seruare, vt & hodierno die, tempore nimirum huius catholicæ & vniuersalis Ecclesiæ visibilis, habet tamen suos Deus occultos, partim in Papismo, partim in Mahumetismo, &c. quos extra ordinem seruat. Illas quoque oportet me adducere. Hactenus admonuit se habere oues alias, nunc vocandas esse dicit, idque necessitate decreti diuini, quod fuit ab æterno, quódque nunc in aduentu Christi implendum est. Adducere hic est vocare exterius. Quòd verò dicitur eas audituras, eo significatur interior & efficax vocatio. Auditio autem ista posita est in fide, per fidem enim respondemus externæ Dei vocationi, quæ sita est in prædicatione Euangelii. Neque putandum est cum Papistis nos ex naturæ beneficio audire vocantem Deum, cùm natura plane surdi & mortui simus, adeo vt nullam facultatem quidem audiendi habeamus, nisi Dominus ipse perforet aures nostras, & indat nobis vitam nouam. Hanc vocationem omnium tam efficacem quid sequetur? Tũ implebitur quod à Propheta dictũ est, Fiet vnum ouile & vnus Pastor. Vide hic quanta efficacia quantaque gratia comitetur primum Christi aduentum, & ipsius in carne manifestationem. Iam virtus Christi patet sesèque porrigit eius gratia ad vniuersas gentes in vnum colligendas, hoc est ad congregandam Ecclesiam visibilem Catholicam in terris. Ante Christi aduentũ & manifestationem in carne, fuit quidem eius efficacia & gratia in terris perpetuò, neque vnquam colleCta fuit Ecclesia sine vnam familiam, siue in vnam gentem, nisi eius vi, efficacia & gratia. Christus enim est heri & hodie, idem est in saecula. Et Christus est agnus ille mactatus inde ab origine mundi. Verùm in aduentu demum ipsius efficacia & gratia
units.tr: To the parable of the shepherd and the sheep there is added a prediction of the calling of the Gentiles. Hence (to return now to our purpose) he says that he has other sheep outside the fold of the Jewish Church. "If you ask why the Lord did not gather into the fold those other sheep which existed in every age, and why he did not bring them together, or rather why he excluded them as if by a wall built up?" I answer: "We must not inquire curiously into the counsels of the Lord, nor seek the reasons for his deeds. We can therefore say that the Lord wished to show the world that he is not bound to the ordinary means, but that he can save men beyond the ordinary way; so that even today, namely in the time of this catholic and universal visible Church, God still has his hidden ones, partly among the Papists, partly among the Mahometans, and so on, whom he preserves beyond the ordinary way. 'I must bring them also.'" Thus far he has admonished that he has other sheep; now he says that they must be called, and this by the necessity of the divine decree, which was from eternity, and which is now to be fulfilled at the coming of Christ. "To bring" here means to call outwardly. But that they are said to hear signifies the inward and effectual calling. This hearing, however, is placed in faith, for through faith we respond to the external calling of God, which is set in the preaching of the gospel. Nor should we think, "with the Papists," that we hear God calling by a benefit of nature, since by nature we are altogether deaf and dead, so that we have no faculty of hearing at all, unless the Lord himself pierces our ears and gives us new life. What will follow from this calling, so effectual for all? Then what was said by the Prophet will be fulfilled: "There will be one fold and one Shepherd." See here how great an efficacy and how great a grace accompanied the first coming of Christ, and his manifestation in the flesh. Now the power of Christ is manifest, and his grace extends to all nations to gather them into one, that is, to gather the visible catholic Church on earth. Before the coming of Christ and his manifestation in the flesh, his efficacy and grace were indeed always present on earth, and the Church was never gathered without his power, efficacy and grace, whether into one family or into one nation. "For Christ is yesterday and today, and the same forever." "And Christ is that Lamb slain from the foundation of the world." But at his coming his efficacy and grace

units.la: Quomodo Christus gentes adducit ad Ecclesiam. Christi se diffudit ad omnes gentes, & omnes in vnum collegit. Neque est quod quisquam id miretur cum omnis omni tempore aduentum Christi praecedete gratia & efficacia extiterit in Ecclesia virtute filij Dei suo tempore in carne manifestandi. Annon oportuit igitur in aduentu ipso ac manifestatione Christi, mortuo iam eo ac glorificato in carne multo maiorem esse ipsius gratiam & efficaciam in hominibus colligendis, vocadis atque seruandis? Quanquam ne in aduentu quidem suo primo perfecta est & impleta gratia & efficacia Christi, vt neque plane perfecta est collectio illa suorum. Verum in secundo demum aduentu Christi id fiet, in quo collectio futura est in vnum omnium electorum, ne vno quidem excepto, & collectio pura electorum: ita vt oues segregandae sint ab haedis, cum adhuc neque omnes ac singuli congregati sint in Ecclesiam visibilem, neque soli electi congregati sint in eam, sed cum iis passim mixti sint hypocritae. At tum quidem hoc quod hic habemus implebitur, Fiet vnum ovile & vnus Pastor. His subiicit Christus; Propterea Pater me diligit. Praedictio est passionis & mortis suae, quam illustrat ex effecto, nempe Patris dilectione; Pater diligit Filium, quia Filius est aeterno genitus: & quia Filius factus est obediens Patri, vsque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Neque vnquam creatura illa tam obediens facta fuit Patri, vt Filius, qui cum in forma Dei esset, non duxit rapinam parem esse cum Deo: sed ipse se exinanivit forma serui accepta. Ex his verbis Christi colligere possumus, Christum toto tempore passionis suae sensisse Dei Patris dilectionem. Nam ex senso illo dilectionis, profecta sunt haec verba, etiam in extremo illo agone, in quo dixit, Deus meus, Deus meus, cur me dereliquisti? & in senso illo irae grauissimo, fuit sensus dilectionis suauissimae, id quod apparet vel ex his verbis (Deus meus, Deus meus,) neque enim Deum suum dixisset, nisi amorem eius sensisset. Atque hoc sensu amoris pa-terni ineffabilis sustentatus est in illo agone. Ita etiam pij percipiunt in obedientia & afflictionibus suis amorem Dei, eoque ita sustentantur, vt etiam in mediis afflictionibus glorientur ex sensu illo amoris Dei. Quis nos separabit a charitate Christi? Hoc est, a sensu charitatis Christi. Vt eam rursus,&c. Hic prædicit gloriam passio-nes insecuturam, idque vt occurreret offensioni Iudæo-rum, qui neque peccata sua, neque miseriam ex peccatis senserunt, ideoque impegerunt in eum, qui & peccata i-psorum, & mortem ac iram Dei ipsis debitam in se trā-stulit. Propter electos quoque hoc subiectum est; nam fides nostra non acquiescit in Christi morte, sed vite-rius se porrigit ad eius resurrectionem. Nam quemad-modum morte sua meritus est nobis omnia, vt remissio-nem peccatorum, vt iustitiam, vitam : ita resurrectione sua efficax est ad applicationem eorum beneficiorum. Quare credendus est a nobis Christus & crucifixus & glo-rificatus. Hic videmus Christum per mediam mortem vidisse vitam eamque gloriosissimam, neque in passione sua sola Dei dilectione, quam inter patiendum sensit, sus-tentatum esse, sed etiam intuitu vitæ ac gloriæ æternæ. Ideo Psalmo 16.9.10. prædictum est de eo in hæc verba, Lætatur cor meum, idcirco, & exultat gloria; etiam caro mea habitat secure, quia non es derelicturus animam meam in sepulchro, &c. Ita etiam pij quique (nam qualia in Christo, talia operatur Spiritus sanctus in piis,) Pij, inquam, præterquam quod sentiant dilectionem Dei in obedientia sua & afflictione, vident quoque eminus, quasi gloriam illam futuram ac vitam æternam, eiusque intuitu sustentantur: non secus ac si quis incedens per arctam, lubricam, ac multis impedimentis constratam semitam, si eminus intueatur exitum latum ac pulchrum, erigitur eo inspecto & confirmatur.
units.tr: How Christ draws the Gentiles to the Church. Christ's grace has spread to all nations and gathered them all into one. Nor is there any reason for anyone to wonder at this, since at every time before the coming of Christ, his grace and efficacy were present in the Church, by the power of the Son of God, who was to be made manifest in the flesh at his appointed time. Ought it not, then, to follow that at the very coming and manifestation of Christ, now that he has died and been glorified in the flesh, his grace and efficacy in gathering, calling and saving men would be much greater? Yet even at his first coming the grace and efficacy of Christ were not perfected and completed, and so that gathering of his people was not wholly perfect either. It will happen only at the second coming of Christ, when there will be a gathering into one of all the elect, not one of them excepted, and a pure gathering of the elect, so that the sheep are separated from the goats. For now neither are all and each gathered into the visible Church, nor are only the elect gathered into it, since hypocrites are mixed with them everywhere. Then, however, what we have here will be fulfilled: There will be one flock and one Shepherd. Christ adds: For this reason the Father loves me. This is a prediction of his passion and death, which he illustrates from its effect, namely the Father's love. The Father loves the Son because the Son has been eternally begotten, and because the Son became obedient to the Father, even to death, death on a cross. Yet no creature was ever made so obedient to the Father as the Son, who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard being equal with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. From these words of Christ we may gather that Christ, throughout the whole time of his passion, felt the love of God the Father. For these words, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?, came even in that final agony from a sense of that love, and in the most severe sense of wrath there was a sense of the sweetest love. This appears even from the words My God, my God: he would not have called him his God unless he had felt his love. By this sense of ineffable fatherly love he was sustained in that agony. So too the godly perceive the love of God in their obedience and afflictions, and are so sustained by it that they even glory in the midst of afflictions from that sense of God's love. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? That is, from the sense of the love of Christ. So that she may again, etc. Here he foretells that glory will follow the sufferings, and this in order to meet the offence of the Jews, who neither perceived their sins nor the misery that comes from sin, and therefore stumbled over him, who transferred to himself both their sins and the death and wrath of God owed by them. This is said also concerning the elect; for our faith does not rest in the death of Christ but reaches further to his resurrection. For just as by his death he merited for us all things, namely the remission of sins, righteousness and life, so by his resurrection he is effective in applying those benefits. Therefore we must believe that Christ was both crucified and glorified. Here we see that Christ, through the midst of death, looked forward to life, and a most glorious life, and that in his passion he was sustained not only by the love of God which he felt while suffering, but also by regard for eternal life and glory. Therefore it is foretold of him in Psalm 16:9–10: My heart rejoices, therefore my glory exults; my flesh also dwells securely, because you will not leave my soul in the grave, etc. So too all the godly (for the Holy Spirit works in the godly such things as are in Christ), in addition to perceiving the love of God in their obedience and affliction, also see from afar that future glory and eternal life, as if from a distance, and are sustained by regard for it. It is like someone walking along a narrow, slippery path, beset with many obstacles, who, if he sees from afar a wide and beautiful exit, is lifted up and strengthened by the sight.

units.la: Nemo tollit eam. Per occupationem interpretatur verba sua quæ dixit, Ego pono animam meam, &c. Putari enim potuisset Iesum positurum animam suam & assumptu-rum eam rursus pro more aliorum hominum. Huic itaque occurrit, docetque penes seipsum esse mortem vitamque suam: hoc enim est quod dicit, se potestatem habere ponendi animam suam, & potestatem habere rursus eam assumendi. Penes neminem est mors vel vita sua, neque potestatem habet quisquam in mortem vel vitam suam: sed Deus est qui solus potestatem habet in mortem & vitam cuiusque, & filio Dei hæc potestas & authoritas est tributa, supra 5.27. At vero Iesus cùm sit Deus & Dei filius; ita in manu sua habuit mortem vitamque suam, vt nemo auferre ab eo animam potuerit nisi ipso volente: & vi Deitatis habitantis in ipso resurrexerit. Nota hic,nō tantùm gloriosam Christi resurrectionem occurrere scandalo mortis & crucis ipsius, verumetiam ipsammet mortem Christi, si quis penitus ad eam attendat,idipsum præstare. Nì ita mortuus est, vt potuerit, si voluisset,nō mori, quia Deus fuit, & Deitas ipsa in morte sese exeruit. Quia enim nocte captus est, vno verbo effecit, vt retrocederent qui ad eum prehendendum venerant, & humi prolaberentur: & cùm redderet Spiritum ea inciderunt signa & miracula, vt Centurio ille prophanus qui ipsum in cruce pendentem custodiebat,obstupefactus dixeret, Vere filius Dei erat iste. Deinde hic obseruamus, necessarium esse quidem, vt in Christi morte videamus hominem, eumque admodum infirmum, deinde in resurrectione videamus hominem, eumque admodum glorificatum, hoc est,naturam nostram supra Angelos quo cueclam.
units.tr: No one takes it away. He explains by way of occupation the words he spoke, I lay down my life, etc. For it might have been supposed that Jesus would lay down his life and take it up again in the way other men do. He therefore meets this and teaches that his death and life are in his own power. For he says that he has power to lay down his life and power to take it up again. No one has power over his own death or life, nor does anyone have authority over his own death or life; but God alone has power over the death and life of each, and this power and authority has been granted to the Son of God (see above, 5:27). But Jesus, since he is God and the Son of God, so held his death and life in his own hand that no one could take his life from him unless he himself willed it, and he rose by the power of the Godhead dwelling in him. Note here that the glorious resurrection of Christ not only meets the scandal of his death and cross, but that the very death of Christ, if one attends closely to it, accomplishes the same thing. He did not die in such a way that, if he had willed, he could not have failed to die, because he was God, and the Godhead itself showed itself forth in his death. For when he was seized by night, with one word he made those who had come to seize him draw back and fall to the ground; and when he yielded up the Spirit, such signs and wonders occurred that the profane centurion who guarded him as he hung on the cross, astonished, said, Truly this man was the Son of God. Next we observe that it is necessary, indeed, that in the death of Christ we see a man, and one very weak; then in the resurrection we see a man, and one greatly glorified, that is, our nature raised above the angels.

units.la: Verùm vt expectemus gratiam & misericordiam ex morte & resurrectione eius necessarium esse præstitum, vt & in morte eius & resurrectione Deum videamus & illum hominem Deum quoque esse: neque enim vel mors eius meritoria fuisset nobis, nisi illa mors Dei fuisset quodammodo in natura nostra habitatis,& sanguis ille Dei fuisset, nimirum propter vnionem illā hypostaticā. Neque rursus resurrectio eius efficax fuisset ad beneficia illa quæ morte promeritus est applicanda nobis, nisi idem Deus fuisset qui resurrexit, hoc est, nisi Deus quodammodo resurrexisset in natura nostra. Ergo oportet & in morte Christi Deum quodammodo morientem in carne nostra videre, & in resurrectione & vita Deum resurgentem quodammodo in carne nostra videre. Atque hinc est illa fidei μυστηρίον, hinc est tota nostra consolatio.
units.tr: But in order that we may look for grace and mercy from his death and resurrection, it was necessary that both in his death and in his resurrection we should see God, and that this man should also be God. For his death would not have been meritorious for us had not that death of God been in some way in our nature, and that blood been the blood of God, namely on account of that hypostatic union. Nor again would his resurrection have been effective for applying to us those benefits which he merited by death, unless the same God had risen, that is, unless God had in some way risen in our nature. Therefore we must see in the death of Christ God in some way dying in our flesh, and in the resurrection and life we must see God in some way rising again in our flesh. From this comes that mystery [μυστήριον] of faith, and from this comes all our consolation.

units.la: Hoc mandatum. Hanc potestatem mortis & vitæ accepit a Patre. Nam Pater in æterna illa Filij generatione communicauit cum eo ab æterno eam potestatem & Dei omnipotentiam. Christus hic dum prædicat potestatem illam suam plane diuinam in morte resurrectione, non obliuiscitur interea Patris sui, sed ei iustam suam gloriam tribuit; ut nos discamus, eius exemplo, quoties mentionem facimus eorum quæ Deus per nos vel fecit vel facturus est, toties Deo gloriam tribuere. Sic Paulus ait, Gratia eius erga me non fuit inanis, sed amplius quàm illi omnes laboraui. Tum addit per correctionem, Non ego tamen, sed gratia Dei quæ mecum est. Hic Deo gloriam suam tribuit. Sed notandum est discrimen inter Christum & nos, cùm de factis nostris loquimur. Christus hic prædicat se moriturum sua ipsius potestate, & sua ipsius potestate deinde resurrecturum: At nemo nisi regum quidem ita de se loqui poterit sine blasphemia: hoc enim acerbè reprehenditur in Assyrio, quòd se fecisse omnia sua virtute, sua sapientia, sua prudentia, prædicârit. Quid, inquit Deus, An securis gloriabitur contra cædentem ipsa? Causa discriminis est, quia homines alij quicunque, tantùm sunt instrumenta & ministri per quos Deus ipse sua potestate agit. At verò filius Dei Iesus Christus non est instrumentum, sed cum Deo principalis est efficiens atque agens cum eadem pariqe potestate, maiestate & gloria, etsi ea quidem à Patre communicata, idque ab æterno. Pater meus operatur usque adhuc, & ego operor, dixit supra cap. 5. 17.
units.tr: This commandment. He received this power over death and life from the Father. For in that eternal generation of the Son, the Father communicated to him from eternity that power and the omnipotence of God. Here Christ, while he proclaims his own wholly divine power in death and resurrection, does not forget his Father in the meantime, but ascribes to him his due glory, so that we may learn from his example that whenever we mention the things God has done or will do through us, we should always ascribe glory to God. So Paul says: His grace toward me was not in vain, but I laboured more abundantly than all of them. Then he adds by way of correction: Yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me. Here he gives his glory to God. But a difference must be noted between Christ and us when we speak of our deeds. Christ here declares that he will die by his own power, and then by his own power will rise again. But no one, except kings perhaps, can speak of himself thus without blasphemy; for this is harshly rebuked in the Assyrian, who boasted that he had done all things by his own strength, wisdom and prudence. What, says God, will the axe boast against the one who cuts with it? The reason for the difference is that other men, whoever they are, are only instruments and ministers through whom God himself acts by his own power. But the Son of God, Jesus Christ, is not an instrument; rather, together with God he is the principal efficient and agent, with the same power, majesty and glory, though indeed that power is communicated to him by the Father, and from eternity. My Father is working until now, and I am working, he said above in chapter 5:17.

units.la: 19 Dissidium igitur rursum ortum est inter Iudæos propter istos sermones.
units.tr: 19 Therefore a division arose again among the Jews because of these words.

units.la: 20 Dicebant autem multi eorum, Dæmonium habet & insanit. Quid eum auditis?
units.tr: 20 Many of them said, "He has a demon and is out of his mind. Why do you listen to him?"

units.la: 21 Alij dicebant, Hæc verba non sunt dæmoniaci: num dæmonium potest cæcorum oculos aperire?
units.tr: 21 Others said, "These are not the words of a demoniac. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?"

units.la: IN his verbis effectus quidam est sermonis præcedentis. Nam verba Christi sine effectu certè aliquo abire non possunt: verùm hic effectus verborum eius alius atque alius est, in aliis atque aliis. Nam alios excæcat & indurat, alios verò illuminat & emollit. Quærat hic aliquis, cùm vnus idémque sermo sit, cur in diuersis tam diuersum & contrarium effectum sortiatur? Simile quid quæro & ego vicissim, cùm vnus idémque calor sit solis cur tam diuersum & contrarium effectum habeat in luto & in cera? Annon respondebit quis, Ob diuersam temperiem quæ in luto est & cera, & aliam atque aliam in istis affectionem, naturæque qualitatem? Ita hic plane dicendum est, non eandem esse cordis dispositionem in omnibus hominibus: ideóque pro dispositione illa diuersa alium atque alium existere effectum verbi Dei in cordibus eorum. At, dicet aliquis, Anno per naturam eadem dispositio est cordis in omnibus hominibus, vtpote prorsus, vt sic dicam, lutea, vel potius lapidea, adeo vt per naturam omnium citra exceptionem corda obdurescant ad verbum Dei prædicatum? Respondeo, ita quidem esse si naturam spectes, sed discrimen hoc quodcunque est oriri dico ex gratia: Nam Deus est solus qui discernit. Quis te discernit? Quid autem habes, quod non accepetis? Sed hic aliquid præterea dicendum est; Fieri quidem potest vt duo aliqui homines, qui pares sunt cæcitate & cordis duritie, & nihildum de Christo audierunt, sed idiotæ sunt ac infideles, ingrediantur vna ad audiendum Christi verbum. Fieri etiam potest vt ex his alter cuadat deterior audito verbo, alter vero eodem audito melior: quæ nunc causa est huius effectus tam discrepantis, præsertim in cordibus similiter affectis? Respondeo hic aliam causam necessario quærendam a dispositione ipsorum cordium, & ad efficaciam & potentiam verbi Dei confugiendum, qua ipsum differt a sole & efficientibus omnibus naturalibus. Nam res naturales efficientes contra naturam rei obiectæ operari non possunt. Sol non potest ceram indurare, vt neque lutum liquefacere. At verò verbum Dei potens est ad operandum, contra naturam obiecti sui: potest enim cor hominis quod natura sua propendet ad duritiem & audito verbo induratur, potest tamen verbum illud ipsum eor dissoluere, & contra ipsius naturam emollire. Verum vt hoc effectum est maximum: ita non nisi rarum est. Ideoque hic scriptum est, multos dixisse Christum dæmonium habere, alios vero, & eos quidem paucos, eum defendisse. Legimus vnius Lydiæ, inter cæteras mulieres quæ conuenerant, Paulum loquentem audierant, cor adapertum esse. Nunc ex induratione ista multorum, aliorum vero illuminatione minatione certè aliqua, obseruandi sunt effectus quidé diuersi, qui in hoc textu sese offerunt, quorum primus est dissensio inter ipsos orta. Neque enim possunt corda hominum indurata & emollita inter se consentire, nec illi quidem pater & filius sint, mater & filia, vir & vxor. Quę enim communio est lucis cum tenebris? Quare quotquot sine delectu admittunt quamcunque quorumcunque hominum societatem, nebulonum, ganeonum, Papistarum, Apostatarum, excommunicatorum, illi satis ostendunt mentes suas nondum serió conuersas & illuminatas esse Dei verbo, quicquid de numero garriat de fide & religione. Videmus deinde aliud effectum, quotquot indurati erant ex Iudæis, illi inuehuntur in Dominum. Alij eum defendunt: Quotquot indurantur verbo Dei prædicato, illi inuehuntur & exacerbantur in eum qui verbum prædicat, etsi fingas eum esse Dominum ipsum: Unde Christus, Odit me mundus, quoniam ego testor de eo opera eius mala esse. Quotquot verò illuminantur illo verbo, illi contra ampletuntur eum, qui verbum prædicat, etiam homunculonem aliquem, cum Dei sit minister. Quare quoties videmus tantum factiuum & odium Ministrorum Dei in hac gente, non aliam causam profecto eius rei quàm multitudinis indurationem & exacerbationem ad verbum hoc prædicatum afferre possumus. Ex hoc enim & aliis fructibus cum verbo Euangelij pugnantibus, ex tot homicidiis, tot adulteriis, blasphemiis aliisque id genus, quam aliâ causam coniicere possumus, nisi verbum hoc prædicari ad indurationem & exacerbationem hominum non paucorum? Tertiò videmus in induratis his magnam esse impatientiam, & quem verbum prædicatum indurat, illi quidem videntur etiam promissiones suauissimæ, amaissimæ esse. Contrà, quem illuminat verbum, id non fit sine summam suauitatem. Neque enim aperitur cor illud, nisi summa cum voluptate. Unde Petrus, Credentes, inquit, exultatis gaudio ineffabili & gloriosò.
units.tr: This is a certain effect of the preceding discourse. For the words of Christ cannot pass without some effect, but this effect of his words is different and varied, in different people. For they blind and harden some, but enlighten and soften others. Someone may ask: since it is one and the same word, why does it produce such diverse and contrary effects in different people? I in turn ask something similar: since the heat of the sun is one and the same, why does it have such diverse and contrary effects on mud and on wax? Will not someone answer: because of the different temperament of mud and wax, and their different affections and natural qualities? So here we must plainly say that the disposition of the heart is not the same in all men; and therefore, according to that diverse disposition, the effect of the word of God in their hearts is different. But someone will say: is the disposition of the heart by nature the same in all men, being altogether, so to speak, clay or rather stone, so that by nature the hearts of all, without exception, harden against the preached word of God? I answer that it is so if you look at nature, but I say that this difference, whatever it is, arises from grace, for God alone is the one who discerns. "Who makes you to differ? And what do you have that you did not receive?" But something more must be said here. It can indeed happen that two men who are equal in blindness and hardness of heart, and have heard nothing of Christ, being untaught and unbelieving, enter together to hear the word of Christ. It can also happen that after hearing it one of them becomes worse, and the other, having heard the same, becomes better. What now is the cause of this so discordant effect, especially in hearts similarly disposed? I answer that another cause must necessarily be sought in the disposition of the hearts themselves, and we must take refuge in the efficacy and power of the word of God, in which it differs from the sun and from all natural agents. For natural agents cannot act against the nature of the thing acted upon. The sun cannot harden wax, nor melt mud. But the word of God is powerful enough to act against the nature of its object: for the heart of man, which by nature inclines to hardness, is hardened when it hears the word, yet that same word can break that heart open and soften it against its nature. But as this effect is the greatest, so it is also rare. Therefore it is written here that many said Christ had a demon, but others, and those indeed few, defended him. We read that the heart of Lydia, one among the other women who had gathered and had heard Paul speaking, was opened. Now from this hardening of many and the enlightening of others, certainly with some wonder, we must observe the different effects that present themselves in this text, the first of which is the dissension that arose among them. For hearts that are hardened and softened cannot agree with one another, even if they are father and son, mother and daughter, husband and wife. For "what fellowship has light with darkness?" Therefore, whoever without discrimination admit any fellowship whatever with any men, scoundrels, gluttons, Papists, apostates, excommunicates, sufficiently show that their minds have not yet been seriously converted and enlightened by the word of God, whatever they chatter about faith and religion. We see next another effect: all who were hardened among the Jews rage against the Lord. Others defend him. Whoever is hardened by the preached word of God rages and is inflamed against him who preaches the word, even if you pretend that he is the Lord himself; hence Christ says, "The world hates me, because I testify of it that its works are evil." But whoever is enlightened by that word, on the contrary, embraces him who preaches the word, even if he is some little man, since he is a minister of God. Therefore, whenever we see so much strife and hatred against the ministers of God in this nation, we can certainly assign no other cause for it than the hardening and inflaming of the multitude against this preached word. For from this and from other fruits that fight against the gospel, from so many murders, so many adulteries, blasphemies and the like, what other cause can we conjecture, except that this word is preached to the hardening and inflaming of not a few men? Thirdly, we see in these hardened ones a great impatience, and the most sweet and lovely promises, which the preached word hardens them against, seem to them quite bitter. On the contrary, he whom the word enlightens is not enlightened without the greatest sweetness. For that heart is not opened except with the greatest joy. Hence Peter says, "Believing, you exult with joy unspeakable and full of glory."

units.la: Hæc verba non sunt Dæmoniaci. Duo hic afferuntur argumenta defensionis Christi: primum est ab eius verbis, secundum est ab eius facto illo in sanando homine caeco. Sed notandus est ordo argumentorum: primum
units.tr: These are not the words of one possessed. Two arguments are brought here in defence of Christ: the first is from his words, the second from his deed in healing the blind man. But the order of the arguments must be noted: the first

units.la: {y} Repetitio ex 2. Corinth. 6.14. orditur à verbis Domini: quo significatur eos magis affectos & commotos verbis eius posterioribus, quàm facto illo priori. Commoti etiam sunt facto, sed secundo loco. Mouent igitur opera Dei, præsertim extraordinaria & miraculosa, sed magis mouent eius verba sine quibus conuersio cordis fieri non potest. Facta & opera reddere possunt attonitum, & præparare cor hominis ad fidem & conuersionem: sed verba sunt Domini quæ conuertunt animum: Unde Danid, postquam magnifica eius facta & opera prædicauit, subiecit: Lex Domini integra est, reficituens animum, &c. Iam verò postquam ministerio verbi conuersum est cor cuiusque, iam incipit vera æstimatio operum Dei. Nemo enim vnquam æstimauit opera Dei pro dignitate sua, aut Deum in operibus suis glorificauit vt decuit, nisi is cuius animus primùm verbo Dei conuersus fuit. Is verò, qui verbo iam conuersus est, in operibus Dei videt ipsius gloriam ac maiestatem, eúmque in iis glorificat. Atque is est qui solus veram voluptatem capit ex his Dei operibus, vt ex Sole eiúsque luce, ex cælis his quos aspicimus, ex elementis, ex terra eiúsque ornamentis omnibus, ex arboribus, ex frugibus; ex quibus inspectis etiam maiorem voluptatem capit fidelis aliquis, etsi ad eū hæreditario iure non spectent, sed ad alium quàm infidelis qui tamen est earum rerum Dominus. Neque enim veram voluptatem capere quenquam posse existimo ex Dei operibus & ex creaturis, nisi qui in Deum credit, eúmque in ipsis potest glorificare. Nota præterea in hoc argumento priori, verbum Dei habere notam suam, maiestatem, spiritum & potentiam, qua facilè discernatur ab omnibus aliis aliorum verbis, sed hanc notam ij vident soli qui eodem illo spiritu intus obsignati sunt. Alij etiam prophani obstupefieri quidem possunt, illo Dei verbo, & cum admiratione illud audire vt de ministris illis Pontificum & Pharisæorum legimus, supra cap. 7. 46. cùm reuersi sunt ad ipsos, Nunquam ita loquutus est homo, vt homo iste? Sed illa admiratio, apprehensio qualiscunque statim euanescit, quia verbo illo non reformantur. Num dæmonium. Hic vide quod supra docuimus, diabolum vel diabolicum hominem, ordinem naturæ in miraculis
units.tr: {y} Repetition from 2 Corinth. 6.14. It begins with the words of the Lord, by which it is signified that they were moved and affected more by his later words than by that earlier deed. They were also moved by the deed, but in second place. So the works of God move, especially the extraordinary and miraculous ones, but his words move more, and without them a conversion of the heart cannot take place. Deeds and works can astonish, and prepare the heart of man for faith and conversion, but the words of the Lord are what convert the soul. Hence David, after he had proclaimed God's magnificent deeds and works, added: "The law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul," etc. Now indeed, once the heart of each person has been converted through the ministry of the word, the true estimation of God's works begins. For no one has ever valued God's works according to their worth, or glorified God in his works as he ought, unless his mind was first converted by the word of God. He, however, who has already been converted by the word sees in God's works his glory and majesty, and glorifies him in them. And this is the one who alone takes true delight from these works of God, as from the sun and its light, from these heavens which we behold, from the elements, from the earth with all its adornments, from trees and fruits; in contemplating these, even a believer takes greater delight, although they do not belong to him by hereditary right, but to another than the unbeliever, who nevertheless is the lord of those things. For I think that no one can take true delight in the works of God and in creatures unless he believes in God and can glorify him in them. Note further in this earlier argument that the word of God has its own mark, majesty, spirit and power, by which it is easily distinguished from the words of all others; but only those see this mark who have been sealed inwardly by that same Spirit.
