Others, even profane people, may indeed be astonished at that word of God, and hear it with admiration, as we read of those ministers of the chief priests and Pharisees, above chapter 7.46, when they returned to them: "Never has a man spoken like this man!" But that admiration, whatever kind of grasp it is, immediately vanishes, because they are not reformed by that word. "Does a demon...?" Here note what we taught above: the devil, or a diabolical man, does not in truth reverse the order of nature in working miracles, but only imposes upon the eyes of men, and this by divine permission, so that by God's just judgment those who love lies more than truth are blinded. We have assigned the cause of this matter above, namely that God does not exert that extraordinary power...

units.la: Psal.19.8. raculis suis æddendis re vera non inuertere, sed imponere hominum oculis duntaxat, idque diuina permissione; vt iusto Dei iudicio excæcentur quicunque mendacia magis diligunt quàm veritatem. Causam huius rei assi-gnauimus supra, nempe quia Deus non exerit illam potentiam extraordinariam, quæ est in peruertendo naturæ ordine, adhoc vt mendacia & errores pugnantes cum ipsius veritate constabiliantur.
units.tr: ...in working his miracles, not in truth overturning them but only imposing on the eyes of men, and that by divine permission, so that by God's just judgment those are blinded who love lies more than the truth. We have shown the cause of this above, namely that God does not exercise that extraordinary power which lies in overturning the order of nature, in order that lies and errors contrary to his truth may be established.

units.la: 22 Facta sunt autem encænia Hierosolymis, & hyems erat.
units.tr: 22 Now the feast of dedication was held at Jerusalem, and it was winter.

units.la: 23 Eambulabat Iesus in templo, in porticu Salomonis.
units.tr: 23 Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon's porch.

units.la: 24 Cinxerunt igitur eum Iudæi, & dixerunt ei, Quousque animam nostram suspendis? Si tu es Christus ille, dic nobis aperte.
units.tr: 24 Then the Jews surrounded him and said to him, How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.

units.la: SEcũda pars capitis est, in qua est nouum colloquium, & nouus sermo Domini habetur. Primùm metio fit comitiorum & conuentus populi: describitur autem partim à tempore, partim à loco. Tempus est festum encœniorum: quod festum institutum fuit à Iuda Machabæo & fratribus, quo tempore expulso Antiochi præsidio ex urbe, cultus Dei restitutus est, & templum quod prophanatum, fuit denuò consecratum. In memoriam huius consecrationis & dedicationis templi voluit Iudas Machabæus solenne hoc festum quotannis celebrari. 1. Mac. 4. Ex tempore comitiorum notamus frequentiam populi quæ solebat esse in festis diebus Hierosolymis, ac proinde notamus opportunum tempus à Domino electum esse, quo nimirum quamplurimos haberet auditores. Quod ad tempus hyemale adiectum, illud factum est, vel ad designandum tempus huius festi, vel ad gravitudinem huius historiæ, vt in historiis fieri solet. Tum locus comitiorum designatur, nimirum templum & porticus Solomonis, id est, ædificata ad eius instar, quam olim Solomon ædificauerat, 1. Regum. 8. 3. Hic deambulat Christus expectans, vt videtur, populi comitia; locus quoque notat frequentiam populi, vtpote amplus; siue mauis notari circumstantia loci apertam docendi rationem, qua se vsum fuisse ipse Dominus ostendit qua nocte comprehendebatur. Vt aduersus latronem exiuistis cum gladys & fustibus, vt comprehenderetis me: quotidie apud vos sedebam docens in templo, nec prehendistis me. Ex hoc tempore tam opportuno, & loco tam commodo illud tantum noto, istas circumstantias temporis & loci non esse negligendas a pastore, sed quaerendum opportunum tempus & commodum locum in quo quis doceat populum, pro mensura gratiae cuiusque. Quoniusque animâ. Sermonem inchoant Iudaei & queruntur: siue id serio, siue simulate faciant in medio relinquimus. Verum tamen, reipsa suspensi erant animis & fluctuantes, quia in Christo non requiescebant, sine quo nulla quies, nulla par conscientiae. Videntur sibi homines sine eo acquiescere in nugis & vanitatibus suis, cuiusmodi infinita sunt in Papismo. Sed quid aliud faciunt, quàm multiplicant dolores suos qui alienum dotant, vt est in Psalmo 16. 4. In Christo vero solida est pax, Venite ad me, inquit, omnes qui onerati & fatigati estis, & ego faciam vt requiescatis. Deinde notabis cum his Iudaeis, eo ingenio esse quosdam homines, imo multos vbique tenebras, vt in meridiana luce caecutiant, & nihil prorsus videant, hoc est praesente Christo in Euangelio suo gloriosissimo dubij sunt & anxij, neque eum apprehendere possint, corde enim sunt tam male affecto. Nihilominus tamen isti culpam transferunt in Christum ipsum & Euangelium, non secus acsi aliquis productus in lucem meridianam occludat oculos, tum queratur Solem non lucere. Istiusmodi sunt caeci isti, qui cum ad oblatam lucem scripturarum claudant oculos, blasphemant tamen ac queruntur, Scripturas Dei mancas, mortuas, mutas, obscuras: & quid non?
units.tr: The second part of the chapter contains a new conversation and a new discourse of the Lord. First, mention is made of the assembly and gathering of the people; it is described partly by the time and partly by the place. The time is the feast of Encaenia, which was instituted by Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, at the time when, the garrison of Antiochus having been expelled from the city, the worship of God was restored and the temple, which had been profaned, was consecrated anew. In memory of this consecration and dedication of the temple, Judas Maccabeus wished this solemn feast to be celebrated every year. 1 Mac. 4. From the time of the gathering we note the crowds of people who were accustomed to come to Jerusalem on festal days, and so we note that the opportune time chosen by the Lord was one when he would have very many hearers. As for the addition of the wintry season, it was made either to mark the time of this feast or for the solemnity of this narrative, as is usual in histories. Then the place of the gathering is named, namely the temple and Solomon's porch, that is, a building modelled on the one Solomon had once built, 1 Kings 8. 3. Here Christ walks, apparently waiting for the assembly of the people; the place also indicates the great number of people, being spacious. Or, if you prefer, the circumstance of the place may be noted as showing the open manner of teaching which the Lord himself showed he had used on the night he was seized: As against a robber you have come out with swords and clubs to seize me. Daily I sat with you teaching in the temple, and you did not seize me. From this so opportune a time and so convenient a place I note only this: these circumstances of time and place are not to be neglected by a minister, but one should seek an opportune time and a convenient place in which to teach the people, according to the measure of each one's grace. How long will you keep our soul in suspense? The Jews begin the discussion and complain. Whether they do this in earnest or in pretence, we leave undecided. Yet in truth they were held in suspense and wavering in their minds, because they did not rest in Christ, without whom there is no rest and no peace of conscience. Men seem to themselves to rest without him in their trifles and vanities, of which there are endless kinds in Papism. But what else do they do than multiply their sorrows, who hasten after another god, as Psalm 16. 4 says? In Christ alone there is solid peace: Come to me, he says, all you who are burdened and weary, and I will give you rest. Next, with these Jews you will note that some men, indeed many everywhere, are of such a disposition that in the midday light they grow dim and see nothing at all. That is, although Christ is present in his most glorious gospel, they are doubtful and anxious and cannot lay hold of him, for their hearts are so ill disposed. Nevertheless, they transfer the blame to Christ himself and the gospel, just as if someone brought out into the midday light should shut his eyes and then complain that the sun does not shine. Such are those blind men who, when the light of the Scriptures is offered, close their eyes, and yet blaspheme and complain that the Scriptures of God are maimed, dead, dumb, obscure, and what not?

units.la: 25 Respondit eis Iesus, Dixi vobis nec creditis: Opera quae ego facio in nomine Patris mei, haec testantur de me.
units.tr: 25 Jesus answered them: I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father's name, these bear witness of me.

units.la: 26 Sed vos non creditis: non enim estis ex ovibus illis meis, sicut dixi vobis.
units.tr: 26 But you do not believe, for you are not of my sheep, as I told you.

units.la: 27 Oues illae mea vocem meam audiunt, & ego go eas agnosco, & sequuntur me.
units.tr: 27 My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.

units.la: CHristus dum respödet, defendit se dupliciter, simul & eos convincit duplicis contumaciæ. Primùm defendit id quod dixit iis se Christum esse, simulque convincit eos contumaciæ in verbum suum. Nec creditis, inquit. Deinde defendit id quod dixit se opera & miracula ita edidisse in nomine Patris, quæ testarentur eum filium Dei esse; hūc enim vsum habebat miracula Christi, ideóque maiora erant miraculis omnibus ante eum à Mose & Prophetis editis, vt supra vidimus) simul etiā convincit eos contumaciæ in opera ipsius. Hic notabis ex hac ingeminatione infidelitatis, quam subiicit prius instrumento fidei, nempe verbo, deinde posteriori, nempe operibus: notabis singula ista media quibus vtitur Deus ad fidem, si interea permaneat quis infidelis, augere singulis gradibus infidelitatem. Verbum auget infidelitatem, & quoties prædicatur toties auget: opera augent infidelitatem, verbum auget infidelitatem, & quoties infidelis quis videt opera Dei, præsertim extraordinaria, totiens augetur duritiēs cordis. Vt verbo dicam, omnia augent duritiem & infidelitatem eius, in cuius animo non operatur Dominus per Spiritum suum sanctum. Res prosperæ augent eam, res aduersæ augent, tota denique vita nihil est aliud quàm progressus quidam in infidelitate & duritie, quam imbibit per omnes sensus continuò. Ea est miseria hominis, cùm Deus per verbum suum in ipso non est efficax. Interà fit fere vt ille nihil sentiat, non percipiat cor suum contrahere duritiē, donec, vt hic factum est, tandem à Domino ad reddendam factorum rationem vocetur: tum autem renocat ei in memoriam Dominus tum singulas rationes, quibus ipse visus est ad eum adducendum ad fidem, tum singulos gradus duritiei ipsius. Quòd si hoc contigerit post tempus gratiæ, tum pro singulis rationibus & mediis fidei, & pro singulis gradibus infidelitatis multiplicabitur iustitia Dei gradus iudicij. Neque enim impunè quis vel semel auditum verbum contemnit, neque etiam impunè contenitur aliquod opus Dei vt discamus magnifacere hanc Dei bonitatem in nobis tot modis ad fi-
units.tr: In answering, Christ defends himself in two ways, and at the same time convicts them of a twofold obstinacy. First he defends what he said, that he is the Christ, and at the same time convicts them of obstinacy towards his word: Nec creditis, he says, you do not believe. Then he defends what he said, that he had performed works and miracles in my Father's name, which bear witness that he is the Son of God. For this was the purpose of Christ's miracles, and so they were greater than all the miracles performed before him by Moses and the Prophets, as we saw above. At the same time he convicts them of obstinacy towards his works. Here you will note from this repeated charge of unbelief, which he brings against first the instrument of faith, namely the word, and then the second, namely the works, that each of these means which God uses to bring about faith, if a man remains unbelieving meanwhile, increases his unbelief at each step. The word increases unbelief, and as often as it is preached, so often it increases it. Works increase unbelief; and as often as an unbelieving man sees the works of God, especially extraordinary ones, so often is the hardness of his heart increased. To put it in a word, all things increase the hardness and unbelief of the one in whose mind the Lord does not work through his Holy Spirit. Prosperous things increase it, adverse things increase it; in short, the whole of life is nothing but a certain progress in unbelief and hardness, which a man imbibes continually through all his senses. This is the misery of man, when God through his word is not effective in him. Meanwhile it commonly happens that he perceives nothing and does not notice his heart contracting hardness, until, as happened here, he is at last called by the Lord to give an account of his deeds. Then the Lord recalls to his memory each of the reasons by which he was led to be brought to faith, and each of the steps of his hardness. If this happens after the time of grace, then for each of the reasons and means of faith, and for each of the steps of unbelief, the justice of God's judgment will be multiplied. For no one escapes punishment for despising the word even once heard, nor for resisting any work of God; so that we may learn to magnify this goodness of God in us, which has tried so many ways to bring us to faith.

units.la: In incredulos & contumaces Dei iudicium. dem adducendis. Non enim.Ratio est infidelitatis huius, ab eius principio altius repetito, nepe quia reprobi sunt: hoc innuit sæpius iam dictum esse à se. Vbi nota, cum quis finem augendæ infidelitatis non facit, & obfirmădi animum suum aduersus omnem rationem, qua vtitur Deus ad ipsum lucrifaciendum, tum quidem id signum esse reprobationis. Sed Dominus qui fuit Patri à consilio in reprobandis hominibus, probè nouit hoc. Nos autem parcè reprobationis sententiam pronuntiemus etiā in maximè desperatos: habet enim Dominus suum tempus quo vocet vnumquemque, & illud nonnullis vocādis admodum ferum est, vt in latrone illo, qui vnà cum Christo cruci affixus est. Sed videndū hic est diligentius consilium Domini. Hoc subiectum esse videtur per occupationem. Putari enim potuit aliquid derogatū fuisse verbo & operibus Domini, quòd isti, & tot numero manerent increduli, hoc est, quòd non essent hæ rationes in his efficaces ad fidem & conuersionē ipsorum: huic occurrit, quòd reprobi sint. Quod etiam nobis in mentem venire debet, in tot homicidiis, totadulteriis, totque maleficiis in tam clara luce perpetratis, idque sine resipiscentia, tum nobis, inquit, in mente venire debet, hæc sententia Domini, Nō omnes esse electos, imò multos esse reprobos: qui autem sint hi nouit Dominus. Tu ratiocinari apud nos debemus ad multos non pertinere Euangelium, nisi ad eos indurandos & conuincendos. Quibus consideratis tantum abesse ab eo debemus, vt offendamur Euangelio, vt è contrà, si Euangelii in nobis ipsis efficax esse sentiamus, lætemur, & existimemus nos Deo totos obstrictos, qui cùm alij maneant cæci, nos ad Euangelij prædicationem oculos mentis adapertos habeamus. Oues meæ. Ratio est cur nó sint oues ipsius proprietate: Audiunt, inquit, vocem meam; hoc est credūt sermoni meo. Fides est argumentum electionis, vt infidelitas & contumacia reprobationis. Hauddubiè autem se consolatur Christus hac re, Quòd oues saltem ipsius, rebellantibus aliis, ipsum sequuturæ sint & auditurę: ita fidelis Pastor quisquis est, se consolari potest hac sententia in rebellione multorum, nempe quòd oues Domini saltem ipsum in nomine Domini loquentem audituræ.
units.tr: Judgment of God on the unbelieving and the obstinate. The reason for this unbelief is traced from its beginning, namely that they are reprobate. This the Lord has often hinted at already. Here note that when someone does not stop increasing his unbelief and hardening his mind against every reason by which God seeks to win him, that is indeed a sign of reprobation. But the Lord, who was the Father's counsellor in the reprobation of men, knows this well. We, however, should pronounce the sentence of reprobation sparingly, even on the most desperate, for the Lord has his own time in which he calls each one, and for some who are called that time is very late, as with that thief who was crucified together with Christ. But here the counsel of the Lord must be considered more carefully. This seems to be introduced by anticipation. For it might have been thought that something was detracted from the word and works of the Lord because these men, and so many of them, remained unbelieving, that is, because these reasons were not effective in them for their faith and conversion. This is met by the fact that they are reprobate. This too must come to mind for us: in so many murders, so many adulteries, and so many crimes committed in such clear light, and without repentance, this saying of the Lord must come to our minds, that not all are elect, indeed that many are reprobate; but who they are the Lord knows. We ought to reason among ourselves that the gospel does not pertain to many, except to harden and convict them. Having considered these things, we ought to be so far from being offended at the gospel that, on the contrary, if we feel the gospel to be effective in ourselves, we should rejoice and think ourselves wholly bound to God, who, while others remain blind, has opened the eyes of our minds to the preaching of the gospel. My sheep. This is the reason why they are not his sheep, by their own property: They hear, he says, my voice; that is, they believe my word. Faith is the mark of election, as unbelief and obstinacy are the mark of reprobation. Christ indeed takes comfort in this, that his own sheep, while others rebel, will follow him and hear him. So any faithful minister may take comfort from this saying amid the rebellion of many: that the Lord's sheep will at least hear him speaking in the name of the Lord.

units.la: Electorum & reproborum discrimen, quid nos doceat.
units.tr: The difference between the elect and the reprobate, and what it teaches us.

units.la: Fides, electionis argumentū.
units.tr: Faith is the argument of election.

units.la: Pastorum consolatio.
units.tr: The comfort of ministers.

units.la: In maxime desperatos quomodo agendum. dituræ sint.Et ego eas agnosco.Hæc causa est cur ipsum audituræ sint, quia ipse cognovit eas. Neque enim nos cognoscimus Dominum, nisi prius ab eo cogniti fuerimus. Cognitio autem ista non est tantum illa præcognitio, quæ fuit ab æterno, sed est cognitio in tempore efficax. Efficacem voco cognitionem, cum certiores fiunt electi de illa Domini cognitione, idque per internam vocationem. Ante illud tempus non minus insolentes sunt & feroces quàm ipsi reprobi, vocati verò interius iam mansuescunt, & mirum in modum delectantur voce Domini sui, ipsúmque internoscunt, non secus atque infans vocem maternam. Amicus sponsi qui stat & audit, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi, inquit Iohannes Baptista.
units.tr: How to deal with those in utter despair. Will they hear? And I know them. This is the reason they will hear him: because he has known them. For we do not know the Lord unless we have first been known by him. This knowing, however, is not merely that foreknowledge which existed from eternity, but is an effective knowledge in time. I call it effective knowledge when the elect are made more certain of that knowledge of the Lord, and this through inward calling. Before that time they are no less insolent and fierce than the reprobate themselves, but once they are inwardly called they now grow gentle, and they take wonderful delight in the voice of their Lord, and they recognise him, just as an infant recognises its mother's voice. The friend of the bridegroom who stands and hears rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom's voice, says John the Baptist.

units.la: 28 Et ego vitam æternam do eis, nec peribunt in æternum, neque rapiet eas quisquam è manu mea.
units.tr: 28 And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand.

units.la: 29 Pater ille meus qui mihi dedit eas, maior omnibus est: neque quisquam potest eas eripere è manu Patris mei.
units.tr: 29 My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of my Father's hand.

units.la: 30 Ego & Pater unum sumus.
units.tr: 30 I and the Father are one.

units.la: NE quis putet frustra vel audituras oues vocem Dei, vel sequuturas Dominum, proponit mercedem; & quam illam? Vitam, & illam quidem æternam, & quæ non miscebitur cum morte, neque enim morientur in æternum. Tum ne quis obiiceret, At oues ipsæ infirmæ sunt, & prædæ sunt multis hostibus, diabolo, mundo & variis tentationibus, ut sunt oues bestiæ ipsæ innocuæ, & prædæ bestiis aliis rapacibus quibuscunque, ut cani, vulpi, leoni, vrso, lupo, &c. Omnibus hostibus opponit manum suam, tanquam solam aduersariam: Neque rapiet quisquam è manu mea. Non quidem opponit robur omnium & firmitatem ipsarum, sed robur ac potentiam suam, quæ quo illæ magis infirmæ sunt, eo magis ipsi conspicitur atque apparet. Potentia mea, inquit Dominus, per infirmitatem perficitur. Similiter Petrus cum de hæreditate illa æterna & in cœlis nobis seruata loquutus est, occurrit huiusmodi offensioni, quæ est ex infirmitate nostra,cùm subiicit, qui virtute Dei custodiùtur per fidē ad salutem, &c. Nisi enim idē Deus qui vitam in nobis æternam in cœlis conseruat, nos in terris conseruet ac custodiat ad illam vitam suo tempore reuelandam, nos, qua sumus infirmitate, ipsi in medio tot tantorúmque aduersariorum quotidie millies periremus. Pater qui dedit. Ostendit neminem rapturum oues suas è manu sua, ex eo quod nemo rapturus sit eas è manu Patris sui. Cõsequens probat, quia ego & Pater vnum sumus, nempe, sententia, potentia & gloria. Hinc sequitur quod si nemo rapturus sit eas è manu Patris, nemo quoque rapturus sit eas è manu ipsius. Assumptionem probat, Nā Pater, inquit, qui dedit mihi eas maior est omnibus: Ergo nemo rapturus est eas è manu Patris: Ergo Christus deducit sidem nostram ad hoc fundamentum, nimirum quòd ipse sit vnus cum Patre Deus. Vt igitur sit fides in Christum Iesum vt credamus eum posse seruare nos ab omnibus inimicis nostris, necesse habemus, vt videamus in Christo Deitatem, in facie eius personam Patris, cùm sit character personæ ipsius; in facie eius gloriam Dei, cùm sit splendor gloriæ ipsius: in manu ipsius manum ac potentiam Patris; denique in illo totam illam Dei Patris maiestatem. Id voluit Dominus Iudæos cernere, etiam tum cùm humiliatus est in carne, vt cõstat ex hoc loco. Et illi quidē potuerunt in humilitate carnis ipsius idipsum intueri. Nam nemo vnquam loquutus est vt ille, nemo operatus est vnquam vt ille: etiam in ipsa cruce potuit conspici eius Deitas, & prophanus ille Centurio coactus est eum Dei filium pronunciare. Potuerunt igitur inspicere Christi gloriam in ipsa humilitate ipsius: & inspexerunt quidem ij quibus dati sunt oculi. Commoratus est, inquit, inter nos, plenus gratiæ & veritatis, & spectauimus gloriam eius, gloriam vnigeniti egressi à Patre. At dices, Iudæis quidem illis qui Dominum habuerunt corpore præsentem fuit sit facile, videre eius gloriam ac maiestatem. Nobis autem à quibus absens est corpore, non ita facile est. Respondeo ex efficacia Christi, & ex illa eius potentia, vt loquitur Apostolus, quam qui credimus ipsi in nobis sentimus, non modò videmus, sed persentiscimus etiam gloriam illam ipsius. Hic autem sensensus potentiæ Christi nunquam existeret ex fide in Christum, nisi is Deus esset benedictus in sæculum, Amen. Iam cognito eo quod Iesus Christus idem Deus sit, deinde sentimus nos teneri eius manu, sentimus nos pariter apprehendi manu Patris ac Dei. Cùm autem sentimus nos prehendi manu Patris ac Dei, tum quidem videmur nobis firmi esse, & extra omne periculum positi, etiam in media morte. Neque enim putandum est non sentire nos penitus apprehensionem illam Dei, a Deo apprehendentis: cum Apostolus dicat, Quis nos separabit a charitate Christi? Hoc est priuabit nos sensu illo dilectionis ipsius: in qua radicati & fundati sumus a Deo, quia principiū illud est etiam natura ipsa notum, nempe Deus est maior omnibus. Videmur autem nobis in tuto esse cum apprehensi sumus a Deo, quia principiū illud est etiam natura ipsa notum, nempe Deus est maior omnibus. Nota deinde Et Deum fundamentum, in quo fundata est vita æterna, est autem manus illa Dei apprehendens nos, non tam manus nostra apprehendens Deum quàm Dei manus apprehendens nos: Fateor etiam nos manu nostra Deum prehendere, nempe fidei manu, ideoque seruari. Seruamur enim virtute Dei per fidem 1. Petr. 1. 5. Verum primum omnium haec apprehensio existit ex apprehensione Dei ea, qua Spiritu suo sancto corda nostra apprehendit: Nam Spiritus Dei est, qui excitat in nobis fidem. Idem innuit Apostolus, cum dicit se apprehendentem metam illam vitæ æternæ, apprehensum esse a Christo: Atque eam ces se causam cur ipse apprehendat metam. Deinde dico fidem nostram adeo infirmam esse nonnunquam, ut nisi conscientia nostra nos admoneret, interea nos apprehendi a Deo, & eius quasi manu teneri, quid de nobis fieret? Postremo illud addo etiam, ante fidem ingenitam & vocationem efficacem, electos manu Dei conseruari secreto quodam pacto ad fidem & vitam futuram.
units.tr: Lest anyone think that the sheep will hear the voice of God in vain, or follow the Lord in vain, he sets out the reward: and what reward? Life, and indeed eternal life, which will not be mingled with death, for they shall not die for ever. Then, lest anyone should object, "But the sheep themselves are weak, and are the prey of many enemies: the devil, the world and various temptations, just as sheep are harmless beasts and the prey of other rapacious beasts of every kind, such as dogs, foxes, lions, bears, wolves, and so on," he sets his hand against all enemies, as though it were the only one opposed to them: No one shall snatch them out of my hand. He does not set against them the strength and firmness of the sheep themselves, but his own strength and power, which becomes all the more visible and evident the weaker they are. My power, says the Lord, is made perfect in weakness. Likewise Peter, when he speaks of that eternal inheritance reserved for us in heaven, meets the offence that arises from our weakness, when he adds: who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation, and so on. For unless the same God who preserves eternal life for us in heaven also preserves and guards us on earth until that life is revealed in its time, we, by reason of our weakness, would perish a thousand times a day in the midst of so many and so great adversaries. The Father who gave. He shows that no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand, from the fact that no one will snatch them out of the hand of his Father. The consequence he proves, because I and the Father are one, namely in judgement, power and glory. From this it follows that if no one will snatch them out of the Father's hand, no one will also snatch them out of his own hand. He proves the assumption: for the Father, he says, who gave them to me is greater than all. Therefore no one will snatch them out of the Father's hand. Therefore Christ brings our faith down to this foundation, namely that he is God, one with the Father. So, if there is to be faith in Christ Jesus, so that we believe that he can keep us from all our enemies, we must see the Deity in Christ, in his face the person of the Father, since he is the express image of that person; in his face the glory of God, since he is the brightness of his glory; in his hand the hand and power of the Father; and finally in him the whole majesty of God the Father. This the Lord wished the Jews to perceive, even when he was humbled in the flesh, as is clear from this passage. And indeed they could behold this very thing in the humility of his flesh. For no one ever spoke as he did, no one ever worked as he did: even on the cross his Deity could be seen, and that profane centurion was compelled to declare him the Son of God. They were able, therefore, to behold the glory of Christ in his very humility: and indeed those to whom eyes were given did behold it. He dwelt, says John, among us, full of grace and truth, and we beheld his glory, the glory of the only-begotten who came from the Father. But you will say that for those Jews who had the Lord present in the body it was easy to see his glory and majesty. For us, from whom he is absent in body, it is not so easy. I reply: from the efficacy of Christ, and from that power of his, as the Apostle speaks, which we who believe in him feel in ourselves; we not only see that glory of his, but even perceive it. Moreover, this sense of the power of Christ would never arise from faith in Christ unless he were God, blessed for ever, Amen. Now that it is known that Jesus Christ is the same God, we then feel ourselves held in his hand, we feel ourselves likewise apprehended by the hand of the Father and of God. When we feel ourselves held by the hand of the Father and of God, then indeed we seem to ourselves to be firm and placed beyond all danger, even in the midst of death. For we must not think that we do not wholly feel that apprehension of God by which God lays hold of us, since the Apostle says: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? That is, he will not deprive us of the sense of that love of his, in which we are rooted and grounded by God, because this principle is known even by nature itself, namely that God is greater than all. We seem to ourselves to be safe when we have been apprehended by God, because this principle is known even by nature itself, namely that God is greater than all. Note next that God is the foundation on which eternal life is founded; and it is that hand of God apprehending us, not so much our hand apprehending God as the hand of God apprehending us. I admit that we also lay hold of God with our own hand, namely the hand of faith, and so are kept. For we are kept by the power of God through faith (1 Pet. 1.5). But first of all, this apprehension arises from that apprehension of God by which he apprehends our hearts through his Holy Spirit: for it is the Spirit of God who stirs up faith in us. The Apostle hints at the same thing when he says that he apprehends that goal of eternal life, and that he has been apprehended by Christ, and that this is the reason why he apprehends the goal. Next I say that our faith is at times so weak that, unless our conscience warned us that in the meantime we are being apprehended by God and held as it were in his hand, what would become of us? Lastly I add this also: before implanted faith and effectual calling, the elect are kept in the hand of God in a certain secret manner, for faith and the life to come.

units.la: 31 Sustulerunt ergo rursum lapides Iudæi ut eum lapidarent.
units.tr: 31 Therefore the Jews again took up stones to stone him.

units.la: 32 Respondit eis Iesus, Multa bona opera exhibui vobis ex Patre meo: propter quod illorum operum me lapidatis?
units.tr: 32 Jesus answered them, "I have shown you many good works from my Father: for which of those works do you stone me?"

units.la: Qui fidei nostrae infirmitatem sua potentia sublouat.
units.tr: How he supports the weakness of our faith by his own power.

units.la: 33 Responderunt ei Iudæi, dicentes, Ob bonum opus non lapidamus te, sed ob blasphemiam, idest, quia tu homo cùm sis, facis teipsum Deum.
units.tr: 33 The Jews answered him, saying, "We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, that is, because you, being a man, make yourself God."

units.la: HOc effectum est scilicet verborum Christi in obstinatis illis Iudæis; Acti sunt in rabiem, hæc tamen rabies non caruit prætextu quodam legis illius quæ in blasphemos & pseudoprophetas lata est, Deut 17. Ex hoc effectu coniicere potes quónam animo quæsierint de Christo supra, & qualénam fuerit illud desiderium eius manifestò cognoscendi, verúmne an fictum. Aperta enim cófessio nunc cos ad insaniā redigit. Sunt hypocritæ isti his similes, qui nihil magis velle videntur quàm veritatis cognitionem, profitentúrque animú suum paratum ad recipiendam lucem doctrinæ, & veritatis informationem. Verùm cùm iam apparuit lux, & illata est quasi in animum eorum vix illa doctrinæ cœlestis, tum quidem frendent cordibus, stridént dentibus, & irruentes in lucis illius ministros, lapidáť eos, & indignis quibusque modis tractant. Quid aliud significat hoc quàm in animo iis non fuisse conuertere se ad Deū & veritatē amplecti, verùm totam eorum voluptatē in tenebris & cordis duritie collocatam esse? Respondit eis Iesus. Domi-nus responso hoc suo obiicit eis paucis verbis multa peccata. primùm iniustitiam in eum qui bene operatus est; deinde ingratitudinem in eum qui in ipsorum gratiam, ad eorum nimirum conuersionem & salutem operatus sit. Tertiò, ingratitudinem in Deum ipsum & Patrem, cùm dicit, Demonstravi multa opera ex Patre meo. Postremò, hæc omnia ea verborum formula proposuit, & ea visus est interrogatione, vt compunctis conscientia rabiem ad tempus represserit. Erhoc observuamus persequutionem quamquè piorum multa simul peccata implicare, iniustitiam, ingratitudinem, eamque non simplicem. Paulus iam conuersus persequutionem suam non potuit satis exaggerare. Eram, inquit, blasphemus & persecutor, & iniuriosus. Sed excantur ita rabie sua persequutores quique, vt ista nō perspiciant, donec Deo eos ad rationem reddendam vocante compungantur conscientiis, simúlque reprimatur. Responderunt ei Iudæi. Co-hibetur hibetur quidem manus eorum, sed non os: nam ratione facti conantur reddere, etiam cum insaniunt & aperte Christum oppugnant. Hoc non est novum persequuto- ribus istis cum ratione insanire, ut dici solet: neque de- sunt qui persequutiones & caedes piorum teterrimas excusent. Verum hoc magis movet, quòd zelum Dei praetexant: quid aliud, quaeso, faciunt quàm vlcisci vt scili- cet blasphemum? Sic isti hodierno die persequuntur. sed quos? Haereticos scilicet & Ecclesiae hostes. Sed quod te- medium invenias nisi patientiam & bonam conscientiam quam opponas adversus calumnias & obiectas haereses, blasphemias, & si quid tale est? Nota hic blasphemi de- finitionem veram quidem, sed falso Christo attributam etiam homini nedum Deo & Dei filio. Blasphemus enim is est proprie qui vel Deo detrahit quod ipsi proprium est, vel Deo affingit quod in ipsius maiestatem omnino non potest competere.
units.tr: This was the effect of Christ's words on those obstinate Jews. They were driven into a rage, yet this rage did not lack some pretext from that law which was given against blasphemers and false prophets, Deut. 17. From this effect you may infer with what intention they had asked about Christ above, and what kind of desire it was to know him plainly, whether genuine or feigned. For now his open confession drives them to madness. There are hypocrites like these, who seem to desire nothing more than knowledge of the truth, who profess that their minds are ready to receive the light of doctrine and to be instructed in the truth. But when the light has appeared, and that heavenly teaching has barely been brought, as it were, into their minds, then they gnash with their hearts, grind their teeth, rush upon the ministers of that light, stone them, and treat them with every unworthy outrage. What does this signify except that in their minds there was no intention of turning to God and embracing the truth, but that all their pleasure was fixed in darkness and hardness of heart? Jesus answered them. By this reply the Lord charges them, in a few words, with many sins: first, injustice toward him who has done good; then, ingratitude toward him who has acted for their own grace, that is, for their conversion and salvation; thirdly, ingratitude toward God himself, the Father, when he says, I have shown you many works from my Father. Lastly, he has set all these things before them in the form of a question, and it seems that by this question he checked their rage for the time, their consciences being pricked. From this we observe that the persecution even of the godly involves many sins at once: injustice, ingratitude, and that not a simple kind. Paul, once converted, could not sufficiently exaggerate his own persecution: I was, he says, a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insulter. But persecutors are so blinded by their rage that they do not perceive these things until, God calling them to give an account, their consciences are pricked and their rage is at the same time restrained. The Jews answered him. Their hand is indeed restrained, but not their mouth: for they try to answer with reasons, even when they rage and openly attack Christ. It is not new for such persecutors to rage with reason, as the saying goes; nor are there lacking those who excuse the most foul persecutions and slaughters of the godly. But what moves us more is that they pretend zeal for God. What else, I ask, do they do but take vengeance, as on a blasphemer? So these men persecute even today. But whom? Heretics, to be sure, and enemies of the Church. But what remedy can you find except patience and a good conscience, which you set against slanders, objected heresies, blasphemies, and whatever is of that sort? Note here the definition of blasphemy, which is true indeed, but wrongly ascribed to Christ, and ascribed even to a man, let alone to God and the Son of God. For a blasphemer, properly speaking, is one who either takes away from God what is proper to him, or attributes to God what cannot at all belong to his majesty.

units.la: 34 Respondit eis Iesus, Nonne scriptum est in lege vestra, Ego dixi, Dij estis?
units.tr: 34 Jesus answered them, Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?

units.la: 35 Si illos dixit deos ad quos sermo Dei factus est, & non potest solvi scriptura:
units.tr: 35 If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken:

units.la: 36 Mene quem Pater sanctificavit & misit in mundum, vos dicitis, Tu blasphemas, quia dixi, Filius Dei sum?
units.tr: 36 Do ye say of him, whom the Father hath sanctified and sent into the world, Thou blasphemest, because I said, I am the Son of God?

units.la: 37 Si non facio opera Patris mei, nolite credere mihi.
units.tr: 37 If I do not the works of my Father, believe me not.

units.la: 38 Sin vero illa facio, etiamsi mihi non creditis, operibus tamen credite, ut cognoscatis & credatis Patrem in me esse, & me in eo.
units.tr: 38 But if I do them, though ye believe not me, believe the works: that ye may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in him.

units.la: OPponit iis Dominus scripturam veteris testamenti, quod nomine legis hic appellat, est enim hoc testimonium desumptum ex Psalmo 82.6. Ego dixi, in- quit Dominus, quod dij estis. Nomen deorum Magistra- tibus tribuitur, idque dicente Deo, ut sciamus non te- mere & fortuito Magistratum quemquam fieri, sed verbo Dei ad eum locum vocari. Hoc scripturae fundaméto posito, ita argumentatur Dominus à minori ad maius. Si dij vocati sunt illi ad quos sermo Dei factus est: nempe dicente illis Deo, Ego dixi quod dij estis: Nam sic interpretatur illud, Ego dixi. Si hoc, inquam, sit, sequitur me non ideo blasphemum, quòd dixerim me filiū Dei esse: at prius verum est, ergo posterius. Ratio assumptionis est: Scriptura solui non potest. Propositionem suam siue connexionem probat à speciali quadam sanctificatione, obsignatione & missione sui, vt supra: κατ' ἐξοχὴν enim dicit se sanctificatum & missum, cùm & reges & magistratus omnes sanctificentur à Deo, ab eòque mittantur. Cæterùm sanctificatio ista est Christi mediatoris vocatio: & qua Deus est, deitatis enim respectu sanctificatus est donis infinitis illis quidem, & omne modum excedentibus: & qua homo est, humanitatis enim ratione sanctificatus est donis supra omnem rem creatam, & vnctus est oleo supra socios. Verùm de hac sanctificatione ita loquitur illis Dominus, vt de re illis coperta, vtpote quam cognitam habere potuerunt ex effectis illis gratiæ illius quæ in ipso erat, nempe ex operibus, de quibus proximè & ex verbo. Nam ex his elucet gratia Christi, & Sanctificatio ipsius mirifica: ex sanctificatione rursus apparet eum superiorem omni creatura, imò Deum esse. Quare perpetuò oculi conuertendi ad effecta Christi. Vide, hic redarguit & conuincit eos ex scriptura, & ea quidem scriptura, quam ipsi tanti faciebant, nimirum Lege. Hæretici & obstinati per scripturas sunt conuincendi. Quibus ipsi, quemadmodū experimur in Papistis hodierno die, malùt renunciare, quam medaciis suis cum scriptura sacra aperte pugnantibus valedicere, vel etiam cedere veritati. Hinc sunt illæ in scripturam sanctam blasphemiæ, mutila est, manca est, mortua est, & quid non? Ad derogandam scripturæ authoritatem ista omnia. Si non facio. Offert nunc Dominus se iis explorandum ex operibus suis, & ex iis iudicandum de se ex operibus. Deinde filius sit necne, & permittit iis ne credant ipsi, nisi convicti operibus ipsius. Ex quo videmus ex operibus externis iudicium fieri de homine, qualis sit & quo modo affectus animo, bonusne an malus sit. Ostende mihi fidem tuam ex operibus tuis, & ego ostendam tibi ex operibus meis.
units.tr: The Lord sets before them the Scripture of the Old Testament, which here he calls by the name of the law; for this testimony is taken from Psalm 82:6: I said, says the Lord, that you are gods. The name of gods is given to magistrates, and this by the word of God, so that we may know that no magistrate is made by chance or accident, but is called to that place by the Word of God. With this foundation of Scripture laid, the Lord argues from the less to the greater: If those are called gods to whom the word of God came, namely when God said to them, I said that you are gods (for so he interprets the words I said), then, I say, if this is so, it follows that I am not blasphemous for having said that I am the Son of God; but the first is true, therefore the second. The reason for the assumption is: the Scripture cannot be broken. He proves his proposition, or the connection, from a special sanctification, sealing and sending of himself, as above: for he says that he is sanctified and sent par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], since kings and all magistrates are sanctified by God and sent by him. Moreover, this sanctification is the calling of Christ the Mediator: and insofar as he is God, for in respect of his deity he was sanctified with gifts that are indeed infinite and exceed every measure; and insofar as he is man, for in respect of his humanity he was sanctified with gifts above every created thing, and he was anointed with oil above his fellows. But the Lord speaks to them of this sanctification as of a matter hidden from them, inasmuch as they could have known it from those effects of the grace that was in him, namely from the works just mentioned and from the Word. For from these the grace of Christ and his wonderful sanctification shine forth; and again from the sanctification it appears that he is above every creature, indeed that he is God. Therefore our eyes must always be turned to the effects of Christ. See, here he refutes and convicts them from Scripture, and indeed from that Scripture which they valued so highly, namely the Law. Heretics and obstinate men are to be convicted by the Scriptures. Like the Papists in our own day, they would rather renounce them than bid farewell to their lies, which openly fight against holy Scripture, or even yield to the truth. Hence come those blasphemies against holy Scripture: it is mutilated, it is maimed, it is dead, and what not? All of this is to detract from the authority of Scripture. If I do not. The Lord now offers himself to them to be tested by his works, and to be judged by them concerning himself, by his works: whether he is the Son or not. And he allows them not to believe him unless they are convinced by his works. From this we see that judgment is made of a man from his outward works, what he is like and how he is disposed in mind, whether he is good or bad. Show me your faith from your works, and I will show you my faith from my works.

units.la: Iacob. 2. 18. meis fidem meam, inquit Apostolus. Quòd si cor cuiusque sit sanctificatum, profecto quæ ex corde proficiscuntur omnia dicta & facta sapiant sanctitatem aliquam necesse est. Quòd si rursus prophanum sit cor, tum verba ab eo prophana, & facta prophana existant oportet. Esau dictus est prophanus: Cur autem? quia unico edulio vendidit ius suum primogeniti. Contemptus integritatis & verbi divini arguit prophanitatem cordis utcunque sint homines alioqui politici, ac ciuilibus istis virtutibus ornati. Videtur hoc temere factum quòd se ex operibus iudicandum tam corruptis iudicibus obtulerit. Quibus profecto facile fuit damnare omnia eius opera: proculdubio ex bona operum suorum conscientia profecta est ista audacia. Nam homines freti bona conscientia operum suorum & iustitia illa quam vocant bonæ conscientiæ, sese offerre solent explorandos & iudicandos ex operibus suis, etiam corruptis & iniquis iudicibus. Enimuerò si veniat (inquit Apostolus) qui alium Iesum prædicet, quam non prædicauimus, aut si spiritum alium accipiatis quem non accepistis, aut Euangelium aliud quod non accepistis, recte eum toleraueritis. Ecce iudicium sui fieri vult ex Euangelio à se prædicato, sic ut si quis excellentius aliquod Euangelium prædicaturus sit, Corinthij ipsum tolerent, ac Paulo præferant. Quod si tum fiat, ut iniquè & corruptè iudicentur opera à corruptis & iniquis iudicibus, quid reliquum est nisi ut sustententur viri boni cadè illa conscientia sua bona, ut à Paulo factu legimus? Mihi vero pro minimo est quod à vobis diiudicer, aut ab humano iudicio: Imò nec meipsum diiudico. Nullius enim rei mihi conscius sum. Nam si conscientia non condemnat quemquam, etiam iniquis hominum iudiciis oppressum, profecto is absoluitur à Deo. Quòd si verò cor ipsius condemnet ipsum, potentior est Deus corde ipsius, hoc est condemnat eum pariter. Sed hic notandum præterea in hoc facto Domini, quòd ipse cognouerit conuictos istos conscientia, quòd opera ipsius à Patre essent, id quod appareret ex eo quod sequitur: nam nihil habent quod operibus ipsius opponant: persequuntur tamen eum, ut videas facilè, quàm obdurati fuerint aduersus veritatem etiam agnitam & suam ipsorum conscientiam. Etiamsi. Hæc est altera permissio, qua quidem concedit iis ut non credant statim ipsi convicti iam operibus ipsius, sed credant ipsis potius operibus. Vide quàm leniter & modestè agat cum iis Dominus & ut se obliviscatur, ad hoc, ut si fieri possit ipsos lucretur. Quoniam enim persona ipsius offendebantur, ideo largitur iis id, ut ad tempus non credant ei quòd sit filius Dei. Postulat autem ipsorum salus, ut primo quoque tempore credat operibus ipsius, quæ Dei sunt. Hic Christi exemplo admonentur Pastores ut sese ac sua omnia negligant, ad hoc ut si fieri possit lucrifaciant fidei suæ commissos. Admonentur rursus omnes ut attendant non tam ad hominum personas, quàm ad ipsum verbum Dei ab iis prædicatum, ne propter offensionem personarum amittant gratiam. Quòd si ea in nobis esset fames verbi Dei, quæ esse debet, profectò non usque adeo hæreremus in his externis; neque enim famelicus aliquis, & qui correptus est extrema fame recusabit cibum etiam ab eo oblatum quem tamen non multum diligit. Sed nos quia iam saturati sumus non verbo Dei, sed affectibus nostris vitiosis, quæ ob oculos sunt perpetuo versamur, ut Paulus loquitur. Vt cognoscatis. Hic finis est credere operibus, ut nimirum tandem cognoscant et agnoscant Filium unum esse cum Patre: hoc enim est, quod ait, me esse in Patre, & Patrem esse in me, eodem enim sensu dictum est cum eo quod habetur supra vers. 30. Ego & Pater unum sumus. Quare vtcunque permittat iis, ut ad tempus non credant in ipsum quòd filius Dei sit: tamen huc tandem redeundum esse docet, ut credant in ipsum. In quo differt magnus ille Pastor ab omnibus aliis pastoribus. Sed sine iactura salutis fieri non potest, ut perpetuò offendamus & impingamus in personam magni illius pastoris, nempe Christi. Is enim est salutis author, & ad quem nos verbum Dei deducit paritèr & opera eius omnia.
units.tr: James 2:18. Show me your faith by your works, says the Apostle. If the heart of each person is sanctified, then surely everything that proceeds from the heart must necessarily have some holiness in its words and deeds. Conversely, if the heart is profane, then the words and deeds that come from it must be profane. Esau was called profane. Why? Because he sold his birthright for a single meal. Contempt for integrity and the divine word shows a profane heart, however civil such men may otherwise be and however adorned with those civic virtues. It seems he acted rashly in offering himself to be judged by his works before such corrupt judges. Those judges could easily have condemned all his works, and that boldness surely came from the good conscience of his own works. For men who rely on a good conscience about their works, and on that righteousness which they call a good conscience, are accustomed to offer themselves to be tested and judged by their works, even before corrupt and unjust judges. Indeed, if someone comes (says the Apostle) preaching another Jesus than we have preached, or if you receive another spirit which you have not received, or another gospel which you have not received, you would rightly bear with him. See, he wants himself to be judged by the gospel he preached, so that if someone were to preach a more excellent gospel, the Corinthians would tolerate him and prefer him to Paul. But if it happens that works are judged unjustly and wrongly by corrupt and unjust judges, what is left except that good men be sustained by that good conscience of theirs, as we read was done by Paul? For me it is a very small thing to be judged by you, or by human judgment. Indeed I do not even judge myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself. For if conscience condemns no one, even when he is oppressed by the unjust judgments of men, then surely he is acquitted by God. But if his own heart condemns him, God is greater than his heart, that is, He likewise condemns him. But here we must further note in this action of the Lord that he knew his accusers were convicted by their conscience, that his works were from the Father. This appears from what follows, for they have nothing to set against his works, yet they pursue him. You may easily see how hardened they were against the truth, even the truth they recognised and their own conscience. Even if. This is the second concession, by which he allows them not to believe at once, though already convicted by his works, but rather to believe the works themselves. See how gently and modestly the Lord deals with them, and how he forgets himself, so that, if possible, he may win them. For since they were offended at his person, he grants them this, that for the time being they need not believe that he is the Son of God. Yet their salvation requires that they believe his works, which are the works of God, at the first opportunity. Here by Christ's example ministers are admonished to disregard themselves and all their own concerns, so that, if possible, they may gain those committed to their faith. Again, all are admonished to attend not so much to the persons of men as to the very word of God preached by them, lest through offence at the persons they lose grace. But if we had in us the hunger for the word of God which we ought to have, we would surely not cling so much to these external things. For a hungry man, one seized by extreme hunger, will not refuse food even when it is offered by one whom he does not much love. But we, since we are already satisfied not with the word of God but with our own depraved affections, which are always before our eyes, keep turning round and round, as Paul puts it. That you may know. The purpose of believing the works is this: that at last they may know and acknowledge that the Son is one with the Father. For this is what he means when he says that I am in the Father and the Father in me, since it is said in the same sense as what is found above at verse 30: I and the Father are one. Therefore, however much he allows them for a time not to believe that he is the Son of God, he teaches that they must nonetheless return to this, that they believe in him. In this the great Shepherd differs from all other ministers. But it cannot happen, without loss of salvation, that we keep offending and stumbling over the person of that great Shepherd, namely Christ. For he is the author of salvation, and the word of God leads us equally to him and to all his works.

units.la: 39 Rursus studebant eum prehendere: sed exiit ex eorum manu.
units.tr: 39 Again they sought to seize him, but he escaped out of their hand.

units.la: 40 Abiitque rursus ad trajectum Iordanis, in eum { }eum locum vbi primum fuerat Iohannes, cum baptizaret, mansit ibi illic.
units.tr: 40 And he went away again beyond the Jordan, into the place where John had first been baptizing, and he stayed there.

units.la: 41 Multi autem venie bant ad eum, & dicebant, Iohannes quidem signum nullum edidit, quaecunque autem de isto dixit, vera erant.
units.tr: 41 And many came to him, and said, John indeed did no sign, but all the things that John said of this man were true.

units.la: 42 Et multi crediderunt in eum.
units.tr: 42 And many believed in him.

units.la: PERmisit iis iudicium, sed illi indicta causa eum prehendere volunt & occidere. Nihil enim habet quod obiiciant aduersus opera eius, verum os iis obturatur, indurantur tamen aduersus eum etiam conuicti conscientia, eumque persequuntur, ut videas indurationis perpetuo comitem esse persequutionem & crudelitatem, praesertim vero cum induratur quis & obfirmatur adversus agnitam veritatem & suam ipsius conscientiam, cuiusmodi fuit illa Pauli, cum dicit, Blasphemus & persequutor, & iniuriosus eram, sed mei misertus est Deus, quia ignorans id faciebam fidei expers. 1. Timoth. 1. 13. Huiusmodi persequutio misericordiam consequitur. Altera vero est cum cognitione & conscientia conuicta, cuiusmodi fuit illa Pharisaeorum, haec aegre impetrat misericordiam & veniam. Sed ut redeamus: illud verum fixumque manet, indurationem & infidelitatem perpetuo comitem habere crudelitatem: ut e contra fides comitem habet misericordiam. Nam quid est fides aliud, quam sensus misericordiae Dei in Christo, quam qui sentit, is profecto omnium miseretur propter Dominum, etiam inimicorum suorum? Odit quidem Dei inimicos & quaerit ut vel conuertantur vel confundantur, non tamen delectatur eorum pernicie, qua Dei sunt creaturae, sed eorum iusta poena delectatur, quia Dei hostes sunt. Estque hoc ingenium ipsius Dei, qui non delectatur perditione creaturae suae, & miseretur etiam reprobórum pereuntium, absque tamen praeiudicio iustitiae suae & iustae irae. Sed exiuit ex eorum. Quod fugerit, ex infirmitate humana fuit: quod autem cum solus esset & undique obsessus ac circumseptus tot inimicis ad apprehendendum cum & occidendum coniuratis, id docuimus tum suis diuinitatis ac potentiae admirabilium. lis, huiusmodi, inquam, potentiæ, per quam etiam in infirmitate illa carnis elucentem, certiores fieri potuerunt aduersarij de eo quod erat in controuersia, nepe eum Deum esse ac Dei filium. Non enim potuisset aliquis, qui homo tantum esset, explicare sese e manibus tot inimicorum. Ergo hoc & huiusmodi factis ostendit Dominus neminem potuisse eripere sibi vitam inuito, sed ipsum eam deponere pro voluntate sua, rursusque eam tollere pro arbitratu suo, vt ipse dixit supra, hoc capite, versu 18.
units.tr: He allowed them judgment, but they, without any cause heard, want to seize and kill him. For they have nothing to set against his works, but their mouths are stopped; yet they are hardened against him even when convicted by conscience, and they persecute him. You may see that persecution and cruelty always accompany hardening, especially when a man is hardened and made obstinate against a truth he has recognised and against his own conscience. Such was Paul's case when he said: "I was a blasphemer, a persecutor and injurious; but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly, in unbelief." 1 Timothy 1:13. Persecution of this kind is followed by mercy. But the other kind, carried on with knowledge and against a convicted conscience, such as that of the Pharisees, obtains mercy and pardon only with difficulty. But to return: this truth stands fixed, that hardening and unbelief always have cruelty as their companion, just as faith has mercy as its companion. For what is faith but a sense of God's mercy in Christ? Whoever has this sense surely has compassion for all men for the Lord's sake, even for his enemies. He indeed hates God's enemies and seeks either that they be converted or confounded; yet he takes no delight in their destruction, since they are creatures of God, but he delights in their just punishment, because they are God's enemies. And this is the very disposition of God himself, who takes no pleasure in the perdition of his creature and has compassion even on the reprobate who perish, yet without prejudice to his justice and just wrath. But he went out of their hand. That he fled was due to human weakness. But that, though he was alone and surrounded on every side by so many enemies conspiring to seize and kill him, he showed the admirable things of his divinity and power, this we have taught before. By such power, I say, which shone forth even in that infirmity of the flesh, his adversaries could be made more certain of what was in dispute, namely that he is God and the Son of God. For no one who was merely a man could have extricated himself from the hands of so many enemies. Therefore by this and such deeds the Lord shows that no one could take his life from him against his will, but that he lays it down at his own pleasure and takes it up again at his own discretion, as he himself said above in this chapter, verse 18.

units.la: Abiitque rursus. Cum Hierosolymis, vbi erat concursus totius populi & gloria Iudææ, non esset locus Christo, non tamen caruit loco in quem se reciperet & in quo maneret. Mansit in deserto, vbi ante eum manserat Iohannes Baptista. Dominus quantisper ipsi placet manere in his terris, cum expellitur ex vno loco, tamen non destituitur plane loco in quo manendum sit. Si celebres & magnificæ regiones ac vrbes vetera non patiantur cum apud se commorari, saltem desertæ regiones eum recipient. Nostra ista regio, si veniat in comparationem cum aliis plerisque regionibus, quid est aliud quàm desertum quoddam? placuit tamen Domino, plerisque aliis derelictis inter nos commorari. Quod si nos eum ingratitudine nostra reiecerimus, supersunt adhuc deserta loca in quæ, derelictis nobis, sese conferet, & in quibus sedem suam figet. Multi autem. Vt non caruit loco Dominus quo fugeret, & in quo commoraretur, ita non caruit Ecclesia cui annuntiaret Euangelium. Dominus enim priius ex lapidibus excitabit filios Abrahamo, quàm non verax erit in promissione sua facta Patribus, & non habebit Ecclesiam. Nam vbicunque locorum agit, & vbicunque placet ipsi erigere vexillum verbi sui, necesse est eo multos confluere: odorantur enim e longinquo homines Dominum, non secus atque aquilæ odorantur cadauer, vt Dominus ipse loquitur. Hoc etiam applicari potest ad Pastores Ecclesiæ, qui si semel vocati fuerint à Deo ad prædicationem Euangelij, profecto impossibile est eos plane destitui iis qui ipsos audiant: quod si alioqui nolent, alij tamen volent audire. Quare magis solliciti sint de certitudine vocationis suæ, quàm de iis qui ipsos
units.tr: And he went away again. Although at Jerusalem, where the whole people were gathered and the glory of Judea was, there was no place for Christ, he was not without a place to withdraw to and remain in. He stayed in the wilderness, where John the Baptist had stayed before him. While it pleases the Lord to remain on these lands, when he is driven out of one place he is not entirely left without a place in which to stay. If famous and magnificent regions and cities will not suffer him to dwell among them, the deserted regions will at least receive him. Our own region, when compared with many other regions, is little more than a kind of wilderness; yet it has pleased the Lord to dwell among us while passing over many others. But if we reject him through our ingratitude, there are still deserted places to which he will betake himself once we have been abandoned, and in which he will fix his seat. Many, however. Just as the Lord was not without a place to flee to and remain in, so the Church was not without people to whom he might proclaim the gospel. For the Lord will sooner raise up children to Abraham from the stones than fail to be true to his promise made to the Fathers, and he will not lack a Church. For wherever he works, and wherever it pleases him to raise the banner of his word, many necessarily flock together; for men scent the Lord from afar, just as eagles scent a carcass, as the Lord himself says. This may also be applied to the ministers of the Church: if they have once been called by God to preach the gospel, it is certainly impossible for them to be utterly left without those who will hear them. If some are unwilling otherwise, others will still be willing to hear. Therefore ministers ought to be more concerned about the certainty of their calling than about those who are to hear them.

units.la: Neque discipulis, quibus Euangelium annuntiatur. Matth. 24. 28. ipsos sunt audituri. Et dicebant. Hic est sermo eorum de Christo. Primum, praeferunt eum Iohani Baptistae: nam scipulorū, cum dicunt Iohannem nullum signum edidisse, simul innuunt Dominum, qui tot signa edat, Iohanne maiorem esse. Videri quidem potest hoc dictum cum cotemptu aliquo Iohannis Baptistae, & in ipsius aliquo opprobrium. Sed reipsa nihil ideo detrahitur, vel Iohanni Baptistae, vel prophetae alicui, vel cuiquam denique homini minum, quod excellat Dominus. Hoc agnouit ipse Baptista ubi conquerentibus discipulis ipsius, quod ipse prae Christo contemptus esset, respondit & dixit, Homo non potest recipere quidquam, nisi fuerit datum ei e caelo, &c. Ex quibus apparet eum lubenter cessisse Christo, & voluisse euanescere, ut Christi gloriae locus esset. Sed quod hoc non sit dictum in contemptum Iohannis Baptistae, verba quae sequuntur satis declarant: Quaecunque de isto dixit vera erant. Quibus verbis praedicant Iohannem verum esse testem Christi interea dum Christum Iohanni praeferunt. Quid aliud requirat Iohannes, aut quisquam omnium Prophetarum, aut quisquam denique pastorum, nisi hoc ut cohonestetur hoc nomine, quod verus testis Christi exiterit? Quae enim nostra in caelis gloria, nisi ea quae de nobis a Domino feretur sententia, quod veri fuerimus in terris testes ipsius? non poterit maior ista dari homini gloria, aut de eo quiddam maius praedicari. Et multi illic. Hoc est effectum Christi apud istos, nimirum credunt. Fundamenta fidei huius petenda sunt, primum ex iis quae ab ipsis dicta sunt de Christi potentia illa in edendis miraculis demonstrata, deinde ex eo quod quae de eo praedicta sunt ab Iohanne, omnia completa sunt. Haec sunt proculdubio fulcra fidei firmissima, potentia Christi quae sentimus ex verbo, ex operibus ipsius, etiam ex sermone crucis, qui iis qui seruantur est potentia Dei. Deinde harmonia illa & consensus inter praedicationes prophetarum & rerum praedictarum eventus. Nam nihil est de Christo praedictum, quod non factum sit ac euenerit suo tempore: nihil rursus eucnit nisi quod praedictum est. Omnia enim etiam quae leviora videri possent de Christo, ut partitio illa vestium, & sors iacta super tunicam ipsius, praedicta sunt a prophetis, adeo ut nihil desideraret possit quo excitetur & confirmetur in nobis fides in Christum Iesum: si nō ipsi nobis defuerimus. Huic sit omnis gloria, Amen.
units.tr: Nor to the disciples, to whom the gospel is announced (Matt. 24:28), who are to hear them. And they said: "This is what he said about Christ." First, they set him above John the Baptist: for in saying that John performed no sign, the disciples at the same time imply that the Lord, who performs so many signs, is greater than John. It may indeed seem that this was said with some contempt for John the Baptist, and as a kind of reproach to him. But in truth nothing is taken away from John the Baptist, or from any prophet, or indeed from any man, by the fact that the Lord excels. John the Baptist himself acknowledged this, when his disciples complained that he was despised in comparison with Christ; he answered and said, "A man cannot receive anything unless it has been given him from heaven," etc. From these words it appears that he gladly yielded to Christ and wished to fade away, so that there might be room for the glory of Christ. But that this was not said in contempt of John the Baptist, the words that follow make sufficiently clear: "Everything he said about this man was true." By these words they proclaim John to be a true witness of Christ, even while they set Christ above John. What else could John, or any of the prophets, or indeed any of the ministers, desire, except to be honoured by this title, that he has proved to be a true witness of Christ? For what glory is ours in heaven, except the verdict the Lord pronounces about us, that we have been true witnesses of him on earth? No greater glory can be given to a man, nor anything greater be said of him. And many believed there. This is the effect of Christ among them, namely that they believed. The foundations of this faith are to be sought, first, from what they themselves said about the power of Christ displayed in performing miracles, and then from the fact that all the things foretold of him by John have been fulfilled. These are without doubt the firmest supports of faith: the power of Christ, which we perceive from his word, from his works, and also from the message of the cross, which to those who are being saved is the power of God. Next, that harmony and agreement between the predictions of the prophets and the events of the things foretold. For nothing has been foretold of Christ that has not come to pass and happened in its time; and again, nothing has happened that was not foretold. For even those things that might seem minor concerning Christ, such as the division of his garments and the lot cast upon his tunic, were foretold by the prophets, so that nothing more could be desired by which faith in Christ Jesus might be stirred up and confirmed in us, if we ourselves do not fail. To him be all glory. Amen.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Hoc capite continetur historia Lazari à Christo excitati à morte. Primò autem occurrunt ea quae excitationem miraculosam antecesserunt ad versum usque 43. Secundò habetur excitatio ipsa miraculosa, verf. 43. & 44. Tertiò, eventus sine ea quae excitationem miraculosam consecuta sunt, ad finem capitis.
units.tr: This chapter contains the story of Lazarus, raised from death by Christ. First come the events that preceded the miraculous raising, down to verse 43. Second, the raising itself, verses 43 and 44. Third, the events that followed the miraculous raising, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAP. XI.

units.la: 1 AEgrotabat autem quidam nomine Lazarus, à Bethania, vico Mariæ & Marthæ sororum ipsius.
units.tr: 1 Now a certain man named Lazarus was sick, from Bethany, the village of Mary and Martha, his sisters.

units.la: 2 (Maria autem ea erat, quæ unxit Dominum unguento, & extersit pedes eius capillis suis, cuius frater Lazarus ægrotabat.)
units.tr: 2 (It was that Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, and whose brother Lazarus was sick.)

units.la: 3 Miserunt ergo sorores eius ad ipsum, dicentes, Domine ecce, quem amas ægrotat.
units.tr: 3 So his sisters sent to him, saying, Lord, behold, he whom you love is sick.

units.la: PRIMA pars capitis & prima occasio redeundi. Quidam nomine Lazarus ægrotabat. Tum is describitur ex loco illo in quo habitabat, Bethania; quæ rursus describitur ex duabus mulieribus sororibus Lazari, quæ ibi pariter degebant. Abiistis describitur locus, quia nomen earum celebre erat tunc temporis ob insignem ipsarum pietatem & Christi observantiam. Nota ex hac prima occasione eiectus fuit ex Iudæa Christus, sed statim post revocatur ægroti huius causa. Fieri quidem potest ut petulanter ad tempus in Christum insultemus ipsiusque expellamus, sed eo diu carere non possunt homines, adeo natura obnoxij sunt miseriis & & calamitatibus omnis generis: Solus autem & verus medicus, solus cōsolator est Iesus Christus. At quis eum accersit? Lazarus aegrotus accersit eū, accersunt eū sorores Lazari, quae cū eo iā prius consuetudine habuerunt, & viderunt illā gratiā, quae in ipso fuit. Non tantum qui miseri sunt accersunt Christum, neque tantum, qui miseriā suam ipsi sentiunt, sed etiam qui habent aliquem gustum gratiae illius quae est in ipso: Nemo, inquit, potest venire ad me, nisi quem Pater traxerit. Trahuntur autem non inuiti, sed sensu quasi longe suauissimo illius gratiae, quae in ipso residet. Maria autem. Inseritur descriptio quaedam Mariae, cuius meminit proximè, non tantum ut discernat eam ab aliis mulieribus, quae plures erant illo tempore eo nomine appellatae. Erant enim Maria Deipara, Maria Magdalena, Maria Cleopae uxor, Maria mater Iacobi minoris, Maria mater Iohannis Marci; denique Maria ista Marthae soror, de qua Lucae cap.10.39. Verum non ideo tantum, ut distinguat eam ab aliis eiusdem nominis, inseritur haec descriptio Mariae, sed ut commendetur mulier hoc erga Christum facto suo toti posteritati. Neque enim quisquam est qui insigniter diligit Christum in hac vita & dilectionem illam suam vel agendo, vel etiam patiendo declarauerit, qui non insignietur praeclaro aliquo nomine & posteritati commendabitur. Ob fidem, inquit Apostolus, maiores nostri testimonio ornati sunt, Abel testimonio iustitiae, Henoch testimonio quod placuisset Deo, &c. Nihil est quod aeque commendat hominem, & in vita hac, & post vitam hanc, quàm fides in Christum. De hoc autem Mariae facto, leges plura cap.12. quod sequitur. Neque enim existimo hoc quod hic narratur effectum fuisse, nisi post Lazarum excitatum ex mortuis. Leges etiam de hoc facto Matth.26.6. Et Marc.14.1. Quod quidem idem est reipsa, sed circumstantiis quibusdam aliud. Vnxit pedes, inquit Iohannes postea cap.12.3. Vnxisse videtur & caput & pedes, sed Iohannes duntaxat pedum meminit, ut videtur, ad facti maiorem commendationem. De vnguento leges cap.12.3. Quòd Maria accepta libra vnguenti Nardi liquidae multi pretij, vnxerit pedes Domini, &
units.tr: This is the first part of the chapter and the first occasion for Christ's return. A certain man named Lazarus was sick. He is described by the place where he lived, Bethany; and that place is in turn described by the two sisters of Lazarus who lived there with him. The sisters are described by name, because their name was famous at that time for their remarkable piety and their devotion to Christ. Note that Christ was driven out of Judea on this first occasion, but he is called back at once because of this sick man. People may indeed insult Christ wantonly for a time and drive him away, but they cannot do without him for long, so much are they by nature subject to miseries and calamities of every kind. The only true physician and the only comforter is Jesus Christ. Who summons him, then? Lazarus, who is sick, summons him; his sisters summon him, who had already been acquainted with him and had seen the grace that was in him. Not only those who are wretched summon Christ, nor only those who feel their misery, but also those who have some taste of that grace which is in him. No one, he says, can come to me unless the Father draws him. They are drawn, however, not unwillingly, but by a sense, as it were, of the most sweet grace that dwells in him. But Mary. A certain description of Mary is inserted, the one he mentioned just before, not only to distinguish her from the other women, who were many at that time bearing that name. For there were Mary the mother of God, Mary Magdalene, Mary the wife of Cleophas, Mary the mother of James the Less, Mary the mother of John Mark; and finally this Mary, the sister of Martha, of whom we read in Luke 10:39. But this description of Mary is not inserted only to distinguish her from others of the same name; it is also inserted so that this woman, by her deed toward Christ, may be commended to all posterity. For there is no one who loves Christ notably in this life and shows that love either by acting or even by suffering, who will not be marked with some distinguished name and commended to posterity. By faith, says the Apostle, our forefathers were commended by testimony: Abel by the testimony of righteousness, Enoch by the testimony that he pleased God, and so on. There is nothing that commends a man equally in this life and after this life as faith in Christ. You will read more about this deed of Mary in chapter 12, which follows. I do not think that what is narrated here was done before Lazarus was raised from the dead. You may also read about this deed in Matthew 26:6 and Mark 14:1. It is indeed the same deed in reality, but differs in certain circumstances. She anointed his feet, John says later in 12:3. She seems to have anointed both head and feet, but John, as it seems, mentions only the feet, for the greater commendation of the deed. About the ointment you may read in 12:3: that Mary, taking a pound of very costly liquid nard ointment, anointed the feet of the Lord and wiped them

units.la: Mariae sororis Lazari descriptio. postea eos exterserit capillis suis. Nota igitur, nō peper-cit sumptibus, emit libra vnguenti multi pretij, quod po-derabat & numerabat Iudas, vt postea videbimus
units.tr: Description of Mary, sister of Lazarus. afterwards with her hair. Note, then, that she spared no expense: she bought a pound of very costly ointment, which Judas weighed and reckoned, as we shall see later.

units.la: Vnguento hoc pretioso non cis-put modò, sed & pedes & imas corporis partes vnxit. Putabat enim pedes Domini magis pretiosos quàm quodnis vnguentum etiam pretiosissimum. Sed quid di-co non pepercisse eā sumptibus, ne sibi quidè pepercit: sed ornamentum illud capitis à natura datum, capillos suos adhibuit ad extergendos ipsius pedes. Putabat enim linteum quodcunque vel pretiosissimum vile esse prae pedibus Domini. vnde igitur extitit hoc factum? Necesse est illud profectum sit ab insigni aliquo animi asse-ctu. Necesse est effusum sit in Domini intereacor mu-lieres interius, dum vnguentum exterius effusum est in eum. Ergo ex insigni quadam dilectione Christi exstit hoc factum. Fuerunt enim & sunt nonnulli qui Christū effusè & propensè diligunt. Charitas Christi, inquit Apostolus, constringit nos, id est constrictos & occupatos tenet omnes sensus nostros: & quę causa? Quia hoc statuit, nos fuisse mortuos & eum pro nobis mortuum. Quisquis sentit primam mortem hæc quæ est in peccatis & ottensis: deinde liberationem illam quæ est per Christum, is mirum in modum diligit Christum, & obuiam quasi it tantæ charitati. Quid tum? Quare, inquit Apostolus, æquum est vt nos non amplius viuamus nobis, sed viuamus illi qui pro nobis mortuus est. Ita Maria hoc loco, ex tantæ dilectionis ipsius Christi sensu, eum vicissim dilexit, adeo vt illius causa non sumptibus modò, sed ne corpori quidem suo pepercerit; imò ne vitæ quidem, si ita opus fuisset, pepercisset. Verum Lucæ 7.37 &c. Legi-mus de singulari quodam amore mulieris cuiusdā pec-catricis quo Dominum est prosequuta. Superauit illa Mariam in eo quòd non modò vnguento, sed lachrymis etiam pedes Domini vnxerit: vna autem lachrymula ex corde contrito effusa, pluris est quàm omne vnguentum quantumuis pretiosum. Vnguentum enim quantumuis pretiosum reponunt Apothecarij, qui vocantur, in pixi-dibus suis terrenis. At Dominus omnem lachrymā quæ
units.tr: With this precious ointment she anointed not only the head but also the feet and the lowest parts of the body. For she thought the feet of the Lord more precious than any ointment, however costly. But why do I say that she spared no expense, when she did not even spare herself? She used that ornament of the head which nature gave her, her hair, to wipe his feet. For she thought any cloth, however costly, worthless compared with the feet of the Lord. Whence, then, did this deed arise? It must have come from some remarkable affection of the mind. It must have been poured out inwardly in the heart of the woman, while the ointment was poured out outwardly upon him. Therefore this deed came from a remarkable love of Christ. For there have been, and still are, some who love Christ abundantly and with all their hearts. The love of Christ, says the Apostle, constrains us, that is, it holds all our senses constrained and occupied; and why? Because it is established that we were dead, and that he died for us. Whoever perceives the first death, which is in sins and offences, and then that deliverance which is through Christ, loves Christ wonderfully and meets such love, as it were, halfway. What then? Wherefore, says the Apostle, it is right that we should no longer live to ourselves, but live to him who died for us. So Mary in this place, from her sense of the great love of Christ himself, loved him in return, so that for his sake she spared not only her money but not even her body; indeed, had it been necessary, she would not have spared even her life. But we read in Luke 7:37 etc. of the singular love of a certain sinful woman with which she followed the Lord. She surpassed Mary in this, that she anointed the feet of the Lord not only with ointment but also with tears; and a single tear poured out from a contrite heart is worth more than any ointment, however precious. For the so-called apothecaries keep even the most precious ointment in their earthly boxes. But the Lord keeps every tear

units.la: cx ex corde contrito promanat, in vtre suo reseruat. At quid mouit illam mulierem ad hoc vt sic faceret? Dilexit, inquit Dominus, multum. Quaobrem: quia multum ei remissum fuit. Cui autem multum remittitur, is multum diligit: cui vero paululum remittitur, paululum diligit. Habes itaque in his mulieribus insignis ac singularis cuiusdam erga Christum dilectionis exemplum. Sed de hac re postea erit agendum pluribus.
units.tr: that flows from a contrite heart in his own bottle. But what moved that woman to do this? She loved much, says the Lord. Why? Because much had been forgiven her. For the one to whom much is forgiven loves much; the one to whom little is forgiven loves little. You have therefore in these women an outstanding and singular example of love toward Christ. But more will have to be said about this matter later.

units.la: Miserunt ergo. Secunda occasio profectionis & reditus Christi in Iudaeam: Accersitur a Maria & sorore ipsius Martha. Summa legationis haec est, Domine, ecce is quem amas aegrotat. Non dicunt quidem, Ecce Lazarus aegrotat, sed, Ecce is quem amas aegrotat. Allegant enim pro argumento petitionis suae amorem illum Domini ipsius, quo Lazarum prosequutus est. Quasi dicant, Domine propter amorem illum quo Lazarum fratrem nostrum ipse prosequeris, veni, & fer opem. Non allegat quidem dilectionem illam qua Lazarus Dominum prosequutus est, procul dubio enim is Dominum vicissim dilexit. Neque sic loquuntur, Domine, ecce is, qui te amat, aegrotat. Causa est, quia fundamentum beneficiorum Dei erga nos non est dilectio nostra, neque quicquam quod in nobis est, quantumuis etiam regenitis, sed Dei ipsius gratuitus fauor ac misericordia.
