Quare fundamentum omnium petitionum nostrarum non oportet esse quicquam quod in nobis sit, sed id tantum quod in ipso Deo est, Dei ipsius gratia in Christo & misericordia. Fiducia enim nostra non consistit nisi in Dei ipsius dilectione quam firmam & immutabilem esse scimus. Quamobrem Paulus ex sensu illo dilectionis Dei in Christo clamat, Quis nos separabit a charitate Christi? Videndum autem diligenter, vt dum in medium proferimus charitate illam Dei inter precandum, serium ipsius sensum habeamus: quem si habuerimus, profecto non frustra effundemus preces nostras.
units.tr: So they sent. This is the second occasion for Christ's departure into Judea and his return: he is summoned by Mary and by her sister Martha. The sum of the message is this: Lord, behold, he whom you love is sick. They do not say, Behold, Lazarus is sick, but, Behold, he whom you love is sick. For they plead as the ground of their request that love of the Lord himself with which he regarded Lazarus. As if they said: Lord, because of that love with which you regard Lazarus, our brother, come and bring help. They do not allege the love with which Lazarus regarded the Lord, for without doubt he loved the Lord in return. Nor do they speak thus: Lord, behold, he who loves you is sick. The reason is that the foundation of God's benefits toward us is not our love, nor anything that is in us, however much we are even regenerate, but the free favour and mercy of God himself. Therefore the foundation of all our petitions ought not to be anything that is in us, but only that which is in God himself, the grace of God in Christ and his mercy. For our confidence rests on nothing except the love of God himself, which we know to be firm and unchangeable. Therefore Paul, from that sense of the love of God in Christ, cries out: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? But we must take care, while we bring that love of God into the midst in prayer, to have a serious sense of it; if we have that, surely our prayers will not be poured out in vain.

units.la: 4 Iesus autem hoc audito, dixit, Morbus iste non est immissus ad mortem, sed pro Dei gloria, vt per eum morbum glorificetur Filius Dei.
units.tr: 4 When Jesus heard this, he said, This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified through it.

units.la: 5 Diligebat autem Iesus Martham & sororem eius, & Lazarum.
units.tr: 5 Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister, and Lazarus.

units.la: 6 Vt ergo audiuit illum ægrotare, tum quidem mansit duos dies in eo loco vbi erat.
units.tr: 6 When therefore he heard that he was sick, he remained two days still in the place where he was.

units.la: 7 Deinde postea dixit discipulis, Eamus in Iudæam rursus.
units.tr: 7 Then after this he said to the disciples, Let us go into Judea again.

units.la: RESpondet Dominus, ac primùm quidem consolationem ministrat, deinde verò statuit ad Lazarum venire: Morbus, inquit, iste non est mortifer vel ad mortem. Mortem intelligit spiritualem & æternam. q.d. Morietur quidem Lazarus, sed non propter peccatum, sic vt mors ipsius sit futura peccati poena: verùm propter Dei gloriam quæ apparebit in eo ex mortuis excitando. Gloriam autem Dei definit quodammodo per glorificationem Filij. Quia vt Filius est splendor gloriæ eius, neque conspicitur gloria Patris nisi in facie Filij, ita non glorificatur Pater nisi in Filio suo. Nota igitur, nō semper immittit Dominus morbum alioqui lethalem, vt perdat ipsum hominem vel puniat peccatum. Ita supra de cæco illo loquutus est, Neque iste peccauit neque parentes eius vt cæcus nasceretur, sed oportet opera Dei manifesta fieri in eo. Immittit igitur suis morbos lethales ad suam ipsius gloriam, & ad ipsorum bonum, vt tandem glorificetur Dominus in resurrectione Lazari. Estque hoc discrimen inter lethalem morbum qui immittitur electis, & cum qui reprobis immittitur. Qui electis immittitur, non immittitur in eum finem vt ipsi perdantur, vel supplicium de peccatis ipsorum sumatur, satisfecit enim plenè pro iis omnibus Iesus Christus. Qui autem reprobis immittitur morbus lethalis, id eo fine fit vt perdantur ipsi & plectantur propter peccata sua in Dei iustitia, quia sunt illi extra Iesum Christum, eiusque iis mors hactenus temporaria nihil aliud quàm principium inferorum & mortis æternæ. Diligebat autem Nunc accingit se ad iter Dominus, & consilium capit abeundi ad Lazarum prout rogatus erat à sororibus ipsius. Causa autem cur paret se ad iter est quòd dilexerit Dominus duas sorores simul & fratrem. Ex quo nota, non temere sorores supra in petitione sua protulisse in medium dilectiolectionem qua Dominus profequutus est Lazarum, dicentes, Domine, ecce is quem amas aegrotat. Neque quisquam nostrum temere vnquam adducet pro fe dilectionem Dei. Demus nos operam vt eam penitus sentiamus & pro nobis adducamus, reliquum permittamus Deo: nunquam autem futurum est, vt frustra illud faciamus: imo vero non metuendum ne concipiamus vel praedicemus nimiam Dei erga nos charitatem. Neque enim capere potest animus noster immensam illam charitatem, qua nos in Christo prosequitur. Quare precatur Apostolus, vt Ephesij fundati ac radicati in hac Dei charitate valeant aflequi cum omnibus sanctis quae fit illa longitudo, latitudo, profunditas & sublimitas illius charitatis Dei, & valeant cognoscere charitatem illa Christi omni cognitione superiorem. Ecce superat captum nostrum dilectio Dei in Christo: Neque in concipiendo nimia charitate vnquam erramus, peccamus autem in eo, quod ne millesimam eius partem persentiscamus & animo concipiamus. Nota rursus, Deum cum rogatur a nobis & inuocatur ad nos adiuuandos, recusare non posse quin audiat nos & veniat ad nos suo tempore. Vsque-adeo mouetur prolata in medium illa dilectione qua nos prosequitur, vnde & nos debemus ei quantum per ipsius gratiam licet, has vices rependere, vt nos simus ei rogemur ab aliis, propter charitatem Dei audiamus eos, & opem miseris fratribus feramus. Nota denique hoc loco non tantum permotum esse Dominum dilectione qua Lazarum ipsum aegrotantem prosequutus est ad hoc vt veniret ad eum, sed praeterea permotum dilectione Mariae & Marthae, quae pariter precabantur eum vt veniret, & preces pro fratre suo fundebant. Ex quo dicimus bonum esse habere fratres huiusmodi aut sororas aut cognatos aut amicos, denique quoscunque qui pro nobis rogent Dominum, quóique Dominus ipse diligat: Quanquam enim diligat nosipsos Deus & mouecatur illa dilectione qua nos ipsos prosequitur, tamen non parum adiuuant nos preces fidelium. Atque haec, de causa cur accingat se ad iter, dicatq; discipulis suis, Eamus rursum in Iudaeam. Verum non statim abit, neque nisi post biduum elapsum abit, permittitque Lazarum c Dei con-
units.tr: The Lord answers, and first offers consolation, and then decides to go to Lazarus. This sickness, he says, is not deadly or unto death. By death he means spiritual and eternal death. As if to say: Lazarus will indeed die, but not on account of sin, so that his death would be the punishment of sin; rather, it will happen for the glory of God, which will appear in him when he is raised from the dead. He defines the glory of God in some measure through the glorification of the Son. For just as the Son is the brightness of his glory, and the glory of the Father is seen only in the face of the Son, so the Father is glorified only in his Son. Note, then, that the Lord does not always send a sickness that would otherwise be fatal, in order to destroy the man himself or to punish sin. So he spoke above of the blind man: Neither did this man sin, nor his parents, that he was born blind, but that the works of God should be made manifest in him. The Lord therefore sends his people deadly sicknesses for his own glory and for their good, so that in the resurrection of Lazarus the Lord may at last be glorified. And there is this difference between the deadly sickness that is sent to the elect and that which is sent to the reprobate. That which is sent to the elect is not sent with the aim that they should perish, or that punishment for their sins should be exacted from them, for Jesus Christ has fully satisfied for all of them. But the deadly sickness that is sent to the reprobate is sent for this end: that they themselves may perish and be punished in God's justice for their sins, because they are outside Jesus Christ, and for them that temporal death is nothing else than the beginning of hell and of eternal death. Now he loved: the Lord now prepares himself for the journey and resolves to go to Lazarus, as his sisters had asked him. The reason why he makes ready for the journey is that the Lord loved the two sisters and the brother together. From this note that the sisters did not rashly bring forward, in their petition, the love with which the Lord had embraced Lazarus, saying, Lord, behold, he whom you love is sick. Nor will any of us ever rashly bring forward the love of God on his own behalf. Let us take pains to feel it deeply and to bring it forward for ourselves, and leave the rest to God. It will never happen that we do this in vain; indeed, there is no need to fear that we may conceive or proclaim too great a love of God toward us. For our mind cannot grasp that immense love by which he embraces us in Christ. Therefore the Apostle prays that the Ephesians, being rooted and grounded in this love of God, may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, breadth, depth and height of that love of God, and may be able to know the love of Christ, which surpasses all knowledge. Behold, the love of God in Christ exceeds our grasp; we never err in conceiving too great a love, but we sin in that we do not feel and conceive even a thousandth part of it. Note again that when God is asked by us and called upon to help us, he cannot refuse to hear us and to come to us in his own time. So greatly is he moved by the love with which he embraces us, which has been brought forward; whence we also ought to repay this favour to him as far as his grace allows, so that when we are asked by others, for the love of God we hear them and bring help to our afflicted brethren. Finally, note in this place that the Lord was moved not only by the love with which he embraced Lazarus, the sick man, to come to him, but also by his love for Mary and Martha, who together were asking him to come and poured out their prayers for their brother. From this we say it is good to have such brothers or sisters or kinsmen or friends, indeed whoever pray to the Lord for us, since the Lord himself loves them. For although God loves us and is moved by the love with which he embraces us, yet the prayers of the faithful help us no little. And so much for the reason why he prepares himself for the journey and says to his disciples, Let us go again into Judea. Yet he does not go at once, nor does he go until two days have passed, and he allows Lazarus to die before he goes.

units.la: TT viuis prius discedere quàm abeat. Vt hoc scias amorem Dei non efficere vt ipse præueniat tempus illud quod præfixit nobis adiuuandis, ac proinde vt nos discamus non metiri dilectionem Domini mora illa sua & tarditate, vt nobis videtur, ad nos veniendi, sed cum patientia & precibus, semper sentientes interea & allegantes illius erga nos charitatem, expectemus. Ita enim visum est Domino exercere patientiam & explorare obedientiam & fidem nostram.
units.tr: Know this: the love of God does not cause him to anticipate the time he has appointed for helping us, and so we should learn not to measure the love of the Lord by that delay and slowness of his in coming to us, as it seems to us, but to wait with patience and prayers, always feeling and reckoning in the meantime his love toward us. For so it seemed good to the Lord, to exercise our patience, to test our obedience and our faith.

units.la: 8 Dicunt ei discipuli, Rabbi, modò studebant te Iudæi lapidare, Et rursum illuc abis?
units.tr: 8 The disciples say to him, Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?

units.la: 9 Respondit Iesus, Nonne duodecim sunt horæ diei? si quis ambulet interdiu, non impingit: quia lucem huius mundi videt.
units.tr: 9 Jesus answered, Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world.

units.la: 10 Si quis autem ambulet noctu, impingit: quia lux ei non adest.
units.tr: 10 But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.

units.la: Discipuli Christi laborant dissuadere ei reditum in Iudæam: prætendunt quidem magis quàm re ipsa cogitant curam ipsius Christi. Nam te ipsa magis moventur studio sui ipsorum: metuunt enim sibi ne eum sequentes incidant in vitæ discrimen, simulque cum eo lapidentur. Non aperte dicunt hoc, sed obscure significant. Pudet nos palam recusare crucem, sed nihil non prætexunt homines, quo eam subterfugiant. Rursus hic notabis, exemplo Christi, non tentari opus aliquod Dei gloriæ inserviens sine impedimentis, nõ solùm iniectis à diabolo & ab apertis inimicis, sed etiam ab iis qui nobis coniunctissimi sunt. Vide similiter impeditum Christum. Matth. 16. 22. 23. Nonne duodecim. Hæc verba fi accommodes ad Christum ipsum, hæc erit sententia apo doseos, q. d. Ego habeo diem mihi præscriptum à Patre, cuius singulæ horæ sunt numeratæ, tempus nimirum vocationis meæ, qua oportet me defungi in terra ad redemptionem hominum. Durante hoc spatio impossibile est me impingere. Necesse enim est absoluam munus mihi impositum. Similis locus fuit supra cap. 9. 4. Oportet me operari eius opera qui misit me donec dies est, &c. Sin accommodes hæc ad discipulos, quod magis fafaciendum videtur: nam animat eos ad se sequendum alioqui meticulosos; sin, inquam, accommodes ad discipulos, hæc erit sententia apodoseos: q.d.Iam dies est & quandiu habetis me vobiscum, habetis diem. Nam ego lux sum mundi, supra cap.9. Quare metanquam præeunte face, tutò ibitis, neque impingetis: me verò non præeunte necesse est vos non solum, sed & omnes impingant, & vt dictum est capite 9. Nox erit mediscedente, in qua qui non exultarunt in luce mei præsentis, impingent. Nota igitur: nos omnes non minùs nunc vocamurà Christo, quàm tunc tèporis Apostoli. Eamus, inquit nobis omnibus. Sed quoniam irum in cælos: hæc enim est vocatio nostri, & vita ista nostra nihil est re ipsa nisi peregrinatio. Verum difficilis est & ardua via, obsita spinis & tribulis, hoc est mille impedimentis milleque terroribus, adeo vt vix liceat nobis impunè pedem in quouis loco ponere. Quod remedium est nisi lucis illius? qua videamus vbi pedem figamus & audacter progredi animo. Sed quæ erit lux? non ista profectò mundi huius. Nam hac luce huius solis & huius lunæ multi sunt errores, & mundus perpetrat opera tenebrarum in ea, homicidia, adulteria, furta, &c. quæ plane via est quæ ducit ad interitum. Quæ igitur lux erit? non naturæ huius. Nascimur enim omnes cum aliqua luce naturæ, sed vix assulsit nobis, cùm euanescit & derelinquit nos in ipso limine. Qua igitur luce opus est? nempe luce illa mundi, qui Christus est. Ego, inquit sum lux mundi. Et sola est lux illa qua præeunte nobis non offendemus. At inquies, qui Christum sequuntur tamen impinguntur, & eum sequuti multi martyres de medio sublati sunt? Resp. Dum vocat nos Christus, vocat ad vitam æternam. Iam hæc mors temporanea sequentibus Christum nihil est aliud, quàm ianua qua cœlos ingredimur. Quare qui sequitur Christum, cùm moritur non tum sicitur impingere. Quod de morte dico, intelligo pariter omnibus in hac vita afflictionibus: nam omnia cooperantur in bonum iis qui diligunt Deum.
units.tr: The disciples of Christ labour to dissuade him from returning to Judea. They put it forward as a matter of concern for Christ himself, but in fact they are moved more by regard for themselves: for they fear that, following him, they may fall into peril of life and be stoned together with him. They do not say this openly, but signify it obscurely. Men are ashamed to refuse the cross openly, yet they will pretend anything to escape it. Here again you will note, from the example of Christ, that no work serving the glory of God is attempted without hindrances, not only those thrown in by the devil and by open enemies, but also those from men most closely joined to us. See Christ similarly hindered: Matt. 16. 22, 23. Are there not twelve hours? If you apply these words to Christ himself, the sense of the apodosis will be this, as if to say: I have a day prescribed to me by the Father, whose individual hours are numbered, namely the time of my calling, in which I must discharge in the earth what is needed for the redemption of men. While this span lasts, it is impossible for me to stumble, for I must finish the task laid upon me. A similar passage occurred above in chapter 9, verse 4: I must work the works of him who sent me, while it is day, etc. But if you apply these words to the disciples, which seems the better course, for it encourages them to follow him when otherwise they would be fearful, then the sense of the apodosis will be this: As if to say: Now it is day, and as long as you have me with you, you have the day. For I am the light of the world, as above in chapter 9. Therefore, walking as if by a going-before torch, you will go safely and will not stumble; but without me going before you, you must stumble, not only you but everyone, and, as was said in chapter 9, night will come when I depart, in which those who did not rejoice in the light of my presence will stumble. Note, then: we are all now called by Christ no less than the Apostles were at that time. Let us go, he says, to all of us. For he is calling us to go to heaven: this is our calling, and this life of ours is in truth nothing but a pilgrimage. But the way is difficult and steep, beset with thorns and thistles, that is, with a thousand hindrances and a thousand terrors, so that scarcely can we set a foot down anywhere with impunity. What is the remedy except that light, by which we may see where to plant our foot and boldly advance in mind? But what will that light be? Certainly not this light of the world. For in this light of this sun and this moon there are many errors, and the world commits in it the works of darkness: murders, adulteries, thefts, and so on, which is plainly the way that leads to destruction. What light then will it be? Not the light of nature. For we are all born with some light of nature, but it hardly shines upon us before it fades and leaves us on the very threshold. What light then is needed? Namely that light of the world, which is Christ. I am the light of the world, he says. And that light alone, going before us, will keep us from stumbling. But you will say: those who follow Christ are nevertheless made to stumble, and many martyrs who followed him have been taken out of the way? I answer: when Christ calls us, he calls us to eternal life. Now this temporal death, to those who follow Christ, is nothing other than the gate by which we enter heaven. Therefore he who follows Christ, when he dies, does not then stumble. What I say of death I understand equally of all the afflictions in this life, for all things work together for good to those who love God.

units.la: Hæc ait: & postea dixit eis, Lazarus amicus ille noster dormit: sed proficiscor, vt à somno excitem eum.
units.tr: He said these things, and afterwards he said to them, "Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep."

units.la: 12 Dixerunt ergo discipuli eius, Domine, si dormit, seruabitur.
units.tr: 12 Then said his disciples, "Lord, if he sleep, he shall do well."

units.la: 13 Hoc autem dixerat de ipsius morte: at illi putarunt eum de dormitione somni.
units.tr: 13 Howbeit Jesus spake of his death: but they thought that he had spoken of taking of rest in sleep.

units.la: 14 Tunc ergo Iesus dixit eis aperte, Lazarus mortuus est.
units.tr: 14 Then said Jesus unto them plainly, "Lazarus is dead."

units.la: 15 Et gaudeo propter vos (ut credatis) me illic non fuisse, sed eamus ad eum.
units.tr: 15 "And I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, to the intent ye may believe; nevertheless let us go unto him."

units.la: 16 Dixit autem Thomas, qui dicitur Didymus, condiscipulis, Eamus & nos, ut moriamur cum eo.
units.tr: 16 Then said Thomas, which is called Didymus, unto his fellow disciples, "Let us also go, that we may die with him."

units.la: POstea, inquit Iohannes, dixit eis de Lazaro mortuo. Nō statim, cùm iussit ire & sequi ipsum, caulam expositi. Ita exercet Deus fidem & patientiam nostram. Iubet nos oculis quasi clausis ipsum sequi, non tamen citra promissionem. Iussit Abrahamum ipsum sequi, sed terram non nominauit, Veni, inquit, in terram quam ego demonstrauero tibi, & faciam te in nomē magnum. Quòd si eum fuerimus sequuti, eique simpliciter confisi, tandem videbimus non sine causa, vel eum iussisse vt ipsum sequeremur, vel nos sequutos esse. Sed ponderanda sunt verba Domini. Lazarus, inquit, amicus noster. Non dicit nudè Lazarum mortuum, sed titulo amici eum insigniens dicit, Amicus noster dormit. q.d. Homo qui nos diligit, & quem nos vicissim diligimus, dormit. Deus ornat honorificis titulis suos amicos in hac vita, & honorificat mentionem facit eorum post hanc vitam. Loquitur autem de eo vt amico etiam nunc, etsi mortuus erat. Amicus Christi non moritur. Christi sumus amici in hac vita: amicitiae sumus eius post hanc vitam. Ex quo sequitur animi cum Christi nunquam intermori. Nam dixit Christus Deum non esse mortuorum, sed viuorum: hoc est mortuos non esse in foedere cum eo. Nam Deus est eorum quotquot in foedere sunt eius. Ita etiam non sunt mortui, qui in gratia & amicitia sunt cum Christo. Tertiò, notandum quòd eum vocet amicum pariter & discipulorum lorum suorum. Christus cum Ecclesia sua & membris Ecclesiæ singulis communes amicos & inimicos habet. Dixit Deus Abrahamo, Benedicam benedicentibus tibi, & maledicam maledicentibus tibi. q.d. Communes tecum amicos & inimicos sum habiturus. Tum hoc notandum quòd non dicat eum mortuum, sed molliori vocabulo vtatur, dicátque Lazarum dormire. Non fit tamen quia Hebræi mortem somni vocabulo indicarunt, sed voluit Dominus hac voce innuere mortem hanc primam non tam appellandam mortis nomine quàm somni vocabulo. Nam mortis nomen sonat interitum creaturæ. Significat igitur eum non interiisse, sed ad tempus conquiescere, & suaviter quasi dormire. Sic supra dixit morbum Lazari non esse ad mortem. Nota igitur, Mors hæc temporaria amicorum Christi, non tam mors dicenda est quàm suavis quidâ somnus, quia in Christo obdormierunt, hoc est illi per fidem insiti mortui sunt. Sed proficiscor. Vt mors amicorum Christi non est proprie mors, sed somnus dicenda,ita resurrectio ex mortuis, non est nisi expergefactio quædam ex somno. Ita Dauid loquitur: cum expergiscar, inquit, id est resurgam ex mortuis, satiabor imagine tua. Et in alio Psalmo scriptum est, Dominum mane quodam excitaturum suos, quasi mors nihil sit aliud, quàm quædam quasi requies, & resurrectio sit excitatio ex somno quæ fit matutino tempore, quo nimirum venturus est Dominus.
units.tr: Afterwards, says John, he told them about Lazarus, who was dead. He did not explain at once when he bade them go and follow him. So God exercises our faith and patience. He bids us follow him as if with our eyes closed, yet not without a promise. He bade Abraham follow him but did not name the land: "Go," he said, "into the land that I shall show thee, and I will make thee a great name." If we follow him and trust him simply, we shall in the end see that he either commanded us to follow him for a good reason or that we did so for a good reason. But the words of the Lord must be weighed. "Lazarus," he says, "our friend." He does not call Lazarus merely dead, but marks him with the title of friend and says, "Our friend sleepeth," as if to say: the man who loves us, and whom we love in return, sleeps. God adorns his friends in this life with honourable titles, and after this life he makes honourable mention of them. He speaks of Lazarus as a friend even now, though he was dead. The friend of Christ does not die. We are Christ's friends in this life; we are his friends after this life. From this it follows that souls never die with Christ. For Christ said that God is not the God of the dead but of the living; that is, the dead are not in covenant with him. For God is the God of all who are in his covenant. So those who are in grace and friendship with Christ are not dead. Thirdly, it should be noted that he calls him a friend, and likewise his disciples' friend. Christ has friends and enemies in common with his Church and with each of its members. God said to Abraham, "I will bless those who bless you, and curse those who curse you," as if to say: I shall have friends and enemies in common with you. Next, it should be noted that he does not say that Lazarus is dead but uses a gentler word and says that Lazarus sleeps. Yet this is not because the Hebrews signified death by the word sleep; rather the Lord wished by this word to hint that this first death is to be called not so much by the name of death as by the word sleep. For the name of death means the destruction of a creature. So it signifies that Lazarus had not perished, but was resting for a time, and as it were sleeping sweetly. So above he said that the sickness of Lazarus was not unto death. Note, then, that this temporary death of Christ's friends is to be called not so much death as a sweet sleep, because they fall asleep in Christ, that is, they who are grafted into him by faith are dead. "But I go." As the death of Christ's friends is not properly death but is to be called sleep, so the resurrection from the dead is nothing but a certain waking out of sleep. Thus David speaks: "When I awake," he says, that is, when I rise from the dead, "I shall be satisfied with thy likeness." And in another Psalm it is written that the Lord will awake his own at a certain morning, as if death were nothing but a kind of rest, and the resurrection an awakening out of sleep which takes place at morning time, when of course the Lord is to come.

units.la: Dixerunt ergo. Videntur quidem congratulari cū Domino, quod Lazarus convalesceret: sed paulò altior est conclusio. Ergo non opus est illuc eas: hanc conclusionē reticent, satis tamen intelligi poterit. Nam turpe est exprimere sepenumero quod cogitat animus adversus Dominum, & pudet afferre prætextus illos & effugia quæ excogitamus ad vitandam crucem. Difficile & perquam difficile est adducere nos ad nostri ipsorum abnegationem. Sane si sic aperte conclusissent discipuli ex cogitatis verbis Domini, nempe iis, quæ de somno Lazari dixit, captiosa fuisset conclusio & astuta, ac verba Domini detorsissent ad institutum. Sed ignoratio verborum Domini, quæ apparet ex versu sequenti eos ex parte excusat. Bene esset obstinatis istis Papistis qui tot
units.tr: "Then said they." They seem indeed to rejoice with the Lord that Lazarus was recovering; but their conclusion is a little deeper. "Therefore there is no need for us to go there." They keep this conclusion to themselves, yet it may be understood well enough. For it is shameful to express often what the mind thinks against the Lord, and we are ashamed to bring forward those pretexts and evasions which we devise to avoid the cross. It is hard, very hard, to bring ourselves to self-denial. Indeed, if the disciples had openly drawn such a conclusion from the words of the Lord, namely from what he had said about the sleep of Lazarus, the conclusion would have been captious and crafty, and they would have twisted the words of the Lord to their own purpose. But their ignorance of the Lord's words, which appears from the following verse, partly excuses them. It would be well for those obstinate Papists, who gather so many heretical conclusions from Scriptures twisted to their own purpose, if, I say, they understood nothing in Scripture.

units.la: Papistis ... hereticas conclusiones colligunt ex scripturis detortis ad institutum suum, si, inquam, illi nihil in scripturis intelligerent. Lazarus mortuus est. Dominus hoc ipso quod aperte iis loquitur exponitque sua verba, satis ostendit quàm tolerans sit suorum, & perferat infirmitates eorū, praesertim vero discipulorum suorum, quorum nō modo ignorantiam, sed nimium crucis metum perfert tam patienter: sed voluit discipulos suos reseruari ad miraculum & miraculosam conuersionem de qua Actor. 2. Insignis enim mutatio breui tempore in iis fuit. Primum enim cum caperetur Dominus dispersi sunt, & subterfugerunt crucem: at vero non multo post cum Christus ascendisset in caelos, capti ac caesi in concilio Iudaeorum gauisi sunt quòd digni habiti essent, qui pro nomine Iesu contumelia afficerentur. Et gaudeo propter vos. Obiici potuit ab iis adhuc quodammodo iter detrectantibus; Ad quid igitur postquam mortuus est abis ad eum? Si abeundum fuit, tempestiuè fuit abeundum. Huic occurrit Dominus, propter vos, inquit, hoc factum est, vt vos credatis. Dictum est supra pro gloria Dei hoc factum? Respondeo, ista inter se non pugnare: nam quae fecit vnquam Deus magnificè pro gloria sua, ea facta sunt quoque pro salute Ecclesiae. Huiusmodi erant omnia Christi miracula. Sed quaeri potest, Annò hoc durum videtur, quòd mortuus sit Lazarus in eum finem vt discipuli crederent? Videtur enim charè redempta illa discipulorum fides. Imò vilis est redemptio animae alicuius, quae fit per temporariam istam mortem. Nam Christus ipse morte sua quam pro nobis passus est, satis ostendit quàm charae sint animae nostrae. Quòd si profecto redimeretur anima vnius, morte aeterna alterius, tū quidem hoc graue videri posset: sed cùm is qui moritur recuperat vitam suam, & perdendo quasi vitam, inuenit eam, vt de Lazaro videbimus postea, profecto vili redimitur vita aeterna morte ista temporaria. Sed eamus. Hactenus sermo fuit cum discipulis, nunc ingreditur Dominus iter suum. Dixit ergo Thomas. Animat Thomas condiscipulos suos etiam ad mortem cum Domino perferendam, siquidem ita necesse sit. Thomas animosus est & promptus ad crucem, sed coactè, non sponte sua, vt verba satis docent. Subeunda autem est crux sponte ac voluntate nostra, alioqui nihil facimus. Gaudeo, inquit Apostolus, & gratulor omnibus si pro libamento super hostia sacrificioque fidei vestrae offerar. Atque hiipsi Apostoli post hoc tempus & Christi ascensionem, longè alio modo se cruci offerebant.
units.tr: ...the Papists gather so many heretical conclusions from Scriptures twisted to their own purpose; if, I say, they understood nothing in Scripture. "Lazarus is dead." By the very fact that he speaks plainly to them and explains his words, the Lord sufficiently shows how tolerant he is of his own, and how he bears with their weaknesses, especially those of his disciples, whose ignorance and excessive fear of the cross he endures so patiently. But he wished his disciples to be kept for the miracle and the wonderful conversion spoken of in Acts 2. For the change in them was remarkable and happened in a short time. At first, when the Lord was seized, they were scattered and fled from the cross; but not long after, when Christ had ascended into heaven, they were seized and beaten in the council of the Jews, and rejoiced that they were thought worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus. "And I am glad for your sakes." This could be objected by those who were still somewhat reluctant to go: "Why then, since he is dead, do you go to him? If we must go, we ought to have gone in good time." To this the Lord replies: "This has happened for your sakes, that you may believe." It was said above that this happened for the glory of God. Do these agree? I answer that they do not conflict; for whatever God has ever done magnificently for his own glory has also been done for the salvation of the Church. Such were all the miracles of Christ. But it may be asked: does it seem harsh that Lazarus died so that the disciples might believe? For that faith of the disciples seems to have been bought at a high price. Indeed, the redemption of a soul is cheap when it is effected through this temporary death. For Christ himself, by the death which he suffered for us, has sufficiently shown how dear our souls are. If indeed the soul of one man were redeemed by the eternal death of another, then this might seem grave; but since he who dies recovers his life, and by losing it, as it were, finds it, as we shall see later about Lazarus, certainly eternal life is bought cheaply by this temporary death. "But let us go." Hitherto the discourse was with the disciples; now the Lord begins his journey. "Then said Thomas." Thomas encourages his fellow disciples to endure death with the Lord also, if it must be so. Thomas is brave and ready for the cross, but under compulsion, not of his own accord, as the words sufficiently show. The cross, however, must be borne willingly and of our own accord, otherwise we accomplish nothing. "I rejoice," says the Apostle, "and congratulate you all, if I am offered upon the sacrifice and service of your faith." And these same apostles, after this time and Christ's ascension, offered themselves to the cross in a very different way.

units.la: 17 Venit ergo Iesus, & invenit eum quartum iam diem in monumento agere.
units.tr: 17 So when Jesus came, he found that he had lain in the grave four days already.

units.la: 18 Erat autem Bethania prope Hierosolymam ferè stadiis quindecim:
units.tr: 18 Now Bethany was near to Jerusalem, about fifteen furlongs off:

units.la: 19 Multique ex Iudaeis venerant ad Martham & Mariam, ut consolarentur eas de fratre suo.
units.tr: Many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother.

units.la: 20 Martha ergo ut audiit Iesum venire, occurrit ei: Maria verò domi sedebat.
units.tr: Martha therefore, when she heard that Jesus was coming, went to meet him; but Mary sat at home.

units.la: DOminus deuenit eò quò tendebat: verum ante miraculum editum narratur quaedam, quorum hoc est I. de spatio temporis quo in sepulchro iacebat conclusus Lazarus, eo nimirum fine, ut conspiciatur quanta sit potentia Domini in homine non modò mortuo, sed sepulto, neque id modò, sed iam putrescente excitando ex mortuis. In eo conspicitur eius potentia & efficacitas fortis roboris, quòd non modò putrescens cadauer excitet ex mortuis, sed in pulverem resolutum sit, ut nihil iam testet iudicio vel hominum vel Angelorum. Tantum id nobis videndum, ut quod ait Apostolus, obdormiamus in Christo, decumbamus in sepulchrum cum fide in admirabilem illam Dei potentiam. Erat autem. Hoc est secundum quod narratur ante miraculum aedi-tum. Conditio sororum Marthae & Mariae quae fuerit post mortuum iam fratrem. Erant autem sorores duae in moerore constitutae, multi Iudaeorum venerunt ad eas consolandi gratia: In causa fuit quia Bethania prope Hierosolymam erat. Ergo haec fuit conditio sororum; Erant in moerore positae. Neque enim damnant scripturae hunc affectum doloris, ut neque alios, quia naturales sunt. Deus autem naturae opifex est. Sed damnant scripturae excessum, corruptionem & ἀπάθειαν in affectibus. Vetat scriptura ne excedat luctus nostèr modum fidei & spei. Non prohibet omnino luctum, sed prohibet ne lugeant sicut caeteri, qui spem non habent: Atque ne excedant modum in luctu, Dominus opportunè suis consulit, mittitque ad eos qui ipsos consolentur. Consolationis rationem praescribit Apostolus eodem loco. Consolatur autem à spe resurrectionis. Credimus, inquit Ie-sum mortuum esse, &c. Deinde ne putarent mortuos postponendos in adventu Domini, neque tam citò occursuros Domino, quàm alios qui tum viui reperiuntur: huic occurrit, Nos, inquit, qui reliqui erimus, &c. tandem subjicit, Consolamini alij alios his sermonibus. Hic igitur finis erat cur multitudo Iudaeorum Bethaniam venerit: sed alium praeterea finem spectabat Dominus, ut frequentes interessent miraculo edendo, multi crederent, à multis ipse glorificaretur. Deus igitur cum nos aliquò proficiscimur, saepe aliud intuetur quàm nos. Nos itaque debemus parati esse in omnem eventum, &c nos Deo committere: hoc etiam videndum, ut quod nobis propositum habemus perpetuò bonum sit, quod contigisse video huic multitudini. Tum quidem melius erit nobiscum, & id quod praeter expectationem evenit nostro bono erit; id quod factum est istis, quorum multi credentes domum reuersi sunt. Martha ergo videtur non tum domi fuisse cùm de adventu Christi audiret: Nam ita Maria quoque de eo audiuisset, simulque in occursum Christi iuisset. Cur autem iuerit ei nondum vicum ingressò obuiam, conspicitur ex sequentibus eius cum Christo verbis, ut nimirum conquereretur de obitu fratris, & remedium, si fieri posset, inueniret. Maria autem sedebat domi in luctu, una cum iis qui ipsam consolabantur. Nam videtur acerbius tulisse fratris mortem quàm tulit eam sororis Martha. Quò magis pii, eò magis fere maestiores, cùm iustae occasiones se offerunt.
units.tr: The Lord came to the place where he was heading. But before the miracle is related, several things are told, the first of which concerns the length of time that Lazarus lay shut up in the tomb. The purpose, no doubt, is that we may see how great the Lord's power is, not only in a man who is dead, but in one who is buried, and not only buried but already decaying, when he raises him from the dead. In this we see his power and effectiveness of strong might, because he not only raises a decaying corpse from the dead, but one that has been reduced to dust, so that nothing remains to bear witness before the judgment of men or angels. We must see only this: that when the Apostle says we sleep in Christ, we lie down in the grave with faith in that wonderful power of God. But. This is according to what is related before the miracle is performed. The condition of the sisters Martha and Mary after their brother had already died. Two sisters were in mourning, and many of the Jews came to them to console them. The reason was that Bethany was near Jerusalem. So this was the condition of the sisters: they were in mourning. For the Scriptures do not condemn this feeling of grief, any more than they condemn others, since they are natural; and God is the author of nature. But the Scriptures condemn excess, corruption and apatheia [ἀπάθειαν] in the affections. Scripture forbids our mourning to exceed the measure of faith and hope. It does not forbid mourning altogether, but it forbids us to mourn as others do who have no hope. And so that they do not exceed the measure in mourning, the Lord opportunely provides for his own and sends to them those who may console them. The Apostle prescribes the manner of consolation in the same place. He consoles from the hope of resurrection: "We believe, he says, that Jesus has died," and so on. Then, lest they think that the dead will be put behind in the coming of the Lord, and will not meet the Lord as soon as those who are found alive at that time, he meets this concern: "We who remain, he says," and so on; and finally he adds, "Comfort one another with these words." This, then, was the reason why a great crowd of Jews came to Bethany; but the Lord had another purpose besides, namely that many might be present at the performing of the miracle, that many might believe, and that he might be glorified by many. So God, when we set out somewhere, often looks at something other than what we look at. We ought therefore to be prepared for every outcome, and to commit ourselves to God; this too must be seen, that what we have proposed to ourselves may always be good, as I see happened to this crowd. Then indeed it will be well with us, and what happens beyond our expectation will be for our good; as it was for those, many of whom returned home believing. Martha therefore seems not to have been at home when she heard of Christ's coming; for otherwise Mary too would have heard of it, and would have gone out together with her to meet Christ. Why she went out to meet him before entering the village is clear from her words to Christ that follow: namely, that she might complain of her brother's death, and find a remedy, if one could be found. Mary, however, sat at home in mourning, together with those who were consoling her. For she seems to have borne her brother's death more bitterly than Martha bore the death of her brother's sister. The more pious people are, the more they are usually saddened, when just occasions present themselves.

units.la: 21 Dixit autem Martha Iesu, Domine, si fuisses hic, frater meus non fuisset mortuus:
units.tr: 21 Martha therefore said to Jesus, Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.

units.la: 22 Sed & nunc scio fore ut quascunque petieris à Deo, det tibi.
units.tr: 22 But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, he will give you.

units.la: 23 Dixit 23 Dicit ei Iesus, Resurget frater tuus.
units.tr: 23 Jesus said 23 Jesus says to her, Your brother will rise again.

units.la: 24 Dicit ei Martha, Scio resurrecturum in resurrectione, vltimo illo die.
units.tr: 24 Martha says to him, I know that he will rise again in the resurrection, on the last day.

units.la: 25 Dixit ei Iesus, Ego sum resurrectio & vita; qui credit in me, etiamsi mortuus fuerit, vivet.
units.tr: 25 Jesus said to her, I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live.

units.la: 26 Et quisquis vivit & credit in me, non morietur in aeternum. Credis hoc?
units.tr: 26 And whoever lives and believes in me will never die for ever. Do you believe this?

units.la: 27 Ait illi, Etiam, Domine, ego credo te esse Christum illum filium illum Dei, qui in mundum venturus erat.
units.tr: 27 She said to him, Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world.

units.la: Statim queritur Martha in hunc sensum, Si hic fuisses non fuisset mortuus frater. Ergo cur non venisti tempestiue? Videtur adhuc impatienter ferre absentiam Domini, etiam mortuo iam ac sepulto fratre. Quàm difficulter ferimus voluntatem Domini, si quando quae nobis ingrata sunt accidant. At Martha postea cum videret excitatum fratrem, idque in Dei gloriam & vtilitatem multorum, in quibus fides vel tum primum ingignebatur, vel confirmabatur, tum, in quam, cum euentum tam gloriosum conspiceret, ei satisfactum est, ita vt si optioni eius datum fuisset, tractum rursus ageretur, nollet aliter fieri, noller interfuisse Dominum dum moreretur frater. Ita etiam nos, cum videbimus euentu eorum quae facit Dominus, quę pro tempore nobis ingrata & acerba videntur, tum quidem ea aliter euenisse nollemus, Deumque in euentis glorificabimus. In primis autem cum videbimus & sentiemus in nobis ipsi gloriosam illam corporum resurrectionem, tum quidem aequis animis feremus mortem tum nostram, tum eorum qui in hac vita nobis coniunctissimi fuerunt. Sed expendamus argumentum querelae. Si hic, inquit, fuisses, Laudabile illud est quod fidem habeat in Domino, mitas & firmitas quod is potuerit impedire ne frater obiret morte, quod etiam persuadeat sibi dilectum Domino fratrem, vt dilectum etsupra Iesus dilexit Mariam, Marthain & Lazarum. Laudabile, inquam, hoc est. Sed vnde illi haec inducia, quod non fuisset mortuus, si ipsi Dominus ad
units.tr: Martha at once complains to this effect: "If you had been here, my brother would not have died. Why then did you not come in time?" She still seems to bear impatiently the Lord's absence, even though her brother was already dead and buried. How hard we find it to bear the will of the Lord when things that are unwelcome to us happen! But afterwards, when Martha saw her brother raised, and that for the glory of God and the benefit of many, in whom faith was then first kindled or confirmed, and when she saw so glorious an outcome, she was satisfied, so that if she had been given the choice and the matter were to be replayed, she would not wish it done otherwise, would not wish the Lord had been absent while her brother was dying. So too we, when we see the outcome of the things the Lord does, which for the time seem unwelcome and bitter to us, will then indeed not wish them to have turned out otherwise, and we will glorify God in the outcomes. Above all, when we see and feel in ourselves that glorious resurrection of bodies, then indeed we will bear calmly both our own death and the death of those who have been closest to us in this life. But let us weigh the argument of her complaint. "If you had been here," she says, it is commendable that she has faith in the Lord, in his meekness and firmness, that he could have prevented her brother from dying; and that she persuaded herself that her brother was beloved of the Lord, as Jesus had loved Mary, Martha and Lazarus, beloved above the rest. This, I say, is commendable. But whence did she derive the assurance that he would not have died, if the Lord himself had been present?

units.la: Carnis ... volua ... oblu&atis effigies fuisset? Neque enim voculam aliquam habuit exore Domini de ea re. Hic igitur excedit limites fidei. Nam fides non extendit se vltra limites verbi: fides est ex auditu, auditus autem per verbum Dei. Bonum est credere Dominum potentem esse simul & amantem nostri. Neque vnquam satis concipere possumus magnitudinem potentiae & dilectionis eius. Charitas Christi, inquit Paulus, omni cogitatione superior est. Sed cum venit in ad particulares liberationes ex temporariis periculis, de quibus multas habemus promissiones & revelationem nullam, tum quidem credendum est Deum posse nos liberare, sed velle nos statim inde eximere, non est temere credendum. Tres apud Danielem cap.3. Adolescentes Schadrac, Mesfac & Abednego, cum apprehensis iis, Tyrannus obiiceret; Quis Deus eripere vos poterit e manu mea? Responderunt, Potest quidem Deus noster nos eripere, sive erepturus est, sive non. Hoc illi, q. d. Et eius sapientiae committamus velint annon. Et tenserunt quidem reipsa eum voluisse: ut videas quam bonum sit nos fidei & voluntati Dei totos committere. Tum quidem vel hanc praesentem vitam recuperavimus, vel certe longe meliorem. Sed & nunc. Correctio, qua se colligit & sperat in Domino adhuc emendari posse, quae facta sunt de fratre ipsius, nempe eum vitae restituere posse: Spe-rat autem hoc freta potentia Domini. Nam hoc piis familiare est sperare in rebus alioqui quae videtur desperatae. Atque spes ea ac fides impatientiae modum imponit, eamque mitigat. Dicit ei Iesus, Resurget. Nō tam spectat Dominus magnam illam infirmitatem fidei, qua quasi nube inuoluta erat mulieris fides, quàm spectat scintillam illam fidei, in media nube, quasi emicantem & scintillantem: Neque arundinem, ut dicitur, quassatam Mat. 12. 20 tam confringet, aut linum fumigans extinguet. Sed ea quantulamcunque mulieris fidem fouet ac nutrit suaui promissione resurrectionis ad vitam. Hoc enim vnicum solatium est aduersus mortem, & in morte, vel nostra, vel nobis coniunctorum, si cogitemus Dominum his vocibus nos affari, Resurges tu, resurget frater tuus, resurget in patri, &c. Verba autem haec videntur dicta esse a Domino, non tam de resurrectione ad vitam hanc, ad quam etiam
units.tr: ...if the Lord himself had been present? For he had not received any word from the Lord's mouth about this matter. Here, then, she goes beyond the limits of faith. For faith does not extend itself beyond the limits of the Word: "faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God." It is good to believe that the Lord is both powerful and loving toward us. And we can never sufficiently conceive the greatness of his power and love. The love of Christ, says Paul, is superior to all thought. But when it comes to particular deliverances from temporal dangers, about which we have many promises but no particular revelation, then indeed we must believe that God is able to deliver us, but that he is willing to release us from them at once, is not to be believed rashly. In Daniel chapter 3 there are three young men, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who, when they were seized, were challenged by the tyrant: "What god will be able to snatch you out of my hand?" They answered: "Our God is indeed able to deliver us, whether he will deliver us or not." That is, they meant: "And let us commit ourselves to his wisdom, whether he wills it or not." And they indeed showed in fact that they wanted him to do so: that you may see how good it is for us to commit ourselves wholly to the faith and will of God. Then indeed we either recover this present life, or certainly obtain a far better one. But even now. This is a correction, by which she collects herself and hopes in the Lord that something can yet be amended in what has been done about her brother, namely that he could be restored to life; and she hopes for this, relying on the power of the Lord. For it is characteristic of the godly to hope in things which otherwise seem desperate. And this hope and faith sets a limit to impatience, and softens it. Jesus says to her, "Your brother will rise again." The Lord does not so much regard the great weakness of her faith, by which the woman's faith was enveloped as by a cloud, as he regards that spark of faith, shining and glittering in the midst of the cloud. Nor will he, as it is said, break a bruised reed (Matt. 12:20) so utterly, or extinguish smoking flax. Rather, however small it is, he nourishes and sustains the woman's faith with the sweet promise of resurrection to life. For this is the only comfort against death, and in death, whether our own or of those joined to us, if we think of the Lord addressing us with these words: "You will rise, your brother will rise, your father will rise," and so on. These words, however, seem to have been spoken by the Lord not so much concerning the resurrection to this life, to which even Lazarus rose, as concerning the resurrection to that glorious life. For the Lord saw that the woman was too much fixed on this life, as if her brother's happiness lay in this life; and therefore he wishes to lift up her soul to a higher view of a better life. Thus a man...

units.la: Ephes.3.19. Rom.10.17. etiam resurrexit Lazarus quàm de resurrectione ad vitam illam gloriosam. Nam vidit Dominus mulierem nimiùm affixam huic vitæ, quasi felicitas fratris sit posita in hac vita: ideóque animam eius erigere vult ad altiorem intuitum vitæ melioris. Sic hominem illum paralyticum in primo congressu alloquutus est Remittuntur tibi, inquit, peccata tua. Domini oculus etiam ad cœlestia cœlestibus illis fixus: Ea sunt quæ primum promittit, quasi spiritualia & spiritualia sunt quæ primum offert. Quòd si alia vel promittat vel spiritualia det, ea promittit & dat, ut nos per ea & vitam trahit Christus. Meliora ac spiritualia, & credamus posse Dominum cœlestia dare, ut de paralytico illo dictum est. Ut autem sciatis, inquit, filium hominis habere potestatem remittendi peccata: Surge & tolle grabatum & ambula, dixit homini.
units.tr: Ephes.3.19. Rom.10.17. Lazarus also rose again, not so much for the resurrection to this life as for the resurrection to that glorious life. For the Lord saw that the woman was too fixed on this life, as if her brother's happiness lay in this life, and so he wants to lift up her soul to a higher view of a better life. So he addressed that paralytic at their first meeting: Your sins are forgiven you, he said, your sins. The Lord's eye is fixed on heavenly things even while he deals with them: he first promises what is spiritual, and what he first offers is spiritual. But if he promises other things or gives spiritual gifts, he promises and gives them so that through them Christ draws us to life. Let us believe that the Lord can give heavenly and better, spiritual things, as was said of that paralytic. "But that you may know," he said, "that the Son of Man has power to forgive sins: rise, take up your bed and walk," he said to the man.

units.la: Scio resurrecturum. Intellexit Dominum loquentem Lucas fidei de ultima resurrectione, & fidem in eam profitetur, interea tantum beneficium videtur eleuare, quia non statim accipit promissionem resurrectionis ad hanc vitam: magis enim sensit vitam istam quàm tum vixit quàm alteram illam & futuram. Ita nos omnes magis sentimus hanc vitam, & sapimus quæ ad eam spectant, quàm illam alteram & quæ ad ipsam pertinent. Ideóque leviora videntur nobis spiritualia & cœlestia, dum hic vivitur. At cùm plenè percipiemus illa, cùm videbimus resurrectionem illam gloriosam, tum retrospicientes ac reflectentes oculos ad hanc vitam quam nunc viuimus, videbitur ea nobis præ illa nihil esse. Speranda nunc est ea eius magnitudo, quàm nunc totam non possumus capere, eàque ipse sustinedi sumus. Dixit ei Iesus, Ego. Cōmoratur Dominus in hac resurrectione, & mulierem in ea instituit diligentius. Nam imprimis necessarium est, eam cognoscere, & in eam credere. Ergo vt cognoscat resurrectionem, primùm eam deducit ad fidem in se. Nam credere resurrectionem extra Christum phantasma est, cuiusmodi fuit tum Pharisaeorum, qui credebant resurrectionem, & tamen Christum reiiciebant. Idem dico de cæteris Dei in Christo beneficiis, vita æterna, remissione peccatorum quæ frustra creduntur extra Christum, per quem, & propter quem ea in nos conseruntur. Etiamsi mortuus. Hic est primus fructus fidei in Christum: etsi mortuus fuerit, spiritualiter nimirum (nam spiritualem mortem, spiritualem vitam hic potissimum spectat Dominus) Venit hora, inquit Dominus supra cap. 5. cum mortui audient vocem Filij Dei & qui audierint vivent: Et de se Apostolus, Vitam, inquit, quam nunc vivo in carne, vivo per fidem filij Dei qui dilexit me Ea est efficacia Christi qua non citius attingitur fide nostra, quam ex morte in vitam nos exsuscitet. Et quisquis vivit.
units.tr: I know that he will rise again. Martha understood that the Lord was speaking of the last resurrection, and she professes faith in it; yet she seems to pass over so great a benefit, because she does not at once accept the promise of resurrection to this life. For she felt more keenly this life, the life she then lived, than that other future life. So we all feel this life more, and savour the things that belong to it, than that other life and the things that pertain to it. Hence spiritual and heavenly things seem lighter to us while we live here. But when we fully perceive them, when we see that glorious resurrection, then, looking back and turning our eyes to this life which we now live, it will seem to us to be nothing in comparison. We must now hope for its greatness, which we cannot now grasp in full, and by which we are sustained. Jesus said to her, I am. The Lord dwells on this resurrection and instructs the woman in it more carefully. For first of all it is necessary that she know it and believe in it. So that she may know the resurrection, he first brings her to faith in himself. For to believe in the resurrection apart from Christ is an illusion, such as that of the Pharisees, who believed in the resurrection and yet rejected Christ. I say the same of the other benefits of God in Christ: eternal life and remission of sins are believed in vainly apart from Christ, through whom and on account of whom they are bestowed upon us. Even if he is dead. This is the first fruit of faith in Christ: even if he has died, that is, spiritually (for it is spiritual death and spiritual life that the Lord chiefly has in view here). The hour is coming, says the Lord above in chapter 5, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. And the Apostle speaks of himself: The life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me. Such is the efficacy of Christ, that our faith no sooner lays hold on him than he raises us from death to life. And whoever lives.

units.la: Hic alter est fructus fidei in Christum, quasi diceret, Qui iam vivens credit in Christum, vivet in aeternum. Non enim tantum vita est ex Christo, sed vitae continuatio; Ideo Apostolus Rom.6. Ex resurrectione Christi, deducit non vitam solum, sed vitam aeternam: Ut Christus ipse postquam resurrexit non iterum moritur, sed vivit in aeternum. Vide igitur, per fidem in Christum is qui mortuus est resurgit ad vitam. Deinde per eandem fidem qui vivit perpetuat vitam suam in aeternum. Sed qua vi sequuntur haec ex fide in Christum? Ego sum, inquit, resurrectio. Vi resurrectionis Christi, qui est primitiae obdormientium, ut vocat eum Apostolus 1. Corinth.15. Resurgimus ad vitam quotquot credimus in eius resurrectionem: Vi deinde vitae eius gloriosae, quam post resurrectionem vivit, nos qui perpetuo ante oculos habemus eius vitam, vivimus in aeternum. Tria in Christo nobis credenda sunt: Mors, & crux eius, Resurrectio eius ex morte, vita denique gloriosa postresurrectionem. Credendo in mortem morimur peccato, credendo in resurrectionem, resurgimus ad vitam, credendo in vitam illam Christi gloriosam permanemus in vita in aeternū. Etiamsi, inquit Apostolus, externus nester homo corrumpitur, tamen interne renovatur quotidie: 2. Cor.4. Et quamvis corpus morti obnoxium sit propter peccatum, tamen spiritus vita est propter iustitiam. Et ipsum illud corpus quod resolvitur, rursus colligetur, si spiritum Christi in nobis permanentem habemus. Cur autem Christi mors, resurrectio, vita tam efficaces sint in nobis, in causa est, quod Dominus spiritus est; ubi autem est Spiritus Domini, ibi tollitur velamen mortis & liberamur, atque nos intuentes, quia spiritus est, transformamur
units.tr: This is the second fruit of faith in Christ, as if he were saying: whoever, while still living, believes in Christ, will live for ever. For life comes from Christ not only as life, but as its continuance. Therefore the Apostle in Romans 6 draws from the resurrection of Christ not life only, but eternal life: just as Christ himself, after he rose, does not die again but lives for ever. See, then: through faith in Christ, he who was dead rises to life. Then, through the same faith, he who lives makes his life last for ever. But by what power do these things follow from faith in Christ? I am, he says, the resurrection. By the power of the resurrection of Christ, who is the firstfruits of those who sleep, as the Apostle calls him in 1 Corinthians 15, we rise to life, as many as believe in his resurrection. Then by the power of his glorious life, which he lives after the resurrection, we who keep his life constantly before our eyes live for ever. Three things must be believed about Christ: his death and cross; his resurrection from death; and finally his glorious life after the resurrection. By believing in his death we die to sin; by believing in the resurrection we rise to life; by believing in that glorious life of Christ we remain in life for ever. Even though, says the Apostle, our outward man is wasting away, yet our inward man is renewed day by day (2 Cor. 4). And although the body is subject to death because of sin, yet the spirit is life because of righteousness. And that very body which is dissolved will be gathered together again, if we have the Spirit of Christ dwelling in us. Why the death, resurrection and life of Christ are so effective in us is because the Lord is Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, the veil of death is taken away and we are set free, and beholding him, since he is Spirit, we are transformed.

units.la: Rom.8.11. 1. Corinth. 15.17-18. mamur in eandem imaginem ex gloria in gloriam.
units.tr: Rom.8.11. 1. Corinth. 15.17-18. transformed into the same image, from glory to glory.

units.la: Credis hoc? Vrget in specie mulieris fidem. Quoties promissiones in genere fiunt, eaeque sub conditione fidei, toties meminerimus a Deo nos vrgeri in specie singulos an credamus. Nam reipsa id facit ac vrget fidem, etsi nunc non expressa voce, vt tunc vrgebat Marthae fidem. Quare demus operam, vt ei respondeamus, quemadmodum Martha. Est enim ea suauis resonantia & quasi echo, dum Dominus dicit, Credisne? Nos autem respondemus, Credo. Requite faciem meam: requiro. Est enim haec efficax vocatio. Sed quid respondet? Credo, inquit, terre. Per velum carnis tum quidem humile (ita enim appellat illud Apost. ad Heb. cap. 10.) intuetur gloriam filii Dei, neque enim impedit velum illud quantumuis in speciem abiectum, etiam crucifixum: non enim prohibet oculum fidei quominus videat gloriam Dei in ignominiosa carne. Imo vero velum carnis nobis prodest intuentibus gloriam Dei, cuius alioqui tantus splendor est, vt eam intueri non sustineamus, nisi inducto quasi carnis velo. Sed notandum quod dicit, se credere in filium Dei. Qui venturus erat in mundum. Hoc nobis omnibus faciendum. Oportet enim credere in Christum non alium, sed eundem illum, qui praedictus fuit a Prophetis, & quem veteres expectabant venturum. Ideoque & illi referendi sunt ad praedicationes illas de Christo, quae conferendae sunt cum euentu, ad hoc vt & fides nostra in Christum confirmetur, & Deus in veritate promissionum suarum glorificetur: Amen.
units.tr: Do you believe this? He presses Martha's faith in a particular case. Whenever promises are made in general, and those under the condition of faith, let us remember that God presses each of us individually to ask whether we believe. For he does indeed do this, and presses faith, even though now not with an expressed voice, as he then pressed Martha's faith. So let us take pains to answer him as Martha did. For it is a sweet response, a kind of echo, when the Lord says, Do you believe? And we answer, I believe. Hear my face: I seek. For this is an effective calling. But what does she answer? I believe, she says, Lord. Through the veil of the flesh, humble as it then was (for so the Apostle calls it in Hebrews 10), she beholds the glory of the Son of God. For that veil does not hinder her, however lowly it appears and even crucified: it does not prevent the eye of faith from seeing the glory of God in the shameful flesh. Indeed the veil of the flesh helps us who look upon the glory of God, whose splendour is otherwise so great that we could not bear to look upon it unless the veil of flesh were, as it were, drawn over it. But note that she says she believes in the Son of God. Who was to come into the world. This must be done by all of us. For we must believe in Christ, not another, but the very one who was foretold by the Prophets and whom the ancients expected to come. Therefore they too must be referred to those predictions about Christ, which must be compared with the outcome, so that our faith in Christ may be confirmed, and God may be glorified in the truth of his promises. Amen.

units.la: 28 Et cum haec dixisset, abiit, & clam vocauit Mariam sororem suam, dicens, Praeceptor adest, & te vocat.
units.tr: 28 And when he had said this, he went away and secretly called Mary his sister, saying, The Master is here and calls you.

units.la: 29 Illa vt audiuit, surgit cito & venit ad eum.
units.tr: 29 As soon as she heard it, she rose quickly and came to him.

units.la: 30 (Nondum autem venerat Iesus in vicum: sed erat in eo loco, vbi occurrerat ei Martha.)
units.tr: 30 (Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was in the place where Martha had met him.)

units.la: 31 Iudei ergo qui domi erant cum ea, & consolabantur eam, labantur eam, quum vidissent Mariam cuísur-rexisse, & exisse sequuti sunt ea dicentes, Abit ad monumentum, vt illic fleat.
units.tr: 31 So the Jews who were in the house with her, comforting her, when they saw Mary rise quickly and go out, followed her, saying, She is going to the tomb to weep there.

units.la: NVnc docet qui fuerit Mariæ cum Christo congressus. Vocatur à Martha sorore & quidem clàm vocatur: Deus enim clàm secretos suos vocat ad se,& e-uocat è reliquo mundo. At quid agebat Maria? Lugebat non tantum (vt facilè credi potest de muliere tam pia) mortem fratris,sed & miseriam naturæ nostræ, quam in morte fratris tanquam in speculo intuebatur. Pij enim quoties vident mortem istam, toties recordantur lapsus nostri, & defectionis à Deo, & defectionem illam lugent. Ergo tum mæsta & lugens euocata est. Quos ineuenit Deus lugentes in hoc mundo & dolentes, sed dolentes secundum Deum, eos euocat ad gaudium, Beati, inquit, Christo qui lugent, nam ipsi consolationem recipient. Concedo quidem illud, in ipso mœrore ac dolore piorum plus gaudij inesse, & verae lætitiæ, quàm in risu huius mundi: Nam cum suspiriis inenarrabilibus coniunctum est gaudium ineffabile. At gaudium istud in hac vita impurum est. Tempus autem erit cum fruentur pij puro gaudio, & quo abstergentur omnes lachrymæ ab oculis eorum. Illa vt audiuit. Hæc est obedientia Mariæ: sed notandum quantopere festinet. Cùm efficax est Dei vocatio, dici non potest quàm cito sequuntur eam homines, alioqui occupati rebus istis mundanis quàm maximè seriis. Mathæus,cùm publicanus esset, sedebat ad telonium: Christus autem prætereiens, Sequere me, inquit: Ille autem relicto telonio statim Christum sequutus est. At cùm quis est in mœrore,tum mœror ipse stimulus quidam est virgétque vt sequatur Christum, nihilque suauius est ea voce, Venite ad me qui onerati & fatigati estis & inuenietis requiem animabus vestris. Præsertim si Christi præcessit gustus aliquis, & si gustauit quisquam benignus sit Dominus,id quod Mariæ, de qua loquimur contigisse certum est. Tum enim cum Paulo suspirat oneratus,cupiens immortalitatem illam inducere. Nondum autem. Designat obiter locum in quo erat Christus quo tempore vocaret Mariam. Nondum, inquit
units.tr: Now he teaches what Mary's meeting with Christ was like. She is called by her sister Martha, and indeed she is called secretly: for God calls his own secretly to himself and calls them out from the rest of the world. But what was Mary doing? She was mourning, not only (as is easily believed of such a pious woman) her brother's death, but also the misery of our nature, which she saw in her brother's death as in a mirror. For the godly, whenever they see that death, are reminded of our fall and our defection from God, and mourn that defection. So she was then sad and mourning when she was called. Those whom God finds mourning and grieving in this world, but grieving according to God, he calls to joy. Blessed, he says, are those who mourn in Christ, for they will receive comfort. I grant indeed that in the very sorrow and grief of the godly there is more joy and true gladness than in the laughter of this world: for an inexpressible joy is joined with unutterable sighs. But that joy is impure in this life. Yet a time will come when the godly will enjoy pure joy, and when all tears will be wiped from their eyes. As soon as she heard it. This is Mary's obedience, but note how quickly she hastens. When God's call is effective, it cannot be said how quickly men follow it, though otherwise they are occupied with worldly things, most serious indeed. Matthew, when he was a tax collector, was sitting at the tax booth; but Christ, passing by, said, Follow me. And he, leaving the tax booth at once, followed Christ. But when someone is in sorrow, the sorrow itself is a kind of goad and spurs him to follow Christ, and nothing is sweeter than that voice, Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and you will find rest for your souls. Especially if some taste of Christ has gone before, and if someone has tasted how kind the Lord is, which it is certain happened to Mary, of whom we speak. For then, burdened, he sighs with Paul, desiring to put on that immortality. Not yet, however. He briefly indicates the place where Christ was when he called Mary. Not yet, he says,

units.la: Matth.9.9 · Matth.11.28 · 1.Cor.5.4 · Ioan.20. quit, venerat in vicum, fortasse metuens sibi à persequutione Iudæorum, nam paulò ante voluerunt eum appre-hendere, vt supra cap. 10. vers. 39. Quando Domino res est cum ingrato populo, non statim ingreditur ad eum, sed foris quasi stans, euocat suos ad se quo lubet modo, siue ad hanc ipsam vitam alibi degendam, siue ad vitam illam alteram & beatam.
units.tr: ...went into the village, perhaps fearing persecution from the Jews, for shortly before this they had wanted to seize him, as above in chapter 10, verse 39. When the Lord has to deal with an ungrateful people, he does not go straight to them but stands, as it were, outside and calls his own to himself in whatever way he pleases, either to live elsewhere in this present life or to that other and blessed life.

units.la: Iudæi ergo. Illi ignari vocationis huius eam insequebantur. Non nouit mundus iste quónam abeant pij vo-cati & euocati ex mundo, à Domino suo. Existimabant Iudæi abiuisse eā ad sepulchrum fratris pro more, vt ibi deflerent eum, quærens scilicet incitamentum quoddam luctus; Quasi vero non satis sit inordinatus affectus nostræ naturæ, eiúsque satis magna sit intemperies, nisi prouocemus eum omnibus modis ad Deum irritandum. Verum veniunt Iudæi isti vnà cum Maria ad Christum, fidemque recipiunt ex inspecto miraculo, vt postea videbimus. Bene nobis est, cū in societate piorū degimus, præstat lugere cum piis, quàm ridere cū mundo. Nam qui participes fiunt luctus piorum, participes sient quoque gaudio eorum etiam inspecto. Notandum etiam est quomodo sunt Iudæi isti vocati ad Christum: præter expectationem suam ad eum accedunt, fidemque in eum consequuntur. Variis enim modis vocat suos Dominus; alios vocat ita, vt admoneat eos quò eant, quomodo nos vocamur hodierno die, quo nimirum dicitur, Venite ad Christum. Alios vocat de improuiso & ita regit secreta sua prouidentia, vt ad ipsum veniant; cùm tamen illi ipsi nihil minus cogitent, quàm Christum, quo modo vocata est ex Sichem Samaritana illa mulier ad Christum sedentem ad fontem Iacobi supra cap. 4. Sed qualiscunque demum sit vocatio, beati sunt qui ad Christum vocantur, eúmque aliqua ex parte apprehendunt in hac vita.
units.tr: The Jews therefore. They, ignorant of this calling, pursued her. This world does not know where the godly who are called and summoned out of the world go, to their Lord. The Jews thought she had gone to her brother's tomb according to custom, to weep for him there, seeking, of course, some stimulus to grief. As if the disordered affection of our nature were not strong enough, and its intemperance great enough, unless we provoked it in every way to anger against God! But these Jews come to Christ together with Mary and receive faith from the miracle they witnessed, as we shall see later. It is good for us, when we live in the company of the godly, to mourn with the godly rather than to laugh with the world. For those who share the grief of the godly will also share their joy, once they have seen it. We must also note how these Jews were called to Christ: they came to him beyond their own expectation and obtained faith in him. For the Lord calls his people in various ways. Some he calls in such a way that he shows them where to go, as we are called today, when it is said, Come to Christ. Others he calls unexpectedly, and by his secret providence so orders things that they come to him, although they themselves think of Christ least of all; so the Samaritan woman from Sychar was called to Christ, who was sitting by Jacob's well, as above in chapter 4. But whatever the manner of calling, blessed are those who are called to Christ and lay hold of him in some measure in this life.

units.la: Maria verò quum venisset eò vbi erat Iesus, visò eo, accidit ad eius pedes, dicens ei, Domine, si fuisses hic, non esset mortuus frater meus.
units.tr: Now when Mary came to the place where Jesus was, she saw him, fell at his feet and said to him, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died."

units.la: Iesus autem vt vidit eam flentem & Iudeos, qui vnà venerant cum ea flentes, infremuit spiritu, & turbauit seipsum.
units.tr: When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her weeping, he groaned in spirit and was troubled in himself.

units.la: 34 Et dixit, Vbi posuistis eum? Dicunt ei, Domine, veni & vide.
units.tr: 34 And he said, "Where have you laid him?" They say to him, "Lord, come and see."

units.la: 35 Lachrymatus est Iesus.
units.tr: 35 Jesus wept.

units.la: 36 Dixerunt ergo Iudaei, Ecce quomodo amabat eum!
units.tr: 36 So the Jews said, "See how he loved him!"

units.la: 37 Quidam autem ex ipsis dixerunt, Non poterat hic qui aperuit oculos caeci, facere vt & iste non moreretur?
units.tr: 37 But some of them said, "Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the blind, have kept this man from dying too?"

units.la: 38 Iesus ergo, rursum fremens apud semetipsum, venit ad monumentum. Erat autem spelunca, & lapis erat ei impositus.
units.tr: 38 Jesus therefore, groaning again within himself, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone had been laid against it.

units.la: COnuenit Maria Christum, viso eo accidit ei ad pedes priusquam loquatur aliquid: non ita ante eam Martha soror. Ex quo deprehenditur maiorem notitiam Christi & maiorem ex notitia reuerentiam fuisse Mariae quàm Marthae. Nam quo maior est notitia Domini, eò magis coram ipso humiliamur perpetuò. Praeterea magis deiecta fuit Maria quàm Martha soror, & in maiori luctu. Quo enim maior est dolor, & humiliatio animi, eorum maior est humiliatio & corporis & animi cùm coram Deo comparemus. Dicens ei, Domine, Ita alloquitur Dominum, vt ante eâ Martha soror. Laudanda est ista fides, vt anteà diximus, quae credit in Domini potentiam simul & dilectionem. Nunquam enim satis possumus eam pro magnitudine sua concipere aut eloqui. Sed unde, quaeso, illud constabat quòd si interfuisset, frater non fuisset mortuus? Nihil enim de Deo credendum est, nisi quod verbo eius revelatum habemus. Valeant bonae intentiones, valeant non scriptae traditiones, & caeteraque figmenta hominum. Iesus ergo. Fleuit Maria, fleuerunt Iudaei, qui vnà cum ipsa erant. Haec est illa naturalis & misericordia, qua moemur vel natura ipsa erga miseros. Affectus profecto inter caeteros impriimi laudabilis, & in quo referimus maximè ipsum Deum. Nam Deus charitas est, 1.Iohan.4.16. Hunc igitur affectum maximè oppugnat Satan, qui omnem misericordiam plane sibi excussit. Sed videdum nobis est vt affectus iste, quemadmodum & cæteri omnes sanctificentur. Sanctificantur autem & purgantur corda nostra affectúsque omnes per fidem.
units.tr: Mary met Christ; when she saw him she fell at his feet before she said anything. Martha her sister did not do so before him. From this it appears that Mary had greater knowledge of Christ, and that her reverence arising from that knowledge was greater than Martha's. For the greater our knowledge of the Lord, the more we are constantly humbled before him. Moreover, Mary was more cast down than her sister Martha, and in greater grief. For the greater the sorrow and humbling of the mind, the greater the humbling of both body and mind when we come before God. Lord: she addresses the Lord as Martha her sister did not. This faith deserves praise, as we said before, for it believes both in the Lord's power and in his love. For we can never sufficiently conceive or express it, in proportion to its greatness. But how, I ask, could she be sure that, had he been present, her brother would not have died? For we must believe nothing about God except what he has revealed to us in his Word. Let good intentions, unwritten traditions and the other inventions of men be gone. Jesus therefore. Mary wept, and the Jews who were with her wept. This is that natural compassion by which we are moved even by nature towards the wretched. It is certainly a praiseworthy affection among the rest, and one in which we chiefly reflect God himself. For God is love, 1 John 4:16. Satan, who has altogether cast off all mercy from himself, attacks this affection most of all. But we must take care that this affection, like all the others, be sanctified. Our hearts and all our affections are sanctified and purified through faith.

units.la: Prius igitur opus est sentiamus apud animos nostros misericordiam illam Dei in Christo Iesu, quàm verè misericordes in alios simus. Paulus Ephesios hortatur, vt sint benigni & misericordes, vt condonent alij aliis offensas suas. Sed quod exemplum misericordiæ ipsius proponit: Sicut, inquit, vobis condonavit Deus in Christo: quo significatur quod diximus, non commoueri vera misericordia, nisi eos qui priùs ipsi senserunt misericordiam illam Dei in Christo. Quòd cùm ita sit, profectò ista immunitis truculentia satis arguit complures nunquam, ne prioribus quidem labris gustasse misericordiam illam Domini in Christo Iesu.
units.tr: Therefore it is necessary first that we feel in our hearts that mercy of God in Christ Jesus, before we are truly merciful to others. Paul exhorts the Ephesians to be kind and merciful, forgiving one another their offences. But the example of mercy he sets before them is this: as God for Christ's sake forgave you. By this is signified what we have said, that true mercy is not stirred unless in those who have first themselves felt that mercy of God in Christ. Since this is so, that cruelty of the unmerciful surely proves that many have never tasted, even with their lips, that mercy of the Lord in Christ Jesus.

units.la: Infremuit Spiritu. Dominus intuitus communem luctum, & ipse vnà commouetur. Affectus sine dubio hic humanus est, sed purus, sanctúsque. Quanto autem affectu misericordiæ commotus est Christus vel hinc apparet, quòd non solùm imbutus fuit affectu humano, sed, vt loquitur author ad Hebræos, in omnibus tentatus fuerit similiter ac nos, excepto peccato. Idque in eum finem, vt disceret misereri. Neque id tantum, verùm in affectu illo humano fuit Deus, & misericordia illa Dei infinita, excitans quasi illum humanum affectum, eúmq; mouens ac gubernans. Nos ipsi in nobis experimur quantopere moueat affectum nostrum Spiritus illte Dei quem ad mensuram tantùm accepimus. Excitat enim in nobis suipiria inenarrabilia, excitat gaudium ineffabile; quanto igitur magis oportet Spiritum illum qui datus est in Christo, non ad mensuram commouere ipsius affectum? Sed quantus fuerit Christi effectus misericordiæ, præstat ex effecto suo discere. Sic enim dilexit mundum, vt pro eo mortuus sit. Et dixit, Vbi. Miseretur aliquì nostri Deus priusquam nos ipsi sentiamus miseriam nostram: nam ex gratia ipsius sensus est tam miseriæ quàm misericordiæ: Sed vbi nos dolentes miseriam nostram videt, dici non potest quantopere noftri misereatur,attingatúrq; ipse nostra miseria. Nã Spi- ritus ipsius est,qui,vt ait Apostolus,intercedit pro nobis gemi- tibus inenarrabilibus,& ipse nouit sensum spiritus sui,eóq; cómouetur.Vbi igitur videt nos sentire nostram ipsorū miseriam, ad ipsúmque supplices confugere, dici non potest quàm citò ad nos adiuuandos properet. Beati i- gitur,qui lugent, quemadmodum ipse dixit, nam con- solationem recipient. Lachrymatus est.Affectus iam erum pit,prius enim infremuit spiritu,nunc autem effundun- tur lachrymæ: Lachrymæ etiam,Dei filium decuerunt. Dixerunt ergo. His duobus versibus habemus iudicium Iudæorum de Christi lachrymis. Quidam,Ecce,inquiût, quo modo amabat eum. Rectè ex lachrymis coniecturam faciunt de amore:nam misericordia est ex amore: quos enim diligimus,eorum miseriæ commiseremur,& quo magis diligimus,eo maior est misericordia. Cùm igi- tur tanta fuerit Christi dilectio, tum Lazari tunc, tum etiam nunc suorum omnium; quantam dicemus esse misericordiam, qua prosequitur suos dum videt eos miseros? Quare rectè colligūt ex misericordia dilectio- nem Christi, de qua etiam supra.Christus,inquit Iohã- nes, diligebat Marthã, Mariam & Lazarum. Quidam autem.Hoc aliorum iudicium est,quo responderi videtur quodammodo superiori sententiæ: q.d.Si tantopere eum dilexit,cur non morti occurrit? Potuit enim is qui sanauit oculos cæci, eum in vita conseruare.
