Ecce me- tiuntur dilectionem Christi morte & afflictionibus: quasi verò Christus non sinat obire mortem, imò non ipse efficacia sua morte hac prima ac temporaria assi- ciat eos quos diligit,ob eas causas quas ipse nouit,nem- pe ob gloriam suam quæ coniuncta est perpetuò cum bono suorum.Quorsum igitur,dices,miseretur morien- tium vel mortuorum , si ipse agens sit & efficax in eorū morte?Vide quid efficiat hæc misericordia Lazaro,pro- sequitur eum donec resurgat, & è mortuis excitetur: prosequitur suos in morte vel mortuos misericordia Dei,donec ipsos excitet in illo die; vt taceam misericor- dia hac ita illis sanctificari mortem & sepulchrum, vt ex pœna peccati euadat ianua cæli.Laudandum hoc in iis præterea, quòd ex opere illo in sanando oculos cæci obobseruauerint eius potentiam, quòd possit liberare nos etsi de voluntate eius nihil statuamus, non tamen eò deueniunt, vt credant eum iam mortuum & sepultum Lazarii posse ex mortuis & sepulchro excitare. Ex quo vides, quàm difficilis semper extiterit fides in resurrectionem mortuorum; neque enim natura oculis tam videre possumus. Est, fateor, in natura ipsa quod persuasionem nostram adiuuet, cuiusmodi est illud seminis ne mortuo exemplum quod putrefit: deinde emittit herbam vel rum, quàm plantam, quod est apud Paulum 1. Corinth. 15. At verò difficilis, nisi fidei oculo non perfectè videtur resurrectio, praesertim verò illa gloria nostri ipsorum. Nam etiam reprobi coguntur agnoscere resurrectionem corporum cum terrore & tremore: at nunquam persuadent sibi, forent ipsi gloriosi ex mortuis resurgant. Iesus ergo rursus sepulchra fumens. Nempe ex aspecto, vt videtur, sepulchrorum nam vt suorum quo Christus induit se affectu misericordiae, ita iisdem rebus oculo Christus intuetur commotus est ad misericordiam quibus nos, sed nihil frustra ab illo fit: hoc enim quod sepulchrum Lazari intuitus infremuerit & misericordia motus fuerit, efficit vt Lazarus ex sepulchro excitaretur. Sic etiā sepulchra suorum nunc clementer intuetur quasi è cælo, illi suo tempore resurrecturi sunt, neque prius cessabit intueri, quàm eos excitauerit. Tū sequitur descriptio quaedam sepulchri his verbis, Erat autem spelunca, &c. hanc ego praeterco
units.tr: He groaned in spirit. The Lord, looking upon the common grief, is himself moved along with them. Here the affection is no doubt human, but pure and holy. How great was the affection of mercy with which Christ was moved may be seen from this: he was not only endowed with human feeling but, as the author to the Hebrews says, was tempted in all things as we are, without sin. And this was so that he might learn to show mercy. Nor is that all: God himself, and his infinite mercy, were in that human affection, as it were stirring up that human feeling, moving and governing it. We ourselves experience in ourselves how greatly the Spirit of God moves our affection, which we have received only in measure. For he stirs up in us unutterable sighs and inexpressible joy. How much more, then, must we suppose that the Spirit who was given in Christ does not move his affection only in measure? But how great Christ's effect of mercy was, it is better to learn from its effect. For God so loved the world that he gave himself up for it. And he said, Where? God shows mercy to some of us before we ourselves feel our misery; for both the sense of misery and of mercy come from his grace. But when he sees us grieving over our misery, it cannot be said how greatly he has mercy upon us and how deeply our misery touches him. For it is his Spirit, who, as the Apostle says, makes intercession for us with groanings that cannot be uttered, and he himself knows the mind of his own Spirit, and is moved by it. Therefore, when he sees us feeling our own misery and fleeing as suppliants to him, it cannot be said how quickly he hastens to help us. Blessed, then, are those who mourn, as he himself said, for they will receive comfort. He wept. The affection now breaks out; for before, he groaned in spirit, and now tears are poured out. Tears too became the Son of God. Therefore they said. In these two verses we have the judgement of the Jews on Christ's tears. Some say, See how he loved him! They rightly make a conjecture about his love from his tears, for mercy springs from love: for those whom we love we pity in their misery, and the more we love, the greater our mercy. Since then the love of Christ was so great, both towards Lazarus then and towards all his people now, how great must we say the mercy is with which he attends to his people when he sees them in misery? Therefore they rightly infer from mercy the love of Christ, of which also above: Christ, says John, loved Martha, Mary and Lazarus. But some of them. This is the judgement of others, which seems in some way to answer the previous opinion: as if to say, if he loved him so much, why did he not come to meet death? For he who healed the eyes of the blind could have kept him alive. Behold, they measure the love of Christ by death and afflictions, as if Christ did not allow death to come, or rather, by his own efficacy, subjects those whom he loves to this first and temporal death for reasons that he himself knows, namely for his own glory, which is always joined with the good of his people. Why then, you will say, does he have mercy on the dying or the dead, if he himself is active and effective in their death? See what this mercy does for Lazarus: it attends him until he rises and is raised from the dead. The mercy of God attends his people in death or when they are dead, until he raises them up on that day; not to mention that by this mercy death and the grave are so sanctified for them that they escape through the gate of heaven from the punishment of sin. It is also to be praised in them that from that work of healing the blind man's eyes they observed his power, that he is able to deliver us, even if we make no judgement about his will; yet they do not come to believe that he can raise Lazarus, already dead and buried, from the dead and the tomb. From this you see how difficult faith in the resurrection of the dead has always been; for by nature we cannot see it with our eyes. There is, I admit, something in nature that helps our persuasion, such as the example of the seed which, when it rots, sends up a blade or rather a plant, as Paul has it in 1 Corinthians 15. But the resurrection is seen only with difficulty, and not fully except with the eye of faith, especially that glory of our own. For even the reprobate are compelled to acknowledge the resurrection of the body with terror and trembling; but they never persuade themselves that they themselves will rise from the dead in glory. Jesus therefore, groaning again. Clearly he is moved by the sight of the tombs, as it seems. As Christ put on the affection of mercy for his own, so he looks upon the same things with the eye of mercy that we do; but nothing is done by him in vain. For that he groaned and was moved to mercy as he looked upon the tomb of Lazarus brings it about that Lazarus is raised from the grave. So too he now looks with compassion upon the graves of his people, as if from heaven; they are to rise at their own time, and he will not cease to look upon them until he has raised them up. Then follows a description of the tomb in these words, It was a cave, and so on; this I pass over.

units.la: 39 Ait Iesus, Tollite lapidem. Dicit ei Martha, soror eius qui mortuus fuerat, Domine, iam olet: quatuor enim diērumest.
units.tr: 39 Jesus said, Take ye away the stone. Martha, the sister of him that was dead, saith unto him, Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days.

units.la: 40 Dicit ei Iesus, Nonne dixi tibi, fore, si crederis, vt videas gloriam Dei?
units.tr: 40 Jesus saith unto her, Said I not unto thee, that, if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God?

units.la: 41 Sustulerunt ergo lapidem e loco vbi mortuus ille fuerat positus. Iesus autem sustulit sursum oculos, & dixit, Pater, gratias ago tibi quòd me audieris.
units.tr: 41 Then they took away the stone from the place where the dead was laid. And Jesus lifted up his eyes, and said, Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me.

units.la: 42 Ego verò sciebam me semper a te audiri: sed propter turbam circumstantem hoc dixi, vt credātne àte missum esse.
units.tr: 42 And I knew that thou hearest me always: but because of the people which stand by I said it, that they may believe that thou hast sent me.

units.la: 43 Et cùm hæc dixisset, clamauit voce magna, Lazare, adesdum foras.
units.tr: 43 And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth.

units.la: 44 Tum qui fuerat mortuus, prodiit pedes & manus vinctus fasciis; facies autem eius sudario erat obuincta: dicit eis Iesus, Soluite eum, & sinite abire.
units.tr: 44 And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go.

units.la: IN edendis miraculis Christus si quid seruile fuit faciendum, ipse ad id non admouere manum suam est solitus, vt supra vidimus in cõuertenda aqua in vinum cap. 2. Ita enim etiam in humilitate carnis retinuit maiestatem & dignitatem suam: potuit autem vel verbo admouisse lapidem hunc, sed voluit ipsos habere partes quoque suas in isto opere, & ministros quasi operis esse, vt manibus quodammodo contrectarent illud miraculum, neque videretur illud elusio aliqua, & fascinatio oculorum: opera Dei vsque adeo sunt tractabilia; nihil facit Christus in nobis etiam per Spiritum regenerationis, nisi quod sentiri & quodammodo contrectari potest. Dicit ei Martha. In exemplo Marthę videmus quàm arctè astricti sumus naturæ isti, ac naturæ ordini. Si quid consentiens sit naturæ, statim illi assentimur: si quid pugnet cum naturæ ordine, tantum abest vt id futurum credamus, vt etiam stultitiam idipsum putemus. Spiritualia enim ista, dicit Apostolus, quæ superant naturæ captum, videntur nobis stultitia. Quare oportet hos supra naturam & erigi & erectos sustineri, nam erecti sumel, nisi sustentemur perpetuò Dei manu, statim recidimus in terram istam, vt natura ipsa terreni sumus: id quod exemplo Marthæ discimus, quæ paulo ante professa est se credere, at nunc impedit quantum in se est infidelitate sua opus Christi. Nam vt de hoc quoq; aliquid admoneam, vt fide nostra promouemus quasi opus Dei, ita infidelitate ipsum impedimus. Non quòd detrahamus aliquid potentiæ diuinæ, sed quòd nos ipsos indignos faciamus, in quos Deus illam suam potentiam exerat. Dilata, inquit, os tuum & ego implebo illud bonis. Dicit ei Iesus, Nonne Reprehensio quædam est. Gloriam
units.tr: In performing his miracles, Christ was accustomed not to put his own hand to any menial task that had to be done, as we saw above in the changing of water into wine, chapter 2. In this way he kept his majesty and dignity even in the humility of the flesh. He could have moved this stone by a word alone, but he chose to let the others have their share in the work and to be, as it were, the ministers of the work, so that they might handle the miracle with their own hands, and it should not seem to be some illusion or trick of the eyes. The works of God are indeed so tangible: Christ does nothing in us, even through the Spirit of regeneration, that cannot be felt and in some sense handled. Martha says to him. In Martha's example we see how tightly we are bound to this nature of ours and to the order of nature. If something agrees with nature, we immediately assent to it; if something runs against the order of nature, we are so far from believing it will happen that we even think it foolishness. For the Apostle says that these spiritual things, which exceed the grasp of nature, seem to us folly. So we must be lifted above nature and, once lifted, be sustained, for once raised up, unless we are held up constantly by the hand of God, we fall straight back to that earth from which, by nature itself, we are made. We learn this from Martha's example: a little before she professed that she believed, but now she hinders, as far as she can by her unbelief, the work of Christ. For, to add something on this point as well: just as we advance the work of God by our faith, so we impede it by our unbelief. Not that we take anything away from the divine power, but that we make ourselves unworthy of having that power exerted upon us. Open thy mouth wide, he says, and I will fill it with good things. Jesus says to her, Did I not say that? There is a kind of rebuke here. By the glory of God he means that miraculous work, in which the power and glory of God shine forth.

units.la: Psal. 89. 11. fiam autem Dei intelligit opus illud miraculosum, in quo elucet potentia & gloria Dei. Vide hic, Martha, quæ prius professa est se credere, reprehenditur tamen quòd non credat, cùm iam ad rem ipsam ventum est. Facile quidem est profiteri fidem. Etiam pij & qui alioqui re-ipsa credunt, tamen cùm ad rem ventum est, fatiscunt, dum nimirum vident tot iniici impedimenta. Verbi gratia, Credimus nunc vitam æternam post mortem hanc: sed in ipsa morte & in agone, vbi incidunt tot vn-dequaque tentationes, quàm difficile est fidem retine-re? Tum opus est maximè huiusmodi admonitionibus & exhortationibus ad fidem. Sustulerunt ergo lapidem. Pro-cedit opus: nam etsi nos infidi sumus, tamen ille fidelis manet, & pugnat lenitate & clementia cum nostra in-gratitudine. Attollens sursum. Hic gestus est eius, antequam exordiatur preces & gratiarum actionem. Elevatione oculorum indicatur cordis elevatio: nam cor elevat oculum, & animus proprie est qui intuetur Deum: trahit tamen secum sensum corporis: quo significat non prius desiturum hunc Spiritum sanctum, quàm non oculum modò, sed totum corpus & totum hominem Deo præsentem sistat.
units.tr: Psal. 89. 11. Behold here, Martha, who previously professed that she believed, is nonetheless rebuked for not believing, now that the matter itself has come to the point. It is indeed easy to profess faith. Even the pious, and those who otherwise believe in fact, nevertheless falter when the matter comes to the test, since they plainly see so many obstacles thrown in their way. For example, we now believe in eternal life after this death; but in death itself and in the agony, when temptations rise on every side, how hard it is to keep hold of faith! Then there is great need for admonitions of this kind and exhortations to faith. They took away the stone. The work goes forward: for although we are faithless, he nevertheless remains faithful, and he contends with our ingratitude through gentleness and mercy. Lifting up his eyes. This is his gesture before he begins his prayers and thanksgiving. By the lifting of the eyes the lifting of the heart is indicated: for the heart lifts up the eye, and it is the mind that properly looks upon God; yet it carries with it the sense of the body, by which he signifies that this Spirit will not cease until he presents to God not only the eye but the whole body and the whole man.

units.la: Tum precatur, Pater, gratias ago tibi quòd audieris me. Hæc verba innuunt præcessisse petitionem aliquam, aliquo temporis intervallo. Quando igitur petiuit à Patre, vt hoc ipsi concederet? De manifesta petitione nihil legimus, neque affirmare audemus: hoc scimus Dominum semper secretò & apud animum suum in precibus versatum, & de suo & salute eorum meditatum. Etiam hoc tempore apparet eum priusquam in gratiarum actionem erupisset, cum Patre suo priuatim egisse, etiam eo ipso tempore quo infremuit Spiritu. Has autem secretas preces & meditationes insequuta est vox.
units.tr: Then he prays, Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me. These words imply that some petition had gone before, at some interval of time. When, then, did he ask the Father to grant him this? We read nothing of an open petition, and we dare not affirm one. This we know: the Lord was always engaged in prayer in secret and within his own mind, and was meditating on his own and their salvation. At this time too it appears that before he broke out into thanksgiving he had dealt privately with his Father, even at that very time when he was troubled in spirit. Upon these secret prayers and meditations the voice followed.

units.la: Quo discimus si precari velimus bene, oportere vt vox sequatur animi meditationem, & animus sit occupatus in Deo & cælestibus illis, priusquam os aperiatur ad eloquendum: hæc enim est ad preces apertas, & ad vocem præparatio: nam non præparato prius corde, & prophano adhuc manente animo, preces non sapiunt Deum, aut eius Spiritum sanctum. Quare sic viuere debemus in terris, vt interea simus municipes regni cælorum, hoc est, vt Paulus alibi ait, vt spectemus continuo non ea quæ cernuntur, sed ea quæ non cernuntur. Ego vero sciebam. Occupatio est. Putari enim potuit à circumstantibus nouum vel difficile id fuisse quòd à Patre sit exauditus, quòd gratias agat præsentibus iis, præter solitum fortassis. Huic igitur occurrit, Sciebam, inquit, me à te audiri semper, non nunc tantùm dum gratias ago. Dominus quocunque tempore gratiam aliquam petiit, ea obtinuit: cuius causa fuit (vt prætereamus hoc quod deitas habitet corpore raliter in humana natura, & maiestatem illam, quasi sibi domesticam habeat, adeo vt quocunque tepore quodcunque petierit id impetrarit:) conformitas voluntatis Christi etiam hominis cum voluntate Dei, vt nihil vnquam nisi quod Patri visum est petierit, adeo vt quo tempore in illa agonia totus attonitus fuit dixitque, aufer à me poculum hoc, continuò tamen eam vocem quasi correxerit, seque ad voluntatem patris sui conformarit, Verùm, inquiens, non vt ego volo, sed vt tu vis. Quòd si igitur Deus audiat petitionem nostram, qui tamen imperfecte regeniti sumus, in quibus caro pugnat aduersus Spiritum, & lex in membris rebellat legi mentis, hoc est, in quibus nunquam in hac vita est plena hæc conformitas. (Nouit enim quis sit sensus sui Spiritus qui pro nobis interpellat suspiriis inenarrabilibus) quanto magis audit illum, in cuius precibus summa est conformitas, & cuius perfectione tum nos ipsi, tum preces nostræ, noitraque omnia sanctificantur, & grata sunt in conspectu Dei? Sed propter turbam. Hic finis est apertæ significationis, q. d. Hoc dixi vt conspiciant hanc virtutem edendi huius miraculi ex cælo esse & exte: ac proinde me à te missum esse. Fieri enim non potest vt virtutem & gratiam huiusmodi accipiat aliquis, nisi à Deo sit missus. Gratia igitur arguit vocationem Dei. Gratiam autem Dei arguunt preces, & gratiarum actio. Qui ergo velit testari coram hominibus se gratiam à Deo accepisse, habeat ipsi gratiam etiam in publico, ipsumque in gratia sua palam glorificet.
units.tr: From this we learn that if we wish to pray well, the voice must follow the meditation of the mind, and the mind must be occupied in God and in those heavenly things, before the mouth is opened to speak. For this is the preparation for open prayer and for the voice: for if the heart is not first prepared, and the mind still remains profane, prayers do not savour of God or of his Holy Spirit. Therefore we ought so to live on earth that meanwhile we are citizens of the kingdom of heaven; that is, as Paul says elsewhere, that we should continually look not on the things which are seen, but on the things which are not seen. But I knew. This is an occupatio. For the bystanders might have thought that it was something new or unusual that he was heard by the Father, that he gave thanks in the presence of these people, perhaps beyond his usual custom. To this he therefore replies: I knew, he says, that I was always heard by thee, not only now while I give thanks. The Lord, whenever he asked for any grace, obtained it. The cause of this was (to pass over the fact that the deity dwells bodily in human nature, and possesses that majesty as if it were its own, so that at whatever time he asked for whatever, he obtained it) the conformity of the will of Christ, even as man, with the will of God, so that he never asked for anything except what seemed good to the Father. So much so that when, in that agony, he was wholly stricken with fear and said, Take this cup from me, nevertheless at once he corrected, as it were, that utterance, and conformed himself to the will of his Father, saying, Nevertheless, not as I will, but as thou wilt. If then God hears our petition, though we are only imperfectly regenerate, in whom the flesh fights against the Spirit and the law in our members rebels against the law of the mind, that is, in whom this conformity is never complete in this life (for he who intercedes for us with groanings which cannot be uttered knows what the mind of his Spirit is), how much more does he hear him in whose prayers the conformity is perfect, and by whose perfection both we ourselves, and our prayers, and all that is ours are sanctified and acceptable in the sight of God? But because of the people. Here ends the plain meaning, as if he said: I said this so that they may see that the power of performing this miracle is from heaven and from outside, and therefore that I was sent by thee. For no one can receive such power and grace unless he has been sent by God. Grace therefore proves the calling of God. Now prayers and thanksgiving prove the grace of God. Therefore whoever wishes to bear witness before men that he has received grace from God should have that grace also in public, and openly glorify him for his grace.

units.la: Et cùm hæc dixisset. Hactenus gratiarum actio fuit, sequitur nunc ipsum opus & miraculum. Clamauit igitur voce
units.tr: And when he had said these things: so far there has been thanksgiving; now follows the work itself and the miracle. He cried out, therefore, with a voice

units.la: Cur Christus semper exauditus fuerit a Patre. Ratio, à minori ad maius. Petitionis apertæ significationis. Altera capitis pars. voce magna.Non quidem quòd virtus sit in voce, vel magna, vel submissa: sed verba Domini erant Spiritus & vita, & Petrus dixit Domino, Verba vitæ æternæ habes, supra cap.6. Cùm tamen voluit Dominus efficax esse in hominibus, vsus est altiori voce, vt supra cap. 7. in vltimo die magni festi clamauit: Si quis sitit, veniat ad me & bibat. Ita in vltimo illo die, Dominus venturus est cum voce exhortationis, voce Archangeli, & cum tuba Dei.
units.tr: Why Christ was always heard by the Father. The argument is from the less to the greater. Of a petition with a clear meaning. The second part of the chapter. With a loud voice. Not that power lies in the voice, whether loud or soft; but the words of the Lord were spirit and life, and Peter said to the Lord, You have the words of eternal life, above in chapter 6. Yet when the Lord willed to be effective among men, he used a louder voice, as above in chapter 7, where on the last day of the great feast he cried out, If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. So on that last day the Lord will come with the voice of exhortation, the voice of the archangel, and the trumpet of God.

units.la: Notandum etiam, quòd eum non tangat manu, non inspiret illi animam, neque etiam quòd iubeat surgere, sed quòd statim requirat ab eo functione vitæ, iubeatque exire foras. Hoc arguit potentiam eius, qui vocat ea quæ non sunt, tanquam sint, qui requirit à mortuis actiones viuentium. In causa est, quòd Dei vocatio sit efficax ad vitam ad existentiam rei vocatæ tribuendam. Quod cùm ita sit, laborandum est, vt hanc vocationis Dei efficaciam in nobis sentiamus, dum requirit à nobis fidem & opera sanctificationis, ad quæ non minus natura inepti sumus, quàm qui naturaliter mortui sunt ad actiones vitales & naturales. Tum qui fuerat. Hoc effectum est efficacis vocationis Dei. Ostendit autem verba Christi vitam esse & Spiritum, & Christum ipsum met vitam esse. Nam nemo habet verba vitæ, nisi qui vita est. Ego sum, inquit, resurrectio & vita, sup. vers. 25. & cap. 5. Dedit filio Pater vitam in semetipso habere. Hoc etiam effecto arguitur ab eo esse vitam istam naturalem: A quo enim est vita illa Spiritualis, ab eo pariter est vita naturalis, vtpote inferior ac deterior, cū vel scintilla aliqua vna vitæ Dei, præstantior est tota vita hominis. Resurrectio autem ista Lazari est quasi præludium ad resurrectionem illam futuram, & in ea quasi initium illius potentiæ ostendit, quam totam profundet in gloriosa illa resurrectione non tam ad vitam naturalem in coniunctione ista corporis & animi positam, quàm ad vitam spiritualem. Seminatur enim, ait Apostolus, corpus animale, excitatur spirituale. Formam exponit qua resurrexit Lazarus. Manus & pedes. Potuit Dominus vel verbo dissoluisse illa vincula, sed voluit astantes Iudæos manibus quasi tractare miraculum, cùm iuberet eos vincula illa dissoluere, vt supra iussit manibus amouere la-
units.tr: It is also to be noted that he does not touch him with his hand, does not breathe life into him, nor even bid him rise, but straightway demands of him the functions of life and orders him to come out. This shows his power, who calls those things which are not as though they were, and who demands the actions of the living from the dead. The cause is that God's call is effective to bestow life and existence on the thing called. Since this is so, we must labour to feel this effective call of God in ourselves, while he requires of us faith and the works of sanctification, to which we are no less unfit by nature than those who are naturally dead are unfit for vital and natural actions. Then he who had been dead came out. This is the effect of God's effective call. It also shows that the words of Christ are life and spirit, and that Christ himself is life. For no one has the words of life unless he is life himself. I am the resurrection and the life, above at verse 25; and in chapter 5, The Father has given to the Son to have life in himself. From this effect it is also shown that this natural life is from him: for from whom comes that spiritual life, from him equally comes natural life, as something inferior and lesser, since even a single spark of the life of God is more excellent than the whole life of man. Moreover, this resurrection of Lazarus is as it were a prelude to that future resurrection, and in it he shows as it were the beginning of that power which he will display in full in that glorious resurrection, not so much for natural life, which consists in the union of body and soul, as for spiritual life. For it is sown a natural body, says the Apostle, it is raised a spiritual body. He sets out the manner in which Lazarus rose. Hands and feet. The Lord could have loosed those bonds by a word, but he willed, as it were, to handle the miracle with the hands of the bystanding Jews, when he bade them loose those bonds, just as above he bade them remove with their hands the stone laid on the tomb.

units.la: {1} 1. Cor. 15. 44 pidem sepulchro impositum.
units.tr: {1} 1. Cor. 15. 44 the stone laid upon the sepulchre.

units.la: 45 Multi ergo ex Iudæis qui venerant ad Mariam, & conspexerant quæ fecerat Iesus, crediderunt in eum.
units.tr: 45 Many therefore of the Jews who had come to Mary, and had seen what Jesus did, believed in him.

units.la: 46 Quidam autem ex eis abierunt ad Pharisæos, & dixerunt eis quæ fecerat Iesus.
units.tr: 46 Some of them, however, went away to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.

units.la: Hic effectus est ex miraculo alius atque alius in aliis atque aliis adstantibus. Nam per eum idque miraculū alio atque alio modo operatur in aliis atque aliis,& secreta sua potentia non minus, adeóque magis efficax est in iis quàm fuit in corpore Lazari excitando. Dum enim Lazarum excitat ad hanc vitam, multos ex Iudæis præparat ad vitam spiritualē. Multos etiā eodem miraculo indurat, sua ipsorum culpa ac malitia,& iudicium exercet de quo supra cap. 9. Ego veni in hunc mundum ad exercendum iudicium, & ut qui vident caeci fiant, & qui non vident, videant. Huiusmodi sunt tum verba, tum facta Christi, quae exterius operatur in mundo. Non enim cū loquitur Christus, vel cum opdratur exterius, ita non modo, sed interea, & per ea interius operatur, vel hoc, vel illo modo in cordibus suis. Quare nunquam otiosi spectatores & auditores operum & verborum Christi esse debemus. Verum demus opera, ut per externa tanquam instrumenta sentiamus internam efficaciam ad conversionem & vitam aeternam. Caveamus autem omnibus modis ne sentiamus nobis animum indurari ad illa, alterum enim horum necessarium est.
units.tr: This effect of the miracle is different in different bystanders, and different in different ways. For through him, and through that same miracle, he works in different ways in different people, and by his secret power no less, and indeed more effectively, in them than he did in the body of Lazarus when he raised it. For while he raises Lazarus to this life, he prepares many of the Jews for spiritual life. Yet by the same miracle he also hardens many, through their own fault and malice, and exercises that judgement of which he speaks above in chapter 9: I came into this world for judgement, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind. Such are the words and deeds of Christ, which he works outwardly in the world. For when Christ speaks, or when he works outwardly, he does not work only outwardly, but at the same time and through these things he works inwardly in their hearts, in this way or that. Therefore we must never be idle spectators and hearers of the works and words of Christ. Rather, let us take the works, so that through external things, as through instruments, we may perceive the inward efficacy towards conversion and eternal life. But let us by all means take care that we do not perceive our minds hardened against them, for one of these two must happen.

units.la: 47 Et congregati sunt summi sacerdotes & Pharisæi, ac dicebant, Quid faciemus? Nam hic homo multa signa edit.
units.tr: 47 Then the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered a council and said, What shall we do? For this man performs many signs.

units.la: 48 Si omittimus eum ita, omnes ei credent: venientque Romani, & delebunt tum locum nostrum, tum gentem.
units.tr: 48 If we let him alone like this, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and destroy both our place and our nation.

units.la: 49 Unus autem ex ipsis Caiaphas, Pontifex maximus anni illius, dixit eis, Vos nihil scitis:
units.tr: 49 But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, You know nothing at all,

units.la: 50 Nec cogitatis conducere nobis, ut unus homo moriamoriatur pro populo, & tota gens non pereat.
units.tr: 50 nor do you consider that it is expedient for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish.

units.la: 51 Hoc autem ex semetipso non dixit: sed cùm esset Pontifex maximus anni illius, prophetauit fore, vt Iesus pro gente moreretur:
units.tr: 51 Now he did not say this of himself; but being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was to die for the nation,

units.la: 52 Nec tantùm pro ea gente, sed vt etiam filios Dei dispersos cogeret in vnum.
units.tr: 52 and not for that nation only, but that he might also gather together into one the scattered children of God.

units.la: 53 Ab illo ergo die consultabant vnà vt trucidarent eum.
units.tr: 53 From that day therefore they took counsel together to put him to death.

units.la: Concilium cogitur aduersus Christum. Coeunt autem primarij sacerdotes & Pharisæi, legis vindices. Institutio diuina erat de vno Pontifice, qui ad vitam fungi solebat illo munere. Verum in hoc, vt in aliis, violata est institutio ac ordinatio Dei, ac multos pontifices simul creauerunt, qui tamen quotannis vicissim in officio essent. Hoc autem anno fungebatur officio Caiaphas. Conuocarunt igitur concilium solenne, quod Sanhedrin vocarunt. De huiusmodi concilio coacto aduersus Christum antehac non legimus. Legimus quidem subita commotione petitum Christum a plebe Iudæorum & multitudine. Legimus etiam cap. 7. supra, Pontifices & Pharisæos emisisse ministros suos ad eum apprehendendum. Sed concilium initum non legimus tâ solenne; in quo determinatum sit de morte Christi. Post tempus, de mediis eû è medio tollendi egerunt, de quibus intelligedus est vers. 53. postea. Quæ causa tâ solenis concilij? hora mortis Christi appropinquabat, prout autè appropinquabat, invalescebat eorū malitia, quæ eum ad morte vsq; prosequuta est: Res enim mali ominis est cum videmus consilia capere aduersarios aduersus Christum & veritatem eius. Prætendunt enim certam perniciem aliquam, nisi contra statuerit Dominus. Sed videamus consilium eorum ac deliberationem. Deliberationis quæstio hæc est, An sinendus est Iesus? Quid faciemus? inquiunt, hoc est, Sinemúsne eum an non? Tum in negantem partem argumentantur. Si sinemus eum, tum venient Romani & perdent locum hunc & gentem totam. In deliberando illud tanquam fundamentum substernunt: Oportere consistere gentem suam: quòd si autem cum ea no possit vna consistere Christus, tum è medio tollendus est. Ea est prudentia carnis: præsentem statum respiciut, cum quo si Christus, si religionis puritas consistere possit, tum Christum & religionem recipiunt: Sin minus, valedicunt Christo, valedicunt religioni: quasi vero Christus & religio ipsis & politiæ inseruiant. Nam contra politia & totus hic mundus Christo & religioni. Contrà verò, hæc est sapientia Dei, cùm in deliberando subsistenitur primùm Christus, subsistenitur religio. Deinde clauduntur quasi oculi ad euentum omnem quem in manus quasi resignamus. Atque hanc esse veram, vnicam ac solidam deliberandi rationem conspicitur ex hac ipsa re, quam in manibus habemus. Nam isti præfe-rentes conditionem suam Christo, ac metuentes ne sit Christus interetur, gens periret, ideo Christum sustulerunt e medio. Hac ipsa autem de causa, quia eum sustulerunt, iusto Dei iudicio factum est, vt venerint Romani, qui ciuitatem & gentem totam perdiderint. Sed quomodo sequitur hoc, Quòd si sinatur Christus, Romani venturi sunt & perditur locum ac gentem? Nam, inquiut, multa miracula edit, hinc omnes crediturì sunt in eum, & deceptionem factum à Romano imperio, quo fiet vt Romani venturi sint & perdituri locum & gentem istam. Vident igitur atque hoc vltrò confitentur, eú multa æderc miracula, hoc est, vident & cõfitentur Dei potentiam & virtutem esse in eo: attamen concludunt perdendum. Annon hoc est aperte pugnare cum Deo & bellum ei indicere? Quod si profecto ignari essent virtutis Dei, quæ in ipso fuit, aliquo modo excusabiles essent: sed cùm ipsi fateantur suo ore, cum edere multa miracula, qui possunt excusari? Blasphemus fui, inquit Paulus, item pers-quator, item iniurius; sed mei misertus est Domi-nus. At cur? quia, inquit, per ignorantiam feci. Discè igitur quanta sit hominum sibi derelictorum audacia etiam in Deum ipsum & in coelos. Non caruerunt suis prætextibus, scio, Res illis fuit non cum Deo, sed cum Iesu nescio quo: & tamen is edidit miracula ipsorum confessione. Vide, quod agnoscunt, quod confitentur, tamen volunt videri se illud ipsum non agnoscere, & contra
units.tr: A council is convened against Christ. The chief priests and the Pharisees, the guardians of the law, come together. The divine institution was that there should be one high priest, who was accustomed to discharge that office for life. But in this, as in other things, the institution and ordinance of God was violated, and they created many high priests at once, who nevertheless were to hold office in turn each year. In this year Caiaphas held the office. They therefore summoned a solemn council, which they called the Sanhedrin. We do not read of any such council gathered earlier against Christ. We read indeed that Christ was sought by the common people and the crowd in a sudden commotion. We also read, above in chapter 7, that the high priests and Pharisees sent their servants to seize him. But we do not read of a council convened so solemnly, in which it was determined concerning the death of Christ. Afterwards they debated the means of removing him, and verse 53 below is to be understood of this. What was the cause of so solemn a council? The hour of Christ's death was drawing near, and as it drew near their malice grew stronger, and it pursued him even to death. For it is an ill omen when we see adversaries taking counsel against Christ and his truth. For they pretend some certain destruction unless the Lord should decide otherwise. But let us look at their counsel and deliberation. The question of their deliberation is this: Is Jesus to be allowed to go on? What shall we do? they say, that is, shall we let him alone or not? Then they argue on the negative side. If we let him alone, the Romans will come and destroy this place and the whole nation. In deliberating they lay down this as a foundation: that their nation must continue to exist; and if Christ cannot continue to exist together with it, then he must be removed. Such is the prudence of the flesh: it looks to the present state, and if Christ and the purity of religion can continue alongside it, then they receive Christ and religion; but if not, they bid farewell to Christ and bid farewell to religion, as though Christ and religion were serving them and their politics. Whereas on the contrary politics and this whole world are against Christ and religion. On the contrary, this is the wisdom of God: when in deliberating we first consider Christ, religion is considered too. Then, as it were, our eyes are closed to every outcome, which we surrender as into the hands of God. And that this is the true, only and solid method of deliberating is seen from this very matter which we have in hand. For those who preferred their own condition to Christ, and feared that Christ would be the ruin of the nation, therefore removed Christ from the midst. And for this very reason, because they removed him, by the just judgement of God it came about that the Romans came and destroyed the city and the whole nation. But how does it follow that if Christ is allowed to go on, the Romans will come and the place and nation will perish? For, they say, he performs many miracles; hence all will believe in him, and the Roman empire will be deceived, with the result that the Romans will come and destroy this place and nation. They therefore see, and of their own accord confess, that he performs many miracles; that is, they see and confess that the power and virtue of God is in him. Yet they conclude that he must be destroyed. Is this not plainly to fight against God and declare war upon him? If indeed they were ignorant of the power of God which was in him, they would be somewhat excusable; but since they themselves confess with their own mouth that he performs many miracles, who can excuse them? I was a blasphemer, says Paul, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I obtained mercy from the Lord. And why? Because, he says, I did it in ignorance. Learn therefore how great is the audacity of men abandoned to themselves, even against God himself and against heaven. They did not lack their pretexts, I know. Their affair was not with God, they say, but with some Jesus or other; and yet he performed miracles, by their own confession. See: what they acknowledge, what they confess, they still wish to seem not to acknowledge it, and on the contrary

units.la: Malu consilium con sultoribus pessimum. conscientiam excusare volunt factum suum. Nemo enim inuenitur facile tam impudens, qui Deum vt Deū oppugnet: verum colorat quisque rem aliquo prætextu, & ipse sibi vult oculos eripere, ne Deum illum videat, quem oppugnat. Ita est hodierno die: Aduersarij scientes oppugnant Christum & veritatem eius, & tamen nolunt videri id facere: neque tantum oculis aliorum imponunt, sed & suis. Vnus autem ex ipsis. Sacerdotem vocat illius anni. Nam institutio diuina de sacerdotibus summis peruersa fuit. Cùmque Dei institutoordinatum fuerit, vt vnus esset, vno tempore Pontifex, qui advitam eo fungeretur munere, institutum hoc immutatum fuit, & multi simul erant pontifices, quorum tamen vnus vno anno & vicissim fungeretur officio pontificali. Notandum autem est huius quodnam fuerit hominis suffragium. Vos, inquit, nescitis. Vide superbiam prudentiæ huius mundi. Sapientes huius mundi lacuri suffragium suum, id faciunt cum opinione quadam sapientiæ suæ, & contemptu aliorum. At sapientia Dei humilis est, & de se modestè sentit, alios autem magnifacit. Sed videndum est suffragium. Expedit, inquit, vt vnus moriatur pro populo. Suffragio & sententia sua prodit malitiam in Christum. Sapientes huius mundi, vt superbi sunt in quoscunque, ita in Christum ac crucem eius malitiosi sunt quàm maximè. Consilia eorum & omnes machinationes sunt ad crucem Christi destruendam, etsi nonnunquam assententur, captandi fauoris gratia. Nam φεύγοντα τὰς σαρκὸς ἐστὶ ἐνιμικιτία ἀδυερσὺς Θεὸν. Ergo suffragium fert quòd expediat vt vnus moriatur pro populo. Vide cæcitatem sapientiæ mundanæ, eum per quem erat salus populo adiudicari oportuit morti. Quid aliud hoc fuit, quàm iugulum hominis succidere, vt seruare-tur reliquum corpus? Neque enim iste putauit virtute temerito mortis Christi seruandum populum. Prophetæ enim qui prædixerunt Christo moriendum pro populo, nunquam id consilij dederunt, vt ipse interficeretur. Sed vt rem ostendam apertius; fuit hæc quidem prophetia, fuit quoque consilium. Prophetia bona, consilium malum. Vt propheta fuit, non fuit ab ipso, vt dicitur versu sequeti, vt verò consilium, ab ipso fuit. Quid igitur? annon ipse intellexit vocem suam, vt Prophetæ superiores? Qui vt Petrus ait, inquisiuerunt in articulum temporis quo Christus passurus erat. Respondeo hunc vt Prophetas & sanctos illos Dei homines non habuisse reuelationem aliquam: sed cum ipse peruersum consilium daret, eo quasi inscio rexit eius linguam, vt olim linguam Balaami, sic vt prophetaret. Quod autem non vt veteres illi Prophetæ prophetabat, apparet vel ex eo quod ignorabat illud mysterium de quo tamen prophetauit. Nam Apostolus, de sapientia Dei loquens, quæ in mysterio occulta est, hanc, nemo, inquit, principum huius mundi cognouit, nam si cognouissent, Dominum gloriæ non crucifixissent. Quare in prophetando non cognouit illud mysterium, quod virtute mortis Christi mundus esset seruandus. Ergo etiam suggerente etiam Deo eiusque spiritu non omnes prophetant eodem modo? Respondeo, non: Quosdam enim inter prophetandum sanctificat corde, alios vero non sanctificat. Prophetas veteres sanctificauit, hunc non sanctificauit. Imo reuelationem ipsam & mentis scientiam considerees, non eodem modo administrat eam omnibus inter prophetandum: Nam quorundam linguam flectit, vt Balaami, quin potius vt Asinæ cui insidebat Balaam, quæ quid loqueretur non agnouit ipsa. Ita etiam iste quid loquutus est ignorauit: ipse nihil intellexisse videtur interea nisi consilium perversum. Notanda deinde hoc loco, quantum honoris Deus attribuerit officio illi pontificali. Virtute officii illius prophetauit iste, non autem persona. Non est quod hoc sibi arroget Pontifex Romanus, hoc est Antichristus, cum non sit post Christum pontificem in Ecclesia Dei Pontifex vllus. Similis quidem est in hoc Caiaphæ Pontifici, quod consilia eius omnia suaduersus Christum, sed in prophetia & veritate pronuntianda non est similis. Nec tantum pro ea gente. Iohannes prophetiam hanc extendit ad gentes dispersas, quæ virtute aduentus Christi & mortis eius collectæ sunt. Virtute quidem Christi venturi & futuræ mortis ipsius collectæ sunt Iudæi. At vero virtute Christi præsentis, & mortis præsentis collectæ sunt etiam gentes. Ex quo nota maiorem efficaciam Christi post aduentum, quàm quæ fuit ante aduentum. Latius enim se porrigit ad omnes, & vniuersalis est omnium vocatio. Neque externa modo vocatio fusior est, & latius sese diffundit; sed & interna. Nam vt ait author ad Hebraeos; Ante Christi aduentum & Christum Pontificem clausum fuit quodammodo regnum coelorum, & pauci ad id ingressi sunt: nempe prioris Tabernaculi sacrificiis nondum patefactum fuisse coelum, vt postea. Post vero Christum, vt ipse Christus loquitur, vis affertur regno coelorum, & violenti rapiunt illud.
units.tr: Bad counsel is the worst counsel for those who give it. They want to excuse their deed to their own conscience. For no one is easily found so shameless as to oppose God as God. Rather, each person colours the matter with some pretext, and wants to blind himself so that he does not see the God he opposes. So it is today: the adversaries knowingly oppose Christ and his truth, and yet they are unwilling to seem to do so. They deceive not only the eyes of others but their own as well. And one of them. He calls him the high priest of that year. For the divine institution concerning the high priests had been perverted. Whereas by God's institution it had been ordained that there should be one high priest at a time, who would hold that office for life, this arrangement was changed, and there were many high priests at once, of whom one held the priestly office for a single year and then in turn. It must be noted whose opinion this was. "You," he says, "know nothing." See the pride of the wisdom of this world. Worldly wise men, when they give their opinion, do so with a certain confidence in their own wisdom and with contempt for others. But the wisdom of God is humble, thinks modestly of itself, and esteems others highly. But we must consider the opinion itself. "It is expedient," he says, "that one man die for the people." By his opinion and judgment he betrays his malice against Christ. Worldly wise men, as they are proud towards everyone, are most malicious towards Christ and his cross. Their counsels and all their schemes are directed at destroying the cross of Christ, even if sometimes they flatter, to win favour. For "the friendship of the world is enmity against God" [ἡ φιλία τοῦ κόσμου ἔχθρα ἐστὶ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν]. Therefore he gives the opinion that it is expedient for one man to die for the people. See the blindness of worldly wisdom: he through whom salvation was to be granted to the people ought to be handed over to death. What else was this than to cut a man's throat so that the rest of the body might be saved? For he did not think that the people were to be saved by the power of Christ's death. The prophets who foretold that Christ must die for the people never gave the counsel that he himself should be killed. But to show the matter more plainly: this was indeed a prophecy, and also a counsel. A good prophecy, an evil counsel. As prophecy it was not from himself, as the following verse says; but as counsel it was from himself. What then? Did he not understand his own words, as the earlier prophets did, who, as Peter says, inquired into the time at which Christ was to suffer? I answer that he had no revelation such as the prophets and holy men of God had. But since he himself gave a perverse counsel, God, as it were without his knowledge, governed his tongue, just as he once governed the tongue of Balaam, so that he prophesied. That he did not prophesy as those ancient prophets did is clear even from the fact that he did not know the mystery about which he nonetheless prophesied. For the Apostle, speaking of the wisdom of God which is hidden in a mystery, says: "None of the rulers of this world knew it; for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." Wherefore, in prophesying, he did not know that mystery, that the world was to be saved by the power of Christ's death. Therefore, even when God and his Spirit prompt, do not all prophesy in the same way? I answer: no. For he sanctifies some in heart while they prophesy, but not others. He sanctified the ancient prophets; this man he did not sanctify. Indeed, if you consider the revelation itself and the knowledge of the mind, he does not administer it in the same way to all who prophesy. For he bends the tongue of some, as that of Balaam, or rather as that of the ass on which Balaam rode, which did not know what it was saying. So this man also did not know what he was saying; he himself seems to have understood nothing except the perverse counsel. Next, note in this place how much honour God has attributed to that priestly office. By the power of the office this man prophesied, not by his own person. The Roman Pontiff, that is the Antichrist, has no reason to claim this for himself, since after Christ there is no pontiff in the Church of God. He is indeed like Caiaphas in this, that all his counsels are against Christ; but in prophesying and declaring the truth he is not like him. Nor was it for that nation alone. John extends this prophecy to the scattered nations, who were gathered by the power of Christ's coming and death. Indeed, the Jews were gathered by the power of Christ's coming and future death; but the Gentiles were gathered by the power of Christ present and his death present. From this note the greater efficacy of Christ after his coming than before it. For it reaches more widely to all, and the calling of all is universal. Not only the external calling is broader and spreads more widely, but the internal calling too. For as the author to the Hebrews says: before Christ's coming, and while Christ was still high priest, the kingdom of heaven was in some sense closed, and few entered it; namely, heaven had not yet been opened by the sacrifices of the earlier Tabernacle, as it was afterwards. But after Christ, as Christ himself says, violence is done to the kingdom of heaven, and the violent take it by force.

units.la: Ab illo ergo. Conclusum est in praecedenti Concilio Cócilium moriendum esse Christo. Consultatio haec est de memorium impiorum diis. Neque enim Satan, vbi captum est consilium malè agendi, vnquam quiescere finit homines priusquam illud exequantur. De Iuda videbimus postea quòd diabolus diis tollen indiderit cordi ipsius, vt traderet Christum. Iohan.13. Post di Christi haec vero dicitur, cùm Dominus porrexisset illi offam, quòd ingressus sit Satan in eum. Primò significatur instinctu diaboli eū consilium cepisse perdedi magistri sui. Secundò, eū confirmatū in eo cōsilio, sic vt nunquā acquiescere potuerit priusquā exequeretur quod apud se decreuerat. Ideo Christus dixit ei, Quod facis, fac citò. Quod significauit eū coquiescere nō potuisse, priusquam exequeretur quod decreuit. Quid sibi vult hoc hodierno die quòd hostes veritatis quiescere nō possunt, sed semper aliquid moliuntur aduersus veritate & veritatis defensores? Nimirū consilium iam esse captum in Concilio illo Tridentino petendi iugulū Christi & Christianorū omnium. Quare videndum nobis est primùm omnium quaenam consilia capiamus. Vt bona capiamus; bonum enim est semper bona capere, quale Dauid cepit, Psal. 39.1. Dixeram, Obseruabo vias meas ne peccem. Et Paulus, Decreueram nihil inter vos scire nisi Iesum Christum, eumque crucifixum. Equidem concedo tentari nos prauis affectionibus quibusque, vt concupiscentia, vt ira, vt libidinis illicita, sed cauendum ne concipiat concupiscentia, vtrum Iacobo loquar. Conceptio enim concupiscentiae est consilium malum. Deinde cauendum, vbi concepit, ne pariat, vt idem loquitur, id est, ne erumpat in peccatum quod actuale vocant: nam peccatum gignit mortem; sed praestat primò motui concupiscentiae resistere;
units.tr: Therefore from that. It was concluded in the previous council that Christ must be killed. This consultation concerns the plots of the impious. For Satan, once a plan of doing evil has been formed, never lets men rest before they carry it out. We shall see later that the devil put into the heart of Judas the thought of betraying Christ (John 13). After the morsel, it is said that when the Lord had handed him a piece of bread, Satan entered into him. First, it is signified that by the prompting of the devil he formed the plan of betraying his master. Second, that he was confirmed in that plan, so that he could not rest until he carried out what he had decided within himself. Therefore Christ said to him: "What you do, do quickly" (John 13:27). This signified that he could not rest until he carried out what he had resolved. What does it mean today that the enemies of the truth cannot rest, but always contrive something against the truth and its defenders? Doubtless a plan has already been formed at that Council of Trent to attack the throat of Christ and of all Christians. Therefore we must first of all consider what counsels we ourselves adopt. Let us adopt good ones; for it is always good to adopt good counsels, as David did: "I had said, I will observe my ways, that I may not sin" (Psalm 39:1). And Paul: "I had determined to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified" (1 Cor. 2:2). I concede that we are tempted by various evil affections, such as lust, anger, and forbidden desires; but we must take care lest lust conceive, as James puts it. For the conception of lust is an evil counsel. Next, once it has conceived, we must take care lest it bring forth, as the same writer says, that is, lest it break out into the sin which they call actual sin. For sin brings forth death. But it is better first to resist the motion of lust.

units.la: Vnde Paul. Irascimini & ne peccate, hoc est quod subiun-git ibidem, Ne occidat sol super iracundiam vestram; Ne da-te locum diabolo. Peccare hoc loco est, quod dicit Iacobus, concipere & motu concupiscentiæ assentiri. Sic enim datur locus diabolo. Illic vetat ne consilium mali agen-di capiatur, vt illi detur, hominem alioqui ad iram esse pronum.
units.tr: Hence Paul: "Be angry, and do not sin" (Eph. 4:26), which is followed in the same place by "Let not the sun go down upon your wrath" and "Give no place to the devil." To sin in this place is what James speaks of: to conceive and to assent to the motion of lust. For in this way a place is given to the devil. There the apostle forbids that an evil counsel be formed, so that no place is given to it, since man is otherwise prone to anger.

units.la: Iesus ergo palam. Caret sibi Dominus vsque ad illam horam, qua ipsi moriendum fuit, & ita cauet, vt tamen interea bene agat in deserto illo in quod confugit. Sci-uit Dominus oportuisse se tandem in eorum manus in-cidere, sed tamen non temere se coniecit in discrimen ante tempus præscriptum. Verum seruauit se operi suo quod ipsi à Patre impositum fuit in terris peragendum. Neque enim vel vnum diem frustrà contriuit. Idem fa-ciendum est nobis. Seruemus nos horæ nostræ, & ita seruemus, vt interea semper promoueamus illud com-mune opus Domini, alioqui conseruatione non sumus digni. Quorsum enim seruaremur nisi bene agerem us? Nascimur enim & viuimus ad Dei gloriam promouen-dam. Quod si possimus vel vnum diem redimere, quo Ecclesiæ prosimus, etsi insequenti die nobis moriendum sit; tamen vnum illum diem in lucro debemus deputa-re. At quomodo scimus nos, quando cauendum & su-giendum, quando moriendum sit? Admirabilis hic est Dei prouidentia: quandiu ipsi opus est opera nostra, nos seruat mirabiliter. Ita Petrũ ad morte producendũ eri-puit. Ita Paulũ per mare, per terras conseruauit: At per-secto opere suo fine miraculo aliquo fuit & Petrũ & Pau-lũ mori & interfici à persequutoribus vtrumque, vt scia-mus nos non tam seruari ad fruendum vita hac, quàm ad opus Dei exequendum. Certiores etiam facit suos quodammodo quando viuendum, quando moriendũ.
units.tr: Jesus therefore openly. The Lord takes care of himself until the hour when he had to die, and so he takes such care that meanwhile he still does good in the wilderness to which he withdrew. The Lord knew that he must at last fall into their hands, but he did not rashly throw himself into danger before the appointed time. Rather he preserved himself for the work which had been imposed on him by the Father to be carried out on earth. For he did not waste even one day in vain. We must do the same. Let us preserve ourselves for our hour, and let us so preserve ourselves that meanwhile we always advance that common work of the Lord; otherwise we are not worthy of being preserved. For why would we be preserved, unless we did good? We are born and live to advance the glory of God. And if we can redeem even one day, by which we may profit the Church, even though we must die the following day, yet we ought to count that one day as gain. But how do we know when we must take care and flee, and when we must die? God's providence here is wonderful: as long as our work is needed by him, he preserves us wonderfully. So he snatched Peter from being led out to death; so he preserved Paul through the sea and over lands. But when his work is finished, by some miracle or other both Peter and Paul were to die, and to be killed by their persecutors, so that we may know that we are preserved not so much to enjoy this life as to carry out the work of God. He also makes his people, in some measure, more certain of when they must live and when they must die.

units.la: Paulus Romæ in vinculis detentus pollicetur sibi vitæ protractionem aliquam. Quid eligam, inquit, ignoro, co-arcter enim vtrimque. Et postea confisus, inquit, nisi me per-mansurum esse. Postea tamen ad Timotheum scribens, Labor, inquit, & tempus meæ resolutionis instat, &c. In fine eiusdem ad Timotheum Epistolæ, cum promittit sibi ereptionem, quam, quæso, ereptionem promittit, aut à quo demũ malo liberatione? An ex præsenti discrimine ereptionem? Eripiet, inquit, me ab omni opere malo, seruabitque cælesti suo regno, cui sit omnis gloria in sæcula sæculorum, Amen. Sed quò confugit Dominus? In regionem, inquit, quæ est prope desertum. Hostes Christi ferè occupant opima quæque loca, & iucunda, adeò vt si qui volunt pie in deserto viuere in Christo Iesu, his necessario cum Christo in desertum sit fugiendum, in eóque viuendum. Examus igitur ad Christum extra castra opprobrium eius portantes. Nostri tamen homines adeo abripiuntur suauitate huius terræ, & opimis quibusque regionibus, vt Hispania, vt Galliis, vt Italia, &c. vt in discrimen vocent sed religionis veritatem gratia rerum istarum, & malint illic esse cum periculo tum vitæ, tum religionis, quàm hic in solitudine cum Christo, & mediocri viuendi ratione. Magnus quæstus est pietas cum animo sua sorte contento.
units.tr: Paul, held in chains at Rome, hopes for some lengthening of his life. "What I shall choose," he says, "I do not know, for I am hard pressed on both sides." And afterwards, trusting, he says, "that I shall remain." Yet later, writing to Timothy, he says, "The time of my departure is at hand," and so on. At the end of the same letter to Timothy, when he promises himself deliverance, what deliverance, I ask, does he promise, or from what evil does he expect liberation at last? Is it deliverance from the present danger? "The Lord," he says, "will deliver me from every evil work and will preserve me for his heavenly kingdom, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen." But whither has the Lord withdrawn? "Into a country," he says, "that is near the wilderness." The enemies of Christ occupy almost every rich and pleasant place, so that those who wish to live godly in Christ Jesus must of necessity flee with Christ into the wilderness and live there. Let us go out, then, to Christ outside the camp, bearing his reproach. Yet our own people are so carried away by the sweetness of this earth and by its fertile regions, that they expose the truth of religion to danger for the sake of such things, as in Spain, in France, in Italy and elsewhere, and prefer to be there, with danger both to life and to religion, rather than here in solitude with Christ and a modest way of living. Godliness with a mind content with its lot is great gain.

units.la: 55 Prope autem erat Pascha Iudæorum: & ascenderunt multi Hierosolymam ex illa regione ante Pascha, vt purificarent se.
units.tr: 55 "Now the Passover of the Jews was nigh: and many went up out of the country to Jerusalem before the Passover, to purify themselves."

units.la: 56 Quærebant ergo Iesum, & loquebantur alij cum alijs in templo stantes; Quid videtur vobis, an venturus non est ad festum?
units.tr: 56 "Then sought they for Jesus, and spake among themselves, as they stood in the temple, What think ye, that he will not come to the feast?"

units.la: 57 Dederant autem primarij Sacerdotes & Pharisæi mandatum, vt si quis nosset vbi esset, indicaret, vt prehenderent eum.
units.tr: 57 "Now both the chief priests and the Pharisees had given a commandment, that, if any man knew where he were, he should shew it, that they might take him."

units.la: S Equitur nunc ad finem vsque capitis quid Iudei ipso absente egerint aduersus eum, quid multitudo item; quid denique principes populi Sacerdotes & Pharisæi, nempe tertium post baptismum Domini. De primo vidimus capite 2. De secundo cap.5. Hoc tertium illud est in quo immolatus est verus ille agnus Paschalis. Instante igitur Pascha te multi ascenderunt Hierosolymam ad purificandum se; id factum est non ordinatione diuina, sed inuentione & traditione quadam sua. Quare purificatio ista, non tam purificatio videtur esse, quàm pollutio. Nam quotquot sunt purificationes nostræ sine præscripto Dei, & contra præscri-ptum Dei, tot sunt pollutiones & inquinationes conscientiæ. Inuenta enim ab hominibus purificatio, nunquam sanctificat conscientiam, vt loquamur cum Apostolo. Habemus autem hic partes & populi & principū aduersus Christum furentium, vt sciamus appropinquāte illa mortis hora malitiam hominum cuiusque generis agnoscere. Ita fit de membris Christi quoties eorum morte & migratione glorificandus est Dominus. Malitia enim hominum omnis generis & conditionis augescere solet, adeo vt hoc sit signum horæ appropinquantis quoties videmus malitiæ nullum modum fieri. Neque enim vidimus in superioribus Paschatibus huiusmodi conspirationem fieri, quia scilicet non adeo appropinquabat hora Domini. Sed videndæ sunt partes & populi & principum. Quærebant ergo Christum. Pars populi sunt, quærunt Christum, nempe vt indicent eum Sacerdotibus & Pharisæis, vt appareat ex sequenti versu non autem inuenientes dicunt, Quid videtur vobis? Quo sermone ostendunt non tam sitim gratiæ Christi, quàm sanguinis ipsius. Neque enim eo fine quærunt, vt participes sint gratiæ eius, sed vt satisfaciant libidini Sacerdotum & Pharisæorum simul, & malitiæ suæ ipsorum. Vide insaniam multitudinis. Non existimant viuere se posse, nisi authorem ac fontem vitæ interficiant, neque enim eo fine eum prosequuntur, vt per mortem eius, vitam consequantur. Neque quisquam conscius proditionis & mortis Christi id vnquam respexit. Quotquot gratiam Christi expectarunt, chara erat eius vita eiusque conseruatio, vt discipulis, vt Mariæ, vt Marthæ, &c. Ita plane sentiendum est de multitudine impiorum hodierno die. Non putant sibi viuendum in mundo, nisi columnas & lumina huius mundi, adeoque Euangelium ipsum tollant de medio, vt columnis succisis corruat mundus, ipsosque repente opprimat. Hoc quidem certum est, neque tamen illi, quæ est eorum dementia, hoc vident. Dederunt autem primary. Hoc est factum principum aduersus Christum & fundamentum superioris facti multitudinis. Nam si quid delirat multitudo, præsertim in rebus religionis, in causa fere sunt princi-
units.tr: It now follows, to the end of the chapter, what the Jews did against him in his absence, what the multitude did likewise, and finally what the rulers of the people, the chief priests and the Pharisees, did; namely, at the third Passover after the baptism of the Lord. We saw the first in chapter 2, the second in chapter 5. This third is the one in which that true Paschal Lamb was sacrificed. Since the Passover was at hand, many went up to Jerusalem to purify themselves. This was done not by divine appointment but by their own invention and tradition. Wherefore this purification seems to be not so much a purification as a pollution. For however many purifications we devise without the prescription of God, and against his prescription, so many are pollutions and defilements of conscience. For a purification invented by men never sanctifies the conscience, to speak with the Apostle. Here, however, we have the parts both of the people and of the princes raging against Christ, so that we may know that as that hour of death draws near, the malice of men of every kind is revealed. So it happens with the members of Christ whenever the Lord is to be glorified by their death and departure. For the malice of men of every kind and condition is wont to increase, so that this is a sign of the approaching hour: whenever we see no limit to malice. Indeed, we did not see such a conspiracy at the earlier Passovers, because, of course, the hour of the Lord was not yet so near. But the parts of the people and of the princes must be examined. "They sought therefore Jesus." Part of the people are these, who seek Christ, namely, that they may betray him to the priests and Pharisees, as appears from the following verse. But they do not say this when they fail to find him: "What think ye?" By which words they show a thirst not so much for the grace of Christ as for his blood. For they do not seek him to the end that they may share in his grace, but to gratify the lust of the priests and Pharisees and, at the same time, their own malice. See the madness of the multitude. They do not think they can live unless they kill the author and fountain of life; indeed they do not pursue him with the aim of gaining life through his death. Nor did any who was privy to the betrayal and death of Christ ever have this in view. All who looked for the grace of Christ held his life and its preservation dear, as did the disciples, Mary, Martha and others. So must we plainly judge of the multitude of the ungodly in our own day. They do not think they can live in the world unless they remove the pillars and lights of this world, and so take the Gospel itself out of the way, so that the world, with its pillars cut down, may fall and suddenly crush them. This is certainly true, yet they do not see it, such is their folly. "And the rulers gave commandment." This was the deed of the princes against Christ, and the foundation of the earlier deed of the multitude. For if the multitude goes mad, especially in matters of religion, the princes are for the most part to blame.

units.la: Principum aduersus Christum conatus. principes.Si enim illi officium facerent, vulgus in ordinem facilè cogeretur. Vnde Dominus non denuntiat iudicium aduersus populum & multitudinem, sed aduersus authores aberrationis eorum. Non, inquit, væ vobis populus Iudæorum, sed væ vobis, Scribæ & Pharisæi, hypocritæ, quoniam præcluditis regnum cælorum coram hominibus, &c. Ita quoque fiet de hoc regno. Nam si defectio à Christo euentura est vnquam, væ illud non tam ad plebem, quàm ad principes pertinebit. Verum si cæci fuerint cæcorum duces, ambo in foueam ruent. Sed dici non potest quàm graue futurum est iudicium principum & procerum, præsertim istorum qui machinantur religionis subuersionem: si defectio populi ab hac sinceritate religionis & veritate futura sit vnquam. Maneat precamur nobiscum Christus, cum veritate verbi sui, ad finem vsque. Huic sit omnis honor & gloria: Amen.
units.tr: The attempts of the princes against Christ. For if those princes did their duty, the common people would easily be brought into order. Hence the Lord does not pronounce judgment against the people and the multitude, but against the authors of their error. "Not," he says, "Woe to you, people of the Jews," but "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut up the kingdom of heaven before men, etc." So too it will be with this kingdom. For if ever a falling away from Christ is to come, that woe will apply not so much to the common people as to the princes. But if the blind are leaders of the blind, both will fall into the pit. Yet it cannot be said how grievous the judgment of the princes and nobles will be, especially of those who plot the overthrow of religion, if ever a falling away of the people from this purity of religion and truth is to come. May Christ, we pray, remain with us, with the truth of his word, to the end. To him be all honour and glory. Amen.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM
units.tr: Argument

units.la: Capitis huius partes sunt 5.
units.tr: The parts of this chapter are five.

units.la: Primò, narratur quomodo Dominus cùm venisset Bethaniam, ibi cœna exceptus sit à sororibus Lazari, & quomodo in illa cœna à Maria sorore Lazari unctus sit, quidque inde euenerit ad versf. vsque 11.
units.tr: First, it is related how the Lord, when he had come to Bethany, was received there at supper by the sisters of Lazarus, and how at that supper he was anointed by Mary, the sister of Lazarus, and what followed from this, to verse 11.

units.la: Deinde, quomodo Hierosolymam asello vectus, lætis populi acclamationibus & congratulationibus sit exceptus, & quid inde euenerit, vsque ad versum 20.
units.tr: Then, how he was carried into Jerusalem on an ass and received with joyful acclamations and congratulations from the people, and what followed from this, to verse 20.

units.la: Tertiò, additur sermo eius quem ad discipulos habuit de sua morte, item de sui abnegatione & confessione, tum de luce verbi sui, vsque ad versum 37.
units.tr: Thirdly, his speech to the disciples is added, in which he spoke of his death, and likewise of self-denial and confession, and then of the light of his word, to verse 37.

units.la: Quartò, exponitur causa cur plerique in eum non crediderint: Et cur qui dam ex primoribus non ausi sint eum confiteri: vsque ad versum 44.
units.tr: Fourthly, the reason is explained why many did not believe in him, and why some of the leaders did not dare to confess him, to verse 44.

units.la: Postremò, narratur sermo Domini de fide & incredulitate tate, nempe cur in ipsum credendum sit, & unde fides illa oriatur, & cur incredduli merito condemnentur: ad finem usque capitis.
units.tr: Lastly, the Lord's discourse on faith and unbelief is related: namely, why one must believe in him, whence that faith arises, and why unbelievers are rightly condemned, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: 1 Esus ergo sex ante Pascha diebus venit in Bethaniam, ubi erat Lazarus ille qui fuerat mortuus, quem suscitaverat a mortuis.
units.tr: 1 Jesus therefore, six days before the Passover, came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom he had raised from the dead.

units.la: 2 Fecerunt igitur ei cœnam illic, & Martha ministrabat: Lazarus autem unus erat ex iis qui simul discumbebant cum eo.
units.tr: 2 So they made him a supper there, and Martha served; but Lazarus was one of those who reclined at table with him.

units.la: 3 Maria vero accepta libra unguenti Nardi liquidæ multi preti, unxit pedes Iesu, & extersit pedes eius capillis suis: domus autem impleta est odore unguenti.
units.tr: 3 Mary then, taking a pound of ointment of spikenard, very precious, anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.

units.la: Hoc capite primum habemus profectionem Christiin Bethaniam vicum Hierosolymis propinquum: deinde Hierosolymam. Primum ergo dicit, Sex ante Pascha diebus Ut prius fugit in desertum cum nondum appropinquaret hora mortis præstituta: ita nunc appropinquante illa hora vltro redit, & se non minus lubens coniicit in manus eorum, per quos ordinatum fuit à Deo, ut ipse occideretur, quam illi eum apprehensum cupiebant. Testatur hoc summa voluntate Christum pro nobis mortuum, & verum esse quod dixit supra cap. 10. Nemo tollit animam meam à me, sed ego pono eam à meipso. Pij quique ac Dei servi moti spiritu Christi eiusque exemplo non minori animi promptitudine, ubi censent diem quo Deum morte sua glorificent appropinquare, Deo quasi ac morti obuiam veniunt, quam ante fugiebant, cum nondum appropinquaret ille dies, cumque esset quod in vita ageret cum iis Deus. Paulus primum fugit Damasco, deinde Hierosolymis Cæsaream: postea vero cum iam pene cursum suum consumsummasset, vt ipse ad Timotheum loquitur, cúmque ei iter versus Hierosolyma instituenti prædictum esset ab Agabo propheta vinciendum esse eum Hierosolymis & tradendum in manus gentium, cúmque precarentur fratres, qui vnà erant, ne Hierosolyma ascenderet, & cum lachrymis quidem precarentur : Quid facitis, inquit eis, flentes & comminuentes cor meum? Nam ego non solùm vinciri, sed & mori paratus sum Hierosolymis pro nomine Domini Iesu. Imò pij absoluto cursu gaudent offerri pro eorum, quos fide imbuerunt suo ministerio, confirman- da. Si, inquit Apostolus, pro libamento offerar super hostia, sa- crificióque fidei vestræ, gaudeo ac gratulor omnibus vobis.
units.tr: In this chapter we have first Christ's journey to Bethany, a village near Jerusalem, and then his journey to Jerusalem. He first says, Six days before the Passover. As before, when the hour of his death was not yet near, he fled into the wilderness; so now, when that hour is approaching, he returns of his own accord and casts himself no less willingly into the hands of those through whom God had ordained that he should be killed, than they were eager to seize him. This testifies, with the greatest willingness, that Christ died for us, and that what he said above in chapter 10 is true: No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of myself. Godly people and servants of God, moved by the Spirit of Christ and following his example with no less readiness of mind, when they judge that the day is near on which they will glorify God by their death, go to meet God and death as if to meet them, which before they had fled, while that day was not yet near, and while God still had work for them to do in this life. Paul first fled to Damascus, then from Jerusalem to Caesarea; but later, when he had almost finished his course, as he himself writes to Timothy, and when it had been foretold to him by the prophet Agabus that he would be bound at Jerusalem and delivered into the hands of the Gentiles, and when the brethren who were with him begged him not to go up to Jerusalem, and begged him even with tears, he said: What do you mean, he said to them, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. Indeed, godly people, having finished their course, rejoice to be offered up for the sake of those whom they have imbued with faith by their ministry, to confirm them. If, says the Apostle, I am being poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice and congratulate all of you.

units.la: Venit igitur primùm Christus Bethaniam vtpote Hierosolymis locum propinquum, vt ei postea ingredienti Hierosolyma, obuiam egrederetur populus cúmque gloriosè exciperent & comitarentur, vt narratur postea.
units.tr: Christ therefore first came to Bethany, since it was a place near Jerusalem, so that when he afterwards entered Jerusalem, the people might come out to meet him, and receive and accompany him in glory, as is related afterwards.

units.la: Venit etiam Bethaniam, tanquam locum commodum Iudæproditori ex quo se subduceret, & cum Pontificibus & Pharisæis pactionem faceret de Christo perdendo. Bethania describitur nunc, non quidem à Maria & Martha, vt suprà cap.11. sed ab illo miraculo in Lazaro excitato ex mortuis; ab opere nimirum Dei. A Dei operibus & speciali præsentia denominandæ sunt in primis & ciuitates & regiones. Bethel primùm appellata est Luz: sed Deo se offerente illi Iacobo Bethel vocata.
units.tr: He came also to Bethany as a convenient place for Judas the betrayer, from which he could withdraw and make a bargain with the chief priests and Pharisees to destroy Christ. Bethany is now described, not indeed by Mary and Martha as above in chapter 11, but by that miracle wrought on Lazarus raised from the dead; that is, by the work of God. Cities and regions are above all to be named from the works of God and from his special presence. Bethel was first called Luz, but when God revealed himself to Jacob, it was called Bethel.

units.la: Neque est hoc inane nomen quod à Deo sumi solet: Daniel enim in oratione sua ad Deum hinc argumentatur ad misericordiam obtinendam: Miserere, inquit, ciuitatis quæ vocata est de nomine tuo. q.d. quæ habuit specialem præsentiam tuam, atque hinc nomen obtinuit. Efficax autem est argumentum. Nam dona & vocatio Dei ἀμεταμέλητα sunt: nisi misericordiæ omnem aditum præcludat nostra ingratitudo.
units.tr: Nor is this an empty name, such as God is wont to bestow. For Daniel in his prayer to God argues from this to obtain mercy: Have mercy, he says, on the city which is called by your name. That is, the city which had your special presence and from this obtained its name. And the argument is effective. For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance [ἀμεταμέλητα]: unless our ingratitude shuts off every approach to mercy.

units.la: Ad quos venit Bethaniam, & quibus tandem se tanquam socium adiunxit? Non quibusuis, sed Mariæ, Marthæ, Lazaro. Et, vt alij Euangelistæ narrant, Simoni leproso qui parauit ei cœnam. Christus post varias iactationes, variáque certamina, vltimum & grauissimum conflictum cum ira Dei, cum Satana & hominibus tentatus, voluit apud suos quasi ad tempus respirare, & consolationem ex iis aliquam accipere, vicissimque ministrare. Nam & Dei serui, quibus haec vita nihil aliud est quàm continuum certamen ac conflictus, cupiunt apud suos respirare non vnquam, vt possint quae supersunt perferre ad finem vsque: Beati autem sunt qui eos recreant. Vide quid de Onesiphoro praedicet Paulus. Praestet misericordiam Deus Onesiphori familiae: quoniam saepe me recreauit, &c. Videndum deinde quàm officiosè illi inseruierint omnes ad quos se recepit. Simon leprosus apparat illi conuiuium: Lazarus vna accumbit, Martha ministrat, Maria inungit. Occupati sunt omnes, sed non vno eodemque modo occupati, verum alio atque alio modo. Inseruiunt tamen illi omnes in suo genere. Sic nos cum Christum habemus nobiscum in verbo suo praesentem, quae quidem non minus efficax est praesentia quàm ea qua cum fuit, parati esse debemus ad illi inseruiendum, ac singuli in vocatione sua: Rex in vocatione sua, Subiecti in vocatione quisque sua, Minister in vocatione sua. Nam, vt Paulus ait de se, Deo seruire debemus omnes in Euangelio filii sui. Denique siue edimus siue bibimus siue quid facimus, faciamus omnia ad illius gloriam. Cùm paramus coenam, Christo paremus: dum accumbimus, cum Christo accumbamus: dum ministramus, Christo ministremus: dum videmur profundere supra modum, vt Maria Christo, id faciamus ad eum quasi inungendum.
units.tr: To whom did he come at Bethany, and with whom did he finally join himself as a companion? Not with just anyone, but with Mary, Martha and Lazarus, and, as the other evangelists relate, with Simon the leper, who prepared a supper for him. Christ, after various troubles and manifold conflicts, having been tested in his final and most grievous struggle with the wrath of God, with Satan and with men, wished to take a breath, as it were for a time, among his own, and to receive some comfort from them, and in turn to minister to them. For the servants of God, to whom this life is nothing but a continual struggle and conflict, always desire to refresh themselves among their own, so that they may bear what remains to the end; and blessed are those who refresh them. See what Paul says of Onesiphorus: May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me, etc. Next we should see how diligently all those to whom he withdrew served him. Simon the leper prepares a banquet for him; Lazarus reclines with him; Martha serves; Mary anoints. All are busy, but not all in one and the same way; rather, in different ways. Yet all of them serve him in their own kind.
