So too, since we have Christ present with us in his word, which is no less effective a presence than that in which he was with them, we ought to be ready to serve him, each in his own calling: A king in his calling, subjects each in their calling, a minister in his calling. For, as Paul says of himself, we ought all to serve God in the gospel of his Son. In short, whether we eat or drink or do anything else, let us do all things to his glory. When we prepare a meal, let us prepare it for Christ; while we recline, let us recline with Christ; while we serve, let us serve Christ; when we seem to pour out beyond measure, as Mary did, let us do so as if to anoint Christ.

units.la: Omnes igitur isti bene occupati sunt in excipiendo tanto hospite: sed si comparationem facias, videbitur Maria elegisse potissimam partem. hoc tempore Dominus id commendat tanquam optimum opus. Bonum, inquit, opus operata est erga me. Ob quod erat commendanda posteritati. Quid sibi vult autem hoc? nempe muliebrem istam propius sensisse quid in Christo fuerit, quàm quemuis aliorum etiam discipulorum hoc tempore. Quod ipsum quoque altius initium habuit. Sensit enim quàm graue sit peccatum: sine sensu enim peccati non est sensus illius suavitatis quae in Christo est. Mirum autem est quàm diligant ipsi Dominum, qui senserunt primum quàm amarum sit peccatum: deinde quàm suauis sit Dominus. Charitas Christi, inquit Paulus, constringit. stringit nos.Quorsum autem? quia, inquit, hoc statuimus quod cum omnes mortui essemus, ille unus pro nobis omnibus mortuus sit, ut nimirum ipsi in posterum quod superest vitae viviamus. De peccatrice muliere legimus, Quod stans apud pedes Domini retro flens coepit rigare pedes eius, &c. Dominus autem ipse postea illud factum interpretatur profectum ab insigni dilectione, qua rursus profecta est exsensu multorum peccatorum, primum perpetratorum, deinde remissorum. Sed factum hoc Mariae diligentius noran-dum est: primum enim erupit fides & amor erga Christum in liberalitatem: Non parcit sumptibus in emen-do pretiosissimo unguento: quo illum totum a capite ad pedes unxit. Nam etsi de capite non fiat mentio a nostro Euangelista, tamen illud ex aliis satis conspicitur. Meminit autem Iohannes pedum potissimum, ex pedibus totum intelligens. Nam si pedes, hoc est una parte, quanto magis caput & suprema parte? Qui vero diligunt Christum non tantum opes suas, non tantum lachrymas, id quod fecit peccatrix mulier, sed & vitam & sanguinem suum pro illo & ad illum quasi unguendum profundent. Neque auari isti, qui ne vel unum quidem stipem eius causa expendere volunt (quicquid Deum iactitent) ex animo unquam dilexerunt Dominum. Deinde notandum est factum summae obedientiae ac reverentiae: fides enim & charitas Christi cum reverentia & submissione tam animi quam corporis coniuncta est, & cum neglectu corporis huius & ornamentorum eius, quae omnia Christi pedibus libenter subiiciunt: Neque enim qui pluris faciunt externum hunc hominem quam internum & occultum illum hominem cordis, ut cum Petro loquar, unquam illi se Christo, sic ut Maria, humiliant, aut ita eum diligunt. Notandum denique effectum huius operis Mariae. Domus, inquit, impleta est odore unguenti, nempe corporalis illius. Quanto magis Ecclesia impletur suavi odore unctionis illius spiritualis Christi, qua unctus est oleo laetitiae supra consortes suos, hanc unctionem spiritualem eiusque odorem percipimus non minus nos, nunc ex praesentia Christi quae est in Spiritu & verbo suo, quam illi tum odorem perceperunt unctionis corporalis ex praesentia eius corporali.
units.tr: All of them, then, were well employed in receiving so great a guest; but if you make a comparison, Mary will seem to have chosen the better part. At this time the Lord commends her deed as an excellent work. She has done a good work, he says, for me. For this reason it was to be commended to posterity. What does this mean? Surely that this woman had a closer sense of what was in Christ than any of the other disciples at this time. This too had a deeper beginning: for she perceived how grievous sin is, since without a sense of sin there is no sense of that sweetness which is in Christ. And it is wonderful how much they love the Lord who first perceived how bitter sin is, and then how sweet the Lord is. The love of Christ, says Paul, constrains us. Why so? Because, he says, we are convinced that since all have died, he died for all, so that those who live should henceforth live for themselves. We read of the sinful woman that she stood behind at the feet of the Lord, weeping, and began to wash his feet with her tears, etc. The Lord himself afterwards interpreted that deed as proceeding from a remarkable love, which in turn proceeded from the sense of many sins, first committed and then forgiven. But this deed of Mary's is to be noted more carefully: for first, faith and love toward Christ broke out into generosity. She does not spare expense in buying the most precious ointment, with which she anointed him all over, from head to foot. For although the head is not mentioned by our evangelist, it is nonetheless sufficiently seen from the others. John mentions the feet especially, understanding the whole from the feet. For if the feet, that is one part, why not much more the head and the highest part? Those who truly love Christ pour out not only their wealth, not only tears, as the sinful woman did, but also their life and blood for him, and to anoint him. The covetous, who do not wish to spend even a single coin for his sake, have never loved the Lord from the heart, whatever they may boast of God. Next, we should note that this was a deed of the highest obedience and reverence: for faith and love toward Christ are joined with reverence and submission of both mind and body, and with neglect of the body and its adornments, all of which they gladly subject to Christ's feet. Indeed, those who value the outward man more than the inward and hidden man of the heart, to use Peter's words, never humble themselves before Christ as Mary did, nor love him in this way. Finally, we should note the effect of Mary's work: the house, he says, was filled with the fragrance of the ointment, namely that bodily fragrance. How much more the Church is filled with the sweet fragrance of that spiritual anointing of Christ, with which he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows. We perceive this spiritual anointing and its fragrance no less now, from the presence of Christ which is in his Spirit and word, than they then perceived the fragrance of the bodily anointing from his bodily presence.
Luke 7.38, etc.

units.la: 4 Dixit ergo quidam ex discipulis eius, nempe Iudas Simonis filius Iscariotes, qui erat eum producturus,
units.tr: 4 Then one of his disciples, namely Judas Iscariot, son of Simon, who was going to betray him, said:

units.la: 5 Quare hoc unguentum non vaniit trecentis denarijs, & datum est pauperibus?
units.tr: 5 "Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?"

units.la: 6 Dixit autem hoc, non quod pauperum ipsi cura esset, sed quia fur erat, & marsupium habebat, & ea quae mittebantur gestabat.
units.tr: 6 He said this, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief; he had the money bag and carried what was put into it.

units.la: 7 Dixit ergo Iesus, Omitte eam, in diem funerationis meae seruauit istud.
units.tr: 7 Jesus therefore said, "Leave her alone; she has kept this for the day of my burial."

units.la: 8 Pauperes enim semper habebitis vobiscum, me vero non semper habebitis.
units.tr: 8 "For you will always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me."

units.la: Opponit se Iudas optimo facto: Nam quo melius opus eo magis resistitur. Describitur autem Iudas primum a nomine, deinde a parente, tertio a gente, quarto a facto quod perpetraturus erat: proditurus erat Iesum, hoc nomē retinet apud omnes Euangelistas, vocatur-que Iudas proditor. Verum cum Spiritus sanctus imponit nomen, altius est eius rei fundamentum. Cum imponit nomē bonum, & cum prodit memoriae nomen alicuius ad decus, tum id argumento est bene esse illi animae: vt cum de Maria ista dicitur, quod vbicunque praedicatum fuerit hoc Euangelium, hoc quod haec fecit ad memoriam ipsius celebrabitur. At vero cum insignit aliquem malo nomine, commendatque posteritati tanquam malum, tum id argumento est male agi cum eo homine cuiusque anima. Alij Euangelistae scribunt hoc dictum fuisse etiam aliis discipulis, Matthaeus omnibus sine discrimine, Marcus certis quibusdam. Verisimile quidem est ortum esse malum a Iuda, deinde grassatum per alios. Nam in hominum numero & coetu aliquo, qui primus murmurat, is quasi flabellum est aliis incitandis ad malum, vt sumus omnes natura contagioni huic obnoxij. At quid dixit Iudas? Quare, inquit, hoc unguentum. Alij habent dictum cum indignatione quadam. Marcus addit fremuisse aduersus mulierem: vt est, significat hoc loco Iudas id quod expresse dicitur.
units.tr: Judas opposes the best deed. For the better the work, the more it is resisted. Judas is described first by his name, then by his father, third by his family, and fourth by the deed he was about to commit: he was going to betray Jesus. He keeps this name in all the Evangelists, and he is called Judas the betrayer. But when the Holy Spirit gives a name, the foundation of the matter goes deeper. When he gives a good name, and when the name of someone is handed down to posterity for honour, this is a sign that the soul of that person is well: as when it is said of this Mary that wherever this Gospel is preached, what she has done will be told in memory of her. But when he marks someone with a bad name and commends him to posterity as wicked, this is a sign that the soul of that man is in bad case. The other Evangelists write that this saying was made also by other disciples: Matthew says by all of them without distinction, Mark by certain ones. It is indeed likely that the evil began with Judas and then spread through the others. For in any company of men, the one who first murmurs is like a bellows for stirring others to evil, since we are all by nature exposed to this contagion. But what did Judas say? "Why," he said, "this ointment?" Others have it that he spoke with a certain indignation. Mark adds that he grumbled against the woman; as the word is, Judas here signifies what is expressly stated.

units.la: Matt.26.13 Marc.14.9 tür apud alios Euangelistas, profusionem fuisse. Ad quid, inquiunt alij, profusio ista. Sic hodierno die existimant homines totum illud quod in Christum, in Euan-gelium eius, in Euangelij ministros erogatur, profun-di & inutiliter abiici, ídque cum indignatione & fre-mitu in eos qui paulò liberaliùs agere volunt. In causa est quia plerisque Christus inane tantùm nomen: Verbum autem Euangelij perfunctorię, &externę quasi politiæ gratia hominibus prædicari videtur. Vno verbo, spiritualia sunt imaginaria: corporalia & temporia solida, vt quæ manibus tractari possunt: Non enim minus est crassum cor istis hominibus, crassus animus, quàm crassa est manus eorum corporea. Neque ea quæ sunt Dei, sed ea quæ sunt hominum sapiunt. Dixit autem hoc. Iohannes quo animo sit hoc ab eo dictum ipse obi-ter inserit. Innuit ergo hunc tantum prætextum fuisse aliquem, cuiusmodi solent prætendere isti homines, qui bona hæc mundana quæcunque inuident præconibus verbi Dei, & præclari quidem sunt illi in speciem, sed Deus non irridetur. At quæ vera causa? fur erat, inquit, deinde marsupium habebat. Quid inde? voluit illud omne clam subducere, si seme\ fuisset missum in marsupium illud quod portabat. Nam si furi credatur marsupium, si officium aliquod quod emolumenti aliquid habet, is furabitur proculdubio. Si furi credatur quæstoris officium, furabitur.
units.tr: Matt. 26.13; Mark 14.9. In the other Evangelists it is called a waste. "To what end," they say, "is this waste?" In the same way people today think that everything that is given to Christ, to his Gospel, and to the ministers of the Gospel is wasted and thrown away uselessly, and they do this with indignation and grumbling against those who wish to act a little more generously. The reason is that for most people Christ is only an empty name, and the word of the Gospel seems to be preached to men only as a matter of outward form, as a kind of polite courtesy. In a word, spiritual things are imaginary, while bodily and temporal things are solid, since they can be handled with the hands. For these men's heart is no less gross, their mind no less gross, than their bodily hand is gross. They do not savour the things that are of God, but the things that are of men. But he said this. John himself inserts in passing with what mind this was said by him. He hints therefore that this was only a pretext, such as those men are wont to put forward, who grudge all these worldly goods to the heralds of the Word of God; and they are indeed splendid in appearance, but God is not mocked. But what was the true cause? He was a thief, he says, and then he had the money bag. What follows? He wished to steal off all that money secretly, if it had been put into that money bag which he carried. For if a money bag is entrusted to a thief, or any office which brings some profit, he will undoubtedly steal from it. If the office of a treasurer is entrusted to a thief, he will steal.

units.la: Dixit ergo Iesus, Sine eam. Non est negotium facessen-dum iis, qui Christo inseruiunt, etsi illud mundus capere non possit quid agant. Decætero, inquit Paulus, nequis molestias mihi exhibeto: etenim stigmata Domini nostri Iesu Christi in corpore meo porto. Tum excusat factum: vbi no-ta eius modestiam. Nam statim obiicit Iudæ furacem a-nimum, neque voluit eum retrahere à facto illo scelé-rato, ad quod destinatus erat: sed finit pergere quò ten-debat. Fundamentum facti & proditionis fuit auaritia: Non illud statim euertit, sed patitur pullulare. Ita agere solet cum iis Deus, quos iusto suo iudicio ad exitium destinauit: sinit progredi continuò in flagitio, donec tandem in perniciem ruant. Excusat igitur factum tanquam extraordinarium: Vt non sit quod Papistæ sumptus vel profusiones potius, quæ fiunt in templis ipsorum,hoc exemplo excusent. Fuit enim hoc factum extraordinarium affirmante illud Christo: figurabat enim breui futuram ipsius sepulturam: At illi trahunt ad ordinarias profusiones in res superfluas ac inutiles. Notandum etiam, quòd Maria,quum hoc ageret, præsenserit mortem Christi & sepulturam breui futuram: atque ex hac quidem præsensione tota fuit illa voluptas in Christo cui pro peccatis mundi simul & ipsius moriendum fuit.Caiaphas quoque prophetauit illi moriendum,sed lato discrimine: Caiaphas consilium dedit. At verò Maria, vt & pij omnes quotquot vnquam in eum crediderunt,damnarunt illud factum. Nam hoc tenendum fundamenti loco,Quotquot virtute mortis Christi vnquam senserunt, mortem & crucifixionem illam, vt à sceleratis erat manibus, nunquam approbarunt. Sic enim Petrus sceleratas vocat manus eorum qui Christum in crucem egerunt. Pauperes enim. Tum respondet præextui illi, quo vsi sunt pauperum: significat autem extraordinarias istas impensas esse. Deinceps autem post discessum ipsius erogandum esse pauperibus. Neque se iā postquam ascenderit in cœlos, voluptatem capturum ex sumptuoso aliquo cultu, cuiusmodi est iste Papistarum hodierno die,verùm simplici. Sumptus autem superfluos, & quod redundat erogandum esse in pauperes.
units.tr: Jesus therefore said, "Leave her alone." Those who serve Christ must not be harassed, even though the world cannot grasp what they are doing. For the rest, says Paul, let no one cause me trouble, for I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus Christ in my body. Then he excuses the deed, where you may note his moderation. For at once he sets against Judas his thieving spirit, and he did not wish to draw him back from that wicked deed to which he was destined, but allowed him to go on to where he was heading. The foundation of the deed and of the betrayal was avarice. He did not at once overturn it, but let it sprout. God usually deals in this way with those whom by his just judgment he has destined to destruction: he lets them go on continually in wickedness until at last they fall to their ruin. He therefore excuses the deed as extraordinary, so that the Papists cannot use this example to excuse their expenses, or rather their extravagances, which are made in their temples. For this deed was extraordinary, since Christ affirmed it: he was foreshadowing his burial, which was soon to come. But they drag it into ordinary extravagance on superfluous and useless things. It is also to be noted that Mary, in doing this, foresaw the death of Christ and his burial, which was soon to come; and from this foreknowledge all her joy was in Christ, for whom it was necessary to die for the sins of the world and for his own sake as well. Caiaphas too prophesied that he must die, but with a wide difference: Caiaphas gave counsel. But Mary, like all the godly who have ever believed in him, condemned that deed. For this must be held as a foundation: all who have ever felt the power of the death of Christ have never approved that death and crucifixion, insofar as it came from wicked hands. Thus Peter calls wicked the hands of those who drove Christ to the cross. For the poor. Then he answers that pretext which they used about the poor; but he signifies that these were extraordinary expenses. And afterwards, after his departure, the poor must be given what is to be spent. Nor, once he has ascended into heaven, will he take pleasure in any sumptuous display of worship, such as that of the Papists today, but in a simple one. Superfluous expenses, and whatever overflows, must be given to the poor.

units.la: 9 Cognouit ergo turba multa ex Iudæis eum illic esse: & venerunt non propter Iesum tantum,sed etiam vt Lazarum viderent, quem excitarat à mortuis.
units.tr: 9 So a great crowd of the Jews learned that he was there, and they came not only because of Jesus, but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead.

units.la: 10 Consultarunt autem primarij sacerdotes, vt Lazarum etiam trucidarent:
units.tr: 10 But the chief priests took counsel to kill Lazarus also,

units.la: 11 Quia multi ex Iudæis propter eum abibant, & credebant in Iesum.
units.tr: 11 because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.

units.la: HOc ex curiositate quadam factum est: nam vbi fe-mel fax Euangelij accensa est,confluunt multi:sed multi sunt qui non nisi curiositatis causa confluunt, vt admirentur & obstupescant, voluptatique in externis vel verbis vel factis capiant. Admirabilis, fateor, est Christus, teste Esaia: mirabilia sunt dicta & facta eius: sed si non fuerit nisi admiratio & stupor quidam, profecto ij qui hodierno die admirantur, fortasse cras die eum persequentur: vt à Nazaraeis factum legimus, qui primum mirati sunt verba illa gratiosa, quae profecta sunt ex ore eius, deinde paulo post ita offensi sunt in eo, vt cum è montis summitate dare praecipitem voluerint. Luc. 4. 29. Quare vnà cum admiratione externarum rerum oportet esse sensum internae gratiae, & eo animo ad Christum accedere debemus nos qui peccatores sumus, vt ex plenitudine eius accipiamus nonnihil: quo quidem animo ad eum peccatrix mulier, quae lachrymis lauit pedes ipsius. Sed hoc notandum, quod Lazarum etiam videre voluerint. Voluit enim Dominus Lazarum, in quo est editum illud miraculum, quiddam stupendum & esse & manere: vt eo viso atque audito ad Christum adducerentur homines. Consultarunt autem. Hoc effectum est proximè superioris: Consilium etiam vt Lazarum trucidarent. Saeviunt homines non in Christum, non in Deum solum: sed in omnia quae inserviunt divinae gloriae, idque Dei & Christi ipsius causa. Nam persequutoribus perpetuò res est cum Deo primùm: neque vnquam persecutio Ecclesiae esset nisi Dei eiusque nominis causa. Notandum verò, quòd qui persequuntur, sint ij quos minime omnium oportuit, Sacerdotes, Pharisaei, typi videlicet Christi, assertores legis divinae. Ex omnibus inimicis & hostibus Dei gravissimi sunt ij qui falsò vendicant sibi titulos ecclesiasticorum hominum, ac authores sunt malitiae aliorum: Insputant enim aliquid in aliorum animos ex felle illo amaritudinis, quo ipsi toti oppleti sunt.
units.tr: This happened from a certain curiosity. For once the torch of the Gospel is lit, many flock together. But there are many who flock together only from curiosity, to wonder and be astonished, and who take pleasure in outward words or deeds. Christ is admirable, I admit, as Isaiah testifies: his words and deeds are wonderful. But if there is nothing in it but a certain wonder and amazement, then surely those who today admire him will perhaps tomorrow persecute him, as we read was done by the Nazarenes, who at first wondered at the gracious words that proceeded from his mouth, and then shortly after were so offended at him that they wanted to throw him headlong from the summit of the mountain. Luke 4.29. Therefore we who are sinners must approach Christ with a sense of inner grace together with the admiration for outward things, and with that mind to receive something of his fullness; with which mind the sinful woman came to him, who washed his feet with her tears. But this is to be noted: that they wished also to see Lazarus. For the Lord willed that Lazarus, in whom that miracle was displayed, should both be and remain something astonishing, so that by seeing and hearing him men might be brought to Christ. But they took counsel. This followed directly from what was said before: they also took counsel to kill Lazarus. Men rage not only against Christ and against God, but against everything that serves the divine glory, and this for the sake of God and Christ himself. For persecutors always have to do with God first; nor would there ever be persecution of the Church except for the sake of God and his name. It is to be noted, however, that those who persecute are the very ones who least of all ought to do so: priests and Pharisees, namely the types of Christ, the defenders of the divine law. Of all the enemies and foes of God, the most grievous are those who falsely claim for themselves the titles of churchmen and are the authors of others' malice. For they infuse into the minds of others something from that gall of bitterness with which they themselves are entirely filled.

units.la: Postero die turba multa quae venerat ad festum, cum audissent Iesum venire Hierosolymam,
units.tr: On the next day a great crowd that had come to the festival, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem,

units.la: 13 Acceperunt termites palmarum, & prodierunt ei obviam, & clamabant Hosanna, Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini, Rex ille Israelis.
units.tr: 13 They took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, and cried, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel."

units.la: SEquitur profectio Christi Hierosolyma versus: primum autem de iis agitur, qui eunt ei obuiam: sunt autem non quidem cives Hierosolymorum, qui in conspectu habuerunt perpetuo templum, sacrificia, & religionis exercitia, non sacerdotes ipsi, non Pharisaei legis interpretes. Nam in hoc obtinet illud vulgatum, Qui templo praesentiores, eo fere absentiores a Deo: ac multitudo est & turba quae ascendit ad Pascha celebrandum: quod si hi, quorum maxime interest, Christum nolunt agnoscere, profecto hi, quorum non tam interest, id faciunt: quod si proue-ctiores nolunt facere, at pueri & infantes id facient. Id quod etiam factum est hoc tempore, cum Domino in templo acclamaret pueri Hosanna filio Dauidis: & Christus factu defenderet, Nunquam, inquit, legistis quod ex ore infantium ac lactentium perfecisti laudem? ibidem. Imo lapides ipsi id facient, si homines cessaue-rint, ut dixit Dominus eodem illo tempore, Si hi, inquit, silauerint, mox lapides clamabunt. Quanquam hi ipsi qui ingressi sunt, nonnisi impetu quodam abrepti sunt ad id faciendum: demus igitur operam, ut quando egredimur ad Christum glorificandum, id faciamus animo constanti, & ex proposito perseuerandi. Quae autem causa cur egressa sit turba? Audierunt, inquit, ipsum aduentare. Sparsus est rumor aduentus eius in urbem, imo secreto quodam motu, tum excitati sunt animi eorum. Cuius id antehac non euenit, cum Dominus iam antea saepius ingressus sit in urbem, nemo tamen iuit ei obuiam, nemo excepit laetis acclamationibus, aut regem salutauit? Respondeo, Dominus hoc primum tempore voluit ingredi ut Rex, voluit crucem auspicari a gloria, voluit regem se ostendere, antequam sacerdotis partes in altari crucis peragerent, ut agnoscerent homines Dominum gloriae crucifixum esse. Atque hinc fuit, ut secreta illa vis regiae authoritatis excitarit animos multitudinis ad eum tanquam regem excipiendum. Vt enim cum nouus aliquis rex terrenus ingreditur in urbem aliquam, populus vniuersus concitatur ad eum excipiendum cum strepitu & tubae sonitu: ita excitantur hoc tempore Christi, Spiritus quadam interna efficacia. Ea enim est efficacia procedens a Christo, si quando se tanquam rege mundo vult ostendere vt omnes excitentur: & in extremo illo die, cum venturus est vt iudex, concutientur & dissoluentur a facie eius caeli & terra. At quomodo instructa multitudo egreditur? acceperunt, inquit, ramos palmarum. Hoc soliti sunt facere in festo tabernaculorum celebrando vt ostenderent laetitiam suam ob memoriam beneficij praeteriti, quod post liberationem & exitum ex Aegypto fecerit Dominus eos habitare in tabernaculis. Sic hoc quoque tempore similem laetitiam ostendit populus, cum nouum suum Regem Christum exciperet. Ergo ita instructa multitudo ei occurrit, & obuiam venit.
units.tr: SWhat follows is Christ's journey toward Jerusalem. First, we consider those who go out to meet him. These are not the citizens of Jerusalem, who always had the temple, the sacrifices and the exercises of religion before their eyes, nor the priests themselves, nor the Pharisees, the interpreters of the law. For the common saying holds here: those nearest the temple are often furthest from God. Yet there is a crowd and a throng that goes up to celebrate the Passover. If those who are most concerned do not want to acknowledge Christ, those for whom it matters less will certainly do so. And if their elders refuse, children and infants will do it. This is what happened at this time, when boys in the temple cried out "Hosanna to the son of David" to the Lord, and Christ defended what they did: "Have you never read that from the mouths of infants and sucklings you have brought forth praise?" Ibid. Indeed, the stones themselves will do it if men fall silent, as the Lord said at that same time: "If these," he said, "should be silent, the stones will immediately cry out." Yet those who went in were only carried away by a kind of impulse to do this. Let us therefore take care that, when we go out to glorify Christ, we do so with a steady mind and a resolve to persevere. But what was the reason the crowd went out? "They heard," it says, "that he was coming." The rumour of his arrival spread through the city, and indeed by some secret movement their minds were stirred. Why had this not happened before, since the Lord had already entered the city many times, yet no one went out to meet him, no one received him with joyful acclamations or greeted him as king? I answer: the Lord wished to enter at this time as King. He wished to begin the cross from glory, and to show himself as king before he carried out the priestly part at the altar of the cross, so that people would recognise that the Lord of glory was crucified. Hence it was that this secret power of royal authority stirred the minds of the multitude to receive him as king. For just as when some new earthly king enters a city, the whole people is roused to receive him with noise and the sound of trumpets, so at this time the Spirit of Christ stirs people by a certain inward efficacy. For this is the efficacy that proceeds from Christ whenever he wishes to show himself to the world as king, so that all are roused; and on that last day, when he comes as judge, the heavens and the earth will be shaken and dissolved before his face. But how did the crowd go out, equipped as it was? "They took," it says, "branches of palm trees." They were accustomed to do this in celebrating the Feast of Tabernacles, to show their joy at the memory of the benefit received after the Lord, having freed them and brought them out of Egypt, made them dwell in tents. So at this time too the people showed a similar joy when they received their new King, Christ. Thus the crowd, so equipped, ran to meet him and came out to him.

units.la: Quum autem occurrit laeta acclamatione & quasi cantico eum excipit, Hosanna, inquiens. Vox haec contracta est; integra autem est Psal. 118. 25. Serua nunc. Vsus fuit eius in festo Tabernaculorum. Psalmo autem citato, praedicitur quasi acclamationem hanc futuram hoc tempore. Itaque nunc laeta acclamatione accipiunt nouum regem. Matth. 11. 9. dicitur Hosanna filio Dauid, & Hosanna qui est in altissimis. Marc. 11. 9. Hosanna qui es in altissimis. apud Lucam, cap. 19. verf. 38. nulla fit huius vocis mentio. Quod ad reliquam acclamationem: Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini, Matth. 21. 9. habetur. Marci vero 11. 10. addit, Benedictum regnum patris nostri Dauid. Lucas 19. 38. addit, Pax in caelis, & gloria in locis altissimis. Ex his videmus secreto Dei Spiritus motu turbam agnouisse Christum Regem suum. Quae autem facit omnino tria sunt: Agnoscit salutem pertinere ad Christum Dauidis filium, Hosanna filio Dauid. Deinde precatur salutem, Hosanna o qui es in locis altissimis: Tertio benedicit Christo regi: Benedictus qui venit, &c. Vides igitur materiam gaudij & ineffabilis laetitiae in Christi regno esse: de quo non est cogitandum, nisi cum gaudio, non loquendum nisi cum voce benedictionis & precationis. Semper precandum est, vt aduentiat ipsius regnum vt ipsum perficiatur.
units.tr: When they came to meet him, they received him with a joyful acclamation, almost like a song, saying "Hosanna." This cry is shortened; the full text is in Psalm 118:25: "Save now." It was used at the Feast of Tabernacles. By quoting the psalm, the cry is foretold as one that would be raised at this time. So now they receive the new king with a joyful acclamation. In Matthew 21:9 it is said, "Hosanna to the son of David, and hosanna in the highest." In Mark 11:9, "Hosanna, he who is in the highest." In Luke 19:38 there is no mention of this cry at all. As for the rest of the acclamation, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord," it is found in Matthew 21:9. Mark 11:10 adds, "Blessed is the kingdom of our father David." Luke 19:38 adds, "Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest places." From these we see that the crowd, by the secret motion of God's Spirit, recognised Christ as their King. Their acclamation has three parts. First, they acknowledge that salvation belongs to Christ, the son of David: "Hosanna to the son of David." Then they pray for salvation: "Hosanna, O you who are in the highest places." Third, they bless Christ the King: "Blessed is he who comes," and so on. You see, then, that the matter of joy and inexpressible gladness lies in Christ's kingdom. We should think of it only with joy, and speak of it only with words of blessing and prayer. We must always pray that his kingdom may come, so that it may be brought to perfection.

units.la: 14 Nactus autem Iesus asellum, insedit ei, sicut scriptum est,
units.tr: 14 And Jesus, finding a young donkey, sat upon it, as it is written:

units.la: 15 Ne time filia Sionis: Ecce rex tuus venit, insidens pullo asinae.
units.tr: 15 "Fear not, daughter of Zion: behold, your king comes, sitting on a colt of an ass."

units.la: 16 Hæc autem non cognouerunt discipuli eius primò, sed cum glorificatus esset Iesus, tunc recordati sunt hæc esse scripta de eo, & sese hæc illi præstitisse.
units.tr: 16 His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written of him, and that they had done these things to him.

units.la: HActenus in hac Christi profectione & ingressu in urbem partes fuerunt turbæ: Nunc de ipso Christo agitur. Nactus, inquit, asellum. Historiam pleniorem videre apud alios Matthæi 21. Marc. 11. Luc. 19. Dum appropinquaret Bethphage, &c. In quo hoc tantum nota, delegisse sibi eum non equum, sed asellum cui insideret, ut vel ea re distingueret inter gloriam regis cœlestis, & regum terrestrium, qui delectantur externa pompa & splendore. Confirmatur hoc factum testimonio Prophetæ. Ita Matthæus, ut impleretur, inquit, quod dictum est per Prophetam dicentem, &c. Ergo ut Deus verus videretur in prædictionibus suis, hoc factum est, ut loquitur David, ut tu iustificeris in sermonibus tuis. Hic enim finis est omnium euentuum, nempe ut glorificetur Deus in veritate sua. Porro nihil est quod Christo accidat, quod non idem prædictum; nihil, inquam, ne id quidem quod videri posset mundo animaduersione non ita dignum. Cuiusmodi est illa partitio vestium ipsius, & hoc loco sefio in asello: habent ista singula momentum suum. Praeterea cum videmus euentum rerum singularum quae Christo obtigerunt sic respondere prædictionibus, id nobis persuadere debet hunc ipsum esse Messiam illum, non autem alium. Neque enim vnquam in alio ita completæ sunt prophetiæ, aut etiam implebuntur, etsi Iudæi in suam ipsorum perniciem ad alios de quibus ipsi somniant prophetias istas de Christo detorquere studeant. Hæc autem. Nunc sunt discipulorum partes, quorum ignorantia crassa reprehenditur, vel ex scriptura testimonio proximo. Scriptura enim conuincit ignorantiæ, præsertim eos quorum maxime interest ipsam cognoscere, cuiusmodi erant discipuli Christi tum temporis, qui vel turba ista cæciores videntur fuisse. Quid enim ageret turba ipsi nescierunt. Sed de ignorantia discipulorum quæ fuerit ante Christi glorificationem diximus antea. Tum per correctionem quandam narrat hanc
units.tr: Up to this point in Christ's journey and entry into the city, the crowd has had the parts. Now the account turns to Christ himself. "Finding," it says, "a young donkey." For a fuller account see Matthew 21, Mark 11 and Luke 19: "When he drew near to Bethphage," and so on. Here note only this: he chose for himself not a horse but a young donkey to sit on, so that by this alone he might distinguish the glory of the heavenly King from that of earthly kings, who delight in outward pomp and splendour. This act is confirmed by the testimony of the prophet. Thus Matthew: "that it might be fulfilled," he says, "which was spoken by the prophet, saying," and so on. Therefore, that the true God might be seen in his predictions, this happened, as David says, "that you may be justified in your words." For this is the end of all events, namely that God may be glorified in his truth. Moreover, there is nothing that happens to Christ that was not foretold; nothing, I say, not even what might seem to the world too trivial to notice. Of this kind is the division of his garments, and here the riding on the donkey: each of these has its own weight. Besides, when we see that the events of the particular things that happened to Christ so correspond to the predictions, this ought to persuade us that he is that very Messiah, and no other. For the prophecies were never so completely fulfilled, nor will they be fulfilled, in any other, even though the Jews, to their own destruction, strive to apply those prophecies about Christ to others whom they imagine. "But these things," it says. Now comes the part of the disciples, whose gross ignorance is rebuked, even from the testimony of Scripture just quoted. For Scripture convicts ignorance, especially in those who most need to know the matter, such as the disciples of Christ at that time, who seem to have been even blinder than that crowd. For they themselves did not know what the crowd was doing. But we have already said above what the disciples' ignorance was before Christ's glorification. Then, by a kind of correction, he now tells this whole matter, namely that this Scripture became known to the disciples at its proper time, that is, when Christ was glorified.

units.la: {ignorantia} Discipuli Christi ignoratia. hanc totam rem, vt & scripturam illam innotuisse suo tempore discipulis, nempe cum glorificatus est Christus. Disce igitur omnis notitiae rerum caelestium fonte esse Christi glorificatione. Ex ea enim est Spiritus sanctus, qui illuminat mentes nostras: supra cap.7. Nondum, inquit, erat Spiritus sanctus, quia nondum erat Iesus glorificatus. Ergo Spiritus sanctus procedit ex Christo glorificato. Neque vel fuit, vel futura est vnquam in posterum notitia rerum caelestium, nisi virtute illius glorificationis vel futurae, vel praesentis. Est enim omnis notitia nostra quasi radius quidam ab illo sole gloriae quae est in Christo & humana etiam Christi natura, diffusus in mentes nostras. Sed Spiritus sanctus quo nos ducit? Recordati sunt, inquit, haec esse scripta. Spiritus sanctus ducit nos ad scripturas sacras, iisque tanquam instrumento vtitur ad corda nostra illuminanda. Nota igitur tria hoc loco cognitionis nostrae principia, glorificationem Christi, Spiritum sanctum & verbum Dei scriptum. Spiritus virtute glorificationis operatur, per verbum autem tanquam per instrumentum operatur.
units.tr: {Ignorance} The ignorance of Christ's disciples. Learn, then, that the glorification of Christ is the source of all knowledge of heavenly things. For from it comes the Holy Spirit, who illuminates our minds. Above, in chapter 7: "The Holy Spirit was not yet," he says, "because Jesus was not yet glorified." Therefore the Holy Spirit proceeds from the glorified Christ. Nor has there been, or will there ever be in time to come, any knowledge of heavenly things except by the power of that glorification, whether future or present. For all our knowledge is, as it were, a ray from that sun of glory which is in Christ, and in his human nature too, diffused into our minds. But to what does the Holy Spirit lead us? "They remembered," it says, "that these things were written." The Holy Spirit leads us to the sacred Scriptures and uses them as an instrument to enlighten our hearts. Note, then, the three principles of our knowledge mentioned in this place: the glorification of Christ, the Holy Spirit, and the written Word of God. The Spirit works by the power of the glorification, but works through the Word as through an instrument.

units.la: 17 Testabatur vero turba quae erat cum eo, quod Lazarum vocasset e monumento, & suscitasset eum a mortuis.
units.tr: The crowd that was with him bore witness that he had called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead.

units.la: 18 Propterea etiam occurrit ei turba, quia audierat eum edidisse hoc signum.
units.tr: For this reason also the crowd went out to meet him, because they had heard that he had performed this sign.

units.la: 19 Pharisaei ergo dixerunt inter se, Videtis nos nihil proficere? Ecce, mundus eum sequutus est.
units.tr: So the Pharisees said among themselves, "Do you see that you are gaining nothing? Look, the world has gone after him."

units.la: REdit ad partes turbae, narratque non tantum acclamasse Hosanna, Benedictus, &c. sed praeterea testimonium tulisse de miraculo hoc insigni, in excitando ex mortuis Lazaro: ideoque illi exiuisse obuiam. Luc. 19.37. dicit magna voce laudasse Deum de omnibus virtutibus quas viderant. Iohannes autem hoc loco vnius miraculi ac virtutis vnius praesertim meminit, vtpote maximi miraculi & maximè recentis. Miracula Christi omnia virtute Christi regis fiebant in operibus planè regiis. Iam vero à virtute spirituali, non terrestri aliqua edebantur miracula. Ideoque illum vt regem, non qui
units.tr: He returns to the crowd and relates that they not only shouted "Hosanna," "Blessed," etc., but also bore witness to this remarkable miracle, the raising of Lazarus from the dead, and that this was why they went out to meet him. Luke 19.37 says they praised God with a loud voice for all the mighty works they had seen. John, however, here mentions one miracle and one power in particular, as being the greatest miracle and the most recent. All Christ's miracles were done by the power of Christ the King, and they were clearly royal works. But the miracles were performed by a spiritual power, not by any earthly one. So they received him and glorified him as king, not of an earthly but of a spiritual kingdom.

units.la: Glorificatio Christi fons omnis notitiae salutaris. dem terrestrem, sed spiritualé excipiunt ac glorificant. Totus enim honor iste à turba ei tum delatus, spiritualis est, ad spiritualem regem pertinens, non autem terrestris ac mundanus. Nam quod ad terrestrem hunc honorem, regnum enim ipse renuit supra cap. 6. 15. cùm turba in deserto apprehensum eum regem, ventris sui saginandi gratia constituere ac creare voluisset. Pharisæi ergo. Nunc sunt partes Pharisæorum. Eorum quidem erat imprimis Christum regem excipere, sed illi tantū ab eo absunt, vt contra grauiter ferant honorem hunc ab aliis ipsi deferri. Nam qui non faciunt Deo ipsi officium suū, illi ægre ferunt ab aliis fieri; & qui ipsi nolunt ingredi in regnum cælorum, precludunt aditum ad cælos omnibus aliis quantum in se est. Imò Deo & piis hominibus inuident, vel tantillum honoris ab aliis delati. Inuident honorificam aliquam eorum mentionem; vt supra vidimus, cùm Ministri Pontificum reuersi sunt ac renunciarent, nunquam loquutum hominem vt Christus loqueretur: Num, inquiunt Pharisæi, & vos seducti estis? Iohann. 7.47. Sic postea Nicodemo eius aliquam defensionem suscipienti infensi sunt ibidem. Paulus huius malitiæ & progressus in peccato causam aperit: cùm de his ipsis Iudæis loquitur, à quibus Christus est crucifixus, & qui proprios Prophetas & Apostolos exegerūt: Ira Dei, inquit, occupauit eos ad extremum vsque. Quid inde? Semper, inquit, complent peccata sua: q.d. peccati nullū modum faciunt, donec eius mensuram impleuerint tandē. Nota hic rursus, impij & persecutores nihil proficiunt. Quare, inquit Danid, gentes tumultuantur & populi meditātur inane? Ecce omnia frustra fiunt: id quod ipsi cogüntur confiteri hoc loco. Videtis, inquiunt, vt nihil proficere, ecce mundus eum sequitur. Imò ne tum quidem profecerūt, cùm eum apprehensum crucifixerunt: nam idem gloriosè post statim resurrexit. Neque proficiunt quicquam persequutores Ecclesiæ, etiam cùm videntur triumphare de Ecclesia prostrata eiusque membris, id quod sentient demum extremo illo die quo Ecclesia glorificabitur, ipsi autem confundentur.
units.tr: The glorifying of Christ is the source of all saving knowledge. For the whole honour that the crowd then paid him was spiritual, belonging to a spiritual king, and not earthly or worldly. As for that earthly honour, he himself refused the kingdom, as we saw above in chapter 6.15, when the crowd wanted to seize him as king in the desert and make him king, for the sake of filling their bellies. "The Pharisees, therefore." Now comes the part of the Pharisees. It was certainly their task above all to receive Christ as king, but they are so far from doing so that, on the contrary, they take it badly that this honour is paid to him by others. For those who do not perform their own duty to God are displeased when others do it, and those who themselves refuse to enter the kingdom of heaven block the way to heaven for everyone else as far as they can. Indeed, they begrudge God and godly men even the slightest honour paid to them by others. They begrudge any honourable mention of them, as we saw above, when the officers of the chief priests returned and reported that no man had ever spoken as this man speaks: "Have you too been deceived?" say the Pharisees. John 7.47. So afterwards they were hostile to Nicodemus when he undertook some defence of him there. Paul discloses the cause of this malice and of its progress in sin, when he speaks of these very Jews, by whom Christ was crucified, and who drove out their own prophets and apostles: "The wrath of God," he says, "has come upon them to the uttermost." What follows? "They always fill up their sins," he says, that is, they make no limit to sin until at last they have filled up its measure. Note here again that the wicked and the persecutors gain nothing. "Why," says David, "do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?" Behold, all things are done in vain, which the Pharisees are here compelled to confess: "You see that you are gaining nothing; look, the world has gone after him." Indeed, they did not gain anything even when they seized him and crucified him, for he rose again gloriously straight afterwards. Nor do the persecutors of the Church gain anything, even when they seem to triumph over the Church cast down and over its members. They will feel this at last on that final day when the Church is glorified, while they themselves are confounded.

units.la: 20 Erant autem quidam Græci ex iis qui ascendunt dunt vt adorent in festo.
units.tr: Now there were certain Greeks among those who went up to worship at the feast.

units.la: 21 Isti venerunt ad Philippum, qui erat à Bethsaida Galilaeae, & rogarunt eum, dicentes, Domine, Volumus Iesum videre.
units.tr: These came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, "Sir, we wish to see Jesus."

units.la: 22 Venit Philippus & dicit Andreae: Andreas rursum & Philippus dicunt Iesu.
units.tr: Philip came and told Andrew; then Andrew and Philip told Jesus.

units.la: 23 Iesus autem respondit eis, dicens, Venit hora ut glorificetur filius hominis.
units.tr: But Jesus answered them, saying, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified."

units.la: 24 Amen autem dico vobis, nisi granum frumenti ceciderit in terram, & mortuum fuerit, ipsum solum manet: si vero mortuum fuerit, multum fructum affert.
units.tr: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit."

units.la: 25 Qui amat animam suam, perdet eam, & qui odit animam suam in hoc mundo, in vitam aeternam custodiet eam.
units.tr: "He who loves his life loses it, and he who hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life."

units.la: 26 Si quis mihi ministrat, me sequatur: & ubi ego fuero, illic & minister meus erit: & si quis mihi ministraverit, honorabit eum Pater.
units.tr: "If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my servant will be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honour him."

units.la: HIstoria quaedam est de Graecis qui consueverant adorandi gratia Hierosolyma ascendere. Haec autem adiecta est, vt ostendatur quàm admirabilis fuerit Christus, & vt ostendatur quàm admirabilis fuerit Christus, & vt aeternatur via sequenti ipsius concioni Christi. Quod autem desiderant Graeci Christum videre, id magis ex curiositate quadam fuit, quàm studio participandi gratiae eius. Nobis autem videndum est, vt Deus Pater trahat nos ad Christum, non autem studium novitatis: hoc est, vt impulsi sensu peccati ac miseriae nostrae Christum adeamus. Venite, inquit, ad me omnes qui fatigati estis & onerati, & ego faciam vt requiescatis. Rursus allecti sensu dulcedinis & gratiae ipsius; Expetamus lac illud sincerum, si modo gustavimus quàm benignus sit Dominus. Haec duo sunt, quae excitant in nobis mirificam sitim ac desiderium admirabile praesentiae eius. Nos, inquit Paulus, qui primitias Spiritus habemus apud nosipsos suspiramus adoptionem expectantes no-stram,id est,redemptionem corporis nostri. Venit Phi-lippus. In Philippo & Andrea perspicimus quidem humanitatem, sed ignorantiam rursus satis crassam, qui Christum voluerunt esse in externa ista hominum admiratione, quasi vero ille ab hominibus gloriam caperet. Sed errorem eorum verba Christi indicant, Corrigit enim eos his verbis: Venit tempus quo glorificetur filius hominis.q. diceret: Non requiro gloriam ab hominibus, neq; postulo vt in admiratione sim apud homines, praesertim cum propediem futurum sit, vt ego vera illa ac caelesti gloria glorificer a Patre meo. Qui nondum viderunt caelestem illam gloriam, de alia non cogitant quàm terrestri ista. At qui caelestem vel gloriam, vel divitias, vel voluptates inspexerunt semel, illi quidem non tanti faciunt mundum hunc, gloriam huius mundi, divitias huius mundi, voluptates huius mundi: ignominiam, paupertatem, &c. mirapatientia tolerant. Abraham, Isaac & Iacob contenti sunt habitare tam diu in terra non sua, in tabernaculis. Quae autem expectabant ciuitatem illam habentem fundamenta, cuius artifex & conditor est Deus. Quotquot autem toti sunt in venanda gloria huius mundi & captandis diuitiis, illi profecto satis produnt se non vidisse quae sit gloria, quae opes illae caelestes, aut oculos supra ista terrena nondum eleuasse.
units.tr: There is a story about the Greeks who used to go up to Jerusalem to worship. It is added so that the greatness of Christ may be shown, and so that his following sermon may be made more attentive. As for the Greeks' desire to see Christ, this arose more from a certain curiosity than from zeal to share in his grace. But we ought to see to it that the Father draws us to Christ, and not a desire for novelty; that is, that, moved by a sense of our sin and misery, we come to Christ. "Come to me," he says, "all you who are weary and heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matt. 11:28). Again, we are drawn by a sense of his sweetness and grace: "Let us desire the pure milk, if indeed we have tasted how gracious the Lord is" (1 Pet. 2:2–3). These two things stir in us a wonderful thirst and an admirable longing for his presence. Paul says, "We who have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan inwardly as we wait for adoption, the redemption of our bodies" (Rom. 8:23). "Philip came." In Philip and Andrew we indeed see humanity, but again a rather gross ignorance, since they wished Christ to be found in that external admiration of men, as if he sought glory from men. But the words of Christ point out their error, for he corrects them with these words: "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified." As if he said: I do not seek glory from men, nor do I ask to be admired among men, especially since it will shortly come to pass that I shall be glorified by my Father with that true and heavenly glory. Those who have not yet seen that heavenly glory think of nothing but this earthly glory. But those who have once looked upon heavenly glory, or riches, or pleasures, do not esteem this world, the glory of this world, the riches of this world, the pleasures of this world, as much as they should; they endure disgrace, poverty, and so on with wonderful patience. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were content to dwell for so long in a land not their own, in tents, because they looked for the city which has foundations, whose architect and builder is God (Heb. 11:9–10). But all who are wholly intent on hunting the glory of this world and seizing riches clearly show that they have not seen what true glory is, nor what those heavenly riches are, nor have they yet lifted their eyes above these earthly things.

units.la: Amen dico vobis. Innuit per correctionem quandam moriendum sibi esse priusquam glorificaretur, simulque mortis scandalum aufert, similitudine quadam significans tantum abfuturam ab eo mortem ipsius, vt gloriam illam ipsius futuram imminuat, vt e contra eam fit mirifice auctura. Vt enim granum frumenti nisi ceciderit in terram, & mortuum fuerit, non fructificat, &c. Ita ego nisi prius mortuus fuero, tam gloriosus euadere non potero. Sin mortuus fuero, gloriosus exurgam, instar culmi qui enascitur ex emortuo semine: & gloriam meam late diffundam in omnes, omnibusque ero tanquam fructus quidam quo vescentur, non secus ac spica ac frumentum. Vide hic Christi mortem tantum abesse ab eo vt gloriam ipsius impediat, vt e contra promoueat eam quàm maximè, atque adeo nobis quoque eam inseruire faciat. Expedit, inquit, vobis vt ego abeam, nisi enim abiero, Consolator ille non veniet ad vos. Si autem profectus fuero, mittam eum ad vos. Disce etiam hic mortem nostram nihil aliud esse quàm sementum quoddam nostri. Ita enim loquitur Apostolus, Seminatur corpus corruptionis, non ...
units.tr: "Truly, truly, I say to you." By a certain correction he hints that he must die before he is glorified, and at the same time he removes the scandal of death, signifying by a kind of likeness that his death will be so far from diminishing his future glory that, on the contrary, it will wonderfully increase it. For just as a grain of wheat, unless it falls into the earth and dies, does not bear fruit, and so on, so unless I first die, I shall not be able to become so glorious. But if I die, I shall rise glorious, like the stalk that springs up from the dead seed, and I shall spread my glory widely among all, and I shall be to all as a fruit on which they may feed, just as the ear and the grain are. See here that the death of Christ is so far from hindering his glory that, on the contrary, it advances it as much as possible, and so makes it serve us also. "It is expedient for you that I go away," he says, "for unless I go away, that Comforter will not come to you. But if I depart, I will send him to you" (John 16:7). Learn here also that our death is nothing other than a sowing of ours. For the Apostle speaks thus: "It is sown a perishable body, it is raised..." (1 Cor. 15:42).

units.la: Sed vt seminemus vnà cum Christo viuendum est: nam si complantati sumus cum eo, conformatione mortis eius, nimirum etiam resurrectionis conformatione coalescemus, nam nisi cum eo seminemur & plantemur, cum eo non resurgemus. Visus etiam mortis nostrae quotquot sumus Christi membra hic addisci potest.
units.tr: But if we are to sow together with Christ, we must live together with him. For if we have been planted together with him in the likeness of his death, we shall certainly also grow together in the likeness of his resurrection. Unless we are sown and planted with him, we shall not rise with him. The likeness of our death, as many of us as are Christ's members, can also be learned here.

units.la: Est autem vt renascamur quasi & reuiuiscamus. Paulus enim in morte eam necessitatem ponit ad vitam, vt nisi moriamur aut certè mutemur aliquo modo, non reuiuiscamus. Demens, inquit, quod tu seminas non viuificit nisi mortuum fuerit. Experientia etiam ipsa pij quique in hac vita discant eum esse mortis visum: nam mortificatione nostri quae est in hac vita eò pertinere experimur: sicut Paulus ait, Externus noster homo corrumpitur: sed interinus renouatur quotidie. Qui amat animam suam. Secundò occurrit mortis scandalo, quasi dicat, tantùm abesse vos oportet ab eo vt offendamini cruce mea, vt eam imitari debeatis. Qui enim amat animam suam, subaudi melius quàm me, perdet eam: hoc enim comparatè accipiendum est, vt & id quod sequitur: Qui odit. Tantum itaque abesse ab eo debemus vt morte Christi aut afflictione seruorum ipsius offendamur: vt etiam eligamus pariter cum iis mori & affligi. Christus, cùm Petrus offenderetur, praedicta à se cruce sua, postquam eum verbo reprehendit, Si quis, inquit ei, vult post me venire, abneget seipsum & crucem suam tollat ac sequatur me. q.d. Offenderis quidem tu Petre, praedictione ista crucis meae; sed nisi sustuleris crucem tuam, non eris me dignus, neque aptus qui me sequaris. Sic Paulus Timotheo, Ne pudeat, inquit, te testimonij Domini nostri; Neque te pudeat mei, qui captivus sum ipsius: sed esto particeps afflictionum Euangelij ex potentia Dei. Imòvel ea re honorari nos existimare debemus, si affligamur Christi causa, vt Apostoli exiftimârunt: qui postquam caesi essent ac dimissi, gaudentes profecti sunt à conspectu concilij, quòd digni habiti essent qui pro nomine Iesu contumelia afficerentur. Et Paulus ad Phi-lippenses, Vobis datum est, inquit, in Christi negotio, non modò in eum credere, sed etiam pro eo affligi. E con-trà autem Dominus animat eos ad crucem. Qui odit, animam suam. Odit, inquam, comparate. Nam quando amor Dei & nostri ipsorum non possunt consistere, tum amor Dei, odium autem animae nostrae esse debet. Videntur prima facie contraria esse ista, odisse animam & custodire eam. Verum, contextus ipse satis rē expedit: dicit enim, custodiet eam in vitam aeternā. Ergo qui odit animam quod ad hanc vitam, seruat eam quòd ad aeterna. Ergo dum exponimus periculo vitam hanc, videndum vt eam cum meliori vita permutemus. Neque enim temerè animam & vitam istam debemus prodigere, sed consideranda est diligenter causa, vt honesta ac iusta de causa, praesertim religionis & Christi eam profundamus. Neque enim prius abiiciendā est ista vita quàm de meliori constituerit, & eam cum aeterna illa commutemus. Non quidem quod profusio huius vitae digna sit aeterna illa. Non sunt paria quae praesenti tempore perpetimur futurae gloriae in nobis retegendae: sed quòd in eum qui vitam suam obtulit ideo, vt nos in aeternum viuamus, profundamus hanc vitam. Vita Christi oblata vel sola promerita est nobis vitam. Nos pro eo vitam nostram exponere debemus vt ei grati videamur, qui ideo mortuus est & resurrexit, vt viuentibus & mortuis dominetur. Si quis mihi ministrat. Tertiò, remo-uet scandalum. q. d. Tantū abesse debet ab eo, vestram damini cruce mea, vt è contra si velitis mihi ministrare, oporteat vos crucem vestram tollere, & sequi me: nam sequi Christum, est crucem suam tollere, & abnegare ipsum ac sequi Christum. vide Matth. 16. cap. Quo loco dicit, Si quis vult post me venire abneget seipsum, & tollat crucem suam & sequatur me. Volunt quidem omnes in otio & in omnium rerum affluentia ministrare Christo & Hierosolymis securè sedentes, videre egredientem Christum ex urbe, & crucem suam portantem. At verò vt insequias Christo, necesse est sequaris eum cum cruce tua ad mortem ipsam vel ignominiosissimam. Exea-mus, mus, inquit Apostolus, extra castrum opprobrium eius portantes. Et ubi ego fuero, illic. Ne putent se sine mercede ministraturos Christo, ostendit quae sit futura conditio eorum. Primum quoad locum in quo sunt habituri: deinde quoad aestimationē in eo loco futuram. Quoad locum: Vbi ego fuero, inquit, illic minister meus erit. Hoc precibus petit a Patre cap.17. Quoad aestimationem vero, honorabit, inquit, eum Pater. Nemo igitur frustra inseruit Domino, verum merces cuiusque est magna. Id autem quotquot vident putant illi quidem maiores divitias esse in afflictionibus quas sustinent Domini causa, quam quae sunt in toto hoc mundo, ut de Mose dicitur, quod putarit maiores divitias probrum Christi, quā thesauros Ægyptiorum. Et quae causa? Intuebatur enim in praemij largitionem. Quorum vero oculi non aperiuntur ad hoc videndum aliquo certè modo, id nūquā expectant futurum, & incredibile iis videtur. Atque inde est quod mundus nihil velit pati Christi causa, quod nullam aliam gloriam videant, quàm mundi istam gloriam: qua amissa putant de omni gloria actum esse.
units.tr: Now we are reborn, as it were, and brought back to life. For Paul makes death the necessary condition of life, so that unless we die, or at least are changed in some way, we shall not be brought back to life. Foolish man, what you sow is not made alive unless it dies. Let every godly person also learn in this life that there is a likeness of death, through experience itself: for we experience this in the mortification of ourselves, which is found in this life. As Paul says, Our outward man is decaying, but our inward man is renewed day by day. He who loves his life is the second answer to the scandal of death, as if he were saying: you must be so far from being offended by my cross that you ought to imitate it. For whoever loves his life, that is, loves it more than me, will lose it. This must be understood comparatively, as is also the case with what follows: whoever hates (his life). We ought therefore to be so far from being offended by the death of Christ or the affliction of his servants that we choose to die and suffer with them. When Peter was offended by Christ's prediction of his cross, Christ rebuked him in words and said: If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross and follow me. That is, you are indeed offended, Peter, by this prediction of my cross; but unless you take up your cross, you will not be worthy of me, nor fit to follow me. So Paul to Timothy: Do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me, his prisoner; but share in the afflictions of the gospel by the power of God. Indeed, we ought rather to think ourselves honoured if we are afflicted for Christ's sake, as the apostles thought, who, after they had been beaten and dismissed, departed rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus. And Paul to the Philippians: It has been granted to you in the cause of Christ, he says, not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him. On the contrary, the Lord encourages them to the cross: whoever hates his life. I say "hates" comparatively. For when the love of God and of ourselves cannot stand together, then the love of God must prevail and hatred must be felt toward our own life. These statements seem at first sight contradictory, to hate one's soul and to keep it. But the context itself explains the matter sufficiently: for it goes on, he will keep it unto eternal life. So whoever hates his soul as regards this life keeps it as regards eternal life. Therefore, while we expose this life to danger, we must see to it that we exchange it for a better life. For we ought not to squander this life and soul rashly, but the cause must be carefully considered, so that we spend them for an honourable and just cause, especially for religion and Christ. Nor should this life be cast away before we have decided on a better one, and exchanged it for that eternal life. Not that the spending of this life is worthy of that eternal life: the sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed in us. But we spend this life on him who offered his own life so that we might live for ever. The offered life of Christ alone has merited life for us. We ought to expose our lives for him, so that we may appear grateful to him who therefore died and rose again, that he might be lord of both the living and the dead. If anyone serves me. Thirdly, he removes the scandal. That is, you ought to be so far from being offended by my cross that, on the contrary, if you wish to serve me, you must take up your cross and follow me. For to follow Christ is to take up one's cross, and to deny oneself and follow Christ. See Matthew 16, where he says, If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross and follow me. All men indeed wish to serve Christ in idleness and in an abundance of all things, sitting safely in Jerusalem, and to see Christ going out of the city carrying his cross. But to follow Christ truly, you must follow him with your cross, even to death, however shameful it may be. Let us go out, says the apostle, outside the camp, bearing his reproach. And where I am, there. So that they may not think they will serve Christ without reward, he shows what their condition will be: first as to the place where they will be, and then as to the esteem they will have in that place. As to the place: where I am, he says, there my servant will be. He asks this of the Father in prayer in chapter 17. As to the esteem, the Father, he says, will honour him. No one therefore serves the Lord in vain, but each one's reward is great. Those who see this think indeed that the riches in the afflictions which they endure for the Lord's sake are greater than all that is in this world, as it is said of Moses that he considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt. And why? For he looked to the recompense of the reward. But those whose eyes are not opened to see this in some way, never expect it to come, and it seems incredible to them. And hence it is that the world wishes to suffer nothing for Christ's sake, because they see no glory other than this worldly glory; having lost it, they think all glory is at an end.

units.la: 27 Nunc anima mea turbata est, & quid dicam? Pater, liberame ab hac hora: sed propterea veni in horam hanc.
units.tr: 27 Now my soul is troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause I came to this hour.

units.la: 28 Pater, glorifica nomen tuum. Venit ergo vox è cælo, dicens, Et glorificavi & rursus glorificabo.
units.tr: 28 Father, glorify your name. Then came a voice from heaven, saying, I have both glorified it and will glorify it again.

units.la: INcidit in eum repentina perturbatio & subitus quidem sensus ita Dei: ideo interpellat sermone, & conqueritur de ea. Non fuit quidem ista perturbatio leuis, aut vulgaris aliqua animi molestia, qualis solet incidere in nos vulgò, & cuiusmodi quoque per naturam humanam obnoxius fuit Christus: Sed fuit oppressio illa & angustia de qua Apostolus Rom. 2. cum de inferis loquitur, Oppressio & angustia aduersus omnem animam hominis perpetrantis malum. Luc.22, vocatur ἀγωνία, quam ipse Christus expressit Matth. 26.38. Marc.14.34. Vnde quaque tristis est anima mea vsque ad mortem. Verum vt de ea re paulò particulariūs dicamus, sita fuit partim in praesenti dolore, partim in metu graviori. Praesens dolor fuit ex praesenti eoque vehementissimo sensu in omnibus facultatibus animi : horribilis irae divinae. Verum ex verbis Marci 14. 33. partes eius designari possunt. Coepit, inquit, Iesus ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι καὶ ἀδημονεῖν, expavescere & gravissime angi. Ergo positus fuit praesens dolor in pauore quodam primum, deinde in angore summo. Pauor fuit, ex subito ac veloci sensu irae vehementissimae in omnibus animae facultatibus. Initium enim inferorum solet esse a subita commotione. Cum dicent, inquit Apostolus, Pax & tuta omnia, tum repentinum immineat exitium. Exemplo est Belsazar. Experiuntur idem reprobi omnes in separatione illa misera animae & corporis. Gravissimus angor autem ex eo apparuit quod omnes animae facultates propter incumbentem iram reliquerunt functiones suas, abreptaque sunt ad succurrendum communi dolori. Ipse autem oblitus est ad tempus operis redemptionis, & concussus totus ineffabili horrore divini indicii, occupabatur tota in eo. Haec autem proveniebant non ex peccato, sed ex mera natura infirmitate. De metu autem maioris iudicii impendentis, vide Heb. 5. 7. Fuit autem metus iste maioris irae magisque impendentis: ea enim reprobo rum apud inferos conditio est, quod metuent sibi perpetuo a maiori iudicio & ira impendente: & ea erit natura illius irae, quae nunquam perficietur. Verum vis irae insequens praecedentem continuo excipiet. Iam vero dolor iste & metus, & omnino ἀγωνία, quam sensit, penitus animo perspecta fuit in precibus, ac iis quidem intensis, imo coniunctis cum strenuis clamoribus & lachrymis. Perspecta fuit in sudore qui fuit quasi grumi sanguinis descendentes in terram. Si quaeras quid interea agebat Deitas: an tum distracta fuit ab humana in Christo natura? Respondeo non fuisse distractam, sed continuisse se eam, donec pateretur natura humana: quod si enim se exeruisset in gloria sua, tum pati eum impossibile fuisset. Sed ad institutum ista accommodanda sunt, videlicet quae verba ex quibus perpessionibus & commotionibus sunt profecta. Primum autem est quaerimonia illa, Vndequaque tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem. Sed enim in graui angore huiusmodi voces, lamentationes
units.tr: A sudden disturbance fell upon him, and a sudden sense of God's [anger]; therefore he speaks and complains about it. This disturbance was indeed no slight or ordinary vexation of the mind, such as commonly falls upon us, and such as Christ too was subject to through human nature. It was rather that oppression and anguish of which the apostle speaks in Romans 2 when he speaks of hell: Oppression and anguish upon every soul of man that does evil. In Luke 22 it is called agony, which Christ himself expressed in Matthew 26:38 and Mark 14:34: My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death. But to speak of this matter somewhat more particularly: it consisted partly in present sorrow and partly in greater fear. The present sorrow was from a present and most vehement sense, in all the faculties of the mind, of the dreadful wrath of God. Its parts can, however, be indicated from the words of Mark 14:33. Jesus, he says, began to be greatly amazed and to be very heavy (ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι καὶ ἀδημονεῖν), to be astonished and to be sorely distressed. The present sorrow therefore consisted first in a kind of terror, and then in extreme anguish. The terror arose from a sudden and swift sense of the most violent wrath in all the powers of the soul. For the beginning of hell is usually a sudden shock. When they shall say, says the apostle, Peace and safety, then sudden destruction comes upon them. Belshazzar is an example. All the reprobate experience the same in that miserable separation of soul and body. The extreme anguish, moreover, appeared from this, that because of the wrath bearing down upon him, all the faculties of the soul abandoned their functions, and were drawn away to help with the common sorrow. He himself, for a time, forgot the work of redemption, and, shaken entirely by the unspeakable horror of divine judgement, was wholly occupied with it. These things arose not from sin, but from mere natural weakness. As to the fear of the greater judgement impending, see Hebrews 5:7. This fear was of a greater wrath and one more imminent: for it is the condition of the reprobate in hell that they fear perpetually a greater judgement and wrath impending upon them, and such will be the nature of that wrath, which will never be finished. But the force of the wrath that follows will continually succeed the preceding. Now this sorrow and fear, and altogether the agony which he felt, was fully displayed in his prayers, and indeed in intense ones, joined even with vigorous cries and tears. It was displayed in a sweat which was like drops of blood falling down to the ground. If you ask what the Deity meanwhile was doing: was it then separated from the human nature in Christ? I answer that it was not separated, but restrained itself until human nature suffered; for if it had revealed itself in its glory, it would have been impossible for him to suffer. But these things must be applied to our purpose, namely, which words proceeded from the sufferings and the commotions. The first is that complaint: My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death. But in such severe anguish, cries and lamentations are wrung from us.

units.la: Luc. 22. 44. tiones & querelæ nobis exprimi. Notanda tamen quedam temperies: neque enim est huiusmodi vox insana & desperationis plena, cuiusmodi sunt voces improborum apud inferos. Quid dicam? Vox hæc existit ex summa perplexitate & anxietate animi. Nam in angore summo est summa perplexitas, adeo ut quis vel quid dicat, vel quid faciat plane nesciat. Dominus quidem inuenit euasionem. At reproborum hæc erit vox perpetua, Quid dicam? Quid faciam? Quia ex illa perplexitate & angore nunquam explicabuntur.
units.tr: Luc. 22. 44. Laments and complaints are expressed in us. Yet a certain restraint must be noted here: this cry is not mad and full of despair, as are the cries of the wicked in the underworld. What shall I say? This cry arises from the utmost perplexity and anxiety of mind. For in extreme anguish there is extreme perplexity, so that a person plainly does not know what to say or what to do. The Lord indeed finds a way out. But for the reprobate this will be a perpetual cry, What shall I say? What shall I do? because they will never be released from that perplexity and anguish.

units.la: Pater, conserua. Vox hæc existit ex obliuione quadam operis suscepti redemptionis humanæ. Nam ex agonia est obliuio omnium rerum, nisi præsentis doloris: conuertit tamen se ad Patrem: quo significatur non desitum fuisse cum omni plane sensu paternæ dilectionis. Neque enim quis inuocat Patrem nisi ex sensu dilectionis eius. Reprobi apud inferos nunquam se ad Deum conuertent ad deprecandum poenā, quia nullo sensu amoris eius afficientur; E contra vero nihil præter extremam iram sensuri sunt in æternum. Sed propterea veni. Vox est se memoriamque suam quocunque modo colligentis. Similis est illi, Verum non quid ego velim, sed quid tu: Marc. 14.36. Ego velim, nimirum, ex infirmitate naturæ humanæ, quæ tamen est sine peccato. Sensus est, Propterea veni in hanc horā, id est, propter hanc ipsam causam, ut patiar missus sum. Reprobi apud inferos nunquam ita sese colligent, verum in æternum occupabuntur in dolore. Pater, glorifica. Prius, oblitus operis ad quod perficiendum missus est, occupatus fuit in leuando præsenti dolore, deprecatúsque est iram Patris. Nunc vero contrà oblitus cogitat de gloria paterna, exoptátq; eam etiam cum passione & morte sua. Ita contingere solet piis sæpe in afflictionibus grauioribus. Ad tempus obliuiscuntur rerum aliarum, & cogitat de præsenti dolore. At vero rursus eriguntur & obliti sui de Deo cogitant, déque eius gloria. Quid deiicis te, anima mea? inquit Dauid, Spera in Domino. Reprobi apud inferos perpetuò sui erunt memores, nunquam vero gloriæ diuinæ, quā nullo vnquam tempore hoc modo exoptabunt. Imò vero sui liberationem expetent cum iactura, si fieri posset,
units.tr: Father, preserve me. This cry arises from a certain forgetfulness of the work of human redemption that he had undertaken. For in agony all things are forgotten except the present pain. Yet he turns himself to the Father, which signifies that his sense of the Father's love had not failed him in any way at all. For no one calls upon the Father except from a sense of his love. The reprobate in the underworld will never turn to God to plead for relief from punishment, because they will feel nothing of his love; on the contrary, they will feel nothing but his extreme wrath for ever. But for this reason I came. This is a cry of one gathering himself and his thoughts together in whatever way he can. It is like that other saying, Not what I will, but what you will: Mark 14.36. "I will," that is, from the weakness of human nature, which nevertheless is without sin. The sense is: For this reason I came to this hour, that is, for this very cause I was sent, that I should suffer. The reprobate in the underworld will never gather themselves in this way, but will be occupied with pain for ever. Father, glorify. Before, forgetful of the work for which he was sent, he was occupied with easing the present pain, and he begged to escape the Father's wrath. Now, on the contrary, forgetful of himself, he thinks of the Father's glory and desires it, even with his suffering and death. So it often happens to the pious in heavier afflictions: for a time they forget other things and think only of the present pain. But then again they rise up, forget themselves, and think of God and of his glory. Why are you cast down, my soul? says David, Hope in the Lord. The reprobate in the underworld will always remember themselves, but never the divine glory, which they will never at any time desire in this way. Rather, they will seek their own deliverance at the cost of loss, if it could be done, [of the divine glory].

units.la: Humiliationis Christi pro nobis testimonium.
units.tr: A testimony to Christ's humiliation for us.

units.la: Victoria Christi, & Ecclesiæ consolatio.
units.tr: Christ's victory and the consolation of the Church.

units.la: Afflictionum grauissimarum typus.
units.tr: A type of the most grievous afflictions.

units.la: Psal. 42.11. diuinæ gloriæ. Venit ergo vox è cælo dicens ei, &c. Id est, Perficiam gloriam in te ac cruce tua, quemadmodum in te eam inchoaui. Ergo nihil impedire potest quin Deus gloriam nominis sui ad summum perducat. Beati autem sunt qui eam cum Christo ferió possunt exoptare. Sic enim futurum est, ut illi sint diuinæ gloriæ participes: neque exoptanda est Dei gloria tantum ut in aliis ea perficiatur, in aliorum cruce & ignominia: sed imprimis ut in nobis ipsis, ut cum pudore nostro & perditione etiam Deus, si quidem ita velit, glorificetur. Sic Moyses expungi suum nomen petiuit e libro vitæ, ut consuleretur diuinæ gloriæ. Sic Paulus optauit se esse anathema diuinæ gloriæ causa .
units.tr: Psal. 42.11. The divine glory. So a voice came from heaven saying to him, etc. That is: I will bring my glory to completion both in you and in your cross, just as I have begun it in you. Therefore nothing can hinder God from bringing the glory of his name to its height. Blessed are those who can desire it with Christ in the same way. For thus it will come about that they share in the divine glory. Nor is the glory of God to be desired only so that it may be accomplished in others, in their cross and shame; but above all in ourselves, so that God, if he so wills, may be glorified even by our shame and ruin. So Moses asked that his name be blotted out of the book of life, that the divine glory might be promoted. So Paul wished himself to be anathema for the sake of the divine glory.

units.la: 29 Et turba quæ adstabat audiuerunt & dixerunt, Tonitruum factum est: Alij dicebant, Angelus ei loquutus est.
units.tr: 29 The crowd that stood by heard it and said, It thundered. Others said, An angel has spoken to him.

units.la: 30 Respondit Iesus & dixit, Non propter me hæc vox exiit, sed propter vos.
units.tr: 30 Jesus answered and said, This voice came not because of me, but because of you.

units.la: 31 Nunc iudicium ad est mundi huius: Nunc princeps ille mundi huius eiicietur foras.
units.tr: 31 Now is the judgment of this world: now the prince of this world will be cast out.

units.la: 32 Et ego si sublatus fuero è terra, omnes traham ad meipsum.
units.tr: 32 And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all men to myself.

units.la: 33 (Hoc autem dicebat significans qua morte futurum erat ut moreretur.)
units.tr: 33 (Now he said this, signifying by what death he was to die.)

units.la: 34 Respondit ei turba, Nos audiuimus ex lege, Christum manere in æternum: Quomodo igitur tu dicis oportere tolli filium hominis? Quis est iste filius hominis?
units.tr: 34 The crowd answered him, We have heard from the law that Christ remains for ever: how then do you say that the Son of man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of man?

units.la: VAriè sentit turba de audita voce illa; alij peius, alij melius sentiunt, vtriq; tamen à vero aberrant. Dacta fuit hęc vox è cælo, vt ait Dominus, postea illorum causa, vt hoc quasi miraculo & portento admoniti, crederent eum esse missum à Deo & Messiam: sed adeo excæcati sunt & indurati, vt tamen de Messia nihil cogitauerint. Amiserunt enim doctrinam de miraculis Messiam declarantibus, omnésque eius futuras petefactiones à Prophetis plane prædictas: non minus hodierno die cæcutiunt homines & indurantur ad verbum Dei, quod alij vt confusum quiddam instar tonitrus accipiunt: alij vt vocem non tam Dei quàm hominum intelligunt: pauci admodum sunt qui de ea recte sentiant. Non propter me. Subest quædam reprehensio: q.d. Cùm vox hæc extiterit propter vos, nempe vt vos credatis me {a}à Deo missum esse, vt loquitur supra 11. 41. tamen non intellexistis eam. Omnia evenerunt Christo nostra causa: miracula testificata sunt de eo nostra causa: implerus thesauro illo omnis gratiæ, vt nos ex plenitudine eius haurire mus, neque tamen ad nos pertinere ista sentimus, in quæ tamen Angeli, ad quos minus spectant, desiderant introspicere: & ipsæ res creatæ, vt loquitur 1. Pet. 1. 12. Apostolus, exertis capitibus exspectant & desiderant.
