Ilæ natura quodammodo expectant revelationem gloriæ filiorum Dei: nos natura abhorremus ab ea: pauci admodum qui acceperunt primitias Spiritus sancti suspirantes cum expetunt, vt loquitur Apostolus ibidem: adeo vt videas nos natura ipsa deteriores mutis ac brutis creaturis. Nunc damnatio. Postquam respirauit Christus, & pœtt ingentem illum doloris sensum, sese collegit: profert autem duo effecta mortis suæ longe excellentissima, damnationem certorum, salutem aliorum. Damnatio est mundi & Satanæ: Salus est hominum tam ex gentibus quàm Iudæis. Nunc, inquit, damnatio mundi huius adest, hoc est, vt appropinquat mors mea; ita appropinquat mundi damnatio, siue iudicium. Mundum hic intelligo peccantem; &, vt magis proprie loquar, ipsum peccatum, quod regnat in mundo. Aliter intelligitur hoc verbum, cùm dicitur à Domino, Non veni in mundum vt condemnem eum, &c. Quare loquitur de damnatione peccati, de qua Paulus, Deus missô filio suo ipsum, conformato carni peccato obnoxiæ, idque propeccato condemnauit peccatum in carne. Alibi verò dicitur pr crucem petemisse inimicitias, hoc est, peccatum quod diuisit inter nos & Deum. Item, dicitur crucifixisse mundum: Absit, inquit, à me gloriari, nisi in cruce Domini nostri Iesu Christi, per quem mundus mihi crucifixus est, &c. Item, Illud inquit, scientes crucifixum cum eo veterem nostrum hominem. Ergo hic intelligo damnationem & interemptionem peccati illius, quo in aduentu Christi abundauit mundus, &quod iam inde ab Adamo ad Mosem regnauit in mundo. Lex autem praeterea introiit, non vt aboleret peccati regnum; sed, inquit, vt augeretur offensa. Quamobrem regnaunt peccatum ab Adamo ad Christum, & perpetuo eius regnum auctum est. Quantum autem fuerit peccati & mortis regnum, satis dicti potest ex Paulo: Palam est ira Dei aduersus omnem impietatem & iniustitiam hominum, hoc est, impietatem & iniustitiam omnis generis, cuius species deinceps numeratae sunt. Sed ratio abolendi peccati mirifica fuit, & ea inuenta est ab ipso Deo: de qua mundus nunquam ne suspicari quidem potuit; nempe abolitum esse regnum peccati & mortis per mortem. Facile intelligit mundus aboleri posse peccatum & mortem per vitam: sed per mortem aboleri posse non intelligit. Vnde astantes Christo crucifixo in ludibrium dixerunt, Nunc seruua te qui seruas alios: nimirum putabant eum non potuisse seruare a morte quemquam qui ipse mortuus esset. Sed vocatis sermo crucis, inquit Apostolus, est Dei potentia & sapientia: & nihil ad vitam efficacius est illa ipsa cruce. Exhibes in mortem Christi regenerat nos, abolétque veterem hominem. Nunc princeps. Damnatio est Satanae, qui peccati author est. Nam vita huius mundi est secundum principe cui potestas est aeris, &c. Dicitur autem princeps huius mundi, quia per peccatum & mortem regnat in mundo: vt enim, teste Paulo, Regnum Dei positum est in iustitia, & pace, & gaudio per Spiritum sanctum; sic regnum Satanae positum est in iniustitia & morte. Vnde ipse propter peccatum, per quod regnat, dicitur rector tenebrarum. Propter mortem per quam regnat dicitur imperium mortis habere. Appropinquante Christi morte maxime saeuiit Diabolus, vnde postea dicit Dominus, Venit princeps huius mundi, hoc est, paulo post in me toris viribus irruet: sed non habet in me quicquam, id est, nihil potest in me nisi quod ipsi permissum est a Patre. Cum autem Dominus affigeretur cruci, grauissimum tum conflictum habuit cum impuris illis omnibus Spiritibus, quos accepit, expoliauit & palam traduxit in triumpho. Crux autem erat instar ftar currus triumphalis. Post illud tempus diaboli victi sunt omnes ac superati: ideóque à Iuda in Epistola sua dicuntur reseruari catenis ferreis sub caligine ad iudicium magni illius diei. Victi, inquam, sunt & captiui: etsi dicatur diabolus à Petro circumite more rugientis leonis, quærens quem deuoret: à Paulo vero Deus huius mundi & agere in filijs infidelitatis, nondum tamen plenè perfectæque victus. Tum autem omnino superabitur, cùm secundò aduenerit Christus, quo tempore sic gloriabitur aduersus omnem aduersariam potestatem: Vbi tua, ô mors victoria? Vbi tuus, ô sepulchrum, stimulus? Stimulus verò mortis est peccatum: Vis autem peccati lex. Et ego si sublatus fuero, nempe in crucem, vt sequens versus exponit, trahàm omnes ad me ipsum, quasi è curru triumphali exporrecta manu sursum traham ad me omnes, pedibus vt & ipsi pariter mecum de diabolo, peccato & morte triumphent. Nam hæc est victoria quæ vicit mundum, nempe fides vestra. Dixit suprà mirum videri mundo quòd Christus morte sua vicerit peccatum & mortem. Ita non minus mirum est quòd crucifixus homo aliciat ad se omnes. Facilè credat quis, omnes se recipere ad gloriosum aliquem: at verò stultitia videtur mundo quòd quis se conferat ad ignominiosum & crucifixum. Neque vero aquilæ frequentiores conuolant ad cadauer, vt vtar hac similitudine, quo in negotio visus est ipse Christus, quàm ad Christum peccatores, qui tenentur sensu aliquo peccatorum suorum. Et crux Christi est vocatis Dei sapientia & potentia, quæ mundo est stultitia & impotentia. Nos audiuimus. Respondet turba ad id quod dixit, Si sublatus fuero. Nihil attendit ad hæc effecta iudicij & saluis, sed studet eum carpere in hoc verbo: verum est quod asserit de perpetuitate Messiæ, nam vetus scriptura est eius rei plena: sed falsum est quòd putet nihil illic haberi de eius morte, id quod cõuincit vel vnus ille locus Prophetæ, Ductus est tanquam ouis ad mactationem, &c. Tum de perpetuitate eius agit ibidem Propheta; generationem eius quis numerabit? Verùm erroris causa hæc fuit, falsa nimirum opinio de regno Messiæ mundano, & mundana eius gloria. Quòd autem nihil de morte eius quærebant in scripturis, in causa
units.tr: Many people take that voice from heaven in different ways: some think worse of it, some better, yet both sides stray from the truth. As the Lord says, the voice came from heaven for their sake, so that, warned by it as by a kind of miracle and portent, they might believe that he was sent by God and was the Messiah. But they were so blinded and hardened that they still did not think of the Messiah at all. For they had lost the teaching about the miracles that declared the Messiah, and all his future sufferings, which the Prophets had plainly foretold. No less today do people grow blind and hardened toward the word of God. Some take it as a confused sort of thunder; others understand it as the voice of men rather than of God; very few think rightly about it. Not for my sake. There is a certain rebuke here, as if to say: although this voice came for your sake, namely so that you would believe that I was sent by God, as he says above in 11:41, you nevertheless did not understand it. All things happened to Christ for our sake. The miracles bore witness to him for our sake. He is filled with that treasury of all grace, so that we may draw from his fullness. Yet we do not think these things belong to us, although the angels, to whom they matter less, long to look into them, and the created things themselves, as the Apostle says in 1 Pet. 1:12, stretch out their heads and long for them. They in their nature wait in some way for the revealing of the glory of the sons of God. We by nature shrink from it. Very few have received the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit, and sigh while they long for it, as the Apostle says in the same place. So much so that you may see that we, by our very nature, are worse than dumb and brute creatures. Now is the judgment. After Christ had taken breath and borne that immense sense of grief, he gathered himself together. He then sets forth two effects of his death, far the most excellent: the condemnation of some, the salvation of others. The condemnation is of the world and of Satan; the salvation is of men, both from the Gentiles and from the Jews. Now, he says, the judgment of this world is at hand, that is, as my death draws near, so the condemnation of the world, or judgment, draws near. Here I understand the world to mean the sinful world, and, to speak more precisely, sin itself, which reigns in the world. This word is understood otherwise when the Lord says, I did not come into the world to condemn it, etc. Therefore he speaks of the condemnation of sin, of which Paul says, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh. Elsewhere it is said that by the cross he put to death enmity, that is, the sin which divided us from God. Likewise it is said that he crucified the world: God forbid, he says, that I should glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me, etc. Likewise: knowing this, he says, that our old man was crucified with him. Therefore here I understand the condemnation and destruction of that sin by which the world abounded at the coming of Christ, and which had reigned in the world from Adam to Moses. Moreover the law came in besides, not to abolish the reign of sin, but, he says, so that the offence might increase. Wherefore sin reigned from Adam to Christ, and his reign was perpetually increased. How great the reign of sin and death was may be sufficiently told from Paul: The wrath of God is revealed against all the ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, that is, ungodliness and unrighteousness of every kind, whose species are then enumerated. But the method of abolishing sin was wonderful, and it was devised by God himself. The world could never even suspect it: namely, that the reign of sin and death was abolished through death. The world easily understands that sin and death can be abolished through life, but it does not understand that they can be abolished through death. Hence those standing by the crucified Christ mocked him, saying, He saved others; let him now save himself. Surely they thought he could not save anyone from death, since he himself had died. But, as the Apostle says, to those who are called, the word of the cross is the power and wisdom of God, and nothing is more effective for life than that very cross. Through the death of Christ he regenerates us and puts off the old man. Now the prince. The condemnation is of Satan, who is the author of sin. For the life of this world is according to the prince of the power of the air, etc. He is called the prince of this world because he reigns in the world through sin and death. For, as Paul bears witness, the kingdom of God consists in righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit; so the kingdom of Satan consists in unrighteousness and death. Hence he is called the ruler of darkness on account of the sin through which he reigns, and is said to have the dominion of death on account of the death through which he reigns. As the death of Christ drew near, the Devil raged most fiercely, and so the Lord afterwards says, The prince of this world is coming, that is, shortly he will rush against me with all his strength; but he has nothing in me, that is, he can do nothing against me except what the Father has permitted him. When the Lord was fastened to the cross, he then had a most grievous conflict with all those unclean spirits whom he took on, and he stripped them and led them openly in triumph. The cross was like a triumphal chariot. From that time all the devils were conquered and overcome. Therefore Jude in his Epistle says that they are kept in chains of iron under darkness until the judgment of that great day. They were conquered, I say, and made captive, although Peter says that the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour, and Paul calls God's enemy the god of this world and says he works in the sons of unbelief. Yet he is not wholly and perfectly conquered. He will be utterly overcome when Christ comes a second time, at which time he will glory thus against every adversary power: Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O grave? The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. And I, if I be lifted up, namely on the cross, as the following verse explains, will draw all men to myself. As from a triumphal chariot, with outstretched hand, I will draw all men upward to myself, so that they may triumph together with me over the devil, sin and death. For this is the victory that has overcome the world: namely your faith. He said above that it seems strange to the world that Christ by his death conquered sin and death. So it is no less strange that a crucified man draws all to himself. One may easily believe that all betake themselves to someone glorious; but to the world it seems folly that anyone should resort to one who is shamed and crucified. Nor do eagles fly more often to a carcass (to use this comparison, in which Christ himself appeared) than sinners fly to Christ, who are touched by some sense of their sins. And the cross of Christ is the wisdom and power of God to those who are called, which to the world is folly and weakness. We have heard. The crowd responds to what he said: If I be lifted up. They take no notice of these effects of judgment and salvation, but they strive to catch him in this word. It is true, what they assert about the perpetuity of the Messiah, for the Old Testament is full of this matter. But it is false that they think nothing there is said about his death, which is refuted even by that one passage of the Prophet: He was led as a sheep to the slaughter, etc. Then the same Prophet, in the same place, speaks of his perpetuity: who shall declare his generation? But the cause of their error was this: a false opinion about the worldly kingdom of the Messiah and his worldly glory. That they did not seek anything about his death in the Scriptures, the cause is

units.la: Ioan. 1.6. 1. Pet. 5.8. 2. Cor. 4.4. Cor. 15.55. Satan sub Ecclesiæ per morte Christi capitis contritus. 1. Ioh. 5.4. Matth. 24.28. Iudicium carnis nű quam acquiescit Deo. Esai. 53.7.8 Origo malï. fuit quòd sine sensu fuerint & peccati sui, & iustitiæ di* uinæ, cui non satisfit nisi per mortē, vel peccatoris ipsius vel mediatoris æquivalentem. Quòd si de peccato suo cogitassent, nouissent quoq; ea loca veteris Scripturæ in quibus prædicta Messiæ & Mediatoris mors. Verùm sa- nus nō eget medico. Illud autem certissimum est, Qui- cunque nihil cogitant de peccato suo, illi quidem Chri- stum eiúsque passionem pro nihilo habent.
units.tr: John 1.6. 1 Pet. 5.8. 2 Cor. 4.4. 1 Cor. 15.55. Satan is crushed under the Church through the death of Christ the head. 1 John 5.4. Matt. 24.28. The carnal judgment never submits to God. Isa. 53.7, 8. The origin of evil was that they had no sense either of their sin or of divine justice, which is not satisfied except through death, either that of the sinner himself or that of an equivalent mediator. If they had thought about their sin, they would also have known those passages of the Old Scripture in which the death of the Messiah and Mediator is foretold. But the healthy have no need of a physician. Yet this is most certain: whoever thinks nothing about his own sin, that man counts Christ and his passion as nothing.

units.la: 35 Dixit igitur eis Iesus, Adhuc paruo tem- pore lux vobiscum est. Ambulate dum lucem ha- betis, ne vos tenebræ deprehendant, nam qui ambu- lat in tenebris, nescit quò vadat.
units.tr: Then Jesus said to them, Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you, for he who walks in darkness does not know where he is going.

units.la: 36 Dum lucem habetis credite in lucem, vt filij lucis sitis. Hæc loquutus est Iesus, & cum abijssset occultauit se ab eis.
units.tr: While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may be sons of light. Jesus spoke these things, and then he departed and hid himself from them.

units.la: NOn respondet directè ad quæstionem Iudæorum proximam: sed hoc quasi sumpto, Quod Messias sit, Quod lux mundi, monet vt ambulent in luce dum lucem habent. Sic Iudæis hodierno die qui de persona Messiæ disputant, dubitantque de eius aduentu respondendum, Dum lucem habetis credite. Sic etiam nostris hominibus, qui toti in personis ministrorum hærent, iisque offenduntur, vt Iudæi olim persona Christi: Quin potius credite in lucem dum lucem habetis. Nam illud verissimum, Qui personis hominum maximè offenduntur, illi minimè omnem lucem vident in eáque ambulant, & beati sunt qui inoffenso cursu pergunt ad diem Iesu Christi, qui beatum pronunciat eum qui non fuerit offensus in eo. Ambulate, inquit, Ambulare primum omnium est credere, vt sequens versus exponit. Deinde reliqua officia Christianorum hominum facere, & viuere vt dignum est Euangelio ac fide in Christum. Dies hic datus est homini ad ambulandum & laborandum cuique in sua vocatione. Ita dies ille spiritualis & splendor Christi datus est ad laborem & iter faciendum: Neque tam milití laborandum est in sua vocatione, aut Agricolæ in sua (vtar enim his Pauli similibus) quàm Christiano homini in sua. Paulus adeo intenso cursu ferebatur versus scopum ad palmam supernæ illius vocationis in Christo Iesu, ut vultum quasi retroflexerit ad eam curriculi partem quam iam confecerat, sed semper enitebatur ad metam. Fateor equidem in die isto Euangelij, dies mali sunt, ut loquitur Apostolus, multaque occurrunt impedimenta, via spinis strata est, via lubrica est: Sed, inquit Paulus, redimenda est occasio, redimenda, inquam, omnibus, imò vita ipsa, ad hoc ut dum lucet dies ambulemus. Videmus quòd si cui necessarium aliquod iter conficiendum sit, si dies luceat supernè, eum ægrè abstinere ab itinere, etsi via subtus difficilis sit ac salebrosa. Ita dum dies hic Euangelij lucet pergendum perpetuò, etsi impedimenta se iniiciant permulta. Sed videnda sunt argumenta admonitionis; Primum est à breuitate diei, Adhuc, inquit, ad paruum tempus, q.d. Breue quidem tempus lucis huius & corporalis præsentiæ meæ superest: Ergo ambulate, &c.
units.tr: He does not answer directly the question the Jews had just asked, but, taking for granted that he is the Messiah and the light of the world, he urges them to walk in the light while they have it. So today the answer to Jews who dispute about the person of the Messiah and doubt his coming must be: While you have the light, believe. So too for our own people, who are wholly fixed on the persons of ministers and are offended by them, as the Jews of old were offended by the person of Christ. Rather, believe in the light while you have the light. For this is most true: those who are most offended by the persons of men are the least able to see any light and to walk in it. Blessed are those who run their course without stumbling toward the day of Jesus Christ, who pronounces blessed the one who is not offended in him. Walk, he says. To walk is first of all to believe, as the following verse explains, and then to perform the remaining duties of Christian men, and to live in a manner worthy of the gospel and of faith in Christ. This day is given to man to walk and to labour, each in his own calling. So that spiritual day and the splendour of Christ are given for labour and for the journey. A soldier must not labour in his calling more than a farmer in his (I shall use Paul's own similes), nor either more than a Christian in his. Paul was borne with such intense effort toward the goal, toward the prize of that heavenly calling in Christ Jesus, that he seemed to turn his face back towards the part of the course he had already run, yet he always strove toward the mark. I grant indeed that in this day of the gospel the days are evil, as the Apostle says, and many hindrances meet us, the way is strewn with thorns, the way is slippery. But, says Paul, the opportunity must be redeemed, redeemed, I say, by all, indeed by life itself, so that while the day shines we may walk. We see that if someone has a necessary journey to complete, and the day shines overhead, he hardly refrains from travelling, even though the road beneath is difficult and rough. So while this day of the gospel shines, we must press on continually, even though many obstacles throw themselves in our way. But the arguments of this admonition must be considered. The first is drawn from the shortness of the day: Yet a little while, he says, a little time, as if to say: only a short time remains of this light and of my bodily presence. Therefore walk, and so on.

units.la: Videmus operarios in brumali die maximè intensis viribus operari, & dum imminet nox maximè laborare. Idem nobis faciendum propter breuitatem spiritualis huius diei. Sic Paulus hortatur ad serium studium rerum cœlestium, Tempus, inquit, contractum est imposterum: ut & qui uxores habent sint ut non habentes, &c. Præsentiam suam corporalem breui tempore substractum iri significat, ita ut ea substracta illi non amplius diem habituri sint. Sic supra. Quæreris me, inquit, & non inuenietis, &c. Quid, inquies, annon substracta è terris corporali Christi præsentia, manset tamen lux illius, adeóque præsentia non minor in Euangelio isto quod post ascensionem clarius cœpit prædicari? Respond. Ita quidem facturum, sed eâ Euangelij lucem nihil profuisse contemptoribus corporalis præsentiæ, imò obfuisse iis potius magisque eos excæcasse & induratos. Nam sic euenire solet, Qui contemnunt lucem, iis vel eripitur lux, vel si reliqua maneat, excæcat & indurat eos iusto Dei iudicio. Quod quidem effectum est Euangelij hodierno die in irrisoribus istis & contemptoribus, qui tam multi viuunt in hac tanta Euangelij luce. Ne vos tenebræ. Secundum est argumentum admonitionis. Minatur tenebras discessurum lucis exceptuaras. Graue est priuari luce; sed grauius est vitam agere in tenebris: graue est destitui & excludi coelo, sed grauius includi inferno. Et ita quidem se habent diuina iudicia. Non sunt tantum priuationes lucis & coelestis gaudij, sed simul immittuntur tenebrae & inferi. Sunt qui lubentius ferrent priuationem coelestis lucis ac gaudij: & vt perfruantur gaudio hoc mundano, lubenter pacisceretur cum Deo se non quaesituros vnquam gaudium coeleste. Verum hoc eos male habet quod praeterquam quod passuri sint amissionem coelestis lucis,eiiciendi sint in tenebras exteriores. Tu quatu malu fit ex tenebris ostedit. Nam qui ambulat. q.d. Ambulabit quidem in tenebris aliquis, sed nescit quonam abiturus sit. Operabitur quidem, sed erunt opera tenebrarum: ambulabit, sed in peccatis & offensis, vt est vita huius mundi, secundum principem cui potestas est aeris, &c. Quod si etiam aliquid erit quod in conspectu hominum laudabile videbitur, vt si quis ciuile quid, morale vel politicum gesserit (quae via fecerunt ethnici illi, qui sine Deo, sine Christo fuerant) illud tamen opus tenebrarum erat, quia sine fide, sine respectu gloriae Diuinae futurum est: sine fide enim non placemus Deo. Quare, vt verbo dicam, quicquid facit quis in tenebris, nescit quid faciet, siue illud malum sit in se quod facit, siue bonum illud sit alioqui & in se. Operantis enim respectu & eius personae respectu quae non est accepta Deo, malum est, Deoque ingratum. Verum experientia docuit non solum huius populi, sed & aliorum post Christum eiusque ascensionem, quod ij qui reiecerunt Christum Euangelium, iis ademptu sit non tantum Ecclesia, sed & e medio eorum sublata sit respublica, iusto Dei iudicio. Neque amplius certis legibus permissum est iis viuere, sed omnium rerum confusio & subuersio insecuta sit. Id quod & nobis euenturum est, si vnquam iusto Dei iudicio remota fuerit a nobis lux ista Euangelij.
units.tr: We see labourers in the winter day working with the utmost strength, and labouring hardest when night is at hand. We must do the same because of the shortness of this spiritual day. So Paul exhorts to earnest pursuit of heavenly things: The time, he says, is shortened henceforth, so that those who have wives be as though they had none, and so on. He signifies that his bodily presence will be withdrawn in a short time, so that once it is withdrawn they will no longer have the day. So above: You will seek me, he says, and you will not find me, and so on. What, you will say, if the bodily presence of Christ is withdrawn from the earth, does his light nevertheless remain, and is his presence therefore no less in this gospel, which after the ascension began to be preached more clearly? I reply: it is so indeed, but the light of the gospel has profited nothing to the despisers of his bodily presence; rather it has harmed them, dazzled them the more, and hardened them. For it usually happens that those who despise the light either have it taken away, or, if it remains, it blinds and hardens them by the just judgment of God. This has indeed come to pass in our own day in those mockers and despisers, who live in such great numbers in this so great light of the gospel. Lest the darkness. This is the second argument of the admonition. He threatens that darkness will overtake those who have let the light go. It is grievous to be deprived of light, but more grievous to live in darkness; grievous to be cut off and shut out from heaven, but more grievous to be shut up in hell. And so indeed the judgments of God stand: they are not merely deprivations of light and heavenly joy, but at the same time darkness and hell are sent in. There are those who would more willingly bear the loss of heavenly light and joy, and who, so as to enjoy this worldly pleasure, would gladly bargain with God that they will never seek heavenly joy. But this troubles them, because, besides suffering the loss of heavenly light, they are to be cast into outer darkness. How evil it is, he shows from the darkness itself: For he who walks. As if to say: someone will indeed walk in darkness, but he does not know whither he is going. He will indeed work, but his works will be works of darkness; he will walk, but in sins and offences, as is the life of this world, according to the prince who has power over the air, and so on. And if there is anything that seems praiseworthy in the sight of men, as if someone has done something civil, moral or political (such as those heathen did who were without God and without Christ), that work was still a work of darkness, because it is done without faith, without regard to the glory of God: for without faith we cannot please God. Therefore, to put it in a word, whatever anyone does in darkness, he does not know what he is doing, whether the thing he does is evil in itself or otherwise good in itself. For with respect to the doer, and with respect to his person, which is not acceptable to God, it is evil and unpleasing to God. Experience has taught, not only of this people but also of others after Christ and his ascension, that those who have rejected Christ and the gospel have lost not only the Church but also, by the just judgment of God, the commonwealth itself has been taken away from among them. Nor is it any longer permitted them to live under settled laws, but confusion and overthrow of all things has followed. This will also happen to us, if ever, by the just judgment of God, this light of the gospel is removed from us.

units.la: Dum lucem habetis. Repetit admonitionem, vt magis moueat, adiicitque argumentum a participatione lucis & illuminatione ex luce & ambulatione in luce futura. Vt filij, inquit, lucis sitis. Qui ambulant in luce ista mundana, illuminantur ab ea & apparent, praesertim occuoculus luce quasi accenditur: ita qui ambulant in luce Euangelij, illuminantur ab ea luce, & mentes accendun-tur, adeo vt ipsi iam luminaria totidem in mundo lucentia in medio pravæ generationis habeantur vocen-turque ab Apostolo: Lucentia, inquam, tum opere ac sin-ceritate vitæ, tum verbo, dum sermonem vitæ prætendunt aliis. Omnes plurimi faciunt eos, qui lucent inter alios luce hac mundana, quanti igitur faciendi qui lucent cœlesti illa luce? Hæc loquutus est Iesus. Nimirum ordinarium medium sequutus est ad se conseruandum in vita ad momentum illud vsque, quod à Patre ipsi erat præstitutum. Sic quoque nobis faciendum, tantisperdum non venit ea hora qua Deus in morte nostra glorificandus est (quam etiam indicabit suis Dominus certis signis & circumstantiis) debemus magnificare vel vnius dici vsuram quã prostimus aliis, vt Christus fecit, qui priuatim suos instituit, eo ipso quo se occultauit tempore: debemus, inquam, interea prodesse aliis, secus enim vita ista indigni sumus, nisi vitam impendamus in Dei gloriam & hominum salutem.
units.tr: While you have the light. He repeats the admonition so as to move them more, and adds an argument from the sharing of light, from being enlightened by the light, and from walking in the light that is to come. That you may be, he says, sons of light. Those who walk in this worldly light are enlightened by it and made visible, especially as the eye is kindled by light; so those who walk in the light of the gospel are enlightened by that light, and their minds are kindled, so that they are themselves regarded as so many lights shining in the world in the midst of a crooked generation, and are called by the Apostle lights: shining, I say, both by the work and sincerity of their life and by the word, while they hold out the word of life to others. Everyone values very highly those who shine among others with this worldly light; how highly, then, ought we to value those who shine with that heavenly light? Jesus spoke these things. Surely he followed the ordinary means of preserving himself in life until that moment which had been appointed him by the Father. So too we must do: as long as that hour has not come in which God is to be glorified in our death (which the Lord will indicate to his own by certain signs and circumstances), we ought to make the most of even a single day's use which we owe to others, as Christ did, who instructed his own privately at the very time when he hid himself. We ought, I say, meanwhile to be of use to others, for otherwise we are unworthy of this life, unless we spend our life for the glory of God and the salvation of men.

units.la: 37 Cum autem tot signa coram eis edidisset, non credebant in eum.
units.tr: 37 But although he had performed so many signs before them, they did not believe in him.

units.la: 38 Vt sermo Esaiæ Prophetæ impleretur, quem dixit, Domine quis credidit sermoni nostro, & brachium Domini cui revelatum est?
units.tr: 38 That the word of the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, which he spoke: Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?

units.la: 39 Propterea non poterant credere, quia iterum dixit Esaias,
units.tr: 39 For this reason they could not believe, because Isaiah said again:

units.la: 40 Excæcauit oculos eorum, & obdurauit cor-da eorum: ne videant oculis & intelligant corde, & se convertant, & sanem eos.
units.tr: 40 He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts, lest they should see with their eyes and understand with their heart, and turn, and I should heal them.

units.la: 41 Hæc dixit Esaias, quando vidit gloriam eius, & loquutus est de eo.
units.tr: 41 Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke of him.

units.la: Videtur inde ab hoc loco ad versum 44. exponi qui fuerit affectus omnium operum Christi, in hoc populo. Quum, inquit, tot miracula, &c. q.d. Quamuis tot dixisset fecisset que iam inde ab eo tempore, quo ingressus est officium hoc Mediatoris, ad hoc vt saluum facet-
units.tr: It seems that from this place to verse 44 the attitude of this people to all the works of Christ is set out. When, he says, he had done so many miracles, etc. That is: although he had said and done so many things from the time when he began this office of Mediator, to save the

units.la: Philip. 2. 15
units.tr: Phil. 2. 15

units.la: Christi sapientia, & constantia in munere exequendo.
units.tr: The wisdom and steadfastness of Christ in carrying out his office.

units.la: Quarta causa pars effectum miraculorum Christi in poret & conuerteret ad Deum populum hunc: tamen in tanta luce verborum factorúmque illi cæci manserunt & increduli. Habent hic quo se cōsolentur ministri Euangelij, fideles præsertim, qui hoc dicere possunt: Quibus nihil reliquerim, quo ad fidem perduci potuit populus ille, tamen incredulus mansit: Quemadmodum hic Spiritus de Christo, déque laboribus quibus ipse defunctus est prædicauit. Paulus, Testor, inquit, me purum esse à sanguine vestrorum omnium & non subterfugisse quo minus annuntiarem vobis totum Dei consilium. Quod si autem id de se testari non posset minister, tum sanguis populi increduli requiretur abeo. Quare videndum illi perpetuò vt Dei bona fragrantia sit, & in iis qui pereunt, & in iis qui seruantur. Vt sermo Esaiæ. Ne quis putaret aliquid detractum Christo aut efficaciæ verbi & operum eius, propterea quod Iudæi manserunt increduli, huic respondet, atque occurrit, ostendens ita oportuisse fieri, neque aliter fieri potuisse, quin increduli manerent: Deus enim id prædixit per Prophetam Esaiam. Necessitas sequelæ hinc apparet, quod opponeat Deum veracem esse in omnibus prædictionibus suis. Ergo, inquit, dicam, & non eueniet? q.d. Necesse est ita eueniat, vt ego prædixeram. Necessitas sequelæ etiam hinc paret, Quod nihil prædicat Deus, quod non præordinauit futurum ab æterno. Nihil autem præordinauit ab æterno quod non suo tempore permittat fieri, aut etiam operetur efficaciter. Neque propterea habent quo se exeusent mala instrumenta, & infideles ipsi. Quod vel ex his verbis Euangelistæ apparet. Quum, inquit, tot miracula ediderit, &c. Quibus verbis significat malitiam & obstinationem eorum, qua maliciosè obstinateque se opposuerunt miraficis Christi operibus. Ecclesia dicit, Nihil à Pilato & Herode & reliquis factum Christo quod non decreuerit manus & consilium Dei: nec tamen excusatos habet, quod ex definito Dei consilio omnia fecerint: Imò, inquit, sceleratis manibus ipsum affixum ligno interemerunt. Necessitas enim hæc decreti & prædictionis Domini neminem cogit; Imò vero cum ea consistit creaturæ libertas & voluntas, vnde est quod decretum creaturam non excusat. Discimus hic nihil à creatura fieri tam tā male & impiè, quin in illo glorificetur Deus, vel ideo quod inde conspiciatur eum verum esse in sermonibus suis, aut immutabilē in decreto suo. Hinc etiam habent quo se consolentur ministri, quando vident se frustra laborasse, vt loquitur Apostolus. Et eos quibus praedicarunt Christum infideles manere: erigendi enim oculi sunt ad decretum Dei, vt hic Christus respexit hanc Prophetæ praedicationem haudquaquam dubiè, & quiescendum in illa Dei æterna sanctaque voluntate. Interea autem semper videndum ne negligentia aut oscitantia ipsius ministri hoc factum sit, vt populus non crediderit.
units.tr: Although the effect of Christ's miracles was to move and turn this people to God, yet in so great a light of words and deeds they remained blind and unbelieving. Here the ministers of the Gospel, and especially the faithful, have something to comfort themselves with, since they can say: "Although I have left nothing undone by which that people might be brought to faith, they remained unbelieving." So the Spirit also preached about Christ and about the labours by which he himself was worn out. Paul says: I testify that I am clean from the blood of you all, and that I have not shrunk from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. But if a minister could not testify this about himself, then the blood of the unbelieving people would be required at his hand. Therefore he must always take care that he is a sweet fragrance of God, both among those who perish and among those who are saved. That the word of Isaiah. Lest anyone should think that anything was taken away from Christ or from the efficacy of his word and works because the Jews remained unbelieving, the evangelist meets and answers this, showing that it had to happen so, and could not have happened otherwise than that they would remain unbelieving, for God foretold this through the prophet Isaiah. The necessity of this inference appears from the fact that God is true in all his predictions. "Shall I say, and will it not come to pass?" That is: it must come to pass as I had foretold. The necessity of this inference also appears from the fact that God foretells nothing which he has not predestined from eternity to be future. But he has predestined nothing from eternity which he does not permit to be done at its time, or even effectively bring about. Nor, for that reason, do wicked instruments and unbelievers themselves have any excuse. This appears even from these words of the evangelist: when he had done so many miracles, etc. By these words he signifies their malice and obstinacy, by which they wickedly and stubbornly opposed the miraculous works of Christ. The Church says: "Nothing was done to Christ by Pilate and Herod and the rest that the hand and counsel of God had not decided beforehand; yet they are not excused because they did everything by the determined counsel of God. Rather, they killed him, fastening him to the tree with wicked hands." For this necessity of the decree and prediction of the Lord compels no one. Indeed, the freedom and will of the creature stands alongside it, and so it is that the decree does not excuse the creature. Here we learn that nothing is done by a creature so badly and impiously that God is not glorified in it, if only because thereby it is seen that he is true in his words and unchangeable in his decree. Hence also the ministers have something to comfort themselves with, when they see that they have laboured in vain, as the Apostle says, and that those to whom they preached Christ remain unbelievers. For their eyes must be lifted up to the decree of God, as Christ looked upon this prophecy of Isaiah without any doubt, and they must rest in that eternal and holy will of God. Meanwhile, however, one must always take care that it has not happened through the negligence or carelessness of the minister himself that the people did not believe.

units.la: In testimoniis ex Esaia Propheta adductis non immorabimur. Primum scriptum est Esaiæ 53.1. In quo Propheta, vt typus quidam Christi, queritur de incredulitate populi & obstinatione aduersus Euangelium, eiúsque praedicationem, non tantùm quæ fuit illo tempore, quo ipse concionatus est, sed multò magis quæ futura erat tempore ipsius Christi. Quis credidit, inquit, &c. q.d. Vel nemo vel pauci. Et brachium Domini, hoc est, potentia Dei, seu Euangelium quod potentia Dei est ad salutem omni credenti. Est enim Euangelium quasi brachium Dei è cœlo porrectum ad erigendos omnes si fieri possit, in cœlum, quod adeo patet, sese adeo late ostendit, vt qui illum non vident sint ex numero eorum qui pereunt. Propterea non. Necessitatem ex repetita denuntiatione colligit, Non poterant, inquit, quia iterum dixit. Neque enim frustra fiunt repetitiones iudiciorum Dei, sed necessitatem quandam imponunt & impossibilitatem effugiendi. Excæcauit. Modus quo excæcati sunt eorum oculi apparet ex verbis eiusdem Prophetæ: Audiant, inquit, continenter, videant continenter. Ergo continenter audiendo & videndo, excæcati sunt. Atqui ea videtur causa illuminationis. Respondeo id ita esse iis qui recipiunt Euangelium neque ei obnituntur, aliis verò incredulis & contemptoribus causa est summæ excæcationis & indurationis. Hæc dixit. Euangelista accommodat hæc testimonia ad Christi tempora, quæ emi-nus ipse vidit. Ita Lucas & Paulus, hæc & huiusmodi testimonia de summa Iudæorum induratione applicant ad Christi tempora. Nam illud certissimum est, in summa luce, qualis fuit illa Christi tempore, summa est induratio in obstinatis: Tenebrae enim non tam excaecant quam lux nisi Deus suo Spiritu simul animum hominis reformet cum verbum Euangelij praedicatur. Atque haec est causa cur maior fit excaecatio atque induratio. Et plura opera tenebrarum etiam nunc in clara luce Euangelij quam olim in tenebris illis Papismi. Nimirum id fit iusto Dei iudicio, quia homines Euangelium passim contemptim habent.
units.tr: We shall not dwell long on the testimonies brought from the prophet Isaiah. The first is written at Isaiah 53.1. In it the prophet, as a certain type of Christ, complains of the unbelief of the people and their obstinacy against the Gospel and its preaching, not only the preaching that was in his own time, when he himself preached, but much more the preaching that was to be in the time of Christ himself. Who has believed, he says, etc. That is: either no one or only a few. And the arm of the Lord, that is, the power of God, or the Gospel, which is the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes. For the Gospel is, as it were, the arm of God stretched out from heaven to lift up all, if that were possible, into heaven; and it shows itself so widely and so openly that those who do not see it are among the number of those who perish. For this reason they could not. He draws the necessity from the repeated declaration: "They could not," he says, "because he said again." For the repetitions of God's judgements are not made in vain, but they impose a certain necessity and an impossibility of escape. He has blinded. The manner in which their eyes were blinded appears from the words of the same prophet: Hear, he says, continually, see continually. Therefore by continually hearing and seeing, they were blinded. And yet this seems to be the cause of enlightenment. I answer that this is so for those who receive the Gospel and do not resist it, but for others who are unbelieving and contemptuous it is the cause of the greatest blindness and hardening. He said these things. The evangelist applies these testimonies to the times of Christ, which he himself saw from afar. So Luke and Paul apply these and similar testimonies about the great hardening of the Jews to the times of Christ. For this is most certain: in the highest light, such as there was in Christ's time, there is the greatest hardening in the obstinate. For darkness does not blind so much as light does, unless God at the same time reforms the mind of man by his Spirit when the word of the Gospel is preached. And this is the reason why blindness and hardening become greater. And there are more works of darkness even now in the clear light of the Gospel than there were of old in the darkness of Popery. This surely happens by the just judgement of God, because men hold the Gospel in general contempt.

units.la: 42 Verumtamen etiam ex primoribus multi crediderunt in eum: sed propter Pharisaeos hoc non profitebantur, ne synagoga moverentur.
units.tr: 42 Nevertheless, even among the chief men many believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they did not confess it, lest they be put out of the synagogue.

units.la: 43 Dilexerunt enim gloriam hominum potius quam gloriam Dei.
units.tr: 43 For they loved the glory of men rather than the glory of God.

units.la: Correctio est superioris sententiae indefinitae versu 37. excipit enim multos qui crediderunt Christo. Nam Euangelium non adeo ineffi-cax est, ut neminem faciat credere, neque qui a Deo missus est, praedicandum Euangelium usque adeo frustra currit, ut cum Apostolo loquar, ut neminem feruet. Necesse enim est aliqui certe illius sermoni fidem habeant, et aliquibus sit odor vitae ad vitam. Sed ex quo genere hominum sunt qui credunt? Ex primoribus, ex quo nimirum hominum genere qui omnium difficillime credit. Videte, inquit Paulus, vocatione vestra, fratres, pauci nobiles, pauci potentes, pauci sapientes secundum hunc mundum. At vero cum visum est Deo exerere potentia per verbum Euangelij sui et sermonem crucis, tum Euangelium subuertit omnem munitionem et sublimitatem quae sese extollit adversus cognitionem Dei, captiuamque ducit omnem cogitationem ad obediendum Christo. Sed propter Pharisaeos. Usque adeo difficile est granum illud fidei in corde latitans elicere ac educere in apertum: hoc est, linguam soluere ad confessionem Christi ac veritatis, adeo ut nisi adsit noua gratia, non sit futura confessio. Sine autem confessione non est salus. Ore fit confessio ad salutem. Sed quid impedit confessionem? metus Pharisaeorum, ne synagoga moverentur. De Excommunicatione supra prà à nobis dictum est. Metus inimicus est confessioni & libertati: metus, inquam, amittendi huius mundi, huius vitæ, honoris, diuitiarum, voluptatum, &c. In viris autem principibus maximè valet hic affectus, qui maximam partem huius mundi occupant, adeo vt pauperibus & iis qui minus possunt, sæpe bene consultum sit, cùm ventum est ad confessiones. Sed altius aperit fundamentum huius metus. Dilexerunt enim gloriam hominum potius quàm gloriam Dei. Amor huius mundi inimicus, causa est tanti metus amittendi eius. Quamobrem vt sit mali- spiritus roboris in die probationis, necesse est discamus non amare mundum, hoc est, necesse est abnegemus nosipsos, & mortificemus affectus nostros, totaque vita nostra progressus sit in mortificatione. Atque ita demum fiet vt mortificata philautia ista, cesset metus, & expulso spiritu timiditatis, succedat spiritus roboris, qui os aperit ad liberam confessionem. Christus supra 5.44. putat impossibile esse vt credant ij qui diligunt gloriam hominum. Quomodo vos potestis credere cū gloriam alij ab aliis captetis, & gloriam quæ à Deo solo proficiscitur non quæratis?
units.tr: This is a correction of the preceding general statement in verse 37, for it excepts the many who believed in Christ. For the Gospel is not so ineffective that it makes no one believe, nor is the Gospel that is preached by one sent from God run in such vain that, to use the Apostle's words, it warms no one. For it is necessary that some certainly give credence to his word, and that for some it be a fragrance of life unto life. But from what class of people are those who believe? From the chief men, that is to say, from that class of men who believe most hardly of all. See, says Paul, your calling, brethren: not many wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble. But when it has seemed good to God to exert his power through the word of his Gospel and the preaching of the cross, then the Gospel overthrows every fortress and height that raises itself against the knowledge of God, and leads every thought captive to obey Christ. But "because of the Pharisees": it is so hard to draw out and bring into the open that grain of faith lying hidden in the heart, that is, to loosen the tongue to confess Christ and the truth, that unless new grace is present, there will be no confession. But without confession there is no salvation: "with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." But what hinders confession? The fear of the Pharisees, lest they be put out of the synagogue. I have spoken above about excommunication. Fear is the enemy of confession and of freedom: the fear, I say, of losing this world, this life, honour, riches, pleasures, and so on. This affection has the greatest force among leading men, who occupy the greater part of this world; so much so that it is often well arranged for the poor and for those who are less able, when it comes to confessions. But more deeply it reveals the foundation of this fear: For they loved the glory of men rather than the glory of God. The love of this world is the enemy, and it is the cause of so great a fear of losing it. Therefore, that there may be a strength of spirit in the day of trial, we must learn not to love the world, that is, we must deny ourselves and mortify our affections, and the whole course of our life must be a progress in mortification. And so at last it will come about that, with this self-love mortified, fear ceases, and the spirit of timidity being cast out, the spirit of strength follows, which opens the mouth to free confession. In John 5.44 Christ holds it to be impossible that those who love the glory of men should believe. "How can you believe, when you seek glory from one another, and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?"

units.la: 44 Iesus autem clamauit & dixit, Qui credit in me, non credit in me, sed in eum qui misit me.
units.tr: 44 Jesus cried out and said, "Whoever believes in me does not believe in me only, but in him who sent me."

units.la: 45 Et qui conspicit me, conspicit eum qui misit me.
units.tr: 45 "And whoever sees me sees him who sent me."

units.la: 46 Ego lux in mundum veni, vt quisquis credit in me, in tenebris non maneat.
units.tr: 46 I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me should not remain in darkness.

units.la: HÆc vltima est concio Christi, habita ad populum, nam rursus prodiit ex occulto, in quo se abdidit, & conseruauit ad horam præstitutam. His autem verbis iis quasi valedicit, hortatur eos ad fidem, quæ est summa omnium exhortationum & argumentum omnium præcipuum, Modus autem loquendi est cum clamore: nempe vtex-hortatio maiori vehementia percelleret eorum aures simul & animos. Luctatur enim cum eorum incredulitate, omnibus modis, verbis, operibus & clamoribus ingeminatis. Argumentum primum est duobus versibus, à pari fide parìque intuitu Patris qui misit ipsum. q.d. Ne-
units.tr: This is the last sermon of Christ, delivered to the people. For he came out again from the hiding-place in which he had concealed himself and kept himself until the appointed hour. With these words he bids them farewell, and he exhorts them to faith, which is the sum of all exhortations and the chief subject of them all. The manner of speaking is with a cry, namely so that the exhortation might strike their ears and minds with greater force. For he wrestles with their unbelief in every way, repeating his points in words, deeds and cries. His first argument is in two verses, from the equal faith and the equal sight of the Father who sent him. That is to say, Do not-

units.la: ZZ fide, parimo est qui non cupiat videre Patrem, eúmque & quę in eo sunt omnia apprehendere ad vitam æternam. At qui me videt, Patrem videt. Qui in me credit, in Patrem credit: Ergo credite in me. Fundamentum huius assumptionis supra fuit. Ego & Pater unum sumus, nempe essentia & maiestate. Christus est splendor gloriæ paternæ est imago inconspicui Dei. Qui ergo vult videre maiestatem illam divinam in Patre eámque apprehendere, convertat oculos ad filium. Vis intueri infinitam illam iustitiam? Vide filium. Vis intueri infinitam illam potentiam? Vide filium. Vis intueri infinitam illam sapientiam? Vide filium. Vis denique intueri infinitam illam misericordiam Patris, & φιλανθρωπίαν, quam videre maximè interest peccatoris? Vide filium, eúmque intuere. Sed qualem eum? Commendat, inquam, charitatem suam erga nos Deus, quòd filius pro impiis & peccatoribus mortuus est, & sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut unigenitum suum dederit pro eo. Ergo in Christo demum crucifixo, & pro nobis mortuo, videmus suum maximam illam & ineffabilem misericordiam. Et primus quidem ac iucundissimus aspectus Christi est, cum peccator Christi crucem intuetur: nam in ea cernitur illa misericordia Dei, qua peccatorem liberat ab omni peccato, & sermo crucis primum omnium est audiendus, quia sermo est misericordiæ. Paulus dixit, Absit a me gloriari, nisi in cruce Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Item, non decreveram quicquam scire inter vos, nisi Christum eúmque crucifixum. Et cur? quia in cruce Christi conspicitur illa misericordia ineffabilis. Quod si quis satis sentiret onus peccatorum suorum, & perciperet quanta passus sit Christus pro peccatis ipsius, tam insigne profecto in illa passione misericordiam illam & dilectionem Dei admiraretur, nempe latitudinem, longitudinem, altitudinem, profunditatem de qua Paulus Ephes. 3. Fateor, longè iucundissimus aspectus est Christi glorificati, in eo enim gloriificato videmus Dei potentiam, & ut cum Apostolo loquar, efficacitatem fortis roboris ipsius qua glorificauit primum Christum, deinde nos cum eo. Sed primus, & quem primum requirit peccator, aspectus Christi est crucifixi illius. Nam primum misericordiam sibi pastulat animus miseri peccatoris cuiusque.
units.tr: ...faith, for there is no one who does not desire to see the Father, and to lay hold of Him and of all that is in Him, unto eternal life. "He who sees me sees the Father; he who believes in me believes in the Father. Therefore believe in me." The ground of this assumption was given above: "I and the Father are one," namely in essence and majesty. Christ is "the brightness of the Father's glory and the express image of the invisible God." Therefore whoever wishes to see that divine majesty in the Father and to lay hold of it, let him turn his eyes to the Son. Do you wish to behold that infinite justice? Look at the Son. Do you wish to behold that infinite power? Look at the Son. Do you wish to behold that infinite wisdom? Look at the Son. Do you wish, finally, to behold that infinite mercy of the Father, and His φιλανθρωπία [love of humankind], which it matters most for the sinner to see? Look at the Son, and gaze upon Him. But what sort of Son? "God commends His love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners Christ died for us" and "God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son for it." Therefore it is in Christ, crucified at last and dead for us, that we see that greatest and ineffable mercy of God. And the first and most welcome sight of Christ is when the sinner looks upon the cross of Christ: for in it is discerned that mercy of God by which He frees the sinner from all sin, and the word of the cross is to be heard first of all, because it is the word of mercy. Paul said, "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Likewise, "I determined to know nothing among you, except Jesus Christ and him crucified." And why? Because in the cross of Christ that ineffable mercy is seen. But if anyone felt sufficiently the burden of his sins, and perceived how much Christ suffered for his sins, he would certainly marvel at that remarkable mercy and love of God shown in that passion, namely the breadth, length, height and depth of which Paul speaks, Ephesians 3. I grant that the sight of the glorified Christ is far more pleasant, for in Him glorified we see the power of God, and, to speak with the Apostle, the working of the strength of His might, by which He glorified first Christ, then us with Him. But the first sight, and the one the sinner seeks first, is of Christ crucified. For the mind of every wretched sinner first demands mercy.

units.la: Ego lux in mundum. Secundum est argumentum a li-beratione a tenebris: ita enim non manebit in tenebris. Tenebrae sunt non hae corporeae, vt noctis, quae profecto satis graues essent futurae mortali, si perpetuo sine lucis & diei vicissitudine permanerent. Neque rursus sunt tenebrae priuatio oculorum corporalium, quae ipsa satis grauis est caeco & oculis priuato. Sed hae tenebrae sunt tenebrae illae spirituales, & caecitas mentis, quam Apostolus definit σκοτισμένοι siue mentem obtenebratam & alienatam a vita Dei, propter ignorantiam quae est in ipsis ex obduratione cordis.Quod si palpitans in tenebris his corporeis caecus aliquis euocaretur ex iis ab alio qui promitteret apertionem oculorum, profecto laeta esset illa vox caeco. Non minus ignari Dei palpitant in tenebris, & nesciunt quo vadunt, vt Apostolus de Athenien-sibus dixit, & Dominus supra vers. 35. An non igitur debet haec laeta vox Christi esse, dicentis, Veni ad me (venire enim credere est) & e tenebris illis mentis te eripiam, ostendamque viam ac rationem salutis totam. Sed tenebras istas spirituales non ita sentimus: & qui apud inferos agit, vt dici solet, non credit alios esse caelos. Qui semel sensit illas tenebras & vidit lucis illius caelestis scintillam aliquam, is profecto nihil sentit grauius quam tenebras has, neque secus sed opprimi sentit, quam si foeda caligine & fumo suffocaretur. Certamen autem illi est cum tenebris perpetuum, vt tandem ex iis eluctetur. Verum quae ratio sequelae? Qui credit in me non manet in tenebris. Ego, lux veni in mundum. Lux dispellit tenebras luce diurna oriente, fugiunt tenebrae nocturnae: ita oriente illo sole iustitiae, fugit illa nox iniustitiae, quae occupauit mundum ante Christi aduentum in carne. Sed hoc discrimen est: lux ista diei & corporea facit, vt omnes in luce appareant & omnes omnium quemque oculos illuminat, velint, nolint. At vero lux illa Christi apparet, non nisi eos illuminat qui delectantur luce. Qui credit, inquit, in me, non manet in tenebris.
units.tr: I am the light come into the world. The second argument is from deliverance from darkness: for thus he will not remain in darkness. These are not bodily darknesses, such as that of night, which would surely be grievous enough for mortals if they lasted forever without the alternation of light and day. Nor again are they the privation of bodily eyes, which is itself grievous enough for a blind man deprived of sight. These are rather spiritual darknesses, and the blindness of mind which the Apostle defines as darkened [σκοτισμένοι], that is, a mind obscured and alienated from the life of God, through the ignorance that is in them from the hardening of the heart. If a blind man, groping in those bodily darknesses, were called out of them by another who promised to open his eyes, that voice would surely be joyful to the blind man. No less do those ignorant of God grope in darkness, and they do not know where they are going, as the Apostle said of the Athenians, and the Lord above, at verse 35. Ought not then this to be the joyful voice of Christ, saying: "Come to me" (for to come is to believe), and I will snatch you out of those darknesses of the mind, and show you the way and the whole manner of salvation? But we do not feel those spiritual darknesses in this way; and he who lives in hell, as it is commonly said, does not believe that there are other heavens. Whoever has once felt those darknesses, and has seen some spark of that heavenly light, surely feels nothing more grievous than these darknesses, and he feels himself oppressed no less than if he were choked by foul mist and smoke. He has a perpetual struggle with the darknesses, that at length he may struggle out of them. But what is the reasoning of the consequence? He who believes in me does not remain in darkness. I, the light, have come into the world. Light dispels darkness: when the daylight rises, the darkness of night flees. So, when that Sun of righteousness rises, that night of unrighteousness flees, which had occupied the world before Christ's coming in the flesh. But there is this difference: that daylight, being bodily, makes all things appear in the light, and illumines everyone's eyes, whether they wish it or not. But the light of Christ does not appear in that way, and it illumines only those who delight in the light. He who believes in me, he says, does not remain in darkness.

units.la: 47 Si quis autem audierit verba mea, & non crediderit, ego non damno ipsum. Non enim venit vt damnem mundum, sed vt seruem mundum.
units.tr: 47 And if anyone hears my words and does not believe, I do not judge him. For I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world.

units.la: 48 Qui reiecit me, nec recipit verba mea, habet qui condemnet ipsum: sermo quem loquutus sum, ille damnabit eum vltimo illo die.
units.tr: 49 For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me himself gave me commandment what to say and what to speak.

units.la: 49 Quia ego ex meipso non sum loquutus, sed qui misit me Pater ipse mihi mandauit quid dicam & quid loquar.
units.tr: 49 For I have not spoken of myself, but the Father who sent me himself gave me commandment what I should say and what I should speak.

units.la: 50 Et scio mandatum eius vitam æternam esse. Quæ igitur ego loquor, prout dixit mihi Pater ita loquor.
units.tr: 50 And I know that his commandment is eternal life. Therefore what I speak, I speak just as the Father has told me.

units.la: TErtium argumentum, quo si nolint moueri, suaui promissione aspectus & apprehensionis Dei, neque ereptione illa ex tenebris, coguntur quasi credere graui comminationi damnationis æternæ. Nam verbum Euangelij promittit primum suauiter, deinde comminatur grauiter: & non minus seuere, adeoque magis, quàm verbum ipsum legis. Verùm hoc differt à lege, quòd id quod iubet det, lex autem non det. Qui non credit, priuatur vita, vel hoc ipso, quod non credit, hoc est, non dignatur eam apprehendere, & sibi in manum quasi sumere. Et hæc quidem poena satis grauis est, quod quis priuetur cœlesti illa suauitate. Verùm præterea qui non credit condemnatur, adiudicatúrque morti æternæ, quia nullum est medium cuiquam: vel enim viuendum in æternum, vel moriendum in æternum: & quia infidelitas non nuda priuatio est, sed contemptus gratiæ, Quime reiicit, inquit, hoc est, contemnit: verf.48. Verùm quis iudex erit au condemnabit? Non ego, inquit, condemno eum, nam enim, &c. Christus in primo suo aduentu cum esset iudex mundi, sic tamen deposuit personam Iudicis vt nihil in se nisi summam mansuetudinem, & amorem tantum, non iram patris sui apparere voluerit, ad hoc vt omnes ad se alliceret. Nam ab iis, quos videmus pollere potestate ad vitam & necem, abhorrere solemus. Quare de eo prædictum fuit, Seruus meus, dilectus meus in quo acquieuit anima mea, non litigabit neque clamabit, neque audiet quisquam in plateis vocem eius, arundinemChristus quo sensu dicat se non venisse vt damnet mundum. nem quassatam non confringet. Quibus verbis significat summam illam mansuetudinem Christi futuram in primo ipsius aduentu: At in secundo aduentu induet personam iudicis,& horribilis conspicietur iis, qui ipsi non crediderunt in hac vita. Tum videbunt filium hominis venientem in nubibus cœli cum potentia & gloria multa. Quare notandum quòd dicit in præsenti tempore, Ego non condemno, non autem non condemnabo. Quis igitur futurus est iudex? Sermo, inquit, quem loquutus sum. q.d. Etsi nullus futurus sit iudex alius, atqui cessante omni iudice vel verbum hoc solum quod ego pronuncio, iudicabit & condemnabit. Putant homines prædicatum hoc verbum Euangelij statim euanescere, & ipsi quantum efficere possunt, dant operam ne id memoriæ ipsorum imprimatur. Atillo die recens erit memoria tum verbi prædicati, tum personarum ipsarum quæ prædicarunt ipsum, & conscientia accusabit grauissimè ob contemptum, verbum Euangelij grauior erit iudex quàm verbum legis. Et Moses accusabit magis ob contemptum Christi, quàm ob violatam legem ipsam moralem. Ne putate, inquit, supra Iohan. 5. me accusaturum vos. Est qui vos accuset, Moses in quo vos speratis. Nam Mosen non audierunt. An Mosen legem prædicantem vel scribentem non audiuerunt? Non, sed Euangelium scribentem. Moses enim, inquit, scripsit de me. Infidelitas autem peccatum grauissimum erit in illo iudicio. Hæc, inquit, est condemnatio mundi, quod lux venit in mundum, & homines magis diligunt tenebras quàm lucem Iohan. 3. Quia ego ex. Ratio est cur sermo condemnabit mundum, ab authore eius Deo. Necesse est enim sermo à tali tanto que authore profectus, efficaciam suam habeat in damnandis contemptoribus, quocunque demum mistro vtatur, & per quodcunque demum instrumentum loquatur: instrumenti enim vilitas non efficit quominus verbum sit efficax, siue ad vitam, siue ad mortem, & ipsum instrumentum fidele est bona fragrantia Christi Deo & in iis qui pereunt, & in iis qui seruantur. Et scio mandatum. Occupatio; Obiici potuit hûc effectum verbi Dei grauem esse nimis, nempe damnationem. Verba quæ ego loquor vobis, inquit Christus, Spiritus & vita sunt: Ioh. 6.
units.tr: THe third argument, by which, if they will not be moved by the sweet promise of seeing and laying hold of God, nor by that rescue out of darkness, they are compelled, as it were, to believe by the heavy threat of eternal damnation. For the word of the Gospel first promises sweetly, then threatens gravely, and no less severely, indeed more so, than the word of the law itself. But this differs from the law: what it commands, it gives; the law, however, does not give. He who does not believe is deprived of life, even by this very fact that he does not believe, that is, he does not deign to lay hold of it and take it, as it were, into his hand. And this punishment is indeed heavy enough, that a man is deprived of that heavenly sweetness. But moreover, he who does not believe is condemned and adjudged to eternal death, because there is no middle course for anyone: for one must either live forever or die forever. And because unbelief is not a bare privation, but a contempt of grace. He who rejects me, he says, that is, despises me: verse 48. But who will be the judge, or who will condemn? "I," he says, "do not condemn him; for indeed, etc." Christ, at his first coming, though he was the judge of the world, nevertheless laid aside the person of a judge in such a way that he wished nothing to appear in himself but the highest gentleness and love only, not the anger of his Father, so that he might draw all to himself. For we are wont to shrink from those whom we see possessing power over life and death. Therefore it was foretold of him: My servant, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased, shall not strive nor cry, nor shall anyone hear his voice in the streets; a bruised reed he shall not break. By these words he signifies that the highest gentleness of Christ would be present at his first coming. But at his second coming he will put on the person of a judge, and will be seen as dreadful by those who did not believe in him in this life. Then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and glory. Hence it is to be noted that he says in the present tense, "I do not condemn," not "I will not condemn." Who then is to be the judge? The word, he says, which I have spoken. That is to say: though there will be no other judge, yet, with every other judge set aside, this word alone which I proclaim will judge and condemn. Men think that the preached word of the Gospel quickly fades away, and they themselves, as far as they can, take care that it is not impressed upon their memory. But on that day the memory will be fresh, both of the word preached and of the very persons who preached it; and conscience will accuse most severely on account of contempt. The word of the Gospel will be a graver judge than the word of the law. And Moses will accuse more on account of contempt of Christ than on account of the violated moral law itself. Do not think, he says, that I shall accuse you before the Father, John 5. There is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope. For they did not hear Moses. Did they not hear Moses preaching or writing the law? No, but Moses writing the Gospel. For Moses, he says, wrote of me. Unbelief, moreover, will be the gravest sin in that judgment. This, he says, is the condemnation of the world, that light has come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, John 3. For I did not. The reason why the word will condemn the world is that its author is God. For a word that proceeds from so great and such an author must have its efficacy in condemning the despisers, whatever minister it uses, and through whatever instrument it speaks. For the meanness of the instrument does not prevent the word from being effective, whether unto life or unto death; and the instrument itself is faithful, a sweet savour of Christ to God, both among those who perish and among those who are saved. And I know the commandment. An objection: it might be said here that the effect of the word of God is too grievous, namely damnation. The words that I speak to you, says Christ, are spirit and life: John 6.

units.la: Ioh. 6. Quíque fidem habet verbo Christi, sentit reipsa viuifi-cũ,vt Petrus,Ad quě,inquit, abibimus? verba vitæ æternæ habes Iohan.6. Effectum autem damnationis & mortis verbi est per accidens, nempe eorum respectu, qui verbum contemnunt. Vbi enim in cor durum incidit & refractarium,illud ipsum deterius reddit solito, ac magis obduratum,sumpta, vt loquitur Apostolus Rom.7.occasione ex verbo Dei quod in se sanctum ac bonum est. Deo igitur in Christo sit omnis honor & gloria:Amen.
units.tr: John 6. Whoever has faith in the word of Christ actually experiences its life-giving power, as Peter did when he said: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life" (John 6). But the word's effect of condemnation and death is incidental, and it concerns those who despise the word. For when it falls on a hard and unyielding heart, it makes that heart worse than before and more hardened, because, as the Apostle says (Rom. 7), sin takes occasion from the word of God, which is holy and good in itself. To God therefore, in Christ, be all honour and glory. Amen. ## ARGUMENT

units.la: ARGVMENTVM
Hoc capite primùm est historia lotionis pedum discipulorum Christi, simúlque sermo eius continuus ad discipulos habitus ad verf.vsque 22.
units.tr: In this chapter, first, is the account of the washing of the disciples' feet, together with Christ's continuous speech to the disciples, from verse 1 to verse 22.

units.la: Secundò, occasione proximi sermonis & querela de se per vnum discipulorum prodendo, de Iuda Iscariote agitur nominatim, eius habetur quædam designatio & designationis effectus, tum in discipulis aliis, tum in ipsomet Iuda,ad verf.31.
units.tr: Second, on the occasion of the preceding speech and his complaint that one of the disciples would betray him, Judas Iscariot is named. There is a certain designation of him and the effect of that designation, both in the other disciples and in Judas himself, up to verse 31.

units.la: Tertiò, egressoiam Iuda discipulos commonefacit atque instruit ad verf.36.
units.tr: Third, after Judas has gone out, he admonishes and instructs the disciples, up to verse 36.

units.la: Postremò, Petro confidenter promittenti constantiam in vita eius defendenda, prædicat lapsum, nempe sui abnegationem, ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Finally, when Peter confidently promises constancy in defending his life, he foretells his fall, namely his denial, to the end of the chapter. ## CHAP. XIII.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
1 ANte festum autem Paschæ, sciens Iesus venisse horam illam suam qua digrederetur ex hoc mundo ad Patrem, quum dilexisset suos illos qui erant in mundo,vsque ad finem dilexit eos.
units.tr: 1 Now before the feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father, having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end.

units.la: 2 Et cœna peracta (cùm diabolus iam immisisset in cor Iudæ filij Simonis, Iscariota, vt proderet eum)
units.tr: 2 And supper being ended, the devil having now put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, to betray him,

units.la: 3 Sciens Iesus Patrem omnia dedisse sibi in manus, & se à Deo prodiisse, & ad Deum abire:
units.tr: 3 Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he was come from God and went to God,

units.la: 4 Surgit à cœna, & deponit pallium: acceptoque linteo præcinxit se.
units.tr: 4 riseth from supper and laid aside his garments; and took a towel and girded himself.

units.la: 5 Deinde immisit aquam in peluim, & cœpit lauare pedes discipulorum, & extergere linteo quo erat præcinctus.
units.tr: 5 After that he poureth water into a bowl, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded.

units.la: HOC tertiū est Pascha post Baptismū Christi & initam functionem. De primo vidimus capite tertio, de secundo capite 5. Nunc de tertio, in quo verus ille agnus Paschalis, Agnus Dei qui tollit peccata mundi immolatus est & occisus. Sciens. Prima occasio, propinquitas mortis, quam describit hoc loco per migrationem quandam in regnum cœleste. Vt intelligamus mortem piorum ac fidelium, qui similiter vt Christus ipse moriuntur, non perditionem aliquam esse, sed migrationem ex mundo in cœlos. Vnde Paulus cùm de morte loquitur, Probamus, inquit, potius migrare & ire ad Dominum habitatum. Nam in mundo dum sumus, peregrè agimus à Domino, Quod ex hac occasione discimus id nimirum est: Moueat Christum breuitas temporis ad hoc exemplum humilitatis, & ad seriò informandos discipulos. Ita breuitas temporis huius vitæ & migrationis propinquitas, nos incitare debent ad officium sedulò faciendum, & ad alios, quantum fieri à nobis potest, promouendum. Adhuc, inquit Christus, superiori capite, ad paruum tempus lux vobiscum est, ambulate in luce dum lucem habetis. Et Paulus, Quia tempus contractum est impositerum, qui uxores habent sint vt non habentes, qui gaudent vt non gaudentes, &c. Hoc est, nihil istarum rerum vnicè agamus, sed studeamus Deo placere imprimis. Imprimis autem Pastores admonere debet breuitas temporis, vt quod est eorum officium, aliis præeant, & verbo & vita; Non, inquam, verbo solo, sed vita quoque; oportet enim ipsi ingrediantur eandem illam salutis viam, quam aliis demonstrant verbo. Paulus qui docuit viam illam qua itur
units.tr: This is the third Passover after Christ's baptism and the beginning of his office. We saw the first in chapter 3 and the second in chapter 5. Now we come to the third, in which that true Paschal lamb, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world, is sacrificed and slain. "Knowing." The first occasion is the nearness of death, which he describes here as a kind of migration into the heavenly kingdom. Thus we understand that the death of the godly and faithful, who die as Christ himself died, is not any destruction but a migration from the world to heaven. Hence Paul, speaking of death, says: "We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord" (2 Cor. 5). For while we are in the world we are abroad from the Lord. From this occasion we learn this: the brevity of time should move Christ to this example of humility, and to earnestly instruct the disciples. So the brevity of this life and the nearness of our departure should urge us to perform our duty diligently, and to advance others as far as we can. "Yet a little while," says Christ in the preceding chapter, "is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light" (John 12). And Paul: "The time is short; it remains that those who have wives be as though they had none; those who rejoice as though they rejoiced not," and so on (1 Cor. 7). That is, we should not pursue these things alone, but above all strive to please God. Above all, the brevity of time ought to admonish ministers that, as is their office, they go before others, both by word and by life. I say, not by word alone but also by life; for they must themselves walk the same path of salvation which they show to others by word. Paul, who taught the way by which one goes

units.la: 1. Cor. 7. 29. ad coelos, Estote, inquit, imitatores mei. Ergo ipse praecessit & ingressus est prior viam eam quam docuit. Praesertim autem praeire debent Pastores exemplo humilitatis: Nam per humilitatem & humilem quasi viam ad sublimitatem coelestem itur. Christus inanitus est priusquam ad summam illam sublimitatem exaltatus est.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 7. 29. to heaven, says: "Be ye followers of me" [Estote imitatores mei]. Therefore he himself went before and entered first upon the way which he taught. Especially ministers ought to go before in the example of humility, for through humility, and as it were by a humble way, one goes to heavenly exaltation. Christ emptied himself before he was exalted to that supreme height.

units.la: Quum dilexisset suos. Altera occasio sive causa potius, & facti fundamentum dilectio. Movit Christū dilectio illa summa ad faciendū omnia quaecunq; fecit nostra causa. Movit eū dilectio ad summā illam humilitatē, qua se ad crucē & inferos ipsos humiliavit. Movit ad hoc exemplū humilitatis. Non satis movet angustia temporis ad curā aliorum habendam, nisi adsit quoque amor. Imo vero, quo angustius est tempus, eo magis sollicitē curamus nosipsos, nisi adsit amor quo alios prosequamur. Sunt qui, si vel ipsis bene sit, vel de ipsis actum sit, nihil pensi habent, licet omnes ties posterorum sursum deorsum voluantur: At qui proximum vixit & posteros etiam in mortis puncto curat sedulo, quomodo se habituri sint, & exporrecta quasi manu omnes ad coelos erigere conantur.
units.tr: "Since he had loved his own." The second occasion, or rather cause, and the foundation of the deed, is love. That great love moved Christ to do all the things he did for our sake. Love moved him to that supreme humility by which he humbled himself even to the cross and to hell itself. It moved him to this example of humility. The shortness of time is not enough to move us to care for others unless love is also present. Indeed, the shorter the time, the more anxiously we care for ourselves, unless there is love by which we care for others. There are those who, whether it goes well or ill with themselves, make no account of anything, even though all the generations of posterity are tossed up and down. But he who lives for his neighbour, and takes diligent care for posterity even at the point of death, how they shall fare, and as it were with hand outstretched, strives to lift all of them up to heaven.

units.la: Et coena facta. Rufus designat tempus facti, sed particularius. Coenam hanc intelligo, non victimam illam qua cum discipulis comedit Pascha, & instituit Coenam Dominicam: hoc enim factum est, ut supra vidimus, ante Pascha. Quum diabolus. Tertio loco notatur tempus a Iudae proditione. Ad notandum autem facti illius ac proditionis atrocitatem, tribuit illam diabolo authori, hoc est peflimo authori peflimum factum. Ita enim solemus pessima quaeque facinora, peflimo authori diabolo adscribere: ita tamen ut homines non sint excusabiles: Nam omnium facinorum ipsi in se causam habent, & ignem quasi in se concipiunt. Diabolus autem flabellum est. Tempus hoc adductum est ad amplificandum factum, nam etsi constitit Christo de proposito Iudae, deque morte decreta, tamen neglecto se morteque sua, curam agere voluit discipulorum quos post se essent relicturus in mundo. Nam illud est ingenium piorum quorumque, quod etsi intelligant male sibi fore, tamen modo benefaciant Ecclesiae nihil curant. Sic Paulus, cum scirer parata sibi vincula & afflictionem Hierosolymis, lymis,cùm eò ascensurus esset: Tamen,inquit,nullius rei rationem habeo, imò vita mea mihi non est chara, vt peragam cursum meum cum gaudio. Præterea ex hoc tempore videmus consultò voluisse Christum edito exemplo hoc humilitatis in conspectu discipulorum, vitam suam, & extremum quasi actum vitæ claudere: vt nimirum quod in postremo viderunt, illud maximè imitarentur in tota vita. Neque enim iam postremò miraculum aliquod voluit edere, sed exemplum hoc humilitatis commendans, nimirum, magis humilitatem nobis quàm donum miraculorum, significans eos esse magis imitatores Christi, qui humilitatem eius sequuntur, quàm qui miracula, & ea quæ extra ordinem fecit.
units.tr: "And supper being ended." Again he marks the time of the deed, but more particularly. I understand this supper not as that sacrifice by which he ate the Passover with the disciples and instituted the Lord's Supper; for that was done, as we saw above, before the Passover. "When the devil..." The third mark of time is taken from Judas's betrayal. To note the atrocity of that deed and betrayal, he ascribes it to the devil as its author, that is, the most wicked deed to the most wicked author. For we are accustomed to ascribe all the worst crimes to the most wicked author, the devil; yet so that men are not thereby excused. For they themselves have the cause of all their crimes within themselves, and they kindle the fire within themselves. The devil is only the bellows. This time is introduced to magnify the deed. For although it was settled for Christ that Judas had made his purpose and that death was decreed, nevertheless, disregarding himself and his own death, he willed to care for the disciples whom he was to leave behind in the world.
