Nota & symbolum scholæ Christi, fateor, est cognitio & professio Christi: sed certior est charitatis illa nota, Vel ideo, cùm professio sit in verbis, charitas sit in operibus. Non diligamus, inquit Iohannes, verbo & lingua, sed opere & veritate. Imò vero nisi charitas confirmet hominibus fidem & professionem, iactatio fidei inane quoddam est argumentum. Ostende mihi fidem tuam ex operibus tuis, ait Iacobus. Ex his sequitur frustra gloriari homines in fide & professione, nisi prodeant cum nota ac sigillo charitatis: frustra homicidas, oppressores, raptores, fures, adulteros, &c. gloriari de Christo, & fide Christiana, quia factis Christum negant.
units.tr: Brotherly love, in what sense Christ's new commandment. For he writes love on the fleshly tables of the heart; hence John calls it the old doctrine, namely as to its substance itself. But it is new in the same place as to the form and manner of handling it, because the darkness is passing and the true light now shines, namely illuminating hearts and reforming minds, so that the doctrine of love may be effective. It should be noted that the Lord did not by chance always have love on his lips. For, as is commonly said, the mouth speaks out of the abundance of the heart. The heart of the Lord was filled with love, with love of men and [φιλαδελφια, brotherly love]. Hence that love burst forth and was poured out in the admonition of others. For those who love themselves diligently admonish others. But those who are estranged from love find nothing pleasing except hatreds and dissensions, and they become the authors of all disturbances. As I have loved, I say. He sets his own example before us, by which we are admonished that it is not enough to command love to others unless we go before them by our example, and persuade them of love not so much by words as by life. Now how greatly the Lord went before us in love has been made known in fact. For no greater love can there be than that by which someone dies for his friend; and he commends love to us in that he died for his enemies. Moreover, for the example of the Lord's love to move us, it is necessary that we feel deeply in our hearts how greatly he has loved us; that is, as I may speak with the Apostle, that we feel the love of God poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. Otherwise, the bare example of so great a love will certainly not move us. For the sense of that love loosens our hearts, with an unspeakable sweetness, into love, first of him who has loved us so greatly, and then into love of our neighbour for his sake. By this all. The second point is an argument from the fact that love is a certain mark by which it is known that we are disciples of Christ, educated in his school. For Christ especially trains his own in love, and has as it were engraved it on their hearts, the law being written in their hearts, as I may speak with the Prophet. Thus it comes about that love is the sign and mark of the disciples of Christ, and that those who wish to show the world that they have been educated in the school of Christ should love one another very much. The mark and badge of the school of Christ is, I grant, the knowledge and profession of Christ; but that mark of love is more certain. Moreover, since profession is in words, love is in deeds. Let us not love, says John, in word and tongue, but in deed and truth. Indeed, unless love confirms the faith and profession of men, the boasting of faith is an empty argument. Show me your faith from your works, says James. From these things it follows that men boast in vain of faith and profession unless they come forth with the mark and seal of love; murderers, oppressors, robbers, thieves, adulterers and so on boast in vain of Christ and the Christian faith, because by their deeds they deny Christ.

units.la: Domine, quò abis. Petro interea hæret in memoria significatio illa discessionis, ideòque petit quonam abeat? Peccat quidem in eo primùm quòd virtutem & efficaciam Christi præsentia eius corporali metiatur: Peccat deinde, quòd fiducia quadam carnis præsumat eum sequi (idque apparet ex sequeti communicatione) quocunque demum sit abiturus. Verùm hoc in eo laudatur, quòd non patiatur libenter Dominum à se avelli. Sed enim quàm benignus esset Dominus, ut ipse loquitur in Epistola sua: & sensit eum verba vitæ æternæ habere. Longè aliter responderunt Pharisæi & Iudæi supra cap. 6. 68. Longè aliter responderunt Pharisæi & Iudæi supra cap. 7. 35. Anibit, inquiunt, ad dispersos Græcos? & cap. 8. 22. an seipsum interfecturus est: cum contemptu nimirum hæc dixerunt. Qui enim sentiunt quantum bonum sit in præsentia Domini, eius discessum ferunt iniquissimo animo. Qui verò non gustarunt quàm suavis sit Dominus, eius discessum susque deque ferunt, eòque gaudet potiùs: quasi verò sit solidum aliquod gaudium sine Domino. Quo ego abeo. Dominus præterito ac dissimulato eo in quo peccatum est à Petro, respondet benignè, ac promittit eum sequuturum ipsum suo tempore. Omnes preces nostræ & sermones ad Deum commisti sunt peccato. Unde si nobiscum ageret ex iustitia sua, nihil à nobis profectum acceptaret. At Dominus nō frangit arundinem quassatam, & linum fumigans non extinguit: hoc est cùm aliquem sensum deprehendit sui Spiritus pro nobis in media infirmitate nostra interpellantis, eum statim agnoscit, ac nos gratos habet in Christo. ftolesu. Tantum est habere vel granum fidei & dile-ctionis: nam quod incepit in nobis opus bonum, ipse perficiet. Nota rursus ex eo quod admonet non posse ipsum nunc sequi, discipulos Christi non statim potentes esse ac firmos ad eum sequendum, hoc est tollendu crucem suam & eum sequendum: Verum habere eos incrementum suum, & paulatim adolescere & crescere in virum perfectum: adeo vt tandem ferendo sint. Verum Dominus est qui hoc nouit: nos autem ipsi experimur, Dominus est qui nos certiores facit de imbecillitate nostra, nos non secus ac pueri, qui putant se etiam in infirma illa aetate multa posse perpeti, fallimur, & ignoramus quid possimus ipsi sufferre. Quare non possum. Iam bis admonitus est de sua infirmitate, semel vna cum caeteris discipulis, iterum seorsim: nec tamen definit sibiipsi ac suis viribus confidere, adeo difficulter adducitur quis ad cognoscendum infirmitatem virium suarum vt sapenumero non nisi experientia, quae stultorum est magistra, eo adducantur. Concedo, nunquam satis Deo confidere potest quisquam, sed quo magis confidit Deo, eo magis diffidit sibi. Contra, quo magis confidit sibi, eo minus confidit Deo. Paulus dicit se afflictum grauiter in Asia, consilium motus coepisse, vt non consideret sibi, sed ei qui excitat mortuos. Ecce fiducia in Deum est cum diffidentia nostri & in nobis ipsis. Si roges quaenam haec fuerit Petri fiducia, Responsio facilis est ex verbis Domini sequentibus, in quibus inanem istam fiduciam reprehendit. Animam tuam. Reprehendit Dominus inanem illam Petri fiduciam: q. d. Tantum abest ab eo vt pro me animam tuam ponituris, &c. Qui confidunt carni, hoc audient a Domino, quod hic audiuit Petrus & reipsa demum experientur, quam inanis sit illa fiducia. Adeo tamen caeci sunt vt non patiantur se corrigi, postquam reprehensi sunt: & caecutiunt ad omnium admonitiones. Na Petrus, etiam adhuc non depositu inanem illam fiduciam, neque aduertit ad verba Domini, sed ea statim dedit obliuioni, vt apparet ex Matth. 26.75. vbi admonitus est recordatus esse verborum Domini. Vide igitur quanta caecitate feramur, donec tandem experiamur quam natura fragiles simus.
units.tr: Lord, where are you going? Meanwhile that saying about his departure remains fixed in Peter's memory, and so he asks where Jesus is going. He sins first in this, that he measures the power and efficacy of Christ by Christ's bodily presence. He sins again in that, with a certain fleshly confidence, he presumes to follow him wherever he is going (as the reply that follows makes clear). Yet in this he is commended, in that he does not willingly suffer the Lord to be taken from him. But how kind the Lord was, as he himself says in his Epistle, and he perceived that Christ had the words of eternal life. The Pharisees and Jews answered quite differently, see above chap. 6.68. The Pharisees and Jews answered quite differently, see above chap. 7.35: Will he go, they say, to the Greeks who are scattered? and chap. 8.22: Will he kill himself? They spoke these words with plain contempt. Those who sense how great a good it is to be in the Lord's presence bear his departure with a most unhappy mind. But those who have not tasted how sweet the Lord is take his departure lightly and rejoice in it rather, as though there were any solid joy apart from the Lord. Where I am going. The Lord, passing over and ignoring the sin Peter committed, answers kindly and promises that Peter will follow him in his own time. All our prayers and words offered to God are tainted with sin. Hence, if he dealt with us according to his justice, he would accept nothing that we have done. But the Lord does not break a bruised reed, nor quench the smoking flax: that is, when he perceives in us some sense of his Spirit interceding for us in the midst of our weakness, he at once acknowledges it, and holds us acceptable in Christ. Even a grain of faith and love is enough, for he who has begun the good work in us will himself bring it to completion. Note again, from his saying that Peter cannot follow him now, that the disciples of Christ are not at once able and strong enough to follow him, that is, to take up their cross and follow him. Rather, they have their own growth, and gradually they grow up and increase into a perfect man, so that at last they become able to bear it. The Lord is the one who knows this; we ourselves learn by experience that the Lord is the one who makes us aware of our weakness. Like children, who think they can endure many things even at that tender age, we are mistaken and do not know what we ourselves can bear. Why can I not? He had already been warned about his weakness twice, once together with the other disciples and again privately. Yet he still does not cease to trust in himself and his own strength, so hard is it for anyone to come to know the weakness of his powers that very often men are led to it only by experience, which is the teacher of fools. I grant that no one can ever trust God enough, but the more a man trusts God, the less he trusts himself; on the other hand, the more he trusts himself, the less he trusts God. Paul says that he was grievously afflicted in Asia, and that he had come to the resolve not to trust in himself but in him who raises the dead. Behold, trust in God goes together with distrust of ourselves and of our own powers. If you ask what this trust of Peter was, the answer is easy from the Lord's following words, in which he rebukes that empty trust. Your life. The Lord rebukes Peter's empty trust, as if to say: far from laying down your life for me, etc. Those who trust in the flesh will hear from the Lord what Peter heard here, and in the end they will experience for themselves how empty that trust is. Yet they are so blind that they will not allow themselves to be corrected after they have been rebuked, and they grow blinder at every warning. For Peter, even now, did not lay aside that empty trust, nor did he heed the words of the Lord, but at once forgot them, as appears from Matt. 26.75, where, when admonished, he remembered the words of the Lord. See, then, with what blindness we are carried along, until at last we learn how weak we are by nature.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM
units.tr: ARGUMENT

units.la: Tribus capitibus sequentibus, nempe 14.15. & 16. habetur sermo Domini ad discipulos suos extremus, quem scilicet ad eos habuit, partim in ipsa caena ultima, partim post caenam.
units.tr: In the three following chapters, namely 14, 15 and 16, we have the Lord's last discourse to his disciples, which he delivered to them partly at the Last Supper itself, and partly after the supper.

units.la: Hoc autem capite primum consolatur discipulos contra scandalum mortis suae, & contra suum ab ijs decessum ad versum 5.
units.tr: In this chapter, first, he comforts the disciples against the scandal of his death and against his departure from them, to verse 5.

units.la: Secundò, Thomam primùm, deinde Philippum, interpellantes sermonem Domini, ipse erudit atque instruit, ad versum 12.
units.tr: Second, he instructs and teaches Thomas first and then Philip, who interrupt his discourse, to verse 12.

units.la: Tertiò, redit ad consolationem illam discipulorum institutam, eámque persequitur ad versum 22.
units.tr: Third, he returns to the comfort of the disciples already begun, and pursues it to verse 22.

units.la: Quartò, Iudas Iacobi frater eum interpellat verf. 22.
units.tr: Fourth, Judas, the brother of James, interrupts him at verse 22.

units.la: Quintò, Christus quaestione illa neglecta ac praeterita pergit in instituta doctrina & consolatione ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Fifth, Christ, setting aside and passing over that question, goes on with the teaching and consolation already begun, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAP. XIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 14

units.la: 1 E turbator cor vestrum: creditis in Deum, etiam in me credite.
units.tr: 1 Let not your heart be troubled: you believe in God, believe also in me.

units.la: 2 In domo Patris mei habitationes multae sunt: alioqui dixissem vobis.
units.tr: 2 In my Father's house are many mansions: otherwise I would have told you.

units.la: 3 Praeficiscor paraturus vobis locum, & quum profectus fuero, & parauero vobis locum, rursum veniam, & assumam vos ad meipsum: ut ubi ero ego, & vos sitis.
units.tr: 3 I go to prepare a place for you, and when I have gone and prepared a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, that where I am, there you may be also.

units.la: 4 Et quò abeam scitis, & viam scitis.
units.tr: 4 And you know where I am going, and you know the way.

units.la: NE perturbentur eius discessu, de quo iam praemonuit, consolatur eos hoc capite, & deinceps ad caput usque 18. In hoc reprehendendi sunt, quòd nullam gratiam, substracta semel corporali praesentia, expectarint à Domino. Verùm habemus hic quod discamus exemplo: Nempe quemadmodum praesente Christo cor hominis tranquillatur, ita absente eo cor hoc.
units.tr: They are not to be troubled by his departure, of which he has already forewarned them. He comforts them in this chapter and onward to verse 18. In this they are to be blamed, because once Christ's bodily presence was taken away they expected no grace from the Lord. Yet here we have an example to learn from: just as a man's heart is calmed while Christ is present, so his heart is troubled while he is absent.

units.la: {y} Prima capitis pars. hominis perturbatur. Fieri quidem potest, vt mundani consopiantur ad tempus securitate aliqua carnali. Verum nulla pax improbis, ait Dominus: scilicet pax vera: Et pij qui semel gustârunt quàm benignus sit Dominus, reipsa experiuntur sine Christo nullam esse consolationem. Creditis in Deum. Argumentum contrapræ turbationem cordis, à fide sumptum, Credite, inquit, in me. Fides in Christum absentem mihi strat consolationem. Iustificati fide pacem habemus apud Deum. Rom. 5. Fides enim efficit præsentiam aliquam: est enim subsistentia rerum quæsperantur, & demonstratio eorum quæ non videntur. Argumentum hoc non nudè & simpliciter proponitur, sed comparatè, facta cum fide in Deum comparatione: quasi dicat, Quemadmodum creditis in Deū, ita credite in me. Nam ego & Pater, vt supra dictum est, vnum sumus. Quare fides in Christum non est præiudicio fidei in Deum Patrem, vt neque fides in Spiritum sanctum præiudicio est fidei in Patrem & filium. Nam vnus idemque Deus est, etsi personæ in vna illa Dei natura distinctæ sint. Nihil autem vetat quo minùs sit fides in plures personas, modo essentia vna sit eadémque. At in plures Deos essentia aliosque atque alios fides esse non potest. Quia fides non potest niti, nisi vna re & substantia. Estque hoc argumentum, quòd vnus sit Deus, & quòd vna sit natura Patris, Filij & Spiritus sancti, à fide quæ ipsa profectò alioqui tribus his non posset niti. Quare non est præiudicio, fides in Filiū, fidei in Patrē: Imò vero, non potest esse fides in Patrem nisi per Filiū, quia est imago eius. Non enim potest fides penetrare ad cum qui habitat in luce inaccessa, nisi per Filium & eum quidem in carne nostra humiliatum: in quo solo lucet nobis gloria paterna, misericordia eius, iustitia eius, potentia eius, sapientia eius, &c. Atque hoc quidem videtur significari his verbis, quorum sensus videtur hic esse: Creditis in Deum, idque vestra ipsorum confessione, tum igitur credite in me, sine quo non potestis in Deum credere.
units.tr: The first part of the chapter. The heart of a man is troubled. It may indeed happen that worldly people are lulled for a time by some carnal security. But, says the Lord, there is no peace for the wicked, meaning true peace. And the godly, who have once tasted how kind the Lord is, find by experience that without Christ there is no comfort. You believe in God. Against the troubling of the heart he argues from faith: Believe, he says, in me. Faith in Christ, though he is absent, gives me comfort. Being justified by faith, we have peace with God (Rom. 5). For faith brings about a kind of presence, since it is "the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen" (Heb. 11). This argument is not put forward bare and simple, but by comparison, the comparison being made with faith in God: as if he said, As you believe in God, so believe in me. For I and the Father are one, as was said above. Therefore faith in Christ does not detract from faith in God the Father, just as faith in the Holy Spirit does not detract from faith in the Father and the Son. For God is one and the same, although the persons are distinct within that one divine nature. Nothing forbids faith to be placed in several persons, provided the essence is one and the same. But faith cannot be placed in several gods with different and different essences, because faith cannot rest on anything but one thing and one substance. And this argument, that God is one and that the nature of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is one, is drawn from faith, which otherwise could not rest on these three at all. Therefore faith in the Son is no prejudice to faith in the Father. Indeed, faith in the Father cannot exist except through the Son, because he is the image of him. For faith cannot penetrate to him who dwells in unapproachable light, except through the Son, and that Son humbled in our flesh, in whom alone the glory of the Father shines for us: his mercy, his justice, his power, his wisdom, and so on. And this seems to be signified by these words, whose sense seems to be this: You believe in God, and that by your own confession; therefore believe in me also, without whom you cannot believe in God.

units.la: In domo. Secundum argumentum consolationis est ab ipsorum bono. Abeo, inquit, paraturus vobis locum in domo patris mei. q. d. Nisi ego abiero, nullus in domo Patris mei futurus est vobis locus. Nullus, inquam, fuit locus in cœlo vel Patribus qui vixerunt ante manifestationem Christi in carne, & eius ascensionem; vel iis qui fuerunt, sunt, futuri sunt in mundo post eius manifestationem & ascensionē, nisi solius ascensionis Christi virtute. Patres invenerunt locum in cœlis virtute ascensionis futurae: Nos vero virtute ascensionis praeteritae. Virtus eadem est & ante ascensionem & post ascensionem, sed alia atque alia est eius mensura: minor virtus ante ascensionem, ideo pauciores tum ingressi sunt cœlos. Stante priore tabernaculo, nondum patefacta est via ad sanctuarium. Maior virtus Christi post ascensionem, ideo plures nunc ingrediuntur cœlos quàm tūc. Vis, inquit Dominus, affertur regno cælorum, & violenti rapiunt illud: innuens multitudinem omnium gentium, quæ, iā patefacta in cœlos via per Christi ascensionē, irrumpunt quasi in cœlos. Sed quæras cur non nisi virtute ascensionis Christi, & non nisi eo nobis præeunte eatur ad cœlos? Respondeo non esse iter ad cœlos nisi per sanguinem, quo satisfit iustitiæ Dei ob peccata hominum, absque sanguine non est remissio peccatorum. Ideo Pontifex non ingressus est terrestre illud sanctuarium sine sanguine. At Christus ingressus est sanctuarium non manufactum, per sanguinem non hircorum & taurorum: sed per suum sanguinem: Ergo non patet ingressus ad cœlum cuiquam, nisi prægresso Christo, hoc est sine eius ascensione. Nihil autem prodest cuiquam illa ascensio Christi, per sanguinem, nisi sit fides in eius sanguinem, neque vllinisi qui credunt in eum crucifixum, virtute ascensionis eius locum habent in cœlis vllum. Ante argumentum ipsum substratum est eius quoddam quasi fundamentum: nempe hoc, In domo Patris mei multæ sunt habitationes. Ante Christi ascensionem sunt quidem multæ habitationes: hoc est, extat Deo cœlestis illa gloria, cuius nos participes sumus qui sine Christo destituimur gloria Dei. Verum non nisi virtute ascensionis Christi præparantur nobis illæ eædem mansiones, nam alioqui occlusæ sunt omnes. Dicam præterea: habitationes sunt in cœlis quæ sufficiant infinitis mundis capiendis: Imo virtus est in ascensione Christi ad præparandum locum infinitis etiam mundis, nedum
units.tr: In my Father's house. The second argument of comfort is taken from their own good. I go, he says, to prepare a place for you in my Father's house. That is, unless I go away, there will be no place for you in my Father's house. No place, I say, was there in heaven for the fathers who lived before the manifestation of Christ in the flesh and his ascension, nor for those who are, have been, or will be in the world after his manifestation and ascension, except by the power of Christ's ascension alone. The fathers found a place in the heavens by the power of the ascension to come; we by the power of the ascension already past. The power is the same both before and after the ascension, but its measure is different and different: the power was less before the ascension, and therefore fewer then entered heaven. While the first tabernacle was still standing, the way into the sanctuary was not yet opened. The power of Christ after the ascension is greater, and therefore more now enter heaven than then. The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, says the Lord, and the violent take it by force, indicating the multitude of all nations, who, now that the way into heaven has been opened through Christ's ascension, break in as it were into heaven. But you may ask why one goes to heaven only by the power of Christ's ascension, and only with him going before us? I answer that there is no way to heaven except through blood, by which the justice of God is satisfied for the sins of men, and without blood there is no remission of sins. Therefore the high priest did not enter that earthly sanctuary without blood. But Christ entered the sanctuary not made with hands, not by the blood of goats and bulls, but by his own blood. Therefore no one has an open way into heaven except with Christ having gone before, that is, without his ascension. But that ascension of Christ through blood profits no one unless there is faith in his blood, and none but those who believe in him crucified have any place in heaven by virtue of his ascension. Before the argument itself there lies, as it were, a certain foundation: namely this, In my Father's house there are many mansions. Before Christ's ascension there indeed are many mansions: that is, that heavenly glory exists with God, of which we are partakers, we who without Christ are deprived of the glory of God. But those same dwelling places are prepared for us only by the power of Christ's ascension, for otherwise all are closed. I will say further: there are in heaven dwelling places sufficient to hold infinite worlds. Indeed there is power in Christ's ascension to prepare a place even for infinite worlds, not to speak of

units.la: Mansiones cœlestes à Christo parantur & patefiunt. iis omnibus hominibus qui in hoc vno mundo sunt. Sed causa est in hominibus ipsis qui desunt sibi, neque credunt in illum sanguinem quo praeparantur nobis illa in coelis loca. Alioqui dixissem. q.d. Nisi ita quidem reipsa esset, & multae essent in domo Patris mei mansiones, non ita dixissem vobis, quod in re fuisset dixissem vobis. Non enim institutum est mihi pascere animos vestros inani spe. Discite igitur, quae promittit Dominus in verbo suo grandia sunt, & magnifica quae de coelis loquitur. At vero nisi ita esset re ipsa, non ita loqueretur: Imo res ipsa maior est verbis: & nos sentiemus reipsa, ubi eo ventum fuerit, omnia maiora ipsis verbis, ut de Regina Sabae dicitur quod confessa sit se vidisse maiora in aula Salomonis, quam quae sermonibus hominum adiplam perlata fuerant. Illud enim verissimum est, Oculus non vidit, auris non audiuit, neque ingressa sunt cor hominis, quae praeparauit Deus iis qui ipsum diligunt.
units.tr: Heavenly mansions are prepared and opened by Christ for all the men who are in this one world. But the fault lies in the men themselves, who fail themselves and do not believe in that blood by which those places in heaven are prepared for us. Otherwise I would have told you. That is: Unless it really were so, and there were many mansions in my Father's house, I would not have said it to you in this way; for it would have been to tell you something untrue, had it not been so in fact. For it is not my purpose to feed your minds with empty hope. Learn, then, that what the Lord promises in his word is great, and that what he says of heaven is magnificent. Indeed, unless it were so in fact, he would not speak in this way. Nay, the reality is greater than the words; and when we arrive there, we shall experience in fact that all things are greater than the words themselves, as it is said of the Queen of Sheba that she confessed she had seen greater things in the court of Solomon than had been reported to her by the talk of men. For this is most true: "Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him."

units.la: Et cum profectus fuero. Hoc tertium argumentum est a secundo Christi aduentu, ad ipsos glorificandos. Magna consolatio est in fide, quia Christum quodammodo praesentem credentibus efficit. Maior consolatio est, cum audimus praeparari nobis locum in coelis: hoc est, cum audimus eadem qua nunc viuimus mutatum iri in aspectum. Verum adhuc plenam illam consolationem impedit conscientia infirmitatis nostrae. Neque enim nobis sunt vires, quibus ascendamus ad loca nobis parata. Ideo cum audimus Christum rediturum & assumpturum nos ad se, iam perfecta est consolatio. Hinc fit ut fideles oculos habeant in coeli intentos, expectantes illustrem illum aduentum & redemptionem corporis sui. Expectant quidem cum suspiriis ac desiderio admirabili: verum simul cum gaudio spei ineffabili. Quod si in spe & expectatione tantum sit gaudium, quantum tum futurum est cum eum praesentem videbimus & in possessionem illam coelestem mittemur?
units.tr: And when I have gone. This third argument is from Christ's second coming, for the glorifying of themselves. There is great comfort in faith, because it makes Christ in some way present to believers. Greater comfort is there when we hear that a place is being prepared for us in heaven, that is, when we hear that the very life we now live will be changed into the sight of him. Yet the full measure of that comfort is still hindered by the awareness of our weakness. For we have no strength by which we may ascend to the places prepared for us. Therefore when we hear that Christ will return and take us to himself, the comfort is now complete. Hence it comes about that the faithful keep their eyes fixed on heaven, waiting for that glorious coming and the redemption of their body. They wait indeed with sighs and wonderful longing, but at the same time with the joy of an inexpressible hope. But if there is so much joy in hope and expectation, how great will it be when we see him present and are sent into that heavenly possession?

units.la: Et quo ego abeam. Hoc est argumentum consolationis quantum: quasi dicat, Interea donec ego venio consolamini vos vel cognitione huc tam loci, ad quem ego primum, deinde vos iturie stis, quam viae qua ad locum illo. Jum veniendum est: vtrumque enim noftis. Qui peregre agit, si non compertum habeat quo tandem loca requieturus sit,ea re grauiter commoueri solet. Quòd si locum quidem noscat,neque tamen viam teneat,grauiter commouetur. Quòd si vero & locum nouerit & viam, iam spe illuc perueniendi gaudet. Ita fit de nobis qui peregrè agimus in hac vita à Domino. Qui neque locum in quo requieturus sit nouit, neque viam cognitam habet,is profecto necesse est grauiter commoueatur. At qui vtrumque cognouit, & locum & viam, is profecto necesse est requiescat in spe.Quare cognitio tum loci ad quem,tum viæ per quam insignem consolationem nobis ministrat. Ignorantia autem istarum rerum comitem habet dolorem & animi deiectionem,præsertim in eo qui non sentit quietem in rebus his terrenis.
units.tr: And where I am going. This is an argument for consolation, as if he said: "Meanwhile, until I come, take comfort in knowing both the place to which I am going first and you afterwards, and the way by which one must travel to that place, for you know both." Whoever travels abroad, if he does not know for certain the place where he will finally rest, is usually made very anxious by this. But if he knows the place, yet does not know the road, he is still deeply troubled. But if indeed he knows both the place and the road, he already rejoices in the hope of arriving there. So it is with us, who are travelling abroad from the Lord in this life. One who knows neither the place where he is to rest nor the road he must take is certainly bound to be deeply troubled. But one who knows both the place and the road is certainly bound to rest in hope. Therefore the knowledge both of the place to which we go and of the way by which we go gives us a remarkable consolation. Ignorance of these things, however, is accompanied by sorrow and dejection of mind, especially in one who finds no rest in these earthly things.

units.la: 5 Dicit ei Thomas, Domine, nescimus quò abeas, quomodo igitur possumus viam scire?
units.tr: 5 Thomas said to him, Lord, we do not know where you are going; how then can we know the way?

units.la: 6 Dicit ei Iesus, Ego sum Via illa & Veritas illa & Vita illa; Nemo venit ad Patrem nisi per me.
units.tr: 6 Jesus said to him, I am the Way and the Truth and the Life; no one comes to the Father except through me.

units.la: 7 Si noffetis me, Patrem etiam meum nosfetis, & iam nunc noftis eum, & vidistis eum.
units.tr: 7 If you had known me, you would have known my Father also; and from now on you know him, and have seen him.

units.la: THomas contradicit quidem in speciem Domino, sed non est ista vera contradictio. Nam Dominus loquutus est de inchoata & confusa quadam notitia, quam acceptam habet ipse qui arundinem quassatam non frangit, & linum fumigans non extinguit. Thomas autem loquutus est de notitia & cognitione diluncta ac perfecta. Cōsistere autem possunt ista, cognitio inchoata affirmata, & notitia perfecta negata. Sic de Prophetis veteribus dicimus, quòd cognouerunt vocationem gentium, cùm eam prædixerunt. Paulus tamen dicit ministerium illud absconditū fuisse à sæculis: Nisi malimus ita respondere, Christum nempe loquutum esse de ea cognitione quæ esse debuit & esse potuit, si discipuli sattis intenti fuissent. Nam quoties illis prædicauit cœlos? quoties de Patre loquutus est? Quoties viam recta quasi digito demonstrauit? Ego, inquit, lux mundi sum, vt supra vidimus. Quare discipuli nimiam ofcitantiam suam proprodiderunt. Nam segnes erant admodum in proficiendo, tantisperdum praesentem habuerunt Dominum. Disce hoc loco ordine cognitionis nostrae ex verbis Thomae, Non novimus, inquit, locum, quomodo igitur viam? Ergo notitia loci praecedit notitiam viae, & primum hoc conoscendum est, esse gloriam, & quae sit illa gloria: Deinde de via eo perveniendi quaerendum. Nam meta ad quam tendimus primum omnium debet esse ante oculos, & ante omnia cognoscenda est, deinde via qua eo perveniturl ingredienda est. Scriptura de via hac loquitur potissimum, & de via hac multa nos praedicamus, de Christo & gratia per illum. Quisquis autem ad lectionem & praedicationem Scripturarum velit proficere, necesse est notitiam habeat penitus animo insitam de gloria quod sit, & quae sit aliquo certe modo: secus, inutiliter & legit & audit. Ego sum via. Christus dum praesupponit eos notitiam aliquam loci simul & eius ad quem profecturus esset, habuisse, eam nunc silentio praeterit, postea tamen de ea dicturus. Ego, inquit, sum via. Tum duobus verbis sequentibus vocem hanc metaphoricam quasi interpretatur, Veritate & vita. Primum ergo videndum cur Christus veritas dicatur. 1. Christus est verax. Sed scimus filium Dei venisse & dedisse nobis mentem, ut cognoscamus illum qui verax est, & simus in verace illo, in filio eius Iesu Christo. 2. Ipse plenus veritatis est, & ex essentia ipsa verus. Vidimus eum supra cap. 1. 14. plenum gratia & veritate. Nam Deitatis plenitudo inhabitat in eo corporaliter. 3. Omnis veritas procedit ab eo. Lex per Mosem data est, gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum. 4. Omnis veritas est de eo tanquam materia subiecta. Quicunque Spiritus confitetur Iesum Christum venisse in carnem, Spiritus est Dei, &c. Fundamentum nemo potest ponere praeter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus. 5. Omnis veritas est in illo, hoc est, rata est in illo. Quotquot enim sunt promissiones Dei, in illo sunt etiam & in ipso sunt, amen: id est, in illo consistunt ac fundantur. Nam sine illo omnia corruunt, in eius enim sanguine consistit omnium veritas. Christus ergo, quia verus est, quia plenus veritatis, quia ab illo est veritas, quia de illo est veritas, quia in illo est veritas: ideo merito veritas appellatur. Vita Christus dicitur Christus: 1. quia viuit. 2. quia per se viuit: Pater dedit filio vitam in semetipso habere. 3. Quia per eam omnia viuunt, & nos quoque viuimus naturalem istam vitam primum per eum. In ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux illa hominum, hoc est, ipse viuificauit homines in ipsa creatione. Viuimus etiam per eum supernaturalem il-lam ac spiritualem vitam, & lux illa in tenebris lucet, id est, postquam tenebrae iam inductae sunt in animum hominis, ipse illuminat animos hominum spirituali illa vita. Ergo quia viuit Christus, quia viuit per se ipse, quia per ipsum omnia, ideo Christus vita dicitur. Quare vt de via ad Patrem dicamus, vno verbo via est Christus. Sed dupliciter consideratur. 1. vt veritas, deinde vt vita. per Christum primum, vt veritas est, proficiscendum est ad Patrem; deinde per eum vt vita est. Veritas enim prima pars viae est, vita secunda est: ergo per veritatem primo ingrediendum. Quid illud est? hoc est, credendum est in Christum, quod veritas sit, quod verba eius omnia vera sint. Deinde ingrediendum est per viam. Quid illud est? hoc est, credendum est in Christum, quod vita sit, & quod omnis vita ab eo sit & per eum. Prima pars viae, quae veritas est, necessario nos ducit ad secundam: Nam sermo veritatis, si credatur, efficax est ad vitam in nobis gignendam. Verba quae ego loquor vobis, spiritus sunt & vita sunt. & Petrus eodem capite, quo abiimus? inquit, nam verba vitae aeternae habes. Quare ex sensu illo vitae, quae est ex sermone veritatis, ad hoc adducimur vt credamus eum vitam esse. Non enim posset nos viuificare ille sermo, nisi ipse qui loquitur, esset vitae fons. Ingressi igitur secundum hanc viae partem, & in ea progressi, tandem peruenimus ad vitam illam aeternam, quae est in conspectu Patris. Huc redeunt haec omnia, quae diximus, vt credamus in Christum. Ergo via est Christus, professio est fidei, fideque progressus. Ne au-tem existimaretur alias esse vias, quibus ad coelos tendamus, statim subiicit, Nemo nisi per me venit ad Patrem. q.d. Ego adeo sola sum via ad Patre, vt non sit alia. Fingunt sibi homines multas vias esse ad coelos: his plenus est Papismus, sed ad coelos vna tantum est, eaque angusta, ad inferos lata est via: hoc est, plures sunt viae, quae ad inferos deducunt.Quare teneamus nos hanc via quam-tuis angustam, relictis omnibus ambagibus, quotquot cogitamus ad Patrem & gloriam illam cœlestem peruenire.
units.tr: THomas indeed seems to contradict the Lord, but this is not a true contradiction. For the Lord spoke of a inchoate and confused kind of knowledge, which he has who does not break the bruised reed nor quench the smoking flax. Thomas, however, spoke of a distinct and perfect knowledge. Yet these things can stand together: an inchoate knowledge may be affirmed, and a perfect knowledge denied. So we say of the ancient Prophets that they knew the calling of the Gentiles when they foretold it. Yet Paul says that this ministry was hidden from the ages. Unless we would rather answer thus: that Christ spoke of the knowledge that ought to have been and could have been present, if the disciples had been sufficiently attentive. For how often did he preach to them of heaven? How often did he speak of the Father? How often did he point out the straight way, as it were with his finger? I am the light of the world, he says, as we saw above. Therefore the disciples revealed their excessive dullness. For they were very slow to make progress, as long as they had the Lord present with them. Learn here, from Thomas's words, the order of our knowledge: We do not know, he says, the place; how then the way? Therefore the knowledge of the place precedes the knowledge of the way. First of all we must know that there is a glory, and what that glory is; then we must inquire about the way of arriving there. For the goal toward which we strive ought to be before our eyes first of all, and must be known before all else; then the way by which one reaches it must be entered upon. Scripture speaks chiefly of this way, and about this way we preach much: about Christ, and about grace through him. But whoever wishes to make progress in reading and hearing the Scriptures must necessarily have a knowledge of glory planted deep in his mind, both what it is and in some sure measure what it is like; otherwise he reads and hears to no purpose. I am the way. Christ, while presupposing that they had some knowledge of the place to which he was about to go, now passes over it in silence, though he will speak of it afterwards. I, he says, am the way. Then, with the two following words, Truth and life, he as it were explains this metaphorical word. Let us first consider why Christ is called the truth. (1) Christ is truthful. But we know that the Son of God has come and given us a mind to know him who is true, and that we may be in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. (2) He is himself full of truth, and true by his very essence. We saw him above in chapter 1:14, full of grace and truth; for the fullness of the Godhead dwells in him bodily. (3) All truth proceeds from him: the law was given through Moses, grace and truth through Jesus Christ. (4) All truth has him as its underlying matter: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is of God, etc.; no one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. (5) All truth is in him, that is, it is established in him: for all the promises of God are in him yea, and in him Amen; that is, they stand and are founded in him. For without him all things fall, since the truth of all things rests in his blood. Christ is therefore rightly called truth, because he is true, because he is full of truth, because truth is from him, because truth is concerning him, because truth is in him. Life: Christ is called Christ (1) because he lives; (2) because he lives of himself: the Father has given to the Son to have life in himself; (3) because by him all things live, and we too live that natural life, first through him. In him was life, and the life was the light of men; that is, he quickened men in creation itself. We also live through him that supernatural and spiritual life, and the light shines in darkness; that is, after darkness has already been brought into the human mind, he illuminates men's minds with that spiritual life. Therefore, because Christ lives, because he lives of himself, because all things are through him, Christ is called life. So, to speak of the way to the Father in one word: the way is Christ. But he is considered in two respects: (1) as truth, and then (2) as life. Through Christ, first as he is truth, we must make our way to the Father; then through him as he is life. For truth is the first part of the way, life the second; therefore we must enter first through truth. What is this? It means that we must believe in Christ, that he is the truth and that all his words are true. Then we must go on through the way. What is this? It means that we must believe in Christ, that he is life, and that all life is from him and through him. The first part of the way, which is truth, necessarily leads us to the second. For the word of truth, if it is believed, is effective in begetting life in us. The words that I speak to you are spirit and are life; and Peter in the same chapter: Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life. Therefore, from the sense of life which comes from the word of truth, we are led to believe that he is life. For that word could not quicken us unless he who speaks were the fountain of life. Having entered, then, upon this part of the way, and having made progress in it, we at last arrive at that eternal life which is in the sight of the Father. All these things that we have said come back to this: that we believe in Christ. Therefore Christ is the way, and the profession of faith is the way, and progress comes by faith. But lest it be thought that there are other ways by which we may strive toward heaven, he immediately adds, No one comes to the Father except through me; as if to say: "I am so much the only way to the Father that there is no other." Men imagine for themselves many ways to heaven; Popery is full of these. But there is only one way to heaven, and it is narrow; the way to hell is broad; that is, there are more ways that lead down to hell. Therefore let us hold to this way, however narrow it is, leaving behind all the windings of those who think they can reach the Father and that heavenly glory by any other means.

units.la: Si me nossetis. Nunc per reprehensionem docet Thomam & cæteros locum eum & personam eam ad quam ipse primùm iturus sit: deinde ipsi post eum discipuli sui. Patrem etiam meum nossetis. Ignorantia Patris fundamentum indicat ignorantiæ filij. q. d. Hoc ipso quod dicitis vos ignorare Patrem, significatis vos ignorare me: nam si noùissetis me, cognouissetis Patrem. Ergo, ignorantes Patrem, ignoratis me. Necessitas hæc omnibus imposita est vt cognoscant Patrem: in eo enim felicitas nostra est posita. At quomodo videbimus Patrem, cùm habitet in luce inaccessa, cùm sit inconspicuus, & cùm dictum sit, Deum nemo vidit vnquam? Respondeo, ipse per se & immediatè videri & conspici à quoquam non potest: quo modo intelligenda sunt superiora testimonia: at per filium & in facie filij videri potest. Hinc dicitur imago Dei, & imago inconspicui Dei, & splendor gloria & character personæ eius. Ergo qui Filium videt, Patrem videt, id quod vsque adeo verum est, vt si cùm videmus filium in Euangelio suo crucifixum & glorificatum, non videamus in eo Patrem, naturam eius, iustitiam eius, potentiam eius, sapientiam eius, denique misericordiam eius, profectò neipsum quidem filium satis videre & cognoscere dicamur. Nam, sicut ipse dicit, si me nouissetis, patrem nouissetis. Et iam nunc cognoscitis. Correctio est, quasi dicat, Quod dico vel significo vos Patrem ignorare, & reprehendo vos eo nomine, quin imò cognoscitis Patrem nunc, & iam antea cognouistis & vidistis eum. Ergo necesse est ex his duo sequantur, primùm cognouerunt patrem reipsa: deinde ignorarunt se cognitum habuisse Patrem. Quemadmodum si quis cognoscat & videat eum hominem, qui pater sit, ignoret interea eum sibi patrem esse, hoc est non cognoscat eũ hoc nomine. Quod autem cognouerunt & viderunt Patrem reipsa ex eo verum est, quòd filium, qui est imago Patris, cognitum habuerunt. Quod verò nescierint interea eum quem in Filio viderunt, Patrem esse, inde
units.tr: If you had known me. Now, by way of rebuke, he teaches Thomas and the others about the place and the person to which he himself is about to go, and then his disciples after him. You would have known my Father also. Ignorance of the Father reveals the root of ignorance of the Son. The sense is: by the very fact that you say you do not know the Father, you show that you do not know me, for if you had known me, you would have known the Father. So, since you do not know the Father, you do not know me. This knowledge is required of all, that they know the Father, for our happiness lies in it. But how shall we see the Father, since he dwells in light inaccessible, since he is invisible, and since it has been said that no one has ever seen God? I answer: he cannot be seen or beheld by anyone through himself and immediately; this is how the earlier testimonies must be understood. But he can be seen through the Son and in the face of the Son. Hence the Son is called the image of God, and the image of the invisible God, and the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person. Therefore whoever sees the Son sees the Father. This is so true that if, when we see the Son crucified and glorified in his Gospel, we do not see in him the Father, his nature, his justice, his power, his wisdom and finally his mercy, we are surely said not even to see and know the Son sufficiently. For, as he himself says, if you had known me, you would have known the Father. And from now on you know him. This is a correction, as if he said: what I say or mean, that you do not know the Father, and I rebuke you for it, is not so; rather, you know the Father now, and you have already known and seen him before. Therefore it must follow from these things that, first, they really knew the Father; and second, they did not realise that they had the Father known to them. It is like someone who knows and sees a man who is a father, and yet does not recognise that this man is his own father, that is, does not know him by this name. That they really knew and saw the Father is true from the fact that they had known the Son, who is the image of the Father. That they did not know in the meantime that the one they saw in the Son was the Father comes from this: they did not yet have in hand the principle that must be known first, namely that the Son is the image of the invisible God, and (as is said later) that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, that is, that they are one in nature, essence and entire majesty. Therefore, since there is no firm comfort in seeing the Father and his glory shining in the Son unless this principle is first known, that the Son is the image of the Father (for otherwise we will not know that this is the glory of the Father which we otherwise behold in the Son), this principle must above all be known by us; and unless this is first known, that the Son is the image of the Father, we must not come to the preaching of the Gospel of Christ, that is, we must not come to Christ, who seems to us to be in vain unless the Father is seen in him.

units.la: Discipuli quomodo Patrem cognouisse dicantur. fuit quòd principium hoc quod imprimis cognoscendum fuit non cognitum habuerint, nempe quòd Filius sit imago inconspicui Dei, & (vt dicitur postea) Pater in Filio sit & Filius in Patre: hoc est, vnum sint natura, essentia, & tota maiestate. Quare, cùm non sit solida consolatio, cùm Patrem eiúsque gloriam in Filio resplendétem videmus, nisi cognito prius hoc principio, quòd sit Filius imago Patris; secus enim ignorabimus eam esse Patris gloriam, quam in filio alioqui intuemur: profectò imprimis nobis cognoscendum est hoc principium, & non nisi hoc prius cognito, quòd Filius sit imago Patris, veniendum ad praedicationem Euangelij Christi, hoc est ad Christum veniendum, qui frustra videtur à nobis, nisi in eo Pater videatur.
units.tr: How the disciples are said to have known the Father. (Continued from the preceding paragraph.) Now, the disciples are said to have known the Father because they had not yet grasped the principle that must be known first, namely that the Son is the image of the invisible God and, as is said afterwards, that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. Hence, since the sight of the Father and his glory shining in the Son gives no solid consolation unless this principle is known first, we must above all know this principle, and not come to the preaching of the Gospel of Christ until we have first known that the Son is the image of the Father.

units.la: 8 Dicit ei Philippus, Domine, ostende nobis Patrem, & sufficit nobis.
units.tr: Philip saith unto him, Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us.

units.la: 9 Dicit ei Iesus, Tantum temporis vobiscum sum, & non noscis me? Philippe, qui vidit me, vidit Patrem, quomodo igitur tu dicis, Ostende nobis Patrem?
units.tr: Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Shew us the Father?

units.la: 10 Non credis me in Patre, & Patrem in me esse? Verba quae ego loquor vobis, à meipso non loquor: sed Pater qui in me manet ipse facit opera.
units.tr: Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? the words that I speak unto you I speak not of myself: but the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works.

units.la: 11 Credite mihi me in Patre, & Patrem in me esse: sin minus, propter ipsa opera credite mihi.
units.tr: Believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father in me: or else believe me for the very works' sake.

units.la: PHilippus ex discipulis alius prodit quoque suam ignorantiam, neque ignorantia modo, sed indocilitatem & tarditatem in concipiendo. Nam ex verbis illis, quae dixit Dominus (si me nouissetis, Patrem nouissetis) satis intelligere potuit illud principium quòd Filius sit imago Patris. Verùm non aduertit, interea prodit quae commendatione aliqua digna sunt: vt desiderium videndi Patris, vt αὐτάρκεια ex eo semel inspecto. Nam sufficientia tum demum est verè, cùm Patrem videmus, in cuius conspectu est satietas gaudiorum. Ergo desideriũ hoc videndi Patris aliquo modo leuius reddit ignorantiae {a}tiæ peccatum. Ignorantia enim si sit desiderium cognitionis paulò magis tolerabilis est: Nam beatum prædicat eum Dominus qui esurit ac sitit iustitiam: quoniam ipse,inquit, saturabitur. At si ignorantia sit prorsus sine desiderio emergendi ex ea, vel(quod deterius est) multa cum voluptate conquiescendi in tenebris ignorantiæ, illud nullo pacto tolerabile est,& argumento est,(si non tempestiue corrigatur) futurarum tenebrarum;quas Dominus vocat tenebras exteriores,quarum initium est tenebræ istæ ignorantiæ in hac vita. Tantum tempus. Dominus non tam respiciens tarditatem quàm desiderium cognoscendi cum cum lenitate ac patientia instituit. Reprehendit quidem, sed cum lenitate & doctrina, vt relinqueret discipulis suis & nobis omnibus exemplum lenitatis in docendo, reprehendendo, &c. Atque ita pro culdubiò voluit discipulos sentire, quàm tardi & indociles ipsi essent, vt maiori cum patientia ac lenitate tardos & indociles alios perferrent. Sed ad rem. Summa reprehensionis hæc est: Cur dicis, Ostende nobis Patrem? Fundamentum substernit reprehensionis suæ; Qui me vidit, Patrem vidit. Tum subsumit, sed cum reprehensione: At me videtis & cognoscitis: alioquin tantum temporis frustra collocasseris. Ergo &c. Rursus illud fundamentum resoluit in principium suum superius: Pater manet in me & ego in Patre. Hoc est, ego & Pater unum sumus, vel ego sum imago Patris. Ex his discimus eos qui ignorant Deum, trahendos esse ad hoc principium, quòd Filius sit imago Patris. Hoc enim cognito primum, tum illud cognoscetur; Qui vident Filium, vident Patrem: atque omnem operam suam in eo collocaturi sunt vt filium intueantur in Evangelio suo. Verba quæ ego loquor. Duobus argumentis ipsis sensibus obuiis ostendit Patrem & Deum inconspicuum in ipso esse: hoc est quod dicitur, plenitudinem Deitatis in ipso habitare corporaliter. Primum est à verbis ipsius: secundum est à factis, quæ arguunt Deum in ipso esse, & quæ etiam conuicerunt aduersarios quòd in ipso esset saltem Dei aliqua præsentia & diuinitas aliqua, vt ministros Pharisæorum & Sacerdotum, qui reuersi renunciarunt, Nunquam loquutum aliquem, vt ipse loquutus cst: & Pharisæos qui ex opere illo ædito in restituendo cæco cap.9. supra collegerunt diuinum hominem & nō peccatorem esse. At verò id fideles multò magis viderunt, quibus verba ipsius vita fuerunt. Verba, inquit Petrus, vitæ æternæ habes. Nos etiam dum prædicatur Evangelium Christi, sentimus inde vitam ad nos profluere, quod profectò arguit Christum, cuius hic est sermo, vitam esse & Deum esse: alioquin non esset ipse efficax ad vitam. Credite mihi me. Hactenus consolatus est discipulos suos, nunc eos exhortatur: Exhortatur autem primùm ad fidem in ipsum. Supra interrogauit Philippum annon crederet se in Patre esse & Patre in se: hoc est, se vnum esse cum Patre: nunc ad fidem eum hortatur. Credere enim Deum in Christo esse, hoc est in infirma natura humana corporaliter habitare difficile est, & cùm natura ipsa pugnat. Vnde Dominus Petro, cùm confiteretur ipsum esse Christum Dei filium; Beatus es, inquit, Simon filius Ionæ: nam caro & sanguis hoc non revelavit tibi, sed Pater meus qui est in cælis. Hoc est, natura non docuit te istam confessionem & fidem. Vt autem difficillimum est hoc credere, & naturam longè exuperat: ita necessarium est adeo ad salutem, vt sine fide illa non sit salus. Hinc sequitur, quòd cùm à natura alienum sit, & tamen necessarium, oportere nos ex natura exire, & supra naturam efferri, ad hoc vt videamus Deum in Christo habitantem. Nam animalis vel naturalis homo non est capax eorum quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Sin minus propter ipsa. Argumentum est ab Operibus: q. d. quòd si nullum est argumentum aliud, quo credatis, saltem moveamini ros opera mea. In operibus vis quædam est ad impellendum quemuis vel inuitum, eò vt videat & confiteatur in Christo diuinum aliquid inesse: & opera sunt testimonium ad cogendum aduersarios. Verùm adhuc vt sit fides, accedat oportet testis, non tam cogens quàm blandè alliciens corda nostra. Oportet enim fidem voluntariam esse. Est autem is Spiritus Dei sanctus, qui persuadet & mutat ac renouat cor nostrum, sine quo & opera & verbum damnationi potius quàm saluti inseruiunt. Opus quidem habemus his ipsis testimoniis, fateor, quæ cogunt, & inuitos alioqui trahunt ad hoc, vt fides sit in Christo.
units.tr: Philip, another of the disciples, also betrays his ignorance, and not only his ignorance but his slowness and dullness in understanding. For from the words the Lord had spoken (if you had known me, you would have known the Father) he could well have understood that principle, that the Son is the image of the Father. But he does not notice this, and in the meantime he shows some things worthy of commendation: his desire to see the Father, and a self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια] that comes from having once beheld him. For sufficiency is truly found only when we see the Father, in whose sight is the fullness of joys. So this desire to see the Father in some measure makes the sin of ignorance lighter. For if ignorance is a desire to know, it is somewhat more tolerable, since the Lord pronounces blessed those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled. But if ignorance is entirely without desire to rise out of it, or (what is worse) if one rests in the darkness of ignorance with much pleasure, that is by no means tolerable, and it is a sign (if it is not corrected in time) of coming darkness, which the Lord calls outer darkness, whose beginning is this darkness of ignorance in this life. So long a time. The Lord, looking not so much at their slowness as at their desire to know, teaches with gentleness and patience. He does rebuke, but with gentleness and instruction, so that he might leave to his disciples, and to us all, an example of gentleness in teaching, in rebuking, and so on. And thus he doubtless wished the disciples to feel how slow and dull they themselves were, so that they might bear with slow and dull others with greater patience and gentleness. But to the matter. The sum of this rebuke is: why do you say, Shew us the Father? He lays the foundation of his rebuke: he who has seen me has seen the Father. Then he adds, but with rebuke: but you see and know me; otherwise you would have spent so much time in vain. Therefore, etc. Again he resolves that foundation into his earlier principle: the Father abides in me and I in the Father. That is, I and the Father are one, or I am the image of the Father. From these things we learn that those who do not know God must be drawn to this principle, that the Son is the image of the Father. For once this is known first, then that other truth will be known: those who see the Son see the Father; and they will direct all their effort to behold the Son in his Gospel. The words that I speak. By two arguments, both obvious to the senses, he shows that the Father and the invisible God is in him, which is what is meant by saying that the fullness of the Godhead dwells in him bodily. The first is from his words; the second is from his deeds, which prove that God is in him, and which convinced his adversaries that in him there was at least some presence of God and some divinity, as the servants of the Pharisees and the chief priests, who came back and reported, Never man spake like this man; and the Pharisees, who from that work done in restoring the blind man (chapter 9 above) concluded that this man was of God and not a sinner. But the faithful saw this much more clearly, for his words were their life. Peter says, Thou hast the words of eternal life. We too, when the Gospel of Christ is preached, feel life flowing to us from it, which surely proves that Christ, of whom this is the message, is life and is God, for otherwise he would not be effective unto life. Believe me. Thus far he has comforted his disciples; now he exhorts them. He exhorts them first to faith in himself. Above he asked Philip whether he did not believe that he was in the Father and the Father in him, that is, that he is one with the Father; now he exhorts him to faith. For to believe that God is in Christ, that is, that God dwells bodily in weak human nature, is difficult, and nature itself fights against it. Hence the Lord said to Peter, when he confessed that he was Christ, the Son of the living God: Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona, for flesh and blood hath not revealed this unto thee, but my Father who is in heaven. That is, nature did not teach you this confession and faith. And just as it is most difficult to believe this, and it far surpasses nature, so it is necessary for salvation, so that without this faith there is no salvation. Hence it follows that, since it is alien to nature and yet necessary, we must go out of nature and be raised above nature, so that we may see God dwelling in Christ. For the natural or animal man is not able to receive the things of the Spirit of God. Or else. This is an argument from works: as if to say, if there is no other argument by which you may believe, at least be moved by my works. In works there is a certain force for driving on anyone, even unwilling, so that he sees and confesses that something divine is in Christ; and the works are a testimony to compel the adversaries. Yet for faith to exist, a witness must come, not so much compelling as sweetly drawing our hearts. For faith must be voluntary. This witness is the Holy Spirit of God, who persuades, changes and renews our heart, without whom both works and word serve condemnation rather than salvation. I grant that we indeed need these very testimonies, which compel and otherwise draw the unwilling to this, that there be faith in Christ.

units.la: 1.Cor.2.14. Christum. Verùm nisi praeterea testetur Spiritus sanctus, & blandè nos alliciat, nihil proderit nos cogi, imò oberit potiùs. Nam certam damnationem augebit in illo die.
units.tr: 1.Cor.2.14. Christ. But unless the Holy Spirit also bears witness and gently draws us, it will profit us nothing to be compelled; indeed it will rather harm us, for it will increase our certain condemnation on that day.

units.la: 12 Amen, amen dico vobis, qui credit in me, opera quæ ego facio, & ipse faciet, & maiora istis faciet. Nam ego ad Patrem meum proficiscor.
units.tr: Verily, verily, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and he will do greater works than these, for I am going to my Father.

units.la: 13 Et quicquid petieritis nomine meo, hoc faciam ut glorificetur Pater in filio.
units.tr: And whatever you ask in my name, that I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.

units.la: 14 Si quid petieritis in nomine meo, ego faciam.
units.tr: If you ask anything in my name, I will do it.

units.la: NUnc ad credendum allicit, ut supra quodammodo coegit: Allicit autem à bono ipsorum, quòd talia opera ipsi sint operaturi, & his maiora per fidem in ipsum. Unde nota fidem, si cui bono sit, nobisipsis bono esse. Non enim Deus eget fide nostra, nobis autem vsque adeo necessaria est, ut sine ea beati esse non possimus. Implet enim nos omni bono, & aptos reddit ad omnia bona opera: quòd si non ad miraculosa illa opera, quæ iam cessarunt (quæ ipsa per fidem operati sunt iam olim in primitiva illa Ecclesia: Nam per hæc cognoscebantur fideles, tum quòd daemonia eicerent & linguis loquerentur, Marc. 16. 17. 18.) quæ, inquam, iam cessarunt: certè aptos reddit ad opera charitatis, quæ miraculosis illis longè sunt praestantiora. Sunt enim hæc testimonia, totidem electionis nostræ, & plus gaudij secum afferunt, quàm miraculosa illa omnia. Dominus discipulis suis, qui postquam miracula in populo ediderunt ad ipsum cum gaudio sunt reuersi: Gaudete, inquit, potius quod nomina vestra sint inscripta cælis. Verùm hic oritur quæstio, An discipuli operati sunt maiora quàm ipse Christus? Respondeo id ita quidem fuisse, sed virtute Christi. Rursus quæritur, An virtute Christi operati sint maiora quàm ipsemet Christus in sua persona? Respondeo id ita quidem fuisse, quia Christus humiliatus per se operatus est in terris agens, Christus verò glorificatus per discipulos suos operatus est. Christus autem glorificatus efficacior est in seruis suis, quàm cùm humiliatus fuit in sua ipsius persona: quod vel solum huius rei argumentum, quòd postquam ascendit in cælos, totius mundi conuersio insequuta sit, quod non tum contigit cùm præsens ageret in terris, latente tunc deitate ipsius, &(vt cum Apostolo loquar) quodammodo exinanita. Nam ego ad Patrem. Hęc causa est, cur maiora operati illi sint: Ipse, inquit, abeo ad Patrem, & statim glorificabor in potentia. Hæc autem potentia sese exeret in terris per vos, veltrúmque ministerium. Vide, hîc causam reddit maiorum operum à glorificatione sua statim futura. Vnde sequitur, quòd cùm Christi potentia, omnia hæc opera futura sint, à Christi gloria nihil detractum, imò eius gloriam per ea petefactum iri. Et quicquid petieritis. Hæc est altera quasi causa, & alterum fundamentū maiorum operum, preces ipsorum, potentiam hanc Christi glorificati è cælis quasi detrahentium. Nam, vt sit in nobis, & in terris efficax illa potentia, quæ in cælis tam latè se diffundit, opus est fide nostra & precibus ordinariis, nimirum instrumentis à Deo ordinatis, ad hoc, vt potentia ipsius in terras deuehatur. Quod Sancti Apostoli in Actis precati sunt Dominum, vt Christus vellet ederet per manus ipsorum signa & miracula, idque ab eo impetrarunt; id ipsum locum habet in aliis operibus, quæ omnia vi & potentia Christi fiunt, & quæ non impetratur nisi fide, & precibus. Quòd autem Deus non sit tam efficax in nobis per bona opera, in causa est segnities ista nostra, qui non precamur Deum nostrum vt oportet. Vt glorificetur Pater in filio. In potentia filij glorificatur Pater; nam potentia filij, Patris quoque est: est enim filij eadem cum Patre essentia & maiestas. Verùm hoc non prætereundum est, quòd cùm Christus de potentia sua exerenda in operibus eorum loquatur, Patris sui reminiscatur interea, ipsiúsque gloriæ. Ea re docemur in omnibus & dictis & factis nostris, Deum ante oculos habere: nam semper cauendum est ipsius gloriæ, & ad eam destinanda sunt omnia nostra, sive dicta, sive facta: quia ex ipso & per ipsum, & in ipso sunt omnia: Rom. 11. 36. Si quid petierit. Rursus promittit se ad preces eorū operaturum miis, vt hoc ipsum quod supra dixit eodē sensu, & iisdem verbis, iis magis persuadeat: vbi notandum. dum quòd dicit se hoc facturum, non autem ipsos facturos. Christus enim ipse est qui edit miracula potentia sua, quam nō transfundit quidem in ministros suos, sed eam in se reseruat, & ex sese effundit, vsus tamē ministerio hominum, vel loquentium, vel operantium.
units.tr: Now he draws us to believe, as above he in a sense compelled us. But he draws us by their own good, because they themselves are going to perform such works, and greater works through faith in him. Hence note that faith is good for us, if it is good for anyone. For God has no need of our faith, but we need it so much that we cannot be blessed without it. For it fills us with every good and makes us fit for all good works. And if not for those miraculous works, which have now ceased (which they themselves performed through faith in that early Church, for by these the faithful were recognised, both because they cast out demons and because they spoke with tongues, Mark 16.17-18), which, I say, have now ceased, then certainly it makes us fit for works of charity, which are far more excellent than those miraculous ones. For these are testimonies of our election, as many as there are, and they bring with them more joy than all those miracles. The Lord said to his disciples, who, after they had worked miracles among the people, returned to him with joy: Rejoice, he said, rather that your names are written in heaven. But here a question arises: did the disciples do greater works than Christ himself? I answer that they did, but by the power of Christ. Again it is asked: did they do greater works by the power of Christ than Christ himself did in his own person? I answer that they did, because Christ, in his humiliation, worked on earth by himself, while Christ glorified worked through his disciples. Now Christ glorified is more effective in his servants than when he was humiliated in his own person. The only proof of this matter is that after he ascended into heaven the conversion of the whole world followed, which did not happen while he was present and acting on earth, his deity then being hidden and (to speak with the Apostle) in a sense emptied. For I am going to the Father. This is the reason why they did greater works: he says, I am going away to the Father, and I shall at once be glorified in power. This power, however, will show itself on earth through you and your ministry. See, here he gives the reason for the greater works from his glorification, which is to come at once. Hence it follows that, since all these works will be done by the power of Christ, nothing is taken from the glory of Christ; rather, his glory will be advanced by them. And whatever you ask. This is the second quasi cause and the second foundation of the greater works: their prayers, as it were drawing down this power of the glorified Christ from heaven. For that power, which is so widely diffused in heaven, may be effective in us and on earth, our faith and ordinary prayers are needed, that is, the means ordained by God, so that his power may be brought down to earth. What the holy Apostles prayed to the Lord in the Acts, that Christ would work signs and miracles through their hands, and what they obtained from him, has the same place in other works, all of which are done by the power and might of Christ, and which are obtained only by faith and prayer. But that God is not so effective in us through good works is due to our sloth, since we do not pray to our God as we ought. That the Father may be glorified in the Son. The Father is glorified in the power of the Son, for the power of the Son is also the Father's; for the Son has the same essence and majesty as the Father. But this must not be passed over: when Christ speaks of his power to be exercised in their works, he at the same time calls to mind his Father and his glory. We are taught by this to keep God before our eyes in all our words and deeds, for the glory of God must always be guarded, and all our things, whether words or deeds, must be directed to it, because from him and through him and in him are all things (Rom. 11.36). If you ask anything. Again he promises to act on their prayers, so that what he said above he might persuade them of more strongly, in the same sense and in the same words. Here it must be noted that he says that he will do this, not that they will do it. For it is Christ himself who works miracles by his power, which he does not indeed transfuse into his ministers, but keeps in himself and pours out from himself, yet using the ministry of men, whether speaking or working.

units.la: 15 Si diligitis me, mandata mea seruate.
units.tr: If you love me, keep my commandments.

units.la: 16 Ego vero rogabo Patrem, & alium aduocatum dabit vobis, vt maneat vobiscum in aeternum.
units.tr: And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, that he may remain with you forever.

units.la: 17 Nempe Spiritum illum veritatis quem mundus non potest recipere, quia non conspicit eum, nec nouit eum: Vos autem nostis eū, quia apud vos manet, & in vobis erit.
units.tr: Namely the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him; but you know him, because he remains with you and will be in you.

units.la: 16 Non relinquam vos orbos: Redeo ad vos.
units.tr: I will not leave you orphans; I come back to you.

units.la: HÆc est secunda exhortatio ad obseruationem mandatorum ipsius: hic intellige illud nouum mandatum vt alij alios diligant. Argumentum petit a dilectione. Sic, inquit, ostendetis quod me absentem diligatis, si obseruaueritis mandata mea. Seruus aliquis, qui diligit dominum suum, omnia facit ad voluntatem domini: tum autem maximè cum peregrè abest dominus se fidelem exhibet. Quæ autem facit causa domini, cum summa alacritate facit omnia & gaudio: Charitas enim laboriosa est, fateor, sed in ea magnum est solatium & gaudium. Quòd si quis requirat argumentum an seruus hic absentem dominum diligat: in primo argumentum est, quo non aliud certius, quòd domino suo absenti sedulò seruiat. Similiter seruus qui ex animo diligit absentem Dominum Iesum, dat operam, vt faciat omnia quæ Domino Iesu accepta sunt, maximè absente ipso Domino: cui tum inseruit tanta cum alacritate, vt lubentius eius causa patiatur omnia, quàm quis faciat aliquid alterius causa. Adeo vt, si requiras signum dilectionis Christi, hoc nimirum illud est, quod quis ex animo studeat ei obedire, & facere voluntatem eius, expectans perpetuò reditum illū Domini sui gloriosum, in quo bene erit ei. Nam, vt ait Dominus, Beatus seruus ille quem cum venerit dominus eius, inuenerit ita facientem: nam præficiet eum seruum omnibus bonis suis. Contrà re
units.tr: This is the second exhortation to keep his commandments. Here understand that new commandment, that they should love one another. He draws his argument from love. Thus, he says, you will show that you love me in my absence, if you keep my commandments. Any servant who loves his master does everything according to the master's will, and most of all when the master is far away he shows himself faithful. Whatever he does for his master's cause, he does with the greatest eagerness and joy; for love is laborious, I grant, but in it there is great comfort and joy. But if anyone asks for the proof that this servant loves his absent master, the first proof is that no other is more certain: that he diligently serves his absent master. Similarly, the servant who from his heart loves the absent Lord Jesus takes care to do all the things that are acceptable to the Lord Jesus, most of all while the Lord himself is absent. He serves him then with such eagerness that he gladly suffers everything for his sake, more than anyone does anything for another's sake. So that, if you seek the sign of love for Christ, it is surely this: that one earnestly strives to obey him and to do his will, always expecting his glorious return, in which it will be well with him. For, as the Lord says, Blessed is that servant whom his master, when he comes, finds so doing; for he will set him over all his goods. On the contrary

units.la: rò si absente domino sit seruus, qui non studeat eius voluntati obsequi, sed omnia faciat pugnantia cum voluntate domini sui absentis, odio persequatur fratrem, verberet, occidat, scortetur, furetur, &c. is plane demonstrat se odisse dominum absentem. Nam ista non tam indicia sunt odij in homines quàm in Deum ipsum, qui hæc prohibuit, vt non fit opus vt se excusent isti eo prætextu quòd non sint hæc facta in Dominum ipsum. Nam tum palam dicet Dominus in aduentu suo secundo, Hæc in se facta esse & in odium ipsius. Vide formulam futuri iudicii, Matth. 25. Ego autem precabor. Alterum argumentum exhortationis ad obseruationem mandatorum suorum, à bono illo quo absens compensabit eos, quo etiam futurum est, vt ipsi possint aliquo modo in mediis miseriis & persequutionibus facere ipsius voluntatem. Ego, inquit, intercessione mea procurabo à Patre vt veniat ad vos Consolator alius, qui meam absentiam compensabit. Hinc conspicitur Christum præsentem consolatorem fuisse discipulis suis, & corporalem ipsius præsentiam ipsis fuisse magno solatio. Viderunt enim plenum gratia ac veritate, & ex plenitudine illa mensuram gratiæ singuli perceperunt. Vnde Petrus non patiebatur se diuelli ab eius latere, Ad quem abibimus? inquit: nam verba vitæ æternæ habes. Præsens etiam custodiebat discipulos tanquam pueros, & adhuc non maturos afflictionibus perferendis, de quo ipso conquesti sunt discipuli Iohannis Baptistæ, quòd cum ipsi crebrò ieiunarent, ipsius discipuli non ieiunarent. Respondit Dominus non potuisse filios thalami præsenti sponso lugere. Ita agit cum suis Dominus omni tempore, quos conseruat ab iniuriis, & afflictionibus tantisper du maturescant & sint ferendo. Ex hoc etiam loco discimus subtracta à discipulis semel corporali præsentia Domini, expositos fuisse eos omnibus periculis ac molestiis: ac tum illud euenisse, quod prædictum fuit olim discipulis Iohannis, tempus affuturum quo subtraheretur ab iis sponsus, atque tum quidem eos ieiunaturos.
units.tr: if the servant, while his master is absent, does not strive to obey his will, but does everything contrary to the will of his absent master, persecutes his brother with hatred, beats, kills, commits fornication, steals, and so on, he plainly shows that he hates his absent master. For these are not so much signs of hatred toward men as toward God himself, who forbade them; so there is no need for those men to excuse themselves on the pretext that these deeds were not done against the Lord himself. For then the Lord will say openly at his second coming that these things were done against him and in hatred of him. See the form of the future judgment, Matt. 25. But I will pray. The second argument for the exhortation to keep his commandments comes from the good with which he will recompense them in his absence, by which it will also come about that they can in some way do his will amid miseries and persecutions. I, he says, by my intercession will procure from the Father that another Comforter come to you, who will make up for my absence. Hence it is seen that Christ was a present comforter to his disciples, and his bodily presence was a great comfort to them. For they saw him full of grace and truth, and from that fullness each one received a measure of grace. Hence Peter would not allow himself to be torn from his side: To whom shall we go? he said; for you have the words of eternal life. Being present, he also guarded his disciples as children, not yet mature enough to bear afflictions; of this very thing the disciples of John the Baptist complained, that while they often fasted, his disciples did not fast. The Lord replied that the sons of the bridechamber could not mourn while the bridegroom was present. So the Lord deals with his people at all times, whom he preserves from injuries and afflictions, for as long as they need to mature and be made fit to endure. From this passage too we learn that, once the bodily presence of the Lord was withdrawn from the disciples, they were exposed to all dangers and troubles; and then that happened which was foretold long ago to the disciples of John, that a time would come when the bridegroom would be taken from them, and then indeed they would fast.

units.la: Hinc fuit quòd absente Domino opus haberent consolatore, qui ipsos tot tantisque miseriis obsessos solaretur. Atque id quoque de omnibus nobis verum est, diabodiabolum ex absentia Christi captare occasionem persequendi Ecclesiam, & circumire quaerentem quem deuoret, ad hoc, vt si fieri posset, simul ac semel omnes ad defectionem sollicitet ac perdat ante reditum illum Domini secundum. Quantum autem is profecerit in eo, testis est vniuersalis illa defectio in regno Antichristi, & nisi consolatorem spiritum absente Domino etiam nunc haberemus, profecto eo adigeremur, vt succumberemus afflictionibus atque miseriis. Ex hoc enim loco discimus Dominum nunquam ita suos deserere, quin aliquam suae praesentiae copiam ipsis faciat, & absente nunc corpore, praesentem magis Spiritu, quantum fuit cum praesens esset corpore, ac vna versaretur cum discipulis. Absens enim plane glorificatus est ad dextram Patris sui, & in glorificato exeruit se illa potentia Dei, quae habitat in homine. Praesens autem in terris inanita fuit ac obscurata magna ex parte plenitudo illa deitatis in ipso corporaliter habitans, tantisperdum opus illud redemptionis humanae absoluceret. Quare absens efficacior est per Spiritum suum, quam cum praesens ageret cum discipulis: Et reipsa quidem discipuli expertu sunt plus consolationis in Christo absente inesse quam in praesente. Omnis enim consolatio in Christo Iesu est per Spiritum ipsius. Consolatio in eo ante adventum primum fuit per Spiritum suum in patribus, & in Prophetis: Consolatio in adventu fuit per Spiritum sanctum in Apostolis, aliisque quotquot vnquam in eo consolationem habuerunt. Consolatio quae iam est absente Christo, est per Spiritum sanctum. Consolatio in futuro seculo, erit per eundem Spiritum sanctum, adeo vt Spiritui qui est ac manet a Christo maior tribuenda sit consolatio, quam praesentiae corporali: etsi quidem praesentia corporis hoc efficiat, vt magis efficax sit Spiritus in credentibus, id quod nos omnes expectari sumus olim cum praesentem eum habebimus, praesertim glorificatum: Tum enim tanta vis Spiritus ab eo procedet, vt transformet nos in imaginem gloriae ipsius.
