Quod autem in discipulis tam efficax non fuit praesentia Christi corporalis, in causa fuit, quòd nondum esset glorificatum corpus, in quo tanta vis est vt glorificatum iam corpus, absens tanto interuallo, efficacius tamen fit per Spiritum sanctum, quàm fuit nondum glorificatum corpus ipsius præsens.
units.tr: Hence it was that, with the Lord absent, they needed a Comforter to console them, who were beset by so many and such great miseries. And this is true of all of us as well: the devil seizes the occasion of Christ's absence to persecute the Church and goes about seeking whom he may devour, in order to stir up and destroy, if possible, all of them at once and together, before the Lord's second return. How far he has succeeded in this is witnessed by that universal apostasy in the kingdom of Antichrist. And unless we still had the Comforter, the Spirit, even now, while the Lord is absent, we would certainly be driven to give way under afflictions and miseries. For from this passage we learn that the Lord never so forsakes his people as not to give them some measure of his presence, and that, though he is now absent in body, he is present by his Spirit, just as much as when he was present in body and lived together with the disciples. For he has been glorified, wholly absent, at the right hand of his Father, and in his glorified state that power of God which dwells in man has come forth into full view. But while he was present on earth, that fullness of deity dwelling in him bodily was for the most part emptied and obscured, for as long as that work of human redemption was being completed. Therefore he is more effective through his Spirit in his absence than when he acted present with the disciples. And indeed the disciples found by experience that there was more consolation in Christ absent than in Christ present. For all consolation in Christ Jesus is through his Spirit. Consolation in him before his first coming was through his Spirit in the fathers and in the prophets. Consolation at his coming was through the Holy Spirit in the apostles and in all others who ever had consolation in him. The consolation which now exists, Christ being absent, is through the Holy Spirit. Consolation in the future age will be through the same Holy Spirit, so that the consolation must be ascribed to the Spirit, who is and remains from Christ, rather than to his bodily presence. Although, indeed, the bodily presence brings this about, that the Spirit is more effective in believers, which we all expect will be the case when we have him present with us, especially glorified. For then such power of the Spirit will proceed from him that he will transform us into the image of his glory. But the reason why the bodily presence of Christ was not so effective in the disciples was that his body was not yet glorified; and in a glorified body there is such power that a body glorified, though absent at so great a distance, becomes nonetheless more effective through the Holy Spirit than his body was when it was present and not yet glorified.

units.la: Nunc videamus à quo proficiscatur Consolator iste. Quem dabit, inquit, Pater meus. Ipse dicit postea se missurum hunc spiritum cap.15.verf.16. Sed nihil est hic discrepatiæ. Spiritus enim primùm procedit à Patre, qui primus exist̃it in Trinitate: deinde à filio qui secundus existit in illa Trinitate. Hunc ordinem innuit eodem loco citato, Quem ego, inquit, mittam à Patre, à quo nimirum primùm procedit. Sed hoc obseruádum, quòd Spiritum sanctum Patri tribuat, vt & omnia quæ ad opus redemptionis in Christo pertinent, primùm Patri tribuantur, vt nos ex eo discamus omnia in opere redemptionis Patri primùm tribuenda esse, à quo etiam vocatus est filius ad opus illud redemptionis, vt nos cognoscentes omnia esse à Patre, illi gloriam tribuamus omnem, sed per filium & Spiritum sanctum. Modus autem quo datur à Patre Spiritus ille Consolator innuitur his verbis; Ego autem Patrem. Est autem per intercessionem Christi preces autem has effudisse videtur in hac vita. Nam precatur in eam sententiam cap.17. Sed notandum hic quàm operosa res sit impetrare Spiritum Dei sanctum, vt & quamcunque gratiam in Christo Iesu, quæ non tantùm sanguine procuratur meritorio, sed etiam intercessione eius ipsius qui meritus est: hoc est, non tantùm merito Christi obtinetur, sed etiam efficacia. His modis impetratus Spiritus sanctus manet in æternum: manet in medius tentationibus & afflictionibus. Nam nemo, inquit, gaudium vestrum (quod est effectum Spiritus sancti) tollet à vobis. Imò verò quo graviores sunt afflictiones, eo firmius adhæret Spiritus, magisque nos consolatur. Non magis auferri potest Spiritus sanctus, quàm mors Christi, eiúsque intercessio inaniri. Nò magis auferri potest gratia superstructa super fundamento illo Iesu Christo (Nam quotquot sunt promissiones Dei, in eo sunt etiam, & in eo sunt, amen. 2. Cor.1.20. id est, stant solidè, ac ratæ fiunt) non magis, inquam, quàm ipsum illud fundamentum Iesus Christus potest eruì. Nempe Spiritum. Cõsolatorem quem dixit nomine suo designat, Spiritum veritatis.
units.tr: Now let us see from whom this Comforter proceeds. "Whom the Father," he says, "will give." He himself says afterwards that he will send this Spirit (chap. 15, verse 16). But there is no discrepancy here. For the Spirit proceeds first from the Father, who exists first in the Trinity, and then from the Son, who exists second in that Trinity. He indicates this order in the passage cited, "whom I," he says, "will send from the Father," from whom, of course, he first proceeds. But this must be observed: he ascribes the Holy Spirit to the Father, so that, as with everything that pertains to the work of redemption in Christ, the Father is first credited with it, so that from this we may learn that everything in the work of redemption is to be attributed first to the Father, by whom the Son also was called to that work of redemption; that we, knowing that all things are from the Father, may ascribe to him all glory, but through the Son and the Holy Spirit. The manner in which that Comforter, the Spirit, is given by the Father is indicated by these words: "But I will pray the Father." It is by the intercession of Christ, and it seems that he poured out these prayers during this life. For he prays to this effect in chapter 17. But it should be noted here how laborious a matter it is to obtain the Holy Spirit of God, and whatever grace in Christ Jesus is procured not only by his meritorious blood but also by the intercession of him who merited it. That is, it is obtained not only by the merit of Christ but also by his efficacious intercession. The Holy Spirit, obtained in these ways, remains for ever; he remains in the midst of temptations and afflictions. "For no one," he says, "will take your joy" (which is the effect of the Holy Spirit) "from you." Indeed, the heavier the afflictions, the more firmly the Spirit clings to us and the more he comforts us. The Holy Spirit can no more be taken away than the death of Christ can be made void, or his intercession be emptied. Grace built upon that foundation, Jesus Christ, cannot be taken away any more, I say, than Jesus Christ himself, that very foundation, can be uprooted. (For "all the promises of God are in him, and in him is Amen," 2 Cor. 1.20, that is, they stand firm and are made valid.) "Namely the Spirit." The Comforter whom he has named, he designates as "the Spirit of truth."

units.la: Eius nomen, nempe Spiritus veritatis.
units.tr: His name, namely the Spirit of truth.

units.la: Propter quem.
units.tr: On account of whom.

units.la: Quo modo datur.
units.tr: How he is given.

units.la: A patre cur procedere dicatur.
units.tr: Why he is said to proceed from the Father.

units.la: Iohã. 16.21 veritatis appellans ab effecto suo in nos docendo veritatem: vt poltea hoc capite, & in deducendo nos in omnem veritatem, vt postea capite 16.13. Ex hac appellatione apparet nullam esse in nobis veritatem, absque hoc spiritu: sed nos natura vanitate & mendaciis repletos esse. Notandum rursus quod quia Spiritus est veritatis, ideo Consolatorem esse: Nam cognitio veritatis causa est consolationis, & Spiritus Dei dum nos agnoscere facit, primum peccatum & miseriam nostram, secundo liberationem nostram in Christo gratuitam, tertio gratitudinem nostram ob tantum beneficium in nos collatum, operatur in cordibus nostris consolationem solidam, ac vnicam eam, & in vita, & in morte. Contrà vero vbi non est triplex hæc cognitio per Spiritum veritatis subministrata, nulla ibi est consolatio, vel in vita, vel in morte. Tantum positum est in cognitione.
units.tr: John 16.21, calling him the Spirit of truth from his effect in us, in teaching the truth, as later in this chapter, and in leading us into all truth, as later in chapter 16, verse 13. From this appellation it appears that there is no truth in us apart from this Spirit, but that by nature we are filled with vanity and lies. It should be noted again that because the Spirit is of truth, he is therefore the Comforter. For knowledge of the truth is the cause of consolation. And the Spirit of God, while he makes us recognise first our sin and misery, secondly our free liberation in Christ, and thirdly our gratitude for so great a benefit conferred upon us, works in our hearts a solid consolation, and the only one, both in life and in death. On the contrary, where this threefold knowledge, supplied by the Spirit of truth, is not present, there is no consolation there, either in life or in death. Everything rests on knowledge.

units.la: Quem mundus non potest. Amplificatio huius beneficij Spiritus veritatis, à mundi conditione. Ex hac oppositione conspicitur, non nisi rarum ac singulare esse Spiritus sancti ac veritatis donum: vt non sit quod Papistæ obiiciant multitudinem suam, hoc est, mundum, qui non amplectitur hanc quam nos, Dei gratia, profitemur veritatem. Tantum enim abesse ab eo debemus, vt putemus causam nostram deteriori loco esse, vt è contrà, vel ob hoc ipsum pluris faciamus singulare hoc ac non vulgare cognitionis ac veritatis beneficium; Deo semper gratias agentes, quod nos exemerit à mundo hoc, & ex illa sece papistica eduxerit, ac transtulerit in lucem suâ admirabilem. Notandum quod dicit, Mundum non posse recipere. Non dicit simpliciter (non recipit) sed negat omnem potentiam ac libertatem, quam vocant arbitrij. Hæc impotentia naturæ est in omnibus hominibus, eleatis pariter & reprobis. Nam animalis homo non est capax rerum quæ sunt Spiritus Dei: sunt enim illi stultitia, nec potest eas cognoscere: sed Deus est qui discernit.
units.tr: "Whom the world cannot." An amplification of this benefit of the Spirit of truth, from the condition of the world. From this contrast it is evident that the gift of the Holy Spirit and of truth is rare and singular, not common, so that the Papists have nothing to object in their multitude, that is, the world, which does not embrace the truth that we, by the grace of God, profess. We ought to be so far from thinking our cause to be in a worse position on that account that, on the contrary, we should value this singular and uncommon benefit of knowledge and truth all the more, always giving thanks to God that he has freed us from this world and has drawn us out of that papistical darkness and brought us into his own marvellous light. It should be noted that he says the world cannot receive. He does not simply say "it does not receive," but denies every power and freedom which they call free will. This impotence of nature is in all men alike, the elect and the reprobate. For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God: they are foolishness to him, nor can he know them; but it is God who discerns.

units.la: Gratia discrimen facit, non natura: nam alios, dum per verbuum suum offert iis Spiritum sanctum, non mouet aut flectit ad hoc, vt eum recipiant. Alios verò mouet, & in ipsis efficax est per eundem illum Spiritum suum, in verbo oblatum: Estque hæc secunda quædam gratia: Ex gratia enim est quod offerat, vel incogitantibus, Spiritum sanctum in verbo Euangelij, ex gratia rursus est quod recipiatur idem ille Spiritus, vt contra in solidum gloria sit eius per Iesum Christum. Amen.Quia non videet eum. Haec ratio est, cur non possit mundus recipere Spiritum, vel cur nullum sit desiderium Spiritus in mundo: nempe quia ignoti nulla cupido est. Nos eo quod cognoscimus quid boni sit in re quapiam, ideo illud appetimus.Ignoti vero nulla cupido est. Sifcires, inquit Christus Samaritanae, donum Dei, & eum qui dicit tibi, Da mihi potum, tu peteres ab eo, & daret tibi aquam vitae. Quo significat ignorantiam tanti doni in causa fuisse cur mulier Samaritana non modo neget ipsi potum aquae, verum etiam cur non petat ab ipso potum aquae illius viuae. Ita res habet in Spiritu Dei. Nam qui non gustarunt, quam suauis sit Dei Spiritus, non possunt ij eum appetere: Quare danda opera est, vt semel Spiritum Dei videamus, & degustemus aliquam eius suauitatem. Cognitus semel Spiritus Christi, accendit in cordibus mirifi-cum ipsius desiderium, nam plenus est gaudij ac consolationis. Beatus autem qui esurit ac sitit, hoc est, qui afficitur desiderio gratiae: nam ipse saturabitur.
units.tr: Grace makes the difference, not nature. For to some, when he offers them the Holy Spirit through his word, he does not move or bend them to receive him; but to others he does move, and the same Spirit, offered in the word, is effective in them. And this is a second grace. For it is by grace that the Holy Spirit is offered in the word of the Gospel even to the unthinking; and again by grace that the same Spirit is received, so that in return glory may be his entirely through Jesus Christ. Amen. "Because it does not see him." This is the reason why the world cannot receive the Spirit, or why there is no desire for the Spirit in the world: namely, because there is no longing for what is unknown. Since we know what is good in some thing, therefore we desire it; but there is no longing for the unknown. "If you knew," Christ said to the Samaritan woman, "the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, Give me a drink, you would ask him, and he would give you living water." By this he signifies that ignorance of so great a gift was the cause why the Samaritan woman not only refused him a drink of water but also did not ask him for a drink of that living water. So it is with the Spirit of God. For those who have not tasted how sweet the Spirit of God is, they cannot desire him; therefore care must be taken that we see the Spirit of God once and taste some sweetness of him. Once the Spirit of Christ is known, he kindles in hearts a wonderful desire for himself, for he is full of joy and consolation. Blessed indeed is he who hungers and thirsts, that is, who is seized by a desire for grace, for he himself shall be satisfied.

units.la: Vos autem cognoscitis. Per occupationem docet quae sit discipulorum conditio, & quam contraria sit conditioni hominis mundi. Obiici enim ab iis potuit; An nostra conditio eadem est cum mundi huius conditione, & an nos versamur in eadem Spiritus sancti ignorantia? Respondet Dominus conditionem eorum longe aliam esse a mundi ista conditione, & ipsos non haerere in iis tenebris, sed Spiritum illum sanctum cognitum habere. Ex quo discimus, quod quoties audimus de infelici ista mundi conditione in tenebris iacentis, sine Deo, sine Christo, sine Dei Spiritu, toties oculos in nosipsos convertendos esse, videndumque an eadem sit nostra quae mundi est conditio, & excutiendus animus an aliqua sit in nobis Spiritus sancti notitia & percepito, necne. Pleriq; figunt in infelici hoc mundo oculos suos, ipsi insultant, ipsum miserum iactant, cum tamen ipsi non minus caeci sint ac miseri, quam mundus. Causam addit cur cognitum Spiritum habeant: Quia, inquit, apud vos manet. Notitia rei
units.tr: You, however, know him. By an occupatio he shows what the condition of the disciples is, and how far it differs from the condition of the people of the world. For they could have objected: is our condition the same as the condition of this world, and do we live in the same ignorance of the Holy Spirit? The Lord answers that their condition is far different from the condition of this world, and that they do not remain in the darkness but have known that Holy Spirit. From this we learn that whenever we hear of the unhappy condition of the world lying in darkness, without God, without Christ, without the Spirit of God, we must turn our eyes upon ourselves, and see whether our condition is the same as the world's, and examine our minds whether or not there is in us some knowledge and perception of the Holy Spirit. Many fix their eyes on this unhappy world, mock it and boast over its wretchedness, although they themselves are no less blind and miserable than the world. He adds the reason why they have the Spirit known to them: Because, he says, he remains with you. The knowledge of a thing

units.la: {a} Quibus Spiritus S. fit cognitus, rei alicuius,est ex praesentia rei aliqua, vt notitia hominis existit ex familiari consuetudine quae est cum ipso: ita & is Spiritum sanctum nouit qui habet Spiritum cum ipso quasi habitantem, ac familiariter eo vtitur. Agnoscit is quidem quàm efficax sit Spiritus ad cognitionem & ad consolationem, quia nimirum habitat nō tantum vnà nobiscum, sed etiam in nobis, vt ex verbis sequentibus apparet, & in vobis erit. Amplificatio est rationis proximae, coniungit enim cum ea promissionem incrementi Spiritus, & maioris efficaciae futurae post suam ad cælos ascensionem & glorificationem. Non relinquam. Ad maiorem confirmationem fidei eorū, promissionem proximam repetit, sed verbis aliis. Nam reditus hic Domini non intelligendus est is, qui futurus est vltimo illo die de quo supra versu tertio: sed reditus est per maiorem Spiritus sui efficaciam post glorificationem sui ad dextram Patris. Ex hoc conspicitur eos solos non esse orphanos, qui gaudent Spiritus praesentia, qua si careant, orphani sunt, & omnibus fraudibus & periculis expositi: etsi illi ipsi videantur sibi habere vniuersi huius mundi praesidium: quam rursus qui habet, etsi ab omnibus destituantur, praesidium tamen habent, quo muniuntur ipsi aduersus diabolum & mundum: orphanis ac viduis atque peregrinis nominatim promittit Deus praesentiam suam: Vide Deuter. 10.18. Psalm. 68.6. & 146.9. Ergo cum habeant isti promissionem hāc sibi peculiariter factam, videndum est iis praesertim, vt sentiant Dei per Spiritum suum sanctum praesentiam, & spes eorum sit in Deo, qui tam benignè se offert iis peculiari quadam promissione. Cùm autem nemo omnium sit, qui non sentiat in se mille defectus, omnibus autem miseris ac egenis promissio facta sit praesentiae Domini, profectò omnibus videndum est, vt sentiat in tanta inopia praesentiam illam Dei, quae supplet omnes defectus nostros, Cui sit omnis gloria, Amen.
units.tr: {a} Those to whom the Holy Spirit is known have knowledge of a thing from its presence, just as a person's acquaintance arises from familiar intercourse with him. So too he knows the Holy Spirit who has the Spirit with him as one dwelling there, and makes familiar use of him. Certainly he recognises how effective the Spirit is for knowledge and for consolation, because he dwells not only with us but also in us, as appears from the words that follow: and shall be in you. This is an amplification of the nearer reason; for it joins to it the promise of an increase of the Spirit and of greater efficacy after his ascension into heaven and glorification. I will not leave you. For the greater confirmation of their faith he repeats the nearer promise, but in other words. For this return of the Lord is not to be understood as the coming on that last day spoken of above in verse three; it is a return through the greater efficacy of his Spirit after his glorification at the right hand of the Father. From this it is seen that those alone are not orphans who rejoice in the presence of the Spirit; without it they are orphans, exposed to all frauds and dangers, even though they seem to themselves to have the protection of the whole world. Conversely, those who have the Spirit, even if they are abandoned by all, still have a protection by which they are guarded against the devil and the world. God promises his presence by name to orphans, widows and strangers: see Deut. 10.18, Ps. 68.6 and 146.9. Therefore, since they have this promise made to them in a peculiar way, they above all must see to it that they feel God's presence through his Holy Spirit, and that their hope is in God, who offers himself so kindly to them by a particular promise. Since there is no one who does not feel in himself a thousand defects, and since the promise of the Lord's presence is made to all the wretched and needy, certainly all must take care to feel in such great want that presence of God which supplies all our defects. To whom be all glory, Amen.

units.la: 19 Adhuc paululum, & mundus me non amplius conspiciet, vos autem conspicietis me: quia ego viuo, vos etiam viuetis.
units.tr: 19 Yet a little while, and the world will no longer see me, but you will see me; because I live, you also will live.

units.la: 20 In illo die vos cognoscetis me esse in Patre.
units.tr: 20 In that day you will know that I am in the Father.

units.la: Fidei discipulorum confirmatio promissa, peculiari quadam ratione.
units.tr: The confirmation of the disciples' faith is promised, in a peculiar manner.

units.la: Discipulorum Christi officium. meo, & vos in me, & me in vobis.
units.tr: The duty of Christ's disciples. ...my, and you in me, and I in you.

units.la: 21 Qui tenet mandata mea, & seruat illa, is est qui diligit me, qui autem diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo: & ego diligam eum, & ipsi conspicuum exhibebo meipsum.
units.tr: 21 He who holds my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me; and he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and will manifest myself to him.

units.la: REpetit iam quartò promissionem illam Spiritus sancti, idque per oppositionem & antithesin conditionis huius mundi, quo maius appareat beneficium erga suos, vt supra obseruauimus. Repetitio autem ista non frustra fit, ea enim significatur quàm difficile sit credere, & sperare futuram gratiam. Ideo ante primum aduentum Christi perpetuò inculcata est promissio aduentus illius Christi futuri, atque adeo difficile est credere in Christum venturum in gloria secundo tempore, vt nunquam satis repeti & inculcari possint promissiones aduentus eius. Tot sunt impedimenta fidei & extra nos & intra nos! Sed videamus verba. Ante promissionem Spiritus, per oppositionem, significatur quæ sint futura conditio mundi, hoc est eorum qui primum vi-lum Christi aduentum despexerunt, siue Pharisæi fuerunt, siue alij, Adhuc, inquit, paululum & mundus me non amplius conspiciet, hoc est redeuntem in Spiritu suo non videbunt, quia nimirum contempserunt primum illum aduentum in carne humiliata. Nam qui contemnunt Christum vno modo præsentem, illi alio præsentem non conspicient. Qui contempserunt Christum in prima illa præsentia in carne humiliata, illi non viderunt præsentem in verbo & Spiritu. Et qui contemnunt nunc præsentem in verbo & in Spiritu, non videbunt in vltimo illo aduentu glorificatum. Contemptores tamen isti, quæ est eorum securitas, certò expectant se visuros Christum in aduentu suo secundo, & pollicentur sibi participes fore se gloriæ ipsius. Similes sunt prophano Esauo, qui vendidit ius primogenituræ suæ vnico edulio: saturatus iam securè surrexit, ac promisit interea se hæredem futurum, donec audiret benedictionem sententiâ Dei & Patris sui à se transfatam in Iacobum fratrem. Sic & contemptores isti non sentient se priuatos esse cælo, donec illam sententiam maledictionis audie-rint, quo quidem tempore, quanquam cum Esauo la-chrymabuntur, non tamen inuenient locum resipiscen-tiæ. Tum sequitur promissio facta discipulis: Vos autem, inquit, conspicietis me. Aspectus hic fuit Christi præsentis per Spiritum suum sanctum. Nam Spiritus per verbum operans sensibus quodammodo repræsentat Christum, & eius præsentia aliqua ipsos implet, exhibet eum oculis videndum. Unde Paulus dicit Christum crucifixum esse ob oculos eorum: auribus præbet audiendum. Vox enim ista Euangelii, Christi ipsius magis est, quàm ministrorum eius, offert manibus tractandum, & gustui quodammodo gustandum. Unde Apostolus, si modò gustástis quàm benignus sit Dominus. Ex hoc sensu Christi, qui est per fidem, videmus fidem nostram, Spiritum sanctum qui excitat fidem, & uno verbo promissionem istam Christi non esse rem aliquam leuem aut imaginariam, verùm nihil esse ea magis sensile, nihil efficacius ad omnem consolationem. Quia ego viuo Ratio subiecta cur conspecturi sint discipuli posthac Domini suum. Quod si quid impedimento futurum sit, quo minus me conspecturi sitis, sanè id erit mors, vel mea, vel vestra, sed ego viuo, & vos viuetis: Ergo nota phrasin, Ego viuo, inquit, non autem ego viuam: significat enim se ab æterno viuere, & in æternum, ac proinde in semetipso vitam habere, ut habemus Iohan. 5. Sic supra cap. 8. 58. Priusquam, inquit, Abraham fieret ego sum: Non dixit, fui: quo significat se essentiam suam ab æterno habere, ac proinde per se esse, non per alium. Ex his igitur loquutionibus colligero potes Christum Deum esse. Nam hæ loquutiones Deo soli proprie sunt, qui est, Eheie, & qui per se viuit. Nos autem per ipsum viuimus & mouemur ac sumus. Illud etiam nota, vitam esse causam cur conspiciamus Christum: Vita enim in genere causa est sensus omnis & in specie aspectus. Causa cur videant homines terrena ista, est vita ea qua sunt imbuti: sic causa cur videant homines cœlestia illa, est vita aliqua necessario, non naturalis ista, quæ oculos magis excæcat ne videant illa cælestia, quàm videndi facultatem aliquam ministrat. Animalis homo non est capax eorum, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei: sunt enim illi stultitia. Quare, vt alibi Paulus loquitur, vt sapientes simus, oportet stultos priùs fieri, & mori naturæ corruptæ ac sapientiæ carnis. In illo die vos. Amplificat beneficium illud futuri aspectus ex adiunctis: Eo, inquit, die quo me aspicietis, videbitis duas res maximas: Primùm vnionem mei & Patris, secundò κοινωνίαν vestri & mei. Inspecto Christo videtur illa vnitas essentiæ ac gloria Patris ac filij, quia dum credit quis in Christum, apprehendit simul infinita omnia, infinitam potentiam, & quæ sit excellens illa magnitudo potentiæ ipsius in nobis qui credimus, infinitam misericordiam, & vno verbo maiestatem illam Dei vniuersam, vnde facile apud animum suum colligit Christum esse vnirum Patri in essentia illa vna ac gloria Deitatis. Quod autem conspiciatur vnio illa Christi & nostri ex inspecto Christo, & fide in eum, vel inde apparet quoddam credimus in Christum, percipiamus gaudium ineffabile ac gloriosum, sentiamus pacem, & vt dicam verbo, sentiamus εὐρηκέναι quandam ineffabilem. Sensus autem iste ἐνωσις esse non potest, nisi sit coniunctio aliqua ἕνωσις Christi & nostri: Nam ἕνωσις est ex κοινωνία. Quare ex hac in Christū, & eo inspecto, percipimus duo maxima beneficia: primum quòd seruator noster sit vnum cum Patre, & Deus sit, par Patri in gloria ac maiestate: secundum quòd nos vnum sumus cum filio & Patre. Nisi demum essent hæ quas dixi coniunctiones ac vniones, nos profecto nunquam eam in Christo vim & efficaciam per fidem percipeteremus, neque suggum hunc vitalem ex eo vnquam hauriremus.
units.tr: He now repeats for the fourth time that promise of the Holy Spirit, and does so by way of opposition and antithesis to the condition of this world, so that the benefit towards his own may appear greater, as we have observed above. This repetition is not made in vain, for it signifies how difficult it is to believe and hope for future grace. Therefore before the first coming of Christ the promise of his future coming was constantly pressed, and so hard is it to believe that Christ will come in glory at the second time, that the promises of his coming can never be repeated and pressed enough. So many are the hindrances to faith, both outside us and within us! But let us look at the words. Before the promise of the Spirit, by way of opposition, is signified what the condition of the world will be, that is, of those who despised the first coming of Christ, whether they were Pharisees or others. Yet, he says, a little while, and the world will no longer see me, that is, they will not see him returning in his Spirit, because they have despised that first coming in humbled flesh. For those who despise Christ present in one way will not see him present in another. Those who despised Christ in that first presence in humbled flesh did not see him present in the Word and the Spirit. And those who now despise him present in the Word and in the Spirit will not see him glorified at that last coming. Yet these despisers, in their security, confidently expect to see Christ at his second coming, and promise themselves that they will share his glory. They are like the profane Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal; satiated, he rose up in security, and meanwhile promised himself that he would be the heir, until he heard the blessing of God and his Father transferred by sentence to Jacob his brother. So too these despisers will not perceive that they are deprived of heaven until they have heard that sentence of malediction; at which time, although they will weep with Esau, they will not find a place for repentance. Then follows the promise made to the disciples: But you, he says, shall see me. This sight is of Christ present through his Holy Spirit. For the Spirit, working through the Word, in some way presents Christ to the senses, and fills them with a certain presence of him, and displays him to be seen by the eyes. Hence Paul says that Christ crucified was set before their eyes; he offers him to be heard by the ears. For that voice of the Gospel belongs to Christ himself more than to his ministers; it offers him to be handled by the hands, and in a manner to be tasted by the palate. Hence the Apostle: if indeed you have tasted how gracious the Lord is. By this sense of Christ, which is through faith, we see our faith, and the Holy Spirit who stirs up faith; and in one word, this promise of Christ is not a light or imaginary thing, but nothing is more perceptible to the senses, nothing more effective for all consolation. Because I live: this is the reason added why the disciples will see their Lord henceforth. If anything should hinder you from seeing me, surely that will be death, either mine or yours; but I live, and you will live. Therefore note the phrase: he says, I live, not I will live; for he signifies that he has life from eternity and to eternity, and so has life in himself, as we have in John 5. So above in chapter 8, verse 58: Before he says Abraham was made, I am. He did not say, I was; by which he signifies that he has his essence from eternity, and therefore is through himself, not through another. From these expressions, then, you can gather that Christ is God. For these expressions belong properly to God alone, who is, Ehyeh, and who lives through himself. But we live through him, and are moved and exist. Note this also: life is the cause why we see Christ. For life in general is the cause of all sense, and in particular of sight. The cause why men see earthly things is the life with which they are imbued; so the cause why men see those heavenly things is a life of a necessarily different kind, not the natural one, which rather blinds the eyes so that they do not see those heavenly things than supplies any faculty of seeing. The natural man is not capable of the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him. Therefore, as Paul says elsewhere, to be wise we must first become foolish and die to corrupt nature and the wisdom of the flesh. In that day you: he amplifies that benefit of the future sight from its attendant circumstances. On that day, he says, when you see me, you will see two very great things: first, the union of me and the Father; second, the κοινωνία of you and me. Looking upon Christ, that unity of essence and glory of the Father and the Son is seen, because when anyone believes in Christ he at the same time apprehends all things infinite: infinite power, and that excellent greatness of his power in us who believe, infinite mercy, and in one word that whole majesty of God; whence he easily gathers in his mind that Christ is one with the Father in that single essence and glory of the Deity. That this union of Christ and ourselves is seen from looking upon Christ and faith in him, appears from this: when we believe in Christ we perceive an ineffable and glorious joy, we feel peace, and, to say it in a word, we feel a certain ineffable εὕρηκα. But this feeling cannot be an ἕνωσις unless there is some conjunction, a ἕνωσις of Christ and of us; for ἕνωσις comes from κοινωνία. Therefore from this looking upon Christ we perceive two very great benefits: first, that our Saviour is one with the Father, and is God, equal to the Father in glory and majesty; second, that we are one with the Son and the Father. Unless these conjunctions and unions which I have mentioned existed, we would certainly never perceive that power and efficacy in Christ through faith, nor ever draw this vital juice from him.

units.la: Qui tenet præcepta mea. id est, corde iis adhæret, vel inscriptam legem corde habet, Et seruat ea. Nempe in vita sua: Is ille est qui diligit me, id est, reipsa restatur se diligere me. Quorsum ista repetitio? Sciuit Dominus futuros vltimis hisce temporibus post decessum suum, qui eadem & charitatem prætensuri essent vitæ malæ. Ideo digito demonstrat quasi eū hominē qui diligit se: Is est, inquit, qui obseruat mandata mea: dilectio enim cernitur in opere. Filioli, inquit Iohannes, ne diligamus verbo, neque lingua solùm, sed opere & veritate. Christus fide iam apprehensus, vel habitans in corde per fidem, efficax est in vita. Vbi
units.tr: "He who keeps my commandments," that is, who adheres to them in his heart, or has the law written in his heart, "and keeps them," namely in his life: "he is the one who loves me," that is, he truly shows that he loves me in deed. Why this repetition? The Lord knew that in these last times after his departure there would be people who would claim the same love while living wicked lives. So he points, as it were, with his finger at the man who loves him: "He," he says, "is the one who observes my commandments," for love is seen in works. "Little children," says John, "let us not love in word, neither in tongue only, but in deed and in truth." Christ, already laid hold of by faith, or dwelling in the heart through faith, is effective in life. Where

units.la: 1. Ioh. 3. 18. Vbi non est vita, vbi non sunt bona opera, ibi non est Christus. Qui autem diligit me, diligetur à Patre. Ne videretur sibi frustra diligere & obseruare mandata ipsius, ostedit non absque fructu aliquo eos dilecturos Christum: Qui diligit Christum filium, Pater eum diliget: compensabitur amore mutuo eóque Paterno. Non sunt ita accipienda hæc verba quasi nos priores diligamus Deum. Imò dilexit nos cum inimici essemus, imò dilexit nos cum nondum essemus. In hoc est charitas, inquit Iohannes, non quod nos dilexerimus nos, nempe priores, sed quod ipse (prior scilicet) dilexerit nos, & miserit filium suum, vt esset propitiatio pro peccatis nostris. Necesse est vt sensus charitatis Dei, eiusdem in cordibus nostris, priusquam nos diligamus Deum. Necesse est perfundat corda nostra suavi sensu dilectionis suæ, antequam nos eum diligamus. Tu quidē ex sensu charitatis ipsius, exsistit dilectio nostra in eum mutua. Fluit enim charitas nostra tanquam riuulus quidam ex pleno illo fonte charitatis Dei. Tum vbi obuiam iimus per charitatem mutuam dilectioni Dei, Deus vi-cissim nobis venit obuiam, & ipse amoris principium est, semperque amore nos & prævenit, & subsequitur: quia amor eius infinitus est, vt inquit Paulus, In charitate radicati, valeatis assequi cum omnibus sanctis, quæ sit illa longitudo, latitudo, profunditas & sublimitas, & cognoscere charitatem illam Christi omni cognitione superiorem. Charitas autem nostra modica est & finita, & nisi perpetuo alerctur, succedente quasi illa Dei charitate (quæ est eius imbecillitas) mox extingueretur: Et reipsa quidem sentimus quàm egre & difficulter excitemur beneficiis etiam maximis, ad Deum redamandum. Et ego diligam eum. Ad amorem Patris adiungit amorem filij: Quem enim Pater amat, filius eundem amat, & é contrà: Imò vnus idémque est amor Patris & filij; vt vna eadémque essentia est Patris & filij, vna maiestas, vna gloria, ita vna eadémque charitas est Patris & filij, loquor de filio Christo, vt Deus est & λόγῳ. Alioqui enim affectus humanus in Christo homine est qui exuperat omnem charitatem creaturæ, & impletus est quasi charitate illa Dei infinita. Sed hic sermo est de charitate filij, & λόγῳ potissimum; atque de se ΥΣΛΟΓΩ & Dei filio loquitur. Ergo vna eadémque est
units.tr: 1 John 3.18. Where there is no life, where there are no good works, there Christ is not. "And he who loves me," he says, "will be loved by the Father." Lest it seem to him that he loves and keeps his commandments in vain, he shows that those who love Christ will not go unrewarded: he who loves the Son will be loved by the Father, and will be repaid with mutual, indeed fatherly, love. These words are not to be taken as if we first love God. Rather he loved us while we were enemies, indeed while we did not yet exist. "In this is love," says John, "not that we loved him first, but that he (namely, first) loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins." It is necessary that the sense of God's love be poured into our hearts before we love God. It is necessary that our hearts be flooded with the sweet sense of his love before we love him. Indeed, our love for him, returned in mutual affection, arises from the sense of his love. "For our love flows like a little stream from that full fountain of God's love." Then, when we meet God's love with our mutual love, God in turn comes to meet us, and he himself is the beginning of love, and always both goes before us with love and follows after us, because his love is infinite, as Paul says: "Being rooted in love, that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, breadth, depth and height, and to know the love of Christ which surpasses all knowledge." Our love, however, is small and finite, and unless it is constantly nourished, with God's love succeeding it (which is his condescension toward our weakness), it would soon be extinguished. And indeed we experience how hard and reluctantly we are stirred to love God in return, even by the greatest benefits. "And I will love him." To the love of the Father he adds the love of the Son: for whom the Father loves, the Son loves too, and conversely. Indeed the love of the Father and of the Son is one and the same, just as the essence of the Father and the Son is one and the same, one majesty, one glory; so the love of the Father and the Son is one and the same, I speak of the Son Christ as God and as the Word [λόγῳ]. For otherwise the human affection in Christ the man exceeds all creaturely love, and is filled, as it were, with that infinite love of God. But here the discourse is about the love of the Son, and chiefly as the Word [λόγῳ]; and he speaks of himself, the Word himself [ΥΣΛΟΓΩ], and the Son of God. Therefore the love of the Father and the Son is one and the same.

units.la: cont="true" charitas Patris & filij. Si autem de perceptione illius charitatis sermo fiat, prius in persona filij percipi eam, vel ipsa experientia discunt credentes. Experimur enim nullum vel aspectum, vel sensum charitatis Dei, hoc est, nullum accessum esse ad lucem illam inaccessam, in qua habitat Deus nisi per filium, qui est splendor gloriæ ipsius, & imago inconspicui Dei. Tum charitatem Patris & filij ex effecto & fructu suo demonstrat. Et, inquit, conspicuum ei exhibebo meipsum. Loquitur de præsentia ea quæ per Spiritum sanctum fit & fuit post ascensum & glorificationem Christi. In conspectu suo videtur Dominus ponere magnum momentum, quasi hoc sit beneficium, quo vel maxime exerit dilectionem suam, si det se videndum ac conspiciendum. Quantum autem sit hoc beneficium non cognoscunt nisi ij, qui quàm miseri sunt sine Christo eiusque præsentia sibi sunt conscij. Qui enim valet non eget medico. Hoc est qui est sine sensu peccati & miseriæ suæ, non agnoscit quantum boni sit in Christo. Vnde ipse Dominus, Venite ad me omnes, qui fatigati & onerati estis; & invenietis requiem animabus vestris.
units.tr: The love of the Father and the Son is one and the same. But if the discourse is about the perception of that love, believers learn by experience itself that it is first perceived in the person of the Son. For we experience no sight or sense of God's love, that is, no access to that inaccessible light in which God dwells, except through the Son, who is the brightness of his glory and the image of the invisible God. Then he shows the love of the Father and the Son from its effect and fruit. "And," he says, "I will manifest myself to him." He speaks of that presence which comes through the Holy Spirit and has come since the ascension and glorification of Christ. The Lord seems to place great weight on being seen, as if this were the benefit by which he chiefly displays his love, if he gives himself to be seen and beheld. But how great a benefit this is, only those know who are conscious of how wretched they are without Christ and his presence. For "he who is well has no need of a physician." He who is without a sense of his sin and misery does not recognize how much good there is in Christ. Hence the Lord himself: "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and you will find rest for your souls."

units.la: 22 Dicit ei Iudas, non ille Iscariotes, Domine, Quid est cur te sis nobis conspicuum exhibiturus, & non mundo?
units.tr: 22 Judas says to him, not Judas Iscariot, "Lord, why is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?"

units.la: 23 Respondit Iesus & dixit ei, Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum seruabit, & Pater meus diliget eum, & ad eum veniemus, & apud eum habitabimus.
units.tr: 23 Jesus answered and said to him, "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him."

units.la: 24 Qui non diligit me, sermones meos non seruat, & sermo quem auditis non est meus, sed eius qui misit me, nempe Patris.
units.tr: 24 He who does not love me does not keep my words; and the word which you hear is not mine, but his who sent me, namely the Father's.

units.la: 25 Hæc loquutus sum vobis, apud vos manens.
units.tr: 25 I have spoken these things to you while still remaining with you.

units.la: 26 Aduocatus autem ille, id est, Spiritus sanctus, quem mittet Pater in nomine meo, ille vos docebit omnia, & in memoriam revocabit vobis omnia quæ dixi vobis.
units.tr: 26 But that Advocate, that is the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things, and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.

units.la: Hic fuit Iudas frater Simonis & Iacobi, consanguineus Domini, ex duodecim vnus qui scripsit Epistolam hanc Iudæ, quam in manibus habemus hodierno die. Miratur quodammodo quod cum tanta sit gratia Domini, is non extendat eam advniuersum mundum,sed ad paucos duntaxat aliquot. Sic mirantur homines quotidie,cum tamen hoc admiratione sit dignū, sit potius,quòd Dominus, vel vnius alicuius miseretur,cum omnes in eodem sit reatu. Ipsi Angeli admirantur tantam Dei misericordiam,dum intuentur mysterium salutis humanæ.Et pij oēs magis ad id obstupescūt quòd videant Deum erga se misericordem,quā quod videant & sciant reiectos esse alios complures. Paulus inducit corruptam rationem quærentem de electione quorundam & reprobatione aliorum. Quasi vero ab æterno oportuit Deum omnes pariter eligere, Annon,inquiunt, iniustus est Deus, quod paribus paria non impertiatur? Respondet Paulus non aliter quàm ex Dei voluntate, qui quos vult eligit, quos vult repudiat. Siue igitur in tempore Dominus aliis præbeat se inspiciendum, aliis vero deneget præsentiam suam, glorificemus ipsum in misericordia & in iustitia sua. Siue ab æterno eligat alios,repudiet vero alios, reuereamur ipsius voluntatem, semperque de omnibus eius actionibus, siue ab æterno, siue in tempore, reuerenter sentiamus,& ipsi omne gloriam in omnibus operibus suis, etsi nos causas non statim intelligamus,ipsi,inquam,omnem gloriam tribuamus,in sempiternum.
units.tr: This Judas was the brother of Simon and James, a kinsman of the Lord, one of the twelve, who wrote this Epistle of Jude that we have in our hands today. He wonders in a way that, since the grace of the Lord is so great, he does not extend it to the whole world, but only to a few. So men daily wonder, though it is rather a matter for admiration that the Lord shows mercy to even one, since all are in the same guilt. The angels themselves marvel at so great a mercy of God, as they look upon the mystery of human salvation. And all the godly are amazed more that they see God merciful towards themselves, than that they see and know that many others have been rejected. Paul introduces a corrupt reasoning that inquires about the election of some and the reprobation of others. As if God ought from eternity to have chosen all alike! "Is God not unjust," they say, "in not bestowing equal things on equals?" Paul answers only that it is according to God's will: "he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens." Whether, then, in time the Lord grants to some that he may be seen, and to others denies his presence, let us glorify him in his mercy and in his justice. Whether from eternity he elects some and rejects others, let us reverence his will, and always think of all his actions, whether from eternity or in time, with reverence; and let us ascribe to him all glory in all his works, even if we do not at once understand the reasons; to him, I say, let us give all glory, for ever.

units.la: Respondit ei Iesus. Videtur non respondere ad interrogationem, sed insistere in priori exhortatione quæ fuit ad obseruationem sermonum suorum, quo significat non tam curiosè inquirendum in causas operum Dei, quàm obediendū esse voluntati ipsius: neque tam quærendam causam cur tot sint quibus deneget præsentiam sui,& gratiam quàm ingrediendum viam eam, qua & præsentiam ipsius & gratiam nos ipsi assequamur: Est autem ea vt diligamus eum, diligentes autem eum obseruemus mandata ipsius. Sic enim si faciamus,Deus nos vicissim diliget, & veniet ad nos, & mansionem faciet apud nos, hoc est, dabit nobis præsentiam suam, non ascedimus cam quidem ad breue tempus, sed in perpetuum. Om-nino enim Christiana professio non tam cernitur in lo-quendo & quaerendo, quàm in agendo. Christum enim discere, teste Apostolo, est exuere veterem hominem & induere nouum. Qui non diligit. Immoratur adhuc in ex-hortatione: Nunc autem à contrario, vel à consequente contrarij suadet ad obseruationem sermonis ipsius: Nā qui non obseruat mandata mea, is non diligit me. Non diligere Deum, est consequens contrarij: q.d. Is qui non obseruat mea mandata, hac ipsa inobedientia sua satis arguit se non diligere me. Ergo vt obedientia testatur de dilectione: ita inobedientia testatur de odio Dei, te-statur, inquam, factum & opus non lingua & verbum. Nam nihil facilius est quàm immundum cor fucare lingua mendaci: nihil rursus difficilius, quàm cor malū & infidele bene agere. Non est possibile, ait Dominus, arborem putrem fructus bonos ferre. Fieri quidem po-test vt malus in speciem bene agat, sed re ipsa non bene agit, neque ad finem in bene agendo potest perseuerare. Illud etiam naturale est linguae, tegere hypocrisin cor-dis. At vero manus hypocrisin detegit, & linguam men-dacij coarguit, Qui dicit, inquit Iohannes, Novi Dominum, & tamen mandata eius non seruat, is mendax est, & veritas in eo non est. & postea, qui dicit, Diligo Deum, & fratrem suum oderit, mendax est. Quis autem agnit mendacem? nempe opus & manus arguunt medacem linguam. Sermo quem auditis. Adhuc persistit in eadem illa exhortatione, quae est ad obedientiam. Nunc enim ducit eos quasi manu ad authorem omnium sermonum ipsius, nempe os ipsius Dei & Patris. Quo discimus omnem fontem fidei ac obedientiae veras, esse os Dei. Nititur enim fides veritate, quae ex ea proficiscitur, ex fide rursus obedientia est. Vnde discimus exemplo Christi, si quando volumus vel fidem, vel obedientiam persuadere, discimus, inquam, animos hominum subuechendos esse ad audiendā quasi ipsius Dei vocem, vt in ea conquiescant. Neque enim potest animus conquiescere in voce creaturae cuiusquā, vel hominis, vel Angeli. Neque authoritas Ecclesiae, vel hominum potest esse fundamentum fidei nostrae, etsi dicant Papistae nos ideo habere fidem scripturae, quia Ec-clesia clesia de ea testatur, quod sit verbum Dei. Nisi enim scriptura ipsa de se testaretur, quod ex Deo esset, & verbum Dei esset, profecto authoritas Ecclesiæ afferentis, id nobis nunquam probaret, aut fidem eius rei faceret. Nam fundamentum ac principium, quo nititur fides, oportet sit ipsamet Dei loquentis vox ac testimonium.
units.tr: Jesus answered him. He seems not to answer the question, but to persist in the earlier exhortation to keep his words, by which he signifies that one must not inquire too curiously into the causes of God's works, but must obey his will; nor ought one to seek so much the cause why he denies his presence and grace to so many, as to enter the way by which we ourselves may attain both his presence and his grace. This way is that we love him, and loving him keep his commandments. For if we do so, God in turn will love us, and will come to us and make his dwelling with us, that is, he will give us his presence, not for a short time only, but forever. For indeed the Christian profession is seen not so much in speaking and asking as in doing. For to learn Christ, as the Apostle witnesses, is to put off the old man and put on the new. He who does not love. He still lingers in the exhortation: now, however, from the contrary, or from the consequence of the contrary, he persuades them to keep his word: for he who does not keep my commandments does not love me. Not to love God is the consequence of the contrary: as if to say, he who does not keep my commandments, by this very disobedience proves enough that he does not love me. Therefore, as obedience bears witness to love, so disobedience bears witness to hatred of God; it bears witness, I say, by deed and work, not by tongue and word. For nothing is easier than to disguise an unclean heart with a lying tongue; and again nothing is harder than for an evil and faithless heart to act well. It is not possible, says the Lord, for a rotten tree to bear good fruit. It is indeed possible that an evil man may act well in appearance, but in fact he does not act well, nor can he persevere to the end in acting well. It is also natural for the tongue to cover the hypocrisy of the heart. But the hand exposes hypocrisy, and convicts the lying tongue. "He who says," says John, "'I know the Lord,' and yet does not keep his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him." And afterwards: "He who says, 'I love God,' and hates his brother, is a liar." Who then recognizes the liar? Surely the deed and the hand convict the lying tongue. The word which you hear. He still persists in the same exhortation, which is to obedience. For now he leads them, as it were by the hand, to the author of all his words, namely the mouth of God himself, the Father. Whence we learn that the mouth of God is the true source of all faith and obedience. For faith rests on the truth that proceeds from it, and obedience in turn follows from faith. Hence we learn from the example of Christ that when we wish to persuade anyone of faith or obedience, we must, I say, lead men's minds to hear, as it were, the very voice of God himself, so that they may rest in it. For the mind cannot rest in the voice of any creature, whether man or angel. Nor can the authority of the Church or of men be the foundation of our faith, even if the Papists say that we therefore have faith in Scripture because the Church bears witness that it is the word of God. For unless Scripture itself testified of itself that it is from God and is the word of God, the authority of the Church asserting it would never prove this to us, nor create faith in the matter. For the foundation and principle on which faith rests must be the very voice and testimony of God speaking.

units.la: Hæc loquutus fuin. Obiicere potuerunt discipuli, non se satis intelligere aut capere, quæ dixit: imo ipse Dominus senserat eos non satis intelligere, vt qui sit cordium scrutator, huic occurrit loqui se duntaxat nunc, & semen quasi spargere: Postea mittendum esse Spiritum sanctum, qui idem docturus esset & subministraturus eorum cordibus, & interioribus animis, quæ ipse inculcaret auribus. Nota igitur primum, nudam esse efficaciam verbi, ne verbi quidem Dei, sine interno doctore Spiritu sancto. Et nisi, vt dixit supra, ἀποδιδοῦναι sinus. Nisi enim Spiritus ad verbum externum prædicatum, illuminet mentes nostras, & aperiat corda nostra, nihil vnquam proficiemus audiendo. Nota rursus non comitari perpetuò internum illum Spiritum doctorem vocem Ministri exterius docentis, ne in suis quidem: & fidelibus ipsis sæpe verbum Dei prædicatum quasi librum clausum: id quod de incredulis scriptum est. Id autem fit ad nos humiliandos: & hinc discimus non despondendum animum, quoties non percipimus eam ex verbo quam debemus consolationem, sed cum patientia expectandum & serumonem perpetuò spargendum à Ministris, recipiendum autem ab auditoribus, consolantes nos ipsos vel hac sola re, quod semen illud verbi Dei sit immortale, hoc est non nesciat, etsi ad tempus suffocetur, nō magis quam ipse Deus, à quo est illud semen, mori. nescit: Vnde dicitur immortale semen Dei viui & manet in æternum. Et nos ipsi id experimur, nos sepe consolationem capere ex eo ipso verbo in necessitatib9 nostris, quod tamen ofcitanter accipimus cum ipsum prædicaretur aut legeretur. Consolator autem ille. Huic consolatori potius officium docendi tribuit, & tamen non doctorem appellauit, sed consolatorem: vt innuat doctrinam eius ad consolationem tendere, & sola quidem doctrina Spiritus est hodie quæ consolatur animos nostros. Fateor equidem nos consolationem capere ex doctrina & ministerio hominum, sed id fit, quia ministerij hominum comes est Spiritus sanctus, secus nulla vera existit consolatio ex doctrina hominum. Ergo cùm sentimus consolationem ex verbo & Euangelio prædicato, id quoque adaugere debet consolationem nostram, quòd eum doctorem habeamus, & certi fimus ex effecto illo consolationis præsentem nobis esse Dei Spiritum. Quem mittet Pater. Mittit Pater Spiritū sanctum in nomine Filij, hoc est per filium Mediatorem & intercessorem, vt ipse dixit supra, Ego precabor Patrem, &c. Nam Spiritus sanctus & omnia dona Spiritus per Mediatorem ad nos vsque perueniunt, & per ipsius humiliati sanguine primum ac mortem, deinde & ipsius glorificati efficacia. Vnde dictum est, Ascendit in sublime & dedit dona hominibus. Postea cap. 15. 26. dicitur filius mittere Spiritū à Patre: hoc idem est re cum eo quod hic dicitur, nempe, Patrem mittere Spiritum sanctum per Filium, vel in nomine Filij. Vtrobique enim obseruatur Patrē esse fontem Spiritus sancti & omnium donorum ipsius. Deinde Filium esse per quem omnia ad nos perveniunt, non vt instrumentum quidem, sed principalem efficientem cum Patre: verum ordine duntaxat secundum à Patre suo. Ille docebit vos omnia. Hoc officium est consolatoris Spiritus, docere omnia. Ne autem promiscuè omnia etiam hominum figmenta hic accipiantur, addit, Omnia quæ dixi vobis. Obseruatum est supra verbum non esse efficax ad consolationem in cordibus sine Spiritu. Hic autem nota Spiritū non operari sine verbo Dei & Christi. Verbum Christi intelligo, primum quod Prophetæ veteres loquuti sunt. Nam per Spiritum Christi loquuti sunt, teste Petro. Deinde intelligo, quòd Christus ipse loquutus est. Tertiò, quòd post eū Apostoli. Quartò, verbi Christi nomine intelligo quod à Mose & Prophetis ac Apostolis scriptis est traditū ex imperio æterni Dei, vt ait Apostolus. Nam quodcunque dictum est, vel à Prophetis vel à Christo & Apostolis, id totū reipsa scripto mandatum est. Vel hic vnus locus sufficit ad damnandum omnes siue Mahumetanos siue Papistas, siue hæreticos alios, vt Anabaptistas, qui acsi Scripturæ Dei non essent perfectæ & perfecta esset in iis revelatio voluntatis ac consilij Dei, de salute nostra, revelationes alias Spiritus, præter has quæ in verbo scriptę sunt, tradunt docéntque; non tam ab hac revelatione pendendum quæ in verbo scripta est, quàm ab aliis revelationibus Spiritus præter verbum & contra verbum.
units.tr: These things I have spoken. The disciples could have objected that they did not sufficiently understand or grasp what he had said. Indeed the Lord himself had perceived that they did not understand enough, and as the searcher of hearts he meets this by saying that for now he is only speaking, and as it were sowing seed. Afterwards the Holy Spirit is to be sent, who would teach the same things and supply them to their hearts and inmost souls, impressing on their ears what he himself had said. Note first, then, that the efficacy of the word, even of the Word of God, is bare without the Holy Spirit as inward teacher. And unless, as he said above, the Spirit gives back [ἀποδιδοῦναι] what is sown, we shall never profit by hearing. For unless the Spirit illumines our minds and opens our hearts to the external word that is preached, we shall never make any progress by listening. Note again that the inward Spirit as teacher does not perpetually accompany the voice of the minister who teaches outwardly, not even in the faithful themselves; and often the Word of God, though preached, is to them like a closed book, which is what is written of unbelievers. This happens to humble us, and from it we learn not to lose heart whenever we do not receive from the word the consolation we ought to receive, but to wait with patience, and meanwhile the ministers must keep sowing the word continually and the hearers must receive it. We may console ourselves with this one thing alone: that the seed of the word of God is immortal, that is, it does not perish, though for a time it may be choked, no more than God himself, from whom that seed comes, dies. Hence it is said: the immortal seed of the living God abides for ever. We ourselves also experience this, that we often receive consolation in our needs from that very word, which nevertheless we took up carelessly when it was being preached or read. The Comforter, however, whom the Father will send. The Father sends the Holy Spirit in the name of the Son, that is, through the Son as Mediator and intercessor, as he himself said above: I will pray the Father, and so on. For the Holy Spirit and all the gifts of the Spirit reach us only through the Mediator, and through the blood and death of his humiliation first, and then through the efficacy of his glorification. Hence it is said: He ascended on high and gave gifts to men. Later, in chapter 15:26, it is said that the Son sends the Spirit from the Father. This is in substance the same as what is said here, namely that the Father sends the Holy Spirit through the Son, or in the name of the Son. For in both places it is observed that the Father is the fountain of the Holy Spirit and of all his gifts, and that the Son is the one through whom all things come to us, not indeed as an instrument, but as principal efficient cause together with the Father, though only second in order from his Father. He will teach you all things. This is the office of the Comforter Spirit, to teach all things. Lest, however, all things be taken here indiscriminately, including the inventions of men, he adds: all the things that I have said to you. It was observed above that the word is not effective for consolation in hearts without the Spirit. Here, however, note that the Spirit does not work without the Word of God and of Christ. By the word of Christ I understand, first, what the ancient prophets spoke, for they spoke by the Spirit of Christ, as Peter bears witness. Second, I understand what Christ himself spoke. Third, what the Apostles spoke after him. Fourth, by the word of Christ I understand what was handed down in writing by Moses, the prophets and the Apostles by the command of the eternal God, as the Apostle says. For whatever was spoken either by the prophets or by Christ and the Apostles, all of it has in fact been committed to writing. This one passage alone is enough to condemn all, whether Mahumetans, or Papists, or other heretics such as the Anabaptists, who teach that, as if the Scriptures of God were not complete and as if the revelation of God's will and counsel concerning our salvation were not perfect in them, there are other revelations of the Spirit besides those contained in the written word; and that we must depend not so much on the revelation that is written in the word as on other revelations of the Spirit apart from the word and against the word.

units.la: 27 Pacem relinquo vobis, pacem illam meam do vobis: non prout mundus dat, ego do vobis. Ne turbator cor vestrum, neque formidato.
units.tr: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.

units.la: 28 Audivistis me dixisse vobis, Abeo & redeo advos. Si diligeretis me, gauderetis utique quod dixerim, Proficiscor ad Patrem, nam Pater maior me est.
units.tr: Ye have heard how I said unto you, I go away, and come again unto you. If ye loved me, ye would rejoice, because I said, I go unto the Father: for my Father is greater than I.

units.la: 29 Et nunc dixi vobis, Priusquam fiat, ut cùm factum fuerit credatis.
units.tr: And now I have told you before it come to pass, that, when it is come to pass, ye might believe.

units.la: 30 Non loquar amplius multa vobiscum: venit enim princeps mundi huius, sed in me non habet quicquam.
units.tr: Hereafter I will not talk much with you: for the prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me.

units.la: 31 Sed ut norit mundus quod ego Patrem diligo: & prout mādauit mihi Pater, ita facio. Surgite, abeamus hinc.
units.tr: But that the world may know that I love the Father; and as the Father gave me commandment, even so I do. Arise, let us go hence.

units.la: HActenus fuerunt exhortationes, nunc redit ad consolationem illam initio capitis huius inceptam. Est autem hoc argumentum consolationis, à pace illa quam discedens relicturus sit iis. Alludit sine dubio ad vsitatum illum Hebraeis salutandi modum, quo pacem alij aliis optare consueuerunt, hoc est omnem prosperitatem ac felicē in omnibus rebus successum: ita Dominus breui discessurus valedicit discipulis suis, ac pacem iis relinquit. Tum addit, pacem illam meam do vobis: q.d. Non tantùm relinquo pacem, vel pacem opto, vt sint homines, sed do pacem eam quam opto. Christus enim efficax est ad dandum pacē illam, quam ipse sanguine suo promeruit est. Neque do pacem tantùm, sed do, inquit, meam pacem, vnde pax Dei vocatur: Et Deus pacis dicitur, & Apostoli optant perpetuò gratiam & pacem à Deo & Christo Iesu : ergo Christus significat non dare sc pacem alienam,sed suam ipsius. Porrò videtur speciale quandam pacem innuere, dum suam dicit, nempe μακάρια & bonæ conscientiæ pacem. Nam ea Christi pax est proprie, vt quæ sit ex bona conscientia; hoc est, conscientia remissionis peccatorum. Bona autem conscientia sit ex Christi sanguine vel fide in eum. Christi sanguis, inquit Apostolus, purgabit conscientiam nostram à mortuis operibus ad serviendum Deo viuo : hoc est purgabit à peccatis, ergo pax hæc bonæ conscientiæ, cùm profluat a Christi sanguine, merito Christo tribuitur, & intelligi dicitur hoc loco Patris nomine. Rursus addit, non vt mundus dat, ego do vobis. Cùm enim etiam det mundus pacem aliquo modo, discrimen statuit inter donum suum & donum mundi. q. d. Quòd si mundus dat pacem, dat eam perfunctorie tantum, & verbo tenus, non reipsa : imò sæpe non sincerè & ex corde. At ego do pacem non ore tantum, neque corde tantum, sed opere. Ergo discrimen statuit in dandi modo. Notandum hic, quàm serio iis commendet pacem quotuplici cum repetitione: vt satis appareat ipsum non tantum pacem iis relinquere, sed etiam animum suum. At ita quidem se res habet; Christus in eos quos diligit non tantum beneficia sua, sed & ipsum animum suum & interiores affectus omnes effundit. Ex pace ita explicata infert consolationis conclusionem, Ne turbetur cor vestrum. Vbi enim non est pax Christi, ibi nihil nisi cordis perturbatio. Carnale enim hanc securitatem quæ multorum est, nunquam pacem dixerim, sed signum subiti exitij: cùm dicent pax & tuta omnia, tum extremum imminet iis exitium. Contrà verò, vbi pax est Christi, ibi solida tranquillitas & securitas cordis, quæ est etiam in mediis periculis. Nam pax Dei, quæ superat omnem cognitionem, præsidio est cordibus nostris, ac mentibus nostris in Christo Iesu.
units.tr: Up to this point these have been exhortations; now he returns to the consolation begun at the start of this chapter. The subject of this consolation is the peace that he is about to leave to them as he departs. He undoubtedly alludes to the customary Hebrew manner of greeting, in which people were accustomed to wish one another peace, that is, every prosperity and a happy outcome in all affairs. So the Lord, about to depart shortly, bids his disciples farewell and leaves them peace. Then he adds: my peace I give unto you, as if to say: I do not merely leave peace, or wish peace for people, but I give the peace that I wish. For Christ is able to give that peace, which he himself merited by his blood. Nor does he give peace only, but he says he gives my peace, whence it is called the peace of God, and God is called the God of peace, and the Apostles constantly wish grace and peace from God and Christ Jesus. Therefore Christ signifies that he is not giving a peace foreign to himself but his own. Moreover, he seems to point to a certain special peace when he says my peace, namely the peace of a blessed [μακάρια] and good conscience. For that is properly Christ's peace, as it arises from a good conscience, that is, the conscience of the forgiveness of sins. A good conscience, however, comes from the blood of Christ or from faith in him. The blood of Christ, says the Apostle, shall purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God: that is, it will purge us from sins. Therefore this peace of a good conscience, since it flows from the blood of Christ, is rightly attributed to Christ, and it is said here to be understood in the name of the Father. Again he adds: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. For although the world too gives peace in some way, he draws a distinction between his gift and the gift of the world. As if to say: if the world gives peace, it gives it only perfunctorily and in word, not in deed, and often not sincerely and from the heart. But I give peace not with the mouth only, nor with the heart only, but in deed. So he draws the distinction in the manner of giving. It should be noted here how earnestly he commends peace to them, with such repetition, so that it is quite clear that he leaves them not only peace but also his own mind. And indeed it is so: Christ pours out on those whom he loves not only his benefits but also his own mind and all his inward affections. From peace so explained he draws the conclusion of consolation: Let not your heart be troubled. For where there is no peace of Christ, there is nothing but disturbance of heart. I would never call that carnal security which belongs to many a peace, but rather a sign of sudden destruction: when they say peace and all is safe, then destruction is at hand for them. On the contrary, where there is Christ's peace, there is solid tranquillity and security of heart, which is present even in the midst of dangers. For the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, is a guard to our hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.

units.la: Audiuistis me dixisse vobis. His verbis videtur modesta quædam reprehensio Apostolorum, quòd non statim perceperint consolationem ex verbis ipsius : ea enim re ostendunt se non diligere Dominum suum vt oportet. Atque hoc exemplo Christi consolantis discipulos suos, discipuli nimia præsentiæ cor poralI affixi.
units.tr: You have heard me say to you. These words seem to be a mild rebuke of the Apostles, because they did not at once receive comfort from his words. By this they showed that they did not love their Lord as they ought. And by this example of Christ, who comforts his disciples, we learn that the disciples were too attached to his bodily presence.

units.la: Thil.4.7. discimus, consolationes saepe temperandas esse reprehensionibus. Nam affectus nimis profusus ac intemperanter ac inordinatè se effundens sistedus est reprehensione aliqua, qualis est illa Dauidis, cùm animam suam nimis deiectam in exilio illo suo ac perturbatam his verbis increpat ac corrigit, Quid deiecis te, anima mea? quid perstrepis in me? Spera in Domino. Sed expendenda sunt verba. Primum fundamentum reprehensioni subiternit, superius illud ipsius dictum, quo admonuit de ipsius discessu. Interea etiam consolatus est eos à reditu ipsius, nempe per Spiritum sanctum. Super hoc fundamentum extruit reprehensionem suam. Si diligeretis me, tantum abfuisset ab eo, ut illud meum dictum vos consternaret ut econtrà ex illo dicto, quo dixi me ad Patrem meum proficisci, summam consolationem cepisset: At non gaudetis, ergo hoc ipso arguitis vos non diligere me, ut oportet. Probatur autem quod gaudendum iis fuisset ex profectione ad Patrem, ex Patris gloria ac maiestate quam comparatè proponit. Pater, inquit, maior me est. Ratio enim est, acsi dixisset, Nam Pater gloriosus est, & ego ubi ad eum profectus fuero veniam in communionem illius gloriae, adeóque ero illi in gloria aequalis. Quòd dicat Patrem ipso maiorem esse, id accipiendum est de officio quo Patre inferior est, officio, inquam, mediatoris, quod requirit exinanitionem filij & obedientiam summam. In hac autem exinanitione & obedientia quoad officium ipsius, manet aequalis Patri persona & essentia. Nam inaequalitas officij non facit inaequalitatem personae & essentiae: vel, ut Cyrillus dixit, missio & obedientia non tollunt aequalitatem potentiae & essentiae. Hic locus ita expositus nihil faciet pro illo mendacio Arrij, qui Filium Patri inaequalem dixit, utpote Deum quendam creatum. Ex hac Domini reprehensione, qua reprehendit eos quòd non consolationem ceperint ex illis ipsius verbis, id primum cōspicimus; Omnia Christi & dicta & facta erga suos pertinere ad ipsorum consolationem: etsi ea sit hominum caecitas & affectuum πάθος, ut saepe in deteriorem partem ei interpretentur, & ex materia quae gaudij per se, faciant sibi materiam doloris ac perturbationis animi, Non commendo hic
units.tr: Thil.4.7. We learn that consolations must often be tempered with rebuke. An emotion that pours itself out too freely and without order or measure needs some rebuke, such as David's, when he chides and corrects his soul, cast down and troubled in that exile of his, with these words: Why are you cast down, my soul? why do you make such an uproar within me? Hope in the Lord. But the words must be weighed. First, he lays the foundation of his rebuke in that earlier saying of his, in which he warned them of his departure. Meanwhile he had also consoled them about his return, namely through the Holy Spirit. Upon this foundation he builds his rebuke. If you loved me, far from that saying of mine dismaying you, you would rather have taken the greatest consolation from the saying in which I said that I am going to my Father, and you would have taken the greatest consolation. But you do not rejoice; therefore by this very fact you show that you do not love me as you ought. It is proved that they ought to have rejoiced at the departure to the Father, from the Father's glory and majesty, which he sets forth by way of comparison. "The Father," he says, "is greater than I." For the reasoning is as if he had said: the Father is glorious, and when I have gone to him I shall come into a share of that glory, and so I shall be equal to him in glory. As for his saying that the Father is greater than he, this must be understood of the office by which he is inferior to the Father, the office, I say, of mediator, which requires the emptying of the Son and his utmost obedience. But in this emptying and obedience, with respect to his office, the person and essence remain equal to the Father. For inequality of office does not make inequality of person and essence; or, as Cyril said, mission and obedience do not abolish equality of power and essence. This passage, so expounded, will do nothing for that lie of Arius, who said that the Son is unequal to the Father, as though he were some created god. From this rebuke of the Lord, in which he reproves them because they did not take consolation from his words, we first perceive this: all of Christ's words and deeds toward his own serve their consolation, even though men's blindness and passion [πάθος] are such that they often interpret them for the worse, and from a matter that is in itself a cause of joy, make for themselves a cause of grief and disturbance of mind. Here I do not commend that feeling [αἴσθησιν], as I may call it, the Stoic insensibility, by which no one is moved by any pain at the adversities that often befall us. But this I want: grief ought always to be mingled with perpetual joy in the Lord and not be despaired of, since we know that all things work together for good to those who love God, and that a Christian should always rejoice, even when he grieves most. Here we also learn what a perverse love is, and this from the example of the disciples. Those men indeed loved the Lord, but not rightly, because they did not rejoice that he was to be glorified before the Father. True love rejoices in the good and glory of the one who is loved; therefore that is not true love which grieves over the good of the one who is loved, even though such grief arises from ignorance, as it did in these Apostles. Hence, above all, there is need of knowledge and understanding, by which the affections of our mind are directed, and without which no motion of the mind is right and no affection is well ordered.

units.la: {a} Psal. 42. αἰσθησιν illam, vt sic dicam, insensibilitatem Stoicam, qua nemo dolore aliquo commoueatur, ex iis quae saepe aduersa eueniunt: Sed hoc volo, oportere dolorem perpetuo gaudio in Domino permistum esse ac non despera-tum, cum illud sciamus, omnia conferre in bonum di-ligentibus Deum: & Christiano homini semper gau-dendum esse, etiam tum cum dolet maximè. Discimus hic quoque quisnam sit praeposterus amor, idque ex exemplo discipulorum. Dilexerunt illi quidem Domi-num sed non rectè, quia non gauisi sunt quod glorifi-candus esset apud Patrem. Verus amor gaudet bono & gloria eius qui diligitur: ergo hic non est verus amor, qui dolet propter bonū eius qui diligitur: etsi dolor ille sit ex ignorantia, cuiusmodi fuit iste Apostolorū. Quare imprimis opus est notitia & cognitione, qua dirigun-tur affectiones animi nostri, & sine qua nullus motus animi rectus, nullus affectus directus.
units.tr: Psalm 42. I do not mean that insensibility of the Stoics, as I may call it, by which no one is moved by any pain at all at the adversities that often befall us. Rather I say this: sorrow ought always to be mingled with a perpetual joy in the Lord, and not be despaired of, since we know that all things work together for good to those who love God; and a Christian ought always to rejoice, even when he grieves most. Here we learn also what kind of love is misdirected, and this from the example of the disciples. Those men did indeed love the Lord, but not rightly, because they did not rejoice that he was to be glorified before the Father. True love rejoices in the good and the glory of the one who is loved; therefore that is not true love which grieves over the good of the one who is loved, although that grief arises from ignorance, such as was the grief of those Apostles. Hence there is first need of knowledge and understanding, by which the affections of our mind are directed, and without which no motion of the mind is right and no affection is well directed.

units.la: Et nunc dixi. Hic est finis omnium praedictionum Christi, vt credamus Iesum esse Christum illum. No-tandum quod non dicat simpliciter, dixi vobis priusquam fieret, vt credatis: sed addit hoc, vt cum factum fuerit credatis. Significat tum demum confirmari fidem, cum praedictionem sequitur eventus. Fides quidem est, fateor, ex praedictione nuda, cuiusmodi fuit illa fides Patrum ante Christi adventum, ex nudis Prophetarum praedictionibus. Verum tum demum confirmatur fides, cum eventus sequitur praedictionem. Nos igitur qui su-mus in regno Christi, materiam certe habemus maioris fidei, maioris consolationis quàm habuerunt Patres, qui non tantum Prophetas habemus, sed Euangelium, in quo narrantur omnia illa, quae de Christo Prophetis praedicta sunt iam perfecta ac consummata esse. Unde Christus nos beatos pronuntiauit. Beati sunt oculi, qui vi-dent quae vos videtis.
units.tr: And now I have said it. This is the end of all the predictions of Christ: that we may believe that Jesus is that Christ. It is to be noted that he does not simply say, "I have told you before it came to pass, that you may believe," but adds this: "that when it has come to pass you may believe." He signifies that faith is then at last confirmed, when the outcome follows the prediction. It is true, I grant, that faith arises from a bare prediction, such as was the faith of the Fathers before the coming of Christ, from the bare predictions of the Prophets. But faith is then truly confirmed when the outcome follows the prediction. We therefore, who are in the kingdom of Christ, certainly have grounds for a greater faith and a greater consolation than the Fathers had, for we have not only the Prophets but the Gospel, in which are related all those things which were foretold of Christ by the Prophets, now shown to be fulfilled and completed. Whence Christ pronounced us blessed: "Blessed are the eyes which see the things that you see."

units.la: Non loquar amplius. Hic videtur sermonem illum suum cum discipulis suis collatum abrumpere ac concludere. Rationem reddit ex eo quòd appropinquante illa hora mortis Christi à Patre destinatae, appropinquauit dia-bolus, appropinquârunt eius satellites & ministri eius ad carnificinam illam exercendam, & exequendum de-cretum. cretum Dei. Neque diabolus tantùm in ministris illis ac instrumentis suis Christum est aggressus, vt Iuda, vt reliquis: sed ipse cum legionibus impurorum Spirituum, venit aduersus Christum: & tum maximè in eum omnes insultarunt, cùm ex cruce penderet, putantes tum de Christo se triumphaturos, atque ita omnem spem redemptionis humanæ sublaturos, & Deum gloria sua, quæ in solo Christo residet, spoliaturos. Testis est huius rei Apostolus quū dicit Christum triumphasse de diabolis, & spoliatos eos palam traduxisse.
