Disce rursus hoc loco exemplo Christi: cùm videmus nobis ex Dei voluntate migrãdum ex hac vita, siue citet nos ipse per morbum, siue per afflictionem aliam quamcunque, oportere vt præparemur ad obuiis vlnis occurrendum mortì, illud scientes, mortem hanc temporariam ad vitam æternam, ingressum esse. Sed in me non habet. Occupatio: An igitur potestatem in te habet diabolus? Respõdetnihil iuris aut potestatis in se habere diabolum. Occurrit igitur scandalo crucis suæ. Spiritus sanctus in Scripturis præcisè admodum notat has mortis Christi circumstantias, quòd ex decreto Patris æterno passus sit. Act.2.&4. quòd à Patre in tempore traditus sit morti: quòd filius ipse se tradiderit sua sponte aut voluntate. Gal.1.&2.Heb.9. His circumstantiis circumscripta est mors Christi, ideo vt intelligamus inuito, vt loquuntur, Deo nihil factum de Christo, vt occurratur scandalo crucis Christi, quod certè ęsset, si inuito Deo eum ad supplicium traptum fuisse videremus, vt denique videamus Christi passionem ac mortem, obedientiam Dei fuisse. Nam voluntas facit obedientiam, siue agat quis, siue patiatur. Quòd si Christus millies mortem passus fuisset, si non summa voluntate passus fuisset, profectò morte sua, neque pro nobis satisfecisset, neque nobis iustitiam aut vitam promeritus fuisset.
units.tr: I will not speak much more. Here he seems to break off and end his discourse with the disciples. He gives the reason: because the hour of Christ's death, appointed by the Father, was drawing near, the devil drew near, and his satellites and ministers drew near to carry out that butchery and to execute the decree of God. Nor did the devil assail Christ only through those ministers and his instruments, such as Judas and the others; but he himself came against Christ with the legions of unclean spirits, and then most of all they all insulted him as he hung on the cross, thinking that they would triumph over Christ then, and so would take away all hope of human redemption and strip God of his glory, which resides in Christ alone. The Apostle is a witness to this matter when he says that Christ triumphed over the devils and openly led them away spoiled. Learn again here from the example of Christ: when we see that we must depart from this life by the will of God, whether he summons us by sickness or by any other affliction, we must prepare ourselves to meet death with open arms, knowing that this temporary death is an entrance into eternal life. But he has no hold on me. Objection: Does the devil then have power over you? Answer: The devil has no right or power whatever over him. Thus he meets the scandal of his cross. The Holy Spirit in the Scriptures very precisely notes these circumstances of Christ's death: that he suffered by the eternal decree of the Father; that he was delivered over to death by the Father in time; that the Son himself gave himself up of his own accord and will. Acts 2 and 4; Gal. 1 and 2; Heb. 9. By these circumstances the death of Christ is circumscribed, so that we may understand that nothing was done to Christ against the will of God, as they say, and so that the scandal of the cross of Christ may be met; which would certainly be a scandal if we saw him dragged to punishment against the will of God; and so that finally we may see that the passion and death of Christ were the obedience of God. For the will makes the obedience, whether one acts or suffers. But if Christ had suffered death a thousand times, and had not suffered with the highest will, he would certainly not by his death have satisfied for us, nor would he have merited for us righteousness or life.

units.la: Sed vt notit. Finis passionis propediem futurę ostenditur, vt ex fine appareat eum non esse in potestate diaboli. Finis est vt ex obedientia ipsius conspiciatur ac manifestum fiat mundo quanto amore patrem suum amplestatur. Nota igitur obedientiam filij præcipuè non ex amore hominum, & φιλανθρωπία, sed ex amore illo æterno ac infinito erga Patrem suù profectum esse: qui tàtus fuit, vt cùm ipsę esset parDeo, ac in forma Dei, sese exinaniuerit forma serui accepta ac obediens factus sit Patri ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Atque hinc factum, vt Pater eum vicissim dilexerit. Dilectionem autem illam suam Pater manifestauit, eò quòd filium humiliatum exaltauerit, ac dederit ei nomen supra omne nomen quod nominatur, vt in nomine Iesu Christi omne genu flectatur, cœlestium, terrestrium ac infernorum. Vt autem agendi istam rationem inter Patrem & Filium ad nos ipsos accommodemus; Obedientia erga homines & humilitas vera, ex amore est: humilitatem & obedientiam sequitur mutuus amor. Ex quo videmus amoris mutui & pacis inter homines causam esse humilitatem qua alij alios vicissim sibi præferunt. Contrà, nota superbiæ ac factus fontem, esse odium ac contemptum hominum animis nostris innatum. Ex quo rursus sequitur contemptus ac odium mutuum. Atque hinc videmus factum ac superbiam causam esse contentionis, dissidiorum ac schismatum. Nota hic præterea finem præcipuum obedientiæ Christi, non hunc esse, vt inde manifestum fieret quantopere dilexerit homines, sed quantopere dilexerit Patrem suum. Nam propter Patrem dilexit hominem, & vt obediret Patri, mortuus est pro homine. Quòd si hic quæras, quid hoc ad mundum hunc, quòd manifestum illi fiat, Filium Patrem ita dilexisse, vt ipsi ad mortem crucis obediens factus sit? Respondeo, Cùm creatura videt Filium æqualem gloria & maiestate, sese tamen ita exinaniuisse, Patris sui causa, mouetur ad obedientiam tum erga Patrem ipsum, tum erga homines alios. Ergo æquales suos, etiam erga inferiores præstandam. Cuius rei etiam exemplum habent in Christo qui sese humiliauit ad lauandos pedes discipulorum suorum. Re vera autem non est vera humilitas & modestia, ne erga homine quidem, nisi ex inspecta priùs humilitate Christi. Nā Christus inspectus refingit animum nostrum ad humilitatem, & veram virtutem quamcunque. Hic, si quæras rursus, quid ad nos, aut quid boni ad nos peruenit, quod Patri humiliemur? Respondeo fœlicitatem nostram in eo posita quòd Pa-
units.tr: But observe. The end of the passion that is soon to come is shown, so that from the end it may appear that he is not in the power of the devil. The end is that from his obedience it may be seen and made manifest to the world how greatly he embraced his Father in love. Note therefore that the obedience of the Son proceeded chiefly not from love of men and love of mankind [φιλανθρωπία], but from that eternal and infinite love toward his Father; which was so great that, though he was equal to God and in the form of God, he emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross. And hence it came about that the Father in turn loved him. The Father showed that love by exalting the humbled Son, and giving him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth. But to accommodate that manner of acting between the Father and the Son to ourselves: true obedience and humility toward men comes from love; mutual love follows humility and obedience. From this we see that the cause of mutual love and peace among men is the humility by which they mutually prefer one another. On the contrary, note that pride and self-regard are the source of hatred and contempt of men, innate in our minds. From this again follows mutual contempt and hatred. And hence we see that pride is the cause of strife, dissensions and schisms. Note here besides that the chief end of Christ's obedience was not that it might be made manifest how greatly he loved men, but how greatly he loved his Father. For he loved man for the sake of the Father, and in order to obey the Father he died for man. But if here you ask what it matters to this world that it should be made manifest to it that the Son so loved the Father that he became obedient to him unto the death of the cross? I answer: when the creature sees the Son, equal in glory and majesty, yet so emptying himself for the sake of his Father, he is moved to obedience both toward the Father himself and toward other men. Therefore equals should show it also toward their inferiors. Christians also have an example of this in Christ, who humbled himself to wash the feet of his disciples. Indeed there is no true humility and modesty, not even toward men, unless humility is first looked upon in Christ. For Christ, looked upon, reshapes our mind to humility and to every true virtue. Here, if you ask again, what does it concern us, or what good comes to us, that we are humbled before the Father? I answer that our happiness is placed in this, that we…

units.la: Humilitas humanæ societatis vinculum.
units.tr: Humility is the bond of human society.

units.la: Superbia contentionum materer.
units.tr: Pride is the matter of contentions.

units.la: Christus cur pro nobis mortuus.
units.tr: Why Christ died for us.

units.la: Quid obedientia Christianos doceat. tri humiliemur, ipsi obediamus, ipsum-glorificemus. Hoc enim est caput omnium beneficiorum Dei Spiritualium & temporalium, vt Deo grati simus ipsúmque glorificemus in Christo Iesu, cui cum Patre sit omnis gloria. Amen. Surgite. Ex his verbis apparet eum locum mutasse, & egressum esse domo, absoluto iam hoc sermone; neque video quomodo aliter interpretari possint hæc verba.
units.tr: What obedience teaches Christians. ...that we are humbled before the Father, that we obey him, and that we glorify him. For this is the head of all God's spiritual and temporal benefits: that we be grateful to God and glorify him in Jesus Christ, to whom with the Father be all glory. Amen. Arise. From these words it appears that he changed place and left the house, this discourse now being finished; nor do I see how these words can be interpreted otherwise.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Hoc capite Christus sermonem superiori capite institutum continuat, & tria potissimum agit.
units.tr: In this chapter Christ continues the discourse begun in the previous chapter, and chiefly does three things.

units.la: 1. Hortatur discipulos ad constantiam in fide, docens eos per fidem sibi tanquam palmites viti esse insitos, ad vers. 8.
units.tr: 1. He exhorts the disciples to constancy in faith, teaching them that through faith they are grafted into him as branches into the vine, up to verse 8.

units.la: Deinde hortatur eos ad studium pietatis, ac imprimis ad mutuam dilectionem, à vers. 8. ad versum usque 18.
units.tr: Then he exhorts them to zeal for godliness, and above all to mutual love, from verse 8 to verse 18.

units.la: Postremò consolatur eos contra odium ac persequutionem mundi, à versu 18. usque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Finally he comforts them against the hatred and persecution of the world, from verse 18 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAP. XV.

units.la: 1 Ego sum vitis illa vera, & Pater meus est Agricola ille.
units.tr: 1 I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.

units.la: 2 Omnem palmitem in me non ferentem fructum tollit: & omnem quæ fert fructum, purgat vt plus fructus afferat.
units.tr: 2 Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away; and every one that beareth fruit he purgeth, that it may bring forth more fruit.

units.la: 3 Iam vos puri estis propter sermonem quem loquutus sum vobis.
units.tr: 3 Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you.

units.la: 4 Manete in me & ego in vobis manebo; sicut palmes non potest ferre fructum à semetipso, id est, nisi manserit in vite: ita nec vos, nisi in me manseritis.
units.tr: 4 Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine, no more can ye, except ye abide in me.

units.la: DDd
units.tr: DDd

units.la: HOC capite pergit in exhortationibus & consolationibus. Primo hortatur ad mutuam coniunctionem ipsorum & sui: deinde hortatur ad mutuā dilectionem aliorum erga alios. Exhortationi ad mutuam coniunctionem cum Christo præmittit generalem denuntiationem simul & promissionem. Atque ita eos præparat ad vnionem illam ipsam, ad quam adhortatur. Denuntiatio autem est aduersus infructuosos vitis ramos, quod tandem ij à Patre abscindentur: promissio est ad ramos vitis fructuosos, quibus pollicetur incrementum purgationis ac regenerationis, ac proinde incrementum fructuum continuum. Denuntiationi simul & promissioni fundamēta quædā sua substernit. 1. Quòd Filius sit vera illa vitis. 2. Quòd Pater sit Agricola. Vt de illo primo fundamēto dicamus: Consuevit Christus, vti satis conspici potest ex hoc Euangelio, per similitudinem quandam & allusionem ad res necessarias & vitales ad hanc vitam, digito quasi demonstrare plenitudinem illam gratiæ, quæ in ipso est. Sic [?]ixit, Ego sum panis ille vivificus: Iohan. 6. 48. Et ego sum lux mundi: Iohan. 8. 12. Ego sum via, veritas & vita: Iohan. 14. 6. Et hoc in loco, Ego sum vera illa vitis. Ergo Christus est panis ad pascendos animos: Christus est lux ad illuminandum tenebras nostras: Christus est via, qua recta itur ad cœlos & ad Patrem: denique est vitis quæ suppeditat vitalem illum & generosum succum membris suis, tantundem ramis sibi insertis. Comparatione autem istarum rerum dicitur verè panis, verè lux, verè vitis. Quod ipse proprie & essentialiter ista omnia sit, creaturæ autem non nisi accidentaliter & participatione quædam veri illius succi vitalis, qui in ipso est ad vitam æternam. Atque hæc de primo fundamento. Alterum est, quòd Pater sit agricola. Similitudo ista & comparatio non est in omnibus. Nam agricola non suppeditat succum suum viti, quum succus illi viti naturalis sit: tantùm labori suo eum foveat. Pater dat filio & communicat ab æterno totam illam vitam filij. Sicut Pater habet vitam in se, ita dedit filio habere vitam in semetipso: Iohan. 5. 26. Sed comparatio est in iis tantùm partibus officij quę sequuntur.q.d.vt Agricola amputat inutiles ramos,purgat autem vtiles & fructuosos : ita & pariter inutilia & corrupta membra amputat, vtilia vero purgat,vt magis fructuosa sint. Ex his fundamentis illud discimus, Patrem eum esse Agricolam, qui sit radix quasi & principium vitae omnis,Filium vero vitem esse per quam vita illa a Patre in nos deriuatur, nos tanquam ramos totidem ei insitos. Nota rursus extra Christum nullam ne potentiam quidem esse ad bonos fructus & opera : neque nos esse per naturam extra Christum, magis aptos ad fructum ferendum,quam est aridum lignum ad fructum aliquem producendum. Omnem palmitem. Hactenus fundamenta per comparationem vitis & agricolae, & per similitudinem officiorum Agricolae proposita. Notanda sunt primum in textu vocabula quaedam, vt ramorum & fructuum. Rami & palmites,hic sunt Ecclesiae visibiles, tam veris membris, quam hypocritis consistantes. Quotquot enim ore confitentur Iesum,pro Ecclesiae & Christi membris censentur. Fructus sunt opera bona, quae sunt instar fructus vitis,vbi enim hausit illum quasi succum vitalem membrum aliquod Christi, necesse est erumpat succus in fructum, non minus succus palmitis in fructum suum.
units.tr: Here he goes on with exhortations and consolations. First he urges their union with himself and with him; then he urges them to mutual love one towards another. Before the exhortation to union with Christ he sets down a general warning together with a promise, and so prepares them for that very union to which he exhorts them. The warning is against the unfruitful branches of the vine: that at last these will be cut off from the Father. The promise is for the fruitful branches, to whom he pledges an increase of purging and regeneration and therefore a continual increase of fruit. Under this warning and promise he lays certain foundations of his own: 1. That the Son is the true vine. 2. That the Father is the husbandman. To speak of the first foundation: Christ is accustomed, as can be seen well enough from this Gospel, by a certain comparison and allusion to things necessary and vital for this life, to point as it were with his finger to that fullness of grace which is in him. So he said, I am the living bread: John 6:48. And I am the light of the world: John 8:12. I am the way, the truth and the life: John 14:6. And in this place, I am the true vine. Therefore Christ is the bread to feed souls; Christ is the light to illuminate our darkness; Christ is the way by which one goes straight to heaven and to the Father; finally, he is the vine which supplies that vital and noble sap to his members, and as much to the branches grafted into him. By comparison with these things he is said truly to be bread, truly light, truly vine. He himself is all these properly and essentially, while creatures are these only accidentally and by a certain participation in that true vital sap which is in him for eternal life. So much for the first foundation. The second is that the Father is the husbandman. This likeness and comparison does not hold in every respect. For the husbandman does not supply his own sap to the vine, since that sap is natural to the vine; he only nourishes it by his labour. The Father gives to the Son, and from eternity communicates to him, the whole of that life of the Son. As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself: John 5:26. But the comparison holds only in those parts of the office which follow. That is, as the husbandman cuts off useless branches and cleanses the useful and fruitful ones, so likewise the Father cuts off the useless and corrupt members, and cleanses the useful ones so that they may be more fruitful. From these foundations we learn this: that the Father is the husbandman, who is as it were the root and beginning of all life, while the Son is the vine through whom that life is derived from the Father to us, as branches grafted into him. Note again that outside Christ there is no power even for good fruits and works, nor are we by nature outside Christ any more apt to bear fruit than dry wood is to produce any fruit. Every branch. Hitherto the foundations have been set out by the comparison of the vine and the husbandman, and by the likeness of the husbandman's duties. First, certain words in the text must be noted, such as branches and fruits. Branches and shoots here are the visible churches, consisting of true members as well as hypocrites. For all who confess Jesus with their mouth are counted as members of the Church and of Christ. Fruits are good works, which are like the fruit of the vine: for where a member of Christ has drawn in that vital sap, the sap must burst out into fruit, no less than the sap of the shoot bursts into its fruit.

units.la: Vt hic locus intelligatur,comparatio quaedam facieda est inter Agricolam & Patre Iesu Christi. 1. Agricolae curae est imprimis vinea sua, quia in ea est voluptas tota & commoditas vitae huius. Deo Patri curae est vitis sua Iesus Christus, quia animus eius acquiescit in Filio suo,& gloria Patris tota in Filio residet. 2. Agricola,si quae vitis sit quam diligit, in numerato habet omnes eius palmites: Deus Pater in numerato habet omnia filij sui membra,sive verè sint membra, sive hypocritae sint. In parabola nuptiarum filij, Non effugiet oculos regis ille vnus hypocrita,qui inter caeteros assedit mensae,non indutus veste nuptiali. Matth.22.11. 3. Agricola suo tempore & anni statis ac commodis tempestatibus ramos & palmites arescentes & infructuosos succidit, rursus fructuosos purgat:ita Pater Iesu Christi suo tempore hypocritas separat ab Iesu Christo & ab Ecclesia sua: purgat autem suos vt viberiorem fructum reddant.
units.tr: To understand this place, a comparison must be made between the husbandman and the Father of Jesus Christ. 1. The husbandman's chief care is his vineyard, because all his pleasure and the comfort of this life lie in it. To God the Father his vine is Jesus Christ, because his mind rests in his Son, and all the Father's glory resides in the Son. 2. If the husbandman has a vine that he loves, he has all its branches in his reckoning; God the Father has in his reckoning all the members of his Son, whether they are truly members or hypocrites. In the parable of the marriage of the king's son, that one hypocrite who sat at the table among the others, not clothed in a wedding garment, did not escape the king's eyes: Matt. 22:11. 3. The husbandman, at the proper time and in the suitable seasons of the year, cuts off the withered and unfruitful branches and shoots, and again cleanses the fruitful ones. So the Father of Jesus Christ at his proper time separates the hypocrites from Jesus Christ and from his Church, but cleanses his own so that they may bear more abundant fruit.

units.la: Atque hoc postremum est quod denuntiatur & promittitur. Videmus toto hoc loco plantatam vitem, omnium quae unquam fuerunt amoenissimam ac pulcherrimam, constantem suis partibus, radice, trunco vel stipite, ramis ac palmitibus suis. Radix est ipse Deus Pater, fons ac radix vitae omnis: is transfundit vitem suam in stipitem qui filius est: Filius deinde transmittit aliquam vitae suae partem in nos, qui quasi rami ac palmites sumus: Nos denique pleni illo succo erumpimus in fructus, qui sunt bona opera: non minus adeoque magis suavia, quam sunt fructus vitis, sapiunt enim vitam Dei & succum illum vitalem, qui in nos a Patre per Filium transfusus est. Fateor, sapiunt opera nostra ex parte amaritudinem naturae nostrae quae no tota expurgata est, sed id nos consolatur, quod Pater agricola nos palmites magis magisque expurget ad hoc ut opera, & plura sint & magis perpurgata. Videmus deinde quam necessarium sit ut continuos progressus faciamus, certe aliquo modo in regeneratione & regenerationis fructibus. Quod si illud necessarium sit ut continuo nos purget Pater, profecto necesse est ut continuo purgemur. Hinc sequitur quod si nullum regenerationis incrementum nullo tempore senserimus in nobis, id argumento esse, nullum habere nos argumentum, quod viui palmites simus inserti in vite illa Iesu Christo. Iam vos puri. Occupatio: Denuntiatio illa abiectionis terrefaceret discipulos suos, tempestive admonet eos, non esse in eo genere palmitum, qui excindendi sunt, sed esse ex palmitibus puris & fructiferis. Ex quo discimus ubi denuntiationes huiusmodi fiunt excutiendos esse nos & videndum nobis, an ex iis sumus ad quos pertinent iudicia illa denuntiata. Cognoscemus autem, si hoc viderimus, An puri simus necne, An viua Christi membra simus necne. Quod rursus cognoscitur ex fructibus nostris, qui electionem & vocationem nostram ipsorum nobis confirmant. Porro, si puri simus reipsa, & an Christus habitet in nobis ipsa, facile percipitur ex vita Christi agentis in nobis. Si enim viuit Christus in nobis, necesse est illud sentiamus cum Paulo, Non amplius viuo ego, inquit, sed viuit in me Christus. Per sermonem. Hic modus est quo expurgati sunt nempe per verbum Christi. Purificatis, inquit Petrus, animabus vestris, auscultando veritati per Spiritum. Spiritus est & vita, hoc est instrumentum Spiritus sancti ad regenerationem & vitam æternam efficiendam. Et verbum Dei, inquit Petrus ibidem, est immortale illud semen regenerationis.
units.tr: And this last is what is threatened and promised. We see throughout this passage a planted vine, the most pleasant and beautiful of all that have ever been, consisting of its parts: root, trunk or stock, branches and shoots. The root is God the Father himself, the source and root of all life; he pours his vine into the stock, which is the Son. The Son then passes some part of his life into us, who are as it were branches and shoots. Finally we, filled with that sap, burst out into fruits, which are good works: no less, and indeed more sweet, than the fruits of the vine, for they taste of the life of God and of that vital sap which has been poured into us from the Father through the Son. I admit that our works partly taste of the bitterness of our nature, which has not been wholly purged; but this consoles us, that the Father the husbandman purges us as branches more and more, so that our works may be both more numerous and more thoroughly cleansed. We see further how necessary it is that we make continual progress, certainly in some way in regeneration and in the fruits of regeneration. If it is necessary that the Father purge us continually, surely it is necessary that we be continually purged. Hence it follows that if we have never at any time perceived any increase of regeneration in ourselves, this is a sign that we have no evidence that we are living branches grafted into that vine, Jesus Christ. Now ye are clean. Occupatio: That threat of rejection might terrify his disciples, so he timely reminds them that they are not in that class of branches which are to be cut off, but are among the clean and fruitful branches. From this we learn that wherever threats of this kind are made, we ought to examine ourselves and see whether we are among those to whom those announced judgments pertain. We shall know this if we see whether we are clean or not, whether we are living members of Christ or not. This again is known from our fruits, which confirm to us our own election and calling. Moreover, whether we are really clean, and whether Christ dwells in us, is easily perceived from the life of Christ working in us. For if Christ lives in us, we must feel it with Paul: I live no longer, he says, but Christ lives in me. Through the word. This is the means by which they were cleansed, namely through the word of Christ. Purifying your souls, says Peter, by obeying the truth through the Spirit. The Spirit is also life: that is, the word is the instrument of the Holy Spirit for effecting regeneration and eternal life. And the word of God, says Peter in the same place, is that immortal seed of regeneration.

units.la: 4 Manete in me, & ego in vobis manebo: sicut palmes non potest ferre fructum a semetipso, id est nisi manserit in vite: ita nec vos nisi in me manseritis.
units.tr: 4 Abide in me, and I will abide in you: as the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, that is, unless it abides in the vine, so neither can you, unless you abide in me.

units.la: 5 Ego sum vitis, vos palmites: is qui manet in me, & ego in eo maneo, hic fert fructum multum: nam seorsum a me nihil potestis facere.
units.tr: 5 I am the vine, you are the branches: he who abides in me, and I in him, the same bears much fruit: for apart from me you can do nothing.

units.la: 6 Nisi quis in me manserit, abiectus extra vineam statim ut palmes arescet: deinde colligitur isti palmites, & in ignem abiiciuntur & ardent.
units.tr: 6 If anyone does not abide in me, he is cast out of the vineyard as soon as the branch withers; then these branches are gathered up, thrown into the fire, and burn.

units.la: 7 Si manseritis in me, & verba mea in vobis manserint, quicquid volueritis, petite, & fiet vobis.
units.tr: 7 If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you will, and it shall be done for you.

units.la: PRæmissa generali doctrina, & præparatis animis discipulorum ad exhortationem, & recipienda quasi exhortationis argumenta: nunc incipit exhortari ad perseuerantiam in illa vnione & coiunctione cum ipso. Notanda sunt verba: Non ait quidem, manete mecum & ego vobiscum: Sed, manete in me & ego in vobis. Qua quidem phrasi notatur arctius quoddam coniunctionis genus. Nota igitur: membra Christi non tam dicuntur manere in Christo, quomodo homines dicuntur simul manere & vnà habitare, quàm manere & vnà habitare in Christo, quo modo rami manent in arbore, & membra corporis in capite suo. Rursus Christus non tam dicitur cum membris suis manere, & cum iis habitare, quàm in iis manere, vt arbor in ramis suis, & caput in membris & corpore; hoc est cum membris suis coniunctum est arctiori vinculo. Vt igitur paucis de hac coniunctione Christi & nostri dicamus: Non est ea quidem corporalis vel naturalis, etsi ea sit arctior naturali quauis: nulla enim tam arctè per naturam coniuncta sunt, quin possint separari: At nos à Christo separari non possumus semel illi verè insiti. Est autem coniunctio haec spiritualis. Spiritualem dico, quia spirituali modo fit, per vincula nimirum spiritualia, non per neruos & ligamenta, per quae fit coniunctio ista corporalis, sed per Spiritum & fidem. Christus enim prior dimittit è coelo spiritum suum sanctum ad nos: nos deinde vicissim fidem nostram ipsius spiritu excitatam, ad eum sursum versus mittimus. Dico per Spiritu simul & fidem: quia coniunctio haec oportet sit mutua, nósque vicissim eum amplectamur. Dico illum priorem dimittere coelitus ad nos Spiritum suum, quia quicquid boni in nobis est, & virium quibus nos eum amplectamur, illa excitantur per eum, eiúsque beneficio. Nos diligimus eū, quia ille prior dilexit nos. Rursus perseuerantia vel in amore, vel in fide ex illo pendet, quia enim perseverat ipse in nobis diligendis, ideo nos perseveramus in illo diligendo; quia ipse manet in nobis per Spiritum suum, ideo nos manemus in illo per fidem nostram. Quare quoties ipse requirit in nobis vel fidem, vel perseuerantiam; toties obsecremus nos eum, vt velit dare nobis Spiritum suum & manere in nobis per Spiritum suum.
units.tr: Having laid down the general teaching, and having prepared the minds of the disciples for exhortation and for receiving the arguments of exhortation, he now begins to exhort them to perseverance in that union and communion with himself. The words must be noted. He does not say, "Remain with me, and I with you," but "Abide in me, and I in you." By this phrase a closer kind of union is indicated. Note, then: the members of Christ are not said to abide in Christ in the way that people are said to remain together and dwell together, but to abide and dwell in Christ, as branches remain in a tree and the members of the body in their head. Again, Christ is not said so much to remain with his members and dwell with them, as to remain in them, as a tree in its branches, and the head in the members and the body; that is, he is joined to his members by a tighter bond. To say briefly something about this union of Christ and ourselves: it is not corporeal or natural, although it is closer than any natural union. For nothing is so tightly joined by nature that it cannot be separated; but once we have truly been grafted into Christ, we cannot be separated from him. This union is spiritual. I call it spiritual because it takes place in a spiritual manner, through spiritual bonds, not through sinews and ligaments, by which that bodily union is made, but through the Spirit and faith. For Christ first sends his Holy Spirit down to us from heaven; then we in turn send our faith, stirred up by his Spirit, upward toward him. I say through the Spirit and faith together, because this union must be mutual, and we must in turn embrace him. I say that he first sends his Spirit down to us from heaven, because whatever good is in us, and the powers by which we embrace him, are stirred up by him and by his kindness. We love him because he first loved us. Again, perseverance, whether in love or in faith, depends on him: for because he himself perseveres in loving us, therefore we persevere in loving him; because he himself abides in us through his Spirit, therefore we abide in him through our faith. Wherefore, as often as he requires in us either faith or perseverance, so often let us beseech him to be willing to give us his Spirit and to abide in us through his Spirit.

units.la: Sicut palmes. Hoc est primum argumentum perseuerantiae. Nisi, inquit, vos in me manseritis, non potestis fructum ferre. Explicatur similitudine vitis. Sicut, inquit, palmes non potest ferre fructum à semetipso, id est, nisi in vite manserit. Conclusio est, Ergo manete in me, & ego in vobis. Argumentum hoc non alia ratione mouet quam quasi necessitas ferendorum fructuum impositta est, supra in illa denuntiatione. Omnem palmitem in me non ferentem fructum tollit Pater. Ergo necessitas haec est fructuum, qua non ferentes fructu in illo, amputandi sunt & abiiciendi. Quare ita demum mouet nos hoc argumentum, si intelligamus hanc necessitatem. Ideo, vt adducamur ad fidem in Christum, duo sunt nobis necessaria cognitu. Primò vt intelligamus necessitatem ferendorum fructuum. Huius rei admonuit Dominus Nicodemum: Nisi, inquit, quis regenitus fit, non videbit regnum gnum coelorum: deinde vt intelligamus extra Christū nullam vim esse ferendorum fructuum. Quantum absint(vt hoc obiter dicam)Papistæ hodierno die à doctrina fidei, qui hominibus inculcant liberum arbitrium, in natura reliquas vires, bona opera quæ per naturam fiunt,&c. Quantum,inquam,absint illi à doctrina fidei, vel ab eo vt fidem hominibus persuadeant, videri potest ex hac Christi doctrina. Neque enim ad fidem in Christum adducimur, nisi illud prius persuasum habeamus quod postea dicitur, Sine Christo nihil posse nos facere, & non esse nos sine eo nisi arida ligna nulli vsui nisi combustioni apta. His positis ac cognitis iam constringitur aliquis ac cogitur necessitate ad Christum confugere, nisi malit excindi ex vite ac prorsus perire.
units.tr: As the branch. This is the first argument for perseverance. Unless, he says, you abide in me, you cannot bear fruit. It is explained by the likeness of the vine: as the branch, he says, cannot bear fruit of itself, that is, unless it abides in the vine. The conclusion is: therefore abide in me, and I in you. This argument moves us in no other way than as a necessity of bearing fruit laid upon us, as in the warning above. The Father takes away every branch in me that does not bear fruit. Therefore this is the necessity of fruit, by which those not bearing fruit in him must be cut off and cast away. Hence this argument moves us only if we understand this necessity. So, that we may be brought to faith in Christ, there are two things we must know. First, that we understand the necessity of bearing fruit: the Lord warned Nicodemus of this, "Unless one is born again, he will not see the kingdom of God." Second, that we understand there is no power to bear fruit outside Christ. (To say this in passing: how far the Papists of today, who teach people about free will, and about the remaining powers in nature, and good works done by nature, etc., are from the doctrine of faith, or from persuading people of faith, can be seen from this teaching of Christ. For we are not brought to faith in Christ unless we are first persuaded of that which is said afterwards: "Without Christ we can do nothing," and that without him we are nothing but dry wood, fit for no use except burning.) Once these things are laid down and known, a person is constrained and compelled by necessity to flee to Christ, unless he prefers to be cut off from the vine and utterly perish.

units.la: Ego sum vitis. Hoc alterum est argumentum perseuerantiæ in fide; Qui manet in me & ego in illo, hic fert fructum multum. Substrata sunt ei primum duo fundamenta: Ego sum vitis, vos palmites. Ergo vt palmites manentes in vite ferunt fructum multum, ita vos manentes in me feretis fructum multum. Nam absque me. Occupatio: Annon nisi manentes in te possimus ferre fructum? huic occurrit, Sine me non potestis quicquam facere. Vt superius argumentum cogebat ad fidem in Christum: ita hoc argumentum allicit ad fidem, & perseuerantiam in ea, præsertim eos qui delectantur in fructibus vitæ sanctæ ac bonis operibus, sentiúntque quàm aridi sunt natura sua, & quàm inepti ad bona opera. Alios autem non mouet, vtpote eos qui delectantur vitæ impuritate ac malis operibus, cuiusmodi sunt hodierno die plerique. Notandus est ordo accommodatus ad naturam nostrā. Prius enim cogendi sumus quodammodo, ac necessitate quadam præparandi quàm allician-di: quæ est obstinatio naturæ nostræ. Tunc enim promissionibus locus erit, vbi necessitas imposita est, & comminationes iam præcesserunt. Ex hoc & superiori argumento illud etiam apparet, quo loco sunt habenda bona opera: Apparet enim fidem in Christum ad bona operadestinari, tanquam ad finem suum. Electi sumus in Christo, ait Apostolus, ad hoc vt sancti simus: & illuxit nobis gratia Dei salutifera, erudiés nos vt abnegata impietate & cupiditatibus mundanis sobriè, iustè, & piè viuamus in præsenti seculo. Adeo vt nisi quis conetur sobriè, iustè & piè viuere, non illuxerit gratia Dei animo ipsius.
units.tr: I am the vine. This is the second argument for perseverance in faith: He who abides in me, and I in him, the same bears much fruit. Two foundations are laid for it first: I am the vine, you the branches. Therefore, as branches abiding in the vine bear much fruit, so you, abiding in me, will bear much fruit. For apart from me [you can do nothing]. Objection: can we not bear fruit unless we abide in you? To this he replies: Apart from me you can do nothing. As the previous argument compelled us to faith in Christ, so this argument draws us to faith and perseverance in it, especially those who take delight in the fruits of holy life and good works, and feel how dry they are by nature and how unfit for good works. It does not move others, namely those who delight in an impure life and evil works, as most people do today. The order is to be noted, as suited to our nature. For we must first be compelled, in a way, and prepared by a certain necessity, before we are drawn; such is the obstinacy of our nature. For promises have their place only where necessity has been imposed and threats have already gone before. From this and the previous argument it also appears in what place good works are to be held: for it appears that faith in Christ is directed to good works as to its end. We are chosen in Christ, says the Apostle, to be holy; and the saving grace of God has dawned upon us, teaching us to renounce ungodliness and worldly lusts, and to live soberly, righteously and godly in the present age. So that unless someone strives to live soberly, righteously and godly, the grace of God has not dawned in his mind.

units.la: Nisi quis. Hoc tertium est argumentum à feruore illo ignis qui deuoraturus est aduersarios, vt loquitur Apostolus ad Hebræos. His autem gradibus peruenitur ad illum ignem Qui non manent in Christo, eiiciuntur extra vineam: hoc est, separantur ab Ecclesia certè illa vera & inuisibili, vtut maneant in hac visibili ad tempus: tū eiecti extra vineam arescunt statim. Nulla enim vita, nulla gratia Christi, nisi in societate Ecclesiæ Christi. Hinc arescentes colliguntur, & in ignem coniecti arldent. Hi sunt gradus, quibus ad inferos peruenitur. Quisquis velit effugere vltimum, caueat sibi à primo, & videat diligenter ne patiatur se à Christo auelli, quòd si contingat ab eo aliquando deflecti, ne maneat extra eū: Nam manentes extra illum, continuò præcipitantur, donec in ignem illum præcipites ferantur. Hoc argumentum graue est, & ad eos pertinet potissimum, qui non mouentur promissionibus, hoc est, ad obstinatos qui delectantur impura vita & acerbis fructibus, hoc est operibus mortuis. Quales hodierno die passim quamplurimos reperias: cum his agendum est seueriùs, & obiiciendus iis feruor ignis illius, vt certè terrore illius ignis cohibeantur ac reprimantur, si nolint promissionibus induci ad credendum. Opus est etiam credentibus hoc argumento, ad hoc vt ne sinant Christum sibi elabi, vel latum vnguem ab ipso declinent, vel ad dextram vel ad sinistram. Qui & ipsi vt in Christo manentes, omnem suauitatem, refrigerium & pacem experiuntur: ita vbi vel paululùm egressi fuerint extra Christum, sentiunt se verberari quasi illa flamma ignis. Nam extra Christum nihil nisi ira & ignis, quæ si non statim sentiatur: attamen argumentum eius est vel maximum securitas ista carnalis, & stupor qui solet desinere in sensum acerrimum atque acerbissimum.
units.tr: Unless someone. This is the third argument, from that fervour of fire which is about to devour the adversaries, as the Apostle speaks to the Hebrews. Now by these steps one comes to that fire. Those who do not abide in Christ are cast out of the vineyard, that is, they are separated from the Church, that true and invisible one, although for a time they remain in this visible one; then, cast out of the vineyard, they wither at once. For there is no life, no grace of Christ, except in fellowship with the Church of Christ. Hence the withered are gathered up, and cast into the fire, and burn. These are the steps by which one arrives at hell. Whoever wishes to escape the last should beware of the first, and see carefully that he does not allow himself to be torn away from Christ; but if it should happen that he is ever turned aside from him, let him not remain outside him. For those remaining outside him are immediately cast headlong, until they are carried headlong into that fire. This argument is grave, and pertains above all to those who are not moved by promises, that is, to the obstinate who delight in an impure life and bitter fruits, that is, dead works. You will find very many such people everywhere today; with these we must deal more severely, and the fervour of that fire must be set before them, so that, if they will not be led by promises to believe, they may at least be restrained and checked by the terror of that fire. This argument is also needed by believers, so that they do not allow Christ to slip from them, nor turn aside from him even a little, either to the right or to the left. Those who, abiding in Christ, experience all sweetness, refreshment and peace, when they have gone even a little outside Christ, feel themselves beaten as if by that flame of fire. For outside Christ there is nothing but wrath and fire; and if this is not felt at once, yet the greatest proof of it is that carnal security and stupor, which usually ends in a most sharp and bitter feeling.

units.la: Si manseritis in me. Quartum est argumentum perseuerantiæ in illa cum Christo vnione: Si manseritis, inquit, in me, & verba mea in vobis manserint, hoc idem est cum eo quod dixit supra, Et ego in vobis. Nā manet Christus in nobis per verbum & Spiritum suum. Dum enim credimus verbo ipsius, ipsum apprehendimus: apprehenditur enim Christus in hac vita in verbo & sacramentis. Quicquid voluerit is. Hoc est argumentum illud, quo promittitur volenti & petenti omnis gratia. Argumentum quidem ad motum valet, sed iis demum, qui sensum miseriæ & inopiæ suæ aliquem habent. Quorsum enim attinet promittere illi, qui nihil desiderat, nullum sensum indigentiæ suæ habet? promittere, inquam, illi aliquid quod supplear illum qui in eo est defectum. Qui valet non eget medico: at ei qui afficitur sensu inopiæ suæ, & agnoscit se destitutum gloria Dei, abalienatum à vita Dei, vt cum Apostolo loquar, nihil illi iucundius est hac promissione, nihil non faciet is vt supplaeatur defectus naturæ multiplex. Quamobrem ad audiendas huiusmodi exhortationes & promissiones præparandi sumus sensu miseriæ ac inopiæ nostræ, si audiendo proficere velimus. Nota hoc loco, quibus gradibus perveniatur ad gratiam Christi. Immediate præcedit gratiam aliquam petitio: Petite, inquit, & fiet vobis. Petitionem antecedit voluntas & desiderium, Quicquid volueritis, inquit, petite. Desiderium oritur ex sensu inopiæ ac miseriæ, cum quo coniunctus est necessario dolor secundum Deum. Nam, inquit Apostolus, Onerati suspiramus. Quisquis sentit onus illud peccati & mortalitatis, is suspirat. Sensus autem iste cum dolore, oritur ex Spiritu illo sancto qui intercedit pro nobis suspiriis inenarrabilibus. Nos qui primitias Spiritus habemus, suspiramus. Spiritus hic dictat suspiria, & ingignit nobis huc sensum, qui ex fide est in Christum. Postquam credidistis obsignati estis Spiritu illo promissionis sancto. Concedo Spiritum antecedere & gignere fidem: sed per fidem tamen accipimus eiusdem Spiritus incrementum. Ergo fides in sanguine Christi principium est omnis gratiæ. Fluit enim omnis gratia ex illo sanguine, ipsiusque merito: per efficaciam autem Spiritus sancti, qui comitatur sanguinem illum Christi nobis applicatur gratia. Ergo fides principium est gratiæ: fidem sequitur Spiritus sanctus, Spiritum sanctum sequitur sensus miseriæ ac inopiæ : sensum illum sequitur ingens desiderium, desiderium sequitur petitio, petitione obtinetur gratia. His fundamentis precum iactis, necesse est obtineamus quicquid gratiæ petimus. Sermo enim hic est de spirituali in Christo gratia & benedictione.
units.tr: If you abide in me. This is the fourth argument for perseverance in that union with Christ: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you," which is the same as what he said above, "And I in you." For Christ abides in us through his Word and his Spirit. For while we believe his word, we lay hold of him, since Christ is apprehended in this life in the Word and the sacraments. Whatever he will. This is the argument by which all grace is promised to the one who wills and asks. It is indeed an argument that moves, but only those who have some sense of their own misery and poverty. For what is the point of promising something to one who desires nothing and has no sense of his need? I say, promising him something to supply the lack in him. "He who is well has no need of a physician." But to one who feels his poverty and acknowledges that he is destitute of the glory of God and alienated from the life of God, to use the Apostle's words, nothing is more welcome to him than this promise; he will do everything so that his manifold defect of nature may be supplied. Therefore, if we wish to profit by hearing such exhortations and promises, we must be prepared by a sense of our misery and poverty. Note here by what steps one comes to the grace of Christ. Some request immediately precedes grace: Ask, he says, and it will be given you. Before the request comes will and desire: Whatever you will, he says, ask. Desire arises from a sense of poverty and misery, and with this is necessarily joined godly sorrow. For, says the Apostle, we groan, being burdened. Whoever feels that burden of sin and mortality, he groans. This sense, however, together with sorrow, arises from that Holy Spirit who intercedes for us with unutterable groanings. We who have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan. This Spirit dictates the groanings and engenders in us this sense, which comes from faith in Christ. After you believed, you were sealed with that Holy Spirit of promise. I grant that the Spirit goes before and begets faith; yet through faith we nevertheless receive the increase of that same Spirit. Therefore faith in the blood of Christ is the beginning of all grace. For all grace flows from that blood and by its merit; but grace is applied to us through the efficacy of the Holy Spirit, who accompanies that blood of Christ. Therefore faith is the beginning of grace; the Holy Spirit follows faith, a sense of misery and poverty follows the Spirit, a great desire follows that sense, a request follows desire, and by request grace is obtained. With these foundations of prayer laid, it is necessary that we obtain whatever grace we ask for. For the discussion here concerns spiritual grace and blessing in Christ.

units.la: 8 In hac re glorificatus fuerit Pater meus, vt fructum multum adferatis, & eritis mei discipuli.
units.tr: 8 In this is my Father glorified, that you bear much fruit, and you will be my disciples.

units.la: 9 Prout dilexit me Pater, ita & ego dilexi vos: manete in illa mea charitate.
units.tr: 9 As the Father has loved me, so I also have loved you; abide in that my love.

units.la: 10 Si mandata mea seruaueritis, manebitis in charitate mea: sicut ego patris mei mandata seruaui, & maneo in eius charitate.
units.tr: 10 If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love.

units.la: 11 Haec loquutus sum vobis, vt gaudium illud meum in vobis maneat, & gaudium vestrum plenum siat.
units.tr: 11 I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and your joy may be made full.

units.la: Hactenus fuit prima exhortatio ad perseuerantiam in illa vnione cum Christo: Nunc hortatur ad producendum fructus illa vnione dignos. Vt adseueraui, inquit, fructum multum. Requirit vt abundent bonis operibus. Oportet abundare bonis operibus eos, qui Christo insiti sunt, in eoque manent, qui tam plenus est omni gratia & veritate. Argumentum primum est a gloria Patris: In hoc, inquit, glorificatus est Pater meus. Quotquot mouentur hoc argumento, necesse est præparentur zelo Dei, nihil mouetur argumento ab eius gloria petito. Quare multum refert quomodo præparemur ad Dei verbū audiendum. Multis enim modis præparandus est animus, si cum fructu velimus audire. Nota hoc loco egregium imprimis bonorum operum effectum, Dei nimirum glorificationem, qua nihil prius ac potius est, & quæ finis esse debet omnium actionum nostrarum. Papistæ ad nihil vtilia putant esse bona opera, nisi operantem iustificent ac feruent. Ad hoc vt respondeamus, tenendum est orationem hanc quia dicit, Ferte fructum multum, translatam esse a palmitibus de quibus supra: vt enim illi viti insiti ferunt fructum, ita & nos quasi Christo insiti, producimus quasi fructum & vuas. Iam com-
units.tr: Thus far was the first exhortation to perseverance in that union with Christ. Now he exhorts them to produce fruits worthy of that union. As I have said, he says, much fruit. He requires that they abound in good works. Those who are grafted into Christ and abide in him, who is so full of all grace and truth, must abound in good works. The first argument is from the Father's glory: In this, he says, my Father is glorified. Whoever is moved by this argument must be prepared by zeal for God, since nothing moves a man except an argument drawn from his glory. Hence it matters much how we are prepared to hear the Word of God. For the mind must be prepared in many ways if we wish to hear with profit. Note here above all the outstanding effect of good works, namely the glorifying of God, than which nothing is more important or more to be desired, and which ought to be the end of all our actions. The Papists think that good works are useful for nothing unless they justify the doer and make him fervent. To answer this, we must hold that this saying, "Bear much fruit," is taken from the branches mentioned above: just as the branches grafted onto the vine bear fruit, so we, grafted as it were into Christ, produce as it were fruit and grapes. Now, having reached the second part of the comparison, let us explain the whole matter by the comparison with the branches.

units.la: Secunda causa pitis pars, discipulos ad producendum fructus sua vnione cum Christo gnos admonens.
units.tr: Second reason. Admonishing the disciples to produce fruit from their union with Christ.

units.la: Ratio. Pater cælestis in eo glorificatur.
units.tr: Reason. The heavenly Father is glorified in this.

units.la: Cōtrà, Superstitiosi seipsos nō Deum glorificare volunt. comparatione palmitum exponamus totam hanc rem. Fructus palmitis & vuæ,non suppeditant quidem vitam palmiti:Neque ideo viuit palmes,quia fructum fert,sed contra fructum fert quia viuit, & vita ipsa in palmite producit fructum. Neque tamen propterea nullus est visus fructus palmitum:Inseruit enim in primis recreandis & exhilarandis hominibus. Ita planè res habet in nobis, qui bona opera producimus. Bona opera nostra non sunt causæ vel iustitiæ,vel vitæ nostræ: Neque ideo iustificamur aut viuimus,quia bona operamur: sed ideo bene operamur, quia iam iustificati & seruati sumus. Neque tamen putandum est propterea nullum esse visum bonorum operum. Nam, vt hoc præteream,iis confirmari electionem & vocationem,iustitiam & vitam nostram in Christo acceptam, vt hoc, inquam,prætereā, quis illud non intelligit,bona opera & hominum ædificationi& Deiglorię inseruire?qui visus est longè maximus. Vxores subiectæ sint viris suis, vt etiam si qui non obediunt sermoni per vxorum conuersationem absque sermone lucrifiant. Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, vt videntes bona opera vestra glorificent Deum qui est in cælis. Agnoscentes nimirum,omnia bona opera ex illo tanquam fonte dimanare. Et eritis mei. Hoc alterum argumentum est, quo suadet bona opera,ab ipsorum commodo:Eritis,inquit, mei discipuli. Hoc est, idé quod dixit supra cap.13.Ex hoc omnes cognoscent vos esse discipulos meos,si charitatem habueritis aliù in alios.Nota igitur disciplinam Christi esse,vt bene agamus, bene operemur, omnémque doctrinam in schola Christi traditam siue fidei sit, siue resipiscentiæ, huc pertinere, vt homines recte sanctéque viuant in præsenti seculo. Quamobrem illi demum proficiunt in schola Christi, qui bene viuunt, qui autem optimè viuunt, optimè proficiunt: Qui nihil boni in vita agunt, nihil proficiunt: Qui mala omnia perpetrant, quid illis cum Christo?
units.tr: On the contrary. Superstitious people wish to glorify themselves, not God. The fruit of the branch and of the grape does not indeed supply life to the branch. Nor does the branch live because it bears fruit; rather it bears fruit because it lives, and life itself produces fruit in the branch. Nor, however, is the fruit of the branches therefore without visible value: it serves above all to refresh and gladden men. So it stands plainly with us who produce good works. Our good works are not causes either of our righteousness or of our life; nor are we justified or made alive because we do good works, but we do good works because we are already justified and saved. Nor, however, should it be thought that good works have no visible effect. For, to pass over this, that election and calling, our righteousness and life accepted in Christ, are confirmed by them, who does not understand that good works serve the edification of men and the glory of God, which is by far the greatest visible effect? Let wives be subject to their husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives. So let your light shine before men, that seeing your good works they may glorify God who is in heaven. Acknowledging, of course, that all good works flow from him as from a fountain. And you will be my disciples. This is the second argument, by which he urges good works from their own advantage: You will be, he says, my disciples. This is the same as what he said above, in chapter 13: By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love one for another. Note therefore that the discipline of Christ is this: that we act well and do good, and that all doctrine taught in the school of Christ, whether of faith or of repentance, aims at this, that men live uprightly and holily in the present age. Therefore those alone make progress in the school of Christ who live well; those who live best make the best progress; those who do nothing good in life make no progress; those who commit all manner of evil, what have they to do with Christ?

units.la: Pront dilexit.Deinceps hortatur ad fundamenta bonorum operum,charitatem in Deum, & dilectionem hominum. Ex his enim omnia bona opera quæ in vita fiūt promanant. Quod igitur ad charitatem erga Deum ait, Manete in illa mea charitate:hoc est,Perseuerate me diligere re. Hęc enim phrasis est vsitata huic Apostolo, Qui manet, inquit, in charitate, in Deo manet: Hoc est, qui diligit, in Deo manet. Argumentum est à Christi ipsius dilectione, qua illos prosequutus est, Ego, inquit, dilexi vos; Ergo, &c. Daclaratur Christi dilectio cōparatione simili. Sicut Pater dilexit me, ita ego dilexi vos, Ergo, &c. Significat non vulgarem dilectionem suam erga ipsos, neque plane talem, qualis esse solet dilectio à creatura promanās, sed tale esse qualis est creatoris ipsius & Dei amor. Nota igitur Christum non tantum nos priorem dilexisse,
units.tr: As the Father has loved. Next he exhorts them to the foundations of good works: love of God and love of men. For from these all the good works done in life flow forth. Therefore what he says about love towards God, Abide in that my love, means: persevere in loving me. For this is a common expression with this Apostle: He who abides, he says, in love, abides in God: that is, he who loves abides in God. The argument is drawn from Christ's own love, by which he has cherished them: I, he says, have loved you; therefore, etc. Christ's love is set forth by a similar comparison: As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you. Therefore, etc. It signifies that his love towards them is not an ordinary love, nor plainly such as usually flows from a creature, but is such as is the love of the Creator himself and of God. Note therefore that Christ has not only loved us first,

units.la: vt est, Nos diligimus eum, quia ipse dilexit nos prior, &c. Sed etiam talem esse eius erga nos amorem, qualis est ille Dei amor, hoc est infinitum & incomprehensibilem: cuius longitudinem, latitudinem, profunditatem & altitudinem nemo potest comprehendere, & qui superat omnem cognitionem. Nosipsi sentimus effundi eum in corda nostra copiosa copia per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis: sed totum semel comprehendere in hac vita non possumus: In altera vero vita stupebimus ad admirabilem illam dilectionem. Nequeuamen etiam tum animus creaturae etiam glorificatae poterit infinitam illam totam comprehendere, quae in Deo est. Salte id scimus quòd illa charitate toti implebimur, cum Deus erit omnia in omnibus. Si mandata mea. Quomodo fieri possit vt maneant in charitate ipsius: siue ipsum diligant, ostendit ex effecto charitatis. q. d. hoc argumento declarabitis vos me diligere, si obseruaueritis mandata mea. Nam dilectio Christi quae in corde est, otiosa esse non potest, quin oportet eam se exerere in obedientia & obseruantia mandatorum ipsius, adeo vt qui nihil boni agunt in vita, & tamen iactitant dilectionem Christi, mentiantur. Sed de hac re satis dictum est, cap. 14. Tantum hoc nūc addimus, ex hoc loco conspici obedientię & bonorum operum principia ac fundamenta quędam. Primum est, dilectio qua Christum amplectimur: secundum est dilectio, qua Christus nos prior amplectitur. Quamobrem in obedientia & bonis operibus alicuius hominis, offerunt se inspicienda nobis hæc duo fundamenta, neque colligendum est ex hac obedientia hominem tantum diligere Christum, sed etiam ipsum hominem. minem à Christo diligi; quod quidem fundamentum est longè fortissimum. Re vera autem diligit eum Deus, cuius ministerio & obedientia velit uti, atque is beneficij loco reputet illud, quòd Deus ipsum in ministerio suo collocarit. Unde Paulus gratias agit Deo in Christo quod ipsum fidelem duxerit, utque ipsum in ministerio suo collocarit.
units.tr: as it is written, We love him, because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). But his love toward us is also of the same kind as God's love, that is, infinite and incomprehensible, whose length, breadth, depth and height no one can comprehend, and which surpasses all knowledge. We ourselves feel it poured out into our hearts in abundant measure through the Spirit Holy, who has been given to us; but we cannot grasp it all at once in this life. In the other life we shall stand amazed at that wonderful love. Yet even then the mind of a creature, even a glorified one, will not be able to comprehend that whole infinity which is in God. At least we know that we shall be filled entirely with that love, when God will be all in all. If my commandments: he shows how they can remain in his love, or love him, from the effect of love. As if he said: by this argument you will show that you love me, if you keep my commandments. For the love of Christ that is in the heart cannot be idle; it must of necessity show itself in obedience and observance of his commandments, so that those who do nothing good in life, yet boast of Christ's love, are liars. But enough has been said on this matter, in chapter 14. We add only this now: from this passage can be seen certain principles and foundations of obedience and good works. The first is the love by which we embrace Christ; the second is the love by which Christ embraces us first. Therefore, in the obedience and good works of any man, these two foundations present themselves for us to examine, and from this obedience we should not conclude only that the man loves Christ, but also that the man is loved by Christ, which foundation is by far the strongest. In truth God loves the man whose ministry and obedience he wishes to use, and that man counts it a benefit that God has placed him in his ministry. Hence Paul gives thanks to God in Christ that he counted him faithful and placed him in his ministry.

units.la: Sicut & ego. Suum exemplum proponit iis, ad hoc ut ostendant seipsum diligere ex observatione mandatorum. Nam & ipse Dominus dilectionem erga patrem suum hoc modo declarauit ac manifestam fecit. Christus exemplar esto summæ dilectionis & obedientiæ, qui cum esset in forma Dei, nec duxit rapinam æquale esse cum Deo, tamen exinaniuit se, accepta serui forma, & obediens factus est Patri ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Imò non tantùm æquali subiecit se, sed & inferioribus se. Lauit discipulorum pedes, ut vidimus superius cap.13. & non indulsit sibi, sed aliis. Rom.15.3. Hoc Christi dilectionis & obedientiæ exemplum vsque adeo necessarium, ut nisi ipsum habeamus ante oculos, non possimus vel diligere, vel obedire. Christi enim obedientia est fidei in eu, quę fingit formatq; animos nostros ad veram obedientiam. Habemus itaq; in Christi obedientia non vnum tantùm commodum, sed plura. Nam præterquam quòd in eius obedientia iustificemur & seruemur, ipsa nobis in imitationem quantum fieri potest transenda est. Hoc autem non præterereundū diximus, quod non tantùm hoc loco, sed & aliis, suum exemplum proponat, & doctrinam vel exhortationem suam suo loco commendat. Tum enim efficax est doctrina, cùm vita docentis eam confirmat.
units.tr: As I also have. He sets forth his own example to them, so that they may show that they love him by keeping his commandments. For the Lord himself declared and made manifest his love toward his Father in this way. Christ is the example of supreme love and obedience, who, though he was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, yet emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross. Indeed he subjected himself not only to his equal but also to his inferiors. He washed the disciples' feet, as we saw above in chapter 13, and did not please himself but others (Rom. 15.3). This example of Christ's love and obedience is so necessary that unless we keep it before our eyes we can neither love nor obey. For Christ's obedience is faith in him, which shapes and forms our minds to true obedience. In Christ's obedience we therefore have not one advantage only but many. For besides being justified and preserved by his obedience, we must also imitate it as far as we can. We must not pass over this point, that he sets forth his own example not only in this place but elsewhere too, and commends his teaching or exhortation in its place by his own life. For teaching is effective when the life of the teacher confirms it.

units.la: Hæc loquutus sum. Concludit superiores omnes exhortationes, & eas commendat in genere ex fine suo: quasi diceret, Omnes istæ ineæ exhortationes vobis sunt vtui, traduntque ad vestrum gaudium. Christi, ut sic loquar, finis est gaudium: initium autem eius, fateor, est dolor resipiscentiæ. Nam per resipiscentiam accessus est ad ipsum: sed finis eius est gaudiū. Vbi enim fruemur illo aspectu longe iucundissimo, tum quidem gaudebimus supra modum: Ita omnes eius sermones spectant ad gaudium; nominatim autem huiusmodi, qui sunt de communione cū eo,de bonis operibus, de dilectione ipsius. Nam in his rebus omnibus materia est gaudij, vt quæ bonam efficiunt conscientiam,ex qua lætitia est De cō-munione illa cum Patre & filio,postquam dixisset Iohānes, subiecit, Hæc scripsi vobis, vt gaudium vestrum plenum sit. Notandum, quòd gaudium hoc primùm vocet suū, deinde quòd vocet ipsorum. Nam Christi gaudium primum est, quantum ab ipso est: deinde nostrum est, quantum ad nos pertinet,nobisque datur.Ex quo intelligi potest, quodnam sit gaudium Christiani hominis. Est autem participatio illius gaudij ineffabilis, quod in ipso Deo est. Deus natura ipsa totus gaudium est. Nos autem consortes sumus diuinæ naturæ. Philosophi illi veteres multum diúque disceptarunt de felicitate humana. Ex his quidam in voluptate & gaudio felicitate collocarunt. In genere quidem non erraru̇nt, cum felicitas hominis spirituale sit gaudium, quale est felicitas Dei,quod tum demum plenum erit,cum omnes lachrymæ abstergentur ab oculis nostris, & Deus erit omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: These things I have spoken. He concludes all the preceding exhortations and commends them in general from their end, as if to say: all these exhortations of mine are useful to you and lead to your joy. The end of Christ, so to speak, is joy; its beginning, I admit, is the sorrow of repentance. For through repentance there is access to him, but its end is joy. When we enjoy that most delightful sight, then indeed we shall rejoice beyond measure. Thus all his words look toward joy, especially those of this kind which concern communion with him, good works, and love of him. For in all these things there is matter for joy, since they make a good conscience, and from a good conscience comes gladness. Concerning that communion with the Father and the Son, after saying this John added, These things I have written to you, so that your joy may be full. It should be noted that he first calls this joy his, and then that he calls it theirs. For Christ's joy is his first, insofar as it comes from him; then it is ours, insofar as it pertains to us and is given to us. From this it can be understood what the joy of a Christian man is. It is a participation in that ineffable joy which is in God himself. God by his very nature is wholly joy, and we are partakers of the divine nature. Those ancient philosophers disputed long and much about human happiness. Some of them placed happiness in pleasure and joy. In general they were not wrong, since human happiness is a spiritual joy, such as the happiness of God is, which will be full only when all tears are wiped from our eyes and God will be all in all.

units.la: 12 Hoc est mandatum illud meum, vt diligatis alij alios,prout dilexi vos.
units.tr: 12 This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you.

units.la: 13 Maiorem charitatem nullus habet, quàm istam,vt quispiam animam suam deponat pro amicis suis.
units.tr: 13 Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.

units.la: 14 Vos amici mei eritis, si feceritis quæcunque ego mando vobis.
units.tr: 14 You are my friends, if you do whatever I command you.

units.la: DIxit supra, Si mandata mea seruaueritis;nunc quod sit illud mandatum,ipse ostendit.Eitquehoc secundum fundamentum bonorum operum,quæ supra commendauit,dilexio nempe proximi. Superius autem fuit dilectio Dei. Nota igitur: dilectio Dei exploratur obseruatione mandati ipsius, vt supra. Mandatum autem, quo exploratur dilectio Christi & Dei, nunc videmus esse non tam mandatum primæ quàm secundæ legis tabulæ. Nam tabulam secundam Deus voluit esse quasi Lydium lapidem, quo exploretur vera obedientia præceptorum primæ tabulæ, & charitas illa quæ in prima legis legis tabula præcipitur: Adeo vt si quis non dilexerit proximum suum iuxta secundam tabulam, certè is non diligat Deum iuxta primam legis tabulam. Contráque, qui dilexerit proximum suum iuxta secundam legis tabulam, is verè diligat Deum suum iuxta primam. Hoc autem notandum, quanto amore prosequatur Christus membra sua, cum velit charitatem illam, quam nos erga ipsum profitemur in membra sua transferri, vt ipsis prosit. Dixit enim supra hac re ostendi quòd ipsum diligant, si obseruauerint mandata ipsius: deinde nunc mandatum ipsius profert in medium, nempe dilectionem proximi, ac si amandaret eum, qui profiteatur se diligere Dominum ad diligendum membra ipsius quæ in terris agunt. Neque verò hoc dico, quasi, Christus nolit a nobis ipsum diligi: verum illud intelligo, Christum delectari plurimùm nostro erga ipsum amore: velle tamen eum vt ille amor reipsa ostendatur in amando proximum & benefaciendo ipsi. Nam nihil opus habet Dominus beneficiis nostris, vt qui in se sit beatissimus & omni sufficiens. Opus autem habent ipsius membra quæ in terris sunt & maxima quæque ex iis indigent ope minimorum abie&tissimorûmque quorumque. hoc professus est Dauid, Bonum, inquit, meum nihil ad te, sanctis qui in terra sunt in quibus est tota oblectatio mea, subaudi, me coserua. Notandum quod requirat amorem mutuum: nam non vniuntur inter se nisi mutuo amore homines, neq; membra illa Christi continentur in vno illo corpore, nisi vicissim sese diligant. Qui enim diligitur, neque ipse vicissim diligit, is non adhæret corpori. Adhæremus enim corpori magis beneficio nostræ ipsorum dilectionis, quàm aliorum qui nos diligunt. Prout dilexi. Suo exemplo commendat amorem proximi, vt supra amorem erga Deum: vt illud conspiciatur verum esse, nempe Christum exemplum esse veræ dilectionis cuiuscunque, &, quod ad amorem proximi attinet, tam necessarium esse Christi exemplum, vt, nisi ipsi sentiamus Christum diligere, nunquam nos proximum diligere possimus: dilectio enim nostra, siue erga Deum sit, siue erga hominem, resultat ex Christi erga nos charitate, eiúsque sensu, quo perfunduntur corda nostra. Estque quasi repercussio
units.tr: He said above, "If you keep my commandments"; now he shows what that commandment is. This is the second foundation of good works, which he commended above, namely love of neighbour; above was love of God. Note, then: love of God is tested by keeping his commandment, as above. The commandment by which the love of Christ and of God is tested is now seen to be not so much the commandment of the first table of the law as of the second. For God willed the second table to be, as it were, a touchstone by which true obedience to the precepts of the first table is tested, and that love which is enjoined in the first table of the law is tested. So that if anyone has not loved his neighbour according to the second table, he certainly does not love God according to the first. On the contrary, whoever has truly loved his neighbour according to the second table of the law truly loves God according to the first. It should be noted, however, with how great love Christ embraces his members, since he wishes the love we profess toward him to be transferred to his members, so that it may profit them. For he said above that it will be shown in this matter that they love him, if they keep his commandments; then he now brings forward his commandment, namely love of neighbour, as if he were commanding the one who professes to love the Lord to love the members of him who are working on earth. I do not say this as if Christ did not want to be loved by us; rather I understand this: that Christ delights greatly in our love toward him, yet wills that this love be shown in fact by loving the neighbour and doing him good. For the Lord has no need of our benefits, being in himself most blessed and sufficient for all. But his members who are on earth have need, and the greatest of them need the help of the least and most abject of all. David professed this: "My good is nothing to you; to the saints who are on earth, in whom is all my delight," supply, "preserve me." It should be noted that he requires mutual love, for men are not united among themselves except by mutual love, nor are those members of Christ held together in that one body unless they in turn love one another. For one who is loved and does not in turn love does not cling to the body. We cling to the body more by the benefit of our own love than by that of others who love us. As I have loved. By his example he commends love of neighbour, as above he commended love of God, so that this is seen to be true: Christ is the example of true love of any kind, and, as far as love of neighbour is concerned, Christ's example is so necessary that unless we ourselves feel that Christ loves us, we can never love our neighbour. For our love, whether toward God or toward man, arises from Christ's love toward us and from the sense of it, with which our hearts are suffused. And it is, as it were, a reflection

units.la: Ps. 16. 2. 3. quaedam radiorum amoris ipsius, quibus nostra corda verberantur.
units.tr: Ps. 16. 2. 3. certain rays of his love, by which our hearts are struck.

units.la: Maiorem hac. Magnitudinem dilectionis suae erga ipsos edocet comparatione illius amoris, qui inter homines maximus esse potest. Maiorem hac charitatem nemo habet, ut quis animam suam ponat pro amicis suis: At ego animam meam pro vobis pono: Ergo maior charitas haberi no potest. Nota igitur quod sit indicium charitatis maximae, nempe, si quis pro fratre suo ponat animam suam. Fateor equidem, magna charitas est, cum quis pro amico ponit animam. Vix, inquit Paulus, pro bono quis moriatur. At haec charitas longe maior est qua quis pro inimico ponit animam suam, neque eiusmodi amor inter homines reperitur. Christus autem pro inimicis suis mortuus est. Ergo singulari quodam amore, cuius exemplum nullum extat inter homines, nos prosecutus est. Verum facile est verbo, singulare dicere & mirificum; sed in eo difficultas est tota, ut animo singularem & infinitum comprehendamus, vel, sicut dicit Paulus, ut assequamur cum omnibus sanctis, quae sit eius longitudo, latitudo, sublimitas & profunditas, &c. Cognoscitur autem & percipitur non alia re, quam fiducia illa, quod mortuus sit Christus pro vnoquoque nostrum. Necesse est enim corda nostra perfundantur prius eius sanguine, hoc est, sentiamus per sanguinem eius remissa esse peccata nostra, quam charitas eius effundatur in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum. Vbi autem imbibit sanguinem eius cor nostrum, simul etiam imbibit charitatem, nosque vicissim eum diligimus accensi iam sensu charitatis eius. Atque ita inseparabili vinculo charitatis mutuae cum eo coniungimur ac gloriamur cum Apostolo, Quis nos separabit a charitate Dei? V os amici mei. Occupatio, quasi dixissent discipuli, cum tantopere diligas amicos, annon amici sumus, ut ad nos pertineat dilectio tua? Respondet amicos esse, sed quadam lege atque conditione, nempe si seruauerint omnia mandata eius: Nos exemplo discipulorum, si quando audimus huiusmodi sententias, ut est haec de charitate Christi qua amicos prosequitur, debemus continuo in nosipsos descendere & explorare, in amici eius simus. Quod non alia
units.tr: Greater than this. He shows the greatness of his love for them by comparison with the greatest love that can exist among human beings: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends" (John 15:13). "But I lay down my life for you." Therefore no greater love can be had. Note, then, what is the sign of the greatest love: that someone lay down his life for his brother. I grant indeed that it is great love when someone lays down his life for a friend. Paul says: "Scarcely will anyone die for a good man" (Rom. 5:7). But a love by which someone lays down his life for an enemy is far greater, and such love is not found among human beings. Yet Christ died for his enemies. Therefore he has embraced us with a unique love, of which there is no example among human beings. It is easy to say "unique" and "wonderful" in words, but the whole difficulty lies in grasping in our minds that love which is unique and infinite, or, as Paul says, in being able to comprehend with all the saints what is its length, breadth, height and depth (Eph. 3:18). It is known and perceived by nothing other than that confidence that Christ died for each one of us. For our hearts must first be bathed in his blood, that is, we must feel that our sins have been forgiven through his blood, before his love is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5:5). Where our heart has drunk in his blood, it also at once drinks in his love, and we in turn love him, now kindled by the sense of his love. And so we are joined to him by the inseparable bond of mutual love, and we glory with the Apostle: "Who shall separate us from the love of God?" (Rom. 8:35, 38). "You are my friends." It is as if the disciples had objected: "Since you love your friends so much, are we not your friends, so that your love applies to us?" He answers that they are friends, but on a certain law and condition, namely if they keep all his commandments. When we hear such sayings as this one about the love of Christ, with which he embraces his friends, let us, following the example of the disciples, examine ourselves at once and see whether we are among his friends. We shall know this better by no other means than by feeling our minds inclined to his obedience. For obedience produces the awareness that we persevere in covenant and friendship with God. We should not conclude from this passage that Christ dies for us because we are his friends and have loved him first; rather, on the contrary, because he died for us, we love him and become his friends. But it is necessary that this effect of his death be realised in us in this life; otherwise his death does not truly pertain to us. Christ therefore dies for friends, and indeed not for those who were friends before his death. For it is necessary that we become his friends at least by the power of his death; he dies for friends who are made friends through his death and by the power of his death.

units.la: Rom.5.7. Eph.3.18.19. Rom.5.5. Rom.8.34.38. alia ratione cognoscemus melius, quàm si sentiamus animos nostros pronos ad eius obedientiam: Nam obedientia gignit conscientiam, quòd perstemus in foedere & amicitia cum Deo. Non est colligendum ex hoc loco, quòd ideo Christus moriatur pro nobis, quia nos eius amici sumus,priorésque nos eum diligamus, cùm è contrà,quia is pro nobis mortuus est, nos eum diligamus, eiúsque amici efficiamur. Sed id necessarium est, vt sit hoc effectum mortis eius in nobis in hac vita: secus profectò non ad nos pertinet mors eius. Moritur ergo Christus pro amicis, & iis quidem non ante ipsius mortem amicis. Nam necesse est saltem vi mortis eius amici illi fiamus: sed pro amicis,qui per mortem & virtute mortis ipsius amici reddcuntur.
units.tr: Rom. 5:7. Eph. 3:18, 19. Rom. 5:5. Rom. 8:34, 38. We shall know this better by no other means than if we feel our minds inclined to his obedience. For obedience gives rise to the conscience that we persevere in covenant and friendship with God. It should not be gathered from this passage that Christ dies for us because we are his friends, and that we love him first; rather, on the contrary, because he died for us, we love him and become his friends. But it is necessary that this effect of his death be realised in us in this life; otherwise his death does not truly pertain to us. Christ therefore dies for friends, and indeed not for those who were friends before his death. For it is necessary that we become his friends at least by the power of his death; he dies for friends who are made friends through his death and by the power of his death.

units.la: 15 Non amplius dicam vos seruos, quia seruus nescit quid faciat Dominus ipsius; vos autem dixi amicos, quia omnia quæ audiui à Patre meo, nota feci vobis.
units.tr: 15 I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you all that I heard from my Father.

units.la: 16 Non vos me elegistis, sed ego elegi vos, & constitui vos vt abeuntes fructum feratis, & fructus vester maneat: vt quicquid petieritis à Patre in nomine meo, det vobis.
