units.tr: 16 You did not choose me, but I chose you, and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain, so that whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he may give you.

units.la: 17 Hæc mando vobis, vt diligatis alij alios.
units.tr: 17 These things I command you, that you love one another.

units.la: OCcupatio: At serui dicendi sumus potius quàm amici. Respondet, Non amplius dicam vos seruos; Erant quidem serui Apostoli, non creatione tantum, quomodò creatura quæcunque serua est creatori suo, sed etiam redemptione. Nam ideo Christus & mortuus est, & resurrexit ac revixit, vt viuis & mortuis dominaretur. Ideo Paulus profitetur se postea non sibi victurū, sed Christo,qui pro eo mortuus est & resurrexit. Neque tantùm iure redemptionis serui erant Apostoli, sed etiā vocationis:nam legatus seruus est eius à quo legatur. Erant itaque Apostoli serui quidem, sed erant præterea amici. Nam qui seruus est iure redemptionis, is quoque amicus est Christo necessario, & tanquam amicus stat & audit vocem sponsi,ac gaudio gaudet propter vocem eius:imò fråter est Christi,& Spiritum accepit adoptionis, per quem clamat, abba, Pater.Cur igitur, inquies, negat se dicturum eos seruos? Respondeo hoc dictum esse ex communi sorte seruorum, prout in more tum fuit. Nam serui vulgò erant mancipia, quæ non habebantur amicorum loco,neque cum iis consilia sua communicabant domini, sed metu supplicij in officio continebantur. Habet quidem Christus,fateor, seruos huiusmodi quàm plurimos. Nam in magna domo nõ sunt tantum vasa aurea & argentea,sed lignea & testacea, &c alia quidem ad decus, alia verò ad dedecus. Huius generis serui,serui sunt quidem iure creationis,sed non redemptionis, quare neque amici, multò minus fratres sunt Christi.Neque enim acceperunt Spiritum adoptionis,sed Spiritũ seruitutis ad metum: sunt enim sub perpetuo metu, quia malè sunt sibi conscij. Seruiunt quidē Deo ac Christo, sed non legi ipsius expressæ, ac voluntati in verbo reuelatæ: verum decreto Dei ac voluntati ipsius non reuelatæ seruiunt necessario. Nihil enim facere possunt, nisi quod manus Dei & consilium eius decreuerunt fieri. Ergo hoc modo negat Dominus discipulos suos seruos sibi esse, aut numerados à se in hoc seruorum numero.Videndũ autē nobis est, qualia simus vasa,& in quo genere seruorum in domo Christi. Apostolus autem eo loco, vbi vasorum discrimē fecit,signũ dedit quo dignoscamus qualia simus vasa. Si quis,inquit,seipsum ab his,nēpe mundi inquinamentis,expurgarit, erit vas ad decus sanctificatum & accommodū vsibus Dei,&c.Ergo non alia re dignoscitur melius quàm sanctificatione,quod quidem effectum est necessarium electionis & iustificationis. Nota ex eo quod dicit, Omnia quæ audiui, Christum qui venit è sinu Patris totum Dei consilium de salute humana cum discipulis suis communicasse: quod Apostoli postea mundo totum annuntiarunt. Nã post glorificationem Domini Spiritus sanctus docebat eos omnia,& suggessit eis omnia ea quæ dixit ipse Dominus, quomodo vnà cum iis in terra ageret, supra 14. 26.id quod profitetur Paulus,Non enim subterfugi, inquit, quominus annuntiarem vobis omne Dei consilium.Sed quęstio est de scriptis Apostolorum:Annon omnia quæ à Christa
units.tr: An objection: but we are called servants rather than friends. He answers, "I will no longer call you servants." The Apostles were indeed servants, not only by creation, as every creature is a servant to its creator, but also by redemption. For Christ died, rose and came to life again so that he might be Lord of both the living and the dead. Therefore Paul declares that afterwards he would live not for himself but for Christ, who died and rose for him. The Apostles were servants not only by the right of redemption but also by the right of calling, for an envoy is the servant of the one who sends him. So the Apostles were indeed servants, but they were also friends. For one who is a servant by right of redemption is necessarily also a friend of Christ; and as a friend he stands and hears the voice of the bridegroom, and rejoices with joy at his voice. Indeed he is a brother of Christ, and has received the Spirit of adoption, by whom he cries, "Abba, Father." Why, you will ask, does he deny that he will call them servants? I answer that this is said in accordance with the common lot of servants, as was the custom at that time. For servants were generally slaves, who were not regarded as friends, and whose masters did not share their plans with them, but kept them in duty through fear of punishment. Christ indeed has, I grant, very many servants of this kind. For in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware, some for honour and others for dishonour. Servants of this kind are indeed servants by the right of creation, but not of redemption; therefore they are not friends, much less brothers of Christ. For they have not received the Spirit of adoption, but the spirit of servitude leading to fear; for they live under constant fear, because they are conscious of doing wrong. Indeed they serve God and Christ, but not by the expressed law of Christ nor by the will revealed in the Word; rather they necessarily serve the decree of God and his unrevealed will. For they can do nothing except what the hand and counsel of God have decreed should be done. In this way, therefore, the Lord denies that his disciples are servants to him, or counted by him in this number of servants. We must consider what kind of vessels we are, and to which class of servants in the house of Christ we belong. Now the Apostle, at the place where he distinguishes between vessels, gave a sign by which we may recognise what kind of vessels we are: "If anyone," he says, "cleanses himself from these things, that is, from the defilements of the world, he will be a vessel for honour, sanctified and fit for the uses of God" (2 Tim. 2:21). Therefore we are known best by nothing other than sanctification, which is indeed the necessary effect of election and justification. Note from the words "all that I heard" that Christ, who came from the bosom of the Father, communicated the whole counsel of God concerning human salvation to his disciples, which the Apostles afterwards proclaimed to the whole world. For after the glorification of the Lord, the Holy Spirit taught them all things and brought to their remembrance all the things that the Lord himself had said while he lived with them on earth (John 14:26). Paul professes this: "For I did not shrink," he says, "from declaring to you the whole counsel of God" (Acts 20:27). But the question concerns the writings of the Apostles: are not all the things that were first announced by Christ by the living voice, and afterwards preached by the Apostles, also committed to writing?

units.la: Act.20.27 (catchword noted in the text above) sto primùm annuntiata sunt viua voce, deinde ab Apostolis prædicata, annon omnia illa literis commendata sunt? Respondeo, omnia reipsa, & quod ad rem ipsam, & materiam, omnia, inquam, sunt scripta, licet non totidem verbis amplificata: Et affirmamus Christum ipsum, si præsens adesset, non plura dicturū, quòd ad rem ipsam, neque quicquam iis quæ scripta sunt, vel additurum, vel detracturum, vel immutaturum: Non vos me elegistis. Hoc loco constituit vt abeant & doceant gentes omnes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris, filij & Spiritus sancti. Matth.28.19. Quod autem iure suo posset iis mandare, præfatur his verbis, Non vos me elegistis. q.d. Vocatio vestra a me est tota, qui prævenerim vos nihil tale cogitantes. Ergo iure meo constitui vt abeuntes, &c. Quòd Apostolorum vocatio ad id muneris à Christo destinata fuerit, nihil opus est dicere. Nam illud conspicitur ex historia ipsa, vt historia vocationis Petri, vocationis Matthæi, vocationis Pauli, qui & ipse id serio profitetur atq; agnoscit: Postquam, inquit, visum est Deo (qui me separauit ab utero matris, & ex gratia sua vocauit, ) revelare filium suum in me, &c. Ecce quot verbis quàm efficacibus agnoscat vocationem suam à Deo esse. Primùm quidem eam tribuit & Dei beneplacito: deinde electioni Dei ac separationi quæ fuit iam inde ab utero matris, adeóque ab æterno. Tertiò gratiæ Dei. Sed vt hæc prætereiam, videmus hoc loco, quo fine fiat, vt Deus omnes in omni vocatione prævenat gratia sua, nempe eo fine vt ius suum in mandando atque in ordinando obtineat, & vt homines obediant Deo eiusque mandato pareant. Quòd si opinio sit vocationis nostræ aliquam partem in nobis ipsis esse, in nobis esse operahæc quæ vocantur Præparationis, in nobis esse liberi arbitrij assensum, id quod docent aduersarij, profecto illa opinione & detrahitur aliquid Deo, ipsiusque in nos iuri, & nos inflamur ita, vt negemus Deo simplicem obedientiam, cogitantes vocationem nostram non omni ex parte ab eo esse, sed aliqua tantum ex parte. Neque enim est simplex obedientia & agnitio iuris in nos Dei, priusquam nihil in nobis esse boni per naturam agnoscamus. Vt abeuntes fructum. Constituit, vt abeuntes fructum adferant: neque id modo, sed vt fructus ipsorum maneat: hoc est, vt perseuerent in fructu adferendo; neque enim satis est bene incepisse, nisi perseueremus ad finem vsque. Palmites ad quos hic allusio est, habent suam tempestatem, qua fructum adferant: At vero membra in Christum insita nullum habent sibi praescriptum certum tempus, non aestatem, non hyemem, non ver, non autumnum, peraeque omni tempestate fructificare oportet. Imprimis vero ministri verbi ad id faciendum tenentur. Praedica sermone, insta opportune, importune, argue, obiurga, exhortare, &c. Bene agitur cum ea in hac vita, qui decernit apud animam suam non conquiescendum, non cessandum a bene agendo in vocatione sua, expectans requiem & sabbatismum suum in caelis futurum, vbi certo requiescet a laboribus suis. Paulus ad illam requiem perpetuo aspirauit, ideoque se fatigauit currendo in stadio huius vitae. Non respicio, inquit, ad ea quae a tergo sunt, sed feror versus metam.
units.tr: Act. 20. 27 (catchword noted in the text above). I answer that all things have been written, both as to the thing itself and as to its substance; all things, I say, are written, although not in the same number of words and expanded. And we affirm that Christ himself, if he were present, would say no more as to the substance, nor would he add to, take away from, or change anything in what has been written. You did not choose me. Here he appoints them to go and teach all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit (Matt. 28. 19). But because he could command them by his own right, he prefaces it with these words: You did not choose me. That is to say: your calling is wholly from me, since I anticipated you when you were thinking of nothing of the kind. Therefore by my right I appointed you to go, and so on. That the calling of the Apostles to this office was determined by Christ needs no argument. For this is clear from the history itself, as in the history of the calling of Peter, the calling of Matthew, the calling of Paul, who himself also seriously professes and acknowledges it: "When it pleased God," he says, "who set me apart from my mother's womb and called me by his grace, to reveal his Son in me, etc." (Gal. 1:15, 16). See with how many and how effective words he acknowledges that his calling is from God: first, he ascribes it to the good pleasure of God; then to the election and separation of God, which was from his mother's womb, and so from eternity; thirdly, to the grace of God. But, to pass over these points, we see here for what end God by his grace anticipates everyone in every calling, namely that he may obtain his right in commanding and ordaining, and that human beings may obey God and submit to his command. But if it is thought that some part of our calling lies in ourselves, that works called preparatory are in us, that the assent of free will is in us, as our opponents teach, then indeed something is taken from God by that opinion, and his right over us is diminished; and we are so inflamed that we deny to God simple obedience, thinking that our calling is not wholly from him but only partly. For there is no simple obedience and acknowledgement of God's right over us before we acknowledge that nothing good is in us by nature. That you should go and bear fruit. He has appointed that they should go and bear fruit, and not only that, but that their fruit should remain; that is, that they should persevere in bearing fruit. For it is not enough to have begun well, unless we persevere to the end. The branches to which this is an allusion have their own season in which they bear fruit; but the members grafted into Christ have no fixed time prescribed for them, not summer, not winter, not spring, not autumn, but they ought to bear fruit equally in every season. Above all, the ministers of the Word are bound to do this: "Preach the word, be urgent in season and out of season, reprove, rebuke, exhort" (2 Tim. 4:2). It goes well for the one who resolves in his soul not to rest or to cease from doing good in his calling, waiting for his rest and sabbath to come in heaven, where he will certainly rest from his labours. Paul always aspired to that rest, and therefore wearied himself running in the race of this life: "I do not look back," he says, "to the things that are behind, but I press on towards the goal" (Phil. 3:13, 14).

units.la: Vt quicquid petieritis. Alterum argumentum ordinationis suae, ex eo quod audiuntur eorum preces factae in Christi nomine. Obscure autem hoc loco occurrit objectioni: Obiici enim potuit multa impedimenta esse quominus fructum ferant, tantum abest, vt perseverent in fructu ferendo. Respondet, Quicquid petieritis in nomine meo, &c. q. d. Credite primum in me, hoc enim est precum fundamentum vnicum, deinde in nomine meo offerte preces vestras. Ij soli preces suas offerunt Deo in Christi nomine, qui in Christum credunt. Nota igitur, non nisi precibus ad Deum obtineri facultatem illam bene agendi in praesenti vita. Initium bene agendi precibus obtinetur, perseuerantia quoque in bene agendo precibus obtinetur. Paulus dum hortatur Ephesios vt sint, hoc est, perseuerent in lucta illa spirituali, commendat iis preces: Semper, inquit, precantes omni prece ac supplicatione. Gratia enim omnis supernè est in Christo absconditiarum et acacia. Neque ad nos descendere potest, neque in nos deriuari, nisi precibus in fide Christi fundatis. Nulla alia vis est quae faciat vt per tantum interuallum, quantum est inter caelos & terras, ad nos vsque deriuetur gratia. Haec sunt quae mandat. Vt armauit eos precibus, ita nunc armat eos dilectione mutua: dilectio haec non tam intelligenda
units.tr: Whatever you shall ask. This is the second argument for his ordaining them: their prayers are heard because they are made in Christ's name. Obscurely, here, he meets an objection. It could be objected that there are many hindrances to their bearing fruit, much less to their persevering in bearing fruit. He answers, Whatever you shall ask in my name, etc. That is, as if he said: first believe in me, for this is the one foundation of prayer; then offer your prayers in my name. Only those who believe in Christ offer their prayers to God in Christ's name. Note, therefore, that the ability to do good in the present life is obtained only through prayer. The beginning of doing good is obtained through prayer, and perseverance in doing good is obtained through prayer as well. When Paul exhorts the Ephesians to be steadfast, that is, to persevere in that spiritual struggle, he commends prayer to them: Praying always, he says, with all prayer and supplication. For all grace is laid up above in Christ, as in a hidden treasury. It can neither come down to us nor be drawn into us, except through prayers founded on faith in Christ. No other power exists that could bring grace down to us across so great a distance as lies between heaven and earth. These are the things he commands. As he has armed them with prayer, so now he arms them with mutual love. This love is not to be understood so much

units.la: Ministrorum verbi officium. 2 Tim. 4. 2. da est ea quæ est erga gregem, quæ ipsa adeo necessaria est, vt, si habeat quis omnem Prophetiam, omnem scientiam, nihil tamen sit sine charitate. Sed non tam intelligenda est hæc charitas, quàm ea quæ esse debet inter Apostolos ipsos vicissim. Nam cooperatij in omni opere opus habent vt vnanimes sint, seque vicissim diligant, alioquin contentionibus & dissidiis commune illud opus interrumpetur necessario. Quod si aliquid videantur bene facere ministri, qui per contentionem & inuidiam faciunt, teste Paulo, nihil sincerè faciunt, & Christum in specie tantùm prædicant: hoc est ambitioni & inuidiæ Christi & Euangelii ipsius prætexunt. Contrà ij soli qui ex charitate faciunt, hoc est, ex dilectione in cooperarios suos, ij soli syncerè Christum prædicant. Videmus Apostolos quoties de cooperariis loquuntur, quibus titulis eos ornent, quantum in eos charitatem indicent: vt Paulus, quoties de Timotheo, de Tito, de Tychico, déque aliis loquitur.
units.tr: The duty of ministers of the Word. 2 Tim. 4. 2. It is that which is owed to the flock, and it is so necessary that if someone has all prophecy and all knowledge, yet he is nothing without love. But this love is to be understood less as that owed to the flock than as that which ought to exist among the Apostles themselves, one with another. For fellow-workers in every task need to be of one mind and to love one another; otherwise that common work will necessarily be interrupted by strife and dissension. If ministers who act through contention and envy seem to do good, yet, as Paul testifies, they do nothing sincerely, and they preach Christ only in appearance: they use the name of Christ and of the Gospel itself as a cover for their ambition and envy. On the contrary, only those who act from love, that is, from affection for their fellow-workers, preach Christ sincerely. We see how the Apostles, whenever they speak of their fellow-workers, adorn them with titles and show how much love they bear them: as Paul does whenever he speaks of Timothy, of Titus, of Tychicus, and of others.

units.la: 18 Si mundus vos odit, scitis me priùs quàm vos, illi odio habitum.
units.tr: 18 If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you.

units.la: 19 Si ex mundo essetis, mundus quod suum est amaret: quia verò ex mundo non estis, sed ego elegi vos ex mundo, propterea odit vos mundus.
units.tr: 19 If ye were of the world, the world would love its own: but because ye are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hateth you.

units.la: 20 Mementote sermonis illius, quem ego dixi vobis, Non est seruus maior domino suo. Si me persecuti sunt, & vos persequentur: si sermonem meum seruauerunt, & vestrum seruabunt.
units.tr: 20 Remember the word that I said unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they have kept my saying, they will keep yours also.

units.la: 21 Sed hæc omnia facient vobis propter nomen meum, quia non nouerunt eum qui misit me.
units.tr: 21 But all these things will they do unto you for my name's sake, because they know not him that sent me.

units.la: TErtio loco instruit atque armat eos patientia, idque suo exemplo tanquam maiori. Odio prosequutus est mundus me ante vos: Ergo patienter ferte odium mundi in vos: Neque enim seruus est supra magistrum suum, vt postea videbimus. Vt igitur priùs exemplum suum proposuit, cùm hortaretur ad charitatem in Deū, ad obseruationem mandatorum eius, ad charitatem in proximum: ita nunc dum patienter ferendum persecutionem hortatur, suum exemplum iis proponit. Chri-
units.tr: In the third place he instructs and arms them with patience, and he does so by his own example, as the greater one. The world persecuted me with hatred before you: therefore bear patiently the world's hatred against you. For the servant is not above his master, as we shall see later. Just as he earlier set forth his own example when he exhorted them to love God, to keep his commandments, and to love their neighbour, so now, while he urges them to bear persecution patiently, he sets his own example before them. Chri-

units.la: Christus igitur omnium virtutum & omnis gratiæ exemplar est maximè viuum & necessarium, adeo, sicut antea dixi, vt nisi Christum in omnibus actionibus instituendis, & tota vita formanda ante oculos habeamus, nihil recte possimus agere in vita. Nisi enim fides sit in Christum primùm, qua ipsum & quæ in eo sunt omnia, eius dilectionem, eius patientiam, &c. aliquo modo intuea-mur, profectò in nobis nulla vera virtus esse potest, fidè enim tanquam pedissequæ totidem sequuntur omnes aliæ virtutes. Itaque Paulus Christi exemplum dum virtutem quamuis nobis commendat præsertim solet proponere, vt quod sit omnium efficacissimum. Ita dum suadet modestiā, Sit is affectus, inquit, in vobis, qui fuit in Christo Iesu. Et dū commendat patientiam & tolerantiam in ferendis infirmis fratribus, Christi affert exemplum; Etenim, inquit, Christus non indulsit sibi ipsi, &c. post quæ continuò subiicit, Quæ scripta sunt ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, vt per patientiam & consolationem scripturarum spem habeamus. Ministrat igitur scriptura tum maximè dum loquitur de Christo consolationem & patientiam.
units.tr: Christ, therefore, is the most living and necessary pattern of all virtue and all grace; so much so, as I said before, that unless we keep Christ before our eyes in ordering all our actions and in shaping our whole life, we can do nothing rightly in life. For unless there is faith in Christ first, by which we look upon him and all that is in him, his love, his patience, and so on, in some way, truly no real virtue can exist in us; for faith is followed, like an attendant, by all the other virtues. And so Paul, when he commends any virtue, is accustomed especially to set Christ's example before us, since it is the most powerful of all. Thus when he urges modesty, he says, Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus. And when he commends patience and tolerance in bearing with the weak brethren, he brings forward Christ's example: For, he says, Christ did not please himself, etc. Immediately after these words he adds, Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope. Scripture therefore supplies consolation and patience most of all when it speaks of Christ.

units.la: Si ex mundo essetis. Alterum argumentum quo hortatur ad patienter tolerandū odium mundi. Mundus vos odit, quòd non sitis ex mundo; est autem à causa odij quæ est quòd non sint ex mundo. Ideo enim odit eos mundus, quòd nod sint ex mundo. Cùm itaque ea sit causa odij, patienter tolerandum odium mundi. Causam odij ostendit ex contraria amoris causa; Quòd si essent ex mundo, mundus eos diligeret. Nota igitur, cùm mundus propensè amat aliquem, id argumento esse quòd non sit Deo probatus. Nam non absque causa amaret cum mundus: nisi enim aliquid quod suū est, videret in ipso inesse, vtpote conformitatem & configurationem cum seculo præsenti, vt loquitur Apostolus, profectò nō eū amaret. Fieri quidè potest, vt aliquando mundus diligat eum qui verè bonus est, sed id fit nunquam causa boni, sed particulari aliqua de causa, vt cognationis, affinitatis, aut commodi alicuius. Contrà verò, cùm mundus odit aliquem, id argumento est, quòd verè bonus est. Non enim, nisi causa aliqua subesset, odisset eum mundus, & aliquid quod Dei est in ipso inesset. Fieri enim potest vt mundus odio habeat sceleratum aliquem, vt homicidam, vt manifesto maleficum: verùm peccatum nunquam odit sincerè, hoc est, vt peccatum est, & Dei offensio, sed qua ratione priuatum aliquod malum ad ipsos accedit. Verbi gratia, qua ratione politia & Respublica, quam etiam aliquam esse cupiunt prophani alioqui homines, violatur ac perturbatur. Quod de hominibus dicimus, id quoque de religione dici potest. Neque enim vel ea religio quâ amat mundus approbanda est, vel ea quam odit mundus recusanda. Neque enim multitudo illa, quam iactitant isti, nota est Ecclesiæ Dei veræ. Sed hoc tantùm obiter attingo, tantùm istud addo, materiam patientiæ inesse in odio mundi. Imò verò id scimus experientia: Nō citiùs odisse mundum, quàm amet Deus, & quo maius est mundi odium, eo maiorem esse Dei dilectionem. Nā afflictio, inquit Paulus, efficit patientiam, patientia, experientiam, nempe diuini fauoris & charitatis de qua postea ibidem. Charitas, inquit, Dei effusa est in cordibus nostris.
units.tr: If ye were of the world. This is the second argument by which he exhorts them to bear the world's hatred patiently. The world hates you because you are not of the world; and the cause of the hatred is that you are not of the world. For the world hates you because you are not of the world. Since, then, this is the cause of the hatred, the world's hatred must be borne patiently. He shows the cause of the hatred from the opposite cause of love: If you were of the world, the world would love you. Note, therefore, that when the world strongly loves someone, this is a sign that he is not approved by God. For the world would not love him without a cause: unless it saw in him something that is its own, namely conformity and likeness to the present age, as the Apostle says, it would surely not love him. It is indeed possible that the world sometimes loves one who is truly good, but this never happens because of his goodness, only for some particular reason, such as kinship, affinity, or some advantage. On the contrary, when the world hates someone, this is a sign that he is truly good. For unless some cause lay behind it, the world would not hate him, and something of God's would be in him. For the world may hate someone wicked, such as a murderer, or one manifestly evil; but it never hates sin sincerely, that is, as sin and an offence against God, but only insofar as some private evil touches its own interests. For example, insofar as the polity and commonwealth, which even profane men otherwise desire to have, is violated and disturbed. What we say of men may also be said of religion. For neither is that religion which the world loves to be approved, nor is that which the world hates to be rejected. Nor is that multitude, which those men boast of, a mark of the true Church of God. But I touch on this only in passing; I add only this, that the material of patience lies in the world's hatred. Indeed we know this from experience: God's love is no less quick to come than the world's hatred, and the greater the world's hatred, the greater God's love. For affliction, says Paul, produces patience, patience produces experience, namely of divine favour and love, of which he speaks later in the same place. The love of God, he says, has been poured out in our hearts.

units.la: Mementote. Tertium argumentum est patientiæ à suo ipsius exemplo simili. Quicquid fecerunt mihi, facient vobis: si oderunt me, odio persequentur vos: si seruauerunt sermonem meum, vestrũ quoque seruabunt. Contenti autem esse potestis ea conditione quæ vobis mecũ communis est. Ratio est, Quia non est seruus domino suo maior. Atque hoc est fundamentum, quo nititur argumentum illud, quo vsus est supra cap. 13. cùm suo exemplo ad humilitatem commoueret. Quòd si velimus exemplo Christi, vel humiles esse, vel patientes in afflictionibus, id considerandaum est quod sit Christus nobiscum comparatus, & quantum nobis superemineat: Est enim Dominus noster. Rursus, quid sumus nos cum eo comparati? Sumus enim serui Christi, longè infra Christum. His positis argumentandum est, Quòd si Dominus omnia passus sit, profectò pudebit seruos si non aliquid saltem passi fuerint. Nam quid sunt quæcunque nos patimur ad ea quæ Christus pro nobis est passus? Contrà colligemus honori esse seruis, si admittantur ad communionem passionum domini sui, idque pro domino suo.
units.tr: Remember. The third argument is for patience, drawn from his own similar example. Whatever they have done to me, they will do to you: if they hated me, they will persecute you with hatred; if they kept my word, they will keep yours also. You may be content, however, with the condition which is shared with you by me. The reason is, because the servant is not greater than his lord. And this is the foundation on which rests that argument which he used above in chapter 13, when he moved them to humility by his own example. If we wish, by Christ's example, to be either humble or patient in afflictions, we must consider how Christ stands compared with us, and how far he surpasses us: for he is our Lord. Again, what are we when compared with him? For we are servants of Christ, far below Christ. Having laid this down, we must argue thus: if the Lord has suffered all things, surely the servants will be ashamed if they have suffered at least nothing. For what are all the things we suffer compared with what Christ has suffered for us? On the contrary, we shall conclude that it is an honour for servants to be admitted to fellowship in their lord's sufferings, and that for their lord's sake.

units.la: Atque Apostoli flagris caesi ideo gauisi sunt, quòd digni habiti essent pro nomine Iesu contumeliam pati. Sed ex argumento obseruamus communia esse haec Domino cum seruis suis & membris omnibus, quòd pariter diligantur pariterque odio habeantur, eosdem amicos habeant, eosdem inimicos. Verum notandum odium hoc, vt & amorem, semper initium sumere ab ipso domino. Nam qui amat seruum domini, is prius amat dominum ipsum: vt non sit quod homines praetendant dilectione Domini, cum seruos ipsius & ministros praesertim verbi odio prosequuntur.
units.tr: The apostles were also beaten with rods and rejoiced for this very reason, that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus. From this argument we observe that these things are shared by the Lord with his servants and all his members: they are loved alike and hated alike, and have the same friends and the same enemies. It must be noted, however, that this hatred, like love, always begins with the Lord himself. For whoever loves the servant of the Lord first loves the Lord himself. So there is no room for men to pretend love for the Lord while they pursue his servants and ministers, especially the ministers of the Word, with hatred.

units.la: Sed haec omnia. Quartum argumentum, à bona & honesta causa, cur odio prosequatur eos mundus. Est autem causa ea Christi & Dei. Odium enim eorum primum omnium pertingit ad Deum Patrem, deinde ad filium, postremo ad seruos. Significat ergo negotium esse mundo primum omnium cum Deo Patre, quem tamen agnoscere & amare simulabant Scribae & Pharisaei: putabant enim se interea amasse Deum, cum Christum & discipulos ipsius persecuti sunt. Sed Christus hoc loco aperte dicit odium eorum primum omnium ad Deum pertinere. Ita hodierno die dum ministros verbi insectantur conuitiis, & in eos omnibus modis iniurij sunt, interea tamen iactitant Christum & Euangelium, quasi verò ij ament Christum & Euangelium, qui seruos Christi & Euangelij praecones oderunt. Nota deinde patientiae materiam magnam in bona honestaque causa esse. Mala enim causa nunquam ministrabit in afflictionibus patientiam: veluti si quis vt fur, vt homicida, vt maleficus patiatur. Nam mala causa efficit malam conscientiam, mala conscientia pudefacit. Quòd si quis dum patitur ob malam causam, gaudium interea Spiritus sentiat & patiens sit, profecto id non habet ex causa ipsa quae peccatum est, sed ex remissione peccati per Christum Iesum: nam remissio peccati purgat conscientiam: ex bona autem conscientia, laetitia est & gaudium per Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: But all these things. This is the fourth argument, drawn from a good and honourable cause, for why the world hates them. The cause is that of Christ and of God. Their hatred reaches first of all to God the Father, then to the Son, and finally to the servants. Therefore the meaning is that the world's quarrel is first of all with God the Father, whom the scribes and Pharisees pretended to acknowledge and love, for they thought in the meantime that they loved God, while they persecuted Christ and his disciples. But Christ here plainly says that their hatred pertains first of all to God. So today, while they harass the ministers of the Word with insults and wrong them in every way, they nevertheless boast of Christ and the Gospel, as if those who hate the servants of Christ and the preachers of the Gospel could really love Christ and the Gospel. Note next that there is great matter for patience in a good and honourable cause. A bad cause will never supply patience in afflictions, as when someone suffers as a thief, a murderer or a criminal. For a bad cause produces a bad conscience, and a bad conscience brings shame. But if someone who suffers for a bad cause feels the joy of the Spirit in the meantime and is patient, this certainly does not come from the cause itself, which is sin, but from the forgiveness of sin through Jesus Christ. For forgiveness of sin cleanses the conscience, and from a good conscience comes gladness and joy through the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Contrà verò bona causa ministrat in afflictionibus patientiam, & gaudium bonae conscientiae. Beati sunt qui propter iustitiam persecutionem patiuntur. Ex causis autem bonis, optima est Christi & veritatis causa, quae etiam ipsa gaudium maximum suppeditat. Nam, vt ait Petrus, Qui patiuntur propter Christum, & gloria & Dei Spiritus su-per eos requiescit. His est Spiritus omnis patientiae, consolationis & gaudii. Testes huius rei fuerunt Martyres, qui exquisitissima quaeque supplicia patientissime tolerarunt, & in mediis tormentis haerentes gauisi sunt tamen, cum admiratione & summo stupore omnium spectantium.
units.tr: On the other hand, a good cause supplies patience in afflictions and the joy of a good conscience. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake. Among good causes, the best is the cause of Christ and of truth, which also itself supplies the greatest joy. For, as Peter says, those who suffer for Christ, the glory and the Spirit of God rest upon them. To them belongs the Spirit of all patience, consolation and joy. The martyrs were witnesses of this, who most patiently endured the most exquisite tortures, and who, while held fast in the midst of torments, nevertheless rejoiced, to the wonder and great amazement of all who looked on.

units.la: 22 Si non venissem, & loquutus essem iis, peccatum non haberent, nunc autem non habent quod praetexant peccato suo.
units.tr: 22 If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin.

units.la: 23 Qui me odit, is etiam Patrem meum odit.
units.tr: 23 He who hates me hates my Father also.

units.la: 24 Si opera non fecissem inter eos quae nemo alius fecit, peccatum non haberent: nunc autem & viderunt, & oderunt tum me tum Patrem meum.
units.tr: 24 If I had not done among them works which no one else did, they would not have sin; but now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father.

units.la: 25 Sed oportet vt impleatur sermo, qui in Legeipsorum scriptus est, Oderunt me immerito.
units.tr: 25 But this happened so that the word written in their Law might be fulfilled: They hated me without cause.

units.la: DEinceps exaggerat illud ipsorum odium in se. Primum argumentum est ex eo quod locutus sit iis. Nam hoc ipso quod locutus sit iis reddit ipsorum aduersus se odium inexcusabile. Ex sermone enim ipsius ipsum cognouerunt. Cognitum igitur eum oderunt. Significat igitur ex cognitione odium, ac proinde ex malitia. Vides igitur radicem odij persequutionis eorum, nempe radicem illam amaritudinis, hinc ignorantia, ex ignorantia rursus persequutio. Non omnis, fateor, persequutio est ex aequo ex malitia, etsi perpetuo aliqua subsit: Verum quaedam est persecutio ex zelo quodam Dei, magis quam ex malitia, vt fuit illa Pauliante conuersionem: Quod ad zelum, inquit, persequutus sum Ecclesiam, ideoque misericordiam se consecutum dicit. Prius, inquit, persecutor fui, sed ideo misertus est mei Deus, quia ex ignorantia feci, expers fidei, hoc est ex caeco quodam zelo. At malitiosa persequutione, hoc est ea quae est ex malitia, non nisi aegre & difficulter admodum consequitur misericordiam. Radix enim illa amaritudinis difficilli me euellitur ex animo. Nota rursus Christum ipsiusque Euangelium respectu mundi non alio pertinere, nisi vt inexcusabiles reddantur in illo die. Id quod Paulus dixit de luce illa quæ in natura reliqua est, quæ eò pertinebat, vt homines reddérentur inexcusabiles. Vide quæ diximus in locu huic valde non absimilem supra,Si cæci essetis,non haberetis peccatum.
units.tr: Next he magnifies their hatred toward himself. The first argument is from the fact that he spoke to them. For by the very fact that he spoke to them, he makes their hatred toward himself inexcusable. For they came to know him from his speech. Having come to know him, they hate him. This means that the hatred springs from knowledge, and therefore from malice. You see, then, the root of their persecution, namely that root of bitterness; from this comes ignorance, and from ignorance again persecution. I admit that not every persecution comes from malice, though some malice is always present. But there is a persecution that springs from a certain zeal for God rather than from malice, such as that of Paul before his conversion: As to zeal, he says, I persecuted the Church, and therefore he says he obtained mercy. Before, he says, I was a persecutor, but God had mercy on me because I acted in ignorance, lacking faith, that is, from a certain blind zeal. But malicious persecution, that is, persecution that comes from malice, obtains mercy only with great difficulty and hardly at all, for that root of bitterness is pulled out of the heart with difficulty. Note again that Christ and his Gospel, with respect to the world, have no other purpose than to make them inexcusable on that day. This is what Paul said of that light which remains in nature, whose purpose was to make men inexcusable. See what we said above on a passage not very unlike this one: If you were blind, you would not have sin.

units.la: Qui me odit. Secundum argumentum quo exaggerat illud odium,ex eo quod pariter oderunt Patrem. Nam hæc coniuncta sunt necessariò, odium Christi & odium Dei. Oderunt homines eos qui sunt discipuli ac membra Christi, quia aliquid Christi habent & Spiritu eius imbuuntur. Oderunt homines Christum ipsum, quia Deum habet in se corporaliter habitantem, vt loquitur Apostolus. Ergo odium mundi præcipuè est adversus ipsum Deum. Miretur aliquis qui possunt homines odisse Deum. Deus lux est. Qui autem peruerse agit (dixit Christus supra 3.) odit lucem vel istam solis. Nam, vt ait Paulus, Interdiu composite ambulandum est,&c. Quanto magis illam verbi diuini lucem, quæ penetrat ad conscientias vsque? Quanto magis Deum ipsum qui lux est? cuius meminisse non possunt sine horrore & detestatione; & quoties affulget conscientiis eorum, eius tantam lucem sustinere non possunt. Vides igitur quantum interfit inter Deum & hominem qualis ipse natura sua est. Non tam pugnant lux & tenebræ quàm Deus & homo, neque finis erit huic pugnæ, his inimicitiis, priusquam is qui dixit vt è tenebris lux existeret, splendeat in cordibus nostris,& tenebras istas quibus per naturam involuimur dispellat.
units.tr: He who hates me. The second argument by which he magnifies that hatred is from the fact that they hate the Father equally. For the hatred of Christ and the hatred of God are necessarily joined together. Men hate those who are the disciples and members of Christ, because they have something of Christ and are imbued with his Spirit. Men hate Christ himself, because he has God dwelling in him bodily, as the Apostle says. Therefore the hatred of the world is chiefly directed against God himself. Someone may wonder how men can hate God. God is light. But whoever does wicked things (as Christ said above, chapter 3) hates the light, even the light of the sun. For, as Paul says, we must walk properly as in the daytime, etc. How much more, then, that light of the divine Word which penetrates even to the conscience? How much more God himself, who is light? Men cannot remember him without horror and detestation; and whenever he shines upon their consciences, they cannot bear so great a light. You see, then, how great is the difference between God and man, as he is by his very nature. Light and darkness do not fight so much as God and man do, and there will be no end to this struggle, to these enmities, until he who said, Let light shine out of darkness, shines in our hearts and dispels those shadows in which we are wrapped by nature.

units.la: Si opera non fecissem. Tertium argumentum quo exaggerat eorum in se odium. Est autem ab operibus suis, vt illud primum fuit à dictis suis. Et hoc quoque argumento ab operibus, iisque nonnulgaribus, arguit eos ex cognitione ea quæ per opera subministrata fuit ipsum odisse: atque ideo ex malitia quadam id fecisse. Opera hoc loco intelligo miraculosa illa ac prodigiosa quæ eiusmodi erant, cuiusmodi nemo alius vnquam operatus est, si modum agendi respicias, si etiam rationem habeas multitudinis illorum operum: Nam & Dominus suo nomine fecit omnia. Alij ante eum Dominj mini nomine, & nemo ante eum tot miracula edidit, quot ille, vt, inquam, eiusmodi erant, ita de eo testaban-tur. Opera, inquit, quæ ego facio testantur de me. In operibus autem eius intuiti sunt diuinam illam in ipso maiesta-tem, non tantum amici & ij quibus vsus est familiariter. (Viderunt enim cum plenum gratia ac veritate, & glo-riam eius tanquam gloriam unigeniti à Patre.) Sed & ipsi inimici, vt Pharisæi cap.9. supra; Si peccator esset an posset signa ista edere? Et ex Pharisæis illi, qui confiteri illum noluerunt, tamen conuicti erant conscientiis suis, ac peccarunt in Spiritum sanctum. Vt autem relictis iis, qui illum viderunt operantem & audiuerunt loquentem, veniamus ad nos ipsos qui hoc sæculo viuimus: Euangelium istud de Christo & sermo ille crucis Christi, qui vocatus est potentia Dei, & Dei sapientia, satis arguit Christum esse Dominum illum gloriæ: Imo Euangelium istud vel repugnantes & aduersarios conuincit maiestate illa & gloria, quæ in tanta sermonis simplicitate elucet: deinde hic obseruamus, etiam ex cognitione homines obstinatos odisse Dominum.
units.tr: If I had not done works. The third argument by which he magnifies their hatred toward himself. It is drawn from his works, as the first was from his words. By this argument also, from works, and those not ordinary ones, he proves that they hated him from knowledge, which was supplied through the works, and therefore that they did it out of a certain malice. By works in this place I understand those miraculous and prodigious deeds which were of such a kind that no one else ever did the like, if you look at the manner of acting, and if you also take account of the number of those works. For the Lord did all things in his own name. Others before him acted in the name of the Lord, but no one before him performed so many miracles as he did; and, as I said, such were these works, and they bore witness to him. The works, he says, which I do bear witness to me. In his works they saw that divine majesty in him, not only his friends and those with whom he lived intimately (for they saw his glory, full of grace and truth, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father). But also his enemies, such as the Pharisees in chapter 9 above: If this man were a sinner, could he do these signs? And among the Pharisees, those who would not confess him were nevertheless convicted by their own consciences, and sinned against the Holy Spirit. But leaving aside those who saw him working and heard him speaking, let us come to ourselves who live in this age. This Gospel about Christ and that message of the cross of Christ, which is called the power of God and the wisdom of God, sufficiently proves that Christ is that Lord of glory. Indeed, this Gospel convicts even those who resist and oppose it by that majesty and glory which shines forth in such simplicity of speech. Then we observe here that even from knowledge men can be obstinate and hate the Lord.

units.la: Et viderunt, inquit, & oderunt. Tolerabile quidem esset illud, si ignari odissent Dominum, at cum scientes oderint, qui potest illud tolerari? Dictum est supra, fateor, quod ex ignorantia Patris oderunt Filium, eumque sunt persequuti: sed hic nihil contrarium. Nam hæc duo consistunt, quod & ex cognitione oderint, & ex ignorantia. Primum quidem cognouerunt, deinde lumen illud cognitionis extinxerunt: hinc est ignorantia & odium Christi: Nam his quasi gradibus progrediuntur homines ad peccatum perpetrandum; primum cognoscunt Deum & bonum & malum. Cognouerunt, inquit, Deum. Deinde cognitioni illi obluctantur, eamque conantur extinguere: Vt visum est vs Deum in notitia non retinere. Hinc ignorantia, hinc amissio conscientiæ & dedolentia: hinc denique omnis proteruia. Nam profecto non prouunt prius homines ad fœda facinora quæque perpetranda quæ sese excæcarint, ac oculos sibi eripuerint, conscientiamque suam quasi cauterio resecuerint. id mirum est quod primum omnium agunt, excutiunt sibi omnem sensum, reddúntque se ipsi stupidos, vt deinde sine impedimento, &c, vt loquitur Apostolus, ἀ πλεονεξίᾳ perpetrent omnē impuritatem. Illud enim non possunt obtinere, tam præcipites feruntur, nisi prius remoueatur omne obstaculum cognitionis & conscientiæ. Denique nota hic causam quæ tollit prætextum peccati, nempe cognitionem. Cognitio enim præcedens tum peccato omni sequenti, tum etiam ignorantiæ, quæ proxima antegreditur peccatum ipsum, excusationem omnem aufert: prius enim cognitionem & notitiam habent homines quàm ignari fiant: ex malitia autem sese excæcant. Quò autem cognitio maior est, eò minor est excusatio. Neque verò tamen aufert excusationem cognitio: verùm auget peccatum. Homicidium peccatum est per se, item adulterium, &c. sed cùm accedit ad hæc cognitio, iam peccatum duplicatum est: loquor de ea cognitione præsertim quæ ex verbo Dei est. Nam cùm cognitio quæ est ex natura augeat peccatum, profectò cognitio quæ est ex verbo ipsius Dei multum magis ipsum auget, & certè tolerabilius erit Sodomæ & Gomorrhæ in illo die, quàm nobis, si in tanta Euangelij luce, sine resipiscentia peccauerimus. Sed oportet. Nevideatur illud odium inuito quasi Deo fuisse, Christus tetriùs huic occurrit, cauétque diuinæ gloriæ & potentiæ, quæ ideo salua est, quòd nihil in Christum, vel cogitatum vel factum sine eius vel prædictione in tempore, vel prædestinatione ab æterno. Hoc videas passim, quoties mentio fit in scripturis sacris vel persecutionis vel crucis Christi, nihil factum esse in Christum sine Deo eiusq; ordinatione. Id etiam ipsum locū habet in omnibus maleficiis quæ eueniunt quotidie in mundo: ex decreto enim & permissione Dei fiunt omnia, ideo inuito Deo dici non possunt fieri. Nam decretum etiam permissiuum tollit inuitū: interea autem non excusantur qui malè agunt, & instrumenta sunt per quæ exequitur Deus decreta sua, vel hac ratione quòd malè agentes scientes & volentes malè agant. Neque verò decretum vel necessitas diuini decreti nos excusat dum aliquid facimus contra voluntatem illam Dei reuelatam. Quod ad locum citatum attinet, is est ex Psal.35.19. qui legis nomine exprimitur. Nam omnis prophetia quid est aliud, quàm legis quædam appendix? Atque omnes prophetæ veteres sub lege erant, ideóque omnia eorum dicta & scripta ad legem referuntur.
units.tr: And they have seen, he says, and hated. It would be tolerable if they hated the Lord out of ignorance, but how can it be tolerated when they hate him knowingly? I admit that it was said above that they hate the Son and persecute him because they do not know the Father. But that is not contrary to what is said here. For both hold together: they hate him both from knowledge and from ignorance. They first knew, and then they quenched that light of knowledge. From this come ignorance and hatred of Christ. For men advance to committing sin by steps like these: first they know God and good and evil. They knew, he says, God. Then they struggle against that knowledge and try to extinguish it: as they did not like to retain God in knowledge. From this come ignorance, the loss of conscience and insensibility, and finally every kind of shamelessness. For men do not, before they commit any foul deeds, first blind themselves, tear out their own eyes and cut off their conscience as with a cautery. What is remarkable is that the first thing they do is shake off all feeling and make themselves stupid, so that they may then, without hindrance, as the Apostle says, [ἀπλεονεξίᾳ] commit every impurity in greediness. For they cannot carry through that, they are not driven so headlong, unless first every obstacle of knowledge and conscience is removed. Finally, note here the cause that takes away the pretext of sin, namely knowledge. For prior knowledge takes away all excuse both for every following sin and for the ignorance which immediately goes before the sin itself. For men first have knowledge and understanding before they become ignorant, but they blind themselves out of malice. And the greater the knowledge, the smaller the excuse. Yet knowledge does not in fact remove excuse; rather it increases sin. Murder is a sin in itself, and likewise adultery, and so on. But when knowledge is added to these, the sin is already doubled. I speak especially of that knowledge which comes from the Word of God. For if the knowledge which comes from nature increases sin, surely the knowledge which comes from the very Word of God increases it much more, and certainly it will be more tolerable for Sodom and Gomorrah in that day than for us, if we sin in such a great light of the Gospel without repentance. But it must be so. Lest that hatred seem to have happened against the will of God, as it were, Christ meets it more firmly, and guards the glory and power of God, which is safe because nothing is thought or done against Christ without his foreknowledge in time or predestination from eternity. You may see this everywhere, whenever mention is made in the Holy Scriptures of either persecution or the cross of Christ: nothing was done against Christ without God and his ordination. This also holds in all the evil deeds that happen daily in the world: for all things come about by the decree and permission of God, and therefore they cannot be said to happen against the will of God. For even a permissive decree removes the unwillingness; yet meanwhile those who act wickedly are not excused, and they are the instruments through which God carries out his decrees, and this is so because those who act wickedly do so knowingly and willingly. Nor does the decree, or the necessity of the divine decree, excuse us when we do something against that will of God which has been revealed. As for the passage cited, it is from Psalm 35:19, which is named by the expression "the law." For what is any prophecy but a kind of appendix to the law? And all the ancient prophets were under the law, and therefore all their sayings and writings are referred to the law.

units.la: 26 Cùm autem venerit Aduocatus ille quem ego mittam vobis à Patre, Spiritus, inquam, ille veritatis, qui à Patre emanat, ille testabitur de me.
units.tr: 26 But when that Advocate comes whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit, I say, of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness of me.

units.la: 27 Sed & vos testabimini, quoniam à principio mecum estis.
units.tr: 27 And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.

units.la: HActenus digressus est Christus in exaggeratione peccati & odij Iudæorum illorum obstinatorum, nunc reuertitur ad discipulos suos, eósque duobus argumentis consolatur ad finem usque capitis. Primum ex eo est, quod per Spiritum sanctum intus testificabitur de se. Aliis autem tantùm extra testatus est per verbum & per opera sua, interea tamen non flexit intus corda eorum. Magna sunt, fateor, externa hæc testimonia, magnum est audire Christum loquentem, magnum videre operantem: sed sine interno Spiritus testimonio nihil, imò plus mali quàm boni adportant. Neque prodesset hodierno die cuiquam audire Christum ipsum loquentem, videre operantem, tractare manibus, si non interea acciperet Spiritum sanctum. Et certius meliúsque est testimonium illud per Spiritum Christi, qui intus & in corde offert Christum, quasi videndum & audiendū, adeóque tractandum: Melius, inquam, est certiúsque hoc Spiritus sancti testimonium, vel solum sine illis, quàm illa omnia sine hoc. Et discipuli ipsi Christi maiorem ac firmiorem testificationem de Christo acceperunt post Christi ascensionem, beneficio nimirum Spiritus huius sancti, quàm etiam tunc habuerunt cùm Christus vnà cum ipsis commoraretur. In causa fuit, quòd per Spiritum Christum alioqui absentem, non iam manibus corporeis, sed corde suo tractarunt cum pace & consolatione ineffabili: ideóque Spiritus sanctus testificans, consolator est dictus. Notandum quòd dicit se missurum Spiritum sed à Patre: quo quidem significat à Patre primùm procedere Spiritum, deinde à se. Eodem sensu dixit superiori capite, Patrem missurum Spiritum in nomine suo: Pater enim mittit Spiritum per Filium, vel Filius mittit eum a Patre. Cum igitur ab utroque emanet idem Spiritus, necesse est de utroque testificetur, & de Patre & de Filio: verum de Patre per Filium, in quo Patrem videndum exhibet. Sed & vos testabimini. Secunda consolatio: Vos quoq; de me testabimini. Causa autem addita est, Quia a principio mecum estis. Conversatio haec corporalis discipulorum quae fuit una cum Christo reddidit eos testes auritos & oculatos, praeparauitq; eos ac confirmauit ad testificationem futuram. Unde Iohannes ait, Quod spectauimus, quod audiuimus, quod manus nostrae tractarunt, id vobis annuntiamus. Verum praecipuum testificationis eorum fundamentum fuit post Christi discessum, utpote testimonium illud Spiritus in cordibus ipsorum, quod quidem vsque adeo firmum est fundamentum, ut etiam ij qui non viderunt Christum oculis istis corporeis, ac loquentem cum auribus suis audiuerunt, aut manibus istis contrectarunt, ij, inquam, habentes internam hanc testificationem Spiritus sancti, de eo loquantur, adeo confidenter, adeo evidenter, ut si eum vidissent oculis, & cum eo conversati fuissent. Neque enim ab aspectu tantum ipsius Christi habemus id ut de eo cum fiducia loquamur, sed multo magis a Spiritu sancto, qui in corde nostro est id obtinemus. Nemo enim potest dicere ipsum Dominum nisi per Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: HAving so far digressed, Christ, in magnifying the sin and hatred of those stubborn Jews, now turns back to his disciples and comforts them with two arguments to the end of the chapter. The first is this: that by the Holy Spirit he will bear witness of himself inwardly. He had indeed borne witness to others only outwardly, through the Word and through his works, yet he had not bent their hearts from within. These external testimonies are great, I admit: it is a great thing to hear Christ speaking, a great thing to see him working. But without the inward testimony of the Spirit they are nothing, indeed they bring more harm than good. Nor would it profit anyone today to hear Christ himself speaking, to see him working, to handle him with their hands, if in the meantime they did not receive the Holy Spirit. And that testimony through the Spirit of Christ, who inwardly and in the heart presents Christ as if to be seen and heard, and so to be handled, is more certain and better. I say it is better and more certain: this testimony of the Holy Spirit, even alone without those outward things, is better than all those things without this. And the disciples of Christ themselves received a greater and firmer testimony about Christ after his ascension, by the benefit, of course, of this Holy Spirit, than they had even when Christ dwelt together with them. The cause was that through the Spirit they handled Christ, who was otherwise absent, no longer with bodily hands but with their heart, with peace and an indescribable consolation. Therefore the Holy Spirit, bearing witness, is called Comforter. It is to be noted that he says he will send the Spirit, but from the Father: by which he signifies that the Spirit proceeds first from the Father and then from himself. In the same sense he said in the previous chapter that the Father would send the Spirit in his name: for the Father sends the Spirit through the Son, or the Son sends him from the Father. Since, then, the same Spirit proceeds from both, he must bear witness of both, of the Father and of the Son; but of the Father through the Son, in whom he presents the Father to be seen. But you also will bear witness. This is the second consolation: you also will bear witness of me. The cause is added: because you have been with me from the beginning. That bodily fellowship of the disciples which they had with Christ made them witnesses by hearing and by sight, and prepared and strengthened them for the testimony to come. Hence John says, What we have seen, what we have heard, what our hands have handled, that we proclaim to you. But the chief foundation of their testimony was after Christ's departure, namely that testimony of the Spirit in their hearts. This foundation is so firm that even those who did not see Christ with those bodily eyes, nor heard him speaking with their ears, nor handled him with those hands, these, I say, having this inward testimony of the Holy Spirit, speak of him so confidently and so evidently as if they had seen him with their eyes and had lived with him. For we have the ability to speak of him with confidence not only from the sight of Christ himself, but much more we obtain it from the Holy Spirit, who is in our heart. For no one can say that Jesus is the Lord except by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Sermonem duobus superioribus capitibus institutum continuat. Primum, praedicat mala ipsis eventura a Iudaeis, usque ad versum 5. Deinde, consolatur eos rursum contra tristitiam quam conceperant ex futuro ipsius decessu, usque ad versum 29. Postremo, praedicit eis futuram ipsorum fugam: ipsisque contra eam consolatur.
units.tr: He continues the discourse begun in the two preceding chapters. First, he foretells the evils the Jews will bring upon them, down to verse 5. Then he consoles them again against the sorrow they had conceived from his coming departure, down to verse 29. Finally, he foretells their future flight and consoles them against it.

units.tr: The second argument of consolation.

units.tr: The efficacy of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: 1 Æc loquutus sum vobis, vt ne offenda-mini.
units.tr: 1 "These things have I spoken unto you, that ye should not be offended."

units.la: 2 Mouebunt vos synagogis: imò veniet tempus quum quisquis trucidabit vos putabit se cultum præstare Deo.
units.tr: 2 They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the time will come when whoever kills you will think he is rendering worship to God.

units.la: 3 Et hæc facient vobis, quia non nouerunt Patrem neque me.
units.tr: 3 And they will do these things to you, because they have not known the Father or me.

units.la: 4 Sed hæc loquutus sum vobis, vt cùm venerit hora illa, memineritis eorū, nempe quòd ego hæc dixerim vobis. Hæc autem vobis à principio non dixi, quia vobiscum eram.
units.tr: 4 But I have spoken these things to you so that, when that hour comes, you may remember them, namely that I said them to you. I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you.

units.la: HOC capite prosequitur sermonem illum quem iam coepit conferre cum discipulis iam inde à capite 14. Primùm autem concludit illam exhortationem ad patientiam, quam instituit capite superiori sub finem. q.d. Hæc quæ dixi de odio mundi, quod quidē vos perpessuri estis, ideo à me dicta sunt, ne offendamini: hoc est, ne post meum discessum, vbi reipsa experiemini odium illud mundi, & persequutionem, offendamini & impingatis in Euangelium. Christus quidem cum cruce coniunctus est necessariò, & Euangelium de Christo comitem habet afflictionem. Esto particeps, inquit Paulus, afflictionum Euangelij. Iam verò à nulla re magis abhorret caro & sanguis, hoc est natura nostra, quàm à cruce & afflictionibus, adeo vt ψυχικῷ duntaxat homini, planè omnis ad Christum aditus sit præclusus: Requiritur enim vt supra naturam euehatur quisque, & potentia Dei sustentetur, interim dum perrumpit ad Christum, per medias afflictiones, dico potentiam Dei: Nam non minùs datum est persecutionem pati pro Christo, quàm in Christum credere. Et esto particeps afflictionum Euangelij, dicit Timotheo, ex potentia Dei. Cùm hæc ita se habeant, profectò nulla alia re magis opus est nobis, quàm hac, vt toto hoc tempore, quo Euangelio sine persequutione fruimur, præperamur ad afflictiones futuras tolerandas. Præparatione autem eò magis opus est, quòd omnia prope diem futuras afflictiones comminentur. Christus enim cùm iam appropinquaret tempus persecutionis sui, admonuit discipulos. Monebunt vos synagogis. Particularius iis prædicit afflictionum genus: primùm eiectionem è synagogis, deinde etiā mortem ipsam. Quo admonemur non vnum tantùm afflictionum genus comitari Christum, & Euangelii ipsius: sed omne genus afflictionum, leuissimum simul & graujssimum, imò mortem ipsam, & mortis quidem genus exquisitissimum quodque. Experti sunt hæc discipuli Christi; primùm eiecti sunt ex synagogis, tum in eos denuntiatum est ne loquerentur in nomine Christi. Postea ad carcerem ventum, hinc ad flagra, postremò mortè multati sunt. Quamobrem nemo præscribat sibi ipse mensuram aliquam afflictionum, sed præparet se ad toleranda omnia, quæ visum erit Deo cuique admetiri. Ita Christus Petro: Cùm iunior esses, incinxisti teipsum, cingebas & ibas quò volebas. Cùm autem senueris, extendes manus tuas, & alius te cinget, & transferet quò noles. Quo significaret passurum Petrum, non quæ visa erant ipsi, sed ad arbitrium & libidinem eorum passurum qui ipsum persequuturi erant Dei tantùm permissione. Ergo præparari debemus nos singulí ad extrema quæque toleranda. Neque enim si negauerimus Christum ob intolerabilem grauitatem supplicij cuiusquam, ideo inexcusabiles erimus. Verùm si recusauerimus perpeti vel exquisitissima tormenta propter eum, ipse nos in illo die abnegabit. Quanquam est quod nos consoletur, nonenim maius erit onus quod imponet nobis quàm erunt vires quas dabit vt illud onus sustineamus, & vna cum tentatione præstabit euasionem. Nam momentanea leuitas afflictionum conficit æternum pondus excellenter excellentis gloriæ. Denique afflictiones comperientur ese laudi & gloriæ & honori cùm patefiet Iesus Christus. Putabit se cultum præstare Deo. Vide causam persecutionis, iudicium nimirum peruersum, quod interea dum mortè afficient discipulos, putabunt se Deo seruire. Grauissima quæque persecutio semper fuit sub prætextu aliquo honesto.
units.tr: In this chapter he continues the discourse he has been holding with the disciples since chapter 14. First, however, he concludes the exhortation to patience that he began at the end of the previous chapter. The sense is: "I have told you of the hatred of the world, which you are certainly going to suffer, so that you may not be offended, that is, so that after my departure, when you experience that hatred of the world and persecution in fact, you may not be offended and stumble over the Gospel. Christ is necessarily bound up with the cross, and the Gospel of Christ has affliction as its companion. Be a partaker, says Paul, of the afflictions of the Gospel. Now nothing is more repugnant to flesh and blood, that is, to our nature, than the cross and afflictions; so much so that for the merely psychic [ψυχικῷ] man every approach to Christ is completely closed off. For each person must be lifted above nature and sustained by the power of God while he breaks through to Christ through the midst of afflictions; I mean the power of God. For it has been granted no less to suffer persecution for Christ than to believe in Christ. And he says to Timothy, be a partaker of the afflictions of the Gospel, according to the power of God. Since these things stand so, there is certainly nothing we need more than this, that during this whole time in which we enjoy the Gospel without persecution, we prepare ourselves to endure the afflictions to come. Such preparation is all the more necessary because nearly every day threatens future afflictions. For when the time of his persecution was already drawing near, Christ warned the disciples: They will put you out of the synagogues. He foretells more particularly the kind of affliction: first expulsion from the synagogues, and then even death itself. By this we are admonished that Christ and his Gospel are accompanied not by one kind of affliction only, but by every kind of affliction, the lightest and the heaviest alike, indeed death itself, and each of the most exquisite kinds of death. The disciples of Christ experienced this: first they were thrown out of the synagogues; then it was commanded against them that they should not speak in the name of Christ. Afterwards they came to prison, then to the lash, and finally they were punished with death. Therefore let no one prescribe for himself some measure of afflictions, but let him prepare himself to endure all things that God shall see fit to measure out to each. So Christ said to Peter: When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished. But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and carry you where you do not wish. By this he signified that Peter would suffer not what seemed good to himself, but according to the will and lust of those who were going to persecute him, and only by the permission of God. Therefore we each ought to prepare ourselves to endure the utmost extremities. For if we deny Christ because the severity of someone's punishment is unbearable, we will not on that account be without excuse. But if we refuse to suffer even the most exquisite torments for his sake, he himself will deny us on that day. Yet there is something that comforts us: the burden he lays on us will not be greater than the strength he gives us to bear it, and along with the temptation he will provide the way of escape. For the momentary lightness of affliction works for us an eternal weight of glory, surpassingly excellent. Finally, afflictions will be found to be for praise and glory and honour when Jesus Christ is revealed. He will think he is rendering worship to God. Note the cause of the persecution: a perverse judgment, namely that while they put the disciples to death, they will think they are serving God. The most severe persecutions have always been carried on under some honourable pretext.

units.la: 2. Corinth. 4. 17.

1. Pet. 1. 7. honestissimo, quoque maior crudelitas erat, eo semper fuit praetextus speciosior. Nullus autem omnium praetextus honestior & speciosior est quam sit religionis ac cultus diuini praetextus. Ergo sub praetextu religionis crudelitas semper maxima fuit. Postquam enim ia excaecati sunt homines a diabolo ac falsa aliqua religione, tum saevire coeperunt. Nullum hominum genus magis saevit ac furit in Christianos quam Antichristus cum sti asseclis suis, sub praetextu nescio quo religionis ac cultus diuini. Sub praetextu enim religionis maxime furit diabolus, eaque committit quae pudeat vel ipsum diabolum palam perpetrare. Exemplo erit in omnem posteritatem illa strages Gallicana, & crudelitas illa quae facile vincit omnem crudelitatem, quae vnquam antea audita est.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 1. 7. The more honourable the pretext, the greater the cruelty; and always the more specious the pretext. Yet none of all pretexts is more honourable and more specious than the pretext of religion and the worship of God. Therefore cruelty has always been greatest under the pretext of religion. For once men had been blinded by the devil and by some false religion, they began to rage. No race of men rages and storms against Christians more than Antichrist with his followers, under some pretext of religion and divine worship, I know not what. For it is under the pretext of religion that the devil especially rages, and commits deeds that would shame the devil himself to perform openly. The massacre in France will be an example to all posterity, and that cruelty which easily surpasses every cruelty ever heard of before.

units.la: Haec facient vobis. Hic attingit fundamentum persecutionis eorum. Est autem caecitas, atque ignorantia Patris & Filij: hinc peruersum iudicium & prava opinio, hinc denique persecutio. Fundamentum omnium bonarum actionum est mens illuminata luce illa Dei quae est in Christo Iesu: hinc rectum de rebus iudicium, hinc cor recte se inclinans, hinc actiones bonae rectaeque. Quod si oculus, inquit Christus, simplex fuerit, totum corpus, hoc est totum illud, sive interius sit in animo, sive exterius in actionibus externis sit, totum illud lucidum est. At vero, si mens quae est animi oculus, non fuerit illuminata, sed obtenebrata, tum peruertitur iudicium, hinc cor male affectum & peruersum, hinc actiones malae. Nam si oculus tuus, inquit Christus, malus fuerit, totum corpus tuum tenebricosum erit. Tu admiratus tenebras illas tenebras, Si lux, inquit, tua, & quod in te est principium luminis, tenebrae sunt, quantae sunt istae tenebrae? Quamobrem Christum ex oculis nostris nunquam sinamus discedere, sed ipse fulgore suo semper nos irradiet, & cordibus nostris affulgeat, vt habeamus in rebus bonis simul & malis rectum iudicium: non modo in iis quae ad religionem, sed etiam in iis quae ad rempublicam & politicam pertinent. Nemo vel politicus recte sentit de re quaque sine Christo, eiusque luce & tanquam face praelata. Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum & lux itineri meo. Sed haec loquutus. Finem subiungit cur tam speciatim ipsos praemonuerit de afflictionibus futuris: est autem ut recordentur haec a se dicta esse, ac proinde ne imparati inveniantur in die illo afflictionis, verum praeparati & instructi. Nam levius laedit quicquid praevidimus ante. Nota igitur opus esse maxime ut praeparemur auditis sermonibus & praemonitionibus de cruce, antequam coeperit Deus nos ea exercere: sic enim futurum est, ut in die afflictionis Spiritus sanctus subministret nobis ex auditis iam prius illorum consolationem. Nam inter alia hoc officium Spiritus sancti est, revocare in memoriam ea quae audiuimus, iis praesertim temporibus quibus opus est maxime. Illud enim experimur in mediis afflictionibus, nos etiam plus capere consolationis ex verbo Dei aliquando audito & percepto, quam tum percepimus cum primum illud ipsum audiuimus, nimirum id fit quia Spiritus Dei revocat illud nobis in memoriam, & per illud efficax est in cordibus nostris.
units.tr: They will do these things to you. Here he touches on the foundation of their persecution. It is blindness and ignorance of the Father and the Son; from this comes a perverse judgment and a wicked opinion, and from this finally persecution. The foundation of all good actions is a mind illuminated by that light of God which is in Christ Jesus: from this comes a right judgment about things, from this a heart rightly inclined, and from this good and upright actions. For if the eye, says Christ, be single, the whole body, that is, the whole of a man, whether inwardly in his mind or outwardly in his external actions, is full of light. But if the mind, which is the eye of the soul, is not illuminated but darkened, then judgment is perverted, from this comes a heart ill-disposed and twisted, and from this evil actions. For if your eye, says Christ, be evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. You marvel at those darkenings: If the light in you, he says, and the principle of light that is in you, is darkness, how great is that darkness? Therefore let us never allow Christ to depart from our eyes, but let him always shine upon us with his brightness and illumine our hearts, so that we may have right judgment in good things and in bad alike: not only in those matters that pertain to religion, but also in those that pertain to the commonwealth and to politics. No one, even a politician, judges rightly about any matter without Christ, and without his light carried before him like a torch. Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path. But I have spoken these things. He adds the reason why he has warned them so specifically about future afflictions: it is so that they may remember that these things were said by him, and therefore that they may not be found unprepared on the day of affliction, but ready and equipped. For whatever we have foreseen wounds us less. Note, then, that it is especially necessary for us to be prepared by hearing discourses and warnings about the cross before God begins to exercise us in it. For thus it will come about that on the day of affliction the Holy Spirit will supply us with the consolation of those things we heard earlier. For among other things it is the office of the Holy Spirit to bring to memory the things we have heard, especially at those times when there is the greatest need. For we experience this in the midst of afflictions: that we sometimes gain more consolation from a word of God heard and received earlier than we gained when we first heard it. This happens, of course, because the Spirit of God brings back that word to our memory, and through it is effective in our hearts.

units.la: Tum obijci potuit, Cur non antehac nos admonuisti? Respondet, Haec non dixi vobis a principio, quia vobiscum eram. Quasi diceret, Nunc demum praemonui, quia futurum est breui, ut ego discedam a vobis: non autem prius admonui, quia eram vobiscum. Nota quomodo vsus sit Dominus discipulis suis, quantopere iis primis illis temporibus, quibus cum ipsis vna versatus est, indulserit. Noluit eos vel audire semel de afflictionibus illis quas perpeti erant impositurum, nedum aliquid tum primum perpeti. Atque de eo quasi quaesti sunt discipuli Iohannis. Cur cum nos & Pharisaei multum ieiunemus, discipuli vero tui non ieiunant? Respondit Dominus, Numpossunt filij thalami lugere, quandiu cum ijs est sponsus? Venient autem dies cum tolletur ab ijs sponsus, & tunc ieiunabunt. Cum autem iam appropinquaret illud tempus quo discessurus erat, praemonuit de futuris propediem afflictionibus: postquam vero decesserit, obnoxij erat afflictionibus omnis generis: causa autem fuit, quia discipulis concessum erat tempus quo adolescerent. Nondum autem primis illis temporibus peruenerant ad maturitatem: habuerunt quidem etiam tum potentiam aliquam Christi praesentem, sed non tam intra se, quam extra. At vero, vbi Christus
units.tr: Then it could be objected: "Why did you not warn us before?" He answers: I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you. As if he said: "I have given warning only now, because my departure is soon to come; I did not warn you before because I was with you." Note how the Lord indulged his disciples in those first days, when he lived among them. He did not want them even to hear once of the afflictions he was going to lay upon them, much less to suffer any of them at that time. The disciples of John once asked him about this same matter: Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples do not fast? The Lord answered: Can the sons of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast. When the time drew near for his departure, he warned them of afflictions that were soon to come; but after he had gone, they were exposed to afflictions of every kind. The reason was that the disciples were given time in which to grow up. In those first days, however, they had not yet reached maturity. They did indeed have some power from the presence of Christ, but it was more outside them than within them. But when Christ departed from them,

units.la: Spiritus S. officium. Cur hoc tempore Christus disseruit de afflictionib. futuris. Mat. 9.14. Infirmitati suorum consulit Christus. stus ab iis discessit, missus est ad eos consolator ille, qui intus eos corroborauit, & dedit iis Christum in cordibus habitantem: hinc maturi facti sunt & apti euaserunt ferendo oneri. Tum autem maiori cum gaudio perpessi sunt omnia pro Christo, quoad corpus suum absente, quàm tum olim cum in pace & tranquillitate vnà cum Christo præsente viuerent. Ita fit de nobis omnibus: Nam in Christo paulatim adolescimus, tantisper dum ad maturitatem & staturam viri iusti perueniatur, Parcit nobis Dominus tantisper dū non sentit nos maturos satis. At vbi maturos videt & satis confirmatos suis ipsius quidem viribus nō nostris ipsorum, tum quidem onus imponit humeris nostris pro analogia & pro portione virium nostrarum.
units.tr: The office of the Holy Spirit. Why Christ spoke at this time about future afflictions. Matt. 9.14. Christ provides for the weakness of his people. the Comforter was sent to them, who strengthened them inwardly and gave them Christ dwelling in their hearts; from this they became mature and were made fit to bear the burden. And then they suffered everything for Christ with greater joy, while he was absent in body, than they had when they lived in peace and tranquillity with Christ present with them. So it is with all of us. For in Christ we grow up gradually, for as long as it takes to reach maturity and the stature of a righteous man. The Lord spares us for as long as he does not judge us to be mature enough. But when he sees us mature and sufficiently strengthened, not by our own strength but by his, then he lays the burden on our shoulders in proportion to our powers.

units.la: 5 Nunc autem abeo ad eum qui misit me, & nemo ex vobis interrogat me, dicens, Quò abis?
units.tr: 5 But now I go to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, Where are you going?

units.la: 6 Sed quia haec loquutus sum vobis, tristitia impleuit cor vestrum.
units.tr: 6 But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.

units.la: 7 Sed ego veritatem dico vobis, confert vobis vt ego abeam. Nisi enim abiero, Aduocatus ille non veniet ad vos: sin autem profectus fuero, mittam eum ad vos.
units.tr: 7 But I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.

units.la: REprehensio est, q. d. Non potius lætentur decessu eius, quàm de eo doleant: siue quòd intemperanter & supra modum doleant. Potiùs, inquit, quærendum fuit quò abeam, ad hoc vt cognoscentes quò abeā, nēpe ad Patrem, & meo & vestro bono lætare mini. At vero quia dixi me abituru, cor vestrum implebitur tristitia, acsi de me & de vobis actum esset. Discipuli Christi vsque adeo conquiescebant in corporali illa Christi præsentia, vt nihil supra exoptarent: nec de alia felicitate vel illius vel sua ipsorum serio cogitarent. Ideo quoties audierunt aliquid de eius ab ipsis discessu, ita doluerunt, acsi nulla felicitas expectanda esset imposterum. Nam haud dubiè hæc ab aliis fiebant ex carnali quodam sensu. Eo sumus ingenio omnes, vt si requies aliqua concedatur nobis in hac vita, si satis diuitiarum, satis gloriæ, satis voluptatis, satis amicorum & familiarium, non nisi difficillimè patiamur vel nos diuelli ab his ipsis rebus, vel eas diuelli à nobis: neque vel cogitemus vel audiamus de seperatione aliqua, nisi cum dolore.
