I came forth from the Father. This he had said obscurely above, in the parable of verse 16, and now, by the occasion of the words that follow, he states it plainly. It must be observed that he did not at once tell the disciples plainly that he would depart, but in the middle he supplied a manifold matter of consolation, with the evident purpose that they might bear more calmly the plain talk about his departure, which some of them took very badly. From this we learn how gently the Lord spares his own, and that he is unwilling to afflict them with sadness, not only by deed but not even by word. Therefore he instructs and prepares their minds before he brings forward the more grievous matters, so that they may bear them with a calmer spirit. Let this be an example to us for ever, that we never rashly and at once afflict anyone with sadness, and that we always deal with everyone with some gentleness and compassion. I see that Paul did this, who not only urged others to rebuke with teaching and gentleness, but also went before them with his own example, and in every part of his ministry he used gentleness. All his rebukes to the Galatians and the Corinthians indicate this, which we see are always softened and, as it were, seasoned with a certain sweetness. He says that he has therefore not yet come to them, for no other reason than that he might spare them, and afterwards not afflict them with sadness. By this he signifies that he descended to rebukes only unwillingly, and that he abstained from every occasion of reproof. Also worth noting is the form in which he presents this news, both welcome and unwelcome, of his departure. In presenting the welcome and the sad news, he uses a form by which, even in signifying his departure, he consoles them. For he says that he leaves the world and goes to the Father, that is, that he may sit gloriously at his right hand. From this place it will follow that he consoles them more than he ever did while he lived with them on earth. This is exactly how we should act: sad and grievous things should be presented in a form that makes the grievous somewhat lighter. For example, if someone were now to say (which is very grievous and sad) that Christ will depart and migrate from this nation of ours, but that meanwhile it will go well for those who grieve earnestly over his departure.

units.la: 29 Dicunt ei discipuli eius, Ecce nunc aperte loqueris, nec similitudinem vllam dicis.
units.tr: 29 His disciples say to him, Lo, now you speak plainly, and use no figure at all.

units.la: 30 Nunc scimus te scire omnia, nec opus esse tibi, vt quis te interroget: per hoc credimus te à Deo prodiisse.
units.tr: 30 Now we know that you know all things, and that there is no need for anyone to question you; by this we believe that you came forth from God.

units.la: HActenus loquutus est Dominus: nunc respondent discipuli: ac primùm quidem indicant gaudium animi ex intellecto iam ipsius sermone, quem instituit de decessu suo quem supra versu decimosexto obscurè & per parabolam proposuit. Neque enim parum vtilitas est ei, qui cupit discere & proficere in schola Christi, quoties aliquid quod scitu necessarium est aperte dicitur. Neque solum tenentur Ministri verbi sanam ac veram doctrinam proponere, sed etiam ea forma, & iis verbis oportet eam proponere, quæ & competunt in materiam subiectam & intelligi possunt à populo, & si fieri possit etiam ab idiota aliquo: verba enim spiritualia cum spiritualibus rebus coniungenda sunt. Quæ etiam loquimur, inquit Paulus, non sermonibus quos docet humana sapientia, sed quos docet Spiritus sanctus, Spiritualibus, &c. Verba etiam aperta esse debent, & obuia populo, vt supra eodem capite, versu 4. Neque oratio & praedicatio mea, suasit Apostolus, versata est in persuasoriis humanae sapientiae verbis, sed in demonstratione spiritualis potentiae. Et postea: Cuiusmodi ipsem habeamus, multa in loquendo euidentia vtimur. Item cap. 4.3. Quod si tectum est nostrum Euangelium, tectum est iis qui pereunt. Et Galatis dicit ea euidentia praedicatum iis à se Euangelium, vt ob oculos Iesus Christus prius fuerit depictus, inter eos crucifixus. Contrà verò volenti lenti proficere in cognitione veritatis, tristitiam affert obscurus sermo,& animum perplexum relinquit, vt vidimus supra vers.17. Quanti facit Paulus sermonem illum qui est ad captum auditorum accommodatus. Vide 1. Corinth.14.19. Malim in Ecclesia, inquit, quinque verba ex intelligentia mea loqui, vt & alios instituam quàm decem millia verborum lingua. Nunc scimus. Hoc secundum est quod respondent: profitentur Christum ἀρχηγὸν esse, ac proinde credere seipsum à Patre venisse. Nec opus est. Hoc ideo dicunt, quia supra cùm quaererent inter se antequam Christum interrogarent, de eo quod obscurè ab ipso dictum est, Paulisper & non conspicietis me, &c. Cū, inquam, supra quaererent inter se, Christus tum cognouit voluisse eos ipsum interrogare, & interrogationem eorū praeoccupauit. Hic solum quaerendum est quaenam ista sit eorum fides quam profitentur? Profecto non esse illam fidem satis firmam ac solidā apparet ex illa Christi responsione quae sequitur, qua reprehendit huiusmodi fidei venditationem: sed fundamentum eius examinandum est hoc loco: Non quidem dicunt, Dixisti te venisse à Patre, & iturum ad Patrem, ac propterea credimus. Quod si enim fides eorum fundata fuisset in verbo, profecto solidior ea fuisset. Sed cùm nitatur miraculo Christi facto in indicando ipsis sensa mentis suae, profecto non satis firmum est fundamentum. Nam potentia Dei, sapientia Dei, iustitia Dei in operibus, sive ordinariis, sive extraordinariis inspecta, possunt quidem animū praeparare ad fidem ac confirmare eum aliquo modo in fide, sed fidem gignere in animo non possunt: Vnde Paulus de mundo isto, Postquam, inquit, in Dei sapientia mundus non cognovit Deum ex eius sapientia, placuit Deo per stultam praedicationem seruare credentes. Et re vera sermo crucis Christi vtcunque stultus videatur esse mundo, is est qui fidem gignit in cordibus nostris. Est enim potentia Dei, non externa, qualis est illa, quae est in miraculis edendis, sed interna & organum Spiritus sancti est speciale, quo mentem illuminat, & cor aperit. Vide supra cap.9. 1. historiam de eo qui caecus fuerat à nativitate. Is miraculo in se edito, coepit quidem rectè ac reverenter de Christo sentire; sed tamen non credidit,
units.tr: Hitherto the Lord has spoken; now the disciples answer. First they show the joy of their minds at the sermon, now understood, which he had delivered about his departure, and which he had set forth obscurely and by a parable above, at verse 16. For it is of no small use to one who desires to learn and make progress in the school of Christ, whenever something that needs to be known is said plainly. Ministers of the Word are bound not only to set forth sound and true doctrine, but also to set it forth in a form and in words that both suit the matter in hand and can be understood by the people, and, if possible, even by some unlearned person. For spiritual words must be joined with spiritual things. Paul says: we speak these things not in words which man's wisdom teaches, but which the Holy Spirit teaches, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. The words also ought to be plain and open to the people, as the Apostle urged above in the same chapter, verse 4: my speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the power of the Spirit. And afterwards: since we have such a hope, we use great plainness of speech. Likewise chapter 4, verse 3: But if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. And he says to the Galatians that the gospel was preached by him with such clearness that Jesus Christ had first been painted before their eyes, crucified among them. On the other hand, to one who is slow to make progress in the knowledge of the truth, an obscure speech brings sadness, and leaves the mind perplexed, as we saw above at verse 17. How highly Paul esteems that speech which is adapted to the capacity of the hearers! See 1 Cor. 14:19: I would rather speak five words in the Church with my understanding, that I may teach others, than ten thousand words in a tongue. Now we know. This is the second thing they answer: they profess that Christ is the author [ἀρχηγόν] and therefore believe that he came from the Father. There is no need. They say this because above, before they asked Christ, they were questioning among themselves about what he had said obscurely, a little while, and you shall not see me, and so on. Christ, I say, knew that while they were questioning among themselves above, they wished to ask him, and he anticipated their question. Here we need only ask what kind of faith this is that they profess. Surely it is apparent that it is not a sufficiently firm and solid faith, from that answer of Christ which follows, in which he rebukes such a boasting of faith. But its foundation must be examined at this point. They do not say: You said that you came from the Father and would go to the Father, and therefore we believe. For if their faith had been founded on the Word, it would surely have been more solid. But since it rests on the miracle of Christ in showing them the thoughts of their minds, surely the foundation is not firm enough. For the power of God, the wisdom of God, and the justice of God, observed in works, whether ordinary or extraordinary, can indeed prepare the mind for faith and confirm it in faith in some measure, but they cannot beget faith in the mind. Hence Paul, speaking of this world: since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through its wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. And truly the word of the cross of Christ, however foolish it may seem to the world, is what begets faith in our hearts. For it is the power of God, not external, such as that which is in performing miracles, but internal, and it is the special instrument of the Holy Spirit, by which he illumines the mind and opens the heart. See above, chapter 9, verse 1, the history of the man who had been blind from birth. Though a miracle was done in him, he began indeed to think rightly and reverently about Christ, but nevertheless he did not believe, until Christ instructed him by his word.

units.la: 1. Cor.1.22. priusquam Christus verbo suo ipsum instruxisset. Credisne, inquit, in filium Dei?
units.tr: 1. Cor. 1.22. before Christ had instructed him by his word. "Do you believe," he says, "in the Son of God?"

units.la: 31 Respondit ei Iesus, Nunc creditis?
units.tr: 31 Jesus answered them, Do you now believe?

units.la: 32 Ecce venient tempus, & iam venit, quum dispergemini unusquisque ad sua, meque solum relinquetis: sed non sum solus: nam pater mecum est.
units.tr: 32 Behold, the time is coming, and is already here, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me.

units.la: 33 Haec locutus sum vobis, ut in me pacem habeatis. In mundo oppressionem habebitis: sed confidite, ego vici mundum.
units.tr: 33 I have said these things to you, that you may have peace in me. In the world you will have tribulation, but take heart: I have overcome the world.

units.la: CHristus fidem illam, quam iactabant refellit, ex effectis futuris: erant enim ipsum deserturi. Vide igitur quàm euanida sit fides ea quae nititur miraculis, quae non poterit ferre calorem persequutionis, quae etiam in ipsam persequutionem nonnunquam definit supra cap. 2. 23. & deinceps. Multi, inquit, crediderunt in nomine eius, conspicientes signa quae edebat. Sed quid tum de Christo dictum? Noluit se iis credere: cognoscit enim quid esset in homine. Sed quaeres, An fides Apostolorum tantum in miraculis fuerit fundata? Respondeo idem ipsorum etiam in verbo Christi fuisse, & illam quidem veram ac iustificantem. Nam cum Christus discipulis dixisset, Quem me dicitis esse? Respondet Simon Petrus ac dixit, Tu es Christus ille filius Dei viuentis. Ac fiduciam ipsorum carne permistam fuisse satis apparet ex aliis locis & confisos eos fuisse Christo, propter respectus aliquos carnales: praeterquam enim quod Christo praesente, & una comorante cum iis, nihil aduersi sunt perpessi, sperabant enim regem terrenum eum futurum. Et, ut verbo dicam, cognouerunt Christum secundum carnem, hoc est, carnalia & mundana. Sic enim loquitur Apostolus, 2. Corinth. 5. Quod si nihil aliud esset quod id argueret, profecto audacia ista ac superbia cum fide sua, quae tū hoc loco conspicitur cum Matt. 26. 33. 34. vbi Petrus dixit se moriturum prius quàm derelicturus esset Christum. Itidem & alij omnes dixerunt: hoc, inquam, satis arguit fidem, siue fiduciam eorum magis carnalem fuisse. Nam fiducia ista carnis semper superba est: fiducia vero Spiritualis humilis & cum timore con-
units.tr: Christ refutes that faith in which they boasted, by the outcome that was to come: for they were going to desert him. See then how empty is a faith that rests on miracles, a faith that cannot bear the heat of persecution, and that sometimes even ends in persecution itself (see above, ch. 2, vv. 23 and following). "Many," he says, "believed in his name, seeing the signs which he did." But what was said then about Christ? "He would not trust himself to them, for he knew what was in man." But you will ask: was the faith of the apostles founded on miracles alone? I answer that their faith was also in the word of Christ, and that it was indeed true and justifying. For when Christ had said to the disciples, "Whom do you say that I am?", Simon Peter answered and said, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Matt. 16.16). Yet that their trust was mixed with flesh is sufficiently clear from other passages, and that they trusted in Christ on account of certain carnal considerations: for apart from the fact that, while Christ was present and dwelling with them, they suffered no adversity, they hoped that he would be an earthly king. And, to put it in a word, they knew Christ according to the flesh, that is, in carnal and worldly terms. For so the Apostle speaks (2 Cor. 5.16). But even if there were nothing else to prove this, their boldness and pride, along with their faith, which is seen here, would surely do so, compare Matt. 26.33-34, where Peter said that he would die before he deserted Christ. Likewise all the others said the same. This, I say, sufficiently shows that their faith, or rather their confidence, was more carnal. For that carnal confidence is always proud, whereas spiritual faith is humble and joined with fear.

units.la: {a} Discipulorum fides etiam in verbum Christi fuit. Mat. 16. 16
units.tr: {a} The faith of the disciples was also in the word of Christ. Matt. 16.16

units.la: Sed variis infirmitatibus labo- rauit. iuncta. Tu per fidem stas, ne effertor animo, sed time. Ecce cum fide vera coniunctus est timor ex infirmitate naturae, ne per eam deficiamus a fide. Neque tum sequitur fidem cum dubitatione esse coniuncta. Aliud enim est metuere ex infirmitate, aliud est dubitare. Deinde quaeri potest hoc loco, Annon Dominus destruat hac praedictione defectionis eorum totam illam consolationem, quam supra aedificavit. Respondeo non minus necessarium esse deiicere vanam fiduciam ac superbiam animi, quam erigere animum deiectum. Neque praeparationem aliam magis necessariam ante diem persequutionis esse, qua quae est in exploranda fide sive fiducia, sitne ea ex carne & sanguine, an vero ex spiritu: fiducia enim sive confidentia fallit saepe, & natura ista nostra fallax est. Ideo laborandum ut distinguamus inter motus carnis & Spiritus; ac sentiamus nos infirmos natura, ut spiritu firmi simus: potentia enim Christi per infirmitatem perficitur. Sed non sum solus. Ne illud offenderet eos quod dixit se solum relinquendum, hoc per correctionem subiecit. Ex quo discimus non deseruisse Patrem Filium suum unquam, ne tum quidem cum questus est in haec verba, Deus meus, Deus meus, cur me deseruisti? Nam etiam tum Pater naturam humanam in Filio sustinuit sub pondere illo irae divinae, quae alioquin necessario succubuisset. Reliquit tamen eum ad tempus sine consolatione ac laetitia, tum cum in summis mortis doloribus haereret: Quomodo quidem non solet derelinquere Martyres. Sic Paulus ait, Omnes me deseruerunt, sed Dominus mihi adfuit, & me corroboravit. Ecce consolationem & corroborationem. Causa discriminis est, Quia Christus sustinuit peccati poenam nostra vice, & punitus est propter peccata nostra ex ira Dei; ubi nulla est consolatio: Martyres vero affliguntur propter testimonium Christi, quod necesse est fiat cum gaudio inefabili, consolante eos Christo, ob cuius nomen patiuntur.
units.tr: But he laboured under various weaknesses. Joined. "You stand by faith; be not high-minded, but fear" (Rom. 11.20). Behold, fear arising from the weakness of our nature is joined with true faith, lest through that weakness we fall away from faith. Nor does it follow that faith is joined with doubt. For to fear because of weakness is one thing; to doubt is another. Next it may be asked here whether the Lord, by this prediction of their defection, does not destroy all the comfort he had built up above. I answer that it is no less necessary to cast down vain confidence and the pride of the mind than to raise up a downcast spirit. Nor is there any preparation more necessary before the day of persecution than to test faith, or confidence, whether it is of flesh and blood or truly of the Spirit: for confidence often deceives, and our nature is deceitful. Therefore we must labour to distinguish between the motions of the flesh and of the Spirit, and to feel ourselves weak by nature, so that we may be strong in the Spirit, for the power of Christ is made perfect in weakness. "But I am not alone." Lest this should offend them, that he said he must be left alone, he added a correction. From this we learn that the Father never forsook his Son, not even when he cried out in these words, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" For even then the Father sustained the human nature in the Son under the weight of that divine wrath, which otherwise would necessarily have overcome it. Yet he left him for a time without consolation and joy, when he was clinging to the extreme pains of death. This is not how he is wont to forsake martyrs. So Paul says, "All forsook me, but the Lord stood by me and strengthened me" (2 Tim. 4.16-17). Behold, consolation and strengthening. The cause of the difference is this: Christ bore the punishment of sin in our place, and was punished for our sins by the wrath of God, where there is no consolation; but the martyrs are afflicted for the testimony of Christ, which must be borne with inexpressible joy, Christ consoling them, for whose name they suffer.

units.la: Haec locutus sum vobis. Concludit sermonem hunc, significatque tendere ad pacem eorum quaecunque dixit. Ergo hic finis est omnium verborum Christi & totius Euangelij, ut fruamur illa pace Christi. Ergo in pace ista est felicitas nostra. Quid enim aliud est quàm regnum illud cœlorum inchoatum in hac vita? Regnū Dei iustitia est, & pax, & gaudium per Spiritum sanctū. Quare qui nullo certè modo fruitur hac pace, is profectò frustra audit Euangelium, & nihil fructus decerpit vel ex Christo, vel ex beneficiis ipsius. Tum ne forte somniarent pacē eam quæ expers esset omnis afflictionis, subiicit cōtinuò: In mundo oppressionem habebitis, quasi dicat: Ne cogitate pacem meam futuram expertem omnis oppressionis & afflictionis in mundo. Imò verò cogitate pacem meam futuram cum oppressione: Atque ita quidem res se habet. Pax hæc interna conscientiarum est cum externa inquietudine. Cœli sunt cum sensu aliquo inferorum, lætitia est cum dolore, adeóque fluit ipsa ex dolore. Ac tum demum serio lætamur, cùm serio dolemus de peccatis nostris. Armat interea eos adversus oppressionem omnem à finali victoria, qua potientur: eam autem significat dum dicit se vicisse mundum: huius consequens est victoria nostra, si modo fide in ipsum habeamus. Nam hæc est victoria, quæ vicit mundum. Ergo nobis certamen est cum diabolo & mundo, non de victoria ipsa, sed de fide, qua quidem adhæreamus ei qui vicit diabolum & mundum. Nam quòd ad victoriam, iam parta est per Christum. Diabolus autem & mundus iam victi oppugnant fidem nostram: ut nos, si fieri posset, separent ab eo, qui vicit ipsos, ne simus ipsius victoriæ participes, ac proinde pereamus. Quamobrem omnis conatus noster esse debet, non quidem ut nos per nos diabolum & mundum vincamus, sed vtnò sinamus nos vnquam à victore illo Christo diuelli. Atque hæc est spiritualis illa lucta nostra, quam describit Apostolus, Ephes.6. Soli igitur victori Christo sit omnis gloria: Amen.
units.tr: I have said these things to you. He concludes this discourse, and signifies that all that he has said tends to their peace. Therefore this is the goal of all the words of Christ and of the whole gospel, that we may enjoy that peace of Christ. In this peace, then, lies our happiness. For what else is it but that kingdom of heaven begun in this life? "The kingdom of God is righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Rom. 14.17). Therefore he who in no way enjoys this peace certainly hears the gospel in vain, and gathers no fruit either from Christ or from his benefits. Then, lest perhaps they should dream of a peace free from all affliction, he immediately adds: "In the world you will have tribulation," as if to say: Do not think that my peace will be free from all oppression and affliction in the world. Rather, think that my peace will be with oppression: and indeed this is how things stand. This inner peace of conscience is with outward unrest. There is heaven with some sense of hell; joy is with grief, and indeed flows from grief. And we rejoice in earnest only when we grieve in earnest over our sins. Meanwhile he arms them against all oppression by the final victory, which they will obtain; and he signifies it when he says that he has overcome the world. Our victory follows from this, if only we have faith in him. For this is the victory that has overcome the world. Therefore our struggle is with the devil and the world, not over victory itself, but over faith, by which we may cleave to him who has overcome the devil and the world. As for the victory, it has already been won through Christ. The devil and the world, though already conquered, attack our faith, so that, if it were possible, they might separate us from him who has conquered them, lest we share in his victory and so perish. Wherefore all our effort ought to be, not that we overcome the devil and the world by our own strength, but that we never allow ourselves to be torn away from that victorious Christ. And this is that spiritual struggle of ours, which the Apostle describes, Eph. 6. To Christ the victor alone, therefore, be all glory: Amen.

units.la: Ecclesiæ conditio in terris.
units.tr: The condition of the Church on earth.

units.la: Tandem etiam in cœlis.
units.tr: Even in heaven at last.

units.la: Conatus noster quàm esse debet.
units.tr: How our endeavour ought to be.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Hoc capite continetur precatio Christi quam habuit tanquam populi Dei summus sacerdos, quum suum ipsius corpus paulo post in ara crucis oblaturus esset: qua & seipsum & populum suum Patri commendat. Constat autem precatio haec tribus partibus. Primùm enim orat pro se ipso ad versum usque sextum. Deinde pro discipulis, à vers. 6. usque ad 20. Postremò pro reliquis electis, qui per Apostolorum doctrinam credituri erant usque ad finem Mundi.
units.tr: In this chapter is contained the prayer of Christ, which he offered as the high priest of God's people, shortly before he was to offer his own body on the altar of the cross. In it he commends both himself and his people to the Father. The prayer has three parts. First, he prays for himself, to verse 6. Second, he prays for his disciples, from verse 6 to verse 20. Last, he prays for the other elect, who were to believe through the teaching of the Apostles until the end of the world.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: 1 Haec loquutus est Iesus, & sustulit oculos suos in coelum, dixitque, Pater, venit hora illa, glorifica Filium tuum, ut & te Filius tuus glorificet,
units.tr: 1 When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven and said, Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee,

units.la: 2 Sicut dedisti ei auctoritatem in omnem carnem, ut quotquot dedisti ei det ijs vitam aeternam.
units.tr: 2 As thou hast given him power over all flesh, that he should give eternal life to as many as thou hast given him.

units.la: 3 Haec est autem vita aeterna, ut te cognoscant esse illum solum verum Deum, & quem misisti Iesum Christum.
units.tr: 3 And this is life eternal, that they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent.

units.la: CVM Christus, quo tempore in terris ageret, intercesserit pro nobis apud Patrem, partim precibus, partim pretio redemptionis & unico illo sacrificio sui ipsius corporis, profecto inter complures alias quas omni tempore concepit preces, ista, quae hoc capite continetur, oratio imprimis insignis atque excellens, idque sive tempus respicias quo orauit: (orauit autem paulo antequam caperetur à Iudeis & crucifigeretur) sive respicias usum huius orationis. Hac enim oratione paulo ante morte concepta, seipsum consecrauit Deo in sacrificiu aeternum: sive respicias materiam huius orationis.Primùm enim precatur pro gloria sua, qua re quid excellentius inueniri potest, ad ver-sum vsque 6. Deinde orat pro discipulis suis eorùmque conseruatione, inde ad versum vsque 10. Tertiò denique orat in genere pro electis omnibus ab eo versu ad finem vsque capitis: siue denique respicias vim ac virtutem huius orationis quæ non est ad tempus aliquod certum,sed durat in perpetuum, & electi omnes virtute huius orationis seruandi sunt. Quare non immeritò dicetur salus nostra,vt in omnibus Christi precibus, ita in his precibus præsertim, tanquam fundamento quodam suo consistere. Primùm hoc loco est transitio facta per Euangelistam, qua paucis concludit sermonem illum Christi qui cum discipulis fuit. Hæc, inquit, loquutus est Iesus. Deinde proponit Christum precatum esse. Etsu-stulit oculos,&c. Propositio continet gestum precaturi.De hoc gestu legimus supra cap.11.41. dum gratias ageret Patri quòd ipsum audiret,quo nimirum tempore Lazarum ex mortuis exsuscitaret. Hoc corporis gestu externo ostendit oculos mentis eleuatos esse ad Patrem. Proficiscitur enim gestus isti externi(cum sint ac veri) ab aliqua mentis ac cordis interiori affectione: vel ex cordis humiliatione, vt est flexus genuum: vel ex cordis eleuatione, vt est eleuatio oculorum.Optimè au-tem inter se consentiunt duo isti gestus, flexus genuum & eleuatio oculorum, vel etiam manuum. Nam non eleuantur nisi humiliato iam priùs animo: neque datur cuiquam intueri Deum, nisi supplici & ad pedes ipsius abiecto. Sed de gestu eius hactenus:Nunc veniamus ad primam precum partem.Primum est petitio pro se suaque gloria. Pater,inquit,glorifica filium tuum. Dum com-pellat Patrem,simul se Filium vocat:his blandis appel-lationibus satis indicat ex filiali qui dicitur amore se precatū esse.Fieri autem non potest, vt Deus non obuiā veniat filiali amori in precibus, paterno illo suo amore.Quod si velimus Dei paternū erga nos amorem conciliare, videamus vt nos filiali erga ipsum amore precemur,& precemur per Spiritum illum adoptionis, qui testatur in cordibus nostris, nos esse Dei filios, dilatatqj os nostrum, vt clamemus Abba pater.Appellationes igi-tur zut quibus vel Deum vel etiam nosipsos insignimus inter precandum, sapiant illum amorem tenerrimum filiorum erga Patrem suum: cui necesse est Deus occurrat mutuo, ac vicem quasi rependat, precesque nostras exaudiat. Nouit enim Deus, quis sit sensus sui Spiritus. Licet autem nobis in Christo Iesu naturali illo Dei filio rum Deum patrem appellare, tum nos ipsos Dei filios.
units.tr: Since Christ, while he was on earth, interceded for us with the Father, partly by prayers and partly by the price of redemption, that is, by that one sacrifice of his own body, this prayer contained in this chapter is surely outstanding and excellent among the many other prayers he offered at all times. This is so whether you consider the time when he prayed (he prayed shortly before he was seized by the Jews and crucified), or the use of this prayer. For by this prayer, offered shortly before his death, he consecrated himself to God as an eternal sacrifice. Or consider the matter of the prayer. First, he prays for his own glory, than which nothing more excellent can be found, to verse 6. Second, he prays for his disciples and their preservation, from there to verse 10. Third, he prays in general for all the elect, from that verse to the end of the chapter. Finally, consider the force and power of this prayer, which is not limited to a certain time but lasts forever, and by the power of this prayer all the elect are to be kept. So it is rightly said that our salvation rests, as all of Christ's prayers do, but especially these prayers, on this as on a certain foundation. First, the Evangelist makes a transition here, briefly concluding that discourse of Christ which he had with the disciples: These things, he says, Jesus spoke. Then he states that Christ prayed: And lifted up his eyes, and so on. This statement contains the posture of the one praying. We read of this posture above, in chapter 11, verse 41, where he gave thanks to the Father for hearing him, namely at the time when he was about to raise Lazarus from the dead. By this outward bodily posture he shows that his mind's eyes were lifted up to the Father. For outward gestures, which are true signs, arise from some inner affection of mind and heart: either from humbling of the heart, as in the bending of the knees, or from lifting up of the heart, as in the lifting of the eyes. Now these two gestures, the bending of the knees and the lifting of the eyes, or even of the hands, agree very well together. For no one lifts up his eyes unless his mind is already humbled, and no one can look upon God except when he has cast himself down as a suppliant at his feet. But enough of his posture. Now let us come to the first part of the prayer. The first thing is a petition for himself and his own glory. Father, he says, glorify thy Son. While he addresses the Father, he at the same time calls himself the Son. By these tender names he sufficiently indicates that he prayed out of filial love. It is not possible that God should not meet with filial love in prayers, that fatherly love of his own. If we want to win God's fatherly love toward us, let us see that we pray with filial love toward him, and pray through that Spirit of adoption, who testifies in our hearts that we are God's sons, and opens our mouths so that we cry, Abba, Father. Therefore the names by which we designate God, or even ourselves, in praying, should savour of that most tender love of sons toward their father. To this love God must necessarily respond in return, as it were repaying it, and hear our prayers. For God knows what is the meaning of his own Spirit. Yet we may call God our Father, and ourselves God's sons, in Christ Jesus, that natural Son of God.

units.la: Sed videamus petitionis summam, Glorifica, inquit, filium tuum. De gloria ista quam petit, postea habemus verf. 5. Est autem ea gloria quam habuit ipse apud Patrem suum, priusquam mundus exisseret. Exstat insignis locus in Epistola ad Philip. Cum de gloria filii Dei quam ab aeterno cum Patre habuit ante manifestationem in carne, tum de humiliatione ipsius & abdicatione illius gloriae, tum quae ad tempus fuit. Denique de recuperatione eiusdem gloriae, ipsiusque denuo filij exaltatione. Qui, inquit, cum esset in forma Dei, non duxit rapinam esse aequalem esse cum Deo. Hic habes gloriam illam quam tum cum Patre suo habuit ab aeterno. Tum subiungit, Sed ipse exinanivit sumpta serui forma, &c. Hic primus est humiliationis gradus: secundus vero est his verbis, & habitu compertus ut homo, &c. quae est extrema Christi humiliatio. Postremo sequitur gloriae ipsius recuperatio verbis magnificis exposita. Quapropter cum exaltauit Deus, &c. Recuperatae gloriae magnificam & plane huic similem descriptionem habes in epistola ad Ephesios. Quem, inquit, ex mortuis excitauit, & collocauit ad dextram suam in coelis, &c. Loquitur hic Christus, fateor, ut aeternus Pontifex & Mediator noster, hoc est, ut Deus & homo est simul ac Deus. Quare etiam petit sibi humanae naturae glorificationem. Sed illud tamen aperte conspicitur ex versu 5. cum petere praesertim gloriam filij Dei & τῶ λόγῳ petit enim illic esse gloriam quam cum Patre habuit, antequam mundus exisseret. Ea autem est gloria filij Dei. Nam quod ad humanae naturae gloriam, ea effectus est quidem necessario consequens gloriam illam Deitatis habitantis corporaliter in ipsa. Quare ipsam petit tantum ex consequenti. Consistit autem in resurrectione ex mortuis, ascensione in coelos, sessione ad dextram sistat.
units.tr: But let us look at the sum of the petition: Glorify, he says, thy Son. We have about this glory which he asks for, later in verse 5. It is the glory which he had with his own Father before the world existed. There is a notable passage in the Epistle to the Philippians, which speaks of the glory of the Son of God which he had from eternity with the Father before his manifestation in the flesh; then of his humiliation and laying aside of that glory, which was for a time; and finally of the recovery of the same glory and the new exaltation of the Son. Who, it says, being in the form of God, did not count it robbery to be equal with God. Here you have that glory which he had with his Father from eternity. Then it adds, But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and so on. This is the first degree of humiliation; the second is in these words, and being found in fashion as a man, and so on, which is the extreme humiliation of Christ. Last follows the recovery of his glory, set out in magnificent words: Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and so on. In the Epistle to the Ephesians you have a magnificent description of the recovered glory, quite similar to this: Whom he raised from the dead, and set at his own right hand in the heavens, and so on. I admit that Christ speaks here as our eternal High Priest and Mediator, that is, as God and man at once, but as God. Therefore he also asks for the glorification of his human nature. Yet it is clearly seen from verse 5 that he asks especially for the glory of the Son of God, and of the Word [τῷ λόγῳ]. For there he asks for the glory which he had with the Father before the world existed. This glory is the glory of the Son of God. As for the glory of the human nature, it is indeed an effect that necessarily follows from that glory of the Godhead dwelling bodily in it. Therefore he asks for it only as a consequence. It consists in the resurrection from the dead, the ascension into heaven, and the sitting at the right hand of God.

units.la: Petitionis summa. Glorificatio filii Dei. Phil. 2.6. &c. Status multiplex Christi. Cuius gloriae hic mentio habetur. In quo constat. Patris: quæ partes gloriæ, quid sunt aliud quàm effectus quidam gloriæ filij Dei & Deitatis sese manifestantis? Vnde Paulus dicit Christum declaratum esse Dei filium secundum Spiritum sanctificationis per resurrectionem ex mortuis. Cùm enim Deitas se exereret & patefaceret, tum collustrauit quasi radiis gloriæ suæ tabernaculum illud humani corporis, in quo ipse habitat. Non secus acsi inferas in domũ tenebricosam insigne ac gloriosam lucé aliquâ quæ tenebras dispellat, & domũ ipsam radiis suis ac splendore suo illustret. Hactenus fuit petitio gloriæ.
units.tr: The sum of the petition: the glorification of the Son of God. Phil. 2.6, etc. The manifold states of Christ. Here is mention of that glory. What it consists in. Of the Father. What are these parts of glory, but certain effects of the glory of the Son of God and of the Godhead making itself manifest? Hence Paul says that Christ was declared to be the Son of God according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection from the dead. For when the Godhead put itself forth and revealed itself, it then lit up, as it were with the rays of its glory, that tabernacle of the human body in which it dwells. It is as if you were to carry a remarkable and glorious light into a dark house, which would drive away the darkness and fill the house itself with its rays and splendour. So far was the petition for glory.

units.la: Nunc sequuntur argumenta petitionis: primum est à mortis propediem affuturæ præsentia. Venit, inquit, hora illa: Nempe mortis meæ & sacrificij offerendi: ergo me glorifica, & continuò libera à morte illa, quæ non modò in se terribilis futura est; sed etiam ignominiosa in oculis omnium, ac discipulis etiam ipsis offensioni. Quâobrem Christus cùm alias perpetuò gloriam illam, vel gloriæ suæ recuperationem à Patre petiisset, tum hoc tempore maximè eam petiit, quia eum vrgebat iã mortis præsentia. Appropinquante enim morte vrgeri oportet nos ad ferium gloriæ ac vitæ æternæ desiderium. Non enim oportet deponere istam vitam, quam nunc viuimus in carne, nisi certi prius ac persuasi nos recepturos alteram illam & gloriosam. Paulus quidem sciuit cùm terrestris domus hæc tabernaculi, hoc est corporis ipsius dissoluta esset, recepturum se ex Deo ædificium non manufactum, sed æternum in cœlis. Certitudo autem hæc & persuasio firma, precibus ad Deum obtinetur: quibus fit, ut in ipsa morte mittamur in eius possessionem certè aliquam, & non tam moriamur quâ obdormiamus in Christo Iesu, ut cum Apostolo loquar. Eos qui obdormierunt in Iesu adducet cum eo. Vt & filius tuus. Hoc petitionis secundū est argumentū, à gloriæ compensatione, id quod indicat & particula, Et: significat enim parè gloriæ compensationē. Ita enim res habet: Filius Dei copensat Patrem suũ mutua glorificatione. Data enim & communicata sibi à Patre gloriā, totā in Patrē rursus reponit ac reddundare facit: adeo vt nihil plane de Patris gloria decedat, quòd eam totam cum filio suo communicet. Imò verò hinc existit Patris summa gloria.
units.tr: Now follow the arguments of the petition. The first is from the presence of death, which is soon to come: The hour is come, he says: namely of my death and of the offering of the sacrifice. Therefore glorify me, and at once deliver me from that death, which will be not only terrible in itself, but also ignominious in the eyes of all, and even a stumbling block to the disciples themselves. For this reason, although Christ had always asked the Father for that glory, or for the recovery of his glory, he asked for it most of all at this time, because the presence of death was already pressing upon him. For as death approaches, we ought to be urged to a serious desire for glory and eternal life. For we must not lay down this life which we now live in the flesh unless we are first certain and persuaded that we shall receive the other, glorious life. Paul indeed knew that when this earthly house of the tabernacle, that is, of the body itself, was dissolved, he would receive from God a building not made with hands, but eternal in the heavens. This certainty and firm persuasion is obtained from God by prayer, and by prayer it comes about that in death itself we are sent into some real possession of that life, and we do not so much die as fall asleep in Christ Jesus, to use the words of the Apostle: Those who sleep in Jesus, God will bring with him. That thy Son also may: this is the second argument of the petition, drawn from the compensation of glory, which the particle also indicates, for it signifies a like compensation of glory. For the matter stands thus: the Son of God repays his Father with mutual glorification. For having received and been given the glory by the Father, he again puts it all back into the Father and makes it overflow to him, so that nothing at all is taken away from the Father's glory, since he shares the whole of it with his Son. Indeed, from this very thing comes the highest glory of the Father.

units.la: {Rom. 1. 4.} Petitionis argumenta. 1. Mortis instantis consideratio. 2. Gloriæ compensatio. tia, quòd Filium glorificet totámque suam gloriam cum Filio communicet, cùm reflectatur, vt sic loquar, & ad Patrem redeat, illum nimirum in quem sunt omnia, vt ait Apostolus, illa ipsa tota gloria, quam ipse cū filio suo communicauerat. Ita res habet in rebus creatis omnibus, quibus etiam partem aliquam Maiestatis illius & gloriæ suæ impertiuit. Nā nulla est vel scintilla gloriæ cōmunicatæ creaturæ cuiquam, quam non necesse sit in ipsum Deum datorem redundare, velit, nolit ipsa creatura. Quamobrem nobis hic videndū, non tantum vt gloria nobis à Deo communicata, in ipsum Deum redundet, (sed quod hic de Christo dictum est, quod nimirum ipse Patrem glorificaturus sit) vt nos ipsi instrumenta eius simus spontanea ac voluntaria illius gloriæ in ipsam regerendæ: secus profectò gloria nostra conuerteturin dedecus nostrū, & ipse se Deus glorificabit, ac talentum illud datum nobis ad hoc vt lucremur Domino, à nobis auferetur, & cedet in Dei ipsius gloriam sine nobis: ex quo, per quem, & in quem sunt omnia: ipsi sit gloria. Amen.
units.tr: {Rom. 1. 4.} The arguments of the petition: 1. the consideration of the approaching death; 2. the compensation of glory. For the Son glorifies the Father and shares with him the whole of his glory, which, so to speak, is reflected back and returns to the Father, namely to him in whom are all things, as the Apostle says, that very whole glory which he had shared with his Son. So it is with all created things, to which he has also imparted some part of his majesty and glory. For no spark of glory communicated to any creature can fail to return to God, the giver, whether the creature wills it or not. Therefore we must see here not only that the glory communicated to us by God returns to God himself (what is said here of Christ, that he will glorify the Father), but also that we ourselves should be willing and voluntary instruments for returning that glory to him. Otherwise our glory will be turned to our own shame, God will glorify himself, and that talent given to us so that we might gain something for the Lord will be taken from us and will pass to the glory of God without us. From him, through him, and to him are all things; to him be glory. Amen.

units.la: Sicut dedisti ei. Tertium argumentum est petitionis à vitæ æternæ quam tribuit electis postquam iam glorificatus est. Primum autem substernit fundamentum huius tantum beneficii, nempe authoritatem illam in omnem carnem datam sibi à Patre: Nam verba hæc non cū prioribus, sed posterioribus coniungenda sunt: ac si ita legatur contextus: Vt sicut dedisti ei authoritatem in omnem carnem, ita ipse det iis quos dedisti ei vitam æternam. Est igitur huius vitæ æternæ fundamentum authoritas illa quam Pater dedit Filio suo. Authoritas hæc planè regia est, & Christus eam obtinet, vt Rex. Patet autē ea ad omnem carnem, hoc est omnem hominem, ne vno quidem excepto, siue electo illo, siue reprobo: nam etiā reprobos iudicabit, supra cap. 5. Christus Matth. 28. 18. latius extedit eam, cūm dicit sibi à Patre datā omnem authoritatē in cœlis & in terris: ideóque etiam imperium obtinuit in Angelos ipsos, neque id tantùm quatenus Deus, sed etiam quatenus homo. Pater dedit filio authoritatem omnem & iudicium etiam, qua Filius hominis est, Iohan. 5. 27. Ab hac authoritate planè regia pe-
units.tr: As you have given him. The third argument of the petition is drawn from the eternal life which he bestows on the elect, after he has been glorified. Now he first lays the foundation of this so great benefit, namely that authority over all flesh which was given him by the Father. For these words are not to be joined with what precedes but with what follows, so that the sentence reads thus: that, as you have given him authority over all flesh, so he may give eternal life to those whom you have given him. The foundation of this eternal life is therefore the authority which the Father gave to his Son. This authority is truly royal, and Christ holds it as King. It extends to all flesh, that is, to every man, without exception, whether elect or reprobate; for he will judge even the reprobate, as above in chapter 5. Christ extends it more widely in Matthew 28.18, when he says that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him by the Father; and therefore he has also obtained dominion over the angels themselves, and this not only as God but also as man. The Father has given the Son all authority and also judgment, because he is the Son of man, John 5.27. From this truly royal authority the whole of this our ministry

units.la: {3} Vitæ æternæ pro electis petitio. det totum hoc ministerium nostrum. Ideóque postquā dixit, Pater dedit mihi omnem authoritatem, subiecit continuò, Itaque profecti docete omnes gentes baptizantes eos in nomine Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti. Ergo ab authoritate regia est prædicatio ista verbi cum administratione sacramentorum & disciplinæ. Neque verò authoritas ista est ipsorum ministrorum in Ecclesia, verùm authoritas est solius Christi. In hoc enim differt Minister aliquis Ecclesiæ à Magistratu politico: hic est cum imperio & authoritate sua, communicata, nimirum sibi à Deo. At verò Minister Ecclesiæ tantùm Minister est & famulus, non tam cum authoritate aliqua sua, sed cum authoritate Christi. Neque enim dixit Dominus discipulis suis, Ego dedi vobis authoritatem: ergo profecti docete, &c. Sed dixit, Pater dedit Filio authoritatem omnem: ergo profecti docete, &c. Quasi dixisset, Docete meà authoritate ac meo nomine: ac facite officium non dominorum sed servorum ac dispensatorum. Hactenus de fundamento domi vitæ æternæ, nunc de dono ipso: Verùm primùm considerandi veniunt ij quibus dandum sit donum hoc vitæ æternæ. Nonquibusvis sine discrimine dandum est, sed iis tantùm, qui dati sunt Filio à Patre, id est quos Pater ab æterno elegit, & in æterno consilio suo dedit filio. Nam in opere salutis nostræ distinguit scriptura partes Patris à partibus Filij: Pater ab æterno eligit seruandos idque in Filio. In tempore eos vocat per verbum suum, imò trahit intus per Spiritum suum sanctū. Nemo enim potest venire ad Filium, nisi Pater qui misit Filiū traxerit cum. Tum sibi à patre traditos seruat filius. De his distinctis partibus Patris & Filij, vide supra cap. 6. 44. & Epist. Iudae. 1. Vocatis, inquit, à Deo Patre sanctificatis & in Iesu Christo seruatis. Sed hic animaduersione digna est, vt huius doni vitæ æternæ Filius totam gloriam Patri tribuat: Authoritas enim ex qua dat vitam æternam, Patri ascribitur: Tum ij ipsi quibus datur vita, dantur primùm Filio à Patre: vt omnis salutis nostræ gloriam Patri scribat. In causa est, quia vocatio ad munus hoc redemptionis humanæ, à Patre fuit, ideóque Patri tribuere toties Filius omnem gloriam, quoties de parte aliqua redemptionis dicitur.
units.tr: {3} The petition for eternal life for the elect. derives. Therefore, after he said, "The Father has given me all authority," he immediately added, "Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." Thus the preaching of the Word, together with the administration of the sacraments and of discipline, springs from royal authority. Nor is this authority the ministers' own in the Church; it belongs to Christ alone. For in this a minister of the Church differs from the civil magistrate: the magistrate holds authority and power of his own, given to him by God; but the minister of the Church is only a minister and servant, not holding any authority of his own, but acting with the authority of Christ. The Lord did not say to his disciples, "I have given you authority; therefore go and teach," etc. He said, "The Father has given the Son all authority; therefore go and teach," etc. It is as if he had said, "Teach by my authority and in my name, and perform the office not of lords but of servants and stewards." So much for the foundation of the eternal life of the house; now for the gift itself. But first we must consider those to whom this gift of eternal life is to be given. It is not to be given to everyone indiscriminately, but only to those who have been given to the Son by the Father, that is, whom the Father from eternity chose and in his eternal counsel gave to the Son. For in the work of our salvation Scripture distinguishes the parts of the Father from the parts of the Son: the Father from eternity chooses those to be saved, and this in the Son; in time he calls them through his Word, and indeed draws them inwardly through his Holy Spirit. "No one can come to the Son unless the Father who sent the Son draws him" (John 6.44). Then the Son keeps those who have been handed over to him by the Father. On these distinct parts of the Father and the Son, see above chapter 6, verse 44, and Jude, verse 1: "To those who are called, sanctified by God the Father and kept in Jesus Christ." But here it is worth noting that the Son ascribes the whole glory of this gift of eternal life to the Father: the authority by which he gives eternal life is ascribed to the Father, and those very persons to whom life is given are first given to the Son by the Father, so that the whole glory of our salvation is ascribed to the Father. The reason is that the calling to this office of human redemption came from the Father; therefore the Son ascribes all glory to the Father whenever any part of the redemption is spoken of.

units.la: Ioan. 6. 44. demptionis nostræ loquitur. Quòd si Filius vocatus & missus à Patre gloriam totam eorum quæ facit ex ossi-cio suo tribuat: quid, quæso, nobis, qui serni sumus dignaxat in domo Dei, faciendum, qui mittimur à Patre & ab ipso vocamur, ad munus aliquod obeundum, vel in Ecclesia vel etiam in Republica?
units.tr: John 6.44. speaks of our redemption. But if the Son, called and sent by the Father, ascribes the whole glory of the things he does in his office to the Father, what, I ask, should we do, who are servants only in the house of God, who are sent by the Father and called by him to perform some office, whether in the Church or even in the commonwealth?

units.la: Nunc vtde vita ilta æterna paucis dicamus, videamus primùm qui quòrque sint fructus glorificationis Christi. Primùm glorificatur Pater ipse, deinde nos seruamur, vitámque æterna consequimur. Sed vt de vita æterna dicamus: Vita nostra æterna fit vi resurrectionis Christi: Quid enim est aliud vita Spiritualis nostra, quàm scintilla quædam vitæ illius, quæ in Christo ipso vsque adeo abundat? Et quid est Spiritus hic viuificus, qui nobis ad mensuram est datus, quàm portio quasi illius Spiritus vitæ, qui in Christo est non ad mensuram? Insignis est ille locus Pauli; Sicut complantati sumus cum eo similitudine mortis ipsius: ita complantabimur cum eo similitudine vitæ ipsius: quo significat & mortificatione veteris hominis esse virtute mortis & crucis Christi: & viuificationem noui hominis esse virtute vitæ Christi. Si enim non excitatus est Christus, nos adhuc in peccatu nostris sumus. Qui igitur cupit scire certò, an Christus pro ipso mortuus sit, videat is primùm an ipse mortuus sit peccato. Qui rursus scire cupit An Christus pro ipso resurrexerit, videat is an sentiat in se nouâ vitam. Quod si neque mortem peccati, neque nouam vitâ in se sentiat, profectò nihil habet quo sibi persuadeat Christum pro se mortuum esse. Hæc est autem vita. Nunc quæ sit necessitas glorificationis Christi ad vitam æternam, docetur ex definitione quadam vitæ æternæ: Vita æterna est cognoscere Patrem solum esse verû Deum, & quem misit Iesum Christum: At nulla est cognitio vel Patris, vel Filij, nisi glorificetur Filius. Ergo nulla est vita æterna, nisi glorificetur Filius. Huius syllogismi tatum habetur propositio in texu: quod ad verba, hæc est vita æterna vt te solum verum Deum. Non solum Deum dicit, sed solum verû Deû, neque solum verum Deum dicit, vt excludat Filium & Spiritum sanctum, qui sunt vnus idémque cum Patre Deus: sed vt excludat idola gentium & fictos deos qui tum passim in mundo habebantur pro diis. Nota igitur hic, vitam nostram in cognitione positam esse: Neque in cognitione cuiusuis, sed in cognitione fontis ipsius vitae: neque in nuda eius cognitione, sed in cognitione quae posita est in fide ac fiducia in fonte illo acquiescete & hauriente quasi vitam ex illo aeternam. Deus autem Pater is est, qui vitae omnis fons est, tum vitae Filij. Pater enim dedit Filio vitam in semetipso habere supra cap.5. tum vitae omnis rei creatae. Ergo nisi cognitio sit Patris, nulla est vita aeterna: Iam vero non cognoscitur Pater nisi in Filio. Patrem nemo vidit unquam, unigenitus qui est in sinu Patris, ipse declarat eum. Filius autem est splendor gloriae Patris & character personae ipsius. Ergo nulla cognitio Patris est, nisi cognoscatur Filius: ia vero non cognoscitur a nobis filius, neque etiam cognosci poterit (habitat enim lucem inaccessam cum Patre) nisi in humana sua natura. Neque etiam nobis prodesset eum cognoscere nisi carne indutum, in qua pro peccatis nostris mortuus est & resurrexit ad iustificationem nostri. Ergo ad vitam aeternam necessarium est ut cognoscamus Filium in carne manifestatum: ideoque hic dicitur, ut cognoscant eum quem misisti Iesum Christum. Cognoscendus enim est Filius a nobis, ut Messias, ut Iesus, ut Christus. Missus autem est in carne: Iesus est & Servator, ut Deus & homo: Christus & Mediator est ut Deus & homo. Vide in tota hac collectione, obiectum proximum cognitionis illius nostrae quae est ad vitam aeternam, esse humanam Christi naturam. Per hanc penetramus ad cognitionem Filij Dei, quae in ipsa habitat corporaliter. Per Filium Dei peruenimus ad cognitionem Patris, qui est fons vitae, qui est ultimum ac supremum cognitionis nostrae obiectum. Qui autem est ultimus in cognitione, & in quo conquiescit postremo fides nostra, hic est Spiritus vitae & primus fons est. Primum enim vita aeterna a Patre manat, manat autem per Filium & carnem Filij ad nos usque. Ex his vides illud postremo vitam nostram aeternam in cognitione stam esse. Quod si in cognitione, profecto quantos progressus facimus in cognitione & fide, tantos progressus facimus in vita: & cum perficietur cognitio, tum perficietur vita in altero illo saeculo. Io. Sequitur & alterum ex eadem hac positione. Si enim vita est in cognitione, profecto mors est in ignorantia. Paulus enim hæc duo coniunxit, mentem, inquit habentes obtenebratam (hæc est ignorantia) & alienatam à vita Dei (hæc est mors) privatio enim vitæ Dei est mors. Quare quisquis cupit viuere vitam Dei, fugiat ignorantiam quam sequitur mors necessario. Tenebræ autem istæ ignorantiæ, quid, quæso, sunt aliud quàm initium tenebrarum exteriorum, in quibus nihil nisi fletus & stridor dentium?
units.tr: Now let us say briefly what that eternal life is, and let us see first what fruits the glorification of Christ brings. First the Father himself is glorified; then we are saved and obtain eternal life. But to say something of eternal life: our eternal life comes about by the power of the resurrection of Christ. For what else is our spiritual life but a certain spark of that life which abounds so greatly in Christ himself? And what is this life-giving Spirit, which has been given to us in measure, but a portion, as it were, of that Spirit of life which is in Christ not in measure? That passage of Paul is remarkable: "For if we have been planted together with him in the likeness of his death, so we shall be also in the likeness of his life" (Rom. 6.5). By this he signifies that the mortification of the old man comes by the power of the death and cross of Christ, and the quickening of the new man comes by the power of the life of Christ. For if Christ has not been raised, we are still in our sins. Therefore whoever wishes to know for certain whether Christ died for him, let him first see whether he himself has died to sin. Whoever again wishes to know whether Christ rose for him, let him see whether he feels a new life in himself. If he feels neither the death of sin nor a new life in himself, he certainly has no ground for persuading himself that Christ died for him. This, however, is eternal life. Now the necessity of the glorification of Christ for eternal life is taught from a certain definition of eternal life: eternal life is to know the Father, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom he sent. But there is no knowledge either of the Father or of the Son unless the Son is glorified. Therefore there is no eternal life unless the Son is glorified. Only the major premise of this syllogism is contained in the text, namely in the words this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God. He does not say God only, but the only true God, and he does not say the only true God in order to exclude the Son and the Holy Spirit, who are one and the same God with the Father, but to exclude the idols of the nations and the fictitious gods who were then commonly held to be gods throughout the world. Note here, then, that our life consists in knowledge: not in the knowledge of anything whatever, but in the knowledge of the very fount of life; and not in a bare knowledge of it, but in that knowledge which lies in faith and trust, resting in that fount and drawing from it, as it were, eternal life. Now God the Father is the fount of all life, and also of the life of the Son; for the Father has given the Son to have life in himself (above chapter 5), and also the life of every created thing. Therefore, unless there is knowledge of the Father, there is no eternal life. But the Father is not known except in the Son: No one has ever seen the Father; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him. The Son, moreover, is the brightness of the glory of the Father and the express image of his person. Therefore there is no knowledge of the Father unless the Son is known; but the Son is not known by us, nor can he be known (for he dwells in light inaccessible with the Father), except in his human nature. Nor would it profit us to know him unless he were clothed in flesh, in which he died for our sins and rose again for our justification. Therefore for eternal life it is necessary that we know the Son manifested in the flesh; and so here it is said, that they may know him whom you have sent, Jesus Christ. For the Son must be known by us as Messiah, as Jesus, as Christ. He was sent in the flesh: he is Jesus and Saviour as God and man; he is Christ and Mediator as God and man. Observe in this whole passage that the proximate object of that knowledge of ours which leads to eternal life is the human nature of Christ. Through this we penetrate to the knowledge of the Son of God, which dwells in it bodily. Through the Son of God we arrive at the knowledge of the Father, who is the fount of life, and who is the last and highest object of our knowledge. But he who is last in knowledge, and in whom our faith at last rests, is the Spirit and first fount of life. For eternal life flows first from the Father; it flows through the Son and his flesh even down to us. From these things you see that our eternal life consists finally in knowledge. And if it consists in knowledge, then surely as far as we make progress in knowledge and faith, so far we make progress in life; and when knowledge is perfected, then life will be perfected in that other age. From this same position there follows also a second point. If life is in knowledge, then surely death is in ignorance. For Paul joined these two: "having their understanding darkened" (this is ignorance) "and alienated from the life of God" (this is death), for the privation of the life of God is death (Eph. 4.18). Therefore whoever desires to live the life of God should flee from ignorance, which necessarily is followed by death. But those shadows of ignorance, what, I ask, are they but the beginning of the outer darkness, in which there is nothing but weeping and gnashing of teeth?

units.la: 4 Ego te glorificaui in terra, opus consummaui quod dedisti mihi vt facerem.
units.tr: 4 I have glorified you on earth; I have finished the work that you gave me to do.

units.la: 5 Nunc igitur glorifica me tu Pater apud te metipsum ea gloria quam habui apud te priusquam mundus esset.
units.tr: 5 And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence, with the glory I had with you before the world existed.

units.la: QVartum est argumentum petitionis à glorificatione Patris illa anteacta: nititur autem promissione, quasi dicat, Promisisti quod si ego te glorificaturus essem, tu vicissim glorificaturus esses me: At ego te glorificaui: Ergo tu vicissim glorifica me, ô pater. 1. De hac promissione passim in veteri Testamento vt Psal.110.1. Dixit Dominus Domino meo, Sede ad dextram meam, donec ponam inimicos tuos in scabellum pedum tuorum. Potuit quidem Dominus iure promissionis illius quæ est sub conditione perfectæ obedientiæ, vendicare sibi gloriam. Eius enim obedientia patefacta fuit: nullus autem homo post Adami lapsum sibi vitam & gloriam vendicare potest, iure promissionis illius factæ sub conditione perfectæ suæ obedientiæ ac operum. Nullius enim hominis, ne regeniti quidem, obedientia & opera perfecta sunt. Quamobrem nos renuntiantes fœderi quod vocant operum, ad fœdus gratuitum, quod in Christi sanguine perfectaque eius obedientia fundatum est, confugimus, petimúsque vitam & gloriam non propter obedientiam nostram, sed propter solius Christi obedientiam. Atque hoc est illud religionis fundamentum quod nunquam agnoscere volunt Papistæ, qui fœderi operum perpetuo mordicus adhærēt, virtutéque eius vitam ac iustitiam sibi quaerunt. Vt comperiat, inquit Paulus, non habens meam iustitiam, sed eam quae est per fidem. Vide hic, Paulus etiam regenitus suam iustitiam pro damno, imo pro stercore ducit, ut Christi illam iustitiam adipiscatur. Sed ut ad verba veniamus, Ego, inquit, te glorificavi in terra. Tum quae sequuntur verba praecedentia exponunt, Opus consummavi quod dedisti mihi ut facerem. Hoc est illud opus redemptionis humanae omnium maximum. Sed quomodo dicit se perfecisse illud opus, cum nondum quo tempore haec loquutus est mortuus esset? Respondeo quod rum certo, tum propediem futurum erat pro praeterito iamque facto eum fe-cisse. Sed quomodo in praeterito se glorificasse iam Patrem, cum supra dixerit se Patrem glorificaturum im-posterum? Respondeo haec omnia inter se consistere: Christus enim et glorificavit Patrem, priusquam ipse a Patre glorificatus esset, et Patrem glorificavit, postquam iam a Patre esset glorificatus. Glorificavit quidem Patrem, priusquam ipse a Patre glorificatus esset perfecta sua obedientia, in qua sic resplenduit Patris misericordia, et philanthropia illa, ut mundus mirarus eam in ipso potuisse misericordiam invenire, qua Filium suum unigenitum morti pro nobis tradiderit. Glorificavit rursus Patrem iam glorificatus a Patre, sui exaltatione, in qua ita emicuit potentia Patris, ut mundus miratus sit eam in ipso potentiam esse, qua mortuum hominem non modo excitaverit ex mortuis, sed, ut dicit Paulus, exaltavit in summam sublimitatem, ac donavit ei nomen, quod est supra omne nomen, &c. hoc est, collocavit eum ad dextram suam in caelis. Apostolus dicit id factum iuxta efficacitatem fortis roboris ipsius. Tum effectum eius efficacitatis continuo subiiciens. Quem exerut, inquit, in Christo cum excitaret ipsum ex mortuis: neque hoc tantum: Sed, inquit, collocavit ad dextram suam in caelis. Hic maxime conspecta est ipsius potentia. Quamobrem in Christo admirandus est tum in misericordia tum in potentia ipsius. Potest etiam conciliatio esse alia, sed quae eodem redit. Christus in terra glorificavit Patrem in Prophetico & Sacerdotali suo munere: iam vero glorificatus, eum in regali suo munere glorificat: Nam regnum quaesitum Patri suo tradet postea. postquam omnia fuerint subiecta sub pedes eius. Quod autem hic ad nos ipsi applicamus, hoc nimirum est: Christus iam morti proximus, profitetur se in vita hac gloOR ficasse Patrem suum: ita nobis videndum in vita hac, ut morti iam proximi, possimus illud praedicare. Ego Pater glorificavi te in vita: iam quod a Paulo facta legimus: Ego, inquit, iam liber & tempus meae resolutionis instat: certamen illud praeclarum decertavi, cursum consummavi, fidem servavi. Quod superest reposita est mihi iustitiae corona, &c. Sed hoc inter nos & Christum interest. Ipse sic glorificavit Patre, ut potuerit obedientiae suae merito, quae fuit personae illius dignitas, petere a Patre glorificationem sui. Nos vero non ita, quia, ut supra admonuit, obedientia nostra imperfecta est. Quare ita oportet nos obedientiam, Deique cultum profiteri, ut nulla sit interea opinio meriti: contra vero opinio sit indignitatis nostrae. Pharisaeus ille glorificavit Deum cum opinione meriti sui, qui tamen domum reversus est non iustificatus a Deo.
units.tr: The fourth argument for the request is drawn from the glorifying of the Father, which has already taken place. It rests on a promise, as if he said: You promised that if I were to glorify you, you in turn would glorify me. But I have glorified you; therefore, Father, glorify me in turn. 1. This promise appears throughout the Old Testament, as in Psalm 110:1: The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool. By the right of that promise, which was made on condition of perfect obedience, the Lord could indeed claim glory for himself, since his obedience was made manifest. But after the fall of Adam no man can claim life and glory for himself by the right of that promise, which was made on condition of perfect obedience and works. For the obedience and works of no man, not even of a regenerate man, are perfect. Therefore we renounce the so-called covenant of works and flee to the free covenant, which is founded on the blood of Christ and his perfect obedience. We seek life and glory not on account of our own obedience, but on account of the obedience of Christ alone. This is that foundation of religion which the Papists never want to acknowledge: they cling stubbornly to the covenant of works and seek life and righteousness for themselves by its power. That he may be found, says Paul, not having my own righteousness, but that which is through faith. See here how Paul, though regenerate, counts his own righteousness as loss, indeed as dung, so that he may obtain the righteousness of Christ. But let us come to the words. I have glorified you, he says, on earth. The words that follow explain what precedes: I have finished the work that you gave me to do. This is that work of human redemption, the greatest of all. But how does he say that he has finished that work, when he had not yet died at the time he spoke these words? I answer that it was both certain and soon to come, and so he speaks of it as past and already done. But how can he say that he has already glorified the Father in the past, when above he said that he would glorify him in the future? I answer that all these things agree with one another. Christ glorified the Father before he himself was glorified by the Father, and he glorified the Father after he had already been glorified by the Father. He glorified the Father before he himself was glorified, by his perfect obedience, in which the mercy of the Father and that love of mankind shone forth so brightly that the world, marvelling, might find in him that mercy by which the Father delivered his only-begotten Son to death for us. And again he glorified the Father, now glorified by the Father, by his exaltation, in which the power of the Father shone forth so brightly that the world marvelled that this power was in him, by which he raised a dead man not only out of the dead, but, as Paul says, exalted him to the highest height, and gave him a name which is above every name, etc., that is, set him at his right hand in the heavens. The apostle says this was done according to the working of the strength of his might. Then he immediately adds the effect of that working: which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and not only this: but he set him, he says, at his right hand in the heavens. Here above all his power is seen. Therefore in Christ we must marvel both at his mercy and at his power. There may also be another reconciliation of the matter, which comes to the same thing. Christ glorified the Father on earth in his prophetic and priestly office; now, glorified, he glorifies him in his kingly office, for he will afterwards deliver the kingdom to his Father, once all things have been put under his feet. But what we apply here to ourselves is this: Christ, now close to death, declares that he has glorified his Father in this life. So we too must see to it in this life that, when we are close to death, we can proclaim the same: I, Father, have glorified you in my life. Now what we read Paul said: I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, etc. But there is a difference between us and Christ. He glorified the Father in such a way that, by the merit of his obedience, which was the dignity of his person, he could ask the Father to glorify him. We cannot do so, because, as he admonished above, our obedience is imperfect. Therefore we ought to profess our obedience and our worship of God in such a way that there is no thought of merit in the meantime, but rather a sense of our unworthiness. That Pharisee glorified God with a sense of his own merit, yet he went home not justified by God.

units.la: Nunc igitur glorifica. Petitionis conclusio. Ergo Pater glorifica Filium. Sed de loco admonet: Apud temetipsum; hoc est non in terra, ubi ego te glorificavi, sed in caelis apud temetipsum, & ad tuam ipsius dexteram. Nam summa gloria, non est nisi in summo loco ac supremo. Ideo etiam petit postea hoc capite ut ubi ipse est, ibi nos simus, hoc est in caelis, ut perfecta sit gloria nostra. Tum de genere gloriae agit. Non vulgari aliqua gloria petit se glorificari: sed ea quam habuit apud Patrem, priusquam hic mundus existeret, hoc est aequali cum Patre gloria. Apud te, hoc est gloria illa quae in secundam Trinitatis personam competit. Nam supra Iohannes, cum de persona loquitur, inquit, sermo ille erat Deus. Vides hic primum, quaenam sit ea gloria quam petit: nempe gloria est Filii Dei praecipue. Vides rursus eam gloriam ad tempus obscuratam fuisse: Obscuratam dico, non plane e medio sublatam. Nam etiam tum cum assumeret formam servi, & obediens factus esset ad mortem, etiam tum, inquam, non perdidit gloriam illam suam aequalem Patris suae gloriae. Missio enim & obedientia non tollunt aequalitatem potentiae & essentiae. Cocedo qui dem illud, obscuratam fuisse illam gloriam, non tamen lauit.
units.tr: Now therefore glorify me. The conclusion of the request: Father, glorify the Son. But he indicates the place: in your own presence; that is, not on earth, where I glorified you, but in heaven, in your own presence and at your own right hand. For supreme glory exists only in the highest and supreme place. Therefore he also asks later in this chapter that where he is, there we may be, that is, in heaven, so that our glory may be complete. Then he speaks of the kind of glory. He asks to be glorified not with some common glory, but with that which he had with the Father before this world existed, that is, with glory equal to the Father's. In your presence: that is, the glory that belongs to the second person of the Trinity. For above John, speaking of the person, says: that Word was God. Here you see first what kind of glory he asks for: it is the glory of the Son of God especially. You see again that this glory was for a time obscured. I say obscured, not utterly taken away. For even when he took the form of a servant, and became obedient unto death, even then, I say, he did not lose that glory of his, equal to the glory of the Father. For mission and obedience do not take away equality of power and essence. I grant indeed that that glory was obscured, but it was not diminished.

units.la: 1. Corinth. 15.24.&c. Doctrina hinc colligenda Glorificemus Deum in vita & morte. 2. Tim. 4.6. &c. tùm forma serui, sed multò magis tam abiecta & horrenda morte. Dico praeterea Filium habitantem corporaliter in illo corporis tabernaculo ad tépus continuisse se, neque gloriam illam suam exeruisse. Quam profecto si exeruisset à momento conceptionis suæ, glorificasseт humanam naturam: Atque ita pro nobis pati non potuisset. Res similitudine erit illustrior. Sol hic cū obscuratur nube, non tamen amittit naturalem suam lucem, impeditur tamen ne nobis affulgeat: ita filius Dei obscuratus vtraque illa nube, primùm carnis nostræ, deinde mortis, nō tamen amisit naturalem & æqualem cum Patre gloriam ac maiestatem. Ex hoc rursus postremò vides, ecquid petat à Patre. Non quidem gloriam eam quam non habuit, etiam tum cùm peteret eam: neque etiā petit vt exuatur nostra natura: sic enim inutilis nobis efficeretur: sed hoc petit, vt gloria quam etiam tum habuit, sese exereret, & eius quasi radij transpareret per humanam illam quam gestauit naturam, càmque radiis suis totam collucтraret. Et ita quidem factum est. Nam cùm exerceret se Deitas illa in persona Filij habitans, excitatus est Christus homo ex mortuis, ascendit ad coelos, & collocatus est ad dextram Patris. Neque vero vires illius Deitatis habitantis in homine Christo, tantùm extenduntur ad naturam nostram quæ est in ipso Christo, sed latius diffunduntur ad nos vsque qui per fidem ipsi insiti sumus. Cùm verò viuemus per aspectu, tum quidem humile istud corpus nostrum transformabitur ac conformabitur corpori ipsius glorioso, pro efficacitate qua omnia sibi potest subiicere.
units.tr: 1. Corinthians 15:24, etc. The doctrine to be gathered here: let us glorify God in life and in death. 2 Timothy 4:6, etc. ...the form of a servant, but much more so in so abject and dreadful a death. I say further that the Son, dwelling bodily in that tabernacle of the body, restrained himself for a time and did not put forth that glory of his. Indeed, if he had put it forth from the moment of his conception, he would have glorified human nature, and so he could not have suffered for us. The matter will be clearer by a comparison. When the sun is obscured by a cloud, it does not lose its natural light, but it is prevented from shining upon us. So the Son of God, obscured by both those clouds, first of our flesh and then of death, did not lose his natural and equal glory and majesty with the Father. From this, lastly, you see again what he asks of the Father. He asks not for the glory which he did not have, even when he asked for it, nor does he ask that our nature be stripped from him, for thus it would be useless to us; but he asks that the glory which he still had might put itself forth, and that its rays, as it were, might shine through the human nature he bore, and light it up entirely with its beams. And so indeed it came to pass. For when that Deity dwelling in the person of the Son put itself forth, Christ as man was raised from the dead, ascended into the heavens, and was set at the right hand of the Father. Nor do the powers of that Deity dwelling in the man Christ extend only to our nature which is in Christ himself, but they are poured out more widely, even to us who have been grafted into him through faith. And when we shall live by sight, then indeed this lowly body of ours will be transformed and conformed to his glorious body, by that power by which he is able to subject all things to himself.

units.la: 6 Manifestum feci nomen tuum hominibus quos dedisti mihi selectos è mundo: tui erant & mihi eos dedisti: & sermonem tuum seruarunt.
units.tr: I have made your name known to the men whom you gave me out of the world, chosen from it. They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.

units.la: 7 Nunc nouerunt omnia quæ dedisti mihi à te esse.
units.tr: Now they have known that all the things you gave me are from you.

units.la: 8 Quia verba quæ tradidisti mihi, tradidi eis: & ipsi receperunt: & verè norunt me à te prodiisse, & crediderunt me à te missum esse.
units.tr: For the words you gave me I have given to them, and they received them, and truly knew that I came out from you, and they believed that you sent me.

units.la: NVnc precatur pro discipulis suis, vndecim illis. Precatur autem Patrem, vt seruet eos à malo. Argumentum petitionis primum est à vocatione, per prædicationem Euangelij. Vocationis enim beneficium consistit in patefactione Dei in Christo. Vocat enim nos Deus dum patefacit nobis se ac voluntatem suam. Quòd si argumentum petat Dominus à vocatione, quo commendat Patri conseruationem discipulorum suorum: certè argumento nobis debet esse vocatio hæc quæ fit per Euangelij prædicationem, nos custodiri ac conseruari à Patre, ac in æternum coseruatum iri. Vocat enim nos Deus in eum finem vt seruet nos. Quoties igitur sentimus nos vocari, toties spem concipere debemus, nos seruatum iri. Quòd si autem vocati non seruemur, id fit culpa nostra, qui vocati non respondemus, nec fidem habemus verbo prædicato. Quòd si autem vocati respondemus, hoc est, si vocatio nostra efficax sit per fidem, tum profectò vocatio certum est argumentum salutis nostræ. Selectos è mundo. Alterum argumentum est petitionis ab electione illa quæ est ab æterno. Quod si Dominus ab electione commendet Patri conseruationem nostri, profectò electio nobis est argumentum salutis necessarium. Quotquot enim electi sunt, illi necessitate seruantur. Necessitas autem hæc nō impedit, quominus pro salute & conseruatione nostri tum nos ipsi tum alij nostra causa precentur, quemadmodum Christus hoc loco precatur pro electis. Nam non minùs ordinati sumus ac præparati ad media, ad fidem, ad preces, ad bona opera, quàm ad salutem ipsam, adeo vt nisi per hæc media ad vitam spectantia ambulemus, nulla omnino sit vita futura, quia nulla fuit electio ad vitam. Tui erant. Tertium argumentum, quod electionis consequens est, Electi enim Dei sunt. Quòd si Filius ex eo quòd Dei eramus commendet nos Deo Patri, profectò idipsum, quòd Dei sumus, argumento nobis esse debet, quod seruabimur ab eo: nam Deus suos necessariò seruat. Qui autem Dei sunt, illi profectò de ea re certiores fient antequam emigrabunt ex hac vita: Id autem resciunt ex ipsius Spiritu. Nam si verum est quod dixit Paulus, Si quis Spiritum Christi non habet, is non est eius: Spi-
units.tr: Now he prays for his disciples, the eleven of them. He asks the Father to keep them from evil. The first argument of the petition is taken from their calling, through the preaching of the gospel. For the benefit of calling consists in the revelation of God in Christ. God calls us when he reveals himself and his will to us. If the Lord, then, draws on calling as an argument for commending to the Father the preservation of his disciples, surely this calling, which comes through the preaching of the gospel, ought to be an argument for us that we are guarded and preserved by the Father and will be kept for ever. God calls us for the purpose of saving us. Whenever we perceive that we are called, we ought therefore to conceive hope that we shall be kept. But if we who are called are not kept, this happens through our own fault, because we who are called do not answer and do not put faith in the word preached.
