But if we who are called do answer, that is, if our calling is made effective through faith, then surely calling is a certain argument of our salvation. Chosen out of the world. The second argument of the petition is taken from that election which is from eternity. If the Lord commends our preservation to the Father on the ground of election, then surely election is a necessary argument of our salvation. For all who are elect are necessarily kept. This necessity does not, however, prevent us, or others on our behalf, from praying for our own salvation and preservation, just as Christ here prays for the elect. For we are ordained and prepared for the means no less than for salvation itself: for faith, for prayer, for good works. So much so that unless we walk through these means which pertain to life, there will be no life at all for us, because there was no election to life. They were yours. The third argument, which follows from election, is this: the elect are God's. For if the Son commends us to God the Father because we were God's, then surely the very fact that we are God's ought to be an argument for us that we shall be kept by him, for God necessarily keeps his own. Those who are God's will certainly be made more certain of this before they depart from this life, and they learn it from his Spirit. For if what Paul said is true, If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his, then the Spirit, dwelling within us, cannot be idle; he certainly shows himself in that love which he pours into our hearts.

units.la: Secunda pars, precationé Christi, pro suis discipulis cõtinens. ritus autem inhabitans, in nobis otiosus esse non potest: sese certe exerit in charitate illa, quam effundit in cordibus nostris. Et mihi eos dedisti. Argumentum petitionis quartum, ex eo quod dati simus Christo a Patre. Et hoc quoque precationis argumentum, nobis persuasionis est argumentum ac certitudinis, qui sumus seruandi: quod si enim senserimus nos Christo semel datos, profecto firma fides conseruationis ac salutis esse potest. Nam dati Christo etiam adhuc patris sumus: neque enim tantum eramus, sed adhuc sumus. Ideo paulo post dicit nos Patris esse. Praeterea nos non ita dat filio, ut ipse omnem nostri curam abiiciat: contra, hoc ipso quod ei dat nos, conseruat nos. Nam dat nos Mediatori in eum finem, ut ipse nos redimat ac conseruet: Pater enim est Seruator noster per Christum Mediatorem. Obseruari etiam potest hoc loco mutua commendatio, qua Pater & Filius nos sibi invicem commendant: Pater dat nos Filio: Filius rursus precatur Patrem pro nobis: ut nemo non videat, quam solido fundamento nitatur salus nostra, cum Pater & Filius salutem nostram sibi invicem tantopere commendent: neque tantum singillatim suas partes in nobis seruandis agant: sed alter apud alterum pro nobis agat. Argumenta haec adducta quatuor extra nos sunt: nam vocatio, electio, hoc quod Patris sumus, hoc quod dati sumus Christo, haec, inquam, omnia extra nos sunt. Nunc deinceps commendat conseruatione nostri, ab argumento interno & inhaerente in ipsis discipulis, nempe fide: quae nihil aliud est quam sensus, & apprehensio quaedam externorum omnium argumentorum: quae ipsa nisi in nobis insint vel seriùs vel citius in hac vita praesenti, profecto nihil est, quo nobis persuadere possimus illa superiora & externa ad nos pertinere.
units.tr: The second part, containing Christ's prayer for his disciples. And you gave them to me. The fourth argument of the petition, from the fact that we have been given to Christ by the Father. This also is an argument of the prayer that persuades us and gives us certainty, we who are to be kept. For if we perceive that we have once been given to Christ, then a firm faith in our preservation and salvation can surely exist. For we who have been given to Christ are still also the Father's; we were not only so in the past, but we still are. Therefore a little later he says that we belong to the Father. Moreover, he does not so give us to the Son that he himself casts off all care for us; on the contrary, by the very fact that he gives us to him, he keeps us. For he gives us to the Mediator for this purpose, that he himself may redeem and preserve us, since the Father is our Saviour through Christ the Mediator. In this place one may also observe the mutual commendation by which the Father and the Son commend us to each other: the Father gives us to the Son; the Son in turn prays to the Father for us. So everyone can see on what solid foundation our salvation rests, since the Father and the Son so earnestly commend our salvation to each other, and do not merely each perform separately their own parts in keeping us, but each acts on our behalf before the other. These four arguments adduced are outside us: for calling, election, the fact that we are the Father's, and the fact that we have been given to Christ, all these, I say, are outside us. Now he goes on to commend our preservation on the basis of an argument internal and inherent in the disciples themselves, namely faith; which is nothing other than a perception and grasp of all those external arguments. Unless this faith is present in us, sooner or later in this present life, there is surely nothing by which we can persuade ourselves that those former and external things pertain to us.

units.la: Fide autem hanc explicat ex variis suis partibus ac officiis: Nam cum in fide primum fit cognitio: Nunc noverunt, inquit, omnia quae mihi dedisti a te esse &, ut postea sequitur, verè noverunt a te exiisse: Deinde cum in fide sit perceptio siue receptio rei cognitae. Verba, inquit, quae tradidisti mihi, ego tradidi eis, & ipsi acceperunt. Tertiò cum in fide sit conseruatio rei semel receptae: ne hoc quidem praetermittit: Sed, inquit, sermone seruarunt. Postremò uno verbo comprehendit haec
units.tr: He explains this faith from its various parts and offices. For since in faith knowledge comes first: Now they have known, he says, that all the things you gave me are from you, and, as follows afterwards, they have truly known that I came out from you. Then, since in faith there is the perception or reception of the thing known: The words, he says, that you gave me, I have given to them, and they received them. Thirdly, since in faith there is the preservation of a thing once received, he does not omit even this: But, he says, they have kept your word. Lastly, he comprehends all these things in one word: they believed, he says, that I was sent by you.

units.la: Rom. 5. hæc omnia, Crediderunt, inquit, me à te missum esse. Tu videndu quàm varia fidei obiecta efficiat: primum ipsum Christu, cu dicit, Nouerunt me àte prodiisse: crediderunt me à te missum esse: deinde quæ in Christo sunt bona, ipsi à Patre data: Nouerunt, inquit, quæ dedisti mihi, &c. Postremò sermonem, siue verbum Dei, quod est de Christo, deque iis quæ in ipso sunt; hoc est, thesauro illo omnium rerum bonarum ac spiritualium. Neque verò illud silentio prætermittendum est quò refert hæc omnia quæ dicit de fide ipsorum, ad gloriam Patris sui. Dicit enim eos nosse Christum ab eo prodiisse, ab eo missum esse, quæ in Christo sunt à Patre esse, sermonem denique Patris esse: vt Patri sit tota gloria fidei nostræ, & in Iesum Christum ipsum, & in beneficia ipsius, & denique in sermonem illum qui est de Christo, deque beneficiis ipsius. Fides enim in Christum tantum abest ab eo, vt aliquid derogeret gloriæ Paternæ, vt è contra eam augeat quàm maximè: Christum enim omnémque in Christo gratiâ ipsi acceptam referimus, ipsíque omnem in Christo gloriam tribuimus.
units.tr: Rom. 5. See how many different objects of faith he sets forth: first Christ himself, when he says, they have known that I came out from you, they believed that I was sent by you; then the good things which are in Christ, given to them by the Father: they have known, he says, the things you gave me, and so on; and lastly the word, or the word of God, which concerns Christ and the things that are in him, that is, that treasury of all good and spiritual things. Nor must it be passed over in silence that he refers all these things which he says about their faith to the glory of his Father. For he says that they know that Christ came forth from him, was sent by him, that the things which are in Christ are from the Father, and finally that the word is the Father's; so that the whole glory of our faith belongs to the Father, both in Jesus Christ himself, and in his benefits, and finally in that word which is about Christ and about his benefits. For faith in Christ is so far from detracting from the Father's glory in any way that, on the contrary, it increases it as much as possible: for we refer Christ and all the grace in Christ, which has been accepted by us, to him, and we ascribe to him all the glory in Christ.

units.la: 9 Ego pro iis rogo, non pro mundo rogo, sed pro iis quos dedisti mihi: quia tui sunt.
units.tr: 9 I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours.

units.la: 10 Et mea omnia tua sunt, & tua mea sunt: & glorificatus sum in eis.
units.tr: 10 And all my things are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them.

units.la: 11 Et non sum amplius in mundo, sed isti sunt in mundo, & ego ad te venio. Pater sancte, serua eos per nomen tuum, quos dedisti mihi, vt sint vnum prout & nos.
units.tr: 11 And I am no longer in the world, but these are in the world, and I come to you. Holy Father, keep them through your name, those whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we also are.

units.la: HÆctenus argumenta petitionis fuerunt: sequitur eiusdem conclusio, sed obscurior, quasi dicat: Cum totsuppetant mihi argumenta, iure videor mihi pro iis rogare. Qui enim participes facti sunt tot beneficiorum, oportet eos habere commendatos tibi: vt etiam necesse est eosdem à te seruari. Definit autem eos pro quibus rogat, per occupationis speciem quandam, ne videatur pro quibusuis indiscriminatim rogare. Definitione sua excludit à precibus suis mundum, hoc est reprobos: includit vero eos qui ipsi sunt dati à Patre, hoc est, discipulos suos nominatim : vt enim electio illa Dei non est omnium hominum, sed limitata est certo aliquo hominum numero, vt etiam donatio Patris limitata est: neq; enim pro aliis, vel intercessit, vel intercedit quàm pro iis, qui electi sunt primùm, deinde dati filio, ídque fiue intercessionem quę fit per preces, siue intercessionem quæ fit per mortem respicias. Quare vt certi simus de intercessione Christi, necesse est sim.us certi de electione nostra, & de eo quod filio sumus dati à Patre. Nota deobseruāda inde quàm distinctæ sint preces Christi: primùm excludit reprobos, postea autem nominatim excludet Iudam proditorem: deinde pro electis petit non confusè & generatim, sed particulatim pro singulis. Nouit enim Dominus qui sint sui. Idem iudicium planè faciendum est de morte ipsius. Mortuus est non pro reprobis, sed pro electis, & pro electis quidem non generatim, sed sigillatim pro singulis: quos cum se traderet morti, singulos habuit ante oculos : verbi gratia, Petrum, Paulum, &c.
units.tr: Thus far have been the arguments of the petition. There follows its conclusion, but more obscure, as if he were saying: since all my arguments are at hand, I rightly seem to myself to pray for them. For those who have been made partakers of so many benefits ought to be commended to you, just as they must necessarily be kept by you. He defines, however, those for whom he prays, with a certain appearance of an occupation, lest he seem to pray for anyone whatever indiscriminately. By his definition he excludes the world from his prayers, that is, the reprobate; but he includes those who have been given to him by the Father, that is, his disciples, by name. For just as God's election is not of all men but is limited to a certain definite number of men, so too the Father's giving is limited; for he has interceded, or intercedes, for none other than those who are elect first and then given to the Son, whether you look at the intercession which is made through prayers or the intercession which is made through death. Therefore, that we may be certain of Christ's intercession, it is necessary that we be certain of our election, and of the fact that we have been given to the Son by the Father. Note from this how distinct Christ's prayers are: first he excludes the reprobate; afterwards he excludes by name Judas the traitor; then for the elect he asks not confusedly and in general, but particularly, for each one. For the Lord knows who are his own. The same judgment must plainly be made concerning his death: He died not for the reprobate, but for the elect, and for the elect not in general but individually, for each one; when he gave himself over to death, he had each one before his eyes, for example Peter, Paul, and so on.

units.la: Neque enim tantùm motus suæ beneficium in genere offert omnibus : at probè & distinctè nouit eos quibus eam communicat. Ideo Paulus, cum hoc agnosceret dixit, Et vitam quam nunc vivo in carne, vivo per fidem filii Dei, qui dilexit me & tradidit semetipsum pro me. Ecce, dicit Paulus, Christum dilexisse ipsum nominatim, & nominatim se tradidisse pro ipso. Ergo oportuit Christum in morte sua Paulum nominatim ante oculos habuisse, proeoque mortuum esse. Atque hæc quidem consolatione non mediocrem suppeditat: quod particularem nostri curam in morte sua habuerit, & specialem quandam prouidentiam. Specialis enim Dei prouidentia efficax est admodum ad consolationem. Quia tui sunt. Dicit potuit, Si dati sint tibi, quid ad me? Respondet, Imò tui sunt: neque modò tui erant vt supra est dictum, sed tui iunt etiam nunc. Ratio subiecta est ab ipso genere, Quia omnia mea tua sunt, & tua mea sunt. Hoc est, omnia nostra communia sunt: vulgò dicitur, Amicorum omnia sunt communia, in quâ etiam sententiâ loquitur Paulus ad Philemonem, Itaque, inquit, si me socium habes, &c. Ergo amicitia efficit bona communia: sic & matrimonium. Sed arctius est vinculum hoc quod est inter Patrem & filium. Nempe vnius eiusdem essentiæ communio. Communio eiusdem essentiæ efficit, vt sint communia omnia: verùm hoc discrimen est in hac communione: primum ius primum est Patris, secundum verò filij, æquale quidem, sed ordine secundum: ius autem filij est ex donatione Patris: vt enim Pater dedit filio essentiam, ita dedit ei omnia alia. Cùm iam data sint omnia filio, non desinunt tamen esse Patris: quia donatio hæc nihil est aliud quàm communicatio, vt & essentiæ ipsius est communicatio. Quod hic asseuerat Dominus, id fideles reipsa in se ipsi sentiunt. Nemo enim est, qui filij est, quin sentiat se Patris esse. Fides enim simul apprehendit vtrumque. Contrà verò, qui non sentit se filij esse, is profectò sentire non poterit se Patris esse. Spiritus enim sanctus operatur in cordibus nostris sensum aliquem earum rerum, quas vult Deus de nobis fieri.
units.tr: Nor does he merely offer the benefit of his death to all in general: he knows distinctly and particularly those to whom he communicates it. So Paul, recognising this, said: And the life I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. See, Paul says, that Christ loved him by name and gave himself up for him by name. Therefore Christ must have had Paul by name before his eyes in his death, and so died for him. This brings no small consolation, namely that he had a particular care for us in his death and a special providence. For a special providence of God is very effective for consolation. Because they are yours. One might say: If they have been given to you, what is that to me? He answers: Indeed they are yours, and they were not only yours, as was said above, but they are yours even now. The reason is drawn from the general principle: All that is mine is yours, and yours is mine. That is, all things are held in common: as the common saying goes, "Among friends all things are common," and Paul speaks to the same effect to Philemon: "So if you have me as a partner," and so on. Friendship therefore makes goods common; so does marriage. But the bond between Father and Son is closer: namely, the communion of one and the same essence. The communion of one essence makes all things common, yet in this communion there is a difference: the first right belongs to the Father, the second to the Son, equal indeed but second in order. The Son's right, however, comes from the gift of the Father: just as the Father gave the Son his essence, so he gave him all else. Although all things have now been given to the Son, they do not cease to be the Father's, because this giving is nothing other than a communication, just as the communication of his essence is. What the Lord asserts here, the faithful feel in themselves in actual experience. For there is no one who is a son who does not feel that he is also the Father's. Faith grasps both at once. On the other hand, whoever does not feel that he is a son will certainly be unable to feel that he is the Father's. For the Holy Spirit works in our hearts a sense of those things which God wills to be made of us.

units.la: Et glorificatus sum in iis. Redit ad argumenta, éstque hoc argumentum sextum ab ipsius filij gloria, vel glorificatione: quam necesse est coniunctam esse cum salute & conseruatione nostri, qui ipsum glorificamus fide, confessione, & tota nostra conuersatione. His enim mediis glorificamus filium. Quamobrem qui sentiunt in se zelum aliquem gloriæ filij, illi quidem pariter habét fiduciam aliquam salutis suæ, & prouidentiæ Patris erga se speciali: Nam qui honorat filium, is honorat Patrem. Et qui non honorat filium, is non honorat Patrē, qui misit ipsum: Qui autem honorat Patrem, Pater eum honorabit. Et non sum amplius. Hoc argumentum est petitionis septimum, ex eo quod relicturus sit ipsos: Ergo Patri eos commendat toto tempore quo ipse quoad corpus suum abses futurus est. Vides igitur curam Patris, & Spiritum quem mittit Pater absentiam filij in corpore suo supplere ac compensare in nobis conseruandis, tantisperdum rursus filium viderimus in nubibus venientem ad salutem nostram æternam; adeo vt non relinquat nos Christus tanquam orphanos: & hoc quidem reipsa experimur quo ortquot Christi sumus, qui quo magis destituti sumus corporali Christi ipsius præsentia, & rebus omnibus huius mundi, eo præsentiorem habemus consolatorem illum, quem mittit Pater in no-
units.tr: And I am glorified in them. He returns to his arguments, and this is the sixth argument, drawn from the glory or glorification of the Son himself, which must be joined with our salvation and preservation, since we glorify him by faith, confession and our whole conduct. For by these means we glorify the Son. Therefore those who feel within themselves some zeal for the Son's glory also have a certain confidence in their own salvation and in the Father's special providence towards them. For whoever honours the Son honours the Father, and whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him. And he who honours the Father will be honoured by him. And I am no more. This is the seventh argument of the petition, from the fact that he is about to leave them. Therefore he commends them to the Father for the whole time in which he himself will be absent in his body. You see then the Father's care, and that the Spirit whom the Father sends supplies and compensates for the Son's absence in his body by preserving us, until we see the Son again coming on the clouds to our eternal salvation; so that Christ does not leave us as orphans. And indeed we experience this in fact, all of us who are Christ's: the less we are deprived of Christ's bodily presence and of all the things of this world, the more present we have that Comforter whom the Father sends in the name of the Son.

units.la: Communionis inter Patrem & filium, seu ad adoptionis filios etiam peruenit & pertinet. mine filij, Pater sancte. Conclusio petitionis grauis & affectu plena: affectu, inquam, erga Patrem, & affectu erga discipulos suos. Affectus erga Patrem sese exerit in hoc verbo, Pater, quē alloquitur affectu filiali, & cum sanctum appellat, indicat reuerentiam erga Patrem: Sanctitas enim reuerentiam postulat. Cum autem petit, vt conseruet eos in nomine suo, fiduciam significat, qua confidit in nomine Patris, hoc est per ipsius potentiam solam, ipsos conseruari posse. Ergo exiitit petitio ex amore in Patrem, ex reuerentia, ex confidentia. Hanc autem tam sanctam affectionem animi Domini in precibus suis, numero inter praecipua petitionis ipsius argu-
units.tr: This communion between the Father and the Son also reaches and pertains to the sons of adoption. Holy Father. The conclusion of the petition is weighty and full of feeling: feeling, I say, towards the Father, and feeling towards his disciples. His affection towards the Father shows itself in the word Father, which he addresses with filial affection, and when he calls him holy he shows reverence towards the Father, for holiness demands reverence. When he asks that he keep them in his name, he expresses the confidence with which he trusts that they can be kept in the name of the Father, that is, by his power alone. Therefore the petition arises from love towards the Father, from reverence, and from confidence. Moreover this so holy disposition of the Lord's mind in his prayers I count among the chief arguments of his petition.

units.la: menta. Nam si sanctè non afficiatur Dominus in precibus nostris erga Deum, quorsum attinet argumenta, vel infinita eius multitudine? Iacobus ait multum valere depre-cationem iusti efficacem cap. 5. 16. (Ecce, ait, si efficax sit fi-ue feruens) hoc est, existat ex corde quod feruet amore Domini, & quasi ardescit zelo in illum: Non autem, ait, si multa sint petitionis argumenta, dū dicit, Quos mihi dedisti. His enim verbis ore prolatis, corde simul apprehendit discipulos suos, eorumque amore vehementer exardescit, & fidem illam eorum, de qua supra, erga se compensat. Quod etiam non parum momenti habet in precibus. Quorsum enim attinet orare pro quoquam quem non diligimus? Cum autem haec coniuncta sunt in precibus, zelus Dei & amor proximi, profecto verum esse oportet illud Iacobi, Multum valet oratio iusti. In his enim positus est fenor ille & efficacia Spiritus. Non est autem hoc praetereundum, quod iam tertio loco sit repetitum illud argumentum sumptum ab eo quod ipsi dati sint discipuli a Patre. Crebra ista repetitio huius argumenti, indicat hoc argumento magis permotum Dominum ad hoc vt precaretur, quam alio quouis: nempe quod ipsi a Patre concrediti sint, & dati eo fine, vt ipsis ab eo prouideatur, & omnia faciat eorum causa: id quod etiam fecit. Nam mortuus est pro iis qui ipsi dati sunt: vt doceat nihil non faciendum, & ferendum eorum causa, quos Deus curae nostrae commisit, siue familia sit, siue Ecclesia, siue denique respublica. Vt autem id maximè monuit Dominum, nempe quod ipsi essent a Patre, ad preces pro ipsis concipiendas: ita sine dubio argumentum fuit, quo maximè commotus est Pater ad eos conseruandos quos dedit filio. Nam quemadmodum oportet filium orare pro iis, qui ipsi sunt dati à Patre: ita vicissim oportet Patrem audire filium orantem pro iis, quos ipse dedit filio suo. Quos enim videt Pater curã gerere eorum, quos ipsis commisit, & ipse Pater eos curat pariter ac conseruat. Vt sint vnum. In hoc posita est illa, quam petit conseruatio: nempe vt conformes fiant Patri & filio. Conformitas haec est in vnitate: vt quemadmodum ipsi vnum sunt essentia, ita discipuli vnum sint mentibus & animis, hoc est vnanimes sint, vnumidemque scientes. Existit autem haec vnitas inter homines ex vnione & coniunctione quae est cum iis qui vnum sunt essentia: Coniunctio autem haec est per fidem. Qui enim fide coniuncti sunt & vniti cum Patre & filio, illos charitatis vinculo inter se mutuò coniunctos esse necesse est. Exhis illud apparet: quod cùm videmus homines vnanimiter inter se viuere & concorditer, tum quidem dicere possumus, eos conseruari à Deo, ipsiusque curæ esse. Contrà verò cùm videmus nihil nisi contentiones, dissidia, odia inter homines esse, affirmare possumus à Deo destertos eos esse vbique permissos, vt de gentibus scriptum est, praeteritis aetatibus Deum sinuisse eas ipsarum viis incedere.
units.tr: For if the Lord were not holily affected in our prayers towards God, what would be the use of arguments, even if they were infinite in number? James says that the prayer of a righteous man is very powerful in its working (chap. 5, verse 16): "If it is effectual," he says, "or fervent": that is, it comes from a heart that burns with the love of the Lord and is, as it were, kindled with zeal for him. He does not say that the petition must have many arguments. When he says Whom you have given me, he takes his disciples into his heart as he speaks these words, and burns vehemently with love for them, and returns the faith they have towards him, of which we spoke above. This too is of no small weight in prayer. For what is the use of praying for anyone whom we do not love? Since these things are joined in prayer, the zeal of God and the love of our neighbour, that saying of James must surely be true: "The prayer of a righteous man avails much." For in these things lies that power and efficacy of the Spirit. It must not be passed over that this argument, taken from the fact that the disciples have been given to him by the Father, is repeated here for the third time. This frequent repetition of the argument shows that the Lord was moved to pray by this argument more than by any other, namely that they were entrusted to him by the Father and given for this end, that he should provide for them and do all things for their sake, which he did indeed do. For he died for those who were given to him, to teach that nothing should be left undone or unendured for the sake of those whom God has committed to our care, whether a household, or the Church, or indeed the commonwealth. And just as this above all reminded the Lord that they were from the Father, so that he should conceive prayers for them, so without doubt this was the argument by which the Father was most moved to preserve those whom he gave to the Son. For just as the Son ought to pray for those who were given to him by the Father, so in turn the Father ought to hear the Son praying for those whom he gave to his Son. For the Father sees that the Son takes care of those whom he has entrusted to him, and the Father himself likewise cares for and preserves them. That they may be one. In this lies that preservation which he asks for: namely that they become conformed to the Father and the Son. This conformity is in unity: just as they are one in essence, so the disciples should be one in mind and spirit, that is, they should be of one accord, and know the same thing. Now this unity exists among men through the union and conjunction which is with those who are one in essence; and this conjunction is through faith. For those who are joined and united by faith with the Father and the Son must necessarily be joined together with one another by the bond of charity. From this it appears that when we see men living together in unanimity and concord, we may say that they are preserved by God and are under his care. On the other hand, when we see nothing but contentions, dissensions and hatreds among men, we may affirm that they have been forsaken by God and left everywhere to themselves, as it is written of the nations, that in past ages God suffered them to walk in their own ways.

units.la: {a} Conseruatio electorum Dei in quo posita sit.
units.tr: The preservation of God's elect, and in what it consists.

units.la: 12 Quum essem cum iis in mundo ego seruaui eos per nomen tuum: quos dedisti mihi ego custodiui, & nemo ex iis periit, nisi filius ille perditionis, vt Scriptura impleretur.
units.tr: 12 While I was with them in the world, I kept them in your name. Those whom you gave me I have guarded, and none of them has perished except the son of perdition, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled.

units.la: 13 Nunc autem ad te venio & haec loquor in mundo vt habeant gaudium meum plenum apud se.
units.tr: 13 But now I come to you, and I speak these things in the world, that they may have my joy made full in themselves.

units.la: 14 Ego tradidi eis sermonem tuum, & mundus eos odio habuit, quia non sunt ex mundo, prout ego non sum ex mundo.
units.tr: 14 I have given them your word, and the world has hated them, because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.

units.la: ARGUMENTUM petitionis octauum ex eo quod ipse eos, dum cum iis vnà esset, seruarit: hinc rogat Pa-
units.tr: The argument of the eighth petition, drawn from the fact that while he was with them he kept them; hence he asks the Father to keep them after he himself has departed from this world.

units.la: trem, vt eos seruet posteaquam ex mundo hoc ipse migrauerit. Conseruationem illam eorum suam amplificat pluribus verbis & circumstantiis. Prima est a diligentia in seruando seria, quae colligitur ex repetitione verborum quae eiusdem sensus sunt. Seruaui eos, inquit: deinde eos quos dedisti mihi ego custodiui. Nam filius Dei quos seruauit, eos diligenter ac serio seruauit, vt gallina pullos suos, vt ipse in Euangelio de se loquitur. In seruando enim diligentiam & curam adesse oportet: ideo quod vae illud denuntiatum sit a Propheta in eos, qui negligenter fecerint opus Dei, hoc est homines ex voluntate Dei non perdiderint, ea enim est illius denuntiationis sententia, vt ex argumento illius loci apparet: Ierem.48.10. Quanto magis vae erit illis, qui non seruauerint & custodierint eos quos tradidit Dominus ipsis custodiendos. Seruare enim in se melius est quam perdere. Secunda circumstantia est in modo seruandi. Seruabam, inquit, eos per nomen tuum. Hoc est, per tuam virtutem ac potentiam, mihi communicatam: hinc filius conseruationis suae gloriam Patri suo tribuit. Quo etiam nos docet, vt gloriam totam conseruationis eorum ac nostrae ac omnino actionum nostrarum, quoties earum mentionem facimus, gloriam, inquam, totam Deo Patri in Christo filio tribuamus, agnoscentes in nomine ipsius omnia nos facere & fecisse. Tertia circumstantia est in causa conseruationis efficiente siue implente, his verbis: Quos dedisti mihi. Subest enim his verbis conseruationis causa: nam inter caetera quae eum moverunt ad conseruationem adeo diligentem, profecto hic in primis movit, quod discipuli a Patre traditi sint ipsi seruandi. Nam cum multa nos mouete debeant ad custodiendos diligenter eos qui nostrae fidei concrediti sunt, profecto hoc imprimis id efficere debet, quod Pater eos nobis seruandos tradiderit nostraeque fidei commiserit. Paulus dum Presbyteros Ephesios hortatur ad attendendum gregem, In quo, inquit, Spiritus sanctus vos constituit Episcopos. Significans eos teneri & obligari ad attentionem, hoc ipso quod in Ecclesia constituti sint Episcopi: Ecclesiaeque Dei ipsis sit concredita. Quarta circumstantia est ab effecto conseruationis adeo diligentis. Nemo, inquit, quit, ex iis periit nisi filius perditionis. Hoc est, homo addictus perditioni, idque, ut scriptura impleatur. Altior causa est decreti Dei, cuius revelatio quaedam est scriptura. Ergo, sensus est ac si dixisset: ut decretum Dei, quod in scriptura sacra revelatum est, executionem caperet, est itaque finis cur non servatus fit Iudas: Impletio Scriptura, quamquam quidem impleri necesse fuit, ut Deus verus esset & immutabilis. Nota igitur ex tali conservatione, qualis fuit illa Christi, quis effectus sequatur, nempe salus ac conservatio eorum, qui conservantur, exceptis iis solis, qui filii sunt perditionis, hoc est, aeterno Dei decreto perditioni addicti sunt. Filii enim perditionis nulla diligentia conservari possunt. Fieri quidem potest ut ad tempus in externa disciplina conserventur, quod etiam de Iuda verum fuit: verum tandem oportet hypocritas suo tempore manifestari, ac deficere. Qui autem postquam aliquandiu steterunt, tandem deficiunt, viderint illi ne filii sint perditionis. Beati qui perseuerauerint usque ad finem.
units.tr: him to keep them safe after he has departed from this world. He amplifies that preservation of theirs with more words and circumstances. The first is the earnestness of his diligence in keeping them, which is gathered from the repetition of words having the same sense. I have kept them, he says; then, those whom you gave me I have guarded. For the Son of God, those whom he has kept, he has kept diligently and earnestly, as a hen keeps her chicks, as he himself speaks of himself in the Gospel. For diligence and care must be present in keeping, because that woe was pronounced by the Prophet against those who had carried out the work of God negligently, that is, who had not destroyed men according to the will of God; for this is the sense of that threat, as the argument of that passage makes plain: Jer. 48.10. How much more woe shall be upon them who have not kept and guarded those whom the Lord has delivered to them to guard. For to keep is better than to destroy. The second circumstance lies in the manner of keeping. I kept them, he says, through your name. That is, through your power and might, communicated to me. Hence the Son attributes the glory of his preservation to his Father. By this he also teaches us to attribute the whole glory of their preservation, and of ours, and of all our actions whenever we mention them, I say, the whole glory, to God the Father in Christ the Son, acknowledging that in his name we do and have done all things. The third circumstance lies in the efficient or fulfilling cause of the preservation, in these words: whom you gave me. For a cause of the preservation is implied in these words; for among the other things that moved him to such diligent keeping, this surely moved him first, that the disciples had been delivered by the Father to be kept by him. For although many things ought to move us to guard diligently those who have been entrusted to our faith, this above all ought surely to effect it, that the Father has delivered them to us to be kept and has committed them to our faith. When Paul exhorts the elders of Ephesus to attend to the flock, he says, In which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops. Signifying that they are bound and obliged to attentiveness by this very fact, that bishops have been placed in the Church, and the Church of God has been committed to them. The fourth circumstance is drawn from the effect of such diligent preservation. None of them, he says, has perished except the son of perdition. That is, a man given over to destruction, and this so that the Scripture might be fulfilled. The deeper cause is the decree of God, of which Scripture is a certain revelation. Therefore the sense is as if he had said: that the decree of God, which is revealed in holy Scripture, might take effect; this is therefore the reason why Judas was not kept: the fulfilment of Scripture, which indeed had to be fulfilled, so that God might be true and immutable. Note, then, from such a preservation as Christ's was, what effect follows: the salvation and preservation of those who are preserved, with the sole exception of those who are sons of perdition, that is, who have been given over to destruction by the eternal decree of God. For the sons of perdition cannot be kept by any diligence. It can indeed happen that for a time they are kept within external discipline, which was also true of Judas; but at last hypocrites must be made manifest in their time and fall away. Those who, after standing for some time, at last fall away, let them see to it lest they be sons of perdition. Blessed are those who persevere to the end.

units.la: Nunc autem ad te venio. His verbis habemus conclusionem. Haec loquor in mundo. Hoc est, rogo pro iis, dum adhuc sum una cum iis, ut ipsos servet. Amplificata est conclusio, ex eo quod iis post se relictis veniat ad Patrem: quod argumentum quidem fuit septimum supra. Nota primum: Quos Christus cum in terris ageret aliquando conservauit, eos Pater nunc servat in reditum usque filii sui. Fateor equidem, non servauit nos Christus, eo quo olim discipulos suos modo, hoc est, corporali sua praesentia: quia tum non extitimus in rerum natura. At vero in tota illa sua quae in terris fuit obedientia, in intercessione illa sua quae tam per preces, quam per mortem fuit, singulos electos futuros ad consummationem usque mundi ipse spectauit, & ante oculos suos habuit. Quare si conscientiae nostrae testentur nobis filiu etiam tum Dei dilexisse nos & pro nobis singulis se tradidisse, ut Paulus de se loquutus est, si, inquam, ita testentur nobis conscientiae nostrae, iam persuasum id habere possumus, nos patri curae esse. Vide rursus, qua fiducia commendet Dominus Patri suo discipulos suos seruandos. Nempe quia ipse, cum in terris ageret, prior eos servaverat
units.tr: "But now I am coming to you." In these words we have the conclusion. "I say these things in the world." That is, I pray for them while I am still with them, that he may keep them. The conclusion is amplified from the fact that, leaving them behind, he comes to the Father; which argument was indeed the seventh above. Note first: those whom Christ once kept while he was living on earth, the Father now keeps until the return of his Son. "I confess," it is true, Christ did not keep us in the same way as he once kept his disciples, that is, by his bodily presence, because at that time we did not yet exist in the nature of things. But in all that obedience of his which he rendered on earth, and in that intercession of his which consisted as much in prayers as in death, he looked upon the individual elect who were to come until the consummation of the world, and he had them before his eyes. Wherefore, if our consciences bear witness to us that the Son of God has also loved us even now, and has given himself up for each of us, as Paul spoke of himself, if, I say, our consciences bear such witness to us, we can already be persuaded that we are a care to the Father. See again with what confidence the Lord commends his disciples to his Father to be kept. Namely, because he himself, while living on earth, had kept them beforehand.

units.la: Gal. 2. 20. uit.Qua enim fiducia audet quis rogare, pro iis qui ipsi sunt traditi, cum ipse negligens ac tegnis eorum custos extiterit? Imo affirmo nescire eum pro aliis intercedere apud Deum, vt ipse eos conseruare velit, qui ipse curam eorum non habuerit. Preces enim quae ad Deum concipiuntur pro aliis, non tantum ex zelo Dei, sed etiam ex dilectione, & cura eorum pro quibus precamur fiant necesse est. Vt habeant gaudium meum. Hic finis est cur conseruentur a Patre, vt Christi gaudium in iis impleatur. Supra fuit alius quidam finis, nempe vt sint vnû, quemadmodum Pater & filius vnum sunt. quos quidem seruat Pater, seruat eos & ad pacem cum aliis, & ad pacem conscientiarum, quod hic gaudium vocat. Gaudium autem hoc Christi dicitur, quia gaudium a Patre est per filium, & non nisi per Mediatoris sanguinem fluit ad nos laetitia ista & pax conscientiarum, quae superat omnem intellectum. Hoc est, oportet conscientiae nostrae conspergantur prius Christi sanguine per fide in ipsum, quam verum ac solidum gaudeamus gaudium.
units.tr: Gal. 2. 20. For with what confidence would anyone dare to ask for those who have been committed to himself, when he himself has been a careless and sluggish keeper of them? Indeed I affirm that he would not know how to intercede before God for others, that God should wish to preserve those whose care he himself has not had. For prayers that are offered to God for others must be made not only from zeal for God, but also from love and care for those for whom we pray. That they may have my joy. This is the purpose why they are preserved by the Father, that Christ's joy may be fulfilled in them. Above, there was another purpose, namely that they may be one, as the Father and the Son are one. Those whom the Father preserves, he preserves both in peace with others and in peace of conscience, which he calls joy here. This joy is said to be Christ's, because the joy is from the Father through the Son, and this gladness and peace of conscience, which surpasses all understanding, flows to us only through the blood of the Mediator. That is, our consciences must first be sprinkled with Christ's blood through faith in him, before we rejoice in a true and solid joy.

units.la: Ego tradidi eis. Argumentum novum a mundi odio. Mundus eos odit: Ergo tu Pater serua eos. Causam odii mundi addit, Quia ex mundo non sunt: Hoc est, segregati sunt per regenerationem ab inquinamentis mundi hujus. Causam quoque huius rei affert, ex sermone ipsius tradito: Nam sermo Dei regenerat nos, & a mundo ipso segregat. Commendat autem quadam similitudine sui ipsius hoc quod ex mundo non sint. Prout, inquit, ego non sum ex mundo: hoc est, impollutus sum, segregatus a peccatoribus & sublimior caelis factus. Haec autem similitudo commendat nos Deo pariter & exosos reddit mundo. Nam Christus est qui primum omnium odit mundus, hoc est, ipsa lux est, ipsa sanctitas est: hinc deriuatur in eos qui luce & sanctitate illa affecti sunt aliquo modo. Nota: odium mundi argumentum est dilectionis ac conseruationis Dei, idque nos quoque ipsi in nobis sentimus. Nam quanto propius ad mundum accedimus, & ad mundi conuersationem, tanto longius sentimus nos abesse a Deo. Rursus quanto remotiores sumus a mundo, tanto propiores esse nos ipsi sentimus.
units.tr: I have given them. A new argument from the hatred of the world. The world hates them: therefore you, Father, preserve them. He adds the cause of the world's hatred: because they are not of the world. That is, they have been set apart by regeneration from the defilements of this world. He also gives the cause of this matter, from the word delivered by him: for the word of God regenerates us and separates us from the world itself. He commends, by a certain likeness to himself, the fact that they are not of the world. Just as, he says, I am not of the world: that is, I am undefiled, separated from sinners and made higher than the heavens. This likeness commends us to God and at the same time makes us hateful to the world. For Christ is the one whom the world hates first of all; that is, he is the light itself, he is holiness itself; from this it is derived, in some measure, to those who have been endowed with that light and holiness. Note: the hatred of the world is a sign of God's love and preservation, and we ourselves feel this in ourselves. For the nearer we come to the world and to the world's way of life, the farther we feel ourselves to be from God. Again, the more remote we are from the world, the nearer we feel ourselves to be.

units.la: 15 Non rogo vt tollas eos è mundo, sed vt serues illos à malo illo.
units.tr: 15 I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from that evil.

units.la: 16 Ex mundo non sunt, prout & ego non sum ex mundo.
units.tr: They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.

units.la: 17 Sanctifica eos tua veritate, sermo ille tuus veritas est.
units.tr: Sanctify them by your truth; your word is truth.

units.la: Conclusio per occupationem sententiæ alienæ: colligi enim ex dictis potuit, Ergo rogas vt tollantur ipsi è mundo? huic occurrit: Non rogo vt, & c. sed vt serues eos à malo. Hoc est, ab odio & persequutionibus mundi. Nota hic duo remedia aduersus persequutionem mūdi, Vnum est cùm Deus suos tollit è mundo, & ad se colligit: Alterum est, cùm seruat suos in mediis persequutionibus. Ad hæc remedia hoc ordine accedit Deus. Non quidem statim tollit suos è mundo, quinimò sinit eos manere in mundo tantisper dum opus suum eorum ministerio perficiat. Interea autem seruat eos in mundo, & in mediis istis persequutionibus mirabiliter. Vbi autem seruati fuerint aliquandiu, donec nimirum opus suum per eos ipse peregerit, tum ad se eos colligit suo tempore, hoc est, facit eos triumphare de mundo, quos mundus perditos esse opinatus est. Nam cùm tollit suos è mundo, tum liberat eos plenè perfectèque ab omnibus malis.
units.tr: This is a conclusion drawn by anticipating an objection. It could be inferred from what was said: "So you ask that they be taken out of the world?" He answers this: I do not ask that you, etc., but that you keep them from evil. That is, from the hatred and persecutions of the world. Here note two remedies against the persecution of the world. One is when God takes his people out of the world and gathers them to himself; the other is when he keeps them safe in the midst of persecutions. God proceeds to these remedies in this order. He does not take his people out of the world at once; rather, he allows them to remain in the world for as long as it takes to accomplish his work through their ministry. Meanwhile he keeps them in the world, and in the midst of these persecutions, wonderfully. But when they have been kept for some time, until he has finished his work through them, then in his own time he gathers them to himself. That is, he makes them triumph over the world, which thought they were lost. For when he takes his people out of the world, he then frees them fully and completely from all evils.

units.la: Ex mundo non sunt. Argumentum petitionis decimum ex eo quòd non sint ex mundo: hoc est, quòd renati sint, quòd separati sint ab inquinamentis huius mundi, Deóque consecrati. Qua autem re fiat vt renascamur, & à mundo separemur, vidimus suprà: nimirum verbo Dei, quod est immortale illud semen, ex quo renascimur. Commendat autem hanc eorum conditionem similitudine quadam suiipsius: Sicut & ego non sum ex mundo. Frequens est Dominus in his comparationibus. Nam similitudo Christi in re quacunque nostram conditionem commendat, etiam similitudo in ignominia quæ est propter nomen ipsius. Per se quidem conditionem ignominiosam, conditionem facit gloriosam. Quanto magis similitudo in gloria, in sanctitate ac separatione
units.tr: They are not of the world. This is the tenth argument for the petition, from the fact that they are not of the world: that is, that they have been born again, that they have been separated from the defilements of this world, and consecrated to God. We saw above by what means we are born again and separated from the world: namely, by the word of God, which is that immortal seed from which we are born again. He commends this condition of theirs by a certain likeness to himself: Just as I too am not of the world. The Lord often uses such comparisons. For the likeness of Christ commends our condition in any matter whatever, even the likeness in the disgrace that comes for his name. In itself disgraceful, that condition he makes glorious. How much more will the likeness in glory, in holiness and in separation from this world, make us glorious?

units.la: ab hoc mundo, nos gloriosos reddet? Nota ex hoc argumento, Quo remotiores à mundo sumus, eo melius custodimur à Deo. Nam quid aliud est custodiri à Deo, quàm seperari à mundo, ne peccamus cum mundo? Non dico hoc equidem eo animo quòd velim homines in solitudines se recipere, aut omnino monasticâ istam Papistarum vitam sequi, hoc est, vitam mortuam, otiosam ac inutilem vel Ecclesiæ Dei, vel reipublicæ. Sed volo homines in hominum aliorum societate viuere, seperare autem se à mundi huius conuersatione, & vita. Hoc est, quod dicit Apostolus, Inculpatos viuere in medio nationis prauæ ac peruersæ, & splendere inter homines, vt luminaria in mundo, sermonem vitæ praetendentia. Vel, vt in eadem epistola scriptum est, Volo eos ita se gerere in mundo & hominum societate, vt interea sint municipes regni cælorum: inde expectantes ventu-rum seruatorem suum Dominum Iesum Christum. Sanctifica eos. Occasione proximi illius argumenti à separatione eorum à mundo, quæ nihil aliud est re ipsa quàm sanctificatio, petit à Patre, vt velit magis magisque sanctificare discipulos suos. Instrumentum sanctificationis innuit esse veritatem ipsius: hæc quidem est non quæuis veritas. Non enim quæcunque indifferenter veritas sanctificat: sed veritas quæ est in Iesu: qui ipse est via, veritas & vita. Verùm Euangelista verbis sequentibus veritatè hanc definit ex sermone ipsius Dei qui verax est, vel ipsa veritas potius. Nam sermo Dei de Christo, vt est immortale illud semen ex quo primùm renascimur; ita est hac illud sincerum, per quod adolescamus in Christo. Nota, petit vt sanctificentur, hoc est, magis magisque separetur à mundo. Nō satis est semel sanctificari, aut inchoare semel illam à mundo nostri separationem: sed qui sanctus est, sanctificetur adhuc. Modus autem quo progredimur in vitæ sanctimonia, est per preces tam nostras, quàm aliorum. Precatur hic Christus, vt magis magisque sanctificentur ipsius discipuli. Instrumentum verò sanctificationis, est veritas siue sermo veritatis. Precandum igitur est, vt hic sermo perpetuò efficax sit ad sanctificandum nos, adeo vt quoties eum audire conceditur, toties progressum in sanctitate aliquê faciamus.
units.tr: Note from this argument: the further we are from the world, the better we are kept by God. For what else is being kept by God than being separated from the world, so that we do not sin along with the world? I do not say this because I want people to withdraw into solitude, or to follow altogether the monastic life of the Papists, that is, a dead, idle life, useless either to the Church of God or to the commonwealth. I want people to live in the society of other men, but to keep themselves apart from the way and manner of life of this world. This is what the Apostle means when he says that we should live blameless in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, and shine among men as lights in the world, holding out the word of life. Or, as is written in the same epistle, I want them so to conduct themselves in the world and in human society that meanwhile they are citizens of the kingdom of heaven, expecting from there their Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ. Sanctify them. On the occasion of that preceding argument from their separation from the world, which in reality is nothing other than sanctification, he asks of the Father that he would be willing to sanctify his disciples more and more. He indicates that the instrument of sanctification is his own truth; but this is not just any truth. For not every truth sanctifies indiscriminately, but the truth that is in Jesus, who himself is the way, the truth and the life. Yet the Evangelist, in the words that follow, defines this truth as the word of God himself, who is true, or rather truth itself. For the word of God concerning Christ, as it is that immortal seed from which we are first born again, so it is also that pure milk by which we grow up in Christ. Note that he asks that they be sanctified, that is, separated from the world more and more. It is not enough to be sanctified once, or to begin once that separation of ourselves from the world; rather, he who is holy must still be sanctified. The way in which we progress in holiness of life is through prayers, both our own and those of others. Here Christ prays that his disciples may be sanctified more and more. But the instrument of sanctification is the truth, or the word of truth. We must therefore pray that this word may always be effective in sanctifying us, so that whenever we are permitted to hear it, we make some progress in holiness.

units.la: 18 Sicut me misisti in mundum, ita & ego misi eos in mundum.
units.tr: 18 As you sent me into the world, so also I have sent them into the world.

units.la: 19 Et eorum causa ego sanctifico meipsum, ut sint & ipsi sanctificati in veritate.
units.tr: 19 And for their sake I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in the truth.

units.la: S Equuntur huius petitionis argumenta duo. Primum est ex eo quod mittit eos in mundum tanquam Apostolos. Hunc ipsorum apostolatum commendat sui quadam similitudine: ut enim ipse à Patre missus est in mundum, & ita ipse dicit se misisse eos in mundū. Nā & Christus Apostolus fuit quodammodo: Magnus nimirum ille Apostolus professionis nostrae. Verum discrimen in eo fuit quòd Christus missus est immediatè à Patre: Apostoli vero non immediatè à Patre: sed per filium missi sunt. Idem iudicium faciendum est de Prophetis, Evangelistis, Pastoribus & Doctoribus: & ut verbo dicam, de omnibus donis quæcunque in Ecclesiam Dei conferuntur, sunt enim omnia ea à Christo proximè & immediatè. Ascendit longè supra omnes cælos, ut impleret omnia. Dedit itaque ipse alios Apostolos, alios Euangelistas. Nota hic, qui demū mittantur in mundū ad prædicandum Euangelium, oportet quidem ij separentur à mundo: hoc est, sanctificentur, neque configurentur sæculo isti. Nullos autem mittit Dominus, nisi quos aliquo modo ipse sanctificat. Qui autem nulla ex parte sanctificati sunt, sed omnino mundo huic conformes manent, ij profectò non tam à Domino missi sunt, quàm ipsi sua sponte cucurrerunt. Et pro iis ego sanctifico. Argumentum huius petitionis secundum. Ego sanctifico meipsum in hunc finem, ut ipsi sanctificentur, id est, Ego me morti consecro, ut sancti sint ipsi ac tibi consecrati. Est itaque argumentum à fine sanctificationis & consecrationis Christi. Consecratio enim Christi, & mors Christi nos sanctificat & consecrat ad officium & munus quodcunque. Quare, ut sanctissimus in munere quocunque, maximè in ministerio isto, oculi perpetuò figendi sunt in morte illa Christi, ipsiusque per mortem consecratione. Instrumentum autem consecrationis huius nostri & sanctificationis est sermo veritatis, hoc est, nostræ.
units.tr: Two arguments follow for this petition. The first is from the fact that he sends them into the world as Apostles. He commends their apostleship by a certain likeness to himself: just as he was sent by the Father into the world, so he says that he has sent them into the world. For Christ too was in a sense an Apostle, that great Apostle of our profession. But there is this difference: Christ was sent immediately by the Father, whereas the Apostles were not sent immediately by the Father but through the Son. The same judgment must be made concerning prophets, evangelists, ministers and teachers, and, to say it in a word, concerning all the gifts that are bestowed on the Church of God, for all of these come from Christ proximately and immediately. He ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. Therefore he himself gave some as Apostles, and some as evangelists. Note here that those who are finally sent into the world to preach the Gospel must indeed be separated from the world, that is, sanctified, and not conformed to this age. The Lord sends no one except those whom he himself in some way sanctifies. But those who are not sanctified in any part, and remain altogether conformed to this world, have certainly not been sent by the Lord so much as they have run of their own accord. And for them I sanctify. This is the second argument for this petition. I sanctify myself to this end, that they may be sanctified: that is, I consecrate myself to death, that they may be holy and consecrated to you. It is therefore an argument from the end of the sanctification and consecration of Christ. For the consecration of Christ and the death of Christ sanctify and consecrate us to whatever office and duty. Therefore, that we may be holy in any office whatever, and most especially in this ministry, our eyes must always be fixed on that death of Christ and on his consecration through death. The instrument of this consecration and sanctification of ours is the word of truth, that is, of ours.

units.la: Altera commendatio Apostolatus, à fine sanctificationis Christi.
units.tr: The second commendation of the apostleship, from the end of Christ's sanctification.

units.la: Instrumentum sanctificationis nostræ.
units.tr: The instrument of our sanctification.

units.la: sermo ille de cruce, vt vocat eum Apostolus. Hoc enim sermone tanquā instrumento Spiritus sancti, crux Christi ad nos applicatur. Applicata autem crux & apprehensa per fidem nos sanctificat, fide enim purgantur corda nostra.
units.tr: That word about the cross, as the Apostle calls it. For by this word, as the instrument of the Holy Spirit, the cross of Christ is applied to us. And when the cross is applied and apprehended by faith, it sanctifies us, for our hearts are purified by faith.

units.la: 20 Non tantum autem pro istis rogo, sed & pro iis qui per sermonem eorum credituri sunt in me.
units.tr: 20 Yet I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word.

units.la: 21 Vt omnes unum sint sicut tu Pater in me, & ego in te, vt & ipsi in nobis unum sint: vt credat mundus me a te missum esse.
units.tr: 21 That they may all be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me.

units.la: Tertia capitis pars, continens precationem pro quibuscunque credenti bus futuris vsque ad finem mundi.
units.tr: The third part of the chapter, containing the prayer for all believers who will come until the end of the world.

units.la: HActenus pro discipulis precatus est, primum vt seruentur, deinde vt sanctificentur: Nunc in postrema precum istarum parte, precatur pro fidelibus quibuscunque diffundant preces Christi, extendantque se in progressu magis magisque. Primum pro se tantum precatus est, vt Pater ipsum glorificaret: deinde pro discipulis suis precatus est, vt Pater ipsos conseruaret primum, deinde sanctificaret. Tertio nunc orat pro omnibus fidelibus quotquot futuri sunt in Ecclesia ad suum vsque reditum. Gratia enim Christi superabundat: verum non ad alios patet quam fideles, idque non culpa ipsius gratiae, quae patere quidem potest, vel in mille mundos: sed culpa hominum, qui capaces gratiae non sunt: vtpote expertes fidei. Vnde factum est vt precatus sit Christus pro fidelibus: mortuus sit pro fidelibus: promissiones omnes faciat in gratiam fidelium. Verum qua ratione fidem assequimur, non alia quam per verbum Apostolorum, Qui, inquit, per sermonem eorum. Sic enim honorat Dominus Apostolos suos, vt nolit fidem gigni aliter quam per sermonem ipsorum, vel praedicatum, vel scriptum. Non excludit quidem hoc sermonem propheticum, verum excludit omnia somnia hominum & vanitates istas quas venditant non scriptas. Quod autem precatur ipse pro fidelibus, hoc nimirum est, Vt omnes vnum sint. hoc est, vniatur ij in vnum corpus, & vnu nouum hominem, cuius quidem caput est Christus, sine quo nulla horum vnio, ne eorum quidem qui maxime con-
units.tr: Until now he has prayed for the disciples, first that they be kept and then that they be sanctified. Now, in the last part of this prayer, he prays for all the faithful, so that the prayers of Christ may spread and extend further and further as they go. First he prayed only for himself, that the Father would glorify him; then he prayed for his disciples, that the Father would first preserve them and then sanctify them. Third, he now prays for all the faithful, however many there will be in the Church until his return. For the grace of Christ overflows, but it does not extend to anyone other than the faithful. This is not the fault of grace itself, which could indeed extend even to a thousand worlds, but the fault of men, who are not capable of grace, being destitute of faith. Hence it is that Christ prayed for the faithful, died for the faithful, and makes all his promises for the sake of the faithful. But by what means we attain faith? By no other means than through the word of the Apostles: "who believe through their word." For thus the Lord honours his Apostles, so that he will not have faith begotten in any other way than through their word, whether preached or written. This indeed does not exclude the prophetic word, but it excludes all the dreams of men and those vanities which they peddle as unwritten. Now what he prays for the faithful is this: "That they all may be one," that is, that they be united into one body and one new man, whose head is Christ, apart from whom there is no such union, not even among those who seem most closely joined either by nature or by some other bond.

units.la: Finis precū Christi pro quibus credentibus à finē vnionis eorum. coniunčti esse videntur vel natura, vel alia quapiam ratione. Nisi enim in ipso sanctificentur natura aliàque omnia vincula, non vere vniuntur per ea inter sese homines. Per ipsum autem omnium recollectio fit, tum quæ in cœlis sunt, tum quæ in terra. Vide Ephes. 1.10. Colos. 1.20. Vnio ista amplificatur pluribus argumentis; primùm similitudine Patris & filii, qui vnum sunt natura ipsa & essentia: Sicut, inquit, tu Pater. Nulla enim re alia repræsentamus magis Deum ac Trinitatem illâ gloriosam, quàm vnione ista & coalitione quasi in vnū corpus. Deinde innuitur eius causa, dum dicitur, Vt & ipsi in nobis vnum sint: hoc est, vniti nobis ac nobiscum coniuncti. Coniunctio enim cum Christo, quæ fit per fidem, causa est coniunctionis cum Ecclesia & corpore Christi, quæ fit per vinculum charitatis. Postremò finis est vnionis huius: Vt, inquit, credat mundus: hoc est, vt mundus credat, intuitus hanc vnionem membrorum Christi, videlicet Christum à Patre missum; hoc est, diuinum quendam hominem esse, neque id modò, sed Deum ipsum esse. Nam non ab alia vlla virtute fluit hæc hominum vnio inter se, & coniunctio membrorum corporis Christi, quà ad diuina illa: estque hoc certum argumentum deitatis Christi: cuius quidem virtute coalescimus nos in vnum corpus. Virtus enim, qua viuificantur & continentur inter se, cohærentque mutuo membra, à capite tota deriuatur.{a}
units.tr: The end of Christ's prayer for believers, from the end of their union: they seem to be joined either by nature or by some other bond. For unless men are sanctified in him, nature and all other bonds notwithstanding, they are not truly united with one another through those bonds. Through him, moreover, the gathering of all things takes place, both those in heaven and those on earth (see Eph. 1.10; Col. 1.20). This union is enlarged by several arguments. First, by the likeness of the Father and the Son, who are one by nature and essence itself: "As you, Father, are in me." For we represent God and that glorious Trinity by nothing more than by this union and coalition, as it were, into one body. Next, its cause is indicated when it is said, "That they also may be one in us," that is, united to us and joined with us. For the conjunction with Christ, which comes about through faith, is the cause of the conjunction with the Church and the body of Christ, which comes about through the bond of love. Lastly, the end of this union is: "that the world may believe." That is, the world, looking upon this union of the members of Christ, may believe that Christ was sent by the Father, that is, that he is some divine man, and not only this, but God himself. For this union of men among themselves, and the conjunction of the members of Christ's body, flows from no other power than that divine one, and this is a sure argument for the deity of Christ, by whose power we cohere into one body. For the power by which the members are quickened and held together, and cling mutually to one another, is wholly derived from the head.

units.la: 22 Et ego gloriam quam dedisti mihi, dedi eis: vt sint vnum, sicut & nos vnum sumus.
units.tr: 22 And the glory which thou gavest me I have given them; that they may be one, even as we are one.

units.la: 23 Ego in eis, & tu in me, vt sint consummati in vnum, & vt cognoscat mundus quòd tu me misisti, & eos diligas, prout me dilexisti.
units.tr: 23 I in them, and thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one, and that the world may know that thou hast sent me, and mayest love them, as thou hast loved me.

units.la: HActenus argumentum petitionis fuit à fine vnionis; sequitur nunc argumentum alterum à fine gloriæ illius quam Pater dedit filio: filius autem dedit fidelibus; est autem vt vniatur inter se fideles. Gloria hæc à Patre data filio in eo posita esse videtur, quòd Pater sit in filio, quemadmodum sequens versus exponit. Pater enim in æterna illa generatione, totam eandémque es-
units.tr: Hitherto the argument of the petition has been drawn from the end of the union; now follows a second argument, drawn from the end of that glory which the Father gave to the Son: and the Son gave it to the faithful; and it is that the faithful be united among themselves. This glory, given by the Father to the Son, seems to consist in this, that the Father is in the Son, as the following verse explains. For the Father, in that eternal generation, communicated to his Son the whole and the same essence,

units.la: {a} Ecclesiæ Christi felicitas. sentiam suam filio suo communicauit: hinc in eo dicitur esse atque gloriam suam ipsi dare. Nam gloria Patris nihil aliud est quàm gloriosa ipsius essentia. Gloriam autem quam filius dat fidelibus, sequens versus exponit in eo sitam esse quòd filius sit in fidelibus. Nam in regeneratione nostri, filius dat Spiritum sanctum credenti cuique, & diuinæ naturæ consortes nos facit: imò seipse communicat nobis. Nam per fidem Christus inhabitat in cordibus nostris. Atque inde est quod dicatur filius in nobis esse, & gloriam suam nobis tribuere, quæ admodum Pater gloriam suam tribuit filio. Etenim hoc loco similitudinem sic accipio, quòd quemadmodum Pater gloriam suam filio: ita filius gloriam suam nobis det. Tum sequitur finis: Vt sint vnum sicut & nos. Pater & filius vnum sunt, quia Pater est in filio. Quia autem filius est in nobis, non tantùm vnum sumus cum filio, ac cum eo coniungimur: sed etiam vnimur inter nos ipsi, vt membra in corpore mutuo vniuntur. Nam ex fide illa qua vnimur cum Christo capite charitas existit qua tanquam vinculo perfectionis vniuntur inter se membra, atque ita perficiuntur: Nam sequenti versu dicitur (Vt sint perfecti in vnum) Vnio enim membrorum in corpore iplorum perfectio est: perfectio enim membri, vt manus, vt pedis, non quidem in eo est, quod separetur membrum à corpore, sed in coniunctione cum reliquis corporis membris: tum enim officio suo fungendo aptum est. Disce hoc loco efficaciam illam manantem ex coniunctione illa quæ est cum capite Christo, & ex fide in eum, non efficere, vt quis in se omnibus numeris absolutus sit, ac omni donorum genere completus; ita vt nihil egeat communione reliquorum membrorum: verùm efficere eam efficaciam, vt vniatur cum reliquis membris, accipiatque non donum corporis totius, sed donum membri, hoc est, mensuram fidei, vt donum oculi in corpore, donum manus, donum pedis. Quare quisquis separat se à corpore, putatque se omnia in se habere, is nihil habet.
units.tr: The happiness of the Church of Christ. The Father communicated his whole and the same essence to his Son; hence he is said to be in him and to give his glory to him. For the glory of the Father is nothing other than his glorious essence. The verse that follows explains that the glory which the Son gives to believers consists in this, that the Son is in them. For in our regeneration the Son gives the Holy Spirit to every believer, and makes us partakers of the divine nature; indeed he communicates himself to us. For Christ dwells in our hearts through faith. Hence it is said that the Son is in us and gives his glory to us, just as the Father gives his glory to the Son. Here I take the comparison in this way: as the Father gives his glory to the Son, so the Son gives his glory to us. Then the end is stated: That they may be one, as we also are. The Father and the Son are one because the Father is in the Son. But because the Son is in us, we are not only one with the Son and joined to him, but we are also united with one another, as the members are mutually united in the body. For from that faith by which we are united with Christ our head comes the love by which the members are united with one another as by the bond of perfection, and so are made perfect. For the next verse says, That they may be made perfect in one. For the union of the members in the body is their perfection: the perfection of a member, such as a hand or a foot, lies not in its being separated from the body, but in its joining with the other members of the body; for only then is it fit to perform its function. Learn here that the efficacy flowing from that union which we have with Christ our head, and from faith in him, does not make anyone so complete in himself, in every respect, and furnished with every kind of gift, that he needs no fellowship with the other members; rather it has this efficacy, that he is joined with the other members and receives not the gift of the whole body but the gift of a member, that is, a measure of faith, as the eye has its gift in the body, the hand its gift, the foot its gift. Therefore whoever separates himself from the body, and thinks he has everything in himself, has nothing.

units.la: Et vt cognoscat mundus. Hic duplicē habes finem vnionis eius: prior est idem cum illo qui supra fuit vers. 21. vt cognoscat mundus meà te missum esse: posterior est, Vt Ut cognoscat te diligere ipsos, sicut me dilexisti. Prior igitur finis est gloria filij: quae in eo est, quod filius agnoscatur à Patre missus: posterior est gloria Patris, quae in eo est, ut agnoscatur Pater diligere filium. Nam eo splendet maxime Patris gloria, quòd misericors & amans nostri agnoscatur. Sed qualisna est hic amor? nimirum talis qualis est Patris amor erga filium suum, paternus nimirum. Neque enim misisset filium, eúmque pro nobis morti tradidisset, nisi nos dilexisset sicut filium & dilectum suum. Nota hic finem cur Deus congreget in vnum Ecclesiam in terris; hoc est, constituat corpus Christo: nempe ut gloria Patris & filij in ea conspiciatur. Nota etiam ordinem quo cognoscatur gloria Patris & filij. Nimirum primùm agnoscitur filius missus à Patre pro nobis nostrique redemptione: deinde agnoscitur immisso & pro nobis tradito filio amor ille Patris &c.
units.tr: Et ut cognoscat mundus: Here you have a twofold end of that union. The first is the same as the one mentioned above at verse 21, that the world may know that you sent me; the second is that the world may know that you have loved them, just as you loved me. The first end, then, is the glory of the Son, which lies in this: that the Son is acknowledged as sent by the Father. The second is the glory of the Father, which lies in this: that the Father is acknowledged to love the Son. For the glory of the Father shines most brightly in this, that he is recognised as merciful and loving towards us. But what sort of love is this? Surely such as the Father's love towards his own Son, that is, a fatherly love. For he would not have sent the Son and handed him over to death for us, unless he had loved us as his own Son and his beloved. Note here the end for which God gathers the Church into one on earth, that is, establishes a body for Christ: namely, that the glory of the Father and the Son may be seen in it. Note also the order in which the glory of the Father and the Son is known. Namely, first the Son is acknowledged as sent by the Father for us and for our redemption; then, with the Son sent and given up for us, that love of the Father is acknowledged, etc.

units.la: 24 Pater, quos dedisti mihi, velim ut ubi sum ego, & illi sint mecum: ut conspiciant gloriam illam meam quam dedisti mihi: quia dilexisti me ante iactum mundi fundamentum.
units.tr: 24 Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, so that they may behold my glory which you have given me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world.

units.la: 25 Pater iuste, mundus te non novit, ego autem te novi, & hi noverunt me à te missum esse.
units.tr: 25 Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I have known you, and these have known that I was sent by you.

units.la: 26 Et notum ipsis feci nomen tuum, & notum faciam: ut charitas qua dilexisti me, sit in eis, & ego in eis.
units.tr: 26 And I have made your name known to them, and will make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them.

units.la: HActenus petiit pro fidelibus, ut quantisper in hac vita sint, inter se vniantur: Nunc vlterius petit, ut, ubi ipse est, ibi ipsi sint, participéntque cælesti illa gloria vnà cum ipso. Neque enim gratia Christi tantùm est in hac vita, sed vltra hanc vitam in immensum porrigitur. Inchoatur fide, perficitur autem aspectu: ideo dictum est, Ut conspiciant gloriam illam quam dedisti mihi. Verùm conspicere gloriam istam non possumus, nisi, ubi ipse est, ibi simus & nos: hoc est, nisi migremus ex terris in cælos, ubi ipse est, sedétque ad dextram illius maiestatis. Commutare autem terras cum cælis non possumus, nisi nos mutemur ipsi primùm. Mutatio autem nostri vel est per mortem, vel est per id quod vice mortis futurum est, in extremo illo die: quamobrem fi mutare locum velimus, id est, terram cum cælo commutare; ne tam ægre feramus hoc quod mutandi fumus ipsi per mortem. Imò desideremus ea omnia quæ facere possunt ad loci mutationem, & aspectum illum gloriæ filij Dei. Sed qui demum sunt qui terras cum cælis commutaturi sunt? Non alij profecto quàm quos Pater electos ab æterno dedit filio: hos autem, etsi nunc peregrè agant à Domino absentes, hos, inquam, aliquando necesse est ad Dominum præfentes esse & ad eum ire habitatum. Qui fide incedunt in hac vita, eos oportet aspectu incedere in altera. Sed notandus est hic finis migrationis nostræ; nempe ut videamus gloriam Christi. Hic est ille aspectus, de quo Apostolus ait, Per fidem incedimus non per aspectum. Videmus quidem nunc gloriam Domini, sed in speculo. Nos autem, inquit, omnes retecta facie, gloriam Domini ut in speculo intuentes in eandem imaginem transformamur ex gloria in gloriam. Cùm autem ibi erimus vbi ipse est, tum quidem eum perfecte, & coram videbimus: cùm autem videbimus eum sicut est, tum plenè perfecteque ipsi glorificabimur. Nam fi fides nos glorificat ex parte; hoc est, dum eum quasi eminus intuemur, profecto aspectus nos plenè perfecteque glorificabit. Tum etiam cùm videbimus eum coram, nos eum perfecte glorificabimus, & indefinen-ter clamabimus, Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus, Dominus Deus ille omnipotens, &c. Quod autem nunc nö perfecte eum glorificamus, in causa est, quia ipsi nondum videmus perfecte ipsius gloriam. Quia dilexisti hoc est, fundamentum gloriæ filij: nempe dilectio Patris ab æterno. Ex dilectione gloriam meriti poteris. Dilectio est immensa: gloria igitur immensa: dilectio est ab æterno: gloria igitur est ab æterno. Glorifica me Pater ea gloria quam habui apud te priusquam, &c. Dilectio est in æternum: ideo gloria in æternum futura est. Sed notandum quod dum loquitur de gloria sua data sibi à Patre, simul sentiat Patris illâ dilectione. Quaobrem de gloria sua cum gaudio mentionem fecit, & cum lætitia animi ineffabili gloria sua fruebatur. Nam fi quis velit frui donis Dei, hoc est, cum voluptate iis vti, sentiat is necesse est dilectionem Dei, à qua profecta sunt illa dona. Quod si quis cum dono Dei aliquo non sentiat dilectionem, & eam quidem in illo diligente profecto non percipiat is necesse est veram voluptatem ex dono ipso: vera emin voluptas est non tam ex dono ipsius que usu, quàm ex dilectionis Dei sensu illo suauissimo.
units.tr: Hitherto he has prayed for the faithful, that for as long as they are in this life they may be united with one another. Now he prays further, that where he himself is, there they also may be, and share with him that heavenly glory. For the grace of Christ is not only in this life, but extends immeasurably beyond it. It is begun by faith but perfected by sight; therefore it is said, that they may behold the glory which you have given me. Yet we cannot behold that glory unless we also are where he is, that is, unless we migrate from earth to heaven, where he is and sits at the right hand of that majesty. Now we cannot exchange earth for heaven unless we ourselves are first changed. Our change comes either through death, or through that which will take the place of death on the last day. Therefore, if we wish to change place, that is, to exchange earth for heaven, let us not bear it with grief that we must be changed by death. Rather let us desire all those things which can help toward the change of place and toward that sight of the glory of the Son of God. But who are they who are to exchange earth for heaven? Surely none other than those whom the Father from eternity has given as elect to the Son. These, though for now they are abroad, absent from the Lord, these, I say, must at some time be present with the Lord and go to dwell with him. Those who walk by faith in this life must walk by sight in the next. But we must note this end of our migration: namely, that we may see the glory of Christ. This is that sight of which the Apostle says, We walk by faith, not by sight. Now indeed we see the glory of the Lord, but in a mirror. But we all, he says, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory. When we shall be where he is, then indeed we shall see him perfectly and face to face; and when we shall see him as he is, then we shall be glorified fully and perfectly in him. For if faith glorifies us in part, that is, while we behold him as if from afar, sight will certainly glorify us fully and perfectly. Then also, when we shall see him face to face, we shall glorify him perfectly, and we shall cry out without ceasing, Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God, the Almighty, and so on. The reason that we do not now glorify him perfectly is that we do not yet see his glory perfectly. Because you loved me: this is the foundation of the Son's glory, namely the Father's love from eternity. From the love you may gather the glory of his merit. The love is immense; therefore the glory is immense. The love is from eternity; therefore the glory is from eternity. Glorify me, Father, with the glory which I had with you before, and so on. The love is eternal; therefore the glory will be eternal. But we must note that, while he speaks of his glory given to him by the Father, he at the same time feels the Father's love in it. For this reason he mentioned his glory with joy, and enjoyed his glory with an inexpressible gladness of mind. For if anyone wishes to enjoy the gifts of God, that is, to use them with pleasure, he must necessarily feel the love of God from which those gifts proceed. But if anyone, with some gift of God, does not feel the love, and certainly does not perceive that love in the one who loves him, he necessarily lacks true delight in the gift itself. For true delight comes not so much from the gift and its use as from that most sweet sense of the love of God.

units.la: Pater iuste. Facta mentione dilectionis Patris erga se nunc eam petit communicari discipulis suis, pro quibus nominatim rogat ad finem vsque orationis suæ. Argumentum est à fine cognitionis tum suæ tum discipulorum suorum, quæ huc tendit, vt dilectio Patris sit in discipulis: quasi dicat, O Pater & ego te cognoui in hunc finem, & ipsi te cognouerunt ac deinceps cogniturì sunt in eundem finem, vt dilectio tua in eis sit. Ergo tu dilige eos. Verùm verba ipsa videamus. Pater iuste, inquit: rem scilicet iustam petiturus, nempe vt cognoscentes se, diligat Pater, ideo enim iustum eum appellat.
units.tr: Righteous Father. Having made mention of the Father's love toward himself, he now asks that it be communicated to his disciples, for whom he prays by name until the end of his prayer. The argument is drawn from the end of both his knowledge and that of his disciples, which tends to this, that the Father's love may be in the disciples.
