It is as if he said: O Father, I have known you to this end, and they have known you and shall know you further to the same end, that your love may be in them. Therefore, you love them. But let us look at the words themselves. Righteous Father, he says: about to ask a just thing, namely that the Father should love those who know him. Therefore he calls him righteous.

units.la: Quale enim est id quod petimus à Deo natura sua, tale oportet Deum agnoscere tum animo, tum voce: vt si sit opus potentiæ id quod petimus à Deo, oportet eum & agnoscere animo & voce appellare potentem: si sit opus Sapientiæ, sapiente: si sit opus misericordiæ, misericorde: si denique sit opus iustitiæ, iustu. Nam nisi animus apprehendat Deum in natura sua tale, qua, quaelo, fiducia possimus tale quid ab eo precibus nostris flagitare? Ideo ad preces cõcipiendas Deo, opus est imprimis Deũ in natura sua, ac in proprietatibus, quas vocant, essentialibus, pro modulo isto fidei ac cognitionis nostræ, cognitum habeamus. Mundus te non novit. Ex antithesi siue mauis dissimilitudine ignorantiæ mundi huius obstinatæ, commendat suam & suorum cognitionem. Nam quo quid rarius, eo charius. Quò rarior in terra fides, eò charior: quò pauciores fideles, eò pluris sunt apud Deum, & apud homines pluris esse debent. Falsa igitur est ista aduersariorum conclusio, à paucitate eorum qui veritatem profitentur, ad labefactandam veritatem & puritatem istam Euangelij. Quin potiùs contrà; ideo pluris faciendaest ista nostra professio, quòd mundus eam respuat. Et ego quidem si profiteor hanc Euangelij sinceritatem, commendarem Deo, vel hoc nomine profecto id facerem quòd mundus eam ignoret; hoc est, illa ipsa multitudo, quam statuunt aduersarij certissimam Ecclesiae suae notam. Ego autem novi te. Hic habes ipsius Filij cognitionem.Cognitionis nomine intellige etiam agnitionem & omnino omnem filij submissionem & obedientiam, quae tota huc spectat, vt Pater nos diligat. Gratia illa quae supra mensuram omnem Filio data est nos gratos facit Patri, atque ad vtilitatem & certū bonum nostrum pertinet: non autem tantum illa quae in nobis ipsis est nobisque beneficio Filij inhaeret. Omnia Christi tam quae sunt in ipso Christo, quàm quae sunt in nobis beneficio Christi, nobis prosunt ad salutem. Commendat quoque haec cognitio Patris, quam ipse profitetur, personam precantis pro discipulis. Neque enim parum refert, quis sit qui precetur pro nobis, ilne qui Deo acceptus est, an alius: ilne qui Deum cognouit, an alius. Multum enim valet oratio hominis iusti, ait Iacobus. Quare siue pro nobis ipsis, siue pro aliis precemur, videndum perpetuo an personae nostrae Deo sint acceptae: an fides sit in Christum Iesum, qua placemus Deo. Personae autem nostrae si placeant Deo, tum quidem preces nostrae, tum quae Deus per Spiritum suum efficit in nobis, omnia placent, acceptaque sunt ei. Ethi cognouerunt. Nunc de cognitione ipsorum, primum praesente, deinde futura: nam eam quoque promittit. Praesente autem duplici, primum ipsius Filij, quod missus sit à Patre: deinde Patris, manifestante eum Filio ipso ia cognito. Cognitio enim nostra ipsorum, & quae in nobis est tam Patris quàm Filij, non praesens tantum sed etiam futura huc pertinet, vt nos diligat Pater. Neque enim Deus nos diligit tantum propter id quod in Christo est, nobis autem imputatur: sed etiam propter id quod in nobis est, & in nobis beneficio Christi inhaeret. Neque rursus diligit nos Pater propter fidem & cognitionem praesentem & inchoatam duntaxat, sed etiam respectum habet ad incrementum fidei & cognitionis: adeoque ad complementum donorum Christi in nobis futurum. Inde videtur esse, quod vel exigua tantum fide & cognitione praediti, sentiant tamen in se amore Dei mimirisicū. Videas enim pene idiotas,quoad cognitione, qui vix possunt distinctè & aperte proferre vel tria verba de Deo déque Christo, admirabili tamen sensu Dei & amoris ipsius qui est in dilecto illo, affici. Quantula, quæso, cognitio erat ea quam habuit peccatrix mulier illa quæ Christi pedes lauit lachrymis suis & tersit crinibus? Testatur tamen de ea Christus quòd plurimum dilexerit. Diligere autem non potuit Deum priusquam ipsa esset à Deo dilecta. Non enim priores diligimus Deum.
units.tr: For such as the thing we ask of God is by its nature, such ought we to acknowledge God to be, both in mind and in speech. So if what we ask of God is a work of power, we ought to acknowledge him in mind and address him in speech as powerful; if it is a work of wisdom, as wise; if of mercy, as merciful; and finally if it is a work of justice, as just. For unless the mind grasps God in his nature as such, with what confidence, I ask, could we demand such a thing from him in our prayers? Therefore, in order to conceive prayers to God, it is first necessary that we have God known to us in his nature, and in his so-called essential properties, to the measure of our faith and knowledge. The world has not known you. From the contrast, or if you prefer the dissimilarity, with the stubborn ignorance of this world, he commends his own knowledge and that of his people. For the rarer a thing is, the dearer it is. The rarer faith is on earth, the dearer it is; the fewer the faithful, the more they are worth in God's sight, and they ought to be worth more in the sight of men. Therefore that conclusion of our adversaries is false, which argues from the small number of those who profess the truth to the shaking of this truth and the purity of this Gospel. Rather, on the contrary, this profession of ours should be valued all the more because the world rejects it. And indeed, if I profess this sincerity of the Gospel, I would commend it to God, and I would certainly do so on this very ground, that the world does not know it; that is, that very multitude which our adversaries set up as the most certain mark of their Church. But I have known you. Here you have the knowledge of the Son himself. By the name of knowledge understand also acknowledgment, and altogether the whole submission and obedience of the Son, all of which looks toward this, that the Father should love us. That grace which was given to the Son beyond all measure makes us pleasing to the Father, and it pertains to our profit and certain good; not only that grace which is in ourselves and adheres to us by the Son's benefit. All of Christ's gifts, both those which are in Christ himself and those which are in us by Christ's benefit, profit us for salvation. This knowledge also commends the person of the one praying for the disciples, which he himself professes. For it matters not little who it is that prays for us, whether one who is acceptable to God or another, whether one who knows God or another. For the prayer of a righteous man avails much, says James. Therefore, whether we pray for ourselves or for others, we must always see whether our persons are acceptable to God, whether there is faith in Christ Jesus by which we please God. But if our persons please God, then our prayers, and whatever God works in us through his Spirit, all please him and are acceptable to him. And these have known: now of their knowledge, first as present and then as future, for he promises this too. The present knowledge is twofold: first that of the Son himself, that he was sent by the Father; then that of the Father, made manifest by the Son, who is now known. For our knowledge of them, and that which is in us of both the Father and the Son, pertains to this, that the Father should love us, not only in the present but also in the future. For God loves us not only on account of what is in Christ and is imputed to us, but also on account of what is in us and adheres to us by Christ's benefit. Nor again does the Father love us only on account of faith and knowledge that are present and only begun; he also has regard to the increase of faith and knowledge, and thus to the future completion of Christ's gifts in us. Hence it seems that even those endowed with only a small measure of faith and knowledge nevertheless feel the love of God in themselves in a marvellous way. For you may see almost unlearned folk, weak in knowledge, who can scarcely state clearly and distinctly even three words about God and about Christ, yet are moved by a wonderful sense of God and of that love which is in the Beloved. How small, I ask, was the knowledge that the sinful woman had, who washed Christ's feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair? Yet Christ testifies of her that she loved much. But she could not love God before she herself was loved by God. For we do not love God first.

units.la: Hic quoque nota principium, ac progressum, denique incrementum cognitionis nostrę. Principium & causa cognitionis nostrę, est cognitio Filij, qui est in sinu Patris. Nisi enim Filium doctorem haberemus, nunquam quicquam de Deo cognosceremus. Quare vt filius nos doceat, oportet ipse Patrem cognoscat. Progressus autem cognitionis nostrę sic se habet: Primum ipsum Filium, docente nos Filio per verbum & Spiritum sanctum cognoscimus: deinde cognito filio, qui est splendor gloriæ paternæ, cognoscimus Patrem, idque docente & manifestante eum Filio. Iam, quòd ad incrementum attinet, non simul & semel cognoscimus Deū, vt neque simul & semel quæ ad Deum pertinent omnia manifestat Filius: sed paulatim accrescit cognitio nostra, paulatim manifestante Filio. De incremento autem isto, hoc addam: Quàm necessarium est, vt, quem cœpit semel Filius docere, ipsum doceat continuò ad finem vsque; tā necessarium est, vt, qui semel cœpit cognoscere & credere, is progressum aliquem faciat in fide & cognitione: tantum abest, vt qui semel veram illam fidem docente Christo inchoauerit, relabatur & à fide excidat ac Spiritum sanctum amittat. Vt supra admonui personam precantis commendare eos Deo pro quibus precatur: ita nunc admoneo, personam eorum pro quibus precatur Christus, commendare eos ipsos Deo, quòd & ipsi Deum cognoscant. Neque enim parum refert ad efficaciam precum pro quibusnam precemur: pro iisne qui Deo accepti sunt, an pro aliis. Sunt enim pro quibus si Moses, si Samuel stent & intercedant, vt hoc cum Propheta dicam, nihil tamen profuturæ essent iis ipsorum preces; vsque adeo enim Deo displicent. Quamobrem si velimus preces piorum pro nobis Deo esse acceptas, videamus imprimis ut personae nostrae Deo sint acceptae. Vt charitas qua. Hic finis est cognitionis tum Christi tum ipsorum, nempe ut dilectio Dei in ipsis sit: hoc est, non tantum ut Deus eos diligat, sed ipsi in se & in cordibus suis penitus sentiant illam Dei dilectionem, dilexit enim Deus suos ab aeterno. Dilexit etiam tum cum inimici essent. Sed ante fidem & cognitionem Dei in Christo dilectionis illius Dei nullus in nobis sensus est. Dilectio autem ista quam perscntiscimus, non est illa quidem vulgaris aliqua, sed paterna Dei dilectio, communio nimirum dilectionis illius, qua Pater Filium suum diligit. Nam ut alia quaecunque gratia, quae in Filium confertur, & in caput quasi nostrum infunditur, ad nos tanquam ad membra corporis ipsius diffillat, nõsque aliquo certe modo afficit: ita charitas Patris quam in Filium caput nostrum infundit, effunditur, ut loquar cum Apostolo, in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis. Nota autem hic cognitionem istam Dei tendere ad sensum dilectionis ipsius, adeo ut qui nihil dilectionis Dei, animo suo percipiat, is profecto nihil de Deo, ut oportet cognoscat. Et ego in eis. Videtur commendare praesentiam hanc dilectionis Dei quae in ipsis est ex sua ipsius praesentia, tanquam perpetuo comite, quasi dicat, Sic enim futurum est, ut ego in iis sim.
units.tr: Here, too, note the beginning, the progress, and finally the increase of our knowledge. The beginning and cause of our knowledge is the knowledge of the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father. For unless we had the Son as teacher, we would never know anything about God. So if the Son is to teach us, he himself must know the Father. The progress of our knowledge is as follows: first, we come to know the Son himself, while the Son teaches us through the Word and the Holy Spirit; then, having come to know the Son, who is the brightness of the Father's glory, we come to know the Father, and this is by the Son's teaching and revealing him. As for the increase, we do not know God all at once, just as the Son does not reveal everything that pertains to God all at once; rather, our knowledge grows little by little, as the Son makes himself known little by little. On this increase I would add this: just as it is necessary that the Son, having begun to teach someone, should keep teaching him continually to the end, so it is necessary that the one who has begun to know and believe should make some progress in faith and knowledge. Far from it being the case that someone who has begun that true faith under Christ's teaching should slip back, fall away from the faith and lose the Holy Spirit. As I warned above, that we commend to God the persons for whom we pray, so now I warn that we commend to God the persons for whom Christ prays, namely that they themselves know God. For it matters not a little to the efficacy of prayers for whom we pray: for those who are acceptable to God, or for others. For there are some for whom, even if Moses or Samuel stood and interceded, as I put it with the prophet, their prayers would profit them nothing, so greatly do they displease God. Therefore, if we want the prayers of the godly on our behalf to be acceptable to God, let us see first of all that our own persons are acceptable to God. Such as the love by which. This is the end of the knowledge both of Christ and of them, namely that the love of God may be in them: that is, not only that God loves them, but that they themselves feel that love of God deeply within themselves and in their hearts, for God loved his own from eternity. He loved them even when they were enemies. But before faith and the knowledge of God in Christ, there is no sense of that love of God in us. The love, however, which we perceive is not some common love, but the fatherly love of God, namely the fellowship of that love by which the Father loves his Son. For just as every other grace that is bestowed upon the Son, and poured into him as our head, flows down to us as the members of his body and certainly affects us in some way, so the love of the Father, which he pours into the Son our head, is poured out, to speak with the Apostle, in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. Note here that this knowledge of God tends toward the sense of his love, so that whoever perceives nothing of God's love in his mind surely does not know anything of God as he ought. And I in them. He seems to commend this presence of God's love that is in them from his own presence, as a perpetual companion, as if he were saying: "For so it will be, that I am in them."

units.la: Notandum tamen non prius sensum nos habere dilectionis Dei Patris, quàm Filius per fidem in nobis inhabitare incipiat: nam causa cur sentiamus paternam hanc dilectionem, est Filij in nobis inhabitatio per fidem. Inhabitante enim in nobis per fidem Filio Dei, tum comitatur eum dilectio Dei, vita denique & gratia omnis: propter Christum enim per fidem in ipso inhabitantem dixit Paulus, Viuo autem non amplius ego, sed viuit in me Christus, & vitam quam nunc viuo in carne, viuo per fidem filij Dei, qui dilexit me & tradidit semetipsum pro me. Huic gloria in secula seculorum. Amen.
units.tr: It should be noted, however, that we do not have a sense of the love of God the Father before the Son begins to dwell in us through faith; for the cause why we feel this fatherly love is the Son's indwelling in us through faith. For when the Son of God dwells in us through faith, the love of God accompanies him, and finally life and every grace. For it was on account of Christ dwelling in him through faith that Paul said: "I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me; and the life I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Hoc capite aggreditur historiam passionis Domini: Quae universa distribui potest in quatuor principales partes, secundum circumstantiam locorum, ubi ea gesta sunt, quae Domino euenerunt.
units.tr: In this chapter he takes up the history of the Lord's passion. The whole of it can be divided into four principal parts, according to the places where the events that befell the Lord took place.

units.la: Prima pars continet ea quae gesta sunt in horto, a principio huius capitis, usque ad versum 13.
units.tr: The first part contains what was done in the garden, from the beginning of this chapter to verse 13.

units.la: Secunda pars, ea quae gesta sunt in domo Caiaphae summi Sacerdotis.
units.tr: The second part, what was done in the house of Caiaphas the high priest.

units.la: Tertia pars, ea quae gesta sunt in praetorio coram Iudice Pontio Pilato, a versu 28. ad versf. 17. capitis 19.
units.tr: The third part, what was done in the palace before the judge Pontius Pilate, from verse 28 to verse 17 of chapter 19.

units.la: Quarta pars, ea quae gesta sunt in loco supplicii, qui nominatur Calvaria, Hebraice Golgotha, a versu 17. usque ad versum 38. A quo versu ad finem usque capitis 19. continetur historia sepulturae Domini.
units.tr: The fourth part, what was done in the place of execution, called Calvary, in Hebrew Golgotha, from verse 17 to verse 38. From that verse to the end of chapter 19 the history of the Lord's burial is contained.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: 1 Haec cum dixisset Iesus, egressus abiit cum discipulis suis trans torrentem Cedron, ubi erat hortus, in quem introivit ipse & discipuli eius.
units.tr: 1 When Jesus had said these things, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, into which he and his disciples entered.

units.la: 2 Noverat autem eum locum etiam Iudas qui prodebat ipsum, quia Iesus frequenter cum discipulis suis illuc convenerat.
units.tr: 2 Judas also, who betrayed him, knew the place, because Jesus had often met there with his disciples.

units.la: 3 Iudas ergo cum accepisset cohortem, & a primariis Sacerdotibus, ac Pharisaeis ministros, venit illuc cum lanternis, & facibus, & armis.
units.tr: 3 Judas therefore, having taken a band of soldiers and ministers from the chief priests and Pharisees, came there with lanterns, torches and weapons.

units.la: 4 Actenus in hoc Euangelio Dominus egit partes doctoris quae sunt in docendo populum Iudaeorum, proxime autem in instruendo discipulos suos, inde a cap. 13. Nunc agit partes sacerdotis in offerentis, partes. ferendo se pro peccatis nostris. Transitus fuit ad hanc partem per proximam precationem, qua se morti consecrauit. Historia passionis duobus sequentibus capitibus comprehensa est, decimooctauo & decimonono. Ea autem diuidit se apertè in has partes. 1. Est historia passionis in horto. 2. Est historia passionis in aula Caiaphae pontificis maximi. 3. Tertia est historia passionis coram Pontio Pilato iudice. 4. Est historia passionis in loco supplicij Caluaria, siue Hebraicè Golgotha. 5. Est postrema pars humiliationis in fine capitis deciminoni de sepultura ipsius. Historiae passionis in horto, vt est apud hunc Euangelistam, summa est, Capitur Christus ac vincitur. Constat autem his capitibus. Primum sunt partes Christi sese vltrò offerentis manibus eorum, qui ad ipsum apprehendendum vna cum Iuda proditore venerunt. 2. Sunt partes Iudae ingressi cum satellitio ad ipsum apprehendendum. 3. Est colloquium ipsorum & Christi. 4. Est temerarium quoddam Petri factum. 5. Capitur Christus ac vincitur.
units.tr: Hitherto in this Gospel the Lord has played the part of teacher in instructing the Jewish people, and more recently in instructing his disciples, from chapter 13 onward. Now he plays the part of the priest offering himself, bearing our sins. The transition to this part was made by the preceding prayer, in which he consecrated himself to death. The history of the passion is contained in the two following chapters, the eighteenth and nineteenth. It divides itself clearly into these parts: (1) the history of the passion in the garden; (2) the history of the passion in the house of Caiaphas the high priest; (3) the history of the passion before Pontius Pilate the judge; (4) the history of the passion at the place of execution, called Calvary or in Hebrew Golgotha; (5) the final part of his humiliation, at the end of chapter nineteen, concerning his burial. The history of the passion in the garden, as this evangelist gives it, comes to this: Christ is seized and bound. It consists of these parts: (1) Christ, of his own accord, offers himself into the hands of those who came with the traitor Judas to seize him; (2) Judas enters with the armed band to seize him; (3) there is a conversation between them and Christ; (4) there is a rash deed of Peter; (5) Christ is seized and bound.

units.la: Quod igitur ad Christi attinet partes: Hæc, inquit, cùm dixisset Iesus, egressus est cum discipulis suis. Hoc est, postquam discipulos instruxit, & se suoque Deo precibus commendauit, tum secure adit mortem. Tum enim secure & pacato animo nos exponimus periculis, & mortem ipsam adimus, cùm functi sumus officio erga eos qui nobis commissi sunt, & Deo nos nostráque omnia comendauimus. Cum discipulis suis, inquit, egressus est trans torrentem Cedron. Nomen hoc tam vallis est, quæ ab aliis Gethsemane dicitur, quàm torrentis qui per eam fluit, inter vrbem & montem Oliuarum: sicut ex 2. Samuel. 15. 23. apparet. Hic erat hortus in quem Christus vna cum discipulis suis ingressus est, ad hoc, vt peccatum quod per vnius hominis in horto rebellionem, in mundum ingressum est, in horto sua obedientia tolleret. Euangelista noster de induitria praetermisit multa, quae ab aliis de Christi in horto isto passione narrantur, à Matth. 26. 36. &c. Marc. 14. 37. &c. Luc. 22. 39. &c. Apud quos narratur Christum cùm ingressus est hortu aliis discipulis considere iussis, assumpsisse sibi duos, Petrum & Iohannem, qui, vt testes erant gloriae ipsius & transfigurationis quae fuit in monte, ita nunc núc testes essent humiliationis ipsius in horto. Primùm itaque his inspicientibus coepit totus cohorrescere & quosdam mœstus esse: ac clara voce audientibus ipsis, hanc vo-cē edidit: Vndique tristis est anima mea vsque ad mortem. Secundò cùm pergeret in luċta illa & conflictu cum ira Dei Patris, clara voce in hęc verba precatus est, Pater si possibile est, auferà me poculum istud. Tertiò cùm adhuc sensus iræ paternæ ingrauesceret, idem rursus precatus est. Quarto cùm adhuc pergeret in luċta & conflictu illo, tertia vice idem precatus est: quo tempore angelus de cœlo descendit, qui ipsum est consolatus.
units.tr: As to the part of Christ: "When Jesus had said these things, he went out with his disciples," says the text. That is, after he had instructed his disciples and commended himself and them to his God in prayer, then he goes securely to death. For we expose ourselves to dangers securely and with a tranquil mind, and go to death itself, when we have discharged our duty toward those committed to us and have commended ourselves and all that is ours to God. "He went out with his disciples," it says, "across the brook Kidron." This name belongs both to the valley, which is also called Gethsemane, and to the brook that flows through it, between the city and the Mount of Olives, as appears from 2 Samuel 15:23. Here was the garden into which Christ entered together with his disciples, so that his obedience in the garden might take away the sin which entered the world through the rebellion of one man in a garden. Our evangelist has deliberately passed over many things which others narrate about Christ's passion in this garden: Matthew 26:36 ff., Mark 14:37 ff., Luke 22:39 ff. There it is related that when Christ entered the garden, he bade the other disciples sit down, and took with him two, Peter and John, who, as they had been witnesses of his glory at the transfiguration on the mountain, were now to be witnesses of his humiliation in the garden. First, then, while they watched, he began to shudder entirely and to be sorrowful, and, with them hearing, he uttered this word in a loud voice: "My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death." Second, as he continued in that struggle and conflict with the wrath of God the Father, he prayed aloud in these words: "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me." Third, while the sense of his Father's wrath grew heavier still, he prayed the same again. Fourth, while he still continued in that struggle and conflict, for the third time he prayed the same; at that time an angel came down from heaven, who comforted him.

units.la: Postremò cùm non esset finis luċtæ illius, verùm magis magisque ingrauescceret, precatus est prolixius, & ardenter adeo, vt grumi sanguinis visi sint descendere è facie ipsius in terram. Id quod nulli mortalium vnquam contigit: vt facilè videat quis neminè vnquâ in hac vita percussum his tot tantísq; terroribus. Ex ista quæ in horto agonia satis apparet primùm, quodnâ sit pœdus peccati: deinde quodnâ sit pœdus iræ Dei peccatû insequétis. Tertiò quàtus sit amor & philanthropia filij qui tû peccatû nostrû tû iram Dei in sese transtulit. Videmus etiam ex hac agonia, Christû verum esse hominè, non tantùm cû corpore humano, sed etiam anima humana. Nam hæc luċta quâ sensitiræ Dei, in anima fuit & cum anima.
units.tr: Finally, since that struggle had no end but grew heavier and heavier, he prayed at greater length and with such fervour that drops of blood were seen to fall from his face to the ground. This happened to no mortal ever; so one may easily see that no one in this life was ever struck with so many and so great terrors. From this agony in the garden it appears, first, what is the penalty of sin; then, what is the penalty of the wrath of God pursuing sin; third, how great is the love and kindness of the Son, who transferred to himself our sin and the wrath of God. We also see from this agony that Christ was truly man, not only with a human body but also with a human soul. For this struggle, in which he felt the wrath of God, was in the soul and with the soul.

units.la: Interea autem quo tempore ipse ita exercebatur, non oblitus est discipulorum, verùm subinde ad eos reuersus ad vigilandum & orandum hortatus est, ac dormientes eos leniter ac blandè castigauit. Satan enim volens de agonia ista altum silentium impostərum esse, sine dubio sedulo id agebat, vt in altum somnum eos coniiceret, ne huius passionis testes fierent. Verùm Euangelista noster de industria hæc præteriit, contentus indicare quàm sponte ac voluntariè Dominus mortem adierit: dum dicit in eum locum ingressum eum qui Iudæ satis cognitus fuerat. Oportuit enim Christi sacrificium voluntarium esse. Quod si enim voluntarium non fuisset, profectò obedientia erga Patrem non fuisset, expiatio pro peccatis nostris pariter nō fuisset. Quòd si expiatio non fuisset, profectò nobis nihil profuisset. Iohannes itaque in narratione ista passionis Domini, hoc præcipuè attendit, vt id subministraret nobis in morte & passione Domini quo fides nostra niteretur. Nititur autem fides nō morte tantùm & passione, sed voluntaria morte & passione.
units.tr: Meanwhile, at the very time when he was so afflicted, he did not forget his disciples, but from time to time returned to them, exhorted them to watch and pray, and gently and kindly rebuked them for sleeping. For Satan, wishing this agony to remain under deep silence, undoubtedly worked diligently to cast them into a deep sleep, so that they would not become witnesses of this passion. But our evangelist has deliberately passed over these things, content to show how willingly and voluntarily the Lord went to death, when he says that he entered the place which was well known to Judas. For Christ's sacrifice had to be voluntary. If it had not been voluntary, certainly it would not have been obedience toward the Father, and likewise it would not have been an atonement for our sins. And if there had been no atonement, certainly it would have profited us nothing. John, therefore, in this narrative of the Lord's passion, especially attends to this, that he may supply us with what in the death and passion of the Lord our faith may rest upon. Faith rests, however, not on death and passion only, but on a voluntary death and passion.

units.la: Nouerat autem. Hactenus partes fuerunt Christi, sequuntur nunc partes Iudæ proditoris, qui dux & antesignanus fuit his qui Christum deprehenderunt. Ille cùm cognitum haberet locum hunc, cuius ratio subiecta est, Quia Iesus illuc cum discipulis suis frequenter conuenerat, accepit cohortem, & à Pontificibus & Pharisæis ministros, &c. Ergo consuetudo quam tum Christus habuit, causa fuit cur exiret contra Christū. Oportet enim proditorem quemque familiare esse ac domesticum. Christo autem familiaris est quisquis ipsius proditor existit. Videndum itaque quænam familiaritas nobis cū Christo intercedat, vt nō sit ea simulata & hypocritica, sed vera ac ingenua: secus profectò si simulata sit, desinet tandem in apostasiam ac manifestam proditionem Christi, ac veritatis ipsius. Nam Apostatarum istorum nunquam fuit vera cū Christo amicitia. Cum accepisset. Duo hominum genera sunt in hoc Iudæ satellitio: primum est Romanorum, & cohors Romana, quæ precario accepta est à prætore Romano; deinde alterum est Iudæorum, vtpote ministri Sacerdotum & Pharisæorum. Veniunt autem isti instructi primùm facibus & laternis, quia noctè egressi sunt ad eum capiendum: deinde armis, gladiis & fustibus, non secus acsi exiissent aduersus latronem: id de quo ipse Christus tum conquestus est. Quorsum tantum hoc satellitum aduersus hominem inermem & nudum? Arguit hoc profectò malam fuisse Iudæ conscientiam. Nam qui mala conscientia grauati sunt, nulla de causa metuunt: & quorum cordibus non est præsidio pax Dei vel bonæ conscientiæ, vt loquitur Apostolus, illi quidem nunquam satis videntur sibi stipari se posse. Arguit quoque hoc malam conscientiam, quod noctè cum facibus egressus sit: nā qui male agit, atque ideo malè sibi conscius est, odit lucem.
units.tr: Knew. Hitherto the parts have been Christ's; now follow the parts of Judas the traitor, who was the leader and standard-bearer of those who seized Christ. Since he knew this place, the reason for which is added, because Jesus had often met there with his disciples, he took a band, and ministers from the chief priests and Pharisees, etc. So the custom which Christ then had was the cause of his going out against Christ. For it is fitting that every traitor be an intimate and familiar. Now whoever becomes the betrayer of Christ is one who was familiar with him. We must therefore consider what familiarity we have with Christ, that it may not be feigned and hypocritical, but true and sincere; otherwise, if it is feigned, it will at last end in apostasy and manifest betrayal of Christ and of his truth. For those apostates never had a true friendship with Christ. Having taken. There are two kinds of men in this band of Judas: first, the Romans, the Roman cohort, which was obtained on request from the Roman governor; second, the Jews, namely the ministers of the priests and Pharisees. These men come equipped first with torches and lanterns, because they went out at night to seize him; then with arms, swords and clubs, just as if they had gone out against a robber, which is exactly what Christ himself complained of at that time. Why such a band against a man unarmed and naked? This certainly shows that Judas's conscience was evil. For those burdened with an evil conscience fear without any cause; and those whose hearts do not have the peace of God or a good conscience as their protection, as the Apostle says, always seem to themselves never able to be guarded enough. This also shows an evil conscience, that he went out at night with torches; for whoever acts wickedly, and is therefore conscious of wrongdoing, hates the light.

units.la: 4 Iesus itaque sciens omnia quæ ventura erant inse, prodiens dixit eis, Quem quæritis?
units.tr: 4 Jesus therefore, knowing all things that were coming upon him, went forth and said to them, Whom do you seek?

units.la: 5 Responderunt ei, Iesum Nazarenum. Dicit eis Iesus, Ego is sum. Stabat autem cum eis etiam Judas qui prodebat eum.
units.tr: 5 They answered him, Jesus of Nazareth. Jesus said to them, I am he. Judas also, who betrayed him, was standing with them.

units.la: 6 Vt ergo dixit eis, Ego is sum, abierunt retrorsum, & ceciderunt humi.
units.tr: 6 When therefore he said to them, I am he, they went backward and fell to the ground.

units.la: 7 Iterum rogauit eos, quem quaeritis? Illi autem dixerunt, Iesum Nazarenum.
units.tr: 7 Again therefore he asked them, Whom seek ye? And they said, Jesus of Nazareth.

units.la: SEquitur colloquium Christi & ipsorum. Primum de Christo ait Iohannes, quod sciuerit omnia quae euentura erant ipsi, quo significat eum non temere aut per imprudentiam captum esse & passum, sed scientem & probe conscium istarum rerum omnium. Tum addit eum prodiisse in conspectum ipsorum, non sibi fuga consuluisse, aut ab ipsis erutum fuisse e latebris: quo significat, ut sciens passus est; ita quoque eum volentem passum esse prodiens in conspectum ipsorum, ipse prior eos alloquutus est, cumque ij respondissent Iesum a se quaeri, subiecit continuo se eum esse: & interrogatione & responsione satis arguit se summa voluntate passum esse: Arguit praeterea sermone suo tam placido ac miti, se passum esse ut agnum, hoc est summa cum animi mansuetudine: ergo & facto & verbo summam Patri obedientiam praestitam indicat. Atque hoc est quo respicit praecipuè Iohannes, ut commendet credentibus ipsius obedientiam, & ipsius exemplo nobis omnibus obedientiam ut patiamur summa voluntate, scientes quascunque passiones, mortem quamcunque ex Dei voluntate esse. Quamobrem ab instrumentis quibuscunque in hac Dei nostri voluntatem oculos nostros subductos esse oportet. Stabat autem cum.Infertum est hoc de Iuda obiter, ad indicandum partim Domini patientiam, qui prodidorem illum patienter adeo inspexit, partim Iudae ipsius impudentiam & perseuerantiam in cordis illa sui obduratione, qui ausus est faciem Domini sui à se tam turpiter proditi, coram intueri ac sustinere ad tempus aliquod ipsius aspectum. Verum oportet proditorem gnauiter impudentem esse. Et qui semel obstirmarunt cor suum aduersus Dominum, fere gradum reuocare non possunt, aut ad sanam mentem redire, vsque dum se in
units.tr: Here follows the conversation between Christ and them. First, John says that Christ knew all the things that were going to happen to him. By this he signifies that Christ was not seized and made to suffer rashly or through carelessness, but knowingly and fully aware of all these things. Then John adds that Christ came forward into their sight and did not seek safety in flight, nor was he dragged out of hiding by them. By this he signifies that, as he suffered knowingly, so he suffered willingly: coming forward into their sight, he himself addressed them first. When they answered that they were seeking Jesus, he at once added that he was the one. By both his question and their answer, he sufficiently shows that he suffered with the greatest willingness. He shows further, by his speech so calm and gentle, that he suffered like a lamb, that is, with the greatest meekness of spirit. Therefore, by both deed and word, he indicates that he rendered the greatest obedience to the Father. This is chiefly what John has in view: to commend to believers Christ's obedience, and through his example to teach us all to obey, so that we suffer with the greatest willingness, knowing that whatever sufferings and whatever death come from the will of God. Therefore our eyes ought to be drawn away from whatever instruments are used in this, and fixed upon God's will. Now Judas also, who betrayed him, stood with them. This is added in passing, partly to show the Lord's patience, who looked so patiently upon that betrayer, and partly to show the impudence and persistence of Judas himself in that hardening of his heart. He dared to look upon, and for a while to endure the sight of, the face of his Lord whom he had so shamefully betrayed. But a betrayer must be resolutely shameless. And those who have once hardened their heart against the Lord can scarcely retreat a step or return to a sound mind, until they cast themselves into final hardening and destruction.

units.la: KKk extremam obdurationem & perditionem coniiciant. Vt ergo dixit. Hic est effectus quidam responsionis illius Christi tam breuis, tam placidæ, Abierunt, inquit, retrorsum & ceciderunt humi. Ea re voluit Christus admonere id quod de se dixit supra cap. 10. 18. Nemo tollit animam meam à me, sed ego pono eam à me ipso, potestatem habeo ponendi eam & potestatem habeo eam rursus assumendi; hoc est, admonere voluit non penes eos fuisse manus in ipsum iniicere, nisi ipse volens se manibus eorum obtulisset. Voluit etiam admonere de resipiscentia, ut si fieri posset tempestiuè resipiscerent, secus inexcusabiles fierent. Ex his colligi potest & hoc, quòd si vox Christi tam blanda & mitis vsqueadeo efficax fuit ad ipsos prosternendos, quàm efficax ad perdendos impios futura est vox illa Christi irata? & si Christi humiliati vox tam placida, tantam efficaciam habuit, quanta futura est vocis ipsius efficacia in improbos cum glorificatus in illo die hanc sententiam adeo tristem proferet? Maledicti, abite à me in ignem æternum qui paratus est diabolo & angelis eius. Colligere quoque possumus ne vnam quidem voculam quam per os ministrorum & seruorum suorum nunc edit abire in nihilum; quin imo efficax futura est ea vel ad vitam vel ad mortem peccatoris. Neque putandum est aliquid imminui de virtute verbi Dei, quòd ipsum recondatur in vasculo testaceo. Potest enim vel pretiosissimum aliquod vnguetum reseruari in vase testaceo, Hùc thesaurù, inquit Paulus, habemus in testaceis vasculis. Iterum ergo. Qui ceciderunt humi rursus se erigunt, quos ipse sic iterum alloquitur. Admoniti igitur tanta vocis Christi efficacia, non tam intelligunt sibi rem esse & confligere se cum diuina manu ac virtute; neque resipiscunt, sed coeptum persequuntur. Quos enim Deus semel tradidit in mentem omnis iudicij expertem, illi vel ipsis belluis stupidiores euadunt. Equus & mulus si forte ceciderunt humi, id persentiscunt: At hi nihil sentiunt, vt magis similes videantur homines qui non modo per naturam sentiunt, sed etiam ratio cinantur, lapidibus & truncis quàm belluis. Belluæ enim aliquem sensum habent, hi nullum. Belluæ percussæ vident percussorem, hi Dei manu non sentiunt, neque diuinâ virtute discernût.
units.tr: Therefore when he said to them, this is a certain effect of that answer of Christ, so brief and so calm: They went backward, and fell to the ground. By this Christ wished to remind them of what he had said above, in chapter 10:18: No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of myself; I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. That is, he wished to remind them that it was not in their power to lay hands on him unless he himself willingly offered himself to their hands. He also wished to remind them of repentance, so that, if it could be done, they might repent in time; otherwise they would be left without excuse. From these things this too can be gathered: if the voice of Christ, so gentle and mild, was so effective in casting them down, how effective will that angry voice of Christ be in destroying the wicked, when he, now glorified, will utter in that day that sentence so dreadful: Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels. We can also gather that not even one little word which he now utters through the mouths of his ministers and servants will pass away into nothing; rather, it will be effective either unto life or unto death for the sinner. Nor should we think that anything is diminished from the power of God's Word because it is kept in an earthen vessel. For a most precious ointment may be kept in an earthen vase. We have this treasure, says Paul, in earthen vessels. Again, therefore, those who had fallen to the ground rise up again, and he addresses them once more in this way. Having been warned by such great efficacy of Christ's voice, they do not understand that they have to do with the divine hand and power; nor do they repent, but pursue what they had begun. For those whom God has once given over to a mind lacking all judgment become more stupid than the beasts themselves. If a horse or mule happens to fall to the ground, it perceives it. But these perceive nothing, so that men, who not only perceive by nature but are also guided by reason, may appear more like stones and stumps than beasts. For beasts have some sense; these have none. A beast that is struck sees the one who strikes it; these do not perceive the hand of God, nor do they discern the divine power.

units.la: 8 Respòdit Iesus, Dixi vobis me eum esse: ergo si me quæritis, sinite hos abire:
units.tr: 8 Jesus answered, I told you that I am he. If therefore you seek me, let these go their way.

units.la: 9 Vt impleretur sermo quem dixerat, Ex iis quos dedisti mihi non perdidi quicquam.
units.tr: 9 That the word might be fulfilled which he had spoken: Of those whom you gave me I have lost none.

units.la: 10 Simon autem Petrus, quum gladium haberet eduxit eum, & percussit seruum Pontificis maximi, & abscidit auriculam eius dexteram. Erat autem nomen serui Malchus.
units.tr: 10 Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it, struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his right ear. Now the servant's name was Malchus.

units.la: 11 Dicit ergo Iesus Petro, Reconde gladium tuum in vaginam: Calicem quem dedit mihi Pater, non bibam illum?
units.tr: 11 Jesus therefore said to Peter, Put your sword into its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?

units.la: HOmo in speciem simplex ac inermis dum stat coram inimicis suis mox deprehendendus, legem tamen iis imponit; neque se alia lege traditurum sese in manus ipsorum dicit, quàm si permiserint discipulos ipsius abire. Hoc arguit diuinam ipsius potentiam, qua eorum manus quasi constrictæ tenebantur, simulque ipsorum stupiditatem, qui eam tamen non sentiunt, neque à coepto desistunt. Sed quid dicas? Qui semel sunt traditi iusto Dei iudicio in mentem reprobam, ne concussi quidem ipsius Dei potentia vnquam resipiscer, nisi ad potentiam accedat misericordia in Christo, quæ animos eorum flectat & blandè alliciat. Potentia enim si sola sit franget prius præfractum hominem quàm flectet eum. Vide rursus boni Pastoris imaginem, dum sui obliuiscitur, recordatur interea suorum. Hoc enim boni Pastoris est, vt etiam morti proximus, tamen non deponat omnem illorum qui ipsius fideicommissi sunt curam: imò libenter ponat animam suam pro grege suo. Sed hoc obseruandum imprimis, quod quo tempore sua voluntate infirmus fuit in se, eodem tempore potens fuerit in suis ad eos protegendos. Nam ex voluntaria infirmitate traditurus se in manus ipsorum, verbo suo cauit ne discipulos suos vel manu attingerent. Cùm Christus penderet ex ligno in ludibrium, iusserunt vt ipse descenderet, vt qui seruabat alios seipsum seruaret: Nimirum cogitabant ipsum ex infirmitate crucifixum.
units.tr: A man who in appearance is simple and unarmed, while he stands before enemies who are about to seize him, nevertheless lays down a condition for them: he says that he will not give himself into their hands on any other terms than that they let his disciples go. This shows his divine power, by which their hands were held as if bound, and at the same time shows their stupidity, who did not feel that power yet did not desist from their undertaking. But what can one say? Those who have once been given over by the just judgment of God to a reprobate mind will never repent, not even when shaken by the power of God itself, unless mercy in Christ is added to that power, to bend their minds and gently draw them. For power alone breaks a stubborn man before it bends him. See again the image of the good Shepherd: while he forgets himself, meanwhile he remembers his own. For it is the mark of the good Shepherd that, even when near to death, he does not lay down all care for those committed to his charge; indeed he gladly lays down his life for his flock. But this above all is to be observed: at the very time when, by his own will, he was weak as regards himself, at that same time he was powerful among his own in protecting them. For, being about to give himself into their hands by a voluntary weakness, he by his word took care that they should not touch his disciples even with a hand. When Christ hung from the wood in mockery, they bade him come down, so that he who saved others might save himself. Surely they thought that he had been crucified through weakness.

units.la: in suis non potentem fuisse. Sed errarunt. Nam eo ipso tempore quo mortuus pependit ipse ex ligno, virtus ex eo processit, qua seruati sunt non modò discipuli, sed fideles quicunque, & tota denique Ecclesia. Si enim virtus Christi vel momento deficeret, eodem momento periret Ecclesia. Quare etiam dum mortuus penderet e ligno Iesus tum fuit, hoc est seruator. Quòd si igitur Christus mortuus, quoad humanam naturam, potens tamen fuit in suis seruandis: quanta est eius potentia nunc, cùm viuit in coelis ad dextram Dei Patris? Verùm non magis potentiam Christi glorificati vident aduersarij, qui Ecclesiam persequuntur, quàm Christi humiliati & crucifixi illam virtutem quæ in morte se exeruit.
units.tr: But they were mistaken: he was not powerless among his own. For at the very time when he hung dead upon the wood, virtue went out from him by which not only the disciples were saved, but all the faithful, and in short the whole Church. For if the power of Christ had failed for a single moment, the Church would have perished in that same moment. Wherefore even while Jesus hung dead upon the wood, he was then the Saviour. If, then, Christ, though dead as to his human nature, was nevertheless powerful in saving his own, how great is his power now, when he lives in heaven at the right hand of God the Father? Yet the adversaries who persecute the Church no more see the power of the glorified Christ than they saw that virtue of the humbled and crucified Christ which showed itself in his death.

units.la: Vt impleretur sermo quem dixerat. Cautam affert cur seruati sint discipuli: Nempe vt sermo ille Christi impleretur quem protulit cùm preces illas funderet ad Patrem supra cap.17. Etsi autem sermo ille Christi intelligedus sit proprie de conseruatione spirituali, tamen hic accommodatus est ad conseruationem corporalem: in corporali tamen hac intelligitur spiritualis illa conseruatio. Nam conseruatio discipulorum corporalis, tunc temporis secum adportabat conseruationem spiritualem: & periculum corporis coniunctum habuit periculum animæ. Nondum enim erant maturi discipuli ad patiendum quicquam graviùs pro nomine Domini sui. Quòd si igitur nondum satis confirmati, tracti tum fuissent ad supplicium, profectò Domino suo renunciassent: id quod factum illud Petri in abnegando Domino suo propter vocem ancillæ paulò post comprobauit. Ideo hoc tempore ipsis pepercit. Ea enim esse solet Domini erga suos misericordia, vt iis parcat, tantisperdum ipse satis virium iis suppeditet ad hoc vt perseuerando non pereant, sed seruentur. Postquam autem iam satis viribus instructi sunt, onus afflictionum humeris eorum imponit. Id quod postea discipulorum cuique factum est suo tempore. Simon autem Petrus quum gladium habere. Hic insectitur factum Petri qui temerè abscidit Malchi auriculam. Euangelistæ alij hoc factum hoc ordine introducunt: Cùm Iesus sermonem hunc faceret, Iudas, qui vnà cum reliquis stabat, prodiit. Accedens autem ad Dominum.
units.tr: That the word might be fulfilled which he had spoken. He gives the reason why the disciples were preserved: namely, that the saying of Christ might be fulfilled which he uttered when he poured out those prayers to the Father, above in chapter 17. Although that saying of Christ is properly to be understood of spiritual preservation, here it is applied to bodily preservation; yet in this bodily preservation that spiritual preservation is understood. For the bodily preservation of the disciples at that time carried spiritual preservation with it, and danger to the body was bound up with danger to the soul. For the disciples were not yet mature enough to suffer anything more grievous for the name of their Lord. For if they, not yet sufficiently strengthened, had then been dragged off to punishment, they would certainly have renounced their Lord, as Peter's later denial of his Lord, prompted by a servant girl's voice, soon proved. Therefore he spared them at this time. For it is the way of the Lord's mercy towards his own to spare them for as long as he himself supplies them with enough strength that by persevering they may not perish but be saved. But after they have been sufficiently equipped with strength, he lays the burden of afflictions on their shoulders. This was afterwards done to each of the disciples in his own time. Simon Peter, since he had a sword. Here the deed of Peter is taken up, who rashly cut off the ear of Malchus. The other evangelists introduce this deed in this order: while Jesus was speaking these words, Judas, who stood with the rest, came forward. Approaching the Lord,

units.la: {*} 5. Petri temerarium factum. num, ac dicens, Rabbi, osculatus est eum: hoc enim datum est signum à proditore, iis quos secum ducebat ad Dominum capiendum. vide Matth. 26.47. &c. Marc. 14.43. Luc. 22.47. Tum Dominus placidè (decreuit enim omnia ferre patienter & pendere ex Patris sui voluntate) placidè, inquam, Iudam alloquutus est, Amice, tradis filium hominis osculo? Tum in Dominum alij quos vnà secum adducebat, irruperunt. Quod cùm viderent discipuli, interrogârunt Dominum, an vellet gladio se protegi? Petrus non expectato Domini responso, eduxit statim gladium, & seruum Pontificis sic percussit vt ei auriculam dextram amputaret. Serui nomen hic insertum est, quod est Malchus, nimirum vt ex tam speciali ista circumstantia conspiciatur veritas facti huius. Etsi Dei iusto iudicio factum sit vt Malchus, in tam mala causa, pateretur hoc malum: etsi etiam ex zelo hoc factum sit à Petro, tamen factum non laudabile esse apparet, vel ex Christi verbis, quibus Petrum alloquitur. Nam quod ad zelum hunc, is praeposterus fuit: Primùm enim transgressus est limites vocationis suæ: priuatus enim non debuit resistere iis qui accesserunt ad hoc facinus, nō nisi armati aliqua magistratus authoritate. Deinde ex igno rantia hoc factum fuisse apparet ex obiurgatione ea Christi, quæ sequitur cùm dicit, Annon bibam poculum quod dedit mihi Pater? Nescivit Petrus datum hoc à Patre poculum, & necessitatem hanc moriendi pro mundo ipsi impositam esse. Nihil magis vulgare ac vsitatum est nobis, quàm zeli prætextu actiones nostras tueri. Zelus autē si nudus sit, non circumscriptus limitibus vocationis cuiusq;, nō colluströtus luce verbi Dei, hoc est, si nō sit ex cognitione, profectò nō meretur laudē & commendatione. Et, vt dicam quod in re est, certiores regulę actionum nostrarum sunt hæ quas afferam: Primùm vocatio cuiuscumque, vt contineat se quisque intra vocationem suā: deinde lux illa & fax verbi diuini, vt in vocatione nihil faciat, nisi prælata illa verbi face & præeunte conscientia voluntatis Dei. Non reicio equidem zelum: imò zelum Dei in actionibus omnibus maximopere requiro: sed dico oportere zelum illum temperari ac continere primùm limitibus vocationis & muneris cuiusque nostrum: deinde præscripto & conscientia verbi diuini. Quòd si quis zelo vltra ista prouehatur, profectò malè succedet quod quis efficit temerario isto zelo abreptus. Fieri quidem potest,vt actionum initia bona & prospera videantur esse,verùm tandem dabunt pœnas temeritatis suæ, qui ex huiusmodi zelo ad faciendum aliquid prorumpunt. Verùm hodierno die pauci sunt Petro similes,imò paucissimi, adeo vt nunc non tam opus sit vt moueamur ad hoc vt zelum temperemus, quàm ad hoc vt omnino zelum habeamus.
units.tr: {*} 5. Peter's rash deed. And saying, "Rabbi," he kissed him; for this was the sign given by the traitor to those whom he was leading with him to seize the Lord. See Matt. 26:47 etc., Mark 14:43, Luke 22:47. Then the Lord, calmly (for he had resolved to bear all things patiently and to depend on his Father's will), calmly, I say, addressed Judas: Friend, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? Then the others whom he had brought with him rushed upon the Lord. When the disciples saw this, they asked the Lord whether he wished to be protected with the sword. Peter, without waiting for the Lord's answer, at once drew his sword and struck the servant of the High Priest so as to cut off his right ear. The servant's name is inserted here, Malchus, that from this so particular circumstance the truth of this deed may be seen. Although by God's just judgment it came about that Malchus, in so bad a cause, suffered this harm; and although the deed was done by Peter out of zeal, yet it appears that the deed was not praiseworthy, even from the words of Christ with which he addresses Peter. For as to this zeal, it was misdirected: first, because he overstepped the limits of his calling; for, being a private person, he ought not to have resisted those who came to this crime, unless armed with some authority of the magistrate. Then, that the deed was done out of ignorance appears from the rebuke of Christ that follows, when he says, Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me? Peter did not know that this cup had been given by the Father, and that this necessity of dying for the world had been laid upon him. Nothing is more common and usual with us than to defend our actions under the pretext of zeal. But zeal, if it is bare, not bounded by the limits of each person's calling, not illuminated by the light of God's Word, that is, if it does not come from knowledge, certainly does not deserve praise and commendation. And, to say what the matter is, the surer rules of our actions are these which I will set out: first, each person's calling, so that each keeps himself within his own calling; then that light and torch of the divine Word, so that in his calling he does nothing except with that torch carried before him and with his conscience guided by the will of God. I do not, indeed, reject zeal; rather I greatly require the zeal of God in all our actions. But I say that this zeal must be tempered and restrained, first by the limits of the calling and office of each of us, and then by the rule and conscience of the divine Word. If anyone is carried beyond these by zeal, certainly whatever he accomplishes, swept along by that rash zeal, will turn out badly. It can indeed happen that the beginnings of their actions seem good and prosperous; yet in the end those who rush into doing something from such zeal will pay the penalty of their rashness. But in the present day there are few like Peter, indeed very few, so that now we need to be moved not so much to temper our zeal as to have zeal at all.

units.la: Videmus deinde in exemplo isto Petri ( qui in bona alioqui causa,vt defensione Domini fui,præpostero zelo abreptus est)fieri,vt,quibus Christi causam agere propositum est, tamen non ita dextrè rem administrent, vt nihil interea vitij admisceatur. Ea enim est corruptio etiã in renatis adhuc reliqua, quæ facilè contagione sua actiones quæ ips̨ in se bonæ sunt ac laudabiles inficiunt. Quare precādum est assiduè,vt velit Dominus personas nostras magis magisq; sanctificare ad sanctas actiones. Sed pauci sunt hodierno die qui peccant in zelo isto nimio,aut etiam inconsiderato. Pleriq; enim omnes ideo peccamus ,quod sine zelo, sine respectu gloriæ Diuinæ omnia faciamus. Sequitur nunc increpatio Petri, Recon-de, inquit, gladium tuum in vaginam. Non tam irato vultu simul & voce excepit Dominus quemquam ex ipsis persequutoribus, ne Iudam quidem ipsum, quàm hic Petrum,vt scias iudicium incipere à domo Dei, desinere autem in aduersarios. Ratio increpationis subiecta est, sumpta quidem non tam à necessitate ipsi imposita ad bibendum poculum afflictionis à Patre propinatum, quàm à summa voluntate sua obeundi id, quod obire eum ex diuino decreto oportuit. Vides hic Christum ne sui quidem defensionem illegitimam laudare: vt scias Deum nolle iniuriam etiam innocenti factam iniuria repelli. Quòd si enim priuatus aliquis,& qui non est vocatus à Deo, iniuriam repellere velit, arreptóque statim gladio percutere eos qui cum authoritate sunt ( quam Deus sanctam ac inuiolabilem semper esse vult) profectò etsi eam cum plausu excipiant omnes homines, tamen Deus eum hominem non approbabit. Quòd si autem tèminiuriam nolit Deus repelli iniuria, quantopere, quæsò, abhorret ab iniuria quæ innocenti cuiquam infertur? Quòd si Petrum propulsantem iniuriam, idque illegitimè obiurgauit Dominus, quæ erit damnatio eorum, qui iniuriam hanc intulerunt ipsi Domino: hoc est viro innocentissimo ac iustissimo? Euangelistæ alij, Matthæus præsertim 26.51. &c. alias præterea rationes adducunt. 1. Qui gladium accipit (hoc est sibi non datum arripit) gladio percutietur. 2. Ego nihil opus habeo præsidio humano. Quod si enim precatus fuero Patrem, is probauerit daturus est mihi plures quàm duodecim legiones Angelorum. 3. Oportet scripturas impleri, quæ dicunt sic oportere fieri. Tum addit Lucas, Dominum tacta Malchi auricula eum sanauisse. Noluit enim sua causa quèquam violari, aut iniuriam aliquam fieri cuiquam, etsi quàm maximè & iustissimè eam promeritus esset. Poculi nomine hic intelligo afflictionum certam mensuram. Vt enim paterfamilias pocula, id est mensuras certas potus propinat familiæ suæ singulis propinat pocula afflictionum ebibenda, prout ipsi visum est: atque ita quidem propinat, vt necesse sit ipsos quibus propinet ea epotare. Quòd si necessitas nobis impositæ sit, vt hoc debet esse positum vniuersum studium nostrum, vt quod ex necessitate alioqui nobis faciendum est, summa voluntate & prompto animo quantum fieri potest id faciamus. Quòd si enim id fecerimus, licet amarum in principio poculum videatur: tamen in fine suaue comperietur. Quòd si verò non sponte nostra fecerimus, quodtamen necessario faciendum est, tum & in principio & in fine amarum sentiemus propinatum nobis illud poculum. Quare studendum patientiæ in hac vita, in qua collocati sumus eo ipso fine, vt explorentur fides & patientia nostra.
units.tr: We see further in this example of Peter (who, in an otherwise good cause, namely the defence of the Lord, was carried away by misdirected zeal) that those who purpose to carry on Christ's cause do not always manage the matter so skilfully that no fault is meanwhile mingled in. For such is the corruption still remaining even in the regenerate, which easily by its contagion stains the actions that in themselves are good and praiseworthy. Therefore we must pray constantly that the Lord will more and more sanctify our persons to holy actions. But there are few in the present day who sin in that excessive or even inconsiderate zeal. For most of us sin for this reason, that we do everything without zeal, without regard to the divine glory. Now follows the rebuke of Peter: "Put up your sword into its sheath," he says. The Lord did not address any of the persecutors themselves with such an angry look and voice, not even Judas himself, as he did here to Peter, so that you may know that judgment begins at the house of God, but ends in the adversaries. The reason for the rebuke is given, taken not so much from the necessity laid upon him to drink the cup of affliction offered by the Father, as from his supreme willingness to undergo what, by divine decree, he had to undergo. You see here that Christ does not praise even an unlawful defence of himself, so that you may know that God is unwilling for an injury, even one done to an innocent person, to be repelled by injury. For if some private person, one not called by God, wishes to repel an injury, and, seizing a sword at once, strikes those who hold authority (which God always wills to be holy and inviolable), certainly, even if all men applaud him, God will not approve that man. But if God is unwilling for an injury to be repelled by injury, how greatly, I ask, does he abhor the injury inflicted on any innocent person? And if the Lord rebuked Peter for repelling an injury, and that unlawfully, what will be the condemnation of those who inflicted this injury on the Lord himself, that is, on the most innocent and most righteous of men? The other evangelists, Matthew especially (26:51 etc.), add other reasons. (1) He who takes the sword (that is, seizes what has not been given to him) will be struck down by the sword. (2) I have no need of human protection. For if I pray to the Father, he will certainly grant me more than twelve legions of angels. (3) The Scriptures must be fulfilled, which say that it must happen so. Then Luke adds that the Lord, when Malchus's ear was touched, healed him. For he was unwilling that anyone should be harmed on his account, or that any injury be done to anyone, even though that man had most justly and fully deserved it. By the name of the cup I understand here a certain measure of afflictions. For as the head of a household offers his household cups, that is, fixed measures of drink, so the Lord offers to each cups of affliction to be drained, as he sees fit; and he offers them in such a way that those to whom he offers them must drink them off. But if a necessity is laid upon us, then this must be our whole endeavour: that what we must otherwise do from necessity we do with the greatest willingness and a ready mind, as far as we can. For if we do so, the cup, though it may seem bitter at the beginning, will be found sweet at the end. But if we do not do it of our own accord, though it must necessarily be done, then we shall feel that cup offered to us as bitter both at the beginning and at the end. Therefore we must strive for patience in this life, in which we have been placed for this very end, that our faith and patience may be tested.

units.la: 12 Cohors igitur & tribunus & ministri Iudæorum comprehenderunt Iesum, & vinxerunt eum.
units.tr: So the cohort, the tribune and the ministers of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him.

units.la: 13 Et abduxerunt primum ad Annam, erat enim socer Caiaphæ, qui erat Pontifex maximus anni illius: is vero misit eum vinctum ad Caiaphã Pontificem maximum.
units.tr: And they led him away first to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. Now he sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.

units.la: 14 Erat autem Caiaphas is qui consilium dederat Iudæis expedire, vt vnus homo moreretur pro populo.
units.tr: Now Caiaphas was the one who had advised the Jews that it was expedient for one man to die for the people.

units.la: HActenus fuit factum illud Petri temerarium, nunc capitur Dominus ac vincitur. Numerantur autem tem sigillatim qui in eum manus iniecerunt: vt intelligamus non effugere oculum Dei ne vnum quidem aliquem, qui male alioqui facinori perpetrando interest, siue is alicuius sit nominis, siue obscurus sit, & ex sece plebis. Ne mirum cuiquam videatur, quòd cùm prius eos verbo repulerit, nunc se offerat manibus ipsorum capiendum ac vinciendum. Nō id quidem factum quasi victus iam ac superatus fuerit ab iis, neque plus virium habuerit ad resistendum: sed hoc omnibus semel demonstrat quòd potuerit se eripere, nunc vltrò se offert eis: demonstratione enim illa potentiæ suæ facis remouet scandalum infirmitatis, ostenditque se sponte sua infirmum fuisse. Quamobrem quisquis offenditur infirmitate Christi, aduertat ad potentiam illam eius, quæ infirmitatem præcessit. Quin potius intueatur potentiã illam longè diuinissimam, quæ sequuta est infirmitatem & crucem. Nam etsi Christus crucifixus fuit ex infirmitate, tamen viuit ex potentia Dei. Postremò gradus hi passionis Domini attendendi sunt: Primùm captus est, deinde vinctus est. Singuli gradus respondent singulis partibus conditionis nostrae. Nam nos capti fuimus a peccato & morte, nos etiam vincti eramus peccati vinculis. Captus est igitur vt nos liberaremur a captiuitate peccati & mortis: vinctus est vt nos liberaremur a vinculis peccati & mortis. Hanc si fiduciam habeamus, sentiemus, dum in Christum credimus, Christum captum & vinctum, sentiemus, inquam, eodem momento nos liberari a captiuitate & vinculis. Ea enim est efficacia passionis Christi & omnium partium eius, in iis qui in eum credunt.
units.tr: So far that rash act of Peter has been told; now the Lord is seized and bound. The men who laid hands on him are counted one by one, so that we may understand that the eye of God does not escape even one of those who take part in a wicked deed, whether he is of some name or is obscure and of the common people. Let no one think it strange that, after he had earlier driven them back with a word, he now offers himself to their hands to be seized and bound. He did not do this as one already conquered and overcome by them, nor because he had lost the strength to resist. Rather, by this he shows once for all that he could have escaped, and now he offers himself to them of his own accord. For by this display of his power he removes the offence of weakness, and shows that he was weak of his own will. Therefore whoever is offended by the weakness of Christ should look to that power of his which went before the weakness. Nay rather, let him look to that power, far more divine, which followed the weakness and the cross. For although Christ was crucified in weakness, yet he lives by the power of God. Lastly, these stages of the Lord's passion are to be noted: first he was seized, then he was bound. Each stage corresponds to a part of our condition. For we were seized by sin and death; we also were bound with the chains of sin. He was seized, then, that we might be freed from the captivity of sin and death; he was bound that we might be freed from the chains of sin and death. If we have this confidence, we shall feel, while we believe in Christ, that Christ was seized and bound, and we shall feel, I say, that at the same moment we are freed from captivity and chains. For such is the efficacy of the passion of Christ and of all its parts in those who believe in him.

units.la: Et adduxerunt primùm. Hic transit ad eam passionis DoDomini partem, quæ fuit in aula Pontificis. Euangelistæ alij narrant quædam, quæ interuenerunt priusquam Christus adduceretur ad Annam : nempe reprehensos a Christo, sed modestè eos qui ipsum capiebant & vinciebant, quod cum in synagoga & templo docuerit perpetuò vbi eum sine tumultu capere licuit, tamen exierint aduersus ipsum cum gladiis & fustibus, tanquam aduersus latronem quenquam : Verum id ita euenisse, quia nunc ipsorum hora esset : hoc est, tempus à Deo ipsis concessum, in quo potestas tenebrarum vigeret, idque vt scriptura impleretur, Matth. 26. 54. &c. Marc. 14.48.&c. Luc.22.52. &c. Admonuit igitur innocentiæ suæ, admonuit peccati ipsorum, sed illi nihilominus pergunt furere. Narrant quoque alij interea temporis dum Christus caperetur ac vinciretur, disperso fuisse discipulos, & sibi fuga consuluisse, Matth. 26.56. Marc. 14.50. Narrat denique Marcus 14.51.52. Iuuenem quendam amictum sindone super nudum corpus sequutum eos, quo tempore Christum abducerent, ad quem cum conuersi essent quidam, & eum insequuti, derelicta sindone nudus effugit ab eis. Iuuenis hic, quisquis ille fuerit, excitatus forte fuit tumultu ac strepitu nocturno: illi autem in eo persequendo prodiderunt insolentiam suam. Hinc introductum narrat eum Euangelista noster in ciuitatem, & domum Annæ primum adductum, quia forte ea prima sese offerebat (neque enim erat quod illic agerent) nisi dicas voluisse eos gratificari Annæ, quia is erat socer Caiaphæ : proposuerunt enim captum & vinctum Dominum, tanquam gratum quoddam spectaculum omnibus inimicis suis. Caiapham notat Pontificem maximum fuisse illius anni, qua quidem re innuit eam, quæ fuit tum in pontificatu ἀρχιερεύς, vt facile videas nihil tum temporis sani fuisse in illo populo, quorum pontificatus, in quo maximum debebat esse momentum in administranda Ecclesia, ita perturbatus fuit. Nam, vt de pontificatu dicam aliquid, Cum ex præscripto legis Dei, vnum esse Pontificem oportuerit, eumque in eo munere durare ad totum vitæ suæ tempus, tum quidem non vnus, sed multi creabantur simul Pontifices, sic tamen vt vicissim, & in singulos annos. nos, quisque munere illo fungeretur. Fuerunt etiam alii, tum in pontificatu corruptelæ contra legem Dei, ut illud quod ex aliis, & non ex stirpe sola Aaronis eligerentur: ut illud quoque quòd electio non esset penes populum, vel consulto Deo, sed penes Reges vel præsides Ethnicos eos qui imperium in populum obtinebant. Is vero misit. Hactenus de abductione Christi ad Annam. Apud quem nihil actum commemoratur, nisi quod arctius vincierint. Ideo enim dicitur Annam misisse eum vinctum ad Caiapham. De Caiapha narratur, quòd is erat qui consuluerat Iudæis, &c. Hoc repetitum est ex cap. II. 49. &c. Consilium dedit Caiaphas interficendi Christum, sed interea ita gubernauit ipsius linguam Dominus, ut prophetârit. Quemadmodum abusus est lingua Balaami ad pronunciandam benedictionem, cùm ipse maledictionem in populum esset pronuntiaturus. Sed quæri potest quorsum repetatur hoc Caiaphæ consilium siue prophetia hoc loco? Respondeo, ut indicetur adductum fuisse Christum ad inimicitias acerrimum, cuius manus non esset effugiturus. Nam qui dedit consilium tollendi ipsum è medio, is proculdubio eum in manus sibi traditum erat sublaturus è medio. Omnes enim cupiunt quàm maximè consilia quæ ipsi cœperunt adimpleri, improbi præsertim, qui adeo iniquo animo ferunt si non succedat quod ipsi consilium dederunt, ut ipsi se suspendio dent, ut de Achitophele legimus.
units.tr: And they led him first. Here he passes to that part of the Lord's passion which took place in the high priest's court. The other evangelists relate certain things that happened before Christ was led to Annas: namely, that Christ rebuked those who seized and bound him, yet gently; and that although he had taught continually in the synagogue and the temple, where they could have seized him without tumult, they nevertheless came out against him with swords and clubs, as if against some robber. But this happened so because it was now their hour: that is, the time granted to them by God, in which the power of darkness prevails, and this so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, Matt. 26:54 etc.; Mark 14:48 etc.; Luke 22:52 etc. He therefore reminded them of his innocence, he reminded them of their sin, but they nevertheless go on raging. Others also relate that meanwhile, while Christ was being seized and bound, the disciples were scattered and took thought for their own flight, Matt. 26:56; Mark 14:50. Finally Mark (14:51-52) relates that a certain young man, wrapped in a linen cloth over his naked body, followed them at the time they were leading Christ away; and when some turned and pursued him, he left the linen cloth behind and fled from them naked. This young man, whoever he was, was perhaps roused by the tumult and noise of the night; but they, in pursuing him, displayed their insolence. Hence our evangelist relates that he was led into the city and into the house of Annas first, perhaps because that was the first place that offered itself (for they had no business there), unless you say they wished to do a favour to Annas, because he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas. For they set forth the Lord, seized and bound, as a welcome spectacle to all his enemies. He notes that Caiaphas was high priest of that year, by which he hints at the high priesthood as it then was, so that you may easily see that nothing sound remained at that time in that people, whose priesthood, in which the greatest weight should lie in governing the Church, was so disordered. For, to say something about the priesthood: although by the prescription of God's law there ought to be one high priest, and he should remain in that office for the whole of his life, at that time not one but many high priests were created at once, yet in such a way that they took turns, and for single years, each one performing that office. There were also other corruptions of the priesthood contrary to the law of God: that they were chosen from others and not from the line of Aaron alone; and that the choice was not in the hands of the people or was not made with God's counsel, but lay with the kings or the heathen governors who held power over the people. Now he sent him. So far concerning the leading of Christ to Annas. Nothing is recorded as done there, except that they bound him more tightly. For this reason it is said that Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas. Of Caiaphas it is told that he was the one who had advised the Jews, etc. This is repeated from chapter 11:49 etc. Caiaphas gave the counsel of killing Christ, but in the meantime the Lord so governed his tongue that he prophesied, just as the tongue of Balaam was made to utter a blessing, though he was about to pronounce a curse upon the people. But it may be asked why this counsel or prophecy of Caiaphas is repeated here. I answer: so that it may be shown that Christ was led to his most bitter enemies, from whose hands he was not going to escape. For he who gave the counsel to remove him from the midst would certainly be the one to remove him from the midst once he was delivered into his hands. For all wish very much that the counsels they have devised be fulfilled, especially wicked men, who take it so ill in spirit if what they themselves have advised does not succeed, that they hang themselves, as we read of Ahithophel.

units.la: 15 Sequebatur autem Iesum Simon Petrus, & alius discipulus. Discipulus vero ille notus erat Pontifici maximo, & simul introiit cum Iesu in aulam Pontificis maximi.
units.tr: 15 And Simon Peter followed Jesus, and another disciple. Now that disciple was known to the high priest, and went in with Jesus into the court of the high priest.

units.la: 16 Petrus autem stabat extra ad ostium. Exiuit ergo discipulus ille alter qui erat notus Pontifici maximo, & loquutus est ostiariæ, & introduxit Petrum.
units.tr: 16 But Peter stood outside at the door. Then the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the doorkeeper and brought Peter in.

units.la: 17 Dixit ergo Petro ancilla ostiaria, Nonne & tu ex tu ex discipulis es hominis istius? Dicit ille, Non sum.
units.tr: 17 Then the maid who kept the door said to Peter, "Are you not also one of this man's disciples? He says, "I am not."

units.la: 18 Adstabant autem serui & ministri qui prunas congesserant, quia frigus erat, & se ipsos calefaciebant: erat vero cum iis etiam Petrus astans, & se ipse calefaciens.
units.tr: 18 Now the servants and officers, who had made a fire of coals because it was cold, stood there and warmed themselves; and Peter was standing with them and warming himself.

units.la: Obiter inserit historiam defectionis & abnegationis Petri, idque in eum finem vt iustificaretur sermo ille Domini ad Petrum, Antequam gallus vocem mittat ter me abnegabis, Matth.26.34. Marc.14.30. Luc.22.34. Primum in hac historia, Petrus tentat Dominum: deinde ipse a Domino tentatur. Tertio tentationi, quantumuis leui, succumbit. Tentat autem Petrus Dominu, cum eū sequitur licet admonitus supra, quod esset impar tanto oneri. Tentat rursus, quod secundo admonitus, cum repulsam pateretur ab ostiaria Caiaphae, non tamen desierit. Quod ad Petri factum & tentationem, ait, Sequebatur eum Petrus: Sed e longinquo & procul, vt alij Euangelistae obseruant, Matth.26.58. Marc.14.54. Luc.22.54. Sequebatur autem ipse cum alio quodam discipulo, cuius nomen non est hic expressum. Putant quidam hunc fuisse Iohannem illum, qui scripsit hoc Euangelium. Argumento hoc adducuntur, quod quoties ipse de se loquitur, tacito ac suppresso suo ipsius nomine loquatur. Sed alij potius censent discipulum aliū fuisse: non ex illis duodecim vnum, sed alium aliquē, cui charus erat Dominus: ad id autem adducuntur, eo quod notus ac familiaris fuerit Pontifici maximo: Quod de Iohanne homine piscatore & vili, discipulo Christi praesertim, non est verisimile. Cum discipulo illo vnà venit Petrus ad ostium aulae Pontificis: intromittitur discipulus ille alius, quia notus erat Pontifici: Petrus repulsam patitur. Sic autem admonitus non desistitab coepto: sed ibi subsistit, tantisperdū opera illius alterius discipuli intromittitur. Voluit enim is Petro gratificari, cum ea ipsa re perditum eum iuerit. Qua quidem re admonemur, ne, dum volumus amicis nostris consulere, eos perdamus. Sed examinandum paulo
units.tr: He inserts in passing the story of Peter's defection and denial, and this in order to confirm the word of the Lord to Peter, Before the cock crows you will deny me three times, Matt. 26:34; Mark 14:30; Luke 22:34. In this story, first Peter tempts the Lord; then he himself is tempted by the Lord. At the third temptation, however slight, he gives way. Peter tempts the Lord when he follows him, although he had been warned above that he was unequal to so great a burden. He tempts him again, because, having been warned a second time, when he was repulsed by the doorkeeper of Caiaphas, he did not desist. As to Peter's deed and temptation, the text says, Peter followed him, but from a distance and afar off, as the other evangelists observe, Matt. 26:58; Mark 14:54; Luke 22:54. Now he followed with another disciple, whose name is not expressed here. Some think this was that John who wrote this Gospel. They are moved to this by the argument that whenever he speaks of himself he speaks without naming himself. But others rather judge that it was another disciple: not one of the twelve, but some other whom the Lord loved; and they are led to this because he was known and familiar to the high priest. But that this is said of John, a man of fishing stock and humble, and especially a disciple of Christ, is not likely. Peter came with that disciple to the door of the high priest's court; the other disciple is admitted because he was known to the high priest; Peter suffers a repulse. Yet, though warned in this way, he does not desist from what he had begun, but stays there, until he is admitted through the efforts of that other disciple. For that disciple wished to do Peter a favour, and by that very act he ruined him. By this we are admonished not to ruin our friends while we wish to look after them. But let us examine this a little more closely.

units.la: {*} Huius tentationis cunstantię.
units.tr: The constancy of this temptation.

units.la: diligentius hoc Petri factum. Quamuis ex zelo quodā hoc factum ab eo fuerit. Peccauit tamen, primum quidem eo quod admonitus iam à Domino, quòd nondū aptus esset ac satis instructus Dei potentia, ad tollendū crucem suam, & sequendum Dominum suum, tamen non secessit ad tempus, sed insequutus fit Dominum. Semper enim pendendum est ab eius voluntate, & abstinendum nonnunquam ab iis quae alioqui non licita modò, sed maximè laudabilia esse videntur. Cuiusmodi est hoc tollere crucem suam, & sequi Dominū. Quid eo facto laudabilius? tamen si Dominus admonuerit non esse pares nos tanto oneri, omnino abstinendum est. Admonet autem Dominus non esse pares nos magno alicui oneri, si nos in nobis ipsi sentiamus non esse in nobis satis virium ad id obeundum.
