Hinc enim colligere possumus, Dominum id officij nondum à nobis requirere, sed nobis parcere, tantisper dum ad maturitatem perveniamus: deinde peccavit in eo, quòd secundò iam admonitus cum repulsam ab ostiaria pateretur, tamen se subducere noluerit. Potuit enim divina prouidentia hoc factum esse satis animadvertere. Nam quoties aggredimur ad aliquid faciendum, non otiose intueri oportet haec quae in medium incidunt impedimenta, sed ea nos revocare debent ad diligentem institutii nostri consideracionem & examinationem: quo facto, si honestum esse ac licitum quod facere aggredimur, persuadeamur, pergamus in eo quod suscepimus, etiam reluctante diabolo, & superatis iam omnibus impedimentis, si dederit Dominus, id perficiamus. Secus autem si facta iam examinatione non videatur nobis quod facere aggredimur honestum esse ac licitum, continuò desistamus à coepto; praestat enim sero sapere quàm nunquam. Factum hoc Petri, ut ipsum à radicibus suis eruamus, fundatum est procul dubio non in caecitate modò mentis suae, qua non vidit ipse virium suarum tenuitatem, sed in inani quadam fiducia virium suarū, quae huc usque eum perduxit in sequendo Christum Dominum suum. Nam etiam humanae vires & fiducia vitium nostrarum aliquousque nos perducet nonnunquam in sequendo Christum, & patiendo pro nomine ipsius,verùm tandem deficiunt.Quamobrem vires iste quas in nobis esse sentimus, & fiducia ista ac promptitudo animi ad patiendum semper exploranda est, utrùm spiritualis sit an verò carnalis. Cognoscitur autem ex hoc potissimùm spiritualis esse, si ipsa sit cum sensu infirmitatis nostræ ipsorum coniuncta, potentia enim Dei per infirmitatem perficitur.1.Cor.12.9.
units.tr: Peter's act needs a closer look. Although he did it out of a certain zeal, he sinned. First, though the Lord had already warned him that he was not yet ready or sufficiently equipped, in God's power, to take up his cross and follow his Lord, he did not withdraw for a time but followed the Lord anyway. We must always depend on his will and sometimes refrain from things that seem not only lawful but highly praiseworthy. Taking up one's cross and following the Lord is such a thing. What could be more praiseworthy than that? Yet if the Lord warns that we are not equal to so great a burden, we must certainly hold back. The Lord warns that we are not equal to some great task when we feel within ourselves that we do not have enough strength to undertake it. From this we may infer that the Lord does not yet require that duty of us, but spares us until we reach maturity. Second, he sinned in that, though warned a second time, when he suffered rejection by the doorkeeper, he still would not withdraw. Divine providence could have made him notice this. For whenever we set out to do something, we must not look idly at the obstacles that arise in our way; they ought to call us back to a careful consideration and examination of our undertaking. If, once this is done, we are persuaded that what we are attempting is honourable and lawful, we should press on with what we have begun, even while the devil resists, and when all obstacles are overcome, if the Lord grants it, we shall complete it. But if, after examination, what we are attempting does not seem to us honourable and lawful, we should at once abandon our undertaking, for it is better to be wise late than never. Peter's act, to pull it up by its roots, was undoubtedly grounded not only in the blindness of his mind, by which he did not see the weakness of his own powers, but in a certain empty confidence in his own strength. This confidence had brought him thus far in following Christ his Lord. For human strength and the confidence of our powers will sometimes lead us some distance in following Christ and suffering for his name, but in the end they fail. Therefore those powers which we feel within us, and that confidence and readiness of spirit to suffer, must always be tested to see whether they are spiritual or carnal. It is known to be chiefly spiritual if it is joined with a sense of our own weakness, for the power of God is made perfect in weakness. 1 Cor. 12.9.

units.la: Dixit Petro ancilla ostiaria. Hactenus tentavit Dominum Petrus: Nunc vicissim à Domino tentatur. Tentatio quidem levis est; quo autem leuior eo grauius eius peccatum fit. Instrumentum tentationis est non ex militibus vnus aliquis, non vir, sed ancilla: eáque vilis & abiecta, vtpote ostiaria. Verba quibus eum tentat, non ita dura & aspera sunt, sed paulò mitiora. An tu discipulus es, inquit ancilla, hominis istius? Qui maximè sibi suisque viribus confidunt, eos solet Dominus tentare opera vilissimorum quorumque instrumentorum, ad hoc vt sentiant ipsi quàm inanis sit fiducia ista carnalis, & quàm fragiles sint vires humanæ, quæ succumbunt tentationibus adeo leuibus, atque id sentientes non modò succumbant, sed pudefiant. Nam vt spes & fiducia spiritualis non pudefacit: ita fiducia ista carnalis tandem aliquando pudefacit. Non sum. Negat se discipulum esse Christi, atque eadem opera abnegat Christum. Qui enim negat discipulum se esse Christi, is negat Christum: Qui autem negat Christum, vel qui non est cum Christo, is est contra Christum. Qui non est nobiscum, inquit, is est contra nos. Quamobrem non est quòd homines excusent se, eo praetextu, quòd non aperte & ex professo negent Dominum, satis enim est ad rollendum omnem excusationem, & ad reddendum inexcusabiles, si obliquè, & vt loquuntur, indirectè id faciant. In hac autem Petri abnegatione videmus quò tandem recidat humana confidentia, quàm abeat in nihilum, atque id quidem per leuissimas quasque tentationes, vt per ancillæ vocem, imò per motu folij, imò fictos terrores & imaginationes, quas ipsi vltro apud animos suos fingunt sibi homines: vt discant omnes non esse confidentes vllos & fortes praeter eos qui in Domino tales sunt. Stabant autem. Hic designat locum tentationis.
units.tr: The maid who kept the door said to Peter. Hitherto Peter has tempted the Lord; now in turn he is tempted by the Lord. The temptation is indeed slight, but the slighter it is, the graver his sin becomes. The instrument of the temptation is not one of the soldiers, not a man, but a maidservant, and a humble and lowly one at that, a doorkeeper. The words with which she tests him are not harsh or rough but rather mild. You too are a disciple of this man, says the maid. The Lord is accustomed to test those who trust most in themselves and their own powers by means of the humblest and lowliest instruments, so that they may feel for themselves how empty such fleshly confidence is and how frail human powers are, which give way to temptations so slight, and that, feeling this, they not only give way but are put to shame. For as spiritual hope and confidence do not bring shame, so this fleshly confidence at last brings shame. I am not. He denies that he is a disciple of Christ, and in the same act denies Christ. For whoever denies that he is a disciple of Christ denies Christ; and whoever denies Christ, or is not with Christ, is against Christ. He who is not with us, he says, is against us. Therefore people should not excuse themselves on the pretext that they do not openly and expressly deny the Lord. For it is enough to remove every excuse and to render them inexcusable, even if they do it obliquely and, as people say, indirectly. In this denial of Peter we see where human confidence finally falls, how it comes to nothing, and this through the slightest of temptations: through the voice of a maidservant, indeed through the movement of a leaf, indeed through false terrors and imaginings which people themselves invent in their own minds, so that all may learn that there are no confident or brave people except those who are such in the Lord. But they stood. Here he marks the place of the temptation.

units.la: Dominus tentat Petrum & occasionem quandam tentationis Petri, stabat & calefaciebat se vna cum prophanis hominibus & inimicis Christi: vt sciant omnes non fine periculo tentationum nos vnà viuere cum impiis & prophanis hominibus. Suauia quidem videntur ista, Calfieri, edere, bibere &c. Sed condimentum illud tentationum acerbum est ac amarũ. Euangelista Marcus narrat statim post hanc primam Petri abnegationem, sequutum primum gallicinium, quo nimirum Dei prouidentia admoneretur Petrus defectionis suæ, si fieri posset: Marc. 14.68. Sed adhuc ipsius conscientia consopita manebat. Neque enim ij qui coeperunt semel peccato indormiscere, statim aliquo motu aut strepitu excitari solent: verùm ad tempus secure dormiunt donec tandem exstimulati acrioribus & crebrioribus minis simul & iudiciis expergefiant. Neq; etiā expergefiunt aut serio resipiscunt, nisi conuersa prius ad ipsos ac ad cor ipsorum Domini facie, vt de Petro factum legimus: vbi cor conuersum fuerit ad Dominum tolletur velamen.
units.tr: The Lord tests Peter, and Peter's occasion of temptation: he stood and warmed himself together with the profane men and the enemies of Christ, so that all may know that we cannot live together with impious and profane men without danger of temptations. Such things seem pleasant: to warm oneself, to eat, to drink, and so on. But that seasoning of temptations is bitter and sharp. The evangelist Mark relates that immediately after this first denial of Peter there followed the first cock-crow, by which, no doubt, divine providence was admonishing Peter of his falling away, if it could be done. Mark 14.68. But his conscience still lay dormant. For those who have once begun to nod off in sin are not usually roused at once by any movement or noise; rather, they sleep securely for a time until at last, stirred by sharper and more frequent threats and judgments, they wake up. Nor do they wake or seriously return to their senses unless first the face of the Lord is turned upon them and upon their heart, as we read was done with Peter; when the heart is turned to the Lord, the veil is taken away.

units.la: 19 Pontifex maximus interrogauit Iesum de discipulis eius, & de doctrina ipsius.
units.tr: 19 The high priest asked Jesus about his disciples and about his teaching.

units.la: 20 Respondit ei Iesus: Ego palam loquutus sum mundo: ego semper docui in synagoga & in templo, quò vndique Iudæi conueniunt, & in occulto locutus sum nihil.
units.tr: 20 Jesus answered him: I have spoken openly to the world; I have always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where the Jews gather from everywhere, and I have said nothing in secret.

units.la: 21 Quid me interrogas? interroga eos qui audierunt, quid sim ipsis locutus: ecce hi sciunt quæ dixerim ego.
units.tr: 21 Why do you ask me? Ask those who heard what I said to them; behold, these know what I said.

units.la: R Edit ad historiam Christi, eiusque passionem quæ fuit in aula Pontificis. His tempore priora videntur quæ narrat Lucas 22.63.64.65.66. Nam non nisi matutino tempore pertractus est in concilium: postquam iam tota nocte illusus esset ac percussus ab iis, qui ipsum captum ac vinculis constrictum detinebant: Sed nunc videamus quæ acta sint in concilio Pontificis. Non profert quidem in medium Pontifex certa aliquot capita falsæ & hæreticæ doctrinæ aduersus Dominum. Id quod fieri oportuit ad hoc vt formalis, vt vocant, esset in iudicio processus. Neque enim immittendæ in eum fuerunt manus antequam constaret aliquo modo de causa cur caperetur & in iudicium vocaretur.Non profert, inquam, aliquot falsæ doctrinæ capita, sed de doctrina ipsius quærittanquam sibi incognita & hactenus inaudita.Quod autem inquirit in doctrinam, eo innuit eam non posse ferre lucem.Quod quærit de discipulis, eo innuit abipso seductos esse. Respondet Christus de doctrina:Ego palam mundo loquutus sum, &c. Quid me interrogas? Vtscilicet de re ignota, quasi vero doctrina mea suspecta esset. Tum ad eos prouocat, qui ipsum audierant, vt testarentur de doctrina ipsius, quia iis erat ea satis perspecta.Interroga eos, inquit, qui, &c. Nota hic primùm quæ sit malitia hostium veritatis. Eam quidem cognitam habentac perspectam, videri tamen volunt ea ignorare.Cognoscunt etiam non aliam veritatem esse, tamen contra conscientiam in eam inquirunt, non secus ac si mendacium esset. Vide rursus in Christi responso, vt veritas non quærit angulos, sed amat lucem: ita veritas, quoad eius fieri potest, palam prædicáda est, & audiente toto mundo, ad hoc, vt si vocetur vnquam in quæstionem tanquam mendacium, quod ipsum qui dem odit lucè, defendi possit, vel ea ratione sola quòd palam prædicata sit, & prouocari possit ad totum mundum, vt ipse testetur de veritate illa publicè & palam annuntiata. Non hoc ideo dico, quòd negem clam vnquam veritatem esse annunciandam, id quod in persequutione necesse est fieri: sed id volo, quantum potest fieri, veritatem proferendam perpetuò in publicum & palam annuntiandam. Nota rursus, quamuis Christus summa voluntate ac patientia omnia sit passus, capiendum se vltrò obtulerit, manus suas vinciendas sponte sua porrexerit, tamen non patitur, vt veritas aliquid perperiatur, & pro mendacio reputetur: neque vt ipse ṗrofalso doctore ac sedustore habeatur: sed veritati patrocinatur simúlque innocentiam suam tuetur. Sic pati debemus, & patienter quidem pati pro nomine Christi ac veritate ipsius, vt interea non sinamus veritatem ipsam pati aliquid, neque eò adducamur vllis est.
units.tr: It refers to the history of Christ and his passion, which took place in the high priest's house. In time, what Luke relates at 22.63–66 seems to come earlier, for he was not brought before the council until morning, after he had already been mocked and struck the whole night by those who held him captive and bound. But now let us see what was done in the council of the high priest. The high priest does not indeed bring forward some definite articles of false and heretical doctrine against the Lord. This had to be done so that the process in the trial would be, as they call it, formal. For hands were not to be laid on him until it was established in some way why he was seized and called to judgment. I say he does not bring forward some articles of false doctrine, but he asks about his teaching, as if it were unknown to him and hitherto unheard of. But in that he inquires into his teaching, he implies that it cannot bear the light. In that he asks about his disciples, he implies that they have been led astray by him. Christ answers concerning his teaching: I have spoken openly to the world, etc. Why do you ask me? As if he were asking about something unknown, as if indeed his teaching were suspect. Then he appeals to those who had heard him, that they might bear witness to his teaching, because it was well known to them. Ask those, he says, who, etc. Notice here first what the malice of the enemies of truth is. They have the truth known and clearly perceived, yet they want to seem ignorant of it. They know also that there is no other truth, yet they inquire into it against their conscience, just as if it were a lie. See again in Christ's answer how truth does not seek corners but loves the light. So truth, as far as it can be, must be proclaimed openly and with the whole world listening, so that if it is ever called in question as a lie, which indeed hates the light, it can be defended, or by this reason alone, that it was proclaimed openly, and the whole world can be appealed to, so that it may itself bear witness to that truth announced publicly and openly. I do not say this because I deny that truth must ever be proclaimed in secret, which in persecution must necessarily happen; but I wish that, as far as it can be done, truth be always brought forward and announced publicly and openly. Notice again that although Christ suffered everything with the greatest willingness and patience, offering himself to be seized and stretching out his hands of his own accord to be bound, yet he does not allow truth to suffer anything or be counted as a lie, nor himself to be regarded as a false teacher and seducer. Instead he defends the truth and at the same time protects his own innocence. So we ought to suffer, and indeed to suffer patiently, for the name of Christ and for his truth, but in such a way that meanwhile we do not allow the truth itself to suffer anything, nor are we led by any torments to confess that Christ's cause is wicked and unjust.

units.la: 5. Christi responsio de doctrina sua. tormentis, vt confiteamur Christi causam iniquam esse & iniustam. Petrus admonet patiendum esse pro bona honestáque causa. Quo significat patiendum esse pro patrocinio, idque patienter admodum. Paulus dicit afflictum quidem se tanquam facinorosum aliquem ad vincula vsque. At ibidem dixit sermonem Dei non esse vniculu. Quo significauit quidè se in vinculis ipsis aperte testificatum de veritate ac sermone Dei. Atque hoc est quod ab Ephesiis postulat vt precentur pro ipso vt etiam in vinculis liberè loquatur Euangelium & aperto ore.
units.tr: 5. Christ's answer about his teaching. (Torments, so that we confess Christ's cause to be wicked and unjust.) Peter admonishes that we must suffer for a good and honourable cause. By this he means that we must suffer for the defence of the truth, and do so very patiently. Paul says that he was afflicted like a malefactor, even to the point of chains. Yet in the same place he said that the word of God is not bound. By this he indicated that in his chains he bore open witness to the truth and word of God. And this is what he asks of the Ephesians, that they pray for him, so that even in chains he may speak the Gospel freely and with an open mouth.

units.la: 22 Hæc autem cum ipse dixisset, vnus ex ministris qui adstabat, baculo cecidit Iesum, dicens, Itanere sponder Pontifici maximo?
units.tr: 22 When he had said these things, one of the ministers who stood by struck Jesus with a rod, saying, "Is this how you answer the high priest?"

units.la: 23 Respondit ei Iesus, Si male loquutus sum, testificare de malo: sin bene, cur me cædis?
units.tr: 23 Jesus answered him, "If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil; but if well, why do you strike me?"

units.la: 24. Misera igitur eum Annas vinctum ad Caiaphan Pontificem maximum.
units.tr: 24. Annas therefore sent him, bound, to Caiaphas the high priest.

units.la: PAssus est à Pontifice falsam accusationem, patitur nunc verbera à ministro Pontificis, Pontifex egit cum eo contra ordinem iudiciorum receptum ac vsitatum. Nunc minister Pontificis quoque contra formam ac ritum iudiciorum eum verberat. Primùm peccauit minister Pontificis in eo quod percussierit eum, quòd bene loquutus sit, quum defenderet doctrinam suam. Secundò peccauit in eo, quòd re nõ prius iudicata percusserit. Tertiò, quòd etsi iudicata fuisset, non suo tamen loco & tempore percusserit. Sed quid dicas, id semper experientia compertum est, innocentes in iudicium vocatos, iniquius ac contra formam iudiciorum tractatos esse quàm aperte maleficos, homicidas, latrones. In causa est, quia maius est odium peruersorum iudicum aduersus innocentiam ac veritatem, quàm etiā iustorum iudicum aduersus malitiam & iniquitatem: Hinc fit vt ita abripiantur odio ac malitia iniqui iudices, vt omne ius fasque violent in tractanda causa innocentis alicuius. In Christi responsione nota quomodo eum ipse cõuincat & dilemmate, seu cornuto, quod vocant, argumento, vtrinque feriat. Vel bene loquutus sum, vel malè. Si malè, non eram percutiendus, re non priùs iudicata. Sin bene, non eram percutiendus omnino. Ergo quoquò te vertas, non illud effugies quin conuincaris iniuriæ. Vide quomodo constrictum teneat vndique ministrum illum Pontificis, eúmque conuincat iniuriæ. Nihil hoc derogat patientiæ nostræ, interim dum patimur & affligimur, quod iniurię conuincamus aduersarios: Semper enim ius & iniuria in lucem proferri debent, & hominum conscientiæ conuincendæ sunt, ad hoc vt vel resipiscant, vel inexcusabiles reddantur, vt Deus glorificetur, vel in misericordia, vel in iustitia sua.
units.tr: He has suffered a false accusation from the high priest; now he suffers blows from the high priest's servant. The high priest dealt with him contrary to the established and customary order of trials; now the high priest's servant also beats him, contrary to the form and rite of trials. First, the high priest's servant sinned in striking him, since he had spoken well while defending his teaching. Second, he sinned in striking him before the case was decided. Third, even if it had been decided, he struck him not in his proper place and time. But whatever you say, experience has always shown that innocent people summoned to judgment are treated more unjustly, and more contrary to the form of trials, than those openly guilty of crimes, murderers and robbers. The reason is that the hatred of wicked judges against innocence and truth is greater than even the hatred of righteous judges against wickedness and iniquity. Hence it happens that unjust judges are so carried away by hatred and malice that they violate every right and law in handling the case of some innocent person. In Christ's answer, note how he convicts him and strikes him on every side with a dilemma, or so-called horned argument. Either I have spoken well, or badly. If badly, I was not to be struck before the case was decided. But if well, I was not to be struck at all. Therefore, whichever way you turn, you will not escape being convicted of wrong. See how he holds that minister of the high priest bound on every side and convicts him of injustice. This does not detract from our patience, that while we suffer and are afflicted we also convict our adversaries of wrong. For right and wrong must always be brought into the light, and the consciences of men must be convicted, so that either they repent, or are made inexcusable, so that God may be glorified, either in his mercy or in his justice.

units.la: Miserat autem. Redit ad occasione quandam ac fundamentum totius huius passionis, atque ita transit ad sequentem historiam Petri. Significatur autem his verbis non omnino immunem fuisse Annam socerum Caiaphæ, & purum à reatu passionis huius Christi: miserat enim eum ac tradiderat in manus hostis sui capitalis, qui prius consilium dederat occidendi ipsum. Cauendum ne quid nobis rei sit cum sanguine innocentis, ne quouis modo assentiamur cædi ipsius, ne ea delectemur. Ea enim vel sola re fimus rei sanguinis innocentis: neque eius tantum, sed totius sanguinis iusti, inde ab Abele ad Zachariam fuit, vt Christus pronuntiat. Quisquis enim assentitur effusioni sanguinis vnius innocentis, is facile ac multo negotio adducitur, vt assentiatur effusioni sanguinis omnium innocentum quotquot vllo tempore occisi sunt.
units.tr: And Annas had sent him. He returns to the occasion and foundation of this whole suffering, and so passes to the following story of Peter. These words signify that Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, was not wholly free of guilt in this suffering of Christ, and was not clear of the crime: for he had sent him and handed him over into the hands of his mortal enemy, who had earlier given counsel that he be killed. We must take care that we have no share in the blood of the innocent, that we in no way assent to his slaying, nor take pleasure in it. For by this alone we become guilty of innocent blood; and not only of that, but of all the righteous blood shed from Abel to Zechariah, as Christ declares. For whoever assents to the shedding of the blood of one innocent person is easily and with little effort led to assent to the shedding of the blood of all the innocent who have been slain at any time.

units.la: 25 Stabat autem Simon Petrus, & sese calefaciebat: dixerunt igitur ei, Num & tu ex discipulis eius es? Negauit ille, & dixit, Non sum.
units.tr: 25 Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. They said therefore to him, "Are you not also one of his disciples?" He denied it and said, "I am not."

units.la: 26 Dicit ei quidam ex seruis Pontificis maximi, cognatus eius cuius abscinderat Petrus auriculam, Nonne ego te vidi in horto cum eo?
units.tr: 26 One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said to him, "Did I not see you in the garden with him?"

units.la: 27 Rursus ergo negauit Petrus, & statim gallus vocem emisit.
units.tr: 27 Peter therefore denied again, and immediately a cock crowed.

units.la: REuertitur ad defectionem Petri, eiusque duas abnegationes persequitur, secundam & tertiam: nam de prima supra: primum hic est occasio tentationis, secundo, tentatio, tertio abnegatio secunda numero. Occasio est in his verbis: Stabat & calefaciebat. Significatur autem eum post primam illam abnegationem Domini in summa securitate mansisse. Quid? annon postquam abnegasset Dominum, secedendum illi fuit, dolendum ac timendum, ne rursus in id mali incideret? sed nulla re commorus stabat & calefaciebat se vna cum ministris sacerdotum. Peccatum enim perpetuo inducit animis nostris securitatem carnalem. Neque secus ac si qui ex altiori loco cecidit, is ad tempus iacet stupidus ac expers sensus: Ita qui a Deo quasi decidit ac prolapsus est, iacet aliquandiu in stupore expers sensus omnis. Et quo grauior lapsus, eo maior perpetuo stupor ac securitas altior. Imprimis autem peccatum in Christum ac veritatem ipsius securitatem hanc inducere solet animo, vt de Iuda vidimus, qui ex malitia cordis in Dominum suum peccauit: Id etiam Petro contigit, qui tamen ex infirmitate Dominum abnegauit. Occasione securitatis huius tentatur denuo. Qui enim post peccatum securi iacent, ij tentationibus diaboli expositi sunt. Petrus autem iam iterum tentatus, secundo negat Dominum: Non sum, inquit. Securi cum tentantur facile cedunt tentationibus vel leuissimis quibusque. Facile enim est dormientem hominem deturbare vel solo digiti attactu. Atque hactenus secunda fuit Petri abnegatio. Sequitur tertia, quae, vt Lucas refert, interposita quasi hora vna sequuta est secundam. Tanto enim tempore post secundam abnegationem securus permansit. Et illud quidem certum est, contraxisse cum secundo hoc lapsu suo maiorem securitatem, quam quae fuit post lapsum illum primum: Nam quo saepius labimur & deficimus a Deo, eo maiorem subinde cotrahimus securitatem, ac stuporem: ex maiori hac securitate sequitur tertia tentatio. Perfistentibus nobis in stupore & securitate, perfistit diabolus in tentationibus. Tentatus Petrus abnegat Dominum tertia vice: Idque, vt obseruant Matth. 26.74. & Marc. 14.71. cum exce execratione & iureiurando. Abiurat itaque Dominum suum, non abnegat simpliciter. Perseuerante tentatione, perseueramus in lapsu, postremus autem grauissimus est. Addit Iohannes immediatè post tertiam abnegationem gallum vocem misisse. Vocem misit primò post primam abnegationem, vocem misit secundò post tertiam abnegationem, hoc factum est vt constaret veritas prædictionis Christi: cùm diceret, Priusquàm gallus bis vocem miserit, ter me abnegabis. Sic Marcus 14.30. Sed an Petrus admonitus est peccati sui ac defectionis hoc galli cantu? Minimè. Nam Lucas 16.61. addit simul ac vocem misit gallus conuersum Dominum intuitum esse Petrum. Atque hinc factum est vt Petrus recordatus sit sermonis Domini, ac respiuerit ad aspectum eius. Secure dormientes in peccato nulla voce excitamur, nisi voce Domini, quæ sola facit, vt mortui audiant: nulla admonitione permouemur, nisi sola Domini admonitione, solóque eius intuitu: lumen enim cognitionis est in facie ipsius: & postquam cor conuersum fuerit ad Dominum, tolletur velamen. Vt nunc paucis examinemus hæc Petri factum: multis quidem, fateor, modis ab eo peccatum est. Peccauit inani fiducia primùm, qua tractus est post Christum contra vnâ ac alteram admonitionem: Ingressus aulam Pontificis peccauit horribiliter: peccauit quidem non iam ex inani confidentia, sed ex alta securitate ac infirmitate. Interea toto hoc tempore, non negauerim Petro fuisse fidem ac dilectionem aliquam: sed dico oppressam fuisse fidem hanc Petri ac dilectionem, partim infirmitate naturæ, partim securitate carnali: quæ tandem influente eum Christo commiserescete eius, cœpit emergere & in seria quadam resipiscentia sese prodere. Vt igitur in Petro habemus summæ infirmitatis humanæ specimen: ita in eo quoque habemus diuinæ clementiæ exemplum admirabile.
units.tr: He returns to Peter's fall and pursues his two denials, the second and the third; for the first was treated above. Here there is first the occasion of the temptation, second the temptation, third the denial, the second in number. The occasion is in these words: He was standing and warming himself. This signifies that after his first denial of the Lord he remained in complete security. What? Should he not, after denying the Lord, have withdrawn, grieved and feared lest he fall into evil again? Yet, undisturbed by anything, he stood and warmed himself together with the servants of the priests. For sin always brings carnal security into our minds. Just as one who has fallen from a higher place lies for a time stunned and without sense, so one who has, as it were, fallen away and slipped from God lies for a while in stupor, without any sense at all. And the graver the fall, the greater the stupor and the deeper the security that follows. Above all, sin against Christ and his truth is wont to induce this security in the mind, as we saw in Judas, who out of malice of heart sinned against his Lord. This also happened to Peter, who nevertheless denied his Lord out of weakness. By the occasion of this security he is tempted again. For those who lie secure after sin are exposed to the temptations of the devil. Peter, now tempted again, denies the Lord a second time: "I am not," he says. Those who are secure, when tempted, easily yield to the slightest temptations. For it is easy to knock down a sleeping man even by a mere touch of the finger. And so far was Peter's second denial. There follows the third, which, as Luke relates, came after an interval of about an hour following the second. For he remained secure for so long a time after the second denial. And it is certain that by this second fall he contracted greater security than that which followed the first fall. For the more often we slip and fail away from God, the greater security and stupor we gradually contract; from this greater security the third temptation follows. While we persist in stupor and security, the devil persists in temptations. Tempted, Peter denies the Lord a third time; and this, as Matthew 26.74 and Mark 14.71 observe, with curses and oaths. He therefore forswears his Lord, not merely denies him. While the temptation persists, we persist in the fall, and the last is the gravest. John adds that immediately after the third denial the cock crowed. The cock crowed first after the first denial, and crowed a second time after the third denial; this happened so that the truth of Christ's prediction might be established, when he said, "Before the cock has crowed twice, you will deny me three times." So Mark 14.30. But was Peter admonished of his sin and fall by this crowing of the cock? By no means. For Luke 16.61 adds that as soon as the cock crowed, the Lord turned and looked at Peter. Hence it came about that Peter remembered the word of the Lord and repented at his look. We who sleep securely in sin are roused by no voice except the voice of the Lord, which alone makes the dead hear; we are moved by no admonition except the admonition of the Lord alone, and by his look alone: for the light of knowledge is in his face; and once the heart has turned to the Lord, the veil will be taken away. Let us now briefly examine this act of Peter: he sinned in many ways, I confess. He sinned first by vain confidence, by which he was drawn to follow Christ against one or two warnings. Entering the high priest's hall, he sinned dreadfully; he sinned not now from vain confidence, but from deep security and weakness. Yet throughout all this time I would not deny that Peter had some faith and love: but I say that this faith and love of Peter were oppressed, partly by the weakness of nature, partly by carnal security; which, when at last the Lord's compassion for him took effect, began to emerge and reveal themselves in a certain serious repentance. Thus, as in Peter we have a specimen of the utmost human weakness, so in him we also have an admirable example of divine clemency.

units.la: 28 Ducunt ergo Iesum à Caiapha in prætorium. Erat autem mane: & ipsi non introierunt in prætorium, ne polluerentur, sed vt ederent Pascha.
units.tr: 28 They led Jesus therefore from Caiaphas into the praetorium. It was early morning, and they did not go into the praetorium themselves, so that they would not be defiled, but so that they might eat the Passover.

units.la: 29 Prodiit ergo Pilatus ad eos, & dixit, Quā accusationem adfertis aduersus hominem illum?
units.tr: 29 Pilate therefore came out to them and said, "What accusation do you bring against this man?"

units.la: 30 Responderunt & dixerunt ei, Nisi iste esset facinorosus, non tradidissemus eum tibi.
units.tr: 30 They answered and said to him, "If this man were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up to you."

units.la: IN Concilio Pontificum plura in eum facta narrantur. Alij, vt Matt.26.59. & c. Marc.14.55. Luc.22.63. &c. Matthaei narratio copiosissima est: quae autem narrat Matthaeus videntur sequuta esse ea quae ab Iohanne hic narrantur. Hic autem in summa, ordo eorum videtur esse quae in eum facta sunt in aula Pontificis. Primùm Pontifex cùm nihil haberet, quod aduersus eum diceret, tentauit eum, vt ex ipsius ore exciperet materiam accusationis & condemnationis aliquam: deinde, cùm nihil proficeret tentando, tum se conuertit ad subornandos falsos testes. Tum ne cùm hoc quidem modo proficeret, ipse Pontifex iratus surrexit, & ipsum adiurauit per Dominum, An Christus ille esset, quod cùm ipse non diffiteretur, iudicatus est blasphemus, ac proinde reus mortis. Hinc dimissum videtur fuisse concilium sacerdotum ac seniorum. Retentus autem est Christus in aula Pontificis, & a ministris sacerdotum ac Romana cohorte custoditus, interea temporis omne genus iniuriae passus est, verba, verbera & nihil non. Crepusculo autem conuenerunt rursus sacerdotes & seniores, & vt antea ipsum interrogarunt an esset Christus: quod cùm ipse rursus non diffiteretur, reum mortis iudicarunt, hinc deceßum est, ac demissum Concilium. Christum autem abducunt ad praetorium. Atque hic incipit tertia pars passionis ipsius sub iudice politico Pontio Pilato. Sed quorsum abducunt ad Pilatum? An vt ipse exploraret an reus mortis esset necne, & omnino iudicium exerceret? At ipsi sacerdotes iam iudicarunt mortis reum. Vnde colligi potest, non alia de causa abductum Iesum ad Pilatum, quàm vt ipse sententiam damnationis pronunciaret, eúmque confestim interficiendum curaret ex sacerdotum iudicio illo iam habito, fretus scilicet tantùm ipsorum verbo: vt non obscurè colligi potest ex verbis sequentibus, quibus respondent Iudaei Pilato: Si non esset maleficus, non tradidissemus eum tibi. Ergo ciuilis iudicis opera abutun-tur.
units.tr: In the council of the priests many things are reported as done against him. Others, such as Matthew 26:59 and following, Mark 14:55, Luke 22:63 and following, and so on, do the same. Matthew's account is very full, and what Matthew relates seems to have followed what John narrates here. The order of what was done to him in the high priest's hall appears, in summary, to be this. First, since the high priest had nothing to say against him, he tried him, to draw from his own mouth some matter for accusation and condemnation. Then, when he gained nothing by testing him, he turned to suborning false witnesses. Then, since he did not succeed even in this way, the high priest himself rose up in anger and adjured him by the Lord to say whether he was the Christ. When he did not deny it, he was judged a blasphemer and therefore liable to death. From this it seems that the council of priests and elders was dismissed. Christ, however, was kept in the high priest's hall, guarded by the servants of the priests and a Roman cohort, and in the meantime he suffered every kind of abuse: words, blows, and everything else. At twilight the priests and elders gathered again and asked him, as before, whether he was the Christ. When again he did not deny it, they judged him liable to death; then they departed, and the council was dismissed. They lead Christ away to the praetorium. And here begins the third part of his passion, under the civil judge Pontius Pilate. But why do they lead him to Pilate? Was it so that he might examine whether the man was liable to death or not, and exercise judgment at all? But the priests had already judged him liable to death. Hence it can be gathered that Jesus was led away to Pilate for no other reason than that Pilate should pronounce the sentence of condemnation and see to it that he was put to death at once, on the basis of that judgment of the priests already given, relying, of course, only on their word. This can be clearly inferred from the words that follow, in which the Jews answer Pilate: "If he were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you." Therefore they abuse the work of the civil judge, as if he were some sort of executioner. So today the one who falsely calls himself the supreme pontiff imitates that supreme pontiff of the Jews, in that he abuses Christian princes to carry out slaughter against them,

units.la: Ex Matth. quaedam ad secunda parte pertinent. tur, tanquam carnificis cuiusdam: Ita hodierno die is qui se summum pontificem mentitur, imitatur tamen Pontificem illum summum qui inter Iudæos fuit, in hoc, quòd Christianis principibus abutatur ad exercendam carnificinā in eos, quos ipse censet morte dignos. Et vt carnifex aliquis, sibi traditum à iudice reum ac damnatum, non audet non tradere morti: ita neque principes quotquot sese vendiderunt, vt sint serui Antichristi, audent famulitium illud ipsi denegare. Rex Hispaniarum coactus est, ad libidinem inquisitorum pontificiorum, in suum ipsius filium sævire, vt nihil sit simile Caiaphæ, quàm qui se Pontificem summum iactitat hodierno die. Atque hæc de ipsius abductione à Caiapha in prætorium, & ad Pilatum. Iudas autem proditor referente Matthæo 27. 3. & deinceps, cùm videret Iesum à Sacerdotibus iam condemnatum abduci ad Pilatum, ducitur ipse pœnitentia proditionis suæ, & desperabundus seipsum strangulat. Exemplum horrendi iudicij Dei, tam in eos qui Christum vendunt, quàm in eos qui Christum emunt. Nec autem ingressi sunt. Notatur modus quo Iesum abduxerunt in prætorium: Nō quidem ipsi vnà cum eo ingressi sunt, sed solum eum intruxerunt: causa addita est, Ne polluerentur, Nempe vel tactu solo hominis Ethnici Pilati. Sic abstinuerunt ab Ethnicis, non ex diuino mandato, sed ex suo commento. Ratio rursus huius addita est, nempe, Vt ederent Pascha. Nimirum illa nocte ad vesperam. Vide insignes hypocritas, contaminarunt se sanguine innocentissimi hominis, quem ceperunt, vinxerunt, indignis modis tractarunt, & tamen religiosi esse volunt in re nihili, commento nimirum suo ipsorum. Hoc enim est ingenium hypocritarum, quòd cùm se polluerunt fœdo facinore quocunque plusquam superstitiosi sunt in observatione cæremoniarum, siue eę mandatæ sint à Deo, siue ab ipsis inuentæ: potissimum tum autem si ab ipsis inuentæ sint. Sed perinde est: nam obseruatio cultus externi cæremoniarum, etiam à Deo præscriptarum, absque cultu morali vanitas est, imò abominatio est Deo: Vide Esa. 1. 10. Quàm similes sunt Catholici isti sanctuli Iudæis isti. Tota enim istorum sanctimonia & religio est in externis cæremoniis potissimum, quos ipsi sibi effinxerunt, Ne tangito, ne edito: Atque cum hypocritica sua sanctimonia prodeûtes in vulgus mundum decipiunt,& secum in certam perniciem trahunt.Eximit er go ad eos Pilatus.Cedit Pilatus superstitioni eorum, ipse- que ad eos egreditur, quæritque quam afferant aduersus Iesum accusationem. Multò æquius factum à Pilato, quàm à Iudæis: Illi cũm nihil haberent quòd dicerent in eum, ceperunt tamen eum ac vinxerunt, agitarunt in Concilio variis ac indignis quibusque modis, tradiderunt denique interficiendum Pilato præsidi;At Pilatus non prius sedere vult in iudicio quàm crimen discat ex Iudæis & videat delationem ipsorum. Id ita fieri solet, vt etiam Ethnicus aliquis maiori vtatur æquitate in iudicando, quàm ij qui sibi falsò arrogant nomen Ecclesiæ.De Romana illa Ecclesia loquor, quæ iniquiori magisque peruerso iudicio tractat verosChristi seruos & innocentes, quàm paganus aliquis aperte maleficos, adeo vt melius sit bono cuique incidere in manus Turcæ, quàm Papæ & Patrum storum Inquisitorum. Nisi ipse esset maleficus. Respondent præsidi satis superbè, irascunturque quòd etiam incognita prius causa, Christum condemnet, contentus scilicet vel solo ipsorum verbo ac præiudicio. Crimen interea aduersus ipsum aliquod afferunt, ne videantur nihil dicere, nempe quod maleficus sit. Sed accusatio ista generalis nimium est. Qui probant illud, ipsum maleficum esse? Necesse est ad hoc, vt sit legitimum iudicium, particularius aliquid dicant. Quòd si id habuissent, dixissent, credo. Deus in tota hac Christi persecutione, Christi innocentiam vult conspici, simulque Iudæorum in agedo contra ipsum iniquitatem. Idipsum perpetuò factum est in persequutionibus martyrum, in quibus voluit ap parere & innocentiam seruorum suorum, & tyrannidé aduersariorum: vt bonum sit pati pro Christo, vel hac sola causa, quòd Deus inter patiendum & cùm condemnatur ab iniquis iudicibus, nos interea iustificet nostràmque innocentiam asserat. Innocentia enim nostra non intermoritur nobiscum. Nam innocentia sanctorum rum viuit etiam hodierno die in animo simul & in ore piorum hominum.
units.tr: Some of these things from Matthew pertain to the second part. The one who falsely calls himself the highest pontiff is treated as a certain kind of executioner. So today the man who pretends to be the supreme pontiff imitates that high priest among the Jews, in that he abuses Christian princes to carry out slaughter against those whom he himself judges worthy of death. And just as an executioner does not dare to refuse to hand over to death a criminal delivered to him by a judge, so the princes, however many have sold themselves to be slaves of Antichrist, do not dare to deny that servitude to him. The King of Spain was compelled, at the pleasure of the Papist inquisitors, to rage against his own son, so that nothing is more like Caiaphas than the man who boasts today that he is the supreme pontiff. So much for Jesus being led away from Caiaphas to the praetorium and to Pilate. Judas the traitor, as Matthew 27 relates from verse 3 onward, when he saw Jesus, already condemned by the priests, being led away to Pilate, was moved to repentance for his betrayal, and in despair he strangled himself. This is an example of the dreadful judgment of God, both on those who sell Christ and on those who buy him. Nor did they go in. The manner in which they led Jesus into the praetorium is noted: they did not themselves go in together with him, but only had him brought in. A reason is added: lest they be defiled, namely by the mere touch of the Gentile Pilate. Thus they abstained from Gentiles, not by divine command but by their own invention. Again a reason for this is added, namely, that they might eat the Passover, that is, that night at evening. See how notable hypocrites they are: they defiled themselves with the blood of the most innocent man, whom they had seized, bound and treated with unworthy abuse, and yet they wish to be scrupulous in a trifling matter, namely by their own invention. For this is the nature of hypocrites: when they have polluted themselves with some foul crime, they become more than superstitious in observing ceremonies, whether these were commanded by God or devised by themselves, and especially if they were devised by themselves. But it makes no difference, for the observance of external ceremonies, even those prescribed by God, without moral worship is vanity, and indeed is an abomination to God. See Isaiah 1:10. How like these Catholic little saints are to those Jews! For the whole sanctity and religion of these men lies chiefly in external ceremonies, which they have fashioned for themselves: Touch not, taste not. And with their hypocritical sanctity they go forth among the common people, deceive the world, and drag it with them into certain destruction. Pilate therefore came out to them. Pilate yields to their superstition and himself goes out to them, and asks what accusation they bring against Jesus. This was done by Pilate far more fairly than by the Jews. They, though they had nothing to say against him, nevertheless seized and bound him, harassed him in the council in various and unworthy ways, and finally handed him over to the governor to be killed. But Pilate does not wish to sit in judgment until he learns the charge from the Jews and sees their accusation. This is the usual practice, so that even a certain Gentile uses greater fairness in judging than those who falsely claim for themselves the name of the Church. I speak of that Roman Church, which with a more unjust and more perverse judgment treats the true servants and innocent of Christ, more than any pagan treats openly wicked men, so that it is better for any good man to fall into the hands of the Turk than of the Pope and the inquisitors of the Fathers. Unless he himself were a criminal. They answer the governor rather haughtily, and are angry that he condemns Christ even before the cause is known, being content, of course, with their word and prejudgment alone. Meanwhile they bring some charge against him, so as not to seem to say nothing, namely that he is a criminal. But that accusation is too general. Who proves that he is a criminal? For a lawful judgment it is necessary that they state something more particular. If they had had such a thing, they would have said it, I believe. In this whole persecution of Christ God wills that the innocence of Christ be seen, and at the same time the iniquity of the Jews in acting against him. The same has always happened in the persecutions of the martyrs, in which he willed both the innocence of his servants and the tyranny of their adversaries to appear, so that it is good to suffer for Christ, even for this reason alone, that God, while we suffer and are condemned by unjust judges, meanwhile justifies us and asserts our innocence. For our innocence does not die with us. Indeed the innocence of the saints lives even today, in the mind and on the lips of godly men.

units.la: 31 Dicit ergo ijs Pilatus, Accipite eum & secundum legem vestram condemnate eum: itaque Iudaei dixerunt ei, Nobis non licet occidere quenquam:
units.tr: Pilate therefore said to them, Take him and condemn him according to your law. So the Jews said to him, It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.

units.la: 32 Vt sermo Iesu impleretur, quem dixerat, significans qua morte futurum erat vt moreretur.
units.tr: 32 That the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he had spoken, signifying by what death he was to die.

units.la: HAEc videtur serio dicere Pilatus, voluit enim potius aliquid remittere de iure suo, quàm iniquè iudicare ac condemnare hominem innocentem: vt satis appareat meliori conscientia fuisse homine Ethnicum & prophanum, quàm iltos qui Ecclesiae nomen sibi vendicarunt, sed falso. Excitauit itaque Deus Pilatum ad iltos pudefaciendum. Inuenimus etiam Ethnicos cum naturali conscientia, totidem quasi luminaria esse nonnunquam, in medio eorum, qui Deum & Christum volunt profiteri, quorum tamen conscientia est cauterio refecta, vt praedictum est ab Apostolo de falsis iltis doctoribus qui in Ecclesia suborituri essent. In extremo autem illo iudicio surrecturi Ethnici & condemnaturi plerosque ex iis qui Christi nomen professi sunt in hac vita. Nobis non licet occidere. Concedunt Pilato ius suum, & profitentur se nolle temere irrumpere in ius alienum. Attamen reipsa iudicandi potestatem Pilato ademerunt, cùm sine accusatione & delatione criminis cuiusquam contentum esse praeiudicio illo ipsorum voluerint eum, ex eóque statim procedere ad condemnationem innocentis. Melius autem fuisset cum Pilato actum, si totam iudicij summam, sibiipsis vendicassent, ipsi eum condemnassent sine praeside Romano, ipsi ad supplicium cùm pertraxissent. Sic enim non fuisset implicatus miser reatu illo peccati eorum gravissimi. Videntur sibi gratificari se Pilato cū agnoscunt ipsum iudicem in capitalibus illis: at reipsa Pilatum perdunt. Melius etiam ageretur cum principibus, qui Papae totidem sunt asseclae, si postquam ipsi censuerunt misera condicio iudicarunt haereticos esse, qui tamen veri Christiani sunt, fi, inquam, tum non traderentur in manum ciuil-lem ad id condemnarentur & interficerentur: sed ipse Papa cum clero illo suo integrum sibi reseruaret, ipse condemnaret, ipse occideret. Implicantur enim seculares, quos vocant, principes reatu peccati ipsius. Praeterea quod hanc potestatem vltro deferat Pilato, magis ideo peccant. Nam qui nō solum ipse peccat, sed alios offendit ac communicare facit peccato suo, is ea ipsa re gravius peccat. Quam graue est peccatum illias bestiae, quae etiam inebriat tot principes terrae, & communicare facit peccatis suis. Hoc enim auget peccatum ipsius, tantum abest ab eo vt ipsum imminuat aut eleuet. Papistae enim putant se ideo liberatos esse ab innocentium ac piorum sanguine, quod nō ipsi, sed politicus aliquis iudex innocentes condemnet, mortique tradat. Vt sermo Iesu impleretur. Iohannes inserit obiter finem responsionis ipsorum: fuit autem vt sermo ille Christi impleretur quem loquutus est tum, cum innueret quo genere mortis tollendus esset e medio. Nam cum reiicerent a se in Pilatum illud ius occidendi, vna eademque opera fecerunt, vt Christus crucifigeretur. Atque hoc fuit illud genus mortis quod ipse Christus futurum praedixit. Si enim sibi delatum ius continuo arripuissent, profecto Christum non crucifixissent (fuit enim hoc inusitatum genus mortis apud Iudaeos) sed lapidibus obruissent ex lege sua. Vides igitur nihil fieri in hac actione & persequutione ista Christi, nisi Deo disponente omnia dicta ac facta, iuxta illud, Vt facerent quaecunque manus tua & consilium tuum prius definierat facienda. Ergo Herodes, Pilatus, reliquique, quid fuerunt aliud quam tortores & carnifices totidem, iam olim praeordinati a Deo ad executionem voluntatis ipsius. Nota hic rursus, nihil dici a nobis, vel agi, quod non disponatur a Deo ad id producendum, quod ipse iam olim destinauit. Interea tamen non excusantur ij qui male vel loquuntur, vel agunt, vel hac sola de causa, quod interea non Dei voluntatem in loquendo, vel agendo intueantur: verum sua ipsorum peruersa voluntate ad loquendum, vel agendum moueantur. Quamobrem semper nobis laborandum in eo, vt bona Dei instrumenta simus, neque moueamur. ueamur tantùm à Deo, sed bene moueamur: hoc est Dei Spiritu sancto agamur. Sic enim opus suum in nobis co-tonaturus est Dominus.
units.tr: It seems Pilate says this in earnest. He preferred to give up some of his right rather than judge unjustly and condemn an innocent man. So it is clear that this Gentile and profane man had a better conscience than those who claimed the name of the Church for themselves, though falsely. God therefore raised up Pilate to shame them. We also find that Gentiles, with their natural conscience, are sometimes like so many lights in the midst of those who want to profess God and Christ, yet whose conscience has been seared with a hot iron, as the Apostle foretold of those false teachers who were going to arise in the Church. In that last judgment, the Gentiles will rise up and condemn many of those who have professed the name of Christ in this life. It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death. They grant Pilate his right and declare that they do not wish to break rashly into another's right. Yet in fact they took away from Pilate the power of judging. For they wanted him, without any accusation or charge of crime, to be content with their prejudgment, and to proceed from that at once to the condemnation of an innocent man. It would have been better for Pilate if they had claimed the whole sum of judgment for themselves, condemning him without the Roman governor and dragging him to execution themselves. Then the wretched man would not have been entangled in the guilt of their most grievous sin. They seem to please Pilate when they acknowledge him as judge in capital cases, but in fact they destroy him. It would also have been better for the princes, who are so many followers of the Pope, if, after they themselves had judged as heretics those wretched people who are nevertheless true Christians, they had not handed them over to the civil hand to be condemned and killed. Instead the Pope himself, with his clergy, would keep the whole power for himself: he would condemn, he would kill. For the so-called secular princes are entangled in the guilt of his sin. Moreover, they sin all the more because they offer this power to Pilate of their own accord. For whoever not only sins himself but also offends others and makes them share in his sin, sins all the more gravely for that very reason. How grievous is the sin of that beast, which also makes drunk so many princes of the earth and makes them share in its sins! For this increases its own sin; so far is it from diminishing or lessening it. The Papists think they are freed from the blood of the innocent and the pious because it is not they themselves but some political judge who condemns the innocent and hands them over to death. That the word of Jesus might be fulfilled. John inserts in passing the outcome of their answer. It came about that the word Christ spoke then was fulfilled, when he indicated by what kind of death he was to be removed from the world. For when they threw back on Pilate the right to put to death, by one and the same act they brought it about that Christ was crucified, and this was the kind of death that Christ himself foretold would happen. For if they had at once seized the right that had been handed to them, they would certainly not have crucified Christ (for this kind of death was unusual among the Jews), but would have stoned him with stones according to their own law. You see, then, that nothing is done in this action and persecution of Christ except that all things said and done are arranged by God, according to that saying: to do whatever your hand and your counsel had decided beforehand should be done. So Herod, Pilate and the rest were nothing other than so many torturers and executioners, long ago predestined by God for the carrying out of his will. Note here again that nothing is said or done by us that is not ordered by God to bring about what he had long ago appointed. Meanwhile, however, those who speak or act badly are not excused, or excused only for this reason, that in speaking or acting they do not look to the will of God, but are moved to speak or act by their own perverse will. Therefore we must always labour to be good instruments of God, and not merely be moved by God but be moved well, that is, be driven by the Holy Spirit of God. For in this way the Lord will bring his work to completion in us.

units.la: 33 Introiuit ergo rursus in prætorium Pilatus, & vocauit Iesum, dixitque ei, Tu ne es rex ille Iudæorum?
units.tr: 33 Then Pilate entered the palace again, called Jesus, and said to him, Are you the King of the Jews?

units.la: 34 Respondit ei Iesus, A te ipsòne tu hoc dicis, an alij dixerunt tibi de me?
units.tr: 34 Jesus answered him, Do you say this of yourself, or did others tell you about me?

units.la: NEmpe post multa verba vtrò citróque habita, & acceptam à Iudæis declarationem illam quam ipse Christo obiicit, quòd se dixerit Regem Iudæorum. Declarationem hanc Lucas sic fusius explicat, Deprehendimus, inquiunt aduersarij, hominem hunc peruertentem gentem nostram, prohibentem tributa dare Cæsari, dicentem se Christum, id est Regem esse. Ex quo videmus crimen hoc, cuius accusat Pilatus Christum, non inuentum à Pilato ipso, vt & verba sequentia indicant, sed à Iudæis Pilato delatum esse. Verùm examinandum paulò diligentius crimen hoc; non deferunt quidem blasphemum, sed proditorem, adeóque reum læsæ maiestatis, vt qui regnum affectaret: sciuerunt enim quocum sibi res esset, Pilato nimirum, homine prophano & Cæsaris legato. Atque hæc est prudentia filiorum huius sæculi. Rursus non verum est quod deferunt & intentant crimen. Nam tantum abfuit Christus à regni affectatione, vt quærentibus ipsum Iudæis vt regem constituerent, in desertum secessit: docuerit etiam dari Cæsari quæ Cæsaris sunt; denique ipse tributum soluerit suo & Petri nomine. Quare calumnia est ista, cùm deferunt crimen affectati regni. Postremò volunt videri studio Cæsaris hæc dicere, cùm tamen reipsa Cæsarem oderint, ac non nisi odio Christi, hoc criminis detulerint. Quamobrem ad calliditatem & calumniam accedit assentatio. Nihil pensi habent per fasne an per nefas prosequatur id quod impiè faciendum propositum. Quicunque enim causam instituerunt inhonestam ac impiam, his nihil curæ est, quibus mediis, quàm illicitis, vtpote fraude, calumnia, adulatione obtineant causam, ad quam alia ratione pe-
units.tr: Naturally, this followed many words exchanged back and forth, and the accusation the Jews had brought, which he now puts to Christ, namely that he had said he was King of the Jews. Luke explains this accusation more fully: We have found this man perverting our nation, forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king. From this we see that the charge with which Pilate accuses Christ was not discovered by Pilate himself, as the following words also indicate, but was reported to Pilate by the Jews. But this charge must be examined a little more carefully. They do not indeed denounce him as a blasphemer but as a traitor, and so guilty of treason, since he aspired to a kingdom. For they knew with whom they had to deal, namely Pilate, a profane man and Caesar's legate. This is the prudence of the children of this world. Again, what they report and bring as a charge is not true. For Christ was so far from aiming at a kingdom that, when the Jews sought to make him king, he withdrew into the wilderness; he also taught that what is Caesar's should be given to Caesar; and finally he paid the tribute in his own name and Peter's. So this accusation of an aspiration to a kingdom is a calumny. Lastly, they wish to seem to be speaking these things out of zeal for Caesar, when in fact they hated Caesar and brought this charge only out of hatred of Christ. Therefore flattery is added to their cunning and slander. They have no concern whether what they have impiously proposed is pursued by lawful or unlawful means. For those who have undertaken a dishonourable and impious cause care nothing about what means they use to gain their cause, however illicit, such as fraud, calumny or flattery, since their cause cannot be reached by any other way. It is necessary that what has been impiously undertaken be achieved by wicked means.

units.la: Actio Pilati cum Christo.
units.tr: The action of Pilate with Christ.

units.la: Iudæorum astutia sycophantica.
units.tr: The sycophantic cunning of the Jews.

units.la: Iohan.6.15. Matth.22.21. Matth.17.27. Eorundem turpis assentatio. uenire non possunt.Necesse est enim quod impiè suscepptum est, malis mediis obtineatur. Quare videndum perpetuò, vt non nisi honesta quæque in vita suscipiamus & proponamus perficienda, adhoc vt bene viuamus & faciamus omnia. Nunc veniamus ad verba,quibus Pilatus Iesum accusat. Tune,inquit,Rex es Iudæorum? Expectárunt quidem Iudæi Pilatum ex iracundia & animi acerbitate omnia in Christum tum facturum, tum dicturum. Crimen enim læsæ maiestatis odiosum erat admodum. Sed Pilatus ingressus iam ad Iesum,tantum abest ab eo vt faciat in eum quidquam seuerius, vt etiā eum ne alloquatur quidem asperius. Non enim continuò iratus proditorem appellat, sed sedato animo eum alloquitur. Exemplum summæ modestiæ ac æquitatis in homine alioqui prophano: & argumentum animi vacui ab huiusmodi perturbationibus quæ omne iudicium solet peruertere: odio nominatim,quo præcipites ferebantur aduersus eum summi sacerdotes & concilii Iudæorum. Neque enim odit Pilatus Iesum, quin potius conscius innocentiæ ipsius volvit eum absolui & ab odio & persequutione Iudæorum liberari.Quare di-scant iudices exemplo Pilati hominis alioqui Ethnici, cum animis ab omni perturbatione vacuis, accedere ad iudicandum de vita & morte alicuius, ab odio autem præsertim immunes sint:alioqui enim si reus aliquis nō minus innocens sit quàm fuit Christus ipse,eum tamen damnabunt. Quòd si autem condemnetur vel maleficus aliquis ex odio vel ira iudicis cuiusquam, profecto requiretur è manu iudicis illius sanguis ipsius. Videndum itaque vt lege interficiatur reus,non odio iudicis. At te ipso hoc dicu? Christus non statim respondet ad obiectū crimen, sed quærit à quonam sit hoc crimen, ab ipsone Pilato fictum,an Pilato ab aliis significatum.Vult enim Dominus in hac Christi persequutione & passione,conspici quæ sint omnium partes, quæ Sacerdotum ac Iudæorum, quæ Herodis, quæ Pilati, præsertim verò quæ sint Iudæorum partes,vt totum onus iniquitatis illius in eos recidat, neque rei sint tantum peccati sui ipsorum, sed peccati etiam aliorum, Herodis, Pilati, &c. Nam Iudæi & persecutorum Ec-eos peccato suo ac damnatione implicârunt. Excu-sent sent se licet quantum volunt Papistæ: vniuersas tamen sanguis Martyrum ipsis imputatur, quia iudices, qui vocantur seculares, quod in hac re vel faciunt vel fecerūt, ad ipsorum libidinem explendam, totum illud vel faciunt vel fecerunt. Nota tursus quòd velit Dominus Pilatum non tantùm habere oculos defixos in crimine illo intentato à Iudæis, sed in Iudæis ipsis delatoribus, qui ex odio vel malitia animi ipsum sunt persequuti. Non tantùm oportet iudicem attendere ad crimen ipsum quod intentatur, sed ad eos qui illud intentant. Quòd si enim reum odio persequantur capitali, vt Iudæi Christum persequuti sunt, profectò pro iusto crimine calumniam sæpe deferent.
units.tr: John 6:15. Matthew 22:21. Matthew 17:27. Their shameful flattery. Therefore we must constantly take care that we undertake and propose for accomplishment in life only what is honest, so that we may live well and do all things well. Now let us come to the words with which Pilate accuses Jesus. Are you, he says, the King of the Jews? The Jews had indeed expected that Pilate, out of anger and bitterness of mind, would do and say everything against Christ. For the charge of treason was very hateful. But Pilate, having now come to Jesus, is so far from doing anything more severe against him that he does not even address him harshly. For he does not at once call the traitor angry names, but speaks to him with a calm mind. This is an example of great moderation and fairness in a man otherwise profane, and a proof of a mind free from those disturbances that usually pervert all judgment, especially the hatred by which the chief priests and the council of the Jews were rushing headlong against him. For Pilate does not hate Jesus; rather, being aware of his innocence, he wishes him to be absolved and freed from the hatred and persecution of the Jews. Therefore let judges learn from the example of Pilate, a man otherwise a Gentile, to approach the judging of anyone's life and death with minds free from every disturbance, and above all free from hatred. Otherwise, if some accused person is no less innocent than Christ himself was, they will condemn him all the same. And if any evildoer is condemned out of the hatred or anger of some judge, then assuredly the blood of that man will be required at the judge's hand. Care must therefore be taken that a defendant is put to death by the law, not by the hatred of the judge. Do you say this of yourself? Christ does not at once answer the charge laid against him, but asks whose charge it is, whether it was invented by Pilate himself or signified to Pilate by others. For the Lord wills, in this persecution and passion of Christ, that it be seen what each party's role was: that of the priests and Jews, that of Herod, that of Pilate; and above all what the role of the Jews was, so that the whole burden of that iniquity falls back on them, and they are guilty not only of their own sin but also of the sin of others, Herod, Pilate, and so on. For the Jews and the persecutors of the Church have entangled them in their sin and condemnation. Let the Papists excuse themselves as much as they like: the blood of the martyrs is nevertheless imputed to them as a whole, because the judges who are called secular, since in this matter they either do or have done that, do and have done that whole thing to satisfy their lust. Note again that the Lord wishes Pilate to keep his eyes fixed not only on the charge brought by the Jews, but on the Jews themselves who laid it, who from hatred or malice of mind have persecuted him. A judge must attend not only to the charge itself that is brought, but also to those who bring it. For if they persecute a defendant with deadly hatred, as the Jews persecuted Christ, they will often bring a calumny in place of a just charge.

units.la: 35 Respondit Pilatus, Numquid ego Iudæus sum? Gens tua & primarij Sacerdotes tradiderunt te mihi, Quid fecisti?
units.tr: 35 Pilate answered, "Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have handed you over to me. What have you done?"

units.la: 36 Respondit Iesus, Regnum meum non est ex hoc mundo: si ex hoc mundo esset regnum meum, ministri mei certassent, ne traderer Iudæis: nunc autem regnum meum non est hinc.
units.tr: 36 Jesus answered, "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have fought, so that I should not be handed over to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from here."

units.la: 37 Dixit ergo ei Pilatus, Ergo Rex es tu? Respondit Iesus, Tu dicis me regem esse. Ego ad hoc natus sum, & ad hoc veni in mundum vt dem testimonium veritati. Quisquis est ex veritate audit vocem meam.
units.tr: 37 Pilate therefore said to him, "So you are a king?" Jesus answered, "You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice."

units.la: PIlatus paulò magis commotus hæc loquitur: abhorret enim totus ab ista delatione, neque eius author vult æstimari à quoquam, quin potiùs eum transfert in Iudæos: Gens tua, inquit. Primùm itaque se authorem negat, idque eo argumento quòd non sit Iudæus, qui conscius esse posset factorum Christi: deinde qui verè sint authores designat; nempe gens Iudæorum, nominatim autem summi sacerdotes. Vide conscientiam tum innocentiæ Christi, tum calumniæ Iudæorum: hinc enim est quod Pilatus tantopere se purget. Purgat autem se de calumnia ista, quòd ipse eius non sit author. Priusquam Christus se purget de obiecto sibi crimine, Pudet enim hominem quodammodò calumniæ illius tã fœ-dæ. Neque tamen miser à cœpto iudicio in innocente desistit, quin ipsum persequitur. Quid, inquiens fecisti? Difficile enim est ingressò semel iudicium in innocentem pedem suum retrahere, quin se statim ita inuoluit atque implicat, vt se explicare in posterum nequeat, etiamsi cum Pilato, quàm maximè velit innocentem aliquem absoluere, priusquam ore suo cum Pilato eum condemnet. Quare vel ne ingrediatur omnino Iudex in iudicium aduersus innocentem, vel si ingressus sit illud, desistat ab eo quàm primùm viderit obiectam calumniam, vel si progredi malit ad finem vsque absoluat innocentem, & eripiat eum ex fictis crimininationibus persequutorum. Neque enim valet ista excusatio, qua iudex aliquis quærit se excusatum habere: Volui, inquiens, ipse hominem absoluere, inuitus condemnaui, oportuit cedere vel authoritati vel importunitati hominum. Ista non excusarunt Pilatum, neque loco illa manuum de qua audiemus postea à reatu sanguinis Christi miserum abluit. Regnum meum non est. Nunc demum respondet Dominus ad calumniam obiectam, sed quo-dammodò purgat: non quidem liberat se cædę, sed libe-rat se calumnia: non negat se regem præ metu vllo Pilati, vel etiam mortis, sed negat se regem terrestrem, aut regnum suum mundanum esse, vt aduersarij somniarunt: Addit rationem: Quod si regnum meum esset ex hoc mundo, serui mei, &c. hoc est pugnarent cum Iudæis de regno terrestri. Quisquis enim regnum in hoc mundo affectat ad mortem vsque ipsam de regno illo dimicaturus est: Christus autem tantum ab eo abfuit vt pugnaverit, vt è contrà Petrum pugnaturum ipse retraxerit atque castigauerit. Tum repetit atque concludit regnum suum non esse ex hoc mundo. Nota cum non statim vbinam sit regnum illud suum docere Pilatum. Non enim iam tam doctorem in docendo agere voluit quàm sacerdotem in patiendo. Ideóque Pilatum ab incepto retrahere noluit, vt qui sciret sibi nunc moriendum esse Dei decreto ac consilio æterno, & quidem sub Pilato isto iudice moriendum. Tempus est quo Christus non docet. Quare ne sinamus elabi opportunitate: & quoad apappellatur dies hodiernus, ne obdureмus corda nostra. Num igitur Rex es tu? Debebat quidem Pilatus sermonē illum coeptum de regno Christi vlterius persequi, sed homo prophanus & non intelligens quæ ad regnum Dei pertinent, inceptum sermonem accusatione Christi interpellat: prophani ac βεβηλοι isti non modo non possunt prosequi sermonem de rebus spiritualibus & ad alteram vitam spectantibus semel inchoatum, sed etiam interpellant eum sermonibus profanis: neque enim delectantur rebus cœlestibus: neque gustarunt vnquam quàm benignus sit Dominus. Tu dicis me regem esse. Christus ad accusationem respondet: non negat quidem se regem esse, sed Pilatum ipsum, qui regem eum vocauit, testem regni sui appellat. Atque hæc est bona illa professio quam testatam fecit Christus coram Pontio Pilato: qua nimirum confessus est se regem esse. Vide 1. Timoth. 6. 13. Tum ne Pilatus regem aliquem terrestrem exisiimaret eum esse, ostendit prætera finem, cur natus sit in mundo, & in mundum venerit, nempe hunc vt testimonium perhiberet veritati, non regem agat, sed seruum potius, depositā ad tempus Regis persona. Nam Christus cùm esset in forma Dei, non duxit rapinam se parem esse cum Deo, sed se ipse exinaniuit, forma serui accepta. Testimonium veritati perhibuit Christus in terris, vt seruus obediens factus voluntati Patris sui. Tū ne putaretur frustra omnino ipsum de veritate testatum esse in mundo, addit, non frustra se cucurrisse respectu renatorum quos dicit Ex veritate esse, hoc est regenitos esse ex veritate, tanquam immortali semine. Veritas autem hic est sermo veritatis. vide supra cap. 17. 17. Obscure admonet Pilatū. Quod si ipse ex veritate esset, ipsum quoque audituram vocem ipsius. Vide, Dominus redit ad sermonem illum coeptum de rebus coelestibus, post quam interpellatus est a Pilato: idque non modo vt se surget, sed vt Pilatum quoque, si qua ratione id fieri possit, adducat ad fidem, saltem inexcusabilem reddat. Hoc autem obseruatione imprimis est dignum quòd diligentius laboret Dominus in Pilato docendo, & si quidē non nisi parcè id faciat, tamen diligentius in eo docēdo laboret, quàm in Sacerdotibus, aut etiam omnino Iudæis, quos vidit induratos & obstirmatos esse aduersus veritatem. Misertus est autem quodammodo Pilati, quo ipsi ad libidinem suam sunt abusi implendam. Exemplo Domini hoc faciendum nobis est, vt etiam interpellati à prophanis hominibus, tamen non desistamus plane à sermonibus spiritualibus, sed pugnemus cum ipsorum infidelitate, ad hoc vt si fieri possit ipsi ad fidem adducantur, vel certè inexcusabiles reddantur, vt Deus saltem glorificetur in iusto suo iudicio.
units.tr: Pilate speaks these words a little more agitated. He is wholly averse to this accusation, and its author does not wish to be thought well of by anyone, but rather shifts the blame onto the Jews: "Your nation," he says. First, then, he denies that he is the author, and he gives as his reason that he is not a Jew, who could have been aware of Christ's deeds. Then he names the true authors: namely the nation of the Jews, and specifically the chief priests. Notice the consciousness of Christ's innocence and of the Jews' calumny, for this is why Pilate so earnestly clears himself. He clears himself of this calumny on the ground that he is not its author. Before Christ clears himself of the crime charged against him, Pilate is ashamed of such a foul calumny, in some measure. Yet the wretched man does not abandon the judgment he has begun against the innocent man, but still pursues him. "What," he says, "have you done?" For once a judge has set foot in a judgment against an innocent man, it is hard to draw back his foot. He at once becomes so entangled and involved that he cannot extricate himself afterwards, even if he would very much like to absolve some innocent man along with Pilate, before he condemns him with his own mouth. Therefore either the judge should not enter into a judgment against the innocent at all, or, if he has entered it, he should desist as soon as he sees the calumny laid against him; or, if he prefers to proceed, he should absolve the innocent man to the end and rescue him from the fabricated accusations of his persecutors. For that excuse, by which a judge seeks to have himself excused, does not hold good: "I wished," he says, "to absolve the man myself; unwillingly I condemned him; I had to yield either to the authority or to the importunity of men." Such excuses did not excuse Pilate, nor did that washing of hands, of which we shall hear later, cleanse the wretched man from guilt for Christ's blood. "My kingdom is not." Only now does the Lord answer the calumny laid against him, but he clears himself in some measure. He does not indeed free himself from the slaughter, but he frees himself from the calumny. He does not deny that he is a king out of any fear of Pilate or even of death, but he denies that he is an earthly king, or that his kingdom is worldly, as his adversaries had dreamed. He adds a reason: "If my kingdom were of this world, my servants, etc.", that is, they would fight with the Jews over an earthly kingdom. For whoever aims at a kingdom in this world will fight for that kingdom even unto death itself. But Christ was so far from fighting that, on the contrary, he restrained and rebuked Peter when he was about to fight. Then he repeats and concludes that his kingdom is not of this world. Note that he does not at once teach Pilate where that kingdom of his is. For he did not now wish to act as teacher in teaching, so much as priest in suffering. Therefore he was unwilling to draw Pilate back from his undertaking, since he knew that he had now to die by the eternal decree and counsel of God, and indeed to die under this judge Pilate. This is the time in which Christ does not teach. Therefore let us not allow the opportunity to slip away, and while the day called today lasts, let us not harden our hearts. "Are you then a king?" Pilate ought indeed to have pursued further the discourse begun about Christ's kingdom, but being a profane man, who does not understand what pertains to the kingdom of God, he interrupts the begun discourse with an accusation against Christ. Such profane and βέβηλοι men not only cannot follow through a discourse on spiritual things, once begun, and things pertaining to the other life, but they also interrupt it with profane talk. For they take no delight in heavenly things, and they have never tasted how gracious the Lord is. "You say that I am a king." Christ answers the accusation: he does not deny that he is a king, but he calls Pilate himself, who named him king, a witness of his kingdom. And this is that good confession which Christ made before Pontius Pilate, by which he plainly professed that he is a king. See 1 Timothy 6:13. Then, lest Pilate should think that he is some earthly king, he further shows the purpose for which he was born and came into the world, namely that he might bear witness to the truth, not play the king but rather the servant, having laid aside for a time the person of the King. For Christ, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Christ bore witness to the truth on earth, as a servant made obedient to the will of his Father. Then, lest it be thought that he had testified to the truth in the world in vain, he adds that he did not run in vain with respect to those who are reborn, whom he calls "of the truth", that is, born again of the truth as of an immortal seed. Now truth here is the word of truth; see above, chapter 17:17. He admonishes Pilate obscurely: if he himself were of the truth, he would also hear his voice. See, the Lord returns to the discourse begun about heavenly things, after being interrupted by Pilate; and this he does not only to save himself, but to bring Pilate also to faith, if by any means it can be done, or at least to render him inexcusable. This is especially worth observing: the Lord labours more diligently with Pilate in teaching him, and although he does so only sparingly, he nonetheless labours more diligently in teaching him than with the priests, or indeed with the Jews generally, whom he saw to be hardened and obstinate against the truth. He had some pity on Pilate, whom they abused to satisfy their own lust. By the example of the Lord we ought to do likewise: even when interrupted by profane men, we should not altogether desist from spiritual discourse, but contend against their unbelief, so that, if possible, they may be brought to faith, or at least be rendered inexcusable, so that God may be glorified at least in his just judgment.

units.la: 38 Dicit ei Pilatus, Quid est veritas? Et cum hoc dixisset, rursum prodiit ad Iudæos, & dixit eis, Ego nullum invenio crimen in eo.
units.tr: 38 Pilate said to him, "What is truth?" And when he had said this, he went out again to the Jews and said to them, "I find no crime in him."

units.la: 39 Est autem vobis consuetudo, vt vnum dimittam vobis in Pascha: vultisne ergo dimittam vobis regem illum Iudæorum?
units.tr: 39 But you have a custom that I should release someone to you at the Passover. Will you therefore that I release to you the king of the Jews?

units.la: 40 Clamauerunt autem rursum omnes dicentes, Nequaquam istum, sed Barabbam. Erat autem ille Barabbas latro.
units.tr: 40 Then they all cried out again, saying, "Not this man, but Barabbas." Now Barabbas was a robber.

units.la: ANtrea abrupit Pilatus sermonem illum de regno Christi inceptum. Nunc autem cogitur certo quodam modo persequi eundem illum de veritate sermonem, sed ita vt cum fastidio, & contemptu id faciat; neque enim expectat dum respondeat Christus ad interrogatum. Prophani homines vel odiosè interpellant sermonem de rebus cœlestibus, vel si vrgeantur præsius, de rebus quidem illis loquuntur: sed cum fastidio, non studio discendi, sed animo conueniendi: Quia nimirum ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, mundo sunt stultitia. Nondum enim gustârunt quàm benignus sit Dominus, ideo experere non possunt sincerum illud lac sermonis. Rursum venit ad Iudæos. Pilatus cùm inueniret quidem Iesum suaipsius confessione regem esse, verùm non terrenum aliquem, sed, vt ipse putat, imaginarium: (Nam regnū cœlorum prophanis hominibus somniū esse videtur) tantum nunc abest ab eo, vt ipsum morte dignum censeat, vt contrà palam suo ore purget. Politici homines, qui nihil sapiunt nisi terrena ista, si ipsis reliqueris terrena ista ac mundana, nihili faciunt quid quis vel loquatur, vel agat de Deo, de Christo, de regno Christi. Nam ψυχικὸς homini ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei stultitia sunt.
