Lysias tribunus cum de Paulo scribit ad Felicem præsidem, Comperi, inquit, accusari eum de περὶ τῶν νομικῶν quæstionibus legis ipsorum, nullius criminis reum quod sit dignum morte aut vinculis. Nota rursus: in Pilato laudabile illud est quòd suo ore tam præclarum de Christo testimonium perhibeat, sed in eo peccat graviter, quòd interea Christum contemnat animo, tanquam phanaticum, contemnat regnum illud de quo Christus loquutus est, tanquam imaginarium, contemnat veritatem illam, cuius meminit, tanquam fabulam. Qui prophani sunt corde, etiam tum cum pulcherrimè loqui videntur de Deo, de religione, peccant gravissimè. Nam corde interea cœlestia illa omnia irrident, & pro nihilo ea habent, ut iunt ipsi animo prophano. Quamobrem quo animo loquamur de Spiritualibus, prophanóne an sanctificato plurimum refert. Videndumque semper, ut interloquendū de his rebus bene, rectè, sanctèque sentiamus, ad hoc ut sermonem nostrū de hisce rebus Deo approbemus. Est autem vobis. Commemorant alij Euangelistæ accusationem alteram quæ ordine præcessit ea quæ hic deinceps narrantur à Iohanne nostro: nam cùm sacerdotes summi vidissent se nihil profecisse prima illa accusatione, in qua læsæ maiestatis crimen Domino intentarunt, cœperunt tum infinitas calumnias in eum congerere, quibus omnibus Christus nihil respondit: ne vrgente quidem illo Pilato: adeo vt Pilatus admiraretur tam altum hominis silentium. Insistunt sacerdotes, & doctrinam falsam ac blasphemam obiiciunt, quam sparserit Christus inde à Galilæa, Hierusalem usque. Pilatus statim vt audiuit ac certò comperit Galilæum esse Christum, eum continuò ad Herodem amandavit, vtpote Galilææ Tetrarcham: Herodes lætatus est aduentu Christi, à quo expectauit signum aliquod edendum. Verum cùm ne verbum quidem, nedum signum ab eo accepisset: tum ad Pilatum cum contemptu Iesum remisit. Pilatus autem secūda vice eum palam sua voce purgauit, atque innocentem declarauit. De his vide Matth. 27. 12. &c. Marc. 15.3. &c. Luc. 23.3. Hic fortasse cum Pilato quis admiretur tam altum illud Christi silentium, pu-
units.tr: Here Pilate again breaks off the discourse about Christ's kingdom that had begun. But now he is compelled, in a certain manner, to pursue that same discourse about truth, yet he does so with disdain and contempt; for he does not wait until Christ answers the question put to him. Profane men either interrupt discourse about heavenly things with hostility, or, if pressed more closely, they do speak of those things, but with disdain: not with a desire to learn, but with a mind to be done with it. Because, of course, "the things of the Spirit of God are foolishness to the world." For they have not yet tasted how gracious the Lord is, and therefore they cannot relish the pure milk of the word. "He went out again to the Jews." Pilate, though he found that Jesus was a king by his own confession, yet not an earthly one but, as he thinks, an imaginary one (for the kingdom of heaven seems to profane men a dream), is now so far from judging him worthy of death that, on the contrary, he openly declares him innocent with his own mouth. Political men, who know nothing but these earthly things, if you leave them these earthly and worldly things, make no account of what anyone says or does about God, about Christ, about the kingdom of Christ. For "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; they are foolishness to him." When the tribune Lysias writes to the governor Felix about Paul, he says, "I found that he was accused concerning questions of their law, but that he was guilty of no crime worthy of death or of bonds." Note again: in Pilate it is praiseworthy that with his mouth he bears so notable a testimony about Christ, but he sins grievously in this, that meanwhile in his mind he despises Christ as a fanatic, despises the kingdom about which Christ spoke as imaginary, and despises that truth of which he speaks as a fable. Those who are profane in heart sin most gravely even when they seem to speak most beautifully about God and religion. For in their heart they mock all those heavenly things and hold them as nothing, as they say, in their profane minds. Therefore it matters greatly with what mind we speak of spiritual things, whether profane or sanctified. And we must always take care that in speaking of these things we think well, rightly, and holily, so that our discourse about these matters may be approved by God. "But you have a custom." Other evangelists record a second accusation which, in order, came before those things that are narrated here by our John. For when the chief priests saw that they had accomplished nothing by that first accusation, in which they charged the Lord with treason, they then began to heap up endless calumnies against him, to all of which Christ made no answer, not even when Pilate pressed him; so that Pilate marvelled at such a deep silence of the man. The priests persist, and they object a false and blasphemous doctrine which Christ had spread from Galilee even to Jerusalem. As soon as Pilate heard and clearly learned that Christ was a Galilean, he at once sent him on to Herod, as tetrarch of Galilee. Herod rejoiced at Christ's coming, expecting from him some sign to be performed. But when he had received not so much as a word from him, let alone a sign, he sent Jesus back to Pilate with contempt. Pilate, however, a second time cleared him by his own voice openly, and declared him innocent. On these things see Matthew 27:12 etc., Mark 15:3 etc., Luke 23:3 etc. Here perhaps someone, with Pilate, might marvel at that deep silence of Christ, ...

units.la: Iudex idé Christum iustificat, quē postea condenat.
units.tr: The judge himself justifies Christ, whom he afterwards condemns.

units.la: Accusatio noua Sacerdotum adu. Christum.
units.tr: The new accusation of the priests against Christ.

units.la: Herodes & Pilatus lu-dos sibi faciunt de Christo.
units.tr: Herod and Pilate make a game of Christ for themselves.

units.la: Pilatus mi-ratur Christi silentium. tétque hoc factum quadam animi pertinacia, à qua tamen tantum abfuit Christus, vt tunc temporis obedientiam & patientiam ostendere magis non potuerit quo tempore tanquam agnus stans coram tonsore suo, mutus non aperuit os suum, & ne vna quidem vocula vel Patris de se consilium, vel aduersariorum ac persequutorum instítutum impediuit.Ne putet igitur quis Christum Martyribus inferiorem, qui in summis persequutionibus, semper animo fuerunt præsentissimo & maximo, nihilque prætermiserunt cui non respondsum dederint, idque admirabili cum fiducia, animique præsentia. Verum ideo Christus non aperuit os suum, in eum nimirum finé, vt ipsis daretur os suum aperire. Nisi enim Dominus summo cum silentio passus fuisset, profecto ipsi in persequutione siluissent. Nunc redeamus ad contextum nostræ historiæ. Quærit quidem Pilatus quàm potest maximè vt Christum liberet. Nactus igitur opportunitatem ex consuetudine iam recepta ac vsitata apud Iudæos eam auidè persequitur vrgéque. Consuetudo ista non nitebatur lege aliqua Dei, sed contra legem Dei de homicidis puniendis & morte multandis. Inuecta est à præsidibus Romanis, & à Iudæis recepta sub praeclaro scilicet prætextu. Sic enim videri voluerunt dies suos festos ornare, vt festum Paschatis & alios: prsides autem ea ratione voluerunt populo commendare clementiam ac misericordiam suam. Nihil enim principes viros magis comendet quàm clementia, qua fit potissimum vt Dei similitudinem ac imaginem referant. Verum prætextus isti non excusant peccatum, cùm interea in Dei expressam legem impingant: nempe hanc, Oculus tuus non parcat homicidæ. Neque verò est quod quisquam putet à Deo regibus vel magistratibus datam esse eam potestatem, quæ sit supra hanc legem, adeo vt possint pro arbitrio suo homicidæ cuiquâ parcere, cùm nulli vnquam creaturæ, ne angelo quidem, plena ac absoluta potestas in vitam & mortem sit concessa, sic vt occidat quem velit, & quem velit rursus in vita conseruet: cùm ea sit solius Dei in creaturam suam potestas, cuius voluntas est vnica regula omnis iustitiæ. Concedo illud quidem, speciales esse leges quasdam certis ac iustis de causis à viris principibus latas, in quas eam habent potestatem, vt iustis de causis,peccantibus in eas, condonent noxam: Verùm si quæ leges sunt quæ nituntur vniuersali illa ac naturali æquitate, contra eas non esse potestatem affirmo. Huiusmodi est ista lex de capitali pœna homicidæ irroganda. Non nego illud quidem in manu principum esse nonnunquam pœnam mitigare, sed pœnam planè condonare posse eos, nego.
units.tr: Pilate wonders at Christ's silence, and thinks this happened from a certain stubbornness of mind, from which Christ was nonetheless so far removed that at that time he could not have shown obedience and patience more fully: at which time, like a lamb standing before its shearer, he was dumb and did not open his mouth, and not even one little word hindered either the Father's counsel concerning him or the plan of his adversaries and persecutors. Let no one therefore think that Christ was inferior to the martyrs, who in the greatest persecutions always had a most ready and very great presence of mind, and left nothing unanswered, and answered with wonderful confidence and presence of mind. But Christ did not open his mouth for this reason, namely so that they might be given the opportunity to open theirs. For if the Lord had not suffered in the greatest silence, surely they would have fallen silent in persecution. Now let us return to the context of our history. Pilate seeks as eagerly as he can to free Christ. Having therefore found an opportunity in the custom already received and usual among the Jews, he pursues it eagerly and presses it. That custom rested on no law of God, but was against the law of God concerning the punishment and death of murderers. It was introduced by the Roman governors and received by the Jews under a splendid pretext, of course. For they wished it to seem that they adorned their festal days, as the feast of the Passover and the others; and the governors by this means wished to commend their clemency and mercy to the people. For nothing commends princely men more than clemency, by which it happens above all that they bear the likeness and image of God. But these pretexts do not excuse the sin, since meanwhile they strike against the express law of God: namely this, "Your eye shall not spare the murderer." Nor is there anyone who should think that such power was given by God to kings or magistrates as is above this law, so that they could at their pleasure spare any murderer whatever, since full and absolute power over life and death has never been granted to any creature, not even to an angel, so that he may kill whom he wishes and again preserve in life whom he wishes; since that power over his creature belongs to God alone, whose will is the sole rule of all justice. I concede indeed that there are certain special laws enacted by princely men for certain and just causes, over which they have the power to pardon the offence of those who transgress them for just causes. But if there are any laws that rest upon that universal and natural equity, I affirm that there is no power against them. Of this kind is this law concerning the infliction of capital punishment on a murderer. I do not deny that it is sometimes in the hand of princes to mitigate a punishment, but I deny that they can altogether remit it.

units.la: Neque verò est quod obiiciant à bonis etiam principibus condonata esse crimina capitalia admissa aduersus leges istiusmodi vniuersales ac naturales, vt à Dauide, qui morte non puniuit vel Ioabi homicidium, vel Amonis incestum, vel denique Absolonis fratricidium. Frustra istud obiicitur, cùm non exemplis sed legibus videndum sit, vt taceam interea vel iustas causas fuisse, cur Dauid sic egerit, vel certè Dauidem peccasse graviter. De Ioabo res clarior est, quàm vt demonstratione egeat: homines ipsi filij Seruiæ firmiores sunt, dixit Dauid.
units.tr: Nor is there reason for anyone to object that capital crimes committed against such universal and natural laws have been pardoned even by good princes, as by David, who did not punish with death either the murder of Joab, or the incest of Amnon, or finally the fratricide of Absalom. This objection is vain, since one must look not to examples but to laws; to say nothing of the fact that there were either just causes why David acted thus, or certainly that David sinned gravely. Regarding Joab the matter is clearer than it needs demonstration: "The men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too strong for me," said David.

units.la: Neque denique aliquid ponderis habet illud argumentum a priuatis offensis, quas omnes non modo possunt, sed debent ex præscripto Dei condonare ac remittere. Cùm inde sequeretur non modò posse sed debere magistratum omne flagitium ac crimen capitale contra leges, remittere. Quòd si non esset aliud quod argueret iudicia Dei inprimis qui leges naturales & vniuersales violarunt, non datam esse cuiuis regum vel principum hanc potestatem, vt impunè possit condonare crimen capitale contra legem tum Dei, tum naturæ, id ostendi potest vel experientia iudiciorum Dei in ipsos viros principes & eorum posteros: in quorum caput pœna illa quâ flagitiosis hominibus ipsis infligere debebant, deriuata est.
units.tr: Finally, the argument from private offences, which everyone not only can but ought to pardon and remit according to the prescription of God, carries no weight at all. For it would follow from this that a magistrate not only can but must remit every outrage and capital crime committed against the laws. But even if there were no other thing that proved that the judgments of God fall above all upon those who violate the natural and universal laws, and that the power to pardon a capital crime against the law both of God and of nature has not been given to any king or prince, this can be shown even by the experience of God's judgments upon the princes themselves and their posterity: upon whose head has been turned that punishment with which they ought to have inflicted those shameful men.

units.la: E memoria non debet expungi vnquam exemplū illud tristissimum iudicij in Saulem, qui contra mandatum Dei non occidit Agagum Regem Amalekitarum. Hæc de his hactenus, & paulò prolixius quàm instituì, nèpe quia consuetudo ista pessima nimis iamdiu inualuit in nostragente. Nunc videamus quàm serio Pilatus in id incubuit, vt Christum dimitteret: qua quidem de causa non caret sua quadam laude, etsi in hoc vituperio sit dignus, quòd hominem innocentissimum tanquam maleficum cum nota ignominiæ nunquâ delenda voluerit dimittere. Nam vt maleficum aliquem comparauit Dominum cum homine maleficentissimo Barabba. Non satis enim est si Iudex innocentem tantum dimittat, sed requiritur praeterea vt tanquam innocentem dimittat. Deus enim vt vult innocentem viuere, ita vult eum viuere tanquam innocentem, & patefactione innocentiae ac veritatis quaerit gloriam suam. Illud praeterea addo, moriendum potius viro innocenti, quam viuendum cum nota ignominiae, aut recipiendam remissionem criminis eius, cuius tamen ipse non sit conscius. Peccauit igitur Pilatus in modo quo eum dimittere voluit. Verum hoc peccatum Iudaeis ipsorumque malitiae potius imputandum fuit quam Pilato, quandoquidem eorum causa ita fecerit, & hoc eis quasi condonarit, quod maxime cupiebant: nempe Iesum hominem esse flagitiosum & mortem promeritum. Sed quid ad Pilatum Iudaei respondent? Clamauerunt, &c. dicentes, Non hunc. Pilatus Christum comparauit cum Barabba homine flagitiosissimo: ac Iudaei Barabbam Christo praeferunt, quasi vero non ad eo mortis reum, vt Christum Dominum. Multo igitur grauius peccant, quam Pilatus, eo quod capitalius oderint Christi innocentiam, quam Barabbae latrocinia. Illud enim est ingenium impiorum, quod magis odio persequatur virtutes quam vitia; iustitiam quam iniustitiam. Iustitia enim, probitatem ac pietatem propter se oderunt: iniustitiam vero & improbitatem, non quidem propter se & simpliciter oderunt, sed respectu aliquo, quia nimirum improbitate flagitiosorum hominum ipsi aliquo modo inquietantur. Hinc est quod lubentius apud se viuere patiantur pessimos quosque, quam eos qui optimi sunt. Hoc vero non est praetereundum silentio, quod nullum odium adversus cerbitate comparandum sit, cum odio eorum qui Ecclesiae nomen mentiuntur, falsoque sibi arrogant. Quo enim praetextus praeclarior est, eo malum maius latet. Sed Christi partes hic non sunt praetermittendae. Interim patitur iustus, at non absque diuina prouidentia ac dispensatione, quaecunque demum sint partes Iudaeorum, praeferentes ipsi Barabbam hominem seditiosum ac flagitiosum. Dispensatio autem Dei iustissima
units.tr: The most sorrowful example of judgment against Saul must never be erased from memory, who against the command of God did not kill Agag, king of the Amalekites. These things on this matter so far, and somewhat more lengthily than I had intended, namely because this most wicked custom has prevailed too long already among our nation. Now let us see how earnestly Pilate applied himself to this, that he might release Christ. For this cause he does not lack a certain praise of his own, although in this he is deserving of blame, that he wished to release a most innocent man as a malefactor, with a mark of disgrace never to be erased. For he compared the Lord, as a kind of malefactor, with the most wicked man Barabbas. For it is not enough if a judge releases an innocent man only, but it is further required that he release him as innocent. For God, as he wills the innocent to live, so he wills him to live as innocent, and by the manifestation of innocence and truth he seeks his own glory. I add this besides: that an innocent man ought rather to die than to live with a mark of disgrace, or to accept the remission of a crime of which he himself is not conscious. Pilate therefore sinned in the manner in which he wished to release him. But this sin is to be imputed to the Jews and to their malice rather than to Pilate, since he acted thus for their sake, and this he, as it were, granted them, which they most desired: namely that Jesus was a shameful man and deserving of death. But what do the Jews answer to Pilate? "They cried out," etc., saying, "Not this one." Pilate compared Christ with Barabbas, a most shameful man; and the Jews prefer Barabbas to Christ, as if he were not a man condemned to death as Christ the Lord was. Therefore they sin much more gravely than Pilate, in that they hated Christ's innocence more deadly than the robberies of Barabbas. For it is the nature of the wicked that they pursue virtues with hatred more than vices, and justice more than injustice. For they hate righteousness, probity and piety for their own sake; but injustice and wickedness they hate not for their own sake and simply, but with some regard, namely because they are in some way disturbed by the wickedness of shameful men. Hence it is that they more willingly suffer the worst men to live among them than those who are best. Yet this must not be passed over in silence: that no hatred is to be compared with the bitterness of those who falsely take to themselves the name of the Church and boast of it. For the more splendid the pretext, the greater the evil that lies hidden. But the part of Christ is not to be omitted here. Meanwhile the righteous one suffers, yet not without divine providence and dispensation, whatever the part of the Jews may be, preferring Barabbas, a seditious and shameful man, to themselves. But the dispensation of God is most just

units.la: Iudicis prudentia qua- ... ma est, etiam tum cum illi iniustissimè agunt. Nam etsi Christus in se innocentissimus fuerit, tamen in nobis reus fuit mortis: quia in se recepit peccata nostra & reatum nostrum. Hoc est quod habet Apostolus, Qui non novit peccatum, factus est peccatum pro nobis, ut nos essemus iustitia Dei in illo. Quamobrem sic totis animis adhorreamus Iudaeorum facta indignissima in innocentem, ut interea Dei illam dispensationem iustissimam in persona aliquo modo ream, totis animis amplectamur ac reuereamur, & gratias illi immortales agamus, quòd unigenitum suum pro nobis dederit, pro nobis fecerit eum peccatum, pro nobis omnis ignominiae & doloribus omnibus, tam animi quàm corporis exposuerit. Ei igitur sit omnis gloria: Amen.
units.tr: of the judge's wisdom, even when they act most unjustly towards him. For although Christ was most innocent in himself, yet in us he was guilty of death, because he took upon himself our sins and our guilt. This is what the Apostle has: "He who knew no sin was made sin for us, that we might be the righteousness of God in him." Wherefore let us abhor with all our souls the most unworthy deeds of the Jews against the innocent, and yet let us embrace and reverence with all our souls that most just dispensation of God, which in a person in some way guilty, and give him immortal thanks, because he gave his only-begotten Son for us, made him sin for us, and exposed him for us to all ignominy and all sorrows, both of soul and of body. To him therefore be all glory: Amen.

units.la: Argumentum huius capitis iam prefixum est capiti 18.
units.tr: The argument of this chapter is already prefixed to chapter 18.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: 1 Vm ergo assumpsit Iesum Pilatus & flagellauit.
units.tr: 1 Then therefore Pilate took Jesus and scourged him.

units.la: 2 Et milites contexuerunt coronam è spinis, & imposuerunt ipsius capiti, & pallio purpureo induerunt eum:
units.tr: 2 And the soldiers plaited a crown of thorns and put it on his head, and they clothed him in a purple robe,

units.la: 3 Et dicebãt, Aue Rex Iudaeorum: Et bacillis eum cædebant.
units.tr: 3 And said, Hail, King of the Jews! And they struck him with rods.

units.la: HOC capite persistit Euangelista in passione Christi: narrant autem alij Euangelistae paulò fusiùs, alia quae antecesserunt flagellationem Domini. Postquam à Iudaeis electus fuisset Barabbas, reiectus verò Iesus, petiit Pilatus de Iesu, quid co fieret? Responderunt autem Iudæi, Crucifigatur, crucifigatur. Ad hæc Pilatus, Nõn in- tenio, inquit, in eo crimen: Tertia vice igitur Iesum absol-uit, innocentémque pronuntiauit: Matth. 27. 22. &c. Marc.15.12.&c.Luc.23.20.&c. Interea dum Pilatus sedet pro tribunali mittit ad eum vxor, monétque ne sit ei res cum iusto illo, Quia, inquit, multa passa sum hodie in somnis propter eum: Matth.27.19. Diuina prouidentia hoc factū est, tum vt proderetur innocentia Christi (vult enim Deus innocentiam ipsius perpetuò manifestari toto passionis tempore. Decet enim Pontificem nostrum innocentem esse, impollutum, segregatum à peccatoribus. Heb.7.26.) tum causa etiam Pilati, vt is vel desisteret à iudicando innocentem ac iustum illum; vel certè inexcusabilis redderetur. Deus enim etiam destinatos ad interitum inuitat ad resipiscentiam, & perfert multa lenitate vasa iræ coagmentata ad interitum. Vide Rom.2.4.&Rom.9.22. Nam Deus etiam erga reprobos misericordiam suam vult conspici, in admonendo scilicet eos, & inuitando ad se priusquam iustitiam suam exerat in ipsos perdendo. Primum igitur hoc capite conatur, quantum potest Pilatus Iesum absoluere: Vt autem id assequatur, primùm eum flagellandum militibus tradit & ignominiæ exponit. Laudo equidem hominis conatum, sed damno medii quo quod instituit persequitur. Fit enim alterum horum necessario, vt prophani homines ac impij, vel nihil boni vnquam proponant sibi faciendum: vel si proponant, persequantur tamen illud malis mediis ac illicitis. Etsi enim bonum sibi proponant faciendum, tamen non rectè proponunt, hoc est, non ex simplici animo ac oculo proponunt: quia non collimant recta ad Dei gloriam. Hinc fit vt in persequendis mediis tota via aberrent. Nam quid est quod facit vt recta incedamus in hac vita, præter Deū ipsiusque gloriam ante oculos nostros positam? Quod quisquis facit, is non facilè aberrat. Habet enim lucernam ac facem pedibus suis. Videbis igitur Pilatum, si factum ipsius diligentiùs examinaueris, etsi quidem bonum finem alioqui propositum sibi habuerit, tamen non recte eum sibi finem propositum, cum conscientia extorserit istud ab eo vel inuito, potiùs quàm vllus Dei aut vovoluntatis ipsius respectus hominem permouerit. Est autem & alia praeterea causa cur in mediis persequendis erraverit. Vult quidem dimitti Christum, sed ita ut id obtineatur cum gratia & bona venia Iudaeorum. Cum igitur in persequendo id quod bonum erat, pependerit ex libidine pessimorum hominum, fieri non potuit quin a recto declinarit. Qui enim quod bonum est, non nisi salua voluntate ac libidine malorum hominum facere constituerunt, necesse est vel nihil unquam boni faciat, vel si faciant, in faciendo graviter peccent. Nota rursus, quanto magis procedit in mediis persequendis, tanto magis peccat. Qui semel statuit apud se inseruire libidini impiorum hominum, cogitur is subinde in deterius abire, & perpetuo deteriora facere, quibus omnibus nihil tandem proficiet. Nihil enim profecit Pilatus, cum indignissima quaeque fecisset in hominem innocentem ad gratiam Iudaeorum.
units.tr: In this chapter the Evangelist continues with the passion of Christ. The other Evangelists, however, relate in more detail what came before the scourging of the Lord. After the Jews had chosen Barabbas and rejected Jesus, Pilate asked what should be done with Jesus. The Jews answered, "Crucify him, crucify him." Pilate replied, "I find no crime in him." So for the third time he acquitted Jesus and declared him innocent (Matth. 27.22, etc.; Mark 15.12, etc.; Luke 23.20, etc.). Meanwhile, while Pilate sat on the judgment seat, his wife sent to him and warned him to have nothing to do with that just man: "For I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him" (Matth. 27.19). This came about by divine providence, partly so that the innocence of Christ might be made known (for God wills that his innocence be made manifest throughout the whole time of the passion; for it befits our High Priest to be innocent, undefiled, and separated from sinners, Heb. 7.26), and partly for Pilate's own sake, so that he would either cease to judge that innocent and just man, or at least be left without excuse. For God also invites even those destined for destruction to repentance, and bears with great gentleness the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction (see Rom. 2.4 and Rom. 9.22). For God wishes his mercy to be seen even towards the reprobate, namely by admonishing them and inviting them to himself before he exercises his justice by destroying them. First, then, in this chapter Pilate tries, as far as he can, to release Jesus. In order to achieve this, he first hands him over to the soldiers to be scourged and exposed to shame. I indeed praise the man's intention, but I condemn the means by which he pursues what he has undertaken. For it necessarily happens with one of two things that profane and impious men either never propose to themselves anything good to be done, or, if they do propose it, they pursue it by evil and unlawful means. For although they propose something good to be done, they do not propose it rightly, that is, they do not propose it with a simple mind and a single eye, because they do not aim straight at the glory of God. Hence it comes about that in pursuing the means they go wholly astray. For what is it that makes us walk uprightly in this life, apart from God and his glory set before our eyes? Whoever does this does not easily go astray, for he has a lamp and a torch for his feet. You will see, then, if you examine Pilate's action more carefully, that although he had otherwise a good end proposed to himself, yet he did not pursue that end rightly; for he was forced, against his will and against his conscience, to do this, rather than any regard for God or for his will moving him. There is also another reason why he went astray in pursuing the means. He indeed wishes Christ to be released, but in such a way that this is obtained with the goodwill and favour of the Jews. Since, therefore, in pursuing what was good he depended on the lust of the worst men, it could not but be that he would turn aside from the right way. For those who have resolved to do what is good only with the consent and at the pleasure of evil men, must either never do anything good, or, if they do, they sin grievously in doing it. Notice, moreover, that the further one proceeds in pursuing the means, the more one sins. He who has once resolved to serve the lust of impious men is compelled to go from bad to worse and to do worse and worse things continually, and in the end he will gain nothing from all of it. For Pilate gained nothing, though he had done every most shameful thing to an innocent man in order to win the favour of the Jews.

units.la: Non sunt praetereundae hic partes militum. Quod faciant id faciunt iussu praesidis Pilati, flagellant eum, ludibrio habent, non sine ipsius mandato. Cum is qui Iudex est peccat, reatu suo implicat quoscunque inferiores servos & Ministros, usque ad carnificem ipsum. Neque propterea excusantur serui & Ministri. Nam ipsi quoque non carent sua quadam malitia. Saepenumero etiam prioris sunt ad facinora quaeque & flagitia, quam dominini sui, id quod non obscure cernimus in militibus istis, quorum hauddubie maior est in Christum malitia, quam ipsius Pilati. Neque enim ista in eum faciunt animo eum liberandi, quo animo constat Pilatum fuisse. Ideoque cum designantur hi nominatim, qui coacti sunt adversus Christum, Spiritus sanctus seorsim militum istorum meminit. Coacti sunt, inquit, vere aduersus sanctum filium suum Iesum, quem vnxisti, Herodes, Pilatus cum gentibus, & populis Israel. Id quod argumento est etiam milites reos fuisse huius facinoris. Itaque videmus non esse quod sese excusent vulgus hominum, quod ad voluntatem dominorum, principum, iudicum suorum fecerit pessima quaeque: ipsis enim moriendum est propter suum ipsorum peccatum: sanguis autem eorum requiretur e manu dominorum. Postremò hīc sunt partes Christi: ipse patitur indigna omnia, idque ex Dei dispensatione, & ea quidem iustissima. Nam is pro nobis factus est peccatū, hoc est trāsfugna quæqs ... lit in humeros suos peccata nostra. Pater pro iustitia sua neminem patitur ferre impunè, ne eum quidem, qui in gratia alicuius sistit se vadè, ne filium quidem suū pro nobis vadem. Qui quamuis filius esset, tamen ex iis quæ passus est didicit obedientiam. Hoc est, quid & quàm bonum esset obedire voluntati Patris sui, contráque quàm malum esset peccare in Patrem, neque ei auscultare. Neque certè quisquam verè novit, vel quantum boni sit in obedientia, vel quantum mali sit in inobedientia & peccato, nisi adsit sensus aliquis iræ Diuinæ, quæ
units.tr: The part of the soldiers must not be passed over here. What they do, they do by the command of the governor Pilate: they scourge him and mock him, not without his order. When he who is the judge sins, he entangles in his guilt all the inferior servants and ministers, even the executioner himself. Yet the servants and ministers are not thereby excused, for they too are not free from their own malice. Often they are even more prone than their masters to all manner of crimes and wickedness, as we clearly see in these soldiers, whose malice against Christ was doubtless greater than that of Pilate himself. For they do these things to him not with the intention of freeing him, which intention is known to have been Pilate's. Therefore, when those who were compelled against Christ are named individually, the Holy Spirit mentions these soldiers separately. "They were gathered together," it says, "truly against thy holy Son Jesus, whom thou hast anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel" (Acts 4.27). This is evidence that the soldiers too were guilty of this crime. Thus we see that ordinary people have no excuse for doing all manner of wickedness at the will of their lords, princes and judges, for they must die for their own sin, and their blood will be required at the hand of their masters. Lastly, here is the part of Christ: he suffers all these undeserved things, and this by God's disposition, and indeed a most just one. For he was made sin for us, that is, he bore upon his shoulders our sins. The Father, for the sake of his justice, suffers no one to bear the penalty with impunity, not even one who stands surety for another's favour, nor even his own Son as surety for us. Although he was a Son, he nevertheless learned obedience from the things that he suffered: that is, what and how good it is to obey the will of his Father, and on the contrary how evil it is to sin against the Father and not to listen to him. Indeed no one truly knows either how much good there is in obedience or how much evil there is in disobedience and sin, unless there is some sense of the wrath of God, which

units.la: necessariò peccatum persequitur. Bonum enim est nobis, quod nonnunquam Deus nos humiliet. Rursus vi-deo in tota hac passione Dei ira magis magisque in Filium suum ingraue scere. Priùs quidem percusserunt eum: at nunc flagellant, imponunt capiti eius contexta è spinis coronâ. Vt illud facilè appareat, quòd ira Dei magis magisque efferuescat in eos qui resipiscere nesciunt, & reprobos qui in Christo Iesu non reperiuntur, & participes fiunt passionis ipsius. Vnde Paulus de obstinatis Iudæis, Ira Dei, inquit, occupauit eos ad extremum usque. Denique in tota hac passione Christi duo video velle Deū conspici in Filio, & ea quidem valde inter se contraria, vt videtur, nempe vt & innocentissimus conspiciatur &
units.tr: necessarily pursues sin. For it is good for us that God sometimes humbles us. Again I see that throughout this whole passion the wrath of God grows heavier and heavier upon his Son. At first they struck him, but now they scourge him and place upon his head a crown plaited of thorns. This makes it readily apparent that the wrath of God burns ever more fiercely against those who do not know how to repent, and against the reprobate who are not found in Christ Jesus, and who become partakers of his passion. Hence Paul says of the obstinate Jews, "The wrath of God has come upon them to the uttermost" (1 Thess. 2.16). Finally, in this whole passion of Christ I see that God wills two things to be seen in the Son, and indeed two that are very contrary to each other, as it seems: namely that he be seen both as most innocent and as most guilty. Most innocent indeed in himself, but most guilty in us, whose sins he takes upon himself.

units.la: nocentissimus: innocentissimus quidem in se, nocentissimus vero in nobis, quorum peccata in se ipse transfert. Hinc fit vt Pilatus quærat eum dimittere quidè tanquam innocentem: interea autem plectat tanquam nocentem, contra conscientiam suam, consentiente tamen voluntate Dei & iusto Dei iudicio. Hæc duo in Filij sui passione ideo conspici voluit, vt nos videremus aptum eum pro nobis Mediatorem esse, in eòque fide conquiescerēmus. Nisi enim primum videro eum, qui cuasit pro me Mediator in se innocentem esse, profectò non adducar eò, vt credam eum posse peccata mea in se recipere eáque expiare. Nam ne sua quidē expiare poterit, si ipse in sese non sit innocens. Talis, inquit Apostolus, nos decebat Pontifex, pius, innocens, impollutus, segregatus à peccatoribus. bes. Rursus nisi videro eum peccatis meis oneratum, & pro me reum factum, profecto sola ipsius innocentiae conscientia, non me mouebit ad hoc, vt habeā pro Mediatore ac seruatore meo. Quid enim ad me illius innocentia, nisi peccata mea in se transferat, & pro iis satisfaciat? Ex hac consideratione diligenti partim innocentiae Christi, partim reatus quae ipsa conspiciuntur in tota historia istaे passionis ipsius, non dici potest, quàm multiplex ac varia commotio affectuum oriatur: hinc misericordia erga innocentem: sic mulieres Hierosolymitanae eum cum lachrymis insequutae sunt, vsque ad locum supplicii. Hinc dolor, quòd homo in se alioqui innocentissimus mea causa tot tantaque indigna sit passus, & ego eum peccatis meis transfixerim. Hinc laetitia, quòd ego liberatus sim illius reatu à reatu illo meo. Hinc denique admirabilis quidam amor erga eum, qui me tantopere dilexit. Charitas illa Christi, inquit Paulus, constringit nos, vt qui hoc statuerimus, si vnus pro omnibus mortuus fuerit, nempe omnes fuisse mortuos, & illum pro omnibus mortuum esse. Rursus, Cui multum remissum est, multum diligit, ait Christus.
units.tr: Hence it comes about that Pilate seeks to release him as innocent, yet meanwhile punishes him as guilty, against his own conscience, though with the consent of God's will and by the just judgment of God. God willed these two things to be seen in the passion of his Son, so that we might see that he is a fit Mediator for us, and so that we might rest in faith on him. For unless I first see that he who has undertaken to be Mediator for me is innocent in himself, I will certainly not be brought to believe that he can take my sins upon himself and expiate them. For he could not even expiate his own sins if he were not innocent in himself. "Such a High Priest became us," says the Apostle, "holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners" (Heb. 7.26). Again, unless I see him burdened with my sins and made guilty on my behalf, the consciousness of his innocence alone will certainly not move me to hold him as my Mediator and Saviour. For what is his innocence to me, unless he transfers my sins to himself and satisfies for them? From this careful consideration, partly of the innocence of Christ and partly of the guilt that is seen throughout the whole history of his passion, there arises a commotion of the affections so manifold and varied that it cannot be told. Hence pity for the innocent: thus the women of Jerusalem followed him with tears as far as the place of execution. Hence grief, that a man who was in himself most innocent should suffer so many and such great indignities for my sake, and that I have pierced him with my sins. Hence joy, that I am freed by him from that guilt of mine. Hence, finally, a certain wonderful love towards him who loved me so greatly. "The love of Christ," says Paul, "constrains us, since we judge thus: that if one died for all, then all have died; and he died for all" (2 Cor. 5.14–15). Again, Christ says, "He to whom much is forgiven loves much" (Luke 7.47).

units.la: 4 Prodijt ergo rursum Pilatus foras, & dixit eis, Ecce adduco vobis eum foras, vt noueritis me nullum in eo crimen inuenire.
units.tr: 4 Then Pilate went out again and said to them, Behold, I bring him out to you, that you may know I find no crime in him.

units.la: 5 Prodijt ergo Iesus foras, ferens spineam illam coronam, & purpureum illud pallium, & dixit eis Pilatus, Ecce homo.
units.tr: 5 Then Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. And Pilate said to them, Behold the man.

units.la: 6 Cum autem vidissent eum primarij Sacerdotes & eorum ministri, clamauerunt, dicentes, Crucifige, crucifige. Dicit eis Pilatus, Accipite eum vos & crucifigite: ego enim non invenio in eo crimen.
units.tr: 6 When the chief priests and their ministers saw him, they cried out, saying, Crucify, crucify. Pilate said to them, Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no crime in him.

units.la: 7 Responderunt ei Iudaei, Nos legem habemus, & secundum legem nostram debet mori: quia filium Dei fecit.
units.tr: 7 The Jews answered him, We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.

units.la: IAm flagellatum & indignis modis tractatum quaerit Pilatus dimittere, ideoque primum iam quarta vice innocentem pronuntiat, ac ipsius innocentiam palam testatur atque praedicat. Id quod argumento est cum eü flagellandum ac irridendum militibus traderet, contra conscientiam eam quam habuit innocentiae eum id fecisse, verum non nisi respectu maioris boni. Eo enim sunt ingenio prophani & homines, vt multa faciant contra conscientiam mala, ad hoc vt magnum aliquod bonum consequantur. Sed an consequutus est Pilatus id quod propositum boni, hoc est innocentis liberationem? Imo eo pertractus est tandem vt ipsum crucifigeret, cotra conscientiam, quem contra conscientiam flagellavit: Vt non fit quod homines contra conscientiam quid mali faciant, ad id vt bonum consequantur. Ecce adduco eum foras. Iam alia ratione conatur eum eripere, nempe moucndo Iudaeos ad misericordiam. Ideo producit eum in conspectum eorum, cum miserabili illo habitu, & ipse quoque Pilatus ea voce vtitur apud Iudaeos, quae possit inclinate eorum animos ad misericordiam. Hoc autem argumento est, quod quo tempore male tractavit Iesum ac flagellavit in gratiam Iudaeorum, interea temporis misertus sit ipsius ob conscientiam innocentiae. Recte quidem fecit eo quod misertus sit, sed male eo quod non modo contra conscientiam, sed misericordiam quoque illam suam naturale, eum tam indignis modis tractarit: Vt exemplo Pilati nihil in natura nostra esse, non conscientiam innocentiae quod potest nos retrahere a male agendo: Video, inquit Medea, meliora probo que, deteriora sequor. Addo vt qui velit bene agere necesse est euehatur supra naturam istam, & gratiam Spiritus sancti accipiat, quae sola proprie pugnat aduersus corruptam istam naturam, & pugnando tandem vincit.
units.tr: Pilate, wishing to release him, had already had Jesus scourged and treated with shameful indignities, and for the fourth time he now declares him innocent and openly bears witness to and proclaims his innocence. This is shown by the fact that when he handed him over to the soldiers to be scourged and mocked, he did so against his own sense of his innocence, but only for the sake of some greater good. For profane men are so disposed that they often do evil against their conscience in order to obtain some great good. But did Pilate obtain the good he aimed at, that is, the release of an innocent man? Rather, he was at last driven to crucify, against his conscience, the man whom he had scourged against his conscience. So it is not the case that men who do evil against their conscience thereby obtain a good. Behold, I bring him out to you. Now he tries to rescue him by another means, namely by moving the Jews to pity. Therefore he brings him before their eyes in that pitiable condition, and Pilate himself uses words before the Jews that might incline their minds to mercy. Here is the mark of the pity he showed: at the very time he ill-treated and scourged Jesus to please the Jews, he was moved to pity him on account of his awareness of his innocence. He did right in pitying him, but wrong that, against his conscience and against that natural mercy of his, he treated him with such indignities. So Pilate's example shows that nothing in our nature, not even the awareness of innocence, can hold us back from doing evil. "I see the better course and approve it, but I follow the worse," says Medea. I add that whoever wishes to do well must be raised above that nature and receive the grace of the Holy Spirit, which alone truly fights against this corrupt nature and, by fighting, at last conquers it.

units.la: Clamauerunt, dicentes, Crucifige. Pilatus omnia tentauit, quibus adduci posse Iudaeos putauit ad hoc vt dimitteretur innocens Iesus Christus: sed frustra omnia. Nam ipsi perstant immoti, neque vllis rationibus ad id flecti possunt: vt videas induratos vsque adeo aduersus innocentem illum quem alioqui oportuit mori ex aeterno decreto, creto.Interea tamen ij non sunt excusabiles: Nam & ipsi se indurant ex malitia cordis sui.Si hic compares sacerdotes cum Pilato : videbis longè deteriori eos loco esse,quod alioqui oportuit longè meliori esse,vtpote luce illa diuini verbi instructos. Pilatus admonitus semel ab vxore sua,conscientiam innocentiæ ipsius aliquam habet, ideoque miseretur innocentis hominis : At isti obfirmati sunt & obstinati tam aduersus conscientiam,quā misericordiam erga innocentem,etsi sæpius iam admoniti sint a Pilato. Ex hoc sequitur multò grauius Dei iudicium incubuisse istis, quàm Pilato, toto hoc passionis & persequutionis Christi tempore. Nam nullum Dei iudicium grauius esse potest, quàm est istud induratio-nis cordis aduersus Deum, neque aliud certius argumentum est grauissimi & celerrimi iudicij consopitos homines de improuiso tandem occupaturi. Cùm dicent, Pax & tuta omnia, tum repentinum illis imminet exitium. Accipite eum vos. Vt suprà Pilatus voluit potius cedere de iure suo in iudicando quàm Iesum citra accusationem & alicuius criminis delationem iudicare, hoc est contra ordinem & vsitatam iudiciorum formam iudicium exercere : ita quoque nunc eligit potiùs cedere de iure suo in sumendo supplicio de reo,quàm innocentem crucifigendum curare. Laudabile quidem istud in Pilato , nisi quòd à conscientia extortum fit vel inuito. Nam ex conscientia duobus modis fieri dicitur aliquid: vel enim ex conscientia fit aliquid , ita vt quis inuitus cogatur aliquid boni facere, quæ quidem non nisi coacta agendi ratio non adeo meretur commendationem: vel ita fit aliquid ex conscientia, vt quis volens ac lubens maximè, agat boni aliquid, quæ quidem agendi ratio meretur veram commendationem. Si tamen conferatur Pilatus cum sacerdotibus quibus cōscientia quasi cauterio resecta fuit,illorum profectò respectu non mediocrem meretur laudem. Nobis tamen conandum est, vt non solum ex conscientia faciamus quid bonum, sed & summa voluntate illud ipsum faciamus non coacti quidem à conscientia , sed vltro sequentes id quod dictat conscientia.Conscientia enim naturalis est: at vero voluntas ista & animi promptitudo faciendo id quod bonum est, idque propter Deum, non est naturalis, sed plane supernaturalis ac spiritualis: existit enim ex cor-dis interiori illa reformatione ac renouatione. Ratio est cur Pilatus cedat de iure suo: Non patitur Dominus conscientiā Pilati iudicis conquiescere: Conscientia tamen sic agitata non finit hominem desistere, quin continuò innocentem prædicet. Iam enim quarta vice testatur de innocentia Christi. Contrà vero si ad Iudæos & sacerdotes venias, continuò magis magisque ipsi indurantur aduersus innocentem: neque iis potest vlla re satisfieri, nisi effuso sanguine innocentis. Res mira! Annon oportuit istos meliori ac vigilantiori multò conscientia esse, quàm Pilatum: vt qui non tantùm luce naturę, sed etiam verbi Dei informati erant? Nam ex scientia existit conscientia. Sed quid dicas? lucem illam verbi malitiose expunxerunt ex animis suis; hinc sequuta est naturalis iudicium lucis priuatio. Nam cùm ex malitia cordis quis lucem illam verbi ex animo suo delet: Deus iusto suo iudicio, quod reliquum est lucis cum conscientia ipso obliterat ex animo, traditque hominem in mentem reprobam. Quamobrem cauendum ne violemus lucem illam quæ verbum Dei nobis ministrat, quamque innobis accendit, vel hac de causa, ne Deus nos plane stupidos & excæcatos tandem reddat.
units.tr: They cried out, saying, Crucify. Pilate tried every means by which he thought the Jews might be brought to let the innocent Jesus Christ go, but all in vain. For they persist unmoved and cannot be bent to it by any arguments. You see how hardened they were against that innocent man whom, by the eternal decree, he had to die. Yet they are not excusable, for they harden themselves through the malice of their own hearts. If you compare the priests here with Pilate, you will see that they were in a far worse position, though they ought to have been in a much better one, since they were instructed by the light of the divine Word. Pilate, admonished once by his wife, retained some sense of the man's innocence, and therefore he pitied the innocent man. But these men were obstinate and stubborn, both against their conscience and against pity for the innocent, although Pilate had already admonished them many times. From this it follows that God's judgment fell far more heavily upon them than upon Pilate, throughout this whole time of Christ's passion and persecution. For no judgment of God can be heavier than this hardening of the heart against God, and there is no surer sign that men who have grown drowsy will at last be overtaken unexpectedly by the most severe and swift judgment. When they say, "Peace and all is safe," then sudden destruction hangs over them. Take him yourselves. As before, Pilate preferred to give up his right to judge rather than judge Jesus without an accusation and without the charge of some crime, that is, to exercise judgment against the order and customary form of trials. So now too he chooses rather to give up his right to inflict punishment on the accused than to see to the crucifixion of an innocent man. That is praiseworthy in Pilate, except that it was wrung from his conscience even against his will. For there are two ways in which something is said to be done from conscience. Either something is done from conscience in such a way that a man is compelled, unwillingly, to do some good; and such a way of acting, being merely forced, does not deserve much commendation. Or something is done from conscience in such a way that a man acts for some good most willingly and gladly; and such a way of acting truly deserves commendation. Yet if Pilate is compared with the priests, whose conscience was, as it were, seared with a branding iron, he certainly deserves no small praise by comparison with them. Still, we must strive not only to do good from conscience, but to do it with the greatest willingness, not merely compelled by conscience but freely following what conscience dictates. For conscience is natural, but that willingness and readiness of mind to do what is good, and to do it for God's sake, is not natural but altogether supernatural and spiritual, since it arises from that inner reformation and renewal of the heart. The reason Pilate gave up his right is that the Lord does not allow the conscience of Pilate the judge to rest. Yet his conscience, so stirred, does not let him desist from proclaiming the innocent man again and again. For now he bears witness to the innocence of Christ for the fourth time. On the other hand, if you turn to the Jews and the priests, you find them growing ever harder against the innocent man, and nothing can satisfy them except the innocent man's blood poured out. A remarkable thing! Ought they not to have had a far better and more watchful conscience than Pilate, since they were instructed not only by the light of nature but by the Word of God? For conscience arises from knowledge. But what can you say? They maliciously blotted out that light of the Word from their minds, and from this followed the natural deprivation of the power of judging by that light. For when someone out of the malice of his heart deletes that light of the Word from his mind, God, by his just judgment, wipes out from the mind what remains of the light together with conscience, and hands the man over to a reprobate mind. Therefore we must take care not to violate that light which the Word of God supplies to us and kindles in us, if only for this reason: that God not at last make us utterly dull and blinded.

units.la: Nota rursus. Quemadmodū Iudæi clamarunt, Crucige, crucifige: ita clamat Pilatus vicissim, Non inuenio crimen in eo. Clamor alter alteri prorsus contrarius: non tamen citra diuinam dispensationem contingit: habet enim Deus opus hoc perficiendum: nempe vt filius ipsius patiatur, & patiatur quidem vt manifesto innocens, vult enim innocentiam eius in media passione prædicari, & quidem prædicari ab ipso iudice. Ideo contrario plane modo secreta quadam operatione sua afficit iudicem & accusatores Christi. Emollit quidem animos iudicis aliquo certè modo, & conscientiam excitat ad hoc vt perpetuò testetur ipse de Christi innocentia. Contrà vero indurat animos accusatorum, ad hoc vt indesinenter & summa contentione & animi & vocis, vrgeant innocentis mortem. Hinc passus est & crucifixus tanquā innocēs. Hæc vsitata Dei ratio est agendi cum suis quos vult aliquid perperi ad gloriam nominis sui. Contrario vsq; adeo modo afficit eos qui ipsos persequuntur: Alios mouet conscientia innocentiæ ipsorum, alios contrà sic indurat, vt contenti esse non possint re vlla, nisi morte & sanguine ipsorum: ad hoc vt toti mundo manifestum sit dignati eos tanquam innocentes. Sic olim Darius rex permotus est conscientia innocentiæ Danielis, dèque ea testatus est, cùm interea aduersarij in ipsum sic indurati essent, vt eorum libido non nisi sanguine innocentis expleri potuerit. Sic quoque voluit Lysiam, Felicem & Festum testari de innocentia Pauli, cùm Iudæi aduersarij sic obfirmarentur interea aduersus eum, vt mortem eius perpetuò vrgerent. Non ita solet agere Deus cum improbis & maleficis, quorum cùm nulla sit innocentia, non excitat aliquos, qui de ipsorum innocentia testentur, sed sic mouet omnes pariter iudicem & accusatores, alios denique quoscunque, vt conspirent aduersus ipsos, ad tollendas has pestes humani generis de medio. Quâ- obrem vel hac sola de causa videndum vt patiamur perpetuò propter bona causam, ad hoc vt mors nostra gloriosa sit: gloriosa autem est, si vt innocentes & iusti patiamur.
units.tr: Note again. Just as the Jews cried out, "Crucify, crucify," so in turn Pilate cries out, "I find no crime in him." The one clamour is utterly contrary to the other, yet this happens not without the divine dispensation. For God has a work to accomplish here: namely, that his Son should suffer, and suffer as one manifestly innocent, for he wills that his innocence be proclaimed in the midst of the passion, and proclaimed by the judge himself. Therefore, by a secret operation of his own, he works in a quite opposite way upon the judge and the accusers of Christ. Indeed, he softens the judge's mind in some measure and stirs up his conscience so that he may continually bear witness to Christ's innocence. On the other hand, he hardens the accusers' minds so that they urge the death of the innocent man without ceasing, with the utmost effort of mind and voice. Hence he suffered and was crucified as innocent. This is God's usual way of dealing with his own, whom he wills to be afflicted for the glory of his name. He deals in a contrary manner with those who persecute them: some he moves by the awareness of their innocence, while others he hardens so that they can be satisfied with nothing but their death and blood, so that it may be clear to the whole world that they were condemned as innocent. Thus of old King Darius was moved by the consciousness of Daniel's innocence and bore witness to it, while his adversaries were so hardened against him that their lust could be satisfied only with the blood of the innocent. So too God willed that Lysias, Felix and Festus should bear witness to Paul's innocence, while the Jewish adversaries were so obstinately set against him that they continually pressed for his death. God does not usually act thus with the wicked and the evildoers, whose innocence is nil; he does not raise up anyone to bear witness to their innocence, but moves judge and accusers alike, and indeed all others, to conspire against them, so as to remove these plagues of the human race from the midst. For this reason alone, then, we must see to it that we suffer continually for the sake of a good cause, so that our death may be glorious; and it is glorious if we suffer as innocent and righteous men.

units.la: Nos legem habemus. Non quidem vendicant sibi ius crucifigendi Christum, aut omnino infligendi supplicium capitale: nam id tum penes Romanos erat: verum legem suam quandam, & ius legis suæ afferunt, atque ex lege sua eum mortem esse commeritum pronuntiant. Interea temporis vides eos obdurari aduersus Christi innocentiam, quam proximè testificatus est Pilatus. Vides deinde quid iis prosit verbum Dei & legis: nempe verbo illo Dei & lege ipsius excæcantur. Impiis & malitiis omnia conferunt ad excæcationem. Idem quoque facit verbum ipsius Dei, quod suapte natura illuminat mentes hominum: neque id quidem immeritò. Non enim verbo Dei vtuntur, tanquam regula & norma affectionum suarum dirigendarum, sed affectibus suis ipsum subiiciunt: interpretantur ipsum: applicant ipsum pro arbitratu suo, & sensu suo corruptissimo. Id quod faciunt hodierno die Papistæ, quibus non confert verbum nisi ad obdurationem & exitium. Sed videamus quónam modo argumententur isti. Ex lege nostra, inquiunt, Blasphemo moriendum est. At hic est Blasphemus, fecit enim se Dei filium: Ergo ex lege nostra moriendum ipsi. Propositio generalis vera est. Vide Leuit. 24.14. Sed applicatio primum blasphemiae in assumptione, deinde mortis in conclusione, falsa plane & malitiosa est. Impij enim postquam iam veras sententias generales substrauerunt, fere in applicando errant: Verbi gratia, postquam dixerunt, Blasphemo cuique moriendum est, si oderunt personam ream, statim subsumunt & applicant malitiose & ex odio personae blasphemiam illam. At hic est Blasphemus, & concludunt ex odio & malitia animi, Hic est dignus morte. Sin vero personam rei diligant, subsumunt continuo ex corrupto illo amore & affectu non esse Blasphemum: Et concludunt ex eodem corrupto affectu, non causa peruersae applicationis est, cor malum & effectus depravatus. Quare ne contenti simus illuminatione mentis, nisi etiam cor reformetur. Quod si enim non sit cordis reformatio, nulla est cognitio generalis, ne optima quidem, vel per naturam, vel per Dei verbum subministrata, qua non avertatur homo ψυχικὸς & corruptus.
units.tr: We have a law. They do not claim the right to crucify Christ, or to inflict capital punishment at all, for that right then belonged to the Romans. But they do assert a law of their own and the authority of that law, and they declare that by it he has deserved death. Meanwhile you see them hardened against Christ's innocence, which Pilate had just attested. Next, see what the Word of God and the law do for them: by that same Word and law of God they are blinded. Wicked men turn everything to their blindness. The Word of God itself does the same, though it of its own nature enlightens the minds of men, and not undeservedly. For they do not use the Word of God as a rule and norm for directing their affections; they subject it to their affections. They interpret it, and they apply it as they please and in their most corrupt sense. The Papists do this today, for whom the Word brings nothing but hardening and destruction. But let us see how these men argue. "By our law," they say, "the blasphemer must die. This man is a blasphemer, for he made himself the Son of God. Therefore by our law he must die." The general proposition is true; see Lev. 24.14. But the application, first of the blasphemy in the assumption and then of the death in the conclusion, is plainly false and malicious. For after the wicked have laid down true general principles, they generally go wrong in the application. For example, having said that whoever blasphemes must die, if they hate the accused person, at once they maliciously and out of hatred of the person subsume and apply that blasphemy: "But this man is a blasphemer," and they conclude out of hatred and malice of mind, "He is worthy of death." But if they love the person of the accused, they immediately subsume, from that corrupt love and affection, that he is not a blasphemer; and from the same corrupt affection they conclude that he is not worthy of death. The cause of the perverse application is a wicked heart and a depraved will. Therefore let us not be content with enlightenment of the mind unless the heart is also reformed. For if there is no reformation of the heart, there is no general knowledge, not even the best, whether supplied by nature or by the Word of God, from which a man, being a natural [ψυχικὸς] and corrupt man, is not turned away.

units.la: 8 Quum ergo audiuisset Pilatus hunc sermonem, magis timuit.
units.tr: 8 When therefore Pilate heard this saying, he was the more afraid.

units.la: 9 Et rursus ingressus est in praetorium, & dixit Iesu, Vnde es tu? Iesus autem responsum ei non dedit.
units.tr: 9 And he went again into the judgment hall, and said to Jesus, "Whence art thou?" But Jesus gave him no answer.

units.la: 10 Dicit ergo ei Pilatus, Mihi non loqueris? Nescis me potestatem habere crucifigendi te, & potestatem habere te dimittendi?
units.tr: 10 Then Pilate said to him, "Speakest thou not unto me? Knowest thou not that I have power to crucify thee, and have power to release thee?"

units.la: 11 Respondit Iesus, Non haberes aduersus me potestatem ullam, nisi hoc tibi datum esset (superne: propterea qui me tradidit tibi, maius peccatum habet.
units.tr: 11 Jesus answered, "Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above; therefore he that delivered me unto thee hath the greater sin."

units.la: Quemadmodum quo magis Pilatus iudex operam dat vt sacerdotes & Iudaei innocentiae Christi conscientia aliquana afficiantur, eo magis ipsi indurati perstant stant: Ita,quò magis Iudæi accusatores in id incumbunt vt conscientia iudicis consopiatur,eò magis euigilat, & perterretur. Quem Deus vult indurari, is nulla ratione emolliri potest. Imò omnia ipsi ad indurationem inserviunt. Quem rursus Deus vult emolliri & conscientiam habere rei cuiusquam, nulla ratione poterit is indurari: Quin imò iis ipsis quibus indurantur alij, ipse emollescit, ipsaque ei conscientiæ horrores incutiunt. Frustra homo contra Deum sibi in conscientias hominum potestatem arrogat. Nota deinde vel conscientiam istam quæ in natura reliqua est, admonere de Deo, adeo vt sine nullum suppeteret argumentum aliud alius maiestatis, conscientia, vel sola satis magnum sit documentum. Quæ vt admonet de Deo quod sit: ita (id quod non obscurè hic discitur) abhorret à Dei illius & maiestatis iilius sacrosanctæ violatione quacunque, adeo vt si quis Deum violet, necesse sit conscientiam suam ipse prius violet, quæ pro Deo stat, ipsiusque quasi munit ab iniuria perversi cordis nostri: Fateor equidem non ita firmiter stat conscientia, vt non succumbat tandem, stat tamē pro Deo. Pugnauit quidem ad tempus pro Deo Pilati conscientia, sed tandem victa est à cordis malitia. Nihil enim in natura tam bonum reliquum est, quod non naturæ eiusdem malitia subuertatur. Quare cum solus Dei Spiritus ad finem vsque pugnet contra carnem, imprimis is petendus est à Deo, vt ipse in nobis habitet, à quo tandem tota hæc naturæ nostræ corruptela & perversitas abolenda est. Illud præterea non est hic prætereundum, quòd non tantùm conscientia admonuerit Pilatum de Deo, sed etiam de Iesu qui coram ipso stabat, licet in specie tunc vilis & abiectus, quod tamen Deus esset ac Dei filius. Quorsum enim tunc audito filij Dei nomine, nisi admonitus aliquo modo fuisset de Iesu, quòd is esset Dei filius? Unde est quod ego puto extra ordinem conscientiam Pilati de Christo informatā fuisse à Deo. Solet enim Deus improbos & prophanos nonnunquam extra ordinem afficere & affulgere iis luce illa cælesti ac supernaturali. Imo gustu rerum cælestium aliquo imbuere: vt Agrippam Regem, qui audito Paulo dixit se propemodum persuasum, vt Christianus fieret. Verum
units.tr: Just as the more Pilate, the judge, labours to have the priests and the Jews touched by some awareness of Christ's innocence, the more they persist, hardened; so the more the Jewish accusers set themselves to lull the judge's conscience to sleep, the more it wakes and is terrified. Whom God wills to harden, he cannot in any way be softened. Indeed, all things serve his hardening. Conversely, whom God wills to soften and to have the conscience of any guilty person, he can in no way be hardened; indeed, by the very things by which others are hardened, he himself is softened, and the horrors of conscience are struck into him. In vain does man arrogate to himself, against God, power over men's consciences. Note further that even that conscience which remains in nature admonishes us about God, so that, even if there were no other argument for his majesty, conscience alone would be a sufficiently great proof. As it admonishes us about God that he is, so (which is learned here not obscurely) it shrinks from any violation of that God's holy majesty, so that if anyone violates God, he must first violate his own conscience, which stands for God and, as it were, guards him against the injury of our perverse heart. I grant indeed that conscience does not stand so firmly that it never finally gives way; yet it stands for God. Pilate's conscience did indeed fight for God for a time, but in the end it was conquered by the malice of his heart. For nothing so good remains in nature that it is not overthrown by the malice of that same nature. Therefore, since the Spirit of God alone fights against the flesh to the end, above all he is to be sought from God, that he may dwell in us, by whom this whole corruption and perversity of our nature is at last to be abolished. Moreover, it must not be passed over here that conscience admonished Pilate not only about God but also about Jesus, who stood before him, although then in appearance base and abject, that yet he was God and the Son of God. For why otherwise, when the name of the Son of God was heard, would he have been afraid, unless he had been admonished in some way about Jesus, that he was the Son of God? Hence it is that I think Pilate's conscience was informed about Christ by God beyond the ordinary course. For God is accustomed sometimes to affect the wicked and profane beyond the ordinary course, and to shine upon them with that heavenly and supernatural light; indeed, to imbue them with some taste of heavenly things, as with King Agrippa, who, when he heard Paul, said that he was almost persuaded to become a Christian. But

units.la: lux illa, vt etiam gustus ille,quo imbuuntur corda eorū, vix adest cūm rursus abest. Non igitur salutaris est: neque tamen caret suo vsu aliquo, saltem hoc vt ipsos reddat inexcusabiles. Eò praeterea pertinebat haec Pilati illuminatio,quantumuis euanida, vt sacerdotes illos condemnaret quos oportuit, cūm scripturas vilis illius speciei Christi testes haberent.Oportuit,inquam,per vilem illam speciem mediam introspicere in gloriam ac maiestatem filij Dei. Tum etiam valet ad condemnationem istorum hominum, qui sermonis de cruce simplicitate, & humilitate offenduntur: & quę ob oculos sunt,vt Paulus loquitur,tantum adspiciunt.
units.tr: that light, like the taste with which their hearts are imbued, is scarcely present when it is again absent. It is therefore not saving; yet it is not without some use, at least that it may render them inexcusable. Moreover, this enlightenment of Pilate, however fleeting, served also to condemn those priests who ought to have been condemned, since they had the Scriptures and witnesses of that base appearance of Christ. They ought, I say, to have looked through that base appearance into the glory and majesty of the Son of God. It also serves for the condemnation of those men who are offended by the simplicity and humility of the word of the cross, and who, as Paul says, look only at what is before their eyes.

units.la: Et rursus ingressus est prætorium. Et hoc quidem in Pilato laudabile est, quòd persequatur vix dum inchoatam Christi notitiam illam, nempe quòd Dei filius esset, ac discendae veritatis causa quaerat ex eo, vnde fit, sitne à Deo,& filius Dei,nécne? Verùm non est illud cogitandum, quod ex amore veritatis id quaesierit, sed ex metu potiùs mali. Metuebat enim sibi à Christo, siquidem is filius Dei esset, ideóque nihil responsi ab Christo retulit: nempe quia Christus vnà cū cælestibus omnibus rebus in conspectu Pilati vilescebat. Nos autem dum persequimur cognitionem Christi semel inchoatam, ex amore veritatis id faciamus,quòd ex promissione ipsius Christi certisimus cum nos auditurum, Amen, amen dico vobis, quaecunque petieritis à Patre meo in nomine meo, dabit vobis.
units.tr: And he went again into the judgment hall. And this indeed is commendable in Pilate, that he pursues the knowledge of Christ, scarcely yet begun, namely that he was the Son of God, and seeks from him, for the sake of learning the truth, whence he is, whether he is from God and the Son of God or not. Yet we must not think that he asked this out of love of truth, but rather out of fear of harm. For he feared Christ, supposing he were the Son of God, and therefore gave him no answer: namely because Christ, together with all heavenly things, was worthless in Pilate's sight. But we, while we pursue the knowledge of Christ once begun, should do so out of love of truth, since we are most certain from Christ's own promise that he will hear us: "Verily, verily I say unto you, whatsoever you shall ask of my Father in my name, he will give it you."

units.la: At,quòd nihil responderit Christus,in causa fuit, nō solum quod sciebat cælestia Pilato vilescere, id quod iam ante expertus est, cūm de veritate coepisset nonnihil dicere: verùm etiam quia opus illud redemptionis mundi,per sanguinem ipsius à Patre destinatum, impedire noluit. Sed annon hoc durum fuit ( absit dicto blasphemia) non consulere saluti Pilati,ideo vt pręmonereatur illud Dei opus esse? Sed annon,inquit Paulus,habet figulus potestatem in lutum, vt ex eadem massa faciat aliud quidem vas ad decus, aliud vero ad dedecus? Praeterea si Deus glorificaretur, quid refert quid creatura fiat? Quotquot vasa sunt gloriae, illi quidem nunquam satis praedicare se Dei misericordiam & gratiam posse sibi videntur,ex qua gratia ipsi sunt vasa totidem ad salutem. lutem coagmentata, tantum abest ab eo vt velint Deum ideo accusare, quòd vasa irae coagmentauerit ad interitum. Mihi non loqueris? Subiratus ista loquitur. Paulò quidè ante metuit sibi à Deo, & Christo Dei filio: nunc verò in Christum iratus, Deum blasphemat. Vnde apparet euanidum fuisse illum metum. Sed instabilitas Pilati hic obseruanda est: primùm nullo metu, nulla Dei reuerentia attactus est, sed animo fuit plane profano: deinde momento mutatus est ad auditum illud filii Dei nomen.
units.tr: But that Christ answered nothing was due not only to his knowing that heavenly things were worthless to Pilate, which he had already experienced when he began to say something about the truth, but also because he was unwilling to hinder that work of redemption of the world, through his blood, which was determined by the Father. But was it not harsh (let not the word be taken as blasphemy) not to care for Pilate's salvation, so that he might be forewarned that this was God's work? But does not the potter, says Paul, have power over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel to honour and another to dishonour? Moreover, if God is glorified, what does it matter what the creature becomes? All who are vessels of glory seem to themselves never able to praise enough the mercy and grace of God, by which grace they are vessels fitted for salvation; so far are they from wishing to accuse God because he has fashioned vessels of wrath for destruction. Speakest thou not unto me? He speaks these words in anger. A little before, he feared God and Christ, the Son of God; now, angry with Christ, he blasphemes God. From this it appears that that fear was fleeting. But Pilate's instability is to be observed here: first, he was touched by no fear, by no reverence for God, but was wholly profane in mind; then in a moment he was changed on hearing the name of the Son of God. Finally, that fear and whatever reverence he had vanished faster than a word. You may see, after the example of Paul, some who lived dissolutely and wickedly a little before, in a moment affected by some feeling of repentance and reverence for God. Then you may see, a little after, all that repentance and reverence...

units.la: Postremò denique citius dicto euanuit ille metus ac reuerentia illa qualiscunque. Videas ad exemplum Pauli nonnullos, qui paulò ante dissolute ac perdite vixerunt, momento affici aliquo sensu resipiscentiae ac reuerentiae Dei. Tum videas paulò post totam illam resipiscentiam ac reuerentiam in nihilum abire.
units.tr: Finally, in short, that fear and whatever reverence it was vanished faster than it can be told. You may see some, like the example of Paul, who shortly before had lived dissolutely and wickedly, moved in an instant by some sense of repentance and reverence for God. Then, shortly afterwards, you may see all that repentance and reverence come to nothing.

units.la: Quod profecto argumento est animum illis hominibus nunquam verè regnitum fuisse. Sed cùm videri voluerint, vel resipiscentia, vel reuerentia Dei aliqua moueri, fuisse interea animum iis oppletum malitia & felle amaritudinis, illitum autem leuiter & non nisi superficie tenus aliquo sensu illarum rerum: vt si veneno mellis quasi superficiem superinducas. Atque ideo fit, vt suo tempore erumpente insita illa malitia, resipiscentia ac reuerentia quae ad tempus aliqua esse visa est, in fumos abeat. Quare si quisquis velit cor sibi stabiliri gratia, excutiat ipsum oportet, non contentus superficie aliqua boni, videatque vt ager ille cordis sui honestus sit & bonus. Cor enim hominis fraudulentum est super omnia. Neque tantum alios sed ipsum hominem imprimis fallit. Nescis me potestatem.
units.tr: This is certainly evidence that the heart of such men was never truly ruled. But while they wished to seem moved by some repentance or some reverence for God, meanwhile their heart was filled with malice and the gall of bitterness, and only lightly smeared, touched on the surface alone with some sense of those things, as if you were to spread honey over the surface of poison. And so it happens that when that inborn malice breaks out in due time, the repentance and reverence which seemed for a while to be there vanish into smoke. Therefore, if anyone wishes his heart to be made firm by grace, he must search it out himself, not content with some surface show of good, and see whether that field of his heart is sound and good. For the heart of man is deceitful above all things. Nor does it deceive others only, but above all the man himself. "Do you not know that I have power?"

units.la: Haec superbè & blasphemè loquitur: vendicat enim sibi absolutam aliquam, quam vocant, potestatem, atque ita manifesto derogat gloriae Dei, cuius hoc proprium est agere vt velit: quia voluntas ipsius est regula omnis iustitiae. In exemplo hoc Pilati, videmus id naturale esse iis, qui cum potestate sunt, vt cogitent absolutam potestatem se habere.
units.tr: He speaks this proudly and blasphemously. For he claims for himself an absolute power, as they call it, and so manifestly detracts from the glory of God, whose proper property it is to act as he wills, since his will is the rule of all justice. In this example of Pilate we see that it is natural for those who hold power to think that they have absolute power.

units.la: Quamuis enim ad tempus modestiores videri velint, & nihil vel velle, vel agere nisi ex legum & diuinae voluntatis praescripto: (id quod supra vidimus in Pilato, cùm diceret se nolle crucifigere Iesum, quia innocens erat) tamen si eos paululum commoueas & prouoces, quid
units.tr: For although for a time they wish to seem more moderate, and to will or do nothing except by the prescription of the laws and the divine will (as we saw above in Pilate, when he said he was unwilling to crucify Jesus because he was innocent), yet if you stir them up a little and provoke them, you will see what

units.la: Principum misera conditio, nisi sibi diligenter caueat. sentiant de potestate sua statim proferent, & blasphemabunt, vt nunc Pilatus, qui ad iram aliquam provocatus fuisse videtur ab Iesu, quod nihil ipsi quærenti respondisset.Cũ igitur eo sint ingenio Principes huius mundi, & qui cum potestate sunt, profectò videtur mihi superiorem omnem potestatem coniunctam esse cum summo periculo, si qui eam habet, homo ψυχικὸς sit tantum & animalis. Nam homini ψυχικῷ & animali potestatem deferre quid aliud est, quàm insanum aliquem armare gladio?Sumus enim omnes natura insani & amentes,& potestate illa abutimur, non tantum ad perniciem aliorum, sed etiam nostram ipsorum. Quamobrem si alij cuiquam opus est regeneratione per Spiritum Dei sanctum,profectò iis opus est maximè,qui maximam partem nacti sunt rerum earum,quæ sunt mundi huius,in primis autem iis qui cum potestate sunt. Nemo enim regum vnquam fuit,non regenitus, qui non conuerterit ipse suum gladium in viscera sua. Putant quidem ij qui aliis superemimént, tantum vulgo hominum opus esse illa regeneratione & sanctificatione animi,oris, manus, decere autem seomnia etiam impura quaque, vt scortationes,blasphemias,homicidia,&c. Verùm enim altiori loco sunt,& quo pluribus tentationibus expositi sunt, eo magis opus est iis Spiritu illo Dei sancto, qui ipsos sanctificet, & in omnibus actionibus dirigat, nisi malint tentationibus succumbere, & prædæ tandem esse diabolo.
units.tr: The wretched condition of princes, unless they take careful heed of themselves: whatever they feel about their power, they will at once declare, and they will blaspheme, as Pilate now does, who seems to have been provoked to some anger by Jesus because he had made no answer when Pilate asked him. Since princes of this world, and those who hold power, are of such a disposition, it seems to me that all supreme power is surely joined with the greatest danger, if its holder is only a psychical [ψυχικὸς] and animal man. For to entrust power to a psychical and animal man is nothing other than to arm some madman with a sword. For we are all mad and insane by nature, and we abuse that power not only to the destruction of others but also to our own. Wherefore, if anyone at all needs regeneration by the Holy Spirit of God, surely those need it most who have obtained the greatest share of the things of this world, and above all those who hold power. For there has never been a king who was not regenerate and yet did not turn his own sword against his own bowels. Indeed, those who excel others think that only the common crowd needs that regeneration and sanctification of mind, mouth and hand, while they may do all things, even impure ones, such as fornications, blasphemies, homicides, and so on. But the higher their place, and the more they are exposed to temptations, the more they need that Holy Spirit of God who sanctifies them and directs them in all their actions, unless they prefer to succumb to temptations and at last become the prey of the devil.

units.la: Nunc conferenda est vox hæc Pilati, qua se potestatem habere crucifigendi Christum gloriatur, cum illa superiori qua Christum innocentem pronùntiauit. Quid ex his vocibus sequi oportet, nisi hoc, quòd profiteatur potestatem se habere crucifigendi hominem innocentem? At hæc vox latronis potius est quàm iudicis: Ergo idem facit ac si profiteatur se non iudicem legitimum, sed latronem esse.Superbia enim & ambitio homines ad insaniam adigit, & ad stultas quasque & insanas voces, idque iusto Dei iudicio, superbiam illam animi stultitia oris vlciscentis.
units.tr: Now this word of Pilate, in which he boasts that he has power to crucify Christ, must be compared with his earlier word, in which he pronounced Christ innocent. What must follow from these words, except that he professes to have power to crucify an innocent man? But this word is that of a robber rather than of a judge. Therefore he does the same as if he professed himself not a lawful judge but a robber. For pride and ambition drive men to madness, and to every foolish and mad word, and that by the just judgment of God, the pride of the mind avenging itself by the foolishness of the mouth.

units.la: II. Responsionis Christi ad Pilatum partes duæ.
units.tr: II. The two parts of Christ's answer to Pilate.

units.la: Responsio Christi duas habet partes:Prior pars respicit Deum Patrem:Posterior respicit Iudeos Iudæos accusatores.
