Nam cùm duo fuerint à quibus potestas hæc Pilati quam gloriatur se habere in innocentem, profecta sit: Nempe Deus, sine quo nihil fit: & Iudæi qui ipsum tradiderat in manus Pilati, Christi ista respōsio ad vtrosque pertinet: Et primùm quidem ad Deū de quo hoc respondet, Non haberes nisi datum fuisset tibi superne. Sed verba sunt expendenda, quibus dicit, Nisi datum fuisset tibi superne. Verba hæc duobus modis accipi possunt: partim quia omnis potestas est à Deo, & diuina ordinatione, partim quia qui cum potestate est, nihil planè potest, nisi ex Dei efficaci dispensatione ac prouidentia. Significat igitur Christus non vno tantùm modo blasphemum fuisse Pilatum, sed duplici: tum quòd potestatem illam suam à Deo esse non agnosceret, tum quòd Dei prouidentiam efficacem ignoraret. Audita hac blasphemia, Christus qui paulò ante in sua causa siluit, neque respondit Pilato quærenti, vndenam ipse esset, à Deo & Dei filius, qui suam, inquam, gloriam ad tempus passus est obscurari, non obmutuit in causa Patris sui: verùm Patris gloriam vendicauit: contra quàm à nobis fieri solet, qui honori nostræ ipsorum satis diligenter cauemus, blasphemias verò in Deum quascunq; patienter audimus, adeo sine zelo Dei viuitur à nobis? Vides rursus in hoc Christi responso, neminem esse ira in manu aut potestate hominis, quin simul adeoque primum in manu sit Dei, adeo vt vita ipsius & mors ipsius magis pendeant à Dei sententia, quàm ab hominum decreto, & voluntate. Quod quo videant homines, fit nonnunquam, vt qui sententia hominū adiudicati sunt mori, ii sententia Dei eripiantur è morte, vt de Iohanne Ieiunus; contràque qui sententia hominum adiudicati sunt vitæ, sententia Dei moriantur, id quod de Agago rege Amalekitarum legimus, ex eo quod Christus admoneat Pilatum, primùm quòd potestas ipsius à Deo sit: deinde quòd omnia Deo dispensante faciat necessario in magistratu illo suo: ex eo, inquam, discimus requiri in eo omni qui cum potestate est, siue Rex sit, siue præses sit: vt primùm agnoscat se potestatē suam à Deo habere: deinde agnoscat Deum omnia per ipsum efficere, ipsum autem sine Deo dispensante planè nihil. Primū
units.tr: Christ's answer has two parts. The first part concerns God the Father; the second concerns the Jews, his accusers. For since there were two sources from which this power that Pilate boasts he has over the innocent man proceeded, namely God, without whom nothing is done, and the Jews who had handed him over into Pilate's hands, Christ's answer pertains to both. And first indeed it pertains to God, of whom he says, "You would have no power unless it had been given you from above." But the words "unless it had been given you from above" must be weighed. These words can be taken in two ways: partly because all power is from God and by divine ordinance, partly because he who has power can do absolutely nothing except by God's efficacious dispensation and providence. Christ therefore signifies that Pilate was blasphemous in two ways, not in one only: both because he did not acknowledge that his power was from God, and because he was ignorant of God's efficacious providence. Hearing this blasphemy, Christ, who a little before had kept silent in his own cause, and had not answered Pilate when he asked whence he was, and who, though he was God and the Son of God, had for a time suffered his own glory to be obscured, did not keep silent in the cause of his Father, but vindicated his Father's glory. Contrary to what is usually done by us, who take quite diligent care for the honour of ourselves, yet patiently hear whatever blasphemies are uttered against God, so without zeal for God do we live! You see again in this answer of Christ that there is no one whose wrath is in the hand or power of man, but that it is first in the hand of God, so that his life and death depend more on the sentence of God than on the decree and will of men. This is sometimes seen by men: those who by the sentence of men were condemned to die are snatched from death by the sentence of God, as Jonathan was; and conversely, those who by the sentence of men were adjudged to live die by the sentence of God, as we read of Agag, king of the Amalekites. From the fact that Christ admonishes Pilate, first that his power is from God, and then that in that magistracy of his he does everything by God's dispensing, we learn, I say, that it is required of everyone who has power, whether he be king or governor, that first he acknowledge that he has his power from God, and then acknowledge that God effects all things through him, while he himself without God's dispensing is absolutely nothing. First,

units.la: 1. Sam. 15.1 &c. illud quo tandem disceret. Nebucadnetzar septennium totum vixit inter bestias, Dan. 4. Secundum vero, quia non agnouit Rex Assyriæ qui gloriatus est omnia à se facta sua manu ac sapientia, grauissimum aduersus eum iudicium Deus per Prophetam suum denunciat, Esai. 10. 13. &c. Tum non est prætereundum illud quod Christus iam in potestate Pilati constitutus, agnoscat primum potestatem illam à Deo esse, atque ita se volens ei subiecerit: deinde oculos fixos habeat in Dei prouidentia, sine qua nihil potuit in ipsum Pilatus: non, inquam, prætereundum est exemplum hoc Christi, sed eo admonentur quotquot sub potestate viuunt, vt agnoscant potestatem supereminentem quancunque à Deo esse, ideoque eam honorent, eíque sint subiecti propter conscientiam Dei. Admonentur præterea quod si contingat incidere in manus hominum qui cum potestate sunt, interea oculos magis fixos habere debeant in Deo ipsiusque prouidentia, quam in hominibus, tum ad gloriam ipsius Dei, tum ad patientiam & consolationem ipsorum. Dum considerant etiam hærentes in tormentis, tractari se interea non tam manibus hominum, quàm manu Patris sui clementissimi. Nam absque agnitione ista prouidentiæ diuinæ nulla est solida ac vera consolatio, vel in vita, vel in morte.
units.tr: 1. Sam. 15.1 &c. That he might at last learn that. Nebuchadnezzar lived a whole seven years among the beasts, Dan. 4. Secondly, because the King of Assyria, who boasted that all his deeds were done by his own hand and wisdom, did not acknowledge this, God pronounces through his Prophet a most grievous judgment against him, Isa. 10. 13. etc. Next, we must not pass over the fact that Christ, though already placed in Pilate's power, first acknowledges that this power is from God, and thus, willing to be subject to it, and then keeps his eyes fixed on God's providence, without which Pilate could do nothing against him. I say, this example of Christ must not be passed over. By it are admonished as many as live under power, that they acknowledge any supreme power whatever to be from God, and therefore honour it and are subject to it for conscience' sake towards God. They are admonished besides that, if it happens that they fall into the hands of men who hold power, they ought meanwhile to keep their eyes more fixed on God and his providence than on men, both for the glory of God himself and for their own patience and consolation, while they consider, even when they hang in torments, that they are handled meanwhile not so much by the hands of men as by the hand of their most merciful Father. For without this acknowledgment of divine providence there is no solid and true consolation, either in life or in death.

units.la: Propterea qui me tradidit.
units.tr: Therefore he who delivered me up to you.

units.la: Altera pars responsionis Christi ad Pilatum pertinens ad Iudæos & accusatores. Pendere autem vista dentur verba ista non tam ex proximè superioribus quæ tu, Iudæos respiciens, ex verbis illis Pilati quæ habentur vers. 10. superiori versu, quasi dicat: Tu quidem gloriaris de potestate tua, verùm Iudei qui me in potestatem tuam tradiderunt: Quo maior est potestas tua in me, eo grauius peccant, & grauior futura est eorum condemnatio. Hic videmus iram Dei in eos qui tradunt innocentes in manus tyrannorum, & maior est & prior est in traditores, quàm in ipsos tyrannos: Prior fuit in Iudam qui Christum prodidit, qui in Iudæos illos quibus eum prodidit: Interea enim dum Christus à militibus & Iudæis huc atque illuc traheretur, Iudas incidit in manus Dei & in torturam conscientiæ suæ, seseque suspendens miser crepuit medius. Putat quidem Pontifex iste Romanus cum clero suo satis se purum esse.
units.tr: This is the second part of Christ's reply to Pilate, and it concerns the Jews and his accusers. These words seem to depend less on the words immediately above them, which Christ addressed to the Jews, than on Pilate's words in verse 10 above, as if he said: "You boast of your power, but the Jews who delivered me into your power have sinned more gravely. The greater your power over me, the graver their sin and the heavier their condemnation will be." Here we see God's wrath against those who deliver the innocent into the hands of tyrants. It is greater and falls first on the betrayers rather than on the tyrants themselves. It fell first on Judas, who betrayed Christ, and before the Jews to whom he betrayed him. For while Christ was being dragged here and there by the soldiers and the Jews, Judas fell into the hands of God and into the torment of his own conscience, and he hanged himself, and wretchedly burst asunder in the middle. This Roman pontiff, together with his clergy, certainly thinks he is pure enough.

units.la: Act. 1. 18. esse à sanguine innocentum, si tradiderit innocentes, à seiam prius damnatos, in manus magistratus politici. Verum non sic effugiet, quin ira Dei & gravior sit & prior in eum quàm in tyrannos ipsos politicos. Ne sit no bis unquam res cum morte innocentis: tantùmque absimus ab eo ut simus eorum proditores ac traditores, ut ne vllas habeamus partes in ipsorum persequutione, ne carnificis quidem, qui tamen putat se vulgo exemptum omni reatu. Sed historia trium adolescetum Sadraci, Misachi & Abednegonis satis docet ne carnifices quidé effugere Dei iudicium: consumpti enim flamma ignis fuerunt, qui tres eos in fornacè igneum iniecerūt: Daniel.3.
units.tr: Act. 1. 18. He will not be free of the blood of the innocent if he hands over innocent men, whom he has previously condemned, into the hands of the civil magistrate. Yet he will not escape so easily: God's wrath is both heavier and falls first upon him rather than upon the civil tyrants themselves. Let us never have to do with the death of an innocent. Let us be so far from becoming their betrayers and deliverers that we take no part at all in their persecution, not even as executioners, although the executioner commonly thinks himself free of all guilt. But the history of the three young men, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, sufficiently teaches that not even executioners escape God's judgment. For those who threw the three into the fiery furnace were consumed by the flame. Dan. 3.

units.la: Nota cū de Deo loquitur Christus nihil ei mali aut peccati in hoc opere & traditione sui in manus ac potestatē Pilati ascribit: verū eius maiestatem ac sanctitatem asserit à blasphemia Pilati. At cùm de Iudæis qui Christum Pilato tradiderunt loquitur; ipsis peccati grauissimi notā inurit. Mira res! vnū enim idemque opus faciebant Deus & Iudæi illi persequutores Christi. Sed respondeo, non eodem tamen modo: Deus enim in communi isto opere quod faciebat, sanctè faciebat. At illi quod faciebant, id non nisi scelerate faciebant, & à Deo traditum sibi, ij sceleratis manibus tradiderunt Pilato, nihil Dei providentiam, nihil ipsius voluntatem respicientes, sed malitiæ suæ ipsorum morem gerentes. Quicquid faciamus, illud totum faciamus propter Dominum & in Domino: secus enim si Deum ante oculos non habeamus, etiam cùm ex Dei revelata voluntate, & expresso mandato aliquid agimus, peccamus tamen. Deinde faciendum est non tantum dispensante Deo, sed mandante: hoc est secundū voluntatem Dei revelatam faciamus & expressum ipsius verbum, non contenti eo si instrumenta duntaxat sumus voluntatis Dei non revelatæ & efficacis decreti ipsius exequendi. In summa faciamus omnia ex revelata Dei voluntate, & faciamus quidem in Domino.
units.tr: Note that when Christ speaks of God, he ascribes to him nothing evil or sinful in this work, in the handing over of himself into the hands and power of Pilate. Rather, he asserts God's majesty and holiness against Pilate's blasphemy. But when he speaks of the Jews who delivered Christ to Pilate, he brands them with the mark of the gravest sin. A wonderful thing! For God and those Jewish persecutors of Christ did one and the same work. But I answer that not in the same way. For God, in this common work which he was doing, acted holily. But they, in what they did, acted only wickedly, and they handed over to Pilate with wicked hands what had been delivered to them by God. They had regard to neither God's providence nor his will, but served their own malice. Whatever we do, we must do for the Lord and in the Lord. Otherwise, if we do not keep God before our eyes, we sin even when we act on the basis of God's revealed will and an express command. Moreover, we must act not merely under God's permission but at his command: that is, we must act according to God's revealed will and his express word, and not be content with being mere instruments of his hidden will and of the carrying out of his effectual decree. In sum, let us do everything according to God's revealed will, and let us do it in the Lord.

units.la: Ex eo tempore studebat Pilatus eū dimittere: Iudæi vero clamabāt, dicentes, Si hunc dimiseris, non es amicus Cæsaris: quicunque se regem facit, contradicit Cæsari.
units.tr: From that time Pilate was eager to release him. But the Jews cried out, saying, "If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend. Whoever makes himself a king opposes Caesar."

units.la: 13 Pilatus ergo cũ audisset hunc sermonem, eduxit foras Iesum, consedítque in tribunali, in loco qui dicitur Lithostrotos, Hebraicè autem Gabbatha.
units.tr: 13 Therefore when Pilate heard this saying, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat, in a place called the Pavement, but in Hebrew Gabbatha.

units.la: 14 Erat autem Parasceue Paschæ, hora verò quasi sexta : tum dicit Iudæis, Ecce Rex vester.
units.tr: 14 Now it was the Preparation of the Passover, and about the sixth hour. And he said to the Jews, "Behold your King!"

units.la: 15 Illi verò clamauerunt, Tolle, tolle, crucifige eum. Dicit eis Pilatus, Regem vestrum crucifigam? Responderunt primarij Sacerdotes, Non habemus regem nisi Cæsarem.
units.tr: 15 But they cried out, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Shall I crucify your King?" The chief priests answered, "We have no king but Caesar."

units.la: QVanto magis insistit Pilatus cũ Christo agere, tanto magis afficitur conscientia innocentiæ ipsius: quanto magis afficitur cõscientia innocentiæ ipsius, tanto maiori studio ducitur ipsius dimittendi. Nunc itaque in id incũbit vehementius quàm antea, fortasse ad id adductus proximis illis Christi verbis, ad quæ obstupuisse videtur Pilatus. Hunc cõscientiæ tantũ sensum in homine Ethnico ascribere benedictionibus Dei : nihil magis æque requiro in iudice atq; conscientia recti & grauis, in innocentiæ & reatus: nisi tandẽ contra conscientia Christi condemnasset. Cũ enim tandẽ contra conscientia quis cediitma-lo,tũ quæ in se fuit benedictio vertitur ei in maledictionem: & conscientia ex cõsiliaria efficitur carnifex. Si hunc absoluerit. Quanto magis Pilatus insistit pro Christo agere,& pro conscientia, tanto obnixius nituntur illi cõtra Christũ,contraq; conscientia : nunc autem grauius eum pertentat quàm antea: nã antehac tentabant eũ criminibus Christo obiectis, nunc verò ipsum Pilatũ quodãmodo læsæ maiestatis accusant: Id enim innuũt cũ obiiciũt quòd nõ sit amicus Cæsaris, si Iesum absoluat, quia ipse contradicit Cæsari: contradicere enim Cæsari ex eo probant, quòd se regem faciat: Quicunq; se regem facit, contradicit Cæsari: At hic se regẽ facit: Ergo contradicit Cæsari: si ergo hunc absoluueris, nõ es amicus Cæsaris. In summa accusant eũ reipsa læsæ maiestatis. Nota: bona conscientia nunquã libera est à tentationibus, quoq; melior est conscientia, eo graviores sunt tentationes. Vltima autẽ tentatio omniũ grauissima: grauissima autẽ est illa, cũ vr getur quis, vt vel conscientiæ suæ renunciet, vel vitæ. Sed quinam
units.tr: The more Pilate insists on acting for Christ, the more his conscience is moved by Christ's innocence. And the more his conscience is moved by Christ's innocence, the more eagerly he is driven to release him. Now therefore he presses on in this matter more vehemently than before, perhaps moved by those last words of Christ, at which Pilate seems to have been astonished. I require nothing more than this sense of conscience in a heathen man, which God's blessings ascribe to him: nothing is more equal to the judge's conscience of what is right and serious, of innocence and guilt. But if he had at last condemned him against his conscience, then the blessing that was in him would be turned into a curse for him, and his conscience, from counsellor, becomes an executioner. "If he releases him..." As Pilate presses more and more to act for Christ and for conscience, so the others strive more stubbornly against Christ and against conscience. But now they press him more severely than before. For before, they attacked him with the charges brought against Christ; now they accuse Pilate himself, in a way, of treason. For they hint at this when they object that, if he releases Jesus, he is not Caesar's friend, because he himself opposes Caesar. They prove that he opposes Caesar from the fact that he makes himself king: "Whoever makes himself king opposes Caesar. But this man makes himself king. Therefore he opposes Caesar. If therefore you release him, you are not Caesar's friend." In sum, they accuse him in reality of treason. Note: a good conscience is never free from temptations, and the better the conscience, the heavier the temptations. The last temptation is the heaviest of all, and the heaviest is when a man is urged either to renounce his conscience or his life.

units.la: Nouissimus Pilati conatuscir ca Christi liberationem, sed ipse tuinâ grauissima est? Pilato: hoc est homini, cuius Deus est Cæsar, cuius cælum est terra, deniq; qui ipē suā vitra hanc vitā non porrigit. Atq; id quidē satis compertū habet Satū: ideóq; tentatione hanc, qua vrget vel abiectione conscientiæ, vel amissione vitæ huius, tentatione, inquā, hanc doctissimè applicat ad ittiusmodi hominem. Quamobrem si velimus armati esse contra tentationem hanc, ne contenti simus sola conscientia, sed fidè & spē in corde habeamus, quibus cōscientia ipsa fulciatur: his enim qui cælestia illa intuentur, & spē suā porrigūt vltra hāc vitā, facilius erit resistere huiusmodi tētationi: & respondere malle se vitā hāc, & vniuersum hunc mundū semel amittere quā renūtiare bonę cōscietię, cū etiā amissa ilta vita sperēt lōgè meliorē se cōsequuturos. Vt vim tēta tionis externæ, ita vim interne malitię, quę hominem cū cōscietia sua precipitē abripit, notabis hoc loco. Nā Pilatus reluctante conscientia, vi malitię cordis sui iudicium peruerfissimum ac iniquissimum ingressus est.
units.tr: Pilate's final attempt concerning Christ's release is the most grievous of all. He is a man for whom God is Caesar, for whom heaven is earth, and who, in short, does not extend his hope beyond this life. Satan certainly knows this well enough, and so he most skilfully applies this temptation, which presses one either to abandon conscience or to lose this life, to such a man. Therefore, if we wish to be armed against this temptation, we must not be content with conscience alone, but must have faith and hope in our hearts, by which conscience itself is supported. For those who look upon heavenly things and extend their hope beyond this life will more easily resist such temptation, and will prefer to lose this life and this whole world once rather than to renounce a good conscience, since they hope that, even when that life is lost, they will obtain a far better one. Note here both the force of external temptation and the force of inner malice, which violently drags a man headlong along with his conscience. For Pilate, while his conscience resisted, entered by the force of the malice of his heart upon a most perverse and most unjust judgment.

units.la: Pilatus ergo quū audisset. Hac tentatione grauissima inclinatur Pilatus ad iudiciū & condemnationem innocentis, & conscientia ipsius labe fadari incipit. Egreditur ad iudicium, simul secum assumpto Iesu tanquam reo. Locus designatur Lithostrotos Græcè, Hebraicè autem Gabbatha, quasi dicas solium vel pauimentum, lapidibus magnificè extructum & instratum. Item tempus notatur versu sequenti, idque duplíciter, partim à parasceue, siue præparatione Paschæ quam celebraturi erant Iudæi ad vesperam: Erat autem parasceue, partim ab hora diei, quæ sexta fuit Iudæis, nobis verò duodecima. Tempus igitur huius iudicij fuit meridianum. Nota igitur in effectu isto tentationis proximæ, quantam vim habeat tentatio eaqua vigetur, vel conscientiæ bonæ labefactatio, vel vitæ huius amissio in oculis hominis ψυχικοῦ cui sapientiaeit sola vita istam præsentē redimere re tā leuiuscula. Neq; enim videt vita hanc quā viuimus fine conscientia & morte nihil differre, vt quæ fine sensu sit. Sensum enim hominis, qua homo est, nō tā metimur ex externis hisce corporis sensibus, qui nobis cū brutis cōmunes sunt, quā ex interna animi conscietia. Illud hic omitto, cōscientiā illā ipsam, quā tanquā cōsiliariā & admonitricē reiiciūt,
units.tr: Therefore Pilate, when he had heard... Under this gravest temptation Pilate is inclined to the judgment and condemnation of the innocent, and his conscience begins to be stained by the blot. He goes out to the judgment seat, taking Jesus along with him as a defendant. The place is designated as Lithostrotos in Greek [Λιθόστρωτος], but Gabbatha in Hebrew [גַּבַּתָּא], as if you would say a dais or pavement, magnificently built and paved with stones. The time is also noted in the following verse, and doubly: partly by the Preparation, or the day of preparation for the Passover which the Jews were to celebrate in the evening, Now it was the Preparation; partly by the hour of the day, which was the sixth for the Jews but for us the twelfth. The time of this judgment was therefore midday. Note then, in the effect of this near temptation, how great a force a temptation has by which either a good conscience is shaken or this life is lost, in the eyes of a natural [ψυχικοῦ] man, for whom it is wisdom to redeem this present life at so slight a price. For he does not see that the life we live without conscience differs nothing from death, since it is without sense. For we measure a man's sense, insofar as he is a man, not so much by those external bodily senses, which we share with the brutes, as by the inner conscience of the mind. Here I pass over the fact that they reject that very conscience, which they regard as a counsellor and admonisher,

units.la: {14} Tandē impiusone ri malę cō scietiæ suę cumbit. postea redituram esse tanquam carnificem aliquem, cuius quidem lanienam & carnificinam multo grauius laturi sunt, quàm ipsam mortem : imò verò quàm mille mortes. Ecce Rex vester. His verbis Pilatus indicat se nondum omnem plane conscientiam innocentiæ Christi amisisse. Sensus enim est, ac si dicat, Quàm verisimile est quod dicitis hunc misellum regnum affectare, cùm is mendico similior sit, quàm Regi. Verba enim habent irrisionem quandam criminis ipsi obiecti, qua quidem subindicat nihil esse in ipso morte dignum. Vt supra vidimus vim tentationis illius eorum & malitiæ cordis: ita hic videmus vim conscientiæ Pilati, quæ non ita facile excutitur, etiam tum cùm consiliariæ & admonitricis partes agit. Nam postquâ carnificis partes coepit iam agere, tum quidem longè difficillimè excutitur, vsque adeo mordicus adhæret homini, iniectis quasi in animam miseri vnguibus, vt nullis agitationibus, nulla vel fraude vel vi lenti & mitigari potest. Illi verò clamarunt. Hominem semel inclinatum à conscientia sua abalienatum hominé præcipitem agat Satan: quem ita obstupefacit tentationibus & quasi clamoribus, vt conscientiæ suæ vocem intus admonentem audire amplius non possit: quemadmodum legimus Idololatras Iudæos cùm in valle Topheth liberos suos immolarent Deo Ammonitarum Molocho, ad sonos instrumentorum ita obsurduisse, vt miseras illas lamentationes ac vociferationes suorum liberorum audire nequirent. Quamobrè resistendum est principiis, neque pati debemus nos vel latum vnguem abduci à bona conscientia, abductos enim ingeminatis viribus adoriente Satan, & quò volet, ipse præcipitabit. Regem vestrum crucifigam? Adhuc pugnat conscientia Pilati pro Christo, sed admodum infirmiter: vt facile conspiciatur eam iam agere quasi extremâ animâ. Sic enim interrogando dubitare se significat faciatne quod volunt an minus. Nam duo sunt vocum genera, quae ex utraque conscientia procedunt: Unum est dum quis constanter negat se facturum id quod malum est: alterum est, dum dubitat faciatne id, quod malum est, annon: sideoq; interrogat debeatne facere, annon? Quoties audimus suspensas huiusmodi voces, toties de coscientia quod interitui iam proxima sit, coniecturam facere possumus. Non habemus regem. Rursus obiicitur Pilato Caesar tanquam Gorgonis caput. Sed vide istorum hypocrisin: Caesarem, quem oderunt ex animo, praetendunt: eiusque obedientiam praetexunt, ad miseram Pilati conscientiam labefactandam, & ad Christum crucifigendum. Hoc familiare est hypocritis in regno Antichristi: qui cum neque Caesare, neque Deum aut religionem ipsius sincere amant: Caesarem tamen ipsiusque obedientiam praetexunt ad Christum & religionem evertendam: contraque Christum & religionem praetexunt ad Caesarem & supereminentem potestatem subvertendam. Idque non ita pridem factum est ab hypocritis illis Pontificiis adversus Regem Gallorum, quem nescio quo religionis praetextu per fraudem parricidae illi & execrandi proditores e medio sustulerunt.
units.tr: {14} At length the impious man succumbs to his own evil conscience, which he fears will return like some executioner, whose butchery and torture they will bear far more grievously than death itself; indeed, than a thousand deaths. Behold your King. By these words Pilate shows that he has not yet wholly lost every sense of Christ's innocence. For the sense is as if he said: how likely is it that this poor wretch aims at the kingdom, when he looks more like a beggar than a king? The words carry a certain mockery of the crime laid against him, and so hint that there is nothing in him deserving of death. As we saw above, the force of their temptation and the malice of their hearts; so here we see the force of Pilate's conscience, which is not easily shaken off, even when it plays the part of counsellor and admonisher. For once it has begun to play the part of executioner, it is shaken off with far greater difficulty, so firmly does it cling to the man, as if it had fixed its claws into his soul, so that by no agitation, by no force or fraud, can it be softened or calmed. But they cried out. Once Satan has driven a man headlong, having drawn him away from his conscience, he so stupefies him with temptations and, as it were, with shouting, that he can no longer hear the voice of conscience admonishing him within. Just as we read that the idolatrous Jews, when they sacrificed their children in the valley of Topheth to Molech, the god of the Ammonites, were so deafened by the sound of instruments that they could not hear the pitiful lamentations and cries of their own children. Wherefore we must resist beginnings, and we must not allow ourselves to be drawn away from a good conscience even by a finger's breadth; for once drawn away, Satan, attacking with redoubled strength, will hurl us wherever he wills. Shall I crucify your King? Pilate's conscience still fights for Christ, but very feebly, so that it is easily seen to be acting as if at its last breath. For by asking, he shows that he hesitates whether to do what they want or not. For there are two kinds of utterance that proceed from a conscience: one is when a man firmly refuses to do what is evil; the other is when he hesitates whether to do what is evil or not, and so asks whether he ought to do it or not. Whenever we hear such hesitant words, we can conjecture that the conscience is close to perishing. We have no king. Again Caesar is thrown at Pilate like the head of a Gorgon. But see the hypocrisy of these men: they put forward Caesar, whom they hate from the heart, and they pretend to obedience to him, in order to shake Pilate's wretched conscience and to have Christ crucified. This is customary for hypocrites in the kingdom of Antichrist: since they love neither Caesar nor God and his religion sincerely, they nonetheless put forward Caesar and obedience to him in order to overthrow Christ and religion; and against Christ and religion they put forward Caesar and the overriding power, in order to subvert it. And this was done not long ago by those hypocritical Papists against the King of the French, whom, under I know not what pretext of religion, those parricidal and accursed traitors removed by fraud from the midst of men.

units.la: Matthaei cap. 27.
units.tr: Matthew chapter 27.

units.la: 24 Videns autem Pilatus se nihil proficere, sed magis tumultum fieri, accepta aqua abluit manus coram turba, dicens, Innoxius ego sum a sanguine huius iusti: Vos videritis.
units.tr: 24 And when Pilate saw that he could prevail nothing, but that rather a tumult was made, he took water, and washed his hands before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it.

units.la: 25 Et respondens universus populus dixit, Sanguis eius super nos & super filios nostros.
units.tr: 25 Then answered all the people, and said, His blood be on us, and on our children.

units.la: 26 Tunc dimisit eis Barabbam, Iesum autem cum flagellasset, tradidit ut crucifigeretur.
units.tr: 26 Then released he Barabbas unto them: and when he had scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified.

units.la: HActenus Pilatus pro Christo ipsiusque innocentia cuius erat conscius cum importunitate & obstinatione Iudaeorum malitia luctatus est. Coepit autem, obiecto sibi laesae maiestatis crimine collabescere, neque tantoperevergere absolutionem innocentis: Tandem vero referente Matthaeo, cuius hic verba & historiam placuit inserere, cum videret se nihil proficere, assumpta aqua [...] abluit manus, cum hac quasi protestatione facta, Innoxius ego sum a sanguine huius iusti:tum conversus ad Iudaeos, dixit iis, Vos videritis, hoc est, vobis reddenda est ratio. His quidem verbis exonerat se, onerat autem Iudaeos hoc malo, quorum importunitate coactus est condemnare innocentem. Qua in re longe fallitur: nam, ut illud fatear, onus illud sanguinis, tum innocentis Christi, tum Pilati ipsius Iudaeis impositum fuisse: tamen ipse quoque Pilatus reus fuit, & mortuus est pro peccato suo: in persona tamen Pilati notabis errorem, quo se implicant homines ψυχικοί, & quotquot ex verbo Dei non sunt illuminati: putant enim quod si pro veritate, innocentia & bona conscientia iam aliquanto tempore, & ut ipsis videtur satis longo, iam pugnarunt; putant, inquam, tum, si tandem necessitate aliqua & hominum importunitate impediantur ne ad finem usque perseverent, se non obstrictos esse amplius & exoneratos iam si succubant in fine, amittantque bonam conscientiam. Sed falluntur: nam qui non perseveraverit in finem, non coronabitur: neque necessitas ea quae trahit secum eius consensum, qui alio qui ex necessitate facit aliquid, excusat quenquam. Necessitas, fateor, ea quae est absque consensu, & vim asserit plane inuitis: ut si quis externa vi impulsus citra assensum voluntatis suae, sine motu spontaneo membrorum corporis sui, offendat in aliquem: tum fateor eam coactionem & necessitatem excusare. Verum cum quis, metu maioris alicuius mali, ut ipsi videtur, cogitur consentire in malum, & malum perficere, profecto huiusmodi necessitas non excusat: & factum illud non tam in inuitis, quam in voluntariis & spontaneis numerandum est. Huiusmodi fuit factum hoc Pilati. Apparet autem tum ex ceremonia ista lotionis manuum, tum ex verbis protestationis, qua vsus est, adhuc manifeste confidentiam innocentiae Christi aliquam. Pater enim voluit apparere Filii sui innocentiam in tota actione ista, in eius principio, in medio, in fine, in accusatione tota, in condemnatione, in crucifixione denique ipsa, in qua voce Centurionis & militum qui ipsum crucifixerunt, hoc est voce ipsorum carnificum, testatum fecit eum hominem iustum & Dei Filium fuisse. Sic consultum voluit esse Pater non modo gloriæ filij sui, vt tanquam innocês moreretursed etiam fidei ac saluti nostræ : vt nos haberemus Pontificem pium, innocentem, impollutum, segregatum à peccatoribus, & sublimiorem cælis factum.
units.tr: Hitherto Pilate struggled for Christ and his innocence, of which he was aware, against the obstinacy and malice of the Jews, with importunity and resistance. But when the charge of treason was laid against him, he began to waver, and he would not so readily have pressed the acquittal of the innocent. At last, however, as Matthew relates (whose words and account I have thought fit to insert here), when he saw that he gained nothing, he took water and washed his hands, making this as a kind of protestation: I am innocent of the blood of this just person. Then, turning to the Jews, he said to them, See ye to it, that is, you must answer for it. By these words he discharges himself, but he burdens the Jews with this evil, by whose importunity he was compelled to condemn the innocent. In this he is far mistaken: for although, I grant, that burden of blood, both of innocent Christ and of Pilate himself, was laid upon the Jews, yet Pilate himself was also guilty, and died for his own sin. Yet in the person of Pilate you will note the error into which natural men [ψυχικοί] and all who are not enlightened by the Word of God fall: they think that if they have already struggled for a time, and as it seems to them a long enough time, for truth, innocence and a good conscience, and if at last they are hindered by some necessity and the importunity of men from persevering to the end, they are no longer bound and are discharged, even if they give way at the end and lose a good conscience. But they are mistaken: for he who does not persevere to the end shall not be crowned; nor does that necessity which carries with it the consent of him who does something from necessity excuse anyone. The necessity that is without consent, and that plainly forces against the will, I grant, excuses: as if someone, impelled by external force, without assent of his will, without spontaneous movement of the members of his body, strikes someone; then I grant that such compulsion and necessity excuse. But when someone, from fear of some greater evil, as it seems to him, is compelled to consent to evil and to perform it, such necessity truly does not excuse, and the deed must be counted not so much among things done against the will as among things done willingly and spontaneously. Such was this deed of Pilate. It appears, moreover, both from that ceremony of washing the hands and from the words of protestation which he used, that he still manifestly confessed some confidence in Christ's innocence. For the Father willed that the innocence of his Son should appear throughout this whole action: at its beginning, in its middle, at its end, in the whole accusation, in the condemnation, and finally in the very crucifixion itself, in which, by the voice of the centurion and of the soldiers who crucified him, that is, by the voice of the executioners themselves, he made it witnessed that he was a just man and the Son of God. Thus the Father willed to provide not only for the glory of his Son, that he should die as innocent, but also for our faith and salvation: that we might have a holy, innocent, undefiled high priest, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens.

units.la: Apparet rursus ex verbis iis, quibus Iudæos est allocutus, Vos, inquiens, videritis, conscientiam Pilati damnasse præfractam illam Iudæorum obstinatione: adeóque citasse ipsos, vt sisterent sese coram tribunali illo Dei. Neque enim si tua ipsius conscientia sileat quâ maximè, tamen patietur Deus te sine teste esse ac citatore, sive admonitore: excitabit prius conscientiam Pagani alicuius atque Ethnici ad te citandum, quàm citatore & admonitore careas; id quod profectò non fit citra documentum aliquod iudicij ac iræ in te diuinæ, cùm tacente conscientia tua ipsius, quam ordinariè alioqui accusare te & citare oportuit, excitatur alterius etiam prophani hominis conscientia, ad te citandum & admonédū. Interea nihil in historia ista conspicitur, ex quo possumus suspicari conscientiam Pilati ipsum accusasse, aut citasse: cùm tamen accusatione ac citatione esset ipse dignissimus. Pergebat enim deliberato animo ad faciinus indignissimū. Quod si enim cōscientia Pilati ipsum accusasset, profectò longè aliam protestationem ipsi extorsisset, quàm hanc, qua professus est palam se innocium fuisse à sanguine iusti illius: quin potiùs propositi nefandi confessionem aliquam ipsi extorsisset. Sed quæ causa fuerat cur conscientia Pilati nihil ipsum, aut certè parum admodum accusset? Certè non alia, quàm quòd ea male esset informata: decepta enim fuit necessitate illa Pilatum satis excusari, præsertim cùm iam tandiu luctatus fuisset cum obstinata illa Iudæorum malitia. Apparet igitur conscientiam Pilati non recte informatam atque instructam fuisse: neque enim conscientia esse earum potest rerum, quarum non est scientia.
units.tr: It appears again from the words with which he addressed the Jews, See ye to it, he says, that Pilate's conscience condemned that obstinacy of the Jews, and so summoned them to stand before that tribunal of God. For if your own conscience is silent, however much it ought to speak, God will not suffer you to be without a witness and summoner, or admonisher: he will first stir up the conscience of some heathen and pagan to summon you, before you lack a summoner and admonisher; which certainly does not happen without some token of judgment and of divine wrath upon you, since, while your own conscience is silent, which ordinarily ought otherwise to accuse you and summon you, the conscience of another, even a profane man, is stirred up to summon and admonish you. Meanwhile nothing in this story is seen from which we could suspect that Pilate's conscience accused him or summoned him, although he was most worthy of accusation and summons. For he went on, with deliberate mind, to a most unworthy deed. For if Pilate's conscience had accused him, it would surely have extorted from him a very different protestation than this, by which he openly professed that he was innocent of the blood of that just man; rather, it would have extorted from him some confession of his wicked purpose. But what was the cause why Pilate's conscience accused him not at all, or very little? Surely no other than that it was ill-informed: for it was deceived by that necessity, by which Pilate was thought sufficiently excused, especially since he had already struggled so long against the obstinate malice of the Jews. It appears, therefore, that Pilate's conscience was not rightly informed and instructed: for conscience cannot be of those things of which there is no knowledge.

units.la: Quare perpetuò videndum nobis est vt non sanctùm sit conscientia aliqua, sed sit conscientia rectè informata, & incorrupta, præsertim, quòd nulla huiusmodi necessitas, quæ conscientiam aliquem coniunctum habet, nos excusct. Informatio autem recta conscientiæ, ex verbo Dei perendum: quæ sola est regula vitæ & actionum no-
units.tr: Therefore we must always take care that our conscience is not just any conscience, but one that is rightly informed and uncorrupted, especially since no necessity that has a conscience attached to it can excuse us. The right information of conscience, however, must be drawn from the Word of God, which alone is the rule of life and of all our actions.

units.la: Hebr. 7. 26. strarum omnium. Nunc autem de Iudæis nonnihil erit dicendum. De quibus profecto oportet fateri, quod si conscientia innocentiæ Christi effecerit, vt Pilatus à se suisque humeris reiecerit illud onus sanguinis iusti: Sacerdotes reliquíque Iudæi vel nulla conscientia & sensu innocentiæ Christi affecti sunt: cùm in se & in posteros suos tam graue onus reciperent, tam lubenter (nā ignorantia semper audax est ac temeraria) vel certè necesse est ex malitia obstinatissima etiam contra conscientiā, hoc eos fecisse: id quod magis credo: nam malitia non minūs, adeóque etiam magis audax est, quàm ignorantia: & maliitiosi quique atque vindictæ cupidi, diris atque inferis sese devouere nihil morantur, cùm malitia adeo excæcet miseros, vt ne inferos quidem possint discernere. Quòd autem ex malitia magis, quàm ignorātia aliqua fecerint Iudæi id quod fecerút aduersus Christum, testes sunt Prophetæ, testes quoque sunt Apostoli: qui totum hoc factum Iudæorum malitiæ & pertinaciæ adscripserunt. Neque etiam inficior ex malitia factum à Pilato quod fecit ipse in Christum. Sed latum est inter eum & Iudæos discrimen. Nam Pilatus etiam ex infirmitate fecit, nempe ex metu, quem ij incusserunt, ne sceleris reus fieret læsæ maiestatis. Ex metu quoque ne tumultus oriretur in populo. At quæ causa, quæso, metus Iudæis? sola malitia ipsos impulit. Pilatus præterea malitiosus erat, non quidem aduersus lucē & illuminationem Spiritus sansti ex verbo Dei suppeditatam, sed aduersus lucem duntaxat naturæ, & naturalem istam conscientiam. Quæ profecto malitia non efficit peccatū illud in Spiritum sanctum. At Iudæi malitiosè oppugnarunt etiā lucem illam verbi, & Spiritui sancto resisterunt: Vos, inquit Stephanus, seper Spiritui sancto obnitimini, sicut Patres vestri, ita & vos. Vnde cūm peccārint haud dubiò ex iis certè aliqui in Spiritū sanctum, ac proinde finali impœnitentia, qua Deus id genus peccati vlcisci solet percussi fuerint. Quid hic mirì est, etsi in eos inciderit eiusmodi iudiciū, cuiusmodi in nullā vnquā gētē? Vnica .n. obsidione, vt narrat Josephus, occisi sūt vndecies cētū mille, præter eos qui capti sūt, 90. millia. Tādē vrbis excidiū sequutū: & id quod posteris suis ipsi quoqz imprecati sunt, ira Dei occupat eos ad extremum vsque. Sed hoc admiratione magis dignum, quod reliquiae illius populi aliquae sint reseruatae Dei infinita & admirabili misericordia. Hoc iudicio tam horrendo admonentur omnes, ne reos se faciant innocentis sanguinis, praesertim Iesu Christi: quem rursus sibi crucifigunt, & cuius sanguinem conculcant, quotquot veritatem hanc Christi iam cognitam impugnant. Heb. 6. & 10 Admonemur quoque ne temere imprecantes nobis ipsi, recipiamus in nos onera quibus non sumus pares. Nam iusto Dei iudicio fit, ut qui vel verbo temerario aut malitioso se ipsi onerat Dei iudiciis, re ipsa tandem iis iudiciis onerentur.
units.tr: Heb. 7. 26. Now something must be said about the Jews. Of them we must admit that, if the consciousness of Christ's innocence led Pilate to cast off from himself and his shoulders that burden of innocent blood, then the priests and the rest of the Jews were either affected by no consciousness or sense of Christ's innocence, since they took upon themselves and their posterity so heavy a burden, so gladly (for ignorance is always bold and rash), or else they must have done this from the most obstinate malice, even against their conscience. This I think more likely, for malice is no less bold than ignorance, and indeed is even bolder. Malicious men, eager for vengeance, do not hesitate to bind themselves with curses and to hell, since malice so blinds wretched men that they cannot even tell hell apart. That the Jews acted from malice rather than from any ignorance in what they did against Christ is attested by the Prophets, and the Apostles bear witness too, who ascribed this whole deed to the malice and obstinacy of the Jews. Nor do I deny that Pilate also acted from malice in what he did to Christ. But the difference between him and the Jews is wide. For Pilate also acted from weakness, namely from fear, which they inspired in him, lest he be accused of treason as a guilty party, and from fear too lest a tumult arise among the people. But what, I ask, was the cause of the Jews' fear? Malice alone drove them. Moreover, Pilate was malicious not against the light and illumination of the Holy Spirit supplied from the Word of God, but only against the light of nature and that natural conscience. Such malice certainly does not make that sin against the Holy Spirit. But the Jews maliciously assailed even that light of the Word and resisted the Holy Spirit: "You always resist the Holy Spirit," says Stephen, "as your fathers did, so do you" (Acts 7. 51). Hence, since without doubt some of them certainly sinned against the Holy Spirit, they were struck with final impenitence, the penalty with which God is wont to punish that kind of sin. What is surprising here, if such a judgment fell upon them as upon no nation ever? For in one siege alone, as Josephus relates, eleven hundred thousand were slain, besides the ninety thousand who were taken captive. At last the destruction of the city followed, and what they had themselves called down upon their posterity, the wrath of God overtook them to the very end. But this is more worthy of wonder: that some remnant of that people has been preserved by the infinite and wonderful mercy of God. By this most dreadful judgment all are admonished not to make themselves guilty of innocent blood, especially the blood of Jesus Christ, whom they crucify afresh and whose blood they trample underfoot, as many as assail this truth of Christ now known (Heb. 6. and 10.). We are also admonished not to rashly invoke curses upon ourselves and take upon us burdens to which we are not equal. For by the just judgment of God it comes about that whoever burdens himself, by a rash or malicious word, with the judgments of God, is in the end himself actually burdened by those judgments.

units.la: Tunc dimisit eis Pilatus. Pilatus vbi sese exoneravit, referente hic Matthaeo iam rem aggreditur sedulo: Barabbam dimittit, Iesum condemnat: condemnatum denuo flagellat. Idipsum alij fere ad verbum referunt, Marc. 15. Luc. 23. Iohan. 19. 16. Obstupefacta enim semel conscientia, & ut Paulus ait, Ephes. 4. Postea qua coepit quis dedolere, tum is dedit se proteruiae ad patrandam impuritatem. Quamobrem, ut quis velit se seruari a certa pernicie, seruet conscientiam, eiusque sensum aliquem: Quo amisso, quid prohibet quominus quis se praecipitem det in obuia quaeque, & in perniciem denique suam ipsius? Nihil enim potest sensu discernere. Notandum quod habet Marcus hoc fecisse Pilatum, ut Iudaeis gratificaretur ac satisfaceret. Studet fere iudices & viri principes populares esse, sibique populi gratiam conciliare. Quod equidem non prorsus damno, modo id sincere: Sed hoc reprehendo, quod nimis auide captet quidem gratiam peruersae plebis, & id quidem non sine malis quibusque mediis. Rediment enim eam vel dimissione nocentis, vel condemnatione innocentis. Sed quid hoc sequitur? An Pilatus obtinuit gratiam populi huius peruersissimi? Historia habet a populo isto accusatum hunc ob male gestam prouinciam, ut erat quidem vir malus & totus corruptus. Idem necesse est eueniat iis quicunque volunt chare adeo ingrati ac peruersi populi gratiam redimere. Dent operam viri Principes, ut semper bona cum con-
units.tr: Then Pilate released them. When Pilate had discharged himself, Matthew now relates with care what follows: he releases Barabbas, condemns Jesus, and then has him flogged after the condemnation. The others relate almost the same words (Mark 15; Luke 23; John 19. 16). For once conscience has been stunned, as Paul says (Eph. 4), when a man has ceased to feel, then he gives himself over to shamelessness, to commit every impurity. Therefore, if anyone wishes to be kept from certain destruction, let him keep his conscience and some sense of it. Once that is lost, what prevents a man from throwing himself headlong into whatever lies in his way, and finally into his own ruin? For he can discern nothing by sense. It should be noted that Mark says Pilate did this in order to gratify and satisfy the Jews. Judges and men in high office usually strive to be popular and to win the favour of the people. I do not altogether condemn this, provided it is done sincerely. But I find fault with the fact that he eagerly sought the favour of a perverse populace, and that not without every sort of wicked means. For he bought it back either by releasing the guilty or by condemning the innocent. But what follows from this? Did Pilate obtain the favour of this most perverse people? History tells that this same people accused him of misgoverning his province, for he was indeed a wicked man and wholly corrupt. The same must happen to all who wish to buy back the favour of a people so ungrateful and perverse. Let rulers take care always to keep good conscience at the head of their affairs, and let them strive always to present themselves approved before God, if indeed they do not wish to be slaves of the wretchedness and perverse populace, serving its depraved and wayward lusts.

units.la: {a} Iudicis iniquitatis: Praemium iniquitatis suae recipit Pilatus. scientia praesint: studeant semper se probatos Deo sistere, siquidem velint non servi esse miseriae & peruersae plebis, ad inseruiendum eius prauae peruersaeque libidini. Hactenus fuerunt accusatio Domini & condemnatio: nunc prosequemur quae intercesserunt inter condemnationem & crucifixionem, eaque repetemus partim ex Matthaeo, partim ex Marco.
units.tr: {a} Judge of iniquity: Pilate receives the reward of his iniquity. So far have we dealt with the accusation and condemnation of the Lord. Now we shall pursue what took place between the condemnation and the crucifixion, and we shall go through these things partly from Matthew, partly from Mark.

units.la: Matthaei 27.
units.tr: Matthew 27.

units.la: 27 Tum milites praesidis, quum abduxissent Iesum in praetorium, coegerunt ad eum vniuersam cohortem.
units.tr: 27 Then the governor's soldiers, when they had led Jesus into the praetorium, gathered the whole cohort about him.

units.la: 28 Et cum exuissent eum, circumposuerunt ei chlamydem coccineam:
units.tr: 28 And when they had stripped him, they put a scarlet robe around him.

units.la: 29 Et coronam e spinis contextam impoſuerunt capiti, & arundinem in dextram eius, & genu ante eum summisso illudebant ei dicentes, Aue Rex Iudaeorum.
units.tr: 29 And when they had plaited a crown of thorns, they put it on his head, and a reed in his right hand, and kneeling before him they mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews.

units.la: 30 Et cum inspuissent in eum, ceperunt arundinem illam, & verberabant caput eius.
units.tr: 30 And when they had spat upon him, they took the reed and struck his head.

units.la: Marci 15.
units.tr: Mark 15.

units.la: 16 Milites vero abduxerunt eum intra aulam, id est praetorium, & conuocauerunt totam cohortem:
units.tr: 16 The soldiers then led him away within the hall, which is the praetorium, and called together the whole cohort.

units.la: 17 Et induerunt eum purpura, & circumposuerunt ei plexam coronam spineam:
units.tr: 17 And they clothed him in purple, and put a plaited crown of thorns around him.

units.la: 18 Et ceperunt eum salutare, dicentes, Aue Rex Iudaeorum.
units.tr: 18 And they began to salute him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews.

units.la: 19 Et verberabant eius caput calamo, & inspuebant in eum, ac summissis genibus adorabant eum.
units.tr: 19 And they struck his head with a reed, and spat upon him, and bowing their knees they worshipped him.

units.la: Condemnatum itaque Pilatus tradidit militibus, & Iudaeis crucifigendum: illi vero acceperunt eum, idque lubentiori animo, quam tradidit eum Pilatus. Nullus enim iudex est tam paratus ad tradendum innocentem morti, quam parati sunt carnifices & executores ad eum recipiendum. Iustus aliquis iudex non habet fere ad manum, qui exequantur iustam ipsius voluntatem ac sententiam: tiam: At iniustus quisq; ad manum habet perpetuò,qui exequantur peruersam suam sententiam. Saulus impius habuit in promptu Doegum Ahomaeum ad dandū interneconi octoginta quinque Sacerdotes Domini. At Dauid pius Rex, quum vellet vlcisci in homicidia Ioabi hominis perditi & sanguinarij, questus est se neminem habere, qui exequeretur iustissimam suam voluntatem aduersus hominem flagitiosum, hac edita voce, Homines isti filij Seruiæ fiermiores sunt me. Improbitas & improbi frequentes sese offerunt Regibus ad iniusta quæque decreta exequenda. Probitas autem & probitari adinodum inueniuntur. Diabolus multos inuenit Ministros in terris, Deus vero paucos. Iam acceptum lesum è manu Pilati non statim abducunt ad locum supplicio destinatum: verùm abducut iterum in prætorium & in locum prætorij interiorem, vbi eum iam condemnatum, moriquè adiudicatum, liberius & crudeliùs tractant quàm antea. Congregatis enim ibi omnibus lictoribus & carnificibus, nemo omnium inuenitur qui non exerceat in eum aliquod crudelitatis ac indignitatis genus. Rursus coronant spina, rursus exutum vestibus suis induunt purpurea & regia: Arundinem dextra manu gestandam præbent: Tum flexis genibus eum regem salutant: Aue, inquiunt, Rex Iudæorum. Hinc cœperunt in faciem ipsius insputre, & accepta arundine caput eius verberare: Postremò exutum veste regia, ac inducta rursus sua veste, abduxerunt. Res mira! Quòd si quis vel fur vel latro semel morte adiudicetur, ferè patiuntur in pace eum abduci ad locum supplicij, imò verò consolantur aduersus propinquę mortis terrores: etiam ipsi hominis aduersarij sibi satisfactum esse iam putant, vbi vident hominem iam condemnatum ac morti proximum. At Iesum Christum condemnatum & addictum morti, non sinunt tamen conquiescere, aut respirare. Malitia hominum, quæ est in peccatum aut peccatorem aliquê flagitiosum, modum habet aliquê. Malitia verò hominum in innocentem quemcunque & eum qui Christi causa reus peragitur, nullum habet modum. Filij tenebrarum capitaliter oderunt filios lucis: atque ynquam satis possunt satiari ipsorum sanguinis.
units.tr: So Pilate, having condemned him, handed him over to the soldiers and to the Jews to be crucified. But they received him, and with more willing minds than Pilate had handed him over. For no judge is so ready to deliver an innocent man to death as executioners and hangmen are ready to receive him. A just judge seldom has at hand men to carry out his just will and sentence, but an unjust man always has at hand those who will carry out his perverse sentence. The impious Saul had at ready command Doeg the Edomite, to slay the eighty-five priests of the Lord. But David, a pious king, when he wished to avenge the murder of the wicked and bloodthirsty man Joab, complained that he had no one to carry out his most just will against that criminal, and he uttered this word: "These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too strong for me." Wickedness and wicked men frequently offer themselves to kings to carry out any unjust decree, but goodness and good men are found very rarely. The devil finds many ministers on earth, but God few. Now, having received Jesus from Pilate's hand, they do not at once lead him away to the place appointed for execution; rather, they lead him back into the praetorium and into its inner part, where, now condemned and adjudged to death, they treat him more freely and cruelly than before. For when all the lictors and executioners have gathered there, not one of them is found who does not inflict on him some kind of cruelty and indignity. Again they crown him with thorns, again they strip him of his own clothes and put on him purple and royal robes; they give him a reed to carry in his right hand; then, bending their knees, they salute him as king: "Hail," they say, "King of the Jews." Then they began to spit in his face and, taking the reed, to strike his head. Finally, having stripped him of the royal robe and put his own clothes on him again, they led him away. A remarkable thing! If some thief or robber is once adjudged to death, they usually allow him to be led in peace to the place of execution; indeed, they comfort him against the terrors of impending death, and his enemies themselves think they have had satisfaction once they see the man condemned and close to death. But Jesus Christ, though condemned and handed over to death, they do not allow to rest or draw breath. The malice of men against sin, or against some wicked sinner, has some limit. But the malice of men against any innocent man, and against one who is accused for Christ's sake, has no limit. The children of darkness hate the children of light mortally, and they can never be satiated with their blood.

units.la: 2. Sam. 3. 39. Cohorsim piorum: pio-rum rarus numerus. ne. Sed hic attollendi sunt altius oculi ad Deum, cuius isti & istorum carnificum ira & malitia, tantum ministra: & re quidem ipsa, Pater est qui filium suum portantem nunc humeris suis onus illud peccatorum nostrorum ad extremum usque persequitur: Ex eo enim tempore quo incidit in manus istorum carnificum; Deus pater ita filium exagitauit indesinenter, ut ne respirare quidem ipsum sit passus. Quo docemur horrendum esse peccatori, qui est extra Christum, neque particeps fit passionis ipsius, incidere in manus Dei viuentis. Fieri quidem potest, ut is ad tempus aliquod in hac vita securus agat, & falsa quadam fruatur pace, sed vbi semel Deus in eum manum suam iniecit, nulla est ei amplius pax. Neque satis-fit irę Dei, nisi miseri hominis æterno supplicio: adeo ut nunquam satis admiraturus sit miser ille tantam tamque insatiabilem esse Dei iram.
units.tr: 2 Sam. 3.39. The company of the godly: the number of the godly is rare. But here our eyes must be lifted higher, to God, whose anger and malice these men and their executioners are only the instrument of. Indeed, it is the Father who in truth pursues his Son, bearing on his shoulders that burden of our sins, to the very end; for from the time he fell into the hands of these executioners, God the Father so relentlessly harassed the Son that he did not even allow him to draw breath. From this we are taught how dreadful it is for a sinner, who is outside Christ and does not share in his passion, to fall into the hands of the living God. It is true that such a person may for a time live securely in this life and enjoy a certain false peace; but once God has laid his hand upon him, he has no peace any more. Nor is the wrath of God satisfied except by the eternal punishment of the wretched man, so that the miserable man will never be able to marvel enough that God's anger is so great and so insatiable.

units.la: Matthæi 27.
units.tr: Matthew 27.

units.la: 31 Et postquam illusissent ei, exuerunt eum chlamyde, induerúntque vestimentis suis: & abduxerunt eum vt crucifigerent.
units.tr: 31 And after they had mocked him, they took off his cloak, put his own garments on him, and led him away to crucify him.

units.la: 32 Exeuntes autem inuenerunt quendam Cyrenæum, nomine Simonem, hunc angariauerunt vt attolleret crucem eius.
units.tr: 32 As they went out, they found a certain Cyrenian named Simon, and they compelled him to carry his cross.

units.la: Marci 15.
units.tr: Mark 15.

units.la: 20 Quum autem illusissent ei, exuerunt eum purpura, & induerunt eum suis ipsius vestimentis, eduxeruntq; vt crucifigerent eum.
units.tr: 20 When they had mocked him, they took off the purple, put his own garments on him, and led him out to crucify him.

units.la: 21 Praeterea angariarunt praetereuntem quendam Simonem Cyrenaeum, venientem rure, (patrem Alexandri & Rufi) vt attolleret crucem eius.
units.tr: 21 Moreover, they compelled a certain passer-by, Simon the Cyrenian, coming in from the country (the father of Alexander and Rufus), to carry his cross.

units.la: Lucæ 23.
units.tr: Luke 23.

units.la: 26 Quum igitur abduceret eum, prehenso quodam Simone Cyrenæo, qui veniebat rure, impo suerunt ei crucem ferendam post Iesum.
units.tr: 26 As they led him away, they seized a certain Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid the cross on him to carry after Jesus.

units.la: Iohan.
units.tr: John.

units.la: 16 Tunc ergo tradidit eum ipsis vt crucifigeretur. Assumpserunt autem Iesum & abduxerunt.
units.tr: 16 Then therefore he delivered him to them to be crucified. And they took Jesus and led him away.

units.la: 17 Et ipse bajulans crucem suam prodiens venit in eum locum, qui dicitur Caluariæ, Hebraice autem Golgotha.
units.tr: 17 And he, bearing his own cross, went out to the place called Calvary, but in Hebrew Golgotha.

units.la: POstquam Iesum ita exagitatum induerút veste propria, iam educunt & abducūt ad locum supplicij, ipse vero ibat. Nō trahunt quidem inuitum, sed euntem sua voluntate ac sponte abducunt. Dominus enim volens ibat, ac lubens conscius voluntatis Patris sui: neque eo quod innocens esset, ideo minus volēs ibat. Nam innocentes demum sunt qui lubentes adeunt mortem, præsertim ij qui innocentes sunt in Christi illa innocentia. At qui non innocentes sunt, in ipsius illa innocentia, ij quidem nunquā lubentes moriuntur. Fieri potest vt voluntatem aliquam & lubentiam simulent aut certè ignorent quantum mali sit in morte, iis qui nō moriuntur in Domino: at reuera lubentes mori non possunt. Neque profecto vllam in morte veram habēt consolationem, quotquot in morte non habent conscientias purgatas innocentis illius sanguine. Modus ab Iohanne notatur, quo ibat Dominus ad locum supplicij destinatum: Et ipse ibat portans crucem suam. Portabat, vt verisimile est, eam post se trahendo, factum ex more & consuetudine eorum, qui à Romanis damnati erat ad crucem. Coacti enim sunt suam crucem vel furcam ipsi portare in locum eum, in quem defigenda erat. Vnde furcifæri lingua Romanorum dicti sunt. Hic inter eundum inciderūt, referentibus aliis Euangelistis, Matthæo, Marco, Luca, in Simonem quendam Cyrenæum, patrē Alexandri & Rufi, redeuntem rure. Hunc angariauerunt portare crucem Domini, hoc est adiuuare Dominum portanda cruce sua: sic vt ipse Iesus gestans crucem suam præcederet, Simon verò cum adiuuans pone sequeretur. Hoc non est factum à Iudæis aut militibus, ideo vt Christo parcerent: sed quia ei defecerunt ita vires, vt oneri succumberet: neque id mirum, cum & totam noctem præcedentem insomnē duxerit, & nocte illa tota ac die etiam insequenti, vsque ad tempus illud quo abductus est ad locum supplicij, ita fit exagitatus & exercitatus variis modis, vt ne respirare quidem ei licuerit. Christus autem vna cum humana ista natura, in fe recepit omnes infirmitates nostras, excepto solo peccato. Non caret mysterio hoc, quod coactus fit Simon vna gestare crucem Domini: Fuit enim Simon gentilis ex Cyrene quae vrbs quaedam in Africa erat. Adumbrabat igitur vocationem qua vocandae erant ad tollendam crucem Domini: &, vt loquitur Apostolus, ad exeundum extra castra opprobriumque eius portantes. Iudaei crucem Christi, vel ipsum Christum ne digito quidem suo attingere voluerunt: quia cum cruce sua execrabilem hominem exiftimarunt. Fateor quidem Christum factum a Patre execrationem: sed factus est execratio pro nobis, vt nos fieremus Dei benedictio in illo: estque haec sola benedictio nostra, vt coniungamur cum illo, qui pro nobis erat maledictus. Simon vel hac re beatus fuit, quod coactus est tollere crucem Christi. Haec est gentium & nostra omnium, qui ex gentibus oriundi fumus, vera beatitas, vt exeamus e castris portantes opprobrium Christi. Ita enim futurum est, vt fi cum eo simul patiamur, simul cum eo glorificemur.
units.tr: After they had thus harassed Jesus and clothed him in his own garments, they now bring him out and lead him away to the place of execution; but he himself was going. They do not drag him along unwilling, but lead him away as he goes of his own will and accord. For the Lord was going willingly, gladly conscious of the will of his Father; nor was he any less willing to go because he was innocent. For it is the innocent who go gladly to death, especially those who are innocent in that innocence of Christ. But those who are not innocent in his innocence never die willingly. It may be that those who do not die in the Lord feign some willingness, or at least are ignorant of how much evil there is in death; but in truth they cannot die gladly. Indeed, however many do not have consciences cleansed by that innocent blood, they have no true consolation in death at all. John notes the manner in which the Lord went to the appointed place of execution: And he went out bearing his own cross. He was carrying it, as is likely, by dragging it behind him, according to the custom of those condemned by the Romans to the cross. For they were compelled to carry their own cross or gibbet to the place where it was to be fixed. Hence those so punished were called furcifers in the Roman tongue. Here, as they went, they met, as the other Evangelists Matthew, Mark and Luke report, a certain Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, returning from the country. They compelled this man to carry the cross of the Lord, that is, to help the Lord bear his cross, so that Jesus himself went before carrying his cross, and Simon followed behind helping. This was not done by the Jews or the soldiers to spare Christ; rather his strength failed him so that he gave way under the burden. Nor is this surprising, since he had passed the whole previous night without sleep, and through that night and the whole of the following day, until the time when he was led to the place of execution, he was so harassed and worn down in various ways that he could not even catch his breath. Christ, however, together with this human nature, took upon himself all our infirmities, except sin alone. This is not without mystery, that Simon was compelled to carry the Lord's cross along with him. For Simon was a Gentile from Cyrene, a city in Africa. He therefore foreshadowed the calling by which those were to be called to take up the cross of the Lord and, as the Apostle says, to go forth outside the camp bearing his reproach. The Jews would not touch Christ's cross, nor even Christ himself, with a finger, because they judged him a detestable man together with his cross. I grant that Christ was made a curse by the Father; but he was made a curse for us, so that we might become God's blessing in him; and this alone is our blessing, that we are joined with him who for our sake was accursed. Simon was blessed even by this, that he was compelled to take up the cross of Christ. This is the true blessedness of the Gentiles and of all of us who spring from the Gentiles: to go out of the camp bearing the reproach of Christ. For so it will be: if we suffer together with him, we shall also be glorified together with him.

units.la: Lucæ 23.
units.tr: Luke 23.

units.la: 27 Sequebatur autem eum magna multitudo populi & mulierum: quæ & plangebant & lamentabantur eum.
units.tr: 27 A great multitude of people and of women followed him, who both beat their breasts and lamented over him.

units.la: 28 Conuersus autem ad eas Iesus dixit, Filiæ Hierusalem, ne flete de me, verum de vobis ipsis flete, & de liberis vestris.
units.tr: 28 But Jesus, turning to them, said: Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.

units.la: 29 Nam ecce venient dies quibus dicent, Beatæ steriles, & uteri qui non genuerunt, & vbera quae non lactauerunt.
units.tr: 29 For behold, the days will come when they will say: Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that never bore, and the breasts that never gave suck.

units.la: 30 Tunc incipient dicere montibus, Cadite in nos: & collibus, Operite nos.
units.tr: 30 Then they will begin to say to the mountains, Fall on us; and to the hills, Cover us.

units.la: 31 Nam si in virente ligno ista faciunt, in arido quid fiet?
units.tr: 31 For if they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?

units.la: NArrat hic Lucas quod cum Christus abduceretur ad locum supplicij, multitudo populi & mulierū ipsum sit insequuta, spectandi scilicet gratia. Voluit enim pater totam hanc rem peragi in publico quasi orbis theatro, eo nimirum tempore, hoc est Paschatis tempore, quo ex omnibus gentibus non pauci conflu-xerunt Hierosolyma. Voluit toto mundo inspectante accusari filium suum pro tribunali iudicis, condemnari, abduci ad supplicij locum, denique crucifigi. Peccatum quoduis, quantumuis secreto perpetratum, natura sua puniendum est manifesto pudore & confusione. Ideo Christus, cū receperit in se peccata mūdi, oportuit inter alia pati eum manifestam ignominiam, & ad eam ferendam produci in conspectum totius mundi: eo scilicet fine, vt quotquot in Christo reperiuntur peccatores, liberentur, in illo extremo iudicio à manifesta ignominia. Nam quod ad eos, qui tum in Christo non reperientur, ij quidem patientur ignominiam apertam, inspectantibus omnibus Angelis pariter & hominibus: Eritque haec aliquota pars inferorum illorum, quos perpetientur in illo die. Et mulierum. Hic narrat Lucas foeminas Hierosolymitanas prosequutas Iesum, cum lachrymis & lamentis. Hauddubiò istud contigit non citra Dei prouidentiam: vt non tantum in tota accusatione praecedente & in condemnatione innocentis illius perhiberetur testimonium innocentiae ab ipso Pilato iudice: sed etiam non careret innocentiae suae testimonio in ipso itinere per quod ad crucem abducebatur. Vt autem omnia quae Christo euenerunt ad nos aliquo modo trahenda sunt: ita & hoc quoque vsui nobis esse debet: ideo enim Christus innocens deflctus est, vt qui in ipso sunt innocentes, licet in se alioqui peccatores sint, inueniant tamen qui ipsorum innocentiam defleant, si quando vsu venerit vt sint miseri. Inuenient autem maxime in illo iudicio extremo eos qui ipsorum miserabuntur. At qui tum non comperient induti ipsius innocentia, ij quidem
units.tr: Luke here relates that as Christ was led to the place of execution, a multitude of people and women followed him, to watch, of course. The Father wished this whole matter to be carried out in public, as it were in the theatre of the world, at that time, namely the time of the Passover, when not a few came together to Jerusalem from all nations. He wished his Son to be accused before the judge's tribunal in full view of the whole world, condemned, led to the place of punishment, and finally crucified. Any sin, however secretly committed, is by its nature to be punished with manifest shame and confusion. Therefore Christ, when he had taken upon himself the sins of the world, had to suffer, among other things, open disgrace, and to be brought forward before the eyes of the whole world to bear it; clearly with this end, that all who are found in Christ as sinners may be freed from open disgrace at that last judgment. As for those who will not then be found in Christ, they indeed will suffer open shame, with all the angels and men looking on; and this will be a part of that hell which they will undergo on that day. And of women. Here Luke relates that the women of Jerusalem followed Jesus with tears and lamentations. Undoubtedly this happened not without God's providence: so that not only throughout the whole preceding accusation and condemnation of that innocent man was testimony to his innocence given by Pilate the judge himself, but he also would not lack a testimony to his innocence on the very road by which he was led to the cross. And since all that happened to Christ must in some way be drawn to us, so this too ought to be of use to us. For Christ was lamented as innocent so that those who are innocent in him, although in themselves otherwise sinners, may nonetheless find people who lament their innocence, if it should happen that they are wretched. Indeed, they will find those who pity them, especially at that last judgment. But those who then will not be found clothed in his innocence, indeed

units.la: QQq non inuenient qui ipsorum miseriam sint defleċturi aut miserabri: sed omnes tum Angeli & homines electi iustum in ipsos Dei iudicium, sunt approbaturi.
units.tr: will not find anyone who will lament or pity their misery; but all the angels and elect men will then approve God's just judgment upon them.

units.la: Christus audito fletu & lamentis mulierum conuersus ad eas dixit, Filiae Hierusalem, ne flete super me, verum super vos ipsis, & super liberis vestris. Rationem reddit cur super his flendum sit a grauissimo illo iudicio quod correpturum sit vrbem Hierusalem: Quo ipso adumbrat iudicium illud extremum futurum: Iudicium autem quod minatur confirmat a maiori. Si in virenti, inquit, ligno ista faciunt, in arido quid fiet? Viride lignum intelligit IESV, qui innocens & fructuosus fuit in te, etsi in nobis reus. Aridum autem lignum sumus nos qui in nobis ipsis sumus aridi & infructuosi, & ad nullam rem aliam praeterquam ad confusionem vtiles. Fletus causa est sensus miseriae vel nostrae ipsorum, vel aliorum: vt cum συμπα-θέα afficimur & commiseratione aliorum. Fleuerunt igitur mulieres ex συμπαθέα Christi, & ex sensu miseriae ipsius: Quod profecto non plane reprehendit Christus. Dolere enim cum dolentibus laudabile est. Sed desiderat in ipsis sensum miseriae suae aliquem, ex quo fletum hunc & luctum optobebat in primis existere. Praesertim cum Christus miser factus sit peccati & miseriae ipsarum causa: Nostra peccata Christum transfixerunt, vt loquitur Iohannes. Hoc itaque a nobis in tota hac passione Christi, quoties de ea audimus, aduertendum, vt non tam oculos directos habeamus in carnifices & tortores illos, quam in peccata nostra ipsorum, & fletus noster exurgat ex sensu peccati & miseriae nostrae, propter quā Christus indignissima queq; passus est. Hoc tamen hic non praetereundum, quod Christus solas istas mulieres flētes in itinere dignatus sit alloquio, eāsq; solas docuerit: hinc enim discimus; Beatos esse qui lugent & deflet miseriam, vel suam, vel aliorum, quoniam ipsi consolationem accipient. Et Deus habitat in corde contrito.
units.tr: Christ, hearing the weeping and lamentation of the women, turning to them, said: Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but over yourselves and over your children. He gives the reason why they must weep over these things, namely the most grievous judgment that is about to overtake the city of Jerusalem; by this very thing he foreshadows that last judgment which is to come, and he confirms the judgment he threatens by an argument from the greater. If, he says, they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry? By the green wood he means Jesus himself, who was innocent and fruitful in himself, though guilty in us. The dry wood, however, are we, who in ourselves are dry and unfruitful, and useful for nothing but confusion. The cause of weeping is a sense of misery, either our own or another's, when we are moved with sympathy and compassion for others. The women therefore wept out of sympathy for Christ, and from a sense of his misery; which Christ certainly does not altogether blame. For to grieve with those who grieve is praiseworthy. But he desires in them some sense of their own misery, from which this weeping and mourning ought chiefly to arise, especially since Christ was made wretched for the sake of sin, and of the wretchedness of these very women: "Our sins pierced Christ," as John says. Therefore this must be noted by us throughout this whole passion of Christ, whenever we hear of it: that we should direct our eyes not so much at those executioners and torturers as at our own sins, and that our weeping should arise from a sense of sin and of our own misery, on account of which Christ suffered the most unworthy things. Yet this must not be passed over here: that Christ deigned to address these women alone, weeping on the way, and taught these alone. For from this we learn that those are blessed who mourn and weep over misery, whether their own or another's, since they will receive consolation. And God dwells with the contrite of heart.

units.la: Lucae 23.
units.tr: Luke 23.

units.la: 32 Ducebantur autem etiam alij duo, qui erant malefici, cum eo necandi.
units.tr: 32 And there were also led two others, who were evildoers, to be put to death with him.

units.la: EST & hoc quartum quod narrat Lucas, quódque Latrones ad historiam itineris pertinet. Simul cum Iesu ducuntur ad locum supplicij duo insignes latrones: Et hoc quoque ad ignominiam augendam spectat, quæ peccatum necessario consequitur, vel in nobis ipsis, vel in Christo nostra causa, qui vt antea ignominiosus fuit respectu multitudinis eum insequutæ, dum iter faceret ad locum supplicij: ita nunc id accedit ad ignominiam, quòd cum latronibus, tanquam latro, trahatur ad supplicium. Qua in re non tam intueor carnificum ipsorum malitiam, quàm Dei consilium dispensantis totam hanc rem, idque iustissimè. Iesus enim Christus factus pro nobis vas & fideiussor sustinuit onus peccatorum nostrorum, non modò latrocinij, sed aliorum omnium peccatorum, quæcúque cadere possunt in electos Dei: imò sustinuit peccata alterius ex duobus illis latronibus, qui vnà cum ipso ad supplicium trahebatur, vt videbimus postea suo loco. Quamobrem non est quòd miremur, à Patre iustissimo filium tantæ ignominiæ expositum fuisse: verùm miremur potiùs tantam Dei erga nos misericordiam qui nostra causa, vt nos liberaremur ab ignominia, non pepercit vnigenito suo.
units.tr: This is the fourth thing Luke relates, and the robbers belong to the history of the journey. Two notorious robbers are led to the place of execution together with Jesus. This also serves to increase the shame that necessarily follows sin, whether in ourselves or in Christ for our sake. Just as earlier he was disgraced in the eyes of the crowd that followed him while he made his way to the place of execution, so now the shame is increased by being dragged to death as a robber alongside robbers. In this I do not look so much at the cruelty of the executioners as at the counsel of God, who arranged this whole matter, and most justly so. For Jesus Christ, made a surety and guarantor for us, bore the burden of our sins, not only of robbery but of all other sins that can fall upon the elect of God. Indeed he bore the sin of one of those two robbers who were dragged to death with him, as we shall see later in its place. Therefore we should not be surprised that the most just Father exposed his Son to such shame. Rather we should marvel at the great mercy of God toward us, who for our sake did not spare his only Son, so that we might be freed from shame.

units.la: Matthæi 27.
units.tr: Matthew 27.

units.tr: 34 They gave him vinegar to drink, mixed with gall; and when he had tasted it, he would not drink.

units.tr: Luke 23.

units.tr: 17 And he, bearing his own cross, went out into the place which is called the place of a skull, but in Hebrew Golgotha:

units.tr: 18 Where they crucified him, and two others with him, on either side, but Jesus in the middle.

units.la: NVnc de crucifixione eius, ac primum de loco in quo crucifixus est dicendum nonnihil. Vocatur locus Hebraicè Golgotha, quod est interpretatum Caluariæ locus. Non est dubium quin situs fuerit hic locus extra portas vrbis, neque etiam quæstio est quin Christus tanquam reiectaneus quis ac reprobus tractus sit ad supplicium, extra portas vrbis subeundum, id quod sacrificiis legalibus iam olim adumbratum est: nam animalia immolanda cremabantur extra castra: eorum deinde sanguis pro expiatione inferebatur in sacrarium.
