Ita Christus extra vrbem crucifixus est, vt ipse deinde cum sanguine suo ingrederetur in cæleste illud sacrarium, vt esset pro nobis æterna expiatio.Sed de nomine tota est controuersia, cur locus Caluariæ sit appellatus. Putant quidam locum sic dictum, quia Caluaria Adæ primi hominis effossa est ex eodem illo loco, in quo defixa est crux Christi. Sed hanc sententiam vanitatibus & fabulis Papisticis annumero. Putant alij ita dictum locum, quia mortuorum hominum crania & ossa in eum locum congesta reseruabantur. Alij deniq; ex figura loci dictum putant. Fuit enim locus quidam eminens & rotundus, non absimilis hominis demortui cranio vel caluariæ, cuiusmodi solent esse loca illa supplicij extra vrbium portas sita. Et quidem qui eum locum in quo crucifixus fuit Christus viderunt, narrant eam hodierno die loci esse figura, quæ Caluariæ est dea mortui hominis. Sed vtcunq; est, certè est locum fuisse ignominiosum, & in quo supplicio affici consueuerunt malefici quiq; vt vel ex loco ipso in quo supplicium passus est Christus possis discere quanta tum fuerit in eum Iudæorum rabies: quæ quidè vt tu fuit Iudæorū aduersus lucè ipsam, nèpe Iesum Christū acerbissima ita cōtinuò post Christi passionē nō desiit flagrare in yerè Christianos.
units.tr: Now something must be said about his crucifixion, and first about the place where he was crucified. The place is called in Hebrew Golgotha, which is interpreted the place of a skull. There is no doubt that this place lay outside the gates of the city, nor is there any question that Christ, treated as one cast out and rejected, was led to execution to be undergone outside the city gates. This was already foreshadowed in the legal sacrifices: the animals to be offered were burned outside the camp, and their blood was then carried into the sanctuary for atonement. So Christ was crucified outside the city, so that he might afterwards enter with his own blood into that heavenly sanctuary, to be an eternal atonement for us. But the whole controversy is over the name, why the place was called the place of a skull. Some think the place was so named because the skull of Adam, the first man, was dug up from the same spot where the cross of Christ was fixed. But I count this opinion among the vanities and fables of the Papists. Others think the place was so called because the skulls and bones of dead men were heaped together and kept there. Still others think it was named from the shape of the place. For it was a certain raised and rounded spot, not unlike the skull or cranium of a dead man, the kind of places that are usually set outside the city gates for execution. And indeed those who have seen the place where Christ was crucified report that today it has the shape of the skull of a dead man. But however it was, it was certainly an ignominious place, where malefactors were commonly put to death. You may learn from the place itself where Christ suffered how great was the fury of the Jews against him. This fury of the Jews against the very light, namely Jesus Christ, did not cease to blaze in the same bitter way against true Christians even after the passion of Christ.

units.la: Narratio eorum quæ loco & tempore crucifixionis gesta sunt. 1. Locus extra vrbem. Cur ita appellatus. Iudæorum in Christū rabies. nos quosq; & filios lucis.Sed ego hic altius attollo oculos adDei Patris consilium illud,quo filiu suum omnibus modis ignominiosum esse voluit,vt pote peccatum factum pro nobis,vt loquitur Apostolus.Etiam a loco in quo passus est voluit aliquid accedere ad ignominiam filij sui: ita tamen vt ignominiam illam ex loco nihil impedire voluerit gloria filij & gloriosum illum triumphu,qui tanto maior fuit, quato locus fuit ignominiosior. Sed quod nobis ex hoc loco ignominioso in quo Christus est crucifixus discedu est,hic habe.Ii qui in illo extremo iudicio (cuius typus quida & imago quaedam viua videtur mihi hoc Christi iudicium,qui tu pro reprobo habitus est,danatus est vt reprobus,& crucifixus vt reprobus quida) Ii,inqua,quotquot reperientur in illo iudicio extra Christum Iesum,vt omnibus modis ignominiosi futuri sunt: illa locus ille quisquis tande futurus est, in quo diuerabuntur in aeternu ac cruciabuntur,ignominia eorum exaggeraturus est: vt e contra, qui in eo iudicio reperiuntur in Christo, tecti ipsius ignominia,vt ex aliis rebus pluribus gloriosi futuri sunt,ita ex gloriose illo loco,& caelesti illo paradiso,accedet ipsis gloria quadam ineffabilis.Christus enim passus est in loco foedo & ignominioso,vt ij habitet in aeterna gloria in loco gloriose.
units.tr: An account of what was done in the place and time of the crucifixion. 1. The place outside the city. Why it was so named. The fury of the Jews against Christ. ...us also, and sons of the light. But here I lift my eyes higher, to that counsel of the Father by which he willed his Son to be disgraced in every way, as one made sin for us, as the Apostle says. He also willed something to be added to the shame of his Son from the place where he suffered, yet in such a way that the shame of the place did not hinder the glory of the Son and that glorious triumph, which was all the greater as the place was more ignominious. But what is to be drawn for us from this ignominious place where Christ was crucified, let this be held. Those who in that final judgment (of which this judgment of Christ, in which he was counted as reprobate, condemned as a reprobate, and crucified as a reprobate, seems to me a certain type and living image) shall be found outside Christ Jesus, they will certainly be disgraced in every way. That place, whatever it will finally be, in which they will dwell and be tormented forever, will heighten their shame. Conversely, those who are found in Christ in that judgment, covered by his shame, will be glorious in many other things, and from that glorious place and that heavenly paradise there will come to them a certain ineffable glory. For Christ suffered in a foul and ignominious place, so that these might dwell in eternal glory in a glorious place.

units.la: Narrant Matthaeus & Marcus, quod postqua ventum esset ad locu supplicij ante crucifixione, sitienti obtulerint bibendu acetum,cu felle mixtu:ita Matthaeus:Marcus vero appellat vinu myrrhatu. Sed res eadem est, na myrrha habet amarore fellis:de hac potione varie sentiunt. Putat quidam delicata fuisse,& a mulieribus,quae cum fletu & planctu prosequute sunt,oblata,ad hoc vt minus sentiret dolorem du haereret in ta crudeli & laeta morte. Quida vero ideo data hanc potionem ita temperata asserunt, vt mors ipsius accelararetur.Myrrha enim habere facultate ac vim egerendi sanguinis traditur.At ego potione hanc Christo propinata credo a Iudaeis & militibus,idq; in ludibriu: vt aute acetosa erat simul & amara,ita propinatum ex acerbo & amaro animo, idq; ad exacerbandu ipsius dolore.Atq; huic potioni ascribo aliqua passionis Domini partem.Adducor ad hac sententiam, tu propter prophetiam illam quae est Psal. 69. 22,
units.tr: Matthew and Mark relate that when they had come to the place of execution, before the crucifixion, they offered him, as he thirsted, wine to drink mixed with gall. So Matthew; but Mark calls it wine mixed with myrrh. Yet the thing is the same, for myrrh has the bitterness of gall. Opinions differ about this drink. Some think it was a soothing drink, offered by the women who followed him with weeping and lamentation, so that he would feel the pain less and persevere in so cruel and yet joyful a death. Others say that this drink was prepared in such a way so that his death would be hastened, for myrrh is said to have the power of driving out blood. But I believe that this drink was offered to Christ by the Jews and the soldiers, and that in mockery. Just as it was both sour and bitter, so it was offered out of a bitter and harsh spirit, and to increase his pain. And to this drink I ascribe some part of the Lord's passion. I am led to this view by that prophecy in Psalm 69:22,

units.la: OQo iij
units.tr: OQo iij

units.la: In siti mea bibendum dant mihi acetum: tum propter historiam sequentem in qua dicitur Christo pendenti e cruce illudentes attulisse spongiam aceto intinctam, orique ipsius applicasse.Ex hac passionis Christi parte, siti nimirum Christi, primum, deinde potu acetoso ac amaro, licet discere quanta sit sitis futura eorum qui extra Christum compescentur in extremo illo iudicio, cui istud praesens Christi plane ἀνάλογον esse videtur, & in illa siti tam corporis quam animae, quam nulla sit futura ipsorum refrigeratio, quibus nihil nisi poculum amarissimae irae diuinae propinabitur epotandum in aeternum. At quotquot in eo iudicio, in Christo reperientur, ipse Christus erit illis fons aquae viuentis, quam ineffabili cum suavitate haurient in sempiternum. De Christo deinde narratur, Quod cum gustasset, noluit bibere. Abhorrebat nimirum ipsa natura a potu tam amaro. Et Christus etsi vim illatā sibi ab aliis patientissimè tulerit, tamen vim sibi ipsi inferre noluit. Gustasse tamen dicitur potum illū, quem alioqui amarum fuisse satis cognovit: ea nimirum re demonstrans nihil fuisse tam amarū, quod ipse non lubens gustarit, ut nos gustaremus, imo hauriremus, ac potare-mus dulcia ac suavia omnia in aeternum.
units.tr: In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink; and also because of the following narrative, in which it is said that, mocking Christ as he hung from the cross, they brought a sponge soaked in vinegar and applied it to his mouth. From this part of Christ's passion, namely his thirst, and then the sour and bitter drink, one may learn how great will be the thirst of those who are restrained outside Christ in that final judgment. This present scene of Christ seems to be plainly analogous [ἀνάλογον] to that judgment, and in that thirst, both of body and of soul, there will be no refreshment for them, to whom nothing but the cup of the most bitter wrath of God will be poured out to be drunk forever. But whoever in that judgment is found in Christ, Christ himself will be to them a fountain of living water, which they will drink in with ineffable sweetness forever. Next it is related of Christ: When he had tasted it, he would not drink. His very nature shrank from a drink so bitter. And although Christ bore with the greatest patience the violence done to him by others, yet he would not do violence to himself. Yet he is said to have tasted that drink, which he surely knew to be bitter; by this he showed that nothing was so bitter that he did not willingly taste it, so that we might taste it, indeed drink it, and forever drink all things sweet and pleasant.

units.la: Nunc veniendū ad ipsum crucifixionis actū. Sic igitur sitibundū veste sua exuunt, exutum tollunt in crucem, & expansum cruci affigunt perforatis manibus ac pedibus, sicut de ipso praedicatum fuit, foderunt manus meas & pedes meos. Atque iam crucifixo Christo testatus est Deus de caelo eum factum fuisse pro nobis execrationem. Fuit quidem iam inde ab ipsa conceptione ad crucifixionem usque Christus alioqui in se benedictus, maledictus vero fuit propter peccata nostra. Verum maledictio illa & execratio non adeo manifesto inspecta est ante mortem illam crucis execrabilem, de qua scriptum est in lege: Execrabilis quisquis pendet e ligno. Ex illa autē execrabili mortē, qua testatus est Deus Pater execrabilē fuisse ac maledictum filium suum, discimus tandem manifestatum iri execrabili illa apud inferos morte, maledictos esse eos, quotquot extra Christum inuenientur in illo die: de iis loquor quorum peccatum & vetus homo non fuit crucifixus vnà cū Christo crucifixo, & quorum χιγγεφω quod aduersus ipsos erat, cruci Christi affixum, deletum non fuit, & è medio sublatum. Ita enim loquitur Paulus de fœdere illo operum, quo tanquam chirographo suo obligantur omnes peccatores ad mortem execrabilem & æternam. Oportet enim crucifigi in inferis illo die, & in illo iudicio nos ipsos, nisi iam ante cum Christo peccatum nostrum crucifixū fuerit. Quamobrem nihil magis sollicitè curandum in hac vita, quàm hoc, vt certi simus de peccato nostro, & vetere homine, quod cū Christo crucifixus sit. Nulla autè ex re alia id melius cognoscemus, quàm ex continua in hac vita carnis mortificatione: quod quidem necessarium est effectum peccati cū Christo crucifixi. Nā cuius peccatum per Christi crucé & sanguinem semel remissum est, quoad reatum peccati attinet: profectò necesse est per eiusdem Christi Spiritū inhærens in ipso peccatum mortificetur.
units.tr: Now we come to the act of crucifixion itself. So they strip him of his garments, since he is thirsty, lift him up, once stripped, onto the cross, and fix him to it, stretched out, with his hands and feet pierced, as was foretold of him: they pierced my hands and my feet. And when Christ had been crucified, God testified from heaven that he had been made a curse for us. Indeed, from his conception until his crucifixion Christ was in himself blessed, but he was made accursed for our sins. Yet that curse and execration was not so plainly seen before that cursed death on the cross, of which it is written in the law: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. From that accursed death, by which God the Father testified that his Son was accursed and execrated, we learn that at last it will be made manifest that those who are found outside Christ on that day will be accursed by that same accursed death in the underworld. I speak of those whose sin and old man were not crucified together with the crucified Christ, and whose handwriting [χειρόγραφον] against them was not nailed to the cross of Christ, blotted out and taken away. For Paul speaks in this way of that covenant of works, by which all sinners are bound, as by their own handwriting, to a cursed and eternal death. For we must be crucified in the underworld on that day, and at that judgment ourselves, unless our sin has already been crucified with Christ. Therefore nothing in this life is to be cared for more anxiously than this, that we be certain about our sin and the old man, that they have been crucified with Christ. And we shall know this better from nothing else than from the continual mortification of the flesh in this life, which is indeed the necessary effect of sin crucified with Christ. For the sin of him whose guilt has once been remitted through the cross and blood of Christ must certainly be mortified by the Spirit of the same Christ dwelling in him.

units.la: Marci 15.
units.tr: Mark 15.

units.la: 25 Erat autē hora tertia quando crucifixerūt eū.
units.tr: 25 And it was the third hour when they crucified him.

units.la: DE hora illa in qua crucifixus est Christus, nō est hīc planè tacendum. Marcus commemorat cruci affixū hora tertia: quod vt melius intelligatur, opus est videamus, quomodo Iudæi noctem suam ac diem soliti sint partiri. Noctem perinde ac diem in duodecim horas distribuerunt, noctem inchoantes ab occasu Solis, & eã finientes Solis ortu: rursus diem circumscribentes ortu & occasu Solis. Fuit & alia partitio apud eos tam diei quā noctis: noctē enim distribuerunt in quatuor partes, quas totidem vigilias dixerūt, singulis vigiliis tres horas annumerantes. Itidem diem in totidem partes, siue quadrantes, distribuerunt, singulis quadrantibus tres horas adscribentes: primum quadrantem ab ortu Solis, siue primo diluculo numerarunt, & horam primam à prima hora vocârunt: secundum quadrantem ab hora tertia exclusiuè numerarunt, in horam sextam inclusiuè, & tertiā ab hora tertia vocarunt. Tertium quadrantem ab hora sexta exclusiuè numerarunt in horam duodecimam inclusiuè, & nonam dixerunt: ergo tertiæ horæ nomine intelligit Marcus spatium illud trium horarum, siue secundū quadrantem, quem tertiam ab hora diei tertia, à qua in
units.tr: Concerning the hour in which Christ was crucified, we must not be silent here. Mark records that he was fixed to the cross at the third hour. To understand this better, we need to see how the Jews were accustomed to divide their night and day. They divided the night, just as the day, into twelve hours, beginning the night at sunset and ending it at sunrise, and again they bounded the day by sunrise and sunset. There was also another division among them, of both day and night: for they divided the night into four parts, which they called watches, counting three hours for each watch. Likewise they divided the day into as many parts, or quarters, assigning three hours to each quarter. They counted the first quarter from sunrise, or first dawn, and called it the first hour. They counted the second quarter from the third hour, excluding it, up to the sixth hour, including it, and called it the third hour, reckoning from the third hour, with which it began. They counted the third quarter from the sixth hour, excluding it, up to the twelfth hour, including it, and called it the ninth. So by the name of the third hour Mark understands that span of three hours, or the second quarter, which they called the third from the third hour of the day, from which it began.

units.la: Hora prima Iudæorum. choabatur, vocarunt. Apparet autem crucifixum fuisse Christum iam fere completo secundo quadrante, vel tertia hora, quum Iohannes condemnatū Christum scribat hora fermè sexta, hoc est, paulo ante quadrantem tertium, qui sexta ideo dicitur, quod initium capiat ab hora sexta exclusiue, vt modo diximus. Quod si condemnatus est hora fermè sexta, profectò maior pars tertiæ elapsa fuit cum condemnatus est Dominus. Oportuit igitur crucifixum esse, cum iam tota tertia fere esset elapsa, & instaret sexta siue tertius quadrans. Videtur mihi intra vndecimam nostram & duodecimam, si tempus reducatur ad calculum, Dominum & condemnatum, & crucifixum fuisse. Pauxillum enim temporis inter sententiam damnatoriam, & executionem sententiæ interceßit, ita accelerante crucem & mortem Domini Iudæorum malitia, vel potius paterna ira in filium qui obiit vadimonium pro peccatis nostris. Quæ res manifesto est iudicio iudicium illud in reprobos futurum, celeriter perficiedum esse, adeo vt inter sententiam damnatoriā, hac nimirum {Maledicti abite à me in ignem æternum, qui paratus est diabolo & Angelis ipsius} & executione illius sententiæ breuissimum tempus sit interuenturum: quin lata sententia illa condemnationis, celerrime rapiedi sunt ad supplicium æternum. Faxit Dominus, vt in illo die reperiamur in Christo Iesu, & participes cum illo fiamus huius iudicij, quod est imago quæ là viua illius futuri & grauissimi.
units.tr: First hour of the Jews. Now it appears that Christ was crucified when the second quarter was nearly complete, or at the third hour, since John writes that Christ was condemned at about the sixth hour, that is, a little before the third quarter, which is called the sixth because it begins from the sixth hour, excluding it, as we have just said. But if he was condemned at about the sixth hour, then surely most of the third hour had elapsed when the Lord was condemned. Therefore he must have been crucified when almost all of the third hour had passed and the sixth, or third quarter, was at hand. It seems to me that if the time is reckoned exactly, both the condemnation and the crucifixion of the Lord took place between our eleventh and twelfth hours. For only a little time passed between the sentence of condemnation and its execution, since the malice of the Jews hastened the cross and death of the Lord, or rather the Father's wrath against the Son who undertook to answer for our sins. This plainly shows that the judgment to come against the reprobate will be carried out swiftly, so that between the sentence of condemnation, namely this one, {Depart from me, accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels}, and the execution of that sentence, the shortest interval will intervene; indeed, once the sentence of condemnation is pronounced, they will be swiftly dragged away to eternal punishment. May the Lord grant that on that day we be found in Christ Jesus and become partakers with him in that judgment, which is a living image of that future and most grave one.

units.la: Lucæ 23.
units.tr: Luke 23.

units.la: 34 Iesus autē dicebat, Pater, remitte hoc ipsis, nesciunt enim quid faciant: partientes vero vestimenta eius iecerunt sortem.
units.tr: 34 But Jesus said, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." And dividing his garments, they cast lots.

units.la: HIc vnum occurrit, quod Christus videtur fecisse interea dum ipsum cruci affigunt. Precatus est pro iis, qui ipsum crucifixerunt, reliqua ad ignominiam pertinent. Pater, remitte iis, inquit, nesciunt enim quid faciant. Petrus dicit Christum conuitiis affectum, non vicissim conuitiatum, & quòd cum malis afficeretur, non minabatur, sed committebat vindictam ei, qui iuste iudicat. Magnū hoc patientiæ argumentū, quòd iis qui ipsum tantis malis affecerunt, nec comminatus quidem sit, hoc est, nullam vindictæ significatione dederit. Sed quod hic dicit non tantum patientiam, sed misericordiam ac charitatem mirificam significat. Precatus est enim pro iis qui ipsum tantis malis affecerunt, & cruci affixerunt. Verum adhuc maiorem significationem dedit charitatis suæ, hoc ipso quod pro crucifigentibus se voluerit crucifigi. Martyres precati sunt pro iis qui ipsos sunt persequuti: sed nemo martyrū vnquam mortuus est, vt persequutores suos redimeret à morte æterna: hoc solius Christi proprium est. Illud notatu dignum est quod dicit Petrus, commisisse vindictam ei, qui iuste iudicat: hoc enim fundamentum fuit patientiæ Christi tam mirificæ, quòd Deum vindicē spectarit, eíque vindictam commiserit: fieri enim nō potest, vt quis patiens sit ergā eos, qui ipsum persequuntur, nisi is proponat sibi Deum vindicem: rursúsque fieri nō potest, vt quinullo modo paties est, sed vlcisciitur omnes iniurias & as duplo compensat: fieri, inquam, nō potest, vt is cogiet de Deo vindice, aut de extremo illo die, in quo Deus oēs iniurias iustè cōpensaturus est. Sed de hoc quæri potest; Quomodò cōsiftant ista duo, Christū cōmisisse vindictā Deo, & interea precatum pro iis, qui ipsum persequuti sunt? Respōsio facilis est: Lōgè enim aliud est cōmittere vindictā Deo & precibus vindictā expetere. Potest enim quis dū cōmittit Deo iudici vindictā, interea precibus cū Deo contendere, vt non vlcisciatur suo iudicio. Sed videntur mihi conceptæ esse preces istæ causa multitudinis maximè, quæ quod tū faciebat ignorabat. Nam quòd ad Sacerdotes, Scribas & Seniores populi, qui obstinata malitia fecerunt quicquid ab iis factum est, vix dixerim pro iis conceptas esse preces istas, quos satis sciuit Dominus induratos esse, cùm dixerit supra cap.17. 9. Ego non pro mundo oro, sed pro iis quos dedisti mihi. Ergo in gratiā ignarae plebis Iudaicæ & militum, qui ex prophanis & ignaris gentibus fuerunt, conceptę videntur fuisse potissimū preces istæ. Legimus virtute proculdubiò istarum precū ad vnam Petri concionem ter mille ex plebe & multitudine Iudaica, cōuersos esse ad fidē Christi. Imò videtur efficacia harum precū se tū exeruisse aliquo ino co, cū vulgus hominum reuerteretur à spectaculo crucis Christi, tundentes sua pectora: hoc est, aliqua contritione affecti. Sed videamus nunc ipsarum precum formulam; Pater, remitte, inquit, iis. Duo sunt peccati principia, vel enim peccatū est ex contumacia & obstinata malitia, vel est ex ignorantia. Quòd si sit ex malitia, reddit inexcusabiles, & os obturat: quia ignorantiam prætexere non poterunt in illo iudicio. Si ex ignorantia, etsi quidē ea non reddat inexcusabiles, quemadmodū facit malitia, tamē non excusat. Neque is qui ob ignorantiæ peccatū condē nabitur in illo die poterit aperire os suū ad hoc vt dicat, Domine, insciens feci; quare peccatū meum non promeretur mortem. Sed hoc profecto non possumus ignorantiæ denegare, quòd cùm malitia irritet iudicē ad iram & iustitiam: ignorantia ipsum inducat ac flectat ad misericordiam. Nā Christus cùm cruci affigeretur, persequutorum illorum ignorantiā intuitus, cōmotus est ipse proculdubiò erga eos misericordia, & Patre quoque ad misericordiā cōceptis his precibus cōmovit. In summa dicā, In persequutionibus nobis res est, vel cū malitiosis, vel cum ignorantibus. Quòd si cum malitiosis, opus est tum patientia; si verò cum ignorantibus, opus est tum non tantum patientia, sed etiam misericordia. Vt autem patietiam erga obstinatos & malitiosos obtineamus, oportet exemplo Christi Deum vindicem & iustum iudicem intueri: vt verò misericordiam, oportet eiusdem Christi exēplo ipsos homines cæcos ac ignaros ob oculos ponere. Nā quotquot ignari sūt, ij miseri sūt & miserabiles magis, quā sūt ij ipsi innocētes, quos ex igne iātia persequūtur. At erga miseros vtendū misericordia.
units.tr: Here there is one thing that Christ appears to have done while they were fastening him to the cross. He prayed for those who crucified him; the rest pertains to his shame. "Father, forgive them," he says, "for they know not what they do." Peter says that Christ was reviled, not that he reviled in return, and that when he was treated with evil he did not threaten, but committed vengeance to him who judges justly. This is a great argument of patience, that he did not even threaten those who had treated him with such great evils, that is, he gave no sign of vengeance. But what is said here signifies not only patience but also wonderful mercy and charity. For he prayed for those who had treated him with such great evils and fastened him to the cross. Yet he gave an even greater sign of his charity by the very fact that he was willing to be crucified on behalf of those who crucified him. Martyrs have prayed for those who persecuted them, but no martyr has ever died so as to redeem his persecutors from eternal death; this belongs to Christ alone. It is worth noting what Peter says, that he committed vengeance to him who judges justly. For this was the foundation of Christ's so wonderful patience, that he looked to God as avenger and committed vengeance to him. For it cannot happen that someone is patient towards those who persecute him unless he sets before himself God as avenger. And again, it cannot happen that someone who is in no way patient, but takes revenge for every injury and repays it twofold, should think of God as avenger, or of that last day on which God is going to repay all injuries justly. But here a question may be asked: how do these two things agree, that Christ committed vengeance to God, and yet in the meantime prayed for those who persecuted him? The answer is easy: it is one thing to commit vengeance to God, and quite another to seek vengeance by prayers. For someone may, while committing vengeance to God as judge, at the same time strive with God in prayer that he may not take vengeance by his judgment. But these prayers seem to me to have been offered chiefly on account of the multitude, who did not know what they were doing. For as to the chief priests, scribes and elders of the people, who by stubborn malice did whatever was done by them, I would hardly say that these prayers were offered for them, since the Lord knew well that they were hardened, when he said above in chapter 17, verse 9: "I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me." Therefore these prayers seem to have been offered especially for the sake of the ignorant Jewish common people and of the soldiers, who were from profane and ignorant nations. We read that, no doubt by the power of these prayers, at the one sermon of Peter three thousand from the common people and the Jewish multitude were converted to the faith of Christ. Indeed the efficacy of these prayers seems to have shown itself in some way even then, when the crowd of men was returning from the spectacle of Christ's cross, beating their breasts: that is, they were affected by some contrition. But let us now look at the very form of the prayer: "Father, forgive," he says, "them." There are two sources of sin: for sin arises either from stubbornness and obstinate malice, or from ignorance. If it arises from malice, it makes men inexcusable and stops their mouths, because they will not be able to plead ignorance in that judgment. If it arises from ignorance, although this does not make men inexcusable as malice does, yet it does not excuse them either. Nor will one who is condemned for a sin committed through ignorance be able to open his mouth on that day to say, "Lord, I did it unknowingly; therefore my sin does not deserve death." But we certainly cannot deny to ignorance this, that whereas malice provokes the judge to anger and justice, ignorance moves and bends him to mercy. For when Christ was being fastened to the cross, looking upon the ignorance of those persecutors, he was no doubt himself moved to mercy towards them, and by these prayers he also moved the Father to mercy. In sum, I say: in persecutions we have to do either with the malicious or with the ignorant. If with the malicious, there is need then of patience; but if with the ignorant, there is need then not only of patience but also of mercy. Now, to maintain patience towards the obstinate and malicious, we must, following the example of Christ, look to God as avenger and just judge; but to maintain mercy, we must, following the same Christ's example, set before our eyes men who are blind and ignorant. For all who are ignorant are wretched, and more to be pitied than they are innocent, whom they persecute out of ignorance. And towards the wretched one must show mercy.

units.la: Matthæi 27.
units.tr: Matthew 27.

units.la: 35 Postquam autem crucifixerūt eū, partiti sunt eius vestimenta, sortem iacientes: vt impleretur quod dictum est à Propheta, Partiti sunt vestimenta mea, & super vestem meam iecerunt sortem.
units.tr: 35 And when they had crucified him, they parted his garments, casting lots: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, They parted my garments among them, and upon my vesture did they cast lots.

units.la: 36 Et sedentes seruabant eum illic.
units.tr: 36 And sitting down they watched him there.

units.la: 37 Et imposuerunt super caput eius crimen ipsius scriptum, HIC EST IESVS REX ILLE IVDAEORVM.
units.tr: 37 And they set up over his head his accusation written, THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS.

units.la: 38 Tūc crucifiguntur cum eo duo latrones, vnus ad ad dextram, & alter ad sinistram.
units.tr: 38 Then there were crucified with him two robbers, one on the right hand, and the other on the left.

units.la: 39. Qui vero praeteribant, convitiabantur ei, monentes capita sua:
units.tr: 39 And those who passed by reviled him, wagging their heads,

units.la: 40 Et dicentes, Tu qui destruis templum, & triduo aedificas, serva teipsum: si Filius Dei es, descende de cruce.
units.tr: 40 And saying, You who destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself: if you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.

units.la: 41 Similiter autem etiam primarij Sacerdotes illudentes cum Scribis & Senioribus dicebant;
units.tr: 41 Likewise also the chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and elders, said:

units.la: 42 Alios servavit, seipsum non potest servare: si rex Israëlis est, descendat nunc de cruce, & credemus ei.
units.tr: 42 He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he is the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.

units.la: 43 Confidit in Deo, eruat ipsum nunc si placet ei; dixit enim, Filius Dei sum.
units.tr: 43 He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he will have him: for he said, I am the Son of God.

units.la: 44 Idipsum autem etiam latrones, qui crucifixi erant cum eo, exprobrabant ei.
units.tr: 44 The robbers also who were crucified with him reproached him in the same way.

units.la: Marci 15.
units.tr: Mark 15.

units.la: 26 Erat quoque inscriptio criminis ipsius inscripta his verbis, REX ILLE IVDAEORVM.
units.tr: 26 And the inscription of his accusation was written above, THE KING OF THE JEWS.

units.la: 27 Crucifixerunt etiam cum eo duos latrones, unum ad dextram, & alterum ad sinistram eius.
units.tr: 27 With him they also crucified two robbers, one on his right hand and the other on his left.

units.la: 28 Et impleta est Scriptura, quae dicit, Et cum sceleratis numeratus est.
units.tr: 28 And the Scripture was fulfilled which says, And he was numbered with the transgressors.

units.la: 29 Qui vero praeteribant, convitiabantur ei monentes capita sua, & dicentes, Vah, Tu qui destruis templum, & triduo aedificas,
units.tr: 29 And those who passed by reviled him, wagging their heads, and saying, Ah! You who destroy the temple and build it in three days,

units.la: 30 Serva teipsum, & descende de cruce.
units.tr: 30 Save yourself, and come down from the cross.

units.la: 31 Similiter autem & primarij Sacerdotes illudentes dicebat alij ad alios, cum Scribis, Alios servavit, seipsum servare non potest.
units.tr: 31 Likewise also the chief priests mocking said to one another, with the scribes: He saved others; himself he cannot save.

units.la: 32 Christus ille Rex Israëlis descendat nunc de cruce, ut videamus, & credamus. Et qui crucifixi erant cum eo, probris afficiebant eum.
units.tr: 32 Let Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, that we may see and believe. And those who were crucified with him reproached him.

units.la: Lucæ 23.
units.tr: Luke 23.

units.la: 34 Partientes vero vestimenta eius, iecerunt sortem.
units.tr: 34 But dividing his garments, they cast lots.

units.la: 35 Et stabat populus spectans, sannis autem excipiebant eum etiam primores cum eis, dicentes, Alios seruauit, seruet seipsum; si hic est Christus electus ille Dei.
units.tr: 35 And the people stood watching, but the rulers also with them scoffed at him, saying, He saved others; let him save himself, if he is that Christ, the chosen one of God.

units.la: 36 Illudebant autem etiā ei milites, accedentes & acetum ei afferentes:
units.tr: 36 The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him vinegar,

units.la: 37 Dicentes, Si tu es Rex ille Iudaeorum, serua temetipsum.
units.tr: 37 Saying, If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself.

units.la: 38 Erat autem etiam inscriptio scripta super eū literis Gracis & Romanis & Hebraicis; HIC EST REX ILLE IVDAEORVM.
units.tr: 38 There was also an inscription written over him in Greek, Latin and Hebrew letters; THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.

units.la: 39 Vnus autem ex maleficis qui erant suspensi, conuiciabatur ei, dicēs, Si tu es Christus ille, & tesum & nos serua.
units.tr: 39 One of the malefactors who were hanged reviled him, saying, If you are that Christ, save yourself and us.

units.la: 40 Respondens autem alter obiurgauit eum, dicens, Nec tu quidem Deum times, quum in eadem sit damnatione?
units.tr: 40 But the other answering rebuked him, saying, Do you not even fear God, seeing you are in the same condemnation?

units.la: 41 Et nos quidem iuste (nam digna factis recipimus) iste vero nihil indecens fecit.
units.tr: 41 And we indeed justly, for we receive what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing amiss.

units.la: 42 Dixitque Iesu, Domine, memento mei cum veneris in regnum tuum.
units.tr: 42 And he said to Jesus, Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.

units.la: 43 Tum dixit ei Iesus, Amen dico tibi, hodie mecum eris in Paradiso.
units.tr: 43 Then Jesus said to him, Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise.

units.la: Iohannis 19.
units.tr: John 19.

units.la: 18 Vbi crucifixerunt eum, & cum eo duos alios, hinc & hinc, medium autem Iesum.
units.tr: 18 Where they crucified him, and two others with him, on either side, but Jesus in the middle.

units.la: 19 Scripsit autem etiam titulum Pilatus, & posuit super crucem. Erat vero scriptum, IESVS NAZARENVS REX ILLE IVDAEORVM.
units.tr: 19 Pilate also wrote a title and put it on the cross. And it was written, JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS.

units.la: 20 Hunc ergo titulum multi Iudæorum legerunt, quia prope ciuitatem erat locus vbi crucifixus erat Iesus: & erat scriptum Hebraicè, Græcè, & Latinè.
units.tr: 20 Many of the Jews therefore read this title, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city; and it was written in Hebrew, Greek and Latin.

units.la: 21 Dixerunt igitur Pilato primarij sacerdotes Iudæorum, Noli scribere, Rex ille Iudæorum: sed illum dixisse, Rex sum Iudæorum.
units.tr: 21 The chief priests of the Jews therefore said to Pilate, Do not write, The King of the Jews; but that he said, I am King of the Jews.

units.la: 22 Respondit Pilatus, Quod scripsi, scripsi.
units.tr: 22 Pilate answered, What I have written, I have written.

units.la: 23 Milites ergo cum crucifixissent Iesum, acceperunt eius vestimenta (& fecerunt quatuor partes, vnicuique militi partem) erat autem tunica insutilis, à summo contexta tota.
units.tr: 23 The soldiers therefore, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments (and made four parts, a part for each soldier), and the tunic was without seam, woven from the top throughout.

units.la: 24 Dixerunt ergo inter se, Non findamus eam, sed sortiamur de ea cuius futura sit: vt Scriptura impleretur, dicens, Partiti sunt vestimenta mea sibi, & super vestem meam iecerunt sortem. Milites igitur hæc fecerunt.
units.tr: 24 They said therefore among themselves, Let us not tear it, but cast lots for whose it shall be: that the Scripture might be fulfilled, saying, They parted my garments among them, and upon my vesture they cast lots. The soldiers therefore did these things.

units.la: Nunc veniamus ad multiplicem ignominiam illa, qua Christus è cruce pendens affectus est. Primùm ignominia afficitur non mediocri, ex eo quod crucifigantur vna cum ipso duo latrones, ita vt ipse medius, tanquam princeps latronum, cum ipsis ad dextram & ad lævam pendentibus crucifixus sit. Dum ergo in extremo dolore & summis tormentis hæret in cruce, interea maxima ignominia afficitur: qua quidem in re ac circumstantia, vt in aliis omnibus, non tam Iudæos ac malitiam ipsorum intueor, quàm suspicio Deum Patrè, ac ipsius iustitiam, sine cuius efficaci prouidentia ac consilio nihil gestum est in tota hac Filij ipsius crucifixione. Oportet igitur, si oculos erigamus ad Deum eiusque dispensationem, colligamus ex analogia poenæ & peccati, grauissimum fuisse illud peccati onus, adeóque etiam grauius, quàm fuit peccatum illorum latronum, quod Christus pertulit in corpore suo super lignum, vt sic loquar cum Petro. Verùm quidem est, non ideo Mar. 1. Pet. 2. 24 grauius fuisse peccatum, quod graviora sint passi,
units.tr: Now let us come to the manifold ignominy with which Christ, hanging from the cross, was afflicted. First, he is afflicted with no small disgrace in that two robbers are crucified together with him, so that he himself, as it were the chief of the robbers, is crucified in the middle, with the others hanging on his right and left. While he therefore clings to the cross in extreme pain and the greatest torments, he is meanwhile afflicted with the greatest disgrace. In this circumstance, as in all the others, I do not look so much at the Jews and their malice as I behold God the Father, and his justice, without whose effective providence and counsel nothing was done in the whole crucifixion of his Son. It is necessary therefore, if we raise our eyes to God and his dispensation, to gather from the proportion between punishment and sin that the burden of sin was very grievous, and indeed more grievous than the sin of those robbers, which Christ bore in his body on the tree, to speak with Peter. It is true, however, that the sin was not greater because he suffered more grievous things,

units.la: Mar. 1. Pet. 2. 24
units.tr: Mar. 1. Pet. 2. 24

units.la: quàm malefici cuiusuis generis, quoniam Martyres nō sunt passi ob peccatum,& peccati nomine,siue causa,sed Christi causa, qui pro ipsis ac ipsorū peccatis, passus est extrema omnia, & in quo habebant conscientiam remissionis peccatorum suorū omnium. At Christus peccati nomine & causa passus est. Quisquis autem ob peccatum patitur, oportet poenam ex Dei iustitia inflictā, peccato ipsius analogam ac proportionalem esse. Christus pro maximo peccatorum onere perpessus est non tantum extremos dolores è ligno pendens, sed summā quoque ignominiam, cuius quidē cum dolore crescente,perpetuum factum est incrementum.Dum autem intueor extremam istam ignominiam inter cætera peccata nostra quæ pertulit in corpore suo super lignum, occurrit mihi extrema ac intolerabilis ista superbia tum Adami, tum omnium hominum in Adamo, qui Deum conati sumus spoliare sua gloria ac honore. Nunc igitur superbia illa intolerabilis extrema ignominia ac humiliatione compensatur: docetque nos summè superbos,si comperiantur in illo die extra Christum, summa ignominia afficiedos ex iusto Dei iudicio. Ex hac ignominiæ parte & reliquis quæ sequuntur, quibus omnibus affectus est Christus è cruce pendens, tanquam reprobus aliquis ac reiectaneus,cernere licet opus illud redemptionis humanæ, tantum abesse à gloriosa illa pompa quam postulat mundus iste, vt contra nihil fit in speciem eo contemptius atque abiectius: sic enim postulauit Dei iustitia, cuius cum præiudicio nullum oportuit lo-cū fieri misericordiæ. Nam absque sanguinis effusione nulla fit peccatorum remissio. Quare quisquis velit particeps esse misericordiæ ac redemptionis in Christo,primùm omnium oportet vt amplectatur Christi illam crucem ignominiosam, ipsamque intueatur quasi eminus fixam in loco illo ignominioso Golgotha,non longè distito ab vrbe Hierosolymorum. Neque id tantùm, sed oportet quoque ipsum tollere crucem suam & Christum sequi: hoc est, oportet libenter perpeti extrema omnia Christi causa,vt simul cum Christo patiens, simul cum ipso glorificetur. Atque hæc de ignominia quæ fuit in eo quod latrones vnà cum Christo crucifixi erant. Ea autem pro
units.tr: than any malefactor of whatever kind, since the martyrs did not suffer on account of sin, or for the sake of sin, but for the sake of Christ, who for them and for their sins suffered all extremities, and in whom they had the assurance of the remission of all their sins. But Christ suffered in the name and on account of sin. Whoever suffers on account of sin must have his punishment, inflicted by the justice of God, proportionate and commensurate to his sin. Christ, for the greatest burden of sins, suffered not only the extreme pains of hanging from the tree, but also the greatest disgrace, and with the growing pain this disgrace also grew without end. Now while I consider that extreme disgrace, which among our other sins he bore in his body on the tree, there comes to my mind that extreme and intolerable pride both of Adam and of all men in Adam, who tried to strip God of his glory and honour. Now therefore that intolerable pride is compensated by extreme disgrace and humiliation, and it teaches us that the most proud, if they are found on that day outside Christ, will be subjected to the greatest disgrace by the just judgment of God. From this part of the disgrace and the rest that follows, with all of which Christ hanging from the cross was afflicted as some reprobate and outcast, one may discern that that work of human redemption is so far from the glorious pomp that this world demands, that on the contrary nothing is made more contemptible and abject in appearance: for thus the justice of God required, to the prejudice of which no place for mercy ought to be made. For without the shedding of blood there is no remission of sins. Wherefore whoever wishes to be a partaker of mercy and redemption in Christ must first of all embrace Christ's ignominious cross, and look upon it as if fixed at a distance in that ignominious place Golgotha, not far from the city of Jerusalem. And not only this, but he must also take up his own cross and follow Christ: that is, he must willingly undergo all extremities for Christ's sake, so that suffering with Christ he may be glorified together with him. And so much concerning the ignominy which lay in the fact that the robbers were crucified together with Christ. But that

units.la: Heb. 9.22. profecta est à Iudæis pariter & gentibus.
units.tr: Heb. 9.22. proceeded from Jews and Gentiles alike.

units.la: Deinde autem afficiunt eum ignominia singuli ordi-nes seorsim: ac primùm ignominia quidem ipsum assi-cit Pilatus iudex. Pilatus igitur curat scribendum titulum, continentem in se causam crucifixionis, siue crimen: vt vel ex ipso crimine lecto & inspecto haberetur pro malefico & reo læsæ maiestatis. Hoc autem factum est ex consuetudine, ac ea quidem laudabili, quæ obtinuit in populo Dei, in quo, vt iudicia, ita & supplicia cū ipsorum causis & criminibus erant aperta, & in conspectu totius populi administrari solita. Docet hoc exemplum Achanis, qui anathema subduxit. Exemplum Blasphemi in deserto. Exemplum Ionathanis qui à patre suo iudicatus est & condemnatus in medio populi. Habet enim populus aliquas partes, & ius aliquod suum in iudiciis. Neque plane exclusò populo exerceri debent iudicia, neque etiā exscindi aliqui à societate politica, præsertim cum ne summus quidē iudex ille Deus, vltimo die condemnaturus sit ad inferos, reprobū aliquem, siue angelum siue hominem, absque consensu aliquo ac approbatione electorum, qui illo die hinc inde staturi sunt circa tribunal ipsius. Quanto magis hoc faciendum terreno iudici? Hæc quidem causa fuit inscriptionis istius ex vsitata consuetudine: sed alia re permotus ac inducitus est Pilatus, nimirum, vt vlciscereretur obstinationem illam Iudæorum, qua ipse pertractus est inuitus alioqui ad pronunciandam illam mortis sententiam in hominem innocentissimum. Sed magis hic Deum eiusque dispensationem intueor, quàm vel Pilatum vel Iudæos. Proculdubio enim hæc inscriptio fuit ex Dei consilio, in eum finem vt primùm confirmaretur cœleste illud Christi regnum: deinde vt externo hoc quasi signo indicaretur triumphus ille quem triumphauit Christus in cruce, palam traductis imperiis & potestatibus eum. Postremò adumbraretur illud præconium ac Euangelium regni Christi, quod paulo post sequutu-rum erat in omnibus linguis & apud omnes populos. Pilatus enim præco quidem fuit regni Christi, etsi tum dentare minus cogitaret, quàm de regno illo Christi gloriosō. Talis enim prædicator Euangelij fuit, qualem
units.tr: Then the individual orders afflict him with disgrace, each in its own way. First, Pilate the judge afflicts him with disgrace. Pilate therefore arranges for a title to be written, stating the cause of the crucifixion, or the charge, so that from the charge itself, read and inspected, he would be taken for a malefactor and a traitor guilty of treason. This was done by custom, and indeed a praiseworthy one, which prevailed among the people of God, among whom judgments and punishments, together with their causes and crimes, were made public and usually carried out in the sight of the whole people. The example of Achan, who took the accursed thing, shows this. So does the example of the blasphemer in the desert, and the example of Jonathan, who was judged and condemned by his father in the midst of the people. For the people has certain parts and some right of its own in judgments. Judgments ought not to be carried out with the people altogether shut out, nor should anyone be cut off from political society, especially since even God, that supreme judge, will not condemn any reprobate to hell on the last day, whether angel or man, without the consent and approval of the elect, who on that day will stand around his tribunal on every side. How much more must this be done by an earthly judge? This was indeed the reason for the inscription, according to ordinary custom. But Pilate was moved and led by another matter, namely to take vengeance on that obstinacy of the Jews, which otherwise pressed him, unwilling, to pronounce that sentence of death on a most innocent man. Yet here I look more at God and his dispensation than at either Pilate or the Jews. For without doubt this inscription was according to God's counsel, first, so that the heavenly kingdom of Christ might be confirmed; then, so that by this outward sign, as it were, that triumph which Christ triumphed on the cross might be shown, the powers and authorities being openly led in procession. Lastly, the proclamation and gospel of Christ's kingdom, which was soon to follow in all tongues and among all peoples, was foreshadowed. For Pilate was indeed a herald of Christ's kingdom, although at that time he thought less of that glorious kingdom of Christ. For he was such a preacher of the gospel as

units.la: Dei consilium in hac inscriptione. supra vidimus Caiapham prophetā, qui prædixit quod expediens esset, vt vnus pro populo moreretur. Eò autem magis adducor vt attribuam hoc factum Dei providentiæ, quòd videam, posteaquam sacerdotes verba inscriptionis immutari volebant, & pro eo quod scriptum fuit à Pilato, Hic est Iesus Rex ille Iudæorum, scribi voluerunt, quod dixerit se Regem Iudæorum: Pilatum perstitisse in sententia. Constantia illa hominis proculdubio pendebat ab immutabili illo Dei decreto de Christi regno, quòd vsque adeo efficax in Pilato fuit, vt nihil in scripto suo mutare vel voluerit vel potuerit. Atque hoc decretum illud est de quo legimus, Narrabo ex decreto, Iehoua dixit ad me, Filius meus es tu, &c. Atque hæc deignominia qua ipsum affecit Iudex Pilatus.
units.tr: God's counsel in this inscription. Above we saw Caiaphas the prophet, who foretold that it was expedient that one man should die for the people. I am the more inclined to ascribe this deed to God's providence, because I see that when the priests wanted the wording of the inscription changed, and wanted written, instead of what Pilate had written, This is Jesus the King of the Jews, that he said he was King of the Jews, Pilate held to his decision. That steadfastness of the man doubtless depended on God's unchangeable decree concerning Christ's kingdom, which was so effective in Pilate that he neither wished nor was able to change anything in what he had written. This is that decree of which we read: I will declare the decree: the LORD said to me, You are my Son, etc. And these are the disgraces with which the judge Pilate afflicted him.

units.la: Sequuntur nunc carnifices, quos ex verbis Iohannis de partitione vestiū ipsius in partes quatuor facta, collegimus fuisse quatuor numero, ita vt vnicuique carnifici cesserit pars vna. Carnifices igitur Christū è ligno pendentem afficiunt ignominiā, dum ipso inspectante in contemptum ipsius vestes prius direptas, tum cūm eum crucifigerent, nunc viderent in quatuor partes, & super tunicam, quæ fuit insutilis à summo contexta tota, miserunt sortem: implentes nimirum id quod à Propheta fuit prædictum: Partiuntur vestimenta mea inter se, & pro indumento meo, proiciunt sortem. Ex qua prædictione illud discitur, nihil ab ipsis factum esse, quod non determinatum fuerit ab æterno in illo Dei concilio. Nam quod tanto tempore antea prædictum est, ridipsum necessariò ab æterno decretum fuerat. Sed vt de facto ipsorum dicamus: Primùm afficiunt Dominum iniuria, quòd innocentem spolient bonis, ac rebus suis, deinde afficiunt ignominia, quòd spolient vestibus, & nudum exponant ludibrio mundi. Postremò summo contemptu afficiunt, quòd coram & intuente etiam ipso è cruce, direptas vestes inter se diuidant: Afficiunt igitur innocentem iniuria, ignominia & contemptu. Sed ego vt in aliis circumstantiis quæ coniunctę sunt cum passione ista Christi, non tam homines intueor, quàm Deum Patrem: ita hic quoque non tam carnifices respicio, quàm iudicem illum, qui iustus est etiam in hoc facto carnificum, vt in aliis omnibus. Nam, vt de iniuria dicam, iustè passus est hanc iniuriam & direptionem vestium, si Deum intueatur, quia ipse hæsit in cruce vestitus nostris peccatis. Ideo iure vestibus sui spoliatus est, si Deum respicias. Peccator enim, quia peccator est, & nondum est exutus per Christum suo peccato, vt nullum ius habet in vestes etiam vilissimas & sordidissimas quasque: ita si vestibus spolietur, id fit non absque iusto Dei iudicio. In extremo autem illo die iudicij (cui semper à me dictum est, præsens hoc iudicium analogum esse) hac ipsa Christi spoliatione admonemur futurum, vt reprobi qui extra Christum tum comperientur, spolientur ac priuentur omni vsu non solùm vestium, sed omnium Dei creaturarum, quæ ordinatæ sunt à Deo, vel ad necessitatem hominum, vel ad ornamentum, cùm ij qui tum in Christo comperientur, non tantùm induendi sunt illa incorruptione ac gloria Christi, sed etiam mittendi sunt in possessionem cœlorum nouorum & terræ nouæ, regnaturi cum capite suo Iesu Christo in sæcula sæculorum. Nunc autem vt dicam de ignominia illa, qua ipsum afficiunt, dum nudum & exutum vestibus ludibrio omnium exponunt: & hoc quoque si Deum respicias iustissimè factum est, propter peccata nostra, quibus indutus hæsit in cruce. Iustum enim est, vt qui peccatis induitur, vestibus exuatur, ac nudus exponatur. Propheta enim peccatricibus ac delicatulis illis fœminis comminatur nuditatem. Iehova, inquit, pudendum earum nudabit. Inter autem alia supplicia quibus afficiendi sunt reprobi in extremo illo iudicio, hoc sine dubio vnum futurum est, quod nudi non tecta illa corporum fœditate ac deformitate, cum quatum cõspicientur, Nudi, inquam in conspectu Angelorum ac hominum omnium sistentur in illo iudicio, cum ineffabili pudore faciei & confusione. Quo quidem tempore eligent potiùs montibus in ipsos incidentibus ac obruentibus ipsos obtegi, quàm sic coram vniuerso mundo confusi toti stare, nudata ac detecta illa corporum deformitate. Vt autem postremo contemptu illo dicamus: Affirmamus non minus iuste respectu Dei, hoc contemptu affectum Christum, quàm aliis illis malis, de quibus iam dictum.
units.tr: Now come the executioners, whom we gather from John's words about the division of his garments into four parts to have been four in number, so that each executioner received one part. The executioners, therefore, put Christ, hanging on the wood, to shame, while he watched: first they stripped his clothes to hold him in contempt; then, when they crucified him, they saw the garments divided into four parts, and they cast lots for the tunic, which was woven in one piece from top to bottom. They thus fulfilled what the prophet had foretold: "They divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." From this prediction we learn that nothing was done by them that had not been determined from eternity in that counsel of God. For what was foretold so long before must necessarily have been decreed from eternity. But to speak of their deed: first they wrong the Lord by injury, in that they strip the innocent of his goods and possessions; then they afflict him with disgrace, in that they strip him of his clothes and expose him naked to the mockery of the world; lastly, they treat him with the greatest contempt, in that they divide his stripped garments among themselves while he is watching from the cross. They therefore afflict the innocent with injury, disgrace and contempt. But as in the other circumstances connected with this passion of Christ, I look not so much at men as at God the Father, so here too I regard not so much the executioners as that judge who is just even in this deed of the executioners, as in all the others. For, to speak of the injury, he suffered this injury and the stripping of his garments justly, if one looks at God, because he himself hung on the cross clothed with our sins. Therefore he was rightly stripped of his garments, if you regard God. For the sinner, because he is a sinner and not yet stripped of his sin through Christ, has no right even to the vilest and filthiest clothes; so if he is stripped of his clothes, this happens not without the just judgment of God. On that last day of judgment (of which I have always said this present judgment is a figure) we are reminded by this very stripping of Christ that the reprobate, who are then found outside Christ, will be stripped and deprived of every use, not only of clothes but of all God's creatures, which have been ordained by God either for human necessity or for ornament; whereas those who are then found in Christ are not only to be clothed with that incorruption and glory of Christ, but are also to be sent into possession of the new heavens and the new earth, to reign with their head, Jesus Christ, for ever and ever. Now, to speak of the disgrace with which they afflicted him, while they exposed him naked and stripped of clothes to the mockery of all: this too, if you look at God, was done most justly, on account of our sins, with which he hung on the cross. For it is just that he who is clothed with sins should be stripped of clothes and exposed naked. The prophet threatens those sinful and pampered women with nakedness: "Jehovah," he says, "will uncover their shame." Among the other punishments with which the reprobate are to be afflicted at that last judgment, this will undoubtedly be one: that they will be displayed naked, without the covering of that bodily foulness and deformity, when they are seen. Naked, I say, in the sight of angels and of all men they will stand in that judgment, with unspeakable shame of face and confusion. At that time they will choose rather to be covered by mountains falling on them and crushing them, than to stand thus confused before the whole world, with the deformity of their bodies bared and exposed. But to speak of that last contempt: we affirm that Christ was afflicted with this contempt no less justly, with respect to God, than with those other evils already mentioned.

units.la: Nam iustum est apud Deum vt peccator, & qui cum contemptu Dei peccat vicissim contemnatur ac despiciatur. Christus autem hoc peccatum nostrum, nempe contemptum, vna cum aliis gestauit in cruce. Eius autem exemplo admonemur, ad reliquas poenas illas, quas dabunt impij in extremo illo iudicio, contemptum accessurum, vel ex eo quod in conspectu ipso reproborum Sancti illi quos olim in hac vita contemnti pserunt, & indignitatibus multis affecerunt, promouebuntur ad coelestem illam gloriam: qua prosecto re inspecta, augebitur ille dolor reproborum ineffabilis. Haec omnia admonent, quantum boni futurum sit in eo, vt inueniamur in Christo in illo die: contraque quantum mali futurum sit in eo, quod reprobi in ipso non inuenientur.
units.tr: For it is just before God that the sinner, and he who sins in contempt of God, should in turn be despised and held in scorn. Christ, however, bore on the cross this our sin, namely contempt, together with the others. By his example we are admonished that contempt will be added to the other punishments which the wicked will suffer at that last judgment. For in the very sight of the reprobate, those holy ones whom they once despised and treated with many indignities in this life will be advanced to that heavenly glory; and that sight will surely increase the unspeakable grief of the reprobate. All these things admonish us how much good there will be in being found in Christ on that day, and, on the other hand, how much evil there will be in the reprobate not being found in him.

units.la: Sequuntur nunc partes populi adstantis ac spectantis: nam & ipse quoque sua quadam ignominia Domi-num afficit, & sannis acerbissimis excipit. Mouent capita dicentes, vah tu qui templum destruis, & post triduum rursus extruis, descende ex cruce, & serua teipsum. Exprobrant Domino pendenti ex cruce illud di̱ctum de quo iam ante vidimus in hoc Euangelio: Nempe, quod dixerit Dominus, destructurum se templum, non quidem illud Hierosolymitanum, sed templum corporis sui, & illud ipsum rursus post triduum, per gloriosam nimirum resurrectionem, reaedificaturum. Sic autem hoc ei exprobrant vt significent fieri non posse, vt id faciat. Argumentum sumunt a praesenti ipsius conditione, qua pendebat e cruce, e qua non poterat seipsum liberare. Persequar deinde aliorum opprobria & sannas, priusquam aliquid in hunc locum obseruauero, quia dicta sunt omnia in eandē fere sententiam. Sequuntur igitur partes primorum populi, vt summorum Sacerdotum, Seniorum, Scribarum, Pharisaeorum. Exprobrant illi Dominus, quod dixerit se Christum illum Dei Filium: exprobrant autem hoc tanquam ἀδύνατον, & quod fieri non poterat. Argumentum est vt supra ab ignominiosa & infirma illa cruce, a qua se ipse liberare non poterat: Vnde impossibile fuit ipsum Christum illum esse, missum ad alios liberandos. Sequuntur deinde partes militum ipsorum sannæ illi illudentes: offerunt acetum bibendum, simúlque exprobrant, quòd dixerit se regem esse Iudæorum, idque in præiudicium, vt ipsi putabant, regni Cæsaris. Significant autè impossibile esse, vt ipse Rex sit. Argumetū est à cruce illa suptū, ex qua pedebat, vt supra.
units.tr: Now follow the parts of the people standing by and looking on. For he too afflicts the Lord with a certain ignominy of his own and receives him with the bitterest taunts. They shake their heads, saying, "Ah, you who destroy the temple and build it again after three days, come down from the cross and save yourself." They throw in the Lord's face, as he hangs on the cross, that saying which we have already seen earlier in this Gospel: namely, that the Lord said he would destroy the temple, not the one at Jerusalem but the temple of his body, and would raise that same temple again after three days, that is, by his glorious resurrection. They throw this at him in such a way as to signify that it cannot be done. They take the argument from his present condition, in which he hangs from the cross and cannot free himself from it. I will pursue the reproaches and taunts of the others before noting anything on this passage, since all were said to much the same effect. Next come the parts of the chief people: the high priests, elders, scribes and Pharisees. They throw in his face that he called himself the Christ, the Son of God, and they throw it as impossible [ἀδύνατον], something that could not be done. The argument, as above, is from that ignominious and weak cross, from which he could not free himself; whence it was impossible that this Christ should be the one sent to free others. Then come the parts of the soldiers, who mock him with their jeers. They offer him vinegar to drink, and at the same time throw in his face that he called himself king of the Jews, and to the prejudice, as they thought, of Caesar's kingdom. They signify that it is impossible for him to be king. The argument is from that cross on which he hangs, as above.

units.la: Sequuntur postremò partes alterius ex latronibus illis & ipsius blasphemia, nempe eius qui tum pendebat è cruce ad latus Christi alterum. Exprobrat Christo, quòd se Christum vocarit: significat autem illud nō posse fieri. Argumentum autem est à cruce illa, è qua pendebat vnà cum crucifixis latronibus. Videmus itaque idè fere esse, quod ab his omnibus exprobratur: & in hac exprobratione tā multiplici summā Christi humiliationē, & inanitionem. Nam magis hauddubiè his sannis & insultationibus acerbissimis humiliatus est, quàm illis tormē tis corporis in quibus hæsit toto illo tempore. Nā his sannis amarulentissimis egerunt quantum in ipsis fuit, vt Christus ageretur in extremam desperationē: vt facilè videas vel ex his sannis & opprobriis obiectis quàm chare constiterit Christo salus nostra, & quàm miseri fuissemus nos, sine redeptore: denique quàm miseri futuri sint illi, qui in isto redeptore Christo non coperientur in illo iudicio. Nulla autem alia via datur qua cōperiamur in eo quàm refipiscētia: si nimirum serio pœniteat nos illorum peccatorum, quibus ipse tum transfixus est. Dum diligentius expendo, quæ Christo obiiciuntur ac exprobrantur, video nō alia esse, quàm ea de quibus accusatus est, ac ob quæ condemnatus & tandem crucifixus est. Quòd si eorum causa crucifixus est, hæsit in extremis illis tormentis, an non debuit hoc istis satisfacere, sic vt non iam obiiceret hærenti in tormentis exquisitissimis, crimen illud ob quod ea perpessus est? Sed quid dicas, morte sanctorum ac innocētum, nō restinguet sitim illa sanguinis quæ est in Christi ac gratiæ ipsius hostibus: imò hærente iā in extremis ac exquisitissimis tormentis perseq̄ entur conuiciis ac sannis, sic, vt si fieri posset, non tantum corpus interficiant: sed & animā adigant in extremam desperationem: imò post mortem cinerem & ossa persequentur, vt videas quàm acerbum sit & insatiabile illud odium in Christianos quod viget in regno Antichristi. Sed hic Dei prouidentiam magis intueor, qui iustissime ista omnia dispensat: filius enim sustinuit personam nostram, & pertulit in corpore super lignum peccata nostra. Nos autem exemplo Christi, cui tanquam reprobo & abiecto, non desiit illud ipsum crimen obquod crucifixus est obiici & exprobrari, admonemur memoriam peccatorum illorum, ob quae damnabutur reprobi ad inferos, nunquam sepeliendam esse, & conscientiam ipsorum nunquam deiturarn, nō tantum eos accusare, sed etiam subiannare, & ludibrio eos habere, summa cum amarulentia. Tum enim dicet conscientia homicidae, Tu cum in viuis esses, delectatus es homicidio: nunc libera te his inferis, & satia te sanguine. Adultero similiter suum adulterium exprobrabit: Tu qui obleftabas te aliquando foedis libidinibus, nunc satia te supplicis: & sic de caeteris.
units.tr: Last of all come the parts of one of those robbers, and his blasphemy: namely of the one who then hung from the cross at the other side of Christ. He throws in Christ's face that he called himself Christ, and he signifies that this could not happen. The argument is from that cross on which he hung together with the crucified robbers. We see, therefore, that what is thrown at him by all of them is pretty much the same, and in this manifold reproach there is the sum of Christ's humiliation and emptiness. For he was without doubt humbled more by these taunts and most bitter insults than by those torments of the body in which he hung throughout that whole time. For with these most bitter mockeries they did, as far as lay in them, drive Christ to extreme despair. From this you may easily see, even from these taunts and reproaches thrown at him, at what cost Christ purchased our salvation, how wretched we would have been without a Redeemer, and finally how wretched those will be who are not found in that Redeemer Christ at the judgment. Now there is no other way by which we may be found in him except repentance: namely, if we seriously repent of those sins for which he was then pierced. As I weigh more carefully what is thrown at Christ and reproached to him, I see that they are none other than those things for which he was accused, and for which he was condemned and at last crucified. But if he was crucified on account of them, and endured those extreme torments, ought he not to have satisfied for them, so that they could no longer throw at him, as he hung in the most exquisite torments, the crime for which he suffered? But what do you say? The thirst for blood in the enemies of Christ and of grace is not quenched by the death of saints and innocents. Indeed, while he was still hanging in the extreme and most exquisite torments, they pursue him with insults and mockeries, so that, if it were possible, they would not only kill the body but drive the soul into extreme despair. Indeed, after death they pursue his ashes and bones, so that you may see how bitter and insatiable is that hatred of Christians which flourishes in the kingdom of Antichrist. But here I rather regard the providence of God, who most justly disposes all these things: for the Son bore our person and bore our sins in his body upon the wood. As for us, by the example of Christ, who, though treated as a reprobate and outcast, never ceased to have that very crime for which he was crucified thrown at him and reproached, we are warned that the memory of those sins for which the reprobate will be condemned to hell is never to be buried, and that their conscience will never cease, not only to accuse them but also to mock and deride them with the utmost bitterness. For then the conscience of the murderer will say: "When you were alive you delighted in murder; now free yourself from these depths and glut yourself on blood." In the same way the adulterer's conscience will throw his adultery in his face: "You who once indulged yourself in foul lusts, now glut yourself on punishment"; and so on for the rest.

units.la: Video vnam eandemque causam esse, qua offenduntur omnes in Christum eumque ludibrio habet. Est autem ea, crux Christi, quam praesentem omnes intuebantur, & a qua non potuit ipse se liberare, vt illi rebantur. Impossibile enim ipsis videbatur, vt siquin cruce haereret, & in tam obiecto mortis genere, destrutu semel templum intra triduum posset rursus extruere, vt is posset Christi partes agere, vt is deniq; posset regis munere in liberando populo defungi. Sed longe errarunt, quandoquidem illa ipsa crux quantumuis ignominiosa & in specie abiecta, sola ac vnica via fuerit ad haec omnia perficienda. Quid enim cum in cruce haereret, anno eadem opera destruebat templum corporis sui, vt ipsum post triduum gloriosa resurrectione sua reaedificaret? Annon per crucem functus est officio Christi, hoc est Sacerdotis vncti, cum offerret tanquam Sacerdos corpus suum in altari crucis? Annon denique per eandem crucem parabat sibi & suis gloriosum regnum, imo per crucem in cruce triumphabat de inimicis suis omnibus, quos in cruce tanquam in curru triumphali infedes traduxit palam in triumpho, teste Apostolo? Vides igitur quam caecutiuerint miseri isti in hoc crucis Christi negotio, eadem plane est caecitas hominum bodierno die, qui dum intuentur Christianos omnium hominum in specie miserrimos, vinciri, in exilium
units.tr: I see that one and the same cause is why all are offended by Christ and hold him in mockery. That cause is the cross of Christ, which they all saw before them, and from which, as they thought, he could not free himself. For it seemed impossible to them that one who clung to a cross, and in so ignominious a kind of death, could once more destroy the temple and rebuild it within three days, that he could play the part of Christ, and that he could finally discharge the office of king in delivering the people. But they were far wrong, since that very cross, however ignominious and abject in appearance, was the sole and only way to accomplish all these things. For what, while clinging to the cross, was he doing at the same time but destroying the temple of his body, so that he might rebuild it after three days by his glorious resurrection? Did he not by the cross perform the office of Christ, that is, of the anointed Priest, when as Priest he offered his body on the altar of the cross? Finally, did he not by that same cross prepare for himself and his people a glorious kingdom? Indeed, by the cross he triumphed over all his enemies, whom he led openly in triumph, as if on a triumphal chariot, upon the cross, as the Apostle bears witness. You see, then, how blind those wretched men were in this matter of Christ's cross. The very same blindness exists among men today, who, when they see Christians, the most wretched of all men in appearance, bound, cast into exile,

units.la: Coloss. 2.15. [illegible, ~6 letters]iici, coburi & exquisitissimis suppliciis quibusq; afflicti, non modò putant fieri non posse, ut hac via ad vitam perveniant, sed pro ludibrio habent eorū professione, & ipsis insolenter insultant tanquā reprobis & a Deo abiectis. Incausa est quòd nunquā viderūt miseri quid quāmque sit peccatum, quod quidem oportuit tum expiari per crucē ignominiosam, quia ita iustitia Dei & maiestas illa offensa postulabat. Et nunc in nobis perpetuò mortificari per cruces & afflictiones varias.
units.tr: Col. 2.15. [illegible] cast out, burned, and afflicted with the most exquisite punishments of every kind, not only think that it is impossible for them to reach life by this way, but also hold their profession in mockery and insolently insult them as reprobates and outcasts from God. The reason is that those wretched men never saw what sin is, which indeed had to be expiated at that time by the ignominious cross, because the justice of God and that majesty offended demanded it. And now, in us, it must be continually mortified by crosses and various afflictions.

units.la: Quia autē aliquid speciale ac proprium est in opprobrio hoc obiecto a latrone, ait enim, Serua teipsum & nos: ideo ex eius verbis specialis quaedā observatio colligenda est. Quod enim dicit, Serua nos, hoc est me & socium illum meum, satis innuit tormentū in quo haesit mouisse eum ad hanc impatientiā & blasphemiā. Nam afflictiones & tormenta, nisi sanctificentur nobis a Deo, exprimunt e nobis impatientes & blasphemas in Deū ipsum voces, vel in potentiā ipsius, vel in misericordiā, quòd nulla nimirum sit Dei misericordia, vel certè quòd ea nihil ad nos spectet. Afficit quidē ignominia Deum aliquis dū diffidit ipsius erga se misericordiae, sed aperte blasphemat qui negat misericordiā omnino: Vt & summa blasphemia est, dū quis negat potentiam Dei; hoc enim est negare Deum: Deus enim nō est, nisi potens sit, atq; ideo omnipotens. Oportet igitur hunc latronē summè blasphemū fuisse in Deum. In quo profectò homine videor mihi vidēre viuā imaginē reproborū in morte sua: vel enim blasphemi sunt in potētiā Dei, vel in misericordiā, negātes eū omnino, vel certè ei diffidentes, atq; ita miseri auerfuntur se a Deo, quē summè oderūt, & ad cuius aspectū toti côrrem ifcūt. Magna est igitur ac grauis istius miseri blasphemia, sed maior profectò fuit Sacerdotū & Scribarū, quos quidē oportuit Messiā cognitū habere: in eum tamen fuerunt blasphemi, licet iis tormēta nulla blasphemiā expresserint. At latro iste non nisi ignarus Christi & crucifixus in cruce, euomit suā hanc blasphemiā. Tolerabilior quoque est latronis blasphemia in Christum, tū quidem ignominiosum & crucifixum, quàm est illorū hominum hodierno die blasphemia in Christum iam glorificatum in cœlis ad dextram illius maiestatis.
units.tr: Because there is something special and peculiar in this reproach from the robber, for he says, Save yourself and us, a particular observation is to be gathered from his words. For when he says, "Save us," that is, me and my companion, he sufficiently hints that the torment in which he hung moved him to this impatience and blasphemy. For afflictions and torments, unless they are sanctified to us by God, draw from us impatient and blasphemous words against God himself, either against his power or against his mercy, namely that there is no mercy of God at all, or at least that it has nothing to do with us. A man dishonours God when he distrusts God's mercy towards himself, but he plainly blasphemes who denies mercy altogether. Likewise it is the highest blasphemy when someone denies God's power, for this is to deny God: God is not God unless he is powerful, and therefore almighty. It is necessary, then, that this robber was most grievously blasphemous against God. In that man I seem to see a living image of the reprobate in their death: for they blaspheme either God's power or his mercy, denying him altogether or at least distrusting him, and so wretchedly turn themselves away from God, whom they hate most of all, and at whose sight they tremble to the core. Great and grave, then, is the blasphemy of that wretched man; but greater certainly was that of the priests and scribes, who ought indeed to have known the Messiah, yet were blasphemous against him, although no torments drew blasphemy from them. But that robber, being ignorant of Christ and hanging on the cross, vomits forth this blasphemy. The robber's blasphemy against Christ, then ignominious and crucified, is also more tolerable than the blasphemy of those men today against Christ now glorified in heaven at the right hand of that majesty.

units.la: Nunc videndæ sunt partes alterius latronis: Is primũ resipiscit, deinde interior resipiscentia erumpit in fru-ctus suos:qui ipsi sunt primum,reprehensio latronis il-liu› in Christum blasphemi: vbi peccatum suum & me-ritum simul confitetur coram Domino, & iis omnibus qui astiterunt: deinde cŏuersus ad Dominum, precatur, Domine, memento mei cum veneris ad regnum tuum. Argumen-ta reprehensionis tria sunt: Quod reprehendit in altero non est quidem tam externa blasphemia, quàm fons ip-se blasphemiæ qui in corde erat: nempe vacuitas ti-moris Dei,quam arguit illa ipsius blasphemia. Primum igitur argumentum est sumptum à præsenti & communi damnatione, hoc est supplicio. Tu es in eadem damna-tione cum isto & mecum: cur igitur non times Dominum, præsertim cum tam subito sistendus sis in illo iudicio, vbi reddituru es rationem,nō solùm anteactæ vitæ to-tius,sed etiam vel multò maximè blasphemiæ huius in Dominum ? Nota ergo primùm Dei manu graui in-cumbente in aliquem, & ad mortem vsque premente, tum quidem tempus est humiliandi se sub potenti illa Dei manu & timendi Deum,atque tribunal illud for-midabile ad quod paulò post sisti eum oportet. Quod si non faciat, tum profecto arguit se merè stupidum, & rebellem in manum illam Dei,quæ non prius eum deserer, quàm opprimet & conteret. Atque hoc illud est, quod à nobis fieri debet, idque debere fieri arguit latronis resipiscentis ista reprehensio: verum impœni-tentia & blasphemia alterius latronis satis arguit non semper id fieri: sed permanere quosdam in extremis etiam calamitatibus adeo stupidos & obstirmatos ad-uersus Dei manum, vt nihilo magis humilientur & metuant Deum, ipsiúsque terribile illud iudicium, quàm si immunes viuerent ab omni malo. In causa est quòd nullus vnquam vel succus gratiæ in iis homi-nibus fuit. Quomodo autem potest oppressio eum succum exprimere qui non est omnino ? An si lignum aridum premas, succum aliquem exprimes ? Omnes autem sumus natura tanquam lignum aridum. At latro alter oppressus iam & in tormentis hærens re-sipiscit, asserit Christi gloriam, reprehendit socium, con[fragment] consitetur peccatum, veniam postulat. At quis inter istos discreuit? Pares erant natura, pares malis operibus & anteacta male vita, pares denique tormentis. Quod si non ex Christo qui simul crucifixus erat hausisset ille alter salutarem illum quem expresserunt tormenta succum gratiæ, profecto nunquam ne nullis quidem tormentis & mortibus exprimi potuisset. Christus quidem ex æquo crucifixus fuit, medius inter vtrumque, sed non impertiuit ex æquo gratiam suam vtrique. Quamobrem in afflictionibus & tormentis, præsertim in extrema illa agonia rogádus est Christus ipse, vt det nobis succum illum gratiæ, quem conabitur afflictionibus & crucibus exprimere, secus enim nulla vnquam vel guttula elici poterit. Exprimetur quidem tum acerbus hic ac amarulentus naturæ nostræ succus, nempe impatientia, blasphemia, & id genus alia: verùm suauis ille gratiæ succus exprimi non poterit. Illud præterea obseruo in primo hoc reprehensionis argumento: oportere eos qui in communi aliqua miseria detinentur, tantum abesse à sannis & ludibrio, vtè contrà commoueantur misericordia in alios, qui in eadem sunt damnatione ac miseria. Quod si nulla afficiantur erga alios misericordia, id quidem argumento esse plane vacuos eos à timore & reuerentia Dei. Si verò conuitiati fuerint, & exprobrarint aliis miseriam, tum quidem arguunt sese non modò vacuos gratiæ ac timoris Diuini, sed impletos esse felle amaritudinis. Omnes natura sumus peccatores & miseri, decet autem miseros & peccatores misericordia duci erga peccatores & miseros. Et nos quidem iustè. Occupatio est, ne colligeret blasphemus ille latro ex eo quod dictum sit communem & eandem condemnationem omnium eorum qui simul crucifixi sunt commune & idem omnium meritum esse: huic occurrit dicens, Nos quidem, hoc est, ego & tu iustè sumus in communi ista damnatione: At iste nihil insolens fecit.
