Duo sunt his verbis argumenta alia, quibus reprehendit latronem illum blasphemum: primum est, Tu meritus es damnationem & supplicium istud, Ergo non times Deum? Quemadmodum enim oppressio & crux, præsertim verò extrema illa oppressio, quæ est ad mortem vsque, debent in nobis excitare Dei timorem, quantumuis antea stupidis: ita con-fideratio meriti nostri, cùm nobiscum cogitamus nos commeritos esse oppressionem illam & mortem, debet nos multò magis excitare ad timorem Dei & feriam refipifcentiam. Hoc quidem debere fieri docet exemplum latronis huius, qui reprehendit illam alterius blasphemiam. At verò quòd non semper id vsu veniat, docet vicissim exemplum latronis illius blasphemi. In causa est quod etsi quidem fit meritum omnium hominum, tamen non omnes ducantur conscientia meriti fui, ne in mortis quidem punctò & in agonia illa & lucta nouissima. Multi sunt etiam, qui fi afficiantur sensu meriti & peccati fui, tamen non afficiuntur sensu misericordiæ Dei, ac proinde fi timent, timor eorum est seruilis tantùm ac desperatus. Quòd autem ad exemplum alterius & resipiscentis latronis, quidam in morte afficiantur sensu tam meriti fui, quàm misericordiæ Dei, ac proinde timeant timore quodam filiali, id totum iam tribuendum est cruci Christi è qua sola defluxit his sensus iste peccati simul & misericordiæ. Nam quod acciidit latroni resipiscenti, idem quoque & aliis euenire necesse est. Quare vt latro iste debebat illam gratiam foli Christo acceptam ferre, quocum tum vna crucifixus est: ita nos quoque debemus illam gratiam eidem Christo ac foli ei ascribere, quocum vna nos quoque nostro quodam modo crucifixi sumus.
units.tr: Now let us consider the part of the other thief. First he comes to his senses, and then that inner repentance breaks out into its fruits. These are, first, his rebuke of the thief who blasphemed Christ, in which he confesses his own sin and deserving before the Lord and before all those who stood by; and then, turning to the Lord, he prays: Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom. There are three arguments in the rebuke. What he rebukes in the other is not so much the outward blasphemy as the source of the blasphemy, which was in the heart: namely, the absence of the fear of God, which that very blasphemy reveals. The first argument, then, is drawn from the present and shared condemnation, that is, the punishment. You are under the same condemnation as this man and as I am: why then do you not fear the Lord, especially since you are so soon to be brought before that judgment where you must give an account not only of your whole past life but also, and much more, of this blasphemy against the Lord? Note, then, first, that when the hand of God lies heavily upon someone and presses him down to death, that is the time to humble oneself under that powerful hand of God, to fear God, and to fear that dreadful tribunal before which he must soon stand. If a man does not do this, he proves himself merely stupid and rebellious against that hand of God, which will not let him go until it has crushed and broken him. This is what ought to be done by us, and that it ought to be done is shown by the rebuke of the repentant thief. But the impenitence and blasphemy of the other thief sufficiently show that this does not always happen: rather, some people remain, even in the greatest calamities, so stupid and hardened against the hand of God that they are no more humbled and do not fear God or his terrible judgment than if they lived free from every evil. The cause is that there was never any juice of grace in such men. But how can pressure squeeze out juice from what has none at all? If you press a dry stick, will you squeeze out any juice? Yet we are all by nature like a dry stick. But the other thief, already pressed and hanging in torments, comes to his senses, affirms Christ's glory, rebukes his companion, confesses his sin, and asks for pardon. Who, then, made a difference between these two? They were equal by nature, equal in their evil deeds and their wicked past life, and equal finally in their torments. If that one had not drawn from Christ, who was crucified at the same time, the saving juice of grace which the torments pressed out, it could never have been pressed out, not even by torments or deaths of any kind. Christ was indeed crucified on equal terms, placed between the two, but he did not bestow his grace equally on both. Therefore in afflictions and torments, especially in that final agony, Christ himself must be asked to give us that juice of grace which our afflictions and crosses try to press out; for otherwise not even a single drop can be drawn out. Indeed, then there will be pressed out this bitter and acrid juice of our nature, namely impatience, blasphemy, and others of that kind; but that sweet juice of grace cannot be pressed out. Besides this, I observe in this first argument of rebuke that those who are held in some common misery ought to be so far from mockery and jeering that they are moved instead to pity for others who are under the same condemnation and misery. If they show no pity to others, that is plainly a proof that they are empty of the fear and reverence of God. If, however, they have reviled and reproached others for their misery, then they prove that they are not only empty of grace and of the fear of God, but full of the gall of bitterness. We are all sinners and miserable by nature, and it is fitting that miserable sinners be moved by mercy toward other miserable sinners. And indeed we justly so. There is an objection to be anticipated: that the blaspheming thief might infer from the fact that it has been said that all who are crucified together share a common and the same condemnation, that they also share a common and the same desert. The other thief meets this by saying: "We indeed, that is, I and you, are justly in this common condemnation. But this man has done nothing amiss." There are two further arguments in these words against the blaspheming thief. The first is: You deserve this condemnation and punishment; therefore do you not fear God? For just as oppression and the cross, especially that final oppression which goes as far as death, ought to rouse in us the fear of God, however stupid we were before, so the consideration of our own desert, when we reflect that we have deserved that oppression and death, ought to rouse us much more to the fear of God and to a speedy repentance. That this ought to be done is taught by the example of this thief, who rebuked the other's blasphemy. But that it does not always come about in this way is shown in turn by the example of the blaspheming thief. The cause is that although all men certainly deserve it, not all are led by the awareness of their own desert, not even at the very point of death and in that last agony and struggle. There are also many who, even if they are affected by a sense of their own desert and sin, are not affected by a sense of God's mercy, and so if they fear, their fear is merely servile and despairing. But that in the case of the other, repentant thief some people at death are affected by a sense both of their own desert and of God's mercy, and so fear with a certain filial fear, must all be ascribed to the cross of Christ, from which alone this sense of sin and of mercy together flowed. For what happened to the repentant thief must happen also to others. Therefore, just as that thief ought to have borne witness that this grace was received from Christ alone, with whom he was then crucified, so we too ought to ascribe that grace to the same Christ alone, with whom we too in a certain manner have been crucified.

units.la: Non prætereunda est hoc loco confessio ista peccati, libera adeo & aperta, non quidem tam expressa tormentis, quàm suauiter educta ex suaui illo sen-benignitatis Domini. Nam posteaquam quis per su refipifcentiam & conuersionem semel gustauit quàm suauis fit Dominus, tum quidem is pro viribus omnia facit ad gloriam illius, quem tam suauem gustauit: imò non metuit sese ignominiæ exponere, vt Dominus glorificetur. Et re vera ea est ipsissima via, qua consequatur gloriam, & operiat peccata sua, abscondatque ab oculis Domini, fi ea manifesta confessione hominibus palam infpicien-da proponat: contráque qui defugit ignominiam suam, vt Deum ignominia aliqua afficiat, is pro-culdubio ignominiæ exponendus est in illo die Do-mini.
units.tr: Here we must not pass over this confession of sin, so free and open, drawn not so much by torments as sweetly drawn out of that sweet sense of the Lord's kindness. For once someone has, through his own repentance and conversion, tasted how sweet the Lord is, then he does everything he can for the glory of him whom he has tasted as so sweet; indeed he does not fear to expose himself to shame, so that the Lord may be glorified. And in truth this is the very way to obtain glory and to cover one's sins and hide them from the Lord's eyes, if one sets them forth for men to see openly in a frank confession; whereas on the contrary, whoever shrinks from his own shame, so as to put some shame upon God, will undoubtedly be exposed to shame on that day of the Lord.

units.la: Sequitur argumentum reprehensionis 3. ab innocentia: Ipse vero nihil insolens fecit. Hoc est, nihil horum quæ nunc patitur merito suo sibi procurauit: nihil enim morte dignum vnquam perpetrauit. Ergo annon times Deum qui petulans es in istum innocentem? Hic docemur, non iacienda conuitia in innocentem, quem videmus nulla iusta de causa supplicio affici: ea re enim arguimus, nos vacuos esse pietatis & timoris Dei. Innocentes autem sunt homines dum patiuntur, duplici ratione: vel enim non sunt rei illius criminis ob quod ipsi puniuntur, vel si rei sint, & malefici, tamen per eandem & resipiscentiam, innocentes in Christi illa innocentia, euadunt. Priori modo immerito ac iniuste afflicti, non sunt illi quidem in supplicio dum hærent, ludibrio habendi, & sannis excipiendi: imo ne innocentes quidem in Christo ipsiusque illa innocentia, dum in pœnis hærent, illudendi sunt, licet a supplicio ciuili non sint, propterea quod in Christo innocentes sint, eximendi. Hic præterea video Patrem Christi, qui toto illo tempore quo accusatus est filius, coram iudice Pilato, innocentem esse filium declarauit toties, etiam per os ipsius iudicis: quinque etiam tum cum educeretur filius ad supplicium testatus est innocentiam ipsius, per fletum & planctum mulierum Hierosolymitanarum. Video nunc eundem illum Christi Patrem, eandem filii innocentiam testificatam facere, idque opera latronis huius resipiscentis, qui vna cum Christo fuit crucifixus. Ita enim nobis consulit, qui vt nō possumus credere in Mediatore præter eum, qui in nobis reus est: ita non possumus credere nisi in eum qui in se innocens est ac iustus. Talis enim nos decebat Pontifex, pius, innocens, impolutus, &c. Oportet enim Pontificem nostrum innocentem esse. Domine, memento. Posteaquam latro iste reprehendit socium suum, simulque confessus est sua ipsius pecca-ta, iam conuersus ad Dominum supplex veniam pre-tit & vitā catur, & gratiam ac vitam petit. Eum appellat Dominum, quem tamen tanquam seruum aliquem vidit è ligno pendentem. Agnoscit præterea Regem eum dum regnum ipsi ascribit. Petit ab ipso vitam quem vidit moribundum. Ista mirifica sunt omnia. Magis autem mira videbuntur, si primum consideremus personam precantis, qualisnam fuerit ante hoc, & quænam sit eius nunc conditio præsens: deinde si consideremus personam ipsius ad quem is dirigit preces suas: nempe Christi ac ipsius præsentem conditionem. Quod igitur attinet ad personam latronis, si is quidem educatus fuisset in schola Christi, res non ita videretur mira: verùm cùm educatus sit in spelunca latronum, vbi omnem sensum æquitatis & humanitatis prorsus extinxit, adeoque hominem exuit de homine, & belua quædam efferata euasit, viuens latrociniis, rapinis, humano denique sanguine: educatio, inquam, ista, mores hi pristini, arguunt mutationem tam subitam plusquam mirabilem. Iam vero, vt respiciamus præsentem hominis conditionem, Quòd si tum corpore liber fuisset, ita vt posset secure aliquo modo Christum ipsiusque regnum, vitam etiam alteram intueri, res sese tam admiranda non offerret. At cùm hæreret in tormentis iis quæ profectò possunt sensus abstractos ab omni re alia totos occupare in sese: cùmque præterea expectaret extremam carnificum manum, profectò nunquam potuit quis satis id demitari, quod oblitus conditionis illius præsentis, vsque adeo alioqui sensibilis, de conditione illa beata in Christo futura cogitarit. Atque hoc nihilo fuit minùs quàm si is eximis infer-ris in summos cælos transiliisset. Nunc si coiuertas oculos ad personam Christi, ipsiusque quæ tum fuit conditionem: si Christus sese tunc oculis latronis, tanquam regem aliquem gloriosum obtulisset, tum profectò res tanti momenti non videretur. At cùm Christum in eadem damnatione hærentem (vt ipse loquitur) videret, adeoque etiam maiori: (nam latro ille non est impetitus iis conuitiis, quibus est Christus, quæ omnibus tormentis fuerunt procul dubiò grauiora) pro
units.tr: This follows the third argument against the thief, from innocence: But this man has done nothing amiss. That is, he has brought none of the sufferings he now endures upon himself by his own deserts, for he never committed anything worthy of death. Therefore do you not fear God, you who are so insolent toward this innocent man? Here we are taught not to hurl insults at an innocent person whom we see punished for no just cause, for by such behaviour we show that we lack piety and the fear of God. Now people are innocent while they suffer in two ways. Either they are not guilty of the crime for which they are punished, or, if they are guilty and wicked, they nevertheless become innocent through repentance, in the innocence of Christ. In the first way, those unjustly and undeservedly afflicted are, while they remain in punishment, to be mocked and jeered at. But even innocent people, in Christ and in his innocence, while they remain in their sufferings, ought not to be mocked, although they may not be exempt from civil punishment, because they are innocent in Christ. Here I also see the Father of Christ, who throughout the whole time the Son was accused before the judge Pilate, declared the Son innocent so many times, even through the mouth of the judge himself. Indeed, even when the Son was led out to execution, he bore witness to his innocence through the weeping and lamentation of the women of Jerusalem. Now I see that same Father of Christ bearing witness to the same innocence of his Son, and doing so through the work of this repentant thief, who was crucified together with Christ. For just as we cannot believe in any mediator except him who is guilty in our place, so we cannot believe except in him who is innocent and righteous in himself. For such a high priest became us: holy, innocent, undefiled, and so on. For our high priest must be innocent. Lord, remember me. After the thief rebuked his companion and at the same time confessed his own sins, he now turned to the Lord, a suppliant, seeking pardon and asking for grace and life. He calls him Lord, though he had seen him hanging on the wood like some servant. He also acknowledges him as King when he ascribes a kingdom to him. He asks life from him whom he sees dying. All these things are wonderful. They will seem even more wonderful if we first consider the person of the one who prays, what he was before and what his present condition is, and then consider the person to whom he directs his prayers, namely Christ and his present condition. As for the person of the thief, if he had been educated in the school of Christ, the matter would not seem so remarkable. But since he was educated in a den of robbers, where he had utterly extinguished every sense of justice and humanity, and had so stripped himself of humanity that he became a kind of savage beast, living by thefts, plunder and finally human blood, that upbringing and those former manners, I say, prove a change so sudden as to be more than wonderful. Now, if we look at the man's present condition: had he still been free in body, so that he could in some measure securely look upon Christ and his kingdom and the life to come, the matter would not present itself as so admirable. But since he was hanging in those torments, which can certainly occupy the senses entirely, withdrawn from every other thing, and since he was also awaiting the final hand of the executioners, no one could ever sufficiently wonder at this: that, forgetting his present condition, which was otherwise so perceptible, he thought about that blessed condition in Christ that was to come. And this was no less than if he had been snatched up by some miraculous power into the highest heavens. Now if we turn our eyes to the person of Christ and to his condition at that time: if Christ had presented himself to the thief's eyes then as some glorious king, the matter would surely not seem of such great importance. But since he saw Christ hanging in the same condemnation (as he himself puts it), and indeed in a worse one, for the thief was not assailed with those insults that Christ was, which were certainly more grievous than all the torments,

units.la: Status Christi, quem latro tam præclara fide & charitate amplectitur. In mortis supplicio. profecto quod in tam crassa ac densa ignominiae nube, videritamen tantam Christi gloriam, id nunquam potest quis satis admirari. Quod si Christo fuisset vsus familiariter ante hac, si ipsum audisset docentem, si vidisset miracula edentem, cum discipulis ac Apostolis suis, res tum quidem non ita magna videri posset. Verùm cùm primus Christi intuitus, primùm cum eo colloquiu, primus cum eo congressus fuerit in cruce, & in ignominiosa ipsius morte, profecto quòd in tanta morte, tantam vitam quaesierit, res est plus quàm admirabilis. Quis enim Iudaeorum omnium Christum è cruce pendentem tum precatus est? Quis discipulorum? Quis denique Apostolorum? Adeo vt crucifixus iste latro pudefecerit, nō Sacerdotes modò & reliquos Iudaeos, sed discipulos quoque Christi, & Apostolos ipsos, qui quidem omnes tunc temporis in Christo offensi erant: pudefaciat etiam omnes omnium aetatum homines, qui noluerunt credere in Christum, quem quidem ipsi vident, nunc non crucifixum, sed glorificatum ad dextram illius maiestatis. Paulus refert solere eligere sibi Deum res nihili, & quae non sunt, ad pudefaciendum ea quae sunt & alicuius pretij videntur esse in mundo. Quod si hoc alias vnquam viu venit, profecto hoc tempore maximè, in quo abiectus quidem latro electus est ad pudefaciendum omnes principes huius mundi, tam Iudaeos quàm Gentes: & exaltatus est ad humiliandam carnis istam super biam: atque adeo excitatus est, non tanquam exemplar modò, sed tanquam magister quidem fidei & respiscentiae, charitatis & patientiae omnibus, & qui tum exiterunt, & qui venturi sunt ad vltimum vsque Christi aduentum: quos profecto, si non crediderint, in illo die vltimo damnaturus est, in quo vt nunc ignominiosa in cruce erectus ad alios docendos: ita tunc erigendus est gloriosus in coelestesubsellium ac throno, ad testimonium ferendum aduersus incredulos quoscunque. Haec quidem omnia eò pertinent, vt qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur, & qui admiratur, admiretur Dominum. Haec enim à me dicta sunt, non eo fine, vt quis habeat homuncionem istum in admiratione: sed vt Christum admiretur, qui rem reportis tam abiectus in speciem, tatam potentiam, tantam misericordiam erga tam miserum latronem.
units.tr: The condition of Christ, whom the thief embraces with such splendid faith and love, in the punishment of death. Indeed, no one can ever sufficiently marvel that the thief, seeing in such a thick and dense cloud of ignominy the great glory of Christ, sought in so great a death so great a life. If he had been familiar with Christ before, if he had heard him teaching, seen him working miracles, with his disciples and apostles, the matter might then not seem so great. But since his first sight of Christ, his first conversation, his first meeting with him, was on the cross and in Christ's ignominious death, it is truly more than admirable that in so great a death he sought so great a life. For who of all the Jews then prayed to Christ hanging on the cross? Who of the disciples? Who, finally, of the apostles? So that this crucified thief shamed not only the priests and the rest of the Jews, but also the disciples of Christ and the apostles themselves, who all at that time were offended in Christ. He also shames all men of all ages who refused to believe in Christ, whom indeed they now see not crucified but glorified at the right hand of that majesty. Paul relates that God is accustomed to choose things of no account, and things that are not, to shame those that are and seem to be of some worth in the world. If this has ever happened, it has certainly happened most of all in this time, in which the abject thief has been chosen to shame all the princes of this world, Jews as well as Gentiles, and has been exalted to humble that pride of the flesh. And so he has been raised up, not only as an example, but as a teacher of faith and repentance, love and patience, to all who have existed and who will exist until the last coming of Christ. Those whom, certainly, if they do not believe, he will condemn on that last day, when he who now was lifted up in ignominy on the cross to teach others will then be raised up in glory on the heavenly judgment seat and throne, to bear witness against all unbelievers whomsoever. All these things tend to this end: that he who glories should glory in the Lord, and he who admires should admire the Lord. For these things have been said by me not with the aim that anyone should hold this little man in admiration, but that he should admire Christ, who from so abject a appearance brings forth so great power, and so great mercy toward so wretched a thief.

units.la: Quanto in teruallo co fessor & martyr exi mius, oesalios ante cesserit.
units.tr: How far in time the outstanding confessor and martyr surpassed all others before him.

units.la: Latro insignis Magister fidei, respiscentiae, charitatis & patientiae.
units.tr: The thief, a notable teacher of faith, repentance, love and patience.

units.la: Mira omnia in Christi gratia erga suos electos potentia. exercuerit Ipsi igitur sit omnis gloria. Amen.
units.tr: All these wonders display the power Christ exercised in grace toward his elect. To him therefore be all glory. Amen.

units.la: Amen, amen dico tibi. Respondet Dominus, promittitque assueta illa asseveratione, & quasi iureiurando ad maiorem fidem adhibito, Amen, amen, inquiens. Quid autem promittit his verbis? Erus hodie mecum in paradiso: hoc est, eris particeps regni illius mei caelestis. Notatur tempus: hodie, inquit: hoc est, nulla mora interposita eris mecum, sicque non erit periculum ne tui obliuiscar, vbi venero in regnum meum: ecce enim hoc ipso die assumate mecum ad regnum meum. Vbi vero erit cum Christo particeps regni ipsius? Nempe in paradiso. De hoc nomine legis 2. Cor. 12. 4. Apocal. 2. 7. & alibi. Nihil autem aliud eo nomine significatur, quam eam quam vocauit Iohannes 14. 2. domum Patris sui, vbi sunt multae habitationes. Paradisus iste est longe supra omnes caelos, quo concendit Christus post resurrectionem suam. Est locus throni gloriae Dei & aeternae quietis Ecclesiae suae. Sed de nomine hoc satis. Videsin hoc Christi responso quanta sit ipsius facilitas in respondendo etiam latroni recipiscenti, neque enim accipit cuiusquam personam Dominus, modo quis serio resipiscat. Audiit fures, audit latrones, audit adulteros, &c. Neque vero id mirum. Nam is qui praeuenit nos gratia, annon necesse est eum subsequi nos gratia? Is qui dat gratiam, qua fit vt rogemus ipsum, annon necesse est ex gratia quoque audiat rogantes? Spiritus Dei, inquit Paulus, interpellat pro nobis suspiriis inenarrabilibus: haec est prima gratia, qua donat nos Spiritu suo sancto, qui nos docet precari. Tum subiungit, Qui scrutatur corda, nouit quis sit sensus sui Spiritus: Haec secunda gratia est, qua nimirum audit ac intelligit omnia quaecunque precamur nos per Spiritu ipsius. Tota difficultas posita est in prima gratia, paucique admodum ea donantur. At vero vbi quis semel est assequutus primam illam gratiam, facillime iam obtinetur secunda. Necesse enim est, si caelestia illa per Spiritum ipsius petamus, vt nos audiat Dominus. Si enim terrestria ista ab eo petamus, vel ea impetrabimus, vel certe de causa certiores nos tandem faciet, cur non statim petentibus condonarit ea. Ita fiet vt voluntate eius simus contenti, ipsiique gratias agamus quam maximas. Deinde nota, quam liberalis beatus sit Dominus. Neque enim satis habet dare id tantum quod petimus, sed superat vota nostra. Petiuit quidem latro vt ipsius duntaxat reminisceretur,cum veniret in regnum suum: Respondet Dominus,Ecce nunc do tibi quod petis: Insuper autem hodie eris mecum in paradiso,vt non sit periculum,ne tui obliuiscar,cum venero in regnum meum. Pete à Domino satis multa & magna: nam profecto impetrabis plura & maiora. Profecto enim gloria illa futura superatura est spem nostram & expectationem illam omnem,quae fuerat in vita ista praesenti. Etiam si loquamur de terrenis istis,anno multi comperiuntur qui acceperunt à Domino plura, quàm quae vnquam aut fuerunt sibi ipsi polliceri? Dauid air, Vitam petiit, sed regnum mihi dedisti, hoc est, non pri- uatam aliquam vitam & obscuram, sed vitam quam vivuo tanquam Rex in luce populi. Nota postremo summam Christi potentiam in summa humiliatione. Verba enim haec Regis sunt, imo Dei sunt: solus enim Deus cae- los potest promittere, & dare. Verum quidem est deitatem illam in Christo inhabitantem, quo tempore pendebat ex cruce, sese obscurasse, ac quodammodo inaniuisse: second cum enim Christus pati non potuisset, si inhabitans in eo deitas vires suas exeruisset. Attamen non ita continuit se ac delituit deitas in Christo è ligno pendente, quin eodem tempore mirabiliter operata sit, & peream Christus, postquam cum morte aeterna & potestatibus infernorum luctatus est, gloriose triumphauerit insidens in cruce sua, tanquam curru triumphali. Hoc quoque, inter cetera, opus conuersionis huius latronis eidem deitati, ipsiusque potentiae, quam exeruit in cruce, ascribimus. Quod si Christus in extrema humiliatione & in diebus carnis suae potens adeo fuerit ad vitam peccatori largiendam, annon oportet eum nunc in caelis glorificatum mirum in modum potentem esse, cum iam deposita omnis illa carnis infirmitas, & deitas omnes suas vires in Christo exerat, & quasi explicet? Quod si igitur in quoquam homine Christus non sit potens ad vitam, id non est ascribendum profecto alicui defectui potentiae quae sit in Christo iam glorificato, verum defectui fidei, qui in nobis est, fidei, inquam, in Christum, quem videmus nunc in cælis glorificatum : cùm latro hic in eum crediderit quem ante oculos crucifixum, & summæ ignominiæ expositum habebat. Summa omnium quæ diximus de hoc Christi responso, huc redit: Cùm vsque adeo facilis ac promptus sit Dominus ad audiendum nostras preces, eum cum fiducia precemur. Cùm liberalis adeo sit, ab eo petamus quod satis est. Cùm denique potens adeo sit, petamus ab eo cum hac fiducia, quòd possit omnia facere supra ea quæ petimus, aut mente concipimus, pro vi illa agente in nobis.
units.tr: Amen, amen, I say to you. The Lord answers, using that customary affirmation, as if an oath were added for greater assurance, saying, Amen, amen. What does he promise in these words? You will be with me today in paradise: that is, you will share in my heavenly kingdom. The time is noted: today, he says. That is, no delay will intervene, you will be with me, and so there will be no danger that I will forget you when I come into my kingdom, for see, on this very day you will be taken up with me into my kingdom. But where will he share the kingdom with Christ? Certainly in paradise. You read of this name in 2 Cor. 12.4 and Rev. 2.7, and elsewhere. Nothing else is meant by that name than the place John calls, in 14.2, the house of his Father, where there are many dwelling places. That paradise is far above all the heavens, to which Christ ascended after his resurrection. It is the place of the throne of God's glory and of the eternal rest of his Church. But enough about the name. From this response of Christ you see how ready he is to answer even a penitent thief, for the Lord does not regard the person of anyone, provided only that one truly repents. He hears thieves, he hears robbers, he hears adulterers, and so on. Nor is this surprising. For he who went before us in grace, must he not also follow us in grace? He who gives the grace by which we are moved to pray to him, must he not also hear those who pray from grace? The Spirit of God, says Paul, makes intercession for us with groanings that cannot be uttered: this is the first grace, by which he gives us his Holy Spirit, who teaches us to pray. Then he adds, He who searches hearts knows what the mind of the Spirit is: this is the second grace, by which he surely hears and understands all that we pray through his Spirit. The whole difficulty lies in the first grace, and very few receive it. But once someone has obtained that first grace, the second is very easily obtained. For if we ask for heavenly things through his Spirit, the Lord must hear us. If we ask him for earthly things, he will either grant them, or at least in time he will make us aware of the reason why he has not at once granted what we asked. Thus it will come about that we are content with his will, and give him the greatest thanks. Next, note how generous the blessed Lord is. For he is not content merely to give what we ask, but surpasses our prayers. The thief indeed asked only that Christ would remember him when he came into his kingdom. The Lord answers, Behold, now I give you what you ask, and moreover, today you will be with me in paradise, so that there is no danger that I will forget you when I come into my kingdom. Ask the Lord for many great things, for you will surely obtain more and greater. For truly that future glory will surpass our hope and all the expectation that we had in this present life. Even if we speak of these earthly things, how many are found who have received from the Lord more than they ever dared to promise themselves? David says, He asked life of you, and you gave him a kingdom, that is, not some private and obscure life, but the life that one lives as king in the light of the people. Finally, note Christ's supreme power in supreme humiliation. For these are the words of a King, indeed they are the words of God, for God alone can promise and give the heavens. It is true that the deity dwelling in Christ, at the time when he hung on the cross, veiled itself and in some way emptied itself, for Christ could not have suffered if the indwelling deity had put forth its powers. Yet the deity in Christ, hanging from the wood, did not so restrain and hide itself that at the same time it did not work wonderfully, and Christ, after he had wrestled with eternal death and the powers of hell, triumphed gloriously, sitting upon his cross as upon a triumphal chariot. We also ascribe this work of the conversion of this thief, among other things, to that same deity and to the power it put forth on the cross. But if Christ, in his extreme humiliation and in the days of his flesh, was powerful enough to bestow life on a sinner, must he not now, glorified in heaven, be wondrously powerful, since all that weakness of the flesh has been laid aside, and the deity now puts forth, and as it were unfolds, all its powers in Christ? If therefore Christ is not powerful to give life to anyone, this is surely not to be ascribed to any lack of power in Christ, now glorified, but to the lack of faith in us, faith, I say, in Christ, whom we now see glorified in heaven, since this thief believed in him whom he had before his eyes crucified and exposed to the greatest shame. The sum of all we have said about this response of Christ comes to this: since the Lord is so ready and prompt to hear our prayers, let us pray to him with confidence. Since he is so generous, let us ask from him what is enough. Since finally he is so powerful, let us ask him with this confidence, that he is able to do far above all that we ask or conceive in mind, by that power working in us.

units.la: Iohannis 19.
units.tr: John 19.

units.la: 25 Stabant autem iuxta crucem Iesu, mater eius & soror matris eius, Maria Cleopæ vxor, & Maria Magdalene.
units.tr: 25 Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene.

units.la: 26 Quum vidisset ergo Iesus matrem ac discipulum adstantē quem diligebat, dicit matri suæ, Mulier, ecce filius tuus.
units.tr: 26 When Jesus therefore saw his mother, and the disciple standing by whom he loved, he saith unto his mother, Woman, behold thy son!

units.la: 27 Deinde dicit discipulo, Ecce mater tua: & ex illa hora recepit eam discipulus ille domum suam.
units.tr: 27 Then saith he to the disciple, Behold thy mother! And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home.

units.la: NVnc redimus ad Iohannis Euangelium, & historiam illam tractamus, qua Christus matrem suam commendat discipulo illi suo quem dilexit. Christus è cruce pendens, non tantùm passus est, sed & egit. Egit autem vt Rex, quemadmodum iam vidimus in historia illa proxima de latronibus. Nunc verò exerit officium humanæ pietatis erga matrem suam. Primùm autem habemus in hac commendatione matris suæ occasionem commendationis. Est autem in eo, quod viderit notos aliquot stantes iuxta crucem. Primùm autem vidit discipulum quendam suum quem dilexit: is est Iohannes, hac enim periphrasi solet Iohannes se designare in Euangelio suo, idq; facit proculdubiò, ideo quòd non tantùm Christus eum singulari quodam modo dilexerit, sed quòd penitus animo & corde suo, ipse Iohannes perpetuò sensérit illam Christi dilectionem: deinde vidit Christus vnà cũ Iohanne stantes tres mulieres, Mariam matrem suam, MaMariam Cleopæ scilicet vel vxorem, vel filiam, sororem aut Mariæ matris Domini: hoc est, secundum Hebraicam phrasim, cognatam Mariæ matris Domini. Deniq; Mariam Magdalenam, è qua eiecta sunt à Domino septem dæmonia. De Iohanne hoc tantũ annotamus, quod etsi hoc tempore passionis Christi mirabiliter suffocata fuerit fides eius, tamen nõ fuerit extincta penitus. Quòd si enim penitus extincta fuisset, profectò is non fuisset sequutus Dominũ suum ad crucem. Quòd si nulla fuisset in eo spes gloriosæ, post ignominiosam illam mortem, resurrectionis: profectò nunquam sustinuisset oculis intueri tam miserandũ spectaculũ. Procul dubio fides dedit ei audaciam eam qua sequutus est Christum ad crucem usque. Spes vero consolationem ministravit, cùm Christum in tam ignominiosa morte hærentem intuitus est. In mulieribus autem istis video insignem σφγλω & amoris quendam affectũ, qui non patitur ipsas à Christo diuellii: Arnisi fides in ipsis fuisset, profectò naturalis illè amoreas eò nunquam prouexisset, vt Christũ ad crucem euntem sequerentur, & nisi spes aliqua fuisset futuræ gloriæ, post mortem tam probrosam, profectò nunquam sustinuissent oculis intueri tam triste spectaculũ. Nolum, inquit Paulus, vos in ignorantia versari, fratres, quod ad eos attinet qui obdormierunt, vt ne doleatis vt ij qui spem non habet. Quibus quidem verbis significat σφγλω ista & naturale amoris affectũ, si non vna sit cũ ea spes gloriosæ resurrectionis, homine necessario adigere ad desperatũ quendam dolore, in morte eius, quæ is in primis charũ habet. Contrà igitur si adsit in morte eorũ, quos habemus charos, spes illa gloriosæ resurrectionis, non tolletur quidem è medio ingenitus ille amoris affectus, vt neque existens ex eo dolor: sed mitigabitur, & cũ dolore miscebitur lætitia, ex spe nimirũ gloriosæ illius resurrectionis. De mulieribus his hoc postremò addo: Quòd si crux Christi nõ absterruit eas à comitando & sequendo Christum, cùm tamen non nisi obscure admodũ viderint gloriã illã venturam: pudeat nos qui Christũ iã glorificatũ quodãmodò videmus in cælis cruce eius deterreri à sequendo eũ ad crucẽ vsque. Sed videamus nunc verba quibus Dominus matrẽ cõmédat Iohanni discipulo suo. Primũ matrẽ Christus copellat, Mulier, inquiens. Mulierē vocat, non autē matrē, qua appellatione ab ipso vsitata, quandiu in terris vnā cū matre sua egit, facis ipse indicauit oculos suos erectos fuisse, vt alias semper, ita in hora illa mortis potissimum supra carnalia ista, vt vocantur: quae homines magnificiunt in hac vita, cuiusmodi sunt, pater, mater, filius, filia, maritus, vxor, genus, patria, &c. Et suo exemplo nos etiā docet, dum hic viuimus, neminem agnoscere secundum carnē, ne Christum quidem ipsum: Quisquis enim in Christo est noua creatura: vetera praeterierunt, ecce noua facta sunt omnia. In caelesti vero vita illa carnalia ista omnia plane abolebuntur. Neque tum erunt amplius, vel patres, vel filij, vel matres, vel filiae, vel mariti, vel vxores, sed erimus, his rebus omnibus, quae veterem creaturam comitantur, iam abolitis, tanquam Angeli totidem caelestes. Nunc verba Christi, quibus matrem suam alloquitur, Ecce, inquit, filius tuus. Demonstrato nimirum Iohanne, qui vnā iuxta crucem stabat, q.d. Ego quidem migro ex ista vita, Iohannem autem substituo loco meo, vt sit is tibi filius, & mea vice faciat officium erga te filij.
units.tr: Now we return to the Gospel of John and take up that history in which Christ commends his mother to his beloved disciple. Hanging on the cross, Christ not only suffered but also acted. He acted as a King, as we have already seen in the earlier history of the thieves. Now, however, he performs the duty of human devotion toward his mother. In this commendation of his mother, we have first the occasion for the commendation. It lies in the fact that he saw some acquaintances standing near the cross. He first saw a certain disciple of his whom he loved: this is John, for John is accustomed to designate himself in his Gospel by this periphrasis, and he doubtless does so because Christ loved him not only in a singular way but because John himself had felt that love of Christ deeply in his mind and heart at all times. Then Christ saw three women standing with John: Mary his mother; Mary the wife, or daughter, or sister of Cleophas, that is, according to Hebrew idiom, a kinswoman of the mother of the Lord; and finally Mary Magdalene, from whom the Lord had cast out seven demons. Concerning John we note only this: although his faith was wonderfully overwhelmed at this time of Christ's passion, it was not utterly extinguished. For if it had been utterly extinguished, he would certainly not have followed his Lord to the cross. And if there had been in him no hope of glorious resurrection after that shameful death, he would certainly never have endured to look upon so pitiable a sight. Without doubt, faith gave him the boldness by which he followed Christ even to the cross. Hope brought him consolation when he looked upon Christ hanging in so ignominious a death. In these women I see a remarkable [storge] and a certain affection of love, which does not allow them to be torn away from Christ. Unless faith had been in them, natural affection would certainly never have carried them so far as to follow Christ going to the cross, and unless there had been some hope of future glory after so disgraceful a death, they would certainly never have endured to look upon so sad a sight. "I would not have you ignorant, brethren," says Paul, "concerning those who have fallen asleep, that you grieve not as those who have no hope." By these words he signifies that such [storge] and natural affection of love, if there is not joined with it the hope of glorious resurrection, necessarily drives a man to a kind of despairing grief at the death of those whom he holds most dear. On the contrary, therefore, if in the death of those whom we hold dear that hope of glorious resurrection is present, the innate affection of love will not indeed be removed from among us, nor the grief arising from it; but it will be softened, and joy will be mingled with grief, namely from the hope of that glorious resurrection. Concerning these women I add this last point: if the cross of Christ did not frighten them from accompanying and following Christ, although they could see only very obscurely that the glory was to come, then we should be ashamed, who now see Christ already glorified in heaven in some way, if we are deterred by his cross from following him even to the cross. But let us now look at the words by which the Lord commends his mother to his disciple John. First, Christ addresses the mother: Woman, he says. He calls her woman, not mother; by which form of address, which he used while he lived on earth with his mother, he himself showed that his eyes were fixed, as always, and especially in that hour of death, above those carnal things, as they are called, which men magnify in this life, such as father, mother, son, daughter, husband, wife, family, country, and so on. By his own example he also teaches us, while we live here, to acknowledge no one according to the flesh, not even Christ himself: For if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; the old things have passed away, behold, all things have become new. In that heavenly life, however, all these carnal things will be utterly abolished. Then there will be no more fathers or sons, mothers or daughters, husbands or wives, but, with all these things that accompany the old creature now abolished, we shall be as the angels of heaven, every one. Now come the words of Christ by which he speaks to his mother: Behold, he says, your son. Indicating, of course, John, who was standing beside the cross, as if to say: "I indeed depart from this life, but I put John in my place, so that he may be a son to you and in my stead perform the duty of a son toward you."

units.la: Iohannem deinde in eundem sensum alloquitur: Ecce mater tua. q.d. Sit tibi loco matris, & vice mea cura eius agito, eique prouideto, non secus atque matri tuae. Iesus Christus potuit quidem e caelis extra ordinem matre sua in viuis post se manentem protegere, ac procurare quaecunque ei necessaria essent: verum non contempsit ordinatam istam agendi rationem. Sic Ecclesiam suam & fideles omnes potest extra ordinem defendere, alere ac curare omnibus modis: at id facit ordinarie, commendatq; etiam num non minus efficaciter, quam cū matrem suā Iohanni comendarer; commendat, inquam, alios, aliis protegendos & curandos, praesertim autem sexum illum muliebrem, vtpote infirmiorem, tanquam matrem suam comendat virili, vt firmiori, adeo vt quicunque protectus sit ac conseruatus in hac vita a quoquam, debeat eius rei gloriam in solidum Christo Iesu. Nota deinde optime consistere inter se officia primae ac secundae legis tabulae, licet videantur nonnunquam discrepare, vt si quo tempore Deus nos trahat aliquo, parentes, vxores, liberi, alio nos trahant atque auocent. At Christus suo exemplo doceat
units.tr: Then he addresses John in the same sense: Behold your mother. As if to say: "Let her be to you in place of a mother, and in my stead take care of her and provide for her, no less than for your own mother." Jesus Christ could indeed, from heaven, outside the ordinary order, protect his mother, who remained in this life after him, and procure whatever was necessary for her; yet he did not despise this ordered manner of acting. Thus he can defend, nourish and care for his Church and all the faithful outside the ordinary order, in every way; but he does so ordinarily, and he entrusts them, no less effectively than when he entrusted his mother to John, I say, he entrusts others to others to be protected and cared for by them, and especially that female sex, as weaker, he commends, as his own mother, to the manly sex, as stronger, so that whoever is protected and preserved in this life by anyone ought to ascribe the glory of that entirely to Christ Jesus. Note next that the duties of the first and second tables of the law agree very well with one another, although they sometimes seem to conflict, as when God draws us to some place and parents, wives, children draw us away and distract us elsewhere. But Christ by his example teaches

units.la: Filiū aliū suo loco substituit.
units.tr: He substitutes another son in his place.

units.la: 17. Christus officio amici fungitur erga Iohannem discipulū.
units.tr: 17. Christ performs the office of a friend toward his disciple John.

units.la: Conseruatio nostra, vt sit consideranda.
units.tr: Our preservation, to be considered.

units.la: Primae ac secundae tabulae officia cohaerēt, sed ordine suo collocāda. cet nos optimè inter se consistere. Qui sic iam occupatus in Patris sui obedientia, vt sui ipsius sit oblitus: tamè matre suâ intuitus, eius nō est oblitus. Sed nota officiorū ordinem. Christus è cruce, hoc est, è medio perfectissimę illius obedientiæ suæ, matris suæ recordatur. Qua quidè re docemur in officiis faciendis, præcedere quidem officium in Deum, subsequi autem officium in homines, adeóque emanare atque existere officium in hominem, ex illo fonte officij in Deum. Qui quidè ordo adeo necessarius est, vt sine amore & officio erga Deum iam antegressso, nullus queat esse sincerus amor, nullum sincerum officium erga homines. Nihil enim quod fit aut geritur erga quemque sincerum est, nisi id in Domino fiat. Quod si hic ordo invertatur, & ordiaris officium ab homine, & à secunda legis tabula, vt illud raceam nullū posse esse eiusmodi sincerū officium, profectò fieri non poterit, vt Deus officium illud ac cultum acceptū ac gratū habeat. Dicit Christus alibi, Qui non odit patrem & matrem propter me, non est me dignus: quanto igitur magis qui præfert patrem aut matrem Christo, non est Christo dignus? Nota præterea: sunt qui dum vident necessariò sibi decedendum ex hac vita, adeo alieni sunt à naturali illo affectu & ἀστοργίᾳ adeo sunt erga eos, quos post se in vitis relinquunt, vt nihili faciant, quid iam post obitum suum de ipsis futurum sit: imo nihili faciant, si ipsis semel iam sublatis è mundo, mundus hic sit totus ruituus. Agnoscunt enim satis prophanorum istorum hominum voces. Alij sunt in mortis hora, qui, etsi non plane exuant storgen illam & naturalem affectum, tamen ita in eis suffocatur dolore illo mortis, vt, si parentes, si vxor, si liberi, & coniunctissimi quique coram sistantur, tamen nihil de iis cogitent, nullam de iis curam ne vultu quidem præseferant. At Iesus Christus in medio tormentorum, blasphemiarum, luctæ, cum ira Patris & æterna morte, dum intuetur matrem suam, sollicitè eius curam agit, cōmendatque eam discipulo suo dilecto: qua quidem re significatur ἐγὼ istam & natiuum hunc affectum erga matre & alios, quicunque cum ipso natura coniuncti erant, in eo maiorem fuisse, quâ in quouis alio vnquam homine. Neque enim quisquam vnquâ filius extitit, qui tantopererè matrem suam dilexit, vt Iesus suâ, adeo vt, nisi in ipsi simus per fidè, oporteat vel deperdi planè natura insitu affectu hunc, vel certè suffocari, nisi fide, præsertim in illa agonia & mortis articulo sanctificemur. Discè postremò exemplo Christi, qui in extrema agonia & conflictu cū morte æterna & cū inferis ipsis, tam serio tamen commendat matrem Iohanni discipulo suo: discè, inquam, honorem illum lege mandatum non tam positum esse in externa quadam cæremonia, quàm in necessariis officiis quibuscunque, ad quæ facienda in gratiam parentum, non minùs profectò sumus deuincti, quàm sunt ipsi parentes ad officia illa necessaria erga nos, in nobis educandis, nutriendis, erudiendis obligati. Etsi enim non sit natura comparatum, vt liberi parentes diligant æquè ac parentes liberos suos, iuxta illud vulgatum, Charitas non ascendit sed descendit: tamen nisi diligamus parentes, & vicem iis rependamus, ipsis infidelibus, inquit Apostolus, sumus deteriores. Nam etiam Ethnici ipsi hæc officia erga parentes suos præstiterunt. Ex illa hora. Sequitur obedientia Iohannis. Matrem Domini eodem loco quo suam ipsius habet, & domum vna secum deducit. Dominus è cruce cōmendauit Iohanni cutam matris, non quidem ipsius Iohannis, sed suæ: Iohannes paret ac pro sua ipsius matre, Domini matrem habet. Dominus quotidie non è cruce, sed ex cælesti illo throno commendat nobis curam, non quidem suæ matris, sed nostri ipsorum, quæ nos genuit & educauit: At quotusquisq; est qui voci huic Domini auscultat? Verùm non est hoc prætereundum silentio, quod hic Iohannes dicatur duxisse matrem Domini domum suam. Iohannes igitur ex discipulis Christi vnus domum & familiam habuit. Quamobrē stultum est putare discipulos Christi, relictis familiis suis, omnibus facultatibus, Christum nudos & omnium egenos sequutos fuisse. Et plus quā stultum est putare cū Monachis istis & otiosis vētribus, perfectionem in mēdicitate, ac proinde in adulatione potius, quam parasitica esse positam.
units.tr: The duties of the first and second tablets cohere, but they must be arranged in their proper order, and they agree very well with one another. Christ, already so occupied in obedience to his Father that he had forgotten himself, nevertheless, when he looked upon his mother, did not forget her. Note, however, the order of the duties. Christ, from the cross, that is, from the midst of his most perfect obedience, remembers his mother. By this we are taught that in performing our duties the duty toward God comes first, and the duty toward human beings follows, so that the duty toward a human being flows from and exists out of that source, the duty toward God. This order is so necessary that without a prior love and duty toward God there can be no sincere love and no sincere duty toward other people. For nothing that is done toward anyone is sincere unless it is done in the Lord. If this order is reversed, and you begin the duty from the human being and from the second tablet of the law, then, to say nothing of the fact that no such duty can be sincere, it certainly cannot happen that God will regard that duty and worship as acceptable and pleasing. Christ says elsewhere, He who does not hate father and mother for my sake is not worthy of me. How much more, then, is he who prefers father or mother to Christ not worthy of Christ? Note further: there are some who, seeing that they must necessarily depart from this life, are so estranged from that natural affection and unnatural coldness [ἀστοργίᾳ], so indifferent toward those whom they leave behind in life, that they care nothing what will become of them after their death; indeed they care nothing if, once they themselves have been taken out of the world, the whole world should collapse. For they recognise well enough the words of those profane men. Others, at the hour of death, although they do not altogether cast off that natural affection [storge, στοργή], are so overwhelmed in them by the grief of dying that, even if parents, wife, children and all the closest kin are set before them, they think of none of them and do not show the least care for them, not even in their countenance. But Jesus Christ, in the midst of torments, blasphemies, struggle, with the wrath of the Father and eternal death upon him, while he looks upon his mother, takes anxious care of her and commends her to his beloved disciple. By this it is signified that this storge [στοργή] and natural affection toward mother and others, all who were joined to him by nature, was greater in him than in any other man ever. For no son has ever existed who loved his mother so greatly as Jesus did his. So much so that unless we are in him through faith, this natural affection implanted in us must either be utterly lost or at least be stifled, unless we are sanctified by faith, especially in that agony and at the point of death. Finally, learn from the example of Christ, who, in his extreme agony and struggle with eternal death and with hell itself, nevertheless so earnestly commends his mother to John his disciple. Learn, I say, that the honour commanded by the law is not so much placed in some external ceremony as in all the necessary duties which, in order to perform them for the sake of parents, we are no less bound to than parents themselves are bound to those necessary duties toward us in bringing us up, nourishing us and educating us. For although it is not natural for children to love their parents as equally as parents love their children, according to the common saying, Love does not ascend but descends, yet unless we love our parents and repay them in kind, we are, says the Apostle, worse than unbelievers. For even the heathen themselves performed these duties toward their parents. From that hour. There follows the obedience of John. He takes the mother of the Lord to the same place where he has his own mother, and leads her home with him. The Lord from the cross commended to John the care of a mother, not indeed of John's own mother, but of his own; John obeys, and has the mother of the Lord in place of his own mother. The Lord every day, not from the cross but from that heavenly throne, commends to us the care not of his own mother but of our own, who bore us and brought us up. But how few are there who listen to this voice of the Lord? Yet it must not be passed over in silence that here John is said to have taken the mother of the Lord into his own home. John, therefore, was one of Christ's disciples who had a house and a household. Wherefore it is foolish to think that Christ's disciples, having left their families and all their possessions, followed Christ naked and destitute of everything. And it is more than foolish to think, with those monks and idle bellies, that perfection lies in beggary, and therefore rather in flattery than in parasitical begging.

units.la: Matthæi 27.
units.tr: Matthew 27.

units.la: 45 A sexta autem hora, tenebrae factæ sunt super vniuervniuersam regionem vsque ad horam nonam.
units.tr: 45 Now from the sixth hour darkness fell over the whole land until the ninth hour.

units.la: Marci 15.
units.tr: Mark 15.

units.la: 33 Quúmque esset hora sexta, facta sunt tenebrae super vniuersam terram vsque ad horam nonam.
units.tr: 33 And when the sixth hour had come, darkness fell over the whole earth until the ninth hour.

units.la: Lucæ 23.
units.tr: Luke 23.

units.la: 44 Erat autem quasi hora sexta, & tenebrae facta sunt in tota regione vsque ad horam nonam.
units.tr: 44 It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over the whole region until the ninth hour.

units.la: 45 Et obtenebratus est Sol, & anlaum templi fissum est medium.
units.tr: 45 And the sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was torn in the middle.

units.la: HActenus de iis quæ Dominus tã passus est quã egit cũ è ligno crucis penderet: nunc sequitur miraculũ è cælo editum quo tempore pendebat in cruce. Tenebrae factæ sunt super totam terram, Tempus designatum est: cùm esset hora sexta. Causa tenebrarũ subiecta est, quia Sol obscuratus est, hoc est, passus est eclipsin. Diximus suprà de nocte & die Iudaeorum, déque eorum communi partitione, primùm in duodecim horas, deinde in quatuor partes, quas partes noctis dixerunt quatuor vigilias: diei vero quatuor horas: etsi singulæ horæ illæ eorum complexæ sunt in se tres horas. De singulis his diei partibus metio fit in hac historia passionis Domini. Ac primũ quidé de primo mane, vel prima hora qua abductus est in prætoriumad Pilatum Iudicem. Accusatio autem ipsius coram Pilato, durauit vsque ad vltimam partem horæ tertiæ, hoc est, durauit horas circiter quinque: paulò ante sextã, hocest vltima parte horæ tertiæ condemnatus est à Pilato iudice Iohan.19.14. hora tertia, ait Marcus 15.15. crucifixus est, hoc est, vltima parte horæ tertiæ, quæ nobis est vndecima. Nam, vt suprà admonui, inter vndecimam & duodecimam horam condémnatus simul & crucifixus eit Dominus. Hora sexta integra è cruce viuus pédebat: quo tempore tenebrae hæ miraculosæ obortæ sunt, & perpetuatæ ad horam vsque nonam, hoc est, ab hora duodecima nostra, ad horam vsque tertiam pomeridianam: hora denique nona ex angustia animi summa edidit hanc vocem, Eli, Eli, lamma sabachthani. Hac hora quoque expirauit Dominus, hoc est, mortuus est inter tertiam pomeridianam. ridianam & quartam. De hac Solis eclipsi quę causa fuit tenebrarum, quæ totam terram tunc occuparunt, dicam porrò: Illud extra controuersiam est, naturale non fuisse eam Solis eclipsin, cū naturalis Solis eclipsis non contingat nisi in Lunæ deliquio, quo nimirum tempore coniunctio naturalis est duorum planetarum Solis & Lunæ. At hęc eclipsis contigit in plenilunio: nępe tempore Paschatis, quod ex lege Dei celebrari consueuit in plenilunio Martij. Cùm igitur Sol & Luna ex diametro ita esset opposita, ut terræ globus medius interiiceretur inter ea, subitò facta est circumuolutio Lunæ, & interpositio inter aspectum nostrum & Solis faciem: adeo ut sicut scriptum legimus à prophanis quibusdam scriptoribus, ipso meridie conspectæ sint in cælo stellæ: & Dionysius quidem Areopagita cùm non constaret de naturali illius eclipseos causa, dixerit Deum naturæ passum esse. Sed de his sobrie & in eum finem dicendum, ut Dominum in cruce pendentem in miraculo isto admirarentur: nam in summa illa filij sui inanitione, voluit ipse cum glorificare, & testari non tantum de innocentia ipsius quà homo erat: sed de gloria etiam ipsius quà Deus erat. Sunt & hic quoque aliquæ partes mutæ & brutæ creaturæ cęli & terræ: quæ ex officio erga opificē suum testantur ægrè se ferre illas quas tū perpessus est indignitates: ideòq; Sol operit ac velat quasi facie suā, ne tā triste illud spectaculum intueatur. Terra sese cōmouet & hiatus facit: neq; hoc silendū hīc, quòd Deus per mutas, sensus expertes & brutas creaturas instituerit docere homines quos oportuit sentire. At magis stupidi fuerunt, quā muta ac bruta creatura: neq; etiam edito iam hoc miraculo quicquam profecerunt, ut scias vbi quis semel à Deo traditus est in mē tem reprobam, eo magis stupidum & brutum euadere, quàm sit ipsa terra, quam pedibus suis conculcat.
units.tr: Hitherto we have dealt with what the Lord suffered before he was hanged on the wood of the cross; now follows the miracle sent from heaven at the time when he hung upon the cross. The darkness came over the whole earth; the time is marked: when it was the sixth hour. The cause of the darkness is given: because the sun was obscured, that is, it suffered an eclipse. We have said above about the night and day of the Jews, and their common division, first into twelve hours, then into four parts, which parts they called the four watches of the night; but of the day, four hours; although each of those hours of theirs comprised within itself three hours. Mention is made of each of these parts of the day in this history of the Lord's passion. And first of the early morning, or the first hour, when he was led away into the praetorium to Pilate the judge. Now his accusation before Pilate lasted to the last part of the third hour, that is, it lasted about five hours; a little before the sixth, that is, in the last part of the third hour, he was condemned by Pilate the judge (John 19:14). At the third hour, says Mark 15:15, he was crucified, that is, in the last part of the third hour, which for us is the eleventh. For, as I admonished above, the Lord was condemned and crucified between the eleventh and the twelfth hour. In the whole sixth hour he hung alive upon the cross; at which time this miraculous darkness arose, and continued until the ninth hour, that is, from our twelfth hour until the third hour after noon. Finally, at the ninth hour, in the greatest anguish of mind, he uttered this cry: Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani. At this hour also the Lord breathed his last, that is, he died between three and four in the afternoon. Concerning this eclipse of the sun, which was the cause of the darkness that then covered the whole earth, I shall say more: It is beyond dispute that this was not a natural eclipse of the sun, since a natural eclipse of the sun happens only at the new moon, when of course the natural conjunction of the two planets, the sun and the moon, takes place. But this eclipse occurred at the full moon, namely at the time of the Passover, which by God's law was customarily celebrated at the full moon of March. Since therefore the sun and the moon were so opposed along a diameter that the globe of the earth lay between them, there was suddenly a turning of the moon around and an interposition between our sight and the face of the sun; so that, as we read written by certain profane writers, stars were seen in the sky at midday itself; and Dionysius the Areopagite, since it was not certain what was the natural cause of that eclipse, said that God suffered along with nature. But these things must be said soberly and to this end: that they might marvel at the Lord hanging on the cross in this miracle; for in that great emptying of his Son, he wished to glorify him and to bear witness not only to his innocence as he was man, but also to his glory as he was God. There are also here some parts of the dumb and brute creation of heaven and earth, which, from duty toward their maker, bear witness that they took ill the indignities he then suffered; and therefore the sun covers and veils itself, as it were with its face, so as not to look upon so sad a spectacle. The earth moves and makes a gaping chasm; nor should it be passed over here, that God through dumb, senseless and brute creatures has willed to teach men who ought to feel. Yet they were more stupid than the dumb and brute creation: nor did they profit at all even after this miracle had been performed; so that you may know that when anyone has once been given up by God to a reprobate mind, he becomes more stupid and brutish than the very earth which he tramples under his feet.

units.la: Matthæi 27.
units.tr: Matthew 27.

units.la: 46 Circiter verò horam nonam exclamauit Iesus, Eli, Eli, lamma sabachthani: hoc est, Deus mi, Deus mi, cur deseruisti me?
units.tr: 46 And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani: that is, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?

units.la: 47 Quidam autem illic stantium, quum hoc audissent, issent, dicebant, Eliam vocat iste.
units.tr: 47 But some of those standing there, when they heard this, said, "This man is calling Elijah."

units.la: 48 Et statim currens quidam ex istis, quum accepta spongiam impleuisset aceto, & circumposuisset calamo, dedit ei vt biberet.
units.tr: 48 And at once one of them ran, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink.

units.la: 49 Reliqui vero dicebant, Sine, videamus an veniat Elias seruaturus eum.
units.tr: 49 But the rest said, "Leave him alone; let us see whether Elijah comes to save him."

units.la: 50 Iesus autem cum rursus clamasset voce magna, emisit spiritum.
units.tr: 50 And Jesus, crying out again with a loud voice, gave up the spirit.

units.la: 51 Et ecce velum templi scissum est in duas partes a summo vsque ad imum: & terra mota est, & petrae scissae sunt:
units.tr: 51 And behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom; and the earth quaked, and the rocks were split.

units.la: 52 Et monumenta aperta sunt: & multa corpora sanctorum qui dormierant surrexerunt:
units.tr: 52 And the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had slept arose,

units.la: 53 Qui egressi e monumentis post resurrectionem eius, introierunt in sanctam urbe, & apparuerunt multis.
units.tr: 53 And coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many.

units.la: 54 Centurio vero & qui cum eo seruabant Iesum, viso terrae motu, & iis quae facta fuerant, timuerunt vehementer, dicentes, Vere filius Dei erat iste.
units.tr: 54 Now the centurion and those with him who were keeping watch over Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that had happened, feared greatly, saying, "Truly this was the Son of God."

units.la: Marci 15.
units.tr: Mark 15.

units.la: 34 Et hora nona clamauit Iesus voce magna, dicens, Eloi, Eloi, lamma-sabachthani: quod est, si quis interpretetur, Deus mi, Deus mi, cur me deseruisti?
units.tr: 34 And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?

units.la: 35 Et quidam adstantium, quum audissent dicebant, Ecce Eliam vocat.
units.tr: 35 And some of those that stood by, when they heard it, said, Behold, he calleth Elias.

units.la: 36 Cucurrit autem quidam, & impleta spongia aceto, & arundini circumposita dedit ei potum, dicens, Sinite, videamus an veniat Elias ad eum detrahendum.
units.tr: 36 And one ran and filled a spunge full of vinegar, and put it on a reed, and gave him to drink, saying, Let alone; let us see whether Elias will come to take him down.

units.la: 37 Iesus vero emissa voce magna, expirauit.
units.tr: 37 And Jesus cried with a loud voice, and gave up the ghost.

units.la: 38 Et aulaeum templi scissum est in duas partes, a summo vsque ad imum.
units.tr: 38 And the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom.

units.la: 39 Quum vidisset autem Centurio qui adstabat ipsi ex aduerso, eum ita emisso clamore expirasse, dixit, Vere hic homo iste filius erat Dei.
units.tr: 39 And when the centurion, which stood over against him, saw that he so cried out and gave up the ghost, he said, Truly this man was the Son of God.

units.la: Lucae 23.
units.tr: Luke 23.

units.la: 45 Et sol obscuratus est, & aulaeum templi fissum est medium.
units.tr: 45 And the sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was rent in the midst.

units.la: 46 Quumque clamasset voce magna Iesus, ait, Pater in manus tuas depono spiritum meum: & cum haec dixisset expiravit.
units.tr: 46 And when Jesus had cried with a loud voice, he said, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up the ghost.

units.la: 47 Quum vidisset autem Centurio quod factum fuerat, glorificavit Deum, dicens, Vere hic homo iustus erat.
units.tr: 47 Now when the centurion saw what was done, he glorified God, saying, Certainly this was a righteous man.

units.la: 48 Et omnis turba quae simul ad hoc spectaculum accesserat, spectans quae facta fuerant, verberas pectora sua revertebatur.
units.tr: 48 And all the people that came together to that sight, beholding the things which were done, smote their breasts and returned.

units.la: Iohannis 19.
units.tr: John 19.

units.la: 28 Postea cum sciret Iesus reliqua omnia iam esse consummata, ut consummaretur Scriptura, dixit, Sitio.
units.tr: 28 After this, Jesus knowing that all things were now accomplished, that the scripture might be fulfilled, saith, I thirst.

units.la: 29 Vas igitur illic erat positum aceto plenum. Illi vero impleverunt spongiam aceto, & hyssopo circumdatam admoverunt ori eius.
units.tr: 29 Now there was set a vessel full of vinegar: and they filled a spunge with vinegar, and put it upon hyssop, and put it to his mouth.

units.la: 30 Quum autem accepisset Iesus acetum, dixit, Consummatum est: & inclinato capite tradidit Spiritum.
units.tr: 30 When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.

units.la: Hic locus postulat, ut dicamus de angore illo animi quem sensit Dominus interea dū è ligno pendeoret. Doctrina autem de interiori animae angultia melius accipietur, si summam fecero totius Dominicae passionis. Tota Christi in terris vita, quid, quaeso, aliud fuit quàm continua passio? peccatum enim nostrum, quod ipse in se transtulit, & iustitia Dei, non actionem modò, sed multò magis passionem Mediatoris postulauit: nam absque sanguinis effusione, non fit remissio. Finis autem passionis Domini fuit perfecta & abolitio peccati nostri. Ἀπαρτισμὸς autem peccati perfecta requirebat passionem Mediatoris perfectam, sive tempus passionis, sive quantitastatem eius respicias. Quamobrem oportuit Mediatorem, non pati modo, sed perfectè absolutéque pati. Passionem Domini reduco ad tria perpessionum genera. 1. Tentationes. 2. Ignominiam. 3. Poenam & dolorem. Tentationes voco explorationes per diabolū ipsiúsque ministros, quibus sollicitatus est ad hoc, ut deficeret à Deo suo, si id potuisset fieri: nimirum quoties nos in nobis experimur quotidie: si solam tentationem eam quæ fit per peccatum excipias. Nam qui novit peccatū, is per peccatum non est tentatus. Finis omnium tentationum Domini fuit, ut iis qui tentantur posset succurrere. Nunc de secunda passionis specie dicamus, quam diximus fuisse ignominiam. Ignominiam hanc pono in iniusta illa innocentis accusatione, falsis testimoniis, opprobriis, conuitiis, sannis, &c. Nam, ait Paulus, Christus non indulsit sibi, sed, sicut scriptum est, convicia eorum qui conviciantur tibi inciderunt in me. De ignominia ea quam passus est Dominus noster causa, diximus antea non uno in loco. Superest ut dicamus de poena quam passus est, tam animo quàm corpore: idque à primo conceptionis suæ momento per totum vitæ curriculum ad ultimū usque spiritum. Nam vix dum natus est, cùm persequutione Herodis coacta est Mater arrepto infante suo fugere in Ægyptum. Ex eo tempore continuò afflictus est nostra causa, usque dum ingrederetur annum ætatis suæ tricesimum, summúlque Mediatoris officium. Ex quo tempore cœperunt afflictiones eius ingravescere continuò ad horam usque mortis ipsius novissimam. Dicendum autem nobis est præcipuè de poena ea quam passus est Dominus postea quàm iam annum tricesimum ingressus est ad finem usque vitæ, hoc est quas perpessus est totis tribus annis cum annidimidio. Nam tantum temporis superuixit postquam Mediatoris officium in se recepit. His igitur tribus annis continuò & sine intermissione passus est dolores tam animi quàm corporis gravissimos. Non corporis tantum, sed multò magis animi. Nā passus est propter peccata nostra: peccata autem nostra maiora sunt animi quàm corporis. Animus enim quid est aliud natura sua quàm sentina omnium malorum, in quibus exequendis, membris corporis, per se stupidis, tanquam
units.tr: This passage calls for us to speak of that anguish of spirit which the Lord felt while he hung on the wood. But the doctrine of the inward distress of the soul will be better understood if I first give a summary of the whole of the Lord's passion. What, I ask, was the whole life of Christ on earth but a continual passion? For our sin, which he took upon himself, and the justice of God required not only an action but much more a passion of the Mediator; for without the shedding of blood there is no remission. The end of the Lord's passion was the complete abolition of our sin. Now the completion [ἀπαρτισμὸς] of sin required a complete passion of the Mediator, whether you regard the time of the passion or its extent. Therefore the Mediator had to suffer not merely, but to suffer perfectly and absolutely. I reduce the passion of the Lord to three kinds of suffering: (1) temptations; (2) ignominy; (3) punishment and pain. By temptations I mean the trials brought by the devil and his ministers, by which he was urged to fall away from his God, if that could have been done; that is, as often as we experience them in ourselves every day, if you except only that temptation which comes through sin. For he who knows sin is not tempted through sin. The aim of all the Lord's temptations was that he might be able to help those who are tempted. Now let us speak of the second kind of passion, which I said was ignominy. I place this ignominy in that unjust accusation of the innocent, in false witnesses, reproaches, insults, mockings, and so on. For Paul says, Christ did not please himself, but, as it is written, the reproaches of them that reproached thee fell upon me. Concerning the ignominy which our Lord suffered for our cause, I have said before in more than one place. It remains to speak of the punishment which he suffered, in both soul and body, from the first moment of his conception through the whole course of his life to his last breath. For scarcely was he born when, under the persecution of Herod, his mother was forced to take up her infant and flee into Egypt. From that time he was continually afflicted for our sake, until he entered his thirtieth year and the highest office of Mediator. From that time his afflictions began to grow heavier continually, up to the last hour of his death. But I must speak chiefly of the punishment which the Lord suffered after he had entered his thirtieth year, to the end of his life; that is, the sufferings he endured during the whole three years and a half. For he survived only so long after he undertook the office of Mediator. In these three years, then, he suffered continually and without intermission the most grievous pains, both of soul and body. Not of body only, but much more of soul. For he suffered on account of our sins, and our sins are greater in the soul than in the body. For what is the soul by its nature but a sink of all evils, in carrying out which the members of the body, in themselves dull, serve as instruments of unrighteousness.

units.la: {y} Tentationes ... Ignominia ... Poena ... Dolores quam instrumentis totidem iniustitiæ abutitur. Quare oportuit Christũ perpeti dolores animi vel imprimis: quod qui negant, videntur mihi plane neque videre quantum mali sit in peccato, neque quàm infinita sit Dei iustitia ; neque denique quanta sit Christi illa gratia,quam sic eleuant atque inaniunt.Sed redeo ad dolores illos, quos perpessus est Dominus tam animo quàm corpore totis tribus illis annis cum anni dimidio. De doloribus corporis,quia iam satis multa sunt dicta,ideo tantum nunc ex fontibus ipsorum ipsos demonstrabo. Profecti sunt primùm à naturali & insita infirmitate,sed quæ sine peccato : Ex hac infirmitate, esuriit,sitiuit, fatigatus est, non secus atque nos omnes sumus his ipsis obnoxij. Profecti sunt deinde ab interiori animi ægritudine. Oportet enim ( quæ est animi & corporis coniunctio arctissima) συμπάθειαν esse eorum mutuam,simúlque ea pati atque affici. Profecti sunt postremò ab externa vi, præsertim ea quam tum passus est, cùm sceleratis manibus ipsum crucifigerent. Sed de doloribus corporis pro præsenti instituto nostro iam satis : de doloribus animi dicam plura : Vt igitur præteream tristitiam & συμπάθειαν illam quam habuit perpetuò ex inspecta hominum miseria,præsertim verò Iudæorum,ad quos seruandos primùm omnium venit in hunc mundum, tristitiam, inquam, quæ sæpenumerò lachrymas ipsi excussit.Dolores animi ipsius pono præcipuè in illa, quam Lucas cap.22.44. ἀγωνίαν vocauit, hoc est, luctam & certamine cum ira Dei, & cum æterna morte quæ ipsi expressit hanc vocem cùm in horto esset : Tristis est anima mea vndequaque vsque ad mortem, Matth.26.38. In ἀγωνία hac,meo iudicio,cœpit constitui,non tũ tantùm cùm in horto fuit,sed etiam ante illud tempus, vt ex Iohannis 12.27. colligi potest, quo loco in agonia illa constitutus,protulit hæc verba: Nunc turbata est anima mea : Et quid dicam? Pater, conserua me ab hac hora. De hac igitur ἀγωνία, etsi nemo vnquam, vel animo comprehendere, vel voce exprimere eam satis potuit : tamen quantum possum exphrasi Scripturæ colligere, illud afferam in medium:In Scripturis sacris inuenio verba quæ significant tum ἀγωνίαν ipsam, tum ipsius magnitudinem, tum denique gradus & partes ipsius aliquot. Primum Esai. 53.5. Attolitur, inquit, ex iniquitatibus nostris. Verbum illud ad animum pertinet magis, quam ad corpus, significatque ingentem quandam animi angustiam, & vexationem. Psal.116.3. Dolores mortis circumdederunt me, & angores inferni occuparunt me. Ecce dolores & angores inferorum. Matth. 26.38. Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem. En tristitiam animi & eam quidem ex omni parte, & ad mortem usque ipsam animae.
units.tr: {y} Temptations ... Ignominy ... Punishment ... Pains, which the soul abuses as so many instruments of injustice. Therefore it was necessary for Christ to suffer pains of the soul above all. Those who deny this seem to me neither to see how great an evil sin is, nor how infinite the justice of God is, nor finally how great is that grace of Christ which they so lessen and empty. But I return to those pains which the Lord suffered, both in soul and body, during those whole three years and a half. Concerning the pains of the body, since many things have already been said, I will now only show them from their sources. They proceeded first from natural and innate weakness, yet a weakness without sin; from this weakness he hungered, thirsted, and grew weary, just as all of us are subject to these same things. They proceeded next from the inward sickness of the soul. For it is necessary (since the union of soul and body is very close) that there be a mutual sympathy [συμπάθειαν esse], and that they suffer and are affected together. They proceeded lastly from external violence, especially that which he then suffered when the wicked hands crucified him. But concerning the pains of the body, enough for our present purpose; I will say more concerning the pains of the soul. Therefore, to pass over that sorrow and sympathy which he always had from beholding the misery of men, especially of the Jews, for whose salvation he first of all came into this world, a sorrow, I say, which often drew tears from him, I place the pains of his soul chiefly in that struggle which Luke in chapter 22, verse 44, called agony [ἀγωνίαν], that is, a wrestling and conflict with the wrath of God and with eternal death, which forced from him this utterance while he was in the garden: My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death (Matt. 26:38). In my judgement this agony began to be formed not only when he was in the garden, but even before that time, as can be gathered from John 12:27, where, placed in that agony, he uttered these words: Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. Concerning this agony, although no one has ever been able to grasp it sufficiently in mind or express it in words, yet as far as I can gather from the language of Scripture, I will bring forward the following: In the holy Scriptures I find words which signify the agony itself, its greatness, and finally some of its degrees and parts. First, Isaiah 53:5: He is raised up, it says, from our iniquities. That word pertains more to the soul than to the body, and signifies a great distress and vexation of spirit. Psalm 116:3: The sorrows of death compassed me, and the pains of hell gat hold upon me. Behold the sorrows and pains of the lower regions. Matthew 26:38: My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death. Lo, sorrow of soul, and that on every side, even to the death of the soul itself.

units.la: Luc.22.44. Et positus in agonia, hoc est conflictu. Annon conflictus hic fuit cum ira Dei? cum nulla enim re alia in horto procul a discipulis suis positus colluctabatur. Ioh. 12.27. Turbata est anima mea. En perturbationes quae extorsit illi preces quae sequuntur ibidem. Pater, conserva me ab hac hora. Act.2.24. Quem Deus excitavit solutis doloribus mortis. In Graeco contextu legitur verbum ὠδῖν quod significat dolorem, qualis est parturientium, utpote dolor vehementissimus & acutissimus, quo Scriptura solet adumbrare dolores illos inferorum. 1.Thes.5.3. Cum enim dicent, Pax & tuta omnia, tum repentinum eis imminet exitium, sicut dolor partus mulieri uterum ferenti. Marci 14. Gradus etiam aliquot illius doloris designantur, cum dicit: Coepit Iesus ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι καὶ ἀδημονεῖν.
units.tr: Luke 22:44. And being in agony, that is, in conflict. Was this conflict not with the wrath of God? For he wrestled alone in the garden, placed apart from his disciples. John 12:27.
