My soul is troubled. See the disturbances which drew from him the prayers that follow there: Father, save me from this hour. Acts 2:24. Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of death. In the Greek text the word ὠδῖν [ōdin] is read, which means pain, such as that of women in labour, namely a most vehement and piercing pain, by which Scripture is accustomed to shadow forth those pains of hell. 1 Thess. 5:3. For when they say, Peace and all is safe, then sudden destruction hangs over them, as the pain of childbirth comes upon a woman with child. Mark 14. Several degrees of that pain are also marked out, when he says that Jesus began to be ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι [ekthambeisthai, astonished] and ἀδημονεῖν [adēmonein, in anguish].

units.la: Nuncigitur ex Marco & ex aliis persequor, quantum fieri potest, partes doloris illius, quibus tum exercitatus est Iesus. Prima igitur pars est in verbo ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι. E'x- θαμβεῖν voco pavorem illum & horrorem, qui fit ex horribili illa Dei ira, velociter ac subito incidente in omnes animi facultates. Atque haec videtur prima pars dolorum infernorum, qui incutiuntur quasi in ipso inferorum limine: qua reprobi subito percutiuntur & attoniti redduntur. Eam expressit Paulus, cum dicent, Pax & tuta omnia, tum repentinum ys imminet exitium, ut dolor partus mulieri. Exemplum huius partis quoddam habemus in Beltezare rege Babyloniae, qui dum agitaret convivia, blasphemaret ac prophanaret vasa domus Dei, subito horrore percussus est & obstupefactus. Angorem hunc summum insequuta est omnium facultatum animi defectio, qua, relictis functionibus suis occupatae sunt omnes in communi illo dolore subleuando. Ex desectione hac facultatum animi ac sensuum omnium, Christus ad tempus est oblitus operis illius redemptionis humanæ, cui paulò ante tam sollicitè instabat. Oblivionem hanc ascribo non peccato vlli, Christus enim non novit peccatum: sed duntaxat meræ naturali infirmitati. Id enim in nobis ipsi experimur, quòd eo tempore quo graui aliquo dolore premimur, abstrahi solent omnes sensus nostri ab re alia quauis, atque occupari totos circa præsentem illum dolorem. Atque in hac secunda parte tanquam in imagine intuemur secundam partem inferorum qua postquam iam attoniti facti sunt reprobi, ex ira illa velociter & subito incidente, deinde in summo manebunt ac sempiterno angore, ex eadem illa ira perfistente, ac in perpetuum eos opprimente. Atque hæc hactenus. Ex Marco fuerunt duæ partes ἀγωνίας, in qua positus fuit Christus. Apostolus Heb.5.7. his addit tertiam, cum dicit Christum in diebus carnis suæ cum clamore valido & cum lachrymis obtulisse preces atque exauditum ex metu. Tertia igitur luctæ pars fuit horribilis ille metus, quo, cum esset in angore ob præsentem illum iræ intolerandæ sensum, metuit sibi à graviori continuo sequutura. Hanc tertiam partem inferorum esse indico, qua reprobi perpetuò futuri sunt in metu gravioris iræ. Nam iræ in eos cumulandæ nunquam futurus est finis. Atque hæc de agonia Christi, quantum ex verbis sacræ Scripturæ colligi potest.
units.tr: Now, therefore, from Mark and from other passages I follow, as far as possible, the parts of that pain with which Jesus was then exercised. The first part, then, lies in the word ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι [ekthambeisthai]. By ekthambein I mean that fear and horror which arises from that dreadful wrath of God, falling swiftly and suddenly upon all the faculties of the soul. This seems to be the first part of the pains of hell, which are inflicted as it were on the very threshold of hell, by which the reprobate are suddenly struck and made dumbfounded. Paul expressed it when he said: Peace and all is safe, then sudden destruction hangs over them, as pain comes upon a woman in labour. We have an example of this part in Belshazzar, king of Babylon, who, while he was holding feasts, blaspheming and profaning the vessels of God's house, was suddenly struck and stupefied with horror. Upon this highest anguish there followed a failure of all the faculties of the soul, by which, their functions abandoned, all were occupied in relieving that common pain. From this failure of the faculties and of all the senses, Christ for a time forgot the work of human redemption, to which shortly before he had so anxiously applied himself. I ascribe this forgetfulness to no sin, for Christ knew no sin, but merely to natural infirmity. For we ourselves experience this: at the time when we are pressed by some heavy pain, all our senses are usually drawn away from every other matter and occupied entirely with that present pain. And in this second part we see, as in an image, the second part of hell: after the reprobate have become dumbfounded from that wrath falling swiftly and suddenly, they will remain in highest and everlasting anguish, that same wrath persisting and oppressing them forever. So much for this. From Mark there were two parts of the agony (ἀγωνία) in which Christ was placed. The apostle in Heb. 5:7 adds a third, when he says that Christ, in the days of his flesh, with strong crying and tears, offered up prayers, and was heard because of his fear. The third part of the struggle, then, was that dreadful fear by which, being in anguish from the present sense of intolerable wrath, he dreaded that a heavier wrath would follow continually. I declare this third part to be a part of hell, in which the reprobate will forever be in fear of heavier wrath, for there will never be an end to the wrath to be heaped upon them. So much concerning the agony of Christ, as far as can be gathered from the words of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Eam deinde aliquo modo assequi possumus ex effectis suis, precibus scilicet & quærimoniis quas ipsi agonia illa animi interior expressit. Dum enim in horto esset, precatus est Patrem, Auferv à me poculum hoc: qua petitione, (vt diximus) indicat ad tempus se oblitum fuisse operis redemptionis humanæ. Deinde intensius precatus est cum clamore valido & lachrymis. Postremò intensissimè precatus est cum sanguineo sudore. Nam grumi quasi sanguinis descendebant de facie ipsius in terram: quale nunquam adhuc obseruatum est in vllo omnium hominum: vt facilè videas nullum vnquam perinde timuisse mortem ac Christum. Vt rursus facilè iudices mortem eam fuisse æternam, & cruciatus eos fuisse inferorum. Sæpe etiam ex interiori hoc iræ grauissimæ
units.tr: We can then attain it in some measure from its effects, namely the prayers and complaints which that inner agony of the soul drew from him. For while he was in the garden he prayed to the Father, Take this cup from me; by which petition, as we have said, he indicates that he had for a time forgotten the work of human redemption. Then he prayed more intensely, with strong crying and tears. Last of all he prayed most intensely, with bloody sweat, for clots like blood were falling from his face to the ground, which has never yet been observed in any man. So you may easily see that no one ever feared death as Christ did, and you may again easily judge that that death was eternal, and that those sufferings were the torments of hell. Often also, from this inner sense of most grievous wrath,

units.la: Agoniæ seu luctæ Christi cõsideratio ex effectis. uissimæ sensu conquestus est: Nunc turbata est anima mea. Tristis est anima mea vndiquaque ad mortem. Huc pertinet quærimonia illa grauissima quæ in cruce fuit, Deus meus, Deus meus, cur me dereliquisti? Quidem significavit a Deo desertum, sed minimè diuulsum. Non enim in cruce fuit diuulsio naturarum, sed desertio tantùm, qua ad tempus Deitas inhabitans hominem destituit & priuauit omni consolatione, tantisperdum persolueretur pretium illud redemptionis nostri ad vltimum vsque quadrantem. Quòd autem interea Deum semel atque iterum inuocat, eo satis ostendit fiduciam illam suam: non desiit Deo suo adhærescere, ne tum quidem cum nullam ex eo ad tempus sentiret consolationem. Estque hoc discrimen inter Christum, qui nostra causa ad tempus erat tanquam reiectus, & alios reprobos. Christus quidem destitutus fuit omni consolatione, ita tamen vt nō desperaret, sed fiduciam interea temporis inconcussam haberet. At reprobi vt deserentur tandem a Deo, ita Deum ipsi quoque deserent, at de vita plane desperabunt. Ideo vox & clamor eorum futurus est, non hic, Deus meus cur me deseruisti? sed hic, Deus me deseruit. Ista enim vox fiduciæ est, hæc verò minimè. Hactenus de duobus illis fundamentis ac principiis quibus peruenire possumus ad cognitionē ἀρρήτως illius Christi, verbis scripturæ viuis ac significantibus. 2. effectis iis quæ apressit interior animi dolor.
units.tr: (The consideration of Christ's agony from its effects.) ...from the most grievous sense of wrath he complained: Now my soul is troubled. My soul is sorrowful on every side unto death. To this belongs that most grievous complaint on the cross: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? It signified being forsaken by God, but by no means being torn apart. For on the cross there was no separation of the natures, only desertion, by which for a time the Deity dwelling in the man left him bereft and deprived of all consolation, for so long as that price of our redemption was being paid to the last farthing. But that meanwhile he calls upon God once and again shows his trust well enough: he did not cease to cling to his God, not even when for the time he felt no consolation from him. And this is the difference between Christ, who for our sake was for a time as if rejected, and the other reprobate. Christ was indeed deprived of all consolation, yet in such a way that he did not despair, but meanwhile had unshaken trust. The reprobate, however, though at last they are forsaken by God, also forsake God themselves, and will utterly despair of life. Therefore their voice and cry will be not, My God, why have you forsaken me? but, God has forsaken me. For the former word is one of trust, but the latter is by no means so. Thus far concerning those two foundations and principles by which we can come to the knowledge of that Christ, who is unspeakable (ἀρρήτως), through the living and significant words of Scripture. The second is from the effects which the inner anguish of the soul expressed.

units.la: Quia autem omnis cognitio, quæ est de Christo, oportet sit cum sensu aliquo coniuncta (id quod vel ex vno illo ad Philip. loco cognosci potest: vbi postquam dixit Apostolus se omnia ducere damnum & stercora ad hoc vt cognosceret Christum: tum partes illius cognitionis subiicit, 1. Cognitionem resurrectionis, 2. Passionis: Sed qualem, quæso, resurrectionis cognitionem? Vt cognoscā inquit, vim resurrectionis ipsius. Eam resurrectionis cognitionem significat quæ coniuncta sit cum sensu illius potentiæ, quæ promanat è Christi resurrectione ad nostri ipsorum viuificationem. Qualem rursus cognitionem passionis significat? vt cognoscam, inquit, communionem passionis ipsius, &c. Eam passionis cognitionem significat, quæ est coniuncta cum sensu aliquo potentiæ passionis Christi in nobis ipsis ad mortificationem carnis.} Quia, inquam, cognitio Christi debet esse coniuncta cū sensu aliquo, ideóque oportet agoniam illam Christi & maledictionem non cognoscere modò, sed etiam aliquousque sentire. Sentimus autem eam primū quando degustamus illud irę diuinę poculum, quod ipse totum simul ac semel exhausit, hoc est aliquo certè modo sentimus iram illam Dei ob peccatum nostrum & offensū Deum, quā ipse totum simul & semel in se recepit. Sic enim futurū est, vt in hunc modum nobiscū ipsi ratiocinemur. Graue adeo onus mihi incumbit meorum solius peccatorum: Quàm graue igitur oportuit esse onus illud omnium peccatorum mundi, hoc est electorum omnium, quod in se gestauit Christus? Quàm graucm oportuit illam maledictionem esse, quæ omnium electorum peccata insecuta est in Christo, cum maledictio ista, quæ mea solius peccata insequitur, idq; non nisi ad certam aliquam mensuram, maledictio, inquam, ea gravis adeo fit. Illud enim extra controversiā est, solere Deus suos tentare conscientia peccati sui, & iræ ipsius sensu aliquo, vel ob eum finem, vt aliquo certè modo apprehendant animo immensam illam Dei iram quam sustinuit Christus, simulq; assequantur aliquousque, vt cum Apostolo loquar, quæ sit illa longitudo, latitudo, profunditas, & sublimitas: & cognoscant charitatem illam Christi omni cognitione superiorem. Sentimus deinde illam Christi maledictionem, cùm persentiscimus eam misericordiam, pacem conscientiæ & benedictionem, quæ ex illa Christi maledictione ad nos vsq; dimanat. Sic enim nobiscum ratiocinamur; Ego quidem sentio gratiā & pacē. Oportet igitur eam quantulacunq;, charè admodū cōstitisse redemptori meo. Et vt quod in re est dicā: Nō cōsistit misericordia, neq; vllus esse potest gratiæ locus, vel etiā se ipsus, nisi infinitæ iustitiæ & iræ infinita illa maledictione & passione Christi satisfiat prius. Atq; hęc in summa dicta sint de Christi passione ac cruce, de qua institutus sermo, sat scio, iis qui pereunt & sapientibus huius mundi stultitia est: Iis autē qui seruantur est Dei potētia & sapientia. In nulla enim re alia effulget Dei sapientia illa & potentia, quàm in cruce Christi: quo enim stultior,
units.tr: Since every knowledge of Christ ought to be joined with some feeling (as can be recognised from that one passage in Philippians, where, after the apostle says that he counts all things loss and dung in order to know Christ, he then sets out the parts of that knowledge: first, the knowledge of the resurrection; second, of the passion). But what sort of knowledge of the resurrection, I ask? That I may know, he says, the power of his resurrection. He means by this knowledge of the resurrection that which is joined with a sense of that power which flows from Christ's resurrection to the quickening of ourselves. And what sort of knowledge of the passion does he mean again? That I may know, he says, the fellowship of his sufferings, and so on. He means that knowledge of the passion which is joined with some sense of the power of Christ's passion in us, for the mortifying of the flesh. Because, I say, the knowledge of Christ ought to be joined with some feeling, it is therefore necessary not only to know that agony and curse of Christ, but also to feel them to some extent. We feel them first when we taste that cup of divine wrath which he drained entirely and at once; that is, in some sure way we feel that wrath of God on account of our sin and offence against God, which he himself received entirely and at once into himself. For it will come about that we reason with ourselves in this way: the burden of my own sins alone lies heavily upon me; how heavy, then, must have been that burden of all the sins of the world, that is, of all the elect, which Christ bore in himself? How grievous must that curse have been which followed the sins of all the elect in Christ, when that curse which follows my sins alone, and that only to a certain measure, is so grievous! For it is beyond dispute that God is accustomed to test his own by the consciousness of their sin and by some sense of his wrath, if for no other end, at least so that they may in some measure apprehend in their minds that immense wrath of God which Christ endured, and at the same time attain, to use the apostle's words, what is that length and breadth and depth and height, and know that love of Christ which surpasses all knowledge. Then we feel that curse of Christ when we perceive that mercy, peace of conscience and blessing which flows to us from that curse of Christ. For we reason with ourselves thus: I indeed feel grace and peace. It must therefore have cost my Redeemer very dear, however small it may be. And, to say what is the case: mercy does not stand, nor can there be any place for grace, not even for yourself, unless infinite justice and wrath are first satisfied by that infinite curse and passion of Christ. These things, in summary, have been said concerning the passion and cross of Christ, of which the discourse was undertaken. I know well that it is foolishness to those who perish and to the wise of this world; but to those who are saved it is the power and wisdom of God. For in nothing else does that wisdom and power of God shine forth more than in the cross of Christ, for the more foolish...

units.la: 1. Cor. 1. 18. Sapientia, potentia, iustitia, mi {a}tior, eo maior conspicitur sapientia eius, qui per rem in speciem stultam, sapiés adeo opus est operatus: & quo infirmior est crux Christi, eo maior apparet Dei potentia, quiperrem tam infirmam in speciem, opus tam potens operatus est, nempe, salutem humani generis. Quod si profecto ratione salutis nostrae sequutus fuisset, humano iudicio potentem, sapientem & gloriosam, i. eam quam approbat humana ratio, tum profecto tota opens gloria translata fuisset a Deo salutis authore, in ratione illam sive medium illud salutis humano iudicio gloriosam. Omnino id videmus, Deum per stultam & insipida quaeq; media, sive ipsam crucem Christi respicias, sive ministerium crucis & sermonis intuearis, salutem humanam perficere in eum finem, ait Apostolus, ut qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur.
units.tr: 1. Cor. 1. 18. Wisdom, power, righteousness: the more foolish a thing is, the more clearly the wisdom of him who has worked so wisely through something foolish in appearance is seen. And the weaker the cross of Christ is, the more evidently the power of God appears, who through a thing so weak in appearance has accomplished a work so powerful, namely the salvation of mankind. Indeed, if God had followed the course of our salvation by what human judgment considers powerful, wise and glorious, that is, by what human reason approves, then surely the whole glory of the work would have been transferred from God, the author of our salvation, to that means of salvation which is glorious by human judgment. We certainly see this throughout: God brings about human salvation through foolish and contemptible means, whether you look at the cross of Christ itself or consider the ministry of the cross and of the word, to the end, as the Apostle says, that he who glories should glory in the Lord.

units.la: Eliam vocat istu Nunc ad cōtextum historiae reuertor. Cùm Christus exclamasset, Eli, Eli, &c. similitudine vocum Eli & Eliae ludunt Iudaei, & Christo ipsiusq; preci-bus illuserunt, ut, si posset fieri, abrūperent eius fiduciā a Deo suo. Neq; enim tantum quaerebant corporis perniciem, sed & corporis simul atq; animae aeternā. Machinationem hanc Satanae pii quotidie expriuntur, praeser-tim hora illa mortis, nēpe, precum suarum interruptione, & fiduciae suae abruptione, ut si fieri possit, toti pereat in aeternū. Sed hic magis Dei dispensatione, ut séper solėo, inuieor, qui ut Christū intus exercet ira acerbissima, ita dūhac tristi lamētatione quaerit effugiū aliquod foris, vultoprecibus ipsius per acerba calūniam a sycophantis obuia venire. Haec enim omnia a Patre ipsius dispensantur, qui nullā cōcedit filio euasione, nullū effugium, tanti sperdū pretiū illud redemptionis nostrae persoluat ad victimū vīq; quadrante. Qua in re videmus, quā misera futura sit reprobōrum cōditio, qui in inferos semel detrusi, quoquo sese verterint, acerbissima ira excipiendi sunt, neq; vllū erit ipsis effugium, neq; vlla euasio ex toto tantisq; angustiis. Christus qui ad tēpus quasi reprobus fuit, dissoluto iā pretio tandē euasit: At hi nunquā effugiēt. Hęcęō spectāt, ut inquiramus tēpestiuē in Christo esse & passionis ipsius ac redemptionis participes fieri. Cum sciret Iesus reliqua. Sequitur quarta vox in quam erupit Christus tum dum è cruce penderet, cuius Iohannes meminit. Hactenus enim tres ex iis vocibus quas in cruce emisit à nobis abseruatæ sunt: sequuntur nunc tres aliæ, quas ordine persequemur. Omnino enim colligimus ex Euangelistis sex voces ipsi excidisse ex cruce pendenti: Quarum duæ sunt indices misericordiæ, non humanæ modò, qualis fuit illa ad matrem quam Iohanni commendauit, sed etiam Diuinæ, qualis fuit illa ad alterum ex latronibus, Amen, Amen, hodie mecum eris in Paradiso. Duæ deinde sunt tristitiæ indices. Prima ad Deum suum, Eli, Eli, lamma sabachthani. Altera ad astantes quibus clamauit, Sitio. Postremæ duæ videntur lætitiæ indices. Prior quidem qua ex sensu iam absoluti operis redemptionis & persoluti pretij dixit, Consummatum est: Posterior quæ ex sensu præsentis ire Dei ac Patris sui manus, Patri suo iamiam expiraturus animam suam commendauit. E cruce igitur pedens exerit pariter misericordiam, tristitiam & lætitiam animi, hoc est multiplicem affectum. Sed nunc consideranda est quarta vox Christi, quæ tristitiæ fuit, extititque ex anima simul & corpore igne illo furoris Diuini penitus quasi iam arefactis & exustis. Ex hoc igitur sensu iæ Diuinæ, quasi respirans, clamat, Sitio. Cum alias Christus sæpe sitiuerit, tum hoc tempore quo è cruce pendebat maximè siti correptus erat, quæ proculdubio pars nō minima pœnæ fuit & pretij redemptionis illius nostræ. Idcoq; notandum tempus quo petiuit ut liberaretur ab illa tam intolerabili siti, nō autem cum consummata sciret omnia: hoc est pretium redemptionis iam persolutum esse: Ideo scriptum est à Iohanne quòd postquam omnia consummata essent, dixerit, Sitio. Notandum opus hoc redemptionis nostri fuisse vniuersum, admirabilem in modum, ut sic loquar, sitiundum. Ira enim Dei infinita illa ineffabiliter sitiuit sanguinem Mediatoris, eúmque exhausit adeo totum, ut nihil succi vel in animo, vel in corpore reliquum fecerit. Hinc illa nimirum sitis fuit Christi temporalis: quam profecto tamdiu tolerare non potuisset nisi in ipso simul extitisset sitis quædam spiritualis, hoc est summum desiderium implendę obedientiæ Patri debitæ & perficiendę salutis humanę. Sitis enim ista spiritualis Christi, absorpsit quodammodò corporalem illam; admonetque hoc Christi exemplum, oportere tantam esse sitim, tantum desiderium obediendi Deo in nobis esse, vt nihil penśi habeamus, quo sumus in dolore, in qua sitiet ipsius sanctissima voluntate, modo ipsi intera ea obedientiam debitam præstemus. Ante omnia enim requirit Deus obedientiam: Ecce, auscultare est melius sacrificio. Ante omnia debemus nos comparari esse ad obedientiam, quę etsi nos ad tempus in summas angustias redigat, tamen lętum ac gloriosum tandem habebit exitum. Vt perficeretur. Hic finis est cur dixerit, Sitio: vt, inquit, implereretur scriptura, quę habetur Psal.69.22. Quinpotius dant pro alimento meo amarore, et in siti mea bibendū dant mihi acetum. Vt Christus impleuit omnē legis & prophetię apicem, ita hanc prędictionem ipse impleuit, & verius quidem hoc dictum intelligitur de Christo, cuius typus fuit Dauid, quàm de ipso Dauide. Nusquam enim legimus Dauidi datum fuisse acetum, quod biberet: at datum esse Christo hic legimus, ac potatum. Vt autem Christus impleuit suo tempore singula, quę sunt de eo prędicta: ita singula quæ Christo acciderunt in ipsius præsertim passione prædicta sunt. Neque prętermissa est a Prophetis vlla circunstantia, quæ in tempus passionis incidit. Qua de re legendus est Psalmus, 22. & Psalmus 99. & Esaiæ caput 53. Minutiorem ac leuiorem rem aliquam putaret quis hunc acceptum hausturum, vt & illam vestimentorum partitionem. At neutrum omissum est a Prophetis: vt videat Deum magis attentum fuisse in mortem & passionem Christi venturi, quàm in mortem, vel etiam in tam cuiusquam mortalium. Quæ res plane arguit illius personæ, vt etiam mortis ipsius, in qua posita est vita mundi, excellentiam & dignitatem. Eadem res quoque confirmat fidem nostram non mediocriter, dum videmus singulos euentus sic respondere singulis prædictionibus, vt si quis amplius dubitet de Iesu, an sit Christus & Messias promissus, is nihil videat, & si tectum sit aliquibus Euangelium hoc Christi, tectum est iis qui pereunt. Vas igitur illic erat positum. Facile quidem obtenperant voci Christi de siti sua admonentis, sed in ipsius ludibrium. Vas fuit impositum aceto plenum, ut videtur ex consuetudine & more, quo ad manum habebant potum, quem crucifixis & in mediis tormentis haerentibus ministrarent. Spongiam intinctam aceto, & affixa arundini vel calamo hyssopi appoluerunt ipsius ori, ut acetum felle admixtum exugeret. Hoc interpretor ex felle illo amaritudinis quo corda eorum penitus suffusa erant, factum esse. Nam etsi iram Patris ipsius iam pene saturatam & sedatam fuisse docuerunt verba illa superiora, quibus dictum est, Postquam sciret omnia esse consummata, &c. tamen malitia illa Iudaeorum & ira in innocentem nihilo remissior facta est, quin eum persequuti sunt Iudaei in morte, post mortem, post gloriosam denique resurrectionem. Deus si quando laxat habenas impiis ad corrigendum suos, ipsi nullum modum perseqendi facere solent: quaeruntque extremam sanctorum perniciem: Ac nisi Deus refrenaret ipsorum impotentiam, profecto nullum Ecclesiae Dei aut piis quibusvis in terris locum facerent reliquum. Atque hinc fit ut Deus postquam impiis visus est tanquam flagellis totidem ad castigandum suos, qui ipsi nullum modum facere voluerunt, flagella apprehensa in ira sua in ignem coniiciat. Cum ergo accepisset: atqui ante crucifixionem oblatum sibi acetum postquam gustasset noluit bibere. Fieri quidem poterat, ut nunc intolerabili siti illa impulsus, nihil liquidi & frigidi quantumuis acerbi & amari recusare voluerit. At nisi eum spiritualis illa sitis salutis ac redemptionis nostrae impulisset eo, ut nihil nostra causa sustinendum recusare voluerit, profecto felle & aceto sitim restinguere recusasset. Sed ut nostra causa iam ante expotavit poculum illud irae Divinae: ita nunc, cum nondum sit satiata Iudaeorum malitia, nostra similiter causa, poculum irae & malitiae Iudaeorum libenter exhaurit, ut nos hauriremus ex illo fonte, aquam viventem ad vitam nostram aeternam. Consummatum est. Hæc est prima illa vox lætitiæ, quæ è cruce quasi promulgat iam persolutum pretium redemptionis, & absolutum tempus redemptionis humanæ. Hoc quo melius intelligamus, sciendum est Christum habuisse duo opera perficienda: primum opus merendi & acquirendi nobis iustitiam, vitam, cœlos denique ipsos. Hoc quidem opus incepit a primo suo conceptu, absoluit vero ultimo mortis suæ momento. Ergo iam expiraturus promulgat e cruce, tanquam loco aliquo eminentiori opus iam consummatum esse, ideoque persolutum pretium redemptionis nostri, ut non sit reliquus vel unus quadrans persoluendus. Hoc uno verbo continetur ac comprehensa est summa totius Euangelij. Quid enim aliud prædicamus in Euangelio, quàm pretium redemptionis nostræ perfectè iam exsolutum esse? Adeo ut non opus sit cuiquam ad perfectionem pretij quicquam adiicere, ne tantillum quidem: hoc enim est derogare gratiæ Dei, & hostes gratiæ sunt isti cum doctrina illa sua meritorum & satisfactionum humanarum. Alterum opus est missionis nostri in possessionem iustitiæ illius & vitæ quas nobis primo illo opere suo acquisiuit. Hoc opus inchoauit a prima illa resurrectione, in eo etiamnum perfistit; perficiet autem ac consummabit illud demum, cum venturus est ad iudicium extremum: quo tempore audietur vox gloriosa non iam ex cruce ignominiosa, sed ex gloriosoaccæleti illo throno. Vox, inquam, illa eadem, Consummatum est. Verùm altius descendendum videtur ad sensum & affectum illum animi, unde procedit ista vox. Mihi videtur ex sensu iræ paternæ magis iam remissæ, & lætitiæ ac gaudij iam reuersi, profecta. Nam paulò ante dimissionem Spiritus, videtur ille conflictus finem suum sortitus esse: eodem planè modo, quo videmus agi cum fidelibus in ultimo illo suo certamine. Postquam enim aliquandiu conflictati sunt cum sensu aliquo iræ Diuinæ, tum subitò quasi respirantes, vocem victoriæ ac lætitiæ indicem solent emittere. Fideles enim conformes fiunt imagini filij Dei, & in vita & in morte: & hæc ipsa quoque vicissitudo doloris & lætitiæ in ipsos solet cadere, quæ cadec
units.tr: Eliam vocat iste: Now I return to the context of the history. When Christ cried out, Eli, Eli, etc., the Jews played on the likeness of the words Eli and Elias and mocked his prayers, so that, if it were possible, they might break his trust in his God. For they were seeking not only the destruction of his body but the eternal destruction of body and soul together. The godly are daily troubled by this scheme of Satan, especially in the hour of death, namely, the interruption of their prayers and the breaking of their trust, so that, if possible, they might perish utterly for ever. But here, as I often do, I look to the dispensation of God, who while he inflicted the most bitter wrath upon Christ within, sought in this sad lamentation some way of escape without, so that his prayers might be met by the cruel slanders of the sycophants. For all these things are arranged by his Father, who allowed the Son no escape and no way out, until he had paid down the full price of our redemption, not a farthing less. In this we see how wretched will be the condition of the reprobate, who once thrust down into hell, however they turn, shall be received by the most bitter wrath, and there will be for them no escape and no release from such great and utter distress. Christ, who for a time was as if reprobate, at last escaped when the price had been paid; but these shall never escape. These things look to this, that we should inquire in good time whether we are in Christ and become partakers of his passion and of his redemption. Cum sciret Iesus reliqua. There follows the fourth cry which Christ uttered while hanging on the cross, of which John makes mention. Hitherto we have observed three of those sayings which he uttered on the cross; now come three others, which we shall follow in order. For we gather from the Evangelists that six sayings fell from him while he hung on the cross. Of these, two are signs of mercy, not only human, such as that to his mother whom he commended to John, but also divine, such as that to one of the thieves, Amen, Amen, today you shall be with me in Paradise. Then there are two signs of sadness. The first is to his God, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani. The other is to those standing by, to whom he cried, Sitio. The last two seem to be signs of joy. The former, which he spoke from the sense that the work of redemption was now finished and the price paid, Consummatum est. The latter, when, from the sense that the hands of God his Father were now present, he, about to expire, commended his soul to his Father. From the cross, therefore, he displays at once mercy, sadness and joy of mind, that is, a manifold affection. But now we must consider the fourth saying of Christ, which belonged to sadness, and which arose from soul and body together, when, by that fire of divine fury, both had been almost wholly dried up and burnt. From this sense of divine anger, as if taking breath, he cries, Sitio. Although Christ often thirsted, yet at this time, while hanging on the cross, he was seized with the greatest thirst, which was without doubt no small part of the punishment and of the price of that redemption of ours. Hence we must note the time at which he asked to be freed from that so intolerable thirst, and not when, knowing that all things were accomplished, that is, that the price of redemption had now been paid. Therefore John wrote that after all things had been accomplished, he said, Sitio. It must be noted that this whole work of our redemption was, in a marvellous manner, so to speak, a thirsting. For the infinite wrath of God thirsted ineffably for the blood of the Mediator, and drained it so completely that no juice was left in either soul or body. Hence, of course, came Christ's temporal thirst, which he could not have endured for so long unless there had also been present in him a certain spiritual thirst, that is, the highest desire to fulfil the obedience owed to the Father and to accomplish human salvation. For this spiritual thirst of Christ largely swallowed up that bodily thirst; and this example of Christ teaches that in us there ought to be such a thirst, such a desire to obey God, that we count as nothing whatever pain we suffer, in whatever distress we are, provided that in the meantime we render the obedience due to him, in whose most holy will we thirst. For above all God requires obedience: Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice. Above all we ought to prepare ourselves for obedience, which, though for a time it may reduce us to the greatest distress, will nonetheless at last have a joyful and glorious outcome. Ut perficeretur. This is the reason why he said, Sitio: that, he says, the Scripture might be fulfilled, which is found in Psalm 69:22. They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. As Christ fulfilled every jot and tittle of the law and the prophets, so he himself fulfilled this prediction, and this saying is more truly understood of Christ, whose type David was, than of David himself. For nowhere do we read that vinegar was given to David to drink; but here we read that it was given to Christ and drunk. Moreover, just as Christ fulfilled in his time each of the things foretold of him, so each of the things that happened to Christ, especially in his passion, was foretold. Nor did the prophets pass over any circumstance which fell within the time of the passion. Concerning this matter the twenty-second Psalm, the ninety-ninth Psalm and the fifty-third chapter of Isaiah should be read. One might think that this detail, the vinegar, was a rather trivial and light matter to be received, as also the division of the garments. But neither was omitted by the prophets; so that we may see that God was more attentive to the death and passion of the coming Christ than to the death, or even to the death of any mortal whatever. This fact plainly proves the excellence and dignity of that person, and also of his death, in which the life of the world is set. The same fact also confirms our faith not a little, while we see single events so answering to single predictions that, if anyone still doubts about Jesus, whether he is the Christ and the promised Messiah, he sees nothing; and if this Gospel of Christ is hidden from some, it is hidden from those who perish. Vas igitur illic erat positum. They indeed readily obeyed the voice of Christ reminding them of his thirst, but to his mockery. A vessel full of vinegar had been placed there, as seems to be the custom, by which they had at hand the drink which they used to give to those crucified and fixed in the midst of torments. They put a sponge soaked in vinegar, fastened to a reed or a stalk of hyssop, to his mouth, so that he might suck up the vinegar mixed with gall. I interpret this as done from that bitterness of gall with which their hearts were utterly suffused. For although those preceding words, in which it was said, When he knew that all things were now accomplished, etc., showed that the Father's wrath had been almost satisfied and calmed, yet the malice of the Jews and their wrath against the innocent were in no way lessened, so that the Jews pursued him in death, after death, and finally after his glorious resurrection. When God at any time loosens the reins to the impious to correct his people, they are wont to make no measure in persecuting, and they seek the utter destruction of the saints; and unless God restrained their impotence, they would surely leave no place in the earth for the Church of God or for any of the godly. And hence it comes about that God, after he has seemed to the impious as if he were to chastise his own with so many scourges, which they were unwilling to limit, seizes the scourges in his wrath and casts them into the fire. When therefore he had received: but before the crucifixion, having tasted the vinegar offered to him, he would not drink. Indeed it might have been that, impelled by that intolerable thirst, he would not refuse anything liquid and cool, however bitter and sour. But unless that spiritual thirst for our salvation and redemption had driven him to be unwilling to refuse anything for our sake, he would surely have refused to quench his thirst with gall and vinegar. But just as for our sake he had earlier drunk that cup of divine wrath, so now, since the malice of the Jews is not yet satisfied, for our sake likewise he willingly drains the cup of the wrath and malice of the Jews, that we might draw from that fountain the living water for our eternal life. Consummatum est. This is that first cry of joy which from the cross proclaims, as it were, that the price of redemption is now paid in full, and the time of human redemption is complete. That we may understand this better, we must know that Christ had two works to accomplish: the first work of meriting and acquiring for us righteousness, life and finally the heavens themselves. This work he began from his first conception, and completed at the last moment of his death. Therefore, now about to expire, he proclaims from the cross, as from some more lofty place, that the work is now finished, and therefore the price of our redemption paid, so that not one farthing or even one remains to be paid. In this one word is contained and comprehended the sum of the whole Gospel. For what else do we preach in the Gospel, than that the price of our redemption has now been perfectly paid? So that there is no need for anyone to add anything to the perfection of the price, not even the smallest thing; for this is to detract from the grace of God, and those who with their doctrine of human merits and satisfactions are enemies of grace. The second work is the bringing of us into possession of that righteousness and life which he acquired for us by his first work. This work he began from that first resurrection, and in it he still persists; but he will perfect and complete it at last, when he comes to the final judgement: at which time the glorious voice will be heard, no longer from the ignominious cross, but from that glorious heavenly throne. The same voice, I say, Consummatum est. But it seems that we must descend more deeply into the feeling and affection of mind from which this saying proceeds. It seems to me that it proceeded from the sense of the Father's wrath now more relaxed, and of joy and gladness now returned. For shortly before the departure of the Spirit, that conflict seems to have reached its end, in exactly the same way as we see things go with the faithful in their last struggle. For after they have wrestled for a while with some sense of divine wrath, then suddenly, as if taking breath, they are wont to utter a cry, the sign of victory and joy. For the faithful are made conformable to the image of the Son of God, both in life and in death; and this very alternation of sorrow and joy is wont to fall upon them, which fell upon Christ their Lord.

units.la: bat in Christum dominum ipsorum. Quùmque clamassèt voce magna. Hæc est altera illa vox ex lætitia profecta & omnium vltima. Notandum quod dicat Lucas clamasse eum voce magna. Solet quidem vox morientium & eorum qui agunt extremam animam, vel nulla, vel exilis admodum esse, quia destituuntur illo momento naturæ viribus. Quamobrem necesse est colligamus ex voce hac tam magna & alta à Domino edita, paulo ante emissionem Spiritus sui, nondum defecisse naturæ vires, ac per naturam potuisse Christum adhuc superuiuere: vnde & aliud sequitur, supernaturalem in Christo potentiam fuisse eam, qua supra & contra naturam effauit ipse animam suam. Ex quo rursus sequitur, potuisse Dominum contra externam omnem vim ac violentiam retinere in se animam suam. De hoc testatus est iam antea ipse Dominus: Nemo aufert animam meam à me, sed ego potestatem habeo deponendi eam, & habeo potestatem rursus assumendi eam. Quamobrem cùm Pilato indicatum esset vesperi quod iam mortuus esset Iesus, is miratus est, neque enim sine miraculo expirauit Dominus. Atque vt in tota vita admirabilis fuit, qualis à propheta dictus est: ita in morte quoque admirabilis fuit. Sed consideremus quæ fuerunt verba illa quæ simul cum spiritu emisit. Pater, in manus tuas. Vox ista longè alia est à voce illa, paulò ante in cruce edita, Deus meus, Deus meus, &c. Profecta quidem vox illa est ex fiducia quidem, verùm ex sensu lætitiæ ac præsentiæ Dei nullo. At verò vox ista vt ex fiducia animi profecta est, ita ex sensu lætitiæ, quæ reuersa est paulò ante emissù vltimù Spiritù. Dù enim in manus Patris commendat ac deponit spiritum suum, procul dubio sentit Patris sui manum illam suauiter dissoluentem & laxantem quasi Spiritum à corpore. Quamobrem Martyres in morte & inexquisitissimis quibusque supplicijs, nõ sunt quidem imitati priorem illam & vocem, vt qui nõ fuerunt derelicti à Deo, sed senserint lætitiam illam & pacem conscientiæ. Ideóq; vocem hanc posteriorem sunt imitati, Domine, in manus tuas depono spiritum meum. Stephanum legimus ea vsum voce: idem legimus fecisse & alios. Sed quæ obseruamus ex ista Christi voce hæc sunt: Primùm in hominibus spiritum esse, hoc est spiri-
units.tr: bat in Christum dominum ipsorum. And when he had cried out with a loud voice. This is the second cry, the other one that arose from joy, and the last of all. It should be noted that Luke says he cried out with a loud voice. Indeed, the voice of the dying, of those who are breathing their last, is usually either absent or very faint, because at that moment they are deprived of their natural strength. It is therefore necessary to conclude from this voice, so loud and high, uttered by the Lord shortly before he gave up his spirit, that his natural strength had not yet failed, and that through his nature Christ could still have continued to live. From this follows another point: that in Christ there was a supernatural power by which he laid down his soul above and against nature. From this in turn follows that the Lord could keep his soul in himself against all outward force and violence. The Lord himself testified to this earlier: No one takes my life from me, but I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again (John 10.18). Therefore, when it was reported to Pilate in the evening that Jesus was already dead, he marvelled, for the Lord did not expire without a miracle. And just as he was admirable throughout his whole life, as the prophet described him, so he was admirable in death also. But let us consider what words he uttered together with his spirit: Father, into your hands (Luke 23.46). That cry is quite different from the one uttered earlier on the cross, My God, my God, etc. That earlier cry arose indeed from trust, but from no sense of joy or of God's presence. But this cry, as it arose from trust of mind, so also from a sense of joy, which returned shortly before he breathed his last. For while he commends and lays down his spirit into the hands of the Father, he surely feels that the Father's hand is gently loosening and releasing the spirit, as it were, from the body. Therefore the martyrs in death and in the most exquisite tortures did not imitate that former cry, since they had not been forsaken by God, but felt that joy and peace of conscience. Hence they imitated this latter cry: Lord, into your hands I commit my spirit. We read that Stephen used this cry, and we read that others did the same. But what we observe from this voice of Christ is the following: first, that there is in human beings a spirit, that is, a spiritual substance, different from and other than the body; second, that this spirit is separated from the body, so that after the body is dissolved the remainder continues to live; third, that our highest concern and care must be for the separation of the spirit from the body, which is about to depart from the body at any moment. For if this was a care to the Lord, how much more ought it to be to us, who are wretched sinners? There are those who rashly squander and breathe out their soul, like beasts, which at last sink back into nothing. But since we remain either to life after this life or to eternal death, we ought not to let our spirit slip out of our hands until it is certain that it will be received into the hands of our God, who, as Peter says, is the faithful creator of souls (1 Pet. 4.19). This anxiety should be all the greater at the point of death, the greater the devil's diligence is at that very moment to devour us. Finally, it must not be passed over here that God cares for us and is concerned for us, especially in that hour of death, which is seen even from this, that a man from his heart commits his soul to him. For unless he himself began to take hold of our soul with his hand, our soul could certainly never grasp him, nor would our mouth ever commend our soul to him. Bowing his head, he gave up the spirit. So far concerning that last cry which the dying man uttered, and by which he committed his soul to God. Now follows the death of the Lord itself: He gave up, it says, his spirit. For the word means to hand over from one hand to another, namely, the Lord handed over his soul into the hands of his Father, which he did when he said, Father, into your hands I commit my spirit. From this there appears a certain difference between the godly and the ungodly in the midst of death. For while the ungodly die without any true sense of God, the godly on the contrary commend their souls to their faithful Creator, who will keep their deposit until the day of resurrection. But this is worthy of notice, that the mention of the Lord's death has been passed over by none of the Evangelists. As for the other matters, such as those voices of which we spoke a little earlier, they were not all observed or recorded equally by all. But when we come to his death and the separation of his soul from his body, this is the sum of the whole agreement.

units.la: Mors Christi voluntaria. Ioan. 10. 18. Lætitia vnde. spiritualem quandam substantiam diuersam & aliam à corpore: Secundò, separari hunc spiritum à corpore: ita vt post dissolutum corpus reliquum sit ac superuiuat: Tertiò, summam esse oportere sollicitudinem & curam nostram de Spiritu à corpore separando, & iam iam emigraturo ex corpore. Quod si enim id cure fuerit Domino, quanto magis id nobis debet esse, qui miseri sumus peccatores? Sunt qui temere prodigunt & efflant animā suam, vt belluæ, quæ tandem in nihilum recidunt. At cùm maneat nos vel post hanc vitam, vel vita, vel mors æterna, non prius elabi è manibus nostris oportet sinere Spiritum nostrum quàm certò constet eum in manus Dei nostri recipi, qui, vt ait Petrus, fidelis est animarum conditor. Hæc sollicitudo in mortis articulo eo maior esse debet, quo maior est diligentia Diaboli eodem illo momento ad nos devorandos. Non prætermittenda est denique hoc loco, Dei nostri cura & sollicitudo de nobis præsertim in illa mortis hora, quæ vel hinc conspicitur, quod quis ex animo animam suam ipsi commendet: Nam nisi ipse inciperet manu sua apprehendere animā nostram, profectò anima nostra eum nunquam apprehendere posset, neq; etiā os nostrum, vnquā animam nostrā ipsi commendaret. Inclinato capite tradidit spiritū. Hactenus de postrema illa voce, quam moribundus emisit, quàq; commendauit Deo animā suam. Nunc demū sequitur mors ipsa Domini: Tradidit, inquit, spiritū suum. Nam verbū significat e manu quasi in manū, nēpe, Patris sui tradidisse Dominum animā suam, quod tum fecit cùm diceret, Pater, in manus tuas depono animam meam. Ex quo apparet discrimē aliquod piorū & impiorum in media morte. Nā cùm impij sine vero sensu Dei moriātur, pij cōtrā animas suas commendant fideli ipsarū cōditori, qui depositum ipsorum seruaturus sit in diem illum resurrectionis. Illud verò dignum est animaduersione, quod à nullo Euangelistarum prætermissa est mentio mortis Domini. Quod ad alia, vt voces istas de quibus paulò ante diximus, non sunt omnia pariter ab omnibus obseruata, aut commemorata. Quum autem ad mortem eius & separationem animæ à corpore est ventum, sum-
units.tr: Christ's death voluntary. John 10.18. Whence joy. spiritual substance, different from and other than the body. Secondly, this spirit is separated from the body, so that after the body is dissolved the rest remains and lives on. Thirdly, our highest concern and care must be to separate the spirit from the body, which is about to depart from the body. For if this was a concern to the Lord, how much more should it be to us, who are wretched sinners? There are some who rashly squander and breathe out their soul, like beasts, which at last sink back into nothing. But since either eternal life or eternal death remains for us after this life, we ought not to let our spirit slip out of our hands until it is certain that it will be received into the hands of our God, who, as Peter says, is the faithful creator of souls (1 Pet. 4.19). This concern should be all the greater at the point of death, the greater the devil's diligence is at that very moment to devour us. Finally, it must not be passed over here that God cares for us and is concerned for us, especially in that hour of death, which is seen even from this, that a man from his heart commends his soul to him. For unless he himself began to take hold of our soul with his hand, our soul could never grasp him, nor would our mouth ever commend our soul to him. Bowing his head, he gave up the spirit. So far concerning that last voice which the dying man uttered, and by which he commended his soul to God. Now follows the death of the Lord itself: He gave up, it says, his spirit. For the word means to hand over from one hand into another; namely, the Lord handed over his soul into the hands of his Father, which he did when he said, Father, into your hands I lay down my soul. From this there appears a certain difference between the godly and the ungodly in the midst of death. For while the ungodly die without any true sense of God, the godly on the contrary commend their souls to their faithful Creator, who will keep their deposit until the day of resurrection. But it is worthy of notice that the mention of the Lord's death has been passed over by none of the Evangelists. As for the other matters, such as the voices of which we spoke a little earlier, they were not all observed or recorded equally by all. But when we come to his death and the separation of his soul from his body, the sum of all is in harmony.

units.la: Spiritus immortalis cum corpore coniuncti considerationis quid nos doceat.
units.tr: The immortal spirit joined with the body: what this consideration teaches us.

units.la: 24. Mors ipsa Domini nostri Iesu Christi pro nobis.
units.tr: 24. The death of our Lord Jesus Christ itself for us.

units.la: Piorum & impiorum in media morte discrimen. ma est omnium harmonia. Iohānes verò qui oculatus fuit testis istarū rerū, notauit praeterea ipsum morientis gestum, dum dicit inclinato capite eum tradidisse Spiritum. Hoc ad certitudinem mortis designandam pertinet. Quod autem nullus omnium Euangelistarū praetermisit Domini mortem, id nos admonet mortem eius ysqueadeo necessariā fuisse, vt & ipse eam pateretur, ratione m, inquam, illā animę ipsius à corpore: & vt nos eam Christi mortem fuisse certò & indubitatò cognoscereremus. Nam nisi Christus fuisset pro nobis mortuus, Mediator noster non potuisset fieri. Mediatorem enim oportuit mori nō crucifigi tantūm, sed in cruce mori: nā absq; morte nulla est redemptio, nulla peccatorum remissio, nulla deniq; vira. Rursus, nisi nos certò sciremus Mediatorē mortuū esse pro nobis, profectò nihil ex ipso, vel reliqua tota passione ipsius, boni possemus sperare. Fides enim in remissionem peccatorū, iustificationē & vitam aeternā pendet ex fide quę est in morte Christi, qua morte beneficia ista omnia ad nos deriuātur. Apostolus necessitatē mortis ex eo docet, q; sine morte testamentū Christi, in quo quasi legat nobis omnia bona illa caelestia, tanquā filius Dei & heres mundi: Testamētū, inquā, illud ratum ac firmū non foret: vt neq; hominis testamentū ratū esse posset nisi intervenient morte testatoris. Quandiu enim viuit testator, testamentū à sę conditū potest immutare, quādo & quoties libitū est. At verò mortuo iā testatore manet testamentū ratū firmūque. Quod si mors Christi interuenies tā necessaria fuit ad hoc, vt ratū fieret ipsius testamentū; an verò possum ego vel quisquā alius, credere legata illa in testamento Domini, bona ad me peruentura, nisi certò scia eum testamentū suum morte sua clausisse & obsignasse? Quare tantū ab eo absū, vt hīc seruatoris mei morte offendar, vt è contra mors Christi sit causa mihi fidei in remissionem peccatorum, & spei vitę ęternę.
units.tr: The difference between the godly and the ungodly in the midst of death. The sum is in harmony among all. But John, who was an eyewitness of these things, further noted the dying man's very gesture, when he says that he gave up the spirit with his head bowed. This pertains to marking the certainty of his death. And that none of the Evangelists passed over the Lord's death reminds us that his death was so necessary that he himself suffered it, in that manner, I say, of his soul's separation from the body, and so that we might know with certainty and without doubt that it was Christ's death. For unless Christ had died for us, our Mediator could not have come into being. For the Mediator had to die, not merely be crucified, but die on the cross; for without death there is no redemption, no remission of sins, and finally no life. Again, unless we knew for certain that the Mediator had died for us, we could hope for nothing good from him, or from his whole remaining passion. For faith in the remission of sins, justification, and eternal life depends on the faith that rests in the death of Christ, by which death all these benefits flow down to us. The Apostle teaches the necessity of death from this, that without the death of the testator Christ's testament, in which as the Son of God and heir of the world he bequeaths to us all those heavenly goods, would not be valid and firm; just as a man's testament cannot be valid unless the testator dies. For as long as the testator lives, he can change the testament he has made, whenever and however often he pleases. But once the testator is dead, the testament remains valid and firm. If the death of Christ was so necessary for this, that his testament might be valid, can I, or anyone else, believe that those legacies in the Lord's testament, goods destined to come to me, unless I know for certain that he has sealed and closed his testament by his death? Therefore I am so far from being offended at the death of my Saviour that, on the contrary, the death of Christ is the cause to me of faith in the remission of sins and of hope of eternal life.

units.la: Hactenus de Domini morte: nunc videda sunt ea miracula quę morte vel comitata sunt, vel certeē proximē subsequuta immediatē. Quatuor signa & miracula numerātur à Matthęo, Marco & Luca: Auleū tēpli fissū est in duas partes à sūmo ad imum: Terremotus ingens fuit. Ru{a}pes scissæ sunt: Monumenta aperta sunt. Fuit quidē Filij Dei extrema humiliatio & exinanitio in morte, cùm pedibus quasi mortis cōculcatus est. Quo quid abiectius aut contemptius? Interea tamen Pater ipsius non reliquit eũabsque testimoniis, non modò innocentię suæ, vt homo sanctus fuit: sed etiam maiestatis & gloriæ, vt Dei Filius fuit. Et deitas illa Filij in Christo homine habitans, etisi non exeruit statim in homine liberando à morte (neque enim id expediebat) tamen extra Christū hominem eripuit in miracula, quibus testata est eum ipsum hominem qui in morte, eaque tam probrosa pendebat ac hærebat, eum ipsum, in quam, dominum gloriæ & dominum vitæ esse: denique ipsæ creaturæ mutæ & brutæ, ne viderentur deesse nunc creatori suo, modo quodam suo loquutæ sunt & silentibus omnibus hominibus, quantis potuerunt viribus creatorem ac Dominū suum glorificarunt. Dixit Dominus, (de discipulis loquens, qui ipsum faustis acclamationibus excipiebant) Si isti siluerint, lapides clamabūt. Ecce hoc ipso tempore id visu venit. Nā silentibus discipulis, qui omnes pa-titer in eum offensi sunt, lapides & saxa clamant. Quòd si Domino in summa ipsius exinanitione nō defuit testimonium tam locuples gloriæ suę, an putandū glorificato ĩa ad dexterā Patris sui Domino, defuturos eos, qui ipsum glorificabunt? Quanto magis nunc, si homines ad quos id pertinet maximè, defuturi sint officio suo, ipsę mutæ ac brutę creaturæ totidē futuræ sunt præcones gloriæ creatoris sui Christi? Sed singula hæc miracula sigillatim sunt exponēda. Ac primū quidē, quod de velo templi scriptū est, velū templi intelligo parietē intermediū auro obduētum & aulęo intectum, in quo Sanctum Sanctorū, id est interior & sanctior pars templi, diuisum fuit à sancto, & templi parte exteriori. Nō-menobtinuit ab officio: velabat enim & cælabat sacrariū, non tātum à reliquo populo, sed etiā à sacerdotibus ipsis, solo summo sacerdote excepto, qui quotānis semel intra velū ingressus est cū sanguine: hoc est illud velum quod sissū est medium à sūmo ad imū, eàq; re testabatur quodāmodò se assētiri voci illi Domini, qua dixit, Consummatum est. Ac si dictū ab eo fuisset: Cęremonię omnes & umbræ legales impletæ iam sunt hac mea morte atque abolitæ. Velum, hac quasi voce audita, respondet, Amen, cessitque Domino, abdicato iam officio ac ministerio illo suo. Videre autem hoc oportuit Iudæos, quod velo templi accidit, & admoneri eos oportuit ac doceri facto illo tam stupendo: verum cum velum ipsum, hoc est, res surda & muta ad vocem Domini cömotum sit, Iudæi videntes & sentientes, nihil tamen viderunt & senserunt, sed & ad vocem Domini, & ad veli fissionem steterunt immoti: vt videas eos traditos fuisse in mente reprobam, & velamen fuisse impositum cordi ipsorum, quod quidem tolli difficilius fuit, quam scindi velum templi: vt videas rursus quā horribile Dei iudicii sit mens reproba, & maius esse miraculum mutationem obdurati cordis & regenerationem hominis, quā mutationem aliquam quantumuis miraculosam & extraordinariam mutę ac brutę creaturæ. Atque hæc de velo fisso. Nunc de terræ motu dicedū. Agitatione terræ significatur agitatio brachij divini, quo terra hæc sustentatur ac fulcitur. Agitado igitur terram, brachium Dei comminatur absorptionem obstinato & scelerato populo ob indignitatem illam tantā commissam in Dominum gloriæ: & sanè multo iustius absorpsisset eos terra tunc, quàm olim Dathan & Abiram, quando illi quidem Mosi se opposuerint: Iudæi vero isti Domini gloriæ crucifixerint. Verum etsi a terra Iudæi tum non sint absorpti, tamen postea suo tempore terra eos euomuit (cum exportati sunt & trucidati a Romanis) quasi indignos qui intra viscera terræ reciperentur. Atque hodierno etiam die reliquiis illius populi exe crabilis, iusto Dei iudicio nō concedit terra ne vestigiū quidem pedis hæreditario possidendum. Comminatur igitur terra absorptione obstinato populo, sed illi nihil interea cömouetur. Cömota quidē est terra, & agitata voce illa Christi magna: At illi neq; voce illa Domini, neq; terræ agitatione, & voce quasi quæ extremum iudicium comminata est, commouentur. Tam immota quædam res est animus hominis obduratus: & tantū tamque stupendum miraculum est, mutare animum obfirmatum contra Deum. Neque ego tam admirarer terræ motus hodierno die & absorptiones etiam impiorum, quàm admirati soleo Dei admirabilem patientiam in tolerandis tàm diu flagitiosis istis & obstinatis hominibus. Quare non deest nobis miraculum, quandiu est Dei ista tanta lenitas & patientia. Miraculum quoque est conuersio quæcunque impij ad Deum: Verùm omnium miraculorum admirabilissimum est Dei ista lenitas & patientia, erga obstinatos: quam tamen tandem grauitate supplicij compensaturus est iis qui pro duritia sua, & corde quod resipiscere nescit, thesaurizat sibi ipsi iram in diem iræ & patefactionis iusti iudicij Dei. Atque hæc de terræmotu hactenus. Quod ad illam petrarum ruptionem, hęc videntur terræ motum consequuta: sed hoc contigit extra ordinem eo tempore, & proculdubio rupes disruptæ comminabantur Iudæis præsentem oppressionem, qua tamen re illi nihil sunt perterriti. Loquor de principibus populi, ut scias facilius ad vocem Domini disrumpi saxa & rupes, quàm & voce Domini, & operibus quibusque miraculosis afficiuntur indurati hominum animi. Supererat nunc postremum miraculum monumentorum, quæ sese vltrò aperiebant eodem quo Christus expirauit tempori momento. Aperta deinde iacebant usque ad tempus illud resurrectionis Domini. Quo quidem tempore virtute resurrectionis Christi, corpora sanctorum rediuiua è monumentis egressa sunt, & ingressa sanctam ciuitatem, in qua non paucis apparuerunt. Quid autem his factum est postea, & nū redierint in sepulchra sua, nolo hoc curiosius indagare. Id autem mihi videtur in hac re verisimilius, quòd ipsa vnà cum Domino suo sursum in cælos recepta sint. Hoc miraculo docuit Deus obstinatum hunc populum, primùm quidem vim mortis Christi, eam quę est ad mortem abolendam & soluenda sepulchri vincula: deinde verò vim resurrectionis ipsius, eam quæ est ad excitandos nos è morte ac sepulchro. Verùm Iudæi illi magis mortui, quâ mors ipsa, nihil commoti sunt hoc mortis ac sepulchri præconio; vt scias nullis miraculis exterius doceri aut admoneri homines & obstinatos istos, nisi Dominus intus operetur vi Spiritus sui sancti, idque etiam non sine miraculo in animis eorum. Et profectò in conuertendis impiis, magis admirabilis est Deus, quàm alioqui in omnibus externis miraculis edendis. Haątenus igitur dictum est de quatuor istis miraculis editis in morte Domini, quæ ipsa sic inter se temperata esse video, vt primum ac postremum comparata sint ad docendum Iudæos: secundum verò & tertium ad eos perterrendum, iisque denunciandum præsens exitium, hoc quasi temperamentum operũ Dei non est negligenter prætereundum: eo enim docemur Deũ etiam, quo tempore armatus maximè conspicitur aduersus impios, tamen ipsis parcere, & nonnisi tardius eos percutere, admonere verò vt tepestiuè resipiscant, & præueniant iudicium illud quod imminet, vt, si nolint resipiscere, iã cũ oppressi erunt incidente iudicio inexcusabiles fiant.
units.tr: Thus far concerning the death of the Lord. Now we must consider the miracles which either accompanied his death or followed immediately after it. Matthew, Mark and Luke count four signs and miracles: the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom; there was a great earthquake; the rocks were split; and the tombs were opened. Surely in death the Son of God was brought to his lowest humiliation and emptying, when he was trodden under foot, as it were, by death itself. What could be more abject or more contemptible? Yet his Father did not leave him without testimony, not only to his innocence, as a holy man, but also to his majesty and glory, as the Son of God. And that deity of the Son, dwelling in Christ the man, although it did not at once display itself by delivering the man from death (for this was not expedient), nevertheless bore witness, through these miracles and apart from the man Christ, that the very man who hung in death, and in a death so disgraceful, was indeed the Lord of glory and the Lord of life. Lastly, the dumb and irrational creatures themselves, lest they seem to be wanting to their Creator now, spoke after a manner of their own, and, while all men were silent, glorified their Creator and Lord with all the strength they had. The Lord had said (speaking of the disciples, who welcomed him with joyful acclamations): "If these should hold their peace, the stones would cry out" (Luke 19:40). Behold, at this very time it came to pass before our eyes: for while the disciples were silent, having all been offended at him, the stones and rocks cried out. But if the Lord, in the depth of his emptying, did not lack a testimony so rich to his glory, can we suppose that, now that he has been glorified at the right hand of his Father, those who will glorify him will be wanting? How much more, then, if the men to whom this duty chiefly belongs should fail in their office, will the dumb and irrational creatures themselves be just as many heralds of the glory of their Creator, Christ? But these miracles must be expounded one by one. And first, as to what is written of the veil of the temple: I understand by the veil of the temple the intervening wall, overlaid with gold and covered with a curtain, by which the Holy of Holies, that is, the inner and holier part of the temple, was divided from the holy place and the outer part of the temple. It held its name from its office: for it veiled and concealed the sanctuary, not only from the rest of the people, but also from the priests themselves, the high priest alone excepted, who once a year entered within the veil with blood. This is that veil which was torn in the middle from top to bottom, and by this the veil in some measure testified that it assented to that word of the Lord by which he said, "It is finished" (John 19:30). As if it had been said by him: "All the ceremonies and legal shadows are now fulfilled and abolished by this my death." The veil, as though it had heard this voice, answers "Amen," and gave way to the Lord, its office and ministry now laid down. But the Jews ought to have seen what happened to the veil of the temple, and they ought to have been warned and taught by that so astonishing deed. Yet although the veil itself, that is, a deaf and dumb thing, was moved at the voice of the Lord, the Jews, seeing and perceiving, nevertheless saw and perceived nothing, but at the Lord's voice and at the tearing of the veil alike they stood unmoved. So you may see that they were given over to a reprobate mind, and that a veil was laid upon their heart; and this indeed was harder to remove than to rend the temple's veil. And so you may see again how dreadful is the judgment of God upon a reprobate mind, and that the changing of a hardened heart and the regeneration of a man is a greater miracle than any change, however miraculous and extraordinary, in a dumb and irrational creature. So much for the torn veil. Now we must speak of the earthquake. By the shaking of the earth is signified the shaking of the divine arm, by which this earth is upheld and propped up. Therefore, by shaking the earth, the arm of God threatened to swallow up the obstinate and wicked people, on account of that great indignity committed against the Lord of glory; and truly the earth would have swallowed them far more justly than it once swallowed Dathan and Abiram, when those men indeed opposed Moses, but these Jews crucified the Lord of glory. Yet although the Jews were not swallowed up by the earth at that time, nevertheless afterwards, in its own time, the earth spewed them out (when they were carried away and slaughtered by the Romans), as men unworthy to be received within its bowels. And even to this day, by the just judgment of God, the earth does not grant to the remnant of that accursed people so much as a foot's breadth to possess as an inheritance. So the earth threatened the obstinate people with swallowing, yet they meanwhile are not moved at all. The earth was indeed moved and shaken by that great voice of Christ; but they are moved neither by the voice of the Lord, nor by the shaking of the earth, nor by that voice which, as it were, threatened the last judgment. So immovable a thing is the hardened human mind; and it is so great and so astonishing a miracle to change a mind made stubborn against God. Indeed I would not marvel so much at earthquakes today, or at the swallowing up even of the wicked, as I am wont to marvel at the admirable patience of God in bearing so long with these wicked and obstinate men. Therefore we are not lacking a miracle, as long as there is this so great gentleness and patience of God. The conversion of any wicked man to God is also a miracle; but of all miracles the most admirable is this gentleness and patience of God toward the obstinate, which he will nonetheless at last repay with the severity of punishment to those who, by their hardness and a heart that knows not how to repent, store up for themselves wrath against the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God. So much for the earthquake. As to the splitting of the rocks, these seem to have followed the earthquake; but this happened out of its ordinary course at that time, and without doubt the broken rocks threatened the Jews with the present overthrow, yet by this they were in no way terrified. I speak of the leaders of the people, so that you may know that rocks and stones are more easily split at the voice of the Lord than the minds of men are softened, hardened though they be, either by the voice of the Lord or by any miraculous works whatever. There remained now the last miracle, that of the tombs, which opened of their own accord at the same moment in which Christ expired. Afterwards they lay open until the time of the Lord's resurrection. At that time, by the power of Christ's resurrection, the bodies of the saints, come back to life, went out of the tombs, entered the holy city, and appeared to many there. But what became of them afterwards, and whether they returned to their graves, I am unwilling to inquire too curiously. It seems to me more probable in this matter that they were taken up together with their Lord into the heavens. By this miracle God taught this obstinate people, first indeed the power of Christ's death, which is to abolish death and to loose the bonds of the grave; and then the power of his resurrection, which is to raise us up from death and the tomb. Yet those Jews, being more dead than death itself, were not stirred at all by this proclamation of death and of the grave; so that you may know that men, even these obstinate ones, are not taught or admonished by any outward miracles, unless the Lord works inwardly by the power of his Holy Spirit, and that this too happens in their minds not without a miracle. And indeed in the conversion of the wicked, God is more admirable than in performing all outward miracles. So far, then, we have spoken of these four miracles wrought at the death of the Lord. I see that they are so tempered among themselves that the first and the last are arranged to teach the Jews, while the second and the third are meant to terrify them and to announce to them their impending destruction. This kind of moderation in the works of God is not to be passed over carelessly: for by it we are taught that God, even at the very time when he appears most armed against the wicked, nevertheless spares them and strikes them only slowly, and warns them to repent in good time and to forestall the judgment that hangs over them, so that, if they will not repent, they may be left inexcusable when judgment falls upon them while they are already oppressed.

units.la: Centurio verò & qui cum eo. Nunc de effecto quodã miraculorum illorum, quæ edita sunt in morte Christi videndum. Existit quidem, fateor, aliqua commotio in eo populo ac turba quæ adstabat Christo crucifixo: verum ea fit in certis aliquibus non quidem Scribis, non Pharisæis, non Sacerdotibus, non Senioribus & Principibus populi, sed primum voce illa Christi, atque editis miraculis commouetur Centurio homo Ethnicus & prophanus. Verè, inquit, filius Dei erat iste: hoc est, homo iustus & diuinus, vt alibi habemus in Euangelio. Commouentur quoque milites, qui adstabant custodientes Christum, & in eandem ipsi quoque erumpunt vocem. Sed an nemo Iudæorum commotus est? Commota quidem est, fateor, turba, hoc est rudiores, idiotæ, & sex populi, quæ verberans pectora sua reuertebatur. At non sunt commoti Sacerdotes, Scribæ & Pharisæi, &c. Sed quî factum est, vt ij quos maximè oportuit, minimè tamen omnium his miraculis perculsi sint? Responsio facilis est; Erant ij iusto Dei iudicio coniecti in mentem reprobam. Nam sicut visum est iis, ait Paulus, Deum in notitia, quam quidem non solum ex natura, sed etiam ex verbo ipsius habuerunt, Deum, inquam, illum in notitia non retinere: ita tradidit eos Deus in mentem reprobam & omnis iudicij expertem. Atque stupor ille, de quo iam multa Prophetæ prædixerunt, hoc tempore potissimum accidit, quo Iudæi Christum crucifixerunt, & lucem Christi ac Spiritum sanctum oppugnarunt malitiosè adeo & præfracte. fracte. Sunt autem Iudaei isti omnibus saeculis futuris, ac posteris iudicij Dei grauissimi, ac maxime horredi exemplum in perpetuum, admonentque tristissimo illo suo exemplo omnes, vt ante omnia sibi metuant a mente reproba, & duritie illa cordis, ac stupore illo, quo vbi quis percussus est, iam brutis animantibus, imo ipsa terra bruta ac muta deterior euadit. Notandum quod qui erant Christi inimici iam in morte ipsius facti sunt amici. Qui eum crucifixerunt tanquam sontem, nunc eum iustificant tanquam insontem & iustum: denique turba illa quae paulo ante clamabat ac ingeminabat, Crucifige, crucifige: nunc verberans pectora sua reuertitur, atque ea re testificans innocentem crucifixum esse. Causa autem cur isti cogantur Dominum in morte testimoniis suis ornare, fuit, quia prius ipsi viderunt Dominum, tot tantisque adeo miraculis honoratum. Quem enim Dominus honorat, vel in vita, vel in morte, coguntur etiam hostes ipsum honorare: & Martyres illos Dei, quos in vita mundus odit, & ad mortem vsque persequuta est hominum maior pars, tamen illa ipsa mors eorum tam flagrans fuit, & corpora igni combusta tam suauem quasi thuris accensi odorem emiserunt, viqui paulo ante in ipsos saeuierunt, ex acerrimis inimicis summi amici sint facti, & sanguis martyrum, vt dici solet, fermè Ecclesiae Dei euaserit. Paulus dicit ie gaudere & gratulari omnibus iis, si pro libamento offeratur super hostia sacrificioque fidei ipsorum. Quo significat martyrum Dei mortem, quasi libamen esse, quo superimposito redditur fides hominum, quae Deo offerri dicitur, tanquam sacrificium quoddam suaue olens ac flagrans: ergo martyres in morte non hominibus tantum, sed etiam Deo bona sunt fragrantia: vt non sit iam quod quorum mors est sanctificata morte illa Christi Iesu, tantopere sibi metuant a morte.
units.tr: The centurion and those who were with him. Now we must consider the effect that these miracles, performed at the death of Christ, had. There is indeed, I admit, some stirring in the crowd that stood by Christ crucified. But it occurs in certain individuals, not in the scribes, the Pharisees, the priests, or the elders and princes of the people. First, the centurion, a heathen and profane man, is moved by that voice of Christ and by the miracles performed. Truly, he says, this was the Son of God: that is, a just and divine man, as we read elsewhere in the Gospel. The soldiers who stood guard over Christ are also moved, and they too break out into the same words. But was no one among the Jews moved? I admit that the crowd was moved, that is, the cruder and more ignorant folk, the common people, who returned beating their breasts. But the priests, scribes and Pharisees were not moved, and so on. But how is it that those who most ought to have been struck by these miracles were struck least of all? The answer is easy. By the just judgment of God they had been cast into a reprobate mind. For, as Paul says, since they did not think it worth while to have God in knowledge, which they had not only from nature but also from his Word, God gave them over to a reprobate mind and to a mind free of all judgment. And that stupor, of which the prophets had already foretold much, came upon them most of all at this time, when the Jews crucified Christ and assailed the light of Christ and the Holy Spirit so maliciously and stubbornly. Those Jews are, for all future ages and for posterity, a most grievous and most dreadful example of the judgment of God, and by their most sorrowful example they warn everyone above all to fear a reprobate mind, that hardness of heart and that stupor, by which, when someone has been struck, he becomes worse than brute beasts, indeed worse than the dumb and senseless earth itself. It should be noted that those who were enemies of Christ have now, in his very death, become his friends. Those who crucified him as a guilty man now justify him as innocent and just. Finally, that crowd which a little before was shouting and repeating Crucify, crucify, now returns beating its breasts, and by this bears witness that the crucified one was innocent. The reason why these men are compelled to adorn the Lord in his death with their testimonies was that they had first seen the Lord honoured with so many and such great miracles. For whom the Lord honours, whether in life or in death, his enemies too are compelled to honour. And those martyrs of God, whom the world hates in life and whom the greater part of mankind has persecuted even unto death, yet their death was so glorious, and their bodies burned in the fire sent forth a sweet odour as of burning incense, that those who a little before had raged against them became the greatest friends from the bitterest enemies, and the blood of the martyrs, as is commonly said, has almost become the seed of the Church of God. Paul says that he rejoices and congratulates all of them, if his blood is poured out as a libation over the sacrifice and offering of their faith. By this he signifies that the death of the martyrs of God is as a libation, over which the faith of men, which is said to be offered to God, is poured as a certain sweet-smelling and fragrant sacrifice. Therefore the martyrs in death are a sweet fragrance not only to men but also to God. So there is no reason why those whose death has been sanctified by the death of Christ Jesus should be so greatly afraid of death.

units.tr: 53 Now there were many women there, looking on from afar, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him.

units.la: QVæ fuerint partes omnium aliorum, Iudæorum, Gentium, iam vidimus: Ipsi Christum persequuti fuerunt, crucifixerunt, ludibrio habuerunt. Nunc postremò habemus quæ fuerint partes piorum & amicorum Christi interea, dum ista à persequutoribus geruntur. Noti ipsius, qui ipso in vita vsi sunt familiariter, ipsi stant procul. Narratur Iohann. 19. 25. 26. 27. Christum in cruce alloquutum esse matrem suam simul & Iohannem discipulum, quibuscum erant & aliæ duæ mulieres, quarum mentio ibi fit: ergo oportet tum, cum eos alloquutus est Dominus, non stetisse procul. Quamobrem videntur mihi iidem illi stetisse procul inter redeundum domum. Postquam enim Dominus iam expirauit, domum reuersi sunt unà cum reliqua multitudine. Verum amor ille Christi, qui non passus est eos à Christo nisi difficulter admodum diuelli, effecit vt subinde in reditu subsisterent, seseque conuerterent ad Christum, eúmque eminus mœsti intuerentur. Sed vtut res habet, certum est vt impulsi amore Christi ipsum ad crucem sunt comitati, ita nexu eiusdem illius amoris cum illo coniuncti, steterunt intuétes eum: atque vt fides & amor coniunxerunt eos cum Christo, ita idem amor Christi separauit eos à reliqua peruersa multitudine, coniunxitque eos inter se: nam qui per fidem & amorem coeunt in vno capite Christo, ij necessario per idem illud amoris vinculum coaptantur inter se in vnum corpus: contraque qui in vno capite per vnam fidem non coeunt, ij profecto nunquam adolescent in vnum corpus. Nullum est vinculum in natura tam arctum quod coniungat homines inter se, si in vno communi capite Christo non coniungantur: contrà vero etsi nullum naturæ, sanguinis, communis patriæ vinculum intercedat, tamen si cum vno capite Christo coniuncti sint, ij necessitate inter se vinciuntur: neque coniunctionem istam impedit vlla locorum distantia. Dū hanc multitudinem quæ Christo crucifixo vndique adstabat mecum diligentius consIdero, videor mihi tanquam in speculo quodam videre huius mundi vniuersi statum & conditionem. Reuera enim mundus quidam hic adest qui vndiquaque circunstat & circumsepit Christum è cruce pendentem: hic sunt Iudæi, hic gentes, hic Ecclesia falsa & adultera, hic genuina & vera, & in ista multitudine, mali cum malis, boni cum bonis congregantur. Hoc commune est omnibus, quod omnes pariter Christum intueantur.
