Verùm alij alio modo, alij pascunt sibi oculos illo spectaculo, alij saturant malitiosum animum suû sanguine ipsius, alij denique & qui boni sunt ac pij intuentur eum cum mœrore quidem animi, cum animi lætitia tamen coniuncta propter fidem & spem resurrectionis Domini sequuturæ. Ita res se habet hodierno die: omnes quotquot vspiam sunt homines quasi circumstantes Christum pariter intuentur, sed alij alio modo: soli pij enim intuentur ita, vt verû fructum ex ipsius morte & resurrectione percipiant. Obseruandum quòd cùmferè is qui maximè coniunctus est cum aliquo, eû pudeat amici sui, cùm morte patitur probrosam: vt contrà quisquis patitur morte aliquam probrosam, is quidem cupit eam perpeti clam amicis, qui eum soliti sunt in pretio habere: cùm, inquam, ita soleat fieri, ego eò adducor vt credâ istos Christi familiares vidisse in Christi morte aliqua ex parte suam ipsorum vitam, & in ipsius
units.tr: We have already seen what the parts of all the others were: of the Jews and of the Gentiles. They persecuted Christ, crucified him, and held him up to mockery. Now at last we have what the parts of the godly and of Christ's friends were meanwhile, while these things were being done by his persecutors. His acquaintances, who had been on familiar terms with him in his life, stand afar off. It is related in John 19. 25. 26. 27. that Christ, on the cross, spoke to his mother and to the disciple John, with whom were also the two other women mentioned there. Therefore, when the Lord spoke to them, they cannot have been standing afar off. For this reason it seems to me that these same people stood afar off on their way home. For when the Lord had now expired, they returned home together with the rest of the crowd. But that love of Christ, which did not allow them to be torn away from Christ except with great difficulty, caused them from time to time on the way back to stop, to turn towards Christ, and to gaze at him sorrowfully from a distance. But however the matter stands, it is certain that, moved by the love of Christ, they accompanied him to the cross, and, bound by the bond of that same love to him, they stood gazing at him. And just as faith and love joined them with Christ, so the same love of Christ separated them from the rest of the perverse multitude and joined them together. For those who come together in faith and love in the one head, Christ, are necessarily fitted together with one another into one body by that same bond of love. On the other hand, those who do not come together in one head through one faith will certainly never grow into one body. There is no bond in nature so close as to join men to one another if they are not joined in the one common head, Christ. On the contrary, even if no bond of nature, of blood, or of a common country lies between them, yet if they are joined to the one head, Christ, they are necessarily bound together, and no distance of place hinders that union. As I consider this multitude more carefully, which stood on every side about the crucified Christ, I seem to see, as in a certain mirror, the state and condition of this whole world. For indeed there is here a world which surrounds and encircles Christ hanging from the cross on every side: here are the Jews, here the Gentiles, here the false and adulterous Church, here the genuine and true one, and in this multitude the wicked are gathered with the wicked, the good with the good. This is common to all, that they all alike look upon Christ. But they do so in different ways. Some feed their eyes on that spectacle, others satisfy their malicious minds with his blood, and others, finally, those who are good and godly, look upon him with sorrow of mind, yet joined with joy of mind on account of faith and the hope of the Lord's resurrection to follow. So it is with the present day: all who are anywhere men stand, as it were, around Christ and look upon him alike, but in different ways. For only the godly look in such a way as to receive the true fruit from his death and resurrection. It should be observed that, since he who is most closely joined with someone is generally ashamed on his friend's account when he suffers a shameful death, and conversely whoever suffers some shameful death wishes to endure it secretly from the friends who were accustomed to hold him in esteem, since, I say, this is usually how it happens, I am led to believe that those intimate friends of Christ saw in the death of Christ, in some part, their own life, and in his shame their own glory, and that that sacrifice of his was so sweet and fragrant to them that they would rather have died with him than have been torn away from him in death. Of this very thing the Lord in some measure forewarned them, when he said: Where…

units.la: {A}Ab eo ... Quæ aueluntur. ignominia suam ipsorum gloriam & suavè adeo acfragrans fuisse ipsis Christi illud sacrificium, ut moricum ipso maluissent, quàm ab ipso in morte diuelli se passi fuissent. De hoc ipso Dominus quodammodo praemonuit, cùm dixit: Vbi cadauer, ibi congregabuntur Aquilæ. Cùm igitur isti tam arctè ipsi adhæserunt in summa ipsius ignominia, pudeat nos, si non adhæreamus ei nunc in summa ipsius gloria, & si patiamur nos ab eo diuelli vllá morte. Hæc in genere dicta sunto de nomis & amicis Christi, siue viris illis, siue fœminis, qui vnà stabant procul ipsum spectantes. Nunc quia mentio fit mulierum praecipuè, de iis dicendum erit aliquid & obseruandum in primis. Primùm de iis dictum est quòd multæ tum fuerint, de viris non lego quòd multi fuerint: deinde, quòd Christum spectarint, proculdubio cum mœrore tum pariter & lætitia. Tertiò, quòd sequutæ fuerint eum ex Galilæa. Non enim iis molestum fuit facere iter cum eo itineris socio. Quartò, quod ministrantes ipsi venerint vnà cum eo à Galilæa Hierosolyma: neque sibi, neque sumptibus suis ipsæ pepercerant, ad hoc vt fruerentur eo, qui verba vitæ habuit. Nominatim autem mentio fit certarum quarundam mulierum, Mariæ Magdalenæ, Mariæ matris Iacobi minoris & Ioses, denique Salomes, quæ mater erat duorum filiorum Zebedæi. Ipsæ ornantur hoc testimonio & tanquam insigni, quòd cùm in Galilæa versarentur Dominus, assiduè vnà fuerunt, ipsíque ministrarunt. Quo significatur eas nunquam à latere ipsius discessisse. In hac mulierum historia videre licet quàm tenero amore Dominum ipsæ sint prosequutæ: qua quidem re viros omnes, etiam eos qui ipsius discipuli tu fuerunt, pudefecerunt: imò verò Apostolos ipsos quorum nullum legimus tum adfuisse Domino, praeter solum Iohannem. Quare Dominus vicissim honore isto testium mortis suæ, ipsas dignatus est, vt eæ Apostolis etiam ipsis qui morti Domini non fuerunt auš interesse, de morte eius testarentur: & Apostolis tandem praecones essent, quod & fecerunt proculdubiò. Neque verò tantùm honorauit eas Dominus vt testes, verumetiā nomina aliquot mulierum commendauit Spiritui suo sancto memoriæ posteritatis prodenda, in memoriam nimirum {a}mirum sempiternam illius officij quod fecerunt erga Dominum in morte sua. Istarum mulierum exemplo illud videmus, sanctarum quarumque mulierum amore erga Dominum solere esse tenerrimum, & quo simplicior est ille sexus & alienior à sapientia ista humana, quae est secundum hunc mundum & carnem hanc, eo solere eas magis sapere caelestia illa ac spiritualia. Nam si quis sibi videur esse sapiens in hoc saeculo, stultus fiat oportet ut fiat sapiens, hoc est vere sapiens & secundum Deum. Hoc autem in his tanquam in imagine intuemur, amorem illum quo is sexus Deum prosequi soleat: ita in iisdem videmus honorem illum quo Deus eas afficere solet nonnunquam prae virili nostro sexu. In hac autem tam speciali mentione facta quarundam mulierum, colligimus Deum tum cum Christus crucifigeretur habuisse oculum providentiae suae fixum in singulis qui tum aderant & intererant illi spectaculo, & Spiritu suo penetrasse usque ad intimas cogitationes singulorum. Idem quoque fit in omnibus hominum coetibus & concionibus publicis quae fiunt quacunque de causa. Habet Deus singulos & singulorum affectus animi interiores notatos. Quamobrem quoties huiusmodi coetibus nos contingit interesse, videndum nobis est diligenter ut corda nostra probemus Deo ad hoc, ut ab eo veniam laudem reportemus.
units.tr: From him ... which are taken away. Their shame was, for them, a glory so sweet and fragrant that they would rather have died with him than have been torn away from him in his death. The Lord foretold this in some measure when he said: Where the carcase is, there will the eagles be gathered together. Since these followers clung so closely to him in the depths of his shame, we should be ashamed if we do not cling to him now in the height of his glory, and if we allow ourselves to be torn from him by any death. This is what I have to say in general about the friends of Christ, whether men or women, who stood together at a distance, looking on him. Now, since women are mentioned in particular, something must be said about them, and some points must be noted first. First, it is said that there were many of them, while I do not read that there were many men. Second, they watched Christ without doubt with both sorrow and joy. Third, they had followed him from Galilee, for the journey with him as a companion was no burden to them. Fourth, they had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, ministering to him; they had spared neither themselves nor their own means, so that they might enjoy him who had the words of life. By name, mention is made of certain women: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses, and finally Salome, who was the mother of the two sons of Zebedee. They are adorned with this testimony, as with a distinguishing mark, that while the Lord was in Galilee they were constantly with him and ministered to him. By this it is signified that they never departed from his side. In this account of the women we may see with what tender love they followed the Lord. By this they put to shame all the men, even those who were his own disciples, and indeed the apostles themselves, of whom we read that none was present with the Lord at that time except John alone. Therefore the Lord, in return, deigned to honour these women with this honour, as witnesses of his death, so that they might testify of his death even to those apostles who had not been present at it, and so that they might at last be heralds to the apostles; and this they undoubtedly did. Nor did the Lord honour them only as witnesses; he also commended the names of several women to his Holy Spirit, to be handed down to the memory of posterity, that is, as an everlasting memorial of the service they rendered to the Lord in his death. From the example of these women we see that the love of holy women towards the Lord is usually most tender, and that the simpler that sex is, and the more remote from that human wisdom which is according to this world and this flesh, the more they usually relish heavenly and spiritual things. For if anyone seems wise in this age, he must become foolish, so that he may become wise, that is, truly wise and according to God. Yet in these women we see, as in an image, that love with which that sex is wont to pursue God; and in the same women we see that honour with which God, beyond our male sex, sometimes is wont to favour them. In this particular mention of certain women we gather that God, when Christ was being crucified, had the eye of his providence fixed on each of those who were present and who attended that spectacle, and that by his Spirit he penetrated to the innermost thoughts of each. The same happens in all assemblies of men and in public sermons, whatever the cause for which they are held. God has each person and the inward affections of each mind noted. Wherefore, whenever it happens that we attend such gatherings, we must take care to examine our hearts before God, so that we may win approval and praise from him.

units.la: Iohannis 19.
units.tr: John 19.

units.la: 31 Iudaei ergo ut non manerent in cruce corpora Sabbatho, quoniam erat parasceve (erat enim magnus dies illius Sabbathi) rogauerunt Pilatum ut confringerentur eorum crura, ac tollerentur.
units.tr: 31 The Jews therefore, so that the bodies should not remain on the cross on the Sabbath, since it was the Preparation (for that Sabbath was a great day), asked Pilate that their legs be broken and that they be taken away.

units.la: 32 Venerunt ergo milites, & prioris quidem latronis confregerunt crura, & alterius qui crucifixus fuerat cum eo.
units.tr: 32 The soldiers therefore came, and broke the legs of the first thief, and of the other who had been crucified with him.

units.la: 33 Ad Iesum autem cum venissent, ut viderunt eum iam mortuum, non confregerunt eius crura:
units.tr: 33 But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs.

units.la: 34 Sed quidam ex militibus lancea latus eius fodit, & statim exiuit sanguis & aqua.
units.tr: 34 But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.

units.la: 35 Et qui vidit testatur, & verum est testimonium eius, ille, inquam, scit se vera dicere, vt & vos credatis.
units.tr: 35 And he who saw it bears witness, and his testimony is true; he, I say, knows that he speaks the truth, so that you also may believe.

units.la: 36 Facta enim sunt haec vt scriptura impleretur, dicens, Non confringetur vllum os ipsius.
units.tr: 36 For these things were done so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: Not one bone of him shall be broken.

units.la: 37 Et rursus alia Scriptura dicit, Videbunt quem transfixerunt.
units.tr: 37 And again another Scripture says: They shall look on him whom they pierced.

units.la: SEquitur historia sepulturae Christi, verum apud Iohannem legimus primum de corporis ipsius detractione, detrahitur autem & tollitur e cruce, interuentu rogationis & intercessionis Iudaeorum apud Pilatum: ex quo apparet, vt non habuerunt Iudaei potestatem tollendi hominis in crucem, ita neque tollendi e cruce: & iurisdictionem ipsis omnem sublatam fuisse iusto Dei iudicio. Interea illud laude dignum est in politia Romana, quod vt absque sententia iudicis nemo actus est in crucem: ita neque absque sententia & authoritate iudicis nemo sublatus est e cruce. Nihil enim fieri oportet de homine quoquam reo & damnato, sine sententia & authoritate iudicis: & lex Dei iudicialis ac forensis fuit tam de homine tollendo e cruce, quam de homine agendo in crucem. Quare non minus hoc quam illud ad iudicem pertinet, qui legis est vindex. Verum non est omittendum, quinam intercesserint apud Pilatum, pro Christo & aliis e cruce tollendis, vt finis tandem imponeretur non tantum dolori, sed etiam ignominiae eorum. Non intercesserunt pro Christo amici, neque enim ausi fuerunt: sed ipsi inimici quasi aliud agentes id fecerunt, non animo quidem benevolo, nulla ducti misericordia, sed ea occasione, de qua paulo post dicemus. Interea autem quocunque demum modo affecti fuerunt ii, beneficium confertur in Christum, Deo rem ita dispensante, qui etiam inimicos & aduersarios nostros aliud agentes facit cooperari in bonum iis qui diligunt Deum. Cessantibus & desferentibus nos amicis nostris, non defecturi sunt qui nobis consulent, neque defutura sinet media quibus nos suo tempore Deus liberabit, qui etiam nonnunquam sine mediis suos ex omnibus malis eripit. Nunc autē videndum quæ sit rogationis istius summa: Vt confringerentur, inquit, crura eorum ac tollerentur. Vtrum hoc ex vsitato more fieri petierunt nécne ego non disputo, sed id non potest colligi ex contextu. Ex quo apparet eos impulsos ad hanc petitionem, propter festum Pascha, quod si in id tempus non incidisset, videtur Iudæos protollendis crucifixis è cruce, non intercessuros fuisse, sed passuros fuisse eos in cruce hærere non tantùm die illo, & nocte eum insequenti, sed etiam die subsequenti & tantisperdum dum ipsi in cruce expirarent. Petunt quidem Iudæi, vt finis aliquis imponeretur dolori illi in quo tum hæsit Dominus, simúlque ignominiæ. Nam adhuc supereminere eum sunt opinati. Verùm non sine tormentis id petūt fieri. Potuit enim minori negotio simul & pœna Christo pariter & aliis vita eripi, vt id liceat nobis discere, inimicos si quando nobis prosunt, eadem opera nos lædere, & amaritudinem in nos animi sui prodere interea aliquo maleficio. Verùm Deus facit vt etiam illa ipsa amaritudo & acerbitas eorum conferant nobis ad bonum. Notanda hic est efficacia consilij simul & verbi Diuini, quomodo eluceat: Iudæi petunt vt confringantur crura Christi vt postea videbimus. Quia Deus ita non modò in æterno consilio suo prouidit, sed etiam prædixit futurum suo tempore. Tum quidem elucet efficacitas consilij & verbi Diuini, cùm homines sese iis opponunt quibus possunt modis, siue petitionibus, siue mandatis suis. Proculdubio hæ oppositiones ordinatæ sunt à Deo, ad hoc vt illucesceret efficacitas illa consilij & verbi ipsius, & vt mundus conspiciat nihil posse homines consiliis & mandatis suis aduersus Deum, decretū & verbum ipsius. Sed nunc videndum quæ causa eos mouerit ad hanc rogationem: non mouit eos misericordia aliqua erga Deum. Non zelus legis Dei quæ iubebat suspensos de ligno eodem die detrahi è ligno, Deut.21.22.23. Sed superstitio quædam sua ipsos ad id mouit. Fuit enim parasceue eodem illo die, vesperi autem celebrandum festum illud Agni Paschalis. Crastinus verò dies Paschalis, & magnū quod vocabant Sabbathum. Ideóque ne solennitas illa & sanƈta actio funestaretur crucifixis illis hominibus, (Nam crucifixi erant per legem maledicti) rogarunt ut deponerentur quidem illi e cruce, sed extincti priūs & affecti graui quodam tormento.Hypocritæ erant ipsi,& vel terrā ipsam quam terebant pedibus,contaminabant, & tamen metuebant sibi ac sancto illi, in quo sanctificatus fuit mundus, ne scilicet ab eo polluerentur. Iam antea ex eadem superstitione abstinebant à prætorio in quo erat Pilatus. Hoc ingenium est hypocritarum quorum religio tota posita est in externis istis & corporalibus exercitiis, & cūm ipsi polluant omnia, quæ attinguntstamen hæc est eorum vox, Ne attingite, negustate, ne contrectate. Sed videndum nunc, cur Sabbathum magnū dicatur,nimirum quia in illum diem incidebat geminū festum, primum Sabbathi & ordinarium, deinde Paschatis & extraordinarium. Nam Pascha celebrandum fuit pridie illius diei ex Dei præscripto: & Christus ex Dei illo præscripto celebrauit Pascha suum pridie illius diei, nempe ea nocte, qua traditus est à Iuda & captus à Iudæis. Verùm Iudæi quoties pridie Sabbathi celebrandum fuit Pascha, reiecerunt Pascha in Sabbathum, ne populus fatigaretur festis tam coniunctis, & remissior fieret in celebrandis iis,si seorsim essent accepta.
units.tr: THE account of the burial of Christ follows. But in John we read first of the taking down of his body. He is taken down and removed from the cross through the request and intercession of the Jews with Pilate. From this it appears that, just as the Jews did not have the power to lift a man up on the cross, so neither did they have the power to take him down from it; and that all their jurisdiction had been removed by the just judgment of God. Meanwhile, this is praiseworthy in the Roman polity: just as no one was led to the cross without the sentence of a judge, so no one was taken down from the cross without the sentence and authority of a judge. For nothing ought to be done to any man who is accused and condemned without the sentence and authority of a judge; and the law of God, both judicial and forensic, concerned the taking of a man down from the cross as much as the leading of a man up to it. Therefore this belongs to the judge, who is the avenger of the law, no less than that. But it must not be left out who interceded with Pilate, both for Christ and for the others to be taken down from the cross, so that an end might at last be put not only to their pain but also to their shame. Christ's friends did not intercede for him, for they did not dare. But his enemies did it, as if acting for another purpose, not indeed with a kindly mind, nor moved by any pity, but on the occasion that we shall speak of a little later. Meanwhile, however those men were affected, a benefit is conferred upon Christ, God so ordering the matter, who also makes even our enemies and adversaries, while acting for another purpose, work together for good to those who love God. When our friends fail us and desert us, there will not be lacking those who will consult for us, nor will God fail to provide the means by which, in his time, he will deliver us; he who even at times snatches his people out of all evils without means. But now we must consider what the substance of that request was: That their legs, he says, be broken and that they be taken away. Whether they asked this according to the customary practice, I do not dispute; but this cannot be gathered from the context. From this it appears that they were moved to this request by the feast of the Passover; for if that time had not coincided with it, the Jews would not, it seems, have interceded for the taking down of the crucified from the cross, but would have allowed them to hang on the cross not only that day and the night following, but also the day after, and until they expired on the cross. The Jews certainly ask that some end be put to that pain in which the Lord then hung, and at the same time to his shame; for they thought he was still rising above them. But they do not ask for it without torments. For Christ could have been deprived of life, with less trouble and with less punishment, as well as the others; so that we may learn from this that when enemies at any time benefit us, they at the same time seek to harm us, and by some wrong to betray the bitterness of their mind against us. But God causes that even that very bitterness and harshness of theirs should work for our good. The efficacy of God's counsel together with his Word is to be noted here, and how it shines forth. The Jews ask that the legs of Christ be broken, as we shall see afterwards; for God not only foresaw this in his eternal counsel, but also foretold that it would come to pass in its time. Then indeed the efficacy of the counsel and Word of God shines forth, when men oppose themselves to them by whatever means they can, whether by their requests or by their commands. Undoubtedly these oppositions were ordained by God, so that the efficacy of his counsel and Word might shine out, and so that the world might see that men can do nothing against God, his decree and his Word, by their counsels and commands. But now we must consider what cause moved them to this request. It was not some regard for God that moved them: it was not the zeal of the law of God, which commanded that those hanged on a tree be taken down from the tree on the same day (Deut. 21.22.23). It was a certain superstition of their own that moved them to this. For that day was the Preparation, and in the evening the feast of the Paschal Lamb was to be celebrated; and the next day was the Passover, and a great Sabbath, as they called it. Therefore, so that that solemnity and holy action should not be defiled by those crucified men (for the crucified were accursed by the law), they asked that they be taken down from the cross, but first be put to death and subjected to some grievous torment. They were hypocrites; they defiled the very ground they trod upon with their feet, and yet they feared for themselves and for that holy place in which the world was sanctified, lest they should be polluted by it. Already before this, from the same superstition, they had abstained from the praetorium in which Pilate was. This is the nature of hypocrites, whose whole religion consists in these external and bodily exercises; and though they themselves pollute all things they touch, yet this is their cry: Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle. But now we must see why the Sabbath is called great: namely, because a twofold feast fell on that day, the first being the Sabbath, which was ordinary, and then the Passover, which was extraordinary. For the Passover was to be celebrated on the day before that day, by God's prescription; and Christ, according to that prescription of God, celebrated his Passover on the day before it, that is, on the night in which he was betrayed by Judas and seized by the Jews. But the Jews, whenever the Passover had to be celebrated on the day before the Sabbath, pushed the Passover over into the Sabbath, so that the people should not be wearied by festivals so closely joined, and should not be less diligent in observing them if they were received separately.

units.la: Hactenus fuit postulatum Iudæorum: sequitur mandatum Pilati,simul & mandati executio. Milites igitur accepto mandato Pilati, accedunt ad crucifixos, & primùm confringunt crura vnius latronis,deinde alterius. Ecce duo hi latrones, dispares quoad vitā futurā, pares siunt tormentis in hac vita: vt nemo metiatur cōditionem quæ est in Christo Iesu ex præsentis vitæ miseriis. Neque verò putandum est cum aduersariis, remissionē fieri peccati,non etiam pœnæ:quasi verò hæc pœna peccati fuerit, quam passus est latro qui receptus est in gratiam,sine qua, tanquam satisfactione aliqua nostra poturisset is sesi nari, cùm illa Christi pro latrone & pro omnibus nobis satisfactio in sese abundè sit sufficiens. Afflictiones autem omnes quas perpetimur in hac vita, toridem Dei sunt castigationes ad mortificationem reliquiarum istarum, quæ in nobis sunt peccati. Cūm autem venissent ad Christum, inuenerunt eum mortuum, & non confregerunt crura ipsius. Vide hic prouiden-tiam Dei, vt is efficiat quod decretum eit, & praedi-ctum. Per mortem illam Christi miraculosam & ex-traordinariam, vt diximus, impleuit illam praedicatio-nem quae fuerat de comminuendis Christi ossibus, vt stultum sit spretis mediis à Deo ordinatis, pendere prorsus à Dei illa prouidentia: hoc enim est tentare Deum, qui non minus ordinauit media, quàm sinem ipsum ad quem nos media perducunt. Vide hic testes mortis Christi. Milites enim isti qui inueniunt eum mortuum, & non confringunt crura ipsius, totidem sunt testes mortis eius, & praedicant quasi palam eum iam mortuum esse, ac si dicant: Hic iam mortuus est, idque eo testatum facimus omnibus, quòd non confringamus crura ipsius vt aliorum. Quorsum enim attinet confringere crura demortui, & extinguere vitam eam quę iam extincta est? Accedit ad hoc testimonium, eius nimirum militis, qui accepta lancea transfixit latus ipsius. Hic quoque preco fuit quidam mortis Domini: ac si dixisset, Ego indubitatam eius mortem reddam, si sit in ipso aliquid vitę, vel spiritus reliquum. Ecce ego illud totum semel emitto atque effundo. Christus ipse voce illa magna cum precibus ad Patrem coniuncta, Pater, inquiens, in manus tuas depono spiritum meum, iam satis testatus est se mortuum esse: sed Deus voluit ipsos quoque carnifices testatam facere Filij sui mortem. Extremam illam Christi ignominiam (nam morte nihil ignominiosius est & abiectius) Deus testatam esse voluit maximè: vt sciamus quàm necessarium fuerit & Christo mori, & nobis credere Christum mortuum esse ad redemptionem nostri & remissionem peccatorum nostrorum. Sed de testibus his Christi carnificibus, hoc non est praeter-eundum quod aliis profuerint suo testimonio, sibi autem non profuerint, cum Christi persequutores exti-terint. Sunt & hodierno die, qui cum aliis praedicent Euangelium, ipsi reprobi fiunt. Quare videndum nobis, vt loquamur & testemur de Christo, quia ipsi credimus, hoc est quia applicamus ad nos ipsi eam salutem quam aliis praedicamus, vt simul cum aliis per Euangelium Christi conseruemur.
units.tr: Thus far the demand of the Jews; now comes Pilate's command, together with its execution. The soldiers, therefore, having received Pilate's order, come to the crucified men and first break the legs of one thief, then of the other. Behold these two thieves, unlike in their future life, are made alike in their torments in this life, so that no one may judge the condition that is in Christ Jesus by the miseries of the present life. Nor indeed should we think, with our adversaries, that the remission of sin is granted without the remission of punishment too, as if this were the punishment of sin which the thief suffered who was received into grace, without which he could not have been saved, as though by some satisfaction of ours. For Christ's satisfaction for the thief and for all of us is in itself abundantly sufficient. Moreover, all the afflictions we suffer in this life are so many chastisements of God for the mortifying of those remnants of sin which are in us. But when they came to Jesus, they found him already dead and did not break his legs. See here the providence of God, which brings about what has been decreed and foretold. By that wonderful and extraordinary death of Christ, as we have said, he fulfilled the prediction concerning the breaking of Christ's bones. It is foolish, therefore, to set aside the means ordained by God and to depend wholly on that providence; for this is to tempt God, who has ordained the means no less than the end to which the means lead us. See here the witnesses of Christ's death. For those soldiers who find him dead and do not break his legs are so many witnesses of his death, and they proclaim, as it were openly, that he is already dead, as if they said: "He is already dead, and we make this plain to all by not breaking his legs as we do those of the others. For what is the point of breaking the legs of a dead man and extinguishing a life that is already extinguished?" To this testimony is added that of the soldier who, taking a lance, pierced his side. He too was a certain herald of the Lord's death, as if he had said: "I will make his death beyond doubt, if there is any life or spirit left in him. Behold, I let out and pour out the whole of it at once." Christ himself, with that loud voice joined to prayers to the Father, saying, "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit," had already sufficiently testified that he was dead; but God willed that the executioners themselves should also bear witness to the death of his Son. God willed especially to make the last shame of Christ, for nothing is more shameful and abject than death, to be attested, so that we may know how necessary it was both for Christ to die and for us to believe that Christ is dead, for our redemption and the remission of our sins. But concerning these witnesses, Christ's executioners, this must not be passed over: that though they served others by their testimony, they did not serve themselves, since they became persecutors of Christ. There are also in our own day those who preach the Gospel to others and yet become reprobate themselves. Therefore we must take care to speak and bear witness of Christ in such a way that we believe in him, that is, that we apply to ourselves the salvation which we preach to others, so that together with others we may be saved through the Gospel of Christ.

units.la: Et statim exiuit sanguis & aqua. Effusio haec proculdu- bio sanguinis & aquae ex parte aliqua naturalis fuit & ordinaria: cum enim cor sit quasi officina purioris ac vitalis sanguinis, & ϲϰεπαςδιον, hoc est membrana, qua cor integitur, contineat aliquid liquoris aquei, quo calor cordis continuo irrixatur: profecto oportuit effusionem hanc sanguinis & aquae ex corde & ϲϰεπαςδιων transfixis naturalem esse & ordinariam. Dum autem considero adeo abunde, adeoque distincte exiuisse sanguinem & aquam, ut a circumstantibus discerni potuerit aqua a sanguine, profecto adducor eo, ut credam effusionem hanc aliquo pacto extraordinariam & insuetam fuisse. Et ut alia quae inciderunt in morte Christi, ostenderunt Christum non hominem tantum, sed longe plusquam hominem: ita & sanguis hic simul cum aqua effusus plane eum prodidit Dei sanguinem esse, & Christum esse Deum.
units.tr: And immediately there came out blood and water. This outpouring of blood and water was without doubt in some measure natural and ordinary: for since the heart is, as it were, the workshop of the purer and vital blood, and the pericardium [περικάρδιον], that is, the membrane which encloses the heart, contains some watery liquid by which the heat of the heart is continually moistened, it must surely have been that this outflow of blood and water from the heart and the pierced pericardium was natural and ordinary. But when I consider that the blood and water came out so abundantly and so distinctly that the water could be told apart from the blood by those standing by, I am indeed led to believe that this outpouring was in some way extraordinary and unusual. And as the other things that happened at the death of Christ showed that Christ was not only a man but far more than a man, so this blood, poured out together with water, plainly revealed that it was the blood of God and that Christ is God.

units.la: Sed videamus quis fuerit effusi illius sanguinis cum aqua visus. Proculdubio testabantur Christum vere mortuum fuisse, effuso iam vitali illo sanguine: neque tantum de morte testabantur, sed de mortis efficacitate & potentia ad concipiendam remissionem peccatorum & regeneratorum: quae duo beneficia, vna cum sanguine & aqua effusa, sunt ex confesso Christi latere. Per sanguinem enim Christi remissio peccatorum & satisfactio iustitiae Diuinae. Per sanguinem & aquam: hoc est per sanguinem aqueum, purgatur & abluitur inhaerens ista naturae corruptio. Iohannes Apostolus dicit, Christum venisse per aquam, nempe per quam purgatur inhaerens corruptio. Neque per aquam tantum, sed etiam per sanguinem, hoc est per aquam sanguineam, per quam obtinemus remissionem peccatorum nostrorum. Atque hic duplex visus fuit effusi sanguinis & aquae. Tertius hic addi potest: testabatur enim haec effusio finem iam impositum sacrificiis, purgationibus ac lotionibus legalibus, quae tantum umbrae quaedam fuerunt venturi huius sanguinis & aquae, quae simul effusa sunt ex Christi latere. Inter testes terrestres, qui testantur de Christi aduentu, numerantur hi duo quasi testes, sanguis & aqua: ex quo sequitur manere eos testes etiamnum, & testari perpetuo in cordibus nostris, dum
units.tr: But let us see what was the significance of that blood poured out with water. Without doubt they bore witness that Christ was truly dead, since his vital blood had now been poured out. Nor did they bear witness only to his death, but to the efficacy and power of that death for obtaining the remission of sins and the regeneration of the faithful; and these two benefits, together with the blood and water poured out, are acknowledged to come from the side of Christ. For through the blood of Christ comes the remission of sins and the satisfaction of divine justice. Through blood and water, that is, through watery blood, that inherent corruption of nature is cleansed and washed away. The Apostle John says that Christ came by water, namely by which inherent corruption is cleansed. And not by water only, but also by blood, that is, by bloody water, by which we obtain the remission of our sins. And this gives a twofold meaning to the outpouring of blood and water. A third may be added: for this outpouring bore witness that an end had now been put to the sacrifices, purifications and legal washings, which were only shadows of this blood and water to come, which were poured out together from the side of Christ. Among the earthly witnesses who testify to the coming of Christ, these two, blood and water, are counted as if they were witnesses. From this it follows that they remain witnesses still, and continually bear witness in our hearts, while

units.la: Testantur complementu ceremoniarum legis.
units.tr: They bear witness to the fulfilment of the ceremonies of the law.

units.la: Regeneratio & communio. Àum conscientiæ nostræ asperguntur hoc sanguine, & cor nostrum purgatur hac aqua perpetuò. Hanc asper- sionem & purgationem quoties sentimus apud animos nostros, toties testimoniū perhibetur nobis quòd Christus iam venerit in mundum: atque sine hoc sensu, frustra adhibentur alia quæcunque testimonia. Habemus quoque quotidie in Sacramento Baptismi & Cœnæ Dominicæ, huius sanguinis & aquæ symbola quibus oculis nostris repræsentatur. In Sacramento Cœnæ, est symbolum sanguinis, in Sacramento Baptismi, est symbolum aquæ: Ergo sanguis & aqua manent perpetuò, vt testes aduentus Christi: & oculis nostris perpetuò in symbolis illis suis repræsentantur. Atque hæc de his hactenus.
units.tr: Regeneration and communion. Our consciences are sprinkled with this blood, and our hearts are continually cleansed with this water. As often as we feel this sprinkling and cleansing in our minds, so often is testimony given to us that Christ has already come into the world; and without this feeling, any other testimonies whatever are applied in vain. We also have daily, in the Sacrament of Baptism and of the Lord's Supper, symbols of this blood and water, by which they are set before our eyes. In the Sacrament of the Supper there is a symbol of the blood, and in the Sacrament of Baptism a symbol of the water. Therefore blood and water remain continually as witnesses of the coming of Christ, and are continually set before our eyes in those their symbols. And so much for these things so far.

units.la: Et qui vidit testatur. Narrationem proximam de non fractis Christi cruribus, & confosso latere ad effusionem vsque sanguinis & aquæ, confirmat suo testimonio. Testimonium suum aggrauat, primùm quòd qui testatus est, viderit: deinde quòd verum sit. Tertiò quod sciat, hoc est persuasum habeat apud conscientiam, quòd verum sit. Atque hæc eò pertinere dicit vt nos credamus.
units.tr: And he who saw it bears witness. He confirms by his testimony the preceding narrative about the unbroken legs of Christ and the pierced side, down to the outpouring of blood and water. He strengthens his testimony, first because he who bore witness saw it; then because it is true; and thirdly because he knows it, that is, is persuaded in his conscience that it is true. And he says that these things serve to make us believe.

units.la: Notandum quàm serio testetur de iis, quæ arguebant Christum mortuum esse, ac proinde quàm serio testetur de Christi morte. Sæpius de hoc iam admonui, tot testimonia de Christi morte perhibita arguere necessitatem mortis Christi eam fuisse, vt, nisi fuisset mortuus, neque ipse Mediator noster esse potuisset, neque nos potuissemus in eum tanquam Mediatorem credere. Qui nullo sensu tangitur neque peccati sui, neque iustitiæ Dei, quæ mortem peccatoris requirit, fateor eum sùsque deque ferre mortem Christi, nec quicquam pensi habere, siue is mortuus fuerit, siue minùs. At si quem merito mouet conscientia peccati sui, cum sensu iræ diuinæ, is profecto sentiet nullum sibi esse locum misericordiæ & salutis, nisi in morte illa Mediatoris sui. Nota deinde vnde-naam proficiscatur fides nostra: nempe ex testimonio. Sed qualem oportet testem esse? Nempe, primùm, oculatum, deinde eum, qui ipse scit ac persuasum habet verum esse illud quod testatur. Tales autem testes fuerunt Apostoli Christi. Ergo fides nostra nititur ipsorum testimonio. Dixi oportere testem non modò occultum esse, sed credentem. Nam fides etiam testantis, quando nimirum credit is atque ideo loquitur, maiorem fidem facit testimonio. Prodit autem fidem suam quoties μετὰ παρρησίας, & cum spirituali demonstratione edit oracula Dei. Testes Christi hodierno die sunt pastores & doctores in Ecclesia. Sed hoc differunt ab Apostolis, quod non sint testes oculati. Testantur quidem quod sciunt ipsi & credunt, sed non quod oculis viderunt, verùm quod habent ex eorum ore, & scriptis, qui viderunt. Ergo fundamentum fidei omnis, est testimonium non pastorum in Ecclesia, sed Apostolorum. Pastoribus autem non est credendum, nisi quatenus testantur mundo idem quod ante eos oculati illi testestati sunt, quódque scriptis suis reliquerunt. Facta sunt enim hæc, vt impleretur. Subiungit finem eorum quæ proximè narrata sunt. Finis est vt impleretur Scripturæ duæ: prima est Exod.12.46. Secunda est Zachariæ 12.10. Putaret quis rem non esse tanti momenti, siue impleantur Scripturæ, siue non impleantur. Nam, quid, inquit, verbo leuius? Respondeo, primùm Deum nihil vnquam temere loquutum esse, sed certo consilio ad gloriam nominis sui, & salutem Ecclesiæ suæ. Quare non est putandum ipsius verba leuia esse, vt solent esse hominum, qui temerè quidquid in buccam venit statim effutiunt. Quare permagni interest & gloriæ Dei & salutis hominum, vt ipsius verba impleantur. Præterea hoc redundat in Dei gloriam, quod postquam impletum est id quod prædictum est, iam Deus in veritate verbi sui glorificetur. Non est ista diuini honoris pars minima, cùm eum glorificamus in sermonibus suis. Apostoli quoties dicunt hoc vel illud factum esse, vt impleretur hæc vel illa Scriptura, toties Deum glorificant in sermonibus suis. Illud quidem fateor, facile esse glorificare Deum in sermonibus suis, cùm eos iam impletos videmus. At multò difficilius est Deo veritatis gloriam tribuere, cùm nondum sermones ipsius impleti sunt. At verò difficillimum est omnium in verbo suo Deum glorificare, cùm videmus omnia cuenire concontraria verbo ac promissionibus. Promisit vitam, ecce mors adest. Promisit Abrahae semen, ecce enervatum corpus Abrahae & emortua vulua Sarae: & revera quidem ea fides sola veram laudem obtinet, qui exemplo fidei Abrahae contra spem sub spe credit, freta scilicet patientia Dei, quae contra spem & contra omnia impedimenta, siue naturae siue aliarum rerum quarumcunque exequitur necessario quod semel loquutus est Deus; ut Deus appareat verus & iustificetur in sermonibus suis. Nunc reliquum est ut sigillatim examinemus haec testimonia Scripturae, & primum illud Exodi, Non confringetur vllum os ipsius. Moses haec effert de agno Paschali, nunc abrogato, agno, inquam, Paschali qui typus quidam fuit Christi. Iohannes typum ad veritatem accommodat, nempe ad Christum, in quo impleta est illa Scriptura. Sic Paul. verba illa quibus Moses praescribit formam comedendi agni Paschalis; Expurgate vetus fermentum, vt sitis noua massa, accommodat Christo: ex quo discimus, quis sit vsus veteris Scripturae, & Christo aptanda, deque eo intelligenda. Verbi gratia, abiiciedus typus agni Paschalis, retinenda tamen haec verba, Non comminuetis os ex eo, & Christo aptanda. Neque vero putandum proterea vim aliquam afferri veteri Scripturae, eamque in sensum non suum detorqueri. Nam eadem illa Scriptura, etiam in veteri populo, intellecta fuit de Christo, etsi mediate per typos & vmbras. Iam vero abolitis vmbris, intelligenda est de Christo immediate. Alterum testimonium est ex Zachariae 12. desumptum, quo loco est promissio respicientiae facta populo Iudaico, qui Christum persequutus est. Nam eodem illo loco subiecta sunt haec verba: Et flebunt super eo tanquam super vnigenito. Exemplum huius respiciencie videmus Act.2.41. Vbiter mille Iudaei leguntur resipuisse & conuersi esse ad concionem Petri vnicam. Sed verbum, Transfixerunt, notandum est. Transfixerunt Christum primum peccatis suis, quibus procurarunt eius mortem: transfixerunt eum deinde cum ipsum sunt persequuti, crucifixerunt, blasphemarunt, denique lancea huius militis transfixerunt latus ipsius. Ad hanc transfixionem accommodat verbum
units.tr: It should be noted how earnestly he bears witness to the things that were argued against Christ being dead, and therefore how earnestly he bears witness to Christ's death. I have already often pointed out that so many testimonies to Christ's death show that his death was necessary, so that, had he not died, our Mediator could neither have been our Mediator nor could we have believed in him as Mediator. The man who is moved by no sense either of his own sin or of God's righteousness, which requires the death of the sinner, I confess makes light of Christ's death and cares nothing whether he died or not. But if someone is rightly moved by a conscience of his sin, together with a sense of divine wrath, he will surely feel that there is no place for mercy and salvation for him except in the death of his Mediator. Next, note where our faith comes from: namely, from testimony. But what sort of witness ought one to be? First, an eyewitness; second, one who knows for himself and is convinced that what he testifies is true. Such witnesses were the apostles of Christ. Therefore our faith rests on their testimony. I said that the witness ought not only to be an eyewitness but also a believer. For the faith of the one testifying, namely when he believes and therefore speaks, gives greater weight to the testimony. He shows his faith whenever he utters the oracles of God with boldness [μετὰ παρρησίας] and with spiritual demonstration. The witnesses of Christ today are the ministers and teachers in the Church. But they differ from the apostles in this, that they are not eyewitnesses. They indeed testify to what they themselves know and believe, but not to what they saw with their eyes; rather, to what they have received from the mouths and writings of those who did see. Therefore the foundation of all faith is the testimony not of the ministers in the Church but of the apostles. Ministers, however, are not to be believed except insofar as they testify to the world the same things that those eyewitnesses testified before them and left in their writings. For these things were done that it might be fulfilled. He adds the purpose of the things just related. The purpose is that the Scriptures might be fulfilled; the two Scriptures are: the first, Exod. 12.46; the second, Zech. 12.10. One might think the matter is not of such great importance, whether the Scriptures are fulfilled or not. For, as he says, what is lighter than a word? I answer: first, God has never spoken rashly, but with a sure purpose for the glory of his name and the salvation of his Church. Therefore we must not think his words are light, as the words of men often are, who blurt out whatever comes into their mouths. Hence it matters greatly both to the glory of God and to the salvation of men that his words be fulfilled. Moreover, this redounds to God's glory: that once what was foretold has been fulfilled, God is glorified in the truth of his word. This is no small part of the honour due to God, when we glorify him in his sayings. Whenever the apostles say that this or that happened so that this or that Scripture might be fulfilled, they glorify God in his sayings. I admit it is easy to glorify God in his sayings when we see them already fulfilled. But it is much harder to give glory to God as the God of truth before his sayings are fulfilled. Yet it is hardest of all to glorify God in his word when we see everything happening contrary to the word and promises. He promised life; behold, death is at hand. He promised Abraham a seed; behold the body of Abraham is worn out and the womb of Sarah dead. And indeed that faith alone obtains true praise which, following the example of Abraham's faith, believes in hope against hope, relying of course on the patience of God, who, against hope and against all obstacles, whether of nature or of any other things whatever, necessarily carries out what God has once spoken, so that God may appear true and be justified in his sayings. It remains now that we examine these testimonies of Scripture one by one, and first that passage of Exodus: Not a bone of him shall be broken. Moses says this of the Passover lamb, now abrogated, the Passover lamb, I say, which was a certain type of Christ. John applies the type to the truth, namely to Christ, in whom that Scripture was fulfilled. So Paul applies to Christ those words by which Moses prescribes the manner of eating the Passover lamb: Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump. From this we learn what the use of the Old Testament Scripture is, and that it is to be applied to Christ and understood concerning him. For example, the type of the Passover lamb is to be set aside, yet these words, You shall not break a bone of it, are to be retained and applied to Christ. Nor is it to be thought that for this reason some violence is done to the Old Testament Scripture, or that it is twisted into a sense not its own. For that same Scripture was understood concerning Christ even among the ancient people, though mediately through types and shadows. Now indeed, with the shadows abolished, it is to be understood of Christ immediately. The second testimony is taken from Zechariah 12, where there is a promise of repentance made to the Jewish people who persecuted Christ. For in that same place these words follow: And they shall mourn for him as for an only son. We see an example of this repentance in Acts 2.41, where about three thousand Jews are read to have repented and been converted by the single sermon of Peter. But the word they pierced must be noted. They pierced Christ first with their sins, by which they procured his death; they pierced him then when they persecuted him, crucified him, blasphemed him; and finally with the spear of this soldier they pierced his side. The word applies to this piercing.

units.la: Ossa Christi non debuerunt nec potuerunt comminui. Prophetę Iohannes isto in loco. Ex hoc testimonio discimus primùm quanta extiterit huius populi malitia & ingratitudo. Peccatis suis mortem Christi procurarunt, ipsi sua manu transfixerunt eum, cuius mortem peccata ipsorum procurarunt. Est sane hoc summæ ingratitudinis,eum qui pro me se offert morti, eum, inquam,mea manu transfodere. Quis est qui non detestetur istam tantam malitiam? Sed videat ne dum Iudæos damnat, se condemnet: dum veritatem Christi oppugnat,dum persequitur Ecclesiam Christi, dum Christũ vita sua & moribus negat. Nã hic quisquis est, bis trãsfigit Christum. Nota deinde quanta sit Christi misericordia erga Iudæos & Gentiles. cordia : Primùm ex mera sua gratia & misericordia offert se morti pro populo isto : deinde,postquam ab ipsis crucifixus est,ex misericordia eos vocat ad resipiscẽ tiam.Vide igitur vt misericordia sua vincat ipsorũ malitiam: vt non immeritò dictum sit,Cũm peccatum abundauit, gratia superabundauit. Legimus in Apocalypsi testimonium hoc ipsum accómodatum ad secundũ illum Christi aduentum, qui futurus est cum nubibus. Ergo in illo die ,cũm venient electi in occursum Domini,primùm omnium cum fletu & lachrymis eum intuebũtur quem trãsxfierunt, & lugebunt super eo, tanquam super vnigenito:sed paulò post abstergentut omnes lachrymæ,& cum Domino in æternum manebunt, & solidum ac sincerum gaudium gaudebunt.
units.tr: The bones of Christ ought not and could not be broken. The prophet John, in this place. From this testimony we learn first how great the malice and ingratitude of this people was. They procured the death of Christ by their sins; with their own hands they pierced him whose death their sins had procured. Surely it is the height of ingratitude to pierce with my own hand him who offers himself to death for me. Who does not detest such great malice? But let him see to it that, while he condemns the Jews, he does not condemn himself: while he opposes the truth of Christ, while he persecutes the Church of Christ, while he denies Christ by his life and conduct. For whoever he is who does these things, he pierces Christ a second time. Next, note how great the mercy of Christ is toward the Jews and the Gentiles. First, out of his pure grace and mercy he offers himself to death for this people; then, after they have crucified him, out of mercy he calls them to repentance. See, therefore, how his mercy overcomes their malice, so that it is not unjustly said: where sin abounded, grace abounded much more. We read in the Apocalypse that this same testimony is applied to the second coming of Christ, which is to be with the clouds. Therefore on that day, when the elect come to meet the Lord, first of all they will look upon him whom they pierced with weeping and tears, and they will mourn over him as over an only son. But soon after, all tears will be wiped away, and they will remain with the Lord for ever and enjoy a solid and sincere joy.

units.la: Matthæi 27.
units.tr: Matthew 27.

units.la: 57 Cùm autem serum diei esset, venit homo diues ✠Arimathæensis, nomine Iofephus, qui & ipse discipulus fuerat Iesu.
units.tr: 57 When it was now evening, there came a rich man of Arimathea, named Joseph, who himself had also been a disciple of Jesus.

units.la: 58 Is adiit Pilatũ, & petiit corpus Iesu. Tunc Pilatus iussit reddi corpus.
units.tr: 58 He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate commanded that the body be given up.

units.la: 59 Et Iofephus cum accepisset corpus, inuoluit illud sindone pura,
units.tr: 59 And Joseph, having taken the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth.

units.la: 60 Posuitq; in monumento suo nouo quod excideRat in petra, & aduoluto saxo magno ad ostiũ monumenti, abiit.
units.tr: 60 And he laid him in his new tomb, which he had hewn out of the rock, and after rolling a great stone to the door of the tomb, he departed.

units.la: 61 Erat autem illic Maria Magdalene, & altera illa Maria, sedentes contra sepulchrum.
units.tr: 61 Now Mary Magdalene was there, and the other Mary, sitting opposite the sepulchre.

units.la: Marci 15.
units.tr: Mark 15.

units.la: 42 Quum autem serum diei iam esset (quoniam erat parasceue, hoc est ante sabbathum)
units.tr: 42 When evening had now come (because it was the Preparation, that is, the day before the sabbath),

units.la: 43 Veniens Iosephus Arimathaensis, honoratus senator, qui & ipse expectabat regnum Dei, fidenti animo introiit ad Pilatum, & petiit corpus Iesu.
units.tr: 43 Joseph of Arimathea, an honourable senator, who himself also waited for the kingdom of God, came boldly in to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.

units.la: 44 Pilatus autem miratus est si iam mortuus esset, & advocato Centurione interrogauit eum, an iamdudum mortuus fuisset.
units.tr: 44 Pilate marvelled whether he was already dead, and calling the centurion to him, he asked him whether he had been dead for some time.

units.la: 45 Et re cognita ex Centurione, donauit corpus Iosepho.
units.tr: 45 And when he learned this from the centurion, he gave the body to Joseph.

units.la: 46 Is emit sindonem, & detractum eum inuoluit sindone, depositumque in monumento quod erat excisum e petra: & aduoluit saxum ad ostium monumenti.
units.tr: 46 Joseph bought a linen cloth, took him down, wrapped him in the linen, and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock, and rolled a stone to the door of the tomb.

units.la: 47 Maria Magdelene vero & Maria mater Ioseph spectabant vbi poneretur.
units.tr: 47 But Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses watched where he was laid.

units.la: Lucæ 23.
units.tr: Luke 23.

units.la: 50 Tunc ecce quidam nomine Iosephus, senator, vir bonus ac iustus:
units.tr: 50 Behold, there was a man named Joseph, a senator, a good and just man:

units.la: 51 Qui non assensus fuerat consilio ac facto eorum, oriundus Arimathaea ciuitate Iudaeorum: qui & ipse expectabat regnum Dei.
units.tr: 51 who had not consented to their counsel or deed, a native of Arimathea, a city of the Jews, who himself also waited for the kingdom of God.

units.la: 52 Hic, inquâ, veniês ad Pilatum, petiit corpus Iesu.
units.tr: 52 This man, I say, came to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.

units.la: 53 Et detractum illud inuoluit sindone, posuitque illud in monumento quod erat in saxo incisum, in quo nondum quisquam positus fuerat.
units.tr: 53 He took it down, wrapped it in linen, and laid it in a tomb cut in the rock, in which no one had yet been laid.

units.la: 54 Porrò dies erat parasceues, & sabbathum succedebat.
units.tr: 54 Now it was the day of Preparation, and the sabbath was drawing near.

units.la: 55 Subsequutæ etiam mulieres quæ cum eo venerant ex Galilæa, spectarunt monumentum, & quomodo positum esset corpus eius.
units.tr: 55 The women also who had come with him from Galilee followed after, and looked at the tomb and how his body was laid.

units.la: 56 Reuersa vero parauerunt aromata & vnguenta, ac Sabbatho quidem quieuerunt, secundum mandatum.
units.tr: 56 And they returned and prepared spices and ointments, and on the sabbath indeed they rested, according to the commandment.

units.la: Iohannis 19.
units.tr: John 19.

units.la: 38 Post hæc autem rogauit Pilatum Ioseph Arimathæensis (vt qui esset discipulus Iesu, sed occultus propter metum Iudæorum) vt tolleret corpus Iesu: quod permisit Pilatus. Venit ergo, & sustulit corpus Iesu.
units.tr: 38 After this, Joseph of Arimathea (being a disciple of Jesus, but a secret one, for fear of the Jews) asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate permitted it. He came therefore and took away the body of Jesus.

units.la: 39 Venit autem Nicodemus (is qui venerat ad Iesum nocte primum) ferens misturam myrrhæ & aloes libras quasi centum.
units.tr: 39 And Nicodemus also came (he who had first come to Jesus by night), bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds.

units.la: 40 Acceperunt ergo corpus Iesu, & obuinxerunt illud linteis cum aromatibus, sicut mos est Iudæis sepelire.
units.tr: 40 So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the Jewish custom of burying.

units.la: 41 In eo autem loco vbi fuerat crucifixus, erat hortus, & in horto monumentum nouum, in quo nondum quisquam positus fuerat.
units.tr: 41 Now in the place where he had been crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb, in which no one had yet been laid.

units.la: 42 Ibi ergo propter parasceuen Iudæorum quod monumentum illud prope esset, posuerunt Iesum.
units.tr: 42 So there they laid Jesus, because of the Jews' Preparation, since the tomb was near at hand.

units.la: HACtenus fuit historia depositionis Christi è cruce, sequitur historia sepulturæ: vt rogatu Iudæorum depositus fuit è cruce, ita rogatu eiusdem Iosephi sublatus est ac sepultus. Primum est Iosephi descriptio, quam colligimus ex harmonia quatuor Euangelistarum. Describitur primùm à Patria sua. 1. Erat ex Arimathæa ciuitate Iudeæ. 2. A diuitiis, erat diues. 3. Ab officio, erat senator honoratus, nempe ex iis consiliariis magni illius consilij, quod Sanhedrim vocarunt. Sed quorsum externa omnia, nisi sint ipsius hominis qualitates bonæ? Quartò igitur describitur à qualitatibus iis, quæ respiciunt hanc vitam: vir bonus fuit & iustus, ac rectus in omnibus actionibus suis. Sed quid attinet ciuiliter, vt inquiut, & moraliter bonum esse, nisi quis sit pius erga Deum? Ergo quinto loco describitur à fide & spe: exspectauit enim regnum Dei: Quod nimirum inchoatum est in primo Christi aduentu, perficietur autem in altero. Cùm nulla sit spes regni Dei nisi in Christo, sto, ideo in aduentu Christi primo, se illi tanquā disci-pulū dedit: licet in eo deliquerit, quòd se discipulū Chriſti palàm profiteri nō fuerit ausus. Estq; hæc sexta descri-ptionis pars. Septimò, ab officio quodā discipuli in Ma-gistrum suum describitur. Non assensus est vel consilio vel facto eorum, qui Christū crucifixerunt: Et hic quo-que defectus fuit aliquis: Non enim satis est non assen-tiri malo, nisi etiam te opponas fortiter eidem malo: vt Nicodemum fecisse legimus, Iohan. 7. 50. cùm in concilio Pharisæorum aduersus Christum congregato responderet, An lex nostra damnat hominem indiĉta causa? Sed in Consiliariis siue Senatoribus varij solent esse defectus. Quidam enim alioqui viri boni, cùm incidit res aliqua difficilis ac periculosa, se eo consilio substrahūt: Sic enim optimè putant se liberare conscientiam suam, sed peccant: oportuit enim ex officio interesse. Melius tamen faciunt quàm hi qui inter sunt & consentiunt ei quod malum est. Alij sunt qui intersunt quidem, præterea etiam non consentiunt ei quod malum est: hi rectius faciunt. Sed adhuc aliqua re deficiuntur, nam oportuit se opponere malo. Ergo hi demum omnium sunt optimi, qui & intersunt & non consentiunt, sed opponunt sese ei quod conscientia suadet malum esse. At cosiliariorum difficilis est & periculosa conditio, præsertim in Republ. non bene costituta, & in qua principes male sunt affecti. Ego solam hanc regulam ex verbo Dei iis præscribo in tanta difficultate, vt intuentes Dominum, ac ipso cōsultore vtentes, studeant perpetuò seruare bonā cōscientiam. Præstat enim conscientia etiam assentiri ei quod malū est, quàm contra conscientiam alioqui assentiri ei quod in se bonum est. Quod enim ex fide non fit, peccatum est. Non quidē temere factum est, vt vir iste honoratus sepulturam Domini procurarit, ipsūmq; sepelierit, sed diuina prouidentia Dei accidit, non tantū vt omnino sepeliretur Dominus (si forte sese opposuissent Iudæi: nā si obscurus aliquis aut mediocris conditionis homo id tentasset, proculdubio ei opposuisset qui quærebat Dominū ignominia afficere, vt in morte, ita & in sepultura) id accidit, inquā, non tantū ideò vt sepeliretur omnino Dominus, sed vt honorabilis esset ipsius sepultura, quippe ab ho-
units.tr: Thus far was the history of Christ's taking down from the cross; the history of his burial follows: just as he was taken down from the cross at the request of the Jews, so at the request of the same Joseph he was taken away and buried. First is the description of Joseph, which we gather from the harmony of the four Evangelists. He is described first by his homeland: 1. he was from Arimathea, a city of Judea. 2. By his wealth: he was rich. 3. By his office: he was an honoured senator, namely one of those counsellors of that great council which they called the Sanhedrin. But why all these external things, unless they are the good qualities of the man himself? Fourthly, then, he is described by those qualities which concern this life: he was a good and just man, upright in all his actions. But what does it matter to be good in a civil and moral sense, as they say, unless one is also pious toward God? Therefore, fifthly, he is described by faith and hope: for he waited for the kingdom of God, which indeed began at the first coming of Christ, but will be perfected at the second. Since there is no hope of the kingdom of God except in Christ, he gave himself to Christ as a disciple at his first coming, although he sinned in this, that he did not dare to profess openly that he was Christ's disciple. This is the sixth part of the description. Seventhly, he is described by a certain duty of a disciple toward his Master. He did not consent either to the counsel or to the deed of those who crucified Christ, and here too there was some defect. For it is not enough not to assent to evil, unless you also boldly oppose the same evil, as we read Nicodemus did (John 7:50), when in the council of the Pharisees gathered against Christ he answered, "Does our law condemn a man without first hearing him?" But among counsellors or senators various defects are usually found. For some, otherwise good men, when some difficult and dangerous matter arises, withdraw from that council, for they think they thus free their conscience, but they sin, for it was their duty to take part by virtue of their office. Yet they do better than those who take part and consent to what is evil. Others take part, and moreover do not consent to what is evil; these act more rightly. But they still fall short in something, for it was necessary to oppose the evil. Therefore those are the best of all, who both take part and do not consent, but set themselves against what conscience tells them is evil. But the condition of counsellors is difficult and dangerous, especially in a commonwealth not well constituted, and where the princes are ill-disposed. In such great difficulty I prescribe to them only this rule from the word of God: that, looking to the Lord and consulting him, they strive constantly to keep a good conscience. For it is better, for conscience's sake, not to assent even to what is evil than to assent, against conscience, to what is in itself good. For whatever is not done from faith is sin. It was not by chance that this honoured man undertook the Lord's burial and buried him himself, but it came about by the divine providence of God, not only so that the Lord should be buried at all (for if perhaps the Jews had opposed it, since if some obscure or ordinary man had attempted it, without doubt they would have opposed him, as they sought to heap dishonour on the Lord both in death and in burial), this came about, I say, not only so that the Lord should be buried at all, but so that his burial should be honourable, being procured and carried out by an honourable man.

units.la: Difficilis & periculosa eorundem conditio.
units.tr: The difficult and dangerous condition of the same counsellors.

units.la: Honoratus vir procurat sepulturam Christi. norabili viro procurata & administrata. Nā etsi Domini sepultura vltimus fuerit gradus humiliationis ipsius (nā quid aliud est sepeliri & condi humo, quā mortis vinculis captiuū detineri?) tandē Deo Patre ita dispensante sepultura Domini facta est primus exaltationis ipsi9 gradus: hinc gloriosa resurrectio, hinc gloriosa in cœlos ascensio, hinc gloriosa ad Dei Patris dextrā sessio. Verūm quidē est honorē hunc sepulturæ Domini, mundanū aliquem fuisse, verūm Christo Dei Filio factus est initiū gloriæ illius cælestis, quę mundanū ritū est subsequuta. Gloria enim ista mūdi huius, iis qui in Christo Iesu sunt, initiū est ingressus ad gloriā illam cælestē ac ineffabilē. Quod si diligentibus Deum etiā ignominia cedat in gloriā, & omnia cōferunt ipsis ad bonum: quāto magis honor & gloria etiā quę mūdi huius est, cessura est in gloriā ipsorum sempiternam. Iosephus dicitur Christi corpus illud quod tū iacebat in ignominia, voluisse tollere: hauddubiō intuitus est gloriosam ipsius resurrectione, qua futurū erat vt corpus illud in specie vile & ipsum gloriosū fieret, & corpora sanctorum sibi conformia redderet. Profecto vel solus hic respectus gloriæ sanctorum futuræ in resurrectione ipsorum, nos mouere debet ad honorāda ipsorū corpora, & in vita & in morte. Petrus Apostolus, vxoribus honorē deberi admonet, vel hac de causa, no biscū futurę sint cōfortes gratię vitæ. Quod si quis apud nos destinetur ad hereditatē & regnū aliquod terrestre, eū omnes habet in honore, vtpote regē aliquādo futurū: quāto magis fieri id debet in hęrede futuro cælestis illius regni? Vasa aurea, argentea in domo alicuius viri magni in pretio sunt: quāto magis in domo Dei vasa illa gloriæ in pretio esse debēt, ad quę pertinet proprie vniuersa etiā huius mundi gloria: vt & mūdus ipse totus quantus quantus est ipsorū est. Quod autē vasa ignominiæ ista possideant vt plurimū, id fit in ira Dei, cui tādem violentæ vsurpationis reddituri sunt ratione. Dominus autem nonnisi parce mundana ista ac terrestria suis impertit, vt discant meliora ac cælestia quærere.
units.tr: An honourable man arranges Christ's burial. For although the Lord's burial was the last step of his humiliation (for what else is being buried and laid in the earth than being held captive in the bonds of death?), yet, with God the Father so ordaining, the burial of the Lord became the first step of his exaltation: hence the glorious resurrection, hence the glorious ascension into heaven, hence the glorious session at the right hand of God the Father. It is true that this honour of the Lord's burial was somewhat worldly, but for Christ the Son of God it became the beginning of that heavenly glory which followed the worldly rite. For that worldly glory is, for those who are in Christ Jesus, the beginning of entry into that heavenly and ineffable glory. And if even disgrace turns into glory for those who love God, and all things work together for good for them, how much more will honour and glory, even that of this world, turn into their everlasting glory? Joseph is said to have wished to take up that body of Christ which then lay in disgrace; without doubt he looked to its glorious resurrection, by which that body, vile in appearance, was to become glorious itself and to make the bodies of the saints conformed to it. Surely this regard alone for the future glory of the saints in their resurrection ought to move us to honour their bodies, both in life and in death. The Apostle Peter admonishes that honour be given to wives, if only for this reason, that they are fellow heirs of the grace of life. If anyone among us is destined to an inheritance and some earthly kingdom, everyone holds him in honour, as one who will one day be king; how much more ought this to be done for the heir of that heavenly kingdom? Gold and silver vessels in the house of a great man are valued; how much more should those vessels of glory be valued in the house of God, to whom properly belongs the whole glory even of this world, so that the whole world, whatever its extent, is theirs. But that the vessels of dishonour possess these things for the most part happens in the wrath of God, to whom they will at last render account for their violent usurpation. The Lord, however, bestows these worldly and earthly things on his own only sparingly, so that they may learn to seek better and heavenly things.

units.la: Hactenus de persona ipsa Iosephi, nunc sequitur ipsius factū. Cōfidēter adit Pilatū. Antea meticulosus erat, nunc audax euadit. Antea occulte discipulus fuit propter metū Iudæo{a}udeorum: nūc verò apertus abiecto omni metu. In quo discis, quàm efficax sit Dei vocatio, si quādo ei visum est quoquam extricare ex his impedimentis diuitiarū, honoris, nobilitatis, sapientiæ, &c. Fateor quidē, pauci sunt sapientes, potentes, nobiles, quos vocat Dominus. Vix legimus de viris principib9 in Iudæa vocatis à Christo, praeterquā de his nominatim Iosepho & Nicodemo. Vocat tamen aliquot ex his ipsis quos lubet, & cum lubet. Qui autē vocantur, illi quidem perquam difficulter, & quasi camelus per foramen acus, vt dixit Dominus, extrahuntur. Miretur aliquis audentiorem eum factum iam in morte Christi, qui delituit in vita Christi, quo tempore operatus est, qualia nemo ante ipsum, & loquutus est, qualiter nemo vnquam mortalium. Profectò oportuit admirabilem vim quandam inesse morti Christi, qualis & quanta non fuit in vita tota ipsius antea facta. Hanc vim mortis suæ futuram prædixit Dominus. Granum frumenti quod in terram decidit, si non mortuum fuerit, iacet solum: at si mortuum fuerit fructificat. & alibi dixit, Vbi cadaver ibi congregantur aquilæ. Hoc nimirum dixit ad ostendendum, quam efficax ad homines alliciendos ad se suaui illo odore sacrificij sui, futurus esset in morte sua. Hac igitur vi mortis Christi protinus ubiò Iosephus extractus quasi è latebris suis confidenter accessit ad Pilatum: hac quoque extractus Nicodemus è latebris suis accessit ad corpus Christi mortuum vnà cum Iosepho sepeliendum.
units.tr: Thus far concerning the person of Joseph; now follows his deed. He boldly approaches Pilate. Before, he was fearful; now he becomes bold. Before, he was secretly a disciple, for fear of the Jews; but now he is open, with all fear cast aside. In this you learn how effective the calling of God is, when it pleases him to draw someone out of these hindrances of riches, honour, nobility, wisdom, and so on. I admit that few of the wise, the powerful and the noble are called by the Lord. Scarcely do we read of men of rank in Judea being called by Christ, except these two by name, Joseph and Nicodemus. Yet he calls some of these very people whom he pleases, and when he pleases. But those who are called are drawn out with great difficulty, like a camel through the eye of a needle, as the Lord said. Let someone marvel that he who lay hidden during Christ's life became bolder in Christ's death, when he did such things as no one before him had done, and spoke as no mortal ever spoke. Surely some admirable power must have been present in the death of Christ, of a kind and a greatness that was not in the whole of his earlier life. The Lord foretold this power of his death: "A grain of wheat that falls into the ground, if it has not died, remains alone; but if it has died, it bears fruit." And elsewhere he said, "Where the carcass is, there the eagles gather." Surely he said this to show how effective, in his death, the sweet odour of his sacrifice would be for drawing men to himself. By this power of Christ's death, therefore, Joseph, as if drawn from his hiding-places, straightway and boldly approached Pilate; by this same power Nicodemus, drawn from his hiding-places, came to the dead body of Christ to bury it together with Joseph.

units.la: Sequitur petitio Iosephi. Petiit à Pilato vt liceat tollere ac sepelire corpus Domini. Vt suprà obseruauimus non nisi impetrata venia è cruce depositum esse corpus Domini: ita non est praetereundum hoc loco, quod non nisi impetrata prius venia à Pilato, sublatum sit, ac sepulturæ commissum corpus Domini. Haec commendat policiam illam Romanam: nam corpus hominis rei ac condemnati in potestate est iudicis, neque de eo quicquam fieri debet nisi consulto iudice. Notandum autem quòd in tota hac historia passionis Domini, ipse nihil de se fieri voluerit, nisi ex iure: noluit iniuriam illam in se factam in horto, ab iis qui armati erant authoritate aliqua ac potestate magistratus, noluit, inquam, iniuriam illam propulsari contra ius à Petro. Qui cum priuatus esset non debebat resistere magistratui. Noluit deinde cruce tolli nisi confulto Pilato. Hoc enim proculdubiò factum est ex voluntate ipsius Domini. Noluit denique corpus suum tradi sepulturæ nisi bona venia Pilati id fieret. Exemplo nimirum suo nos admonens ne quid de nobis permittamus fieri, quod aliquo modo possit esse alij offensioni & scandalo, efficiatque vt impingat in bo nas leges, & authoritatem ac potestatem magistratus. Sed in his videor mihi aliquid sublimius intueri, nempe oportuisse eum, quò liberaturus esset nos è potestate summi iudicis, & à summa illa iustitia, oportuisse, inquam, cum subiici terreno iudici, & terrenæ iustitiæ in omnibus. Christus enim nostra causa & agendo, & patiendo omnem iustitiam adimpleuit. Non est hic præ-tereunda Dei prouidentia, qua quidem factum est, vt neque vi, neque dolo tolleretur Christi corpus, sed bona cum venia Pilati: nimirum in eum finem, vt ex petitione ista Iosephi mors Christi innotesceret, vt patet ex proximè sequentibus verbis, & ex sepultura Christi quæ illustri ac nobili in loco fuit, ipsius resurrectio innotesceret. Atque hæ sunt duæ quasi columnæ fidei nostræ quæ est in Christum Iesum, quas semper conatus est Satan excitatis subinde hæreticis succidere: sed Deo sit gratia, stant hæ in Ecclesia Dei firmiter ad hodiernum vsque diem, hæreticis illis in inferis iamdudum sepultis.
units.tr: Next comes Joseph's request. He asked Pilate for leave to take up and bury the body of the Lord. As we observed above, the body of the Lord was taken down from the cross only after pardon was obtained; so it should not be passed over here that the body of the Lord was removed and committed to burial only after pardon had first been obtained from Pilate. This commends that Roman polity: for the body of a condemned criminal is in the power of the judge, and nothing ought to be done with it except with the judge's consent. It should be noted too that in the whole history of the Lord's passion he himself wished nothing to be done concerning himself except by right. He did not want that injury, done to him in the garden by men armed with some authority and power of the magistrate, to be repelled by Peter contrary to right. Since Peter was a private person, he ought not to resist the magistrate. Then he did not want to be taken down from the cross except with Pilate's consent; for this was certainly done by the Lord's own will. Finally, he did not want his body handed over to burial except with Pilate's good permission. He was surely admonishing us by his own example not to allow anything to be done concerning ourselves which might in some way be a stumbling-block and scandal to another, and so bring about that it strikes against good laws and the authority and power of the magistrate. But in these things I seem to see something more sublime: namely, that he had to submit to an earthly judge and to earthly justice in all things, in order that he might deliver us from the power of the supreme judge and from that supreme justice. For Christ, both by acting and by suffering on our account, fulfilled all justice. Here the providence of God must not be passed over, by which it came about that the body of Christ was removed neither by force nor by trickery, but with Pilate's good permission: surely to this end, that from this request of Joseph the death of Christ might become known, as is plain from the words that immediately follow, and that from the burial of Christ, which was in an illustrious and noble place, his resurrection might become known. And these are, as it were, two pillars of our faith, which is in Christ Jesus, and which Satan has always tried to cut down by raising up heretics from time to time. But, thanks be to God, these pillars stand firm in the Church of God to this day, those heretics having long since been buried in hell.

units.la: Pilatus autem miratus.Ex his primùm apparet quod dimus: ex hac nimirum petitione Iosephi innotuisse mortem Christi, vel ipsis inimicis: deinde illud quod etiam à nobis iam antea est obseruatum, Christi mortem extraordinariam fuisse. Nam si ordinaria fuit ac vsitata, cur miratus est Pilatus, quod præter consuetudinem crucifixorum tam cito mortuus esset? Extraordinariam hac mortem antea arguebat ipsius Christi vox tam magna illa quam emisit, quo tempore expirauit. Vt mortem extraordinariam hæc arguebant, ita arguebant Christum plusquam hominem fuisse, & in eo fuisse potentiam contrariam potentiæ huic à natura insitæ, per quam adhuc Christus multò diutiùs supereminere poterat. Arguebant, inquam, Christum Deum esse, & mortem illam
units.tr: But Pilate, marvelling. From this first appears what we said: from this very request of Joseph the death of Christ became known, even to his enemies. Then comes what we have already noted, that Christ's death was extraordinary. For if it was ordinary and usual, why did Pilate marvel that he had died so quickly, contrary to the custom with the crucified? That his death was extraordinary was shown earlier by the very great voice that Christ uttered at the time when he expired. As for his death, these things proved it extraordinary, and in the same way they proved Christ to be more than a man, and that in him there was a power contrary to the power implanted by nature, by which Christ could have far surpassed it for much longer. They proved, I say, that Christ was God, and that death...

units.la: Et re cognita.Hactenus fuit petitio Iosephi, nunc concedit Pilatus quod petiuit. Sed notandum quod non tratradat Christum in manus Iosephi, vel concedat sepultu-ram, antequam penitus resciat eum mortuum esse. Hoc ex iure Romano factum. Nam damnatus ad mortem non est trahendus è manu iudicis, antequam constet eum iam mortuum esse. Quod si sic fecerunt viridi arbori, quid fiet aridae? Quod si summo iure egerunt cum innocente, quid de nocentibus & reis futurum est in illo die vltimi iudicij Dei? Certior iam factus quod expirasset Iesus, donauit Iosepho demortui corpus. Hoc humanitatis fuit; vt credibile est ex conscientia innocentiæ Christi, quam nunquam penitus amisit Pilatus. Vtcunque est, humanitatis fuit hoc opus. Quòd si Iosepho restitit cum Caiapha Pontifice, aliis Sacerdotibus, Scribis & Pharisæis, profecto id non impetrasset tam facile. Ijenim non aliam quàm sepultura asini, vt dicitur, Domino permisissent.
