Wondrous is the obstinacy of the disciples in their unbelief, and they teach us plainly by their own example how difficult it is for a man, by nature, to believe the article of the resurrection of the dead: namely that one who has once died and departed from this life can be called back to life. Indeed this is harder to believe for those who are wiser according to the flesh than for those who do not trust so much in the wisdom of the flesh, that is, for men rather than for women. For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him. While these things were going on, other women returned again to the tomb, and as they departed, entirely unaware of what had happened to Magdalene, Jesus met them and greeted them. This story is found in the words that immediately follow.

units.la: Matthæi 28.
units.tr: Matthew 28.

units.la: 9 Vt autem proficiscebantur, vt hoc renuncia-rent discipulis eius, ecce Iesus occurrit eis, dicens, Aue: ille vero accesserunt, & prehenderunt pedes eius, & adorauerunt eum.
units.tr: 9 As they were going to tell his disciples, behold, Jesus met them, saying, "Hail!" And they came up and took hold of his feet and worshipped him.

units.la: 10 Tunc ait eis Iesus, Ne timete, abite, renun-tiate fratribus meis, vt abeant in Galilæam: illic me videbunt.
units.tr: 10 Then Jesus said to them, "Do not be afraid. Go, tell my brothers that they should go into Galilee, and there they will see me."

units.la: 11 Euntibus autem ipsis, ecce quidam ex custodia venerunt in vrbem, & renuntiarunt primaribus Sacerdotibus omnia quæ facta fuerant.
units.tr: 11 While they were on their way, behold, some of the guard came into the city and reported to the chief priests everything that had happened.

units.la: 12 Ipsi vero congregati cum senioribus, consilioque capto, numos multos dederunt militibus.
units.tr: 12 And they, gathering together with the elders and taking counsel, gave a large sum of money to the soldiers,

units.la: 13 Dicentes, Dicite, Discipuli eius noctu venerunt, & exim furati sunt nobis dormientibus.
units.tr: 13 saying, "Say that his disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep."

units.la: 14 Quod si hoc auditum fuerit apud præsidem, nos persuadebimus ei, & securos vos præstabimus.
units.tr: 14 "And if this should come to the governor's ears, we will persuade him and make you safe."

units.la: 15 Ipsi vero accepta pecunia fecerunt sicut erant edocti: & divulgatus est ille sermo apud Iudæos vsq; ad hodiernum diem.
units.tr: 15 So they took the money and did as they had been taught. And this story has been spread among the Jews until this day.

units.la: 16. Secunda apparitio Christi, nempe mulieribus. Primo loco Mariæ occurrit, quia Mariæ desiderium maximè ardens fuit. Secundo loco his mulieribus occurrit, quia proximè post Mariam Dominum desiderarunt. Tertio & postremo discipulis & Apostolis, quia domi desidentes postremi fuisse videntur tacti desiderio & studio Domini. Primis quidem desiderio primùm occurret Dominus: postremis vero desiderio postremò occurret Dominus. Bonum est tangi desiderio Domini, siue primo, siue etiam postremo loco. Sciendum autem est ideo Dominum appropinquare ad nos, quia nos priores ad eum appropinquamus, aut desideramus eum: verùm è contra ideo nos appropinquare ad Dominum, quia Dominus prior appropinquat ad nos. Quoties autem sentimus in nobis desiderium Domini, id argumento est Dominum desiderio nostri affici, & ad nos propiùs accedere. Contrà verò quoties non sentimus in nobis hoc Domini desiderium, id argumento est Dominum à nobis longius abesse. Dicens, Auete. Verbum Græcum est χαίρετε, gaudete, Domini præsentia nunquam est muta, verùm, vt ipsius præsentia gaudij plena est, ita sermone suo ministrat illud gaudium. Nam sermo Domini potens est instrumentum gaudij & salutis. Christus autem, vt est pax nostra, ita veniens ipse euangelizauit pacem. Quare magni faciendum est Christi Euangelium, quod est potentia Dei ad salutem cuiuis credenti. Illi autem accesserunt. Nempe adductae laetitia ex praesentia & sermone illo Domini: laetitiae enim sensus, qui est ex Domini praesentia & verbo, nos inuitat ad amplexus eius, efficitque illam καινωνία, ex qua rursus existit maior laetitia. Nam credentes in eum, inquit Petrus, exultamus gaudio ineffabili ac glorioso. At vero ex κοινωνία illa, quae per aspectum futura est, cum patefiet Dominus noster, erit laus, honor & gloria in saeculum. Videtur Dominus non defugisse mulierum amplexus, eare consulens imbecillitati fidei ipsarum: sic enim futurum erat, vt manibus cum tractantes, certiores fierent de resurrectione ipsius: ideoque sequitur in textu, quod iam amplexu ipsius certiores factae, ipsum adorarunt. Non est autem hoc praeter eundum quod non inuolarint statim in cruices ipsius, sed proiectae ad pedes, eos sunt amplexae. Fides quidem familiaris est, sed non cum contemptu. Coniunctio enim cum Christo est cum capite, nam Christus super omnia caput est etiam ipsi Ecclesiae. Capiti autem debetur reuerentia a corpore suo, & membris corporis: praeterea quisquis vere coniungitur cum Christo, cernit in eo eam maiestatem & gloriam, quae cogat eum ad reuerentiam, etiam dum in hac vita est, quanto magis id fiet in altera, vbi plena perfectaque reuerentia erit, cum plena perfectaque intelligentia? Ne timete. Vox est Christi ad mulieres. Amplexus hic earum videtur cum timore aliquo fuisse, qui profecto non caruit omni culpa, cum praesertim Christus eum vetuerit. Debet quidem haec fidei coniunctio esse absque metu & dubitatione (quam tamen aduersarij nobis commendant) attamen ea est Domini sanctitas, & nostra impuritas, vt necesse sit in hac vita, aliquod impedimentum interuenire, & facere, quo minus pleni sint amplexus. Remedium autem vnicum est, vox ipsa Domini, qualis est ista, Ne metuite: vel ista, Ac
units.tr: 16. The second appearance of Christ, namely to the women. He first met Mary, because her longing was most ardent. Second, he met these other women, because they came next after Mary in longing for the Lord. Third and last, he appeared to the disciples and apostles, who sat at home and seem to have been the last to be touched by the longing for and zeal for the Lord. Those first in longing are first met by the Lord; those last in longing are at last met by the Lord. It is good to be touched by the longing for the Lord, whether in the first place or even in the last. Yet we must know that the Lord comes near to us because we first come near to him or long for him; but on the contrary, we come near to the Lord because the Lord first comes near to us. Whenever we feel in ourselves a longing for the Lord, this is a sign that the Lord is moved by longing for us and draws nearer to us. On the other hand, whenever we do not feel this longing for the Lord in ourselves, this is a sign that the Lord is far from us. Saying, Hail. The Greek word is χαίρετε, rejoice. The presence of the Lord is never silent; as his presence is full of joy, so by his word he supplies that joy. For the word of the Lord is a powerful instrument of joy and salvation. Christ, who is our peace, also came and preached peace. Therefore the gospel of Christ is to be held in high esteem, for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. But they came up. Namely, they were drawn on by the joy that came from the presence and the words of the Lord. For the feeling of joy that comes from the Lord's presence and word invites us to embrace him, and it produces that [κοινωνία] fellowship, from which again arises greater joy. For Peter says, believing in him, we exult with joy unspeakable and full of glory. But from that fellowship, which will be by sight when our Lord is revealed, there will be praise, honour and glory for ever. The Lord seems not to have shunned the women's embraces, consulting in this way the weakness of their faith. For it was to happen that, by handling him with their hands, they would be made more certain of his resurrection; and therefore the text goes on to say that, now made certain by his embrace, they worshipped him. Nor should it be passed over that they did not rush straight at his feet, but, falling down at his feet, they embraced them. Faith is indeed familiar, but not with contempt. For our union with Christ is a union with the head, since Christ is head over all things, even to the Church. Reverence is owed to the head by its body and by the members of the body. Moreover, whoever is truly united with Christ sees in him that majesty and glory which compels reverence, even while in this life; how much more will this happen in the other life, where reverence will be full and perfect, together with full and perfect understanding? Do not be afraid. These are Christ's words to the women. Their embrace seems to have been accompanied by some fear, which certainly was not free from all fault, especially since Christ forbade it. This union of faith ought indeed to be without fear and doubt (which our opponents nevertheless commend to us). Yet such is the holiness of the Lord and our impurity that in this life some hindrance must intervene and prevent the embraces from being full. The only remedy, however, is the very word of the Lord, such as this, Do not fear; or this, And

units.la: Ephes. 2. 14. cedamus cum fiducia ad thronū gratiæ, vt misericordiam conse-quamur, vel alia quæuis istiusmodi, quæ passim in Scri-pturis Dei occurrit. In altera vita, in qua multo gloriosiorem & maiestate omni pleniorem cum cōspiciemus, tamen aspectus eius & coniunctio cum eo erit absque omni timore, quia materia timoris, quæ est naturæ corruptio, & vitium in nobis, non erit amplius, sed charitas Dei erga nos tum implebitur: perfecta enim charitas foras eiicit metum. Abite, annuntiate. Iam bis ab Angelis missæ sunt mulieres ad annunciandum Domini resurrectione discipulis: deinde à Domino missa est Magdalene: neque tamen crediderunt discipuli. Admirabilis Domini patientia fuit in ferenda tanta incredulitate. Admirabilis amor in fratribus appellandis, quos fere puduit Domini sui. Admirabilis cura in iis instituendis, quos emissurus erat ad docendum orbem terrarum: admirabilis sapientia in iis humiliandis pet mulieres magistras, quarum opera fuit vsurus ad eos humiliandos & adducendos sub obedientiam fidei. Non enim minus opus est doctoribus Euangelij humilitate quam cognitione. Sed videamus nunc mandatum quod acceperunt perferendum discipulis: Vt abeant, inquit, in Galilæam. In Galilæam iubet abire: non statuit quidem convenire eos in Iudæa, aut Hierosolymis. Qui eum spreverunt humiliatum in carne, iam glorificatus post resurrectionem eos vicissim spernit. Pollicetur visuros se discipulos in Galilæa, quasi dicat, Non crediderunt aliis annuntiantibus de me, ipsi suis oculis me videbunt in Galilæa. Mira est ista Domini indulgentia, qui licet ij sint infidi, tamen ipse fidus manet, negare seipsum non potest. Et cum abundat eorum peccatum, tum superabundat ipsius gratia: vt vel ij iam sua experientia docerent hoc orbem terrarum, quod dixit Apostolus: Vbi auctum est peccatum, ibi superabundauit gratia. Paulus qui hoc Romanis prædicauit, ipse prius experientia idem didicit. Nam postquam dixit alibi se blasphemum fuisse, persequutorem & iniuriosum, paulo post subiecit, Sed superabundauit gratia Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Eph. 2. 14. let us come with confidence to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy; or any other such word, which occurs everywhere in the Scriptures of God. In the other life, in which we shall see him far more glorious and fuller of all majesty, his sight and our union with him will nevertheless be without any fear, because the matter of fear, which is the corruption of nature and the vice in us, will be no more; but then God's love towards us will be fulfilled, for perfect love casts out fear. Go, tell. Already twice the women had been sent by the angels to announce the Lord's resurrection to the disciples; then the Lord sent Magdalene; yet the disciples did not believe. Admirable was the Lord's patience in bearing such unbelief. Admirable was his love in calling them brothers, whom he was almost ashamed of. Admirable was his care in instructing those whom he was about to send to teach the world; admirable his wisdom in humbling them through women as teachers, by whose work he would humble them and bring them under the obedience of faith. For the teachers of the gospel need humility no less than knowledge. But let us now see the command they received to deliver to the disciples: That they may go, he says, into Galilee. He bids them go into Galilee; he did not decide that they should meet in Judea or Jerusalem. Those who despised him when he was humbled in the flesh, now that he is glorified after the resurrection, in turn despise them. He promises that the disciples will see him in Galilee, as if to say: They did not believe others who announced me; they themselves shall see me with their own eyes in Galilee. Wonderful is this indulgence of the Lord, who, although they are faithless, yet he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself. And where their sin abounds, there his grace superabounds, so that even they, by their own experience, might teach the world what the Apostle said: Where sin has increased, there grace has superabounded. Paul, who preached this to the Romans, had first learned the same by experience. For after saying elsewhere that he had been a blasphemer, a persecutor and an insulter, he added shortly after, "But the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ superabounded."

units.la: Proficiscentibus autem ipsis. Dum haec ita geruntur, quidam
units.tr: As they were going away. While these things were thus taking place, certain men

units.la: Charitatis immensæ Domini nostri exemplum.
units.tr: An example of the immense charity of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Mandatum Christi per mulieres ad discipulos.
units.tr: Christ's command through the women to the disciples.

units.la: Dominus seipsum negare non potest.
units.tr: The Lord cannot deny himself.

units.la: 17. Impii, quoties {a}am è custodibus veniunt in ciuitatem, & principibus Sacerdotum omnia annuntiant quæ fuerant. Isti quidē, neque ab Angelo aliquo, neque à Christo ipso in vrbem cum hoc nuncio missi sunt: acti tamen speciali Dei prouidentia, venerunt ad principes Sacerdotum ista annuntiantes. Ex quibus manifestum fuit eos spe sua fuisse frustratos. Nam miserunt illi custodes resurrectionis Christi obscurandæ gratia, & per vim quasi detinendi Dominum in sepulchro: at Deus remittit eos tanquam totidem testes & nuncios eiusdem resurrectionis: neque etiam de ea testari diligentius potuerunt, si ad testificandum missent codu-cti à Sacerdotibus: vt videas frustra nitentes homines contra Deum, & laborare in iis supprimendis, quæ ipse, vt in lucem veniant iam olim decreuit. Sunt quidem isti eiusdem veritatis præcones, cuius eram ante eos mulieres, sed non eodem modo, neque eodem animo annuntiant idem. Mulieres quidem læto animo annuntiarunt discipulis Christi lætum illud nuncium: at illi sacerdotibus lætum nuntium annunciant ammo tristi. Sunt enim qui rerum alioqui lætarum nonnisi tristes sunt præcones: contraque iidem illi rerum quoque tristium præcones exist-unt læti, prout ipsis arridet non arridet ea quæ annuntiant. Metiuntur enim non ex rerum ipsarum natura, sed ex suo ipsorum perfo affectu. Quare videat quisque, quomodo & quoties noua illa, quæ sunt de Ecclesiæ huius militantis, apud alios commemoret, siue bona ea, siue mala. Videant autem præcones Euangelij Christi vt læto animo lætum hoc nuncium de Christo & pace illa quæ omnibus annuncient. Tunc coacti. Audito hoc nuncio sacerdotes, quid faciunt? 1. Concilium cum Consilio capto redimunt sibi copiosa pecunia linguas militum ad impudenter mentiendum. Mendacium autem habetur his verbis: Dicite, inquiunt, Discipuli eius nocte venerunt, &c. Tum ne metu supplicij recurarent conditionem milites, pollicentur se persuasuros præsidi & securos ipsos præstituros. Proculdubio audito hoc nuncio coepit eos pudere. Qui enim luctantur cum Deo pudefient tandem. Penes nos est pudor faciei, quia peccauimus, inquit Propheta. At pudorem hunc fa-
units.tr: 17. The wicked, as often as some of the guards come into the city and announce to the chief priests everything that had happened. Indeed, these men were sent into the city with this news neither by any angel nor by Christ himself; yet, driven by a special providence of God, they came to the chief priests and announced these things. From this it was clear that they had been disappointed in their hope. For those guards had been sent to obscure the resurrection of Christ, and to hold the Lord, as it were by force, in the sepulchre; but God sends them back as so many witnesses and messengers of the same resurrection, nor could they have testified about it more carefully had they been sent to bear witness at the priests' hire. Thus you may see men struggling in vain against God, and labouring to suppress those things which he himself had long ago decreed should come to light. These men are indeed heralds of the same truth of which the women were before them, but they do not announce it in the same way, nor with the same spirit. The women indeed announced the joyful news to Christ's disciples with a glad heart; but these men announce the joyful news to the priests with a sad heart. For there are some who are only sad heralds of things otherwise joyful, and on the contrary, the same men are glad heralds of sad things, as the things they announce please or displease them. For they measure not by the nature of the things themselves, but by their own disposition. Let each one therefore consider how and how often he relates those new things which concern this militant Church, to others, whether they be good or evil. Let the heralds of the gospel of Christ consider that they should announce this joyful news about Christ and that peace which is for all, with a glad heart. Then they were compelled. When the priests heard this news, what do they do? First, they take counsel and with the council they buy the tongues of the soldiers with a large sum of money, so that they may lie shamelessly. The lie is contained in these words: "Say," they say, "that his disciples came by night, etc." Then, lest the soldiers should take care of their own condition for fear of punishment, they promise that they will persuade the governor and make them safe. Without doubt, when this news was heard, they began to be ashamed. For those who wrestle with God will at last be put to shame. "Shame of face is ours, because we have sinned," says the Prophet. But this shame ...

units.la: Deus vult, aduersus seipsos iuste potentiæ diuinæ testes.
units.tr: God wills that they, rightly, become witnesses against themselves to the divine power.

units.la: Frustra resistunt, Deo, quanuis malo animo deeius operibus garriant.
units.tr: They resist God in vain, although with a malicious mind they chatter about his works.

units.la: Eorundem malignitas.
units.tr: The malice of the same men.

units.la: Sacerdotes, sibi ipsis & pleculæ tur piter & diabolico prorsus animo imponunt. ciei velant, mendacio quasi obducto, ne à populo con-spiciatur, militumque operam ad mendacium hoc ob-ducendum sibi redimunt. Pudor faciei debet quidé nos deducere ad facti pœnitentiam, & peccati confessionē: at qui semel cœperunt peccare in Spiritum Dei sanctū; & in ipsum minet Deum immediatè peccare, ij fere pœ-nitere nesciunt, neque pedem possunt retrahere: verum semper complent peccata sua, quia ira Dei occupauit eos ad ex-tremum usque. Vos semper Spiritui sancto obnitimini, inquit Stephanus. Horribile istud tantæ cōtumaciæ Iudæorum exemplum, debet nobis omnibus documento esse im-perpetuum. Ipsi vero accepta. Ementibus eas Sacerdotibus vendunt linguas suas milites isti ad splendidum & im-pudens mendacium conflandum. Causa erat quia pro-phani erant. Primùm ex gentibus erant, quæ sine Deo in mundo vixerunt; deinde milites erant, quorum rara est pietas ac fides. Prophanus quisque venalem habet linguam, manum, pedem, denique ipsum animum. Pro-fanus Esau vnico edulio vendidit ius suum primogeni-ti. Et cur? quia prophanus. Emptiones & venditiones istæ linguarum & conscientiarū, quæ passim apud nos viget in quacunque hominum conditione, satis indicant nihil subesse præter magnam animorum prophanitatē. Quā-obrem quisquis cupit bonam retinere conscientiam, is studeat sanctificationi: qua quidem retenta in animo, retinetur pariter conscientia: qua verò amissa, amittitur simul conscientia. Et diuulgatus est. Mendacium hoc quod fecerunt isti aduersus resurrectionem Christi, & latè sparsum est per Iudæos, & diu durauit. Ergo si non pri-mo illo conatu sacerdotum obscurata sit Christi resur-rectio, saltem secundo id contigit. Quæ succedunt im-piis aduersus Deum, ego in victoriis nunquam posuero: successus enim sunt infelices. Sed quæ ista victoria, cū & interea manserit hæc persuasio resurrectionis Christi in cordibus piorum, & maneat etiam ac duret in Eccle-sia eadem illa persuasio in hodiernum usque diem? Ta-dem enim vincet veritas. Sed mirum est Iudæos tam ci-tò fidem habuisse mendacio tam splendido & futili. Si surreptum est & furto sublatum corpus Christi mortuū, à quibus est id factū? An à discipulis ipsius? An id credi-bile bile est, timidos aliquot homunciones & inermes, contra Pilatum, contra Cæsarem ipsum, contra Iudæos, contra armatos milites tentasse tam audax facinus? At dormientibus custodibus hoc facinus perpetratum. Sanè securè tum est dormitum in tanto strepitu, quantum oportuit esse in devoluendo tanto lapide. Sed finge dormiuisse, cur non ij fures illos sunt persequuti statim ex somno tam profundo excitati? Quod profecto fuisset factum, si clam loblatū fuisset corpus Christi. Sed quid dicas? Quotquot amorem veritatis non recipiūt, & proinde pereunt, ij leuissimis & futilissimis quibusq; mendaciis inducuntur ad credendum. Antichristi aduentus est ex efficacia Sathanæ cum omni potentia & signis ac prodigiis mendacibus, & cum omni fraude in iis qui pereunt, proeo quod amorem veritatis non receperunt, ut salui fierent.
units.tr: The priests, for their own advantage and with a thoroughly devilish mind, impose on themselves and on the people. They cover the shame of their face with a lie, as if it were drawn over, so that they will not be seen by the people, and they buy the soldiers' service to spread this lie. Shame of face ought indeed to lead us to repent of the deed and to confess the sin. But those who have once begun to sin against the Holy Spirit, and who, as it were, sin against God himself immediately, almost never know how to repent, and cannot draw back their foot. Rather, they always fill up their sins, because the wrath of God has seized them to the very end. You always resist the Holy Spirit, says Stephen. This dreadful example of the obstinacy of the Jews ought to be an everlasting lesson to us all. But they received payment. These soldiers sell their tongues to the priests, who buy them, to fabricate a splendid and shameless lie. The reason was that they were profane. First, they were of the Gentiles, who lived without God in the world; then they were soldiers, among whom piety and faith are rare. Every profane person has a tongue, a hand, a foot, and finally his very mind for sale. Profane Esau sold his birthright for a single meal. And why? Because he was profane. These buyings and sellings of tongues and consciences, which flourish everywhere among us in every condition of men, sufficiently show that there is nothing beneath them except great profanity of mind. Therefore whoever wishes to keep a good conscience should strive for sanctification: if this is kept in the mind, the conscience is kept too; but if it is lost, the conscience is lost at the same time. And it was spread abroad. This lie that these men told against the resurrection of Christ was widely spread among the Jews and lasted a long time. So if the resurrection of Christ was not obscured by the first attempt of the priests, it was at least obscured by the second. I will never count as victories the successes that impious men win against God; for such successes are unhappy. But what victory is this, when meanwhile this persuasion of Christ's resurrection has remained in the hearts of the godly, and that same persuasion remains and endures in the Church up to the present day? For in the end the truth will prevail. But it is remarkable that the Jews so quickly believed a lie so splendid and so flimsy. If the dead body of Christ was snatched away and stolen, by whom was it done? By his disciples? Is it credible that a few timid and unarmed little men attempted so bold a deed against Pilate, against Caesar himself, against the Jews, against armed soldiers? But it is said the deed was done while the guards were asleep. Surely they slept soundly in such a great commotion as must have accompanied the rolling away of so great a stone. But suppose they had slept: why did they not pursue those thieves, roused immediately from such deep sleep? That would certainly have happened if the body of Christ had been carried off secretly. But what do you say? All who do not receive the love of the truth, and therefore perish, are led to believe the lightest and most flimsy lies. The coming of Antichrist is by the working of Satan, with all power and lying signs and wonders, and with all deceit among those who perish, because they did not receive the love of the truth, so that they might be saved.

units.la: Marci 16.
units.tr: Mark 16.

units.la: 12 Posteà autem duobus ex ipsis ambulantibus apparuit alia forma, quum rus proficiscerentur.
units.tr: 12 Afterwards he appeared in another form to two of them as they were walking, when they were going into the country.

units.la: 13 Et illi abierunt, & annunciauerunt reliquis qui nec illis quidem crediderunt.
units.tr: 13 And they went and reported it to the rest, who did not believe them either.

units.la: Lucæ 24.
units.tr: Luke 24.

units.la: 13 Et ecce duo ex ijs ibant eo ipso die in vicum distantem stadiis sexaginta ab Hierusalem, cui vico nomen est Emmaus.
units.tr: 13 And behold, two of them were going that same day to a village about sixty furlongs from Jerusalem, called Emmaus.

units.la: 14 Et colloquebantur inter se de istis omnibus quæ euenerant.
units.tr: 14 And they talked together about all these things that had happened.

units.la: 15 Et factum est dum colloquerentur, & se mutuo rogarent, ipse Iesus accederet & vnà iter faceret cum ipsis.
units.tr: 15 And it came to pass, while they talked and questioned one another, that Jesus himself drew near and went with them.

units.la: 16 Oculi autem eorum tenebantur, ne ipsum agnoscerent.
units.tr: 16 But their eyes were held, so that they did not recognise him.

units.la: 17 Dixit autem eis, Qui sunt hi sermones quos conseritis inter vos ambulates? & quid estis tristes vultu?
units.tr: 17 And he said to them, "What are these words you exchange with one another as you walk? And why are you sad in countenance?"

units.la: 18 Respondens autem alter cui nomen Cleopas dixit ei, Tu solus commoraris Hierosolyma, & non nosti quae in ea facta sunt his diebus?
units.tr: 18 And one of them, named Cleopas, answered and said to him, "Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?"

units.la: 19 Ipse vero dixit eis, Quae? At illi dixerunt ei, Quae facta sunt Iesu Nazareno, qui fuit Propheta, potens reipsa & verbis, coram Deo & toto populo.
units.tr: 19 And he said to them, "What things?" And they said to him, "The things concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a prophet, mighty in deed and word before God and all the people."

units.la: 20 Quomodo eum tradiderunt principes Sacerdotum & Magistratus nostri ut morte damnaretur, & crucifixerunt eum.
units.tr: 20 "How the chief priests and our rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him."

units.la: 21 Nos autem sperabamus illum esse qui redempturus esset Israelem: atqui praeter haec omnia, tertium hunc diem agit hodie ex quo haec facta sunt.
units.tr: 21 "But we hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel. Indeed, besides all this, today is the third day since these things happened."

units.la: 22 Sed & mulieres quaedam ex nobis perculerant nos, quae diluculo venerunt ad monumentum:
units.tr: 22 "But certain women of our company also astonished us, who came early to the tomb,"

units.la: 23 Et non inuento eius corpore venerunt, dicentes se etiam apparitionem Angelorum vidisse, qui dicunt eum vivere.
units.tr: 23 "and did not find his body; and they came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels, who say that he is alive."

units.la: 24 Et abierunt quidam eorum qui erant nobiscum, ad monumentum, & ita invenerunt prout mulieres dixerant, ipsum vero non viderunt.
units.tr: 24 "And some of those who were with us went to the tomb, and found it just as the women had said, but they did not see him."

units.la: 25 Tum ipse dixit eis, O amentes & tardi corde ad credendum omnibus quae loquuti sunt Prophetae!
units.tr: 25 Then he said to them, "O foolish men, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken!"

units.la: 26 Nonne haec oportuit pati Christum, & introire in gloriam suam?
units.tr: 26 "Ought Christ not to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?"

units.la: 27 Et exorsus a Mose & omnibus Prophetis, interpretabatur illis in omnibus Scripturis quae de se scripta erant.
units.tr: 27 And beginning from Moses and all the Prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.

units.la: 28 Appropinquarunt igitur vico in quem proficiscebantur, & ipse simulabat se longius ire.
units.tr: 28 So they drew near to the village to which they were going, and he made as if he would go farther.

units.la: 29 Sed & ipsi adegerunt eum dicentes, Mane nobiscum, quoniam aduesperascit, & inclinauit dies. Ingressus est igitur vt maneret cum eis.
units.tr: 29 But they urged him, saying, "Stay with us, for it is towards evening and the day is now far spent." So he went in to stay with them.

units.la: 30 Et factum est cum accubuisset cum eis, sumpto pane benedixit, & fractum porrexit eis.
units.tr: 30 And it came to pass, when he had sat down at table with them, that he took bread, blessed it, and broke it, and gave it to them.

units.la: 31 Aperti sunt autem eorum oculi, & agnouerunt eum, sed ipse ablatus est ex eorum conspectu.
units.tr: 31 Then their eyes were opened and they recognised him, but he vanished from their sight.

units.la: 32 Tum alter ad alterum dixerunt, Nonne cor nostrum ardebat in nobis dum loqueretur nobis in via, & dum aperiret nobis Scripturas?
units.tr: 32 Then they said to one another, "Did not our heart burn within us while he talked with us on the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?"

units.la: 33 Et surgentes eo ipso momento, reuersi sunt Hierosolymam, & inuenerunt congregatos illos vndecim, & eos qui cum ipsis erant;
units.tr: 33 And they rose up that very hour, returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them,

units.la: 34 Et qui dicebant, Suscitatus est Dominus vere, & conspectus est Simoni.
units.tr: 34 who said, "The Lord has truly risen, and has appeared to Simon."

units.la: 35 Tum ipsi exposuerunt eis quae gesta erant in via, & vt fuerat a se agnitus in fractione panis.
units.tr: 35 Then they related what had happened on the way, and how he had been recognised by them in the breaking of bread.

units.la: Redimus nunc ad testes resurrectionis Christi sanctiores, quàm fuerunt custodes illi de quibus proximè. Eo ipso die quo resurrexit Dominus, ea gesta sunt quae diximus de aliis testibus quibuscunque. Duo discipuli quidem non erant e numero undecim Apostolorum; ex iis enim nominatur vnus Cleopas, alterius nomen supprimitur. Duo hi discipuli ibant in vicum quendam distantem stadiis sexaginta ab vrbe Hierusalem, hoc est miliaribus septem cum dimidio. Vicoautem nomen erat Emmaus. Ibant hi duo desperantes propemodum de redemptione per Christum futura, vt apparet ex sequentibus: ex quo discimus quanta sit Domini gratia, qui non modo non quaerentes se, sed deserentes se, & prope desperabundos praeuenit gratia sua. Quisquis enim inuenit Dominum, is inuenit eum ex gratia ipsius mera. Quidam enim sunt non qui quaerunt eum: quidam sunt qui fugiunt ab eo: Qui autem cum quaerunt, non recte id faciunt, vt
units.tr: We now return to witnesses of Christ's resurrection who are holier than those guards mentioned just before. On the very day the Lord rose, the things we have described happened, with other witnesses of every kind. Indeed the two disciples were not among the eleven apostles; for one of them is named as Cleopas, while the name of the other is suppressed. These two disciples were going to a village about sixty stadia from the city of Jerusalem, that is, about seven and a half miles. The village was called Emmaus. These two were walking, almost despairing of the redemption to come through Christ, as appears from what follows. From this we learn how great the grace of the Lord is, who anticipates with his grace not only those who do not seek him but those who flee from him, and those who are almost in despair. For whoever finds the Lord finds him by his pure grace. For there are some who do not seek him, and some who flee from him; but those who do seek him do not do so rightly, as

units.la: Eo ipso die quo resurrexit Dominus, ea gesta sunt quae diximus. mulieres illæ, quibus hoc exprobrauit Angelus, quòd viuentem inter mortuos quæsiuerint. Sed quotusquisque est, qui quærit ac desiderat secundum illum Domini aduentum? Vt appareat perpaucos habere primitias illas Spiritus sancti, quibus fit vt suspirantes apud se, expectent adoptionem suam, redemptionem corporis sui.
units.tr: On the very day the Lord rose, the things we have described took place. Those women, whom the angel rebuked because they sought the living among the dead. But how few are there who seek and long for that coming of the Lord? So it is clear that very few have those first fruits of the Holy Spirit, by which, groaning within themselves, they wait for the adoption and the redemption of their body.

units.la: Et colloquebatur Hactenus fuit iter, nunc sermones collati in itinere, sunt. Ex quibus conspicitur in illis semen aliquod pietatis & fidei reliquum fuisse, quo sustentati sunt, & quasi supernatarunt, ne penitus in desperationis illo gurgite submergerentur. Quo enim tempore suos deserere videtur Dominus, tamen interea non prorsus destituit eos omni gratia sua, qua sustententur, tantisper dum ipse propius accedes admoueat manum suam salutarem ad eos eripiendos ac liberandos. Et factum est. Disputatio ista & suscitatio non ex malitia aliqua, neque ex curiositate profecta est. Verum ex studio cognoscendi. Huiusmodi autem hæsitationi succurrere solet Dominus. Ipse Iesus accessit. Decet quidem bonos, pios & honestos sermones conferre: nescimus enim quam prope abest Dominus, imo scimus præsentem esse. A cuius præsentia tatum abesse debet ab eo vt abhorreamus, (vt ij qui male sibi conscij obleLtant se malis, siue sermonibus, siue actionibus) abhorreamus, inquâ, ab eius præsentia, vt e contrà eam requiramus potius, & precibus expetamus, ad hoc, vt nos, nostras cogitationes, nostros sermones omnes velit sanctificare: Nulla enim gratia est, nulla lux præter eam, quæ procedit a facie Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Nihil autem bene sanctèque geri potest a quoquam in vita, præterquam ab eo qui ambulat coram eo: hoc est ita ambulat, ac si eum habeat perpetuo præsentem: vt & re ipsa præsens est perpetuò, siue id quis sentiat animo & cogitatione, siue minus id sentiat. Ambulare enim coram Deo, est non tantum habere eum testem vitæ nostræ quasi occulatum: sed etiam testem videre & cogitare animo. Occulti autem. Marcus in suo Euangelio, dicit apparuisse Christum his duobus alia forma. Lucas hic aperte docet non ideo aliam fuisse formam, quod re ipsa mutata sit Domini forma, sed quòd oculi ipsorum tenerentur, ne agnoscerent eum talem, qualis tum erat re ipsa. Mutatio igitur hæc de qua loquitur Marcus nō fuit in ipso, sed in oculis ipsorum. Qua autem forma apparuerit iis nonest expressum. Verisimile autem est apparuisse Dominum forma viatoris, lumbos habens lucciņctos, & baculum manu tenēs: qui mos fuit Iudæorum iter aliquod ingredientium, vt cùm apparuit Magdalenæ erat am habitu & cultu hortulani cuiusdam. An autem reipsa Dominus tum vestibus fuerit indutus non disputo: Constat autem apparuisse eum iis non nisi vestitum, nudum autem ex mortuis resurrexisse eum certum est. Sed vt ista missa faciamus, videmus quod licet oculi & aures cum ipsorum functionibus in cernendo, audiendo, internoscendo a natura sint, tamen ita à natura sint, vt penes Dominum & authorem naturæ sit ipsa natura, qui eam mutat & inuertit pro arbitratu suo, ad hoc vt discamus nos & emēdicare ab eo eas functiones, vt alias aliorum sensuum & membrorum, corporis omnes, & pro acceptis gratias ei agere perpetuas. Quod si fūctiones sensuum nobis sint sic emendicandæ, ac si in natura non essent omnino, & pro Dei beneficiis habendæ: quantò magis functiones animi puræ sanctæque quæ in natura non sunt, imò naturæ sunt contrariæ, à nobis emendicandæ sunt à Deo & beneficiorum Dei loco habendæ? Animalis homo nō est capax eorum quæ sunt Spiritus Dei: quod si igitur datum fuerit nobis intelligere spiritualia, quantum est illud beneficium?
units.tr: And he talked with them. So far there was the journey; now comes the conversation held on the way. From it we see that some seed of piety and faith remained in those men, by which they were sustained and, as it were, kept afloat, so that they were not wholly sunk in the abyss of despair. For at the very time when the Lord seems to forsake his own, he nevertheless does not utterly leave them destitute of his grace, by which they are upheld, until he draws near and stretches out his saving hand to rescue and free them. And it came to pass. This disputation and questioning arose from no malice and no idle curiosity, but from a desire to know. The Lord is accustomed to come to the aid of such doubting. Jesus himself drew near. It is indeed fitting for good, pious and honest men to talk together, for we do not know how near the Lord is; rather, we know that he is present. Given that he is present, we ought to shrink from his presence, as those who are conscious of evil do, who burden themselves with evil words or deeds. Rather, we should seek his presence and ask for it in prayer, so that he may sanctify us, our thoughts and all our words. For there is no grace and no light apart from that which proceeds from the face of our Lord Jesus Christ. Nothing in life can be done well and holily by anyone except by one who walks before him, that is, who walks as if he had him always present, since in fact he is always present, whether a man feels it in mind and thought or feels it less. For to walk before God is not only to have him as a witness of our life, as if he were watching, but also to see the witness and to think of him in the mind. But their eyes were held. Mark, in his Gospel, says that Christ appeared to these two in another form. Luke here plainly teaches that the form was not other because the Lord's form was really changed, but because their eyes were held, so that they did not recognise him as he really was at that time. The change of which Mark speaks, then, was not in him but in their eyes. In what form he appeared to them is not stated. It is likely, however, that the Lord appeared in the form of a traveller, with his loins girded and a staff in his hand, which was the custom of the Jews when setting out on a journey, just as he appeared to Magdalene in the dress and garb of a gardener. Whether the Lord was in fact clothed with garments at that time I do not dispute; it is agreed that he appeared to them only clothed, but it is certain that he rose from the dead naked. But, setting these matters aside, we see that although the eyes and ears, with their functions of seeing, hearing and discerning, are by nature, nevertheless they are so by nature that the nature itself is in the power of the Lord and author of nature, who changes and turns it at his pleasure. This is so that we may learn to beg from him the functions of these senses, as of the other senses and members of the body, and always to give him thanks for what we receive. If the functions of the senses must be begged of him in this way, as if they were not in nature at all and were to be counted as God's benefits, how much more must the functions of the soul, pure and holy, which are not in nature but are even contrary to nature, be begged from God and counted as benefits of God? The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; if therefore it has been given to us to understand spiritual things, how great a benefit that is!

units.la: Dixit autem. Sequitur colloquium Christi & duorum discipulorum. Primùm autem sermonē exorditur Christus, quæritq; de rebus duabus. 1. De sermonibus, quos conWulerunt inter eundum. 2. De dolore animi, qui se in vultu eorum tetrico illo ac tristi prodidit. Ex dolore apparet sermones eos tristes fuisse, non autem lætos, quales nimirū solent esse eorū, qui tristia & ingrata inter se communicant. Ergo tristibus & lamentatibus superuenit Christus. Beati qui lugent, quoniā ipsi consolatione accipient. Doluerunt, fateor, abs re & sine iusta causa: sed præstat dolere propter Christum in re etiam læta, quàm lætari in re aliqua tristi. Discimus enim isto in loco Christum consolatum esse duos hos viatores, licet etiā abs re & fine causa lamentantes offenderit. Obseruandum deinde de Christo, quod vltro quaeuit cau-sum tri-stitiae ipsorum. Non expectat Dominus dum nos prio-res exonereimus curam ac solicitudinem nostram in eius sinum: verum ipse nos prior ad id inuitat ac prouocat, Venite, inquit,ad me omnes, qui fatigati & onerati estis, & ego faciam vt requiescatis. Non tantum inuitat nos verbo, sed & opere ipso nos trahit: Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater qui misit me traxerit eum ipsum, inquitChristus. Tu solus commorans. Profecto non sine causa reprehendit eum Cleopas, quem habuit pro ignoto.
units.tr: And he said. There follows the conversation of Christ with the two disciples. Christ first begins the talk and asks about two things: (1) about the discussions they had held as they went; (2) about the grief of mind that showed itself in the gloomy and sad look on their faces. From the grief it appears that their talk was sad and not cheerful, as is usually the case with those who share sad and unwelcome matters with one another. So Christ came upon them while they were sorrowing and lamenting. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. They grieved, I admit, without cause and without a just reason; yet it is better to grieve for Christ even in a matter that is happy, than to rejoice in some matter that is sad. For in this place we learn that Christ comforted these two travellers, even though he found them lamenting without reason and without cause. Next we should observe concerning Christ that he of his own accord sought out the cause of their sadness. The Lord does not wait until we first unburden the care and anxiety of our hearts into his bosom; rather, he himself invites and provokes us first. Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest, he says. He does not only invite us by word, but also draws us by the work itself: No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him, says Christ. Art thou only a stranger? Surely Cleopas did not rebuke him without cause, when he took him to be a stranger. For it is not fitting, when the works of God are so plain, that anyone should be ignorant of them, and that men should be blind, as they say, in broad daylight. For the enlightenment of some is wonderful, and again the blinding of others is wonderful. And as God is wonderful in his mercy towards his own, so he is also wonderful in his justice towards the reprobate. For the Lord is wonderful in every way.

units.la: Nam non decet, cum vsqueadeo manifesta sunt Dei opera, quemquam eorum esse ignarum, & in meridiana, vt dicitur, luce cacutire homines. Etenim illuminatio quorundam est admirabilis: & rursus quorundam excaecatio admirabilis est. Utque Deus admirabilis est in misericordia sua erga suos, ita quoque admirabilis est in iustitia sua erga reprobos. Omnibus enim modis admirabilis est Dominus. Dixit ijs, Quo? Adhuc persistit Dominus in sancta dissimulatione, pergitque vrgere ac inducere eos vt exonerent curam illam animi. Nam suos etiam reluctantes non statim deserit, verum iterum atque iterum ad se trahit: & si nos infidi simus, ipse fidelis manet, seipsum abnegare non poterit, id est, semper sui similis persistit. Quae facta sunt. Postea quam Cleopas reprehendit Christum, quasi peregrinum, ignarum rerum tam manifestarum, nunc eum docet quodammodo & instituit in iis quae ad Christum pertinent. Sed haec verba ipsi tantum extorta sunt, secreta quadam Christi operatione, qui cum trahit suos ac prouocat ad exonerandum in se curam ac sollicitudinem animi sui, tandem vincit, quia intus agit, atque in nobis efficax est. Immutat quoque impios ac prouocat trahitque eos, sed non sequuntur. Nihil ex iis boni extorquet, quia foris tantum trahit eos, per externos hos sensus, aures, oculos, &c. Sed diligentius expendenda sunt verba. Primum proponit ea quae facta sunt superioribus illis diebus, facta esse Iesu Nazareno: Deinde Iesum describit: Tertio, quae facta sunt in eum exponit. Postremo, factorum illorum quis fuerit effectus in discipulis ipsius, docet.
units.tr: And he said unto them, What manner of communications are these? The Lord still persists in holy dissimulation and goes on urging and leading them to unburden that care of mind. For he does not immediately forsake his own, even when they resist, but again and again draws them to himself. And if we are faithless, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself, that is, he always continues like himself. The things which are come to pass. After Cleopas rebuked Christ as a stranger, ignorant of such plain matters, now he in some measure teaches and instructs him about the things that pertain to Christ. But these words were drawn out of him only by a secret work of Christ, who, when he draws his own and provokes them to unload the care and anxiety of their minds upon him, at last prevails, because he works inwardly and is effective within us. He also changes the impious and provokes and draws them, but they do not follow. He wrings nothing good out of them, because he draws them only from outside, through these external senses, ears, eyes and so on. But the words must be weighed more carefully. First, he sets forth the things that were done in those past days, and that they were done to Jesus of Nazareth. Second, he describes Jesus. Third, he sets out what was done to him. Last, he teaches what effect those deeds had on his disciples.

units.la: Opera Dei nobis cognita esse debent.
units.tr: The works of God ought to be known to us.

units.la: Christus suos vrget vt postea soluetur.
units.tr: Christ urges his people, so that he may afterwards be released.

units.la: Cleopas exponit ea quae Christo paulo ante acciderant.
units.tr: Cleopas sets out what had happened to Christ a little before.

units.la: Summa & partes huius expositionis.
units.tr: The sum and parts of this exposition.

units.la: Quod ad propositionem, Nazarenū vocat deceptus cōmuni illo vulgi errore, à quo, propterea quòd Iesus educatus fuisset Nazarethæ cum Iosepho & Maria matre, existimabatur non tantùm natum eum Nazarethæ, sed etiam Iosephi fuisse filium. Non nego equidem vocarum quoque ab Apostolis Nazarenū, vt à Petro Act. 4.10. à Paulo Act. 26.9. sed ij sic loquuti sunt longè a lo sensu atque animo, non quidem ex errore vulgi, sed ad captum vulgi, qui eum ex eo potissimum nomine habebant cognitum. Iidem autem discipuli duo Nazarethæ cum vulgo putarunt eum natū esse: vt videas quid sit vulgus hominum ac multitudinem sequi in negotio religionis: & verè Ecclesiæ tanquam certam quandam notam constituere multitudidem. Sed ad descriptionē venio: Virum Prophetam vocat primùm: in quo non erauit: Nam & vir fuit Dominus & Propheta, sed nō tantùm vir, vt Cleopas de eo sensisse videtur: nam non Deum, sed Diuinum quendā hominem opinatū fuisse cum verisimile est. Neque tantū Propheta fuit, sed & Rex & Sacerdos maximus: ex quibus officiis nō satis cognitū eum fuisse Cleopæ apparet. Secundò, potentē dicit sermonibus & operibus: & rectè quidē, si potentiam illam & Spiritum illum per quem & loquebatur & operabatur, ipsius Christi Spiritū existimasset. Nā hoc discrimen fuit inter Christū & alios, qui ante eū erant, Prophetas: ipsi vt serui totidem per Christi Spiritū & loquuti sunt & operati, idque in Christi nomine & authoritate. At verò Christus vt Filius & Dominus in domo Dei per suū ipsius Spiritū, & loquutus est & operatus, suo etiam nomine atq; authoritate: vnde cùm alij Prophetæ dicant, Dominus hoc dicit: Christus ait, Amen, amen dico vobis. Quasi dicat, Ego dico meo ipsius nomine, nō tantū Patris. Sed hoc à Cleopa tum ignoratūest, qui putauit eū lūtaxat in albo aliorū Prophetarum fuisse, & aliis simi- lem, etsi fortassis aliis excellentiore (coram Deo.) Hoc testiū est in descriptione; quasi dicat, eū approbatū fuisse à Deo & ab hominibus. Rectè quidē hoc quoque: Nem nemo vnquam Angelorum, nedūm hominum ea approbationem & illud nomen accepit à Deo, quod Christus accepit, Quo filius est nominatus? Cui dixit
units.tr: As to the proposition, he calls him "the Nazarene" because he was deceived by that common error of the crowd. Since Jesus had been brought up at Nazareth with Joseph and Mary his mother, people supposed that he was not only born at Nazareth but was also the son of Joseph. I do not deny that the Apostles too called him the Nazarene, as Peter in Acts 4.10 and Paul in Acts 26.9. But they spoke in that way far from this meaning and intention. They did not do so from the crowd's error, but to suit the crowd's understanding, since the crowd knew him chiefly by that name. Yet these same two disciples of Nazareth thought with the crowd that he had been born there. You may see from this what the crowd of men is, and how much it is to be followed in matters of religion; and indeed the Church, the multitude, is set up as a kind of certain mark of the Church. But I come to the description. First he calls him "a prophet, a man," and in this he was not wrong. For the Lord was both a man and a prophet, but not only a man, as Cleopas seems to have thought. For it is probable that he thought of him not as God but as some divine man. Nor was he only a prophet, but also the great King and Priest; and from these offices it appears that Cleopas did not know him well enough. Second, he says that he was mighty in word and deed. And he was right, if only he had thought that the power and the Spirit by whom he spoke and worked were the Spirit of Christ himself. For this was the difference between Christ and the prophets who came before him: they, as servants, both spoke and worked by the Spirit of Christ, and that in the name and authority of Christ. But Christ, as the Son and Lord in the house of God, both spoke and worked by his own Spirit, and also in his own name and authority. Hence, whereas the other prophets say, "The Lord says this," Christ says, "Amen, amen, I say to you." It is as if he were saying, "I speak in my own name, not only the Father's." But Cleopas did not then know this. He thought that Christ was only one on the roll of the other prophets, and like them, though perhaps more excellent than they, "before God." This bears witness in the description, as if he were saying that he was approved by God and by men. This too is rightly said. For no one of the angels, let alone of men, ever received that approval and that name from God which Christ received: by what name was he given as Son? To whom did he say

units.la: Iesus, vir Propheta. vnquam Angelorum, Filius meus es, ego genui te hodie? Quod vero ad populum attinet, licet neque verbo neque etiā facto à multitudine Iudæorum sit approbatus, tamen conscientiis eorum approbatus est. Vnde extiterunt nō- nunquam hæ aut his similes aliquæ voces: Ab omni æuo non est auditum aliquem aperuisse oculos eius qui cæcus natus fuerit. Et alibi, Nunquam ita loquutus est homo, vt homo iste. Sed illam Dei & Patris approbationem tantùm non cognouit Cleopas, qui filium D. i nondum cognouit, neque etiam cognouit approbatum eum esse à Deo habitante in se corporaliter. Declaratus est enim Filius Dei potenter per Spiritum sanctificationis. Et iustificatus est in Spiritu. Quod autem illud, Coram Deo, sic exponamus, adducimur illo loco Act. 2. 22. in quo in eundem sensum dictum est, eum virum fuisse à Deo approbatum apud eos præstantibus factis, & miraculis & signis. Atque sic quidem descripsit Christum Cleopas iste. In qua descriptione, etsi quæ dicit vera sint omnia: tamen in iis quæ de eo prædicat magnus est defectus: & ne ipse quidem quæ dicit recte ea intelligit: Neque tamen ideo reiectus est à Domino, qui arundinem quassatam non frangit, neque linum fumigans extinguit: sed vel tantillum fidei & dilectionis cum magna ignorantia sæpenumero coniunctum, acceptum habet atque fouet. Et quomodo eum. Nunc de iis quæ Iesu facta sunt agitur. Sunt autem quæ hic narrantur duo. 1. morte damnatus est, 2. crucifixus est. Authores harum rerum erant. 1. Principes Sacerdotum. 2. Magistratus politicus, Pilatus & alij. Si ad ista aduerteris, videbis hæc per indignationem aliquam à Cleopa superioribus subiecta esse, ac si dixisset: Cùm vir talis tantúsque esset, nihilominus illi indignis modis eum tractârunt, &, vt cum Paulo loquar, etsi esset Dominus gloriæ, tamen eum crucifixerunt, hoc est ignominiosissimo mortis genere sustulerunt è medio. Nam pij quique, qui vident illam Dei & Christi gloriam, indignissime solent ferre illius gloriæ violationem, adeo vt sine maxima offensione eam intueri non possint, nisi Deus illa prouidentia, quæ est in omnibus rebus atque actionibus, etiam indignissimis, efficax, eos consolaretur. Vnde Petrus meminit minimè factiillius omnium, quæ vnquam fuerunt indignissimi, nempe crucifixionis Domini gloriæ, ac definito Dei consilio & prouidentia sceleratis manibus crucifixum esse. At impij quod non vident, ideo indignissima quæque perpetrant, sine sensu aliquo & pœnitentia: nam si viderent, profectò sic non auderent. Si, inquit Paulus, cognouissent principes huius seculi, Dominum gloriæ non crucifixissent. Nos autem sperabamus. Ex prima illa narrationis suæ parte colligit Cleopas non esse amplius, quòd sperent eum redemptorem fore Israëli, hoc vsus argumento. Nos sperabamus illum esse, &c. At nunc condemnatus & crucifixus est; Ergo non est quòd speremus amplius eum redemptorem fore Israëli. Vide quàm bene scilicet hoc inferat ex morte eius, planè enim contrarium debuit inferri. Mortuus est, Ergo redemptor futurus. Nulla enim absque sanguinis effusione est remissio peccatorum. Sed isti communi errore decepti, expectarunt promissum illum Christum, gloriosum futurum regem, & vindicem populi mundanum, qui error non tam tum inuasit vulgò, sed etiam discipulos Christi & Apostolos ipsos. Mater duorum filiorum Zebedæi dixit, Domine, Cùm veneris in regnum tuum, fac vt mearum filiorum vnus ad dextram, alter ad sinistram tuam sedeat in regno tuo. Et post resurrectionem, Domine, inquiunt, an hoc tempore restitues regnum Israeli? Vide ergo quid sit in rebus religionis pendere ex sententia vulgi & multitudinis, quam tamen nobis obtrudunt Aduersarij tanquam veræ Ecclesiæ notam aliquam certissimam.
units.tr: Jesus, a man and a prophet. Ever of the angels, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you"? As for the people, although he was not approved in word or deed by the crowd of the Jews, yet he was approved in their consciences. Hence there have sometimes arisen these or similar sayings: From eternity it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one who was born blind. And elsewhere: Never has a man spoken as this man does. But Cleopas did not fully recognise that approval by God and the Father, since he did not yet know the Son of God, nor did he know that he was approved by God dwelling in him bodily. For the Son of God was declared powerfully by the Spirit of sanctification, and was justified in the Spirit. As for how we should explain that phrase "before God", we are led to Acts 2.22, where it is said to the same effect that this man was approved by God among them by mighty works, and miracles, and signs. And so indeed Cleopas describes Christ. In this description, although all that he says is true, yet there is a great deficiency in what he preaches about him, and he himself does not rightly understand what he says. Yet he is not on that account rejected by the Lord, who does not break the bruised reed nor quench the smoking flax; rather, even a little faith and love, joined with great ignorance, he often accepts and cherishes. And how he ... Now we come to what was done to Jesus. There are two things narrated here: first, he was condemned to death; second, he was crucified. The authors of these things were: first, the chief priests; second, the civil magistrate, Pilate and others. If you attend to these matters, you will see that Cleopas adds them above with some indignation, as if he were saying: "Although he was such a man and so great, nevertheless they treated him in unworthy ways, and, to speak with Paul, although he was the Lord of glory, they crucified him, that is, they took him out of the way by the most ignominious kind of death." For all the godly, who see that glory of God and Christ, are wont to bear most indignantly the violation of that glory, so that they cannot look upon it without the greatest offence, unless God, by that providence which is effective in all things and actions, even the most unworthy, comforts them. Hence Peter mentions the most unworthy deed of all that have ever been done, namely the crucifixion of the glory of the Lord, and says that he was crucified by wicked hands according to the determined counsel and providence of God. But the wicked, because they do not see this, commit the most unworthy deeds with no sense or repentance; for if they saw it, they would certainly not dare to do so. "If the rulers of this age had known," says Paul, "they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." But we were hoping. From the first part of his narrative Cleopas concludes that there is no longer reason to hope that he will be the redeemer of Israel, using this argument: We were hoping that he was, etc. But now he has been condemned and crucified; therefore there is no longer reason for us to hope that he will be the redeemer of Israel. See how well, indeed, he draws this inference from his death, for the opposite ought to have been inferred. He has died; therefore he will be the redeemer. For without the shedding of blood there is no remission of sins. But these men, deceived by the common error, expected that promised Christ to be a glorious king and an avenger of the people in worldly fashion. This error had taken hold not only of the crowd at that time, but also of the disciples of Christ and the Apostles themselves. The mother of the two sons of Zebedee said, "Lord, when you come into your kingdom, grant that one of my sons may sit at your right hand and the other at your left in your kingdom." And after the resurrection they say, "Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" See, then, what it is, in matters of religion, to depend on the opinion of the crowd and the multitude, which nevertheless our adversaries thrust upon us as a most certain mark of the true Church.

units.la: Atqui pater. Hæc est secunda pars narrationis Cleopæ de duratione Christi sub morte. Nunc igitur tertius dies est, ex quo mortuus est. Ex hoc quoque & illud concludendum significat, non esse quod sperent amplius redemptorem fore ipsum. Cùm tamen si recte aduertissent ad prædictiones Prophetarum & ipsius etiam Christi recentem illam prædictionem, planè contrarium mortuus sit.
units.tr: But, father. This is the second part of Cleopas' account concerning the duration of Christ under death. Now, therefore, it is the third day since he died. From this too he signifies that the same conclusion must be drawn, namely that there is no reason for them to hope any longer that he himself will be the redeemer. Yet if they had rightly attended to the predictions of the prophets and to Christ's own recent prediction, he has died in exactly the opposite way.

units.la: ZZz inferedum fuisset, in hanc formam: Hic tertius est dies? Ergo dies resurrectionis. Sed scripturas ignorauit, & praedicationis Christi oblitus est. Hinc dies tertius dies fuit illis moestitiae & doloris: vt videas ex ignoratis scripturis fieri, vt ea in quibus est materia spei & consolationis, plane mutentur in materiam desperationis atq; doloris. Sed & mulieres. Tertia pars narrationis Cleopae, continens historiam eorum, quae acciderunt eo ipsa die, qui dies fuit Resurrectionis Domini. Primum est nuncium illud mulierum, quae exierunt ad sepulchrum Domini. Deinde est nuncium discipulorum aliquot, duorum, nempe Petri & Iohannis, superiori illi mulierum non valde absimile. De Christo, ait Cleopas, vtriq; aliquid quidem nunciarut, non tamen viderunt ipsum. Ex quo relinquit intelligendum non reliquam esse spe ipsius videndi imposterum: quia nimirum oculis istis corporeis non viderunt vel mulieres vel discipuli Dominum post ipsius Resurrectionem: ergo nulla spes amplius redemptionis per ipsum. Quasi vero oporteat metiri redemptionem aut Redemptorem ex crasso & corporeo nostro sensu: cum fides vel spes rerum sunt quae non cernuntur corporeis hisce sensibus. Sed in eo quoque peccauit Cleopas, quod dixerit non visum a mulieribus & discipulis Dominum: quandoquidem a Magdalene primum, deinde mulieres aliae ipsum viderint. Sed videntur hi duo discipuli a coetu aliorum discipulorum egressi esse ante reditum mulierum: vt ut sint crassi nimis fuerunt adhuc & ψυχικοί, qui tantum ex corporeo isto sensu toti pendebant; cum qui spirituales sunt spectent ea quae non cernuntur, nempe oculis fidei, quae non cernuntur oculis istis corporeis. Spectamus, inquit Paulus, non ea quae cernuntur, sed ea quae non cernuntur. In hac narrationis tertia parte aliquid recitatur, quod fidem aliquam resurrectionis Christi redoleat, cum dicit Cleopas, non inuentum quidem eum a mulieribus & discipulis: mulieres vero nuntiasse conuenisse se Angelos qui dicerent Dominum viuere. Haec verba indicant eos inclinasse aliquo certe modo in eam sententiam quod Dominus resurrexisset. Vide igitur vt solent homines fluctuare inter spem & metum, & vt recos
units.tr: It ought to have been inferred in this form: "This is the third day; therefore the day of the resurrection." But he was ignorant of the Scriptures and had forgotten the preaching of Christ. Hence the third day was for them a day of sadness and grief. You may see that from the Scriptures not understood, it comes about that those things which contain the matter of hope and consolation are wholly turned into matter of despair and grief. But also the women. The third part of Cleopas' narrative, containing the history of what happened on that very day, which was the day of the Lord's resurrection. First is the report of the women who went out to the Lord's sepulchre. Then comes the report of some of the disciples, two, namely Peter and John, not very unlike that earlier report of the women. Concerning Christ, says Cleopas, they reported something to both, yet they did not see him himself. From this he concludes that there is to be understood no remaining hope of seeing him henceforth: because, of course, neither the women nor the disciples saw the Lord with those bodily eyes after his resurrection; therefore there is no longer any hope of redemption through him. As if indeed it were right to measure redemption, or the Redeemer, by our gross and bodily sense, since faith and hope are of things which are not seen by these bodily senses. But Cleopas also erred in saying that the Lord had not been seen by the women and disciples, since he was first seen by Magdalene and then by other women. But these two disciples seem to have left the company of the other disciples before the women returned. However gross they were, still fleshly and natural [ψυχικοί], wholly dependent on that bodily sense alone; whereas those who are spiritual look at things that are not seen, namely with the eyes of faith, which are not seen with those bodily eyes. We look, says Paul, not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. In this third part of the narrative something is recited which smells of some faith in the resurrection of Christ, when Cleopas says that the women did not find him, and the disciples did not either, but that the women reported that they had met angels who said that the Lord was alive. These words indicate that they had in some way inclined to that opinion, that the Lord had risen. See, then, how men are wont to waver between hope and fear, and how...

units.la: Ignoratio scripturarum fons erroris. Narratio Cleopae post pars, animi extra scripturam fluctuantis ratiocinationes aperiens. Animalis hominis miseria. 1 Cor. 4.18. Inter spe & metum pii extentione e-mergetes fluctuant. recordatio verbi Dei semel annunciati eos sustentet aliquo modo, ne prorsus in desperationem abeant. Quare perpetuo audiendum verbum Dei, quod tum suum vsu habet & efficax est maxime, cum maxime tentamur. Sustentat autem nos & quasi supernatare facit, tanquam perdum Christus manu sua porrecta nos eripiat ex aquis illis desperationis. O amentes & tardi. Hactenus Cleopas. Nunc respondet Dominus: Primum reprehendit eorum socordiam & incredulitatem, deinde eos docet. In reprehensione infideles eos denotat & incredulos, dum primum amentes vocat eos, deinde tardos corde. Infidelitas enim in mente quidem hominis est amentia siue stultitia, in corde vero stupiditas siue tarditas. Quemadmodum fides est in mente quidem sapientia, in corde vero alacritas quaedam & promptitudo; fides autem & infidelitas versantur circa spiritualia, vt sunt scripta Prophetarum & Apostolorum. Quis quis sapit mente, & apprehendit corde spiritualia illa, is est qui non credit: Sapiat licet quaecunque velit terrena & humana, si non interea sapiat spiritualia, is nihil sapit vt oportet: Quantumuis promptus & acutus ad apprehendendum vel omnia terrena ista, si tamen coelestia & spiritualia non apprehendat, stupidus est ac tardus. Non enim ex terrenis & humanis, sed ex Diuinis & coelestibus iudicium faciendum est de vera sapientia mentis pariter & vera apprehensione & promptitudine cordis. Eo quod dicat omnibus quae loquuti sunt, exagerat eorum incredulitatem. q. d. Cum tot sint de Christo a Prophetis scripta, tamen fidem nulli horum adhibetis. Multa dicta & scripta exaggerant infidelitatem non credentium, & iudicium in eos aggravat. Non est hoc praetereundum, quod docturus eos, primum omnium seuera quadam reprehensione excutiat iis torporem illum suum. Quid enim attinet docere stupidos, non prius excusso stupore & incusso iis sensu aliquo amentiae, caecitatis & miseriae ipsorum? Non opportet. Hoc est illud doctrinae caput quod tractandum suscipit. Est autem non tantum de passionibus Christi, sed passionum illarum necessitate: quod oporteat Christum per passionem & mortem statuit.
units.tr: Ignorance of the Scriptures is the source of error. Cleopas's narrative that follows reveals the reasoning of a mind wavering outside Scripture. The misery of natural man (1 Cor. 4.18). Godly people, rising up between hope and fear, waver. The remembrance of the word of God once proclaimed keeps them up in some way, so that they do not altogether fall into despair. For this reason the word of God must always be heard, since it is then most useful and most effective when we are most tempted. It sustains us and makes us, as it were, float above the waters of despair, as if Christ, holding out his hand, were rescuing us from those waters. "O foolish and slow of heart." Thus far Cleopas. Now the Lord answers. First he rebukes their dullness and unbelief, and then he teaches them. In his rebuke he marks them as faithless and unbelieving, first calling them foolish, then slow of heart. For unbelief in the mind is folly or foolishness, but in the heart it is dullness or slowness. Just as faith is wisdom in the mind, but in the heart it is a certain eagerness and readiness; and faith and unbelief are concerned with spiritual things, such as the writings of the prophets and apostles. Whoever is wise in mind and grasps those spiritual things with his heart, is the one who does not believe. However wise he may be in whatever earthly and human matters he wishes, if at the same time he is not wise in spiritual things, he is not wise as he ought to be. However quick and sharp he may be to grasp all these earthly things, if he does not grasp heavenly and spiritual things, he is dull and slow. For judgement about true wisdom of mind, and likewise about true apprehension and readiness of heart, must be made not from earthly and human things but from divine and heavenly ones. By saying "to all the things they have spoken," he heightens their unbelief, as if to say: although so many things about Christ have been written by the prophets, you give faith to none of them. Many sayings and writings heighten the unbelief of those who do not believe and make their judgement heavier. This must not be passed over: before he teaches them, he first, by a certain severe rebuke, shakes off their torpor. For what is the use of teaching the dull unless their stupor has first been shaken off and some sense of their own folly, blindness and misery has been stirred in them? It is not fitting. This is the chief point of doctrine that he undertakes to treat. It concerns not only the sufferings of Christ but the necessity of those sufferings: that it behoved Christ to suffer and die.

units.la: Vocat eos amentes & tardos corde. Incredulitas quid. De vera & falsa sapientia iudicium. ingredi in gloriam suam. Necessitatem autem hanc deinceps confirmat ex testimoniis & prædictionibus Mosis & Prophetarum. Quæ enim prædicta sunt, necessario eueniunt omnia: quia quæ à Prophetis prædicta sunt, ea ipsa à Deo ordinata sunt ab æterno. Est & alia quædam causa huius necessitatis, quæ nos propius attingit: nempe peccatum nostrum, quod Christo est imputatum, propter quod Christus ad tempus aliquod est quasi exclusus è cœlo, & execratio pro nobis factus. Peccatum enim siue id inhæreat siue imputetur perpetuo intercludit aditum ad cœlos, tantisperdum abolitum. Quòd si filius Dei, qui peccatum non nouit, factus tamen est peccatum pro nobis, propter peccatum nostrum, quà homo, exulauit ad tempus è cœlo: quanto magis nos, qui in peccato concipimur & nascimur, non ingredi emur regnum cœlorum, nisi peccatum nostrum fuerit abolitum? Quòd si dicat quis, Christus morte suavia m nobis aperuit ad cœlos, Quorsum igitur opus est nos ipsi affligamur & moriamur? Oportet enim nos per multas oppressiones ingredi regnum cœlorum. Respondeo afflictiones nostras non esse vel satisfactionem, vel partem vllam satisfactionis: Verùm cùm non minùs necesse sit vt mortificetur corrupta nostra natura, quàm vt ipsi iustificemur, mortificatio autem carnis non perficiatur sine afflictionibus, profecto vsque adeo sunt eæ necessariæ, vt nihil magis.
units.tr: He calls them foolish and slow of heart. What unbelief is. Judgement on true and false wisdom. To enter into his glory. He now goes on to confirm this necessity from the testimonies and predictions of Moses and the Prophets. For all things that have been foretold necessarily come to pass, because what the prophets foretold was itself ordained by God from eternity. There is also another cause of this necessity, which touches us more closely: namely our sin, which was imputed to Christ, on account of which Christ was for a time, as it were, shut out from heaven and made a curse for us. For sin, whether it dwells in us or is imputed to us, perpetually blocks the way to heaven until it is abolished. But if the Son of God, who knew no sin, was nevertheless made sin for us, on account of our sin, and as man went into exile from heaven for a time, how much more must we, who are conceived and born in sin, be unable to enter the kingdom of heaven unless our sin has been abolished? But if someone should say, Christ by his death has opened the heavens to us, why then is it necessary for us to be afflicted and to die ourselves? For we must enter the kingdom of heaven through many afflictions. I answer that our afflictions are not satisfaction, nor any part of satisfaction. But since it is no less necessary that our corrupt nature be mortified than that we ourselves be justified, and the mortification of the flesh is not accomplished without afflictions, these are indeed so necessary that nothing is more so.

units.la: Exorsus à Mose.
units.tr: Beginning from Moses.

units.la: Propositum illud doctrinæ suæ caput nunc confirmat: Hoc autem docendi ordine vsum esse tum Dominum, satis conspici potest ex ipso contextu. Nimirum testimonia in medium adduxit. Primùm ex Mose & Prophetis. Deinde prolata est interpretatus de Christo. Postremò interpretata accommodauit ad institutam illam suam propositionem, conclusitque ex iis necessitatem Passionis Christi. Christus quid quæso facit aliud hoc loco quàm prædicat Euangelium? Prædicat autem Euangelium prædicando Mosen & Prophetas. Ergo Euangelium quid est aliud quàm interpretatio quædam & plena declaratio Mosis & Prophetarum. Mosis autem & Prophetarum scripta quid sunt aliud, quàm texta. textus quidam Euangelij? Quamobrem cùm non sit separanda interpretatio, & (vt vocatur) glossa à contextu suo, nemo separet Euangelium à Moise & Prophetis, neque nouum Testamentum à vetere, sicut phanatici quidam senserunt: Vetus scilicet Testamentum iam iisqui sub Euangelio sunt non esse necessarium. Christus prædicando Euangelium interpretatus est Moisen & Prophetas. Apostoli Euangelium confirmarunt testimoniis Moisis & Prophetarum. Nos quoties prædicamus Euangelium substernere quidem debemus scriptum Apostolorum, tanquam primum fundamentum: sed fundare oportet deinde super Apostolos & Prophetas: Prophetas denique ipsos super Moisen. Hinc bene fundata est doctrina super fundamentum illud triplex: & bene fundata ea fides est, quæ super doctrinam illam, vt sic dicam, fundamentalem triplicem, fundata est ac superstructa. Interpretabatur quæ de ipso scripta erant. Ergo Christus omnis doctrinæ siue Euangelicæ, siue Apostolicæ, siue Propheticæ, siue denique Mosaicæ fundamentum est. Vnde Apostolus, postquam dixit superstructos esse eos super fundamentum Apostolorum & Prophetarum, subiecit continuò hæc verba, Cuius imus angularis lapis est Christus. Item: Nemo potest ponere aliud fundamentum præter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus. Et alibi: Finis legis est Christus, in quo nimirum impletur lex. Non veni vt dissolvam legem & Prophetas, sed vt impleam: inquit Christus.
units.tr: He now confirms that point of his teaching which he proposed. That the Lord used this order of teaching can be seen well enough from the context itself. Namely, he brought forward testimonies: first from Moses and the Prophets. Then the things brought forward were interpreted concerning himself. Finally, he applied the things interpreted to that proposition of his, and from them he concluded the necessity of the Passion of Christ. What, I ask, is Christ doing in this place other than preaching the Gospel? But he preaches the Gospel by preaching Moses and the Prophets. Therefore what is the Gospel other than a certain interpretation and full declaration of Moses and the Prophets? And what are the writings of Moses and the Prophets other than the text of which the Gospel is the text's exposition? Therefore, since interpretation and (as it is called) the gloss should not be separated from its text, let no one separate the Gospel from Moses and the Prophets, nor the New Testament from the Old, as certain fanatics have thought: namely, that the Old Testament is no longer necessary for those who live under the Gospel. Christ, in preaching the Gospel, interpreted Moses and the Prophets. The apostles confirmed the Gospel by the testimonies of Moses and the Prophets. When we preach the Gospel we ought indeed to lay down the writings of the apostles as the first foundation; but then we must build upon the apostles and prophets, and finally upon the prophets themselves, upon Moses. Hence doctrine is well founded upon that threefold foundation, and that faith is well founded and built up which is raised upon that threefold, so to speak, foundational doctrine. He interpreted the things that were written about himself. Therefore Christ is the foundation of all doctrine, whether Gospel, or apostolic, or prophetic, or finally Mosaic. Hence the Apostle, after saying that they are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, immediately adds these words: "Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone." Likewise: "No one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ." And elsewhere: "Christ is the end of the law," that is, in whom the law is truly fulfilled. "I came not to destroy the law and the prophets, but to fulfil them," says Christ.

units.la: Appropinquarunt. Hactenus Dominus tanquam viator aliquis duos discipulos instituit in fide Christi. Sequitur nunc historia reuelationis ipsius, appropinquantibus ipsis iam vico Emmaunti. Fingebat se Dominus longius ire. Non est hinc colligendum loquutum esse Dominum secus quàm cogitauit, quod profecto est mentiri. Sed cùm propositum apud se haberet longius ire, & se ab eis subducere, nisi futurum esset vt serio inuitaretur ab ipsis, suppressa conditione, loquutus est quod apud se iam proposuit. Dissimulatio ergo fuit, non in eo quod secus dixerit, quàm sensit & apud animum suum cogitauit (nam proposuit quidem longius abire) verùm in eo quòd conditionem propositi cæl-rit. Quod autem ea fuerit conditio, quam diximus, & in animo fuerit Domino discedere, nisi præstita ab eis conditione ea, satis apparet ex versu sequenti. Exempla huiusmodi multa legas in Scripturis sacris tũ Dei ipsius, tum sanctorum hominum, præsertim iis in locis, in quibus Deus comminatur iudicia nulla expressa conditione. Suppressa autem & quasi dissimulata est conditio ea de causa quam ipse nouit: tentandi nimirum gratia, vel aliqua alia nobis fortassis ignota. Ergo locus hic nihil seruit iis qui mentiri volunt quouis modo: tantùm hoc discimus, tum non curiosè indagandum in Domini consilium, quodcunque ipse capit de nobis, cùm non est visum ei id reuelare: sed studendum vt faciamus voluntatem Domini eam quam ipse iam reuelauit. Hoc autem reuelauit, quod oporteat nos omnibus modis requirere & retinere apud nos præsentiam illam Domini nostri, adeoque etiam adigere istorum exemplo eum vt nobiscum maneat. Atque hoc ipsum seriũ retinendi apud nos Domini studium, argumentum quoddam est propositi ac consilij ipsius, quod nimirum decreuerit nobiscum manere. Qui enim nobis dat velle, dat quoque id quod volumus: & qui implet conditionem propositi, implet quoque propositum ipsum. Contrà, cùm non est studium retinendi apud nos Dominum, id quidem arguit non hoc propositum apud se Dominum, vt nobiscum maneat. Sed ipsi adegerunt. Inuitatus Dominus vna cum iis, ingreditur vicum & domum: vt videas id verum esse, quod dixit Christus violentos rapere regnum cælorum.
