Eos demum qui Christum quodammodo adigunt, & inuitum quasi ac reluctantem retrahunt, habere Christũ secum habitantem. Eos verò qui vim ipsi non afferunt non fieri eius participes aut retinere eius præsentiam. Rursus obseruamus humanitatem non carere mercede sua: & humanos quosq;, hospitales & benignos erga homines pro hominibus Christum excipere hospitio, dictum est Heb. 13.2. Quosdam cum id ignorarent pro hominibus Angelos hospitio excepisse, Abrahamum & Lotum intelligit Gen. 18.3. & 19.8. At nemo est qui non dicat, quod si ipse in Christum incideret, secum lubentissime
units.tr: They drew near. Thus far the Lord, as a certain traveller, instructed two disciples in the faith of Christ. Now follows the story of his revelation, as they were already drawing near the village of Emmaus. The Lord pretended to be going further. We should not conclude from this that the Lord spoke otherwise than he intended, which would indeed be lying. But since he had it in his mind to go further and withdraw from them, unless he should be seriously invited by them, he spoke what he had already resolved in himself, the condition being withheld. That this was the condition we have mentioned, and that the Lord was minded to depart unless that condition had been fulfilled by them, is clear enough from the following verse. You will read many examples of this kind in the holy Scriptures, both of God himself and of holy men, especially in those places where God threatens judgements without any condition expressed. But the condition was withheld and as it were dissembled for the reason that he himself knew: namely for the sake of testing, or for some other reason perhaps unknown to us. Therefore this passage serves nothing for those who wish to lie in any way; we learn only this: that we must not inquire curiously into the Lord's counsel, whatever he has decided about us, since it has not pleased him to reveal it; but we must take care to do the will of the Lord which he has now revealed. He has revealed this: that we ought in every way to seek and to keep with us the presence of our Lord, and indeed to compel him, by the example of these men, to remain with us. And this very earnest zeal for keeping the Lord with us is a certain proof of his purpose and counsel, namely that he has decided to remain with us. For he who gives us the will also gives that which we will; and he who fulfils the condition of a purpose fulfils the purpose itself. On the contrary, when there is no zeal for keeping the Lord with us, this indeed shows that the Lord does not have this purpose, to remain with us. But they compelled him. The Lord, invited together with them, enters the village and the house; so that you may see that what Christ said is true, that the violent take the kingdom of heaven. Those who, in some way, compel Christ, and as it were draw him back unwilling and reluctant, have Christ dwelling with them. But those who do not use force to him do not become partakers of him, nor retain his presence. Again, we observe that humanity does not lack its reward, and that all humane, hospitable and kind people who receive men as guests receive Christ in the persons of men, as it is said in Heb. 13.2. Some, not knowing this, received angels as guests in the persons of men: Abraham and Lot are meant, Gen. 18.3 and 19.8. But there is no one who would not say that if he himself were to meet Christ, he would most gladly with him...

units.la: {a} Huiusmodi dissimulationis piæ exempla. fùmè exceptuτũ hospitio, & nihil non officij erga ipsum prǫstitutū. Ultimo n. die illo dicturi sunt, Domine, Quando te vidimus esurientem, aut sitientem, aut hospitem, aut nudum, aut ægrotum, aut in carcere, & non ministravimus tibi? At qui erga homines nullam exercent benignitatem, profectò nec in Deum possent ipsi esse officiosi aut pij. Legimus quidem de iis, qui cum in homines essent benefici, eos hospitio excepisse, ut ipsis videbatur, pro hominibus Dominum ipsum hospitio excepisse. At nusquam legimus de iis, qui in humaniter se gesserunt erga homines, quod Deum exceperint unquam hospitio. Et factum est cum Simulat Dominus se viatorem, sed sanctitatem non dissimulavit. Sanctus fuit in sermone, in itinere, & sanctificavit discipulos duos, qui unà iter faciebant: Sanctus fuit in accubitu, fracturus enim & distributurus panem benedixit. Dissimula in aliis, ut vis; finge te viatorem, ut vis: nam in sanctitatis officiis ne sit ulla dissimulatio. Nec confirmato te huic seculo, & filiis huius seculi. Diabolus quidem & ministri ipsius transformant se in Angelos lucis: at vero Deus & veri ipsius ministri non transformantur in Angelos tenebrarum. Hoc eos tangit qui conformant se & domi & foris omnium moribus: cum prophani sunt, cum sanctis fingunt sanctitatem.
units.tr: Examples of such pious dissimulation. He was most graciously received as a guest, and every service was offered to him. For on that last day they will say, Lord, when did we see you hungry, or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you? But those who show no kindness to people could certainly not be dutiful or pious towards God. We do read of those who, being generous to men, received as a guest one whom they took to be a man, and so unknowingly received the Lord himself. But we never read of anyone who treated men kindly and yet received God as a guest. And it came to pass, when the Lord feigns to be a traveller, but he did not disguise his holiness. He was holy in his speech, holy on the road, and he sanctified the two disciples who walked with him. He was holy at table, for when he was about to break and distribute the bread, he blessed it. Pretend in other things as you wish, play the traveller as you wish, but let there be no pretence in the duties of holiness. Nor be conformed to this age and to the sons of this age. The devil and his ministers transform themselves into angels of light, but God and his true ministers are not transformed into angels of darkness. This applies to those who conform themselves to the manners of everyone, at home and abroad: when they are profane, they pretend holiness among the holy.

units.la: Et fecit eis. Vide quàm familiariter agat cum iis: semel ab eis non tantum ingressus vicum, sed etiam domum eandem, neque domum tantum, sed & eadem mensa accubuit. Neque id tantum, sed & sua ipsius manus pauit ac nutriuit. Qui semel inuitant Dominum, tò cū eis procedit familiaritatis, ut etiam pascat eos sua ipsius manu, neque tantùm cū iis vescatur corporeo hoc cibo & pascat eos hoc cibo: sed etiam insinuet se in eorum corda & pascat eos ad vitam æternam. Experiatur quis, nū velit Dominus se ut familiariter: vtetur profectò eo familiarius, quàm potuit unquam suspicari. Ecce sto ad ostium, inquit Christus, & pulso, si quis audierit vocem meam & aperuerit ostium, ingrediar ad eum, & cænabo cum eo & ipse mecum. Quibus verbis significat Dominus se superaturum ipsius expectationem, qui cœperit eo ut familiariter. Aperti autem sunt. Cognitus est ab iis Dominus, partim ex visitata illa sua precum formula, partim pulerum.
units.tr: And he did so to them. See how familiarly he dealt with them. Once he had entered not only the village but the very same house with them, and not only the house but also reclined at the same table. And not only that, but with his own hand he fed and nourished them. Those who invite the Lord once find that he proceeds with them in such familiarity that he feeds them with his own hand, and not only eats with them this bodily food and feeds them with it, but also insinuates himself into their hearts and feeds them unto eternal life. Let anyone try whether the Lord will be familiar with him: he will certainly use him more familiarly than he could ever have imagined. Behold, I stand at the door, says Christ, and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and sup with him, and he with me. By these words the Lord signifies that he will surpass the expectation of the one who has begun to be familiar with him. And their eyes were opened. The Lord was recognised by them, partly from that familiar form of prayer of his, and partly from his beauty.

units.la: Exceptionis ordinarie dilutio. Mat. 25. 44.
units.tr: The ordinary excuse of those who receive guests refuted. Matt. 25.44.

units.la: Sanctitas morum & erga Deum reverentia nunquam dissimulanda.
units.tr: Holiness of conduct, and reverence towards God, must never be dissembled.

units.la: Qui Christo sunt familiares, ab eo plus quàm optauerant recipiunt.
units.tr: Those who are familiar with Christ receive from him more than they had hoped.

units.la: Apoc. 3. 20.

Mutatio facta in oculis discipulorum. ex assueta & vsitata agendi ratione, in pane frangendo & distribuendo discipulis suis. Verū cū bis externis coniuncta est interna & efficax operatio per Spiritū suum sanctū, in aperiendis ipsorum oculis. Ex hoc loco, vt ex illo superiori, vbi de continendis eorum oculis dictum est, apparet nullam metamorphosin aut mutationem factam in ipso, sed mutationem tantum factam in eorum oculis. Discimus hic incrementum gratiae: inuitatus ab iis Dominus, non tantum eodem cum iis vsus est hospitio, simul coenauit & ipsos sua manu pauit: sed oculos eorum prius clausos aperuit, seque cognoscendum iis exhibuit: vt discas quantum boni gradatim quasi ad nos peruenias ex consuetudine Domini. Nunc quidem non videmus eum sicut est: sed si vsi fuerimus eo familiariter, suo tempore coram eum intuebimur eique conformabimur. Et ipse ablatus est. Non quidem ex visibili facto est inuisibilis neque mutationem passus est in se aliquam, sed vt antea mutauit eorum oculos, sic vt modum non inspicerent quo ipse ab iis discesserit ac disparuerit. Quod si cui videatur hoc mirū, quòd Dominus tantillo tempore se conspiciendum eis dederit, vt vix eum viderint cum ex eorum oculis sublatus est. Respondeo, quantum satis erat ad fidem resurrectionis, se conspiciendum eis dedit. Quòd si diutius cum eis vna versatus fuisset, iam illud fouisset inanem aliquam spem discipulis, quòd ipsi habituri essent Dominum incolam secum in terris, etiam iam post resurrectionem. Neque enim fieri potuit vt Dominum post resurrectionem haberent conuictorem & socium vitae, qualem habuerunt eum ante mortem. Impossibile enim fuit immortalem iam factum & gloriosum habitare cum mortalibus & vilibus hominum istis corporibus. Quamobrem si cui in animo est habitare cum Domino, cogitet is de migratione & glorificatione corporis sui futura in illo die.
units.tr: A change made in the eyes of the disciples: from his accustomed and usual manner of acting, in breaking and distributing bread to his disciples. But with these outward things there is joined an inward and effective operation through his Holy Spirit, in opening their eyes. From this passage, as from that earlier one where it was said that he held their eyes, it appears that no metamorphosis or change was made in him, but only a change in their eyes. Here we learn the increase of grace: having been invited by them, the Lord not only used the same hospitality with them, dined with them and fed them with his own hand, but also opened their eyes, which had previously been closed, and presented himself to them to be recognised. Thus you may learn how much good comes to us step by step, as it were, from the Lord's familiarity. Now indeed we do not see him as he is, but if we have been familiar with him, in his time we shall look upon him face to face and be conformed to him. And he vanished out of their sight. He did not indeed become invisible by any visible change, nor did he undergo any alteration in himself, but just as before he changed their eyes, so that they did not perceive the manner in which he departed from them and disappeared. But if anyone thinks this strange, that the Lord gave himself to be seen by them for so short a time that they scarcely saw him before he was taken from their eyes, I answer: he gave himself to be seen by them as much as was sufficient for faith in the resurrection. For if he had stayed with them longer, he would have fostered in the disciples some empty hope that they would have the Lord living with them on earth even after the resurrection. For it could not be that after the resurrection they should have him as a companion and sharer of life, as they had him before his death. For it was impossible that he, now immortal and glorified, should dwell with mortals in these vile bodies of men. Therefore, if anyone desires to dwell with the Lord, let him think of the migration and glorification of his body which will come on that day.

units.la: Effectus sermonis Christi in discipulis.
units.tr: The effect of Christ's speech on the disciples.

units.la: Nonne cor nostrum. Hactenus fuit sermo collatus inter Christum & discipulos ipsius: sequitur effectum sermonis Christi in discipulis. Reuocant in memoriam a rdorem illum & sensum, quem iam antea perceperunt animo, cum ipse in itinere exponeret Scripturas quae erant de Christo. Ex illo autem ardore non tantum ex præsenti aspectu colligunt eum qui loquutus est, Christum esse (non enim fuit illa vulgaris aliqua commotio animi, quæ tum fuit excitata in cordibus eorum) Verùm singularis quædam mutatio, arguebatque eum iis loquutum esse, qui simul cum sermone spirabat spiritum illum ignitum quo accensa sunt eorum corda. Secus enim profecto non extitisset ardor aliquis & sensus singularis, qualis solet existere in animis credentium ex sermone ministri alicuius (habet enim etiam homo, ut Paulus, ut Petrus, ministerium Spiritus sancti) & accendit quoque hunc ignem in corde, sed non ea mensura, qua accensus est ignis in corde ipsorum tum per sermonem Christi. Ardor enim ille tantus sese prodebat, non esse nimirum per ministerium hominis tantum, sed per operationem Dei, qui ipsos tum alloquebatur. Qui enim acceperunt discretionis illum Spiritum, hi quidem discernunt Spiritus, & cùm docentes audiunt diiudicant, cognoscuntque quo Spiritu loquatur. Christum autem loquentem discernunt ab aliis. Sed de his satis. Hoc autem notandum, quòd tunc temporis cùm Christus loqueretur in itinere, non collegerunt statim isti ex hoc quem perceperunt animi ardore, Christum eum esse qui loquebatur: verùm nunc demum cùm ipse se prodidit, ardorem illum reuocant in memoriam, ex eóque concludunt præsentiam Domini. Ita solet fieri, ut nimirum in præsentia, non ita distinctè discernamus de sensu illo cordis. Oculi enim nostri adeo ad tempus præstrinc̄ti sunt & notitia adeo confusa. Verùm postea aperiente Deo oculos nostros reuocamus in memoriam sensum illum priorem, & diiudicamus distinctius & limatius. Postquam verò videbimus Christum sicut est, tum quidem omnem hunc sensum & motum quem ex sermone ipsius percipimus, in hac vita in memoriam reuocabimus, deque eo distinctius indicabimus tum, quàm vnquam antea cùm in hac essemus vita. Atque ex eo tum demum colligemus, ac concludemus, Dominum in illo sermone quem audiuimus fuisse nobis præsentem. Quare cùm fructus sensus & ardoris huius quem percipimus ex ver bo Dei nunquam amissuri simus, demus operam in hac vita, vt assiduè ex verbo Dei percipiamus sensum hunc, quàm fieri potest plurimum, & quàm sæpe. Sed vtde ardore isto dicamus nonnihil: Hic est sensus ille, quem ex verbo Dei audito percipimus. Sensus enim hic est instar ardoris & ignis cuiusdam accensi in corde. Spiritus enim qui eum excitat in corde est quasi ignis: vnde etiam igni comparatur. Ipse vos baptizabit Spiritu & igni. Ardor autem hic nihil est aliud, quàm inflammatio quædam omnium affectuum nostrorum erga Deum; præsertim autem amoris, quo eum animo complectimur cum admirabili quadam suauitate. Præcedit autem affectiones nostras cordis apprehensio illa quam fidem appellamus. Ex illa apprehensione sequuntur affectus omnes, eorumque accensio & inflammatio. Ignis autem sic accensus depascit quasi Deum ipsum: vt enim ignis accensus foveretur & augetur materia aliqua combustibili: ita ignis hic in corde nostro accensus nutritur perpetua illa Dei præsentia in Christo Iesu & oleo illo Spiritus sancti pinguissimo. Consumit autem scoriam hanc corruptionis nostræ, eámque paulatim exedit: quòd autem in corde bonum est, illud explorat reddítque pretiosum, vt ignis aurum: nos autem sursum rapit, & subuehit. Vt enim ignis sursum emicat, & grauia quæque, quæ alioqui natura tendunt deorsum, in altum protrudit: ita ignis hic accensus in corde per Spiritum nos alioqui natura nostra graues & terrenos, vi illa sua in altum subleuat. Et surgentes. Haud stenus commemorarunt illum ardorem quo affecti sunt in itinere, & sese consolati sunt paulisper post sublatum ex oculis ipsorum Dominum. Nunc redeunt Hierosolymam quanta possunt celeritate, vt quæ acciderunt & viderunt ac audiuerunt, discipuli ibi congregatis renunciarent. Cùm Hierosolymis egressi iter fecerunt versus Emmauntem, tardè quidem progressi sunt, & nonnisi inuiti admodum, Christo quem pro viatore quodam habuerunt, quæ Hierosolymis acciderant, exposuerunt. At nunc magna cum celeritate redeunt Hieroso tosolyma, neque continere possunt apud se perceptum illud gaudium, aut retinere quae viderunt & audiuerunt. Pij cum tristi sunt animo, neque habent quae narrent nisi tristitia de Christo & Ecclesia ipsius, tum quidem tarde incedunt, tarde loquuntur, tarde faciunt omnia. At vero cum laeto sunt animo & laeta omnia habent, quae narrent alii, tum quidem festini sunt ac celeres, & in eundo & inloquendo: & tunc gaudium illud animo perceptum facile devorat omne taedium, omnem laborem ac molestiam. Haec adeo vera sunt, ut si quis non festinet ad praedicandum Euangelium Christi, ea re satis arguat se nullam adhuc ex Euangelio illo percepisse gaudium.
units.tr: Did not our heart burn within us? Hitherto the conversation between Christ and his disciples has been related; now follows the effect of Christ's speech upon the disciples. They call to mind that burning and feeling which they had already perceived in their minds, when he himself was expounding the Scriptures concerning himself on the road. From that burning they gathered, not only from his present appearance, that the one who spoke was Christ (for that was not some ordinary agitation of mind which was then stirred up in their hearts), but rather a certain singular change, and it showed that he had spoken to them while breathing out, along with his speech, that fiery Spirit by which their hearts were kindled. For otherwise there would certainly not have arisen such a burning and singular feeling as usually arises in the minds of believers from the sermon of some minister (for a man also, like Paul and Peter, has the ministry of the Holy Spirit), and who also kindles this fire in the heart, but not to the same degree as the fire was kindled in their hearts then through the speech of Christ. For that great burning revealed itself as not coming only through the ministry of a man, but through the working of God, who was then addressing them. For those who have received the gift of discerning spirits do indeed discern the spirits, and when they hear teachers they judge, and know by what Spirit he speaks. But they distinguish Christ speaking from others. Yet enough on these points. It must be noted, however, that at the time when Christ was speaking on the road, those men did not immediately conclude from the burning of mind which they perceived that the one who was speaking was Christ; but only now, when he has revealed himself, do they call that burning to mind and from it infer the presence of the Lord. It is usually so, that in the present we do not discern so distinctly that feeling of the heart. For our eyes are so dazzled for the moment, and our knowledge so confused. But afterwards, when God opens our eyes, we recall that earlier feeling and judge it more distinctly and more precisely. Yet when we shall see Christ as he is, then indeed we shall recall in this life all this feeling and motion which we perceive from his speech, and we shall speak of it more distinctly than we ever could while we were in this life. And from that, then at last, we shall gather and conclude that the Lord was present to us in that speech which we heard. Wherefore, since we shall never lose the fruit of this feeling and burning which we perceive from the Word of God, let us take pains in this life to perceive this feeling from the Word of God continually, as much as possible, and as often as possible. But let us say something about this burning: this is that feeling which we perceive from the Word of God when we hear it. For this feeling is like a burning and a kind of fire kindled in the heart. For the Spirit who stirs it up in the heart is as it were fire; hence he is also compared to fire: He will baptize you with the Spirit and with fire. This burning, moreover, is nothing other than a certain inflaming of all our affections towards God, especially of that love by which we embrace him in heart with a wonderful sweetness. But before our affections of heart comes that apprehension which we call faith. From that apprehension all the affections follow, and their kindling and inflaming. Now fire so kindled feeds upon God himself, as a kindled fire is fostered and increased by some combustible matter: so this fire kindled in our heart is nourished by the perpetual presence of God in Jesus Christ and by that most rich oil of the Holy Spirit. It consumes, moreover, the dross of our corruption, and gradually eats it away; and what is good in the heart it tests and makes precious, as fire does gold. But it also lifts us up and bears us aloft. For as fire shoots upward, and thrusts upward all heavy things which by nature otherwise tend downward, so this fire kindled in the heart by the Spirit lifts us up on high by its own power, us who otherwise are by nature heavy and earthly. And rising up. They had not long recalled the burning with which they were affected on the road, and for a little while after the Lord had been taken from their eyes they comforted themselves. Now they return to Jerusalem with all possible speed, so that the disciples gathered there may be told what happened, and what they saw and heard. When they had set out from Jerusalem and made their way towards Emmaus, they had gone slowly and only very reluctantly, and had reported to Christ, whom they took for some travelling companion, what had happened in Jerusalem. But now they return to Jerusalem with great haste, and cannot contain within themselves the joy they have received, nor keep to themselves what they saw and heard. When the godly are sad in mind, and have nothing to tell but sorrow about Christ and his Church, then indeed they walk slowly, speak slowly, do everything slowly. But when they are glad in mind and have joyful things to tell others, then indeed they are quick and swift both in going and in speaking; and then that joy received in the mind easily swallows up all weariness, all labour and trouble. These things are so true that if anyone is not hastening to preach the Gospel of Christ, he thereby sufficiently proves that he has not yet received any joy from that Gospel.

units.la: Et invenerunt congregatos & dicentes. Discipuli congregati Hierosolymis praeveniunt sermone & annunciatione resurrectionis Christi, duos istos qui Emmaunte venerunt. Surrexit, inquiunt, Dominus vere. Causam reddunt a testimonio Simonis Petri, qui post resurrectionem ipsum viderit. Nam visum esse a Petro testatur Paulus. Qui etiam ad communicandum aliis gaudium illud animo perceptum Euangelium Christi, ii ipsi nonnunquam ab aliis praeveniuntur & audiunt ipsi laetum nuncium priusquam fiat eis loquendi copia. Quod si non praeniantur, saltem audiant vicissim, laetum illud nuncium. Quod si non vicissim audiant ex aliis, certe ex illorum eorum nuncio & sermone de Christo audiscit gaudium illud animo perceptum: neque aliis solum praedicant, sed & sibi. Tantum abest ab eo ut decedat aliquid ipsorum gaudio eo quod ipsum cum aliis communicent, ut haec sit ipsissima via qua adaugeatur gaudium illud perceptum.
units.tr: And they found the eleven gathered together, and those who said: The disciples gathered at Jerusalem anticipate, by their words and announcement, those two who came from Emmaus with the news of Christ's resurrection. The Lord, they say, has truly risen. They give as the reason the testimony of Simon Peter, who had seen him after the resurrection; for Paul bears witness that he was seen by Peter. Those who have received the joy of the Gospel of Christ in their minds to share it with others are sometimes anticipated by others, and they themselves hear the joyful news before they have the opportunity to speak. And if they are not anticipated, at least they hear the joyful news in turn. And if they do not in turn hear it from others, certainly from the message and speech of those men about Christ they hear the joy received in their minds; and they preach it not only to others but also to themselves. So far is it from their joy being diminished by sharing it with others, that this is the very way in which the joy they have received is increased.

units.la: Marci 16.
units.tr: Mark 16.

units.la: 14 Postremo vero una sedentibus ipsis undecim conspicuum sese praebuit, & exprobravit incredulitatem eorum, & cordis duritiem, eo quod iis qui ipsum conspexerant suscitatum non credidissent.
units.tr: 14 Last of all, as the eleven were sitting at table, he appeared to them and upbraided them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he was raised.

units.la: Lucae 24.
units.tr: Luke 24.

units.la: 36 Haec autem ipsis loquentibus, stetit ipse Iesus in medio eorum. sus in medio eorum, & dixit eis, Pax vobis.
units.tr: 36 While they were saying these things, Jesus himself stood in the midst of them and said to them, Peace be unto you.

units.la: 37 Consternati vero & expauefacti videbantur sibi Spiritum conspicere.
units.tr: 37 But they were startled and terrified, and supposed that they had seen a spirit.

units.la: 38 Tunc dixit eis, Quid turbati estis, & quare discepta-tiones subeunt corda vestra?
units.tr: 38 And he said to them, Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts?

units.la: 39 Videte manus meas & pedes meos: nam ego ipse sum: Contrectate me, & videte, nā Spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, prout me conspicitis habere.
units.tr: 39 See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.

units.la: 40 Et cùm hoc dixisset, ostendit eis manus ac pedes.
units.tr: 40 And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet.

units.la: 41 Adhuc autem ipsis non credentibus præ gaudio, & mirantibus dixit eis, Habetis hic esculentum aliquid?
units.tr: 41 While they still did not believe for joy and were amazed, he said to them, Have you anything here to eat?

units.la: 42 Tunc ipsi porrexerunt ei partem piscis assi & aliquid ex fauo apiario;
units.tr: 42 And they gave him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb.

units.la: 43 Quæ ille accepit & in eorum conspectu comedit:
units.tr: 43 He took it and ate it in their sight.

units.la: 44 Dixitque eis, Hi sunt sermones quos loquutus sum vobis, quum adhuc essem vobiscum, oportere impleri omnia quæ scripta sunt in lege Mosis & in Prophetis & Psalmis de me.
units.tr: 44 And he said to them, These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that all things must be fulfilled which are written about me in the law of Moses, in the Prophets, and in the Psalms.

units.la: 45 Tunc aperuit eorum mentem, ut intelligerēt Scripturas.
units.tr: 45 Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures.

units.la: 46 Et dixit eis, Ita scriptum est, & ita oportuit Christum pati & resurgere à mortuis tertio die:
units.tr: 46 And he said to them, Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day,

units.la: 47 Et prædicari eius nomine resipiscentiam ac remissionem peccatorum apud omnes Gentes, incipiendo ab urbe Hierosolymorum.
units.tr: 47 and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

units.la: 48 Vos autem estis horum Testes.
units.tr: 48 And you are witnesses of these things.

units.la: 49 Et ecce ego emittam promissum Patris mei in vos: Vos autem manete Hierosolymis, vsquequo induainduamini virtute ex alto.
units.tr: 49 And behold, I will send the promise of my Father upon you; but remain in Jerusalem until you are endued with power from on high.

units.la: Iohannis 20.
units.tr: John 20.

units.la: 19 Quum ergo vespera esset, die illo primo Hebdomadis, & fores essent clausæ illic vbi erant discipuli coacti propter metum Iudæorum: venit Iesus stetitque in medio ipsorum, & dixit, Pax vobis.
units.tr: 19 When therefore it was evening on the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered together for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the midst of them, and said, Peace be unto you.

units.la: 20 Et cum hæc dixisset ostendit eis manus ac latus suum. Gauisi sunt ergo discipuli viso Domino.
units.tr: 20 And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then were the disciples glad when they saw the Lord.

units.la: 21 Dixit autem eis iterum, Pax vobis, sicut misit me Pater, ita & ego mitto vos.
units.tr: 21 Then said he to them again, Peace be unto you: as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you.

units.la: 22 Et cum hæc dixisset, afflauit eos, & dixit eis, Accipite Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: 22 And when he had said this, he breathed on them, and said unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost.

units.la: 23 Si quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis: si quorum retinueritis, retenta sunt.
units.tr: 23 Whosesoever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whosesoever sins ye retain, they are retained.

units.la: 24 Thomas autem unus ex duodecim, qui dicitur Didymus, non erat cum eis, quando venerat Iesus.
units.tr: 24 But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came.

units.la: 25 Dixerunt igitur ei alij discipuli, Vidimus Dominum. Ille verò dixit eis, Nisi videro in manibus eius vestigium clavorum, & immisero digitum meum in vestigium clavorum, & immisero manum meam in latus eius, nequaquam credam.
units.tr: 25 The other disciples therefore said unto him, We have seen the Lord. But he said unto them, Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.

units.la: 26 Octo ergo post diebus rursus erant discipuli eius intus, & Thomas cum eis: Venit Iesus foribus clausis, & stetit in medio ipsorum, & dixit, Pax vobis.
units.tr: 26 And after eight days again his disciples were within, and Thomas with them. Then came Jesus, the doors being shut, and stood in the midst, and said, Peace be unto you.

units.la: 27 Deinde dicit Thomæ, Infer digitum tuum huc, & vide manus meas, & profer manum tuam, & immitte in latus meum, & ne esto incredulus, sed credens.
units.tr: 27 Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.

units.la: 28 Respondit autem Thomas & dixit ei, Domine mi, & Deus mi.
units.tr: 28 And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.

units.la: 29 Dicit ei Iesus, Quia vidisti me, Thoma, credidisti, beati qui non viderunt & crediderunt.
units.tr: 29 Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.

units.la: 30 Multa vero etiam alia signa edidit Iesus in discipulorum suorum conspectu, quae non sunt scripta in hoc libro.
units.tr: 30 And many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book.

units.la: 31 Haec autem scripta sunt, ut credatis Iesum esse illum, Filium illum Dei, & ut credentes vitam habeatis per nomen eius.
units.tr: 31 But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is that Christ, the Son of God, and that believing ye might have life through his name.

units.la: H Actenus de quatuor apparitionibus Christi audiuimus. Prima qua apparuit Magdalenæ, secunda qua apparuit aliis mulieribus, tertia qua apparuit duobus discipulis Emmauntem proficiscentibus : quarta qua Petro, cuius obiter meminit Lucas. Nunc sequitur quinta apparitio Christi post resurrectionem suam. Apparuit enim discipulis in vnum congregatis. Primùm habemus descriptionem quandam congressus huius discipulorum Christi ex variis circumstantiis, quas colligimus ex tribus Euangelistis: primùm ex iis qui in vnum conuenerunt, describitur. Marcus vndecim dicit, cùm tamen Thomas non tum interfuerit: sed maiori parti totius nomen abeo est attributum. Iohannes discipulos generali nomine appellat. Illud obseruo, Christi discipulos toto hoc tempore in vnum conuenisse. In vnum conuenerunt ante passionem, in vnum conuenerunt in passione: stabant enim noti eius procul vt supra. In vnû denique conuenerût post passionem. Quotquot Christi sunt, ii perpetuò propendunt ad vnum corpus coficiendum, & ad mutuò inter se communicandum omnia, siue tristia, siue laeta: prout vnus est Deus Pater, vnum est caput Christus, vnus est Spiritus, vna fides, &c. Consolatio enim membrorum sita est in concionibus & communicationibus. Nam his promissus est consolator ille Spiritus sanctus: & haec qui contemnit, nunquam percepturus est eam quam oportet consolationem. Secunda circumstantia est quid in comitiis illis fecerint,
units.tr: So far we have heard of the four appearances of Christ: the first, to Mary Magdalene; the second, to the other women; the third, to the two disciples going to Emmaus; the fourth, to Peter, which Luke mentions in passing. Now follows the fifth appearance of Christ after his resurrection. For he appeared to the disciples gathered together. First we have a certain description of this assembly of Christ's disciples, drawn from various circumstances that we gather from the three Evangelists. First, it is described from those who came together. Mark says "eleven," although Thomas was not then present, but the whole name is attributed to the greater part. John calls the disciples by a general name. I observe this: Christ's disciples came together in one place throughout this whole time. They came together before the passion, they came together during the passion (for his acquaintances stood afar off, as above), and finally they came together after the passion. All who belong to Christ always tend to form one body and to share everything mutually with one another, whether sad or glad, just as there is one God the Father, one head Christ, one Spirit, one faith, and so on. For the comfort of the members lies in sermons and in fellowship. For it is to these that the promised Comforter, the Holy Spirit, is given, and whoever despises them will never receive that comfort which he ought to have. The second circumstance is what they did in that assembly.

units.la: Marcus dicit sedisse vnà, Lucas addit communicasse inter se ea quæ annunciabantur à variis de resurrectione Domini. Hæc præparatio quædam fuit antegressa aduentum Domini, idque non sine virtute aduentantis & appropinquantis ipsius Domini. Nam appropinquante ad nos Domino, Spiritus ille Domini qui in nobis est sese commouere incipit, excitare in cordibus lætitiam, & os aperire adloquendum, & sermones conferendos de spiritualibus & coelestibus. Spiritus enim præsentit aduentū Domini: & in illo die, quotquot erunt Domini, in aduentu eius erigetatq; attollent capita. Nūquā enim erigerentur attollerēt capita, nisi eis affulgeret eósq; irradiaret lux illa Domini aduentantis. Ergo Dominus cum præcipit discipulis Luc.21. vt erigant & attollant capita, significat vim illam qua id fiet profecturam à se in aduentu illo suo. Tertia circumstantia est temporis quod præsente annotatum est ab Iohanne, fuit autem primus dies hebdomadis, hoc est dies Dominicus, qui ipse dies fuit resurrectionis. Vespera, inquam fuit, illius diei post solis occubitum & sera nox. Nam fuit posteaquam duo illi discipuli reuersi sunt Emmaunte: inclinante autem sole reuersi sunt, vt vidimus supra. Iohannes causam noctu habita sint hæc comitia. Propter metum, inquit, Iudæorum. Hæc enim prudentia in piis requiritur, tempus illud deligant comitiorum suorum, quod opportunum & tutum, siue diurnum, siue nocturnum, nihil refert, modò sancti sint ij qui in vnum conuenerunt. Omne enim tempus sanctum est sanctis, vt & omnia alia. Christus etiam præsentem se sistit suis, quouis tempore, siue diurno, siue nocturno. Quamobrem neque tempora, neque loca, neque quid aliud tam considerandum, quàm persona ipsa, & persone sanctitas. Quarta circumstantia est locus. Non quidem hic peculiariter expressum habemus locum, tantum hoc notat Iohannes, locum fuisse clausum & munitum, procul dubio propter metum Iudæorum. Nam prudentia vt requiritur in tempore comitiorum deligendo, ita quoque in loco. Sanctos autem illos, qui secretum illud & arcanum mysterium inter se communicat, sancti cum mundo non conueniunt.
units.tr: Mark says they sat together; Luke adds that they shared with one another those things which were announced by various people about the resurrection of the Lord. This preparation went before the coming of the Lord, and not without the power of the Lord who was coming and drawing near. For when the Lord draws near to us, that Spirit of the Lord which is in us begins to stir, to arouse joy in our hearts, to open our mouths to speak, and to bring forth words about spiritual and heavenly things. For the Spirit perceives the coming of the Lord; and on that day, all who belong to the Lord will lift up and raise their heads at his coming. For they would never raise their heads unless that light of the Lord coming to them shone upon them and lit them up. Therefore when the Lord commands the disciples (Luke 21) to straighten up and lift up their heads, he signifies the power by which this will be accomplished, which will proceed from him at that coming of his. The third circumstance is the time, which John has noted in the present passage. It was the first day of the week, that is, the Lord's day, which was itself the day of the resurrection. It was, I say, the evening of that day, after sunset, and late at night. For it was after the two disciples had returned from Emmaus, having set out as the sun was declining, as we saw above. John gives the reason why this assembly was held at night: "for fear," he says, "of the Jews." For this prudence is required of the godly: that they choose for their assemblies a time that is opportune and safe, whether by day or by night, it makes no difference, provided that those who come together are holy. For every time is holy to the holy, as is everything else. Christ also presents himself to his own at any time, whether by day or by night. Wherefore neither times, nor places, nor anything else is to be considered as much as the person himself and the holiness of the person. The fourth circumstance is the place. Indeed we do not have the place expressly named here; John only notes that the place was closed and secured, without doubt because of the fear of the Jews. For prudence is required in choosing a place just as in choosing a time of assembly. Now those holy people who share together that secret and hidden mystery do not agree with the world.

units.la: Aduentans ad nos Domini sensus quidam veluti prænuncius. oportet segregari à mundo, & ab eorum comitiis abcerceri prophanos quosque: quod tandem fiet, cum in coelis ad Dominum aggregabuntur, ad quos tum non pertinebit aditus impiis. Hactenus fuit comitiorum istoru descriptio ex variis circumstantiis. Venit Iesus. Sistit se eis Christus extraordinarie, miraculose & repente. Celerrimus enim est motus glorificati corporis. Modus autem miraculosus non est expressus. Colligi autem potest ex eo quod dicitur apud Iohannem clausas fuisse fores. Ideoque de modo varij variè sentiunt. Papistæ, ut figmentum illud suum de præsentia corporis Domini in Coena, quam necessario sequitur unius corporis in variis locis positio, stabiliant; dicunt Domini corpus per ostij clausi corpus penetrasse. Nā si semel hoc obtinea-tur posse duo corpora simul in uno loco esse, eadem ratione illud sequitur, unū corpus esse posse in locis pluribus: sed utrumque cum natura corporis pugnat, nō tantum non glorificati, sed etiam glorificati: ut non sit quod hic nobis de glorificato corpore garriant. Altera sententia est, quod Domini corpore ingrediente, cessserit & rarefactum sit ostij corpus, ingressio autem eo iam rursus coaluerit & consolidatum sit, ut ambulante eo in mari consolidatum est mare, quod statim post redit ad naturam suam: atque hæc sententia non ita aliena est, & eam ferre potest illa Dei omnipotentia cum priore illam non posset ferre, ut quæ contradictionem includat. Tertia opinio est, & quæ maximè mihi probabilis esse videtur, quòd ingrediente Domino apertæ sint fores, ingresso, iam clausæ sint rursus celerrimo quodam motu, Act. 5. & 12. & 16. legimus de subita apertione & occlusione ostiorum, cum Apostoli vel per ministerium Angelorum, vel etiam absque ministerio Angelorum liberati sunt è carcere. De huiusmodi penetratione corporum per corpora nihil legimus, ut neque de rarefactione corporum. Quare mihi videtur maximè probabilis hæc opinio, quæ consentiens est aliis Scripturæ locis. Verum ut ista missa faciamus, videri potest ex hoc loco, Domini aduentum, siue is in misericordia, siue in iustitia sua veniat, esse subitum ac inexpectatum: ut discamus non quidem curiosius inquirere in tempus adventus
units.tr: The approaching of the Lord is a certain sense, as it were, of a forerunner: it is necessary to be separated from the world, and the profane are to be shut out from their assemblies; which will finally happen when they are gathered to the Lord in heaven, to whom access will then not be open to the impious. So far is the description of these assemblies from various circumstances. "Jesus came." Christ presents himself to them extraordinarily, miraculously and suddenly, for the movement of a glorified body is most swift. The mode, however, is not expressed; but it can be gathered from the fact that John says the doors were shut. Therefore people judge the mode differently. The Papists, in order to establish their fiction of the bodily presence of the Lord in the Supper, which necessarily entails the positioning of one body in various places, say that the Lord's body penetrated the body of the closed door. For if once this is granted, that two bodies can be in one place at the same time, by the same reasoning it follows that one body can be in many places; but both are contrary to the nature of a body, not only of a non-glorified body but even of a glorified one, so that they have no reason to chatter to us here about a glorified body. The second opinion is that, when the Lord's body entered, the body of the door yielded and was made rarefied, and after the entry it again coalesced and was consolidated, just as the sea was consolidated when he walked on it, and afterwards returned at once to its own nature. This opinion is not so foreign, and that omnipotence of God can bear it, though it could not bear the former, since it involves a contradiction. The third opinion, which seems to me most probable, is that when the Lord entered the doors were opened, and after he had entered they were closed again by a very swift motion. We read in Acts 5, 12 and 16 of the sudden opening and closing of doors, when the Apostles were freed from prison, either through the ministry of angels or even without the ministry of angels. Of this kind of penetration of bodies through bodies we read nothing, nor of any rarefaction of bodies. Wherefore this opinion seems to me most probable, as it agrees with other passages of Scripture. But setting these things aside, it can be seen from this passage that the coming of the Lord, whether he comes in mercy or in his justice, is sudden and unexpected; so that we may learn not to inquire too curiously into the time of his coming, but to prepare ourselves for the time of the Lord's coming.

units.la: Christus glorificato corpore suis se sistit. uentus ipsius, sed praeparare nos in tempus illud aduentus Domini: Vigilate, inquit, nam nescitis qua hora venturus sit Dominus.
units.tr: Christ, with his glorified body, presents himself to his own. [Let us not be curious about] the coming of the Lord, but prepare ourselves for that time of his coming: Watch, he says, for you do not know at what hour the Lord will come.

units.la: Et dixit eis, Pax vobis. Hoc dixit procul dubio voce illa sua assueta & familiari, quae possit ab iis innotescere. Nam omnibus modis se iis conatur notum perspe-ctumque facere. Illi interea difficulter admodum eum cognoscunt. Sed oportuit pacis hanc optationem efficacem esse, quae profecta est ab eo, qui pacis author fuit. Ipse enim est pax nostra. Cum autem is, qui pax est, euangelizet pacem, tum nisi ferro simus duriores, oportet annunciationem illam in nobis efficacem esse. Homines optare quidem possunt pacem, sed dare eam non possunt. Christus est, qui dum optat pacem dat eam pariter: Pacem illam meam do vobis, non prout mundus dat, ego do vobis. Territi vero. Hoc est effectum praesentiae Christi discipulis, quae confirmare eos debuit, ac fidem illam stabilire quam sermonibus ultro citroque habitis de resurrectione ipsius paulo antea iactitabant. Verum ab eo abfuit, ut illam eorum fidem propemodum exterruerit: mentem, quae paulo ante illuminata fuit, tenebris cecarit: cor, quod paulo ante gaudio suffusum fuit, vanis terroribus concusserit. Subita quidem haec mutatio fuit, ut intelligant omnes quam subitis mutationibus obnoxius sit animus humanus in hac vita, & quam cito dimoveamur bona aliqua constitutione: verum mutationis huius unde initium? Duae enim sunt animae humanae partes, Mens & Cor. Utrum mutatio ista coeperit in mente prius an in corde? Facile conspici potest mutationis initium factum esse in mente. Ideo enim territi sunt & expavefacti corde, quod putarunt se Spiritum conspicere. Ergo Mens primum falsa imaginatione se ipsa decepit, deinde cordi vanos terrores incussit. Hoc ideo observo, ut omnes videant hominis mentis vanitatem, quae tantum abest ab eo, ut inferiores affectus sua luce regat ac moderetur (hoc enim ipsi ex officio incumbit) ut e contra vanis imaginationibus suis & ratiocinationibus eos disturbet, ut necesse sit mentem, cui tamen tantum tribuerunt philosophi, cum primis regenerari.
units.tr: And he said to them, Peace be with you. Without doubt he said this in his usual and familiar voice, so that they could recognise it. For in every way he tries to make himself known and clearly seen by them, but they recognise him with great difficulty. Yet this wish of peace had to be effective, since it came from him who was the author of peace. For he himself is our peace. Since he who is peace also proclaims peace, unless we are harder than iron, that proclamation must be effective in us. Men can indeed wish for peace, but they cannot give it. It is Christ who, in wishing peace, at the same time gives it: My peace I give to you, not as the world gives, I give to you. But they were terrified. This was the effect of Christ's presence on the disciples, which ought to have strengthened them and established the faith that they had been boasting of, in their talk back and forth about his resurrection, a little while before. But far from strengthening that faith of theirs, his presence almost terrified it: it darkened the mind, which a little before had been illuminated; it shook the heart, which a little before had been filled with joy, with empty terrors. This was a sudden change, so that everyone may understand how liable the human spirit is to sudden changes in this life, and how quickly we are moved out of some settled state. But where did this change begin? For there are two parts of the human soul, the mind and the heart. Did this change begin first in the mind or in the heart? It can easily be seen that the beginning of the change was in the mind. For they were terrified and alarmed in their hearts because they thought they saw a spirit. So the mind first deceived itself by a false imagination, and then it struck the heart with empty terrors. I note this so that everyone may see the vanity of the human mind, which is so far from governing and moderating the lower affections by its light (which is its proper duty), that on the contrary it disturbs them by its vain imaginings and reasonings. Hence the mind, to which the philosophers have ascribed so much, must above all be regenerated.

units.la: Mentis nostrae miseria, nisi Christus speciali quadam gratia adsit.
units.tr: The misery of our mind, unless Christ is present by a special grace.

units.la: Animalis hominis vanitas. ac reformari per Spiritum Dei ; renouamini vero Spi- ritu mentis vestræ. Putabant se Spiritum conspicere. Ergo Spiritum intueri non potuerunt sine maximis terroribus. Ea enim est infirmitas mortalis oculi huius corporei, vt eius quod gloriosum est, immortale ac cœleste, aspectum ferre non queat. Mentis etiam ipsius acies, quæ longè acutior esse debet, non sustinet aspectum rerum immortalium ac cœlestium. Culpa est nō tam ipsarum rerum obiectarum, quibus oportet mentes nostras collustrari, quam ipsius mentis: quæ cùm natura sua lippiat non potest sustinere tantum fulgorem, sed ad aspectum earum rerum sese excæcat per innatas illas quæ in ea sunt, tenebras. Quid turbati estis? Dominus reprehendit perturbationem illam cordis, & vanam illam mentis imaginationem. Solus Dominus est qui verbo suo reformat animum hominis male affectum. Atque id primùm facit aliqua vsus fuerita-te, & increpatione: inordinati enim affectus isti cordis nostri in ordinem sunt cogendi vi aliqua maiore : & altitudo ista mentis nostræ euertenda est armis paulò validioribus. Disputationes subeunt corda. Verbum ascendendi in Græco contextu legitur, quo innuit Christus modum eum quo mens hominis dum ipsi obiiciuntur res spirituales, sese exercet & excæcat: est autem per ascensionem cogitationum, ratiocinationum ac imaginationum. Ascendunt enim hæ veluti fumus quidam & caligo ab imo in summum, tantisperdum obiectas res spirituales plane ex oculis nostris eripiant. Sic Philosophi gentium in ratiocinationibus suis euanuerunt. Sic Scholastici Papistarum sese sophistica sua & mundum totum excæcarunt. Hoc igitur verbo admonet Christus ne quoties verbum Dei nobis offertur, nimis indulgeamus ratiocinationibus nostris. Ratiocinamur quidem, sed ne sinamus ratiocinationes nostras ascendere, vt sic loquar, cum Christo. Verum cū sobrietate, cum animo discendi veritatem, cum precibus inquiramus in sanctum illud ac spirituale Dei verbum. Videte manus meas. Hactenus eos reprehendit; nunc vero docet: docet autem primùm se corpus esse, deinde
units.tr: The vanity of the natural man, and that he must be reformed by the Spirit of God: but be renewed in the spirit of your mind. They thought they saw a spirit. So they could not look upon a spirit without the greatest terror. For such is the weakness of this mortal bodily eye that it cannot bear the sight of what is glorious, immortal and heavenly. Nor can the very keenness of the mind, which ought to be far sharper, bear the sight of immortal and heavenly things. The fault lies not so much in the objects themselves, by which our minds ought to be illumined, as in the mind itself: which, since by its nature it is weak-sighted, cannot bear so great a brightness, but blinds itself to the sight of those things by the darkness innate in it. Why are you troubled? The Lord rebukes that disturbance of the heart and that vain imagination of the mind. The Lord alone reforms the ill-disposed spirit of man by his word. And he does this first by some reproof and rebuke: for these disordered affections of our heart must be brought into order by some greater force, and that lofty pride of our mind must be overthrown by somewhat stronger weapons. Reasonings arise in the hearts. The Greek text reads a verb meaning to ascend, by which Christ indicates the manner in which the human mind, when spiritual things are set before it, exercises and blinds itself: namely by the ascent of thoughts, reasonings and imaginings. For these rise like a kind of smoke and mist from below upward, so that they snatch the spiritual things set before us altogether from our eyes. Thus the philosophers of the Gentiles vanished away in their reasonings; thus the Scholastics of the Papists blinded themselves and the whole world with their sophistry. By this word, therefore, Christ warns us that whenever the word of God is offered to us, we should not too much indulge our own reasonings. We do indeed reason, but let us not allow our reasonings to ascend, so to speak, against Christ. Rather, let us inquire into that holy and spiritual word of God with sobriety, with a mind eager to learn the truth, and with prayers. See my hands. Hitherto he has reproved them; now he teaches. He teaches first that he is a body, and then

units.la: Ephes. 4. 23. se non esse Spiritum. Docet autem se corpus esse ex sensu ipso, primum visus, Videte, inquit, deinde tactus, Contrectate, inquit. Videndas autem ostendit & tractandas manus & pedes: in quibus erant perspicua vulnerum recentium vestigia. Docet autem se non esse Spiritum hoc modo: Spiritus, inquit, non habet carnem & ossa. Ego vero ut conspicitis, habeo carnem & ossa. Ergo ego non sum Spiritus. Vide igitur ex sensu & sensibilibus: sensu nimirum visus, sensu tactus: ex visibilibus & tractabilibus se corpus esse non autem Spiritum edocet. Per sensum enim fides & gignitur & confirmatur. Ideoque Dominus spirituales ac coelestes demittit ad sensum istum corporeum. Papistae persuadere volunt nobis, corpus ipsum & sanguine ipsum Domini realiter & localiter esse in Coena Domini. Quod si nos velint docere, eo quo Christus discipulos suos modo docuit, hoc est per sensum & sensibilia, per visum, per tactum, tum aliquid eundem facerent: sed cum id non faciant, neque carnes, ossa & sanguinem ostendant, quae oculis videamus, manibus nostris palpemus, nihil faciunt. Neque nos unquam credemus, ita rem se habere. Neque etiam tenemur credere, imo si crederemus, graviter peccaremus, domininum, & abnegaremus veritatem corporis Domini. Quod non potest consistere sine visibilibus istis & tractabilibus, ne glorificatum quidem: ut no sit quod futilem iam suam distinctionem inter corpus humiliatum & glorificatum nobis offerant. Nota deinde Dominum post resurrectionem retinuisse in manibus & pedibus & latere suo vestigia vulnerum eorum quae inflictae sunt ei in cruce, & cicatrices conspicuas: cum tamen oportuerit glorificatum corpus resurgere sine notis omnibus infirmitatis. Cicatrices autem ex vulneribus acceptis notae sunt aliquae infirmitatis. Sic tamen placuit sese non uno tantum modo demittere nostra causa, & ad spatium quadraginta dierum non ingredi in plenam illam suam gloriam. Valebit enim hoc ad fidem resurrectionis Domini, non modo ipsum Dominum praesentem conspicere, sed videre etiam vulnerum vestigia quae inflicta sunt ei, ut crederent resurrexisse eum ipsum, qui iam no multo ante crucifixus fuit, non autem alium aliquem. Vtrum vero adhuc in coelis iam glorificatus retineat illa ipsa vulnerum vestigia necne, non disputo. Sed hoc scio, nos cum eum videbimus sicut est, & eum conspiciemus, quem transfiximus, nos, inquam tum recentem habituros memoriam illius crucis & illorum vulnerum. Vt enim crux Christi semper futura est in conspectu Patris, ita semper futura est in memoria nostra, ea enim ratione aeternus erit Pontifex & sempiternum sacrificium. Si cut autem pacatur ira Dei, ex inspecta illa eius cruce in sempiternum: sic quoque pacabitur conscientiae nostrae, ex sempiterna eiusdem crucis recordatione. Ex duobus enim principiis exurget laetitia & pax nostra in sempiternum, ex inspectione gloriae praesentis, & ex recordatione crucis praeteritae sempiterna.
units.tr: Eph. 4. 23. that he is not a spirit. He teaches that he is a body from the very senses: first sight, See, he says; then touch, Handle, he says. He shows his hands and feet to be seen and handled, in which there were plain traces of recent wounds. He teaches that he is not a spirit in this way: A spirit, he says, does not have flesh and bones. But I, as you see, have flesh and bones. Therefore I am not a spirit. Notice then that he teaches from the senses and sensible things: from sight and touch, that he is a body and not a spirit, from things visible and tangible. For faith is both born and strengthened through the senses. And therefore the Lord brings down spiritual and heavenly things to this bodily sense. The Papists want to persuade us that the body and blood of the Lord are really and locally present in the Lord's Supper. If they wished to teach us in the way Christ taught his disciples, that is through the senses and sensible things, through sight and touch, they would be doing something to the same effect; but since they do not do this, and do not show us flesh, bones and blood that we may see with our eyes and touch with our hands, they do nothing. Nor will we ever believe that the matter stands so, nor are we bound to believe it; indeed, if we did believe it, we would sin gravely, and deny the truth of the Lord's body. This cannot stand without those visible and tangible things, not even in the glorified body; so their distinction between the humbled and the glorified body, which they now offer us, is futile. Notice further that after the resurrection the Lord kept in his hands and feet, and in his side, the traces of the wounds that were inflicted on him on the cross, and visible scars; yet the glorified body ought to have risen without any marks of infirmity. But scars from received wounds are some marks of infirmity. Nevertheless it pleased him to humble himself in this way, not only once for our sake, and not to enter into his full glory for the space of forty days. For this served to establish the faith in the Lord's resurrection: not only to see the Lord himself present, but also to see the traces of the wounds inflicted on him, so that they might believe that the very one who had been crucified not long before had risen, and not some other. Whether he still retains those very traces of the wounds in heaven now that he is glorified, I do not dispute. But this I know: when we shall see him as he is, and shall behold him whom we pierced, we shall then, I say, have a fresh memory of that cross and those wounds. For as the cross of Christ will always be before the eyes of the Father, so it will always be in our memory; for by that means he will be an eternal High Priest and an everlasting sacrifice. And just as the wrath of God is appeased, from the contemplation of that cross, for ever, so too our conscience will be appeased by the everlasting remembrance of the same cross. For from two sources will arise our joy and peace for ever: from the contemplation of present glory, and from the everlasting remembrance of the past cross.

units.la: Adhuc autem ipsis, prae gaudio, non credentibus. Hactenus docuit eos per sensum & sensibilia. Adhuc autem ipsi non credunt, sed abripiuntur gaudio quodam, atque admiratione: gaudio autem isto & admiratione impedita videtur esse eorum fides. Ideoque dicitur (prae gaudio non credentibus) Quo autem hoc melius intelligatur, sciendum est quod maxime volumus fieri, id fere videri nobis impossibile: adeo ut quis illud euenisse dicat, non statim habeamus fidem. Gaudio tamen aliquo interea afficimur ex nuncio illo, & animus noster abripitur admiratione. Etsi quidem res sit quam vehementissime effectam esse volumus, feruet animus ac totus intumescit prae gaudio. Cum gaudio isto non est coniuncta proprie fides, siquidem fides sit sedati animi & tranquilli, quam rursus sequitur tranquillum & quietum quoddam gaudium, quale conceperunt discipuli Christi, postea cum iam constitisset de Domino suo, quod is ipse esset. Video hoc loco imaginem quandam futurae conditionis nostrae in aduentu illo Domini nostri. In primo aspectu eorum quae occurrus non vidit, neque auris audiuit, neque ingressa sunt cor hominis, abripietur subito gaudio quodam & admiratione animus noster, deinde sequetur sedata quaedam rerum caelestium apprehensio cum gaudio tranquillo in sempiternum. Vt e contra reprobi in primo aspectu
units.tr: Yet they did not believe, because of their joy. So far he has taught them through the senses and by sensible things. Yet they still do not believe; they are carried away by a certain joy and by wonder, and their faith seems to be hindered by that joy and wonder. Hence it is said: "not believing for joy." To understand this better, we should note that the thing we most want to happen often seems almost impossible to us, so much so that, when someone tells us it has happened, we do not believe it at once. Meanwhile we are stirred by some joy at that news, and our mind is carried away by wonder. Even when it is the very thing we most wanted to happen, the mind boils and swells entirely with joy. Faith, properly speaking, is not joined with this joy, since faith belongs to a calm and tranquil mind. Faith is followed by a tranquil and quiet joy, such as the disciples of Christ came to feel afterwards, when it was already established about their Lord that he was indeed himself. In this place I see a certain image of our future condition at that coming of our Lord. At the first sight of those things which "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man," our mind will suddenly be carried away by a certain joy and wonder; then there will follow a settled apprehension of heavenly things, with a tranquil joy, for ever. Conversely, the reprobate, at the first sight

units.la: Spectu & sensu horribilis illius irae, quam tantam esse, nunquam in vita ista suspicati sunt: primùm exhorrescent & attoniti fient supra modum: ēstque haec illa ἐκ ταραχῆς qua perturbatum fuisse legimus Dominum in horto primùm, paulò antequam caperetur. Deinde ἐκ ταραχῆς excipit ἀπηλονία, quae fuit secunda Domini perturbatio: qui sedatior est quidam sensus irae & constans quaedam doloris ineffabilis apprehensio in sempiternum. Vide de his Marc.14.33. Habetis hic escu-lentum aliquod. Ne audita quidem voce & salutatione tam familiari, cognoverunt eum, neque conspectis e- tiam manibus & pedibus, neque denique iam tractatis iis crediderunt: nunc luctatur Dominus cum infidelitate eorum, actionemque corporis propriam profert in conspectum ipsorum. Edere enim & bibere actio est corpora: edit autem non quod opus haberet ipse cibo mortali ac perituro cum esset immortalis iam, & Deoplenus: sed quod sic voluit, actione ista edendi, docere eos veritatem corporis sui, hoc est humiliatio-ne immortalis iam & glorificari corporis voluit eos docere, tunc enim cum iam factus esset immortalis, humilitate fuit. Tota enim vita Domini quantisper in terra moratus est, perpetua quaedam humiliatio fuit. Ante mortem se humiliavit ad mortem usque, mortem autem crucis: cum tamen esset in forma Dei, neque duceret rapinam parem esse cum Deo. Post resurrectionem se humiliavit totos quadraginta dies. Hoc idem obseruo, non tantùm, ut videamus quanta exitere Domini φιλανθρωπία & amor erga homines, sed etiam ut prouocentur omnes ad parem quasi compensationem, & ut sic humilianti se Domino obuiam veniant; praesertim cum etiam adhuc sese quotidie pergat humiliare in ministerio suo. Nam in ministerio hoc suo, inquit Paulus, precatur & orat nos Dominus, ut oblatam illam reconciliationem recipiamus: Quid est Deum humiliare se, si hoc non sit? Dum precatur & orat quotidie nos per legatos & ministros suos ut ipsi reconciliemur. Multiplex humiliatio ista Dei in Christo, ut ex ineffabili est misericordia affertque credentibus gratiam admirabilem, ita si contemnatur, neque recipiatur, necesse est iudicium nostrum multis modis aggrauet in illo die. Deinde ex hac edendi actione illud colligi poterit, Christum post resurrectionem retinuisse facultatem edendi & reliquas etiam facultates, quae vocantur naturales & animales, verum longe alia conditione: iam erant in eo glorificatae omnes & ex naturalibus & animalibus spirituales factae. Sequitur igitur nos quoque post resurrectionem retenturos easdem istas reipsa facultates, glorificatas tamen, & ita oppletas Deo, qui omnia erit in omnibus, ut nihil opus habituri simus istis, quibus nunc indigemus, cibo, potu, &c. Deus enim erit templum nostrum, & lucerna nostra erit agnus, &c. Quantisper in hac vita sumus, in qua Deus in nobis est, non omnia sed aliquid duntaxat, egebimus rebus istis externis ac caducis, quarum profecto usus, argumentum est non quidem perfectionis, sed imperfectionis & infirmitatis, atque adeo mortalitatis nostrae. Quaerere autem quid factum sit hoc cibo, in ventriculum Domini semel ingesto, an concoctio aliqua secuta sit, an conversio, an alimentum, an egestio aliqua excrementorum, parum attinet neque magnum habet usum. Respondere tamen potest eum qui omnia fecit ex nihilo, potuisse nullo negotio tantillum cibi in nihilum conuertere.
units.tr: and sense of that dreadful wrath, which they never suspected in this life to be so great, will first shudder and be stunned beyond measure. This is that "agitation" [ἐκ ταραχῆς] by which we read the Lord was first troubled in the garden, shortly before he was taken. Then after the agitation comes "a calmer state" [ἀπηλονία], which was the second disturbance of the Lord: a more settled sense of wrath, and a constant apprehension of ineffable grief, for ever. See on these things Mark 14:33. Have you anything to eat here? Even when they had heard his voice and so familiar a greeting, they did not recognise him; even when they had seen his hands and feet, and finally when they had handled him, they did not believe. Now the Lord struggles with their unbelief, and he brings his own bodily action before their sight. To eat and to drink is an action of bodies; and he ate, not because he had need of mortal and perishable food, since he was already immortal and full of God, but because he willed, by that action of eating, to teach them the truth of his body, that is, to teach them of his humiliation and of the glorification of his body; for when he was already made immortal, he was still in humility. For the whole life of the Lord, for as long as he dwelt on earth, was a continual humiliation. Before his death he humbled himself even unto death, and the death of the cross; although he was in the form of God, he did not think it robbery to be equal with God. After the resurrection he humbled himself for the whole forty days. I observe this same thing, not only so that we may see how great the Lord's love of humankind and his affection towards men is, but also so that all are provoked to a kind of equal return, and so come to meet the Lord who humbles himself; especially since even now he daily goes on humbling himself in his ministry. For in this ministry of his, as Paul says, the Lord beseeches and entreats us to receive that reconciliation offered to us: what is it for God to humble himself, if this is not so? While he daily beseeches and entreats us through his legates and ministers that we be reconciled to him. This manifold humiliation of God in Christ, which springs from ineffable mercy and brings admirable grace to believers, so if it is despised and not received, must necessarily weigh down our judgment in many ways on that day. Next, from this action of eating it can be gathered that Christ after the resurrection retained the power of eating and also the other faculties which are called natural and animal, but in a far different condition: all of them were now glorified in him, and from natural and animal they had been made spiritual. It follows, therefore, that we too after the resurrection shall retain those same faculties, yet glorified, and so filled with God, who will be all in all, so that we shall have no need of those things we now need, food, drink, and so on. For God will be our temple, and the Lamb will be our lamp, and so on. As long as we are in this life, in which God is in us, we shall need those external and perishable things, not in every respect but only in some measure; their use is certainly a sign not of perfection but of imperfection and weakness, and so of our mortality. But to ask what became of this food, once swallowed into the stomach of the Lord, whether any digestion followed, or any change, or nourishment, or any evacuation of waste, matters little and has no great use. Yet one may answer that he who made all things out of nothing could without any trouble have turned so small an amount of food into nothing.

units.la: Hi sunt sermones. Sequitur concio quaedam habita ad discipulos, in qua primum proponit duas necessitates, alteram de iis quae ipsi acciderunt, passione sua & resurrectione, alteram de praedicatione earundem rerum: deinde constituit eos praedicatores ac testes earundem rerum, confirmatis iis per promissionem Spiritus sancti. Quo autem magis persuadeat venturum Spiritum sanctum, iubet manere Hierosolymis, dum imbuantur virtute ex alto. Ut igitur reuertar ad primam illam necessitatem: hoc syllogismo eam concludit: Quaecunque scripta sunt de me in Mose, Prophetis & Psalmis, oportuit ea omnia impleri; At quae mihi acciderunt, passio, inquam, & resurrectio, de me scripta sunt in Mose, Prophetis & Psalmis: ergo hæc oportuit impleri omnia. Cum propositione coniuncta est tacita reprehensio discipulorum, quod obliti sunt sermonum, quos ante mortem cum apud eos esset, loquutus est. Q. d. Hi sunt sermones, &c. & tamen à vobis obliuioni traditi sunt. Admirabilem videmus tum fuisse ignorantiā discipulorum Christi, qui cum Moses, cum Prophetæ, cum Psalmi pleni essent istarum rerum, quæ Christo suo tempore acciderunt: tamen nihil istorum isti cognoverunt. Ad ignorantiam accessit obliuio quædam admirabilis, quòd cum de his non semel à Domino sint praemoniti, & quidem paulò ante mortem: tamen obliuioni omnia tradiderunt. Obliuionem autem exaggerat eo quod iam viderent, quæ paulò ante prædixit Dominus impleri, nempe passionem, resurrectionem: tamen non sunt recordati: vt videas in istis imaginem ignorantiæ, stupiditatis naturæ notæ, interdum excitati fuerimus à Domino vi Spiritus sancti aperientis oculos mentis nostræ, & reuocantis in memoriam nostram, quæ ex verbo Dei prædixit. Habes rursus in Christo exemplum misericordiæ ineffabilis erga suos, quos non finit in perpetuum torpescere, & ad mortem vsque consopiri, fetos suo tempore expergefacit. Hæc enim ipsa reprehensio istorum est summæ misericordiæ: præstat enim reprehendi & omnibus modis quassari in hac vita, ad hoc vt excitemur ex somno isto tam profundo ac lethali, quàm post hanc vitam in æternum perire. Deinde in propositione habes partitionem veteris testamenti in Moses, Prophetas, & Psalmos. Psalmos à Prophetis distinguit, cum tamen in Psalmis habeantur Prophetiæ de Christo venturo plenissimæ. Distinguit autem eos à Prophetis, vt mihi videtur, propter argumenti principalis diuersitatem. Principale enim argumentum conspicitur ex ipso Psalmorum nomine, quod sint cantiones quas Dauid & cecinit Deo suo, & scriptis post se reliquit. Sub argumento illo tanquam principali continentur Prophetiæ de Christo: Cuius quidem figura quædam eáque expressa maxime & viua extitit Dauid: Eáque etiam re aliqua est differentia inter prophetias Dauidis & aliarum prophetiarum.Dum prophetat Dauid,ipse perpetuo sustinet personam Christi, vt qui fuerit eius typus, & omnia quæ Dauidi acciderunt in vita, typicè ipsi acciderunt: Alij autem Prophetæ non sic inter prophetandum sustinent personam Christi venturi. Alias tamen Psalmi Dauidis aggregantur prophetiis & ipse Dauid Prophetis, cùm veteris testamenti partitio fit in Legem & Prophetas,vtvidimus apud Lucam antea hoc ipso capite. Tum ad assumptionem syllogismi venio. At ita, inquit, scriptum est. Hoc est, scriptū est in Mose, Prophetis & Psalmis de resurrectione Domini. Hanc assumptionem adductis in medium scripturæ locis ex Mose, Prophetis & Psalmis, probatam esse à Domino facile conspici potest ab hoc versu inserto à Luca: nempe quòd Dominus aperuit mentes eorum, vt scripturas intelligerent, ab ipso nimirum tum adductas & allegatas ad probandam assumptionem istam.Nota hoc loco Dominum cum scripturarum allatarum testimonio coniunxisse Spiritum suum sanctum, qui interius aperuit discipulorum mentes, ad hoc, vt allatas à se scripturas possent intelligere. At hæc demum fuit efficax prædicatio & Scripturarum expositio, cùm is qui prædicauit auditores suos, & interius & exterius docuit.Hoc autem Domini proprium fuit, docere interius per Spiritum suum, quos docuit exterius per verbum. Paulus enim plantare potest, Apollos rigare: hoc est exterius docere, sed Dominus est qui dat incrementum, hoc est interius docet. Cùm ad sermonem Pauli apertum est cor Lydiæ purpurariæ, dictum est ibi non Paulum quidem sed Dominum ipsum aperuisse cor Lydiæ vt attenderet iis quæ tum dicebantur à Paulo.Notandum deinde non alias, quàm quo tempore exponerentur Scripturæ, apertum esse cor discipulorum. Ergo ad solam scripturarum explicationem illuminatio ista per Spiritum sanctum, & operatio ista Spiritus in cordibus fit.Valeant igitur omnes illæ reuelationes phanaticorum rum hominum & ϑεοπνευστοι illi sine verbo scripto ip-siusque explicatione. Valeat ille Spiritus Papistarum, quem efficacem dicunt esse & operari ad praedicatio-nem etiam figmentorum humanorum, quę non modo non reperiuntur in scripturis, sed cum iis plane pugnant. Est enim re ipsa non Spiritus Christi, sed efficacia Sathanę: de qua 2. Thess. 2. 9. Notandum hic postremo est quanta sit humanę mentis cęcitas & quanta opere per naturam cęcutiamus ad lucem illam veri Dei: ut non sit quod quis mihi ostentet liberum arbitrium Papistarum: hoc est congenitum illud lumen & rectum iudicium, ut & voluntatem ex aliqua parte rectam: id enim est, quod intelligunt Papistę nomine liberi arbitrij. Nempe aliquid vitę illius Dei, ut eam vocat Apostolus, post lapsum hominis reliquum. Non est, inquam, quod mihi ostentet quis liberum illud arbitrium, cum agitur de verbo Dei recte intelligendo, cum ne mica quidem rectę mentis aut iudicij, rectę voluntatis reperiatur in homine, cum ad Scripturas intelligendas ventum est. Potest quidem aliquid videre beneficio etiam mentis huius naturalis. Sed quàm citò euanescit illud: Et hoc ipsum quod videt atque intelligit iudicio mentis & ratiocinationis suis depravat, ut videre est Rom. 1. Non est deinde quod quis loquatur mihi de ingenio hominis, de naturali solertia, de acumine iudicij, de alijs deniq; idgenus naturę dotibus & facultatibus: praesertim cum hoc habeat Paulus, Si quis, inquit, videtur sibi sapiens esse, fiat stultus ut sit sapiens. Hoc est deponat omnem fiduciam sapientię, ingenij & acuminis sui: accedat autem ad audiendum Dei verbum, tanquam puer aut infans, quemadmodum monuit Christus. In regno enim cœlorum oportet nos pueros esse. Naturalia ista sunt aliquid, fateor, si sanctificentur luce illa Spiritus sancti: Sine Spiritu autem sanctificationis magis obsunt quàm prosunt: φρόνημα enim σαρκὸς inimicitia est adversus Deum. Quaeri hic potest annon iam ante hoc tempus apertae sunt mentes discipulorum, cum iam circiter triennium audiunt docentem Dominum? Respondeo hoc non
units.tr: These are the words. There follows a certain sermon delivered to the disciples. In it he first sets out two necessities: one concerning the things that happened to himself, his suffering and resurrection, and one concerning the preaching of these same things. Then he appoints them as preachers and witnesses of these same things, confirming them with the promise of the Holy Spirit. To persuade them the more that the Holy Spirit is coming, he bids them remain at Jerusalem until they are clothed with power from on high. So, to return to that first necessity, he concludes it with this syllogism: whatever has been written about me in Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms, all of it had to be fulfilled. But what has happened to me, namely the suffering and the resurrection, has been written about me in Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms. Therefore all of this had to be fulfilled. Joined to the premise is a tacit rebuke of the disciples, because they had forgotten the words he spoke to them while he was still with them before his death. It is as if he said: "These are the words," etc., and yet you have let them slip from your memory. We see here the remarkable ignorance of Christ's disciples: although Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms were full of these things that happened to Christ in his time, they understood none of them. To the ignorance was added a certain remarkable forgetfulness, because they had been forewarned of these things by the Lord more than once, and that only shortly before his death; yet they consigned it all to oblivion. He heightens the forgetfulness by the fact that they were already seeing what the Lord had lately foretold being fulfilled, namely the suffering and the resurrection; yet they did not recall it. Here you may see a picture of ignorance and of the stupidity of our nature; and sometimes we are roused by the Lord, through the power of the Holy Spirit opening the eyes of our mind and recalling to our memory what God foretold in his Word. In Christ you have again an example of his unspeakable mercy towards his own, whom he does not allow to grow numb forever, nor to be lulled to death, but awakens them in his own time when they are his cherished ones. For this very rebuke of theirs is a sign of the highest mercy: it is better to be reproved and shaken in every way in this life, so that we may be roused from a sleep so deep and deadly, than to perish forever after this life. Next, in the premise you have the division of the Old Testament into Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms. He distinguishes the Psalms from the Prophets, although the Psalms contain the most complete prophecies of the Christ who was to come. He distinguishes them from the Prophets, as it seems to me, because of the difference in their principal subject. For the principal subject is seen from the very name of the Psalms, that they are songs which David sang to his God and left behind him in writing. Under this subject, as its principal theme, the prophecies concerning Christ are contained. David was a certain figure of him, and a most express and lively one. There is also this difference between David's prophecies and those of the other prophets: while David prophesies, he constantly sustains the person of Christ, as one who was his type, and all that happened to David in his life happened to him typically. The other prophets, however, do not in their prophesying sustain the person of the Christ who is to come in this way. Nevertheless, David's Psalms are numbered among the prophecies, and David himself among the Prophets, since the division of the Old Testament is made into the Law and the Prophets, as we saw earlier in Luke in this same chapter. Now I come to the assumption of the syllogism. But thus, he says, it is written. That is, it is written in Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms concerning the resurrection of the Lord. That this assumption was proved by the Lord, by bringing forward passages of Scripture from Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms, can easily be seen from the verse inserted by Luke: namely that the Lord opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures, the very passages which he himself had then brought forward and alleged in order to prove that assumption.
