Note here that the Lord joined to the testimony of the Scriptures he had cited his Holy Spirit, who inwardly opened the minds of the disciples so that they could understand the Scriptures he had cited. Yet this preaching and exposition of the Scriptures was then effective, since he who preached taught his hearers both inwardly and outwardly. Indeed it was proper to the Lord to teach inwardly through his Spirit those whom he taught outwardly through the Word. For Paul may plant, Apollos water; that is, to teach outwardly; but it is the Lord who gives the increase; that is, he teaches inwardly. When at Paul's sermon the heart of Lydia, the seller of purple, was opened, it is said there that it was not Paul but the Lord himself who opened the heart of Lydia, so that she attended to what was then being said by Paul. Note further that the hearts of the disciples were opened only at the time when the Scriptures were being expounded. Therefore this enlightenment by the Holy Spirit, and this working of the Spirit in hearts, takes place only in the explanation of the Scriptures. Let all those revelations of the fanatical men, and those "God-breathed" ones [θεοπνευστοι], without the written word and its explanation, be of no account. Let that spirit of the Papists be of no account, which they say is effective and works in the preaching even of human inventions, which not only are not found in the Scriptures but plainly contradict them. For in truth this is not the Spirit of Christ but the working of Satan, of which we read in 2 Thess. 2. 9. Finally, it must be noted here how great is the blindness of the human mind, and how much by nature we are blind to that light of the true God. So there is no reason for anyone to show me the free will of the Papists, that is, that innate light and right judgement, and a will that is in some part upright; for this is what the Papists mean by the name of free will: some remnant of that life of God, as the Apostle calls it, left in man after the fall. There is no reason, I say, for anyone to show me that free will when the question is of rightly understanding the Word of God, since not a crumb of a right mind or judgement, of a right will, is to be found in man when it comes to understanding the Scriptures. Indeed a man may see something even by the aid of this natural mind. But how quickly that vanishes! And what he sees and understands he corrupts by his own judgement and reasoning, as may be seen in Rom. 1. Nor is there any reason for anyone to speak to me of man's talent, of natural skill, of the keenness of judgement, or of other gifts and faculties of this kind of nature, especially since Paul says: "If anyone thinks himself to be wise, let him become a fool, that he may be wise." That is, let him put aside all confidence in his wisdom, talent and keenness, and come to hear the Word of God like a child or infant, as Christ taught. For in the kingdom of heaven we must be children. Those natural endowments are something, I grant, if they are sanctified by that light of the Holy Spirit; but without the Spirit of sanctification they do more harm than good, for "the mind of the flesh [φρόνημα σαρκὸς] is enmity against God." Here it may be asked whether the minds of the disciples had not already been opened before this time, since for about three years they had been hearing the Lord teach. I answer that this

units.la: ita intelligendum esse, quasi nulla fuerit omnino cordis eorum apertio ante hoc tempus: sed quod tamen non fuerit ante resurrectionem, quanta post resurrectionem Domini coeperit esse: quo quidem tempore, vt caput ipsum adiit gloriam suam, ita in membris suis coepit esse efficacior, quàm antea. Spiritus enim operatio in membris pendet ex capitis ipsius constitutione. Conclusio, vt ad eam tandem venia-mus, infert necessitatem passionis simul & resurrectionis; atque ideo necessitatem quasi imponit fidei eorum, qua credant eum resurrexisse. Oportet enim ad hoc vt credamus in Euangelium, hoc est in historiam quæ est de Christo, necessitas quædam nobis imponatur: hæc nimirum qua sciamus aliter non potuisse fieri quin Christus pateretur primum, deinde resurgeret iuxta narrationem & historiam Euangelicam. Intelligentes enim necessitatem hanc rei gerendæ, iam facilius eò adducimur ad credendum historiæ rei gestæ. Necessitas autem hæc addiscitur ex prædictionibus Mosis & Prophetarum in veteri scriptura. De prædictionibus enim iis ita nobis sentiendum est, quod impleri eas suo tempore oportuerit. Discè igitur quis sit vsus veteris Scripturæ & prædictionum illarum de Christo, & quàm necessaria sit ad fidem noui testamenti.
units.tr: is not to be understood as though there were no opening of their hearts at all before this time; but that it was not as great before the resurrection of the Lord as it began to be afterwards. At that time, as the Head himself entered into his glory, so in his members it began to be more effective than before. For the working of the Spirit in the members depends upon the constitution of the Head himself. As to the conclusion, to come at last to it: it draws out the necessity of the suffering and the resurrection together; and therefore it as it were imposes a necessity upon their faith, so that they may believe that he has risen. For in order that we may believe the Gospel, that is, the history which concerns Christ, a certain necessity must be laid upon us, namely that we may know that it could not have happened otherwise than that Christ should first suffer and then rise again, according to the narrative and history of the Gospel. For when we understand the necessity of this thing being done, we are the more readily led to believe the history of what was done. This necessity, moreover, is learned from the predictions of Moses and the Prophets in the Old Scripture. For concerning those predictions we ought to think this: that they had to be fulfilled in their own time. Learn therefore what use the Old Scripture and those predictions about Christ have, and how necessary they are to the faith of the New Testament.

units.la: Et prædicari in eius nomine. Hactenus de prima necessitate rerum ipsarum: sequitur altera necessitas prædicationis earum rerum. Ad fidem enim nostram & confirmandam, necessaria est prædicatio Euangelij. Quomodo, inquit Apostolus, invocabunt eum in quem non crediderunt? Quomodo credent ei de quo non audierint? Quomodo autem audient absque prædicante? Quomodo prædicabunt nisi missi fuerint? Ideo Christus cùm sciret hanc necessitatem, veniens ipse Euangelizauit pacem, Et minister dictus est circumcisionis. Ascendens autem in cœlos dedit alios quidem Apostolos, alios vero Prophetas, alios autem Euangelistas, alios autem Pastores & Doctores, qui nimirum omnes prædicarent ad reditum vsque ipsius pacis hoc Euangelium. Dedit quoque Spiritum sanctum, sed eum quidem per prædicationem. {a}nem Euangelij ministrandum. Vnde Paulus vocat Euangelium hoc Spiritus ministerium. Is eius nomine. Circumscriptio est huius prædicationis ex variis circumstantiis; 1. in cuius nomine, hoc est cuius authoritate, nepe Christi. Non est enim aliud nomen sub cælo, quod datum sit inter homines, per quod oporteat nos seruari. Christus ipse suo nomine & authoritate propria prædicauit. Prædicauit enim tanquam authoritatem habens: & dixit, Amen, amen dico vobis: hoc est, meo ipsius nomine dico. Alij autem post Christum omnes prædicant nomine & authoritate Christi, in quorum prædicatione conspicitur ipsius Christi authoritas, si modò Christum habeant ante oculos, & eius solius gloriam in prædicando quærant. Paulus quia dixit se nihil scire, nisi Iesum Christum, eumque crucifixum, ideo dixit postea, se prædicasse cum demonstratione Spiritualis potentiæ. Doctores autem illi Corinthij cùm se potius quàm Dominum spectarint, ideo cum persuasoriis duntaxat humanæ sapientiæ verbis prædicasse dicuntur à Paulo. Quemadmodum igitur ipsum Christi nomen efficax est: ita prædicatio in nomine ipsius efficax est: & Euangelium in ipsius nomine, est potentia Dei in salutem credenti. Hæc autem efficacia Euangelij profluit à nomine & authoritate Christi, arguitque quanta sit potentia ipsius & authoritas, arguit, inquam, ei datam esse omnem authoritatem in cœlis & in terra, & euectum cum in summâ sublimitatem: datúmque illi nomen quod est supra omne nomen.
units.tr: And to be preached in his name. So far concerning the first necessity of the things themselves. There follows a second necessity, that of preaching those things. For the preaching of the Gospel is necessary both to establish and to confirm our faith. How, says the Apostle, shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? How shall they believe him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they be sent? Therefore Christ, knowing this necessity, coming himself preached peace, and was called a minister of the circumcision. Ascending into heaven, however, he gave some indeed to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers, who would all preach this Gospel until his return to bring peace. He also gave the Holy Spirit, but to be ministered through the preaching of the Gospel. Hence Paul calls this Gospel the ministry of the Spirit. In his name. This preaching is delimited by various circumstances: (1) in whose name, that is, by whose authority, namely Christ's. For there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved. Christ himself preached in his own name and by his own proper authority. For he preached as one having authority, and said, Verily, verily, I say unto you, that is, I say it in my own name. But all others after Christ preach in the name and by the authority of Christ, and in their preaching the authority of Christ himself is seen, provided they keep Christ before their eyes and seek his glory alone in preaching. Because Paul said that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified, therefore he later said that he preached with a demonstration of spiritual power. But those Corinthian teachers, looking to themselves rather than to the Lord, are said by Paul to have preached only with persuasive words of human wisdom. Just as the name of Christ itself is effective, so preaching in his name is effective, and the Gospel in his name is the power of God unto salvation to the one who believes. Now this efficacy of the Gospel flows from the name and authority of Christ, and it shows how great his power and authority are; it shows, I say, that all authority in heaven and in earth has been given to him, and that he has been raised to the highest sublimity, and that the name which is above every name has been bestowed upon him.

units.la: Refipiscentiam & remissionem. Hæc sunt quæ in nomine eius prædicare oportet. Duo sunt quibus comprehensum est totum Euangelium: constat enim primùm doctrinâ Refipiscentiæ, deinde doctrina Remissionis peccatorum. Refipiscentiæ doctrina est partim quidem legis: cuius summa est, Maledictus omnis qui non manserit in omnibus quæ scripta sunt in libro legis huius, vt faciat ea. Hinc horrores illi & terrores conscientiæ: partim vero Euangelij doctrina, cuius summa hæc est, Quisquis crediderit seruabitur: hinc dolor ille secundum Deum existit, hoc est, propter offensum tam misericordem & clementem Patrem. Dolor autem hic qui
units.tr: Repentance and remission. These are the things which must be preached in his name. There are two things by which the whole Gospel is comprehended: for it consists first of the doctrine of repentance, and then of the doctrine of the remission of sins. The doctrine of repentance is partly that of the Law, whose sum is, Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of this law, to do them. Hence come those horrors and terrors of conscience. Partly, however, it is the doctrine of the Gospel, whose sum is this: Whoever believes shall be saved. Hence that sorrow arises which is according to God, that is, on account of having offended so merciful and gracious a Father. This sorrow which

units.la: {a} Philip. 2.9. est secundum Deum efficit refipiscentiam & conuersionem ad Deum. In resipiscentia igitur est fides, quia sine fide non fit vlla ad Deum conuersio. Quod autem ad refipiscentiam necessaria sit doctrina Euangelij, apparet ex loco illo, qui est Matth. 3. 2. Resipiscite, inquit, appropinquavit enim regnum coelorum. Ratio resipiscentiae & argumentum hic sumptum est ab aduentu & praesentia Christi, quod est Euangelium de Christo. Doctrina remissionis peccatorum, est doctrina Euangelij, quae resipiscentiae fuit. Nam eadem doctrina, quae efficit resipiscentiam, eadem inquam, remissionis est ministra. Nam non est statuendum resipiscentiam & remissionem peccatorum tempore distincta esse. Eodem enim quo resipiscimus momento, conscientiam habemus remissionis peccatorum nostrorum, & audimus quasi ex ore ipsius Dei, absolutoriam illam sententiam. Fieri quidem potest, ut quis posterius tempore ministret resipiscenti peccatorum remissionem. Si quorum remiseritis peccata, remittentur eis, &c. Atqui eodem temporis momento, quo resipiscimus, Deus dat nobis remissionem peccatorum nostrorum. Ista tamen distincta sunt natura ordine, & prior quidem est resipiscentia, tanquam praeparatio quaedam animi ad remissionem: posterior vero remissio, quae est applicatio gratiae ad animam sic iam praeparatam. Praeparatio ad gratiam est cum dolore aliquo: at applicatio est cum sensu quodam insignis gaudij. Hinc gaudium illud veniens fidelis animae, non sentitur, nisi expressum ex dolore, & ex corde contrito: & gaudium ineffabile ac gloriosum, cum suspiriis inenarrabilibus coniunctum est: hoc est gaudium peccatoris dum hic viuit, ex dolore perpetuo expressum est. Quandiu enim peccatores sumus (sumus autem in tota ista vita) tandiu nos in dolore oportet esse. At vero gaudium nostrum, cum plene perfecteque iam liberati fuerimus a peccato, erit purum ac sincerum, sine dolore. Atque tum abstergentur ab oculis nostris omnes lachrymae: quia nimirum post hanc vitam, non erimus amplius peccatores. Apud omnes gentes. Cum praedicari oporteat omnibus gentibus resipiscentiam, sequitur necessario omnes gentes peccatum inuasisse. Omnes enim peccauerunt & deficiuntur glo-
units.tr: {a} Philip. 2.9. is of God works repentance and conversion to God. Repentance therefore includes faith, since without faith there is no conversion to God at all. That the doctrine of the Gospel is necessary for repentance appears from that passage in Matthew 3.2: Repent, he says, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. The reason for repentance and the argument drawn here come from the coming and presence of Christ, which is the Gospel about Christ. The doctrine of the forgiveness of sins is the doctrine of the Gospel, and it belongs to repentance. For the same doctrine that produces repentance is also the minister of forgiveness. We must not suppose that repentance and the forgiveness of sins are separated in time. For at the very moment we repent, we have the assurance that our sins are forgiven, and we hear that absolving sentence as if from the mouth of God himself. It is indeed possible that someone should afterwards, in time, minister the forgiveness of sins to the penitent: If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them, and so on. Yet at the same moment in time when we repent, God gives us the forgiveness of our sins. These things are nevertheless distinct in nature and order: repentance comes first, as a certain preparation of the mind for forgiveness, and forgiveness comes afterwards, as the application of grace to the soul so prepared. The preparation for grace is with some sorrow, but the application is with a certain sense of remarkable joy. Hence that joy which comes to the faithful soul is not felt except as it springs from sorrow and a contrite heart; and that joy, unspeakable and glorious, is joined with inexpressible sighs. This is the joy of the sinner while he lives here, and it is always expressed through sorrow. For as long as we are sinners (and we are sinners through this whole life), so long we must be in sorrow. But our joy, when we have been fully and perfectly freed from sin, will be pure and sincere, without sorrow. And then all tears will be wiped from our eyes, because, of course, after this life we shall no longer be sinners. Among all nations. Since repentance must be preached to all nations, it necessarily follows that all nations have been overtaken by sin. For all have sinned and fall short of the glo-

units.la: Rom. 3. 23. & 11. 32. ria Dei: & conclusit Deus omnes in contumacia. Ergo resipiscentia praedicanda omnibus gentibus, infert peccati amplitudinem. Rursus cum praedicari oporteat omnibus gentibus remissionem peccatorum, sequitur gratiam Christi ad omnes patere. Iustitia Dei est in & super omnes qui credunt. Ergo remissio peccatorum praedicanda omnibus necessario infert superabundantem gratiam. Nam cum abundat peccatum, superabundat gratia. Ante Christi aduentum gratia Dei conclusa quasi erat intra solius Iudaeae fines: at postquam iam aduenit Christus, intra tam angustos limites concludi non potuit, quia erat magnitudine & copia: ergo oportuit post Christi aduentum copiose iam praedicari gratiam tam copiosam. Quamobrem iniuriam summam necesse est faciant gratiae Dei, qui impediunt ipsius praedicationem. De sacrilegis istis loquor, qui ad se rapuerunt olim bona illa Ecclesiastica quibus oportuit alii dispensatores & ministros gratiae. Incipiendo ab Hierosolym. Etsi omnibus praedicanda sit gratia, tamen admonet Christus id certo quodam ordine oportere fieri: ac primum omnium, Iudaeis, hoc est, veteri illi populo Dei praedicandam esse: Iudaeorum enim in aduentu Christi haec fuit praerogativa ordinis: Vobis necesse fuit primum exponi sermonem Dei, Act. 13. 46. Hunc ordinem in Epistolis Pauli passim seruari videas, idque non solum quoad gratiam, quae est in hac vita, sed etiam quod ad gloriam quae in altera est. Gloria, honor & pax, cuiuis operanti bonum, tum Iudaeo imprimis, tum & Graeco. Contra autem propter contemptum gratiae ad infidelem Iudaeum priori loco pertinebit. Indignatio, oppressio & angustia aduersus omnem animam hominis perpetrantis malum, tum Iudaei imprimis, tum etiam Graeci. Disce ergo quod qui semel praerogatiuam obtinuerunt, semper praerogatiuam obtinebunt, nisi sua ipsorum culpa aliis postponantur.
units.tr: Rom. 3. 23. & 11. 32. ry of God, and God has shut up all under disobedience. Therefore the repentance that must be preached to all nations shows how great sin is. Again, since the forgiveness of sins must be preached to all nations, it follows that the grace of Christ extends to all. The righteousness of God is upon all and over all who believe. Therefore the forgiveness of sins, which must be preached to all, necessarily implies a superabundant grace, for where sin abounds, grace abounds all the more. Before the coming of Christ, the grace of God was, as it were, shut up within the borders of Judea alone; but once Christ had come, it could not be confined within such narrow limits, because of its greatness and abundance. So after Christ's coming it was necessary that so abundant a grace should now be preached abundantly. Therefore those who hinder its preaching do the greatest wrong to the grace of God. I am speaking of those sacrilegious men who have seized for themselves those ecclesiastical goods which ought to have gone to others as stewards and ministers of grace. Beginning from Jerusalem. Although grace is to be preached to all, Christ nevertheless indicates that this must be done in a certain fixed order: first of all it is to be preached to the Jews, that is, to that old people of God, for this was the prerogative of the Jews in the order of Christ's coming: It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you, Acts 13.46. You will see this order kept throughout the Epistles of Paul, and not only with regard to the grace which is in this life, but also with regard to the glory which is in the next: Glory, honour and peace to everyone who does good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. On the other hand, because of contempt for grace, the unbelieving Jew will belong first to the other side: Indignation and wrath, tribulation and anguish, on every soul of man who does evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek. Learn therefore that those who once obtained the prerogative will always keep it, unless by their own fault they are set after others.

units.la: Vos autem estis horum testes Secunda pars sermonis Christi, qua imponit discipulis munus hoc praedicandi, ipsosque emittit ad annunciandum Euangelium. Non enim minus necessaria est missio eorum qui praedicant, quam ipsa praedicatio. Quomodo praedicabunt nisi mittantur? Hoc toto loco obseruo nihil de Christo, ipsius Euangelio,
units.tr: But you are witnesses of these things. This is the second part of Christ's discourse, in which he lays this task of preaching upon the disciples and sends them out to announce the Gospel. For the sending of those who preach is no less necessary than the preaching itself: How shall they preach unless they are sent? In this whole passage I observe nothing about Christ, about his Gospel,

units.la: Discrimen patefactionis. ipsius denique ministris fieri temere: sed omnia necessitate quadam & certa Dei prouidentia. Neque quisquam est fidelium ministrorum, qui non mittatur ab ipso, & cuius non faciat ipse delectum. Quod si nihil horum fiat absque Dei prouidentia, neque etiam ministrorum quisquam praedicet sine speciali illa prouidentia: sequitur ne vnum quidem audire praedicantem ministrum aliquem sine eadem Dei prouidentia. Quemadmodum enim specialis est prouidentia erga praedicatorem Euangelij: ita quoque specialis est prouidentia erga auditorem eiusdem praedicati: vt & praedicator & auditor Deum in prouidentia & in gratia sua glorificet. Et si omnes oportet mitti a Deo: tamen id non fit sine discrimine aliquo.
units.tr: The difference of revelation. Finally, nothing is done rashly to his ministers, but everything happens by a certain necessity and by the sure providence of God. There is no faithful minister who is not sent by him, and whom he does not himself choose. If nothing of these things happens without the providence of God, then no minister preaches without that special providence either. It follows that no one hears even a single minister preaching without the same providence of God. For just as there is a special providence toward the preacher of the Gospel, so there is also a special providence toward the hearer of the same preaching, so that both preacher and hearer glorify God in his providence and in his grace. And although all ought to be sent by God, this does not happen without some difference.

units.la: Quidam enim immediate a Deo sine horum ministerio missi sunt, vt hoc loco Apostoli, & ante eos Prophetae: alij vero, vt hodierno die ministri mediate a Deo mittuntur per hominum ministerium: in quibus mittendis oportet eos quorum interest, & quorum ministerio vtitur Deus, oportet, inquam, diligenter attendere ad Dei voluntatem, an velit eos ab ipsis mitti necne: hoc est, vt ex voluntate Dei mittant eos. Quos enim misit Christus Apostolos, misit eos ex voluntate Dei Patris: hoc est, Deus Pater misit eos per filium Iesum Christum. Sic quos mittunt homines, oportet mittant eos ex voluntate Dei Patris & filij. Cognoscitur autem voluntas Dei & Christi ex illis, vt sic dicam, gratiis & Spiritus sancti donis, quae recensset Apostolus 1. Timoth. 3.1. &c. & Tit. 1.6. Sunt autem ex iis quaedam dona quae cum aliis Christianis communia sunt, quaedam vero quae propria sunt, ex quibus est illa ad docendum & gubernandum aptitudo. Sed non est praetereundum hoc loco, qui demum sint ij quos mittit Dominus: nempe qui paulo ante defecerunt turpiter a Domino suo, qui etiam post resurrectionem tam obstinati fuerunt & ad credendum difficiles. Hi nimirum sunt quos nunc mittit Dominus: vt scias tantum abfuisse ab eo vt fuerint isti idonei, qui a Domino mitterentur (Et ad haec quis idoneus? &, Nec enim idonei sumus ex nobismetipsis ad cogitandum quicquam velut ex nobis ipsis) vt e contra inidonei plane fuerint & inepti, pleni malorum qui cum ministerio ex diametro pugnant. gnarunt, adeo vt ipsi ex tenebris facti sint lux, iuxta illud Pauli, Qui dixit vt e tenebris lux exisseret, is est qui splenduit in cordibus nostris, nempe tenebricosis istis, & splendendo in iis lucem ex tenebris eduxit. Non secus atque in creatione dixit, vt e tenebris lux splendesceret, huius rei insignis quidam testis fuit Apostolus Paulus, qui cum prius esset blasphemus, persequutor, iniuriosus: et blasphemo, persequutore, iniurioso, factus est non modo Christianus, sed Apostolus. Vide igitur quantum fit, quamque operosum illud, dum ex homine, fidelis Dei minister efficitur. Magnum quidem illud est, facere ex homine Christianum hominem: sed illud maius, facere ex homine ministrum Dei, ac dispensatorem mysteriorum Christi. Elegisse autem videtur tales, tamque ad tantum illud ministerium inidoneos: ad hoc, vt Apostoli ipsi primi omnium exempla fierent misericordiae illius diuinae superabundantis omnibus aliis & toti posteritati: vtque ipsi in ministerio suo ostenderent lenitatem erga omnes quantumuis peccatores, conscij nimirum sibi illius suae miseriae, quae fuerat iam ante missionem & Dei vocationem: vnde Paulus non sine experientia sua illud praedicauit, vbi auctum est peccatum, ibi superabundauit gratia.
units.tr: Some were sent immediately by God, without the ministry of men, as the Apostles were in this place, and the Prophets before them. Others, however, as ministers today, are sent by God mediately, through the ministry of men. In sending these, those whom it concerns, and through whose ministry God works, ought, I say, to attend carefully to the will of God, whether he wishes them to be sent by these men or not; that is, that they send them according to the will of God. For those whom Christ sent as Apostles, he sent according to the will of God the Father; that is, God the Father sent them through his Son Jesus Christ. So those whom men send ought to be sent according to the will of God the Father and the Son. The will of God and of Christ, however, is known from those gifts of grace and of the Holy Spirit, so to speak, which the Apostle enumerates in 1 Timothy 3:1 etc. and Titus 1:6. Some of these gifts are common to them with other Christians, while others are peculiar to them, among which is that aptitude for teaching and governing. But it must not be passed over here who exactly are those whom the Lord sends: namely, men who shortly before had shamefully deserted their Lord, and who, even after the resurrection, were so obstinate and slow to believe. These, surely, are those whom the Lord now sends, so that you may know how far they were from being fit men to be sent by the Lord (And who is fit for these things? and, "For we are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves"). On the contrary, they were plainly unfit and unskilled, full of evils, which fight diametrically against the ministry, so that they themselves were made light out of darkness, according to that saying of Paul: "God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, is he who has shone in our hearts," namely in those dark hearts, and by shining in them he drew light out of darkness. Just as in creation he said that light should shine out of darkness, the Apostle Paul was a notable witness to this thing: since before he was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and injurious, he was made not only a Christian but an Apostle, though a blasphemer, persecutor and injurious man. See then how great and how laborious a thing it is when a man is made a faithful minister of God. It is indeed a great thing to make a man a Christian; but it is greater to make a man a minister of God and a steward of the mysteries of Christ. Yet he seems to have chosen such men, so unfit for so great a ministry, for this purpose: that the Apostles themselves might be the first of all examples of that divine mercy which abounds toward all others and toward all posterity; and that in their ministry they might show gentleness toward all, however great sinners, being conscious, of course, of their own misery, which had existed even before their sending and the calling of God. Hence Paul preached, not without his own experience, that "where sin abounded, grace did much more abound."

units.la: Et ecce ego mittam promissum. Animat eos ad suscipiendum in se hoc munus Apostolatus à Spiritu sancto & extraordinariis illis Spiritus sancti donis, quae iam olim promissa sunt: praesertim apud Ioelem Prophetam, vt legimus Act. 2. 7. Effundam ex Spiritu meo in quamuis carnem, &c. Nota hoc in loco primum, filium conferre suo tempore Spiritum & dona Spiritus, quae Pater iam ante promiserat: hinc mensura doni Christi dicitur Ephes. 4.7. Et eodem capite postea vers. 10. vt impleret, inquit, omnia, dedit alios quidem Apostolos, &c. Ex quo sequitur quod hoc superius est & prius, nempe iam filium ante accepisse a Patre omnem gratiam & omnia dona Spiritus sancti, cum ipso Spiritu sancto: & Patrem ea omnia dediisse filio suo primum, non autem nobis. Pater diligit filium, & dedit ei in manum eius omnem potestatem, & in ipso sunt omnes thesauri sapientiae ac cognitionis abscondite. Ex quo sequitur & ea darent. aliud, quod & hoc prius est; nempe meritum Spiritus sancti, & omnium ipsius donorum esse filij solius : qui enim solus primum accepit omnem gratiam, is solus omnem eam promeritus est : omnis autem gratia ista quæ datur nobis charè constitit Christo : nobis enim hanc omnem acquisiuit, non minori pretio quàm sanguinis fui. Quomodo igitur, inquies, Spiritus sanctus cum donis ipsius ad nos peruenit ? Respondeo, non per meritum aliquod nostrum, sed per gratiam Patris & filij meram. Nos ex plenitudine eius accepimus gratiam pro gratia. In ipso est thesaurus omnis cognitionis & sapientiæ : In ipso inhabitat omnis plenitudo deitatis corporaliter. Nos autem in eo fumus complepti : dum nimirum in eum credimus. Atque hæc est beneficentia filij qua quod ipse charè admodum emit, dat nobis gratis. Noftis enim beneficentiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi, &c. 2. Corinth.
units.tr: "And behold, I send the promise." He encourages them to take upon themselves this office of the Apostleship by the Holy Spirit and by those extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit, which had been promised long ago, especially by the Prophet Joel, as we read in Acts 2:17: "I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh," etc. Note first in this place that the Son bestows the Spirit and the gifts of the Spirit at his own time, which the Father had already promised before; hence the measure of Christ's gift is spoken of in Ephesians 4:7. And in the same chapter afterward, verse 10: "that he might fill all things, he gave some indeed as Apostles," etc. From this it follows that this is higher and prior, namely that the Son had already before received from the Father all grace and all the gifts of the Holy Spirit, together with the Holy Spirit himself; and that the Father had given all these things first to his Son, and not to us. "The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand" and "in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." From this it also follows that another thing is prior, namely that the merit of the Holy Spirit and of all his gifts belongs to the Son alone. For he who alone first received all grace is alone the one who merited it all. But all this grace which is given to us has cost Christ dearly: for he obtained all of it for us at no less a price than his own blood. How then, you will ask, does the Holy Spirit with his gifts come to us? I answer: not through any merit of ours, but through the pure grace of the Father and the Son. "We have received of his fullness grace for grace." "In him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily." "And we are complete in him," namely when we believe in him. And this is the bounty of the Son, by which he gives us freely what he himself bought at so great a price. "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ," etc. 2 Corinthians 8:9.

units.la: 8. 9. Sed quod obseruo hoc loco primarium est : Sine Spiritu sancto nihil potest minister. Non sustinuerim quicquam loqui quod non effecerit Christus per me, inquit. Alij in politia quidem aliquid fine Spiritu Christi præstare possunt, freti natura & naturæ donis. Sed in Ecclesia inutilis est quisquis non habet Spiritum illum sanctum, eiusque aliquod donum. Quamobrem Spiritus sanctus ministris Ecclesiæ nominatim promissus est, quippe quorum functio tota Spiritualis est. Neque etiam quisquam est fidelium ministrorum, qui non habeat Spiritum sanctum comitem, id quod & ipse, & alij experiri possunt. Non ego tamen, inquit Paulus, laboravi, sed gratia Dei quæ mecum est. Et alibi dicit fe decertasse secundum efficacitatem ipsius agentem in fe potenter. Item, Quandoquidem, inquit, experimentum quæritis in me loquentis Christi, qui erga vos non est infirmus, sed potens est in vobis. Multa sunt præterea apud Paulum in hanc sententiam, qui in mediis infirmitatibus suis, & in morte etiam ipsa, sensit vitam ac virtutem illam Christi in fe efficaciter agere. Vos autem manete. Quo magis credant fe receptuos propertinens. missum illum Spiritum sanctum, mandat ne exeant
units.tr: But what I observe in this place is of the first importance: a minister can do nothing without the Holy Spirit. "I would not dare to speak anything which Christ has not effected through me," he says. Others indeed in the civil sphere can accomplish something without the Spirit of Christ, relying on nature and the gifts of nature. But in the Church whoever does not have that Holy Spirit, and some gift of him, is useless. For this reason the Holy Spirit is promised by name to the ministers of the Church, since their whole function is spiritual. Nor is there any faithful minister who does not have the Holy Spirit as his companion, which both he himself and others can experience. "Yet not I," says Paul, "but the grace of God which is with me." And elsewhere he says that he has striven according to the working of Christ, who works powerfully in him. Likewise: "Since you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me, who is not weak toward you, but is mighty in you." Moreover there are many things in Paul to this effect, who, in the midst of his weaknesses, and even in death itself, felt that life and that power of Christ working effectively in him. "But you remain," etc. Lest they believe that they are to go out before they have received that Spirit, he commands them not to depart [from Jerusalem] until they have received the Holy Spirit sent to them.

units.la: HicHierosolymis priusquam eum recipiant: hoc est, quodammodo tempus iis receptionis Spiritus praescribit. Dominus enim perpetuo rei promissae aliquam praestat securitatem, & aliquam dat nobis arrham, tantisper dum promissionem suam adimpleat, rationem scilicet habens infirmitatis nostrae. Non enim possumus nos perpetuo a nudo solóque ipsius verbo pendere. Fieri quidem potest, ut ad tempus aliquod verbo ipsius sed adhaereamus: atque hoc modo solet Dominus suorum fidem explorare. Sed id diuturnum esse non potest, nisi cum fide tandem aliquando fit aliquis sensus, & aliqua rei promissae perceptio: & aliqua, ut sic loquar, arrha rei & securitas. Deinde hic nota, ministro non esse prodeundum ad Euangelium promulgandum, nisi sentiat adiungi sibi comitem Spiritum Dei sanctum. Prohibet enim discipulos suos ne exeant, nisi recepto prius Spiritu sancto. Quàm temerè faciant isti, qui freti naturae tantum donis, ingenio, memoria, iudicio naturali, statim consciendunt suggestum, & ex eo loquuntur populo Dei in ipsius nomine, qui non sine iusto Dei iudicio procurant sibi tandem dedecus & ignominiam: & produnt se non missos esse à Domino, sed cucurrisse, cum non fuerint missi.
units.tr: Here, in Jerusalem, before they receive him: that is, in some measure he prescribes the time for their receiving of the Spirit. For the Lord always gives some assurance of the promised thing, and gives us some pledge, until he fulfils his promise, taking account, of course, of our weakness. For we cannot always depend on his bare word alone. It may indeed happen that for a time we cling only to his word; and in this way the Lord is accustomed to test the faith of his people. But this cannot last long, unless at length, with faith, some sense and some perception of the promised thing comes; and some pledge, so to speak, and assurance of the thing. Next, note here that a minister is not to go forth to proclaim the Gospel unless he feels that the holy Spirit of God is joined to him as his companion. For he forbids his disciples to go out unless they first receive the Holy Spirit. How rashly do those act who, relying only on natural gifts, on talent, memory and natural judgment, straightway mount the pulpit, and from there speak to the people of God in his name; and who, not without the just judgment of God, bring upon themselves in the end disgrace and shame, and reveal that they were not sent by the Lord, but ran without being sent.

units.la: Hactenus de sermone Domini ad discipulos suos, ut eum scripto prodidit Lucas. Iohannes in Euangelio suo habet praesertim sermonis Domini partem posteriorem, de missione Apostolorum. Hanc enim paulò fusiùs recitat, quàm Lucas, & paulo aliter. Narrat Iohannes Dominum praefatum esse pacem: Iterum, inquit, dixit eis, Pax vobis. Sic eos praeparavit ad recipiendum sermonem illum quem erat subiecturus continuò de eorum missione. Ad recipiendum enim sermonem Domini, praesertim Euangelium pacis & laetitiae, debemus praeparari pace. Nuntium enim pacis & laetitiae, postulat animum pace praeparatum, ut recipiatur cum pace & cum gaudio: alioquin nihil boni ex eo percipitur. Cùm autem ipsum recipimus cum pace animi & laetitia, tum quanto magis audimus, tanto magis imbibimus gaudium.
units.tr: So far the Lord's words to his disciples, as Luke has recorded them in writing. John, in his Gospel, gives mainly the latter part of the Lord's discourse, on the sending of the apostles. He relates this a little more fully than Luke does, and in a slightly different way. John tells us that the Lord first spoke peace: "Again," he says, "he said to them, Peace be unto you." In this way he prepared them to receive the message he was about to give them directly, concerning their sending. For we ought to be prepared with peace to receive the word of the Lord, especially the Gospel of peace and joy. A message of peace and joy requires a mind prepared by peace, so that it may be received with peace and with joy. Otherwise nothing good is gained from it. When we receive it with peace of mind and gladness, the more we hear it, the more we drink in joy.

units.la: Pace praefationis exoptat. dium illud Spiritus sancti. Quamobrem & nuncios pacis illius Euangelij decet annunciare Euangelium cum præfatione aliqua pacis & lætitiæ, exemplo Domini sui : & qui accedunt ad Euangelium audiendum, debent sese præparare sensu aliquo lætitiæ & gaudij : Gaudij, inquam, ex dolore peccati, & miseriæ nostræ proficiscentis, & cum seria respipiscentia coniuncti : nam id demum gaudium est Christiani hominis in hac vita. Sicut misit me Pater. Hactenus fuit præfatio, sequitur ipse sermo : primum habemus missionem Apostolorum propositam, deinde habemus confirmationem & consolationem eorum, dum primum induit mittendos Spiritus sancti virtute & gratia, deinde armat potestate. De missione autem quia diximus supra, ideo nunc tantum pauca dicemus. Ex hac comparatione qua declaratur eorum missio, primum hoc observo : solum Christum filium Dei, à Patre suo missum immediatè. Hic enim honor est filio proprius, de quo Hebr. 5. 5. Christus non assumpsit sibi honorem ut fieret Pontifex, sed is qui dixerat, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Dedit autem Pater filio suo omnem potestatem mittendi alios, quos quidem ipse mittit vel immediatè, ut Prophetas, ut Apostolos, vel mediatè, ut Pastores & Doctores. Nam quod ad Apostolos, illi quidem missi sunt à Patre, sed mediatè per filium. Ideo Paulus vocat se Apostolum Christi, idque per voluntatem Dei Patris, significans immediatè se missum esse à Christo, mediatè verò à Deo Patre. De Christo verò dicitur, quod is postquam ascendit in cœlos, dederit alios Apostolos, alios Prophetas, &c. Deinde ex hac comparatione observo Apostolatum non modò legitimum esse, sed esse cum authoritate. Is enim qui mittit Apostolos, est missus prior ipse à Patre, hoc est, non modò legitimè est vocatus, sed fuit cum authoritate. Eadem ratio valet & in pastoribus omnibus, ad probandam non modò legitimam eorum esse prædicationem, vocationem, sed etiam cum authoritate aliqua esse coniunctam. Nam quod mittantur à filio patet : Dedit enim alios Pastores & doctores. & doctores. Mittuntur ergo à filio veri pastores in Ecclesia, licet mediatè per hominum ministerium id fiat. Quum igitur mittantur à filio, qui ipse prior missus est à Patre, cum authoritate sint necesse est: Sicut enim filius legatus à Patre sustinet personam Patris: ita pastores missi à filio sustinent quodammodo personam filij. Quare vel obedientia, vel inobedientia in Pastorem, redundat in filium & Patrem: & filius reputat eam sibi & Patri praestitam. Luc. 10. 15. Qui audit, me audit, & qui vos reiicit, me reiicit. Qui vero me temnit, reiicit eum qui misit me. Tertiò observa, tum etiam legitimam esse missionem & vocationem, vel Apostoli, vel Pastoris, cùm mittitur ab eo qui ipse prior missus est: Ergo hi demum legitimi in Ecclesia pastores sunt, qui mittuntur à presbyterio, & ab aliis qui ipsi priores sunt missi. Nominatio quidem sanè sensus est penes populum, at missio tantùm penes presbyterium. Afflavit & dixit eis. Nunc mandos instruit, ac primùm quasi induit gratia Spiritus sancti. Haec afflatio visibilis non fuit illa quidem missio Spiritus, sed symbolum dunta-xat, & sacramentum inspirationis, symbolum dico rei significatae commodum: nam ventus figura est Spiritus sancti non inepta. Vide Iohann. 3. 8. Symbolum autem hic non est mutum illud quidem, sed ad sacramentum accedit verbum, ut & in quibusvis aliis sacramentis, in Baptismo, in Coena Domini, ad declarandum ministrum symbolum ipsum, & ad fidem efficiendam ac proinde ad reddendum symbolum efficax in cordibus eorum. Nam verbum est praecipuè quod fidem efficit, & anima est quasi Sacramenti. Praetereo nunc quàm foedè & praeposterè abutantur Episcopi Pontifices hac actione Domini in creandis sacrificulis suis, qui foetido ore afflantes, dicunt iis, Accipite Spiritum Sanctum, nescientes hoc sacramentum non ordinarium esse, sed extraordinarium in ordinandis extraordinariis hominibus, hoc est, Apostolis Christi usurpantes: quo sacramento donati sunt olim Apostoli extraordinaria quadam gratia. Neque hic locus pugnat cum
units.tr: The Holy Spirit desires that joy through the preface of peace. Therefore, following the Lord's example, those who announce the Gospel of that peace should also announce it with some preface of peace and gladness, and those who come to hear the Gospel should prepare themselves with some sense of gladness and joy. I say joy that springs from grief over sin and our misery, and is joined with genuine repentance, for this is in the end the joy of a Christian in this life. As the Father has sent me. So much for the preface; now comes the discourse itself. First we have the sending of the apostles set forth, then their confirmation and comfort, since first he clothes them with the power and grace of the Holy Spirit, and then arms them with authority. Since we have spoken of the sending above, we will now say only a few things about it. From this comparison, by which their sending is declared, I first observe this: that only Christ, the Son of God, was sent immediately by his Father. For this honour belongs peculiarly to the Son, as Hebrews 5:5 says: Christ did not take to himself the honour of becoming high priest, but he who said to him, You are my Son, today I have begotten you. The Father gave his Son the whole power of sending others, whom he himself sends either immediately, as the prophets and apostles, or mediately, as pastors and teachers. As for the apostles, indeed they were sent by the Father, but mediately, through the Son. Therefore Paul calls himself an apostle of Christ, and that by the will of God the Father, signifying that he was sent immediately by Christ, but mediately by God the Father. Of Christ it is said that, after he ascended into heaven, he gave some apostles, some prophets, and so on. Next, from this comparison I observe that the apostleship is not only lawful but is also held with authority. For he who sends the apostles was himself sent first by the Father; that is, he was not only lawfully called but also had authority. The same reasoning holds for all pastors, to prove that their preaching and calling are not only lawful but also joined with some authority. That they are sent by the Son is plain: for he gave some pastors and teachers. Therefore the true pastors in the Church are sent by the Son, although this happens mediately, through the ministry of men. Since they are sent by the Son, who was himself first sent by the Father, they must necessarily have authority. For just as the Son, as the Father's envoy, bears the person of the Father, so pastors sent by the Son in some measure bear the person of the Son. Hence obedience or disobedience toward the pastor passes over to the Son and the Father, and the Son counts it as done to himself and to the Father. Luke 10:16: He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me. But he who despises me rejects him who sent me. Thirdly, observe that the sending and calling of an apostle or a pastor are lawful only when he is sent by one who was himself first sent. Therefore those alone are lawful pastors in the Church who are sent by the eldership and by others who were themselves first sent. Indeed the naming belongs to the people's judgment, but the sending belongs only to the eldership. He breathed on them and said to them. Now he instructs those who are to be sent, and first clothes them, as it were, with the grace of the Holy Spirit. This visible breathing was not indeed the sending of the Spirit, but only a sign and sacrament of inspiration: I say a sign suited to the thing signified, for the wind is an apt figure of the Holy Spirit. See John 3:8. This sign, however, is not mute, but the word joins the sacrament, as in all other sacraments, in Baptism and in the Lord's Supper, both to declare the sign to the minister and to produce faith, and so to make the sign effective in their hearts. For it is chiefly the word that produces faith, and the soul is, as it were, the life of the sacrament. I pass over now how shamefully and perversely the Papist bishops abuse this action of the Lord in creating their little priests, who breathe with foul mouths and say to them, Receive the Holy Spirit, not knowing that this sacrament is not ordinary but extraordinary, used in ordaining extraordinary men, that is, the apostles of Christ. By this sacrament the apostles were once endowed with a certain extraordinary grace. Nor does this passage conflict with that one in Luke 24:49, in which we read that the Spirit was not then given to him, but that the sending of the Holy Spirit was promised.

units.la: illo qui est Lucæ 24. 49. in quo legimus non tum datum ei Spiritum, sed promissam esse missionem Spiritus sancti. Promissio enim facta est illic plenorum illorum Spiritus sancti donorum, quæ acciderunt postea in die Pentecostes, cum fissæ illæ linguæ igneæ non sine miraculo inciderunt Apostolis: hic vero datum est initium donorum, & rigati sunt duntaxat Spiritu sancto, tantisperdum eo plenius imbuerentur, id quod contigit eo ipso Pentecostes die. Nam intelligendum est nō simul ac semel datum esse Spiritum sanctum cum donis suis discipulis Christi, sed gradatim ac pedetentim. Acceperūt enim quasi primitias Spiritus, quo tempore Dominus humiliatus est in terris: at postquam resurrexit, auctiorem eum acceperunt: postremo vero postquam Dominus est glorificatus, effusus est in eos Spiritus iuxta promissionem factam. Pendet enim gratia corporis ac membrorum, ex ipso capite per analogiam quandam, & proportionem: cumque plene glorificatum est caput, tum quidem ipsum impleuit omnia. Quod autem nos non simus completi hoc tempore & hac ætate, in causa est, quod tristitia afficiamus Spiritum illum sanctum. Sunt enim hæc postrema tempora, in quibus peccata abundant, sic ut ex consolatore Spiritu (quæ est nostra ista ingratitudo) efficiamus nobis testem eum adversus nos in illo die.
units.tr: that one in Luke 24:49, in which we read that the Spirit was not then given to them but that the sending of the Holy Spirit was promised. For the promise was made there of the full gifts of the Holy Spirit, which came afterward on the day of Pentecost, when the tongues of fire descended on the apostles, not without a miracle. Here, however, the beginning of the gifts is given, and they were only sprinkled with the Holy Spirit, so that they might be more fully imbued with him, which happened on the very day of Pentecost. For it must be understood that the Holy Spirit was not given to the disciples of Christ at once and all together with his gifts, but gradually and little by little. They received, as it were, the firstfruits of the Spirit while the Lord was humbled on earth; but after he rose again they received him in greater measure; and finally, after the Lord was glorified, the Spirit was poured out upon them according to the promise made. For the grace of the body and of the members depends on the head itself, by a certain analogy and proportion; and when the head has been fully glorified, then indeed it has filled all things. That we are not filled at this time and in this age is because we grieve that Holy Spirit. For these are the last times, in which sins abound, so that from a comforting Spirit (and this is our ingratitude) we make him a witness against us on that day.

units.la: Si quorum remiseritis. Hactenus induit discipulos suos virtute Spiritus sancti: nunc armat eos potestate. De armis his lege 2. Corinth. 10.4. De hac potestate data Apostolis lege primum Matthei 16.19. vbi Dominus Petrum nominatim compellans simul ad alios sermonem suum dirigit: Et tibi, inquit, dabo claves regni cælorum, &c. deinde de ea lege Matth. 18.18. quo loco omnes pariter compellans ait, Quæcunque ligaueritis in terra, erunt ligata in cælo, &c. Atque hæc potestas data est à Domino ante passionem, post resurrectionem autem iterata est ac repetita, vt legimus hoc loco. Neque tum data est tantum Apostolis & ministerio, quod quidem tunc temporis extraordinarium erat; sed etiam data est ordinario ministerio duraturo ad Christi vsque reditum. Rationes autem
units.tr: If you forgive the sins of any. So far he has clothed his disciples with the power of the Holy Spirit; now he arms them with authority. On these weapons see 2 Corinthians 10:4. On this authority given to the apostles, read first Matthew 16:19, where the Lord, addressing Peter by name, at the same time directs his words to the others: And to you, he says, I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven, etc. Then read Matthew 18:18, where he addresses them all alike and says, Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, etc. This authority was given by the Lord before his passion, but after the resurrection it is conferred again and repeated, as we read in this place. Nor was it given only to the apostles and their extraordinary ministry, which at that time was extraordinary; it was also given to the ordinary ministry, which would last until the return of Christ. The reasons for exercising this power are two.

units.la: Minis terio & extraordinario & ordinario claues data. tem administrandæ huius potestatis duæ sunt. Prima quidem est verbum legis & Euangelij prædicatum: secunda vero est disciplina, quam Ecclesiasticam vocant: illa, hanc tempore debet antecedere. Potestas autem hæc cernitur non in eo proprie vt ministerium remittat peccatum, vel ipsum retineat: nam solius Dei est proprium remittere & retinere peccata: id quod etiam Pharisæi agnouerunt, cum Christo, quem pro homine tantum habuerunt, tanquam blasphemum obiecerunt, quod diceret, Remissa sunt tibi peccata tua. Et apud Esaiam, Ego, ego ipse, ait Dominus, deleo defectiones tuas propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordor. Ergo hoc solius Dei proprium est retinere & remittere peccata. Neque id communicat cum vlla creaturarum, quia pars est gloriæ ipsius, quam non impertit alteri. Neque vero deest iusta huius rei ratio. Si enim proprie loquamur, peccatum in Deum solum committi dicitur: Tibi, tibi soli peccavi, inquit regius Psaltes. Maneat ergo illud, solius Dei esse proprie remittere & retinere peccata: ligare & soluere: hoc est, sententiam pronunciare de remissione & retentione peccatorum. In quo ergo cernitur hæc potestas? Cernitur in promulgatione ac præconio in terris facto sententiæ illius quæ iam lata est in cælis. Neque enim nos statim in cœlos subuehit Deus, vt audiamus hanc sententiam ibi pronunciari, ipse se demittit ad nos, & in ministerio suo ad nos usque descendit de cœlis: ac per ministerium hoc suum sententiam in cœlis iam à se latam promulgat in terris, idque ad nostram vel consolationem, siquidem sententia sit remissionis; vel deiectionem, si sit sententia retentionis peccatorum. Quod si enim ministerium hoc, in quo se humiliat Deus, & per quod rogat ipse & orat nos, vt loquitur Apostolus, à nobis contemnitur, profecto nulla esse potest remissionis peccatorum, & salutis nostræ certitudo. Ergo, vt redeamus, cernitur hæc potestas in promulgatione ac declaratione sententiæ in cœlis iam pronunciatæ ac latæ. Id quod ipsa verba videntur innuere: dicit enim, Quorum remiseritis peccata, ea remissa sunt, in tempore nimirum præterito, quasi dicat, Iā de iis sententia est lata. Vos autem sententiam iam latam in cœlis, promulgatis atque declaratis in terris. Sic dicit, Quorum retinueritis peccata, ea retenta sunt, pręterito vsus tempore: quasi dicat, Iam retenta sunt per sententiam de iis latam in cœlis. Præterea sciendū potestatem ministerio Ecclesiastico siue illi Apostolico & extraordinario, siue huic pastorali & ordinario, concessam quidem iis regiam esse, sed tantum ministeriales. Sic de nobis reputet homo vt de ministris Christi & dispensatoribus mysteriorum Dei. De potestate nostra, inquit, quam dedit nobis Dominus: & ministerium gloriosum. Et conscientiæ quidem hominum ipsorum experiuntur potestatem esse. Quandoquidem, inquit, experimentum quæritis in me loquentis Christi. Si autem eam conferamus cum potestate ciuili, quæ potestas est etiam regia, profecto hac ratione superior erit ciuili. Quia cum ciuilis sit in vitam & bona ista temporaria, potestas hæc Ecclesiastica & ministerialis, est in vitam & bona æterna. Vnde ministerium Spiritus & iustitiæ vocatur. Quòd si quæras cum oporteat præconem certum esse de sententia vdicis, quam sit ipse promulgaturus: qui sciet minister sententiam hanc vel remissionis vel retentionis peccati in cœlis iam pronuntiatam esse, vt ipse deinde possit bona cum conscientia eam promulgare & hominibus declarare? Respondeo non reuelari Ministris extra ordinem hanc Dei sententiam, sed ordinarie per Spiritum nimirum & verbum ipsum, quod habemus in manibus, idque hoc modo: Generalem quidem sententiam habemus in verbo, hanc nimirum (vt de præconio remissionis dicamus priori loco) Quisquis crediderit in Christum, seruabitur Adde ad fidem resipiscentiam, vt dicas, Quisquis crediderit & resipuerit, seruabitur. Ad hoc assumo peculiariter: At hic peccator resipiscit & credit: hinc in conclusione sequitur sententiæ declaratio: Ergo hic seruatur & remissa sunt ei peccata. Rursus generalem sententiam habemus, Qui non credit & resipiscit, iam condemnatus est. Assumo, At hic peccator non credit, neque {q}que resipiscit. Hinc concludo declarationem sententiæ illius in cœlis iam latę, Ergo hic peccator iam condemnatus est & ligatus in cœlo.
units.tr: The keys are given to the extraordinary and to the ordinary ministry. There are two means of administering this power. The first is the preaching of the word of law and Gospel. The second is what they call ecclesiastical discipline. The former ought to come before the latter. This power does not consist properly in the minister forgiving sins or retaining them, for to remit and retain sins belongs to God alone. The Pharisees also recognised this, when they objected to Christ, whom they regarded as merely a man, as a blasphemer because he said, Your sins are forgiven you. And in Isaiah the Lord says, I, I myself, blot out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins. Therefore it is God's alone to retain and remit sins. He does not share this with any creature, because it is a part of his glory, which he does not impart to another. Nor is there a lack of good reason for this. For, to speak properly, sin is said to be committed against God alone: Against you, you alone, have I sinned, says the royal psalmist. Let it stand, then, that it belongs to God alone properly to remit and retain sins, to bind and to loose; that is, to pronounce sentence concerning the remission and retention of sins. In what, then, does this power consist? It consists in the proclamation and public announcement, made on earth, of that sentence which has already been pronounced in heaven. For God does not carry us up into heaven at once so that we might hear this sentence pronounced there. Rather, he humbles himself and in his ministry comes down from heaven to us. Through this ministry of his he makes known on earth the sentence already passed by him in heaven, and he does so for our consolation if the sentence is one of remission, or for our dismay if it is a sentence of retention of sins. For if this ministry, in which God humbles himself, and through which he himself entreats and exhorts us, as the Apostle says, is despised by us, then surely there can be no remission of sins and no certainty of our salvation. Therefore, to return to the point, this power consists in the promulgation and declaration of the sentence already pronounced and passed in heaven. The words themselves seem to indicate this, for he says, Whose sins you remit, they are remitted, in the past tense, as if to say: the sentence concerning them has already been passed; you, however, promulgate and declare on earth the sentence already passed in heaven. So he says, Whose sins you retain, they are retained, using the past tense, as if to say: they have already been retained by the sentence passed on them in heaven. Furthermore, it should be known that the power granted to the ecclesiastical ministry, whether to that apostolic and extraordinary ministry or to this pastoral and ordinary one, is indeed a kingly power, but only a ministerial one. Let a man so regard us, as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Concerning our power, he says, which the Lord gave us, and the glorious ministry. And indeed men's consciences themselves experience it as a power. Since, he says, you seek proof of Christ speaking in me. But if we compare it with civil power, which is also a kingly power, it will surely in this respect be superior to civil power. For civil power extends to this life and temporal goods, whereas this ecclesiastical and ministerial power extends to eternal life and eternal goods. Hence it is called the ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness. But if you ask: since a herald must be certain of the sentence of the judge that he is to proclaim, how will the minister know that this sentence of remission or retention of sin has already been pronounced in heaven, so that he may then promulgate it and declare it to men with a good conscience? I answer that this sentence of God is not revealed to ministers by an extraordinary means, but ordinarily through the Spirit and the Word itself, which we have in our hands, and in this way. We have a general sentence in the Word, namely (to speak first of the proclamation of remission) Whoever believes in Christ will be saved. Add repentance to faith, so that you say, Whoever believes and repents will be saved. To this I add the particular premise: But this sinner repents and believes. From this, in the conclusion, follows the declaration of the sentence: Therefore this man is saved and his sins are forgiven. Again, we have the general sentence, He who does not believe and repent is already condemned. I assume: But this sinner neither believes nor repents. From this I conclude the declaration of that sentence already passed in heaven: Therefore this sinner is already condemned and bound in heaven.

units.la: Thomas autem. Sequitur in Euangelio Iohannis historia particularis de Thoma, ipsiúsque incredulitate. Thomas is fuit qui Didymus est vocatus: de eo primùm legimus, quod coaptatus sit in numerum duodecim Matth.10.3. Deinde habemus eum ægrè tulisse quòd Dominus instituisset profecisci rursus in Iudæam, & erupisse in verba quæ indignationem animi satis magnam prodiderunt: Eamus & nos ut moriamur cum eo, Ioban. 11.16. Postremò hoc loco habemus historiam incredulitatis ipsius, adeóque etiam non mediocris contumaciæ: Nec credidit, nec voluit etiam credere: ut exemplo Thomæ discamus Apostolos Christi non natura, sed gratia discretos fuisse ab aliis hominibus, etiam perditissimis, eósque primùm omnium constitutos fuisse exemplaria totidem & spectacula misericordiæ Dei in Christo Iesu: idque Paulus de se confessus est: Ut essem, inquit, exemplo crediturus ipsis in vitam æternam. Sed de persona hominis hactenus. Apostoli & discipuli reliqui, quibus in unum locum coactis Christus se conspiciendum obtulit, annunciant Thomæ resurrectionem Domini. Occasio præmissa est, quia Thomas aberat tum cùm apparuit aliis Dominus: de causa absentiæ ipsius nō disputo curiosius, siue is tardiùs quàm alij è latibulo suo quò confugerat quando captus est Dominus, proripuerit se, siue occupatus fuerit priuatis suis rebus, interea temporis, dum alij in unum erant coacti, & de Christo ipsiúsque resurrectione inter se inuicem quærebant. Tantùm hoc video, per absentiam ipsius, ipsum priuatum fuisse gratia & præsentia illa Domini, quam alij in illo discipulorum cœtu acceperunt. Vt discamus non sine aliqua iactura nos abesse à sacris cœtibus, quibus promisit Dominus suam præsentiam. Si id fiat per negligentiam, tum minus est mali: sin verò per contemptum fiat, tum ad iacturam quam facimus boni accedit ira Dei ob contemptum ordinationis suæ. Quare primùm omnium quærendum regnum cœlorum ut alia deinde adiiciantur nobis. Opus igitur est ut laboremus. in quærendo regno cœlorum, quod vbi iam consequuti sumus, tum quidem reliqua, quæ ad vitam hanc præsentem tolerandam pertinent,sua sponte accedunt: adeo vt non sit opus vt in iis quærendis nos supra modum fatigemus. De occasione hactenus. Sequitur annunciatio resurrectionis Domini, Vidimus, inquiunt, Dominum. Discipuli alij non inuident Thomæ bonum, quod ipsi absente eo acceperunt: ea enim ipsissima via est adaugendi gratiam iam receptam, si eam cum aliis communicemus, & si talentum Domini apud nos depositum, exponamus ad vsuram. Neque obstet quòd cum labore & aliqua iactura bonorum huius vitæ parta sit ea gratia; quod enim ipsi nos nonnisi difficulter consequuti sumus, & quod auidè ad nos arripuimus (nā vis afferenda est regno cœlorum) id iam non parcè & liberaliter in alios erogemus. Sequuntur partes Thomæ, nempe priusquam admirabilis ipsius incredulitas, qui cum tanta nube oculatorum testium circumseptus esset, tamen nō credidit.
units.tr: But Thomas. There follows in John's Gospel a particular account concerning Thomas and his unbelief. This Thomas is the one called Didymus. Of him we first read that he was counted among the twelve, Matt. 10.3. Then we find him taking it badly that the Lord had decided to set out again for Judea, and bursting out in words that revealed a considerable indignation of mind: Let us also go, that we may die with him, John 11.16. Last, in this passage we have the story of his unbelief, and indeed of no small obstinacy: he did not believe, nor even wished to believe. Let us learn from the example of Thomas that the apostles of Christ were distinguished from other men, even the most abandoned, not by nature but by grace, and that they were the first of all to be set up as so many examples and spectacles of the mercy of God in Christ Jesus. Paul confessed this of himself: That I might be, he says, an example to those who would afterwards believe in him unto eternal life. But so much for the person of the man. The apostles and the other disciples, to whom Christ showed himself to be seen when they had been gathered into one place, announce to Thomas the resurrection of the Lord. The occasion is explained beforehand: Thomas was absent when the Lord appeared to the others. I do not inquire too curiously into the cause of his absence, whether he was slower than the others to emerge from the hiding place to which he had fled when Christ was taken, or whether he was occupied with his private affairs in the meantime, while the others were gathered together and were asking one another about Christ and his resurrection. I see only this: through his absence he was deprived of that grace and presence of the Lord which the others received in that company of disciples. Let us learn that we are not absent from the sacred assemblies, in which the Lord has promised his presence, without some loss. If this happens through negligence, then the harm is less; but if it happens through contempt, then to the loss we incur is added the wrath of God on account of the contempt of his ordinance. Therefore the kingdom of heaven must be sought first of all, so that other things may be added to us afterwards. So we must labour to seek the kingdom of heaven, and once we have attained it, the remaining things that pertain to bearing this present life will of their own accord come to us, so that we need not wear ourselves out beyond measure in seeking them. So much for the occasion. There follows the announcement of the Lord's resurrection: We have seen the Lord, they say. The other disciples do not begrudge Thomas the good which they received in his absence. For this is precisely the way to increase grace already received, if we share it with others, and if we put out at interest the talent of the Lord deposited with us. Nor should it be an objection that this grace was obtained with toil and some loss of the goods of this life; for what we have obtained with difficulty, and have eagerly seized upon (for the kingdom of heaven must be taken by force), we should now bestow upon others not sparingly but generously. Follows the part of Thomas, namely his remarkable unbelief, which, though he was surrounded by so great a cloud of eyewitnesses, nevertheless did not believe.

units.la: Haud dubiè enim primùm exorsa est Magdalene, quæ prima vidit Dominum post resurrectionem ipsius, ac testata est Thomæ (ē vidisse Dominum. Aliæ mulieres idem testatæ sunt. Post eas duo discipuli qui Emmauntem sunt profecti. Deinde Petrus qui ipsum etiam vidit: postremò omnes vna voce idem sunt testati. Thomas ipsorum omnium testimonio nihil cōmotus, mansit incredulus. Vt scias nihil posse proficere omnium etiam oculatorum testium testimonium, nisi adsit principalis ille testis, Spiritus Christi, qui tetetur cordibus nostris, aperiat oculos mentis, & cor nostrum inflectat ad credendum. Absque eo quis non habebit fidem, ne suis quidem ipsius sensibus, id quod in aliis discipulis vidimus supra, qui, cùm in medio eorum staret Christus, & ipsi eum præsentem intuerentur, non tamen crediderunt priusquam Dominus aperuit eorum mentes ad intelligendas Scripturas. vide Luc.24.41.
units.tr: Doubtless it was Magdalene who first began, since she was the first to see the Lord after his resurrection, and she testified to Thomas that she had seen the Lord. The other women gave the same testimony. After them came the two disciples who went to Emmaus. Then Peter, who also saw him. Last of all, they all testified the same thing with one voice. Thomas, unmoved by the testimony of them all, remained unbelieving. So that you may know that the testimony of all the eyewitnesses can accomplish nothing unless that principal witness, the Spirit of Christ, is present, who speaks in our hearts, opens the eyes of the mind, and turns our heart to believe. Without him, no one will have faith, not even through his own senses. We saw this above in the other disciples, who, though Christ stood in their midst and they looked on him as present, did not believe until the Lord opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. See Luke 24:41.

units.la: §6. Quæstio de iudice & interpretatione Canonicæ Scripturæ
units.tr: §6. Question about the judge and the interpretation of the canonical Scripture

units.la: Quæritur hodierno die de principali teste ac iudice primùm authenticæ scripturæ, deinde veræ interpretationis locorum Scripturæ: Quinam certò sciamus hanc Scripturam, quam habemus in manibus esse verbū Dei? & qui sciemus hunc vel illum esse verum Scripturæ sensum? sum? Aduersarij ideo de Scriptura, quòd authentica sit & Dei ipsius verbum; & vera interpretatione Scripturæ constare dicunt, quòd dicat hoc Ecclesia, quòd testatur itaque rem habere Ecclesia. Testimonium enim Ecclesiæ principale ac ferè vnicum argumentum Scripturæ, quòd sit verbum Dei & interpretationis Scripturæ, quòd sit vera ac genuina, statuunt esse. Hinc illæ voces, quòd Ecclesia sit iudex Scripturæ, & interpretationis ipsius. At nos dicimus primarium testem & Scripturæ ipsius, quòd sit verbum Dei: & interpretationis Scripturæ, esse Spiritum illum Dei sanctum testantem in cordibus, aperientem mentes nostras ad Scripturas ipsas intelligendas; neque propterea sequitur quod illi obiiciunt, nos facere Scripturæ ac interpretationis ipsius testem ac iudicē priuatum aliquem Spiritum: quandoquidem dicamus hunc Spiritum per Scripturam, & in Scriptura loqui, ac proinde Scripturæ Spiritum esse. Hic enim Spiritus per Scripturam docet nos Scripturam esse authenticam & ipsum Dei verbum: Rursus per Scripturam docet nos idem Spiritus hanc vel illam esse veram, & genuinam Scripturæ interpretationem. Principalis enim vox Spiritus sancti est Scriptura, quæ nobis esse debet loco viuæ vocis ipsius Dei. Vox autem Ecclesiæ (de vera loquor) est vox quædam Spiritus sancti secundaria. Sed de his hactenus. Ad incredulitatem Thomæ accessit pertinacia quædam & malitia. Non enim credidit, neque etiam credere voluit: ait enim, Nequaquam credam, nisi hisce oculis videro manus & pedes eius; neque id tantum, nisi digitum immisero in vestigia clavorum quibus transfixæ sunt manus eius & perfossi pedes; neq; id tantum, sed addit: Nisi manum meam etiam totam immisero in vulnus lateri eius infixum. Vides hominis pertinaciam: incredulitas enim est cum contumacia coniuncta, qua etiam commonstrata via & patefacta quasi ianua, qua euadamus ex hoc peccati, quo detinemur, quasi carcere: tamen nolumus exire, sed magis nos implicamus peccato nostro. Atque hoc est illud virus & fel amaritudinis, quod inspuit diabolus in naturam nostram, & hic est nexus illè iniustitiæ, quo quasi cathena constricti tenemur per aeternam damnationem, nisi per Christum liberemur. Malum istud Petrus obseruauit in Simone, cum dixit, Video te in felle amaritudinis, & in nexu iniustitiæ positum. Verba eius satis arguunt ad pertinaciam animi accessisse arrogantiam & superbiam: sibi enim visus est plus sapere, quàm cæteri omnes, quorum reprehendit stultitiam & niniam illam credulitatem: eorum autem annunciationem, pro somno habuit. Increduli vt pertinaces sunt, sic etiam superbi, & soli sibi videntur sapere: Sermonem de cruce & resurrectione Christi habet pro stultitia. Credentes in crucem & resurrectionem pro stultis ducimur & fatuis ac deliris. Quare, inquit Paulus, si quis videtur sibi sapere (non enim dicit, Si quis sapit, nam ipsa nihil sapit, qui Christum non sapit) Sed, Si quis, inquit, videtur sibi sapere, stultus fiat vt fiat sapiens; hoc est, renunciet sapientiæ carnis, quæ nequit consistere cum sapientia Dei.
units.tr: Today the question is about the principal witness and judge, first of the authentic Scripture, and then of the true interpretation of the passages of Scripture: how can we be certain that this Scripture which we hold in our hands is the Word of God? And how shall we know that this or that is the true sense of Scripture? Our opponents say that Scripture is authentic and the Word of God, and that its true interpretation is established, because the Church says so and testifies that the matter stands so. They hold that the testimony of the Church is the chief, and almost the only, argument that Scripture is the Word of God and that the interpretation of Scripture is true and genuine. Hence those phrases, that the Church is the judge of Scripture and of its interpretation. But we say that the primary witness both that Scripture is the Word of God and that its interpretation is true is that Holy Spirit of God who testifies in our hearts and opens our minds to understand the Scriptures themselves. Nor does it follow from this, as they object, that we make some private spirit the witness and judge of Scripture and its interpretation, since we say that this Spirit speaks through Scripture and in Scripture, and is therefore the Spirit of Scripture. For this Spirit teaches us through Scripture that Scripture is authentic and is the very Word of God. Again, through Scripture the same Spirit teaches us that this or that interpretation is the true and genuine interpretation of Scripture. For the principal voice of the Holy Spirit is Scripture, which ought to stand for us in place of the living voice of God himself. The voice of the Church (I speak of the true Church) is a secondary voice of the Holy Spirit. But enough on these matters. To Thomas's unbelief was added a certain obstinacy and malice. For he did not believe, nor did he even want to believe. He says: "I will by no means believe unless I see with these eyes his hands and feet; nor only that, unless I put my finger into the marks of the nails by which his hands were pierced and his feet wounded; and not only that, but he adds: unless I put my whole hand into the wound fixed in his side." You see the man's stubbornness. For unbelief is joined with contumacy, which, even when the way has been shown and a door opened, as it were, by which we may escape from this sin that holds us, as from a prison, still does not want to come out, but rather entangles itself more in its sin. This is that poison and gall of bitterness which the devil breathes into our nature, and this is that bond of iniquity by which, as if bound with a chain, we are held for eternal damnation unless we are freed through Christ. Peter noticed this evil in Simon when he said: "I see you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity." His words sufficiently show that arrogance and pride had come to the obstinacy of his mind. For he seemed to himself to know more than all the others, whose foolishness and excessive credulity he rebuked, while he regarded their announcement as a dream. Unbelievers are as proud as they are stubborn, and they seem wise to themselves alone. They regard the message of the cross and resurrection of Christ as foolishness. We who believe in the cross and resurrection are counted as fools, madmen and lunatics. Hence Paul says: "If anyone seems to himself to be wise" (for he does not say, "If anyone is wise", since one who does not know Christ is wise in nothing), but "If anyone," he says, "seems to himself to be wise, let him become a fool so that he may become wise"; that is, let him renounce the wisdom of the flesh, which cannot stand together with the wisdom of God.

units.la: Contumaciam autem istam Thomæ, video esse, non quidem absolutam & citra omnem exceptionem: sed, vt sic dicam, conditionalem. Non enim ait, Non credam omnino, sed ait, Non credam nisi videro, &c. Alia est contumacia conditionalis, vt ista Thomæ: alia vero absoluta & simplex, vt illa Sacerdotum & Pharisæorum, cum nunciatum est iis resurrexisse Dominum a militibus qui sepulchrum Domini muniebant. Annunciantibus enim iis resurrexisse Dominum, non tam fidem non habebat, quàm fidem habere nolebant: ideoque contumacia Thomæ veniam accepit, ipsique remissa est. Contumacia vero Sacerdotum & Pharisæorum, ipsis non remissa est: verum vt manserunt increduli, ita perierunt. Quamobrem cauendum à contumacia præsertim absoluta illa quæ tandem efficit peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, & irremissibilis est. Obserua hoc loco denique, fundamentum incredulitatis & contumaciæ huius Thomæ, adeoque totius huius mali fontem, fuit autem sensus iste crassus & corporalis.Nam fidei suæ fundamentum sensum oculorum suorum & manuum sibi substrauit. Non peccauit quidem ideo, quòd omnino desiderauerit oculis videre, & manibus contrectare Dominum: ipse enim Dominus alios discipulos docuit supra, per sensum visus simul & tactus. Atque hodierno etiam die infirmitatis nostræ rationem habens, docet nos in sacramentis per eosdem istos sensus. Sed ideo peccauit Thomas, quod fidem sic alligauerit sensui, vt nisi spectare & contrectare eum daretur, professus fit tā aperte & obstinatè se credere noluisse, quòd Dominus resurrexisset. Quare desideremus quidem & expetamus videre Dominum hisce oculis corporeis. Id enim desiderarunt, quotquot pij vnquam fuerunt, quibus tamen non est datum oculis corporeis eum cernere. Reges & Prophetæ eum videre cupierunt. Abraham videre cupiuit diem eius. Simeon cupiuit eum videre. Ergo desiderare quidem nobis permittitur, sed cauendum ne fidem Christi sic alligemus sensui oculorum, vt recusemus credere nisi spectemus & contrectemus visu siue tactu: imò verò quod maius est, fides in promissionem non est sic alliganda nesensui quidem cordis interiori & arrhaboni Spiritus sancti, qui in pijs fidem solet consequi, vt recusemus fidem habere in verbum & promissionē, nisi semper adsit sensus ille gaudij & arrhabonis consequens fidei. Vix enim tres passus confecit in fide, qui nondidicit ex nudo solóq; Dei verbo nonnunquam pendere, id quod factum est à Dauide, quo tempore semel atq; iterum dixit, In Deo laudabo verbum eius, Psal. 56. & 11.
units.tr: I observe that Thomas's obstinacy was not absolute and without any exception, but, so to speak, conditional. For he does not say, "I will not believe at all," but he says, "I will not believe unless I see," and so on. There is a conditional obstinacy, such as Thomas's, and there is an absolute and simple obstinacy, such as that of the priests and Pharisees, when they were told by the soldiers who guarded the Lord's tomb that the Lord had risen. For when they announced that the Lord had risen, they were not so much without faith as unwilling to have faith. Therefore Thomas's obstinacy received pardon and was forgiven him. But the obstinacy of the priests and Pharisees was not forgiven them; rather, as they remained unbelieving, so they perished. Wherefore we must beware above all of that absolute obstinacy which at last produces the sin against the Holy Spirit, and which is unforgivable. Observe finally in this place the foundation of Thomas's unbelief and obstinacy, and so the source of all this evil: but this sense was gross and bodily. For he laid as the foundation of his faith the sense of his own eyes and hands. He did not sin indeed because he desired to see the Lord with his eyes and to handle him with his hands at all.
