For the Lord himself taught the other disciples above through the senses of sight and touch together. And even today, taking account of our weakness, he teaches us in the sacraments through these same senses. But Thomas sinned in this, that he so bound his faith to his sense that, unless he was granted to look at and handle him, he professed so openly and stubbornly that he was unwilling to believe that the Lord had risen. Therefore we may indeed desire and long to see the Lord with these bodily eyes. For all the godly who have ever lived have desired this, and yet it has not been given to them to behold him with bodily eyes. Kings and prophets longed to see him. Abraham desired to see his day. Simeon desired to see him. Therefore we are permitted indeed to desire, but we must beware lest we so bind faith in Christ to the sense of the eyes that we refuse to believe unless we see and touch with sight or touch. Indeed, what is greater, faith in the promise ought not to be so bound even to the inner sense of the heart and the earnest of the Holy Spirit, which usually follows faith in the godly, that we refuse to have faith in the Word and the promise unless that sense of joy and earnest which accompanies faith is always present. For scarcely has anyone taken three steps in faith who has not learned at times to depend on the bare Word of God alone. This was done by David, when at one time and again he said: "In God I will praise his word." Ps. 56 [56:10–11].

units.la: Octo igitur post diebus. Sequitur sexta Christi apparitio, idq; in gratiam Thomæ præsertim. Tempus apparitionis notatur octauus dies, nempe ab eo die quo professus est Thomas se non creditur, nisi certa quadam lege & conditione: & ab eo die quo resurrexit Dominus. Nam superiores quinque apparitiones fuerunt eodem ipso die, quo resurrexit Dominus à mortuis. Toto hoc octiduo Thomas mansit incredulus & contumax, vt scias peccato aliquo iam semel commisso soporem induci, & velum quasi attrahi cordi: ex quo fit rursus vt peccetur & admittatur vel idem peccatū, vel certè aliud aliquod. Petrus semel abnegato Domino stupidus factus est: ex stupore prolapsus est in idē peccatū abnegatio-nis. Tertiò deniq; in idem recidit. Dauid post adulteriū, quasi sopitus incidit in homicidiū: post quod socors ac stupidus mansit aliquot menses: Cùm autem quoduis peccatū post se relinquat stuporem aliquē, tū maximè id facit contumacia aduersus verbum Dei & agnitam veritatem. Sicut visum est ijs, inquit Paulus, Deum non tinere in notitia, sic tradidit eos Deus in mentem reprobam. Qua quidem mente reproba significatur extremus stupor, dedolentia, & cauterio reiecta conscientia. Rursus erant discipuli. De ista ingrediendi ad discipulos forma, quia diximus supra, ideo nunc eam silentio praeteribimus: de salutatione quoque diximus, quam quidem oportuit efficacem esse, cum is salutarit, qui pacis author est. Tantum hoc video, quod ubi semel contractus est ille sopor, nulla sit in posterum expergefactio, nisi interueniat Christi praesentia. Quis excitauit Davidem? Annon Christus Dei filius cum mitteret ad eum Nathan Prophetam? Nam Prophetae illi veteres olim loquuti sunt per Christi Domini spiritum. Thomas etiam ex eo stupore nunquam fuisset excusitatus nisi Christus eum interpellasset. Nisi enim misericordia illa Dei, quae est in Christo nos ex sopore hoc nostro excitet, iustitia Dei in nobis affligendis nunquam id factura est: Ne omnia quidem exempla iustitiae & iudiciorum ipsius id effectura sunt. Nam dicit Iudas in epistola sua, eos qui Dei nostri gratiam transferunt ad lasciuiam, ne exemplo quidem terribilis illius iudicij, quod Sodomam & Gomorrham & his finitimas ciuitates occupauit, commotos fuisse: sed similiter sopitos carnem polluisse. Infer digitum. Vide benignitatem Domini: Concedit Thomae quod voluit, etiam quod improbe & per incredulitatem ac contumaciam voluit, etiam inui-tat eum: atque haec citra omnem amarulentiam animi facit: ne quis putet dictum hoc a Domino false & ironice. Nam verba quae continuo subiungit, Ne esto incredulus, sed credens, satis indicant cum summa lenitate & mansuetudine animi haec a Domino dicta esse Thomae. Subest his verbis quaedam reprehensio: sed ea lenitate temperata, ut vix possit deprehendi. Quid est quod hic obseruemus, nisi lenitatem & misericordiam Domini, quam Paulus dicit tantam fuisse, ut sibi non indulserit, ad hoc ut nobis indulgeret? Cum autem multa lenitate vtitur erga quosuis, tum etiam reprobos ipsos, Cuius vult miseretur Christus. Thomas huius diti illustre exemplu. Summa Christi mā fuetudo. Rom.15.3. vt dicitur, An copia benignitatis eius & tolerantiæ ac lenitatis contemnis, ignorans te benignitate Dei ad resipiscentiam deducit? Item, Multa lenitate pertulit vasa irae coagmentata ad interitum: quando ventum est ad suos, in quibus videt scintillam aliquam boni & gratiæ oppressam iam & suffocatam onere corruptionis naturæ huius, tum quidem verum est de eo illud, Arundinem quassatam non frangit, linum fumigans non extinguit. Sed de his satis.
units.tr: After eight days, then. The sixth appearance of Christ follows, and it is made especially for the sake of Thomas. The time of the appearance is marked as the eighth day, namely from the day on which Thomas declared that he would not believe unless under a certain law and condition, and from the day on which the Lord rose. For the five earlier appearances all took place on the very day on which the Lord rose from the dead. Throughout this whole week Thomas remained unbelieving and obstinate. Learn from this that once some sin has been committed, a drowsiness is induced and a veil is, as it were, drawn over the heart, and from this it follows that the same sin, or some other, is committed again. Peter, after denying the Lord once, became dull, and from that dullness he fell into the same sin of denial, and a third time he relapsed into it. David, after his adultery, as if dozing, fell into murder, and after that he remained sluggish and dull for some months. Now, although every sin leaves some stupor behind it, obstinacy against the Word of God and the truth once acknowledged does so most of all. As Paul says, since they did not think it worth while to retain God in their knowledge, so God gave them over to a reprobate mind. By this reprobate mind is signified utmost stupor, insensibility, and a conscience seared as with a hot iron. And again the disciples were there. Since we have spoken above about this manner of entering to the disciples, we will now pass over it in silence; we have also spoken about the greeting, which had to be effective, since he who greeted them was the author of peace. I see only this: once that drowsiness has taken hold, there is no waking up afterwards unless the presence of Christ intervenes. Who roused David? Was it not Christ the Son of God, when he sent the prophet Nathan to him? For those ancient prophets once spoke through the Spirit of Christ the Lord. Thomas too would never have been roused from that stupor unless Christ had addressed him. For unless that mercy of God which is in Christ rouses us from this our drowsiness, the justice of God will never accomplish it by afflicting us; nor will all the examples of his justice and judgments accomplish it. For Jude says in his epistle that those who turn the grace of our God into lasciviousness were not moved even by the example of that terrible judgment which overwhelmed Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities near them, but in the same way were lulled to sleep and defiled the flesh. Put in your finger. See the kindness of the Lord: he grants Thomas what he wished, even what he wished wickedly and through unbelief and obstinacy, and he even invites him; and he does this without any bitterness of mind, lest anyone think that this was said by the Lord falsely and ironically. For the words that he immediately adds, Do not be unbelieving, but believing, sufficiently show that these words were spoken by the Lord to Thomas with the greatest gentleness and meekness of mind. Beneath these words there is a certain rebuke, but tempered with such gentleness that it can scarcely be detected. What do we observe here, except the gentleness and mercy of the Lord, which Paul says was so great that he did not spare himself, in order that he might spare us? And although he uses great gentleness towards everyone, he does so also towards the reprobate themselves: Christ has mercy on whom he wills. Thomas is a notable example of this. The utmost meekness of Christ, as is said in Rom. 15.3. Again, Or do you despise the riches of his goodness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? Likewise, He endured with much patience the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction. When we come to his own, in whom he sees some spark of good and grace, already oppressed and smothered by the burden of this corrupt nature, then indeed what is said of him is true: A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoking flax he will not quench. But enough of these matters.

units.la: Præstat enim gustare reipsa quàm benignus ac suauis sit Dominus, quàm multa verba de eius benignitate facere. Hic quærat fortassis quispiam, quinam consistere potuerit cum natura illa Dei in Christo, & illa ipsius iustitia immutabili hoc quod concesserit Thomæ, id quod tam improbè ab eo postulatum est. Re-spondeo, quòd petierit is videre & tangere Dominum, id quidem per se iniustum & improbum non fuit, sed in eo peccauit, sicut supra vidimus, quod fidem resurrectionis sic sensu astrinxerit, ut professus sit se non crediturum, nisi viso prius & contrectato Domino. Habuit interea hauddubiè spiritualis illius desiderij nonihil, & amore sincero aliquo Dominū est persequutus: ut liceat discere ipsius exemplo Dominum non ita attentum esse ad imperfectionem illā, qua plenæ sunt preces & petitiones eorū, qui sunt ipsius: verum præterita tota illa imperfectione ac corruptione, qua quasi inuoluta est illa fidei eorū & desiderij scintillula, fidei vel tantulæ rationem habere. Nouit enim Dominus quis sit sensus sui Spiritus etiam luctantis in nobis cum innumeris infirmitatibus. Nihil hic expressè habemus de Thoma an iā inuitatus ad id à Domino, digitū inseruerit in vestigia vulnerum, quæ inerat manibus & pedibus eius, & manum immiserit in vulnus inflictū lateri ipsius. Quòd si inuitatus Thomas id fecerit, profectò oportuit insigniter impudentem & obstinatum esse, qui ne Domino ipsi, quem tum vidit præsentem, quem audiuit loquentē crediderit: sed verisimilius est Thomam ad conspectum Dominum, & audita eius vocem totum pudefactū redijsse ad se, ac sese collegisse. Dici enim non potest quā ciró mutetur animus, vel induratissimo cuique, quoties visum est Domino in eo efficax esse. Alij discipuli con-
units.tr: For it is better to taste in fact how kind and sweet the Lord is than to make many words about his kindness. Here perhaps someone will ask how this could be consistent with that nature of God in Christ and with his unchangeable justice, that he granted Thomas what Thomas so wickedly demanded. I answer: that he asked to see and touch the Lord was not in itself unjust or wicked, but he sinned in this, as we saw above, that he bound the faith in the resurrection so tightly to his senses that he professed he would not believe unless he first saw and handled the Lord. Meanwhile he undoubtedly had some measure of that spiritual desire, and he pursued the Lord with some sincere love; so that from his example we may learn that the Lord is not so attentive to that imperfection, with which the prayers and petitions of those who are his are full, but, setting aside all that imperfection and corruption in which the little spark of their faith and desire is, as it were, wrapped, he takes account even of the smallest trace of faith. For the Lord knows the disposition of his Spirit, even when it struggles in us amid countless infirmities. We have nothing here expressly saying whether Thomas, already invited to it by the Lord, put his finger into the marks of the wounds that were in his hands and feet, and put his hand into the wound inflicted on his side. But if Thomas did this at the invitation, he would surely have had to be remarkably shameless and obstinate, not to believe the Lord himself, whom he then saw present and heard speaking. It is more probable that Thomas, at the sight of the Lord and on hearing his voice, was completely abashed, came back to himself, and gathered himself together. For it cannot be said how quickly the mind is changed, even in the most hardened person, whenever it pleases the Lord to be effective in him.

units.la: {?} spectu. specto Domino, & audita eius voce, nō statim crediderunt, vt vidimus suprà: neque tamen sunt notati à Spiritu sancto tanta incredulitate, quanta Thomas fuit. Ille autem, cuius incredulitas supra alios magna apparuit, ad conspectum Dominum & auditam eius vocem statim credidit, erupitque in eam confessionem, de qua audiemus postea. Vt scias non pendere fidem nostram ex nobis, vel ex corde nostro, sic vel secus affecto: verum ex Domini voluntate & misericordia. Non est enim volentis aut currentis, sed miserentis Dei. Dominus meus.
units.tr: The other disciples, at the sight of the Lord and on hearing his voice, did not believe at once, as we saw above; yet the Holy Spirit did not mark them with so great an unbelief as Thomas had. But Thomas, whose unbelief had appeared great beyond the others, at the sight of the Lord and on hearing his voice believed at once, and burst out into that confession of which we shall hear afterwards. So that you may know that our faith does not depend on ourselves, or on our heart, disposed this way or that, but on the will and mercy of the Lord. For it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. My Lord.

units.la: Vox haec erupit proculdubio ex luce subito illata in mentem ipsius, idque ex efficaci illa praesentia Domini: illuminata est mens eius ad videndum Christum Dominum primum qua homo fuit: nam Christus homo est Dominus omnium. Deinde ad videndum Christum qua Deus fuit. Per verbum enim, vt vocat Apostolus ad Hebraeos, carnis & humanae naturae introductus est ad spectandum plenitudinem illam Deitatis in Christo inhabitantem corporaliter. Cum luce ista in mentem illata, apertum est cor Thomae ad amplectendum fide Dominum, quem vidit, simulque Deum quem vidit.
units.tr: This word undoubtedly burst forth from the light suddenly brought into his mind, and that from the effective presence of the Lord: his mind was enlightened to see Christ the Lord first as man, for Christ is man and Lord of all. Then to see Christ as God. For through the word, as the Apostle to the Hebrews calls it, he was brought into the flesh and human nature to behold that fullness of the Godhead dwelling bodily in Christ. With that light brought into his mind, the heart of Thomas was opened to embrace by faith the Lord whom he saw, and at the same time the God whom he saw.

units.la: Hinc est quod vocet non Dominum modo, sed Dominum suum: non Deum modo, sed Deum suum: ex subita hac metis illuminatione primum, deinde cordis apprehensione Domini sui & Dei sui, prolata est vox ac confessio Domini ac Dei aperta ista ac manifesta. Nō legimus huiusmodi confessione editam prius à quoquam aliorum discipulorum: vt videas id verum esse, vel ex hoc exemplo Thomae, quod dici solet: Vltimos esse primos, primos autem nouissimos. Hi paulo ante priores erant fide Thoma: at nunc subito quasi mutatione facta Thomas eos omnes anteuertit. Illi sunt afflati Spiritu sancto: at Thomas, qui tum abfuit, ita est illuminatus vel solo Christi aspectu, vt eruperit in confessionem eam, quae nondum audita est ex quoquam eorum. Haec ideo obseruo, vt videas omnia in solidum gratiae Dei tribuenda esse: & non esse currentis aut volentis, sed miserentis Dei. Haec subita eruptio arguit scintillam aliquam fidei & desiderij, vti diximus, in Thoma fuisse reliquam. Nam sideríum Christi nullum in eo extitisset prius, quomodo sic eum quasi à se desideratum & expetitum fuisset subito amplexus? Sermo enim eius plane prese fert, primùm desiderium Domini ac dolorem aliquem propter amissum, vt ipse putabat, Dominum: deinde gaudium propter inuentum iam eum praeter expectationem. Quia vidisti me, Thoma, credidisti. Agnoscit Dominus fidem Thomae, sed agnoscendo eam eleuat quodammodo, quia non credidit animo priusquam oculis vidit. Non dicit Dominus, Quia contrectasti Thoma, &c. Vnde ego sum in ea sententia, Thomam no contrectasse manibus Dominum: Agnoscit tamen fidem Thomę, simulque commendat fidem eorum qui crediturí sunt, non tamen visuri. Agnoscit fidem Thomae, non autem beatum praedicat propter fidem: sed fidem eorum qui credituri sunt, licet non visuri, praedicat, eósque beatos fore pronunciat. Ex quo colligimus nihilo inferiores esse nos, qui iam credimus cum non viderimus, iis qui crediderunt, quia viderút, praesertim Thoma isto qui noluit credere, priusquam vidit. Beatitudinis autem ista praedicatio, vel ideo efficax est, quòd, vt ait Petrus, Nos qui credimus, cum non viderimus, exultamus gaudio ineffabili ac glorioso. Sed tum demum praedicatio ista beatitudinis efficax futura est, cùm videbimus Dominum sicuti est: quo tempore similes ei erimus. Sed quid est cur tanti faciat Dominus fide eorum, qui non vident? Respondeo, quo quid difficilius obtinetur, eo pretiosius est magisque exploratu, ac maiori etiam laude dignum. Fides autem sine aspectu difficulter obtinetur, eóq; maiore consequitur laudem & commendationem. Vide Petrum 1.Epist.1.7.
units.tr: Hence he calls not only the Lord but his Lord, not only God but his God. From this sudden illumination of the mind first, and then the apprehension of the heart of his Lord and his God, there came forth the voice and open and manifest confession of the Lord and God. We do not read that any confession of this kind was first made by any of the other disciples; so that you may see this to be true, even from this example of Thomas, what is commonly said: the last will be first, and the first last. These had been before Thomas in faith a little while earlier, but now, as if by a sudden change, Thomas outstrips them all. They were inspired by the Holy Spirit; but Thomas, who was absent at that time, was so enlightened by the mere sight of Christ that he burst out into that confession which had not yet been heard from any of them. I note these things so that you may see that all must be ascribed wholly to the grace of God, and that it is not of him who wills or runs, but of God who shows mercy. This sudden outburst shows that some spark of faith and desire, as we said, remained in Thomas. For no longing for Christ would have existed in him before, how else would he so suddenly have embraced him as one desired and sought by himself? For his speech plainly bears the marks, first of a longing for the Lord and some grief for the one he thought was lost, then of joy at having found him beyond expectation. Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed. The Lord acknowledges the faith of Thomas, but in acknowledging it he somehow raises it up, because he did not believe in his mind before he saw with his eyes. The Lord does not say, "Because you have touched me, Thomas," etc. Hence I am of the opinion that Thomas did not touch the Lord with his hands. Yet he acknowledges the faith of Thomas, and at the same time commends the faith of those who would believe without seeing. He acknowledges the faith of Thomas, but does not pronounce him blessed on account of his faith; rather he proclaims the faith of those who will believe, though not seeing, and declares that they will be blessed. From this we gather that we, who now believe though we have not seen, are in no way inferior to those who believed because they saw, especially to that Thomas who was unwilling to believe before he saw. This proclamation of blessedness is effective for this reason, that, as Peter says, we who believe, though we have not seen, rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. But this proclamation of blessedness will be fully effective only when we see the Lord as he is, at which time we shall be like him. But why does the Lord set such store by the faith of those who do not see? I answer: the more difficult a thing is to obtain, the more precious it is, and the more tested, and also more worthy of praise. Now faith without sight is obtained with difficulty, and therefore it obtains the greater praise and commendation. See 1 Peter 1.7.

units.la: Multa igitur etiam. Haec obiter inserta esse videntur historiae resurrectionis, quibus occurrit vanę hominum curiositati. Obiici enim potuit Iohanni, An omnia à Christo edita miracula ab ipso in Euangelio suo essent cōscripta? Respondet multa fecisse Christū quae nō sunt scripta: hinc rursus quæri potuit, Annon igitur Euangelium à te scriptum imperfectum est? Respondet, haec quę scripta sunt satis esse ad fidem & salutem. Videntur quidem ista non suo loco esse dicta: quid enim ista ad historiam resurrectionis pertinent? Respondeo mihi videri Apostolū hic abrupisse sermonem illum institutum tinent. de resurrectione Domini, & conclusisse quodammodo Euangelium suum. Nam capite sequenti in eandem sententiam, & in eadem fere verba concludit historiam suam. Redit tamen postea ad historiam resurrectionis, quam denique in hanc ipsam sententiam concludit. Reuertamur ad miracula a Christo edita: de his enim est occupatio ista & responsio. Quæri rursus potest, An miracula quæ non sunt scripta inutilia erant? Respondeo profuisse eis ad fidem, qui vix erunt eo seculo quo ædita sunt, vt illud taceam, facere etiam ea ipsa non parum ad fidem nostram, dum audimus ac legimus extitisse tum primis illis temporibus tantam miraculorum copiam: & si ea quænam fuerint, distincte non sciamus. Ex quo rursus illud discitur, ea quidem non indigna scriptione & memoria fuisse quæ non sunt scripta, sed sufficere ex plurimis hæc quæ scripta sunt, non à Iohanne tantum, sed etiā ab aliis Euangelistis, caque non pauca. Sed vt de miraculis quædā paulò altius repetamus: Christus cum venit in hunc mundum, multis modis fuit admirabilis, vnde inter alia hoc nomen sortitus est, quo admirabilis est vocatus. Admirabilis fuit quoad personam, Deus enim & homo fuit in vna persona. Admirabilis fuit quoad doctrinam & verbum ab ipso prædicatum: attulit enim admirabilem doctrinæ lucem: admirabilis denique fuit, quoad res gestas & miracula, quæ Deum esse ipsum plane demonstrabant. Doctrina Christi & verbum ab ipso prædicatum proprie inseruiebat fidei. Miracula rursus inseruiebat doctrinæ. Vel enim animos hominum præparabat ad doctrinam recipiendam, vel in recepta iam doctrina fide confirmabant. Doctrina Christi pariter & miracula scripto ex ipsius Christi voluntate comissa sunt, ad fidem & salutem posteritatis. Scripta doctrina nobis habenda est loco viuę vocis ipsius Christi: Miracula scripta habenda sunt nō alio loco, quàm si fieri ea nostris oculis eerneremus: adeo vt non iam sit opus nobis aliis & nouis miraculis, quibus subinde confirmetur doctrina Christi & Apostolorum. Opus erat iis, qui erant in prima illa Ecclesia, cum recens iam tradita esset hæc doctrina, ac mundo noua videretur, & cum Ecclesiæ adhuc esset infantia. At nunc cum iam satis primis illis temporibus confir-
units.tr: Many other things too. These things seem to have been inserted in passing into the history of the resurrection, to meet the empty curiosity of men. For it could be objected to John: were all the miracles Christ performed written down by him in his Gospel? He answers that Christ did many things which are not written. Then again it could be asked: is your Gospel therefore incomplete? He answers that what has been written is enough for faith and salvation. These things indeed seem not to have been said in their proper place, for what do they have to do with the history of the resurrection? I answer that it seems to me the Apostle here broke off the discourse on the resurrection of the Lord which he had begun, and in a way concluded his Gospel. For in the following chapter he concludes his history with the same sentiment and almost the same words. Yet he returns afterwards to the history of the resurrection, which he finally concludes with this very sentiment. Let us return to the miracles performed by Christ, for this discussion and answer concern them. Again it can be asked: were the miracles that were not written down useless? I answer that they profited those who were in the age in which they were performed, not to mention that even those miracles themselves do not little for our faith, while we hear and read that there was such an abundance of miracles in those first times, even if we do not know distinctly what they were. From this again it is learned that those things which were not written were indeed not unworthy of being written and remembered, but that what has been written from very many is sufficient, not only from John but also from the other Evangelists, and not a few of them. But to go back somewhat more deeply concerning miracles: Christ, when he came into this world, was admirable in many ways, whence among other things he obtained the name by which he is called Admirable. He was admirable as to his person, for he was God and man in one person. He was admirable as to his doctrine and the word preached by him, for he brought the admirable light of doctrine. Finally he was admirable as to his deeds and miracles, which plainly demonstrated that he was God. The doctrine of Christ and the word preached by him properly served faith. The miracles in turn served the doctrine, for they either prepared the minds of men to receive the doctrine or confirmed faith in doctrine already received. The doctrine of Christ and the miracles were committed to writing by the will of Christ himself, for the faith and salvation of posterity. Written doctrine is to be held in place of the living voice of Christ himself; written miracles are to be held no differently than if we were seeing them with our own eyes. So there is no longer need for us of other and new miracles by which the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles might be confirmed from time to time. There was need of these for those who were in that first Church, when this doctrine had only just been delivered and seemed new to the world, and when the Church was still in its infancy. But now, since in those first times the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles has been sufficiently

units.la: { } Notes in the margin are printed beside the text in short lines and are transcribed above at their places. confirmata fit miraculis doctrina Christi & Apostolorum, non opus est amplius ea nobis miraculis quotidie confirmetur, nisi velis eam in perpetuum novam manere. Eat nunc & quaeratat qui velit miracula: nō aliud profecto accipiet à Deo, praeter hoc Euangelicae doctrinę planè miraculosum effectum, quod cernitur in gignenda in cordibus nostris fide hac iustificante, in regenerandis nobis, denique in inchoanda in nobis vita illa aeterna. Nam Euangelium Christi sentimus & experimur reipsa potentiam esse Dei ad salutem cuiuis credenti. Quod si quis non cōtentus admirabili isto effecto etiamnū requirat externa nescio quae miracula, satis arguit se nunquam in se sensisse hoc, de quo loquimur, Euangelij effectū: quod profecto nisi tandē senserit in se ex Euangelio hoc scripto ac praedicato, & ex miraculis his scriptis & praedicatis, nunquam futurum est ut sentiat illud, ne si infinita quidem ederentur coram miracula. Doctrina igitur Christi & miracula edita ab eo scriptis cōmissa sunt, ut iam diximus, sed hoc discrimine: Tota Christi doctrina, quod ad subsistentiam, perscripta est, ne vel una quidē sententia, quae ad fidē & salutē necessaria fuit desiderata: at verō nō sunt conscripta omnia numero miracula ea quae ab eo sunt edita: illud nimirū, ut scriberetur tota doctrina exigente fide nostra: hoc verō, nimirum ut scriberentur omnia & singula miracula non exigere fide nostra. Nam regula ac mensura scripti & revelationis non debet esse vana hominum curiositas, quae inexplebilis est, sed fides ac salus nostra, ut ea sufficiant scripta, quae ad fidē & salutem satis sunt. Qui his non contentus, plura adeoque infinita requirit. Veritates, quas vocant, non scriptas, miracula infinita: neq; illi quidem mihi videntur quaerere aliquid ultra & supra vitam aeternam, hoc est phatasmata quaedam, nescio quae sua. Quod si fides Papistę posset omnia simul & semel capere, quaecunque in veteri ac novo testamento scripta sunt, ego profecto hoc ei lubentius largirer, ut praeterea aliquid quaereret & sibi fingeret. At verò cùm fides nostra non posset respondere magnitudine sua iis ipsis quę iam extant scripta, cur fabricat sibi miserallia? Cur assuit veritati Dei, cui non sumus nos pares in hac vita, cur, inquam, assuit huic misero infinitą
units.tr: confirmed by miracles, there is no need that it be confirmed for us daily by miracles, unless you wish it to remain new forever. Let whoever wishes now go and seek miracles: he will surely receive from God nothing other than the truly miraculous effect of the Gospel doctrine, which is seen in begetting in our hearts this justifying faith, in regenerating us, and finally in beginning in us that eternal life. For we feel and experience in fact that the Gospel of Christ is the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes. But if anyone, not content with this admirable effect, still seeks I know not what external miracles, he sufficiently shows that he has never felt in himself that effect of the Gospel of which we speak. Unless at last he feels it in himself from this Gospel written and preached, and from these miracles written and preached, he will never feel it, even if infinite miracles were performed before him. So the doctrine of Christ and the miracles performed by him have been committed to writing, as we have said, but with this difference: the whole doctrine of Christ has been set down in full as far as its substance goes, so that not even one saying necessary for faith and salvation is missing; but not all the miracles he performed have been written down in number. The former was required by our faith, that the whole doctrine be written; the latter, that all and each of the miracles be written, is not required by our faith. For the rule and measure of Scripture and revelation ought not to be the empty curiosity of men, which is insatiable, but our faith and salvation, so that those things suffice which are written and are enough for faith and salvation. Whoever is not content with these, but requires more, and so infinitely more. Unwritten truths, as they call them, and infinite miracles: nor do such people seem to me to seek anything beyond and above eternal life, that is, certain phantasms of their own, I know not what. But if the faith of the Papist could grasp all at once and in a single act whatever is written in the Old and New Testaments, I would gladly grant him that he might seek and invent something else besides. But since our faith cannot match by its greatness even those things which are already written, why does he fabricate miseries for himself? Why does he add to the truth of God, to which we are not equal in this life, why, I say, does he add to this wretched faith an infinite

units.la: CCCc nescio quæ figmenta sua? Sed de his hactenus. Iesum. Hæc summa est fidei. Fides enim est in Iesum, neque illum ipsum qui commoratus est inter Iudæos. De eo autem hoc credendum est, quod sit Christus, primum. Atque hoc ad officium Iesu spectat: est enim Christus officio, hoc est vnctus in regem, in Prophetam & in Pontificem. Deinde de eo credendum est, quòd sit Filius Dei. Hoc ad personam ipsius spectat. Nam persona est Christus proprie vt Deus, & vt Filius Dei. Est enim secunda Trinitatis persona. Humana autem natura Christi non constituit personam, sed assumpta est ad personam, & arctè adeo cum persona Filij coiuncta est, vt totus Christus Deus & homo persona dicatur. Nunc quid ex hac fide ad nos redeat videndum nobis est. Fide enim honoramus Christum, & quasi ad eum in sublime ascendimus. Redit autem per fidem ad nos vita ęaque æterna. Vita autem hæc, est vita Dei: ergo fluit primùm à Filio Dei, & Christo Deo. Quà autem Filius idem Dei, Christus est, ad nos vsque peruenit. Nam primùm quia vnctus est in Pontificem, meritus est nobis vitam. Deinde quà Rex & Propheta est, applicat nobis id quod meritus est, qua Sacerdos, quà Propheta quidem applicat, dum docet nos. Qua rex verò, dum poteter & efficacxer in nobis agit operatúrque. Hæc igitur sunt quæ nobis credenda sunt de Iesu. Atque hic ex fide fructus ab Iesu ad nos vsque peruenit. Sed caro & sanguis non docet nos hanc fidem. Vt enim dicente Paulo, Nemo potest dicere Iesum Dominum, nisi per Spiritum sanctum: ita nemo potest credere Iesum esse Christum & Dei filium, nisi per Spiritum sanctum: de quo etiam admonuit Christus Petrum cùm confessus esset eum esse Dei filium.
units.tr: number of his own I know not what fictions? But so much for these matters. Jesus. This is the sum of faith. For faith is in Jesus, not in him who lived among the Jews. Concerning him this must first be believed, that he is Christ. This relates to his office: for Christ is by office, that is, anointed as King, Prophet and High Priest. Next, it must be believed concerning him that he is the Son of God. This relates to his person. For Christ is properly a person as God and as the Son of God, for he is the second person of the Trinity. The human nature of Christ does not constitute a person, but was assumed into the person and is so closely joined with the person of the Son that the whole Christ, God and man, is called a person. Now we must see what returns to us from this faith. For by faith we honour Christ, and as it were ascend with him on high. But through faith eternal life returns to us. This life, however, is the life of God: therefore it flows first from the Son of God and Christ God. Insofar as he is the Son of God, Christ reaches us. For first, insofar as he is anointed as High Priest, he has merited life for us. Then, insofar as he is King and Prophet, he applies to us what he has merited: as Priest he applies it, and as Prophet he applies it while he teaches us; as King he applies it while he works and effects in us by his power. These, then, are the things that must be believed about Jesus. And here the fruit of faith reaches us from Jesus. But flesh and blood does not teach us this faith. For as Paul says, no one can say that Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit, so no one can believe that Jesus is Christ and Son of God except by the Holy Spirit, of which Christ also admonished Peter when he confessed that he was the Son of God.

units.la: Caro, inquit, & sanguis hæc non retexit tibi, sed Pater meus qui est in cœlis. Atque hæc de his hactenus.
units.tr: "Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." So much for these things for now.

units.la: Argumentum huius capitis iam præfixum est capiti 20.
units.tr: The argument of this chapter has already been prefixed to chapter 20.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAP. XXI.

units.la: 1 POstea seseruersus exhibuit Iesus discipulis, ad mare Tiberiadis. Sic autem exhibuit.
units.tr: 1 After this, Jesus showed himself again to the disciples at the Sea of Tiberias. He showed himself in this way.

units.la: 2 Erant simul Simō Petrus, & Thomas Didymus, & Nathanaël qui erat ex Cana Galilææ, & filij Zebedæi, aliique ex discipulis tum duo.
units.tr: 2 Simon Peter, Thomas called Didymus, Nathanael who was from Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of the disciples were together.

units.la: 3 Dicit eis Simon Petrus, Abeo piscatum. Dicunt ei, Imus & nos tecum. Exierunt & ascenderunt in navigium statim: & illa nocte nihilceperunt.
units.tr: 3 Simon Peter said to them, "I am going fishing." They said to him, "We will come with you too." They went out and immediately got into the boat, and that night they caught nothing.

units.la: 4 Mane verò iam exorto stetit Iesus ad litus: non tamen discipuli Iesum esse.
units.tr: 4 But when morning had already come, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.

units.la: 5 Dicit igitur eis Iesus, Pueri, nunquid obsonij habetis? Responderunt ei, Non.
units.tr: 5 So Jesus said to them, "Children, have you any food?" They answered him, "No."

units.la: 6 Ille dixit eis, Coniicite rete in dextram navigii partem, & inuenietis. Coniecerunt ergo, & non amplius valebat trahere præ multitudine piscium.
units.tr: 6 He said to them, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." So they cast it, and they were no longer able to haul it in because of the great number of fish.

units.la: 7 Dicit ergo discipulus ille, quem diligebat Iesus, Petro: Dominus est. Simon ergo Petrus cùm audisset Dominum esse, amiculum succinxit (erat enim nudus) & abiecit se in mare.
units.tr: 7 Therefore that disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, "It is the Lord." So when Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he tucked his outer garment around him (for he was naked) and threw himself into the sea.

units.la: 8 Alij verò discipuli navigio venerunt (non enim longè aberant à terra, sed circiter cubitis ducentis) trahentes rete plenum piscium.
units.tr: 8 But the other disciples came in the boat (for they were not far from land, but about two hundred cubits away), dragging the net full of fish.

units.la: 9 Ut autem descenderunt in terram, viderunt prunas positas, & piscem impositum & panem.
units.tr: 9 When they came down onto the land, they saw a charcoal fire set there, and fish laid on it, and bread.

units.la: 10 Dicit eis Iesus, Adferte ex piscibus quos modò cepistis.
units.tr: 10 Jesus said to them, "Bring some of the fish you have just caught."

units.la: 11 Ascendit Simon Petrus, & traxit rete in terram, plenum magnis piscibus centum quinquaginta tribus, & cum tot essent non est fissum rete.
units.tr: 11 Simon Peter went up and drew the net to land, full of large fish, one hundred and fifty-three; and although there were so many, the net was not torn.

units.la: 12 Dicit eis Iesus, Venite, prandete. Nullus autem discipulorum audebat illum interrogare, Tu quis es? cum scirent Dominum esse.
units.tr: 12 Jesus said to them, "Come and eat." Yet none of the disciples dared to ask him, "Who are you?", since they knew it was the Lord.

units.la: 13 Venit ergo Iesus, & accipit panem, & dat eis, & piscem similiter.
units.tr: 13 Jesus then came and took the bread and gave it to them, and likewise the fish.

units.la: 14 Ita iam tertio sese exhibuit Iesus discipulis suis, postquam suscitatus fuerat ex mortuis.
units.tr: 14 This was now the third time that Jesus showed himself to his disciples, after he had risen from the dead.

units.la: Equitur post resurrectionem Christi, apparitio eius septima, si singulas seorsim velit quis enumerare, initio sumpto ab illa qua conspectus est primùm omnium à Maria Magdalene: sin verò numerare velit apparitiones, quæ non sunt factæ nisi discipulis in unum congregatis, iam hæc tertia est eius apparitio, ut postea annotat Iohannes. Quo autem die post resurrectionem suam, & post apparitionem proximam apparuerit iam tertia vice, non est id quidem expressum. Locus verò apparitionis huius notatus est: fuit is mare Tyberiadis, quod mare alias Lacus Gennezareth est dictum. Lacus enim Hebraea phrasi mare vocatum est. De hac tà multiplici apparitione Christi & patefactione post resurrectionem, potest quæri: Annon satis fuit semel bisve se discipulis conspiciendum dare? Resp. Hæc ipsa tam credibra apparitio arguit quàm difficile sit & arduum credere in resurrectionem mortuorum: Arguit etiam opus fuisse primis illis testibus multiplici sensu, & patefactione Domini post resurrectionem suam, ut ipsi cum certa persuasione multa, ut Paulus de se loquutus est, postpossent de ea aliis, tum viua voce, tum scripto, ad redi-tum vsque Christi testificari. Ergo patefactio ista Domini tam crebrò iterata est, propter nos. Vnaquæque enim patefactio aliquid addit fidei nostræ: Omnes autem patefactiones coniunctim sumptæ, fide nostrâ quasi consummant, atq; perficiunt. Nobis enim sic cogitandum est, ac si nos ipsi oculis nostris vidissemus Dominum post resurrectionem suam: Quod Petrus vidit ego mecum cogito, neq; etiam fallor me id ipsum vidisse: Quod Iohannes, quod alij oculis suis viderit, ego reputo apud me idipsum me vidisse oculis meis: Et quoties hi ipsi viderunt Dominum, ego cogito me toties vidisse eum. Cùm enim Petrus dicit se oculis aspexisse illius maiestatem, ipse mihi Christum digito quasi demonstrat oculis meis aspiciendum: Et Paulus dum sibi visum esse Dominum prædicat post resurrectionem ipsius, eadem opera demonstrat Dominum mihi videndum. Et Iohannes cùm dicit, Quod spectauimus, quod audiuimus, quod manibus nostris tractauimus, illud iam annuntiamus, eadem opera mihi proponit videndum, audiendum, contrectandum manibus etiam meis Dominum, vt & ipse postea loquitur, impleat gaudium meum. Hic taceo tam multiplicem pa-tefactionem Christi id effecisse, vt ipsi in loquendo pariter, & in scribendo multa vsi fuerint. Nam multiplex sensus significat, hæc vero efficit. Illa autem & libertas in loquendo plurimum valet ad fidem augendam. Erant simul. Hi in vnum coiuerunt, non quidem temere, sed certa Dei prouidentia, quasi cogente eos in vnum, ad hoc vt se iis in vnum coactis conspiciendum offerret. Deus enim cùm insignem aliquam gratiam conferre constituit, suos in vnum congregat, vt cum iis gratiam illam suam communicet. Magna enim gratia & Dei præsentia datur potissimum cœtibus sanctorum. Spiritus sanctus sub figura linguarum dispertitarum instar ignis in die Pētecostes datus est vniuerso cœtui discipulorum. Et hodierno die reipsa experimur omnes Spiritum maximè in nobis efficacem esse dū prædicatur Euangelium in Ecclesia Dei, & in cœtibus sanctorū. Thomas inter alios nunc numeratur. Thomas, inquam,
units.tr: After the resurrection of Christ, his appearance is the seventh, if one wishes to count each one separately, beginning with the one in which he was first seen of all, by Mary Magdalene. But if one wishes to count appearances that were made only when the disciples were gathered together, this is now his third appearance, as John later notes. On what day after his resurrection, and after his immediately preceding appearance, he appeared for the third time, is not indeed stated. The place of this appearance is noted: it was the Sea of Tiberias, which elsewhere is called the Lake of Gennesaret. For the Hebrew idiom calls a lake a sea. Concerning this so frequent appearance and manifestation of Christ after the resurrection, one may ask: was it not enough for him to give himself to be seen by the disciples once or twice? Answer: this very frequent appearance shows how difficult and hard it is to believe in the resurrection of the dead. It also shows that those first witnesses needed the many-sided perception and the manifestation of the Lord after his resurrection, so that with a firm conviction they might be able to bear witness to many things about it to others, as Paul speaks of himself, both by living voice and in writing, down to the return of Christ. Therefore this manifestation of the Lord was repeated so often, on our account. For each manifestation adds something to our faith, and all the manifestations taken together, as it were, complete and perfect our faith. For we must think of it as though we ourselves had seen the Lord with our own eyes after his resurrection. What Peter saw, I think of as seen by me as well, and I do not think I am mistaken in saying that I saw the same thing: what John and others saw with their eyes, I reckon that I too saw with my own eyes; and as often as they saw the Lord, I think I too have seen him that many times. For when Peter says that he saw with his eyes the majesty of that One, he almost points out Christ to me with his finger, to be seen by my eyes; and when Paul declares that the Lord appeared to him after his resurrection, he at the same time shows me the Lord to be seen. And when John says, "What we have seen, what we have heard, what we have handled with our hands, that we now proclaim," at the same time he sets before me the Lord to be seen, heard, and touched with my own hands, so that, as he himself later says, he may fulfil my joy. Here I pass over the fact that such a manifold manifestation of Christ caused them to use many things both in speaking and in writing. For the manifold perception signifies, but this produces. And that freedom in speaking is of very great value for increasing faith. "They were together." These came together into one place, not indeed by chance, but by the certain providence of God, as though God were compelling them into one body, so that, gathered together, they might be offered to be seen by him. For when God determines to bestow some remarkable grace, he gathers his people into one, so that he may share that grace of his with them. For great grace and the presence of God are given especially to assemblies of the saints. The Holy Spirit was given under the appearance of tongues divided, like fire, on the day of Pentecost, to the whole assembly of the disciples. And today we all actually experience that the Spirit is most powerfully effective in us when the Gospel is preached in the Church of God and in assemblies of the saints. Thomas is now counted among the others. Thomas, I say, who was absent at the time when the Lord first gave himself to be seen by the others. But he was present with the others when he revealed himself a second time. Now too he takes part in the company of the others, now that the Lord reveals himself a third time to his disciples. Once led out onto the way of grace, he who had for some time strayed from the way now goes forward together with the others. For to him who has, more will be given; and he who began a good work in us will bring it to completion by the day of Jesus Christ.

units.la: CCcc iij qui aberat quo tempore aliis primum se Dominus conspiciendum dedit. At adfuit vna cum aliis, dum secundo se iis patefecit. Interest nunc quoque aliorum coetui, cum tertia vice se patefacit Dominus discipulis suis. Semel eductus in viam gratiae, qui aliquandiu a via aberrauit,iam pariter cum aliis progreditur.Habenti enim datur : & qui coepit in nobis opus bonum perficiet ad diem Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Once led out onto the way of grace, he who had for some time strayed from the way now goes forward together with the others. For to him who has, more will be given; and he who began a good work in us will bring it to completion by the day of Jesus Christ.

units.la: {a}Abeo piscatum. Non quidem temerè hoc factum est, quòd Thomas,& alij Petrum,cui animus erat segregare se ab aliis,sunt comitati; sed certa Dei prouidentia,qui, vt in vnum suos conuocat, ita conuocatos iam in vnum, conseruat simul ac retinet, eo quo ipsi visum est modo, facitque vt cum aliis vellent se segregare ab aliis, alij se ab iis segregari ac diuelli non patiantur. Haec facit in eum finem,vt Ecclesiae suae in vnum coactae, impertiatur gratiam eam,quae alioqui non daretur dispersis & segregatis.Quod si Petrus alio iuisset, Thomas alio, aliisque alio, dubito an singulis se videndum Dominus praebuisset, quibus coniunctis & in vnum congregatis, praesentiam suam gratificatus est ad admirabilem ipsorum consolationem. Non est hic laborandum valde in eo,quod discipuli & Apostoli Christi iam destinati aliquam, eique multo sublimiori muneri,nempe Apostolatui,redierunt tamen ad vile illud piscandi munus & seruilem occupationem. Nam quanquam iam erant designati, qui Apostolatu fungerentur, tamen nondum erant facti re ipsa Apostoli, antequam virtute ex alto induerentur, & effusus esset in eos Spiritus sanctus in die Pentecostes. Quamobrem prior illa eorum functio nondum fuit plane abdicata. Praeterea nihil hic mihi videtur incommodi, quòd Apostoli etiam ipsi in licita quadam & honesta occupatione,etiam manibus suis sint operati.Id quod Paulus se fecisse dicit non vno in loco;1.Cor.4.12. 1.Thessal.2.9.2.Thess.3.8. Profecti sunt. Eunt illi quidem, vt capiant pisces, & quaeritent sibi victum hunc corpore reum.Dominus interea alio eos auocat,ad recipiendam nimirum ipsius praesentiam, quae tota illa occupatione piscatoria praestantior fuit, & quam Petrus pluris fecit, quam numerosam aliquam piscium copiam,quos etiam omnes
units.tr: {a}"I am going fishing." It was not by chance that Thomas and the others accompanied Peter, who had the intention of separating himself from the others; but it was by the certain providence of God, who, just as he gathers his people into one, so also, once they are gathered into one, keeps and holds them together, in the way that seems good to him, and brings it about that, although some wish to separate themselves from others, the others do not allow them to be torn away and separated. He does this to this end: that the grace which would otherwise not be given to the scattered and separated may be imparted to his Church gathered into one. For if Peter had gone one way, Thomas another, and the others another, I doubt whether the Lord would have offered himself to be seen by each one singly; but having them joined together and gathered into one, he graciously granted them his presence, to their wonderful comfort. Here we need not labour greatly over the fact that the disciples and Apostles of Christ, already designated to an office and to a far higher ministry, namely the apostleship, nevertheless returned to that humble work of fishing and to that servile occupation. For although they had already been appointed to fulfil the apostleship, yet they had not in actual fact become Apostles before they were clothed with power from on high and the Holy Spirit was poured out upon them on the day of Pentecost. For this reason their former work had not yet been wholly abandoned. Besides, nothing here seems to me improper, that the Apostles themselves also worked with their own hands in some lawful and honest occupation. Paul says he did this in more than one place: 1 Cor. 4.12; 1 Thess. 2.9; 2 Thess. 3.8. "They went." They indeed go to catch fish and seek for themselves this food for the body that is liable to perish. Meanwhile the Lord calls them away elsewhere, namely to receive his presence, which was far more excellent than all that fishing business, and which Peter valued more than any large quantity of fish, all of which he too...

units.la: Diligentibus Deum omnia in bonū conferunt. omnes reliquit statim, vbi conspexit iam ac cognouit Dominum: ad quem etiam, vt celeriter perueniret, se in præsens vitæ discrimen coniecit, abiiciendo se in mare, & enatando ad Christum. Sic enim omnes tam actiones quàm passiones suorum conuertit Dominus ad bonum ipsorum, ac inseruire facit vitæ eorum sempiternæ. Vi- dendum est nobis dum quiduis agimus, dum imus pi-scaturi, aut omnino facturi aliquid, eamus cum interioris sensu aliquo dilectionis Dei. Hoc modo futurum est, vt vna eademque opera in cœlos ipsos eamus recta. Et illa nocte nihil. Differt quidem Dominus laborum succes- sum & fructum, vt eum abundantius suo tempore conferret. Sic enim cum suis solet agere: destituit eos ad tempus commodo suo, idque ex instituto & dedita opera, eo nimirum fine, vt tandem eos cumulet benedictione sua. Paulus ad Philemonem de Onesimo seruo fugitiuo scribens, ait, verf. 15. Cuius labore & opera ad tempus priuatus es, vt perpetuum eum reciperes. Simul hoc facit ad Dei gloriam: nam cum perpetuo & sine intermissione laboribus nostris benedicit, tum vix agnoscitur à nobis eius benedictio: imò homines pro Deo sibi benedicunt, sibi sanctificant, & suam quasi manum deosculantur. Cum vero senserunt aliquandiu, se frustra laborasse, postremò vero cumulantur Dei benedictione. Iam clarè benedictionem dignoscunt, & Deo gloriam omnem tribuunt. Maior autem beatitudo in benedictione Dei cernitur, & seria gratiarum actione, quam in ipso illo bono terrestri, quantumcunque illud est quod in nos confertur. Mane autem. Tandem adest Dominus, postquam iam totam noctem cum labore & ærumna operati sunt, idque inutiliter & absque laborum suorum fructu vllo. Sic enim solet Dominus tandem ad suos accedere, postquam iam multum diuque, & sine fructu laborarunt. Venit autem mane: hoc est, suo tempore: nam tempus aduentus Domini matutinum est. Eo enim absente nox & tenebrae sunt: eo veniente oritur lux. Ipse enim lucifer ille est, & sol ille iustitiae, qui aduentu suo dispellit omnes tenebras. Hinc sunt illæ sententiæ Dauidis. Primum, Vespere fecit vt diuersetur fletus, mane verò adest cantus. Deinde, Satiabor cum expergiscar, illo nimirum mane, similitudine tua. Loquitur autem de vltimo & glorioso illo aduentu Domini. Non tamen. Fortasse quia ipsorum continebantur oculi, ne quem videbant praefentem cognoscerent. Tantum hoc obseruamus, Vt Dominus non est quaesitus ab iis: ita iam repertus non est ab iis cognitus: vt videamus quam longe absumus a gratia & a Deo, qui per naturam neque possumus eum quaerere, vel de eo quaerendo semel cogitare: neque etiam fe vltro offerentem possumus cognoscere, nisi ipse aperiat oculos nostros, seque nobis ipse innotescere faciat.
units.tr: Those who love God turn all things to good. He left everything at once, when he saw and recognised the Lord, and to reach him quickly he cast himself into peril of life, throwing himself into the sea and swimming to Christ. For in this way the Lord turns all the actions and sufferings of his people to their good, and makes them serve their everlasting life. We must see to it that whenever we do anything, whenever we go out to fish or undertake anything at all, we go with some inward sense of love for God. In this way it will happen that one and the same work takes us straight to heaven itself. And that night they caught nothing. The Lord indeed delays the outcome and fruit of their labours, so that he may bestow it more abundantly in his own time. For this is how he is accustomed to deal with his people: he leaves them for a time in want, at his own pleasure and on purpose, with the aim, no doubt, that at last he may load them with his blessing. Paul, writing to Philemon about Onesimus the runaway slave, says (v. 15): You were parted from him for a time, that you might receive him for ever. This also serves God's glory. For though he blesses our labours constantly and without interruption, his blessing is hardly recognised by us; indeed people bless themselves, as if for God, sanctify themselves, and kiss their own hand, as it were. But when they have felt for some time that they have laboured in vain, and at last are loaded with the blessing of God, then they clearly recognise the blessing and give all the glory to God. But greater blessedness is seen in the blessing of God, and in earnest thanksgiving, than in that earthly good itself, however great it is that is bestowed upon us. But when morning came. At last the Lord is present, after they had worked the whole night through with toil and hardship, and that to no purpose and without any fruit of their labours. For in this way the Lord is accustomed at last to come to his own, after they have laboured long and to no avail. But when morning came: that is, in his own time; for the time of the Lord's coming is morning. For when he is absent there is night and darkness; when he comes, light rises. He himself is that morning star, and that sun of righteousness, who by his coming scatters all darkness. Hence are those sayings of David: first, At evening weeping may lodge, but in the morning there is singing; then, I shall be satisfied when I awake, that is, in that morning, with your likeness. But he speaks of that last and glorious coming of the Lord. Yet they did not know. Perhaps it was because their eyes were held, so that they did not recognise him standing before them. We observe only this: just as the Lord was not sought by them, so now that he has been found he was not recognised by them; so that we may see how far we are from grace and from God, who by nature can neither seek him nor so much as think once of seeking him, and cannot recognise him even when he offers himself of his own accord, unless he opens our eyes and makes himself known to us.

units.la: Pueri, Numquid. Hic fe incipit iis patefacere; praeparat autem eos ad futurum successum, & laboris fui fructum, ipsiusque Domini benedictionem, per confessionem inopiae suae. Confessionem enim hanc ab iis accipit, dum respondent quaerenti fe nihil obsonij habere. Non enim fatis est ad hoc, vt laboribus nostris benedicat Dominus, fi egeni & inopes fimus: verum requirit Dominus praesertim agnitionem, sensum, adeoque etiam confessionem inopiae nostrae: superbum enim ac inflatum mendicum aliquem aduersatur Dominus. Iacite rete. Potuit quidem fine opera ipsorum nauigium piscibus adimplere, sed voluit benedicere laboribus ipsorum, & non nisi laborantibus dare successum: neque id praetereundum quod etiam haetenus per totam noctem iam fatigatos, miseros, laborare voluerit, ad hoc vt successum iis daret: vt videamus quantopere Dominus requirat industriam & laborem nostrum: non quidem quod propter laborem nostrum bene succedat nobis, cum Deus solus fit is qui dat incrementum, & dat quidem propter fe, & Christum suum, citra vllum hominum meritum.
units.tr: Children, have you any food? Here he begins to reveal himself to them; and he prepares them for the future success and the fruit of their labour, and for the Lord's own blessing, through their confession of their poverty. For he receives this confession from them when they answer his question that they have no food. For it is not enough for the Lord to bless our labours if we are needy and destitute; rather the Lord requires above all the acknowledgement, the sense, and so also the confession of our poverty, for the Lord opposes the proud and puffed-up beggar. Cast the net. He could indeed have filled the boat with fish without their labour, but he chose to bless their labours and to give success only to those who work. Nor is it to be passed over that he wished them, now weary and wretched after toiling through the whole night, to labour on, in order to give them success; so that we may see how greatly the Lord requires our diligence and labour. Not that our success comes because of our labour, since God alone is the one who gives the increase, and gives it for his own sake and that of his Christ, without any merit of men.

units.la: Quod autem labores nostri nihil prosi-cere fine eo; hoc ipse docet nos manifestò, dum finit nos nonnunquam ad fatis diuturnum tempus frustra laborare. Hoc docuit Petrum & alios frustra laborantes & sese fatigantes per totam noctem hoc loco. Requirit tamen labores nostros, quia hoc medium est ordinarium, per quod benedicit nobis Dominus, & officium, ac, vt sic dicam, seruitium Deo a nobis debitum. Dum enim simplici, sincerōque animo feruimus hominibus, nibus, tum non tam hominum servi sumus, quàm ipsius Christi Ephes. 6. 6. Iecerunt ergo rete. Obedientia hæc tam prompta, præstita etiam ignoto, & alicui etiam, vt ipsis videbatur, è vulgo, arguit magnam in iis patientiam ac laborum tolerantiam, quæ etiam tum fuit, postquam iam totam noctem laborassent ad sudorem usque & fatigationem. Fortasse domiti erant & subacti iam diutina fatigatione. Sed patientiam hanc & tolerantiam laborum effecit, vt mihi videtur, potissimum spes successus & benedictionis Dei, suo tandem tempore obuenturæ. Spes enim facit tolerantiam laborum. Tolerantia autem, siue patientia consequitur successum, si modo spes ea in Domino sit, qui nunquam suos plane deserit. Quare sperandum dum viuis, vel ideo vt Deum tuum honores. Fide enim & spe omnis boni venturi à Deo fonte illo bonorum omnium, plurimum glorificatur ipse Deus in misericordia sua.
units.tr: That our labours avail nothing without him, he himself teaches us plainly, in that he allows us at times to labour in vain for a fairly long time. He taught this to Peter and the others here, who laboured in vain and wearied themselves through the whole night. Yet he requires our labours, because this is the ordinary means through which the Lord blesses us, and the duty and, as I may say, the service owed to God by us. For when we serve men with a simple and sincere mind, we are then not so much servants of men as of Christ himself (Eph. 6. 6). So they cast the net. This obedience, so prompt, rendered even to a stranger, and to one who seemed to them to be of the common sort, shows great patience in them and endurance of labours, which continued even after they had laboured through the whole night to the point of sweat and exhaustion. Perhaps they had been subdued and tamed by long fatigue. But this patience and endurance of labours was produced, as it seems to me, chiefly by the hope of success and of the blessing of God, which would come at last in its own time. For hope makes endurance of labours possible. Endurance, or patience, obtains success, provided that hope is placed in the Lord, who never utterly forsakes his people. Therefore one must hope while one lives, if only so that you may honour your God. For by faith and hope in every good thing to come from God, that fountain of all good, God himself is greatly glorified in his mercy.

units.la: Dicit ergo discipulis Is erat Iohannes noster, qui cum effusa esset charitas Dei in corde ipsius per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est ei, sese perpetuò in Euangelio suo hac Christi erga se dilectione depingit & detegit. Dicit hic Petro, Dominus est. Primus hic cognouit Dominum. Aperti autem sunt oculi eius, per miraculum illum quem vidit successum. Vidit enim in eo non modò potentiam, sed etiam liberalitatem ac beneficentiam quandam mirabilem. Hinc statim collegit Dominum fuisse eum, qui in opere, & iaciendo retia direxit manus ipsorum. Sic Dei opera & beneficia, quæ in nos quotidie confert, deducere nos debent ad videndum ipsum Dominum. Si enim ea paulò diligentius aduertamus, deprehendemus in iis digitum Dei, hoc est, characterem quendam potentiæ, misericordiæ & liberalitatis ipsius Dei, vt oculis nostris sublatis in cœlos intueamur Deum omnium opificem & datorem, ipsumque glorificemus; id quod profecto summum bonum nostrum est, nempe Deum nostrum glorificare. Ij autem qui non aduertunt & notant Dei opera, non tantum priuant se hoc bono, sed etiam benedictionem Dei conuertunt sibi in maledictionem.
units.tr: He therefore says to the disciples. This was our John, who, since the love of God was poured out in his heart through the Holy Spirit who was given to him, portrays and reveals himself throughout his Gospel by this love of Christ towards him. He says to Peter, It is the Lord. He was the first to recognise the Lord. And his eyes were opened by the miraculous success he saw. For he saw in it not only power, but also a certain wonderful generosity and beneficence. Straightaway from this he gathered that it was the Lord who had directed their hands in the work and in casting the nets. So the works and benefits of God, which he bestows upon us daily, ought to lead us to see the Lord himself. For if we attend to them somewhat more carefully, we shall detect in them the finger of God, that is, a certain mark of the power, mercy and generosity of God himself; so that, lifting our eyes to heaven, we may behold God the maker and giver of all, and glorify him. This is indeed our highest good, namely to glorify our God. But those who do not notice and mark the works of God not only deprive themselves of this good, but also turn the blessing of God into a curse for themselves.

units.la: Simon ergo Petrus cum audisset. Iohannes quidem cp-
units.tr: Simon Peter therefore, when he heard John indeed ...

units.la: Petrus agnouit Christum per aspectum, Petrus autem per auditum, docente nimirum eum Iohanne. Cognitio deinde Petri erupit in zelum, quo vicissim superior fuit Iohanne doctore suo, qui tamen ipso erat prior fide & cognitione. Zelum hunc Petri accipio verum fuisse, non autem praecipitem aliquem temeritatis impetum. Ex quo colligimus diuersa fuisse dona Iohannis & Petri: hunc quidem zelo, illum vero cognitione excelluisse. Nam illud quod dicitur 1. Corinth. 12. 11. Quod distribuat dona sua cuique prout ipsi visum est admetiri: hoc, inquam, verum fuit etiam de ipsis Apostolis: quorum alij alia dona acceperunt. Iohannes cognitionem Christi excellentem, vt testatur ipsius Euangelium, quod plenum est sublimi de Christo doctrina, praesertim de ipsius Deitate. Petrus vero zelum ardentissimum accepit, quo alios superauit. Paulus dicit se gratiam laborandi maiorem quam omnes alios accepisse: neque enim vnus aliquis ex Apostolis omnia pariter accepit, neque etiam id vtile fuisset, vel ipsi, vel aliis: sic enim is alios fortassis prae se contempsisset, & alij vicissim ei perfectionem illam tantam inuidissent, atque ita corpus fuisset laceratum. Inaequalitas enim ista, & diuersitas donorum est, vt dicit Paulus, quae vincit aptatque inter se corporis Christi membra; non secus atque fit in corpore humano, in quo inaequalitas & diuersitas facultatum, quae singulae sunt in singulis membris, continet inter se membra eiusdem corporis. Obserua deinde, tota nocte superiori fides Iohannis elanguit, sic & zelus Petri: at mane appropinquante iam Christo, & fides Iohannis & zelus Petri vigent ac reuiuiscunt: vt inde discamus gratiam hanc fidei, cognitionis, zeli denique excitari per Christum, qui materia quidem est & obiectum istorum. Fides enim est ex eius luce, quae resplendet in cordibus nostris: Zelus ex ardore Spiritus, qui ab eo procedit accenditque in cordibus nostris hunc ardorem. Is est, inquit Paulus, qui splenduit in cordibus nostris ad praebendum lumen cognitionis gloriae Dei, quae est in facie Iesu Christi. Omnis itaque cognitio Dei est in facie Christi, cuius quasi radij illati in mentes nostras, eas colcollustrat,& in iis fide & cognitione gignunt.Deniq; cū videbimus eum sicuti est,similes gloria ei sumus. Quia nimirum ipsius gloria transformabit nos in eandē imaginem ex gloria in gloriam.
units.tr: Peter recognised Christ by sight, but Peter also by hearing, namely with John as his teacher. Peter's knowledge then broke out into zeal, in which in turn he surpassed John his teacher, who nevertheless was earlier than himself in faith and knowledge. I take this zeal of Peter to have been genuine, and not some headlong rush of rashness. From this we gather that the gifts of John and Peter were different: the one excelled in zeal, the other in knowledge. For what is said in 1 Cor. 12. 11, that the Spirit distributes his gifts to each one as he wills, this, I say, was true also of the Apostles themselves, of whom one received one gift and another another. John excelled in the knowledge of Christ, as his Gospel, which is full of the sublime teaching about Christ, especially about his deity, bears witness. But Peter received a most burning zeal, by which he surpassed the others. Paul says that he received a greater grace of labouring than all the others. For no single one of the Apostles received everything equally, nor would that have been useful, either to himself or to others; for in that case he might perhaps have despised the others on account of it, and they in turn might have envied him so great a perfection, and so the body would have been torn apart. For this inequality and diversity of gifts, as Paul says, is what binds together and fits the members of the body of Christ; just as in the human body the inequality and diversity of faculties, each of which resides in individual members, holds the members of the same body together. Observe further that throughout the preceding night John's faith languished, and likewise Peter's zeal; but when morning drew near and Christ was now approaching, both John's faith and Peter's zeal grew strong and came back to life. From this let us learn that this grace of faith, knowledge and, finally, zeal is kindled through Christ, who is indeed the matter and object of these. For faith comes from his light, which shines in our hearts; zeal from the fire of the Spirit, which proceeds from him and kindles this fire in our hearts. He it is, says Paul, who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God, which is in the face of Jesus Christ. Therefore all knowledge of God is in the face of Christ, whose rays, as it were, falling upon our minds, enlighten them and beget in them faith and knowledge. Finally, when we shall see him as he is, we shall be like him in glory; for indeed his glory will transform us into the same image, from glory to glory.

units.la: Alij autem discipuli navigio. Pauló quidem tardius adueniunt,tamen omnes tandem ad Christum perueniunt. Zelus abripuit Petrum ad Dominum, fides verò & cognitio perducunt Iohannem & alios ad Dominum. Nam fides Christi, licet non coniuncta cum tanto illo zeli feruore, quantus erat in Petro, hominem tamen ad Christum tandem perducit. Sine fide vero certè aliqua, nemo videbit facie Dei. Quod enim Apostolus dixit de sanctimonia, ego non immitò possum idem affirmare de fide.
units.tr: The other disciples come along in the boat, somewhat more slowly, yet all of them at last reach Christ. Zeal snatched Peter away to the Lord, but faith and knowledge led John and the others to the Lord. For the faith of Christ, though not joined with that great fervour of zeal which Peter had, nevertheless brings a man to Christ in the end. Yet without some faith no one will see the face of God. What the Apostle said of holiness, I may not unreasonably affirm of faith as well.

units.la: Trahentes rete. Petrus relicto post se reti, simul piscibus omnibus, celeriter nauit ad Dominum. Iohannes & alij trahentes post se rete piscibus refertum nauigant: vtrique bene. Nam zelus ita abripuit Petrum, vt & rete cum piscibus, & sese suámque vitam neglexerit. Iohannes verò vt cognouit Dominum, ita agnouit hoc ipsius beneficium, quod eam in gratiam eius qui dedit ipsum, voluit secum vnà inferre. Vtrique igitur rectè fecerunt. Vt diuersa sunt dona à Deo hominibus data, ita & actiones variæ sunt pro mensura & varietate donorum. Omnes tamen suo quodam modo bonæ ac laudabiles: & quod in vnius actione deest, id alterius actione suppletur. Quod deerat in actione Petri, id suppletum est actione Iohannis & aliorum. Rursus zelus Petri alios promouit, prouocauitque ad æmulationem aliquam. Quamobrem non sunt reiiciendæ actiones piorum, eo quòd vndique non sint perfectæ singulæ, quasi verò omnia dona simul ac semel vni alicui dederit Dominus. Verum in vnum quasi corpus omnes omnium actiones sunt congerendæ, vt quod in vna actione deest, per alteram suppleatur, & simul sumptis omnibus ac confertim, iam perfectum quadam & integrum actionum corpus habeas. Descendentes in terram. Omnia miraculosa sese iis offerunt: in marinum vident miraculosam captur̄a piscium, dein-de descendentes in terrā inuenerunt miraculosum igne, & apparatum extraordinarium: hoc ideo dispensatū est a Deo, vt non modò resurrexisse Dominum cognoscerent,sed resurrexisse eum cū admirabili potentia: atq; hominem illum qui resurrexit ex mortuis Deum esse intelligerent: sedidit enim ipse in his operibus adeo miraculosis Deitatis suæ specimen aliquod. Iohannes testatur vidisse se gloriam eius, tanquam gloriam unigeniti ex Deo.Iohan.1.14. Gloriam autem hanc Deitatis in Christo deprehendit ex his & similibus ipsius effectis atque operibus. Voluit autem se post resurrectionem suam cognosci ab iis etiam vt Deum & Dei filium: aliter enim cognitio Christi non est salutaris. Non est hic prætereundū silentio, quòd his iam editis miraculis, non tantum docuit discipulos, sed & iis profuit ad alendam præsentem hanc vitam: atque in iis non tantum patefecit potentiam illam diuinam, sed etiā amore quendam erga eos, eorūmque vitam,singulare, vt non tantum hærerent in admiratione potentiæ ipsius,sed vel multò magis fide & amore mutuo eum vicissim complecterentur. Admirari quidem oportet Christū & operā ipsius: nam ipsum vocauit admirabilem Esaias 9.5. Sed sic admirari eum, ipsiusque potentiam ac maiestatem plane diuinam, vt interea coniungamur cum eo per fidem & dilectionem; secus nihil nobis profutura est admiratio.
units.tr: Dragging the net. Peter, leaving the net behind him together with all the fish, swiftly swam to the Lord. John and the others, dragging behind them the net full of fish, sail in: both did well. For zeal so carried Peter away that he neglected both the net with the fish and himself and his own life. John, however, as soon as he knew the Lord, also recognised this benefit of his, and wished to bring it along with him out of gratitude to the one who had given it. Both therefore acted rightly. As the gifts given by God to men are diverse, so their actions are various, according to the measure and variety of the gifts. Yet all are good and praiseworthy in their own way, and what is lacking in one man's action is supplied by another's. What was lacking in Peter's action was supplied by the action of John and the others. Again, Peter's zeal spurred others on and provoked them to some emulation. Therefore the actions of the godly are not to be rejected because each of them is not perfect in every respect, as if the Lord had given all his gifts at once and together to one man. Rather, the actions of all must be gathered into one body, as it were, so that what is lacking in one action is made up by another; and taking them all together, in a heap, you will have a complete and whole body of actions. Going down onto the land. Everything miraculous presents itself to them: on the sea they see the miraculous catch of fish; then, coming down onto the land, they find a miraculous fire and extraordinary preparation. This was arranged by God so that they would recognise not only that the Lord had risen, but that he had risen with wonderful power, and that the man who rose from the dead was God; for in these very miraculous works he displayed some specimen of his Deity. John testifies that he saw his glory, the glory of the only-begotten from God (John 1:14). He grasped this glory of the Deity in Christ from these and similar effects and works of his. Moreover, after his resurrection he wished to be known by them also as God and the Son of God; for otherwise the knowledge of Christ is not saving. It must not be passed over in silence that, with these miracles now performed, he not only taught the disciples but also benefited them by nourishing their present life. In these things he revealed not only that divine power but also a certain singular love towards them and their life, so that they would not only cling in wonder at his power but much more embrace him in return with faith and mutual love. Indeed, one ought to marvel at Christ and his works, for Isaiah called him wonderful (Isa. 9:5). But one must so marvel at him, and at his power and altogether divine majesty, that meanwhile we are joined to him through faith and love; otherwise our admiration will profit us nothing.

units.la: Afferte ex piscibus. Prior orditur sermone Dominus: reuerentia enim Domini eos cohibuit ne ipsi priores cum alloquerentur. Præsentia enim Domini efficax est, vt ad fidem, ita etiam ad reuerentiam & timorē. Exigit autem ab iis ratione illius capturæ admirabilis: quidem significat noluisse se temere abiici ab iis beneficium illud, licet terrenum, à se in eos collatum. Hinc etiam sequitur laudandum factum Iohannis & aliorum qui secum traxerunt ad terram rete piscibus refertum. Sed hoc notandum est quod laboribus ipsorum capturam illam piscium ascribat: Expiscibus, inquit, quos cepistis: quod ideo dicit, vt intelligamus quanti faciat Deus labores nostros suscep-tos ex ipsius voluntate. Etsi enim hi per se quidem inutiles sint, & nos quoque non nisi serui inutiles simus, postquam iam omnia fecimus quæ potuimus: tamen labores nostros, vt vtiles prædicat, & nos quoque commendat vt seruos vtiles pro gratia & mi-
units.tr: Bring some of the fish. The Lord begins the speech first, for his reverence restrained them so that they did not presume to address him first. For the presence of the Lord is effective, producing faith and also reverence and fear. He demands from them an account of that wonderful catch, which indicates that he did not want that benefit, though earthly, bestowed by him upon them to be rashly cast aside. Hence also follows the praiseworthy deed of John and the others who drew the net full of fish to land. But it must be noted that he attributes the catch of fish to their labours: of the fish, he says, which you have caught. He says this so that we may understand how highly God values our labours undertaken by his will. For although these in themselves are indeed useless, and we too are only unprofitable servants once we have done all that we could, nevertheless he declares our labours useful, and commends us too as useful servants, through his grace and

units.la: 5. Colloquium Domini cum discipulis. misericordia sua ipsius, ad nos nimirum tanquam filios suos animandos & provocandos ad pergendum in operre ac labore, cùm hoc sit à Deo ordinatum, & necessariū adeo, vt absque laboribus & operibus, quæ præparauit Deus vt ambularemus in iis, non obtineatur vita æterna. Similiter & eodem sensu, cùm coronat in nobis gratiam suam ex sola meráque gratia, coronam illam vocat mercedem, quasi labores nostri eam sint promeriti: non alio sensu coronam, & gratuitum suum præmiū vocat mercedem, quàm quo reipsa ascribit laboribus nostris & operibus gratiam & beneficium suum gratuitū. Agit enim nobiscum perpetuò, & nobis quasi adblanditur atque indulget nostro bono: vt pater agit cum filiis suis, & iis adblāditur quo eos animet atque provocet perpetuò ad bene agendum. Eodem denique sensu docet nos in Oratione illa quam Dominicam vocant, appellare panem, quem petimus à Deo, panem nostrum acsi nobis deberetur: quem tamen petimus à Deo, tanquam panem ipsius Dei, non autem nostrum. Et hoc quoque ex amore illo paterno & gratia profectum est, quòd dicat nostrum esse, quod tamen reipsa non est nostrum, neque nobis aliquo iure ab ipso debetur. Ascendit Simon Petrus. Petrus qui zelo quodam conueniendi Dominum iam prius abreptus, reliquit post se rete vnà cum capris piscibus: nunc primus omnium mandatum Domini exequitur in extrahendo eodem illo reti, cum piscibus. Quod argumento est Petrum illud tantū Domini beneficium non pro nihilo habuisse tum, cùm eo relicto & in mare se abiecit, & ad Dominum enatauit. Habemus in eius facto imaginem quandam facti pij cuiusque, qui ad tempus adeo subuehitur supra terrena ista omnia, vt nihil de iis cogitet, totus nimirum occupatus in cœlestibus illis, & in fruitione ipsius Domini, cùm ipse sit municeps regni cælorum. Postea verò ex voluntate Domini subsidit quasi, & manum admouet operi pro ratione functionis suæ. Interea autem tempore quantum potest fieri, cor suum habet in cœlis, vbi thesaurus ipsius est. Hoc enim est vti mundo hoc, sic vt cæteron abutaris. Abutitur enim mundo & mundanis istis, qui non modò manum suam admotam habet ad ea, sed etiam cor suum in iis defixum. Et cum tot essent, Quòd non fit fractum rete, tribuit illud secretæ Deipotentiæ. Hoc itaque extraordinariū est, & miraculosum, vt & fuit ante captura illa piscium, vt etiam erant prunæ illæ accensæ, cum reliquo toto apparatu. Hæc omnia nō sine miraculo facta sunt: eo fine vt in Christo iam ex mortuis suscitato deprehenderent inhabitantem corporaliter Deitatis omnem plenitudinem: neque id tantùm, sed vt ipsi viderët Deitatem illam, quæ & ante passionem, & in passione sese obscurauit, nunc in luce quasi prodire, atque etiam ostendere, vt Christus iam incipieret gloriosus eonspici, qui antea in oculis omnium vilis contemptúsque fuerat.
units.tr: 5.
