The conversation of the Lord with the disciples. his own mercy, namely to encourage and provoke us, as his sons, to persevere in work and toil; since this has been ordained by God, and is so necessary that without labours and works, which God prepared so that we should walk in them, eternal life is not obtained. Similarly, and in the same sense, when he crowns his grace in us from grace alone, he calls that crown a reward, as if our labours had merited it. He calls the crown, his freely given prize, a reward in no other sense than that in which he really ascribes his free grace and benefit to our labours and works. For he deals with us perpetually, and as it were flatters us and indulges our good, as a father deals with his sons and flatters them so as to encourage and provoke them constantly to do well. In the same sense, finally, he teaches us in that prayer which they call the Lord's Prayer to call the bread that we ask of God our bread, as if it were owed to us; yet we ask for it from God as the bread of God himself, not ours. This too has come from that paternal love and grace, that he says it is ours, when in reality it is not ours, nor is it owed to us by him under any right. Simon Peter went up. Peter, who had earlier been carried away by a certain zeal to meet the Lord, left behind the net together with the fish; now he is the first of all to carry out the Lord's command in drawing that same net, with the fish. This is evidence that Peter did not count that great benefit of the Lord as nothing, when he left it behind, threw himself into the sea and swam to the Lord. In his deed we have a certain image of every godly person, who for a time is so carried above all these earthly things that he thinks of none of them, being wholly occupied with those heavenly things and with the enjoyment of the Lord himself, since he is a fellow citizen of the kingdom of heaven. Afterwards, however, by the will of the Lord, he settles down, as it were, and puts his hand to work according to the nature of his calling. Meanwhile, as far as it can be done, he keeps his heart in heaven, where his treasure is. For this is to use this world without abusing it. He abuses the world and worldly things who not only has his hand applied to them, but also has his heart fixed upon them. And although there were so many, the fact that the net was not broken he ascribes to the secret power of God. This therefore is extraordinary and miraculous, as the catch of fish was before, as the coals that were lit were too, with all the rest of the preparation. All these things were done not without a miracle, with this end: that in Christ now raised from the dead they might perceive the fullness of the Deity dwelling bodily; and not only this, but that they might see that Deity, which had obscured itself both before the passion and in the passion, now as it were coming forth into the light and even showing itself, so that Christ might now begin to be seen in glory, who before had been cheap and despised in the eyes of all.

units.la: Venite, prandete. Nunc familiarius se gerit erga discipulos suos, & vt iam factis extraordinariis & miraculosis patefecit, se iis tanquam illum Deum omnipotentem: ita nunc ordinaria ista familiari & assueta agendi ratione, probat se iis verum esse hominem, humano corpore indutum, quemadmodum iam antea non Spiritum se, sed corpus actione illa edendi comprobauit. Neque verò interea securus est corporis ipsorum, quos satis scirebat & fessos & famelicos: vt constet Dominum & fidei illorum ac vitæ illius cælestis, & corporis eorum vitæque præsentis vna eadémque opera consuluisse. Suorum enim corpora dum pascit manu sua, animos pariter pascit dum ij è manu ipsius cibum capiunt cum precè & gratiarum actione. Nullus autem discipulorum. Hoc obiter insertum est ab Euangelista, vt doceat quanta cum reverentia Domini vna cū eo accubuerint, simulque quanra cum πληροφορία & certa persuasione. Nemo eorum audebat interrogare eum, Ecquis esset? Ratio subiecta est, Quia sciuerunt quod Dominus esset. Itaque interroga re quod sciuerunt, fuisset nimiæ audaciæ atque impudentiæ. Postquam enim se iam satis reuelauit, vltra quæ rere est audaciæ & impudentiæ, id quod à Pharisæis & Scribis factum legimus. Postquam enim se iis iam satis superque patefecisset tam verbis quàm operibus, Magister, inquiunt, velimus ex te signum videre. Ipse verò respondens dixit eis, Natio mala & adulterina signum quærit, sed signum non dabitur ei, nisi signum illud Ionæ Prophetæ. phetæ. Sic etiam hodierno die, Natio mala est & adul-tera ea, quæ quærit sibi miracula, reuelationes extraor-dinarias, veritates non scriptas aliáque huiusmodi, non contenta hac sola reuelatione Scripturarum, præsertim Scripturæ Noui Testamenti: in qua mysterium Christi plenè perfectéque reuelatum est: & qua profecto reuelatione non aliam clariorem recipiemus, tantisperdum ipse Dominus secunda vice aduenerit. De fide & infidelitate hoc semel admoneo: fides vt est pudica, ita moderata: hoc est ad modū aliquem, non autē supra modū relationes sibi quærit. Infidelitas verò, vt impudens est, immoderato & plus nimio curiosa, neque modum vllum tenet in reuelationibus requirendis: id quod faciit quidē non animo discendi, sed vel tentandi Deum, vel satisfaciendi immoderatæ suæ curiositati. Hic si quæras, An non assiduos nos esse oportet in petendo à Deo cognitionis nostræ incrementum: sicut scriptum est: Petite & dabitur vobis, &c. Luc.11.9. Violenti rapiunt regnum cælorum, Matth.11.12. Dominus etiam sanctā hanc importunitatem commendat Luc.18.1.&c. Respondeo longè differre inter se ista: petere nouam aliquam reuelationem, præter hanc, quam habemus in scripturis Propheticis & Apostolicis: & petere cognitionē earundem harum scripturarum. Cognitionem & mentis illuminationem quotidie maiorem petere à Deo & possumus & debemus: reuelationem verò aliquam ea quæ in Scripturis est clariorem & ampliorem petere nefas est: id enim est negare Christum, cum plena perfectáque reuelatione in mundum venisse: vide de hac re Rom.10.6.
units.tr: Come and eat. Now he deals with his disciples more familiarly. Just as he had shown himself to them, by extraordinary and miraculous deeds, to be that almighty God, so now by this ordinary, familiar and customary way of acting he proves to them that he is a true man clothed in a human body. In the same way, by that act of eating, he had earlier shown that he was not a spirit but a body. Nor, in the meantime, was he careless of their bodies, for he knew well that they were both weary and hungry. So it is clear that the Lord, by one and the same work, cared both for their faith and heavenly life and for their bodily and present life. For while he feeds their bodies with his own hand, he likewise feeds their souls, as they take food from his hand with prayer and thanksgiving. No one of the disciples. The evangelist has inserted this in passing, to teach with how much reverence they reclined at table with him, and at the same time with how much full assurance [πληροφορία] and firm conviction. None of them dared to ask him, Who are you? The reason is added: because they knew that it was the Lord. So to ask what they already knew would have been an excess of boldness and impudence. For since he had now revealed himself sufficiently, to ask further would be a boldness and impudence beyond measure, like the thing we read was done by the Pharisees and scribes. For after he had already revealed himself to them more than enough, both by words and by works, they said, "Teacher, we would like to see a sign from you." But he answered and said to them, "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, but no sign will be given to it, except the sign of the prophet Jonah." So also today, that is an evil and adulterous generation which seeks for itself miracles, extraordinary revelations, unwritten truths and things of that kind, and is not content with this one revelation of the Scriptures, especially the Scripture of the New Testament, in which the mystery of Christ is fully and perfectly revealed. Indeed, we shall receive no clearer revelation than this one until the Lord himself comes a second time. I give this one warning about faith and unbelief: faith, being modest, is also moderate; that is, it seeks revelations within some limit and not beyond measure. Unbelief, however, being shameless, is immoderately and excessively curious, and keeps no limit in demanding revelations. It does this not with a mind to learn, but either to tempt God or to satisfy its immoderate curiosity. Here, if you ask whether we ought not to be constant in asking God for an increase of our knowledge, as it is written, "Ask, and it shall be given you," etc., Luke 11:9; "The violent take the kingdom of heaven," Matt. 11:12; and the Lord also commends this holy importunity, Luke 18:1, etc. I answer that these things differ greatly: to ask for some new revelation, beyond the one we have in the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures, and to ask for knowledge of those same Scriptures. We both can and should ask God each day for greater knowledge and enlightenment of mind; but to ask for any revelation clearer and fuller than what is in the Scriptures is wrong, for that is to deny that Christ has come into the world with a full and perfect revelation. On this matter see Rom. 10:6.

units.la: Hac iam tertia vice.
units.tr: This now the third time.

units.la: Conclusio est patefactionis & apparitionis Domini proximæ, in qui notat quota fuerit ea numero, nempe tertia: quem quidem numerum ego ad patefactiones discipulis in vnum congregatos factis retulerim vt suprà admonui: ideóque in textu legitur, Patefactus est Iesus discipulis. Nā si alias reuelationes magis particulares his generalibus annumerare velis, inuenies Dominum octies iam se patefecisse. 1. Magdalenæ. 2. Aliis aliquot mulieribus. 3. Duobus discipulis inter proficiscendum in vicum Emmauntem. 4. Petro. 5. Fratribus, amplius quàm quingentis, & Iacobo, videt.Cor.15.5. 6. Discipulis Hierosolymis coactis in unum, absente Thoma. 7. Coactis praesente una cum aliis etiam Thoma. 8. Ab his septem numero conspectus est. Toties autem se post resurrectionem patefecit, procul dubio ad fidem faciendam resurrectionis suae, non discipulis tantum, sed etiam nobis: ut nos quoties audimus tot oculatos fuisse testes resurrectionis Domini, & legimus istorum testium scripta; toties capiamus incrementum aliquod fidei nostrae. Sed de hoc iam supra a nobis est dictum satis.
units.tr: The conclusion concerns the coming near of the Lord's manifestation and appearance, in which he notes how many times it was, namely the third. I would refer this number to the manifestations made to the disciples when they were gathered together into one, as I noted above; and so the text reads, "Jesus was manifested to the disciples." For if you wish to add to these general appearances the more particular revelations, you will find that the Lord had already revealed himself eight times: (1) to Magdalene; (2) to some other women; (3) to two disciples while they were going into the village of Emmaus; (4) to Peter; (5) to the brethren, more than five hundred at once, and to James, 1 Cor. 15:5; (6) to the disciples gathered together in Jerusalem, Thomas being absent; (7) to them gathered together, Thomas now being present with the others; (8) he was seen by these seven in number. However, he manifested himself so many times after his resurrection, no doubt to establish faith in his resurrection, not only for the disciples but also for us: so that, as often as we hear that so many eyewitnesses of the Lord's resurrection existed and we read the writings of those witnesses, so often we may gain some increase of our faith. But enough has already been said by us on this above.

units.la: 15 Quum ergo prandissent, dicit Simoni Petro, Simon fili Ionae, diligis me plusquam hi? Dicit ei, Certe, Domine, tu nosti quod amem te. Dicit ei, Pasce agnos meos.
units.tr: 15 When therefore they had dined, he said to Simon Peter, "Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Feed my lambs."

units.la: 16 Dicit ei rursum secundo, Simon fili Ionae, diligis me? Ait illi, Certe, Domine, tu nosti quod amem te. Dicit ei, Pasce oves meas.
units.tr: 16 He said to him again the second time, "Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Feed my sheep."

units.la: 17 Dicit ei tertio, Simon fili Ionae, amas me? Tristitia fuit affectus Petrus quod tertio dixisset ipsi, Amas me? dixitque ei, Domine, tu omnia nosti: Tu nosti quod amem te. Dicit ei Iesus, Pasce oves meas.
units.tr: 17 He said to him the third time, "Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?" Peter was grieved that he had said to him the third time, "Do you love me?" and he said to him, "Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you." Jesus said to him, "Feed my sheep."

units.la: 18 Amen, amen dico tibi, quum esses iunior, cingebas te, & ibas quo volebas: quum autem senueris, extendes manus tuas, & alius te cinget, & transferet quo noles.
units.tr: 18 "Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were younger, you girded yourself and went where you wished; but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and carry you where you do not wish to go."

units.la: 19 Hoc autem dixit, significans qua morte glorificaturus esset Deum. Et cum hoc dixisset, dicit ei, Sequere me.
units.tr: 19 Now he said this, signifying by what death he would glorify God. And when he had said this, he said to him, "Follow me."

units.la: A Bsoluto iam prandio Christus confert sermones cum Petro potissimum, idque eo fine, non quidem ut cum tanquam vicarium suum, vniuerso terrarum orbi praficeret, memor scilicet illius promissionis, ut tradut Pontificii, qua fecit Matth.16.18. Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam: sed ut Petrum, qui tam foeda il-la abla abnegatione Domini sui, se priuauit dignitate Apostolica, in suum locum reponeret, accepta ex eius ore confessione amoris suis erga Dominum, simulque odij tam foedi illius peccati, quod perpetrauit, cùm Dominũ suum tam constanter abnegauit. Restitutus est, fateor, iā prius te ipsa, cùm vnà cum reliquis citra exceptionem Petro demandatum est ministerium Euangelij, & dictū in Apostoleis eis, Sicut misit me Pater, ita ego mitto vos: Verùm hæc eius restitutio, non ita distincta & aperta fuit: nunc vero vt omnem scrupulum eximeret ex animo Petri, & examinis pariter omnium discipulorum, cum Petro agitatorum de ipsius restitutione, adhibitis sex testibus, caeteris nimirum, qui vnà aderant, discipulis: ídque ad magis confirmandam illam ipsius restitutionem. Vrget autem confessionem istam Petri tribus vicibus, ad hoc, vt quemadmodum trina abnegatione abdicauit sese Apostolatu: ita trina confessione restitueretur reponeretúrque in locum suum. Est itaque hic finis proprie serm monis huius, quem cum Petro nominatim confert. Potest etiam hic esse finis, vt iam discessurus abiis, Petro, & aliis qui vnà aderant, & audiebant, seriam Ecclesiæ curam commendaret. Petrum enim compellans nominatum simul alios alloquitur. Verùm ille, de quo iam dixi, præcipuus est huius sermonis finis, nempe vt Petrum, qui abnegatione sua se priuauit dignitate Apostolica, in locum suum per resipiscentiam & confessione restitueret. Ex quo obseruamus ei qui negat Dominum ex infirmitate, id quod Petrus fecit, locum esse resipiscentiæ aliquem; sed Dominum esse qui ad resipiscendam inuitat & peccatorem miserum praeuenit. In aula Caiaphæ post trinam abnegatione reuocauit eum, retrò cum aspiciens. Nunc etiam quod tum inchoatum est, o-ius, absoluit, & ter vrget vnam eandemque confessionem. Sed videamus ipsa Domini verba. Simon, fili Ionæ, diligis me? Non quæritideo quod ignoret, vtrum se diligat nectum: Petrus enim ipse postea fatetur nosse id Dominum. Verùm quærit an diligat ipsum melius, quàm alij? Primum vt reuocet ei in memoriam verborum illam iantiam, qua vsus est Petrus, cùm diceret, Etiamsi omnes offendantur in te, ego nunquam offendar. q.dixisset, Ego diligo te plus quàm alij. Deinde vt reuocet ei in memoriam turpem illam suam defectionem, protestationi illi superiori planè contrariam: quæ dum facit Dominus, acriter pungit hominis conscientiam: ac si dixisset, Petre, diligis me plus quàm hi, sicut gloriatus es ante passionem meam: cùm tamen contra gloriationem illam & professionem turpiter à me desecueris, méque tam constanter semel, iterum, ac tertiò abnegaueris? Sic igitur pungit hominem, sed ea interim cum lenitate & mansuetudine, vt interea nulla asperitas in verbis conspiciatur: simul enim accendit rursus atque reparat amorem Petri erga Dominum defectione illa ipsius & abnegatione iâ aliquo modo labefactatum: & dum obiurgat eü simul consolatur, ac si diceret: Etsi me contra protestationem tuam abnegaueris, tamen locus est veniæ si modò ames me. Nota igitur, vna eademque breui sententia & reprehendit eum & consolatur, deiicit & erigit, vulnerat & alligat vulnus. Expectasset fortasse quis maiorem à Domino seueritatê in obiurgando Petrum in hoc primo, vt videtur, post abnegationem ipsius sermone cum Petro collato: sed amor Domini & philanthropia illa incredfabilis, non passa est eum litigare, clamare, in plateis vociferari, arundinem quassatam frangere, linum fumigas extinguere, sicut de eo prædictum est à Propheta. vide Matth. 12.19.20. Eius autem exemplo admonemur non licere cuiquam reprehendere, nisi ei qui diligit, vt reprehensio sit cum lenitate, ac proinde ad instaurationem atque ædificationem eius qui reprehenditur, non autem ad destructionem. Amor autem mansuetam efficit reprehensionem, mansuetam eruditionem, mansuetā exhortationem, omnes denique partes officij in alios mansuetas ac lenes, id quod Paulus requirit. Eo autem quod ter idem quaerat, sit vt ter idem confiteatur, vt iam postea triplicē abnegatione restitueretur. Triplex enim abnegatio postulabat trinā confessione, vt videbimus postea. Præterea defectio illa Petri exigebat vt nō statim ei credetur. Nota, quotquot apostatā fecerunt, turpiore præsertim, iis non citò credendū, sed multūm prius explorandi sunt: iterum atque iterum sunt quasi perfodiendi, tantisperdum purior illa amoris Dei aqua ex imo cordi
units.tr: Now that the meal is over, Christ speaks with Peter in particular, and he does so with this aim: not, indeed, so that he might set him over the whole world as his vicar, mindful of that promise, as the Papists interpret it, by which he said in Matt. 16:18, "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church"; but so that he might restore Peter, who by that foul denial of his Lord had deprived himself of apostolic dignity, to his own place, by receiving from his mouth a confession of his love for the Lord, and at the same time a hatred of that foul sin which he committed when he so steadfastly denied his Lord. He was indeed already restored, I admit, at the time when the ministry of the gospel was committed to Peter together with the rest, without exception, and it was said to the apostles, "As the Father has sent me, so I send you." Yet this restoration of his was not so distinct and open. But now, so that he might remove every scruple from Peter's mind, and also the doubts of all the disciples, which had been stirred up with Peter about his restoration, he calls six witnesses to it, namely the other disciples who were present; and this is to confirm more firmly that restoration of his. He presses this confession of Peter three times, so that, just as by a threefold denial he had cast himself out of the apostleship, so by a threefold confession he might be restored and put back into his place. This, then, is the proper purpose of this conversation, which he holds with Peter by name. This may also be the purpose: that, about to depart from them, he might commend to Peter, and to the others who were present and listening, the serious care of the Church. For in addressing Peter by name, he speaks at the same time to the others. But the purpose I have already mentioned is the chief purpose of this discourse, namely that Peter, who by his denial had deprived himself of apostolic dignity, should be restored to his place through repentance and confession. From this we observe that for one who denies the Lord out of weakness, as Peter did, there is room for some repentance; but it is the Lord who invites to repentance and goes before the wretched sinner. In the house of Caiaphas, after the threefold denial, he called him back, looking at him. Now too he completes what was then begun, and presses one and the same confession three times. But let us look at the Lord's own words. "Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?" He does not ask this because he does not know whether Peter loves him; for Peter himself afterwards confesses that the Lord knows it. But he asks whether Peter loves him more than the others do. First, so that he might bring to Peter's memory the rash words he used when he said, "Even if all are offended in you, I will never be offended," as if he had said, "I love you more than the others." Then, so that he might bring to his memory that shameful defection of his, which was entirely contrary to that earlier protestation. In doing this the Lord sharply pricks the man's conscience, as if he said, "Peter, do you love me more than these, as you boasted before my passion, when on the contrary you have shamefully deserted me from that boast and profession, and have denied me so steadfastly once, twice, and a third time?" So he pricks the man, but at the same time with such gentleness and mildness that no harshness appears in his words. For at the same time he kindles again and restores Peter's love for the Lord, which had been somewhat weakened by that defection and denial of his; and while he rebukes him, he also consoles him, as if he said, "Although you have denied me, contrary to your protestation, yet there is room for pardon, provided you love me." Note, then, that by one and the same brief saying he both reproves and comforts him, casts down and raises up, wounds and binds the wound. Perhaps someone would have expected from the Lord greater severity in rebuking Peter in this first conversation with him after his denial, as it seems; but the love of the Lord and that incredible kindness of his did not allow him to quarrel, to shout, to cry out in the streets, to break the bruised reed or quench the smoking flax, as was foretold of him by the prophet. See Matt. 12:19, 20. And by his example we are taught that no one may rebuke except one who loves, so that the rebuke may be with gentleness, and therefore for the restoration and building up of the one who is rebuked, and not for his destruction. Love, moreover, makes rebuke mild, teaching mild, exhortation mild; in short, it makes all the duties toward others mild and gentle, which Paul requires. Because he asks the same thing three times, it follows that he is confessed the same three times, so that the threefold denial might afterwards be restored. For a threefold denial required a threefold confession, as we shall see later. Moreover, that defection of Peter required that he should not be believed at once. Note that however many have made shipwreck of the faith, especially those who have fallen more shamefully, they are not to be believed quickly, but must first be tested very thoroughly: again and again they must, as it were, be pierced through, until that purer water of love for God flows out from the bottom of the heart
1 Tim. 2.24, etc. Tit. 3.2.

units.la: Lapsis nō cito, nec temere credendum. dis eorum eliciatur.
units.tr: Those who have lapsed are not to be believed quickly or rashly, until the truth of their repentance is drawn out.

units.la: Etiam Domine, tu nosti. Sequitur confessio Petri, in qua primum obseruamus, quàm amanter respondeat Domino: id profecto arguit interrogationem Domini amorem spirasse, ac suavitate mirifica, cuius quidem sensu attactus animo Petrus, effudit quasi vicissim animum suum & amoris illum effectum in Dominum suum. Non enim nos vnquam priores diligimus Dominum: verum in quia effunditur charitas Dei in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis, ideo nos vicissim Dominum diligimus. Sed obseruandum, quòd cum Dominus coparatè interrogarit eum, Diligis, inquiens, me plusquam hi? Petrus simpliciter respondeat, Amote. Didicit nimirum iam de se mo- deftius & sentire & loqui. Dixit iam antea coparatè, Etsi omnes offendantur in te, ego non offendar: Praeferens, nimirum, esse aliis omnibus in amore erga Christum, & nimium sibi confisus. Ac postquam lapsus est, iam experientia infirmitatis suae edoctus modestior esse coepit. Peccata enim & defectiones piorum conuertuntur perpetuo in ipsorum bonum. Quòd si natura paulo sint arrogantiores nimiumq; sibi confidant, ac prae se alios contemnant, lapsu suo tandem discunt modestiores esse. Tum notandum quòd dum profitetur amore erga Dominum, ipsum testè appellet; atque ideo pauciter facit duo: primum ipsum honorat, tanquam Deum; deinde approbat ei sinceritatem cordis sui. Nam Deus testis dicitur esse non tam confessioni oris, quàm sinceritati cordis. Quamobrem si quis Deum teste appellet, videat sincerè, & ex animo loquatur. Tame homines vulgò, dum mentiuntur, aliterque loquuntur atque sentiunt, Deum sibi teste inuocant. Quid hoc aliud est, quo, quàm Deum vindicè mendacij sui inuocare? Neque prætermittendum, quòd dum cõfitetur amorem illum suum, ipsum Domini sui nomine insigniat. Quod argumentum quidem est reuerentiae. Confessionibus enim & protestationibus, inquibus appellamus Deum, oportet adsit timor Dei iudicium & reuerentia: & non nisi honorificè copellandus est. Deus ille gloriæ & maiestatis plenus. Voces istæ hominum profanæ, petulantes, blasphemæ, quas euomunt coram Deo, fatiurguut nullâ subesse Dei reuerentiâ: imò verò ipsos dicit in corde suo, nõ esse Deum. Cum tertiò repetitur hæc ipsa confessio Petri, additū est eū iam tertia vice interrogatū à Domino, tristē fuisse, & cum tristitia ac mœrore animi confessum fuisse. Tristis fuisse videtur ideo, quod videbatur Dominū non ipsi fidē habere. Nos autē exeo obseruamus in cōfessionibus nostris ad modestiā, ad sinceritatē, ad reuerentiā oportere accedere tristitiā: & eam etiam vrgere Dominū ipsum, qui non desistit à pungendo nos, & vrgendo, priusquam tristitiā aliquam animis nostris excutiat. Postremò obseruandū, quòd eandē cōfessionē tandē vrgeat, nimirū quia ter abnegauerat Dominū suū. Quot enim quasi gradibus defectionis discēditur à Deo, tot rursus gradibus cōfessionis Domini reditur ad eū: & graue aliquod peccatū postulat diutinā resipiscētiā, & inultiplicē cōfessionē tū ad Dei gloriā, tū ad cōfirmationē nostri, quod iā peccatū nostrū sit remissū Deo. Quo enim diuturnior resipiscētia, & quo crebrior confessio, eo remissionis maior firmiórque est fiducia.
units.tr: Yes, Lord, you know. There follows Peter's confession, in which we first observe how lovingly he answers the Lord. This clearly shows that the Lord's question breathed love, and Peter, moved by its wonderful sweetness, poured out his soul in return, as it were, and the effect of that love upon his Lord. For we never love the Lord first; rather, because the love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, for that reason we love the Lord in return. But it should be noted that when the Lord asked him comparatively, Do you love me, he said, more than these? Peter simply answered, I love you. He had by then learned to think and speak of himself more modestly. Earlier he had spoken comparatively: Even if all are offended in you, I shall not be offended. There he set himself above all the others in love for Christ, trusting himself too much. But after his fall, taught by the experience of his own weakness, he began to be more modest. For the sins and failings of the godly are always turned to their good. If by nature they are somewhat arrogant and trust themselves too much, and despise others in comparison with themselves, by their fall they at last learn to be more modest. Next, it should be noted that in professing his love for the Lord, he calls him as witness. In doing so he does two things: first, he honours him as God; second, he vouches for the sincerity of his heart. For God is said to be witness not so much to the confession of the mouth as to the sincerity of the heart. Therefore, if anyone calls God as witness, let him see that he speaks sincerely and from his heart. Yet men commonly, when they lie and speak otherwise than they think, call God to witness. What else is this but to invoke God as avenger of one's own lie? Nor should it be passed over that in confessing his love he names his Lord. This is indeed an argument of reverence. For in confessions and protestations in which we call upon God, there ought to be the fear of God, judgement and reverence, and he must be addressed only with honour. He is the God full of glory and majesty. Those profane, wanton, blasphemous words of men, which they vomit out before God, prove that there is no reverence of God in them; indeed, they say in their heart that there is no God. When this same confession of Peter is repeated a third time, it is added that he, now asked a third time by the Lord, was saddened and confessed with sadness and grief of mind. He seems to have been saddened because he thought the Lord did not trust him. From this we observe that our confessions must approach with modesty, sincerity and reverence, and that sadness must be present; and the Lord himself presses us to this, for he does not cease from pricking and urging us until he has shaken some sadness out of our minds. Finally, it should be noted that he presses the same confession upon him at last, namely because he had denied his Lord three times. For as many steps as one departs from God by falling away, so many steps must one return to God by confessing the Lord; and a grave sin demands a lasting repentance and a manifold confession, both to the glory of God and to the assurance of ourselves that our sin is now forgiven by God. For the longer the repentance and the more frequent the confession, the greater and firmer is the confidence of forgiveness.

units.la: Pasce agnos meos. Hic post cōfessionē sequitur absolutio Petri, q.d. Restituo te in locū Pastoris, volóque te totum hunc amorem, quantus, quantus est, in agnos meos transfundere. Nota ergo: Amor nostēr erga Christū oportet se effundat in officiū erga homines pro ratione vocationis cuiusque, siue politica ea sit, siue Ecclesiastica. Qui enim profitetur verbo amorem erga Christum, neq; interea facit officiū erga homines, is mendax est. Qui dicit, Nouī Deū & mādata eius non seruat, mendax est, & in eo veritas non est. Rursus obseruamus, quòd si non nisi post confessionē amoris erga se Dominus iusserit eū pa-scere gregem suū, omnis recta actio, pro ratione officij cuiusque, procedit ex amore Domini tanquā fonte suo vnico: adeo vt nemo possit rectè, sincerè, ac seriò agere aliquid ex officio, nisi illud totū scaturiat ex eo fonte. Immò incidunt huiusmodi tēpora quibus obiiciuntur impedimenta ea, quæ nisi Christum interea habeamus ante oculos, non sit penes nos superare. Quid loquar de iis difficultatibus, quibus omni ex parte fidelis quisque pastor impetitur, quas profectò impossibile est eum superare, nisi amore Christi absorbeantur illæ omnes: & nisi eum, vt hoc cum Apostolo loquar, constringat amor Christi. Nos stulti, inquit, propter Christum. Resoluit autem hunc amo-
units.tr: Feed my lambs. Here, after the confession, follows Peter's absolution, as if to say: I restore you to the place of a minister, and I want you to pour all this love of yours, whatever its measure, into my lambs. Note, then: our love for Christ ought to pour itself out into duty towards people, according to the calling of each, whether civil or ecclesiastical. For whoever professes with his words love for Christ, yet meanwhile does not perform his duty towards people, is a liar. He who says, I know God, and does not keep his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him. Again we observe that if the Lord has commanded him to feed his flock only after the confession of love for himself, then every right action, according to the calling of each, proceeds from the love of the Lord as from its one source; so that no one can rightly, sincerely and earnestly do anything from his office unless all of it springs from that source. Indeed, times of this kind arise in which obstacles are thrown up which, unless we keep Christ before our eyes in the meantime, it is not in our power to overcome. What shall I say of those difficulties with which every faithful minister is assailed on every side, which it is surely impossible for him to overcome unless all of them are swallowed up by the love of Christ, and unless the love of Christ constrains him, to use the words of the Apostle? We are fools, he says, for Christ's sake. Now he resolves this love
{a} John 2.4.

units.la: {b} 1 Cor. 5.14. 1 Cor. 4.10. amorem nostrum erga Christum in amore Christi erga nos. Postquâ enim hoc dixit, Amor Christi constringit nos, addidit continuò, vt qui sciamus quòd cùm mortui essemus, vnus pro omnibus mortuus est. En fundamentum illud primum omnium officiorū, adeóque omnium quæ reste geruntur in vocatione quacunque. Amor enim ille Domini erga nos excitat in nobis amore mutuum erga Dominum. Hinc Domini causa omnia facimus omnes. Viuimus illi, morimur illi. Vt autem nulla est recta, sincera & seria actio in vita, nisi profluat ea ex amore Christi: nulla est certius argumentum amoris Christi, quàm officium bene rectéque gestum. Contráque nullum certius argumentum est cordis vacui isto amore, quàm officium non fideliter & rectè obitum. Ex pertur-batione illa & corruptione Ecclesiæ Dei quæ fuit Corinthi deprehendit Paulus inflatos illos, vt vocat, doctores non amasse Christum illum, quem prædicarunt, tandemq; vltimo capite, his verbis in eos denunciat, Siquis non amat Dominum Iesum Christum, sit Anathema Maranatha. Anathema enim sunt falsi doctores & mercenarij, non tam quòd corrumpant Ecclesiam Dei, eámque perdant, quàm quòd ipsum Dominum Iesum non amant. Sed diligentius verba sunt examinanda. Primum verbum pascendi & pastoris, quod per metaphoram transfertur ad alia munia quæcunque siue politica, siue Ecclesiastica, in quibus diligentia, cura & sollicitudo quasi pastorum requiritur: præsertim verò in officio Ecclesiastico & in ministerio requiritur diligentia & sollicitudo Pastoris, id quod docet nos Dominus, vel per hanc ipsam triplicem & tam seriam commendationem gregis sui. Christus quidem ipse, si proprie loquamur, Pastor est, & merito hoc sibi nomen vendicat vt proprium, Iohan.10. Nam & grex ad ipsum pertinet, & cibus pariter quo pascitur grex ipsius est. Venenum enim est illud omne, quod non depromitur ex penu illo verbi Christi. Hoc tamen nomen cum ministris & seruis suis quorum opera vritur in pascendo grege suo communicat, eósque ipso nomine honorat, eodémque etiam prouocat eos ad fideliter pascendum & faciendum officium. Sed de Pastoris nomine hactenus satis: nunc de iis qui pascendi sunt. Sunt illi quidem non ferae bestiae, vt sunt lupi, vrsi, leones, &c. sed agni, sed oues: hoc est electi, qui simplices sunt ac innocentes, sicuti agni & oues. Quod quidem sic accipiendum volo; non quod electi sint statim vt agni, sed quòd progressu temporis per verbum & Spiritum cicurentur ij, qui primum fuerunt tanquam leones, vrsi, lupi, tigres, aliaeque ferae bestiae. Nam in natura nullum est discrimen inter electos & reprobos, etiamsi in secreto Dei consilio, ipsiusque praedestinatione, & ipsius denique gratia discrimen sit. Nam Deus solus est, qui discreuit electos suos. Quaeri igitur hic potest, Annon nisi quos videt mites & innocentes tanquam agnos, Pastor debeat aggredi & suscipere pascendos? Respondeo, Oportet eum suscipere pascendos quosuis, tam feras bestias, quàm agnos, ad hoc, vt ex feris bestiis agnos efficiat tandem, si id fieri vllo modo possit. Rursus quaeritur, Annon cum Dominus Petro commendet electos suos, annon eos tantum debet Pastor suscipere docendos & pascendos? Sint illi licet primum; & in primo congressu lupis similiores quàm agnis: sed tamen eos solos commendat Petro isto in loco pascendos. Resp. Commendat quidem proprie Dominus electos, sed interea non excludit reprobos, quibus afferri pabulum vult quoque, si non ad conuersionem & saluteam eorum, saltem ad indurationem & iustam damnationem. Pastores autem vult eos omnes habere pro electis suis eosque pascere tanquam agnos ad vitam aeternam. Non enim est hominum discernere & diiudicare hominum electionem & reprobationem: solus enim Dominus nouit qui sunt sui. Hoc tamen verum esse oportet, non nisi in electis solis collocatum laborem fructuosum & efficacem fore. Nam reprobus rei ipsa nunquam manuescit aut cicuratur. Fieri quidem potest, vt ad tempus induat se agnina pelle, hoc est hypocritam agat, & hypocriseos praetextum sibi assumat: nunquam tamen sincere & ex animo pius ac bonus euadet. Hoc non est praetermittendum quod iubeat pascere non alienos, sed agnos suos. Pasce, inquit, agnos meos, hoc est pretio sanguinis mei redemptos, ac proinde iure meos. Hoc verbum, vt continet argumenmentum cur pascendi agni: Quia, nempe Domini sunt, pretio sanguinis ipsius redempti: ita admonet Pastorem ne habeat gregem Dei, pro suo: neque sibi, hoc est in vsum & commodum suum pascat eum. Ideo Baptista dixit, Qui habet sponsam, sponsus est: Amicus autem sponsi stat & audit eum, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi. Quibus verbis significauit se non sibi, sed Domino qui sponsus est Ecclesiae suae, ambire Ecclesiam Dei aut eam pascere. Et Paulus, Ambio vos, inquit; Zelotypia Dei: praeparaui enim vos quos vni viro (vt virginem puram) sistam, nempe Christo. Sacrilegium enim est omnium teterrimum Christum spoliare sponsa sua, & grege suo empto iam & acquisito tanto illo sanguinis Dei pretio. Iam hoc postremo loco obseruandum occurrit quod ter idem repetat; Pasce, inquit, agnos meos, Pasce oues meas, Pasce oues meas. Absolutio ter repetita, confirmat magis restitutionem illam Petri, & gratiam illam Apostolatus ipsi redditam. Hoc etiam quod non semel tantum, ac vna vice transferat amorem Pastoris in gregem ac Ecclesiam suam: sed ter id faciat, & toties quoties Petrus confessus est se amare Dominum: Hoc, inquam, arguit admirabilem & ineffabilem ipsius erga homines amorem, quos in suum ipsius locum sumogat, in eos translato amore illo, qui ipsi totus debebatur, adeo vt quoties quis profiteatur se Dominum diligere, toties respondeat pascendum esse gregem ipsius.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 5.14. 1 Cor. 4.10. our love toward Christ in Christ's love toward us. For after he had said, the love of Christ constrains us, he at once added, that we know that, since we were dead, one died for all. There is that foundation, the first of all duties, and therefore of all things rightly done in any calling whatever. For that love of the Lord toward us stirs up in us a mutual love toward the Lord. Hence we all do everything for the Lord's sake. We live to him and we die to him. As no action in life is right, sincere and earnest unless it flows from the love of Christ, so there is no surer proof of the love of Christ than a duty well and rightly performed. Conversely, there is no surer proof that a heart is empty of that love than a duty not faithfully and rightly discharged. In the disturbance and corruption of God's Church at Corinth, Paul perceived that those puffed-up teachers, as he calls them, did not love the Christ whom they preached. At last, in the final chapter, he pronounces this against them in these words: If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha. For false and mercenary teachers are accursed not so much because they corrupt God's Church and destroy it, as because they do not love the Lord Jesus himself. But the words must be examined more carefully. First, the word to feed and the word shepherd, which by metaphor is transferred to other offices of any kind, whether civil or ecclesiastical, in which the diligence, care and concern of shepherds are required. Especially in the ecclesiastical office and in the ministry, the diligence and concern of the Shepherd are required, as the Lord teaches us, even through this threefold and so earnest commendation of his flock. Christ himself, properly speaking, is the Shepherd, and rightly claims this name as his own, John 10. For the flock belongs to him, and the food on which the flock feeds is likewise his. For all that is not drawn from that store of Christ's word is poison. Yet he shares this name with his ministers and servants, whose work he uses in feeding his flock, and honours them by the very name, and so also urges them to feed faithfully and to perform their duty. But enough has been said of the name of Shepherd; now of those who are to be fed. They are indeed not wild beasts, such as wolves, bears, lions, etc., but lambs, sheep: that is, the elect, who are simple and innocent, like lambs and sheep. This I wish to be understood thus: not that the elect are at once like lambs, but that, as time goes on, through the Word and the Spirit, those who at first were like lions, bears, wolves, tigers and other wild beasts are tamed. For in nature there is no distinction between the elect and the reprobate, even if there is a distinction in the secret counsel of God, in his predestination, and finally in his grace. For God alone has distinguished his elect. It may therefore be asked here: ought the Shepherd to approach and take on for feeding only those whom he sees as gentle and innocent, like lambs? I answer: he ought to take on for feeding all whatever, wild beasts as well as lambs, so that he may make lambs out of wild beasts in the end, if this can be done by any means. Again it is asked: since the Lord commends his elect to Peter, ought the Shepherd to take on for teaching and feeding only these? Let them be at first, though in the first encounter more like wolves than lambs: yet in that place he commends only these to Peter for feeding. Answer: the Lord indeed commends the elect properly, but meanwhile he does not exclude the reprobate, to whom he also wishes food to be offered, if not for their conversion and salvation, at least for their hardening and just condemnation. But he wishes the Shepherds to regard all of them as his elect, and to feed them as lambs for eternal life. For it is not for men to discern and judge the election and reprobation of men: for the Lord alone knows who are his. Yet this must be true: labour is fruitful and effective only when it is spent upon the elect alone. For the reprobate never in fact becomes tame or domesticated. It may indeed happen that for a time he puts on a lamb's skin, that is, plays the hypocrite, and assumes the pretext of hypocrisy; yet he never becomes truly and from the heart devout and good. Nor should this be passed over: he bids him feed not other people's sheep but his lambs. Feed, he says, my lambs, that is, those redeemed by the price of my blood, and therefore rightly mine. This word, as it contains the reason why the lambs are to be fed, namely that they belong to the Lord, redeemed by the price of his blood, so warns the Shepherd not to hold God's flock as his own, nor to feed it for himself, that is, for his own use and advantage. Therefore the Baptist said, He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him, and rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom's voice. By these words he signified that he did not court the Church of God, or feed it, for himself, but for the Lord, who is the bridegroom of his Church. And Paul says, I court you with a godly jealousy; for I have prepared you to present you as a pure virgin to one husband, Christ. For it is the most abominable of all sacrileges to despoil Christ of his bride, and of his flock, already bought and acquired at the great price of God's blood. Now at this last point it is to be noted that he repeats the same thing three times: Feed, he says, my lambs; feed my sheep; feed my sheep. The threefold repeated absolution confirms more strongly Peter's restoration and the grace of the apostleship restored to him. This also, that he does not transfer the Shepherd's love to his flock and Church only once, on a single occasion, but does so three times, and as often as Peter confessed that he loved the Lord: this, I say, shows his wonderful and ineffable love toward men, whom he takes into his own place, the love which was wholly owed to himself being transferred to them; so that as often as anyone professes that he loves the Lord, so often is he answered that the Lord's flock is to be fed.

units.la: Cum esses iunior. Praemonitio est qua praeparat Petrum, iam restitutum Apostolatui, ad mortem futuram, & eam quidem violentam, qua obsignaturus sit Euangelium a se iam praedicatum. Praemonitione autem hac & praeparatione armat quasi hominem aduersus mortem. Nam tela praeuisa minus laeduntur. In persona Apostoli Petri omnes Pastores, quotquot hscipiunt hoc munus docendi Euangelium, praemonent pariter & praeparat atque armat aduersus mortem, eamque violentam. Etsi enim neque ex reuelatione aliqua particulari id faciat vt tunc fecit, neque omnes sanguine suo statim obsignent Euangelium suum, sed non nisi paucis is honor deferatur, atque ...
units.tr: When you were younger. This is a forewarning by which he prepares Peter, now restored to the apostleship, for a death to come, and indeed a violent one, by which he is to seal with his blood the gospel he has already preached. By this forewarning and preparation he arms the man, as it were, against death. For weapons seen in advance wound less. In the person of the apostle Peter, all Shepherds, as many as receive this office of teaching the gospel, are equally forewarned, prepared and armed against death, and a violent death. For although he does not do this now by any particular revelation, as he then did, and although not all seal their gospel at once with their blood, but this honour is granted to only a few, and the gift of suffering for the name of Christ is given to few...

units.la: DDd d iiij hoc donum patiendi pro nomine Christi detur: tamen ea voluntas Dei est, vt sese præparent assiduè omnem violentam aliquam mortem, qua glorificent Deum. Et fere omnia minantur Pastori mortem: non est ei res cum agnis tantum, etsi mittatur ad pascendos agnos, sed cum lupis & leonibus, præsertim autem cum rugiente illo leone Sathanæ qui dies noctésque obambulat quærens quem devoret, imprimis autem ipsum ouium Pastorem exposcit ad cædem. Eandem etiam præparationem esse oportet ouium, quæ in medio luporum sunt & quæ si effugerint mortem, crucem certè aliquam & afflictionem non sunt effugituræ. Omnes enim qui pie volunt viuere in Christo Iesu, afflictionem patientur. Et oportet per multas tribulationes ingredi regnum cælorum. Quare tam Pastoribus quàm ouibus oportet esse propositum moriendi aliquod, si Deus ita voluerit, & omnes nos debemus esse saltem propositio animi nostri martyres Christi, si non re ipsa. Propositio præmonitionis est per comparationem dissimilium, comparatis inter se priore illa Petri conditione, quæ fuit in iuuentute, & posteriore quæ futura est in senectute, quasi dicat, Naturæ ordo inuertetur in te, Petre. Nam qua ætate par eras afflictionibus, & eas per vires iuuentutis tuæ sustinere poteras, ea ætate non es afflictus, verùm tum omnia pro arbitratu tuo, & ex animi tui sententia fecisti. Profecturus aliquò cingebas te (Alludit ad mores hominum orientalium, qui prælongis & demissis vsi sunt vestibus, quare profecturi aliquò sese ad iter succingebant.) Postquam autem ipse te cinxisti, tum iuisti, quò iubuit. At verò qua ætate futurus es impar afflictionibus, & eas per imbecillitatem senectutis sustinere non posse videberis, ea ætate affligeris. Alius te cinget, hoc est loris astringet & vinctum abducet, quò noles: hoc est, violenta morte morieris. Hic sensus videtur esse verborum Domini quibus, vt videtur, hominem abstertet à tam difficili Apostolatus functione, & tam contraria priori illi vitæ conditione, quæ fuit libera & immunis ab afflictionibus, & in qua ne senectuti quidem & ingrauescenti ætati, quę vacare solet ab omnibus laboribus, parcendum esset. Vocatio illa Domini est, qua ad affli-
units.tr: This is nevertheless God's will: that they should constantly prepare themselves for any violent death by which they may glorify God. Almost everything threatens the Shepherd with death. He has to do not only with lambs, though he is sent to feed lambs, but with wolves and lions, and above all with that roaring lion of Satan who walks about day and night seeking whom he may devour, and who especially demands the Shepherd of the sheep himself for slaughter. The same preparation is also needful for the sheep, who are in the midst of wolves and who, even if they escape death, will certainly not escape some cross and affliction. For all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution. And we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of heaven. Wherefore both Shepherds and sheep must have some purpose of dying, if God so wills, and we all ought at least to be martyrs of Christ in purpose of mind, if not in deed. The forewarning proceeds by comparison of unlike things, setting over against each other that earlier condition of Peter, which was in his youth, and the later one which will be in his old age, as if to say: the order of nature will be reversed in you, Peter. For at the age when you were equal to afflictions, and could bear them by the strength of your youth, you were not afflicted; rather, at that time you did everything at your own pleasure and according to your own mind. You girded yourself when you were about to go somewhere (this alludes to the custom of eastern men, who wore very long and loose garments, so that when about to set out somewhere they tucked them up for the journey). But after you had girded yourself, you went where you wished. But at the age when you will be unequal to afflictions, and will seem unable to endure them through the weakness of old age, you will be afflicted. Another will gird you, that is, bind you with thongs and lead you away bound, where you do not wish to go: that is, you will die a violent death. This seems to be the sense of the Lord's words, by which, as it seems, he turns the man away from so difficult a function of the apostleship, and from a condition of life so contrary to that earlier one, which was free and exempt from afflictions, and in which not even old age and advancing years, which are wont to be free from all labours, would be spared. That calling of the Lord is one by which he is brought to afflictions...

units.la: Violentæ mortis descriptio.
units.tr: A description of violent death.

units.la: Ministerii Ecclesiastici difficultas.
units.tr: The difficulty of the ecclesiastical ministry.

units.la: Præmonitionis propositio per comparationem dissimilium. afflictiones vocat perpetuò, siue vocet pastorem, siue vocet gregem. Eriam statim in initio praemonet du- ram fore conditionem nostram in hac vita: imò vero quibus poterit modis eam audientibus nobis exaggerat. In mundo oppressionem habebitis, dixit discipulis suis ante passionem. Sed addidit continuò, Confidite, ego vici mundum. Promittit enim afflictis finalem victoriam, & in mediis afflictionibus eos ita consolatur, vt magis gaudium adsit afflictis, quàm tibi mundo, atque etiam in media ipsa morte vita sit iis. Vt morientes, inquit Paulus, & ecce viuimus. Rursus video hoc loco non esse quòd fidelis aliquis Pastor certò sibi pollicetur se Christo pariter & lucris, priuilegiis, & libertatibus huius vitae fruiturum. Quod si quis animo fruendi his aggrediatur hoc munus, se ipse fallit, neque recte sentit de munere isto Pastoris. Quare Paulus ingressus munus Apostolatus, omnia haec priuilegia, praerogatiuas omnes, quae aliquando ipsi lucra esse videbantur, pro damnis duxit, imò pro stercoribus, denique seipsum iis inultauit. Fieri quidem potest, vt haec accidant Pastori, & in satis magna rerum istarum omnium affluentia sit. Nam & haec omnia etiam Pastori & ministro verbi sunt à Deo sanctificata. Verùm haec omnia ei praestex expectatione accidant, & his vtatur, ita vt iis non abutatur. Secuti colulit Paulus: semper autem Christum solum pro lucro habeat, qui quidè solus est lucrū, & in vita & in morte. Fieri quidem potest vt alia in vita nobis lucra sint: at verò in morte deficiunt omnia nihilq; nobis prodesse possunt. Christus autem solus qui vicit morte, in morte nobis lucrū est, sine quo profecto mors ista nihil terribilius est. Postremò notandum, quòd Petrus quo tempore liberè viueret, sine Christo, tum quidem visus sit sibi beatè viuere. Id enim obscurè innuit Dominus, dum commemorat priorem illam Petri conditionem, quae fuerat antequam cognosceret Dominum. Atque hoc malo adolescentiores & iuniores sæpè laborant: putat se beatos esse, si cum bona valetudine, libertate & licentia viuendi vt volunt, etiam sine Domino viuat: cùm interea temporis serui sint peccati & miseriae sint miserrima. Liberi enim Domino & iustitiae,
units.tr: The statement of the warning, by way of a comparison of unlike things. He calls them afflictions continually, whether he is calling the minister or calling the flock. He also warns at once at the beginning that our condition in this life will be hard, and indeed he sets it forth in the most vivid ways he can for us who hear him. "In the world you will have tribulation," he said to his disciples before the passion. But he immediately added, "Be of good cheer, I have overcome the world." For he promises the afflicted a final victory, and he so comforts them in the midst of afflictions that the afflicted have more joy than the world has, and that even in the very midst of death there is life for them. "As dying," says Paul, "and behold, we live." Again, I see that in this place there is no reason why any faithful minister should promise himself that he will enjoy Christ together with the gains, privileges and liberties of this life. If anyone takes up this office with a mind to enjoy such things, he deceives himself and does not rightly understand the office of a minister. Therefore Paul, when he entered upon the office of the apostleship, counted all these privileges and all the prerogatives that once seemed to him gains as losses, indeed as dung, and finally he stripped himself of them. It may indeed happen that these things come to a minister, and that he has them in fairly great abundance. For all these things too have been sanctified by God for the minister and the minister of the Word. But they come to him as things he should expect and use in such a way that he does not abuse them. Next Paul added: "and always has Christ alone as gain," who alone is gain, both in life and in death. It may indeed be that other things are gains for us in life; but in death all things fail and can do us no good. Christ alone, who has conquered death, is our gain in death, and without him that death is surely nothing but most terrible. Lastly, it should be noted that Peter, at the time when he lived freely, without Christ, seemed to himself to live happily. The Lord hints at this obscurely when he recalls Peter's former condition, which was before he knew the Lord. And younger and more youthful people often suffer from this evil: a man thinks himself blessed if he lives as he likes, with good health, freedom and licence, even without the Lord; yet in the meantime they are slaves of sin and are most wretched in their miseries. For those who are free from the Lord and from righteousness,

units.la: serui sunt peccati & ininstitiæ necessario: quos autem Filius in libertatem vindicarit, verè liberi sunt: & ubi spiritus Domini, ibi libertas.
units.tr: are necessarily slaves of sin and of unrighteousness; but those whom the Son has set free are truly free, and "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty."

units.la: Quò noles. Ergóne inuitus pertractus est Petrus ad supplicium? Puto hoc dictum comparatè, ac si dixisset, Abducet te, non tam quò tu voles, quàm quò ipse voleris: voluntas enim tua persequutoris tui & tortoris voluntati erit obnoxia. Nisi malis hoc, quod Petrus dicatur nolle, communi naturæ ascribere. Natura enim abhorret à separatione ista corporis & animæ, vt etiam ipsius Christi exemplo licet discere, qui alioqui totus erat compositus ad obedientiam Patris sui. Sed in Petro non tantùm naturæ communi tribuendum est hoc, verùm etiam naturæ corruptæ: cuius etiam tum reliquiæ erant in Petro, quæ continuò nos conantur retrahere ab obedientia Dei. vide Rom. 7.19. Non facio bonum quod volo, sed malum quod nolo, hoc ago. Nota igitur hic Petrum & sanctos martyres quoscunque non omnino vacuos fuisse à mortis metu, sed luctando cum pauore illo summo, victores mortis euasisse: vt non sit quòd nos defugiamus martyrium, ideo quòd in nobis ipsi sentiamus in-firmitatem & metum aliquem: nam profectò victoria in martyrio non minus in eo cernitur, quòd superemus metum hunc naturà insitum, & reliquias corruptionis naturæ, quàm quòd superemus omnia tormenta & supplicia quæque exquisitissima. Et obedientia nostra etiam hoc interno inobedientiæ motu probatur, clarióque eo euadit, quòd reluctante natura & corruptione ista perficiatur. Nunc vt hoc postremo loco dicamus exemplo Petri, afflictiones & morte pro Domino, non posse nos ferre viribus nostris, sed donum esse ipsius Dei. Vobis datum est in Christi negotio non solùm credere in eum, sed etiam pro eo affligi, inquit Paulus. Philip.1.29. Idem iubet Timotheum participem esse afflictionum 2.Tim.1.8. Euangelij ex potentia Dei. Quare assiduos esse oportet nos in precibus nostris ad Deum, vt is velit nos sua illa potentia in afflictionibus sustinere. Hoc autem dixit significans. Euangelista inserit interpretationem verborum Christi. Interpretatur autem verba Christi de Petri morte. sti omnino de morte violenta: non autem, vt Papistæ volunt, de certo aliquo genere mortis violentæ, verbi gratia, crucifixione, quam quidem non præ se ferunt hoc loco verba Christi. Sed obseruandum, quòd non dicat (qua morte esset moriturus) sed, qua mortē esset glorificaturus Deum. Circumscriptio enim est mortis siue martyrij Petri. Nam cum omnium piorum mors glorificet Deum, mors præsertim eorum, qui Christi Euangelium suo sanguine obsignant, hanc speciale laudem ac definitionem obtinet, quòd Deum glorificare dicatur: quia in eorum morte gloriæ diuinæ materia potissimum æternitur: in morte autem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, fuit gloriæ Dei materia maxima: ideo primum omnium sibi hanc laudem & mortis circumscriptionem vendicat, Glorifica, inquit, Pater, nomen tuum, hoc est, Sine moriar in gloriam nominis tui. Proximè vero post mortem Christi, materia gloriæ Dei posita est in morte martyrum: vnde hoc loco mortem Petri dixit Iohannes esse glorificationem Dei. Sic Paulus intentè dixit se exaltasse, vt magnificaretur Christus in corpore suo, siue per vitam, siue per mortem. Hæc commendatio mortis martyrum debet nos ad mortem animare obeundam libenter pro Euangelio Christi obsignando. Sequere me. Nunc surgit Christus, & abiturus præcipit Petro, vt ipsum sequatur: vt hoc sit ei Sacramentum quasi & signum indubitatum futuræ crucis & mortis. Nam sequi Christum est tollere crucem suam, & eum sequi. Simulque eum animat ad crucem, dum se ducem illi proponit, non tantum in morte, sed in resurrectione. Quòdenim sequamur Christum in morte, & habeamus eum pro duce in morte, profectò id aufert à nobis mortis acerbitatem, nam acerba mors est rum demum, qui moriuntur pro peccatis suis. Christus autem in morte præcedens nos, moritur pro peccatis nostris, atque ita aufert mortis amaritudinem, facique vt mors iam sit nobis vitæ quædam porta. Quòd vero sequamur eum in vita & resurrectione, ideo habemus post mortem, vitam & resurrectionem. Nam Christus præit nobis in vita & resurrectione, vt nos cū eo virtute vitæ & resurrectionis ipsius viuamus & resurgamus. Ergo quod Christum praeeuntem nobis & ducem sequamur, id debet nos animare ad fortiter patiendum pro nomine ipsius.
units.tr: Where you do not wish to go. Was Peter then dragged to punishment against his will? I think this is said by way of comparison, as if he had said: "He will lead you not so much where you wish to go as where he himself wishes you to go; for your will will be subject to the will of your persecutor and tormentor." Unless you prefer to ascribe this, that Peter is said to be unwilling, to common nature. For nature shrinks from this separation of body and soul, as can also be learned from the example of Christ himself, who in other respects was entirely disposed to obedience to his Father. But in Peter this should be attributed not only to common nature but also to corrupted nature, of which remnants were still in Peter, which continually try to draw us back from obedience to God. See Rom. 7.19: "I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do." Note therefore here that Peter and all the holy martyrs were not wholly free from fear of death, but by struggling against that greatest dread they escaped as victors over death; so that there is no reason for us to shun martyrdom because we feel weakness in ourselves and some fear; for surely the victory in martyrdom is seen no less in this, that we overcome this fear implanted by nature and the remnants of corrupted nature, than in that we overcome all the most exquisite torments and punishments. And our obedience is proved even by this inward motion of disobedience, and it comes out the clearer because it is accomplished while nature and that corruption resist. Now, to say at this last point, from the example of Peter, that we cannot bear afflictions and death for the Lord by our own strength, but that it is a gift of God himself: "It has been given to you in the cause of Christ not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him," says Paul (Phil. 1.29). He likewise bids Timothy be a partaker of afflictions for the gospel "according to the power of God" (2 Tim. 1.8). Therefore we ought to be constant in our prayers to God, that he may be willing to sustain us in afflictions by that power of his. "But this he said, signifying," the evangelist inserts an interpretation of the words of Christ. He interprets the words of Christ as referring to Peter's death: surely of a violent death, but not, as the Papists want, of some particular kind of violent death, for example crucifixion, which the words of Christ do not in fact express in this place. But it should be observed that he does not say "by what death he would die," but "by what death he would glorify God." For this is a circumscription of the death or martyrdom of Peter. For since the death of all the godly glorifies God, and especially the death of those who seal the gospel of Christ with their blood, this death has the special praise and definition that it is said to glorify God, because in their death the matter of the divine glory is chiefly set forth; but in the death of our Lord Jesus Christ was the greatest matter of the glory of God. Therefore first of all he claims this praise and circumscription of death for himself: "Glorify," he says, "Father, your name"; that is, "Let me die to the glory of your name." Next after the death of Christ, the matter of the glory of God is placed in the death of the martyrs; hence in this place John said that Peter's death was the glorifying of God. Thus Paul also pointedly said that he had exalted himself, so that Christ might be magnified in his body, whether by life or by death. This commendation of the death of martyrs ought to animate us to undergo death willingly, for sealing the gospel of Christ. "Follow me." Now Christ rises and, about to depart, commands Peter to follow him; so that this may be for him a sacrament, as it were, and an indubitable sign of the cross and death to come. For to follow Christ is to take up our cross and follow him. And at the same time he encourages him to the cross, while he sets himself before him as leader, not only in death but in resurrection. For because we follow Christ in death, and have him as leader in death, this surely takes from us the bitterness of death; for death is bitter only to those who die for their own sins. But Christ, going before us in death, dies for our sins, and so takes away the bitterness of death, and makes death now a kind of gate of life for us. And because we follow him in life and in resurrection, we have life and resurrection after death; for Christ goes before us in life and resurrection, so that we may live and rise again with him by the power of his life and resurrection. Therefore, that we follow Christ as going before us and as our leader ought to encourage us to suffer bravely for his name.

units.la: Iohannis 21.
units.tr: John 21.

units.la: 20 Conuersus Petrus videt illum discipulum quem diligebat Iesus, sequentem, qui & recubuerat in coena illa super pectus eius, & dixerat, Domine, quis est ille qui te prodit?
units.tr: 20 Peter turned round and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following, who also had leaned back at that supper upon his breast, and had said, Lord, who is it that betrays you?

units.la: 21 Hunc ergo cum vidisset Petrus dicit Iesu, Domine, hic autem quid?
units.tr: 21 When Peter therefore saw him, he said to Jesus, Lord, and what about this man?

units.la: 22 Dicit ei Iesus, Si velim eum manere donec veniam, quid ad te? tu me sequere?
units.tr: 22 Jesus said to him, If I will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? Follow you me.

units.la: 23 Exiit ergo sermo iste inter fratres, discipulum illum non moriturum: sed non dixerat ei Iesus, Non morietur, sed, Si eum velim manere donec veniam, quid ad te?
units.tr: 23 Then this saying went out among the brothers, that this disciple would not die. Yet Jesus had not said to him, He will not die, but, If I will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?

units.la: 24 Hic est discipulus ille, qui de his testatur, & haec scripsit: & scimus verum esse testimonium eius.
units.tr: 24 This is the disciple who bears witness of these things, and wrote these things; and we know that his testimony is true.

units.la: 25 Sunt autem & alia multa quae fecit Iesus, quae si scribantur singillatim, ne mundum quidem ipsum opinor capturum eos qui scriberentur libros.
units.tr: 25 And there are also many other things which Jesus did, which, if they were written every one, I suppose the world itself would not contain the books that would be written.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: HACtenus fuit sermo mutuus Domini & Petri, quem post piscium capturam vltro citroque contulerunt: sequitur sermo eorundem, qui inter proficiscendum conferebatur. Sermonem quidem prior inchoat Petrus & curiosius interrogat Dominum, vt videbimus. Verum occasio primum in textu venit obseruanda: ea autem continetur his verbis: Conuersus Petrus. Iussit Dominus in se intentum esse eum, seque sequi strenue, adeo vt ne semel retrospiceret: Petrus autem oblitus mandati, & officij sui conuersus est ad Iohannem. Hinc materiam curiositatis suae nactus est, vt videbimus. Quo docemur, quod posteaquam iam a Domino sumus vocati ad sequenquendum ipsum, in quocunque demum munere, ita adeo intenti esse debeamus in Dominum, & serio adeo cogitare de officio, ut non oporteat nobis tantum otij esse a bs re nostra, ut ad alium quem conuersi a Domino, & ab officio nostro, ipsum intueamur, videamusque quid ipse agat in vocatione atque officio suo. Curiositatis enim est ita curare aliena, ut interea nostrorum, quae nobis ipsis ex officio incumbunt obliuiscamur. Paulus in decurrendo illo stadio suo, dixit se non reflexisse oculos ad ea quae a tergo essent, verum contendisse ad ea, quae essent a fronte, ad palmam illam supernae vocationis Dei in Christo Iesu: quibus quidem verbis significauit seriam illam suam in Apostolatu ad quem est vocatus occupationem, & cursum intensissimum: nihil fecisse se quod quouis modo posset ipsum ab officio diuertere. Vidit discipulum quem diligebat. Ex oculis Petri retro a Domino & vocatione conuersis ad Iohannem, sequitur materia scandali & curiositatis: intuitus autem Iohannem recordatur veteris dilectionis Domini & familiaritatis, quae inter ce fuit Iohanni cum Domino: fuit quidem Iohannes dilectus Domino: familiariter in vltima coena recubuit in pectore ipsius, ac tacentibus aliis familiariter interrogauit de proditore. Recordatus igitur Petrus hanc dilectionem & familiaritatem, admiratus est Iohannem pariter non esse inuitatum a Domino, ad id ut ipsum sequeretur. Admiratus autem, oblitus est officij vocationis suae, & curiosius iam coepit indagare de Iohanne, ipsiusque vocatione. Qui vel tantum otij sibi sumit a vocatione sua & officio suo obeundo, ut conuersus ad alium quem, ipsum intueatur, in ipsius vocationem inquirat, profecto vix se conuertet ad alium, quin materiam scandali & remoram sibi inueniat. Nos qui cursum corripimus eo vt propositam spem obtinea- mus, oportet ita intentos esse in praecursorem, qui intra velum pro nobis ingressus est, vt dum fungimur officio nostro, eum nunquam ex oculis nostris decedere patia- mur. Nota rursus ex his verbis, eum qui ia antea accepit multa & non vulgaria illa quidem signa dilectionis Domini, non nunquam tamen ita deseri a Deo, vt & ipse incipiat dubitare, & alij admirari cum sic esse desertum à Domino : cùm tamen non ita se rem habere satisap-pareat ex hoc loco. Nam nihilo nunc remissiorem fuisse dilectionem Domini erga Iohannem, quàm anteaex responsione ipsa Domini subiecta satis conspicitur. Quamobrem non est vel de nobis, vel de aliis temere iu-dicandum ex externis istis. Hic autem quid? subaudi fa-ciet, annon sequetur te dilectus iste tuus discipulus? Hęc est curiosa illa Petri interrogatio, & curiositas non solùm superflua, sed etiam noxia : ex eo autem orta est quod segnescere iam inciperet in vocatione sua, neque eo quo eum decuit studio & contentione animi, Do-minum sit subsequutus : teste enim Apostolo, qui ipsi nihil operis faciunt, ij demum sunt qui curiosè agunt: qui enim maximè satagunt rerum alienarum, hi in sua-rum rerum tractatione maximè solent esse securi. Quare sic curemus quidem aliena, vt cura sit non curiositas: cura aliorum pro vocatione cuiusque praecipitur. Alij aliorum onera portate. At curiositas prohibetur: nam vnusquisque onus suum portabit. Officium cuiusque & vocatio coniuncta est cum aliqua aliorum cura. Hic autem videndum ne cura illa conuertatur in curiositatem: qua quidem fiet, vt tibi plus obfuturus sis, quàm aliis profuturus. Peccauit in eo quoque Petrus, quòd putarit omnes pariter eodem vocari. Ipse vocatus est ad hoc vt Dominum sequeretur ad mortem vsque. Putauit igitur Iohannem oportuisse eodem vocari, cùm tamen in Ecclesia Dei, alij ad alia, atque alia vocentur, & variae sint militiae Christianae species. Aliis quidem pugnandum est ad sanguinis effusionem, aliis verò non item: quamobrem sequi nos oportet, quocunque Domino visum est vocare, permittentes interea alios suo ipsorum Domino, qui vterur iis, prout ipse vult.
units.tr: So far was the mutual conversation of the Lord and Peter, which they held back and forth after the catch of fish. What follows is their conversation, which was carried on while they were walking. Peter, as we shall see, begins the talk and questions the Lord rather inquisitively. But first we must note the occasion given in the text, which is contained in these words: Peter turned round. The Lord had bidden him to keep his attention fixed on him and to follow him earnestly, so that he should not look back even once. But Peter, forgetting the command and his duty, turned round to John. From this he got the matter of his curiosity, as we shall see. Here we are taught that, since we have been called by the Lord to follow him, in whatever office it may be, we ought to be so intent upon the Lord, and to think so seriously about our duty, that we have no leisure to be concerned with other people's business, so as to turn away from the Lord and from our own duty, and look at another, and see what he is doing in his calling and office. For it is the mark of curiosity to attend so closely to other people's affairs that in the meantime we forget what our own duty lays upon us. Paul, in running that race of his, said that he had not turned his eyes to what was behind him, but had strained toward what was before him, toward that prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. By these words he signified his earnest occupation in the apostleship to which he was called, and his most intense course: he had done nothing that could in any way turn him aside from his duty. He saw the disciple whom he loved. From Peter's eyes, turned away from the Lord and his calling, to John, there follows the occasion of offence and curiosity. But when he looked at John, he recalled the old love and familiarity of the Lord, which John had with the Lord. John was indeed beloved of the Lord; at the last supper he had leaned familiarly on his breast, and, when the others were silent, had familiarly asked about the traitor. Peter, therefore, recalling this love and familiarity, wondered that John, likewise, had not been invited by the Lord to follow him. Wondering, however, he forgot the duty of his calling, and now began to inquire more curiously about John and his calling. The man who takes so much leisure from his own calling and the discharge of his office that he turns to look at another and inquires into his calling will hardly turn to another without finding for himself a matter of offence and a hindrance. We who run the race that we may obtain the hope set before us must be so intent upon our forerunner, who has entered within the veil for us, that, while we are doing our duty, we never allow him to leave our eyes. Note again from these words that one who has previously received many, and not ordinary, signs of the Lord's love may yet sometimes be so forsaken by God that he himself begins to doubt, and others wonder that he has been so forsaken by the Lord; yet that this is not so, appears sufficiently from this passage. For the love of the Lord toward John was no less now than before, as is sufficiently clear from the Lord's answer that follows. Therefore we must not rashly judge either ourselves or others from such outward things. And what about this man? Supply: will he not follow you, this beloved disciple of yours? This is that curious question of Peter's, and a curiosity not only superfluous but also harmful. It arose from the fact that he was already beginning to grow slack in his calling, and was not following the Lord with the zeal and effort of mind that became him. For, as the Apostle says, those who do no work themselves are the very ones who act in a curious way; for those who are most busy with other people's affairs are usually most careless in handling their own. Let us therefore so care for other people's affairs that our care is not curiosity: care for others is enjoined according to each one's calling. Bear one another's burdens. But curiosity is forbidden: for each one shall bear his own burden. Each one's duty and calling is joined with some care for others. Here, however, we must take heed lest that care be turned into curiosity; for then it will come about that you will do more harm to yourself than good to others. Peter also erred in this, that he thought all were called alike. He himself was called to follow the Lord even unto death. He therefore thought John ought to be called in the same way, whereas in the Church of God some are called to one thing and some to another, and there are various kinds of Christian service. Some must fight to the shedding of blood, but others need not do so. Wherefore we must follow wherever the Lord has seen fit to call us, while allowing others to belong to their own Lord, who uses them as he wills.

units.la: Si velim eum manere. Sensus est, quasi dicat, Tu quidem nimis curiosè de eo quaeris: esto securus & permittito hoc mihi. Tu verò quod iubeo, fac, & me sequere. Tria sunt quae reprehendit in eo, si quis ad ea attendat diligentius. 1. Reprehendit quòd non pergat ipse in vocatione sua. 2. quòd nimis sit sollicitus de vocatione aliena. 3. est, quod & maximum est, quòd irruptionem aliquam faciat in officium ipsius Domini, non contentus eius voluntate qui prout vult vnicuique distribuit: dum enim dicit Dominus, Si velim, innuit Petrum non satis acquiescere valuntati ipsius, ea nimirum qua voluit Iohannem non sequi ipsum: ideoque vendicat atque asserit sibi suam ipsius potestatem. Plura igitur in curiositate concurrunt peccata. 1. est neglectus functionis propriae. 2. est curiositas in functione aliena, saepe cum iniuria in proximum coniuncta. 3. est iniuria in ipsum Dominum, & irruptio quae fit quodam modo in officium ipsius. Haec omnia quidem deprehendit Dominus in hoc Petri facto, eaque reprehendit. Deprehendit quoque ac reprehendit pariter in omnibus hodierno die quicunque agunt curiose. Interea notandum, quod dum reprehendit Petrum in curriculo suo segnescentem, non deseruerit eum, sed porrecta quasi manu rursus eum apprehenderit transeritque post se: dum enim suos deprehendit Dominus, in ira aliqua sua, non tamen interea obliuiscitur gratiae ac misericordiae: sed simul eos incitat ad pergendum in cursu suscepto, & in vocatione sua: estque perseverantia nostra nihil aliud quam multiplicatio quedam gratiae Dei.
units.tr: If I will that he remain. The meaning is as if he said: You are asking about him too curiously. Be easy and leave this to me. But you do what I command, and follow me. If one attends more carefully to these things, there are three that he rebukes in Peter. (1) He rebukes him because he does not persevere himself in his own calling. (2) Because he is too anxious about another's calling. (3) And what is greatest of all: because he makes some intrusion into the Lord's own office, not content with the will of him who distributes to each one as he wills. For when the Lord says, If I will, he hints that Peter did not sufficiently acquiesce in his will, namely in that will by which he willed John not to follow him; and so Peter claims and asserts for himself a power that is his own. Therefore several sins come together in curiosity: (1) there is neglect of one's own function; (2) there is curiosity about another's function, often joined with wrong done to one's neighbour; (3) there is wrong done to the Lord himself, and an intrusion made in some way upon his office. The Lord indeed detected all these things in this deed of Peter's, and rebuked them. He also detects and rebukes in the same way all those who act curiously on this day. Meanwhile it is to be noted that, while he rebuked Peter for growing slack in his course, he did not forsake him, but, as it were stretching out his hand, took hold of him again and carried him past himself. For when the Lord corrects his own, in some anger, he nevertheless does not forget grace and mercy; rather he at the same time urges them to press on in the course they have undertaken and in their calling. And our perseverance is nothing other than a certain multiplication of the grace of God.

units.la: Nisi enim Dominus gratiam illam suam erga nos multiplicaret, & segnescentes nos in cursu & vocatione nostra, porrecta quasi manu sua apprehensos traheret post se: profecto fieri nequaquam posset ut nos ab eo iam deserti ad finem usque perseveraremus.
