Ex quo nota quàm nihil proficiant homines omnia audiendo, omnia etiam videndo, quantumuis spiritualia & cœlestia, quantouis tempore, nisi pariter συνδιδασκοντοι sint, & accipiant Spiritum sanctum. Iam plusquam triennium audiuerunt operante, hoc ipso tempore viderunt eū cœlesti quadam gloria indutum esse, & tamen nihil adhuc nisi terrestre.
units.tr: They sinned in curiosity, as appears from the Lord's answer. Second, the disciples still dreamed of I know not what earthly kingdom. Third, they wished to reign and triumph before they had fought the contest. From this note how little men profit by hearing everything and even by seeing everything, however spiritual and heavenly it is, and for however long a time, unless they are taught together [συνδιδασκόντοι] with the Holy Spirit and receive him. For more than three years they had heard him, and at this very time they had seen him clothed with a certain heavenly glory, and yet still they thought of nothing but the earthly.

units.la: quid & crassum sapuerunt. Nunc videamus quid responderit eis Dominus. Primùm reprehendit eorum curiositatem: Non est vestrum, inquit. Deinde monet vt cogitent primùm de promissione illa facta Spiritus sancti. Tu de officio suo & Apostolatu. Nota: Christus iamiam discessurus & abiturus in gloriam suam, substic tamen paulisper, & cum spiritu lenitatis & patientiæ admirabili stupidos istos docet ac erudit. Atque ne nunc quidem arundinem quassatam frangit, aut linum fumigans extinguit: verùm, cum omni lenitate & mansuetudine, adeo stupidos tolerat atque docet. Responsio autem eius de hoc nos admonet: velle quidem Dominum vsque adeo attentos esse nos primùm ad officium, ad quod sumus per ipsum vocati in hac vita, deinde ad promissionem gratiæ & vitæ alterius, vt ne tantillum quidem temporis impertiamur curiositati.
units.tr: They were also foolish and rather gross in their understanding. Now let us see what the Lord answered them. First he rebukes their curiosity: It is not yours, he says. Then he advises them to think first of that promise made of the Holy Spirit, and of their own office and apostleship. Note this: Christ, though about to depart and go away into his glory, nevertheless stays a little while and, with a remarkable spirit of gentleness and patience, teaches and instructs these dull men. And even now he does not break the bruised reed nor quench the smoking flax; rather, with all gentleness and meekness, he bears with such dull men and teaches them. His answer admonishes us of this: the Lord wishes us to be so attentive first to the duty to which we have been called by him in this life, and then to the promise of grace and of another life, that we give not even the smallest portion of time to curiosity.

units.la: 1. Absoluto colloquio Christus triumphator & rex noster ascendit in cœlos. Benedicit primùm discipulis suis, tanquam Ecclesiæ sacerdos.
units.tr: 1. When the conversation was finished, Christ, our triumphant king, ascended into the heavens. First he blesses his disciples, as the priest of the Church.

units.la: Hactenus fuit communicatio, sequitur Ascensio in cœlos. Ascensurus benedixit eis manibus in altum sublatis: priusquam enim ipse ascendit in cœlos, gratiam discipulis suis deducit è cœlis: quæ ipsa iam post eius ascensionem in cœlos esset cum iis permansura. Pacem relinquo vobis, pacem illam meam do vobis. Iohan. 14. 27. Reliquit autem eis benedictionem Dei. Benedixit autem eis Dominus iam discedens, vt sacerdos. Sacerdotis enim erat in publico benedicere Dei populo. Benedixit etiam obseruato ritu illo & cæremonia Sacerdotibus in veteri lege vsitata: eleuatis nimirum in altum manibus: Benedixit denique vt sacerdos regalis: iam enim regale illud solium suum erat ascensurus: ideòque benedictionem illam, quæ sacerdoti erat per potentiam illam quæ regis erat, oportuit tum efficacem esse. Homines possunt quidem bene optare, & id quidem ex animo, verùm quod optant non possunt effectum dare, cùm hoc sit solius Dei & Christi proprium. Sed quid obseruandum occurrit? hoc nimirum est, ministerio Euangelij à Christo relictum esse singularem quandam benedictionem. Vidimus iam supra singularem promissionem ministerio factam: Matth. 28. 20. Nunc autem videmus singularem quandam ac particularem benedictionem à Christo
units.tr: So far there has been fellowship; next comes the ascension into heaven. About to ascend, he blessed them with his hands lifted up on high. For before he himself went up into the heavens, he brought grace down from heaven to his disciples, grace which was to remain with them even after his ascension into heaven. "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you" (John 14:27). He left them, then, the blessing of God. The Lord blessed them as he was departing, as a priest does, for it belonged to a priest to bless God's people in public. He also blessed them with the rite and ceremony used by the priests under the old law, namely with hands lifted up on high. Finally, he blessed them as a royal priest, for he was about to ascend to that royal throne of his; therefore that blessing, which belonged to a priest through the power that belonged to a king, had then to be effective. Men may indeed wish well, and sincerely, but they cannot give effect to what they wish, since this belongs to God and Christ alone. But what should we observe here? This, namely, that Christ left to the ministry of the Gospel a unique blessing. We have already seen above the special promise made to the ministry: Matthew 28:20. Now we see that Christ, as he departed, left to the ministry a singular and particular blessing, such as we do not see left even to kings themselves, who are blessed in this blessing of the ministers of the Gospel, as are all others in whatever other callings and functions.

units.la: Ministerii Euangelici summa. sto discedente, ministerio relictam esse, qualem non videmus relictam esse ne ipsis quidem regibus, qui ipsi benedicti sunt in hac benedictione ministrorum Euangelij, vt & alij quicunque in aliis vocationibus & functionibus quibuscunque. Benedictio autem haec fidelis ministerij hodierno etiam die efficax esse percipi tur ex eo, quod sentiamus ipsum esse ministerium iustitiae, ministerium Spiritus sancti: Imo ex eo quod consistat ac duret hoc ipsum ministerium in tanto odio, in tanta persecutione hominum & diabolorum. Nisi enim benedictio illa Christi in eo esset efficax & potens, profecto ipsum infirmum alioqui & in speciem abiectum ac vile in terris consistere nequiret. Post benedictionem videamus deinde Domini in coelos ascensionem. Explicata autem est a Marco, & Luca partim in Euangelio suo, partim in Actis Apostolorum, his servatis circumstantiis. Primum Dominus postquam iam benedixisset recessit ac disiunctus est ab iis aliquanto interuallo. 2. Elevatus est sursum. 3. Susceptus est nube. 4. Susceptus iam in nube ipsis intuentibus ablatus est ab oculis ipsorum. 5. Iam ablatus in nube ferebatur sursum in coelos. In omnibus his circumstantiis, vt gloriosam habemus Domini ascensionem, ita sensibilem eam ac visibilem habemus admodum. Nam cum staret prius in medio eorum, quo possent omnes melius ascendentem videre, paululum recessit ab iis, deinde elevatus est sensim ac pedetentim, ita vt ipsi sensim ascendentem oculis suis prosequi possent. Postea ab obuia nube ipsis videntibus suscepius est. Atque hucusque eum ascendentem in ipsius persona viderunt. Iam autem non vident personam Domini amplius, sed vident nubem illam in qua susceptus est, in coelos sursum ferri. Haec omnia admodum sensibilia & visibilia erunt: non enim nunc momento disparuit, vt vidimus supra momento ablatum fuisse eum a discipulis, quibuscum accumbebat in vico Emmaunte. Tam sensibilem voluit esse ascensione sua proculdubio, vt discipuli videntes, & oculis comprehendentes ipsum, haberent plenam fidei persuasionem: vt habentes plena persuasione & ..., possent deinde mundo eum praedicare.
units.tr: The sum of the Gospel ministry. That this blessing of the faithful ministry is effective even today is perceived from the fact that we feel that it is "the ministry of righteousness, the ministry of the Holy Spirit" (2 Cor. 3); indeed, from the fact that this very ministry endures and survives in such great hatred and persecution by men and devils. For unless Christ's blessing were effective and powerful in it, the ministry, weak and otherwise abject and worthless in appearance, could not possibly survive on earth. After the blessing let us next see the Lord's ascension into the heavens. It is described by Mark and Luke, partly in their Gospels and partly in the Acts of the Apostles, with these circumstances observed. First, when the Lord had blessed them, he withdrew and was parted from them at some distance. Second, he was lifted up. Third, he was received by a cloud. Fourth, already received into the cloud, he was taken from their eyes while they were looking on. Fifth, taken up in the cloud, he was carried upward into the heavens. In all these circumstances, the Lord's ascension is glorious, and likewise very perceptible and visible. For while he had stood before in the midst of them, so that they could all see him ascending better, he withdrew a little from them, then was lifted up gradually and step by step, so that they could follow him ascending with their eyes little by little. Afterwards he was received by a cloud that met him, while they watched. And up to this point they saw him ascending in his own person. But now they no longer see the person of the Lord, but see the cloud in which he was received being carried upward into the heavens. All these things are very perceptible and visible; for he did not vanish in a moment, as we saw above that he had been taken from the disciples in a moment, with whom he was reclining at the village of Emmaus. Without doubt he wished his ascension to be so perceptible, so that the disciples, seeing and grasping him with their eyes, might have full persuasion of faith, and having that full persuasion ... might then be able to preach him to the world.

units.la: FFff ij care cum libertate & euidentia in loquendo. Huiusmodi spem cum habeamus multa in loquendo παῤῥησίαν & euidentia, hoc est, ad viuum, ipsum Dominum ascendentem in coelos repraesentantes, mundus iam firmiter crederet ascendisse Dominum in coelos. Ergo nostri habita est ratio, & Ecclesiae Christi, in hac tam sensibili ac visibili ascensione Domini: & Apostoli non tam sua, quam Ecclesiae causa extiterunt omnium istarum rerum testes oculati.
units.tr: FFff ij care, with freedom and clarity in speaking. Since we have this kind of hope, we have much boldness [παῤῥησίαν] and clarity in speaking, that is, we represent vividly the Lord himself ascending into the heavens, and the world would now firmly believe that the Lord had ascended into the heavens. Therefore account was taken of us and of Christ's Church in this so perceptible and visible ascension of the Lord; and the apostles became eyewitnesses of all these things not so much for their own sake as for the sake of the Church.

units.la: Et sedit ad dextram. Iam ingressus Dominus in coelos altissimos, consedit ad dextram Patris sui. Sede, inquit, ad dextram meam, donec disposuero inimicos tuos in scabellum pedum tuorum. Sedit ad dextram, hoc est, obtinuit omnem potestatem in coelis & in terra, qua filius Dei & Deus Patri aequalis & glorificatus est, ea gloria, quam habuit apud Patrem ante iacta mundi fundamenta. Qua autem homo, exaltatus est supra omnem creaturam, adeo ut Deus per manum hominis gubernet omnia nunc in coelis & in terra. Videmus itaque Dominum a gloria in gloriam transiisse. Discipuli viderunt quidem Ascensionem gloriosam, sed sessionem illam ad dextram Patris longe gloriosissimam non viderunt: neque enim corruptibilis hic & mortalis oculus tantae gloriae capax est. Vidit quidem Stephanus apertos coelos, & Filium hominis adstantem ad dextram illius maiestatis. Sed quantulum, quaeso, fuit illius gloriae, quod ipsum tum revelatum est? Apostoli licet non tum viderint considere ad dextram Patris Filium, tamen eodem ipso momento, quo consedit, experti sunt potestatem illam regiam, ac Dominium Christi quod in omnia obtinuit. Quid enim sibi voluit tantum illud gaudium eorum, quorum paulo post reversi sunt Hierusalem? An non tum regnum Christi in iis fuit efficax ad illud tantum gaudium? Regnum enim Dei est iustitia, & pax, & gaudium per Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: "And sat at the right hand." Now that the Lord has entered the highest heavens, he sits at the right hand of his Father. "Sit," he says, "at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet" (Ps. 110:1). He sat at the right hand, that is, he obtained all power in heaven and on earth, by which the Son of God, equal to the Father and God, is glorified with that glory which he had with the Father before the foundation of the world. But as man, he has been exalted above every creature, so that God now governs all things in heaven and on earth by the hand of man. We see, therefore, that the Lord passed from glory to glory. The disciples indeed saw the glorious ascension, but they did not see that session at the right hand of the Father, far the most glorious; for this corruptible and mortal eye is not capable of such glory. Stephen indeed saw the heavens opened and the Son of man standing at the right hand of that majesty (Acts 7:56). But how small, I ask, was that glory, even when it was revealed to him? Although the apostles did not then see the Son sitting at the right hand of the Father, yet at the very moment when he sat down they experienced that royal power and the lordship of Christ which he obtained over all things. For what did that great joy of theirs mean, the joy with which they returned shortly afterwards to Jerusalem? Was not the kingdom of Christ then effective in them for that very joy? For the kingdom of God is righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom. 14:17).

units.la: 4. Discipuli adorato eo. Ipsi autem adorato eo. Hactenus de Christo dictum. Nunc sequuntur partes discipulorum, & quid nam interea temporis egerint, dum Dominus in coelos ascendit. t. Adorant. 2.Intenti sunt oculis in cœlos. Adorarunt, quia viderunt tantam gloriam, quantam nunquam viderant ante hac. Ergo nunquam ante hac tam impense, tam reuerenter, tam confidenter illi adorarunt Dominum, quàm hoc tempore. Adorarunt quidem iam antea, & coluerunt vt Messiam : sed parua ex parte tantum cognitum. At nunc vident Regem gloriæ & iudicem mundi: ergo oportuit cultum hunc esse maiorem, & liberiorem, quàm vnquam fuerit antea. Quanto enim magis quis videt gloriam Dei, tanto maiori erga eum reuerentia ducitur. Nos nunc quidem adoramus Christum, verum cùm videbimus eum sicuti est, tum adoramus eum multò maiore cum reuerentia, fiducia, libertate: quia scimus quod similes ei erimus, cùm videbimus eum sicuti est: hoc est, conformes erimus imagini gloriæ ipsius, & exuemur tota hac mortalitate & corruptione, qua tum erant induti Apostoli, quo tempore eum ascendentem in cœlos glorificarunt. Ergo in vltimo illo die cultus noster & adoratio nostra prosequemur Christum è cœlis descendentem vincetearn discipulorum Christi, qua tum prosequuti sunt Christum in cœlos ascendentem. Et cùm essent intentis in cœlum oculis. Hoc alterum est, quod fecerunt discipuli interea dum in cœlum ascenderet, prosecuti sunt oculis eum in cœlos ascendentem, quod quidem argumento fuit, corda eorum simul cum Christo in cœlos elevata fuisse. Corda autem eorum sursum elevata sunt vi ac virtute ascensionis ipsius Christi, in quem crediderunt. Nam credentes in Christum, & cum eo per fidem coniunctos, simul cum eo sursum in cœlos tolli oportet per vinculum illud fidei. Nota igitur, oculus noster attollitur in cœlos, quia cor nostrum attollitur in cœlos: cor autem attollitur, quia Christus ascendit in cœlos. Ista autem quæ non est elevatio oculorum ex cordis elevatione, cor elevatum & elevatio cordis ex ascensione Christi, argumento est oculum nostrum, & cor nostrum, adeoque totum hominem, corpus simul & animam in cœlos suo tempore virtute ascensionis Iesu Christi elevatum iri in cœlos, in ipsius gloriosò illo reditu: cui sit omnis gloria. Amen.
units.tr: 4. The disciples, having worshipped him. "And they, having worshipped him." So far we have spoken of Christ. Now follow the parts of the disciples, and what they did meanwhile, while the Lord was ascending into the heavens. 1. They worship. 2. "They were intent with their eyes on the heavens." They worshipped because they saw so great a glory, as they had never seen before. Therefore never before had they worshipped the Lord so earnestly, so reverently, so confidently, as at this time. They had indeed worshipped and honoured him before as the Messiah, but known only in small part. But now they see the King of glory and the judge of the world; therefore this worship had to be greater and freer than it had ever been before. For the more one sees the glory of God, the greater the reverence with which one is moved toward him. We now indeed worship Christ, but when we shall see him as he is, then we shall worship him with much greater reverence, confidence and freedom, because we know that we shall be like him when we see him as he is; that is, we shall be conformed to the image of his glory, and shall put off all this mortality and corruption with which the apostles were then clothed, at the time when they glorified him ascending into the heavens. Therefore on that last day our worship and adoration will accompany Christ descending from the heavens, with that same eagerness of the disciples of Christ with which they then accompanied Christ ascending into the heavens. "And while they were looking up intently into heaven": this is the second thing the disciples did while he was ascending into heaven; they followed him with their eyes as he ascended, which was a sign that their hearts were lifted up into heaven together with Christ. Their hearts were lifted up by the power and virtue of Christ's own ascension, in whom they believed. For those who believe in Christ, and are joined to him through faith, must be raised up together with him into heaven by that bond of faith. Note, then: our eye is lifted up to heaven because our heart is lifted up to heaven; and the heart is lifted up because Christ ascended into heaven. But this, which is not the lifting of the eyes from the lifting of the heart, and the lifted heart and the lifting of the heart from the ascension of Christ, is an argument that our eye, and our heart, and therefore the whole man, body and soul together, will in due time be lifted up into heaven by the power of the ascension of Jesus Christ, at his glorious return: to whom be all glory. Amen.

units.la: Ascendentem oculis prosequuntur discipuli.
units.tr: The disciples gaze after the ascending Lord with their eyes.

units.la: Ecce viri duo. Illis sic adorantibus & intuentibus in coelos, vide quid inciderit. Coelitus a throno Christi mittuntur continuo ad eos legati, ij autem sunt Angeli, numero duo sunt, forma viris similes sunt, vestitu candidi sunt & gloriosi. Nota, vix consedit Christus ad dextram Patris in coelis, cum testatam fecerit discipulis suis, quos post se reliquit in terris, primum potestatem illam suam plane regiam, qua imperat etiam Angelis: deinde, curam suam erga discipulos suos, in quorum gratiam, & ad quorum consolationem, misit coelitus Angelos suos. Haec potestas Christi & cura ista erga suos perpetuo manet eadem in hodiernum visque diem. Viri Galilaei, Sequitur sermo Angelorum ad discipulos. 1. Reprehendunt eos. 2. Consolatur. Reprehendunt, quod cum redeundum esset ipsis Hierusalem, ut ibi expectarent promissum illum Spiritum, quo iam accepto egrediendum fuit, & praedicandum Euangelium ex mandato Domini omni creaturae: cum haec, inquam, facienda essent, reprehendunt eos quod otiosi essent speculatores & contemplatores. Nota, non satis esse, si totos dies stemus vel sedeamus otiosi speculatores, etiam coelos ipsos in quos ascendit Dominus intuentes, verum oportere nos serio occupatos esse in tota vita; interea autem dum occupamur, in sancta aliqua legitimaq; vocatione coelos intueri convenit, & oculos in Deum, in Christum, in futura gloriam intetos habere. Paulus dum spectabat non ea quae cernuntur, sed ea quae non cernuntur; du probabat potius migrare & ad Domini irae habitatum; dum non curabat terrestria, sed gerebat se ut municipe coelorum, unde expectabat venturum seruatorem suum Dominum Iesum Christum: interea temporis quid agebat? Ambimus, inquit, & incolentes & migrantes ei esse accepti, quia factorum omnium reddenda est ratio coram illo tribunali: scientes, igitur, terrorem illum Domini, homines ad fidem adducimus. Quare, ita intenti esse debemus in coelos, ut interea semper aliquid boni in vita faciamus. Neque enim fieri potest, ut aliquid sincere agatur, nisi inter agendum Deum ipsiusque gloriam ob oculos positam habeamus. Quamobrem, damnanda est otiosa ista speculatio Monachorum, & otiosorum ventrium, cum interea nihil boni
units.tr: Behold, two men. While they stand thus worshipping and looking up into heaven, see what happens. Messengers are sent at once from heaven, from the throne of Christ, to them. These are angels, two in number, similar to men in form, bright and glorious in their clothing. Note that Christ had scarcely sat down at the right hand of the Father in heaven, when he first showed to his disciples, whom he left behind on earth, that kingly power of his by which he rules even the angels, and then his care for his disciples, for whose benefit and comfort he sent his angels from heaven. This power of Christ and this care for his people remain the same for ever, even to this day. "Ye men of Galilee," there follows the speech of the angels to the disciples. (1) They rebuke them; (2) they comfort them. They rebuke them because, when they ought to have returned to Jerusalem to wait there for the promised Spirit, by whose coming they were to go out and preach the gospel to every creature according to the Lord's command, they were idly standing as watchers and contemplators. Note that it is not enough to stand or sit idly as watchers all day long, even gazing at the heavens into which the Lord ascended; rather we must be seriously occupied throughout our whole life. Meanwhile, while we are occupied in some holy and lawful calling, it is fitting to look up to heaven and to keep our eyes fixed on God, on Christ, and on future glory. Paul, while he looked not at things which are seen but at things which are not seen, while he preferred to depart and be at home with the Lord, while he did not care for earthly things but conducted himself as a citizen of heaven, whence he waited for his Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, what was he doing in the meantime? "We labour," he says, "whether at home or away, to be acceptable to him, for we must all give an account of our deeds before that judgment seat; knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men to faith." Therefore we ought to be so intent on heaven that in the meantime we always do some good in our life. For nothing can be done sincerely unless, while we act, we keep God and his glory before our eyes. Therefore that idle speculation of monks and of idle bellies is to be condemned, since in the meantime they do no good, and do not help the Church of God, but harm it very much, while they pour their dreams and delusions, about which they have idly thought, into the Church of God to corrupt men's minds. Now let us see the second part of the angels' speech, which consists in comfort. The angels comfort the disciples with the hope of Christ's return, which will be just as glorious as was his ascension. Note therefore that solid comfort lies in the hope of Christ's return; but the other comforts which console us in the bodily absence of our Lord are, I admit, the Holy Spirit and faith. Yet unless we set the Lord's return apart for its proper time, we would by no means have that solid comfort. For if we hoped in Christ only in this life, without the hope of Christ's return and the resurrection of the bodies, we would certainly be "of all men most miserable." We look for the glorifying of our bodies and eternal life at his return. "We look for our Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, to come from heaven, who will change our lowly body and make it like his glorious body." For "when we shall see him as he is, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is." That glorious ascension of the Lord did not then make the bodies of the disciples like his glorious body; but the glorious descent of Christ from heaven will make both theirs and ours like his glorious body. Therefore the comfort in the descent of Christ will be greater than that which was in his ascension. So far the angels.

units.la: Otiosa speculatio prohibita; actio verso praecepta est nobis. faciant, neque Ecclesiæ Dei prosint, sed obsint ei pluri-num, dum somnia sua, & deliria, de quibus otiosi cogitarùt, ingeruntin Ecclesiam Dei ad corrumpendos hominum animos. Nunc videamus secundam sermonis Angelorum partem, quæ posita est in consolatione. Consolantur discipulos Angeli à Christi illo redditu perinde glorioso futuro, atque fuit eius ascensio. Nota igitur, solidam consolationem esse sub spe reditus Christi: sed alia, fateor, quæ nos consolantur in corporali ista absentia Domini nostri, sunt Spiritus sanctus & fides. Verùm nisi separaremus redituum suo tempore Dominum, solidam illam consolationem nequaquam haberemus. Nam si in hac tantùm vita speraremus in Christo, sine spe reditus Christi & resurrectionis corporum, profectò omnium mortalium essemus miserrimi. In reditu eiùs Christi expectamus glorificationem corporum nostrorum & vitâ æternam. Expectamus, nos Seruatorem nostrum Iesum Christum è cœlis venturum, qui transformabit corpus nostrum humile, & conformabit ipsum gloriosofuo corpori. Nam cùm videbimus eum sicuti est, similes ei erimus, quia videbimus eum sicuti est. Gloriosa illa Domini ascensio, non tum conformauit corpora discipulorum, gloriosô ipsius corpori: verùm gloriosus descensus Christi è cœlis conformabit eorum & nostra simul corpora gloriosô ipsius corpori. Quare maior futura est consolatio in descensu Christi, quam quæ fuit in eius ascensu. Hactenus Angeli.
units.tr: Idle contemplation is forbidden; action is rather enjoined upon us. Now what do the disciples do next? First they return to Jerusalem with great joy. They obey, therefore, and obey with great joy. This joy arose partly from what they had seen, namely the glorious ascension of their Lord, and partly from what they had heard from the angels, namely the glorious descent from heaven that was to come at some time. Yet unless Christ, now sitting in heaven at the right hand of the Father, had been effective in them to produce that joy, they would certainly never have conceived such joy in their minds. For joy effected through the Holy Spirit is a most certain sign of the kingdom of Christ, and it shows that the Lord now reigns in heaven; for the kingdom of God is "righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit." Moreover, if you compare the joy which the disciples then felt with all the joy they had ever conceived before, you will certainly see that they had never rejoiced so before, not even when they had the Lord present with them. This shows that the bodily presence of Christ does not bring about and produce joy in our souls, just as his bodily absence does not prevent our joy; rather, joy comes chiefly from that effective working of the Spirit of Christ. Nevertheless these men say that they cannot rejoice in the Lord's Supper unless they have the body of Christ there, bodily and really, as they say, to eat and to devour it. But the cause of this joy must be weighed a little more carefully. They could indeed rightly rejoice when Christ led them out to Bethany, if only because they had such and so great a leader. But now, when they return home alone and forsaken by Christ, what cause of joy lay beneath? I answer: instead of Christ's presence they had faith and hope at the same time; faith, indeed, apprehending him glorified in heaven, and hope, awaiting his glorious return, to come at its appointed time. For faith and hope in this life make up for us the bodily absence of the Lord, and without them there would certainly be no matter of joy in this life for Christian men; but with faith and hope come patience and joy even in the midst of afflictions. Therefore, says Paul, "for which cause I also suffer these things; nevertheless I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day." Here is the cause of patience in afflictions: namely faith in the power of Christ, by which he is able to keep our life, deposited with him in heaven, and hope in his return on that day, on which it is to come about that we receive back from him that deposit of his. "And when they had entered." This is the second thing they do: having now entered Jerusalem together, they go up into the upper room, to share with one another the joy they have conceived about their Lord. For those who rejoice together in Christ, set apart from the world, desire to be and to live together; and indeed they will necessarily live together after this life.

units.la: Nunc deinde quid faciunt discipuli? primùm reuertuntur Hierusalem cum gaudio magno. Parent igitur, & parent cum gaudio magno. Gaudium hoc fuit partim ex eo quod viderunt, nempe gloriosa Domini sui ascensione, partim ex eo quod audiuerunt ex Angelis, nempe gloriosa Domini descensione è cœlis olim futura. Nisi autem Christus sedens iam in cœlis ad dextram Patris efficax in iis fuisset ad istud eorum gaudium, profectò gaudium tantùm nequaquam animo concepissent. Nam gaudium per Spiritum sanctum effectum est certissimum regni Christi, arguitque iam Dominum in cœlis regnare: regnum enim Dei est iustitia, & pax, & gaudium per Spiritum sanctum. Si conferas deinde gaudium illud, quod eo tempore gausunt discipuli, cum omni gaudio quod antehac vnquam conceperunt, profecto videbis eos nunquam ita ante-hac gauisos vt nunc: ne tunc quidem cum praesentem secum haberent Dominum. Id quod arguit corporalem Christi praesentiam, non perficere atque gignere in animis nostris gaudium: vt neque corporalem ipsius absentiam impedire gaudium nostrum: sed gaudium esse praecipue ex efficaci illa operatione Spiritus Christi. Nihilominus tamen isti gaudere non posse se dicunt in Coena Domini, nisi corporaliter, & realiter, vt loquuntur, Christi corpus ibi praesens habeant ad vescendum eo, ipsumque deuorandum. Sed causa huius gaudij adhuc paulo diligentius expendenda est. Potuerunt quidem merito gaudere, cum Christus eos educeret in Bethaniam, vel ideo quod talem tantumque ducem habuerunt. At nunc cum soli & a Christo derelicti reuertuntur domum, quae causa gaudij suberat? Respondeo, pro Christi praesentia habebant fidem simul & spem: fide quidem eum in coelis glorificatum apprehendentem: spem vero expectantem ipsius gloriosum reditum, futurum suo tempore: fides enim & spes in hac vita compensant nobis absentiam Domini corporalem, sine quibus profecto nulla esset Christianis hominibus in vita ista materia gaudij: cum fide autem, & spe, est patientia, est gaudium in mediis etiam afflictionibus. Quam ob causam, inquit Paulus, & haec patior, neque erubesco. Noui enim cui crediderim, & mihi persuasum est eum posse depositum meum in illum diem seruare. Ecce causam patientiae in afflictionibus, fidem nimirum potentiae Christi, qua potest is seruare nobis vitam nostram apud se in coelis depositam: & spem reditus ipsius in illo die, in quo futurum est, vt ipsi ab eo recipiamus depositum illud suum. Et cum introissent. Hoc secundum est quod faciunt, iam ingressi vna Hierusalem, simul ascendunt in coenaculum ad communicandum secum inuicem illud conceptum a se gaudium de Domino suo. Qui enim simul gaudent in Christo, segregati a mundo simul cupiunt esse & viuere: & quidem simul victuri sunt post hanc vitam ne-cef.
units.tr: Now, what do the disciples do next? First, they return to Jerusalem with great joy. So they obey, and they obey with great joy. This joy arose partly from what they had seen, namely their Lord's glorious ascension, and partly from what they had heard from the angels, namely the glorious descent of the Lord from heaven, which was to come in the future. Yet unless Christ, already seated in heaven at the right hand of the Father, had been effectively at work in them for that joy, they could never have conceived such joy in their minds. For the joy that the Holy Spirit produces is the sure pledge of Christ's kingdom, and it shows that the Lord is already reigning in heaven, since the kingdom of God is righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. If you then compare the joy the disciples felt at that time with all the joy they had ever felt before, you will see that they had never rejoiced as they did now, not even when they had the Lord present with them in person. This shows that the bodily presence of Christ does not of itself produce and beget joy in our hearts, just as his bodily absence does not hinder our joy. Joy comes chiefly from the effective working of the Spirit of Christ. Nevertheless, they say that they cannot rejoice at the Lord's Supper unless they have the body of Christ there present to them, bodily and really, as they put it, to eat and to devour. But the cause of this joy must be weighed a little more carefully. They could indeed rightly rejoice when Christ led them out to Bethany, if only because they had such a leader and so great a one. But now, when they return home alone and forsaken by Christ, what ground of joy lay beneath them? I answer: in place of Christ's presence they had faith and hope together. Faith laid hold of him as glorified in heaven; hope looked for his glorious return, which would come in its own time. For in this life faith and hope make up for the bodily absence of the Lord. Without them, there would truly be no matter for joy in this life for Christian people. With faith and hope comes patience, and joy even in the midst of afflictions. This is why Paul says, "For this cause I also suffer these things, yet I am not ashamed. For I know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to keep what I have committed to him until that day" (2 Tim. 1.12). Here is the reason for patience in afflictions: faith, namely faith in the power of Christ, by which he is able to keep safe for us our life, which is laid up with him in heaven; and hope in his return on that day, when we shall receive back from him what we have entrusted to him. And when they had come in. This is the second thing the disciples do. Having now entered Jerusalem together, they go up into the upper room to share with one another the joy they have conceived concerning their Lord. For those who rejoice together in Christ, set apart from the world, desire also to be and to live together. And indeed, they will necessarily live together after this life.

units.la: 2. Tim. 1. 12. cessario. Nam fides, spes, gaudium, in communione sanctorum & acquiruntur & conseruantur. Denique gaudium nostrum perficietur in futura illa cœlesti societate. Extra autem societatem, communionem, & coniunctionem animorum cum sanctis omnibus, nulla fides, nulla spes, nullum gaudium, nulla Chri-sti est gratia. Hinc Paulus, dum loquitur de aliqua Christi gratia, solet dicere eam esse cum omnibus sanctis, vt est Ephef. cap. 3. v. 18. vbi de charitate Dei loquitur, & 1. Thessal. 3. 13. vbi de stabiliendis cordibus nostris in sanctimonia loquitur. Erántque semper in templo. Hoc tertium illud est quod faciunt discipuli, incipiunt iam esse audaciores, & se non continentes in cœnaculo, in templum conuenerunt, vbi vnà cum fratribus Domini & cum mulieribus sanctis, nominatim verò Maria matre Iesu, laudabant & benedicebant Deum. Obserua igitur exercitia ea, quibus in sancta societate, fides, spes & gaudium, conseruantur & augentur. Sunt autem ea preces ad Deum, laudationes, prædicatio Euangelij, Psalmi, hymni, spirituales cantiones, sanctæ denique communicationes. His quidem conseruatur & augetur gratia Christi, & sine his inutiliter fiunt coeuntes Ecclesiastici. Notandum, quòd quanta fieri potuit frequentia, in locum celebrem & publicum conuenerunt. Nam frequentia sanctorum quo maior, locus quo celebrior, eo maior Domini præsentia, maius gaudium Spiritus sancti nobis, maior Deo gloria. Nam si promissa est præsentia Dei priuatim duobus vel tribus, qui in vnum conueniunt in nomine eius, quanto magis promittitur sanctis frequenter coeuntibus, in locum celebrem aliquem & publicum?
units.tr: 2. Tim. 1. 12. necessarily. For faith, hope, and joy are both acquired and preserved in the communion of the saints. Finally, our joy will be made complete in that future heavenly fellowship. But outside the fellowship, communion, and joining of souls with all the saints, there is no faith, no hope, no joy, no grace of Christ. Hence Paul, when he speaks of some grace of Christ, is accustomed to say that it is with all the saints, as in Ephesians 3.18, where he speaks of the love of God, and in 1 Thessalonians 3.13, where he speaks of establishing our hearts in holiness. And they were continually in the temple. This is the third thing the disciples do: they now begin to be bolder, and no longer keeping themselves hidden in the upper room, they gather in the temple, where together with the brothers of the Lord, with the holy women, and especially Mary the mother of Jesus, they praised and blessed God. Notice, then, the exercises by which faith, hope, and joy are preserved and increased in holy fellowship. These are prayers to God, praises, the preaching of the gospel, psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, and finally holy communications. By these grace is preserved and increased in Christ, and without them the gatherings of the Church are useless. It should be noted that they gathered in as large a number as could be, in a famous and public place. For the greater the gathering of the saints, and the more famous the place, the greater the presence of the Lord, the greater the joy of the Holy Spirit for us, and the greater the glory to God. For if the presence of God is promised to two or three who come together in his name in private, how much more is it promised to the saints who gather frequently in some famous and public place?

units.la: Illi vero egressi. Quartum est quod faciunt. Quo etiā comprehensa est summatim historia illa tota, quæ habetur in Actis Apostolorum. 1. Habemus egressum simul & prædicationem discipulorum. Secundò, habemus successum prædicati ab iis Euangelij. Quòd ad primum illud attinet, postquam iam impleti essent gaudio, gratia & donis Spiritus sancti, egressi sunt in ludæam, & in gentes omnes, ad communicandam reliquo mundo gratiam qua ipsi iam erat repleti. Ita nobis quoque faciendum, quotquot in animo habemus praedicare Euangelium Christi. Primum, oportet cōtineamus nos intra priuatos parietes, tantisperdum nos ipsi gratia implea-mus: vel certè eam ad mensuram aliquam accipiamus. Tum vbi ipsi iam accepimus mensuram gratię aliquam, egrediendum est in publicum, & ea ipsa gratia, quam nos accepimus, cum aliis est communicanda, & in alios quasi transfundenda. Sed egressio istorum miraculosa est, & accidit Iudæis longè praeter expectationem suam, siue ipsum Christum respicias, siue discipulos ipsius. Nam quoad Christum, putarunt Iudæi, eum iam in ignominia sepultum esse, & ne nominandum quidem impositerum vnquam nomen ipsius, nisi forte cum execratione & detestatione. Quod ad discipulos, putarunt eos ita perterrefactos tam tristi illo spectaculo Domini sui, vt ne hiscere quidē auderent. Hæc dum Iudæi cogitant secum, & dum securi Christi agunt, ecce de repente prodeunt discipuli gestantes coram ipsis, coram toto mundo, crucifixum illum hominem. Adeo vt in hac egressione eorum, & annunciatione cum tanta παράδοξα, satis videas potentiam illam Christi regis, stupendā, ac plane miraculosam. Nunc de successu etiam est dicendum: Domino, inquit, vnā operante. Successus iste non minus stupendus est quàm egressus eorum fuit, Domino scilicet cooperante, vel potius, Domino operante, illis autem cooperantibus (Dei enim homines συνεργοί sunt) Christo Domino, inquam, cooperante, tum editis miraculis, tum aliis praeterea modis ad confirmandum sermonem Euangelij ab iis praedicatum. In successu igitur, vt in egressu, plane conspicitur Christi regnum & potentia illa coelestis. Equidem, dum solet conferre successum illum Euangelij, qui tantus tum fuit primis illis temporibus, statim post ascensionem Iesu Christi, praedicantibus Apostolis; cum eo, qui nunc est successu, tam exiguo, praedicati a nobis Euangelij, praedicati, inquam, eadem sinceritate, nunc qua tunc fuit; cogor apud animum meum concludere
units.tr: Those who went out. This is the fourth thing they do, and it summarises the whole story recorded in the Acts of the Apostles. First, we have the going out and the preaching of the disciples together. Second, we have the success of the Gospel as preached by them. As to the first, once they had been filled with joy, grace and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, they went out into Judea and to all the nations, to share with the rest of the world the grace with which they themselves were now filled. So we too must act, as many of us as intend to preach the Gospel of Christ. First, we must keep ourselves within private walls until we have been filled with grace ourselves, or at least have received some measure of it. Then, once we have received some measure of grace, we must go out into public, and that very grace which we have received must be shared with others and, as it were, poured into them. But the going out of these men was miraculous, and it came about far beyond their expectation, whether you look at Christ himself or at his disciples. For as regards Christ, the Jews thought that he had already been buried in disgrace, and that his name would never again be spoken except perhaps with curses and detestation. As for the disciples, they thought that they had been so terrified by that sad spectacle of their Lord that they would not even dare to open their mouths. While the Jews were thinking these things among themselves, and while they went about their business secure in Christ's defeat, suddenly the disciples come forth, carrying before them, before the Jews and before the whole world, that crucified man. So that in this their going out and their proclamation of such a paradox you may see plainly the power of Christ the King, astonishing and altogether miraculous. Now we must also speak of the success: "the Lord," it says, "working together" [with them]. This success is no less astonishing than their going out was: namely, the Lord cooperating, or rather, the Lord working, while they cooperated (for men are fellow-workers of God) [συνεργοί], I say, the Lord Christ cooperating, both by the miracles performed and by other means besides to confirm the word of the Gospel preached by them. In the success, then, as in the going out, the kingdom of Christ and his heavenly power are plainly seen. Indeed, when I compare that success of the Gospel, which was so great in those first times, immediately after the ascension of Jesus Christ, with the Apostles preaching, with the present success of the Gospel preached by us, so small, preached, I say, with the same sincerity now as it was then, I am forced to conclude in my own mind

units.la: 1.Cor.3.9. non nisi paucos nunc seruandos restare, præ multitudine eorum, qui seruati sunt primis illis temporibus ad prædicationem Apostolorum. Quod si tectum est Euangelium Christi, rectum est ijs, qui pereunt, vt ait Apostolus. Ergo quòd tam pauci nunc tam difficulter credant,id quidem arguit multos esse, quibus sit pereundum, vtpote destinatos iam olim ad certum exitium: à quo petimus vt liberet suos omnes Deus, per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Amen.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 3.9. that only a few remain now to be saved, in comparison with the multitude of those who were saved in those first times by the preaching of the Apostles. But if the Gospel of Christ is hidden, it is hidden from those who perish, as the Apostle says. Therefore, that so few now believe with such difficulty indeed argues that there are many for whom it is necessary to perish, as having been destined long ago to certain destruction; from which we pray that God deliver all his own, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: FINIS.

units.la: LECTORI S.
units.tr: To the Reader

units.la: Ne sequentes quædam pagellæ vacarent, D. Hieronymi & Augustini dicta quædam describere & addere visum est.
units.tr: Lest the following little pages be empty, I have thought fit to copy out and add some sayings of St Jerome and Augustine.

units.la: Ex Epistola ad Paulinum.
units.tr: From the Letter to Paulinus.

units.la: Matthæus, Marcus, Lucas, & Iohannes, quadriga Domini, & verum Cherubim, quod interpretatur scientiæ multitudo, per totum corpus oculati sunt, scintillæ emicant, discurrunt fulgura, pedes habent rectos, & in sublime tendentes, terga pennata, & ubique volantia, tenent se mutuo, sibiq; perplexi sunt, & quasi in rota volvuntur, & pergunt quocunque eos flatus Spiritus sanctr perduxerit.
units.tr: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, the chariot of the Lord, and the true Cherubim, which is interpreted "a multitude of knowledge," are full of eyes over the whole body; sparks shine forth, lightnings run to and fro; they have straight feet, and their backs are winged, tending upward and flying everywhere; they hold one another fast, and are entangled with one another, and roll as if in a wheel, and go wherever the breath of the Holy Spirit leads them.

units.la: Ex Catalogo scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum.
units.tr: From the Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers.

units.la: Iohannes Apostolus, quem Iesus amavit plurimum, filius Zebedæi, frater Iacobi Apostoli, quem Herodes post Passionem Domini decollauerat, nouissimus omnium scripsit Euangelium, rogatus ab Asiæ Episcopis, aduersus Cerinthum aliósque hæreticos, & maximè tùc Ebionitarum dogma consurgens, qui asserunt Christum ante Mariam non fuisse. Vnde & compulsus est diuinam eius natiuitatem dicere. Sed & aliam causam huius scripturæ ferunt; quòd quum legisset Matthæi, Marci, & Lucæ volumina, probauerit quidem textum historiæ, & vera eos dixisse firmauerit, sed vnius tantum anni, in quo & passus est, post carcerem Iohannis, historiam texuisse. Prætermisso itaque anno cuius acta à tribus exposita fuerant, superioris temporis, antequam Iohannes clauderetur in carcerem, gesta narrauit, sicut manifestum esse poterit iis qui diligenter quatuor Euangeliorum volumina legerint. Quæ res etiá διαφωνίαν, quæ videtur Iohannis esse cum cæteris, tollit. Scripsit autem & vnam epistolam, cuius exordium est, Quod fuit ab initio, quæ ab vniuersis Ecclesiasticis & eruditis viris probatur. Reliquæ autem duæ, quarum primæ principium est, Senior Electa Domina: & sequentis, Senior Caio charißimo, quem ego diligo in veritate; Iohannis presbyteri asseruntur: cuius & hodie alterum sepulchrum apud Ephesum ostenditur: & nonnulli putant duas memorias eiusdem Iohannis Euangelistæ esse. Super quare quum per ordinem ad Papiam auditorem eius venturn fuerit, differemus. Quarto decimo igitur anno, secundam post Neronem persecutionem mouente Domitiano, in Patmon insulam relegatus, scripsit Apocalypsin: quam interpretantur Iustinus Martyr & Irenæus. Interfecto autem Domitiano, & actis eius, ob nimiam crudelitatem, à senatu rescissis, sub Pertinace principe rediit Ephesum: ibique vsque ad Traianum principem perseuerans, totas Asiæ fundauit rexitque Ecclesias, & confectus senio, sexagesimo octauo post passionem Dominianno mortuus, iuxta eandem vrbem sepultus est.
units.tr: John the Apostle, whom Jesus loved most, son of Zebedee, brother of the Apostle James, whom Herod beheaded after the Lord's Passion, last of all wrote the Gospel, at the request of the bishops of Asia, against Cerinthus and other heretics, and especially then against the rising doctrine of the Ebionites, who assert that Christ did not exist before Mary. Hence he was also compelled to speak of his divine birth. But they also report another reason for this writing: that when he had read the books of Matthew, Mark and Luke, he approved indeed their text of the history and confirmed that they had spoken the truth, but that they had woven the history of only one year, the year in which he also suffered, after John's imprisonment. So, passing over the year whose acts had been set out by the three, he narrated the deeds of the earlier time, before John was shut up in prison, as will be plain to those who read the four volumes of the Gospels diligently. This matter also removes the discord which seems to exist between John and the others. He also wrote one epistle, which begins "That which was from the beginning," and which is approved by all the ecclesiastical and learned men. The other two, of which the first begins "The elder to the elect lady," and the following "The elder to Gaius, the beloved, whom I love in truth," are ascribed to John the presbyter; and his second tomb is still shown today at Ephesus; and some think there are two memorials of the same John the Evangelist. We shall deal with this question when, in due order, we come to Papias, his hearer. Therefore, in the fourteenth year, when Domitian stirred up the second persecution after Nero, he was banished to the island of Patmos, and wrote the Apocalypse, which Justin Martyr and Irenaeus interpret. But when Domitian was killed, and his acts, because of his excessive cruelty, were annulled by the senate, under the emperor Pertinax he returned to Ephesus; and there, persevering until the emperor Trajan, he founded and governed all the churches of Asia, and, worn out with age, died in the sixty-eighth year after the Lord's Passion, and was buried in the same city.

units.la: Ex expositione D. Augustini in Euangelium Iohannis, Tract. 1.
units.tr: From St Augustine's exposition of the Gospel of John, Tractate 1.

units.la: IOhannes inspiratus est à Deo, sed tamē homo: quia inspiratus, dixit aliquid: si nō inspiratus esset, dixisset nihil. Quia verò homo inspiratus, non totum quod est dixit, sed, quod potuit homo, dixit: &c.
units.tr: John was inspired by God, yet he was a man: because he was inspired, he said something; if he had not been inspired, he would have said nothing. But because he was a man inspired, he did not say all that is, but what a man could say: etc.

units.la: Qui susceperunt pacem nunciandam populo, contemplati sunt ipsam sapientiam, quantū humanis cordibus potuit contingi, quod nec oculus vidit, nec auris audiuit, nec in cor hominis ascendit. Si in cor hominis non ascendit, quomodo ascendit in cor Iohannis? An non erat homo Iohannes? An forte nec in cor Iohannis ascendit, sed cor Iohannis in eam ascendit? Quodenim ascendit in cor hominis, de imo est ad hominem: quò autem ascendit cor hominis, sursum est ab homine, &c.
units.tr: Those who received the peace to be announced to the people contemplated that wisdom itself, as far as it could be touched by human hearts, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man. If it did not enter into the heart of man, how did it enter into the heart of John? Was John not a man? Or perhaps it did not enter into John's heart, but John's heart rose up into it? For what enters the heart of man comes from below to man; but whither the heart of man rises, it is above man, etc.

units.la: Erat Iohannes de illis montibus de quibus scriptum est, suscipiant montes pacem populo tuo, & colles iustitiam; qui dixit, In principio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat apud Deum, & Deus erat Verbum. Susceperat pacem mons iste, contemplabatur diuinitatem verbi. Qualis istemons erat? quàm excelsus? Transcenderat omnia cacumina montium terrarum, transcenderat omnes campos aeris, transcenderat omnes altitudines syderum, transcenderat omnes choros & legiones Angelorum. Nisi enim transcenderet omnia ista quæ creata sunt, non perueniret ad eum per quem facta sunt omnia.
units.tr: John was one of those mountains of which it is written, Let the mountains receive peace for your people, and the hills righteousness; he who said, In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. That mountain had received peace; it beheld the divinity of the Word. What kind of mountain was this? How lofty? It had surpassed all the peaks of the mountains of the earth, it had surpassed all the plains of the air, it had surpassed all the heights of the stars, it had surpassed all the choirs and legions of angels. For unless it had surpassed all these things that are created, it would not have reached him through whom all things were made.

units.la: Ergo, fratres mei, si vultis intelligere, leuate oculos vestros in montem illum, id est, erigite vos ad Euangelistam, erigite vos ad eius sensum. Sed quia montes isti pacem suscipiunt; non potest autem esse in pace, qui spem ponit in homine: nolite sic erigere oculos in montem, vt putetis in homine spem vestram esse collocatam: & sic dicite, Leuaui oculos meos in montes, vnde veniet auxilium mihi, vt statim subiungatis, Auxilium meum à Domino, qui fecit cœlum & terram. Ergo leuemus oculos in montes, vnde veniet auxilium nobis: & tamen non ipsi montes sunt, in quibus spes nostra ponenda est. Accipiunt enim montes quod nobis ministrent. Ergo vnde & montes accipiunt, ibi spes nostra ponenda est. Oculos nostros cum leuamus ad Scripturas, quia per homines ministratæ sunt Scripturæ; leuamus oculos nostros ad montes, vnde veniet auxilium nobis. Sed tamen & ipsi homines, qui scripserunt Scripturas, non de se lucebant; sed ille erat verum lumen, qui illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum. Mons erat & ille Iohannes Baptista, qui dixit, Non sum ego Christus, ne quisquam, spem in monte ponens, caderet ab illo qui montes illustrat: & ipse confessus ait, Quoniam de plenitudine eius nos omnes accepimus. Ita debes dicere, Leuaui oculos meos in montes vnde veniet auxilium mihi: ne auxilium quod tibi venit motibus imputes: sed sequaris & dicas, Auxilium meum à Domino, qui fecit cœlum & terram.
units.tr: Therefore, my brothers, if you wish to understand, lift your eyes to that mountain, that is, raise yourselves up to the Evangelist, raise yourselves to his meaning. But because those mountains receive peace, and he who places his hope in man cannot be in peace, do not so lift your eyes to the mountain that you think your hope has been placed in man; and say thus: "I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help will come to me," so that you immediately add, "My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth." Therefore let us lift our eyes to the mountains, whence help will come to us; and yet the mountains themselves are not that in which our hope is to be placed. For the mountains receive so that they may minister to us. Therefore, where the mountains too receive, there our hope is to be placed. When we lift our eyes to the Scriptures, because the Scriptures were ministered through men, we lift our eyes to the mountains, whence help will come to us. But yet the men themselves who wrote the Scriptures did not shine by their own light; "but he was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world." That John the Baptist too was a mountain, who said, "I am not the Christ," lest anyone, placing his hope in the mountain, should fall away from him who illumines the mountains; and he himself, confessing, said, "For of his fullness we have all received." So you ought to say, "I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help will come to me," lest you attribute to the mountains the help that comes to you; but you should follow on and say, "My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth."

units.la: LAVS DEO OPT. MAX.
units.tr: PRAISE TO GOD, MOST GOOD AND GREATEST.
